p.seg: Annals I: Annals of Tàizǔ
Tàizǔ Chéngtiān Guǎngyùn Shèngdé Shéngōng Zhàojì Lìjí Rénxiào Ruìwǔ Duānyì Qīn’ān Hóngwén Dìngyè Gāo Huángdì,
whose surname was Àixīnjuéluó,
personal name Nǔ'ěrhāqí.
His ancestors were remnants of the Jīn dynasty.
The progenitor was Bùkùlǐ Yōngshùn,
whose mother was Fókùlún,
said to have conceived after sensing a red fruit.
As he grew older,
he quelled the rebellion of the Sānxìng,
and the multitude revered him as Bèilè.
He resided in the city of É'énlǐ, in the wilderness of Émòhuì east of the Chángbái Mountains,
and called his tribe Mǎnzhōu.
The Mǎnzhōu began from this time.
The Yuán dynasty established a Military-Civilian Myriad-Household Office in that area,
and in the early Míng dynasty, the Jiànzhōu卫 was established.
Several generations later,
Bùkùlǐ Yōngshùn's clan did not govern their people well,
so the people rebelled.
The clan was massacred,
but the youngest son, Fànchá, escaped.
After several more generations,
came Dudū Mèngtèwǔ,
who was Zhàozǔ Yuán Huángdì.
He possessed great wisdom and strategy,
and planned to restore their former glory.
He annihilated his enemies,
and reclaimed their territory.
Thereupon, Zhàozǔ moved to Hètú'ālā by the Sūkèsūxǔ River.
He had two sons: the elder Chōngshàn,
and the younger Chǔyàn.
Chōngshàn had three sons: the elder Tuǒluó,
the second Tuǒyìmó,
and the youngest Xībǎoqí Piāngǔ.
Xībǎoqí Piāngǔ had one son: Dudū Fúmǎn,
who was Xīngzǔ Zhí Huángdì.
Xīngzǔ had six sons: the elder Déshìkù,
the second Liúchǎn,
the third Suǒcháng'ā,
the fourth Juéchāng'ān,
who was Jǐngzǔ Yì Huángdì,
the fifth Bāoláng'ā,
and the youngest Bǎoshí.
Jǐngzǔ inherited his ancestral enterprise,
and resided in Hètú'ālā.
His brothers each built their own cities,
the closest being five *lǐ* away,
the furthest twenty *lǐ* away.
They lived in a circle,
commonly known as Nínggǔtǎ Bèilè,
these being the Six Ancestors.
Jǐngzǔ had five sons: the elder Lǐdūn,
the second É'ěrgǔn,
the third Jièkān,
the fourth Tǎkèshì,
who was Xiǎnzǔ Xuān Huángdì,
and the youngest Tǎchá Piāngǔ.
At that time, the Shuòsènà and Jiāhǔ clans were terrorizing the various tribes.
Jǐngzǔ led Lǐdūn and the other Bèilè to attack and defeat them,
seizing all the tribes within two hundred *lǐ* east of the Wǔlǐng and west of the Sūkèsūxǔ River.
From this, they prospered.
Xiǎnzǔ had five sons,
Tàizǔ being the eldest.
His mother was the Xǐtǎlā clan,
who was Xuān Huánghòu.
She was pregnant for thirteen months before giving birth.
That year was *jǐwèi*,
the thirty-eighth year of Jiājìng of the Míng dynasty.
Tàizǔ had a magnificent bearing,
a broad and expansive will,
deep-seated foresight,
a voice like a bell,
an unforgettable memory,
and a magnanimous disposition.
The lord of the neighboring Gǔlè city, Ātài, was attacked by Míng General Lǐ Chéngliáng.
Ātài was
Wáng Gǎo's son
and Lǐdūn's son-in-law.
Jǐngzǔ took his sons and grandsons to observe.
There was a Níkān Wàilán who
enticed Ātài to open the city gates,
and Míng soldiers entered and massacred them.
Both ancestors (Jǐngzǔ and Xiǎnzǔ) perished in the disaster.
Tàizǔ and his younger brother Shū'ěrhāqí were caught between the armies.
Lǐ Chéngliáng's wife was struck by his appearance
and secretly allowed him to return.
On the way, he met É'yìdū,
who followed him with nine followers.
Upon Tàizǔ's return,
he had thirteen suits of armor.
The Lóngdūn and other clansmen of the Five Cities were jealous of him,
using fear of the Míng as a pretext,
and repeatedly plotted to harm him.
They sent someone to ambush him in the middle of the night,
and his bodyguard Pàhǎi died.
É'yìdū and Ānfèiyánggǔ guarded him very carefully.
Once, they captured a person at night,
and Tàizǔ said:
"Release him,
do not sow resentment."
He sent a messenger to complain to the Míng:
"What crime did our ancestors commit to be massacred by your soldiers?"
The Míng people returned their remains.
He also said:
"Níkān Wàilán is
our enemy.
We wish to capture him."
The Míng people did not allow it.
At that time, Nuòmǐnà, lord of Sà'ěrhǔ city, Gáhāshàn Hāsīhǔ, lord of Jiāmùhú city, and Chángshū, lord of Zhānhé city, led their subordinates to surrender.
Tàizǔ swore an oath with them
and married his daughters to them.
Thus, he conceived the ambition to use military force.
That year was *guǐwèi*,
the eleventh year of Wànlì of the Míng dynasty,
and Tàizǔ was twenty-five years old.
In the fifth month of summer of *guǐwèi*,
Tàizǔ raised an army to attack Níkān Wàilán.
Nuòmǐnà's army did not arrive,
and Níkān Wàilán fled to Jiǎbǎn.
Tàizǔ's army captured Túlán city,
and Níkān Wàilán fled to Hékǒu Tái.
The army pursued him,
approaching the Míng border.
Míng soldiers came out,
and Níkān Wàilán fled to É'ěrhún.
The army's expedition was fruitless,
due to Nuòmǐnà breaking his promise
and revealing the military's schedule.
Tàizǔ killed Nuòmǐnà and his younger brother Nàikēdá.
The Kāngjiā, Lǐdài, and other clansmen of the Five Cities rallied Hādá soldiers to raid Húqǐ village.
Tàizǔ sent Ānfèiyánggǔ and Bāsùn with twelve men to pursue them,
recovering all the plunder and returning.
In the first month of spring of *jiǎshēn*,
they attacked Zhàojiā city
to avenge the Húqǐ village incident.
On the way, they encountered heavy snow,
and the troops asked to return.
Tàizǔ said:
"The city lord Lǐdài is
my kin, a brother of the same surname,
yet he guides Hādá.
How can he be forgiven!"
They pressed on
and eventually captured the city.
Earlier, Lóngdūn instigated Nuòmǐnà to break his promise,
and also sent someone to kill Gáhāshàn Hāsīhǔ.
Tàizǔ collected his bones and buried them.
In the sixth month,
he attacked Sàmǔzhàn
to avenge Gáhāshàn Hāsīhǔ.
He also attacked his partisan, Nèshēn, at Mǎ'ěrdūn stockade,
besieging it for four days and annihilating them.
In the ninth month,
he marched against the Dǒng'è tribe.
Due to heavy snow, the army returned.
Soldiers from the city sallied forth,
but were defeated by twelve cavalrymen.
The Wángjiǎ tribe requested aid to attack Wēngkèluò city.
Tàizǔ went there midway,
burning its outer wall.
Tàizǔ shot from the rooftop,
and enemy soldier É'ěrgǔní shot Tàizǔ,
the arrow piercing his helmet and striking his head.
He pulled out the arrow, shot back,
and killed one of them.
Luókē shot Tàizǔ,
the arrow penetrating his armor and hitting his neck.
He pulled out the arrow shaft, which was twisted,
flesh and blood bursting forth.
Leaning on his bow, he slowly descended,
drank several *dǒu* of water,
his wound severe,
and rode back.
After recovering,
he attacked again
and captured it.
He found É'ěrgǔní and Luókē.
Tàizǔ said:
"They are brave warriors."
He appointed them as Zǔolǐng,
granting them three hundred households.
In the spring, second month of the Yǐyǒu year (1585),
Tàizǔ raided Jièfán.
As he was about to return,
four hundred combined troops from the four cities of Jièfán, Sà'ěrhǔ, Dōngjiā, and Bǎ'ěrdá pursued him.
When they reached Tàilángāng,
the city lords Nèshēn and Bāmùní spurred their horses forward together.
Just as they were about to catch up,
Tàizǔ turned his cavalry to meet the enemy.
Nèshēn's blade cut Tàizǔ's whip.
Tàizǔ swung his saber, striking Nèshēn's back, causing him to fall from his horse.
He then turned and shot Bāmùní,
killing both of them.
The enemy dared not press closer,
and slowly withdrew.
In the summer, fourth month,
he campaigned against the Zhéchéng Tribe.
Due to a great flood,
he ordered all armies to return,
advancing with eighty cavalrymen.
Upon reaching the Húnhé River,
he saw in the distance eight hundred enemy troops arrayed along the river.
Bāoláng'ā's grandson, Zhāqīn Sānggǔlǐ, was afraid
and took off his armor, giving it to someone.
Tàizǔ rebuked him, saying:
"You are usually so mighty among your clan and party;
how can you be so cowardly now!"
and dismissed him.
He alone, with his younger brother Mù'ěrhāqí and close attendants Yánbùlù and Wǔlínggá, charged straight into the enemy.
They killed over twenty people.
The enemy scattered and fled.
They pursued them to Jílín Gāng and then returned.
Tàizǔ said:
"Today's battle,
where four people defeated eight hundred,
is truly a blessing from Heaven."
In the autumn, ninth month,
he attacked Āntǔ Guā'ěrjiā City,
capturing it
and beheading its city lord Nuòyīmóhún.
In the summer, fifth month of the Bǐngxū year (1586),
he campaigned against the Bōyīhún fort of the Húnhé Tribe,
subduing it.
In the autumn, seventh month,
he conquered the Tuōmòhé City of the Zhéchéng Tribe.
Hearing that Níkānwàilán was in É'ěrhún,
he swiftly advanced his troops,
attacking and taking its city,
but could not find him.
Climbing the city walls and looking into the distance,
he saw a man in a felt hat and blue cotton armor,
thinking it was Níkānwàilán.
He pursued him with a single horse
and was surrounded by local people.
He fought bravely despite being wounded,
shooting eight people dead
and beheading one,
before escaping.
After learning that Níkānwàilán had entered the Ming border,
he sent someone to the border officials to request his apprehension,
and sent Zhāisà to behead him.
With the culprit apprehended,
he began paying tribute to the Ming.
In subsequent years, the rewards of silver and silk varied.
In the spring, first month of the Dīnghài year (1587),
he built a city on the southern slope of Hǔlán Hādá,
and for the first time constructed palaces.
He promulgated decrees within his tribe,
prohibiting violence and rebellion,
curbing theft,
and establishing laws and regulations.
In the sixth month,
he attacked the Zhéchéng Tribe,
capturing the mountain fort
and killing its fort lord Ā'ěrtài.
He ordered Éyìdū to lead an army to capture Bǎ'ěrdá City.
Tàizǔ attacked Dòng Chéng,
and its city lord Zhāhǎi surrendered.
In the summer, fourth month of the Wùzǐ year (1588),
Hādá Bèilè Hù'ěrgān came to surrender with his daughter.
Suwán Tribe's Suǒ'ěrguǒ, leading his son Fèiyīngdōng and others, Yá'ěrgǔ fort's Hùláhǔ, leading his son Hù'ěrhàn, and Dǒng'è Tribe's Héhélǐ, all came to surrender with their respective tribes.
They were all treated generously.
In the autumn, ninth month,
he captured the Wángjiǎ City of the Wányán Tribe.
Yèhè Bèilè Nálínbùlù came to surrender with his younger sister, Nàlá Shì,
and a banquet was held to complete the ceremony,
she being the Empress Xiàocí Gāo.
In the spring, first month of the Jǐchǒu year (1589),
he captured Zhàojiā City
and beheaded its city lord Nínggǔqīn.
In the winter, tenth month,
the Ming appointed Tàizǔ as the Dūyù Qiānshì of the Jiànzhōu Guard.
In the spring, first month of the Xīnmǎo year (1591),
he dispatched troops to raid various routes in the Chángbái Mountains,
gathering all their people.
Yèhè requested land,
but he did not grant it.
Yèhè then used military force to plunder our eastern border's Dòngzhài.
In the winter, tenth month, twenty-fifth day of the Rénchén year (1592),
his eighth son, Huángtàijí, was born,
born to Empress Gāo,
who would become Tàizōng.
In the summer, sixth month of the Guǐsì year (1593),
the four tribes of Yèhè, Hādá, Huīfā, and Wūlā combined their forces to invade Hùbùchá.
He dispatched troops to defeat them.
In the autumn, ninth month,
as Yèhè was dissatisfied with us,
it rallied the three Hùlún tribes of Wūlā, Hādá, and Huīfā,
the three Mongol tribes of Kē'ěrqìn, Xībó, and Guà'ěrqá,
and the two Chángbái tribes of Nàyīn and Zhūshělǐ,
a total of nine tribes with thirty thousand troops, to invade.
Tàizǔ sent Wǔlǐkān to scout the enemy.
Upon reaching the Húnhé River,
he intended to cross the river by night
and galloped over the ridge to report.
Tàizǔ said:
"Has the Yèhè army indeed arrived?
Tell the generals to fight at dawn."
At dawn,
he led his troops out,
and announced to the multitude:
"Untie your armguards,
remove your neck-guards;
do not constrain yourselves,
as it is inconvenient for fierce combat."
He further ordered:
"A motley crowd,
their ambitions are not unified.
If we defeat their vanguard,
the army will surely turn and flee.
Our army will seize the opportunity,
and none will not be victorious."
Everyone was inspired.
Tàizǔ ordered Éyìdū to challenge with a hundred men.
Yèhè Bèilè Bùzhāi spurred his horse to meet the challenge,
but his horse hit a tree and fell.
Our soldier Wútán beheaded him.
Kē'ěrqìn Bèilè Míng'ān's horse got stuck in the mud.
He switched to a spare horse and fled.
The enemy was routed.
Our army pursued them northwards,
capturing countless prisoners and spoils,
and brought back Wūlā Bèilè's brother, Bùzhāntài, as a captive.
In the winter, tenth month,
he dispatched troops to campaign against the Zhūshělǐ Route,
capturing its route chief Shūlénggé.
He sent Éyìdū and others to attack the Nàyīn Route,
beheading its route chief Sōuwěnsàikèshí,
because these two routes had assisted the enemy.
In the spring, first month of the Jiǎwǔ year (1594),
Mongol Kē'ěrqìn Bèilè Míng'ān and Kā'ěrkā Bèilè Lǎosa sent envoys to establish good relations.
From then on, Mongol envoys came without interruption.
In the summer, sixth month of the Yǐwèi year (1595),
he campaigned against Huīfā,
capturing Duōbì City
and beheading its city lord.
In the spring, second month of the Bǐngshēn year (1596),
Ming envoys arrived,
accompanied by two Korean officials.
They were treated with due ceremony.
In the autumn, seventh month,
he sent Bùzhāntài back to Wūlā.
It happened that its Bèilè had been killed by his tribesmen,
so Bùzhāntài was established as Bèilè.
In the spring, first month of the Dīngyǒu year (1597),
the four Yèhè tribes requested to restore good relations,
which was granted,
and an alliance was formed.
In the ninth month,
he sent his younger brother Shū'ěrhāqí to pay tribute to the Ming.
In the spring, first month of the Wùxū year (1598),
he ordered his younger brother Bāyǎlá and eldest son Chǔyīng to lead an army to attack Ānchǔlākù,
because of its allegiance to Yèhè.
In the winter, tenth month,
Tàizǔ paid tribute to the Ming.
In the eleventh month,
Bùzhāntài came for a meeting,
and Tàizǔ gave his younger brother's daughter to him as wife.
In the spring, first month of the Jǐhài year (1599),
the route chiefs Wánggé and Zhānggé of the Hǔ'ěrhā Route of the Dōnghǎi Wòjí Tribe came to surrender,
presenting sable and fox furs,
and annual tribute became a regular practice.
In the second month,
he first created the national script.
In the third month,
he opened mines,
mined gold and silver,
and established iron foundries.
Hādá and Yèhè engaged in warfare,
sending a hostage to seek aid.
He sent Fèiyīngdōng and Gágài to guard them.
Hādá then secretly allied with Yèhè,
and the garrison commander reported it.
In the autumn, ninth month,
Tàizǔ attacked Hādá,
storming and capturing the city,
and brought back its Bèilè, Mènggébùlù.
Mènggébùlù harbored rebellious intentions,
which Gágài failed to report,
so both were executed.
In the spring, first month of the Xīnčǒu year (1601),
the Míng dynasty blamed us for destroying Hādá.
Therefore, Ménggébùlù’s son, Wú'ěrgǔdài, was sent back to rule Hādá.
Hādá was invaded by Yèhè and Měnggǔ.
An envoy was sent to complain to the Míng,
but the Míng did not respond.
Another envoy from Hādá announced a famine to the Míng,
but again, there was no response.
Tàizǔ then returned Wú'ěrgǔdài,
took control of his people,
and Hādá was destroyed.
In the twelfth month,
Tàizǔ again paid tribute to the Míng.
This year, the military system was established,
and people were ordered to raise silkworms.
In the spring, first month of the Guǐmǎo year (1603),
we moved to Hètú'ālā,
which was the old residence since Zhàozǔ.
In the ninth month,
Consort Nālāshì died.
She was Empress Xiàocí Gāohuánghòu.
When the consort first fell ill,
she asked to see her mother.
Her brother, Yèhè Bèilè, did not allow her to come,
and so she died.
In the spring, first month of the Jiǎchén year (1604),
Tàizǔ attacked Yèhè,
captured two cities,
and took seven of their strongholds.
The Míng granted us the title of Lónghǔ Jiàngjūn.
In the Yǐsì year (1605),
the outer city walls were built.
Engeděr of the Měnggǔ Kā'ěrkǎ Bāyuētè tribe surrendered.
In the winter, twelfth month of the Bǐngwǔ year (1606),
envoys from Engeděr and five Měnggǔ tribes came to pay tribute,
and honored Tàizǔ as Shénwǔ Huángdì.
This year,
limits were placed on civilian land ownership.
In the spring, first month of the Dīngwèi year (1607),
Mùtèhēi, the chief of Wǎ'ěrkǎ Fēiyōu city, came,
stating that Wūlā had invaded and oppressed them,
and sought to join us.
Shū'ěrhāqī, Chǔyīng, Dàishàn, Fèi'yīngdōng, and Yánggǔlì were ordered to lead troops to relocate five hundred households.
Wūlā dispatched ten thousand troops to intercept and attack,
but they were defeated,
three thousand heads were taken,
and five thousand horses were captured.
The army returned,
and Chǔyīng and others were generously rewarded.
In the summer, fifth month,
younger brother Bāyālā, Éyìdōu, Fèi'yīngdōng, and Hù'ěrhān were ordered to conquer the Wòjí tribe,
and two thousand people were brought back.
In the autumn, ninth month,
Tàizǔ, seeing that Huīfā had repeatedly broken its promises,
personally led a campaign,
conquered it,
and thus destroyed Huīfā.
In the spring, third month of the Wùshēn year (1608),
Chǔyīng and Āmín were ordered to attack Wūlā,
and captured Yíhàn'ālín city.
Bùzhàntài was afraid,
and re-established friendly relations,
bringing fifty Yèhè people as captives,
and also requested a marriage alliance.
This was granted.
This year,
an alliance was formed with Míng generals,
each side agreeing to guard its borders,
and stones were erected at the boundary.
In the spring, second month of the Jǐyǒu year (1609),
a letter was sent to the Míng,
stating:
“Those Wǎ'ěrkǎ living adjacent to Cháoxiǎn belong to us.
Order them to be given to us.”
The Míng envoy returned over a thousand households from Cháoxiǎn.
In the winter, tenth month,
Hù'ěrhān was ordered to conquer Wòjí Hūyělù,
and took full control of it.
In the winter, eleventh month of the Gēngxū year (1610),
Éyìdōu was ordered to lead an army to persuade the chiefs of the Wòjí Nàmdūlǔ various routes to surrender.
On the return, they attacked Yǎlǎn Lù
because it had not submitted,
and had also robbed our people,
and took it.
In the spring, second month of the Xīnhài year (1611),
two thousand men in the country who had no wives were granted spouses,
with different amounts of gold.
In the autumn, seventh month,
son Ābātài, Fèi'yīngdōng, and Ānfēiyánggǔ were ordered to take the Wòjí Wū'ěrgǔchén and Mùlún two routes.
In the eighth month,
younger brother Shū'ěrhāqī died.
In the winter, tenth month,
Éyìdōu, Héhélǐ, and Hù'ěrhān were ordered to lead an army to conquer Wòjí Hǔ'ěrhā,
capturing two thousand people,
and also attracting nearby routes,
obtaining five hundred households.
In the autumn, ninth month of the Rénzǐ year (1612),
Tàizǔ personally campaigned against Wūlā,
because it had repeatedly broken its covenants,
and had also shot an arrow with a whistling tip at the emperor's daughter.
Bùzhàntài resisted them by the river.
The army encamped on the east bank of the river,
captured six cities,
and burned their stored provisions.
Bùzhàntài personally came out to beg for peace.
Tàizǔ severely rebuked him,
but allowed him to send a hostage to make peace,
and garrisoned troops there.
The army returned.
In the spring, first month of the Guǐchǒu year (1613),
Bùzhàntài again sided with Yèhè,
so an army was dispatched to campaign against him.
Bùzhàntài came to meet them with thirty thousand troops.
Tàizǔ personally led the charge into battle,
and the generals fought bravely,
soundly defeating them,
and then entering their city.
When Bùzhàntài reached the city,
he could not enter.
Dàishàn pursued him,
and he fled alone on horseback to Yèhè,
thus destroying Wūlā.
Envoys were sent to demand Bùzhàntài,
but Yèhè did not hand him over.
In the autumn, ninth month,
troops were raised to attack Yèhè,
and a message was sent to the Míng.
The city of Wūsū was surrendered,
and nineteen of its city strongholds were burned.
Yèhè reported the emergency to the Míng,
and the Míng sent an envoy to mediate.
The army returned,
passing through Fǔshùn,
where Míng guerilla commander Lǐ Yǒngfāng came to welcome them.
A letter was given to him, saying:
“There is no ill will with the Míng.”
In the summer, fourth month of the Jiǎyín year (1614),
the emperor's eighth son, Huángtàijí, married a woman from Měnggǔ.
She was the daughter of Mǎnggǔsī of the Kē'ěrqìn tribe,
and the "welcoming of the bride" ceremony was performed.
A Míng envoy came,
calling himself a Dūdū (commander).
The emperor said to him:
“I know you.
You are the scoundrel Xiaō Zǐyù from Liáoyáng.
It's not that I can't kill you,
but I fear it would bring shame to the great nation.
Tell your provincial governor
not to deceive us again.”
In the winter, eleventh month,
troops were dispatched to conquer the Wòjí Yǎlǎn and Xīlín two routes,
and a thousand people were obtained.
In the summer, fourth month of the Yǐmǎo year (1615),
Míng general Zāng Chéngyìn sent people to demand territory,
but this was refused.
All zuǒlǐng (company commanders) were ordered to cultivate land and store grain.
In the autumn, intercalary eighth month,
the emperor's eldest son, Chǔyīng, died.
Previously, Tàizǔ intended to hand over governance to Chǔyīng,
but Chǔyīng was arrogant and headstrong,
and the people's hearts were not with him,
so this plan was halted.
Chǔyīng resented this,
burned a memorial to report to Heaven,
was accused by others,
and hanged himself.
In the winter, tenth month,
generals were sent to conquer the Wòjí Dōnggélǐkù route,
and ten thousand people were obtained.
This year,
the military system was reformed.
Initially, four banners (yellow, red, white, black) commanded the troops.
At this time, four bordered banners were added,
and black was changed to blue.
Five high ministers were appointed to manage state affairs and hear lawsuits,
assisted by ten Zā'ěrgǔqī.
At this point, more and more people surrendered,
and the territory expanded further,
so the various Bèilè and ministers repeatedly urged the emperor to ascend the throne.
In the first year of Tiānmìng, in the spring, first month, Rénshēn day (January 28, 1616),
the emperor ascended the throne,
established the reign title Tiānmìng,
and named the state Jīn.
The various Bèilè and ministers honored him with the title Fùyù Lièguó Yīngmíng Huángdì (Wise Emperor Who Nurtures and Protects Numerous States).
His second son, Dàishàn, was appointed Dà Bèilè.
His nephew, Āmín, was appointed Er Bèilè.
His fifth son, Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài, was appointed Sān Bèilè.
His eighth son, Huángtàijí, was appointed Sì Bèilè.
Éyìdōu, Fèi'yīngdōng, Héhélǐ, Hù'ěrhān, and Ānfēiyánggǔ were appointed as the five high ministers,
collectively managing state affairs.
They were instructed to uphold fairness and integrity,
and strive for good governance.
Hù'ěrhān patrolled the border,
capturing and executing over fifty ginseng thieves.
Míng Provincial Governor Lǐ Wéihàn detained our envoys Gānggǔlǐ and Fāngjínè.
Therefore, ten prisoners were taken from jail and executed at the border,
and Gānggǔlǐ and the others were able to return.
In the autumn, seventh month,
the five grand ministers were forbidden from hearing lawsuits in their private residences.
Hu Huerhán and Ānfēiyánggǔ were ordered to attack the Sàhālián department in Dōnghǎi,
and they captured thirty-six stockades.
In the eighth month,
they crossed the Hēilóng Jiāng.
The river ice had already frozen solid.
They captured eleven stockades,
and then proceeded to the Shǐquǎn, Nuòluò, and Shílāxīn routes,
taking their people back with them.
In the second year, Dīngsì, in the spring, first month,
Míng'ān, Bèilè of the Kē'ěrqìn Mongols, came to court,
and was treated with exceptional courtesy.
In this year,
troops were dispatched to take the scattered tribes and their strategically difficult islands in Dōnghǎi,
taking their people back with them.
In the third year, Wùwǔ, in the second month,
an edict was issued to officers and soldiers to inspect military supplies
and promulgate military regulations.
On the day Rén'yín,
the Emperor attacked Míng,
proclaiming the Seven Great Grievances to Heaven,
and, after sacrificing at the Tángzǐ, set forth.
The army was divided, with the four left banners heading to the two cities of Dōngzhōu and Mǎgēndān,
which they captured.
The Emperor led the troops of the four right banners towards Fǔshùn.
Lǐ Yǒngfāng, a guerrilla commander of Míng Fǔshùn, surrendered.
He was appointed Zǒngbīngguān,
to gather the surrendered people,
and their city was destroyed.
Míng Zǒngbīng Zhāng Chéngyìn and others came in pursuit,
so the army turned back to engage and slay Chéngyìn and his company,
then returned to base.
In the fifth month,
they again attacked Míng,
capturing five fortresses including Fǔ'ān,
destroying the cities,
and bringing back their grain.
In the seventh month,
they entered Yǎhú Guān,
where Míng generals Zōu Chǔxián and others died in battle.
In the winter, tenth month,
Nàhāhā, head of the Hǔ'ěrhā department in Dōnghǎi, came to surrender,
and was granted gifts of varying degrees.
Forty chiefs from various routes of the Shǐquǎn departments came to surrender,
were feasted and rewarded with gifts,
and also granted official positions.
In the fourth year, Jǐwèi, in the spring, first month,
Yèhè was attacked,
and over twenty stockades were captured.
Upon hearing of a Míng army,
they returned.
Míng Jīnglüè Yáng Hào sent an envoy to discuss a truce,
but the Emperor's reply refused it.
Yáng Hào led an army of two hundred thousand to attack,
also summoning troops from Yèhè and Cháoxiǎn,
advancing in four routes.
Dù Sōng's army crossed the Húnhé from the east route, emerging at Fǔshùn and Sà'ěrhǔ.
Liú Tíng's army entered Dǒng'è from the south route.
Scouts reported this.
The Emperor said:
“The Míng troops coming from the south
are trying to lure us south.
There must be heavy troops in the north,
so we should break them first.”
He ordered the Bèilè to advance first.
On the first day of the third month, Jiǎshēn,
in the early morning,
the army set out.
Dà Bèilè Dàishàn discussed the direction of the army's advance.
Sì Bèilè Huáng Tàijí said:
“It is advisable to head to Jièfán.
We have fifteen thousand people building the city,
with many laborers but few soldiers,
so there is concern that they might be caught off guard.”
Èyìdōu said:
“Sì Bèilè's words are correct.”
So they headed towards Jièfán.
Towards noon,
they reached Tàilán Gāng,
and caught sight of the Míng army.
A thousand men were detached to reinforce Jièfán.
The cavalry of Jièfán had already engaged the Míng army as it was half-way across the valley mouth,
attacking their rear,
then retreating to defend Jílín Yá.
Dù Sōng left his troops entrenched at Sà'ěrhǔ,
while he himself attacked Jílín Yá.
When our army arrived,
the laborers also charged down,
pressing upon the Míng army.
At this time,
the Emperor arrived at Tàilán to observe the military situation,
and ordered the main army to attack Sà'ěrhǔ.
As dusk fell, they breached its defenses,
and at night, attacked Sōng's army from both sides.
Sōng could not hold out,
and he, along with his lieutenants Wáng Xuān, Zhào Mènglín, and others, all died.
They pursued the fleeing enemy to Sháoqín Shān,
and the western route army was defeated.
On this day,
Mǎ Lín's army came from Qīnghé and Sānchà in the northeast to Shàngjiānyá.
On the day Yǐyǒu,
Dàishàn, having heard the report,
rushed there with three hundred cavalry.
Mǎ Lín gathered his troops into the trench,
arraying firearms outside,
protected by cavalry.
Another general, Pān Zōngyán, was stationed at Fēifēn Shān, acting as a supporting flank.
The Emperor led the four Bèilè to pursue Dù Sōng's rearguard,
annihilating his army,
and then heard that Mǎ Lín's army had arrived.
The Emperor hastened to climb the mountain and attack from above.
Dàishàn charged into the enemy lines,
Āmǐn and Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài waved their banners and led their troops to follow.
With attacks from above and below,
Mǎ Lín fled,
his副將 (fùjiàng) Mǎ Yán died in battle,
and his entire army collapsed.
They then moved to attack Fēifēn.
The Emperor led the cavalry in a sudden charge,
beheading Zōngyán,
and the northwest route army was defeated,
while the Yèhè troops fled.
At this time, Liú Tíng's southern route army, by a secluded path through Kuāndiàn, had defeated our five hundred garrison soldiers,
and was pressing deep into our territory.
The Emperor ordered Hù'ěrhán to lead a thousand troops as reinforcements,
and garrison commander Tuōbǎo joined him with his remaining soldiers.
On the day Bǐngxū,
the Emperor again ordered Āmǐn to lead two thousand men to follow.
The Emperor arrived at Jièfán,
and sacrificed eight oxen before the battle standard.
On the day Dīnghài,
Dà Bèilè Dàishàn and Sì Bèilè Huáng Tàijí were ordered to defend the south.
They encountered Tíng's crack cavalry, over ten thousand strong, advancing.
Sì Bèilè, with thirty elite cavalry, seized Ābùdálǐ Gāng.
Dàishàn, braving danger, entered their army disguised with Dù Sōng's uniform and banner.
The army fell into disorder.
Sì Bèilè rushed down to join the battle,
slaying Tíng,
and also defeating his rearguard.
They pursued the victory to Fùchá.
Tíng's army inspector Kāng Yìnggān engaged with firearms.
A great wind arose,
and the smoke and flames blew back on them,
again utterly defeating them.
Yìnggān fled,
and the Cháoxiǎn troops surrendered.
In just four days, three routes of the Míng army were broken.
As for the northern route army of Lǐ Rúbǎi,
it was urgently recalled by Yáng Hào's dispatch.
When they reached Húlán,
they encountered twenty of our scout cavalry,
who climbed a hill, sounded conch shells,
shouted, and pursued them.
Rúbǎi's army scattered and fled,
trampling over a thousand more people to death.
On the day Jiǎchén,
the surrendered Cháoxiǎn general Jiāng Hónglì was released to return,
with a letter admonishing his sovereign.
In the fourth month,
Jièfán was then built.
Troops were sent to sweep Tiělǐng,
capturing about a thousand people.
In the fifth month,
Cháoxiǎn envoys came to express gratitude.
In the sixth month,
earlier, Mùhàlián had been sent to pacify the remaining people of the Hǔ'ěrhā department.
By this time, a thousand households were obtained.
The Emperor came out of the city to pacify them,
granting them fields, dwellings, cattle, and horses.
The Emperor led troops to attack Kāiyuán,
captured it,
slayed Mǎ Lín and others,
annihilated their army,
and returned to encamp at Jièfán.
In the autumn, seventh month,
Míng Qiānzǒng Wáng Yīpíng and four others surrendered,
as did the previously surrendered garrison commander Ābùtú;
each was given an official position.
The Emperor attacked Tiělǐng,
and captured it.
That night,
the Kè'ěrkā department of Mongolia came to reinforce Yèhè,
but was defeated.
They were pursued to the Liáohé,
and their Bèilè Jièsài was captured.
In the eighth month, on the *jǐsì* day,
an expedition was launched against Yèhè.
Yèhè had two cities;
Bèilè Jīntáishí defended the eastern city,
while his younger brothers Bùyánggǔ and Bùěrhánggǔ defended the western city.
The army was divided to besiege them.
Their outer walls were demolished,
and the cities were undermined.
When the cities collapsed,
our army entered.
The Fourth Bèilè was ordered to take Jīntáishí’s son Déěrgélè to repeatedly persuade him to surrender,
but Jīntáishí ultimately refused.
He was then seized and hanged.
Bùěrhánggǔ surrendered.
Bùyánggǔ was defiant
and was killed.
Yèhè fell.
The army returned and was stationed at Jièfán.
In the tenth month of winter,
an envoy from Línđānhán of Měnggǔ Cháhāěr came.
His letter contained many insults,
so his envoy was detained.
Envoys from the five tribes of Kāěrkā came to form an alliance to attack Míng.
The Emperor sent his ministers Xīfú and four others to attend the alliance.
Soon after, subordinates from the five tribes came to pledge allegiance,
but the Emperor rejected them.
In this year,
Míng appointed Xióng Tíngbì as Jīnglüè.
In the first month of spring of the fifth year, *gēngshēn*,
the Emperor sent a reply to Línđānhán,
rebuking his insolence.
Our envoy had been detained.
The Emperor also killed his envoy.
In the second month,
Jièsài’s sons Kēshíkètú and Sètèxīěr were bestowed furs and horses,
and were ordered to take turns serving as hostages.
In the third month,
merits were evaluated,
and military ranks were redefined.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Fèi Yīngdōng, the Commander of the Left Wing, General-in-Chief, and First-Class Minister, passed away.
The Emperor personally wept for him.
In the sixth month of summer,
an edict was issued to erect two poles at the gate.
Those who wished to complain were to hang their petitions on the poles,
so that public sentiment could be fully conveyed.
In the eighth month of autumn,
the Emperor attacked Míng
and plundered Shěnyáng.
The Míng troops retreated without a fight,
so he returned.
In the ninth month, on the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Emperor’s younger brother Mùěrhāqí passed away.
The imperial carriage personally attended the funeral,
and then proceeded to Fèi Yīngdōng’s tomb to offer condolences.
In the tenth month of winter,
the capital was moved from Jièfán to Sāěrhǔ.
In this year,
Míng Shénzōng passed away.
Guāngzōng was enthroned,
but soon passed away.
Xīzōng was enthroned.
Jīnglüè Xióng Tíngbì was dismissed,
and Yuán Yìngtài was appointed to replace him.
In the second month of spring of the sixth year, *xīnyǒu*,
the Emperor attacked Míng
and plundered Fèngjí Bǎo,
reaching Wǔjìng Yíng.
In the third month, on the *rénzǐ* day,
the Emperor launched a major assault on Míng Shěnyáng.
Siege equipment was transported by boat
down the Húnhé River.
Shěnyáng’s defenses were well-prepared;
stakes were planted around the moats.
Our army pulled out the stakes and advanced fiercely.
The Míng army fought to the death,
and General-in-Chief Hè Shìxián and others were cut down in battle.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Shěnyáng was entered.
Their relief forces, led by General-in-Chief Chén Cè and others, were defeated at the Húnhé River.
General-in-Chief Lǐ Bǐngchéng was defeated at Báitǎ Pù.
All relief forces fled.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
riding on the victory, the army advanced towards Liáoyáng.
Yuán Yìngtài diverted water to fill the moats,
arranged cannons around the city,
and commanded his troops to sally forth.
They could not hold out and retreated,
defending the city towers.
On the *rénxū* day,
our Right Wing army destroyed the sluice gates,
and the Left Wing army destroyed the bridges.
The Right Wing, under Fù Xīchéng, scaled the city wall.
Hearing this, the Left Wing
all ascended.
The Míng army still fought with torches in the alleys,
but by dawn, they were all routed.
Yuán Yìngtài immolated himself,
and Imperial Censor Zhāng Quán was captured
and died unyielding.
On the *guǐhài* day,
Liáoyáng was entered.
The people of Liáo provided imperial carriages, drums, and music to welcome the Emperor,
shouting "Long live!" along the streets.
Imperial Prince Dégrélè was ordered to sweep south of Liáo.
Wherever he went, people surrendered,
and his troops camped on the city walls,
not entering civilian homes.
In the sixth month,
Èyìdū, the General-in-Chief of the Left Wing and First-Class Minister, passed away.
The Emperor personally attended the funeral
and wept sorrowfully.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *rén yín* day,
a banquet was held for the meritorious generals and soldiers,
and wine and clothes were bestowed.
The people of Zhènjiāng City killed their commander Tóng Yǎngzhēn
and surrendered to Míng general Máoyúnlóng.
In the eleventh month, on the *yǐmǎo* day,
Āmǐn was ordered to attack Máoyúnlóng
and defeated him.
Tái jí Gǔěrbùshí of the Kāěrkā tribe surrendered.
Míng again appointed Xióng Tíngbì as Jīnglüè.
In the first month of spring of the seventh year, *rénxū*, on the *jiǎyín* day,
the Emperor attacked Míng
and assaulted Guǎngníng.
On the *bǐngchén* day,
Xīpíng Bǎo was captured.
Three thousand Míng troops came to resist,
but were defeated.
Their Generals-in-Chief Liú Qú and Qí Bǐngzhōng were cut down,
Patrol Commissioner Wáng Huàzhēn fled,
and Mobile Corps Commander Sūn Dégrōng surrendered the city.
On the *gēngshēn* day,
the Emperor entered Guǎngníng,
forty of its castles surrendered,
and the army advanced towards Shānhǎiguān.
Xióng Tíngbì burned all the villages and forts along the road and fled.
The army then moved north to attack Yìzhōu,
captured it,
and returned to station at Guǎngníng.
Seventeen Bèilè of the Měnggǔ Èlǔtè tribe came to submit.
The Emperor feasted and rewarded them,
granting them various ranks.
All five tribes of Kāěrkā came to pledge allegiance.
In the second month, on the *guǐwèi* day,
the Emperor returned to Liáoyáng.
As Liáoyáng City was dilapidated,
the capital was moved to the banks of the Tàizǐhé River.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the first day, *yǐwèi*,
Ānfēiyánggǔ, a First-Class Minister, passed away.
In the first month of spring of the eighth year, *guǐhài*, on the first day, *rénchén*,
Bākè of the Měnggǔ Zhālǔtè tribe came to pay respects at court,
and was sent back with the hostage prince.
In the fourth month of summer, on the *guǐyǒu* day,
Imperial Prince Ābātài and Dégrélè, and Imperial Grandson Yuètū led troops to attack Bèilè Áng'ān of Zhālǔtè,
because he had killed our envoy.
Áng'ān fled with his family.
Dámùbù pursued him
and was killed by a spear.
Our army, enraged,
advanced and killed Áng'ān and his son,
and also brought back the wives and children of another tribe, Sāngtǔ.
In the sixth month,
women who were already married were warned not to bully their husbands;
violators would be punished.
In the tenth month of winter, on the *dīngchǒu* day,
Hùěrhàn, a First-Class Minister, passed away.
The Emperor personally wept for him.
In the first month of spring of the ninth year, *jiǎzǐ*,
Bèilè Ēnkègéěr of Kāěrkā came to pay respects at court
and requested to move inland.
This was granted,
and troops were sent to resettle his people.
In the second month, on the *gēngzǐ* day,
the Emperor’s younger brother Bèilè Bāyǎlā passed away.
The Emperor sent Kùěěr and others to form an alliance with Tái jí Àobā of Kēěrqìn,
prohibiting communication with Cháhāěr.
In the fourth month,
a mausoleum was constructed on Yánglǔ Shān, northeast of the Eastern Capital,
and Jǐngzǔ and Xiǎnzǔ were reburied there.
This was named Yǒnglíng.
In the fifth month,
Máoyúnlóng raided Huīfā.
Garrison commanders Lénggélǐ and Sūěrdōng'ān pursued and annihilated his forces.
In the eighth month of autumn, on the *rénchén* day,
Héhélǐ, General-in-Chief and First-Class Minister, passed away.
The Emperor heard the news and was deeply saddened,
saying,
"Why does Heaven not leave a single person to send off my old age!"
Máoyúnlóng's troops were farming on Yālù Dǎo.
Lénggélǐ was sent to raid his forces
and annihilated them.
In the first month of spring of the tenth year, *yǐchǒu*, on the *guǐhài* day,
Imperial Prince Mǎnggǔěrtài was ordered to lead troops to Lǚshùn,
attack the Míng garrison,
and demolish its city.
In the second month,
the daughter of Kē'ěrqìn Bèi勒 Zhàisāng came to marry the Fourth Bèi勒 Huángtàijí as a concubine,
and a grand banquet was held to complete the rites.
In the third month, on the day Gēngwǔ,
the capital was moved to Shěnyáng.
After five changes, the capital was finally settled there,
which was called Shèngjīng.
Kā'ěrdá and others were dispatched to campaign against Wǎ'ěrkā.
Upon their return,
they brought 300 of its people to surrender.
In the summer, the fourth month, on the day Jǐmǎo,
the imperial clan member Wángshàn, Vice-General Dázhūhù, and Chē'ěrgé campaigned against Wǎ'ěrkā.
They returned triumphantly,
and were honored with a grand banquet.
In the sixth month, on the day Guǐmǎo,
Máowénlóng's forces attacked Yàozhōu.
The garrison general Yánggǔlì defeated them.
In the autumn, the eighth month,
Tǔmùbù was dispatched to fortify Yàozhōu.
Míng forces came to attack,
but were repelled,
and 700 horses were captured.
Bó'ěrjìn was ordered to campaign against Hǔ'ěrhā,
and brought 500 of their households to surrender.
Yǎhù campaigned against the Guà'ěrqá tribe,
and captured 2,000 of their people.
Máowénlóng attacked Hǎizhōu Zhāngtúnzhài.
The garrison general Jièshā repelled him.
The Emperor issued a prohibition on alcohol throughout the nation.
In the tenth year, Jǐmǎo,
the imperial princes Ābài, Tǎbài, and Bābùtài campaigned against Hǔ'ěrhā,
and returned with 1,500 people.
In the eleventh month, on the day Gēngxū,
Kē'ěrqìn Àobā reported an army from Cháhā'ěr.
The Fourth Bèi勒 Huángtàijí and Ābàtài were dispatched with 5,000 elite cavalry to meet them,
and Líndānhàn fled.
In this year,
Míng envoy Gāodì was appointed Director-General,
and drove the people of Jǐnxī into Shānhǎiguān.
The Níngqián Dao Yuánchónghuàn swore to hold his ground.
In the eleventh year, Bǐngyín, in the spring, the first month, on the day Wùwǔ,
the Emperor raised an army to attack Míng's Níngyuǎn.
Upon reaching Yòutún,
the defending general fled,
and its accumulated grain was seized.
Upon reaching Jǐnzhōu,
all the garrison generals had already fled.
On the day Dīngmǎo,
they arrived at Níngyuǎn.
The Níngqián Dao Yuánchónghuàn, along with Grand General Mǎnguì and Vice-General Zǔdàshòu, held the city firmly.
The weather was cold and the ground frozen,
so excavating the city did not cause it to collapse.
Western cannons were fired from the city walls,
causing considerable casualties to the soldiers,
so the attack was called off.
Wǔnàgé was dispatched to lead Mongol troops to attack Juéhuádǎo,
seizing 2,000 boats,
and burning all their military provisions,
then returned to the capital.
In the second month, on the day Rénwǔ,
the Emperor returned to Shěnyáng,
and said to the Bèi勒s:
"Since I began using military force,
there has been no one who dared to defy me.
What kind of person is Yuánchónghuàn
that he could achieve this!"
In the summer, the fourth month, on the day Bǐngzǐ,
a campaign was launched against the five tribes of Kā'ěrkā,
because they had broken their alliance.
Their Bèi勒 Nángnǔkè was killed,
and they advanced to plunder Xīlāmùlún,
seizing their livestock.
In the fifth month,
Máowénlóng's forces attacked Ānshānyì and Sà'ěrhǔ.
Garrison generals Bābùtài and Bàdǔlǐ defeated them,
capturing their general Lǐliángměi.
On the day Dīngsì,
Kē'ěrqìn Bèi勒 Àobā came to court,
to express gratitude for the assistance.
The Emperor treated him with great courtesy,
and enfeoffed him as Tǔxiètúhán.
In the sixth month,
the Emperor wrote instructions to the Bèi勒s.
In the autumn, the seventh month,
the Emperor was unwell,
and visited Qīnghé Tāngquán (Hot Springs).
In the eighth month, on the day Bǐngwǔ,
the Emperor's illness worsened,
and he returned by boat.
On the day Gēngxū,
upon reaching Àijībǎo,
the Emperor passed away,
and the mourning period was announced in the palace.
He reigned for eleven years,
and was sixty-eight years old.
In the third year of Tiāncōng, he was buried in Fúlín.
Initially, his posthumous title was Wǔ Huángdì,
and his temple name was Tàizǔ.
Later, his posthumous title was changed to Gāo Huángdì,
and eventually accumulated to Chéngtiān Guǎngyùn Shèngdé Shéngōng Zhàojì Lìjí Rénxiào Ruìwǔ Duānyì Qīn'ān Hóngwén Dìngyè Gāo Huángdì.
A commentary states: Tàizǔ was endowed by Heaven with wisdom and courage,
and his divine martial prowess was unparalleled.
He endured tribulations with unwavering integrity,
and in times of adversity, he concealed his brilliance.
As more people pledged allegiance,
resistance and discord gradually vanished.
Since he annihilated the armies of the nine tribes,
his territory expanded daily.
He campaigned for over thirty years,
established a state, and ascended the throne.
The battle of Sà'ěrhǔ effectively concluded his task.
The battle of Sà'ěrhǔ effectively concluded his task.
Moving the capital to Shěnyáng
demonstrated far-reaching vision.
Compared to Qí and Fēng,
there is little to concede.
Annals Two: Annals of Tàizōng, Part One
Tàizōng Yìngtiān Xīngguó Hóngdé Zhāngwǔ Kuānwēn Rénshèng Ruìxiào Jìngmǐn Zhāodìng Lóngdào Xiǎngōng Wén Huángdì,
whose personal name was Huángtàijí,
was the eighth son of Tàizǔ,
and his mother was Empress Xiàocí Gāo.
The Emperor had an imposing and magnificent appearance,
and was exceptionally intelligent and sagacious.
His complexion was like fresh cinnabar,
and he did not shiver in severe cold.
As he grew older, he became increasingly brave and skilled,
proficient in horsemanship and archery.
He was fond of classical texts,
and consulted them tirelessly.
He was benevolent, filial, generous, and compassionate,
possessing a remarkably broad magnanimity.
In the first year of Tiānmìng,
Tàizǔ appointed him as a Héli Bèi勒,
and together with the Great Bèi勒 Dàishàn, Second Bèi勒 Āmǐn, and Third Bèi勒 Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài, they were known as the Four Great Bèi勒s.
The Emperor was ranked fourth,
and was called the Fourth Bèi勒.
When Tàizǔ passed away,
the succession was undecided.
Dàishàn, along with his sons Yuètūo and Sàhālián, believing the Emperor's talent and virtue surpassed all others,
discussed and requested his succession with the other Bèi勒s.
The Emperor declined repeatedly,
but after a long time, he finally accepted.
On the first day of the ninth month, Gēngwǔ, in the eleventh year of Tiānmìng, Bǐngyín,
he ascended the throne in Shěnyáng.
An edict was issued declaring the following year as the first year of Tiāncōng.
Originally,
Tàizǔ had given him his name
by guesswork.
Later, it was learned that the Han called the crown prince
"Huángtàizǐ,"
and the Mongol successor was called
"Huángtáijí,"
the pronunciations of which coincided.
When he ascended the throne,
everyone believed it was Heaven's will.
On the xīnweì day,
an oath was made to Heaven and Earth,
to follow the correct path,
adhere to ritual and righteousness,
foster friendship and love,
fulfill public loyalty,
and admonish all the great bèilè and others.
On the jiǎxū day,
an edict was issued to Hànguan and commoners: for those who privately plot to flee, or order spies to come and go,
even if they are the first to report it, they will not be prosecuted.
Later, however, only those who had fled and were captured would be executed.
On the bǐngzǐ day,
an edict stated:
“The commencement of construction
hinders agricultural work.
Previously, for city walls and border fortifications,
matters of defense,
taxing the people’s labor,
was truly unavoidable.
Henceforth, only dilapidated structures will be repaired,
no new construction will be undertaken,
allowing the people to diligently cultivate their fields.
Mǎnzhōu and Hàn people
shall not be treated differently;
in lawsuits, corvée labor,
fairness and equality must prevail.
Those under the jurisdiction of a bèilè
are not permitted to hunt outside the borders.
Market taxes are for state expenditure,
allowing for trade and commerce.
Those who privately go abroad or evade taxes will be punished.”
On the dīngchǒu day,
Hàn people were ordered to live in separate garrisons from Mǎnzhōu.
Previously, thirteen Hàn able-bodied men formed a village,
assigned as slaves to Mǎnguan.
By this time,
each bèiyù retained only eight men,
the rest were all registered as civilian households,
settled in separate garrisons,
and managed by Hàn officials chosen for their integrity.
Eight gùshān ézhēn were established,
to command the Eight Banners.
Nàmǔtài was appointed as the gùshān ézhēn of the Zhènghuáng Qí,
Éfù Dáěrhàn as the gùshān ézhēn of the Xiānghuáng Qí,
Éfù Héshuòtú as the gùshān ézhēn of the Zhènghóng Qí,
Bóěrjìn as the gùshān ézhēn of the Xiānghóng Qí,
Éfù Gùsāntài as the gùshān ézhēn of the Xiānglán Qí,
Tuōbóhuī as the gùshān ézhēn of the Zhènglán Qí,
Chèěrgé as the gùshān ézhēn of the Xiāngbái Qí,
and Kākèdǔlǐ as the gùshān ézhēn of the Zhèngbái Qí.
Sixteen grand ministers were also established
to assist in governing general affairs
and hear lawsuits of the Eight Banners.
Another sixteen grand ministers were also established
to participate in managing lawsuits,
and were dispatched for military campaigns and garrisoning.
On the yǐweì day,
Ōubā, the Tǔxiètú Hán of the Měnggǔ Kēěrqìn, sent an envoy to offer condolences.
In winter, the tenth month, on the jǐyǒu day,
due to the Měnggǔ Kāěrkā Zhálǔtè tribe breaking their alliance, killing, and plundering,
and secretly communicating with the Míng,
the great bèilè Dàishàn and others were ordered to lead an elite force of ten thousand men to attack them.
First, a letter was sent to declare their crimes.
The emperor escorted them to Púhéshān and returned.
On the guǐchǒu day,
Léngérlǐ and Āshān were separately dispatched to lead a light force of six hundred into Kāěrkā Bālín territory,
to project military might.
On the bǐngchén day,
Ōubā, the Tǔxiètú Hán of Kēěrqìn, and fourteen bèilè including Dàidáěrhàn, each sent envoys to offer condolences.
Dázhūhù campaigned against the Guàěrcá tribe,
captured their people and livestock, and returned.
Yuán Chónghuàn, the Míng Níngyuǎn Xúnfǔ, sent Lǐ Lāmā and Dūsi Fù Yǒujué and others to offer condolences,
and also to congratulate on the accession.
On the jiǎzǐ day,
the great bèilè Dàishàn and others severely defeated the Zhálǔtè,
beheaded their bèilè Èěrzhāitú,
captured bèilè Bākè and his two sons, as well as fourteen bèilè including Lāshīxībù, and returned.
In the eleventh month, on the xīnweì day,
the emperor departed Shěnyáng to welcome the great bèilè Dàishàn,
the army arrived at the border of Tiělǐng Fánhé.
On the guǐyǒu day,
a victory banquet was held,
merits were assessed,
and awards were distributed to the generals and soldiers.
On the wùyín day,
the emperor returned to Shěnyáng.
Tǔěrjì, the bèilè of the Cháhāěr Ālāchuòtè tribe, led one hundred households to surrender.
On the yǐyǒu day,
Fāngjínà and Wēntáshí were sent with Lǐ Lāmā to report to Yuán Chónghuàn,
and a letter was also sent saying:
“Recently, we have ceased hostilities and
sent envoys to offer condolences and congratulations.
As the visitors came with courtesy,
we therefore dispatched officials to express our gratitude.
In the past, when the late emperor went to Níngyuǎn,
he sent an imperial letter proposing peace,
but received no reply.
If you truly wish to cultivate good relations,
reply truthfully in your letter,
without embellishment.”
Chónghuàn did not report this,
but ordered our envoy to return the letter.
Wèizhēng Bābài, son of Zhuólǐkètú Bèilè, brought his family to surrender.
Qīngbātúlǔ Sāngāěrzhāi, bèilè of Kēěrqìn, and Mǎnzhūshīlǐ, táijí, each brought saddles, horses, cattle, and sheep to offer condolences.
In the twelfth month, on the gēngzǐ day,
the sale of weapons to various Měnggǔ principalities was forbidden.
On the rénxū day,
people from Hēilóngjiāng came to offer tribute.
In the first year of Tiāncōng, spring, the first month, on the bǐngzǐ day,
the second bèilè Āmǐn,
and bèilè Jíěrhālang, Ājígé, Dùdù, Yuètūo, Shuòtuō were ordered to lead troops to campaign against Cháoxiǎn.
The emperor said:
“Cháoxiǎn has repeatedly offended us for generations.
Now, Míng’s Máo Wénlóng is near its islands,
harboring our rebellious people.
It is advisable to plan for both.”
Fāngjínà and Wēntáshí were again sent with a letter to Míng’s Yuán Chónghuàn,
explaining that the expedition was due to the Seven Great Grievances,
and proposing peace talks,
as well as the annual amount of tribute.
In the second month, on the jǐhài day,
a letter was sent to persuade Gǔnchūsībāyātúlǔ of the Měnggǔ Nàimàn tribe.
In the third month, on the rénshēn day,
Āmǐn and others conquered Cháoxiǎn’s Yìzhōu,
and separately dispatched troops to attack Tiěshān.
Míng’s defending general Máo Wénlóng fled.
They also conquered Ānzhōu,
advanced to Píngyǎng City,
and crossed the Dàtóng Jiāng.
Lǐ Zōng, the King of Cháoxiǎn, sent an envoy to welcome the army.
Āmǐn and others enumerated his seven crimes,
and still sent an envoy to urge for peace.
Zōng was afraid,
and fled with his wife and children to Jiānghuádǎo,
his eldest son Lǐ Dùn fled to Quánzhōu.
Āmǐn again dispatched Deputy General Liú Xìngzuò to the island to personally convey the message to Zōng.

Zōng sent his clan brother, Prince Yuánchāngjūn Lǐ Jué, to offer one hundred horses, one hundred tiger and leopard furs, four hundred pieces each of brocade and ramie, and fifteen thousand pieces of cloth.
On the gēngzǐ day,
an alliance was made with Cháoxiǎn,
and an agreement was reached to cease hostilities.
On the rénshēn day,
Míng’s Yuán Chónghuàn sent Dù Míngzhōng with Fāngjínà and others with a letter,
as well as a letter from Lǐ Lāmā,
wishing to resolve grievances and cultivate good relations.
However, he requested a reduction in the amount of gold and silks,
and expressed doubt about our military campaign against Cháoxiǎn.
On the xīnsì day,
Āmǐn and others sent an envoy to report the victory.
On the yǐyǒu day,
one thousand Mǎnzhōu soldiers and two thousand Měnggǔ soldiers were ordered to garrison Yìzhōu,
and three hundred Mǎnzhōu soldiers and one thousand Měnggǔ soldiers were ordered to garrison Zhènjiāng City.
Lǐ Zōng was also informed:
“Our retention of troops in Yìzhōu
is to guard against Máo Wénlóng.”
Āmǐn and others then withdrew their troops,
returning with Lǐ Jué.
In the fourth month of summer, on the *jiǎchén* day,
a letter was sent to Yuán Chónghuàn, saying:
“To release hatred and cultivate good relations
is indeed what we desire.
Joseon, out of self-importance, slighted us
and harbored our defectors and fugitives.
We waited several years for them,
but they showed no repentance,
which is why we launched an expedition.
Heaven guided their sincerity,
and our army achieved victory.
Now peace has been made,
yet you deceitfully speak of cultivating good relations
while still sending scouts to reconnoiter
and repairing castles and fortifications.
Our country's generals
are indeed suspicious because of this.
To speak of sincerity and cultivate harmony
must be achieved through material means to complete the ritual.
How could we be greedy and profit from this,
making your country's strength unsustainable?
It can be reduced by half.
Seasonal tributes and gifts
should be as previously agreed.
This would be a blessing for both nations.”
After the letter was completed,
it was heard that Chónghuàn was building Tǎshān, Dàlínghé, Jǐnzhōu, and other cities.
So, the sending of the envoy was stopped,
and the letter was given to Dù Míngzhōng to be returned.
Chónghuàn was further reprimanded, saying:
“When two nations cultivate good relations,
their borders should be clearly defined.
Now you are again repairing border walls
and secretly planning invasion and encroachment.
If the war does not cease,
and Heaven grants Yān and Yún to us,
and your lord unfortunately flees,
his body ruined and reputation destroyed,
what would that be like?
From ancient times, civil officials who are inexperienced merely utter grand words,
often leading to the loss of armies, harm to the people,
and the overthrow of the state.
Previously, the improper appointment of personnel in Liaozuo
resulted in the complete loss of territory east and west of the river.
Do you still think this is not enough of a warning and plan to stir up conflict?”
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
Àmǐn and others returned triumphantly from Joseon.
The Emperor welcomed them at Wǔjìngyíng,
bestowing a suit of imperial clothing upon Àmǐn,
and a horse upon each of the others.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
the merits of the generals and soldiers who campaigned in Joseon were discussed,
and promotions and rewards were granted proportionally.
On the *wùchén* day,
the Emperor returned to Shěnyáng.
On the *yǐchǒu* day,
a letter was sent to the Cháhā'ěr Táijí Jìnóng and Nàimàn Gǔnchū Sībātúlǔ, inviting them to make peace.
In the fifth month, on the *wùchén* day,
Lǐ Jué, the younger brother of the King of Joseon, was sent back to his country.
A banquet was held to bid him farewell,
and he was also given a saddled horse, furs, belts, and other items.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
the Emperor heard that the Ming people were building cities and establishing military agricultural colonies at Jǐnzhōu, Dàlínghé, and Xiǎolínghé,
and that Chónghuàn had not sent a reply letter.
He personally led an army to attack them.
On the *yǐhài* day,
he arrived at Guǎngníng,
and advanced the troops by night.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
the Ming soldiers at Dàlínghé and Xiǎolínghé abandoned their cities and fled,
so Jǐnzhōu was besieged.
Over two thousand Ming soldiers from Táibǎo surrendered,
and all were released to return home.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Jǐ Yòng, the Ming Grand Eunuch defending Liáodōng, and Zhào Shuàijiào, the Grand General, sent envoys to the army to request instructions.
The Emperor sincerely explained the situation to them,
and also permitted Jǐ Yòng to come personally to finalize negotiations.
Jǐ Yòng did not reply,
so Jǐnzhōu was attacked.
When it was on the verge of being taken,
Ming relief troops arrived.
The army retreated five *lǐ* and encamped,
sending messengers to summon troops from Shěnyáng to reinforce the army.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Gùshān Ézhēn Bó'ěrjìn and others arrived with troops.
On the *guǐsì* day,
Níngyuǎn City was attacked,
and over a thousand of its foot soldiers were annihilated.
Afterwards,
Mǎn Guì, the Ming Grand General, sallied forth and formed a battle array.
The Emperor wanted to attack him,
but the three great Bèilè all advised against it.
The Emperor was enraged,
and urged the generals to put on their helmets,
leading Àjígé to charge forward rapidly.
They defeated the vanguard,
pursued them to the foot of Níngyuǎn City,
and utterly destroyed them.
The Bèilè, without donning their helmets, followed.
Jí'ěrhāláng, Sàhālián, and Wǎkèdá were all wounded.
The Jǐnzhōu defenders also sallied forth and engaged in battle,
and our army again met and attacked them.
Yóují Juéluó Bàishān and Bèiyù Bāxī died in battle.
The Emperor attended their funerals,
weeping and offering libations.
Our army returned and encamped at Shuāngshùpù.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
they returned to Jǐnzhōu.
In the sixth month, on the *jǐhài* day,
Jǐnzhōu was attacked.
It was an oppressively hot summer,
and many soldiers were killed or wounded.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
the army returned.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
the Emperor returned to Shěnyáng.
That year,
there was a great famine,
a *dǒu* of rice was worth eight *liǎng* of silver.
Silver was cheap and goods were expensive,
and banditry greatly increased.
The Emperor said with compassion:
“If people turn to banditry due to hunger,
can they all be killed?”
He ordered them to be whipped and released,
and also disbursed treasury funds to relieve the people.
In the seventh month of autumn, on the *jǐsì* day,
the Měnggǔ Āohàn Suǒnuòmùdùléng, Sàichén Zhuólìkètú, and Nàimàn Gǔnchū Sībātúlǔ came to pledge allegiance with their entire nations.
Lǐ Zōng, King of Joseon, sent envoys to express gratitude
and present local products.
Àshídá'ěrhàn and others were ordered to go and reply to them,
and soon Yìzhōu was returned to Joseon.
This month,
Yuán Chónghuàn of Ming was dismissed and returned home.
In the eighth month, on the *xīnhài* day,
the Cháhā'ěr Ālākèchuòtè tribe's Bèilè Bā'ěrbātúlǔ, Nuòméndáilái, and Chuī'ěrzhāmùsū led their followers to surrender.
This month,
Míng Xīzōng died,
and his younger brother, the Prince of Xìn, succeeded to the throne,
who was Emperor Zhuāngliè.
In the ninth month, on the first day of the *jiǎzǐ* cycle,
an edict stated that apart from using cattle for national grand sacrifices and banquets,
the slaughter of horses, mules, cattle, and donkeys was entirely prohibited.
In the eleventh month of winter, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Cháhā'ěr Great Bèilè Ángkūndùléng surrendered.
On the *xīnsì* day,
the Sàhā'ěrcá tribe came to pay tribute.
In the twelfth month, on the first day of the *jiǎwǔ* cycle,
the Cháhā'ěr Ālākèchuòtè Bèilè Tú'ěrzhīyī'ěrdēng surrendered.
In the second year, in the first month of spring, on the *wùzǐ* day,
four chiefs of the Géyīkèlǐ tribe led their subordinates to pay homage.
In the second month, on the first day of the *guǐsì* cycle,
Éyìdū's son Tú'ěrgé and Fèiyīngdōng's son Cháhāní were both appointed as Grand Generals.
Lǐ Zōng, King of Joseon, sent his Grand General Lǐ Lán and others to present local products,
and two thousand *shí* of rice,
further selling one thousand *shí* at a fair price at Zhōngjiāng.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
due to the repeated killing of Qālqīn envoys by the Cháhā'ěr Duōluólètè tribe,
the Emperor personally led an army to campaign.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
the Duōluólètè tribe was attacked and
defeated.
Duō'ěrzhīhātán Bātúlǔ was wounded and fled,
their wives and children were captured,
Táijí Gǔlǔ was killed,
and eleven thousand two hundred people were captured and brought back.
On the *dīngsì* day,
to celebrate the victory,
eight cattle were sacrificed to Heaven.
In the third month, on the *wùchén* day,
the Emperor returned to Shěnyáng.
Bèilè Àmǐn and other officials welcomed him in the suburbs,
performing the embracing ritual.
As his younger brothers Duō'ěrgǔn and Duōduó had meritorious service in the campaign,
Duō'ěrgǔn was granted the title Mò'ěrgēndàiqīng,
and Duōduó was granted the title É'ěrkèchǔhǔ'ěr.
On the *gēngyín* day,
a banquet was held for them to celebrate the bestowal of names.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
gold was given to countrymen without wives,
enabling them to marry.
Bèilè Duō'ěrgǔn was made Gùshān Bèilè.
In the fourth month of summer, on the *bǐngchén* day,
Bālín Bèilè Sàitè'ěr,
Táijí Sàilěng, Āyùshí, Mǎnjūxílí led their followers to surrender.
The Ming again appointed Yuán Chónghuàn as Governor-General of Jì and Liáo.
Chónghuàn had always disliked Máo Wénlóng.
At this time, Máo Wénlóng was occupying Pídǎo,
recruiting people from Liáo,
and would kill those who fled to falsely claim merit,
thus he was promoted to Grand General,
with discretionary powers.
Later, he even sent a letter to us to establish good relations.
The Emperor sent Kēkuò and others with a letter in reply.
Afterwards,
Máo Wénlóng arrested Kēkuò and others and sent them to Yānjīng.
Chónghuàn deceitfully killed Máo Wénlóng for the crime of private communication.
In the fifth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
the Míng people abandoned Jǐnzhōu.
Beìlè Ābātài and others led three thousand soldiers to raid their territory,
destroying the three cities of Jǐnzhōu, Xìngshān, and Gāoqiáo,
and demolishing twenty-one beacon towers east of the thirteen stations.
Previously, Gùtètābùnáng, with his followers, fled from Cháhār and hid in Měnggǔ territory,
killing any who had submitted.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Beìlè Jǐ'ěrhāláng and Háogé were ordered to lead troops to punish Gùtètābùnáng.
On the *yǐyóu* day,
Gùtè was executed,
and his people and livestock, numbering in the tens of thousands, were captured.
The chieftains of the Hǔ'ěrhā tribe, Lǐfótǎ and others, from the coastal area east of Chángbáishān, came to court.
In the eighth month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
peace was negotiated and an alliance established with the Kālāqìn tribe.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
Nàimàn Beìlè Gǔnchūsī was granted the title Dálhàn,
and Zhālǔtè Kābāhǎi was granted the title Wèizhēng.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Cháoxiǎn came to offer tribute.
In the ninth month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
auxiliary troops from the outer vassal states were levied to jointly conquer Měnggǔ Cháhār.
On the *guǐhài* day,
the Emperor led a large army westward.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
they reached Liáoyáng.
The various Beìlè and Táijí from Àohàn, Nàimàn, Kā'ěrkā, Zhālǔtè, and Kālāqìn each came with their troops to rendezvous.
On the *jǐsì* day,
the army was stationed at Chuòluòguō'ěr.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
a banquet was held for the assembled Beìlè.
The various Beìlè of Kē'ěrqìn did not arrive.
Tǔxiètú Hàn Èfù Àobā, Hátánbātúlǔ, and Mǎnjūxílí came as agreed,
requesting to first raid and then merge forces.
The Emperor was enraged,
and sent envoys to urge them.
At this time, Àobā disobeyed orders
and returned directly.
Mǎnjūxílí and Táijí Bādūn presented what they had captured,
and the Emperor granted Mǎnjūxílí the title Dálhànbātúlǔ,
and Bādūn the title Dálhànzhuólìkètú,
bestowing generous rewards.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
the army advanced to attack Xí'ěrhā, Xíbótú, Yīng, and Tāngtú,
conquering them
and capturing countless people and livestock.
In the winter, tenth month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
the army returned.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
an edict was issued to the Beìlè of Àohàn, Nàimàn, Bālín, and Zhālǔtè,
forbidding them from intercepting and killing surrendering people;
violators would be punished.
On the *rényín* day,
the Emperor returned to Shěnyáng.
Because Liú Xìngzuò falsely claimed to have hanged himself
and escaped back to Míng territory,
his mother, wife, and children were imprisoned.
In the twelfth month, on the *dīnghài* day (the first day of the month),
a letter was sent to Tǔxiètú Hàn Èfù Àobā,
enumerating his crimes.
The Bayǎlā tribal chiefs Yī'ěrbīao and others came to offer tribute.
Měnggǔ Guōbì'ěrtú and Zhālǔtè Beìlè Sàiběn and his younger brother Mǎní each led their tribes to submit.
In the third year, spring, first month, on the *gēngshēn* day,
Tǔxiètú Hàn Àobā came to confess his crimes,
was pardoned, and sent away.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
an edict ordered the various tribes of Kē'ěrqìn, Àohàn, Nàimàn, Kā'ěrkā, and Kālāqìn to all abide by the national regulations.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
an edict instructed the various Beìlè to take turns handling government affairs for the three great Beìlè.
In the second month, on the *wùzǐ* day,
an edict instructed the three great Beìlè, the various Beìlè, and the ministers not to extort property from the common people;
violators would be punished.
On the *jǐhài* day,
Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì and Xiàocí Gāohuánghòu were jointly interred at Shízuǐtóushān in Shěnyáng,
with Consort Fùcháshì also interred.
Kā'ěrkā Zhālǔtè Beìlè Dàiqīng, Sāngtǔ, Sānggǔ'ěr, Sānggá'ěrzhài and others led their followers to submit.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
the Emperor made a southern tour,
inspecting border fortresses,
and repairing those that were ruined or weak.
On the *wùshēn* day,
he arrived at Hǎizhōu,
where an old man aged one hundred and three,
his wife one hundred and five,
and his son seventy-three,
were granted an audience and given cattle.
On the *xīnhài* day,
the Emperor returned to Shěnyáng.
In the third month, on the *wùwǔ* day,
military orders for the Měnggǔ tribes were reiterated.
In the summer, fourth month, on the *bǐngxū* day (the first day of the month),
the Wénguǎn (Literary Office) was established,
and Bākèshí Dáhǎi and Gānglín were ordered to translate Hànzì books,
while Kù'ěrtī and Wúbāshí were ordered to record the court's political affairs.
In the fifth month, on the *dīngwèi* day,
the Beìlè of Nàimàn and Zhālǔtè grazed their herds beyond the border,
and voluntarily requested to be punished.
The Emperor pardoned them.
In the sixth month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
an expedition against Míng was discussed,
and the Kē'ěrqìn, Kā'ěrkā, Zhālǔtè, Àohàn, and Nàimàn tribes were ordered to muster their troops,
and also to procure timber in advance to build ships for transporting provisions.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Kālāqìn Bù'ěrgádū Dàiqīng and Táijí Zhuó'ěrbì,
and Tǔmòtè Táijí Āyùshí and others sent envoys to offer tribute.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Tǔmòtè Táijí Zhuó'ěrbìtài and others came to offer tribute.
In the autumn, seventh month, on the *xīnmǎo* day,
Kā'ěrkā Táijí Bàihúndài, Lābātài, and Mǎnjūxílí came from Kē'ěrqìn to court.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
Mèng'ātú led troops to conquer Wá'ěrkā.
On the *yǐwèi* day,
the Kù'ěrkā tribe came to offer tribute.
In the eighth month, on the *gēngwǔ* day,
regulations for rewards and punishments during battle for the Eight Banners were issued.
On the *yǐhài* day,
an edict stated:
"From ancient times to the present,
both civil and military arts have been employed;
civil arts to govern the world,
military arts to overcome enemies.
Now, desiring to revive civil education,
we shall hold examinations for scholars.
All scholars in the Beìlè residences, Mǎn, Hàn, and Měnggǔ,
are ordered to take the examination.
Those who pass will have their conscript labor compensated by others."
In the ninth month, on the *rénwǔ* day (the first day of the month),
the first examination for scholars was held,
two hundred people were selected,
rewarded with varying amounts of silk and cloth,
and exempted from corvée.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
Beìlè Jǐ'ěrhāláng and others returned from raiding the Míng routes of Jǐnzhōu and Níngyuǎn,
capturing an estimated three thousand.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
Ālǔ tribe Dùsīgá'ěrzhìnóng first sent envoys to establish friendly relations.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
Kālāqìn Bù'ěrgádū came to offer tribute.
In winter, in the tenth month, on the day *Guǐchǒu*,
the Emperor personally led an expedition against the Míng.
Soldiers from various Měnggǔ tribes were summoned to gather in sequence.
On the day *Gēngshēn*,
they reached Nàlǐtè Hé.
Five thousand Cháhār people surrendered.
On the day *Rénxū*,
they reached Liáohé.
On the day *Bǐngyín*,
Kē'ěrqìn Àobā, with twenty-three Bèilè, came to meet.
The Emperor gathered the Bèilè and high officials to discuss whether campaigning against the Míng or against the Cháhār would be more advantageous.
All said that Cháhār was distant,
so it was decided to campaign against the Míng.
On the day *Xīnwèi*,
they reached Qīngchéng in Kālāqìn.
The Great Bèilè Dàishàn and the Third Bèilè Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài stopped outside the tents of the other Bèilè.
They entered to see the Emperor and secretly proposed returning the army.
After they withdrew,
Yuètè and others entered to report that the generals were waiting outside to advance.
The Emperor was displeased,
and then said:
"My two elder brothers say that our troops have advanced deeply,
wearing out the army and attacking from afar.
If provisions become scarce and horses are exhausted,
and the enemy surrounds and attacks,
there will be no way to return.
You all saw this coming,
yet you said nothing at first.
Now that I have traveled so far,
you use this as an excuse.
My plan is about to be ruined,
why wait!"
Yuètè steadfastly requested to advance the army.
The eight Gùshān Ézhēn went to Dàishàn and Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài to discuss.
They reached a decision in the middle of the night.
An edict stated:
"I, by the Mandate of Heaven,
have raised an army to attack the Míng.
Those who resist shall be slain;
those who surrender shall not be disturbed.
Captured people,
their parents, wives, and children, shall not be separated.
Do not violate women,
do not strip people of their clothes,
do not destroy houses or utensils,
do not cut down fruit trees,
do not get drunk.
Transgressors will be punished without mercy.
If the Gùshān Ézhēn and others fail to enforce this,
their guilt shall be the same."
On the day *Yǐhài*,
they reached Lǎohé.
Jǐ'ěrhālā ng and Yuètè were ordered to lead the right-wing army to attack Dà'ānkǒu.
Ābātài and Ājígé were ordered to lead the left-wing army to attack Lóngjǐngguān.
The Emperor, with the Great Bèilè Dàishàn and the Third Bèilè Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài, led the main army to follow.
On the day *Dīngchǒu*,
the left-wing army captured Lóngjǐngguān.
Míng Deputy General Yì'ài and Participatory General Wáng Zūnchén came to reinforce,
but both were defeated and killed.
The defending generals of Hàn'érzhuāng and Pānjiākǒu both surrendered.
On the day *Wùyín*,
the Emperor personally supervised the troops in capturing Hóngshānkǒu.
On the day *Xīnsì*,
the Emperor arrived at Zūnhuà.
Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài led the left-wing army from Hàn'érzhuāng to meet him.
A letter was sent to Míng Provincial Governor Wáng Yuányǎ, urging him to surrender.
On the first day of the eleventh month, *Rénwǔ*,
the Bèilè of the right wing led their forces to meet.
Earlier, Jǐ'ěrhāláng and others had captured Dà'ānkǒu,
winning all five battles.
They captured Mǎlányíng, Mǎlánkǒu, and Dà'ānyíng, three cities.
Míng Luówènyù defending general Lǐ Sīlǐ surrendered.
Shānhǎiguān General-in-Chief Zhào Shuàijiào came to reinforce with four thousand soldiers.
Ājígé met and cut him down.
On the day *Jiǎshēn*,
the Bèilè attacked Zūnhuà.
Zhèngbái Qí petty officer Sàmǔhātú was the first to ascend.
The main army followed,
and thus the city was captured.
Míng Provincial Governor Wáng Yuányǎ hanged himself.
The Emperor personally poured a golden goblet of wine and bestowed it upon Sàmǔhātú,
promoting him to Bèiyù,
with hereditary succession without substitution.
He was granted the title Bātúlǔ.
His faults would be pardoned.
As his family was indeed poor,
they were given relief.
Měnggǔ soldiers disturbed and harmed the people of Luówènyù.
An order was issued, stating:
"Any Bèilè or high official who plunders the property of surrendered castles shall be executed.
Those who arbitrarily kill surrendered civilians shall be punished with death.
Those who forcibly take civilian property
shall compensate double what they took."
On the day *Jǐchǒu*,
rewards were given to the generals and soldiers for their merits in capturing the city, with varying degrees.
On the day *Rénchén*,
Participatory General Yīng'é'ěrdài and Literary Official Fàn Wénchéng were left to guard Zūnhuà.
The main army advanced and approached Yānjīng.
There was a Měnggǔ soldier who killed a person and stripped them of their clothes.
The Emperor ordered him to be shot to death.
On the day *Jiǎwǔ*,
they swept through Jìzhōu.
On the day *Yǐwèi*,
they swept through Sānhé.
On the day *Bǐngshēn*,
the left-wing Bèilè went to Tōngzhōu to inspect the river crossing.
Míng reinforcing troops from Dàtóng and Xuānfǔ arrived at Shùnyì.
Bèilè Ābātài and Yuètè defeated them.
Shùnyì surrendered.
The Emperor arrived at Tōngzhōu
and issued an edict to the Míng officials and common people, saying:
"Our nation has long defended the border with loyalty and obedience.
Yèhè is like one nation with us.
The Míng ruler protected Yèhè and insulted us.
This is one of the seven great grievances.
I knew that we would ultimately not be compatible,
therefore I announced to Heaven and raised an army.
Heaven stood by our nation
and bestowed upon us the land east of the river.
Our Tàizǔ Emperor still wished for peace
and for the people to rest.
Your nation did not comply.
Heaven again bestowed upon us the land west of the river.
When I ascended the throne,
I again complied with your nation's request,
intending to relinquish the title of Emperor and call myself Khan,
and hastily made a national seal.
But your nation did not comply.
Now I have raised an army and come.
Those who obey will be appeased;
those who defy will be executed.
It is your ruler who likes to wage war,
just as your ruler kills you.
The wheel of Heaven turns;
nothing goes and does not return.
There are sons of Heaven who become commoners,
and there are also commoners who become sons of Heaven.
Since Heaven protects me,
it made me relinquish the title of Emperor.
May Heaven examine this!"
On the day *Xīnchǒu*,
the main army approached Yānjīng.
The Emperor encamped east of Tǔchéngguān, north of the city.
The two wings encamped to the northeast.
Míng Dàtóng General-in-Chief Mǎn Guì and Xuānfǔ General-in-Chief Hóu Shìlù were stationed at Déshèngmén.
Níngyuǎn Provincial Governor Yuán Chónghuàn and Jǐnzhōu General-in-Chief Zǔ Dàshòu were stationed at Shāwōmén.
The Emperor led the right-wing Great Bèilè Dàishàn,
Bèilè Jǐ'ěrhāláng, Yuètè, Dùdù, Sāhālián, and others,
leading the Báijiǎ Hùjūn and Měnggǔ soldiers, to advance and attack Guì and Shìlù.
He dispatched the left-wing Great Bèilè Mǎnggǔ'ěrtài, Ābātài, Ājígé, Duō'ěrgǔn, Duōduó, Háogé, and others,
leading the Báijiǎ Hùjūn and Měnggǔ soldiers, to meet and attack Chónghuàn and Dàshòu.
Both were defeated.
On the day *Guǐmǎo*,
a Míng eunuch, who had surrendered, was sent with a letter to the Míng to negotiate peace.
On the day *Yǐsì*,
they encamped at Nánhǎizi.
On the day *Wùshēn*,
Yuán Chónghuàn and Zǔ Dàshòu encamped at the southeastern corner of the city,
erecting fences for defense.
Our army pressed close and encamped.
The Emperor led light cavalry to inspect.
The Bèilè requested to attack the city.
The Emperor said:
"The path is narrow and dangerous.
If our soldiers are harmed,
even gaining a hundred cities would not be worth it."
Thus, he stopped the attack.
Previously,
two Míng eunuchs had been captured.
Deputy General Gāo Hóngzhōng,
Participatory General Bāo Chéngxiān, and Níng Wánwǒ were ordered to receive a secret plan.
By this time,
Hóngzhōng and Chéngxiān sat close to the two eunuchs and whispered, saying:
"Withdrawing the troops today
is the best strategy.
Earlier, the Emperor rode alone towards the enemy.
Two of the enemy saw the Emperor and spoke for a long time before leaving.
It is likely that Governor Yuán has made an agreement,
and this matter is settled."
At this time, Eunuch Yáng feigned sleep and secretly listened.
The next day, he was released to return
and reported what he had heard to the Míng Emperor.
Consequently, Chónghuàn was imprisoned.
Dàshòu, in fear,
led his troops to flee to Jǐnzhōu,
destroying Shānhǎiguān as he exited.
The Bèilè and high officials requested to attack the city.
The Emperor said:
"If we attack, we can conquer it,
but I fear harming our good generals and strong soldiers.
I cannot bear it."
So he stopped.
On the *xīnhài* day of the twelfth month, the first day of the lunar month,
the grand army advanced southwards via Hǎizǐ.
They hunted and marched,
heading for Liángxiāng,
and captured its city.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
General Wú Nàgé-kè captured Gù'ān.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Beile Ābātài and Sàhālián were dispatched with a grand sacrifice (tàiláo) to worship at the tombs of Tàizǔ and Shìzōng of the Jīn dynasty.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
they again advanced towards Yānjīng,
defeated Ming troops at Lúgōuqíáo,
and annihilated their forces.
Ming generals Mǎn Guì, Sūn Zǔshòu, Hēi Yúnlóng, and Má Dēngyún, with forty thousand troops, erected barricades south of Yǒngdìngmén.
At dawn on the *dīngmǎo* day,
our army destroyed the barricades and entered,
beheading Mǎn Guì, Sūn Zǔshòu, and over thirty officers from vice-general downwards,
capturing Hēi Yúnlóng and Má Dēngyún,
and seizing six thousand horses,
which were then distributed among the generals and soldiers.
On the *wùchén* day,
Dáhǎi was sent to deliver a letter to the Ming for peace negotiations.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Beile Ābātài and Jí'ěrhāláng plundered Tōngzhōu,
burned its boats,
attacked Zhāngjiāwān,
and captured it.
Dáhǎi placed two copies of the peace negotiation letter outside Āndìngmén and Déshèngmén.
On the *yǐhài* day,
another person was sent to deliver a letter to Āndìngmén.
Neither received a reply.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
the army was stationed at Tōngzhōu.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
Yuètūo, Sàhālián, and Háogé led four thousand troops to besiege Yǒngpíng.
They then captured the cities of Xiānghé and Mǎlányù,
which subsequently revolted again.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
the grand army marched towards Yǒngpíng.
In the spring of the fourth year, on the *xīnsì* day of the first month, the first day of the lunar month,
the grand army arrived at Zhēnzǐzhèn and Shāhéyì,
both of which surrendered.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
they reached Yǒngpíng.
Previously,
Liú Xìngzuò had escaped from our country and returned,
hiding with Chónghuàn.
Now,
he led fifteen Manchu soldiers and five hundred Mongol soldiers he had brought with him, intending to go and defend Shāhé.
Hearing of the grand army's arrival,
he changed course for Tàipíngzhài in Yǒngpíng,
and ambushed and killed Kālāqìn soldiers on the way.
The Emperor was enraged by his ingratitude,
and dispatched Beile Ābātài and others to capture and behead him,
tearing his body apart for public display.
On the *guǐchǒu* day,
the Emperor gave strategies to the generals,
and attacked the city during the night.
Gunpowder within the city ignited spontaneously,
the enemy army fell into great disorder,
and at dawn the city was captured.
Beile Jí'ěrhāláng and others entered the city to pacify it.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
