Zhào Ěrsùn was transferred as the Governor-General of the Three Eastern Provinces,
appointed Imperial Commissioner (*Qīnchāi Dàchén*),
and concurrently managed military affairs of the three provinces.
He was given the additional title of Judicial Commissioner (*Tífǎshǐ*) for the Rèhé Circuit in Zhílì.
On the *xīnyǒu* day,
Zhào Ěrfēng was appointed acting Governor-General of Sìchuān,
and Wáng Rénwén was appointed Minister for Border Affairs of Sìchuān and Yúnnán.
The filial piety of Niè Jíguī, former Provincial Governor of Zhèjiāng, who died grieving for his parents, was announced to the legations.
On the *guǐhài* day,
Zhào Qí, a Hàn Dynasty Confucian scholar, and Liú Yīn, a Yuán Dynasty Confucian scholar, were both enshrined in the Temple of Confucius (*Wénmiào*).
Chinese merchants established the Dàtóng School in Yokohama, Japan,
and a plaque with the inscription
“Educate Talent, Broaden Learning” (*Yùcái Guǎngxué*)
was awarded.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
Huáng Xīng, a Revolutionary Party member, led his party to burn down the Governor-General's Yamen in Guǎngzhōu,
and then drove away.
In the summer, fourth month, on the *xīnwèi* day,
Yáng Wéndǐng requested a delay in abolishing the Green Standard Army and defense forces in Húnán.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
graduates of overseas studies, such as Zhōng Shìmíng and Wāng Xīzhī, were granted the titles of advanced scholars (*jìnshì*) and recommended scholars (*jǔrén*) in law and political science,
and recommended scholars in engineering, with some variations.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Zhào Ěrsùn requested permission to act expediently in personnel and administrative matters,
which was granted.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
the officials of the Governor's and Garrison Commanders' battalions in Shāndōng were abolished.
On the *wùyín* day,
an imperial edict was issued to establish a responsible cabinet.
The regulations for cabinet officials were promulgated.
Yì Kuāng, Prince Qìng, was appointed Prime Minister (*Nèigé Zǒnglǐ Dàchén*),
and Grand Secretaries Nà Tóng and Xú Shìchāng were both appointed Assistant Ministers (*Xiélǐ Dàchén*).
Liáng Dūnyàn was appointed Minister of Foreign Affairs (*Wàiwù Dàchén*),
Shàn Qí as Minister of Civil Affairs (*Mínzhèng Dàchén*),
Zài Zé as Minister of Finance (*Dùzhī Dàchén*),
Táng Jǐngchóng as Minister of Education (*Xuéwù Dàchén*),
Yìn Chāng as Minister of War (*Lùjūn Dàchén*),
Zài Xún as Minister of the Navy (*Hǎijūn Dàchén*),
Shào Chāng as Minister of Justice (*Sīfǎ Dàchén*),
Pǔ Lún as Minister of Agriculture, Industry, and Commerce (*Nónggōngshāng Dàchén*),
Shèng Xuānhuái as Minister of Posts and Communications (*Yóuchuán Dàchén*),
Shòu Qí as Minister of Dependencies (*Lǐfān Dàchén*).
Furthermore, the Prime Minister and Assistant Ministers of the cabinet were all appointed State Councilors (*Guówù Dàchén*).
The Prime Minister and Assistant Ministers of the cabinet also served as Ministers of the Constitutional Review Office (*Xiànzhèng Biāncháguǎn Dàchén*),
and Yì Kuāng, Prince Qìng, continued to manage the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
The Court of Imperial Remonstrance (*Bìdéyuàn*) was established,
with Lù Rùnxiáng as its President (*Yuànzhǎng*),
and Róng Qìng as his Deputy.
The old Grand Council (*Jiù Nèigé*), Office of Military Affairs (*Bànlǐ Jūnjīchù*), and Office for Deliberating on Political Affairs (*Huìyì Zhèngwùchù*) were abolished.
Grand Secretaries (*Dàxuéshì*) and Assistant Grand Secretaries (*Xiébàn Dàxuéshì*) still ranked within the Hànlín Academy.
Officials below Cabinet Academician (*Nèigé Xuéshì*) were abolished.
The Office of Military Advice (*Jūnzhīfǔ*) was established,
with Bèile Zài Tāo and Yù Lǎng both serving as Ministers of Military Advice (*Jūnzhī Dàchén*).
An edict was issued to establish the regulations for the office.
Zhào Ěrsùn, together with Chén Kuílong, Zhāng Rénjùn, Ruì Chéng, and Lǐ Jīngxī, consulted with the Ministers of the Constitutional Review Office to deliberate on the provincial official system.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
Yì Kuāng, Prince Qìng, and Grand Secretaries Nà Tóng and Xú Shìchāng all resigned from their positions as Prime Minister and Assistant Ministers,
but their resignations were not accepted,
and they were urged to immediately assume their duties.
The ban on opium was reiterated,
and the Ministry of Civil Affairs and Ministry of Finance were instructed,
along with provincial Governor-Generals and Provincial Governors, to set a deadline for its complete prohibition.
An imperial edict decreed the nationalization of railways.
Previously,
Shí Chángxìn, a supervising censor (*gěishìzhōng*), had memorialized to criticize the abuses of railway companies formed by merchants and commoners in various provinces,
proposing that the ministers of the relevant ministry should be ordered to nationalize all trunk lines in the country,
while allowing gentry and merchants in various provinces to raise funds to build branch lines themselves.
The emperor approved this
and sent it to the Ministry of Posts and Communications for deliberation.
Now,
the memorial stated:
“China has a vast territory
and distant borders;
there must be major trunk lines crisscrossing the four borders
to facilitate administration and control the central hub.
The previous planning was inadequate,
leading to a chaotic and fragmented railway policy,
without distinguishing between trunk and branch lines,
or considering the people's financial capacity.
A single application
was often approved for commercial operation.
However, after several years,
Guǎngdōng had collected only half its shares,
and built few railways.
Sìchuān had huge debts,
with no means of recovery.
Húnán and Húběi had established companies for many years,
only to incur prolonged losses.
If this continues indefinitely,
I fear that as time passes,
the burden on the people will deepen,
and both superiors and subordinates will suffer its harm.
It is therefore requested that trunk lines be nationalized,
and branch lines be left for the people to construct themselves.
The people should be informed that
all trunk lines established by commercially operated companies in various provinces before the third year of Xuāntǒng
should be immediately reclaimed by the state.
Construction should be expedited,
and all previously approved cases should be nullified.”
Hence this imperial edict.
On the *xīnwèi* day,
a fire occurred in Jílín,
and forty thousand taels of silver were issued for relief.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
Fúqí, the acting General and Vice-Commander-in-Chief of Guǎngzhōu, was granted posthumous honors and compensation.
On the *dīnghài* day,
the National Assembly (*Zīzhèngyuàn*) requested that matters concerning the budget and loans be subject to its deliberation,
but this was not permitted.
On the *wùzǐ* day,
Duān Fāng was reinstated as a Vice-Minister (*Shìláng*) awaiting appointment,
and appointed Minister for Supervising the Yuè-Hàn and Chuān-Hàn Railways (*Dūbàn Yuèhàn Chuānhàn Tiělù Dàchén*).
An edict was issued that vacant positions awaiting appointment should not be memorialized.
An edict was issued that in the autumn of this year, the Imperial Guard and army divisions from the vicinity of the capital would gather for a large-scale exercise in Yǒngpíng Fǔ, Zhílì.
On the *jǐchǒu* day,
Pǔ Wěi, Prince Gōng, was relieved of his position as Minister for Opium Prohibition due to illness,
and Nèlèhè, Prince Shùnchéng, replaced him.
On the *gēngyín* day,
Shèng Xuānhuái, the Minister of Posts and Communications, concluded a loan agreement with banks from Britain, Germany, France, and America.
On the *xīnmǎo* day,
Páng Hóngshū was dismissed,
and Shěn Yúqìng was appointed Provincial Governor of Guìzhōu.
On the *rénchén* day,
Governor-Generals and Provincial Governors were ordered to inform the people that
railways are now state-managed.
From the date of the imperial edict's promulgation,
the rented shares in Sìchuān and Húnán provinces
would also be suspended.
For those collected before the fourth month of the third year of Xuāntǒng,
the Ministry of Posts and Communications and the Minister for Supervising Railways should investigate and memorialize in conjunction with the Governor-Generals and Provincial Governors.
Any local official daring to conceal or not report would be investigated and punished.
Yáng Wéndǐng memorialized that since the imperial edict on the nationalization of trunk railways was heard in Húnán province,
public sentiment was agitated and fearful,
with unusual clamor.
Leaflets were widely distributed,
fearing incitement.
An edict was issued to strictly prohibit this,
and if any lawless elements were to incite trouble,
intending to revolt,
they would be executed without mercy, according to the regulations for punishing rebellious parties.
Zhū Jiābǎo memorialized that the confluence of the Jiāngsū and Ānhuī rivers was an area where bandit gangs frequently appeared,
and successive years of famine had made banditry even more rampant.
He requested to implement the regulations for punishing secret society members and bandits in Húběi and Sìchuān,
with offenders to be dealt with under military law.
On the *bǐngshēn* day,
the postal service, formerly attached to the Maritime Customs Service, was transferred to the Ministry of Posts and Communications.
The fixed land tax for official land in Kūnmíng County, Yúnnán, was abolished.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
disaster relief was provided for Téng and Yì counties in Shāndōng.
In the fifth month, on the day of Gēngzǐ,
acting on the advice of Wáng Shìqí, Grand Courtier of the Court of Judicial Review from Húnán, and other京官 (Jīngguān, Beijing officials),
the collection of house donations and rice and salt donations for road construction in Húnán was suspended.
On Xīnyǒu,
Yáng Wéndǐng reported in a memorial that the Húnán Consultative Bureau stated that the Xiang Road (湘路) could be self-managed,
and they were unwilling to borrow money.
He relayed their request based on the circumstances
and was strictly reprimanded.
Relief silver was granted to overseas Chinese victims in Mexico.
On Rénchén,
the positions of Dūsī (都司) and Shǒubèi (守備) and lower-ranking officers, as well as infantry and cavalry in the Guǎngxī Green Standard Army (Lǜyíng), were abolished.
On Guǐmǎo,
the three prefectures of Yǎn, Yí, and Cáo in Shāndōng,
and Jìníng Zhōu, suffered from disaster.
Thirty thousand taels of treasury silver were issued for relief.
The Sìchuān Consultative Bureau, upon hearing the imperial decree regarding the nationalization of railways, with gentry and commoners alike,
sent numerous letters and telegrams
requesting a delay in the takeover,
and also requested the suspension of the publication of the謄黃 (ténghuáng, official gazette),
submitting their request for Wáng Rénwén to relay.
When Rénwén reported this,
an imperial edict severely rebuked him,
still ordering the swift publication of the謄黃,
to be widely promulgated,
and to provide earnest guidance.
On Yǐsì,
the payment for reclaiming barren land was exempted for poor Banner households in Húnchūn.
On Wùshēn,
the palace examination was held for graduates of study abroad programs, including the Jìnshì (進士) Jiāng Gǔhuái,
and officials were appointed accordingly.
On Yǐmǎo,
Sūn Bǎoqí memorialized that imperial clan members (Zōngzhī) should not interfere in governance,
and was reprimanded.
On Rénzǐ,
Nà Tóng was reinstated
and again appointed Grand Academician of the Wènyuāngé.
On Bǐngchén,
due to the recovery of railway rights, Guǎngdōng
advocated not using government-issued paper currency
but exchanging tickets for silver.
Zhāng Míngqí was instructed to take preventive measures.
On Dīngsì,
the Zīzhèngyuàn (資政院, Consultative Council) presented revised regulations for the Shùjì Xuétáng (速記學堂, Shorthand School).
On Wùwǔ,
the Ministries of Dùzhī (度支, Finance) and Yóuchuán (郵傳, Posts and Communications) jointly memorialized on the method for recovering the main lines of the Chuān, Yuè, and Hàn railways.
They requested the repurchase of company shares from the four provinces of Yuè (Guǎngdōng), Chuān (Sìchuān), Xiāng (Húnán), and È (Húběi),
to be exchanged by the ministry for specially issued national railway shares.
For the Yuè (Guǎngdōng) railway, six tenths would be issued.
For the Xiāng (Húnán) and È (Húběi) railways, the original capital would be returned.
For the Chuān (Sìchuān) railway, over four million taels for actual labor and materials used in Yíchāng
would be given national guaranteed-interest shares,
while the remaining over seven million taels
could either be reinvested as shares
or used for industrial development,
all at their discretion.
An imperial edict ordered Duān Fāng to immediately proceed to the provincial capitals to instruct the governors-general and governors to comply.
Dīng Bǎoquán was relieved due to illness,
and Chén Bǎochēn was appointed Governor of Shānxī.
On Gēngshēn,
Yú Shìméi was appointed Director-General of the Lǐxuéguǎn (禮學館, Institute of Rites).
On Jiǎzǐ,
the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) submitted the official system for subordinate officials of the Grand Secretariat and the official system for the Fǎzhìyuàn (法制院, Institute of Legal System),
and an imperial edict promulgated them.
The Nèigé Chéngxūntīng (內閣承宣廳, Grand Secretariat Bureau of Promulgation) was established,
along with four bureaus: Zhìgào (制誥, Imperial Edicts), Guān (官, Officials), Tǒngjì (統計, Statistics), and Yìnzhù (印鑄, Seals and Casting).
Positions such as Gécchéng (閣丞, Grand Secretary Assistant), Tīngzhǎng (廳長, Bureau Director), and Júzhǎng (局長, Bureau Chief) were established.
The Yuànshǐ (院使, Director) of the Nèigé Fǎzhìyuàn was also established.

The Xiànzhèng Biānchácháng (憲政編查館, Constitutional Compilation and Review Bureau), Lìbù (吏部, Ministry of Personnel), Zhōngshūkē (中書科, Secretariat Scrutiny Office), Jīchá Qīnfèng Shàngyù Shìjiànchù (稽察欽奉上諭事件處, Office for Inspecting Matters of Imperial Edicts), and Pībĕnchù (批本處, Memorial Review Office) were abolished,
with their functions transferred to the Grand Secretariat.
The Fānshūfáng (繙書房, Translation Office) was reassigned to the Hànlínyuàn (翰林院, Hanlin Academy).
The Ministry of War memorialized
to appoint military advisors for the provincial training offices (Dūliàn Gōngsuǒ).
On Yǐchǒu,
the Hànlínyuàn presented the Kāngxī Zhèngyào (康熙政要, Essential Policies of Kangxi) compiled by Jiǎntǎo (檢討, Compiler) Zhāng Qìn.
In the sixth month, on Dīngmǎo,
the Zīzhèngyuàn was ordered to revise its regulations in conjunction with the Grand Secretariat.
Relief was granted for flood disasters in the three Húnán counties of Wǔlíng, Lóngyáng, and Yìyáng.
The gunpowder magazines of the Bǎodìng Army Arsenal and the Army Second Division Exercise Hall both caught fire.
On Gēngchén,
there were floods in Ānhuī;
the embankments in Wǔlǐbēi (五里碑) and Jiǔlián (九連) and other places in Wúwéi Zhōu were breached.
On Xīnsì,
Róng Qìng was appointed President of the Bìdéyuàn (弼德院, Bureau of Admonition and Virtue),
with Zōu Jiālái as Vice President.
Lù Rùnxiáng was relieved as Minister for Opium Prohibition,
and Chén Bǎochēn was relieved as Governor of Shānxī,
to be held in reserve for a Shìláng (侍郎, Vice Minister) position.
Yīkètǎn was relieved as Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Dūcháyùan (都察院, Censorate),
and noted for a Vice Commandant (Fù Dūtǒng) position.
The concurrent position of Prefect of Shùntiān Fǔ was abolished.
On Rénwǔ,
Lù Zhōngqí was appointed Governor of Shānxī.
On Guǐwèi,
Zhào Ěrfēng memorialized that in the recaptured Bātáng DéRóng (巴塘得榮) area,
households and commoners requested to pay land tax,
and over a thousand lamas from Làngzhuāng Sì (浪莊寺) were permitted to return to secular life.
He also memorialized that the households and commoners of Bātáng Lín Kǎshí (巴塘臨卡石) surrendered
and were assigned to the administration of Sānbà Tīng.
On Yǐyǒu,
the banner of Zāsàkè Gùshān Bèizǐ Sānjìmìdōubù (扎薩克固山貝子三濟密都布) in Yīkèzhāo Méng (伊克昭盟) suffered disaster,
and ten thousand taels of treasury silver were issued for relief.
On Bǐngxū,
bandit groups in Dāngá'ěr Tīng (丹噶爾廳) and Xīníng Xiàn gathered to cause unrest;
the government troops dispersed them,
and the chief culprits Lǐ Wàng, Lǐ Tǒngchūn, and Lǐ Guānbójiǎn (李旺、李統春、李官博儉) were executed.
On Xīnmǎo,
the Diǎnlǐyuàn (典禮院, Bureau of Ceremonies) was established,

with positions such as Zhǎngyuàn Dàxuéshì (掌院大學士, Grand Academician of the Bureau), Fù Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì (副掌院學士, Vice Academician of the Bureau), Xuéshì (學士, Academician), and Zhí Xuéshì (直學士, Senior Academician).
Lǐ Diànlín was appointed Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì of the Diǎnlǐyuàn,
with Guō Zēngxīn as Vice.
On Rénchén,
over 2,400 gentry and commoners from Sìchuān, including Luó Lún,
regarding the nationalization of railways,
and the methods determined by Shèng Xuānhuái and Duān Fāng in conjunction with the Ministry of Dùzhī,
which treated the Sìchuān people purely with force
and were not fair,
dared not obey,
and requested a decision.
Wáng Rénwén reported this,
and an imperial edict severely rebuked him
for his repeated impertinent memorials.
A Consul-General was added for Java Island, which was under Dutch rule,
and Consuls for Sùshuǐ (Surabaya) and Sūméndálà (Sumatra).
On Jiǎwǔ,
heavy rains caused rivers to overflow in Chángdé Fǔ, Húnán,
inundating subordinate counties,
and destroying fields and houses.
Sixty thousand taels of treasury silver were issued for relief.
On Bǐngshēn,
concerning the continued agreement on opium prohibition with the British envoy,
the strict prohibition was reiterated,
and Chinese and foreign officials were instructed to earnestly implement it.
In the intercalary sixth month, on Jǐhài,
Bǎo Xī was appointed Minister for Opium Prohibition.
On Gēngzǐ,
Ēn Shòu was relieved due to illness,
and Yú Chénggé was appointed Governor of Shǎnxī.
On Guǐmǎo,
heavy rains in Ānhuī,
and the sudden rise of the Yangtze River tide,
caused flooding in various prefectures and counties along the river.
Fifty thousand taels of treasury silver were issued for relief.
On Gēngxū,
Yú Chénggé was transferred to be Governor of Húnán,
and Yáng Wéndǐng was appointed Governor of Shǎnxī.
On Rénzǐ,
an imperial edict ordered this year's mobilization of the Imperial Guards and the armies of the various nearby garrisons to Yǒngpíng Fǔ for a grand exercise.
Prince Bèi Lè Zǎi Tāo (貝勒載濤), Minister of Military Advising, was ordered to respectfully represent the emperor and personally oversee the exercise.
On Guǐchǒu,
Prince Bèi Zǐ Pǔ Lún (貝子溥倫) and Zhènguógōng (鎮國公) Zǎi Zé (載澤) were ordered to compile and draft grand imperial ceremonies in conjunction with the Zōngrénfǔ (宗人府, Imperial Clan Court).
On Yǐmǎo,
revolutionaries attacked Lǐ Zhǔn (李準), Admiral of the Guǎngdōng Navy, with a bomb;
he was injured but survived.
The former Jílín General Míng Ān (銘安) passed away.
On Bǐngchén,

Zǎi Zhèn (載振), Lù Rùnxiáng (陸潤庠), Zēng Qí (增祺), Chén Bǎochēn (陳寶琛), Dīng Zhènduó (丁振鐸), Yáo Xīguāng (姚錫光), Shěn Yúnpèi (沈雲沛), Chéng Xūn (誠勳), Qīng Ruì (清銳), and Zhū Zǔmóu (朱祖謀) were all appointed Advisory Ministers of the Bìdéyuàn (弼德院),

and State Ministers Yì Kuāng (奕劻), Nà Tóng (那桐), Xú Shìchāng (徐世昌), Liáng Dūnyàn (梁敦彥), Shàn Qí (善耆), Zǎi Zé (載澤), Táng Jǐngchóng (唐景崇), Yìn Chāng (廕昌), Zǎi Xún (載洵), Shào Chāng (紹昌), Pǔ Lún (溥倫), Shèng Xuānhuái (盛宣懷), Shòu Qí (壽耆), as well as Zōnglìng (宗令, Imperial Clan Court Director) Shì Duó (世鐸) of the Zōngrénfǔ, and Grand Minister of the Imperial Household Department Kuí Jùn (奎俊) and Jì Lù (繼祿), all concurrently served as Advisory Ministers of the Bìdéyuàn.
On Dīngsì,
Shàn Qí was transferred to be Minister of the Lǐfān Yuàn (理藩院, Court of Colonial Affairs),
and Guì Chūn (桂春) was appointed acting Minister of Civil Affairs.
Fèng Shān (鳳山) was transferred to be General of Guǎngzhōu,
and Shòu Qí was appointed General of Jīngzhōu.
Yán Kǎi (顏楷) and other chairmen of the Sìchuān Railway Shareholders' Association presented a memorial impeaching the Ministry of Yóuchuán;
Zhào Ěrfēng reported this,
but there was no response.
On Xīnyǒu,
the chief counties of provincial prefectures were abolished
and replaced with local judicial courts.
On Yǐchǒu,
the Grand Secretariat requested a revision of regulations.
On the Rénshēn day of the seventh month,
Zhào Ěrfēng reported that the railways were nationalized,
but the people of Chuān still largely misunderstood,
and collectively demanded [a different approach].
An edict was issued to the Yóuchuán Bù (Ministry of Post and Communications) and the Dūbàn Tiělù Dàchén (Minister Overseeing Railways) to clarify railway shares,
making the methods clear
to dispel public doubts.
On the Jiǎxū day,
Ruìchéng, Zhāng Míngqí, Zhào Ěrfēng, and Yú Chénggé were ordered to jointly manage railway affairs within their respective jurisdictions.
Duān Fāng was ordered to go to Sìchuān to investigate railway matters.
On the Dīngchǒu day,
as the public in Sìchuān was restless
and susceptible to incitement,
Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief) Tián Zhènbāng was ordered to strictly discipline his troops to suppress unrest,
and Duān Fāng was urged to proceed quickly to Sìchuān,
with permission to bring troops.
Zhào Ěrfēng and Yùkūn, along with the Tídū, Sī (Judicial Commissioners), and Dào (Intendants), reported
that the people of Chuān were fiercely contending over the railways,
requesting that the Zīzhèngyuàn (Advisory Council) decide on returning the railways to private commercial management.
This was not allowed,
and Zhào Ěrfēng was again ordered to suppress and disperse them.
On the Jǐmǎo day,
heavy rain fell in various prefectures of Jiāngsū,
causing dikes to burst,
and submerging fields and crops.
Forty thousand taels of silver were issued from the imperial treasury for relief.
The Yǒngdìng Hé burst its banks.
Duān Fāng entered Sìchuān,
and all new and old land and naval forces were placed under his command.
Lù Zhēngxiáng was transferred to be the Chūshǐ Éguó Dàchén (Minister to Russia),
and Liú Jìngrén was made Chūshǐ Héguó Dàchén (Minister to the Netherlands).
On the Xīnsì day,
Zhōngruì was dismissed,
and Guìfāng was appointed Kēbùduō Bànshì Dàchén (Minister Resident at Kobdo).
Pǔfēng was dismissed,
and Sà Yìntú was appointed Kēbùduō Cāncàn Dàchén (Assistant Minister at Kobdo).
On the Rénwǔ day,
rebellion broke out in Sìchuān,

and Zhào Ěrfēng arrested nine people: Pú Diànjùn, president of the Zīyì Jú (Provincial Assembly); Luó Lún, vice-president; Dèng Xiàokě, president of the Bǎolù Tóngzhìhuì (Railway Protection League); Yán Kǎi and Zhāng Lán, presidents of the Shareholders' Association; and Hú Róng, Jiāng Sānchéng, Yè Bǐngchéng, and Wáng Míngxīn.
Soon after, the Tóngzhìhuì gathered a crowd and surrounded the Zǒngdū Shǔ (Governor-General's Yamen),
dispersing only after being attacked.
Relief was provided for the disaster in the four prefectures of Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, Húzhōu, and Shàoxīng in Zhèjiāng.
On the Guǐwèi day,
the Emperor began his studies.
Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretary) Lù Rùnxiáng and Shìláng (Vice Minister) Chén Bǎochēn were his tutors,
and Fùdūtǒng (Deputy Lieutenant-General) Yīkètǎn instructed him in the National Language (Mandarin Chinese) and Qīngwén (Manchu script).
Relief was provided for the flood in Húběi.
On the Jiǎshēn day,
a dike in Chénghǎi Xiàn (Cheng County), Guǎngdōng, burst,
and forty thousand taels of silver were issued from the imperial treasury for relief.
Sìchuānese people residing in the capital held a meeting to discuss the railway issue,
and submitted a petition to the Zīzhèngyuàn (Advisory Council) requesting it to present their case.
Liú Shēngyuán, a representative, was ordered to be arrested and repatriated to his hometown.
The Xuébù (Ministry of Education) was ordered to restrain students from participating in external affairs,
and local authorities were commanded to prohibit gatherings and meetings.
On the Dīnghài day,
floods occurred in Jǐnán and various prefectures and counties in the eastern and western circuits of Shāndōng,
and the private dikes on the upper reaches of the Huáng Hé (Yellow River) again burst.
Fifty thousand taels of silver were issued from the imperial treasury for relief.
Relief was provided for the flood in Fújiàn.
On the Wùzǐ day,
former Liǎngguǎng Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Guangdong and Guangxi) Cén Chūnxuān was ordered to go to Sìchuān
to assist Zhào Ěrfēng in handling suppression and pacification affairs.
On the Jǐchǒu day,
the Jiānguó Shèzhèng Wáng (Regent Prince) reviewed the Jìnwèijūn (Imperial Guard).
On the Guǐsì day,
due to the civil unrest in Sìchuān,
Zhào Ěrfēng was ordered to supervise and command the various armies to swiftly disperse [the rebels],
while distinguishing between good and bad elements for suppression and pacification;
those who were coerced would be pardoned.
On the Jiǎwǔ day,
the wild tribes of Bōmì surrendered.
On the Bǐngshēn day of the eighth month,
Hède (Robert Hart), the Zǒng Shuìwùsī (Inspector-General of Customs), died,
and was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince).
A shrine was ordered to be built in Yīlí for the late Chéngdū Jiāngjūn (General of Chengdu) and former Yīlí Jiāngjūn (General of Yili) Mǎ Liàng.
On the Rényín day,
Qìng Qīnwáng (Prince Qing) Yīkuāng again requested to be relieved of his duties as Nèigé Zǒnglǐ Dàchén (Prime Minister) and Administrator of the Wàiwù Bù (Ministry of Foreign Affairs).
This was not allowed.
On the Jiǎchén day,
the Dúbiāo (Governor-General's Brigade) and Tíbiāo (Provincial Commander-in-Chief's Brigade) of Zhílì were abolished,
along with the officers and cavalry and infantry garrison troops of the Tōngyǒng, Tiānjīn, Zhèngdìng, Dàmíng, and Xuānhuà zhènbiao (Brigades).
The Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief) remained.
On the Bǐngwǔ day,
Jiāngnán Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Jiangnan) Liú Guāngcái was dismissed due to illness,
Zhāng Xūn was transferred to replace him,
and Zhāng Huáizhī was made Gānsù Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Gansu).
On the Dīngwèi day,
the national anthem was established.
On the Gēngxū day,
the Yánzhèng Yuàn (Salt Administration Bureau) was established,
with officials from minister downwards appointed,
and the Yánwù Chù (Salt Affairs Office) was abolished.
Zàizé was ordered to concurrently serve as Yánzhèng Dàchén (Minister of Salt Administration).
On the Guǐchǒu day,
Duān Fāng and Ruìchéng reported
that the Guǎnghàn (Guangzhou-Hankou) and Chuānhàn (Sichuan-Hankou) railways within Húběi province were nationalized,
and the commercial companies were dissolved.
Methods for acquiring railway shares were agreed upon.
An imperial edict commended this,
and awarded gentry for their profound understanding of righteousness.
On the Jiǎyín day,
the Gémìngdǎng (Revolutionary Party) plotted rebellion in Wǔchāng.
The plot was discovered,
thirty-two people were arrested,
and three people, including Liú Rǔkuí, were executed.
Ruìchéng reported this,
and an imperial edict praised him for nipping the disaster in the bud
and quickly restoring order.
He was ordered to strictly interrogate the captured individuals
and pursue those who fled.
On the Yǐmǎo day,
the Xīnjūn (New Army) in Wǔchāng mutinied and joined the Gémìngdǎng (Revolutionary Party).
Zǒngdū (Governor-General) Ruìchéng abandoned the city and fled,
whereupon Wǔchāng fell.
An imperial edict stripped Ruìchéng of his post,
but still ordered him to temporarily assume the duties of Zǒngdū,
to atone for his mistakes by rendering service.
Lùjūn Dàchén (Minister of War) Yìnchāng was ordered to lead an army to suppress the rebellion,
and the Húběi army and reinforcements were all placed under his command.
Sà Zhènbīng led warships and Chéng Yǔnhé led naval forces to reinforce them.
On the Bǐngchén day,
Zhāng Biāo abandoned his camp and fled,
due to collusion between soldiers and bandits.
He was stripped of his title as Húběi Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Hubei),
but was still tasked with suppressing the bandits.
The grand maneuvers at Yǒngpíng were suspended.
The ban on transporting grain in Shānxī and Hénán was lifted.

The military and civilians of Wǔchāng rallied around Lí Yuánhóng, the Tǒnglǐngguān (Brigade Commander) of the Lùjūn Dì'èrzhī Hùnchéng Xié (21st Mixed Brigade of the Army), proclaiming him Dūdū (Military Governor),
and established a jūnzhengfǔ (military government).
Thereafter, various provinces seized territory with their armies and declared independence,
and those elected as leaders all styled themselves Dūdū.
The Gémìngjūn (Revolutionary Army) captured Hànyáng,
raided the arsenal and ironworks,
and occupied Hànkǒu.
On the Dīngsì day,
Yuán Shìkǎi was reinstated as Húguǎng Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Huguang),
and Cén Chūnxuān as Sìchuān Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Sichuan),
both ordered to oversee suppression and pacification affairs.
Bèilè (Prince of the Fourth Rank) Zàitāo was ordered to command the various Jìnwèijūn (Imperial Guard) units to defend the capital region.
On the Wùwǔ day,
Wáng Rénwén was dismissed,
and Zhào Ěrfēng was reinstated as Chuāndiān Biānwù Dàchén (Minister for Border Affairs of Sichuan and Yunnan).
This year's tribute from Fèngtiān was suspended.
On the Jǐwèi day,
Cén Chūnxuān resigned as Sìchuān Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Sichuan).
The imperial edict did not allow it.
Liáng Dūnyàn was urged to come to the capital to serve.
The capital opened public granaries to provide food for the people.
On the Rénxū day,
an imperial edict decreed that all land and naval forces along the Cháng Jiāng (Yangtze River) were to be under the command of Yuán Shìkǎi.
An edict was issued concerning the military operations in Chuān and Chǔ:
those who were originally coerced followers,
if they extricated themselves and returned,
their past actions would not be prosecuted.
Those willing to serve in the army
and capable of capturing and presenting bandit leaders
would be generously rewarded.
Registers of rebel party members should be destroyed,
to avoid implication of others.
Affected areas in both provinces would receive relief and comfort.
The abolition of the Lǜyíng (Green Standard Army) and Xúnfángduì (Patrol and Defense Forces) in various provinces was revoked.
Shòuqí was dismissed,
and Liánkuí was appointed Jīngzhōu Jiāngjūn (General of Jingzhou).
On the Guǐhài day,
by imperial decree of the Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager),
two hundred thousand taels of silver were issued from the imperial treasury to aid the victims of the war in Húběi.
The rivers in Lóngxī and Nánjìng counties in Fújiàn overflowed and dikes burst,
and twenty thousand taels of silver were issued from the imperial treasury for relief.
Due to military operations in Húběi,
Shāndōng and Shānxī provinces were ordered to purchase and transport rice and wheat to supply the army.
On the Jiǎzǐ day,
Fùdūtǒng (Deputy Lieutenant-General) Wáng Shìzhēn was ordered to assist in Húběi military affairs.
On the *yǐchǒu* day of the ninth month, which was the first day of the month,
there was a solar eclipse.
The Zīzhèngyuàn convened its second session,
and an imperial edict exhorted the councilors.
The Húnán New Army mutinied.
Governor Yú Chénggé fled to a warship,
and Huáng Zhōnghào, commander of the Patrol and Defense Battalion and former General of the Guǎngxī Yòujiāng Garrison, died.
On the *bǐngyín* day,
the Shǎnxī New Army mutinied.
Acting Governor and Provincial Administration Commissioner Qián Néngxùn attempted suicide but failed,
and then fled to Tóngguān.
Xi'ān General Wénruì, Vice General Chéngyàn, and Kèméng'é all died.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
the Empress Dowager issued an imperial decree,
releasing 240,000 *liǎng* from the imperial treasury to relieve famine in Zhílì, Jílín, Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Shāndōng, Zhèjiāng, Húnán, and Guǎngdōng provinces,
and establishing a Charity and Relief Association.
On the *wùchén* day,
Zhāng Yīntáng was dismissed,
and Shī Zhàojī was appointed Minister to Italy, Mexico, and Peru.
Revolutionaries killed Guǎngzhōu General Fèngshān with an explosive device.
On the *jǐsì* day,
the Empress Dowager donated funds to the Charity and Relief Association.
The Zīzhèngyuàn stated that Minister of Posts and Communications Shèng Xuānhuái had abused his power and violated laws,
deceived the emperor,
distorted policies,
and caused disaster and chaos,
and was truly the primary culprit for endangering the nation.
An imperial edict stripped him of his office.
Duān Fāng memorialized,
reporting that the origin of the chaos in Sìchuān
was truly caused by conflicts between officials and common people.
He requested the release of Pú Diànjùn, Speaker of the Consultative Council, and Dèng Xiàokě, along with nine others,
and that Xiāo Xiāng, a principal in the Ministry of Justice detained in Húběi, also be exempted from prosecution.
This was granted.
Táng Shàoyí was appointed Minister of Posts and Communications.
Chén Bāngruì was appointed Minister for Relief Affairs in Jiāngsū and Ānhuī.
On the *gēngwǔ* day,
the Empress Dowager released 1,000,000 *liǎng* from the imperial treasury to aid the Húběi army.
Yìnchāng was recalled,
and Yuán Shìkǎi was appointed Imperial Commissioner,
to oversee the suppression and pacification of Húběi,
commanding all armies.
Féng Guózhāng, Chief of the Army General Staff, was ordered to command the First Army,
and Duàn Qíruì, Commander-in-Chief of the Northern Jiāngsū, to command the Second Army,
both under Yuán Shìkǎi's command.
Chūnlù was appointed Guǎngzhōu General.
Condolences and pensions were granted to the deceased Guǎngzhōu General Fèngshān.
Féng Guózhāng fought the revolutionary army at Shèkǒu,
recapturing it.
On the *rénshēn* day,
Ruìchéng, having lost Wǔchāng,
fled aboard a warship,
stealthily escaped the province,
and lived a life of shame.
An imperial edict ordered his arrest and transport to the capital,
to be tried by the Ministry of Justice.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
an imperial edict was issued, blaming himself.
Pǔlún and Zàizé were ordered to draft articles for the constitution,
and report them promptly.
Shìxù, Grand Secretary and President of the Zīzhèngyuàn, resigned due to illness.
Lǐ Jiājū was appointed as his replacement,
and Dáshòu as Vice President.
Guìchūn returned to his post as Vice Minister of the Granaries.
Zhào Bǐngjūn was appointed Acting Minister of Civil Affairs.
Húnán Governor Yú Chénggé was stripped of his office,
but temporarily continued to manage Húnán gubernatorial affairs.
The Shānxī New Army mutinied,
and Governor Lù Zhōngqí died.
The Yúnnán New Army mutinied.
Governor-General Lǐ Jīngxī fled.

Provincial Administration Commissioner Shìzēng, along with Commander Zhōng Línnóng, Expectant Daoist official in charge of military preparations Wáng Zhènjī, and Baggage Train Battalion Commander Fàn Zhōngyuè, all died.
Tāng Shòupotential was ordered to oversee the organization of local militia in Zhèjiāng.
The ban on political parties was lifted.
Those who had been punished during the Wùxū Coup,
and those who had subsequently been suspected of political revolution,
and those who had recently been coerced into surrendering,
were all pardoned.
The Zīzhèngyuàn stated that the cabinet should bear responsibility,
and requested the abolition of the current regulations,
the implementation of a complete cabinet system,
and that imperial relatives and nobles not be appointed.
An imperial edict approved this.
The Shùntiān Prefecture implemented price controls on grain.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
the Jiāngxī New Army mutinied.
Governor Féng Rǔkuí fled to Jiǔjiāng,
and died by taking poison.
The Ānhuī New Army attacked the provincial capital
and was dispersed.
On the *yǐhài* day,
Yuán Shìkǎi was appointed Premier,
and ordered to organize a complete cabinet.
Prince Qìng Yìkuāng was dismissed as Premier,
and appointed President of the Bìdéyuàn.
Nàtóng and Xú Shìchāng were dismissed as Assistant Premiers,
and along with Róngqìng, were appointed Advisory Ministers of the Bìdéyuàn.
Shànqí, Zōu Jiālái, Zàizé, Táng Jǐngchóng, Yìnchāng, Zàixún, Shàochāng, Pǔlún, Táng Shàoyí, and Shòuqí were dismissed as Ministers of State,
and all relieved of their ministerial duties.
Zàitāo was dismissed as Minister of the Army Council,
and Yìnchāng was appointed to that post.
Wèi Guāngtáo was reinstated as Governor-General of Húguǎng,
and ordered to proceed quickly to Húběi.
All land and sea forces and the Yangtze River Flotilla remained under Yuán Shìkǎi's command.
On the *bǐngzǐ* day,
Yuán Shìkǎi was summoned to the capital.
Wáng Shìzhēn was appointed Acting Governor-General of Húguǎng.
Following Zhāng Shàozēng's suggestion,
the Zīzhèngyuàn was ordered to draft the constitution.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
the Zīzhèngyuàn memorialized to adopt constitutional monarchy,
presenting nineteen major articles of faith.
100,000 *liǎng* from the imperial treasury were released to relieve refugees in Sìchuān suffering from military disaster.
On the *wùyín* day,
an imperial edict instructed commanding officers to explain to the people that the court and the people were making a fresh start,
and did not wish to use military force again.
Commanding officers were ordered to strictly enforce discipline
and forbid disturbing the populace.
Wú Lùzhēn, Commander of the Sixth Division, was appointed Acting Shānxī Governor.
Yuán Shìkǎi resigned as Premier,
and a gentle edict encouraged him to remain.
Condolences and pensions were granted to the martyred Shānxī Governor Lù Zhōngqí.
Guìzhōu declared independence,
electing a military governor.
Governor Shěn Yúqìng fled.
The revolutionary army occupied Shànghǎi.
Yuán Shìkǎi ordered the front-line armies to halt their advance.
He then dispatched Prefect Liú Chéng'ēn and Senior Staff Officer Cài Tínggàn to Lím Yuánhóng to persuade him to end hostilities,
but they returned without achieving their objective.
On the *jǐmǎo* day,
an imperial edict permitted revolutionaries to organize political parties according to law.
The Zīzhèngyuàn stated that during the Battle of Hànkǒu,
government troops had brutally killed civilians,
and requested an order for a ceasefire.
Yuán Shìkǎi was ordered to investigate and punish military officers guilty of crimes,
and the state would compensate merchants and civilians for their losses.
Wú Lùzhēn memorialized,
reporting that he had sent officers into the enemy camp to persuade them,
issued an order to cease attacks,
and personally went to Niángzǐguān to appease the revolutionary army.
An imperial edict commended him.
The Guǎngdōng Diplomatic Commissioner's Office was abolished.
Jiāngsū Governor Chéng Déquán sided with the revolutionary army in Sūzhōu,
and declared himself military governor.
The Zhèjiāng New Army mutinied.
Governor Zēngyùn was captured
and later released.
On the *gēngchén* day,
Zhāng Shàozēng, Commander of the Twentieth Division, was granted the title of Vice Minister,
to pacify the Yangtze River region.
Zhāng Shàozēng claimed illness and did not go.
Zhāng Xūn was appointed Minister for Joint Military Affairs of the Southern Ocean.
Zhào Ěrfēng was dismissed,
and Duān Fāng was appointed Acting Governor-General of Sìchuān.
Yuán Shìkǎi was urged to come to the capital.
Wāng Zhàomíng, Huáng Fùshēng, and Luó Shìxūn, suspected political criminals, were released from prison.
On the *xīnsì* day,
Guǎngxī Governor Shěn Bǐngkūn declared himself military governor.
The Ministry of Appointments Bureau caught fire.
On the *rénwǔ* day,
Xú Shàozhēn, Commander of the Jiāngníng New Army, mutinied with his troops.
General Tiěliáng, Governor-General Zhāng Rénjùn, and Commander-in-Chief Zhāng Xūn resisted.
Zhènjiāng fell,
and Zài Mù, Vice General of Jīngkǒu, died.
The Ānhuī New Army mutinied,
and elected Governor Zhū Jiābǎo as military governor.
On the *guǐwèi* day,
an imperial edict specially appointed Yuán Shìkǎi as Premier.
Following the Zīzhèngyuàn's memorial,
and based on the principles of constitutional election,
this appointment was made.
Lǚ Hǎihuán requested that the Charity and Relief Association be expanded according to the Red Cross Society law,
which was granted.
Guǎngdōng declared independence,
electing a military governor.
Governor-General Zhāng Míngqí fled.
The Fújiàn New Army mutinied.
General Púshòu and Governor-General Sōngshòu died.
On the *jiǎshēn* day,
the Empress Dowager issued an imperial decree dismissing Jìlù,
and reinstated Shìxù as Minister of the Imperial Household Department.
Xīliáng was summoned for an audience.
As the court initially made no distinction between Manchu and Han military and civilian populations,
commanding officers were ordered to inform the people of this.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
Shāndōng Governor Sūn Bǎoqí declared independence.
The Shùntiān Prefecture memorialized to establish a Provisional Charity and General Relief Red Cross General Association in the capital.
Bèile Yùlǎng was dismissed as Minister of the Army Council,
and Xú Shìchāng was appointed to that post.
On the *bǐngxū* day,
rewards and pensions were granted to the officers and soldiers who fought and defended Jiāngníng.
Lǚ Hǎihuán was appointed President of the Chinese Red Cross Society,
and concurrently managed the Charity and Relief Association.
The Consultative Councils and New Armies of the Three Eastern Provinces demanded independence.
Governor-General Zhào Ěrxùn refused,
shelved their proposal,
and still ordered them to dissuade the others.
On the *dīnghài* day,

It was decreed that the troops from various garrisons in the environs of the capital, as well as armies from various routes, and the forces under Jiāng Guìtí, should all be subject to Yuán Shìkǎi's command.
On the day of Wùzǐ,
envoys were dispatched to comfort the provinces affected by war,
to solicit public opinion.
It was decreed that provincial governors and viceroys should nominate representatives to come to the capital for a conference.
Zhào Ěrxùn, citing his culpability in the Sichuan affair, requested dismissal,
but an imperial edict disallowed it.
Wú Lùzhēn, having led troops to Shíjiāzhuāng,
was killed by his subordinates.
Censor Wēn Sù impeached Wú Lùzhēn for harboring malicious intentions,
and his rebellious tendencies had become evident.
An imperial edict commanded Chén Kuílóng to investigate.
Wáng Shìzhēn was relieved due to illness,
and Duàn Zhīguì was appointed Acting Governor-General of Húguǎng.
The Yongdìng River closure was completed.
Yuán Shìkǎi arrived in the capital.
On the day of Jǐchǒu,
Zhāng Xíluán was appointed Governor of Shānxī.
Pǔtíng was dismissed,
and Xīliáng was appointed Military Governor of Rèhé.
On the day of Gēngyín,
Yuán Shìkǎi recommended ministers of state.
An imperial edict appointed Liáng Dūnyàn as Minister of Foreign Affairs,
Zhào Bǐngjūn as Minister of Civil Affairs,
Yán Xiū as Minister of Revenue,
Táng Jǐngchóng as Minister of Education,
Wáng Shìzhēn as Minister of the Army,
Sà Zhènbīng as Minister of the Navy,
Shěn Jiābĕn as Minister of Justice,
Zhāng Jiàn as Minister of Agriculture, Industry, and Commerce,
Yáng Shìqí as Minister of Posts and Communications,
Dáshòu as Minister of the Court of Colonial Affairs,
all with vice-ministers to assist them.
Yú Shìméi and Bǎo Xī were appointed Ministers for Revising Laws.
Shàochāng, Lín Shàonián, Chén Bāngruì, Wáng Xù, Wú Yùshēng, and Ēnshùn were all appointed Advisory Ministers of the Bìdé Yuàn (Council of Advisers).
On the day of Xīnmǎo,
Duàn Qíruì was appointed Acting Governor-General of Húguǎng.
Shēng Yǔn was appointed Acting Governor of Shǎnxī,
and placed in charge of military affairs.
On the day of Rénchén,
Zēng Yùn, Governor of Zhèjiāng, was stripped of his post for unauthorized abandonment of duty.
On the day of Guǐsì,
for supervising the attack on the remaining rebels at Mòlíngguān,
where officers and soldiers fought bravely,
Zhāng Xūn was awarded the hereditary title of Second Class Light Chariot Captain.
On the day of Jiǎwǔ,
the Zīzhèng Yuàn (Advisory Council) submitted revised regulations,
which were promulgated.
In the tenth month of winter, on the day of Bǐngshēn,
the Cabinet memorialized regarding matters conflicting with the constitution,
and stopped summoning officials for audiences and memorials.
The Bìdé Yuàn and the Jūnzī Fǔ (Council of Military Consultation) were also restricted.
The old system of daily duty for each yámen was abolished.
Shìxù was again appointed Grand Secretary of the Wényuāngé.
On the day of Wùxū,
Wǔ Tíngfāng, Zhāng Jiàn, Táng Wénzhì, and Wēn Zōngyáo advised the Regent,
requesting support for a republican political system.
On the day of Gēngzǐ,
the nineteen articles of the constitutional creed were sworn before the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple),
with the Regent performing the sacrifice on behalf of the Emperor.
Láo Nǎixuān was appointed Director-General of the Imperial University.
Pǔliáng was dismissed,
and Huáng Màochéng, General of the Xuānhuà Garrison in Zhílì, was concurrently appointed Acting Military Governor of Cháhā'ěr.
On the day of Xīnchǒu,
Zhāng Huáizhī, Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Gānsù, was ordered to assist in the defense of Zhílì.
Chéngdū, Sìchuān, declared independence,
and elected a military governor.
On the day of Rén'yín,
Duān Fāng, Minister for Supervising Railways, expectant Vice-Minister, and Acting Governor-General of Sìchuān, led troops into Sìchuān,
and was near Zīzhōu
when he was killed by his subordinates.
His younger brother Duān Jǐn, who accompanied him,
was also killed.
For his meritorious service in retaking Hànyáng,
Féng Guózhāng was ennobled as a Second Class Baron.
Qīn Wáng Āmù'ěrlíngguī of Kē'ěrqìn was ordered to Fèngtiān,
to confer with Zhào Ěrxùn on Mongolian affairs.
The rebel army attacked Jīnlíng,
and Deputy General Wáng Yǒuhóng died in battle.
On the day of Jiǎchén,
Sūn Bǎoqí renounced independence,
and impeached himself, awaiting punishment.
An imperial edict pardoned him,
and commended the officials and merchants of Shāndōng who did not join the rebellion.
Funds were issued to reward Zhāng Xūn's army.
Liáng Dǐngfēn was awarded the third-rank京堂 (ministerial position),
and was to assist Lǐ Zhǔn in recovering Guǎngdōng.
On the day of Bǐngwǔ,
the revolutionary army captured Jiāngníng,
and General Tiěliáng and Governor-General Zhāng Rénjùn fled to Shànghǎi,
while Zhāng Xūn retreated with his remaining forces to Xúzhōu for defense.
Yuán Shìkǎi signed a temporary armistice agreement with the revolutionary army,
suspending hostilities for three days.
Subsequently, the period was extended repeatedly,
until the day the national polity was decided.
Xú Shìchāng was appointed Minister specifically in charge of training the Imperial Guard.
On the day of Dīngwèi,
Bǎofēn was dismissed,
and Qí Yàolín was appointed Governor of Hénán.
Shòu Xūn was ordered to confer with Yuán Shìkǎi and Xú Shìchāng on military affairs.
On the day of Wùshēn,
the Zhébùzūn Dānbā Hútúkètú declared himself independent,
and expelled Sānduō, the Imperial Resident of Kùlún.
An imperial edict stripped Sānduō of his post.
On the day of Jǐyǒu,
the deceased Fěng Rǔkuí, Governor of Jiāngxī, who died a martyr, was posthumously honored and indemnified.
On the day of Gēngxū,
Zǎi Fēng, the Regent, memorialized the Empress Dowager,
returned the seal of the Regent,
and retired to his princely residence.
By Imperial Edict of the Empress Dowager,
Shìxù and Xú Shìchāng were both promoted to Grand Tutor,
to protect the Emperor.
Duàn Qíruì was ordered to suppress bandits in Dāngyáng, Tiānmén, and other areas.
On the day of Xīnhài,
an imperial edict appointed Yuán Shìkǎi as Plenipotentiary Minister,
and entrusted representatives to go south to discuss the overall situation.
Féng Guózhāng was appointed Military Governor of Cháhā'ěr.
The Zīzhèng Yuàn requested the adoption of the solar calendar,
and freedom for all subjects to cut their hair;
an imperial edict approved both.
On the day of Rénzǐ,
the title of Minister for Training the Imperial Guard was changed to Commander-in-Chief,
and Féng Guózhāng was appointed to it.
Liáng Bì was appointed Military Counselor of the Jūnzī Fǔ.
Sōngshòu, Governor-General of Mǐnzhè, who died a martyr, was posthumously honored and indemnified.
On the day of Bǐngchén,
the Tàipíngshān Cháhàn'áolā coal mine in Hēilóngjiāng province was opened.
On the day of Dīngsì,
the revolutionary army reached Jīngzhōu,
and Hénglíng, Acting Deputy Military Governor of the Left Wing, died there.
On the day of Wùwǔ,
the Cabinet memorialized for the implementation of patriotic bonds.
On the day of Xīnyǒu,
Sūn Bǎoqí was dismissed,
and Hú Jiànshū was appointed Governor of Shāndōng.
On the first day of the eleventh month, Jiǎzǐ,
Yuán Shìkǎi requested the abolition of the old system where officials submitted sealed memorials.
On the day of Yǐchǒu,
Shī Jìyún, former Acting Provincial Judicial Commissioner of Húběi, and Chén Zhōngxìn, former Junior Supervisor of the Imperial Banqueting Court, were ordered to organize militia in Sìchuān.
On the day of Bǐngyín,
Yǐn Chānghéng and Luó Lún of Chéngdū, with their同志軍 (Comrade Army), entered the Governor-General's yámen,
kidnapped and seized Zhào Ěrfēng, former Acting Governor-General of Sìchuān and Minister for Border Affairs of Sìchuān and Yúnnán;
he did not yield
and died.
On the day of Wùchén,
Zhào Guóxián, Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Cháozhōu, Guǎngdōng, who died in service, was posthumously honored and indemnified.
On the day of Rénshēn,
the Empress Dowager decreed the convocation of a provisional national assembly,
to publicly decide on the national polity of a constitutional republic.
Earlier,
Yuán Shìkǎi had dispatched Táng Shàoyí to the south,
to discuss the overall situation with Wǔ Tíngfāng, the representative of the revolutionary army,
choosing Shànghǎi as the negotiation site.
After repeated meetings,
Wǔ Tíngfāng strongly advocated for the abolition of the imperial system and the establishment of a republic,
which Táng Shàoyí could not overturn,
stating that it must first be reported to the emperor for a decision,
and thus he reported it.
Yuán Shìkǎi memorialized requesting the convocation of an imperial conference of princes and ministers,
and ultimately his words were followed.
At this point,
a national conference was scheduled to be held in Shànghǎi
to resolve the national polity.
On the day of Jiǎxū,
seventeen provincial representatives held the election for the provisional president in Shànghǎi,
elected a provisional president,
established a government in Nánjīng,
and named it the Republic of China (Zhōnghuá Mínguó).
On the day of Wùyín,
royal relatives and princes were urged to contribute funds to the army.
Dìngchéng, Chief Justice of the Dàlǐ Yuàn (Supreme Court), was dismissed,
and Liú Ruòzēng replaced him.
On the day of Jǐmǎo,
Yáng Shìqí was dismissed,
and Liáng Shìyí was appointed Acting Minister of Posts and Communications.
On the day of Xīnsì,

Duān Fāng, Acting Governor-General of Sìchuān, Minister for Supervising the Yuè-Hàn and Chuān-Hàn Railways, and expectant Vice-Minister, and his brother, Prefect Duān Jǐn, were posthumously honored and indemnified.
The Yánzhèng Yuàn (Salt Administration Bureau) was abolished.
The Luanzhou Mutiny occurred,
and was pacified.
In Yīlí, Yáng Zànxù, Brigadier-General of the New Army, mutinied,
and General Zhì Ruì died.
On the day of Dīnghài,
the Zhébùzūn Dānbā Hútúkètú was admonished,
and presented with precious items from previous reigns.
On the day of Gēngyín,
Hénglíng, Acting Deputy Military Governor of the Left Wing of Jīngzhōu, who died a martyr, was posthumously honored and indemnified.
On the day of Xīnmǎo,
Yuán Shìkǎi encountered a bomb on the road,
but it missed.
On the day of Rénchén,
Zhāng Huáizhī was concurrently appointed Assistant Minister for Shāndōng Defense.
On the day of Guǐsì,
the relevant authorities were ordered to protect the lives and property of foreigners.
Shū Qīng'ā was ordered to assist in Húběi defense.
Wū Zhēn was appointed Commander of the Gendarmerie,
and martial law was declared in the capital.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day of the twelfth month, which was the first day of the lunar month,
Zhāng Huáizhī was awarded the title of Xúnfǔ.
On the *jǐwèi* day,
former Shānxī Xúnfǔ Lù Zhōngqí was again granted the hereditary rank of Second-Class Qīngchē Dūwèi,
and his son Lù Guāngxī, a Hánlín Yuàn Shìjiǎng who was killed at the same time, was posthumously bestowed the Third-Rank Jīngtáng title.
He was given generous compassion and an honorific posthumous name.
Zhōngqí's wife, Lady Táng, was also honored and commiserated.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
Zhāng Rénjùn was dismissed,
and Zhāng Xūn was appointed acting Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng.
Hú Jiànshū was dismissed,
and Zhāng Guǎngjiàn was appointed acting Shāndōng Xúnfǔ.
Wú Dǐngyuán was appointed to assist in Shāndōng's defense.
On the *jǐhài* day,
the I-lí Jiāngjūn Zhìruì, who died in the line of duty, was posthumously honored and commiserated.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
by imperial edict of the Empress Dowager,
Yuán Shìkǎi was granted the title of First-Class Hóu for his loyalty to the nation.
Élèhún was appointed acting I-lí Jiāngjūn,
and Wénqí was appointed to handle matters for the Tǎěrbāhātái Cānzàn Dàchén.
Lǐ Jiājū was dismissed,
and Xǔ Dǐnglín was appointed Zīzhèng Yuàn Zǒngcái.
The revolutionaries attacked Liángbì with an explosive bullet,
wounding his leg.
He died two days later.
On the *rényín* day,
Yuán Shìkǎi declined the marquisate,
but after repeated earnest refusals, he finally accepted.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
for the recapture of Tóngguān,
ten thousand taels of silver were awarded to the army as a犒軍.
On the *jiǎchén* day,
for his achievements at Hànyáng,
Zhāng Biāo's rank of Tídū was reinstated.
On the *yǐsì* day,
Zhāng Huáizhī was appointed Ānhuī Xúnfǔ.
The Fúzhōu Jiāngjūn Púshòu, who died in the line of duty, was posthumously honored and commiserated.
On the *dīngwèi* day,
Zhāng Xíluán was ordered to Fèngtiān to assist in defense matters,
Lǐ Shèngduó was appointed acting Shānxī Xúnfǔ,
and Lú Yǒngxiáng was appointed to assist in Shānxī's military affairs.
The Jūnzī Fǔ Jūnzīshǐ Liángbì, who was assassinated, was posthumously honored and commiserated.
On the *wùshēn* day,
Wáng Gēng was appointed Jūnzī Fǔ Jūnzīshǐ.
On the *jǐyǒu* day,
by imperial edict of the Empress Dowager,
Yuán Shìkǎi was given full authority
to negotiate terms with the revolutionary army and report to the throne.
At this time, Cén Chūnxuān, Yuán Shùxūn, Lù Zhēngxiáng, Duàn Qíruì, and others requested the swift establishment of a republic
to prevent further suffering of the people.
Therefore, without waiting for the convocation of the national assembly,
it was decided to cede political power,
and thus this decree was issued.
On the *gēngxū* day,
Kūnyuán was appointed to assist in Rèhé's defense.
On the *xīnhài* day,
Sòng Xiǎolián was appointed acting Hēilóngjiāng Xúnfǔ.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
Xú Shìchāng was dismissed as Jūnzī Dàchén.
Shìzēng, the Gānsù Bùzhèngshǐ who died in the line of duty in Yúnnán, was posthumously honored and commiserated.
On the *yǐmǎo* day,
Xīliáng was dismissed,
and Kūnyuán was appointed acting Rèhé Dūtǒng.
On the *dīngsì* day,
unpaid land and grain taxes in Xúzhōufǔ, Jiāngnán, were remitted.
On the *wùwǔ* day,
Yuán Shìkǎi reported to the throne that he had discussed with the Southern representative Wǔ Tíngfāng,
agreeing to a republic,
and submitted eight conditions for the favorable treatment of the imperial family,
four conditions for the treatment of the imperial clan,
and seven conditions for the treatment of the Mǎn, Méng, Huí, and Zàng peoples,
totaling nineteen articles.
The Empress Dowager ordered Yuán Shìkǎi, with full authority, to establish a provisional republican government
and discuss unification methods with the revolutionary army.
Yuán Shìkǎi then, by imperial edict of the Empress Dowager,
proclaimed to China and foreign nations:
"Previously, due to the uprising of the revolutionary army
and the response from various provinces,
the entire land was in turmoil,
and the people suffered greatly.
Yuán Shìkǎi was specially ordered to dispatch representatives to discuss the overall situation with the revolutionary army representatives,
to convene a national assembly, and publicly decide the form of government.
For the past two months,
there has been no definite solution.
North and South are separated,
and both sides are at a stalemate.
Merchants cease their travels,
and scholars are exposed in the wilderness.
As long as the national structure is not decided,
the people will not have peace.
Now, the sentiment of the entire nation
leans largely towards a republic.
The southern provinces
initiated the movement first,
and the northern generals
also advocated it later.
The will of the people
is the will of Heaven.
How can I bear to, for the honor and glory of a single family,
go against the wishes of the myriad people?
Therefore, observing the general trend externally
and the public sentiment internally,
I especially, along with the Emperor, cede the sovereign power to the entire nation,
establishing a constitutional republic.
This will appease the people's desire for peace and order within the country
and align with the ancient sage's principle of 'the world belongs to all.'
Yuán Shìkǎi was previously elected Prime Minister by the Zīzhèng Yuàn.
At this juncture of old and new transitioning,
he should be the means for the unification of North and South.
Let Yuán Shìkǎi, with full authority, organize a provisional republican government
and negotiate unification methods with the revolutionary army.
The ultimate goal is to ensure the people's tranquility
and the peace of the realm,
and to unite the five races of Mǎn, Méng, Hàn, Huí, and Zàng with their complete territories to form a great Zhōnghuá Mínguó.
The Emperor and I can then retire to a life of peace and leisure,
enjoying the years,
receiving the respectful treatment of the citizens,
and personally witnessing the achievement of an excellent governance.
Would this not be wonderful!"
It also said:
"Ancient rulers of the world
prioritized preserving the lives of the people
and could not bear to harm those they were meant to nourish.
The newly established national structure
is solely to first quell the great chaos
and secure lasting peace.
If we go against the will of the majority of the people
and rekindle endless wars,
the overall situation will collapse,
and massacres will follow,
inevitably leading to the tragic suffering of ethnic groups.
This would shock the imperial ancestral temples,
torment the myriad people,
and the subsequent calamities would be unbearable to speak of.
When faced with two evils,
one chooses the lesser.
This is precisely the court's painful dilemma in judging the times and observing changes,
and its compassion for our suffering people.
All you officials and people, both inside and outside the capital,
must earnestly understand this intention,
weigh the advantages and disadvantages for the overall situation,
and not act with hollow pretentiousness
or extreme empty talk,
lest both the nation and the people suffer.
The Mínzhèng Bù, the Bùjūn Tǒnglǐng, Jiāng Guìtí, Fēng Guózhāng, and others are ordered to guard strictly
and guide with earnestness,
so that all may clearly understand the court's intention to conform to Heaven and the people,
and its great impartiality.
As for the establishment of officials and division of duties in the state,
they serve as the standard for the people.
Internally, there are cabinet, bureaus, ministries, and academies;
externally, there are governors-general, governors, provincial administrations, and circuit intendants.
These are to protect and secure the common people,
not established for one person or one family.
All you officials, great and small, both inside and outside the capital,
should deeply reflect on the difficulties of the times
and carefully perform your duties.
It is incumbent upon all chief officials to earnestly admonish and encourage,
not neglecting their posts,
thereby fulfilling my long-cherished intention of loving and cherishing the people."
It also said:
"Previously, due to the critical state of the nation
and the suffering of the myriad people,
the Grand Council was specially ordered to discuss with the revolutionary army the various conditions for the favorable treatment of the imperial family,
to achieve a peaceful resolution.
Now, according to the report,
the conditions for favorable treatment proposed by the revolutionary army,
including the perpetual worship at ancestral temples and imperial tombs,
and the proper repair of the late Emperor's mausoleum to its original state,
have all been fully undertaken.
The Emperor merely abdicates political power,
but does not relinquish his honorable title.
It was also agreed upon eight articles for the favorable treatment of the imperial family,
four articles for the treatment of the imperial clan,
and seven articles for the treatment of the Mǎn, Méng, Huí, and Zàng peoples.
Upon reviewing the report, it is quite comprehensive.
I hereby proclaim to the imperial clan and the Mǎn, Méng, Huí, and Zàng peoples
that henceforth you must remove all boundaries,
jointly maintain peace and stability,
and once again witness the flourishing of the world
and collectively enjoy the blessings of the republic.
I have high hopes for this."
Thereupon, the Emperor abdicated.
A commentary states: The emperor, in his tender years, inherited the throne.
He oversaw the state and acted as regent.
All military and state affairs,
from beginning to end, were handled by him.
Major decisions were all reported to the empress dowager for her final approval.
When the great change arose,
he promptly relinquished political power,
making the realm public.
He was granted perpetual preferential treatment,
thus opening up an unprecedented marvel in history.
Like Yú Bīn (虞賓) in his position,
the culture and institutions were still new.
When right and wrong are settled,
historians often find it difficult.
However, Kǒngzǐ (孔子) compiled the Chūnqiū (春秋),
writing what should be written
and deleting what should be deleted.
What he saw in his own time was detailed more thoroughly than what he heard.
How could the institutional history of a dynasty
be omitted?
Perhaps it is also for the common judgment of all under heaven and future generations?
Treatise on Astronomy One
Among the historical treatises on astronomy,
after the Tiānguānshū (天官書) in the Shǐjì (史記),
only the two treatises from the Jìn (晉) and Suí (隋) dynasties
fully describe celestial bodies, observational instruments, and astromancy.
The Táng (唐) and Sòng (宋) added more detail,
but none were complete.
During the Yuán (元) dynasty,
measurements and observations became more precise and clear,
and prognostication was denser.
However, constrained by its territorial boundaries,
its cultural influence had not yet spread widely.
Many aspects of its governance and astronomical observations were still brief.
The Qīng (清) dynasty unified the entire land of Huáxià (華夏),
with sagely emperors succeeding one another.
Shèngzǔ (聖祖) personally managed the science of numbers,
investigating its utmost subtleties.
He successively created seven new instruments,
measuring the sun, moon, and stars
to the minutest fractions of degrees and seconds;
and surveying the longitudes and latitudes of the imperial map
across the entire vast territory.
Shìzōng (世宗) further, due to accumulated errors over the years,
authorized his observatory officials to adopt the elliptical method.
Gāozōng (高宗) also, finding occasional omissions in the old records of star positions,
personally commissioned the Jīhéng Fǔchén Yí (璣衡撫辰儀) instrument
to conduct renewed observations.
After the pacification of Huíjiāng (回疆) and the two Jīnchuān (金川) regions,
he again ordered a re-measurement of the li cha (里差, meridian difference)
and its inclusion in the shíxiàn (時憲, calendar system).
With clear principles, accurate calculations,
precise instruments, and meticulous methods,
this was
unprecedented in history.
This Treatise on Astronomy
fully records the methods of inference and verification.
The celestial phenomena that were clearly recorded
in the Veritable Records of successive dynasties and by relevant offices
are also all inscribed herein.
After the 60th year of Qiánlóng (乾隆) (1795),
since there were no national historical records to draw upon,
those details are omitted.
Celestial Phenomena, Earth's Body, Meridian Difference
Celestial Phenomena, as stated in the Tiānxiàngpiān (天象篇) of the Lìxiàng Kǎochéng (曆象考成):
"The Tiānwèn (天問) in the Chǔ Cí (楚辭) asks: 'The sphere has nine layers,
who engineered their measures?'
Later calendrical astronomers
stated that heaven has twelve layers.
This does not mean that heaven actually has so many layers;
it means that the sun, moon, and stars revolve in heaven,
each following its own path,
which is what the Chǔ Cí (楚辭) referred to as 'sphere'.
To understand the principle of these spheres,
one must scrutinize the motions of these spheres.
To examine the motions of these spheres,
one must use a perfectly still and unmoving reference,
only then can their waxing and waning be determined.
Indeed, the celestial path is still and specialized,
while celestial movements are direct.
The perfectly still has its own heaven,
which serves as the upper and lower reference for the earth.
Therefore, all moving bodies revolve within it ceaselessly.
If there were no perfectly still reference to verify the utmost motion,
even the Sages would not have been able to achieve their skill.
Humans always observe the heavens from the ground,
and the movements of the seven luminaries can all be obtained;
this is precisely because stillness is used to verify motion.
"Of the twelve layers of heaven,
the outermost is perfectly still and unmoving;
the next is the Primum Mobile,
from which the north and south poles and the equator are determined.
Next are the north-south precession;
next are the east-west precession;
these two layers of heaven,
their motion is very subtle,
so calendrical astronomers temporarily set them aside without discussion.
Next are the Three Enclosures and Twenty-Eight Mansions,
where the fixed stars move.
Next is the path of Saturn;
next is the path of Jupiter;
next is the path of Mars;
next is the path of the Sun,
which is the Ecliptic.
Next is the path of Venus;
next is the path of Mercury;
the innermost is the path of the Moon,
which is the White Path.
The inner and outer positions of these heavens are determined by their distance from the earth.
However, the knowledge of their distance from the earth
is derived from the eclipses and occultations of the various luminaries, and the speed of their movements.
For whatever is eclipsed or occulted must be above,
and whatever eclipses or occults must be below.
The lunar body can obscure the sun's light and cause a solar eclipse;
this is evidence that the sun is far and the moon is near.
The moon can eclipse the five planets,
and the moon and the five planets can in turn eclipse the fixed stars;
this means the five planets are higher than the moon but lower than the fixed stars.
The five planets can also eclipse each other,
which means the five planets each have their own distances.
"Furthermore, the Primum Mobile, with its vast and primordial qi, carries all the heavens in a leftward rotation;
its speed is very fast.
Therefore, those closer to the Primum Mobile
rotate leftward quickly but move rightward slowly.
Gradually moving further from the Primum Mobile,
the leftward rotation is slower, but the rightward movement becomes faster.
Currently, among the rightward movements,
fixed stars are the slowest,
Saturn and Jupiter are next,
Mars is next.
The Sun, Venus, and Mercury are relatively faster, and the Moon is the fastest;
this is further evidence of their relative proximity."
The Rìchán Lìlǐ (日躔曆理) in the Kǎochéng Hòubiān (考成後編) states:
"From the Western methods of Ptolemy to Tycho,
the theories of deferents, epicycles, and equants were established.
In recent times, Kepler, Cassini, and others
also proposed that the deferent is elliptical."
The Yuèlí Lìlǐ (月離曆理) states:
"Since Westerners created the elliptical method,
the distance between the sun and the moon's heaven varies,
which means the center of the moon's deferent advances and recedes.
The distance between the earth's center and the heaven's center
causes the difference between the two centers to vary."
Combining these discussions,
the celestial phenomena are fully covered.
The fixed star heaven has no parallax and no details of secondary epicycles,
therefore, this treatise records the distances of the seven heavens from Saturn downwards to the earth's center,
detailing the findings of observations and calculations.

highest by elliptical method: sixty-three and 77/100 times the earth's radius.
Terrestrial Body. The *Húntiān* school says that Heaven envelops the Earth like an egg wraps its yolk.
The *Nèijīng* states:
"The Huángdì said, 'Is the Earth truly beneath?'
Qíbó replied, 'The Earth is beneath humans,
in the midst of the Great Void.'
He asked, 'What does it rely on?'
He replied, 'The Great *Yì* supports it.'"
The *Dàdài Lǐ* states:
"Shānjūlí asked Zēngzǐ, 'Is it true that Heaven is round and Earth is square?'
Zēngzǐ replied, 'If Heaven were truly round and Earth were square,
then its four corners would not be covered.
Cān once heard from the Master:
"The Way of Heaven is round,
the Way of Earth is square."'"
Shàozǐ, a Sòng Confucian, said:
"What does Heaven depend on?
It depends on Earth.
What does Earth attach to?
It attaches to Heaven.
What do Heaven and Earth depend on and attach to?
They depend on and attach to each other.
In their mutual dependence and attachment,
Heaven depends on form,
and Earth attaches to *qì*."
Chéngzǐ said:
"Based on the sun's shadow, thirty thousand *lǐ* is taken as the center.
If there were a limit,
yet having reached one side as far as fifteen thousand *lǐ*,
the movement of Heaven and Earth would still be as before.
Thus, the 'center' is also merely a 'center of the time'."
He also said:
"The celestial body currently defined by people
is merely determined by what the eye sees.
Where the gaze reaches its limit and sees nothing,
they then assume it is the end.
However, someone once saw ten large stars below the South Pole while at sea.
Thus, the celestial body currently seen is probably not yet definitively determined.
The rising and setting of the sun and moon
do not exceed the thirty thousand *lǐ* range.
However, China only extends to Shànshàn and Shāchē,
which is already fifteen thousand *lǐ*.
If one were to observe the sun from there,
it would still only be within the thirty thousand *lǐ* range.
Bózhún was in Zézhōu
and once ate chives three times,
first eating Huáizhōu chives,
then Zézhōu,
then Bīngzhōu.
This shows that within a few hundred *lǐ*,
the climate already differs by three months.
If this difference is applied to everything,
then it would amount to half a year's difference.
In this way,
there would be those who experience winter solstice here and summer solstice there,
but it is just a matter of winter and summer."
Zhūzǐ's commentary on *Tiānwèn* states:
"The form of Heaven is round like a pellet,
and its rotation also has no tangible form,
but is like the swirling of a strong wind.
The Earth, on the other hand, is the dregs of *qì* that have gathered to form a tangible body.
But because it is bound within the swirling strong wind,
it is able to float steadily in the air for a very long time without falling."
Westerners say that the terrestrial body is spherical,
with people on all sides,
with alternating winter and summer,
and opposite day and night,
which aligns perfectly with the *Nèijīng*, the *Dàijì*, and the words of the Sòng Confucians.
Now, using the circumference of Heaven as three hundred sixty degrees,
if one travels two hundred *lǐ* south,
the North Pole lowers by one degree;
if one travels two hundred *lǐ* north,
the North Pole rises by one degree.
Traveling two hundred *lǐ* east or west along the equator,
the difference in the early or late appearance of a lunar eclipse is also one degree.
Along the latitude circles north and south of the equator,
although the widths differ,
they all correspond to the celestial sphere.
Thus, the great circumference of the Earth is three hundred sixty degrees everywhere,
and its circumference both east-west and north-south is seventy-two thousand *lǐ*.
Calculated using the ancient foot of eight *cùn*,
the circumference is ninety thousand *lǐ*.
Using the ratio of circumference three to diameter one,
the diameter is thirty thousand *lǐ*.
This also matches the ancient saying of thirty thousand *lǐ* as the center.
Therefore, the terrestrial body being spherical
is beyond doubt.
The distances between latitudes and longitudes vary along the great circumference;
these key points are recorded.

The *lǐ* difference (*lǐchā*)
is due to the different north-south and east-west locations where people reside,
thus the celestial zenith and local horizon also differ.
It can be calculated and determined by *lǐ*,
hence the name *lǐchā*.
Its relevance to astronomical observation is immense.
The appearance and disappearance of fixed stars,
the varying length of day and night,
the rising and setting of the Seven Luminaries,
the early or late arrival of solar terms,
and the depth and sequence of eclipses,
all vary because of it.
Only by obtaining the amount of this difference
can the reasons for these variations
all be predicted,
preventing them from being mistaken for anomalies and leading to fabricated explanations.
