Treatise 2: Astronomy, Part 2: Astronomical Instruments
The Hàn dynasty created the armillary sphere (húntiānyí),
said to be based on the surviving system of the jīhéng (armillary sphere and sighting tube).
The Táng and Sòng dynasties both imitated its creation.
It was not until the Yuán dynasty that simplified armillary spheres (jiǎnyí), celestial globes (yǎngyí), observation tables (kuíjǐ), gnomons (jǐngfú), and other instruments were made,
which were more detailed than ancient ones.
During the Míng dynasty, an observatory was built against the city wall inside the Qíhuà Mén gate in Běijīng,
and imitating the Yuán dynasty's designs, an armillary sphere (húnyí), a simplified armillary sphere (jiǎnyí), and a celestial globe (tiāntǐ sānyí) were constructed,
and placed on the platform.
Below the platform were the Gǔjǐng Táng hall, gnomons (guībiǎo), and clepsydras (húleìu);
the early Qīng dynasty continued these practices.
In the eighth year of Kāngxī's reign (1669),
Emperor Shèngzǔ, acting on the advice of the imperial minister Nán Huáirén,
rebuilt six instruments:

the ecliptic equatorial instrument (huángdào jīngwěiyí), the equatorial instrument (chìdào jīngwěiyí), the horizontal azimuth instrument (dìpíng jīngyí), the horizontal altitude instrument (dìpíng wěiyí), the quadrant (jìxiànyí), and the celestial globe (tiāntǐyí).
In the fifty-second year (1713),
the horizontal azimuth and altitude instruments were combined into one instrument.
In the ninth year of Qiánlóng's reign (1744),
Emperor Gāozōng personally designed the Jīhéng Fǔchényí,
which was also placed on the platform.
Now, examining the designs and uses of each instrument,
they are all described in this chapter.
The ecliptic equatorial instrument (huángdào jīngwěiyí):
The instrument has four circles,
each divided into four quadrants,
with each quadrant being ninety degrees.
The outermost large circle, which is fixed and immovable,
is called the tiānyuán zǐwǔ guī (celestial prime meridian gnomon).
Its outer diameter is six chi,
the gnomon's face is one cun three fen thick,
and its side is two cun five fen wide.
The lower half of the gnomon is clamped into a cloud-shaped base.
The half-circle supported above it
is precisely aligned north-south,
vertically upward to the zenith,
and centrally to the horizon.
From above and below the horizon, based on the degrees of rise and set of the northern and southern celestial poles at the capital,
the two poles of the equator are determined.
Next inward is the guòjí zhì quān (polar passing circle),
at evenly divided points around the circumference of this circle,
steel pivots are inserted through the two poles of the equator.
Furthermore, according to the great angular separation between the ecliptic and the equator,
the northern and southern poles of the ecliptic are determined on the polar passing circle.
Ninety degrees from the ecliptic poles, the ecliptic circle (huángdào quān) is installed,
intersecting the polar passing circle at a right angle,
each embedded within the other to join,
making the two circles one entity,
rotating together.
On the two sides of the ecliptic circle,
one shows the twelve zodiacal constellations,
the other shows the twenty-four solar terms.
Their two intersections
correspond to the winter solstice
and the summer solstice.
Next inward is the ecliptic longitude circle (huángdào jīngquān),
which is pivoted on the ecliptic poles with steel pivots.
The diameter of the circle forms a round axle,
with a circumference of three cun.
A cylindrical column is erected at the center of the axle as the latitude pointer (wěibiǎo),
forming a right angle with the side of the longitude circle.
Both the ecliptic circle and the longitude circle are equipped with sliding pointers (yóubiǎo),
and a brass wire serves as a plumb line at the top of the instrument.
The entire instrument is supported by twin dragons,
and further crossbeams are used to support the dragon's feet.
At the four ends of the beams,
each is supported by a lion,
and screw pillars are set to achieve levelness.
If the plumb line is off-center,
rotate the screw pillars;
when the plumb line is straight,
the instrument is level.
Usage:
To find the ecliptic longitude and latitude of a certain star,
one person must first find the previously obtained longitude and latitude of that star on the ecliptic circle,
place the sliding pointer on it,
and pass it through the central column of the north-south axis,
aligning the pointer with the star to set the instrument.
Another person uses a sliding pointer on the longitude circle, passing it over the column,
aligning the pointer with the observed star;
by sliding and positioning it,
the indicator line of the sliding pointer on the longitude circle determines the star's latitude.
Then, with the instrument set, observe the degrees between the two pointers on the ecliptic circle,
which is the star's longitude difference.
Or, when observing the sun or moon,
using a nearby star as a reference,
the procedure is the same.
The chìdào jīngwěiyí (Equatorial Armillary Sphere).
The instrument has three circles.
The largest outer circle
is the tiānyuán zǐwǔ guī (Celestial Meridian Circle).
It is borne by a dragon facing south.
The divisions and pole-setting of the guī
are all the same as those of the huángdào yí (Ecliptic Armillary Sphere).
Ninety degrees from the pole, the chìdào quān (Equatorial Circle) is placed,
intersecting the zǐwǔ guī at a right angle,
and is fixed and unmoving.
The inner surface and upper side of the circle are engraved with twenty-four hours,
each hour having four kè.
The outer surface of the guī is divided into three hundred and sixty degrees,
with the chìdào jīng quān (Equatorial Meridian Circle) placed inside.
With the north and south poles as pivots,
it can rotate east and west,
tangent to the inner surface of the chìdào quān.
The diameter of the jīng quān serves as a circular axle.
A circular column is erected at the center of the axle.
The methods for the yóubiǎo (movable sight), chuíxiàn (plumb line), jiāoliáng (crossbeam), luózhù (screw posts), etc.,
are all the same as those of the huángdào yí.
Regarding its use,
if measuring the time of day for the sun,
then the shíqè yóubiǎo (movable time sight) on the chìdào quān,
which is the tōngguāng ěr (aperture),
is aligned with the nánběi zhóubiǎo (north-south axial sight).
Observing what the yóubiǎo inside the chìdào quān points to,
gives the hour, minute, and second.
For the longitudes of various celestial bodies,
two tōngguāng ěr are used,
which are two jìngbiǎo (diameter sights),
one fixed and one movable on the chìdào quān.
One person peers through the fixed ěr at the nánběi zhóubiǎo,
aligning it with a previously observed star.
Another person moves the movable ěr to align it,
peering at the běnzhóubiǎo (main axial sight) to be straight with the object being measured.
The degree and minute indicated on the chìdào quān between the two ěr
is the difference in longitude between the two objects.
Latitude is also obtained by moving and aligning a tōngguāng ěr on the jīng quān.
The aim is to make the eye, the sight, and the object being measured collinear.
The degree and minute indicated by the jīng quān below the běn ěr, whether north or south of the equator,
is the degree and minute of the object's distance from the equator, north or south.
The dìpíng jīngyí (Horizontal Azimuth Instrument).
The instrument has only one dìpíng quān (horizontal circle),
with a full diameter of six chǐ.
Its planar width is two cùn and five fēn,
and its thickness is one cùn and two fēn.
It is divided into four quadrants,
each ninety degrees.
It is supported by four dragons standing on a jiāoliáng.
At the four ends of the jiāoliáng,
luózhù are installed for leveling.
A vertical column is placed at the intersection of the jiāoliáng,
with its height equal to the dìpíng quān,
precisely at the center of the dìpíng quān.
Additionally, an axle is erected on the dìpíng quān, one to the east and one to the west,
approximately four chǐ high.
Each column has a dragon
coiling upwards,
with a claw extending from the end of each column,
mutually holding a spherical bead.
Below is a vertical axle,
flat and square in shape,
hollowed out like a window lattice,
to house a straight line.
The upper end of the axle enters the bead,
and the lower end enters the center of the vertical column,
allowing it to rotate.
The line within the axle
always serves as the chuíxiàn of the tiānzhǐng (zenith).
There is also a rectangular horizontal sight,
as long as the full diameter of the dìpíng quān,
one cùn thick,
and one cùn and five fēn wide.
A square hole is opened in its center to fit over the lower end of the vertical axle,
allowing it to rotate with the vertical axle.
Its two ends are sharpened to a point,
to indicate the degree divisions of the dìpíng quān.
Furthermore, a line extends from each end,
meeting at the top of the straight line within the vertical axle,
forming two triangles.
Whenever something is to be measured,
the yóubiǎo is rotated
so that the three lines are collinear with the object being measured.
Then, observing what the end of the sight points to,
gives the dìpíng jīngdù (horizontal azimuth) of the object being measured.
The dìpíng wěiyí (Horizontal Altitude Instrument),
which is the xiàngxiànyí (quadrant instrument),
takes one-fourth of a complete circle to measure altitude.
Its arc is ninety degrees,
and its two sides are circular radii,
six chǐ long.
The intersection of the two radii is the center of the instrument.
The instrument frame has vertical columns to the east and west,
each supported by two dragons.
A horizontal beam is mounted above,
and a central column is inserted into the horizontal beam,
allowing the instrument center to rotate.
It points to the two sides of the instrument,
one parallel to the central column,
and one parallel to the horizontal beam.
A short circular column is also erected at the instrument center to serve as a sight.
A kuīhéng (sighting rule) is added,
equal in length to the radius,
its upper end fixed at the instrument center,
and its lower end sharpened
to indicate the degree divisions on the arc surface.
Additionally, a biǎo'ěr (sight aperture) is installed.
When something is to be measured,
the kuīhéng is moved up and down,
peering through the slit of the biǎo'ěr at the circular column,
to make it collinear with the object being measured.
The degree division indicated by the end of the héng
is the dìpíng wěidù (horizontal altitude) of the object being measured.
The jìxiànyí (Sextant Instrument).
Its arc surface is one-sixth of a full circle,
divided into sixty degrees.
It has one arc and one gàn (arm),
the gàn being six chǐ long,
which is the radius of the full circle.
The width of the arc is two cùn and five fēn.
To the left and right of the gàn,
delicate cloud patterns (xìyún jiūmànchī lián) entwine,
serving to secure it.
At the upper end of the gàn is a small héng,
forming a cross with the gàn.
Circular columns serve as sights at the instrument center and both ends of the héng.
A yóubiǎo is provided on the arc surface.
The platform supporting the instrument
is approximately four chǐ high.
A vertical column is planted in the middle
to support the center of gravity of the instrument,
allowing it to rotate left and right,
and tilt up, down, or sideways,
with no limitations.
Hence, it is also called the bǎiyóuyí (All-Purpose Movable Instrument).
Regarding its use,
to measure two celestial bodies,
regardless of their ecliptic or equatorial coordinates,
and to find the angular distance between them on a great circle:
One person peers through the ěr biǎo at the end of the héng at the central column biǎo,
aligning it with one celestial body.
Another person peers through the yóu'ěr biǎo towards the central column biǎo, aligning it with the other celestial body.
The degree division from the end of the héng to below the yóu'ěr biǎo
is the angular distance between the two celestial bodies.
The tiāntǐyí (Celestial Sphere Instrument).
The instrument is a sphere,
six chǐ in diameter,
resembling the celestial vault.
Hence, it is named tiāntǐ (Celestial Body).
A steel axle passes through its center,
with both ends exposed,
attached to the north and south poles of the zǐwǔ guī,
allowing it to rotate.
The base is four chǐ and seven cùn high.
On the base is the dìpíng quān,
eight cùn wide.
At the zǐwǔ positions, there are openings,
for the zǐwǔ guī to pass through.
The width and thickness of the openings are the same as those of the zǐwǔ guī,
so that the two circles intersect at a right angle,
the inner surface is perfectly flat,
and they embrace the instrument from left to right, and up and down.
The surrounding area is left open by five fēn,
to allow the gāohú yóubiǎo (movable altitude arc sight) to move back and forth.
A shí pán (time plate) is also installed outside the zǐwǔ guī,
two chǐ in diameter,
divided into twenty-four hours.
With the north pole as its center,
its pointer, which indicates time,
is also fixed at the north pole,
allowing it to move with the tiāntǐ,
and also to rotate independently.
A geared mechanism is also installed below the base,
to rotate the zǐwǔ guī,
enabling the north pole to rise and fall with the local horizon in various directions.
The limits of the visibility and invisibility of celestial phenomena in various directions
can all be thoroughly observed.
The dìpíng jīngwěi héyí (Combined Horizontal Azimuth and Altitude Instrument).
The wěiyí is placed on the central column of the jīngyí.
Regarding its use,
rotate the wěiyí,
align it with the object being measured with the yóubiǎo,
and obtain the latitude from the wěiyí.
Observe where the edge of the wěiyí intersects the jīngyí,
and the longitude is obtained: one measurement yields both.
The Jīhéng Fǔchén Yí (Armillary Sphere for Observing Celestial Motions)
consists of three concentric constructions.
The outermost one
is the ancient Liùhé Yí (Six-Harmonies Armilla),
but without the horizon circle.
Its upright double rings form the meridian circle.
Both sides are engraved with 360 degrees of the celestial circumference.
Starting from the North and South Poles,
the first degree to the middle is 90 degrees;
this is the celestial longitude.
The obliquely inclined single ring is the Tiāncháng Chìdào Quān (Eternal Equator Circle).
Both sides are engraved with 12 hours of the daily circumference.
Zǐ (midnight) and Wǔ (noon) are positioned at the halfway point of the central void of the meridian double rings,
joining at their middle points;
this is the celestial latitude.
At both the North and South Poles, circular axes are set.
The axes are originally solid within the central void of the meridian double rings,
with the axes pointing inward
to penetrate the rings of the two inner constructions.
Below, it is supported by a cloud-shaped base.
The center of the upward-facing surface has a double groove to receive the double rings.
The center of the eastern face has a cloud-shaped recess to receive the plumb line.
Below, a cross-shaped frame is placed,
with screws applied to level it.
Dragon pillars are erected at both the eastern and western ends of the frame.
The dragon mouths hold pearls,
with holes opened to support the two axes of the Tiāncháng Chìdào (Eternal Equator) for Mǎo (east) and Yǒu (west).
According to the determination of the north-south true line from the observatory,
when the base frame is stably positioned,
then the four directions of the flat plane are correct.
Also, according to the degree and minute of the North Pole's elevation above the horizon at the capital,
counting upward to form one quadrant,
this is the zenith.
According to the degree and minute of the South Pole's depression below the horizon,
counting downward to form one quadrant,
this is the geocenter.
A small nail is placed at the zenith to suspend a plumb line,
so that it hangs directly at the geocenter,
and also precisely against the surface of the double rings.
A plummet is attached to the end of the line,
which also precisely fits into the cloud-shaped recess,
neither touching nor separated.
Then the four directions of the upper and lower vertical planes are also correct,
and the horizon is already contained within them.
Next, the inner construction is the ancient Sānchén Yí (Three-Stars Armilla),
but without the ecliptic circle.
The double rings penetrating the two poles
form the Chìjí Jīngquān (Celestial Equator Meridian Circle).
Each pole has an axial hole
to receive the axis of the celestial longitude,
and both sides are engraved with 360 degrees of the celestial circumference.
Joining at the middle of the Chìjí Quān (Celestial Equator Circle),
and moving co-planar with the Tiāncháng Chìdào (Eternal Equator),
is the Yóuxuán Chìdào Quān (Revolving Equator Circle).
Both sides are engraved with 360 degrees of the celestial circumference,
corresponding to the rotation of the primal mover's equator.
From the South Pole of the Jīngquān (Meridian Circle),
two quadrant arcs are made to support it,
preventing it from tilting or collapsing.
Next, the innermost construction is the ancient Sìyóu Yí (Four-Revolutions Armilla).
The double rings penetrating the two poles
form the Sìyóu Quān (Four-Revolutions Circle).
Both sides are engraved with 360 degrees.
Fixed at the two poles of the Yóuquān (Revolutions Circle) is the Zhíjù (Straight Diameter).
Attached to the center of the Zhíjù is the Kuīhéng (Sighting Bar).
A vertical indicator is set at the middle of the Yóuquān
to point to longitude and time.
A vertical indicator is set to the right of the Kuīhéng
to point to latitude.

Additionally, there are a Jièhú Zhǐ Shídu Biǎo (Auxiliary Arc Time Indicator), a Lìbiǎo (Upright Indicator), a Píngxíng Lìbiǎo (Parallel Upright Indicator), and a Píngxíng Jièhú Biǎo (Parallel Auxiliary Arc Indicator)
to supplement any limitations in measurement.
There are also a Wǎng Jīngdù Biǎo (Longitude Binding Indicator), a Wǎng Shídu Biǎo (Time Binding Indicator), and a Píngxíngxiàn Cè Jīngdù Biǎo (Parallel Line Longitude Measuring Indicator)
to ensure consistency between two measurements.
As for its dimensions:
The meridian circle has an outer diameter of 6 cùn (feet) 3 chǐ (inches),
an inner diameter of 5 chǐ 6 cùn 6 fēn (fen),
a ring surface width of 3 cùn 2 fēn,
a thickness of 9 fēn,
and a central void of 1 cùn.
The Tiāncháng Chìdào (Eternal Equator) has an outer diameter of 6 chǐ 1 cùn 2 fēn,
an inner diameter of 5 chǐ 6 cùn 4 fēn,
a ring surface width of 2 cùn 4 fēn,
and a thickness of 1 cùn 4 fēn.
The Chìjí Jīngquān (Celestial Equator Meridian Circle) has an outer diameter of 5 chǐ 5 cùn 6 fēn,
an inner diameter of 5 chǐ 1 cùn 2 fēn,
a ring surface width of 2 cùn 8 fēn,
a thickness of 8 fēn,
and a central void of 1 cùn 2 fēn.
The Yóuxuán Chìdào (Revolving Equator) has an outer diameter of 5 chǐ 5 cùn 6 fēn,
an inner diameter of 5 chǐ 1 cùn 2 fēn,
a ring surface width of 2 cùn 2 fēn,
and a thickness of 1 cùn 2 fēn.
The Sìyóu Quān (Four-Revolutions Circle) has an outer diameter of 5 chǐ,
an inner diameter of 4 chǐ 6 cùn 8 fēn,
a ring surface width of 1 cùn 6 fēn,
a thickness of 7 fēn,
and a central void of 1 cùn 4 fēn.
The Zhíjù (Straight Diameter) is as long as the circle's diameter,
1 cùn 6 fēn wide,
7 fēn thick,
with a central void of 1 cùn 4 fēn.
The Kuīhéng (Sighting Bar) is 4 chǐ 7 cùn 2 fēn long,
1 cùn 2 fēn square,
with a central void of 1 cùn.
Square bronze caps are applied to both upper and lower ends,
5 fēn thick,
the inner part 3 fēn
and 1 cùn square,
inserted into the tube,
the outer part 2 fēn
and 1 cùn 2 fēn square,
flush with the tube surface,
with a circular hole opened in the center.
The Zhǐ Shídu Biǎo (Time Indicator)
has an overall length of 7 cùn 3 fēn.
Its base is 1 cùn 6 fēn long,
shaped like a square tube,
inserted into the central void of the Sìyóu (Four-Revolutions) double rings,
1 cùn 4 fēn wide.
The horizontal band is 3 cùn 2 fēn long,
5 fēn wide,
with both ends hooked back by 2 fēn,
fastened to the outside of the ring surface.
The indicator is 5 cùn 2 fēn long,
1 cùn wide.
Its side line for indicating time
faces the center of the square tube.
The lower end, 2 cùn 4 fēn long,
3 fēn thick,
is flush with the surface of the Yóuxuán Chìdào (Revolving Equator),
to indicate degrees and minutes.
The upper end, 2 cùn 8 fēn long,
2 fēn thick,
is flush with the surface of the Tiāncháng Chìdào (Eternal Equator),
to indicate hours and quarters.
The Zhǐ Wěidù Biǎo (Latitude Indicator)
is curved in two places,
mounted on the right side of the Kuīhéng (Sighting Bar).
The base is 3 cùn long,
9 fēn wide,
with a curved width of 7 fēn,
equal to the thickness of the Sìyóu Huán (Four-Revolutions Ring).
The curved part is 1 cùn 7 fēn long,
flush with the outer surface of the Sìyóu Huán,
its width reduced by half from the centerline,
for indicating latitude.
The Jièhú Zhǐ Shídu Biǎo (Auxiliary Arc Time Indicator):
its base square tube and horizontal band length and width are the same as the previous Zhǐ Shídu Biǎo.
Below the horizontal band,
from left to right,
an arc back is vertically attached,
9 cùn 3 fēn long,
1 cùn 2 fēn wide,
1 fēn 6 lí thick.
At the end of the arc back,
a flat Zhǐ Shídu Biǎo (Time Indicator) is attached.
Excluding the thickness of the arc back,
it is 5 cùn 2 fēn long,
1 cùn wide.
The distance from the centerline of the indicator's base square tube to the inner edge of the Zhǐ Shídu Biǎo
is 6 cùn 7 fēn,
corresponding to 15 degrees on the Yóuxuán Chìdào (Revolving Equator),
and 1 hour on the Tiāncháng Chìdào (Eternal Equator).
Two Lìbiǎo (Upright Indicators):
they are straight with a flat base.
The indicator height and base length are both 3 cùn 2 fēn,
9 fēn wide,
1 fēn thick.
One indicator has a rectangular hole opened upward,
1 cùn long,
with a straight line remaining in the middle.
5 fēn above that, a circular hole is opened,
4 fēn in diameter,
with a cross line remaining in the middle,
mounted on the upper end of the Kuīhéng (Sighting Bar).
The other indicator has a vertical slit opened downward to the same degree as before,
and a small circular hole opened upward,
mounted on the lower end of the Kuīhéng,
each aligned with the centerline of the sighting bar's surface,
fastened with screws.
Two Píngxíng Lìbiǎo (Parallel Upright Indicators):
they are curved with a flat base.
The base plate is 4 cùn long,
1 cùn 2 fēn wide,
1 fēn thick,
with a central void 3 cùn 2 fēn long,
9 fēn wide.
The indicator is curved like a Gōugǔ (right-angled triangle).
The Gǔ (vertical leg) is straight like an upright indicator,
3 cùn 2 fēn high,
9 fēn wide.
The Gōu (horizontal leg) is horizontally connected to the end of the Gǔ,
5 cùn long,
9 fēn wide,
horizontally fixed at the end of the base plate.
The base plate's central void
covers the outside of the upright indicator's base plate,
clamping the indicator to secure it.
The Píngxíng Jiè Hú Biǎo,
constructed like the Píngxíng Lì Biǎo,
but with an inverted orientation.
One pillar is fixed above the level surface,
measuring four cùn, one fēn, and eight háo high.
Another pillar hangs down from the level surface,
measuring six cùn, two fēn, and eight háo long.
Six fēn below the end of the pillar, a round hole is opened.
Five fēn further down, a rectangular hole is opened.
These are all made in the same manner as those of the Lì Biǎo.
The Wǎn Jīngdù Biǎo is
four cùn long in total
and one cùn, four fēn wide.
Its base is a square tube one cùn, six fēn long
and one cùn, eight fēn high,
which fits between the Sìyóu double rings.
It is secured with screws on the left and right.
Its end has upper and lower faces,
which clamp the Yóuxuán Chìdào.
The upper face is seven fēn wide,
half the width of the base,
and aligns with the central line of the Kuīhéng.
The lower face is secured with a screw.
The Wǎn Shídù Biǎo consists of
inner and outer sections.
The inner section, with its upper, lower, and inner three faces,
is fixed within the inner rule of the Yóuxuán Chìdào.
The end of its upper face
supports the lower part of the outer section.
Two square holes are opened
to receive the square feet of the outer section.
The lower face is secured with a screw.
The outer section, with its upper, lower, and outer three faces,
is fixed to the outer rule of the Tiāncháng Chìdào.
The end of its upper face
covers the top of the inner section.
The lower face is secured with a screw.
For the Píngxíngxiàn Cè Jīngdù Biǎo,
at the two ends of the Zhíjù, perpendicular to the North and South Poles,
copper plates are installed,
shaped like an "I".
They are two cùn, eight fēn square,
equally divided with the two faces of the Zhíjù.
The two principal parts each have a missing rectangle,
one cùn, six fēn long
and seven fēn wide,
which fits into the hollow space of the Zhíjù.
A round hole is opened in the center,
through which the axis of the Tiānjīng passes.
At the four corners, one cùn, nine fēn from the center,
pillars are installed.
They have round tops with holes
for threading straight lines,
parallel to the central diameter of the Zhíjù.
Small rings are fixed below
for attaching the lines parallel to the Chìjīng.
Furthermore, according to the distance of stellar mansions and degrees,
a Chìjīng Píngxíngxiàn Biǎo is installed on the Yóuxuán Chìdào.
Its design shows a semicircle drawn on top,
with a half-square inside.
Starting from the diagonal line,
the initial degree to the horizontal diameter is forty-five degrees.
Its central diameter aligns with the edge line of the Zhǐdù Biǎo.
Two sliding pointers are installed at the center of the semicircle,
each two cùn long,
one cùn, nine fēn from the center.
A small 'umbilicus' (protrusion) is left at the edge,
and a small round hole is opened in the center
for threading a line through.
The upper end is tied to the two rings at the diagonal of the North Pole copper plate.
The lower end passes through the two rings at the diagonal of the South Pole copper plate.
Each is weighted with a plumb bob.
For use:
To measure the time of day,
rotate the Sìyóu Quān east and west,
and tilt the Kuīhéng north and south,
so that sunlight passes squarely through the hole.
Observe the time on the Shídù Biǎo pointed to by the lower pointer of the Sìyóu Quān against the Tiāncháng Chìdào.
This gives the time.
If the sun's image is obstructed by the Chìdào,
use the upper Lì Biǎo of the Kuīhéng for measurement,
ensuring both holes of the pillar are perfectly aligned.
Then observe the time on the Shídù Biǎo.
If obstructed by the Lóngzhù,
use the Píngxíng Lì Biǎo for measurement,
and likewise observe the time on the Shídù Biǎo.
If the Shídù Biǎo is obstructed by the Zǐwǔ Quān,
then use the Jiè Hú Zhǐ Shídù Biǎo instead,
followed by the Píngxíng Lì Biǎo.
To determine the sun's image,
observe the time indicated by the Jiè Hú Zhǐ Shídù Biǎo,
and add one hour.
This gives the result.
To measure longitude:
Take a known fixed star before or after local noon.
Using its equatorial longitude's opposition,
fix the Sìyóu Quān on the Yóuxuán Chìdào with the Wǎn Jīngdù Biǎo.
Then set an arbitrary time,
and using the Wǎn Shídù Biǎo,
at the opposition of that time,
fix the Tiāncháng Chìdào.
Next, bring the Sìyóu Quān to the Yóuxuán Chìdào,
use the Kuīhéng to measure the star accurately,
and rotate it counter-clockwise.
When the set time arrives,
observe the mansion and degree on the Yóuxuán Chìdào pointed to by the Wǎn Shídù Biǎo.
This is the sun's equatorial longitude for the day.
Alternatively, use the sun's equatorial longitude at the current time,
fix it on the Yóuxuán Chìdào with the Wǎn Shídù Biǎo.
Then, using the opposition of the set time,
fix it on the Tiāncháng Chìdào.
When the set time arrives,
use the Sìyóu Kuī to measure the moon or a planet.
Then observe the mansion and degree on the Yóuxuán Chìdào indicated by the Zhǐ Shídù Biǎo,
and add half a circle.
This gives the measured equatorial longitude of the moon or planet.
To measure the longitudinal distance between two luminaries:
Fix the Píngxíngxiàn Cè Jīngdù Biǎo at the initial mansion and initial degree on the Yóuxuán Chìdào.
One person uses this Píngxíngxiàn Biǎo, the two left lines and the two right lines,
and observes the western luminary;
rotating it counter-clockwise.
Another person uses the Sìyóu Kuīhéng to measure the eastern luminary.
The degree and minute on the Yóuxuán Chìdào indicated by the Zhǐ Shídù Biǎo
is the measured equatorial longitudinal distance between the two luminaries.
To measure latitude:
Whenever longitude is obtained,
immediately observe the degree and minute on the Sìyóu Quān indicated by the Zhǐ Wěidù Biǎo.
This gives the measured equatorial latitude.
If there is any obstruction,
replace it as in the method for measuring time.
For stars near the North Pole,
use the Píngxíng Jiè Hú Biǎo for measurement.
Records of Three Astronomical Phenomena: Sun, Moon, Five Planets, and Fixed Stars; Twelve Divisions of the Ecliptic and Equator, and Lodges; Stars at Dusk, Dawn, and Culmination.
Sun, Moon, Five Planets:
From ancient times, those who spoke of the essence of the heavens only knew the sun, moon, and five planets as parts of a celestial sphere.
In recent times, Westerners have made large telescopes
and measured the forms of various luminaries and the various small stars, halos, and gases nearby.
Ancient and modern differ,
so we record the most prominent findings.
The sun's surface has small dark shapes,
which constantly move, completing a full circuit in twenty-eight days.
On the moon's surface, direct sunlight reveals bright features,
while oblique illumination reveals dark features.
Its surface has convexities and concavities,
so even when fully illuminated,
there are faint dark mixed features.
The body of Shǎxīng (Saturn)
is somewhat egg-shaped.
Old measurements said it had two ears on its sides.
Modern measurements show that near its equator, the star's surface is very narrow,
while farther from the equator it is very wide.
There are five small stars arranged beside it.
The closest, the first star,
orbits in about just under two days;
the second star in just under three days;
the third star in just over four and a half days;
the fourth star is slightly larger,
orbiting in sixteen days;
the fifth star orbits in eighty days.
All revolve around Shǎxīng once.
The surface of Mùxīng (Jupiter)
always has parallel dark features.
Outside are four small stars.
The first star orbits in one day and seventy-three kè;
the second star in three days and fifty-three kè;
the third star is slightly larger,
orbiting in seven days and sixteen kè;
the fourth star orbits in sixteen days and seventy-two kè.
All revolve around Mùxīng once.
The surface of Huǒxīng (Mars)
has indefinite dark features within it.
Jīnxīng (Venus) and Shuǐxīng (Mercury) both borrow light from the sun,
exhibiting phases like the moon during conjunction, quadratures, and oppositions.
Fixed Stars (Héngxīng). The Lìxiàng Kǎochéng states:
"The names of fixed stars
appear in the Chūnqiū.
The stars marking the middle of the four seasons, as well as Dǒu, Qiānniú, Zhīnǚ, Shēn, Mǎo, Jī, Bì, Dàhuǒ, Nóngxiáng, Lóngwěi, Niǎodàng, Yuánsì, and Yuányuán,
are scattered throughout the Shàngshū, Yì, Shī, Zuǒzhuàn, and Guóyǔ.
In the Zhōulǐ, the Chūnguān Fángxiàngshì was in charge of the positions of the twenty-eight constellations (èrshíbā xiù),
and the Lǐjì Yuèlìng and Dàdài Lǐ Xiàxiǎozhèng provide a somewhat complete account of the visible and hidden phases of these stars.
In ancient times, people revered Heaven and diligently served the populace,
issuing policies according to the seasons,
all based on stars as markers.
After the Qin burning of books,
the ancient techniques of Xīhé
were no longer verifiable,
and what was transmitted was only the Shǐjì Tiānguānshū,
but its records are brief.
In the Later Hàn, Zhāng Héng said:
'Among the inner and outer officials (constellations), there are one hundred twenty-four constantly bright ones,
three hundred twenty named ones,
totaling two thousand five hundred stars.'
However, his work is not extant.
By the Three Kingdoms period,
the Grand Astrologer (Tàishǐlìng) Chén Zhuó first arranged the star charts by Wū Xián, Gān, and Shí,
totaling two hundred eighty-three officials (constellations)
and one thousand four hundred sixty-four stars.
In the Suí dynasty, Dān Yuánzǐ composed the Bùtiāngē,
enumerating the Three Enclosures (Sān Yuán) and Twenty-Eight Mansions (Èrshíbā Xiù),
totaling one thousand four hundred sixty-seven stars,
which served as a guide for astronomical observation.
However, it did not yet include the celestial coordinates (jīngwěidùshù) for each star.
From the Táng and Sòng dynasties onward,
various scholars, by observing and measuring with astronomical instruments (yíxiàng),
began to record each star's entry into its mansion (rùxiù) and its distance from the celestial pole (qùjí dùfēn),
which was more precise than ancient methods.
"The Xīnfǎ Suànshū Fixed Star Charts (Héngxīng Túbiǎo)
list a total of one thousand two hundred sixty-six stars,
divided into six magnitudes: seventeen first-magnitude stars,
fifty-seven second-magnitude stars,
one hundred eighty-five third-magnitude stars,
three hundred eighty-nine fourth-magnitude stars,
three hundred twenty-three fifth-magnitude stars,
and two hundred ninety-five sixth-magnitude stars.
Additionally, there are four hundred fifty-nine unnamed stars not categorized by magnitude.
In the Kāngxī Rénzǐ year, the Qīn Tiān Jiān newly compiled the Yíxiàng Zhì,
which also divided fixed stars into six magnitudes,
but their numbers differ slightly.
Sixteen first-magnitude stars,
sixty-eight second-magnitude stars,
two hundred eight third-magnitude stars,
five hundred twelve fourth-magnitude stars,
three hundred forty-two fifth-magnitude stars,
and seven hundred thirty-two sixth-magnitude stars,
totaling one thousand eight hundred seventy-eight.
Star gazers, based on what their eyes could discern,
grouped stars that were close together
to form constellations and named them.
Many faint and dim stars
could not be identified.
Therefore, the number of constellations (xīngguān) varied among different schools,
and could not be uniform.
However, the twenty-eight mansions and major stars
are consistent between ancient and modern, and between Chinese and Western traditions."
It also states:
"The motion of fixed stars (héngxīng xíng) is what was formerly known as precession of the equinoxes (suìchā).
Ancient methods all held that fixed stars were stationary
and the ecliptic shifted westward.
Now, it is held that the ecliptic is stationary
and fixed stars move eastward.
If fixed stars were stationary and the ecliptic shifted westward,
then the ecliptic longitude and latitude of fixed stars should differ annually,
and their equatorial longitude and latitude should remain unchanged forever.
Now, measurements show that the ecliptic longitude of fixed stars
moves eastward every year,
while the latitude remains constant.
As for equatorial longitude,
it differs year by year,
and the latitude varies even more significantly.
For stars in the six mansions from Xīngjì to Qúnshǒu,
those south of the celestial equator
had higher ancient latitudes that are now gradually decreasing,
and the opposite is true for those north of the celestial equator.
For stars in the six mansions from Qúnshǒu to Xīngjì,
those south of the celestial equator
had lower ancient latitudes that are now gradually increasing,
and the opposite is true for those north of the celestial equator.
For any star within twenty-three and a half degrees of the celestial equator,
those north of the celestial equator
can cross to the south of the celestial equator,
and those south of the celestial equator
can also cross to the north of the celestial equator.
This clearly shows that fixed stars move eastward along the ecliptic,
and it is not the ecliptic that shifts westward.
The Xīnfǎ Suànshū records that before the Westerner Tycho (Tìgǔ),
some said fixed stars move eastward one degree per century,
others said one degree in seventy-odd years,
or one degree in sixty-odd years,
with revisions over time,
but no definite number was reached,
similar to the repeated revisions of precession by ancient people.
It was not until Tycho
that it was determined fixed stars move eastward by fifty-one seconds annually,
approximately one degree in over seventy years.
This number is close to the precession value determined by Yuán dynasty's Guō Shǒujìng.
Over one hundred forty years have passed since then,
and observations of the heavens
show no discrepancies.
However, star movements are tiny,
and differences only become apparent
after many years.
Thus, Tycho's determined number
should not be rigidly taken as a fixed rate;
rather, it is appropriate to measure and verify it over time
and deduce the number based on celestial movements."
The Yíxiàng Kǎochéng states:
"In Kāngxī year thirteen,
the Supervising Minister (Jiānchén) Nán Huáirén compiled the Yíxiàng Zhì.
The star names that are the same as ancient ones
total two hundred fifty-nine constellations
and one thousand one hundred twenty-nine stars,
which is twenty-four constellations and
three hundred thirty-five stars fewer than the Bùtiāngē.
Furthermore, beyond the established named stars,
five hundred ninety-seven stars were added.
Also, twenty-three constellations
and one hundred fifty stars near the South Pole were added.
In recent years,
after repeated measurements and observations,
many of the celestial coordinates (xīngguān dùshù) in the Yíxiàng Zhì
are still not accurate.
Moreover, the order of many stars is not sequential,
and also needs correction.
Therefore, each star was measured individually,
its coordinates calculated,
its appearance observed,
and its order sequenced,
and these were recorded in charts.
Counting the Three Enclosures and Twenty-Eight Mansions,
the star names that are the same as ancient ones
total two hundred seventy-seven constellations
and one thousand three hundred nineteen stars,
which is eighteen constellations and
one hundred ninety stars more than the Yíxiàng Zhì,
and closer to the Bùtiāngē.
What is particularly consistent with ancient practice
is the sequence of the Twenty-Eight Mansions (èrshíbā xiù cìshè).
From ancient times, the Zīxiù Mansion has always been before
the Shēnxiù Mansion.
However, there is no clear ancient text
stating which star was used as the reference point (jù).
The Tángshū says: 'Anciently, the right shoulder of Shēn was taken as the reference point,'
which is too far off.
The Wénxiàn Tōngkǎo, citing the astronomical treatises of the two Sòng dynasties, says: 'Zī has three stars,
using the southwestern star as reference; Shēn has ten stars,
using the first star west of the middle star as reference.'
Western methods
use the upper-middle star of Zīxiù as reference,
and also the first star west of the middle star for Shēnxiù.
Now, according to our observation, the upper-middle star of Zīxiù is only a little over six minutes ahead of the southwestern star,
and the southwestern star is small,
while the upper-middle star is large.
Thus, it is appropriate to use the upper-middle star as the reference point.
If the first star west of the middle star of Shēnxiù were used as the reference star,
then the ecliptic longitude of Zīxiù would already be over one degree behind Shēnxiù,
and its equatorial longitude would also be over thirty-one minutes behind Shēnxiù.
Now, to maintain sequential order,
we use the first star east of the three middle stars of Shēnxiù as the reference star.
In this way, the ecliptic longitude of Zīxiù is consistently a little less than one degree ahead of Shēnxiù,
which aligns with the Zī-before-Shēn sequence.
The stars of other constellations
are all arranged sequentially,
avoiding the errors of overlap or inversion.
Furthermore, beyond the established named stars,
one thousand six hundred fourteen stars were added.
Those near a certain constellation are named '增星 (zēngxīng)' of that constellation,
with their positions annotated sequentially,
for future reference.
The twenty-three constellations
and one hundred fifty stars near the South Pole,
which are not visible in China,
still follow the old Western measurements.
In total, there are three hundred fixed star constellations
and three thousand eighty-three stars."
The twelve mansions of the ecliptic and equatorial paths, and their corresponding constellations. Ancient people divided the year into twelve mansions, which corresponded to the solar terms.
Therefore, the Winter Solstice was at the center of `Chǒu`.
The Spring Equinox was at the center of `Xū`.
The Summer Solstice was at the center of `Wèi`.
The Autumn Equinox was at the center of `Chén`.
Later generations took the mid-season solar terms,
and the Winter Solstice was at the beginning of `Xīngjì`.
Ancient people did not know that the constellations moved eastward along the ecliptic,
nor did they observe the precession of the equinoxes.
So they named each mansion after the constellation it was in.
Therefore, `Kuí` and `Lóu` constituted `Jiànglóu`,
and `Fáng`, `Xīn`, and `Wěi` constituted `Dàhuǒ`.
Later generations completely retained these names,
but they did not account for the changes in the constellations themselves.
After several millennia,
the so-called Four Symbols of `Cānglóng`, `Xuánwǔ`, `Báihǔ`, and `Zhūquè` even changed their positions.
So, the names of the twelve mansions
merely preserve ancient meanings.
Now, the constellations corresponding to the initial degrees of the twelve mansions, as determined in the `Kāngxī` *jiǎzǐ* year (1684),
and the constellations corresponding to the initial degrees of the twelve mansions, as revised in the `Qiánlóng` *jiǎzǐ* year (1744),
are both recorded below on the left.

Stars at dusk and dawn. Since the `Yú Shū` recorded the stars at dusk in the four mid-seasons,
and the `Yuèlìng` listed stars at dusk and dawn for each month.
However, the star for mid-winter in `Yú Shū` was `Mǎo`,
while in `Yuèlìng`, the star at dusk was `Dōngbì`.
There is a difference of about two thousand years;
the mid-season stars differ by four mansions.
Although this is due to the precession of the equinoxes,
the ancient methods were crude and lacked precise degrees and minutes,
so it is difficult to delve deeply into the matter.
Now, based on the celestial longitude and latitude of fixed stars determined in the `Kāngxī` *rénzǐ* year (1672),
we have calculated and listed the stars at dusk and dawn for each solar term in the `Yǒngzhèng` first year *guǐmǎo* (1723) in this record.
If one seeks the stars at dusk and dawn for each solar term after `Qiánlóng` ninth year *jiǎzǐ* (1744),
one should then calculate them based on the revised celestial longitude and latitude of fixed stars from the `Qiánlóng` *jiǎzǐ* year.

Record Four, Astronomy Four: `Kāngxī` *rénzǐ* Year (1672) Table One of Ecliptic Longitude and Latitude for Fixed Stars
Observing the sun is to rectify time.
Observing the stars is to record days.
The sun travels along the ecliptic,
therefore, to measure fixed stars,
one must determine their ecliptic longitude and latitude.
Moreover, fixed stars move eastward along the ecliptic.
Upon careful examination,
only 51 arcseconds of longitude are added or subtracted each year.
Now, based on the previously measured ecliptic longitudes and latitudes of fixed stars from the `Kāngxī` *rénzǐ* year,
and their north or south direction,
and their magnitudes,
it is compiled into two volumes.
First are listed stars, including famous ones and nearby ones, from `Jiànglóu` (Xū Mansion) to `Chúnwěi` (Sì Mansion),
covering 180 degrees.

Records of the twelve astronomical phenomena, twelve solar eclipses, lunar and five-planet transits, occultations, close approaches, *Tàibái* visible in daytime, solar and lunar changes.
Solar Eclipses. The *Sāntǒng* and *Sìfēn* [calendrical systems],
both had methods for calculating lunar eclipses,
but no methods for calculating solar eclipses.
As solar eclipses might or might not be seen,
might be partial or deep,
and vary by location,
the exact numbers were not known,
making the establishment of a method exceedingly difficult.
Therefore, since ancient times, they were considered especially unusual,
and each eclipse,
was invariably recorded in historical texts.
Later generations' methods for calculating solar eclipses became precise,
yet they were still recorded,
following the new moon.
Those seen in the Imperial Annals (*Běnjì*),
without the eclipse magnitude and the lunar lodge involved,
are all included in this Treatise (*Zhì*),
for those who study calendrical astronomy to examine.

The Moon and the Five Planets' *Língfàn* (Invasion) and *Yǎnjù* (Occultation/Conjunction)
The *Tiānguān Shū* says: "Mutual invasion is a struggle."
It also states:
"Within seven *cùn* there must be an event,"
meaning their latitudes are so close it is like an eclipse.
According to current methods:
When two stars are within three *fēn* of each other, it is a *líng*;
When the Moon and a star are within seventeen *fēn* of each other, it is a *líng*;
Being within one *dù* of each other is a *fàn*;
When one star covers another, it is an *yǎn*.
*Qīntiān Jiān* annually pre-calculates instances where the Moon and the Five Planets enter these limits,
compiling a report and submitting it.
Originally named *Língfàn Shū*,
in the early *Yōngzhèng* years,
it was renamed *Xiāngjù Shū*.
Since it relies on astrological observation,
it also involves calendrical calculation,
each following its original designation,
and also noting the constellation where it occurred.

Annals Vol. 14, Astronomy Section 14: Guest Stars, Meteorites, Cloud *Qì*
Guest Stars: In the *dīngwèi* year, 9th month, on the *bǐngshēn* day of Tàizǔ's reign,
a comet was seen in the east.
In the 3rd year of Tiānmìng, 10th month, on the *bǐngyín* day,
a comet was seen in the east,
its tail five *zhàng* long,
moving gradually northward towards the Běidǒu each night,
and vanished after nineteen days.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì, 11th month, on the *gēngyín* day,
a strange pale white *qì* was seen in Shēn,
moving northwest into Bì.
In the third year of Kāngxī, on the *jǐwèi* day of the tenth month, the new moon began.
There was a star, like a broom, in Zhěn.
It was seen in the east.
On the *dīngmǎo* day,
its tail was seven or eight *cùn* long,
of a dark blue color,
pointing southwest.
On the *dīnghài* day,
its tail was over three *chǐ* long,
pointing northwest,
retrograde to Yì.
In the eleventh month, on the *wùxū* day,
its tail was over five *chǐ* long,
pointing north,
to Zhāng.
On the *gēngzǐ* day,
it reached Jǐng.
On the *guǐmǎo* day,
it moved northwest to Mǎo.
On the *yǐsì* day,
its tail pointed northeast,
to Wèi.
On the *gēngxū* day,
it reached Lóu,
its tail pointing east,
blue in color.
In the twelfth month, on the *rénxū* day,
it reached Kuí,
its body small,
its tail over two *chǐ* long.
In the fourth year, in the second month, on the *jǐsì* day,
an unusual star was seen in the southeast, in Nǚ.
On the *jiǎxū* day,
its tail was seven *cùn* long,
pointing southwest,
pale blue.
On the *dīngchǒu* day,
its tail was over one *chǐ* long,
moving northeast in direct motion to Xū.
On the *xīnsì* day,
it reached Shì,
its body gradually enlarging,
its tail over eight *chǐ* long.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
it reached Bì,
its tail over five *chǐ* long.
In the seventh year, in the first month, on the *jiǎzǐ* day,
a white light appeared in the southwest,
over six *chǐ* long,
its tail pointing southeast.
The prognostication said it was Tiānqiāng.
In the second month, on the *yǐhài* day,
it gradually lengthened to over four *zhàng*,
its tail sweeping Tiānyuàn, Jiǔliú, and Jūnjǐng.
On the *dīnghài* day,
it disappeared.
In the twelfth year, in the second month, on the *guǐsì* day,
an unusual star was seen in Lóu,
as large as a walnut,
white in color,
its tail over one *chǐ* long,
pointing east.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day,
it was still seen.
In the fifteenth year, in the first month, on the *wùzǐ* day,
an unusual star was seen northeast of Tiānyuàn,
white in color.
In the sixteenth year, in the third month, on the *guǐmǎo* day,
an unusual star was seen in the northeast, in Lóu,
its body bright and lustrous,
its tail over one *chǐ* long,
pointing southwest.
The prognostication said it was Hányù.
In the nineteenth year, in the tenth month, on the *wùzǐ* day,
a comet was seen in Yòuzhífǎ,
white in color,
its tail over one *chǐ* long,
pointing west,
moving east very rapidly.
On the *rénzǐ* day,
it became invisible near the sun.
In the eleventh month, on the *bǐngchén* day, the new moon began.
The tail trace was seen in the west at dusk.
On the *rénxū* day, the star body was seen,
pale blue in color,
its tail over six *zhàng* long,
and over two *chǐ* wide,
pointing northeast.
In the twenty-first year, in the seventh month, on the *jǐsì* day,
a comet was seen north of Běihé,
white in color,
its tail over two *chǐ* long,
pointing southwest,
moving northeast very rapidly.
On the *rénshēn* day,
it entered Wǔgōng,
its tail over six *chǐ* long.
In the twenty-second year, in the intercalary sixth month, on the *gēngxū* day,
an unusual star was seen north of Wǔchē and east of Bāgǔ,
white in color,
moving southwest in retrograde motion.
On the *wùchén* day,
it entered Wǔchē.
In the twenty-third year, in the fifth month, on the *jiǎshēn* day,
an unusual star was seen in the Tàiwēiyuán,
eastern part belonging to Zhěn,
white, bright, and large,
moving northeast in direct motion.
On the *yǐyǒu* day,
it moved over four degrees,
to below Yòushètí.
In the twenty-fifth year, in the seventh month, on the *gēngyín* day,
an unusual star was seen in the east,
near the horizon,
white in color,
moving east not rapidly.
On the *dīngyǒu* day,
it had moved a total of sixteen degrees,
to Liǔ,
with a faint tail trace.
On the *rényín* day,
it reached Xīng,
and gradually disappeared.
In the twenty-seventh year, in the tenth month, on the *jǐyǒu* day,
an unusual star was seen in Kuí,
white in color,
for a total of three nights.
In the twenty-ninth year, in the eighth month, on the *jǐyǒu* day,
an unusual star was seen in Jī,
yellow in color,
for a total of two nights.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng, in the ninth month, on the *jǐchǒu* day,
an unusual star was seen below Húshǐ,
white in color,
its body faint,
its radiance over one *chǐ* long,
pointing northwest,
retrograde to Jǐng.
In the 6th month, on the *dīngmǎo* day of the 2nd year of Qiánlóng
an anomalous star appeared to the east of Yòugēng,
white in color,
belonging to Lóu,
moving towards the southwest;
on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
it was still seen.
In the 1st month, on the *dīnghài* day of the 7th year,
an anomalous star was seen in the southeast;
on the *wùzǐ* day,
it rose more than twenty-seven degrees above the horizon,
as large as a pellet,
yellow in color,
with a tail over four feet long,
pointing southwest,
belonging to Chǒu gōng,
outside of Xúxīng in Tiānshìyuán;
it moved retrograde for over forty days and then disappeared.
In the 11th month, on the *jǐhài* day of the 8th year,
a comet appeared between Kuí and Bì,
as large as a pellet,
yellowish-white in color,
with a tail over one foot long,
pointing east,
belonging to Xū gōng;
it moved retrograde until the 1st month, on the *xīnmǎo* day of the 9th year,
for a total of fifty-three days,
traveling over twenty-nine degrees.
In the 3rd month, on the *guǐchǒu* day of the 13th year,
an anomalous star appeared in the east,
as large as a hazelnut,
yellow in color,
with a tail over two feet long,
pointing southwest,
to the south of the third star of Lí gōng;
it moved prograde until the 1st day of the 4th month, on the *jiǎyín* day,
traveling three degrees,
its tail was over one foot long,
its body small and light faint;
on the *rénxū* day,
it reached Téngshé;
on the *yǐchǒu* day,
it reached Wángliáng;
on the *bǐngyín* day,
it disappeared.
In the 5th month, on the *jiǎyín* day of the 14th year,
a propitious star appeared in the east,
as large as a chicken egg,
long and round in shape,
yellowish-white in color,
its light brilliant and moist,
moving not swiftly,
emerging from Tiānjīn,
entering Chúcǎo;
the prognostication said, "Containing glory."
In the 3rd month, on the *rénchén* day of the 24th year,
a comet appeared in the southeast;
on the *jiǎwǔ* day,
it appeared below the first star of Xū,
as large as a hazelnut,
bluish-white in color,
with a tail over one foot long,
pointing southwest,
moving prograde;
on the *guǐmǎo* day,
its body was small and light faint,
its tail was three or four inches long;
on the *wùshēn* day,
it completely vanished.
In the 4th month, on the *wùchén* day,
a comet appeared in the southwest,
above the second star of Zhāng;
on the *jǐsì* day,
it was six degrees from Zhāng,
as large as a hazelnut,
bluish-yellow in color,
its tail light diffused,
over two feet long,
pointing southeast,
moving prograde;
on the *rénshēn* day,
its form and trace were very small;
on the *dīngchǒu* day,
it was even fainter;
on the *jǐmǎo* day,
it gradually dispersed;
in the 5th month, on the *rénwǔ* day,
it completely vanished.
In the 11th month, on the *wùchén* day,
an anomalous star appeared in the southeast,
below the fourth star of Jǐng,
as large as a hazelnut,
bluish-yellow in color,
moving towards the northwest;
on the *guǐyǒu* day,
it had traveled four degrees,
in Wèi,
with a faint trace of a tail;
on the 1st day of the 12th month, on the *dīngchǒu* day,
it completely vanished.
In the 7th month, on the *jiǎchén* day of the 34th year,
a comet appeared in the southeast,
below Mǎo;
on the *dīngwèi* day,
it was as large as a pellet,
bluish-white in color,
with a tail three feet long,
pointing southwest,
moving prograde very swiftly;
in the 8th month, on the *dīngmǎo* day,
it was in the same palace as the sun and disappeared;
in the 10th month, on the *xīnhài* day,
it was seen in the west,
below the second star of Lièshì,
its body and form small,
its tail one foot long;
on the *bǐngzǐ* day,
it completely vanished.
In the intercalary 5th month, on the *jǐyǒu* day of the 35th year,
an anomalous star appeared in the southeast,
to the west of the first star of Tiānbiàn,
as large as a pellet,
bluish-yellow in color;
on the *guǐchǒu* day,
it had moved thirty-two degrees towards the north;
on the *yǐchǒu* day,
it disappeared.
In the 11th month, on the *yǐchǒu* day,
a comet appeared in the southeast,
over one foot long;
on the *bǐngyín* day,
it was below the second star of Liǔ;
on the *wùchén* day,
it was bluish-white in color,
its tail pointing southeast,
moving over ten degrees towards the northwest daily;
on the *gēngwǔ* day,
it became slightly dim;
on the *xīnwèi* day,
it completely vanished.
Falling stars and meteorites: A falling star as large as a *dǒu* (dipper)
occurred in the 9th month, on the night of the *xīnhài* day, the 1st day of the month, in the *wùzǐ* year of Tàizǔ's reign,
when the king was campaigning at Jiǎchéng,
and all the soldiers and horses were startled.
A falling star as large as a basin
occurred in the 9th month, on the *rénshēn* day of the 14th year of Qiánlóng,
emerging from Lóu xiù,
red in color,
entering Tiānyuàn,
with light,
and a tail trace.
A falling star as large as a bowl
occurred in the 11th month, on the *gēngchén* day of the 4th year of Shùnzhì,
traveling northwest from the center of the sky into Shǔ,
with sound,
red in color,
its light illuminating the ground,
startling chickens and dogs.
In the 9th month, on the *xīnsì* day of the 5th year, it was similar,
with a sound like thunder.
In the 6th month, on the *xīnwèi* day of the 15th year,
it traveled from northwest to southeast,
with sound,
red in color,
without light or tail trace.
Meteors like lamps:
On the *wùwǔ* day in the *yín* hour of the fifth month of the fourth year of Shùnzhì (1647),
from northwest to southwest,
its color was blue-white,
with light.
On the *jiǎwǔ* day of the eighth month of the seventh year (1650),
from southeast to northeast,
its color was reddish-yellow,
entering Dǒu,
without light or a tail.
On the *jǐyǒu* day of the fourth month of the eighth year (1651),
it traveled southward from Dī Xiù,
its color blue-white;
on the *wùyín* day of the fifth month,
it traveled southwestward from Kàng Xiù,
its color white,
with many small stars accompanying it,
entering Yì;
on the *bǐngzǐ* day of the third month of the ninth year (1652),
it traveled southwestward from the midheaven,
its color red,
entering Bì;
all had light
and a tail.
On the *bǐngshēn* day of the ninth month,
it entered the Zǐwēi Yuán from the midheaven,
its color red;
on the *bǐngyín* day of the eighth month of the tenth year (1653),
it entered the Tiānshì Yuán from the midheaven,
its color blue-red;
all had light.
On the *jiǎzǐ* day of the fourth month of the twelfth year (1655),
it entered Wēi from Kàng Xiù,
its color reddish-yellow,
with light
and a tail.
On the *guǐyǒu* day,
it emerged from Fáng Xiù,
its color blue-yellow,
entering Wěi;
on the *jiǎshēn* day of the seventh month of the sixteenth year (1659),
it emerged from Niú Xiù,
traveled northeastward,
its color reddish-yellow,
disappearing at Shǔ;
all were without light or a trace.
On the *dīngsì* day of the eighth month of the second year of Kāngxī (1663),
it entered the Zǐwēi Yuán from Xū Xiù,
with small stars accompanying it;
on the *wùshēn* day of the ninth month of the third year (1664),
it entered Kuí from the midheaven;
both were red in color;
on the *wùyín* day of the first month of the sixth year (1667),
it emerged from Guǐ Xiù,
its color blue,
followed by a sound,
entering Tǔsīkōng;
on the *wùzǐ* day of the second month of the seventh year (1668),
it emerged from Dàjiǎo,
its color reddish-yellow,
entering Jī;
on the *jiǎwǔ* day of the ninth month of the twelfth year (1673),
it emerged from Gōuchén,
its color blue-white,
disappearing at Shǔ;
all had light and a tail.
On the *jǐhài* day in the *yǒu* hour of the ninth month of the sixteenth year (1677),
it descended from due north,
its color red-white,
its tail like a snake,
with light.
On the *guǐyǒu* day in the *yǒu* hour of the sixth month of the nineteenth year (1680),
from southwest to northeast,
its sound like thunder,
its tail like a bolt of cloth.
On the *rénwǔ* day of the eleventh month of the twenty-fifth year (1686),
it emerged from Zuǒshū,
its color white,
disappearing at Shǔ,
its tail reaching across the sky.
On the *wùyín* day of the twelfth month,
it emerged from Zhěn Xiù,
its color blue-yellow,
entering Qíguān.
On the *dīnghài* day of the second month of the twenty-ninth year (1690),
it emerged from Hégǔ,
its color yellow,
entering Wěi.
On the *dīngsì* day at the first watch of the first month of the nineteenth year of Qiánlóng (1754),
it emerged from Kuí Xiù,
traveling northwestward;
on the *wùshēn* day at the first watch of the third month of the twenty-second year (1757),
it emerged from the northwest,
descending;
both were blue in color.
On the *jiǎshēn* day at the fifth watch of the intercalary sixth month of the twenty-fourth year (1759),
it emerged from Tǔsīkōng,

Monograph 15: Anomalies (Part 1)
The *Zhuàn* says: "Heaven has three luminaries,
Earth has five phases (Wǔxíng).
Calamities of the Five Phases
are caused by the qi of the Earth.
When water does not moisten downwards,
fire does not blaze upwards,
wood does not bend or straighten,
metal does not follow change,
and earth does not yield crops,
and the crops do not ripen,
this is called losing their nature.
The nature of the Five Phases originates from Earth,
and humans are attached to Earth.
The five human affairs
also correspond to the Earth's Five Phases.
Is this not the original meaning of the *Hóngfàn*?"
The Monograph on the Five Phases in the *Míngshǐ* details these auspicious and anomalous phenomena,
but removes the forced correlation with human affairs.
Its words are indeed correct.
Now, following the example of the *Míngshǐ*,
and also adopting ancient principles,
we supplement the omissions of previous histories.
The *Hóngfàn* says:
"Water's nature is to moisten downwards."
If water does not moisten downwards,
it is a sign of calamity.

All constant cold, constant overcast skies, snow and frost, ice and hail, fish calamities, locust plagues, pig misfortunes, dragon and snake anomalies, horse oddities, human diseases, epidemics, drum portents, meteorites, floods, water changes, black omens, and black auspicious signs are all attributed to water.

On the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month of the first year of Kāngxī,

The red dragon was in front,
the green dragon was behind.
Their scales and armor emitted fire.
Passing over Zǐjiā Dài,
they toppled over a hundred houses
and injured one person.
At midnight on the ninth day of the ninth month,
a fiery dragon was seen.
On the sixteenth day of the fourth month of the second year,
a dragon was seen in Chóngmíng.
A snake,
several *zhàng* long,
with a waist circumference of about three *chǐ*,
and scales,
emitting a red light, emerged southeast of Sāntái.
On the twenty-first day of the fifth month of the third year,
a dragon was seen in Jīngshān,
its scales and armor fully visible.
On the first day of the seventh month,
a great storm and sea surge occurred in Zhènyáng.
A dragon descended upon Míchǎng,
injuring several people.
On the fourth day of the eighth month,
the sky was clear and cloudless,
and a yellow dragon was seen in the southeast.
In the seventh month of the seventh year,
a dragon roamed in front of the county office in Xiánníng.
When the rain cleared,
it could not ascend.
Townspeople tied its neck and paraded it through the market.
In the sixth month of the twelfth year,
a dragon rose from a commoner's house in Mǎpù, Shēnzé.
With a great storm,
it broke through the wall and departed.
On the eighteenth day of the twelfth month,
two dragons were seen hanging in the air in Dānyáng,
departing after some time.
In the summer of the thirteenth year,
a dragon was seen in Yǒngjiā.
There was a great flood in Wànzǎi,
and a dragon emerged.
In the sixth month of the seventeenth year,
a dragon suddenly revealed its head and horns on Dàmù Shān in Xiánníng.
For three days,
its scales and armor shone like red gold.
It flew during the daytime,
carving a river through the mountain,
injuring people and livestock.
On the fifteenth day of the tenth month of the eighteenth year,
a dragon was seen in the southeast of Zhènyáng.
In the tenth month of the twenty-first year,
dragons were seen in Qīngpǔ and Xīnghuà.
In the sixth month of the twenty-sixth year,
a yellow dragon was seen in broad daylight in Zhūjiā Cūn, Huáng Xiàn.
Mist obscured everything,
and firelight flew up.
In the third month of the thirty-sixth year,
a dragon was seen in the Chìshuǐ Hé in Bìjié.
In the eighth month of the fortieth year,
a dragon was seen in Yángjiǎo Cūn, south of Dúshān Zhōu.
On the ninth day of the sixth month of the forty-first year,
a white dragon leaped from flat ground at Áoquán
and flew away.
On the sixth day of the fifth month of the forty-fifth year,
a dragon emerged from the cliffs of Jīnshān,
glowing with golden light.
In the forty-seventh year,
there was a dragon in a well in Língzhōu.
Its head and tail were seen from time to time.
After several days,
suddenly there was a great rain and thunder,
and it soared into the sky and departed.
In the sixth month of the sixtieth year,
a dragon hung in front of the school in Jīntán.
Its fishy odor assailed the nose.
After offering incense and praying,
it soared into the sky and departed.
On the thirteenth day of the seventh month,
there was a great thunderstorm in Nánlóng,
and a dragon was seen west of the city.
In the seventh month of the second year of Yōngzhèng,
a flying dragon was seen in Běiliú.
In the twelfth month,
mist rose from Mùmén Hǎizǐ,
with the appearance of a *jiāolóng* flying out.
In the fifth month,
a dragon rose in Héngzhōu.
In the spring of the seventh year,
a dragon was seen soaring into the sky from Wénwěi Tǎ in Āndìng and departing.
In the fourth month of the ninth year,
a dragon was seen in Ānnán, in the northeast.
In the sixth month,
a dragon was seen on the sandy beach in Qīngpǔ.
In the second month of the second year of Qiánlóng,
a white dragon was seen in Cháoyáng.
In the first month of the third year,
a dragon was seen west of the city in Zhījiāng.
In the ninth month,
dragons fought in Mǎo, Qīngpǔ,
from the southwest to the northeast, entering the sea.
In the fifth month of the fifth year,
there was a great wind in Gāoyóu,
and a white dragon danced in the air,
its scales and armor fully visible.
On the thirteenth day of the sixth month of the sixth year,
a white dragon in Shèwǎng Cūn, Dōng Xiāng, Kūnshān, swept away seventeen houses.
On the twenty-fifth day,
a white dragon in Xíjiā Tán swept away a large boat and two people from Zhōujiā Zhuāng.
It fell onto the riverbank three *lǐ* from Bāchéng Zhèn.
Then it swept away a townsperson named Shèng Mǒu,
threw him to the ground,
and he was unharmed.
On the twelfth day of the sixth month of the ninth year,
a dragon from Fúshān flew into a commoner's building.
In an instant, smoke rose,
and the building was entirely burned.
On the *rénchén* day of the seventh month,
Jiàn [unknown character] 天 suddenly darkened,
and a white dragon's tail hung down over two *zhàng*.
In the eighth month of the twelfth year,
a dragon was seen on Xiǎohuá Shān in Gāozhōu.
On the fifth day of the seventh month of the fourteenth year,
a dragon rose from the bottom of Yǒngfēng Wéi in Gāochún,
its head, tail, scales, and armor all visible.
In the seventh month of the fifteenth year,
a dragon in Qínjiā Diàn, Zhèngníng, broke through a house and ascended.
Immediately, there was a great thunderstorm.
In the autumn of the nineteenth year,
dragons fought in Jùzhì Hé in Jǐnán.
On the twentieth day of the fifth month of the twentieth year,
a fierce wind and sudden rain occurred in Chénghǎi.
Two dragons came from the east,
passing through the east gate of Péngzhōu Suǒ.
They toppled fifty-seven *zhàng* of the city wall
and over three hundred houses.
Some people were crushed to death.
In the sixth month of the twenty-first year,
a dragon slowly descended from the sky in Zhāoshōu, Lóngjǐng area.
On the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month of the twenty-sixth year,
a red dragon was seen in the enclosure between the two rivers of Zhāngtǐ in Jiāzhōu.
On the seventh day of the sixth month,
a fiery dragon was seen in Shímò Cūn, Gāopíng.
On the fourteenth day of the seventh month,
a *jiāolóng* rose from the west river in Xiàhuī Cūn, Tàiyán.
It was two *zhàng* high,
brilliantly colored,
and flew southeast.
Wind and clouds followed it.
On the thirteenth day of the fourth month of the twenty-ninth year,
a black dragon was seen in Tiānmén,
its head, horns, claws, and armor all visible.
In the third month of the forty-third year,
a dragon was seen in Ānqīu.
On the twelfth day of the eighth month of the forty-sixth year,
a group of dragons was seen northeast of Wúshān in Jǔzhōu.
In the fifth month of the fifty-fifth year,
a dragon rose from Zhōushān, Dìnghǎi,
sweeping away fields and houses
and drowning people.
Three days later,
the dragon was chopped into three sections.
Its tail was missing,
and its scales were as large as a sunflower fan.
In the sixth month of the fifty-sixth year,
a red dragon was seen in Lóngwáng Yù, Jǔzhōu,
first large then small,
several *zhàng* long.
The vegetation it passed over was as if burned.
In the spring of the sixtieth year,
a white dragon came from the east to south of Jīnzé Zhèn in Qīngpǔ,
just three or four *chǐ* above the ground.
The roof tiles of the houses it passed over all flew off.
In the sixth year of Jiāqìng,
when the Confucius Temple in Dōnghú was being renovated,
a white dragon was seen riding the wind and flying away.
In the ninth year,
the water of Jìdú Hé in Qǔyáng suddenly surged.
Several dragon carriages were seen wading into the water and disappearing
as the water receded.
In the fifth month of the fourteenth year,
a dragon played in the Jiāngjūn Hé near the City God Temple in Ruìzhōu.
The water rose over a *zhàng*.
In the sixth month of the twentieth year,
a *jiāolóng* rose in Liǔzi Xiàng, Huánggāng,
injuring over one hundred forty people
and submerging countless fields and residences.
In the sixth month of the twenty-first year,
a *jiāolóng* was seen in Yīngwǔ Shuǐ.
In the seventh month of the fourth year of Dàoguāng [道光] (1824),
a dragon was seen at Yuèwàngyán [月望岩] in Máchéng [麻城].
In the jiǎchén [甲辰] month of the seventh month of the fifth year (1825),
a dragon was seen at Fúrónghú [芙蓉湖] in Wǔjìn [武進].
On the fifth day of the sixth month of the sixth year (1826),
a jiāo [蛟] (flood dragon) emerged in Yídū [宜都],
destroying people's homes
and drowning countless people.
On the tenth day of the fifth month of the seventh year (1827),
the Wāngjiāhé [汪家河] river in Fángxiàn [房縣] overflowed,
and a jiāo [蛟] emerged,
destroying countless people's fields.
On the twenty-second day of the eleventh month of the ninth year (1829),
a green dragon was seen in Téngxiàn [滕縣],
approximately dozens of zhàng [丈] long,
with its scales clearly visible.
In the sixth month of the tenth year (1830),
a dragon emerged from Yuánsì [城原寺] in Sōngzīchéng [松滋城],
and ascended over Yángzhōu [洋州].
On the twelfth day of the seventh month,
a jiāo [蛟] rose in Yǒngjiā [永嘉],
splitting mountains as it emerged,
sweeping away fields and dwellings,
and drowning countless people and animals.
In the jiǎshēn [甲申] month of the seventh month of the sixteenth year (1836),
a dragon in Wǔjìn [武進] sank into the ground, forming a pond.
In the fifth month of the twenty-eighth year (1848),
a dragon was seen at Hónghú [洪湖] in Jiānlì [監利].
On the twenty-third day of the seventh month,
five dragons were simultaneously seen in the sky over Tàipíng [太平];
that night, a fierce hurricane arose.
On the seventeenth day of the fifth month of the second year of Xiánfēng [咸豐] (1852),
there was not a single cloud in the sky over Zhījiāng [枝江],
when a white dragon descended upon Wǎyáohú [瓦窰湖],
serpentining for several lǐ [里],
then suddenly soaring away.
On the seventh day of the seventh month of the third year (1853),
a white dragon,
dozens of zhàng [丈] long, was seen in Xīxiāng [西鄉].
On the fifteenth day of the seventh month,
a dragon was seen at Nièkǒu [聶口] in Huángpí [黃陂],
its scales clearly distinct,
lifting boats and sundry objects into the air.
In the eleventh month,
a fierce dragon descended in Xīnàchuān [西納川] in Xīníng [西寧],
its stench detectable for several lǐ [里].
On the twenty-third day of the seventh month of the fifth year (1855),
a great storm with thunder and lightning arose in Shíshǒu [石首],
and in an instant, two dragons ascended tail-to-tail.
In the fifth month of the sixth year (1856),
a two-headed snake was seen in Póyángxiàn [鄱陽縣].
On the eighth day of the fifth month of the seventh year (1857),
a sudden storm with wind and rain struck Zēngshìtáng [曾氏塘] in Láifèngxiàn [來鳳縣];
something over a zhàng [丈] long,
carried by the wind, entered the pond,
resembling an ox in form,
its body adorned with five colors,
its eyes shining brightly,
and water spurted up.
On the seventeenth day of the sixth month of the eighth year (1858),
a dragon entered the city of Yúnmèng [雲夢],
destroying numerous houses,
and circled the city northeastward.
In the third month of the tenth year (1860),
a dragon was seen in Máchéng [麻城].
In the fifth month,
a dragon emerged from Tiān'étáng [天鵝塘] in Sōngzī [松滋],
traversing dry land,
and wherever it passed, all crops were flattened.
In the winter of the eleventh year (1861),
two dragons fought in the sea off Pínghú [平湖].
In the third year of Tóngzhì [同治] (1864),
there was a dragon fight in Sūzhōu [蘇州].
In the first month of the fourth year (1865),
a dragon was seen at Fāngcǎozhōu [芳草洲] in Yíchéng [宜城].
On the fifth day of the fifth month of the sixth year (1867),
three dragons were seen in Gāochún [高淳].
On the twenty-second day of the third month of the tenth year (1871),
there was a dragon fight in Húzhōu [湖州],
with fierce winds and sudden downpours,
uprooting trees and overturning boats.
On the twelfth day of the fifth month,
a dragon was seen in Gāochún [高淳].
By the end of the seventh month,
a jiāo [蛟] emerged from a well in the city.
In the first month of the nineteenth year of Guāngxù [光緒] (1893),
a dragon was seen in a well in Língtái [靈台].
In the tenth month of the twenty-first year (1895),
a dragon was seen at Huìguǎngsì [惠廣寺] in Dàtōng [大通].
In the fourth month of the tenth year of Shùnzhì [順治] (1653),
there were two "mountain horses" in Wúchuān [吳川]: one crossed Shíqiàn [石塹],
the other entered from the southeast corner of the city.
In the seventh month of the third year of Kāngxī [康熙] (1664),
a mare belonging to a commoner in Bìjié [畢節] gave birth to a foal
with five legs.
In the sixth month of the fifth year (1666),
a horse was seen in Ānshì [安市] of Yúchíchéng [魚池城] in Xiàofēng [孝豐],
its mane and tail like those of an ordinary horse,
but with a fleshy saddle on its back;
it roamed the fields,
and after more than a month, its whereabouts became unknown.
In the fifth month of the fifteenth year (1676),
Zhào Háo's [趙豪] mare in Nánlè [南樂], a local student, gave birth to twin foals,
one female and one male.
In the twenty-sixth year (1687),
a mare belonging to a commoner in Píngyuǎnzhōu [平遠州] gave birth to twin foals.
In the second month of the eighth year of Yōngzhèng [雍正] (1730),
a mare belonging to a commoner in Jiāngjīnxiàn [江津縣] gave birth to twin foals.
In the summer of the twenty-first year of Qiánlóng [乾隆] (1756),
a herd of white horses appeared at Tāngkēngzhài [湯坑寨] in Fēngshùn [豐順],
coming out at night to eat grain,
and disappearing when driven away.
In the second month of the twenty-ninth year of Dàoguāng [道光] (1849),
a white mare belonging to a commoner in Zhōnggǔ [中谷] Village, Dìngzhōu [定州], gave birth to two green mules.
In the first year of Tóngzhì [同治] (1862),
a mule and a horse were born from the same womb in Zhènhǎiyíng [鎮海營] in Xīníng [西寧].
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì [順治] (1651),
Mister Wú Quán's [吳全] wife, Lady Lǚ [呂氏], in Shèxiàn [歙縣] gave birth to four sons at once.
In the first year of Kāngxī [康熙] (1662),
Mister Xú Wéipíng's [徐維平] wife in Láiyáng [萊陽] gave birth to a son with four eyes, four arms, and four legs.
In the eleventh year (1672),
Mister Guō Hǎogāng's [郭好剛] wife, Lady Fēng [馮氏], in Jìnzhōu [晉州] gave birth to four sons at once.
In the thirteenth year (1674),
the wives of two brothers, whose surname is unknown, in Dōngyáng [東陽]
were both pregnant;
when they gave birth,
one gave birth to a catfish
with a fish head and a snake body;
the other gave birth to a macaque
with all its hands and claws complete.
In the sixteenth year (1677),
Péng Wànchūn's [彭萬春] daughter in Bìjié [畢節], seven years old, had smallpox,
and when she recovered,
she changed into a boy.
In the spring of the seventeenth year (1678),
a commoner's wife in Qīnghé [清河] gave birth to a headless child,
with two eyes on its breasts
and its mouth on its navel;
could it have been a Xíngtiān [形天] type?
In the fifth month of the twenty-fifth year (1686),
Mister Léi's [雷氏] daughter in Zhōngzhōu [忠州] transformed into a male,
and later became a monk.
In the thirty-second year (1693),
Wáng Bāngyàn's [王邦彥] wife in Dézhōu [德州] gave birth to four sons at once.
In the thirty-fourth year (1695),
Zhāng Zìfù's [張自富] wife, Lady Wáng [王氏], in Chángzhì [長治] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the thirty-seventh year (1698),
Yuè Shù's [岳戍] wife, Lady Lǐ [李氏], in Bǎo'ānzhōu [保安州] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the thirty-eighth year (1699),
Cháng Tōng's [常通] wife in Lùchéng [潞城] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the thirty-ninth year (1700),
a woman of the Lù [陸] family in Húzhōu [湖州] gave birth to a son
with two heads and four arms.
In the forty-first year (1702),
Jiǎ Wénjǔ's [賈文舉] wife in Xīníngxiàn [西寧縣] gave birth to four sons at once.
In the summer of the forty-fourth year (1705),
Zhāng Ruòzhī's [張若芝] wife in Shíshǒuxiàn [石首縣] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the forty-sixth year (1707),
Mister Tán's [譚某] daughter in Wúxiàn [吳縣] transformed into a man.
In the fifty-third year (1714),
a commoner's wife in Guǎngyuán [廣元] gave birth to two snakes,
which were unharmed;
Gāo Wànyán's [高萬言] wife in Láiyángxiàn [萊陽縣] gave birth to four sons at once.
In the sixth month of the fifty-fourth year (1715),
Sūn Zǐfāng's [孫子芳] wife in Dōngpíngzhōu [東平州] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the fifty-sixth year (1717),
Tán Shàngyuán's [檀上元] wife, Lady Hóng [洪氏], in Dōngliú [東流] gave birth to three sons at once;
Mister Zhāng's [張某] wife in Yǐngshàng [潁上] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the fifty-seventh year (1718),
Xíng Xù's [邢序] wife in Xìnyángzhōu [信陽州] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the fifty-eighth year (1719),
Zhào Zìxiǎn's [趙自顯] wife in Xīnghuàxiàn [興化縣] gave birth to three sons at once;
Jiǎ Zéyí's [賈則宜] wife in Zhàochéng [趙城] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the fifty-ninth year (1720),
Mister Wáng's [王某] wife in Hándān [邯鄲] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the sixty-first year (1722),
Shǐ Biàn's [史徧] wife in Jùyěxiàn [鉅野縣] gave birth to three sons at once.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng
a certain commoner's wife in Pí Xiàn gave birth to three boys at one time.
Lǐ Fúkuí's wife, a commoner in Qīngzhōu, gave birth to two boys and one girl at one time.
Liú Jùqīng's wife, a commoner in Gāomì, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Páng Shì, Mǎ Shàobù's wife, a commoner in Cháo Xiàn, gave birth to three boys at one time.
In the autumn of the second year
Máo Qǐměi's wife, a commoner in Nánlíng, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Jiǎ Sānpìn's wife, a commoner in Fényáng, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Wáng Zhīzuǒ's wife, a commoner in Jiǎnzhōu, gave birth to three boys at one time.
In the second month of the third year
Zhēn Yǎngwǔ's wife, a commoner in Qíhé, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Guō Shì, Qín Shùxián's wife, a commoner in Lùchéng, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Wǔ Shì, Hǎo Shìhuì's wife, a commoner in Xiāngyuán, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Liú Shì, Zhāng Guózé's wife, a commoner in Yángchéng, gave birth to three boys at one time.
In the fourth year
Xú Láizhèn's wife, a commoner in Táo Xiàn, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Lì Xīngqí's wife, a commoner in Xiānglíng Xiàn, gave birth to three boys at one time.
In the fifth year
Liú Hǔ's wife, a commoner in Dōnghé Xiàn, gave birth to three boys at one time.
Lǐ Zhēn's wife, a commoner in Yángchéng, gave birth to three boys at one time.
In the sixth year
Rèn Wàntōng's wife, a commoner in Dìngxīng Xiàn, and Liú Zhìlóng's wife, a commoner in Yúcì, both gave birth to three boys at one time.
A commoner's wife in Dōngshān Cūn gave birth to fish.
Tián Yǔ's wife, a commoner in Tíngshān Xiàn, gave birth to three boys at one time.
