Chapter Twenty: The Shíxiàn Calendar
The Dàtǒng (Grand Unification) calendar of the Míng dynasty
was based on the Shòushí (Season-Granting) calendar of the Yuán dynasty.
After the Chénghuà reign,
eclipses were often inaccurate.
At the end of the Wànlì reign,
Xú Guāngqǐ, Lǐ Zhīzǎo, and others translated Western books into a new method,
which accurately predicted eclipses and planetary transits,
but it was not yet put into practice.
After Shìzǔ established the capital,
he abolished the old Míng calendar
and made calculations according to the new method,
which became the Shíxiàn calendar used for over two hundred and sixty years.
Xú Guāngqǐ and others had earnestly debated the issue,
but at the time, their efforts were blocked and not implemented.
That it became the basis for the new dynasty's calendar reform,
was this not the will of Heaven?
Shèngzǔ was proficient in calendrical studies;
he decided to use the method of uniform rotation to align the Seven Luminaries
and set the Jiǎzǐ year of Kāngxī as the epoch.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
following the request of the calendrical officials,
the calculation method was changed to the elliptical method,
and the Guǐmǎo year of Yōngzhèng was set as the epoch.
During the Dàoguāng reign,
the calendrical officials, finding discrepancies in the seconds and minutes of eclipses,
adjusted the original numbers based on actual measurements,
and set the Jiǎwǔ year of Dàoguāng as the epoch.
From Kāngxī to Dàoguāng,
the method of astronomical calculation was revised three times.
However, the calendar with the Jiǎwǔ epoch of Dàoguāng only contained a star catalogue.
As for calculating solar and lunar eclipses and planetary motions,
the books were not yet completed.
The Westerner Johann Adam Schall von Bell (Tāng Ruòwàng),
who collaborated with Xú Guāngqǐ in translating the new method,
used forty-two points to demonstrate the precision of the Western method and the inadequacy of the Chinese method.
The students of astronomy were uniformly convinced.
Méi Wéndǐng from Xuānchéng diligently studied celestial calculations,
tracing back from the Shòushí calendar to the methods of various schools since the Sāntǒng and Sìfēn calendars.
He also extensively researched the Jiǔzhí and Huíhuí (Islamic) methods,
and then reconciled them with the new method.
He thoroughly understood their origins,
and investigated their similarities and differences.
Eventually, due to his accomplished scholarship, he gained the recognition of Shèngzǔ.
Thus, for scholars of astronomical calculation,
they began to understand the consistency between Chinese and Western learning,
and were no longer bewildered by the new method.
Ferdinand Verbiest (Mùnígé) entered China at the same time as Johann Adam Schall von Bell (Tāng Ruòwàng).
He transmitted his learning to Xuē Fèngzuò from Zīchuān.
Wáng Xíchǎn from Wújiāng independently created a new method,
which he used to predict solar and lunar eclipses
with not a second or a fraction of a second of error.
The methods of these two schools
were not officially adopted by the court astronomers,
yet their precision
might have surpassed that of the court officials.
Now, for the Shíxiàn Calendar Chapter,
we will elaborate on its astronomical calculation, the Seven Luminaries, the Four Additional Influences, fundamental principles, and mathematical methods in this essay.
The important arguments from various scholars that contribute to mathematical principles
are also summarized and recorded.
The Míng Dàtǒng calendar and the Huíhuí (Islamic) calendar,
which were used in the early Kāngxī period,
are discussed in detail in the Míng History,
so they will not be elaborated upon here.
Evolution of Astronomical Calculation
In the sixth month of the first year of Shùnzhì,
Tāng Ruòwàng stated:
“In the second year of Chóngzhēn of the Míng dynasty, I came to the capital,
and then I revised the old calendar according to the new Western methods.
Now, I present a diagram of the solar eclipse predicted by the new method for the first day of the eighth month of this year,
including the extent in minutes and seconds as observed in the capital and various provinces,
as well as its starting and ending positions.
I respectfully submit this diagram,
and I request that an official be dispatched at the appointed time to measure it.”
This was granted.
In the seventh month,
Ruòwàng again presented his celestial predictions.
In this month, the Lǐbù stated:
“The Qīntiānjiān has adopted the new method,
and its calculations are complete.
We request that it be given a new name
and promulgated throughout the realm.”
Ruì Qīnwáng said:
“It should be named 'Shíxiàn,'
to signify the court's utmost intention to conform to Heaven and govern the people.”
This was granted.
At noon on the bingchén day, the first day of the eighth month,
there was a solar eclipse of two minutes and forty-eight seconds.
Grand Secretary Féng Quán,
together with Ruòwàng, went to the Guānxiàngtái to measure and report on it.
Only the new method perfectly matched the observations,
while both the Dàtǒng and Huíhuí calendars showed errors in time.
An imperial edict stated:
“The old methods have accumulated errors over a long time,
and this is not due to miscalculation by the officials or students.
Since the new method closely aligns with celestial movements,
the Qīntiānjiān should study it diligently and not be negligent.”
In the tenth month,
the Shíxiàn calendar for the second year of Shùnzhì was promulgated.
Ruòwàng again stated:
“The regulation of human time
depends entirely on the solar terms' entry into the palaces and the sunrise and sunset times.
Now, the day, hour, minute, and second of the solar terms, and the sunrise and sunset times,
are all calculated according to the varying distances.
I request that these be published in the Shíxiàn calendar.”
This was granted.
In the eleventh month,
Ruòwàng was appointed to oversee the Qīntiānjiān.
Ruòwàng and others stated:
“We have calculated the minutes and seconds of the lunar eclipse according to the new method,
and we have re-determined the list of books to be presented annually,
deleting duplicates
to avoid confusion.”
In the sixth month of the second year,
Ruòwàng and others stated:
“The old method predicts a solar eclipse of slightly more than three minutes at chénshí on the jǐmǎo day, the first day of the twelfth month of this year.
The Huíhuí method predicts an eclipse of slightly less than one minute.
According to the new method,
it should only be slightly more than half a minute,
and it will occur before sunrise,
not visible above the horizon.
We request that an official be dispatched at the appointed time for measurement.”
This was granted.
At the appointed time, it was cloudy and rainy,
so the verification was halted.
In the eleventh month,
Ruòwàng presented the Chóngzhēn Lìshū, translated by Míng Grand Secretary Xú Guāngqǐ, renamed as Xīnfǎ Lìshū.
The emperor ordered its distribution to the officials and students of the Qīntiānjiān for study,
and also ordered it to be deposited in the Shǐguǎn,
and promoted Ruòwàng to the rank of Tàicháng Sìqīng.
In the tenth year,
Ruòwàng was granted the title Tōngxuán Jiàoshī,
to commend his diligent work.
Ruòwàng's method
takes the wùchén year of Tiāncōng as its epoch.
It divides the celestial sphere into three hundred and sixty degrees.
The Sun's mean motion in one day is fifty-nine minutes, eight seconds, nineteen wēi, forty-nine xiān, and thirty-six máng.
Its highest annual motion is forty-five seconds.
In the wùchén year, its mean distance from the winter solstice is fifty-three minutes, thirty-five seconds, and thirty-nine wēi.
Its highest distance from the winter solstice is five degrees, fifty-nine minutes, and fifty-nine seconds.
The Moon's mean motion in one day is thirteen degrees, ten minutes, thirty-five seconds, and one wēi.
Its proper motion is thirteen degrees, three minutes, fifty-three seconds, and fifty-six wēi.
Its true node moves three minutes and ten seconds.
The lunar apogee moves six minutes and forty-one seconds.
In the wùchén year, its mean distance from the winter solstice is six gōng, one degree, fifty minutes, fifty-four seconds, and forty-six wēi.
Its proper distance from the winter solstice is six gōng, twenty-five degrees, thirty-two minutes, fifteen seconds, and thirty-four wēi.
Its true node's distance from the winter solstice is one gōng and fourteen seconds.
The lunar apogee's distance from the winter solstice is eleven gōng, six degrees, and nineteen minutes.
The planet Saturn's mean distance from the winter solstice should be eleven gōng, eighteen degrees, fifty-one minutes, and fifty-one seconds.
Its highest motion this year from the winter solstice is nine gōng, eight degrees, fifty-seven minutes, and fifty-nine seconds.
The difference between its mean motion and its highest motion, which is its equation,
is two gōng, nine degrees, fifty-three minutes, and fifty-two seconds.
Its true node's motion from the winter solstice is six gōng, seven degrees, nine minutes, and eight seconds.
In a common year, its mean motion is twelve degrees, thirteen minutes, and thirty-one seconds.
Its highest motion is one minute, twenty seconds, and twelve wēi.
Subtracting the highest motion from the mean motion,
we get twelve degrees, twelve minutes, and fifteen seconds,
which is its annual equation.
In a leap year, its mean motion is twelve degrees, fifteen minutes, and thirty-five seconds.
Its equation is twelve degrees, fourteen minutes, and fifteen seconds.
Its true node's annual motion is forty-two seconds.
The planet Jupiter's mean distance from the winter solstice should be eight gōng, twenty-eight degrees, eight minutes, and thirty-one seconds.
Its highest motion this year is eleven gōng, twenty-seven degrees, eleven minutes, and fifteen seconds.
The difference between its mean motion and its highest motion, which is its equation,
is nine gōng, zero degrees, fifty-seven minutes, and sixteen seconds.
Its true node's motion is six gōng, twenty-four degrees, forty-one minutes, and fifty-two seconds.
In a common year, its mean motion from the winter solstice is one gōng, zero degrees, twenty minutes, and thirty-two seconds.
Its highest motion is fifty-seven seconds and fifty-two wēi.
Subtracting the two numbers,
we get one gōng, zero degrees, nineteen minutes, and thirty-four seconds,
which is its annual equation for a common year.
In a leap year, its mean motion from the winter solstice is one gōng, zero degrees, twenty-five minutes, and thirty-one seconds.
Its equation is one gōng, zero degrees, twenty-four minutes, and thirty-three seconds.
Its true node's annual motion is fourteen seconds.
The planet Mars's mean distance from the winter solstice should be five gōng, four degrees, fifty-four minutes, and thirty seconds.
Its highest motion this year is seven gōng, twenty-nine degrees, thirty minutes, and forty seconds.
The difference between its mean motion and its highest motion, which is its equation,
is nine gōng, five degrees, twenty-three minutes, and fifty seconds.
Its true node's motion is three gōng, seventeen degrees, two minutes, and twenty-nine seconds.
In a common year, its mean motion from the winter solstice is six gōng, eleven degrees, seventeen minutes, and ten seconds.
Its highest motion is one minute and fourteen seconds.
Subtracting the two numbers,
we get six gōng, eleven degrees, fifteen minutes, and fifty-five seconds.
In a leap year, its mean motion from the winter solstice is six gōng, eleven degrees, forty-eight minutes, and thirty-six seconds.
Its equation is six gōng, eleven degrees, forty-seven minutes, and twenty-one seconds.
Its true node's annual motion is fifty-three seconds.
The planet Venus's mean distance from the winter solstice should be the same as the Sun's,
which is zero gōng, zero degrees, fifty-three minutes, thirty-five seconds, and thirty-nine wēi.
The difference between its mean motion and its highest motion, which is its equation,
is six gōng, zero degrees, fifty-six minutes, and fifty-five seconds.
Its appearance and disappearance begin from its furthest point,
which is zero gōng, nine degrees, eleven minutes, and seven seconds.
Its highest motion is at six gōng, zero degrees, sixteen minutes, and six seconds.
In a common year, its distance from the winter solstice is eleven gōng, twenty-nine degrees, forty-five minutes, forty seconds, and thirty-eight wēi.
Its proper equation is eleven gōng, twenty-nine degrees, forty-four minutes, and seventeen seconds.
Its appearance and disappearance motion is seven gōng, fifteen degrees, one minute, and fifty seconds.
Its highest motion is one minute and twenty-one seconds.
In a leap year, its distance from the winter solstice and its proper motion increase by fifty-nine minutes and eight seconds.
Its appearance and disappearance motion increases by three degrees, six minutes, and twenty-four seconds,
which is its motion in one day.
Venus's true node is sixteen degrees before its highest point,
which is five gōng, fourteen degrees, and sixteen minutes.
Its motion is extremely minute,
thus its rate has not been determined,
but there is no great difference from its highest motion.
The planet Mercury's mean distance from the winter solstice should be the same degree as the Sun's.
The difference between its mean motion and its highest motion, which is its equation,
is twenty-nine degrees, twenty minutes, and two seconds.
Its appearance and disappearance begin from its furthest point,
which is three gōng, twenty-nine degrees, fifty-four minutes, and sixteen seconds.
Its highest point is at eleven gōng, zero degrees, fifty-two minutes, and forty-two seconds.
In a common year, its distance from the winter solstice is also the same degree as the Sun's.
Its proper equation is eleven gōng, twenty-nine degrees, forty-three minutes, and fifty-one seconds.
Its appearance and disappearance motion, after three full cycles, is one gōng, twenty-three degrees, fifty-seven minutes, and twenty-six seconds.
In a leap year, its equation is twelve gōng, zero degrees, forty-two minutes, and fifty-nine seconds.
Its appearance and disappearance motion, after a full cycle, is one gōng, twenty-seven degrees, three minutes, and fifty-two seconds.
Its true node's motion, or rather, its being at the same degree as its highest point, is difficult to ascertain,
thus we dare not determine it.
Ruòwàng (Johann) discusses the forty-two main points of the new methods: First, celestial and terrestrial longitudes and latitudes.
Heaven has longitudes and latitudes;
the Earth also has them.
Two hundred and fifty *lǐ* correspond to one degree of the heavens,
for both longitude and latitude.
Second, various planets in different heavens.
The various planets vary greatly in their altitudes and distances from each other,
refuting the error of the old calendar which considered them to be concentric.
Third, different centers.
The Sun's proper circle is not concentric with the Earth.
The distance between the two centers
varies throughout history.
Fourth, atmospheric refraction error.
The Earth has an atmosphere;
without a pre-determined atmospheric refraction correction, precise agreement cannot be achieved.
Fifth, calculation methods differ from ancient methods.
Celestial measurement uses spherical triangles,
and calculations use a table of trigonometric functions (sines and tangents).
Sixth, all measurements and calculations use the ecliptic.
Measuring the heavens with an equatorial instrument,
the obtained longitudes do not match.
The new methods use ecliptic longitude,
applying a table for converting between ecliptic and equatorial coordinates,
thus achieving precise agreement with celestial movements.
Seventh, revising all corrections.
Starting from the *jǐmǎo* day, midnight, after the winter solstice in the *wùchén* year, the second year of Tiāncōng.
Eighth, finding the true *jiéqì* (solar terms).
The old methods used mean *jiéqì*,
which were not true *jiéqì*;
now revised.
Ninth, true limits of acceleration and deceleration.
Using the *Shòushí* calendar's *xiāofēn* (decrement minute) as the mean year,
and then adding or subtracting the difference between the highest and lowest points
to determine the fixed year.
Tenth, measuring the two equinoxes with a gnomon.
The old methods measured the winter solstice with a *guībiǎo* (gnomon and ruler),
which was not the best method.
Now, the spring and autumn equinoxes are used,
which are more precise than the two solstices.
Eleventh, the Sun's rising and setting and the limits of dawn and dusk.
Calculated starting from the capital (Jīngshī),
with additions and subtractions for different locations.
Twelfth, unequal day and night.
The difference is more than one *kè* (quarter-hour);
one reason is that the ecliptic's motion is slower in summer and faster in winter,
another reason is the varying distances between the ecliptic and equatorial planes,
so the rates of degrees are not equally divided.
Thirteenth, revising the time divisions.
Dividing day and night into ninety-six *kè*.
Fourteenth, different methods for intercalary months.
The old methods used mean *jiéqì* to set intercalary months,
which was incorrect.
Now revised to use the celestial degrees traversed by the Sun to determine the *jiéqì*.
Fifteenth, lunar additions and subtractions.
There is only one addition/subtraction for new moons and full moons;
for other days, there are two or three others,
with varying average numbers.
Sixteenth, the Moon's varying altitude, speed, and slowness.
The Moon's movement is slowest at its highest point in its orbit
and fastest at its lowest point.
The five planets follow the same principle.
Seventeenth, the varying speed of the Moon's appearance after the new moon.
One reason is its own varying speed of motion,
another is the inclination of the ecliptic's ascent and descent,
and a third is whether the Moon's orbit (báidào) is north or south in latitude.
Eighteenth, nodal motion additions and subtractions.
When the Moon is at a node,
seeking it by mean motion will certainly not match.
Therefore, an addition/subtraction is introduced for the mean motion of the nodes.
Nineteenth, lunar latitude distance in degrees.
The old methods stated the ecliptic and lunar orbit (báidào) were five degrees apart,
unaware that there are still gains and losses outside of new and full moons.
The maximum distance
is five and one-third degrees.
Twentieth, occurrence or non-occurrence of eclipses.
For a lunar eclipse, the distance from the ecliptic in latitude is compared with the sum of the radii of the Moon and the Earth's shadow.
For a solar eclipse, the distance is compared with the sum of the radii of the Sun and Moon.
If the distance is small, there is an eclipse;
if large, there is no eclipse.
Twenty-first, different eclipse limits for the Sun and Moon.
For a lunar eclipse, the Moon's orbit (tàiyīn) and the Earth's shadow circle are tangent.
This is compared by their two apparent radii to the angular distance of the lunar orbit (báidào) from the ecliptic.
Then, from the angular distance, the nodal period is deduced to determine the eclipse limit.
For a solar eclipse, parallax must be added to obtain the angular distance.
Twenty-second, differences and similarities in the magnitude of solar and lunar eclipses.
For a lunar eclipse, the angular distance is the actual distance between the center of the Moon and the center of the Earth's shadow.
For a solar eclipse, it is the distance between the centers of the Sun and Moon.
However, a solar eclipse is based on apparent distance, not actual distance.
Twenty-third, actual eclipse and central eclipse.
The straight line from the Earth's center to the ecliptic is taken as the primary axis.
If the Sun, Moon, and five planets are all on this line,
then it is an actual eclipse.
If the Moon and the five planets are each on the circumference of their own epicycle,
and the straight line from the Earth's center extends to the ecliptic,
and the centers of the two epicycles are both on the line,
then it is a central eclipse.
Twenty-fourth, apparent eclipse.
A solar eclipse has an actual eclipse in the heavens
and an apparent eclipse seen by people.
The apparent eclipse is based on the observer's eye and the ground.
Twenty-fifth, the ecliptic's ninety degrees as the central limit for east-west differences.
Regarding the zenith, the altitude difference is directly downward.
The north-south difference is obliquely downward.
But for the east-west difference, only the central limit line is directly downward,
and outside of it, all are obliquely downward.
Regarding its path, the north-south difference is the leg (*gǔ*),
the east-west difference is always the base (*gōu*),
and the altitude difference is always the hypotenuse (*xián*).
At the central limit, the leg and hypotenuse become one line,
and there is no base.
Twenty-sixth, the three parallaxes.
Taking the Earth's radius as one side,
the distance of the Sun and Moon from the Earth as another side,
and the altitude of the two luminaries as a third side,
a triangle is formed.
This is used to obtain the altitude difference.
Then, shifting southward changes the latitude to obtain the north-south difference.
By shifting left or right within the ninety-degree limit of the ecliptic, the latitude changes,
obtaining the east-west difference.
Twenty-seventh, the three external differences.
The east-west, north-south, and altitude differences
all arise from the Earth's diameter.
The three external differences do not arise from the Earth's diameter but from the atmosphere.
First,
the clear atmospheric refraction difference;
second,
the clear atmospheric diameter difference;
third,
the epicycle diameter difference.
Twenty-eighth, inconsistent eclipse ingress and egress times.
This refutes the theory of bisection of the two times.
The new methods use apparent motion to deduce variable times,
thus making clear the reason for inconsistent eclipse ingress and egress times.
Twenty-ninth, different eclipse calculations.
Various regions calculate the eclipse times and magnitudes of solar eclipses based on the Earth's diameter.
Thirtieth, solar eclipse variations.
According to calculations, an eclipse should occur but is not actually seen.
This must be because the north-south difference at this day and place changes to an east-west difference.
This happens only once or twice in a thousand years,
but it is not impossible.
Thirty-first, predicting past and verifying future.
The various tables of the new methods,
tracing backward and extending forward,
are clear at a glance,
requiring no effort.
Thirty-second, the five planets relative to the Sun.
In the old methods, the number of days for conjunction and invisibility
was sometimes more, sometimes less,
determined only by section markers,
thus inevitably having errors.
Now corrected.
Thirty-third, precise agreement of invisibility and visibility.
The old methods for the invisibility and visibility of the five planets only used the ecliptic's angular distance,
which was incorrect.
Now corrected.
Thirty-fourth, the latitudes of the five planets.
The Moon's proper orbit (tàiyīn běndào) obliquely intersects the ecliptic,
thus giving rise to angular distances and both lunar and solar calendars.
The same applies to the five planets.
The new methods meticulously calculated each,
which the old methods could not do.
Thirty-fifth, invisibility and visibility of Venus and Mercury.
Venus may be in conjunction with the Sun but not invisible.
Mercury may be separated from the Sun but not visible.
A single measurement with an armillary sphere can reveal this,
which the old methods could not achieve.
Thirty-sixth, measuring the five planets.
To measure the five planets, fixed stars must be used as a reference.
Thirty-seventh, eastward shift of fixed stars.
Fixed stars use the ecliptic pole as their pole.
Each constellation's angular distance from a star is sometimes close to the celestial pole,
or sometimes far from the celestial pole.
This is due to the different poles of the ecliptic and equatorial planes,
not because the angular distances of stars have different motions or change positions.
Thirty-eighth, defining six grades of stellar magnitudes.
This was unheard of before.
Thirty-ninth, clarifying doubts about the Milky Way.
The new methods measure with telescopes,
showing that the Milky Way is formed by countless small stars clustered together.
Fortieth, deleting and revising the four subsidiary points (sìyú).
Luó is the direct intersection of the Moon's orbit (báidào),
Jìdū is the central intersection,
and Yuèbèi is the point of the Moon's highest altitude.
As for the remaining Zǐ'ài,
there are no numbers to define it.
The *Míng Shǐ* (History of Ming) conflated it;
now all are revised and deleted.
Forty-first, measuring instruments.
Those added by the new methods include:

the quadrant, the universal astrolabe, the horizontal astrolabe, the crossbow-astrolabe, the celestial ring and armillary sphere with limiting instruments, the universal equatorium with simple plane, and the full ecliptic-equatorial instrument.
And the newly manufactured telescope
is especially important for star measurements.
Forty-second, sundials.
These include the horizontal sundial, the three-gables sundial, the universal sundial, and the light-transmitting sundial.
In addition, there are star dials and moon dials
for nighttime measurement.
What Ruòwàng said
largely used the new methods to criticize the shortcomings of the old techniques.
However, the essence of the new methods
is also fully contained herein.
In the fourth month of the fourteenth year,
Wú Míngxuàn, the head of the previous Huíhuí Division and Autumn Official, said:
"My ancestor Mòhé Yìlǐ and eighteen other families,
originally from the Western Regions,
came to court to present their profound learning and re-translate texts in the *jǐwèi* year of the Kāihuáng reign of the Suí dynasty.
They were appointed as officials of the sun.
For 1059 years,
they specialized in observing the movements of the constellations to determine auspiciousness and inauspiciousness.
Each year, they calculated the transgressions of the Moon and the Five Planets,
made astrological predictions,
and forecasted solar and lunar eclipses.
It became a fixed rule to submit our written reports for approval.
In the third year of Shùnzhì,

Tāng Ruòwàng, who held the seal of this Directorate, ordered our division that there was no need to report on solar and lunar eclipses, transgressions of the Moon and the Five Planets, or astrological predictions.
I have examined the Seven Luminaries calculated by Ruòwàng,
and Mercury is supposed to be hidden and invisible in the second and eighth months.
Yet, Mercury was still seen in the east on the twenty-ninth day of the second month,
and was visible in the evening of the twenty-fourth day of the eighth month.
As this relates to astrological predictions,
I dare not fail to report the truth.
I beg to re-establish the Huíhuí Division
to preserve this unique learning."
The memorial was sent to the relevant department.
At that time, Yáng Guāngxiān, a military student from Xīn'ān Guard, knocked on the imperial gate and submitted a "Treatise on Exposing Errors,"
criticizing the errors in Tāng Ruòwàng's new methods,
and further stating:
"The five characters 'according to the new Western methods'
in the *Shíxiàn Calendar* are especially inappropriate."
He also submitted a "Deliberation on Selection,"
criticizing Ruòwàng for using the *Hóngfàn Wǔxíng* for the burial date of Róng Qīnwáng,
whereby the orientation, sun, and moon all violated taboos and brought ill omen.
In the twelfth month of the third year of Kāngxī,
the Ministry of Rites discussed
"to change the five characters 'according to the new Western methods'
on the *Shíxiàn Calendar* to the two characters 'approved by memorial.'"
This was adopted.
In the fourth year,
the deliberative princes and others stated: "The traditional method of 100 *kè* per day
was changed to 96 *kè* by the new method;
the order of the Twenty-Eight Mansions
was altered by Tāng Ruòwàng, moving the constellations of Zī and Cān;
furthermore, Zǐ'ài was deleted from the Four Remnants.
All these are inappropriate.
In the selection of dates, the proper Five Elements were not used,
but the *Hóngfàn Wǔxíng* were used,
leading to the orientation, sun, and moon all violating taboos and bringing ill omen.
The matter is grave.
Tāng Ruòwàng and the divisional officials should be sentenced to *língchí* or beheaded accordingly."
An imperial edict granted Tāng Ruòwàng leniency and exempted him from death;
Lǐ Zǔbái and four other officials of the *Shíxiàn* Division were all executed.
Thus, the old *Dàtǒng* method was reinstated,
and Yáng Guāngxiān was put in charge of the Directorate's affairs.
Guāngxiān repeatedly declined in memorials,
but was not permitted.
Guāngxiān was not proficient in the science of astronomical calculation.
In the seventh year of Kāngxī,
he claimed that there would be a intercalary twelfth month in the following year.
He later realized his mistake
and reported it himself,
but the *Shíxiàn Calendar* had already been issued.
An edict was then issued to the entire empire to stop the intercalary month.
In the same year, Wú Míngxuǎn, Vice Director of the Directorate, stated:
"The ancient methods are erroneous,
and the reports from the Five Official Divisions and the Huíhuí Division are inconsistent.
Corrections should be made immediately."
This was sent to the Ministry of Rites for deliberation.
The Ministry of Rites reported back:
"The calculations of the Seven Luminaries, specifically the two stars Venus and Mercury, by Gē Jìwén and others of the Five Official Divisions, are too erroneous.
The Seven Luminaries calculated by Registrar Chén Yùxīn have not been verified by observation
and also contain errors.
The Seven Luminaries calculated by Vice Director Wú Míngxuǎn are closer to celestial phenomena
and should therefore be adopted.
The Directorate officials, together with the officials of the four divisions,
should continue to measure sundial shadows daily to determine the solar terms
and observe the Moon and the Five Planets at night to determine their movements."
This was adopted.
In the eleventh month,
the Westerner Nán Huáirén stated that the various methods currently in use did not conform to celestial phenomena.
Consequently, Nán Huáirén, Lì Lèisī, Ān Wénsī, and Directorate officials Mǎ Yòu, Yáng Guāngxiān, Wú Míngxuǎn, and others were summoned to the Dōnghuá Gate.
Grand Secretary Lǐ Wèi conveyed the imperial decree:
"The setting of time is a crucial state affair.
You must not harbor old grudges,
thinking yourselves right and others wrong.
What is right should be followed,
what is wrong should be corrected,
aiming always for the utmost perfection."
In the twelfth month,
Nán Huáirén impeached Wú Míngxuǎn for errors in the *Shíxiàn Calendar* for the eighth year of Kāngxī he had produced,
and this was submitted to the deliberative princes, Nine Ministers, and Censors for discussion.
The deliberative princes and others stated:
"We request that ministers be dispatched to verify with Nán Huáirén and others."
Tú Hǎi, Lǐ Wèi, and eighteen other individuals were then sent to the Imperial Observatory for verification.
In the second month of the eighth year,
the deliberative princes and others reported back:
"Tú Hǎi and others went to the Imperial Observatory for verification,
and Nán Huáirén's statements all matched,
while Wú Míngxuàn's statements were all erroneous.
When asked, Directorate Director Mǎ Yòu and others also stated that Nán Huáirén's calculations indeed conformed to celestial phenomena.
We humbly believe that although the 100 *kè* method has been in use for a long time,
since Nán Huáirén's 96 *kè* method conforms to celestial phenomena,
it should naturally be adopted.
Furthermore, Nán Huáirén stated that Luóhóu, Jìdū, and Yuèbèi are used in calculations
and thus listed after the Seven Luminaries,
but the star Zǐ'ài is useless
and should not be included.
Therefore, starting from the ninth year of Kāngxī,
the calendar using 96 *kè* should be implemented."
At this time, Míngxuàn said,
"I only know astronomy,
but not calendrical computation."
Guāngxiān said,
"I do not know calendrical computation,
only calendrical principles."
Guāngxiān's words were especially disrespectful
and he was stripped of his office.
In the third month,
Nán Huáirén was appointed Vice Director of the Directorate of Astronomy.
Previously, the Directorate officials, following ancient methods, calculated that an intercalary month should be placed in the twelfth month of the eighth year of Kāngxī.
Nán Huáirén stated that *Yǔshuǐ* (Rain Water) is the mid-solar term of the first month,
and on the twenty-ninth day of that month, it coincided with *Yǔshuǐ*.
Thus, this would be the first month of the ninth year of Kāngxī,
and no intercalary month should be placed.
The intercalary month should be in the second month of the following year.
Many Directorate officials sided with Huáirén,
followed his words,
and moved the intercalary month to the second month of the ninth year.
Thus, both the *Dàtǒng* and Huíhuí methods were abolished,
and only the Western method was exclusively used,
as it was at the beginning of Shùnzhì's reign.
In the eighth month,
Nán Huáirén impeached Yáng Guāngxiān for falsely accusing Tāng Ruòwàng of rebellion.
The deliberative princes and others discussed
"Tāng Ruòwàng should be reinstated as 'Tōngwēi Jiaoshī,'
and given a posthumous award according to his original rank.
Yáng Guāngxiān should be subject to the reverse penalty."
An imperial edict stated
"no deliberation."
In the second month of the thirteenth year,
the newly constructed astronomical instruments were completed and reported.
Nán Huáirén was promoted to the honorary title of Tàicháng Sìqīng.
In the second month of the fourteenth year,
an edict instructed Vice Director Ān Tài to study ancient calendrical methods under Hé Jūnxī.
In the second month of the fifteenth year,
the Directorate of Astronomy reported a solar eclipse on the first day of the fifth month.
Vice Director Ān Tài, using ancient methods, calculated that the eclipse should be 5 fen and 60 seconds.
Nán Huáirén's new method calculated it to be only 20 *wēi*, 3 fen, and 1 second.
On the appointed day, they ascended the platform for observation.
At the peak of the *yǒu* hour, the eclipse reached its maximum,
nearly 1 fen.
At the beginning of the *xū* hour, it returned to its full state.
The fractions calculated by the ancient method were far off,
and the new method also did not match very well.
Nán Huáirén said:
"This is due to the effect of the clear misty vapor.
Misty vapor can make small objects appear large."
In the seventh month of the seventeenth year,
the Directorate of Astronomy presented the *Kāngxī Yǒngnián Biǎo* in thirty-two volumes.
In the tenth month of the twenty-second year,
the Directorate officials completed the calculation of the Shèngjīng Ninety-Degree Table.
Previously,
Nán Huáirén had reported:
"The altitudes of the North Pole vary across provinces,
and thus the times and magnitudes of conjunctions and eclipses are all different.
These all rely on the Ninety-Degree Table for each province.
Previously, the altitude of the North Pole in Shèngjīng was unknown,
so the Ninety-Degree Table for the capital was used.
Now, it has been measured that the North Pole in Shèngjīng is two degrees higher than that of the capital.
I request that the Ninety-Degree Table be calculated according to its altitude."
This was adopted.
At this point,
the Shèngjīng Ninety-Degree Table was presented,
and an edict stated
"to be observed forever."
In the tenth month of the forty-first year,
Grand Secretary Lǐ Guāngdì presented three scrolls of astronomical and calendrical queries by Méi Wéndǐng, a gòngshēng from Xuānchéng.
The Emperor said:
“I have paid attention to calendrical calculations for many years,
and I can determine the right and wrong of this matter.”
He then personally annotated and returned them.
The details are found in Méi Wéndǐng’s biography.
Méi Wéndǐng discussed the similarities and differences between Chinese and Western methods, saying:
“The adoption of the new calendar today
is a combination of their strengths
to supplement the deficiencies of the old methods,
not a complete abolition of ancient methods in favor of new techniques.
Indeed, the Western calendar shares more than one point of similarity with the Chinese method.
What it calls the highest epicycle and declination for the five planets
is the Chinese method's Yíngsuō Lì (Expansion-Contraction Calendar),
and for the moon,
it is the Chízài Lì (Slow-Fast Calendar).
What it calls the annual cycles of the five planets
is the Chinese method's duànmù (segmentation).
What it calls the eastward movement of fixed stars
is the Chinese method's suìchā (precession).
What it calls the solar terms determined by the sun's passage through the mansions
is the Chinese method's dìngqì (fixed qi).
What it calls the variations in true solar terms across different provinces
is the Chinese method's lǐchā (longitudinal difference).
However, the Chinese method speaks of yíngsuō and chízài,
while the Western explanation clarifies their principles by referring to the highest and lowest points;
the Chinese method speaks of duànmù,
while the Western explanation clarifies their principles by referring to annual cycles;
the Chinese method speaks of suìchā,
while the Western explanation clarifies their principles by referring to the eastward movement of fixed stars.
Thus, what the Chinese calendar describes are the 'what is so' of movements,
while what the Western calendar deduces are the 'why it is so' principles.
This is its valuable aspect.
As for dìngqì and lǐchā,
the Chinese calendar originally had these methods,
but they were not applied in the calendar itself;
they were not absent in ancient times and only present now.
What is truly new in the Western calendar
is the latitudes of the five planets.
In the Chinese calendar, latitudes
were only applied to the sun and moon,
and the five planets had not been addressed in this way.
Now, the Western calendar for the five planets has nodes and latitudinal movement,
explained with the same clarity as the sun and moon.
This is a major deficiency in the Chinese calendar,
which has been supplemented by the Western method.
Thus, for points of similarity with the Chinese method,
it has clarified the 'why it is so';
and for the deficiencies of the Chinese method,
it has provided supplements.
Therefore, our accumulated observations
are further corroborated by their theories,
and their theories, which might seem hard to believe,
are proven to be true by our accumulated observations.
Even if a sage were to reappear,
they would surely adopt and utilize both.”
In the tenth month of the fiftieth year,
the Emperor issued an edict to the Grand Secretaries and others:
“I have always paid attention to astronomy and calendrical methods.
The major points of the Western method are not incorrect,
but in the division of minutes and degrees,
errors inevitably accumulate over time.
This year, at the summer solstice,
the Qīntiān Jiān reported it as 'wǔzhèng sānkè' (noon, three kè).
I carefully measured the sun's shadow
and found it to be 'wǔchū sānkè jiǔfēn' (noon, three kè, nine fēn).
Even a slight discrepancy at this time
might lead to a much greater difference decades later.
It is like money and grain:
though a 'wēichén' (tiny dust particle) or 'miǎohū' (a fraction of a second) seems insignificant,
when totaled,
it accumulates from little to much.
This matter has factual evidence,
unlike the arguments of scholars which can be filled with empty words to shirk responsibility.”
He also commanded the Ministry of Rites to recruit personnel skilled in computational methods,
personally examined them at the imperial audience,
and selected 42 people, including Gù Cóng.
In the fifth month of the fifty-first year,
the Emperor traveled to the Bìshǔ Shānzhuāng,
and summoned Méi Juéchéng, grandson of Méi Wéndǐng, to the imperial temporary residence.
Previously, he had ordered Chén Hòuyào, professor of Sūzhōu Prefecture;
Hé Jūnxī's sons Hé Guózhù and Guózōng, both Qīntiān Jiān Wǔguānzhèng;
the official student Míng'āntú;
and Chéng Dé, former Qīntiān Jiān Jiānfù,
to all accompany him and serve.
The Emperor personally instructed and questioned them,
allowing them to pose difficulties as if between master and disciple.
When Juéchéng arrived,
his responses pleased the Emperor,
and he was subsequently assigned to serve in the inner court with Hòuyào and others.
In the fifth month of the fifty-second year,
the revision of works on lǜlǜ (pitch pipes) and computational methods began.
Qínwáng Yǔnzhǐ, the fifteenth imperial son Yǔnbì, and the sixteenth imperial son Yǔnlù were appointed to oversee the compilation.
Hé Guózōng and Méi Juéchéng were appointed as compilers.
Chén Hòuyào, Wèi Tíngzhēn, Wáng Lánshēng, Fāng Bāo, and others served as proofreaders.
The compiled books
were presented daily to the Emperor,
who personally made corrections.
In the fourth month of the fifty-third year,
the Emperor instructed Qínwáng Yǔnzhǐ and others:
“The framework of ancient calendars is very good,
but their numerical values have become inaccurate over time.
When revising the books, we should follow the framework of ancient calendars,
but use current numerical values for calculations.”
In the tenth month,
he further decreed:
“The height of the North Pole and the obliquity of the ecliptic are of utmost importance.
These should be measured daily behind the Dànníng Jū.”
A quadrant instrument was then constructed,
five chǐ in diameter,
made of bronze.
By day, it measured the sun's altitude;
by night, it measured the stars Gōuchén and Dìxīng.
Additionally, two zhōngbiǎo, two zhèngbiǎo, and two dàobiǎo were made,
all four chǐ high.
The zhōngbiǎo measured the center of the sun's shadow;
the zhèngbiǎo and dàobiǎo measured the shadows of the sun's upper and lower edges.
However, the fractional parts of the sun's shadow obtained from the six gnomons were often inconsistent.
Méi Juéchéng said:
“With tall gnomons and faint shadows,
the fractional parts are difficult to ascertain accurately,
a problem that has plagued astronomers since ancient times.
In the past, Guō Shǒujìng made a bronze gnomon,
with two dragons at its ends,
raising the crossbeam to forty chǐ.
Because its shadow was indistinct,
he created a 'jǐngfú' (shadow tally) to obtain a solid shadow.
Its construction involved a bronze leaf two cùn wide,
its length twice its width,
with a tiny hole in the center, like a needle's eye or a mustard seed.
It had a square wooden base,
and one end was fitted with a pivot
allowing it to open and close.
By adjusting one end,
its needle could be tilted,
higher to the north and lower to the south,
moving back and forth within the indistinct shadow.
Sunlight passing through the hole,
no larger than a millet grain,
faintly revealed the crossbeam within.”
So, six jǐngfú were made, imitating Guō Shǒujìng's design from the Yuán Shǐ,
and used according to the method.
Only then did the fractional parts of the shadow become perfectly accurate.
Measurements yielded a North Pole height of 39 degrees, 59 minutes, 30 seconds at Chàngchūnyuán,
which was four minutes and thirty seconds higher than the imperial observatory in the capital.
The obliquity of the ecliptic was 23 degrees, 29 minutes,
which was two minutes less than previous measurements.
In the eleventh month,
Qínwáng Yǔnzhǐ and others stated:
“Guō Shǒujìng, in creating the Shòushí Lì (Calendar for Granting Seasons),
dispatched people to 27 locations for distributed measurements,
thus achieving close agreement.
Now, in addition to daily measurements at Chàngchūnyuán and the observatory,
for eight provinces such as Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, Yúnnán, Sìchuān, Shǎnxī, Hénán, Jiāngnán, and Zhèjiāng,
where lǐchā is particularly pronounced,
we request that people be sent to measure daily
to obtain true values.
This way, the lǐchā to the east, west, north, and south, as well as the radius of the sun's celestial sphere,
will all have concrete evidence.”
This was approved.
In the second month of the fifty-eighth year [of Kāngxī's reign],
because the number of calendar calculators was insufficient for use,
an imperial edict instructed the Lǐbù to select candidates from the Měngyǎngzhāi examinations.
Twenty-eight people, including Fù Míng'ān, were chosen
and ordered to work in the Xiūshūchù.
In the sixtieth year,
the imperially compiled book on algorithms was completed,
and given the name Shùlǐ Jīngyùn.
An edict stated:
"This book is bestowed upon Méi Wéndǐng, one copy,
and he is ordered to diligently proofread it."
His grandson, Méi Juéchéng, was dispatched to deliver the book to him.
In the sixth month of the sixty-first year,
the draft of the calendar book was completed,
along with those on lǜlǚ and algorithms,
together forming the Lǜlì Yuānyuán in one hundred juan: one part was Lìxiàng Kǎochéng, upper and lower volumes;
one part was Lǜlǚ Jīngyì, upper and lower volumes;
a supplement;
and one part was Shùlǐ Jīngyùn, upper and lower volumes.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
Lìxiàng Kǎochéng was promulgated to the Qīntiānjiān,
which became the Kāngxī Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ.
Starting from the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
the compilation of the Shíxiànshū strictly followed the methods of Lìxiàng Kǎochéng.
It was also agreed that the imperially compiled books
did not need to be managed by the Qīntiānjiān;
the Westerners who managed the calendar methods were appointed as Jiānzhèng.
In the sixth month of the eighth year,
Jiānzhèng Míng'āntú stated:
"The movements of the sun and moon,
over long periods, gradually diverge,
and methods must be continually revised
to achieve close agreement.
Your servants, following the imperially compiled Lìxiàng Kǎochéng to calculate the shíxiàn,
and based on the estimations of Jiānzhèng Dài Jìnxián and Jiānfù Xú Màodé,
have noticed a slight discrepancy.
Regarding the solar eclipse on the first day of this month,
your servants jointly observed it,
and the actual measurement did not match the calculated fractions.
We humbly request an imperial edict to Dài Jìnxián and Xú Màodé for detailed revision and repair."
This was approved.
In the fourth month of the tenth year,
the revised tables for the sun's ecliptic longitude and the moon's anomaly were completed.
In the fourth month of the second year of Qiánlóng,
Gù Cóng, who was assisting in the affairs of the Lìbù Shàngshū, stated:
"Emperor Shìzōng approved the words of the observatory officials,
requesting the compilation and revision of the two tables for the sun's ecliptic longitude and the moon's anomaly,
to calculate the conjunctions of the sun and moon,
as well as their passage through zodiacal houses,
new moons, full moons, first quarters, and last quarters,
the varying lengths of day and night,
and also their eclipses and transits,
totaling thirty-nine pages,
to be appended to the end of the tables in Lìxiàng Kǎochéng.
Upon investigation, the compiler of these tables
is the Western Jiānzhèng Dài Jìnxián;
those capable of using these tables
are the Western Jiānfù Xú Màodé and Wǔguānzhèng Míng'āntú.
It is proposed to appoint Dài Jìnxián as the Zǒngcái,
and Xú Màodé and Míng'āntú as Fùzǒngcái,
to diligently examine and verify,
and to add diagrams and explanations.
Should there be any places within Lìxiàng Kǎochéng that warrant modification,
they should also be ordered to carefully correct them."
An imperial edict stated:
"Let Gù Cóng be solely in charge of this."
In the fifth month,
Cóng again stated:
"I humbly request that Méi Juéchéng be appointed Zǒngcái,
and Hé Guózōng assist as Fùzǒngcái."
This was approved.
In the eleventh month,
Prince Zhuāng Yǔnlù was appointed Zǒnglǐ.
In the fourth month of the third year,
Prince Zhuāng Yǔnlù and others stated:
"In the book Lìxiàng Kǎochéng,
the only change in numbers is a reduction of two fen in the greatest obliquity of the ecliptic;
the rest still follow the old methods of the Western mathematician Tycho.
Among the Westerners in the Kāngxī era were Cassini and Flamsteed, who
developed ideas that Tycho had not fully explored.
There are three main points: first, regarding the difference in the apparent radius of the sun,
formerly set at three fen,
now measured to be only ten seconds;
second, regarding the difference in atmospheric refraction,
formerly set at thirty-four fen at the horizon, and
at an altitude of forty-five degrees,
only five seconds,
now measured to be only thirty-two fen at the horizon, and
at an altitude of forty-five degrees,
still fifty-nine seconds;
third, that the proper orbits of the sun, moon, and five planets are not perfect circles,
but are all ellipses,
with longer diameters at the ends
and shorter diameters at the sides.
Due to these three points,
both longitudes and latitudes show slight discrepancies.
Dài Jìnxián and others were familiar with these theories,
but because they had not been verified,
they dared not immediately accept them as correct.
During the solar eclipse on the new moon of the sixth month of the eighth year of Yōngzhèng,
the old method calculated nine fen and twenty-two seconds,
while the new method calculated eight fen and ten seconds.
Compared with actual measurements,
the new method was closer.
Therefore, it was approved to re-compile the new tables for the sun's ecliptic longitude and moon's anomaly,
to be appended to Lìxiàng Kǎochéng.
Your servants, having been ordered to revise and supplement the table explanations and diagrams,
calculated using the new table for the sun's ecliptic longitude that
the vernal equinox is later by about thirteen kès than before,
the autumnal equinox is earlier by about nine kès than before,
and both the winter and summer solstices are later by about two kès.
However, upon measuring the sun's altitude at noon,
only the winter solstice is higher by about two fen than before;
the summer solstice and autumnal equinox differ by merely twenty to thirty seconds.
This is because measurements are taken on the ground,
while calculations are based on the earth's center.
The currently determined differences in the apparent radius of the earth and atmospheric refraction are both different from before,
hence calculations sometimes differ by several kès,
but measurements ultimately do not deviate significantly.
As for establishing the method based on elliptical orbits,
although calculations are more complex,
adjusting old numbers to match celestial movements
is quite innovative.
Your servants have clarified the principles and numbers,
and written nine chapters on the sun's ecliptic longitude along with its tables.
We humbly request your imperial decision,
to be attached after Lìxiàng Kǎochéng,
and titled Yùzhì Hòubiān.
Whatever has been explained in the previous book
will not be redundantly restated."
This was reported and noted.
In the seventh year,
Prince Zhuāng Yǔnlù and others presented ten juan of books on the sun's ecliptic longitude, moon's anomaly, and passage through zodiacal houses,
which became the Yōngzhèng Guǐmǎo Yuánfǎ.
In the tenth month of the ninth year,
Jiānzhèng Dài Jìnxián and others stated:
"The Língtái Yíxiàng Zhì originally stated that stars differ by about one degree every seventy years.
A long time has passed,
so it should be revised.
At the time of the revision of the Zhì in the thirteenth year of Kāngxī,
the greatest obliquity of the ecliptic differed from current measurements.
The tables listed
should be individually supplemented and revised.
The Three Enclosures and Twenty-eight Mansions, as well as various other stars,
differ in number between past and present,
and should also be rectified."
An imperial edict instructed Prince Zhuāng, È'ěrtài, and Zhāng Zhào to deliberate and report.
In the eleventh month,
it was agreed to keep the three individuals jointly in charge.
In this year, the names Luóhóu and Jìdū were revised,
and Zǐqì was added as one of the Sìyú.
In the seventeenth year,
Prince Zhuāng Yǔnlù and others stated that the stars listed in Yíxiàng Zhì
were often out of order.
They were now corrected sequentially,
resulting in thirty juan of books,
which were given the name Yíxiàng Kǎochéng.
In this month, Prince Zhuāng and others again reported on the revision of the fixed star longitude and latitude tables,
and the reordering of the twenty-eight mansions, placing Zī before Shēn.
An imperial edict instructed the Dàxuéshì to consult with the Jiǔqīng and report.
In the twelfth month,
Dàxuéshì Fù Héng and others stated:
"We request that starting from the nineteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the mansion for the day in the Shíxiànshū
be changed to Zī first, Shēn second."
This was approved.
Later, the Qīntiānjiān found a calculation error for Saturn, deducting thirty fen from its parallel motion,
leading to gradual discrepancies between the eclipses and transits and the original calculations
from the Qiánlóng era to the early Dàoguāng era.
In the eighth month of the eighteenth year of Dàoguāng (1838),
Jìngzhēng (敬徵), the Minister of Works managing the affairs of the Imperial Astronomical Bureau (Qīntiānlán), stated:
"Since I, your servant, began managing the Bureau's affairs in the fourth year of Dàoguāng (1824),
I have examined the instruments on the observation platform.
The obliquity of the ecliptic (huángchì dàjù) instruments made in the thirteenth year of Kāngxī (1674)
all indicated twenty-three degrees and thirty-two minutes.
When the Jīhéng Fǔchényí (璣衡撫辰儀) was re-made in the ninth year of Qiánlóng (1744),
the obliquity of the ecliptic measured
was twenty-three degrees and twenty-nine minutes.
This shows that the original instruments were no longer consistent with celestial movements,
and now almost a hundred years have passed,
so even the Fǔchényí has errors.
I have replaced the axis of the Fǔchényí
and re-positioned all other instruments.
I have also newly made one small quadrant instrument
to allow officials and students to measure the sun's movement by day
and the moon and stars by night.
Whenever there is a solar term or an eclipse,
if the measured actual numbers do not match the calculations,
a detailed examination is conducted.
It was found that due to discrepancies in the sun's latitude,
the measured obliquity of the ecliptic was slightly smaller than before,
its value being only twenty-three degrees and twenty-seven minutes.
From the variations in the timing of the solar terms,
it was determined that there were irregular advances and retreats in the sun's celestial longitude.
The sun's celestial longitude is the basis for all calculations,
and all other celestial bodies follow it.
Moreover, to calculate the sun's movement,
the 'annual actual' (suìshí) and 'seasonal response' (qìyìng) differences, referred to as the 'lowest celestial longitude' (běntiān zuìbēi xíngdù), are used as a basis.
It is proposed that beginning from the jiǎwǔ (甲午) year, the fourteenth year of Dàoguāng (1834), as the base year,
according to the actually measured numbers,
the original numbers be slightly adjusted,
so that the calculated timings of the sun's movement and solar terms
appear closer to the actual measured numbers.
As for the moon's celestial longitude,
eclipses are the major means of verification.
Recent lunar eclipses measured
were mostly earlier than originally predicted,
and fewer were later.
Therefore, adjustments were made to the moon's mean motion (píngxíng), proper motion (zìxíng), and nodal motion (jiāoxíng).
According to the currently proposed mean motion,
still using the old numbers for all inequalities,
three lunar eclipses were calculated after the fourteenth year of Dàoguāng (1834).
Except for the one in the third month of the seventeenth year (1837) where only the initial partial eclipse was seen,
and the one in the ninth month where the sky was cloudy and could not be measured,
only the lunar eclipse on the fifteenth day of the ninth month of the sixteenth year of Dàoguāng (1836) was measured.
It was close to the calculations with the new numbers,
but being only one eclipse,
it cannot yet be relied upon,
and still requires continuous verification.
The lunar eclipse of the fifteenth day of the eighth month of this current year is approaching.
We have respectfully calculated the time, magnitude, and direction using the newly proposed numbers,
comparing them to the original calculations which show differences in minutes and seconds,
and have separately prepared a clear list to be presented.
At the appointed time, we, your servants, will measure hourly
and then report the actual findings in a memorial."
This was reported and acknowledged.
In the sixth month of the twenty-second year (1842),
Jìngzhēng and others again stated:
"Whenever there is a solar or lunar eclipse,
calculations using the newly proposed numbers
are all close to the actual measurements.
For the solar eclipse on the first day of the sixth month of this year,
the new calculation differed from the actual measurement by only a few seconds.
This indicates that the newly proposed numbers
leave no doubt for the sun's movement,
and are also closely aligned for the moon's movement.
Now, we propose to first measure the fixed stars
to align with their movements,
and then examine the sun's path (rìchán) and the moon's nodes (yuèlī)
to ensure they conform to celestial movements.
We request to take the jiǎwǔ (甲午) year, the fourteenth year of Dàoguāng (1834), as the epoch,
and according to the new numbers for the sun's movement and the obliquity of the ecliptic,
to revise the tables of fixed star and ecliptic/equatorial longitudes and latitudes.
Also, during the calculations,
to thoroughly examine the movements of the five planets and the moon,
so that the books on fixed stars, the five planets, solar and lunar eclipses, etc.,
can be completed in due course."
This was granted.
In the seventh month of that year,
Jìngzhēng was appointed Chief Editor for calendar revision,
and Zhōu Yúqìng (周餘慶), the Censor-General (Jiānzhèng), and Gāo Yù (高煜), the Assistant Censor-General (Zuǒ Jiānfù), were appointed Deputy Chief Editors.
In the seventh month of the twenty-fifth year (1845),
thirteen scrolls each of the Ecliptic Longitude and Latitude Tables and the Equatorial Longitude and Latitude Tables were presented,
one scroll of the Moon and Five Planets Distance Table,
four scrolls of the Milky Way Boundary Table,
and one scroll each of the Comprehensive Study of Fixed Stars, the Star Head Celestial Song, and the General Record of Fixed Stars,
as the continuation of the Yíxiàng Kǎochéng (儀象考成).
However, the sections on solar and lunar eclipses and the movements of the five planets were still missing and incomplete.
At that time, Sī Tíngdòng (司廷棟), the Dōngguānzhèng (冬官正), compiled a new method for parallax in transgressions (língfàn shìchā),
using spherical trigonometry for calculations,
to determine the ecliptic longitude and high arc triangle by limiting the distance to Earth's height and the star's distance from the ecliptic pole,
which was simpler than the old method.
After Qiánlóng,
among the calendar officials capable of improving old methods,
Sī Tíngdòng was the only one.
Among those who understood calendrical science without being calendar officials,
after Méi Wéndǐng (梅文鼎), Xuē Fèngzuò (薛鳳祚), and Wáng Xīchǎn (王錫闡),
Jiāng Yǒng (江永), Dài Zhèn (戴震), Qián Dàxīn (錢大昕), and Lǐ Shànlán (李善蘭) were particularly prominent.
Their elucidation of Chinese and Western calendrical principles
truly far surpassed that of Xú Guāngqǐ (徐光啟), Lǐ Zhīzǎo (李之藻), and others.
Treatise 21, Calendar 2: Celestial Calculation Methods (Tuībù Suànshù)
The methods used in the new celestial calculation system
are plane triangles,
spherical triangles,
and ellipses.
Now, I will summarize their main principles,
verify the origins of their establishment,
and test the practicality of the numbers used,
totaling sixteen methods,
presented in this chapter.
A plane triangle is formed
by the intersection of three straight lines.
The lines are sides,
and the empty space enclosed by two lines is an angle.
There are right angles,
which are one-quarter of a full circle,
like angle jiǎ (甲) in the shape Jiǎyǐbǐng (甲乙丙).
There are acute angles,
less than one-quarter,
like angles yǐ (乙) and bǐng (丙).
There are obtuse angles,
more than one-quarter,
like angle wù (戊) in the shape Dīngwùjǐ (丁戊己).
(Diagram data not available yet)
Regardless of the magnitude of an angle,
it always has its corresponding eight lines (bāxiàn).
These are sine (zhèngxián), versine (zhèngshǐ), secant (zhènggē), tangent (zhèngqiē),
and the four lines of the complementary angle (the degree subtracted from ninety degrees).
For example, if jiǎyǐ (甲乙) is the original degree,
then bǐngyǐ (丙乙) is the complementary degree.
Sine is yǐwù (乙戊),
versine is jiǎwù (甲戊),
secant is gēngdīng (庚丁),
tangent is gēngjiǎ (庚甲),
cosine is yǐjǐ (乙己),
coversine is bǐngjǐ (丙己),
cosecant is xīndīng (辛丁),
cotangent is xīnbǐng (辛丙).
If rénguǐ (壬癸) is the original degree,
then chǒuguǐ (丑癸) is the complementary degree.
Sine is guǐchén (癸辰),
versine is rénchén (壬辰),
cosine is guǐmǎo (癸卯),
coversine is chǒumǎo (丑卯),
cosecant is zǐyín (子寅),
cotangent is chǒuyín (丑寅).
Since rénguǐ (壬癸) exceeds ninety degrees, there is no proper secant or tangent.
We borrow zǐwèi (子未) of guǐwǔ (癸午) as the secant,
and wǔwèi (午未) as the tangent.
If the exact ninety degrees, chǒurén (丑壬), is the original degree,
then there is no complementary degree.
The radius chǒuzǐ (丑子) is the sine,
the radius rénzǐ (壬子) is the versine.
There is also no secant or tangent,
nor any cosine, coversine, cosecant, or cotangent.
Anciently, the full circumference of a circle was set at three hundred and sixty degrees,
one-quarter was called a quadrant,
being ninety degrees.
Each degree has sixty minutes,
each minute has sixty seconds,
(Diagram data not available yet) and each second has sixty micros.
The radius of the circle was one hundred thousand,
later changed to ten million.
The eight lines for each degree and each minute are calculated
and listed in tables.
When calculating triangles,
within ninety degrees,
if one wishes to use a certain degree and a certain line,
one takes it from the table,
and calculates the line.
If one wishes to know a certain degree,
one matches it in the table.
For angles exceeding ninety degrees,
if one wishes to use sine, secant, tangent, and the four complementary ones,
one subtracts the degree from half a circumference,
and takes the remainder from the table.
If one wishes to use versine,
one takes the cosine and adds the radius to it.
Once a certain line is obtained,
if one wishes to know a certain degree,
one matches it in the table and names the remainder after subtracting it from half a circumference.
There are five methods for calculating plane triangles:
1. Given two sides and the angle opposite one of them, to find the angle opposite the other side:
Let the known side be the first ratio,
the sine of its opposite angle be the second ratio,
and the other known side be the third ratio.
Multiply the second and third ratios,
and divide by the first ratio.
The result is the fourth ratio,
which is the sine of the unknown opposite angle.
For example, in the diagram, side Jiǎyǐ (甲乙) is known,
angle Dīng (丁) opposite to it is known,
side Yǐdīng (乙丁) is another known side,
and angle Jiǎ (甲) is the unknown opposite angle.
The principle behind this is that two successive proportions are condensed into one.
In the diagram, Yǐdīng (乙丁) is to the radius,
as Yǐbǐng (乙丙) is to the sine of angle Dīng (丁).
The method should first be to take the radius as the first ratio,
the sine of angle Dīng (丁) as the second ratio,
and Yǐdīng (乙丁) as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio, which is the perpendicular line Yǐbǐng (乙丙).
Having obtained Yǐbǐng (乙丙),
Jiǎyǐ (甲乙) is to the radius
as Yǐbǐng (乙丙) is to the sine of angle Jiǎ (甲).
Then, take Jiǎyǐ (甲乙) as the first ratio,
Yǐbǐng (乙丙) as the second ratio,
and the radius as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is naturally the sine of angle Jiǎ (甲).
Then, combining and calculating,
multiply the first ratio (radius) of the first step by the first ratio (Jiǎyǐ (甲乙)) of the second step to form a common first ratio.
Multiply the second ratio (sine of angle Dīng (丁)) of the first step by the second ratio (Yǐbǐng (乙丙)) of the second step to form a common second ratio.
Multiply the third ratio (Yǐdīng (乙丁)) of the first step by the third ratio (radius) of the second step to form a common third ratio.
The result is the fourth ratio,
which is the product of the fourth ratio (Yǐbǐng (乙丙)) of the first step and the fourth ratio (sine of angle Jiǎ (甲)) of the second step.
It should still be divided by Yǐbǐng (乙丙)
to obtain the sine of angle Jiǎ (甲).
Since it must be divided later,
it is better not to multiply it in the first place.
The Yǐbǐng (乙丙) within the common second ratio is multiplied by the third ratio.
Multiplication and division cancel each other out,
so Yǐbǐng (乙丙) can be omitted.
Also, the radius within the common third ratio is multiplied by the second ratio.
The radius within the common first ratio is also the divisor.
Multiplication and division cancel each other out,
so the radius can also be omitted.
Therefore, we simply take Jiǎyǐ (甲乙) as the first ratio,
the sine of angle Dīng (丁) as the second ratio,
and Yǐdīng (乙丁) as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the sine of angle Jiǎ (甲).
2. Given two angles and the side opposite one of them, to find the side opposite the other angle:
Let the sine of the known angle be the first ratio,
its opposite side be the second ratio,
and the sine of the other known angle be the third ratio.
The result is the fourth ratio,
which is the unknown opposite side.
The principle for this is fully contained in the method for finding an angle given an opposite side;
a reverse consideration makes it self-evident.
3. Given two sides and the included angle, to find the two unknown angles:
Let the sum of the two sides adjacent to the known angle be the first ratio,
and their difference be the second ratio.
Subtract the known angle from half a circumference.
The remainder is the exterior angle.
Halve it,
and take its tangent as the third ratio.
The result is the fourth ratio,
which is the tangent of half the difference angle.
Consult the table to get the degree.
Add it to half the exterior angle;
this is the angle opposite the slightly larger side adjacent to the known angle.
Subtract it;
the remainder is the angle opposite the slightly smaller side adjacent to the known angle.
The principle here lies in the plane triangle.
When three angles are joined,
they must collectively form half a circumference.
As shown in the triangle Jiǎyǐbǐng (甲乙丙),
the perpendicular bisector Jiǎdīng (甲丁)
divides it into two right-angled triangles.
A right angle is half of a rectangle.
All four angles of a rectangle are exactly ninety degrees.
In a right-angled triangle, the two acute angles diagonally cut a rectangle.
One of these angles is a certain amount more than half of ninety degrees,
and the other is a certain amount less than half of ninety degrees.
This is naturally the case when a line passes straight through.
Therefore, the angle on the right side of Jiǎ (甲) must combine with angle Yǐ (乙) to be ninety degrees,
and the angle on the left side of Jiǎ (甲) must combine with angle Bǐng (丙) to be ninety degrees.
Considering the right-angled triangles, when angle Dīng (丁) is added to each,
they both become half a circumference,
forming an acute-angled triangle.
Removing angle Dīng (丁),
the sum of the three angles still constitutes half a circumference.
Therefore, besides the one known angle,
even if the individual degrees of the remaining two angles are unknown,
it is known that their sum
is the remainder of half a circumference minus this angle.
Another principle lies in similar triangles.
As shown in triangle Bǐnggēngwù (丙庚戊),
sides Bǐnggēng (丙庚) and Bǐngwù (丙戊) and angle Bǐng (丙) are known.
Extend Bǐnggēng (丙庚) to Bǐngjiǎ (丙甲).
Connect Bǐngwù (丙戊) to Jiǎwù (甲戊),
which represents the sum of the two sides.
Cut Bǐngwù (丙戊) at Bǐngdīng (丙丁),
forming Wùdīng (戊丁),
which represents the remainder after subtracting the two sides.
Draw the dashed line Gēngdīng (庚丁).
Bǐnggēng (丙庚) and Bǐngdīng (丙丁) are of equal length.
The two angles inside the circle at Gēngdīng (庚丁) must be of the same degree.
These are both half the exterior angle of angle Bǐng (丙),
equal in degree to Jiǎxīn (甲辛) and Xīngēng (辛庚).
The angle at Gēng (庚) outside the circle
is half the difference by which the angle Gēng (庚) of the original shape is greater than angle Wù (戊);
this is half the exterior angle.
Taking Gēngdīng (庚丁) as the ratio to the radius,
then Jiǎgēng (甲庚) is the ratio to the tangent of half the exterior angle Dīng (丁).
Radius and tangent always form a right angle.
It is also because two chords drawn inside the circle, Jiǎgēng (甲庚) and Gēngdīng (庚丁), will always form a right angle.
Again, draw line Dīngjǐ (丁己)
parallel to Jiǎgēng (甲庚).
Gēngdīng (庚丁) is still the ratio to the radius,
and Dīngjǐ (丁己) is the ratio to the tangent of half the difference angle at Gēng (庚) outside the circle.
The larger triangle Wùjiǎgēng (戊甲庚) and the smaller triangle Wùdīngjǐ (戊丁己),
since Wùjiǎ (戊甲) and Wùdīng (戊丁) are on the same line,
and Jiǎgēng (甲庚) and Dīngjǐ (丁己) are parallel,
are naturally similar.
Therefore, the sum of sides Jiǎwù (甲戊) is the first ratio,
the difference of sides Wùdīng (戊丁) is the second ratio,
and the tangent of half the exterior angle Jiǎgēng (甲庚) is the third ratio.
The result is the fourth ratio,
which is naturally the tangent of half the difference angle Dīngjǐ (丁己).
4. Given two angles and the included side, to find the unknown angle:
Sum the two known angles,
and subtract from half a circumference.
The remainder is the result.
The principle for this is fully contained in the method for finding two unknown angles given two sides and the included angle.
5. Given three sides, to find the angles:
Let the largest side be the base.
Sum and subtract the middle and smallest sides.
Multiply the two results.
Divide by the largest side.
Take this result and add it to the largest side, then halve it; this is the larger segment of the base.
Subtract this result from the largest side, then halve it; this is the smaller segment of the base.
Then, take the middle side as the first ratio,
the larger segment of the base as the second ratio,
and the radius as the third ratio.
The result is the fourth ratio,
which is the cosine of the angle opposite the smallest side.
Alternatively, take the smallest side as the first ratio,
the smaller segment of the base as the second ratio,
and the radius as the third ratio.
The result is the fourth ratio,
which is the cosine of the angle opposite the middle side.
The principle here lies in finding Pythagorean triples and comparing two squares.
As shown in the diagram, Jiǎbǐng (甲丙), the middle side, and Jiǎyǐ (甲乙), the smallest side, are both hypotenuses.
Yǐbǐng (乙丙), the largest side, is divided by Dīng (丁).
Dīngbǐng (丁丙) and Dīngyǐ (丁乙) are both bases (gōu).
The perpendicular line Jiǎdīng (甲丁) is the height (gǔ).
The sum of the squares of the base and height is always the square of the hypotenuse.
Since the height Jiǎdīng (甲丁) is common to both shapes,
the square of the larger hypotenuse Jiǎbǐng (甲丙) is greater than the square of the smaller hypotenuse Jiǎyǐ (甲乙)
by the same amount that the square of the larger base Dīngbǐng (丁丙) is greater than the square of the smaller base Yǐdīng (乙丁).
Also, the comparison of two squares
is always equal to the product of the sum and difference of their square roots.
As shown in the diagram, Wùyínréngēng (戊寅壬庚) is the larger square,
minus the smaller square Jǐmǎoxīngēng (己卯辛庚).
The remainder is the irregular rectangle Wùjǐmǎoxīnrénwù (戊己卯辛壬寅曲矩形).
Move Mǎoguǐrénxīn (卯癸壬辛) to Guǐyínchǒuzǐ (癸寅丑子),
forming a straight rectangle.
Its length, Wùchǒu (戊丑),
is naturally the sum of the square root of the larger square Wùyín (戊寅) and the square root of the smaller square Mǎoxīn (卯辛).
Its width, Wùjǐ (戊己),
is naturally the difference between the square root of the larger square Wùgēng (戊庚) and the square root of the smaller square Jǐgēng (己庚).
Therefore, in triangle Jiǎyǐbǐng (甲乙丙),
the sum of Jiǎbǐng (甲丙) and Jiǎyǐ (甲乙) is their sum,
and their subtraction is their difference.
The product of these two numbers
is like the product of the sum and difference of Bǐngdīng (丙丁) and Dīngyǐ (丁乙).
Dividing by Bǐngyǐ (丙乙)
naturally yields their difference.
Adding and subtracting Bǐngwǔ (丙午) and halving each
naturally gives Bǐngdīng (丙丁) and Yǐdīng (乙丁).
Having obtained Bǐngdīng (丙丁) and Yǐdīng (乙丁),
take Bǐngjiǎ (丙甲) and Yǐjiǎ (乙甲) respectively as the ratios to the radius.
Bǐngdīng (丙丁) and Yǐdīng (乙丁) will naturally be the ratios to the cosines.
These five methods,
four do not require calculation,
and one cannot be calculated.
To find the opposite angle given the opposite side,
if the two known sides are equal,
then the required angle must be equal to the known angle.
To find the opposite side given the opposite angle,
if the two known angles are equal,
then the required side must be equal to the known side.
Given two sides and the included angle,
if the two known sides are equal,
then the two required angles must be exactly half of the known exterior angle.
To find an angle given three sides,
if two sides are equal,
then half of the unequal side serves as the base;
if three sides are equal,
then the triangle is equilateral, with all three angles being sixty degrees,
all not requiring calculation.
However, to find the opposite angle given the opposite side,
if the number of units for one known side is small,
the opposite known angle is acute;
but if the number of units for one known side is large,
and one seeks the opposite angle,
it is impossible to know whether it is acute or obtuse,
thus it cannot be calculated.
For all problems where sides or angles are incomplete,
one can obtain them by cross-referencing.
A spherical triangle
is formed by the intersection of three great circles,
and its sides are also measured in degrees.
Ninety degrees is considered "complete" (a quadrant),
less than ninety degrees is "small,"
and more than ninety degrees is "large."
Its angles, acute, obtuse, or right, are similar to those of a planar triangle.
There are seven calculation methods:
First, to find the opposite angle given the opposite side.
Take the sine of the known side as the first ratio,
the sine of the opposite angle as the second ratio,
and the sine of another known side as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the sine of the required opposite angle.
The principle here is also a simplification of two proportionalities into one.
As shown in diagram Jiǎ-Yǐ-Bǐng,
knowing sides Jiǎ-Yǐ and Bǐng-Yǐ and angle Bǐng,
find angle Jiǎ.
Draw a perpendicular arc Yǐ-Xīn.
The ratio of the radius to the sine of angle Bǐng
is the same as the ratio of the sine of Yǐ-Bǐng to the sine of Yǐ-Xīn.
The method is to take the radius as the first ratio,
the sine of angle Bǐng as the second ratio,
the sine of Yǐ-Bǐng as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the sine of Yǐ-Xīn.
Once the sine of Yǐ-Xīn is obtained,
the ratio of the sine of Jiǎ-Yǐ to the sine of Yǐ-Xīn
is the same as the ratio of the radius to the sine of angle Jiǎ.
Thus, take the sine of Jiǎ-Yǐ as the first ratio,
the sine of Yǐ-Xīn as the second ratio,
the radius as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the sine of angle Jiǎ.
However, as multiplication and division cancel out,
it can be simplified.
Second, to find the opposite side given the opposite angle.
Take the sine of the known angle as the first ratio,
the sine of the opposite side as the second ratio,
and the sine of another known angle as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the sine of the required opposite side.
The principle here is self-evident upon re-examination.
Third, given two sides and the included angle,
whether acute or obtuse,
to find the unknown side.
Take the radius as the first ratio,
the cosine of the known angle as the second ratio,
arbitrarily take the tangent of one known side as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
designated as tangent.
Consult the table to get the degree,
subtract it from the other known side,
the remainder is the divided side.
Then, take the cosine of the previously obtained degree as the first ratio,
the cosine of the initially used side as the second ratio,
the cosine of the divided side as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the cosine of the unknown side.
If the original angle is obtuse,
and the divided side is large,
this side is small;
if the divided side is small,
this side is large.
If the original angle is acute,
and the divided side is small,
this side is small;
if the divided side is large,
this side is large.
The principle here is a simplification of three proportionalities into two.
As shown in diagram Jiǎ-Bǐng-Dīng,
knowing sides Jiǎ-Bǐng and Jiǎ-Dīng and angle Jiǎ,
draw a perpendicular arc Bǐng-Yǐ in the middle.
The ratio of the radius to the cosine of angle Jiǎ
is the same as the ratio of the tangent of Jiǎ-Bǐng to the tangent of Jiǎ-Yǐ.
The first calculation is easier to understand.
After dividing Jiǎ-Dīng at Yǐ,
and obtaining the divided side Dīng-Yǐ,
the ratio of the cosine of Jiǎ-Yǐ to the radius
is the same as the ratio of the cosine of Jiǎ-Bǐng to the cosine of Bǐng-Yǐ.
The method is to first take the cosine of Jiǎ-Yǐ as the first ratio,
the radius as the second ratio,
the cosine of Jiǎ-Bǐng as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the cosine of Bǐng-Yǐ.
Once the cosine of Bǐng-Yǐ is obtained,
the ratio of the radius to the cosine of Yǐ-Dīng
is the same as the ratio of the cosine of Bǐng-Yǐ to the cosine of Dīng-Bǐng.
Thus, take the radius as the first ratio,
the cosine of Yǐ-Dīng as the second ratio,
the cosine of Bǐng-Yǐ as the third ratio,
to find the fourth ratio,
which is the cosine of Dīng-Bǐng.
However, since multiplication and division cancel out,
