If the angle included by two sides is right,
then by multiplying the cosines of the two known sides and dividing by the radius,
the cosine of the unknown side is obtained directly,
the principle being self-evident.
If both known sides are either large or small,
this side is small;
if one known side is small and the other is large,
this side is large.
Fourth, given two angles and the included side,
to find the unknown angle.
Treat the angles as sides,
and the side as an angle,
and solve in reverse;
obtain the degree,
then take its reverse;
both the solving and the taking are subtracted from a semicircle.
Fifth, given two sides and the two angles opposite them,
either acute or obtuse,
to find the unknown side and angles.
Take the radius as the first ratio.
Arbitrarily take the cosine of one known angle as the second ratio.
Take the tangent of the side opposite the other known angle as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio,
name it a tangent,
and look it up in the table for degrees.
Again, apply the method using the other known angle and a side to find it,
and again obtain a degree.
Observe if the original two known angles are both acute or both obtuse;
if they are the same, then add the two obtained degrees;
if they are different,
then subtract the two obtained degrees.
In both cases, this addition or subtraction yields the unknown side.
Then, according to the first method, find the angle opposite the side,
and the unknown angle is obtained.
If the original other angle is obtuse,
and the side opposite the first angle used is greater than the later obtained degree,
this angle is obtuse.
If the side opposite the first angle used is smaller than the later obtained degree,
this angle is acute.
If the original other angle is acute,
and the side opposite the first angle used is smaller than the later obtained degree,
this angle is obtuse.
If the side opposite the first angle used is greater than the later obtained degree,
this angle is acute.
The principle here lies in the difference between whether the perpendicular arc is inside or outside the figure,
and how the angles are divided into acute or obtuse,
and the sides vary in size,
and their corresponding relationships of front, back, left, right, up, down, toward, and away.
As in the figures Jiǎ-Yǐ-Bǐng [甲乙丙],
where angles Jiǎ [甲] and Yǐ [乙] are both acute,
two acute angles face each other,
therefore the perpendicular arc Bǐng-Dīng [丙丁]
is taken from the middle for correction
and is inside the figure.
In the figure Jǐ-Bǐng-Gēng [己丙庚],
angles Jǐ [己] and Gēng [庚] are both obtuse,
two obtuse angles face each other,
therefore the perpendicular arc Wù-Bǐng [戊丙] is also inside the figure.
In the figure Gēng-Bǐng-Yǐ [庚丙乙],
angles Gēng [庚] and Yǐ [乙],
one acute and one obtuse, are opposite,
the perpendicular arc Bǐng-Dīng [丙丁]
is corrected from the outside
and is naturally outside the figure.
When it is inside the figure, it divides the base into two,
the two obtained segment lengths,
such as Yǐ-Dīng [乙丁] and Dīng-Jiǎ [丁甲],
combine to form one base like Yǐ-Jiǎ [乙甲],
thus it is appropriate to add them.
When it is outside the figure,
it extends the remainder of the base,
the two obtained segment lengths,
such as Gēng-Dīng [庚丁] and Yǐ-Dīng [乙丁],
overlap without covering,
the base is like Gēng-Yǐ [庚乙],
thus it is appropriate to subtract them.
The correspondence of acute and obtuse, and large and small,
should also be carefully examined as in the diagram on the right.
If the two known sides opposite the two known angles include a right angle,
then one obtained degree is the unknown side,
the principle is also self-evident.
Sixth, given three sides to find an angle,
take the product of the sines of the two sides adjacent to the desired angle as the first ratio.
Take the radius squared as the second ratio.
The difference between the two sides is the remainder for the comparative arc.
Take its versine and subtract the versine of the opposite side from it as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio,
which is the versine of the desired angle.
The principle here is that a two-step proportion is simplified into a one-step proportion.
As in the figure Jiǎ-Rén-Yǐ [甲壬乙],
to find angle Jiǎ [甲],
its versine is Chǒu-Dīng [丑丁].
The method should take the sine of side Jiǎ-Yǐ [甲乙], Yǐ-Bǐng [乙丙], as the first ratio.
Take the radius Yǐ-Jǐ [乙己] as the second ratio.
The difference between the two sides' comparative arc versine Yǐ-Kuí [乙癸] and the opposite side's versine Yǐ-Mǎo [乙卯], which is Kuí-Mǎo [癸卯] (same as Xīn-Zǐ [辛子]), as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio as Rén-Xīn [壬辛].
Then take the sine of side Jiǎ-Rén [甲壬], Wù-Xīn [戊辛], as the first ratio.
Take Rén-Xīn [壬辛] as the second ratio.
Take the radius Jǐ-Dīng [己丁] as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio as Chǒu-Dīng [丑丁].
The versine of angle Jiǎ [甲] is also obtained through multiplication and division,
hence the simplification.
Seventh, given three angles, either acute or obtuse, to find a side,
treat the angles as sides,
and inversely find their angles.
Once the angles are found,
take them as sides again.
Both finding and taking always involve subtracting from a semicircle.
The principle here is in the secondary figure,
as in the figure Jiǎ-Yǐ-Bǐng [甲乙丙],
the degree of angle Jiǎ [甲] is Dīng-Wù [丁戊],
and subtracting it from a semicircle gives Wù-Jǐ [戊己].
Its degree must be the same as side Zǐ-Xīn [子辛] of the secondary figure Zǐ-Xīn-Wǔ [子辛午].
This is because Chǒu-Mǎo [丑卯] is the intersection point Chǒu [丑] of angle Yǐ [乙],
and arc Jiǎ-Yǐ [甲乙] must be a right angle.
Dīng-Wù [丁戊] is the intersection point Wù [戊] of angle Jiǎ [甲],
and arc Jiǎ-Yǐ [甲乙] must also be a right angle.
Since a single Jiǎ-Yǐ [甲乙] intersects both arcs Chǒu-Xīn [丑辛] and Wù-Xīn [戊辛] to form right angles,
then both arcs must be ninety degrees.
The nature of spherical triangles is thus.
Since Wù-Xīn [戊辛] is ninety degrees,
Zǐ-Jǐ [子己] is also ninety degrees.
Removing the overlapping Wù-Zǐ [戊子],
Jǐ-Wù [己戊] is naturally the same as Zǐ-Xīn [子辛].
Therefore, Gēng-Kuí [庚癸] must be the same as Zǐ-Wǔ [子午],
and Mǎo-Wèi [卯未] may not be the same as Wǔ-Xīn [午辛];
all principles are as such.
And since the complementary angles of this figure are all sides of that figure,
the complementary angles of that figure must be sides of this figure,
hence by inversely taking them, they are obtained.
If three angles include a right angle,
excluding the right angle,
take the sine of one angle as the first ratio,
the cosine of another angle as the second ratio,
and the radius as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio,
which is the cosine of the side opposite the other angle.
The principle here also relates to the secondary figure,
but treats the right angle and one angle as angles of the secondary figure,
and adds or subtracts quadrants to the other angle as the side opposite the angle in the secondary figure.
The representation differs slightly.
Among these seven methods,
only in finding sides and angles from each other
are there cases where acute or obtuse, and large or small, cannot be determined.
However, there are no such problems in astronomical calculations,
so they are not fully listed.
Among these seven problems, there are some aspects of finding sides and angles that are not exhausted,
which can be obtained by mutual application.
An ellipse is a circular surface with longer diameters at both ends and shorter diameters at its waist.
However, it must be drawn with a compass
before calculations can be performed.
The method of drawing it is
to arbitrarily take two points as centers,
one point as a boundary,
and fix a needle at each.
Encircle them with a silk thread,
and use a pencil at the end to mark the boundary.
When the needle is guided and rotated,
an ellipse is formed.
As in the figure with points Jiǎ [甲], Jǐ [己], Wǔ [午],
drawing it according to the method
forms the ellipse Chǒu-Wǔ-Sì-Wèi [丑午巳未].
Yín-Chǒu [寅丑] and Yín-Sì [寅巳] are the major semi-axes.
Yín-Wǔ [寅午] and Yín-Wèi [寅未] are the minor semi-axes.
Yín-Jiǎ [寅甲] is the focal distance.
Jǐ-Jiǎ [己甲] is twice the focal distance.
The length Jiǎ-Wǔ [甲午] is the same as Yín-Sì [寅巳],
and also the same as Yín-Chǒu [寅丑],
and Jǐ-Wǔ [己午] is similar;
the sum of these two lengths
is always equal to Chǒu-Sì [丑巳].
If the Wǔ [午] needle is guided to Shēn [申],
although the lengths Jiǎ-Shēn [甲申] and Shēn-Jǐ [申己] differ,
their sum remains constant.
Jiǎ-Wǔ [甲午] is equivalent to the major semi-axis, like a hypotenuse (弦).
The focal distance is like a base (勾).
The minor semi-axis is like a height (股).
Knowing any two of these,
the unknown third can be found using the Gōu-Gǔ [勾股] method.
If calculating the area,
take the squared ratio of a flat surface, 400000000, as the first ratio.
Take the ratio of a circular surface, 314159265, as the second ratio.
Multiply the major and minor diameters to get a rectangle as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio,
which is the area of the ellipse.
If calculating the mean semi-axis,
multiply the major and minor semi-axes
and take the square root to get it.
However, a line starting from center Jiǎ [甲],
rotating clockwise from Chǒu [丑],
as shown in the figure to Xū [戌],
the area enclosed between Jiǎ-Chǒu [甲丑] and Jiǎ-Xū [甲戌],
also has a corresponding angle.
To find the angle and area from each other,
there are four methods:
First, to find the area from the angle:
Take the radius as the first term of the ratio;
the sine of the known angle as the second term;
twice the difference between the two foci as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the ordinate of twice the difference between the two foci,
the perpendicular line being like Jǐyǒu.
Again, take the radius as the first term;
the cosine of the known angle as the second term;
twice the difference between the two foci as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the boundary degree area line.
The extended line is like Jiǎyǒu.
The ordinate of twice the difference between the two foci is the square of the perpendicular.
Add the extended line
to the sum of Jiǎxū and Jǐxū, which is equal to the major diameter of Sìchǒu, to get the sum of the base and hypotenuse.
Divide this to get the difference.
The sum and difference added together and halved give the chord Jǐxū.
Subtract this from the major diameter to get the line Jiǎxū.
Again, take the radius as the first term;
the sine of the known angle as the second term;
the line Jiǎxū as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the side Xūhài.
Again, take the minor diameter as the first term;
the major diameter as the second term;
the side Xūhài as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the side Chénhài.
Again, take the major semi-diameter Yínchén (which is equal to Yínchǒu) as the first term;
the radius as the second term;
the side Chénhài as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the sine.
Compare with the table to get the degrees.
Again, take half a full circle (180 degrees converted to seconds) as the first term;
half the circumference of a circle (3.1415926) as the second term;
the obtained degrees converted to seconds as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the proportional arc line.
Again, take the radius as the first term;
the major semi-diameter as the second term;
the proportional arc line as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the arc line Chénchǒu.
Multiply this by the major semi-diameter and halve it
to get the area of the circular segment Yínchénchǒu.
Again, take the major semi-diameter as the first term;
the minor semi-diameter as the second term;
the area of the circular segment as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the area of the elliptical segment Yínxūchǒu.
Then, multiply the difference between the two foci (Yínjiǎ) by the side Xūhài and halve it.
Subtract this from Yínxūchǒu
to get the area cut between Jiǎxū and Jiǎchǒu.
The principle for this is fully contained in the main diagram, plane trigonometry, and spherical trigonometry;
the method is extremely precise.
Second, to find the angle from the area:
Take the square of the line Jiǎchǒu (which is obtained by subtracting the major semi-diameter from the difference between the two foci) as the first term;
the square of the intermediate radius as the second term;
the area between Jiǎxū and Jiǎchǒu as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the intermediate area,
like Jiǎdīkàng.
Consider the area of the elliptical segment as 360 degrees.
Take the area of one degree as the divisor.
Divide by this to get the angle enclosed between Jiǎxū and Jiǎchǒu.
The principle for this is the ratio of similar figures.
However, Jiǎkàng and Jiǎdī are of the same length,
while Jiǎxū is longer than Jiǎchǒu.
Since the difference is not much,
they are treated as the same number.
If Xū is extended to the focus,
the actual difference between Jiǎchǒu and Jiǎxīn is large.
It is still necessary to use the previous method to find the line Jiǎxū.
Assume Jiǎxū and Jiǎxīn are approximately the same for calculation.
Third, to find the area by approximation from another area:
Take the known area,
such as Xīnjiǎchǒu in the diagram.
Divide it by the area of one degree
to get the degrees of the area.
Let these degrees be the angle,
at the ordinate of twice the difference between the two foci, like Gēngjǐchǒu.
Take the radius as the first term;
the sine of angle Jǐ as the second term;
twice the difference between the two foci as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the perpendicular line Jiǎzǐ.
Again, take the radius as the first term;
the cosine of angle Jǐ as the second term;
twice the difference between the two foci as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the segment Jǐzǐ.
Jiǎzǐ is the square of the perpendicular.
The remainder when Jǐzǐ is subtracted from the major diameter is the sum of the base and hypotenuse.
Divide this to get the difference between the base and hypotenuse.
The sum and difference added together and halved give the line Jiǎgēng.
Again, take the line Jiǎgēng as the first term;
the perpendicular line Jiǎzǐ as the second term;
the radius as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the sine of angle Gēng.
Add the obtained degrees to angle Jǐ to get angle Gēngjiǎchǒu.
Then, use the method of finding area from angle
to find the area Gēngjiǎchǒu.
Subtract the area Xīnjiǎchǒu from it, the remainder being like Gēngjiǎxīn.
Then, use the method of finding angle from area
to find the degrees.
Add these to angle Gēngjiǎchǒu
to get angle Xīnjiǎchǒu.
Fourth, to find the angle by approximation from another angle:
Take the known area, as in the previous method, as the area degrees,
such as Chǒujiǎdīng.
Let these degrees be the angle,
at the center of the ellipse, like Dīngyǐxīn.
Take the minor semi-diameter as the first term;
the major semi-diameter as the second term;
the tangent of the assumed angle as the third term.
The fourth term thus found is the tangent of angle Dīngyǐguǐ.
Compare with the table to get the degrees.
Then, draw the line Bǐngchǒu at the ordinate of twice the difference between the two foci, at Bǐng.
Let angle Chǒubǐngjiǎ be equal to angle Guǐyǐdīng.
Then extend the line Bǐngchǒu to Yín,
making Chǒuyín equal to Jiǎchǒu.
Then Bǐngyín is equal to the major diameter.
Also draw the line Jiǎyín,
forming triangle Jiǎyínbǐng.
Use the tangent method for external angles to find angle Yín.
Double it to get angle Chǒu of figure Jiǎbǐngchǒu.
Add it to angle Bǐng to get angle Chǒujiǎdīng.
The principle here is that angle Guǐyǐjiǎ is greater than the area degrees of Chǒujiǎdīng,
which is angle Zǐyǐguǐ.
These degrees are then used for the previous supplementary calculation of Xīnjiǎgēng,
as the difference is not significant.

Record 22, Shíxiàn 3, Kāngxī Jiǎzǐ Yuán Fǎ Shàng (The first volume describes the origin of the calendar method;
the middle volume records the regular orbits of the seven luminaries and fixed stars;
the lower volume records the distances of various planets.)
Origin of the Calendar Method for Solar Path:
To find the true north-south line by facing south.
Use a perfectly level platform
and draw several concentric circles.
Erect a gnomon at the center of the circles and observe the sun's shadow.
Mark where the tip of the gnomon's shadow touches the circle.
Observe the two points (left and right) on the same circle and connect them with a straight line;
this is true east-west.
From the exact center of the east-west line, draw a perpendicular line towards the center of the circles;
this is true north-south.
Compared with a compass in the capital city,
it deviates by more than four degrees to the east.
(In the 17th year of Qiánlóng, it was changed to two degrees and thirty minutes.)
To measure the altitude of the North Celestial Pole to determine the celestial sphere.
Around the winter solstice,
use instruments to measure the altitude of the star Gōuchén as it rises above the horizon.
In the Yǒu-time (5-7 PM), this star is above the North Pole.
Wait for it to gradually turn and rise,
until it stops rising.
In the Mǎo-time (5-7 AM), this star is below the North Pole.
Wait for it to gradually turn and descend,
until it stops descending.
Take the average of the highest and lowest altitudes
to be the altitude of the North Pole.
Fixed stars have no terrestrial radius difference.
Gōuchén is also very high above the ground,
and the atmospheric refraction difference is also minimal,
so the number is accurate.
Using this, the altitude of the North Pole measured at Chàngchūnyuán was 39 degrees, 59 minutes, and 30 seconds.
To find the terrestrial radius difference to verify the discrepancy between geocentric true altitude and surface apparent altitude.
At noon on Jiǎzǐ day in the fifth month of the 54th year of Kāngxī (1715),
the altitude of the sun measured at Chàngchūnyuán was 73 degrees, 16 minutes, and 23 micro-minutes.
At the same time, the altitude of the sun measured at Guǎngzhōu Fǔ, Guǎngdōng, was 90 degrees, 6 minutes, 21 seconds, and 48 micro-minutes.
The distance from the equator to the zenith at Chàngchūnyuán was 39 degrees, 59 minutes, and 30 seconds.
The distance from the equator to the zenith at Guǎngzhōufǔ was 23 degrees and 10 minutes,
deviating 3 degrees and 33 minutes to the west.
It was eight days after the summer solstice,
when the sun's path was highest.
Using plane trigonometry, the ratio of the terrestrial radius to the sun's distance from the earth's center was derived
as 1 to 1162.
Again, at noon on Bǐngshēn day in the third month of the 55th year of Kāngxī (1716),
the altitude of the sun measured at Chàngchūnyuán was 53 degrees, 3 minutes, 38 seconds, and 10 micro-minutes.
At the same time, the altitude of the sun measured at Guǎngzhōufǔ, Guǎngdōng, was 69 degrees, 54 minutes, 8 seconds, and 36 micro-minutes.
It was eight days after the spring equinox,
when the sun's path was at its mean distance.
The ratio of the terrestrial radius to the sun's distance from the earth's center was derived
as 1 to 1142.
Then, comparing the ratio of the sun's highest position to the radius of its celestial sphere (10179208) with the ratio of the terrestrial radius (1162),
and comparing this to the ratio of the sun's lowest position to the radius of its celestial sphere (9820792) with the terrestrial radius,
we get 1121.
Having obtained the distances of the three limits from the earth's center,
the terrestrial radius difference for each degree was derived using plane trigonometry.
To find the distance between the ecliptic and the equator to correct the ecliptic.
In the 53rd year of Kāngxī (1714),
the summer solstice noon solar altitude was repeatedly measured at Chàngchūnyuán,
yielding an apparent altitude of 73 degrees, 29 minutes, and a few seconds.
Adding the terrestrial radius difference of 50 seconds,
the true altitude obtained was 73 degrees and 30 minutes.
Subtracting the local equatorial altitude of 50 degrees and 30 seconds,
the remainder was 23 degrees, 29 minutes, and 30 seconds,
which is the greatest distance between the ecliptic and the equator.
Using spherical trigonometry, the declination for each degree was derived.
To calculate the atmospheric refraction to verify the amount by which atmospheric gases make small objects appear large and low objects appear high.
During the Wànlì 萬曆 reign of the Míng 明 dynasty,
the Westerner Tycho [Brahe], at a latitude of 55 degrees and some minutes north of the equator in his country,
measured the maximum refraction above the horizon as 34 minutes.
Above the horizon,
this refraction gradually decreases,
and at 45 degrees,
it is 5 seconds.
Higher than that, there is no refraction.
His method of calculation is as follows:
If the observed altitude of the sun is 10 degrees, 34 minutes, 42 seconds,
its distance from the meridian is 83 degrees.
At that time, the sun's position was 3 degrees, 36 minutes into the Jiànglóu 降婁 mansion,
and its distance north of the equator was 1 degree, 26 minutes.
The distance of the North Pole from the zenith was 50 degrees, 0 minutes, 30 seconds.
Using these three values—distance from the meridian, distance north of the equator, and distance of the North Pole from the zenith—
a spherical triangle is constructed.
The true altitude of the sun is calculated as 10 degrees, 27 minutes, 53 seconds.
Subtracting this from the observed altitude,
and adding the parallax of 2 minutes, 57 seconds,
gives 9 minutes, 46 seconds,
which is the atmospheric refraction for 10 degrees, 35 minutes above the horizon.
This method is still followed.
To measure the tropical year to determine the mean daily motion.
On the Guǐwèi 癸未 day of the second month in the 54th year of Kāngxī 康熙 (1715), at noon,
the sun's altitude was measured at Chàngchūnyuán 暢春園 as 50 degrees, 0 minutes, 32 seconds, 35 micro-seconds.
Adding the parallax of 1 minute, 56 seconds, 5 micro-seconds,
the true altitude is 50 degrees, 2 minutes, 28 seconds, 40 micro-seconds.
(The parallax added here
still uses the old numbers from the new computational treatises.
The actual parallax and the ratio of the sun's distance from the earth's center,
at its highest, lowest, and mean distances,
were not determined until the following year.
Retrospective calculations showed no difference,
hence no change was made.
As for calculating the parallax,
it is taken at the vernal equinox and eight days after the summer solstice,
also following old calculations.
The actual highest limit
is measured over several days
and is not pre-determined.
Since the mean distance at summer solstice was not yet determined,
the tropical year was also determined by the lowest point.
The ratio of the highest and lowest points
is found during eclipses.
The westward offset of Guǎngzhōu Fǔ 廣州府
was obtained by first measuring the timing of lunar eclipses.)
Subtracting this from the equatorial altitude of 50 degrees, 0 minutes, 30 seconds,
the remainder is 1 minute, 58 seconds, 40 micro-seconds,
which is the sun's latitude north of the equator.
Knowing that the vernal equinox occurred before noon,
using this latitude and the maximum obliquity of the ecliptic, a spherical triangle is constructed,
from which the ecliptic longitude is calculated as 4 minutes, 57 seconds, 43 micro-seconds,
which is the sun's longitude past the vernal equinox.
The next day, at noon,
the latitude was measured again,
and the sun's longitude past the vernal equinox was calculated as 1 degree, 4 minutes, 6 seconds, 3 micro-seconds.
Subtracting the two longitudes past the vernal equinox, the remainder is 59 minutes, 8 seconds, 20 micro-seconds for one day's motion.
By proportion, the vernal equinox on this day was at the 3rd *kè* 刻 and 14th minute of *sìchū* 巳初, 10 seconds, 48 micro-seconds.
Again, on the Wùzǐ 戊子 day of the second month in the 55th year of Kāngxī 康熙 (1716), at noon,
the sun's altitude was measured at Chàngchūnyuán 暢春園 as 49 degrees, 54 minutes, 49 seconds, 51 micro-seconds.
Calculating according to the method,
the vernal equinox on this day was at the 3rd *kè* 刻 and 2nd minute of *shēnchū* 申初, 55 seconds, 48 micro-seconds.
The total distance between the two vernal equinoxes is 365 days, 5 hours, 3 *kè* 刻, 3 minutes, 45 seconds,
which is the tropical year.
Using this value,
and dividing it into the circumference of the heavens,
the daily mean motion is obtained.
To calculate the equation of the center and the apogee to determine the anomaly.
After the two solstices in the 56th year of Kāngxī 康熙 (1717),
the sun's altitude at noon was measured daily at Chàngchūnyuán 暢春園.
Its longitude was calculated,
and the actual motion for that day and the next was compared.
It was calculated that on the Jiǎxū 甲戌 day of the fifth month, at the 1st *kè* 刻 and 40 seconds, 45 micro-seconds of *chénzhèng* 辰正, it entered the 7th degree of the Wèi 未 mansion.
On the Yǐhài 乙亥 day, at the 1st *kè* 刻 and 14 minutes, 57 seconds, 27 micro-seconds of *sìchū* 巳初, it entered the 8th degree of the Wèi 未 mansion.
On the Dīngchǒu 丁丑 day of the eleventh month, at the 1st *kè* 刻 and 12 minutes, 57 seconds, 41 micro-seconds of *zǐzhèng* 子正, it entered the 7th degree of the Chǒu 丑 mansion.
On the night of this day, at the 3rd *kè* 刻 and 12 minutes, 27 seconds, 47 micro-seconds of *zǐchū* 子初, it entered the 8th degree of the Chǒu 丑 mansion.
These two sets of numbers are used to establish the method.
As shown in the diagram, point Jiǎ 甲 is the center of the Earth,
which is also the center of the *zōngdòng tiān* 宗動天 (primum mobile).
Yǐ 乙, Bǐng 丙, Dīng 丁, Wù 戊 form the ecliptic,
concentric with the *zōngdòng tiān* 宗動天.
Yǐ 乙 is the summer solstice,
Bǐng 丙 is the autumnal equinox,
Dīng 丁 is the winter solstice,
and Wù 戊 is the vernal equinox.
Let point Jǐ 己 be the center,
and draw the circle Gēng 庚, Xīn 辛, Rén 壬, Guǐ 癸,
which is the eccentric sphere.
Gēng 庚 is the apogee, corresponding to the Zǐ 子 mansion on the ecliptic.
Rén 壬 is the perigee, corresponding to the Chǒu 丑 mansion on the ecliptic.
Yín 寅 and Mǎo 卯 are the mean distances.
Draw the line Gēngchǒu 庚丑 through the two centers Jǐ 己 and Jiǎ 甲,
which bisects this sphere and the ecliptic into two semicircles.
From summer solstice Yǐ 乙 to winter solstice Dīng 丁,
draw the line Yǐdīng 乙丁,
which cuts the left half of the eccentric sphere, making it greater than half a year.
From autumnal equinox Bǐng 丙 to vernal equinox Wù 戊,
draw the line Bǐngwù 丙戊,
which cuts the lower half of the eccentric sphere, making it smaller than half a year.
Now, the time from the 7th degree of the Wèi 未 mansion to the 7th degree of the Chǒu 丑 mansion
is 182 days, 16 hours, 12 minutes, 16 seconds, 56 micro-seconds,
which is greater than half a year by 1 hour, 17 minutes, 54 seconds, 26 micro-seconds.
The time from the 8th degree of the Wèi 未 mansion to the 8th degree of the Chǒu 丑 mansion
is 182 days, 14 hours, 27 minutes, 30 seconds, 20 micro-seconds,
which is smaller than half a year by 26 minutes, 52 seconds, 10 micro-seconds.
Thus, we know that the 7th degree of the Wèi 未 mansion is before the apogee, like Chén 辰,
and the 8th degree is after the apogee, like Sì 巳.
The 7th degree of the Chǒu 丑 mansion is before the perigee, like Wǔ 午,
and the 8th degree is after the perigee, like Wèi 未.
Adding these two (large and small) numbers,
and comparing their ratio to the ratio of one degree of Chén 辰-Sì 巳 or Wǔ 午-Wèi 未,
is the same as the ratio of the amount greater than half a year to the Chén 辰-Zǐ 子 or Wǔ 午-Chǒu 丑 arc.
This gives 44 minutes, 36 seconds, 48 micro-seconds.
Adding this to the 7 degrees of Yǐchén 乙辰 or Dīngwǔ 丁午,
gives the degrees by which the apogee and perigee pass the two solstices.
Since the apogee and perigee have an annual motion,
these are combined to form a calculation,
determining the degree by which the mean distance passes the autumnal equinox in this year.
Using the proportional method, it is calculated that the mean distance was passed on the Bǐngwǔ 丙午 day, after the autumnal equinox, at the 1st *kè* 刻 and 13 minutes, 49 seconds of *sìzhèng* 巳正.
If it were on the ecliptic,
it should have moved 90 degrees from the apogee Zǐ 子 to Yín 寅,
which would be 7 degrees, 44 minutes, 36 seconds, 48 micro-seconds of the Chén 辰 mansion.
From actual measurements,
it is less than 2 degrees, 3 minutes, 9 seconds, 40 micro-seconds in Shēn 申.
Checking its tangent,
we get 358416, which is the equation of the center between Jǐ 己 and Jiǎ 甲, assuming the radius of this sphere is ten million.
Also, in this year, at Chàngchūnyuán 暢春園, the vernal equinox was measured to be on the Guǐsì 癸巳 day of the second month, at the 2nd *kè* 刻 and 6 minutes, 47 seconds of *hàichū* 亥初.
Lìxià 立夏 (start of summer) was on the Jǐmǎo 己卯 day of the third month, at the 2nd *kè* 刻 and 1 minute, 36 seconds of *hàizhèng* 亥正.
The autumnal equinox was on the Gēngzǐ 庚子 day of the eighth month, at the 2nd *kè* 刻 and 4 minutes, 3 seconds of *shēnchū* 申初.
The number of days between each was counted,
and the mean daily motion was calculated.
As shown in the diagram, Jiǎ 甲 is the center of the Earth.
Yǐ 乙, Bǐng 丙, Dīng 丁, Wù 戊 are the ecliptic.
Wù 戊 is the vernal equinox,
Sì 巳 is the summer solstice,
Bǐng 丙 is the autumnal equinox,
Gēng 庚 is the winter solstice,
and Xīn 辛 is Lìxià 立夏.
Zǐ 子, Chǒu 丑, Yín 寅, Mǎo 卯 are the eccentric sphere.
Rén 壬 is the center of the sphere.
At the vernal equinox, the sun is at Zǐ 子.
At Lìxià 立夏, it is at Guǐ 癸.
At the autumnal equinox, it is at Yín 寅.
Chǒu 丑 is the apogee.
Mǎo 卯 is the perigee.
To find the equation of the center between Rén 壬 and Jiǎ 甲,
and to find the angle Xīn Jiǎ Yǐ 辛甲乙,
which is the distance of the apogee from Lìxià 立夏.
Using the right triangle Jiǎchénzǐpíng 甲辰子平 and the right triangle Rénjǐjiǎ 壬己甲,
Rénjiǎ 壬甲 is found to be 358977,
which is 561 ten-millionths more than the previous number.
The angle Jiǎ 甲 is also found to be 53 degrees, 38 minutes, 25 seconds, 55 micro-seconds,
which is the distance of the apogee from Lìxià 立夏.
Subtracting the distance from summer solstice to Lìxià 立夏 (45 degrees),
gives the apogee at 8 degrees, 38 minutes, 25 seconds, 55 micro-seconds after the summer solstice.
All these numbers do not match the previous ones.
Therefore, the method of using the deferent and epicycle for the equation of the center was adopted.
To determine the motion of the apogee and the radii of the deferent and epicycle to determine the anomaly.
In the 17th year of Kāngxī 康ī (1678),
the apogee was measured to be 7 degrees, 4 minutes, 4 seconds after the summer solstice.
In the 56th year (1717),
the apogee was measured to be 7 degrees, 43 minutes, 49 seconds after the summer solstice,
approximately moving eastward by 1 minute, 1 second, 10 micro-seconds per year.
The radius of the deferent is set to ten million.
Three-quarters of the equation of the center is the radius of the epicycle,
and one-quarter is the radius of the equant.
As shown in the diagram, Jiǎ 甲 is the center of the Earth,
which is also the center of the deferent.
Yǐ 乙, Bǐng 丙, Dīng 丁, Wù 戊 form the deferent.
The circles marked left, right, up, down are the epicycles.
The smallest circle is the equant.
Yín 寅 is the sun's apogee,
and Chén 辰 is the perigee.
The center of the epicycle moves clockwise along the circumference of the deferent starting from the winter solstice, representing the mean motion.
The center of the equant moves counter-clockwise along the circumference of the epicycle starting from the perigee, representing the argument of latitude.
The comparison of the motions of the two circles
is the motion of the perigee.
The sun moves clockwise along the circumference of the equant.
When the equant is at the apogee or perigee,
it is closest to the center of the deferent,
like Yín 寅 and Chén 辰.
When the equant is at the mean distance,
it is furthest from the center of the deferent,
like Mǎo 卯 and Jǐ 己.
Its motion, being twice that of the accumulated point of the equant,
does not match the numbers of the old eccentric sphere.
To establish the limits of twilight in minutes to determine dawn and dusk,
it is measured to be within 18 degrees below the horizon,
before sunrise and after sunset.
The origin of the method for lunar anomaly:
To determine the mean motion (parallelism).
According to the method of the Westerner Hipparchus,
one hundred and twenty-six thousand, zero hundred and seven days and four kè (quarters of an hour) is set as the interval between two eclipses when their rates align,
from conjunction to opposition and then to apogee and perigee,
all returning to their initial states.
Calculating the accumulated total within this period,
there are four thousand two hundred and sixty-seven conjunctions and oppositions,
and four thousand five hundred and seventy-three apogees and perigees.
Set the accumulated total of days and kè as the dividend (實, *shí*).
Divide it by the number of conjunctions and oppositions,
to get the conjunction and opposition quotient (策, *cè*).
Then, set the celestial circumference as the dividend.
Divide it by the conjunction and opposition quotient,
to get the daily mean motion of the Moon relative to the Sun.
Add the daily mean motion of the Sun,
to get the daily mean motion of the Moon along the White Path (lunar ecliptic) longitude.
Again, set the accumulated total of days and kè as the dividend.
Divide it by the number of apogees and perigees,
to get the apogee and perigee fraction (分, *fēn*).
Set the celestial circumference as the dividend.
Divide it by the apogee and perigee fraction,
to get the Moon's daily proper motion.
Subtract the daily White Path longitude from the daily proper motion,
to get the daily highest motion (apogee motion).
To derive the radius of the epicycle and the apogee to verify acceleration and deceleration.
The Westerner Tycho measured three lunar eclipses:
For the first eclipse, the Sun was at seven degrees, thirty-five minutes, forty-seven seconds, and fifty-three wēi of the Quánshǒu Palace (鶉首宮) on the day,
and the Moon was at the same degrees, minutes, and seconds from the Xīngjì Palace (星紀宮),
when the Moon's motion was at the beginning of its slowest limit.
For the second eclipse, the Sun was at the beginning degree of the Shòuxīng Palace (壽星宮),
and the Moon was at the same degree from the Jiànglóu Palace (降婁宮),
when the Moon's motion was at nearly half of its slowest initial limit.
For the third eclipse, the Sun was at two degrees, fifty-four minutes, zero two seconds, and forty-nine wēi of the Xīngjì Palace,
and the Moon was at the same degrees, minutes, and seconds from the Quánshǒu Palace,
when the Moon's motion was at the beginning of its fastest limit.
The interval from the first eclipse to the second eclipse was one thousand one hundred and eighty days, twenty-two hours, fourteen minutes, and zero four seconds,
with a true motion difference of eighty-two degrees, twenty-four minutes, twelve seconds, and zero seven wēi,
a mean motion difference of eighty degrees, twenty-one minutes, and ten seconds,
and a proper motion difference of three hundred and eight degrees, forty-seven minutes, zero seven seconds, and twenty-seven wēi.
The interval from the second eclipse to the third eclipse was one thousand nine hundred and eighteen days, twenty-three hours, zero five minutes, and fifty-seven seconds,
with a true motion difference of ninety-two degrees, fifty-four minutes, zero two seconds, and forty-nine wēi,
a mean motion difference of eighty-five degrees, zero twenty-five seconds,
and a proper motion difference of two hundred and thirty-one degrees, twelve minutes, fifty-two seconds, and thirty-three wēi.
Using planar trigonometry, the radius of the epicycle was found to be eight thousand seven hundred parts out of one hundred thousand parts of the deferent (本天) radius.
Also, the apogee motion was derived,
calculated to be thirty-seven degrees, thirty-four minutes, and thirty-four seconds past the apogee on the first new moon of the first year of Chóngzhēn (崇禎).
However, when generally derived from these three lunar eclipses,
the number for the epicycle radius did not match,
thus an equant (均輪) was postulated.
To establish the motion of four wheels to determine acceleration and deceleration.
The Westerner Tycho, based on actual measurements,
divided the radius of the epicycle into three parts,
retaining two parts as the radius of the epicycle,
and one part as the radius of the equant.
This method follows it.
The center of the epicycle starts from the winter solstice of the deferent, revolving clockwise for the mean motion,
adding an eccentric (負均輪) circle.
Its radius is the radius of the new epicycle,
plus the number of the radius of the second epicycle (次輪).
Its center is the same as the center of the epicycle.
The epicycle moves eccentrically,
without proper motion,
moving the center of the equant from the apogee counter-clockwise,
traveling along the circumference of this circle,
as the argument of proper motion (自行引數).
Tycho also posited the second epicycle at the Earth's center,
and added a second equant (次均輪).
This method changes it,
setting the center of the second epicycle to move along the circumference of the equant,
starting from the closest point clockwise as the doubled argument (倍引數),
its radius being two hundred and seventeen thousand parts out of ten million parts of the deferent radius.
The center of the second equant moves along the circumference of the second epicycle,
starting from new and full moons,
revolving clockwise from the point closest to the Earth's center on the second epicycle,
traveling twice the angle of the Moon from the Sun as the doubled elongation (倍離),
its radius being one hundred and seventeen thousand five hundred parts out of ten million parts of the deferent radius.
The Moon moves along the circumference of the second equant,
revolving counter-clockwise from the lowest point of the second equant,
also traveling the doubled elongation.
As shown in the diagram, 甲 (Jiǎ) is the Earth's center,
which is the center of the deferent.
乙丙丁戊 (Yǐ-Bǐng-Dīng-Wù) is an arc of the deferent.
丙甲 (Bǐng-Jiǎ) is the radius.
戊 (Wù) is the highest point of the half-wheel (半輪).
癸 (Guǐ) is the lowest.
酉 (Yǒu) is the highest point of the eccentric circle.
丑 (Chǒu) is the lowest.
壬 (Rén) is the farthest point of the equant.
辛 (Xīn) is the closest.
寅 (Yín) is the farthest point of the second epicycle.
亥 (Hài) is the closest.
土 (Tǔ) is the uppermost point of the second equant.
木 (Mù) is the lowermost.
This shows the equant center at the apogee and also at new/full moon.
Another diagram shows the Moon at 戌 (Xū),
which means the equant has revolved counter-clockwise,
and is also at new/full moon.
The radii of the second epicycle and second equant are obtained at the quadratures (上下弦)
and when the proper motion is at three or nine palaces (三宮或九宮), accumulating measurements to obtain
the maximum mean number of seven degrees, twenty-five minutes, and forty-six seconds.
Its tangent is one million three hundred and four thousand.
Subtract from this the epicycle and equant, along with their radii.
Halve the remainder,
which is the radius of the second epicycle.
Between the two quadratures and new/full moon,
when the proper motion is at three or nine palaces, accumulating measurements shows that
the mean number often does not match the calculation,
with a difference of up to forty-one minutes and zero two seconds.
By method, its radius is sought,
and the radius of the second equant is obtained.
To determine the nodal period (交周) using two lunar eclipses.
On the full moon (望, *wàng*) of the *gēngshēn* day in the eleventh month of the thirteenth year of Shùnzhì (順治), at eighteen hours, forty-four minutes, and fifteen seconds after *zǐzhèng* (midnight),
the lunar eclipse lasted fifteen minutes and forty-seven seconds,
south of the ecliptic.
The Sun was at ten degrees, thirty-nine minutes of the Xīngjì Palace,
three degrees, forty-nine minutes past its lowest point.
The Moon's proper motion was three palaces, twenty-seven degrees, forty-six minutes.
On the full moon of the *bǐngwǔ* day in the twelfth month of the thirteenth year of Kāngxī (康熙), at three hours, twenty-three minutes, and twenty-six seconds after *zǐzhèng*,
the lunar eclipse lasted fifteen minutes and fifty seconds,
south of the ecliptic.
The Sun was at twenty-one degrees, fifty-two minutes of the Xīngjì Palace,
fourteen degrees, twenty-one minutes past its lowest point.
The Moon's proper motion was three palaces, twenty-five degrees, twenty-four minutes.
The accumulated interval between them was two hundred and twenty-three months.
Using Hipparchus's (依巴谷) new moon quotient (朔策) fixed number five thousand four hundred and fifty-eight as the first rate (一率),
the nodal return (交終) fixed number five thousand nine hundred and twenty-three as the second rate (二率),
and two hundred and twenty-three months as the third rate (三率),
we get the fourth rate (四率) as two hundred and forty-one and five thousand four hundred and fifty-one five thousand four hundred and fifty-eighths,
which is the number of nodal returns between the two lunar eclipses.
Then, multiply the accumulated interval between the two lunar eclipses, six thousand five hundred and eighty-five days, eight hours, thirty-nine minutes, and ten seconds,
by the Moon's daily mean longitude.
Divide by the number of nodal returns,
to get one million two hundred and ninety thousand eight hundred and twelve seconds, with a remainder of eight seven nine five nine eight,
which is the degree of each nodal forward motion.
Subtract this from the total seconds in a celestial circumference,
leaving five thousand one hundred and eighty-seven seconds, with a remainder of one two zero four zero two,
which is the degree of each nodal retrograde motion.
Then, divide the accumulated interval in days and minutes between the two lunar eclipses by the number of nodal returns,
to get twenty-seven days and two one two two three three,
which is the nodal period in days and minutes.
Then, divide the degree of each nodal retrograde motion by the nodal period in days and minutes,
to get three minutes, ten seconds, and thirty-seven wēi,
which is the daily retrograde motion of the two nodes.
Add this to the Moon's daily mean motion,
to get thirteen degrees, thirteen minutes, forty-five seconds, and thirty-eight wēi,
which is the Moon's daily motion relative to the node.
Because the difference in the Moon's proper motion between the two eclipses is two and a half degrees,
and the difference in the eclipse magnitude is three seconds,
there is a difference of one wēi from Hipparchus's determined motion relative to the node.
Hipparchus's determined number is still used.
To determine the maximum inclination of the White Path (lunar ecliptic) to the ecliptic (黃白大距度) and the mean node (交均) to fix the nodal motion.
When the Moon leaves the ecliptic at the beginning degree of the Quánshǒu Palace,
and is ninety degrees from the node to the north of the ecliptic,
wait until it reaches the meridian to measure it,
obtaining the altitude.
Subtract the equatorial altitude and the latitude of the ecliptic-equatorial distance.
One measurement at new/full moon
gives a maximum inclination of four degrees, fifty-eight minutes, and thirty seconds;
another at quadratures
gives a maximum inclination of five degrees, seventeen minutes, and thirty seconds,
which are used to establish the method.
As shown in the diagram, 甲 (Jiǎ) is the ecliptic pole.
乙丙丁戊 (Yǐ-Bǐng-Dīng-Wù) is the ecliptic.
Add the two inclination degrees and halve them
to get the mean value of the maximum inclination of the White Path to the ecliptic,
which serves as the radius, such as 巳甲 (Sì-Jiǎ),
to draw the epicycle, such as 巳庚辛壬 (Sì-Gēng-Xīn-Rén).
Also, subtract the two inclination degrees and halve them to get the radius, such as 巳癸 (Sì-Guǐ),
to draw the equant, such as 癸子丑寅 (Guǐ-Zǐ-Chǒu-Yín).
Its center revolves counter-clockwise along the epicycle,
moving three minutes and ten seconds and more daily.
The pole of the White Path follows the equant,
starting from the closest point,
revolving counter-clockwise,
traveling the doubled elongation.
When it reaches 癸 (Guǐ), the maximum inclination is 乙卯 (Yǐ-Mǎo);
when it reaches 丑 (Chǒu), the maximum inclination is 乙辰 (Yǐ-Chén).
Moving through the half of 子丑寅 (Zǐ-Chǒu-Yín), the nodal motion is fast.
Moving through the half of 寅癸子 (Yín-Guǐ-Zǐ), the nodal motion is slow.
To determine the difference in the radius of the Earth as seen from the Sun.
At Chàngchūnyuán, the altitude of the Moon was measured to be 62 degrees, 40 minutes, 51 seconds, and 43 microseconds.
Simultaneously, at Guǎngzhōu Fǔ, Guǎngdōng, the altitude of the Moon was measured to be 79 degrees, 47 minutes, 26 seconds, and 12 microseconds.
At that time, the Moon was in the initial degree of the third mansion of its proper motion,
and its distance from the Sun was 180 degrees.
Using this as the method,
and employing a plane triangle, the ratio of the Earth's radius to the Moon's distance from the Earth's center when it is at its mean distance
was derived as 1 to 56.72.
Following this method, when the Moon was in the initial degree of the first mansion of its proper motion and 90 degrees from the Sun, a measurement was taken.
The ratio of the Earth's radius to the Moon's distance from the Earth's center when it is at its highest
was found to be 1 to 61.98.
Furthermore, when the Moon was in the initial degree of the sixth mansion of its proper motion and 90 degrees from the Sun, a measurement was taken.
The ratio of the Earth's radius to the Moon's distance from the Earth's center when it is at its lowest
was found to be 1 to 53.71.
Then, using a plane triangle, the difference in the Earth's radius for each degree was calculated.
To examine the hidden and visible, early and late appearances of the Moon to distinguish between *tiǎo* and *nà*.
One test is for the three mansions before and after the spring equinox.
The ecliptic rises obliquely and descends perpendicularly.
At sunset, the Moon is high above the horizon,
appearing swiftly after the new moon.
For the three mansions before and after the autumn equinox,
the ecliptic rises perpendicularly and descends obliquely.
At sunset, the Moon is low above the horizon,
appearing late after the new moon.
Before the last quarter, being hidden late or hidden early is the opposite.
Another test relates to being north of the ecliptic,
where it appears early and is hidden late.
Being south of the ecliptic is the opposite.
Another test relates to its apparent slow motion,
where both appearing and being hidden are late;
and for apparent fast motion,
both appearing and being hidden are early.
Principles for establishing the method of eclipses:
To determine the apparent diameters of the Sun and Moon to ascertain the depth of the eclipse magnitude.
Using both the direct and inverse gnomon,
the shadow at noon is taken in each case
to determine its altitude.
The difference between the two altitudes is taken as the apparent diameter of the Sun.
After several years of precise measurement,
the maximum apparent diameter of the Sun was found to be 29 minutes, 59 seconds,
and the minimum apparent diameter was 31 minutes, 5 seconds.
Using a wall as a gnomon,
with its western edge aligned with the meridian line,
a person stands north of the gnomon,
at an fixed position.
When the western limb of the Moon touches the meridian line,
the time is noted from the clock.
After the entire body of the Moon has passed,
when its eastern limb just leaves the meridian line,
the time is again noted from the clock.
The difference between the two times
is converted into degrees to get the apparent diameter of the Moon.
After several years of precise measurement,
the maximum apparent diameter of the Moon was found to be 31 minutes, 47 seconds,
and the minimum apparent diameter was 33 minutes, 42 seconds.
To determine the radius of the Earth's shadow to ascertain the degree of light.
With the ratio of the Earth's radius to the Sun and Moon's distance from the Earth's center already obtained,
and the true values of the apparent diameters of the Sun and Moon also obtained,
we then have the ratio of the apparent diameters of the Sun and Moon from their highest to lowest, and the Earth's radius, to the actual diameters of the Sun and Moon.
For a solar eclipse, whether a person on Earth sees it or not.
For a lunar eclipse, the Sun shines on the back of the Earth, forming a dark shadow.
Since the Sun is large and the Earth is small,
a conical shape is formed.
Since the Sun has high and low positions,
the Earth's shadow has varying lengths and widths.
Since the Moon has high and low positions,
its entry into the shadow has varying depths.
All these can be predicted and incorporated into the method.
The radius of the Earth's shadow is always larger than what is actually measured.
During the lunar eclipse in the eighth month of the *wùxū* year of Kāngxī 56 (1717 CE),
its actual elongation was 2 mansions, 3 degrees, 41 minutes, 3 seconds,
and its distance from the Earth's center was 57.41 Earth radii.
The measured latitude was 36 minutes, 18 seconds north of the ecliptic.
The Moon's radius was 16 minutes, 10 seconds.
The eclipse magnitude was 23 minutes, 30 seconds.
Then, using the ecliptic latitude, the latitude of the white path was determined at the maximum eclipse.
The distance in latitude was added to the eclipse magnitude,
and the Moon's radius was subtracted from the sum,
leaving 43 minutes, 46 seconds,
which was the radius of the Earth's shadow.
If calculated according to the theory,
with the Sun at its highest
and the Moon at its mean distance,
the Earth's shadow radius should be 48 minutes, 34 seconds.
When scaled by the actual measured value,
it should be 44 minutes, 43 seconds,
a difference of 3 minutes, 51 seconds.
This difference indicates that the Sun's rays extend beyond its actual body
and can erode the Earth's shadow.
By comparing the actual measurement with the calculation,
the "degree of light" of the Sun was determined to be 6.37 times the Earth's radius.
As shown in the diagram,
Jiǎ is the center of the Earth,
Wù Jǐ is the diameter of the Earth,
Yǐ Dīng is the shadow cast by the Sun,
the end of which reaches Gēng.
Xīn Rén represents the overflowing light that erodes the shadow,
gradually narrowing until
it completely disappears at Chǒu.
(Diagram data not available yet)
Principles for establishing the method of planetary motion for the five planets:
To determine the mean motion of Saturn.
Ancient measurements determined it to be 21,551.3 days,
with equal degrees and minutes from the fixed stars,
and equal distances from the Sun.
Saturn completes 57 conjunctions with and oppositions to the Sun during its synodic cycle.
The accumulated mean days are taken as the dividend,
and the number of synodic cycles, 57, as the divisor.
Dividing yields the synodic period.
Then, taking 360 degrees as the dividend for each cycle,
and dividing by the synodic period, yields the daily motion relative to the Sun.
Subtracting this from the Sun's daily mean motion
yields Saturn's daily mean motion.
This method is still followed.
To use three oppositions of Saturn to determine the radii of its epicycle and deferent and its apogee to establish its waxing and waning.
During the Wànlì reign of the Míng dynasty,
the Westerner Tycho measured three oppositions of Saturn.
For example, the first opposition occurred when the Sun was at 1 degree, 3 minutes, 27 seconds of the jūzī mansion,
and Saturn was at the same degree, minute, and second in the qúnwěi mansion.
The second opposition occurred when the Sun was at 21 degrees, 47 minutes, 39 seconds of the jūzī mansion,
and Saturn was at the same degree, minute, and second in the qúnwěi mansion.
The third opposition occurred when the Sun was at 16 degrees, 51 minutes, 28 seconds of the jiànglóu mansion,
and Saturn was at the same degree, minute, and second in the shòuxīng mansion.
The interval from the first to the second opposition was 11,343 days, 5 hours, 36 minutes,
with an actual motion difference of 20 degrees, 44 minutes, 12 seconds,
and a mean motion difference of 19 degrees, 59 minutes, 54 seconds.
The interval from the second to the third opposition was 755 days, 20 hours, 31 minutes,
with an actual motion difference of 25 degrees, 3 minutes, 49 seconds,
and a mean motion difference of 25 degrees, 19 minutes, 16 seconds.
Using non-concentric circles and applying plane triangles,
the difference between the two centers was derived as 1,162,000 ten-millionths of the radius of the deferent,

To determine the mean motion of Jupiter.
Ancient measurements determined it to be 25,927.617 days.
Jupiter completes 65 conjunctions with and oppositions to the Sun during its synodic cycle.
The accumulated mean days are taken as the dividend,
and the number of synodic cycles, 65, as the divisor.
Dividing yields the synodic period.
(Diagram data not available yet) Then, taking 360 degrees as the dividend for each cycle,

Ancient measurements determined that in 2,919 days and 667/1000ths of a day,

Set the accumulated mean days as the dividend,
and 5, the number of revolutions of the planet in its second epicycle, as the divisor.
Dividing gives the period.
Using 360 degrees for each revolution as the dividend,
and dividing by the period,
gives Jīnxīng's (Venus's) daily mean motion in the second epicycle.

Method for calculating the Sun's ecliptic motion: To find the `Tiānzhèng` Winter Solstice,
take the full year (length),
multiply it by the number of years minus one from the epoch year,
to get the cumulative mean points.
Add the `qìyìng` to get the total cumulative points.
(For calculating past dates,
subtract the `qìyìng` to get the total cumulative points.)
If the number of days exceeds the `jìfǎ` cycle, remove the multiples of it,
the remainder is the day `fēn` for the `Tiānzhèng` Winter Solstice.
(For calculating past dates,
take the remainder and subtract it from the `jìfǎ` cycle,
the result is the day `fēn` for the `Tiānzhèng` Winter Solstice.)
Starting from the first day, `Jiǎzǐ`,
convert its remainder to `kè-xiàfēn`,
and properly collect it as hours and `kè`.
(A full day, 10,000 `fēn`, is the first ratio,
the remainder is the second ratio,
`kè-xiàfēn` is the third ratio,
the fourth ratio obtained is for hours and `fēn`.
Every 60 `fēn` is taken as one hour,
every 15 `fēn` is taken as one `kè`.)
The initial time starts at `Zǐzhèng`,
add the `sùyìng` to the cumulative mean points,
if it exceeds the `sùfǎ` cycle, remove the multiples of it,
the result is the day `fēn` for the lunar mansion corresponding to the `Tiānzhèng` Winter Solstice,
starting from `Jiǎo Sù` on the first day.
To find the parallel motion,
take the full day as the first ratio,
the Sun's daily mean motion as the second ratio,
the remainder of the `Tiānzhèng` Winter Solstice subtracted from the full day as the third ratio,
the fourth ratio obtained is the number of seconds for the year's root.
Then, take the Sun's daily mean motion,
multiply it by the number of days from the current day to the day after the Winter Solstice,
the result is in seconds.
Combine it with the annual root,
and collect it in houses, degrees, and minutes,
to get the parallel motion.
To find the *shíxíng* (actual motion),
set the lowest annual motion (*zuìbēi suìxíng*),
and multiply it by the number of accumulated years.
Then set the lowest daily motion (*zuìbēi rìxíng*),
and multiply it by the number of days after the winter solstice.
Add the two numbers together,
and add the lowest anomaly (*zuìbēi yìng*).
(For superior examination, subtract the lowest anomaly.)
Use the result as the argument (*yǐnshù*) by subtracting the uniform motion (*píngxíng*).
Using a plane triangle,
take two-thirds of the radius of the epicycle (*běnlún bànjìng*) as the side opposite the right angle,
and take the argument as one angle.
Find the side opposite the angle and double it.
Then find the side opposite the other angle,
and add or subtract it from the radius of the deferent (*běntiān bànjìng*).
(If the argument is from the third palace to the eighth palace, add;
if from the ninth palace to the second palace, subtract.)
Again using a plane triangle,
take the doubled number as the shorter side,
and the number resulting from adding or subtracting the radius of the deferent as the longer side,
with the right angle between the two sides.
Find the angle opposite the shorter side as the equation of the center (*jūnshù*).
Set the uniform motion and add or subtract the equation of the center.
(If the argument is from the first palace to the fifth palace, add;
if from the sixth palace to the eleventh palace, subtract.)
This yields the *shíxíng*.
To find the stellar longitude (*sùdù*),
multiply the annual precession (*suìchā*) by the accumulated years.
Add this number to the ecliptic stellar longitude from the *Jiǎzǐ Fǎyuán* calendar (*Jiǎzǐ Fǎyuán huángdào sùdù*).
This is the stellar determinant for the current year (*běnnián sùqín*).
Subtract the *shíxíng* from it.
The remainder is the daily stellar longitude of the sun (*rìchán sùdù*).
If the *shíxíng* is less than the *sùqín* to be subtracted,
subtract after decrementing by one constellation.
To find the daily constellation for a given date (*jìrì zhísù*),
set the number of days after the winter solstice,
add the winter solstice,
and remove full cycles according to the calendar day method.
Beginning from the *jiǎzǐ* day,
add the constellation of the winter solstice,
and remove full cycles according to the constellation method.
Beginning from *Jiǎoxiù* (Horn),
this yields the daily constellation for the given date.
To find the exact time of the solar terms (*jiéqì shíkè*),
the sun's transit at the first degree of the first palace (丑 *Chǒu*,

the fifteenth degree is Clear and Bright (*Qīngmíng*).
The first degree of the fifth palace (酉 *Yǒu*,
*Dàliáng* asterism)
is Grain Rain (*Gǔyǔ*);
the fifteenth degree is Beginning of Summer (*Lìxià*).
The first degree of the sixth palace (申 *Shēn*,
*Shíshěn* asterism)
is Grain Full (*Xiǎomǎn*);
the fifteenth degree is Grain in Ear (*Mángzhòng*).
The first degree of the seventh palace (未 *Wèi*,
*Qúnshǒu* asterism)
is Summer Solstice (*Xiàzhì*);
the fifteenth degree is Minor Heat (*Xiǎoshǔ*).
The first degree of the eighth palace (午 *Wǔ*,
*Qúnhuǒ* asterism)
is Major Heat (*Dàshǔ*);
the fifteenth degree is Beginning of Autumn (*Lìqiū*).
The first degree of the ninth palace (巳 *Sì*,
*Qúnwěi* asterism)
is Limit of Heat (*Chǔshǔ*);
the fifteenth degree is White Dew (*Báilù*).
The first degree of the tenth palace (辰 *Chén*,
*Shòuxīng* asterism)
is Autumn Equinox (*Qiūfēn*);
the fifteenth degree is Cold Dew (*Hánlù*).
The first degree of the eleventh palace (卯 *Mǎo*,
*Dàhuǒ* asterism)
is Frost's Descent (*Shuāngjiàng*);
the fifteenth degree is Beginning of Winter (*Lìdōng*).
The first degree of the twelfth palace (寅 *Yín*,
*Xīmù* asterism)
is Minor Snow (*Xiǎoxuě*);
the fifteenth degree is Major Snow (*Dàxuě*).
For all these, if the sun's *rìchán* at midnight (*zǐzhèng*) has not yet reached the degree of the solar term palace,
then the solar term occurs on that day;
if it has already passed the degree of the solar term palace,
then the solar term occurs on the next day.
Then, subtract the *shíxíng* of this day from the *shíxíng* of the next day to obtain the first ratio.
Divide the daily *kè* and *fēn* by two to get the second ratio.
Subtract the *shíxíng* at midnight of this day from the degree of the solar term palace to get the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained will be the minutes after midnight.
Convert this to *shíkè*,
and that is the exact initial time of the solar term.
If the *shíxíng* exactly matches the degree of the solar term palace without any remainder,
then it is the first *kè* of midnight.
To find the exact time of the solar terms for various provinces,
all are based on the capital (*Jīngshī*),
and adjusted according to the deviation in longitude.
For every degree of deviation,
add or subtract one-quarter of a *shí* (hour).
(If it deviates to the east, add;
if to the west, subtract.)
To calculate the time method for solar terms,
convert the mean motion (*jūnshù*) of the day of the solar term to a time difference (*jūnshù shíchā*),
and reverse its addition or subtraction.
Also, use the radius as the first ratio,
the cosine of the greatest obliquity of the ecliptic (*huángchì dàjù*) as the second ratio,
and the tangent of the ecliptic degree (*huángdào dù*) of the current solar term as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained will be the tangent of the equator (*chìdào zhèngqiē*).
Check the table to find the degree,
and subtract it from the ecliptic degree.
The remainder, converted to time, is the difference in ascending degree time (*shēngdù shíchā*).
After the two equinoxes, it is added;
after the two solstices, it is subtracted.
All these are added to or subtracted from the exact time of the solar term,
to get the time in use for the solar term.
To find the declination (*jù wěidù*),
use the radius of the deferent as the first ratio,
the sine of the greatest obliquity of the ecliptic as the second ratio,
and the sine of the *shíxíng*'s degree before or after the spring and autumn equinoxes as the third ratio.
(If the *shíxíng* is from the first degree of the third palace to the last degree of the fifth palace,
subtract it from the third palace;
the remainder is before the Spring Equinox.
If from the first degree of the sixth palace to the last degree of the eighth palace,
then subtract the third palace;
this is after the Spring Equinox.
If from the first degree of the ninth palace to the last degree of the eleventh palace,
subtract it from the ninth palace;
the remainder is before the Autumn Equinox.
If from the first degree of the twelfth palace to the last degree of the second palace,
then subtract the ninth palace;
this is after the Autumn Equinox.)
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Check the table to find the declination.
If the *shíxíng* is from the third palace to the eighth palace,
its latitude is north of the equator;
if from the ninth palace to the second palace,
its latitude is south of the equator.
To find the times of sunrise, sunset, and day and night,
use the radius of the deferent as the first ratio,
the tangent of the altitude of the North Pole (*běijí gāodù*) as the second ratio,
and the tangent of the current day's declination as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Check the table to find the equatorial degrees before or after *mǎo* (east) and *yǒu* (west) for sunrise and sunset.
Convert this to time,
(one degree converts to one-quarter of an hour,
all mentions of converting to time follow this rule)
to get the minutes from *mǎo* and *yǒu*.
By adding or subtracting from the *mǎo* and *yǒu* times,
the times of sunrise and sunset are obtained.
(Before the Spring Equinox and after the Autumn Equinox,
add to *mǎo* proper for sunrise,
and subtract from *yǒu* proper for sunset.
After the Spring Equinox and before the Autumn Equinox,
subtract from *mǎo* proper for sunrise,
and add to *yǒu* proper for sunset.)
Then double the minutes from *mǎo* and *yǒu*,
and add or subtract it from half the duration of day or night,
to get the times of day and night.
(After the Spring Equinox, add to get the day duration,
and subtract to get the night duration;
after the Autumn Equinox, it is the reverse.)
