Method for Calculating Lunar Positions:
To find the celestial noon winter solstice (*tiānzhèng dōngzhì*),
it is the same as the sun's transit.
To find the mean motion of the Moon (tàiyīn),
place the accumulated integral (zhōng jīfēn),
add the minor remainder (xiǎoyú) of the qi-response (qìyìng) (details in "Solar Path (Rìchán)"),
(the Sun is not used here;
the same applies below),
subtract the minor remainder of the winter solstice (dōngzhì) of the celestial prime (tiānzhèng),
to get the accumulated days (jīrì).
(For upward calculation, subtract the minor remainder of the qi-response
and add the minor remainder of the winter solstice of the celestial prime.)
Multiply this by the daily mean motion of the Moon,
and remove the full circumference in seconds;
the remainder is recorded as degrees and minutes of the palace (gōngdùfēn).
Add this to the mean anomaly (píngxíngyìng) of the Moon,
to get the Moon's annual root (niángēn).
(For upward calculation, subtract.)
Then place the daily mean motion of the Moon,
multiply it by the number of days from the next day after the winter solstice of the celestial prime,
the result is in seconds.
Record this as degrees and minutes of the palace,
and combine it with the annual root,
(remove multiples of twelve palaces)
to get the Moon's mean motion.
To find the motion of the Lunar Node (yuèbèi),
multiply the accumulated days (see previous section;
the same applies below)
by the daily motion of the Lunar Node,
remove the full circumference in seconds;
the remainder is recorded as degrees and minutes of the palace.
Add this to the anomaly of the Lunar Node (yuèbèiyìng),
to get the Lunar Node's annual root.
(For upward calculation, subtract.)
Then place the daily motion of the Lunar Node, multiply it by the number of days from the next day after the winter solstice of the celestial prime,
the result is in seconds.
Record this as degrees and minutes of the palace,
and combine it with the annual root,
(remove multiples of twelve palaces)
to get the motion of the Lunar Node.
To find the mean motion of the true ascending node (zhèngjiāo),
multiply the accumulated days by the daily mean motion of the true ascending node,
remove the full circumference in seconds;
the remainder is recorded as degrees and minutes of the palace.
Subtract this from the anomaly of the true ascending node (zhèngjiāoyìng),
(if the anomaly of the true ascending node is insufficient for subtraction,
add twelve palaces before subtracting)
to get the true ascending node's annual root.
(For upward calculation, add.)
Then place the daily mean motion of the true ascending node,
multiply it by the number of days from the next day after the winter solstice of the celestial prime,
the result is in seconds.
Record this as degrees and minutes of the palace,
subtract it from the annual root,
(if the annual root is insufficient for subtraction,
add twelve palaces before subtracting)
to get the mean motion of the true ascending node.
To find the Moon's mean motion for a given time (yòngshí tàiyīn píngxíng),
use the time conversion of the daily mean value of the Sun (tài yáng jūnsù biànshí) (details in "Solar Path (Rìchán)"),
to get the time difference of the mean value (jūnsù shíchā).
(If the mean value is added,
the time difference is subtracted;
if the mean value is subtracted,
the time difference is added.)
Then convert the remainder from the subtraction of the Sun's daily ecliptic longitude (huángjīngdù) and equatorial longitude (chìjīngdù) (details in "Solar Path (Rìchán)")
into time,
to get the time difference of ascending degree (shēngdù shíchā).
(After the equinoxes, it is added;
after the solstices, it is subtracted.)
Then add or subtract the two time differences,
to get the total time difference (shíchā zǒng).
(If the two time differences have the same sign in addition/subtraction,
they are added to get the total;
if positive, it remains positive;
if negative, it remains negative.
If they have different signs,
they are subtracted to get the total;
if the positive number is larger, the total is positive;
if the negative number is larger, the total is negative.)
Convert this to seconds,
and multiply by the Moon's hourly mean motion to get the product (shí).
Divide this by the number of seconds in one degree,
the result is in seconds.
Record this as degrees and minutes,
to get the time-difference motion (shíchāxíng).
Add or subtract this from the Moon's mean motion,
(if the total time difference is positive, subtract;
if negative, add)
to get the Moon's mean motion for a given time.
To find the first true motion (chūshíxíng),
place the Moon's mean motion for a given time,
subtract the motion of the Lunar Node,
to get the argument (yǐnshù).
Using a plane triangle,
take half the radius of the epicycle (běnlún) as the side opposite the right angle,
and the argument as one angle;
find the three sines of the opposite angle.
Then find the side opposite the other angle,
and add or subtract it from the radius of the deferent (běntiān).
(For arguments from the ninth palace to the second palace, add;
for arguments from the third palace to the eighth palace, subtract.)
Again using a plane triangle,
take the three sines as the shorter side,
and the added/subtracted deferent radius as the longer side,
with the right angle between the two sides;
find the angle opposite the shorter side as the first equation of the center (chūjūnsù),
and also find the side opposite the right angle.
(This is the line from the nearest point of the second epicycle to the center of the Earth.)
Then place the Moon's mean motion for a given time,
add or subtract the first equation of the center,
(for arguments from the first palace to the fifth palace, subtract;
for the sixth palace onwards, add)
to get the first true motion.
To find the *báidào shǐxíng* (actual lunar position on the white path):
Set the initial actual position.
Subtract the actual position of the sun on this day to get the *cìyǐn* (secondary argument)
(which is the lunar argument of anomaly).
Using a plane triangle,
with the line from the nearest point of the secondary epicycle to the Earth's center as one side;
twice the *tōngxián* (chord) of the *cìyǐn* (with the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the *cìyǐn* as the second ratio,
the radius of the secondary epicycle as the third ratio,
the fourth ratio obtained and doubled is the *tōngxián*)
as another side.
Add the initial mean anomaly (*chū jūnsù*) to the argument (*yǐnsù*) minus half a circle in degrees (if the argument is less than half a circle,
subtract it from half a circle;
if it exceeds half a circle,
subtract half a circle from it).
Then, add or subtract
the *cìyǐn* from the quadrant in degrees (if the *cìyǐn* is less than a quadrant,
subtract it from the quadrant;
if it exceeds a quadrant or three quadrants,
subtract the quadrant or three quadrants and
use the remainder;
if it exceeds two quadrants,
subtract two quadrants,
and then subtract the remainder from the quadrant
to get the *cìyǐn* from the quadrant in degrees).
(For subtraction from the *chū jūnsù*:
if the *cìyǐn* passes a quadrant or three quadrants, add it;
if it does not pass a quadrant or passes two quadrants, subtract it.
The opposite applies for addition to the *chū jūnsù*.)
This forms the included angle.
(If the sum exceeds a full circle,
subtract it from a full circle and
use the remainder as the included angle.
If the sum is exactly half a circle or the subtraction leaves no remainder,
then there is no second mean anomaly.
If the *cìyǐn* is at the initial degree
or exactly half a circle,
there is also no second mean anomaly.)
The angle opposite the *tōngxián* is the second mean anomaly (*èr jūnsù*).
(If there is no *chū jūnsù*:
with the distance from the center of the secondary epicycle to the Earth's center as one side,
the radius of the secondary epicycle as one side;
the doubled *cìyǐn* as the included angle,
if the *cìyǐn* exceeds half a circle,
subtract it from a full circle and
use the remainder;
at the highest point, it is the included interior angle;
at the lowest point, it is the included exterior angle;
the angle opposite the radius of the secondary epicycle is the *èr jūnsù*.)
Then determine its sign (plus or minus).
(Add the *chū jūnsù* to the degree of the mean epicycle center's distance from the lowest point
to get the *jiājiǎn fànxiàn* (addition/subtraction limit).
If the *fànxiàn* is exactly ninety degrees,
the sign of the *èr jūn* addition/subtraction is the same as the *chū jūn*.
If the *fànxiàn* is less than ninety degrees,
subtract it from ninety degrees,
double the remainder
to get the *jiājiǎn dìngxiàn* (fixed limit for addition/subtraction).
If the *chū jūn* is subtracted,
use the doubled *cìyǐn*;
if the *chū jūn* is added,
use the remainder of the doubled *cìyǐn* subtracted from a full circle,
and compare both with the *dìngxiàn*.
If the *fànxiàn* exceeds ninety degrees,
subtract ninety degrees,
double the remainder
to get the *jiājiǎn dìngxiàn*.
If the *chū jūn* is added,
use the doubled *cìyǐn*;
if the *chū jūn* is subtracted,
use the remainder of the doubled *cìyǐn* subtracted from a full circle,
and compare both with the *dìngxiàn*.
If it is greater than the *dìngxiàn*,
the sign of the *èr jūn* addition/subtraction is the same as the *chū jūn*;
if it is smaller than the *dìngxiàn*, it is the opposite.)
Also, find the side opposite the angle,
which is the distance from the center of the secondary mean epicycle to the Earth's center.
Then, using this line and the *cìyǐn*,
use a plane triangle,
with the distance from the center of the secondary mean epicycle to the Earth as one side,
the radius of the secondary mean epicycle as one side,
and the doubled *cìyǐn* as the included angle.
(If the *cìyǐn* exceeds half a circle,
subtract it from a full circle and
use the remainder.)
The angle opposite the radius of the secondary mean epicycle is the third mean anomaly (*sān jūnsù*).
Determine its sign (plus or minus).
(If the doubled *cìyǐn* is less than half a circle, it is plus;
if it exceeds half a circle, it is minus.)
Then, add or subtract the *èr jūnsù* and *sān jūnsù*
to get the *èrsān jūnsù* (combined second and third mean anomalies).
(If both mean anomalies have the same sign, add them;
if they have different signs, subtract them.)
Add or subtract this from the initial actual position.
(If both mean anomalies are plus, it is still plus;
if both are minus, it is still minus.
If one is plus and one is minus,
if the plus value is larger, it is plus;
if the minus value is larger, it is minus.)
This is the *báidào shǐxíng*.
To find the *huángdào shǐxíng* (actual lunar position on the ecliptic):
Using a spherical triangle,
with the mean value of the *huángbái dàjù* (greatest ecliptic latitude) as one side,
half the difference of the *dàjù* as one side,
and the doubled *cìyǐn* as the included angle.
(If the *cìyǐn* exceeds half a circle, subtract it from a full circle and
use the remainder.)
The side opposite the angle is the *huángbái dàjù*.
Also, the angle opposite half the difference is the *jiāojūn* (nodal anomaly).
Add or subtract the *jiāojūn* from the *zhèngjiāo píngxíng* (mean position of the ascending node).
(If the doubled *cìyǐn* is less than half a circle, it is minus;
if it exceeds half a circle, it is plus.)
This yields the *zhèngjiāo shǐxíng* (actual position of the ascending node).
Then add or subtract six *gōng* (palaces or signs) to get the *zhōngjiāo shǐxíng* (actual position of the descending node).
Set the *báidào shǐxíng*.
Subtract the *zhèngjiāo shǐxíng*
to get the *jùjiāo shǐxíng* (distance from the node).
With the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the cosine of the *huángbái dàjù* as the second ratio,
the tangent of the *jùjiāo shǐxíng* as the third ratio,
the fourth ratio obtained is the tangent of the ecliptic.
Consult the table to get the degrees and minutes,
subtract it from the *jùjiāo shǐxíng*,
the remainder is the *shēngdùchā* (difference in right ascension).
Add or subtract this from the *báidào shǐxíng*.
(If the *jùjiāo shǐxíng* does not pass a quadrant
or passes two quadrants, it is subtracted;
if it passes a quadrant or three quadrants, it is added.)
This is the *huángdào shǐxíng*.
To find the *huángdào wěidù* (ecliptic latitude):
With the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the *huángbái dàjù* as the second ratio,
the sine of the *jùjiāo shǐxíng* as the third ratio,
the fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Consult the table to get the *huángdào wěidù*.
From the first to fifth *gōng* of the *jùjiāo shǐxíng* is north ecliptic latitude;
from the sixth to eleventh *gōng* is south ecliptic latitude.
To find the *sìzhǒng sùdù* (four types of mansion degrees):
Following the method for finding *sùdù* from the sun's position,
obtain the *běnnián huángdào sùqín* (ecliptic mansion division for the current year).

Depending on whether the *huángdào shǐxíng*, *yuèbèi xíng* (lunar apogee position), and *zhèngjiāo*, *zhōngjiāo shǐxíng* in degrees and minutes are sufficient to subtract from a certain mansion within the *sùqín*, subtract it.
The remainder is the *sìzhǒng sùdù*.
To find the *jìrì zhísu* (mansion of the day):
Same as the sun's position.
To find the *jiāogōng shíkè* (time of crossing a palace):
Subtract the *tàiyīn běnrì shǐxíng* (actual lunar position on this day) from the *cìrì shǐxíng* (actual lunar position on the next day). (If it has not yet passed the palace, use this day;
if it has passed the palace, use the next day.)
The remainder is the first ratio.
The *kèxiàfēn* (fractions of a *kè*, 1/100 of a day) is the second ratio.
The remainder of the *tàiyīn běnrì shǐxíng* (excluding the palace)
subtracted from thirty degrees is the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the *jùzǐzhèng fēnshù* (minutes from midnight).
Collect it according to the method
to get the *jiāogōng shíkè*.
To find the *tàiyīn chūrù shíkè* (times of moonrise and moonset):
Find the equivalent equatorial longitude for the sun's ecliptic longitude on this day.
Then, using a spherical triangle,
with the moon's distance from the ecliptic pole as one side,
the distance from the ecliptic pole to the celestial north pole as one side
(i.e., the *huángchì dàjù* (obliquity of the ecliptic)).
The moon's distance from the winter solstice ecliptic longitude as the included exterior angle.
(If it exceeds half a circle, subtract it from a full circle and
use the remainder.)
The opposite side obtained is the moon's distance from the celestial north pole in degrees.
Subtract it from ninety degrees
to get the equatorial latitude.
(If it is less than ninety degrees,
subtract it from ninety degrees,
the remainder is north latitude.
If it exceeds ninety degrees,
subtract ninety degrees,
the remainder is south latitude.)
Also, find the angle near the celestial north pole,
which is the moon's distance from the winter solstice equatorial longitude.
Then, with the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the tangent of the height of the celestial north pole as the second ratio,
the tangent of the moon's equatorial latitude as the third ratio,
the fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Consult the table to get the moon's ingress and egress equatorial degrees before and after *mǎozhèng* (true sunrise/6 AM) and *yǒuzhèng* (true sunset/6 PM).
(If the moon is north of the equator,
it rises before *mǎozhèng*
and sets after *yǒuzhèng*;
if the moon is south of the equator,
it rises after *mǎozhèng*
and sets before *yǒuzhèng*.)
Add or subtract this (subtract for before, add for after)
from the moon's equatorial distance from the sun.
(This is obtained by subtracting the sun's equatorial longitude from the moon's equatorial longitude.)
The result is converted to hours.
Count from *mǎozhèng* and after *yǒuzhèng*.
(From *mǎozhèng* for rising,
from *yǒuzhèng* for setting.)
The time obtained,
plus the time for the moon's motion at that moment,
(approximately thirty minutes per hour,
which is two parts per hour),
gives the *tàiyīn chūrù shíkè*.
To determine the conjunctions, first quarter, opposition, and last quarter:
The limit for conjunction (héshuò) is when the actual path of the Moon and the actual path of the Sun are in the same palace (gōng) and the same degree (dù).
Three palaces (gōng) away is the limit for the first quarter (shàngxián).
Six palaces (gōng) away is the limit for opposition (wàng).
Nine palaces (gōng) away is the limit for the last quarter (xiàxián).
In all cases, if the Moon has not yet reached the limit, it is considered the current day.
If it has already passed the limit, it is considered the next day.
Then, subtract the actual path of the Moon for the current day from that for the next day, and similarly for the Sun.
The two remainders are compared to form the first ratio (yīlǜ).
The minutes and seconds are divided into the second ratio (èrlǜ).
Add the limit to the actual path of the Sun for the current day (for the first quarter, add three palaces (gōng);
for opposition, add six palaces (gōng);
for the last quarter, add nine palaces (gōng)).
Then, subtract the actual path of the Moon for the current day.
The remainder is the third ratio (sānlǜ).
The fourth ratio (sìlǜ) thus obtained represents the minutes from zǐzhèng (midnight).
By applying this method,
the times for conjunction, first quarter, opposition, and last quarter are obtained.
To determine straight ascent (zhèngshēng), oblique ascent (xiéshēng), and horizontal ascent (héngshēng):
On the day of conjunction,
the Moon's actual path from zǐgōng (15 degrees) to yǒugōng (15 degrees) is straight ascent.
From yǒugōng (15 degrees) to the beginning of wèigōng is oblique ascent.
From the beginning of wèigōng to yíngōng (15 degrees) is horizontal ascent.
From yíngōng (15 degrees) to zǐgōng (15 degrees) is oblique ascent.
To determine whether a month is long or short:
Compare the preceding conjunction with the current conjunction.
If the Heavenly Stems (rìgān) are the same, the preceding month is long.
If they are different, the preceding month is short.
To determine an intercalary month (rùnyuè):
Use the months of the two preceding and succeeding years that contain the winter solstice (dōngzhì) as the standard.
If there are thirteen months (yuè) in between,
the month without a central qi (zhōngqì) is designated as the intercalary month,
following the preceding month.
If there are two months without a central qi (zhōngqì) in one year,
the earlier one without a central qi (zhōngqì) is designated as the intercalary month.

Method for calculating Saturn (tǔxīng), Jupiter (mùxīng), and Mars (huǒxīng):
To determine the Celestial Zenith Winter Solstice (tiānzhèngdōngzhì),
refer to the solar ephemeris (rìchán) for the same day.
To calculate the average motion (píngxíng) of the three stars (sān xīng):
Multiply the accumulated days (jīrì) (for details, see Moon's anomaly (yuèlí)) by the star's daily average motion (měirìpíngxíng).
Subtract full circumferences (zhōutiān) in seconds.
The remainder is converted to palaces (gōng), degrees (dù), and minutes (fēn), which is the accumulated daily motion (jīrìpíngxíng).
Add this to the star's average position (běnxīngpíngxíngyīng)
to obtain the star's annual root (běnxīngniángēn).
(If calculating for earlier dates, subtract.)
Then, take the star's daily average motion (měirìpíngxíng).
Multiply it by the number of days from the Celestial Zenith Winter Solstice (tiānzhèngdōngzhì) to the desired date.
Add this result to the annual root (niángēn)
to get the star's average motion (běnxīngpíngxíng).
To calculate the highest motion (zuìgāoxíng) of the three stars (sān xīng):
Multiply the accumulated days (jīrì) by the star's highest daily motion (běnxīngzuìgāorìxíng).
Add this result to the star's highest position (běnxīngzuìgāoyīng)
to get the highest annual root (zuìgāoniángēn).
(If calculating for earlier dates, subtract.)
Then, take the star's highest daily motion (běnxīngzuìgāorìxíng).
Multiply it by the number of days from the Celestial Zenith Winter Solstice (tiānzhèngdōngzhì) to the desired date.
Add this result to the annual root (niángēn)
to get the star's highest motion (běnxīngzuìgāoxíng).
To calculate the conjunction motion (zhèngjiāoxíng) of the three stars (sān xīng):
Multiply the accumulated days (jīrì) by the star's conjunction daily motion (běnxīngzhèngjiāorìxíng).
Add this result to the star's conjunction position (běnxīngzhèngjiāoyīng)
to get the conjunction annual root (zhèngjiāoniángēn).
(If calculating for earlier dates, subtract.)
Then, take the star's conjunction daily motion (běnxīngzhèngjiāorìxíng).
Multiply it by the number of days from the Celestial Zenith Winter Solstice (tiānzhèngdōngzhì) to the desired date.
Add this result to the annual root (niángēn)
to get the star's conjunction motion (běnxīngzhèngjiāoxíng).
To calculate the initial true motion (chūshíxíng) of the three stars (sān xīng):
Take the star's average motion (běnxīngpíngxíng).
Subtract the highest motion (zuìgāoxíng)
to obtain the argument (yǐnshù).
Using a plane triangle (píngsānjiǎoxíng):
The side opposite the right angle is formed by subtracting the radius of the deferent (běnlún) from the radius of the epicycle (jūnlún).
The argument (yǐnshù) is one angle.
Calculate the side opposite the argument angle (yǐnshùjiǎo) and the side opposite the other angle.
Again, using a plane triangle (píngsānjiǎoxíng):
The shorter side is formed by adding the side opposite the argument angle (yǐnshùjiǎo) to the chord of the epicycle (jūnlúntōngxián) (for method of finding the chord,
see Moon's anomaly (yuèlí)).

The longer side is formed by adding or subtracting the side opposite the other angle to the radius of its celestial sphere (běntiānbànjìng) (if the argument (yǐnshù) is from the 3rd to the 8th palace (gōng), subtract;
if from the 9th to the 2nd palace (gōng), add).
The right angle is between the two sides.
The angle opposite the shorter side thus obtained is the initial mean anomaly (chūjūnshù).
Also, the side opposite the right angle thus obtained is the distance from the center of the second epicycle (cìlún) to the center of the Earth (dìxīnxiàn).
Add or subtract the initial mean anomaly (chūjūnshù) to the star's average motion (běnxīngpíngxíng)
(if the argument (yǐnshù) is from the 1st to the 5th palace (gōng), subtract;
if from the 6th to the 11th palace (gōng), add)
to obtain the star's initial true motion (běnxīngchūshíxíng).
To calculate the star's true motion in its own path (běndàoshíxíng):
Subtract the star's initial true motion (běnxīngchūshíxíng) from the Sun's actual path (tàiyángshíxíng) for the current day
to obtain the secondary argument (cìyǐn).
(This is the distance from the Sun's degree (rìdù).)
Using a plane triangle (píngsānjiǎoxíng):
One side is the distance from the center of the second epicycle (cìlún) to the center of the Earth (dìxīnxiàn).
Another side is the radius of the second epicycle (cìlún) (only for Mars (huǒxīng) does the radius of the second epicycle (cìlún) vary;
the method for finding it is detailed later).
The included exterior angle is the secondary argument (cìyǐn) (if it exceeds a half-circumference, subtract it from a full circumference and use the remainder).
Calculate the angle opposite the radius of the second epicycle (cìlún) to obtain the secondary mean anomaly (cìjūnshù).
Also, calculate the side opposite the secondary argument angle (cìyǐnjiǎo) to obtain the distance from the star to the center of the Earth (xīngjùdìxīnxiàn).
Then, add or subtract the secondary mean anomaly (cìjūnshù) from the initial true motion (chūshíxíng)
(addition or subtraction is opposite to that for the initial mean anomaly (chūjūn))
to obtain the star's true motion in its own path (běnxīngběndàoshíxíng).
To calculate Mars's (huǒxīng) true radius of the second epicycle (cìlún):
Designate Mars's (huǒxīng) full diameter of the deferent (běnlún quánjìng) as 20,000,000, which is the first ratio (yīlǜ).
The maximum eccentricity of its orbit (běntiāngāobēidàchā) is the second ratio (èrlǜ).

The versed sine of the epicycle center's distance from its lowest point (jūnlúnxīnjùzuìbēizhīzhèngshǐ) is the third ratio (sānlǜ) (subtract the argument (yǐnshù) from a half-circumference to get the epicycle center's distance from its lowest degree (jūnlúnxīnjùzuìbēidù)).
The fourth ratio (sìlǜ) thus obtained is the eccentricity difference of its orbit (běntiāngāobēichā).
Then, designate the Sun's full diameter of the deferent (tàiyángběnlúnquánjìng) as 20,000,000, which is the first ratio (yīlǜ).
The maximum eccentricity of the Sun's orbit (tàiyánggāobēidàchā) is the second ratio (èrlǜ).

The versed sine of the Sun's argument (tàiyángyǐnshù) for the current day is the third ratio (sānlǜ) (if the argument (yǐnshù) exceeds a half-circumference, subtract it from a full circumference and use the remainder).
The fourth ratio (sìlǜ) thus obtained is the Sun's eccentricity difference (tàiyánggāobēichā).
Then, take Mars's (huǒxīng) minimum radius of the second epicycle (zuìxiǎocìlúnbànjìng).
Add the two eccentricity differences (gāobēichā) to it
to obtain Mars's (huǒxīng) true radius of the second epicycle (cìlúnshíbànjìng).
To calculate the star's true ecliptic motion (huángdàoshíxíng):
Take the star's initial true motion (běnxīngchūshíxíng).
Subtract the star's conjunction motion (běnxīngzhèngjiāoxíng)
to obtain the argument from conjunction (jùjiāoshíxíng).
(This is the distance from the center of the second epicycle (cìlún) to the conjunction point.)
Then, the radius of its celestial sphere (běntiānbànjìng) is the first ratio (yīlǜ).
The cosine of the angle of intersection between its path and the ecliptic (huángdào) is the second ratio (èrlǜ).
The tangent of the argument from conjunction (jùjiāoshíxíng) is the third ratio (sānlǜ).
The fourth ratio (sìlǜ) thus obtained is the tangent.
Consult the table to find the ecliptic degree (huángdàodù).
Subtract this from the argument from conjunction (jùjiāoshíxíng)
to obtain the ascent difference (shēngdùchā).
Add or subtract this from the true motion in its own path (běndàoshíxíng)
(if the argument from conjunction (jùjiāoshíxíng) is not in the first or second quadrant, subtract;
if it is in the first or third quadrant, add)
to obtain the star's true ecliptic motion (běnxīnghuángdàoshíxíng).
To find the observed latitude of the three stars (Sānxīng),
take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the angle of intersection between the star's path and the ecliptic as the second ratio,
and the sine of the true motion relative to the node as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is a sine,
from which, by consulting the table, the initial latitude is found.
Then, take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the initial latitude as the second ratio,
and the distance of the epicycle center from the geocentric line as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the star's distance from the ecliptic line.
Next, take the star's distance from the geocentric line as the first ratio,
the star's distance from the ecliptic line as the second ratio,
and the radius of the celestial sphere as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is a sine.
By consulting the table, the observed latitude of the star is found,
and its north-south direction is determined accordingly.
(From the first to the fifth palace of true motion relative to the node is north of the ecliptic;
from the sixth to the eleventh palace is south of the ecliptic.)
To find the ecliptic longitude and the day number,
this is the same as for the sun's position.
To find the time of crossing the palace (jiāo gōng),
this is the same as for the moon's apogee/perigee (yuè lí).
To find the fixed limits for the morning and evening visibility/invisibility (fú jiàn dìng xiàndù) of the three stars,
the star's true ecliptic motion coinciding in palace and degree with the sun's true motion is considered "conjunction and invisibility" (hé fú).
After hé fú, as the star gradually moves away from the sun,
it becomes "morning appearance" (chén jiàn) in the east, moving prograde.
Prograde motion gradually slows down,
and after reaching its slowest point, it retrogrades, which is called "stationary and retrograde" (liú tuì).
When it first retrogrades a semi-circle away from the sun, it is called "retrograde opposition" (tuì chōng).
The day after tuì chōng is "evening appearance" (xī jiàn).
Retrograde motion gradually slows down,
and after reaching its slowest point, it moves prograde, which is called "stationary and prograde" (liú shùn).
At the beginning of prograde motion, it gradually accelerates and approaches the sun again,
until it reaches hé fú,
which is "evening invisibility" (xī bù jiàn).
The limits for its visibility/invisibility are:
Sātīng 11 degrees,
Mùxīng 10 degrees,
Huǒxīng 11.5 degrees.
If, a certain number of days before or after hé fú,
the sun's true motion and the star's true motion are close to this limit,
then use the star's true ecliptic motion on that day,
applying spherical trigonometry.
The angle of intersection between the equator and the horizon is one known angle,
(for evening,
use the internal angle after the vernal equinox,
and the external angle after the autumnal equinox;
the opposite for morning.)
The true motion's distance from the vernal/autumnal equinox is the opposite side.
The maximum obliquity of the ecliptic is another known angle.
From this, the unknown opposite side is found.
Then, using the two known sides opposite the two known angles,
find the other unknown angle,
(for evening,
use the internal angle after the autumnal equinox,
and the external angle after the vernal equinox;
the opposite for morning.)
This is the height above the horizon at the limit.
Then, use spherical trigonometry,
with a right angle,
and the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the horizon,
(which is the height above the horizon at the limit.)
The star's visibility/invisibility limit
is the arc opposite the intersecting angle.
Find the arc opposite the right angle,
which is the ecliptic distance from the sun.
(If the star has no latitude distance on the ecliptic,
this is the fixed limit.)
Also use spherical trigonometry,
with a right angle,
and the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the horizon.
The star's latitude distance is the arc opposite the intersecting angle.
Find the arc between the two angles,
which is the addition/subtraction difference.
By adding or subtracting it from the ecliptic distance from the sun,
(add for south latitude,
subtract for north latitude.)
The fixed visibility/invisibility limit is obtained.
Observe if the star's distance from the sun is close to the fixed limit.
If it is a certain number of days before hé fú,
then that day is "evening invisibility";
if it is a certain number of days after hé fú,
then that day is "morning appearance."
To find the time of hé fú for the three stars,
when the sun's true motion is about to reach the star's true motion,
that is the day of hé fú;
if it has already passed the star's true motion,
that is the next day of hé fú.
To find the time,
subtract the star's daily true motion from the sun's daily true motion (i.e., the difference between the true motions of today and tomorrow)
as the first ratio.
The rest is the same as finding the new and full moon for yuè lí.
To find the time of tuì chōng for the three stars,
when the star's ecliptic true motion and the sun's true motion are about half a circle apart,
that is the day of tuì chōng;
if it has already passed half a circle,
that is the next day of tuì chōng.
The method for finding the time
is to add the sun's daily true motion and the star's daily true motion as the first ratio.
The rest is the same as before.
To find the time of same degree (tóng dù),
add or subtract the daily true motions of the two stars (subtract if both stars move in the same direction;
add if one is prograde and one is retrograde)
as the first ratio.
The fractional part of the hour is the second ratio.
The distance between the two stars is the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the fraction from midnight (zǐ zhèng).
Add it to the time to get the result.
This applies to all five planets.

Method for calculating Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng:
To find the winter solstice (tiān zhèng dōng zhì),
this is the same as for the sun's position.
To find the parallel motion of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng's primary body (běn xīng),
this is the same as for Sātīng, Mùxīng, and Huǒxīng.
To find the highest motion of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng,
this is the same as for Sātīng, Mùxīng, and Huǒxīng.
To find the visibility/invisibility parallel motion of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng,
this is the same as for the primary body's parallel motion.
To find the nodal motion (zhèng jiāo xíng) of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng,
set the primary body's highest parallel motion,
subtract 16 degrees for Jīnxīng,
and add or subtract 6 palaces for Shuǐxīng,
and the result is obtained.
To find Jīnxīng's initial true motion,
use the primary body's argument (yǐn shù) to find the initial mean anomaly (chū jūn shù),
and add or subtract it from the primary body's parallel motion
to get the primary body's initial true motion.
And to find the distance of the epicycle center from the geocentric line,
this is the same as for Sātīng, Mùxīng, and Huǒxīng.
To calculate the initial true motion of Shuǐxīng (Mercury):
Use a plane triangle.
Take the radius of the epicycle as one side,
and the radius of the deferent as another side.
The angle enclosed by them is the triple of the argument as the outer angle.
(If it exceeds a semicircle, subtract it from a full circle
and use the remainder.)
Find the side opposite to this angle,
and also the angle opposite to the deferent radius.
Then use another plane triangle.
Take the radius of the celestial sphere as the greater side,
and the side opposite to the angle as the smaller side.
The angle opposite to the deferent radius, added to or subtracted from the deferent’s distance from its apogee,
(If the argument is less than a semicircle,
subtract it from a semicircle;
if it exceeds a semicircle,
subtract a semicircle;
this is the deferent’s distance from its apogee.
The method of addition and subtraction
is to add if the triple argument does not exceed a semicircle,
and subtract if it exceeds a semicircle.)
is the enclosed angle.
Calculate the angle opposite the smaller side, which is the initial mean anomaly,
and also calculate the side opposite the angle, which is the distance from the secondary epicycle center to the geocenter.
Add or subtract the initial mean anomaly from Shuǐxīng’s parallax,
(For arguments from the 1st to 5th mansions, subtract;
from the 6th to 11th mansions, add.)
to get Shuǐxīng’s initial true motion.
To calculate the true motion of Jīnxīng (Venus) and Shuǐxīng during their morning/evening apparitions and disappearances:
Place the planet's parallax for apparition/disappearance,
and add or subtract the planet's initial mean anomaly.
(For arguments from the 1st to 5th mansions, add;
from the 6th to 11th mansions, subtract.)
This gives the result.
To calculate the ecliptic true motion of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng:
Use a plane triangle.
Take the planet's distance from the secondary epicycle center to the geocenter as one side,
and the planet's secondary epicycle radius as another side.
The angle enclosed by them is the planet's true motion for apparition/disappearance as the outer angle.
(If it exceeds a semicircle, subtract it from a full circle
and use the remainder.)
Calculate the angle opposite to the secondary epicycle radius, which is the secondary mean anomaly,
and also calculate the side opposite to the angle, which is the planet's distance from the geocenter.
Add or subtract the secondary mean anomaly from the initial true motion.
(For true motion during apparition/disappearance from the 1st to 5th mansions, add;
from the 6th to 11th mansions, subtract.)
This gives the planet's ecliptic true motion.
To calculate Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng’s true motion relative to the secondary node:
Take the planet's initial true motion,
and subtract the planet's true motion at the ascending node,
to get the true motion relative to the node.
Add this to the planet's true motion for apparition/disappearance,
to get the planet's true motion relative to the secondary node.
To calculate Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng’s apparent latitude:
Take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio.
The sine of the angle of intersection between the planet's secondary epicycle and the ecliptic as the second ratio.
(For Jīnxīng, there is only one angle of intersection;
for Shuǐxīng, the angle of intersection varies.
The actual angle of intersection must be calculated and used;
the method is detailed later.)
The sine of the planet's true motion relative to the secondary node as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is a sine.
Consult the table to get the planet's secondary latitude.
Then, take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the planet's secondary latitude as the second ratio,
the planet's secondary epicycle radius as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the planet's distance from the ecliptic.
Then, take the planet's distance from the geocenter as the first ratio,
the planet's distance from the ecliptic as the second ratio,
the radius of the celestial sphere as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is a sine.
Consult the table to get the planet's apparent latitude,
and determine its north or south direction.
(From the 1st to 5th mansions is north of the ecliptic;
from the 6th to 11th mansions is south of the ecliptic.)
To calculate Shuǐxīng's actual angle of intersection:
Take a radius of ten million as the first ratio.
The node correction in arcseconds as the second ratio.
(For true motion relative to the node from the 9th to 2nd mansions, use the correction for the ascending node;
from the 3rd to 8th mansions, use the correction for the mean node.
Also, apply it according to north or south.)
The sine of the true motion relative to the node as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the angle difference.
Take the angle of intersection,
(The method of using the angle of intersection is the same as using the node correction.)
and add or subtract the angle difference.
(For true motion relative to the node from the 9th to 2nd mansions, if the planet is north of the ecliptic, add;
if south, subtract;
for the 3rd to 8th mansions, it is the reverse.)
This gives the actual angle of intersection.
To calculate the ecliptic mansion degree and the date,
same as the Sun's motion.
To calculate the time of passing through mansions,
same as the Moon's distance.
To calculate the fixed limits for Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng’s morning/evening apparitions and disappearances:
When the planet's true motion is in the same mansion and degree as the Sun's true motion, it is an inferior conjunction,
after which it gradually moves away from the Sun;
in the evening it is seen in the west, moving direct.
The direct motion gradually slows,
and at its slowest point, it reverses to retrograde motion.
Initially, while retrograde, it gradually approaches the Sun,
then it disappears in the evening,
and again becomes aligned with the Sun at the same degree, which is a superior conjunction.
From this point, it again gradually moves away from the Sun,
and is seen in the east in the morning.
It is still retrograde, gradually slowing,
and at its slowest point, it reverses to direct motion.
Initially, while direct, it gradually speeds up,
and again approaches the Sun,
until it reaches inferior conjunction,
then it disappears in the morning.
The limits for their apparition and disappearance
are five degrees for Jīnxīng,
and ten degrees for Shuǐxīng.
The method for calculating these fixed limits
is the same as for Tǔxīng (Saturn), Mùxīng (Jupiter), and Huǒxīng (Mars),
by observing when the planet's distance from the Sun approaches the fixed limit.
For example, a certain number of days before inferior conjunction,
is the day it disappears in the morning;
a certain number of days after inferior conjunction,
is the day it appears in the evening;
a certain number of days before superior conjunction,
is the day it disappears in the evening;
a certain number of days after superior conjunction,
is the day it appears in the morning.
To calculate the time of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng's inferior conjunction:
Observe when the planet's true motion is about to reach the Sun's true motion, which is the day of inferior conjunction;
when it has passed the Sun's true motion, it is the day after inferior conjunction.
The method for calculating the time
is the same as the method for calculating the times of new and full moons for the Moon's distance.
To calculate the time of Jīnxīng and Shuǐxīng's superior conjunction:
Observe when the Sun's true motion is about to reach the planet's true motion, which is the day of superior conjunction;
when it has passed the planet's true motion, it is the day after superior conjunction.
The method for calculating the time
is the same as the method for calculating the times of retrograde oppositions for Tǔxīng, Mùxīng, and Huǒxīng.
For fixed stars, use the numbers
found in the Sun's motion.
Method for predicting fixed stars: To calculate ecliptic longitude,
subtract one from the number of years since the Kāngxī Rénzǐ year,
to get the accumulated precession,
and multiply by it.
Convert this to degrees and minutes,
and add it to the ecliptic longitude from the Kāngxī Rénzǐ year's fixed star table,
to get each fixed star's longitude for the current year.
To calculate equatorial longitude and latitude:
Use a spherical triangle.
Take the star's distance from the ecliptic pole as one side,
the obliquity of the ecliptic as another side,
and the angle between the current year's star position and the summer solstice as the enclosed angle.
Calculate the angle opposite the side representing the star's distance from the ecliptic pole.
Before the summer solstice, use the degree directly;
after the summer solstice, subtract from a full circle and use the remainder.
Starting from the first degree of the Xīngjì mansion,
this gives the equatorial longitude for each fixed star.
Then calculate the side opposite the original angle,
and subtract it from a quadrant;
the remainder is the equatorial latitude.
(Subtracting from a quadrant means north;
subtracting from a quadrant means south.)
To find the culminating star:
Take the current kě (quarter-hour) and fēn (minute) as the first ratio.
The remainder after subtracting today's Sun's true motion from tomorrow's Sun's true motion as the second ratio.
The set time converted to fēn as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
and add it to today's Sun's true motion,
to get the Sun's ecliptic longitude at this time.
Using a spherical triangle,
derive the Sun's equatorial longitude.
Convert the set time to equatorial degrees (one shí (hour) becomes fifteen degrees,
one fēn becomes fifteen minutes,
one miǎo (second) becomes fifteen seconds.)
Add or subtract a semicircle.
(If less than a semicircle, add a semicircle;
if more than a semicircle, subtract a semicircle.)
This gives the Sun's degree from noon at this time.
Add this to the Sun's equatorial longitude,
to get the equatorial longitude of the meridian at this time.
Observe which fixed star's equatorial longitude for the current year matches this,
that is the culminating star.

Method for Predicting Lunar Eclipses:
To find the Winter Solstice in the *Tiān Zhèng* month,
use the *Rì Chén* method.
To find the *Jì Rì*:
Add one day to the number of days from the *Tiān Zhèng* Winter Solstice
to get the *Jì Rì*.
To find the initial *Shuò*:
First find the accumulated days and the *Yuè Lí*.
Take the accumulated days and subtract the *Shuò* value
to get the *Tōng Shuò*.
(For calculations from the top, add.)
Divide by the *Shuò Cè*,
and add one to the quotient to get the accumulated *Shuò*.
The remainder is subtracted from the *Shuò Cè* to get the initial *Shuò*.
(For calculations from the top, the quotient is the accumulated *Shuò*,
no need to add one.
The remainder is the initial *Shuò*,
no need to subtract.)
To find the Moon's entry into the eclipse limit:
Take the accumulated *Shuò*,
multiply it by the Moon's nodes *Shuò Cè*,
remove any full circles (in seconds),
the remainder is the accumulated *Shuò* Moon's nodes.
Add the initial *Shuò* Moon's nodes value
to get the initial *Shuò* Moon's nodes.
(For calculations from the top, take the initial *Shuò* nodes value and subtract the accumulated *Shuò* nodes.)
Then add the Moon's nodes *Wàng Cè*,
and repeatedly add the nodes *Shuò Cè* thirteen times,
to get the mean Moon's nodes for each month's *Wàng*.
Check which month's nodes fall within the eclipse limit
to identify the month of the eclipse.
(Nodes between 5th *gōng*, 15 degrees, 06 minutes and 6th *gōng*, 14 degrees, 54 minutes,
and between 11th *gōng*, 15 degrees, 06 minutes and 1st *gōng*, 14 degrees, 54 minutes,
are all within the eclipse limit.)
Then check the true nodes in detail.
To find the mean *Wàng*:
Multiply the number of months the Moon enters the eclipse limit by the *Shuò Cè*,
add the *Wàng Cè*,
then add the initial *Shuò* day fraction and the *Jì Rì*,
remove any full *Jì Fǎ*,
the remainder is the mean *Wàng* day fraction.
Starting from the first day with *Jiǎzǐ*,
determine the *gānzhī* of the mean *Wàng*,
and use the *kè* and *fēn* to include its remainder,
processing it according to the method.
Starting from the initial hour *Zǐ Zhèng*,
obtain the hours, *kè*, minutes, and seconds.
To find the Sun's mean motion:
Take the accumulated *Shuò*,
add the number of months the Moon enters the eclipse limit to get the *Tōng Yuè*,
multiply by the Sun's mean motion *Shuò Cè*.
Remove any full circles (in seconds),
add the initial *Shuò* Sun's mean motion value,
(for calculations from the top, subtract.)
Then add the Sun's mean motion *Wàng Cè*,
and that is the result.
To find the Sun's mean apogee:
Take the *Tōng Yuè*,
multiply by the Sun's apogee *Shuò Cè*,
remove any full circles (in seconds),
add the initial *Shuò* Sun's apogee value,
(for calculations from the top, subtract.)
Then add the Sun's apogee *Wàng Cè*,
and that is the result.
To find the Moon's mean apogee:
Take the *Tōng Yuè*,
multiply by the Moon's apogee *Shuò Cè*,
remove any full circles (in seconds),
add the initial *Shuò* Moon's apogee value,
(for calculations from the top, subtract.)
Then add the Moon's apogee *Wàng Cè*,
and that is the result.
To find the Sun's true apogee:
Using the Sun's mean apogee,
find the Sun's equation of the center according to the *Rì Chén* method.
Using the Moon's mean apogee,
find the Moon's primary equation of the center according to the *Yuè Lí* method.
Add or subtract the two equations of the center to get the distance arc.
(If both equations have the same sign, subtract;
if different signs, add.)
Use the Moon's distance from the Sun's mean motion per hour as the first rate,
one hour converted to seconds as the second rate,
the distance arc converted to seconds as the third rate,
to find the fourth rate as the distance time in seconds.
Then determine its sign (add or subtract).
(If both equations have the same sign,
if the Sun's is larger, keep the sign;
if the Sun's is smaller, reverse it;
if one equation is added and one subtracted,
the sign follows the Sun's.)
Then use one hour converted to seconds as the first rate,
the Sun's apogee per hour as the second rate,
the distance time in seconds as the third rate,
to find the fourth rate in seconds.
Convert it to degrees and minutes,
which is the Sun's apogee arc.
(According to the sign of the distance time.)
Add or subtract it from the Sun's mean apogee
to get the true apogee.
To find the Moon's true apogee:
Use one hour converted to seconds as the first rate,
the Moon's apogee per hour as the second rate,
the distance time in seconds as the third rate,
to find the fourth rate in seconds.
Convert it to degrees and minutes,
which is the Moon's apogee arc.
(According to the sign of the distance time.)
Add or subtract it from the Moon's mean apogee
to get the true apogee.
To find the true *Wàng*:
Using the Sun's true apogee,
re-calculate the equation of the center to get the Sun's true equation,
and also find the Sun's distance from the Earth's center line.
(This is the side opposite the right angle of the second plane triangle of the true equation.)
Using the Moon's true apogee,
re-calculate the equation of the center to get the Moon's true equation,
and also find the Moon's distance from the Earth's center line.
(The method is the same as for the Sun.)
Add or subtract the two true equations to get the true distance arc.
(Adding and subtracting is the same as for the distance arc.)
According to the previous method for finding distance time,
find the true distance time in hours and minutes.
Add or subtract it from the mean *Wàng*,
(adding and subtracting is the same as for the distance time)
to get the true *Wàng*.
(If adding exceeds 24 hours,
the true *Wàng* advances one day;
if there is not enough to subtract,
borrow one day as 24 hours for subtraction,
and the true *Wàng* recedes one day.)
To find the true nodes:
Use one hour converted to seconds as the first rate,
the Moon's nodes per hour as the second rate,
the true distance time converted to seconds as the third rate,
to find the fourth rate in seconds.
Convert it to degrees and minutes,
which is the nodes distance arc.
Add or subtract it from the Moon's nodes,
(according to the sign of the true distance time.)
Then add or subtract the Moon's true equation,
to get the true nodes.
If the true nodes fall within the definite eclipse limit,
there will be an eclipse.
(Between 5th *gōng*, 17 degrees, 43 minutes, 05 seconds and 6th *gōng*, 12 degrees, 16 minutes, 55 seconds,
and between 11th *gōng*, 17 degrees, 43 minutes, 05 seconds and 1st *gōng*, 12 degrees, 16 minutes, 55 seconds,
is the definite eclipse limit.
If it does not fall within this limit,
no further calculation is necessary.)
To find the Sun's true ecliptic longitude:
Use one hour converted to seconds as the first rate,
the Sun's mean motion per hour as the second rate,
the true distance time converted to seconds as the third rate,
to find the fourth rate in seconds.
Convert it to degrees and minutes,
which is the Sun's distance arc.
(According to the sign of the distance time.)
Add or subtract it from the Sun's mean motion,
and then add or subtract the Sun's true equation,
to get the ecliptic longitude.
Then use spherical trigonometry to find the equatorial longitude.
(Refer to the section on *Yuè Lí* for finding the Moon's rising and setting times.)
To calculate the actual new moon or full moon time for practical use,
take the daily true mean time difference as the mean time difference,
and the difference in rising degrees (the difference in celestial longitudes between the ecliptic and the equator
) converted to time as the rising degree time difference.
Add or subtract these two time differences to get the total time difference.
(The method for addition and subtraction
is detailed in the section "Calculating the Moon's Anomaly for Practical Use with Parallel Time.")
Add or subtract this from the actual new moon or full moon
to get the practical time of the actual new moon or full moon.
(Those within nine *kè* before sunrise and after sunset
can observe the eclipse.
Those beyond nine *kè* are entirely in daytime,
so there is no need to calculate them.
To calculate the time of maximum eclipse,
take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the cosine of the great distance between the ecliptic and the equator as the second ratio,
and the tangent of the true node's circumference as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the tangent.
Look up the table to find the node's circumference at maximum eclipse.
Subtract this from the true node's circumference
to get the node's circumference rising degree difference.
Then add the Moon's one-hour anomaly value to the Moon's true anomaly,
calculate it according to the method for the initial mean of the Moon's anomaly,
which gives the posterior mean.
Add or subtract this posterior mean with the Moon's true mean.
(If both means have the same sign, subtract;
if different signs, add.)
The resulting number is then added or subtracted with the Moon's one-hour distance from the Sun in parallel.
(If both means are positive, add if the posterior mean is larger,
subtract if smaller.
If both means are negative, subtract if the posterior mean is larger,
add if smaller.
If one mean is positive and one is negative,
the addition or subtraction follows the posterior mean.)
This gives the Moon's true motion relative to the Sun.
Then, convert the Moon's true motion relative to the Sun to seconds as the first ratio,
one hour converted to seconds as the second ratio,
and the node's circumference rising degree difference converted to seconds as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is in seconds.
Convert this to hours and minutes
to get the time interval to maximum eclipse.
Add or subtract this from the practical time of the actual new moon or full moon.
(For the true node's circumference, the first and sixth mansions indicate subtraction,
and the fifth and eleventh mansions indicate addition.)
This gives the time of maximum eclipse.
To calculate the latitude of maximum eclipse,
take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the great distance between the ecliptic and the equator as the second ratio,
and the sine of the true node's circumference as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Look up the table to find the latitude of maximum eclipse.
(For the true node's circumference, the first and fifth mansions indicate north,
and the sixth and eleventh mansions indicate south.)
To calculate the Moon's radius,
take the Moon's highest distance from Earth as the first ratio,
the Earth's radius proportion as the second ratio,
and the Moon's distance from the geocenter line minus the radius of the secondary epicycle as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the Moon's distance from Earth.
Then, take the Moon's distance from Earth as the first ratio,
the Moon's true radius as the second ratio,
and the radius of the celestial sphere as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Look up the table to find the Moon's radius.
To calculate the radius of the Earth's shadow,
take the Sun's highest distance from Earth as the first ratio,
the Earth's radius proportion as the second ratio,
and the Sun's distance from the geocenter line as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the Sun's distance from Earth.
Then, take the Sun's radius in light minutes minus the Earth's radius as the first ratio,
the Sun's distance from Earth as the second ratio,
and the Earth's radius as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the length of the Earth's shadow.
Then, take the length of the Earth's shadow as the first ratio,
the Earth's radius as the second ratio,
and the radius of the celestial sphere as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Look up the table to find the Earth's shadow angle.
Then, take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the tangent of the Earth's shadow angle as the second ratio,
and the length of the Earth's shadow minus the Moon's distance from Earth as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the width of the Earth's shadow entered by the Moon.
Then, take the Moon's distance from Earth as the first ratio,
the width of the Earth's shadow as the second ratio,
and the radius of the celestial sphere as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the tangent.
Look up the table to find the radius of the Earth's shadow.
To calculate the magnitude of the eclipse,
take the Moon's full diameter as the first ratio,
ten tenths as the second ratio,

and the combined diameter (the combined radii of the Moon and the Earth's shadow) minus the difference in latitude at maximum eclipse (if the combined diameter is less than the latitude difference, there is no eclipse)
as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the magnitude of the eclipse.
To calculate the times of first contact and last contact,
take the cosine of the latitude at maximum eclipse as the first ratio,
the cosine of the combined diameter as the second ratio,
and the radius of ten million as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the cosine.
Look up the table to find the arc distance of first and last contact.
Then, convert the Moon's true motion relative to the Sun to seconds as the first ratio,
one hour converted to seconds as the second ratio,
and the arc distance of first and last contact converted to seconds as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is in seconds.
Convert this to hours and minutes
to get the time interval to first and last contact.
Add or subtract this from the time of maximum eclipse
to get the times of first and last contact.
(Subtract for first contact,
add for last contact.)
To calculate the times of totality and emergence from totality,
take the cosine of the latitude at maximum eclipse as the first ratio,
the cosine of the difference between the two radii as the second ratio,
and the radius of ten million as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the cosine.
Look up the table to find the arc distance of totality and emergence from totality.
Then, convert the Moon's true motion relative to the Sun to seconds as the first ratio,
one hour converted to seconds as the second ratio,
and the arc distance of totality and emergence from totality converted to seconds as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is in seconds.
Convert this to hours and minutes
to get the time interval to totality and emergence from totality.
Add or subtract this from the time of maximum eclipse
to get the times of totality and emergence from totality.
(Subtract for totality,
add for emergence from totality.)
To calculate the total duration of the eclipse,
double the time interval to first and last contact,
and you will get it.
To calculate the Moon's ecliptic longitude and latitude,
take the Sun's ecliptic longitude,
add or subtract six mansions.
(If it exceeds six mansions, subtract six mansions;
if less than six mansions, add six mansions.)
Then add or subtract the arc distance of maximum eclipse,
and further add or subtract the ecliptic-equatorial rising degree difference.
(The method for calculating the rising degree difference
is detailed in the section "Calculating the Moon's Anomaly for Ecliptic True Motion.")
This gives the Moon's ecliptic longitude.
To calculate the latitude,
see the Moon's anomaly.
To calculate the Moon's equatorial longitude and latitude,
see the section "Calculating the Moon's Anomaly for Rising and Setting Times."
To calculate the *xiù* degree,
it is the same as the Sun's motion.
To calculate the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the horizon,
convert the time of maximum eclipse to equatorial degrees.
(Every four minutes converts to one degree.)
Then subtract three mansions from the Sun's equatorial longitude.
(If it cannot be subtracted, add twelve mansions and then subtract.)
The remainder is the Sun's equatorial degree distance from the vernal equinox.
Add these two numbers.
(Subtract a full circle if it exceeds one.)
This gives the equatorial degree distance from the vernal equinox to the prime meridian.
Subtract this from a half circle
to get the equatorial degree distance from the vernal equinox to the prime meridian east or west.
(If it exceeds a half circle,
subtract a half circle,
and it is prime meridian west.
If it is less than a half circle,
remove the half circle subtraction,
and it is prime meridian east.)
If the equatorial degree distance from the vernal equinox to the prime meridian east or west crosses a quadrant,
subtract it from a half circle,
and the remainder is the equatorial degree distance from the autumnal equinox to the prime meridian east or west.
(The autumnal equinox's east-west distance from the prime meridian
is opposite to the vernal equinox's.)
Subtract the vernal and autumnal equinox's east-west distance from the prime meridian from ninety degrees.
The remainder is the equatorial degree distance from the vernal and autumnal equinox to the horizon.
This is then used as one side of a spherical triangle,

with the great ecliptic-equatorial distance and the angle of intersection between the equator and the horizon (i.e., the altitude above the equatorial horizon; this is used for the vernal equinox west of the prime meridian and the autumnal equinox east of the prime meridian;
if it is the vernal equinox east of the prime meridian or the autumnal equinox west of the prime meridian,
then subtract this degree from a half circle and use the remainder)
as the two adjacent angles.
The opposite angle obtained
is the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the horizon.
(For the vernal equinox east of the prime meridian and the autumnal equinox west of the prime meridian,
the obtained number is the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the horizon.
For the vernal equinox west of the prime meridian and the autumnal equinox east of the prime meridian,
subtract the obtained number from a half circle,
and the remainder is the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the horizon.)
To find the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the high arc:
Take the sine of the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the horizon as the first ratio (率, lǜ);
the sine of the angle of intersection of the equator and the horizon as the second ratio (率, lǜ);
the sine of the degrees of the equinoxes' distance from the horizon and the equator as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
The fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained is a sine.
Consult the table to find the degrees of the equinoxes' distance from the horizon and the ecliptic.
Next, observe the equinoxes that are above the horizon.
Subtract the Moon's ecliptic longitude from the third and ninth palaces (三宮, Sāngōng and 九宮, Jiǔgōng).
(For the spring equinox, subtract from the third palace (三宮, Sāngōng);
for the autumn equinox, subtract from the ninth palace (九宮, Jiǔgōng).)
The remainder is the Moon's ecliptic distance from the equinoxes.
(If the degrees of the equinoctial palace are greater than the degrees of the Moon's palace,
it is before the equinoxes;
if the reverse is true, it is after.)
Then, add or subtract the degrees of the equinoxes' distance from the horizon and the ecliptic, and the Moon's ecliptic distance from the equinoxes.
This gives the Moon's ecliptic distance from the horizon.
(If the equinoxes are west of noon,
add if the Moon is after the equinox;
subtract if it is before.
If the equinoxes are east of noon, the reverse applies.)
Then observe whether its limit is east or west.
(If the equinoxes are west of noon,
if the Moon's ecliptic distance from the horizon is less than ninety degrees, it is limited to the west (限西, xiànxī);
if it exceeds ninety degrees, it is limited to the east (限東, xiàndōng).
If the equinoxes are east of noon, the reverse applies.)
Then, take the cosine of the Moon's ecliptic distance from the horizon as the first ratio (率, lǜ);
the radius of the celestial sphere as the second ratio (率, lǜ);
the cotangent of the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the horizon as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
The fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained is a tangent.
Consult the table to find the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the high arc.
To find the fixed angle of intersection for first contact and last contact:
Set the circumference of the greatest eclipse.
Add or subtract the arc distance of first contact or last contact.
This gives the circumference of first contact or last contact.
(Subtract to get first contact;
add to get last contact.)
Then, take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio (率, lǜ);
the sine of the maximum distance between the ecliptic and the Moon's path (黃白大距, Huángbái Dàjù) as the second ratio (率, lǜ);
the sine of the circumference of first contact as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
The fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained is a sine.
Consult the table to find the latitude of first contact.
Then, take the sine of the circumference of last contact as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
(The first and second ratios (率, lǜ) are the same as before.)
The fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained is a sine.
Consult the table to find the latitude of last contact.
(For the circumference, the first palace (初宮, Chūgōng) and fifth palace (五宮, Wǔgōng) are north latitude;
the sixth palace (六宮, Liùgōng) and eleventh palace (十一宮, Shíyīgōng) are south latitude.)
Then, take the sine of the sum of radii as the first ratio (率, lǜ);
the sines of the latitudes of first contact and last contact as the respective second ratios (率, lǜ);
a radius of ten million as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
For each, the fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained is a sine.
Consult the table to find the angular difference between the two latitudes for first contact and last contact.
Add or subtract the angular difference between the two latitudes from the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the high arc.
This gives the fixed angle of intersection for first contact and last contact.
(For first contact, if limited to the east (限東, xiàndōng),
add if south latitude;
subtract if north latitude.
If limited to the west (限西, xiànxī),
subtract if south latitude;
add if north latitude.
For last contact, the reverse applies.)
If there is no angular difference in latitude for first contact and last contact,
then the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the high arc is the fixed angle of intersection.
To find the azimuth of first contact and last contact:
If the eclipse is limited to the east (限東, xiàndōng),
and the fixed angle of intersection is within forty-five degrees,
first contact is lower-left,
and last contact is upper-right.
If it is beyond forty-five degrees,
first contact is left-lower,
and last contact is right-upper.
If it is exactly ninety degrees,
first contact is directly left,
and last contact is directly right.
If it exceeds ninety degrees,
first contact is left-upper,
and last contact is right-lower.
If the eclipse is limited to the west (限西, xiànxī),
and the fixed angle of intersection is within forty-five degrees,
first contact is upper-left,
and last contact is lower-right.
If it is beyond forty-five degrees,
first contact is left-upper,
and last contact is right-lower.
If it is exactly ninety degrees,
first contact is directly left,
and last contact is directly right.
If it exceeds ninety degrees,
first contact is left-lower,
and last contact is right-upper.
(In the capital (京師, Jīngshī), the quadrant of the ecliptic and the horizon is always south of the zenith,
so the azimuth is determined thus.
If it is north of the zenith, the reverse applies.)
To find the magnitude of the partial eclipse in minutes and seconds:
Subtract the time of sunrise or sunset on the current day
(if first contact or greatest eclipse is before sunset,
it is a partial eclipse at setting, use sunset time.
If greatest eclipse or last contact is after sunrise,
it is a partial eclipse at rising, use sunrise time.)
from the time of greatest eclipse.
The remainder is the time distance of the partial eclipse.
Take one hour converted to seconds as the first ratio (率, lǜ);
the actual change in degrees of the Moon's distance from the Sun in one hour, converted to seconds, as the second ratio (率, lǜ);
the time distance of the partial eclipse, converted to seconds, as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
The fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained is in seconds.
Record it in degrees and minutes.
This is the arc distance of the partial eclipse.
Then, take a radius of ten million as the first ratio (率, lǜ);
the cotangent of the arc distance of the partial eclipse as the second ratio (率, lǜ);
the cosine of the latitude of greatest eclipse as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
The fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained is a cotangent.
Consult the table to find the arc distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse.
Then, take the Moon's full diameter as the first ratio (率, lǜ);
one-tenth as the second ratio (率, lǜ);
the remainder after subtracting the arc distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse from the sum of radii as the third ratio (率, lǜ).
The fourth ratio (率, lǜ) thus obtained
is the magnitude of the partial eclipse in minutes and seconds.
To find the times of lunar eclipses in various provinces:
Convert the longitudinal difference of each province from the capital (京師, Jīngshī) into time
(for every degree of difference,
the time difference is four minutes).
Add or subtract this from the lunar eclipse time in the capital (京師, Jīngshī).
This gives the result.
(Add for east,
subtract for west.)
To find the azimuth of lunar eclipses in various provinces:
Using the equatorial altitude of each province and the lunar eclipse time,
calculate it according to the method for determining azimuth in the capital (京師, Jīngshī).
This gives the result.
To draw a lunar eclipse diagram:
First, draw two lines, one horizontal and one vertical,
intersecting at a right angle.
The horizontal line represents the ecliptic;
the vertical line represents the ecliptic meridian.
Use the radius of the Earth's shadow to draw a circle from the center to represent the umbra (闇虛, ànxū).
Next, use the sum of radii as the measure to draw an outer empty circle (外虛圈, wàixūquān),
which defines the limits of first contact and last contact.
Then, use the difference between the two radii as the measure to draw an inner empty circle (內虛圈, nèixūquān),
which defines the limits of total eclipse and reappearance of light.
Then, on the outer empty circle, along the vertical line, either left or right,
take five degrees as a mark.
Observe the first palace (初宮, Chūgōng) and eleventh palace (十一宮, Shíyīgōng) of the actual circumference and make a mark to the right;
the fifth palace (五宮, Wǔgōng) and sixth palace (六宮, Liùgōng) and make a mark to the left.
Then, draw a line from the mark through the center of the circle to the lower circumference of the outer empty circle.
This is the lunar path meridian.
On this line, measure the latitude of greatest eclipse from the center of the circle to make a mark.
This is the location of the Moon's center at greatest eclipse.
From this, draw a cross-horizontal line.
This is the lunar path (白道, Báidào).
The points where it intersects the inner and outer empty circles
are the locations of the Moon's center for the four limits before and after greatest eclipse.
Finally, use the Moon's radius as the measure and draw small circles at each of the five limit Moon centers.
The images of the five limits are then complete.
Calculation of Solar Eclipses
The Sun's actual radius is 507.
For the rest, see the method for calculating solar eclipses from lunar eclipses.
To find the Winter Solstice (冬至, Dōngzhì) in the first month (天正, Tiānzhèng):
Same as the Sun's longitude.
To find the number of days in the calendar cycle (紀日, Jìrì):
Same as lunar eclipses.
To find the first new moon (首朔, Shǒushuò):
Same as lunar eclipses.
To find when the Moon enters the eclipse limit:
Same as the method for finding the mean synodic period of each month's full moon in lunar eclipses,
but without using the full moon ephemeris (望策, wàngcè).
This is the mean synodic period of each month's new moon.
Observe which month's synodic period enters the edible limit.
That is the month with an eclipse.
(From 5th palace 9 degrees 08 minutes to 6th palace 8 degrees 51 minutes,
and from 11th palace 21 degrees 09 minutes to 1st palace 20 degrees 52 minutes,
all are edible limits.)
