To find the Moon's mean Equation of Center (太陰平引, Tàiyīn Píngyǐn):
The above four items
are all the same as the method for finding the mean full moon in lunar eclipses,
but without adding the full moon ephemeris (望策, wàngcè).
To find the Sun's true Equation of Center (太陽實引, Tàiyáng Shíyǐn):
Same as lunar eclipses.
To find the Moon's true Equation of Center (太陰實引, Tàiyīn Shíyǐn):
Same as lunar eclipses.
To find the true new moon (實朔, Shíshuò):
Same as the method for finding the true full moon in lunar eclipses.
To find the true synodic period (實交周, Shíjiāozhōu):
Same as lunar eclipses.
Observe when the true synodic period enters the eclipse limit for an eclipse.
(From 5th palace 11 degrees 45 minutes to 6th palace 6 degrees 14 minutes,
and from 11th palace 23 degrees 46 minutes to 1st palace 18 degrees 15 minutes,
are the true new moon edible limits.)
To find the Sun's actual ecliptic longitude and equatorial longitude:
Same as lunar eclipses.
To find the time of the true new moon,
it is the same method as finding the time of the true full moon for a lunar eclipse.
(If the time of the true new moon
is before sunrise or after sunset
by more than five *kè* [刻],
then it is nighttime
and need not be calculated.)
To find the time of greatest eclipse,
the method is the same as for finding the moment of greatest eclipse for a lunar eclipse.
To find the equatorial degrees from the equinoxes to the meridian at the time of use,
subtract three *gōng* [宮] from the sun's equatorial longitude.
(If it is insufficient to subtract,
add twelve *gōng* and then subtract.)
This is the sun's equatorial degrees after the vernal equinox.
Then convert the time of greatest eclipse into equatorial degrees,
add or subtract half a circumference.
(If it exceeds half a circumference, subtract half a circumference;
if it is less than half a circumference, add half a circumference.)
This is the sun's true equatorial degrees from the meridian.
Add the two numbers.
(If it totals a full circumference, remove it.)
If the number does not exceed a quadrant,
it is the equatorial degrees west of the meridian from the vernal equinox.
If it exceeds one quadrant,
subtract it from half a circumference;
the remainder is the equatorial degrees east of the meridian from the autumnal equinox.
If it exceeds two quadrants,
then subtract two quadrants;
the remainder is the equatorial degrees west of the meridian from the autumnal equinox.
If it exceeds three quadrants,
subtract it from a full circumference;
the remainder is the equatorial degrees east of the meridian from the vernal equinox.
To find the ecliptic degrees from the equinoxes to the meridian at the time of use,
take the cosine of the greatest angle between the ecliptic and equator as the first ratio,
the radius of the celestial sphere as the second ratio,
and the tangent of the equatorial degrees from the equinoxes to the meridian as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the tangent.
Check the table to get the ecliptic degrees from the equinoxes to the meridian at the time of use.
To find the ecliptic-equator difference in latitude at the noon of the time of use,
take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the greatest angle between the ecliptic and equator as the second ratio,
and the sine of the ecliptic degrees from the meridian as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Check the table to get the ecliptic-equator difference in latitude at the noon of the time of use.
To find the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian circle at the time of use,
take the sine of the ecliptic degrees from the meridian as the first ratio,
the sine of the equatorial degrees from the meridian as the second ratio,
and the radius of the celestial sphere as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Check the table to get the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian circle at the time of use.
To find the *gōng* [宮] degrees of the ecliptic at the noon of the time of use,
take the ecliptic degrees from the equinoxes to the meridian at the time of use.
For the vernal equinox, add or subtract three *gōng*.
(If west of the meridian, add three *gōng*;
if east of the meridian, subtract from three *gōng*.)
For the autumnal equinox, add or subtract nine *gōng*.
(If west of the meridian, add nine *gōng*;
if east of the meridian, subtract from nine *gōng*.)
This gives the *gōng* degrees of the ecliptic at the noon of the time of use.
To find the height of the ecliptic at the noon of the time of use,
take the equatorial altitude
(the remainder after subtracting the quadrant from the altitude of the north pole).
Add or subtract the ecliptic-equator difference in latitude at noon.
(Add for ecliptic *gōng* 3 to 8;
subtract for *gōng* 9 to 2.)
This gives the result.
To find the horizontal quadrant distance of the ecliptic from the meridian at the time of use,
take the cosine of the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian circle as the first ratio,
the radius of the celestial sphere as the second ratio,
and the tangent of the height of the ecliptic at noon as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the tangent.
Check the table to get degrees and minutes.
Subtract this from ninety degrees;
the remainder is the degrees and minutes of the horizontal quadrant distance of the ecliptic from the meridian.
To find the *gōng* degrees of the horizontal ecliptic quadrant at the time of use,
add or subtract the degrees and minutes of the horizontal quadrant distance from the meridian with the *gōng* degrees of the ecliptic at noon.
(For the *gōng* degrees of the ecliptic at noon, add for *gōng* 1 to 5;
subtract for *gōng* 6 to 11.
If the height of the ecliptic at noon exceeds ninety degrees,
then reverse the addition and subtraction.)
This gives the result.
To find the moon's distance from the boundary at the time of use,
subtract the *gōng* degrees of the horizontal ecliptic quadrant at the time of use from the sun's ecliptic longitude.
The remainder is the moon's degrees from the boundary.
Observe whether the boundary is east or west.
(If the sun's ecliptic longitude is greater than the *gōng* degrees of the horizontal ecliptic quadrant, it is east of the boundary;
if smaller, it is west of the boundary.)
To find the height of the boundary from the horizon at the time of use,
take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian circle as the second ratio,
and the cosine of the height of the ecliptic at noon as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the cosine.
Check the table to get the height of the boundary from the horizon.
To find the moon's height arc at the time of use,
take the radius of the celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the height of the boundary from the horizon as the second ratio,
and the cosine of the moon's distance from the boundary as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the sine.
Check the table to get the moon's height arc.
To find the angle of intersection of the ecliptic height arc at the time of use,
take the sine of the moon's distance from the boundary as the first ratio,
the cotangent of the height of the boundary from the horizon as the second ratio,
and the radius of the celestial sphere as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the tangent.
Check the table to get the angle of intersection of the ecliptic height arc.
To find the angle of intersection of the white path height arc at the time of use,
take the angle of intersection of the ecliptic height arc.
Add or subtract the greatest angle between the ecliptic and the white path.
(For *gōng* 1 and 11 of the intersection around greatest eclipse,
if the moon is east of the boundary, add;
if west of the boundary, subtract.
For *gōng* 5 and 6, it is the reverse.)
This gives the result.
(If it exceeds ninety degrees,
east of the boundary becomes west of the boundary,
and west of the boundary becomes east of the boundary.
If it is insufficient to subtract, reverse the subtraction.
Then, if the horizontal ecliptic quadrant is south of the zenith,
the horizontal white path quadrant is north of the zenith;
if the horizontal ecliptic quadrant is north of the zenith,
the horizontal white path quadrant is south of the zenith.)
To find the sun's distance from the earth,
refer to the section "Finding the Radius of the Earth's Shadow" in lunar eclipse calculations.
To find the moon's distance from the earth,
refer to the section "Finding the Moon's Radius" in lunar eclipse calculations.
To find the vertical difference at the time of use,
use a plane triangle
with the earth's radius as one side
and the sun's distance from the earth as another side.
Subtract the moon's height arc at the time of use from a quadrant;
the remainder is the included angle.
Find the angle opposite the side of the sun's distance from the earth.
Subtract one quadrant;
this is the apparent altitude of the sun.
Subtract it from the moon's height arc;
the remainder is the difference in the sun's distance from the earth's radius.
Then use another plane triangle
with the earth's radius as one side
and the moon's distance from the earth as another side.
Subtract the moon's height arc at the time of use from a quadrant;
the remainder is the included angle.
Find the angle opposite the side of the moon's distance from the earth.
Subtract one quadrant;
this is the apparent altitude of the moon.
Subtract it from the height arc;
the remainder is the difference in the moon's distance from the earth's radius.
Subtract the two differences in earth's radius
to get the vertical difference.
To find the horizontal difference at the time of use,
take a radius of ten million as the first ratio,
the cosine of the angle of intersection of the white path height arc as the second ratio,
and the tangent of the vertical difference as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the tangent.
Check the table to get the horizontal difference at the time of use.
To find the approximate time of greatest eclipse,
take the moon's actual daily motion converted to seconds as the first ratio,
one hour converted to seconds as the second ratio,
and the horizontal difference converted to seconds as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is seconds.
Collect this in hours and minutes;
this is the minutes of difference for the approximate time.
Add or subtract it from the time of greatest eclipse.
(If the moon is west of the boundary, add;
if east of the boundary, subtract.
This is determined by whether the angle of intersection of the white path height arc changes or does not change its boundary.)
This gives the approximate time of greatest eclipse.
To find the equatorial degrees from the equinoxes to the meridian at the approximate time,
calculate it by converting the approximate time of greatest eclipse into equatorial degrees.
The rest is the same as the previous method for the time of use.
All subsequent sections follow this pattern,
but all calculations use the degrees and minutes of the approximate time.
To find the ecliptic degrees from the equinoxes to the meridian at the approximate time.
To find the ecliptic-equator difference in latitude at noon at the approximate time.
To find the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian circle at the approximate time.
To find the *gōng* degrees of the ecliptic at noon at the approximate time.
To find the height of the ecliptic at noon at the approximate time.
To find the horizontal quadrant distance of the ecliptic from the meridian at the approximate time.
To find the *gōng* degrees of the horizontal ecliptic quadrant at the approximate time.
To find the moon's distance from the boundary at the approximate time,
take the sun's ecliptic longitude.
Add or subtract the horizontal difference at the time of use
(according to the sign of addition/subtraction for the approximate time difference).
This is the moon's ecliptic longitude at the approximate time.
Subtract this from the *gōng* degrees of the horizontal ecliptic quadrant at the approximate time
to get the moon's distance from the boundary at the approximate time.
The rest is the same as for the time of use.
To find the height of the boundary from the horizon at the approximate time.
To find the moon's height arc at the approximate time.
To find the angle of intersection of the ecliptic height arc at the approximate time.
To find the angle of intersection of the white path height arc at the approximate time.
To find the vertical difference at the approximate time.
To find the horizontal difference at the approximate time.
To find the *shíshèn* (moment of greatest obscuration) apparent motion,
double the *dōngxīchā* (east-west difference) of the given time and subtract the *dōngxīchā* of the proximate time;
then you will obtain it.
To find the *shíshèn* true time:
take the apparent motion, converted to seconds, as the first ratio;
the *jùfēn* (arc difference) of the proximate time, converted to seconds, as the second ratio;
the *dōngxīchā* (east-west difference) of the given time, converted to seconds, as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is in seconds.
Convert this into hours and minutes,
which is the true time *jùfēn*.
Add or subtract this from the given time of *shíshèn*
to obtain the *shíshèn* true time.
(The addition/subtraction sign is the same as that for the proximate time *jùfēn*.)
To find the *zhēntuán shí chūnqiūfēn jùwǔ chìdào dù* (true time vernal/autumnal equinox distance from noon equatorial degrees):
convert the *shíshèn* true time into equatorial degrees and calculate it.
The rest is the same as the method for the given time.
The following items are calculated similarly,
but all calculations use true time degrees and minutes.
To find the *zhēntuán shí chūnqiūfēn jùwǔ huángdào dù* (true time vernal/autumnal equinox distance from noon ecliptic degrees).
To find the *zhēntuán shí zhèngwǔ huángchì jùwěi* (true time noon ecliptic-equatorial difference in latitude).
To find the *zhēntuán shí huángdào yǔ zǐwǔquān jiāojiǎo* (true time angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian).
To find the *zhēntuán shí zhèngwǔ huángdào gōngdù* (true time noon ecliptic arc degrees).
To find the *zhēntuán shí zhèngwǔ huángdào gāo* (true time noon ecliptic altitude).
To find the *zhēntuán shí huángpíng xiàngxiàn jùwǔ* (true time distance of the ecliptic plane quadrant from noon).
To find the *zhēntuán shí huángpíng xiàngxiàn gōngdù* (true time ecliptic plane quadrant arc degrees).
To find the *zhēntuán shí yuè jùxiàn* (true time Moon's distance from the limit):
set the Sun's ecliptic longitude,
add or subtract the *dōngxīchā* (east-west difference) of the proximate time
(according to the addition/subtraction sign of the true time *jùfēn*),
to obtain the true time Moon's ecliptic longitude.
The rest is the same as for the given time.
To find the *zhēntuán shí xiàn jùdì gāo* (true time limit's distance from Earth altitude).
To find the *zhēntuán shí tàiyīn gāo hū* (true time Moon's altitude arc).
To find the *zhēntuán shí huángdào gāo hū jiāojiǎo* (true time angle of intersection of ecliptic altitude arcs).
To find the *zhēntuán shí báidào gāo hū jiāojiǎo* (true time angle of intersection of white path altitude arcs).
To find the *zhēntuán shí gāoxiàchā* (true time altitude difference).
To find the *zhēntuán shí dōngxīchā* (true time east-west difference).
To find the *zhēntuán shí nánběichā* (true time north-south difference):
take a radius of ten million as the first ratio;
the sine of the true time *báidào gāo hū jiāojiǎo* (white path altitude arc intersection angle) as the second ratio;
the sine of the true time *gāoxiàchā* (altitude difference) as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is a sine.
Consult the table to find the *zhēntuán shí nánběichā* (true time north-south difference).
To find the *shíshèn* apparent latitude:
follow the method for finding the *shíshèn jùwěi* (distance from latitude) in a lunar eclipse
to obtain the actual latitude.
Add or subtract the true time *nánběichā* (north-south difference) from it
to get the *shíshèn* apparent latitude.
(If the white path quadrant is south of the zenith,
and the latitude is south, add,
and the apparent latitude remains south;
if the latitude is north, subtract,
and the apparent latitude remains north.
If the latitude is north and the *nánběichā* is greater than the actual latitude,
then subtract inversely, and the apparent latitude becomes south.
The opposite applies if the limit is north of the zenith.)
To find the Sun's radius:
take the Sun's distance from Earth as the first ratio;
the Sun's actual radius as the second ratio;
the radius of this celestial body as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is a sine.
Consult the table to find the Sun's radius.
To find the Moon's radius,
refer to the lunar eclipse section.
To find the magnitude of the eclipse (*shífēn*):
take the Sun's full diameter as the first ratio;
ten parts as the second ratio;
the combined radii (the sum of the Sun's and Moon's radii)
minus the apparent latitude as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the *shífēn*.
To find the time of first contact (*chūkúi*) and last contact (*fùyuán*):
take the cosine of the *shíshèn* apparent latitude as the first ratio;
the cosine of the combined radii as the second ratio;
a radius of ten million as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is a cosine.
Consult the table to find the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú* (arc distance).
Also, take the Moon's actual motion relative to the Sun, converted to seconds, as the first ratio;
one hour, converted to seconds, as the second ratio;
the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú*, converted to seconds, as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is in seconds.
Convert this into hours and minutes,
which is the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùshí* (time distance).
Add or subtract this from the *shíshèn* true time
to obtain the time of first contact and last contact.
(Subtract for *chūkúi*,
add for *fùyuán*.)
To find the *chūkúi chūnqiūfēn jùwǔ chìdào dù* (first contact vernal/autumnal equinox distance from noon equatorial degrees):
convert the *chūkúi yòngshí* (first contact given time) into equatorial degrees and calculate it.
The rest is the same as for the given time.
The following items are calculated similarly,
but all calculations use *chūkúi* degrees and minutes.
To find the *chūkúi chūnqiūfēn jùwǔ huángdào dù* (first contact vernal/autumnal equinox distance from noon ecliptic degrees).
To find the *chūkúi zhèngwǔ huángchì jùwěi* (first contact noon ecliptic-equatorial difference in latitude).
To find the *chūkúi huángdào yǔ zǐwǔquān jiāojiǎo* (first contact angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian).
To find the *chūkúi zhèngwǔ huángdào gōngdù* (first contact noon ecliptic arc degrees).
To find the *chūkúi zhèngwǔ huángdào gāo* (first contact noon ecliptic altitude).
To find the *chūkúi huángpíng xiàngxiàn jùwǔ* (first contact distance of the ecliptic plane quadrant from noon).
To find the *chūkúi huángpíng xiàngxiàn gōngdù* (first contact ecliptic plane quadrant arc degrees).
To find the *chūkúi yuè jùxiàn* (first contact Moon's distance from the limit):
set the Sun's ecliptic longitude,
subtract the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú*,
then add or subtract the true time *dōngxīchā* (east-west difference)
(according to the addition/subtraction sign of the true time *jùfēn*),
to obtain the *chūkúi tàiyīn huángdào jīngdù* (first contact Moon's ecliptic longitude).
The rest is the same as for the given time.
To find the *chūkúi xiàn jùdì gāo* (first contact limit's distance from Earth altitude).
To find the *chūkúi tàiyīn gāo hū* (first contact Moon's altitude arc).
To find the *chūkúi huángdào gāo hū jiāojiǎo* (first contact angle of intersection of ecliptic altitude arcs).
To find the *chūkúi báidào gāo hū jiāojiǎo* (first contact angle of intersection of white path altitude arcs).
To find the *chūkúi gāoxiàchā* (first contact altitude difference).
To find the *chūkúi dōngxīchā* (first contact east-west difference).
To find the *chūkúi nánběichā* (first contact north-south difference).
To find the *chūkúi shìxíng* (first contact apparent motion):

subtract and combine the *chūkúi dōngxīchā* (first contact east-west difference) and the *zhēntuán shí dōngxīchā* (true time east-west difference) (if *chūkúi* and *shíshèn* are in the same limit, subtract;
if *chūkúi*'s limit is east and *shíshèn*'s limit is west, combine)
to get the difference;
then add or subtract the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú* to get the apparent motion.
(For subtraction,
if the eclipse is in the east limit, subtract if *chūkúi dōngxīchā* is large,
add if small.
The opposite applies if the eclipse is in the west limit.
For combination, always subtract.)
To find the *chūkúi* true time:
take the *chūkúi shìxíng* (first contact apparent motion), converted to seconds, as the first ratio;
the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùshí* (time distance), converted to seconds, as the second ratio;
the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú* (arc distance), converted to seconds, as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is in seconds.
Convert this into hours and minutes,
which is the *chūkúi jùfēn* (arc difference).
Subtract this from the *shíshèn* true time
to obtain the *chūkúi* true time.
To find the *fùyuán chūnqiūfēn jùwǔ chìdào dù* (last contact vernal/autumnal equinox distance from noon equatorial degrees):
convert the *fùyuán yòngshí* (last contact given time) into equatorial degrees and calculate it.
The rest is the same as for the given time.
The following items are calculated similarly,
but all calculations use *fùyuán* degrees and minutes.
To find the *fùyuán chūnqiūfēn jùwǔ huángdào dù* (last contact vernal/autumnal equinox distance from noon ecliptic degrees).
To find the *fùyuán zhèngwǔ huángchì jùwěi* (last contact noon ecliptic-equatorial difference in latitude).
To find the *fùyuán huángdào yǔ zǐwǔquān jiāojiǎo* (last contact angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the meridian).
To find the *fùyuán zhèngwǔ huángdào gōngdù* (last contact noon ecliptic arc degrees).
To find the *fùyuán zhèngwǔ huángdào gāo* (last contact noon ecliptic altitude).
To find the *fùyuán huángpíng xiàngxiàn jùwǔ* (last contact distance of the ecliptic plane quadrant from noon).
To find the *fùyuán huángpíng xiàngxiàn gōngdù* (last contact ecliptic plane quadrant arc degrees).
To find the *fùyuán yuè jùxiàn* (last contact Moon's distance from the limit):
set the Sun's ecliptic longitude,
add the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú*,
then add or subtract the true time *dōngxīchā* (east-west difference)
(according to the addition/subtraction sign of the true time *jùfēn*),
to obtain the *fùyuán tàiyīn huángdào jīngdù* (last contact Moon's ecliptic longitude).
The rest is the same as for the given time.
To find the *fùyuán xiàn jùdì gāo* (last contact limit's distance from Earth altitude).
To find the *fùyuán tàiyīn gāo hū* (last contact Moon's altitude arc).
To find the *fùyuán huángdào gāo hū jiāojiǎo* (last contact angle of intersection of ecliptic altitude arcs).
To find the *fùyuán báidào gāo hū jiāojiǎo* (last contact angle of intersection of white path altitude arcs).
To find the *fùyuán gāoxiàchā* (last contact altitude difference).
To find the *fùyuán dōngxīchā* (last contact east-west difference).
To find the *fùyuán nánběichā* (last contact north-south difference).
To find the *fùyuán shìxíng* (last contact apparent motion):

subtract and combine the *fùyuán dōngxīchā* (last contact east-west difference) and the *zhēntuán shí dōngxīchā* (true time east-west difference) to get the difference (if *fùyuán* and *shíshèn* are in the same limit,
subtract;
if *shíshèn*'s limit is east and *fùyuán*'s limit is west,
combine);
then add or subtract the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú* to get the apparent motion.
(For subtraction,
if the eclipse is in the east limit, add if *fùyuán dōngxīchā* is large,
subtract if small.
The opposite applies if the eclipse is in the west limit;
for combination, always subtract.)
To find the *fùyuán* true time:
take the *fùyuán shìxíng* (last contact apparent motion), converted to seconds, as the first ratio;
the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùshí* (time distance), converted to seconds, as the second ratio;
the *chūkúi* and *fùyuán jùhú* (arc distance), converted to seconds, as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is in seconds.
Convert this into hours and minutes,
which is the *fùyuán jùfēn* (arc difference).
Add this to the *shíshèn* true time
to obtain the *fùyuán* true time.
To find the total duration of the eclipse (*shíxiàn zǒngshí*):
combine the *chūkúi jùfēn* and *fùyuán jùfēn*;
then you will obtain it.
To find the Sun's ecliptic *sùdù* (lodging degrees),
same as the Sun's station (*rìchán*).
To find the Sun's equatorial *sùdù*:
using the method for finding equatorial longitude and latitude for fixed stars, obtain the *běnnián chìdào sùqín* (equatorial lodging degrees for the current year);
the rest is the same as the method for finding the ecliptic for the Sun's station.
Calculate the intersection angle for the initial and final contacts.
Obtain the apparent latitudes for the initial and final contacts.
(Same method as for maximum eclipse.)
To find the difference in latitude angles for each.
Add or subtract each from the angle of intersection with the ecliptic's high arc.
This gives the determined intersection angle for the initial and final contacts.
The method is the same as for a lunar eclipse.
To find the azimuth of initial and final contacts:
If the eclipse occurs in the eastern limit,
and the determined intersection angle is within forty-five degrees,
the initial contact is upper-right,
and the final contact is lower-left.
If beyond forty-five degrees,
the initial contact is right-upper,
and the final contact is left-lower.
If exactly ninety degrees,
the initial contact is directly right,
and the final contact is directly left.
If beyond ninety degrees,
the initial contact is right-lower,
and the final contact is left-upper.
If the eclipse occurs in the western limit,
and the determined intersection angle is within forty-five degrees,
the initial contact is lower-right,
and the final contact is upper-left.
If beyond forty-five degrees,
the initial contact is right-lower,
and the final contact is left-upper.
If exactly ninety degrees,
the initial contact is directly right,
and the final contact is directly left.
If beyond ninety degrees,
the initial contact is right-upper,
and the final contact is left-lower.
(In Jīngshī, the yellow flat quadrant is always south of the zenith,
so the azimuth is determined this way.
If north of the zenith, it's the reverse.)
To find the magnitude of the partial eclipse (in fen and miao),
take the time of sunrise or sunset on the current day (if initial contact or maximum eclipse is before sunrise,
it is a partial eclipse at sunrise,
use the sunrise fen;
if maximum eclipse or final contact is after sunset,
it is a partial eclipse at sunset,
use the sunset fen).
Subtract this from the true time of maximum eclipse.
The remainder is the duration of the partial eclipse.
Then, convert the duration of the initial and final contacts into seconds as the first ratio.
Convert the apparent motion of initial and final contacts into seconds as the second ratio.
(If the partial eclipse is before maximum eclipse,
use the apparent motion of initial contact;
if the partial eclipse is after maximum eclipse,
use the apparent motion of final contact.)
Convert the duration of the partial eclipse into seconds as the third ratio.
The calculated fourth ratio will be in seconds.
Convert it into degrees and fen,
which is the arc distance of the partial eclipse.
Also, take a radius of ten million as the first ratio.
The cotangent of the arc distance of the partial eclipse as the second ratio.
The cosine of the latitude distance at maximum eclipse as the third ratio.
The calculated fourth ratio will be a cotangent.
Consult a table to find the distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse.
Then, take the full diameter of the Sun (Tàiyáng) as the first ratio.
Ten fen as the second ratio.
The combined diameter minus the distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the magnitude of the partial eclipse in fen and miao.
To find the solar eclipse times and magnitudes for various provinces,
take the time of maximum eclipse used in Jīngshī,
and add or subtract according to the east-west deviation of each province.
This gives the time of maximum eclipse used for each province.
Then, according to the altitude of the North Pole for each province,
calculate it using the Jīngshī method,
and it is obtained.
To find the solar eclipse azimuth for various provinces,
use the intersection angle of the ecliptic's high arc and the apparent latitudes of initial and final contacts for each province.
Calculate its determined intersection angle,
and it is obtained.
The method for drawing solar eclipse diagrams is the same as for lunar eclipses.
However, only the radii of the Sun (Tàiyáng) and Moon (Tàiyīn) are used as measures,
to draw a large virtual circle,
representing the path of the Moon's (Tàiyīn) center during initial and final contacts.
The inner virtual circle is not used,
as there are no limits for total eclipse and reappearance of light.
For conjunctions and occultations, the numbers used
include the motions of the Seven Luminaries, fixed stars (héngxīng), and eclipses.
To calculate conjunctions and occultations:
To find when a conjunction/occultation enters its limit:
For the Moon (Tàiyīn) conjuncted/occulting a fixed star,
take the longitude of the Moon (Tàiyīn) on the current and next day.
Consult the table of fixed star (héngxīng) longitudes and latitudes for the current year.
If a certain star's latitude does not exceed ten degrees,
and its longitude is within this limit,
then it is an entry into the conjunction/occultation limit.
Then check whether the Moon (Tàiyīn) is above or below the stars within the limit.
(If both the star and Moon (Tàiyīn) latitudes are north of the ecliptic,
the one with the greater latitude is above;
the one with the lesser latitude is below.
If both are south of the ecliptic, it's the reverse.
If one is south and one is north,
the northern one is above,
the southern one is below.)
If the Moon (Tàiyīn) is above,
use if the two latitudes are within two degrees of each other.
If the Moon (Tàiyīn) is below,
use if within one degree.
If the distance is within seventeen fen, it is an occultation (líng).
If beyond eighteen fen, it is a conjunction (fàn).
If latitudes are the same, it is an occultation (yǎn).
For the Moon (Tàiyīn) conjuncted/occulting the Five Planets (Wǔxīng),
if the Moon's (Tàiyīn) longitude on the current day is before the star and on the next day is after the star, it is considered an entry into the limit.
The rest is the same as for conjunctions/occultations with fixed stars.
For the Five Planets (Wǔxīng) conjuncted/occulting fixed stars,
use if the two latitudes are within one degree of each other.
If the distance is within three fen, it is an occultation (líng).
If beyond four fen, it is a conjunction (fàn).
The rest is the same as for the Moon (Tàiyīn).
For the Five Planets (Wǔxīng) conjuncted/occulting each other,
the faster moving one is the conjunctor/occultor star.
The slower moving one is the star being conjuncted/occulted.
If their speeds are the same but one is direct and one is retrograde,
then the direct moving star conjuncts/occults the retrograde moving star.
In all cases, if this star's longitude on the current day is before that star, and on the next day is after that star, it is considered an entry into the limit.
The rest is the same as for conjunctions/occultations with fixed stars.
To find the daily motion in degrees:
For the Moon (Tàiyīn) conjuncted/occulting a fixed star,
simply use the Moon's (Tàiyīn) true daily motion in degrees as the daily motion.
For conjuncted/occulting the Five Planets (Wǔxīng),
add or subtract the Moon's (Tàiyīn) true daily motion in degrees and the star's true daily motion in degrees.
(If the star is direct, subtract;
if retrograde, add.)
This is the daily motion.
For the Five Planets (Wǔxīng) conjuncted/occulting fixed stars,
use the star's true daily motion in degrees as the daily motion.
For the Five Planets (Wǔxīng) conjuncted/occulting each other,
add or subtract the true daily motions in degrees of the two stars.
(If both are direct or both are retrograde, subtract;
if they move in different directions, add.)
This is the daily motion.
To find the time of conjunction/occultation:
Convert the daily motion in degrees to seconds as the first ratio.
The fen below a ke as the second ratio.
Convert the degree difference from the current day's zǐzhèng to seconds as the third ratio.
The calculated fourth ratio will be in fen.
Convert it into shi and ke,
starting from zǐzhèng,
and it is obtained.
To find the Moon's (Tàiyīn) parallax during conjunction/occultation:
(The parallax of the Five Planets (Wǔxīng) is very small,
and can be disregarded.)
Take the fen below a ke as the first ratio.
Convert the Sun's (Tàiyáng) true daily motion in degrees to seconds as the second ratio.
Convert the conjunction/occultation time to fen as the third ratio.
The calculated fourth ratio will be in seconds.
Convert it into degrees and fen,
add it to the Sun's (Tàiyáng) true motion at zǐzhèng on the current day.
This is the Sun's (Tàiyáng) ecliptic longitude at the current time.
Calculate the east-west difference and north-south difference according to the solar eclipse method.
To find the Moon's (Tàiyīn) apparent latitude:
Take the Moon's (Tàiyīn) true latitude.
Add or subtract the north-south difference.
(The method of adding and subtracting
is the same as for a solar eclipse.)
And it is obtained.
To find the Moon's (Tàiyīn) distance from the star:
Add or subtract the Moon's (Tàiyīn) apparent latitude and the star's latitude.
(If both are north or both are south, subtract;
if one is north and one is south, add.)
This gives the Moon's (Tàiyīn) distance from the star.
Use if the distance is within one degree.
To find the apparent time of conjunction/occultation:
Convert the Moon's (Tàiyīn) true hourly motion to seconds as the first ratio.
Convert one hour to seconds as the second ratio.
Convert the east-west difference to seconds as the third ratio.
The calculated fourth ratio will be in seconds.
Convert it to fen,
and add or subtract it from the conjunction/occultation time.
(If the Moon (Tàiyīn) is west of the limit, add;
if east, subtract.)
This gives the apparent time of conjunction/occultation.
Record of the 25th Shíxiàn Calendar (Shíxiànlì), Volume 6, First Method of Yōngzhèng Guǐmǎo:
Origin of the reform of the Solar Ephemeris (Rìchán):
Redefining the true length of the year to balance changes.
The true length of the year in ancient times was longer, but now it is shorter.
Therefore, there is a method of increase and decrease in calendar granting.
That determined by the Westerner Tǐgǔ
subtracted three ten-thousandths from Guō Shǒujìng's.
However, Nàduān and others repeatedly measured it,
stating that Tǐgǔ's subtraction was excessive.
They determined it to be 365.2423344201415 days,
which is slightly more than one ten-thousandth greater than Tǐgǔ's determination.
Dividing the 360 degrees of the full circle by this,
gives the daily mean motion,
which is slightly more than five xiān less than Tǐgǔ's determination.
This method uses it.
Revising the obliquity of the ecliptic and latitude to determine expansion and contraction.
The maximum obliquity of the ecliptic,
which was wide in ancient times, is now narrow,
constantly decreasing without increasing.
Westerners, namely Lì Zhuólǐ and Gáxīní, measured the maximum obliquity of the ecliptic to be 23 degrees, 29 minutes,
which is 2 minutes, 30 seconds less than that determined by Dìgǔ,
and 1 minute less than that determined by Kèbái'ěr.
This method uses it.
Carefully examining the atmospheric refraction to eliminate discrepancies.
The Westerner Dìgǔ realized that the atmosphere surrounds the Earth,
and the sun, moon, and stars shine from outside the atmosphere.
When a person on the ground views them, they are affected by the atmosphere,
which must make them appear higher.
However, the light rays from the sun, moon, and stars, upon entering the atmosphere,
must refract downwards.
Therefore, within the atmosphere, the light ray and the line of sight converge, becoming one.
Outside the atmosphere,
they diverge into two.
The angle formed by the intersection of these two lines
is the angle of atmospheric refraction.
However, there was no arithmetic for it.
Gáxīní repeatedly and meticulously investigated,
stating that although the divergence of the line of sight and the light ray varies,
their convergence occurs at a fixed point.
A line drawn from the Earth's center through this convergent point to the circumference
is the atmospheric secant.
The line of sight forms an angle with the secant,
and the light ray also forms an angle with the secant.
Subtracting these two angles
yields the angle of atmospheric refraction.
Therefore, at the North Pole, at an altitude of 44 degrees,
repeated precise measurements were taken,
yielding a maximum refraction at the horizon of 32 minutes, 19 seconds.
The thickness of the atmosphere was found to be 6095 ten-millionths of the Earth's radius.
The ratio of the sines of the angle of the line of sight and the angle of the light ray
Using this, the atmospheric refraction for each degree can be derived.
This method uses it.
As shown in Figure A, 甲 (jiǎ) is the Earth's center;
乙 (yǐ) is the ground surface;
丙乙 (bǐngyǐ) is the thickness of the atmosphere;
丑甲 (chǒujiǎ) is the secant;
癸乙 (guǐyǐ) is the line of sight;
子戊 (zǐwù) is the light ray;
癸戊子 (guǐwùzǐ) is the angle of atmospheric refraction;
癸寅 (guǐyín) and 子卯 (zǐmǎo) are the two sines.
Carefully examining the parallax to distinguish between various factors.
On the 14th night before the second and minute count of the Rénzǐ year of Kāngxī 11 (1672), at midnight,
Mars was in opposition to the Sun.
The Westerner Gáxīní, in the country of Fùlángjìyà, measured Mars' distance from the zenith to be 59 degrees, 40 minutes, 15 seconds.
Lì Shí'ěr, on the island of Gáyēnà, on the same meridian, measured Mars' distance from the zenith to be 15 degrees, 47 minutes, 5 seconds.
At the same time, instruments with telescopes capable of measuring seconds and fractions of a second were used
to measure the distance between the nearest fixed star on the meridian
and Mars.
Gáxīní's observation showed Mars to be 15 seconds lower.
Since fixed stars have no parallax to be used in formulating the law,
using a planar triangle,
Mars' maximum parallax at the horizon was calculated to be 25 seconds,
with a remainder of 0.37.
Furthermore, based on the ratio of Mars' distance from Earth to the Sun's distance from Earth, as measured by Gēbáiní and Dìgǔ,
which is 100 to 266,
using the method of inverse proportion,
the Sun's maximum parallax at the horizon when at mean distance was found to be 10 seconds.
The difference for each degree
is proportional to the radius and the sine.
This method uses it
to find the ratio of the Earth's radius to the celestial radius of the Sun.
At mean distance, it is 1 to 20,626;
at aphelion, it is 1 to 20,975;
at perihelion, it is 1 to 20,277.
The maximum parallax at the horizon is 9 seconds, 50 micro-seconds at aphelion,
and 10 seconds, 10 micro-seconds at perihelion.
Using the area of an ellipse as parallelism to adjust the mean value.
Since the time of the Westerner Kèbái'ěr,
repeated precise measurements have been made,
and the maximum difference in anomaly is only 1 degree, 56 minutes, 12 seconds.
To deduce the anomaly for each degree:
around aphelion,
the epicycle errs small,
the deferent errs large;
around perihelion,
the epicycle errs large,
the deferent errs small.
Thus, by halving the maximum anomaly difference
and checking its sine,
169,000 is obtained as the difference between the two centers.
Taking the distance from the celestial center to the aphelion and perihelion as 10,000,000,
an ellipse is drawn.
Lines are drawn from the Earth's center
to divide its area equally,
representing parallel degrees.
The angle subtended by these lines is the actual degree
to deduce the anomaly.
This falls between the values obtained from the epicycle and deferent.
However, calculating this for each degree
was difficult without arithmetic.
Gáxīní and others then established methods for calculating areas and angles,
which, when verified against actual measurements,
were found to be perfectly consistent.
This method uses it.
As shown in Figure A, 甲 (jiǎ) is the Earth's center;
乙 (yǐ) is the celestial center;
丁 (dīng) is the aphelion;
丙 (bǐng) is the perihelion;
戊己 (wùjǐ) is the mean distance.
The area divided into sections is parallel,
and the angle of the corresponding circle circumference is the actual ecliptic longitude.
Revising the perihelion longitude to correct the argument.
The Westerner Gáxīní and others measured the annual parallel motion to be 1 minute, 2 seconds, 59 micro-seconds, 51 pico-seconds, 8 atto-seconds,
which is 1 second, 49 micro-seconds and some more than the Jiǎzǐ Yuán Fǎ method.
This method uses it.
Revising the position of parallel motion to correct the New Year.
Using the determinations of the Westerner Gáxīní,
it was calculated that the winter solstice of the Yōngzhèng Guǐmǎo year (1723) occurred on the Bǐngshēn day, at the third *kè* and eleventh *fēn* of the Chǒu hour, with some remainder,
which is two *kè* later than the Jiǎzǐ Yuán Fǎ method.
On the next day, at the first *kè* of the Zǐ hour, the perihelion passed the winter solstice by 8 degrees, 7 minutes, 32 seconds, 22 micro-seconds,
which is 17 minutes, 35 seconds, 42 micro-seconds more than the Jiǎzǐ Yuán Fǎ method.
The origins of the revised lunar anomaly method:
To determine the Moon's true distance from Earth and its maximum anomaly,
which varies with time,
in order to achieve adaptability.
Since the Westerner Kèbái'ěr initiated the elliptical method,
Nàduān and others repeatedly measured lunar anomalies.
When the Sun was at the Moon's mean distance, the maximum equation of the center was found to be 4 degrees, 57 minutes, 57 seconds,
with the difference between the two centers being 433,190.
When the Sun was at the Moon's apogee,
or at the Moon's perigee, the maximum equation of the center was 7 degrees, 39 minutes, 33 seconds,
with the difference between the two centers being 667,820.
After the Sun passes the Moon's apogee or perigee,
the difference between the two centers gradually decreases;
after the mean distance,
the difference between the two centers gradually increases.
When the Sun is 45 degrees before or after the Moon's apogee or perigee,
the difference between the two centers is moderate.
Also, when the Sun is at the Moon's apogee or perigee,
the highest anomaly is always fast,
stopping at 45 degrees after the apogee or perigee.
When the Sun is at the Moon's mean distance,
the highest anomaly is always slow,
stopping at 45 degrees after the mean distance.
This is similar to the Sun and Moon's expansion and contraction (anomaly) and acceleration and deceleration,
but the cycle is doubled.
Therefore, taking the Earth's center as the center,
and adding the maximum and minimum values of the difference between the two centers and halving them,
550,505 is obtained
as the radius of the highest epicycle.
Subtracting and halving them,
117,315 is obtained
as the radius of the highest deferent.
The center of the deferent revolves clockwise along the circumference of the epicycle,
moving at the highest parallel degree.
The true celestial center revolves clockwise along the circumference of the deferent, starting from the farthest point,
moving at twice the degree of the Sun's distance from the Moon's highest point.
Using a planar triangle,
the highest true mean value is derived.
Also, the difference between the two centers for each hour is calculated
to find the area.
Similar to the method for calculating the Sun's anomaly,
this is used to find the acceleration and deceleration,
and is called the first equation.
This method uses it.
As shown in Figure E, 戊 (wù) is the Earth's center;
甲壬癸子 (jiǎrénquǐzǐ) is the epicycle;
乙丁丑丙 (yǐdīngchǒubǐng) is the deferent.
Both 丙 (bǐng) and 丁 (dīng) are the true celestial center.
丙 (bǐng) is the farthest point,
丁 (dīng) is the nearest point.
The difference between the two centers 戊丙 (wùbǐng) is large,
the elliptical area 己庚 (jǐgēng) is small.
The difference between the two centers 戊丁 (wùdīng) is small,
the elliptical area 辛申 (xīnshēn) is large.
Adding an average value to account for the equation of time.
Since the time of the Westerner Kèbái'ěr,
Nàduān and others repeatedly measured and tested,
finding that after the Sun is at perihelion, the Moon's parallel motion is always slow,
while the highest parallel motion and the quadrature parallel motion are always fast.
The opposite is true after the Sun is at aphelion.
Therefore, when the Sun is at the mean distance,
the Moon's parallel motion has a difference of 11 minutes, 50 seconds;
the highest parallel motion has a difference of 19 minutes, 56 seconds;
the quadrature parallel motion has a difference of 9 minutes, 30 seconds.
The difference for each degree in between
is always proportional to the Sun's mean distance mean value and the Sun's per-degree mean value,
and is called the "first average."
This method uses it.
Added two mean anomalies to average the area.
Since the time of the Westerner Isaac Newton (Nàiduān),
repeated precise measurements have been made,
revealing that when the Sun is at the apogee or perigee of the Moon's orbit, the Moon's parallel motion is always slower,
stopping at 45 degrees after the apogee/perigee.
In the middle of the Moon's orbit, relative to the apogee/perigee, the opposite is true.
However, the greatest cumulative retardation or acceleration
occurs exactly at 45 degrees,
and the difference when the Sun is at its highest (apogee) versus its lowest (perigee)
is also not uniform.
Therefore, it was determined that when the Sun is at its highest,
the maximum difference at 45 degrees after the midpoint of the Moon's apogee/perigee is 3 minutes and 34 seconds;
when the Sun is at its lowest,
the maximum difference at 45 degrees after the midpoint of the Moon's apogee/perigee is 3 minutes and 56 seconds.
After the apogee/perigee is a subtraction,
after the midpoint is an addition.
The difference in the daily distance of the Moon from its highest point for each degree
is proportional to the radius and the sine of twice the degree of the Sun's distance from the Moon's highest point.
The difference in the Sun's distance from the Earth for each degree

is also proportional to the ratio of the cube of the Sun's apogee/perigee distance from the Earth to the cube of the Sun's current distance from the Earth, which is the same as the Sun's highest distance from the Earth.
This is called the two mean anomalies (èrpíngjūn).
This method is used in the present work.
Added three mean anomalies to account for the node difference.
Since the time of the Westerner Isaac Newton (Nàiduān),
it was determined that the celestial north pole (báijí) circulates around the node mean wheel, at twice the degree of the Sun's distance from the node.
Thus, it was determined that after the Sun passes the two nodes (intersections of the ecliptic and lunar path, Huángbái liǎngjiāo),
the Moon's parallel motion is slightly slower;
after the Sun passes the great distance from the nodes (Huángbái dàjù),
the Moon's parallel motion is slightly faster;
the maximum difference is 47 seconds.
After the two nodes is a subtraction,
after the great distance is an addition.
The difference for each degree
is proportional to the radius and the sine of twice the degree of the Sun's distance from the node.
This is called the three mean anomalies (sānpíngjūn).
This method is used in the present work.
Re-established the two mean anomalies to correct for apogee/perigee.
Since the time of the Westerner Giovanni Domenico Cassini (Gásīní),
repeated measurements and observations have determined that when the Sun is 45 degrees before or after the highest syzygy (new moon or full moon, Shuòwàng),
the maximum difference is 33 minutes and 14 seconds;
when the Sun is 45 degrees before or after the lowest syzygy,
the maximum difference is 37 minutes and 11 seconds.
After syzygy is an addition,
after the two quarters (first and last quarter, liǎngxián) is a subtraction.
The two mean anomalies of the Moon's distance from the Sun for each degree
are proportional to the radius and the sine of twice the degree of the Moon's distance from the Sun.
The difference in the two mean anomalies of the Sun's distance from its highest point for each degree

is also proportional to the ratio of the cube of the Sun's apogee/perigee distance from the Earth to the cube of the Sun's current distance from the Earth, which is the same as the Sun's highest distance from the Earth,
similar to the two mean anomalies (èrpíngjūn).
This method is used in the present work.
Re-established the three mean anomalies to match the total sum.
Since the time of the Westerner Giovanni Domenico Cassini (Gásīní),
measurements were taken when the sum of the Moon's distance from the Sun and the Moon's apogee distance from the Sun's apogee was 90 degrees.
Except for the difference in the last mean anomaly,
this difference is equal to when the Moon's distance from the Sun or the Moon's apogee distance from the Sun's apogee alone is 90 degrees.
Measurements were also taken when the sum of the Moon's distance from the Sun and the Moon's apogee distance from the Sun's apogee was 45 degrees.
Again, except for the last mean anomaly,
this difference is equal to when the Moon's distance from the Sun or the Moon's apogee distance from the Sun's apogee alone is 45 degrees.
Thus, it was determined that the difference in the Moon's three mean anomalies
is an addition within half a cycle of the total degrees of the Moon's distance from the Sun and the Moon's apogee distance from the Sun's apogee,
and a subtraction outside half a cycle.
The maximum difference at 90 degrees and 270 degrees is 2 minutes and 25 seconds.
The difference for each degree
is proportional to the radius and the sine of the total degrees.
This method is used in the present work.
Added the last mean anomaly to account for the distance in degrees.
Since the time of the Westerner Giovanni Domenico Cassini (Gásīní),
measurements showed that when the Sun and Moon apogees are at the same degree, or the Sun and Moon are at the same degree, there is only one difference in distance,
which means there are only three mean anomalies.
If the two apogees have a difference in degrees,
and the Sun and Moon also have a difference in degrees,
then, in addition to the three mean anomalies,
after the new moon (shuò) there is a further difference and retardation,
and after the full moon (wàng) there is a further difference and acceleration.
However, when the Moon's apogee distance from the Sun's apogee is 90 degrees, and the Moon's distance from the Sun is also 90 degrees,
there are no three mean anomalies,
and the difference is instead at its maximum.
Therefore, it is known that in addition to the three mean anomalies,
there is also a last mean anomaly (mòjūn).
The 90-degree distance of the Moon's apogee from the Sun's apogee is divided into nine limits (intervals),
each measured when the Moon's distance from the Sun is 90 degrees:
when the two apogees are 90 degrees apart,
the difference is 3 minutes;
80 degrees,
the difference is 2 minutes and 39 seconds;
70 degrees,
the difference is 2 minutes and 19 seconds;
60 degrees,
the difference is 2 minutes;
50 degrees,
the difference is 1 minute and 43 seconds;
40 degrees,
the difference is 1 minute and 28 seconds;
30 degrees,
the difference is 1 minute and 16 seconds;
20 degrees,
the difference is 1 minute and 7 seconds;
10 degrees,
the difference is 1 minute and 1 second.
The difference for each degree in between
is found using proportional means.
The difference for each degree of the Moon's distance from the Sun
is proportional to the radius and the sine of the Moon's distance from the Sun.
After the new moon (shuò) is a subtraction,
after the full moon (wàng) is an addition.
This method is used in the present work.
Re-established the node mean anomaly and the great distance from the nodes to match the differences.
Since the time of the Westerners Isaac Newton (Nàiduān) and Giovanni Domenico Cassini (Gásīní),
it has been measured that when the Sun is at the two nodes,
the maximum inclination angle (jiāojiǎo) is 5 degrees, 17 minutes, and 20 seconds;
when the Sun is 90 degrees from the node,
the minimum inclination angle is 4 degrees, 59 minutes, and 35 seconds.
After syzygy (new moon or full moon),
the inclination angle further increases.
As the Sun's distance from the node and the Moon's distance from the Sun gradually increase,
it gradually becomes larger,
reaching an additional 2 minutes and 43 seconds when the Sun is 90 degrees from the node and the Moon is also 90 degrees from the Sun.
The maximum node mean anomaly (jiāojūn)
is 1 degree, 29 minutes, and 42 seconds.
The sum of the maximum and minimum inclination angles is taken and halved,
which gives the epicycle (běnlún) revolving around the ecliptic pole (huángjí);
the difference is halved,
which gives the deferent (jūnlún) carrying the celestial north pole (báijí).
The full radius of the deferent is divided into five parts;
one part is taken,
and the increase after syzygy is removed from it,
which gives the full radius of the small wheel (xiǎolún) of maximum increase,
placed on the lunar path (báidào).
The remainder is the full radius of the small wheel of the node mean anomaly.
The difference between this and the full radius of the deferent
is the full radius of the negative small wheel (fùxiǎolún),
concentric with the deferent.
The deferent moves negatively,
not independently.
The center of the deferent moves along the circumference of the epicycle,
rotating counter-clockwise,
which is the parallel motion of the node.
The center of the small wheel of the node mean anomaly is on the circumference of the negative small wheel,
starting from the farthest point,
rotating clockwise,
moving at twice the degree of the Sun's distance from the node.
The celestial north pole (báijí) is on the circumference of the small wheel of the node mean anomaly,
starting from the farthest point,
rotating counter-clockwise,
and its motion is again doubled.
The small wheel of increase on the lunar path
has the closest circumference.
The point on the ecliptic (huángdào)
is tangent to the lunar path at syzygy (new moon or full moon).
Its full radius varies in size according to twice the degree of the Sun's distance from the node,
always equal to the versed sine (zhèngshǐ) corresponding to the maximum increase within the small wheel.
Also, within the current full radius, the versed sine corresponding to twice the degree of the Moon's distance from the Sun is taken as the angle subtended.
Verification against actual measurements
shows perfect agreement.
This method is used in the present work.

The origin of the revised method for eclipses:
Using the true longitude of the Sun and Moon from the ecliptic for two consecutive sidereal days to determine the true new and full moons.
First, calculate the mean new and full moons to find the month of the conjunction.
Next, calculate the ecliptic longitudes of the Sun and Moon for the mid-night of the current day and the next day to find the time of the true new and full moons.
Then, calculate the Sun and Moon's longitudes for the current time and the next time to determine the exact moment by proportion.
This differs from the Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ, which only uses two days and considers the yellow and white paths to be in the same longitude.
Using the oblique distance between two longitudes to find the exact time of the greatest phases of solar and lunar eclipses and the true distance between their centers.
Since the ecliptic and lunar path are not originally parallel,
the Sun and Moon's longitudes are often obliquely distant.
If the Sun is considered stationary,
then the Moon would appear to move along an oblique distance line.
Therefore, the line of closest distance between the two centers
does not form a right angle with the lunar path,
but forms a right angle with the oblique distance line.
When the distance arc changes,
it is not proportional to the Moon's true motion relative to the Sun,
but to the oblique distance.
As shown in the diagram, Jiǎ-Yǐ is the ecliptic,
Wù-Yǐ is the lunar path,
Jiǎ-Wù is the latitude of the true new/full moon distance,
Jiǎ-Guǐ is the Sun's true hourly motion,
Wù-Chǒu is the Moon's true hourly motion.
Suppose the Sun is stationary and Guǐ coincides with Jiǎ,
then the Moon is not at Chǒu but at Yín.
Wù-Yín is the oblique distance line between the two longitudes for one hour,
Jiǎ-Mǎo forms a right angle with Wù-Yín,
which is the line of closest distance between the two centers.
Wù-Mǎo is the arc of the greatest phase of the eclipse.
All these arcs are treated as straight lines,
and calculated using plane triangles.
For the first contact and last contact,
the combined diameters are used as the hypotenuse in a right triangle calculation.
Revising the ratio of the true diameters of the Sun and Moon to the Earth's diameter.
The Westerner Mò Jué manufactured a telescopic instrument
and measured the apparent diameter of the Sun to be 31 minutes 40 seconds at its highest,
32 minutes 12 seconds at its mean distance,
and 32 minutes 45 seconds at its lowest.
The apparent diameter of the Moon is 29 minutes 23 seconds at its highest,
31 minutes 21 seconds at its mean distance,
and 33 minutes 36 seconds at its lowest.
Using these numbers, the true diameter of the Sun is calculated to be 96.6 times the Earth's diameter,
and the true diameter of the Moon is 27 percent of the Earth's diameter,
with a remainder of 0.26 and a bit more.
The Sun's parallax is 15 seconds.
This method uses these values.
Revising the method for calculating the shadow radius and shadow difference.
Add the differences in the radii of the Sun, Moon, and Earth,
then subtract the Sun's radius;
the remainder is the true shadow radius.
Furthermore, during a lunar eclipse, the Sun is below the Earth,
and the atmosphere obscures sunlight.
The apparent diameter of the Earth's shadow is larger than its true diameter by approximately 1/69th of the difference between the Moon's and Earth's radii;
this is the shadow difference.
As shown in the diagram, in triangle Jiǎ-Dīng-Xīn,
the two interior angles Dīng and Xīn are equal to the exterior angle Rén-Jiǎ-Xīn.
Angle Dīng is the difference between the Sun's and Earth's radii,
(Diagram data is still missing) Angle Xīn is the difference between the Moon's and Earth's radii.
(Line Jiǎ-Dīng is approximately equal to the Sun's radius Jiǎ-Bǐng,
line Jiǎ-Xīn is approximately equal to the Moon's radius Jiǎ-Jǐ,
as their angles correspond to the Earth's radius Jiǎ-Yǐ.)
The angle Bǐng-Jiǎ-Dīng, which is opposite to Rén-Jiǎ-Jǐ, is the Sun's radius.
Therefore, by adding angles Dīng and Xīn,
angle Rén-Jiǎ-Xīn is obtained.
Subtract angle Rén-Jiǎ-Jǐ from it,
the remainder, angle Jǐ-Jiǎ-Xīn,
is the true shadow radius.
Revising the method for calculating the true time of the greatest phase of a solar eclipse and the apparent distance between the two centers.
Treat arcs as straight lines,
and use plane triangles.
Using the true distance between the two centers at the time of the greatest phase as one side,
the difference in altitude at that time as another side,
and the angle of intersection between the white longitude high arc at that time as the included angle,
the opposite side is found,
which is the apparent distance between the two centers.
Also, find the angle opposite to the true distance between the two centers.
Then assume another time,
(Set forward if eastward,
set backward if westward.)
and find the true distance between its two centers and the difference in altitude as two sides.
Subtract the angle of intersection of the white longitude high arc from the angle of the assumed time's distance arc;
the remainder is the included angle.
Find the opposite side,
which is the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time.
Also find the angle opposite to the true distance between the two centers.
Now, compare the angles of intersection of the white longitude high arcs at the current time and the assumed time,
and subtract the angle opposite to the true distance between the two centers at the current time.
Then add the angle opposite to the true distance between the two centers at the assumed time,
and subtract from the full circumference to get one angle.
Use the apparent distances between the two centers at the current time and the assumed time as the two sides enclosing this angle.
Find the opposite side, which is the apparent motion.
Find the point where its perpendicular bisector intersects the apparent motion,
which is the true time of the greatest phase of the eclipse.
The perpendicular line is the apparent distance at the true time.
(The above additions and subtractions
are stated for setting backward.)
Then, using the obtained true time,
re-examine whether the apparent distance between the two centers matches the calculated perpendicular line;
if it does, that is the determined true time.
As shown in the diagram, Qián is the Sun's center,

The perpendicular bisector Rén-Chǒu is the apparent distance at the true time.
The method for first contact and last contact is the same,
but the combined diameter is used as the limit for verifying the true time.
For an eclipse at the horizon,
the horizontal is the boundary, and the apparent distance between the two centers is directly calculated,
without using apparent motion.

Then use a planar triangle,
with twenty million as one side,
twice the difference between the two centers as another side,

for the six outer palaces, subtract from a full circle to use the remainder.)
Find the angle opposite twice the difference between the two centers;

Set the parallel (píngxíng);

from the sixth to the eleventh palace, subtract.)

Method for calculating lunar motion: To find the true winter solstice,
follow the Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ.
To find the Moon's (Tàiyīn) parallel motion,
follow the Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ.
To find the apogee's (zuìgāo) parallel motion,
follow the Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ to find the motion of the Moon's nodes (Yuèbèi xíng).
To find the nodes' (zhèngjiāo) parallel motion,
follow the Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ.
To find the effective parallel (yòng píngxíng),
take the Sun's (Tàiyáng) maximum mean as the first ratio,
the Moon's (Tàiyīn) first maximum mean as the second ratio,
and convert the Sun's (Tàiyáng) mean for the current day into seconds as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained will be in seconds.
Convert this into minutes (fēn)
(the same applies hereafter)
for the Moon's (Tàiyīn) first mean.
Then, take the maximum mean of the apogee (zuìgāo zuìdà píngjūn) as the second ratio
(the first and third ratios are as before).
The fourth ratio obtained is the apogee's (zuìgāo) mean for the current day.
Then, take the maximum mean of the nodes (zhèngjiāo zuìdà píngjūn) as the second ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the nodes' (zhèngjiāo) mean for the current day.
Record its plus or minus sign.
(The Moon's nodes (Tàiyīn zhèngjiāo) are opposite to the Sun's (Tàiyáng);
the apogee (zuìgāo) is the same as the Sun's.)
Add or subtract each from its parallel motion (píngxíng)
to get the Moon's (Tàiyīn) second parallel motion, and the effective apogee (yòng zuìgāo) and effective nodes (yòng zhèngjiāo).
From the Sun's (Tàiyáng) actual position (shíxíng), subtract the effective apogee (yòng zuìgāo)
to get the distance from the Sun to the Moon's apogee (rì jù yuè zuìgāo).
Subtract the effective nodes (yòng zhèngjiāo)
to get the distance from the Sun to the nodes (rì jù zhèngjiāo).
Next, take a radius of 10 million as the first ratio.
Add or subtract the Sun's (Tàiyáng) mean (jūnshù) from the Sun's (Tàiyáng) argument (yǐnshù) to get the actual argument (shíyǐn).
Take its cosine as the second ratio.
Take twice the difference between the Sun's two centers (Tàiyáng bèi liǎngxīn chā) as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained is the component (fēngǔ).
Then, take the sine of the actual argument (shíyǐn) as the second ratio
(the first and third ratios are as before).
The fourth ratio obtained is the vertical component (gōu).
Add or subtract the component (fēngǔ) from the full diameter of 20 million
(add for the actual argument within the third palace and outside the ninth palace;
subtract for outside the third palace and within the ninth palace)
to get the sum of the chord and the leg (gǔxián hé).
From this, find the chord.
Then subtract it from the full diameter
to get the distance from the Sun to the Earth's center (rì jù dìxīn shù).
Square this number and then multiply by itself again to get the cubic product (lìfāngjī).
Subtract this from the Sun's (Tàiyáng) apogee cubic product (zuìgāo lìfāngjī)
to get the cubic difference for the current time (běnshí lìfāngjiào).
Then, take a radius of 10 million as the first ratio,
each of the two maximum means of the apogee and perigee (gāobēi zuìdà èr píngjūn) as the second ratio,
and the sine of twice the distance from the Sun to the Moon's apogee (rì jù yuè zuìgāo bèidù zhèngxián) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio for each,
which gives the two means of the apogee and perigee for the current time (běnshí gāobēi èr píngjūn).
Then, take the large difference in cubic product between the apogee and perigee (gāobēi lìfāng dàjiào) as the first ratio,
the cubic difference for the current time (běnshí lìfāngjiào) as the second ratio,
and the remainder after subtracting the two means of the apogee and perigee for the current time (běnshí gāobēi èr píngjūn) as the third ratio.
Add the fourth ratio obtained to the second mean of the apogee for the current time (běnshí zuìgāo èr píngjūn)
to get the second mean for the current time (běnshí èr píngjūn).
Record its plus or minus sign.
(If twice the distance from the Sun to the Moon's apogee is less than half a cycle, subtract;
if it exceeds, add.)
Again, take a radius of 10 million as the first ratio,
the third maximum mean (zuìdà sān píngjūn) as the second ratio,
and the sine of twice the distance from the Sun to the nodes (rì jù zhèngjiāo bèidù zhèngxián) as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the third mean (sān píngjūn).
Record its plus or minus sign.
(If twice the distance from the Sun to the nodes is less than half a cycle, subtract;
if it exceeds, add.)
Then, set the second parallel (èr píngxíng),
and add or subtract the second and third means (èr sān píngjūn)
to get the effective parallel (yòng píngxíng).
To calculate the *chūshíxíng* (primary true motion),
use a plane triangle.
Take the radius of the highest epicycle as one side,
and the radius of the highest deferent as another side.
Subtract the *rìjùyuè zuìgāo bèidù* (highest multiple of the Sun-Moon distance) from half a circumference.
The remainder is the included angle.
Calculate the angle opposite the deferent radius.
This is the *zuìgāo shíjūn* (highest true equation),
recording its sign.
(If the *rìjùyuè zuìgāo bèidù* is less than half a circumference, it's plus;
if it exceeds, it's minus.)
Then, calculate the side opposite the original angle.
This is the *běnshí liǎngxīnchā* (current epoch's difference between the two centers).
Add or subtract the *zuìgāo shíjūn* to or from the *yòng zuìgāo* (highest value) to get the *zuìgāo shíxíng* (highest true motion).
Subtract the *yòng píngxíng* (mean parallel) from the *zuìgāo shíxíng* to get the *tàiyīn yǐnshù* (Moon's argument).
Again, use a plane triangle.
Take ten million units of radius as one side,
and the *běnshí liǎngxīnchā* as another side.
Subtract the *tàiyīn yǐnshù* from half a circumference; the remainder is the included angle.
Calculate the angle opposite the *liǎngxīnchā*.
Add it to the original angle.
This again becomes the included angle.
Calculate the angle opposite the ten million units of radius.
This is the *píngyuán yǐnshù* (mean circle argument).
Now, take the radius of the main celestial sphere as the first ratio,
the sine of the *běnshí liǎngxīnchā* as the sine,
and find its cosine from the table as the second ratio.
Take the tangent of the *píngyuán yǐnshù* as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the tangent.
Look it up in the table to get the *shíyǐn* (true argument).
Subtract it from the *tàiyīn yǐnshù* to get the *chūjūnshù* (initial equation).
Place it in the *yòng píngxíng* (mean parallel).
Add or subtract the *chūjūnshù* to it.
(If the argument is from the 1st to 5th *gōng* (house), it's subtraction;
from the 6th to 11th *gōng*, it's addition.)
This gives the *chūshíxíng*.
To calculate the *báidào shíxíng* (true motion in the white path),
place the *chūshíxíng*.
Subtract today's *běnrì tàiyáng shíxíng* (Sun's true motion for this day).
This is the *yuèjùrì* (Moon's distance from the Sun).
Now, take ten million units of radius as the first ratio,
and the *gāobēi zuìdà èrjūnshù* (two largest equation numbers for apogee and perigee) as the second ratio.
Take the sine of the *yuèjùrì bèidù* (multiple of Moon's distance from Sun) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio for each.
These are the *běnshí gāobēi èrjūnshù* (current epoch's two equation numbers for apogee and perigee).
Also, take the *gāobēi lìfāng dàjiào* (larger value of the apogee/perigee cubic comparison) as the first ratio,
and the *běnshí lìfāngjiào* (current epoch's cubic comparison) as the second ratio.
Subtract the *běnshí gāobēi èrjūnshù*; the remainder is the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio.
Add it to the *běnshí zuìgāo èrjūnshù* (current epoch's two highest equation numbers).
This is the *běnshí èrjūnshù* (current epoch's two equation numbers),
recording its sign.
(If the *yuèjùrì bèidù* is less than half a circumference, it's plus;
if it exceeds, it's minus.)
Now, place the *yuèjùrì*.
Add or subtract the *èrjūn*.
This is the *shíyuèjùrì* (true Moon's distance from the Sun).
Place the *tàiyáng zuìbēi píngxíng* (Sun's lowest mean parallel).
Add or subtract six *gōng*.
This is the *rì zuìgāo tàiyīn zuìgāo shíxíng* (Sun's highest, Moon's highest true motion).
Subtract the Sun's highest from it.
This is the *rìyuè zuìgāo xiāngjù* (highest Sun-Moon separation).
Add it to the *shíyuèjùrì*.
This is the *xiāngjù zǒngshù* (total separation).
Take ten million units of radius as the first ratio,
the *zuìdà sānjūn* (largest third equation) as the second ratio,
and the sine of the *xiāngjù zǒngshù* as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio.
This is the *sānjūnshù* (third equation number),
recording its sign.
(If the total is less than half a circumference, it's plus;
if it exceeds, it's minus.)
Also, take ten million units of radius as the first ratio.
Use the *rìyuè zuìgāo xiāngjùdù* (degree of highest Sun-Moon separation) with the mean proportion.
Take the *běnshí liǎngxián zuìdà mòjūn* (current epoch's largest last equation of the two chords) as the second ratio.
Take the sine of the *shíyuèjùrì* as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio.
This is the *mòjūnshù* (last equation number),
recording its sign.
(If the *shíyuèjùrì* is less than half a circumference, it's subtraction;
if it exceeds, it's addition.)
Now, place the *chūshíxíng*.
Add or subtract the *èrjūn*, *sānjūn*, and *mòjūn*.
This gives the *báidào shíxíng*.
To calculate the *huángdào shíxíng* (true motion in the ecliptic),
use a plane triangle.
Take the radius of the orthogonal epicycle as one side,
and the radius of the orthogonal deferent as another side.
The *rìjù zhèngjiāo bèidù* (multiple of the Sun's distance from the node) is the included exterior angle.
(If the *bèidù* exceeds half a circumference,
subtract half a circumference
and use the remainder.)
Calculate half the difference between the two angles opposite the two sides.
Subtract it from the *rìjù zhèngjiāo*.
The remainder is the *zhèngjiāo shíjūn* (true equation of the node).
Add or subtract it (if the *rìjù zhèngjiāo bèidù* is less than half a circumference, it's plus;
if it exceeds, it's minus)
to the *yòng zhèngjiāo* (value for the node).
This is the *zhèngjiāo shíxíng* (true motion of the node).
Place the *báidào shíxíng*.
Subtract the *zhèngjiāo shíxíng*.
This is the *yuèjù zhèngjiāo* (Moon's distance from the node).
Again, take ten million units of radius as the first ratio,
and the versine of the *rìjù zhèngjiāo bèidù* as the second ratio.
(If the *bèidù* exceeds half a circumference,
subtract it from a full circumference
and use the remainder.)
Take half the difference of the *huángbái dàjù* (greatest distance between ecliptic and white path) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio.
This is the *jiāojiǎo jiǎnfēn* (nodal angle decrement).
Also, take half of the *zuìdà jùrì jiāfēn* (greatest Sun-distance increment) as the third ratio.
(The first and second ratios are as before.)
Calculate the fourth ratio.
This is the *jùjiāo jiāchā* (nodal distance increment difference).
Again, take ten million units of radius as the first ratio,
and the versine of the *shíyuèjùrì bèidù* as the second ratio.
(If the *bèidù* exceeds half a circumference,
subtract it from a full circumference
and use the remainder.)
Take half of the *jùjiāo jiāchā* as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio.
This is the *jùrì jiāfēn* (Sun-distance increment).
Place the *zuìdà dàjù* (greatest major distance).
Subtract the *jiāojiǎo* (nodal angle).
Add the *jiǎnfēn* and *jùrì jiāfēn*.
This is the *huángbái dàjù*.
Now, take ten million units of radius as the first ratio,
the cosine of the *huángbái dàjù* as the second ratio,
and the tangent of the *yuèjù zhèngjiāo* as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the tangent.
Look it up in the table to get the *huángdào jùjiāodù* (ecliptic nodal distance).
Subtract it from the *yuèjù zhèngjiāo*.
The remainder is the *shēngdùchā* (ascending degree difference).
Add or subtract it to the *báidào shíxíng*.
(If the *yuèjù zhèngjiāo* is in the 0th, 1st, 2nd, 6th, 7th, or 8th *gōng*, it's subtraction;
in the 3rd, 4th, 5th, 9th, 10th, or 11th *gōng*, it's addition.)
This gives the *huángdào shíxíng*.
To calculate the *huángdào wěidù* (ecliptic latitude),
follow the *Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ* (Method of the *Jiǎzǐ* Epoch).
To calculate the four kinds of *sùdù* (lodging degrees):
for *Yuèbèi* (Lunar Apogee), use the *zuìgāo shíxíng*;
for *Luó* (Ascending Node), use the *zhèngjiāo shíxíng* plus or minus six *gōng*;
for *Jìdū* (Descending Node), use the *zhèngjiāo shíxíng*;
the rest follow the *Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ*.
To calculate the *jìrì zhísù* (lodging star of the recorded day).
To calculate the *jiāogōng shíkè* (time of crossing houses).
To calculate the *tàiyīn chūrù shíkè* (times of Moonrise and Moonset).
To calculate the *héshuò xiánwàng* (new moon, first quarter, full moon, last quarter).
To calculate the *zhèngshēng*, *xiéshēng*, *héngshēng* (right ascension, oblique ascension, horizontal ascension).
To calculate the *yuè dàxiǎo* (Moon's size).
To calculate the *rùnyuè* (intercalary month),
all follow the *Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ*.
To determine the monthly ordinates (yuèlìng),
when the sun is in Juézǐ,
it is Jiànyín (the first month),
the east wind thaws the ice,
hibernating insects begin to stir,
fish ascend bearing ice,
otters sacrifice fish,
migratory geese fly north,
and plants begin to sprout.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Jiànglóu,
it is Jiànmǎo (the second month),
peaches begin to blossom,
orioles sing,
hawks transform into doves,
swallows arrive,
thunder then sounds,
and lightning begins.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Dàliáng,
it is Jiànchén (the third month),
paulownia trees begin to blossom,
field mice transform into quails,
rainbows first appear,
duckweed begins to grow,
cooing doves flutter their feathers,
and hoopoes descend onto mulberry trees.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Shíshěn,
it is Jiànsì (the fourth month),
mole crickets sing,
earthworms emerge,
snake gourds grow,
bitter vegetables blossom,
delicate grasses wither,
and the wheat harvest arrives.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Quánshǒu,
it is Jiànwǔ (the fifth month),
mantises hatch,
shrikes begin to sing,
mockingbirds fall silent,
deer shed their antlers,
cicadas begin to sing,
and pinellia grows.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Quánhuǒ,
it is Jiànwèi (the sixth month),
warm winds arrive,
crickets dwell in walls,
hawks begin to swoop,
decaying grass turns into fireflies,
the earth is moist and the heat is muggy,
and heavy rains occur frequently.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Quánwěi,
it is Jiànshēn (the seventh month),
cool winds arrive,
white dew descends,
cold cicadas sing,
hawks then sacrifice birds,
heaven and earth begin to become solemn,
and grains are harvested.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Shòuxīng,
it is Jiànyǒu (the eighth month),
wild geese arrive,
swallows return,
birds prepare for winter,
thunder begins to cease,
hibernating insects seal their burrows,
and waters begin to dry up.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Dàhuǒ,
it is Jiànxū (the ninth month),
wild geese arrive as guests,
sparrows enter the great waters and become clams,
chrysanthemums have yellow blossoms,
jackals then sacrifice beasts,
plants turn yellow and fall,
and hibernating insects all burrow down.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Xīmù,
it is Jiànhài (the tenth month),
waters begin to freeze,
the earth begins to freeze,
pheasants enter the great waters and become large clams,
rainbows hide and are not seen,
heavenly qi rises,
earthly qi descends,
and a blocked and closed state forms winter.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Xīngjì,
it is Jiànzǐ (the eleventh month),
horned owls do not sing,
tigers begin to mate,
Lychee sprouts emerge,
earthworms knot,
deer shed their antlers,
and springs move.
These are the six hòus.
When the sun is in Yuánxiāo,
it is Jiànchǒu (the twelfth month),
geese face north,
magpies begin to nest,
pheasants crow,
chickens lay eggs,
migratory birds are fierce and swift,
and the surface of waters and marshes becomes solid.
These are the six hòus.
Each five dù (degrees) constitutes one hòu.
It is obtained by calculating according to the palace degrees.
For the numbers of the five planets,
to calculate the movement of the five planets,
it is the same as the Yuánfǎ of Jiǎzǐ.
However, the parallel movement of Sàtuxīng (Saturn) should be reduced by thirty fēn (minutes).
For the numbers of the fixed stars,
see the astronomical treatise.
The method for calculating fixed stars
is the same as the Yuánfǎ of Jiǎzǐ.
For the numbers of Zǐqì,
the winter solstice on the first day of the first month (Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì) in the Jiǎzǐ year of Qiánlóng 9 (1744) is the Yuánfǎ.
(The winter solstice was in the eleventh month of the Guǐhài year.)
Zǐqì moves 126 miǎo (seconds) per day,
with a remainder of 720777.
Zǐqì should be at 7th palace, 17 dù, 50 fēn, 14 miǎo, 53 wēi.
To calculate Zǐqì,
and to find the movement of Zǐqì,
it is the same as the method for finding the parallel movement of the sun.
To find the lunar lodge degrees,
it is the same as for the sun.
In Zhì 26, Shíxiàn 7, the Yuánfǎ from Yōngzhèng Guǐmǎo (1723) onward.
Numbers for lunar eclipses.
The朔cè is 29 days, 53059053.
The望cè is 14 days, 765295265.
