The cycle of the lunar node (Tàiyīn Jiāozhōu) at New Moon (Shuòcè) is 110413 miǎo,
with a remainder of 92441334.
The cycle of the lunar node (Tàiyīn Jiāozhōu) at Full Moon (Wàngcè) is 6th palace, 15 dù, 20 fēn, 06 miǎo, 58 wēi.
The mean distance of the Moon's semidiameter difference from Earth is 57 fēn, 30 miǎo.
The maximum solar semidiameter difference from Earth is 10 miǎo.
The mean distance of the sun from the Earth's center is 10 million.
The mean distance of the moon from the Earth's center is 10 million.
The mean apparent radius of the sun is 16 fēn, 6 miǎo.
The mean apparent radius of the moon is 15 fēn, 40 miǎo, 30 wēi.
The New Moon (Shuò) should be on the 15th day, 12633.
The first New Moon (Shǒushuò) lunar node cycle should be 6th palace, 23 dù, 36 fēn, 52 miǎo, 49 wēi.
For the remainder, see the sun's ecliptic longitude and the moon's latitude.
Method for calculating lunar eclipses.
To find the winter solstice on the first day of the first month (Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì),
to find the calendar day (Jìrì),
to find the first New Moon (Shǒushuò),
and to find the moon's entry into the eclipse limit,
it is all the same as the Yuánfǎ of Jiǎzǐ.
If the moon's mean node cycle for a certain month enters the eclipse limit,
then that month has an eclipse.
(The node cycle from 5th palace, 14 dù, 51 fēn to 6th palace, 15 dù, 9 fēn,
and from 11th palace, 14 dù, 51 fēn to 1st palace, 15 dù, 9 fēn,
are all within the eclipse limit.)
Then examine it in detail at the actual time of the precise conjunction.
To find the mean Full Moon (Píngwàng),
it is the same as the Yuánfǎ of Jiǎzǐ.
To find the actual Full Moon (Shíwàng) and actual time (Shíshí),
first find the general time (Fànshí),
using the comparison of the actual movements of two days,
which is the same as the method for finding New and Full Moons in the Jiǎzǐ Yuánfǎ.
Next, set two times, before and after,
and for each, find the actual ecliptic movements of the sun and moon.
Then use the comparison of the actual movements of the two times
to obtain the actual Full Moon and actual time.
Also, at the actual time, find the actual ecliptic movements of the sun and moon,
and observe if the moon's distance from the precise conjunction at this time enters the limit for an eclipse.
(From 5th palace, 17 dù, 43 fēn to 6th palace, 12 dù, 17 fēn,
and from 11th palace, 17 dù, 43 fēn to 1st palace, 12 dù, 17 fēn,
are all within the eclipse limit.)
To find the time used for the actual Full Moon (Shíwàng Yòngshí),
use the method for finding the sun's mean number and ascending degrees at the actual time,
which is the same as the Yuánfǎ of Jiǎzǐ.
(This is also the same when comparing sunrise and sunset.)
To calculate the precise time of greatest obscuration (食甚時刻),
use a plane triangle.
Take the real movement of the Mínggōng (太陰白道) in one hour, converted to seconds, as one side.
(Compare the real movements of the current hour and the next hour.)
Take the real movement of the Sun's ecliptic (太陽黃道) in one hour, converted to seconds, as another side.
Take the great angular distance between the Sun and Moon (黃白大距) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望) as the included angle.
The angle opposite the shorter side obtained is the difference in the oblique distance intersection angle (斜距交角差).
Add this to the great angular distance between the Sun and Moon (黃白大距) at the exact moment (實時)
to get the ecliptic intersection angle of the oblique distance (斜距黃道交角).
Then, take the sine of the difference in the oblique distance intersection angle (斜距交角差) as the first ratio.
Take the Sun's real movement in one hour as the second ratio.
Take the sine of the great angular distance between the Sun and Moon (黃白大距) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the oblique distance between the two longitudes in one hour (一小時兩經斜距).
Then, take the radius of ten million (千萬) as the first ratio.
Take the cosine and sine of the ecliptic intersection angle of the oblique distance (斜距黃道交角) as the second ratios, respectively.
Take the Moon's real ecliptic latitude (實緯) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratios for each,
which are the real latitude at greatest obscuration (食甚實緯) (north/south same as the Moon's real ecliptic latitude at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望))
and the arc of distance (距弧).
Then, take the oblique distance between the two longitudes in one hour (一小時兩經斜距) as the first ratio.
Take one hour converted to seconds as the second ratio.
Take the arc of distance at greatest obscuration (食甚距弧) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the time of distance at greatest obscuration (食甚距時).
Add or subtract this from the time used at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望用時).
(Subtract if the Moon's distance from the node (月距正交) is in the first or sixth mansion (初宮、六宮);
add if in the fifth or eleventh mansion (五宮、十一宮).)
This gives the precise time of greatest obscuration (食甚時刻).
To calculate the Sun's and Moon's real pulls (實引),
set the Sun's pull value (引數) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望).
Add or subtract the Sun's mean anomaly (均數) for the current hour
to get the Sun's real pull (太陽實引).
Then, set the Moon's pull value (引數) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望).
Add or subtract the Moon's initial mean anomaly (初均數) for the current hour
to get the Moon's real pull (太陰實引).
To calculate the Sun's and Moon's distances to Earth (距地),
use a plane triangle.
Take the product of the Sun's longitude (日躔倍) and the difference between the two centers (兩心差) as the side opposite the proper angle (正角).
Take the Sun's real pull (太陽實引) as another angle.
(For within the third mansion (三宮內), use the original degree;
for beyond the third mansion (過三宮), subtract from the sixth mansion (六宮);
for beyond the ninth mansion (過九宮), subtract from the full circumference (全周);
use the remainder.)
The side opposite the Sun's real pull (太陽實引) obtained is the leg (勾).
Also, the side opposite the originally unknown angle obtained is the fractional leg (分股).
Add or subtract this from twenty million (二千萬).
(Add if the real pull (實引) is within the third mansion (三宮內) or outside the ninth mansion (九宮外);
subtract if outside the third mansion (三宮外) or within the ninth mansion (九宮內).)
This is the sum of the leg and hypotenuse (股弦和) and the leg (勾).
Calculate the leg (股).
Add or subtract this from the fractional leg (分股).
(Subtract if the real pull (實引) is within the third mansion (三宮內) or outside the ninth mansion (九宮外);
add if outside the third mansion (三宮外) or within the ninth mansion (九宮內).)
This gives the Sun's distance to Earth (太陽距地).
Similarly, calculate using the product of the Moon's distance from the node (月離倍) and the difference between the two centers (兩心差) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望).
This gives the Moon's distance to Earth (太陰距地).
To calculate the radius of the real shadow (實影半徑),
take the Moon's distance to Earth (太陰距地) as the first ratio.
Take the Moon's mean distance to Earth (中距太陰距地) as the second ratio.
Take the difference between the Moon's mean maximum Earth radius (中距太陰最大地半徑差) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the Moon's maximum Earth radius difference for the current hour (本時太陰最大地半徑差).
Then, divide this by sixty-nine
to get the shadow difference (影差).
Then, take the Sun's distance to Earth (太陽距地) as the first ratio.
Take the Sun's mean distance to Earth (中距太陽距地) as the second ratio.
Take the Sun's mean apparent radius (中距太陽視半徑) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the Sun's apparent radius (太陽視半徑).
Subtract this from the Moon's maximum Earth radius difference for the current hour (本時太陰最大地半徑差).
Then, add the Sun's maximum Earth radius difference (太陽最大地半徑差).
This is the shadow radius (影半徑).
Then, add the shadow difference (影差).
This is the real shadow radius (實影半徑).
To calculate the Moon's apparent radius (太陰視半徑),
take the Moon's distance to Earth (太陰距地) as the first ratio.
Take the Moon's mean distance to Earth (中距太陰距地) as the second ratio.
Take the Moon's mean apparent radius (中距太陰視半徑) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the Moon's apparent radius (太陰視半徑).
To calculate the magnitude of the eclipse (食分),
take the Moon's full diameter (太陰全徑) as the first ratio.
Take ten units converted to six hundred seconds as the second ratio.
Subtract the real latitude at greatest obscuration (食甚實緯) from the combined radii (併徑) (combined radii of the real shadow and apparent Moon).
Convert the remainder to seconds as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is in seconds.
Convert this to minutes.
This is the magnitude of the eclipse (食分).
To calculate the times of first contact (初虧) and last contact (復圓),
take the sum of the combined radii (併徑) and the real latitude at greatest obscuration (食甚實緯), converted to seconds, as the first ratio.
Take their difference, converted to seconds, as the last ratio.
Calculate the mean ratio, which is in seconds.
Convert this to minutes.
This is the arc of distance for first contact and last contact (初虧、復圓距弧).
Then, take the oblique distance between the two longitudes in one hour (一小時兩經斜距) as the first ratio.
Take one hour converted to seconds as the second ratio.
Take the arc of distance for first contact and last contact (初虧、復圓距弧) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the time of distance for first contact and last contact (初虧、復圓距時).
Add or subtract this from the precise time of greatest obscuration (食甚時刻).
This gives the times of first contact and last contact (初虧、復圓時刻).
(Subtract for first contact;
add for last contact.)
To calculate the times of totality (食既) and emergence of light (生光),

take the sum of the difference between the two radii (兩徑較) (remainder after subtracting the real shadow and apparent Moon radii) and the real latitude at greatest obscuration (食甚實緯), converted to seconds, as the first ratio.
Take their difference, converted to seconds, as the last ratio.
Calculate the mean ratio, which is in seconds.
Convert this to minutes.
This is the arc of distance for totality and emergence of light (食既、生光距弧).
To calculate the time of distance for totality and emergence of light,
the method is the same as for first contact and last contact.
(If the eclipse magnitude is within ten parts,
these two limits do not exist.)
To calculate the total duration of the eclipse (食限總時),
use the same method as in the Jiǎzǐ Yuán (甲子元).
To calculate the Moon's ecliptic longitude, latitude, and mansion degree (經緯宿度) at greatest obscuration (食甚太陰黃道經緯宿度),
take one hour converted to seconds as the first ratio.
Take the Moon's real movement in the white path (太陰白道實行) in one hour as the second ratio.
Take the time of distance at greatest obscuration (食甚距時) converted to seconds as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the Moon's real movement for the time of distance (距時月實行).
Add or subtract this from the Moon's real movement in the white path (太陰白道實行) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望).
(Adding/subtracting is the same as for the time of distance at greatest obscuration.)
This gives the Moon's ecliptic longitude (黃道經度) at greatest obscuration.
Then, set the Moon's distance from the node (月距正交) at the exact moment of conjunction or opposition (實望).
Add or subtract the Moon's real movement for the time of distance (距時月實行).
This gives the Moon's distance from the node (月距正交) at greatest obscuration.
Then, calculate the ecliptic longitude, latitude, and mansion degree (黃道經緯宿度) again,
same as for the Moon's distance from the node (月離).
To calculate the Moon's equatorial longitude, latitude, and mansion degree (赤道經緯宿度) at greatest obscuration,
take the radius of ten million (千萬) as the first ratio.
Take the sine of the Moon's ecliptic longitude (黃道經度) from the vernal/autumnal equinox (春、秋分) at greatest obscuration (食甚太陰) as the second ratio.
(If the Moon's ecliptic longitude at greatest obscuration is less than the third mansion (三宮),
subtract from the third mansion;
if beyond the third mansion,
subtract the third mansion;
if beyond the sixth mansion,
subtract from the ninth mansion;
if beyond the ninth mansion,
subtract the ninth mansion.)
Take the cotangent of the Moon's ecliptic latitude (黃道緯度) at greatest obscuration as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the cotangent.
Look up the table to get the arc of the Moon's distance from the two equinoxes (距二分弧) and the angle of intersection with the ecliptic (黃道交角).
Add or subtract the great angular distance between the ecliptic and equator (黃赤大距).
(If the Moon's ecliptic longitude at greatest obscuration is from the ninth mansion to the third mansion,
add for south latitude,
subtract for north latitude;
both are south of the equator,
if reversed to subtract, it is north.
From the third mansion to the ninth mansion, adding/subtracting is reversed.)
This is the arc of the Moon's distance from the two equinoxes (距二分弧) and the angle of intersection with the equator (赤道交角).
Then, take the cosine of the arc of the Moon's distance from the two equinoxes (距二分弧) and the angle of intersection with the ecliptic (黃道交角) as the first ratio.
Take the radius of ten million (千萬) as the second ratio.
Take the tangent of the Moon's ecliptic longitude (黃道經度) from the vernal/autumnal equinox (春、秋分) at greatest obscuration (食甚太陰) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the tangent of the arc of the Moon's distance from the two equinoxes (距二分弧).
Then, take the radius of ten million (千萬) as the first ratio.
Take the cosine of the arc of the Moon's distance from the two equinoxes (距二分弧) and the angle of intersection with the equator (赤道交角) as the second ratio.
Take the tangent of the arc of the Moon's distance from the two equinoxes (距二分弧) as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio, which is the tangent.
Look up the table for the equatorial longitude (赤道經度) from the vernal/autumnal equinox (春、秋分).
Add or subtract the third and ninth mansions.
(If the Moon's ecliptic longitude at greatest obscuration is less than the third mansion,
subtract from the third mansion;
if beyond the third mansion, add the third mansion.
If beyond the sixth mansion,
subtract from the ninth mansion;
if beyond the ninth mansion, add the ninth mansion.)
This gives the Moon's equatorial longitude (赤道經度) at greatest obscuration.
To calculate the latitude and mansion degree (緯度宿度),
use the same method as in the Jiǎzǐ Yuán (甲子元).
To find the angle of intersection of the ecliptic high arc at first contact and last contact,
take the radius of ten million as the first ratio.
The sine of the greatest distance between the ecliptic and the equator is the second ratio.
The sine of the ecliptic longitude of the shadow's distance from the vernal and autumnal equinoxes is the third ratio.
The fourth ratio thus obtained is a sine,
which, checked against the table, yields the shadow's distance from the equator in degrees.
(The shadow's distance from the vernal and autumnal equinoxes in degrees is the same as the sun's.
When the sun is north of the equator,
the shadow is south.
When the sun is south of the equator,
the shadow is north.)
Then, take the cosine of the ecliptic longitude of the shadow's distance from the vernal and autumnal equinoxes as the first ratio.
The cotangent of the greatest distance between the ecliptic and the equator is the second ratio.
The radius of ten million is the third ratio.
The fourth ratio thus obtained is a tangent,
which, checked against the table, is the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the equatorial right ascension.
Then, use a spherical triangle,
taking the distance from the celestial north pole to the zenith as one side,
and the sum or difference of the shadow's distance from the equator and ninety degrees as another side.
(Subtract if north,
add if south.)
The exact time of first contact and last contact (if it exceeds twelve o'clock,
subtract it from twenty-four o'clock)
is converted into equatorial degrees,
each serving as the included angle.
Thus, find the angle opposite the distance from the celestial north pole to the zenith.
Each of these is the angle of intersection of the right ascension high arc,
which is added to or subtracted from the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the equatorial right ascension.
(If the moon is in the six palaces before the summer solstice,
and the eclipse occurs after *zǐzhèng*, subtract it,
which is called *xiànxī*.
If the eclipse occurs before *zǐzhèng*, add it.
If it exceeds ninety degrees,
subtract it from a half-cycle,
which is called *xiàndōng*.
If it does not reach ninety degrees,
then do not subtract it from a half-cycle,
and it becomes *xiànxī*.
The opposite applies to the six palaces after the summer solstice.)
This yields the angle of intersection of the ecliptic high arc for each.
(If the eclipse is at *zǐzhèng*,
the shadow is at noon,
and there is no angle of intersection of the right ascension high arc,
then the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the equatorial right ascension is the angle of intersection of the ecliptic high arc.
Before the summer solstice, the moon is *xiànxī*;
after, it is *xiàndōng*.)
To find the angle of intersection of the combined diameter high arc at first contact and last contact,
take the combined diameter as the first ratio.
The true latitude at greatest eclipse is the second ratio.
The radius of ten million is the third ratio.
The fourth ratio thus obtained is a cosine,
which, checked against the table, yields the angle of intersection of the combined diameter and the true latitude.
(If there is no true latitude at greatest eclipse,
then there is no such angle,
nor is there an angle of intersection of the combined diameter and the ecliptic.)
Then, set ninety degrees,
add or subtract the angle of intersection of the oblique distance and the ecliptic,
to obtain the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the true latitude at first contact and last contact.
(At greatest eclipse, if the moon's distance is exactly at the first or sixth palace,
subtract for first contact,
add for last contact.
If at the fifth or eleventh palace,
add for first contact,
subtract for last contact.)
Subtract each of these from the angle of intersection of the combined diameter and the true latitude
to get the angle of intersection of the combined diameter and the ecliptic at first contact and last contact.
(If the angle of intersection of the combined diameter and the true latitude is small,
the north-south distance from the latitude is the same as at greatest eclipse.
If large, the opposite applies.)
Add or subtract this from the angle of intersection of the ecliptic high arc.
(For first contact *xiàndōng* and last contact *xiànxī*,
add if latitude is south,
subtract if latitude is north.
For first contact *xiànxī* and last contact *xiàndōng*,
the addition/subtraction is reversed.)
This yields the angle of intersection of the combined diameter high arc for each.
(If there is no angle of intersection of the combined diameter and the ecliptic,
then the angle of intersection of the ecliptic high arc is the angle of intersection of the combined diameter high arc.)
To find the azimuth of first contact and last contact,
take the angle of intersection of the combined diameter high arc as the fixed intersection angle.
The method is the same as for *Jiǎzǐ Yuán*.
However, for the initial degree of the angle of intersection of the combined diameter high arc, first contact in *xiàndōng* is directly below,
and in *xiànxī* is directly above.
Last contact in *xiàndōng* is directly above,
and in *xiànxī* is directly below.
(Determined according to the north polar altitude of Jīngshī,
same method as *Jiǎzǐ Yuán*.)
To find the magnitude of the eclipse in *fēn* and *miǎo*,
use the oblique distance of the two longitudes,
not the moon's distance or the sun's true motion.
The rest is the same as the *Jiǎzǐ Yuán* method.
To find the azimuth of the eclipse,
use the distance between the two centers during the eclipse,
and do not use the combined diameter to find the various intersection angles,
as in determining the azimuth of first contact and last contact.
Before greatest eclipse, it is the same as first contact.
After greatest eclipse, it is the same as last contact.
To find the time and azimuth of lunar eclipses for various provinces,
the principle is the same as the *Jiǎzǐ Yuán* method.
To draw the lunar eclipse diagram,
it is the same as the *Jiǎzǐ Yuán* method.
Solar Eclipse Data
The sun's light division is fifteen *miǎo*.
The rest can be found under solar track, lunar distance, and lunar eclipse.
Method for Calculating Solar Eclipses
To find *Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì*,
to find the day count,
to find the first new moon,
to find when the moon enters the eclipse limit,
all are the same as for lunar eclipses,
except that *wàngcè* is not used.
This is the moon's orbital period from new moon each month.
Observe which month falls within the eclipseable limit,
and that is the month with an eclipse.
(The orbital period from five palaces, eight degrees, forty-two minutes to six palaces, nine degrees, fourteen minutes,
and also from eleven palaces, twenty degrees, forty-six minutes to first palace, twenty-one degrees, eighteen minutes,
are all within the eclipseable limit.)
To find the mean new moon,
to find the true new moon and true time,
all are the same as the method for finding the full moon in lunar eclipses,
except that *wàngcè* is not added.
Observe when the moon's distance at this time enters the eclipse limit from its direct intersection, which means there is an eclipse.
(From five palaces, eleven degrees, thirty-four minutes to six palaces, six degrees, twenty-two minutes,
and also from eleven palaces, twenty-three degrees, thirty-eight minutes to first palace, eighteen degrees, twenty-six minutes,
are the limits for an eclipse.)
To find the time used for the true new moon,
it is the same as finding the time used for the true full moon in a lunar eclipse.
(Comparing it with sunrise and sunset,
it is the same as the *Jiǎzǐ Yuán* method.)
To find the time used for greatest eclipse,
it is the same as the method for finding the time of greatest eclipse in a lunar eclipse.
To find the true influence of the sun and moon,
To find the distance of the sun and moon from the Earth,
all are the same as for lunar eclipses.
To find the difference in elevation of the horizon,
first find the moon's maximum geocentric semidiameter difference for the current day;
the method is the same as for lunar eclipses.
Then subtract the sun's maximum geocentric semidiameter difference
to get the difference in elevation of the horizon.
To find the sun's true semidiameter,
first find the sun's apparent semidiameter;
the method is the same as for lunar eclipses.
Subtract the sun's light division from it
to get the sun's true semidiameter.
To find the moon's apparent semidiameter,
the method is the same as for lunar eclipses.
To find the ecliptic longitude and constellation degree of the sun at greatest eclipse,
finding the longitude is the same as finding the moon's white path in a lunar eclipse;
finding the constellation degree is the same as for the sun's track.
To find the equatorial longitude, latitude, and constellation degree of the moon at greatest eclipse,
use the greatest distance between the ecliptic and the equator;
the method is the same as finding the moon's ecliptic in a lunar eclipse.
To find the angles of intersection of the ecliptic and equator, the ecliptic and white path, and the equator and white path,
take the cosine of the sun's distance from the vernal and autumnal equinoxes in ecliptic longitude at greatest eclipse as the first ratio.
The cotangent of the greatest distance between the ecliptic and the equator is the second ratio.
The radius of ten million is the third ratio.
The fourth ratio thus obtained is a cotangent,
which, checked against the table, yields the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and equator.
(After the winter solstice, the ecliptic longitude is west of the equatorial right ascension;
after the summer solstice, it is east.
If the sun is at the solstices,
then there is no such angle.)
Also, the previously obtained angle of intersection of the oblique distance and the ecliptic
is the angle of intersection of the ecliptic and the white path.
(At true new moon, if the moon's distance is exactly at the first or eleventh palace,
the white path is west of the ecliptic longitude;
if at the fifth or sixth palace,
it is east of the ecliptic longitude.)
The two intersection angles are added or subtracted
to give the angle of intersection of the equator and the white path.
(If both intersection angles are eastward or both are westward, they are added.
The eastward or westward direction of the white path relative to the equatorial right ascension follows this.
If one is eastward and one is westward, they are subtracted.
The eastward or westward direction follows the larger angle.
If they cancel out completely,
then there is no such angle.
If there is no angle of intersection of the ecliptic and equator,
then the ecliptic and white path angle is the same as the equator and white path angle,
and their eastward/westward directions are also the same.)
To find the sun's distance from noon in equatorial degrees for the time in use,
subtract the time in use at greatest eclipse from twelve o'clock.
The remainder is converted into equatorial degrees,
yielding the sun's distance from noon in equatorial degrees for the time in use.
To find the intersection angle of the celestial equator and the altitude circle at the specific time,
use a spherical triangle.
Take the distance from the celestial north pole to the zenith as one side,
and the distance from the Sun to the celestial north pole as another side.
(If the celestial declination is south,
add ninety degrees;
if it is north,
subtract it from ninety degrees.)
Use the degree of the Sun's distance from the meridian equator at the specific time as the included angle.
The angle obtained opposite to the distance from the celestial north pole to the zenith
is the intersection angle of the celestial equator and the altitude circle at the specific time.
(Before noon, the celestial equator is east of the altitude circle;
after noon, the celestial equator is west of the altitude circle.
If the Sun is at true noon,
then there is no such angle.)
To find the distance from the Sun to the zenith at the specific time,
use the sine of the intersection angle of the celestial equator and the altitude circle at the specific time as the first ratio,
the sine of the distance from the celestial north pole to the zenith as the second ratio,
and the sine of the Sun's distance from the meridian equator at the specific time as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained will be a sine.
Consult the table to find the Sun's distance from the zenith.
To find the difference in altitude at the specific time,
use ten million (as) the radius as the first ratio,
the difference in horizontal altitude converted to seconds as the second ratio,
and the sine of the Sun's distance from the zenith at the specific time as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained will be in seconds.
Receive it in minutes
as the difference in altitude at the specific time.
To find the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the specific time,
add or subtract the intersection angle of the celestial equator and the altitude circle at the specific time and the intersection angle of the celestial equator and the ecliptic,
to obtain the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the specific time.
(If they are both east or both west, add them.
The ecliptic's position, east or west of the altitude circle, remains the same.
If one is east and one is west, subtract them.
The east or west position follows the larger angle.
If there is no intersection angle of the celestial equator and the ecliptic,
or no intersection angle of the celestial equator and the altitude circle,
then name the existing angle as such,
with both east and west positions being the same.
If both angles are absent,
or cancel out when subtracted,
then there is no such angle.
The specific time at the moment of greatest eclipse is the true time.
The difference in altitude at the specific time and the true latitude at the moment of greatest eclipse,
added if south and subtracted if north,
gives the apparent distance between the two centers at the moment of greatest eclipse.
To find the apparent angle between the two centers at the specific time,
if the Moon is north of the ecliptic,
take the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the specific time.
If the Moon is south of the ecliptic,
take the exterior angle of the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the specific time.
(The true distance's east or west position relative to the altitude circle
is the same as that of the ecliptic if the Moon is north,
and opposite if it is south.)
Both are the apparent angle between the two centers at the specific time.
(If the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle exceeds ninety degrees,
south latitude is treated as north latitude,
and north latitude as south latitude.)
To find the true angle between the two centers at the specific time,
use a plane triangle.
Take the true distance between the two centers at the moment of greatest eclipse at the specific time as one side,
(which is the true latitude at the moment of greatest eclipse.)
Take the difference in altitude at the specific time as one side,
and the apparent angle between the two centers at the specific time as the included angle.
The result obtained is the true angle between the two centers at the specific time.
To find the apparent distance between the two centers at the specific time,
use the sine of the true angle between the two centers at the specific time as the first ratio,
the true distance between the two centers at the specific time as the second ratio,
and the sine of the apparent angle between the two centers at the specific time as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the apparent distance between the two centers at the specific time.
(If the ecliptic is west of the altitude circle,
and the apparent distance between the two centers is greater than the combined radius,
or there is no eclipse, or it has not yet begun, etc.,
the specific time is the true time of first contact.
If it is east of the altitude circle, it is the true time of last contact and restitution.
If it is smaller than the combined radius,
west of the altitude circle is between first contact and greatest eclipse,
east is between restitution and greatest eclipse.)
To find the assumed time of greatest eclipse,
take the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the specific time: eastward for forward,
westward for backward.
A larger angle implies further
and a smaller angle implies closer.
(Further means not exceeding nine *kè*,
closer may be several *fēn*.)
Measure the interval of several minutes before or after the specific time
as the assumed time of greatest eclipse.
To find the minute difference for the assumed time,
subtract the specific time of greatest eclipse from the assumed time of greatest eclipse
to get the minute difference for the assumed time.
To find the arc difference for the assumed time,
use one hour converted to seconds as the first ratio,
the oblique distance between the two longitudes for one hour as the second ratio,
and the minute difference for the assumed time converted to seconds as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the arc difference for the assumed time.
To find the angle to the arc difference for the assumed time,
use the true latitude at the moment of greatest eclipse as the first ratio,
the arc difference for the assumed time as the second ratio,
and ten million (as) the radius as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained will be a tangent.
Consult the table to find the angle to the arc difference for the assumed time.
To find the true distance between the two centers at the assumed time,
use the sine of the angle to the arc difference for the assumed time as the first ratio,
the arc difference for the assumed time as the second ratio,
and ten million (as) the radius as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the true distance between the two centers at the assumed time.
To find the Sun's distance from the meridian equator at the assumed time,
to find the intersection angle of the celestial equator and the altitude circle at the assumed time,
to find the Sun's distance from the zenith at the assumed time,
to find the difference in altitude at the assumed time,
and to find the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the assumed time:
these five items above
are all the same as for the specific time,
but all calculations use the degrees and minutes of the assumed time.
To find the apparent angle between the two centers at the assumed time,
if the Moon is north of the ecliptic,
subtract the angle to the arc difference for the assumed time from the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the assumed time.
If the Moon is south of the ecliptic, add them,
and then subtract from a semicircle.
The remainder is the apparent angle between the two centers at the assumed time.
(For subtraction,
if the angle to the arc difference is small,
the true distance's east or west position relative to the altitude circle is the same as that of the ecliptic.
If the angle to the arc difference is large, it is opposite.
For addition and then subtraction from a semicircle,
the true distance's east or west position relative to the altitude circle
is always opposite to that of the ecliptic.)
If the two angles are equal and subtract to zero,
or if they add up exactly to one hundred and eighty degrees,
then there is no intersection angle,
and also no true angle between the two centers at the assumed time.
In this case, subtract the true distance between the two centers at the assumed time from the difference in altitude at the assumed time.
The remainder is the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time.
(If the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle exceeds ninety degrees,
south latitude is treated as north latitude,
and north latitude as south latitude.)
To find the true angle between the two centers at the assumed time,
and to find the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time,
both are the same as for the specific time.
To find the difference in the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the assumed time,
subtract the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the specific time from the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the assumed time.
This is the result.
To find the angle of the altitude circle intersecting the apparent distance at the specific time for the assumed time,
add or subtract the difference in the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle at the assumed time and the true angle between the two centers at the specific time.
This is the result.
(Subtraction for north latitude,
addition for south latitude.
If the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude circle exceeds ninety degrees,
it is the opposite.)
To find the apparent angle of motion for the assumed time,
add or subtract the angle of the altitude circle intersecting the apparent distance at the specific time for the assumed time and the true angle between the two centers at the assumed time.
This is the result.
(If both true distances are east of the altitude circle,
or both are west,
then subtract;
if one is east and one is west,
then add.
If the sum exceeds a semicircle,
subtract it from a full circle
and use the remainder.)
If there is no true angle between the two centers at the assumed time,
and the difference in altitude at the assumed time is greater than the true distance between the two centers at the assumed time,
then the angle of the altitude circle intersecting the apparent distance at the specific time for the assumed time is the apparent angle of motion for the assumed time.
If the difference in altitude at the assumed time is smaller than the true distance between the two centers at the assumed time,
then subtract the angle of the altitude circle intersecting the apparent distance at the specific time for the assumed time from a semicircle.
The remainder is the apparent angle of motion for the assumed time.
To find the apparent distance angle for the assumed time,
use a plane triangle.
Take the apparent distance between the two centers at the specific time as one side,
the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time as one side,
and the apparent angle of motion for the assumed time as the included angle.
The result obtained is the apparent distance angle for the assumed time.
To find the apparent motion for the assumed time,
use the sine of the apparent distance angle for the assumed time as the first ratio,
the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time as the second ratio,
and the sine of the apparent angle of motion for the assumed time as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the apparent motion for the assumed time.
To find the apparent motion for the true time,
use ten million (as) the radius as the first ratio,
the cosine of the apparent distance angle for the assumed time as the second ratio,
and the apparent distance between the two centers at the specific time as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the apparent motion for the true time.
To find the apparent distance between the two centers for the true time,
use ten million (as) the radius as the first ratio,
the sine of the apparent distance angle for the assumed time as the second ratio,
and the apparent distance between the two centers at the specific time as the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained
is the apparent distance between the two centers for the true time.
When seeking the true time of maximum eclipse,
use the apparent motion at the assumed time as the first ratio,
the time difference in minutes at the assumed time as the second ratio,
the apparent motion at the true time as the third ratio,
and find the fourth ratio,
which is the minute difference for the true time of maximum eclipse.
Add or subtract this from the time of maximum eclipse
(if the declination of the moon is to the west of the high arc, add;
if to the east of the high arc, subtract)
to obtain the true time of maximum eclipse.
To find the true time’s distance arc,
to find the true time’s angle to the distance arc,
to find the true time’s actual distance between the two centers,
the above three items
follow the same method as for the assumed time,
but all calculations use degrees and minutes of the true time.
To find the true time’s solar distance from the meridian of the celestial equator in degrees,
to find the true time’s intersection angle of the right ascension and the high arc,
to find the true time’s solar distance from the zenith,
to find the true time’s difference in height,
to find the true time’s intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc,
to find the true time’s angle of apparent distance between the two centers,
to find the true time’s angle of actual distance between the two centers,
to verify the true time’s apparent distance between the two centers,
the above eight items
follow the same method as for the use time,
but all calculations use degrees and minutes of the true time.
To find the correction for the true time’s intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc,
the method is the same as for the assumed time,
but calculations use degrees and minutes of the true time.
To find the true time’s intersection of the high arc and the apparent distance angle at the assumed time,
the method is the same as for the assumed time,
but addition and subtraction differ.
(If the moon is north of the ecliptic,
the assumed time and true time’s actual distances between the two centers are on the same side, east or west, of the high arc,
only the declination of the moon differs.
If the assumed time’s intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc is small, add;
if large, subtract.
If the declination of the moon is also the same,
it is the opposite.
If the two actual distances are one east and one west,
then both are subtracted.
If the moon is south of the ecliptic,
if the assumed time’s intersection angle is small, add;
if large, subtract.)
If there is no assumed time’s angle of actual distance between the two centers,
and the assumed time’s difference in height is greater than the assumed time’s actual distance between the two centers,
then the true time’s correction for the intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc
is the true time’s intersection of the high arc and the apparent distance angle at the assumed time;
if the assumed time’s difference in height is less than the assumed time’s actual distance between the two centers,
then subtract the true time’s correction for the intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc from half a circumference,
the remainder is the true time’s intersection of the high arc and the apparent distance angle at the assumed time.
(If the intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc exceeds 90 degrees,
southern latitude is treated like northern latitude,
and northern latitude like southern latitude.)
To find the verified true time’s apparent motion angle,
the method is the same as for the assumed time.
If the assumed time’s actual distance coincides with the high arc,
and there is no east or west,
if the assumed time’s difference in height is greater than the assumed time’s actual distance between the two centers,
then subtract;
if smaller, add.
If the true time’s correction for the intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc is equal to the assumed time’s angle of actual distance between the two centers,
and is subtracted completely with no remainder,
then the true time’s angle of actual distance between the two centers
is the verified true time’s apparent motion angle.
Or if they add up exactly to half a circumference,
then subtract the true time’s angle of actual distance between the two centers from half a circumference,
which is the verified true time’s apparent motion angle.
To find the verified true time’s apparent distance angle,
to find the verified true time’s apparent motion,
the above two items
follow the same method as for the assumed time,
but calculations use degrees and minutes of the verified true time.
To find the fixed true time’s apparent motion,
(If the fixed true time’s apparent motion is equal to the verified true time’s apparent motion,
then the true time of maximum eclipse is the fixed true time.
If it is greater or smaller,
use the following method to find it again.)
To find the fixed true time’s apparent distance between the two centers,
the above two items
follow the same method as for the true time,
using degrees and minutes of the verified true time for calculation.
To find the fixed true time of maximum eclipse,
use the verified true time’s apparent motion as the first ratio,
the remainder after subtracting the true time’s minute difference from the assumed time’s minute difference as the second ratio,
the fixed true time’s apparent motion as the third ratio,
and find the fourth ratio,
which is the minute difference for the fixed true time.
Add or subtract this from the assumed time of maximum eclipse
(if the declination of the moon is to the east of the high arc, if the assumed time’s minute difference is small, subtract;
if large, add.
If the declination of the moon is to the west of the high arc,
it is the opposite.)
to obtain the fixed true time of maximum eclipse.
To find the magnitude of the eclipse,
multiply the sun’s actual semi-diameter by two as the first ratio,
ten parts as the second ratio,
and the remainder after subtracting the fixed true time’s apparent distance between the two centers from the sum of the diameters as the third ratio,
and find the fourth ratio,
which is the magnitude of the eclipse.
To find the assumed time before first contact and after last contact,
if the declination of the moon is to the west of the high arc,
and the apparent distance between the two centers at the time of maximum eclipse is not far from the sum of the diameters,
then use the time of maximum eclipse as the assumed time before first contact;
if smaller, take a time earlier;
if larger, take a time later,
measuring the difference in minutes before or after the time of maximum eclipse
to be the assumed time before first contact.
Subtract this from the fixed true time of maximum eclipse,
add the remainder to the fixed true time of maximum eclipse,
to obtain the assumed time after last contact.
If the declination of the moon is to the east of the high arc,
first find last contact,
then first contact,
the principle is the same.
To find the assumed time before first contact’s minute difference,
to find the assumed time before first contact’s distance arc,
to find the assumed time before first contact’s angle to the distance arc,
(If the assumed time before first contact is before the time of maximum eclipse, it is west;
if after the time of maximum eclipse, it is east.)
To find the assumed time before first contact’s actual distance between the two centers,
the above four items
follow the same method as for the assumed time of maximum eclipse,
but calculations use degrees and minutes of the assumed time before first contact.
To find the assumed time before first contact’s solar distance from the meridian of the celestial equator in degrees,
to find the assumed time before first contact’s intersection angle of the right ascension and the high arc,
to find the assumed time before first contact’s solar distance from the zenith,
to find the assumed time before first contact’s difference in height,
to find the assumed time before first contact’s intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc,
the above five items
follow the same method as for the time of maximum eclipse.
To find the assumed time before first contact’s angle of apparent distance between the two centers,
the method is the same as for the time of maximum eclipse,
but addition and subtraction differ,
(If the moon is north of the ecliptic,
and the two angles are both east or both west,
then add;
if one is east and one is west,
subtract.
If the moon is south of the ecliptic,
it is the opposite.
Also subtract from half a circumference.
If the intersection angle of the declination of the moon and the high arc exceeds 90 degrees,
then southern and northern latitudes are mutually exchanged.)
The rest is the same as for the assumed time of maximum eclipse.
To find the assumed time before first contact’s angle of actual distance between the two centers,
to find the assumed time before first contact’s apparent distance between the two centers,
the above two items
follow the same method as for the time of maximum eclipse,
but calculations use degrees and minutes of the assumed time before first contact.
To find the assumed time after first contact,
if the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time before first contact is less than the sum of the diameters,
then take a time earlier;
if greater, take a time later,
observing the magnitude of the difference,
measuring a certain number of minutes earlier or later,
to be the assumed time after first contact.
Subsequent calculations for each item
are all the same as for the assumed time before first contact,
but calculations use degrees and minutes of the assumed time after first contact.
To find the correction for the apparent distance at first contact,
subtract the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time before and after first contact,
and this is obtained.
To find the correction for the assumed time at first contact,
subtract the minute differences at the assumed time before and after first contact,
and this is obtained.
To find the correction for the apparent distance from the sum of diameters at first contact,
subtract the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time after first contact from the sum of the diameters,
and this is obtained.
To find the fixed true time of first contact,
use the correction for the apparent distance at first contact as the first ratio,
the correction for the assumed time at first contact as the second ratio,
the correction for the apparent distance from the sum of diameters at first contact as the third ratio,
and find the fourth ratio,
which is the minute difference for the true time of first contact.
Add or subtract this from the assumed time after first contact
(if the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time after first contact is greater than the sum of the diameters, add;
if smaller, subtract)
to obtain the true time of first contact.
Then, using the true time of first contact, follow the previous method to find its apparent distance between the two centers.
If it is indeed equal to the sum of the diameters,
then the true time of first contact is the fixed true time of first contact.
The true time’s angle of actual distance between the two centers at first contact is the azimuth angle of first contact.
If it is greater or smaller,
then compare the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time before and after first contact (whichever is closer to the sum of the diameters)
with the apparent distance between the two centers at the verified true time,
and proportionally calculate according to the method
to obtain the fixed true time of first contact.
All items for finding the assumed time before last contact
follow the same method as for first contact,
but calculations use degrees and minutes of the assumed time before last contact.
To find the time of restoration after total eclipse,
observe the apparent distance between the two centers at the assumed time before restoration. If it is less than the sum of the diameters,
then take a later time.
If it is greater than the sum of the diameters,
then take an earlier time.
Examine the magnitude of the difference.
Measure a certain number of divisions earlier or later,
and this will be the assumed time for restoration.
Each item is calculated in sequence,
all in the same way as for the previously assumed time,
but using the degrees and minutes of the later assumed time for separate calculations.
To find the apparent distance difference at restoration,
to find the assumed time difference at restoration,
to find the sum of apparent distances difference at restoration,
to find the true time of restoration—
these four items
are all the same as the method for the initial phase,
but use the degrees and minutes of restoration for separate calculations.
To find the total duration of the eclipse,
take the true time of initial phase
and subtract the true time of restoration,
and the result is obtained.
To find the fixed angle of intersection for the initial phase and restoration,
if the moon's celestial longitude at the initial phase is east of the high arc,
subtract the initial phase azimuth from half a circumference.
If it is west of the high arc,
use the initial phase azimuth directly.
For restoration, the opposite applies: these are all fixed intersection angles.
To find the azimuth for the initial phase and restoration,
the method is the same as for the Jiǎzǐ Yuán,
but for the fixed intersection angle, if the initial degree of the moon's celestial longitude at the initial phase is east of the high arc, it is considered directly above (north);
if west, directly below (south).
For restoration, if east, it is considered directly below (south);
if west, directly above (north).
To find the sunrise and sunset divisions during the partial eclipse,
the method is the same as for the Jiǎzǐ Yuán.
To find the distance in time during the partial eclipse,
subtract the sunrise and sunset divisions from the time of greatest eclipse,
and the result is obtained.
To find the distance arc during the partial eclipse,
the method is the same as for the assumed time of greatest eclipse,
but use the distance in time during the partial eclipse for separate calculations.
To find the intersection angle between the eclipsed right ascension and the high arc,
use the cosine of the declination difference between the ecliptic and celestial equator as the first ratio,
the sine of the altitude of the north pole as the second ratio,
and ten million as the radius for the third ratio.
The fourth ratio obtained will be the cosine,
and checking the table yields the intersection angle between the eclipsed right ascension and the high arc.
To find the intersection angle between the eclipsed celestial longitude and the high arc,
the method is the same as for the time of greatest eclipse,
but use the degrees and minutes of the partial eclipse for separate calculations.
To find the angle opposite the distance arc during the partial eclipse,
to find the actual distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse,
to find the angle opposite the apparent distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse—
these three items
are the same as the method for the assumed time of greatest eclipse,
but use the degrees and minutes of the partial eclipse for separate calculations.
To find the angle opposite the actual distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse,
use the difference in altitude above and below the horizon.
The remaining methods are the same as for the time of greatest eclipse.
To find the apparent distance between the two centers during the partial eclipse,
the method is the same as for the time of greatest eclipse,
but use the degrees and minutes of the partial eclipse for separate calculations.
To find the eclipse magnitude in divisions during the partial eclipse,
it is the same as finding the eclipse magnitude,
using the distance during the partial eclipse for calculations.
To find the azimuth during the partial eclipse,
for those before the greatest eclipse,
use the method for the initial phase.
For those after the greatest eclipse,
use the method for restoration.
To find the time and azimuth of the solar eclipse for each province,
the principle is the same as the Jiǎzǐ Yuán method.
To draw the solar eclipse map,
the method is the same as the Jiǎzǐ Yuán method.
To draw the terrestrial map of the solar eclipse,
take the divisions where the eclipse is most visible,
each division being one limit.
(Stopping at the twenty-first limit.)
Then take the times when the eclipse is visible, early or late,
each *kè* being one limit.
(Stopping at the ninety-sixth limit.)
Through cross-calculation,
deduce the altitude above/below the north pole and the east/west deviation for various places where the eclipse is visible.
Then connect them on a map according to the degrees.
Also, according to the names of various places corresponding to altitudes and deviations on the complete terrestrial map,
fill them in one by one.
For distances, use numbers
related to the moon's departure and the movements of the five planets and fixed stars.
The method for calculating distances
is the same as the Jiǎzǐ Yuán method for calculating conjunctions and oppositions.
Astrological calculation tables:
The two methods of Jiǎzǐ Yuán and Guǐmǎo Yuán,
apart from this method,
all involve calculations using tables.
Their main principles are described in this section.
Jiǎzǐ Yuán Method:
First is the annual root table,
which uses the year, day, and lunar mansion as its framework.
Starting from the year of the epoch, it extends forward three hundred years,
obtaining for each year the apparent positions of the Sun at midnight on the day following the winter solstice (Tiānzhèng Dōngzhì Cìrì Zǐzhèng) and its lowest mean motion,
listed as the Sun's annual root table.
The Moon's and its highest, and orthogonal mean motions,
are listed as the Moon's annual root table.
The five planets and their highest, orthogonal, and retrograde/direct mean motions
are listed as each planet's annual root table.
Second is the annual mean motion table,
which uses the number of days as its framework.
From one day to three hundred and sixty-six days,
it accumulates the mean motions of the Sun, Moon, and five planets, as well as their lowest, highest, orthogonal, and retrograde/direct mean motions,
each listed as an annual mean motion table.
Third is the daily mean motion table,
which uses hours, minutes, and seconds as its framework,
aligned in three layers with degrees, minutes, and seconds.
From one to sixty,
it accumulates the mean motions of the Sun, Moon, and five planets, as well as their highest, orthogonal, retrograde/direct, moon-to-sun distance, Moon's argument, and nodal period mean motions,
each listed as a daily mean motion table.
Fourth is the equation table,
which uses the argument as its framework,
pre-calculating the advance and retreat, and acceleration and deceleration for each degree and minute,
and listing them fully in the table.
The Moon has additional second and third equation tables,
which use the argument and the moon-to-sun distance as frameworks,
listed horizontally and vertically,
to derive the second and third equations,
fully listed in the table.
For the four planets Sātǔ, Mùxīng, Jīnxīng, and Shuǐxīng,
the primary equation and its division, and the secondary equation and its comparison,
are listed together in one table.
For Huǒxīng, the primary equation and the distance from the epicycle center to Earth, the epicycle's proper radius, and the difference in the Sun's apogee/perigee,
are listed together in one table.
All of these are equation tables.
Fifth is the declination table,
which uses ecliptic degrees as its framework,
listing the corresponding north-south declinations from the celestial equator,
forming the ecliptic-equatorial declination table.
Using the Moon's distance from the node as its framework,
it divides the great ecliptic-ecliptic separation into six limits,
listing the corresponding north-south declinations from the ecliptic,
forming the ecliptic-lunar declination table.
Sixth is the ascension table,
which uses ecliptic degrees as its framework,
listing the corresponding equatorial degrees,
forming the ecliptic-equatorial ascension table.
Seventh is the ecliptic-equatorial intersection angle table,
which uses ecliptic degrees as its framework,
taking the corresponding ecliptic-equatorial intersection angles and listing them in the table.
Eighth is the ascension difference table,
which uses the Moon's and five planets' distance from the node and ecliptic longitude as frameworks,
listing the comparison of their respective ecliptic degrees,
each forming an ascension difference table.
Ninth is the time difference table,
which uses the ecliptic as its framework,
taking the change in time corresponding to the comparison of equatorial degrees,
listed as the ascension time difference table.
Also, using the argument as its framework,
it takes the change in time corresponding to the mean motion,
listed as the mean motion time difference table.
Tenth is the terrestrial radius difference table,
which uses actual altitude as its framework,
taking the respective terrestrial radius differences for the Sun, Moon, and the three planets Huǒxīng, Jīnxīng, and Shuǐxīng,
each listed as a table.
Eleventh is the atmospheric refraction difference table,
which uses actual altitude as its framework,
taking the corresponding atmospheric refraction difference,
listed as a table.
Twelfth is the actual motion table,
which uses the argument as its framework,
taking the actual motions of the Sun, Moon, and the Moon's distance from the Sun,
each listed as a table.
Thirteenth is the nodal mean distance limit table,
which uses the Moon's distance from the Sun as its framework,
taking the corresponding nodal mean motion and distance limit,
listed together in one table.
Fourteenth is the initial new moon root table,
which uses the year, day, and lunar mansion as its framework.
Starting from the year of the epoch, it extends forward three hundred years,
taking the corresponding date and time in hours, minutes, and seconds of the initial new moon, and the Sun's mean motion,
the Sun's and Moon's arguments,
and the Moon's nodal period.
These five items are listed together in one table.
Fifteenth is the new moon and full moon calculation table,
which uses the month number as its framework.
From one to thirteen,
it takes the corresponding new moon and full moon calculations and the Sun's mean motion for new moon and full moon calculations,
the Sun's and Moon's arguments for new moon and full moon calculations,
and the Moon's nodal period for new moon and full moon calculations.
These ten items are listed together in one table.
Sixteenth is the apparent radius table,
which uses the argument as its framework,
taking the corresponding solar radius, lunar radius, lunar distance from the Earth's shadow radius, and shadow difference.
These five items are listed together in one table.
First, the Table of Lunar Travel for Eclipses,
which takes the distance from the eclipse maximum to the latitude (緯分) as its main index.
From the first division to the sixty-fourth division,
it takes the sum of the two radii of the Sun (Tàiyáng), Moon (Tàiyīn), and Earth's (Dì) shadow,
from twenty-five divisions to sixty-four divisions,
arranged in vertical and horizontal columns.
It then lists the corresponding lunar travel in divisions and seconds
to form a table.
The difference and sum of the two radii of the Moon (Tàiyīn) and Earth's (Dì) shadow are used in the same way.
Second, the Table of Yellow-level Quadrants,
which takes the zodiacal longitude (Huángdào gōngdù) at true noon as its main index.
It divides the altitude of the North Pole (Běijí) from sixteen degrees to forty-six degrees into thirty-one limits.
It lists the corresponding distance of the spring equinox from noon, the yellow-level quadrant, and the distance of the limit from the Earth's (Dì) altitude,
all three in one table.
Third, the Table of the Intersection Angle of the Ecliptic (Huángdào) High Arc, which takes the distance of the Sun (Rì) from the limit as its main index.
From the first degree to the ninetieth degree,
it divides the distance of the limit from the Earth's (Dì) altitude from twenty degrees to eighty-nine degrees into seventy limits.
It lists the corresponding intersection angle of the ecliptic (Huángdào) high arc to form a table.
Fourth, the Table of the Solar (Tàiyáng) High Arc,
whose method of listing is the same as the Table of the Intersection Angle of the Ecliptic (Huángdào) High Arc.
Fifth, the Table of East-West and North-South Differences,
which takes the intersection angle in degrees as its main index.
From the first degree to the ninetieth degree,
and the altitude difference from one division to sixty-three divisions,
arranged in vertical and horizontal columns.
It lists the corresponding East-West difference and North-South difference
in the same table.
Sixth, the Table of Latitude Difference Angle,
which takes the combined radius as its main index.
From thirty-one divisions to sixty-four divisions,
and the distance from the latitude from one division to sixty-four divisions,
arranged in vertical and horizontal columns.
It lists the corresponding latitude difference angle to form a table.
Seventh, the Table of Planetary (Xīng) Distance from the Ecliptic (Huángdào),
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the distance from the intersection as its main index.
It lists the corresponding numbers of the planetary (xīng) distance from the ecliptic (Huángdào) for each planet (xīng) as a table.
For Mercury (Shuǐxīng) alone, the intersection angle is divided into twenty limits, from four degrees, fifty-five divisions, thirty-two seconds to six degrees, thirty-one divisions, two seconds.
Eighth, the Table of Planetary (Xīng) Distance from Earth (Dì),
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the planet (xīng) from the Sun (Rì) as its main index.
It lists the corresponding planetary (xīng) distance from the Earth (Dì) in the table.
Ninth, the Table of Mercury's (Shuǐxīng) Distance Limit,
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the distance from the intersection as its main index.
It lists the corresponding distance limit to form a table.
Tenth, the Table of the Five Planets' (Wǔxīng) Visibility/Invisibility Distance from the Sun's (Rì) Ecliptic (Huángdào) Degrees,
which takes the planetary (xīng) ecliptic (Huángdào) travel table as its main index.
It lists morning and evening, ascending and descending.
It lists the corresponding ecliptic (Huángdào) degrees of each planet (xīng) from the Sun (Rì),
all in one table.
Eleventh, the Table of the Five Planets' (Wǔxīng) Visibility/Invisibility Distance from the Sun (Rì) Adjustment Differences,
whose method of listing is the same as the Ecliptic (Huángdào) Degrees Table,
but it does not distinguish the five planets (wǔxīng),
but rather the North and South of the ecliptic (Huángdào) from one degree to eight degrees.
Additions from the Guǐmǎo Yuánfǎ:
First, the Table of Solar (Tàiyáng) Distance from the Earth's (Dì) Center,
which takes the actual solar (tàiyáng) attraction as its main index.
It lists the corresponding true number and logarithm of the solar (tàiyáng) distance from the Earth's (Dì) center
in the table.
Second, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) First Mean,
which takes the solar (tàiyáng) attraction value as its main index.
It lists the corresponding lunar (tàiyīn) first mean, highest mean, and orthogonal mean
in the table.
Third, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Second Mean,
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the Sun (Rì) from the Moon's (Yuè) highest point as its main index.
It lists the corresponding second mean when the Sun (Tàiyáng) is at its highest, and the difference in altitude in seconds,
all in the table.
Fourth, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Third Mean,
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the Moon (Yuè) from the orthogonal point as its main index.
It lists the corresponding third mean to form a table.
Fifth, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Highest Mean and the Distance of the Epicycle Center from Earth (Dì),
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the Sun (Rì) from the Moon's (Yuè) highest point as its main index.
It lists the corresponding highest mean and the number of the epicycle center's distance from the Earth (Dì),
all in the table.
Sixth, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Second Equalization,
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the Moon (Yuè) from the Sun (Rì) as its main index.
It lists the corresponding second equalization and the difference in altitude when the Sun (Tàiyáng) is at its highest,
all in the table.
Seventh, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Third Equalization,
which takes the total distance as its main index.
It lists the corresponding third equalization in the table.
Eighth, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Last Equalization,
which takes the actual zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the Moon (Yuè) from the Sun (Rì) as its main index,
and the maximum distance between the Sun (Rì) and Moon (Yuè),
arranged in vertical and horizontal columns.
It lists the corresponding last equalization to form a table.
Ninth, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Orthogonal True Equalization,
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the Sun (Rì) from the orthogonal point as its main index.
It lists the corresponding orthogonal true equalization in the table.
Tenth, the Table of Intersection Angle Addition,
which takes the zodiacal longitude (gōngdù) of the Sun (Rì) from the orthogonal point as its main index.
It lists the corresponding addition and difference for the distance from the intersection,
all in the table.
Eleventh, the Table of Ecliptic (Huáng) and Lunar (Bái) Latitude Distance,
whose method of listing is the same as the Table of Ascensional Difference.
Twelfth, the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Distance from the Earth's (Dì) Center,
which takes the actual lunar (tàiyīn) attraction as its main index.
It lists the corresponding maximum and minimum differences between the two centers, the lunar (tàiyīn) distance from the Earth's (Dì) center, and the multiple divisions,
all in the table.
For those with the same name but different content:
The Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) First Mean is divided into three limits: large, medium, and small.
The Table of Ecliptic (Huáng) and Lunar (Bái) Ascensional Difference lists the minimum intersection angle and large and small difference in seconds.
The Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Earth's (Dì) Radius Difference and the Table of Lunar (Tàiyīn) Actual Travel are both divided into two limits: large and small.
Records of the Twenty-seven Shíxiàn Bāl língfàn Shìchā Xīnfǎ, Part One (During the Dàoguāng reign,
compiled by Sī Tíngdòng, the head of the Bureau of Astronomy (Qīntiānjiān) Autumn (Qiūguān) Department;
it is more precise than the old method,
appended to the end of the volume
for reference.)
When calculating the actual time (Yòngshí):
The calculation of the travel of various luminaries
is all based on the Sun (Tàiyáng);
and the actual travel of the Sun (Tàiyáng)
is rooted in its mean travel.
The method of calculation
always begins at Zǐzhèng (midnight) each day.
Here, Zǐzhèng
refers to Píng Zǐzhèng (mean midnight),
which is the position where the point of the Sun's (Tàiyáng) mean travel aligns with the initial moment of Zǐzhèng.
The current calculation of time (shíkè),
although using the actual travel between two Zǐzhèngs as a proportion,
the result obtained is also the point aligned with the mean travel.
Thus, the point aligned with the actual travel
naturally has differences of advancement or retardation.
If the Sun (Tàiyáng) is at its lowest point and its actual travel is greater than its mean travel,
then the point aligned with the Sun (Tàiyáng) must be to the east of the mean travel.
In terms of time (shíkè),
it is "not yet reached."
If the Sun (Tàiyáng) has passed its highest point and its actual travel is less than its mean travel,
then the point aligned with the Sun (Tàiyáng) must be to the west of the mean travel.
In terms of time (shíkè),
it is "already passed."
Therefore, the mean number that should be added, converted to time, becomes the time difference that should be subtracted;
the mean number that should be subtracted, converted to time, becomes the time difference that should be added.
This is because of the distinction between the Sun's (Tàiyáng) mean and actual travel,
which gives rise to the time difference from the mean number.
However, the path of the Sun (Tàiyáng) is the ecliptic (Huángdào),
while the basis for time (shíkè) is the equator (Chìdào).
Because the ecliptic (Huángdào) and equator (Chìdào) are obliquely intersected,
there must be a difference in ascensional degrees (chādù) for the same rising.
For example, after the two equinoxes (Èrfēn), the equator (Chìdào) is smaller than the ecliptic (Huángdào),
and its difference should be subtracted.
In terms of time (shíkè), it is "not yet reached."
After the two solstices (Èrzhì), the equator (Chìdào) is larger than the ecliptic (Huángdào),
and its difference should be added.
In terms of time (shíkè), it is "already passed."
Therefore, the difference in ecliptic (Huáng) and equatorial (Chì) ascensional degrees (shēngdù chā) obtained by the method of right spherical triangles
is converted into hours and minutes.
After the two equinoxes (Èrfēn), it is added;
after the two solstices (Èrzhì), it is subtracted.
This is because of the distinction between ecliptic (Huángdào) and equatorial (Chìdào) longitudes,
which gives rise to the time difference from ascensional degrees.
According to the two differences arising from the Sun's (Rì) travel at the current time,
each is added to or subtracted from the mean time to obtain the actual time (Yòngshí).
Only by using the actual time (Yòngshí) can other numbers be calculated.
Therefore, calculating the actual time (Yòngshí) is also the first priority for eclipses (Jiāoshí),
which is the first calculation for solar (Rì) and lunar (Yuè) eclipses.

To find the time difference from the vernal equinox to noon, the quadrant degrees of the ecliptic mean anomaly, and the distance from the limit to the height of the Earth.
To calculate the parallax of the moon's occultations and transits,
one must indeed follow the method in the later chapters for finding the three differences of a solar eclipse.
However, their applications differ.
The east-west difference for a solar eclipse is used to find the apparent distance arc,
while the north-south difference is used to find the apparent latitude.
The apparent distance arc and apparent latitude are then used to find the apparent separation and apparent motion.
Since the moon travels along the white path (白道),
it must be based on the white-level quadrant (白平象限).
However, for the distances of the five planets from fixed stars, and the distances of the five planets from each other,
the moment of separation is taken as the time when their ecliptic longitudes are the same,
and the number representing their north-south separation in ecliptic latitude is taken as their vertical distinction.
As for the moon's distance from the five planets and from fixed stars,
the moment of occultation or transit is also taken as the time when their ecliptic longitudes are the same,
without further inquiry into the white path longitude.
How, then, does it relate to the white-level quadrant?
Nevertheless, its use of the east-west difference to determine the advance or retreat of apparent time,
and its use of the north-south difference to determine the magnitude of apparent latitude,
in order to fix the distance of the apparent separation,
all involve differences in ecliptic longitude and latitude.
Therefore, it must be based on the palace degrees of the ecliptic-level quadrant (黃平象限).
The ecliptic-level quadrant
is the midpoint of the ecliptic's semicircle above the horizon.
Considering that the ecliptic intersects the equator obliquely,
the midpoint of the equator's semicircle above the horizon
always falls on the meridian,
whereas the midpoint of the ecliptic's semicircle above the horizon
varies over time.
This is because the ecliptic pole, starting from the negative ecliptic pole circle, rotates daily counter-clockwise with the celestial sphere,
completing one revolution around the celestial pole.
If the ecliptic pole is south of the celestial pole,
then the winter solstice is at local noon,
and the ecliptic rises and sets obliquely.
If the ecliptic pole is north of the celestial pole,
then the summer solstice is at local noon,
and the ecliptic rises and sets directly,
and the ecliptic-level quadrant also exactly aligns with the meridian.
If the ecliptic pole is west of the celestial pole,
then the vernal equinox is at local noon,
and the ecliptic is inclined,
rising from the northeast and setting in the southwest,
and the ecliptic-level quadrant is then east of local noon.
If the ecliptic pole is east of the celestial pole,
then the autumnal equinox is at local noon,
and the ecliptic rises from the southeast and sets in the northwest,
and the ecliptic-level quadrant is then west of local noon.
Thus, the orientation of the ecliptic
differs with time.
Therefore, by using each degree of the ecliptic,
one calculates the ecliptic-level quadrant and its height above the horizon (限距地高) to construct a table.

To find the jù-xiàn-chā.
The term jù-xiàn-chā
refers to the difference in degrees between the Moon's position and the huáng-píng quadrant.
In the old method, the Moon's distance from the limit (jù-xiàn) was set at ninety degrees.
Because the ecliptic (huáng-dào) spans the heavens,
its orientation varies with time.
The portion that is above the horizon
is always a semi-circle.
Its central point
is ninety degrees from the horizon, both to the east and to the west.
Therefore, using the ninety-degree limit
was to observe whether the Moon was above or below the horizon.
If the Moon's distance from the limit exceeded ninety degrees,
it was considered to be below the horizon
and thus not included in calculations.
However, this method takes the ecliptic as the basis for calculation.
Considering that the Moon's path (bái-dào) intersects the ecliptic obliquely,
the Moon's travel along the bái-dào
always entails a latitude difference, north or south, from the ecliptic.
For those with southern latitude, the Moon rises early and sets late.
When the Moon is at the horizon,
its distance from the huáng-píng quadrant is less than ninety degrees.
For those with northern latitude, the Moon rises late and sets early.
When the Moon is at the horizon,
its distance from the huáng-píng quadrant has already exceeded ninety degrees.
Therefore, the ninety-degree standard is insufficient as a basis.
Hence, a method was established to find this difference,
similar to the concept of the "jù-rì jiā-jiǎn-chā" (add/subtract difference from the Sun) for the five planets' occultations and reappearances in relation to the Sun's limit.
This method uses the altitude of the limit from the horizon and the Moon's latitude from the ecliptic,
calculated according to the law of spherical right triangles.
Indeed, the orientation of the ecliptic
rotates counter-clockwise with the heavens,
and its ascending, descending, direct, and oblique movements
differ from time to time.
When it is directly ascending and directly descending,
the altitude of the limit from the horizon in Jīng-shī reaches over seventy-three degrees.
When the altitude is large,
the jù-xiàn-chā corresponding to the Moon's latitude becomes smaller.
When it is obliquely ascending and obliquely descending,
the altitude of the limit from the horizon in Jīng-shī is only over twenty-six degrees.
When the altitude is small,
the jù-xiàn-chā corresponding to the Moon's latitude becomes larger.
If the Moon's latitude is at its maximum,
this difference can reach over ten degrees.
This is why the jù-xiàn-chā must be established.
Therefore, based on the altitude of the huáng-píng quadrant from the horizon in Jīng-shī,
the corresponding jù-xiàn-chā for each degree of the Moon's true ecliptic latitude is calculated to create a table.
For example, assume the altitude of the limit from the horizon in Jīng-shī is thirty-four degrees,
and the Moon's true ecliptic latitude is five degrees, both north and south.
We need to find the jù-xiàn-chā.

And the angle wù-jǐ-bǐng is vertically opposite to the angle yǐ-jǐ-gēng,
so their degrees are also equal.
If the Moon is exactly at a direct or middle intersection,
coinciding with point jǐ on the ecliptic,
it is precisely on the horizon.
Then wù-jǐ is the Moon's distance from the limit, ninety degrees.
If it exceeds ninety degrees,
