To find the intersection angle of the ecliptic longitude arc and the Moon's distance from the zenith.
The old method of calculating the three anomalies for a solar eclipse
was originally based on the `Huángpíng Xiàngxiàn` (Yellow Equator Quadrant).
Since the `Kǎochéng Qiánbiān` (Former Compilation of Astronomical Calculations) stated that the three anomalies originate from the Moon,
and the Moon's longitude and latitude are `Báidào` (white path) longitude and latitude,
using the `Báidào` is more precise than using the `Huángdào` (yellow path).
Therefore, to find the three anomalies, the angle of the Moon from the `Báipíng Xiàngxiàn` (White Equator Quadrant)
is taken as the basis, using the `Báidào` high arc intersection angle and the Moon's high arc.
The `Hòubiān` (Later Compilation) modified this method
by using the `Báijīng` (white longitude) high arc intersection angle and the Sun's distance from the zenith to find the three anomalies.
To find the `Báijīng` high arc intersection angle,
it is obtained by adding or subtracting the angle between the `Chìjīng` (red longitude) high arc intersection angle and the `Chìbái` (red-white) two longitudes.
It does not involve finding the Moon's distance from the `Báipíng Xiàngxiàn`.
This method is considerably more computationally efficient than the previous one.
Now, for calculating parallax,
it involves finding the apparent distance and apparent time when a star and the Moon have the same `Huángdào` longitude.
Therefore, the three anomalies should be determined from the `Huángpíng Xiàngxiàn`.
In this case, the method could originally imitate the `Hòubiān` by not seeking the `Huángpíng Xiàngxiàn` directly, but instead finding the `Huángjīng` (yellow longitude) high arc intersection angle.
(This is the complementary angle of the `Huángdào` high arc intersection angle.)
However, without comparing the Moon's distance from the `Huángpíng Xiàngxiàn` with its distance from the local horizon,
it is impossible to know whether the Moon is above or below the horizon.
Therefore, when calculating the intersection angle now,
we first determine the Moon's east-west distance from the `Huángpíng Xiàngxiàn`, the elevation of the `Huángpíng Xiàngxiàn` from the horizon, and the Moon's distance from the `Huángjí` (Yellow Pole).
Then, following the method in the `Hòubiān` of using oblique spherical triangles to find the `Chìjīng` high arc intersection angle and the Sun's distance from the zenith,
the `Huángjīng` high arc intersection angle and the Moon's distance from the zenith can be obtained.

From the zenith (no data for the diagram) draw perpendicular arc `Jiǎ-Hài`,

calculate angle `Shēn` as 56 degrees, 2 minutes, 51 seconds,

Still using the oblique spherical triangle `Jiǎ-Mǎo-Shēn`,
apply the opposite side-opposite angle method
to calculate arc `Jiǎ-Shēn` as 53 degrees, 43 minutes, 24 seconds,
which is the Moon's distance from the zenith.
Calculating the Moon's distance from a star and the apparent time of occultation.
The Moon's high arc above the horizon,
calculated from the center of the Earth, is the true altitude.
What is seen from the Earth's surface is the apparent altitude.
The difference between them
is the radius parallax.
When the Moon is on the horizon,
its distance from the zenith is 90 degrees.
The difference is greatest,
and the sine of the angle is the radius at that location.
As the Moon rises,
its distance from the Earth gradually increases.
The higher it is from the Earth,
the smaller the difference.
The amount of this difference
corresponds to the sine of the Moon's distance from the zenith at that time.
Thus, using the method of proportion, the altitude difference at that time is obtained.
Once there is an altitude difference,
there is a distinction between apparent longitude and true longitude.
The difference between apparent longitude and true longitude
is the east-west difference.
The difference between apparent latitude and true latitude
is the north-south difference.
Now, to calculate the three anomalies,
we follow the `Hòubiān`'s method for calculating the three anomalies in a solar eclipse using planar triangles.
While the `Hòubiān`'s three-anomaly diagrams are drawn on a flat surface,
we now use a diagram that measures a sphere from a sphere
to calculate the three anomalies.
The resulting north-south difference
is compared with the Moon's true latitude at that time
to obtain the apparent latitude.
By comparing the apparent latitude with the star's latitude,
we determine the relative north-south position of their distances.
The resulting east-west difference
is proportional to the Moon's true motion in one hour,
to obtain the time difference from the apparent time.
By identifying whether the Moon's distance from the limit is east or west, and adding or subtracting the time of occultation,
the apparent time of occultation is obtained.
Previously, we calculated that on the 6th day of the 3rd month of the Rénchén year in the 12th year of Dàoguāng (March 27, 1832),
at Xū-zhèng-èrkè-bāfēn-shíjiǔmiǎo (7:32:19 PM), the Moon was in conjunction with the fourth star of Sīguài.
The angle between the ecliptic and the altitude arc was 56 degrees, 2 minutes, and 51 seconds.
The Moon's distance from the zenith was 53 degrees, 43 minutes, and 24 seconds.
On this day, the maximum lunar horizontal parallax difference was 60 minutes and 7 seconds.
The Moon's true ecliptic latitude was south 3 degrees, 30 minutes, and 27 seconds.
The fourth star of Sīguài's ecliptic latitude was south 3 degrees, 11 minutes, and 44 seconds.
In one hour, the Moon's true motion was 36 minutes and 33 seconds.
We need to calculate the apparent time of the star-moon conjunction in minutes and seconds.
As shown in Figure A, Jiǎ (甲) is the zenith.
The circle formed by Jiǎ (甲), Wèi (未), Chén (辰), and Sì (巳) represents the ecliptic meridian.
The line Chén (辰), Wǔ (午), Sì (巳) is the horizon.
Mǎo (卯) is the ecliptic pole.
Wèi (未), Wǔ (午), Xīn (辛) represent the ecliptic.
Point Wèi (未) is the ecliptic quadrant's degree.
Arc Wèi (未) Chén (辰) is the distance from the limit to the ground altitude.
This is equal to the distance from Mǎo (卯) Jiǎ (甲) (ecliptic pole) to the zenith.
Shēn (申) is the Moon.
Zǐ (子) is the fourth star of Sīguài.
They are both on the ecliptic at Yǒu (酉).
Point Yǒu (酉) is the ecliptic longitude of the Moon and the star.
Arc Yǒu (酉) Wèi (未) is the Moon's distance west of the limit.
Zǐ (子) Yǒu (酉) is the star's distance from the ecliptic, south latitude 3 degrees, 11 minutes, and 44 seconds.
Shēn (申) Yǒu (酉) is the Moon's true distance from the ecliptic, south latitude 3 degrees, 30 minutes, and 27 seconds.
Arc Shēn (申) Mǎo (卯) is the Moon's distance from the ecliptic pole.
Jiǎ (甲) Shēn (申) Xū (戌) is the altitude arc.
Shēn (申) Jiǎ (甲) is the Moon's distance from the zenith, 53 degrees, 43 minutes, and 24 seconds.
Angle Mǎo (卯) Shēn (申) Jiǎ (甲) is the angle of intersection between the ecliptic and the altitude arc, 56 degrees, 2 minutes, and 51 seconds.
This is the opposite angle to Xū (戌) Shēn (申) Hài (亥).
Their degrees are equal.
These are true degrees calculated from the center of the Earth (no diagram data available yet).
However, people live on the surface of the Earth, which is higher than the Earth's center.
Therefore, the apparent altitude is always lower than the true altitude.
When the Moon is at the horizon,
its horizontal parallax is at its maximum,
which is currently 60 minutes and 7 seconds.
Thus, according to the method for calculating the difference in altitude at this time in the following chapter,
the ratio of the radius to the sine of arc Jiǎ (甲) Shēn (申) is the same as the ratio of the maximum horizontal parallax to the difference in altitude at this time.
The difference in altitude at this time is found to be 48 minutes and 28 seconds.
Like the division of Shēn (申) Huǒ (火),
point Huǒ (火) is the Moon's apparent altitude.
From point Huǒ (火), draw a line Huǒ (火) Mù (木) parallel to the ecliptic,
forming a right triangle Shēn (申) Mù (木) Huǒ (火).
(Since the arc degree is very small,
it is calculated as a straight line,
which is the same principle as calculating the three differences for solar eclipses in the following chapter.)
In this figure, Mù (木) is the right angle.
We have angle Shēn (申), the intersection angle of the ecliptic and the altitude arc.
We have side Shēn (申) Huǒ (火), which is the difference in altitude at this time.
We calculate side Mù (木) Huǒ (火) to be 40 minutes and 12 seconds, which is the east-west difference.
We calculate side Shēn (申) Mù (木) to be 27 minutes and 4 seconds, which is the north-south difference.
Adding this to Shēn (申) Yǒu (酉), the Moon's true latitude,
we get Mù (木) Yǒu (酉), the Moon's apparent latitude, 3 degrees, 57 minutes, and 31 seconds.
Subtracting Zǐ (子) Yǒu (酉), the star's latitude,
we get arc Zǐ (子) Mù (木) as 45 minutes and 47 seconds,
which is the apparent distance from the Moon to the fourth star of Sīguài as seen by a human observer, with the Moon below the star.
The star and the Moon share the longitude of point Yǒu (酉),
so they are conjoined.
Now the Moon's apparent altitude is at Huǒ (火),
and although its apparent latitude differs to Mù (木),
its distance from star Zǐ (子) is still within one degree.
The apparent longitude of point Huǒ (火) on the ecliptic differs to Tǔ (土).
Therefore, at this time, although the star's longitude is at Yǒu (酉),
the Moon's apparent longitude at point Tǔ (土) is to its west.
This means it has not yet reached it.
However, the division of Tǔ (土) Yǒu (酉) is equal to Huǒ (火) Mù (木).
Therefore, by using the ratio of the Moon's true motion in one hour to the east-west difference Huǒ (火) Mù (木),
we get the distance in minutes for one hour as 6 minutes,
which is the time it takes for the Moon to travel Huǒ (火) Mù (木).
Adding this to the time when the Moon's apparent altitude reaches point Huǒ (火),
we get Hài-chū-èrkè-shísìfēn-shíjiǔmiǎo (9:24:19 PM),
which is the apparent time when a human observer sees the Moon at point Mù (木) with the star,
sharing the longitude of point Yǒu (酉).
Calculating the apparent time of the Moon's distance from the limit:
The apparent time of the Moon's distance from the limit
must be greater than the true time of the Moon's distance from the limit,
because when its apparent longitude difference causes a change in the distance,
the Moon and the star will advance or recede as the sky moves westward.
Generally, when the Moon's altitude decreases due to horizontal parallax,
there will certainly be a difference between the apparent longitude and true longitude, and between the apparent latitude and true latitude.
Now, considering the ecliptic quadrant being to the south of the zenith on the ground,
the apparent latitude always differs southward.
If the true latitude is north,
the apparent latitude is always smaller than the true latitude,
and the difference is subtracted.
If the true latitude is south,
the apparent latitude is always greater than the true latitude,
and the difference is added.
Therefore, even if the true distance between stars and the Moon with south latitudes is within one degree,
there are cases where the apparent distance turns out to be outside one degree.
Conversely, even if the true distance between stars and the Moon with north latitudes is outside one degree,
there are cases where the apparent distance turns out to be within one degree.
(Those with a north-south distance greater than one degree are not considered to be in conjunction,
so they are not used.)
As for the difference in apparent longitude,
the maximum difference in monthly travel can be up to two hours.
During these two hours,
all celestial bodies rotate counter-clockwise with the sky,
almost reaching one quadrant.
Therefore, the difference in apparent longitude
is related to the advance or retreat of the Moon's motion.
For example, if the Moon is west of the ecliptic quadrant,
the apparent longitude differs westward,
and the apparent time must be later than the true time.
If the Moon is east of the ecliptic quadrant,
the apparent longitude differs eastward,
and the apparent time must be earlier than the true time.
As a result, there are cases where the star and Moon are not yet below the horizon at the true time,
but they are already below the horizon at the apparent time;
or where the star and Moon have already risen above the horizon at the true time,
but they have not yet risen above the horizon at the apparent time.
Therefore, after calculating the true time,
one must compare the Moon's distance from the ecliptic quadrant with the horizon limit degree,
to determine whether the Moon is above or below the horizon at that time.
(If the Moon's distance from the limit is less than the horizon limit degree,
the Moon is above the horizon;
if it is greater than the horizon limit degree,
the Moon is below the horizon.)
If the Moon's distance from the limit is slightly less than the horizon limit degree,
the star and Moon must be above the horizon at the true time,
but may be below the horizon at the apparent time.
The difference
is the counter-clockwise rotation degree of all celestial bodies corresponding to the apparent longitude difference in the Moon's travel distance.
Now, we take the smallest true longitude, apparent longitude difference, and corresponding counter-clockwise rotation degree as the apparent longitude difference.
(The method is described in the section on calculating the horizon limit degree in the next volume.)
Subtract this from the horizon limit degree
to obtain the apparent horizon limit degree,
and compare it with the Moon's distance from the limit.
If the Moon's distance from the limit is less than the horizon limit degree but greater than the apparent horizon limit degree,
then even if the Moon is above the horizon at the true time,
it must be below the horizon at the apparent time.
(Since it is known that the Moon must be below the horizon,
such cases are discarded.)
If the Moon's distance from the limit is less than the apparent horizon limit degree,
then the Moon is above the horizon at the apparent time.
However, there are still exceptions,
because the apparent longitude difference always uses the smallest numbers.
If the Moon's true path is not determined by the apparent time,
and we recalculate the Moon's distance from the limit,
then whether the Moon is actually above or below the horizon at that time
cannot be accurately determined.
Therefore, after obtaining the apparent time,
we must carefully examine the Moon's true latitude and its distance from the limit at the true time.
If the true latitude is south and the Moon's distance from the limit exceeds 60 degrees,
or if the true latitude is north and the Moon's distance from the limit exceeds 70 degrees,
(if the Moon's distance from the limit at the true time is within this range,
the Moon must be above the horizon at the apparent time.)
In all such cases, we recalculate the Moon's distance from the ecliptic quadrant at the apparent time.
If this degree is greater than the horizon limit degree,
then the Moon is below the horizon at the apparent time,
and is still not used.
Only if this degree is less than the horizon limit degree
can it be confirmed that the Moon must be above the horizon at the apparent time,
and this can be verified by actual measurements.
This is why apparent differences must be meticulously calculated
before they can be adopted and used.
Record 28, Shíxiàn (時憲) 9, New Method for Apparent Differences in Conjunctions, Part 2
Calculating the Equation of Time (Jūnshù Shíchā)
Using the Sun's argument in degrees and minutes for the current day,
(rounding up 30 seconds to one minute for use.)
Consult the table for the equation of time for the Sun's longitude in the following chapter,
find the corresponding value,
and obtain the equation of time (Jūnshù Shíchā),
noting the addition or subtraction sign.
(If the argument has zero minutes,
use intermediate proportion to find it.)
Calculating the Right Ascension Difference (Shēngdù Shíchā)
Using the Sun's true ecliptic motion in degrees and minutes for the current day,
(rounding up 30 seconds to one minute for use.)
Consult the table for the right ascension difference for the Sun's longitude in the following chapter,
find the corresponding value,
and obtain the right ascension difference (Shēngdù Shíchā),
noting the addition or subtraction sign.
(If the true motion has zero minutes,
use intermediate proportion to find it.)
Calculating the Total Time Difference (Shíchā Zǒng)
Add or subtract the equation of time (Jūnshù Shíchā) and the right ascension difference (Shēngdù Shíchā)
to get the total time difference (Shíchā Zǒng).
If both time differences have the same sign (both plus or both minus),
then add them to get the total time difference,
keeping the sign (plus remains plus,
minus remains minus).
If the two time differences have opposite signs (one plus, one minus),
then subtract them to get the total time difference.
If the larger number is positive, the total is positive;
if the larger number is negative, the total is negative.
Calculating the True Time of Conjunction (Língfàn Yòngshí)
Take the time of conjunction,
add or subtract the total time difference,
to get the true time of conjunction (Língfàn Yòngshí).
Calculating the Sun's Ecliptic Longitude at This Time
Take 1440 minutes in a full day (周日, zhōurì) as the first ratio.
Subtract the actual solar positions (太陽實行, tàiyáng shíxíng) of the two days (本日, běnrì and 次日, cìrì) (subtracting seconds,
and carrying over 1 minute for every 30 seconds [or more];
degrees are converted to minutes) as the second ratio.
Convert the time of the eclipse (凌犯時刻, língfàn shíkè) to minutes as the third ratio.
The calculated fourth ratio is added to the actual solar position of the current day (本日太陽實行, běnrì tàiyáng shíxíng),
to obtain the ecliptic longitude of the Sun at the current time (本時太陽黃道經度, běnshí tàiyáng huángdào jīngdù).
To find the distance from the vernal equinox to noon at the current time (本時春分距午時分, běnshí chūnfēn jù wǔshífēn):
Using the ecliptic longitude of the Sun at the current time,
(carry over 1 degree for every 30 minutes [or more]),

consult the right column of the Yellow-Flat Quadrant Table (黃平象限表, Huángpíng Xiàngxiàn Biǎo) for the distance from the vernal equinox to noon (春分距午時分, chūnfēn jù wǔshífēn) and add it to the eclipse duration (淩犯用時, língfàn yòngshí).
Subtract 12 hours from this.
(If the subtraction is not possible,
add 24 hours before subtracting.)
This yields the distance from the vernal equinox to noon at the current time.
(Discard every 24 hours.)
To find the magnitude of the yellow-white arc at the current time (本時黃白大距, běnshí huángbái dàjù):
Take 1440 minutes in a full day as the first ratio.
Subtract the magnitudes of the yellow-white arc (黃白大距, huángbái dàjù) of the two days as the second ratio.
Convert the eclipse time to minutes as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio.
Add or subtract this from the magnitude of the yellow-white arc of the current day.
(If the magnitude of the yellow-white arc of the current day is larger, subtract;
if smaller, add.)
This gives the magnitude of the yellow-white arc at the current time.
To find the distance of the Moon from the orthogonal point at the current time (本時月距正交, běnshí yuèjù zhèngjiāo):
Take 1440 minutes in a full day as the first ratio.
Convert the difference between the Moon's distance from the orthogonal point for the two days into seconds as the second ratio.
Convert the eclipse time to minutes as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio.
Convert this to degrees, minutes, and seconds,
and add it to the Moon's distance from the orthogonal point of the current day,
to get the Moon's distance from the orthogonal point at the current time.
To find the Moon's true latitude (太陰實緯, tàiyīn shíwěi):
Take the radius as the first ratio.
Take the sine of the magnitude of the yellow-white arc at the current time as the second ratio.
Take the sine of the Moon's distance from the orthogonal point at the current time as the third ratio.
(If the Moon's distance from the orthogonal point at the current time exceeds the 3rd quadrant,
subtract it from the 6th quadrant. If it exceeds the 6th quadrant, subtract the 6th quadrant.
If it exceeds the 9th quadrant,
subtract it from the 12th quadrant,
using the remainder.)
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the sine of the Moon's true latitude.
Consult the table to find the Moon's true latitude,
and record whether it is north or south.
(If the Moon's distance from the orthogonal point at the current time is between the 1st and 5th quadrants, it is North.
If between the 6th and 11th quadrants, it is South.
If the Moon's distance from the orthogonal point at the current time is exactly in the 1st or 6th quadrant,
then there is no true latitude.
If it is exactly in the 3rd or 9th quadrant,
then the magnitude of the yellow-white arc at the current time is the true latitude.
The 3rd quadrant is North,
and the 9th quadrant is South.)
To find the yellow-flat quadrant (黃平象限, huángpíng xiàngxiàn) and the quadrant distance to the Earth's height (限距地高, xiànjù dìgāo):
Using the distance from the vernal equinox to noon at the current time,
consult the Yellow-Flat Quadrant Table,
and record the number corresponding to the closest time and minutes,
which is the yellow-flat quadrant.
Then look at the left side and record the quadrant distance to the Earth's height,
which is the quadrant distance to the Earth's height.
To find the star's longitude (星經度, xīngjīngdù):
For the selected star,
consult the ecliptic longitude of this star recorded in Volume 26 of the Yíxiàng Kǎochéng (儀象考成) table,
and add the precession.
(The table uses the *jiǎzǐ* (甲子) year of Qiánlóng 9 (乾隆九年) as the epoch.
To Dàoguāng 14 (道光十四年), *jiǎwǔ* (甲午),
is 90 years.
One degree, sixteen minutes, and thirty seconds of precession should be added.
Thereafter, 51 seconds of precession are added annually.)
This gives the star's longitude for the current year.
If calculating the longitude of the five planets (五星經度, wǔxīng jīngdù):
Take 1440 minutes in a full day as the first ratio.
Convert the eclipse time to minutes as the second ratio.
Take the actual daily movement of the star (一日星實行, yīrì xīng shíxíng) as the third ratio.
(Subtract the actual movements of the star on the two days [本次日兩實行, běncìrì liǎng shíxíng]
to obtain the actual daily movement of the star.)
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the star's actual movement for the given time (距時星實行, jùshí xīng shíxíng).
Add or subtract this from the star's longitude for the current day.
(Add if direct motion, subtract if retrograde motion.)
This gives the star's longitude at the current time.
To find the star's latitude (星緯度, xīngwěidù):
For the selected star,
record its ecliptic latitude as listed in Volume 26 of the Yíxiàng Kǎochéng table.
(No precession.)
Record whether it is north or south.
If calculating the latitude of the five planets:
Take 1440 minutes in a full day as the first ratio.
Convert the eclipse time to minutes as the second ratio.
Take the daily difference in star latitude (一日星緯較, yīrì xīng wěijiào) as the third ratio.
(If the latitudes of the two days are both south or both north,
subtract them to get the star's latitude difference.
If one is south and one is north,
add them to get the star's latitude difference.)
Calculate the fourth ratio.
Add or subtract this from the star's latitude for the current day.
(If the latitude of the current day is larger, subtract;
if smaller, add.
If the sum is the third ratio,
the calculated fourth ratio must be subtracted from the latitude of the current day,
and the north/south designation remains that of the current day.
If the calculated fourth ratio is greater than the star's latitude,
then subtract the star's latitude from the calculated fourth ratio,
and the north/south designation should be the same as the next day.)
This gives the star's latitude at the current time,
and record whether it is north or south.
To find the Moon's distance from the quadrant (月距限, yuèjù xiàn):
Subtract the yellow-flat quadrant from the star's longitude,
to obtain the Moon's distance from the quadrant,
and record whether it is east or west.
(If the star's longitude is larger, it is east of the quadrant;
if smaller, it is west of the quadrant.
If one of the star's longitude or the yellow-flat quadrant is within the 3rd quadrant and the other outside the 9th quadrant,
the one within the 3rd quadrant should be added to 12 quadrants before subtracting.)
If the Moon's true latitude (太陰實緯, tàiyīn shíwěi) obtained is within 60 degrees south or
within 80 degrees north,
there is no need to calculate the horizontal limit (地平限度, dìpíng xiàndù).
If the latitude exceeds 60 degrees south,
or exceeds 80 degrees north,
then calculate the horizontal limit.
To find the difference from the limit (距限差, jùxiànchā):
Using the quadrant distance to the Earth's height (限距地高, xiànjù dìgāo) and the Moon's true latitude in degrees and minutes,
consult the Difference from Limit Table (距限差表, Jùxiànchā Biǎo) and record the corresponding number at the intersection of the row and column,
which is the difference from the limit,
and record whether to add or subtract.
(South latitude subtracts, north latitude adds.)
To find the horizontal limit:
Set 90 degrees,
add or subtract the difference from the limit,
to get the horizontal limit.
From the horizontal limit, subtract the minimum apparent longitudinal difference (最小視經差, zuìxiǎo shìjīngchā) of 8 degrees, 55 minutes, and 17 seconds,
to obtain the apparent horizontal limit (視地平限度, shìdìpíng xiàndù).
If the Moon's distance from the quadrant is greater than the apparent horizontal limit,
it means the Moon is below the horizon,
and no further calculation is needed.
(Because the Moon is closest to the Earth,
its apparent motion varies over time.
Therefore, the minimum apparent longitudinal difference is used to determine the apparent limit.
Based on the minimum quadrant distance to the Earth's height,
when the Moon is at its southernmost point on the ecliptic,
the minimum ecliptic height arc intersection angle (最小黃經高弧交角, zuìxiǎo huángjīng gāo hú jiāojiǎo) is found to be 26 degrees, 6 minutes, and 24 seconds.
Using the minimum Moon-Earth radius difference and the fastest actual lunar motion,
the minimum distance in minutes (距分, jùfēn) is found to be 37 minutes and 8 seconds.
Converted to equatorial degrees, it is 9 degrees and 17 minutes.
Its corresponding minimum ecliptic degree is found to be 8 degrees, 31 minutes, and 34 seconds.
Adding the minimum east-west difference (最小東西差, zuìxiǎo dōngxīchā) of 23 minutes and 43 seconds,
gives the minimum apparent longitudinal difference of 8 degrees, 55 minutes, and 17 seconds.
However, when the Moon is at its highest point,
the Earth-radius difference is minimal,
but its actual lunar motion must be slower,
so the distance in minutes becomes larger.
Taking all the minimum values here
might lead to omissions.)
To find the distance from the pole in minutes (距極分邊, jùjí fēnbīan):
Take the radius as the first ratio.
Take the cosine of the Moon's distance from the quadrant as the second ratio.
Take the tangent of the quadrant distance to the Earth's height as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the tangent of the distance from the pole in minutes.
Consult the table to find the distance from the pole in minutes.
To find the Moon's distance from the ecliptic pole (月距黃極, yuèjù huángjí):
Set 90 degrees,
add or subtract the Moon's true latitude.
(South adds, north subtracts.)
This gives the Moon's distance from the ecliptic pole.
To find the Moon's distance in minutes (距月分邊, jùyuè fēnbīan):
Subtract the distance from the pole in minutes from the Moon's distance from the ecliptic pole,
to get the Moon's distance in minutes.
To find the ecliptic height arc intersection angle (黃經高弧交角, huángjīng gāo hú jiāojiǎo):
Take the sine of the Moon's distance in minutes as the first ratio.
Take the sine of the distance from the pole in minutes as the second ratio.
Take the tangent of the Moon's distance from the quadrant as the third ratio.
Calculate the fourth ratio,
which is the tangent of the ecliptic height arc intersection angle.
Consult the table to find the ecliptic height arc intersection angle.
(If the Moon's distance from the quadrant is zero degrees,
meaning the Moon is exactly in the yellow-flat quadrant,
then the ecliptic longitude and the height arc coincide,
and there is no ecliptic height arc intersection angle.)
To find the Moon's actual attraction (月實引, yuè shíyǐn) for the current and next day:
Add or subtract the initial mean value (初均, chūjūn) of the current day from the Moon's attraction value (月引數, yuèyǐnshù) of the current day,
to get the Moon's actual attraction for the current day.
Add or subtract the initial mean value of the next day from the Moon's attraction value of the next day,
to get the Moon's actual attraction for the next day.
To find the Moon's actual attraction at the current time (本時月實引, běnshí yuè shíyǐn):
Take 1440 minutes of a Zhou rì as the first ratio.
Convert the Língfàn shí Kè into the second ratio.
Subtract the two actual positions of the Moon for the current day
(carrying over a minute if seconds are 30 or more), and convert degrees to minutes.
) as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio.
Convert it into degrees and minutes,
and add it to the Moon's actual position for the current day
to get the Moon's actual position for the current hour.
To find the distance from the celestial heart to the earth for the current hour and day:
Take 1440 minutes of a Zhou rì as the first ratio.
Convert the Língfàn shí Kè into the second ratio.
Subtract the two celestial heart-to-earth distances for the current day as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio.
Add or subtract it from the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current day.
(If the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current day is large, subtract;
if small, add.)
This yields the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current hour and day.
To find the distance difference:
Subtract the smaller distance-to-earth value from the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current hour,
to get the distance difference.
To find the Moon's distance from the zenith:
Take the sine of the angle of intersection of the ecliptic altitude arc as the first ratio.
Take the sine of the altitude of the limiting distance from the earth as the second ratio.
Take the sine of the Moon's distance from the limit as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio, which is the sine of the Moon's distance from the zenith.
Consult the table to get the Moon's distance from the zenith.
(If there is no angle of intersection of the ecliptic altitude arc,
then subtract the altitude of the limiting distance from the earth from the Moon's distance from the ecliptic pole.)
To find the difference in the Moon's radius of the earth:
Using the Moon's actual position for the current hour (carrying over a degree if it reaches 30 minutes)
and the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current hour and day,
consult the appended table of the difference in the Moon's radius of the earth for eclipses
to find the corresponding value,
which is the difference in the Moon's radius of the earth.
If the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current hour and day varies (near or far),
calculate it using the ratio of the distance difference.
To find the altitude difference for the current hour:
Take the radius as the first ratio.
Take the sine of the Moon's distance from the zenith as the second ratio.
Take the difference in the Moon's radius of the earth as the third ratio.
(If predicting the Língfàn of the five planets,
except for the two planets, Tǔxīng and Mùxīng, which have no difference in the radius of the earth,
Huǒxīng, Jīnxīng, and Shuǐxīng all have a difference in the radius of the earth.
Then, observe the planet's position.
From the 10th palace 15 degrees to the 1st palace 15 degrees,
is the highest limit.
From the 1st palace 15 degrees to the 4th palace 15 degrees,
and from the 7th palace 15 degrees to the 10th palace 15 degrees,
is the middle limit.
From the 4th palace 15 degrees to the 7th palace 15 degrees,
is the lowest limit.
According to the limit corresponding to the planet's position,
find the maximum difference in the radius of the earth for that planet.
Subtract it from the difference in the Moon's radius of the earth
to get the difference in altitude between the planet and the Moon at the horizon,
as the third ratio.)
Find the fourth ratio,
which is the altitude difference for the current hour.
To find the east-west difference:
Take the radius as the first ratio.
Take the sine of the angle of intersection of the ecliptic altitude arc as the second ratio.
Take the altitude difference for the current hour as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio,
which is the east-west difference.
(If there is no intersection angle,
then there is no east-west difference,
the altitude difference is the north-south difference,
and the Língfàn use time is the Língfàn apparent time.)
To find the north-south difference:
Take the radius as the first ratio.
Take the cosine of the angle of intersection of the ecliptic altitude arc as the second ratio.
Take the altitude difference for the current hour as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio,
which is the north-south difference.
To find the Moon's apparent latitude:
Add or subtract the north-south difference from the Moon's actual latitude
to get the Moon's apparent latitude,
and note the north or south sign.
(If both latitudes are south, add them, and it remains south.
If both latitudes are north, subtract them, and it remains north.
If the north-south difference is large,
then subtract in reverse, changing north to south.)
To find the Moon's distance from the star:
Add or subtract the star's latitude from the Moon's apparent latitude
to get the Moon's distance from the star,
(noting whether the Moon is above or below the star.)
If both latitudes are north or both are south, then subtract;
(If the Moon's latitude is greater,
north is above,
south is below;
if the Moon's latitude is smaller,
north is below,
south is above.)
If one latitude is south and one is north, then add.
(If the Moon's latitude is north, it is above;
if the Moon's latitude is south, it is below.)
If both latitudes are the same,
and they subtract to zero,
it is a lunar occultation of a star.
This is used for distances within one degree;
if the distance is greater than one degree,
it is a large latitude,
not used,
and calculation is unnecessary.
To find the Moon's actual motion:
Using the Moon's actual position for the current hour (carrying over a degree if it reaches 30 minutes)
and the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current hour and day,
consult the appended table of the Moon's actual motion for eclipses
to find the corresponding value,
which is the Moon's actual motion.
If the celestial heart-to-earth distance for the current hour and day varies (near or far),
calculate it using the ratio of the distance difference.
To find the difference in minutes:
Take the Moon's actual motion as the first ratio.
Take the east-west difference as the second ratio.
Take one hour converted to 3600 seconds as the third ratio.
Find the fourth ratio,
which is the difference in minutes,
and note whether to add or subtract.
(If the Moon is east of the limit, subtract;
if the Moon is west of the limit, add.)
To find the Língfàn apparent time:
Take the Língfàn use time.
Add or subtract the difference in minutes
to get the Língfàn apparent time.
(If the Língfàn use time is not enough to subtract the difference in minutes,
add 24 hours and then subtract.
The resulting Língfàn apparent time will be for the previous day.
If adding results in 24 hours or more, remove 24 hours.
The resulting Língfàn apparent time will be for the next day.)
Times before sunrise or after sunset are used;
times after sunrise and before sunset
are during daylight,
and are not used.
If the Moon is in south latitude,
and the Moon's distance from the limit exceeds 60 degrees,
or if the Moon is in north latitude,
and the Moon's distance from the limit exceeds 70 degrees,
the following method must be used to calculate it.
To find the apparent time of the vernal equinox's distance from noon:
Take the current hour's vernal equinox distance from noon.
Add or subtract the difference in minutes
to get the apparent time of the vernal equinox's distance from noon.
(If the current hour's vernal equinox distance from noon is not enough to subtract the difference in minutes,
add 24 hours and then subtract;
if adding results in more than 24 hours, remove 24 hours.)
To find the apparent time's ecliptic horizontal quadrant:
Using the apparent time of the vernal equinox's distance from noon in hours and minutes,
consult the Ecliptic Horizontal Quadrant Table,
select the closest value to the time in hours and minutes,
and record the corresponding number.
This yields the apparent time's ecliptic horizontal quadrant.
To find the apparent time's Moon's distance from the limit:
Take the star's longitude.
Subtract it from the apparent time's ecliptic horizontal quadrant
to get the apparent time's Moon's distance from the limit.
Values where the degree is less than the horizontal limit degree are used;
if it is greater than the horizontal limit degree,
the Moon is below the horizon,
and it is not used.
Ecliptic Horizontal Quadrant Table:
The Ecliptic Horizontal Quadrant Table is based on the north pole altitude of Jīngshī (Beijing) at 39 degrees 55 minutes,
and the maximum distance between the ecliptic and equator at 23 degrees 29 minutes.
According to ecliptic longitude,

for each degree, the vernal equinox distance from noon in hours and minutes, the ecliptic horizontal quadrant in palaces and degrees, and the altitude in degrees and minutes of the limit distance from the earth
are derived and listed in three sections.
The table name
“Chūnfēn jù Wǔ”
refers to
the time in hours and minutes derived from the degrees of the right ascension of the vernal equinox from noon.
“Huáng píng xiàngxiàn”
refers to
the palace and degree of the ecliptic horizontal quadrant for the current hour.
“Xiàn jù dì gāo”
refers to
the altitude of the ecliptic horizontal quadrant from the horizon for the current hour.
The table starts from the beginning of the 3rd palace
because the Sun's ecliptic longitude at the beginning of the 3rd palace is the vernal equinox,
which is the start of the vernal equinox's distance from noon.
Method for using the tables:
Take the degree and minute of the sun's ecliptic longitude for the current time.
Consult the table for the corresponding time interval from the vernal equinox to noon (Chūnfēn jùwǔ shífēn 春分距午時分).
Add the time for the phenomenon's occurrence (Língfàn yòngshí 淩犯用時).
If the sum is greater than 12 hours, subtract 12 hours.
(If it is less than 12 hours, add 24 hours before subtracting.)
The result is the time interval from the vernal equinox to noon for the current time.
Based on this time interval,

find the closest time interval in the table to determine the corresponding ecliptic quadrant degree and minute (Huángpíng xiàngxiàn gōngdù jí xiàndù dìgāo fēn 黃平象限宮度及限距地高度分) and the distance from the ecliptic limit to the horizon in degrees and minutes (xiàndù dìgāo fēn 限距地高度分).
This will yield the desired ecliptic quadrant and the distance from the ecliptic limit to the horizon.
Example: Suppose the sun's ecliptic longitude is one palace and fifteen degrees (yī gōng shíwǔ dù 一宮十五度),
and the time for the phenomenon's occurrence (Língfàn yòngshí 淩犯用時) is 19 hours and 45 minutes.

To find the time interval from the vernal equinox to noon (Chūnfēn jùwǔ 春分距午), the ecliptic quadrant (Huángpíng xiàngxiàn 黃平象限), and the distance from the ecliptic limit to the horizon (xiàndù dìgāo 限距地高):
First, consult the table. For an ecliptic longitude of one palace and fifteen degrees, the corresponding time interval from the vernal equinox to noon is 21 hours, 9 minutes, and 54 seconds.
Add the time for the phenomenon's occurrence, 19 hours and 45 minutes.
Subtract 12 hours.
(If the result exceeds 24 hours, subtract 24 hours.)
This gives 4 hours, 54 minutes, and 54 seconds,
which is the required time interval from the vernal equinox to noon.
Then, use this time to find the closest value in the table,
which is 4 hours, 54 minutes, and 51 seconds.
The corresponding ecliptic quadrant is five palaces, sixteen degrees, fifty-nine minutes, and twenty-seven seconds,
which is the required ecliptic quadrant degree and minute.
The corresponding distance from the ecliptic limit to the horizon is 72 degrees, 49 minutes, and 58 seconds,
which is the required distance from the ecliptic limit to the horizon.
If the ecliptic longitude has fractional minutes (língfēn 零分),
if it is 30 minutes or more, it is rounded up to one degree.
No interpolation is used
because the difference for each degree is very small.
Table of the difference from the limit (Jùxiànchā biǎo 距限差表)
The table of the difference from the limit lists sections by height from the limit to the horizon.
The first column lists the minutes of the moon's true latitude (Tàiyīn shíwěidù fēn 太陰實緯度分).
The middle column lists the north and south of the ecliptic.
The difference from the limit, from the first degree and ten minutes to five degrees and seventeen minutes,
is subtracted if the latitude is south (wěinán 緯南),
and added if the latitude is north (wěiběi 緯北).
Method for using the table:
Take the degree of the distance from the limit to the horizon and the moon's true latitude.
Find the number where their row and column intersect,
which is the required difference from the limit.
Example: Suppose the distance from the limit to the horizon is 28 degrees,
and the moon's latitude is 4 degrees and 20 minutes south of the ecliptic.
To find the difference from the limit:

Consult the row for a distance from the limit to the horizon of 28 degrees and the column for the moon's true latitude of 4 degrees and 20 minutes. The difference from the limit is 8 degrees and 12 minutes.
This is the required difference from the limit.
Since the latitude is south of the ecliptic,
this is a subtractive difference.
The distance from the limit to the horizon is taken in whole degrees.
If the distance from the limit to the horizon has 30 minutes or more,
it is rounded up to one degree.
If it is less than 30 minutes, it is discarded.
The moon's true latitude is taken in intervals of ten minutes.
If the moon's true latitude has fractional minutes,
if it is 5 minutes or more, it is rounded up to ten minutes.
If it is less than 5 minutes, it is discarded.
No interpolation is used
because the difference for each degree and minute is very small.
Zhì 29 Dìlǐ 1
Having Qīng risen in the East,
it has gone through five or six generations.
Tàizǔ and Tàizōng vigorously campaigned and managed,
possessing the eastern lands.
They first pacified Hādá, Huīfā, Wūlā, Yèhè, and all the Nínggǔtǎ regions.
Thereupon, the twenty-five old vassal Zāsàkè tribes and fifty-one banners all entered the imperial domain.
Shìzǔ entered the pass to eliminate the bandits,
establishing the capital at Yāndū,
and possessed the eighteen provinces of Zhōngguó,
governing the entire realm,
thereby establishing singular supremacy.
Shèngzǔ and Shìzōng drove far and wide,
expanding territory and opening frontiers.
They also acquired the new vassal Khalkha (Kā’ěrkā) four tribes and eighty-two banners,
Qīnghǎi four tribes and twenty-nine banners,
and from Hèlánshān, the Ölöts (Èlǔtè) extended to the two Zàng (Tibet) regions.
The nations of the four directions,
all embraced our imperial influence.
Coming to Gāozōng,
he pacified the greater and lesser Jīnchuān,
recovered Zhǔngá'ěr and the Huíbù,
and the felt-and-milk-product peoples across more than twenty thousand *lǐ* north and south of Tiānshān,
were arrayed with headwear and robes,
relying on Hàn like heaven.
From then on,
to the east, as far as Kùyèdǎo belonging to Sānxìng,
to the west, as far as Xīnjiāng Shūlè to Cōnglǐng,
to the north, as far as Wàixīng'ānlǐng,
to the south, as far as Yáshān in Guǎngdōng Qióngzhōu,
none failed to kowtow and submit to the interior,
sincerely belonging to this dynasty.
How glorious!
Such a feat had not been seen since Hàn and Táng.
After Mùzōng's restoration,
Táiwān and Xīnjiāng were reorganized into provinces.
Upon Dézōng's succession,
Fèngtiān, Jílín, and Hēilóngjiāng were further changed to Dōng Sānsěng (Three Eastern Provinces),
sharing the same customs as the inner lands: with over seventeen hundred prefectures, departments, sub-prefectures, and counties.
East of Táng's Sānshòuxiángchéng,
guarding the border gates to the south,
reaching the Sōnghuā Jiāng to the east,
bordering the Great Desert to the north,
was Inner Mongolia (Nèi Ménggǔ).
Beyond it, crossing the vast desert (Hànhǎi),
obstructed by Xīng'ān,
to the east bordering the Hēilóng Jiāng,
to the west crossing the Ā'ěrtài Shān,
was Outer Mongolia (Wài Ménggǔ).
Reinforced by defenses,
and linked by marriages,
these were all pacified and brought to tranquility by the successive emperors,
hence for over two hundred years,
none dared to harbor dissenting intentions.
When Tàizōng campaigned against the disobedient states in the four directions,
Cháoxiǎn (Joseon) was the first to submit,
and was granted a title and enfeoffed as a king.
In the sixth year of Shùnzhì,
Liúqiú submitted a memorial and paid tribute,
becoming a permanent vassal in the East.
Subsequently, nations such as Ānnán, Xiāmluó, Miǎndiàn, Nánzhǎng, and Sūlù requested to offer tribute and declared themselves subjects,
and were listed as southern tributary states.
During Gāozōng's reign,
the Western Regions (Xīyù) were pacified,
Bālèsī, Héndūstǎnd, Àiwūhǎn, Bádákèshān, Bùhār, Bóluò'ěr, Tǎshíkè'ān, Ānjíyán, Hàohǎn, Dōng Xī Bùlǔtè, Zuǒ Yòu Hāsàkè,
and the various Huíbù of Kǎnchēdī,
successively joined the empire,
coming to offer tribute and be recognized as kings.
East, west, north, and south,
the territory expanded by tens of thousands of *lǐ*,
the vastness of the domain,
can be said to be extreme.
By the late dynasty,
the great powers rose all around,
eying like tigers and swallowing like whales.
All the nations that offered tribute through multiple interpreters and engaged in trade,
were fragmented,
and all were carried away by the powerful.
In the early Qīng dynasty, the demarcation of territory and frontiers,
largely followed the Míng system.
Over the years, there were gains and losses,
and each generation differed.
The changes in rivers and waterways,
the additions and deletions of prefectures and counties,
and the divisions and mergers of borders,
are all detailed in the gazetteers,
and also measured using the North Star to determine altitude and deviation,
to delineate the vastness, extent, and intricate curves of the internal and external boundaries,
for the convenience of the court's management.
Zhílì
Zhílì: The territory of the Jì and Yǎn prefectures in Yǔgòng.
During the Míng dynasty, it was Běijīng,
and the Běipíng Bùzhèngshǐsī and Wànquán Túdūhuīshǐsī were established.
In the early Shùnzhì reign of the Qīng dynasty,
the capital was established,
becoming Zhílì Province.
One governor-general was appointed,
named Xuāndà.
(Stationed in Dàtóng, Shānxī,
governing Xuānfǔ.
Abolished in the 13th year of Shùnzhì.) Three governors were appointed: one named Shùntiān,
(stationed in Zūnhuà,
governing Shùntiān and Yǒngpíng prefectures.
Abolished in the early Kāngxī reign.) one named Bǎodìng,
(stationed in Zhēndìng,
governing Bǎodìng, Zhēndìng, Shùndé, Guǎngpíng, Dàmíng, and Héjiān prefectures.
Abolished in the 16th year of Shùnzhì.) one named Xuānfǔ.
(Stationed in Xuānfǔzhèn,
governing Yánqìng and Bǎo'ān departments.
Abolished in the 8th year of Shùnzhì.) In the 5th year,
the Governor-General of the three provinces of Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Hénán was established.
(Stationed in Dàmíng.)
In the 16th year,
it was changed to Zhílì Governor.
(Moved to Zhēndìng the following year.)
In the 8th year of Kāngxī,
it was again moved to Bǎodìng.
In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng,
it was again changed to Governor-General.
The Fǔyǐn's old seat of government in Shùntiān
became the fixed system.
(Before this, in the 18th year of Shùnzhì, an additional Zhílì Governor-General was established,
also stationed in Dàmíng.
In the 5th year of Kāngxī, it was changed to Governor-General of three provinces,
and abolished in the 8th year.)
In the 32nd year of Kāngxī,
Xuānfǔzhèn was changed to Xuānhuà Fǔ.
(Yánqìng and Bǎo'ān departments were subordinated to it.)
In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng,
Rèhé Tīng was established,
and Zhēndìng was changed to Zhèngdìng.
In the 2nd year,
five directly governed departments of Dìng, Jì, Jìn, Zhào, and Shēn were added,
and Zhāngjiākǒu Tīng was established.
In the 3rd year,
Tiānjīn Wèi was promoted to a directly governed department,
and in the 9th year to a prefecture.
In the 10th year,
Duōlúnnuò'ěr Tīng was established.
In the 11th year,
Rèhé Tīng and Yì Zhōu were both made directly governed departments.
In the 12th year,
Dúshíkǒu Tīng was established.
(Jìn Zhōu was subordinated to Zhèngdìng.)
In the 7th year of Qiánlóng,
Chéngdé was still Rèhé Tīng.
In the 8th year,
Zūnhuà was promoted to a directly governed department.
In the 43rd year,
Rèhé Tīng was again promoted to Chéngdé Fǔ.
In the 2nd year of Guāngxù,
Wéichǎng Tīng was established.
(Subordinated to Chéngdé.)
In the 30th year,
Cháoyáng Fǔ was established.
(Jiànpíng was established under it the following year.)
In the 33rd year,
Chìfēng Xiàn was promoted to a directly governed department.
(Kāilǔ and two other counties were established under it.)
Currently, apart from the Jīngyǐn,
it governs eleven prefectures,
seven directly governed departments,
three directly governed sub-prefectures (tīng),
nine scattered departments,
one scattered sub-prefecture (tīng),
and one hundred and four counties.
Its northern boundary reaches the border of the Abāgá Yòuyì Qí of Inner Mongolia;
Its eastern boundary reaches the border of Níngyuǎn Zhōu, Fèngtiān;
Its southern boundary reaches the border of Lánfēng Xiàn, Hénán;
Its western boundary reaches the border of Guǎngníng Xiàn, Shānxī.
Its breadth is 1,230 lí,
and its length is 2,630 lí.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
the total number of households was 4,995,495,
and the population was 23,613,171.
(Its mountains: Héngshān, Tàiháng.
Its rivers: Sānggān (which is Yǒngdìng), Hūtúo (which is Zǐyá), Wèi, Yì, Zhāng, Bái, Luán.
Its strategic passes: Jǐngxíng, Shānhǎi, Jūyōng, Zǐjīng, Dàomǎ, and other passes;
Xǐfēng, Gǔběi, Dúshí, Zhāngjiā, and other strategic mouths.
For transport, there are waterways: from Tiānjīn southeast to Zhīfú, Shànghǎi,
northeast to Yíngkǒu,
east to Rénchuān in Cháoxiǎn (Korea), and Chángqí (Nagasaki) in Rìběn (Japan).
Railways: Jīngjīn,
Jīnyú,
Jīnghàn,
Zhèngtài,
Jīngzhāng.
Postal routes: east out of Shānhǎiguān reaching Shèngjīng Suīzhōng,
west out of Zǐjīngguān reaching Língqiū, Shānxī,
south across the plain reaching Dézhōu, Shāndōng,
north out of Gǔběikǒu reaching Rèhé.
Telegraph lines: northwest to Kùlún (Ulaanbaatar),
southwest to Tàiyuán;
from Tiānjīn northeast to Fèngtiān;
submarine cable from Dàgū east to Zhīfú.)
Shùntiān Fǔ: (In the early Míng dynasty, it was called Běipíng Fǔ.
Later, Běijīng was built,
and it was changed again.
Since the Liáo dynasty, all capitals were located here.
In the sixth year of Zhèngtǒng,
it was first named Jīngshī.
It administered six zhōus and
twenty-five xiàns.
) In the early Shùnzhì reign,
a Fǔyǐn, Fǔchéng, and Zhìzhōng were appointed for Jīngshī.
The Shùntiān Xúnfǔ was stationed at Zūnhuà,
and this post was abolished in the early Kāngxī reign.
In the fifteenth year,
Zūnhuà was elevated to a zhōu.
In the twenty-seventh year,
four Lù Tóngzhī were appointed,
to separately administer the subordinate zhōus and xiàns.
(They were assigned to the Tōngyǒng and Bàchāng circuit-dao.
They were also jointly overseen by the Zhílì Zǒngdūd.
) In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
ministers from the various boards and ministries were again appointed to concurrently manage the affairs of the fǔ,
by special imperial appointment,
without a fixed number of officials.
In the ninth year,
Nínghé was established.
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng,
Zūnhuà was again elevated to a Zhílìzhōu,
with Yùtián and Fēngrùn subordinate to it.
It was 440 lǐ wide
and 500 lǐ long.

Nánjīng,
now southwest of the city,
was the fortified city of Táng dynasty's Yōuzhōu military governor.
The Jīn dynasty expanded it.
By the Yuán dynasty, the old site gradually disappeared.
The Yuán dynasty's Dàdū
then encompassed the areas outside today's Āndìngmén and Déshèngmén.
In the early Míng dynasty, the northern part of the city wall was shrunk,
and the Yuán system was also changed.
In the early Yǒnglè reign,
the southern city was re-expanded,
which was again different from the old system of Hóngwǔ.
Today, the Imperial City has a circumference of eighteen lǐ.
Inside Zhèngyángmén is called Dàqīngmén;

The county has one post station.

Fèngtiān: In the territory of Yǔgòng's Qīng and Jì provinces.
(Shùn divided its northeast into Yōu and Yíng.
Xià retained Qīng and Jì.
Shāng changed it to Yíngzhōu.

it was Yōuzhōu.

it was Liáodōng Dūzhīhuǐshǐ Sī.
) In the 3rd month of the 10th year of Qīng Tiānmìng,
the capital was set at Shěnyáng.
In the 8th year of Tiāncōng,
it was honored as Shèngjīng.
In the 1st year of Shùnzhì,
all the Míng guards and stations were abolished,
and Neì Dàchén, Fù Dūtǒng,
and the Eight Banners garrisons were established.
In the 3rd year,
Neì Dàchén was changed to Ángbāng Zhāngjīng,
and the seal of Zhènshǒu Zǒngguǎn was granted.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī,
Ángbāng Zhāngjīng was changed to Zhènshǒu Liáodōng Děngchù Dìfāng Jiāngjūn.
In the 4th year,
it was changed to Zhènshǒu Fèngtiān Děngchù Dìfāng Jiāngjūn.
In the 3rd month of the 33rd year of Guāngxù,
the Jiāngjūn was abolished,
and the Dōngsānsheng Zǒngdū and Fèngtiān Xúnfǔ were established,
changing it into a province.
North to Táonán;
(bordering Hēilóngjiāng.)
South to Lǚshùnkǒu;
(maritime boundary southeast,
bordering Cháoxiǎn by the Yālù Jiāng.)

East to Āntú.

Its breadth was 1,800 lǐ,
and its length was 1,750 lǐ.
The North Pole's elevation ranged from 39 degrees 40 minutes to 44 degrees 15 minutes.
It was 4 to 12 degrees east of Jīngshī.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
the registered households numbered 1,655,733,
and the population was 10,696,004.
It administered a total of eight fǔ,
five zhílì tīng,
three tīng,
six zhōu,

(Note: Shèngjīng,
in the 5th year of Tiāncōng, was enlarged and repaired based on the Míng Shěnyáng Wèichéng.
The city wall was 9 lǐ and 332 bù in circumference,
3 zhàng 5 chǐ high,
1 zhàng thick,
with battlements 7 chǐ 5 cùn high,
and a total of 651 embrasures.
There were eight gates: on the east, the left was Fújìn,
the right was Nèizhì;
on the south, the left was Déshèng,
the right was Tiānyòu;
on the west, the left was Huáiyuǎn,
the right was Wàirǎng;
on the north, the left was Dìzài,
the right was Fúshèng.
Each gate had a tower and barbican,
in addition to corner towers.
In the center of the four cities was Dàzhèng Diàn,
the place where Tàizōng held court.
To the west of the palace was the Dànèi.
Facing south was Dàqīng Mén,
inside the gate was Chóngzhèng Diàn,
in front of the palace to the east was Fēilóng Gé,
to the west Xiángfèng Gé.
Directly north of Chóngzhèng Diàn was Fènghuáng Lóu,
north of the tower was Qīngníng Gōng.
To the east of the palace were Yǎnqìng Gōng and Guānsuī Gōng,
to the west Yǒngfú Gōng and Línzhǐ Gōng.
In front of Fènghuáng Lóu,
to the east was Shīshàn Zhāi,
south of the zhāi was Rìhuá Lóu;
to the west Xiézhōng Zhāi,
south of the zhāi was Xiáqǐ Lóu.
East of Chóngzhèng Diàn was Yíhé Diàn,
behind the palace was Jièzhǐ Gōng,
behind the gong was Jìngdiǎn Gé.
West of Chóngzhèng Diàn was Díguāng Diàn,
behind the palace was Bǎojí Gōng,
behind the gong was Jìsī Zhāi,
behind the zhāi was Chóngmó Gé.
West of the Dànèi was Wénsù Gé,
a place for storing books.
To the southeast was Tàimiào.
The silver treasury was south of Dàzhèng Diàn,
the weaving treasury was south of the Dànèi.
The Hùbù, Lǐbù, and Gōngbù were east of the silver treasury,
the Xíngbù and Bīngbù were west of the weaving treasury.
The Yùshǐ Gōngshǔ was in the northeast corner of the city.
Outside it, the guānchéng was built in the 19th year of Kāngxī,
7 chǐ 5 cùn high,
and 32 lǐ 48 bù in circumference.
There were eight gates: on the east, the left was Xiǎodōng Guān,
the right was Dàdōng Guān;
on the south, the left was Dànán Guān,
the right was Xiǎonán Guān;
on the west, the left was Dàxī Guān,
the right was Xiǎoxī Guān;
on the north, the left was Xiǎoběi Guān,
the right was Dàběi Guān.
Inside the guānchéng, to the south was Tiāntán,
to the east were Dìtán and Tángzi,
in the southwest corner were Shèjì Tán and Léiyǔ Tán,
in the southeast corner were Xiānnóng Cí and Jìtián.
In the southwest corner of Jìtián, two water gates were set up,
guiding the Xiǎoshěn Shuǐ to flow out from the gates,
its lower course emptying into the Húnhé.
Its famous mountains were Yīwūlǘ and Sōnglíng.
Its major rivers were Liáo Hé and Hún Hé.
Its important strategic points were Shānhǎiguān, Fènghuángchéng, and Wēiyuǎnbǎo.
Its boat routes: from Yíngkǒu southwest to Tiānjīn,
south to Zhīfú,
southeast to Cháoxiǎn's Rénchuān.
Its railways: those belonging domestically were
Yíngyú;
those belonging to Japan were
the Dōngqīng Zhīlù built by Russia.
Its telegraph lines: west to Tiānjīn,
southwest Lǚshùn,
southeast Fènghuáng and Āndōng,
northeast Jílín.

Jílín: The ancient domain of the Sùshèn state.
(In the early Míng dynasty,
it was the territory of the Nú'érgān Dū Sī,
governing 184 guards and 20 garrisons.
Later, it belonged to the Huīfā, Wūlā, and Yèhè of the three Chángbái Shān tribes and the four Hùlún tribes,
also encompassing the northern borders of Hādá and the lands of the Dōnghǎi tribes.
)In the early Qīng dynasty,
a Manchu city was built in the wilds of Émòhuì at Èduōlǐchéng.
In the 10th year of Shùnzhì (1653),
an Āngbāng Zhāngjīng and two Fùdūtǒng were stationed to guard Nínggǔtǎ.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī (1662),
it was changed to Nínggǔtǎ Jiāngjūn.
In the 15th year (1676), it was relocated,
and changed to Jílín Jiāngjūn.
Earlier, in the 10th year (1671), one Fùdūtǒng was relocated to be stationed in Jílín,
and in the 33rd year (1694), to Bódōunà.
In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng (1725),
a Jílín Ālèchǔkā Fùdūtǒng was re-established.
In the 5th year (1727),
a Sānxìng Fùdūtǒng was added.
In the 7th year of Guāngxù (1881),
a Húnchūn Fùdūtǒng was established,
along with three prefectures: Jílín, Bīnzhōu, and Wǔcháng.
In the 8th year (1882),
Jílín Tīng was promoted to Fǔ.
Later, Chángchūn, Xīnchéng, and Yīlán were added,
each governing a varying number of counties.
In the 33rd year (1907), a province was established,
the Jiāngjūn was changed to Xúnfǔ,
and all Fùdūtǒng and similar posts were abolished.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng (1911),
the southwest, northwest, southeast, and northeast four routes were designated as four circuits (dào).
In total, it administered eleven prefectures (fǔ),
one sub-prefecture (zhōu),
five departments (tīng),
and eighteen counties (xiàn).
To the west, it reached Yītōngzhōu,
bordering Shèngjīng;
to the east, it reached the Wūsūlǐ Jiāng,
bordering Russia's Dōnghǎi Bīnshěng;
to the north, it reached the Sōnghuā Jiāng,
bordering Hēilóngjiāng;
to the south, it reached the Túmén and Yālù Jiāng,
bordering Cháoxiǎn.
Its breadth was over 2,400 lǐ,
and its length was over 1,500 lǐ.
Its northern latitude ranged from 41 degrees 30 minutes to 45 degrees 40 minutes.
Its longitude relative to Jīngshī (Beijing) ranged from 9 degrees 8 minutes to 13 degrees 10 minutes east.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng (1911),
it had 739,461 households,
and a population of 3,735,167.

From Húnchūn eastward to Hǎishēnwǎi,

Its tribes,

From the mouth of the Hùntóng Jiāng west to Hēilè'ěr,
the Jìlèimí tribe resided there,
which is the Jìlèimǐn of the Jīn Shǐ;

the Hèzhékālā resided there,

By the Treaty of Àihún in the 8th year of Xiánfēng (1858),
the mouth of the Wūsūlǐ Jiāng was made the new boundary,
losing over 2,000 lǐ of land,
but for Jí, this was only its northeast corner.
By the Treaty of Běijīng in the 11th year (1861),
from the mouth of the Wūsūlǐ Jiāng, flowing upstream to the Sōngāchá Hé,
crossing Xīngkǎi Hú west to the mouth of the Báilíng Hé,
then crossing the Dàsuīfēn Hé south to the mouth of the Húbùtú Hé,
then south and west to the old boundary east of the Túmén Jiāng mouth was ceded to Russia.
The mouth of the Húbùtú Hé at Wūzhákù Biānkǎ became the new boundary,
losing several thousand lǐ more,
thus there was no longer any river mouth entering the sea within Jí's jurisdiction.
In the 12th year of Guāngxù (1886),
the Hēidǐngzi boundary survey

so the "tǔ"
character boundary marker
30 lǐ inland from the mouth of the Túmén Jiāng became the new Sino-Russian boundary.
Also, in the northeastern sea, Kùyè Dǎo,

was 300 to 400 lǐ wide
and over 2,000 lǐ long.
To its northwest was Túcèsútú Shān,
on its shaded side were the Shèwǎláng tribe, and on its sunny side the Fèiyǎkā tribe.
To the south was Ādāngjí Shān,
on its eastern side the Sōngkuòluò tribe, and to its south the Éhènlángchūn tribe,
and further south the Yǎdān tribe,

Being distant, they could not arrive regularly,

Later, it belonged to Sānxìng.

Volume 32, Geography 4, Hēilóngjiāng
Hēilóngjiāng: The northern border of the ancient Sùshèn kingdom.
In the Míng dynasty, it was administered by the Nú'ěrgān Dūsī.
In the early Qīng dynasty, there were various tribes such as the Suǒlún and Dáhū'ěr,
scattered across the lands inside and outside Hēilóngjiāng, along the É'ěrgǔnà Hé and Jīngqílǐ Jiāng.
During the Tiāncōng and Chóngdé reigns,
they were progressively conquered.
In the 22nd year of Kāngxī, the Rakeshà were vanquished,
and the General Guarding Hēilóngjiāng and Other Places, and the Assistant Military Governor, were first established and stationed in Àihún Chéng on the eastern bank of the river.
Soon after, they were moved to Mò'ěrgēn.
In the 37th year,
the Assistant Military Governor was moved to Qíqíhā'ěr.
In the 38th year,
the General also moved there,
and it thus became the provincial capital.
Later, additional Assistant Military Governors were set up for Mò'ěrgēn, Hēilóngjiāng, Hūlán, Hūlúnbèi'ěr, and Bùtèhā.
Towards the end of Guāngxù's reign,
half of these posts were abolished,
and various departments, prefectures, and counties were established instead.
In the 33rd year,
the General was removed,
the Hēilóngjiāng巡fǔ (Provincial Governor) was appointed,
it was reformed into a province,
all Assistant Military Governor posts were abolished,
and the local official system was changed.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
it comprised three Circuits,
seven Prefectures,
six Departments,
one Subprefecture,
and seven Counties.
One additional Prefecture,
eleven Directly Administered Departments,
and five Counties were proposed to be established.
To the south, it bordered Jílín along the Sōnghuā Jiāng.
To the west, it bordered the Russian-held Sàbàihālé Province and the Chēchén Hàn Qí of Outer Měnggǔ along the É'ěrgǔnà Hé.
To the southwest, it adjoined the Wūzhūmùqìn Zuǒyì, Kē'ěrqìn Yòuyì Zhōng, Qián, and Hòu banners of Inner Měnggǔ.
To the east, it still bordered Jílín at the confluence of the Sōnghuā and Hēilóng rivers.
To the north and northeast, it bordered the Russian-held Āmù'ěr Province.
Its breadth was over 2,800 lǐ,
and its length was over 1,500 lǐ.
Its latitude ranged from 45 degrees 50 minutes to 52 degrees 50 minutes North.
Its longitude ranged from 3 degrees 40 minutes to 16 degrees 20 minutes East of Jīngshī (Beijing).
(Note: Regarding the old boundaries of Hēilóngjiāng,
Yáng Bīn's "Liǔbiān Jìlüè" states:
"The territory under the Àihún General
extended east to the sea,
and west to the Russian border at Nǐbùchǔ."
Nǐbùchǔ is Níbùchǔ,
now known in Russian as Nerchinsk.
The Àihún General was the Hēilóngjiāng General;
this was the boundary in the early Qīng dynasty.
From the mouth of the Ānbāgé'ěrbìqí Hé,

All streams and rivers south of the range flowing into Hēilóngjiāng belonged to China,
while those north of the range belonged to Russia.
China and Russia divided along the range;
this was the boundary of the Treaty of Níbùchǔ in the 28th year of Kāngxī.
From where the É'ěrgǔnà Hé enters Hēilóngjiāng
to where Hēilóngjiāng meets Sōnghuā Jiāng,
the area south and west belonged to Hēilóngjiāng Province,
while the area north and east belonged to Russia.
China and Russia divided along the river;
this was the boundary of the Treaty of Àihún in the 8th year of Xiánfēng.
Níbùchǔ is over 500 lǐ west of the Ānbāgé'ěrbìqí Hé.
It was originally the territory of China's Màomíng'ān, Bùlātè, and Wūliánghǎi tribes.
During the Chóngdé reign,
it was stealthily occupied by the Russians,
who built a city there and resided in it,
encroaching upon and plundering the Suǒlún and Dáhū'ěr tribes,
causing border troubles for over 30 years.
In the 28th year of Kāngxī, the boundary was set,
and it was then given to Russia,
thus shrinking the old boundary by over 500 lǐ.
As for the old territory south of Wàixīng'ānlǐng,
and north and east of Hēilóngjiāng,
it was perhaps over 3,700 lǐ.
Although its mountains, rivers, tribes, and cities/settlements now belonged to Russia,
they are also recorded here
so as not to forget their origin.
Wàixīng'ānlǐng is the great northern branch of Kūnlún.
The southern branch of the Kūnlún mountain range
forms the Liángzhōu Nánshān,
the Hèlánshān,
the Yīnshān,
and the Nèixīng'ānlǐng.
The northern branch forms the Cōnglǐng,
the Tiānshān,
the Ā'ěrtài Shān,
the Kěntè Shān,
and the Wàixīng'ānlǐng.
"Inner" and "Outer"
are in reference to Hēilóngjiāng.
Other mountains such as Dǒusèshān, Ròuyángshān, Zhūdèhèshān, NènDānhādālāshān, Dálètìshāshān, Ālālāshān, Dàosīhādá, Cháhāyànhādá, and Màohādá
are all branches of Wàixīng'ānlǐng,
and are located northeast of the river.
Regarding rivers, the Ānbāgé'ěrbìqí Hé is the starting point of the Kāngxī old boundary into the main river.
From here eastward,

The *fǔ* territory occupies the lower reaches of the Hūlán Hé,
with the Sōnghuā Jiāng bordering its south.
With its long rivers and numerous branches,
it provides ample irrigation.
The soil is fertile
and is known as a grain-producing area.
After the 13th year of Yōngzhèng
military colonies and settlements were established,
and reclamation efforts were made daily.
During the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns [1851-1875],
vagrants from Zhílì and Shāndōng who migrated outside the Pass
competed to work as laborers in the colonies and settlements.
As time passed,
they privately bought and sold land,
their occupied land grew daily,
and their numbers increased.
Successive generals then memorialized for civil reclamation,
increased and reformed civil officials,
and the *fǔ* became a pioneer
in the provincial system.

The Gānhé flows in from the northwest.

it joins the Kūnhé on its right.
