The 64 villages east of the river were there.
South of the Jīngqílǐ Jiāng,
north of the Hēilóngjiāng,
and east to the boundary set by the *fēngduī* in the 9th year of Guāngxù.
There are the Bólègé'ěrqìn Hé and Bó'ěrhélǐ'èmé.
It spans 140 *lǐ* north-south,
and 50 to 70 *lǐ* east-west.
According to the treaty of the 8th year of Xiánfēng,
this was the permanent residence of the people of this banner.
During the Gēngzǐ Incident,
the Russians violated the treaty and drove them out,
even disturbing the right bank of the river,
coercing tens of thousands of elderly residents to be drowned in the river by officials.
When the peace treaty was concluded,
in the 32nd year of Guāngxù, only the land on the right bank was recovered.
The 64 villages have not yet been reclaimed.
Now, the *tīng* territory only comprises three townships in the west, south, and north.
There are over 100,000 *shǎng* of undeveloped land in the Xùnbiélā section,
which was opened for cultivation at the end of Guāngxù.
Three stations were previously established: from Èlètǎ'ěrqí in Nènjiāng, 85 *lǐ* northeast to Kùmù'ěr within the *tīng*'s jurisdiction;
another 35 *lǐ* to Èyǔ'ěr;
and another 100 *lǐ* to Hēilóngjiāng city,
which is the seat of the *tīng*.
These are the ten stations on the northern route from the provincial capital.
Furthermore, from the *tīng*, traveling south to Bìlā'ěrhùi, it meets the Xīndào from Hǎibì.
Traveling north through the forest reaches Mòhé,
where newly established Huò'ěrmòjīn and Qílèkè *kǎlún* are located.
The commercial port
is located between Tóudào Gōu and Èrdào Gōu north of the city.
It was opened by the Sino-Japanese treaty in the 31st year of Guāngxù.
According to records, in the middle of Yōngzhèng,
thirteen *kǎlún* were established.
In the 8th year of Xiánfēng,
China and Russia divided the river as a boundary.
For example, Yīmǎbìlā'áng'ā, Jīngqílǐ Hé, Wūlǔmùsūdān, Niǔlèmen Hé, and the confluence of the Hēilóng and Húntóng two rivers.
Five *kǎlún* went to the Russian territory on the left bank,
while on the right bank, eight were added to the east and three to the west.
In the 12th year of Guāngxù,
to protect the Mòhé gold mines,
twenty-three more were added, including Xī'ěrgēntǔhādá,
connecting to Zhū'ěrtèyī of Hūlúnbèi'ěr city.
Further southeast, five more were added: Chèlèshān, Xùnhé, Kuò'ěrfēiyīn Hékǒu, Jípǔxùn Hé, and Tíyīn Hé,
making a total of five,
for a grand total of thirty-nine *kǎlún*.
After the Gēngzǐ chaos,
all *kǎlún* were destroyed.
South of the Xùnhé was allocated to Xīngdōng Dào.
In the 34th year,
starting from the mouth of the È'ěrgǔnà Hé
down to the mouth of the Xùnhé,
twenty new *kǎlún* were established: Luògǔhé,
Nàqīnhādá,
Mòhé,
Wūsūlǐ,
Bā'ěrbōlì,
Āmù'ěr,
Kāikùkāng,
Ānluó,
Yīxīkěn,
Wōxīmén,
Āngān,
Cháhāyàn,
Wànghādá,
Hūmǎ'ěr,
Xī'ěrgēnqí,
Qīlā,
Zhákèdáhuòluò,
Huò'ěrqìn,
Huò'ěrmòjīn,
Qīkèlè.
Each *kǎ* has one officer and thirty soldiers.
Five *kǎ* have one *kǎ* officer,
and ten *kǎ* have one general *kǎ* officer.
Of the thirty *kǎ* soldiers,
ten patrol,
and twenty are assigned to open up wasteland for cultivation.
They rotate shifts,
and the grain they obtain serves as a stipend for the officers and soldiers.
When the land is productive and the harvest is abundant,
land is granted and salaries are stopped.
Hēihé Fǔ: (900 *lǐ* northeast of the provincial capital.
Originally named Dàhēihétún.) In the 34th year of Guāngxù,
the *fǔ* was established,
belonging to Àihún Dào.
(To the west: Notable branches of the Nèi Xīng'ānlǐng mountains,
Yāntǒng, Báishí, Kùmù'ěr Shìwéi Shān, Èlèkè'ěr Shān.
The Hēilóngjiāng comes from the north,
forming the boundary with Russia.
It receives the Hūmǎ'ěr Hé on its right,
entering the territory.
South to Xī'ěryīqí Kǎlún,
it joins the Dānhé, Kuānhé, Qīlā, Kānī, Kùlún, Kèlǔlún, Dàyàn, Huòlìgēbì, Fǎbiélā, Èní, Ālèkāmù rivers.
Further east, it passes north of the city.
Further south,
it receives the Jīngqílǐ Jiāng on its left,
and the Wūkèsà Hé on its right,
entering Àihún.
To the north is the Hūmǎ'ěr Hé,
originating from the Yīlèhūlǐ Shān.
It has four sources from north and south,
which converge and flow east into the territory.
The Wōlìkè, Kùlèguǒlǐ, Chuònuò, Zhákèdáqí Hé flow in from the west.
Further east is Hū'ěrhā,
flowing east into the Hēilóngjiāng.
Its source and course are approximately seven to eight hundred *lǐ*.
Its banks are where the *Èlúnchūn* people of the Kùmǎ'ěr tribe, who offered sable, fished and hunted.
On the south bank is the ancient city of Hūmǎ'ěr.
The *fǔ* seat was formerly a Sino-Russian trading port.
Initially, mutual trade was less than one-thousandth of that at the river and sea ports.
After the river was divided,
trade prospered.
Since they vigorously developed Hǎilánpào,
and also during the Gēngzǐ Incident,
Chinese merchants flocked to their territory,
commerce flourished daily for them,
while ours sharply declined.
However, the *fǔ* seat, protecting Àihún to the south,
is truly a crucial border defense point.
There are over 100,000 *shǎng* of undeveloped land in the Fǎbiélā section,
which was opened for cultivation in the 34th year of Guāngxù.
One official and commercial road: 80 *lǐ* south to Àihún city.
The rest are waterways,
relying on Russian steamboats for travel.
Four new *kǎlún* were established: Xī'ěrgēnqí,
Qīlāzhákèdá,
Huòluò,
Huò'ěrqìn.
Hūlún Zhílì Tīng: (860 *lǐ* northwest of the province.
This is the city of Hūlúnbèi'ěr Fùdūtǒng.
Ancient Shìwéi kingdom.
There is Shìwéi Shān.
During the Míng dynasty, it belonged to the Duǒyán Sān Wèi.)
In the 34th year of Guāngxù (1908),
it was established by converting the Hūlúnbèi'ěr city.
The Hūlún Bīngbèi Dào was stationed in the *tīng*.
It is over 1,100 *lǐ* wide,
and 1,600 *lǐ* long.
The North Pole is at 49 degrees and 35 minutes latitude.
The capital is 2 degrees and 2 minutes to the east.
(The Nèi Xīng'ān Lǐng is to the east.
The mountain range runs north from the Suǒyuè'ěrjì Shān,
forming the Yīlèhūlǐ'ālín,
then turns east,
with its remaining branches winding westward along the north and south banks of the Hǎilā'ěr Hé;
the right bank of the É'ěrgǔnà Hé is within the *tīng*'s territory,
and all its waters originate here.
The Hǎilā'ěr Hé flows out from the western foothills of the range,
westward through Chuōluó'ěr,
north of Chá'ěrbāqí Shān,
south of Nàdū'ěr and west of Zhádùn,
further west through Tènánkè,
and further west the Yīmǐn Hé,
all converge here.
It passes north of the city,
joins the Mò'ěrgēn Hé,
and enters Lúbīn.
To the northwest, it joins the É'ěrgǔnà Hé and enters Shìwéi.
To the north: the Gēnhé receives various rivers from the west of Èluónuò'ěr,
and further west enters the É'ěrgǔnà Hé.
To the south is Dá'ěrbīn Chí,
from which the Hā'ěrhā Hé flows out,
westward converging into Bèi'ěr Chí.
The Wū'ěrshùn Hé flows out from the pond,
northward into Hūlún Chí.
The *tīng*'s territory serves as pastures for the Suǒlún, Xīnbā'ěrhǔ, Èlǔtè, and Chénbā'ěrhǔ banners.
Also, north of the Hǎilā'ěr Hé, there is the Tuōhé Lù Xiélǐng,
governing the Èlúnchūn people.
Eight old posts were established: from Yá'ěrbókètái in Xībùtèhā, fifty *lǐ* west to Yī'ěrkètè in the *tīng*,
another fifty *lǐ* to Hū'ěrgèyī,
another fifty *lǐ* to Shūdūkèyī,
another sixty *lǐ* to Yàkèsà,
another fifty *lǐ* to Hālāhéshuò,
another sixty-five *lǐ* to Zhálāmùtài,
another fifty-two *lǐ* to Hākè'émó,
and another sixty *lǐ* to Hūlúnbèi'ěr Chéng,
which is the seat of the *tīng*.
It was the seventeenth post on the western route from the provincial capital.
During the Gēngzǐ Incident (1900),
the post stations were destroyed,
and all travel thenceforth was via the Dōngqīng Tiělù.
Also, 320 *lǐ* southwest, at Bùyětúbù'ěrdū, is the Yěshòuníng Sì,
on the road from Zhāngjiākǒu.
Eight *lǐ* north of the temple is a large market,
where in the eighth month of each year,
Inner and Outer Mongols gather for trade.
Three new *kǎlún* (guard posts) were established: namely Mèngkèxīlǐ,
É'ěrdénítuóluóhuī,
and Kùkèduōbó,
with Kùkèduōbó as the general *kǎlún*.
To the southwest is the Zhū'ěrbótè Yánchí (salt lake).
The Dōngqīng Tiělù enters the territory from Lúbīn,
passes north of the city,
and enters the territory of Xībùtèhā.
There are nine railway stations: Wángōng, Wūgǔnuò'ěr, Hǎilā'ěr, Hākè, Zhá'ěrmù, Yàkèshén, Miǎndùhé, Wūnán'ěr, and Yīlìkèdōu.
As a treaty port,
it was opened for trade by the Sino-Japanese agreement in the eleventh month of the 31st year of Guāngxù (December 1905).
Regarding the Hūlún border *kǎlún*,
since the border demarcation with Russia in the 5th year of Yōngzhèng (1727),
twelve *kǎlún* were established, including Cháhàn'áolā and Sūkètèyī,
named "Outer *Kǎlún*".
In the 11th year (1733),
fifteen more *kǎlún* were established inside the Outer *Kǎlún*, including Kùlǐduō'ěrtèlè and Mòlèjīn,
spaced one or two hundred *lǐ* from the Outer *Kǎlún*,
named "Inner *Kǎlún*".
In the 7th year of Xiánfēng (1857),
due to the great distance between inner and outer posts,
they were relocated to be
thirty to forty *lǐ* apart,
to facilitate mutual patrolling.
Three *kǎ* were changed to three *tái*,
and new names were given,
but later they were all dilapidated and undocumented.
In the 10th year of Guāngxù (1884),
to prevent Russians from crossing the border to mine gold,
from Hēilóngjiāng Chéng, along the right bank of the É'ěrgǔnà, north of the Hūlún Zhū'ěrtèyī *kǎlún*,
five more were added, including Mòlǐlèkè,
making a total of seventeen Outer *Kǎlún*.
These were all destroyed in the Gēngzǐ Incident (1900).
In the 34th year (1908),
a reorganization was carried out,
starting from Tǎ'ěrbāgāndáhū Shān,
extending to the mouth of the É'ěrgǔnà Hé,
twenty-one were re-established,
fifteen retaining their old names,
and six newly named:
Tǎ'ěrbāgāndáhū,
Cháhàn'áolā,
Ābāgāitú (the above belong to Lúbīn);
Mèngkèxīlǐ,
É'ěrdénítuóluóhuī,
Kùkèduōbó (Kùkèduōbó is the general *kǎlún*,
the above belong to Hūlún);
Bātú'ěrhéshuò,
Bāyǎsīhūlángtúwēndū'ěr,
Húyù'ěrhéqí,
Bāyànlùkè,
Zhū'ěrtèyī,
Mòlǐlèkè,
Bìlā'ěrhé,
Niú'ěrhé,
Zhū'ěrgānhé (Zhū'ěrgānhé is the general *kǎlún*);
Wēnhé,
Chángdiàn,
Yīmùhé,
Qígānhé,
Yǒng'ānshān,
Élèhādá (the above belong to Shìwéi).
Previously, Russians had crossed the border to cultivate land and cut grass;
by this time, they were expelled,
and Hūlún established a Border Cultivation General Bureau,
with a branch office in Lúbīn.
The Russians complied with regulations and paid taxes,
and Chinese people obtaining permits for trade
came and went in an endless stream.
This occurred in the winter month of the 34th year of Guāngxù (1908).
Also, the sixteen old *kǎlún* southwest of Hūlún
were all for defending against the Kǎ'ěrkǎ.)
Lúbīn Fǔ: (One thousand one hundred and sixty *lǐ* northwest of the province.
Originally named Mǎnzhōulǐ,
it was the first station of the Dōngqīng Tiělù entering China.
) In the 34th year of Guāngxù,
it was initially planned to establish Mǎnzhū Fǔ,
later renamed,
and belonged to Hūlún Dào.
(East: The É'ěrgǔnà Hé enters from Hūlún,
flows northwest,
and near Àbāgāitú Shān,
divides into two branches.
One flows southwest,
becoming the Dálán'èluò Mùhé,
entering Hūlún Chí.
Its main stream flows northeast from the west side of the mountain,
becoming the É'ěrgǔnà Hé.
It makes a great turn here,
like a person bending their back to pass an object with their hand.
É'ěrgǔnà,
in Mongolian, means "to pass an object with the hand."
The Hǎilār Hé turns into the É'ěrgǔnà Hé,
splitting into two branches,
one flowing along the east bank,
called Hǎilār Hékǒu,
and one flowing along the west bank,
called É'ěrgǔnà Hé,
which reunite further north,
entering the Hēilóng Jiāng.
From Àbāgāitú Shān downwards, it is the boundary water between China and Russia.
In the 28th year of Kāngxī,
boundary markers were erected by the Níbùchǔ Treaty.
The Kèlǔlún Hé enters from the Kǎ'ěrkǎ Department,
and the Dálán'èluò Mùhé branches off from the Hǎilār Hé,
both entering Hūlún Chí,
where the water accumulates without flowing out,
thus Hūlún is a salt lake.
To the southeast is the Wū'ěrshùn Hé,
flowing out of Bèi'ěr Chí,
and flowing north into Hūlún Chí.
Its right bank is the territory of Hūlún Tīng,
with pastures of the Xīnbā'ěrhǔ banners.
There were formerly six Sino-Russian boundary *Èbó*: namely Tǎ'ěrgē Dágù,
Càhǎn Wūlǔ,
Bólúotuóluó Hǎi,
Suǒkètú,
É'ěrdǐlǐtuóluó Hǎi,
and Àbāhāyītú.
This was the 63rd *Èbó* of the Sino-Russian border east of Kùlún.
The Qiàkètú Treaty of the 5th year of Yōngzhèng established this as the end of the *Èbó*.
Southwest of Tǎ'ěrbāgàn Dáhū Shān is the Kǎ'ěrkǎ boundary,
with Manchu and Mongolian boundary markers,
which demarcate Hūlún and Kǎ'ěrkǎ,
replaced every ten years.
There are three newly established *Kǎlún*: namely Tǎ'ěrbāgàn Dáhū,
Càhǎn Áolā,
and Àbāgāitú.
To the north is the Jīnyuán Biānbǎo.
The Dōngqīng Tiělù enters Chinese territory from the Russian Sàbàikēlè Province,
passes east of the prefectural seat,
and enters Hūlún Tīng.
It has four stations: Mǎnzhōulǐ,
Zángāng,
Zhālàinà'ěr,
and Hèlèhóngdé.
It is a commercial port,
opened by a Sino-Japanese agreement.
It has a customs house.
Xīngdōng Dào: (1,500 *lǐ* northeast of the provincial capital.
In the Míng dynasty, this was the territory of Hēilóngjiāng,
and places such as Sùwēn Hé Wèi and Zhēnhé Suǒ.
)In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
the Suí-Lán Hǎidào of Suíhuà Chéng was relocated to the area east of the Nèi Xīng'ān Lǐng,
and renamed Xīngdōng Bīngbèi Dào,
specializing in reclamation, forestry, and mining affairs.
In the 34th year,
its office was established north of Tuōluó Shān,
serving as the prefectural seat.
It administered two counties.
(The Nèi Xīng'ān Lǐng range enters from Àihuī,
runs south as the watershed between the Nèn Jiāng and Hēilóngjiāng,
and to the northeast and east of Hǎilún, it forms the watershed between Hēilóngjiāng and Sōnghuājiāng,
known as Bùlún Shān,
and Fó sī Hēng Shān,
ending at the confluence of the Hēilóng Jiāng and Sōnghuā Jiāng,
called Xiǎo Xīng'ān Lǐng.
Hēilóngjiāng enters from Àihuī, joined by the Xùn Hé,
and flows southeast.
The upper source of the Kē'ěrfēn Hé is called É'ěrpí Hé.
Further southeast,
it receives the Gáchí Hé from the right bank,
and the Xīdūlǐ, Gǔlèkùlā, Bìhǎn Yìn, Qídá, Mòlǐ, Wūyún, and other rivers,
which flow in from the southwest.
Further southeast,
it receives the Jiālè Hé and Fǔ Hé from the right bank.
It bends south,
and the Jiāyīn Hé flows in from the west.
Then it flows south, passing east and then south of the prefectural seat.
The Qiūtái Hé flows in from the west in a winding course.
Bending east,
it receives the Fē'ěrfǎ'èmú Shuǐ, Bùzhàn Hé, and Yīlǐ Hé from the right bank,
and converges with the Sōnghuā Jiāng.
To the north is the Xùn Hé,
and flowing east is the Zhàn Hé,
which joins the Ā'ěrqìn on the right bank,
and flows into Hēilóngjiāng.
Its left bank is the territory of Àihuī.
To the west: Dūlǔ;
further west: Tāngwàng,
which on its right bank joins the Yīchūn Zhálǐ Hé;
further west: Bālán Hé,
which flows east and then bends south,
all entering Tāngyuán.
The prefectural seat is located on the right bank of Hēilóngjiāng,
facing Ètúnsōngyóuzi across the river.
To the northwest: the confluence of the Zhàn Hé and Xùn Hé;
the upper section has Bìlá'ěr and Èlúnchūn Xiélǐng.
The Èlúnchūn were originally hunting tribes,
unacquainted with writing, farming, or planting,
and were deceived by the Russians.
In the late Guāngxù era,
pacification and settlement were first proposed.
Xīngdōng Dào concurrently served as *xiélǐng*,
establishing reclamation bureaus and schools.
To the west of the Xīng'ān Lǐng is Lóngmén Zhèn;
on the south bank of Hēilóngjiāng are Zhàoxīng Zhèn and Yùxīng Zhèn,
where reclamation is flourishing.
There are three official and commercial roads: formerly, there was a road from Qíqíhā'ěr to Guānyīn Shān;
in the 34th year of Guāngxù,
a new road was opened from Xīngdōng, passing through Yāntǒng Shān to Tāngyuán,
which was the southwest road;
and another road from Guānyīn Shān, passing through Tāngyuán territory to Sānxìng,
which was the west road.
In the 2nd year of Xuāntǒng,
the Hǎibì Dào was newly opened,
allowing access from Bìlá'ěr to Hǎilún.
)Dàtōng Xiàn (520 *lǐ* southwest of the prefectural seat.
Originally Chónggǔ'ěrkù Zhàn,
one of the five stations north of the Jiāng River in Jílín.
Established in the 31st year of Guāngxù,
it was a county subordinate to Yīlán, Jílín.
In the 34th year, its affiliation was changed.
To the north, the Nèi Xīng'ān Lǐng mountain range winds around,
while the south is all flat plains.
To the south: the Sōnghuā Jiāng enters from Mùlán,
flows east, then northeast into Tāngyuán;
its right bank is Fāngzhèng, Jílín.
To the west: Chàlín, Xiǎoqiáozǐ, Fùlāhún, Tóudào, Èrdào, Sāndào, Sìdào Shāhé, Zhuǎnxīnhú, Èrdàohézǐ,
all flow south into the Sōnghuā Jiāng.
The right bank of Èrdàohézǐ is Mùlán territory.
To the east is the Dàtōng Hé,
after which the county is named.
Further east are the Wūlāhún, Dàgǔdòng, and Xiǎogǔdòng rivers,
which also flow south into the Sōnghuā Jiāng.
The left bank of Xiǎogǔdòng Hé is Tāngyuán territory.
The Wūlāhún Hé flows west,
converging into two lakes,
called Sānjí Pào and Èrlóng Tán.
The land beside the lakes is fertile and rich.
One station road.
In the 27th year of Qiánlóng,
Jílín borrowed land north of the river to establish five stations.
From present-day Bīnzhōu, crossing the river and heading east into the county,
were Fó sī Héng,
Fùlāhún,
Chónggǔ'ěrkù (which is the county seat),
È'ěrgúmùsuǒ,
and further east connected to the present-day Miàogá Shān Zhàn of Tāngyuán,
reaching Sānxìng Chéng.
In the late Guāngxù era,
the affiliation of the stations was changed,
and all established postal bureaus.
)Tāngyuán Xiàn (350 *lǐ* southwest of the prefectural seat.
In the Míng dynasty,
Túnhé Wèi.
Túnhé is Tāngwàng Hé.
Established in the 31st year of Guāngxù,
it was a county subordinate to Yīlán, Jílín.
In the 34th year, its affiliation was changed.
To the north lies the southern foothills of the Xiǎo Xīng'ān Lǐng mountain range,
and to the south it is close to the Sōnghuā Jiāng;
the land is flat.
The Sōnghuā Jiāng enters from Dàtōng,
flows northeast,
passes east of the county seat,
and converges with Hēilóngjiāng.
Within the county, the Sōnghuā Jiāng flows very circuitously,
with dense and mixed trees on its banks;
the navigation route is like a crawling earthworm.
Its right bank is Yīlán, Fùjǐn, and Línjiāng of Jílín.
To the south: the Tāngwàng Hé enters from Xīngdōng,
flows south,
receives the Rúyì Hé,
Wādān, Sūlābālán, and Xiǎogǔdòng Hé,
all flowing southeast into the Sōnghuā Jiāng.
The right bank of Xiǎogǔdòng Hé is Dàtōng territory.
To the northeast are Xiānglán,
and to the west Bànjié, Hèjīn, Gèjié, Huā'ěrbù, Ālíngdá, Hèlì, and other rivers,
which on the left bank join Wútóng, Púyā, and Élèmì to form the Dài Hé,
all flowing southeast into the Sōnghuā Jiāng.
The Hēilóngjiāng has a branching stream that flows out
into the Sōnghuā Jiāng,
into which the Xiǎohēi Hé flows from the west.
With its winding harbors and channels,
resembling irrigation ditches,
this is a remote and fertile region.
There is the Gāojiātún Xún sī.
In the 2nd year of Xuāntǒng,
the Élèmì Hé Zhāolái Zhèn was established,
where there is the Dōngyì Gōngsī,
and on the Hèlì Hé there is the Xīngdōng Gōngsī,
both engaged in reclamation.
The county territory from southwest to northeast is
narrow and long for over a thousand *lǐ*;
if fully developed,
ten counties could be established.
The southwest is somewhat prosperous,
while the northeast is only just beginning.
The station road from Miàogá Shān Zhàn crosses the river to Sānxìng;
there is also a road from Xīngdōng Yāntǒng Shān reaching the southwest of the county,
and the west road from Guānyīn Shān passing through the county to Sānxìng.
In the late Guāngxù era,
new postal bureaus were established at Gèjié Hé and Wādān Hé.
Zhàozhōu Zhílìtīng: (Fán,
nán.
Six hundred *lǐ* southeast of the provincial capital.
Míng dynasty,
Sācháhédù,
which is Sānchàhédù.
) In the 32nd year of Guāngxù (1906),
a *tīng* was established on land reclaimed from the Hòuqí of Guōěrluósī.
(South: The Sōnghuā Jiāng enters from Jílín Bódōunà,
converges with the Nèn Jiāng,
flows eastward,
receives water from Bóěrgūhā Pō,
passes south of the city,
then further east receives water from Liánhuā Pō, Xiàdàijíchuán Kǒu, Sāndàogāngzi, and Làozhōuchuán Kǒu,
entering Hūlán.
The right bank forms the boundary of Jílín Xīnchéng and Shuāngchéng.
West: The Nèn Jiāng enters from Āndá,
flows south,
receives water from Wūlánnuòěr,
and empties into the Sōnghuā Jiāng.
The right bank forms the boundary of Dàlài.
The *tīng*'s territory is flat and vast.
North City Pào flows south and converges to form Chādámǎ Pō,
its lower course pooling in the sand.
To the northeast is the Zhàodōng Fēnfáng Jīnglì.
Three old stations were established: from Tāláhā Zhàn in Āndá south to Gǔlú in the *tīng*'s territory,
then south to Wūlánnuòěr,
and further south to Màoxīng.
These are the ten stations on the southern route.
There were also eight stages on the southeastern route,
four of which were within the *tīng*'s territory.
Starting from Màoxīng Zhàn,
east to Bōěrjīhātái,
then east to Chábùqíěr,
then east to Ònīduōtú,
then east to Bùlākè,
and then east into Hūlán territory.
One official-commercial road: from Màoxīng west to Guōěrluósī Gōngfǔ,
then west crossing the Nèn Jiāng via Bājiāchuán Kǒu into Dàlài.
Northeast of the *tīng* are five stations.
The commercial port,
to the southwest at Xìnxiǔgāngzi,

a strategic point along the river.
It was designated a commercial port for future development at the end of Guāngxù's reign.
The Dōngqīng Tiělù enters from Āndá,

There are two railway stations: Hāncǎogāng and Mǎngōu.

pí,
nán.
Two hundred ten *lǐ* southwest of the provincial capital.

Míng dynasty,
Táoěrhédù and the territory of Zhuōěrhé.
) In the 30th year of Guāngxù (1904),

North: Tǎzichéng and Jǐngxīngzhèn have two *fēnfáng jīnglì*.
There were two old Mongolian stations: starting from Bǔkuí Zhàn,

Three official-commercial roads: one goes north out of Jǐngxīngzhèn to the provincial capital;

Along the Nèn Jiāng at Hāláhéshuò,

fán,

Āndá,

(West: The Nèn Jiāng enters from Lóngjiāng,

Three old stations were established: from Tèmùdéhè Zhàn in Lóngjiāng south to Wēntuōhuān within the *tīng*'s jurisdiction,

Products:

Tiěshānbāo Hé.

Shìwéi Zhílì Tīng: (In the 34th year of Guangxù,

Among them, the Gēnhé is the largest,

Both banks are fertile plains and rich land,

The È'ěrgǔnà Hé flows west of the Tīng's seat,

There is the Hālā'ěr (which is the Jílālín Hé),
the Méilèkā (which is the Níbùchǔyuē nèi zhī hé), Sùnhé, È'ěrqímù, Bìlā'ěr, Bìlākèchǎn, Gǔ'ěrbùqí, Jílínzǐ, Āmùpí, Niú'ěr, Zhū'ěrgān, and Wēnzhū Hé.
All of these flow in from the southeastern mountains.

There are the Wūmǎ, Dà Jígēdá, and Xiǎo Jígēdá,

It then turns again and flows northeast.
There is the Yīmù Hé,
and over twenty other small rivers,

Among them, the Niú'ěr Hé is the largest,

At the river mouth, there are two areas of flat land on the left and right,
with fertile soil.
After the È'ěrgǔnà Hé receives the Gēnhé and Niú'ěr Hé,
its waters become large and rapid,
flowing directly into the Hēilóngjiāng.
And Jílālín is a central location,
hence the Tīng's administration is located there.
Fifteen new border defense kǎlún were established

Niú'ěr Hé,
Zhū'ěrgān Hé General Kǎlún,
Wēnhé,

Yǒng'ānshān,

The most important road from Jílālín south to Tǎ'ěrbāgāndáhū Shān is over 700 lǐ.
North from there to Zhū'ěrgān Hé is over 350 lǐ,

From Zhū'ěrgān to the mouth of the È'ěrgǔnà Hé is over 550 lǐ,

In the upper reaches of the Gēnhé, there is a path leading out to Xībùtèhādámò'ěrgēn.
È'ěrgǔnà civilian boats only reach Jílālín;

In winter,
ice sleds can be driven on the river,

Volume 33 Geography 5 Jiāngsū
Jiāngsū: The territory of the three prefectures of Yáng, Xú, and Yù from the Yǔgòng.
During the Míng dynasty, it was Nánjīng.
In the second year of Qīng Shùnzhì, it was reorganized as Jiāngnán Shěng,
and a Bùzhèngshǐ Sī was established.
A Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū was appointed (governing Jiāngnán and Jiāngxī,
stationed in Jiāngníng.
A Huáiyáng Zǒngdū was also established,
but was soon abolished.)
along with a Jiāngníng Xúnfǔ.
(Administered from Sūzhōu.
A Fèng Lú Ānhuī Xúnfǔ was also established,
but was soon abolished.)
In the eighteenth year,
nine prefectures were separated: Ānqìng, Huīzhōu, Níngguó, Chízhōu, Tàipíng, Lúzhōu, Fèngyáng, Huái'ān, Yángzhōu,
and four independent departments: Xú, Chú, Hé, Guǎngdé.
These belonged to Ānhuī,
and were administered by the Jiāngnán Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
Ānhuī established a Xúnfǔ.
In the third year,
the Jiāngběi Àncháshǐ was delegated to govern there.
In the fifth year,
Yángzhōu, Huái'ān, and Xúzhōu were again placed under Jiāngnán.
In the sixth year,
Jiāngnán changed to its present name.
The Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ was changed to the Ānhuī Bùzhèngshǐ Sī,
(stationed in Jiāngníng.)
and the Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ to the Jiāngsū Bùzhèngshǐ Sī,
(administered from Sūzhōu.)
It governed seven prefectures: Jiāngníng, Sūzhōu, Chángzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Zhènjiāng, Yángzhōu, Huái'ān,
and one independent department: Xúzhōu.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
the four departments of Tàicāng, Pī, Hǎi, and Tōng were promoted to independent departments.
In the eleventh year,
Xúzhōu was promoted to a prefecture,
and Pī reverted to a department,
subordinate to it.
In the twenty-fifth year of Qiánlóng,
the Ānhuī Bùzhèngshǐ Sī was moved to Ānqìng,
and a Jiāngníng Bùzhèngshǐ Sī was additionally established.
The four prefectures of Jiāngníng, Huái'ān, Xú, and Yáng were separated,

Gazetteer 34, Geography 6, Ānhuī [Ānhuī]
Ānhuī: the domain of Yǔgòng's Yáng, Xú, and Yù three zhōus.
During the Míng dynasty, it belonged to Nánjīng.
In the second year of Qīng Shùnzhì (1645),
it was reorganized as Jiāngnán Shěng,
with the establishment of the Fèngyáng Xúnfǔ and Ānlúchítài Xúnfǔ,
who also managed military affairs for the Cāojiāng,
and were jointly commanded by the Huáiyáng Zǒngdū.
In the sixth year (1649),
all were abolished.
In the eighteenth year (1661),
Jiāngnán's Left and Right Bùzhèngshǐs were established,
with the Left Bùzhèngshǐ governing the nine fǔs of Ānqìng, Huīzhōu, Níngguó, Chízhōu, Tàipíng, Lúzhōu, Fèngyáng, Huái'ān, and Yángzhōu,
as well as the four zhílìzhōus of Xú, Chú, Hé, and Guǎngdé,
stationed in Jiāngníng.
In the first year of Kāngxī (1662),
Ānhuī was first established as a provincial capital,
and a Xúnfǔ was re-established,
stationed in Ānqìng.
In the third year (1664),
Jiāngnán divided one Ànchásǐ to govern here.
In the fifth year (1666),
Yángzhōu, Huái'ān, and Xúzhōu were ceded back to the Jiāngníng Right Bùzhèng.
In the sixth year (1667),
the Left Bùzhèng was changed to the Ānhuī Bùzhèngshǐ Sī.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (1723),
the Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū was given jurisdiction over the three provinces of Ānhuī, Jiāngsū, and Jiāngxī.
In the second year (1724),
the three zhōus of Yǐng, Bó, and Sì, belonging to Fèngyáng Fǔ,
and Liù'ān Zhōu, belonging to Lúzhōu Fǔ,
were elevated to zhílìzhōus.
In the thirteenth year (1735),
Yǐngzhōu was elevated to a fǔ,
and Bózhōu was demoted again to belong to Yǐng.
In the twenty-fifth year of Qiánlóng (1760),
the Ānhuī Bùzhèngshǐ also moved from Jiāngníng to be stationed here.
To the east, it borders Lìshuǐ, Jiāngsū;
to the west, Máichéng, Húběi;
to the south, Péngzé, Jiāngxī, and Suì'ān, Zhèjiāng;
to the north, Lùyì, Hénán.
It spans seven hundred thirty-five lǐ from east to west,
and six hundred sixty-six lǐ from north to south.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng (1911),
there were three million one hundred forty-two thousand one hundred eighty-four registered households,
and sixteen million two hundred twenty thousand nine hundred fifty-two people.

four subordinate zhōus,
and fifty-one xiàns.

Shānxī: The domain of Jìzhōu according to the Yǔgòng.
In the early Qīng dynasty, it continued the Míng system as a province,
and established a Zǒngdū and a Xúnfǔ.
At the end of Shùnzhì’s reign,
the Zǒngdū was abolished.
In the fourth year of Kāngxī,
Yànpíng Dào was established by combining Jìnán and Jìběi.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
Guīhuà Tīng was established.
In the second year,
eight Zhílì Zhōu were added.
(Píngdìng, Xīn, Dài, Bǎo, Xiè, Jiàng, Jí, Xí.)
In the third year,
two Fǔ were added.
(Níngwǔ, Shuòpíng.)
In the sixth year,
Pú and Zé two Zhōu were both elevated to Fǔ,
and Guīsuī Dào was established.
In the fourth year of Qiánlóng,
Suīyuǎn Tīng Tóngzhī was added.
In the twenty-fifth year,
five Tōngpàn were further added to the territories belonging to Guīsuī.
(Guīhuàchéng, Qīngshuǐhé, Sàlāqí, Hélíngé'ěr, Tuōktuōchéng.)
They, along with the two Tīng of Guī and Suī, all belonged to Guīsuī Dào.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Guīhuàchéng Tōngpàn was abolished.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Jízhōu was reassigned to Píngyáng Fǔ,
and Huòzhōu became a Zhílì Zhōu.
Currently, it governs nine Fǔ,
ten Zhílì Zhōu,
twelve Tīng,
six Zhōu,
and eighty-five Xiàn.
Its eastern border is Jǐngxíng, Zhílì;
(three hundred seventy-five lǐ.)
its western border is Wúbǎo, Shǎnxī;
(five hundred five lǐ.)
its southern border is Jìyuán, Hénán;
(seven hundred thirty lǐ.)
its northern border is the grassland of Sìzǐ Bùluò, Nèi Ménggǔ.
(One thousand one hundred lǐ.)
Its width is eight hundred eighty lǐ,
and its length is one thousand six hundred twenty lǐ.
The elevation of the North Pole ranges from thirty-four degrees fifty-seven minutes to forty-one degrees fifty minutes.
It is located three degrees four minutes to five degrees forty-five minutes west of Jīngshī.
It is one thousand two hundred lǐ northeast of Jīngshī.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng,
it had one million nine hundred ninety thousand thirty-five registered households,
and nine million two hundred nineteen thousand nine hundred eighty-seven people.
(Its famous mountains: Guǎncén, Tàiháng, Wángwū, Léishǒu, Dǐzhù, Xīchéng, Héng, Huò, Jùzhù, Wǔtái.

Shāndōng: The region of Qīng, Xú, Yǎn, and Yù four provinces according to Yǔgòng.
The Míng dynasty established the Shāndōng Chéngxuānbùzhèngshǐsī.
The early Qīng dynasty followed this system.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
Tài'ān, Wǔdìng, and Bīn Departments from Jìnán Fǔ were elevated,
as were Jìníng, Cáo, Yí, and other six Departments from Yǎnzhoū Fǔ, becoming Zhílìzhōu.
In the eighth year,
Jìníng Zhōu still belonged to Yǎnzhoū Fǔ.
In the twelfth year,
Wǔdìng and Yí two Departments were elevated to Fǔ,
and Bīn Zhōu's affiliation was changed to Wǔdìng.
In the thirteenth year,
Tài'ān and Cáo two Departments were elevated to Fǔ.
In the forty-first year of Qiánlóng,
Jìníng and Línqīng were again elevated to Zhílìzhōu.
In total, it administered ten Fǔ,
two Zhōu,
eight non-direct Zhōu,
and ninety-six Xiàn.
It was located south of the Capital.
East to the Great Sea;

and its length was 800 lǐ.
Its latitude ranged from thirty-four degrees thirty-five minutes to thirty-eight degrees twenty minutes.
Relative to the Capital, its longitude ranged from one degree twenty-five minutes west to six degrees forty minutes east.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng,
registered households numbered five million three hundred seventy-seven thousand eight hundred seventy-two,
and the population was thirty-one million three thousand six hundred ninety-four.

Shǎnxī Shěng: The territory of Yúgòng's Yōng and Liáng two zhōu.
In the Míng dynasty, the Shǎnxī Děngchù Zuǒ, Yòu Chéngxuānbùzhèng Shǐsī were established,
with their capital in Xī'ān.
In the early Qīng dynasty, this was continued,
and a xúnfǔ was established,
with his seat in Xī'ān.
Also, a zǒngdū was established,
concurrently administering Sìchuān.
Soon after, this was changed to administer Shān and Shǎn.
In the 9th year of Yōngzhèng,
it exclusively administered Shǎn and Gān,
with its seat in Xī'ān.
In the 13th year,
it again administered Sìchuān.
In the 13th year of Qiánlóng,
the concurrent administration was abolished.
In the 19th year,
it concurrently held the office of Gānsù Xúnfǔ.
In the 24th year,
it was changed to Shǎngān Zǒngdū.
In the 29th year,
it was moved to Lánzhōu, Gānsù,
which then became the fixed system.
In the 2nd year of Kāngxī,
the four fǔ of Líntáo, Gǒngchāng, Píngliáng, and Qìngyáng were separated to establish Gānsù Shěng,
and the Yòu Bùzhèng Shǐ's seat was moved there.
In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng,
the six zhōu of Shāng, Tóng, Huá, Yào, Gān, and Bīn of Xī'ān Fǔ,
and the three zhōu of Fū, Suídé, and Jiā of Yán'ān Fǔ,
were promoted to zhílì zhōu.
In the 9th year,
Yúlín Wèi was changed to a fǔ.
In the 13th year,
Tóng Zhōu was promoted to a fǔ,
while Huá was demoted back to a zhōu under its jurisdiction,
and Yào was also demoted back to a zhōu under its former jurisdiction.
In the 1st year of Qiánlóng,
Jiā was demoted back to a zhōu under Yúlín.
In the 48th year,
Xīng'ān Zhōu was promoted to a fǔ.
Its eastern border is Hénán Wénxiāng;

Vol. 39, Geography 11, Gānsù
Gānsù: the territory of Yǒngzhōu (south also including Liángzhōu) in Yǔgòng.
In the Míng dynasty, it was the land of Shǎnxī Bùzhèngshǐ Sī and Shǎnxī Xíngdū Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī.
In the early Shùnzhì [reign] of the Qīng dynasty,
following the Míng system,
a Gānsù Xúnfǔ was established,
stationed in Níngxià.
(The Níngxià Xúnfǔ was soon abolished.)
In the fifth year (1648),
the Gānsù Xúnfǔ was moved to Lánzhōu.
In the third year of Kāngxī [reign] (1664),
Shǎnxī was divided into the Left and Right Bùzhèngshǐ Sī,
with the Right Bùzhèngshǐ Sī stationed in Gǒngchāng,
governing four prefectures as before.
In the sixth year (1667),
the Shǎnxī Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ Sī was renamed Gǒngchāng Bùzhèngshǐ Sī.
In the seventh year (1668),
it was again renamed Gānsù Bùzhèngshǐ Sī,
and its seat moved to Lánzhōu.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng [reign] (1725),
the Xíngdū Zhǐhuīshǐ Sī and various *wèisuǒ* were abolished,
and Gānzhōu, Liángzhōu, Níngxià, Xīníng were reorganized,
and Sùzhōu, along with Qín and Jiē two *zhōu*, were promoted to Zhílìzhōu.
In the third year of Qiánlóng [reign] (1738),
Líntáo Fǔ was abolished and moved to Lánzhōu,
and thus its name was changed.
In the twenty-fourth year (1759),
Ānxī Fǔ was established.
In the twenty-ninth year (1764),
the Xúnfǔ was abolished,
and the Shǎnxī Gān Zǒngdū was stationed in Lánzhōu,
performing the duties of a Xúnfǔ.
In the thirty-eighth year (1773),
Zhènwèi Fǔ was established in Bālǐkūn, and Díhuà Zhílìzhōu in Wūlǔmùqí.
In the thirty-ninth year (1774),
Ānxī Fǔ was downgraded to a Zhílìzhōu.
In the forty-second year (1777),
Jīngzhōu was promoted to a Zhílìzhōu.

Huàpíngchuān Zhílìtīng was established.

In the twelfth year of Guāngxù [reign] (1886),
Xīnjiāng was reorganized into a province,
and Díhuà and Zhènwèi were detached and assigned to it.

Jiāngxī shěng: The territory of Yángzhōu in Yǔ Gòng.
The Míng dynasty established the Jiāngxī Xúnfǔ
and the Chéngxuān Bùzhèngshǐ Sī
and the Nángàn Xúnfǔ.
The early Qīng dynasty followed this.
In Shùnzhì four years (1647),
the Zǒngdū of Jiāngnán, Hénán, and Jiāngxī was established.
(Governed from Jiāngníng.)
In six years (1649),
Hénán was removed from its jurisdiction.
In nine years (1652),
the seat of government was moved to Nánchāng.
(It was soon returned to its former seat.)
In eighteen years (1661),
the Jiāngxī Zǒngdū was established.
In Kāngxī four years (1665), it reverted to its former status.
Earlier, in three years (1664), the Nángàn Xúnfǔ was abolished,
made permanent.
In Qiánlóng eight years (1743),
Liánhuā Tīng was additionally established in Jí'ān.
In nineteen years (1754),
Gànzhōu's Níngdū Xiàn was elevated to a zhílì zhōu.
In thirty-eight years (1773),
Gànzhōu's Dìngnán Xiàn was elevated to a tīng.
In Guāngxù twenty-nine years (1903),
Gànzhōu's Guānyīngé Tōngpàn was changed to Qiánnán Tīng.
In thirty-three years (1907),
Tónggǔ Yíng was changed to a tīng,
subordinate to Ruìzhōu.

四川 (Sìchuān): The domain of 梁州 (Liángzhōu) in the 禹貢 (Yǔgòng).
In the Ming dynasty, the 四川等處承宣布政使司 (Sìchuān Děngchù Chéngxuānbùzhèngshǐsī) was established.
The early Qing dynasty followed this.
In the second year of Shùnzhì (順治)
四川省 (Sìchuān Shěng) was established,
and a Xúnfǔ (巡撫) was set up,
with its seat in 成都 (Chéngdū).
In the fourteenth year
a 四川總督 (Sìchuān Zǒngdū) was added.
In the fourth year of Kāngxī (康熙)
烏撒 (Wūsā) was changed to be under 貴州 (Guìzhōu).
In the seventh year
a 川湖總督 (Chuānhú Zǒngdū) was established,
stationed in 湖北荊州 (Húběi Jīngzhōu).
In the ninth year
it was moved to 駐重慶 (zhù Chóngqìng).
In the nineteenth year
it was again changed to 川陝甘總督 (Chuānshǎngān Zǒngdū),
stationed in 陝西西安 (Shǎnxī Xī'ān).
In the sixth year of Yōngzhèng (雍正)
東川 (Dōngchuān), 烏蒙 (Wūméng), and 鎮雄 (Zhènxióng) were changed to be under 雲南 (Yúnnán);
遵義 (Zūnyì) was changed to be under 貴州 (Guìzhōu);
馬湖 (Mǎhú) province was merged into a zhōu (州);
建寧衞 (Jiànníng Wèi) was changed to 寧遠府 (Níngyuǎn Fǔ);
and the three zhōu (州) of 錦 (Jǐn), 茂 (Mào), and 達 (Dá), along with 資縣 (Zī Xiàn), were all promoted to Zhílì Zhōu (直隸州).
In the seventh year
雅州 (Yǎzhōu) was promoted to a Fǔ (府).
In the twelfth year
the two zhōu (州) of 嘉定 (Jiādìng) and 潼川 (Tóngchuān) were promoted to Fǔ (府);
忠州 (Zhōngzhōu) was promoted to Zhílì Zhōu (直隸州);
and 黔彭直隸廳 (Qiánpéng Zhílì Tīng) was established.
In the first year of Qiánlóng (乾隆)
酉陽土司 (Yǒuyáng Tǔsī) was changed to 酉陽直隸州 (Yǒuyáng Zhílì Zhōu);
and 永廳 (Yǒngtīng) was promoted to Zhílì Tīng (直隸廳).
In the fourteenth year
a 四川總督 (Sìchuān Zǒngdū) was again specifically established,
the Xúnfǔ (巡撫) was abolished,
and the Zǒngdū (總督) concurrently managed the affairs of the Xúnfǔ (巡撫),
with its seat in 成都 (Chéngdū).
In the twenty-fifth year
松潘衞 (Sōngpān Wèi) was changed to 松潘直隸廳 (Sōngpān Zhílì Tīng);
雜古腦 (Zágǔnǎo) was changed to 理番直隸廳 (Lǐfān Zhílì Tīng).
In the twenty-sixth year
石砫土司 (Shízhù Tǔsī) was changed to 石砫直隸廳 (Shízhù Zhílì Tīng).
In the seventh year of Jiāqìng (嘉慶)
達州 (Dázhōu) was promoted to 綏定府 (Suídìng Fǔ).
In the thirtieth year of Guāngxù (光緒)
打箭鑪廳 (Dǎjiànlú Tīng) was promoted to Zhílì Tīng (直隸廳).
In the thirty-second year
the 督辦川滇邊務大臣 (Dūbàn Chuāndiānbianwù Dàchén) was established,
stationed in 巴塘 (Bātáng).

Prefecture.

)Formerly administered six zhōu [prefectures]
and twenty-five xiàn [counties].
In the 16th year of Shùnzhì,
Luójiāng was absorbed into Déyáng,

In the 1st year of Kāngxī,
Chóngníng was absorbed into Pí,

In the 9th year,
Huáyáng was absorbed into Chéngdū.

Huáyáng was re-established,

Wènchuān and Bǎo subordinate to Mào,
Zīyáng, Rénshòu, and Jǐngyán subordinate to Zī.
Wēi was also absorbed into Bǎo.
In the 6th year,
the four counties of Chóngníng, Shuāngliú, Péng, and Zhāngmíng were re-established and belonged to the prefecture.
In the 7th year,
Zhāngmíng was transferred to Lóng'ān.

Gazetteer, Volume 46, Geography, Part 18, Táiwān
Táiwān: An ancient wilderness,
not connected to Zhōngguó,
it was called Dōngfān.
(During the Kāihuáng reign of the Suí dynasty,
Hu Bēn Chén Líng was dispatched to scout Pēnghú and its thirty-six islands.
In the 42nd year of Jiājìng of the Míng dynasty,
the sea bandit Lín Dàoqián plundered the coastal prefectures and counties.
Dūdū Yú Dàyóu attacked him,
pursuing him to Pēnghú,
where Dàoqián fled into Táiwān.
In the 1st year of Tiānqǐ,
Yán Sīqí from Mǐn led Japanese people to occupy the land.
After a long time,
it was seized by the Dutch.
)In the 18th year of Shùnzhì of the Qīng dynasty,
the sea bandit Zhèng Chénggōng drove out the Dutch and occupied it,
illegally establishing Chéngtiān Fǔ,
naming it Dōngdū,
and setting up two counties:
Tiānxīng
and Wànnián.
His son Zhèng Jīng changed Dōngdū to Dōngníng Shěng
and elevated the two counties to zhōu.
In the 22nd year of Kāngxī, it was pacified,
and Táiwān Fǔ was established,
subordinate to Fújiàn Shěng,
administering three counties.
In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng,
Zhānghuà Xiàn was added,
administering four counties.
In the 13th year of Guāngxù,
it was reorganized as a province.
(On the *gēngwǔ* day of the ninth month of the 13th year of Guāngxù,
Mǐnzhè Zǒngdū Yáng Chāngjùn and Táiwān Xúnfǔ Liú Míngchuán jointly submitted a memorial,
which briefly stated:
"Táiwān's territory,
from north to south, spans over 700 *lǐ*,
and from east to west, it is nearly 200 *lǐ* at its narrowest,
and perhaps 300 or 400 *lǐ* at its widest.
Lofty mountains and great rivers
interconnect high and low areas.
The area previously governed
was merely a line south of the mountains,
thus only three counties were sufficient and even more than enough.
Subsequently, as the wilderness was progressively opened,
numerous *tīng* administrations were added, yet it was still insufficient.
In the 1st year of Guāngxù,
Shěn Bǎozhēn requested the establishment of Táiběi Fǔ and its counties to secure the northern route,
and also moved the Tóngzhī's seat to Bēinán to manage the 'rear mountains,'
thereby giving the entire Táiwān official system
a rudimentary structure.
However, at that time, the situation
did not involve selecting critical measures for improvement,
nor was it a plan for lasting peace and stability.
We, your ministers, have collectively deliberated and discussed,
and humbly believe that the method of establishing administrations
relies on strategic terrain and power,
and the way to divide governance
values impartiality.
The governance of Tái Shěng
is considered more difficult than that of the interior,
yet the area of each county
is conversely larger than those in the interior.
For example, counties like Zhānghuà, Jiāyì, Fèngshān, Xīnzhú, and Dànshuǐ,
range from over 200 *lǐ* to 300 *lǐ* in length and width,
making it impossible to reach them in an emergency.
Moreover, defense is the key to governing Táiwān,
and if the jurisdiction is too broad,
it is difficult to be comprehensive in observation,
and if control is too loose,
communication is often impeded.
As for the middle and northern routes of the 'rear mountains,'
they stretch three to four hundred *lǐ*,
with only scattered forts established in sections,
and no dedicated officials stationed for governance.
The previous remote control was
also difficult to exercise effectively.
Now, at the beginning of reorganization,
when all neglected affairs are to be revived,
if we do not make appropriate changes,
how can responsibilities be fixed for the long term?
Last September,
I, Míngchuán, personally went to the central route to supervise the suppression of rebellious indigenous tribes,
observing the terrain along the way.
And according to various local officials,
maps and explanations of the strategic passes, roads, fields, mountains, and streams within their jurisdiction
were drawn and presented.
Furthermore, reports on the cultivated land successively submitted by officials in charge of pacifying indigenous tribes and assessing land taxes
have been received.
We have carefully planned for the entire situation, both front and rear mountains,
identifying what should be added,
what should be changed,
and what should be abolished.
Upon investigation, the Qiáozītú area of Zhānghuà,
surrounded by mountains and winding rivers,
opens up into a plain in the middle,
presenting a grand and spacious vista.
It is also centrally located for the entire Táiwān.
Following the proposal of the former Xúnfǔ Cén Yùyīng,
we propose establishing the provincial capital there.
The northern and eastern parts of Zhānghuà are to be divided to establish the principal prefecture, named Táiwān Fǔ,
with its capital county named Táiwān Xiàn.
The original Táiwān Fǔ and county are to be renamed Táinán Fǔ and Ānpíng Xiàn.
East of Jiāyì and
south of Zhānghuà,
from Zhuóshuǐ Xī to Gūshíguī Xī,
by adjusting the boundaries, forming a square of over 400 *lǐ*,
we propose adding a county named Yúnlín Xiàn.
The area around Xīnzhú's Miáolì Jiē
controls the entrance to the interior mountains,
connecting to Dàhú in the east,
with many newly reclaimed wilderness lands along the mountains.
We propose adding a county named Miáolì Xiàn in the southwestern parts of Xīnzhú,
combining it with the original Zhānghuà,
and the Púlíshè Tōngpàn,
making one *tīng* and four counties,
all subordinate to Táiwān Fǔ.
The post of Lùgǎng Tóngzhī
should be abolished.
North of Dànshuǐ,
Sandiaolǐng controls the east,
with many indigenous settlements,
and is too far from the county seat.
Jīlóng is the primary gateway to Táiběi.
With trade and port construction,
foreign relations are complex.
Currently, coal mines are being developed,
railways are being built,
and merchants and common people are gathering,
making pacification and appeasement even more crucial.
We propose to divide the four northeastern forts of Dànshuǐ,
and place them under the jurisdiction of Jīlóng Tīng.
The originally established Tōngpàn is to be changed to a Fúmín Lǐfān Tóngzhī,
to enhance his authority.
This is a general outline of the additions and changes for the 'front route.'
As for the situation in the 'rear mountains,'
the north is defined by Sū Xī as the main pass,
and the south by Bēinán as the key area.
The central control point
is Shuǐwěi.
This place is directly east-west with the proposed Yúnlín Xiàn.
Currently, a road of over 190 *lǐ* has been opened,
passing through Dānshèlǐng and Jíjí Jiē to reach Zhānghuà.
It will connect to the provincial capital,
establishing a central route,
connecting the front and rear like a pulse,
truly serving as the key to Táidōng.
We propose adding a Zhílì Zhōuzhīzhōu,
named Táidōng Zhílì Zhōu,
with Yílán as its western boundary
and Héngchūn as its eastern boundary,
measuring over 500 *lǐ* in length,
and approximately 40 *lǐ* to over 10 *lǐ* in width,
all under the jurisdiction of this Zhōu,
and still subordinate to the Táiwān Bīngbèi Dào.
The old seat of Bēinán Tīng
is proposed to be changed to a Zhílì Zhōu Tóngzhī.
South of Shuǐwěi,
it is to be changed to Huāliángǎng Tīng.
Within it, there are already several thousand *mǔ* of cultivated land.
Outside, the sea mouth is several *zhàng* deep.
To inspect merchant ships
and manage the common people and indigenous tribes,
we propose adding a Zhílì Zhōu Pàn,
to be permanently stationed there,
all subordinate to Táidōng Zhílì Zhōu.
This is a general outline of the additions for the 'rear route.'
We respectfully note that Táiwān's territory, taxes, and labor services
are daily increasing and expanding,
and are no longer the same as the old situation of loose administration and temporary placement.
Adapting to local conditions
seems impossible to further delay.
Moreover, in recent years, the 'raw indigenous tribes' have assimilated,
their primitive nature initially brought into order,
making it even more necessary to guide and soothe them in different ways
to achieve real results.
To integrate the distant and enlighten the near
requires officials everywhere.
We, your ministers, being involved in the situation,
dare not rashly change things
to disrupt the old regulations,
nor dare we be content with deficiencies and simplify matters
to lose the foundation of wealth and prosperity.
We have weighed the gains and losses to find a compromise
and hope to reach a satisfactory solution."

and both it and the main channel flow northwest into the sea.

Guǎngdōng: The southern extremity of Yángzhōu according to Yǔ Gòng.
During the Míng dynasty, a *bùzhèngshǐsī* was established,
governed from Guǎngzhōu.
In the early Qīng dynasty, following the Míng system,
it was designated as a province.
In the Yōngzhèng era,
Liánzhōu and Chéngxiāng were elevated to Jiāyìng Zhōu,
both directly administered.
In the Jiāqìng era,
Nánxióng was demoted to a *zhílì zhōu*,
then soon restored to its former status,
Fógāng was added,
Nánxióng was again demoted to a *zhōu*,
Liánshān was added.
In the Tóngzhì era,
Yángjiāng was elevated to a *tīng*,
Chìxī was added.
In the Guāngxù era,
Qīnzhōu and Yázhōu were elevated,
Wànzhōu was demoted.
It comprised six *dào*,
nine *fǔ*,
seven *zhílì zhōu*,
three *zhílì tīng*,
four *sàn zhōu*,
one *sàn tīng*,
and seventy-nine *xiàn*.

Its northeast is seven thousand five hundred seventy *lǐ* from the capital.

Volume 48, Geography 2, Guǎngxī
Guǎngxī: The southern border region of Jīngzhōu in Yǔgòng.
In the Yuán dynasty, the Guǎngxī děngchù Xíngzhōngshūshěng was established.
In the Míng dynasty, it was renamed Chéngxuānbùzhèngshǐsī.
In the early Qīng dynasty, a province was established,
and a Xúnfǔ and Bùzhèng were set up to govern it jointly.
A Liǎngguǎng Zǒngdū was appointed.
In the second year of Kāngxī (1663),
a Zǒngdū was separately established for Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī.
In the fourth year, it reverted to the former system.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (1723),
it was again divided.
The next year, it was again unified.
In the sixth year (1728),
the Yúnguì Zǒngdū was concurrently given jurisdiction over Guǎngxī.
In the twelfth year (1734),
it reverted to the former system again,
with the seat in Guǎngdōng's Zhàoqìng Fǔ,
later moved to Guǎngzhōu Fǔ.
Initially, it administered nine fǔ.
(Guìlín, Liǔzhōu, Qìngyuǎn, Sī'ēn, Pínglè, Wúzhōu, Xúnzhōu, Nánníng, Tàipíng.
) In the fifteenth year of Shùnzhì (1658),
Sìchéng Tǔzhōu was promoted to a fǔ,
and soon after renamed Jūnmín Fǔ.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng (1725),
Yùlín and Bīnzhōu were promoted to Zhílì Zhōu.
In the fifth year (1727),
Sìchéng reverted to a fǔ.
In the seventh year (1729),
Zhèn'ān Fǔ was established.
In the twelfth year (1734),
Bīnzhōu was demoted and subordinated to Sī'ēn Fǔ,
and Xīlóng Zhōu was promoted to Zhílì Zhōu.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng (1742),
Xīlóng Zhōu was demoted and subordinated to Sìchéng Fǔ.
In the first year of Guāngxù (1875),
Bǎisè Tīng was promoted to Zhílì Tīng.
In the twelfth year (1886),
Guīshùn Zhōu was promoted to Zhílì Zhōu.
In the eighteenth year (1892),
Shàngsī Zhōu was promoted to Zhílì Tīng.
Its northeast is 7,460 lí from Jīngshī.
To the east, it reaches Húnán's Dàozhōu;
) To the west, it reaches Guìzhōu's Pǔ'ān;
) To the south, it reaches Guǎngdōng's Xìnyí;
) To the north, it reaches Húnán's Chéngbù Xiàn;
) Its width is 2,810 lí,
and its length is 2,960 lí.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng (1911),
it had 1,274,544 households,
and a population of 8,746,747.
It administered eleven fǔ,
two Zhílì Tīng,
two Zhílì Zhōu,
eight tīng,
fifteen zhōu,
forty-nine xiàn,
twenty-four tǔzhōu,
four tǔxiàn,
and thirteen tǔsī.
Those in Qìngyuǎn were called Zhǎngguānsī.
(Its famous mountains: Yuèchéng, Línhè, Jùlòu, Yánghǎi, Dàróng.
Its great rivers: Líjiāng, Qiánjiāng, Yùjiāng, Xiāngjiāng.
Post roads: The northeast crosses Yuèchéng Qiáo to reach Húnán's Yǒngzhōu;
the southwest crosses Kūnlún Guān to reach Lóngzhōu;
the southeast reaches Guǎngdōng's Fēngchuān.
Telegraph lines: The northeast reaches Chángshā,
the southeast reaches Guǎngzhōu,
and the west connects to Qìngyuǎn.
Railways: From Lóngzhōu, it exits via Zhènnán Guān to reach Ānnán's Liàngshān.)

they were in the northern part of the Shàngjīng Dào.
In the Jīn dynasty, they belonged to Běijīng Lù.
In the Yuán dynasty, they belonged to Shàngdū Lù.
In the Míng dynasty, they were occupied by Mongols,
who called themselves Wūzhūmùqìn,
a Khān clan of Cháhār.
Because Lín Dān Khān was tyrannical,
Bèilè Duōěrzì (Dorji) and Sāilèng (Sereng) went to seek refuge with the Kāěrkā (Khalkha).
)In the eighth year of Tiāncōng, they surrendered and returned,
and Duōěrzì was enfeoffed as Qīnwáng,
leading the Right Wing,
while Sāilèng was enfeoffed as Bèilè,
leading the Left Wing,
both titles hereditary.
Their territory bordered Suǒlún (Solon) to the east,
Hàoqítè (Khöchid) to the west,
Bālín (Bairin) to the south,
and Hānhǎi to the north.
It was three hundred sixty *lǐ* wide
and four hundred twenty-five *lǐ* long.
(The tribute route was through Dúshíkǒu.) The Wūzhūmùqìn Right Wing (its Zhásàkè (Jasagh) resided at Bākèsūěrhātái Shān,
nine hundred twenty-three *lǐ* northeast of Gǔběikǒu.
It was one thousand one hundred sixty-three *lǐ* south of Jīngshī.
Its pasturage included the Yīnjáhā Hé (Inzhakh River) which flowed into the sands,
and the Húlúgǔěr Hé (Khulugul River),
which pooled in Ādákènuòěr (Adakh Nor).
It bordered the Left Wing to the east,
Bālín (Bairin) to the south,
the Hàoqítè (Khöchid) Left Wing to the west,
and the Chēchén Hàn (Chechen Khan) Central Right Banner to the north.

and two hundred ten *lǐ* long.
The altitude of the North Star was forty-four degrees forty-five minutes.
It was one degree ten minutes east of Jīngshī.
Its mountains included: to the east, Ruìlù Shān,
Mongolian name Bùhútú.
To the west,
Dàxiǎo Huángyīng Shān and Hēi Shān, Mongolian name Kālā tú.
To the northwest,
Shuāng Shān, Mongolian name Hèyuèěr Édé, and Wūlìyátái Shān.
To the northeast,
Sàiyīn Ēndūěr Shān.
Its waters included: to the southeast, Hèěrhóng Hé (Khökhöng River),
whose source was Gámùěrzhàn (Gamurzhan),
flowing west into Lúshuǐ (Reed Water).
Tú Hé, also known as Húlúgǔěr (Khulugul),
whose source was northeast of Gǔshíkèténg (Khüshigdteng),
named Āěrdátú Hé (Ardatu River),
flowing northwest into the Right Wing,
becoming Húlúgǔěr Hé (Khulugul River),
then flowing north into Ādákě Chí (Adakh Lake).
) The Wūzhūmùqìn Left Wing (its Zhásàkè resided at Kuísūtuólóhǎi on the Òěrhǔ Hé (Örkhu River),
one thousand one hundred sixty *lǐ* northeast of Gǔběikǒu.

Its pasturage was west of Suǒyuèěrzì Shān (Soyorji Mountain).
It had the Òěrhǔ Hé (Örkhu River),

Kùliètú (Kürietü) to the south,
Dáláisūtú (Dalai Süütü) to the west,

It was two degrees twenty minutes east of Jīngshī.

To the north,
Sèěrbǎng Fēng.
Its waters included: to the northeast, Sèyěěrqí Hé,
whose source was Hāláotú Pō (Khaoltu Lake),

To the southeast, Yīnjáhā Hé (Inzhakh River),

Shuǐjīng Zhù:

In the early Qīng dynasty, a system was established
for three grades of sacrifices: the Huánqiú, Fāngzé, Qígǔ, Tàimiào, and Shèjì were grand sacrifices (dàsì).

Heavenly Spirits (Tiānshén), Earth Deities (Dìqí), Grand Duke of Jupiter (Tàisuì), Morning Sun (Zhāorì), Evening Moon (Xīyuè), Emperors of Past Dynasties (Lìdài Dìwáng), Former Teacher (Xiānshī), and Former Farmer (Xiānnóng) were medium sacrifices (zhōngsì).
Temples for Former Physicians (Xiānyī) and others,
and shrines for Worthies (Xiánliáng), Manifesting Loyalty (Zhāozhōng), and others were group sacrifices (qúnsì).
During the Qiánlóng era,
the regular rain ceremony (chángyú) was changed to a grand sacrifice,
and the Former Silkworm (Xiāncán) to a medium sacrifice.
During the Xiánfēng era,
Guānsheng and Wénchāng were changed to medium sacrifices.
At the end of the Guāngxù era,
the Former Teacher Kǒngzǐ was changed to a grand sacrifice;
this was a special honor.
The Son of Heaven sacrificed to Heaven and Earth, the Ancestral Temple (Zōngmiào), and the Altars of Soil and Grain (Shèjì).
If there was a reason,
an official would be dispatched to perform the sacrifice.
For medium sacrifices,
the emperor might personally sacrifice or dispatch an official.
For group sacrifices,
officials were always dispatched.
There were thirteen grand sacrifices: on the first xīn day of the first month, Qígǔ;
in the first month of summer, chángyú;
on the winter solstice, Huánqiú;
all of these were sacrifices to Hàotiān Shàngdì;
on the summer solstice, Fāngzé sacrificed to Huángdìqí;
in the four second months of the seasons, the Tàimiào received offerings,
and at the end of the year, there was the joint sacrifice (xiápjì);
in the middle months of spring and autumn,
on the first wù day,
sacrifices were made to Shèjì;
on the first dīng day, sacrifices were made to Xiānshī.
There were twelve medium sacrifices: at the spring equinox, Zhāorì;
at the autumn equinox, Xīyuè;
in the first month of spring and the day before the new year's eve, sacrifices were made to Tàisuì and Yuèjiāng;
in the middle month of spring, sacrifices were made to Xiānnóng;
in the last month of the season, sacrifices were made to Xiāncán;
in the middle months of spring and autumn, sacrifices were made to Lìdài Dìwáng, Guānsheng, and Wénchāng.
There were fifty-three group sacrifices: in the last month of summer, sacrifices were made to the God of Fire (Huǒshén);
in the middle month of autumn, sacrifices were made to the City God of the Capital (Dūchénghuáng);
in the last month of the season, sacrifices were made to the God of Cannons (Pàoshén).
In the middle months of spring and winter, sacrifices were made to Xiānyī;
in the middle months of spring and autumn, sacrifices were made to the two pools of Black Dragon (Hēilóng) and White Dragon (Báilóng) as well as various Dragon Gods (Lóngshén);
the River God Temple (Héshénmiào) at Yùquánshān, Kūnmínghú, Huìjì Shrine (Huìjìcí);

as well as the shrines for Xiánliáng, Zhāozhōng, Shuāngzhōng, Jiǎngzhōng, Bāozhōng, Xiǎnzhōng, Biǎozhōng, Jīngyǒng, Ruìzhōng Qīnwáng, Dìngnán Wǔzhuàng Wáng, the two Kèxī, Hóngyì Wénxiāng Qínxiāng and other gentlemen.
The Northern Pole Saintly Protector True Lord (Běijí Yòushèng Zhēnjūn) and the City God of the Eastern Peak (Dōngyuè Dūchénghuáng)
were sacrificed to on the Emperor's Birthday (Wànshòujié).
There were also special ceremonies performed according to the occasion,
such as performing the Shìdiàn (ceremony) for Xiānshī during inspections of schools,
performing the Shìdiàn for Tàixué (Imperial Academy) to celebrate achievements,
and making a reverent announcement to Chuánxīndiàn during Imperial Lectures (Yùjīngyán).
As for the Five Peaks (Yuè), Four Marches (Zhèn), Four Seas (Hǎi), Four Rivers (Dú),
imperial tombs and temples (Dìwáng Língmiào),
Xiānshī's birthplace Qūlǐ,
and the temple of Yuánsheng Zhōugōng,
when the emperor traveled and visited these places,
he might sacrifice personally
or not.
During major celebrations,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices.
The sacrifices performed in various provinces,
such as those to Shèjì,
Xiānnóng,
Wind and Thunder (Fēngléi),
local mountains and rivers (Jìngnèi Shānchuān),
Chénghuáng,
Lìtán (Altar for Hungry Ghosts),
imperial mausoleums (Dìwáng Língqǐn),
Xiānshī,
Guāndì,
Wénchāng,
shrines for famous officials (Mínghuàn) and worthies (Xiánliáng),
and special shrines for famous ministers (Míngchén) and loyal exemplary figures (Zhōngjié),
as well as those who averted disasters and protected the people,
were all promulgated to the authorities (yǒusī),
with annual sacrifices in spring and autumn.
As for family temples (jiāmiào) of Qīnwáng and below,
sacrifices were made to the founding ancestor (shǐfēngzǔ) and the five generations of gāo, zēng, zǔ, and ní.
Officials of all ranks down to commoners (pǐnguān dàishìshùrén) sacrificed to the four generations of gāo, zēng, zǔ, and ní.
Other sacrifices, either for specific reasons
or following local customs,
as long as they did not violate the sacrificial regulations (sìdiǎn),
were not prohibited.
This is an overview.
As for the altars and spirit tablets,
sacrificial offerings,
fasting and pious declarations,
and all regulations and ritual procedures,
their differences and similarities are detailed,
their intricacies recorded,
with nothing omitted or repeated,
so that observers may examine and understand them.
Regulations for the Altars and Enclosures In the tenth year of Tiāncōng,
a site was chosen in Shèngjīng
to build the Yuánqiú and Fāngzé Altars.
After offering sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
the reign title was changed to Chóngdé.
The Heaven Altar was round,
with three tiers.
The top tier had nine layers,
with a circumference of one zhàng and eight chǐ;
the second tier had seven layers,
with a circumference of three zhàng and six chǐ;
the third tier had five layers,
with a circumference of five zhàng and four chǐ: all three chǐ high.
The outer wall had a circumference of one hundred thirteen zhàng.
The Earth Altar was square,
with two tiers.
The top tier was six zhàng square,
two chǐ high;
the lower tier was eight zhàng square,
two chǐ and four cùn high.
The outer wall had a circumference of one hundred thirty-three zhàng.
The regulations were very simple.
When Shìzǔ established his capital in Yānjīng,
the Yuánqiú Altar was built outside Zhèngyángmén, in the southern suburbs,
and the Fāngzé Altar outside Āndìngmén, in the northern suburbs.
The regulations were then expanded.
The Yuánqiú Altar faced south,
with three tiers.
The top tier was five zhàng and nine chǐ wide,
nine chǐ high;
the second tier was nine zhàng wide,
eight chǐ and one cùn high;
the third tier was twelve zhàng wide,
the same height as the second tier.
The bricks used for paving totaled one, nine, seven, five, which are yang numbers.
There were four ramps leading out,
each with nine steps.
The balustrade pillars were capped with blue glazed tiles.
The inner enclosure was round,
with a circumference of ninety-seven zhàng, seven chǐ, and five cùn,
eight chǐ and one cùn high.
There were three gates on each of the four sides,
each gate having two pillars.
There was one furnace for burning firewood and one pit for burying offerings.
The outer enclosure was square,
with a circumference of two hundred four zhàng, eight chǐ, and five cùn,
nine chǐ and one cùn high.
The four gates were like those of the inner enclosure.
Behind the north gate was the Huángqióngyǔ,
facing south,
circular in design.
It had eight pillars arranged in a circle,
with double eaves and a golden roof.
The base had a circumference of thirteen zhàng and seven cùn,
nine chǐ high.
There were three ramps leading out,
with fourteen steps each.
The east and west wings each had five bays,
with one ramp leading out,
seven steps.
The roofs of the main hall and wings were all covered with blue glazed tiles.
The surrounding wall had a circumference of fifty-six zhàng, six chǐ, and eight cùn,
one zhàng and eight cùn high.
Three gates were set up on the south side.
Outside the outer enclosure gates, to the north, were the Shénkù and Shénchú, each with five bays,
facing south.
There was one well pavilion.
To its east were the storehouses for sacrificial vessels, musical instruments, and palm mats.
Further east were a well pavilion and a slaughter pavilion.
The inner wall of the altar was round to the north,
the rest was square.
There were four gates: Dàiyuán to the east,
Zhāohēng to the south,
Guǎnglì to the west,
Chéngzhēn to the north.
North of Chéngzhēn was the Dàxiǎngdiàn.
The altar was round,
facing south.
There were twelve pillars inside and outside each,
with four central "dragon well" pillars.
It had a golden roof,
with triple eaves,
covered with blue, yellow, and green glazed tiles.
The base had three tiers,
with three ramps leading out on the north and south,
and one ramp leading out on the east and west.
The upper two tiers each had nine steps,
the third tier had ten steps.
The east and west wings had two layers,
the front each with nine bays,
the rear each with seven bays.
In front was the Dàxiǎngmén,
its roof covered with green glazed tiles,
with three ramps leading out front and back,
each with eleven steps.
To the southeast were a furnace for burning firewood and a pit for burying offerings,
designed like those of the Yuánqiú Altar.
The inner enclosure had a circumference of one hundred ninety zhàng, seven chǐ, and two cùn.
There were four gates.
Behind the north gate was the Huánggāndiàn,
facing south,
with five bays,
covered with blue glazed tiles.
There were five ramps leading out,
each with nine steps.
Outside the eastern brick gate were seventy-two long corridors,
with connecting eaves and continuous ridges,
extending north to the Shénkù and well pavilion.
Further northeast was the slaughter pavilion,
a place to shelter from rain and snow during the offering of sacrificial meat.
The outer surrounding wall had gates on the east, west, and north,
connecting to Chéngzhēn on the south.
Further northwest was the Zhāigōng,
facing east.
The main hall had five bays,
with three ramps leading out,
the central one with thirteen steps,
the left and right ones each with fifteen.
On the left was a bronze figure for fasting and purification,
on the right was a time-marking tablet.
The rear hall had five bays,
the left and right side halls each with three bays.
The inner palace wall was one hundred thirty-three zhàng, nine chǐ, and four cùn square.
There were three central gates,
and one each on the left and right.
It was surrounded by a moat,
crossed by three stone bridges.
To the northeast was a bell tower.
The outer palace wall was one hundred ninety-eight zhàng, two chǐ, and two cùn square,
with moats and bridges similar to the inner design.
Outside the Guǎnglì gate, to the northwest, was the Shénlèguān,
facing east.
In the center was the Níngxīdiàn,
with five bays.
Behind it was the Xiǎnyòudiàn,
with seven bays.
To the west was the Xīshēngsuǒ,
facing south.
Further west was a bell tower.
The surrounding wall of the Dàxiǎngdiàn connected to the Yuánqiú Altar on the south,
and turned east and west to the north in a circular shape.
The inner wall was one zhàng and one chǐ high,
the base nine chǐ thick,
the top seven chǐ thick,
with a circumference of one thousand two hundred eighty-six zhàng, one chǐ, and five cùn.
The outer wall was one zhàng, one chǐ, and five cùn high,
the base eight chǐ thick,
the top six chǐ thick,
with a circumference of one thousand nine hundred eighty-seven zhàng and five chǐ.
There were two gates facing west,
arranged parallel north and south.
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng,
the Zhāigōng was repaired,
and the Shénlèguān was changed to a office.
In the twelfth year,
the inner and outer walls were repaired,
and the Yuánqiú Altar was rebuilt,
further expanding its regulations.
The top tier had a diameter of nine zhàng,
the second tier fifteen zhàng,
the third tier twenty-one zhàng,
one, nine, three, five, three, seven—
all celestial numbers.
The total of the three tiers was forty-five zhàng,
conforming to the meaning of "nine-five".
The measurements adhered to the ancient chǐ,
equivalent to eight cùn and one fēn of the construction chǐ,
also in agreement with the "nine-nine" numbers.
The altar surface was paved with nine layers of bricks.
The central circular surface of the top tier
was surrounded by nine rings,
with the number of bricks accumulating from one nine to nine nines.
The second and third tiers similarly increased in turn.
On the top tier, each side had eighteen [steps],
the second tier twenty-seven each,
the third tier forty-five each,
all accumulating to a multiple of nine.
Multiplying by four,
the total was three hundred sixty,
corresponding to the degrees of the heavens.
Its height was: top tier five chǐ and seven cùn,
second tier five chǐ and two cùn,
third tier five chǐ.
The balustrades, pillars, and steps all conformed to the current chǐ.
There was a slight difference in the increase or decrease of ancient and modern measurements,
but using nine as the standard resolved it.
Furthermore, the altar surface was changed to mugwort-leaf blue stone,
the platform surface of the Huángqióngyǔ was paved with blue and white stone,
and the outer altar surface of the Dàxiǎngdiàn was paved with golden bricks.
The halls, palaces, gates, and walls within the altar were all blue glazed tiles.
In the sixteenth year,
the Dàxiǎngdiàn was renamed Qínián.
The roofs, eaves, gates, wings, and inner and outer enclosure walls within the altar were all changed to blue glazed tiles,
while those far from the altar remained as before.
Soon after, a south gate was added to the outer wall of the Tiāntán,
and a bell and drum tower to the inner wall.
Thereafter, sacrifices at the Tiāntán were entered through the new south gate,
while sacrifices at the Qíniándiàn were still entered through the north gate.
In the twentieth year,
the Shénlèsuǒ was changed to a bureau.
The layout for the three altars of Tiānshén, Dìqí, and Xiānnóng:
Once completed,
the stairs all emerged from the four sides,
located outside the Zhèngyángmén.
The Xiānnóngtán is positioned to the southwest,
its circumference is forty-seven zhàng,
and its height is four chǐ five cùn.
To the southeast is the Guāngēngtái,
which is set up during the plowing ceremony.
In front is the jítán,
and behind it is the Jùfúdiàn.
To the northeast is the Shéncāng,
with a circular granary in the center.
In front is the Shōugǔtíng,
and behind it is the Jìqìkù.
Outside the south gate of the inner wall,
the Shénqítán is located there.
The Shéntán is positioned to the east,
five zhàng square,
and four chǐ five cùn five fēn high.
To the north are four stone niches,
carved with cloud patterns,
for separate sacrifices to Yún, Yǔ, Fēng, and Léi.
The Qítán is positioned to the west,
ten zhàng wide,
six zhàng long,
and four chǐ high.
To the south are five stone niches,
carved with mountain and water patterns.
For separate sacrifices to Yuè, Zhèn, Hǎi, and Dú.
The square enclosures of the two altars
both have a circumference of twenty-four zhàng,
and a height of five chǐ five cùn.
The main gates are divided into south and north,
the rest are like the Rìtán and Yuètán.
Furthermore, outside the east gate of the inner wall, to the north, is the Zhāigōng,
with five jiāng,
a rear hall,
side halls,
and tea and dining rooms.
During the Qiánlóng era,
the Zhāigōng was renamed Qìngchénggōng.
The outer wall of the altar has a circumference of one thousand three hundred and sixty-eight zhàng.
There are two gates, south and north,
facing east.
The south gate enters the Xiānnóngtán,
and the north gate enters the Tàisuìdiàn.
The main hall has seven jiāng,
with eleven xiáng on both the east and west sides.
In front of it is the Bàidiàn,
and one liáolú.
The Xiāncántán,
built in the ninth year of Qiánlóng,
is located in the northeast corner of the Xīyuàn,
its design is similar to the Xiānnóng.
It has a diameter of four zhàng,
a height of four chǐ,
with stairs emerging from four sides.
The main hall has three jiāng,
facing west.
To the east is the Cǎisāngtái,
three zhàng two chǐ wide,
four chǐ high,
with stairs emerging from three sides.
In front is the Sāngyuántái,
in the middle are the Jùfúdiàn and the Jiǎnguǎn,
and behind is the Zhīshì.
There are side halls,
surrounded by palace walls.
East of the wall is the Yùcánhé,
crossed by two bridges.
East of the bridges are three Cánshǔ,
and twenty-seven Cánshì,
all facing west.
The outer wall has a circumference of one hundred and sixty zhàng.
The Xiānnóngtán in each province, prefecture, and county has dimensions similar to the Shèjìtán,
the rest are according to the system.
Number of divine tablets, sacrificial vessels, offerings, jade, silk, and sacrificial animals: The divine tablets
at the first level of the Huánqiú
have the principal position for Hàotiān Shàngdì,
facing south.
There are eight accompanying positions,
starting from Tàizǔ up to Xuānzōng,
facing east and west.
All positions are covered with canopies.
The second level has subordinate positions:
to the east Dàmíng,
followed by Xīngchén.
To the west Yèmíng,
followed by Yún, Yǔ, Fēng, and Léi.
During regular Yú sacrifices, such as those in winter solstice, grand sacrifices, and grand Yú sacrifices,
there are subordinate deities but no accompanying imperial ancestors.
The order of positions for Qígǔ is similar to the first level of the Huánqiú,
without canopies.
At the first level of the Fāngzé,
the principal position is for Huángdìqí,
facing north,
with imperial ancestors and lineage ancestors arranged as accompanying deities,
facing east and west.
The second level has subordinate positions:
to the east Wǔyuè,
Qǐyùn, Lóngyè, and Yǒngníng Sānshān,
followed by Sìhǎi.
To the west Wǔzhèn,
Tiānzhù and Chāngruì Èrshān,
followed by Sìdú.
When making announcements to Tiāndì due to specific events,
no accompanying or subordinate positions are set up.
In the seventeenth year of Shùnzhì,
a combined sacrifice was held at the Dàxiǎngdiàn,
where the principal position had Tiāndì on the left
and Dìqí on the right,
facing south.
Tàizǔ to the east
and Tàizōng to the west
accompanied them.
There were twelve altars for subordinate sacrifices:
Dàmíng was positioned to the east,
followed by Xīngchén, Wǔyuè, Qǐyùn, Sìhǎi, Tàisuì, and Míngshān Dàchuān.
Yèmíng was positioned to the west,
followed by Yún, Yǔ, Fēng, Léi, Wǔzhèn, Tiānzhù, Lóngyè, Sìdú, Dìwáng, and Tiānxià Shénqí.
At the Shèjìtán, stone tablets are planted in the center,
with separate divine tablets
for the principal positions.
Dàshè to the east,
Dàjì to the west.
Facing north.
To the east, Hòutǔ Jùlóngshì accompanied,
to the west, Hòujìshì.
Without canopies.
The niches under the altar used wood.
At the Rìtán, Dàmíng is to the east,
without canopies.
At the Yuètán, the principal position is Yèmíng,
accompanied by Běidǒu, the Twenty-eight Xiù, and Zhōutiān Xīngchén,
all under one canopy.
At the center of the Tiānshéntán,
on the left is Yúnshī,
followed by Fēngbó;
on the right is Yǔshī,
followed by Léishī,
facing south.
At the center of the Dìqítán are the Wǔyuè,
on the right are the Wǔzhèn,
followed by Sìhǎi;
on the left are the Wǔlíng,
followed by Sìdú,
facing north.
To the right side are the mountains and rivers of Jīngshī,
to the left side are the mountains and rivers of Tiānxià.
Without canopies.
For the Shénqí positions in various provincial prefectures, zhou, and counties,
at the center are Yún, Yǔ, Fēng, Léi;
on the left are Shānchuān,
on the right are Chénghuáng.
The divine tablets of the Jiāotán
are enshrined in the Huángqióngyǔ, Huánggāndiàn, and Huángqíshì.
The divine tablets of Shénqí, Shèjì, Rìyuè
are enshrined in the Shénkù,
and are moved to the altar location during sacrifices.
The divine tablets in the sleeping chambers and niches of the Tàimiào and Fèngxiāndiàn
are moved to the imperial thrones in the front halls during sacrifices.
As for the niches in the Chuánxīndiàn, Lìdài Dìwáng, and Xiānshī temples,
they are sometimes separate, sometimes combined,
without a fixed system.
Sacrificial vessels:
For the principal position at the Huánqiú,
three *jué* (goblets),
one *dēng* (food stand),
two *fǔ* (rectangular vessels) and *guǐ* (round vessels), ten *biān* (bamboo baskets) and *dòu* (wooden stands),
one *fěi* (bamboo container), *zǔ* (sacrificial table), and *zūn* (wine vessel) each.
Subordinate positions are the same.
Only for Dàmíng and Yèmíng, thirty *zhǎn* (cups),
and two *yèmíng xíng* (liquid vessels) each.
Yún, Yǔ, Fēng, Lěi follow Yèmíng.
For regular *yú* (rain-seeking sacrifice) like the Winter Solstice, Grand Sacrifices, and Grand *Yú*,
the principal and subordinate positions both have six *biān* and two *dòu*.
For Announcement Sacrifices, the principal position is the same.
For the Fāngzé Prayer-for-Grain Altar's principal and subordinate positions,
and the Fāngzé's attendant positions,
all follow Huánqiú.
*Zhǎn* and *xíng* follow Yèmíng.
For seasonal offerings at Tàimiào,
the Emperor and Empress share the same table,
both with three *jué*,
two *fǔ* and *guǐ*,
twelve *biān* and *dòu*,
and one *dēng*, *xíng*, *fěi*, and *zǔ* each.
*Zūn* are the same for the front and rear halls.
For *xiá* (combined ancestral) sacrifices, it's like seasonal offerings,
each table in the East Wing has three *jué*,
two *fǔ* and *guǐ*,
ten *biān* and *dòu*,
and one *xíng*, *fěi*, and *zǔ* each.
There are eight tables for *zūn* in total,
divided into two sets,
with *jué* and *xíng* doubled.
The West Wing is the same,
but with one *fǔ* and *guǐ*,
and four *biān* and *dòu*.
For Announcement Sacrifices,
the central and rear halls both have six *biān*,
and two *dòu*.
For the Shèjì Altar's Dàshè and Dàjì,
both have one jade *jué*,
two pottery *jué*,
one *dēng*, *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each,
and two *xíng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each.
Subordinate positions are the same,
but all *jué* are pottery.
For Prayers and Announcements,
six *biān*,
and two *dòu*.
For provincial sacrifices to Shèjì,
six *jué*,
one *xíng*,
four *biān* and *dòu*,
and one *fǔ*, *guǐ*, *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each,
as for Dàshèjì.
For Rìtán, Yuètán, Xiānnóng, and Xiāncán Altars,
all have three *jué*,
thirty *zhǎn*,
ten *biān* and *dòu*,
two *xíng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each,
and one *dēng*, *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each.
Provincial sacrifices to Xiānnóng are like sacrifices to Shèjì.
For Tiānshén Altar, four tables,
for all prayers and sacrifices, a total of twelve *jué*,
each using six *biān*, two *dòu*, one *zūn*, and one *fěi*.
The Dìqí Altar is the same,
but with seven tables and a total of twenty-seven *jué*.
For Reciprocal Sacrifices to Shénqí,
each table is the same as Rìtán,
but without *zhǎn*.
For provincial sacrifices to Shénqí,
three *jué*,
four *biān* and *dòu*,
two *xíng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each,
and one *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each.
For seasonal inspections and sacrifices to Yuèzhèn and Hǎidú, it's the same.
For Reciprocal Sacrifices, one *xíng* is added;
for incidental special sacrifices, two are still used.
The rest are the same.
For sacrifices made by officials, there are no *dēng* or *zhǎn*.
The Tàisuì Hall follows Xiānnóng,
and reciprocal sacrifices are also the same.
For Prayers,
six *biān* and two *dòu*,
no *zǔ* is presented.
The principal position for Xiānshī follows Huánqiú,
but only two *xíng* are used.
The Four Complements follow the principal position,
but only eight *biān* and *dòu* are used,
without *dēng*.
For the Twelve Worthies' positions,
each has three *jué*,
one *xíng*,
one *fǔ* and *guǐ*,
four *biān* and *dòu*,
with two *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* shared.
The two positions in both wings share a table,
one *jué* per position,
a total of six *jué* offered,
with two *fěi* shared,
six *zūn* and *zǔ* each,
one *fǔ* and *guǐ* each,
and four *biān* and *dòu* each.
For inspecting schools and performing the Shìdiàn, it's the same.
In the 33rd year of Qiánlóng,
the Imperial Household provided one Zhōu tripod, *zūn*, *yóu*, *léi*, *hú*, *fǔ*, *guǐ*, *gū*, and *jué* each,
displayed in Dàchéng Hall,
for use as ritual vessels.
For Chóngshèng Temple, the principal position has five tables,
each table has three *jué*,
eight *biān* and *dòu*,
two *xíng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each,
and one *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each.
The subordinate position has five tables,
three *jué*,
four *biān* and *dòu*,
one *xíng*, *fěi*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each,
with two *zǔ* shared,
and two *zūn*.
The two wings have three tables,
each table is the same as the subordinate position,
but with two *fěi* shared.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
the *biān* and *dòu* for the principal position of Xiānshī were increased to twelve,
and for Chóngshèng Temple to ten.
The ritual vessels for Quèlǐ, provincial Wénmiào, and Chóngshèng Temple follow Tàixué.
For Lìdài Dìwáng, the principal position has sixteen tables,
each table has three *jué*,
one *dēng*,
two *xíng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each,
ten *biān* and *dòu*,
one *fěi*,
with seven *zǔ* shared,
and seven *zūn*.
The subordinate positions in the two wings have twenty tables,
each table has twelve *jué*,
two *xíng*,
four *biān* and *dòu*,
one *fǔ*, *guǐ*, and *fěi* each,
with four *zǔ* shared,
and four *zūn*.
For Chuánxīn Hall, the principal position has nine tables,
each table has three *jué* and *zūn* each,
one *xíng* and *fěi* each,
and two *biān* and *dòu*.
The subordinate position has two tables,
each table has three *jué*,
two *biān* and *dòu*,
and one *xíng*, *fěi*, and *zūn* each.
For Guāndì and Wénchāng Dìjūn, both have three *jué*,
ten *biān* and *dòu*,
two *xíng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each,
and one *dēng*, *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each,
but the rear hall has eight *biān* and *dòu*.
All provinces follow the capital's style.
For Xiānyī Sānhuáng positions,
each position has three *jué*,
ten *biān* and *dòu*,
and one *fǔ*, *guǐ*, *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each.
The two wings have six tables,
each table has one *guǐ* and *fǔ*,
two *fěi* and *zūn* each,
four *biān* and *dòu*,
and a total of six *jué*.
For Dūchénghuáng, three *jué*,
ten *biān* and *dòu*,
two *xíng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ* each,
and one *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each.
For Huǒshén and Dōngyuè Temple,
all have five fruit plates,
and one *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each.
Hēilóngtán, Yùquánshān, the various Lóngshén Temples at Kūnmínghú, Huìjì Temple, and Héshén Temple all have three tables,
each table has three *jué*,
two *fǔ* and *guǐ*,
ten *biān* and *dòu*,
and one *fěi*, *zǔ*, and *zūn* each.
Initially, it followed the old Ming dynasty system.
The sacrificial offerings at altars and temples adhered to ancient regulations,
but the utensils were made of porcelain.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
they were changed to cast bronze.
