In the 13th year of Qiánlóng,
an imperial edict stated that sacrificial offerings should emulate ancient practices,
and ordered court officials to convene a discussion.
Thus, regulations were established for *biān* (bamboo baskets) to be woven from bamboo,
*dòu* (vessels) from silk and satin,
and lacquerware.
Suburban altars used pure lacquer,
while the Tàimiào used painted designs.
As for the *dòu*, *dēng*, *fǔ*, and *guǐ*,
suburban altars used pottery,
the Tàimiào only used *dēng* of pottery,
while others used wood,
lacquer,
and were adorned with gold and jade.
*Xíng* (cups) were cast bronze adorned with gold.
As for *zūn* (wine vessels), suburban altars used pottery.
For the Tàimiào, the Chūxīzūn for spring, Xiàngzūn for summer, Zhùzūn for autumn, Húzūn for winter, and Shānzūn for the joint sacrifice
were all cast bronze.
For sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, *jué* (cups) used gourds;
the Tàimiào used jade;
the two side-chambers used pottery.
For the main positions at the Shèjì,
one was jade, two were pottery.
For the accompanying positions, pure pottery was used.
Additionally, *dòu*, *dēng*, *fǔ*, *guǐ*, *xíng*, and *zūn* were all pottery.
The sacrifices to the Sun, Moon, Xiānnóng, and Xiāncán also followed this.
For emperors, venerated teachers (Xiānshī), Guāndì, Wénchāng, and other shrines,
all used bronze.
All pottery had to distinguish colors:
Yuánqiū, Qígǔ, and Chángyú were cyan;
Fāngzé, Shèjì, and Xiānnóng were yellow;
Rìtán was red;
Yuètán was white.
The pottery *dēng* at the Tàimiào
had a yellow base with colorful decorations;
all others were white.
For holding silk, bamboo *fěi* (baskets) were used,
the color matching their utensils.
For carrying sacrificial animals, wooden *zǔ* (platters) were used,
painted with cinnabar lacquer.
Plates for hair and blood used pottery,
their color also matching their utensils.
In the 19th year of Jiāqìng,
it was stipulated that the *fǔ*, *guǐ*, *dòu* of the Tàimiào and all bamboo *biān* for sacrifices
were to be repaired every three years.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
the *jué* for Xiānshī were changed to jade.
Sacrificial Offerings:
The contents of *biān* and *dòu* were each twelve items.
*Biān* contained molded salt, dried fish, dates, chestnuts, hazelnuts, water chestnuts, foxnuts, dried venison, white cakes, black cakes, dried gruel, and rice flour cakes.

*Dòu* contained pickled leeks, minced meat paste, pickled celery cabbage, minced venison, pickled celery, minced rabbit, pickled bamboo shoots, minced fish, sliced spleen, pork chops, thin gruel, and thick gruel.
For ten items,
*biān* omitted dried gruel and rice flour cakes;
*dòu* omitted thin gruel and thick gruel.
For eight items,
*biān* omitted white and black cakes;
*dòu* omitted sliced spleen and pork chops.
For four items,
*biān* only contained molded salt, dates, chestnuts, and dried venison;
*dòu* only contained pickled celery cabbage, minced venison, pickled celery, and minced rabbit.
For *biān* with six items,
they contained dried venison, dates, hazelnuts, grapes, peach kernels, and lotus seeds.
For *dòu* with two items,
they only contained minced venison and minced rabbit.
One *dēng* (vessel)
contained plain broth (Tàigēng).
Two *xíng* (cups)
contained seasoned broth (Hégēng).
Two *fǔ* (vessels)
contained rice and millet.
Two *guǐ* (vessels)
contained broomcorn millet and foxtail millet.
Jade, Silk, and Sacrificial Animals: Jade was in six grades.
For the Supreme Lord (Shàngdì), a cyan *bì* (disk);
for the Imperial Earth Spirit (Huángdìqí), a yellow *cóng* (tube);
for the Great Land Altar (Dàshè), a yellow *guī* (tablet);
for the Great Harvest Altar (Dàjì), a cyan *guī*;
for the Morning Sun Altar (Zhāorì), a red *bì*;
for the Evening Moon Altar (Xīyuè), a white *bì*.
According to the old system,
jade was used for regular spring and autumn sacrifices at the Shèjì Altars,
but not for prayers.
In the 34th year of Qiánlóng,
when there was a drought and prayers for rain were held,
an edict stated:
"Jade is for protecting and sheltering abundant grains,
to prevent partial disasters of flood and drought;
therefore, the responsible officials are specifically ordered to use jade for the rites."
From then on, this became a permanent rule.
Silk was in seven grades:
Firstly, the Jīaosi Zhìbó (Suburban Sacrifice Regulated Silk), used for the Northern and Southern Suburbs.
For Shàngdì, twelve cyan pieces;
for Dìqí, one yellow piece.
Secondly, the Lǐshén Zhìbó (Spirit Worship Regulated Silk), used for Shèjì and below.
For Shèjì, four black pieces;
for Dàmíng, one red piece;
for Yèmíng, one white piece;
the Sun and Moon were the same.
For the Stars and Big Dipper, seven white pieces,
and one each of cyan, red, yellow, and black.
For Heavenly Spirits, Clouds, Rain, Wind, and Thunder,
one each of cyan, white, yellow, and black.
For the accompanying positions at Fāngzé,
the five sacred mountains (Yuèzhèn) each had five,
in five colors.
The five imperial tombs (Wǔlíngshān) had five white pieces.
The Four Seas (Sìhǎi) used colors corresponding to their directions.
The Four Great Rivers (Sìdú) had four black pieces.
For Dìqí, two yellow pieces,
three each of cyan and red,
seven black, and twelve white.
Xiānnóng and Xiāncán both had one cyan piece.
For Xiānshī's main and accompanying positions,
the twelve philosophers,
the two side-chambers,
Chóngshèngcí's main position,
and its Eastern and Western side-chambers,
all used one white piece each.
The positions for various emperors, Guāndì, Wénchāng's main position and rear hall,
Tàisuì's main position,
Běijí Yòushèng Zhēnjūn, and Dōngyuè Dūchénghuáng were also the same.
However, Xiānyī's main position had three;
Chóngshèng's accompanying positions had four;
Tàisuì's two side-chambers had twelve;
Huǒshén had one red piece.
Thirdly, the Gàosì Zhìbì (Announcement Sacrifice Regulated Silk), used for prayers and reports.
For Qígǔ, Yúsì, and announcements at Yuánqiū, all had one cyan piece;
for announcements at Fāngzé, one yellow piece.
Fourthly, the Fèngxiān Zhìbì (Ancestor Worship Regulated Silk), used for accompanying positions at suburban sacrifices and the Tàimiào.
Yuánqiū and Fāngzé accompanying positions each had one;
emperors and empresses at the Tàimiào had one for each position.
Fifthly, the Zhǎnqīn Zhìbì (Royal Kinsmen Regulated Silk), used for imperial princes honored as accompanying sacrificers.
Each position in the Eastern side-chamber of the Tàimiào had one.
Sixthly, the Bàogōng Zhìbì (Meritorious Officials Regulated Silk), used for meritorious officials honored as accompanying sacrificers.
Each position in the Western side-chamber of the Tàimiào had one.
The three types (Fèngxiān, Zhǎnqīn, Bàogōng) were all white;
Zhàozhōng and other shrines were the same,
and woven with Manchu and Han characters.
Seventhly, plain silk (Sùbó).
Each position in the two side-chambers of the Dìwángmiào had one;
the two side-chambers of the Xiānyīmiào had a total of four;
other sacrifices also preferred plain silk.
Sacrificial Animals were in four grades:
Firstly, *dú* (calf);
secondly, *tè* (single ox);
thirdly, *tàiláo* (grand sacrifice);
fourthly, *shàoláo* (lesser sacrifice).
Colors preferred were reddish-brown or dark.
Yuánqiū and Fāngzé used *dú*;
Dàmíng and Yèmíng used *tè*;
Heavenly Spirits, Earth Spirits, Tàisuì, Sun, Moon, Stars, Clouds, Rain, Wind, Thunder, Shèjì, Yuèzhèn, Hǎidú, Tàimiào, Xiānnóng, Xiāncán, Xiānshī, Emperors, Guāndì, and Wénchāng used *tàiláo*.
The Western side-chamber of the Tàimiào,
the accompanying philosophers in the Wénmiào, Chóngshèngcí, the two side-chambers of the Dìwángmiào,
and the rear halls of Guāndì and Wénchāng,
used *shàoláo*.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
Chóngshèng's main position was changed to *tàiláo*.
Provincial deities, Shèjì, Xiānnóng, Guāndì, Xiānyī's accompanying positions, and all collective sacrifices used *shàoláo*.
Huǒshén, Dōngyuè, and Xiānyī's main positions,
and Dūchénghuáng,
all used *tàiláo*.
*Tàiláo* comprised one sheep, one ox, and one pig.
*Shàoláo* comprised one sheep and one pig.
For Grand Sacrifices, abstinence lasts ninety days;
for Medium Sacrifices, sixty days;
for Collective Sacrifices, thirty days.
For Grand Sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
five days beforehand, a Qīn Wáng inspects the sacrificial animal;
two days beforehand, the Lǐ Bù Shàng Shū inspects the sacrificial animal;
one day beforehand, at the hour of Zǐ, the animal is slaughtered.
When the Emperor offers sacrifice at the Tiān Tán,
two days beforehand, at the hour of Yǒu, the animal is slaughtered.
For the Tàimiào, Shèjì, and Xiānshī, three days beforehand;
for Medium Sacrifices, two days beforehand.
The Lǐ Bù Shàng Shū leads the Tàicháng Sī to inspect the sacrificial animal,
and one day beforehand, at dawn, the animal is slaughtered.
Only for the Xīyuè sacrifice is it slaughtered at dawn on the day itself.
According to regulations,
officials from the Cháyuàn, Lǐ Bù, Tàicháng, and Guānglù supervise the slaughter.
For Collective Sacrifices, only the Tàicháng Sī carries it out.
In the seventeenth year of Qiánlóng (1752),
it was stipulated that for Grand and Medium Sacrifices, the Guānglù Qīng supervises the slaughter.
Originally,
for Grand Sacrifices at the Jiāotán,
the Emperor would stay in the Zhāigōng some days beforehand
to inspect the altar, sacrificial vessels (biāndòu), and sacrificial animals (shēngláo).
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng (1742),
it was reformed that one day beforehand, the Emperor would proceed to the Huánqiū to inspect the altar;
the officiants for separate offerings would proceed to the Shénkù to inspect the biāndòu,
and to the Shénchú to inspect the shēngláo.
Later, it was stipulated that on the day of inspecting the altar,
the Emperor would personally proceed to the Huángqióngyǔ and Huángqiándiàn to offer incense.
Traditionally,
when inspecting the biāndòu and shēngláo,
it was either personally supervised
or not.
In the thirty-fifth year (1770),
it was stipulated that officials be dispatched to manage the affairs,
and this became the norm thereafter.
Sacrifice Dates: For sacrifices at the Jiāo and Miào,
two years before the sacrifice, in the tenth month,
the Qīn Tiān Jiān would first divine auspicious dates.
One year beforehand, in the first month,
a memorial listing the auspicious dates and the fixed dates for various sacrifices was presented.
This was then announced throughout the empire.
The Tàicháng Sì would, according to the sacrifice dates, memorialize for approval in advance,
but it was actually overseen by the Lǐ Bù.
When Shìzǔ assumed the throne,
he decreed that sacrifices should be divided into ranks
and offered at appropriate times.
Since then, the dates for Grand, Medium, and Collective Sacrifices were successively regulated and
established as precedents.
In the seventh year of Jiāqìng (1802),
it was further stipulated that if Grand or Medium Sacrifices fell on an inauspicious day, the date would not be changed.
During the Xiánfēng reign,
it was further stipulated that for the spring and autumn sacrifices to Guāndì and Wénchāng, inauspicious days should not be used.
Regarding the time of sacrifices,
in the thirteenth year of Shùnzhì (1656),
an edict stated that for sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, the Emperor should leave the palace at the fifth watch;
for Shèjì and Tàimiào, at dawn.
In the twelfth year of Kāngxī (1673),
following Tàizōng's old system,
altars and temples used dawn;
Xīyuè used the hour of Yǒu.
In the eighth year of Jiāqìng (1803),
an edict stated that sacrificial rites
should be performed between the hours of Yín and Mǎo,
conforming to the ancient meaning of "starting affairs at dawn" in the Rítuál Classics.
For all personally conducted Grand Sacrifices,
the responsible department would set the time,
and the chief officiant, attendants, and accompanying officiants would await.
Those who arrived early or late on a whim
would be impeached by the Yùshǐ.
Fasting and Abstinence: In the third year of Shùnzhì (1646),
regulations for fasting and abstinence for suburban sacrifices were established.
In the eighth year (1651),
it was stipulated that for Grand Sacrifices (three days) and Medium Sacrifices (two days), wooden abstinence plaques should be placed in public offices.
Ten days before the sacrifice,
a register of those observing abstinence was sent to the Tàicháng.
On the appointed day, no legal cases were tried,
no banquets were held,
no music was listened to,
no overnight stays in the inner palace,
no alcohol or meat,
no visiting the sick or condoling the bereaved,
no worshipping other deities or sweeping tombs.
Those who were ill or in mourning should not participate.
For Grand and Medium Sacrifices,
the Tàicháng Sī presented abstinence plaques and bronze figures to be placed on the yellow table at the Qiánqīng Mén.
Three days before a Grand Sacrifice,
the Emperor observed abstinence within the inner palace
and issued an edict of warning.
The decree stated:
"You, all my officials,
shall purify your hearts and concentrate your minds,
each diligently performing your duties.
Should any dare to be disrespectful,
the state has established punishments.
Be reverent and not negligent!"
One day before the sacrifice,
the plaques and bronze figures were removed and sent to the Zhāigōng,
and the Emperor proceeded to the altar to observe abstinence overnight.
In the fourteenth year (1657), for the sacrifice at Huánqiū,
abstinence was observed in the inner palace for two days,
and in the Zhāigōng within the altar precinct for one day.
Accompanying officiants observed abstinence in their public offices,
and for Huánqiū, within the altar precinct.
In the fifth year of Yōngzhèng (1727),
Yùshǐ and others were dispatched to inspect the altar.
In the ninth year (1731),
an edict ordered the Kē and Dào officials to observe abstinence during sacrifice periods.
The following year,
following the Ming dynasty's system of sacrifice plaques, abstinence plaques were made,
and accompanying officiants were commanded to wear them
to prevent irreverence.
In the fourth year of Qiánlóng (1739),
a minister of rites memorialized that
for Grand Sacrifices at the Jiāotán,
the Tàicháng Qīng would, four days beforehand, list the abstinence period
and present the plaques and bronze figures to be placed at the Qiánqīng Mén for two days, and in the Zhāigōng for one day.
For the Tàimiào and Shèjì, they were placed at the Qiánqīng Mén for three days.
For Medium Sacrifices,
three days beforehand, they were presented
and placed at the Qiánqīng Mén for two days.
They were removed and returned on the day of the sacrifice.
For the Empress's sacrifice to Xiāncán,
the presentation was similar.
However, they were placed in the Jiāotài Diàn by inner eunuchs for three days.
In the seventh year (1742),
it was stipulated that for suburban sacrifices and abstinence,
the Emperor would stay in the inner palace for two days,
and in the Zhāigōng within the altar precinct for one day.
Princes and Dukes stayed in their mansions,
the rest in their public offices,
all for two days.
They would proceed to the Zhāigōng outside the altar for one night's abstinence.
If an official was dispatched to offer sacrifice on behalf of the Emperor,
Princes and Dukes did not participate.
For sacrifices at the Tàimiào and Shèjì,
Princes, Dukes, and all officials observed abstinence as before,
all for three days.
For sacrifices to the Sun, Moon, Emperors, Xiānshī, and Xiānnóng,
Princes and Dukes observed abstinence for two days,
but not if a substitute official was dispatched.
For the Empress's sacrifice to Xiāncán,
abstinence was for two days;
Princesses, Fújìn, and official ladies accompanying the sacrifice
observed abstinence for two days beforehand.
In the twelfth year (1747),
an edict decreed that for suburban sacrifices, Qígǔ, and Dàyú,
on the day of the sacrifice, an oath of warning should be proclaimed,
and accompanying officiants should gather at the Wǔ Mén to perform the rites,
which aligned with the ancient intention of all officials receiving a warning.
After the responsible department submitted the ritual,
it was carried out.
It was later abolished.
However,
Ministers were strictly ordered to observe abstinence in their public offices,
and the chief imperial guards and other inner ministers observed abstinence in the Zǐjìn Chéng.
Violators would be punished.
Originally,
when observing abstinence in the Zhāigōng, drums and horns were sounded.
In the fourteenth year (1657), an edict stated:
"For those observing abstinence, the ears should not listen to music.
Confucius said: 'Having fasted for three days,
if one uses one day for this,
one still fears disrespect.
How can one beat drums on the second day?'
He meant that one should not scatter one's resolve.
Blowing horns and beating drums
to augment military display
is not in line with the meaning
and should not be used."
Thus, it was ceased.
In the nineteenth year (1754),
it was decreed that all officials should write the admonitory decree on plaques,
and three days beforehand,
display them in their public halls
to serve as a warning.
In the thirteenth year of Jiāqìng (1808),
an edict admonished those involved in abstinence and those supervising the rituals
to follow old regulations and uphold the solemnity of the sacrificial rites.
At the beginning of Xuāntǒng,
when the Jiānguó Shèzhèng Wáng acted on behalf of the Emperor,
the Emperor observed abstinence within the palace,
and the presentation of abstinence plaques and bronze figures was discontinued.
In the eighteenth year of Jiāqìng's reign,
when Lín Qīng's rebellion arose,
it was pacified within a few days.
The emperor happened to perform the grand sacrifice at the Yuánqiū.
An edict was issued that on the day before, upon arrival at the altar, he was not to ascend the imperial carriage (niǎn),
but would proceed from the palace to the Huángqióngyǔ and enter the zhāigōng.
He would also ride in a sedan chair (jiānyú),
in acknowledgment of the great blessing.
When Xuāntǒng succeeded to the throne,
the regent (jiānguó) performed the suburban sacrifices on his behalf.
On the day of the sacrifice, he would proceed to the altar
without fasting and spending the night there.
Officials did not greet or send him off.
When entering or exiting, ascending or descending,
he still used the right gate,
and performed the rites on the right steps.
The position for bowing was set up in a second tier,
slightly behind the emperor's position.
The yellow canopy was removed.
He would receive the sacrificial meat (zuò) at the place of ritual performance.
After completing this,
he would be presented with the blessed wine and sacrificial meat.
The rest followed the procedure for the emperor's personal sacrifice.
Suburban Sacrifices with Co-worship (Pèixiǎng): In the fifth year of Shùnzhì, on the winter solstice,
the sacrifice at the Yuánqiū was performed,
with Gāozǔ (Tàizǔ) enshrined as co-worshipped.
In the fourteenth year, an edict stated:
"Tàizǔ initiated the imperial enterprise,
and Tàizōng continued the imperial achievements.
Their merits and virtues are equally grand,
and both should be honored with sacrifices."
Thereafter, in the grand sacrifices to Heaven and Earth,
Tàizōng was also enshrined as co-worshipped.
Thus, for the Qígǔ sacrifice on the first Xīn day,
Tàizǔ's spirit tablet was placed to the east of the Shàngdì position,
and after auspicious divination, Tàizōng's tablet was placed to its west.
For the summer solstice, the co-worship at the Fāngzé remained as per the original rite.
In the seventeenth year,
the rite of combined sacrifice at the Dàxiǎngdiàn was performed,
but it was soon abolished.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī, on the winter solstice,
the sacrifice at the Southern Suburb was performed.
Following the suggestion of the ritual officials,
Shìzǔ was enshrined to co-worship Shàngdì.
Nine days later,
he was enshrined to co-worship Huángdìqí,
and the rites were performed at the Fāngzé.
In the ninth year,
the Qígǔ sacrifice also followed this.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
Shèngzǔ was enshrined for co-worship at the Dàxiǎngdiàn,
followed by Tàizōng.
In the winter of the thirteenth year,
when Gāozōng succeeded to the throne,
he issued an edict stating:
"My Imperial Father Shìzōng,
whose virtue matches the creation of the universe,
should be sacrificed to at the suburban altars."
He commanded that the rites be deliberated upon and reported.
The deliberators suggested that in the second year of Qiánlóng, on the winter solstice, he be co-worshipped at the Yuánqiū;
in the third year, on the first Xīn day of the first month of spring, he be co-worshipped at the Dàxiǎngdiàn;
and on the summer solstice, he be co-worshipped at the Fāngzé.
The emperor's intention was that if the co-worship occurred after his enshrinement in the ancestral temple,
the summer solstice would be close and the winter solstice far.
If the Fāngzé was co-worshipped first,
the sequence would already be disparate.
If awaiting the Southern Suburb sacrifice,
the timing would again be too long.
Examining the old precedents,
Shìzǔ and Tàizōng were co-worshipped with Heaven and Earth,
and without exception, the Yuánqiū always preceded the Fāngzé,
sometimes on the next day, sometimes after ten days,
the rites were clearly established.
Consulting the Classics and Commentaries,
during the Chéng Zhōu period, Hòujì was co-worshipped with Heaven in the suburban sacrifice,
and King Wén was worshipped in the ancestral temple in the Míngtáng,
which is what the Yuèlíng refers to as
"in the last month of autumn,
the grand sacrifice to Dì."
The Zhào Gào states,
"On the Dīngsì day, three days later, offer sacrifices in the suburbs."
Commentators explain that this was not a regular sacrifice but a sacrifice to Heaven,
to announce the enthronement.
In the third year of Huángyòu during the Sòng dynasty,
the Dàqìngdiàn was used as the Míngtáng,
and Heaven and Earth were worshipped together,
with three sages assisting.
In ancient times, suburban sacrifices were performed according to circumstances,
not necessarily fixed on the two solstices.
Therefore, an edict was issued that the grand ceremony for Shìzōng's co-worship with Heaven the following year
should proceed according to this.
After a year,
an auspicious day before the summer solstice was chosen to enshrine Shìzōng for co-worship at the Yuánqiū.
The rest followed the deliberation.
Previously, the ritual for ascent to co-worship presented by the Board officials
did not include the "first audience with Shàngdì."
The emperor said:
"When my Imperial Father was enshrined in the ancestral temple,
he first met the ancestors,
and then ascended to his seat.
Now performing co-worship,
to first meet Shàngdì,
is truly appropriate in meaning."
Subsequently,
the relevant department drew up the ritual and submitted it.
Thus, for the sacrifice at the Southern Suburb, Shìzōng's spirit tablet was presented for audience with Shàngdì.
On the summer solstice, for the sacrifice at the Fāngzé,
he was presented for audience with Huángdìqí.
His position was next to Shìzǔ.
Thereafter, all ascensions to co-worship always included a first audience,
which became the norm.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
Gāozōng was enshrined for co-worship.
In the first year of Dàoguāng,
Rénzōng was enshrined for co-worship.
Both followed the established ritual.
After thirty years,
the emperor was unwell,
and issued a posthumous decree to abolish the "Jiaopèi" (郊配) sacrifice.
It roughly stated:
"The Dì (禘) and Jiāo (郊) sacrifices to ancestors and lineage
have been highly regarded since ancient times.
In Our dynasty, from the first Tàizǔ (太祖) to Rénzōng (仁宗),
their profound benevolence and deep kindness
make it truly fitting for them to receive offerings at the Jiaotán (郊壇),
a grand ritual for honoring one's origins.
If this practice is followed endlessly for generations,
it will only invite more criticism from future generations.
Therefore, this cannot but be limited."
When Wénzōng (文宗) ascended the throne,
he immediately ordered Wáng Dàchén (王大臣) to convene a discussion.
Lǐ Qīnwáng Quánlíng (禮親王全齡) and others unanimously stated:
"The great departed emperor's merits and virtues shone brightly,
and the Jiaopèi must not be changed.
We request to continue to follow the established precedent."
Lǐbù Shìláng Zēng Guófān (禮部侍郎曾國藩) submitted a memorial, saying:
"Regarding the abolition of the Jiaopèi,
there are two reasons why I dare not comply,
and three reasons why I dare not violate it.
The great departed emperor's benevolence and kindness
were in harmony with the vast creation,
feeding our myriad people,
just as Hòujì (后稷) was entitled to be paired with Heaven.
He governed the empire for thirty years,
without a single day of leisure,
without a moment of irreverence,
pure and unceasing,
just as Wénwáng (文王) was entitled to be paired with Shàngdì (上帝).
If he truly possesses the substance to be jointly offered,
how can I, as a minister, feel at ease
by penning a document to elevate him to this pairing?
This is the first reason I dare not comply.
The great departed emperor's virtue was so profound as to be divine;
even if there were no precedent to cite,
one should still submit a request.
How much more so, when there is an established precedent,
dare one overstep even slightly!
The saying goes: 'The ruler acts on his intentions;
the minister acts on the regulations.'
While those above may harbor humility,
those below should uphold established rules.
This is the second reason I dare not comply.
The scale of the altar and enclosure
has fixed dimensions;
every brick and stone
is arranged according to the Nine-Five Yang numbers,
and cannot be increased or altered.
Inside the tent, there is only room for sacrificial vessels,
and outside, there is almost no spare ground.
The great departed emperor worried that tens of thousands of years later,
some might propose enlarging the altar and enclosure,
or shrinking the tent's dimensions.
Therefore, he set this restriction,
setting an example himself.
If the solemn decree for discussion
has not yet been decided and implemented,
then who among later generations would dare commit a great impropriety?
Eventually, it would lead to modifying the foundation
and lightly changing old regulations.
This is the first reason I dare not violate.
During the Chuígǒng (垂拱) era of the Táng (唐) dynasty,
Gāozǔ (高祖), Tàizōng (太宗), and Gāozōng (高宗) were all offered sacrifices at the Jiaosì (郊祀).
In the eleventh year of Kāiyuán (開元),
following Zhāng Yuè's (張說) proposal,
Tàizōng and Gāozōng were removed.
During the Jǐngyòu (景祐) era of the Sòng (宋) dynasty,
Yìzǔ (藝祖), Tàizōng, and Zhēnzōng (真宗) were all offered sacrifices at the Jiaosì.
In the seventh year of Jiāyòu (嘉祐),
following Yáng Tián's (楊畋) proposal,
Tàizōng and Zhēnzōng were removed.
In our dynasty, during the Shùnzhì (順治) era,
the Dàxiǎngdiàn (大饗殿) held joint sacrifices,
but later that ritual was also abolished.
The great departed emperor worried that tens of thousands of years later,
some might cite the old precedents of Táng and Sòng
and rashly abolish the sacrifice.
Therefore, he issued an edict stating that only the Son of Heaven may discuss rituals;
if even increasing the number of paired deities is not permitted,
how could abolishing a sacrifice even arise?
This is the second reason I dare not violate.
Our dynasty governs with filial piety,
and posthumous decrees are particularly weighty.
Shèngzǔ (聖祖) dared not disobey the posthumous decree of Xiàozhuāng Wén Huánghòu (孝莊文皇后),
and did not dare to immediately inter her in the underground palace.
Rénzōng dared not disobey the posthumous decree of Gāozōng,
thus, despite his great accomplishments and glorious deeds,
his temple name did not receive the 'Zǔ' (祖) appellation.
If this can be violated,
where is the family law?
Furthermore, he repeatedly emphasized,
humbling himself,
and elevating his ancestors—
great filial piety and great deference,
a virtue unsurpassed throughout history.
This is the third reason I dare not violate.
Silently considering Your Majesty's profound filial heart,
not elevating him to the pairing would be a lack of ritual,
but hastily elevating him would be disobedience,
and would also bring future worries.
On a future day, during the Jiaosì,
if the emperor considers the departed instruction
and looks to the ten thousand generations,
he might be startled and uneasy,
and the ritual officials would have no excuse for blame."
The emperor largely approved of his words.
Later, he again broadly consulted the court for opinions,
and personally issued an imperial edict,
stating:
"The people of Zhōu (周) sacrificed to Hòujì at the Jiaosì.
During the Táng, Sòng, and Míng (明) dynasties,
sometimes three ancestors were jointly offered,
or several emperors were distributed to be paired.
In Our dynasty, throughout successive holy reigns,
none failed to offer the pairing.
However, as the number of paired deities increases,
the altar system has its fixed limits.
The late emperor's virtues and benevolence
are on par with those of the ancestral emperors;
it should be as requested.
After the Fùlǐ (祔禮) is completed,
he shall still be elevated to the pairing,
and at the same time, embodying the posthumous instruction,
the restriction shall be clearly shown.
From now on, the paired positions for the Jiaosì
shall be set at three Zǔ and five Zōng (宗),
to be a permanent standard."
Thus, in the summer of the second year of Xiánfēng (咸豐) for the great sacrifices at Yuánqiū (圜丘) and Fāngzé (方澤),
and in the spring of the third year for the Xīnqígǔ (上辛祈穀) sacrifice,
Xuānzōng (宣宗) was offered the pairing,
his position next to Gāozōng.
In the eleventh year,
the emperor passed away.
Mùzōng (穆宗) felt that regarding the grand Jiaopèi ceremony,
the posthumous decree had set it at three Zǔ and five Zōng,
which made his sacred heart uneasy.
So he convened his ministers for discussion,
and also respectfully sought counsel from the two empresses dowager.
Lǐ Qīnwáng Shìduó (禮親王世鐸) and others memorialized successively, saying:
"Ritual values appropriateness,
and filial piety demands upholding the will.
The posthumous instructions of two reigns
should be respectfully followed."
The emperor reluctantly agreed to this.
Consequently, Wénzōng's Jiaopèi was suspended.
In the first year of Tóngzhì (同治),

Zhāng Xīróng (張錫嶸), the provincial education commissioner of Yúnnán (雲南), citing the meaning of "strictly honoring the father and pairing him with Heaven" from the Míngtáng (明堂) chapter of the Xiàojīng (孝經),
suggested that in late autumn, the Dàxiǎngdiàn for sacrificing to Shàngdì should
offer Xiǎnhuángdì (顯皇帝) as a paired deity.
Shìduó and others further explained this using the Qīndìng Xiàojīng Yǎnyì (欽定孝經衍義),
stating that alternating offerings and joint sacrifices
were not appropriate according to ritual.
The discussion was then dropped.
Qígǔ (Prayer for Grain)
During the Shùnzhì reign, it was decreed that in the first month of the year, on the first xīn day, sacrifices would be offered to Shàngdì at the Dàxiǎngdiàn
to pray for grain for the people.
The Emperor would personally attend and perform the rites,
similar to the Winter Solstice ceremony.
However, there would be no subsidiary altars,
and no burning of firewood.
In the seventeenth year [of Shùnzhì],
an edict stated that for the grand ceremony of offering sacrifices to the Emperor (Shàngdì),
there should be no differences.
Thereafter, praying for grain and burning firewood became standard practice,
and the combined sacrifices to Shàngdì and all deities, formerly held at the Dàxiǎngdiàn, were moved to the Yuánqiū.
In the twenty-ninth year of Kāngxī,
Shèngzǔ personally composed the prayer text.
In the forty-eighth year,
the Emperor fell ill
and was unable to attend in person,
so an official was dispatched to act on his behalf.
At that time, jiāng, zhè, lǔ, and yù (regions) suffered successive floods and droughts,
so he still personally composed a prayer text to pray for them.
By custom,
if the first xīn day fell before the fifth day of the first month,
the next xīn day would be used instead.
In the eighth year of Yōngzhèng,
the first xīn day was the second day of the first month.
Because of the New Year's Day banquet, the [Ministry] officials
requested a ten-day postponement,
but this was not permitted.
Fasting and purification were observed as usual beforehand.
In the thirteenth year, on the tenth day of the first month, which was a xīn day,
spring had not yet begun.
The Emperor said:
"This is not in accordance with the principle of receiving the yang energy."
He commanded the ritual officials to deliberate.
They reported:
"According to the Lǐyuè Lìng (Ritual Monthly Ordinances),
on the day of Lìchūn (Beginning of Spring),
the Son of Heaven welcomes spring in the eastern suburbs,
and then prays to Shàngdì for grain.
This rite is originally held after Lìchūn.
We request to follow the precedent of using the next xīn day,
or the first xīn day after Lìchūn."
This was adopted.
In the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng,
héqīnwáng and others, considering the Dàxiǎng (Grand Sacrifice) as an autumn thanksgiving rite,
distinct in meaning from praying for grain,
requested a change of name.
The assembled officials also stated that it was not the original system of the Míngtáng,
and the continued use of the name Dàxiǎng
did not match the reality.
An imperial edict was issued,
changing the name to
"Qínián" (Prayer for Good Harvest).
For all Qígǔ ceremonies,
the imperial carriage proceeded to the Nánjiāo (Southern Suburbs).
Inside the Xītiānmén (West Heaven Gate), on the west side of the Shénlù (Spirit Path), the Emperor would descend from his palanquin,
enter the left gate of the Qínián (Temple),
and proceed to Huánggān Gōng (Palace of Imperial Heaven) to offer incense.
After the ceremony,
he would go to the Qínián Tán (Altar of Prayer for Good Harvest) to inspect the ritual positions,
and upon completion,
exit through the left gate, ascend the palanquin, and proceed to the Zhāigōng (Palace of Abstinence).
In the thirty-seventh year,
it was further stipulated that on the day before, the palanquin would enter the Xītiānmén,
and from the Zhāigōng, the Emperor would ride an imperial sedan chair eastward,
stopping at the left gate of the Xīzhuānchéng (Western Brick City).
He would then walk to the Huánggāndiàn (Hall of Imperial Heaven) to offer incense,
and upon completion,
return to the Zhāigōng,
while the qīnwáng would inspect the altar positions.
On the day of the sacrifice, he would leave the Zhāigōng,
ride a palanquin
to the center of the Yǒngdào (Avenue),
change to an imperial sedan chair,
and descend on the west side of the Shénlù.
From the Zhuānchéng, he would walk to the awning,
enter the left gate,
and the rites would be the same as those at the Yuánqiū.
In the forty-seventh year, on the fourth day of the first month, which was a xīn day,
the ritual officials previously requested to change it to the next xīn day for convenience.
The Emperor said:
"If the first xīn day falls before the third day of the first month,
it requires a year-long preceding period of fasting;
if it falls before the fourth day,
it is due to the empress dowager's birthday blessings.
The current situation is not like those past,
why should it be changed?
It shall remain the first xīn day,
and this shall be established as a precedent."
He further decreed:
"Praying for grain in the first month of spring
is to welcome the yang energy
and herald auspicious signs for agriculture.
Consulting the Classics and Commentaries,
it should be the first xīn day after Lìchūn,
not the first xīn day after Yuándàn (New Year's Day).
However, if it falls at the beginning of the month,
fasting should commence in the previous twelfth month.
However, the communal sacrifice at the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple)
is a major rite,
and worshipping gods in the palace
is a national custom.
If these are performed during the fasting period,
it seems not to be a way of exclusive and focused reverence."
Therefore, he referred it to the court officials for deliberation.
Soon after, they reported:
"The first xīn day should be determined based on the one occurring after Lìchūn.
Instead of using the xīn day in the twelfth month,
it is better to use the xīn day in the first month
to emphasize the beginning of the year.
If it falls before the third day,
then it should be changed to the next xīn day.
If it falls before the fourth day,
then one day of fasting is required,
and on that day, as the Emperor has not yet entered the Zhāigōng,
the palace worship ceremonies
will not interfere with each other.
There is no need to change the date."
This was approved.
In the fourth year of Xiánfēng,
during the Qígǔ ceremony,
the Emperor suffered from a chronic illness,
and he commanded the ritual officials to appropriately reduce the ceremonies.
Shìláng Sòng Jìn requested to follow the old practice of sending a substitute.
The Emperor said:
"This is not lightly altering old regulations;
one should respond to Heaven with sincerity, not with mere formalities.
This meaning should be understood by all."
Yúsì (Rain Sacrifice)
This had never been performed outside the Pass.
In the fourteenth year of Shùnzhì, due to a summer drought,
Shìzǔ first prayed for rain at the Yuánqiū.
Three days of fasting were observed beforehand.
Light-colored caps and robes were worn,
slaughtering was forbidden,
and legal proceedings were suspended.
On the appointed day,
the Emperor, in plain clothes, walked to the altar,
the path was not cleared,
and no imperial guard of honor was displayed.
On the altar were placed wine, fruits, incense, lamps, prayer silks, and cooked beef jerky and relish.
During the sacrifice, no music was played,
no auxiliary deities were set up,
no jade offerings were made,
and no blessed wine was drunk or sacrificial meat received.
The rest was as per the Winter Solstice sacrifice rituals.
For the Fāngzé, Shèjì, and various other altars for deities,
officials were dispatched to officiate the sacrifices.
After rain was received,
three days later,
officials were dispatched to offer thanksgiving sacrifices.
The establishment of the Emperor personally praying at the suburban altars began from this point.
Three years later, there was another drought.
An auspicious day was chosen, and fasting was observed.
The Emperor walked to the Nánjiāo
and personally offered a solemn prayer.
At that time, there was not a single cloud in the sky,
but soon after, there was heavy rain.
The thanksgiving sacrifice was performed as before.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī, due to a summer drought,
an edict commanded all officials to reflect and reform,
and the Ministry of Rites prayed for rain.
The following year,
the Emperor personally prayed.
Thereafter, personal sacrifice became customary.
In the twenty-sixth year,
he personally composed a prayer text and offered it,
and rain immediately fell.
He also once set up an altar within the palace,
kneeling in prayer for three days and nights,
eating only plain food daily.
Four days later,
he walked to the Tiāntán (Temple of Heaven) to pray,
and rain poured down suddenly.
He walked back to the palace,
his clothes and shoes soaked.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng,
Censor Xú Yǐshēng submitted a memorial, stating:
“The Spring and Autumn Annals tradition says: ‘When dragons appear, perform the yù ritual,
to pray for nourishing rain for all grains.’
The Book of Rites – Laws of Sacrifices says: ‘Yú Zōng,
sacrifices for floods and droughts.’
The Book of Rites – Monthly Ordinances says: ‘For the yù ritual,
the emperor uses grand music,
commands all counties to perform yù sacrifices,
and sacrifices to all dukes and high ministers who have benefited the people,
to pray for a bountiful harvest.
This is the regular yù ritual.’
The Rites of Zhōu says: ‘The Rice Cultivator [official] in times of severe drought [should] together perform yù and collect [taxes].’
The Spring and Autumn Annals records twenty-one yù rituals,
some of which were performed twice in a month,
indicating severe drought.
This is also performing yù due to drought.
Examining the meaning of yù, it is to sigh and pray for rain.
Its system [involved]
establishing an altar next to the southern suburban area,
hence the southern gate of Lǔ was called Yúmén.
It was abolished in the Western Hàn dynasty,
and prayers for drought were then offered at suburban altars and ancestral temples.
In the Jìn dynasty, in the Yǒnghé era, an altar was erected in the southern suburb.
Emperor Wǔ of Liáng first moved it to the east [of the capital]
and changed burning sacrifices to burying them in pits.
Emperor Tài of Táng restored the old system.
In the Sòng dynasty, in the first month of summer, sacrifices were offered to Shàngdì.
The Míng dynasty established an altar east of Tàiyuán Mén.
Once the system was established,
prayers were offered in times of drought.
Our dynasty has no altar for the yù sacrifice;
the ritual system seems incomplete.
An altar should be established according to the terrain,
to conform to the ancient meaning.”
The matter was referred to the ritual officials for deliberation.
The deliberation stated:
“When dragons appear in the first month of summer,
a day should be chosen to perform the regular yù ritual,
sacrificing at Huánqiū,
with the enshrined ancestors as co-sacrificers.
The four subsidiary altars
should all be in accordance with the rites.
If there is drought after the first month of summer,
then following the Táng system,
sacrifices should be offered to the gods of heaven and earth, the altars of grain and soil, and the ancestral temples.
Prayers should be offered every seven days.
If insufficient,
then prayers should still be offered separately.
If the drought is severe,
a grand yù ritual should be performed.
The old regulations stipulated
that prayers for rain must include distant sacrifices to the Four Seas;
this was now abolished.
For the grand yù ritual,
sixteen child dancers should be used,
dressed in dark robes,
divided into eight rows,
holding feather screens.
After three libations,
the music stops,
and then the dance is performed.
Eight chapters of the Imperial Poem ‘Yúnhàn’ are sung.
When finished,
the burning sacrifice is observed.
The rest is the same as the regular yù ritual.
For praying for clear weather after prolonged rain,
it is appropriate to follow the Spring and Autumn Annals tradition of beating drums and using sacrificial animals,
consulting the general study of the yíng sacrifice system,
beating drums and sacrificing a young animal.
For the yíng sacrifice at the state gate,
if the rain does not stop,
then drums are beaten and sacrificial animals are used at the altar of the soil god.
Separate prayers are abolished,
and Buddhist and Daoist officials erecting altars and chanting scriptures are stopped.
For the altars for ploughed fields in the provinces, prefectures, and counties
they should still follow the precedent of the fourth year of Yōngzhèng.
When the regular yù ritual is performed in the first month of summer,
if there is drought,
first sacrifice to the mountains and rivers within the jurisdiction,
then to the altars of grain and soil.
If there is excessive rain and a prayer for clear weather is needed,
it should follow the model of the capital.”
In the seventeenth year,
additional music for rain prayers and thanksgiving sacrifices was introduced.
In the twenty-fourth year,
when the regular yù ritual brought no rain,
the Emperor walked to the Shèjì Tán to pray,
still using jade.
In the sixth month, for the grand yù ritual,
he personally composed the prayer text
and established the ritual procedures.
The day before,
the Emperor, in ordinary attire, would inspect the prayer tablet,
go to the altar and fast overnight,
remove the imperial entourage,
and stop the music.
When leaving the palace, he would ride a horse,
and the accompanying ministers would follow in ordinary attire.
Upon reaching the southern suburb,
he would walk to the altar
and offer incense at the designated positions.
On the day of the sacrifice,
the Emperor, wearing a rain hat and plain clothes, would walk and pray,
and the accompanying officials would do likewise.
There would be no burning of firewood,
no presenting of sacrificial meat,
no drinking of blessed wine, or receiving of sacrificial meat.
After three libations,
the child dancers would perform the feather dance and sing poems,
then withdraw,
all according to the ceremony.
The Emperor would lead the officials in three bows,
remove the offerings,
and observe the burning sacrifice.
After the completion of the rites,
he would return to the palace.
In the thirty-seventh year,
the Emperor, due to old age,
ordered that the ritual procedures be appropriately reduced to resemble those of Huánqiū.
In the eighteenth year of Jiāqìng,
as the Imperial Astronomical Bureau frequently chose Lìxià for the yù ritual,
which greatly deviated from ancient meaning,
an imperial decree ordered that a propitious day be chosen a few days after Lìxià.
This was established as a precedent.
In the sixth month of the twelfth year of Dàoguāng, for the grand yù ritual,
he personally composed the prayer text,
reflecting on his own faults.
That evening, it rained.
Thanksgiving was offered according to the usual ceremony.
Censor Chén Zhuō requested a renewed earnest prayer.
The Emperor said:
“The Laws of Sacrifices include both prayers and thanksgiving.
To treat thanksgiving as prayer
is not in accordance with the rites.
Do not exceed the old system.”
That year, the empress, Dìng Huánghòu, performed the ritual offering to the First Silkworm Goddess.
A silkworm house was established,
and the spirit tablet of Xīlíngshì, the goddess of the First Silkworm, was reverently installed in advance.
On the appointed day, at the *chén* hour, first quarter,
the empress, in ceremonial robes, rode the phoenix palanquin out of the palace.
Upon reaching the left gate of the Inner Altar Enclosure, she dismounted
and entered the Hall of Robing,
followed by the imperial consorts and concubines.
After washing,
she ascended the central steps
and took her bowing position on the southern steps.
Six prostrations,
three kneelings,
and three bows were performed.
The ritual of giving thanks for good fortune and sacrificial meat was reduced by one (meaning two were performed instead of three).
No eulogy was read.
Wine was offered three times.
During all bows and kneelings,
the imperial consorts and concubines performed the rites below the altar.
The rest was according to the ceremony for offering to the God of Agriculture.
The ritual completed, she returned to the palace.
The next day,
the ritual of personally plucking mulberry leaves was performed.
Before this, a terrace had been built north of the mulberry fields,
with two "silkworm mothers" (cánmǔ)
and twenty-seven "silkworm women" (cánfù) appointed.
One superintendent (cángōnglìng) and one assistant superintendent (cángōngchéng) were in charge of the affair.
The empress observed a one-day vegetarian fast.
The imperial consorts, concubines, and others who participated in plucking mulberry leaves also completed their fasts.
On that day, at dawn,
the princesses and others of the mulberry attendance class waited inside the South Gate.
At the *sì* hour, first quarter,
the empress exited the palace,
followed by the imperial consorts and concubines,
and proceeded to the Western Park (Xīyuàn),
entering the Hall of Robing.
The ceremonial announcers guided the imperial consorts, concubines, princesses, and others to their positions for plucking mulberry leaves.
The master of ceremonies requested the empress to perform the rite.
She then went to the center north of the mulberry rows.
Two assistant ritual officers
presented a basket and a hook.
The empress held the hook in her right hand
and the basket in her left,
and walked eastward along the outside of the rows.
The palace eunuchs raised colored flags,
sounded gongs and drums,
and sang songs of mulberry plucking.
After the empress plucked three times, eastward and westward,
the singing ceased.
The assistant ritual officers reverently received the basket and hook.
The empress then went to the Mulberry Viewing Terrace (Guānsāngtái).
Subsequently, the imperial consorts, concubines, princesses, and others plucked five times,
and the noblewomen plucked nine times.
This concluded the plucking.
The silkworm mother knelt facing north.
The master of ceremonies held up the basket and handed it to her.
She reverently received it and withdrew.
She then chopped the leaves,
handed them to the silkworm women,
who scattered them onto the silkworm trays.
The empress then went to the Cocoon Hall (Jiǎnguǎn).
The ceremonial announcers guided the imperial consorts and concubines to perform their rites, which concluded.
They returned to the palace.
When the silkworm affairs were completed,
the silkworm mother and silkworm women selected cocoons and placed them in baskets to present.
A propitious day was chosen for the ritual of processing cocoons.
The empress again went to the altar and presided over the weaving room,
reeling three basins of silk.
She then personally distributed the raw silk to the silkworm women to conclude the matter.
Soon after, Assistant Minister Sāndé submitted a memorial stating:
"The personal silkworm ritual
is a grand ceremony unseen for generations.
I request that the regulations for the altar site and palace buildings,
and the date of the commencement and completion of construction,
be transmitted to the Imperial Historiography Academy (Shǐguǎn)."
An imperial edict approved it.
In the third month of the ninth year,
the empress first personally performed the silkworm ritual according to the established ceremony.
Later, Dìng Hòu did not personally attend,
but sent a consort to act on her behalf.
The rites were performed below the steps,
ascending and descending from the eastern steps.
She did not drink the blessed wine, receive the sacrificial meat,
nor participate in the accompanying sacrifices.
In the fourteenth year,
the Ministry of Rites requested that a consort be sent to perform the sacrifice.
At that time, the Imperial Noble Consort (Huáng Guìfēi) had not yet been formally established as the Empress (Zhèngwèi Zhōnggōng).
The Emperor issued an edict saying:
"The consort who acts on behalf
acts on behalf of the Empress.
If her position is not yet formally established,
what can she act on behalf of?"
Therefore, he ordered the ministers of the Imperial Household Department (Nèifǔ Dàchén) to perform the rites.
Only when the Empress was officially enthroned
did she personally attend the offerings.
Thereafter, sometimes she personally attended,
sometimes officials officiated,
or a consort acted on her behalf;
all were carried out by imperial decree.
As for the sacrifices offered by the provinces (xíngshěng),
only in the fifty-ninth year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that the annual sacrifices to the Silkworm God at the Xuānyuán Huángdì Temple in Zhèjiāng, and the Silkworm God shrines in Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu prefectures,
be included in the sacrificial canon.
The sacrificial vessels were to be the same as those for the God of Agriculture.
Deities of the Earth (Dìqí): In the early years of Shùnzhì,
after the Five Sacred Mountains (yuè), Four Lesser Mountains (zhèn), Four Seas (hǎi), and Four Rivers (dú) were assigned to receive accompanying sacrifices at the Altar of Square Earth (Fāngzé),
an Altar of Earth Deities was again built.
Located west of the Altar of Heaven (Tiāntán),
it also worshipped the famous mountains and great rivers of the realm.
In the third year,
it was decreed that one official be sent to the Northern Lesser Mountain (Běizhèn) and Northern Sea (Běihǎi) combined;
one to the Eastern Sacred Mountain (Dōngyuè), Eastern Lesser Mountain (Dōngzhèn), and Eastern Sea (Dōnghǎi);
one to the Western Sacred Mountain (Xīyuè), Western Lesser Mountain (Xīzhèn), and Jiāngdú River;
one to the Central Sacred Mountain (Zhōngyuè), Huáidú River, and Jìdú River;
one to the Northern Sacred Mountain (Běiyuè), Central Lesser Mountain (Zhōngzhèn), Western Sea (Xīhǎi), and Hédú River;
one to the Southern Lesser Mountain (Nánzhèn) and Southern Sea (Nánhǎi);
and one specifically to the Southern Sacred Mountain (Nányuè).
Before departure,
an official was first dispatched to observe a one-day fast,
perform two kneelings and six bows,
and conduct the three offerings ritual.
In the eighth year,
the mountain of Yǒnglíng Mausoleum in Xīngjīng was enfeoffed as Qǐyùn;
the mountain of Dōngjīng Mausoleum as Jìqìng;
the mountain of Fúlíng Mausoleum as Tiānzhù;
and the mountain of Zhāolíng Mausoleum as Lóngyè.
All were listed for sacrifice at the Altar of Earth (Dìtán).
In the sixteenth year,
the Dōngjīng Mausoleum was moved to be interred with Xīngjīng,
and the sacrifice to Jìqìng Mountain was abolished.
The following year,
following the suggestion of the ministers of rites,
the worship of Běiyuè was changed to Húnyuán.
In the second year of Kāngxī,
Fènglái Mountain was bestowed the name Chāngruì,
and it was also sacrificed to.
In the sixth year,
officials were sent to offer sacrifices as per the initial system.
Only Nánzhèn and Nánhǎi each had a separate official dispatched.
In the sixteenth year,
an imperial edict elevated the rank of the Chángbái Mountain God to be worshipped like the Five Sacred Mountains.
From that year, the seasonal distant sacrifices were never omitted.
In the twenty-fourth year,
during the Eastern Tour, the Tàiyuè Mountain was sacrificed to.
The Emperor's name was not written on the prayer tablet.
A fast was observed the day before.
The Grand Master of Ceremonies (Tàicháng) carried the prayer tablet, incense, silk, and wine cups;
the relevant officials prepared the sacrificial offerings and livestock.
On the appointed day, wearing the dragon robe,
the Emperor departed from his temporary palace.
Music was prepared but not played.
Upon reaching the temple, he dismounted from his palanquin.
He entered the central gate,
waited in the tent,
came out after washing,
and proceeded to the bowing position in the center of the hall,
performing two kneelings and six bows.
The presentation and offering were according to the usual ceremony.
He did not drink the blessed wine or receive the sacrificial meat.
The following year,
the worship of Běiyuè and Húntóng Jiāng was again changed.
After two years,
the distant sacrifices began.
In the first month of the thirty-fifth year,
to pray for blessings for the populace,
ministers were first dispatched to make separate sacrificial announcements
to the Five Sacred Mountains: namely Dōngyuè Tàishān, Nányuè Héngshān, Zhōngyuè Sōngshān, Xīyuè Huàshān,
and Běiyuè Héngshān.
The Five Lesser Mountains: namely Dōngzhèn Yíshān, Nánzhèn Kuàijīshān, Zhōngzhèn Huòshān, Xīzhèn Wúshān, and Běizhèn Yīwūlǘshān.
The Four Seas: namely Dōnghǎi, Nánhǎi, Xīhǎi, and Běihǎi.
The Four Rivers: namely Jiāngdú, Huáidú, Jìdú, and Hédú.
Also, Wūlā Chángbái Shān.
The comprehensive worship of rivers and lofty mountains began from this point.
The following year,
the northern desert was pacified,
and sacrifices were dispatched to the mountains, lesser mountains, seas, and rivers as before.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
Jiāngdú was bestowed the title Hánhé;
Hédú as Rùnyù;
Huáidú as Tōngyòu;
and Jìdú as Yǒnghuì.
Dōnghǎi was also bestowed as Xiǎnrén;
Nánhǎi as Zhāomíng;
Xīhǎi as Zhènghéng;
and Běihǎi as Chónglǐ.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
Tàiníng Mountain was enfeoffed as Yǒngníng,
and was appended to the sacrifices at the Altar of Earth, following precedent.
Wherever the emperor's inspection tours arrived,
sacrifices were offered at imperial tombs and temples.
During major celebrations,
sacrifices and announcements were made similarly.
In the twenty-first year of Kāngxī's reign,
after the suppression of the rebellion in Diān,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices,
distribute eulogies, incense, and silk,
and bestow one yellow umbrella,
two imperial standards, and two dragon banners.
All successful military campaigns
were celebrated with sacrifices according to the established rites.
In the twenty-third year,
during the Southern Tour,
passing through Jiāngníng,
the emperor visited the tomb of Míng Tàizǔ
and offered oblations.
He issued an edict to officials to inspect and
protect the tomb guards.
Five years later,
during an inspection of Kuàijī,
sacrifices were offered at Yǔ Líng.
The emperor's personal name was inscribed in the sacrificial text,
and the rite of three kneelings and nine prostrations was performed.
When the imperial cortege stopped in Jiāngníng,
sacrifices were offered at Míng Tàizǔ Líng,
following the same ceremony as for Yǔ.
During regular tours, when offering sacrifices at imperial tombs,
the ceremony was similar to that for temples,
typically involving two kneelings and six prostrations.
This was considered a special ceremony.
In the thirty-eighth year,
during another Southern Tour,
seeing that Míng Tàizǔ Líng was dilapidated,
an edict was issued, following the precedent of the Zhōu and Sòng dynasties,
to grant one official post to a descendant of the Míng imperial clan,
to ensure perpetual guardianship.
In the forty-second year,
during the Western Tour,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices at Nǚwā Shì Líng.
Upon arriving in Shǎn,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices at all tombs along the way.
Only for the sacrifices to Zhōu Wén and Wǔ was the emperor's personal name inscribed in the sacrificial text,
out of reverence for the Sages.
In the sixty-first year,
a posthumous edict was issued,
stating:
"Míng Tàizǔ rose from commoner status,
united the realm,
and his achievements surpassed those of the Hàn, Táng, and Sòng rulers.
In the latter years of his dynasty, there were natural disasters,
internal strife among officials,
and external banditry,
leading to the overthrow of the state.
Examining his successors,
none showed obvious signs of depravity or neglect;
it was likely due to the mandate of heaven.
Moreover, many of the institutional systems and structures
of our dynasty are based on theirs.
It is fitting to seek out their collateral branches,
grant them suitable noble ranks,
and enable them to perform sacrifices in spring and autumn."
Shìzōng succeeded to the throne,
and consequently granted Zhū Zhīlián the hereditary title of first-class Marquis.
He was dispatched to Jiāngníng and Chāngpíng to offer sacrifices,
and this became a regular annual practice thereafter.
There had historically been two tombs of Dì Yáo: one in Píngyáng
and one in Púzhōu.
Gǔlín, southeast of Púzhōu,
was the ancient Léizé.
In the first year of Qiánlóng's reign,
after repairs and rectification,
Gǔlín was designated as the original site,
while the oblations in Píngyáng continued as before.
The tombs and temples of Shénnóng and Yú Shùn were also repaired,
and tomb guardians were appointed.
In the eleventh year,
because Shǎnxī was an ancient capital region
with many imperial tombs,
local officials were ordered to investigate those not recorded in the collected statutes
and to have local authorities protect them.
In the thirteenth year,
the imperial carriage visited Qūfù,
offering oblations at Shàohào Líng.
Thereafter, all Eastern Tours included personal sacrifices by the emperor.
In the sixteenth year,
one descendant of the Sī clan was selected
and granted a hereditary eighth-rank official post
to oversee sacrifices at Yǔ Líng.
At Nǚwā Líng in Zhàochéng,
there was formerly a statue in the temple.
The emperor condemned its irreverence,
removed it,
and replaced it with a spirit tablet,
forbidding private prayers.
In the eighteenth year,
the emperor visited Tàilíng.
After the ceremony,
he proceeded to Fángshān to offer sacrifices at Jīn Tàizǔ Líng,
and bestowed official titles, ranks, and monetary gifts upon his descendant, Wányán Shì.
In the twenty-sixth year,
it was decreed that officials would be dispatched for imperial tombs, the Five Sacred Mountains and Four Great Rivers, and the shrines of the Former Master (Confucius).
In the forty-first year,
a Minister of Rites stated:
"Regarding Yáo's tomb mentioned in the standard histories,
the geography treatises of the two Hàn dynasties state: 'In Chéngyáng, Jìyīn Commandery, there is Yáo's mound and a spiritual terrace.'
Liú Xiàng's biography states 'buried in Jìyīn'.
The geography treatise of the Jìn dynasty states: 'Chéngyáng is where Shùn fished,
Yáo's mound is to the west.'
The rites treatise of the Sòng History states: 'It is in Gǔlínshān, east of Léizé in Púzhōu.'
The various accounts in Lǚ Shì Chūnqiū,
Dìwáng Shìjì,
the works cited in Shuǐjīngzhù,
Kuòdìzhì,
Tàipíng Huányǔjì,
Lù Shǐ,
and Jígǔlù,
all align with the standard histories.
Since the Yuánhé era of the Later Hàn,
sacrificial rites have been performed at that location.
Although Míng Hóngwǔ changed the place of sacrifice to Dōngpíng,
it remained within the territory of Lǔ, which is consistent.
In the early Qiánlóng period,
Gǔlín was designated as Yáo Líng,
correcting historical errors,
a practice that can be maintained for ten thousand generations.
Henceforth, sacrifices and announcements
shall follow the old regulations.
As for the other tomb in Píngyáng,
officials shall offer sacrifices there,
following the Dōngpíng precedent."
Subsequently,
Yǐn Jiāquán, a Grand Administrator of the Court of Judicial Review, requested to abolish the sacrifices to Míng Xuānzōng and Shìzōng.
The court deliberated and concluded:
"Xuānzōng had good governance,
and should not be criticized for one or two matters.
However, Shìzōng executed loyal officials and favored sycophants,
which is consistent with historical records,
so his sacrifices should be suspended."
This was agreed to.
In the forty-ninth year,
during a Southern Tour to Jiāngníng,
sacrifices were offered at Míng Tàizǔ Líng.
The Minister of Rites presented the ceremony,
involving three libations,
with one prostration for each libation.
The emperor ordered that the ceremony for Shàohào Líng be used instead,
involving two kneelings and six prostrations,
without the need for libations,
and this was established as a regulation.
In the fiftieth year,
the emperor visited Tāngshān.
Passing through Chāngpíng,
he personally offered libations at Míng Chéngzǔ Líng,
had it repaired,
and also rebuilt the sacrificial hall at Dìnglíng,
and reinstated the sacrifices for Shìzōng.
In the first year of Jiāqìng's reign,
the practice of dispatching officials was abolished,
and imperial edicts instructed the Deputy Military Governors and General Commanders of each province to perform the rites.
In the ninth year,
the emperor visited the Eastern Tombs.
Passing through Pánshān,
he inspected the Míng Tombs.
According to custom,
the emperor would go to Chánglíng to offer libations and oblations,
and dispatch princes and high officials to offer oblations at the other tombs.
On that day, Rénzōng personally went,
and after three libations,
he performed three prostrations.
The distant sacrifices to Yuán Tàizǔ and Shìzǔ Líng
were traditionally held outside Dèshèng Mén,
south of Chàngchūnyuán and Yuánmíngyuán.
The emperor considered this location inappropriate.
He ordered that thereafter, for celebratory ceremonies,
a new site be chosen north of Qīnghé and south of Chāngpíng to perform the rites.
In the sixteenth year of Dàoguāng's reign,
it was decreed that the spring and autumn sacrifices at the Míng Tombs
should be performed by the hereditary Marquis,
or, if unavailable, by the highest-ranking official of their clan,
or by a dispatched unranked minister,
making this a permanent system.
In the seventh year of Guāngxù's reign,
an edict was issued prohibiting the cultivation of land near the Míng Tombs.
Chuánxīn Diàn In the fourteenth year of Shùnzhì
emperor, the jīngyán (imperial lectures on the classics) were held following the Míng dynasty system.
Sacrifices were offered to the Former Teacher Kǒngzǐ at the Hóngdé Diàn.
In the tenth year of Kāngxī, the practice was resumed,
with officials dispatched to offer sacrifices.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Chuánxīn Diàn was designed and built,
located to the east of the Wénhuá Diàn.
In the center, offerings were made to the Imperial Teachers Fúxī, Shénnóng, and Xuānyuán;
the Emperor Teachers Yáo and Shùn;
and the Kingly Teachers Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ.
They faced south.
To the east was Zhōu Gōng,
to the west Kǒngzǐ.
The sacrificial vessels were on par with those at imperial ancestral temples.
Each year, when the Emperor was to attend the jīngyán,
a Grand Secretary was dispatched beforehand to respectfully announce it.
Sacrifices at the Chuánxīn Diàn began from this time.
The following year,
when the Emperor was about to attend the jīngyán,
an edict stated:
"The former sages and former teachers,
who transmitted the Way and established the lineage,
shine like the sun and stars.
I, though distantly, inherit their philosophy of mind,
and emulate it without ceasing,
gradually approaching spontaneity.
Applying this to governance and education,
I hope not to deviate from the sages and worthies.
I shall personally go and perform the rites."
On the day of sacrifice, incense and candles were prepared,
one xíng (a type of sacrificial vessel),
two biān and two dòu (sacrificial vessels) each,
and silk and jǔe (wine cups) were offered.
The prayer was read,
and thus the sacrifice was performed.
The Emperor wore the gǔnfú (ceremonial robes)
and performed the two kneelings and six bows ritual.
The Crown Prince, when attending lectures in spring and autumn,
also first offered sacrifices and made announcements.
On the first and fifteenth day of each month, the Tàicháng Qīng was dispatched to offer wine, fruit, and incense.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was decided that the respectful announcement ritual would be performed on this very day,
and it became a regular practice thereafter.
In the sixth year of Qiánlóng,
the Emperor personally sacrificed at the Chuánxīn Diàn.
In the sixtieth year, upon abdicating,
he performed it again.
During the reigns of Rénzōng, Xuānzōng, and Wénzōng,
they all personally went to make respectful announcements.
Later, the practice was discontinued.
The regulations for the jīngyán
are detailed elsewhere in the Jiālǐ (Auspicious Rites).
Zhìshèng Xiānshī Kǒngzǐ In the first year of Chóngdé,
a temple was built in Shèngjīng,
and Grand Secretary Fàn Wénchéng was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Yánzǐ, Zēngzǐ, Zǐsī, and Mèngzǐ were appointed as co-worshippers.
It was decided that the Shìdiàn ritual would be performed on the dìng day of the middle month of spring and autumn.
Shìzǔ established the grand capital,
making the Guózǐjiān in the capital the imperial academy,
and erected a Wénmiào (Confucian Temple).
Its layout was standard,
facing south.
The Xīchíjìng Mén faced west.
In front was the Dàchéng Mén,
inside which were twenty-four halberds arranged in rows,
ten stone drums,
and eleven rooms each in the east and west halls,
facing north.
The Dàchéng Diàn had seven rooms,
with three stepped exits.
The two side corridors each had nineteen rooms,
with east and west arranged rooms like those inside the gate,
facing south.
The main hall of the Qǐshèng Cí had five rooms,
and the two side corridors each had three rooms.

The liáolú (incinerator), yìkǎn (burial pit), shénkù (spirit storehouse), shénchú (spirit kitchen), zǎishēngtíng (slaughtering pavilion), and jǐngtíng (well pavilion) were all built according to regulations.
In the second year of Shùnzhì,
it was decreed that Kǒngzǐ be referred to as Dàchéng Zhìshèng Wénxuān Xiānshī Kǒngzǐ.
On the shàngdìng day of spring and autumn,
one Grand Secretary was dispatched to perform the sacrifice,
two Hanlin officials made sub-offerings,
and the Jìjiǔ sacrificed at the Qǐshèng Cí,
with former worthies and former scholars joining as co-worshippers.
If there was a reason,
it was changed to the cìdìng or xiàdìng day.
On the first day of the month,
the Jìjiǔ performed the Shìcài ritual,
setting out wine, celery, jujubes, and chestnuts.
The Four Co-Worshippers of the Former Teacher received three offerings,
the Ten Sages in the two side corridors,
and the Jiānchéng and others made sub-offerings.
On the fifteenth day of the month,
the Sīyè offered incense.
In the center, the Former Teacher Kǒngzǐ was worshipped,
facing south.
The Four Co-Worshippers were: Fùshèng Yánzǐ,
Zōngshèng Zēngzǐ,
Shùshèng Zǐsīzǐ,
and Yàshèng Mèngzǐ.
The Ten Sages were: Mǐnzǐ Sǔn, Rǎnzǐ Yōng, Duānmùzǐ Cì, Zhòngzǐ Yóu, Bǔzǐ Shāng, Rǎnzǐ Gēng, Zǎizǐ Yǔ, Rǎnzǐ Qiú, Yánzǐ Yǎn, and Zhuānsūn Zǐshī,
all facing east and west.

Those co-worshipped in the west corridor were: Former Worthies Dàntái Miè míng, Mì Bùqí, Yuán Xiàn, Gōngyě Cháng, Nángōng Shì, Gōng Āi, Shāng Qú, Gāo Chái, Qīdiāo Kāi, Fán Xū, Sīmǎ Gēng, Shāng Zé, Yǒu Ruò, Liáng Zhān, Wūmǎ Shī, Rǎn Rú, Yán Xīn, Bó Qián, Cáo Xù, Rǎn Jì, Gōngsūn Lóng, Qīdiāo Túwén, Qín Shāng, Qīdiāo Duō, Yán Gāo, Gōngxī Chì, Rángsì Chì, Rèn Bùqí, Shízuò Shǔ, Gōngliáng Rú, Gōngxià Shǒu, Gōngjiān Dìng, Hòu Chù, Kuàng Dān, Xīróng Diǎn, Hǎnfù Hēi, Yán Zǔ, Róng Qí, Jùjǐng Jiāng, Zuǒrén Yǐng, Qín Zǔ, Zhèng Guó, Xiàn Chéng, Yuán Kàng, Gōngzǔ Jùzī, Lián Jié, Yān Jí, Shúzhòng Huì, Yuè Kài, Gōngxī YúRú, Dí Hēi, Guī Xùn, Kǒng Zhōng, Chén Kàng, Gōngxī Diǎn, Qín Zhāng, Yán Zhīpú, Bùshū Chéng, Shī Zhīcháng, Qín Fēi, Shēn Chéng, Yán Kuài, Zuǒqiū Míng, Zhōu Dūnyí, Zhāng Zài, Chéng Hào, Chéng Yí, Shào Yōng, Zhū Xī,
totaling sixty-nine people;

Former Scholars Gōngyáng Gāo, Gǔliáng Chì, Fú Shèng, Kǒng Ānguó, Máo Cháng, Hòu Cāng, Gāotáng Shēng, Dǒng Zhòngshū, Wáng Tōng, Dù Zǐchūn, Hán Yù, Sīmǎ Guāng, Ōuyáng Xiū, Hú Ānguó, Yáng Shí, Lǚ Zǔqiān, Luó Cóngyàn, Cài Chén, Lǐ Tóng, Lù Jiǔyuān, Zhāng Shì, Xǔ Héng, Zhēn Déxiù, Wáng Shǒurén, Chén Xiànzhāng, Xuē Xuān, Hú JūRén,
totaling twenty-eight people.
In the Qǐshèng Cí,
the Qǐshèng Gōng's tablet was in the center,
facing south.
The co-worshippers' tablets were: Former Worthies Yán Wúyáo, Zēng Diǎn, Kǒng Lǐ, Mèngsūn Shì,
facing east and west.
Those co-worshipped in the two side corridors were: Former Scholars Zhōu Fǔchéng, Chéng Xiàng, Cài Yuándìng, Zhū Sōng.
In the ninth year,
Shìzǔ inspected the academy
and performed the Shìdiàn ritual for the Former Teacher.
Kings, dukes, and all officials
fasted and attended the sacrifice.
Beforehand,
the Yǎnshèng Gōng led the hereditary Wǔjīng Bóshì of the Kǒng, Yán, Zēng, Mèng, and Zhòng clans,
five members of the Kǒng clan,
and two members each of the Yán, Zēng, Mèng, and Zhòng clans,
to the capital.
All descendants of the five clans who held official posts in the capital also participated in the sacrifice.
That year, one Nánzōng Bóshì of the Kǒng clan was appointed
to oversee sacrifices in Xī'ān.
In the fourteenth year,
Investigating Censor Zhāng Wénguāng stated:
"Conferring posthumous princely titles surely misrepresents the sage,
and the four characters 'Dàchéng Wénxuān'
are also insufficient to fully express the sage.
It is fitting to change the inscription to 'Zhìshèng Xiānshī'."
This was adopted.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī,
the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè music was bestowed upon the imperial academy.
In the twenty-second year,
the Emperor personally inscribed the characters
"Wànshì Shībiǎo"
on a plaque, which was hung in the Dàchéng Diàn
and also distributed to educational institutions in the provinces.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Emperor composed a preface for the praise of Kǒngzǐ and four praises for Yán, Zēng, Sī, and Mèng,
which were carved into stone.
Their texts were proclaimed and distributed to the provinces.
In the fifty-first year,
because Zhūzǐ greatly illuminated the sagely learning,
he was promoted to the ranks of the Ten Sages,
his position after Bǔzǐ.
Soon after, Sòng dynasty scholar Fàn Zhòngyān was ordered to be co-worshipped.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
an edict posthumously enfeoffed Kǒngzǐ's five ancestors with princely titles.
Thus, Jīnmùfù Gōng was titled Zhàoshèng,
Qífù Gōng as Yùshèng,
Fángshú Gōng as Yíshèng,
Bóxià Gōng as Chāngshèng,
and Shúliáng Gōng as Qǐshèng.
The Qǐshèng Cí was renamed Chóngshèng.
Zhàoshèng's tablet was in the center,
Yùshèng to the left,
Yíshèng to the right,
Chāngshèng next to the left,
and Qǐshèng next to the right,
all facing south.
The co-worshippers remained as before.
In the second year,
during the academy inspection and Shìdiàn ritual,
Shìzōng noted that among the worthies enshrined in the temple courtyard,
some who had been removed should be reinstated,
or some who were missing should be added,
and which ones should be enshrined in the Chóngshèng Cí.
He ordered court officials to deliberate.
When the deliberations were presented,
the Emperor said:
"Dài Shèng and Hé Xiū are not pure scholars;
Zhèng Zhòng, Lú Zhí, Fú Qián, and Fàn Níng adhered to a single school of thought,
and are somewhat inferior to the pure and profound Zhèng Kāngchéng.
As for the other scholars, whether they are truly suitable
should be re-examined and decided."
The revised deliberations were presented.
Thus, six individuals were reinstated for worship: Lín Fàng, Qú Yuàn, Qín Rǎn, Yán Hé, Zhèng Kāngchéng, and Fàn Níng.
Twenty individuals were added for worship: Kǒngzǐ's disciples Xiàn Dǎn, Mù Pí;
Mèngzǐ's disciples Yuèzhèngzǐ, Gōngdūzǐ, Wàn Zhāng, Gōngsūn Chǒu;
from Hàn, Zhūgě Liàng;
from Sòng, Yǐn Tūn, Wèi Liǎowēng, Huáng Gàn, Chén Chún, Hé Jī, Wáng Bǎi, Zhào Fù;
from Yuán, Jīn Lǚxiáng, Xǔ Qiān, Chén Hào;
from Míng, Luó Qīnshùn, Cài Qīng;
and from the current dynasty, Lù Lóngqí.
One person was inducted into the Chóngshèng Cí:
Sòng dynasty scholar Héngqú Zhāng Zǐdí.
Soon after, to avoid the given name of the Former Teacher,
the character
"Yì"
was added to form
"Qiū."
The place name was to be pronounced like "qī,"
except for the character
"Huánqiū,"
which remained unchanged.
In the eighth month of the fourth year, on the *Zhòngdīng* (middle *dīng*) day,
Shìzōng personally attended the *shìdiàn* ceremony.
Initially,
there was no system for personal imperial sacrifice during the two spring and autumn rites;
it was at this time that it was first established.
The sacrificial animals (*xīshēng*) and food vessels (*biāndòu*) were in accordance with the *Dīng* sacrifice.
The ritual involved two kneels and six bows,
offering silk and presenting wine goblets.
The standing position was changed to kneeling.
The eulogy was still read,
but the Emperor did not partake of the blessed wine (*yǐnfú*) or receive the sacrificial meat (*shòuzuò*).
The Shàngshū offered sacrifices to the Four Consorts (Sìpèi),
while the Shìláng offered sacrifices to the Eleven Sages (Shíyīzhé) in the two side halls (*liǎngwǔ*).
The following year,
the 27th day of the eighth month was designated as the birth anniversary of the Former Teacher (Xiānshī).
Officials, commoners, and soldiers
were to fast for one day,
making it a permanent custom.
Another year later,
the imperial inscription
"Unprecedented Since the Creation of Mankind"
(*Shēngmín Wèiyǒu*) plaque
was bestowed and hung as per previous practice.
In the eleventh year,
the ritual for the personal imperial sacrifice was established:
three incensings in front of the incense table.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
an edict ordered the replacement of the yellow tiles on the Dàchéng Diàn and its gate
with green tiles for the Chóngshèng Cí.
The sacrifice to the Yuán dynasty Confucian scholar Wú Chéng was reinstated.
In the third year,
Yǒu Zǐruò was elevated to the Twelve Sages (Shí'èrzhé),
his position after Bǔ Zǐshāng.
Zhū Zǐ’s position was moved after Zhuānsūn Zǐshī.
That year, on the *Shàngdīng* (first *dīng*) day,
the Emperor personally inspected the academy and attended the *shìdiàn*.
He departed in a solemn carriage,
descending from the palanquin outside the temple gate.
Upon entering the central gate,
he waited in the main antechamber (*dàcì*),
then went out to wash his hands.
He entered the Dàchéng central gate,
ascended the steps,
offered incense three times,
and performed the two kneels and six bows ceremony.
Officials in charge then performed the offerings in sequence.
In the main hall,
the officiating sacrifice officials ascended the east and west steps,
entered the left and right gates,
and proceeded to the altars of the Four Consorts and Twelve Sages.
The officiating sacrifice officials in the two side halls proceeded separately to the altars of the Former Worthies (Xiānxián) and Former Confucian Scholars (Xiānrú).
After offering incense and making the libations,
the Emperor bowed three times.
The second offering (*yàxiàn*) and final offering (*zhōngxiàn*) followed the initial procedure.
The use of three offerings for the *shìdiàn* began here.
For sacrifices at the Chóngshèng Cí,
the bowing position was below the steps.
The officiating sacrifice official ascended the east steps,
entered the left gate,
and, after offering incense at the altar of the Founding Sage King (Zhàoshèngwáng),
the officiating sacrifice officials ascended the east and west steps,
entered the left and right gates,
and proceeded separately to the altars of the consorts and the accompanying altars in the two side halls to offer incense,
performing three kneels and nine bows.
The offering of silk and reading of the eulogy
were performed during the first offering.
A total of three offerings
completed the ceremony.
From then on, this became the regular format.
In the eighteenth year,
the sacrificial items for the *Dīng* sacrifice at the Imperial Academy (Tàixué) were revised
to use a "minor animal sacrifice" (*shàoláo*) according to the Qùelǐ precedent.
The Twelve Sages had one table each on the east and west,
and the two side halls had three tables each.
For the Four Consorts in the Chóngshèng Cí,
the two side halls had one table each on the east and west.
The altars of the Twelve Sages each had one piece of silk,
with two baskets (*fěi*) collectively for the east and west.
For the separate offerings,
in the main hall, east and west,
officials from the Hànlín Academy each presented three goblets.
In the west hall, four officials from the Guózǐjiàn
collectively presented three goblets.
For the Twelve Sages in the two side halls, students undergoing training (*yìyè zhūshēng*) were used to present goblets.
The order of positions in the two side halls was determined,
arranged according to historical accounts and chronological sequence.
In the thirty-third year,
the renovation of the Temple of Literature (Wénmiào) was completed,
and the main gate's
"Temple of the Former Teacher"
(*Xiānshī Miào*) plaque was enlarged.
The main hall and its gate were named
"Great Accomplishment" (*Dàchéng*).
The Emperor personally inscribed the plaque
and composed a stele inscription.
Ten vessels were selected from the imperial collection of *zūn* and *yí*
— one *xīzūn*, *léiwénhú*, *zǐjué*, *nèiyányǒu*, *kānghóujué*, *dǐngméngguǐ*, *léiwéngū*, *zhàozhòngguǐ*, *sùxǐ*, and *xīshǒuléi* each —
and bestowed upon the imperial academy (Chéngjūn).
In the fiftieth year,
the new Bìyōng was completed,
and the Emperor personally delivered lectures,
with the *shìdiàn* ceremony performed as before.
During the Jiāqìng period,
the ceremony of imperial visit to the Bìyōng was held twice.
In the second year of Dàoguāng, an edict granted Lú Zōngzhōu,
in the third year Tāng Bīn,
in the fifth year Huáng Dàozhōu,
in the sixth year Lù Zhì and Lǚ Kūn,
and in the eighth year Sūn Qífēng,
the privilege of being enshrined among the Former Confucian Scholars.
In the eighth year,
Wáng Zèngfāng, the Húběi Education Commissioner, requested the enshrinement of Chén Liáng.
The Emperor rejected the proposal, stating that
his words and deeds were not verifiable.
Not long after,
Censor Niú Jiàn made a similar request for Lǐ Yóng.
The Board's discussion was favorable,
but the Emperor denounced it.
In the sixteenth year,
an edict decreed that Kǒngzǐ should not be enshrined in the same temple as Buddhist and Daoist figures.
Thereafter, Sòng minister Wén Tiānxiáng and Sòng Confucian scholar Xiè Liángzuǒ were again included in the sacrifices.
In the early Xiánfēng period,
