Former Worthy Gōngmíng Yí,
Sòng ministers Lǐ Gāng and Hán Qí were added to the sacrifices.
In the third year, in the second month, on the *Shàngdīng* day,
the *shìcài* ceremony was performed.
Six days later,
the Emperor lectured at the Bìyōng.
From the descendants of sages and worthies
to the students of the Imperial Academy,
a multitude gathered around the bridge to listen.
In the seventh year,
Mèng Pí, Kǒngzǐ's elder brother, was added to the sacrifices in the Chóngshèng Cí.
Former Worthy Gōngsūn Qiáo was added to the sacrifices in the Sacred Temple (Shèngmiào).
Sòng minister Lù Xiùfū and Míng Confucian scholar Cáo Duān were also included.
In the tenth year,
following the advice of the ritual officials,
the criterion for the grand enshrinement ceremony
was determined to be the elucidation of sacred learning and the transmission of the Daoist tradition.
Others, according to their conduct,
were placed in the categories of Loyal and Righteous (*Zhōngyì*), Famous Officials (*Mínghuàn*), or Local Worthies (*Xiāngxián*).
As for distinguished ministers and great輔,
those already enshrined in the Imperial Ancestral Temples (*Dìwáng Miào*)
should not be deliberated upon again.
In the second year of Tóngzhì,
Censor Líu Yùnán argued that the new regulations for accompanying sacrifices were too strict,
preventing figures like the Sòng Confucian scholar Huáng Zhèn from being included.
He feared this might cause distress to public sentiment and customs.
The Emperor criticized him for being pedantic and mistaken.
That year, Rǔ people Máo Hēng,
Míng scholars Lǚ Liú and Fāng Xiàorú were also included in the sacrifices.
Consequently, the order of added sacrificial positions was revised,
each arranged according to historical era.

Then Gōngyáng Gāo, Fú Shèng, Máo Hēng, Kǒng Ānguó, Hòu Cāng, Zhèng Kāngchéng, Fàn Níng, Lù Zhì, Fàn Zhòngyān, Ōuyáng Xiū, Sīmǎ Guāng, Xiè Liángzuǒ, Luó Cóngyàn, Lǐ Gāng, Zhāng Shì, Lù Jiǔyuān, Chén Chún, Zhēn Déxiù, Hé Jī, Wén Tiānxiáng, Zhào Fù, Jīn Lǚxiáng, Chén Hào, Fāng Xiàorú, Xuē Xuān, Hú Jūfāng, Luó Qīnshùn, Lǚ Kūn, Líu Zōngzhōu, Sūn Qífēng, and Lù Lóngqí were placed in the east hall.

Gǔliáng Chì, Gāotáng Shēng, Dǒng Zhòngshū, Máo Cháng, Dù Zǐchūn, Zhūgé Liàng, Wáng Tōng, Hán Yù, Hú Yuàn, Hán Qí, Yáng Shí, Yǐn Tūn, Hú Ānguó, Lǐ Tóng, Lǚ Zǔqiān, Huáng Gàn, Cài Chén, Wèi Liǎowēng, Wáng Bó, Lù Xiùfū, Xǔ Héng, Wú Chéng, Xǔ Qiān, Cáo Duān, Chén Xiànzhāng, Cài Qīng, Wáng Shǒurén, Lǚ Kūn, Huáng Dàozhōu, and Tāng Bīn were placed in the west hall,
and their portraits were drawn and distributed to all provinces.
In the seventh year,
Sòng minister Yuán Xiè and Former Confucian scholar Zhāng Lǚxiáng were added to the sacrifices.
In the first year of Guāngxù,
Former Confucian scholar Lù Shìyí was added.
Thereafter, Hàn Confucian scholar Xǔ Shèn, Liú Dé the King Xiàn of Héjiān,
Former Confucian scholar Zhāng Bóxíng,
and Sòng Confucian scholars Fǔ Guǎng, Yóu Zuò, and Lǚ Dàlín were all enshrined.
In the twentieth year, in the middle of autumn, on the *Shàngdīng* day,
the Emperor personally attended the *shìdiàn*,
and the ritual of partaking of the blessed wine and receiving the sacrificial meat was reinstated.
In the twelfth month of the thirty-second year, winter,
the worship was elevated to a Grand Sacrifice.
Regarding the sacrificial rites for the Former Sage,
since the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì periods of the Míng dynasty,
it had already been set at eight rows of dancers (bāyì),
and twelve biān and dòu vessels.
In the ninth year of Jiājìng,
following Zhāng Cōng's suggestion,
it was first demoted to a Medium Sacrifice.
During the Kāngxī era,
Wang Shìzhēn, the Libationer, once requested to consider adopting the Chénghuà and Hóngzhì systems,
but the deliberation was long and not implemented.
At this point, the Emperor ordered the officials of rites to prepare a ceremony and submit it.
They reported:
"Kǒngzǐ’s virtue rivals the two great [heaven and earth],
his Way surpasses that of a hundred kings.
From the Hàn to the Míng dynasties,
the ceremonies were often incomplete.
Our Holy Ancestor (Shèngzǔ) performed the Shìdiàn (Sake-offering ceremony) at Quèlǐ,
with three kowtows and nine prostrations,
and a curved handle yellow canopy
left for the temple courtyard.
Shìzōng attended the Yǒng (Imperial College),
only stating he was 'going to the school.'
He offered incense, silk, and wine before the altar,
kneeling but not standing.
Yellow tiles adorned the temple,
and he was enfeoffed as king in five generations.
On his birthday, a fast was observed,
and his sacred name was respectfully avoided.
Gāozōng's Shìdiàn
followed the methods of Shèngzǔ,
personally performing three offerings,
establishing it as a regular ceremony.
The veneration of his virtue and recognition of his merits
far surpassed previous generations.
This already subtly implied the intention to elevate it to a Grand Sacrifice.
Shìzōng’s imperial decree stated: 'The Way of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, and Wǔ
relies on Kǒngzǐ not to fall into disuse.
The Book of Lúnyǔ,
in particular, is essential for daily use,
enabling the moral principles of myriad generations to be clear,
names to be distinguished,
people's hearts to be upright,
and customs to be virtuous.
This is why he is said to be 'unique among all living beings.'
The imperial instructions are resplendent,
consistent from beginning to end.
Although academic factions are currently diverse,
the display of reverence
is sufficient to achieve the great effect of rectifying the classics and uplifting the people."
After the memorial was submitted,
the Wénmiào (Confucian Temple) was accordingly re-roofed with yellow tiles,
eight rows of dancers were used for the music,
and military dances were added.
The Emperor personally attended the Shìdiàn.
When there was an event, a prince was sent as a substitute.
Grand Secretaries (Dàxuéshì) were used for the separate offerings to the Four Co-Worshipped,
and Ministers (Shàngshū) were used for the Twelve Sages in the two side halls.
On the day of the sacrifice, one entered through the left gate of the Dàchéng Hall,
ascended the steps, and entered through the left gate of the main hall.
The three kowtows and nine prostrations were performed.
Incense was offered,
and silk and wine were presented while kneeling.
The three offerings were all personally performed.
The departure was also the same.
When a substitute was sent, Ministers (Shàngshū) were used for the Four Co-Worshipped,
and Vice Ministers (Shìláng) for the rest.
They entered and exited through the right gate,
and did not drink the blessed wine or partake of the sacrificial meat.
The Chóngshèng Cí (Temple for Honoring Sages) was originally designated for a prince to preside over the sacrifice.
If substituting for the Shìdiàn,
then a Grand Secretary was used for it.
Vice Ministers were used for the separate offerings to the co-worshipped figures,
and Grand Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé Xuéshì) for the western side hall.
The rest remained as before.
In the thirty-fourth year,
the system of nine bays, three steps, and five platforms for the Wénmiào was established.
Censor Zhào Qǐlín requested that Wáng Fūzhī, Huáng Zōngxī, and Gù Yánwǔ be admitted for co-worship.
This was sent to the Board for deliberation.
Previously, acting Vice Minister of the Board of Rites Guō Sōngtāo and Húběi Education Commissioner Kǒng Xiánglín had requested Fūzhī for co-worship,
and Jiāngxī Education Commissioner Chén Bǎochēn had requested Zōngxī and Yánwǔ for co-worship,
but both were rejected.
At this time, the Board deliberated and stated:
"These three men lived during the late Míng dynasty,
and resolutely championed profound study of the classics for the nation.
Their moral character and scholarship,
and their reverence for the Way, were practiced concurrently.
However, Fūzhī’s Huáng Shū
consisted of various chapters,
whose purport was based on the Chūnqiū;
Zōngxī’s Míngyí Dàifǎng Lù,
with its chapters 'Yuán Jūn' and 'Yuán Chén,'
derived its meaning from Mèngzǐ,
and seemed somewhat extreme.
Only Yánwǔ was truly pure in his purity.
Yánwǔ should be approved for co-worship,
while Fūzhī and Zōngxī await a final decision."
The Emperor ordered that all three be co-worshipped.
At the Wénmiào in Quèlǐ,
when there was an event, a sacrificial proclamation was made,
following the previous sacrificial proclamation text.
The spring and autumn sacrifices were the same as those at the Imperial Academy (Tàixué).
During the Kāngxī era,
Shèngzǔ personally performed the sacrifice during his eastern tour,
and the Board of Rites prepared the ceremony.
On the day after his stop,
the Emperor wore the imperial robe (lónggǔn),
and the imperial procession's regalia was fully displayed.
He performed two kowtows and six prostrations.
Officials were dispatched to offer separate sacrifices to the co-worshipped figures, the Ten Sages, the two side halls, and the Qǐshèng Cí (Temple for Enlightenment and Sageliness).
All accompanying officials,
civil officials from Prefect (Zhīfǔ) and above, military officials from Brigadier General (Fùjiàng) and above,
the Duke Yǎnshèng, and the employed descendants of various clans,
all attended the sacrifice.
The Emperor's heart was still uneasy,
and he ordered further deliberation.
Soon after, it was decided that both welcoming and sending off the spirits would involve three kowtows and nine prostrations,
with only minor differences in the musical pieces compared to the Imperial Academy.
The Taichang Temple musicians and dancers could be sent in advance to practice.
The Emperor personally composed the prayer text.
On the day of the sacrifice, he proceeded to the temple.
Upon reaching the front of the Kuíwén Gé (Pavilion of the Star of Literature), he dismounted from his carriage.
He rested briefly at the fasting place,
then exited from the main hall,
entered the Dàchéng Mén (Gate of Great Accomplishment),
ascended the main hall, and after completing the Shìdiàn,
he lectured on books in the Shīlǐ Táng (Hall of Poetry and Rites).
After the ceremony,
he inspected the carriages, clothing, and ritual vessels in the temple courtyard.
He changed into his ordinary attire
and rode to Kǒnglín (Confucius Forest),
where he knelt to pour wine,
three libations,
and performed three prostrations.
Silver and silk were bestowed upon the Duke Yǎnshèng and others, varying by rank.
The curved handle yellow canopy was left displayed in the temple courtyard.
The land of Kǒnglín was expanded,
and its taxes were exempted.
A temple stele was erected,
with the Emperor's calligraphy carved into the stone.
A temple for Zǐsīzǐ (Zisi) was also built,
modeled after the temples of Yán, Zēng, and Mèng.
In the thirty-second year,
the renovation of the Wénmiào was completed.
The Imperial Princes went to offer sacrifices,
performing the rites at the Xìngtán (Apricot Altar).
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
the Qǔfù temple suffered a disaster.
Officials were dispatched to Quèlǐ to offer sacrifices and comfort.
An imperial edict ordered ministers to rebuild it,
and also commanded the Quèlǐ司樂 (Director of Music) to send people to the Tàicháng (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) to learn music and dance.
The robes and hats were all to be made according to the Tàixué style.
In the eighth year,
the temple was completed,
with yellow tiles and painted beams,
all modeled after palace architecture.
All the dēng, guǐ, fǔ, xíng, biān, dòu, zūn, and jué vessels
were bestowed from above.
Steles were erected according to old custom.
A special imperial edict commanded the Fifth Imperial Prince to go and perform the sacrifice.
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng,
the musical pieces for the sacred temple at Quèlǐ were finalized.
In the twenty-third year,
the eastern tour and personal sacrifice followed the previous system.
Ministers were dispatched to sacrifice at the dedicated temples of Yán, Zēng, Sī, and Mèng.
The Emperor's eulogies for the Four Worthies were carved into stone.
Regarding the musical instruments required for the Shèngjīng school palace,
it was only in the Qiánlóng era that the Prefect (Fǔyǐn) was ordered to construct them according to the imperial ritual vessel illustrations.
The bózhōng (large bell) and tèqìng (special chime stone)
were made in the inner court,
and specially bestowed upon the Imperial Academy and school palaces in various provinces.
The Vice Prefect (Fǔchéng) was also ordered to select dancers who were skilled in music to be sent to the Tàicháng to practice the dances.
Thereafter, because Rèhé became a place for seasonal imperial tours,
schools (hóngxù) were established there.
The altar arrangement in the Dàchéng Hall was set according to the Tàixué style,
and the sacrificial and musical instruments were also the same.
As for the Shìdiàn in various provincial prefectures, departments, and counties,
the local Seal-bearing officials presided over the sacrifice.
The rites were like those of the Tàixué,
and this was implemented in the early Shùnzhì era.
In the fifth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was stipulated that the Governors-general (Dū), Governors (Fǔ), and Education Commissioners (Xuézhèng) of each province should lead their subordinates in offering sacrifices on the dīng day.
When the Education Commissioner arrived for examinations,
they first proceeded to the Wénmiào to perform rites.
Prefectural, departmental, and county officials led their subordinates to perform them in the Wénmiào of their administrative seat.
In the sixth year of Qiánlóng,
an imperial edict commanded that ancestral worthies and former Confucians be enshrined in the school palaces of the direct provinces.
In the early Tóngzhì era,
a diagram showing the order of position for co-worshipped former Confucians was issued.
At the end of Guāngxù,
when it was elevated to a Grand Sacrifice,
the regulations, ritual vessels, music, dances, and sacrificial offerings for the Chóngshèng Cí in the Wénmiào of various provinces
were all made to align with those of the Tàixué,
and the ceremonial procedures strictly followed the old customs.
Wénchāng Dìjūn During the Chénghuà reign of the Míng dynasty,
the original temple was rebuilt.
It was located outside Dì'ānmén in Jīngshī,
but had long been dilapidated.
In the fifth year of Jiāqìng (1800),
the bandits in Tóngjiāng were pacified.
Initially, the bandits had spied on Zītóng,
and seeing the banners on the temple mountain,
retreated.
Thereupon, the emperor personally inscribed the plaque
“Huàchéng Qídìng”
to commemorate
the extraordinary achievement.
Funds from the imperial treasury were allocated to rebuild the temple.
It was completed in the summer of the following year.
Rénzōng personally paid his respects with nine prostrations,
and issued an edict stating:
“The Emperor Lord Wénchāng presides over the literary destiny,
honoring the sacred and repelling evil.
He is revered throughout the realm
along with Guānshèng,
and it is fitting that he be included in the sacrificial canon.”
Thereupon, Grand Secretary Zhū Guī composed a stele inscription,
briefly stating:
“The Wénchāng star is recorded in the Tiānguān Shū,
which says: ‘The six stars of the Dǒukuí,
called Dàikuāng, form the Wénchāng Gōng.’
This is it.
The Shàngshū mentions ‘yin six zōng’.
Kǒng’s commentary quotes Zhèng Xuán saying: ‘All are heavenly deities.
Sīzhōng and Sīmìng,
are the fifth and fourth stars of Wénchāng respectively.’
The Zhōulǐ Dàzōngbó states: ‘Offer a yuǒliáo sacrifice to Sīzhōng and Sīmìng.’
Zhèng’s commentary refers to the Wénchāng star.
Thus, the worship of Wénchāng
began in the time of Yú,
was established in the Zhōulǐ,
and was even included in suburban sacrifices during the Hàn and Jìn dynasties.
The Yuánmìng Bāo says: ‘The supreme general establishes martial might,
the second general rectifies left and right,
the noble minister manages literary affairs,
and the Sīlù rewards meritorious scholars.’
Thus, the duties of official rank, emolument, and imperial examinations have long been established.
It also says that the Emperor Lord was Zhāng Zhòng in the early Zhōu dynasty,
distinguished by filial piety and fraternity;
during the Suí and Táng dynasties, he was Wáng Tōng.
Referring to Lǐ Shāngyǐn’s poem about the Zhāng Yàzǐ Temple,
and reading Sūn Qiáo’s eulogy to the Zītóng Shénjūn,
the Huà Shū states: In the Kaiyuan reign of Táng, he was appointed Zuǒchéng.
The Tōngkǎo states: Xīzōng enfeoffed him as Jìshùn Wáng.
Sòng Zhēnzōng changed his title to Yīngxiǎn.
Zhézōng added the title Fǔyuán Kāihuà Wénchāng Sīlù Dìjūn.
The Yuán dynasty added the title Hóngrén.
This can be verified.”
The Ministry of Rites then finalized the resolution.
The spring sacrifice was held on the third day of the second lunar month, his birthday.
The autumn sacrifice,
in the middle of autumn, on an auspicious day, the rites were performed,
with a high minister dispatched.
The front hall housed the main deity,
while the back hall worshipped his ancestors.
The sacrificial rites were like those for Guāndì.
In the sixth year of Xiánfēng (1856),
he was elevated to a medium sacrifice.
Officials from the Ministry of Rites requested to raise the temple steps,
expand the regulations,
and send a prince to preside over the sacrifice.
For the back hall, the chief official of the Tàicháng Temple would personally attend,
performing two kneeling bows and six prostrations,
with six musical performances,
and a eight-row civilian dance.
This was approved.
Officials in charge of Wénchāng temples in the provinces and prefectures would offer sacrifices at the appointed times.
For those without temples,
a temporary altar would be set up in a public office for the sacrifice.
After the ceremony,
the altar and offerings were removed, and the祝帛 (zhùbó, sacrificial silk) was sent for burning.
Sacrifice to the Banners In the tenth year of Tiānmìng (1625),
after settling Shěnyáng and
returning the army to Hùhúnhé,
a bull was slaughtered to sacrifice to the banners.
In the first year of Tiāncōng (1627), when campaigning against Cháoxiān,
and returning triumphantly the following year,
banners were erected and heaven was worshipped.
From then on, it became customary to sacrifice to the banners when setting out on campaigns and when returning to the capital.
At that time, the banners were worshipped along with Guāndì in his temple.
After Shìzǔ entered the pass,
the 'gazing sacrifice' (wàngjì) was first performed.
Whenever the emperor personally led a campaign, on an auspicious day for departure,
a large imperial yellow dragon banner (yùyíng huánglóng dàdú) would first be erected outside the inner gate of the Tángzǐ.
Eight large banners for the Eight Banners and eight large banners for the Huǒqìyíng (Firearms Camp) would be set up on either side,
arrayed behind it,
all facing north.
The emperor, wearing military attire and a saber,
would leave the palace on horseback,
and dismount at the Tángzǐ street gate.
After the ritual in the circular hall,
he would exit the inner gate to pay respects to the banner deities,
leading the campaigning generals and soldiers in three kneeling bows and nine prostrations,
without announcement.
After the ceremony, music would play,
and the imperial carriage would set off.
The chief imperial bodyguards (lǐng shìwèi nèidàchén) and the banner bodyguards (sīdú shìwèi) would lead the imperial guards, carrying the banners and following.
Upon triumphant return, a sacrifice would be offered.
On the appointed day, the imperial carriage and retinue (fǎjià lǔbù) would be arranged
from five li outside the suburb up to the Tángzǐ gate.
When the carriage reached the suburb,
the emperor would dismount and bow to the banners as prescribed.
When generals were dispatched on campaigns, the same ritual was observed.
When Shèngzǔ returned triumphantly from his campaign against Gá'ěrdān,
on the following day, an altar was erected outside Āndìngmén,
and sacrifices were offered to the accompanying military banners,
using a grand animal sacrifice (tàiláo).
This was the first time a high minister was dispatched to perform the ceremony.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
it was established that a sacrifice would be offered every three years.
All banners were stored in the Imperial Household Department,
and brought out for the sacrifice.
For sacrifices to the banners in the provinces,
military officers in military attire were dispatched to perform the rites.
Sacrifice to the Cannons In the fifth year of Tiāncōng (1631),
red-coat cannons (hóngyī pào) were cast,
inscribed with "Tiānyòu Zhùwēi Dàjiāngjūn".
They were then carried to destroy Zǐzhāngtái
and capture Dàlínghé.
The practice of carrying red-coat cannons during military campaigns began here.
Subsequently, an edict ordered Hàn army soldiers to carry cannons when entering the pass.
After Shìzǔ established his capital in Yānjīng,
a system was established to offer sacrifices on the first day of the last month of autumn each year.
The cannon positions would be arranged at Shāguōcūn near Lúgōuqíao,
an altar would be set up on the ground,
facing west.
The Dūtǒng of the Eight Banners' Hàn army would preside over the ceremony,
with banners arrayed on the flanks,
using fruits and a small animal sacrifice (shàoláo).
At the appointed time, beginning with the Xiānghuáng Banner cannon position,
the Dūtǒng, wearing his embroidered robe,
would offer incense,
perform three kneeling bows and nine prostrations,
three libations,
and read the prayer.
The other seven cannon positions would follow the same procedure.
The Fùdūtǒng and others would assist in the sacrifice in order.
When Shèngzǔ returned triumphantly,
an altar was set up outside Déshèngmén,
with offerings similar to the banner sacrifice.
Shìzōng also stipulated a sacrifice every three years.
In the fourteenth year of Qiánlóng (1749),
the Mǎnzhōu Huǒqìyíng (Manchu Firearms Camp) began to sacrifice to the deities of the Eight Banners' mother and child cannons.
The Zǒngtǒng presided over the sacrifice,
following the Hàn army's cannon ritual.
Later, it was stipulated that the Mǎnzhōu cannon sacrifice would follow the Hàn army's precedent,
going to Lúgōuqíao in the last month of autumn to practice with cannons,
and holding the sacrifice on that very day.
In the thirtieth year,
prayer tablets were first used for the cannon sacrifice,
and special sacrificial vessels were also provided.
Group Sacrifices
Former Physicians Initially, following the old Míng dynasty practice,
sacrifices were offered at Jǐnghuì Diàn of the Tàiyīyuàn (Imperial Academy of Medicine)
on the first jiǎ day of the second lunar month each year,
with an official dispatched to perform the rites.
The Three Sovereigns (Sān Huáng) were worshipped:
Fúxī in the center,
Shénnóng on the left,
and Huángdì on the right.
The Four Associates (Sì Pèi) were:
Gōumáng, Fēnghòu, Zhùróng, and Lìmù.
In the eastern hall were Jiùdàijì, Qíbó, Bógāo, Shàoshī, Léigōng, Yīyǐn, Chúnyúyì, Huàtuó, Huángfǔmì, Cháoyuánfāng, Wéicízàng, Qián Yǐ, and Liú Wánsù, fourteen individuals.
In the western hall were Guǐyúqū, Yúfù, Shàoyú, Tóngjūn, Mǎshīhuáng, Biǎnquè, Zhāng Jī, Wáng Shūhé, Gé Hóng, Sūn Sīmiǎo, Wáng Bīng, Zhū Gōng, Zhāng Yuánsù, and Zhū Yānxiū, fourteen individuals.
The Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) presided over the sacrifice.
Officials from the Imperial Academy of Medicine
made separate offerings in the two halls.
The ritual involved three kneeling bows and nine prostrations,
and three libations.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
officials of the Imperial Academy of Medicine were ordered to all perform ritual fasting and attend the sacrifice.
There were two Dū Chénghuáng Miào.
The old Shěnyáng Chénghuáng Miào,
from the Yuán to the Míng dynasties,
its sacrificial rites were never discontinued.
After the Qīng dynasty established its capital,
it was elevated to a Dū Chénghuáng Miào,
and officials performed sacrifices there at appointed times.
As for the one in Yānjīng,
a temple was built inside Xuānwǔmén.
In the middle autumn of Shùnzhì eight years (1651),
the Tàicháng Qīng was dispatched to offer sacrifices,
which became an annual custom.
A grand sacrifice (Tàiláo) was used,
and the ritual offerings were like those for worshipping the former physicians.
On Wànshòu Jié, officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices,
with the addition of fruits.
In the Yōngzhèng reign,
ministers were instead dispatched,
and later, princes were again commanded to perform the rites.
The Jìnchéng Chénghuáng Miào was built in the northwest corner of the Forbidden City.
The Huángchéng Chénghuáng Miào was built inside Xī'ānmén,
named Yǒngyòu Gōng.
On Wànshòu Jié or in late autumn,
ministers of the Nèifǔ were dispatched to preside over the sacrifice,
using a lesser sacrifice (Shǎoláo).
The Běijí Yòushèng Zhēnjūn Miào
was built outside Dì'ānmén, east of Rìzhōng Fāng Bridge,
named Língxiǎn Xiǎnyòu Gōng.
In the Shùnzhì reign,
it was initially stipulated that officials be dispatched to sacrifice on Wànshòu Jié,
but later ministers were dispatched instead.
Five fruit platters, fifteen cake and pastry platters, and three tea cups were arranged, and the rites involved three genuflections and nine kowtows.
The Huǒshén Miào
was built west of Rìzhōng Bridge.
In the early Kāngxī reign,
it was stipulated that the Tàicháng Qīng be dispatched to sacrifice on the twenty-third day of the sixth month each year,
but later ministers were dispatched instead.
A lesser sacrifice (Shǎoláo) was used.
In the Yōngzhèng reign,
it was changed to a grand sacrifice (Tàiláo).
Initially, white silk was used,
but in the Qiánlóng reign, it was changed to red.
Other procedures were the same as the ritual for Běijí.
The Dōngyuè Miào
was located outside Cháoyángmén,
with annual sacrifices on Wànshòu Jié.
For the sacrifices to the Dragon Gods:
The Hēilóngtán Miào was built on the summit of Jīnshān in the northwest.
Shèngzǔ and Shìzōng personally composed stele inscriptions.
In Qiánlóng five years (1740),
it was granted the title
"Zhāolíng Pèizé."
The Yùquánshān Miào,
in Qiánlóng nine years (1744), was granted the title
"Huìjì Cíyòu."
The Kūnmínghú Cí,
formerly named Guǎngrùn Língyǔ Cí,
was granted the title
"Ānyòu Pǔjì."
In the Jiāqìng reign,
it was additionally granted
"Pèizé Guǎngshēng."
When there was a drought in the Jīngjī,
the Emperor personally prayed at the Hēilóngtán Miào.
In Qiánlóng forty-six years (1781),
it was granted the title
"Zhāolíng Guǎngjì."
During the Jiāqìng reign,
it was finally included in the sacrificial canon,
and ministers without fixed rank were dispatched to offer sacrifices at Huìjì Cí.
The Héshén Miào was built inside Qǐchūnyuán,
worshipping Tiānhòu, the Dragon Gods, and the River Gods,
with sacrifices in both spring and autumn,
and ministers of Yuánmíngyuán were dispatched to conduct the affairs.
The rituals and offerings were all in accordance with those of the Dū Chénghuáng Miào.
As for those sacrifices without fixed times or locations,
and those specifically offered by officials at appointed times:
For the gods of Hòutǔ Sīgōng,
a system was established in the early Shùnzhì reign:
Whenever there was a major construction project,
altars were built on either side in that area,
a decorated tent was erected,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices,
using a lesser sacrifice (Shǎoláo) with cakes and fruits.
For major constructions involving the installation of a *wěn* (ridge ornament),
sacrifices were offered to the Liúlí Yáoshén (god of the glazed tile kiln) and various Gate Gods,
following the rites for Sīgōng.
During the Xiánfēng reign,
the Sīgōng god of Chūnyǔ Xuān in Yuánmíngyuán was granted the title Zhāoxiū Fūxī Zhēnjūn,
and Tǔmǔ was titled Fūrén.
Ministers of the Nèifǔ were commanded to offer sacrifices in spring and autumn.
For the Sījī Shén:
In the late Shùnzhì reign, a weaving bureau (Zhīzào Jú) was established,
and sacrifices and announcements began to be made,
presided over by the chief official of the Lǐbù.
For the Sīcāng Shén:
Of the three granaries in Tōngzhōu,
only the Xīcāng (West Granary) previously had a shrine.
Of the seven granaries within the capital,
only the Yòuyì Xīngpíng Cāng had a shrine,
which was renovated during the Yōngzhèng reign.
Thereafter, a temple was established at the Hǎiyùn Cāng of the Zuǒyì.
Of the five granaries outside the capital,
a temple was established at the Chújì Cāng,
and spirit tablets were all set up.
The Cāngchǎng Shìláng presided over the sacrifices,
using a lesser sacrifice (Shǎoláo) and fruits,
with the granary supervisor accompanying the worship,
performing two genuflections and six kowtows.
All these sacrifices commenced at dawn,
and those participating in the sacrifices all wore court attire;
this was the general outline.
As for shrines established in Jīngshī by special imperial decree,
they are fully detailed in later sections.
If, in the direct provinces, there were those who had performed meritorious deeds for the people in mitigating disasters and averting calamities,
they would be granted enfeoffment titles and
have exclusive shrines built,
where local officials would regularly offer sacrifices according to the canon.
In Shìzǔ's reign,
Héshén Sòng Xièxù was worshipped in Sùqiān.
In Shèngzǔ's reign,
Zhūgě Liàng was worshipped in Chéngdū;
Tiānhòu Sòng Lín Shì Nǚ was worshipped in Fújiàn and various other provinces.
In Shìzōng's reign,
Měng Jiàngjūn Yuán Liú Chéngzhōng was worshipped in various provinces.
Previously, Zhílì Zǒngdū Lǐ Wéijūn reported:
"During a locust plague,
the locals prayed at the Měng Jiàngjūn Miào,
and the affliction was immediately removed."
Thereupon, imperial edicts were issued for temples to be built and sacrifices offered in all provinces.
Later, Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū Zhā Bìnà also stated:
"Wherever Měng Jiàngjūn Miào were worshipped, there was no locust damage,
while places without temples all suffered disaster."
He was reprimanded.
The edict stated:
"For floods, droughts, and locust disasters,
frontier officials should reflect and reform,
not merely engage in prayers."
Wǔ Yuán was worshipped in Qiántáng,

In the twenty-seventh year of Guāngxù (1901),
when the two Empresses Dowager (Liǎnggōng) travelled west,
upon their return to the capital,
the imperial boat crossed the river
without being disturbed by waves,
thus the titles of all the Great Kings and Generals were specially augmented.
All those who received sacrifices were granted titles,
which are not fully recorded;
only the most notable are documented here.
Some were already enfeoffed in previous dynasties and received additional titles now,
while others were first enfeoffed in the current dynasty and later received multiple additional titles;
these are all omitted.
By established rule,
a title of forty characters would not be further augmented;
there were exceptions,
but these were not part of the regular system.
Only the Jīnlóng Sìdàwáng received an additional title beyond forty characters, "Xīhù,"
and the Tiānhòu received up to sixty characters,
further bestowed with "Jiāyòu."
The Five Sacrifices (Wǔsì)
initially followed the old system,
being collectively offered annually at the west wing of the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Tàimiào) at the end of the year.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì (1651), a new regulation was established:
the household gods (Sīhù Shén) were worshipped outside the palace gates in the first month of spring,
the kitchen gods (Sīzào Shén) in front of the grand kitchen in the first month of summer,
the central hearth god (Zhōngliú Shén) on the steps of the Tàihé Diàn in the last month of summer,
the gate gods (Sīmén Shén) west of the Wǔmén in the first month of autumn,
and the well gods (Sījǐng Shén) in front of the grand kitchen's well in the first month of winter.
The two sacrifices to the central hearth and the gate gods
were managed by the Tàicháng Sì,
while the three sacrifices to the household, kitchen, and well gods
were managed by the Nèiwùfǔ.
Thus, separate sacrifices began,
but soon reverted to the old practice.
When the Shèngzǔ Emperor reformed the sacrificial code,
these were again abolished,
and special sacrifices were also suspended.
Only on the twenty-third day of the twelfth month
was the kitchen god worshipped in the palace as a regular custom.
The Bālà (八蜡) Sacrifice.
In the early Qīng (清) dynasty, this was held outside Shěngjīng (盛京).
The temple was built inside the South Gate.
In spring and autumn, an altar was set up for a distant sacrifice.
After Shìzǔ (世祖) entered the Pass,
this practice was still continued.
In the tenth year of Qiánlóng (乾隆)
an imperial edict abolished the Là (蜡) Sacrifice.
At that time, court officials still strongly requested the continuation of the ancient Là (蜡) Sacrifice.
Gāozōng (高宗) decreed:
"The rite of the Grand Là (蜡) Sacrifice
originated from Yīqí (伊耆).
The Three Dynasties continued it.
The ancient system is extremely distant,
and the commentaries are mixed and conflicting.
The Eight Là (八蜡) were associated with insects.
Later Confucians argued that pests that harm crops should not be sacrificed to.
The 'Yuèlìng' (月令) states: 'Pray for a bountiful year to the Tiānzōng (天宗).'
This is the Là (蜡) Sacrifice.
The commentary says 'sun, moon, stars, and constellations,'
so the deities presided over are not the Eight Gods.
As for gathering all things to seek their enjoyment,
with so many gods, their positions are even harder to determine.
Là (蜡) and Là (臘) have different robes and caps.
Some say Là (臘) is Là (蜡),
while others say Là (蜡) comes after Là (蜡).
Since the Hàn (漢) dynasty, Là (臘) was performed but not Là (蜡).
From the Wèi (魏) and Jìn (晉) dynasties onwards,
its abolition and establishment were inconsistent.
Some indulged in the theories of the Five Elements,
even including the Heavenly Emperor, the Human Emperor, and the Dragon, Qílín (麟), and Vermilion Bird,
resulting in one hundred and ninety-two seats,
which commentators considered a breach of禮 (lǐ).
Sū Shì (蘇軾) said: 'Welcoming cats makes them cat-cadavers,
welcoming tigers makes them tiger-cadavers.
This is close to what actors do.'
Thus, its practice has long resembled a play.
For this reason, it was abolished and not practiced during the Yuán (元) and Míng (明) dynasties.
Moreover, the various gods of the Là (蜡) Sacrifice,
such as the First Farmer (先嗇), the Controller of Agriculture (司嗇), the sun, moon, stars, constellations, mountains, forests, rivers, and marshes,
are worshipped at separate altars and temples.
Folk festivals and thanksgiving
also borrowed from the Là (蜡) Sacrifice to celebrate camaraderie in the villages.
However, each followed its own customs,
and was never constrained by ceremonial rituals.
Let them all be abolished."
From then on, there was no longer any Là (蜡) Sacrifice.
Sacrifice to the Lì (厲) Spirits. According to the Míng (明) system,
from the capital (Jīngshī 京師) down to the commanderies and counties (jùnxiàn 郡縣),
all offered sacrifices at the Lì (厲) Altar.
In the early Qīng (清) dynasty, the capital was Shěngjīng (盛京),
and the Lì (厲) Altar was built outside the Dìzài (地載) Gate.
After Shìzǔ (世祖) entered the Pass,
there is no record of the Lì (厲) Sacrifice in Jīngshī (京師).
Only in the provinces, the City God (Chénghuáng 城隍) was worshipped together with the gods of the Shénqí (神祇) Altar.
On the first and fifteenth days of each month, officials would go to the temple to offer incense.
They would perform two kneelings and six prostrations.
If the rain or sunshine was delayed beyond the expected time, prayers would be offered.
Furthermore, the City God presided over the Lì (厲) Altar sacrifices.
In the early Shùnzhì (順治) era,
altars were set up in the prefectures (fǔ 府), departments (zhōu 州), and counties (xiàn 縣) of the provinces, on the northern outskirts of the city.
Annually, on Qīngmíng (清明) Day, the fifteenth day of the seventh month, and the first day of the tenth month,
three sheep, three pigs, three shí (石) of cooked rice, incense, candles, wine, and paper offerings were used to sacrifice to the un-worshipped ghosts and spirits of the locality.
In prefectures, it was called Jùnlì (郡厲);
in counties, Yìlì (邑厲).
Before the appointed date, the sacrificial offerings were prepared.
Officials would go to the City God Temple to announce the Lì (厲) Sacrifice.
On the day, a sacrificial furnace was set up south of the altar.
The spirit tablet of the City God was placed in the center of the altar.
Kneeling before the spirit tablet,
three sticks of incense were offered.
The rite involved three prostrations.
After sending off the offerings by burning,
three libations of wine were poured.
Then, retreating,
the spirit tablet was returned to its original position.

Record of Sixty Rites, Part Four (Auspicious Rites, Part Four). Tángzǐ (堂子) Sacrifice to Heaven. Kūnníng Gōng (坤寧宮) Sacrifices to Gods. Setting out offerings on festive days. Sacrificing to gods for blessings. Fèngxiān Diàn (奉先殿). Shòuhuáng Diàn (壽皇殿). Ānyòu Gōng (安佑宮) (with Suīchéng Diàn (綏成殿) attached). Mǎnzōu Tiàoshén (滿洲跳神) Ceremony.
Tángzǐ (堂子) Sacrifice to Heaven. In the early Qīng (清) dynasty, starting from Liáoshěn (遼瀋),
there was a rite of setting up poles to sacrifice to Heaven.
Also, in a quiet chamber, sacrifices were made to the gods of the Altar of Soil and Grain (Shèjì 社稷) and other deities.
This was called the Tángzǐ (堂子).
It was built outside the Nèizhì (內治) Gate, east of the city.
This embodied the meaning of the ancient Míngtáng (明堂) where all gods were worshipped.
After Shìzǔ (世祖) established the capital in Yànjīng (燕京),
following the national customs,
a site was chosen outside the Cháng'ān (長安) Left Gate,
and the Tángzǐ (堂子) was still built there.
In the very center was the Xiǎngdiàn (饗殿),
with five bays,
facing south,
where all the gods were gathered for worship,
covered with yellow glazed tiles.
In front was the Bàitiān Yuándiàn (拜天圜殿),
facing north.
In the center was a stone seat for the divine pole.
Slightly behind it,
the two wings were divided into six rows each,
with six tiers in each row.
Imperial princes (Huángzǐ 皇子) were in the first tier,
followed by princes of the first rank (Qīnwáng 親王), princes of the second rank (Jùnwáng 郡王), Bèilè (貝勒), Bèizǐ (貝子), and Gōng (公),
each according to their row order,
all facing north.
To the southeast was the Shàngshéndiàn (上神殿),
with three bays,
facing south.
The sacrificial rites varied,
but the New Year's Day worship of Heaven and the triumphant return from expeditions were considered important,
and were both personally performed by the Emperor.
Other monthly sacrifices, pole sacrifices, Buddha bathing sacrifices, and horse sacrifices
were usually delegated to the responsible officials.
After the establishment of the Chóngdé (崇德) era,
it was formalized that
on New Year's Day each year,
the Emperor, leading Qīnwáng (親王), Fānwáng (藩王), down to the Vice-Commander-in-Chief (Fùdūtǒng 副都統), would perform the rites.
Soon, it was limited to Bèilè (貝勒) only,
then again limited to Jùnwáng (郡王) only,
and even delegated guards to hang paper and silk offerings.
Whenever the Emperor personally sacrificed,
on the twenty-sixth day of the twelfth month, preceding the event,
officials from the Imperial Household Department (Nèifǔ 內府) would go to Kūnníng Gōng (坤寧宮) to request the morning and evening sacrificial spirit tablets.
The divine sedan chair was then installed and,
carried by imperial eunuchs.
Eight imperial guards and four lanterns led the procession.
Six ritual slaughter officials (Sīzǔguān 司俎官),
one master of ceremonies (Zhǎngyí Sī 掌儀司),
and ten imperial bodyguards
guided it to the Xiǎngdiàn (饗殿) for offerings.
Morning and evening incense offerings were made as usual.
According to custom,
the paper and silk offerings hung on the spirit tablets,
accumulated at the end of the month, were stored in bags.
On New Year's Eve, they were sent to the Tángzǐ (堂子)
and burned together with clean paper and the divine poles.
At that time, Nèifǔ Dàchén (內府大臣), leading the Chief Scribe (Zhǎngshǐ 長史) and imperial bodyguards, would hang twenty-seven new paper and silk offerings.
At dawn,
the Emperor would leave the palace in a sedan chair,
accompanied by the participating princes and dukes.
Upon reaching the inner gate of the Tángzǐ (堂子), they dismounted,
entered the central gate,
proceeded to the Yuándiàn (圜殿) to take their kneeling positions,
facing south.
The Emperor led all officials in performing the three kneelings and nine kowtows.
After completion,
the imperial procession returned.
The next day,
the spirit tablets were returned to the palace.
In the eleventh year of Kāngxī (康熙)
an edict declared that the New Year's Day Tángzǐ (堂子) worship rite should be clearly prepared,
using chanters (Míngzànguān 鳴贊官).
The following year,
Han officials were excluded from participating in the sacrifice.
In the twenty-ninth year
an edict instructed imperial princes to accompany the Emperor in performing the rites.
After the Nèifǔ Dàchén (內府大臣) presented paper and silk offerings in the Yuándiàn (圜殿), the Crown Prince (Huángtàizǐ 皇太子) presented his paper and silk offerings.
Shòuhuángdiàn. The old system had three chambers,
located northeast of Jǐngshān.
The sacred images of Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, Shìzǔ, and the empresses
were previously enshrined in Tǐrén'gé.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
an imperial decree ordered the censor Mǎng Húlí to paint the imperial portrait of Shèngzǔ,
to be enshrined in the central hall of Shòuhuángdiàn.
On imperial birthdays, death anniversaries, New Year's Day, and other festivals,
the emperor would lead the imperial princes and close-kin princely nobles to pay respects and offer sacrifices.
Whenever the rituals for entombment in the imperial mausoleum and enshrinement in the Tàimiào were completed,
the emperor would personally visit to offer sacrifices.
He would usually pay respects once a month,
sometimes even three times.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
the sacred image of Shìzōng was enshrined in the eastern chamber.
Thereafter, the sacred images of successive reigns
were enshrined in the eastern and western chambers in order,
which became a permanent custom.
In the third year,
it was decreed that the emperor should proceed to Shòuhuángdiàn to perform rites when visiting the imperial mausoleums, going on provincial tours, or returning to the capital.
Soon after, it was decreed that the rites for the Wànshòu Festival should be performed in the same manner as other festivals.
In the thirteenth year,
it was relocated and rebuilt in the center of Jǐngshān,
following the design of Ānyòugōng.
The main hall had nine chambers,
the left and right side halls each had three bays,
and the eastern and western wing halls each had five bays.
It was completed that winter.
Gāozōng personally composed an inscription,
its eulogy reading:
"Only Yáo was majestic,
only Shùn was double-illumined;
our ancestors took them as models.
Not contentious, not anxious,
benevolence permeated, righteousness cultivated;
our ancestors emulated them.
To expand the benevolence of the benevolent emperors,
to manifest the laws of the imperial emperors,
this is the duty of the humble one.
To inherit, to continue,
to be bright, to be clear;
this is what the humble one contemplates.
The heavenly journey, the cloudy demise,
spring dew, autumn frost—
my heart is filled with sorrow.
My father enshrined the imperial portraits of the ancestors
here in Shòuhuáng,
and I continue to follow him.
The design is grand and proper,
thus planned and constructed;
the work must not be rushed.
Ascending and descending, relying and leaning,
residing and receiving sacrifices in this chamber,
the image of 'soup and wall' is attained.
May it bless my descendants,
to continue for ten thousand generations,
nay, for ten million.
Observe virtue here,
do not deviate or turn away;
bear it in mind with reverence."
In the fifteenth year,
an imperial edict stated:
"In previous dynasties, the imperial portraits were enshrined
mostly in temples,
and separate pure halls
had no fixed location.
I reverently recall the founding and establishment by the imperial ancestors;
their manifest legacy is here.
Forever cherishing their former grace,
our admiration is ever new.
To conform to the rites of the temple's ancestral worship,
this aligns with the system of the imperial household.
Therefore, the sacred images of the imperial ancestors and empresses should be welcomed and enshrined in Shòuhuángdiàn.
On New Year's Eve, they should be collectively invited and hung for display,
and libations and offerings solemnly made."
Thereupon, the imperial portraits of Shèngzǔ and Shìzōng were enshrined,
and the imperial portraits of Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, and Shìzǔ were welcomed from Tǐrén'gé.
It was then decreed that on New Year's Eve, they should be reverently hung,
and fresh fruits and meat sauces offered.
On New Year's Day, a grand sacrifice would be held,
offering porcelain wares, bambooware, and bean vessels as sacrifices,
and also burning incense and performing rites.
On the second day, offerings would be made as on New Year's Eve.
After the rites, they would be respectfully stored.
Furthermore, on New Year's Day, the emperor would perform rites at Tángzi and Fèngxiāndiàn,
and upon completion,
proceed to Shòuhuángdiàn to perform rites.
On New Year's Eve and the second day,
the imperial princes were ordered to take turns.
On the Shàngyuán Festival, pastries and delicacies were offered.
In autumn, the sacred images were displayed,
with the Palace Secretariat reverently managing the affairs.
That year, the sacred images of successive reigns were completed,
and the emperor personally visited to enshrine them,
performing a grand sacrifice.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
an imperial edict stated that the divine portraits enshrined in Shòuhuángdiàn
began with Shèngzǔ.
Whenever a death anniversary or birthday occurred,
the emperor should personally pay respects,
to instruct his descendants to follow this practice.
The same applied to Ānyòugōng.
Ānyòugōng is located in the northwest corner of Yuánmíngyuán.
Its construction began in the fifth year of Qiánlóng,
and was completed in the eighth year.
The main hall had nine chambers,
with vermilion doors and yellow eaves,
like the system for sleeping temples.
In the central niche hung the imperial portrait of Shèngzǔ,
to its left Shìzōng,
and to its right Gāozōng.
Before the niches were displayed utensils, books, and personal garments,
with a set of Zhōnghé Sháoyuè arranged together.
When the emperor was in residence at the garden,
on the birthdays of the successive emperors,
death anniversaries,
festivals,
and the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
he would offer incense and perform rites.
When visiting the imperial mausoleums, departing on provincial tours, or returning to the capital,
he would personally visit to report.
Gāozōng personally composed an inscription,
which briefly stated:
"The offerings on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month are a remnant system from the Western Hàn's Yuanmiao.
The Shén'yùdiàn in the Sòng dynasty also originated from this meaning,
being the place for enshrining the imperial portraits of successive reigns.
During the Shàngyuán Festival, lantern towers were erected; during the Hánshí Festival, swings were set up—
compared to the Hàn, preparations were complete.
However, the widespread construction of such halls across prefectures and states,
and the offering of sacrifices in Buddhist monasteries,
were criticized by discerning individuals.
Our imperial ancestor Shèngzǔ's grace and benevolence spread widely,
reaching remote towns and desolate valleys.
Those who drank of his virtue but did not know it,
and the descendants, officials, and commoners
who personally received his education,
justly sang his praises with deep admiration, and this never ceased.
Therefore, my imperial father Shìzōng reverently enshrined the imperial portrait in Shòuhuángdiàn,
paying respects on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
and also made offerings as per ritual at Chàngchūnyuán,
which was favored by my imperial ancestor.
This had the sincerity of the Hàn and Sòng in preparing all objects and rites,
without the drawback of the Sòng era's excessive sacrifices leading to disrespect.
I, the humble one, with trepidation inherit the imperial legacy,
mindful that Yuánmíngyuán was the imperial garden of my imperial father.
I have built a hall of nine bays,
reverently enshrining my imperial ancestor within it,
and enshrining my imperial father in the eastern chamber as a consort.
This is what is called 'rites arising from righteousness';
since it has been established,
none dare abolish it."
Yǒngyòusì is located next to Wànshùyuán in the Rèhé Summer Resort.
It was built in the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng.
It has a five-bay tower,
enshrining the imperial portraits of Shèngzǔ, Shìzōng, and Gāozōng.
The Yúnshān Shèngdìlóu enshrines the imperial portrait of Rénzōng.
The furnishings are all the same as Ānyòugōng.
When the imperial carriage arrived, they would be hung for enshrinement,
and stored away after the emperor returned.
In the vermilion courtyard was displayed Gāozōng's imperial inscription,
which briefly stated:
"A Buddhist temple was founded,
named Yǒngyòu.
Not only do the bells, fish, and Buddhist chants
suffice to allow the thirty-six scenes to bear witness to the Dharma;
but where the imperial ancestor's sacred sun shone,
even ten thousand years hence,
descendants, officials, and commoners
will forever feel as if he is present.
This is like Śākyamuni's Gijjhakūṭa mountain,
the vajra dharma seat,
protected by devas and nāgas;
and thus, the means by which to continue the ancestral path, to soothe parents,
to pray for blessings, and to nourish aspirations
is also entrusted here."
Rénzōng's imperial inscription "Yǒngyòusì Zhānlǐ Jìjì"
also shows deep affection for his ancestors and father.
During the Dàoguāng era,
the imperial portraits were moved to Jìdétáng for enshrinement,
which was renamed Suíchéngdiàn.
In the central chamber was Shèngzǔ,
to its left Shìzōng,
to its right Gāozōng,
in the next left chamber Rénzōng,
and thereafter, the imperial portraits of successive reigns
were still hung in the left and right chambers in order.
In the fifth year, in winter,
Zháo Wáng 澤王 was posthumously honored as Zhào Zǔ 肇祖,
Qìng Wáng 慶王 as Xīng Zǔ 興祖,
Chāng Wáng 昌王 as Jǐng Zǔ 景祖,
Fú Wáng 福王 as Xiǎn Zǔ 顯祖.
They, along with their four empresses, were enshrined in the rear hall,
and offerings were made to them according to the seasonal sacrifice rites.
In the eighth year,
Empress Xiàoduānwén 孝端文皇后 was interred in the ancestral temple.
The spirit tablets were presented before Tàizǔ 太祖, the Empress Dowager, and Tàizōng 太宗,
and the three跪 nine拜 (three kneelings and nine prostrations) ritual was performed on her behalf.
Her position was next to Tàizōng,
and then a further one跪 three拜 (one kneeling and three prostrations) was performed.
After this was completed,
the grand sacrifice was carried out.
For sacrifices in the rear hall, officials were dispatched.
Whenever an interment took place,
a notification was sent out the day before.
On the day itself, the presentation, enshrinement, and grand sacrifice were performed,
and this was established as a precedent.
In the eighteenth year,
Shìzǔ 世祖 was interred in the ancestral temple,
his position being to the west side of Tàizǔ,
facing east.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī 康xī,
Empress Xiàokāngzhāng 孝康章皇后 was interred in the ancestral temple,
her position being next to Shìzǔ.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Empress Xiàozhuāngwén 孝莊文皇后 was interred in the ancestral temple.
At the appointed time, the spirit tablets of Shìzǔ and Empress Zhāng 章后 were moved aside,
and the presentation ritual was performed.
Her position was next to Empress Wén 文后.
For all spirit tablets interred in the ancestral temple,
the junior avoids the senior,
and this was followed thereafter.
In the fifty-seventh year,
Empress Xiàohuìzhāng 孝惠章皇后 was interred.
Some deliberated that since Empress Xiàokāng 孝康 had been interred for a long time,
her position should be next.
Grand Secretary Wáng Yàn 王掞 argued,
"Your Majesty's sagely filial piety reaches heaven.
When the Grand Empress Dowager was interred in the ancestral temple previously,
she was not placed above Empress Xiàoduān 孝端.
Would you now place Empress Xiàokāng above Empress Xiàohuì?"
The deliberators did not agree,
but the Emperor indeed considered it incorrect,
and ordered it to be rectified.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng 雍正,
the ritual ministers stated:
"In ancient times, when emperors and kings were interred in the Grand Ancestral Temple,
their empresses must be offered sacrifices alongside them.
The Zhōu 周 dynasty sacrificed in the Bìgōng 閟宮,
the Hàn 漢 dynasty in separate chambers,
and the Táng 唐 and Sòng 宋 dynasties had the Kūnyí 坤儀 and Fèngcí 奉慈 Halls to express filial thoughts.
Since then, for those who shared the ancestral temple,
the first character of the empress's title was the same as the temple name.
For those who sacrificed in separate temples,
they only had an posthumous name but no temple name.
Their positions might be one emperor and one empress,
or one emperor and two empresses.
Sòng Tàizōng 宋太宗 and Huīzōng 徽宗 had four empresses interred successively,
the ritual system differed.
In our dynasty, Tàizǔ had three empresses,
only Xiàocí 孝慈 was interred in the temple and called Gāohòu 高后.
Tàizōng had two empresses,
Xiàoduān and Xiàozhuāng were both called Wénhòu 文后.
Shìzǔ had three empresses,
Xiàohuì and Xiàokāng were both called Zhānghòu 章后.
Xiàoxiàn 孝獻 was only sacrificed in the Xiàolíng 孝陵 Offering Hall,
this was the established rule.
Now that Shèngzǔ 聖祖 is to be interred in the ancestral temple,
Rénxiào 仁孝 should be enshrined as his consort,
it is indeed appropriate for them to share the sacrifices.
However, the temple name 'Rén' 仁
duplicates the honorary posthumous title.
It should be changed to Xiàochéng 孝誠.
And Xiàogōng 孝恭, who embodied maternal virtues,
should also be interred alongside.
As for Xiàozhāo 孝昭 and Xiàoyì 孝懿,
a detailed discussion among court officials is needed."
Soon after, a decision was reached:
"From the Xià 夏 and Shāng 商 dynasties down to the Six Dynasties,
all had one emperor and one empress.
Táng Ruìzōng 唐睿宗 had two empresses,
Sòng Tàizǔ had three empresses,
and Tàizōng had four empresses.
On the system of interment in the ancestral temple,
Zhū Zǐ 朱子 and other Confucians held no differing opinions.
Carefully examining previous records,
Xiàozhāo and Xiàoyì should be called Rénhuánghòu 仁皇后 along with Xiàochéng and Xiàogōng,
and interred together in the Grand Ancestral Temple."
This was followed.
According to the ritual,
one primary empress,
one subsequently established,
and one birth mother,
were arranged in order.
First Xiàochéng,
then Xiàozhāo,
then Xiàoyì,
then Xiàogōng.
Here, the spirit tablets of the emperor and empresses
were arranged in order on the east side,
facing west,
their position being next to Tàizōng.
In the second year of Qiánlóng 乾隆,
Shìzōng 世宗 and Empress Xiàojìng 孝敬后 were interred in the ancestral temple,
their position on the west side,
facing east,
next to Shìzǔ.
In the forty-second year,
Empress Xiàoshèng 孝聖后 was interred,
next to Xiàojìng.
The following year,
Gāozōng 高宗 went to Shèngjīng 盛京,
and relocated and built the four ancestral temples to the east of the Dàqīng Mén 大清門.
It was eleven zhàng (丈) one chǐ (尺) five cùn (寸) in length from north to south,
and ten zhàng three chǐ five cùn in width from east to west.
The main hall had five bays,
and the east and west side halls each had three bays.
There were three main gates,
and one east and one west gate.
Ministers were commanded to supervise its completion.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng 嘉慶,
Gāozōng and Empresses Xiàoxián 孝賢 and Xiàoyí 孝儀 were interred in the ancestral temple,
their position on the east side,
facing west,
next to Shèngzǔ.
In the first year of Dàoguāng 道光,
Rénzōng 仁宗 and Empress Xiàoshú 孝淑后 were interred in the ancestral temple,
their position in the west sequence,
facing east,
next to Shìzōng.
In the thirtieth year,
Xuānzōng 宣宗 left a will regarding the matter of interment in the ancestral temple,
which generally stated:
"The Rítuals for the Son of Heaven specify seven ancestral temples.
The Zhōulǐ 周禮 (Rites of Zhou) 'Xiǎozōngbó' 小宗伯 chapter differentiates between ancestral temples (miào 廟) and distant ancestral altars (tiāo 祧), and the system of zhāo-mù (昭穆).
The Hàn dynasty had seven ancestral temples and six chambers,
the Táng dynasty nine generations and eleven chambers,
the Sòng dynasty nine generations and twelve chambers.
The discussions on ritual were numerous
and varied.
Our dynasty, from Tàizǔ to Rénzōng,
has exactly seven chambers.
If we do not consider both ancient and modern practices,
we will surely become a laughingstock to future generations.
I, with my meager virtue, inherited the foundation.
How dare I presume to be compared to my ancestors?
Interment in the ancestral temple is absolutely not permissible.
The Fèngxiān Diàn 奉先殿, Shòuhuáng Diàn 壽皇殿, and Ānyòu Gōng 安佑宮, as the original ancestral temples,
their system may remain unchanged."
Thereupon, the matter was submitted to court officials for deliberation.
Then Qínwáng Quánlíng 禮親王全齡 and others advocated following established precedents.
Assistant Minister Zēng Guófān 曾國藩 also stated:
"It is absolutely impossible to comply.
In ancient times, the ancestral altar (tiāo) was for ancestral temples where the relationship of kinship had become distant,
referring to the seven temples.
However, there were those whose kinship became distant but were not moved to the ancestral altar (tiāo),
these were necessarily those whose generational virtues were sought after,
and were not counted among the seven temples.
Such as the three rulers of Yīn 殷 and King Wén 文 and King Wǔ 武 of Zhōu.
The late Emperor is the paternal temple (mí miào 禰廟) for His Majesty,
not comparable to the seven temples where kinship has become distant.
Moreover, his merits and virtues were all-encompassing,
and he should be considered a chamber that, along with the former emperors and ancestral lines,
will not be moved to the ancestral altar for a hundred generations.
Furthermore, even feudal lords and grandees still have temple sacrifices,
how much more so for one as revered as the Son of Heaven?
How can we abolish the rite of interment?"
The Emperor granted his request.
The edict stated:
"The seven ancestral temples for the Son of Heaven
are merely a regular system of ritual,
not referring to chambers that are not to be moved to the ancestral altar (tiāo).
For the Imperial Father to be interred in the ancestral temple and called Zōng 宗,
is in accordance with the system."
Thus, in the second year of Xiánfēng 咸豐,
Xuānzōng and Empresses Xiàomù 孝穆, Xiàoshèn 孝慎, and Xiàoquán 孝全 were interred in the ancestral temple,
their position in the east sequence,
facing west,
next to Gāozōng.
The following year,
Empress Xiàohéruì 孝和睿皇后 was interred,
next to Xiàoshú.
Wénzōng 文宗 was raised by Grand Empress Dowager Kāngcí 康慈 in his youth.
In the eleventh year, when the Emperor passed away,
Mùzōng 穆宗, fulfilling the late emperor's last wish,
bestowed the honorary posthumous title of Xiàojìng 孝靜.
In the first year of Tóngzhì 同治,
she was interred in the ancestral temple, next to Xiàoquán.
In the fourth year,
Wénzōng and Empress Xiàodé 孝德 were interred in the ancestral temple,
their position in the west sequence,
facing east,
next to Rénzōng.
At this time, the central hall of the Grand Ancestral Temple had all nine bays arranged in order.
When Mùzōng passed away,
his ancestral tablet had yet to be enshrined.
In the third year of Guāngxù (1877),
Dūn Qīnwáng Yìcóng and others personally went to survey the site,
and deliberated on what was appropriate.
Shìjiǎng Zhāng Pèilún requested to follow the system of the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties,
establishing a permanent ancestral temple (shìshì) for Tàizōng,
which would not be removed for a hundred generations.
He proposed extending the side walls of the rear hall to the left and right, and building a shìshì on each side.
Shìláng Yuán Bǎohéng stated that under the Zhōu system, the shìshì was next to the Tàizǔ temple,
above the zhāomù order.
Later generations, while in the same hall but different rooms,
accorded respect to the nearest ancestors.
He requested that the central hall, to the left and right of Tàizǔ, be made into a nine-bay shìshì,
with two bays extended to the east and west,
and separate temples for six generations of kin, arranged by zhāomù, built.
Tàizǔ would be in the center,
with six bays on each side,
forming the left and right shìshì.
Tàizǔ to Mùzōng would all be considered unremovable for a hundred generations,
without waiting for the end of kinship to be progressively moved.
In the vacant spaces to their left and right,
two more temples would be built,
each with three bays,
for three zhāo and three mù,
successively moving in,
thereby saving relocation.
Hónglú Sì Qīng Xú Shùmíng said:
“In ancient times, the temple was in front and the sleeping hall behind.
The temple was for sacrifices,
which is the front hall today;
the sleeping hall was for storing robes and crowns,
which are the central and rear halls today.
What needs to be discussed now
is merely the sleeping hall for storing robes and crowns.
A sleeping hall should be built to the left of the central hall,
while sacrifices would still be held in the front hall.
All ancestors and imperial ancestors (lièzǔ, lièzōng),
unremovable for a hundred generations,
if a shìshì were built next to the rear hall,
it would conversely seem to be above Tàizǔ.
Only by increasing the sleeping chambers
would the zhāomù order be maintained.”
Regarding other proposals,
most generally favored the shìshì.
Some suggested that the rear hall should be expanded,
with the spirit tablets of the four ancestors moved into it.
It would be converted into a shìshì,
with Tàizōng moved into the central room.
Mùzōng's enshrinement in the temple,
placed in the fourth room on the west side of the central hall,
was the suggestion of Tōngzhèngshǐ Xīzhēn.
Some proposed building shìshì on both sides of the central hall,
two to the east and one to the west,
with Tàizǔ's tablet enshrined in the center.
Among the seven temples, one eastern temple would enshrine Tàizōng,
and two temples would enshrine Shèngzǔ;
one western temple would enshrine Shìzǔ.
Six kin temples would be built on both sides of the front hall,
enshrining those from Shìzōng downwards,
thus preventing disorder in the zhāomù.
This was the suggestion of Shǎozhānshì Wénzhì.
Some proposed building two zhāomù shìshì on both sides of the central hall,
but constructing square halls,
each with five bays both longitudinally and horizontally,
moving Tàizōng to the zhāo shìshì,
and Shìzǔ to the mù shìshì,
both facing north in the central bay.
Shèngzǔ would reside in the zhāo shìshì,
in the first bay facing east.
The central hall would still enshrine Tàizǔ.
Each of the zhāo and mù sections would have four bays,
with the spirit tablets of the successive emperors moved up in order.
When Mùzōng was enshrined,
he would be in the third zhāo bay.
This was the suggestion of Sīyè Bǎotíng.
Subsequently,
the Grand Secretariat (Géyì) decided that altering the ancestral temple system in such a complex way
was not advisable.
Lǐ Qīnwáng Shìduó and others said:
“Rather than clinging to ancient precedents,
it is better to adhere to established rules.
The central hall of the Tàimiào has nine bays;
the central bay remains as it is,
with four bays on each side to the east and west.
We request to renovate and decorate it, as was done in the early Dàoguāng period.
The second and third bays to the east will be for the zhāo positions,
where the spirit tablets of Tàizōng and his two empresses, Shèngzǔ and his four empresses, Gāozōng and his two empresses, and Xuānzōng and his four empresses will be arrayed in order.
The second and third bays to the west will be for the mù positions,
where the spirit tablets of Shìzǔ and his two empresses, Shìzōng and his two empresses, Rénzōng and his two empresses, and Wénzōng and Xiàodé Hòu will be arrayed in order.
In the future, when Mùzōng and Xiàozhé Hòu are enshrined,
their position will be after Xuānzōng.”
When this proposal was submitted,
Chún Qīnwáng Yìxuǎn approved it,
and memorialized:
“This embodies reverence in adaptation,
and is more appropriate than other suggestions.
However, the number of temple bays is limited,
while the imperial lineage is endless.
Renovation is not the ultimate solution.
The removal of ancestral tablets (tiāomiào) is an established system throughout the dynasties,
and cannot be avoided.
We request an imperial decree that from now on,
the provision of 'not removing for a hundred generations' should not be invoked.
Instead, the rite of removal when kinship ends should be followed,
so that this great institution may endure with heaven and earth.”
At that time, Xú Shùmíng strongly advocated Xuānzōng's dying wish,
considering the expansion of rooms in the Hàn and Táng dynasties to be wrong.
The current use of the precedent of adding niches in the Fèngxian Diàn,
in millions of years,
makes further additions difficult.
It is appropriate to follow the ancestral instructions
and pre-determine the zhāomù order.
Nèigé Xuéshì Zhōng Pèixián also spoke to this effect,
and Hónglú Sì Shǎoqīng Wénshuò even requested the construction of Mùzōng's sleeping temple.
Wénzhì and Bǎotíng, in particular, strongly argued that combining niches was crude
and not a permanent system.
The two empress dowagers, having no other recourse,
again referred the matter to the imperial princes and ministers for deliberation,
and also consulted Zhílì Zǒngdū Lǐ Hóngzhāng.
Lǐ Hóngzhāng said:
“According to the Zhōu Guān,
when artisans construct a state,
the shìshì and míngtáng
are limited to five rooms.
Zhèng's commentary states
that the five rooms are all in one hall.
According to this,
Zhūzǐ's diagram of the shìshì and kin temples arranged southward in sequence
does not entirely conform to the system.
As for building sleeping halls or increasing square halls,
these are not found in ancient systems.
What Lǐ Qīnwáng and others said
is not without merit.
In the ancestral temple system of our dynasty,
the spirits of the ancestors
are gathered in one room.
If they were suddenly moved or changed,
how would the spirits find peace?
The Tàimiào has double walls,
courtyards, terraces, and halls,
each with an established form.
Considering ancient and modern practices,
changing the temple is not convenient.
Establishing a system according to the times,
it is appropriate to follow the precedent of adding niches to the Fèngxian Diàn.
Some deliberators might consider it too simple.
Upon examining ancient rites, enshrinement in the temple often involved successive movements,
but only changing decorations or eaves,
not greatly altering the old temple.
Today's niche seats are like the 'kǎnshì' (recessed chambers) of the Jìn and Sòng dynasties.
Jìn Huáyuán suggested that the temple hall should be limited by the capacity for the spirit tablets,
without being bound by a fixed number.
Wáng Dǎo and Wēn Jiào discussed it back and forth,
and only then were kǎnshì added.
The Sòng dynasty added eight rooms,
which Cài Xiāng diagrammed.
How is today's addition of niches
different from this?”
He further stated:
“The Fèngxian Diàn is the ancient yuánmiào,
which is different from the Tàimiào.
However, during the Yōngzhèng era, it was decreed that the spirit tablets in the Fèngxian Diàn and the Tàimiào should be identical.
Established precedents can be followed,
and one cannot say that the system of adding niches cannot be emulated in the Tàimiào.
As for the removal (tiāocài), though it is a regular practice,
there is no clear ritual text for the chamber where the removed tablets are stored.
Zhèng Kāngchéng said that during the Zhōu dynasty, removed tablets were stored in the Tàimiào and the permanent ancestral temples of civil and military officials,
meaning that removed tablets coexisted in the same temple as unremoved ancestors.
Hence, the temple was also called 'tiāo'.
The Jìn dynasty stored them in the western side chambers,
which was questioned as non-ritualistic at the time,
but later generations adopted it as a precedent.
Confucian scholars considered the ancient 'tiāo jiāshì' (removed side chambers) to be rather an arbitrary term.
Since the current temple is different from ancient ones,
the matter of removal should not be lightly discussed.
Only what Chún Qīnwáng presented
is capable of guiding His Majesty to great magnanimity
and adapting the temple system to suit the circumstances.”
From this, the decision was finally made.
In the fifth year,
Mùzōng and Empress Xiàozhét were enshrined in the ancestral temple.
They were placed in the eastern row,
facing west,
next to Xuānzōng.
In the seventh year,
Empress Xiàozhēn ascended and was enshrined,
next to Xiàodé.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
Empress Xiàoqīn ascended and was enshrined,
next to Xiàozhēn.
That year, the matter of Dézōng's enshrinement in the ancestral temple was deliberated.
The ritual officials stated:
"Brothers share the same zhāomù sequence,
but the Mù position is left empty in one chamber."
The other officials who debated the rites,
those who emphasized the imperial lineage,
believed that different zhāomù sequences would be inconvenient;
those who emphasized the imperial succession,
in turn, believed that the same zhāomù sequence would be inappropriate.
However, Grand Secretary Zhāng Zhīdòng alone advocated:
"In ancient times, there was the rite of removing ancestral tablets from the temple (tiāoqiān),
so brothers' zhāomù sequence ought to be the same.
Now, without the rite of tiāoqiān,
brothers' zhāomù sequence can be different."
The deliberation was then settled.
That autumn,
an imperial edict stated:
"In our dynasty's temple system,
in the front hall, from Tàizǔ downwards, the seven generations all face south,
while from Xuānzōng downwards, the three generations are arranged to face east and west,
which differs from what the ancients called Mù facing north and Zhāo facing south.
The Mù and Dé temples,
both being 'not to be removed for a hundred generations,'
should adhere to Zhūzǐ's theory,
arranging zhāomù by left and right,
and not by zhāomù as a measure of seniority or inferiority.
Rites arise from righteousness;
one should not, due to discrepancies in classical interpretations,
adhere too rigidly.
Dézōng's enshrinement in the ancestral temple
shall be in the middle hall, in the fifth Mù position, next to the western column;
in the front hall, the position shall be in the Mù position west of Wénzōng's seat, facing east.
This embodies the principle of concurrent enshrinement from previous reigns,
comforts the spirits of the past emperors in heaven,
and shall be established as a permanent regulation.
The order of positions in the Fèngxiān Hall shall also follow this."
Seasonal Sacrifices In the early days of Tàizōng's establishment of the state,
on Qīngmíng and New Year's Eve,
he personally visited Tàizǔ's mausoleum,
which is where the seasonal sacrifices began.
In the first year of Chóngdé,
the Grand Ancestral Temple was completed.
There were seasonal sacrifices in the four first months (mèng),
fresh offerings every month,
and sacrifices on imperial birthdays, death anniversaries, Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, and at the end of the year.
In the fifth month, cherries were offered,
and an order was given to present them to the Grand Ancestral Temple.
All newly harvested fruits and grains
were first offered before being presented to the emperor,
and this was established as a rule.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
the system of seasonal sacrifices was established:
in the first month of spring, a day in the first ten days was chosen;
in the three other first months, the first day of the month was used;
and the musical performance had six movements.
In the second year,
an order was given to perform sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple according to the Fèngxiān Hall's rituals,
including reading the prayer and performing the sacrifice.
Officials were dispatched to sacrifice at the Fúlíng, Zhāolíng, and the four ancestral temples,
offering only incense, candles, wine, and fruit,
without reading prayers.
On the first day of the seventh month,
the autumn sacrifices to the Grand Ancestral Temple and the four ancestral temples,
and the Zhōngyuán sacrifice to the mausoleums,
all used cattle and sheep.
Soon after, it was stipulated that the sacrificial rites for the four ancestral temples should follow those of the capital,
using raw sacrificial animals.
Furthermore, cooked beef was used for sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple,
and the offering of cooked meat (jìnzuò) was abolished.
In the eighth year,
the system of imperial personal sacrifices was established,
with drinking of sacrificial wine (yǐnfú) and receiving of sacrificial meat (shòuzuò) as at the Altar of Heaven (Huányuánqiú).
Music was played, and both civil and military ceremonial dances (yìwǔ) were performed.
In the twelfth year of Kāngxī,
following the advice of ritual officials,
sacrifices at the Grand Ancestral Temple
were to begin at dawn.
In the spring of the twenty-fourth year,
after personally performing the sacrifice,
an edict stated:
"I have seen the ceremonial officer announce the prayer,
and when it came to my name,
his voice was not elevated.
The rites state that a son's name is called before his father,
and descendants refer to their ancestors by name;
how can this be treated lightly?
Henceforth, let this be a warning."
In the eleventh year of Yōngzhèng,
Shìzōng noted that there was no incense offering at temple sacrifices
and no kneeling presentation for silk (bó) and wine (jué),
and ordered Grand Secretaries and ritual officials to deliberate on adding these.
Soon after, they reported:
"Among the great sacrifices, none is more important than the Altar of Heaven,
and no filial offering is greater than that matching heaven.
The rites of the ancestral temple
should be considered alongside those of the Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì).
On the day of sacrificing at the Shèjì,
the Emperor personally goes to offer incense,
and the Grand Ancestral Temple should naturally follow suit.
As for silk and wine, if they are not personally presented,
and the Emperor stands at the bowing position,
it is because it is considered secondary to the Altar of Heaven.
It is best to retain the old ritual."
This was approved.
It was also decreed that the spirit tablets in the Grand Ancestral Temple should follow the system of the Fèngxiān Hall,
with the revered ancestor placed in the center.
Officials of the Tàicháng Temple were requested to present the tablets,
and imperial guards were used for offering silk and wine,
but this was later changed to using imperial clan officials.
Upon Gāozōng's ascension,
it was decreed that during the three years of mourning,
when sacrificing at the temple, the Emperor should wear court robes and music should be played as before,
but for fasting and purification, plain clothes should be worn,
and the cap should have a tassel.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
following the advice of ritual officials,
the honorific posthumous titles of the successive emperors were inscribed on the prayer tablet.
When the incense and silk were sent for burning, they would pass through the central path,
and the Emperor would turn to stand on the east side,
waiting for the officials carrying the prayer and silk to exit,
then return to his position,
as in the sacrifices at the Altar of Heaven.
Soon after, it was decreed that incense should be offered daily,
with the temple guardian officials performing the rites.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, officials from the Tàicháng Temple were used.
Later, this was changed to using imperial clan princes and dukes in rotation.
In the twelfth year,
an edict stated that imperial clan officials should be used for offering silk and wine at the Grand Ancestral Temple,
to familiarize them with rites and temper their character.
The Zōngrénfǔ (Imperial Clan Court) princes and dukes were commanded to supervise,
and later it was again stipulated that Juéluó (Collateral Imperial Clan) officials should be used for offering silk and wine in the rear hall.
According to established practice,
for temple sacrifices,
the Emperor would leave the palace by carriage,
change to a sedan chair outside the Tàihémén.
Upon entering the street gate,
to the right of the spirit path,
he would walk into the south gate,
and proceed to the temporary resting place outside the Jǐmén.
He would enter and ascend the eastern steps,
enter the front hall gate,
and take his bowing position.
After the ceremony was completed,
he would exit as he entered.
All entrances were made from the left.
In the thirty-seventh year,
as the Emperor grew older,
some ceremonial procedures were slightly reduced.
When entering the temple,
he would change to entering by sedan chair from the Quēzuǒmén into the northwest gate,
and outside the temple's north gate,
enter by carriage.
He would proceed to the foot of the eastern steps outside the Jǐmén.
He would walk through the gate,
ascend the steps, and enter the hall.
After performing the rites,
he would exit in the same manner.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
the seating order for the seasonal sacrifices in the front hall was established.
Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, Shìzǔ (the Emperor's father) and his empress all faced south.
Shèngzǔ (the Emperor's father) and his empress were in the eastern position facing west.
Shìzōng (the Emperor's father) and his empress were in the western position facing east.
Gāozōng (the Emperor's father) and his empress were in the secondary eastern position facing west.
Subsequent emperors and empresses followed this seating order.
In the spring seasonal sacrifice of the eighth year,
the ritual officials divined a propitious day, the sixth day of the first month.
Rénzōng observed three days of fasting prior.
It happened to coincide with Gāozōng's death anniversary,
and the colors of the attire did not match,
so it was ordered to change to the eighth day.
Thereafter, all spring sacrifices were performed on the eighth, ninth, or tenth day of the first lunar month.
In the fourth year of Dàoguāng,
an edict stated that the offering of sacrificial wine and meat (xièfúzuò) at temple sacrifices should follow the rites of the Shèjì,
with princes, dukes, and all officials performing the three kneelings and nine prostrations.
When Mùzōng and Dézōng first ascended the throne,
seasonal sacrifices and grand quinquennial sacrifices were performed by proxy by imperial princes;
only after taking personal control of government did they personally attend.
During the Xuāntǒng reign, the Prince Regent performed them on behalf of the emperor.
祫祭 (Xiáji) — The joint ancestral sacrifice. Historically, the dì and xiá sacrifices were performed separately.
The discussions on ritual were varied,
but lacked adherence to ancient teachings.
The Qīng system had xiá but no dì.
The practice of offering sacrifices in the ancestral temple on New Year's Eve
actually began with Tàizōng.
Shìzǔ adopted this practice
and established it as a sacrificial ceremony.
In Shùnzhì sixteen years (1659),
Yuán Màogōng, the Left Vice Censor-in-chief, requested the performance of the xiá sacrifice
to manifest filial governance.
Thus, it was decided that the grand xiá would be held on the day before New Year's Eve,
moving the spirit tablets from the rear and middle halls to the front hall.
The Four Ancestors and Tàizǔ faced south,
and Tàizōng was positioned in the east, facing west.
The day before, officials were dispatched to inform the rear and middle halls,
and to observe fasting and inspect the sacrificial animals.
On the appointed day, Shìzǔ personally attended,
the ritual being like the seasonal sacrifices.
From then on, this became an annual custom.
Soon after, it was stipulated that the music and dance for the xiá sacrifice would be performed outside the hall.
