During the Kāngxī era,
the censor Lǐ Shíqiān requested the performance of the dì sacrifice.
The ritual minister Zhāng Yùshū submitted a memorial, stating:
"Studies of the ritual system show inconsistencies regarding the dì sacrifice.
Some say that the Yú and Xià dynasties performed dì to Huángdì,
and the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties to Dìkù,
all of whom were co-sacrificed at the Altar of Heaven;
some say that the ancestor from whom one originated was the 'sense-born emperor,'
and was sacrificed in the southern suburb;
some say that the Altar of Heaven, the Altar of Earth, and the Ancestral Temple constituted the three dì sacrifices: earlier scholars have all refuted these as incorrect.
Regarding the dì sacrifice in the Ancestral Temple,
the explanations are particularly inconsistent.
Some say that dì only extended to demolished temples,
while others say that the 'Chángfā' poem was for the Yīn dì,
and the 'Yǒng' poem for the Zhōu dì,
and that both the existing and demolished temples were sacrificed together.
Only Zhào Kuāng and Lù Chún of the Táng dynasty believed that dì was different from xiá,
and did not include all temples.
Kings established the temple of the progenitor,
and traced the emperor from whom the progenitor originated,
co-sacrificing the progenitor with him,
hence it was called dì.
As for one xiá every three years,
and one dì every five years,
this explanation originated with Hàn scholars,
and later generations followed it.
The dì rituals of Hàn, Táng, and Sòng
did not investigate the origin of the progenitor,
but merely combined the ancestors of all temples within a five-year period,
performing the xiá-dì in the Ancestral Temple.
Generally, there was a dì sacrifice before the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
but its system is not detailed.
After the Hàn and Táng dynasties, there was the name dì,
but it was indistinguishable from xiá.
Zhōu took Hòujì as its progenitor,
and Dìkù as his origin,
but there was no position for Kù in the Grand Temple,
so the xiá sacrifice did not include him.
Only during the dì sacrifice was Kù's position established,
with Jì co-sacrificed.
When applied to later generations,
it could not be fully harmonized.
Therefore, Sòng Shénzōng abolished the dì ritual.
In the early Hóngwǔ era of Míng, some requested its implementation,
but the general consensus did not lead to its execution.
During the Jiājìng era,
a vacant position was established
to sacrifice the Imperial Progenitor Emperor,
with Tàizǔ co-sacrificed;
this matter was inappropriate,
and the ritual was soon abolished.
When the state was first established,
honorable titles were posthumously conferred upon the Four Ancestors,
and temples were erected for their worship,
starting from Zhàozǔ.
Tàizǔ's merits and virtues were profound,
and he should be the ancestral temple lord for ten thousand generations,
but tracing his origin,
Zhàozǔ was most prominent in founding the great enterprise.
Currently, in the Grand Temple sacrificial rituals,
the four seasonal sacrifices are performed separately in the front and rear halls,
to express their respective veneration.
At year-end, the xiá sacrifice is performed in the front hall,
to collectively present their reverence.
Several libations are offered in a year,
and benevolence, filial piety, sincerity, and reverence
have already reached their utmost.
A dì sacrifice every five years
is not necessarily needed."
Thus, the proposal was dismissed.
In Qiánlóng thirty-seven years (1772), during the grand xiá,
the Emperor personally went to Zhàozǔ's position to offer incense,
while the rest of the imperial sons and princes went separately
to their positions to perform the rituals according to the usual ceremony.
The ritual proceedings for visiting the temple were reduced, similar to the seasonal sacrifices.
In sixty years (1795), as the abdication was approaching,
he personally offered incense at all nine temples.
In Jiāqìng four years (1799),
it was decided that for the year-end xiá sacrifice,
the seating arrangement in the front hall would be the same as for the seasonal sacrifices.
In Xiánfēng eight years (1858),
Wénzōng's illness had just subsided,
and a prince performed the xiá sacrifice on his behalf,
however, before the sacrifice, he still personally went to bow and kneel.
As for the xiá sacrifice performed at specific times,
ancient rites stipulated that after the three-year mourning period for the Son of Heaven,
the spirits of the ancestors were gathered for sacrifice,
which was called the jí sacrifice (auspicious sacrifice).
In Yōngzhèng two years (1724),
Zhū Shì, Minister of Personnel, stated:
"Your Majesty is supremely benevolent and greatly filial,
mourning for three years as if it were one day.
Now that the mourning period is complete,
I request a xiá sacrifice at the Grand Temple,
signifying the return to auspiciousness and the release from sorrow."
The decree was approved.
In the second month of the following year (1725),
the Emperor went to the temple to perform the xiá sacrifice,
following the ceremony of the year-end grand xiá.
Thereafter, the xiá sacrifice performed after the completion of mourning followed this precedent.
Addition of Posthumous Titles and Epithets. In Chóngdé one year (1636),
Tàizōng received the honorary title,

and posthumously enfeoffed the progenitor as Zéwáng (King Zé), his great-grandfather as Qìngwáng (King Qìng), his great-great-grandfather as Chāngwáng (King Chāng), and his grandfather as Fúwáng (King Fú).
He conferred the honorable posthumous titles of Wǔ Huángdì (Martial Emperor) upon Tàizǔ and Xiàocí Huánghòu (Empress Xiàocí).
On that very day, he personally sacrificed at the Grand Temple.
The next day,
all officials presented their congratulations.
In Shùnzhì one year (1644),
jade tablets and jade seals were presented to Tàizǔ, Empress Xiàocí, and Tàizōng,
and enshrined in the Grand Temple.
The tablets were eight inches and eight fen long,
three inches and nine fen wide,
and four fen thick.
There were tens of tablets,
with ascending and descending dragons engraved on the front and back pages.
The seals were four inches and two fen square,
one inch and five fen thick,
with a knob two inches and seven fen high,
four inches and two fen long,
and three inches and five fen wide.
The seal cases were made of gold.
All tablets and seals for the Grand Temple were made of jade,
of a bluish-white color.
The inscription on the tablets used the lí style (a formal, solemn script),
and the inscription on the seals matched the posthumous titles,
reading
"Seal of Emperor Mǒu Zǔ Mǒu Zōng Mǒu Huángdì,"
and for empresses,
"Seal of Empress Mǒu."
In five years (1648),
Zewáng was posthumously honored as Zhàozǔ Yuán Huángdì (Progenitor Emperor Yuán),
and his consort as Yuán Huánghòu (Empress Yuán);
Qìngwáng as Xīngzǔ Zhí Huángdì (Progenitor Emperor Zhí),
and his consort as Zhí Huánghòu (Empress Zhí);
Chāngwáng as Jǐngzǔ Yì Huángdì (Progenitor Emperor Yì),
and his consort as Yì Huánghòu (Empress Yì);
Fúwáng as Xiǎnzǔ Xuān Huángdì (Progenitor Emperor Xuān),
and his consort as Xuān Huánghòu (Empress Xuān).
After enshrinement,
the rites were performed like the seasonal sacrifices.
Three days later,
congratulations were offered as per ceremony.
In seven years (1650),
the honorable posthumous title was conferred upon Xiàoduān Wén Huánghòu (Empress Xiaoduanwen).
In nine years (1652),
jade tablets and seals were presented to the emperors and empresses of the Four Ancestors.
In eighteen years (1661),
the honorable posthumous title was conferred upon Shìzǔ.
Before the date, a fast was observed,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices and inform Heaven, Earth, the Ancestral Temple, and the Altars of Land and Grain.
On the appointed day,
the Dì, in plain clothes, proceeded to the Tàihémén.
After inspecting the cè and bǎo,
the Dàxuéshì placed them in a decorated palanquin,
which was borne by xiàowèi.
It was led by the Imperial staff,
and the Emperor's carriage followed.
The Wánggōng and all officials knelt and waited at their assigned positions,
then followed.
Upon arriving outside the main gate of the Shòuhuángdiàn, the Dì alighted from his carriage,
entering through the left gate,
while the decorated palanquin entered through the right gate.
Two Dàxuéshì knelt and respectfully placed the cè and bǎo on the altar.
The Dì took his position
and led the assembled officials in the ritual of three kneelings and nine kowtows.
The Zàn yǐn intoned,
"Kneel,"
then intoned,
"Present the cè."
The Dàxuéshì bearing the cè knelt on the left
and advanced to present it to the Dì.
When finished,
it was handed to the Dàxuéshì kneeling on the right, who placed it on the central altar.
The Zàn yǐn intoned,
"Present the bǎo,"
and the procedure was as before.
The Zàn yǐn intoned,
"Proclaim the cè."
The official proclaiming the cè knelt and declared:
"The posthumous title is 'Tǐtiān Lóngyùn Yīngruì Qīnwén Dàdé Hónggōng Zhìrén Chúnxiào Zhāng Huángdì,'
and the temple name is 'Shìzǔ.'"
After the proclamation of the cè was complete,
the Zàn yǐn intoned,
"Proclaim the bǎo,"
and the ceremony was likewise.
The ritual of three kneelings and nine kowtows was performed,
and offerings were made simultaneously.
When finished,
the silk cè, bǎo, and zhùbó were taken to the liao place to be burned.
Two Dàxuéshì,
bearing the xiāngcè and xiāngbǎo, led the catafalque to its place of interment,
performing one kneeling and three kowtows.
The next day, an imperial edict was issued to the empire.
Whenever posthumous titles were conferred upon a deceased Dì or Hòu,
the xiāngcè and xiāngbǎo were presented before the jīyán,
then interred at the shānlíng.
The juàncè and bǎo were sent to the liao,
and the yùcè and yùbǎo were buried in the Tàimiào after a propitious date was divined.
Subsequent practices followed this pattern.
Initially, Tàizǔ's posthumous title was "Chéngtiān Guǎngyùn Shèngdé Shénggōng Zhàojì Lìjí Rénxiào Wǔ Huángdì,"
and Tàizōng's was "Yìngtiān Xīngguó Hóngdé Zhāngwǔ Kuānwēn Rénshèng Ruìxiào Wén Huángdì."
Shèngzǔ, in continuing the imperial legacy,
added six characters,
"Ruìwǔ Hóngwén Dìngyè,"
to Tàizǔ's title,
and changed his temple name to Gāohuángdì.
To Tàizōng's title,
four characters, "Lóngdào Xiǎngōng,"
were added,
and his temple name remained as before.
Following the advice of the ritual officials,
the ceremony was to be performed after Shìzǔ's enshrinement in the ancestral temple.
The following year,
a posthumous title was conferred upon Cíhé Huángtàihòu.
In the twenty-seventh year,
a posthumous title was conferred upon Xiàozhuāng Tàihuángtàihòu.
In the fifty-seventh year,
a posthumous title was conferred upon Xiàohuì Huángtàihòu.
She was
Shèngzǔ's birth mother.
On the day of her enshrinement in the ancestral temple,
it was ordered that her spirit tablet be placed above Cíhé's.
In the winter of the sixty-first year,
Shìzōng instructed his court officials,
"The late Huángkǎo succeeded to the throne,
and should naturally be referred to as Zōng.
However, the classics state: 'An Zǔ has accomplishments, a Zōng has virtue.'
The late Huángkǎo personally established peace,
and while his succession was a matter of preserving the established order,
his achievements were those of a founder.
It is fitting to elevate his title to Zǔ,
to match his great accomplishments.
Deliberate on this thoroughly."
The deliberation stated:
"According to the Lǐjīng,
the Yǒuyúshì sacrificed to Huángdì in the dì ritual and to Kù in the jiāo ritual.
They venerated Zhuānxū as Zǔ and Yáo as Zōng.
Yet the 'Shùn Diǎn' states: 'Shùn arrived at the Wénzǔ.'
The commentary identifies this as Yáo's temple.
'Returned and arrived at the Yìzǔ' is further interpreted as Yáo's ancestor.
Combining this with venerating Zhuānxū as Zǔ,
there would be three Zǔ.
Chén Xiángdào of the Sòng dynasty said: 'Anyone who is co-sacrificed to Heaven may be called Zǔ.'
The Guóyǔ records Zhǎn Qín saying that the Yǒuyúshì revered Gāoyáng as Zǔ and sacrificed to Yáo in the jiāo ritual,
which is why Yáo was called Wénzǔ.
From Zhuānxū to Yáo,
all were descendants of Huángdì,
thus all were called Zǔ.
Furthermore, the Zhōulǐ Dàzōngbó mentions: xiá, dì, zhuīxiǎng, cháoxiǎng.
The commentary explains: 'In ancient times, in the ancestral temple, all ancestors were gathered and sacrificed to in the cháomiào,
hence the xiá ritual was called cháoxiǎng.
Considering the gathering of all ancestors insufficient,
they further performed the dì ritual for their ultimate progenitor,
hence the dì ritual was called zhuīxiǎng.'
The 'progenitor' refers to the founding ancestor,
and those below him are called 'all ancestors.'
Thus, all from the founding ancestor downwards can be called Zǔ."
Another proposal for the posthumous title stated:
"When an emperor's achievements are grand and flourishing,
he may invoke the ancient meaning of 'Zǔ has accomplishments' and be referred to as Zǔ.
We humbly believe that only a sage can magnify profound virtue,
and only an Zǔ can manifest great accomplishments."
The proposal was submitted
and approved by the Dì.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
a posthumous title was thus conferred,
and the temple name Shèngzǔ.
He further decreed:
"Tàizǔ, Tàizōng, and Shìzǔ, three sages in succession,
had towering achievements and profound virtues.
Xiàozhuāng, Xiàokāng, and Xiàohuì assisted in the prosperity and initiated auspicious eras,
their beautiful virtues flowing forth as blessings.
It is fitting to add further posthumous titles
to express filial piety."
Thereupon, additional posthumous titles were conferred:
Tàizǔ was styled Duānyì,
Tàizōng was styled Jìngmǐn,
and Shìzǔ was styled Dìngtǒng Jiànjí.
And Xiàocí, Xiàoduān, and the three empresses
all had their posthumous titles honored.
At that time, the Gōngbù enshrined the spirit tablets in the temple chambers,
decorating them with lacquer and gold.
One Zhōngshū official and one Hànlín official each wrote the new posthumous titles.
A memorial was submitted requesting two Dàxuéshì to perform the Tiánqīng ritual,
first reverently informing Tiāndì and Shèjì.
On the appointed day,
Shìzōng, in ceremonial robes, proceeded to the Tàimiào to perform the ritual of conferring posthumous titles.
After completion,
he returned to the palace,
changed into imperial robes,
and proceeded to the Fèngxiān Diàn to offer sacrifices.
Subsequent practices followed this pattern.
In the sixth year,
the jade bǎo and yùcè for the successive emperors and empresses, as well as the cè and bǎo for Shèngzǔ Huángkǎo and Huángbǐ, were carved and completed,
and enshrined in the Tàimiào.
The ceremony was as follows:
In a purified chamber of the Tàimiào, a yellow altar was set up,
with decorated curtains on both sides.
The cè and bǎo were displayed in the center.
Wáng and ministers, in court robes, attended to the affairs.
The Dì, in ceremonial robes, respectfully inspected them,
performing one kneeling and three bows.
They were then placed in a decorated palanquin,
and the procession proceeded as in the earlier ceremony.
After being placed on the altar,
the Dì entered and performed the ritual as before.
The cè and bǎo were collected in the central hall
and stored separately in golden caskets.
The Dì, in turn, offered incense,
performing one kneeling and three bows.
The ritual was completed.
Upon Gāozōng's ascension to the throne,
he added further posthumous titles to the successive emperors and empresses,
decreeing:
"While there are regulations for the auspicious titles in the ancestral temple,
the sincerity of repaying one's origins is endless.
To express this utmost feeling,
it is not bound by constant rules."
In the forty-fifth year of Qiánlóng,
observing that the jade colors of the cè and bǎo from previous dynasties were uneven,
an order was given to select skilled artisans to carve fine jade from Hétián.
Two years later, the work was completed.
After a reverent inspection,
they were enshrined in the Tàimiào according to ritual.
The sixteen sets of old ones
were ordered to be sent to the Shèngjīng Tàimiào,
reverently stored with jade seals and golden cords.
From then on, whenever Dì or Hòu were enshrined in the temple,
separate cè and bǎo were prepared and sent to Shèngjīng,
becoming a permanent regulation.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
Rénzōng upheld the bequeathed instruction
and established a regulation:

The posthumous titles of successive emperors, having already reached twenty-four characters, and those of successive empresses, having already reached sixteen characters, would no longer be considered for additions.
In the second year of the Kāngxī Emperor's reign (1663),
the site for the tomb of Shìzǔ (the Shùnzhì Emperor) was chosen at Fèngtái Shān in Zūnhuà
and named Xiàolíng.
Before this, Shìzǔ had been hunting here.
He stopped his horse, looked around, and said:
"The imperial aura of this mountain is verdant and dense;
it can serve as my longevity palace."
He then took off his waist-sash and threw it,
and instructed his attendants, saying:
"The place where the sash falls shall be the burial site."
When the mausoleum was completed,
everyone was amazed that it was such an auspicious location.
The festivals of Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Dōngzhì, and Suìmù were designated as the four major annual sacrifices.
Additionally, the underground palaces of Fúlíng and Zhāolíng were rebuilt.
Upon completion of the work,
a solemn announcement was made upon the enshrining of the tablets,
and sacrifices were offered as for a grand banquet (dàxiǎng).
The spirit tablets were placed in Lóng'ēn Diàn.
Shrines, precious beds, curtains, quilts, and clothes racks were made following the style of the Tàimiào.
Whenever officials visited the mausoleum for official business,
those of the third rank and above performed their rites outside the luóchéngmén (walled city gate).
On a day of sacrifice,
officials of the second rank and above were permitted to enter the city to accompany the mausoleum guardians in offering sacrifices.
Upon returning,
they would pay their respects and take leave.
Whenever visiting the mausoleum,
one would proceed eastward through the shímén (stone gate).
Princes (wáng) and Bèi勒 would perform three genuflections and nine kowtows outside Lóng'ēn Mén.
The duty officer would open the gate.
Bèizi and officials of the third rank and above did not do so;
all were guided by the officials in charge of sacrifices.
On a day of sacrifice, this was exempted.
At this time,功德碑 (monuments of merit and virtue) were erected at the three mausoleums.
Thereafter, whenever a mausoleum was built,
a stele was erected,
following the established practice.
In the eighth year (1669),
the four seasonal grand sacrifices were standardized.
Duluó Bèi勒 and below,
but above the rank of Fèngguó Jiāngjūn and Juéluó Nán, were dispatched to perform the rites.
In the autumn of the following year,
the emperor escorted the Tàihuáng Tàihòu and Huáng Tàihòu, accompanied by the empress, to visit Xiàolíng.
The day before,
he personally made an announcement at the Tàimiào.
The next day, the imperial procession set forth.
The imperial regalia (lǔbù) were displayed,
but no music was played.
Upon arriving at the mausoleum,
the Tàihuáng Tàihòu sat on the east side of the fāngchéng (square city),
offered wine, and expressed grief.
The Huáng Tàihòu, leading the empress and others, stood in front of the mínglóu (spirit tower),
performed six obeisances, three genuflections, and three kowtows,
then expressed grief and offered wine,
and kowtowed three more times.
They returned to the temporary imperial residence (xínggōng).
All visits of the Huáng Tàihòu to mausoleums followed this precedent.
The next day,
the emperor again visited Lóng'ēn Diàn
to perform the dàxiǎng ritual.
The day after that,
a yellow tent was set up in front of the hall,
paper offerings were burned,
and a prayer text was read to offer sacrifices.
The ceremony concluded.
Returning to the capital,
an announcement was again made at the Tàimiào.
Two days later,
the emperor ascended the Tàihé Diàn,
and all officials presented their congratulations.
In the autumn of the following year,
the imperial carriage arrived in Shèngjīng.
After visiting Fúlíng and Zhāolíng,
the emperor summoned the generals and others, bestowed wine upon them,
and instructed the chief and deputy supervisors of the mausoleum guardians, saying:
"Your duty is to oversee the sacrifices.
You must personally and reverently supervise all sacrificial offerings,
ensuring utmost sincerity and respect,
to accord with Our filial piety."
Upon returning, he received congratulations at Dàqīng Mén,
hosted a banquet for his ministers,
and presented awards to the mausoleum officials and soldiers.
For Yǒnglíng, princes and high ministers were dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Officials were also dispatched to the tombs of Yǐng Qīnwáng, Kèqín Jùnwáng, Zhíyì Gōng Fèi Yīngdōng, and other meritorious nobles to pour libations.
On the day of return to the capital,
an announcement was made at the temple as per custom.
In the twenty-first year (1682),
after the pacification of Diān (Yúnnán),
the emperor visited the mausoleums in both capitals
according to the initial rites.
Upon returning to the capital,
a solemn announcement was made at Fèngxiān Diàn.
From then on, visiting the mausoleums and offering sacrifices became a regular practice after quelling rebellions.
In the sixtieth year (1721),
on the sixtieth anniversary of his accession to the throne,
the emperor commanded Shìzōng (the Yōngzhèng Emperor) to lead the imperial princes and grandsons to Shèngjīng.
The imperial princes offered sacrifices at Zhāolíng,
the imperial grandsons at Yǒnglíng,
and the emperor personally went to Fúlíng for the grand sacrifice.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (1723),
the mausoleum of Shèngzǔ (the Kāngxī Emperor) was named Jǐnglíng.
The following year,
the Qīngmíng sacrifices were offered according to regulations.
In the eighth year (1730), on the Dōngzhì festival,
which coincided with the death anniversary of Shèngzǔ,
the Board of Rites stated that for major mausoleum sacrifices,
a tàiláo (grand offering of ox, pig, and sheep) should be used,
with offerings of silk and wine cups,
and the reading of a prayer text.
Officials dispatched to preside over the sacrifice were to wear court attire.
In the thirteenth year (1735), for the grand sacrifices of Qīngmíng and Dōngzhì,
the practice was changed to dispatching dukes in rotation.
On the full moon day (wàngrì) of the seventh month,
generals, assistant ministers, and others presided over the sacrifices.
For the new moon (shuò), full moon (wàng), and death anniversaries (jìchén),
it was decided that the chief supervisor (zǒngguǎn), holding the official seal (guānfáng), would preside over the sacrifices,
performing the three genuflections and nine kowtows ritual.
In the first year of Qiánlóng (1736),
six imperial clansmen, including the Fǔguó Jiāngjūn, were commanded to relocate and be stationed in Shěnyáng,
and were granted land and residences,
to perform sacrifices at the appropriate times of the year.
In the second year (1737),
an edict was issued changing the presiding officials for the new moon and full moon sacrifices to Bèi勒, dukes, and ministers in rotation.
Concerned about inconsistent ceremonial procedures,
two Master of Ceremonies (zànlǐláng) were added to guide the entry and exit,
though they still did not chant the rites.
In the third year (1738), on Qīngmíng,
the emperor visited Shìzōng's Tàilíng.
In the sixth year (1741),
the four seasonal grand sacrifices for the three mausoleums were standardized.
For sacrifices on death anniversaries,
two stationed generals were designated to perform the rites.
In the seventh year (1742),
wine cup stands (juédiàn) were added to the three mausoleums
to prepare for the rituals.
In the eighth year (1743),
it was decided that visiting mausoleums should follow the same procedure as the emperor's personal sacrifices at the Tàimiào,
and this was incorporated into the ceremonial regulations.
Subsequently,
the emperor escorted the Huáng Tàihòu to visit the ancestral mausoleums.
The ritual procedures followed the precedent of the Kāngxī period.
Thereafter, all three visits were conducted in the same manner.
In the autumn of the forty-third year (1778),
after visiting Yǒnglíng and Fúlíng,
an edict was issued stating:
"Reflecting on the old territories of Liáoshěnyáng,
having toured them repeatedly,
my heart reveres the old traditions,
hoping they will never be forgotten.
The flourishing and peaceful reign of the imperial lineage
is all due to the arduous founding efforts of the past.
Future generations of descendants
should look upon these original peaks and be inspired to ponder,
and bow before the pines and cypresses to gain enlightenment.
They should silently reflect on how to continuously receive Heaven's favor
and how to successfully continue the legacy of their ancestors.
They should understand the difficulty of maintaining what has been established,
and diligently avoid any decline.
Thus, may the flourishing prosperity
last for myriad years.
Otherwise,
if they disregard the old capital,
and dread distant travels,
or merely visit the ancestral mausoleums by chance,
unmoved and indifferent,
treating it like sightseeing historical sites,
this is to forget their roots.
Shèngjīng is a fundamentally important place,
the origin of our auspicious beginnings.
Future generations must personally experience and observe it.
Do not fail to heed Our words!"
In the fifth year of Jiāqìng (1800), on Qīngmíng,
the emperor went to Chāngruì Shān to visit Gāozōng's Yùlíng.
First, the earth-spreading ceremony (fūtǔ) was performed,
followed by the grand sacrifice (dàxiǎng).
The mausoleum officials had prepared clean earth in baskets in advance.
When the emperor changed into plain white robes in the dressing chamber,
the attending officials, dressed in plain robes,
removed the tassels from their hats,
and followed to the fāngchéng.
The relevant officials presented yellow cloth shoe covers.
The emperor put them on,
and his attendants did likewise.
They ascended from the eastern stone steps to the east side of the stone balustrade of the bàochéng (precious city).
The mausoleum ministers presented the earth in baskets.
Following the imperial carriage, they knelt and offered it at the earth-spreading spot.
The emperor respectfully took it and spread it.
When finished,
he handed back the basket,
descended,
and removed his shoe covers.
Then he changed into his imperial robes,
with tassels reattached to his hat,
and the attending officials also changed.
The Board of Rites requested to proceed with the grand sacrifice.
The emperor went to Lóng'ēn Diàn to perform the rites,
read the prayer,
and made three offerings.
Generally, on Qīngmíng Day, when visiting the imperial tombs and adding soil,
during the mourning period,
the Emperor personally performed the rites.
Ten years later,
the Emperor first visited Yǒnglíng.
He wore plain clothes,
and proceeded to the steps behind Qǐyùndiàn Hall,
where he performed three kneelings and nine kowtows.
The relevant officials presented the offering table.
He performed three kowtows and three libations.
After completing the rites,
he expressed sorrow.
The next day, in court attire, he performed the grand sacrifice.
Visiting Fúlǐng and Zhāolíng was done in the same manner.
Later, due to discrepancies and errors in the sacrificial vessels,
Shìchén, the Shìláng of the Lǐbù in Shèngjīng, was dismissed from his post.
An edict was issued stating,
"Fēngpèi is the old capital;
ministers should not forget it."
This edict was circulated to all public offices,
indicating the importance attached to these sacrifices.
In the eighth year of Dàoguāng,
when visiting Yùlíng and Chānglíng,
the Grand Councilors followed the Emperor into the gate.
This was commanded to be established as a precedent.
In the ninth year,
the Empress Dowager was escorted to Shèngjīng to visit the three imperial tombs,
following the established rites.
In the first year of Xiánfēng, the Eastern Tombs were visited;
in the fifth year, the Western Tombs were visited.
When Empress Xiàozhēn visited Tàilíng,
female tomb officials acted as guides.
Upon entering the gate, everyone proceeded from the left.
Rituals were performed in front of the Mínglóu tower,
consisting of six bows, three kneelings, and three kowtows.
Female officials presented the offering table.
The Empress performed three kowtows and three libations,
and expressed sorrow during the Western sacrifice.
Next, visiting Chānglíng and Mùlíng followed the initial rites.
During the Tóngzhì and Guāngxù eras, these practices were followed entirely.
From Xiàolíng and Jǐnglíng downwards,
Shìzōng's tomb is Tàilíng,
Gāozōng's Yùlíng,
Rénzōng's Chānglíng,
Xuānzōng's Mùlíng,
Wénzōng's Dìnglíng,
Mùzōng's Huìlíng.
All are located in the two prefectures of Yì and Zūnhuà in Zhílì,
and are referred to as the Eastern and Western Tombs.
The Eastern Tombs are on Fèng táishān Mountain,
also known as Chángshān Mountain;
the Western Tombs are in Tàipíngyù Valley,
also known as Yǒngníngshān Mountain.
Both are dedicated to Fāngzé.
Officials for offerings were appointed,
and estates were established.
For the grand sacrifice in the Lóng'ēndiàn Hall, sacrificial prayers and silks were used.
On that day, bright lanterns were lit.
One ox, two sheep, and four wine vessels were used.
The Emperor and Empress shared the same altar position.
One set of offerings for honoring ancestors was arranged,
eighteen vessels for soup, rice, dried meat, and mincemeat,
and sixty-five vessels for pastries and fruits.
The sacrificial animals were placed on a zǔ (sacrificial stand),
and silks were placed in baskets.
Wine was poured into zūn (vessels),
supported by a zhōu (stand).
A coarse cloth covered the spoon implements.
If an Imperial Noble Consort was co-worshiped,
she would be positioned to the west, facing east,
with one plain silk,
and eleven fewer vessels for pastries and fruits.
During the Winter Solstice and festive celebrations, expressions of sorrow were omitted.
When officials were dispatched to perform sacrifices, court attire was worn.
They ascended and descended from the west steps,
and entered and exited through the right side of the gate.
When imperial princes visited the tombs,
they dismounted at the xiàmǎbēi (dismounting stele),
and ascended the left steps outside Lóng'ēnmén Gate.
They performed three kneelings and nine kowtows,
without pronouncements
or libations.
For concubine burial grounds, officials were appointed as per regulations,
a xiǎngdiàn (sacrificial hall) was built,
and spirit tablets were set up.
Quarterly, officials were dispatched to offer wine,
performing two kneelings and six kowtows,
without pronouncements.
They entered and exited through the left gate of the hall.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, the offering officials performed the rites.
During the Guāngxù era,
when the Emperor visited the Western Tombs,
he proceeded to the burial ground of Imperial Noble Consort Zhuāngshùn.
He performed one kneeling, three kowtows, and three libations.
He also issued an edict to the ritual ministers,
stipulating that sacrificial items and rituals should be of superior quality.
Thereafter, on Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Winter Solstice, and death anniversaries, princes and dukes were dispatched to offer sacrifices,
with pastries and fruits increased to sixty-five vessels.
In the early Xuāntǒng era,
Dézōng was buried in Xīnglóngyù,
named Chónglíng.
The burial grounds for imperial princes were the same as those for concubines.
During the Jiāqìng era,
the Emperor personally visited the burial ground of Imperial Crown Prince Duānhuì,
performing three offerings and three libations.
Accompanying officials also performed the rites,
with one kowtow for each offering.
This ritual was recorded in the Collected Statutes.
Chapter 62: Rites 6 (Auspicious Rites 6) Zhāozhōngcí, Xiánliángcí, meritorious officials' dedicated shrines, imperial clan's family temples, family sacrifices for officials and commoners.
Zhāozhōngcí. In the second year of Yōngzhèng, an edict stated:
"The Rites of Zhōu has officials for recording achievements.
For all those who have rendered meritorious service,
their names are written in the Tàicháng (Bureau of Ceremonies),
and they are sacrificed at the Dàzhēng (Grand Sacrifice).
The Book of Sacrifices states,
'Those who die in diligent service shall be sacrificed.'
This is to honor virtue and reward merit,
and to encourage loyalty and integrity.
Since Tàizǔ founded the dynasty,
generals and ministers,
and officials who defended territories,
who gave their lives to protect the nation,
are truly commendable and pitiable.
It is appropriate to establish a shrine in the capital,
to be sacrificed to for generations.
Those subordinate officers and soldiers who died in the line of duty
shall also be enshrined on the left and right.
This will commend and illustrate their achievements,
so that those near and far who observe and hear
may be inspired to feel loyalty and righteousness,
and biographies shall also be written for them to be passed down permanently."
Thereupon, a shrine was built inside Chóngwénmén Gate.
Annually, in the middle months of spring and autumn,
an auspicious day was chosen,
and officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Princes, dukes, and ministers were positioned in the main hall.
Seven altars were arranged,
with one sheep and one pig.
On the left, three altars,
each with one sheep and one pig.
The right side was similar.
Each altar had one plain silk, three wine cups, and five fruit plates.
Other officials were positioned in the two side halls and the rear main chamber,
each with five altars.
The two corridors each had three altars.
All had one sheep and one pig each,
as a general count.
For the soldiers enshrined,
there were thirty-six altars,
each with one plate of pork, three wine cups, and two kinds of fruit.
The Tàichángqīng presided over the sacrifice,
with the Sīguān (officials in charge) in the side halls and rear chambers performing their respective offerings.
In the sixth year,
the shrine was completed,
and named
"Zhāozhōng."
An imperial calligraphic plaque was bestowed,
reading
"Biǎojiǎng Zhōngxūn" (Commending Loyal Merits).

In the early Yōngzhèng reign (1723),

For all who had been commended and honored,
their tablets were placed in the temple,
and sacrifices were offered in spring and autumn.
In the 41st year of Qiánlóng (1776),
it was decreed that all officials of the Míng dynasty who died for the country,
having already received posthumous titles,
were also permitted to be enshrined.
Moreover, scholars (zhūshēng), commoners (wéibù), mountain recluses (shānqiáo), and hidden urbanites (shìyǐn)
who fulfilled their aspirations by dying for righteousness,
were also to follow the previous precedent.
In the 7th year of Jiāqìng (1802),
it was first ordered that temples of manifest loyalty (Zhāozhōng Cí) be built in the prefectural cities of each province,
or appended to the Guāndì and Chénghuáng temples.
All civil and military officials, as well as soldiers and local militia (xiāngyǒng), who died in battle
were to be enshrined according to their籍 (records/origins).
Officials of the Eight Banners of the 2nd rank and above who had already been enshrined in the capital's temple
were still permitted to be enshrined in the temples at the location of their death in battle.
Fifty people shared one niche,
with their tablet placed in the center.
For soldiers and militiamen, a hundred or several tens shared one tablet,
arranged on both sides,
with those from the garrison placed above those from the Green Standard Army.
In the two sacrifices of spring and autumn,
the local officials personally attended,
using a lesser offering (shǎoláo),
with fruits, incense offering, silk offering, and three libations as per ceremony.
In the 2nd year of Tóngzhì (1863),
Zēng Guófān's request was granted,
and a Zhāozhōng Cí was built in Jiāngníng,
to sacrifice the Hunan naval and land forces who died in battle.
Officials and gentry who resisted valiantly and were later restored were also permitted grand sacrifices,
and special temples were built for them.
Women who died as martyrs
also had separate temples of chastity and valor (Zhēnliè Cí) erected for them.
Xiánliáng Cí (Temple of Worthies) In the 8th year of Yōngzhèng (1730), an imperial edict stated:
"In ancient times, at the great ancestral sacrifices,
all who bestowed laws upon the people
and stabilized the nation through their toil
were listed in the sacrificial canon
and received bright oblations.
Since the founding of our dynasty,
illustrious ministers and great assistants
have appeared one after another.
Some had merits that extended to the battle-axe,
others possessed integrity as harsh as ice and frost.
Since they have established a model for all,
they ought to be honored with sacrifices.
This will inspire
generations of ministers to observe and be moved to strive,
knowing whom to admire and emulate.
Thus, may good and capable people rise with joy,
fulfilling Our great expectations.
In the capital, a site should be chosen to build a temple,
named 'Xiánliáng' (Worthy and Capable),
with sacrifices offered in spring and autumn,
forever glorifying this grand ceremony."
Consequently, a temple was built to the west of Di'ānmén,
with the main hall and rear chambers each having five bays,
and east and west wings.
Annually, in the middle months of spring and autumn,
an auspicious day was chosen,
and an official was sent to offer sacrifices.
Before the main hall, each altar had one plain silk, one sheep, one pig, and five plates of fruit.
The rear chambers had the same fruits,
but only one set of sacrificial animals and silk shared an altar.
The official presiding over the sacrifice wore a python robe,
knelt twice, kowtowed six times, and offered three libations.
The rest followed the usual ceremony.
Thereupon, it was unanimously agreed that Yíxián Qīnwáng (Prince Yí of the First Rank) Yǔnxiáng,
whose foundational meritorious service to the imperial clan was paramount,
should be ranked first.
Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretary) and Gōng (Duke) Túhǎi,
Gōng (Duke) Làitǎ,
Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretary) Zhāng Yīng,
Shàngshū (Minister) Gù Bādài, Mǎ'ěrhàn, Zhào Shēnqiáo,
Hédào Zǒngdū (Grand Canal Governor-General) Jìn Fǔ, Qísūlè,
Zǒngdū (Governor-General) Yáng Zōngrén,
Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor) Chén Bīn,
were all selected for enshrinement.
Thereafter, those who successively entered the temple included:
Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretary) Fàn Wénchéng, Bākèshídáhǎi, Ālántài, Lǐ Zhīfāng, Wú Tián, Zhāng Yùshū, Lǐ Guāngdì, Fùníng'ān, Zhāng Pénghé, Níng Wánwǒ, Wèi Yìjiè, Ésèhēi, Wáng Xī;
Lǐng Shìwèi Nèidàchén (Minister of the Imperial Bodyguard) Fúshàn, Fèiyánggǔ, Yǐndé;
Shàngshū (Minister) Lì Dùnà, Xú Cháo, Yáo Wénrán, Wèi Xiàngshū, Tāng Bīn;
Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief) Zhāng Yǒng, Wáng Jìnbǎo, Sūn Sīkè, Shī Láng;
Zǒngdū (Governor-General) Zhào Liángdòng, Yú Chénglóng, Fùlǎtǎ, Mèng Qiáofāng, Lǐ Guóyīng;
Dūtǒng (Brigade-General) Féng Guóxiàng, Lǐ Guóhàn, Gēntè;
Tǒnglǐng (Commander) Mǎngyītú;
Jiāngjūn (General) Ā'ěrnà, Àixīng'ā, Fóníliè;
Fùdūtǒng (Deputy Brigade-General) Chǔkù Bātúlǔ.
The following year, the temple was completed,
and an imperial inscription was bestowed, reading
"Chóng Zhōng Niàn Jiù" (Revere Loyalty, Remember the Old),
and tablets were set up for sacrifice.
The front hall was presided over by Nèidàchén (Minister of the Interior) or Sǎnzhi Dàchén (Minister without specific portfolio), Shàngshū (Minister), or Dūtǒng (Brigade-General).
The rear chamber used Taìchángsì Zhǎngguān (Officials of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
On the day of enshrinement,
their descendants all participated in the ceremony.
In spring and autumn, officials were sent to accompany the sacrifices.
In the twelfth year,
sacrifices were offered to Grand Secretaries Tián Cóngdiǎn and Gāo Qíwèi.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
an imperial decree ordered that all ministers enshrined who had not yet been granted posthumous titles should be retroactively granted them.
That year, sacrifices were offered to Yang Míngshí, who held the title of Shàngshū and concurrently served as Jìjiǔ;
Grand Secretary Zhū Shì;
Imperial Minister Hāshìtún;
and Shàngshū Mǐsīhàn.
In the fifth year,
sacrifices were offered to Governor-General Lǐ Wèi.
The following year,
sacrifices were offered to Shàngshū Xú Yuánmèng,
and Provincial Governor Xú Shìlín.
In the tenth year,
the positions in the shrine were reorganized.
The Yíxián Qīnwáng was enshrined in the center of the front hall.
All other ministers were placed in a single niche in the rear chamber.
Those who were earliest in generational order were placed first;
the rest were arranged in rows to the left and right,
according to generational order and rank.
Grand Secretaries were placed in front,
followed by Lead Imperial Guards, Imperial Ministers, Shàngshū, Dūtǒng, Jiāngjūn, Zǒngdū, Qiánfēng Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng, Tídū, Shìláng, Xúnfǔ, and Fùdūtǒng,
listed in descending order.
For hereditary nobles whose sons or grandsons were appointed Shàngshū or Dūtǒng,
or whose Marquises or Earls served as Shìláng or Fùdūtǒng,
their placement still depended on their official rank.
Subsequently, those enshrined included
the Chāoyǒng Qīnwáng Cèlíng,
who was placed in the niche to the left of the Yíxián Qīnwáng.

Illustrious ministers included Grand Secretaries Mǎ Qí, Yīsāng'ā, Fúmǐn, Huáng Tíngguì, Jiǎng Pǔ, Shǐ Yízhí, Liáng Shīzhèng, Láibǎo, Fù Héng, Yǐn Jìshàn, Chén Hóngmóu, Liú Lún, Liú Tǒngxūn, Shūhèdé, Gāo Jìn, Yīng Lián, Xú Běn, and Gāo Bīn;
Assistant Grand Secretary Zhàohuì;
Left Censor-in-Chief Lābùdūn;
Shàngshū Wāng Yóudūn, Lǐ Yuánliàng, and Ālǐgǔn;
Qián Chénqún, who held the title of Shàngshū;
Dūtǒng Fù Qīng;
Jiāngjūn Héqǐ, Yīlètú, and Kuílín;
Governor-Generals Nàsūtú, Chén Dàshòu, Kārjíshàn, Hènián, Wú Dáshàn, Hé Huì, Yuán Shǒudòng, Fāng Guānchéng, Sàzài; and Tídū Xǔ Shìhēng;
and Provincial Governors Pān Sīqǔ, È Bì, Lǐ Hú, and Fù Hóngliè.
Fù Hóngliè from the Yōngzhèng era,
and Lābùdūn and Fù Qīng from the Qiánlóng era,
were both enshrined in the Zhāozhōng Cí,
and now are again enshrined as worthy individuals.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
those enshrined included Grand Secretaries Fúkāng'ān, Āguì, Liú Yǒng, Wáng Jié, Zhū Guī, Dài Qūhēng, and Dǒng Gào;
Shàngshū Dǒng Bāngdá, Péng Yuánruì, and Fèng Kuān;
and Governor-General È Huī.
During the Dàoguāng reign,
those enshrined included Grand Secretaries Fùjùn, Cáo Zhènyōng, Tuōjīn, Chánglíng, Lú Yìnpǔ, Wénfú, and Wáng Dǐng;
Assistant Grand Secretaries Wāng Tíngzhēn and Chén Guānjùn;
Shàngshū Huáng Yuè and Lóngwén;
Jiāngjūn Yùlín;
Governor-Generals Yáng Yùchūn and Táo Shù;
and Governor-General of Waterways Lí Shìxù.
During the Xiánfēng reign,
those enshrined included Grand Secretaries Pān Shì'ēn, Wénqìng, and Yùchéng;
Assistant Grand Secretary Dù Shòutián;
Shìláng Dù È;
and Provincial Governor Hú Línyì.
During the Tóngzhì reign,
those enshrined included Grand Secretaries Guìliáng, Qí Jùnzǎo, Guān Wén, Wō Rén, Zēng Guófān, Ruìcháng, and Jiǎ Zhēn;
Wēng Xīncún, who held the title of Grand Secretary;
Assistant Grand Secretary Luò Bǐngzhāng;
and Governor-Generals Shěn Zhàolín and Mǎ Xīnyí.
Those enshrined during the Guāngxù reign were
Gōngzhōng Qīnwáng Yìxīn;

illustrious ministers Grand Secretaries Wénxiáng, Yīngguì, Quánqìng, Zàilíng, Zuǒ Zōngtáng, Língguì, Bǎoyún, Ēnchéng, Fúkūn, Zhāng Zhīwàn, Línshū, Élèhébù, Lǐ Hóngzhāng, Rónglù, Yùdé, Kūngāng, Chónglǐ, and Jìngxìn;
Assistant Grand Secretaries Shěn Guìfēn and Lǐ Hóngzǎo;
Jiāngjūn Chángshùn;
Governor-Generals Shěn Bǎozhēn, Dīng Bǎozhēn, Cén Yùyīng, Zēng Guóquán, and Liú Kūnyī;
Tídū Sòng Qìng;
and Provincial Governor Zhāng Yáo.
Those initially enshrined in the Xuantǒng reign were
only five individuals: Grand Secretaries Wáng Wénsháo, Zhāng Zhīdòng, Sūn Jiānài, and Lù Chuánlín,
and Assistant Grand Secretary Dài Hóngcí.
Regarding the Xiánliáng Cí (Shrines for Worthy Officials) in various provinces:
In the tenth year of Yōngzhèng,
an imperial edict stated:
"Shrines shall be built in the provincial capitals
for all civil and military ministers serving outside the capital
who are loyal, brave, majestic, and beloved,
and whose merits are widely recognized,
so that they may receive sacrifices
to encourage those in office.
For example, Jiāngjūn Cài Liáng,
Tídū Zhāng Qǐyún,
and Zǒngbīng Sū Dàyǒu and Wèi Zhùguó
are worthy of such selection."
It was established that
the spring and autumn sacrifices would follow the same dates as in the capital,
with the Zhīfǔ presiding over the sacrifices,
and the offerings and rituals also being the same.
Special Shrines for Meritorious Officials: In the eleventh year of Shùnzhì,
an imperial edict ordered the construction of a shrine for Kǒng Yǒudé.
The site was chosen three lǐ outside the Zhāngyìmén gate,
and it was named Dìngnán Wǔzhuàng Wáng Cí,
with his two consorts enshrined alongside him.
In the third year of Kāngxī,
it was decreed that spring and autumn sacrifices should be regularly performed.
Later, the Kèxī Gōng Cí was built outside the Āndìngmén gate,
enshrining the First-Class Duke Èbìlóng and his county princess, Shūshūjuéluó Shì.
Subsequently, Lead Imperial Guard Yǐndé
and Shàngshū Ālǐgǔn, along with his wife,
were also enshrined alongside during the Qiánlóng era.
Those built during the Yōngzhèng reign included
the Qínxiāng Gōng Cí outside the Cháoyángmén gate,
enshrining Dìngnán Jiāngjūn Tóng Túlái and his wife;
his eldest son Zhōngyǒng Guógāng and second son Duānchún Guówéi were
both enshrined alongside due to their military achievements.
The Wénxiāng Gōng Cí outside the Déshèngmén gate
enshrined Grand Secretary Túhǎi.
Standing parallel to the Kèxī Cí outside the Āndìngmén gate
was the Hóngyì Gōng Cí,
enshrining Guānglù Dàfū Éyìdōu,
with his wife also enshrined alongside.
Those built during the Qiánlóng reign included
the Kèxī Gōng Cí outside the Dōng'ānmén gate,
enshrining Imperial Minister Hāshìtún and his wife;
his son Chéng'ēn Gōng Mǐsīhàn and grandson Lǐ Róngbǎo;
and later, his great-grandson Grand Secretary Fù Héng was also enshrined alongside.
The Shuāngzhōng Cí inside the Chóngwénmén gate
enshrined Left Censor-in-Chief Lābùdūn and Dūtǒng Fù Qīng.
That they combined Zhāozhōng and Xiánliáng and then rebuilt a special shrine
was incomparable to others.
The Jīngyǒng Cí outside the Dì'ānmén gate
enshrined Jiāngjūn Míngruì,
and Dūtǒng Zhālāfēng'ā,
Tǒnglǐng Guānyīnbǎo,
and Zǒngbīng Lǐ Quán, Wáng Yùtíng, and Défú were also subsequently enshrined alongside.
The Ruìzhōng Qīnwáng Cí was outside the Cháoyángmén gate,
enshrining Duō'ěrgǔn and his six Fújìn.
During the Jiāqìng era,
a shrine for Grand Secretary Fúkāng'ān was built
called "Jiǎngzhōng" (Commending Loyalty),
outside the Dōng'ānmén gate.
A shrine for Dūtǒng Èlèdēngbǎo was called
"Bāozhōng" (Praising Loyalty),
outside the Dì'ānmén gate.
During the Guāngxù era,
a shrine for Kē'ěrqìn Qīnwáng Sēnggélínqìn was built
called "Xiǎnzhōng" (Manifesting Loyalty),
inside the Āndìngmén gate.
A shrine for Grand Secretary and Earl Lǐ Hóngzhāng
was called "Biǎozhōng" (Exemplifying Loyalty),
inside the Chóngwénmén gate.
During the Xuāntǒng era,
a combined shrine for Lìshān and Liányuán was built outside the Xuānwǔmén gate.
For all special shrines in the capital,
on auspicious days in the mid-months of spring and autumn,
the Tàicháng Qīng would be dispatched to offer sacrifices.
One "lesser sacrifice" (shǎoláo) and five types of fruit were used.
Only for the two shrines of Tóng Túlái and Hāshìtún,
three shǎoláo and fifteen types of fruit were used.
The Jīngyǒng Cí used shǎoláo as usual,
but also fifteen types of fruit.
Each spirit tablet received one piece of silk and three cups of wine,
which was consistent across all shrines.
In the seventh year of Jiāqìng,
it was first decreed that the officiating ministers performing the rites should wear python robes and official insignia.
For those in the provinces,
the local officials would offer sacrifices in spring and autumn.
Here, the most meritorious are recorded.
The building of the Zhōngjié Cí in Húguǎng to enshrine Left Governor-General Xú Yǒng
marked the beginning of building special shrines in the provinces.
During the Kāngxī era,
Guǎngxī built the Shuāngzhōng Cí,
enshrining Mǎ Xióngzhèn and Fù Hóngliè.
Then Fújiàn enshrined Fàn Chéngmó, Chén Qǐtài, Wú Wànfú, and Gāo Tiānjúe;
Yúnnán enshrined Gān Wénkūn.
During the Yōngzhèng era,
Qīnghé enshrined Jìn Fǔ and Qí Sūlè;
Kāifēng enshrined Tián Wénjìng.
Shèngjīng enshrined the Yíxián Qīnwáng.
During the mid-Qiánlóng era,
an imperial edict ordered that the four Jùnwáng, Tōngdá, Wǔgōng, Huìzhé, and Xuānxiàn,
and the four Qīnwáng, Lǐliè, Ráoyú, Zhèngxiàn, and Yǐngyì, be also included,
and the shrine renamed Xiánwáng Cí.
Later,
the two Qīnwáng, Ruìzhōng and Yùxuān,
and Kèqín Jùnwáng
were also collectively enshrined.
Jī Zēngyún and Gāo Bīn
were jointly enshrined in the Qīnghé shrine with Jìn Fǔ and others.
Yīlí enshrined Bāndì and Èróng'ān,
while Lābùdūn and Fù Qīng even had shrines built for them as far as Xīzàng (Tibet).
During the Jiāqìng era,
Wǔwēi built the Shuāngliè Cí,
enshrining Hán Zìchāng and Hán Jiāyè;
Tóng'ān enshrined Lǐ Chánggēng;
Chéngdū enshrined Délèngtài;
Hánchéng and Huáxiàn enshrined Qiáng Kèjié.
During the Dàoguāng
reign, Lǐ Shìxù was enshrined in Jiāngnán;
Fāng Zhènshēng, Mǎ Bùqú, and Chén Yùwēi in Táiwān;
Yáng Yánliàng in Zhàochéng;
Guān Tiānpéi and the father and son Chén Liánshēng in Hǔmén;
Yùqiān in Zhènhǎi;
Gě Yúnfēi, Zhèng Guóhóng, and Wáng Xīpéng in Dìnghǎi;
Hǎilíng in Jīngkǒu;
and Chén Huàchéng in Bǎoshān.
During the Xiánfēng
reign, Chángruì, Chángshòu, and Ā'ěrjīng'ā were enshrined in Guǎngxī;
Lín Zéxú in Xī'ān and Sūzhōu;
Jiǎng Wénqìng in Ānqìng;
Jiāng Zhōngyuán in Lúzhōu;
Liú Ténghóng in Ruìzhōu;
Xiàng Róng and Zhāng Guóliáng in Jiāngníng and Sūzhōu;
Jí'ěrháng'ā in Jīngkǒu,
with Bēngkuò and Liú Cúnhòu also enshrined there;
Shuānglái and Qú Ténglóng in Yángzhōu;
Lǐ Kūnyuán in Lìshuǐ and Hǔshù;
Tóng Jiàn and Xiè Zǐchéng in Tiānjīn;
Tǎqíbù in Chángshā and Jiǔjiāng;
Lǐ Xùbīn in Húguǎng, Jiāngxī, and Ānhuī;
Luó Zénán in Jiāngxī and Húguǎng;
and also jointly enshrined with Ráo Tíngxuǎn in Guǎngxìn.
Xiāngxiāng later separately enshrined Zénán, Wáng Zhēn, and Liú Ténghóng.
Xiāo Qǐjiāng in Húnán and Jiāngxī;
Hú Línyì in Húguǎng;
later also enshrined in Ānqìng.
Luó Ràodiǎn in Zūnyì.
During the Tóngzhì
reign, Guān Wén and Hú Línyì were jointly enshrined in Húběi;
Lǐ Mèngqún in Lúzhōu;
Ruìchāng, Wáng Yǒulíng, Zhāng Yùliáng, and others in Zhèjiāng;
Luó Zūndiàn in Hángzhōu;
Xióng Jiànyì in Fùyáng;
Zhào Jǐngxián in Húzhōu;
Yuán Jiǎsān in Chénzhōu, Ānqìng, Línhuái, and Huái'ān;
Jiāng Zhōngyì in Nánchāng and Qīngyáng;
Lǐ Xùyí in Ānhuī and Húguǎng;
later jointly enshrined with Duōlóng'ā in Qiánshān.
Chéng Xuéqǐ in Ānqìng, Sūzhōu, and Jiāxīng;
Duōlóng'ā in Hénán, Ānhuī, Shǎnxī, and Jílín;
later jointly enshrined with Línyì in Ānqìng.
Lǐ Chéndiǎn in Jiāngníng, Ānqìng, and Jí'ān;
Zhāng Yùnlán in Húnán, Fújiàn, and Guǎngdōng;
Sēnggélínqìn in Cáozhōu, Tiānjīn, and Méngchéng;
later also enshrined in Fèngtiān.
Péng Yùjú in Húnán, Jiāngsū, and Ānhuī;
Cáo Rénměi and others in Húguǎng;
Luò Bǐngzhāng in Sìchuān and Húnán;
Liú Sōngshān in Shǎn and Gān;
Mǎ Xīnyí in Jiāngníng and Ānqìng;
Zēng Guófān in Jiāngníng, Húnán, Húběi, Ānhuī, and Zhílì;
later jointly enshrined with Guóquán in Kāifēng.
Zhāng Liàngjī and Pān Duó were jointly enshrined in Chángshā;
Mùkèdéng'é in Bāyàndài;
Zāsàkè Qīnwáng Xībó'ěr in Hāmì;
Wú Jiābīn in Nánfēng;
Jiǎng Wèiyuǎn, Huáng Rùnchāng, and others in Guìzhōu.
Thereupon the Ministry of Rites stated:
"The special shrines in each province should be built on vacant land,
without encroaching on people's residences,
and it is forbidden to alter or destroy historical monuments, famous sites, and shrines and tombs of saints and sages."
This was approved.
During the Guāngxù
reign, Wú Wénróng was enshrined in Yángzhōu and Huángzhōu;
Liú Diǎn in Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Mǐn, Zhè, and Gānsù;
Shěn Bǎozhēn in Jiāngnán, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, and Táiwān;
Guō Sōnglín in Jiāngsū, Jiànfú, Shāndōng, and Húnán;
Wú Chángqìng in Jiāng, Zhè, Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Hénán;
later also enshrined in Cháoxiǎn.
Zuǒ Zōngtáng in Mǐn, Zhè, Shǎn, Gān, Xīnjiāng, and Jiāngníng;
Bào Chāo in Sìchuān, Húnán, Jiāngxī, Ānhuī, and Jiāngsū;
Jīn Shùn in Shǎn, Gān, and Jílín;
Yáng Yùkē in Dàlǐ and Zhènnán;
Liú Chángyòu in Jiāngxī, Guǎngxī, Yúnnán, and Xīnníng;
Cén Yùyīng in Yún, Guì, and Guǎngxī;
Zhōu Shèngbō in Ānhuī and Shāndōng;
later jointly enshrined with Shèngchuán and Dài Zōngqiān in Jǐnán.
Péng Yùlín in Húguǎng, Jiāngxī, Jiāngníng, and the West Lake of Zhèjiāng;
Quán;
Zhāng Yào in Hénán, Ānhuī, Húběi, Zhílì, Gān, and Xīn;
Zhōu Shèngchuán in Ānqìng, Jiāngníng, and Qīngxiàn;
Chén Guóruì in Shāndōng and Jiāngsū;
Yán Jìngmíng in Shāndōng and Shǎnxī;
Liú Jǐntáng in Húnán, Gān, and Xīn;
Liú Míngchuán in Ānhuī and Fújiàn;
Dīng Bǎozhēn, Yáng Chāngjùn in Shāndōng, Sìchuān, Zhōu, Chángshā, and Lánzhōu;
Lǐ Hóngzhāng in Jiāng, Zhè, Hénán, Zhílì, and Shāndōng;
Sòng Qìng in Zhílì, Fèngtiān, Hénán, and Ānhuī;
Niè Shìchéng in Ānhuī and Lútái;
Liú Kūnyī in Húnán, Jiāngxī, Ānhuī, and Jiāngníng;
Féng Zǐcái in Guǎngxī, Yún, and Guì;
Zēng Guóhuá in Ānhuī and Húnán;
Táo Mó in Gān and Xīn;
Mǎ Yùkūn in Zhílì and Ānhuī;
Yīng Hàn in Ānhuī;
Dèng Shàoliáng in Húnán and Xuānchéng;
Xiāo Fúsì in Jiāngnán;
Táo Shù, Lín Zéxú, Zōu Mínghè, Fúzhūhóng'ā in Jiāngníng;
Wú Táng in Qīng, Huái, and Xúzhōu;
with Yáo Guǎngwǔ and others also enshrined there.
Téng Xuéyì and Táng Dìngkuí in Xúzhōu;
Zhāng Zhīwàn in Huái'ān;
Ruǎn Yuán and Jiǎng Yìlǐ in Hángzhōu;
Zhāng Hécái in Huái and Yáng;
Wú Kūnxiū in Nánchāng;
Luó Sījǔ in Dōngxiāng;
Wō Rén in Hénán;
Lǐ Tángjiē in Wēnxiàn;
Liú Róng and Zēng Wàngyán in Xī'ān;
Yíxián Qīnwáng, Wénqiān, Dīng Shòuchāng in Tiānjīn;
Chéng Zhàolín in Língshòu and Bǎodìng;
Wú Kědú in Shùntiān Jìzhōu;
Pān Zǔyìn in Bǎochí;
Jīn Yùnchāng in Xīnjiāng;
Three Sages Shrine was built in Fèngtiān,
enshrining Wénxiáng, Chóngshí, Dūxīng'ā;
also enshrining Zuǒ Bǎoguì, Yīkètáng'ā, Chángshùn.
Jīn Fú, Yán Mào, Fù Jùn, Xī Yuán in Jílín;
Wáng Kǎitài in Fújiàn Táiwān;
Wǔsù Qīnwáng Háogé in Sìchuān Xīchōng;
Chén Hóngmóu in Língguì;
Zēng Bìguāng, Hán Qǐ, Lí Péijìng in Guìyáng.
At that time, various provinces vied to request the establishment of special shrines,
but an edict forbade such excess.
The Xuāntǒng reign did not last long,
yet Léi Zhèngwǎn was enshrined in Húběi, Ānhuī, Shǎn, Gān, and Fèngtiān;
Chéng Wénbǐng in Zhílì, Shāndōng, Hénán, and Ānhuī;
Pān Wàncái in Ānhuī and Měnggǔ Qí;
Dǒng Lǚgāo in Héfèi;
Niú Shīhán in Wōyáng;
Xú Yòngyí, Xǔ Jǐngchéng, Yuán Chǎng in Hángzhōu Xīhú,
known as
the "Three Loyal Ones."
Chǎng was also enshrined in Wúhú.
From then on, Lián Yuán was enshrined in Bǎochí;
Zhāng Zhīdòng in Wǔchāng;
Wáng Wénsháo in Chángshā;
Mǎ Wéiqí in Chéngdū;
Dīng Tǐchāng in Qínzhōu;
Xià Yùxiù in Kūnmíng.
These are all the major ones.
For the others, the border officials submitted requests,
and the Ministry of Rites deliberated and responded.
The events are recorded in the Veritable Records,
and the dates can be verified,
there are still more than can be enumerated.
Throughout the Qīng dynasty,
the many aides who followed the Dragon [i.e., the emperor]
rose from beyond the passes.
When quelling the Three Feudatories,
most were Hàn generals from the Northwest.
When pacifying the rebel bandits in the Three Provinces,
Shu generals rose in competition.
When pirates were rampant in the Southeast Sea,
Mǐn commanders emerged one after another.
Xiāng and Chǔ military officials
pacified the Yuè Rebellion.
In the campaign to suppress the Niǎn,
Ān generals participated.
Among them, those who completed their loyalty and died in defense
were especially numerous in shrines.
As for the general shrines for meritorious officials,
during Shìzōng's reign,
the Zhōngyǒng Shrine was built in Lánzhōu.
During Rénzōng's reign,
the Zhāngzhōng Shrine was built in Kāshígá'ěr.
During the Tóngzhì Restoration,
Húnán had the Biǎozhōng Shrine;
Xiāngxiāng and Píngjiāng had the Zhōngyì Shrine;
Dòngtíng Jūnshān, Xiāngxiāng, and Guìyáng had the Zhāozhōng Shrine.
Other places like Húkǒu Shízhōngshān for the navy,
Jīnlíng for the Xiāng Army land forces,
Chǔ Army navy,
Wúsōng for the outer sea navy,
Táiwān for the Huái and Chǔ armies,
Sūzhōu, Wǔchāng, Bǎodìng, Lúzhōu, Cháohú, Jǐnán, Wúxī, and other places for the Huái Army,
ensured that all who fought and sacrificed their bodies
received offerings of incense and sacrifices of blood;
their purpose was all to manifest loyalty.
In addition, the Banner garrisons in Jiāngníng and Jīngkǒu,
the officials and gentry of the Jīnlíng military camp,
the Wǔyì Army in Wǔchāng,
the Sōngwǔ Army in Chéngdū,
the Yì Army in Jǐnzhōu,
and various Zhāozhōng Shrines,
along with the Zhōngyì, Zhāozhōng, Wèizhōng, Zhōngliè, and other shrines in various prefectures and counties,
served to reward those who died for their achievements,
and are too numerous to count.
The sacrificial rites and offerings followed previous procedures.
Ancestral Temples for the Imperial Clan In the first year of Chóngdé,
it was decreed that enfeoffed princes of the imperial clan should establish ancestral temples.
In the fifth year of Shùnzhì,
an imperial edict stated that if a prince had no heir,
his spirit tablet would be enshrined in the west side hall of the rear hall of Tàimiào.
Those with descendants
should establish separate temples for their sacrifices.
During the mid-months of the four seasons and at the end of the year, they would attend the secondary sacrifices at Tàimiào.
Upon completion,
they would return to their residences to perform their own rituals.
Regarding offerings of new produce,
anything not yet presented at Tàimiào
was not permitted to be privately offered at the family temple.
At that time, Zhūang Qīnwáng established one temple.
Lǐ Qīnwáng, Xùn Qīnwáng, and Qiān Qīnwáng shared one temple.
Ráoyú Jùnwáng and Duānzhòng Qīnwáng shared one temple.
Yǐng Qīnwáng and Shùnchéng Jùnwáng shared one temple.
Yù Jùnwáng had one temple.
Kèqín Jùnwáng and Yǎnxǐ Jùnwáng shared one temple.
In the ninth year of Yōngzhèng,
Yíxián Qīnwáng established one temple.
For the family sacrifices of qīnwáng's heirs apparent and jùnwáng,
a temple of seven bays was built,
with the central five bays forming the main hall,
and the left and right sides partitioned by walls to create side chambers.
Behind the beam in the north of the hall were five rooms.
The central room enshrined the founding prince,
The tablets of the great-great-grandparents, great-grandparents, grandparents, and parents were arranged in order as two Zhāo and two Mù,
Zhāo on the east and Mù on the west.
When the kinship ties became distant, their tablets would be moved.
Those moved from the Zhāo position
had their spirit tablets stored in the east side chamber.
The two Zhāo positions were then elevated into one room,
and two rooms were used to enshrine the elevated and associated tablets.
Those moved from the Mù position
were stored in the west side chamber,
and their elevation and association were similar.
To the south was the central gate,
and further south, the temple gate,
with side gates to the left and right.
The courtyard was divided into east and west side halls,
the east for storing robes and caps,
and the west for ritual vessels and musical instruments.
The temple had a double-eaved roof,
vermilion pillars,
painted rafters,
green tiles,
and red plastered walls.
Inside the gate was a furnace for burning silk.
Outside was a room for slaughtering sacrificial animals,
facing west.
A propitious day was chosen in the middle month of each of the four seasons.
In mid-spring, the tablets of those moved were brought out for the collective feast.
According to the rites,
in the hall, the founding ancestor had a dedicated altar table,
in the central position,
facing south.
To the left, in the east side chamber, the tablets of those moved shared an altar table.
Next were the two Zhāo, sharing an altar table,
facing east.
To the right, in the west side chamber, the tablets of those moved shared an altar table.
Next were the two Mù, sharing an altar table,
facing west.
Slightly to the west, one altar table for incense and silk was set up,
and one altar table for libation vessels.
Each altar table had one sheep and one pig,
two xíng (meat broth vessels), two fǔ (grain vessels), and two guǐ (food vessels),
and eight biān (bamboo dishes) and eight dòu (wooden dishes) each.
Each position had one piece of silk, three ceremonial cups (jué), and six musical instruments.
Descendants of the same ancestor,
of adult age and above,
would attend the sacrifice at the appointed time.
Officials of the mansion would accompany them,
with the ritual master (tōngzàn) and subordinate officials performing the duties.
For offering incense, silk, and ceremonial cups, descendants would be used.
Three days beforehand,
the principal worshipper would fast in an outer chamber,
and all others would also fast.
At dawn on the day of the sacrifice,
the principal worshipper would enter in court attire,
taking his position in the exact center under the hall eaves.
His elder uncles and brothers participating in the sacrifice would stand on the east steps,
and his younger brothers and sons would stand below the east steps.
Positions were arranged by generation difference,
and within each generation, by age.
Officials and subordinates would stand below the west steps,
arranged by rank.
All would face north.
At clear light,
two senior youths would proceed to the room of the founding ancestor,
and four others would proceed separately to the east and west side chambers,
and the Zhāo and Mù rooms.
Each would respectfully place the spirit tablets on the altars.
For Zhāo,
the father's tablet was on the right, the mother's on the left.
For Mù,
the father's tablet was on the left, the mother's on the right.
They would kneel,
bow once,
and rise.
The principal worshipper would wash his hands,
take his position, and the music for welcoming the spirits would begin.
He would proceed to the altar of the founding ancestor and offer incense three times,
then proceed in turn to each of the moved ancestral altars to offer incense.
He would lead his clan members in the ritual of two kneels and six kowtows.
Offering silk, pouring libations, presenting offerings, and reading the prayer were all performed according to custom.
After the three offerings were completed,
he would proceed to the altar of the founding ancestor, kneel to receive the ceremonial cup and the sacrificial meat,
bow three times,
remove the dishes,
send off the spirits,
with two kneels and six kowtows.
He would then proceed to the burning pit to observe the burning.
Upon completion of the rites,
the spirit tablets would be returned to their rooms,
and they would withdraw.
The sacrificial meat would be divided and distributed among the clan members.
For the rites of seasonal sacrifices,
five altar tables were set up in the hall.
The founding ancestor and his consort occupied the central position, facing south.
The great-great-grandparents, great-grandparents, grandparents, and parents
were arranged to the left and right according to Zhāo and Mù.
Each altar table had one sheep and one pig,
and the rest was as per the collective feast system.
For seasonal offerings of new produce,
on the appointed day, the principal worshipper would rise early,
lead his sons and younger brothers in full dress into the temple,
clean the hall,
set up the altar tables,
and arrange six plates each of fruits and delicacies.
Each position had two chopsticks and three cups.
The rooms would be opened,
and they would proceed in turn to each altar table, kneel, and offer incense,
bow three times.
The sons and younger brothers would offer wine to all.
The principal worshipper would perform two kneels and six kowtows,
and the sons and younger brothers would follow suit.
When finished,
the rooms would be closed,
and they would withdraw.
For making announcements due to affairs,
four plates each of fruits and delicacies were offered,
and the rites were the same as for offering new produce.
Visiting the temple on the first and fifteenth days of the month was also similar.
For Bèilè, Bèizǐ, and imperial clan gōng, the family ancestral temple had five bays,
with three forming the hall.
Behind the beam in the north, five rooms were divided,
enshrining the founding ancestor and four generations.
Side chambers on both sides enshrined the tablets of those moved due to distant kinship.
The temple did not have a double-eaved roof,
the gate was not fully painted,
but the rest was as for qīnwáng.
For the collective feast,
the founding ancestor had a dedicated altar table,
with one sheep and one pig.
The moved tablets in the east side chamber and the two Zhāo had a dedicated altar table,
with one sheep and one pig each.
The moved tablets in the west side chamber and the two Mù were also similar.
For seasonal sacrifices, each had a dedicated altar table.
Zhāo and Mù each shared the same sacrificial animals.
The biān and dòu were each reduced by two compared to qīnwáng.
No music was used.
The rite was one kneel and three kowtows.
For seasonal offerings, four plates of fruits were offered.
Announcements were made when there were affairs,
and visits were made on the first and fifteenth days.
The rest was according to the qīnwáng's rites.
Family Sacrifices of Officials, Scholars, and Commoners. For officials' families, the ancestral temple is situated to the east of the living quarters.
For ranks one to three, the temple has five bays.
Three bays form the hall,
with walls on the left and right delimiting it.
To the north is a side chamber (夾室 jiāshì),
and to the south are rooms.
The courtyard has two covered corridors (廡 wǔ);
the eastern one stores clothing,
and the western one stores sacrificial vessels.
The courtyard is enclosed by a wall.
For ranks four to seven, the temple has three bays.
The middle bay is the hall,
with side chambers (夾室 jiāshì) and rooms to the left and right,
and covered corridors (廡 wǔ).
For ranks eight and nine, the temple has three bays.
The middle bay is wide,
and the left and right bays are narrow.
The courtyard has no covered corridors (廡 wǔ).
Clothing and sacrificial vessels are stored in chests,
arranged in the east and west corridors.
Behind the hall are four chambers,
where the spirit tablets of the Gāozǔ (great-great-grandfather), Zēngzǔ (great-grandfather), Zǔ (grandfather),
and Ní (father) are enshrined,
with Zhaō on the left and Mù on the right.
The Bǐ (ancestress) is paired with the Dī (principal wife),
facing south.
Ancestors above the Gāozǔ (great-great-grandfather),
whose generational ties have expired, are moved to the Tiáo.
Those moved from the Zhaō position
have their spirit tablets stored in the eastern side chamber (夾室 jiāshì);
those moved from the Mù position
have their spirit tablets stored in the western side chamber (夾室 jiāshì).
Moving to chambers and joining the temple
both follow the Zhaōmù generational sequence.
The east and west corridors serve as additional sacrificial positions (祔位 fùwèi).
Elder and younger paternal uncles, grandfathers, brothers, and adult sons and nephews who died without issue or died young
have their names written in ink on tablets according to their generation,
males to the east and females to the west,
facing east and west respectively.
Regarding the number of sacrificial animals and vessels:
for ranks one to three,
one sheep and one pig.
Each table has two cutting boards (俎 zǔ),
two soup bowls (鉶 xíng) and two food containers (登 dēng),
and six bamboo baskets (籩 biān) and six wooden platters (豆 dòu).
For ranks four to seven,
a special pig (特豕 tèshǐ).
One table, one cutting board (俎 zǔ),
and four bamboo baskets (籩 biān) and four wooden platters (豆 dòu).
For ranks eight and below,
a pork shoulder, not specially slaughtered (不特殺 bù tèshā).
One table, one cutting board (俎 zǔ),
and two bamboo baskets (籩 biān) and two wooden platters (豆 dòu).
Annual sacrifices are performed in the middle month of each season on an auspicious day.
Reading of the invocation (祝 zhù), assisting the ritual (贊禮 zànlǐ), and holding the libation cup (執爵 zhíjué) are all done by the children and younger relatives.
All sons and grandsons who have reached the age of capping (成年 chéngnián)
attend the sacrifice.
Three days before,
the host and those involved observe a fast.
At the fifth watch (五鼓 wǔgǔ) on the day of sacrifice,
the host wears court robes,
and the assembly wears formal attire,
and enters the temple.
The host waits at the bottom of the eastern steps.
Clan members wait in the east and west of the courtyard,
following the Zhaōmù generational sequence.
The principal wife (主婦 zhǔfù) leads the other women in formal attire,
goes to the kitchen to supervise the cooking.
Once the soup is ready,
they enter the eastern room to arrange the bamboo baskets (籩 biān) and wooden platters (豆 dòu),
and place the soup bowls (鉶 xíng), food containers (豋 dēng), spoons (匕 bǐ), chopsticks (箸 zhù), vinegar (醯 xī), and sauces (醬 jiàng) in readiness.
At dawn,
the eldest of the sons and younger relatives opens the chambers,
brings out the spirit tablets, and places them on the ritual tables (几 jī).
At the Zhaō position, the Kǎo (father) is on the right and the Bǐ (mother) is on the left.
Those performing additional sacrifices set up the eastern and western additional sacrificial positions (祔位 fùwèi).
The host ascends from the eastern steps,
washes,
and stands at the bowing position beneath the central eaves.
Respected clan members stand on the two steps;
those of lower status stand at the bottom of the steps.
All face north.
The host goes before the incense table, kneels,
offers incense three times,
presents a libation cup,
rises,
returns to position,
and leads the clan in one kneel and three bows.
The host goes before the Gāozǔ (great-great-grandfather)'s table and offers a libation cup.
The offerings before the Zēngzǔ (great-grandfather)'s, Zǔ (grandfather)'s, and Ní (father)'s tables are completed in the same manner.
Those performing additional sacrifices offer wine to all the additional sacrificial positions (祔位 fùwèi).
The invocation (祝 zhù) is read.
For each offering,
the principal wife (主婦 zhǔfù) leads the other women in making offerings,
kowtows once, and rises.
The first offering (初獻 chūxiàn) includes spoons (匕 bǐ), chopsticks (箸 zhù), vinegar (醯 xī), and sauces (醬 jiàng).
The second offering (亞獻 yàxiàn) includes soup (羹 gēng), rice (飯 fàn), and sliced meat (肉胾 ròuzì).
The third offering (三獻 sānxiàn) includes pastries (餅餌 bǐngěr), fruits (果 guǒ), and vegetables (蔬 shū).
At the completion of the offering,
the host kneels before the incense table,
and the invoker (祝 zhù) conveys the blessings (嘏 gǔ) from the ancestral fathers to the host.
The host tastes the wine and food,
returns the vessels to the invoker (祝 zhù),
kowtows once, rises,
returns to position,
sees off the spirits,
and performs one kneel and three bows.
After supervising the burning (of sacrificial items),
the participants depart.
The host leads the sons and younger relatives in returning the spirit tablets,
offering incense, and performing the rites.
The sacrificial vessels are removed,
the doors are closed,
and they withdraw.
The sacrificial food is consumed at midday.
For ranks three and above,
seasonal sacrifices are performed fully.
For ranks four to seven,
two sacrifices are performed (in spring and autumn).
For ranks eight and nine, one sacrifice is performed (in spring).
All participants,
regardless of status, are present.
The host respectfully enters the席 xí (mat/seat),
pours wine for the respected elders.
The eldest of the sons and younger relatives leaves his seat to pour wine for the host.
The elderly and young exchange toasts in a lively manner.
When the ceremony is over,
all depart.
The mats are removed,
and the kitchen staff and servants must consume all the remaining sacrificial food.
On festive occasions (令節 lìngjié) when new produce is offered,
for ranks one to three,
each table has four plates of fruit and four dishes of delicacies.
For ranks four to seven,
two plates of fruit are reduced.
For ranks eight and nine, two dishes of delicacies are also reduced.
However, the provision of soup and rice is the same for all.
On the first and fifteenth days of the month, tea is offered.
Two vessels on the food table.
The ritual for offering tea is simultaneous with the main sacrifice.
For common scholars' families,
a shrine (龕 kān) is set up to the north of the main hall (寢堂 qǐntáng),
with planks dividing it into four chambers,
enshrining Gāozǔ (great-great-grandfather), Zēngzǔ (great-grandfather), Zǔ (grandfather), and Ní (father).
The Bǐ (ancestress) is paired with them.
The positions are as in the officials' ritual,
facing south.
Adult relatives within the mourning attire grades (服親 fúqīn) who died without issue
have their names written on paper according to their generation as additional sacrificial positions (祔位 fùwèi).
After the ceremony,
these are burned,
no tablets are erected.
On each of the four seasonal festivals,
the spirit tablets are brought out for offering.
Two plates of cooked grain (粢盛 zīshèng),
four dishes of meat, fruits, and vegetables,
two bowls of soup,
and two bowls of rice.
A fast is observed beforehand.
The evening before the offering,
the principal wife (主婦 zhǔfù) prepares the food in her room.
At dawn,
the host wears auspicious clothing,
leads the sons and younger relatives in bringing out the spirit tablets and arranging them on the incense table,
Zhaō to the east and Mù to the west.
Additional sacrificial positions (祔位 fùwèi) are set up on the west corridor table.
The host stands at the bottom of the eastern steps.
The assembly stands to the east and west according to their generation.
After the host offers incense,
he performs one kneel and three bows,
and rises.
The principal wife (主婦 zhǔfù) leads the other women out of the room to offer spoons (匕 bǐ), chopsticks (箸 zhù), vinegar (醯 xī), and sauces (醬 jiàng),
kneels,
kowtows,
and withdraws.
The host goes before the tables,
in sequence pours wine and offers cooked food,
kneels,
kowtows,
and rises.
The sons and younger relatives offer to the additional sacrificial positions (祔位 fùwèi).
When finished,
the sacrificial text is read.
For the second offering (再獻 zàixiàn),
the principal wife (主婦 zhǔfù) offers rice and soup.
For the third offering (三獻 sānxiàn), pastries (餅餌 bǐngěr) and seasonal vegetables are offered.
After the host leads the clan in performing the rites,
the sacrificial text and sacrificial positions (祭位 jìwèi) are burned,
the spirit tablets are returned,
the vessels are removed, and they withdraw.
The sacrificial food is consumed at midday.
One sacrifice is performed in spring.
Tea is offered on the first and fifteenth days of the month.
If there is an important event, it is announced.
All involve one kneel and three bows.
In commoners' family sacrifices,
a shrine is set up in the north of the main chamber,
where the tablets of the high ancestor (gāo zǔ), great-great-grandfather (zēng zǔ), grandfather (zǔ), and father (ní) are enshrined.
On festivals, fresh offerings are presented.
The altar does not exceed four vessels,
with soup and rice.
On that day, they rise early.
The mistress of the house prepares the dishes.
The master leads his children and younger brothers to conduct the sacrifice with reverence.
All rituals are like those of a common scholar, but slightly simpler.
On the first and fifteenth of the month, tea is offered,
and incense and lamps are lit to perform the rites.
Reporting affairs is also done in the same way.

Treatise on Sixty-Three Rites, Rituals Seven (Auspicious Rites One): Ascension Ceremony, Abdication Ceremony, Empress Dowager's Regency Ceremony, Emperor's Assumption of Personal Rule Ceremony, Grand Court Audience Ceremony, Daily Court Audience Ceremony (with Imperial Gate Audience appended), Grand Emperor Emeritus's Three Major Festivals Congratulatory Audience Ceremony, Grand Empress Dowager's, Empress Dowager's, Empress's Three Major Festivals Congratulatory Audience Ceremony, Grand Banquet Ceremony, Bestowal of an Honorable Title or Auspicious Title Ceremony (with Bestowal of Honorable Titles on Imperial Consorts and Concubines appended), Enfeoffment of the Empress Ceremony (with Enfeoffment of Concubines appended), Enfeoffment of the Crown Prince Ceremony (with Crown Prince's Birthday appended), Enfeoffment of Various Princes Ceremony (with Enfeoffment of Princesses appended).
Second are the Auspicious Rites (jiā lǐ).
Those pertaining to the Son of Heaven
are the ceremonies of court audiences, banquets, enfeoffments, and imperial lectures (jīng yán).
Those performed by commoners
are the village drinking rites (xiāng yǐn jiǔ lǐ).
And the rites of marriage
are the same for both high and low.
The Rites of Zhōu (Zhōu Guān) state:
"To unite the myriad people with auspicious rites."
In governing the state and administering the lands,
there is nothing that does not follow this.
Here, the major ones are listed,
along with similar ceremonies,
and compiled into this chapter.
Ascension Ceremony: In the early Qīng dynasty, Tàizǔ (太祖) founded the enterprise,
established the reign title Tiānmìng (天命).
On the first day of the first month, he ascended the throne.
The Bèilè (貝勒) and all officials gathered before the hall,
standing in order according to their wings.
When the Emperor entered the hall,
all knelt.
The Eight Grand Ministers (bā dà chén) stepped out of their ranks,
knelt and presented a memorial to confer an honorable title.
An attendant received it,
knelt before the Emperor, and read it aloud.
The Emperor descended from his seat,
burned incense and announced to Heaven,
then led the Bèilè and all officials in performing the rites,
three genuflections and nine kowtows.
When finished,
he returned to his seat.
The Bèilè, etc., each led their banner members in offering congratulations.
Tàizōng (太宗) ascending the throne was also like this.
In the tenth year of Tiāncōng (天聰),
the reign title was changed to Chóngdé (崇dé),
and the dynastic title was established as Dàqīng (大清).
Three days prior, oaths and warnings were issued,
an altar was built,
and imperial equipage (lú bù) was prepared.
On the appointed day,
the Emperor led all officials to the Temple of Heaven (Tiān Tán) to respectfully make an announcement.
When the ceremony was complete,
the official bearing the imperial seal (yù bǎo) proceeded first.
The Emperor ascended the altar from the middle steps and took his seat.
The Bèilè, etc., performed three genuflections and nine kowtows.
When finished,
everyone knelt.
The Bèilè arranged themselves on the left and right.
The official bearing the seal knelt and presented it.
The Emperor received the seal,
then passed it to an official of the Grand Secretariat (Nèi Yuàn).
All officials performed the rites as before.
When finished,
all knelt.
The official designated to read stood to the east of the altar, holding the memorial in Mǎn (滿), Měng (蒙), and Hàn (漢) scripts.
He read them sequentially.
When all officials had completed the rites,
they returned to their positions,
music was played,
and the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
The next day, the Emperor held court.
All officials presented memorials of congratulations,
performing three genuflections and nine kowtows.
Next, the executive officials performed rites as in the previous ceremony.
Thereupon, a banquet was bestowed,
and an amnesty edict was promulgated.
Eight years later,
Shìzǔ (世祖) succeeded to the throne.
Officials were dispatched to announce to the altars and temples as in the initial rites,
but without setting up imperial equipage,
playing music,
or bestowing a banquet.
On the first day of the tenth month of Shùnzhì (順治)元年 (the first year),
the capital was established in Yānjīng (燕京).
