Prior to this, officials of the Grand Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Sì) cleared the altar precincts,
and the Directorate of Ceremonial (Sīlǐ Jiān) set up seats and altars.
On the appointed day,
officials were dispatched to announce to the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain (shè),
the grand imperial equipage (dà jià lú bù) was prepared.
The Emperor wore his sacrificial robes,
exited through Dàqīng Mén (大清門),
proceeded to the Southern Suburb (Nán Jiāo),
and announced to Heaven and Earth.
When the ceremony was complete,
he was led into the eastern tent of the Temple of Heaven to change into ceremonial robes.
Upon his imperial seat,
all officials knelt.
The Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) led one Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) to ascend from the eastern steps,
kneel facing north in the exact center.
One Scholar (xuéshì) respectfully took the seal from the altar table and handed it to the Grand Secretary,
who received it with reverence
and delivered an address saying:
"The Emperor rules over all nations;
all princes, civil and military officials are filled with boundless joy."
When finished,
he passed it to the Scholar.
The Scholar knelt to receive it,
placed it on the altar table,
and returned to his position.
When the officials completed the rites,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
Officials of the Court of State Ceremonial (Hónglúsì) set up the imperial table in the center of Huángjí Mén (皇極門).
A memorial table was set up to the east of the eaves.
Princes and Bèilè, etc., stood in order north of the Inner Golden Water Bridge (Nèi Jīnshuǐ Qiáo).
Civil and military officials stood in order south of the bridge,
all facing east and west.
Music began.
When the Emperor took his seat, it stopped.
Whips cracked.
Executive officials completed the rites on the steps
and took their positions.
The princes led all officials in presenting memorials.
When the rites were completed,
whips cracked,
and the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
Nine days later, on a jiǎzǐ (甲子) day,
an edict was promulgated according to regulations.
Shèngzǔ (聖祖) inherited the enterprise.
Officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices to Heaven and Earth, and the Imperial Ancestral Temple (Zōngshè).
The Emperor, in mourning attire, proceeded to the imperial couch (jī yán) and performed three genuflections and nine kowtows,
reverently announcing his acceptance of the mandate.
He went to the side hall to change into ceremonial robes,
then proceeded to the palaces of the Grand Empress Dowager (Tàihuáng Tàihòu) and the Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu),
performing three genuflections and nine kowtows at each.
Then he rode in his palanquin out of Qiánqīng Mén (乾清門),
and presided in Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿),
where the Grand Ministers of the Interior (Nèi Dàchén) and other executive officials performed rites.
Then he presided again in Tàihé Diàn (太和殿),
where princes, dukes, and all officials presented memorials and performed rites as per regulations.
No reading aloud,
no music,
no banquet was held.
Princes and dukes entered,
were granted tea, and then
returned to the palace.
He reverted to mourning attire,
retired to the mourning hut (shān cì),
and promulgated an edict.
Shìzōng (世宗) succeeded to the great lineage,
following all previous ceremonies,
except for abolishing the granting of tea.
From Gāozōng (高宗) onwards, those who succeeded to the throne as crown princes all followed the same.
Ceremony for Abdication and Succession. The ancient ceremony for imperial abdication.
Initially, Gāo Zōng (高宗) reigned for a long time.
He once declared that he would relinquish power upon reaching eighty-six years of age.
When the sixtieth year of Qián Lóng (乾隆) arrived,
an imperial edict stated:
"Since ancient times, when emperors abdicated,
it was either due to their own idleness and recklessness
or due to many pressing affairs at the time.
The hurried abdication and succession
offered no commendable rituals.
Now the nation is in its prime,
so discuss the ceremonies in detail and report them."
Thereupon, an auspicious date was chosen, and the heir apparent's position was determined,
with the following year designated as the first year of the heir emperor.
The ritual officials presented the ceremonial protocols.
Before the appointed date, officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices to the ancestral temples and the altars of earth and grain.
On the day, the relevant department set up the imperial throne in the Tài Hé Diàn (太和殿).
There were two side tables,
a precious table in the center,
and slightly to the south, two stands facing east and west;
an edict table by the eastern pillar,
a memorial table by the western pillar,
and stands facing north and south;
a yellow table stood in the middle of the imperial steps.
Inside the balustrade, a kneeling mat for the heir emperor was laid.
Before the hall, imperial paraphernalia were displayed,
and outside the gate, imperial palanquins were positioned.
Outside the Wǔ Mén (午門) were five imperial chariots, trained elephants, ceremonial horses, yellow canopies, and cloud-patterned trays.
Under the eaves, the Zhōng Hé Sháo Yuè (中和韶樂) orchestra was stationed;
outside the gate on the imperial steps, the Dàn Bì Dà Yuè (丹陛大樂) orchestra was stationed.
Academicians of the Grand Secretariat placed the edict of abdication on the eastern table,
officials from the Board of Rites placed the congratulatory memorial on the western table.
Grand Secretaries and others proceeded to the Qián Qīng Mén (乾清門) to request the imperial seal and placed it on the left side table.
Two Grand Secretaries stood separately under the two eaves.
Princes, dukes, and all civil and military officials stood in their assigned order.
Envoys from Cháo Xiǎn (朝鮮), Ān Nán (安南), Xiān Luó (暹羅), and Guō Ěr Kē (廓爾喀) lined up at the end of the rows.
Officials from the Directorate of Astronomy proceeded to the Qián Qīng Mén to announce the time.
The heir emperor, in court attire, emerged from the Yù Qìng Gōng (毓慶宮).
At this time, two attendant Grand Ministers of the Interior, leading twenty imperial guards, assembled outside the Qián Qīng Mén.
Two chief officials of the Board of Rites, acting as guides, stood at the foot of the gate steps.
Ten leading Grand Ministers stood at the foot of the steps behind the hall.
The Supreme Emperor, in ceremonial robes, rode in his palanquin.
The heir emperor followed, with various officials leading and attending.
The Wǔ Mén rang bells and drums.
Upon reaching behind the hall, the palanquin was lowered.
The Supreme Emperor ascended to the throne in the Zhōng Hé Diàn (中和殿).
The heir emperor stood inside the hall, facing west.
Officials from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices guided the assisting ministers to their positions.
Without a vocal usher,
they performed the nine prostrations.
Those attending the ceremony swiftly exited
to their positions in the outer court.
The Zhōng Hé Sháo Yuè began to play,
performing the "Yuán Píng Zhāng" (元平章).
The Supreme Emperor then proceeded to the Tài Hé Diàn.
The heir emperor stood in attendance as before.
When the music ceased,
whips cracked three times at the foot of the steps.
The Dàn Bì Dà Yuè began to play,
performing the "Qìng Píng Zhāng" (慶平章).
The heir emperor proceeded to the kneeling position.
Princes and dukes stood on the imperial steps,
while civil and military officials and tributary envoys stood below the imperial terrace.
The herald announced,
"Kneel!"
The heir emperor, leading the multitude of officials, knelt.
The herald announced,
"Proclaim the memorial!"
The official proclaiming the memorial entered,
carrying the memorial to the center beneath the eaves and knelt.
Two Grand Secretaries knelt to his left and right.
The memorial was unrolled.
The music ceased.
After the proclamation,
the memorial was returned to its original table,
and the official withdrew.
The herald announced,
"Rise!"
The heir emperor withdrew to stand on the left side,
facing west.
Two Grand Secretaries guided him to kneel before the throne.
The left Grand Secretary requested the imperial seal,
and kneeling, presented it to the Supreme Emperor.
The Supreme Emperor personally bestowed it upon the heir emperor.
The heir emperor knelt to receive it.
The right Grand Secretary knelt to accept it,
and placed it on the right side table.
The heir emperor proceeded to the kneeling position.
Music began.
The herald announced,
"Kneel,
Prostrate,
Rise!"
He led the multitude of officials in performing the nine prostrations.
The herald announced,
"Withdraw!"
The music ceased,
and the ceremony concluded.
Whips cracked as before.
The Zhōng Hé Sháo Yuè began to play,
performing the "Hé Píng Zhāng" (和平章).
The Supreme Emperor returned to his palace.
Court eunuchs had already set up musical instruments.
The Supreme Emperor took his place in the inner hall.
Princesses,
Fù Jìn (福晉),
and imperial grandsons, great-grandsons, and great-great-grandsons who had not yet been granted titles,
performed the rites of congratulation.
The heir emperor changed into ceremonial attire,
respectfully awaiting in the warm pavilion of the Bǎo Hé Diàn (保和殿).
Academicians of the Grand Secretariat had already placed the edict of abdication and the imperial seal on the central table in the Tài Hé Diàn.
Officials from the Board of Rites placed the congratulatory memorial for ascension on the eastern table.
Attendants and guides assembled outside the Bǎo Hé Diàn.
The Directorate of Astronomy announced the time.
The heir emperor proceeded to the Zhōng Hé Diàn.
Attendants performed the rites according to their ranks,
without vocal ushering.
After the rites were completed,
the heir emperor proceeded to the Tài Hé Diàn to ascend the throne.
Music played,
then stopped.
The memorial was proclaimed,
and rites were performed,
all in accordance with the previous format.
After the rites were completed,
they withdrew,
and resumed their positions.
Grand Secretaries advanced,
carrying the edict,
exited through the central gate,
and handed it to the Minister of Rites.
The Minister knelt to receive it,
rose,
placed it on the yellow table,
and performed three prostrations.
He then carried the edict again and placed it on the cloud-patterned tray.
An official from the Bureau of Ceremonial knelt to receive it,
rose,
and exited through the central pathway.
The ceremony concluded,
all withdrew,
and the heir emperor returned to his palace.
Grand Secretaries and others proceeded to the Qián Qīng Mén to send off the imperial seal.
The Board of Rites respectfully engraved and promulgated the imperial edict.
Ceremony for Ruling from Behind a Screen. In the eleventh year of Xián Fēng (咸豐),
Wén Zōng (文宗) passed away,
and Mù Zōng (穆宗), who was very young, succeeded to the throne.
Censor Dǒng Yuán Chún (董元醇) memorialized, requesting that the Empress Dowagers temporarily take charge of state affairs.
This pleased the empress dowagers.
Wang ministers and others were ordered to discuss the protocol for ruling from behind a screen.
When their deliberations were submitted,
the empress dowagers' imperial decree still stated,
"Ruling from behind a screen is not what we wish to do,
but because current affairs are difficult,
and the Wang ministers and others cannot be without direction,
we reluctantly grant the request."
So it was.
Thus, on the first day of the eleventh lunar month,
the Emperor, accompanied by the two Empress Dowagers, held court in the Yǎng Xīn Diàn (養心殿).
Princes, dukes, and ministers gathered outside the hall gate,
performing rites as prescribed.
Whenever internal and external officials were summoned for audience,
the two Empress Dowagers and the Emperor would jointly hold court in the Yǎng Xīn Diàn.
A screen would be hung in front of the Empress Dowagers.
Or if a certain minister was summoned for an audience,
the Prince Regent and Grand Ministers of the Imperial Presence would take turns announcing it.
When external officials were granted audience,
they would hold court in the front hall of the Yǎng Xīn Diàn.
The Prince Regent and Grand Ministers of the Imperial Presence, leading imperial guards, would stand in their respective ranks.
A screen would be hung in front of the Empress Dowagers, and a table set up.
The names and titles of the various officials would be presented,
and proposed imperial decrees drafted in advance,
then separately recorded and annotated.
Before the Emperor, a table was set up.
Various chief officials would, as usual, submit green-headed slips.
The Prince Regent and others would respectfully place them on the table.
Audiences would proceed according to standard protocol.
The Empress Dowagers would simply affix their seals to certain names internally.
After this,
they would hand them to the Wang ministers to transmit the decrees.
As for memorials of greetings from officials,
three copies were to be submitted.
For military reports from various provinces and routes,
whenever an imperial decree needed to be issued,
the Prince Regent and others would request instructions, draft the decree,
and present it for review and promulgation the next day.
However, the wording and composition
were still based on the Emperor's intent,
and when proclaimed to officials,
the decree should be written with the character
"Zhèn" (朕).
In the thirteenth year of the Tongzhì reign (1874),
Dézōng succeeded Wénzōng to the throne.
The imperial princes and high officials again requested the Two Empresses Dowager to govern from behind the curtain,
and all was approved in accordance with the established precedents from the early Tongzhì reign.
In the sixth year of the Guāngxù reign (1880),
Empress Dowager Cí'ān passed away,
and Empress Dowager Cíxǐ began to govern exclusively from behind the curtain.
It was decreed that she would relinquish power after thirteen years.
However, Dézōng, considering the still-difficult times,
continued to have her preside over audiences
and deliver instructions from the throne,
with a gauze screen set up to obscure her.
Ceremony for Assuming Personal Rule: In the first month of the twelfth year of the Tongzhì reign (1873),
the Two Empresses Dowager relinquished power.
Mùzōng conducted the ceremony for assuming personal rule.
Beforehand, envoys were dispatched to make announcements to Heaven, Earth, the ancestral temples, and the altars of land and grain.
On the appointed day, the imperial procession for the Empresses Dowager and the imperial procession for the Emperor were arranged.
A ceremonial table was set up at the gate of the Cínínggōng.
Inside the threshold, a kneeling mat for the Emperor was laid out.
Inside the Tàihédiàn, a rescript table was placed on the east side,
a secondary ceremonial table to the east,
and one central table on the imperial steps (dān bì).
Outside the Wǔmén, a dragon palanquin and an incense palanquin were set up.
Academicians of the Nèigé presented the Emperor's congratulatory memorial, placing it in a casket,
and then carried it out.
Grand Secretaries followed to outside the Yǒngkāng Zuǒmén.
A Grand Secretary received the casket
and proceeded to the Cíníngmén.
Ascending the east steps,
he placed it on the table
and withdrew.
Eunuchs carried the table in
and placed it east of the imperial throne in the Cínínggōng.
Academicians of the Nèigé presented the imperial rescript and placed it on the yellow table in the hall.
Officials of the Lǐbù presented the congratulatory memorials from princes and officials, placing them on the secondary yellow table to the east.
The congratulatory memorials from generals, commanders-in-chief, and garrisons were placed inside the dragon palanquin.
Officials of the Hónglúsì led princes of the first rank and below,
up to princes of the "eight distinguished families" and above, as well as Mongol princes, to assemble outside the Lóngzōngmén.
Officials not belonging to the "eight distinguished families" and below, up to second-rank officials and above, assembled outside the Chángxìnmén.
Third-rank officials and below assembled outside the Wǔmén.
At the time announced by the Qīntiānjiān,
the Emperor, in ceremonial attire, rode in a palanquin out of the Lóngzōngmén.
Upon arriving outside the Yǒngkāng Zuǒmén, he dismounted.
Princes and below followed.
Upon reaching the Cíníngmén,
the Emperor ascended the east steps
and stood facing west, to the left of the gate.
The four lecturers of the Rìjiǎng Guān stood on the west steps,
facing east.
The leading officials, along with the imperial guards, stood at the end of the imperial procession,
divided to the left and right.
The Empress Dowager emerged and took her seat in the Cínínggōng.
The Zhōnghé music began,
playing the "Yù Píng Zhāng" movement.
She ascended the throne,
and the music ceased.
The Emperor went to his kneeling position.
The Dān Bì music began,
playing the "Yì Píng Zhāng" movement.
Princes, high officials, imperial guards, and others stood in order, facing upwards.
The usher called out,
"Bow and kneel!"
The Emperor, leading his officials, performed three kneelings and nine prostrations.
At this time, two censors were placed beneath the west pillar,
along with two ushers.
At the end of the imperial procession and outside the Wǔmén, two censors, two Lǐbù officials, and two ushers were stationed,
serving as ceremonial assistants.
Ushers were also placed inside and outside the Yǒngkāng Zuǒmén and other gates,
to relay commands to the outside.
Officials outside the Wǔmén followed and performed the ritual.
The usher called out,
"Ritual complete!"
The Emperor returned to his position.
Princes and officials returned to their standing positions.
The Empress Dowager returned to her palace.
The Minister of the Lǐbù announced,
"Ritual complete!"
Only then did the Emperor return to his palace.
Shortly after, he reappeared and presided in the Zhōnghédiàn.
After the attending officials completed their ceremony,
they quickly exited and stood in the outer court.
The Emperor then presided in the Tàihédiàn.
Music began,
he ascended the throne,
music ceased,
and three whips were cracked.
Princes and all officials performed the ritual.
The proclamation of memorials and issuance of edicts were all according to the previous system.
Guāngxù's thirteenth year (1887), Dézōng's assumption of personal rule, followed this pattern.
Grand Court Ceremony: In the first year of the Tiānmìng reign (1616),
the New Year's Day celebration of congratulations began,
and court ceremonies were instituted.
In the sixth year of the Tiāncōng reign (1632),
the newly established court ceremonies were implemented,
from which the current court lineup originated.
In the first year of the Chóngdé reign (1636),
the ceremonies for presenting memorials on New Year's Day and celebrating imperial birthdays were established.
In the eighth year of the Shùnzhì reign (1651),
New Year's Day, Winter Solstice, and the Emperor's Birthday (Wànshòu Shèngjié) were designated as the three great festivals.
In the eighth year of the Kāngxī reign (1669),
the musical compositions for the principal court assembly were established,
and these were performed on all three great festivals.
During the Grand Court, salutations and congratulations were offered.
Officials from princes downwards, as well as princes from outer dependencies and envoys, all took their positions in the ranks.
The responsible department arranged the imperial procession and musical instruments according to regulations.
A yellow table was set up on the east side of the Tàihédiàn.
At dawn,
princes (wáng), imperial princes of the second rank (bèilè), and imperial princes of the third rank (bèizǐ) assembled at the Tàihémén.
Officials not belonging to the "eight distinguished families" and below assembled outside the Wǔmén.
The Lǐbù placed the memorials in the palanquin.
Soldiers carried them to outside the Wǔmén, where they were placed on both sides,
then the memorials were carried into the Tàihédiàn and placed on the tables.
The Hónglú Qīng led the princes (wáng) and bèilè to stand on the imperial steps (dān bì).
Ushers led the assembled officials and the officials presenting memorials to enter through the two side gates (yè mén),
and stand in order on the imperial courtyard (dān chí).
Officials from Cháoxiǎn (Korea) and Měnggǔ (Mongolia) entered through the west side gate,
standing at the end of the west rank.
Two censors overseeing the ceremony stood under the west eaves, facing east.
Four each stood on the imperial steps (dān bì) and imperial courtyard (dān chí), facing each other east and west.
Eight stood at the end of the east and west ranks.
Four ushers stood under the hall eaves,
and similarly on the imperial steps (bì) and courtyard (chí).
Six officials of the Luánjíwèi were in charge of cracking the whip at the three steps of the south staircase on the imperial steps (dān bì).
At the time announced by the Qīntiānjiān,
the Emperor emerged and presided in the Zhōnghédiàn.
After the attending officials completed their ceremony,
they quickly exited to the outer court to attend to matters.
When the imperial carriage departed,
the vanguard and rear guard followed the established rites.
Bells and drums sounded at the Wǔmén.
The Zhōnghé music began.
The Emperor proceeded to the Tàihédiàn.
The music ceased.
Inner Grand Ministers stood divided in front and behind.
Imperial guards were positioned behind them for protection.
Four officials from the Qǐjūzhù stood behind the golden pillars on the west side.
Grand Secretaries,
Academicians,
lecturing and reading academicians,
and Senior and Junior Supervisors of Instruction stood under the east eaves.
Censors (yùshǐ) and Vice Assistant Censors-in-Chief stood under the west eaves.
Officials of the Luánjíwèi called out,
"Crack the whip!"
Ushers called out,
"Form ranks!"
Princes and all officials took their kneeling positions.
The official proclaiming the memorial presented it,
and knelt facing north directly below the hall.
Two Grand Secretaries unrolled the memorial.
After the proclaiming official finished reading,
it was placed back on the original table.
The Dān Bì music began,
and all officials performed three kneelings and nine prostrations.
They withdrew
and returned to their original standing positions.
Officials of the Hónglúsì led the envoys from Cháoxiǎn and others.
Officials of the Lǐfànyuàn led the envoys from Měnggǔ to their kneeling positions.
They performed three kneelings and nine prostrations.
The Dān Bì music began.
After the ceremony was complete,
the music ceased.
They withdrew and stood as before.
Seats were granted.
All officials, including foreign envoys, performed one kneeling and three prostrations at their standing places,
then sat in order.
After tea was served,
three whips were cracked again.
The Zhōnghé music began.
The imperial carriage returned to the palace.
The music ceased, and the officials withdrew.
Initially established,
external officials would pay tribute and audiences on New Year's Day.
They would gather in front of the Bǎohé Diàn to perform the rites.
After the 26th year of Kāngxī, this practice was abolished.
In the 6th year of Qiánlóng,
it was stipulated that congratulatory ceremonies for the Emperor's Birthday (Shèngjié) would be performed while the Emperor was on tour (xíngzài).
In the 24th year,
the seating order for officials during Grand Audiences (dàcháo) was determined,
and red-lacquered wooden plaques were set up.
In the 54th year,
two additional Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn) chief officials and
thirty-six officials from the Bureaus (Kē) and Circuits (Dào) were added.
They were positioned along the sides of the 'Grade Mountains' (pǐnjí shān) to maintain order during the audience.
Also, in the early years of Gāozōng's reign,
civil officials of the third rank and above, and military officials of the second rank and above, were granted tea.
Others, only the record-keepers and foreign envoys, participated.
In the 2nd year of Jiāqìng, the practice of granting tea was abolished.
According to regulations (lìng jiǎ),
banquets were held at noon on New Year's Day (Yuándàn) and the Emperor's Birthday (Wànshòu Jié).
On the day after the Winter Solstice (Dōngzhì Jié), congratulations were received.
On the Emperor's Birthday, the Tàimiào was first visited,
then rites were performed at the Empress Dowager's (Huángtàihòu) palace.
Upon completion,
congratulations were received.
Civil and military officials in the directly administered provinces (zhíshěng) would, on the three major festivals,
all set up incense altars,
and, dressed in court attire, face the palace (wàngquē) to perform the rites.
Manchu, Mongol, and Han Banner armies (hànjūn) were divided into two wings,
while Han officials were divided into civil (east) and military (west).
Regular Audience Ceremony (Chángcháo Yí) After Tàizǔ established his reign title (jiànyuán) in the bingchén year,
he became even more diligent in state affairs.
He held court every five days,
burned incense to heaven,
and proclaimed ancient wise sayings, virtuous deeds, and the reasons for success or failure, rise or decline,
to admonish his officials and people.
However, this was not yet established as a fixed system.
In the early years of Chóngdé,
ceremonial regulations were first established,
including the setting up of the Grand Imperial Procession (dàjià lǔbù).
Officials from princes downwards, in court attire,
would wait for the Emperor to emerge from the palace,
and music would begin.
Upon reaching the hall,
and ascending the throne,
the music would cease.
Seats would be granted,
and all officials, according to their ranks,
would prostrate once and take their seats.
Officials from the Boards (Bù) and Censorate (Yuàn) would step forward to present their memorials.
After completion, the Emperor (jià) would return to the palace.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì,
Minister (Gěishì Zhōng) Wèi Xiàngshū said:
"According to past practice, there were New Moon (shuò) and Full Moon (wàng) audiences,
as well as morning audiences (zǎocháo), evening audiences (wǎncháo), inner audiences (nèicháo), and outer audiences (wàicháo).
Even if we cannot follow the old system entirely now,
I request that court be held three times a month,
to fulfill the sincere intention of diligent governance."
Yáng Huáng also said:
"The old rule for officials to hold court eleven times a month
seems too frequent.
Now, officials come to court daily to present memorials,
which is not less than eleven audiences.
It should be fixed that court attendance rites are performed on the 5th, 15th, and 25th of each month."
From then on, the system of holding court on days ending in five (féng wǔ shìcháo) was established.
Soon after, it was stipulated that officials for presentation (jiàncháo), farewell (cícháo), and thanks (xiè'ēn)
would all perform their rites on regular audience days.
When the Emperor presided over the Tàihé Diàn,
after presentations were concluded,
seats and tea were granted,
all in accordance with regular protocol.
If the Emperor did not attend the hall on that day,
officials would perform their rites outside the Wǔmén.
Tributary envoys from outer vassals (wàifān)
also performed their rites on regular audience days.
If they needed to return quickly,
they were not bound by the audience schedule,
and would proceed directly to the Wǔmén to perform their rites.
The same applied to external officials who needed to proceed quickly to their posts.
It was also stipulated that during regular audiences in the hall,
princes and dukes (wánggōng) would sit in order along the sides within the hall.
In the 8th year of Kāngxī,
it was stipulated that officials below dukes, marquises (hóu), and earls (bó) would be divided into six ranks,
and sit in order.
Later, this was changed to nine ranks.
In the 9th year,
an edict was issued to the Censorate (Dūchá Yuàn) to investigate impropriety among princes and high officials (wáng dàchén).
In the 20th year,
糾儀御史 (Jiūyí Yùshǐ, Rectifying Ceremonial Censors) and staff were established for regular audiences.
In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng,
four imperial guards (shìwèi) were dispatched to supervise the court ranks.
It was stipulated that on audience days, before dawn,
two Hónglú Sì officials would lead officials of the left and right wings into the Xīyè Mén to sit in their designated places.
When the drum sounded strictly,
they would stand up and listen to the announcement.
From the south side of the imperial standard (zhàng), they would be led forward,
their ranks tidied,
and perform the rites as prescribed.
In the early years of Qiánlóng,
an edict ordered all officials, great and small, to sit in their ranks at dawn,
following the example of imperial court officials.
In the 16th year,
an edict instructed the ministers of the Boards and Censorate (Bù Yuàn Dàchén) to oversee and lead their subordinates,
attending their ranks on schedule for regular audiences,
without absence or neglect.
In the 9th year of Guāngxù,
the court system was revised.
For all newly appointed officials,
the Hónglú Sì would list their names and titles and submit them to the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé).
On the appointed day, the Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shàngshū) and the Hónglú Qīng would request the Emperor to attend the hall,
and lead the officials to give thanks and perform the rites.
Princes, dukes (wánggōng), and all other officials would attend behind the imperial procession (lǔbù).
If the Emperor did not attend the hall,
civil and military officials would sit in their ranks outside the Wǔmén.
The time for this was
chénzhèng in spring and winter,
and mǎozhèng in summer and autumn.
In case of rain, snow, or national mourning, it would be excused.
On days when officials sat in their ranks,
Hónglú Sì officials would position them according to their wings.
Princes and dukes (wánggōng) gathered outside the Tàihé Mén,
two ranks each on the east and west.
All officials gathered outside the Wǔmén,
nine ranks each on the east and west.
Four Rectifying Ceremonial Censors (Jiūyí Yùshǐ) and four staff members from the Ministry of Personnel (Lì Sīyuán) and Ministry of Rites (Lǐ Sīyuán) each,
were positioned at the beginning and end of the ranks,
all facing west and looking north.
At the appointed time, the staff members of the Ministries of Personnel and Rites (Lì Lǐ Sīyuán) would receive the official names and titles.
The Rectifying Ceremonial Censors (Jiūyí Guān) would patrol the ranks for inspection,
then return to their positions and sit.
After a while,
they would exit in sequence.
The Ceremony of Attending to Government at the Palace Gate.
In the early Qīng dynasty, it was established
that government affairs were attended to daily,
always at the main gate.
The Jiǔqīng, Kēdào officials would all assemble to present their memorials,
which was the regular practice.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
the 御門 (Yùmén) ceremony was first formally established.
Whenever memorials from the Boards and Censorates had not yet received an imperial edict,
the memorials would be sent to the Nèigé.
When a certain number had accumulated,
an imperial edict would be issued for a specific day to attend to affairs at the Yùmén.
On that day,
in the center of the Qiánqīngmén, an imperial couch, a screen, and a desk for memorials were set up.
At dawn,
the ministers from the Boards and Censorates who were to present memorials, along with their accompanying officials, would all gather in the courtyard.
The emperor would ascend the throne.
The imperial guards would stand to his left and right.
The Jìzhùguān would ascend the western steps,
and the officials from the Boards and Censorates would ascend the eastern steps,
each taking their place and kneeling.
The Shàngshū would be in front,
the Shìláng behind,
and the accompanying officials even further back.
One Shàngshū would carry a memorial box, turn and advance,
proceed to the memorial desk,
kneel and present it on the desk,
rise,
retreat slightly,
hasten to the eastern pillar,
and then turn to the head of the row.
Kneeling,
he would orally present a certain matter.
When finished,
he would rise,
retreat slightly,
and lead his subordinates down the steps on the left.
Regarding the order of presenting memorials:
the Boards of Hù, Lǐ, Bīng, and Gōng would take turns at the head of the presentation.
The Sānfǎsī would be directly in the third row.
The Lìbù would be directly in the sixth row.
The Zōngrénfǔ would be placed before the Boards and Censorates.
The Hàn, Zhān, Kēdào, and the Jiǔqīng presenting jointly would be after the Boards and Censorates.
Each would advance and present their memorials according to their turn, as before.
When the Lìbù presented memorials,
they would also lead eight officials from various departments who were on duty for their audience.
After the audience was completed,
they would then withdraw.
Two Nèigé Shìdú Xuéshì would ascend the eastern steps,
go to the desk, kneel,
lift the memorial box,
rise,
and withdraw.
The Hàn, Zhān, Kēdào, and imperial guards would all withdraw.
At that time, one Mǎn Xuéshì appointed to read memorials,
carrying the memorial box, would ascend the eastern steps,
turn and withdraw.
The Dàxuéshì would follow,
kneeling according to their rank.
The Jìzhùguān would advance slightly and stand facing east.
The Xuéshì carrying the box would go to the desk, kneel, open the box,
take out the memorials, and present them in order.
The emperor would issue and proclaim his edicts.
After the Dàxuéshì and others received the edict,
they would rise,
descend the eastern steps.
The Jìzhùguān would descend the western steps.
The imperial carriage would return to the palace.
When memorials were presented,
Hànlín officials were ordered to record them,
starting from Shùnzhì second year.
Before this, memorials were presented in spring and summer at Mǎo Zhèng,
and in autumn and winter at Chén Chū.
In Kāngxī twenty-first year,
it was decreed to extend the Yùmén session time.
Spring and summer were changed to Chén Chū,
and autumn and winter to Chén Zhèng.
Two years later,
Censor Wèi Zhípú requested a schedule of every five days or every two or three days.
Shèngzǔ decreed:
“Governance must be diligent and meticulous,
and there should be no interruptions from beginning to end.”
In the twenty-fifth year,
two Kēdào officials each were appointed to attend the sessions,
ranking above the Qǐjūzhùguān.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Qǐjūzhùguān were abolished.
The Hànlín who attended the sessions
were ordered to withdraw immediately after presenting memorials.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
the Qǐjūzhùguān were re-established,
with two more added.
Four Biānjǐan were also ordered to attend the sessions,
ranking above the Kēdào.
In Qiánlóng second year,
Xuīxiū, Biān, and Jiǎn officials were ordered to wear prayer beads,
following the example of Kēdào officials,
to maintain the solemnity of the court ceremony.
In Jiāqìng eighteenth year,
it was decreed that when memorials were proclaimed and edicts received,
the Yùqián Dàchén and imperial guards should not withdraw.
This was established as a rule.
The Ceremony for the Tàishàng Huángdì at the Three Major Festivals. In Jiāqìng first year,
Gāozōng abdicated the throne to Rénzōng,
and was honored as Tàishàng Huángdì.
The ceremony of court greetings was established.
On the designated day, the ceremonial carriage, imperial regalia, and ceremonial music were arranged as in the abdication ceremony.
Three desks were set up in the Tàihédian.
The memorial pavilion was carried to the Wǔmén.
The congratulatory memorial was placed on the eastern desk,
and writing brushes and inkstones on the western desk.
At dawn,
princes, dukes, and all civil and military officials in court robes,
and foreign envoys in their national attire,
gathered beneath the palace gate.
The emperor, in ceremonial robes,
awaited in the Nuǎngé of the Bǎohédian.
The Tàishàng Huángdì departed by palanquin,
descended at the northern steps of the Tàihédiàn.
The Zhōnghé Sháoyuè began,
playing the Yuánpíng Zhāng.
He ascended to the throne in the hall,
and the music ceased.
The emperor stood facing west inside the hall.
The whip cracked thrice.
The announcer
called "Páibān!"
The Dānbì Dàyuè began,
playing the Qìngpíng Zhāng.
The emperor went to his bowing position,
facing north.
At this time, Hónglú officials led the assembled ministers and foreign envoys to stand in their solemn rows.
The announcer called "Jìn!"
The announcer called "Guì!
Kòu!
Xīng!"
The emperor led the assembled ministers in the three-kneels and nine-kowtows ceremony.
When finished,
the emperor returned to his position and stood.
The crowd withdrew
and returned to their rows.
The music ceased.
The whip cracked.
The Zhōnghé Sháoyuè began,
playing the Hépíng Zhāng.
The Tàishàng Huángdì returned to his palace,
and the music ceased.
The emperor ascended the hall.
The assembled ministers presented their memorials and performed the rituals as prescribed.
The Ceremony for the Tàihuáng Tàihòu, Huáng Tàihòu, and Huánghòu at the Three Major Festivals.
In Shùnzhì eighth year,
it was decreed that on New Year's Day, at the foot of the Cínínggōng steps, the ceremonial regalia and musical instruments for the Huáng Tàihòu would be set up.
The Huáng Tàihòu would enter the palace,
and the music would begin.
She would ascend the throne,
and the music would cease.
The emperor, leading the Nèidàchén and imperial guards, would proceed to the palace and perform the three-kneels and nine-kowtows ceremony.
When finished,
princesses and Fújìn below them,
and Dūtǒng, Zǐ, and Shàngshū’s wives above them,
would perform the six-solemn bows, three-kneels, and three-kowtows ceremony.
Music would play as before,
and a grand banquet would be held.
The Winter Solstice and the Emperor's Birthday were similar,
except that the banquet was omitted on the Winter Solstice.
In Kāngxī eighth year,
it was decreed that on New Year's Day, the ceremonial carriage of the Tàihuáng Tàihòu and Huáng Tàihòu, the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè, and the Dānbì Dàyuè would all be set up.
The emperor, leading the princes, dukes, ministers, imperial guards, and officials from Dūtǒng, Zǐ, and Shàngshū upwards,
would first proceed to the Tàihuáng Tàihòu's palace,
and then to the Huáng Tàihòu's palace,
performing the rites as prescribed.
When finished,
the Huánghòu, leading the princesses, Fújìn, and official wives, would also perform the rites in the same manner.
In the twenty-first year,
it was decreed that officials presenting memorials from the capital and outside
should gather outside the Wǔmén to perform the rites.
Soon after, Jīuyí Yùshǐ were appointed,
stationed outside the palace gate and at the end of the ceremonial procession outside the Wǔmén,
to strictly supervise the proceedings.
In the twelfth year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that second-rank imperial women (mìngfù) be allowed to join the ranks for congratulatory ceremonies for the Empress Dowager.
Later, an edict was issued for hereditary nobles (shìjué) to include baron-ranked men in their court salutations.
In the twenty-fifth year of Jiāqìng,
an edict stated that on the three grand festivals for the Empress Dowager,
generals (jiāngjūn), governors-general (dū), provincial governors (fǔ), military commanders (tí), and brigade-generals (zhèn) should all present congratulatory memorials,
and the practice of submitting yellow folded scrolls with祝文 (zhùwén) was abolished.
On New Year's Day of the first year of Dàoguāng,
the Grand Secretaries first presented the Emperor with congratulatory memorials,
after which the Emperor led his officials to the palace to perform the rites.
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
the Empress Dowager and the Emperor jointly held court at Cínínggōng to receive congratulations.
The following year,
this was changed to Yǎngxīndiàn.
Princes (wáng), dukes (gōng), and officials of the second rank and above
assembled outside Cíníngmén,
while those of the third rank and below assembled outside Wǔmén.
Korean envoys were placed at the end of the western ranks.
They performed the rites according to their ranks,
without a master of ceremonies' call (bùzàn).
The Winter Solstice and the Emperor's Birthday (Shèngshòu Jié) followed the same protocol.
However, during years of grand celebration,
after the Empress Dowager ascended the throne,
the practice of publicly reading memorials (xuānbǐao) was added.
In the second year of Guāngxù,
on the Empress Dowager's birthday (Shèngshòu),
the Emperor personally presented the memorial,
and the rest of the ceremony remained the same.
The Empress (Huánghòu) previously had no ceremony for receiving congratulations from officials.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
it was decreed that on New Year's Day, congratulatory ceremonies be held,
with full ceremonial guards (yízhàng).
After the Empress finished performing rites at the Empress Dowager's palace,
she would return to her own palace,
where princesses (gōngzhǔ) and imperial women (mìngfù) would all proceed to her palace to offer congratulations.
The Winter Solstice and the Empress's Birthday (Qiānqiū Jié) followed the same protocol.
During the Kāngxī era,
it was decreed that the Empress should first proceed to the Grand Empress Dowager's palace,
then to the Empress Dowager's palace to perform rites.
Upon returning to her palace, she would ascend her seat.
From princesses to the wives of princes of the first degree (zhènguó jiāngjūn),
and from dukes (gōng) and marquises (hóu) to the wives of ministers (shàngshū),
all would perform the rites in court attire.
In the sixth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was first ordered that on the Empress's Birthday (Qiānqiū Jié), princes (wáng), dukes (gōng), and all officials should wear their蟒袍 (mǎngpáo) and embroidered rank badges (bǔfú).
This practice was subsequently approved.
On the Qiānqiū Jié of an Imperial Noble Consort (Huáng Guìfēi) who managed the six palaces,
the ceremony was the same as that for the Empress.
Grand Banquet Ceremony: All customary state banquets
were overseen by the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù),
supplied by the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglùsì),
and arranged by the Bureau of Imperial Cuisine (Jīngzhànsī).
Banquets for the establishment of a new reign and the settling of the capital:
In the early Chóngdé period,
Tàizōng changed the reign title and established a new dynasty,
holding a banquet at Dǔgōngdiàn.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
when the capital was established in Yānjīng,
a banquet was held, and a throne was set in the center of Huángjí Mén.
The Emperor ascended the throne,
granted seats to all officials,
and bestowed tea and offered wine.
All performed one kneel and one kowtow.
After the banquet, thanks were offered with the initial rites.
On that day, during the banquet,
several imperial eunuchs (nèijiān) performed kowtows and dances in advance.
An edict stated:
"During grand congratulatory ceremonies,
eunuchs are not permitted to follow the Míng dynasty system of joining the ranks and performing rites."
The suppression of eunuchs began with this act.
New Year's Day Banquet:
In the early Chóngdé period,
regulations were established:
a banquet was held at Chóngzhèngdiàn.
Princes (wáng), beile (bèilè), beise (bèizi), dukes (gōng), etc., each presented their own food, livestock, and wine.
Outer vassal princes (wài fān wáng) and beile (bèilè) did likewise.
In the tenth year of Shùnzhì,

it was ordered that imperial princes (qīnwáng), imperial heirs (shìzǐ), commandery princes (jùnwáng), as well as outer vassal princes (wài fān wáng) and beile (bèilè), each present livestock and wine.
If insufficient,
the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglùsì) would supplement it.
The imperial banquet was provided by the Directorate of Imperial Foods (Shàngshànjiān).
This practice was abolished in the thirteenth year of Kāngxī,
but reinstated several years later.
In the twenty-third year,
roast meat (fánzhì) was changed to soups and stews (yáogēng),
and silver vessels were removed.
Princes (wáng) and below presented different grades of soups, stews, and banquets.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
the New Year's Day banquet ceremony was established.
On that day, at the hour of sì (9-11 a.m.),
inner and outer princes (wáng), dukes (gōng), and taisha (táijí) assembled at Tàihémén in court attire.
Civil and military officials assembled at Wǔmén.
The imperial banquet was set before the throne.

Grand ministers of the interior (nèi dàchén), ministers of the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ dàchén), and chief officials of the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) and the Court of Colonial Affairs (Lǐfānyuàn) supervised the seating arrangements.
A yellow canopy was erected on the imperial platform (dānbì),
and gold vessels were displayed beneath it.
Behind the imperial procession (lǔbù), a blue canopy was erected,
and various seats were arranged.
Officials of the Court of State Ceremonials (Hónglúsì) led officials in.
Officials of the Court of Colonial Affairs (Lǐfānyuàn) led outer vassal princes (wáng) and dukes (gōng) in.
The Emperor proceeded to Tàihédiàn,
ascended the throne.
The Zhōnghé Sháolè music began.
Princes (wáng) and ministers took their places inside the hall.
Civil officials of the third rank and military officials of the second rank and above took their places on the imperial platform (dānbì).
The rest took their places under the blue canopy.
All performed one kowtow,
and sat.
Tea was bestowed.
Grand music began on the imperial platform (dānbì).
Princes (wáng) and below knelt at their seats,
then performed another kowtow.
After the Emperor finished drinking tea,
imperial guards (shìwèi) served tea to princes (wáng) and ministers.
Officials of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglùguān) served tea to all officials.
They then performed another kowtow at their seats.
After drinking,
they performed another kowtow,
and the music stopped.
The tablecloths were unveiled.
Officials of the Bureau of Ceremonials (Zhǎnyísī) individually held kettles, wine cups (jué), and gold goblets (zhī).
Grand music began.
All officials rose.
Officials of the Bureau of Ceremonials (Zhǎnyísī) held the kettles and poured wine into the wine cups (jué).
The minister designated to present wine (jìnjúe dàchén) approached and knelt,
and then all knelt.
Officials of the Bureau of Ceremonials (Zhǎnyísī) handed the wine cups (jué) to the minister.
The minister ascended from the central steps (zhōngbì),
knelt before the Emperor, and presented the wine.
He rose,
descended from the right steps (yòubì),
returned to his position,
performed one kowtow,
and all officials kowtowed.
The minister rose,
ascended again from the right steps (yòubì),
knelt to receive the wine cup (jué),
returned to his position,
and knelt.
Officials of the Bureau of Ceremonials (Zhǎnyísī) received the empty wine cup (xūjué) and withdrew.
They held the goblet (zhī) and filled it with wine,
and by imperial command, bestowed wine upon the minister who had presented the wine.
Princes (wáng) and below rose.
Officials of the Bureau of Ceremonials (Zhǎnyísī) stood and handed the goblet (zhī).
The minister knelt to receive the wine cup (jué),
performed one kowtow,
finished drinking,
waited for the recipient of the wine cup (jué) to withdraw,
performed another kowtow,
rose,
and returned to his seat.
All officials sat.
The music stopped.
The Emperor consumed his meal.
Zhōnghé Qīnglè music began.
Food from each banquet table was distributed,
with one goblet (zhī) of wine each,
following the same procedure as serving tea.
The music stopped.
Mongolian music and songs were presented.
After this,
ministers performed the Mǎn Dǎo dance.
The Mǎn Dǎo dance offered longevity.
The paired dances were then performed.
Music and songs accompanied them.
The Wǎ'ěrkā Shì dance began,
accompanied by Mongolian music and songs.
Then more group dances were performed.
Each time they withdrew, they performed one kowtow.
Various acrobatic performances were then presented.
After completion,
all officials performed three kowtows.
Grand music began.
Whips were cracked.
Sháolè music began,
and the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
The Dōngzhì (Winter Solstice) feast.
During the Shùnzhì reign, it was established to follow the ceremony of Yuándàn (New Year's Day),
but later it was often suspended.
The Yuánhuì (New Year's Gathering) feast.
Whenever there was a New Year's Day court gathering,
which was a regular annual event,
or on the occasion of the Wànshòu (Emperor's Birthday) celebration,
or a decennial national celebration,
a special feast ceremony would be held.
In the 35th and 55th years of the Qiánlóng reign,
the emperor personally composed songs for the Yuánhuì,
and the feast ceremony remained as before.
However, after the wine was served,
the Qìnglóng dance would be performed,
the officers of music would sing,
and the dancers, wearing masks,
would ride on yùmǎ (wooden horses),
to perform the Yángliè dance.
The musicians playing string instruments like the zhēng and ruǎn, and clappers,
would perform their skills in turn.
During the Xǐqǐ dance,
the high officials would enter,
perform the three kòutóu (kowtows),
and dance in formation to the sound of the singing.
When the singing ceased,
the jiā (pipes) would be played,
and the Barbarian tribes would perform a joint concert.
Officials from the Imperial Household Department would lead the Cháoxiǎn pái (Korean entertainers),
and children from Huíbù (Muslim regions) and Jīnchuān Fānbù (Jinchuan Barbarian tribes) would perform various acrobatics,
which were slight variations.
The Qiānqiū (Thousand Autumns) feast.
This was an institution created in the 52nd year of the Kāngxī reign,
held at Chàngchūnyuán (Garden of Joyful Spring).
All incumbent officials from the provinces, retired Han officials, and commoners,
aged 65 and above, up to 90, were included.
Their sons and grandsons, or members of the imperial clan, would hold the cups and serve drinks,
and food items would be distributed.
An edict forbade them from standing,
to show special favor.
In the 50th year of the Qiánlóng reign,
a feast was held at Qiánqīnggōng (Palace of Heavenly Purity),

attended by kings, dukes, internal and external civil and military officials, retired officials, gentry, soldiers, aged farmers, merchants, and foreign tributary kings, dukes, and tàijí (Mongol nobles),
Huíbù and Fānbù local officials and headmen,
and Cháoxiǎn peíchén (Korean tributary ministers),
all over the age of sixty,
totaling more than three thousand people.
Ministers aged 70 and above,
and others aged 90 and above,
were allowed to be supported by their children and grandchildren to attend the feast.
The oldest individuals,
such as Guō Zhōngyuè, who was 105 years old and held the title of Sīyè (Director of Studies),
were allowed to approach the fǔzuò (imperial throne) alongside first-rank officials,
and personally receive wine from the emperor.
After the feast,
precious gifts were awarded according to rank.
It was held again in the first year of Jiāqìng's reign,
with the feast set in Huángjídian (Hall of Imperial Supremacy).
Three thousand fifty-six people attended the feast,
and five thousand people received awards.
From the highest officials to the lowest,
down to the common soldiers,
as well as the tribute envoys from Ménggǔ (Mongolia), Huíbù, Fānbù, Cháoxiǎn (Korea), Ānnán (Annam), Xiānluó (Siam), and Guō'ěrkā (Gurkhas),
regardless of their age,
all gathered in the imperial courtyard.
It was indeed a grand ceremony.
The Dàhūn (Grand Wedding) feast.
In the 8th year of the Shùnzhì reign,
after the grand wedding ceremony,
a feast was held following the Yuándàn ceremony.
Offerings of livestock and wine were also presented to the Empress Dowager,
and this was imitated thereafter.
The Gēngjí (Plowing Ceremony) feast.
It was held in the 11th year of the Shùnzhì reign,
and named
"Láojiǔ" (Labor Wine).
The Kǎixuán (Victory Return) feast.
It began in the 7th year of the Chóngdé reign.
In the 13th year of the Shùnzhì reign, it was formally established that
victorious generals, upon audience with the emperor, would be granted a feast.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
after the pacification of Jīnchuān,
a feast was held at Yíngtái;
after the pacification of Huíbù,
a feast was held at Fēngzéyuán;
and after the pacification of both Jīnchuān,
a feast was granted at Zǐguānggé (Pavilion of Purple Light).
At that time, captured Fānbù children who were skilled in Guōzhuāng and Jiǎsīlǔ dances,
and Fānbù shamanic nàxì (exorcism plays),
were also ordered to perform during the feast,
and this became a regular practice.
In the 8th year of the Dàoguāng reign,
after the pacification of Huíjiāng (Muslim borderlands),
a feast was granted at Zhèngdàguāngmíngdiàn (Hall of Uprightness and Luster).
On that day, the grand general offered a cup of wine for the emperor's longevity,
the emperor personally bestowed wine,
and ordered the imperial guards to distribute wine to the ministers who had participated in the campaign,
the rest followed the usual ceremony.
The Zōngshì (Imperial Clan) feast.
In the 11th year of the Qiánlóng reign,
a feast was held at Yíngtái,
granted to imperial princes and dukes.
By imperial decree, they were seated according to seniority,
and performed family rites.
They were also led to Shūqīngyuàn liúbēitíng (Flowing Cup Pavilion at the Garden of Purity and Serenity) for sightseeing,
and given wine and fruits.
In the 48th year,
a feast was held at Qiánqīnggōng,
attended by the imperial princes, kings, dukes, and 1,308 imperial clan members holding third and fourth-rank titles.
Those who could not attend due to other duties were all given awards,
totaling two thousand people.
In the 9th year of Jiāqìng,
a feast was held at Dūndiàn,
largely similar to the Yíngtái feast.
The Wàifān (Foreign Tributary) feast.
It was held annually on New Year's Eve at Bǎohédiàn (Hall of Preserving Harmony),
granted to Ménggǔ (Mongol) kings and dukes.
The seating, serving of tea, offering of wine, serving of drinks, musical performances, and expression of gratitude,
all followed the Yuánhuì ceremony.
When they came to court to present tribute,
or to escort family members to an imperial audience,
either an imperial grace feast was bestowed,
or a feast was held at the Lǐbù (Board of Rites),
with preparations made according to imperial decree.
Regarding tribute missions from various nations,
such as envoys from Cháoxiǎn, Ānnán, Liúqiú, and Hélán (Holland) coming to the capital,
there were also customary feasts.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
Myànliàn (Myanmar) envoys attended a feast at Wànshùyuán (Garden of Ten Thousand Trees),
where their five kinds of national musical instruments were played in a joint performance.
Thereafter, whenever feasts were held,
music from Zhǔnbù (Dzungar region), Huíbù, Ānnán, Myànliàn, and Guō'ěrkā was always performed.
Furthermore, during the Shùnzhì reign,
it was established that the Xiāngshì (Provincial Examinations) feast would be held at Shùntiānfǔ (Shuntian Prefecture),
and the Huìshì (Metropolitan Examinations) and Jìnshì chuánlú (Imperial Examination Graduates' Proclamation) feasts would be held at the Lǐbù.

Other events such as Línyōng (Imperial visit to the Imperial Academy), Jīngyán (Imperial Lecture), Xiūshū (Compilation of Books), Chūjǔ rìjiǎng (First Daily Lecture), Língxìng hànlínyuàn (Imperial Visit to the Hanlin Academy), and Shànxiě shénpái (Writing of Ancestral Tablets),
also involved customary feasts.
When Yǎnshènggōng (Duke Yansheng) and Zhèngyī Zhēnrén (Perfected Person of Orthodox Unity) came to court,
and during the compilation of Shílù (Veritable Records) and Huìdiǎn (Collected Statutes), feasts were always held at the Lǐbù.
Ceremony for conferring honorific titles and auspicious titles. In the early Qīng dynasty, during the reigns of Tàizǔ and Tàizōng,
all officials conferred honorific titles,
and the ceremony was the same as that for the emperor's enthronement.
During the Kāngxī reign,
officials and commoners collectively petitioned to confer an honorific title.
On the occasion of the emperor's 60th birthday,
they again made a plea.
Shèngzǔ (Emperor Kāngxī) decreed that such words were of no benefit to governance,
and refused to allow it.
Even after Gāozōng (Emperor Qiánlóng) pacified the frontiers,
kings and high officials still requested to confer an honorific title,
but it was not accepted.
Only when a new emperor ascended the throne,
and honored his mother as Huángtàihòu (Empress Dowager) and the Empress Dowager as Tàihuángtàihòu (Grand Empress Dowager),
were honorific titles conferred.
When the nation held a grand celebration,
auspicious titles were conferred,
either of two or four characters,
progressively added to show respect.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì’s reign,
a reverent title was bestowed upon Empress Xiàozhuāng.
Her honorific title was
“Zhāoshèng Císhòu.”
Prior to the ceremony, sacrifices and announcements were made.
The Emperor personally submitted the memorial.
On the appointed day, the Emperor’s ceremonial carriage was displayed in the Tàihe Hall,
and the Empress Dowager’s ceremonial carriage was displayed in the Cíníng Palace.
All offerings and arrangements were ready.
Princes and dukes gathered at the Tàihe Gate,
ministers gathered at the Right Wing Gate,
and all other officials gathered at the Wǔ Gate,
standing in divided wings.
The Emperor ascended the hall,
the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè began to play,
performing the “Hǎishàng Pántáo” movement.
After the Emperor had reviewed the imperial decree and seal,
the officiating officials placed them separately inside pavilions.
The Luányí guards carried them,
the decree pavilion in front,
the seal pavilion behind.
The Emperor led his officials, following the imperial carriage to the Cíníng Gate.
Entering the palace, they stood on the east of the steps.
The Assistant Minister of Rites and Grand Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat presented the imperial decree and seal,
and the Grand Academicians presented and read the texts of the decree and seal,
standing by the left side.
The Emperor proceeded to the bowing position,
while princes, dukes, and all officials stood according to their ranks.
The Empress Dowager ascended her palace seat,
the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè began to play,
performing the “Yù Píng” movement.
She ascended the throne,
and the music ceased.
The announcer called
“Kneel!”
The Emperor led his officials in kneeling.
The announcer called
“Present the decree!”
A Grand Academician knelt on the right side and presented it.
He rose,
and withdrew.
The Emperor received the decree,
and respectfully offered it.
A Grand Academician knelt on the left side to receive it.
He rose,
and placed it on the central table.
The announcer called
“Present the seal!”
The ceremony proceeded as before.
The announcer called
“Proclaim the decree!”
The official appointed to proclaim the decree went before the table, knelt facing north,
opened the case, proclaimed the text,
then put it back.
He rose,
and withdrew.
The announcer called
“Proclaim the seal!”
The same procedure was followed.
It was then placed back on the original table.
Four palace women lifted the table and placed it on the palace steps.
The Dānbì Grand Music began to play,
performing the “Yì Píng” movement.
The Emperor led his officials in three kowtows and nine prostrations.
Officials outside the Wǔ Gate received and relayed instructions, performing the rites with their ranks.
When the ceremony was complete,
the Empress Dowager rose from her seat.
The Zhōnghé Sháoyuè began to play,
performing the “Lǚ Píng” movement.
She returned to her palace.
The Empress led the six palaces and princesses and others to the palace to offer congratulations.
The next day,
the Emperor presided at the Tàihe Hall.
Princes, dukes, and all officials presented memorials to offer congratulations.
An imperial edict was issued according to the established system.
That year, the grand wedding ceremony was completed,
and the ceremony for bestowing honorific titles was also conducted in the same manner.
In the first year of Kāngxī’s reign,
an honorific title was bestowed.
As it was a period of mourning,
no memorials were submitted,
no ceremonies were held,
and no court congratulations took place.

All grand wedding ceremonies, assumption of personal rule, enthronement of an Empress, successful military campaigns, grand celebrations of an Empress Dowager, and bestowal of honorific titles were to follow the usual procedures.
In the forty-first year of Qiánlóng’s reign,
after the pacification of Jīnchuān,
an honorific title was bestowed.
The Empress Dowager instructed that the Emperor was advanced in age,
and should not be overly fatigued.
She ordered that the decree and seal be prepared in advance,
and that the rites be performed at the appointed time,
but the proclamation of the memorial texts was to be omitted.
This was followed thereafter.
In the ninth year of Dàoguāng’s reign,
after the pacification of Huíjiāng,
an honorific title was bestowed upon the Empress Dowager.
The King of Miàndiàn (Myanmar) sent envoys to present a gold-leaf congratulatory memorial.
This marked the beginning of Burmese kings presenting memorials.
The formal investiture of Grand Consorts with decrees and seals followed the previous ceremony,
except that eunuchs carried the table to be placed before the Grand Consort’s seat.
The Emperor performed the rites,
and the Grand Consort rose and stood aside from her seat.
The next day, the court reception of congratulations in the hall was the same.
If an official was dispatched to conduct the matter,
the Minister of Rites, in court attire, would proceed to the Grand Secretariat.
The decree and seal would be carried out,
and he would accompany the Grand Academicians to escort them.
Upon reaching the palace gate,
eunuchs would enter to present them to the Grand Consorts and Grand Imperial Concubines.
After they were received,
the ceremony was complete.
Initially, decrees and seals were made of gold.
During the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns, fine jade was also used.
After Dàoguāng, they were made exclusively of jade.
All formal investitures of Imperial Noble Consorts and Noble Grand Imperial Concubines
used decrees and seals.
Grand Consorts used decrees and impresses.
Grand Imperial Concubines used decrees.
Ceremony for the Enthronement of the Central Palace: In the first year of Chóngdé’s reign,
Empress Xiàoduānwén, as the legitimate primary consort, was formally installed in the central palace,
and the enthronement ceremony was first performed.
On that day, a yellow tent was set up in front of the Qīngníng Palace.
Inside the tent, a yellow table was placed,
and to its east, the table for the decree and seal.
Princes, dukes, and officials gathered at the Chóngzhèng Hall.
The Emperor presided in the hall and reviewed the decree and seal.
The chief envoy and deputy envoy, holding their credentials,
and the officiating officials, carrying the decree and seal, proceeded to the front of the yellow tent.
The Empress came out to receive them.
The envoys respectfully placed the decree and seal on the table,
standing facing west.
The text of the decree was proclaimed.
It was written in Mǎn, Méng, and Hàn scripts.
It was then successively handed to the right palace woman.
The palace woman knelt to receive it and presented it to the Empress.
The Empress successively knelt to receive it,
and passed it to the left palace woman,
who also knelt to receive it.
It was placed on the yellow table.
The subsequent proclamation and reception of the seal also followed this procedure.
The envoys exited,
and reported back.
The Empress led the princesses, fújìn, and court ladies to the Chóngzhèng Hall to perform six bows, three kowtows, and three prostrations before the Emperor.
When finished,
she returned to her palace and ascended her seat.
The consorts led the princesses and others in performing rites.
Princes, dukes, and officials presented memorials to offer congratulations,
and a banquet was granted as per usual.
In the sixteenth year of Kāngxī’s reign,
Empress Xiàozhāorén was enthroned.
Prior to this, the rites of Nàcǎi and Dàzhēng were retrospectively performed, as in a grand wedding ceremony.
The Emperor personally went to the Fèngxiān Hall to offer sacrifices and announce.
Officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices and announce at Heaven and Earth, and the Rear Hall of the Imperial Ancestral Temple.
On the day itself, a table for the credentials was set in the center of the Tàihe Hall,
with offerings to the east and west;
to the left and right, one table each was set,
with offerings to the north and south.
The Emperor presided in the hall and reviewed the decree and seal.
Princes, dukes, and officials stood in order.
The chief envoy and deputy envoy stood on the imperial steps,
facing north.
The official proclaiming the imperial decree stood to the left of the central hall door.
The imperial decree was proclaimed, saying:
“On such and such a date,
Consort Mǒushì is enthroned as Empress.
You are commanded to hold the credentials and perform the ceremony.”
Thereupon, the chief and deputy envoys held the credentials and proceeded forward.
The guards carried the decree and seal pavilions out through the Xiéhé Gate,
to the Jǐngyùn Gate.
The decree, seal, and credentials were handed to the eunuchs,
who respectfully carried them to the palace gate.
The Empress came to receive them.
When the ceremony was completed,
the eunuchs exited
and returned the credentials to the envoys.
The envoys reported back.
The Emperor led his officials to the palaces of the Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager to perform rites.
The next day,
the Empress, in ceremonial dress, went to both palaces and before the Emperor’s seat to perform rites.
In the second year of Qiánlóng’s reign,
Empress Xiàoxiánchún was enthroned,
following the usual procedure.
An imperial edict was commanded to be issued,
and this was established as a family law.
In the first year of Jiāqìng’s reign,
Empress Xiàoshūruì was established.
On the day of the enthronement,
after the Grand Emperor’s qiānqiū banquet and return to the palace,
the Emperor and Empress went forward to perform rites.
The Emperor presided in the hall.
The chief and deputy envoys held the credentials.
When the ceremony was complete,
they first proceeded to the Grand Emperor’s palace gate to report back.
The rest followed the usual procedure.
The enfeoffment of concubines,
also began in the first year of Chóngdé.
The Four Consorts were enfeoffed on the same day.
At the appointed time, envoys were ordered to hold the ceremonial scepter and enfeoff them according to ritual.
The consorts, leading princesses (gōngzhǔ), imperial daughters-in-law (fújìn), and court ladies (mìngfù), proceeded before the Emperor to perform six bows, three kowtows, and three full prostrations.
The same was done before the Empress.
Before a consort, they performed four bows, two kowtows, and two full prostrations.
The consorts, facing each other, each performed two bows, one kowtow, and one full prostration.
During the Kāngxī reign,
the Noble Consort (guìfēi) and seven concubines (pín) were enfeoffed on the same day as the Empress (zhōnggōng).
The various concubines received a patent (cè) but no seal (bǎo).
In the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that the Imperial Consort (huángfēi) should manage the affairs of the six palaces,
and her status should be elevated.
The sacrifices and proclamations (jìgào) were to follow the ceremonies for enfeoffing the Empress.
The next day, she paid respects to the Empress Dowager (huángtàihòu),
kneeling and bowing to the left of the imperial walkway.
In the third year of Dàoguāng,
an edict stated that thereafter, the sacrifices and proclamations for enfeoffing concubines (pín) would be abolished,
even if they were enfeoffed on the same day as a consort (fēi).
This was to be established as a regulation.
Ceremony for Establishing the Crown Prince (huángtàizǐ) In the fourteenth year of Kāngxī,
the Emperor's legitimate son, Yǔnrèng, was established as the Crown Prince.
Sacrifices and proclamations were made in advance.
The jade (yù), silk (bó), incense (xiāng), and tablets (bǎn)
were all personally inspected by the Emperor.
On the appointed day, the Emperor held court in the main hall and issued the decree,
which was the same as establishing the Empress.
The principal envoy (zhèngshǐ) presented the patent (cè),
and the deputy envoy (fùshǐ) presented the seal (bǎo).
After the rituals were completed,
the principal and deputy envoys reported back.
The Emperor, leading the Crown Prince, performed sacrifices and proclamations at the Fèngxiān Diàn.
The Crown Prince knelt on a mat placed outside the threshold.
He also went to the Emperor's and Empress's palaces to perform rituals.
The next day,
the Emperor held court to receive congratulations and issued edicts as per normal ceremony.
Princes (wánggōng) presented memorials (jiān) before the Crown Prince to offer congratulations.
The Crown Prince proceeded to the Wǔyīng Diàn to perform rituals with imperial princes (qīn) and princely dukes (jùnwáng), and others.
Civil and military officials from outside the capital also presented congratulatory memorials as per ceremony.
On the Crown Prince's birthday (qiānqiūjié),
the Crown Prince first proceeded to the Fèngxiān Diàn to offer sacrifices,
then went before the Emperor to perform rituals,
returned to the Yùqìng Gōng,
and then proceeded to the Dūnběn Diàn to receive congratulations.
Princes and all officials performed two kowtows and six full prostrations.
After completion,
he returned to his palace,
and the multitude of officials withdrew.
Subsequently, Yǔnrèng was repeatedly deposed and reinstated,
and the succession remained unsettled until the Emperor's later years.
Fifty years later,
Grand Secretary Wáng Yàn submitted seven confidential memorials,
requesting the establishment of the foundation of the state (i.e., naming a successor).
In the sixtieth year,
he reiterated his previous request,
which angered the Sacred Emperor.
It was not until after the Qiánlóng and Jiāqìng reigns
that an explicit edict was issued declaring no Crown Prince would be established,
a practice previously unknown since the founding of the dynasty.
Ceremony for Enfeoffing Various Princes (zhūwáng) In the first year of Chóngdé,
it was decreed that on the day of enfeoffment,
princes (wáng) and princely lords (bèilè) would stand in order before the Chóngzhèng Diàn.
Officials from the Inner Court would present the imperial patent (zhìcè) and seal (yìn) on a table,
awaiting the imperial decree for enfeoffment.
All the princes would kneel.
The official announcing the patent and the official presenting the patent would both stand to the east of the table.
After the announcement was completed in sequence,
the patent and seal would be presented to the various princes.
The princes would respectfully receive them,
then hand them over to their attendant officials,
and return to their positions.
After the ceremony was completed,
they would follow the official bearing the patent to the Qīngníng Gōng,
and perform rituals before the Emperor and Empress,
three kowtows and nine full prostrations.
Then they would exit the Dàqīng Mén.
The various princes would congratulate each other,
all performing two kowtows and six full prostrations.
Upon returning to their residences,
their consorts (fújìn) and ladies (fūrén) would each perform congratulatory rites.
Residence officials (fǔliáo) would offer congratulations to the various princes,
performing two kowtows and six full prostrations.
Bèilè's staff would perform one kowtow and three full prostrations.
In the twelfth year of Kāngxī, a regulation was established:
for all enfeoffments,
two principal and deputy envoys would be selected.
The day before,
a scepter table (jiécè àn),
an incense table (xiāng àn),
and a patent and seal table (cèbǎo àn) would be set up in the hall.
Imperial guards and musical instruments would be fully displayed before the hall.
At the appointed time,
the principal and deputy envoys would proceed to the Tàihé Diàn to receive the scepter and depart.
Imperial guards (jiàowèi) would carry the patent and seal pavilion (cèbǎo tíng) to the prince's mansion.
The prince, leading his residence officials, would kneel to receive them outside the gate.
The principal and deputy envoys would place the patent, seal, and scepter separately on their respective tables,
standing to the east of the scepter table.
The prince would stand to the west of the table.
After the rituals were completed,
the prince would proceed to the incense table and kneel,
listening to the proclamation of the imperial patent.
The envoys would present the patent and seal.
The prince would respectfully receive them,
return to his position,
and perform rituals as before.
The envoys would return the scepter and report back.
The prince, leading his residence officials, would kneel to see them off.
Music would be played for both receiving and sending off.
The document for enfeoffing an imperial prince (qīnwáng) was called a "seal" (bǎo);
for a princely duke (jùnwáng), it was an "imprint" (yìn).
A bèilè received a patent (zhìcè) but no imprint.
The rituals for offering thanks were the same.
Initially,
for enfeoffing the heir of an imperial prince (qīnwáng shìzǐ), a gold patent was used.
For a princely duke, a gilded silver patent was used.
A bèilè was granted a patent of appointment (gàomìng).
Later, this was changed to paper patents.
In the tenth year of Xiánfēng,
an edict decreed that patents for enfeoffing imperial princes should be made of gilded silver.
However, since Gōng Qīnwáng Yìxīn's princely title was hereditary,
a gold patent was still to be made for him.
For the enfeoffment of a princess (gōngzhǔ),
when the enfeoffment envoys arrived,
the princess, leading her maids, would greet them to the right of the ceremonial gate.
The envoys would bear the imperial patent inside
and place it on a yellow table before the gate,
then move it inside the canopy in front of the hall.
The princess would ascend the western steps,
performing six bows, three kowtows, and three full prostrations.
After the proclamation was read,
it would be handed to a maid.
The princess would kneel to receive it
and perform rituals as before.
The envoys would report back
and be seen off outside the ceremonial gate.
On that day, the Emperor would ascend the throne.
The princess would proceed before the Emperor,
then enter the Empress's palace,
performing six bows, three kowtows, and three full prostrations in both instances.
Next, she would proceed before the various consorts,
each time performing four bows, two kowtows, and two full prostrations.
Upon returning to her residence,
her household staff would offer congratulations.
Other procedures were the same as for enfeoffing an imperial prince.
For both gǔlún gōngzhǔ and héshuò gōngzhǔ,
those of the same generation were enfeoffed as eldest princess (zhǎng gōngzhǔ).
The elder ones were enfeoffed as grand eldest princess (dàzhǎng gōngzhǔ).
All were granted gold patents.

Treatise 64, Rites 8 (Auspicious Rites 2) Grand Wedding Ceremony. Ceremony for Imperial Princes' Weddings (with ceremonies for princes and dukes appended). Ceremony for Princesses' Marriages (with ceremonies for princely daughters and below appended). Marriage Rites for Officials and Commoners. Ceremony for Imperial Tours of Schools (with visits to the Imperial Academy appended). Imperial Lectures (with daily lectures appended). Examination of Scholars. Proclamation of Edicts (with reception of edicts appended). Presentation of Books. Presentation of Memorials and Petitions. Imperial Tours of Inspection. Village Archery and Drinking Rites.
The Grand Wedding Ceremony. In the *wùzǐ* year of Tàizǔ's (太祖) early Qīng (清) reign,
Nàlínbùlù (納林布祿), the *bèilè* (貝勒) of the Yèhè (葉赫) state, sent his sister to marry [the Emperor].
The Emperor, with the *bèilè* (貝勒) and others, welcomed her.
A grand feast was held,
and the ceremony was completed.
At that time, the ceremonial procedures had not yet been finalized.
After Tàizōng (太宗) ascended the throne,
the ceremony of enthronement was performed.
It was not until the eighth year of Shùnzhì (順治) (1651),
when Shìzǔ's (世祖) grand wedding took place,
that the ceremony for installing an Empress was first established.
Prior to the date, an auspicious day was chosen for the betrothal ceremony (*nàcǎi* 納采).
The day before [the ceremony],
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices to the suburban altars (*jiāo, shè* 郊、社) and the Tàimiào (太廟) (Imperial Ancestral Temple).
On the appointed day, at dawn,
a ceremonial table for the imperial insignia (*jié'àn* 節案) was set up in the Tàihé Diàn (太和殿).
The ceremonial gifts were arranged on the imperial staircase (*dānbì* 丹陛),
and decorated horses were displayed below.
The principal and副 envoys waited to the east of the imperial courtyard (*dānchí* 丹墀).
The officiating herald (*míngzàn guān* 鳴贊官) announced the proceedings.
After the envoys performed three跪 and nine prostrations,
they ascended the eastern steps
and stood on the imperial staircase.
The official who proclaimed edicts (*xuānzhì guān* 宣制官) transmitted the imperial edict.
The envoys knelt.
The edict stated:
"We now take a certain daughter of the Mǒu (某) clan as Empress.
We command you, Our ministers, to proceed with the imperial insignia (*jié* 節) and perform the betrothal ceremony."
The Grand Secretary (*dàxuéshì* 大學士) entered,
bore the imperial insignia out,
and presented it to the principal envoy.
The principal envoy received it,
and together with the副 envoy, rose
and proceeded to descend the left side of the middle steps.
The attendant officials placed the ceremonial objects into decorated palanquins.
The honor guard led the procession,
and imperial guards led the horses, following.
They exited through the middle gate of Tàihé Mén (太和門)
and proceeded to the Empress's residence (*hòudǐ* 后邸).
The Empress's father, in court attire, knelt to welcome them on the right side of the road outside the gate.
Upon entering,
the envoys placed the imperial insignia on the central table.
The attendant officials arranged the ceremonial objects on the left and right tables,
and displayed the horses in the courtyard.
The envoys proclaimed the imperial edict for the betrothal ceremony (*nàcǎi* 納采),
and then, in sequence, presented the ceremonial objects to the Empress's father.
The Empress's father knelt to receive them,
rose,
and, leading his sons and younger brothers, bowed towards the palace.
The envoys exited,
kneeling to see them off as they had been greeted.
One day before [the wedding],
the grand presentation of wedding gifts ceremony (*nàzhēng* 納徵) was performed.
The relevant department prepared the ceremonial objects for the grand presentation,
and dispatched envoys to transmit the imperial edict,
following the procedures of the betrothal ceremony.
The day before the grand wedding,
officials were again dispatched to offer sacrifices [to the altars].
On the appointed day, the imperial equipage (*lúbù* 鹵簿) and ceremonial music (*yuèxuán* 樂懸) were all prepared.
The Emperor proceeded to the Tàihé Diàn (太和殿) to inspect the imperial scroll (*cè* 冊) and imperial seal (*bǎo* 寶).
The imperial edict stated:
"The Emperor, respectfully obeying the august decree of the Empress Dowager (*huángtàihòu* 皇太后),
shall take a certain daughter of the Mǒu (某) clan as Empress.
Now, on this auspicious month and propitious day,
with all ceremonial objects and imperial documents prepared,
We command you, Our ministers, to respectfully escort her with due ceremony."
Envoys were dispatched according to the procedures for enthroning an Empress.
The envoys followed the imperial scroll and seal palanquins, exiting through the Xiéhé Mén (協和門).
The imperial carriage returned to the palace.
At this time, the Empress's honor guard was arranged at her residence.
When the investing envoys arrived,
the Empress's father, leading his relatives in court attire, welcomed them outside the gate.
The Empress, in ceremonial attire, welcomed them in the courtyard.
