The Empress's mother, leading all the female relatives, all knelt in court attire.
The envoys bore the imperial scroll and seal in and placed them on the table.
The Empress knelt facing north-south at the table.
Officials of the Inner Court (*nèiyuàn guān* 內院官) stood facing west.
They read the texts of the imperial scroll and seal,
and then presented them, in order, to the left female official.
The female official knelt to receive them and presented them to the Empress.
The Empress reverently received them,
and then handed them to the right female official,
who also knelt to receive them,
and placed them in a casket on the table.
The Empress rose,
performed six bows, three跪, and three kowtows.
After the ceremony was completed,
she ascended the imperial sedan chair (*niǎn* 輦).
The female officials bore the casket and placed it in a decorated palanquin.
Drums and music led the procession,
followed by the honor guard,
and then the phoenix sedan chair (*fèngniǎn* 鳳輦).
The Empress's parents knelt to see her off, as they had knelt to welcome her.
When the sedan chair reached the Xiéhé Mén (協和門),
the ceremonial carriages stopped.
The female officials bore the casket forward and placed it in the central palace (*zhōnggōng* 中宮).
The sedan chair entered through the central gate,
and at the steps of the Tàihé Diàn (太和殿), the Empress descended from the sedan chair and entered the palace.
The Emperor proceeded to the Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿),
and, leading the various princes, went before the Empress Dowager (*huángtàihòu* 皇太后) to perform salutations.
After this was completed,
the various princes withdrew.
The Emperor proceeded to the Tàihé Diàn (太和殿),
and bestowed a feast upon the Empress's father and relatives.
Princes (*wánggōng* 王公) and all civil and military officials were also present.
The Empress Dowager (*huángtàihòu* 皇太后) proceeded to the Wèiyù Gōng (位育宮),
which was the Bǎohé Diàn (保和殿),
and bestowed a feast upon the Empress's mother and relatives.
Princesses (*gōngzhǔ* 公主), imperial consorts (*fújìn* 福晉), and noblewomen (*mìngfù* 命婦) were all present.
Three days later,
the Emperor again proceeded to the Tàihé Diàn (太和殿).
Princes (*wánggōng* 王公) and all civil and military officials presented memorials to offer congratulations,
and an imperial edict was issued as per regulation.
The Empress's parents and brothers were bestowed with clothing and articles of varying grades.
In the eleventh year [of Shùnzhì (順治)], at the grand wedding,
three days later,
after the Empress paid her respects to the Empress Dowager (*huángtàihòu* 皇太后),
the feast began.
In the fourth year of Kāngxī (康熙), at the grand wedding,
a betrothal feast (*nàcǎi yàn* 納采宴) was held at the Empress's residence.
Three princesses (*gōngzhǔ* 公主) and three wives of senior officials (*fǔchén mìngfù* 輔臣命婦) were present,
as were Inner Grand Ministers (*nèidàchén* 內大臣), Imperial Bodyguards (*shìwèi* 侍衞), and officials from *gōng* (公) rank downwards, and civil officials of the second rank and above.
The grand presentation of wedding gifts (*dàzhēng* 大徵) also followed the same procedure.
The Empress's grandparents and parents were bestowed with clothes.
Thanksgiving was offered as per ceremony.
On the appointed day,
when the envoys arrived bearing the imperial scroll and seal,
after the Empress reverently received them,
the Imperial Astronomical Bureau (*Qīn tiān jiān* 欽天監) announced the auspicious time.
The Empress ascended the imperial sedan chair (*niǎn* 輦).
Four noblewomen (*mìngfù* 命婦) led the way,
and seven followed behind,
all on horseback.
Inner Grand Ministers (*nèidàchén* 內大臣) and Imperial Bodyguards (*shìwèi* 侍衞) followed,
and withdrew at the steps of the Tàihé Diàn (太和殿).
The Empress descended from the sedan chair.
Eunuchs bearing the imperial scroll and seal led her to the Zhōnghé Diàn (中和殿).
The noblewomen withdrew.
Attendant noblewomen (*zhíshì mìngfù* 執事命婦) welcomed her and accompanied her into the palace.
The eunuchs bearing the imperial scroll and seal handed them to the eunuchs guarding the imperial treasures (*shǒubǎo nèijiān* 守寶內監),
and withdrew.
The Emperor went before the Grand Empress Dowager (*tàihuángtàihòu* 太皇太后) and the Empress Dowager (*huángtàihòu* 皇太后) to perform salutations,
and proceeded to the hall and bestowed a feast as before.
The Empress Dowager (*huángtàihòu* 皇太后), leading the wives of senior officials (*fǔchén mìngfù* 輔臣命婦), entered the palace,
and bestowed a feast upon the Empress's mother and relatives.
Princesses (*gōngzhǔ* 公主) and imperial consorts (*fújìn* 福晉) were not present.
At the *yǒu* (酉) hour (5-7 PM),
a feast was held in the palace,
and the shared cup ceremony (*héjǐn lǐ* 合巹禮) was performed.
The next day,
the Empress paid respects and morning audience to the two Empresses Dowager.
Three days later, she received congratulations,
and an imperial edict was issued as per usual custom.
In the eleventh year of Tóngzhì (同治),
the betrothal ceremony (*nàcǎi* 納采), grand presentation of wedding gifts (*dàzhēng* 大徵), dispatch of the imperial scroll (*fācè* 發冊), and respectful escort (*fèngyíng* 奉迎) [ceremonies]
all strictly followed the established pattern.
However, at the appointed time when the Empress ascended the imperial sedan chair,
the envoys rode horses ahead,
eunuchs supported her,
and Inner Grand Ministers (*nèidàchén* 內大臣) and others rode alongside.
Outside the Wǔmén (午門),
nine phoenixes and curved canopies led the way.
When they reached the Qiánqīng Mén (乾清門),
the dragon palanquins stopped.
The envoys and others withdrew.
Officials from the Ministry of Rites (*Lǐbù* 禮部) bore the imperial scroll and seal and placed them on the left and right tables in the Jiāotài Diàn (交泰殿),
then withdrew.
The imperial sedan chair entered the Qiánqīng Gōng (乾清宮).
All attendants withdrew,
and imperial bodyguards closed the folding screens.
Imperial consorts (*fújìn* 福晉) and noblewomen (*mìngfù* 命婦) attended the sedan chair as it entered the palace.
A shared cup feast (*héjǐn yàn* 合卺宴) was held in the palace,
and the ceremony was completed.
In the fifteenth year of Guāngxù (光緒), at the grand wedding,
six days later,
the Empress first paid respects to the Empress Dowager (*huángtàihòu* 皇太后).
Another two days later,
the Emperor received congratulations.
The remaining procedures were the same.
Imperial Prince's Wedding Ceremony. First, the marriage is decreed.
Ministers and their wives, who are of advanced age and have long-standing marriages, are selected to assist in the affair.
The **fú jìn**'s father, wearing a python robe, proceeds to the **Qián Qīng Mén**,
kneels facing north.
A minister, facing west, conveys the imperial decree:
"We hereby assign the daughter of **Mǒu** as consort to Imperial Prince **Mǒu**, to be his **fú jìn**."
The **fú jìn**'s father performs the three跪九拜 (three kneelings and nine kowtows)
and retires.
A propitious day is chosen.
Inner ministers and imperial guards are selected to accompany the Imperial Prince to the **fú jìn**'s home to perform the betrothal (**wén dìng**) ceremony.
The **fú jìn**'s father, wearing ceremonial robes, greets them outside the gate.
The Imperial Prince ascends to the hall and bows.
The **fú jìn**'s father returns the bow,
bowing three times,
then stands.
The meeting with the **fú jìn**'s mother proceeds likewise.
Taking leave,
the **fú jìn**'s father escorts them outside the main gate.
For the gift-giving (**nà cǎi**) ceremony,
the responsible office prepares the ceremonial gifts and silks,
and also prepares clothes, saddles, and horses bestowed upon the **fú jìn**'s parents.
An Inner Household Minister and Palace Superintendent Imperial Guard are appointed as envoys.
Upon arriving at the gate,
the **fú jìn**'s father welcomes them into the central hall.
After expressing gratitude,
a feast is held.
Ministers accompany the **fú jìn**'s father in the central hall for the feast,
while imperial wives and female officials accompany the female relatives in the inner chambers.
When finished,
the envoys return to court to report.
The day before the wedding,
the **fú jìn**'s family delivers the trousseau to the Imperial Prince's palace.
On the day itself,
the Imperial Prince proceeds to the Emperor and Empress to perform rites.
If the marriage is to a concubine,
then he also proceeds to their residence.
When the auspicious time arrives,
the **Luán Yí Wèi** prepares a decorated palanquin.
An Inner Household Minister, leading twenty subordinates and forty guards, proceeds to the **fú jìn**'s residence to welcome her.
The decorated palanquin is placed in the hall.
A female official announces
"Ascend the palanquin."
The **fú jìn** ascends,
and her parents and family all see her off.
Palace guards carry the palanquin.
Female officials follow,
exiting the main gate and riding horses.
Upon reaching outside the Forbidden City gate,
everyone walks, following the palanquin inside.
They dismount at the Imperial Prince's palace gate.
Female officials lead her into the palace.
When the time for the wedding cup (**hé jǐn**) ceremony arrives,
the Imperial Prince faces west,
the **fú jìn** faces east,
and they perform two bows.
Each takes a seat.
A female official pours and mixes wine and presents it.
Both drink.
After three courses of wine and dishes,
they rise
and again perform two bows.
At this time, the palace is adorned with hangings and decorations.
A feast is set,
attended by the **fú jìn**'s parents, relatives, ministers, and imperial wives.
The ceremony is completed.
The next day, the Imperial Prince and **fú jìn** rise early
to pay respects to the Emperor and Empress.
Female officials lead the Imperial Prince to stand slightly in front on the left,
where he performs three kneeling and nine kowtows.
The **fú jìn** stands slightly behind on the right,
performing six deep bows, three kneelings, and three kowtows.
When meeting the concubines who bore children,
the Imperial Prince performs two kneelings and six kowtows,
and the **fú jìn** performs four deep bows, two kneelings, and two kowtows.
After nine days,
she returns to her parents' home (**guī níng**).
After the feast,
they return together,
not staying past noon.
For the wedding ceremonies of princes and dukes,
the system was standardized during the **Chóng Dé** era.
Whenever a **qīn wáng** (prince of the first rank) marries the daughter of a court official,
on the day of the gift-giving (**nà cǎi**),
officials of the princely residence serve as envoys.
A feast is held on this day,
with abundant meat and wine.
The wedding day feast is likewise.
Clothes, saddles, and horses are bestowed upon the bride's parents according to regulations.
If the bride is the daughter of an outer **fān qīn wáng** (prince of the first rank), **jùn wáng** (prince of the second rank),
**bèi lè** (prince of the third rank),
or **tái jí**,
the ceremonial items differ according to their rank.
For the wedding day feast,
the number of sacrificial animals varies appropriately.
For the betrothal and marriage of a **shì zǐ** (heir apparent),
**jùn wáng** (prince of the second rank),
**bèi lè** (prince of the third rank),
**bèi zǐ** (prince of the fourth rank),
**zhèn guó gōng** (duke of the first rank), and **fǔ guó gōng** (duke of the second rank),
the ceremonial items and the meat and wine for the feast days
decrease in number successively,
all having different grades.
During the **Shùn Zhì** era,
the wedding system was further reformed.
It was stipulated that those below the rank of **bèi lè** were forbidden from using pearls and satin.
When an imperial marriage is granted,
princes and dukes proceed to the **Zhōng Hé Diàn** or **Wèi Yù Gōng** to express gratitude.
If their son has not yet received a title,
his wedding ceremony follows that of his father.
If he has received a title, it follows his rank.
In the early **Kāng Xī** reign,
it was first ordered that princes and dukes could exchange cloth for satin for the gift-giving (**nà cǎi**) ceremony,
while other customs remained the same.
Princess's Marriage Ceremony. On the day the marriage is decreed,
the **é fù** (imperial son-in-law), wearing a python robe, proceeds to the East Steps of the **Qián Qīng Mén**,
kneels facing north.
The assisting minister stands facing west.
The imperial decree is announced:
"Princess **Mǒu** is chosen to be married to **É Fù Mǒu**."
He respectfully accepts the decree,
expresses gratitude, and retires.
For the initial betrothal,
a day is chosen to proceed to the **Wǔ Mén**,
to offer the "nine-nine" gifts,
which is the gift-giving (**nà cǎi**) ceremony.
Camels, horses, feasts, sheep, and wine are presented in the prescribed numbers.
An imperial decree directs the distribution to the responsible offices.
The next day, a banquet is held.
The **é fù**, leading his family members, proceeds in court attire to the Empress Dowager's palace to pay respects.
After the rites are completed,
they gather at the **Bǎo Hé Diàn**.
The Emperor ascends the throne.
The **é fù** and others perform three kneelings and nine kowtows.
After the imperial feast is laid out,
the minister in charge of presenting wine kneels and offers it.
The Emperor accepts and drinks.
Wine is then bestowed upon the ministers,
who kneel and drink it.
At this time, the **é fù** and others perform only one bow.
After the banquet is cleared, they express gratitude,
performing one kneeling and three bows.
Exiting to outside the **Nèi Yòu Mén**,
they perform three kneelings and nine kowtows,
then retire.
All expressions of gratitude before the Emperor are announced by an official.
Before the Empress's palace, there is no announcement.
On this day, the **é fù**'s family members proceed to the Empress Dowager's and Empress's palaces for banquets, as prescribed.
The day before the princess's marriage (**lí jiàng**),
the **é fù** proceeds to the palace gate to express gratitude.
Inner Household officials, leading **Luán Yí** guards, deliver the trousseau to the **é fù**'s residence.
Inner Supervisors and imperial wives, accompanied by female attendants, arrange the items.
On the day itself,
the **é fù**'s family prepares the "nine-nine" gifts,
such as saddles, horses, and armor,
proceeds to the **Wǔ Mén** to respectfully present them.
A banquet is held as in the initial betrothal ceremony.
When the auspicious time arrives,
the princess, in ceremonial robes, proceeds to the Empress Dowager, Emperor, Empress, and the concubines who bore her, to perform rites.
Imperial wives assist her in ascending the palanquin,
lowering the curtain.
Palace guards carry her out of the palace.
The ceremonial guard is fully arrayed,
with lanterns and torches leading the way.
**Fú jìn**, **fū rén**, and imperial wives follow in palanquins,
proceeding to the **é fù**'s residence to perform the wedding cup (**hé jǐn**) ceremony.
On this day, ninety tables are set for the feast.
If the princess marries into an outer **fān** (vassal state),
only meat and wine are used.
Nine days after the marriage,
she returns to the palace to express gratitude.
The princess enters the palace to perform rites.
The **é fù** proceeds to outside the **Cí Níng Mén**, **Qián Qīng Mén**, and **Nèi Yòu Mén** to perform rites.
In the eighth year of **Tiān Mìng** (1623),
**Tài Zǔ** (**Nurhaci**) held court in the Eight-sided Palace,
instructing princesses on women's virtues,
not to disrespect their husbands
or act with arbitrary arrogance.
Violators would be punished.
At the time, it was considered the beginning of kingly transformation.
Subsequently, it became custom
that the **é fù** and his parents, upon seeing the princess, would all bend their knees and offer greetings (**kòu ān**).
If a gift was bestowed, they would kowtow.
This was to follow ancient precedents.
However, in the twenty-first year of **Dào Guāng** (1841),
Emperor **Xuān Zōng** deemed it improper ritual,
and slightly reformed the ceremonies.
The **é fù**, upon seeing the princess, would stand respectfully to express reverence.
The princess would stand and reply.
The maternal uncle and aunt, upon seeing the princess, would stand upright to express reverence.
The princess would likewise.
When presenting gifts,
all would stand upright,
exempt from bending the knee,
to emphasize the hierarchy of human relations,
and this was enacted as a regulation.
They also established the "Nine-Nine Rites" to be performed upon arriving at the wedding,
and abolished feasts.
Thereafter, the abolition of feasts became the norm.
The following year,
the initial "Nine Sheep" betrothal gift was changed.
This was followed subsequently.
During the Tóngzhì reign,
it was stipulated that when a Gōngzhǔ returned home for a visit (guīníng),
the Èfù was exempted from performing the salute at the inner right gate,
with the rest following the previous ceremony.
For the marriage ceremony (yúguī lǐ) of a Jùnzhǔ,
during the Chóngdé reign,
the betrothal gifts (pìnyí) for a Qīnwáng marrying off his daughter were set:
saddles and horses, and armor (jiǎzhòu) totaling fifteen.
If marrying into an outer feudatory (wàifān),
Qīnwáng and those below them would present camels, horses, and sheep as betrothal gifts,
according to the "seven-nine count."
There were eight accompanying maids (yìngbì),
and five households of male and female servants.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
the betrothal gifts for court officials were:
saddles and horses, and armor, seven of each.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
it was stipulated that a Jùnwáng would have six accompanying maids,
and four households of male and female servants.
For marrying off daughters to court officials, saddles and horses were seven,
while the betrothal gifts (nàcǎi) from outer feudatories were reduced compared to the Chóngdé reign.
For Jùnzhǔ and those below,
i.e., Xiànzhǔ, Jùnjūn, Xiànjūn, Xiāngjūn, for their marriage ceremonies,
the provisions were successively reduced.
In the eighth year of Kāngxī,
it was stipulated that when Jùnzhǔ and Xiànzhǔ returned home for a visit,
their maternal families were prohibited from providing Manchu servants,
but were limited to eight Mongol or Han servants.
For Jùnjūn down to Xiāngjūn,
there were six Mongol or Han servants.
For daughters of Jiāngjūn down to Zōngshì,
there were four.
In the thirty-fifth year of Qiánlóng,
court officials were no longer required to present betrothal gifts,
but outer feudatories continued as before.
No banquets were held.
Marriage Rites for Officials and Commoners: For officials arranging marriages,
a matchmaker must first be sent to convey a letter,
then an auspicious day is chosen for the betrothal gifts (nàcǎi).
From Gōng, Hóu, Bó down to ninth-rank officials,
the ceremonial items were reduced according to official rank.
The principal host wears auspicious attire,
instructs a son or junior relative to act as envoy,
and attendants carry the ceremonial items to the woman's residence.
The woman's principal host, in auspicious attire, greets them.
The attendants arrange the ceremonial items in the courtyard,
present the letter and deliver the message.
The principal host receives the letter,
announces it at the ancestral temple, and serves wine to the guests.
After the guests retire,
they are seen off at the gate,
and the envoy returns to report.
On this day, a banquet is held with sacrificial animals and wine.
For Gōng, Hóu and those below,
the numbers differed accordingly.
The day before the wedding,
the woman's family sends someone with a broom and dustpan to the groom's house,
to arrange bedding, mattresses, and utensils.
On the appointed day,
the groom's family prepares the "cup-joining banquet" (héjǐn yàn) in advance.
The groom waits in auspicious attire,
with ceremonial retinue ready.
The groom, following his father's command, personally goes to receive the bride,
proceeding to the woman's residence in a decorated sedan chair.
The woman's principal host announces to the ancestral temple,
saying:
"The such-and-such daughter of this house,
will today return to the such-and-such clan."
Then she is crowned with a hairpin and given instructions.
She returns to the inner chamber for the libation ceremony,
with the father on the east and mother on the west.
The daughter emerges in formal attire,
bows twice facing north.
Attendants pour wine for the daughter.
The father instructs her on the proper way to manage a family,
and the mother ties her apron and handkerchief,
reiterating the father's instructions.
The daughter acknowledges without objection.
When the groom arrives,
he enters the gate and bows twice.
He presents the wild goose,
then exits.
The matron covers the daughter's head with a sunshade,
and she exits.
The groom bows and descends.
The daughter, led by the matron, ascends the sedan chair.
The honor guard leads the procession,
and attendants follow behind the sedan chair.
The groom returns first.
When the sedan chair reaches the gate,
the groom leads her up the west steps,
into the chamber, crossing the threshold.
An accompanying maid spreads the groom's mat on the east side,
and the bridal attendant spreads the bride's mat on the west side.
After completing the cross-bowing,
they sit facing each other at the feast.
Food is brought in.
After eating,
the accompanying maid and bridal attendant take goblets and fill them with wine,
offering them to the groom and bride to drink.
For the third drink, they use the "cup-joining" gourd.
After finishing the drinks,
the groom exits.
The accompanying maid and bridal attendant arrange the bedding and pillows.
The groom enters,
and the candles are extinguished.
On this day, the banquet is the same as for the betrothal gifts.
If an official's son has not yet assumed office,
the rites follow those of his father;
those who have assumed office follow their respective ranks.
The marriage rites for scholars follow those of ninth-rank officials.
For commoners' betrothal gifts,
the number of head ornaments is limited to four,
the sedan chair is not decorated with colorful silks,
and the rest is the same as for scholars.
On the third day of the marriage,
the host and hostess lead the new bride to visit the ancestral temple.
If there is no temple,
they visit the paternal ancestors (zǔ, ní) in the chamber,
following the usual announcement ceremony.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
regulations were established:
for Han people's betrothal and marriage,
for fourth-rank officials and above,
silk fabrics and head ornaments were limited to eight items,
and food items to ten categories.
Fifth-rank and below reduced by two,
eighth-rank and below reduced by another two.
For soldiers and commoners, coarse silk and fine silk, and fruit boxes were also limited to four items.
On the wedding day for officials,
their official retinue was used,
with six lanterns and twelve drummers and musicians.
For those without rank,
there were four lanterns and eight drummers and musicians.
Extravagance was forbidden;
officials and commoners alike were not allowed to use monetary gifts.
Shìxué Yí (Regulations for Imperial Visits to the Imperial Academy) In the first year of the Shùnzhì reign,
the emperor went to the Tàixué (Imperial Academy) to perform the Shìdiàn (Sacrificial Ceremony to Confucius).
Prior to this, the Yǎnshèng Gōng and Wǔjīng Bóshì (Erudites of the Five Classics) arrived.
Five descendants of the Sage (Confucius),
two descendants each of the Yuánshèng (Confucius's father), his wife, and the Zhé (Confucius's worthy disciples)
traveled by post-carriage to the capital.
The children and grandchildren of various clans who were currently serving as court officials,
as well as teachers and students from various official schools, and Jìnshì (Metropolitan Graduates), Jǔ (Provincial Graduates), and Gòng (Tribute Scholars),
all participated in observing the ceremony.
The Nèigé (Grand Secretariat) proposed the Classics and the Sū (Book of Documents),
and the Jìjiǔ (Libationer) and Sīyè (Assistant Libationer) prepared the讲章 (lecture notes) and presented them to the emperor.
On the appointed day,
a large imperial canopy was set up to the east of the Dàchéng Mén (Gate of Great Accomplishment).
In the Yílún Táng (Hall of Moral Principles), a yellow imperial tent was set up with the imperial throne.
In front of the tent was an imperial desk,
and to its left and right were two lecture desks.
The Jìjiǔ and others presented the讲章 and their copies for the lecture,
with the Sū on the left and the Jīng (Classic) on the right,
displayed on the desks.
The emperor, in ceremonial attire, rode in a palanquin to the academy.
The Jìjiǔ and Sīyè, leading officials and students, knelt to welcome him to the right of Chéngxián Jiē (Street of Accomplished Sages).
The imperial carriage entered the tent,
and the emperor proceeded to the Dàchéng Diàn (Hall of Great Accomplishment) to perform the Shìdiàn.
After the ceremony,
he exited, changed into a formal robe,
and proceeded to the Yílún Táng,
entering the imperial lecture tent.
He ascended the throne.
Princes and dukes stood on the steps,
while civil and military officials stood below the steps.
The Yǎnshèng Gōng led the Bóshì and descendants of various clans,
and the Jìjiǔ and others led the officials and students to their bowing positions.
They performed the ritual of three kowtows and nine prostrations.
After this,
from the princes and dukes down to the nine high ministers, all were successively granted seats.
Soon after, they knelt inside the hall,
performing one kowtow.
The Hónglú (Court of Imperial Entertainments) official announced
"Jìn Jiǎng" (Begin the Lecture).
The Jìjiǔ and Sīyè entered,
stood facing north,
and the attendant officials moved the Classic desks before the emperor.
The lecturing officials were granted seats.
The Jìjiǔ and others performed one kowtow
and sat down.
They lectured in sequence.
Hànlín and Zhànshì (Academicians and Supervisors of Imperial Instruction) officials of the fourth rank and below,
as well as Guānjiān (Supervising Officials), Shīrú (Teachers), Bóshì, descendants of sages and worthies, and students pursuing studies, listened in a circle.
After the lecture,
they withdrew,
and all who had listened also withdrew.
They returned to their positions and stood in order,
kneeling to listen to the imperial decree.
The decree stated:
"The Way of the Sages
is like the sun at its zenith.
By lecturing, practicing, and embracing it,
you can use it to assist in governance.
You, teachers and students, should strive for this."
The Jìjiǔ and others performed three kowtows and nine prostrations
and withdrew.
Tea was granted,
and all the officials received and drank it.
One kowtow,
and the ceremony was completed.
As the imperial carriage departed,
all knelt to see it off.
The next day,
the Guānjiān, Bóshì, and students presented their thanks.
The emperor presided at the Tàihé Diàn (Hall of Supreme Harmony).
Gifts and rewards were bestowed according to regular ceremony,
and the Yǎnshèng Gōng and other officials were hosted for a banquet by the Lǐbù (Board of Rites).
Three days later,
an imperial edict was issued to the Tàixué,
commanding students to exert themselves.
The Yǎnshèng Gōng was granted official robes and headwear,
and the Guānjiān and Bóshì and others received one suit of clothes.
Assistant instructors and students received differing amounts of silver.
In the eighth year of Kāngxī,
Emperor Shèngzǔ performed the Shìdiàn at the Tàixué
and lectured on the Classics, all in accordance with established practice.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
an edict stated:
"The grand ceremony of 'Shìxué' (Imperial Visit to the Academy)
should not be referred to as 'xìng' (imperial visit implying pleasure).
Henceforth, change 'xìng'
to 'yì' (imperial visit implying solemnity)."
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
an order was given for the Bóshì of the Mǐn, Rǎn, Yán, Bǔ, Zhuānsūn, and Duānmù clans to accompany the sacrifice and observe the ceremony,
following the precedent of the five clans.
The following year,
the emperor personally visited the academy for Shìxué.
Thirty-two descendants of sages and worthies, as well as the Dōngyě clan, came to observe the ceremony.
They were sent to the academy for study.
The emperor immediately summoned the Yǎnshèng Gōng and others and personally admonished them,
saying:
"Since you are descendants of sages and worthies,
you should have the heart of sages and worthies,
not merely read their books.
You must personally practice and implement their teachings,
striving to have no regrets in your actions,
only then will you not betray your learning.
You must diligently contemplate and strive,
to inherit and continue the transmission of their spiritual legacy."
On the first Dīng day of the third month in the third year,
the emperor personally went to the Tàixué to perform the Shìcài (Vegetable Offering) ceremony.
Six days later,
he presided over lectures at the Pìyōng (Imperial College).
Princes, dukes, and high ministers,
descendants of sages and worthies,
and even students of the Tàixué,
gathered in the thousands around the bridge gates and the Bìshuǐ (Jade-Green Water).
When the order for the Lín Yōng (Imperial Presence at Pìyōng) was issued,
an auspicious date was chosen.
Attendant officials set up the imperial tent outside the Dàchéng Mén.
In the Pìyōng Diàn, on the steps, Zhōnghé Sháoyuè (Central Harmony and Shao Music) was played.
Inside the Tàixué Mén, Dānbì Dàyuè (Great Music of the Vermilion Steps) and Qīngyuè (Pure Music) were played.
Inside the hall, the Classic desks and lecture desks were all prepared as before.
After the emperor completed the Shìdiàn and went to the Yílún Táng,
he changed into a formal robe
and proceeded to the Pìyōng.
Bells and drums were sounded at the Tàixué.
He ascended the throne,
music was played,
and it ceased with rhythm.
An official announced
"Qí Bān" (Form ranks).
Lecturing officials, attendant officials, and disciplinary officials took their bowing positions.
The official announced
"Guì" (Kneel),
"Kòu" (Kowtow),
"Xīng" (Rise).
They performed the ritual of two kowtows and six prostrations,
and rose.
If the Yǎnshèng Gōng came for an audience,
he would lecture first.
From the Grand Secretary down to the students, they stood in separate ranks.
After the ceremony was completed,
the Mǎn (Manchu) lecturing officials entered,
performed one kowtow,
and took their seats
to lecture on the Sishū (Four Books).
The emperor elucidated the meaning of the books
and proclaimed it to his officials and workers.
All officials and students around the bridge knelt and listened.
After finishing, they rose.
The Jìjiǔ lectured on the Classics,
and the emperor elucidated the meaning of the Classics as in the initial ceremony.
The rest was the same as the Shìxué Yí.
Before this, Cáo Xuémǐn, a censor, had submitted a memorial saying:
"It is appropriate to consult ancient regulations
and construct a Pìyōng at the Guózǐjiān (Imperial Academy)."
This was rejected by the Board's deliberation.
By the forty-ninth year,
the newly constructed Guóxué (National Academy) was completed.
The following year, when the emperor was to preside over the Pìyōng,
he ordered ministers to regulate and dredge the circular water,
and all ritual and music were fully implemented.
A special imperial edict commended Xuémǐn,
and also ordered Korean envoys to observe the ceremony with the ranks.
After the ceremony,
rewards were granted differently.
The next day, descendants of sages and worthies and students were given additional gifts of silk.
In the third year of Dàoguāng, during Lín Yōng,
it was ordered that students with hereditary privileges should attend the lectures in advance.
The emperor admonished the Guānjiān, saying:
"Transforming the people and establishing customs
is founded on schools.
Promoting the worthy and nurturing virtue
is the responsibility of teachers.
Scholars prioritize character and insight.
Gradual influence and immersion
have their origins.
You, supervising ministers, are the model for these many scholars.
You should uphold the art of teaching,
correct the models,
not be ostentatious,
nor be stubborn.
Be filial at home and respectful to elders abroad,
choose friends and be close to teachers.
Only then can a good custom be formed
to continue the splendid legacy of the sages."
In the first month of the year,
the imperial carriage traveled to Lǔ,
to perform rites before the Former Teacher,
and lecture on scholarship at Quēlǐ.
Two descendants of the Sages and Worthies were pre-selected as lecturing officials,
and Hanlin officials were tasked with drafting the lecture chapters.
The day before,
the Kuíwén Pavilion was grandly arranged,
and the imperial seat was set up in the Shīlǐ Hall.
An imperial desk was placed in front,
and lecture desks were arranged under the western eaves.
On the appointed day,
the lecture chapters and their duplicates were displayed on the desks.
The Emperor departed from the temporary imperial residence,
and the Yǎnshèng Gōng, in ceremonial attire, led the Wǔjīng Bóshì and members of various clans to kneel and welcome him on the right side of the temple gate.
The Emperor entered,
proceeded to the Dàchéng Hall to offer sacrifices to Kǒngzǐ,
following the ceremony for the top Dīng day.
The imperial carriage then left,
and the Emperor proceeded to the Shīlǐ Hall,
and ascended the throne.
Officials from the Yǎnshèng Gōng downwards followed,
stood in order in the courtyard,
and performed the three kneelings and nine kowtows.
When this was completed,
the lecture began.
The lecturing officials knelt once, kowtowed three times,
and rose.
After the lectures on the classics and books were completed,
all retired.
The imperial carriage then visited Kǒnglín.
The next day,
the Yǎnshèng Gōng and others were granted silk, gold, and books in varying amounts.
Disciples from various clans who possessed literary merit and good conduct were selected to be presented to the Tàixué.
All who had entered officialdom
were advanced one rank.
The ceremony for the Jīngyán initially followed the Ming dynasty system,
where Grand Secretaries did not typically concurrently serve in the Jīngyán.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì (1652),
it was held once in the middle month of spring and autumn,
and only then were Grand Secretaries ordered to preside over Jīngyán affairs.
Ministers, Left Censor-in-chiefs, Commissioners of the Office of Transmission, Grand Judges of the Court of Judicial Review, and Academicians attended the session,
with two Hanlin officials delivering the lectures.
An imperial desk and lecturing officials' desks were prepared in advance,
with lecture chapters and duplicate copies displayed,
literature on the left and classics on the right.
When the time came,
the Emperor, in everyday attire, proceeded to the Wénhuá Hall,
while the Recording Officials stood west of the pillar,
facing east.
The lecturing officials and others knelt twice and kowtowed six times,
then rose,
and stood in order on the left and right,
with the attending officials standing behind them.
The Ceremony Supervising Officials stood in the eastern and western corners.
The Announcer called out
"Jìn Jiǎng" (Begin the Lecture),
and the lecturing officials went before the desks, knelt,
kowtowed three times,
rose,
and took their places at the left and right desks.
They first lectured on the Four Books and then the Classics,
before returning to their positions.
The Emperor then read out imperial treatises in both Manchu and Chinese.
After all officials had knelt and listened,
the Grand Secretaries presented a memorial expressing their gratitude and delight.
They rose,
descended the steps, and performed the two kneelings and six kowtows.
When this was completed,
the Emperor proceeded to the Wényuān Pavilion,
where he granted seats and tea.
When the ceremony was concluded,
he returned to the palace.
A banquet was held in the Běnrén Hall.
After the banquet,
thanks were offered.
In the tenth year of Kāngxī (1671), a Jīngyán was held,
and Grand Secretary Xióng Cìlǚ was appointed as lecturing official,
presiding over Jīngyán affairs.
Shortly thereafter,
Shèngzǔ considered the spring and autumn lectures to be too infrequent,
and consequently issued an edict for daily lectures to be held in the Hóngdé Hall.
In the twenty-fourth year (1685),
the system was formalized,
designating Grand Secretaries, Left Censor-in-chiefs, Vice Ministers, and Grand Academicians of the Imperial Household Department as Jīngyán lecturing officials.
In the second month,
the Wénhuá Hall was completed,
and a grand ceremony was held.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he was in mourning,
and no lectures were held.
On an auspicious day in the eighth month of the third year of Yōngzhèng (1725),
an edict stated:
"All emperors who govern the realm
rely on classical learning.
I have received ancestral instruction,
and constantly study the classics.
To savor the Way and research the classics
is truly the foundation for governing and pacifying the people.
Now that the mourning period has ended,
it is imperative to proceed with these lectures."
Thus, the lectures were resumed as per custom.
In the fifth year of Qiánlóng (1740),
an edict stated:
"The establishment of the Jīngyán
is intended to offer admonitions and guidance.
Recently, the presented lecture chapters
contain too many laudatory phrases,
which completely deviates from the ancient spirit of inquiry and caution.
When a ruler governs,
they rightly rely on using antiquity to verify the present,
and offering what is beneficial and rejecting what is not.
It is essential to present matters clearly and thoroughly,
hoping to benefit governance and scholarship,
and thereby truly align with the practical meaning of classical studies."
In the seventh year (1742),
it rained on the day of the Jīngyán,
and the ceremonial officials, according to custom, requested a postponement.
The edict stated:
"When Duke Wén of Wèi went hunting and encountered rain,
he still did not break faith with the gamekeeper.
How much more so for this great ceremony,
which has already been preceded by sacrificial announcements?
How could it be appropriate to postpone it?
The officials in charge
may wear rain gear and stand in their ranks,
temporarily suspending the rituals of kneeling on the steps and bestowing tea in the hall.
Henceforth, in case of rain, follow this precedent."
The Hànlín Academy was solely responsible for daily lectures,
which ceased only the day before the winter and summer solstices.
In the fourteenth year (1749),
as the presented lectures on classics and history
gradually became mere formalities,
an edict ordered their cessation.
In the fifty-first year (1786),
the Emperor presided over the Jīngyán,
and bestowed a banquet upon the ceremonial officials who attended,
divided into eastern and western ranks,
specifically commanding the performance of cautionary poems.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
Zhāng Péngzhǎn submitted a memorial requesting that Hanlin and Censorate officials daily present interpretations of classics and memorials.
An imperial edict rebuked him for being impractical.
When Wénzōng ascended the throne,
Zēng Guófān requested the restoration of the old daily lecture system,
but it was blocked by departmental deliberation.
The following year, the first year of Xiánfēng (1851),
in the first month,
a special imperial decree was issued ordering Hanlin and Imperial Household Department officials to take turns on duty,
and the Emperor personally set the topics,
so that they would write lecture notes,
and present them for imperial review on separate days.
Up until the period of Guāngxù and Xuāntǒng,
this practice was still followed.
Regulations for Policy Examinations During the Tiāncōng reign,
the imperial examination system was first established.
In the early Shùnzhì reign,
the Jǔrén who passed the metropolitan examination gathered at Tiān'ānmén for an examination.
In the fifteenth year,
the examination was changed to be held on the dānchí (imperial terrace) of the Tàihédiàn,
and the system of policy examinations conducted from beneath the imperial pavilion (línxuān cèshì zhì) was instituted.
One day beforehand,
yellow desks were set up in the very center of the imperial steps (dānbì)
and in the east wing inside the Tàihédiàn,
respectively.
Examination tables were prepared under the eaves of the east and west galleries.
On the appointed day, at dawn,
officials of the Nèigé, in court attire, brought the examination questions and placed them on the desks inside the hall.
The Emperor ascended the Tàihédiàn,
while princes, dukes, and all officials stood by.
Officials of the Hónglúsì led the Gòngshì to stand below the imperial steps.
The Dàxuéshì took the questions and handed them to the Lǐbù officials,
who received them kneeling,
placed them on the desk on the imperial steps,
and kowtowed three times.
They then lifted the desk and descended the left steps,
placing it in the center of the imperial path.
The Dújuǎnguān and Zhíshìguān each performed three kneeling kowtows and nine prostrations.
All the Gòngshì did likewise.
After this was completed,
the imperial carriage returned to the palace.
The examination tables were moved to the left and right of the dānchí,
facing north.
Lǐbù officials distributed the questions,
the Gòngshì received them kneeling,
kowtowed three times,
and took their seats at the tables.
After completing their policy essays,
officials responsible for receiving and sealing the papers waited under the eaves of the left wing.
The sealed papers were collected and placed into examination chests.
The Shōuzhǎngguān sent them to the Dújuǎnguān for review.
The Emperor did not ascend the hall,
officials below the rank of prince did not assemble,
and the imperial guard of honor (lǔbù) was not displayed.
The review of the papers was completed in three days.
On the next day,
the top ten papers were arranged, and their rankings were determined,
then sealed and presented for imperial inspection.
The Emperor ascended the western warm chamber of the Yǎngxīndiàn.
After deliberating,
the Dújuǎnguān were summoned in,
and the Emperor personally assigned the grades (jiǎ-yǐ) and handed them over.
They then went out to unseal the papers,
and in order, transcribed the names onto green-headed slips (lǜtóuqiān).
Ten men were led into the Qiánqīngmén,
to await below the western steps.
The Emperor ascended the palace,
and the Dújuǎnguān carried the slips in,
presenting them kneeling.
The Yǐnbānguān led the ten men to kneel in the middle of the imperial steps.
Their names and ancestries were announced in order.
They rose
and retired.
The Emperor personally designated three persons for the first class (yījiǎ)
and seven for the second class (èrjiǎ),
handing the slips to the Dújuǎnguān,
who received them kneeling,
rose,
and retired,
leading the ten men to stand below the western steps.
The imperial carriage returned to the side palace (biàndiàn).
The ten men exited first.
The Dújuǎnguān carried the papers to the Hóngběnfáng,
and after filling in the rankings,
handed them to the Nèigé to inscribe the gold list (jīnbǎng).
On the day of the Chuánlú ceremony,
the lǔbù was displayed,
musical instruments (yuèxuán) were set up,
and princes, dukes, and all officials stood in attendance.
The Gòngshì all wore official robes,
with three-branch, nine-leaf top hats (sānzhī jiǔyè dǐngguān),
and stood at the end of the ranks.
The Emperor ascended the Tàihédiàn,
and the Dújuǎnguān and other officials performed rites as before,
presenting and receiving the list as in the policy question ceremony.
Hónglúsì officials led the Gòngshì to their positions,
where they knelt to hear the pronouncement.
The imperial decree stated:
"On a certain date,
policy examinations were held for all Gòngshì of the empire.
Those of the first class are granted the degree of Jìnshì Jíyǐ,
those of the second class are granted the degree of Jìnshì Chūshēn,
and those of the third class are granted the degree of Tóng Jìnshì Chūshēn."
When "Yījiǎ yīmíng Mǒu"
(First Class, First Name, So-and-so) was announced,
he was ordered to step forward and kneel.
The second and third names were announced in the same manner.
When "Èrjiǎ yīmíng Mǒu děng ruògān míng"
(Second Class, First Name, So-and-so and several others) and "Sānjiǎ Mǒu děng ruògān míng"
(Third Class, So-and-so and several others) were announced,
they did not step forward,
but performed three kneeling kowtows and nine prostrations together.
They then retired to stand.
Lǐbù officials carried the list out through the central path,
followed by the Yījiǎ Jìnshì.
The other Jìnshì exited through the left and right side gates.
The list was placed in a dragon pavilion (lóngtíng),
and three kowtows were performed again.
Guards (jiàowèi) carried the pavilion,
preceded by drums and music,
and displayed it outside the Dōngcháng'ānmén.
Three days later, it was returned to the Nèigé.
Then, the Shùntiānfǔ prepared parasols and an entourage to escort the Zhuàngyuán to his residence.
Five days later,
the Zhuàngyuán, accompanied by all the Jìnshì, submitted a memorial of gratitude following the usual ceremony.
In the fifty-fourth year of Qiánlóng,
the palace examination (Diànshì) was changed to be held in the Bǎohédiàn.
This became the permanent rule thereafter.
Regulations for Issuing Imperial Edicts In the early Qīng dynasty, imperial edicts (zhàoshū) used three scripts: Manchu, Mongolian, and Chinese.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
it was formalized to use two scripts: Manchu and Chinese.
On the day an edict was issued,
the lǔbù was arranged in front of the Tàihédiàn.
Inside the dānchí, yellow parasols and cloud trays (yúnpán) were set up, and an edict desk was placed to the east of the hall.
A yellow desk was placed in the middle of the imperial steps.
Outside the Wǔmén, a lóngtíng and an incense pavilion (xiāngtíng) were prepared.
An auspicious cloud golden phoenix (duǒyún jīnfèng) was pre-positioned in the phoenix mouth (zhìkǒu) of the Tiān'ānmén tower.
To its east, an edict-announcing platform (xuānzhàotái) was erected.
Princes, dukes, and all officials, in court attire, gathered at the Wǔmén.
Nèigé Xuéshì presented the edict to the Qiánqīngmén, and after its use,
unfolded it on the yellow desk.
The Emperor ascended the hall.
After princes, dukes, and all below performed their rites,
the Dàxuéshì presented the edict to the Lǐbù Shàngshū beneath the eaves of the hall.
The Shàngshū received it kneeling,
and placed it on the desk on the imperial steps.
After performing rites,
the edict was placed inside a cloud tray,
covered with a yellow parasol.
Lǐbù officials carried the tray out through the central path, passing the Tàihémén.
All officials followed to outside the Wǔmén,
where it was placed in the lóngtíng.
Upon reaching the south of the bridge outside the Tiān'ānmén,
the edict was placed on a yellow desk on a high platform.
All officials stood facing north in their respective ranks.
The annunciation official stood facing west on the platform.
The assembly knelt to listen to the pronouncement.
First, the Manchu text was pronounced,
then the Chinese text.
The assembly performed three kneeling kowtows and nine prostrations.
The official bearing the edict took the auspicious cloud to support the edict,
which was tied with colorful cords,
and lowered from the mouth of the golden phoenix.
Lǐbù officials received it,
and again placed it in the lóngtíng.
It was carried out through the Dàqīngmén
to the Lǐbù,
where an incense desk was set up facing the imperial palace,
and the Shàngshū led his subordinates in performing rites.
The edict was transcribed onto yellow paper (ténghuáng)
and distributed to all provinces.
If the Emperor did not ascend the hall,
all officials merely waited south of the bridge outside the Tiān'ānmén,
and the rest of the ceremony was the same.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
it was formalized that
whenever an edict arrived,
the local authorities would prepare a lóngtíng, banners, and attendants to welcome it in the suburbs.
The imperial envoy (cháoshǐ) dismounted,
placed the edict in the lóngtíng,
facing south,
while the local officials (shǒutǔguān) faced north and performed rites.
Drums and music led the procession,
with the imperial envoy following on horseback.
Upon reaching the public office (gōngxiè),
all officials first entered and stood in order.
When the lóngtíng reached the courtyard,
the imperial envoy stood to the east.
After the rites were completed,
the edict was presented to the official responsible for reading it aloud (zhǎndúguān).
He received it kneeling,
and all officials knelt.
After the pronouncement was completed,
the edict was handed back to the imperial envoy,
again placed in the lóngtíng,
and kneeling kowtows were performed as in the initial rite.
They then retired.
The chief administrator (chánglì) transcribed it onto yellow paper
and distributed it to all subordinate jurisdictions.
Wherever the edict passed,
all officials of prefectures (fǔ), departments (zhōu), counties (xiàn), and garrisons (wèi) within a five-lǐ radius
all came out of the city gates to welcome and send it off.
Regulations for Submitting Books.
When the *Shílù* and *Shèngxùn* are compiled,
a propitious day is chosen for their submission.
The Emperor holds court to receive the books,
and the princes, dukes, and all officials offer congratulations.
The *Yùdié* and *Běnjì* follow a similar procedure.
In the eleventh year of Kāngxī,
when the *Shìzǔ Shílù* was completed,
one day prior,
a memorial table was set up to the east of the stairs of the Tàihédian,
and the *Shílù* tables were arranged below the stairs.
On the day itself, imperial equipage was prepared,
and musical instruments were displayed.
The supervising officials presented the memorial in a memorial pavilion,
the compiling officials presented the *Shílù* in an ornamented pavilion,
and the princes, dukes, and all officials assembled to perform the rites as usual.
Stewards then carried the fragrant pavilion and the ornamented pavilion out through the central path,
the memorial pavilion by the left.
The supervising officials followed to the Dānchí of the Tàihédian,
where they presented the *Shílù* and the memorial, arranging them separately on tables.
The Emperor ascended the throne,
and the Hónglú official announced the submission of the *Shílù*;
music began.
The Lǐbù official raised the *Shílù* table and ascended via the central path,
reaching outside the palace gate.
The Emperor rose from his seat,
and the music stopped.
The table was brought in,
and then the Emperor sat.
The table was placed in the center of the Bǎohédian.
The supervising officials stood in a neat row below the steps.
When the announcer said,
"Kneel,"
they all knelt.
When the announcer said,
"Submit the memorial,"
the official designated to read the memorial knelt and read it aloud.
When finished,
music began,
and all officials performed the three kneelings and nine kowtows,
then retreated to stand,
and the music stopped.
The officials knelt again,
and the official designated to read the memorial spoke on their behalf, saying:
"Your humble servants, certain princes [surname] and others, together with the civil and military officials, respectfully state that
the divine accomplishments and sacred virtues of Emperor Shìzǔ
have been compiled into a book,
shining brightly for ten thousand generations.
Your servants are filled with joy and delight,
and it is appropriate to offer congratulations."
The Hónglúqīng then announced an imperial decree in reply, saying:
"Emperor Shìzǔ's accomplishments and virtues rival heaven;
the *Shílù* has been compiled.
Our heart is filled with joy and celebration,
which we share with you, Our officials."
After the announcement,
the rites were performed as before.
Tea was bestowed,
and all performed one kowtow.
The imperial carriage returned.
The supervising officials brought the *Shílù* to the Qiánqīngmén,
handed it over to the great palace,
and then withdrew.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
the *Shèngzǔ Shílù* and *Shèngxùn* were submitted together,
which later became the regular practice.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
it was decided that the *Shílù* and *Shèngxùn* should be stored in the Huángshǐchéng.
The supervising officials were sent to deposit them in golden caskets,
and copies were stored in the Nèigé.
In the twelfth year of Jiāqìng,
the procedure for raising the table and presenting the books was revised,
and imperial clan officials from *Bèizǐ* downwards were chosen to manage the affair.
From Rénzōng onwards,
the Emperor still went to the Huángshǐchéng to offer incense,
as in the old regulations.
When the *Yùdié* was submitted,
no memorial was presented,
and no imperial decree was announced.
The supervising officials followed the ornamented pavilion into the Zhōnghédian,
placed it on a table,
and opened the four central chests.
The Emperor stood and reviewed it,
and after the entire book was presented and viewed,
it was sent to the Huángshǐchéng.
If it was compiled every ten years,
or if the Emperor did not hold court,
he would view it in the palace.
All *Shílù*, *Shèngxùn*, and *Yùdié*
were also sent to Shèngjīng for honored storage.
From the first year of Qiánlóng, the *Běnjì* began to be submitted.
A propitious day was merely chosen to store it in the Huángshǐchéng.
As for the *Fānglüè*, two copies were submitted:
one stored in the Shǐchéng,
and one handed over to the Lǐbù for publication.
When the almanac (*Shíxiànshū*) was completed,
the Qīn Tiānjian officials submitted it annually on the first day of the tenth month,
and it was also bestowed upon princes, dukes, and all officials.
The rite of distributing the calendar was performed at Wǔmén.
When distributed to the direct provinces,
the governors-general and governors received the calendar according to the usual ceremony.
Regulations for Submitting Memorials and Letters. For the Emperor's birthday (*Wànshòujié*), New Year's Day (*Yuánrì*), and Winter Solstice (*Chángzhì*),
princes, dukes, and all officials in the capital each submitted memorials.

Generals, military governors, deputy military governors, governors-general, governors, provincial commanders-in-chief, and brigade-generals in the provinces each submitted congratulatory memorials and letters,
which were collected and sent to the Board via courier.
On the appointed day, a memorial table was set up at the left pillar of the Tàihédian.
The memorials were arranged in an ornamented pavilion,
carried to outside the Wǔmén,
and presented on the table.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
the memorials were read and the rites performed, after which
all memorials and letters were sent to the Nèigé for storage.
For the Empress Dowager's birthday (*Huángtàihòu Shèngshòu*) and the Empress's birthday (*Huánghòu Qiānqiū*),
the memorials and letters from princes and civil and military officials, both inside and outside the capital,
were all presented outside the Wǔmén.
After the rites,
they were also sent to the Nèigé.
Initially, the memorials used three-style scripts,
but later, only Chinese script was used,
except for Manchu banner garrisons who used Manchu script.
In advance, the Nèigé drafted and finalized the format and issued it,
to be respectfully submitted when due.
For the congratulatory memorials on the three great festivals,
those in the capital referred to themselves as
"Your humble servants, certain princes [surname] and others,"
"various princes, *Bèilè*, and civil and military officials";
those in the provinces referred to themselves as
"Your humble servants, certain officials [surname] and others,
with sincere joy and delight,
bowing and prostrating ourselves, respectfully state,"
and at the end said:
"Your servants are filled with boundless awe and reverence for the heavens and the sage,
and with the utmost joy and delight,
hereby present this memorial to offer congratulations and to inform."
The procedure for submitting to the Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager was the same.
For the crown prince's letter format,
the initial declaration of officials was the same,
and the end said:
"Your servants are filled with boundless joy and exuberance,
hereby present this letter to offer congratulations and to inform."
Initially,
for New Year's Day and Winter Solstice,
civil and military officials of the fifth rank and above in the direct provinces each submitted congratulatory memorials and letters,
while for the Emperor's birthday (*Wànshòujié*), only memorials to the Emperor were submitted,
all collectively submitted by the respective superiors.
Governors-general and governors did not submit memorials or letters;
for any major ceremony,
they submitted a formal report to offer congratulations.
Later, it was ordered that for memorials and letters from each province, one general "fire-token" (urgent dispatch pass) be used for the entire province,
and a special envoy be dispatched to deliver them.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
as provincial administration commissioners and deputy commanders were unable to personally convey their memorials and letters,
the practice of attaching their submissions to others was abolished.
It was also decreed that for the Empress's birthday (*Huánghòu Qiānqiūjié*), New Year's Day, and Winter Solstice,
the submission of congratulatory letters (*jiān*) be permanently discontinued.
For the Crown Prince's celebrations,
officials in the capital assembled to offer congratulations,
but did not prepare letters (*jiān*),
and provincial officials were also exempt from offering congratulatory letters.
In the sixtieth year,
Gāozōng abdicated,
taking the title *Tàishàng Huángdì*.
The format for congratulatory memorials was:
"Your imperial son [surname], leading the princes and high ministers, respectfully reports that
on New Year's Day of a certain year,
the *Tàishàng Huángdì* personally bestowed the great imperial seal,
and Your imperial son respectfully received the benevolent command.
Therefore, I respectfully lead the princes, civil and military high ministers, and others in presenting this memorial to offer congratulations."
At the end, it said:
"Your imperial son and all ministers are filled with boundless admiration, joy, and delight,
and hereby present this memorial to offer congratulations and to inform."
The format for congratulatory memorials on the Emperor's enthronement
only stated,
after "bowing and prostrating ourselves":
"We respectfully greet the completion of His Majesty's reception of the imperial seal,
and the commencement of his reign and era.
We respectfully present this memorial to offer congratulations."
The rest followed the previous format.
The Grand Imperial Tour Ritual. When the Emperor inspects the provinces and observes the people,
a special grand ceremony of periodic tours is held.
After selecting an auspicious day,
the Emperor, in his travelling attire,
rides his palanquin out of the palace,
leading the Imperial Bodyguards, Grand Ministers, and others, along with the Forbidden Army, to guard and escort the Imperial carriage.
All officials, in their travelling attire, ride on horseback and depart in order.
Where the Imperial carriage passes,
unauthorized followers, accompanying officials, military officers, or civil servants are prohibited from disturbing the people or trampling crops.
All provisions of food and fodder
are defrayed from the public treasury.
Nearing the border,
the Dū, Fǔ, Tí, and Zhèn officials lead their subordinates to welcome the Emperor on the right side of the road.
The gentry and elders welcome him from various distances.
Once the Imperial carriage stops,
the border officials and others pay court outside the temporary camp gate.
The next day,
rites are performed for the sacred mountains (Fāngyuè),
and sacrifices are made to former emperors and ancient teachers.
All these the Emperor personally attends.
For shrines and tombs of famous worthies, officials are dispatched.
Officials are received in audience,
and questions are asked about local customs and popular sentiments.
The Emperor personally inspects river defenses,
giving instructions and strategies.
Those who present poems and prose are summoned for examination,
and the most outstanding are promoted to office.
He reviews the troops of the regional garrisons,
taking the opportunity to discern their talent and martial prowess.
When passing through prefectures and counties,
he grants remissions and exemptions from taxes,
enquires after the elderly,
and bestows special favors.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì (1651),
a system was established:
when the Emperor undertakes a tour,
a separate set of incense and treasures is specially made to be carried along,
and all seals for the accompanying officials are cast,
adding
the character "Xíngzài" (temporary residence or traveling court).
Memorials from the ministries and censorial offices
are collated by the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat),
and sent to the Xíngzài every three days.
The presentation of local products where the Imperial carriage passes is prohibited.
It was also stipulated that wherever the Imperial carriage passes,
local officials within a hundred *lǐ* must welcome and send off the Emperor on the right side of the road.
In the twenty-third year of Kāngxī (1684),
when Emperor Shèngzǔ (Kāngxī Emperor) made his southern tour,
it was decreed that accompanying princes, dukes, grand ministers, and officials from ministries and offices must follow the Imperial carriage in order of their departure.
Subsequently, he made five southern tours to Jiāngzhè (Jiangnan and Zhejiang),
personally offered sacrifices at Dàiyuè (Mount Tài) in Tàian,
crossed the river and sacrificed to the River God,
went to Jiāngníng (Nanjing) to visit the mausoleum of Míng Tàizǔ,
made four visits to Wǔtái,
and one visit to Xī'ān.
Generally, he prohibited extravagance and emphasized practicality,
diligently attending to the affairs of the people.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
the Empress Dowager was often escorted on southern tours,
such as to Hénán,
to Wǔtái,
and to Shāndōng and Tiānjīn.
Wherever the Imperial carriage (Cuìhuá) arrived,
the common people benefited from its blessings.
He made six tours to Jiāngzhè,
where he assessed key engineering projects,
and extensively constructed dikes and dams.
Even though this consumed millions in public funds, he did not regret it.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
he toured Wǔtái Qīngliángshān,
bestowing celebrations and favors,
following the precedents of Kāngxī.
The Village Drinking Ritual. In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
following the old system of the Míng dynasty,
it was ordered that the capital prefecture and the prefectures, departments, and counties of the direct provinces
should hold the ritual in the school temple
on the full moon of the first spring month and the new moon of the first winter month each year.
The day before,
the officiants arranged the seats in the lecture hall and practiced the ritual.
Retired officials were designated as the Grand Guests (Dàbīn),
positioned to the northwest;
those excellent in both age and virtue were the Secondary Guests (Cènbīn),
positioned to the northeast;
next were the Introducers (Jiè),
positioned to the southwest;
below the Guests were the Third Guests (Sānbīn);
positioned behind the Guests, Host, Introducers, and Secondary Guests;
the officials of the prefecture, department, or county served as the Host (Zhǔrén),
positioned to the southeast.
For Shùntiān Fǔ, the Fǔyǐn (Prefect) served as the Host,
one Sīzhèng (Director of Rituals) was responsible for raising the goblet (yángzhì),
assumed by a Teaching Official (Jiàoguān).
Two assistants for guiding (zànyǐn) and two for reading the statutes (dúlǜ) were appointed,
assumed by Licentiate Scholars (Shēngyuán).
On the day, the officiants led the sacrificial animals and prepared the dishes.
The Host, with his subordinates, went to the school,
and then invited the Guests.
When the Guests arrived,
they were welcomed outside the gate,
the Host on the east and the Guests on the west.
After three bows and mutual deference, they ascended,
facing each other and bowing twice.
The Guests took their seats,
and the Secondary Guests and Introducers were invited in,
following the Guests' ritual.
Once in position,
the announcer called "Yángzhì!"
The Sīzhèng ascended from the western steps,
stood facing north,
and the Guests and Host all stood up.
The announcer called "Yī!" (bow),
the Sīzhèng bowed,
and the Guests, Introducers, and others returned the bow.
The officiants lifted the cover, poured wine into the goblet, and handed it to the Sīzhèng.
The Sīzhèng raised the goblet and spoke, saying:
"Respectfully, our imperial court,
following ancient statutes,
promotes the etiquette of ritual education,
and holds the village drinking ritual.
This is not merely for eating and drinking;
rather, all of us, old and young,
should encourage one another.
As ministers, be loyal;
as sons, be filial;
let there be order between old and young;
elder siblings be friendly, younger siblings respectful;
internally, be harmonious with clan members;
externally, be at peace with fellow villagers.
Let no one neglect or fall short,
thereby shaming their parents."
After reading,
the announcer called "Yǐnjiǔ!" (drink wine),
and the Sīzhèng drank standing.
The announcer called "Yī!" (bow),
and all bowed.
The Sīzhèng returned to his position,
and the Guests and Introducers all sat.
The announcer called "Dúlǜlìng!" (read the statutes),
the Licentiate Scholars went to the table, stood facing north,
and all rose and bowed together.
They read:
"The statutes state:
For all village drinking rituals,
order the old and young,
discuss the worthy and good,
distinguish the treacherous and stubborn.
Those advanced in age and outstanding in virtue are placed in the upper ranks;
those pure and diligent follow closely.
Distinguish by age.
Those who violate the law or rules shall not be allowed to participate.
Otherwise, they shall be judged for violating the regulations.
Should anyone dare to be noisy or behave improperly,
the one who raised the goblet shall correct them."
After reading, they returned to their positions.
The announcer called "Gōngzhuàn!" (serve dishes),
and the officials set out the dishes.
The announcer called "Xiànbīn!" (present to the guest),
and a goblet was handed to the Host.
The Host received it
and placed it at the Guests' seats.
He then withdrew slightly,
bowed twice,
and the Guests returned the bow.
The same was done for the Secondary Guests.
All sat,
and the officials poured wine for everyone.
The announcer called "Yǐnjiǔ!" (drink wine),
wine was served three to five rounds,
and three kinds of soup.
When finished,
the dishes were removed.
The Secondary Guests, Host, and subordinate officials stood on the east,
and the Guests and Introducers on the west,
all bowing twice.
The announcer called "Sòngbīn!" (send off the guests),
and all bowed three times,
exited,
and withdrew.
In the first year of the Yōngzhèng reign,
an edict stated:
“The rite of rural conviviality (xiāngyǐnjiǔlǐ) is for honoring the aged and respecting the virtuous.
Its institution is ancient.
On the day of its observance in Shùntiān Fǔ,
the officials of the Ministry of Rites shall supervise it as a regular practice.”
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng,
owing to the lack of uniformity in the rural conviviality system across the provinces,
or its frequent omission for years.
The old ceremony, as depicted in illustrations, featured a Dàbīn, Jièbīn, Yībīn, Èrbīn, Sānbīn,
and a Yīzuàn, Èrzuàn, Sānzuàn,
with many confusing titles.
According to the ancient *Yílǐ*:
“If the guests (bīn) have followers (zūn),
they are the various dukes and grandees (gōngdàfū).”
The commentary states:
“The modern text reads it as zuàn.
These are officials from the locality who have reached the rank of grandee,
coming to assist the host in entertaining the guests.
They are those whom the host honors and whose methods he follows.”
The *Dàijì* states:
“The zuàn sits in the northwest,
to assist the host.”
It describes how the host personally invites the main guest (bīn) and the secondary guest (jiè),
with elaborate rituals of bowing, offering and returning toasts, and polite refusals,
but not a single word mentions the zuàn.
This is what is meant by
“not interfering with the host’s main ceremony.”
Subsequently, for the bīn and jiè of rural conviviality,
the relevant authorities (yǒusī) should select elders (qíshēn) and those of great virtue (shuòdé) for these roles.
Alternatively, if prominent officials residing in the countryside come to observe the rite,
they should sit in the northeast according to ancient rites.
If there are none, it is better to omit them
than to establish the title of zuàn.
In the fiftieth year,
it was ordered that the rural conviviality should be held annually without fail.
Each time the rite was performed,
the six chapters of the Emperor's "Bǔshēng Shī" were played.
The procedure was:
wine was offered to the guest (xiànbīn),
the guest returned the toast to the host,
and wine circulated several times.
The musicians (gōng) ascended,
played the se,
and sang "Lùmíng."
After three rounds of wine for the guest, host, and others below,
the food steward (sīzhuàn) served soup,
the sheng and qing instruments began,
playing "Nángāi,"
with an interlude song of "Yúlì,"
and the sheng playing "Yóugēng."
The wine steward (sījué) served wine in sequence.
After the food steward served soup three times,
the ensemble played together,
singing "Guānjuī."
The musicians announced
“the music is complete,”
and the food was cleared away.
The guest and host all rose and bowed twice.
The guest and secondary guest departed,
and the host escorted them outside the gate,
following the initial reception ceremony.
Originally,
all expenses for the rural conviviality were drawn from public funds.
From the late Dàoguāng era,
these funds were reallocated for military provisions,
and management was consequently shifted to local organizations.
Other matters proceeded according to old practices.
However, its observance was rare.

Volume 65: Rites 9 (Military Rites): Imperial Expeditions, Triumphant Returns, Appointing Generals for Expeditions, Reporting Victories, Accepting Surrender, Presenting and Receiving Captives, Grand Reviews (including Joint Reviews and Beijing Training), Autumn Hunts, Rites for Eclipses
The third section is Military Rites.
The great affairs of the state
are sacrifices and warfare.
The *Zhōuguān* system prescribed six armies
and managed nine punitive expeditions,
with authority belonging to the Sīmǎ.
However, for major military campaigns and grand field exercises,
the rites were overseen by the Zōngbó.
This was to teach troop management, army deployment, encampment, and grand reviews,
while incorporating the ceremonies of sōu, miáo, xǐ, and shòu
for the sacrifices of shè, yuè, bāng, and zhēng.
Thus,
military drills had a purpose,
and the killing of beasts was a ritual.
The military achievements of the Qīng dynasty were splendid.
All rites related to military expeditions, accepting achievements, training, and hunting expeditions
were extremely well-established.
Therefore, based on ancient principles,
the important matters were recorded separately
and compiled into this chapter.
In ancient times, for solar eclipse rescue rites,
the tàipú assisted in drumming,
which also belonged to the summer officials (xiàguān).
Now, these are similarly appended here.
Imperial Expeditions: In the third year of Tiānmìng,
Tàizǔ issued a book on military training methods.
He personally led infantry and cavalry to campaign against the Míng,
visited the Tángzǐ,
and wrote the Seven Grievances to heaven,
which marked the beginning of imperial expeditions.
In the first year of Chóngdé,
Tàizōng campaigned against Cháoxiǎn.
Prior to the expedition, he swore an oath to heaven and reported to the ancestral temple,
issued military regulations,
and divided the troops into left and right wings.
On the appointed day,
the imperial carriage departed from Fǔjìn Mén,
the imperial retinue (lǔbù) was arrayed,
and conch shells were blown, and music played.
He respectfully visited the Tángzǐ,
performing three prostrations and nine kowtows.
Outside, eight daò were erected,
and sacrifices were offered as before.
After the rites, the journey began.
In the thirty-fifth year of Kāngxī,
when suppressing Gá'ěrdān,
the Emperor personally led the six armies (liùshī) out through the central route.
Three days prior,
sacrifices were offered to the suburban altars (jiāo), ancestral temples (miào), and Tàisuì.
On the scheduled day, sacrifices were sent to the gods of roads, cannons, and fire.
The Emperor wore his campaign attire and carried his sword,
riding out of the palace,
accompanied by inner grandees and others for protection.
At Wǔmén, bells and drums were sounded,
soldiers blew horns and conch shells,
and sacrifices were made to the Tángzǐ and the Dàoshén as per custom.
The welcoming music began,
playing "Yòupíng Zhāng."
The imperial carriage exited the capital gate,
proceeding to the troop assembly point,
where two cannon shots were fired.
The banner armies followed,
and princes, dukes, and all officials escorted the emperor.
The soldiers formed neat ranks,
and in order, guarded the imperial procession.
At each encampment, the terrain was surveyed,
the imperial camp was established in the center,
with other camps encircling it,
enclosed by a curtain wall,
and a banner gate erected to the south.
Outposts (chìhòu) were positioned far out,
and camp drums (diāodǒu) were strictly enforced.
Twenty-one patrol posts were set up,
with inner grandees leading the imperial guard (qīnjūn) for night watch.
Outside, a net-like enclosure was established,
with three gates: east, west, and south.
Eight patrol posts were set up,
with commanders of the guard (hùjūn tǒnglǐng) leading the Yǔlín army for patrols.
Loud talking was prohibited,
and entry and exit were strictly controlled.
Further outside, tents formed a double camp,
with four gates,
each guarded by ten men.
The accompanying officials
lined up outside the double camp.
The main army divided into wings to graze horses,
and crossing ranks was forbidden.
When the imperial carriage halted at a temporary camp,
all armies stopped.
Accompanying officials reported matters as usual.
When the night watch first began,
the watch drums were strictly beaten,
pedestrians were halted,
and inner and outer imperial guards patrolled in turns.
At the fifth watch,
a bell rang at the imperial camp,
and horn calls arose from the vanguard camp.
At the first drum of the watch,
the outer camps ate breakfast and prepared their gear;
at the second drum,
the vanguard broke camp;
at the third drum,
the left, right, and rear armies dispatched their baggage trains,
and accompanying officials waited outside the banner gate.
At daybreak,
a cannon shot signaled the imperial departure.
Wherever the six armies passed,
local officials welcomed them within their jurisdiction;
senior officials went beyond their borders to welcome them.
Outer princely dukes (wàifān wánggōng) and their gentry (shēnjī) knelt to receive them,
all performing inspection ceremonies simultaneously.
As the army marched,
sacrifices were sent as needed to the gods of wind, rain, mountains, and rivers,
and watchtowers were maintained within the army.
Shèngzǔ personally inspected
and organized the troops.
He ascended the banner gate,
reviewed the generals and soldiers,
and upon reaching Xībā Tái,
envoys delivered an imperial edict to Gá'ěrdān.
The enemy, seeing the grand army,
abandoned their armor and fled.
The Emperor led the vanguard on a swift advance to Tuōnuò,
then dispatched generals to pursue,
and then returned.
Gá'ěrdān (Galdan) had not yet repented.
That autumn,
the Emperor went on an inspection tour to the northern frontier.
He announced that he was going beyond the Great Wall to test falcons,
and traveled with a reduced retinue.
In the tenth month,
he reached Bái Tǎ,
and stayed at Nánguān.
Mongol princes and others presented gifts in an endless stream.
The Emperor bestowed food upon the victorious soldiers,
had them brought near his seat, and distributed gifts to all.
The next day,
he further ordered imperial meals to be distributed to the army.
More than a month later,
he arrived at Hū Tǎn Hé Shuò,
crossed the river,
and those who surrendered came one after another.
Gá'ěrdān submitted,
and then the army returned.
The following year,
the Emperor personally led the northern expedition for the third time.
The departure ceremony was as before,
and he stopped at Héng Chéng.
He ordered the local high officials to welcome the imperial carriage at the river.
At that time, Hāmì captured Gá'ěrdān's son and sent him to the military camp.
Many from the Èlǔtè (Oirat) tribe defected.
Gá'ěrdān died by taking poison.
The Emperor returned by boat from the Yellow River.
Victorious Return. In the second year of Chóngdé,
Tàizōng (Hong Taiji) conquered Cháoxiǎn (Joseon Korea).
On the day the army returned,
the ruler and his ministers came out ten *lǐ* outside the city to see off the imperial carriage,
performing the three kneelings and nine kowtows as per ritual.
Upon returning, he sent two high officials to escort them.
When the imperial carriage set off,
the standard-bearer was immediately sacrificed to in front of the army.
Local officials greeted the Emperor on the road.
After the imperial carriage passed,
they followed the army to the next stop to receive orders,
and were granted wine from afar while seated.
When they were twenty *lǐ* from Shèngjīng,
Zhèng Qīnwáng (Prince Zheng) and others met them, bearing congratulatory memorials.
They then cleared the path in advance,
set up a yellow tent,
and waited for the imperial carriage to arrive,
kneeling to welcome it on the left side of the road.
The Emperor entered the tent and sat down.
The princes and others knelt to present their memorials,
which the Grand Secretary received.
After the reading was completed,
the princes and others performed the three kneelings and nine kowtows.
Then a grand banquet was held.
After the banquet, they departed.
Upon reaching Shèngjīng,
they performed rites at the Tángzǐ (Manchu ancestral temple)
and then returned to the palace.
In the thirty-fifth year of Kāngxī,
Shèngzǔ (Kangxi Emperor) campaigned against Gá'ěrdān,
defeated him,
and returned to Tuōnuò.
Upon entering triumphantly,
he burned incense to thank Heaven.
Entering the marching camp,
the Grand Secretaries and others presented congratulatory memorials.
Princes, dukes, and all officials offered congratulations.
The remaining Mongol princes and others welcomed the imperial carriage and performed rituals.
The Khalkha Zásàkè (Jasagh) and others gathered at the east gate of the camp to request an audience,
all kowtowing and shouting "Long live!"
They were granted tea and a banquet,
and received silver and goods of varying amounts.
Along the way, those who welcomed and offered gifts, bowing down,
came in great numbers.
Upon reaching Qīnghé,
the imperial princes, princes, dukes, and all ministers knelt to welcome him five *lǐ* outside the city.
The Eight Banners military officers and the gentry and commoners of the near-capital region also burned incense and hung colorful silks,
supporting and leading their families, prostrating themselves.
He ordered the vanguard not to disturb the imperial procession,
and those who gathered around numbered in the millions,
their cheers like thunder.
The Emperor paid respects at the Tángzǐ as usual.
The following year,
the northern desert was pacified,
and the return of the army was also like this.
After returning to the palace,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices at the suburban altars, the altars of earth and grain, and the imperial ancestral temple,
and to all deities.
He visited the imperial tombs,
and received congratulations in the imperial hall.
Officials from all direct provinces presented memorials,
and edicts were issued according to regulations.
The Emperor personally inscribed and carved stones,
and erected a stele at the Imperial Academy.
Dispatching Generals. In the first year of Chóngdé,
