Tàizōng ordered Ruì Wáng (Prince Rui) Duō'ěrgǔn (Dorgon) and others to lead an army to campaign against Míng.
He personally went to see them off,
offering sacrifices at the Tángzǐ and to the standard-bearer deity,
following the ceremony for a personal expedition.
He then proceeded to the drill ground,
and gave instructions and warnings to the generals and soldiers.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
Yīng Wáng (Prince Ying) Ājìgé (Ajige) was appointed as Jìngyuǎn Dàjiàngjūn (Generalissimo who Pacifies the Distant),
to campaign against the roving bandits,
and was granted an imperial edict and seal.
The ceremony was as follows:
Outside Wǔmén (Meridian Gate), the imperial procession was arranged.
On the steps, a yellow tent was set up,
and an imperial seat was placed.
The imperial edict and seal were displayed on a table east of the eaves.
Princes, dukes, and all officials assembled.
The Emperor ascended the seat.
The Generalissimo led the generals on expedition to the kneeling position to bow.
Ministers of the Interior Court then presented and read the imperial edict in Manchu, Mongolian, and Chinese.
The imperial edict and seal were handed to the Generalissimo.
When completed,
they departed.
In the thirteenth year,
it was decreed that on the day before the army set out,
clothes, horses, bows, and swords would be customarily granted in front of Wǔmén,
and all officials going on expedition would be summoned
to be personally instructed on strategy.
A banquet was granted.
On the day of departure,
all waited in military attire outside Wǔmén.
The imperial edict and seal were granted as per the initial ritual.
In the thirteenth year of Kāngxī,
generals were ordered to be dispatched separately to Húguǎng and Sìchuān.
After the ceremony,
the Emperor went out Cháng'ān Yòumén (Right Gate of Chang'an) to see them off.
The prince leading the expedition, along with all officials, proceeded to the place where troops were arrayed.
The Ministry of Rites set up an ancestral tent.
The Court of Imperial Entertainments prepared tea and wine.
Inner Ministers and others led them to express gratitude.
Their departure was
as before.
If the Emperor did not personally see them off,
then a *qīnwáng* (prince of the first rank) or Inner Minister would go.
During the campaign against Gá'ěrdān,
Fèiyánggǔ (Fiyanggū) was first summoned from Guīhuà Yì (Guihua Post) to be Fúyuǎn Dàjiàngjūn (Generalissimo who Soothes the Distant).
On the day he arrived, he was rewarded with a banquet.
Shèngzǔ presided at the Tài hé Mén (Hall of Supreme Harmony).
Ministers sat in the corners.
The generals on expedition and the ministers responsible for transporting provisions sat to the north left and right of the Jīnshuǐ Qiáo (Golden Water Bridge).
Music was played, and various performances were staged.
The Generalissimo was ordered to advance before the Emperor,
who personally bestowed a cup of wine.
After kneeling to receive it and drinking it with a kowtow,
the Dūtǒng (General) and Fù Dūtǒng (Deputy General) advanced next,
and attendants were ordered to bestow wine upon them.
Cānlǐng (Lieutenant Colonels) and below stood in rows of ten,
kneeling to drink on the steps.
He further ordered the ministers to ensure all soldiers had drunk and eaten,
and bestowed imperial蟒幣 (dragon robes/silk) upon those who partook in the banquet,
other silks upon the rest,
and cloth upon the soldiers.
After expressing thanks and departing together,
the Grand Secretary then presented the imperial edict and seal to the Generalissimo.
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng,
it was decreed that on the day before dispatching generals, the ancestral temple should be notified.
On the day of departure, the Fèngxiān Diàn (Hall for Worshipping Ancestors) was notified,
and an official was dispatched.
If a general was appointed *Dàjiàngjūn* while already leading an army on the frontier,
then a chief envoy and a deputy envoy would be ordered
to carry the imperial edict and seal there.
The Generalissimo, with his subordinates, would await at the drill ground.
In the main hall, a yellow table was set up,
displaying the imperial edict and seal.
The Generalissimo knelt.
The chief envoy read the edict and presented it.
The deputy envoy read the seal inscription and presented the seal.
The Generalissimo received them with reverence, in turn,
and passed them to the accompanying officials on his left and right.
They performed the three kneelings and nine kowtows.
After the ceremony, they carried them into the main camp.
In the 14th year of Qiánlóng,
three ceremonies were established for appointing generals:
First, when the Grand General Jīnglüè went forth on campaign, receiving the imperial seal and edict,
the Emperor would personally bestow them from his imperial presence.
Second, the Fúshè ritual.
Before setting out on campaign,
report was made to the Fèngxiān Diàn,
rites were performed at the Tángzi,
and a sacrifice was offered to the banner (dú).
Third, the Zǔdào ritual.
When the Jīnglüè was about to depart,
the Emperor would personally see him off and bestow wine,
and command high officials to accompany him to the outskirts of the city,
where a Zǔzhàng and a banquet were arranged.
The details of these rituals were as previously specified.
There were two ceremonies for military campaigns:
First, the troop formation.
The vanguard of the Jīnglüè would display the imperial military weapons,
followed by the command arrows (lìngjiàn),
then the imperial seal (chìyìn),
then the standard flags (biāoqí),
with the main army corps bringing up the rear.
The number of command arrows and standard flags was twelve each.
Second, the meeting with local officials.
When the Jīnglüè passed through a territory,
the Jiāngjūn, Dū, and Fǔ, dressed in python robes (mǎngfú), would go outside the city walls to greet him.
Civil officials, from Sīdào downwards, and military officials, from Zǒngbīng downwards,
would kneel on the right side of the road and in the hall.
The Jīnglüè would sit in the main seat,
the Jiāngjūn, Dū, and Fǔ would sit to the side,
and civil Sīdào and military Tídū officials and below
would perform the Tíngcān salute.
The departure and escort were as in the previous ceremony.
If the imperial seal and edict were not bestowed in the imperial palace,
then the imperial cortege (lǔbù) and court music (yuèxuán) were omitted,
and officials without specific duties would not assemble.
In the 34th year,
Grand Secretary Fùhéng was appointed Jīnglüè for military affairs in Yúnnán.
Gāozōng did not ascend to the main hall,
did not perform rites at the Tángzi,
did not offer sacrifice to the banner,
and did not personally see him off.
An Imperial Academy scholar (Nèigé Xuéshì) brought the imperial seal and edict to the Tàihé Diàn.
The Jīnglüè and others waited beforehand at the steps of the imperial platform,
while two Grand Secretaries stood outside the hall.
At the appointed time, the Jīnglüè ascended the steps,
and the seal-bearing official, following the Grand Academy scholar, entered, presented the imperial seal and edict, and exited.
The Jīnglüè knelt to receive them.
Upon completion of the ceremony,
the official bearing the imperial seal and edict went first,
the Jīnglüè followed,
and at the foot of the steps,
the imperial seal and edict were placed in a decorated palanquin.
A yellow parasol was displayed in front,
imperial guards were arrayed,
and the imperial bodyguards (shìwèi) accompanying the campaign led the way,
while all others followed behind,
stopping at the Jīnglüè's residence.
The imperial seal and edict were displayed on a table in the hall.
On the appointed day, the procession would set forth solemnly.
Reporting victory. In the early Yuán of Tiāncōng,
Cháoxiān reported a victory,
and the army returned.
The imperial carriage exited the city,
stopping in the wilderness by Wǔjìng Yíng.
An imperial tent (xíngwò) was set up about a *lǐ* away from the imperial camp.
The Emperor, accompanied by the various Bèilè, advanced a few paces beyond the imperial tent,
and stood mounted to await the triumphant return.
When they arrived,
they arrayed themselves in order,
erected banners, worshipped Heaven,
and entered for an audience.
The Emperor stepped down from his position to welcome them.
The various Bèilè performed the kneeling and prostrating salute,
and a banquet was bestowed.
In the 1st year of Chóngdé,
upon the triumphant return from the campaign against Míng,
Tàizōng led his officials ten *lǐ* outside the city to welcome and commend them.
The Wáng, Bèilè, and others formed ranks in order,
erected banners, blew conches,
and the Emperor led them in worshipping Heaven with three kneelings and nine prostrations.
After completion,
the Emperor ascended his seat.
The Wáng and Bèilè presented the victory memorial,
which the Grand Secretaries received,
and had read before the Emperor.
After completion, they knelt and kowtowed as per ritual.
An imperial edict was issued for the Bǎojiàn ceremony (embrace and audience).
Thereupon, the Wáng and Bèilè advanced before the Emperor, performed one kneeling and three prostrations,
and were bestowed seats and a banquet as before.
In the 2nd year of Shùnzhì,
Nánjīng was pacified,
and Prince Yù returned with his army.
Shìzǔ went to Nányuàn to welcome and commend him.
More than ten large banners were erected,
as in the initial ceremony.
In the 13th year,
it was decreed that for victorious Wáng and high officials returning from campaign,
one Wánggōng and accompanying high officials would be dispatched to commend them in the suburbs.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī,
it was decreed that on the day following a triumphant return,
the Emperor would hold court.
Upon completion of the ceremony,
generals and others were exempted from performing salutes,
and for the banquet, tables and seats were dispensed with,
only sacrificial animals were provided.
In the 21st year,
when Grand General Bèizi Zhāngtài and others returned triumphantly from Yúnnán,
the imperial carriage went to Lúgōuqiáo to welcome and commend them, pausing there.
Officials made preparations,
and the following day, the imperial carriage arrived,
and all worshipped Heaven together,
establishing this as a customary practice.
In the 14th year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that upon the successful conclusion of a victorious campaign,
sacrifices should be offered to Heaven and Earth, the ancestral temples and altars, and the imperial mausoleums.
Sacrifices should be made to the former teachers (xiānshī),
steles should be erected at the Tàixué,
and literati officials should be ordered to compile the strategies for pacification for future generations.
When the Grand General Jīnglüè's army returned,
before entering the city,
court officials were dispatched to commend them in the suburbs.
The Emperor held court,
and the Jīnglüè, leading the meritorious officials, expressed gratitude
and surrendered the imperial seal and edict.
The ceremony was the same as for receiving the edict.
After the banquet ceremony was completed,
the Ministry of War assessed merits and achievements,
and distributed titles and rewards accordingly.
Thereafter, when General Dìngbiān Zhàohuì and others, and General Dìngxī Āguì and others returned triumphantly,
Gāozōng always stopped at the Huángxīnzhuāng Traveling Palace,
built a platform for the suburban commendation,
and all officials assembled.
A yellow tent was set up in the center,
facing south,
with eight blue canopies on each wing,
facing east and west.
The platform was to the south of the tent,
with left and right banners erected upon it,
and an imperial kneeling cushion in the middle.
To the east and west, there was one red pillar each for dismounting.
The Emperor, in his dragon robe (lónggǔn), proceeded to the platform.
Conches were blown,
and battle music (náogē yuè) was played.
The generals and accompanying high officials and soldiers were all in armor,
kneeling outside the red pillars, awaiting the imperial carriage.
The Emperor took his position for the salute,
and the generals and all officials were arrayed in eastern and western ranks.
When the official of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Hónglúguān) intoned
"Kneel,"
they all knelt.
He intoned
"Kowtow,
Rise."
The Emperor worshipped Heaven,
performing three kneelings and nine prostrations,
and the generals and others followed suit.
Upon completion,
the Emperor entered the tent and ascended his seat.
The Wánggōng and all officials stood under the eastern canopy.
After the ceremony,
the Emperor exited the tent and mounted his steed.
The triumphal song was played,
the chapter "Chàng Huáng Wēi" was performed,
and the imperial carriage returned to the traveling palace.
The rest followed the precedents from the Kāngxī era.
In the 5th year of Xiánfēng,
Qīn Wáng Sēnggélínqìn of Kē'ěrqìn pacified the rebellion in Gāotáng.
When he returned to court,
Wénzōng presided from the Yǎngxīndiàn,
performed the Bǎojiàn ceremony,
and offered extensive commendation.
Previously, when he departed on campaign, he was granted the seal of a Cānzàn Dàchén (Minister assisting in military affairs)
and bestowed the Nèikùní Sùguāng Dāo.
At this time, these were simultaneously offered and returned.
Receiving surrender. In the spring of the 2nd year of Chóngdé,
the King of Cháoxiān confessed his crimes and requested surrender.
Thereupon, an altar was built on the east bank of the Hàn Jiāng.
A yellow tent was set up.
The imperial carriage departed the camp,
and music played.
After crossing the river and ascending the altar,
the imperial cortege was arranged.
The King of Cháoxiān, with his accompanying officials, came walking to pay respects to the court.
An official was dispatched to meet them about a *lǐ* away.
They were led in.
The Emperor led them in worshipping Heaven,
then ascended his seat.
The King and others prostrated themselves on the ground, confessing their crimes.
The official intoned
"Perform the three kneelings and nine prostrations ritual."
They were bestowed seats,
with the King's position above the Qīn Wáng,
and his sons' positions among the Bèilè's sons.
A banquet was bestowed,
their captives were returned,
and the King and those below him were granted sable robes.
In the sixth year,
Mongolian Bèilè (貝勒) and others pledged allegiance.
After an audience,
they were commanded to compete in archery,
strongmen were chosen for wrestling,
and a banquet was granted for them to fully enjoy themselves.
This was a special honor.
All tribute items presented were rejected.
In the fourteenth year of Qiánlóng (乾隆),
a regulation was proposed that whenever surrenders were accepted on the military front,
a swift memorial should be submitted.
It was approved.
Then a grand proclamation was written and displayed to both the court and the public.
An altar was built to the left of the main camp,
facing south.
A marker was erected a hundred paces south of the altar,
and a large flag was raised,
bearing the words
"By Imperial Edict, Accepting Surrender."
The surrendering parties would stand beneath it.
The Jīnglüè Dàjiāngjūn (經略大將軍) would emerge in military attire,
with drumming, blowing of horns, and cannon fire,
accompanied by the Cānzàn Dàchén (參贊大臣) and others on horseback.
Upon approaching the altar,
the surrendering parties would prostrate themselves facing north.
The Jīnglüè (經略) would ascend the altar and sit upright.
The Cānzàn (參贊) would all sit,
the generals would stand to the side,
and the rest would stand in solemn ranks.
The surrendering parties would crawl on their knees to the foot of the altar,
bowing their heads and begging for their lives.
The Jīnglüè (經略) would proclaim the Emperor's benevolent intent,
and bestow appropriate rewards.
Drumming and horns would sound loudly from the camp gate.
The surrendering parties would repeatedly kowtow in gratitude,
rise,
and withdraw.
Presenting and Receiving Captives: In the early Qīng (清) dynasty, Tàizǔ (太祖) and Tàizōng (太宗) conquered the frontiers with military might,
capturing a great many prisoners.
At that time, there was no fixed custom for presenting and receiving them.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng (雍正),
after Qīnghǎi (青海) was pacified,
captives were brought to the capital,
and it was then decided to first choose an auspicious day to present them at the ancestral temple and the altars of earth and grain.
Captives had white cords tied around their necks.
When they reached the street gate of the Tàimiào (太廟), they stood facing north.
The sacrificial official arrived in court attire.
The captives prostrated themselves,
and the ceremony coincided with a feast.
The same was done when they reached the street of the Shèjì (社稷) altars.
The sacrificial official entered the altar to offer sacrifices,
the ceremony being the same as for spring and autumn prayers and reports.
The captors led the captives out.
The next day,
the Emperor ascended the Wǔmén (午門) tower to receive the captives.
An imperial seat was placed directly in the center,
a yellow canopy was spread under the eaves,
the imperial equipage was arrayed north and south of the palace gate,
followed by imperial horses.
Imperial carriages were arrayed south of the Jīnshuǐ Qiáo (金水橋),
followed by trained elephants.
Princes, dukes, and all officials assembled.
The officers leading the captives stood outside the golden drums,
with the captives following behind.
Once the ranks were arrayed,
the Emperor, in his dragon robe,
emerged from the palace in his imperial carriage.
Upon reaching the Tàihé Mén (太和門),
grand music, cymbals, and horns played,
and golden drums vibrated.
He ascended the tower and took his seat.
An official announced,
"Present the captives!"
Grand music played on the imperial steps,
performing the Qìngpíng Zhāng (慶平章).
Officials from the Hónglú Sì (鴻臚寺) led the officers in,
where they stood facing north.
An official announced,
"Perform the ceremony!"
The captives entered and prostrated themselves.
An official from the Bīngbù (兵部) knelt and reported,
"The captives seized from the pacification of such-and-such a place
are respectfully presented before Your Majesty.
We await Your Majesty's command."
The imperial decree stated:
"The presented captives are to be handed over to the Xíngbù (刑部)."
The chief official of the Xíngbù (刑部) knelt to receive the decree,
and then led the shackled captives out.
Grand music played on the imperial steps,
and princes, dukes, and all officials performed the usual ceremonies.
If imperial grace spared them from execution,
then an imperial decree would be proclaimed releasing their bonds.
The captives would kowtow,
and the officers would lead them out.
On that day, the officers were given a banquet by the Bīngbù (兵部).
The next day, they were granted various caps, shoes, silver, and silk.
Whenever territories were pacified,
the ceremony for receiving captives was the same.
During the Qiánlóng (乾隆) era,
the empire's territory expanded daily.
In the twentieth year,
the Zhǔngá'ěr (準噶爾) were crushed and pacified.
Dáwǎqí (達瓦齊) and Luóbúzàng Dānjīn (羅卜藏丹津) from Qīnghǎi (青海) were captured and brought in cages,
one after another.
This ceremony was performed twice in one year.
Five years later,
Huíjiāng (回疆) was finally pacified,
and Cánlācùjìn (攢拉促浸) was suppressed.
All these events were successively celebrated with grand ceremonies.
Within six years,
songs of triumph were sung four times.
Contemporaries considered this the era of utmost prosperity.
Grand Military Review: In the seventh year of Tiāncōng (天聰),
Tàizōng (太宗) led the Bèilè (貝勒) and others to supervise and drill the armies,
practicing formations.
This marked the beginning of grand military reviews.
In the thirteenth year of Shùnzhì (順治),
it was decided to hold one every three years,
and this was established as a regulation.
Soon after, the Emperor visited the Nányuàn (南苑),
commanding the Nèi Dàchén (內大臣) and others to don armor,
reviewing their equestrian skills and archery,
and also demonstrating a large-scale hunt to his officials.
In the twelfth year of Kāngxī (康熙),
a military review was held at Nányuàn (南苑).
Shèngzǔ (聖祖) donned armor,
ascended the Liàngyīngtái (晾鷹臺),
and took his seat in a yellow tent.
Nèi Dàchén (內大臣), Dūtǒng (都統), and others each led their troops,
while princes, Bèilè (貝勒), and others each led their banner dependents,
all proceeding from west to east.
Once arrayed,
guns fired and horns sounded.
They formed a battle array from east to west,
and were deployed in divisions according to their wings.
After the review,
targets were ordered to be set up on a platform.
The Emperor personally shot five arrows,
all hitting the mark.
He then rode and shot,
hitting the mark with a single shot.
He then took off his armor, granted a banquet,
and returned.
Subsequently, reviews were held
sometimes at Lúgōuqiáo (盧溝橋),
sometimes at Yùquán Shān (玉泉山),
or sometimes at Duōlúnnuò'ěr (多倫諾爾).
The location was not fixed,
nor was the timing limited to three years.
In the thirty-fourth year,
the Emperor again visited Nányuàn (南苑) for a review.
The Eight Banners were divided into three teams.
The Emperor, with his imperial sons, donned armor,
attended by Nèi Dàchén (內大臣) and others.
Behind them, three dragon banners were raised,
and the imperial bodyguards of the Upper Three Banners followed.
All the camps of cavalry, household guards, vanguards, and artillery were reviewed.
Standing before the army,
conch shells blew,
drums were beaten,
and troops carrying deer antlers advanced in formation.
Armored soldiers waved red flags,
and guns and cannons fired in unison.
Gongs sounded to stop,
then drums were beaten again,
and guns and cannons fired as before.
This was done nine times.
The first advance was five zhàng (丈),
and the second advance was also the same.
By the tenth advance,
guns and cannons fired continuously without interruption.
The deer antlers were opened to form eight gates.
The first team exited,
followed by the second and third teams.
Once arrayed,
the gates closed,
horns sounded,
and they advanced with shouts.
Both wing teams advanced like a flock of geese.
Gongs sounded to recall the troops.
They stood in their original formation,
then slowly turned in formation,
with the first team bringing up the rear.
After the review,
they returned to the imperial temporary palace,
where rewards and punishments were explicitly ordered.
Before the review,
soldiers were granted food.
After the review,
they were granted wine.
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1729),
Shìzōng visited Nányuàn
to inspect the chariot and cavalry camp soldiers.
He issued an edict, saying:
"This is merely one aspect of training.
To defeat an enemy in battle
depends on assessing the situation and judging the circumstances,
with divine insight and clarity.
It lies with the individual;
how can mere formations be sufficient to control the enemy?"
On that day, during the drill,
formations were arranged according to position and flag color.
Later, during the Northern Expedition,
victories were frequently achieved through chariot warfare.
In the second year of Qiánlóng's reign (1737),
a grand review was held.
He visited Nányuàn
and resided in the imperial tent-palace.
Once the troops were assembled,
the infantry marched forward in neat ranks.
A distance of ten zhàng was the standard,
and other rituals were similar.
According to regulations,
on the day of a grand review,
the imperial escort was displayed outside the temporary palace.
When the carriage departed,
Náo Gē Dà Yuè (martial music) was played,
performing the Zhuàng Jūn Róng Zhāng (Chapter on Strengthening Military Appearance).
Upon return,
Qīng Yuè (pure music) was played,
performing the Chàng Huáng Wēi Zhāng (Chapter on Extending Imperial Majesty).
During any drill, three cannon shots were fired;
the same applied when the imperial carriage departed and returned.
On the same day, all banners were granted feasts, sheep, pigs, firewood, and charcoal.
Until the Jiāqìng period,
all was carried out according to previous custom.
The joint review was an institution initiated by Kāngxī in the thirtieth year of his reign (1691).
At that time, the Khalkha had recently submitted,
and Shèngzǔ desired to train them in laws and regulations.
He specifically ordered a joint review at Shàngdū Qī Xī.
Thereupon, their various tribes were gathered,
along with the vassal kings and Tàijí of the forty-nine banners,
who had encamped a hundred lǐ away in advance.
When the imperial carriage left the capital,
the soldiers of the Upper Three Banners followed,
while the soldiers of the Lower Five Banners came from Dúshí to join.
Camps were pitched and outposts established.
The three banner guards formed one camp,
positioned in the center.
The Eight Banner vanguards formed two camps,
the five banner guards formed ten camps,
and the firearm camp soldiers formed four camps,
encircling the imperial camp.
The vanguards formed four outposts,
and the guards formed twenty-four outposts,
each establishing their tents and dwellings,
residing around the camp.
The encampments of the Mongols and Khalkha were moved to within fifty lǐ,
but entry into the outposts was forbidden.
Rewards were classified into nine grades,
and seats were arranged in seven rows.
A net-city was set up with the imperial tent,
an imperial couch precisely in the center,
two traveling tents on each side,
and all ceremonial regalia and musical instruments were provided.
Banquets were held in order.
The Mongol kings and others sat on the left,
the Khalkha on the right.
Dances were practiced in sequence,
and all skills were demonstrated.
Thereupon, the Khalkha Khans, Jì nóng, Nàyán, and others were ordered to advance before the emperor,
and were bestowed cups of wine,
while the rest were distributed by the imperial guards.
The ceremony concluded.
The next day, each camp took its position,
displaying large cannons.
The Emperor donned his armor,
and after the review, proclaimed an edict,
removing their Khān titles,
and bestowing upon them the noble ranks of Wáng, Bèilè, Bèizǐ, and Gōng.
The Tàijí were divided into four grades,
comparable to the forty-nine banners.
They were granted gifts according to their grades,
with added grace and courtesy,
and the rest as per ritual.
For the training of the Beijing garrisons,
joint drills were held four times a year in the last month of spring and autumn.
In spring, they wore armor;
in autumn, regular uniforms.
The camp and formation regulations were the same as for the grand review.
In mid-spring and early autumn, they ascended the city walls by banner to practice sounding conch shells.
The Ministry of War dispatched officials to inspect them,
which became an annual custom.
The Guard and Elite Cavalry Camps performed mounted archery drills three times a year;
the Vanguard and Guard Camps performed mounted archery drills once every three years.
The Grand Ministers of the Imperial Household and the Banner Dutǒngs supervised these.
As for military exercises in the provinces,
the Dūdū, Fǔ, Tí, and Zhèn served as military commanders.
On the day of frost in the last month of autumn each year,
they reviewed drills at the exercise ground.
Military tents were set up in advance.
At dawn on the appointed day,
officers and soldiers donned armor and formed ranks.
A large banner was erected in the center,
and the military commander led the officers and soldiers in a salute.
Military music played,
and the jié yuè (commander's insignia) led the way.
They thoroughly inspected the formations,
then returned and ascended the commander's platform.
After entering the tent,
the commander of the central army presented the formation diagrams
and requested permission for a joint drill.
Thereupon, flags were waved,
three cannon shots were fired, horns sounded, and drums beaten.
When the drums sounded, the army advanced;
when the gongs sounded, they halted.
The firing of muskets in formations followed the Beijing garrison system.
After the review,
officers and soldiers were tested in mounted archery,
rewards and punishments were clearly declared,
and the soldiers were feasted and honored.
The training of the grain transport river forces was the same as the Eight Banners.
Naval drills and defenses,
and sea-going signals,
varied by province.
Annually in the last month of spring or autumn, or in summer,
when the tide was calm and the wind favorable,
they would board warships and arrange formations,
unfurling sails and harnessing the wind,
sounding horns and firing cannons,
all in accordance with military regulations.
The Green Standard Navy followed the same.
Autumn Hunt: Since Qīng Tàizǔ rose to prominence in the eastern frontier,
he led his subjects in military training and hunting as military exercises.
Tàizōng continued this practice.
Shìzǔ unified all of China,
frequently visited Nányuàn,
and ordered restrictions on travel and encirclement for the hunt.
Thus began the establishment of the grand hunt escort regulations.
In the first year of Kāngxī's reign (1662),
it was stipulated that for the imperial carriage's hunting excursions and encampments, one Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng (Commander of the Guards) and one Yíngzǒng (Camp Commander) each were appointed,
to lead officers and soldiers to survey the terrain in advance.
The Wǔbèi Yuàn (Armaments Office) set up the mobile camp
and erected the tent-palace.
It was enclosed by a yellow-painted wooden wall,
with banner gates erected,
covered by yellow curtains.
Outside this was a net-city,
where guards and troops were stationed,
not to go beyond their designated areas.
In the tenth year (1671),
the wooden wall was abolished and replaced with yellow curtains.
In the twentieth year of Kāngxī's reign (1681),
he visited beyond the Great Wall
and hunted in Nánshān.
Soon after, he exited Shānhǎi Guān,
then proceeded to Wūlā,
engaging in archery and hunting personally at both locations.
Two years later, in the sixth month (1683),
he visited Gǔběikǒu and hunted there.
This was the beginning of the Mùlán hunting expedition.
Mùlán is 400 lǐ north of Chéngdé Fǔ,
belonging to Wēngniútè.
Previously, a vassal king had offered it as a hunting ground,
spanning over 1,300 lǐ,
with dense forests,
lush water and grass,
where herds of beasts gathered and bred.
From then on, the autumn hunt ceremony was held,
with occasional expeditions in winter.
In the thirty-third year (1694),
the Hǔqiāng Yíng (Tiger Spear Camp) was established,
divided among the Upper Three Banners,
with a Zǒngtǒng (Commander-in-Chief) and a Zǒnglǐng (General Commander) appointed.
During the grand hunt,
if ferocious beasts were encountered,
spears were arrayed to follow them.
It was also ordered that garrison soldiers in various provinces should participate in seasonal hunts annually as a regular practice.
In the sixty-first year (1722),
he again visited beyond the Great Wall for a hunting expedition,
bestowing clothes and other items upon the Mongol kings and dukes,
establishing this as a permanent system.
In the eighth year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1730),
the Eight Banner people were ordered to practice foot-hunting,
with each banner hunting two or three times.
In the early years of the Qiánlóng reign,
a Grand Minister in charge of the mobile imperial camp was appointed,
to whom all matters concerning setting out, hunting, lodging, and guarding were entrusted.
In the sixth year,
Cóng Dòng, a censor, submitted a memorial requesting a temporary suspension of the imperial hunt.
The emperor issued an edict saying:
"In ancient times, the four seasonal hunts (sōu, miáo, mǐn, shòu)
were for practicing military skills through field hunting.
The imperial hunts of Our Imperial Ancestor
not only benefited the military
but also upheld the principles of governance.
Furthermore, visiting the various Mongolian banners according to the calendar,
and bestowing special favor upon them,
was a particularly grand strategy for cherishing those far away.
Moreover, during times of war,
when numerous levies were made,
the imperial hunt was occasionally suspended,
but promptly resumed thereafter.
How much more so now, with a long period of peace,
people have grown accustomed to ease and comfort,
and their archery and horsemanship are gradually declining from their former state.
How can we not invigorate them?
This autumn, for the Mùlán imperial hunt,
the prefectures and counties passed through
will have three-tenths of their assessed taxes remitted
as a permanent precedent."
There were over sixty hunting grounds.
Each year for the grand autumn hunt,
either eighteen or nineteen enclosures,
or twenty enclosures,
would be used, changing every other year.
For the location of the enclosure,
the date would always be announced in advance,
specifying where it would begin,
where it would proceed,
and where it would conclude and be closed,
and these places would be pre-arranged.
On the appointed day, officials and soldiers would go to the ground and array themselves,
awaiting the imperial presence at the enclosure.
A heavy enclosure would be set up at the starting point,
with soldiers from the Hǔqiāng Battalion and hunters from various departments specifically assigned to shoot any beasts that escaped from within the enclosure.
Whenever Gāozōng went hunting,
the forty-nine old banners, as well as the Khalkha and Qīnghǎi divisions, would follow in shifts,
with measures for pacification and cohesion being meticulously observed.
By the time the Western Regions were pacified,
distant banners such as the left and right Khassak,
the East and West Burut,
Andijān,
and Bukhārā,
came to court one after another,
fearing they might be late.
The Tǔ'ěrhùt also brought their entire populace tens of thousands of *lǐ* to the court.
The Emperor once comforted them at the Bùgùtú Chāng'ā,
and then bestowed upon it the name
"Yīmián,"
which in the national language means "reaching the ultimate extremity."
In the twentieth year,
the layout was revised: the net-city and connected tents were set at one hundred seventy-five,
three banner-gates were established,
and military banners called 'Golden Dragon' were erected at intervals.
About ten *zhàng* outside the net-city and connected tents was the outer city,
with two hundred fifty-four connected tents,
four banner-gates were established,
and military banners called 'Flying Tiger' were erected at intervals.
Sixty *zhàng* outside the outer connected tents,
the area was guarded all around,
with forty tents erected,
each displaying its banner,
and the Eight Banners guards were solely responsible for this.
The regulations were thus detailed and precise.
For all autumn hunts,
the garrison commanders would select capable officers to go to the capital for training in advance.
Annually,
the Mongolian banners selected one thousand two hundred fifty men as imperial huntsmen,
known as
"enclosure walls,"
to assist in the surrounding efforts.
When the time came,
the Emperor, in military attire and on horseback, would leave the palace,
escorted in a manner similar to an imperial tour.
Once settled in the mobile imperial camp,
soldiers were forbidden from trampling crops or disturbing officials and common people,
and night travel was prohibited.
Violators were punished according to the law.
The Grand Minister in charge of the hunt would arrive at the site,
array the troops by banner,
erect a yellow banner in the center as the central army,
and erect red and white banners at the two wings obliquely as markers.
At the ends of the two wings, called 'Wūtúlí' in the national language,
blue banners were erected as markers,
all under the command of the central army.
The ministers in charge of the hunt were led by princes and grand ministers,
with Mongolian kings, princes, and *tàijí* as deputies.
The two Wūtúlí were each led by three Bātúlǔ imperial guards who would ride,
forming a continuous circle,
from far to near.
There were two types of enclosure systems:
riding into the mountains and forests,
encircling but not closing, was called 'Xíngwéi',
which in the national language is 'Ādámì'.
For a closed enclosure,
before the fifth watch (about 3-5 AM), the minister in charge of the hunt would lead the various officers and soldiers on the hunt to inspect the size and distance of the mountains and rivers,
detour outside the hunting ground,
sometimes thirty or fifty *lǐ*,
sometimes seventy or eighty *lǐ*,
all arriving at the "viewing city."
This was the closed enclosure,
which in the national language is 'Wūtúlí Āchàmì'.
The "viewing city"
was the yellow curtain city.
Once the enclosure was closed,
the imperial huntsmen at the Wūtúlí would remove their hats, holding them up with their whips,
and loudly shout
"Mǎ'ěrgá,"
which in Mongolian means "hat."
This sound would be relayed to the central army
three times in total.
When the central army knew the enclosure was closed,
it would slowly advance with its banners.
Before sunrise,
the Emperor would ride from the mobile imperial camp to the viewing city to rest briefly,
awaiting the arrival of the blue banners.
Then the imperial carriage would emerge,
the Emperor would put on his bow case and quiver,
and enter the central army to survey the situation within the enclosure.
All advances and halts, fast or slow,
were commanded by verbal edicts and gestures.
When a beast broke through the enclosure,
arrows were fired to kill it.
The Grand Ministers and imperial guards would shoot those that escaped outside the enclosure,
and the accompanying officials would pursue and shoot.
If fierce beasts were encountered,
the tiger-spear officers and soldiers would follow.
If there were too many beasts within the ground,
one side would be opened to let them escape,
and those outside the enclosure were still forbidden from chasing and shooting.
After the beasts were captured,
they were sorted by type and presented.
When the imperial carriage returned to the temporary palace,
this was called "dispersing the enclosure."
The captured game was distributed to the escorts,
and the grand autumn hunt ceremony was concluded,
with feasts and rewards varying by rank.
Deer calling:
When deer begin to call,
it is usually after Báilù,
and by imitating their call,
they can be lured close.
This method differed from daily practice.
The imperial guards and others would divide into three teams,
marching about ten *lǐ* out from the camp,
and would await the imperial decree to stop the third team.
After another four or five *lǐ*,
the second team would stop.
After another two or three *lǐ*,
nearing the deer-calling spot, the first team would stop.
At this time, there were only about ten horsemen among the accompanying officials.
The Emperor would order deer to be shot;
the whole group would crane their necks awaiting the imperial decree,
and the three teams would then arrive before the Emperor in succession.
When Gāozōng hunted at Mùlán,
he personally rode a famous steed,
commanding the imperial guards to lead him deep into the mountains.
Upon seeing a herd of deer,
he ordered an imperial guard to hold up a fake deer head and make a "yōuyōu" sound,
luring a doe close,
then quickly shot it with an arrow,
and drank its blood.
This not only strengthened him
but also accustomed him to hardship.
During the Jiāqìng reign, the autumn hunt followed this example.
Responding to a Solar Eclipse: In the first year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that
in the event of a solar eclipse,
all civil and military officials in the capital would go to the Ministry of Rites to perform the rescue ritual.
In the fourteenth year of Kāngxī,
this was changed so that the Qīn Tiān Jiān would calculate the exact time in minutes and seconds,
the Ministry of Rites would verify it,
and then inform the various provincial officials.
Its ritual:
whenever there is a solar eclipse,
the Commandants and Vice-Commandants of the Eight Banners Manchu, Mongolian, and Han Armies lead their subordinates to be on alert in their respective departments,
and perform the rescue ritual.
The Shùntiān Fǔ then instructs its officials to go to the ministries to clean the halls and offices.
Inside and outside, incense altars are set up.
On the open platform, censers and candlesticks are arranged.
Behind them, seating mats are spread for the hundred officials to prostrate.
Officials of the Luání Wèi arrange golden drums and bells on both sides of the ceremonial gate.
The Shǐ of the Yuèbùshu offers a drum and waits below the platform,
all facing the sun.
Officials of the Qīntiān Jiān report the initial obscuration of the sun.
The Míngzàn chants,
“Qíbān!” (All ranks!)
The hundred officials wear plain clothes,
divided into five rows,
with one head official from the Lǐbù leading each row.
The Míngzàn chants,
“Jìn!” (Advance!)
The Míngzàn chants,
“Guì! (Kneel!)
Kòu! (Prostrate!)
Xīng!” (Rise!)
Music plays,
and all perform three genuflections and nine kowtows,
then rise.
The head of the ranks goes before the altar and offers three sticks of incense,
then returns to position.
The Míngzàn chants,
“Guì!” (Kneel!)
and all kneel.
The Míngzàn chants,
“Fágǔ!” (Beat the drums!)
The Shǔshǐ offers the drum and advances,
kneeling on the left side.
The head of the ranks strikes the drum three times.
Golden drums and bells ring simultaneously.
They take turns offering incense,
kneeling reverently and waiting for the sun to become whole again.
When the drums stop,
the hundred officials change into auspicious clothes,
and perform the ritual as before.
When finished,
all withdraw.
On this day, two officials from the Cíji Sì of the Lǐbù and two Doctors from the Qīntiān Jiān
go to the Guānxiàng Tái to conduct observations.
An incense altar is set up facing the sun.
From the initial obscuration to the full recovery,
the ritual is performed as prescribed.
For a lunar eclipse,
the rescue ritual is performed at the Zhōngjūn Dūdū Fǔ,
later changed to Tàicháng Sì,
following the solar eclipse ritual.
In the provinces, during solar and lunar eclipses,
each region performs the rescue ritual according to the estimated time and duration calculated by the Qīntiān Jiān.
It is performed at the offices of the Governors-General and Governors in provincial capitals,
and at the various public offices in prefectures, departments, sub-prefectures, and counties.
Teaching officials supervise the ceremony,
student scholars act as guides,
and Yin-Yang officials report the time.
As for leading the ranks in performing the ritual,
one Governor-General or Governor and one chief official take charge.
The offering of incense, beating of drums, and reverent kneeling
are the same as in the rescue ritual in the capital.

Records Volume 66: Rites 10 (Guest Rites) General Rites for Tributary States; Rites for Tributary Missions from Mountain, Sea, and Other States; Rites for Enfeoffing Tributary States by Imperial Edict; Rites for Foreign Envoys to Have an Audience; Rites for Meetings between Imperial Princes and Princes of the Inner and Outer Domains; Rites for Meetings between Capital Officials; Rites for Meetings between Provincial Officials; Rites for Meetings between Scholars and Commoners
The fourth category is Guest Rites.
In the early Qīng dynasty, there were two categories of tributary states,
divided under the Lǐfān Yuàn and the Zhǔkè Sī.
Those under the Lǐfān Yuàn were
the Khalkha Mongols,
Tibet, Qīnghǎi, and Gurkha;
those under the Zhǔkè Sī were
Cháoxiǎn (Korea),
Yuènán (Vietnam),
Nánzhǎng (Lan Xang),
Miǎndiàn (Burma),
Sūlù (Sulu),
Hélán (Holland),
Xiāmluó (Siam),
and Liúqiú (Ryukyu).
Although there was a slight distinction in closeness,
in terms of rites, all were considered vassals.
Western nations
were initially also considered part of the tributary system.
However, from the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns onwards,
European influence (wind) and Asian influence (rain)
became increasingly pressing.
When envoys came and went,
treaties were concluded on equal terms,
and in terms of rites, they became rivals.
Indeed, the Book of Odes mentions
“there are guests,”
and historical records speak of
“relations with neighbors.”
Regardless of whether they are vassal states or allied states,
ultimately,
those who come are all guests.
We are the hosts,
and all matters to be handled
are guest rites.
This compilation details their rituals and procedures,
and the Rites for Meetings between Imperial Princes and Princes and Hundred Officials, and the Rites for Meetings between Scholars and Commoners
are also appended.
General Rites for Tributary States: In the early Qīng dynasty,
the three Khalkha Khans of Northern Mongolia simultaneously offered tribute.
When the northern desert was pacified,
the policy of appeasement gradually extended afar.
North of the Hánhǎi,
west of the Qiānghuāng,
the Öölöt of Qīnghǎi,
and the Dzungar of Tibet
were all incorporated into the empire's territory.
Holland also received an imperial edict, was recognized as a king,
and listed among the tributary states.
Thereafter, the number of arrivals increased.
They were ordered to guard their borders, perform their duties, and offer tribute.
The Lǐfān Yuàn was established to govern them.
During the Chóngdé reign,
regulations were established:
If Bèilè and others from the outer Mongol tribes had great merits,
they would be enfeoffed as Hèshuò Qīnwáng,
or Duōluó Jùnwáng,
or secondly, Duōluó Bèilè.
An envoy would be sent with an imperial letter to perform the enfeoffment.
Upon entering the territory,
the Bèilè would come out five *lǐ* to greet him,
kneeling to await the imperial charter's passage,
then follow on horseback.
Upon arrival at the manor,
an incense altar was set up in the center.
The envoy would place the charter upon it,
then stand to the left.
The Bèilè would perform one kowtow and three genuflections.
After completing,
he would rise,
then kneel again.
The envoy would present the charter.
After the announcing official read it,
it was placed back on the original altar.
The Bèilè performed three kowtows,
then rose.
Receiving the charter was like the initial rite.
The Bèilè and the envoy would perform six kowtows facing each other.
The envoy would sit on the left,
the Bèilè on the right.
When the matter was concluded,
the Bèilè would personally see him off as before.
Whenever imperial edicts, rewards, or gifts arrived, the same procedure was followed.
When inner and outer Zāsàkè held a league meeting,
it occurred once every three years.
An envoy carried the imperial decree, and the welcoming and sending-off rites were the same.
From kings downwards,
those who offered annual tribute
were divided into rotating annual shifts,
and performed rites at the end of the ranks.
Their seating position was one rank lower than inner Qīnwáng, Bèilè, Bèizi, and Gōng,
and there were differences in banquets and rewards.
In the 59th year of Kāngxī,
annual regulations for audiences were established.
The twenty-four Mongolian tribes were divided into two shifts,
and the Khalkha Zāsàkè and others into four shifts.
In the 4th year of Yōngzhèng,
the Emperor, mindful of the distant toil of the kings and Tàijí of the forty-nine banners,
decreed a change to three shifts,
with an audience every two years.
In the 8th year of Xiánfēng,
due to the long journey and burden of the Mongolian Khans and others,
an edict ordered the suspension of annual shifts.
Those who served before the Emperor
continued their rotating duties as before.
As for the ceremonial procedures for tribute,
each banner sent one person quarterly to manage the affairs,
and annually presented horses, sheep, and wine as tribute.
These were submitted to the Lǐbù via the Lǐfān Yuàn.
The Zhōuyuǎn Qīnglìsī was in charge
of all regulations concerning tribute and rewards.
Regulations for Tribute from Mountain and Sea Nations All nations, at the appointed time, shall offer tribute.
They shall dispatch attendant ministers to court.
Their reception, banquets, and賜 (cì) [gifts]
shall be managed by the Lǐbù.
Upon approaching the border,
the local senior officials shall issue postal tallies (yóufú)
and select several civil and military officers to escort them.
The responsible authorities shall provide lodging and provisions
and dispatch soldiers to guard them.
Along the route, escorts shall be changed
until they reach the Jīngjī.
Upon arrival,
they shall be led into the guest hostel.
At the appointed time, their numbers shall be verified,
and their food and drink shall be distributed evenly.
The next day,
they shall prepare a memorial (biǎowén) and local products (fāngwù),
and the attendant officials, each dressed in their respective attire,
shall proceed to the Lǐbù and wait below the steps.
Officials from the Yízhìsī shall set up a memorial table in the hall.
At dawn,
the Qīng (qīng) of the Huìtóngsìyìguǎn shall lead the tribute envoys to the Lǐbù.
One Shìláng shall stand to the left of the table,
and two Yízhìsī officials shall stand separately to the left and right pillars.
The Guǎnqīng shall ascend first
and stand west of the left pillar.
Two Tōngshì and two Xùbān, respectively,
shall lead the tribute envoys to ascend the steps and kneel.
The principal envoy shall present the memorial,
which the Guǎnqīng shall respectfully receive
and hand to the Shìláng,
who shall place it on the table
and return to his position.
The envoys shall perform the three kneeling and nine kowtowing salutations
and rise.
They shall withdraw,
led out by the Guǎnqīng.
Lǐbù officials shall send the memorial to the Nèigé to await instructions,
and the tribute items shall be handed over to the responsible authorities.
If it coincides with a grand court audience or a regular court audience,
the Xùbān shall lead the tribute envoys to line up at the end of the west rank,
awaiting the announcement to perform the rites as customary.
If it is not a court audience day, the Lǐbù shall first report.
If an audience is granted,
the Guǎnqīng shall instruct them in advance on the protocol.
On the appointed day, the Emperor shall ascend the hall.
The Lǐbù Shàngshū shall lead the tribute envoys in,
with the Tōngshì following.
Upon reaching the Dānchí, after performing the rites,
they shall ascend from the west steps,
with the Tōngshì again following them.
They shall kneel outside the palace gate.
The Emperor shall offer condolences and inquire,
the Shàngshū shall transmit the message,
and the Tōngshì shall relay it.
The tribute envoys shall offer their replies,
the Tōngshì shall translate,
and the Shàngshū shall present it on their behalf.
When finished,
they shall withdraw.
If exceptional favor is shown,
then after performing the rites at the Dānchí,
they shall be led into the right gate of the hall
and stand at the end of the right wing of ministers,
with the Tōngshì standing slightly behind.
They shall be granted seats and tea,
and shall kowtow and kneel along with the ministers.
After drinking,
the condolences and inquiries shall be transmitted and answered as before.
Upon leaving the court,
they shall be given imperial food and drink,
and then withdraw.
The next day, they shall proceed to the Wǔmén to express gratitude.
The Lǐbù shall memorialize requesting the bestowal of gifts upon the king and the granting of banquets to the tribute envoys.
Once the imperial decree is received,
the responsible authorities shall display the bestowed items to the left of the Wǔmén road.
The Guǎnqīng shall lead the tribute envoys to stand facing east,
the Shìláng shall stand facing west,
and all responsible officials shall be in their ranks.
The tribute envoys shall proceed to the west steps, perform three kneelings and nine kowtows.
Officials from the Zhǔkèsī shall present the bestowed items to the tribute envoys,
who shall receive them kneeling.
In order, gifts shall be bestowed upon the tribute envoys and their attendant officials and retinue,
all receiving them kneeling.
The proclaimer shall call out
"Rise,
Kowtow"
as customary.
They shall withdraw,
and be granted a banquet by the Lǐbù.
When the tribute envoys are about to return to their country,
the Guānglùsì shall prepare sacrificial animals, wine, fruits, and vegetables.
The Shìláng shall host a banquet at the guest hostel,
and the escort and provisions shall be arranged as before.
All provincial capitals passed through shall feast them,
with one official from the Sīdào overseeing the matter.
Lodging and provisions shall be provided daily,
generally with abundant generosity.
In the early Shùnzhì reign,
regulations were established:
for tributary missions from various nations,
bearing memorials and local products,
the limit was three ships,
with one hundred people per ship,
and twenty tribute attendants.
In the thirteenth year (1656),
Tsagan Khan of Russia dispatched an envoy to offer tribute.
As he was unfamiliar with court etiquette,
his tribute was rejected,
and he was sent back.
The next year, he again presented a memorial and tribute,
the journey taking three years.
The memorial still did not conform to the proper format.
Shìzǔ, considering that foreign nations were adapting to civilization,
deemed it appropriate to be accommodating,
to grant some imperial favor,
and issued a decree ordering him not to have an audience.
In the thirty-second year of Kāngxī (1693),
Russia again dispatched an envoy, Izbrandt Ides, to court.
The Emperor first granted him an audience,
bestowed a seat and food.
In the fifty-ninth year (1720),
the Portuguese envoy, Filippo de Ferrari, had an audience.
The Emperor was in the Jiǔjīng Sānshì Diàn.
The envoy entered the left gate of the hall,
ascended the left steps,
and advanced to the imperial seat kneeling to present the memorial.
The Emperor received the memorial,
the envoy rose,
and exited.
All entrances and exits involved three kneelings and nine kowtows.
He was granted a seat and tea,
and expressed gratitude as customary.
Initially,
when envoys from Liúqiú, Ānnán, and Xiāmluó came,
all council ministers would assemble,
and they would be granted seats and tea.
In the first year of Qiánlóng (1736),
an edict ordered this to cease.
At that time, the number of attendant ministers from vassal states increased,
so the responsible authorities were ordered to distribute the Huángqīng Zhígòngtú [Illustrations of Tribute-Bearers of the Imperial Qing]
to instruct those who would come from afar.
In the first month of the forty-seventh year (1782),
a banquet was held at Zǐguānggé,
attended by attendant ministers from Cháoxiǎn, Liúqiú, and Nánzhǎng.
After the banquet,
precious items were bestowed.
In the fiftieth year (1785),
a Banquet for a Thousand Elders (Qiānsǒu Yàn) was held.
It was specifically ordered that Cháoxiǎn attendant ministers celebrating the New Year (Hèzhèng) who were over sixty years old should be appointed as principal and deputy envoys,
attend the banquet, and compose poems.
Five years later (1790),
King Nguyễn Quang Bình of Ānnán came to the capital to offer birthday felicitations.
His ceremonial rank was set,
placing him between the Qīnwáng and Jùnwáng,
while his attendant ministers remained at the end of the ranks.
In the fifty-eighth year (1793),
England offered tribute.
Envoy George Macartney and others had an audience.
He stated that he was not accustomed to kneeling and kowtowing,
but when he reached the imperial presence,
he knelt and prostrated himself naturally.
In the first year of Jiāqìng (1796),
another Qiānsǒu Yàn was held,
attended by Cháoxiǎn, Ānnán, Xiāmluó, and Gyalpo Druk Tashi Dorje of Gorkha, who offered nine kowtows,
"kneeling before the Great Emperor: Your humble servant has heard that the rebel bandits in Húnán were causing trouble,
leading to the Emperor's mighty wrath,
and troops were dispatched to suppress them.
Now they have been pacified; hearing this brings joy and comfort.
Your humble servant has received profound imperial grace,
and respectfully presents humble local products
and a memorial,
kowtowing to congratulate the imperial joy.
Your humble servant has always been favored by imperial grace,
regarded as a child of the people,
with only one heart to submit
and live harmoniously with neighboring states.
Your humble servant Yángbù is far from the capital,
and is still young.
I humbly beg to be treated as a servant,
to be kindly instructed and guided,
so that the grace I receive may not be shallow."
and so forth.
His tribute items totaled twelve,
with such simple words and respectful intention.
In the twenty-first year (1816),
England again dispatched an envoy to offer tribute.
Officials informed him that he must perform the kneeling and kowtowing rites,
whereupon Lord William Amherst and others claimed illness and did not have an audience.
The Emperor was enraged,
decreed that he be sent back to his country,
and canceled the banquet and bestowal of gifts.
Thereafter,
British envoys no longer came to court.
In the ninth year of Dàoguāng (1829),
after the pacification of Huíjiāng,
an honorable title was bestowed upon the Empress Dowager.
The King of Miǎndiàn dispatched an envoy to present a golden leaf memorial,
an unprecedented act.
Traditionally,
Liúqiú (Ryukyu) presented tribute once every two years.
In the 19th year of the reign,
an imperial edict changed the frequency to once every four years.
At that time, King Shàng Yù (Shō Iku) consulted with the Fújiàn (Fujian) governor, Wú Wénróng (Wu Wenrong),
stating that Liúqiú (Ryukyu) was near the sea
and often suffered from strong winds.
When tribute was offered in a timely manner,
winds and rains were harmonious and smooth,
and the harvest was abundant that year.
Tribute ships entering and exiting Fújiàn (Fujian) territory
were given the annual seasonal calendar (shí xiàn shū),
allowing them to act according to the seasons.
The land did not produce medicines,
relying on ships to bring them back for use.
Furthermore, the art of maritime navigation (zhēn fǎ)
could not be mastered without constant practice.
If the frequency were changed to once every four years,
it was feared that harvests would be uneven,
people would not be taught the seasonal work,
medicines would be lacking,
and knowledge of the compass (zhēn pán) would become rusty.
He requested a return to the old system for convenience.
The request was granted.
It was also ordered that the children of accompanying officials could follow the tribute envoys to study in the imperial academy.
In the 34th year of Guāngxù (Guangxu),
Guō'ěrkā (Gorkha) presented tribute.
The chief envoy Gájī (Gajee) was awarded a second-rank robe,
and the deputy envoy a fourth-rank robe.
When they performed their duties,
their attire would follow their respective ranks,
which was unprecedented.
Regarding tribute frequency,
Cháoxiǎn (Joseon) came annually,
Liúqiú (Ryukyu) once every two years,
Ānnán (Annam) twice every six years,
Xiāmluó (Siam) every three years,
Hélán (Holland) and Sūlù (Sulu) every five years,
Nánzhǎng (Nanjiang) every ten years,
each coming once.
Other distant places had no fixed tribute schedule.
Regarding tribute items,
each presented its native products;
non-native products were not to be offered.
Cháoxiǎn (Joseon), Ānnán (Annam), Liúqiú (Ryukyu), Miǎndiàn (Myanmar), Sūlù (Sulu), and Nánzhǎng (Nanjiang) all had regular items,
while others presented whatever they wished.
Rituals for Imperial Investiture of Vassal States: The Qīng (Qing) dynasty, since Tàizōng (Taizong)'s conquest of Cháoxiǎn (Joseon),
carved a stone tablet at Sāntiándù (Samjeondo).
Thereafter, Ānnán (Annam), Liúqiú (Ryukyu), and other countries
successively requested investiture,
and envoys were sent to all of them.
For others who turned towards the empire,
undeterred by distant seas or
arduous mountain paths,
imperial letters of commendation were issued,
given to their envoys to carry back, and that was all.
During the Chóngdé (Chongde) reign,
regulations were established:
All foreign states demonstrating allegiance
would be granted imperial edicts and noble titles.
Memorials and letters submitted
were to be signed with the Qīng (Qing) dynastic year.
If a tributary state had no heir to succeed to the throne,
it would send an accompanying official to request an imperial mandate.
The Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) would memorialize for the dispatch of one chief and one deputy envoy, each carrying a credential (jié), to confer investiture.
They would be specially granted a first-rank Qílín (Kylin) robe to honor their mission.
On the day of their departure,
the Gōngbù (Ministry of Works) would provide banners and entourages,
and the Bīngbù (Ministry of War) would provide carriages.
The investiture envoys would proceed to the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites).
One official from the Yízhìsī (Department of Rituals and Ceremonies) would hold the credential,
and another would hold the imperial edict and decree.
They would hand these to the chief officials of the department,
who would then present them to the chief and deputy envoys,
who would receive them kneeling.
They would rise,
change into traveling attire, and depart by carriage.
Upon approaching the border,
the country's border officials would prepare lodgings, transport, and horses.
Along the route,
local officials would kneel in welcome.
Upon arriving in the capital,
the succeeding king would send accompanying officials to welcome them in the suburbs,
performing three genuflections and nine kowtows.
The envoys would be saluted with one genuflection and three kowtows.
They would be invited into the residence,
where the imperial edict, credential, and dragon pavilion would be displayed.
The rituals would be performed as prescribed.
The king would pay respects to the envoys with three kowtows,
but they would not respond.
A day would be chosen,
and the king, leading his accompanying officials, would proceed to the residence.
After the ceremony,
the king would return first.
The envoys would dismount at the steps.
The chief envoy would hold the credential,
and the deputy envoy would hold the imperial edict and decree.
They would enter the palace and place them on a table,
then retreat and stand on the east side.
The king, leading all officials, would stand facing north,
perform three genuflections and nine kowtows.
They would rise
and proceed to kneel before the investiture position.
The deputy envoy would hand the imperial rescript to the official designated to read it aloud.
After reading,
the king would perform the ritual as before,
then exit and wait outside the gate.
When the envoys exited,
the king would kneel to see them off.
After a short while,
the king would go to their residence to offer congratulations.
When the envoys returned to the imperial court,
the king would then draft a memorial (biǎo wén),
prepare local products,
and send an accompanying official to the imperial court to express gratitude.
If an imperial funeral rite (yù jì) was combined with investiture,
the funeral rite would first be conducted at the ancestral temple.
The imperial funeral eulogy (yù jì wén) would be displayed on a table,
with the envoys standing on either side.
The crown prince would kneel and kowtow as before,
then retreat and stand to the left of the spirit tablet.
The eulogy would then be read aloud,
and all would bow low.
After reading,
they would rise.
The ritual of sending off the burnt offerings would be performed,
and the envoys would withdraw.
Next, the investiture ceremony would be held,
with rituals identical to the preceding ones.
When the imperial edict and decree were handed to the envoy to bring back,
the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites) would set up a table at the Wǔmén (Meridian Gate),
positioned centrally,
with the Shàngshū (Minister) standing to the left of the table.
Officials from the Yízhìsī (Department of Rituals and Ceremonies) would lead the envoy from the residence,
hand over the imperial edict and decree.
The rank-setter (xù bān) would guide him to kneel before the table,
and the giving and receiving would follow the prescribed rules.
He would then retreat to the west of the imperial courtyard (dān chí),
perform three genuflections and nine kowtows.
With the ceremony complete,
he would return to present them to the king.
The expression of gratitude was similar.
Ritual for Foreign Public Ministers' Audience: In the early Kāngxī (Kangxi) reign,
overseas foreigners began to present tribute.
The central court received them
with slightly different courtesies than for vassal states.
Nán Huáirén (Ferdinand Verbiest), an official of the Qīntiānjiān (Imperial Astronomical Bureau), was granted the title of Gōngbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Ministry of Works).
When summoned to an imperial audience,
he was permitted to stand by,
not performing the kneeling and kowtowing rituals.
During the Yōngzhèng (Yongzheng) reign,
the Roman Pope sent an envoy to the capital.
Shìzōng (Yongzheng Emperor) permitted him to follow Western rites,
and even shook his hand.
In the late Qiánlóng (Qianlong) period,
the British envoy Mǎgélǐ (George Macartney) was granted an audience.
The ritual officials discussed the ceremony with him.
He spoke of the protocol for an audience with the British King,
and a special imperial decree permitted the use of Western rites.
On the day of the banquet,
the emperor personally bestowed a goblet of wine.
Once commercial treaties were established,
diplomatic missions became frequent.
During the Xiánfēng (Xianfeng) and Tóngzhì (Tongzhi) reigns,
foreign envoys often sought an audience.
At that time, due to differing ritual systems,
such requests were strongly rejected.
In the Tóngzhì (Tongzhi) period,
British and French envoys earnestly requested audiences repeatedly,
but we still insisted on Chinese protocols,
not responding to them.
They even said,
"It is appropriate to quickly cultivate good relations.
Obstructing their audience
is to be stingy with guest etiquette."
In the twelfth year,
Mùzōng assumed personal rule.
Envoys from the Great West (Europe) jointly requested an audience,
presenting their credentials.
They first stated they would use Western etiquette,
bowing three times at the waist.
Court officials strongly argued against its inconvenience.
The Zhílì Governor-General Lǐ Hóngzhāng suggested,
briefly stating:
"When previous emperors summoned Western envoys,
the various nations had not yet established treaties,
and the envoys were not yet stationed in the capital.
Although the national power was strong,
it did not compare to today.
Yet, they could still be governed by the regular ceremony of ascending the hall to receive memorials.
However, during the Jiāqìng reign,
when the British envoy came to court,
the three kneelings and nine kowtows were already not performed.
Subsequently, treaties were concluded,
and they were treated as formidable equals.
It was not appropriate to bind them with the禮 (lǐ) due to subordinates.
To refuse to meet them
seems not to align with sentiment.
To insist on kneeling and bowing
seems to show a lack of broad perspective.
We should simply take their reverence as sufficient,
and pardon their insufficient禮 (lǐ).
It is only proper to discuss and establish regulations,
to be mutually observed.
When the various envoys come,
allow one audience,
but no second audience.
Allow them to be seen together at one time,
but not to request individual audiences.
This should deter their covetousness.
Furthermore,禮 (lǐ) changes with the times.
Our dynasty has established customs for treating tributary states,
but no fixed禮 (lǐ) for treating friendly nations.
The recent commercial treaties
are truly a change unseen for several millennia.
The nation has no precedent for such禮 (lǐ),
nor did the ancient sages foresee and establish such禮經 (lǐjīng).
It is up to us to weigh the current situation and adapt expediently to establish the standard."
At that time, Gōng Qīnwáng, who was in charge of the Zǒnglǐ Gèguó Shìwù Yámén, repeatedly argued over the kneeling and bowing rituals,
but the envoys remained firm as before.
It was difficult to ultimately thwart their wishes,
so a memorial was presented,
and an imperial edict explicitly granted permission.
In the summer of that year,

the Japanese envoy Fùdǎo Zhǒngchén, the Russian envoy Wōliángmǎlǐ, the American envoy Lóu Fěidí, the British envoy Wēi Tuǒmǎ, the French envoy Rè Fúlǐ, and the Dutch envoy Fèi Guǒsūn had an audience at the Zǐguāng Gé,
presenting their credentials,
acting according to the agreed-upon regulations.
During the reception,
the Emperor sat or stood as he pleased,
bestowing tea and wine,
grace emanating from above.
The envoys inquired about his well-being,
and respectfully offered congratulatory remarks.
They were not to speak of matters
before being asked.
Western etiquette dictates that a subject bows three times when seeing the monarch;
this was now changed to five bows.
Envoys were granted an initial audience upon arrival,
but no further ones.
Subsequent bearers of credentials were to follow this precedent.
The禮式 (lǐshì) was diagrammed and rehearsed in advance,
the location of the audience,
and the specific month, day, and time,
were all to await imperial instructions.
This was the general outline.
In the sixteenth year of Guāngxù,
the envoy to Britain, Xuē Fúchéng, submitted a memorial stating:
"For audiences with various envoys,
clear regulations must be established.
Whenever an envoy first arrives in a country,
its sovereign invariably grants an audience and offers words of comfort.
After the envoy has paid respects,
he bows and withdraws,
without discussing public matters.
This is a universal custom.
Recently, I heard that the ministers resident in the capital,
because they have not been received during the day,
have not been without private discussions.
In past years, the British envoy Wēi Tuǒmǎ used pretexts to avoid being admitted for an audience,
leading to many demands in the Yāntái Treaty,
clinging to empty formalities while suffering actual losses,
which was not a wise strategy.
Now, we should follow the precedent set in the twelfth year of Tóngzhì,
and act accordingly.
Regarding禮節 (lǐjié),
an imperial edict can be issued to the relevant department before the audience,
allowing for flexibility in both Chinese and Western禮 (lǐ).
This grants them discretion.
In this way,
even if they perform Western禮 (lǐ),
it will not damage our institutional integrity."
And so on.
From then on, this became a standing rule.
In the twenty-seventh year,
when the allied forces suppressed the Boxer Rebellion,
the various nations demanded changes to the rituals.
They stipulated that all envoys meeting together
must do so in the Tàihé Diàn.
An envoy from a single nation requesting an individual audience
must do so in the Qiánqīng Gōng.
When presenting credentials,
an imperial sedan chair must be dispatched to receive them,
the envoy dismounting before the palace gate,
and being escorted back after the ceremony.
When bringing credentials and memorials,
they must enter through the central gate,
and the Emperor must personally receive them.
If a banquet is set in the Qiánqīng Gōng,
the Emperor must personally take his seat.
Later, it was further granted that joint audiences could be changed to the Qiánqīng Gōng,
and the sedan chairs used would be yellow.
Thereupon, Qìng Qīnwáng Yìkuāng and others, considering the distinction of 'heaven and earth, superiority and inferiority,'
could not comply with every single demand.
So, they negotiated with the various envoys,
which lasted several months,
before the three matters of riding yellow sedan chairs, audiences in the Tàihé Diàn, and dismounting before the palace steps were deliberated and modified,
and the dispute finally ceased.
The ceremony for foreign princes having an audience
began in the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù.
When German Prince Heinrich (Hēnglì) had an audience,
the Emperor proceeded to the Yíhé Yuán,
and was enthroned in the Rénshòu Diàn.
Prince Heinrich entered in formal attire,
presented his credentials,
and the Emperor offered words of comfort.
Afterward,
Heinrich wished to have an audience with the Empress Dowager,
and the Emperor, acting on her imperial decree, met him on her behalf.
On that day, at the hour of sì (9-11 a.m.),
the Emperor was in the Yùlán Táng.
Heinrich, accompanied by the German envoy Hǎi Jìng and others, entered.
Officials from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs led them to rest briefly in a tent outside the east side gate of the hall.
When the imperial carriage arrived,
the retinue followed the usual procedure,
cracked the whip three times,
and the Emperor ascended the throne.
Qìng Qīnwáng and others attended on either side.
The high official of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs led Heinrich and the others in through the central gate,
bowed once facing north,
walked a few steps and bowed again,
and bowed once more before the dragon pillars.
Then, they presented the credentials,
and Qìng Qīnwáng descended the left steps to receive them,
placing them on a jade table.
Heinrich and the others bowed again,
the Emperor nodded in response,
and offered words of comfort in the national language.
Qìng Qīnwáng knelt to the left of the table to hear the imperial words,
then descended the steps,
and translated the pronouncements into Chinese.
After the German translator finished translating,
Heinrich and the others bowed again,
and the Emperor again nodded in response.
Heinrich and the others retreated a few steps and bowed again,
retreated to the left of the hall,
and bowed once more.
The ceremony was complete.
Ceremonies for the mutual greeting of inner and outer princes. In the first year of Chóngdé,
the ritual for the mutual greeting of imperial clan (Zōngshì) and outer vassal (Wàifān) Qīnwáng, Jùnwáng, Bèilè, and Bèizi was established.
When the guest reaches the gate,
officials of the prince's mansion report,
the host descends the steps to greet,
the guest declines,
the host ascends.
The guest and his retinue enter through the central gate,
the guest goes to the left,
the host goes to the right.
They perform the mutual greeting ceremony:
two kneelings and six kowtows,
then stand in order of precedence.
Attending officials ascend the east steps,
performing the ceremony likewise.
They rise,
enter the right gate,
and sit behind the guest.
Serving attendants offer tea,
the guest receives tea,
kowtows,
the host returns the kowtow.
After drinking tea and conversing,
attending officials approach the front pillars,
kneel,
kowtow,
rise,
and exit.
The guest leaves his seat, kneels and kowtows,
the host returns the kowtow,
and both rise.
When the guest departs,
the host descends the steps to see him off,
and the officials see him to outside the gate.
If an Outer Vassal Junwáng is seen,
the host welcomes and sees him off outside the main hall,
without descending the steps.
Upon meeting,
the guest performs two kowtows and six bows,
and the host responds with half of that.
When the guest takes leave,
he performs a kowtow,
and the host responds with a kowtow but no bow.
The rest follows the ceremony for a Qīnwáng.
If an Outer Vassal Beìlè is seen,
the host leaves his seat to welcome him,
but does not exit the hall.
The guest faces north and performs kowtows as before,
and the host receives him standing.
The host then sits properly at his seat,
and the guest sits attendantly.
Upon taking leave, the guest performs a kowtow,
and the host receives him standing but does not see him off.
The rest follows the ceremony for a Junwáng.
If an Outer Vassal Beìzǐ or Gōng is seen,
a subordinate official of the host's residence leads the guest into the hall,
and the kowtows are the same.
Upon taking leave, they still perform kowtows,
and the host receives them while seated.
The rest follows the ceremony for a Beìlè.
If an Outer Vassal Qīnwáng sees a Junwáng,
the host welcomes and sees him off inside the main gate,
and the rest is the same as when a Qīnwáng meets a Qīnwáng.
A Junwáng seeing a Junwáng is also like this.
If an Outer Vassal Beìlè sees a Junwáng,
it is according to the禮 (lǐ) of a Junwáng seeing a Qīnwáng.
From this point downward, when guest and host meet,
the protocol is progressively reduced.
If an Outer Vassal Qīnwáng sees a Beìlè,
the host welcomes and sees him off outside the gate.
The guest enters,
the host follows,
and upon meeting, each performs one kowtow and three bows.
An Outer Vassal Junwáng and Beìlè seeing a Beìlè is the same.
If an Outer Vassal Beìzǐ or Gōng sees a Beìlè,
the guest performs one kowtow and three bows,
and the host receives him kneeling and with clasped hands.
When an Outer Vassal Wáng or Beìlè sees a Beìzǐ,
both guest and host perform one kowtow and one bow and then sit,
this is what is different.
Protocol for Beijing Officials Meeting Each Other: In the first year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that
when Beijing court officials of equal rank meet,
when the guest reaches the gate,
the host welcomes him inside the main gate,
bows and leads the guest in.
Upon reaching the steps,
the host defers for the guest to ascend,
the guest on the west, the host on the east.
Upon reaching the main hall,
the host defers for the guest to enter,
and both face north and perform two prostrations.
Rising,
the host sets the guest in the proper seat facing west.
The guest declines,
but the host insists,
and eventually the guest sits properly.
The guest returns the gesture, setting the host in the proper seat facing east, also like this.
The guest takes his seat,
receives tea,
bows,
and the host returns the bow.
After drinking tea and conversing,
they bow to each other to take leave.
The guest descends the steps,
the host sees him off to the gate,
and they bow to each other again.
The guest declines to be seen off,
but the host insists,
sees the guest off outside the main gate,
watches the guest board his carriage or mount his horse,
and then withdraws.
A Shàngshū or Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ seeing a Dàxuéshì is the same.
If the guest is one rank lower,
the host quickly moves to the proper seat for the guest,
and declining is also like this.
The rest of the ceremony is the same.
Officials of the two- to lower-rank Beijing bureaus, Hànlǐn, Zhǎn, Kē, and Dào seeing a Dàxuéshì:
The host welcomes inside the Yímén and
sees off outside the main gate,
but does not watch them board their carriage or mount their horse.
Kē and Dào officials seeing a Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ, Fù Dū Yùshǐ, or Shàngshū follows the same ceremony.
Officials of the fifth to eighth ranks seeing a Dàxuéshì:
The host welcomes at the foot of the hall steps,
the guest goes to the eastern steps,
and the host leads him in.
The guest faces north and bows,
declines,
and then performs three bows,
while the host faces east and returns the bows.
The guest quickly moves to the proper seat for the host,
declines,
but is firmly invited,
and eventually sits properly and bows to each other.
The guest faces west, and the host faces northeast.
After the guest finishes his business,
he takes leave,
and performs three bows as before.
The host sees him off outside the second gate.
Hànlǐn, Zhǎn, Kē, and Dào officials seeing two- or three-rank officials
follow the protocol for a guest one rank lower.
Seeing four- or five-rank officials,
it is the same as the protocol for officials of equal rank.
Subordinate officials of the Gé, Bù, Sì, and Jiān seeing their superior:
For the first meeting,
they wear court attire and proceed to the office,
ascend from the eastern steps,
present their credentials and sit at the table,
face the superior in order and perform three bows,
and the superior rises from his seat to return the bows.
Then they withdraw.
If it is a casual meeting,
it is like a fifth-rank official seeing a Dàxuéshì.
Protocol for Guóxuéshēng seeing a Guózǐshī:
For the first meeting,
they prepare a name card,
wear court attire and proceed to the academy,
ascend the hall from the eastern steps,
face north and perform three bows,
and the teacher receives them standing.
They stand attendantly on the left side,
face west to receive instruction,
and when finished,
perform three bows and withdraw.
If it is a casual meeting,
they announce their name,
and wait to be summoned before entering.
The teacher welcomes them at the top of the steps,
the disciple ascends,
and bows.
The teacher enters the door,
the disciple follows,
faces north and performs two prostrations,
