and the teacher faces west and returns the bows.
The disciple quickly moves to the teacher's proper seat,
the teacher bids him to sit,
and the disciple bows facing north.
The teacher's seat is on the northeast side,
the disciple's on the west.
When tea arrives,
they bow,
ask questions,
and bow.
To take leave,
they face north and perform three bows,
and the teacher returns them all.
When seeing them out,
the teacher walks ahead,
the disciple follows behind,
and outside the second gate,
the disciple performs three bows,
and only withdraws after the teacher has entered.
Hànlín Yuàn Shùjíshì seeing a Dàxuéshì
is the same as seeing a Jiàoxí Shùjíshì.
In all cases when Beijing court officials meet on the road and must avoid each other:
If their ranks are equal,
they take separate paths.
Next, they yield the way.
Next, they rein in their horses and wait for the other to pass.
Next, they dismount.
Only an Imperial Envoy, if he encounters someone who should avoid him,
may simply take a separate path.
Furthermore, for military officials of the rank of Míngōng, Hóu, Bó, or lower,
but Nán or higher,
and civil officials of the rank of Dàxuéshì or lower,
but Jiǔqīng or higher,
they may use one horse as a lead.
If they meet on the road, they all dismount and avoid each other.
Protocol for Civil and Military Officials of the Provinces Meeting Each Other: During the Shùnzhì era,
it was stipulated that when a Dū, Fǔ, Xuézhèng, Hécáo Zǒngdū,
Yánzhèng,
or Xúnshì Yùshǐ meet,
their seating arrangements are parallel.
All others follow their respective ranks in performing rites.
In the eighth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was stipulated that when officials of the provinces meet,
if their ranks are equal,
when the guest arrives at the office,
the clerk reports,
the gate is opened,
and the guest enters through the central gate,
dismounting from his carriage or horse at the eaves of the outer hall.
The host welcomes him at the front of the eaves,
bows and leads the guest in.
Upon reaching the main hall,
both perform two prostrations.
The proper seating, taking one's place, offering tea, and taking leave
are the same as the ceremony for Beijing court officials.
Subordinate officials seeing their superiors:
They dismount from their palanquins and horses outside the camp gate,
and enter through the left gate.
For a first meeting, they present a name card,
and report for duty.
When civil officials of the circuit (Sīdào) see a governor-general or governor (Dūfǔ),
they are welcomed behind the screen in the hall.
Upon reaching the main hall (Tīngshì),
during the court salutation (Tíngcān), they are granted exemption from prostrating.
They bow three times,
and the Dūfǔ returns each bow.
The Dūfǔ sits in the main seat,
and the Sīdào sits in a side seat.
When ordered to sit,
they bow.
When tea arrives,
they bow.
All bows are returned as before.
When taking leave,
they bow three times as at the beginning.
They are escorted to outside the screen door,
where the Sīdào bows three times.
They wait for the Dūfǔ to enter,
then bow three more times,
and hasten out.
The Dūfǔ returns the visit with a name card the next day.
If it is an audience for official business,
they wear everyday attire and state their full title and name,
bow three times, and take their seats.
The rest is as before.
When prefects (Fǔ), subprefects (Tīng), magistrates (Zhōu), and county magistrates (Xiàn) have an audience,
they are exempted from prostrating during the court salutation.
Fǔ and Tīng bow,
and the bow is returned.
Zhōu and Xiàn bow,
and the bow is received while standing.
They are not escorted,
nor are visits returned.
When assistant officials (Zuǒ'èr) and others have an audience,
they kneel once and kowtow three times,
without bowing or sitting.
When Fǔ, Tīng, Zhōu, and Xiàn see a Sīdào,
it is the same as a Sīdào seeing a Dūfǔ.
When Zuǒ'èr and other officials see a Sīdào,
it is the same as seeing a Dūfǔ.
When assistant prefects (Tóngzhī) and subprefects (Tōngpàn) see a prefect (Zhīfǔ),
their card addresses them as "junior student" (Wǎnshēng),
they enter through the central gate,
and the rites of host and guest are observed.
When Zhōu and Xiàn educational officials (Jiàozhí) see a Dūfǔ,
the ceremony is like that of Zuǒ'èr seeing a Sīdào,
without welcoming or escorting.
When seeing a Zhīfǔ,
they are welcomed and escorted outside the screen door.
When seeing an assistant prefect (Fǔcuì),
they are welcomed and escorted under the eaves of the hall.
The rest is the same.
When seeing a Zhōu or Xiàn,
the ceremony is the same as Tóngzhī and Tōngpàn seeing a Zhīfǔ.
When Sīdào, Fǔ, and Tīng see an education commissioner (Xuézhèng),
they enter through the central gate,
the rites are those of host and guest,
and the welcoming and escorting extend to outside the hall eaves.
If the Xuézhèng's rank is high,
the ceremony is like seeing a Dūfǔ.
When Zhōu and Xiàn see them,
they perform the court salutation and sit in a side seat,
and the host returns the bow but not the prostration.
When a salt commissioner (Yùnshǐ) sees a Dūfǔ or a salt censor (Yányuàn),
it is the same as a Sīdào.
From the Yùnshǐ and sub-commissioner (Yùnpàn) downwards, the etiquette gradually decreases.
When military officials below the rank of brigade-general (Fùjiàng) see a provincial commander-in-chief (Tídū),
for a first meeting, they state their title and name and report for duty,
and if they are wearing armor, they are told to be exempted,
and change into official attire with a sword.
Commandants (Dūsī) and garrison commanders (Shǒubèi) are not exempted;
they kneel to announce their names,
sit on the ground,
and are not served tea.
The rest of the ceremony decreases according to rank,
the same as for civil officials.
In the 13th year of Shùnzhì,
regulations for meetings between civil and military officials in the provinces were established.
When a Tídū sees a governor-general (Zǒngdū),
they enter through the central gate,
dismount at the ceremonial gate,
and bow three times upon ascending the hall.
The Zǒngdū sits in the main seat,
and the Tídū sits in a side seat.
Welcoming and escorting do not extend beyond the hall eaves.
If the Tídū also holds a hereditary position,
the Zǒngdū faces west,
and the Tídū faces east.
When taking leave,
they are escorted to under the hall eaves,
and seen off to their mounted horse.
When a commander-in-chief (Zǒngbīng) has an audience,
they dismount outside the ceremonial gate,
and if they are to sit, they take a subservient seat.
Welcoming and escorting stop at the top of the steps.
When seeing a governor (Xúnfǔ),
they are treated with the rites of host and guest, but with equal status.
Below this, the etiquette decreases according to rank.
Regarding meetings between Manchu and Han officials,
a general (Jiāngjūn) and deputy lieutenant-general (Fùdūtǒng) meet a Dū, Fǔ, Tí, or Zhèn as equals.
Officials below Sīdào see a Jiāngjūn as they would a Zǒngdū,
and see a Fùdūtǒng as they would a Zǒngbīng.
A brigade commander (Xiélǐng) and a regimental commander (Cānlǐng) see a Dūfǔ like a Sīdào,
a company commander (Zuǒlǐng) and a defender (Fángyù) like a Zhīfǔ,
and a commander of the metropolitan cavalry (Xiāoqíjiao) like a Zhōu or Xiàn.
For those not under a unified command,
the rites of host and guest are always observed.
When students of the Confucian academy (Rúxué Dìzǐyuán) see their teachers (Xuélǎo),
it is the same as students of the Imperial Academy (Guózǐshēng) seeing teachers of the Imperial Academy (Guóxué Shī).
Rites for meetings between gentry and commoners: When a guest reaches the gate,
an attendant announces the name,
the host comes out to welcome them outside the main gate,
and bows them in.
Upon reaching the inner gate and the steps, they bow again as at first.
Upon ascending the hall,
both face north and bow twice.
Rising,
the host and guest mutually take their main seats.
At the table,
the guest is to the east and the host to the west.
They drink tea,
and when conversation is finished,
the guest withdraws,
bowing.
Upon reaching the steps and the inner gate,
they bow,
and take leave.
The host returns all bows.
They are escorted to outside the main gate,
bowing as at first.
Rites for juniors seeing elders: Upon reaching the gate, they announce their name,
wait outside,
and are summoned by the elder to enter for the audience.
They ascend the steps,
face north and bow twice,
and the elder faces west and returns the bow.
When ordered to sit,
they take a subservient seat according to the elder's seating position.
When tea arrives,
they bow.
When conversation is finished,
they report their departure,
and bow three times.
All bows are returned;
they are not escorted out.
If an elder comes to visit,
the junior welcomes and escorts them outside the main gate.
The rest is as the previous ceremony.
Seeing a friend of one's father
is the same as seeing an elder.
Rites for students (Shòuyè Dìzǐ) seeing their teachers (Shīzhǎng):
For a first meeting,
before the teacher comes out,
the student enters first,
arranges the mat in the main position,
and waits below the hall.
When the teacher comes out and summons them,
they then offer the gift (Zhì) and enter,
place the gift on the mat,
face north and bow twice,
and the teacher stands and returns the bow.
Rising,
they respectfully inquire about the teacher's well-being.
Only when ordered to sit do they take a subservient seat.
If a question is asked,
they rise to answer.
When taking leave,
they bow three times,
and are not escorted.
For regular meetings, they take a subservient seat.
If they request instruction, they rise.
If they ask for further explanation, they rise.
If the teacher gives instruction,
they stand to listen.
Only when ordered to sit do they sit.
If the teacher asks a question,
they still rise to answer.
Entering in the morning and leaving in the evening, they always bow once.
With fellow students,
they are arranged by age.
Record 67, Rites 11 (Rites of Mourning 1): Imperial Funeral Rites, Empress Funeral Rites, Imperial Consort (Guìfēi) and other Funeral Rites.
Fifth are inauspicious rites.
For the three-year mourning period,
from the Son of Heaven to the common people,
regardless of noble or humble status, it is one and the same.
There are clear filial piety observances that govern and illuminate,
from the funeral rites of empresses and emperors above,
down to the mourning regulations for officials and commoners below,
which are established according to the circumstances and expressions of feeling,
and are detailed in the Huìdiǎn and Tōnglǐ.
Herein they are compiled by category in sequence,
with additions and deletions across successive dynasties,
as clear as a mirror.
Funeral Rites for the Emperor In the tenth year of Tiānmìng,
Tàizǔ passed away.
Officials and commoners, near and far,
wailed and wept as if mourning their own parents.
Five days later,
the imperial carriage was respectfully brought out of the palace,
and the coffin was placed in the northwest corner of Shěnyáng city.
According to the state regulations,
on New Year's Eve and New Year's Day, music and dances were traditionally presented,
but these were all abolished at this time.
At that time, the Eastern Realm was newly established,
and the regulations were not yet detailed.
In the eighth year of Chóngdé,
Tàizōng passed away.
Males, from qīnwáng down to niúlǔ zhāngjīng and the Crown Prince of Cháoxiǎn;
females, from gōngzhǔ down to the wives of fèngguó jiāngjūn,
gathered in front of Qīngníng Gōng,
approached the sacrificial table to burn incense,
knelt and poured libations three times,
stood up,
and wailed.
Gùshān ézhēn, āngbāng zhāngjīng, officials below chéngzhèng, and noblewomen gathered outside the Dàqīng Mén,
stood in order and wailed.
The next day,
the coffin was respectfully moved to Chóngzhèng Diàn.
Princes, dukes, and all officials cried and wailed morning and evening for three days.
As for their places of fasting,
princes, bèilè, bèizi, and dukes returned to their residences;
officials of the ministries and courts lodged in their offices;
idle officials proceeded to Dǔgōng Diàn;
gùshān ézhēn and other officials and noblewomen
returned home on the evening of the next day.
When Shìzǔ ascended the throne,
he was only six years old.
It happened to be extremely cold,
and an attendant offered him a sable robe,
but he refused to wear it,
saying:
"If it were yellow,
I would wear it myself.
Only because it is red,
I will not wear it."
On that day, no imperial procession was arranged,
and no music was played.
Princes and high ministers said that since he had already ascended the throne,
his hat should be adorned with a plume.
Thereupon, all military and civilian personnel adorned their hats with plumes.
Officials were temporarily prohibited from weddings, banquets, and gatherings,
but commoners were not restricted.
Then, a mournful imperial edict was issued to Cháoxiǎn and Měnggǔ,
stating:
"Our August Father, with his profound virtue and grand achievements,
was loved and revered by the subject states.
On a certain day of this month,
he ascended to be a guest among the dragons (passed away).
All officials and commoners, both within and outside the realm,
are without exception sorrowful.
Let all subject states be informed.
The rites of sacrifice and burial
shall all follow frugality and simplicity.
Furthermore, we shall adhere to the ancient system,
substituting days for months,
and mourning attire shall be shed after twenty-seven days."
Upon the arrival of the edict,
the king and his subordinates performed the mourning rites as before.
At this time, they were still outside the Great Wall.
In the eighteenth year of Shùnzhì,
Shìzǔ passed away.
Shèngzǔ cut his queue and put on mourning attire.
Princes, dukes, all officials, princesses, fùjìn,
down to clan women, zuǒlǐng, third-rank imperial guards, and noblewomen above,
males removed their hat plumes and cut their hair,
females removed their hair ornaments and cut their hair.
After the great encoffinment,
the coffin was respectfully moved to Qiánqīng Gōng.
A sacrificial table was set up,
and libations were offered three times a day: morning, late afternoon, and noon.
The Emperor personally went to the Shàngshí to pour libations,
bowed three times,
stood,
and wailed.
Princes, dukes, high ministers, princesses, fùjìn, xiànjūn, and wives of imperial clan dukes approached the sacrificial table.
Vice Commandants-in-chief and above stood in order outside Qiánqīng Mén.
Han civil officials went outside Jǐngyùn Mén.
Military officials went outside Lóngzōng Mén.
All wore white mourning clothes
and cried and wailed morning and evening,
for a total of three days.
Outer vassal ministers were given white cloth for their mourning attire.
By the fourth day,
princes, dukes, and all officials observed fasting and lodged for a total of twenty-seven days.
After this, they cried and wailed once a day.
Military and civilian personnel removed their mourning attire.
Music and marriages
were suspended for officials for one hundred days,
and for military and civilian personnel for one month.
For one hundred days, official documents were written with blue ink,
and official seals were stamped in blue.
Slaughter was forbidden for forty-nine days.
In the capital, from the day of the grand mourning,
temples and monasteries each rang their bells thirty thousand times.
The next day, the imperial will was promulgated at Tiān'ānmén.
All ministers wore plain clothes
and performed the three kowtows and nine prostrations.
After the proclamation,
they wailed.
The Lǐbù copied the edict
and promulgated it to all provinces.
Officials awaiting appointment, imperial academy students, clerks, scribes, monks, and Daoists
all wore plain clothes and proceeded to the Shùntiān Fǔ office,
crying and wailing morning and evening for three days.
When the edict reached the provinces,
the chief officials, leading their subordinates, wore plain clothes and went out to the suburbs to kneel and receive it.
Upon entering the public office, they performed the rites,
listened to the proclamation, and wailed.
They shed their mourning attire after twenty-seven days,
and noblewomen did likewise.
Military and civilian males and females shed their mourning attire after thirteen days.
The rest was as in the capital.
For the Yīndiàn,
twenty-one food tables were arranged,
eleven wine vessels,
nine sheep,
and ninety thousand sheets of paper money.
The eulogy was read.
The Emperor went to the sacrificial table and wept.
Crying was echoed both inside and outside.
Libations were poured.
He led the assembly in three bows,
wailed,
and burned the offerings.
The Qǐdiàn was set up like the Yīndiàn ceremony.
On the appointed day, the coffin was respectfully placed on the Dàshēng Yú.
Libations were poured three times,
and sacrifices were made at all passing gates and bridges.
The Emperor followed, weeping bitterly,
and all ministers followed in order.
Upon approaching Jǐngshān,
those inside and outside gathered in order,
awaited the arrival of the spiritual carriage,
knelt, and wailed.
After the coffin was respectfully placed in Shòuhuáng Diàn,
a sacrificial table was set up.
The Emperor poured libations three times,
bowing once for each libation,
and his sorrow was endless.
The Empress Dowager comforted him again and again,
and only then did he return to the palace.
The next day, the first sacrifice was performed,
and the Emperor shed his mourning attire.
The day after, the Yìjì was performed.
After a full month, the Yuèdiàn was performed.
From then on, Yuèdiàn was performed within one hundred days,
and Yuèdiàn was performed within one year.
The rites were all similar to the Yīndiàn,
only the offerings and paper money presented differed.
After a full year, the final sacrifice was offered,
but no eulogy was read.
They conferred an honored posthumous title and temple name.
Reverently they announced it at the suburban altars, the ancestral temples, and the altars of the soil and grain.
On the appointed day, outside the funerary palace, the imperial procession was displayed,
music was played.
The Grand Secretaries respectfully placed the imperial title document (cè) and seal (bǎo) on a table,
bowed three times,
and withdrew.
The emperor, in plain clothes, proceeded to the Tàihé Mén.
After inspecting them,
he knelt once and bowed three times,
then withdrew and stood on the east side.
The Grand Secretaries went before the table,
again bowed three times,
and respectfully placed the cè and bǎo inside the decorated pavilion,
following the initial ritual.
Cavalry guards carried them,
the imperial guard led the way,
the imperial carriage followed.
Princes, dukes, and all officials first assembled outside the Xiéhé Mén,
knelt to welcome,
then followed outside the main gate of the Shòuhuáng Diàn.
The cè and bǎo pavilion entered,
reaching the eaves.
The emperor entered through the left gate.
The head official of the Board of Rites first respectfully placed the silk cè and bǎo on the central table,
then withdrew.
The Grand Secretaries went before the pavilion, bowed three times,
and respectfully placed the incense, cè, and bǎo on the left table.
The emperor took his position,
and led the assembly in three跪nine bows.
A Grand Secretary, from the left table, respectfully presented the cè on bended knee.
The emperor offered the cè,
handed it to a Grand Secretary on his right,
who received it kneeling,
and placed it on the central table.
Presenting the bǎo was also done in the same manner.
Then the cè was proclaimed.
The proclaiming official, holding the silk cè, proclaimed it,
bowed three times,
and withdrew.
The ceremony for proclaiming the bǎo was the same.
The emperor led the assembly in performing the rites as before.
He then proceeded before the offering table for the sacrifice,
laid out silk,
read the invocation,
offered wine three times,
as per custom.
The silk cè and bǎo were burned,
and the ceremony concluded.
The next day, an edict was issued as prescribed.
Within a hundred days, the inner and outer groups assembled for the preface,
read the invocation, cried, and offered sacrifices as in the initial ceremony.
On this day, the spirit tablet was inscribed.
One Grand Secretary entered the Guāndé Diàn,
went before the spirit tablet to be enshrined in the ancestral temple and offered incense,
then respectfully carried the tablet to the Shòuhuáng Diàn and placed it on a table outside,
and bowed three times.
One Manchu and one Han Grand Secretary each went before the incense table and again bowed three times.
After the inscription was filled with blue pigment,
the rites were performed as before.
The tablet was respectfully placed on a yellow palanquin,
and proceeded to stop before the Guāndé Diàn.
The Grand Secretaries entered the hall,
went before the spirit tablet to be enshrined in the Fèngxiān Diàn and bowed three times,
then respectfully placed the tablet on an anjuan palanquin,
which followed behind the yellow palanquin,
exiting the Jǐngshān East Gate,
and entering the Dōnghuá Mén.
The emperor, in plain clothes, knelt to welcome them inside the Jǐngyùn Mén,
and followed them to the Qiánqīng Mén,
where the palanquins stopped.
The emperor went before both spirit tablets, bowed three times to each,
placed them on tables one after another,
made three offerings,
and nine bows.
The ceremony was completed.
An auspicious day was chosen for the enshrinement.
The xiángjí ceremony.
The grand sacrifice was performed like the initial sacrifice.
After it concluded,
the emperor ascended the hall,
and held an audience with his officials.
On Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, Dōngzhì, and Sùichú,
offerings were made as appropriate for the season.
Once an auspicious day for burial was divined,
the coffin was to be moved to the imperial tomb.
Three days beforehand,
envoys were dispatched to inform Heaven, Earth, and the imperial altars.
The day before,
an ancestral offering was made,
the ceremony was as for the qǐdiàn.
Previously, princes and ministers, citing ancient rites,
had only allowed the imperial carriage to escort a short distance,
but this was not permitted.
However, an imperial decree from the Empress Dowager was received,
and they had no choice
but to reluctantly obey the compassionate command.
On the appointed day, inner and outer groups assembled.
The emperor went to the coffin, poured wine,
performing all rites and showing all grief.
The assisting ministers, leading the officiating officials, respectfully placed the coffin on the palanquin to begin the procession.
The imperial procession led the way,
the cè and bǎo followed behind.
The emperor cried out, clinging to the palanquin.
After it had passed,
he walked to outside the Dōng'ān Mén and wept while making an offering.
All officials followed him.
At every gate and bridge passed,
a sacrifice was made.
At stopovers along the way,
offerings were made morning and evening.
Princes performed the rites,
all officials expressed their sorrow.
Within a hundred lì, the local officials, in plain clothes, knelt to welcome on the right side of the road.
Upon reaching the tomb,
offerings were made as they were along the way.
Prior to the grand burial,
assisting ministers and officials of the third rank and above were dispatched to the tomb to make offerings.
Three days beforehand,
reverent announcements were made as in normal announcement ceremonies.
On the appointed day, the assisting ministers went to the coffin to announce the removal,
poured wine three times,
and respectfully placed the coffin on the palanquin.
All officials lined up in order,
knelt, and expressed their sorrow.
After the palanquin had passed,
they cried and followed.
Upon reaching the underground palace,
princes and ministers respectfully carried the coffin inside.
The cè and bǎo were placed on the left and right,
and the stone gate was closed.
The assisting ministers led the assembly in pouring wine three times,
expressed sorrow,
and the imperial procession and ceremonial instruments were burned.
When the Xiǎng Diàn was completed,
the spirit tablet of Shìzǔ was respectfully installed,
and offerings were made as in seasonal sacrifices.
After twenty-seven months,
a joint sacrifice was made at the Tàimiào,
as in the year-end joint sacrifice.
In the 61st year of Kāngxī,
the Shèngzǔ passed away.
During the grand shrouding,
princes, dukes, and ministers were ordered to enter the Qiánqīng Mén to gaze upon the coffin.
Imperial sons and grandsons were ordered to perform rites on the Dānchí platform.
Princesses, fùjìn, and others all gathered before the Jǐyán Diàn.
The emperor and all imperial sons put on mourning clothes.
The East Wing was designated as a mourning hut (yǐlú).
The imperial will was issued,
instructing the officials of rites to revise and add to the ceremonial procedures.
At the appointed time, the emperor stood outside the Qiánqīng Gōng,
facing west.
A Grand Secretary respectfully carried the imperial will out from the central path.
The emperor knelt,
waited for it to pass,
then returned to his mourning quarters.
The Grand Secretaries exited the Qiánqīng Mén.
The Minister of Rites bowed three times and received it kneeling.
The rest was as with previous imperial wills.
After twenty-seven days, they were to shed their mourning clothes.
The emperor said:
"To wear mourning is the way of a child towards a parent.
The twenty-seven-day mourning period,
it is truly difficult to comply with."
All officials, considering the paramount importance of state affairs,
requested compliance with the imperial will to remove mourning clothes.
He did not agree.
They again presented a memorial saying:
"The filial piety of the Son of Heaven has always been different from that of scholars and commoners.
The Xiàojīng says:
'The Son of Heaven displays filial piety by extending his virtuous teachings to the populace and spreading them throughout the four seas.'
The Shū Jīng refers to Gāozōng's liángyīn,
and Dù Yù of the Jìn Dynasty considered it a text on grieving in heart after shedding mourning clothes.
This is because the sovereign presides over the ancestral temples and altars of soil and grain,
and sacrifices are auspicious rites,
which must be performed after mourning clothes are removed.
If mourning is not removed after twenty-seven days,
the sacrificial ceremonies will inevitably be incomplete."
They again kowtowed and earnestly pleaded,
and only then did he consent.
After shedding mourning clothes,
he still moved his residence to the Yǎngxīn Diàn,
living in fasting and plain clothes for three years.
The imperial coffin was respectfully placed in the Shòuhuáng Diàn,
and food was offered three times daily.
He withdrew to the Guāndé Diàn and sat on the ground.
Matters were reported to him there.
After the evening offering was completed,
he would then return to the yǐlú.
The assembled officials deliberated on advancing a respectful posthumous title.
The emperor personally pricked his finger, circling with blood the
characters "Shèngzǔ".
The ritual officials presented the ritual protocols, but they were not satisfactory,
so they were revised.
Previously, announcements were made to the Fèngxiān Diàn.
On the appointed day, after reviewing the imperial register and seals,
the emperor performed one kneel and three bows.
He stood east-side, facing west,
waiting until the pavilion carrying the imperial register and seals had departed before returning to the palace.
He proceeded to the mourning hall, leaning by the hut in respectful waiting.
At that time, tribute offerings from Cháoxiǎn arrived,
and were set before the sacrificial table.
All officials assembled.
Officials from the Hónglú Sì introduced the envoys,
who stood south of the ceremonial guard,
facing north,
performing three kneels and nine bows.
An official was sent to read the document,
offering three libations,
with one bow for each libation.
The assembled multitude and the envoys all expressed sorrow and performed the rituals.
The envoys again performed two kneels and six bows,
burned offerings,
and withdrew.
The foreign vassal, the Àohàn Wáng, requested an audience with the coffin,
which was granted.
From then on, envoys from the Měngfān all gained permission to enter for an audience, which became customary.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
when the coffin was to be moved to the Jǐnglíng offering hall,
court officials cited the rites of the Sòng and Míng dynasties,
stating that the successor emperor should not personally escort the coffin.
The emperor did not consent.
The ritual officials discussed that after the coffin was interred in the underground palace,
the spirit tablet for the Tàimiào would be inscribed,
and a prince would be respectfully ordered to return it to the capital.
The emperor said:
"During the late Míng, emperors did not personally escort the coffin,
hence the kings and high officials acted on their behalf.
Since I am going personally,
I should naturally personally escort it back."
Two days before the relocation,
announcements were also sent to Hòutǔ and the gods of Chāngruì Shān.
On the appointed day,
the emperor went to the coffin to offer libations,
led the multitude in three bows,
and after expressing sorrow,
quickly stood by the eastern side of the main gate.
As the coffin emerged,
he knelt,
expressing sorrow.
He ascended the great funerary carriage,
kneeling on its left.
The ritual official performed a sacrifice to the carriage,
kowtowing three times.
When the funerary procession set off,
the emperor followed on foot.
Upon reaching the eastern gate of Jǐngshān,
he waited for the overnight stop.
Upon reaching Jǐnglíng,
the emperor knelt to receive it outside the Red Gate,
expressing sorrow.
He followed on foot,
arriving at Sāndòng Qiáo,
where he knelt and waited.
The great funerary carriage was lowered, and the coffin was placed on a smaller carriage,
and respectfully enshrined in the offering hall.
A sacrificial table was set,
and the imperial register and seals were arranged.
Three libations were offered,
and three bows performed,
completing the ceremony.
The emperor could not bear to part,
but the assembled officials invoked the Empress Dowager.
Having no choice,
he returned to the imperial carriage the next day.
The kings and high officials requested to hold court,
but the emperor, stating that the coffin was not yet permanently interred,
ordered a temporary delay.
After persistent requests,
it was eventually carried out.
After the burial date was set,
on the morning of the appointed day, the emperor went to Jǐnglíng to offer sacrifices,
weeping and mourning in great sorrow,
offering three libations and three bows,
then quickly moving to kneel and weep outside the mausoleum gate to wait.
As the imperial hearse entered the underground palace,
he again offered three libations and three bows,
then exited to wait in the tent.
The inscription of the spirit tablet and the Yu sacrifice followed the usual rites,
after which the spirit tablet was respectfully returned to the capital and enshrined in the Tàimiào.
As the twenty-seven months were nearing completion,
the request of the Minister of Personnel, Zhū Shì, was granted
for a grand ancestral sacrifice at the Tàimiào,
which was announced to officials and commoners.
When Shìzōng died,
the funeral rites entirely followed the precedents of Jǐnglíng.
The next day, for the morning sacrifice,
a select few kings, Bèizi, and Dukes were specifically chosen to view it inside,
while others assembled in the corridor of the Qiánqīng Gōng to perform the rites.
Thereafter, princes, dukes, high officials, Éfù, and Tàijí who arrived for the first time
were all allowed to request permission to view.
Thirty members of the imperial clan and twenty Jiéluó were also ordered to take turns in offering sacrifices to express their grief and remembrance.
When the imperial will was issued,
the Grand Secretaries carried it to the eaves of the Qiánqīng Gōng.
The emperor personally received it,
placed it on a table,
and performed three bows.
The Grand Secretaries also went before the imperial table and performed three bows.
As the will exited the central gate,
the emperor knelt to receive it,
waited for it to pass,
then returned to his mourning hut.
When the will reached the provinces,
soldiers, civilians, men, and women changed into mourning attire for twenty-seven days.
When the coffin was moved to the Yōnghé Gōng,
the emperor followed on foot.
The assembled officials advised against it, but he did not yield,
and consequently resided in that palace.
He only returned after the twenty-seventh day.
Within the month, he visited daily.
After the first month, it was once every other day.
After the second month, it was once every three days.
At that time, the Emperor wished to observe a three-year mourning period.
The court officials requested to shorten it to one month for each year,
but this was not permitted.
He ordered a detailed examination of the rites and ceremonies.
Soon, the proposed regulations were submitted:
"One,
regarding sacrifices:
According to the 'Wáng Zhì' chapter of the Lǐ Jì, 'during the three years of mourning, no sacrifices are offered,
except for sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, the gods of the soil and grain (Shèjì),
and affairs conducted after removing the sash of mourning.'
The commentary states, 'One dares not set aside the exalted for the humble.'
This implies that during the three-year period, these should inherently be performed personally.
Míng Lǚ Kūn stated that ancestors are not less important than parents,
and offering sacrifices should not be delayed by mourning.
How can they be neglected for long?
Indeed, as Heaven and kinship are of one principle,
sacrifices at the ancestral temple
should also be performed concurrently.
We humbly propose: For all major sacrifices at the suburban altars (Jiāo), ancestral temples (Miào), Shèjì, and Fèngxiān Diàn,
the Emperor shall personally attend and perform the rites,
or dispatch officials to respectfully deputize,
all with music.
He shall fast and purify beforehand,
wear plain clothing,
with tassels and cords on his hat,
inspect the prayer tablets,
and don ceremonial robes.
For 朝日 (Cháorì),
夕月 (Xīyuè),
and offerings to emperors, former teachers (Xiānshī), and former farmers (Xiānnóng),
officials shall be dispatched to perform the rites,
all in ceremonial robes with music.
On the appointed day, the hat and robes shall be as during the fasting period.
Sacrifices to gods within the palace
shall be held after one hundred days.
Jīngyán lectures and plowing ceremonies (Gēngjí)
shall be held after the mourning attire is changed.
Two,
regarding court audiences:
These pertain to major ceremonies.
The New Year's Day (Yuándàn) grand audience
is observed by all nations,
and the court ritual is of utmost importance.
We humbly propose: Within the twenty-seven months,
for the New Year's Day audience,
the Emperor shall ascend the Tàiwò Diàn in auspicious attire,
without proclamations or
music.
Regular audiences shall be the same.
Three,
regarding attending to state affairs at the palace gate (Yùmén Tīngzhèng):
This is a matter of great importance in the imperial system.
In the past, Sòng Rénzōng observed three years of mourning
and changed his attire when presiding over court.
During Xiàozōng's time,
after twenty-seven days,
officials requested him to attend to state affairs.
Citing the text that 'wearing a ceremonial cap and robes, he came out to the Yingmén gate,' they earnestly requested,
and permission was granted.
Examining historical records,
this has been the custom since ancient times.
We humbly propose: Routine matters and audiences shall all be conducted in the Biàndiàn,
and only after one hundred days shall the Emperor attend at the palace gate.
Four,
regarding hats and robes:
As for the system of 'Liàngyīn,'
former scholars said there was no ancient evidence.
History records that Wèi Xiàowén Dì and Táng Dézōng, after removing their mourning attire, still wore plain clothes and unbleached silk headscarves when attending to state affairs.
Although Sòng Rénzōng adopted the system of shortening the mourning period,
he changed his attire when presiding over court,
but within the palace, the three-year mourning period was observed.
This is because white mourning clothes cannot be worn at court.
Those in previous dynasties who observed three years of mourning
only wore plain clothes within the palace.
We humbly propose: Within one hundred days, wear white mourning clothes.
After one hundred days, change to plain clothes.
When visiting the funerary altar (Jīyán), still wear white mourning clothes.
When attending to state affairs at the palace gate or visiting the Empress Dowager's (Huáng Tàihòu) palace, wear plain clothes,
with tassels and cords on the hat.
When ascending the main hall for court audiences, change to auspicious attire.
For sacrifices and all other ceremonies, wear ceremonial robes.
Upon completion of the twenty-seven-month mourning period,
the rites shall be as those for the hundred-day ceremony,
with sacrifices offered and mourning attire removed.
Five,
regarding palace attire regulations:
The Emperor and Empress are of one body; their attire regulations cannot differ.
After twenty-seven days, the Empress shall wear plain clothes.
For ceremonies, she shall change to ceremonial robes.
When visiting the Jīyán, she shall still wear white mourning clothes.
Imperial consorts (Fēipín) shall also follow this.
Imperial princes (Huángzǐ) shall be the same as all other princes (Zhūwáng).
Six,
regarding princes, dukes, and officials in the capital:
They shall remove their mourning attire after twenty-seven days.
For ceremonies, court audiences, and attendance in groups, they shall wear auspicious attire.
When managing affairs in their offices or presenting memorials at court, they shall wear plain clothes,
with tassels and cords on their hats.
When visiting the Jīyán, they shall remove their hat tassels.
All offices shall use vermilion seals on their memorials."
The decree was approved.
On the first day of the first year of Qiánlóng's reign,
as it was the beginning of his reign,
the Emperor held a regular audience in the Tàiwò Diàn.
This was abolished the following year
and established as a precedent.
When the coffin was to be moved to Tàilíng,
the Emperor went to the coffin and completed the rites.
The Empress Dowager (Huáng Tàihòu) also offered three libations.
The rest remained as before.
According to previous custom, on Qīngmíng, Zhōngyuán, the end of the year, and national days of mourning (Guójì), rites were performed in court attire,
and then mourning was expressed in plain clothes.
Only on Dōngzhì was the plain attire not changed.
As the coffin had not yet been buried,
and the Emperor was still in mourning,
he approved the request of the ritual officials.
The officiating officials performing the sacrifices did not wear hat tassels
and still wore plain clothes.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
during mourning for Gāozōng,
the procedures followed the precedent of Tàilíng,
except that when the imperial edict reached the provinces,
civil and military officials, along with gentry and elders, removed their hat tassels and wore plain clothes to go out of the city to kneel and welcome it.
They then entered their public offices to perform the rites.
After the proclamation was heard,
they expressed sorrow
and only then donned mourning attire,
weeping before the coffin for three days.
Officials, civil servants, soldiers, and common people, from the day of the great event,
did not shave their hair for one hundred days.
For the grand funeral,
the Emperor personally led the coffin in the imperial funeral carriage into the underground palace.
Furthermore, as the grand ceremony of the New Year's audience had already been held in the first year,
it was not to be held again within the twenty-seven months.
Rénzōng died at Rèhé.
Six days later,
the coffin arrived in Jīng.
Only then was the grand embalmment performed,
and it was enshrined in the Dànbó Jìngchéng Diàn.
Four more days later,
the imperial edict was promulgated.
Ritual officials escorted the dragon palanquin
and dispatched it to the capital via post.
According to old regulations,
from the Empress Dowager downwards, all wore plain clothes after twenty-seven days.
Xiàohé Ruì Huánghòu changed to white mourning clothes
and only changed after one hundred days.
When the coffin was about to arrive,
the officials went out of the city to weep and welcome it.
The Emperor returned first,
and waited at Āndìngmén and Dōnghuámén to weep and welcome it.
He followed on foot into the Dà Nèi,
and it was enshrined in the Qiánqīng Gōng.
Approving the proposal of the ritual officials,
as the mourning period had reached twenty-seven days,
the mourning attire was to be removed after the grand sacrifice.
Also, the offerings before the Jīyán,
the display of the imperial carriages and ceremonial guards,
the assembly of officials, and the use of blue seals by all offices
were all to cease after the grand sacrifice.
Xuānzōng died.
The coffin was moved to Yuánmíngyuán
and enshrined in the Zhèngdà Guāngmíng Diàn.
The Yǎnshèng Gōng happened to be in the capital.
When the two-week anniversary sacrifice occurred,
he was ordered to go to the garden to attend the rites.
Wénzōng died at Rèhé.
Following Xuānzōng's precedent,
the coffin was moved to the Dōnglíng.
Mùzōng was still young.
The officials, citing the precedent of Kāngxī's second year,
requested the Emperor only to escort it a short distance.
In the second year of Tóngzhì, when the mourning attire was removed,
by imperial decree from the two Empress Dowagers (Liǎng Gōng Huáng Tàihòu),
all celebrations and banquets
were to await the completion of the imperial tomb affairs.
Mùzōng and Dézōng died,
and this precedent was followed in both cases.
From the time that Shìzōng personally selected the auspicious site for the Tàilíng mausoleum,
the construction required the use of the imperial treasury.
He also issued an edict not to build stone statues,
pitying the human labor.
Xuānzōng was buried in Mùlíng,
with simple regulations.
Later, during the Tóngzhì era,
Assistant Minister Sòng Jìn suggested that the Dìnglíng project should follow the example of Mùlíng.
Although the court officials were constrained by established precedents,
the system did not allow for any slight extravagance.
At the time, it was praised for its frugality.
In the early Xuāntǒng era,
when building Chónglíng for Dézōng,
several million from the treasury were disbursed.
Royal relatives and high-ranking officials presided over the affair,
diverting funds to construct their private residences,
resulting in the mausoleum remaining unfinished for over three years.
After the abdication,
the authorities allocated funds for its completion.
By the time of the burial,
the work was barely halfway done,
hence it was relatively modest compared to the old system.
Empress's Funeral Rites
Empress Yèhènálā Shì passed away.
After three years,
she was buried at Níyǎmǎnshān.
In the third year of Tiāncōng,
she was interred with Tàizǔ in Fúlíng,
the regulations for which were very simple.
After entering Shānghǎi Guān,
whenever there was a major event for a successive empress,
ministers were specially appointed to oversee the funeral rites,
and the Board of Rites meticulously discussed the details.
In the fourth month of the sixth year of Shùnzhì,
Empress Bóěrjìjítè Shì of Tàizōng passed away.
Her coffin was enshrined within the palace,
and an altar was set up in the main hall.
A vermillion banner was erected outside the gate, to the right.
From the highest-ranking princes to the lowest-ranking commanders,
princesses, fújìn, and noble ladies all gathered.
Shìzǔ led the assembly in donning mourning clothes.
The initial sacrifice, grand sacrifice, extended sacrifice, monthly sacrifice, hundred-day sacrifice, and other rites
were the same as those for a grand funeral.
In the seventh year,
she was posthumously honored with the title Xiàoduānwén Huánghòu,
and buried in Zhāolíng.
Shèngzǔ's mother, Empress Dowager Cíhé, Tóngjiā Shì,
passed away in the second month of the second year of Kāngxī.
When she first fell ill,
the Emperor, who was then eleven years old,
attended to her day and night.
When her condition worsened,
he ceased eating and sleeping.
Upon her death, he cut his hair and donned mourning clothes,
weeping and wailing in sorrow.
He took no food or drink,
moving his close attendants to tears.
He still ate three meals a day,
while princes and high officials cried twice a day in shifts.
Marriages were suspended,
music ceased,
soldiers and civilians removed their hat tassels,
and noble ladies removed their ornaments,
for twenty-seven days.
Other restrictions lasted for seven days.
After four days,
officials on duty removed their hat tassels
and wore plain white.
On the fifth day, an edict was issued,
and civil and military officials in plain clothes tearfully welcomed it.
Upon entering their public offices, they performed the kowtow three times and nine bows,
listened to the declaration of mourning,
and performed the rites as before.
They cried morning and evening for three days.
They wore white cloth,
and military personnel and civilians, male and female, wore plain clothes like those in the capital.
She was posthumously honored with the title Xiàokāngzhāng Huánghòu.
The coffin was moved to Bànshàng.
The Emperor poured libations, performed the rites, and cried out in sorrow.
The Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager, considering the Emperor's young age,
only personally saw her off.
She was interred with Shìzǔ in Xiàolíng
and enshrined in the Tàimiào.
In the fifth month of the twelfth year,
Empress Hèshèlǐ Shì passed away.
Court was suspended for five days.
People wore plain white,
and three offerings were made daily.
Officials inside and outside the court gathered, wearing plain cloth,
and cried morning and evening for three days.
The coffin was moved to the temporary burial palace at Běishāhé Gǒngfèngchéng,
and the Emperor personally saw it off.
From the initial mourning to the hundredth day,
he also personally offered sacrifices.
At that time, there was a military campaign against the Three Feudatories (Sānfān),
and fearing that public mourning and wearing mourning clothes in the provinces would easily cause confusion,
the mourning rites were exempted,
but other things remained as before.
She was posthumously titled Rénxiào.
After three weeks,
sacrifices were offered as at a mausoleum.
Later, she was buried at Chāngruìshān.
Upon Shìzōng's ascension,
she was posthumously titled Xiàochéngrén Huánghòu.
In the second month of the seventeenth year,
Empress Niǔhùlù Shì passed away.
Her funeral arrangements were similar to those of Empress Rénxiào.
She was posthumously titled Xiàozhāo.
Shìzōng added the posthumous title Rén.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Shìzǔ's mother, Bóěrjìjítè Shì, passed away.
Before this, when the Grand Empress Dowager was ill,
the Emperor personally attended her.
He walked to the southern suburbs to pray,
wishing to reduce his own lifespan to extend her compassionate longevity.
He personally composed a prayer,
the words of which were earnest and sincere.
When the Grand Minister of Sacrifices read it aloud,
tears flowed down his cheeks.
After suffering this great loss,
he cried incessantly.
He lived in a mourning hut, sleeping on the ground,
and emaciated himself excessively,
to the point of fainting and vomiting blood.
From that day on,
officials inside and outside gathered,
crying three times a day.
After four days, they cried twice a day.
Officials and common people observed a vegetarian fast for twenty-seven days.
Temples and monasteries each rang their bells thirty thousand times.
Official documents used blue seals,
memorials used vermillion seals,
and imperial edicts had blue endorsements.
When the New Year's Eve and New Year's Day arrived,
the assembled ministers requested the Emperor to temporarily return to the palace,
but he refused.
He only ordered the cessation of crying for one day on New Year's Day.
The Board of Rites deliberated and proposed the posthumous title Xiàozhuāngwén Huánghòu.
The Emperor, however, felt that she had not long ascended to heaven,
and it was truly unbearable for him
to immediately change her honorable title to a posthumous one.
He issued an edict that after her enshrinement in the burial garden,
she should be honored with the posthumous title during sacrifices.
When the coffin was moved for enshrinement on the evening of its departure,
his sorrowful longing was overwhelming.
Those around him strongly urged him to ascend the imperial carriage,
but he firmly refused to mount it,
cutting the carriage reins,
and walked mournfully alongside.
Whenever the coffin bearers rotated,
he would kneel prostrate and weep at length,
until he reached the temporary burial palace,
his face pale and feet weary,
his grief felt across the streets.
He also issued an imperial decree that upon returning to the palace, he would still reside in a tent outside the Qiánqīngmén.
He also resolved to observe three years of mourning,
unable to bear replacing months with days.
Ministers repeatedly memorialized him to end the mourning,
and over five hundred imperial academy students also pleaded for him to restrain his grief and follow the rites.
The Emperor, emaciated and weeping loudly,
reluctantly put aside his mourning attire,
but every memory caused him pain,
and this did not change for three years.
Earlier, when the Grand Empress Dowager was critically ill,
she instructed the Emperor, saying:
"Tàizōng's coffin has been enshrined for a long time.
The inferior should not disturb the superior,
so it is not suitable for joint burial.
If a separate burial ground were to be constructed,
it would inevitably be laborious and costly.
My heart is attached to you and your father,
and I cannot bear to be far away,
so it would be appropriate to reside in Zūnhuà."
The Emperor then selected a site south of Xiàolíng to build a sacrificial hall,
where the coffin was enshrined,
called the "Temporary Enshrinement Hall,"
and officials were appointed to offer sacrifices according to the Xiàolíng system.
It was not until Shìzōng rebuilt the underground palace,
named Zhāoxīlíng,
that the grand burial finally took place.
Shèngzǔ's Empress Rén, Tóngjiā Shì,
passed away in the seventh month of the twenty-eighth year.
This was only the second day after she was elevated from concubine to empress.
The Emperor suspended court and personally attended,
composing four poems to mourn her.
She was posthumously titled Xiàoyì,
and her funeral rites were similar to those of Xiàozhāo.
Shìzǔ's Empress, the Bó'ěrjìjítè clan,
died in the twelfth month of the fifty-sixth year.
Previously, when her illness was very grave,
the officials of rites requested that the funeral ceremonies be conducted according to those of Empress Xiàokāng.
The Emperor said:
"When Empress Xiàokāng passed away,
I was barely ten years old,
and the regents managed the funeral,
so the rites may not have been fully observed.
Later, I saw the funeral ceremonies of Empress Rénxiào,
which were quite clear in their arrangements.
If a major event occurs,
all discussions should proceed accordingly."
When she died,
the Emperor happened to have a foot ailment.
He was carried near the ritual table and mat,
and donned mourning attire while on his couch.
He cried and fainted,
recovering after a while.
The assembled officials knelt around him and earnestly pleaded,
whereupon he reluctantly allowed himself to be carried to a side hall.
When the coffin was about to be moved to the funerary palace,
a preliminary offering ceremony was set up.
The officials of rites requested that a prince be sent as a substitute.
The Emperor said:
"This is the first offering,
and I must personally perform it.
How can this rite be performed again in Níngshòu Gōng?"
On that day, he sent a substitute to present the libation cups,
but still performed the rites from his couch beside the ritual table and mat.
When the coffin began its journey,
he was carried on his couch, weeping as he saw it off.
After passing out of the west gate of Níngshòu Gōng,
he looked up and could no longer see the funeral carriage.
Only then did he cease his sorrow,
and returned to his mourning hut.
For the grand sacrifice,
his foot ailment had slightly improved,
so he personally went to the funerary palace to perform the rites.
Her posthumous title was Empress Xiàohuìzhāng,
and she was buried in Xiàodōnglíng.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
Shìzōng's mother, Empress Dowager Rénshòu Wūyǎ, died.
Her funeral rites were like those of Empress Xiàohuì.
Her posthumous title was Empress Xiàogōngrén,
and she was interred with Shèngzǔ in Jǐnglíng.
At that time, the Emperor was observing mourning for Shèngzǔ,
and resided in Yǎngxīn Diàn.
When this mourning period ended,
he continued with the mourning for the Empress Dowager.
The regents cited Shèngzǔ's funeral rites and requested that the *xiá* sacrifice be performed after the mourning period concluded.
The Emperor said:
"The sorrow of a child for their parents' death is the same,
but the rites for Emperors and Empresses
and the state's system
are different.
Now that the period for my Imperial Mother's removal of mourning attire has arrived,
we shall choose an auspicious day to make offerings and report to Fèngxiān Diàn,
without issuing an edict to the court and the outside world for this."
In the ninth month of the ninth year,
Shìzōng's Empress, the Nàlā clan, died.
The Emperor wore plain white mourning attire for thirteen days before removing it.
She was moved to Tiáncūn.
After three full years,
the seasonal offerings at the funerary palace were the same as the rites at Shāhé funerary palace,
except that the officials performing the sacrifices changed their embroidered badges.
When Gāozōng ascended the throne,
he bestowed the respectful posthumous title of Empress Xiàojìngxiàn.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
she was interred with Shìzōng in Tàilíng.
In the third month of the thirteenth year,
the Emperor escorted the Empress Dowager on an eastern tour,
and Empress Fùchá accompanied them.
She died upon returning to Dézhōu.
The Emperor personally composed a lament for her death.
As the funeral procession approached,
princes, dukes, and high officials assembled at the reed palace in Tōngzhōu.
The Imperial sons offered sacrifices,
and mourned and performed the rites.
Upon its arrival,
the assembled officials, in plain attire, knelt to greet it at Cháoyáng Mén.
Princesses and close relatives of princes' wives gathered at Chúxiù Gōng.
Wives of various princes and titled ladies gathered outside Dōnghuá Mén,
all in mourning attire, kneeling to greet the coffin.
It was then enshrined in Chángshòu Gōng.
The Emperor personally attended to don mourning attire,
and suspended court for six days.
For the mourning of the Central Palace,
since Empress Xiàochéngrén,
the regulations for funeral rites in the provinces and directly governed areas had not been carried out for a long time.
At this time, the princes and high officials said:
"The *Zhōu Lǐ* states that for the Queen, one wears coarse mourning clothes,
and the commentary explains that all officials wear *zīcuī* (a less severe form of mourning),
meaning there is no difference between internal and external officials.
The *Míng Huìdiǎn* records the Empress's funeral rites,
where thirteen Chief Provincial Administrations, together with Zhílì and the Ministry of Rites, requested an imperial envoy to announce the death.
Officials, soldiers, and common people in the outer provinces
were to observe the same mourning attire as in the capital.
Now that the great departed Empress has passed away,
it is a day when all four seas share in the sorrow.
Therefore, civil and military officials in the outer provinces should be ordered to wear mourning attire according to the regulations."
This was followed.
Her posthumous title was Xiàoxián.
In the fifth month,
court officials memorialized, saying:
"Although the Empress is the consort,
her position is respected by the system of rites.
Ascending the hall to hold court
is a matter of established regulations.
For the funeral rites of Empress Xiàoxián,
the ancestral system should be followed.
After one hundred days, the Emperor will ascend the hall, and civil and military officials and envoys from foreign states will perform their respects in court attire as in normal rites.
The Emperor observed two months of abstinence and purification rites,
and held court at the palace gate.
The assembled officials wore court attire without hanging pearls,
and after the ceremony, reverted to plain attire.
After one hundred days, if court is held at the palace gate,
the assembled officials will wear regular attire with pearls,
so as to conform to the distinctions in the system of rites."
The Emperor said:
"For the funeral rites of Empress Xiàoxián,
I have considered both ancient and modern practices,
without personal bias.
Examining the funeral of Empress Xiàojié Chén in the seventh year of Jiājìng of the Míng dynasty,
Zhāng Cōng cited ancient rites,
saying: 'For mourning attire, princes cease wearing it for periods of one year or less,
this is specifically for collateral one-year mourning.
However, for the death of a wife, originally three years of mourning are observed,
reduced to one year,
which certainly is not a cessation.
The sovereign should observe one-year mourning for the Empress,'
and so on.
Now, according to the memorialized proposal,
regarding ascending the hall and performing music,
all major court ceremonies and sacrificial rites
shall naturally follow the established examples.
However, for regular daily court sessions,
only bells and drums shall be struck,
and musical instruments shall be displayed but not played.
By the first month of next year,
when the one-year period will be approaching,
all ceremonies shall revert to normal practice."
At that time, Jiāng Xīnghàn, a Commander of the Yízhōu garrison, and Jīn Wénchún, the Prefect of Jǐnzhōu, shaved their heads during the national mourning period.
The responsible authorities reported this,
and the Ministry was ordered to apprehend and punish them.
It was also reiterated
that the ancestral system prohibited shaving within one hundred days,
and violators would be executed.
This edict was recorded in the *Huìdiǎn*.
In the thirty-first year,
Empress Nàlā died.
At that time, the Emperor was at Rèhé,
and the princes and high officials remaining in the capital reported it.
An imperial edict stated:
"Since her enthronement,
the Empress has not displayed any lack of virtue.
Last year, when accompanying the Empress Dowager on the southern tour,
her temperament suddenly changed from the norm,
and she did not fully fulfill her filial duties.
She ought to be deposed.
However, her title is still retained.
Her funeral rites shall follow the precedent for a Noble Consort,
to be handled by the ministers of the Imperial Household Department."
Rénzōng's mother, the Wèijiā clan,
died in the first month of the fortieth year while holding the rank of Noble Consort.
An imperial edict proclaimed her as Imperial Noble Consort Lìngyì,
and ordered the eighth, twelfth, and fifteenth Imperial sons,
and Imperial grandson Miándé and others to wear mourning.
She was buried in Shèngshuǐyù.
Subsequently, Rénzōng was established as Crown Prince,
and she was then posthumously granted the title of Empress Xiàoyí,
and her spirit tablet was moved to Fèngxiān Diàn.
Later, the temple title was further elevated to Empress Chún,
and then her spirit tablet was moved to the Tàimiào.
Gāozōng's mother, the Suíqìng皇太后 Niǔhùlù Shì,
passed away in the first month of the forty-second year.
The Emperor wore mourning for a hundred days,
like during Shìzōng's funeral,
and for the remainder, continued to wear plain clothes.
He personally composed the honorific posthumous title Xiàoshèng Xiàn Huánghòu.
Ritual officials submitted funeral protocols,
citing the precedent from the ninth year of Yōngzhèng,
that within twenty-seven months, if major events such as suburban sacrifices or ancestral temple ceremonies occurred,
plain clothes should be worn for the offerings,
and music should be set up but not played.
The Emperor said:
"The ceremonies for suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples are of great importance
and should not be slightly diminished due to a grand mourning."
He then referred the matter to the Grand Councilors for deliberation.
Soon after, the proposed deliberation was submitted:
"For major sacrifices at the suburban altars and ancestral temples,
officials should be dispatched to make offerings,
music should still be played,
and court attire should be worn for the rituals.
For regular sacrifices, plain clothes should be worn for offerings,
and music should be set up but not played."
The edict was approved.
An imperial edict was issued,
stating that from the day it reached the provincial capitals,
marriages should be suspended,
for princes, dukes, and all officials for a hundred days,
and for military and common people for one month.
Music should be stopped,
for princes, dukes, and all officials for one year,
and for military and common people for a hundred days.
Other regulations remained unchanged.
Previously, the mourning rites of past dynasties
regarding clothing and ritual after a hundred days
were not recorded in the Collected Statutes.
At this time, the Grand Councilors were ordered to consult with the high-ranking officials responsible for funeral rites to deliberate in detail.
They submitted a proposal for the ceremonies of ascending the throne and holding court.
The imperial decree was issued:
"The New Year's court assembly
need not be held within twenty-seven months.
As for daily court sessions,
they shall resume after a hundred days."
Regulations were also established for imperial attire:
"One,
within a hundred days, white mourning clothes.
After shedding mourning clothes for a hundred days,
plain clothes for twenty-seven months.
When approaching the spirit tablet,
the cap should have its tassel removed.
One,
within a hundred days, for sacrifices to the suburban altars, the Altars of Soil and Grain, and the Altar of the Sun,
officials should be dispatched to perform the rites.
On fasting days,
plain clothes and a cap with a tassel attached.
After a hundred days,
the Emperor shall personally proceed to perform the rites.
Also, during the fasting period,
ordinary clothes without pearl ornaments.
When reviewing the sacrificial prayers,
and staying overnight at the altar in advance,
ordinary clothes with pearl ornaments.
On the day of sacrifice, court attire and music shall be used.
Upon returning to the palace, music should be set up but not played.
One,
after a hundred days, for sacrifices, the imperial dragon robe and jacket.
Within a hundred days, for sacrifices at the Fèngxiān Diàn, a cap with a tassel, and a blue robe and jacket.
After a hundred days, a cap with a pearl finial, a blue robe, and a golden dragon jacket.
One,
within twenty-seven months, for sacrifices to the Altar of the Moon, Emperors, Ancient Teachers, and Ancient Farmers,
officials shall be dispatched to perform the rites.
One,
for sacrifices to the great gods in the palace,
after a hundred days, the Emperor shall personally proceed to perform the rites,
wearing a dragon robe, a blue jacket, and pearl ornaments.
One,
after twenty-seven days,
if it is New Year's Day,
for seven days before and after, a sable jacket with pearl ornaments.
After a hundred days,
when holding court at the Wǔmén,
ordinary clothes without pearl ornaments.
One,
after twenty-seven days and within a hundred days,
audiences and receptions shall all be held in the private hall,
wearing white mourning clothes.
For the Emperor's birthday,
ordinary clothes for seven days.
One,
when reviewing the memorial tablet and seal of the late Empress Dowager,
plain clothes with a cap with a tassel,
and a fasting token worn in advance for the fast.
One,
when reviewing the imperial genealogy,
court attire.
One,
in the twelfth month for sealing the imperial seals,
and in the first month for opening the imperial seals,
the imperial dragon jacket.
One,
the reading of the imperial edicts for the civil and military graduates shall not take place in the main hall.
One,
the Imperial Lectures and the plowing ceremony
shall be held after twenty-seven months.
One,
for the mountain tomb rituals,
within twenty-seven months for visiting the imperial tombs,
a blue robe and jacket,
a cap with its tassel removed.
When traveling to and from,
caps shall have tassels attached.
One,
for the consorts in the inner palace,
after shedding white mourning clothes after twenty-seven days,
ordinary clothes for twenty-seven months.
On New Year's Day and the Emperor's birthday,
auspicious clothes for seven days.
Within a hundred days, for the ritual of silkworm cultivation,
a princess or a fùjìn shall be dispatched to respectfully perform it on behalf of the empress.
Court attire.
After a hundred days and within twenty-seven months,
the ritual shall be performed as before,
with auspicious clothes.
As for civil and military officials,
white mourning clothes for twenty-seven days,
plain clothes within a hundred days,
caps with tassels,
in summer, caps with rain tassels.
When approaching the spirit tablet, tassels shall still be removed.
One,
within a hundred days, for sacrifices to the suburban altars, ancestral temples, altars of soil and grain, and the Altar of the Sun,
officials shall be dispatched to respectfully perform them on behalf of the Emperor.
In advance for inspecting the sacrificial animals, all shall wear plain clothes.
On the day of sacrifice,
the main officiant and all functionaries shall wear court attire.
Music shall be played.
After a hundred days and within twenty-seven months,
they shall personally proceed to perform the rites.
On fasting days, ordinary clothes with pearl ornaments,
when reviewing sacrificial prayers, inspecting sacrificial animals, and staying overnight at the altar, they shall wear a badge of office.
In winter, sable jackets with pearl ornaments.
On the day of sacrifice,
court attire and music shall be used.
One,
after a hundred days, for sacrifices at the Tángzi,
all shall wear python robes, badges of office, and pearl ornaments.
Within a hundred days, for sacrifices at the Fèngxiān Diàn,
blue robes and jackets,
caps with tassels.
After a hundred days, badges of office and pearl ornaments.
One,
after a hundred days, for sacrifices to the Altar of the Moon, Emperors, Ancient Teachers, and Ancient Farmers,
officials shall be dispatched to perform the rites,
all wearing plain clothes for fasting.
On the day of sacrifice,
court attire,
and music shall be played.
Within a hundred days, plain clothes shall be worn for the rites,
and music shall be set up but not played.
One,
within twenty-seven months, if New Year's Day falls on a day when sacrifices are made at the Tángzi,
all officials shall wear python robes, badges of office, and pearl ornaments.
For the three days before and after, and for the seven days before and after the Emperor's birthday, ordinary clothes with pearl ornaments shall be worn.
One,
after twenty-seven days and within a hundred days, officials granted an audience
shall wear blue robes and jackets.
After a hundred days, blue jackets.
One,
after a hundred days and within twenty-seven months,
for ascending the throne, regular court, and sitting in attendance, court attire shall be worn.
On the first and fifteenth day of the lunar month, ordinary clothes with pearl ornaments shall be worn.
One,
for the imperial coffin's transfer to the mountain tomb,
attending officials shall wear blue robes and jackets and caps with tassels removed during the journey.
After the ceremony is completed,
and the spirit tablet returns to the capital,
and for attending officials visiting the imperial tombs after a hundred days,
they shall wear blue robes and jackets on the journey,
caps with tassels attached.
On the day of visiting the tombs, the same applies.
Upon returning to the capital,
they shall revert to short-lapel robes and riding jackets.
One,
within a hundred days, raincoats and rain caps shall all be blue.
After a hundred days, rain caps shall be according to rank,
and raincoats shall remain blue.
This also applies to imperial princes and below."
The edict was approved.
In the fourth month,
the Empress Dowager was interred at Tàidōng Líng.
The imperial coffin passed by Tàilíng,
and it was ordered to temporarily stop by the roadside.
The Emperor performed rites towards the imperial tomb on behalf of the deceased,
and this was established as a regulation.
Upon reaching the mausoleum, on the second day, a xiǎngdiàn lǐ (banquet and offering ceremony) was held.
Initially,
the emperor considered that the old term in the "Collected Statutes"
"qiǎndiàn" (sending-off offering)
was inappropriate.
He ordered the literati officials to investigate its origin.
The Grand Secretaries stated:
"The term 'qiǎndiàn'
has no explicit mention in the Rít jīng (Classics of Rites).
It is only found in Kǒng Yǐngdá's commentary on the Shì sāng lǐ (Ritual for a Scholar's Funeral),
and has been used ever since the Táng dynasty.
It seems Kǒng Yǐngdá merely used the term 'qiǎnchē' (sending-off cart) for the cart carrying wrapped sacrificial animals on the day of the burial in the Yí lǐ (Book of Rites),
and then took the character 'qiǎn' to name the offering,
which is an forced and inappropriate connection.
Re-examining the Yí lǐ,
for the sacrifice performed before departure,
'the cloth covering the wrapped sacrificial animals is removed.'
Zhèng Kāngchéng's commentary states: 'This symbolizes the return of the guests' sacrificial vessels after the banquet.'
Moreover, the Lǐ jì zá jì (Miscellaneous Records of the Book of Rites) says: 'After a grand banquet,
the platters of the three sacrificial animals are rolled up and returned to the guest lodging,
which is done out of sorrow.'
Zhèng's commentary states: 'Returning the guests' sacrificial vessels after the banquet signifies the filial son's sorrow at his parent's departure.'
Thus, the sacrifice performed before departure
originally used the xiǎng lǐ (banquet ritual).
The old term 'qiǎndiàn'
seems
not as appropriate as 'xiǎngdiàn'."
An imperial edict was issued to the relevant department to correct and adopt this.
In the fourth month of the forty-fourth year,
the emperor went to the mausoleum to shed his mourning attire.
He issued an edict saying:
"When I previously suffered the great loss of my imperial father,
I intended to observe the three-year mourning period.
However, in accordance with the compassionate decree of the Holy Mother,
it was shortened to one hundred days.
Though the plain white clothes were removed,
the mourning remained.
Subsequently, during the great mourning of the Holy Mother,
it did not continue beyond one hundred days.
This is not to say that I valued the former greatly and the latter lightly.
It is because at that time, my physical strength was at its peak,
and I could have completed the three-year mourning period.
Now, I am approaching seventy years old;
if I were to observe it now and fail to fully perform the rites,
my heart would feel even more uneasy."
Rénzōng Huánghòu Xǐtálà Shì (Empress Xǐtálà of Rénzōng)
died in the second month of the second year of Jiāqìng.
By imperial decree of the Tàishàng Huáng (Retired Emperor),
her funeral rites were to be those of an empress.
It was changed to five days of suspended court sessions and seven days of plain attire.
During the offering and libation ceremonies,
the imperial princes and others wore mourning clothes according to the regulations.
Officials and common people all wore plain attire for seven days,
without removing their hat tassels
or letting their hair grow.
Soon after, an edict was issued stating that during the period of suspended court sessions,
memorials should still be submitted,
and various audiences should not be abolished.
Officials presenting memorials and officials granted audiences
were all to wear ordinary attire without jade pendants.
All marriages were suspended, and music ceased;
for officials, this lasted twenty-seven days,
for military personnel and common people, seven days,
and the rest followed the usual rites.
She was posthumously granted the title Xiàoshú,
and subsequently buried in Tàipíng Yù.
In the first month of the thirteenth year,
Xuānzōng Huánghòu Niǔhùlù Shì (Empress Niǔhùlù of Xuānzōng) died.
At the time, she was in the position of a Fújìn (imperial consort),
and was temporarily interred in the garden tomb at Wángzuǒ Cūn.
In the twenty-fifth year, when the emperor ascended the throne,
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Xiàomù Huánghòu.
It was proposed to change the garden tomb to an imperial tomb.
The Ministry of Rites stated:
"The regulations for the garden tomb are not yet complete.
For the great sacrifice on the death anniversary
and the small sacrifices on the first and fifteenth of the lunar month,
please follow the precedent of Xiàoshú Hòu's temporary coffin palace."
The imperial order was approved.
Subsequently, Grand Secretaries Dài Jūnyuán and others were ordered to survey and select Bǎohuá Yù.
Later, due to water seepage in the underground palace,
in the eleventh year of Dàoguāng,
she was reburied in Lóngquán Yù.
Two years later,
Xuānzōng Huánghòu Tóngjiā Shì (Empress Tóngjiā of Xuānzōng) died.
The emperor suspended court sessions for nine days
and wore plain attire for thirteen days.
She was posthumously granted the title Xiàoshèn.
Another two years later,
a burial site was chosen,
sharing the auspicious ground with Empress Xiàomù.
In the first month of the twentieth year,
Huánghòu Niǔhùlù Shì (Empress Niǔhùlù) died.
The emperor wore a blue gown and jacket for thirteen days before shedding them,
and still wore plain attire for the memorial offerings.
She was posthumously granted the title Xiàoquán.
She was also buried in Lóngquán Yù.
In the twelfth month of the twenty-ninth year,
Rénzōng Huánghòu Niǔhùlù Shì (Empress Niǔhùlù of Rénzōng) died.
She was posthumously granted the title Xiàohérùi Huánghòu.
At the time, the emperor was seventy years old.
He shed the plain white mourning clothes after twenty-seven days,
and died a few days later.
In the third year of Xiánfēng,
she was buried in Chāngxī Líng.
The day after Empress Xiàohé died,
Wénzōng Hòu Sàkèdá Shì (Empress Sàkèdá of Wénzōng) died in the position of a Fújìn.
The Imperial Household Department managed the funeral,
and she was interred in Tiáncūn.
In the first month of the following year, when the emperor ascended the throne,
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Xiàodé Huánghòu,
and her funeral rites were previously revised
to those of a great mourning ceremony.
In the fourth year of Tóngzhì,
she was interred together with Wénzōng in Dìng Líng.
Kāngcí Huáng Guì Tàifēi (Imperial Noble Consort Dowager Kāngcí)
was Xuānzōng's Imperial Noble Consort.
In the seventh month of the fifth year of Xiánfēng,
she was honored as Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager).
She died shortly after.
The emperor observed one hundred days of mourning according to regulations.
She was posthumously granted the additional title Xiàojìng,
enshrined in Fèngxiān Diàn,
and Mù Líng Fēi Yuán (Mausoleum of Concubines at Mù Líng) was changed to Mùdōng Líng.
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
the ancestral temple posthumous title 'Chéng' was added,
and she was enshrined in the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple).
In the second month of the first year of Guāngxù,
Jiāshùn Huánghòu Ménggǔ Ālǔtè Shì (Empress Ménggǔ Ālǔtè of Jiāshùn) died.
Less than one hundred days had passed since Mùzōng's mourning.
After the emperor shed his plain white mourning clothes,
he led his officials in observing mourning for twenty-seven days,
with rites as in previous cases.
She was posthumously granted the title Xiàozhéyì Huánghòu.
In the fifth year,
she was interred together with Mùzōng in Huì Líng.
Cí'ān Huáng Tàihòu (Empress Dowager Cí'ān),
of the Niǔhùlù clan,
was the empress of Wénzōng.
She died in the second month of the seventh year.
She was posthumously granted the title Xiàozhēnxǐan Huánghòu,
and buried in Dìngdōng Líng.
In the tenth month of the thirty-fourth year,
Cíxǐ Tàihuáng Tàihòu (Grand Empress Dowager Cíxǐ) died one day after Dézōng.
The Ministry of Rites was ordered to propose a generous deliberation.
It was subsequently proposed that imperial edicts should use blue ink for one hundred days,
and memorials should be presented fifteen days later.
Princes, dukes, officials, princesses, Fújìn, and noblewomen were to weep and mourn three times daily for twenty-seven days.
Officials were to suspend marriages for a year,
and cease music for twenty-seven months.
The military and civilians in the capital were to cease sacrifices for twenty-seven days,
and the rest was as per the grand mourning rites.
She was posthumously granted the title Xiàoqīnxǐan Huánghòu,
and buried in Dìngdōng Líng.
Funeral rites for Gui Fei (Noble Consorts) and others:
In the early Shùnzhì period,
regulations were established that for the funerals of Fēi (Consorts)
and Bìn (secondary consorts),
the Imperial Household Department was responsible,
and imperial instructions were to be sought when necessary.
In the fourth year of Kāngxī,
Shòukāng Tàifēi Bóěrjìjítè Shì (Consort Dowager Shòukāng, of the Bóěrjìjítè clan) passed away.
The emperor suspended court sessions for three days,
and within the Grand Palace and among the imperial clan, everyone wore plain attire.
Princes, dukes, high officials, princesses, Fújìn, and noblewomen all gathered.
For the first sacrifice,
one hundred forty thousand units of paper money,
ten thousand units of painted satin,
thirty-one banquets,
one ox,
eighteen sheep,
and nine jars of wine
were displayed, and a eulogy was read for the sacrifice.
The next day for the second sacrifice,
ten thousand units of paper money,
five banquets,
three sheep,
and three jars of wine were displayed.
The grand sacrifice was the same as the first sacrifice.
For the preliminary sacrifice during the relocation,
twenty thousand units of paper money,
thirteen banquets,
five sheep,
and five jars of wine were displayed.
Seasonal sacrifices followed the usual practice.
Mourning Rituals for Crown Princes, Imperial Princes, and Imperial Princes' Primary Consorts Mourning rituals for the Crown Prince:
According to the ancestral statutes of the Qīng
dynasty, no heir apparent was formally established.
However, in the third year of Qiánlóng
when the Second Imperial Prince, Yǒnglián, passed away,
Gāozōng decreed:
"Yǒnglián was my嫡子 (dìzǐ, direct descendant/eldest son by the principal wife).
Though not formally enfeoffed,
the grand plan for establishing him as heir had already been decided.
His rites should be observed as for a Crown Prince."
The Ministers of Rites then reported:
"The mourning rites for a Crown Prince
are not recorded in the Collected Statutes.
According to old regulations,
if a child died young,
mourning clothes were not worn.
It is now proposed that
the Emperor wear plain clothes
and cease court for seven days.
If personally attending the libation ceremony,
the hat finial should be removed.
The ministers in charge of the funeral, the dispatched princes and dukes, and the Crown Prince's attendants shall all wear mourning clothes.
The Nèiwùfǔ (Imperial Household Department) captains, and the household guards and cavalry commanders under the household control
— a total of six hundred people —
shall also wear mourning clothes, to be removed on the day of the first sacrifice.
Upon receiving the decree, officials in the directly-governed provinces
shall all remove their hat finials and wear plain clothes for three days.
Marriages shall be suspended, and music ceased.
In the capital, this lasts for forty days;
in the provinces, half that duration.
There is no precedent for a young deceased to have a soul banner.
