However, we request to follow the mourning ceremony for Huáigīn Wáng during the Yōngzhèng
period, where a soul banner was still used.
When outer Mongolian princes,驸马 (fùmǎ, imperial sons-in-law), princes, dukes, Tàijí, princesses, and Fújìn and Gùnjǔ enter the capital during the mourning period,
men shall remove their hat finials,
and women shall remove their head ornaments.
Korean envoys shall wear plain clothes for seven days.
The coffin shall be made of paulownia wood."
At the opening ceremony, the Emperor personally poured wine as a sacrifice,
and personally oversaw the coffin's relocation.
The head of the Board of Rites sacrificed to the hearse.
At the first sacrifice, internal and external officials gathered.
The Emperor went to the funeral hall and poured three cups of wine as an offering.
At each offering, the multitude bowed once.
On this day, mourning clothes were removed and hair shaved.
Before conferring the posthumous title,
an announcement was dispatched in advance to the rear hall of the Tàimiào (Imperial Ancestral Temple) and the Fèngxiān Diàn (Hall for Worshipping Ancestors).
The posthumous title was Duānhuì.
The rites were completed.
The Board of Rites issued the order to all provinces
and sent a dispatch to the King of Cháoxiǎn (Korea),
stating that upon receipt of the document, he should lead his hundred officials in plain clothes,
and military and civilians should cease marriages and music for three days.
Eight years later,
he was buried in the Zhūhuáshān (Zhu Hua Mountain) mausoleum. Mourning rituals for Imperial Princes:
In the fifteenth year of Shùnzhì,
when Rónggīn Wáng passed away,
the funeral arrangements were more elaborate than for an ordinary Prince.
He was buried in the Huánghuāshān (Huang Hua Mountain) mausoleum.
During the Kāngxī
reign,
regulations were established:
for any Imperial Prince who died young,
a small, vermilion coffin was prepared,
and he was interred in Huánghuāshān.
Only a grave pit was dug for a flat burial,
without a mound or a stele.
In the sixth year of Yōngzhèng,
the Eighth Imperial Prince, Fúhuì, passed away.
The Emperor ceased court,
and everyone in the Dà Nèi (Forbidden City) wore plain clothes for three days.
No sacrifices were made to the gods.
An edict commanded a princely burial.
Thirteen years later,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as a Prince
with the posthumous title Huái.
In the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the Imperial Prince Yǒngcóng, only two years old, passed away.
The Emperor stated:
"Although I had secretly decided
to make him heir,
it was not as formally declared as for Crown Prince Duānhuì.
His mourning rites should be superior to those of an ordinary Imperial Prince."
At the grand sacrifice, the Emperor personally attended and offered libations,
conferring the posthumous title Dàomǐn,
and later posthumously enfeoffing him as Zhégīn Wáng.
Two years later,
the Eldest Imperial Prince, Yǒnghuáng, passed away.
His coffin was made of fir wood.
His Fújìn and Imperial Grandson Miándé and others cut their hair and removed their ornaments,
wearing mourning clothes for one hundred days and then removing them,
and plain clothes for twenty-seven months.
The assembled princes and dukes removed their mourning clothes on the day of the grand sacrifice.
The Board of Rites requested to move the coffin on the third day
and cease court for three days.
The edict changed this to five days.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Dìnggīn Wáng
with the posthumous title Ān.
The Emperor personally attended and offered libations at both the first sacrifice and the grand sacrifice.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Third Imperial Prince, Yǒngzhāng, passed away.
An edict commanded the funeral to follow the standard for a Gùnwáng (Prince of a Commandery).
Court ceased for two days.
Everyone in the Dà Nèi and the imperial clan wore plain clothes for five days.
No sacrifices were made to the gods.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as Xúngùnwáng.
In the forty-first year,
the Twelfth Imperial Prince, Yǒngjì, passed away.
An edict commanded the funeral to follow the standard for a Zōngshì Gōng (Imperial Clan Duke).
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
he was posthumously enfeoffed as a Bèilè.
In the eleventh year of Dàoguāng,
the Eldest Imperial Prince, Yìwěi, passed away.
An order commanded the funeral to follow the standard for an Imperial Prince.
The gathering of princesses, Fújìn, and noblewomen was suspended.
No stele was erected in the mausoleum.
He was posthumously enfeoffed as a Bèilè
with the posthumous title Yǐnzhì.
Thirty years later,
he was promoted to Gùnwáng. Mourning for Imperial Princes' Primary Consorts:
By established regulation,

the Heir Apparent of a Qīngwáng (Prince of the First Rank), those below a Duōluó Gùnwáng (Prince of the Second Rank), and those down to Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn (General by Grace), Gùlún Gōngzhǔ (Princess of the First Rank), Hèshuò Fújìn (Primary Consort of a Prince of the Second Rank) and below, down to Gùshān Gégé (Princess of the Second Rank), and the wives of Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn, all gathered.
Morning offerings included a food banquet,
and midday included a fruit banquet.
At the first sacrifice, one soul banner was used,
along with 120,000 pieces of paper money,
twenty-five food banquets,
fifteen sheep,
seven jars of wine,
and a eulogy was read.
For subsequent offerings, 3,000 pieces of paper money were displayed,
twelve food banquets,
and seven sheep and seven jars of wine each.
The ceremonies for the hundredth day, first anniversary, and the four seasonal offerings were the same.
In the thirteenth year of Jiāqìng,
when Xuānzōng was still the Second Imperial Prince,
his Fújìn, Niǔhùlù
Shi, passed away.
The Emperor ordered that mourning clothes be worn immediately,
to be removed after the first sacrifice.
For Imperial Princes' Fújìn who had not yet established their own residences, the rules for a Qīngwáng's Fújìn were followed.
The coffin and its cover were both red.
As there was no ceremonial procession,
a golden-yellow cover was specially bestowed.
The ceremonial procession still followed the standard for a Qīngwáng's Fújìn,
but the flag color used was bordered white.
This was established as a regulation.
In the seventh year of Dàoguāng,
when Imperial Prince Yìwěi's Fújìn, Guā'ěrjiā Shì, passed away,
the internal and external gatherings and the pre-arrival reception at the temporary resting place were suspended.
In the eleventh year,
she was posthumously enfeoffed as Bèilè Fūrén (Bèilè's Wife).
After selecting an auspicious day, an official was dispatched to the funeral hall with a paper册 (cè, scroll/register)
to read the eulogy and offer sacrifice.
Mourning Rituals for Princes of the First Rank and their Primary Consorts, etc. In the ninth year of Shùnzhì,
upon news of a Qīngwáng's death,
court ceased for three days.
For a Shìzǐ (Heir Apparent of a Qīngwáng) or Gùnwáng, it was two days.
Later, this was changed so that for a Bèilè (Prince of the Third Rank) and below, court did not cease.
For burial equipment,
from Qīngwáng down to Bèilè, colored coffins were used,
with five layers of matting.
For Bèizi (Prince of the Fourth Rank) down to Fǔguógōng (Duke of the Second Rank), the coffins were the same,
with three layers of matting.
For Zhènguó Jiāngjūn (General of the First Rank) and below, vermilion coffins were used,
with one layer of matting.
Upon death, ceremonial guards were arranged.
For Qīngwáng, fifteen saddled horses and loose horses;
for Shìzǐ and Gùnwáng, fourteen each;
for Bèilè, thirteen each;
for Bèizi, twelve each;
for Zhènguógōng (Duke of the First Rank), ten each;
for Fǔguógōng, eight each;
for Zhènguó Jiāngjūn, seven whip horses;
for Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (General of the Second Rank), five;
for Fèngguó Jiāngjūn (General of the Third Rank), four;
for Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn, three.
All within and outside the Prince's household wore mourning clothes,
to be removed on the day of the grand sacrifice.
Internal and external officials removed their hat ornaments and wore plain clothes to gather,
each according to their respective regulations.
Zhènguó Jiāngjūn and below did not attend the funeral.
Princesses, Fújìn, and noblewomen attending the funeral
required an Imperial decree on a case-by-case basis.
For Qīngwáng down to Fǔguógōng,
there were two Imperial sacrifices,
with an official dispatched to the tomb to read a eulogy and offer sacrifice.
The Zōngrénfǔ (Imperial Clan Court) requested the bestowal of a posthumous title,
and drafted the inscription for the stele.
The Gōngbù (Board of Works) erected the stele and built the pavilion.
For Bèilè and below, steles were self-erected,
and burial expenses were granted with varying amounts.
For Zhènguó Jiāngjūn down to Fèngguó Jiāngjūn, two sacrifices were granted,
with one eulogy.
The erection of a stele and bestowal of a posthumous title
required an Imperial decree on a case-by-case basis.
Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn were granted sacrifices without a eulogy,
no stele was erected,
and no posthumous title was granted.
When a son of a Qīn Wáng, Zhì Gōng, who had been married, passed away,
saddles and horses were bestowed by Xǔ Chén,
and the sacrificial offerings were to be made according to the examples for their parents,
except that no official was dispatched to offer sacrifices.
Unmarried young sons were not to have tombs built.
For burial periods,
a Qīn Wáng observed a full year,
a Jùn Wáng seven months,
and a Bèizi and below five months.
It was also decreed that for the mourning of a Qīn Wáng Fújìn and below,
internal and external gatherings were to be held as prescribed.
The ceremonial guards were arranged according to their noble rank.
A Qīn Wáng Fújìn, Cè Fújìn, and Shìzi Fújìn received one imperial sacrifice.
In the twelfth year,
it was decreed that for the mourning of a princess married to an outer vassal,
one imperial sacrifice was given,
and an official was dispatched to the tomb to read the eulogy and offer sacrifices.
In the fourth year of Kāngxī,
it was decreed that the bestowal of posthumous titles from Bèilè down to Rù Bā Fēn Gōng required an imperial decree.
In the ninth year,
it was decreed that for the mourning of a Qīn Wáng down to a Fǔguó Gōng,
the officials of their respective mansions were to wear mourning attire.

For the twelve branches of Lǐ Qīn Wáng, Sù Qīn Wáng, Chéngzé Qīn Wáng, Jìngjǐn Qīn Wáng, Ráo Yú Qīn Wáng, Zhèng Qīn Wáng, Kèqín Jùn Wáng, Kèxī Bèilè, Jìngníng Bèilè, Gù'ěrmǎhóng Bèizi, and Fúlèihēi Gōng,
all those who were descended from these branches,
including themselves and the officials of their mansions and their titled ladies, were to wear mourning attire.
Those not of these branches who attended the mourning removed their hat plumes.
Attending officials acted according to their masters.
Honored relatives were exempt from mourning attire.
In the fifty-second year,
it was decreed that when the birth mother of a Bèilè died,
mourning arrangements were to be made as for a principal wife,
and an official was dispatched to read the eulogy and offer sacrifices.
In the fifty-fourth year,
it was decreed that a Gǔlún Gōngzhǔ with descendants
was permitted to request the erection of a stele and the bestowal of a posthumous title.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
by imperial decree, it was deliberated and decided that henceforth, the emperor's descendants would observe the five grades of mourning attire.
When observing the mourning of an uncle or brother,
they would, as per custom, submit a memorial and attend the mourning.
For the various princes and below,
regardless of their rank,
when observing mourning for a Xiǎogōng and above,
they were to attend the mourning and don mourning attire.
The period for Qī (one year) was sixty days, Dàgōng (nine months) one month, and Xiǎogōng (five months) seven days before removal.
In the third year of Qiánlóng,
it was further decreed that the mourning attire for Qī was removed on the day of the grand sacrifice, Dàgōng on the day of the first sacrifice, and Xiǎogōng on the day of the funeral procession.
In the twenty-first year,
an imperial edict stated that the bestowal of posthumous titles for a Zhū Wáng's Cè Fújìn required an imperial decree,
and sacrifices were not to exceed once,
and the giving of sacrificial texts was abolished.
In the thirty-sixth year,
it was decreed that Bèilè, Bèizi, and Gōng holding a first-rank official position were permitted to request a posthumous title,
while Zhèngguó Jiàngjūn and Fǔguó Jiàngjūn holding a first-rank official position were permitted to request funeral gratuities.
In the fortieth year,
it was decreed that any Cè Fújìn who was the birth mother of a Wáng, etc.,
was permitted to request imperial sacrifices,
reduced by one grade from that of a Dǐ Fújìn.
In the fifty-sixth year,
when the Fūrén of Zhèngguó Gōng Jìnchāng passed away,
an imperial edict abolished the imperial sacrifice;
subsequently, this served as a precedent.
In the seventeenth year of Jiāqìng,
when Yìshòu, the son of Bèilè Miánhéng, passed away,
an order was issued to posthumously confer upon him the title of Wèi Rù Bā Fēn Fǔguó Gōng.
Henceforth, if a member of the imperial clan was posthumously enfeoffed as a Gōng,
it was invariably treated as Wèi Rù Bā Fēn,
and this was established as a regulation.
Funeral ceremonies for princesses and below:
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì,
it was decreed that the mourning for a Gǔlún Gōngzhǔ was to be treated like that of a Qīn Wáng Fújìn,
a Héshuò Gōngzhǔ like that of a Shìzi Fújìn,
a Jùnzhǔ like that of a Jùn Wáng Fújìn,
a Xiànzhǔ like that of a Bèilè Fūrén,
a Jùnjūn like that of a Bèizi Fūrén,
and a Xiànjūn like that of a Zhèngguó Gōng Fūrén.
In the twelfth year,
it was decreed that for princesses married to outer vassals down to Xiànzhǔ, an imperial eulogy was to be given,
and an official was dispatched to the tomb to read the libation.
For Jùnjūn and below,
no eulogy was given for sacrifices.
In the twenty-fourth year of Dàoguāng,
it was decreed that when a princess died,
the Nèi Wù Fǔ was to request an imperial decree,
and if an official was ordered to manage the mourning,
all rites and ceremonies
were to be reported to the Lǐ Bù for deliberation.
Upon receiving the imperial decree,
another dispatch was sent to various departments for execution.
The Èfù would manage the mourning himself.
The Lǐ Bù should report on the assembly place.
For the mourning of princesses and below,
the assembly required a temporary imperial decree.
If approval was granted,
a dispatch was sent to the Zōngrén Fǔ and the Five Banners for circulation.
For those who had not yet married or received enfeoffment,
the Nèi Wù Fǔ managed the mourning,
and no assembly was held.
Funeral ceremonies for Chún Xián Qīn Wáng and his Fújìn: In the sixteenth year of Guāngxù,
when Chún Qīn Wáng Yìxuǎn died,
it was decreed that he be referred to as
"Huángdì Běnshēng Kǎo" (the Emperor's birth father).
The Emperor observed mourning for a full year,
wearing plain white for eleven days,
and suspended court as such.
Within the year, when in the private palace, he continued to wear plain clothes.
On New Year's Day, when visiting the Tángzi,
proceeding to Cíníng Gōng,
and receiving homage at Tàihé Diàn,
he wore ceremonial attire.
However, when ascending the throne, no memorials were proclaimed,
music was arranged but not played,
and banquets for imperial relatives and court officials were suspended.
The Emperor's name was written on the sacrificial texts and stele inscriptions.
For the initial sacrifice, grand sacrifice, and removal to the imperial tomb, he wore a dark blue robe and jacket,
removed the hat plume,
and personally performed the rites.
Regulations for the ancestral temple system, sacrifices, and burial were also established.
The tile colors for the main hall and main gate of the temple
used yellow glazed tiles in the center,
and green glazed tiles for the ridge of the hall and the surroundings of the main gate.
Sacrifices were offered with the rites of the Son of Heaven.
Seasonal sacrifices were performed
on the first day of the lunar month in the four mid-seasons,
and on the anniversary of death, he personally offered sacrifices.
Burial was conducted with the rites of a Qīn Wáng.
The Emperor personally composed the stele inscription,
and he was posthumously titled Xián.
In the thirty-second year,
when his Fújìn Yèhènālā Shì died,
she was referred to as
"Huángdì Běnshēng Bǐ" (the Emperor's birth mother),
and her funeral ceremonies followed the precedent of Chún Xián Qīn Wáng.
Anniversaries of Death: In the tenth year of Shùnzhì,
it was decreed that on the anniversaries of death for the Three Mausoleums of Shèngjīng and Xīngjīng,
the tomb-guarding officials were dispatched to perform the rites,
offering wine and fruit,
without reading eulogies
or presenting silk.
In the twelfth year,
it was revised that officials be dispatched on anniversaries of death,
with the Lǐ Bù presenting a memorial for imperial instruction.
In the third year of Kāngxī,
it was again decreed that on the anniversaries of death for the Three Mausoleums, sacrifices were to be offered before the spirit tablet in the Lóng'ēn Diàn by unveiling the curtain.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
after the period of mourning for the Shèngzǔ had concluded,
the Emperor, with boundless sorrow and admiration,
wished to follow the sacrificial rites observed during the three-year mourning period,
and he submitted this for deliberation by the ministers of rites.
Soon after, the deliberation was presented,
and it was decided that according to the precedent of annual sacrifices,
one prince, duke, or high official from the capital or the imperial mausoleums would be dispatched to preside over the sacrifice,
and one-third of the princes, dukes, and officials in the capital would attend as accompanying sacrificers.
This was established as a regulation.
In the thirteenth year,
when Gāozōng succeeded to the throne,
it was deliberated and decided that on the anniversary of Shèngzǔ's death,
it would follow the grand seasonal sacrifices at the mausoleums,
using a grand animal sacrifice (Tàiláo),
offering silk and libation cups,
reading eulogies,
with an official dispatched to preside over the sacrifice,
and all mausoleum officials would attend as accompanying sacrificers,
abolishing the dispatch of capital officials.
Henceforth, the anniversaries of death for successive emperors and empresses
would always be observed as per this precedent.
According to regulations,
on the anniversaries of death for emperors and empresses,
all internal and external personnel wore plain clothes,
banquets were suspended,
music ceased,
and judicial matters were not handled.
The Emperor proceeded to the rear hall of Fèngxiān Diàn to offer incense and perform rites.
When performing the sacrifice to the Southern Suburbs,
the Emperor reviewed the prayer tablet.
On an anniversary of death,
he wore a dragon robe, dragon jacket, and prayer beads,
while attending officials wore python robes, embroidered jackets, and prayer beads.
When reviewing the prayer tablets for the Northern Suburbs, ancestral temples, altars to the gods of land and grain, and other medium sacrifices,
all wore dragon jackets and prayer beads,
and attending officials all wore official robes with insignia squares and prayer beads.
During the fasting period for grand sacrifices,
he wore everyday clothes and prayer beads,
and accompanying and attending officials also did the same.
If a sacrifice day coincided with an anniversary of death,
during the performance of rites, sacrificial attire and music were used,
but after the rites, plain clothes were resumed.
Bestowal of Sacrifices and Burials: When Shìzǔ first entered the pass,
following the precedents from the Chóngdé period,
for Gōng of extraordinary rank, and Gōng of the first, second, and third ranks who died,
officials were dispatched to offer sacrifices three times;
for Zǐ and Fù Dūtǒng, twice;
for Cānlǐng and Zuǒlǐng, once.
For those who died in battle or had meritorious service,
officials were dispatched to manage the mourning,
which was determined by imperial decision.
In the third year of Shùnzhì (1646),
it was stipulated that for civilian Gōng, Hóu, Bó, Zǐ concurrently serving as Nèidàchén, Dūtǒng, Dàxuéshì, Shàngshū, or Zhènshǒu Jiāngjūn who passed away,
a memorial stele would be erected upon imperial decree,
and a single memorial ceremony held.
For hereditary Gōng, Hóu, Bó, Zǐ who died in office within three years,
only sacrificial offerings would be given,
without a memorial inscription,
and no stele would be erected.
For officials of the second and third ranks who died,
sacrificial offerings would be given.
If they had completed a full three-year term, a memorial inscription would be given.
Those with military achievements
were eligible to request the erection of a stele.
In the thirteenth year (1656),
it was decided that for Zuǒlǐng, Yuánwàiláng, and Zhǔshì who completed a full three-year term,
sacrificial offerings and a memorial inscription would be given.
Those who had not completed the term would receive no memorial inscription.
The same applied to those who retired.
In the fifteenth year (1658),
it was stipulated that for chief officials of boards and courts whose rank was elevated to the first or second品 (rank),
a memorial ceremony would be held and a stele erected.
Those of the third rank who had completed a full three-year term were treated similarly.
If they had not completed the term,
only a memorial ceremony would be held.
Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng, Fùdūtǒng, Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng, and Bùjūn Zǒngwèi, upon completing their examination, were treated as third-rank officials.
If they were Bónán,
they could receive a memorial ceremony and have a stele erected.
Cānlǐng and Qiánfēng Cānlǐng who completed a full three-year term
would receive a memorial ceremony,
but no stele would be erected.
Fourth-rank Qīng and Shàoqīng who completed their examination were treated similarly;
otherwise, no memorial inscription would be given.
Those who died in battle, regardless of rank,
were eligible for a special imperial posthumous grant.
Nèidàchén, Dūtǒng, Dàxuéshì, Shàngshū, Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng, Fùdūtǒng, Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng, Shìláng, Xuéshì, and Bùjūn Zǒngwèi who retired with their original rank
were treated the same for memorial ceremonies and stele erection.
Incumbent Qīngchē Dūwèi, Zuǒlǐng, Jìdūwèi, Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, and Zhǔshì
received a memorial ceremony, but no stele inscription.
For hereditary Gōng, Hóu, and Bó who held official positions,
posthumous grants were given according to their official positions;
otherwise, only sacrificial offerings were given.
In the seventeenth year (1660),

it was stipulated that for those who personally attained the ranks of civilian Gōng, Hóu, Bó, Zǐ, as well as Dūtǒng who held the position of Nèidàchén, and Zhènshǒu Jiāngjūn, a full burial would be granted.
Dàxuéshì,
Shàngshū,
Zuǒ/Yòu Dūyùshǐ with elevated rank and Gōngbǎo status,
were granted a full burial equivalent to a first-rank official.
Those without additional titles or elevated rank were granted a full burial equivalent to a second-rank official.
Shìláng without concurrent titles or elevated rank who completed their full term
were granted a full burial equivalent to a third-rank official;
those who had not completed the term received half of it.
Fourth-rank Qīng, Shàoqīng, or those concurrently holding the title of Shàoqīng,
were treated as fourth-rank officials,
and only sacrificial offerings were given.
Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng, Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng, Fùdūtǒng, and Bùjūn Zǒngwèi who completed their full term were granted a full burial;
those who had not completed the term received half of it,
and a memorial ceremony was held once.
From military officers of Cānlǐng and civil officials of Lángzhōng downwards,
no sacrificial offerings were given.
Those who died in battle were treated as before.
In the eighteenth year (1661),
it was stipulated that for civilian Gōng, Hóu, Bó who personally attained their ranks, burial arrangements would be made,
and a memorial ceremony held once,
with additional ceremonies by special imperial favor.
Dūtǒng, Nèidàchén, Dàxuéshì, Shàngshū, Yòu Dūyùshǐ, Zǐ, Zhènshǒu Jiāngjūn, and officials with additional titles or elevated rank to the first or second品,
were all granted burial arrangements according to their rank,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
Third-rank Shìláng, Xuéshì, Tōngzhèngshǐ, and Dàlǐsìqīng who completed their full term were granted a full burial;
those who had not completed the term received half of it,
and a memorial ceremony was held once.
Cānlǐng, Xiélǐng, Lángzhōng, Zuǒlǐng, and third-rank Shìwèi, Hùwèi Guān who died in battle
received a memorial ceremony once.
Han civil officials of the first, second, or third rank who completed their full term
all received a memorial ceremony and burial arrangements;
those who had not completed the term received half of it,
and a memorial ceremony was held once.
Outside officials from Bùzhèngshǐ and Ànchásǐ downwards
followed the regulations for capital officials.
Military officials with additional titles from Fùjiāng upwards
were granted burial arrangements,
and a memorial ceremony held once;
the same applied to those without concurrent titles who completed their full term;
those who had not completed the term received half of it,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
Zhīxiàn and Shǒubèi and above who died in battle
were granted burial arrangements according to their posthumously conferred rank,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
All Manchu and Han civil and military officials who retired from their original posts
received the same posthumous grants as incumbent officials.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī (1670),
it was stipulated that for Gōng, Hóu, and Bó who personally attained their ranks or inherited them, a full burial would be granted,
an official dispatched to read the memorial text,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
Nèidàchén, Dūtǒng, Zǐ-rank Sǎnzhíchén, Dàxuéshì, Shàngshū, Zuǒ Dūyùshǐ, Zǐ, hereditary Zǐ, Zhènshǒu Jiāngjūn, and Tídū,
were all granted a full burial according to their rank,
an official dispatched to read the memorial text,
and a memorial ceremony held once.

Nán-rank Sǎnzhíchén, Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng, Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng, Fùdūtǒng, Shìláng, those who personally attained the rank of Nán, Xuéshì, Fù Dūyùshǐ, Zǒngdū, Zǒngbīng Guān, and Xúnfǔ with elevated rank to the second品,
were all granted a full burial according to their elevated rank,
an official dispatched to read the memorial text,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
Third-rank Shìláng, Xuéshì, Fù Dūyùshǐ, Xúnfǔ, Tōngzhèngshǐ, and Dàlǐsìqīng,
upon completing their full term, were granted a full burial;
those who had not completed the term received half of it,
and an official was dispatched to read the memorial text,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
Bùzhèngshǐ were granted a full burial,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
For Yúnqíwèi and third-rank Shìwèi and above,
and civil officials of Zhīxiàn and military officials of Shǒubèi and above who died in battle,
a full burial was granted according to their posthumously conferred rank,
and a memorial ceremony held once.
In the twenty-fourth year of Dàoguāng (1844),
the rites for bestowing sacrificial offerings to Wáng, Gōng and below were established.
On the day of the ceremony,
honor guards were arranged in the main hall.
Before the spirit tablet, a ritual table was placed,
displaying the bestowed sacrificial items.
Self-prepared sacrificial items were arranged on the left and right.
Before the table, the position for the dispatched official to offer libations was set.
To the east, a table for the invocation text was set,
facing north.
To the south, a burning pit for paper offerings was set,
with paper and silk provided.
When the dispatched official arrived,
the chief mourner, leading kinsmen and subordinate officials, would kneel and welcome him outside the main gate.
An official from the Lǐbù would carry the memorial inscription and enter through the central gate,
placing it on the east table.
The dispatched official would follow,
take his position standing,
and the chief mourner and all below would take their positions kneeling.
After the official who read the invocation text finished reading,
the dispatched official would kneel and offer three libations,
bowing once for each libation.
Zhènguó Jiāngjūn and below would offer libations standing.
The chief mourner would lead the assembly in performing the rites.
After completion,
they would rise,
lament,
and burn the memorial inscription.
The chief mourner would lead the assembly in looking towards the imperial palace to give thanks,
performing three kneeling bows and nine prostrations.
The dispatched official would exit,
and be seen off kneeling outside the main gate.
For bestowing posthumous titles, Qīnwáng typically used one character,
while Bèilè and below, and civil and military ministers used two characters.
For Jùnwáng's posthumous titles,
the Ming dynasty system of using two characters was still followed,
though occasionally one character was used.
During the reign of Shèngzǔ (Kāngxī Emperor),
when posthumous titles were retrospectively bestowed upon Jùnwáng,
both Manchu and Han texts used one character,
thus establishing the new rule.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì (1652),
it was stipulated that upon hearing of the death of a Qīnwáng or below,
the Zōngrénfǔ would request a posthumous title,
and the Nèiyuàn would draft the stele inscription.
In the fourth year of Kāngxī (1665),
it was decided that when bestowing posthumous titles upon various Wáng,
an additional character would be added to their granted title.
For Bèilè and below, up to Bārùfēng Gōng,
the decision of whether to grant a title required an imperial decree.
In the thirty-sixth year of Qiánlóng (1771),
by imperial decree, it was deliberated and decided that Bèilè to Fǔguógōng who concurrently held first-rank positions would be granted posthumous titles,
still requiring an imperial decree.
Those who concurrently held second-rank or lower positions, or no positions, would no longer be granted posthumous titles.
According to regulations,
for officials of the first rank and above, the decision of whether to grant a posthumous title required the emperor's adjudication.
Officials of the second rank and below were not eligible to request one.
Those who did receive posthumous titles
were usually by special imperial decree,
either for diligence and hard work,
or for integrity and righteousness,
or for literary merit,
or for military achievements.
This was an exceptional honor
to encourage and inspire.
Before the Jiāqìng and Dàoguāng eras,
the bestowal of posthumous titles was strict,
and it was often the case that those who reached the first rank, who by precedent should have received one, did not.
In the reign of Shìzōng (Yǒngzhèng Emperor),
First-rank Gōng Fúshàn,
Dàxuéshì Wèi Yìjiè,
Jiāngjūn Fónílè and Mǎngyītú,
Dūtǒng Féng Guóxiāng,
Shàngshū Tāng Bīn, Xú Cháo, Mǎěrhǎn and others,
who were highly esteemed and influential,
were enshrined in the Xiánliáng Temple.
It was not until the early years of Gāozōng (Qiánlóng Emperor)
that they finally received retrospective posthumous titles.
This grand ceremony of changing names
was truly not easy to obtain.
According to the imperial decree,
for those granted a posthumous title, the Lǐbù (Board of Rites) would seek imperial approval,
and then inform the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat) to have the典籍 (Dianjí) draft it.
By the reign of Mùzōng,
Grand Secretary Zhuó Bǐngtián changed the practice to the Hàn Piàoxiān (Chinese style memorial slips),
and it was solely managed by the Shìdú (Reader).
Grand Secretaries and those appointed to the Hánlín Yuàn (Hanlin Academy)
were eligible to receive the posthumous title
"Wén".
There were also cases where individuals received the title Wén by special imperial grace.
The Shìdú would propose eight characters,
and the Grand Secretary would select four characters.
For others, sixteen characters would be proposed,
and the Grand Secretary would select eight,
all subject to imperial final decision.
For military officials who received the title Wén,
such as the Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén (Minister of the Imperial Bodyguard) Suǒní (Sonin), who received the title Wénzhōng,
it was an exceptional honor.
However,
"Wénzhèng"
was not permitted to be proposed;
it was only granted by special imperial grace.
For civil officials, from a third-rank Qīng (Minister) internally, and from a Bùzhèngshǐ (Provincial Administration Commissioner) externally,
it was not customary to grant posthumous titles.
However, Yùshǐ (Censor) Lù Lǒngqí was titled Qīngxiàn,
Shìjiǎng Xuéshì (Lecturer of the Hanlin Academy) Qín Chéngyè was titled Wénjié,
and Tàicháng Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) Táng Jiàn was titled Kèshèn.
These were exceptions made out of respect for scholarly officials,
and deep consideration for imperial tutors,
and did not follow standard procedure.
In Xiánfēng's third year (1853),
the Lǐchén (Ministers of Rites) memorialized to establish that civil officials of the second rank who died as martyrs
should be granted posthumous titles equivalent to first-rank officials.
For example, for Ánchásǐ (Provincial Judicial Commissioner) who received generous compensation,
the Lǐbù could also invoke this precedent to petition.
After the military campaigns,
many officials at the Dào (Circuit), Fǔ (Prefecture), Zhōu (Department), and Xiàn (County) levels died in service,
and border officials would memorialize for them,
disregarding the usual regulations.
For military officials who died in service,
those below Cāncóng (Battalion Commander)
were to be considered for compensation as if they were Fùjiàng (Brigade General);
those below Xiélǐng (Assistant Commander)
were to be considered for compensation as if they were Fù Dūtǒng (Deputy Lieutenant General): all could invoke the new regulations to memorialize for this.
However, those whose military achievements were incomplete
were not permitted to use the character
"Xiāng".
By the twelfth year (1863),
an edict stated:
"Henceforth, for civil and military officials
whose official ranks do not customarily qualify for posthumous titles,
no petitions should be made indiscriminately."
At this point, the restrictions became somewhat stricter.
In Guāngxù's fourth year (1878),
Guìzhōu Xúnfǔ (Governor of Guizhou) Lí Péijìng petitioned for a posthumous title for the dismissed Zǒngdū (Governor-General) Hè Chánglíng.
The imperial decree stated that the institution of posthumous naming
did not allow for abuse or presumption,
and issued a stern admonition,
and also sent Lí Péijìng to the Board of Civil Office for deliberation.
There were also cases of posthumous titles being revoked,
such as Shěn Déqián and Biàn Sānyuán.
This was either due to re-evaluation of their lives
or revelations after their deaths,
leading to the removal of their official ranks and the toppling of their memorial tablets,
as a warning.
Regarding the posthumous titles of the Korean kings,
they were formerly also drafted by the Nèigé.
Subsequently,
because the proposed characters sometimes touched upon the given names of their past kings,
it was changed to having their country propose eight characters themselves,
which were then submitted for the emperor's final decision.
Imperial Rites for Foreign Vassals
In Shùnzhì's thirteenth year (1656),
it was decreed that for the funerals of Mongol vassal Qīnwáng (Princes of the First Rank) and others,
officials would be dispatched to deliver sacrificial texts to be read at the tomb,
and the chief mourner, with his subordinates, would kneel to receive them.
After the rites,
they would face the imperial palace to give thanks, performing the three kneelings and nine kowtows.
From kings downwards,
the sacrifices were conducted as before,
but the sacrificial animals and items
varied in grandeur according to their rank.
For those with significant achievements,
memorial tablets were erected and generous compensation granted,
with special dispatch of ministers and imperial guards,
all by imperial grace.
For the deaths of Qīnwáng and Jùnwáng (Princes of the Second Rank) Fùjìn (Princess Consorts),
sacrifices were dispatched as per custom.
For Bèilè (Princes of the Third Rank) down to Gōng Fūrén (Duchesses),
sacrifices were dispatched,
but without sacrificial texts.
When news arrived of the deaths of the Korean king's mother consort, queen, or crown prince,
the Lǐchén petitioned for imperial compensation,
and envoys (a principal and a deputy) were dispatched to deliver sacrificial items, incense, and paper money for the imperial sacrifice.
In Qiánlóng's fifty-first year (1786),
when the Korean Crown Prince Lǐ Xié passed away,
the Lǐbù reported it.
An imperial decree stated that Korea had always maintained its vassal status,
and was most notably respectful and obedient,
and ordered double the usual sacrificial items to be given,
showing exceptional benevolence.
In Jiāqìng's tenth year (1805),
when news arrived of the death of King Lǐ Gǒng's great-grandmother, the Zhūangshùn Wángfēi (Princess Zhuangshun),
a single sacrifice was bestowed.
When the kings of Liúqiú (Ryukyu) and Yuènán (Vietnam) died,
upon notification of mourning,
envoys were dispatched for imperial sacrifices,
and silver and silk were also given.
For the deaths of their mothers, consorts, or crown princes,
no mourning was announced,
and no imperial compensation was granted.
If an envoy fell ill and died in Beijing,
a petition for imperial compensation rites would be submitted,
a coffin and sacrifice would be bestowed,
and burial in their homeland was permitted.
Funeral Rites for Officials
According to regulations,
when an official fell ill, they were moved to the main chamber; when critically ill, a will was written.
Officials of the third rank and above prepared a memorial of their last wishes.
Crying only commenced after death.
A chief mourner and chief mourner's wife were appointed.
The various attendants responsible for the funeral arranged the coffin.
Dukes and Marquises used plain wood,
while Hou (Marquises), Bo (Earls), and first-rank officials used vermilion coffins.
An obituary was announced.
A deathbed and curtained hall were set up,
and bathing implements were arranged.
Then the "hán" (placing of items in the mouth) ceremony took place.
For third-rank officials and above, small pearls and jades were used.
For seventh-rank officials and above, five pieces of gold and wood shavings were used.
The deceased was dressed in layers of clothing:
one set of everyday attire,
and court robes, caps, and belts according to their rank.
The next day was the minor shrouding,
with the shrouding bed placed east of the hall.
Shrouding garments were added:
for third-rank officials and above, five layers,
three lined and two unlined;
for fifth-rank officials and above, three layers,
two lined and one unlined;
for sixth-rank officials and below, two layers,
one lined and one unlined: all made of silk.
One lined quilt was also used.
The day after that was the major shrouding and sealing of the coffin.
A spirit bed was set up east of the coffin,
and a spirit seat in front of the coffin.
An offering table was arranged.
The chief mourner and all sons resided in a mourning hut.
Clan members each wore their respective mourning attire.
Morning and evening offerings of dishes and meals were made.
At noon, cakes and pastries were offered.
On the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month,
the morning offering was a grand sacrifice,
with more elaborate dishes and fruits.
For the first sacrifice,
a feast table with a sheep and wine was arranged,
and paper money was prepared.
For a Gōng (Duke), fifteen tables were set,
seven sheep,
and forty thousand pieces of paper money;
for a Hou (Marquis), twelve tables,
and thirty-six thousand pieces of paper money;
for a Bo (Earl), twelve tables,
and thirty-two thousand pieces of paper money: all with six sheep.
For a first-rank official, ten tables,
five sheep,
and twenty-eight thousand pieces of paper money;
for a second-rank official, eight tables,
four sheep,
and twenty-four thousand pieces of paper money;
for a third-rank official, six tables,
and twenty thousand pieces of paper money;
for a fourth-rank official, five tables,
and sixteen thousand pieces of paper money: all with three sheep.
For a fifth-rank official, four tables,
and twelve thousand pieces of paper money;
for sixth and seventh-rank officials, three tables,
and ten thousand pieces of paper money: all with two sheep.
Clan members gathered,
and the chief mourner and others performed two bows,
crying and offering sacrifices according to ritual.
After the final sacrifice,
those observing "dàgōng" (second degree of mourning) changed into plain clothes.
The same applied to the grand sacrifice.
After the initial sacrifice,
those observing "qīfú" (first degree of mourning) changed into plain clothes.
After a hundred days, a sacrifice was offered and hair was shaven.
Burial took place after three months.
The burial ground for a first-rank official was ninety *bù*,
the mound was one *zhàng* and six *chǐ* high,
decreasing successively down to twenty *bù* with a mound two *chǐ* high, then stopping.
It was enclosed by a wall.
For a Gōng, Hóu, or Bó, the perimeter was forty *zhàng*,
with four households to guard the tomb;
for second-rank officials and above, the perimeter was thirty-five *zhàng*,
with two households;
for fifth-rank officials and above, the perimeter was thirty *zhàng*,
with one household;
for sixth-rank officials and below, the perimeter was twelve *zhàng*,
with only two people to guard it.
For officials from Gōng down to the second rank,
stone figures, *wàngzhù* pillars, and two each of stone tigers, sheep, and horses were used.
Third-rank officials had no stone figures,
fourth-rank officials had no stone sheep,
and fifth-rank officials had no stone tigers.
For the tomb gate, a stele was carved.
For a Gōng, Hóu, or Bó, the *chīshǒu* was three *chǐ* two *cùn* high,
the stele body was nine *chǐ* high,
three *chǐ* six *cùn* wide,
and the *guīfū* was three *chǐ* eight *cùn* high.
First-rank officials used a *chīshǒu*,
second-rank officials a *qílínshǒu*,
and third-rank officials a *tiānlù bìxiéshǒu*.
Fourth to seventh-rank officials used a round top and square base.
The top, compared to a Gōng, Hóu, or Bó, successively decreased by two *chǐ* down to one *chǐ* eight *cùn* and stopped.
The stele body successively decreased by five *cùn* down to five *chǐ* five *cùn* and stopped.
The width successively decreased by two *cùn* down to two *chǐ* two *cùn* and stopped.
The base successively decreased by two *cùn* down to two *chǐ* four *cùn* and stopped.
For carving the burial epitaph (*kuàngzhì*), two stone slabs were used:
one for the cover,
inscribed with "Tomb of such-and-such official";
the other for the base,
inscribed with the name, native place, three ancestral generations, birth year, death and burial month and day, and the burial place of descendants.
For women, the posthumous honors followed those of their husband and sons/grandsons.
The two stones faced each other,
bound with iron,
and buried in the tomb.
For making the coffin carriage (*jiùyú*),
a bamboo grid was used on top,
adorned with colorful silk,
with curtains hung on the sides,
tassels hanging from the four corners,
and silk banners (*zēnghuāng*) and silk awnings (*zēngwéi*) both in blue.
Gōng, Hóu, and Bó used five-colored woven silk;
first and second-rank officials used gold-brocaded silk;
fifth-rank officials and above painted clouds and *qì*;
sixth and seventh-rank officials used plain silk without decoration.
It was carried on poles.
Fifth-rank officials and above used red poles;
sixth and seventh-rank officials decorated with red chalk.
Painted *shà* fans were used to screen the coffin:
four for fifth-rank officials and above;
two for sixth and seventh-rank officials.
Two funeral cloths (*yǐnbù*),
one meritorious cloth (*gōngbù*),
and one spirit carriage (*língchē*).
Burial objects (*míngqì*) followed local customs.
An auspicious day was chosen for the funeral procession (*fāyǐn*).
The evening before, an ancestral offering (*zǔdiàn*) was made.
The next day, a farewell offering (*qiǎndiàn*) was made,
and all attendees for the burial gathered.
A Gōng had eight saddled horses,
successively decreasing down to two.
The ceremonial retinue led the way,
guided by red streamers (*dānzhào*) and inscription banners (*míngjīng*).
During the Mǎn dynasty, red streamers were used;
during the Hàn dynasty, inscription banners were used.
Upon reaching the tomb site,
the burial took place.
Sacrifices were made to Hòutǔ,
the spirit tablet was inscribed,
solemnly placed,
the spirit entered the carriage,
then the return wailing,
followed by the *Yú* ritual.
Sheep, wine, and paper/silk offerings varied according to rank.
After the sacrifice was completed,
the second *Yú* was performed on a soft day,
and the third *Yú* on a hard day.
One hundred days later, the "cessation of wailing" (*zúcū*) occurred.
The next day, the spirit tablet was inducted into the family ancestral temple (*fùjiāmiào*).
After one year, the minor *Xiáng* sacrifice (*xiǎoxiáng*) was performed.
After two years, the major *Xiáng* sacrifice (*dàxiáng*) was performed,
and the spirit tablet was moved into the temple.
The invocator read the memorial address,
and the chief mourner prostrated five times.
After this,
the spirit tablet was re-inscribed,
and an east chamber was set up at the temple,
where the ancestral tablet (*tiāozhǔ*) was enshrined and stored in a side chamber.
Then the spirit seat (*língzuò*) was removed.
One month later, the *Tán* sacrifice (*tán*) was performed.
The mourning period up to this point totaled twenty-seven months.
The chief mourner went to the temple to respectfully perform the *Tán* ritual.
For those who heard of the death while away,
upon receipt of the訃 (fù) notice,
they changed clothes,
wailed,
and hastened to the funeral (*bēnsāng*).
Upon arriving home, they leaned on the coffin and wailed,
and the next day donned mourning clothes (*chéngfú*).
The mourning period began on the day the訃 (fù) notice was received.
Other rules were the same.
If one heard of a death requiring mourning for less than a year (*qī*),
they changed clothes, set up a spirit tablet, and wailed.
If they hastened to the funeral,
they donned mourning clothes upon arriving home.
If an official was in office,
for the death of anyone other than their biological parents,
even if it required one year of mourning,
they still continued their official duties
and did not hasten to the funeral.
Upon hearing the訃 (fù) notice,
they changed clothes, set up a spirit tablet, and wailed.
They observed mourning while in private residence,
but when entering the public office to handle affairs, they still wore regular attire.
Those in one-year mourning (*qīsāngzhě*)
did not participate in court audiences or sacrifices for the year.
After the mourning period was complete,
they set up a spirit tablet and wailed in their private residence,
and then removed the mourning.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì,
it was decreed that the funeral rites for the parents of all officials would follow the rank of their sons,
and that wives' mourning for their husbands would follow the same principle.
The ranks of sons and the ranks of wives for their husbands were treated similarly.
In the twenty-sixth year of Kāngxī,
acting in plays and gambling during mourning were prohibited.
Whenever an official died at his post,
or his parents or wife died,
he was permitted to enter the city to handle affairs.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
an imperial edict stated that Beijing Manchu and Han civil and military officials, upon experiencing a parent's death,
could return to their offices to handle affairs after one hundred days,
while continuing to observe mourning in private.
Participation in sacrifices and court audiences was suspended.
In the twenty-fourth year of Dàoguāng,
it was decreed that commoners below the rank of Duke and above military and civilian commoners observe twenty-seven months of mourning,
during which they could not hold banquets or play music,
could not marry wives or take concubines,
and their household gates could not replace old couplets.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
the Ministry of Rites proposed unifying Manchu and Han mourning regulations.
From then on, Manchu officials, upon the death of a parent, resigned their positions,
consistent with the practice for Han officials.
Funeral rites for scholars and commoners: In the early years of Shùnzhì,
regulations were established.
When a scholar or commoner died,
a red coffin was used,
with one layer of inner coffin (*chèn*),
and one saddled horse.
The initial sacrifice used funeral banners (*yǐnfān*),
one thousand each of gold and silver paper money,
three sacrificial feasts,
and one sheep.
The grand sacrifice was the same.
The sacrifices on the hundredth day and one-year anniversary
were half of the initial sacrifice.
The coffin was kept for one month before burial,
and burial took place after three months.
For tomb sacrifices, the amount of paper money, wine, and food was fixed.
According to general rites,
a scholar's burial clothes included one outer garment (*liǎn yī*) and one inner garment (*fù chán*),
one inner quilt (*fù qīn*),
one set of everyday clothes for *xí*,
three pieces of gold or silver powder for the mouth stuffing (*hán*),
and an inscription banner (*míngjīng*) was used.
Commoners used one inner quilt (*fù qīn*),
three pieces of silver powder for the mouth stuffing (*hán*),
and a spirit tablet (*húnbó*) was erected.
A scholar's burial ground perimeter was twenty *bù*,
and the mound was six *chǐ* high.
The tomb gate had a stone tablet (*jié*),
with a round top and square base.
Two burial epitaphs (*kuàngzhì*) were used,
as per official regulations.
The coffin carriage (*jiùyú*) had a bamboo grid on top with hanging tassels,
the poles were decorated with red chalk,
and there were no *shà* fans.
Two funeral cloths (*yǐnbù*),
one meritorious cloth (*gōngbù*).
One spirit carriage (*língchē*).
Burial objects followed local customs.
A commoner's burial ground was nine *bù*,
and the mound was four *chǐ* high.
There was a burial epitaph (*zhì*) but no stone tablet (*jié*).
The coffin carriage used a cloth quilt to cover the coffin,
with no curtains or canopy.
The two ends of the poles were decorated in black,
and the middle in red chalk.
Other aspects largely imitated those of ranked officials,
but with reduced scale.
In the early years of the Yōngzhèng reign,
it was stipulated that for deceased military personnel and commoners,
five sets of clothes should be placed with the body,
and one saddle and horse.
For the initial sacrifice,
there were two sacrificial feasts,
and one sheep.
The grand sacrifice was the same;
regular sacrifices were halved.
For officials and Imperial Academy students, the coffin cover was made of blue silk;
for military personnel and commoners, it was made of spring cloth.
In the thirteenth year [of Yōngzhèng],
an edict stated:
“We hear that the people in the outer provinces are extravagant in funerals,
even gathering relatives and neighbors,
holding feasts and drinking heavily,
calling it ‘noisy mourning’ (nào sāng).
Furthermore, various entertainments are displayed at the funeral site during interment.
Not only is this unreasonable,
it is also heartless.”
Governors-general and governors were ordered to strictly prohibit these bad customs,
and violators were to be punished.
Another edict said:
“Auspicious and inauspicious events follow different paths
and must not interfere with each other.
Thus, for a marriage that takes place outside the three-year mourning period but the betrothal occurs within it,
the Spring and Autumn Annals still deemed it improper.
The pain and grief of a three-year mourning period
are profound and immense.
Yet, ignorant people, unaware of ritual teachings,
fearing they might not be able to marry after observing mourning,
hastily proceed with it while their parents are critically ill or before the interment is complete.
We deeply pity them.
From now on,
from officials in court
down to Imperial Academy students,
this regulation must not be violated.
As for servants and commoners,
who are poor and have no one to rely on,
if their parents are bedridden
and rely on their daughters-in-law to prepare food,
they may proceed with welcoming the bride and serving meals.
The marriage ceremony, however, should be completed only after the illness has recovered or the mourning period is over.”
In ancient times, rituals did not extend to commoners.
Is this what that refers to?
Zēngzǐ asked:
“If the groom’s parents die while he is on his way to welcome the bride,
the woman should change into a plain deep garment (shēnyī) and a white headband (gǎo zǒng) to rush to the mourning.”
This is also the same meaning.
Mourning Regulations (Fúzhì): In the third year of Shùnzhì,
mourning dress regulations were established,
with diagrams included in the laws,
and promulgated throughout the empire.
In the fourth year of Dàoguāng,
the Dà Qīng Tōng Lǐ (Comprehensive Rites of the Great Qīng) was expanded and compiled.
The caps, clothes, headbands, and shoes recorded therein
largely followed previous dynastic customs.
There are five types of mourning clothes: The zhǎncuī (cut-edge sackcloth) mourning garment,
made of coarse unhemmed hemp cloth,
with edges unstitched.
Hemp cap and headband (dié),
straw shoes,
and a bamboo staff.
Women wear hemp shoes and do not carry a staff.
The qīcuī (even-edge sackcloth) mourning garment,
made of fine hemmed hemp cloth,
with edges stitched.
Hemp cap and headband,
grass shoes,
and a paulownia staff.
Women still wear hemp shoes.
The dàgōng (major mourning) garment,
made of coarse white cloth,
with cap and headband similar to it.
Shoes edged with raw silk cloth.
The xiǎogōng (minor mourning) garment,
made of slightly finer white cloth,
with cap and shoes as before.
The sīmá (fine hemp) garment,
made of fine white cloth,
with headband similar.
Plain shoes without embellishments.
There are eight periods of mourning: The zhǎncuī of three years:
A son for his father or mother;
for his stepmother (jìmǔ), kind mother (címǔ), adoptive mother (yǎngmǔ), legitimate mother (dímǔ), or birth mother (shēngmǔ);
one who is adopted (wéi rén hòu zhě) for his adoptive father or mother;
the son's wife observes the same.
An unmarried daughter for her father or mother, and a married woman who was divorced and returned home observes the same;
a legitimate grandson (dí sūn) as the main inheritor (chéng zhòng) for his paternal grandfather or grandmother, or great-great-grandfather or great-great-grandmother;
a wife for her husband;
a concubine for the head of the household observes the same.
The qīcuī with staff for one year (zhàng qī):
The legitimate son (dí zǐ) and other sons for a concubine mother (shùmǔ);
the son's wife observes the same;
a son for a remarried mother (jià mǔ) or divorced mother (chū mǔ);
a husband for his wife;
a legitimate grandson (dí sūn) when his paternal grandfather is alive, as the main inheritor for his paternal grandmother.
The qīcuī without staff for one year (bù zhàng qī):
For paternal uncles or aunts, or their wives;
for blood brothers or sisters;
for the children of blood brothers or sisters, and unmarried daughters thereof;
for an adoptive father with whom one resided, where there are no paternal relatives of dàgōng rank or higher for either party;
a paternal grandfather for his legitimate grandson;
a father or mother for their legitimate eldest son or other sons;
for the wife of the legitimate eldest son;
for an unmarried daughter;
for a son who has been adopted by another;
a stepmother for her eldest son or other sons;
a grandson for his paternal grandfather or grandmother;
an unmarried granddaughter or a married granddaughter observes the same;
a married daughter for her father or mother;
one who is adopted for his birth father or mother;
an unmarried daughter or a married daughter without a husband or son for her brothers or sisters, and her nephews or unmarried nieces;
a married daughter for her brothers who have succeeded their father;
a wife for the sons of her husband's brothers, and for their unmarried daughters;
a concubine for the father, mother, wife, eldest son, other sons, and her own sons of the head of the household.
The qīcuī of five months:
For paternal great-grandfathers or great-grandmothers;
a daughter, even if married, does not reduce her mourning.
The qīcuī of three months:
For paternal great-great-grandfathers or great-great-grandmothers;
a daughter, even if married, does not reduce her mourning;
for an adoptive father with whom one formerly resided;
for an adoptive father with whom one resided, where both parties have paternal relatives of dàgōng rank or higher.
The dàgōng of nine months:
A paternal grandfather for his grandson or unmarried granddaughter;
a paternal grandmother for all her grandsons;
a father or mother for all their daughters-in-law and married daughters;
paternal uncles or aunts, or their wives, for their nephews' wives and married nieces;
one who is adopted for his brothers or paternal aunts, or unmarried sisters;
once adopted,
mourning for all birth relatives is reduced by one degree;
the wife of one who is adopted for her husband's birth father or mother;
for one's own first cousins (táng xiōngdì) and unmarried first cousins (táng jiěmèi);
for married paternal aunts or sisters;
for the sons of one's brothers who have been adopted by another;
a married daughter for paternal uncles or aunts of her own clan (běn zōng);
for brothers of her own clan and their sons;
for paternal aunts or sisters of her own clan and unmarried daughters of her brothers;
a wife for her husband's paternal grandparents and paternal uncles or aunts.
The xiǎogōng of five months:
For paternal granduncles or grandaunts;
for first cousins once removed (táng bóshú fùmǔ) and married first cousins;
for second cousins (zài cóng xiōngdì) and unmarried second cousins;
for the sons of first cousins and their unmarried daughters;
for paternal grandaunts through a cousin and paternal grandaunts of the same generation who are unmarried;
a paternal grandfather for his legitimate grandson's wife;
for the grandsons of brothers and their unmarried granddaughters;
for maternal grandparents;
for the brothers or sisters of one's mother;
and for the sons of sisters;
one who is adopted for his married paternal aunts or sisters;
a wife for the grandsons of her husband's brothers and their unmarried granddaughters;
for her husband's paternal aunts, sisters, brothers, and her husband's brothers' wives;
for the sons of her husband's first cousins and their unmarried daughters;
a married daughter for her first cousins of her own clan and unmarried sisters.
The sīmá of three months:
A paternal grandfather for all his grandsons' wives;
a paternal grandmother for her legitimate grandson's wife and all her grandsons' wives;
paternal great-great-grandfathers or great-great-grandmothers for their great-grandsons or great-great-grandsons;
for a wet nurse;
for clan great-grandfathers or great-grandmothers;
clan paternal uncles or aunts;
for clan brothers or sisters and unmarried clan sisters;
for clan great-grandaunts, clan grandaunts, and unmarried clan aunts;
for the great-grandsons of brothers and their unmarried great-granddaughters;
for the sons of second cousins and their unmarried daughters;
for married paternal grandaunts, paternal aunts, and second cousins;
for the sons of paternal aunts and the sons of maternal uncles;
for maternal cousins;
for one's wife's father or mother;
for a son-in-law;
for maternal grandsons and maternal granddaughters;
for the wives of brothers' grandsons;
for the wives of first cousins;
for the wives of first cousins' sons;
a wife for her husband's great-great-grandfathers or great-great-grandmothers;
for her husband's paternal granduncles or grandaunts, and her husband's paternal grandaunts who are unmarried;
for her husband's first cousins once removed (táng bóshú fùmǔ) and paternal aunts of the same generation who are unmarried;
for her husband's first cousins and the wives of her husband's first cousins;
for her husband's first cousins (táng jiěmèi);
for the sons of her husband's second cousins and their unmarried daughters;
for her husband's married first cousins (táng jiěmèi);
for the wives of her husband's first cousins' sons and their grandsons and unmarried granddaughters;
for the wives of her husband's brothers' grandsons and her husband's married brothers' granddaughters;
for her husband's brothers' great-grandsons and their unmarried great-granddaughters;
a married daughter for paternal granduncles or grandaunts of her own clan and paternal grandaunts who are unmarried;
for paternal uncles or aunts of her own clan (cóng bóshú fùmǔ) and paternal aunts of the same generation who are unmarried;
for the sons of first cousins of her own clan and their unmarried daughters.
In the fortieth year of Qiánlóng,
Emperor Gāozōng specially permitted a sole son to concurrently serve two ancestral lines (jiān tiāo),
thus establishing the rule for jiān tiāo.
Jiān tiāo was a pragmatic measure to complement the classics,
adequately filling the gaps in ancient rites.
The collected statutes (Huìdiǎn) mourning regulations differentiate between major lineage (dàzōng) and minor lineage (xiǎozōng),
with the major lineage being more important.
The major lineage observes mourning according to the main article of the mourning regulations,
while one who concurrently serves two ancestral lines (jiān tiāo) observes mourning according to the reduced mourning period.
In the ninth year of the Dàoguāng reign,
the ministers of rites further deliberated on the mourning rites for two ancestral lines (liǎng tiāo fúzì).
For a son who, being an only child, inherited the ancestral sacrifices of two branches (fēn chéng liǎng fáng zōng tiāo),
he was to observe three years of zhan cuī mourning for his father and mother,
and qi cuī bù zhàng qī mourning for his paternal grandparents.
If the father passed away,
the principal grandson (dí sūn) who was the chief mourner (chéng zhòng)
would observe three years of zhan cuī mourning.
For his own biological relatives (běn shēng qīn shǔ), the mourning grade was reduced by one degree from the regular mourning.
For descendants, concerning their biological relatives, mourning rites were determined solely by their adopted lineage (suǒ hòu zōng zhī qīn shǔ).
In the tenth year of the Tóngzhì reign,
the request of the ministers of rites was approved,
concerning the mourning rites for a concubine of the concurrently inherited ancestral line (jiān tiāo shù mǔ).
According to the established regulations, one would observe qī mourning for the concurrently inherited father and mother,
and xiǎo gōng mourning for the concurrently inherited concubine.
For one who, as a son of the main branch (dà zōng), concurrently inherited a minor branch (xiǎo zōng), or one who, as a son of a minor branch, concurrently inherited the main branch,
the main branch was considered primary (dà zōng wéi zhòng).
Therefore, qī nián mourning was observed for the concubine of the main branch,
and xiǎo gōng mourning for the concubine of the minor branch.
For one who, as a son of a minor branch, concurrently inherited another minor branch,
the biological parents were considered primary (suǒ shēng wéi zhòng).
Therefore, qī nián mourning was observed for the biological concubine,
and xiǎo gōng mourning for the concurrently inherited concubine.
As for those who were adopted (chū sì) but did not concurrently inherit two ancestral lines,
the adopted lineage was considered primary (suǒ hòu wéi zhòng).
Therefore, qī nián mourning was observed for the concubine of the adopted lineage,
and xiǎo gōng mourning for the biological concubine.
Since qī nián mourning was reduced to xiǎo gōng,
the mourning observed by the concurrently inherited concubine for her concurrently inherited son also followed this rule.
Zhì chapter sixty-nine, Yuè part one.
The record states:
“For bringing peace to superiors and governing the people,
nothing is better than lǐ (rites).”
“For transforming customs and changing traditions,
nothing is better than yuè (music).”
Music,
it is that which examines the spirits, receives guests,
classifies things, and expresses merit,
through its virtuous fragrance offering profound praise to the Supreme Lord.
When the sagely Way spreads in all directions,
sound and governance are connected;
thus, there are choreographed dances (zhuì zhào zhī róng)
and sounds of flutes and pipes (shāo yuè zhī yīn),
clothing them in its brilliance,
and anointing their strategies and achievements,
thereby bringing peace to the people.
The people are free from lamenting weariness, distress, or injury,
and from rebellious, licentious, arrogant, and dissolute intentions.
Only then can the Yǎ and Sòng be created.
Indeed, when the Sānmiáo tribe submitted, the Sháo dance was performed;
when the eleven-part tax was established, sòng oū were chanted;
when the Xuánniǎo song was sung, the prosperity of Shāng arose;
when the Língtái music was played, the Way of Zhōu flourished.
When the royal court lost its hold,
the spirits did not bestow blessings.
By the Spring and Autumn period,
there was great chaos.
Kǒng Ní (Confucius) compiled the Shī Jīng (Classic of Poetry),
placing the Shǔ Lí in the Guófēng,
and equating the virtue of kings with that of feudal lords,
making it clear that the Yǎ could not be restored.
Later, the tyrannical Qín dynasty arose,
and the Yuè Jīng (Classic of Music) was destroyed by dust.
The music of Zhèng and Wèi
began from this point,
and although songs were performed in suburban temples,
their sounds did not reach the lower classes.
There was no mention of disturbing the people or equalizing education.
Nonetheless, throughout successive dynasties,
none failed to elaborately present the Nányǎ,
composing their own suburban odes,
upholding the difficulty of ancestral achievements,
and extolling the manifest imperial merits,
examining and comparing bells and chimes,
and establishing intricate ceremonies.
Although the vastness of the three (Wǔ Dì) and five (Sān Huáng) sovereigns
was brilliantly of the same style,
the yearning to hear Sháo music
made them strive even harder for it.
This is what previous admonitions criticized,
likening it to chanting at night.
The Qīng dynasty originated from a remote and distant land;
initially, their worship of spirits and sacrifices to Heaven
followed border customs.
When Tàizǔ received the Mandate of Heaven,
he began to adopt Chinese customs.
During the Tiānmìng and Chóngdé reigns,
Wǎěrkā was conquered,
Cháoxiǎn submitted,
and Cháhāěr was pacified.
Their palace musical instruments (gōng xuán) were acquired,
to be used for entertainment with envoys from the four borders.
When Shìzǔ entered the passes (rù guān),
he restored the old systems of the Míng dynasty.
There was the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè,
used for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, and court assemblies.
There was the Dānbì Dàyuè,
used by princes, dukes, and all officials for congratulatory ceremonies.
There were the Zhōnghé Qīngyuè and Dānbì Qīngyuè,
used for banquets within the palace.
There was the Lúbù Dǎoyíngyuè,
used for imperial tours.
They also created ráo gē fǎ qǔ (military songs and ritual music),
to rouse martial spirit and hatred for enemies,
and to proclaim the eight winds (bā fēng),
matching the short flutes of the Hàn dynasty.
As for the old Manchu dances,
called mǎng shì,
they were usually performed by descendants of renowned families,
and depicted stories from Liáoshěn,
showing postures of waving banners and spears, drawing arrows, galloping horses, and charging into battle,
with movements of bending and stretching, advancing and retreating, nimble and agile, bowing and looking up.
Their songs differed from those of Hàn,
and were not promulgated by the Tàicháng (Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
Perhaps this was to signify the continuation of their heritage and the establishment of their lineage,
never forgetting the former kings?
Shèngzǔ and Gāozōng
took the initiative in musical creation,
their ministers not having the keen hearing of Shī Kuàng,
and the sovereigns surpassing the excellence of Jī Dàn.
They harmonized sounds with metal and stone instruments,
and proclaimed their virtues to the heavens.
Imperial orders and imperial creations
were most splendid at this time.
However, observing their command for court musicians to harmonize the pitch,
and summoning Xían Hēi to perform songs,
it was not that they failed to cultivate talent and forge structure,
making all four corners follow suit.
Yet, after two successions,
the celebratory songs gradually declined.
Wèi Wén (Emperor Wèi Wén Dì) felt like sleeping upon hearing it,
and Jì Zhá observed it without criticism.
This shows that the excellence of music
reveals the rise and fall of a state.
Songs of praise reside among the people;
they are not self-generated.
Yet, throughout the three ancient periods,
there was never a prior realization
of this,
which is truly regrettable.
Examining Qīng music,
it generally followed the Míng precedents,
with six pitches and seven beginnings (liù jiān qī shǐ),
truly inheriting what was lost from antiquity,
measuring short reeds (bù zhǐ hé),
and testing resonance with ash-filled tubes.
This is how Shén Gǔ was able to stop the flow (sè liú),
and Lì Shǒu was able to bend his steps.
To revive the lost primordial sounds,
and restore genuine simplicity,
to promote our Huá (Chinese) music,
and reject Western melodies,
to purify desires and refine nature,
even a single thread (yī yán) might achieve this.
If it can protect the classics and admonitions,
it might be found here.
One must learn from previous models;
then we will be superior.
What is recorded in the National Archives (guó chéng)
regarding the order of musical instruments and numerical calculations,
and the discussion of pipes, lutes, and strings,
is splendidly well-ordered,
and can be called cultured.
Now, I have extracted its essentials
to be compiled into a simple record.
Tàizǔ first established himself on the eastern frontier,
suppressing chaos with military force.
The sounds and objects were simple and unadorned,
largely following the old customs of Liáo.
In the first year of the Tiānmìng reign,
he ascended to the throne in Shěnyáng.
When the various Bèilè and all officials offered congratulations and wished him longevity in court,
the ceremonial music for the imperial cortege (lúbù) was first established.
In the eighth year,
the music for victory celebrations, worship of Heaven, and banquets was determined.
In the eighth year of Tàizōng's Tiāncōng reign,
the music for armies to pay respects at the Tángzi and worship Heaven, and the music for New Year's Day court audiences, were further established.
In the ninth year,
the theatrical performances (zá jù) on New Year's Day were discontinued.
Earlier, the Méilè Zhāngjīng, Zhāng Cúnrén, submitted a memorial, saying:
“New Year's Day court audiences
are matters of great importance.
Theatrical farces and jests
are not suitable for display in the palace hall.
According to precedent,
when the Eight Banners hold banquets,
only yǎyuè (ritual music) is to be used.”
This was followed.
In the eighth year,
a decree was issued: for the morning sacrifice to the sun, seven pieces of music were to be played.
The musical movements used
For welcoming the spirits, the music was to be Yínxī (寅曦);
for offering jade and silks, Cháoxī (朝曦);
for the first offering, Qīngxī (清曦);
for the second offering, Xiánxī (咸曦);
for the final offering, Chúnxī (純曦);
for clearing away the food, Yánxī (延曦);
and for sending off the spirits, Guīxī (歸曦).
For the evening sacrifice to the moon, six pieces of music were to be played.
The musical movements used
"Guāng" (光).
For welcoming the spirits, the music was to be Yíngguāng (迎光);
for offering jade and silks and the first offering, Shēngguāng (升光);
for the second offering, Yáoguāng (瑤光);
for the final offering, Ruìguāng (瑞光);
for clearing away the food, Hánguāng (涵光);
and for sending off the spirits, Bǎoguāng (保光).
All these were zhōnghé sháoyuè (中和韶樂).
For the three major festivals celebrating the Huángtàihòu (皇太后) and Huánghòu (皇后),
and for the emperor's grand wedding ceremonies,
all used dànbì dàyuè (丹陛大樂).
For sacrifices to Zhēnwǔ (真武), Dōngyuè (東嶽), and the Chénghuáng Miào (城隍廟),
the Jiàofāng Sī (教坊司) performed music as for common sacrifices.
In this year, the request from the Lǐbù (禮部) was also granted
to revise the number of ceremonial dances, musical movements, and musical instruments.
The grand music for ancestral temple sacrifices was performed inside the hall.
The civil and military ceremonial dancers were arranged, and all musical movements, ending songs, and musical instruments were set up.
An additional 570 dancers were appointed to fill the old quota.
Subsequently, it was also decreed that for regular court audiences and ascending the throne, the zhōnghé sháoyuè (中和韶樂) would play Lóngpíng (隆平);
for princes, dukes, and all officials performing rites, the dànbì dàyuè (丹陛大樂) would play Qìngpíng (慶平);
for foreign vassals performing rites, the dànbì dàyuè (丹陛大樂) would play Zhìpíng (治平);
and for returning to the palace, the zhōnghé sháoyuè (中和韶樂) would play Xiǎnpíng (顯平).
For plowing the sacred field and offering sacrifices to the Xiānnóng (先農),
seven musical movements were played.
They used
"Fēng" (豐).
For welcoming the spirits, the music was to be Yǒngfēng (永豐);
for offering silks and the first offering, Shífēng (時豐);
for the second offering, Xiánfēng (咸豐);
for the final offering, Dàfēng (大豐);
for clearing away the food, Lǚfēng (屢豐);
for sending off the spirits, Bàofēng (報豐);
and for observing the burial, Qìngfēng (慶豐).
After the ceremony,
at the imperial fasting palace,
the grand music for escorting and welcoming played Tiānxià Yuè (天下樂);
for ascending the seat, Wànsuì Yuè (萬歲樂);
for officials performing rites, the dànbì dàyuè (丹陛大樂) played Cháotiānzǐ (朝天子);
for banquets and wishing longevity, Sānyuè Sháoguāng (三月韶光);
and for serving food, the qīngyuè (清樂) played Tàiqīng Gē (太清歌).
For the xiápū (祫祭) at the Tàimiào (太廟), for welcoming the spirits, Zhēnpíng (貞平) was played;
for offering silks and the first offering, Shòupíng (壽平);
for the second offering, Jiāpíng (嘉平);
for the final offering, Yōngpíng (雍平);
for clearing away the food, Xīpíng (熙平);
and for sending off the spirits, Qīngpíng (清平).
For the grand sacrifice to Heaven, Earth, and all gods in the Dàxiǎng Diàn (大享殿),
nine musical movements were played.
They used
For welcoming the spirits, the music was to be Yuánhé (元和);
for offering jade and silks, Jǐnghé (景和);
for presenting sacrificial meat, Sùhé (肅和);
for the first offering, Shòuhé (壽和);
for the second offering, Ānhé (安和);
for the final offering, Yǒnghé (永和);
for clearing away the food, Xiéhé (協和);
for sending off the spirits, Tàihé (泰和);
and for observing the burning and burial, Qīnghé (清和).

For grand celebrations such as conferring honorary titles and seals upon the Huángtàihòu (皇太后), honoring the Tàifēi (太妃), establishing the Empress, and the imperial examinations in the Tàihé Diàn (太和殿),
special decrees were issued regarding the music to be used.
Thereafter, when visiting Shèngjīng (盛京) and paying respects at the imperial tombs,
as well as presenting the Shílù (實錄) and Yùdié (玉牒), the same practices applied.
In the early Kāngxī (康熙) reign,
as Shèngzǔ (聖祖) ascended the throne as a youth,
he simply followed the old system,
making no changes.
In the eighth year,
a decree was issued to specify the music for morning audiences and felicitations for the emperor, grand empress dowager, empress dowager, and empress during the three major festivals.
For the emperor ascending the throne on New Year's Day, the zhōnghé sháoyuè (中和韶樂) played Yuánpíng (元平);
for returning to the palace, Hépíng (和平).
For ascending the throne on the Winter Solstice, Suípíng (遂平) was played;
for returning to the palace, Yǔnpíng (允平).
For ascending the throne on the emperor's birthday (Wànshòu Jié), Qiánpíng (乾平) was played;
for returning to the palace, Tàipíng (太平).
For officials performing rites, the dànbì dàyuè (丹陛大樂) played Qìngpíng (慶平);
for foreign vassals, Zhìpíng (治平).
For the Tàihuángtàihòu (太皇太后) ascending the throne, Shēngpíng (升平) was played;
for returning to the palace, Héngpíng (恆平);
for performing rites, Jìnpíng (晉平).
For the Huángtàihòu (皇太后) ascending the throne, Yùpíng (豫平) was played;
for returning to the palace, Lǚpíng (履平);
for performing rites, Yìpíng (益平).
For the Huánghòu (皇后) ascending the throne, Shúpíng (淑平) was played;
for returning to the palace, Shùnpíng (順平);
for performing rites, Zhèngpíng (正平).
However, as the officials had practiced for a long time,
the musical phrases and rhythms
became harsh and out of place.
The musicians, responding to their duties,
were like the ritual masters,
only recording the clanging and dancing.
Since the time of Shìzǔ (世祖),
he had repeatedly instructed the music officials to rehearse the ceremonial dances, sounds, appearance, and etiquette.
He once admonished the Grand Secretaries, saying:
"For all sacrifices in various places,
the music played by the Tàicháng Sì (太常寺) is not harmonious.
Music is a grand ceremony for sacrifices;
only when the sounds, appearance, and etiquette fully match the song texts
can it achieve perfection.
Therefore, summon the Tàicháng Sì (太常寺) officials and strictly admonish them."
By the eleventh year,
Shèngzǔ (聖祖) also instructed the ritual officials:
"Be diligent in reverence for sacrifices,
practice assiduously,
do not remain negligent as before,
and thereby profane the clear ordinances."
In the twenty-first year,
the Three Feudatories were suppressed,
and the empire was at peace.
Zuǒfù Dūyùshǐ (左副都御史) Yú Guózhù (余國柱) first requested the rectification of the musical movements for suburban sacrifices, ancestral temples, court audiences, and banquets.
The emperor said:
"The musical movements for sacrifices
are essential for the achievements of an era.
The Lǐbù (禮部) and Hànlín Yuàn (翰lín yuàn) should convene and deliberate on this matter and report back."
Soon, a memorial was submitted:
"From ancient times, temple music
was originally used to praise the virtues and accomplishments of ancestors.
For the current dynasty's suburban altars and ancestral temple sacrifices, the musical movements,
with the song name 'Píng' (平),
have been followed for a long time.
For the sacrifices to Tàizǔ (太祖), Tàizōng (太宗), and Shìzǔ (世祖) at the Tàimiào (太廟),
it is appropriate to follow the old custom.
However, the tunes for court audiences and banquets
are not fully refined.
It is advisable to order the relevant departments to consult ancient practices and adapt them to current needs,
to seek the origins of sound and rhythm,
and to establish the standards for elegant performances."
This was approved.
Consequently, Grand Secretary Chén Tíngjìng (陳廷敬) was ordered to re-compose the various chapters of court music.
However, these still followed the old Ming Dynasty style;
although they aimed for grandeur and richness,
they were like mere singing,
with the five notes and two alterations
following errors and losing their proper arrangement.
As Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is the foundation of all things,
none of the officials could speak of it.
The emperor, being modest,
also did not have time to reform it.
In the twenty-third year,
during his eastern tour, he visited Quèlǐ (闕里),
personally offered sacrifices at Kǒnglín (孔林),
displayed the imperial procession,
and played the grand music for escorting and welcoming, with its musical movements and dances.
Beforehand, the Tàicháng Sì (太常寺) was ordered to send music officials to practice there,
the same as for the Tàixué Xiānshī Miào (太學先師廟).
In the twenty-ninth year,
