due to the recent submission of the Khalkha,
a special joint inspection ceremony was held,
with the display of the imperial procession
and the playing of ráo gē dà yuè (鐃歌大樂).
At this, the emperor felt the decay of ritual and music,
and thus began to aspire to the task of creating new works.
In the thirty-first year [of Kāngxī's reign],
the emperor was in the Qiánqīng Gōng.
He summoned the Grand Secretaries and the Nine Ministers,
pointed to the Diagram of the Five Sounds and Eight Winds, and said to them:
"The ancients said that when the twelve *lǜ* were established,
and then applied to the eight musical instruments,
the eight instruments would harmonize.
When played to Heaven and Earth,
the eight winds would harmonize.
All things auspicious,
and propitious omens that could be brought forth,
would all arrive without fail.
This means that the matters related to musical temperament are of great importance.
However, the origin of the twelve *lǜ*
is not precisely known.
The calculations mentioned in the *Lǜlǜ Xīnshū*
exclusively use the method of 'diameter one, circumference three'.
If this method were correct,
then all calculations would be correct;
if it were erroneous,
then nothing would be correct.
I observe that the method of 'diameter one, circumference three'
cannot possibly be correct.
For if the diameter is one *chǐ*,
then the circumference should be three *chǐ*, one *cùn*, four *fēn*, one *lí* and a remainder.
If this is accumulated to one hundred *zhàng*,
the difference would be fourteen *zhàng* and a remainder.
If we extrapolate upwards from this,
can the errors and discrepancies even be spoken of?"
He then took out various diagrams of squares and circles and said to his ministers:
"What is referred to as 'diameter one, circumference three'
can only calculate the numbers of a hexagon.
If one calculates a circle's circumference, there must be a remainder.
I observe that the method of 'radius, *gōu*, and *gǔ*' in the table of eight lines is extremely precise.
All circular figures can be calculated using square methods.
The art of extracting square roots
comes from this.
If the *huángzhōng* pipe is nine *cùn* long,
with an empty circumference of nine *fēn*,
its volume is eight hundred and ten *fēn* cubed –
this is taken as the standard *lǜ*.
This is an old saying.
If its *fēn* and *cùn* are expressed in terms of *chǐ*,
then the ancient and modern *chǐ* systems differ;
we should use the measurements of Heaven and Earth as the standard.
Only the theory of 'intervening eight generating each other',
where sounds, high and low,
cyclically generate each other,
and return to the original note,
must involve eight intervals;
this is an immutable principle."
He then ordered musicians to take flutes and *sè* lutes and carefully tune them in sequence.
Upon reaching the eighth sound,
it returned to the original note.
The Emperor said:
"Is this not the meaning of 'intervening eight generating each other'?"
All the ministers replied:
"It is truly as Your Sacred Instruction states,
beyond what we humble servants have heard or seen."
In the thirty-fourth year,
the system for sounding horns, beating drums, and striking gongs during grand military reviews was established.
In the first month of the forty-ninth year,
on the occasion of Empress Xiàohuìzhāng's seventieth birthday,
he again issued an edict to the Ministry of Rites, saying:
"The *Mǎkèsì* dance
is a grand Manchu banquet ceremony,
a rite of utmost solemnity.
By tradition, it is performed by princes and high officials.
This year, on the Grand Empress Dowager's seventieth birthday,
I am also fifty-seven years old,
and wish to personally dance and offer a toast."
On that day, a banquet was held in the Empress Dowager's palace with music playing.
The Emperor danced before her, offered a goblet,
and only ceased when joy was at its peak.
The Emperor, having profoundly studied musical temperament,
appointed Lǐ Guāngdì as a Grand Secretary of the Wényuán Gé at that time.
As an esteemed elder, Lǐ Guāngdì was consulted.
He presented his compiled *Dàsīyuè Shìyì* and *Lè Lǜ Lùn Biàn*.
Thereupon, he submitted a memorial, saying:
"Rites and music cannot depart from one for an instant,
nor can they fail to be practiced throughout the world for a single day.
Since the Hàn dynasty,
rites and music have collapsed and deteriorated,
not conforming to the spirit of the Three Dynasties for over two thousand years,
and music even more so.
For even with the clearly recorded rhythms, chapters, instruments, and *lǜlǜ* in various classics,
the multitude of explanations
ultimately cannot be unified,
let alone the subtle and profound principles
that harmonize with Heaven and Earth!
Now, the four seas are filled with decadence,
morality is degraded,
ranks and statuses are indistinguishable,
and extravagance and usurpation cannot be stopped;
connections lack proper order,
and disputes cannot be forbidden.
The *Jì* says: 'Without a foundation, nothing stands;
without elucidation, nothing progresses.'
That which is spiritual and clear is the foundation;
that which is raised and put into practice is the elucidation.
It is fitting to seek out and summon renowned scholars,
and even those well-versed in ancient and modern times,
to look back to the Xià and Shāng dynasties,
and closely examine from the Hàn and Táng dynasties onwards,
to thoroughly investigate, weigh, and determine,
to establish a great canon for the current era,
to purify the world and serve as a model for myriad generations."
Grand Secretary Zhāng Yùshū also stated:
"The study of musical temperament and mathematics
has been lost for a long time.
Errors have been transmitted and copied,
and no one has been able to identify their mistakes;
profound meanings and subtle mechanisms
have not been explored for their essence.
We, your humble servants, personally listen to your instructions,
yet we only momentarily awaken,
and then become confused when recalculating;
how can officials and common people both inside and outside the court
commonly understand?
It is appropriate that Your Majesty specially adjudicate and decide,
compile them into a book,
and promulgate it throughout the four directions,
for everyone to study and practice.
This will correct the accumulated errors in calculations throughout history,
and establish an excellent method for harmonious sound for ten thousand generations,
benefiting both scholarship and governance."
The Emperor was reluctant to refuse the requests of his ministers.
In the fifty-second year,
he therefore issued an edict to revise various *lǜlǜ* books,
establishing an academy in the Méngyǎng Zhāi.
He sought out those throughout the realm who were proficient in musical temperament.
Lǐ Guāngdì recommended Wèi Tíngzhēn from Jǐngzhōu, Méi Juéchéng from Níngguó, and Wáng Lánshēng from Jiāohé to serve as compilers.
Wáng Lánshēng was a scholar previously selected by Lǐ Guāngdì.
He had an innate understanding of musical temperament.
Zhū Zǐ's *Qín Lǜ Túshuō*
contained many erroneous characters.
Wáng Lánshēng corrected them by discerning the intent,
making them clearly understandable.
When summoned to serve at court,
those involved in compiling and editing were all refined scholars,
but Wáng Lánshēng's scholarship was uniquely profound.
He also frequently sought moderation with the Emperor,
and whenever there was a point of doubt,
the Emperor would personally resolve it.
Their method first clarified that *huángzhōng* is the root of the twelve *lǜlǜ*.
They used longitudinal and horizontal millet grains to determine ancient and modern standards of measurement.
The modern *chǐ* of eight *cùn* and one *fēn*
was equivalent to the ancient *chǐ* of ten *cùn*.
One hundred horizontal millet grains
were equivalent to eighty-one longitudinal millet grains.
The *Hàn Zhì* states:
"The length of *huángzhōng*
is measured by the width of one medium-sized *zǐgǔ jùshǔ* grain.
Ninety *fēn* constitute the length of *huángzhōng*,
with one *fēn* being one unit."
Width refers to the horizontal dimension.
Ninety *fēn* constituting the length of *huángzhōng* clearly indicates
that *huángzhōng* is accumulated from ninety horizontal millet grains.
Using the measure of horizontal millet grains to compare with longitudinal millet grains,
which is the ratio of the ancient *chǐ* to the modern *chǐ*:
let the ancient *chǐ* be the first ratio,
the modern *chǐ* be the second ratio,
and the ancient *chǐ* length of *huángzhōng* (nine *cùn*) be the third ratio.
From this, the fourth ratio is derived as seven *cùn*, two *fēn*, nine *lí*,
which is the modern *chǐ* measure of *huángzhōng*.
The *Lǜlǜ Xīnshū* states: *huángzhōng* is nine *cùn* long,
with an empty circumference of nine *fēn*,
resulting in a volume of eight hundred and ten *fēn* cubed.
If we again set the ancient *chǐ*,
its volume is eight hundred and ten *fēn* cubed.
Dividing by ninety *fēn*,
we get a cross-sectional area of nine square *fēn*.
Using proportional calculation,
the line lengths are equal,
but the areas are different.
Let the standard circular area of one hundred thousand be the first ratio,
the square area of one hundred twenty-seven thousand three hundred twenty-four be the second ratio,
and the current cross-sectional area of nine square *fēn* be the third ratio.
From this, the fourth ratio is derived as eleven *fēn*, forty-five *lí*, ninety *háo*.
Taking the square root gives three *fēn*, three *lí*, eight *háo*, five *sī*, one *hū*,
which is the diameter of *huángzhōng* in ancient *chǐ*.
Calculating the circumference,
we get ten *fēn*, six *lí*, three *háo*, four *sī*, six *hū*.
Then, comparing the volume in ancient *chǐ* to the volume in modern *chǐ*:
one hundred *fēn* (ancient *chǐ*) cubed,
which is one million *fēn* cubed, is the first ratio.
Eighty-one *fēn* (modern *chǐ*) cubed,
which is five hundred thirty-one thousand forty-one *fēn* cubed, is the second ratio.
The *huángzhōng* volume of eight hundred ten *fēn* cubed is the third ratio.
From this, the fourth ratio is derived as four hundred thirty *fēn*, four hundred sixty-seven *lí*, two hundred eleven *háo*,
which is the volume of *huángzhōng* in modern *chǐ*.
Dividing this by the modern *chǐ* length of seven *cùn*, two *fēn*, nine *lí*,
we get a cross-sectional area of five *fēn*, ninety *lí*, forty-nine *háo*.
Calculating the diameter gives two *fēn*, seven *lí*, four *háo*, one *sī*, nine *hū*.
Thus, the longitudinal length, volume, cross-sectional area, and diameter of the *huángzhōng* pipe were determined.
Once the huángzhōng was established,
the method of making lǜlǚ of the same diameter was then devised.
It took the accumulated volume of millet grains as its measure,
and it was verified by subtracting or adding one-third.
Subtracting one-third from huángzhōng
generated línzhōng downwards.
Adding one-third to línzhōng
generated tàicù upwards.
Subtracting one-third from tàicù
generated nánlǚ downwards.
Adding one-third to nánlǚ
generated gūxǐ upwards.
Subtracting one-third from gūxǐ
generated yìngzhōng downwards.
Adding one-third to yìngzhōng
generated ruíbīn upwards.
Adding one-third to ruíbīn
generated dàlǚ upwards.
Subtracting one-third from dàlǚ
generated yīzé downwards.
Adding one-third to yīzé
generated jiázhōng upwards.
Subtracting one-third from jiázhōng
generated wúshè downwards.
Adding one-third to wúshè
generated zhònglǚ upwards.
Again, doubling them,
from ruíbīn down to yìngzhōng,
and halving them,
from huángzhōng down to zhònglǚ,
all are six.
Discarding Jīng Fáng’s theory of changing lǜ,
the gōng sound was set between huángzhōng and dàlǚ.
Huángzhōng serves as gōng,
followed by tàicù responding as shāng,
followed by gūxǐ responding as jué,
followed by ruíbīn responding as biànzhēng,
followed by yīzé responding as zhēng,
followed by wúshè responding as yǔ,
followed by half huángzhōng responding as biàngōng.
These are called the five sounds and two changes of the yang lǜ.
Reaching half tàicù becomes qīnggōng,
still corresponding to huángzhōng.
Dàlǚ serves as gōng,
followed by jiázhōng responding as shāng,
followed by zhònglǚ responding as jué,
followed by línzhōng responding as biànzhēng,
followed by nánlǚ responding as zhēng,
followed by yìngzhōng responding as yǔ,
followed by half dàlǚ responding as biàngōng.
These are called the five sounds and two changes of the yin lǚ.
Reaching half jiázhōng becomes qīnggōng,
still corresponding to dàlǚ.
They successively become gōng for each other,
selecting sounds by compromise,
thus forming categories without being mixed.
Testing it with a xiāo or dí,
gōng corresponds to gōng,
fán corresponds to shāng,
liù corresponds to jué,
wǔ corresponds to biànzhēng,
yǐ corresponds to zhēng,
shàng corresponds to yǔ,
chǐ corresponds to biàngōng.
Huángzhōng is the lower gōng (low gōng),
dàlǚ is the higher gōng (high gōng),
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Tàicù is the lower fán (low fán),
jiázhōng is the higher fán (high fán),
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Gūxǐ is the lower liù (low liù),
zhònglǚ is the higher liù (high liù),
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Ruíbīn is the lower wǔ (low wǔ),
línzhōng is the higher wǔ (high wǔ),
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Yīzé is the lower yǐ (low yǐ),
nánlǚ is the higher yǐ (high yǐ),
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Wúshè is the lower shàng (low shàng),
yìngzhōng is the higher shàng (high shàng),
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Doubling them,
then double wúshè and double yìngzhōng become the right biàngōng (chǐ) character of the gōng sound,
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Double yīzé and double nánlǚ become the right lower yǔ (shàng) character of the biàngōng,
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Double ruíbīn and double línzhōng become the right lower zhēng (yǐ) character of the lower yǔ,
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Halving them,
then half huángzhōng and half dàlǚ become the left biàngōng (chǐ) character of the yǔ sound,
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Half tàicù and half jiázhōng become the left shàogōng (gōng) character of the biàngōng,
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
Half gūxǐ and half zhònglǚ become the left shàoshāng (fán) character of the shàogōng,
thus distinguishing qīng and zhuó.
This is why ancient music started with xiàzhēng and ended with qīngshāng.
With huángzhōng as the single diameter,
its varying lengths
create the twelve lǜlǚ,
further aided by doubling and halving,
to obtain the complete five sounds and two changes.
From this, musical instruments were made.
Using the volume of huángzhōng as the base,
adding and subtracting fractions,
all are compared using the length and diameter of huángzhōng.
A large addition reaches eight times,
so the length and diameter also double.
A small reduction reaches one-eighth,
so the length and diameter also halve.
There are twelve tubes for the regular lǜlǚ,
six doubled tubes,
and six halved tubes.
There are fifty-six huángzhōng-shaped tubes,
also six doubled tubes,
and six halved tubes.
The same-shaped tubes then generate eleven same-diameter tubes,
totaling one thousand three hundred sixty-eight tubes.
The system is established according to these numbers,
to examine their measurements,
and to discern their sounds.
A tube eight times the huángzhōng,
its sound corresponds to the zhuógōng (low gōng) of the regular huángzhōng lǜ.
A tube seven times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the qīnggōng (high gōng) of the dàlǚ lǜ.
A tube six times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the zhuóshāng (low fán) of the tàicù lǜ.
A tube five times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the qīngshāng (high fán) of the jiázhōng lǜ.
A tube four times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the zhuójúe (low liù) of the gūxǐ lǜ.
A tube three and a half times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the qīngjúe (high liù) of the zhònglǚ lǜ.
A tube three times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the zhuóbiànzhēng (low wǔ) of the ruíbīn lǜ.
(Three times should correspond to zhònglǚ,
but now it is a semitone higher and corresponds to ruíbīn,
probably because the tube body is gradually smaller,
making the sound easily distinguishable.
It is necessary to add half of the regular huángzhōng volume
to three times its volume
to correspond to the qīngjúe (high liù) of the zhònglǚ lǜ.
The principle of half volume
arises from this.)
A tube two and a half times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the qīngbiànzhēng (high wǔ) of the línzhōng lǜ.
A tube two and a quarter times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the zhuózhēng (low yǐ) of the yīzé lǜ.
(A tube two times the huángzhōng
does not correspond to yīzé, but rather between two and a half and two times it begins to correspond.
It is necessary to halve the half volume again,
making it one-quarter,
and add it to two times,
then the fraction matches.
The principle of one-quarter
arises from this.)
A tube two times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the qīngzhēng (high yǐ) of the nánlǚ lǜ.
A tube one and three-quarters times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the zhuóyǔ (low shàng) of the wúshè lǜ.
A tube one and two-quarters times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the qīngyǔ (high shàng) of the yìngzhōng lǜ.
A tube one and one-quarter times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the zhuóbiàngōng (low chǐ) of the half huángzhōng lǜ.
A tube one and one-eighth times the huángzhōng,
corresponds to the qīngbiàngōng (high chǐ) of the half dàlǚ lǜ.
(This tube is closest to the regular huángzhōng.
To obtain the fraction that matches qīnggōng,
one-quarter is halved again,
making it one-eighth,
and added to the fraction of the regular huángzhōng,
then its sound begins to correspond.
The principle of one-eighth
arises from this.)
Following this, the pitch of the zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾) pipe corresponds to the lǜ of bàn Tàicù (半太簇).
The zhuó gōng (濁宮) and dī gōng (低工) will then harmonize with the pipe that is eight times the size of Huángzhōng (黃鍾), producing the same sound.
Decreasing in sequence:
a pipe that is seven-eighths the length of zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾)
corresponds to the lǚ of Dàlǚ (大呂);
a pipe that is six-eighths the length
corresponds to the lǜ of Tàicù (太簇);
a pipe that is five-eighths the length
corresponds to the lǚ of Jiázhōng (夾鍾);
a pipe that is four-eighths the length
corresponds to the lǜ of Gūxǐ (姑洗);
a pipe that is three and a half eighths the length
corresponds to the lǚ of Zhònglǚ (仲呂);
a pipe that is three-eighths the length
corresponds to the lǜ of Ruíbīn (蕤賓);
a pipe that is two and a half eighths the length
corresponds to the lǚ of Línzhōng (林鍾);
a pipe that is two and a quarter eighths the length
corresponds to the lǜ of Yízé (夷則).
(This one-quarter of an eighth
is precisely one thirty-second of zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾);
at this point, the principle of thirty-seconds emerges.)
A pipe that is two-eighths the length
corresponds to the lǚ of Nánlǚ (南呂);
a pipe that is one and three-quarter eighths the length
corresponds to the lǜ of Wúshè (無射);
a pipe that is one and two-quarter eighths the length
corresponds to the lǚ of Yìngzhōng (應鍾);
a pipe that is one and one-quarter eighths the length
corresponds to the lǜ of bàn Huángzhōng (半黃鍾);
a pipe that is one and one-eighth eighths the length
corresponds to the lǚ of bàn Dàlǚ (半大呂).
(This one-eighth of an eighth
is precisely one sixty-fourth of zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾);
at this point, the principle of sixty-fourths emerges.)
And a pipe that is one-eighth the length
corresponds to zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾)
and is half the length and half the diameter of zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾).
From eight times Huángzhōng (黃鍾) down to one-eighth Huángzhōng (黃鍾),
all twelve lǜ lǚ (律呂) of the same diameter are present,
and all form a single key with five sounds and two biến (變).
Extending and deducing from this:
if the accumulated length of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is increased to sixty-four times,
then the pipes of the same form will have a length and diameter four times that of zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾);
if the accumulated length of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is decreased to one sixty-fourth,
then the pipes of the same form will have a length and diameter one-quarter that of zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾).
The pipe of the same form with sixty-four times the accumulated length corresponds to zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾);
the pipe of the same form with fifty-six times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is seven sixty-fourths correspond to Dàlǚ (大呂);
the pipe of the same form with forty-eight times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is six sixty-fourths correspond to Tàicù (太簇);
the pipe of the same form with forty times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is five sixty-fourths correspond to Jiázhōng (夾鍾);
the pipe of the same form with thirty-two times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is four sixty-fourths correspond to Gūxǐ (姑洗);
the pipe of the same form with twenty-eight times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is three and a half sixty-fourths correspond to Zhònglǚ (仲呂);
the pipe of the same form with twenty-four times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is three sixty-fourths correspond to Ruíbīn (蕤賓);
the pipe of the same form with twenty times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is two and a half sixty-fourths correspond to Línzhōng (林鍾);
the pipe of the same form with eighteen times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is two and a quarter sixty-fourths correspond to Yízé (夷則);
the pipe of the same form with sixteen times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is two sixty-fourths correspond to Nánlǚ (南呂);
the pipe of the same form with fourteen times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is one and three-quarter sixty-fourths correspond to Wúshè (無射);
the pipe of the same form with twelve times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is one and two-quarter sixty-fourths correspond to Yìngzhōng (應鍾);
the pipe of the same form with ten times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is one and one-quarter sixty-fourths correspond to bàn Huángzhōng (半黃鍾);
the pipe of the same form with nine times the accumulated length and the pipe of the same form that is one and one-eighth sixty-fourths correspond to bàn Dàlǚ (半大呂);
the pipe of the same form that is one sixty-fourth still corresponds to zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾).
Thus, the twelve lǜ lǚ (律呂) with the same diameter but different forms,
by combining their lengths as multiples or halves, achieve the function of xuángōng (旋宮).
And the Huángzhōng (黃鍾) pipes of the same form but different diameters,
by increasing or decreasing their actual lengths,
also achieve the function of xuángōng (旋宮).
The creation of instruments and the search for sounds
are unified here.
Nevertheless,
the five sounds and two biến (變) for pipes and strings differ from each other.
After the Hàn (漢) and Táng (唐) dynasties,
all followed the theories of Sīmǎ (司馬) and Huáinán (淮南),
mistakenly applying the method of dividing by three and adjusting by one (sānfēn sǔnyì zhī shù 三分損益之術)
to the order of the five sounds and two biến (變) for pipe tones,
and then taking the string divisions for the five sounds of the Guǎnzǐ (管子)
and forcibly applying them to the twelve lǜ lǚ (律呂).
If one tries to cut bamboo to make a pipe and blow it,
the half-lǜ of Huángzhōng (黃鍾)
does not harmonize with Huángzhōng (黃鍾);
rather, what harmonizes with Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is the half-lǜ of Tàicù (太簇).
This shows that the theory of "double and half correspondence"
applies to string tones, not pipe tones.
Furthermore, if Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is gōng (宮),
its zhēng (徵) sound does not correspond to Línzhōng (林鍾) but to Yízé (夷則).
This shows that the theory of "gōng (宮) generating zhēng (徵) by dividing by three and adjusting by one"
applies to string divisions, not pipe lǜ (律).
When deriving sounds from string divisions,
the sound of the full string and the half string correspond,
but the half-lǜ is one tone lower than the full lǜ.
This is because the physical nature of a string
relies on human effort to pluck it and produce sound.
A full string is long,
so its sound is slow (lower in pitch),
and a half string is short,
so its sound is fast (higher in pitch).
Within the range of long and short, slow and fast,
the principle of full and half correspondence is embedded.
The physical nature of a pipe is hollow;
it relies on human breath entering it to produce sound.
Therefore, for pipes of the same diameter,
their full and half lengths do not correspond.
To find a correspondence,
the diameter must be halved.
This is why zhèng Huángzhōng (正黃鍾) and a pipe that is one-eighth of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) correspond and produce the same sound.
Due to the difference between full and half,
the divisions for the five sounds and two biến (變) generated from the first to the eighth tone of pipe lǜ (律) and string divisions also differ.
For pipe lǜ (律), the full length of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is the first tone of the gōng (宮) sound;
then the half of Tàicù (太簇) is the eighth tone, shàogōng (少宮).
In between, the full Tàicù (太簇) is the second tone, shāng (商);
Gūxǐ (姑洗) is the third tone, jué (角);
Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is the fourth tone, biànzhēng (變徵);
Yízé (夷則) is the fifth tone, zhēng (徵);
Wúshè (無射) is the sixth tone, yǔ (羽);
the half of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is the seventh tone, biàngōng (變宮).
From the first tone to the eighth tone,
there are seven full divisions.
If string divisions hypothetically take the full division of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) as the first tone of the gōng (宮) sound,
then the half of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is the eighth tone, shàogōng (少宮).
In between, the division of Tàicù (太簇) is the second tone, shāng (商);
the division of Gūxǐ (姑洗) is the third tone, jué (角);
the division of Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is the fourth tone, biànzhēng (變徵);
the division of Línzhōng (林鍾) is the fifth tone, zhēng (徵);
the division of Nánlǚ (南呂) is the sixth tone, yǔ (羽);
the division of Yìngzhōng (應鍾) is the seventh tone, biàngōng (變宮).
For each string division,
from gōng (宮) to shāng (商),
shāng (商) to jué (角),
jué (角) to biànzhēng (變徵),
zhēng (徵) to yǔ (羽),
yǔ (羽) to biàngōng (變宮),
all are full divisions;
but from biànzhēng (變徵) to zhēng (徵),
and biàngōng (變宮) to shàogōng (少宮),
only half a division is obtained.
From the first tone to the eighth tone,
it sums to six full divisions.
Therefore, string tones cannot be divided according to the twelve lǜ lǚ (律呂).
For example, if the string is set to the character chǐ (尺) for the doubled Wúshè (無射) biàngōng (變宮),
then the division of xiàzhēng (下徵) is obtained.
(The character hézì (合字) for the doubled Wúshè (無射) biàngōng (變宮)
is the current hézì (合字) for the dí (笛) and tóuguǎn (頭管).
Any musical piece that places the first string
must obtain the division of xiàzhēng (下徵),
and only then are the positions of the five tones correct.
Therefore, the common practice of using the tóuguǎn (頭管) hézì (合字) to set one string of a qín (琴) as the gōng (宮) of Huángzhōng (黃鍾)
is precisely because one string must be set with the hézì (合字)
to obtain the division of xiàzhēng (下徵).)
If the string is set to the character gōng (工) for the gōng (宮) sound of Huángzhōng (黃鍾),
the division of xiàyǔ (下羽) is obtained;
if the string is set to the character fán (凡) for the shāng (商) sound of Tàicù (太簇),
the division of biàngōng (變宮) is obtained;
if the string is set to the character liù (六) for the jué (角) sound of Gūxǐ (姑洗),
the division of gōngxián (宮絃) is obtained;
if the string is set to the character wǔ (五) for the biànzhēng (變徵) sound of Ruíbīn (蕤賓),
the division of shāngxián (商絃) is obtained;
if the string is set to the character yǐ (乙) for the zhēng (徵) sound of Yízé (夷則),
the division of juéxián (角絃) is obtained;
if the string is set to the character shàng (上) for the yǔ (羽) sound of Wúshè (無射),
the division of biànzhēng (變徵) is obtained;
and if the string is set to the character chǐ (尺) for the biàngōng (變宮) of bàn Huángzhōng (半黃鍾),
the division of zhēngxián (徵絃) is still obtained.
Now, if we borrow the division of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) as the full division of the gōngxián (宮絃),
and its first tone is still set to the lǜ of Huángzhōng (黃鍾),
then the second tone is limited by the division of Tàicù (太簇),
and its sound also corresponds to the lǜ of Tàicù (太簇).
The third tone then changes to the division of Jiázhōng (夾鍾),
and its sound begins to correspond to the lǜ of Gūxǐ (姑洗).
If the division of Gūxǐ (姑洗) is still used,
then the sound will change and correspond to the lǚ of Zhònglǚ (仲呂).
The fourth tone then changes to the division of Zhònglǚ (仲呂),
and its sound corresponds to the lǜ of Ruíbīn (蕤賓).
If the division of Ruíbīn (蕤賓) is still used,
then the sound will change and correspond to the lǚ of Línzhōng (林鍾).
The fifth tone will be the division of Línzhōng (林鍾) and correspond to the lǜ of Yízé (夷則).
The sixth tone will be the division of Nánlǚ (南呂) and correspond to the lǜ of Wúshè (無射).
The seventh tone then changes to the division of Wúshè (無射),
and its sound begins to correspond to the lǜ of bàn Huángzhōng (半黃鍾).
If the division of Yìngzhōng (應鍾) is still used,
then the sound will change and correspond to the lǚ of bàn Dàlǚ (半大呂).
This is how the gōngxián (宮絃) division, due to its full string's first tone being set to the lǜ of Huángzhōng (黃鍾),
changes into the division of a yǔxián (羽絃).
Alternatively, if the division of Huángzhōng (黃鍾) is taken as the full division of the gōngxián (宮絃),
and the seven tones of the main string are each desired to be limited by the divisions of the seven tones within the gōngxián (宮絃),
then the first tone must be set to the lǜ of Gūxǐ (姑洗).
Dividing it in sequence,
this is how the gōngxián (宮絃) division, due to its full string's first tone being set to the lǜ of Gūxǐ (姑洗),
obtains the division of a gōngxián (宮絃).
Yet another way is to take the hézì (合字) of the dí (笛) and tóuguǎn (頭管), which is now set as the doubled lǜ of Wúshè (無射), as the full division of the gōngxián (宮絃).
Dividing the first tone in sequence,
the division of xiàzhēngxián (下徵絃) is obtained.
This is how the gōngxián (宮絃) division, due to its full string's first tone being set to the hézì (合字) of the dí (笛),
changes into the division of a zhēngxián (徵絃).
If string tones are set according to lǜ lǚ (律呂),
then the string divisions subtly shift accordingly.
If the sequence of seven tones is named according to string divisions,
then the musical modes (gōng diào 宮調) will not accord with lǜ lǚ (律呂).
This is due to the different ways pipe lǜ (律) and string divisions generate sound and obtain divisions,
and thus the xuángōng zhuǎndiào (旋宮轉調) of string music
also differs from that of pipe music.
The two modes, Qīng and Zhuó, each have seven *diào*,
some of which are identical to wind instruments,
some of which can be made identical,
and some of which cannot.
Only the Gōng *diào* is identical;
the five notes and two transformations all correspond correctly.
Those that can be made identical
are the Shāng *diào* and Zhēng *diào*, where the five notes, the main sound, and the two transformations are borrowed.
Those that cannot be made identical
are the Jiǎo *diào*, Biànzhēng *diào*, Yǔ *diào*, and Biàngōng *diào*, within which the Qīng and Zhuó sounds are mixed.
If they are played solely with string instruments
and not accompanied by wind instruments,
there are only four *diào*;
the remaining three *diào* all transition into the string instrument Gōng *diào*.
Therefore, the *Rítual of Zhōu* (Zhōulǐ)'s Grand Director of Music (Dàsīyuè)'s three Gōng,
and the *Hàn Shū*'s (Hàn Zhì) three systems (sāntǒng),
all take the three *diào* as their standard.
The so-called three systems are:
The first is the Heavenly System (Tiāntǒng),
with Huángzhōng as the Gōng.
This is the Huángzhōng Gōng pitch, with the Yǔ starting the *diào*.
Gūxǐ's Jiǎo pitch establishes the Gōng,
and the main *diào* is thus the Gōng *diào*.
The second is the Human System (Réntǒng),
with Tàicù as the Gōng.
This is Tàicù's Shāng pitch, with the Yǔ starting the *diào*.
Ruíbīn's Biànzhēng establishes the Gōng,
and the main *diào* is thus the Shāng *diào*.
The third is the Earthly System (Dìtǒng),
with Línzhōng as the Gōng.
This is the string instrument Zhēng subdivision as Yǔ,
actually the wind instrument Yízé's Zhēng pitch, with the Yǔ starting the *diào*.
Half Huángzhōng's Biàngōng establishes the Gōng,
and the main *diào* is thus the Zhēng *diào*.
In the *Suí Shū*'s (Suí Zhì) account, Zhèng Yì said: "Examining the *lǜlǚ*,
within the seven pitches,
three pitches are discordant."
At that time, when comparing pitches and *lǜlǜ*,
some used wind instruments to verify string instruments,
and some used string instruments to verify wind instruments.
Thus, four *diào* were harmonious,
and three *diào* were discordant,
which are the two transformed *diào* and the Jiǎo *diào*.
(In the Biànzhēng *diào* and Yǔ *diào*, only one pitch among the five main pitches is discordant.
However, the Yǔ *diào* can still stand as a distinct *diào*,
while the Biànzhēng *diào* transitions into the Gōng *diào* pitch names.
As for the Jiǎo *diào* and Biàngōng *diào*,
two or three pitches among the five pitches are discordant,
largely resembling the Gōng *diào* pitch names,
and thus cannot form a distinct *diào*.)
The *Táng Shū* (Táng Zhì) records four Gōng and twenty-eight *diào*,
which generally define the twelve *lǜlǚ* based on the divisions of string instruments.
Hence, there are names like Zhènggōng Dàshí and Gāodàshí.
Now, by examining the harmony or disharmony of string and wind instruments,
to distinguish between the separate or combined use of Yang *lǜ* and Yin *lǚ*,
we realize that the twenty-eight *diào* in the *Táng Shū* only considered string instruments,
not wind *lǜlǜ*.
And the three systems used by the ancients
actually utilized the harmonious combination of wind and string instruments.
Therefore, there are four key aspects to string instrument music: First,
to determine the pitch name of a string instrument corresponding to a certain *lǜlǜ*,
thereby obtaining the precise division of that string.
Second,
string instrument *diào* cannot be successively transposed in sequence.
Therefore, taking the Gōng *diào* as the standard,
some strings remain unchanged,
while other strings are either tightened by one semitone
or loosened by half a semitone,
thus forming a *diào*,
and the divisions of the seven pitches for each string change accordingly.
Third,
although string instrument *diào* do not have two transformations,
when tuning strings and selecting pitches,
one must carefully examine the pitches of the two transformations
and calculate their divisions
to grasp their organization;
otherwise,
the Gōng *diào* has no standard to refer to.
Fourth,
in string instrument Gōng *diào*,
only Gōng, Shāng, and Zhēng can be harmonized with the *lǜlǜ* for use.
The other four *diào* have discordant Yin and Yang,
or are mixed into the Gōng *diào* pitch names,
and cannot form distinct *diào*.
If these four points
are analyzed meticulously,
then the methods for string instrument *xuángōng zhuǎndiào* will be complete.
As the study of music became obscure,
speakers since ancient times offered divergent and abundant theories,
with no consensus.
Sīmǎ Qiān (Zǐcháng) and Bān Gù (Mèngjiān) already had differing views.
During the Suí and Táng dynasties, ritual music (dēnggē)
mixed with Sogdian (Sūzhībó) and Kuchean (Gūcí) music.
If one applies the *lǜlǜ* to it,
the divine skill of the blind musician (Shéngǔ) was not inherited,
akin to the loss of poetry.
During the Sòng dynasty, people like Lǐ Zhào, Hé Xiàn, Fàn Zhèn, and Cài Yuándìng,
showed some ambition to restore ancient practices,
but only relied on empirical verification,
or even embellished their theories with explanations of Yin and Yang "outer walls."
It was the Ming dynasty prince Zhū Zàiyù who first discussed *lǜlǜ* measurements using Gougu (Pythagorean theorem).
He was inherently skilled in mathematics,
added precise ratios,
and based his work on practical measurements.
The thousand-year-old errors in wind instrument and string divisions
were thus finally corrected.
The following year, his book was completed,
divided into three sections: "Correcting the *Lǜlǜ* and Examining Sounds" (Zhènglǜ Shěnyīn),
which elucidated the starting numbers of Huángzhōng,
and the principles of increasing and decreasing *lǜlǜ* based on length, volume, area, and circumference, as well as the method of *xuángōng* for wind and string *lǜlǜ*;
"Harmonizing Sounds and Establishing Music" (Héshēng Dìnglè),
which clarified the essentials of making instruments from the eight materials (bāyīn),
and detailed the similarities and differences between ancient and modern practices;
and "Coordinating Modes and Arranging Melodies" (Xiéjūn Dùqǔ),
which took the principles of rhythm and meter taught by the Portuguese (Bō'ěrdūhā'ěr guórén) Xu Rìshēng and the Italian (Yìdàlǐyà guórén) Délǐgé,
and verified them with the *lǜlǜ* and Gōng *diào* methods recorded in classics and histories,
allocating them to the two notational systems of Yin and Yang,
and was bestowed the name *Lǜlǜ Zhèngyì*.
Lánshēng, Tíngzhēn, and others were all granted the *jìdì* degree
and promoted in office to varying ranks.
Afterwards, an edict was issued to revise and correct the pitches of the Zhōnghé music pieces,
stating:
"The Zhōnghé music pieces performed in the palace
all follow the Ming dynasty style,
with lines of varying lengths
and a structure resembling *cí* poetry.
Because this was deemed inelegant,
Grand Secretary Chén Tíngjìng and others were commanded to revise and compose them.
The structure of the chapters now uses four-character lines,
but the musicians, being unfamiliar with the new pitches,
still sing them by piecing together long and short lines to fit the rhythm.
Now that the old *diào* have been rediscovered,
the Gōng-Shāng rhythm is very harmonious.
It is imperative that the words and phrases of the songs also follow the rhyme,
so that the chapters are clear and the Gōng pitches are harmonious.
Let the Hanlin of the Nánshūfáng, together with the Grand Secretaries,
carefully deliberate and report."
In the eleventh month of that year, during the winter solstice,
the emperor personally sacrificed at the Huánqiū,
using the newly established *lǜlǜ* and music.
In the 54th year,
the Huánqiū altar was rebuilt,
with sixteen bronze bells and jade chimes each.
In the 55th year,
the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè was promulgated to the Confucian Temples in the provinces (zhíshěng).
Initially,
the music pieces had been revised to use "Píng",
but the provinces still used "Hé".
It was then, following the request from the Ministry of Rites,
that the new system was first promulgated.
In the second year of Shìzōng Yōngzhèng's reign (1724),
thirty-six songs for the plowing ceremony (gēngjí) were established.
For the banquet music during the plowing ceremony,
when presenting the feast,
the court orchestra played the "Rain and Sunshine Timely" (Yǔyáng Shíruò) movement;
when presenting wine,
the wind and string instruments played the "Bumper Harvest of Five Grains" (Wǔgǔ Fēngdēng) movement;
when presenting dishes,
the *qīngyuè* played the "Every Household Prosperous and People Content" (Jiāgěi Rénzú) movement.
The lyrics for these
were all composed by Grand Secretary Jiǎng Tíngxí.
Later, regulations were also set for music during sacrifices:
the Fēngbó Temple sacrifice and the Jiàofāngsī were to provide music;
the Léishī and Yúnshī Temples sacrifices were to have music provided by the Héshēngshǔ.
For official and commoner weddings,
officials (pǐnguān) were not allowed to have more than twelve drummers and musicians,
and students (shēng), imperial students (jiān), military personnel (jūn), and commoners (mín)
were not allowed to have more than eight musicians.
These were enacted as regulations.
Gāozōng ascended the throne.
He was keen on making new regulations and systems.
Prince Zhuāng, Yǔnlù, had been supervising the revision of the three books on law and mathematics since the time of Shèngzǔ,
and by this time he still managed musical affairs.
In the sixth year of Qiánlóng,
when the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè was performed in the palace,
the emperor felt that the melodies and rhythms were not harmonious with the lyrics.
He then ordered Prince Hé, Hóngzhòu, to test them together with Yǔnlù.
Yǔnlù then said:
"According to the old system of the Míng dynasty,
the musical lyrics were composed of lines of five, six, or seven characters,
and the rhythm of the melody followed accordingly.
Both the lyrics and the melody had eight lines,
thus their lengths were harmonious.
Now, if the palace music is fixed at four characters per line,
it would be no different from the music for the altars and temples.
Only by re-establishing the musical lyrics,
which is crucial for grand ceremonies,
should the Grand Secretary and the Ministry of Rites be consulted to deliberate on the twelve compositions of the musical lyrics in detail,
and then the Hànlín Academy be ordered to revise and present them."
Soon after, Grand Secretary È'ěrtài and others deliberated:
"Among the twelve compositions of musical lyrics,
only Shúpíng and Shùnpíng compositions have eight lines per chapter.
The other ten compositions have ten lines per chapter,
with four characters per line.
However, when judged by the melody,
each chapter has eight lines,
with six, seven, or eight characters per line.
To combine a ten-line, four-character musical lyric
with an eight-line, six, seven, or eight-character melody,
the length and intonation
are unlikely to be entirely harmonious.
Therefore, the number of characters per line in the musical lyrics
should be adjusted to match the rhythm of the melody.
Each chapter should be composed of eight lines,
and lines are not restricted to four characters."
The proposal was approved.
The old Zhōnghé music's bianzhong had four extra *yí zé* bells placed before the *huáng zhōng* bell,
and the emperor doubted their correctness.
He also inquired of his officials about the "doubled pitches" of the bianzhong and the reason why some were set up but not played.
At that time, Zhāng Zhào, as an Assistant Minister of Justice, assisted Yǔnlù in managing the ministry.
He was renowned for his knowledge of music.
He reported:
"The system of bianzhong
consists of sixteen bells per frame.
The eight *yáng lǜ* are in one suspension,
placed above;
the eight *yīn lǜ* are in another suspension,
placed below.
*Yáng* from *yáng*,
*yīn* from *yīn*.
The *lǜ lǚ* system
must have 'doubled' (bèi) and 'half' (bàn) pitches
to ensure the completeness of high and low, clear and turbid sounds,
thus achieving the function of tonal modulation.
Therefore, the *yáng lǜ* have *bèi ruí bīn*, *bèi yí zé*, and *bèi wú shè* before *huáng zhōng*,
and *bàn huáng zhōng*, *bàn tài cù*, and *bàn gū xǐ* after *wú shè*.
The *yīn lǜ* have *bèi lín zhōng*, *bèi nán lǚ*, and *bèi yìng zhōng* before *dà lǚ*,
and *bàn dà lǚ*, *bàn jiá zhōng*, and *bàn zhòng lǚ* after *yìng zhōng*.
Pitches lower than *bèi ruí bīn*
are too low and muffled,
and pitches higher than *bàn zhòng lǚ*
are too high and sharp,
hence they are not used.
The bianzhong does not have *bèi ruí bīn* or *bèi lín zhōng*,
nor does it have the six half-pitches.
This is because the eight bianzhong
produce harmonious and moderate sounds,
which are sufficient for use.
The low range does not reach *bèi ruí bīn* or *bèi lín zhōng*,
and the high range does not reach the six half-pitches.
Their order is arranged
from low to high,
from turbid to clear.
*Bèi yí zé* and *bèi wú shè* should be before *huáng zhōng*,
and *bèi nán lǚ* and *bèi yìng zhōng* should be before *dà lǚ*,
following the same principle as the lengths of flutes
and the thickness of zither strings.
In the panpipes, the two pipes for *bèi yí zé* and *bèi wú shè* are before *huáng zhōng*,
and the two pipes for *bèi nán lǚ* and *bèi yìng zhōng* are before *dà lǚ*.
On the zither, the two strings for *bèi zhǐ* and *bèi yǔ* are before the *gōng* string.
If the positions of zither strings or panpipe tubes were exchanged,
the sounds would not be harmonious.
Therefore, the arrangement of the bianzhong is the same as that of stringed and wind instruments."
He further reported:
"A frame of bianzhong
has eight bells on top and eight below.
The upper ones are *yáng lǜ*,
the lower ones are *yīn lǜ*.
Regarding the rules for striking,
during sacrifices at the Southern Suburbs, temple rites, and grand court ceremonies,
*huáng zhōng* is used as the *gōng* note.
For the Northern Suburbs and the Altar of the Moon,
*dà lǚ* is used as the *gōng* note.
When *huáng zhōng* is used as *gōng*,
the upper bells are struck.
When *dà lǚ* is used as *gōng*,
the lower bells are struck.
During court audiences, the lower bells are exchanged and placed on top to be struck,
it does not mean that the eight lower bells are not struck.
Also, the eight bells originally only produced seven notes.
When *gū xǐ* is the *gōng* note,
and *huáng zhōng* starts the tune as the 'gōng' character,
*bèi yí zé* and *wú shè* become *biàn zhǐ*,
and *tài cù* becomes *biàn gōng*.
These three bells are not part of the tune,
hence they are not struck.
Outside of the 'gōng' character tune,
only two bells are not struck.
If *tài cù* is taken as the *gōng* note,
and *bèi wú shè* starts the tune as the 'chǐ' character,
then *bèi yí zé*, *wú shè*, and *tài cù* three bells are all struck,
while *huáng zhōng* becomes *biàn gōng*,
and *yí zé* becomes *biàn zhǐ*,
and these two bells should then not be struck.
However, due to tradition, *huáng zhōng* tune has always been considered *huáng zhōng gōng*.
Confucian scholars, not knowing music,
believed that *huáng zhōng* is the origin of sound and energy,
the mother of all things,
and using it for sacrifices and court audiences brings good fortune,
otherwise, misfortune.
They do not realize that when *huáng zhōng* is the *gōng* note,
its first sound is *xià yǔ*.
Excluding *biàn gōng* and *biàn zhǐ* which are not part of the tune,
*shāng*, *jiǎo*, *zhǐ*, *yǔ* must be used alternately.
If every sound were *huáng zhōng*,
as Yàn Zǐ said about a zither playing only one note,
who could listen to it?
Moreover, the music of *Dà Wǔ*
actually used *wú shè* as the *gōng* note,
as recorded in the *Guó Yǔ*.
*Wú shè* is the end of the *yáng lǜ*,
yet King Wǔ used it.
Therefore, it is clear
that it is perfectly acceptable
for each of the twelve months to use its corresponding *lǜ* as the *gōng* note."
The emperor approved this,
and ordered it to remain as before.
At that time,
the Qīng dynasty had flourished for over a hundred years.
Ancient learning had begun to sprout,
and many Confucian scholars like Máo Qílǐng, Lǐ Gōng, Hú Yànshēng, and Jiāng Yǒng wrote extensively on the subject of music,
with their textual research becoming increasingly meticulous.
The emperor also admired the grandeur of the nine-fold performance of the Xiāosháo music,
composing poems and compiling odes,
courageous in making reforms,
hoping to achieve great peace through culture.
Although a book on music had been compiled during the reign of the Shèngzǔ Emperor,
it mostly focused on pitches and rhythms,
but the musical sections lacked notation,
and did not correspond to the sounds.
There was a director of harmony, Gāo Wànlín,
who, advanced in years, refined the pitches,
and revised the *gōng* [keynote] scores,
but this was only for the music of the altars and ancestral temples.
For court assemblies and clear singing,
the previous errors were still followed.
Zhào then requested to continue compiling the treatise on pitches and temperaments,
stating,
"The lost ancient canons
should be corrected and rectified."
This was granted.
A bureau was opened for compilation,
and Yǔnlù was again commanded to oversee the matter.
Soon after,
the officials of the bureau submitted a proposal:
"Regarding the notation for the music of altars and temples,
the Heavenly Altar, Imperial Ancestral Temple, and Altar of the Morning Sun all use Huángzhōng as the *gōng*;
the Altar of the Earth and Altar of the Evening Moon use Dàlǚ as the *gōng*.
This is close to the Southern Qí practice of only using Huángzhōng,
but also incorporates both *qīng* [clear] and *zhuó* [濁] [heavy] modes.
As for Dàlǚ,
though its meaning has merit,
the bells within the *biānzhōng* must include some that are set up but not played,
similar to the reproach of 'mute bells' before the Suí dynasty.
Our Emperor's creations establish the age,
continuing a brilliant legacy.
It is appropriate to extensively research and thoroughly investigate,
to assist in this grand ceremony.
Indeed, when speaking of rites and music, one must adhere to the accomplishments of the Zhōu dynasty.
However, the Zhōu dynasty is distant,
and its texts are insufficient for verification.
What can be examined
is best found in the *Zhōu Lǐ*.
But the *Zhōu Lǐ*'s statements that the Yuánzhōng is the *gōng* for sacrificing to Heaven, Hánzhōng for sacrificing to Earth, and Huángzhōng for sacrificing to the ancestral temple,
do not specify what pitch Yuánzhōng and Hánzhōng are.
Zhèng Kāngchéng took Yuánzhōng to be Jiázhōng
and Hánzhōng to be Línzhōng.
Sacrificing to Earth with Línzhōng
is indeed a good interpretation.
However, why Línzhōng is also called Hánzhōng
is without basis.
Only by analyzing the sequence of the six *lǜ* [pitches]
is there Hánzhōng but no Línzhōng,
thus knowing that Hánzhōng is Línzhōng.
However, among the six *lǜ*, there is Jiázhōng but no Yuánzhōng.
To take Yuánzhōng as Jiázhōng,
saying that Jiázhōng is born between Fáng and Xīn constellations,
and Fáng and Xīn are great stars,
the Bright Hall of the Celestial Emperor,
is to use the words of the warring states' astrologers Gān Gōng and Shí Shēn,
to explain the system of the Duke of Zhōu seven hundred years prior.
This is certainly not thorough scholarship.
Lǐ Guāngdì said that sacrificing to Heaven uses Huángzhōng as the *gōng*,
and sacrificing to the ancestral temple uses Yuánzhōng as the *gōng*,
with Yuánzhōng and Huángzhōng alternating,
which scholars have followed without change.
Measuring this against the text of the spring *dì* sacrifice,
which takes place in the month of Jiázhōng,
it seems reasonable,
but it also stems from personal opinion.
The *Zhōu Lǐ* originally states that sacrificing to Heaven uses Yuánzhōng as the *gōng*;
immediately below it says Huángzhōng is the *jiǎo* [third note of the pentatonic scale].
In a single chapter of music,
there is no principle where Huángzhōng is both the *gōng* [first note]
and the *jiǎo*.
In the sequence of the six *lǜ*,
each *qīng* and *zhuó* has one mode.
Huángzhōng and Dàlǚ are paired for sacrificing to the celestial deities;
Tàicù and Yìngzhōng are paired for sacrificing to the terrestrial deities;
Gūxǐ and Nánlǚ are paired for sacrificing to the four directions;
Ruíbīn and Hánzhōng are paired for sacrificing to mountains and rivers;
Yízé and Zhònglǚ are paired for honoring Jiāng Yuán;
Wúshè and Jiázhōng are paired for honoring ancestors.
The order of the pitches determines the hierarchy of the deities.
However, when *lǜ* and *lǚ* are used together,
between *qīng* and *zhuó*,
some are in the same mode,
some are in different modes,
making it difficult to implement
in practice.
Therefore, successive dynasties all wished to emulate the Zhōu system,
but struggled to find a reliable basis.
For court audiences and banquets, the *lǜ* of the respective month should be used as the *gōng*.
This is the most accepted theory.
Huángzhōng occupies the Zǐ position,
the governing principle of Heaven.
The Qián trigram is in Hài,
and Zǐ is before Hài,
the beginning of the twelve earthly branches.
Huángzhōng generates Línzhōng downwards;
Línzhōng occupies the Wèi position,
the governing principle of Earth.
The Kūn trigram is in Shēn,
with Yang moving forward and Yin moving backward,
so Wèi is before Shēn.
From Zǐ to Wǔ are seven *lǜ*,
and the Way of Heaven is complete.
From Wèi to Chǒu are seven *lǜ*,
and the Way of Earth is complete.
Thus, Huángzhōng belongs to Heaven,
Línzhōng belongs to Earth.
Línzhōng generates Tàicù upwards;
Tàicù occupies the Yín position,
the governing principle of humanity.
Therefore, it is used for sacrificing to the ancestral temple.
This embodies the ancient scholars' saying that 'all things originate from Heaven,
and humans originate from ancestors.'
Guāngdì also praised Zǔ Xiàosūn for his unique foresight,
and among the music used throughout history,
this is the closest to antiquity.
Your humble servants' foolish opinion is

that we should follow the method of *xuán gōng zhuǎn diào* [changing the key and shifting the mode] established in the Shèngzǔ Emperor's *Lǜ Lǚ Zhèng Yì* (Correct Meaning of Pitches and Temperaments),
changing the music for the Altar of the Earth to use Línzhōng as the *gōng*,
and the music for the Imperial Ancestral Temple to use Tàicù as the *gōng*.
The Altar of the Grain God is also associated with Earth,
and should also be changed to use Línzhōng as the *gōng*.
The moon rises in the west,
Yǒu [the earthly branch corresponding to west]
is the correct position of the west.
Moreover, the autumn equinox sacrifices to the moon,
which is the month of Jiànyǒu.
The Altar of the Evening Moon should be changed to use Nánlǚ as the *gōng*.
If the Altar of the Morning Sun is considered in terms of the sun in the east and the moon in the west, and the sun in Mǎo and the moon in Yǒu,
it should use Jiázhōng as the *gōng*.
However, Jiázhōng is Yin while the sun is Yang;
considering the meaning that the human heart belongs to the sun,
it is appropriate to change to Tàicù as the *gōng*.
For court assemblies and banquets,
they should all follow Táng dynasty's Zǔ Xiàosūn's theory,
using the *lǜ* of their respective months as the *gōng*.
The Altar of the First Farmer,
which is for agricultural matters,
should use Gūxǐ as the *gōng*.
For the Temples of Emperors of Past Dynasties and the Temple of Kǒngzǐ, sacrifices are made in spring and autumn;
Jiázhōng for spring and Nánlǚ for autumn as the *gōng*.
The Altar of the Grand Year should use Tàicù, the *lǜ* of the beginning of the year, as the *gōng*."
The memorial was submitted,
but the music for the Empress Dowager and Empress ascending their seats and returning to their palaces still lacked determined pitches and temperaments.
Therefore, the officials of rites were ordered to convene a discussion.
Yǔnlù deliberated, saying:
"For the music of the Empress Dowager and Empress, the appropriate pitches and temperaments
were extensively researched in previous canons,
but no clear text was found.
However, all twelve *lǜlǚ* are generated from Huángzhōng;
thus, Huángzhōng is the origin of sound and *qì*.
But since it is exclusively used in the Southern Suburb to honor the Supreme Emperor,
it is naturally inconvenient to propose its use.
Moreover, *lǜ* corresponds to Qián [Heaven],
and *lǚ* corresponds to Kūn [Earth];
the origin of Kūn indeed should use *lǚ*.
Dàlǚ is the *lǚ* of Huángzhōng.
Therefore, it is proposed that the Empress Dowager's music use Dàlǚ as the *gōng*.
The *Lǐ Jì* states: 'The Son of Heaven is the sun;
the sun and moon follow each other from east to west without ceasing,
this is the Way of Heaven.'
Yǒu is the correct position of the moon.
Drawing upon the meaning of 'Empress as the moon,'
it is proposed that the Empress's music use Nánlǚ as the *gōng*."
Prince Lǚ, Yǔntáo, deliberated, saying:
"The bureau officials proposed Dàlǚ as the *gōng* for the Empress Dowager's music,
and Nánlǚ as the *gōng* for the Empress's music.
Your humble servant believes that Dàlǚ and Nánlǚ are both Yin *lǚ*.
The Emperor once issued an edict: 'For all grand celebration ceremonies,
the Empress Dowager's palace should use Yang *lǜ*.'
According to the old system, all grand ceremonies
used Huángzhōng as the *gōng*.
I request that the old system be followed.
For the Emperor's three major festivals—Winter Solstice, New Year's Day, and His Majesty's Birthday—
and the Empress Dowager's and Empress's three major festivals,
Huángzhōng should be used as the *gōng*."
The Emperor replied:
"Dàlǚ
is the *lǚ* of Huángzhōng.
Since Huángzhōng is used to honor the Supreme Emperor,
Línzhōng to honor the Empress of Earth,
and Tàicù to honor the ancestral temple,
and the Empress Dowager's music is proposed to use Dàlǚ,
the order of Dàlǚ
is after Nánlǚ.
If the Empress's music already uses Nánlǚ,
this places her before the Empress Dowager.
Moreover, the Fāngzé Altar uses the *lǚ* Ruíbīn,
with Línzhōng as the *gōng*.
and the Altars of Soil and Grain should also be distinct."
He therefore ordered a re-discussion.
Thereupon, the palace scholars requested that the music for the Empress Dowager be set to the gōng of Nánlǚ,
and for the Altars of Soil and Grain sacrifices in the second month of spring and autumn, on the first wù day,
the gōng should be Jiázhōng and Nánlǚ.
This was approved.
In the seventh year,
Yǔnlù and others again memorialized:
"For the Grand Empress Dowager's ascent to the throne and return to the palace, the Zhōnghé Sháolè is used;
for ceremonies, the Dānbì Lè is used,
which is the same as for the Emperor.
However, the Empress Dowager and Empress both use the Dānbì Lè.
Upon consulting the Zhǎngyí Sī (Office of Ceremonies),
from ancient times, for ascent to the throne and return to the palace, the Zhōnghé Sháolè has always been used.
When Chén Tíngjìng drafted the musical compositions,
considering that the Empress Dowager and Empress dared not be the same as the Grand Empress Dowager,
he named it Dānbì.
We request to revert to the old practice,
and compose separate musical pieces."
Soon after, it was decided that for the Empress Dowager's ascent to the throne in Cíníng Gōng, the Zhōnghé Sháolè should play Yùpíng;
for the Emperor leading the princes and officials in performing rites, the Dānbì Dàlè should play Yìpíng;
for returning to the palace, the Zhōnghé Sháolè should play Lǚpíng.

The Empress leading the Imperial Noble Consorts, Noble Consorts, Consorts, Concubines, as well as Princesses, Fújìn, and Noble Ladies in performing rites at the palace, should follow the same practice.
For the Emperor's three major festivals, when appearing at the open veranda, returning to the palace, and ascending to the throne in the inner hall, the Zhōnghé Sháolè should play Yuánpíng;
for the Empress leading the Imperial Noble Consorts, Noble Consorts, Consorts, and Concubines in performing rites, the Dānbì Dàlè should play Yōngpíng;
for descending from the throne, the Zhōnghé Sháolè should play Hépíng.
For the Empress's three major festivals, when ascending to the throne, the Zhōnghé Sháolè should play Shúpíng;
for performing rites, the Dānbì Dàlè should play Zhèngpíng;
for descending from the throne, the Zhōnghé Sháolè should play Shùnpíng.
For the Emperor's banquets, serving of tea, and granting of tea, the Dānbì Qīnglè should play Hǎiyǔ Shēngpíng Rì;
for serving of wine and granting of wine, it should play Yùdiàn Yún Kāi;
for serving of dishes and granting of food, the Zhōnghé Qīnglè should play Wànxiàng Qīngníng.
For the Empress Dowager's three major festivals, her ascent to the throne, return to the palace, and performance of rites should be the same as for celebrations.
The lyrics played for banquets, serving of tea, wine, and dishes should be the same as the Emperor's.
At this time, Xú Yǐshēng, the Supervising Censor for Shāndōng Circuit, memorialized:
"In ancient times, there was the ceremony of Yújì,
which was for praying for abundant rain for the hundred grains.
Its system
was to build an altar beside the southern suburb.
Our dynasty's ritual system is complete,
only the Yújì has no altar enclosure.
I humbly request an imperial edict for the ritual officials to extensively seek precedents,
carefully examine the system,
and emulate the ancient rite of 'dragon appearing, then performing Yú' (Lóng Xiàn Ér Yú),
to select a location and erect an altar."
The Emperor sent down his memorial,
and Grand Secretary È'ěrtài and others deliberated, saying:
"In the first month of summer,
the Azure Dragon constellation appears in the east,
to pray for abundant rain for the hundred grains,
hence 'dragon appearing, then performing Yú'.
In the Yonghe (永和) era of the Jìn (晉) dynasty,
a Yú altar was built according to the suburban altar system,
to pray to the Supreme Lord and all deities.
If there was a drought, rain was prayed for.
In the Táng (唐) dynasty, Yú sacrifices were performed in the southern suburb,
and later the Yú rites were performed at the Yuánqiú.
For the Yú rites during droughts after the first month of summer in the capital of successive dynasties,
prayers were offered once every seven days.
The Táng system was the most judicious.
Your ministers deliberate that its system should be emulated.
In ancient grand Yú, two ranks of dancing children were used,
dressed in black robes,
each holding feather screens,
singing the poems of Yúnhàn.
Now, His Majesty has composed eight chapters of poems in the style of Yúnhàn,
His Sacred thoughts are earnest,
and the Imperial compositions are incisive.
Sixteen dancing children should be used,
in black robes,
in eight rows,
holding feather screens.
When the music for the final offering stops,
the announcer announces: 'Dancing children sing poems.'
After the singing,
the ceremonial burning is observed.
The Zhǎngyí Sī is ordered to select those with clear and bright voices to fill these roles.
The feather screens should follow the style of the 'Imperial Dance' in the Zhōu Lǐ.
The rites and ceremonies should be the same as the regular Yú in the first month of summer.
The Altars of the Supreme Lord, Soil and Grain, Ancestral Temples, and Grand Age Deity all have existing musical compositions,
only the Altar of Deities is lacking.
An edict should be issued to the Lǜlǚ Guǎn to compose and submit them."
Thereupon, it was decided that for Yú sacrifices to the Celestial Deities, they should follow the Yuánqiú,
with Huángzhōng as the gōng;
for the Terrestrial Deities, they should follow the Fāngzé,
with Línzhōng as the gōng.
The music should use seven movements:
for welcoming the deities, play Qífēng;
for presenting silk, play Huáfēng;
for the initial offering, play Ānfēng;
for the second offering, play Xīngfēng;
for the final offering, play Yífēng;
for removing dishes, play Héfēng;
for sending off the deities, play Xīfēng.
In this year, a dedicated Music Department was established.
All sacrificial music managed by the Tàicháng Sì and Shénlè Guān,
court assembly and banquet music managed by the Héshēng Shǔ and Zhǎngyí Sī,
and ceremonial procession music managed by the Luán'yí Wèi,
were all subordinated to it.
Ministers of the Lǐ Bù and Nèiwù Fǔ, as well as ministers from various boards and offices who were knowledgeable in music, were to oversee it.
It established Shǔzhèng, Shǔchéng, Shìcóng, Dàizhào, Gōngfèng, Gōngyòngguān, drummers, and musicians,
collectively called Shǔlì (Departmental Officials),
and their titles were distinguished by the musical instruments they managed.
Those for bells were called Sīzhōng, for chimes Sīqìng,
and for qín, sè, shēng, xiāo, likewise.
Also, Daoist priests were prohibited from serving as musicians in the Tàicháng Sì.
Initially,
many of the Míng (明) dynasty's music and dance performers were selected from Daoist acolytes.
When Shìzǔ established the capital,
this practice was continued,
but the Daoists became lax and irreverent,
which discerning individuals lamented.
It was not until this time that the abuse was finally reformed.
Subsequently, following the advice of the palace scholars,
the music for the ploughing ceremony (Gēngjí) was established.
Before the Gēngjí, seeds were presented.
The guiding and welcoming music led the procession.
On the day,
the Héshēng Shǔ and its subordinates stood respectfully to the south of the decorated canopy.
(The system of decorated canopies
was abolished twenty-three years later.)
Fourteen persons sang the harvest chants,
six persons each managed gongs, drums, clappers, flutes, shēng, and xiāo.
Fifty persons carried colored flags.
After the sacrifice,
the Gēngjí rite was performed.
Upon completion of the rite,
the guiding and welcoming music began.
When the imperial carriage arrived at the inner gate of the fasting palace,
the music stopped,
and the Zhōnghé Sháolè began.
When the Emperor arrived at the rear hall,
the music stopped.
After reporting the completion of the ploughing of an acre (zhōngmǔ),
the Zhōnghé Sháolè began.
When the Emperor arrived at the fasting palace,
and ascended to the throne,
the music stopped.
The officials offered congratulations and performed rites,
and the Dānbì Dàlè began.
For serving tea and granting tea, the Zhōnghé Sháolè began.
When the Emperor rode in his palanquin out of the palace,
the Héshēng Shǔ's ceremonial procession grand music played simultaneously.
For banquets, serving tea, and granting tea, "Rain and Sun Timely" was changed to Xǐ Chūnguāng.
For serving wine and granting wine, "Abundant Harvest of Five Grains" was changed to Yúnhé Diézòu.
For serving dishes and granting food, "Families Provided, People Content" was changed to Fēnghé Rìlì.
The musical pieces for ascending to the throne and returning to the palace were the same as for the regular court audience in the third month.
The Dānbì music for officials performing rites was the same as for New Year's Day.
It was also decided that for the sacrifice to the Ancestress of Sericulture (Xiāncán), the musical instruments should include sixteen fāngxiǎng,
two yúnluó, two sè, two zhànggǔ, two pāibǎn,
four qín, six xiāo, six dí, six shēng,
and one jiàngǔ.
For the Empress's mulberry-picking song, the instruments should include two jīngǔ, two pāibǎn,
six xiāo, six dí, six shēng.
The musical pieces for officials dispatched to offer sacrifices were the same as for communal sacrifices.
It was also decided that for the banquet given to the Yǎnshèng Gōng, the music should play Zhūsì Fāyuán Cháng.
For the banquet of the Zhèngyī Zhēnrén, it should play Shàngqīng Bìluò.
For the banquet of civil jinshi, it should play Qǐ Tiānmén.
For military jinshi, it should play Héqì Qià.
For the village drinking ceremony, Lùmíng, Sìmǔ, and Huánghuáng Zhě Huá (three chapters) were sung.
The shēng played the Emperor's compositions supplementing Nángāi, Báihuá, Huáshǔ (three chapters).
Interspersed, Yúlí, Nányǒu Jiāyú, and Nánshān Yǒu Tái (three chapters) were sung.
The shēng played the Emperor's compositions supplementing Yóugēng, Chóngqiū, Yóuyí (three chapters).
The ensemble played Zhōunán Guānju, Gétán, Juǎněr (three chapters),
and Zhàonán Quècháo, Cǎifán, Cǎipíng (three chapters).
In the ninth month of the eighth year,
when Gāozōng made an eastern inspection tour to Shèngjīng,
the imperial guard was fully equipped.
Drum and wind instruments on horseback led the procession.
The next day, the Dānbì Dàlè was set up at the Liǎngyuè Tíng.
The Lǐ Bù set up a dragon pavilion,
placed congratulatory memorials,
and used the guiding and welcoming music.
When the Emperor arrived at Chóngzhèng Diàn,
and ascended to the throne, the Zhōnghé Sháolè played Yuánpíng.
When the princes and ministers performed rites and read memorials, the Dānbì Dàlè played Qìngpíng.
When the Korean tributary officials paid respects, the Dānbì Dàlè played Zhìpíng.
When issuing edicts and granting tea, the Zhōnghé Sháolè played Hépíng.
On that day, the Zhōnghé Dānbì Qīnglè played during the banquet at Chóngzhèng Diàn was the same as for the banquet at Tàihé Diàn.
The Màkèshì Dance was changed to the Qìnglóng zhī Wǔ,
and the Shìdé zhī Wǔ was also added.
Soon after, it was decided that within the music and dance, the large and small màhù were to be the Yángliè Wǔ.
The bamboo horses ridden by the dancers were Yúmǎ,
and the màhù were masks.
Ministers performing a dance to offer longevity were performing the Xǐqǐ Wǔ.
Those who sang the compositions were called Sīzhāng.
Those who rode bamboo horses were called Sīwǔ.
Those who plucked the pípá were called Sīpípá.
Those who played the xiánzi were called Sīsānxián.
Those who played the zhēng were called Sīzhēng.
Those who beat the jie were called Sījié.
Those who beat the pāibǎn were called Sīpāi.
Those who clapped their hands were called Sībiàn.
In the ninth year,
the Emperor personally visited the Hànlín Yuàn.
An edict commanded the music department to set up music.
Upon ascending the throne, Lóngpíng was performed.
The Chancellor of the Hànlín Yuàn, leading the hundreds of officials, performed the rituals and played Qìngpíng.
Tea was presented and bestowed, with Wénwù Jīnghuá Shèng performed.
An imperial banquet was presented with Yùshǔ Yán Yīng performed; wine was presented and bestowed with Yángé Yún Nóng performed.
The hundreds of officials expressed gratitude with Qìngpíng performed.
Upon returning to their offices, Xiǎnpíng was performed.
In that year, six musicians of the Tàicháng Sì were dismissed.
Musical instruments were added for the Altars of Heavenly Spirits and Earthly Deities.
The ritual ministers were instructed that
for the New Year's Eve banquet in the Bǎohé Diàn for the Mongolian princes and others,
first Mongolian music should be played,
followed by the Qìnglóng Dance.
For the New Year's Day banquet in the Tàihé Diàn for the princes and high officials,
these should be used interchangeably.
This was decreed as a regulation.
Since the Emperor ascended the throne,
music regulations were frequently changed,
with reforms, abolitions, diminutions, and additions,
all decided by his sagacious judgment.
The multitude of officials, eager to comply with the imperial will,
busied themselves with patching things up,
not possessing the discernment of Zhāng Qián'guī or Wàn Bǎocháng.
The Emperor pondered Lóngwēi Huànhuàn,
and thus specially decreed the clarification and standardization of various musical pieces for court assemblies and banquets.
Beginning in the seventh year with the standardization of musical pieces for suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples,
it was completed in the eleventh year.
For court assemblies:
on New Year's Day, the Emperor's Zhōnghé Yuè;
upon ascending the throne, Yuánpíng;
upon returning to the palace, Hépíng.
On the winter solstice, Zhōnghé Yuè;
upon ascending the throne, Suìpíng;
upon returning to the palace, Yǔnpíng.
For the Emperor's birthday (Wànshòu), Zhōnghé Yuè;
upon ascending the throne, Qiánpíng;
upon returning to the palace, Tàipíng.
For the Lantern Festival (Shàngyuán), Zhōnghé Yuè;
upon ascending the throne, Yípíng;
upon returning to the palace, Shēngpíng.
For regular court sessions, Zhōnghé Yuè;
upon ascending the throne, Lóngpíng;
upon returning to the palace, Xiǎnpíng.
For inner court rituals, Dānbì Yuè Yōngpíng.
For rituals by princes and hundreds of officials, Dānbì Yuè Qìngpíng.
For foreign vassals, Dānbì Yuè Zhìpíng.
For the Empress Dowager's three major festivals, Zhōnghé Yuè;
upon ascending the throne, Yùpíng;
upon returning to the palace, Lǚpíng;
Dānbì Yuè Yìpíng.
For the Empress's three major festivals, Zhōnghé Yuè;
upon ascending the throne, Shúpíng;
upon returning to the palace, Shùnpíng;
Dānbì Yuè Zhèngpíng.
For suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples: At the Yuánqiú Altar, for welcoming the spirits, Shǐpíng;
for presenting jade and silk, Jǐngpíng;
for presenting sacrificial meat, Xiánpíng;
for the first offering, Shòupíng;
for the second offering, Jiāpíng;
for the final offering, Yǒngpíng;
for removing the offerings, Xīpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Qīngpíng;
for observing the burning sacrifice, Tàipíng.
At the Fāngzé Altar, for welcoming the spirits, Zhōngpíng;
for presenting jade and silk, Guǎngpíng;
for presenting sacrificial meat, Hánpíng;
for the first offering, Dàpíng;
for the second offering, Ānpíng;
for the final offering, Shípíng;
for removing the offerings, Zhēnpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits and observing the burial, Níngpíng.
For the Prayer for Harvest (Qígǔ): for welcoming the spirits, Qípíng;
for presenting jade and silk, Suīpíng;
for presenting sacrificial meat, Wànpíng;
for the first offering, Bǎopíng;
for the second offering, Rángpíng;
for the final offering, Ruìpíng;
for removing the offerings, Wòpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Zīpíng;
for observing the burning sacrifice, Gǔpíng.
For the Rain Sacrifice (Yú Jì): for welcoming the spirits, Àipíng;
for presenting jade and silk, Yúnpíng;
for presenting sacrificial meat, Xūpíng;
for the first offering, Línpíng;
for the second offering, Lùpíng;
for the final offering, Zhānpíng;
for removing the offerings, Língpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Dànpíng;
for observing the burning sacrifice, Pèipíng.
For seasonal sacrifices at the Tàimiào:
for welcoming the spirits, Yípíng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Mǐpíng;
for the second offering, Fūpíng;
for the final offering, Shàopíng;
for removing the offerings, Guāngpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, returning to the palace, and observing the burning sacrifice, Yìpíng.
For the joint sacrifice (Xiápíng): for welcoming the spirits, Kāipíng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Sùpíng;
for the second offering, Xiépíng;
for the final offering, Yùpíng;
for removing the offerings, Chénpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, returning to the palace, and observing the burning sacrifice, Chéngpíng.
For the Altars of Land and Grain (Shèjì): for welcoming the spirits, Dēngpíng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Màopíng;
for the second offering, Yùpíng;
for the final offering, Dūnpíng;
for removing the offerings, Bópíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Lèpíng;
for observing the burial, Zhēngpíng.
For the Prayer for Rain and Thanksgiving Sacrifice at the Shèjì Altar: for welcoming the spirits, Yánfēng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Jièfēng;
for the second offering, Zīfēng;
for the final offering, Pèifēng;
for removing the offerings, Suīfēng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Yífēng;
for observing the burial, Bófēng.
For the Morning Sun Sacrifice (Zhāorì): for welcoming the spirits, Yínxī;
for presenting jade and silk, Cháoxī;
for the first offering, Qīngxī;
for the second offering, Xiánxī;
for the final offering, Chúnxī;
for removing the offerings, Yánxī;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Guīxī.
For the Evening Moon Sacrifice (Xīyuè): for welcoming the spirits, Yíngguāng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Shēngguāng;
for the second offering, Yáoguāng;
for the final offering, Ruìguāng;
for removing the offerings, Hánguāng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Bǎoguāng.
For successive Emperors (Lìdài Dìwáng): for welcoming the spirits, Zhàopíng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Xīngpíng;
for the second offering, Chóngpíng;
for the final offering, Tiánpíng;
for removing the offerings, Chúnpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits and observing the burning sacrifice, Kuāngpíng.
For the First Teacher (Xiānshī): for welcoming the spirits, Zhaōpíng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Xuānpíng;
for the second offering, Zhìpíng;
for the final offering, Píng;
for removing the offerings, Yìpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Dépíng.
For the First Farmer (Xiānnóng): for welcoming the spirits, Yǒngfēng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Shífēng;
for the second offering, Xiánfēng;
for the final offering, Dàfēng;
for removing the offerings, Lǚfēng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Bàofēng;
for observing the burial, Qìngfēng.
For the First Silkworm Cultivator (Xiāncán): for welcoming the spirits, Xiūpíng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Chéngpíng;
for the second offering, Jūnpíng;
for the final offering, Qípíng;
for removing the offerings, Ròupíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Qiàpíng.
For Heavenly Spirits and Earthly Deities (Tiānshén Dìqí): for welcoming the spirits, Qífēng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Huáfēng;
for the second offering, Xīngfēng;
for the final offering, Yífēng;
for removing the offerings, Héfēng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Xīfēng.
For the Grand Controller of the Year (Tàisuì): for welcoming the spirits, Bǎopíng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Dìngpíng;
for the second offering, Gǔpíng;
for the final offering, Fùpíng;
for removing the offerings, Yíngpíng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Fēngpíng.
For the Prayer for Rain and Thanksgiving Sacrifice at the Tàisuì Altar: for welcoming the spirits, Xūfēng;
for presenting silk and the first offering, Yífēng;
for the second offering, Jìnfēng;
for the final offering, Xiéfēng;
for removing the offerings, Yìngfēng;
for bidding farewell to the spirits, Qiàfēng.
For the Emperor's return to the palace after sacrificing at altars and temples, the procession music was Yòupíng.
For celebratory ceremonies, the procession music was Xǐpíng.
The lyrics for all of these were commanded to be re-written by Confucian officials,
and the Son of Heaven personally decided them,
dividing and proportioning them to match the rhythm.
If they fit, the original was kept;
if not, the lyrics were changed, and the tune altered.
Compared to the old regulations, there were additions and subtractions.
The "Lǜlǚ Zhèngyì Hòubiān" (Sequel to the Orthodox Meaning of Music Theory) was also completed in this year.
It included sections on "Sacrificial Music,"
"Court Assembly Music,"
"Banquet Music,"
"Procession Music," and
"Imperial Journey Music."
It further meticulously examined the differences in reforms, abolitions, diminutions, and additions from previous dynasties,
resulting in "Studies on Musical Instruments," "Studies on Musical Systems," "Studies on Musical Pieces," and "Studies on Standards of Measurement."
It also elucidated the methods used by the Sagely Ancestor to judge sounds, standardize musical systems, and harmonize instruments,
resulting in "Thirty-Five Chapters on Music Inquiries."
Generally, it was detailed in its palace music scores,
but regarding the origins of the pitches,
and the divisions and combinations of pipe sounds and string lengths,
it entirely followed the Sagely Ancestor,
without any new innovations.
The Emperor himself wrote the preface to it.
In the second month of the thirteenth year,
the emperor made an eastern tour to Shāndōng,
where he sacrificed at Dàiyuè.
The Grand Secretaries and others memorialized:
"Mount Tài has historically not used music.
According to the 'Dà Sī Yuè' chapter of the Zhōu Lǐ, 'Play Ruíbīn, sing Hánzhōng, and dance Dàxià to sacrifice to mountains and rivers.'
Now that a grand ceremony is specially held,
ranking it with Dàizōng,
we request to follow the ancient practice of using music,
and instruct the Ministry to compose the musical scores."
Thereupon, an imperial edict decreed six musical compositions,
using
"Fēng".
In the tenth month,
Zhāng Guǎngsì and Nàqīn had long made no progress in their campaign against Jīnchuān.
The emperor specially appointed Grand Secretary Fùhéng as Jinglüè,
and sent him out with the army,
performing the ritual of bestowing the battle-axe.
On that day, the emperor presided at the Tài hé Diàn,
with imperial carriages, honor guards, and musical instruments arranged as usual.
When he ascended the throne,
the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè played Lóngpíng.
The Jinglüè knelt to receive the imperial seal and perform the ritual.
The Dānbì Dàyuè played Qìngpíng.
The Jinglüè followed the minister bearing the imperial seal down the east steps.
The music stopped.
When the emperor returned to the palace, the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè played Xiǎnpíng.
On the day of the mǎ sacrifice, the great banners of the Eight Banners were erected south of the inner gate outside the Tángzi.
Soldiers holding conch horns were lined up.
The emperor's palanquin left the palace.
Music was arranged but not played.
Upon reaching the red stakes,
the conch horns sounded.
The emperor entered through the street gate and dismounted from his palanquin.
The conches stopped.
The ritual was performed.
The conches sounded again.
After the ritual before the banners was completed,
they went out to the red stakes.
The conches stopped.
The welcoming music began.
