When the imperial carriage arrived outside the Dōng Cháng'ān Mén,
the emperor ascended to the military tent
and took his seat.
He bestowed wine upon the Jinglüè.
All the officers joining the expedition carried their quivers.
They declined,
and set off.
Upon returning to the palace,
the welcoming music played.
The following year, upon their triumphant return,
a banquet was held at Fēngzé Yuán.
The emperor presided at the tent-hall.
When tea was presented and bestowed, Jǐngyùn Qiánkūn Tài was played.
When the master of ceremonies presented the cups and pitchers, Shèngdé Dànfū was played.
When food was presented, Rìyào Zhōngtiān was played.
Later, when Zhào Huì pacified the Western Regions
and Āguì recaptured Jīnchuān,
this same ritual was used for their triumphant returns,
but Jǐngyùn Qiánkūn Tài was changed to Shèngwǔ Guāngzhāo Shì,
Shèngdé Dànfū to Yǔdiàn Xiátōng,
and Rìyào Zhōngtiān to Shèngzhì Xiáchāng.
The Dé Lóng Wǔ was changed to Dé Shèng zhī Wǔ.
All the Zhōnghé musical compositions were augmented with martial celebratory phrases
to boast of the emperor's achievements.
The emperor also personally composed thirty chapters of triumphal songs,
and increased the nǎo songs by sixteen chapters,
which were performed during the suburban encampment.
Their sound and appearance were grand and magnificent,
surpassing antiquity.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Governor of Jiāngxī reported the discovery of eleven ancient bells
and submitted their diagrams.
The emperor showed them to his court officials,
who identified them as bózhōng.
He ordered the casting of
twelve pitch-standard bózhōng according to the bell's pitch and dimensions,
to be used for the special suspension in the Zhōnghé.
After they were completed,
the emperor personally composed their inscriptions.
Yǔnlù and others also requested the creation of twelve special qìng,
to complement the bózhōng,
carved from Khotan jade.
In the thirty-third year,
the musical compositions for the Guān Dì Miào were finalized,
with one chapter each for welcoming the deities, sending off the deities, and the three presentations.
In the eighth month of the forty-fifth year,
for Gāozōng's seventieth birthday,
nine chapters of Xǐqǐ Wǔyuè were added.
From then on, whenever there was a major celebration,
new musical compositions were regularly created.
In the fifty-second year,
Prince Yǒngróng was ordered, along with Zōu Yìxiào and Zhuāng Cúnyǔ, to re-establish the musical scores of the Shī Jīng,
correcting the errors of Zhèng Shìzǐ Zài Yù.
In the fifty-eighth year,
the Ministry of Music was again ordered to practice the music of Ānnán, Guō'ěrkā, Cū Miǎndiàn, and Xì Miǎndiàn.
Thus, the music of the Qīng Dynasty
under this emperor underwent several changes.
In the first year of Rénzōng Jiāqìng's reign,
two chapters of the Tàishàng Huángdì's grand festivals for the imperial hall and Zhōnghé Sháoyuè were added,
one chapter of Dānbì Dàyuè,
one chapter of Dānbì Dàyuè for rituals within the palace,
one chapter of Yányàn Zhōnghé Qīngyuè, two chapters of Dānbì Qīngyuè, and nine chapters of Qìnglóng Wǔyuè.
Also, two chapters of the Tàishàng Huángdì's imperial hall and Zhōnghé Sháoyuè were added for the Qiānsǒu Yàn at the Huángjí Diàn.
Thereafter, when presiding over the Yōng,
visiting the Hànlín Yuàn, performing sacrifices at the Wénchāng Miào,
praying for clear weather at the Shèjì Tán, and during the emperor's birthday,
musical compositions were always added.
In the eighth year,
the performance of Ānnán music at banquets was ordered to stop.
On New Year's Day of the fourteenth year,
during the banquet at the Tài hé Diàn,
it was ordered that Korean, Huíbù, Jīnchuān, and Miǎndiàn music and dances, among others, be performed.
When Qìnglóng Wǔ or Xǐqǐ Wǔ were performed,
they were immediately presented.
Four additional ministers joined the formation dance.
This became the annual custom.
During the reigns of Xuān and Wén,
governance was effortless,
and the palace orchestra was merely a formality.
Although there were additions and innovations,
they were not related to grand ceremonies.
In the late years of Dézōng Guāngxù's reign,
military music was created following the example of European and American nations.
Also, the grand sacrifice to the former teacher was elevated,
increasing the number of yìmǔ,
and the national anthem was revised.
The compositions were repeatedly unsettled for many years,
until the abdication,
with many never implemented.

The rhythm of music
is formed by *shēngdiào*.
*Shēng* refers to
the seven notes of *wǔshēng èrbiàn*;
*diào* refers to
that which harmonizes the seven notes for mutual use.
The origin of *shēngdiào*
inherently comes from *xuángōng*,
which differs depending on the variations in pitch pipes (*guǎnlǜ*) and string lengths (*xiándù*) for the seven notes.
The ancient method of *xuángōng*
combined bamboo (wind instruments) and silk (string instruments) together.
Since the Suí Dynasty,
only string sounds were used to clarify the divisions of the *wǔshēng*,
and the *lǜlǚ xuángōng*
subsequently lost its transmission.
As for *xuángōng*,
any of the twelve *lǜlǚ* can serve as *gōng*,
establishing a principal *jūn*,
each governing seven notes,
and all twelve *lǜlǚ* can function as the *wǔshēng èrbiàn*.
*Shēngdiào* implies that
the *shēng* stands alone as a *shēng*,
and the *diào* stands alone as a *diào*.
Moreover, *diào* has distinctions such as *zhǔdiào*, *qǐdiào*, and *zhuǎndiào*.
Therefore, when *zhuǎndiào* is combined with *xuángōng*,
it is named *gōngdiào*.
When the *wǔshēng èrbiàn* rotate through the fourteen notes of the two *jūn* (clear and turbid),
they form ninety-eight notes;
these are the complete notes.
However, although *diào* takes *gōng* as its principal,
*gōng* also stands alone as *gōng*,
and *diào* also stands alone as *diào*.
For example, if *gōng* establishes the principal of a *jūn*,
and the note *xiàyǔ*
is again greater than *gōng*,
it thus becomes the head of the *diào*.
This is what the ancients called "*gōng zhú yǔyīn*".
If *yǔ* is the *zhǔdiào*,
and *gōng* establishes the *gōng*,
once the positions of the seven notes of a *jūn* are fixed,
then the *èrbiàn* notes do not initiate a *diào*,
and notes that do not align with the starting note of the *diào* also do not initiate a *diào*.
This is because if *yǔ* initiates the *diào*,
*zhǐ* is before it,
and *biàngōng* is after it.
These two notes are close to *yǔ*,
resulting in confused sounds.
Moreover, *biànzhǐ* is the sixth note,
and also does not align with the starting note of *yǔ*.
This is why notes in the *èrbiàn* positions,
and the *wǔzhèngshēng* in the *zhǐ* position,
are all not allowed to initiate a *diào*.
As for stopping a *diào*,
it also takes notes compatible with the principal *diào*,
and can conclude with a note capable of initiating a *diào*.
Notes in the *èrbiàn* and *zhǐ* positions
are also not used.
The note that establishes the *yǔ* position as the head of the *diào*,
if it starts from its own *shēng*,
is the principal *diào*.
If the starting note and the fifth note are *yǔ*,
it aligns secondary to *jué*.
If the starting note and the third note are *yǔ*,
it aligns secondary to *gōng*,
and the *jūn* and *diào* correspond.
If the starting note and the fourth note are *yǔ*,
it aligns with *shāng* and can transition in and out.
Thus, the principal *diào* is one *diào*;
those starting from the *gōng* position form one *diào*;
those starting from the *jué* position form one *diào*;
and those starting from the *shāng* position form yet another *diào*.
(Those starting from the *yǔ*, *gōng*, and *jué* positions are considered *zhèng* (principal/correct);
those starting from the *shāng* position are considered *jiǎjiè* (borrowed/temporary),
hence it is said they can transition in and out.
This is like what is said in compositions about transitioning in and out of a certain *gōng* and *diào*.
For "transitional alignment":
the head of the *xiàyǔ* mode to *jué* is the fifth position;
the third note of *shāng* to the eighth note of *zhèngyǔ* is also the fifth position.)
One *jūn* has four *diào*;
seven *jūn* have twenty-eight *diào*.
Combining the fourteen *jūn* of clear and turbid
results in fifty-six *diào*.
When musicians compose,
the method for transitioning between the seven *diào*
is that a *sìzì* starting from *sì* is a *zhèngdiào*.
(When musicians change *diào*,
they all use the *sìzìdiào* as a standard.
With *sì*, *yǐ*, *shàng*, *chǐ*, *gōng*, *fán*, *liù*, *qī* arranged in positions,
whichever character falls into the *sìzì* position
is named as that *diào*.
This is just like the method of rotating *xuángōng* with *wǔshēng èrbiàn* in sequence,
taking the *sìzì* as the *yǔ* position for initiating the *diào*.)
*Yǐzì* starting from *sì* is *Yǐzìdiào*;
*Shàngzì* starting from *sì* is *Shàngzìdiào*;
*Chǐzì* starting from *sì* is *Chǐzìdiào*;
*Gōngzì* starting from *sì* is *Gōngzìdiào*;
*Fánzì* starting from *sì* is *Fánzìdiào*;
*Hézì* starting from *sì* is *Hézìdiào*.
(This refers to flute finger holes.)
In *Sìzìdiào*, *yǐ* and *fán* are not used.
In *Yǐzìdiào*, *shàng* and *liù* are not used.
In *Shàngzìdiào*, *chǐ* and *wǔ* are not used.
In *Chǐzìdiào*, *gōng* and *yǐ* are not used.
In *Gōngzìdiào*, *fán* and *shàng* are not used.
In *Fánzìdiào*, *hé* and *chǐ* are not used.
In *Hézìdiào*, *wǔ* and *gōng* are not used.
This is like when *yǔshēng* is the *zhǔdiào*,
the notes corresponding to *biàngōng* and *biànzhǐshēng* are not used.
Furthermore, in *Sìzìdiào*, *yǐ* and *fán* cannot initiate a *diào*,
and *liùzì* also cannot initiate a *diào*.
This is like when *yǔshēng* is the *zhǔdiào* in the *yǔ* position,
the *èrbiàn* cannot initiate a *diào*,
and *zhǐshēng* also cannot initiate a *diào*.
The rotation of these seven characters in the seven *diào*
is equivalent to the *wǔshēng èrbiàn* rotating to become *gōng*.
*Gōngdiào shēngzì*
are truly a single entity.
Analyzing it,
there are four categories: First is the positioning of the seven notes (*Qīshēng Dìngwèi*),
where the *wǔshēng èrbiàn* establish fixed positions.
From *xiàyǔ* to *zhèngyǔ*,
they are arranged as eight in total,
clearly showing the principle of *gé bā xiāngshēng* (generation at an octave interval).
By observing the *shēngzì lǜlǚ* of the *xiàyǔ* position,
one knows which *gōng* and which *diào* it is.
By observing the *shēngzì lǜlǚ* of the *gōng* position,
one knows which *diào* and which *gōng* it is.
By observing the *èrbiàn* positions,
one knows which *shēngzì* and which *lǜlǚ* should be avoided.
Second is *Xuángōng Zhǔdiào*,
where the *wǔshēng èrbiàn* rotate below the fixed positions of the seven notes (*Qīshēng Dìngwèi*).
These are also divided into eight positions.
For example, if *yǔshēng* is placed below *xiàyǔ*,
and *gōngshēng* is placed below the *gōng* position,
then *gōngshēng* establishes the *gōng* while *yǔshēng* is the *zhǔdiào*.
Another example: if *shāngshēng* is placed below *xiàyǔ*,
and *biànzhǐ* is placed below the *gōng* position,
then *biànzhǐ* establishes the *gōng* while *shāngshēng* is the *zhǔdiào*.
Third is *Héshēng Qǐdiào* (harmonizing and initiating *diào*),
using the twelve *lǜlǚ*, including their doubled and halved forms, for preparedness.
According to the generated notes,
each follows its *jūn* and is sequenced below the *xuángōng*.
Furthermore, each *diào* initiated by notes harmonious with the *diào* head is noted below its corresponding *lǜ* and *lǚ*,
to rectify the names of each *diào*.
For example, if *Huángzhōng* establishes the *gōng*,
then *Yízé* establishes the *xiàyǔ* position to be the *zhǔdiào*.
*Bèiwúshè* and *zhèngruíbīn* (as *èrbiàn* notes) do not initiate a *diào*,
and *zhèngyízé* (as a *zhǐ* note) also does not initiate a *diào*.
Therefore, the one that initiates the *diào* using *bèiyízé* is the *Zhèngyǔdiào*.
Initiating with *Huángzhōng gōngshēng* makes it *Zhènggōng*.
Initiating with *Tàicù shāngshēng* makes it *Zhèngshāng*.
Initiating with *Gūxiǎn juéshēng* makes it *Zhèngjué*.
These are the four *diào* of *Zhènggōng*.
If *Dàlǚ* establishes the *gōng*,
then *Bèinánlǚ* establishes the *xiàyǔ* position as the *zhǔdiào*.
The one used to initiate the *diào* is *Qīngyǔdiào*.
Initiating with *Dàlǚ gōngshēng* makes it *Qīnggōng*.
Initiating with *Jiázhōng shāngshēng* makes it *Qīngshāng*.
Initiating with *Zhònglǚ juéshēng* makes it *Qīngjué*.
These are the four *diào* of *Qīnggōng*.
The remaining establishments of *gōng* and *zhǔdiào*
all follow this example.
Fourth is *Yuèyīn Zìsè* (musical note character designations),
where the character designations assigned by *lǜlǚ xiāo dí*
follow the *shēngdiào* and are ordered accordingly,
listed under the *lǜlǚ*.
For example, *Huángzhōng* is the *gōngzì*.
The *xiāo* corresponding to *Huángzhōng* is the *gōngzì*,
and the *dí* corresponding to *Huángzhōng* is the *wǔzì*.
All are noted under the *Huángzhōng* fundamental *lǜ*.
*Dàlǚ* is the *gāogōngzì*.
And the *gāogōng* of the *xiāo* and *gāowǔ* of the *dí* are also noted under the *Dàlǚ* fundamental *lǜ*.
The character that establishes the *yǔ* position
is the *zhǔdiào*.
The character that establishes the *gōng* position
is the established *gōng*.
Characters in the *èrbiàn* positions
are not used, nor are those in the *zhǐ* position used to initiate a *diào*.
When these four categories are arranged into a table,
the principles of *xuángōng*, *zhuǎnshēng* (changing notes), *zhǔdiào*, and *qǐdiào* become clear.
With *Huángzhōng gōngshēng* establishing *gōng*,
*Bèiyízé xiàyǔ* is the *zhǔdiào*, making it *Shàngzìdiào*.

The theory that string sounds conform to the *lǜlǚ*
originated with the *Huáinánzǐ*.
The *Huáinánzǐ* based it on the *Guǎnzǐ*.
The *Guǎnzǐ* states:
"When preparing to produce the five sounds, for all initial notes,
first establish one and multiply it by three,
then divide by four to match the nine-nines (81),
with this produce the initial *Huángzhōng xiǎosù* to form *gōng*.
Take three parts and add one part,
making one hundred and eight, which is *zhǐ*.
Not without taking three parts and removing a suitable multiple,
with this produce *shāng*.
Take three parts and return to their original position,
with this form *yǔ*.
Take three parts and remove a suitable multiple,
with this form *jué*."
When examining string sounds,
regardless of the full length of a certain string,
it is set as the initial sound.
Then, halve it,
dividing it equally into two.
Its sound then harmonizes with the initial sound, forming the eighth sound.
Next, take the full length of the initial sound,
then divide it by four,
remove one part and use three parts.
Its sound corresponds to the fourth sound of the full-length initial sound.
This measure is between the full-length initial sound and the half-length eighth sound,
also equally divided into two parts.
This is what the *Guǎnzǐ* refers to as,
"When preparing to produce the five sounds, for all initial notes,
first establish one and multiply it by three,
then divide by four to match the nine-nines (81)."
"First establish one and multiply it by three"
means taking the full length of the initial sound as one unit,
and multiplying it by three.
The resulting number is three times greater than the full length.
"Divide by four to match the nine-nines (81)"
means taking this three-times full length,
dividing it into four parts and taking one of them,
to match the measure of nine-nines, eighty-one,
which is the division for the *gōng* sound.
"Xiǎosù"
means "sù,"
which is white silk,
or processed silk,
referring to a small string.
It means that the sound of this measure is established as the *gōng* position.
Other strings smaller than this string
all take this as their principal.
Therefore, it is said, "with this produce the initial *Huángzhōng xiǎosù* to form *gōng*."
"By eighty-one, adding one part of three makes one hundred and eight, which is *zhǐ*,"
refers to the full length of the initial sound of this string.
(This is the number for *zhǐ* generated downwards from the *gōng* string.)
Then, from one hundred and eight,
remove one part of three,
making seventy-two,
which is *shāng*.
From *shāng* seventy-two,
add one part of three,
making ninety-six,
which is *yǔ*.
From *yǔ* ninety-six,
remove one part of three,
making sixty-four,
which is *jué*.
Sīmǎ Shì's *Lǜshū* states that the numbers for *zhǐ* and *yǔ* are smaller than *gōng*.
The *Guǎnzǐ* states that the numbers for *zhǐ* and *yǔ* are larger than *gōng*
because it uses multiples of *zhǐ* and *yǔ*,
referring to *xiàzhǐ* and *xiàyǔ*.
If the initial string starts from *xiàzhǐ*,
this is the meaning of the *Báihǔtōng*'s "string sounds valorize *zhǐ*."
Now, let us meticulously deduce the numbers using the method of subtracting and adding one-third.
*Huángzhōng* and *zhèngzhǐ* both generate seventy-two upwards,
forming *zhèngshāng*.
*Zhèngshāng* generates ninety-six upwards,
forming *xiàyǔ*.
Generating downwards produces forty-eight,
forming *zhèngyǔ*.
*Xiàyǔ* and *zhèngyǔ* both produce sixty-four,
forming *zhèngjué*.
*Zhèngjué* generates eighty-five upwards,
(remainder 0.33)
forming *biàngōng* which is lower than the *gōng* sound.
Generating downwards produces forty-two,
(remainder 0.66)
forming *biàngōng* which is higher than the *yǔ* sound.
The *biàngōng* lower than the *gōng* sound
and the *biàngōng* higher than the *yǔ* sound
both produce fifty-six,
(remainder 0.88)
forming *biànzhǐ*: this is *zhuójūn*.
*Biànzhǐ* generates seventy-five upwards,
(remainder 0.85)
forming *qīnggōng*.
*Qīnggōng* generates one hundred and one upwards,
(remainder 0.13)
forming *qīngxiàzhǐ*.
Generating downwards produces fifty,
(remainder 0.56)
forming *qīngzhǐ*.
*Qīngxiàzhǐ* and *qīngzhǐ* both produce sixty-seven,
(remainder 0.42)
forming *qīngshāng*.
*Qīngshāng* generates eighty-nine upwards,
(remainder 0.89)
forming *qīngxiàyǔ*.
Generating downwards produces forty-four,
(remainder 0.94)
forming *qīngyǔ*.
*Qīngxiàyǔ* and *qīngyǔ* both produce fifty-nine,
(remainder 0.93)
forming *qīngjué*.
Generating upwards produces seventy-nine,
(remainder 0.91)
forming *qīngbiàngōng* which is lower than *qīnggōng*.
Generating downwards produces thirty-nine,
(remainder 0.33)
forming *qīngbiàngōng* which is higher than *qīngyǔ*.
The *qīngbiàngōng* lower than *qīnggōng* and the *qīngbiàngōng* higher than *qīngyǔ* both produce fifty-three,
(remainder 0.27)
forming *qīngbiànzhǐ*: this is *qīngjūn*.
From *gōng* to *shāng*,
*shāng* to *jué*,
*jué* to *biànzhǐ*,
*zhǐ* to *yǔ*,
and *yǔ* to *biàngōng*,
all are whole divisions.
However, from *biànzhǐ* to *zhǐ*,
and *biàngōng* to *gōng*,
are only half divisions.
The *Qǐyīmpiān* of the *Guǎnzǐ*
and Sīmǎ Shì's *Lǜshū* both represent the fundamental five notes.
The *Huáinánzǐ* first recorded the numbers for the two *biàn* notes,
but they should not be named after the twelve *lǜlǚ*.
What is particularly noteworthy
is the division of the two *biàn* notes
and the theory that their ratio to the principal notes is either harmonious or erroneous.
What is called *Yìngzhōng*
is the *biàngōng* measure of the string sound.
What is called *Ruíbīn*
is the *biànzhǐ* measure of the string sound.
The string sound *biàngōng* on the first string (*xiàzhǐ*) is the third sound,
residing in the third position,
just like the *jué* sound on the *gōng* string, which is in the third position.
Although the sound is different,
its division precisely matches the measure of a principal sound.
Therefore, it is said that *Gūxǐ* generates *Yìngzhōng*,
which is harmonious when compared to a principal sound.
The *biànzhǐ* on the first string (*xiàzhǐ*) is the seventh sound,
residing in the seventh position,
just like the *biàngōng* on the *gōng* string, which is in the seventh position.
Although the sound is also different,
its division is that of a *biàn* sound.
Therefore, it is said that *Yìngzhōng* generates *Ruíbīn*,
which is erroneous when not compared to a principal sound.

The methods for string notes to rotate through gōng and change dǐao
are four. First,
if a string note is set to correspond to a certain lǜlǚ sound character,
then the degree of that string is obtained.
For example, if the doubled Wúshè pitch is set to the biàngōng-hé character,
then the degree for the zhǐ string is obtained;
if the Huángzhōng pitch is set to the gōng-sì character,
then the degree for the yǔ string is obtained;
if the Tàicù pitch is set to the shāng-yǐ character,
then the degree for the biàngōng string is obtained;
if the Gūxǐ pitch is set to the jiǎo-shàng character,
then the degree for the gōng string is obtained;
if the Ruíbīn pitch is set to the biànzhǐ-chǐ character,
then the degree for the shāng string is obtained;
if the Yīzé pitch is set to the zhǐ-gōng character,
then the degree for the yǔ string is obtained;
if the Wúshè pitch is set to the yǔ-fán character,
then the degree for the biànzhǐ string is obtained.
These are the correct degrees for tuning the seven notes of a yánglǜ mode.
The degrees for tuning the seven notes of a yīnlǚ mode are also similar.
The pitches of the strings cannot be shifted sequentially;
they must be based on the gōngdiào (宫调) mode.
Therefore, the seven notes change accordingly.
For example, the zither's standard tuning is gōngdiào.
In its shāngdiào (商调) mode, each of the seven strings is raised one pitch,
but strings six and seven are too quick and easy to change.
Or if the biàngōngdiào (变宫调) mode lowers each of the seven strings one pitch,
then strings one and two are too slow and cannot produce sound.
Therefore, in gōngdiào, the seven strings are established as the standard.
When shifting modes,
some of the seven strings change,
some do not change,
some should be tightened,
and some should be loosened.
Amidst the shifting of the strings, the gōngdiào mode revolves.
For instance, if strings one, three, and six are all loosened by one管律 (guǎnlǜ) pitch,
which is half a degree on the string,
while the remaining strings are not moved,
it shifts to shāngdiào.
This is because in zhènggōngdiào (正宫调), strings one and six are set to the pitch of bèiwúshè (倍無射).
The biàngōng (变宫) character "hé" (合) obtains the zhǐ (徵) string's division,
which lowers to the pitch of bèiyízé (倍夷则).
The yǔ (羽) sound's character "fán" (凡) shifts the jué (角) string's division,
so string three is set to the pitch of gūxǐ (姑洗).
The jué (角) sound's character "shàng" (上) obtains the gōng (宫) string's division,
which lowers to the pitch of tàicù (太簇).
The shāng (商) sound's character "yǐ" (乙) shifts the yǔ (羽) string's division.
Strings two, four, five, and seven do not move,
still corresponding to their original pitches.
However, strings two and seven, which originally obtained the yǔ (羽) string's division,
shift to the zhǐ (徵) string's division.
String four, which originally obtained the shāng (商) string's division,
shifts to the gōng (宫) string's division.
String five, which originally obtained the jué (角) string's division,
shifts to the shāng (商) string's division.
Regarding the pitch of bèiwúshè,
the biàngōng (变宫) character "hé" (合) as the zhǐ (徵) string's division
transforms into biànzhǐ (变徵), corresponding to the pitch of bèiyìngzhōng (倍應鍾);
qīngbiàngōng (清變宮) is high six,
corresponding to the pitch of gūxǐ.
The jué (角) sound's character "shàng" (上) as the gōng (宫) string's division
transforms into biàngōng (变宫), corresponding to the pitch of zhònglǚ (仲吕);
qīngjué (清角) is high shàng (上).
These two divisions are not used in the two transformations.
Because string three is set to the pitch of tàicù,
the shāng (商) sound's character "yǐ" (乙) obtains the yǔ (羽) string's division to start the mode.
String four, which originally obtained the shāng (商) string's division,
shifts to the gōng (宫) string's division to establish gōng (宫).
Therefore, it is called shāngdiào.
For example, if strings two, four, five, and seven are all tightened by half a guǎnlǜ pitch,
which is also half a degree on the string,
while the remaining strings are not moved,
it shifts to juédiào (角调).
This is because in zhènggōngdiào, strings two and seven are set to the pitch of huángzhōng (黃鍾).
The gōng (宫) sound's character "sì" (四) obtains the yǔ (羽) string's division,
which raises to the pitch of dàlǚ (大呂);
qīnggōng (清宫) is high five, shifting the zhǐ (徵) string's division.
String four is set to the pitch of ruíbīn (蕤賓).
The biànzhǐ (变徵) character "chǐ" (尺) obtains the shāng (商) string's division,
which raises to the pitch of línzhōng (林鍾);
qīngbiànzhǐ (清變徵) is high chǐ (尺), shifting the gōng (宫) string's division.
String five is set to the pitch of yízé (夷则).
The zhǐ (徵) sound's character "gōng" (工) obtains the jué (角) string's division,
which raises to the pitch of nánlǚ (南呂);
qīngzhǐ (清徵) is high gōng (工), shifting the shāng (商) string's division.
Strings one, three, and six do not move,
still corresponding to their original pitches.
However, strings one and six shift to the jué (角) division,
and string three shifts to the yǔ (羽) division,
but the transformed biànzhǐ (变徵) and biàngōng (变宫) are not used.
Because string three corresponds to the pitch of gūxǐ,
the jué (角) sound's character "shàng" (上) obtains the yǔ (羽) string's division to start the mode.
String four, which originally obtained the shāng (商) string's division,
raises to the jué (角) string's division,
shifting to the gōng (宫) string's division to establish gōng (宫).
Therefore, it is called juédiào.
For example, if only string five is tightened by half a guǎnlǜ pitch,
which is also half a degree on the string,
it shifts to biànzhǐdiào (變徵調).
String four corresponds to the pitch of ruíbīn.
The biànzhǐ (变徵) character "chǐ" (尺) obtains the yǔ (羽) string's division to start the mode.
String five, which originally obtained the jué (角) string's division,
raises to the biànzhǐ (变徵) division,
shifting to the gōng (宫) string's division to establish gōng (宫).
Therefore, it is called biànzhǐdiào.
For example, if only string three is loosened by one guǎnlǜ pitch,
which is half a degree on the string,
it shifts to zhǐdiào (徵调).
Because string five corresponds to the pitch of yízé,
the zhǐ (徵) sound's character "gōng" (工) obtains the yǔ (羽) string's division to start the mode.
Strings one and six, which originally obtained the zhǐ (徵) string's division,
shift to the gōng (宫) string's division to establish gōng (宫).
Therefore, it is called zhǐdiào.
For example, if strings one, three, and six are loosened by one guǎnlǜ pitch,
and string four is loosened by half a guǎnlǜ pitch,
both being half a degree on the string,
it shifts to yǔdiào (羽调).
Because strings one and six correspond to the pitch of bèiyízé,
the yǔ (羽) sound's character "fán" (凡) obtains the yǔ (羽) string's division to start the mode.
Strings two and seven, which originally obtained the yǔ (羽) string's division,
raise to the biàngōng (变宫) division,
shifting to the gōng (宫) string's division to establish gōng (宫).
Therefore, it is called biàngōngdiào.
One,
although the pitches of string instruments in various modes have no secondary changes,
when setting the strings and taking notes,
one must carefully examine the sounds of secondary changes,
and must calculate the divisions of secondary changes.
For example, in one mode of the Yánglǜ,
speaking of the divisions of the seven notes of the zhǐ string,
the open string sound is the first note of a full division.
Its second note, corresponding to the yǔ string, is the yǔ division.
Its third note, corresponding to the biàngōng string, is the biàngōng division.
Up to the seventh note, corresponding to the biànzhǐ string, it is the biànzhǐ division.
The eighth note still corresponds to the full string,
thus it returns to the first note.
Each division corresponds to its respective string,
and also to its respective lǜ.
Calculating their divisions,
the first note zhǐ to the second note yǔ,
and the third note yǔ to the third note biàngōng,
are all full divisions.
The third note biàngōng to the fourth note gōng,
is only a half division.
The fourth note gōng to the fifth note shāng,
the fifth note shāng to the sixth note jué,
and the sixth note jué to the seventh note biànzhǐ,
are all full divisions.
The seventh note biànzhǐ to the eighth note zhǐ,
is also a half division.
Speaking of the divisions of the seven notes of the gōng string,
the open string sound is the first note of a full half.
Its second note, corresponding to the shāng string, is the shāng division.
The note corresponding to the jué string is the jué division.
The third to seventh notes, corresponding to the biàngōng string, are the biàngōng division.
The eighth note still corresponds to the full string.
However, the fourth note biànzhǐ to the fifth note zhǐ,
and the seventh note biàngōng to the eighth note gōng,
are all only half divisions.
From the string division corresponding to the Yǐ character of the shāng sound of Tàicù to the string division corresponding to the Shàng character of the jué sound of Gūxǐ,
and from the string division corresponding to the Fán character of the yǔ sound of Wúshè to the string division corresponding to the Hé character of the biàngōng sound of Bànhuángzhōng,
the interval must be a half division.
Therefore, the divisions of the seven notes of each string do not change,
but there is a distinction of interleaving in the corresponding lǜ.
Within the full and half divisions,
the gōng mode turns.
Taking the seven strings of the gōng mode as a standard,
and referring to the seven notes of the zhǐ string in each mode,
the zhǐ of the shāng mode
is the yǔ of the gōng mode transformed into a zhǐ division.
For the yǔ of the gōng string,
the open string's first note is yǔ.
Its biàngōng and biànzhǐ are at the second and sixth notes.
This means the interval from the second note to the third note,
and from the sixth note to the seventh note,
is a half division.
Now, if the open string is transformed into zhǐ,
then biàngōng and biànzhǐ are at the third and seventh notes.
This means the interval from the third note to the fourth note,
and from the seventh note to the eighth note,
is a half division.
Therefore, the open string's fixed Gōng sound, Sì character of the Huángzhōng lǜ does not change.
The second note then corresponds to the Shāng sound, Yǐ character of the Tàicù lǜ,
the interval between them being a full division for the third note.
If we take the Jué sound, Shàng character of the Gūxǐ lǜ,
then the interval from the second note to the third note is a half division,
which is still the same as the yǔ of the gōng mode.
Thus, one must take the Qīngjué, Gāoshàng of the Zhònglǚ lǜ.
Only then does the string length in between obtain a full division.
Its fourth note still corresponds to the Biànzhǐ, Chǐ character of the Ruíbīn lǜ.
This is because from Tàicù Yǐ character to Gūxǐ Shàng character is a half division.
Adding the half division of Zhònglǚ Gāoshàng,
we get one full division.
And from Zhònglǚ Gāoshàng to Ruíbīn Chǐ character is a half division.
This is why from the second note to the third note we get a full division,
which is from yǔ to biàngōng.
And from the third note to the fourth note is a half division,
which is from biàngōng to gōng.
The fifth note still corresponds to the Zhǐ sound, Gōng character of the Yízé lǜ.
The sixth note still corresponds to the Yǔ sound, Fán character of the Wúshè lǜ.
From the fourth note to the fifth note,
and from the fifth note to the sixth note,
also obtain full divisions.
Up to the seventh note, if we take the Biàngōng, Hé character of the Bànhuángzhōng lǜ,
then the interval from the sixth note to the seventh note is a half division,
also the same as the yǔ of the gōng mode.
One must take the Qīngbiàngōng, Gāoliù of the Bàndàlǚ lǜ.
Only then does the string length in between obtain a full division.
Its eighth note still corresponds to the Gōng sound, Sì character of the Huángzhōng lǜ, the same as the first note.
This is because from Wúshè Fán character to Bànhuángzhōng Hé character is a half division.
Adding the half division of Bàndàlǚ Gāoliù,
we get one full division.
And from Bàndàlǚ Gāoliù to Huángzhōng Sì character is a half division.
This is why from the sixth note to the seventh note we get a full division,
which is from jué to biànzhǐ.
And from the seventh note to the eighth note is a half division,
which is from biànzhǐ to zhǐ.
The zhǐ of the jué mode
is the biàngōng of the gōng mode mixed with the yǔ of the qīnggōng mode, transformed into a zhǐ division.
For the biàngōng of the gōng mode, the open string's first note is biàngōng.
Biànzhǐ is at the fifth note.
This means the interval from the first note to the second note,
and from the fifth note to the sixth note,
is a half division.
For the yǔ of the qīngshāng mode, the open string's first note is qīngyǔ.
Its qīngbiàngōng and qīngbiànzhǐ are at the second and sixth notes.
This further means the interval from the second note to the third note,
and from the sixth note to the seventh note,
is a half division.
Now, if the open string is transformed into zhǐ,
then the interval from the third note to the fourth note,
and from the seventh note to the eighth note,
is a half division.
If the first note is still set to the Shāng sound, Yǐ character of the Tàicù lǜ,
then the full division obtained from the first note zhǐ to the second note yǔ
must be taken from the Qīngjué, Gāoshàng of the Zhònglǚ lǜ.
Its original mode's yǔ string
would then also correspond to the Qīngjué, Gāoshàng of the Zhònglǚ lǜ.
This would mean the qīngjué mode is not the true jué mode.
Therefore, we take the Jué sound, Shàng character of the Gūxǐ lǜ as the true jué mode.
Hence, for modes starting on the yǔ string,
one must take the true jué sound of Gūxǐ,
and the yǔ division of the zhǐ string must also correspond to the Gūxǐ lǜ.
Thus, the open string's first note of the zhǐ string in the jué mode
is half a tone lower than the open string's first note of the biàngōng string in the true gōng mode.
Taking the open string's sound of the yǔ string in the qīnggōng mode,
the Qīnggōng, Gāowǔ of the Dàlǚ lǜ,
only then do its divisions align.
This is because the yǔ sound of the original mode obtains the true jué lǜ.
The second note corresponds to the Jué sound, Shàng character of the Gūxǐ lǜ, as the yǔ division.
The third note corresponds to the Biànzhǐ, Chǐ character of the Ruíbīn lǜ, as the biàngōng division.
The fourth note corresponds to the Qīngbiànzhǐ, Gāochǐ of the Línzhōng lǜ, as the gōng division.
The fifth note corresponds to the Qīngzhǐ, Gāogōng of the Nánlǚ lǜ, as the shāng division.
The sixth note corresponds to the true Biàngōng, Liù character of the Bànhuángzhōng lǜ, as the jué division.
The seventh note corresponds to the true Gōng, Sì character of the Huángzhōng lǜ, as the biànzhǐ division.
The eighth note still corresponds to the Qīnggōng, Gāowǔ of the Dàlǚ lǜ.
Then, the interval from the third note Ruíbīn to the fourth note Línzhōng is a half division.
The interval from the seventh note Huángzhōng to the eighth note Dàlǚ is a half division.
These are precisely the two half divisions from biàngōng to gōng,
and from biànzhǐ to zhǐ of the original mode's zhǐ string.
The zhǐ of the biànzhǐ mode
is the gōng of the gōng mode transformed into a zhǐ division.
For the gōng of the gōng mode, biànzhǐ and biàngōng are at the fourth and seventh notes.
This means the interval from the fourth note to the fifth note,
and from the seventh note to the eighth note,
is a half division.
Now, if the open string is transformed into zhǐ,
then the interval from the third note to the fourth note,
and from the seventh note to the eighth note,
is a half division.
Shifting the half division from the fourth note to the fifth note of the gōng of the gōng mode
to the half division from the third note to the fourth note,
then the fourth note takes the Qīngzhǐ, Gāogōng of the Nánlǚ lǜ.
The interval from the third note Yízé to the fourth note Nánlǚ is a half division.
The interval from the seventh note Tàicù to the eighth note Gūxǐ is a half division.
The zhǐ of the zhǐ mode
is the shāng of the gōng mode transformed into zhǐ.
For the shāng of the gōng mode, biànzhǐ and biàngōng are at the third and sixth notes.
This means the interval from the third note to the fourth note,
and from the sixth note to the seventh note,
is a half division.
Now, if the open string is transformed into zhǐ,
then the interval from the third note to the fourth note,
and from the seventh note to the eighth note,
is a half division.
Shifting the half division from the sixth note to the seventh note of the shāng of the gōng mode
to the half division from the seventh note to the eighth note,
then the seventh note takes the Qīngjué, Gāoshàng of the Zhònglǚ lǜ.
The interval from the third note Wúshè to the fourth note Bànhuángzhōng is a half division.
The interval from the seventh note Zhònglǚ to the eighth note Ruíbīn is a half division.
The zhǐ of the yǔ mode
is the jué of the gōng mode transformed into a zhǐ division.
For the jué of the gōng mode, biànzhǐ and biàngōng are at the sixth and fifth notes.
This means the interval from the second note to the third note,
and from the fifth note to the sixth note,
is a half division.
Now, if the open string is transformed into zhǐ,
then the interval from the third note to the fourth note,
and from the seventh note to the eighth note,
is a half division.
Shifting the half division from the second note to the third note, and the half division from the fifth note to the sixth note of the shāng of the gōng mode,
to the half division from the third note to the fourth note, and the half division from the seventh note to the eighth note,
then the third note takes the Qīngbiàngōng, Gāowǔ of the Bàndàlǚ lǜ.
The sixth note takes the Qīngjué, Gāoshàng of the Zhònglǚ lǜ.
The seventh note takes the Qīngbiànzhǐ, Gāochǐ of the Línzhōng lǜ.
The interval from the third note Bàndàlǚ to the fourth note Huángzhōng is a half division.
The interval from the seventh note Línzhōng to the eighth note Yízé is a half division.
The zhǐ of the biàngōng mode
is the biànzhǐ of the gōng mode mixed with the jué of the qīnggōng mode, transformed into a zhǐ division.
For the biànzhǐ and biàngōng of the gōng mode, they are at the first and fourth notes.
This means the interval from the first note to the second note,
and from the fourth note to the fifth note,
is a half division.
For the jué of the qīnggōng mode, biànzhǐ and biàngōng are at the second and fifth notes.
This further means the interval from the second note to the third note,
and from the fifth note to the sixth note,
is a half division.
Now, if the open string is transformed into zhǐ,
then the interval from the third note to the fourth note,
from the seventh tone to the eighth tone
constitutes a half-step.
Herein, the *Lǚ* of Nánlǚ's *qīngzhēng gāogōng* is set as the first tone of the *sǎnsheng*.
From the third tone, Huángzhōng, to the fourth tone, Dàlǚ, constitutes a half-step.
From the seventh tone, Yízé, to the eighth tone, Nánlǚ, constitutes a half-step.
This is the method for the string tones to set the seven *yánglǜ* modes which are used in rotation.
When setting the seven *yīnlǚ* modes for establishing the *yǔ* divisions,
they must also be based on the *yīnlǚ*.
The mixed use of *yīn* and *yáng* for each string and each division is also similar.
First,
among the various modes of string tones,
only *gōng* and *shāngzhēng* can harmonize with *lǜlǚ* for use.
The seven tones of each string in the *gōng* mode
all correspond to one *jūn* of the *yánglǜ*.
(The divisions of the two altered seven tones are also like this.)
The seven tones of each string in the *qīnggōng* mode and the divisions of the two altered seven tones
all correspond to one *jūn* of the *yīnlǚ*.
This is why the string tone *gōng* mode can harmonize with *lǜlǚ*.
The five principal tones of each string in the *shāng* mode
all correspond to the *yánglǜ*,
only the two altered tones convert to the *yīnlǚ*.
In the *qīngshāng* mode, only the two altered tones are mixed into the *yánglǜ*.
This is why the five principal tones of the *shāng* mode can harmonize with *lǜlǚ*.
The five principal tones and the altered *gōng* tone of each string in the *zhēng* mode all correspond to the *yánglǜ*,
only the altered *zhēng* tone takes from the *yīnlǚ*.
In the *qīngzhēng* mode, only the altered *zhēng* tone is mixed into the *yánglǜ*.
This is also why the five principal tones and the altered *gōng* tone of the *zhēng* mode can harmonize with *lǜlǚ*.
As for the five principal tones within the *jué* mode,
the *zhēng* string, *gōng* string, and *shāng* string all correspond to the *yīnlǚ*,
while the two altered tones conversely obtain the *yánglǜ*.
Furthermore, the *shāng* tone *yǐ* character and the *yǔ* tone *fán* character
cannot be used in any string or any division.
These two tone characters are left the same as in the *gōng* mode.
The mixing of *yīn* and *yáng* in the five tones and two altered tones of the *qīngjué* mode is also like this.
Therefore, the *jué* mode cannot harmonize with *lǜlǚ*.
Within the five principal tones of the *biànzhēng* mode, the *gōng* string corresponds to the *yīnlǚ*,
and the two altered tones also obtain the *yánglǜ*.
The *yǔ* tone *fán* character cannot be used in any string or any division.
In the *qīngbiànzhēng* mode, the *gōng* string is also mixed into the *yánglǜ*.
Therefore, the *biànzhēng* mode cannot harmonize with *lǜlǚ*.
However, it only borrows one tone,
which makes it the same as the *gōng* mode's tone characters.
Compared to the *jué* mode, it is more correct.
Within the five principal tones of the *yǔ* mode, the *jué* string corresponds to the *yīnlǚ*,
and the two altered tones correspond to the *yīnlǚ*.
In the *qīngyǔ* mode, the *jué* string and the two altered tones correspond to the *yánglǜ*.
Although it cannot harmonize with *lǜlǚ*,
based on the string tones, it is still one of the modes with all seven tones complete.
Within the five principal tones of the *biàngōng* mode, the *zhēng* string and *gōng* string both correspond to the *yīnlǚ*,
while the two altered tones conversely obtain the *yánglǜ*.
Furthermore, the *shāng* tone *yǐ* character and the *yǔ* tone *fán* character
cannot be used in any string or any division.
These two tone characters are left the same as in the *jué* mode.
The mixing of *yīn* and *yáng* in the five tones and two altered tones of the *qīngbiàngōng* mode is also like this.
Therefore, it also cannot harmonize with *lǜlǚ*.
*Gōng* Mode
*Zhēng* First String,
sets the *lǜ* of double Wúshè.
The altered *gōng* (*hé*) character
obtains the division of lower *zhēng*.
*Yǔ* Second String,

obtains the division of lower *yǔ*.

*Jué* Fifth String,

obtains the division of the *jué* string.

*Zhēng* Sixth String,
sets the *lǜ* of half Huángzhōng.

obtains the division of the *zhēng* string.
*Yǔ* Seventh String,

*Zhēng* Sixth String,

*Yǔ* Seventh String,

The string sounds on the right are for `Xuán Gōng Zhuǎn Diào` (revolving Gōng and changing keys).
Based on the qín strings,
Taking the Yǔ string as the starting note for the main key.
Therefore, for `Xuán Gōng` modulation, `Huángzhōng` is taken as the principal Zhǐ, and the Yǔ position of the second string is established as the Gōng key.
The `Lǜlǚ Hòubiān` (Later Compilation of Lǜlǚ), based on the seven notes,
Takes Gōng as the principal note.
If Huángzhōng is Gōng,
then the Gōng division sound of the string corresponds to Huángzhōng,
the Shāng division corresponds to Tàicù,
the Jué division corresponds to Gūxǐ,
the Biànzhǐ division corresponds to Ruíbīn,
the Zhǐ division corresponds to Yízé,
the Yǔ division corresponds to Wúshè,
the Biàngōng division corresponds to half Huángzhōng.
(That is, double Wúshè.)
If Dàlǚ is Gōng,
the divisions of the seven notes correspond to the negative lǚs similarly.
Speaking of divisions,
then the Gōng division that corresponds to Huángzhōng is the division of Huángzhōng,
the Shāng division is the division of Tàicù,
the Jué division is the division of Gūxǐ,
the Biànzhǐ division is the division of Ruíbīn.
As for the Zhǐ division that corresponds to Yízé,
it is not the division of Yízé,
but is the division of Línzhōng.
The Yǔ division that corresponds to Wúshè,
is also not the division of Wúshè,
but is the division of Nánlǚ.
The Biàngōng division that corresponds to half Huángzhōng,
is not the division of half Huángzhōng,
but is the division of Yìngzhōng.
If Dàlǚ is Gōng,
the Biànzhǐ division then becomes the division of Biàn Línzhōng,
the Zhǐ division then becomes the division of Yízé,
the Yǔ division then becomes the division of Wúshè,
the Biàngōng division then becomes the division of Biàn Huángzhōng.
Their yīnyáng each have seven modes,
each mode has seven strings.
A detailed table can be found in `Yuèwèn` (Music Inquiries),
not fully recorded here.

Three chapters for the banquet at Fēngzéyuán: music for serving tea and wine on the imperial steps,
music for serving dishes in the Zhōnghé style.
Chapter on "Jǐngyùn Gānkūn Tàizhī Zhāng" for serving tea. The propitious fortune of the universe is vast and peaceful,
the eight directions return to its embrace.
Swiftly removing the invaders,
the battle clouds over Yùlěi clear.
A sealed memorial reaches the imperial steps,
the Son of Heaven's countenance brightens, proclaiming to his officials.
Displaying grand strategies,
applying extraordinary talents,
achieving great deeds and returning victoriously.
Forever pacifying the borders,
the spring colors of Jǐnjiāng dispel the mists.
Human effort marvelously substitutes for divine work,
matching the achievements of Fāngshú's military campaigns.
Merits recorded on banners and flags,
honored with jade tablets and scepters.
(Verse 1) By decree,
by decree specially proclaimed,
how different from Jífǔ's eulogy for the pacification of Huái?
Strategic planning in the tent yields swift success.
Celebrating clarity and peace,
a banquet is held at Pénglái,
auspicious light radiates, illuminating the screen walls.
Warm and harmonious,
auspicious qi comes from the south.
(Verse 2) Returning and feasting, policies are set forth,
the beacon fires of peace report boundless joy.
The five domains display their glory,
all regions are tranquil, ascending the spring terrace.
Carriages and books, jade and silks,
greatly bestowed, as vast as Heaven.
As vast as Heaven,
rewards for meritorious service are celebrated,
titles are conferred, shining on the Sāntái.
(Verse 3) Recalling the severe winter,
the flags and banners unfurled their colors;
rejoicing this spring,
the reed pipes and drums harmonize.
All due to the sagely decision of the imperial court.
Changing the seasons,
sweeping away floating clouds and dust.
(Verse 4) Our martial might is glorified, revered by many,
praising their excellence,
coming to pay tribute and pledge allegiance across the world.
Offering tribute to the Golden Terrace,
why must we wash weapons by the Yúhǎi?
Making a boat ultimately relies on timber for crossing rivers.
Timber for crossing rivers,
also assists in governance and tempering the immortal cauldron.
(Verse 5) Looking to the future,
weapons are laid down.
Receiving protection,
amnesty and leniency are granted.
Wild beasts are scattered,
phoenixes sing in harmony.
Barbarian regions are pacified, bringing universal blessings,
treasures and gifts joyfully fill the steps.
(Verse 6) Flower petals lightly sift down,
fragrant clouds gather,
the great cosmic order turns, and warmth arrives.
Pulling at almond cheeks,
blushing peach complexions.
Gazing at the full baskets,
harvesting auspicious fruits,
they are already arranged on the jade table.
Spring and grace endure,
delighting the imperial heart,
matching the imperial bounty.
(Verse 7) The three halls rejoice in harmony,
a thousand officials are happy and jubilant,
the joy of Yáo and Shùn is happily reenacted.
Knowing there is joy,
forever without suspicion,
gazing at the full baskets,
harvesting auspicious fruits,
they are already arranged on the jade table.
Spring and grace endure,
delighting the imperial heart,
matching the imperial bounty.
(Verse 8) The encounter between enlightened ruler and worthy officials shines for a thousand generations,
rejoicing in the triumphant return of the army,
cheers rising from both within and without.
Magnificent achievements are sung in unison,
grand plans are marked in the annals of history.
(Receding with obeisance)
Chapter on presenting wine: The Sage's Virtue is broadly manifested.
The Emperor's might is spread far and wide, aided by the Prime Minister.
Bestowed with the battle-axe, leading the vanguard,
He pacifies and stabilizes with divine martial prowess.
(First stanza) The Shu (巴蜀) bandits run rampant,
He oversees from the imperial court, holding the military seal.
Then the frosty halberds point west,
And feathered cavalry hasten south.
His awe is profound,
His reputation precedes him to distant borders,
His eminence is majestic,
His punitive campaigns precisely strike the weak and isolated.
Looking up at the Three Terraces,
Power is wielded by the Left Chancellor;
Entrusted with exclusive command,
His star shines in the central pivot.
The campaign is close at hand,
Victory is swift.
(Second stanza) Exerting martial prowess and governing with wisdom, holding to the sagely counsel,
Immediately upon arriving at the front,
He sends news of victory,
How splendid his ambition, shining brightly!
He clearly establishes strict discipline for the military,
Commands to victory with divine assistance.
The Eight Trigram Formation (八陣圖) of wind and clouds,
His strategic plans serve as a model.
He encourages public loyalty,
Busily propagates virtuous teachings.
He restores the lands,
And pardons the ignorant and stubborn.
(Third stanza) Receiving the sagely calculations,
The heavenly army eradicates,
Why worry about the winding paths of Shu (蜀道)?
Divining a swift campaign,
He soars like an eagle from the capital (上都).
The sun is cold and frozen,
The plank roads enter the clouds,
The fierce wind is strong,
Snow covers the roads.
Riding sleds,
He exerts himself diligently.
(Fourth stanza) Suddenly the camp is opened like Xìliǔ (細柳),
Warmth is like holding padded silk.
Solemnly receiving the heavenly mandate,
His spiritual power shakes the eight regions.
He eliminates the night-raiders,
Grasping the key is like crushing dry leaves.
He pacifies disturbances,
Sharpens spears and lances,
Cultivates civil virtues,
Displays shields and feathers,
Boosts morale,
Loyalty and trust are mutually fostered.
(Fifth stanza) They compete to show sincerity,
Regretting their resistance in difficult terrain.
Coming to surrender with hands bound,
Like fish in a boiling pot.
He opens the net of Tāng (湯),
Swiftly proclaims the victory report;
Comforting Yáo's (堯) heart,
He avoids punitive expeditions.
(Sixth stanza) The triumphant return of the army is celebrated,
News of victory first reported,
Bugles and drums hasten the vanguard.
Not alarming the chickens and dogs, all are safe and settled,
His illustrious reputation rivals the strong crossbow (強弩).
A unified and peaceful reign for ten thousand years of joy,
The military's aggressive spirit subtly dissipates, becoming a timely rain.
(Seventh stanza) Gentle breezes waft,
A beautiful vista unfolds,
Receiving imperial favor, already drunk, they hasten like ényù (鵷鷺).
They truly assist in counsel, connecting hearts and minds,
The imperial treasury often seen protected by wind and clouds.
The upright court, with one virtue, celebrates peace and prosperity,
How can spring light compare to the vastness of imperial favor?
(Eighth stanza) Immersed in abundance,
Bestowed with a grand feast.
Three cups are proposed,
Bowing to accept the imperial wine,
Feasting on imperial cuisine.
Waves ripple,
Soaked in refreshing dew.
They compete to raise their goblets,
Offering longevity and many blessings.
How beautiful the prime of life,
Spring overflows the cloud-paths.
The Emperor, governing wisely, opens a prosperous era,
Light floats in jade goblets,
Radiance reflects on golden doors.
(Ninth stanza) Abundant and extraordinary blessings,
The multitude sings with joy,
His prestige spreads across the six directions,
His position is weighty, like the Three Dukes (三孤).
Presenting excellent counsel,
Pacifying the borders when sent out,
Truly serving as a pillar of the central court.
They eagerly await the Emperor's agreement (都俞),
Assisting like Táng (唐) and Yú (虞).
All officials solemnly approach,
Shouting "Long live the Emperor!" at the palace steps.
The officials are numerous,
Bowing and rejoicing.
Melodious and resonant,
Sheng (笙) and yú (竽) play on forever.
For ten thousand years,
The jade candle burns peacefully.
The Yellow River is clear, the seas are calm, the golden basin (金甌) is secure,
Honor thrives with tiger-and-bamboo tallies,
Joy fills hats and robes.
(Tenth stanza) The days lengthen,
The season is warm and mild,
All creatures revive from this,
Precious incense rises spirally from the imperial censer.
Fragrant túdū (酴酥) wine overflows jade jars.
Thinking of those years,
Resting by algae and rushes,
How different is today's Hào Yàn (鎬燕) from the past?
Celebrating the prosperity of the imperial court,
Singing of the harmonious encounter between ruler and minister,
The dawning sun illuminates the imperial residence.
(Concluding remarks)

celebrating the reign of Yáo,
and the gentle air is warm and beautiful.
Tender willows are lush and verdant,
vibrant plums flutter,
and distant lands will forever cease the smoke of war.
Cloud-capped peaks rise on all sides to greet the imperial tent,
and myriad layers of rosy clouds reflect the imperial banquet.
Strategies are proclaimed,
urgent military dispatches are conveyed,
and ministers and officials leap with joy and delight.
(Section 1) Gentle breezes, beautiful sun, and auspicious clouds appear;
the celestial gates of the nine heavens open the palace halls.
Sheng and huáng music accompanies the peaceful banquet,
with achievements inscribed in the Qílín Pavilion, and royal strategies made manifest.
Ministers assist in governing the realm,
their actions echoing the statutes of Yáo,
and weapons are sheathed as the people turn to goodness.
(Section 2) How admirable!
The merits of Wèi Huò come one after another,
and strategies for border defense can be planned.
Punishments are justly administered,
and military steps are never amiss.
The army's strength is reinforced,
and military camps are overseen.
The sagely might is brightly displayed, manifesting Heaven's punishment;
since they have come to court,
why bother with a difficult assault?
Blessings flow like rivers,
wine gushes like springs;
all bask in deep imperial favor.
(Section 3) The píxiū are commanded,
mountains are contained within Yǔ’s domain,
the comet (chánqiāng) is swept away,
and the wind is harmonious like Shùn’s zither.
To inspire awe is added to refined poetry,
carriages rumble,
drums resonate deeply.
(Section 4) The imperial army returns,
its might unparalleled,
benevolent decrees and names are engraved on bells and tripods.
The borders are pacified and secured,
and conflicts cease in remote corners of the world.
Wondrous feats are achieved in Cáncóng’s bird-paths,
and high-held cups of rosy wine connect to the Big Dipper.
Banners and flags flutter like willows in the warm spring breeze,
and the loyalty of a sunflower heart basks in the sun.
(Section 5) The six dishes for immortals,
seasoned with salt and plum,
are shared from forbidden delicacies.
On the jade steps, they dance with joy,
hanging sun and moon,
opening twin pheasant fans.
All rejoice that Heaven's will aligns with human will,
appreciating the spring scenery of the nine heavens,
listening fully to the warbling of orioles.
The beautiful scenery is abundant,
from watching incense rise from golden ní,
to flowers blooming in the imperial garden.
(Section 6) The daytime water clock turns,
the clear rosy clouds are splendid;
thereafter, may they be like oars and rain,
the grand officials in harmony like strings and zithers.
The Yúnsháo music is splendidly arranged,
colorful honor guards are arrayed,
inviting joy, and things become even more beautiful.
When the Emperor is blessed,
conflicts are settled, weapons are put away,
civil governance is refined, and military might is put aside.
(Section 7) Enchantingly,
they toast with immortal peaches,
urging the dawn arrow.
Beyond the flowers,
tall banners turn.
Governance reaches supreme order,
the world is at peace.
For billions of years,
weapons are abolished, and punishments are set aside,
diligence and effort are offered in homage.
Rejoicing this morning,
most unforgettable,
is the Emperor's grace and Heaven's favor.
(Section 8) Aiding transformation and harmonizing the primal forces,
they follow in the footsteps of Zhōu Shào,
with renowned worthies gathered to spread their influence throughout the world.
Great blessings fully descend and illuminate,
and gracious light should universally spread.
Not merely three thousand armored soldiers,
the supreme foundation is held high, rejoicing in eternal stability.
(Recitative)
The 25th year of Qiánlóng,
victory parade in the western border,
banquet at Fēngzé Yuán, three chapters. Presenting tea, presenting wine, clear music in the imperial courtyard;
presenting dishes, clear music of harmony.
Chapter on Presenting Tea, "The Sagely Might Shines Throughout the World" The sagely might shines throughout the world,
and all things are prosperous.
Behold the pacification of the barbarians,
the jade frontier scrolls away clouds and rainbows,
the expansion of territory has surpassed Hàn’s Guānxī,
succeeding in glorious plans that trace back to ancient records.
In the morning, axes are granted;
in the evening, war drums sound,
just as the three armies play their drums and trumpets,
celebrating military success.
Their merits in the green annals are incomparable,
Heaven's favor consoles the Emperor's heart.
Jífǔ's pacification of the Huái River is a modest comparison,
his achievements manifest like soaring eagles,
his honor shared with dragon guards.
(Section 1) How admirable!
How admirable is the bearing of Yàfū.
Clear skies open, willows brush against the vanguard banner,
heroic winds sweep away the Lóulán forts.
Expanding written script and carriages,
a grand foundation for ten thousand miles,
a stream of immortal music winds around the vermilion steps.
Incense from the imperial censer,
auspicious mists wafting.
(Section 2) Throwing down spears and doffing armor, a gathering of wind and clouds,
gentlemen and ladies are joyful and peaceful.
They receive blessings with compassion and benevolence,
the nine heavens are close at hand, fearing Heaven's majesty.
The ranks of phoenixes and egrets,
gather like scattered stars.
Like scattered stars,
on Yáo's steps,
dancers with shields and feathers perform on the dragon steps.
(Section 3) Recalling the past,
Yīlí was greatly pacified;
rejoicing this morning,
Huíbù is entirely returned.
Ráo songs are sung in unison, shining with banners and flags,
looking back,
it spread from east to west.
(Section 4) Imperial plans are all due to Heaven's bestowed wisdom,
acting opportunely,
diligently reviewing despatches late into the night.
Strengthening the frontier,
moon bows and star arrows are all elite.
Evil influences are pacified, whales are slain,
allowing axes to drive away the people's ailments.
(Section 5) Listening to the sound of the wind,
like the cry of cranes.
On the path ahead,
trees and grasses become cavalry.
Welcoming baskets of food,
filled with fine silks,
singing in front and dancing behind, all loyal like sunflowers,
turning to gaze at the brilliant light.
(Section 6) The sound of bugles and drums urges on,
beacon fires are relayed,
auspicious light rises everywhere on the spring terrace.
Continuing great achievements,
recording on monumental steles,
in times of peace,
extolling great beauty.
Immortal banquets bestowed at Péngchí,
for billions of years,
gathering the imperial blueprint,
conforming to the emperor's way.
(Section 7) Fortune corresponds to a prosperous era,
armies are numerous and well-ordered,
the imperial banquet is set, gazing at clouds and sun.
Majesty is formidable,
virtue is lofty,
in times of peace,
extolling great beauty.
Immortal banquets bestowed at Péngchí,
for billions of years,
gathering the imperial blueprint,
conforming to the emperor's way.
(Section 8) Continuing songs of joy, reaching the times of Táng and Yú,
behold the valiant master-ministers bowing respectfully.
Illustrious achievements portend great joy,
harmony opens an era of longevity.
(Recitative)
Chapter on Offering Wine and the Far-Reaching Yǔdian. Yǔdiàn far-reaching and connected,
the Zhōujiāng is distantly controlled, relying on good pillars.
Punishment succeeds,
phoenixes are drawn to the court.
(First Stanza) Our Emperor sits in serene dignity,
military dispatches and strategies are given to the supreme general,
stabilizing and expanding the Huái region,
and bringing the northern deserts to join.
Bearing jade and silk,
Dàyuān divides into left and right,
contributing precious jades,
Bùlǔ fills east and west.
A shower of special grace,
wolves and jackals are freed from the net;
thinking of ingratitude,
owls and tigers display ferocity.
The pheasant alliance is broken,
a mantis's arm claims dominance.
(Second Stanza) The military discipline is strict and the commander-in-chief loyal,
hoisting the campaign banner,
sweeping across the rainbow,
charging through northern snow and fierce winds,
warm as if holding floss, all are joyous.
The morale of the vanguard boasts surplus courage,
a million *píxiū* are mighty,
wind and clouds are commanded at a glance,
laughing at the puny clowns filled with terror.
Startling evil spirits,
wild boars and piglets scatter.
(Third Stanza) Displaying our might,
the royal army is solemn and harmonious,
relying on this to exhaust the defiant.
Surely a bird overturning its precarious nest needs no wind.
Fish in a pot,
their tracks cannot escape;
tigers hiding in a crag,
their power cannot be tolerated.
Riding armored horses,
sweeping away mad youths.
(Fourth Stanza) Awaiting the wind to clear the three burrows,
the Tiānshān moon hangs like a bow.
Further comforting the hundred pheasants,
banners and flags obscure the sky.
Let wolves run and hide in thickets,
the demonic aura cannot hide its tracks.
Crossing Xī'ěr,
like withered stalks are urged,
approaching Bátá,
like gushing springs.
Meeting the righteous banner,
the prime culprits are utterly destroyed.
(Fifth Stanza) Competing to embrace allegiance,
rejoicing in favor.
Desiring to be royal subjects,
vying to offer *qiúgòng*.
Gazing at Shùn's steps,
black and yellow are offered as tribute.
Reaching Yáo's court,
memorials are consecutively sealed.
(Sixth Stanza) Upon the return of the army,
the public announcements are well-crafted,
the tribes of the western frontier are all stirred by the news.
It is not about displaying military prowess in remote wilds,
the grand design naturally continues the ancestral legacy.
The great mandate of the holy dynasty is renewed at once,
meritorious achievements for a thousand years receive Heaven's favor.
(Seventh Stanza) The imperial heart is pleased,
ceremonies and banquets are held solemnly,
attending the three palaces, hurrying like phoenixes.
Nourished by the deep dew, songs and praises are formed,
the *Juàn'ē* is continued, singing Zhōu poetry again.
The wise and upright celebrate "Dūyú" this day,
washing armor in the Heavenly River is known to be needless.
(Eighth Stanza) The reed ashes rise,
the pitch corresponds to *gōng*.
Silver snow falls profusely,
garden trees are carved from jade.
The song of *Dìdù* blends,
the sound is winding,
harmonizing with feather pipes and bells.
Competing to receive favor,
bowing to receive glass goblets.
Joy at the clear weather,
the light radiant and bright,
the golden *ōu* is forever solid, mountains and rivers are important.
Spring brings auspicious grass,
joy overflows from propitious pines.
(Ninth Stanza) Clouds gather suddenly,
clear rosy clouds bake at midday,
all officials stand reverently,
jade pendants tinkle.
Immortal retinue majestic,
*zhīgài* exquisite,
truly shining like pearls and glistening like jade.
Playing *shīméng*,
leisurely *shēng* and *yōng*,
great achievements and rich merits,
reciting ancestors and singing of clans.
Bright and brilliant,
*Ānshí* comes in red,
rustling and rustling,
Wǎnmǎ from the east.
Bowing on carpets,
with hairpins and ribbons in dignified array,
the three cups of wine are weighty with solemnity.
Cranes hear the calls and responses,
phoenixes harmonize with the rustling.
(Tenth Stanza) Drunk in the immortal kitchen,
the flower clock lasts long,
sending cattle home and releasing horses signifies success achieved,
receiving the Emperor's grace like clear wine is an honor.
Míngjiá on the jade steps are lush and green,
thinking of the prosperity built in Yānhào in those years,
the joyful songs of celebration are the same then and now.
Rejoicing in auspicious mists in the revolving palace,
further, the emperor's residence is surrounded by stars,
a whole court reverently bows, offering precious goblets.
(Concluding Remarks)
Chapter on Presenting Food: The Sagely Rule, Distant and Prosperous. The sagely rule is distant and prosperous;
records chronicle auspicious signs;
the six directions look up to the double radiance;
the day of transformation extends long.
Auspiciousness opens the golden gate;
its illumination truly covers distant lands.
Stars and clouds brilliantly embrace the heavenly blessing;
wind and rain are harmonious, assisting the imperial feast.
Grand and expansive is the chapter;
the 彗星 (huìxīng) is calmed;
imperial might widely spreads to distant regions.
(Section 1) Golden stalks and jade dew melt on immortal palms;
Yáo’s (Yáo) sky and a clear sun illuminate golden plaques.
Outside the general's quarters, a cold majesty is vast;
sheathing spears, presenting goblets, spring clouds abound.
In the Qílín Gé (Qílín Gé), meritorious names are recorded;
the boundless waves of grace spread wide;

(Section 2) Imagining the great enterprise,
divine achievements surpass those of the Hàn (Hàn) and Táng (Táng);

Military might vigorously spreads;
soldiers and horses gallop.
Heaven’s punishment is declared;
barbarian lands are reached;
the court’s plans and calculations sweep like wind and thunder;
holding military strategies,
commanding the army.
Celebrating peace and stability;
carrying banners and standards;
returning in triumph, the army dances and sings.
(Section 3) Outside Yúguān (Yúguān),
rainbow banners and tiger tents;
looking at the border cities,
like beehives and ant nests;
all people, like infants, come to submit.
Cleansing the desert;
annihilating the Sirius (Tiānláng) star.
(Section 4) Returning and disarming,

from Cōngshān (Cōngshān) to Púhǎi (Púhǎi), a hundred flowers fragrant.
Spirits high, vigor strong;
discussing merits and drinking to the utmost, the famed generals first.
Golden goblets are successively invited for prior rewards;
Western Region grapes are beautiful and fragrant.
All admire the imperial way, without partiality;

(Section 5) Harmonious light, gentle and vast;
drinking from jade goblets;
rare delicacies and a hundred brews.
Dew on water smartweed, abundant;
gazing respectfully,
the heavenly countenance, like the clear firmament.
The chief steward’s six dishes are seasoned in a golden cauldron;
served before the imperial banquet,
pheasant-feather fans brightly open in pairs.
Clouds and mist in myriad forms;
gazing at this resplendent auspicious aura,
like the three immortal mountains and Pénɡlánɡ (Pénɡlánɡ).
(Section 6) Receiving the banquet’s joy;
imperial grace flourishes;
from now on, no alarms from watchtowers;
armor is cleansed and stored.
Precious talismans are abundant and fragrant;
auspicious omens line up;
heaven's heart bestows abundant blessings.
Widely spreading civil virtues;
further increasing wealth and dispelling grievances;
the sound of the xūn (xūn) and qín (qín) blends.
(Section 7) Gazing upon and bathed in imperial benevolence;
expressing the awe of the multitudes;
like flowers and willows blossoming before spring;
immortal peaches bestowed at the banquet;
grace is widespread, virtue boundless.
Taking off battle robes,
fierce warriors leap with joy;
still intending to have their images drawn in the Qílín Gé (Qílín Gé).
Pacifying the beacons of war;
wishing for long reception of heavenly bestowed divine blessings.
(Section 8) Wine and music;
grace and bounty joyfully spread throughout the court.
Coming to enjoy, coming to submit is constant;
laying down arms and cultivating culture, observing the signs of good governance.
How is this different from chanting of the expansive Luòshǔi (Luòshǔi);

Jìnchá Tú Zhàohóngjī Zhī Zhāng —The “Offering Tea for the Grand Foundation” Chapter. The grand foundation is established,
a joyous omen of peace and happiness.
At the splendid banquet, receiving immense favor and solemn rites,
tea is bestowed by imperial decree.
(Verse 1) Attending the auspicious feast, bathed in grace,
respectfully and orderly, maintaining solemn decorum,
with phoenix fans opening wide, gazing at the emperor's proximity.
The celestial sphere revolves,
robes hang gracefully.
The great harmony and propitious fortune bring repeated jubilation;
when governance is peaceful,
the principle is self-cultivation and family regulation.
(Verse 2) Accumulating virtue at the splendid gates welcomes abundant blessings,
auspiciousness gathers in the women's quarters, nurturing a virtuous empress;
imperial favor begins from now.
Receiving imperial decrees and edicts, bathed in gracious splendor,
enfeoffed with five ranks,
bestowing noble titles upon descendants.
Bestowing upon descendants,
inheriting great bounty,
blessings and prosperity frequently bestowed.
(Verse 3) Officials gather,
performing rites in the vermilion court.
Playing stringed and wind instruments,
singing odes on the imperial steps.
Princes and feudal lords assist at the imperial gate,
playing exquisite music,
listening to all harmonize in joy.
(Verse 4) Internal and external harmony achieves perfect governance,
an auspicious omen.
Heaven and earth are set in their positions,
celebrating the propitious time,
welcoming good fortune and joy.
Sharing the glory of intertwining auspicious tree branches,
and abundant, double-headed wheat ears.
Double-headed wheat ears,
like King Wén's benevolent rule, beginning with the *Juán'ěr* and *Línzhǐ* odes.
(Verse 5) Spreading great auspiciousness,
assisting in good governance,
extending to distant descendants,
like a rainbow and lightning, auspicious.
Matching heaven and earth,
ordering the four seasons.
Lutes and zithers harmonize, joyfully,
the empress dowager is pleased.
(Verse 6) The scene is bright with auspicious light,
celestial music resounds,
imperial tea is bestowed by the heavenly household.
The dew from the bronze dew-collecting plates,
poured into jade cups,
oranges passed in handkerchiefs,
plums offered on trays,
carrying a rare fragrance in sleeves.
Close to the jade table,
near the imperial presence,
extending the joyous banquet.
(Verse 7) Rivers are beautiful, mountains are splendid,
rites are clear, music is complete,
auspicious omens for a myriad generations, surpassing Jī and Sì.
Clouds intertwine like a canopy,
phoenixes arrive in stately procession,
living under the benevolent rule of Yáo,
wandering in the age of Shùn,
imperial relatives and honors are bestowed.
Close to the jade table,
near the imperial presence,
extending the joyous banquet.
(Verse 8) Wine shared in street goblets, rich grace extended,
joyful and harmonious,
feelings fully expressed.
Nine blessings successfully achieved,
the three luminaries foretell auspiciousness.
(Receding verses)
Jìnjiǔ Bǎoshàn Xiángkāi Zhī Zhāng —The “Offering Wine with Auspiciously Opening Fans” Chapter. Auspicious fans open,
golden incense burners waft fragrance at the joyous gathering.
Everlasting harmony in poetry,
spring fills three thousand realms.
(Verse 1) Fortune flourishes and heaven and earth are in harmony,
all under heaven, people together enjoy the spring terrace.
Behold, the golden goblet first gleams,
and a new jade melody is composed.
Smoke gently curls,
auspicious light illuminates the imperial willows,
joy overflows,
felicity rises to the palace scholar trees.
The imperial wind spreads,
the transformation of Zhōunán begins,
singing of the sagely rule,
grace comes from the northern palace.
Poetry harmonizes with the water caltrops,
joy encompasses the orchid terrace.
(Verse 2) The auspicious rites are newly completed, embracing a hundred blessings,
together, joy soars,
spreading throughout the nine realms,
the praises of numerous descendants and the Qílín are in harmony.
All look up to the grand rites, as the empress approaches,
imperial presence and joyful feast, delightful and harmonious.
Officials gather, displaying talent,
imperial music pleases the sage heart.
Welcoming abundant blessings,
universal celebration of peace in heaven and earth.
Singing of the correct beginning,
approaching the jade steps.
(Verse 3) Grape wine fills the jade goblets, old vintage,
fragrance fills the myriad longevity cup.
See the solemn banquet begin at the Jade Hall.
Tones are clear and strong,
Kuí's melodies harmonize.
Rhythm is clear and bright,
phoenix pipes urge.
Joy and blessings,
come from heaven.
(Verse 4) Hear the *Jūzhōu* ode recited,
clouds and mist splendidly open.
And phoenix sheng pipes play in succession,
Xiáosháo music harmonizes beautifully.
Just as spring returns to heaven,
palace flowers pile up like brocade.
The clepsydra flows slowly,
days seem like years,
light sparkles,
cups are like the sea.
Celestial music plays,
the realm is like Pénglái.
(Verse 5) Spreading the fragrant banquet,
arranging it on both sides of the steps.
Abundant dishes from Yáo's kitchen,
peach fruits from the Jade Terrace.
As wine is poured leisurely,
its taste is like sweet nectar.
All bow in praise,
together drink from golden goblets.
(Verse 6) Emerald goblets,
parrot cups,
jade and gems glitter with brilliant light.
Drinking in harmony, enjoying the spread of benevolent influence,
imperial benevolence is vast, like heaven.
Heaven and earth together offer auspicious omens,
the abundant celebration is universally embraced.
(Verse 7) Rites are complete,
virtuous intent is broad,
the imperial palace's transformation arises from a peaceful heavenly heart.
Longevity cups are even more joyful, presented with rhinoceros horns,
harmonious sounds like phoenixes soaring and luan birds fluttering.
Auspiciousness widely celebrates throughout the world,
the customs of "Ernan" are truly unparalleled.
(Verse 8) Concentrating abundant blessings,
pleasing the sage heart.
Drum and bell sounds urge,
qin and se sounds harmonize,
elegant and eulogistic poems are composed.
Singing of the pepper's proliferation,
the lingering melody lingers.
Chanting of the melon's continuous growth,
joyful dance of two palace colors.
Celebrating peace and prosperity,
further wishing for the longevity of the emperor and empress.
Orderly and respectfully meeting at the auspicious gathering,
imperial sentiment is profound,
the emperor's rule is majestic.
(Verse 9) Offering sacrifices like Yǔ bowed,
on the steps of Shùn and Yáo.
Golden minced fish and jade sliced meat,
precious goblets and jade wine vessels.
Happily attending the banquet,
hurrying together,
auspicious gathering, auspicious guests, joyful and harmonious.
A thousand auspicious omens arrive,
ten thousand blessings come.
Wine like the Huái River,
grace covers the whole world.
All officials gather,
ranked among the thorns and scholar trees,
advancing all,
everyone a salt-and-plum (talented minister).
See the bright sun shine, clouds open,
pearls and jades combine, light sparkling.
The blessings of the Great Plan spread,
auspicious praises harmonize.
(Verse 10) Receiving vast blessings,
for a myriad years,
opening the golden gates,
bowing at the jade steps.
The morning sun and gentle breeze greet the imperial platform,
colorful imperial guards like clouds arranged.
Walking on floral tiles,
as if ascending the spring terrace,
the palace water clock slowly urges.
Joy and harmony boundless,
bathed in vast imperial grace,
five-colored clouds high holding purple glow cups.
(Receding verses)
Chapter on Serving Food for Heaven and Earth in Perfect Peace. Heaven and earth are in perfect peace,

Heaven presides over great creation,
Earth's function is to nourish life,

The regalia of Yú Shùn’s glorious reign,

Dances in the alleys and songs in the thoroughfares,

the harmony and joy of all lands are most flourishing.
(Section 2) How fortunate!
Smoke wafts from incense burners, auspicious mists entwine,
noble relatives gather, adorned with official caps.
Wine is poured into jade goblets,
music is played on silver sheng.
Rejoicing in the grand assembly,
bearing special honor,

Dewdrops are abundant,
pearls spill from golden stems.
