Oh, how glorious is the August Qīng dynasty,
receiving its mandate from Heaven.
Its grand fortune extends brightly,
for ten thousand myriad years.
Heaven inaugurates auspicious seasons,
propitious *jiē míng* grass appears on the steps.
All myriad nations share one world,
the Sacred Longevity is a thousand years.
Verily, from our ancestors,
the foundation was laid in È Yān.
On the mountains of Chángbái,
magpies held a vermilion fruit in their beaks.
Continuously, like gourds and melons,
long will their auspiciousness flourish.
Our revered ancestors were born auspiciously,
accumulating blessings and renewed glory.
The old territory was greatly expanded,
eastward reaching the edge of the sea.
Saints succeeded saints,
inheriting it for eternal generations.
(Chapter 1) Illustrious divine accomplishments,
like a dragon rising and soaring.
With thirteen armored warriors,
his deeds began to emerge.
He avenged and quelled the rebellion,
first conquering Tú Lún.
With a single pointing of his divine spear,
he struck terror into powerful neighbors.
The nine surnames secretly encroached,
but were swept away without a trace.
The five tribes of Měnggǔ,
came to submit to the great name.
The Míng army, in four columns,
was annihilated in five days.
The capital was established at Liáoshěn,
the capital city was majestic.
The battle clouds were five-colored,
the river ice solidified at night.
Heaven aids the virtuous,
who rise in response to the opportune moment.
(Chapter 2) Heaven bestowed sagacity,
covering and protecting the lesser states.
Distant ones submitted, near ones returned,
and cultured virtue was broadly spread.
The four quarters came to pledge allegiance,
gathering like clouds and following like shadows.
Long-term officials were established,
to oversee all affairs.
Therefore, national script was created,
like Jié's writings and Xī's drawings.
Sounds harmonize with fundamental tones,
unchanging for ten thousand ages.
Therefore, the military system was established,
with colorful banners fluttering majestically.
Some pure, some interspersed,
forever pacifying the eight directions.
Grand plans were laid,
great enterprises were brought to fruition.
Boundless blessings were bestowed,
fortune gathered for a thousand generations.
(Chapter 3) Enlightening and assisting wise heirs,
brightly expanding previous accomplishments.
Manifesting and honoring eminent virtues,
to widely receive heavenly blessings.
Waverers were appeased and embraced,
Cháoxiǎn submitted in good faith.
They eternally served as the eastern dependency,
and were granted *guī zàn* ceremonial jade.
Thirty-five commanderies,
bowed their heads and declared themselves vassals.
Westward, reaching the land of Buddhism,
interpreters came as guests from afar.
He cleansed and campaigned against Míng,
displaying his army in Qí and Lǔ.
Sweeping through the suburbs like lightning,
he took nothing despite having it.
He seized territory in Sōngxìng,
and repeatedly annihilated enemy forces.
Winning every one of a hundred battles,
thereby accumulating great merits.
(Chapter 4) The Emperor's virtue spread widely,
receiving the illustrious name.
The nation was established, and the era named,
permanently establishing the Great Qīng.
He harmonized the nine kindred,
and the human relationships were regulated.
He honored virtue and befriended the worthy,
making them his arms and legs, heart and backbone.
The Three Institutes were opened,
to learn from the past and revere Confucianism.
Suburban sacrifices and ancestral rites,
were performed to adorn the imperial blueprint.
Ranks and offices were assigned,
the Six Boards managed governance.
All officials faithfully discharged their duties,
setting an example for all nations.
His might awed all under Heaven,
his virtue matched the firmament.
He respectfully carried on without ceasing,
with eminent achievements and abundant merits.
(Chapter 5) The Emperor received the divine implements,
unifying the world.
He eliminated great bandits,
and the universe was cleansed.
Once he donned his military attire,
it was like a timely sweet rain.
He widely proclaimed his military achievements,
becoming the lord of gods and men.
He personally attended to major state affairs,
rectifying discipline and setting order.
He established rites and composed music,
manifesting norms and regulations.
He accepted counsel and appointed the worthy,
prudent in minor matters and far-sighted.
He established laws and reviewed punishments,
setting a standard for ten thousand generations.
He was diligent and frugal,
founding the dynasty with sincerity and generosity.
The mandate was renewed,
he held himself with trepidation and industry.
(Chapter 6) The sagacious and divine one established the supreme standard,
his Way surpassed a hundred kings.
For sixty-one years,
his fortune and longevity were long-lasting.
Heaven endowed him with sagacity,
he ascended the throne in his youth.
He served the Two Empresses Filially,
his virtue renowned through a thousand ages.
The three rebels stirred,
but were utterly suppressed in one fell swoop.
The sea turbulence was forever quelled,
the waves subsided, the whales calmed.
He personally led the six armies,
campaigning three times in the desert.
His awe was stern, his embrace benevolent,
he rooted out the stubborn and supported the weak.
He achieved the accomplishments of Yǔ,
and made inspection tours like Yú.
Throughout the land,
none failed to respect and love him.
(Chapter 7) Heaven operates robustly,
the divine sage modeled himself after it.
Diligent in study and governance,
he served as both ruler and teacher.
"No idleness" was his maxim,

One person's toil and worry,
pacified these myriad nations.
With civil and military strategies,
the land was tranquil, and Heaven brought perfection.
Moderation established the ultimate standard,
like the ringing of jade and the striking of metal.
For ten thousand myriad years,
his light and glory were observed and extolled.
Respecting Heaven and diligent for the people,
he embodied the primordial and acted as a sage.
Heaven's scrutiny was greatly manifest,
the succeeding kings were reverent.
They modeled themselves on the August Ancestor,
and the imperial fortune would endure long.
(Chapter 8) The beautiful blueprint shines brightly,
the six directions are harmonious and prosperous.
Stars glow and clouds are splendid,
wind and rain come in due season.
All receive auspicious blessings,
the jade candle is harmoniously regulated.
The imperial rule is mild,
the Way shines through the imperial records.
Spreading east and covering west,
harmonizing north and pacifying south.
All who came by ladder and boat with tribute,
reached Yáo's steps.
Like the rising sun and the waxing moon,
myriad bows receive blessings.
They strike the ground and sing in the streets,
shouting "Sōng" and offering splendid congratulations.
The magnificent rites are orderly,
the praises are overflowing.
Continuing the glorious legacy of the ancestors,
forever celebrating peace and prosperity.
(Chapter 9)
In Jiāqìng First Year,
the Supreme Emperor held a banquet,
with the nine chapters of celebratory music and dance.
Oh, greatly exalted [Tàishàng],
your auspicious blessings come from Heaven.
The calendrical cycle of sixty years began anew,
and propitious omens circulated.
The *bǐngchén* year inaugurated the new cycle,
and a precious mandate was personally received.
Heaven's compassion was silently invoked,
and the ancestral achievements were respectfully upheld.
The initial vow was fulfilled,
not exceeding the previous era.
A prime successor was bestowed,
to greatly carry on the ancestral sacrifices.
On the first day of the first lunar month,
a double radiance auspiciously commenced.
In the grand court, the transmission was enacted,
again bestowing boundless blessings.
Maintaining integrity and adhering to the mean,
the mental transmission was respectfully observed.
Rivaling the merits of [Xùn] and [Huá],
the world ascended to benevolence and longevity.
(Chapter 1) The Sage holds the talisman,
reverently and solemnly attending to affairs.
The majestic [Tài] Altar, so solemn,
fully embodies the rich rituals.
Facing south, he takes his position,
personally undertaking every necessary action.
Praying for a good harvest in the *xīn* month,
and divining with the dragon for rain.
Ascending and descending to the spiritual deities,
with sincere sacrifices and fragrant offerings.
The four seasons are perfectly harmonized,
and all spirits enjoy the offerings.
Rain and sun, cold and heat,
wind and timeliness.
The eight governmental concerns are reverently pondered,
and the nine regions are purely harmonious.
Longevity increases beyond the elder years,

Receiving abundant blessings,
they respond collectively and are numerous.
(Chapter 2) His plans and achievements are gloriously carried on,
the foundation of blessings for ten thousand myriad generations.
Appearing before Heaven,
the fragrant offerings ascend, clearly accepted.
With deep longing, like for a dish of soup,

Rising early, ever vigilant,
the precious records are perused.
Four times visiting the secondary capital,

Recalling the arduous founding,
and the establishment of the nation.
His prestige extended through the arc and arrow,
and civilization was perfected through caps and robes.
Respectfully following former decrees,
diligently, never forgetting.
Succession after succession,
gloriously continuing the inherited rule.
For ten thousand years,
may these blessings be granted.
(Chapter 3) The Sage governs,
managing all myriad affairs.
With utmost sincerity and enduring perseverance,
he is diligent every day.
Reverence is a sign of longevity,
and vigor is the essence of [Qián].
His insight illuminates the eight directions,
and he applies himself diligently throughout the ten *guǐ* (hours).
With crimson brush, he reviews memorials,
and in the vermilion hall, he holds audiences.
He encourages agriculture by personally plowing,
and demonstrates righteousness through imperial tours.
He inspects dikes and dams,
for rivers and seas.
He practices military skills,
and bestows generosity upon border regions, proclaiming joy.
Pure and ceaseless,
thus bestowing great longevity.
Steadfastly preserving peace,
who among past records can compare?
(Chapter 4) The people respond like grass,
the Sage's grace like spring.
The great mechanism silently operates,
the universe is united in benevolence.
Five times exempting adult taxes,
three times remitting grain taxes.
Waiving debts and easing levies,
his grace penetrates deep into the marrow.
He consults on agriculture,
extending its benefits to all territories.
When reports come from remote corners,
great bounties are generously bestowed.
The people's hidden grievances are illuminated,
the best officials are selected.
Prisons are justly reviewed and cases reversed,
reliant on comfort and guidance.
Heaven and Earth cover and sustain,
Sun and Moon illuminate.
Ineffable is the Emperor's power,
truly receiving Heaven's heart.
(Chapter 5) The Sage's plans are far-reaching,
his cultural virtue widely spread.
The Way is exalted like a golden mirror,
its image beautiful like a jade pivot.
Rites are corrected in illustrated books,

The Four Treasuries are arranged,

In lecture halls, theories are expounded,

In the circular bridge, drums are beaten,

Literary compositions number three thousand,

The Milky Way shines with order,

He educates and instructs the people,

Precious timbers like *piánnán* and *méizǐ*,

(Chapter 6) The imperial achievements are glorious and resplendent,
continuing military prowess.
Distant lands bring tribute,
remote barbarians follow his influence.
The [Zhǔn] Department and the [Huí] lands,

Twenty thousand square *yú* of territory,
settlement and cultivation thus initiated.
The [Jīnchuān] region was pacified again,
the [Qióng] and [Bó] tribes razed.
Towering ships awed,
the sea islands were pacified.
[Miǎnmèng] knocked at the passes,
[Jiāonán] reached the imperial court.
[Wèizàng] rested in meditation,

Ten great achievements were proclaimed,
surpassing [Yǔ] and [Tāng].
Stubborn [Miáo] submitted,
continuing the glory of [Zǐguāng].
(Chapter 7) The model of the five blessings,

The auspicious beginning of a hundred million years,

The precious seal
"Ten Complete,"
the hall's inscription
"Four Gains."
The *jiǎzǐ* cycle is explored,
the fundamental origin derived from the *Yì*.
Greatly opening the gate of longevity,

Precious archives are expounded,
magnificent celestial phenomena clearly displayed.
The foundation of virtue,
the accumulation of blessings.
Auspicious documents radiate brilliance,

May your blessings be as ninefold as the [Rú] River,
and extend to the eight directions.
May the double radiance continue to shine,

(Chapter 8) The [Tàishàng] established virtue,
achieving both the "Five Sages" and "Three Sovereigns."
Greatly esteemed, yet yielding,

Plants and animals flourished,

Sons and emperors receive his countenance,

The source of auspiciousness further spreads,

The jade map records its essence,

Pure blessings accumulate,

Gloriously commencing the imperial era,

The cycles of time gather and flourish,

May his sagely lifespan be everlasting,

(Chapter 9) [Qiánlóng] twenty-sixth year,

Great blessings abound like mountains and seas,

(Chapter One) The year is Xīnsì,

(Chapter Eight) Like the rising sun,
like the waxing moon.

(Chapter Ten) Great filial piety is manifest,

(Chapter Nineteen) May the Holy Mother enjoy abundant health and ease,

(Chapter Twenty)
In the thirty-sixth year of Qiánlóng,

All blessings arrive completely,

(Chapter One) In the year of Chóngguāng Màomǎo, the seasons renew,

All the people,

(Chapter Seventeen) Her compassionate countenance is joyful and at ease,

The high ministers held to righteousness,
Angry and wishing to annihilate them.
But the Emperor's virtue favors life,
Saying they should be spared wholesale execution.
Six articles were agreed upon,
Which they piously and fearfully followed.
They reverently received the imperial grace,
The net was loosened, and benevolence was shown.
They greatly reformed their hearts.
Crawling, they rushed to him.
Clearing roads and building altars,
Fragrant clouds enveloped the path.
The Emperor's benevolence spread widely,
Overflowing the six directions.
Reviving the withered and decaying,
Granting them new life.
Indeed, the Mǎn troops,
Completed their task in a month.
How could it be so swift?
It relied on the Imperial strategy.
Divine merits shone brightly,
Heaven and earth were opened wide.
The nine-layered victory plan,
Its brilliance matched the sun and moon.
Engraved on jade,
Recorded in histories.
The grand ceremony was completed,
The music of peace was played.
The great achievement was accomplished,
The celebratory banquet was attended.
Great harmony pervaded,
Filling the universe.
Auspicious clouds intertwined,
Like pearls strung on a thread of constellations.
Tribute ships and precious gifts,
For hundreds of millions of years.
In the twenty-fifth year of Qiánlóng,
The pacification of the Xīyù,
A banquet,
The first chapter of the Déshèng Dance and Music.
Ancestral ambitions were continued and accomplished,
eradicating distant rebels.
Plans were drawn up with composure,
expanding the territory by twenty thousand lǐ.
Rivers and plains were surveyed,
and then administered as fields.
Imperial strategies were profound and far-reaching,
in alignment with Heaven's will.
The Qēlēng (車楞) had internal strife,
begged for grace, and submitted.
They were granted peerages as kings and dukes,
and their dependents were cared for.
The guǐyù (鬼蜮) Àqiú (阿酋)
crawled to the imperial court.
He was favored with a vassalage,
wielding the yue (鉞) and leading expeditions.
Dáwǎqí (達瓦齊) was captured,
but was granted a new life and pardoned.
Mindful of his military service,
he was grandly enfeoffed and promoted.
Àqiú (阿酋), being cunning and deceitful,
would soon face Heaven's punishment.
He vainly hoped for what was not his due,
and rebelled mid-journey.
He was fickle and two-faced,
abandoning his wife and children.
His retainers scattered;
such a great villain deserved this.
Drawing water for ten thousand lǐ,
wishing to extinguish the prairie fire.
Like that mad chieftain,
he needlessly burned himself.
He fled to Éluósī (俄羅斯),
where pestilence claimed his life.
Distant lands respected the king,
and thus offered him at the border.
Mǎnzhōu Suǒlún (滿洲索倫)
crossed the waves and flew over.
Their valor was irresistible,
they ascended steep ridges.
They captured the fugitives,
and seized their livestock.
They took their sons and daughters,
like destroying rotten wood.
Wherever bows and arrows reached,
the enemy strongholds could not resist.
They hastily sought to escape like rabbits,
terrified and helpless.
Ignorant rebel masses,
causing chaos and change.
With imperial virtue nurturing them,
the orphaned and solitary found life.
How could it be said that the army was exhausted?
How could it be said that military might was abused?
Seizing the opportune moment and converging,
how could one bear not to pacify the distant lands?
Those previously imprisoned were released
from their confinement.
As soon as they returned to Kùchē (庫車),
rumors spread.
Only that wicked leader
was incomparably disloyal to his sovereign.
Unmindful of imperial grace,
who could not gnash their teeth?
Once Yīlí (伊犁) was pacified,
all the tribes submitted.
Long-term plans were made in advance,
to gather all the Huízú (回族).
Two villains escaped and fled,
generals were ordered to pursue and intercept them.
They crossed their lairs,
and arrived directly at Bādá (巴達).
Imperial guards were dispatched,
thus their situation was understood.
The Huí (回) chieftain bowed his head and knocked it,
offering the heads of his enemies and showing sincerity.
Records from the distant past cannot be traced,
but historical annals are all there.
Such annihilation of bandits
has never had an equal.
The zhānqiāng (欃槍) was completely swept away,
the world ascended to peace.
The army was dispatched justly,
and the inner and outer lands were eternally purified.
The emperor's wisdom and sincerity,
worked tirelessly day and night.
Achieving great accomplishments,
the sacred heart was pleased.
Those who follow me prosper,
those who oppose me perish.
Fearing neglect in distinguishing,
Heaven's words are clearly manifest.
Rewards and enfeoffments were granted for meritorious service,
bravery was recognized and names conferred.
These great rewards were brightly proclaimed,
their splendor made manifest.
The chief villains were eliminated,
and great success was achieved.
Like spring nurturing all things,
virtue accords with purity and tranquility.
In the eighth year of Dàoguāng (道光),
Huíjiāng (回疆) was pacified again.
At the banquet,
Dèshèng Wǔyuè Èrshízhāng (德勝舞樂二十章).
In the sacred reign of Dàoguāng (道光),
virtue spread throughout the vast world.
Tributes and gifts were offered,
with reverence and devotion.
(Chapter 1) These foolish Huí (回) rebels,
petty scoundrels evading punishment.
Hidden in remote wildernesses,
daring to be the leaders of war.
(Chapter 2) Like a herd,
their malicious aura spread.
Crossing passes and secretly instigating,
they did not restrain themselves and burned.
(Chapter 3) The Emperor, majestically enraged,
commanded the display of might.
Go forth and suppress the rebellion,
capture them and return.
(Chapter 4) At Húnbāshí Hé (渾巴什河),
our reputation was first established.
Then Kēpíng (柯坪) was annihilated,
leaving no remnants.
(Chapter 5) At Shāgǎng (沙崗),
our troops attacked.
The three villages were swept clean of their lairs,
success achieved in ten days.
(Chapter 6) After a month of success,
the four cities were swiftly recovered.
The Bókè (伯克) knelt in welcome,
praising the divine speed.
(Chapter 7) No red without fox,
no black without crow.
Wherever the bow-star pointed,
they all bowed to their guilt.
(Chapter 8) The Emperor grieved for the eight cities,
and remitted their taxes.
The aged celebrated joyfully,
like sweet rain from the nine heavens.
(Chapter 9) Oh, how brilliant are the imperial plans,
ten articles widely promulgated.
The criminals must be apprehended,
let them not delay punishment.
(Chapter 10) Let no punishment be delayed,
let no expeditionary force wait.
Return victoriously in sequence,
to rest from their toil.
(Chapter 11) The four mountains vast,
scouts circled them.
Where the ominous birds flew,
court bows were drawn.
(Chapter 12) The year was at an end,
the masses eagerly marched.
With staves they beat the bandits,
at Ātúshén Zhuāng (阿圖什莊).
(Chapter 13) We pursued, they fled,
from dusk till dawn.
Reaching Tiěgài Shān (鐵蓋山),
their escape route was suddenly cut off.
(Chapter 14) Then they lost their horses,
then they dragged their soldiers.
Their short blades were seized,
and they were bound with long ropes.
(Chapter 15) City willows first sprouted,
relay riders galloped.
City dwellers lined the roads,
gazing at the red flags from afar.
(Chapter 16) Bows were put away, sashes bestowed,
reported to Heaven and ancestors.
Returning to the benevolent Empress Dowager,
who greatly received blessings.
(Chapter 17) Stone tablets were erected to record the events,
captives received at the imperial gate.
A joyful banquet was initiated,
dew-drenched and cloud-needing.
(Chapter 18) The fine wine was excellent,
the dance troupe entered to assist.
Both young and old bowed their heads,
May our Emperor live for ten thousand years!
(Chapter 19) Imperial might is glorious,
imperial grace is long-lasting.
Satiated with benevolence and righteousness,
may he live for ten thousand years without bounds!
(Chapter 20)
Dàyàn Jiāchuī Yuè Liùshíqīzhāng (大宴笳吹樂六十七章) (established in the seventh year of Qiánlóng (乾隆)).
Mùmǎ Gē (牧馬歌) The joy of the sovereign,
relies on this discipline.
The joy of the myriad people,
relies on our monarch.
Families are well-ordered,
by the strength of the husband.
Friends are successful,
by the virtue of harmony and unity.
Ancient Song: The eight kinds of formation and destruction,
are truly the norm of the human world.
Fallen into the net of delusion,
bound by the lock of desire and the reins of emotion.
Foolish people without knowledge,
rejoice in this unending splendor.
Clinging to emptiness as existence,
how can their fallacious words be fitting?
Rúyì Bǎo: Not cleansing the mind with the sūtras,
possessing original nature yet ignorant.
Not embracing the Buddhayāna,
preaching wondrous practices, yet listening confusedly.
Auspicious Sign: One leader emerges,
all nations honor and cherish him.
Profound grace, vast and overflowing,
universally benefits the common people.
A hundred flowers bloom gloriously,
delighting the eye for a day.
Abhiṣeka’s precious light,
subdues all multitudes.
Sincerely Moved Words: How truly awe-inspiring!
Accomplishing with utmost sincerity.
How truly surpassing!
Exhausting one's abilities.
How truly genuine!
Words without embellishment.
How truly diligent!
Never daring to rest.
Chapter of Auspicious Celebrations: There is a ruler, sagacious and enlightened, surpassing Dài Tiān;
there are ministers, respectful and diligent, surpassing descendants.
A capable wife manages the household better than a man;
the Rúyì treasure pearl is found only in a filial son.
Chanting of the Resemblers: Eliminate one's own sins,
relying on the Buddha's true words.
If one wishes to cure illness,
only good medicine exists.
The Bodhi lamp,
leads sentient beings out of darkness;
the wisdom comb,
combs through the entanglements of the six desires.
Jūn Mǎ Huáng: The water of the great sea is immeasurable,
how can the treasures of the heavenly storehouse ever cease?
Harmonious good friends are infinitely beneficial,
the sagely ones' counsel and teachings are boundless.
Chant of Lofty Virtue: When the ruler is benevolent,
he is the father of the multitude.
When the noble person is peaceful,
all follow and attach themselves.
How excellent is that wise person,
who truly serves as a teacher.
Hiding wisdom and harboring selfishness,
is truly a bane to the people.
Well Done Song: Only peace and harmony,
are what the mind desires.
Without doubt or apprehension,
friends are blessed.
Song of the Land of Joy: To share wealth with others,
is the greatest kindness.
To bestow wisdom upon others,
is surely even greater.
Tà Yáo Niáng: The sun is about to rise,
the morning star shines brilliantly.
Longevity is indicated by this,
his eyebrows are prominent and auspicious.
Thirty is strong,
fifty is late twilight.
None are closer than the grandmother,
none are more revered than the grandfather.
Eulogy and Prayer: My horse prances lightly,
moving like flowing water.
Outstanding talents fill the seats,
friends and kin rejoice with pleasure.
Clans and in-laws,
are all rich and noble.
Pouring wine for joy,
it is both abundant and delicious.
Slow Song: Fifteen for joy and eighty for decline,
youthful looks and flourishing beauty turn to sadness in late twilight,
grandmother is dearest, grandfather is most revered.
Táng Gōngzhǔ: Following the king's path,
faults and errors are rare.
Acting according to one's station,
why then doubt?
Song of Sincere Devotion: Nothing fails,
when following the Way.
Long without separation,
in accordance with parental affection.
Míngguāng Qǔ: Behold the sun and moon,
emitting light in the empty sky.
Sagely ruler and sagely mother,
shining brilliantly, worshipped by tens of thousands.
Jíxiáng Shī: The brightness of the sun and moon,
will surely illuminate with glory.
The brightness of the sagely ruler,
reaches all the multitude.
Sagely and Enlightened Times: Encountering sagely and enlightened times,
truly is my blessing.
Grace and favor universally bestowed,
truly is my good fortune.
Subtle Words: Sudden changes and transformations,
follow their natural course.
Like that mirage,
my remaining life is fleeting.
During Auspicious Peace: Commit no evil deeds,
Bodhisattvas.
Acting recklessly in darkness and delusion,
leads to falling into the three evil paths.
Song of Good Governance: What is the origin of the sūtras?
Their origin is the宗 (Zōng).
What is the origin of the body?
Grandmother and grandfather.
What is the origin of sin?
Burning anger.
What is the origin of blessing?
Harmony and peace.
Words of Longevity: No words are unsuitable for the Way,
like ten thousand streams flowing to the ocean.
Only the deluded words of external paths,
draw their own well and remain unconnected.
Yǎotiǎo Niáng: The timid wild beast,
desires to preserve its body.
The diligent common people,
desire to protect their descendants.
Zànlù: Those foolish people,
only know their own bodies.
These wise people,
their hearts encompass all people.
Chant of the Four Sages: The six desires entwine,
making one cling to this fleeting life.
Alas, like a fleeting glimpse of a white colt,
it is like a dream, like lightning.
Hè Shèngcháo: Compassion and skillful means,
forever cut off doubt and attachment.
The Pure Land of Ultimate Bliss,
neither perishes nor is born.
Yīngliú Xíng: To act knowingly,
is how the wise and enlightened proceed.
To act unknowingly,
is the company of the foolish and ignorant.
To act after deliberation,
is the mark of the extraordinary pioneer;
to act impulsively and recklessly,
is truly of the lowest sort.
Jiāngù Zǐ: The horse prances lightly,
the body cannot find peace.
Reflecting on this body,
it is inherently impermanent.
The horse gallops vigorously,
life cannot find tranquility.
Reflecting on this life,
it is inherently unborn.
Yuè Yuán: The virtue of a good horse,
can be verified in the field.
The conduct of good friends,
is revealed through interaction.
Huǎn Gē: What is a good horse?
It is what the rider thinks of.
What are good friends?
Those respected over time.
Zìchún Cí: Only the Emperor's power,
can summon and pacify; the parents' power, can free from worry.
Riding a splendid steed, galloping forth,
relying on a mighty hero to draw the bow.
Měi Fēngjūn: Arrogance and self-aggrandizement,
are truly not benevolent.
Hoarding wealth for oneself,
will not last long, it will be divided into four.
Only those who are not discerning,
are not cautious and fearful.
Malicious thoughts constantly sprout,
who can live with them?
Shàonián Xíng: Alas, abandoned in the caves,
why not spread one's fragrant reputation afar?
Alas, growing old in the wilderness,
why not forever leave behind a good name?
Chant of the Four Heavenly Kings: Alas for Běi Máng,
whose renown is proclaimed.
Běi Máng, alas,
whose green annals remain unchanged.
Wǎnzhuǎn Cí: Gaze at that central forest,
luxuriant with ten thousand trees.
Sandalwood has fragrance,
born uniquely.
All beings are like this,
bustling and numerous.
The parents of the people,
one person stands out as the head.
Tiělí: Flying and soaring,
relying solely on wings.
Becoming sound and rhythm,
relying solely on the mind as the guide.
To hit the target when shooting,
relying solely on the finger.
To interact well,
harmony is constant.
Mùpòzhū. A chick forms from an embryo,
the merit of incubation and transformation.
Feathers are used as a ceremony,
the abundance of bestowed life.
To guide those who are ignorant and unenlightened,
is solely the merit of the Sages.
To clarify one's fundamental nature,
it truly lies within oneself.
Hǎohéqǔ. Diligent and wise,
how can one not be cherished?
Indulging in this small pleasure,
supreme joy is hard to attain.
Zhāngfù. Heaven's light shines impartially,
the Sages' teachings are without distinction.
Their counsels and instructions are vast,
mirroring this without obscurity.
Tiānmǎyín. Qíjì horses do not flock with lame donkeys,
wild geese do not associate with sparrows.
Zōuyú beasts do not approach foxes,
Sages and wise ones do not befriend the ignorant and lowly.
Dàlóngmǎyín. Who knows this illusory body,
yet keeps this Buddha nature secret?
Who does not regress,
when Buddha's grace comes to bear witness?
The virtuous may fall,
who knows their ailment?
The lowest may suddenly rise,
who knows their competition?
Shǐtiáolǐ. Blessings and wisdom, naturally bestowed by Heaven,
truly hard to encounter.
Perceptive and accomplished people,
how can they be easily met?
Zhuīfēngzhěmǎ. Lush and verdant,
the mountain has fragrant orchids.
Bright and splendid,
the head has a beautiful topknot.
Huíbōcí. The wise sovereign is truly outstanding,
the excellent ministers are rarely matched.
Worthy ones assist the royal house,
let no one cling to perverse ways like pests.
Chángyù. Let noble conduct be followed,
the common people are worthy of pity.
One should widely love the multitude,
and not defy loyal words.
Píngdiào. Qíjì horses suit my physique,
bow case and quiver guard my body.
Good words serve my path,
classics and histories nourish my heart.
Yóuzǐyín. Ascending that high mound,
I think of my old home.
I cherish two people,
who do not leave the door of the hall.
Climbing that towering peak,
I think of my old home.
I cherish two people,
who do not leave the walls.
Píngdiàoqǔ. If emperors are not idle,
Heaven and Earth will be harmonious and peaceful.
If princes are diligent and quick,
the multitude of people will prosper and thrive.
Gāoshìyín. When the sun rises,
Heaven is the constant.
When people act,
the ruler is the standard.
When water flows,
it follows hollows and fills them.
When mares roam,
it is the nature of colts.
Zāishēngmíng. Not coveting wealth and bribes,
but moved by the respectful hearts of brothers.
Not greedy for food and drink,
but moved by the sincere devotion of elders.
Gāozāixíng. How to achieve great peace?
Gazing reverently at the imperial road.
What is constant in human life?
Carefully preserve this precious body.
What the people cannot forget,
is a good name shining over the divine realm.
Descendants flourishing continuously,
hundreds of millions and more.
Sānzhāng. Revere the Buddha's command,
like the nourishing sweet rain.
Do not commit evil deeds,
sowing the seeds of suffering.
Yuányīn. The body is impermanent,
like flowers in autumn.
Fame is impermanent,
like thunder that does not linger.
Wealth is impermanent,
like bees brewing honey;
Water is impermanent,
like the sea producing foam.
Lángān. The worthy admire the worthy,
the unworthy do not admire the worthy.
Bees stop when they see flowers,
dragonflies fly away gracefully.
Sīzāixíng. A thousand pieces of gold or a precious horse,
are not as good as what ancestors bequeathed.
Having tasted all fruits,
is not as sweet as mother's milk.
Fǎzuòyǐn. Lightning is fearsome,
as the time of bright summer arrives.
Frost is fearsome,
as the five grains are about to be harvested.
Calamity is fearsome,
born of joy.
Is there anything not fearsome?
Remembering the first descent of the soul.
Jiēyǐncí. The burning house has no coolness,
the path of suffering has no joy.
Who can carry one on the bird's path?
Jānbufú is hard to set foot on.
Huàdǎocí. The realm of Jānbufútí,
is like that high mountain,
difficult to cross.
When this present time is gone,
the vast ocean stretches endlessly,
truly hard to cross.
Qībǎo'ān. Look at that embankment,
the water will not overflow.
When a ruler shepherds the people,
there will be no dispersal.
Though the flying bird is tired,
it would rather not fall to the ground.
A noble man is steadfast in poverty,
to death he does not waver.
Duǎngē. Alas, the joys of my life,
are like the waxing and waning of the Yellow Oriole.
I feel the swift passage of beautiful time,
like the green color on leaves.
When youth is in its prime,
let us rejoice and prolong the day.
Xīzhào. Time, oh time,
beyond time there is no time.
When time has passed,
what joy is there to have?
When the Yellow Oriole has set,
there will surely be little warmth.
When the light of day has dimmed,
it will be gloomy and dark.
Guīguóyáo. Oh, the glorious and sacred era,
abundant like a benevolent ruler.
Cherished, oh cherished,
day by day more distant, more divided.
There are also good friends,
like brothers and sisters.
Day by day more distant, more separated,
unable to reach out remotely.
Sēngbǎoyín. Sincerely commit and take refuge,
then one is safe and auspicious.
Like the Buddha's pagodas and temples,
why then be far apart?
Harmonious and joyful, indulging in it,
hands and feet supporting each other.
Like elder and younger sisters,
why then be far apart?
Póluóményǐn. Ghee must become clarified butter,
father will become grandfather.
Sand must become a mound,
mother will become an old woman.
Sānbùluò. Try to observe the Three Realms,
bubbles rise and bubbles burst.
Like autumn clouds,
suddenly rising, suddenly vanishing.
Wǔbùluò. How swiftly the flowing water rushes,
my life is like this journey.
Though there are Sages and virtuous people,
who can linger for a little while?
In the 25th year of Qiánlóng,
the Western Regions were pacified,
a banquet was held,
a chapter of music was played on the horn.
The Chánghé gate is resplendent,
Bells and chimes resound.
Cracking whips enforce reverence,
The Emperor thus enjoys peace and comfort.
Blessed by Heaven's pure grace,
Ancestral virtue accumulates blessings.
Calmly and steadily settling the realm,
Truly ascending to grand governance.
The Sagely virtue extensively spreads,
Its brilliance reaching far and near.
Like stars circling the North Star,
All tribes gather and cease resistance.
Benevolent grace covers and protects,
Vast as the boundless ocean.
Vying to pledge allegiance,
Rushing to pay homage.
Laws and institutions are fully prepared,
Victorious plans are accomplished.
The unruly hordes of villains,
File in to offer sincerity.
Heaven's might trembles them,
Minor potentates are awestruck and vigilant.
The great sovereign is solely benevolent,
None do not become subjects.
The Sagely teachings extensively spread,
Touching hearts and minds with bowed heads.
Yuèkū shares the same customs,
Surpassing ancient and modern times.
Distant strategies are in accord,
Remote regions are at peace and well.
The virtue of pacification and appeasement,
Spreads to distant wildernesses.
The great creative power's achievements are immense,
Abundantly moistening the entire earth.
Lofty and magnificent virtue,
Lasts for millions of years.
In the eighth year of Dàoguāng,
Huíjiāng was pacified again.
At the banquet,
Kājī pipes played the Jiǔzhāng music.
How glorious is the imperial might,
Manifest throughout the nine domains.
Huíjiāng is now settled,
Drinking to celebrate the victorious return.
(Chapter One) Huíjiāng is completely controlled,
Pacified by the pure Emperor.
Fearing the divine and obeying the teachings,
Solidifying our frontier.
(Chapter Two) These foolish rebellious descendants,
Escaped punishment for two generations.
Setting themselves ablaze like a prairie fire,
The law cannot be lenient.
(Chapter Three) War chariots advanced westward,
Like clouds and rainbows.
Three victories in one month,
The four cities awaited them.
(Chapter Four) The four cities are now pacified,
The villainous factions are eradicated.
Bows drawn and [missing character] stretched,
How could the evil birds remain?
(Chapter Five) The Hui hamlets were near,
Where owls gathered.
Tracking them down, pursuing relentlessly,
The iron stronghold was greatly imposing.
(Chapter Six) Bound with white sashes,
Reported with red flags.
New year brings joy,
The imperial heart is filled with delight.
(Chapter Seven) In the past, we sang of chariots departing,
Now we sing of gathering ferns.
Receiving blessings from the heavenly ancestor,
Returning good to the benevolent Empress's chambers.
(Chapter Eight) Auspicious offerings are truly appropriate,
Extensive indeed is the bestowed grace.
Holding up the wine cup and bowing,
May His Majesty live for ten thousand years.

Dàhéqǔ: Following the great foundation,
Revering the enlightened spirits.
With a single, utmost sincerity,
Diligently serving the divine.
Lofty and majestic great sovereign,
Forever establishing the common people.
Cherishing and supporting with all hearts,
Bowing their heads, they come as subjects.
Considering the impermanence of human life,
It is proper to diligently cultivate good deeds.
Truly, when all actions are good,
There will be peace in the end, and the spirits will hear.
Rǎnsīqǔ: The great sovereign is most sagely,
His teachings spread across the land.
Bringing peace and order to all nations,
They kneel and serve the Lord.
Gōngmò: Greatly manifest is the venerable Empress,
Her benevolence embraces all regions.
The nation's talents respectfully assist,
Collaborating to uphold the nation's norms.
People from all corners of the land,
Their sincerity widely extends.
All bow their heads in reverence,
Relying on and upholding the sagely Emperor.
Yǎzhèngcí: Illustrious and sagely enlightened,
No distance is beyond his illumination.
Multitudes of common people,
No thought of disobedience.
Primal transformation with a benevolent heart,
Doing good and eradicating evil.
In the land of the Sage,
There is long life and eternal joy.

spreading widely,
the king's carriage sounds with clanging.
Wine, sweet wine, and reed instruments,
drinking from Yáo's goblet,
singing of Shùn's land.
(Seventh Verse) With ease and rest,
leading to tranquility and nourishment,
yellow-robed children and white-haired elders look up with joy,
the voice of education reaches distant lands.
Truly fragrant,
various scents waft,
all eight steeds are well-trained.
Brocade spreads out,
unifying chariots and scripts,
standardizing measures.
Unifying chariots and scripts,
standardizing measures.
(Eighth Verse) The imperial tour and sagely writings come from the heavens,
spreading benevolence,
waves of grace ripple forth.
Joyfully encountering the enlightened and good,
harmonious sounds echo and blend.
(Ninth Verse)
His sagacious plans were uniquely executed, achieving martial success;
At the western peak of Tiānzhù, eternal peace was proclaimed.
Observing the moon and divining the wind has been passed down since ancient times;
Listen now to the sound of today's victory song.
(Poem 1) In previous years, the army returned from Yīlí,
With a renowned king brought captive in humble bonds.
To the west of heaven, the lunar constellations all bowed like stars;
The barbarians' realm opened remotely from Mèigǔ.
(Poem 2) Both younger and elder brothers, in desperate straits,
Two Huāmén were long imprisoned in the barbarian court.
Suddenly, the imperial army descended from the nine heavens,
First granting the grace of rebirth by breaking their chains.
(Poem 3) They were bestowed permission to return to their old units, with much honor and grace,
Tasked with pacifying the remaining barbarians, freeing them from the net.
May the Qílián Shān be used as a whetstone,
And may Púlièi Hǎi not stir up waves.
(Poem 4) How could it be that the hawk-eyed ones ultimately defied transformation,
Instead unleashing owl-like cries, inciting rebellious dust?
The northern grasses equally received the dew from heaven,
While the yellow sands alone betrayed the spring of the frontier.
(Poem 5) The vast net of heaven was originally wide,
But the utterly wicked must be eradicated.
Day and night, calmly, a grand strategy was devised,
A detached force was again dispatched to seize the cruel ones.
(Poem 6) Ladders and battering rams fiercely assailed Kùchē's walls,
The fleeing rebels, in panic, indeed fled back.
Who knew the surrendering people vied to offer allegiance,
While a few stray souls luckily escaped the ruined nest.
(Poem 7) The tiger tally conveyed the decree from the cinnabar clouds,
The battlements and banners shone brightly in a single morning.
Suddenly, the Three Gates took on a new appearance,
And the Grand Marshal was again appointed Huò Piáoyáo.
(Poem 8) One army quickly secured Shāyǎ'ěr,
And soon captured all of Ākèsū.
Thousands of miles, swift as wind, swept like lightning,
The great army directly pressed upon the isolated enemy city.
(Poem 9) Like ants gathering and bees swarming for three months,
Like bears crouching and tigers lurking, each worth a thousand.
The army's might, like mountains, was inherently unshakable,
The vile sort vainly taught their spears to turn back.
(Poem 10) No need for provisions to be packed for the journey,
Gladly, supplies were already found in the enemy city.
Why marvel at the miraculous rain of grain?
The earth left "fire-rice" awaiting the divine army.
(Poem 11) How could heavenly nectar be scooped to fill the Big Dipper,
In the vast land-sea of Shuōlè Chéng?
Suddenly, it was reported that a wondrous spring appeared as wells were cleared,
The entire camp sang and danced, bowing to the King's enlightenment.
(Poem 12) Flying squirrels knew their tricks were exhausted,
Cannons flying through the forest echoed with the wind.
Lead pellets were picked up and then used to annihilate the rebels,
Indeed, assisting the Heavenly Court's fire attack.
(Poem 13) Ten thousand cavalry descended from the sky,
Chasing the wind, they had already passed Fúyún Duī.
The alternating soldiers aligned with divine strategy,
Exactly like a surprise army, they captured the fort and returned.
(Poem 14) Six cities, like lips and teeth, guarded Hétián,
Overnight, surrender flags were passed from fort to fort.
What harm if five li confused Zhuōyě,
Turning to ride the dense fog to pacify the wolf smoke.
(Poem 15) All the barbarians followed the order like the wind,
Their allied tribes, hand in hand, bowed together.
Their Huízì tables were presented through multiple interpreters,
Joyfully becoming subjects, conversing through translators.
(Poem 16) As embroidered banners unfurled, the sharp army divided,
The Gēbì desert's wind and sand gathered the evening clouds.
In the middle of the night, the enemy camp was collectively terrified,
Startled by generals descending from the heavens.
(Poem 17) Attacking from front and back with combined strength,
Their claws and teeth entirely blunted, how could they escape?
The heavenly wind scattered their ant-like formation,
Hiding in holes, like prisoners in a jail.
(Poem 18) Yèěrqímù's gate was wide open,
Hāshíhā'ěr city stood majestic.
The scenery here was unknown in ancient times,
Now, only the heavenly army comes.
(Poem 19) Heads bowed along the path to welcome the banners,
The dry marsh had long scorched with stirring sand.
Most wondrous was the transformation by the divine,
The Rain Master now also greeted the imperial army.
(Poem 20) Long rumored, women and children looked to the clouds like rain,
Now hearing cheers responding to drums and gongs.
Kneeling, they offered carved trays, vying to present fruits,
Grapes and蒟jiǔ醬jiàng could not compare.
(Poem 21) How fortunate these distant lands to be under the堯Yáo heaven,
From now on, their cities will be bustling markets.
Light taxes only for alfalfa,
The same written script first used to exchange money.
(Poem 22) The strong army divided its paths to attack Dāohuán,
Battling for days, the plants and trees became lush.
Pursuing relentlessly into the night, sounds and shadows vanished,
On the mountaintop, the bright moon was a bent bow.
(Poem 23) Tens of thousands vied to advance, the enemy's morale crumbled,
Cheers from mid-sky brought down the circling eagles.
Even now, people passing Yīxīěr,
Still feel the thunder shaking the azure sky.
(Poem 24) The universe was known of old to have a direction,
Now terrified by the irresistible divine spear.
Every head bowed in submission,
At night, the watch drums were silent.
(Poem 25) Generals joined the formation, flying feathered arrows,
Brave warriors in the heat of battle wielded decorated halberds.
The surrendering barbarians, receiving orders, were like hawks and hounds,
Could the逃táo flee and escape before the mountain?
(Poem 26) Their remnants temporarily preserved in Qínà'ěr,
Their cunning lair in Bùhái was hard to find.
The white magpie banner flew high, carrying the rebel's head,
The imperial envoy personally presented the victorious dispatch.
(Poem 27) Flea-like lungs and dung beetle arms could not sustain themselves,
With kin estranged and followers defecting, where could they go?
Light swords cut through formations, crushing light cavalry,
Again reported, scattered and bearing the bodies of the fallen.
(Poem 28) The victorious dispatch, swift as a star, came from distant lands,
In the imperial garden, the clouds and things showed early signs of spring.
Before the reed ashes stirred, spring arrived,
Auspicious flowers vied to bloom, shining in all directions.
(Poem 29) The joyful news reached the imperial women's quarters, where the day was long,
Together enjoying the empress's blessings and the prosperity of the times.
Respectfully praising the martial achievements and boundless longevity,
And all gazing upon the light of the sun and moon.
(Poem 30) Mountains and rivers vied to tell of the regional records,
Customs and traditions vied to circulate the Royal Gathering Map.
On this day, the western frontier extended over twenty thousand li,
Kūnlún still remained in the eastern corner.
(Poem 31) The joyous land of Mòjiālè was once boasted of,
How could it be that they became frogs in a well?
From then on, the Western Regions increased in joyful color,
Truly teaching that the land belonged to the heavenly family.
(Poem 32) As the rising sun dawned, the primal images opened,
The eight directions and seven celestial bodies were on the jade platform.
Lǔsīnàmò knew to respectfully obey,
Coming together to the Míng steps to offer respects at the new moon.
(Poem 33) Ten thousand ancient ice mountains and snowy peaks were at leisure,
All were taught to present tribute and join the court assembly.
Where were the plum blossoms' spring wind flutes?
A bamboo channel connected to Yùguān.
(Poem 34) The merit of presenting severed heads was recorded in the academy,
And imperial writings were carved on distant mountain peaks.
Just look, the Milky Way illuminated inside and outside,
Every character the heart of the two classics of Táng and Yú.
(Poem 35) When success was achieved, the divine imperial strategy was admired,
Measuring the sea and touching the disk, the truth was not yet fully seen.
Lofty discussions illuminated and awakened the ignorant,
All admired the ultimate principles that distinguished heaven and man.
(Poem 36) Jade tablets and ritual discs were displayed at the sacred altar, heavenly gifts,
Jade scepters and badges announced the grand plan in the pure temple.
The glorious grand ceremony, with all offering blessings,
The emperor's heart was solemn, naturally accumulating auspiciousness.
(Poem 37) The sun shone, the wind was warm, the phoenix tower was open,
In the nine heavens, cinnabar decrees and auspicious clouds floated.
The pervasive dew covered the land, bestowing widespread grace,
Amidst the sounds of victory, benevolent favor flowed.
(Poem 38) His splendid achievements all stemmed from his sagacious decisions,
Even the deeds of the Three Sovereigns and Five Emperors are hard to name.
Now, a short whip collects lands beyond the heavens,
The seasonal calendar merely shows the fifth watch.
(Poem 39) Feathers danced, bows were cased, the six armies rested,
Merit was celebrated, and banquets held, bowing before the imperial steps.
This humble subject wishes to compose a fife melody,
Ashamed to hold a brush without the words for the Zhu Lù.
(Poem 40)
In the 41st year of Qiánlóng,
The pacification of Jīnchuān,
Thirty victory songs composed by Emperor Gāozōng.
On the 24th of the Mid-Autumn Festival night, at the hour of Chǒu (1-3 AM),
a red banner was delivered to the Mùlán camp.
I was already awake, awaiting military dispatches,
who would have thought I would witness this tonight?
(Poem 1) Seven thousand *lǐ* (li) away, the road is long and arduous;
from over ten days, now eight days.
It is evident that all hearts share a single will;
how excellent that the rewards for their actions are clearly shown.
(Poem 2) The most important rebel stronghold is Lèwéi,
along with Xiǎolián and Gálàyī.
The momentum to break them like bamboo is formed, it should be within days;
may the swift delivery of the victory news be without hindrance.
(Poem 3) Why the clamor in the temporary camp in the middle of the night?
It is the red banner arriving at the gate.
Five years of diligent effort, shared by those above and below,
great achievements collectively bathed in heavenly grace.
(Poem 4) A single red lantern guiding the red banner,
in an instant, everyone in the temporary camp knew.
Old departments and new vassals all congratulated;
when has a victory report ever been like this in ancient times?
(Poem 5) A promise was made to my sons concerning their journey;
upon seeing the red banner, immediately a memorial was presented.
Although my compassionate heart already knew of the joy,
I further dispatched imperial guards to report to Shānzhuāng.
(Poem 6) A rebel stronghold was broken, and a flying cavalry rode;
there was no time to explain all the details.
The generals who exerted their strength should be generously rewarded;
first showing this harbinger of success, adding encouragement is appropriate.
(Poem 7) The previous surrender was merely to cease hostilities;
this time, the victory report is a sweeping clear-out.
Receiving heaven's favor with reverence, how can I not be comforted?
But until the military campaign is fully accomplished, my heart cannot rest.
(Poem 8) Burning the midnight oil is my rightful duty;
joyful and sleepless, how can I sleep?
Thus, I know that the matter of *jīchǐ* (clogs worn by Xie An) truly exists;
compared to that, the disparity in importance is vast.
(Poem 9) Three victories anticipated within a month;
at this time, military affairs are precisely related.
Capturing them and sweeping their lairs, singing of Qídìng's (Qi Ding) success;
I await their triumphant return to Jiāotái.
(Poem 10) In the *jiǎwǔ* year, I paused my imperial progress at Táohuā Sì (Tao Hua Si);
military dispatches were right here, looking down from the window.
How fortunate that today I am still in this place,
a single star flying amidst the green willows.
(Poem 11) Lèwéi reported victory in the temporary camp at night,
coinciding with the return journey from the imperial mausoleum during the day.
In an instant, ten thousand people all showed joy;
may the light of the sun and moon forever eliminate warfare.
(Poem 12) The three strongholds still linger for over a month;
how can the six armies, fighting bravely, spare them?
Where firearms intensely attack all around,
the paltry fish at the bottom of the pot will soon be rotten.
(Poem 13) From over ten days, it arrived in eight days via relay stations;
a single red banner, ten thousand horses flying.
The various tribes lining the road were both joyful and fearful;
it is the nation's celebration, and the nation's might.
(Poem 14) Dangerous mountains and rivers pacified the evil villains;
the deep-rooted cunning traps utterly destroyed.
From now on, all tribal territories will be at peace;
bullying and deceit will cease from this point.
(Poem 15) Cáncóng's (Cancong) extremely perilous hidden evil atmosphere,
a hundred battles achieved success, unheard of in ancient times.
With *dōngdōng* (dong dong) drumbeats, the sound of triumph is presented;
the Qiāng (Qiang) children bow their heads, seeing off the general.
(Poem 16) Numerous strongholds stand like forests in ten thousand mountains,
breaking through perils and charging, enduring all hardships.
The achievements all rely on the strength of the army and generals;
a single red banner enters Táoguān (Tao Guan).
(Poem 17) Jiāng Wéi's (Jiang Wei) conquest area was called Wéizhōu (Weizhou);
the envious barbarians left behind their ballads.
Today, Lèwéi becomes an internal territory;
Wúyōu Chéng (Wuyou Cheng) is truly without worry.
(Poem 18) I waited for victory through winter and into spring;
just as it was about to be completed, I felt frequent anxiety.
Tonight, I can finally rest assured;
tomorrow, I will inform the military commanders to be cautious.
(Poem 19) Today, the rebel nests are overturned,
Qídìng (Qi Ding) can now cease warfare.
Do not let the triumphal songs be heard too easily,
for five years of effort are fortunately accomplished in one day.
(Poem 20) Jiāotái (Jiao Tai) is still this Jiāotái;
how fortunate to have such a grand event again after rebuilding.
Do not say that several years have passed with separation;
my spirit is infused as if accompanied daily.
(Poem 21) Meritorious ministers lead the bowing before the spiritual banners;
soldiers blow conch shells, displaying mighty military bearing.
Music plays, battle songs are sung, they come forward to pay homage;
the family law of punishing barbarians will endure for ten thousand years.
(Poem 22) In the *jǐsì* year, the army returned from a surrender;
in the *gēngchén* year, the imperial suburban sacrifice was grand.
To let cattle return to the pastures and horses return to the fields was my original aspiration;
how could I expect to see two such triumphs?
(Poem 23) Five years to pacify the Zhuňbù (Zhunbu) and return to the city;
the small bandits of Jīnchuān (Jinchuan) are similar to before.
I commend my officers and soldiers for their long-standing animosity towards the enemy;
I cannot but feel increased compassion for them.
(Poem 24) The perilous terrain, coupled with the firm resolve of the multitude,
forest strongholds, step by step, they battled forward.
It was more difficult than past events by many times;
my comfort constantly stems from the resolve.
(Poem 25) They dug tunnels to live in and avoid firearms,
finally, they came out of the barbarian city with hands bound.
Greedy for life like ants, they are indeed so;
was their word sincere, when gathering their clan to be burnt?
(Poem 26) They toiled for five springs and autumns;
the treacherous plank roads seemed like smooth postal routes.
Along the road, red flowers and green willows;
who would regret seeking a marquisate?
(Poem 27) Taking off their military attire, they put on auspicious robes;
imperial commendations and special rare graces.
With one heart, they exerted their efforts and achieved the greatest;
then the imperial stable was opened, granting six flying horses.
(Poem 28) Jīnchuān (Jinchuan) cleansed of war, never again to have trouble;
what became of the arrogant ones in the shallow pond?
Near and far, Lángxiāng (Langxiang) has many common people;
all came joyfully to hear the triumphal song.
(Poem 29) How could the triumphal song be easily heard?
Five years of arduous toil for all the armies.
I myself never rested at midnight,
sharing so many worries with them.
(Poem 30)
In the 55th year of Qiánlóng,
when Gāozōng reached his eightieth year,
Péng Yuánruì (彭元瑞), Minister of Personnel, compiled imperial poems into three hundred chapters of the Wànshòu Qúgē (萬壽衢歌).
When the emperor returned to the palace from Yuánmíngyuán (圓明園),
he presented them as a prelude.
And with pacification within and suppression without,
order established and merits achieved,
ministers also frequently presented memorialized works.
In the 20th year of Kāngxī,
Yè Fāng'ǎi (葉方藹) presented Huángyǎ (皇雅),
namely "Jīngqiū Shí'èrzhāng" (涇丘十二章),
eulogizing the acceptance of surrender;
namely "Guānlǒng Shí'èrzhāng" (關隴十二章),
for pacifying Lǒngyòu (隴右);
namely "Nánjì Shíyīzhāng" (南紀十一章),
for pacifying Mǐn (閩);
namely "Jùjìn Shíyīzhāng" (巨浸十一章),
for pacifying sea pirates.
Xú Jiāyán (徐嘉炎) presented Ráo Gē Gǔchuī Qǔ (鐃歌鼓吹曲),
namely "Shènghuáng Chū" (聖皇出),
signifying the emperor receiving the Mandate;
"Liáoshuǐ Diàn" (遼水奠),
for pacifying the Cháhār (察哈爾) rebellion;
"Ān Lǒngyòu" (安隴右),
for pacifying Wáng Fǔchén (王輔臣);
"Yùzhāng Fān" (豫章翻),
for pacifying the Jiāngxī (江西) rebels;
"Sǎo Qīmǐn" (掃七閩),
for pacifying Gěng Jīngzhōng (耿精忠);
"Hǎibō Píng" (海波平),
for expelling Zhèng Jǐn (鄭錦);
"Píng Wǔyáng" (平五羊),
for suppressing Shàng Zhīxìn (尚之信);
"Guìshuǐ Shēn" (桂水深),
for pacifying Guǎngxī (廣西);
"Jiān Qúkuí" (殲渠魁),
meaning Wú Sānguì (吳三桂) died,
and the rebel faction dispersed;
"Dòngtíng Hú" (洞庭湖),
for pacifying Húnán (湖南);
"Shōu Chéngdū" (收成都),
for pacifying the entire Shǔ (蜀) region;
"Kè Qiányáng" (克黔陽),
for pacifying Guìzhōu (貴州);
"Dìng Kūnmíng" (定昆明),
for executing Wú Shìfán (吳世璠),
and pacifying the entire Diān (滇) region;
"Wéndé Wǔ" (文德舞),
for announcing the achievement of success.
In total, fourteen chapters.
Yuán Yòu (袁佑) also presented "Píng Diān Ráo Gē" (平滇鐃歌),
namely "Shèng Tóngtiān" (聖同天),
"Chūshī Chū" (出師初),
"Huáng Yǐ" (皇矣),
"Yú Shuò" (於鑠),
"Shì Mǔ" (氏畝),
"Xī Yèláng" (昔夜郎),
"Wànfāng Píng" (萬方平),
"Yú Dū" (於都),
"Shěn Tiānxīn" (審天心),
"Shān Shí" (山石),
in total, ten chapters.
In the 23rd year of Kāngxī,
when Shèngzǔ (聖祖) toured Quèlǐ (闕里),
Xú Yuánwén (徐元文) presented "Dōngxún Yǎ" (東巡雅), thirteen chapters.
Lǐ Zhènyù (李振yù) presented "Qīncí Quèlǐ Yǎ" (親祠闕里雅), one piece.
Gù Qiān (顧汧) presented "Shèngzhèng Yǎ" (聖政雅),
"Dōngshān Shízhāng" (東山十章),
and "Nánxūn Shízhāng" (南勳十章).
Jīn Jūjìng (金居敬) presented "Jiàxìng Quèlǐ Yuèfǔ" (駕幸闕里樂府), twelve chapters.
In the 28th year of Kāngxī,
when Shèngzǔ made a Southern Tour,
Zhào Zhíxìn (趙執信) presented "Nánxún Yuèfǔ" (南巡樂府), four chapters: namely "Dōngnán Chūn" (東南春),
signifying no disturbance on the roads;
"Suìxīng Yáo" (歲星謠),
signifying exemption from taxes;
"Jiāngshuǐ Qīng" (江水清),
signifying officials understanding law and being incorruptible;
"Táohuā Rán" (桃花然),
signifying changing local customs.
Péng Huìqí (彭會淇) also presented "Nánxún Fēngyáo" (南巡風謠), ten chapters.
In the 36th year of Kāngxī,
when personally campaigning in the desert,
and the Èlǔtè (厄魯特) fled,
Chén Tíngjìng (陳廷敬) presented "Shèngwǔ Yǎ" (聖武雅), three pieces:
"Wéi Tiān" (惟天), eleven chapters,
speaking of first arriving in the desert,
securing the border and defeating the enemy,
and the flourishing military achievements;
"Huáng Yǐ" (皇矣), eleven chapters,
speaking of pacifying and attracting the people;
"Wǔ Chéng" (武成), eleven chapters,
speaking of capturing the wicked and exterminating the兇,
and the great completion of military achievements.
Wáng Shìzhēn (王士禛) presented "Píng Běi Yǎ" (平北雅), one piece.
Dù Zhēn (杜臻) presented "Píng Mòběi Ráo Gē Gǔchuī Qǔ" (平漠北鐃歌鼓吹曲): namely "Yáng Shèngwǔ" (揚聖武),
"Shén Jījié" (神幾捷),
"Zhì Jīntāng" (峙金湯),
"Bò Zhìshòu" (踣猘獸),
"Tiānsì Huáng" (天駟蝗),
"Tiānxíng Jiàn" (天行健),
"Jǐng Gūchú" (穽孤雛),
"Fú Tiānzhū" (伏天誅),
"Qú Gēfán" (衢歌繁),
"Wǔgōng Chéng" (武功成),
"Guāng Zhījiǎn" (光芝檢),
"Chén Wánghuì" (陳王會),
in total, twelve chapters.
Chén Lùn (陳論) presented "Shèngwǔ Gōngchéng Ráo Gē Gǔchuī Qǔ" (聖武功成鐃歌鼓吹曲): namely "Shèngwǔ Zhāo" (聖武昭),
"Xíng Tiāntǎo" (行天討),
"Qián Jìgào" (虔祭告),
"Mìng Jiàngshuài" (命將帥),
"Jiāxiáng Yìng" (嘉祥應),
"Sān Chūsài" (三出塞),
"Guǎng Zhāolái" (廣招徠),
"Dà Wúwài" (大無外),
"Kǎigē Huán" (凱歌還),
"Cí Zūnhào" (辭尊號),
in total, ten chapters.
Sòng Jùnyè (宋駿業) presented "Píng Běi Yǎ" (平北雅): "Chéng Mìng" (成命), nine chapters,
speaking of the Son of Heaven personally leading troops out of the frontier,
pacifying the border dust,
and bringing peace to the myriad people;
"Huáng Yòu" (皇祐), nine chapters,
speaking of the Son of Heaven again leaving the frontier,
assessing military provisions,
and making opportune decisions;
"Tiān Jiàn" (天監), nine chapters,
speaking of the Son of Heaven a third time leaving the frontier,
the wicked and ugly being utterly defeated,
submitting to heavenly punishment,
and achieving great success.
Shěn Hán (沈涵) presented "Shèngjià Běixún Ráo Gē" (聖駕北巡鐠歌), four chapters: "Fǔ Wànguó" (撫萬國),
speaking of the emperor's might pointing north,
and the Èlǔtè fleeing afar;
"Chéng Fǎjià" (乘法駕),
speaking of the imperial carriage touring the border,
and the Khālkha (喀爾喀) earnestly showing sincerity;
"Zǐtán Gāo" (紫壇高),
speaking of virtue harmonizing heaven and man,
and sweet rain repeatedly falling;
"Liùlóng Xuán" (六龍旋),
speaking of returning to the palace for purification and rituals,
and personally visiting the northern suburbs.
Jiāng Chényīng (姜宸英) presented "Píng Shāmò Huángōng Kǎigē" (平沙漠還宮凱歌), seven chapters: "Huáng Yǐ" (皇矣),
eulogizing the imperial decision;
"Yǒu Shān Cuīwéi" (有山崔嵬),
narrating the auspicious omen;
"Cóngjūn Lè" (從軍樂),
for the generals and soldiers;
"Jué Dàmò" (絕大漠),
eulogizing divine might;
"Èr Yí Lè" (二儀樂),
for cherishing life;
"Xióng Hú" (雄狐),
praising the generals' ability to comprehend divine strategy,
and achieve great success;
"Gē Kǎixuán" (歌凱旋),
celebrating the pacification of rebels and the early return of the imperial carriage.
In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng,
Qián Chénqún (錢陳羣) presented "Qīnghǎi Píngdìng Ráo Gē" (青海平定鐃歌),
namely "Mí Zhī Qióng" (麋之窮),
"Zéimǔ Fú" (賊母俘),
and "Qū Qúnchǒu" (屈羣醜), three chapters.
In the 8th year of Qiánlóng,
Shěn Déqián (沈德潛) presented "Yèlíng Qìngchéng Yuèfǔ" (謁陵慶成樂府),
namely "Shèng Dàxiào" (聖大孝),
"Fā Luánlù" (發鑾輅),
"Shèngjīng Lè" (盛京樂),
"Yè Sānlíng" (謁三陵),
"Huái Zǔliè" (懷祖烈),
"Lǐ Chéngyàn" (禮成宴),
"Qúnfān Cháo" (羣蕃朝),
"Dàshòu Yuè" (大狩閱),
"Yǒngxī Lèi" (永錫類),
and "Liùlóng Huí" (六龍迴), ten chapters.
Wàn Chéngcāng (萬承蒼) also presented "Dì Jiàn" (帝鑒), ten chapters.
In the 14th year of Qiánlóng,
Liáng Shīzhèng (梁詩正) presented "Píngdìng Jīnchuān Yǎ" (平定金川雅): "Yǒu Yì" (有繹), five chapters,
eulogizing the launching of the campaign;
"Róng Chē" (戎車), four chapters,
for eliminating the two villains;
"Fán Yún" (繁雲), five chapters,
for the surrender of the tribal chiefs;
"Luán Biāo" (鸞鑣), five chapters,
for announcing the achievement of success.
Mèng Lín (夢麟) also presented "Shèngwǔ Yuǎnyáng Yǎ" (聖武遠揚雅), one piece.
In the 42nd year of Qiánlóng,
Chéng Jǐngyī (程景伊) presented "Píngdìng Liǎng Jīnchuān Yǎ" (平定兩金川雅), four pieces: namely "Bāoniè" (苞蘖), ten chapters,
describing Zànlā (纘拉) initiating the conflict,
dispatching troops for expedition,
and eventually pacifying them;
"Yín Wēi" (寅威), seven chapters,
describing Suǒnuòmù (索諾木) harboring our rebels,
holding dangerous positions and resisting orders,
selecting and dispatching troops,
and assessing military strategy to crush the strong and sharp;
"Zhōu Lù" (周陸), ten chapters,
describing the military's might and the ministers' efforts,
successfully executing the wise strategy,
All the multitudes of villains were captured;
military merit was achieved.
The ten chapters of joyful triumph
manifest the sacred martial prowess.
The celebratory rites
are extended boundlessly.
The elegant eulogies,
ranking the auspicious praises of the various ministers,
though not yet promulgated by the Music Office,
contain matters worthy of record by the officials in charge,
and are appended at the end.
Treatise 76: Music 8
The musical system of the Qīng Dynasty
included the Zhōnghé Sháoyuè, Dānbì Dàyuè, Zhōnghé Qīngyuè, Dānbì Qīngyuè, Dǎoyíng Yuè, Náogē Yuè, Hécísānggē Yuè, Qìngshénhuānyuè, Yànyuè, Cìyànyuè, and Xiāngyuè.
The instruments varied according to their specific use.
All are listed and fully described
in the order of the music departments.
The musical instruments acquired from tributary states
are listed under the Yànyuè,
which were not detailed in ancient times,
and thus cannot be omitted.
However, only their names and forms are recorded;
as for their measurements and acoustic principles,
these are preserved by the relevant officials.
The Zhōnghé Sháoyuè,
used in altars and temples,
includes one bózhōng,
one tèqìng,
sixteen biānzhōng,
sixteen biānqìng,
one jiàngǔ,
six chí,
two páixiāo,
two xūn,
ten xiāo,
ten dí,
ten qín,
four sè,
ten shēng,
two bófu,
one zhù,
one yù,
and one huī.
For the Temple of the Former Teacher (Xiānshī Miào),
there are six qín, xiāo, dí, and shēng each,
four chí,
with the rest being the same.
For imperial tours and sacrifices to the Five Sacred Mountains (Fāngyuè),
the bózhōng and tèqìng are not used;
there are four qín, xiāo, dí, and shēng each,
two sè and chí each,
with the rest being the same.
For use in the halls and on the steps,
there are four xiāo,
four dí,
two chí,
four qín,
two sè,
eight shēng,
with the rest being the same.
The bózhōng
are made of cast bronze,
totaling twelve,
corresponding to the twelve lǜ.
Their design features a smaller upper diameter
and a larger lower diameter,
a larger longitudinal diameter,
and a smaller horizontal diameter.
They have thirty-six nipples (rǔ).
The two corners hang downwards.
Each of the twelve bells has its own stand (jù),
with varying sizes and designs.
The bell of Huángzhōng
has two luán measuring one chǐ eight cùn two fēn two lí in height,
and a yǒng length of one chǐ zero bā fēn.
They gradually decrease in size down to the bell of Yìngzhōng,
which has two luán measuring nine cùn six fēn in height,
and a yǒng length of five cùn six fēn eight lí.
The bell of Huángzhōng
is used in the eleventh month;
the bell of Dàlǚ
is used in the twelfth month;
the bell of Tàicù
is used in the first month;
the bell of Jiázhōng
is used in the second month;
the bell of Gūxǐ
is used in the third month;
the bell of Zhònglǚ
is used in the fourth month;
the bell of Ruíbīn
is used in the fifth month;
the bell of Línzhōng
is used in the sixth month;
the bell of Yízé
is used in the seventh month;
the bell of Nánlǚ
is used in the eighth month;
the bell of Wúshè
is used in the ninth month;
the bell of Yìngzhōng
is used in the tenth month.
There are four shǔn and jù for the bells,
all painted gold. The upper shǔn has dragon heads carved on both sides,
a golden luán standing on its spine,
its beak holding a five-colored tassel.
The dragon's mouth is similar,
hanging down to the base.
The middle shǔn has an "yè" (protruding ornament),
carved with clouds and dragons.
The attached shǔn has yellow velvet cords tied to suspend the bells.
The two jù on either side
are supported by five-colored crouching lions.
Below is the base (fū),
and on the base is a wall,
carved with mountain and water shapes.
The jù for Huángzhōng, Dàlǚ, and Tàicù have the same measurements;
the jù for Jiázhōng, Gūxǐ, and Zhònglǚ have the same measurements;
the jù for Ruíbīn, Línzhōng, and Yízé have the same measurements;
the jù for Nánlǚ, Wúshè, and Yìngzhōng have the same measurements.
They are not displayed together when in use;
for example, if Huángzhōng is the Gōng note,
then only the bell of Huángzhōng is suspended.
The other months follow this pattern.
The tèqìng
are made of Hetian jade (Hétián yù),
totaling twelve,
corresponding to the twelve lǜ.
Their shape is an obtuse-angled rectangle.
The long leg is called gǔ,
and the short leg is called gǔ.
Both sides are carved with cloud and dragon patterns,
with a hole for a cord to suspend them.
Each of the twelve qìng has its own stand (jù),
with varying sizes and designs.
The qìng of Huángzhōng
has a gǔ length of one chǐ four cùn five fēn eight lí,
and a gǔ length of two chǐ one cùn eight fēn seven lí.
They gradually decrease in size,
down to the qìng of Yìngzhōng,
which has a gǔ length of seven cùn six fēn eight lí,
and a gǔ length of one chǐ one cùn five fēn two lí.
The smaller ones are thicker in substance.
The qìng of Huángzhōng
is seven fēn two lí nine háo thick,
gradually increasing to the qìng of Yìngzhōng,
which is one cùn two fēn nine lí six háo thick.
The qìng of Huángzhōng
is used in the eleventh month;
the qìng of Dàlǚ
is used in the twelfth month;
the qìng of Tàicù
is used in the first month;
the qìng of Jiázhōng
is used in the second month;
the qìng of Gūxǐ
is used in the third month;
the qìng of Zhònglǚ
is used in the fourth month;
the qìng of Ruíbīn
is used in the fifth month;
the qìng of Línzhōng
is used in the sixth month;
the qìng of Yízé
is used in the seventh month;
the qìng of Nánlǚ
is used in the eighth month;
the qìng of Wúshè
is used in the ninth month;
the qìng of Yìngzhōng
is used in the tenth month.
There are also four shǔn and jù for the qìng;
only the upper shǔn has phoenix heads carved on both sides,
and the base is decorated with reclining mallards,
with white feathers and red beaks.
The twelve qìng are not displayed together;
one is suspended for the relevant month,
the same as the bózhōng.
The biānzhōng
are made of cast bronze,
with sixteen bells on a single stand (jù),
corresponding to the twelve principal lǜ and four doubled lǜ.
(Yízé, Nánlǚ, Wúshè, and Yìngzhōng each have a doubled lǜ.)
Eight are Yīn and eight are Yáng.
Their external shape is elliptical,
and their size is uniform,
but their internal height, internal diameter, and volume differ.
The thickness of their solid bodies
gradually increases.
The first doubled Yízé bell
is one fēn three lí three háo thick,
up to the sixteenth Yìngzhōng bell,
which is two fēn eight lí four háo thick.
The shǔn and jù are painted gold;
the upper shǔn has dragon heads carved on both sides,
the middle and lower shǔn are both carved with auspicious clouds,
and golden hooks are attached to suspend the bells.
The two jù are supported by five-colored crouching lions,
below which is the base (fū),
carved with mountain and water shapes.
Biānqìng
are made of Língbì stone or jasper.
Sixteen qìng are arranged on a single stand (jù),
corresponding to the twelve fundamental pitches and four doubled pitches
(the same as biānzhōng).
There are eight for yīn and eight for yáng.
All are obtuse-angled rectangles,
of the same size and construction.
The side length is seven cùn, two fēn, nine lí.
The face length is one chǐ, nine fēn, three lí, five háo.
Only the thickness of the body
increases progressively.
The first doubled Yíjié qìng
is six fēn, six háo, eight sī thick.
Down to the sixteenth Yìngzhōng qìng,
it is one cùn, two fēn, nine lí, six háo thick.
The construction of the frame (sǔn jù) is the same as for biānzhōng,
except that the upper sǔn is carved with phoenix heads on the left and right.
The base (fū) is decorated with reclining ducks,
with white feathers and vermillion beaks.
Jiàngǔ
have a wooden frame covered with leather,
and are mounted on a post.
The diameter of the face is two chǐ, three cùn, four lí.
The length of the frame is three chǐ, four cùn, five fēn, seven lí.
The frame has square holes pierced halfway through it,
through which the post passes, extending upwards to support a canopy,
and downwards to the base.
The canopy is domed at the top and square at the bottom.
Its top is painted gold,
and decorated with a golden luán bird.
The drum is supported by curved wood,
with four prongs embracing the frame.
The base has four feet,
each decorated with a reclining lion.
It is struck with two drumsticks (fú),
which have straight handles and round heads.
All drumsticks are made this way.
There are two chí.
Both are made from sections of bamboo,
intermittently bound with silk,
and played by blowing horizontally.
One hole on top serves as the embouchure.
Five holes open outwards,
one hole opens inwards,
and two additional holes open downwards side-by-side as sound holes.
The end of the tube has a bottom,
with one hole opened in the middle.
A bamboo node is left above the embouchure to close off the sound.
One Gūxǐ chí
has a diameter of eight fēn, seven lí.
From the embouchure to the end of the tube,
its length is nine cùn, nine fēn, five lí, nine háo.
It is used in yáng months.
One Zhònglǚ chí
has a diameter of eight fēn, three lí, two háo.
From the embouchure to the end of the tube,
its length is nine cùn, five fēn, two lí, five háo.
It is used in yīn months.
Páixiāo
are made from a collection of bamboo pipes,
their shape, with varying lengths, resembles phoenix wings.
There are sixteen pipes,
eight for yīn and eight for yáng,
all of the same diameter but different lengths.
The top has a mountain opening (shānkǒu) and is played by single blowing.
There are no side holes.
From left to right,
two doubled pitches (Yíjié,
Wúshè)
and six fundamental pitches (lǜ) are arranged to harmonize with the yáng jùn (mode).
From right to left,
two doubled pitches (Nánlǚ,
Yìngzhōng)
and six fundamental pitches (lǚ) are arranged to harmonize with the yīn jùn.
The names of the lǜ and lǚ are engraved on each pipe's surface.
They are placed in a wooden box (dú),
with their embouchures aligned.
The box is made of wood,
shaped like a small table,
hollow in the middle to receive the pipes.
There are two xūn.
They are made of fired clay,
both oval in shape like a goose egg,
sharp at the top and flat at the bottom.
There are four holes in the front,
two holes in the back,
and one hole at the top.
They are held and blown with the hands.
One Huángzhōng xūn
has an inner height of two cùn, two fēn, three lí.
Its belly diameter is one cùn, seven fēn, one lí, seven háo.
Its bottom diameter is one cùn, one fēn, six lí, eight háo.
It is used in yáng months.
One Dàlǚ xūn
has an inner height of two cùn, one fēn, three lí, three háo.
Its belly diameter is one cùn, six fēn, four lí, two háo.
Its bottom diameter is one cùn, one fēn, one lí, seven háo.
It is used in yīn months.
There are two xiāo.
They are made from sections of bamboo.
Both have a mountain opening (shānkǒu) at the top.
Five holes open in the front,
one hole opens in the back,
and two sound holes
open opposite each other on the sides.
One Gūxǐ xiāo
has a diameter of four fēn, three lí, five háo.
From the mountain opening to the sound holes,
its length is one chǐ, five cùn, eight fēn, four lí, two háo.
It is used in yáng months.
One Zhònglǚ xiāo
has a diameter of four fēn, one lí, six háo.
From the mountain opening to the sound holes,
its length is one chǐ, five cùn, one fēn, five lí, two háo.
It is used in yīn months.
There are two dí.
They are made from sections of bamboo.
Both are intermittently bound with silk,
and have dragon heads and tails added to their ends.
There is one hole on the left,
which is a separate embouchure.
The next hole is covered with a bamboo membrane.
There are six holes on the right,
all opening upwards.
Two sound holes
open opposite each other on the sides.
The two end holes
also open upwards.
One Gūxǐ dí
has a diameter of four fēn, three lí, five háo.
From the embouchure to the far right end,
its total length is one chǐ, two cùn, five fēn, one lí, seven háo.
It is used in yáng months.
One Zhònglǚ dí
has a diameter of four fēn, one lí, six háo.
From the embouchure to the far right end,
its total length is one chǐ, one cùn, nine fēn, seven lí, two háo.
It is used in yīn months.
The qín
has a top made of paulownia (tóng)
and a bottom made of catalpa (zǐ),
lacquered.
It is wide at the front, narrow at the back, round on top, flat on the bottom, and hollow in the middle.
Its total length is three chǐ, one cùn, five fēn, nine lí.
There are two holes on the bottom.
The upper one is called Lóngchí (Dragon Pool),
the lower one Fèngchí (Phoenix Pool).
Inside the belly are two pillars, Tiānzhù (Heaven Pillar) and Dìzhù (Earth Pillar).
Tiānzhù is round
and located below the shoulder.
Dìzhù is square
and located above the waist.
There are seven strings in total,
all vermillion.
The first string has 108 strands (lún).
The second string has 96 strands.
The third string has 81 strands.
The fourth string has 72 strands.
The fifth string has 64 strands.
The sixth string has 54 strands.
The seventh string has 48 strands.
There are seven pegs (zhěn)
and thirteen markers (huī).
The decorations, Yuèshān and Jiāowěi, are made of red sandalwood (zǐtán).
The huī are made of mother-of-pearl (luóbàng).
The zhěn are tied with yellow velvet cords (róngxùn).
It is supported by a lacquered table (jǐ).
The body of the sè is made of paulownia (tóng),
lacquered.
It is wide at the front, narrow at the back, round on top, flat on the bottom, high in the middle, and curved downwards at both ends.
Its total length is six chǐ, five cùn, six fēn, one lí.
There are two holes on the bottom,
which are called yuè.
The front yuè has four openings.
The back yuè is round on top and flat on the bottom.
There are twenty-five strings in total.
All strings have 243 strands (lún).
The middle string is yellow,
and the ones on both sides are vermillion.
Bridges (zhù) are set to harmonize the strings.
The bridges have no fixed positions,
each is adjusted according to the mode (gōngdiào).
The string holes are decorated with mother-of-pearl (luóbàng).
It is supported by two golden tables (jǐ).
Shēng (笙) 2.
Purple bamboo is cut to make the pipes,
which are planted in a ring within a gourd.
The gourd may also be replaced by wood.
All pipes number seventeen,
bound together with bamboo.
The base is full and the tip tapers.
Near the bottom, the base of each pipe is half-cut to expose a cavity.
Thin copper sheets are used for the reeds,
each dotted with a wax bead.
Above each, a sound hole is made according to its corresponding lǜ-lǚ (律呂).
Half of the gourd is fitted with a short, oval mouthpiece,
its end raised.
In the center is a square hole,
and a separate long mouthpiece, shaped like a phoenix's neck,
is placed into this short mouthpiece's square hole.
The end is the blowing hole.
Air enters through the blowing hole,
causing the reeds to vibrate and produce sound.
The xiǎo shēng (小笙) is made like the dà shēng (大笙) but is smaller.
It also has seventeen pipes,
but the first, ninth, sixteenth, and seventeenth pipes have no reeds.
There are thirteen pipes with reeds in total.
The rest is identical to the dà shēng.
Bó fǔ (搏拊),
like a drum but smaller.
The diameter of its head is seven cùn (寸), two fēn (分), nine lí (釐).
The circumference of its frame is one chǐ (尺), four cùn, five fēn, eight lí.
On the frame are two golden coiled dragons,
holding small golden rings in their mouths.
These are tied with a yellow velvet cord,
and it is placed horizontally on a stand.
When used, it is hung around the neck
and struck with both left and right hands.
Each time the jiàn gǔ (建鼓) is struck once,
the bó fǔ is struck twice to keep the rhythm.
Zhù (柷),
made of wood.
It is shaped like a square dòu (斗),
wider at the top and narrower at the bottom.
On the center of three sides, there are raised round shapes to receive the strike.
On one side, there is a round hole in the center for sound to emerge.
It is supported by a stand.
The striking tool is called zhǐ (止).
Yǔ (敔),
made of wood.
It is shaped like a crouching tiger.
On its back are twenty-seven serrated carvings.
It is supported by a stand.
It is played with a zhēn (籈),
which is made of bamboo.
Half of it is split into twenty-four stems,
which are scraped horizontally across the serrations.
Huī (麾),
made of yellow silk.
It is embroidered with nine-bend cloud dragons.
