The top is adorned with blue silk,
embroidered with a red sun.
Within the sun, the characters Zhōnghé (中和) are embroidered.
Above, the Sāntái (三台) stars are embroidered.
To the left, the Běidǒu (北斗).
To the right, the Nándǒu (南斗).
Horizontal wooden bars are placed at the top and bottom of the silk.
The upper one is carved with twin dragons.
The lower one is shaped like mountains and water.
All are gold.
Zhū gāng (朱杠),
its upper part curved into a dragon's head to suspend the huī.
When the huī is raised, the music begins.
When the huī is lowered, the music stops.
Dānbì Dàyuè (丹陛大樂)
is used for all ceremonies where the emperor receives congratulations in the palace hall and for ritual performances within the palace.
Its instruments are: Xìzhú (戲竹) 2,
Dà gǔ (大鼓) 2,
Fāngxiǎng (方響) 2,
Yúnluó (雲鑼) 2,
Xiāo (簫) 2,
Guǎn (管) 4,
Dí (笛) 4,
Shēng (笙) 4,
Zhànggǔ (杖鼓) 1,
Pāibǎn (拍板) 1.
(The xiāo, dí, and shēng are the same as those in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè (中和韶樂)).
Xìzhú,
made by splitting bamboo.
There are two of them,
each with fifty stems.
They are red,
supported by a gold-painted hu-lu (壺盧).
Below it is a handle,
also red.
Each person holds one,
standing on the Dānbì (丹陛).
When they are brought together, the music begins.
When they are separated, the music stops.
(The sound of xì (戲) is the same as huī,
and its use is also the same as huī).
Dà gǔ,
a wooden frame covered with leather.
The diameter of its head is three chǐ, six cùn, four fēn, five lí.
The height of the frame is three chǐ, two cùn, four fēn.
A bronze resonator is installed inside.
The drumhead is yellow,
painted with five-color cloud dragons.
The frame is red,
painted with intertwining dragons.
Four golden rings are on the sides of the frame.
It is supported by a red stand.
The stand has hooks,
which hook the rings to suspend the drum horizontally.
The stand is six chǐ high.
The drummers step onto it to strike the drum.
Fāngxiǎng,
made of steel.
They are rectangular in shape.
Sixteen pieces share the same frame (jù, 虡).
They correspond to the twelve primary lǜ (律) and four supplementary lǜ.
(Same as biānzhōng (編鐘) and qìng (磬)).
Their form and material are all the same.
Only their thickness varies.
The thickness of the bèi yīzé (倍夷則) is
three fēn, three háo (毫), four sī (絲).
It progressively increases to the thickness of the yìngzhōng (應鍾),
which is six fēn, four lí, eight háo.
The upper third of the back has a horizontal ridge.
Its upper end is perforated,
and tied with a yellow velvet cord,
suspended from the jù and leaning diagonally.
It is struck with a small steel mallet.
All sections of music use the same (fāngxiǎng),
except for the Mǎshàng Kǎigē Yuè (馬上凱歌樂) which uses eight of them,
one for each person,
who hold and strike them.
Yúnluó,
cast from bronze.
Ten pieces share the same frame.
They correspond to four primary lǜ and six semi-lǜ.
(Gūxǐ (姑洗), Ruíbīn (蕤賓), Yízé (夷則), Wúshè (無射) are the four primary lǜ;
the six semi-lǜ range from bàn huángzhōng (半黃鍾) to bàn wúshè).
All have holes pierced on four sides,
and are tied to the frame with yellow velvet cords.
Four are in the middle,
three on the left, and three on the right,
forming a nine-palace pattern in three rows.
One piece protrudes above.
Their thickness determines their order.
The bottom right piece corresponds to the lǜ of Gūxǐ,
with a thickness of two lí, five háo, two sī.
It progressively increases to the topmost piece,
which corresponds to the lǜ of bàn wúshè, with a thickness of five lí, nine háo, eight sī.
Guǎn (管) is also known as tóuguǎn (頭管).
Made of hard wood or bone/horn.
There is one large and one small.
Both have seven holes in front and one hole at the back.
A reed mouthpiece (lú shào, 蘆哨) is fitted at the end of the pipe,
inserted into the pipe and blown.
The dà guǎn (大管) uses a Gūxǐ lǜ guǎn as its body.
Its diameter is two fēn, seven lí, four háo.
From the bottom of the reed mouthpiece to the end,
its length is five cùn, seven fēn, six lí.
The xiǎo guǎn (小管) uses a Huángzhōng (黃鍾) bànjī (半積) type pipe as its body.
Its diameter is two fēn, one lí, seven háo.
From the bottom of the reed mouthpiece to the end,
its length is five cùn, six fēn, two háo.
Both are bound at intervals with silk,
and decorated at both ends with ivory.
Zhànggǔ,
with two heads, upper and lower.
Iron rings covered with leather,
then fitted onto a wooden frame.
It has a slender waist.
The frame height is one chǐ, nine cùn, four fēn, four lí. The waist diameter is two cùn, eight fēn, eight lí.
The diameters of the two ends are eight cùn, one fēn each.
The diameters of the upper and lower faces are one chǐ, two cùn, nine fēn, six lí each.
The drumheads and frame are all yellow,
painted with five-color cloud dragons,
and edged with green leather decorative coins (yǎnqián, 掩錢).
Six golden hooks are attached to the upper and lower edges,
interlaced with yellow velvet cords.
The waist is bound.
The waist is decorated with green leather charred-leaf patterns (jiāoyè wén, 焦葉文).
It is struck with red bamboo strips.
Pāibǎn,
made of hard wood.
Three pieces on the left and three on the right.
Two holes are pierced horizontally near the top,
connected with yellow velvet cords.
They are clapped together to keep the rhythm.
Zhōnghé Qīnglè
is used for the ceremony of enfeoffing a venerable person,
banquets and presentation of dishes.
It is also used for hanging lanterns on New Year's Eve and Yuánxī.
Its instruments are: two yúnluó,
two dí,
two guǎn,
two shēng,
one zhànggǔ,
one shǒugǔ,
and one páibǎn.
(The dí and shēng are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháolè;
the yúnluó, guǎn, and bǎn are the same as in Dānbì Dàlè.)
The zhànggǔ is similar to that in Dānbì Dàlè but smaller,
either half the size
or two-thirds the size.
The shǒugǔ
has a wooden frame covered with leather.
Its face diameter is nine cùn one fēn two háo;
its waist diameter is one chǐ two fēn four lí.
A handle pierces the frame;
it is held and struck.
Dānbì Qīnglè
is used for banquets and the presentation of tea and wine,
and also for bestowing tea at Lín Yōng.
All musical instruments are the same as in Zhōnghé Qīnglè.
Dǎoyíng Yuè and Náogē Yuè
are used for the emperor's comings and goings.
When the luánjià lǔbù is used, Dǎoyíng Yuè is played.
When the qíjià lǔbù is used, the Xíngxìng Yuè of Náogē is played.
When the fǎjià lǔbù or dàjià lǔbù is used, Dǎoyíng Yuè is interspersed with Náogē Yuè.
However, when proceeding to altars or temples for major sacrifices, Dǎoyíng Yuè and Náogē Yuè are set up but not played.
For all three major festivals when memorials are presented, and when shílù, shèngxùn, or yùdié are presented,

and also for personal plowing, personal sericulture, calendrical announcements, issuance of edicts, palace examinations, sending out examination results, and welcoming the kiss [of the examination results],
for all occasions where the imperial retinue precedes the emperor's entry and exit,
Dǎoyíng Yuè is played.
The music of Náogē includes Lǔbù Yuè.
It has one section,
called Náogē Gǔchuī.
It has Qiánbù Yuè.
It has one section,
called Qiánbù Dàlè.
(Also called Dàhǎnbō.)
It has Xíngxìng Yuè.
It has three sections: called Míngjiǎo,
Náogē Dàlè,
and Náogē Qīnglè.
It has Kǎixuán Yuè.
It has two sections: called Náogē
and Kǎigē.
Lǔbù Yuè and Qiánbù Dàlè are arranged side-by-side,
also called Jīngǔ Náogē Dàlè.
For all yuánqiú, qígǔ, and chángyú ceremonies,
when the dàjià lǔbù is used, the three sections of Qiánbù Dàlè, Náogē Gǔchuī, and Xíngxìng Yuè are all displayed.
For Fāngzé,
when the fǎjià lǔbù is used,
Qiánbù Dàlè and Náogē Gǔchuī are displayed.
For Tàimiào, Shèjì, and various medium sacrifices,
when the fǎjià lǔbù is used,
Náogē Gǔchuī is displayed.
The same applies to court assemblies using the fǎjià lǔbù.
When receiving captives from the imperial tower,
when the fǎjià lǔbù is used,
Jīngǔ Náogē Dàlè is displayed.
For imperial tours and grand reviews,
when the qíjià lǔbù is used,
Míngjiǎo Náogē Dàlè and Náogē Qīnglè are displayed.
For triumphant returns and suburban welcoming ceremonies,
Náogē is played.
For the return of the imperial carriage and the review of troops,
Kǎigē is played.
Dǎoyíng Yuè uses two xìzhú,
six guǎn,
four dí,
two shēng,
two yúnluó,
one dǎoyínggǔ,
and one páibǎn.
(The shēng and dí are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháolè;
the xìzhú, yúnluó, guǎn, and bǎn are the same as in Dānbì Dàlè.)
The dǎoyínggǔ
is made like a large drum but smaller.
Its face diameter is two chǐ four fēn eight lí;
its frame height is one chǐ six cùn two fēn.
It is painted with five-colored clouds and dragons,
and has a bronze resonator inside its belly.
Four golden rings are attached to the sides,
tied with yellow velvet cords.
Two people carry it,
striking it with vermilion mallets.
Náogē Gǔchuī uses forty-eight lónggǔ,
twenty-four huàjiǎo,
eight dàtóngjiǎo,
eight xiǎotóngjiǎo,
two jīn,
four zhēng,
twelve dí,
four zhànggǔ,
and four páibǎn.
(The dí are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháolè;
the bǎn are the same as in Dānbì Dàlè.)
The lónggǔ
has a wooden frame covered with leather.
Its face diameter is one chǐ five cùn three fēn six lí;
its frame height is six cùn four fēn eight lí.
The face, frame, decoration, and golden rings are all the same as the dǎoyínggǔ.
The rings are tied with yellow velvet cords.
When moving, it is hung from the neck;
when displayed, it is placed on a stand.
The stand has three gathered bamboo poles,
pierced by a pivot to support it.
The huàjiǎo
is made of wood,
hollow inside and wide in the belly,
with sharp ends.
It is five chǐ four cùn six fēn one lí two háo long.
It is bound at the top and bottom with bronze,
and bound in the middle with five sections of rattan,
lacquered.
A wooden reed is inserted into the end of the horn to blow it;
the reed is seven cùn two fēn nine lí long.
The dàtóngjiǎo,
also called dàhào,
is cast in bronze,
in two sections, upper and lower.
Its shape is like a bamboo tube,
narrow at the base and wide at the end,
with a spherical shape in the middle.
The upper section is inserted into the lower section;
when used, it is pulled to extend it.
Its total length is three chǐ six cùn seven fēn two lí.
The xiǎotóngjiǎo,
also called èrhào,
is cast in bronze,
in two sections, upper and lower.
The upper section is straight;
the lower section flares out.
Each has a spherical shape connecting them,
and is pulled and inserted like the dàtóngjiǎo.
Its total length is four chǐ one cùn four lí.
The dàjiǎo has a large body and a low sound;
the xiǎojiǎo has a slender body and a high sound,
not determined by length.
The jīn
is cast in bronze.
Its face is flat,
with a diameter of one chǐ four cùn five fēn eight lí,
and a depth of two cùn two fēn seven lí five háo.
Two holes are drilled in the side,
through which yellow velvet cords are tied and passed through a wooden handle;
it is lifted and struck.
The zhēng
is cast in bronze,
shaped like a plate.
Its face is flat,
with an opening diameter of eight cùn six fēn four lí,
a depth of one cùn two fēn nine lí eight háo,
and an edge width of eight fēn six lí four háo.
Six holes are drilled,
in pairs side by side,
encircled by a wooden frame,
which also has holes.
They are connected by yellow velvet cords.
Two bronze rings on the left and right
are tied with yellow velvet cords.
It is hung from the neck and struck.
The zhànggǔ is the same as in Dānbì Dàlè,
except its face is painted with flowing clouds,
with a tàijí symbol in the center.
Qiánbù Dàlè
uses four dàtóngjiǎo,
four xiǎotóngjiǎo,
and four jīnkǒujiǎo.
(The dàtóngjiǎo and xiǎotóngjiǎo are made the same as in Náogē Gǔchuī.)
The jīnkǒujiǎo,
formerly called suǒnà,
is a wooden pipe
with golden mouthpieces at both ends,
narrow at the top and flaring at the bottom.
The pipe length is nine cùn eight fēn nine lí.
The golden mouthpiece at the top of the pipe is two cùn one fēn six lí long,
gourd-shaped,
with two small bronze plates added.
The golden mouthpiece at the bottom of the pipe is four cùn eight fēn six lí long,
with the pipe carved like alternating bamboo sections.
It has seven holes in front
and one hole in back.
A reed is inserted into the end of the pipe to blow it.
For Ráo Gē Dà Yuè (Grand Ráo Song Music),
eight Jīnkǒujiǎo are used,
two Tónggǔ,
one Tóngdiǎn,
one Jīn,
one Bá,
and one Xínggǔ.
(The Jīnkǒujiǎo are the same as in Qiánbù Dà Yuè;
the Jīn are the same as in Ráo Gē Gǔ Chuī.)
The Tónggǔ are
cast from bronze.
Their shape is like a Jīn.
The diameter of the face is nine inches, seven fen, two li.
The center rises eight fen, one li,
with a diameter of two inches, six fen, seven li, three hao.
Two holes are pierced along the rim,
through which yellow silk cords are threaded to hang and strike them.
The Tóngdiǎn
are made like a Tónggǔ but smaller.
The Bá are
cast from bronze.
The diameter of the face is six inches, four fen, eight li.
The center rises one inch, two fen, nine li, six hao,
with a diameter of three inches, two fen, four li.
A hole is pierced and a cord threaded through;
they are clapped together to harmonize the music.
The Xínggǔ
is also called Luógǔ.
It has a wooden frame covered with leather,
larger at the top and smaller at the bottom.
The face and frame are painted and decorated like a Lónggǔ.
There are four bronze rings,
through which yellow silk cords are threaded.
When traveling, it is slung over a horse;
for formations, it is placed on a stand.
For Ráo Gē Qīng Yuè (Clear Ráo Song Music),
two Yúnluó are used,
two Dí,
two Píngdí,
two Guǎn,
two Shēng,
one Jīn,
one Bá,
one Tóngdiǎn,
and one Xínggǔ.
(The Dí and Shēng are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè;
the Yúnluó and Guǎn are the same as in Dānbì Dà Yuè;
the Jīn are the same as in Ráo Gē Gǔ Chuī;
the Bá, Tóngdiǎn, and Xínggǔ are the same as in Ráo Gē Dà Yuè.)
The Píngdí
are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè,
except they do not have dragon heads or tails.
For Xíngxìng Yuè (Processional Music),
the numbers for Ráo Gē Dà Yuè and Ráo Gē Qīng Yuè are combined,
and augmented with eight Dà Tóngjiǎo,
eight Xiǎo Tóngjiǎo,
and two Ménggǔjiǎo.
(The Dà Tóngjiǎo and Xiǎo Tóngjiǎo are the same as in Ráo Gē Gǔ Chuī.)
The Ménggǔjiǎo
is also called Ménggǔ Hào.
It is made of wood,
hollow in the middle and flaring at the end,
composed of two sections, upper and lower.
There are two designs for the horn, male and female.
The internal diameter of the upper opening of the male horn is three fen, four li, five hao.
The internal diameter of the upper opening of the female horn is two fen, eight li, five hao.
Both have a bronze mouthpiece attached to the end of the tube,
into which a horn reed is inserted for playing.
The male produces a deep sound,
the female a clear sound.
For Ráo Gē, four Dà Tóngjiǎo,
four Xiǎo Tóngjiǎo,
eight Jīnkǒujiǎo,
four Jīn,
two Luó,
two Tónggǔ,
four Náo,
four Bá,
two Xiǎo Hé Bá,
four Huā Kuānggǔ,
four Déshènggǔ,
four Hǎidí,
four Yúnluó,
six Xiāo,
six Dí,
six Guǎn,
six Chí,
and six Shēng are used.
(The Dà Tóngjiǎo, Xiǎo Tóngjiǎo, and Jīn are the same as in Ráo Gē Gǔ Chuī;
the Jīnkǒujiǎo are the same as in Qiánbù Dà Yuè;
the Tónggǔ and Bá are the same as in Ráo Gē Dà Yuè;
the Xiāo, Dí, Chí, and Shēng are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè;
the Yúnluó and Guǎn are the same as in Dānbì Dà Yuè.)
The Luó
is made like a Tónggǔ but thicker;
its sound is lower and smaller than a Tónggǔ.
The Náo are
cast from bronze.
The diameter of the face is one chi, two cun.
The center rises,
a hole is pierced and a cord threaded through,
and they are clapped together.
The Xiǎo Hé Bá
are made like Bá,
with a face diameter of seven cun, nine fen.
The center rises,
a hole is pierced and a cord threaded through,
all the same as the Bá.
The Huā Kuānggǔ
is a waist drum (yāogǔ).
It has a wooden frame covered with leather,
a face diameter of one chi, five cun, two fen,
and a frame height of one chi, six cun,
painted with floral patterns.
The stand is made of sandalwood,
with four intersecting cross-legs,
and the drum is suspended by a bronze ring and struck.
The Déshènggǔ has
a wooden frame covered with leather,
a face diameter of one chi, six cun, one fen,
and a frame height of five cun, eight fen,
painted with clouds and dragons.
The stand has four posts,
and the drum is suspended above and struck.
The Hǎidí
is made like a Jīnkǒujiǎo but smaller,
with a total length of nine cun, five fen.
For Kǎigē (Triumphal Music), four Yúnluó,
eight Fāngxiǎng,
two Bá,
two Dà Hé Bá,
two Xīng,
two Tóngdiǎn,
two Tiào,
four Xiāo,
four Dí,
twelve Guǎn,
four Shēng,
two Zhànggǔ,
and two Pāibǎn are used.
(The Xiāo, Dí, and Shēng are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè;
the Yúnluó, Guǎn, and Zhànggǔ are the same as in Dānbì Dà Yuè;
the Bá and Tóngdiǎn are the same as in Ráo Gē Dà Yuè.)
The Fāngxiǎng
are made like those in Dānbì Dà Yuè.
Eight of them are used,
one for each person,
held and struck.
The Dà Hé Bá
are made like Bá,
with a face diameter of one chi, one cun, eight fen.
The center rises,
a hole is pierced and a cord threaded through,
and they are clapped together.
The Xīng are
cast from bronze.
The mouth diameter is one cun, eight fen,
and the depth is one cun.
The center rises,
each has a round hole pierced,
through which a cord is threaded,
and they are clapped together.
The Tiào are
cast from bronze.
The face diameter is two cun, seven fen,
the mouth diameter is three cun, one fen, five li,
and the depth is six fen.
A hole is pierced and a cord threaded through,
and they are struck with a wooden piece.
The Pāibǎn consist of three pieces,
two are bound together,
and one is used to strike them.
Hé Cí Sāng Gē Yuè (Rice-song and Mulberry-song Music)
is used for the imperial plowing and imperial sericulture ceremonies.
For the imperial plowing, six Jīn,
six Gǔ,
six Xiāo,
six Dí,
six Shēng,
and six Pāibǎn are used.
For the imperial sericulture, two Jīn,
two Gǔ,
six each of Xiāo, Dí, and Shēng,
and two Pāibǎn are used.
(The Xiāo, Dí, and Shēng are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè;
the Bǎn are the same as in Dānbì Dà Yuè.)
The Jīn are made like those in Ráo Gē Gǔ Chuī but slightly smaller.
The mallet is made of yellow leather,
gourd-shaped,
with a red handle.
The Gǔ
are made like Lónggǔ but slightly smaller,
suspended from the neck and struck.
Qìngshén Huānlè (慶神歡樂)
is used for all group sacrifices.
Its instruments are two yúnluó (雲鑼),
two guǎn (管),
two dí (笛),
one shēng (笙),
one gǔ (鼓),
and one pāibǎn (拍板).
It is only augmented for the sacrifices to the First Silkworm Empress (先蠶), Guāndì (關帝), and Wénchāng (文昌).
(The dí, shēng, and gǔ are the same as those in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè (中和韶樂);
the yúnluó, guǎn, and bǎn are the same as those in Dānbì Dàyuè (丹陛大樂).)
There are nine types of Yànyuè (宴樂): the first is Duìwǔ Yuè (隊舞樂),
the second is Wǎěrkā Bù Yuè (瓦爾喀部樂),
the third is Cháoxiān Yuè (朝鮮樂),
the fourth is Ménggǔ Yuè (蒙古樂),
the fifth is Huíbù Yuè (回部樂),
the sixth is Fānzǐ Yuè (番子樂),
the seventh is Kuòěrkā Bù Yuè (廓爾喀部樂),
the eighth is Miǎndiàn Guó Yuè (緬甸國樂),
and the ninth is Ānnán Guó Yuè (安南國樂).
There are three types of Duìwǔ (隊舞): the first is Qìnglóng Wǔ (慶隆舞),
which is used for all court assemblies in the palace and celebratory banquets;
the second is Shìdé Wǔ (世德舞),
used for banquets of the imperial clan;
the third is Déshèng Wǔ (德勝舞),
used for victory banquets.
The three dances are of the same form,
all being dances with musical accompaniment.
Their instruments are one zhēng (箏),
one xīqín (奚琴),
three pípá (琵琶),
three sānxián (三絃),
sixteen jié (節),
and sixteen pāi (拍).
The zhēng
resembles a sè (瑟) but is smaller.
It is made of hollowed paulownia wood,
measuring four chi (尺), seven cùn (寸), three fēn (分), eight lí (釐), and five háo (毫) in total length.
It has fourteen strings,
each string having fifty-four lún (綸),
with bridges set according to the respective melodic mode.
It has two holes at the bottom.
The front is square;
the back is round on top and flat on the bottom.
The entire body is gold,
and the four sides are painted with gold kuí lóng (夔龍).
The bridge and tail edge are made of red sandalwood (zǐtán);
the string holes are decorated with ivory.
The xīqín
is made of hollowed paulownia wood
and has two strings.
It has a dragon head
and a square neck.
The body (cáo) length is equal to the neck.
The back is round with a concave middle,
covered with a board.
At the end of the body, a round peg is set,
and a leather buckle is applied to fasten the strings.
The lower lip of the dragon head serves as the string-notch (shānkǒu),
hollowed out to receive the strings.
It is wound with two tuning pegs (zhóu),
one on each side,
and a wooden bow with eighty-one horsehair strands is used to play it.
The pípá
is made of hollowed paulownia wood,
has four strings,
a curved head, and a long neck.
It has a flat front and a round back,
with a wide, oval body (fù).
A soundboard (fùshǒu) is applied to the front of the body (cáo).
The middle of the curved head serves as the string-notch.
Four sandalwood tuning pegs (tánzhóu) are set to fasten the strings,
two on each side.
Above the string-notch, four "elephants" (xiàng) are made of boxwood;
below, thirteen "grades" (pǐn) are made of bamboo,
pressed to produce sound.
The two sides of the waist are crescent-shaped.
Inside the body, fine steel bars form the "gall" (dǎn).
The strings from the string-notch to the soundboard
measure two chi, one cùn, and six fēn in length.
The first string is decorated with vermillion.
The sānxián
is made of sandalwood,
has a long neck,
a square body (cáo),
and rounded corners,
covered with snake (huī) skin.
The neck (bǐng) passes through the middle of the body (cáo).
The end of the neck at the end of the body is covered with wood.
Holes are pierced to pass the strings.
The lower half of the spoon-shaped head (chítóu) is hollowed out to receive the strings,
which are fastened with three tuning pegs,
two on the left and one on the right.
The jié
is made of woven bamboo resembling a winnowing basket,
vermilion in color,
with a tiger shape on the back.
Two round bamboo sticks are used,
scraped to mark the jié.
The pāi
consists of four pieces of red sandalwood (zǐtán) skin.
Three are bundled together,
and one is used to strike them.
When Tàizǔ (太祖) pacified the Wǎěrkā Bù (瓦爾喀部),
he obtained their music,
which was included in the Yànyuè,
and this became the Wǎěrkā Bù Yuèwǔ (瓦爾喀部樂舞).
It uses four bìlì (觱篥)
and four xīqín.
(The xīqín are the same as those in Duìwǔ Yuè.)
The bìlì
is a reed pipe with three holes.
It has a golden mouthpiece,
flares at the bottom,
and has a small hole in the middle.
The reed (huáng) is opened at the end of the pipe,
the opening of the reed being four cùn, five fēn, and three lí from the end of the pipe.
During Tàizōng's (太宗) time,
the music of the Cháoxiān Guó (朝鮮國) was obtained
and included in the Yànyuè,
becoming the Cháoxiān Guó Pái (朝鮮國俳).
It uses one dí,
one guǎn,
and one páigǔ (俳鼓).
(The dí is the same as in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè;
the guǎn is the same as in Dānbì Dàyuè.)
The páigǔ is like a lónggǔ (龍鼓) but smaller,
and is hung around the neck to be played.
When Tàizōng pacified Cháhāěr (察哈爾),
he obtained their music,
which was included in the Yànyuè,
becoming the Ménggǔ Yuèqǔ (蒙古樂曲).
There are jiāchuī (笳吹)
and Fānbù Hézòu (番部合奏),
both being music of Duōěrdēmì (掇爾多密),
managed by the Shíbāng Chù (什幫處).
Jiāchuī uses one hújiā (胡笳),
one zhēng,
one húqín (胡琴),
and one kǒuqín (口琴).
(The zhēng is the same as that used in Duìwǔ Yuè,
but only has six strings.)
The hújiā
is a wooden pipe with three holes.
Horns are applied to both ends,
and the end flares upwards.
From the blowing hole to the end,
it measures two chi, three cùn, nine fēn, and six lí.
The húqín
is made of hollowed wood,
has two strings,
a dragon head,
and a square neck.
The body (cáo) is elliptical and tapers at the bottom,
covered with leather.
Outside the body, a wooden pin like a hairpin is set to fasten the strings.
Below the dragon head is the string-notch,
hollowed out to receive the strings,
which are fastened with two tuning pegs,
one on each side.
A wooden bow with eighty-one horsehair strands is used to play it.
The kǒuqín
is made of iron,
with one handle and two prongs.
A reed (huáng) is set in the middle,
with its end protruding outside the prongs.
It is held horizontally in the mouth,
and sound is produced by vibrating the reed with the tongue
and by breathing in and out.
Fānbù Hézòu
uses one yúnluó,
one xiāo (簫),
one dí,
one guǎn,
one shēng,
one zhēng,
one húqín,
one pípá,
one sānxián,
one èrxián (二絃),
one yuèqín (月琴),
one tíqín (提琴),
one zházhēng (軋箏),
and one huǒbùsī (火不思),
and one pāibǎn.
(The xiāo, dí, and shēng are the same as in Zhōnghé Sháoyuè;
the yúnluó and guǎn are the same as in Dānbì Dàyuè;
the zhēng, pípá, and sānxián are the same as in Duìwǔ Yuè.)
Húqín,
Èrxián,
has a bamboo neck and coconut body,
with a *tóng* wood soundboard.
The body's diameter is three *cùn* eight *fēn* four *lí*.
It is circular,
unlike the *húqín* used with *jiāchuī*, which is oval and tapers downwards.
The pegbox is hollowed out to accommodate the strings,
which are wound by two pegs,
both on the right.
The strings, from the pegbox to the bridge,
are two *chǐ* three *fēn* five *lí* two *háo* long.
They are bowed with a bamboo bow strung with eighty-one horsehairs.
Èrxián
is made of camphor wood,
with a *tóng* wood soundboard.
It is rectangular in shape,
with a hole in the bottom.
The soundboard is fitted with a handrest like a *pípá*.
The curved head is hollowed out to accommodate the strings,
wound by two pegs,
one on each side.
The strings are two *chǐ* three *cùn* four *lí* long.
It has seventeen frets,
pressed to produce sound.
Yuèqín
is made of sandalwood,
has four strings,
and a *tóng* wood soundboard.
It has an octagonal, curved neck,
with the neck running through the body.
The soundboard is fitted with a handrest.
The curved neck is hollowed out to accommodate the strings,
which are wound by four pegs,
two on each side.
The strings are two *chǐ* three *cùn* four *lí* long,
and it has seventeen frets,
the same as the *Èrxián*.
Tíqín
has four strings.
Its body is made of rounded wood,
covered with python skin and hollow underneath.
A bamboo neck runs through the body,
protruding beyond the body's end.
A wooden cover presses the strings.
The end of the neck is hollowed out to accommodate the strings,
which are wound by four pegs,
all on the right.
It is bowed with a bamboo bow strung with horsehair,
bowed between the four strings.
Yàzhēng
is similar to a *zhēng* but smaller,
carved from *tóng* wood,
and has ten strings.
It has bridges at the front and back.
The strings between the bridges are one *chǐ* six *cùn* one *fēn* eight *lí* long.
Each has a movable bridge,
and it is bowed with a wooden rod.
Huǒbùsī
is similar to a *pípá* but thinner,
with four strings.
It has a *tóng* wood neck,
with its lower half carved out for the body,
covered with python skin.
The curved head is hollowed out to accommodate the strings,
wound by four pegs,
all on the right.
The strings, from the pegbox to the bridge, are one *chǐ* seven *cùn* seven *fēn* four *lí* long.
Pāibǎn
consists of three pieces of *zǐtán* wood.
Two are bound together,
and struck with the third.
When Gāozōng pacified Huíbù,
he acquired their music,
which was placed at the end of court banquets.
These are the musical instruments of Huíbù:
one Dábù,
one Nágálá,
one Hā'ěrzhákè,
one Kā'ěrnài,
one Sàitā'ěr,
one Lābābǔ,
one Bālāwàn,
and one Sū'ěrnài.
Dábù
has a wooden frame covered with leather,
shaped like a hand drum but without a handle.
There are two sizes, large and small.
One face has a diameter of one *chǐ* three *cùn* six *fēn* five *lí* two *háo*.
The other face has a diameter of one *chǐ* two *cùn* two *fēn* four *lí*.
Both are yellow,
with a painted colorful lion on the face,
and are struck with the fingers.
Nágálá
has an iron frame covered with leather,
larger at the top and smaller at the bottom,
shaped like a marching drum.
There is a small ring on the side,
tied with a yellow felt cord.
Two drums are linked together,
and struck with a stick on each side.
Hā'ěrzhákè
is shaped like a *Húqín*,
with a coconut body,
covered with horsehide.
It has an upper wooden neck
and a lower iron neck.
A hole is opened in the middle of the body's bottom,
and three small holes are opened on the side.
Two strands of horsehair serve as strings,
passing from the pegbox to the back.
They are wound by two pegs,
one on each side,
and attached to the lower iron neck.
Below the horsehair strings are ten steel strings,
attached to the upper wooden neck
and the lower iron neck,
with five pegs on each side.
Separately, a wooden rod serves as a bow,
strung with over eighty horsehairs,
which bows the horsehair strings,
producing sound sympathetic to the steel strings.
Kā'ěrnài
resembles the common *yángqín*.
It has eighteen steel strings.
It is carved from hollowed wood,
straight on the left and curved on the right.
The left side has a bridge like the *yuèshān* of a *qín*,
to secure the root of the steel strings.
The ends of the steel strings are fitted with wooden pegs,
similar to the *zhěn* of a *qín*,
entering the right end.
They are arranged in two alternating layers of height,
and the pegs are turned to adjust the tension of the strings.
It is plucked with finger picks
or a wooden plectrum.
Throughout, it has double strings,
except for the first, which is a single string.
Sàitā'ěr
is shaped like a dagger.
It has two silk strings
and seven steel strings.
A wooden neck runs through the body,
the bottom of which is covered with leather.
The face is flat and the back is round.
The neck has twenty-three threaded frets,
like the frets of a *pípá*.
The strings are wound by nine pegs.
Two pegs at the end of the neck wind the silk strings.
Three pegs are on two faces,
and four pegs are on the left side,
winding one double steel string
and six single strings.
It is plucked with finger picks
or a wooden plectrum to play the silk strings,
producing sound sympathetic to the steel strings.
Lābābǔ
has five silk strings
and two steel strings.
A wooden neck runs through the body.
The body is shaped like half a bottle,
its bottom covered with leather.
The curved head is hollowed out to accommodate the silk strings,
wound by five pegs,
two on the left and three on the right.
Two pegs on the right side of the curved head wind the steel strings.
It is plucked with finger picks
or a wooden plectrum to play the silk strings,
producing sound sympathetic to the steel strings.
Bālāwàn
is a wooden pipe,
narrow at the top and wide at the bottom,
decorated with copper.
It is shaped like a *tóuguǎn* but has a bottom,
with small holes to emit sound.
The pipe is nine *cùn* four *fēn* long in total.
Seven holes are on the front,
and one hole is on the back.
A reed mouthpiece is fitted on the pipe for blowing.
Sū'ěrnài,
also named Suǒnà,
is a wooden pipe,
decorated with copper at both ends,
narrow at the top and wide at the bottom,
shaped like a *jīnkǒujiǎo* but smaller.
Seven holes are on the front,
one hole is on the back,
and one hole is on the left side.
A reed mouthpiece is fitted on the copper pipe for blowing.
Gāozōng平定Jīnchuān,
acquired its music.
Later, when the Bānchán É'ěrdéwéi from Hòuzàng came to court,
he presented his music.
Both were placed at the end of the banquet music,
and were called Fānzi yuè.
The music of Jīnchuān: called Ā'ěrsàlán,
called Dàguōzhuāng,
called Sìjiǎolǔ.
It used one Déli,
one Bóqiě'ěr, one Délèwō.
Déli,
resembles a suǒnà but smaller.
Bóqiě'ěr,
consists of two bronze plates,
round, six inches in diameter,
raised in the center,
with a hole for a cord,
struck together left and right.
Délèwō,
is similar in shape to a dábu.
The music of Bānchán: called Zhāshílúnbù,
used two Déli,
one Bāwāng,
one Cāngqīng,
four Lóngsīmǎ'ěrdélèwō.
The Déli is similar to that of Jīnchuān music,
but slightly larger in form.
Bāwāng,
resembles a lǎbābù,
with seven strings.
Cāngqīng,
is made like a yúnluó.
Lóngsīmǎ'ěrdélèwō,
resembles a nágálá but made of bronze,
with a face diameter of one foot three inches,
a sharp bottom,
and a frame height of one foot.
Gāozōng 평정Guō'ěrkā,
acquired its music,
which was placed at the end of the banquet music,
and was called Guō'ěrkā Yuèwǔ.
It used one Dábulā,
three Sàlángjì,
one Dānbùlā,
one Dálā,
two Gōnggǔlī.
Dábulā,
resembles a nágálá,
with one side covered with leather.
There are two types: one has a full body and a sharp bottom,
the other has a slightly full bottom that gradually tapers.
Leather straps are tied all around,
connected by colored silk threads,
suspended from the waist,
and struck together with both left and right hands.
Sàlángjì,
is carved from wood,
with four leather strings,
and nine iron strings.
The neck is three inches long,
hollowed out inside,
and decorated on the surface with a Buddha figure carved from fish teeth.
The handle is five inches two fen long,
the trough surface is three inches wide,
hollowed out from the top,
and covered with leather.
The middle part is tapered like a crescent moon,
bound with yellow leather.
The bottom is oval,
with holes drilled in the neck to accommodate the leather strings,
two on each side.
The axis handle face has nine holes,
arranged diagonally from right to left,
like scales,
each holding an iron string.
There are nine axes,
all on the right,
five above and four below.
A bridge is set on the trough surface,
with nine holes in the middle for the iron strings,
and supporting the leather strings above.
A bow made of soft wood with horsehair is used to rub the leather strings,
which resonate with the iron strings to produce sound.
Dānbùlā,
is carved from paulownia wood,
using a large gourd as the soundbox,
with a straight handle,
a flat face and a rounded back,
four iron strings,
wound onto four tuning pegs,
two above,
one on each side.
On the handle are two iron pieces serving as string rests,
one with a hole for strings,
the other supporting the strings.
Dálā,
consists of two bronze plates,
round, two inches one fen in diameter.
Raised in the center,
with a hole,
tied with colored silk threads,
struck together left and right.
Gōnggǔlī,
are bronze bells,
connected with colored silk threads,
fifty bells per string,
a total of four strings.
When singing, two people tie them to their thighs,
and leap with both feet to produce sound.
In the 53rd year of Qiánlóng,
Miǎndiàn Guó became a vassal,
and presented its music,
which was placed at the end of the banquet music,
and was called Miǎndiàn Guó Yuè.
There are two types, coarse and fine: coarse Miǎndiàn music,
used one Jiēnèidādōuhū,
one Jīwānxiékū,
one Nièdōujiāng,
one Niènièdōujiāng,
one Jiémǎngnièdōubù.
Jiēnèidādōuhū,
is a wooden frame covered with leather,
with a knob on the frame,
tied with silk,
suspended horizontally from the neck,
and struck with the hand.
Jīwānxiékū,
is similar in form to a yúnluó,
there are eight of them,
four above and four below,
all suspended on a frame.
The frame is propped up from behind with two pieces of wood,
and played by leaning it diagonally.
Nièdōujiāng,
is a wooden tube with a bronze mouthpiece,
gradually flaring towards the bottom,
with seven holes in front,
and one hole behind.
A bronze whistle is set at the end of the tube,
with a reed whistle added on top,
and the joint between the tube and the bronze mouthpiece
is covered with a bronze pick.
Niènièdōujiāng,
is shaped like a jīnkǒujiǎo but smaller,
a wooden tube with a wooden mouthpiece,
the rest is the same as Nièdōujiāng.
Jiémǎngnièdōubù,
consists of two bronze plates,
round, three inches five fen in diameter.
Raised in the center,
with a hole,
threaded with leather,
struck together left and right.
Fine Miǎndiàn music,
used one Bādálā,
one Bàngzhá,
one Zǒnggǎojī,
one Mìqióngzǒng,
one Déyuēzǒng,
one Bùlěi,
one Jiēzú.
Bādálā,
has a wooden soundbox,
shaped like a boat,
total length two feet seven inches five fen.
The front and rear ends are shaped like mountain peaks,
the tips of the two peaks
are strung with silk cord.
Twenty-two bamboo plates are arranged and threaded,
all one inch wide.
The first plate is five inches two fen long,
three fen five li thick;
subsequently, the length gradually increases and the thickness gradually decreases,
until the last plate, which is one foot one inch five fen long,
and one fen thick.
It is struck with a mallet made of bamboo wrapped in cotton.
Bàngzhá,
is a wooden frame covered with leather,
larger at the top and smaller at the bottom.
The face diameter is six inches one fen,
the bottom diameter is four inches,
the frame height is one foot.
Leather straps are tied all around,
and struck with the hand.
Zǒnggǎojī,
has thirteen strings,
a curved handle,
a continuous soundbox,
the handle curves like a scorpion's tail.
The soundbox surface is covered with leather,
with four round holes for sound emission.
Along the belly of the soundbox, there is a hand rest,
with thirteen holes,
for tying the strings,
each diagonally drawn to the handle and fastened,
played with the hand.
The Mìqióngzǒng
has three strings,
is made of wood,
and is fish-shaped.
Its body is rectangular,
with a long groove carved along the underside of the belly,
without a bottom.
Scales are carved on both sides.
Five frets are set on the surface.
It has nine small round holes for sound emission:
four in front,
four in the middle,
and one at the back.
The head is sharp and projects upward,
carved with whiskers, horns, large teeth, and round eyes.
The tail is also sharp.
A copper nut is placed on the neck.
Three vermilion strings are attached.
The tail has a ring to secure the strings.
Holes are pierced on the sides,
where pegs are installed,
two on the left and one on the right.
It is played by hand.
The Déyuēzǒng
has three strings,
is made of wood,
hollow inside,
and is fan-shaped.
The middle section curves inward on both sides.
Holes are partially drilled in the neck to secure the strings.
It is secured with three pegs,
two on the left and one on the right.
A piece of wood is attached at the end of the soundbox to tie the strings.
It is played by bowing with a wooden bow strung with over eighty horsehairs.
The Bùlěi
is a tube made of bamboo.
The upper end is half-stoppered with wood to form the mouthpiece.
Seven holes face forward,
one hole faces backward,
and the uppermost hole faces forward.
A bamboo membrane is added.
The Jiēzú
consists of two cast copper pieces.
Each has an aperture of 1.8 *cùn*.
They are raised in the middle
with holes pierced through for a cord,
and are struck together by the left and right hands.
In the 54th year of Qiánlóng,
music from the Ānnán state was acquired
and placed at the end of banquet music.
This became the Ānnán Yuèwǔ.
It uses one Gàigǔ,
one Gàipāi,
one Gàishào,
one Gàitán Xiánzi,
one Gàitán Húqín,
one Gàitán Shuāngyùn,
one Gàitán Pípá,
and one Gài Sānyīnlüo.
(In the vernacular of Ānnán,
the names of all musical instruments
begin with the character Gài.)
The Gàigǔ
has a wooden frame covered with leather,
open at the bottom.
Its diameter is 8.4 *cùn*.
It is supported by a stand.
It uses two bamboo mallets,
or it is held with the left hand
and struck with the mallet by the right hand.
The Gàipāi
uses three sandalwood clappers:
one has linked coins attached to its upper end,
one has goose teeth carved on its back,
and one has saw teeth on its right side.
The left hand holds and strikes two clappers together,
the linked coins producing a sharp sound.
The right hand holds the one with saw teeth
and uses it to strike the goose teeth,
creating a varied sound.
The Gàishào
is a transverse flute,
a tube cut from bamboo,
lacquered,
with twenty-one sections.
The first hole on the left is the embouchure.
Next, a bamboo membrane is added.
It has six holes on the right
and two holes at the end, all facing upward.
Two holes on the sides face opposite each other.
Both ends are decorated with horn.
The Gàitán Xiánzi
has three strings
and is made of sandalwood.
The soundbox is rectangular and oval,
with both sides covered with snakeskin.
The spoon-shaped head is hollowed out to secure the strings.
It is secured with three pegs,
two on the left and one on the right.
The Gàitán Húqín
has two strings
and a bamboo neck.
The soundbox is tube-shaped,
slightly bulging at the bottom.
The front is covered with snakeskin.
The curved head is hollowed out.
Both pegs pass from back to front to secure the strings.
The strings, from the nut to the bridge,
are 1.8 *chǐ* long.
The rest follows the system of the Húqín of the Fānbù Hélè.
The Gàitán Shuāngyùn
is like a Yuèqín
with four strings
and is made of sandalwood.
The soundboard is made of *tóng* wood
and is shaped like a full moon.
Its diameter is 1.16 *chǐ*.
Its thickness is 1.8 *cùn*.
The curved neck is hollowed out to secure the strings.
It is secured with four pegs,
two on the left and two on the right.
On the soundboard there is a bridge,
and seven frets below the nut,
all made of sandalwood.
The Gàitán Pípá
has four strings
and is made of hollowed *tóng* wood.
Its total length is 3 *chǐ*.
The neck is hollowed out to secure the strings.
It is secured with four pegs,
two on the left and two on the right.
Four *xiàng* (frets) are set on the upper part,
and ten *pǐn* (frets) are arranged below.
The strings, from the nut to the bridge,
are 2.14 *chǐ* long.
The Gài Sānyīnlüo
consists of three cast copper gongs
linked by an iron ring
and arranged like the character 品 (pǐn).
The top one has a diameter of 2.45 *cùn*.
The right one has a diameter of 2.38 *cùn*.
The left one has a diameter of 2.3 *cùn*.
It is supported by a sandalwood handle,
and the mallets are made of horn.
For Cìyànlè (banquet music):
It is used for banquets after the Jīngyán ceremony,
for banquets for the civil, military, provincial, and metropolitan examinations,
for banquets for the Yǎnshènggōng,
and for banquets for the Zhèngyī Zhēnrén.
Its instruments are: two Yúnluó,
two *dí*,
two *guǎn*,
two *shēng*,
one *gǔ*,
and one *pāibǎn*.
(The *dí*, *shēng*, and *gǔ* are the same as in the Zhōnghé Sháolè.
The Yúnluó, *guǎn*, and *bǎn* are the same as in the Dānbì Dàlè.)
For Xiānglè (local music):
It is used for the spring and autumn *shìdiàn* ceremonies in prefectural, departmental, and county schools.
Its instruments are: one *huī*,
sixteen biānzhōng,
sixteen biānxìng,
six *qín*,
two *sè*,
two páixiāo,
four *xiāo*,
six *dí*,
two *chí*,
six *shēng*,
two *xūn*,
one jiàngǔ,
two *bófǔ*,
one *zhù*,
and one *yǔ*.
(All are made in the same manner as those of the Zhōnghé Sháolè.)
For the Xiāngyǐnjǐu ceremony, one Yúnluó,
one fāngxiǎng,
two *qín*,
one *sè*,
four *xiāo*,
four *dí*,
four *shēng*,
one shǒugǔ,
and one *pāibǎn* are used.
(The *qín*, *sè*, *xiāo*, *dí*, and *shēng* are the same as in the Zhōnghé Sháolè.
The Yúnluó, fāngxiǎng, and *bǎn* are the same as in the Dānbì Dàlè.
The shǒugǔ is the same as in the Qīnglè.)
Jié,
(Used in Zhōnghé Sháolè.
) Nine layers of yak tails,
covered with gold leaves,
bound with green leather.
Crimson pole,
the top curved into a dragon's head to hold the yak tails.
Frames are erected one on the east and one on the west,
each frame having two jié.
Musicians hold them to regulate the dance.
(The jié directs the civil dance,
the jīng directs the martial dance.
Jīng is also called jié,
its form is the same as the jié.
Gān,
(Used in Zhōnghé Sháolè.
) Made of wood,
with a guī-shaped top.
The upper half is painted with five-colored clouds and dragons,
the lower half with intertwined dragons,
edged with five-colored feather patterns.
The middle is a white ground,
with vermilion writing:
"Rain and sun in season,
the four seas forever clear.
Granaries full,
the eight directions tranquil.
Observe the three, eternally settled,
obtain the one, thus righteous.
All deities receive their offices,
all nations come to court."
There are eight phrases in total,
one phrase for each yì.
The back of the gān is crimson,
with two horizontal bands.
A curved wooden piece is inserted in the middle.
Martial dancers hold it in their left hand.
Qī,
(Used in Zhōnghé Sháolè.
) Made of wood,
axe-shaped.
Black back, white blade.
Crimson handle.
Martial dancers hold it in their right hand.
Yǔ,
(Used in Zhōnghé Sháolè.
) Wooden handle,
planted with pheasant feathers,
held by a gilt dragon's head.
Crimson handle.
Civil dancers hold it in their right hand.
Yuè,
(Used in Zhōnghé Sháolè.
) Six-holed bamboo pipe,
crimson.
Civil dancers hold it in their left hand.
There are two types of dances: those used for offering sacrifices to gods are called yìwǔ,
those used for banquets are called duìwǔ.
All yìwǔ use gān and qī for martial dances,
and yǔ and yuè for civil dances.
Gān and qī are called the "dance of martial achievement,"
yǔ and yuè are called the "dance of civil virtue."
For sacrifices, the first offering uses martial dances,
the second and final offerings use civil dances.
Only at the temples of the Former Teacher (Kǒngzǐ) and Wénchāng, the first, second, and final offerings all use civil dances.
As for the Great Yú ceremony,
sixteen boys wear black robes,
hold yǔyì,
sing and perform the Huángwǔ.
All of these belong to the yìwǔ category.
Those belonging to the duìwǔ category
were initially called Mǎngshìwǔ,
(also called Mǎkèshìwǔ).
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng,
it was renamed Qìnglóngwǔ.
Within it, the Great and Small Mǎhù were divided into Yánglièwǔ,
which was the martial dance,
and the dance performed by high officials offering longevity was Xǐqǐwǔ,
which was the civil dance.
In that year, during a tour to Shèngjīng,
a banquet was held for the imperial clan,
and the Shìdéwǔ was added.
In the fourteenth year,
after the pacification of Jīnchuān,
a triumphant banquet was held,
and the Déshèngwǔ was also added.
The three dances had the same form,
each with its own musical scores.
For Yánglièwǔ,
thirty-two people wearing masks were used.
Half wore yellow painted cloth,
half wore black sheepskin.
They leaped and somersaulted,
imitating exotic beasts.
Eight people rode Yúmǎ,
armored with bows and arrows,
advancing in two wings.
They faced north, bowed once,
then rose.
They circled and chased,
imitating the Eight Banners.
One beast was struck by an arrow,
and the group of beasts submitted in fear,
symbolizing martial achievement.
For Xǐqǐwǔ,
twenty-two high officials,
dressed in court robes and ceremonial swords, entered.
They bowed three times,
rose,
and retreated to the east side, standing facing west.
They advanced in pairs,
bowed three times after the dance,
and withdrew.
The next group advanced in succession following the previous ritual.
This is the general outline of the duìwǔ.
Besides these, there are the music and dances of the Four Borders: to the east are Wǎ'ěrkā and Cháoxiǎn;
to the north is Ménggǔ;
to the west are Huí, Fān, and Guō'ěrkā;
to the south are Miǎndiàn and Ānnán.
All are presented together at the end of the banquet music.
For the Wǎ'ěrkā tribal music and dance,
there are eight dancers.
All wear red cloud-patterned satin robes with satin floral patches,
large fox fur hats.
They stand ready to the west of the Dānbì.
Before the music begins,
they advance and bow three times,
then withdraw.
Eight musicians
advance in two wings,
kneel on one knee,
and play Wǎ'ěrkā music.
The dancers advance and dance,
forming pairs.
After each pair finishes dancing,
they bow three times,
and withdraw.
For the Cháoxiǎn (Joseon) performers,
there is one each for flute, pipe, and drum skills.
All wear felt hats
with carved gold tops,
blue cloud-patterned satin robes,
brown cloud-patterned satin vests,
and blue silk sashes.
One performer leader
wears a mask,
a dark blue satin hat
with a red tassel,
a red cloud-patterned satin robe,
white silk long sleeves, a green cloud-patterned satin tiger-patched vest,
and a cross-patterned blue silk sash.
Fourteen acrobats
wear short red clothes.
They stand on both sides of the Dānbì.
The performer leader advances from the right wing,
stands facing north,
and gives an address in Gāolí (Korean) language.
The flute, pipe, and drum players advance from the right wing,
stand facing northeast.
The acrobats advance from the left wing,
from east to west,
each displaying their skills.
For Ménggǔ music,
there is kā-flute playing.
Four instrument players
and four lyricists
all wear python-patterned robes,
standing beside the Dānbì.
For the Fān (Tibetan) ensemble,
there are fifteen instrument players.
They also all wear python-patterned robes,
standing beside the Dānbì,
entering together with the kā-flute group.
They bow once,
kneel on one knee,
and play Ménggǔ music.
For Huí (Muslim) music,
there are eight instrument players.
All wear brocade clothing, silk trousers, variegated spun silk spliced-sleeve robes,
brocade-faced cloth trousers, Wōduàn-edged Huíhuí hats,
dark blue satin boots,
and green silk shoulder guards.
Two dancers,
two plate dancers,
all wear kàozi brocade waistbands and spun silk spliced-sleeve robes.
Four large Huízǐ acrobats
all wear kàozi variegated spun silk spliced-sleeve robes,
and five-colored silk Huíhuí small caps.
Two small Huízǐ
wear variegated silk clothing and silk trousers.
All stand ready below the Dānbì.
After the Cháoxiǎn (Joseon) performers display their skills,
they ascend the Dānbì to perform music.
The dancers begin to dance,
and the plate dancers accompany the dance.
When finished,
the small Huízǐ acrobats follow to display their skills.
Foreigners' Music.
From Ā'ěrsàlán in Jīnchuān,
three musicians play instruments,
three dancers dance.
They perform a lion dance.
The lion is seven feet long,
covered in multi-colored fur.
Its foreign name is Sēnggéyǐ.
The lion handler wears clothes of mixed colors,
holding a rope
tied to a juggling ball,
of five colors.
Its foreign name is Sēnggéyǐ Ālākā.
Dàguōzhuāng,
its foreign name is Dàlāgáde.
Ten dancers perform.
Two people dance hand-in-hand.
One wears a python robe,
with a feather,
and hanging beads,
with two sashes, yellow and blue, draped diagonally,
crossing like a cross.
The other wears a blue robe,
with hanging beads,
with two sashes, yellow and purple, draped diagonally,
crossing like a cross.
Sìjiǎolǔ,
its foreign name is Délèbù.
Six dancers perform,
wearing dancing helmets,
whose foreign name is Dámào.
Each inserts six chicken feathers,
whose foreign name is Dámòyǐ.
They have rattan shields tied to their backs,
whose foreign name is Sàisīdān.
They wear waist knives on their belts,
whose foreign name is Jiānggéyǐ.
They hold bows in their left hands,
whose foreign name is Démùníyě.
They hold arrow quivers in their right hands,
whose foreign name is Bólā.
Holding five arrows,
whose foreign name is Gé bìyǐ.
They dance facing each other.
Bānchán's Zháshílúnbù,
whose foreign name is Bólāgá.
Six musicians play instruments.
Ten foreign children dance,
each wearing a long sash,
holding an axe,
whose foreign name is Shālèbiē.
They dance and sing Buddhist chants.
Guō'ěrkā music and dance.
Six musicians play instruments.
All wear Huízi clothes,
and red sheepskin boots.
Two of them wrap their heads with foreign brocade,
the rest with red and green cloth.
Five singers sing.
All wrap their heads with red and green cloth.
One wears a green silk garment,
and red embroidered shoes.
The rest wear Huízi clothes and red sheepskin boots.
Two dancers perform.
All wear red and green silk garments,
wearing scarlet felt hats,
gold and silver threaded scarves,
and red embroidered shoes.
Their waists are all tied with various colored cloths.
Each dancer ties a string of copper bells to each foot,
called Gōnggǔlǐ.
They leap and make sounds.
Singing and dancing are performed together.
Crude Miǎndiàn music.
Five musicians play instruments.
Six singers sing.
All wear their hair long and tied with red,
in Miǎndiàn clothing and headwear.
Refined Miǎndiàn music.
Seven musicians play instruments.
All wear their hair long and tied with red,
and blue satin short jackets.
Four dancers perform.
Wearing shimmering satin short jackets,
all with multi-colored skirts,
their waists are tied with foreign brocade,
wearing tied scarves.
Singing is accompanied by crude music,
dancing is accompanied by refined music.
Ānnán Kingdom music.
Nine musicians play instruments.
All wear Dào scarves,
and yellow oriole embroidered Taoist robes,
with blue satin sashes.
Four dancers perform.
Wearing python robes,
their crowns and sashes are the same as the instrumentalists.
They dance holding colorful fans.

Record 77: Carriages and Attire 1: Emperor's Five Carriages; Emperor's Palanquin and Carriage; Empress's Carriage and Chariot (with Empress Dowager's Carriage and Chariot attached); Imperial Noble Consort and below's Carriages and Chariots; Prince and below's Carriages and Chariots; Prince's Consort and below's Carriages and Chariots; Officials outside the capital's Carriages and Chariots (with commoners attached); Ladies of Rank's Carriages and Chariots.
From Yú Dǐng's embroidered garments,
the system of "trailing robes" was created.
The distinctions of carriages and attire,
thus shone forth as a common practice.
The Xià dynasty's headwear and the Yīn dynasty's carriages,
showed different styles, simple and refined.
Coming to the Zhōu dynasty,
it learned from the two preceding dynasties.
Officials for caps and chariots,
officials for attire and banners.
Each with specialized officers,
with clear rites and complete provisions.
From Qín and Hàn onwards,
each dynasty had its differences.
The number of ranks became increasingly complex,
as fully recorded in previous chapters.
In the early Míng, wooden carriages,
were used for suburban sacrifices,
valuing simplicity over elaborate carving,
which was also commendable.
The Qīng's Tàizǔ,
rose in the eastern frontier,
diligently pursuing distant strategies,
and wore military attire.
Tàizōng inherited the mantle,
and then established the capital in Liáo.
In the sixth year of Tiāncōng,
he had already ordered the ritual officials to review and establish ceremonial guards,
and because of the problem of changing clothes and forgetting ancestors,
he learned from Jīn and Yuán.
The national customs of clothing and headwear,
all followed the old style.
Never forgetting one's origins,
to be shown to future generations.
Shìzǔ entered the pass,
and ruled over Zhōngxià.
Military achievements were established,
and culture gradually flourished.
During the Kāngxī and Yōngzhèng reigns,
there were continuous additions and revisions.
Court regulations and national splendor,
were already brilliant.
Even Gāozōng,
was able to inherit the tradition of attire.
Ruling with peace and harmony,
he employed Confucian officials.
Established the "Three Compendia" (Sāntōng),
deciphering ancient texts and compiling records.
The number of the five carriages,
was revised to conform to the Zhōuguān.
Comparing ancient and present,
detailed illustrations of ritual vessels were provided.
Thus, for imperial conveyances,
many additions and revisions were made.
The ceremonial regulations of this dynasty,
were at their most elaborate at this time.
From then on,
succeeding generations, high and low,
generally followed previous regulations,
and there were no extravagant changes.
Investigating these systems,
this chapter is dedicated to them.
The section on Lǔbù (Imperial Equipage),
includes escorts.
During the Guāngxù and Xuāntǒng eras,
naval and land forces emerged.
Flag designs and uniforms,
underwent a sudden transformation.
Already seen in the Military Records,
they are not repeated here.
Seals, treasures, stamps, and tallies,
are used to signify trust.
Dragon, tortoise, insect, bird,
each with different knob and script.
Successive dynasties followed them,
all relying on them as legal standards.
Detailed established styles,
all based on rank differences.
Also, since the opening of maritime trade,
international relations became paramount.
For exchanges and gifts,
orders of merit (Bǎoxīng) were replicated.
With distinctions of name and rank,
to honor wearers.
Towards the late period,
new systems gradually proliferated,
including titles of nobility,
which were not in practice for long.
Such matters,
are only briefly mentioned here.
In the early Qīng dynasty, the Míng dynasty's old system was retained.
There were the *Yùlù*, *Dàlù*, *Dàmǎniǎn*, and *Xiǎomǎniǎn* conveyances,
which, along with the *Xiāngbùniǎn*, were collectively known as the Five Carriages (*wǔniǎn*).
The *Dàcháorì* was displayed east of the Tàihé Mén.
Also, there were the *Liángbùniǎn*, *Dàyíjiào*, *Dàjiào*, *Míngjiào*, and *Zhéhémíngjiào*.
All of these were managed by the Left Office.
During the Great Sacrifices of the Winter Solstice and the Sacrifices to Fāngzé in the Summer Solstice, the *Liángbùniǎn* was used.
On the day of ascending the throne hall, it was also displayed east of the Tàihé Mén.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng (1742),
it was decreed that when the emperor personally performed the rites for the Great Sacrifices,
he would travel in a palanquin out of the palace
and then transfer to a carriage (*niǎn*) at the Tàihé Mén.
After the sacrifices, he would return to the palace,
again using a palanquin.
In the eighth year (1743),
the *Dàlù* was renamed *Jīnlù*,
the *Dàmǎniǎn* was renamed *Xiànglù*,
the *Xiǎomǎniǎn* was renamed *Gélù*,
the *Xiāngbùniǎn* was renamed *Mùlù*,
and the *Yùlù* remained unchanged.
These were known as the Five Chariots (*wǔlù*),
managed by the Luányí Wèi.
During the Great Court Assemblies,
they were displayed outside the Wǔ Mén.
In the thirteenth year (1748),
an imperial edict stipulated the use of the Five Chariots,
starting from the Southern Suburbs sacrifices of that year.
A new *Yùniǎn* was constructed,
and the *Liángbùniǎn* was renamed *Jīnniǎn*.
These were known as the Two Carriages (*èrniǎn*).
It was also decreed that the *Dàyíjiào* would be the *Lǐyú*,
the *Zhéhémíngjiào* would be renamed *Qīngbùyú*,
and the *Dàjiào* would be designated *Bùyú*.
These were known as the Three Palanquins (*sānyú*).
For the Southern Suburbs sacrifices, the *Yùniǎn* was used.
For the Northern Suburbs, Tàimiào, and Shèjì Tán sacrifices,
the *Jīnniǎn* was used.
For the *Cháorì*, *Xīyuè*, *Gēngjí*, and other minor sacrifices,
the *Lǐyú* was used.
During the Great Court Assemblies,
they were all displayed outside the Tàihé Mén.
For imperial progresses, the *Qīngbùyú* was used.
When the imperial carriage entered or exited, the *Bùyú* was used.
The carriages and palanquins for imperial princes
were only to be constructed after their enfeoffment.
Here, we compile what is recorded in the *Lǐqìtú*.
Those stipulated before Qiánlóng are considered the initial system,
appended by category,
for reference and scrutiny.
The Emperor's *Yùlù* was
made of wood, painted vermillion,
with a round canopy and a square base,
standing one *zhàng* two *chǐ* one *cùn* high (approx. 3.9 meters).
The canopy was three *chǐ* one *fēn* high (approx. 0.99 meters),
decorated in blue,
with four jade-inlaid round plaques.
It was topped with a golden round finial one *chǐ* two *cùn* nine *fēn* high (approx. 0.42 meters),
supported by a carved golden "hanging cloud" eaves eight *chǐ* one *cùn* long (approx. 2.6 meters),
adorned with three layers of gold-carved cloud plaques.
There were also three layers of blue satin draperies,
embroidered with intertwining golden clouds, dragons, and feathers.
Four embroidered golden blue satin straps
were attached to the base.
The four posts were six *chǐ* seven *cùn* nine *fēn* high (approx. 2.17 meters),
each five *chǐ* six *cùn* apart (approx. 1.8 meters),
painted with golden clouds and dragons.
Vermillion curtains hung at the doors,
three on each of the four sides.
The seat was eight *chǐ* five *cùn* long (approx. 2.74 meters)
and eight *chǐ* four *cùn* wide (approx. 2.71 meters),
encircled by a vermillion railing,
decorated with interspersed gold and colorful designs.
Floral carpets covered the interior of the railing.
The Cloud Dragon Throne was in the center,
one *chǐ* three *cùn* high (approx. 0.42 meters)
and two *chǐ* nine *cùn* wide (approx. 0.93 meters).
Each of the two wheels had eighteen spokes,
carved with flowers and adorned with gold.
They were fitted with two axles and shafts,
twenty-two *chǐ* nine *cùn* five *fēn* long (approx. 7.4 meters),
with golden dragon heads and tails adorning both ends.
The base was eleven *chǐ* one *cùn* five *fēn* long (approx. 3.6 meters)
and eight *chǐ* four *cùn* in diameter (approx. 2.71 meters).
At the back, a *tàicháng* banner was erected,
with twelve streamers,
also made of blue satin,
embroidered with the sun, moon, and five planets.
The streamers were embroidered with the twenty-eight constellations.
All the tassels were embroidered with golden dragons,
and five-colored silk tassels hung below.
It used a bundled bamboo vermillion pole.
To the left was added a *xījí* (ceremonial halberd),
to the right was decorated a dragon head,
and both were adorned with five vermillion yak-tail flags (*máo*),
with blue silk ribbons hanging down.
For ascending, five steps were used,
with vermillion and golden railings on both sides.
It was pulled by one elephant,
with vermillion velvet traces.
When displayed,
two barriers (*xíngmǎ*) supported the shafts.
These were also straight vermillion poles,
with copper tips at both ends.
(The initial system:
The dimensions of the *Yùlù* were the same as the *Dàlù*.
The flat platform above the carriage, the bead-drop panel, wheel spokes, felloes, hub, axle ends, and all ropes for the shafts were also the same.
However, it lacked the twelve compartments beneath the flat platform and the eight compartments on the left and right.
The two front pillars of the carriage pavilion
were decorated with raised and gilded ascending dragons.
The dimensions of the pavilion pillars, railings, and seats,
as well as the door panels, decorative elements, and all constructions beneath the soft seats inside the pavilion,
were entirely the same as the *Dàlù*.
The only difference was that the screens were carved with five cloud-dragons in agarwood color outlined in gold,
and beneath the screens, the three lower panels were carved with three cloud-dragons in agarwood color outlined in gold.
Beneath these, cloud panels were carved in the same number,
which was slightly different from the *Dàlù* system.
The carriage roof, round platform, celestial wheel, and all front constructions of the carriage pavilion,
as well as the *Tàicháng* banner, steps, and barriers,
were all the same as the *Dàlù*.)
The Jīnlù
also has one elephant yoked.
It has a round canopy and a square chassis,
decorated in yellow,
with four gold round plates attached.
Three layers of yellow satin curtains hang down.
Four ties,
also made of yellow satin,
are attached to the chassis.
At the rear, a large banner is erected,
with twelve streamers,
each embroidered with a gold dragon.
The rest is made according to the style of the Yùlù.
(Note: The name Jīnlù
was changed from Dàlù.
In its initial design,
the Dàlù was one zhàng, three chǐ, nine cùn, and five fēn high,
and eight chǐ, two cùn, and five fēn wide.
On the carriage was a flat platform,
with front and rear railings and "goose wings" (yànchì), and four dangling rúyì ornaments.
Beneath the "dripping pearl" (dīzhū) board were two shafts,
each over two zhàng, two chǐ, and nine cùn long,
both adorned with vermilion, gilded copper dragon heads and tails,
with scales and leaf-shaped pieces attached.
Beneath the flat platform was a square box,
with vermilion frames on all four sides,
twelve compartments at the front and back,
inside of which were blue grounds painted with five-colored clouds and cranes,
and eight compartments on the left and right,
with blue grounds on top and green grounds below,
painted with six beasts and birds each.
There were two wheels,
pierced by an axle,
each wheel having eighteen spokes and felloes,
all vermilion,
adorned with gilded copper engraved flower and leaf pieces.
Inside each wheel was a hub,
adorned with gilded copper engraved lotus petal wheel discs.
Iron pins were inserted into the ends of the axle on both sides,
adorned with gilded copper engraved dragon-head tube cores.
The axle was wrapped with red velvet for the various ropes of the shafts.
The carriage pavilion was six chǐ, seven cùn, and nine fēn high,
with four columns each five chǐ, eight cùn, and four fēn long.
The plinth seat was nine cùn, five fēn high,
with front and rear columns engraved with gold cloud-dragon patterns,
and mountains and waters below.
The main door was five chǐ, one cùn, nine fēn high,
and two chǐ, four cùn, nine fēn wide.
The left and right doors were each two chǐ, two cùn, five fēn wide,
with twelve carved wood agarwood-colored panels with gilded auspicious grass designs around the top.
At the front left and right were two hinged doors each,
with complete visible tenons,
all vermilion,
adorned with gilded copper engraved flower and leaf pieces.
The hinged doors were woven with yellow silk cord.
At the rear was a vermilion screen,
in front of which were three upper hinged doors,
carved in agarwood color with five gilded cloud dragons.
Above was a vermilion panel,
engraved with one gold cloud dragon.
The middle three hinged doors
had three agarwood-colored gilded cloud dragons.
The lower three hinged doors
had gilded cloud panels matching their number.
Behind the screen, the upper three hinged doors
had three vermilion engraved gold dragons.
The next had gold engraved cloud panels matching their number.
The middle three hinged doors
had four vermilion engraved gold dragons.
The next had agarwood-colored gilded cloud panels matching their number.
The lower three hinged doors
also had agarwood-colored cloud panels matching their number.
All were adorned with gilded copper engraved flower and leaf pieces.
Inside the pavilion, a vermilion frame was woven with yellow silk cord,
and the soft seat had four large yellow velvet ropes dangling,
with lotus-shaped pendant stones hanging below.
Above were flower rugs and straw mats,
and a large red gold-woven brocade mattress.
There was one vermilion chair,
its backrest carved with one agarwood-colored gilded cloud dragon,
below which was carved one cloud panel,
and one vermilion "fortune and longevity" (fúshòu) panel,
along with a complete set of yellow gold-woven chair covers, seat cushions, and four surrounding chair skirts.
Yellow silk curtains surrounded it,
or yellow silk gauze was used.
Outside the pavilion were ten red curtains with blue brocade edges,
each with two yellow silk cords for pulling the curtains,
and complete yellow copper rings.
The carriage roof and round platform were three chǐ, one fēn high,
topped with a gilded copper crouching dragon,
with an inverted and upright lotus seat,
one chǐ, two cùn, nine fēn high, from which four yellow velvet ropes for climbing the roof hung.
The platform was two cùn high,
topped with vermilion.
Below it, the outer four sides had agarwood-colored grounds,
with gilded clouds and green decorations.
Inside the carriage cover pavilion were gold-leafed *dǒugǒng* brackets,
supporting a vermilion framed precious canopy,
with eight corners,
covered with yellow brocade,
named Huángwū.
The center and surroundings were embroidered with nine five-colored cloud dragons.
There were three layers of "heavenly wheels" (tiānlún),
vermilion,
on which were placed eighty-one carved wood gold-leafed "dragon-gleaming leaf" (lóngyàoyè) panels.
Between the three layers were painted five-colored clouds,
and the number of backing panels also matched.
Below the platform, the four sides were adorned with yellow copper,
with three layers of golden yellow brocade water-drip ornaments,
each layer having eighty-one pleats,
interspersed with embroidered five-colored cloud dragon patterns.
From the four corners hung blue brocade sashes,
each embroidered with three five-colored rising dragons.
The four corners of the round platform were connected to the carriage seat panels with yellow silk round cords for climbing the roof,
and gold-leafed wooden fish.
In front of the carriage pavilion were two sets of left and right corner railings,
and one straight railing at the back with left and right corner railings,
all vermilion.
Inside were inlaid carved wood gold-leafed dragons,
interspersed with five-colored clouds.
The three railings had a total of twelve columns,
each column topped with one carved wood gold-leafed crouching dragon,
and gilded five-colored decorative lotus-wrapped columns.
Inside the railings, flower rugs and straw mats were placed all around.
Behind them stood two Tàicháng banners,
made of yellow cloud satin,
both with twelve streamers.
Each streamer was embroidered with one rising dragon inside and out.
There were two vermilion assembled bamboo poles,
the left pole's banner waist embroidered with the sun, moon, and Big Dipper,
and the pole top used a gilded copper dragon head.
The right pole's banner waist embroidered with *fú* characters,
and the pole top used a gilded copper *jǐ* (halberd).
Each was adorned with two gilded copper bells,
and twelve red tassels hung down,
with gilded copper precious canopies above,
and blue silk streamers below.
There was one stepping ladder,
made of vermilion wood,
adorned with gilded copper engraved flower and leaf pieces.
There were two "horse racks" (xíngmǎ jià),
made of vermilion wood,
adorned with gilded copper leaf pieces,
with yellow velvet flat cords threaded through the top.
One yellow cloth-faced silk-lined carriage cover, one oiled silk raincoat,
one red oiled folding ladder, one red oiled grappling hook each.
Two gold-leafed copper precious vases,
along with carved wood gold-leafed inverted and upright lotus seats,
carved flower and exotic grass gold-leafed elephant saddles, harnesses, and felt cages each.
The Xiànglù,
has four服馬 (fúmǎ) and
six驂馬 (cānmǎ).
It is fitted with movable rings and bells,
with a round canopy and a square chariot body (zhěn).
Its height is one zhàng, one chǐ, three cùn.
The canopy is two chǐ, six cùn, five fēn high.
It has four red-decorated, ivory-inlaid round plaques.
Three layers of red satin aprons hang down,
with four ties,
also made of red satin,
attached to the chariot body.
The four pillars are six chǐ, four cùn, nine fēn high,
each separated by five chǐ, eight cùn.
The seat is one zhàng, five fēn long
and nine chǐ, one cùn wide,
encircled by a vermilion railing (zhūlán).
There are three shafts (yuán),
each two zhàng, two chǐ, three cùn long.
The chariot body is one zhàng, five fēn long,
with a diameter of nine chǐ, one cùn.
At the rear is erected a large vermilion banner (dàchì),
with twelve streamers (yóu),
each embroidered with a golden phoenix.
The rest of its construction is the same as the Yùlù.
(Note: The Xiànglù was a redesign of the Dàmǎniǎn.
In its original design,
the Dàmǎniǎn was one zhàng, two chǐ, five cùn, nine fēn high
and eight chǐ, nine cùn, five fēn wide.
It had two shafts,
each two zhàng, five cùn, nine fēn long.
The flat platform, dripping pearl board, spokes, felloes, hub, axle caps, and all the harnessing ropes on the palanquin were
all like those of the Dàlù.
It also lacked the decorations of twelve anterior and posterior compartments and eight left and right compartments below the flat platform.
The palanquin pavilion was six chǐ, four cùn, nine fēn high,
vermilion.
The four pillars were five chǐ, five cùn, four fēn long.
The railing seat was as high as the palanquin pavilion.
Its upper perimeter had twelve carved wooden, aloeswood-colored, gold-painted cloud panels.
The bottom also had the same.
The door was five chǐ, nine fēn high,
and two chǐ, four cùn, five fēn wide.
The width of the left and right doors was two cùn less.
There were two panels each at the front and sides,
and three panels at the rear,
fully equipped with transparent lattices (míngcì),
all vermilion,
adorned with gold-painted copper chased floral leaf decorations.
The center of the panels was woven with yellow silk cord.
Inside the pavilion was a soft seat,
covered with a plain blanket.
The rest of its construction was the same as the Dàlù.
The palanquin roof and circular plate were two chǐ, six cùn, five fēn high,
both top and bottom vermilion.
The palanquin canopy was blue-decorated.
The bronze dragons, lotus pedestals, precious canopies, and yellow coverings were all made like those of the Dàlù.
The three layers of celestial wheels were also like them.
At the front of the palanquin pavilion was a straight railing,
at the rear a straight railing with corner turns,
and on the left and right two railings,
inlaid with cord-ringed panels,
all vermilion.
The four panels had a total of twelve pillars,
the carved decorations at the top of each pillar were the same as the Dàlù.
Inside the railings were spread plain blankets and straw mats.
The Tàicháng flag, foot ladder, barrier horse (xíngmǎ), curtain cover (xiǎnyī), and rain cover (yǔyī) were also like them.
However, the lù was drawn by elephants,
and the niǎn by horses,
so the decorations of saddles, cruppers, bridles, and bell tassels were all prepared for them.)
The Mùlù,
has two服馬 (fúmǎ) and
four驂馬 (cānmǎ).
It is fitted with movable rings and bells,
with a round canopy and a square chariot body (zhěn).
Its height is one zhàng, one chǐ, six cùn, five fēn.
The canopy is three chǐ, six cùn, one fēn high.
It has four black-decorated, huālí-inlaid round plaques.
Three layers of black satin aprons hang down,
with four ties,
also made of black satin,
attached to the chariot body.
The four pillars are six chǐ, five fēn high,
each separated by five chǐ, one cùn.
The seat is nine chǐ long
and eight chǐ, eight cùn wide,
encircled by a vermilion railing (zhūlán).
There are three shafts (yuán),
each two zhàng, one chǐ long.
The chariot body is nine chǐ long,
with a diameter of eight chǐ, eight cùn.
At the rear is erected a large banner (dàhuī),
with twelve streamers (yóu),
each embroidered with Divine Martial (Shénwǔ).
The rest of its construction is entirely like that of the Yùlù.
(Note: The Mùlù was a redesign of the Xiāngbùniǎn.
In its original design,
the Xiāngbùniǎn was one zhàng, two chǐ, five cùn high.
The seat was three chǐ high,
with a square width of eight chǐ, two cùn, five fēn.
The palanquin seat was vermilion,
its perimeter had twelve carved wooden, polychrome cloud, wholly gold-leafed dragon panels,
interspersed with wholly gold-leafed upright and inverted lotus pedestals.
Below the seat were twenty carved wooden, gold-lined, polychrome cloud panels.
Below the seat were four shafts;
the two central shafts were three zhàng, five chǐ, nine cùn long,
the left and right shafts were two zhàng, nine chǐ, five cùn long with a surplus,
all vermilion,
adorned with gilded bronze dragon heads and tails,
with eight yellow cord-ringed loops for pulling the shafts.
The palanquin pavilion was six chǐ, five fēn high,
its four pillars each five chǐ, eight cùn long.
The railing was two cùn, five fēn high,
also all vermilion.
Its upper perimeter had twelve carved wooden, aloeswood-colored, gold-painted fragrant herb panels,
adorned with gold-painted bronze lù-shaped chased floral leaf decorations.
The door was two cùn taller than the Dàmǎniǎn,
and its width was the same.
The left and right doors were two chǐ, two cùn wide.
At the front and left-right sides were two vermilion 十字槅 (shízìgé) panels each,
with eight carved aloeswood-colored, gold-painted cloud dragon panels,
and the same number of cloud panels below,
all adorned with gold-painted copper chased floral leaf decorations.
Inside the pavilion were spread floral carpets and straw mats,
a large red brocaded gold-threaded silk cushion,
and one vermilion carved gold dragon chair.
The construction from the backrest downwards was the same as the large and small Dàmǎniǎn.
The palanquin roof and circular plate were two chǐ, six cùn high with a surplus,
with a gilded bronze crouching dragon top.
The rest of the construction was the same as the large and small Dàmǎniǎn.
The celestial wheels were also made in the same way.
At the front of the palanquin pavilion were two left and right corner-turning railings,
and at the rear one straight railing with left and right corner turns,
all vermilion,
inlaid with carved wooden, gold-leafed dragons,
interspersed with polychrome clouds.
The three panels had a total of twelve pillars,
the carved decorations at the top of each pillar were the same as the Dàlù.
Inside the railings were spread floral carpets and straw mats all around.
Inside the pavilion was one carved wooden, wholly gold-leafed sword mountain,
one vermilion footrest,
and a complete set of yellow satin covers.
There was one foot ladder,
made of vermilion wood,
adorned with six carved gold-leafed flying dragon and polychrome cloud cord-ringed panels,
twelve gold-painted polychrome water panels,
and four crouching dragons,
all adorned with gold-painted copper chased floral leaf decorations.
Its curtain covers and rain covers were all made according to the specifications of the large and small Dàmǎniǎn.)
A Géluò (革輅)
has one shaft horse,
three outriggers.
It is also fitted with movable rings and bells,
a round canopy and a square carriage bed.
Its height is one zhàng (丈), one chǐ (尺), three cùn (寸).
The canopy is two chǐ (尺), five cùn (寸), five fēn (分) high.
It is adorned with four mud-silver decorated bridle bits and round yellow leather pieces.
Three layers of white satin valances hang down,
with four ties,
also made of white satin,
attached to the carriage bed.
The four pillars are five chǐ (尺), five cùn (寸), nine fēn (分) high.
The seat is one zhàng (丈), six chǐ (尺) long
and eight chǐ (尺), three cùn (寸), five fēn (分) wide,
encircled by a vermilion balustrade.
There are two shafts,
each one zhàng (丈), nine chǐ (尺), five fēn (分) long.
The carriage bed is one zhàng (丈), six cùn (寸) long,
and eight chǐ (尺), three cùn (寸), five fēn (分) in diameter.
At the back, a Dàbái (大白)
with twelve streamers is erected.
Each streamer is embroidered with a golden tiger.
The rest of the construction is identical to the Yùlù (玉輅).
(Note: The change from Xiǎomǎniǎn (小馬輦) to Géluò (革輅)
began in the eighth year of Qiánlóng (乾隆).
Initially,
the Xiǎomǎniǎn (小馬輦) was one chǐ (尺) less in height and width than the Dàmǎniǎn (大馬輦).
The two lower shafts were one zhàng (丈), nine chǐ (尺), five fēn (分) long.
The flat platform, drip-bead board, spokes, and felloes were all the same as the Dàmǎniǎn (大馬輦).
The sedan pavilion was five chǐ (尺), five cùn (寸), nine fēn (分) high,
and vermilion.
The four pillars were five chǐ (尺), four cùn (寸), five fēn (分) long.
The threshold was one cùn (寸), four fēn (分) high,
with twelve pieces of agarwood-colored, gold-painted cloud panels carved around the top,
and likewise below.
The door was five chǐ (尺) high
and two chǐ (尺), two cùn (寸), five fēn (分) wide.
The width of the left and right doors was reduced by a little over one cùn (寸).
In front, on the left and right, there were two latticework panels each,
with all their bright wooden teeth intact,
all vermilion,
and adorned with gilt-brass engraved floral leaf pieces.
The core of the latticework was woven with yellow thread braids.
At the back, there was a vermilion screen,
carved with five agarwood-colored, gold-painted cloud dragons,
and three agarwood-colored, gold-painted cloud dragon braid-ring panels,
the number of cloud panels also being the same.
The perimeter was also adorned with gilt-brass engraved floral leaf pieces.
On the vermilion board of the pavilion seat, a plain felt mat and straw mat were laid,
with a red woven gold brocade cushion.
Outside, there were four red curtains.
The seat, backrest, and other parts below were all the same as the Dàmǎniǎn (大馬輦).
The sedan roof and round platform were one cùn (寸) lower than the Dàmǎniǎn (大馬輦).
The top was decorated with a gilt-bronze precious pearl finial.
The lotus base, precious canopy, and other ornaments,
as well as the heavenly wheel and other structures in front of the sedan pavilion,
were also the same as the Dàmǎniǎn (大馬輦).
The Yùniǎn (玉輦)
is made of vermilion wood,
with a round canopy and a square base.
Its height is one zhàng (丈), one chǐ (尺), one cùn (寸).
The canopy is two chǐ (尺) high.
It has four blue decorations and jade-mounted round plaques.
It is topped with a golden round finial,
