supported by openwork gold hanging clouds.
Four curved beams hang down,
ending in golden cloud leaves.
Two layers of blue satin valances hang down,
pleated all around.
Four ties,
made of yellow wool,
are attached to the corners of the base.
The four pillars are five chǐ (尺), three cùn (寸) high,
each five chǐ (尺) apart,
and painted with cloud dragons.
The door is four chǐ (尺), eight cùn (寸) high.
In winter, blue felt door curtains are used,
replaced by vermilion curtains in summer,
edged with black satin,
three on each of the four sides.
The base is two chǐ (尺), four cùn (寸) high.
The upper part is seven chǐ (尺), six cùn (寸) square.
The lower part is seven chǐ (尺), seven cùn (寸) square.
It is adorned with two layers of panels,
the upper painted with colorful clouds,
the lower painted with golden clouds,
and encircled by a vermilion balustrade,
one chǐ (尺), six cùn (寸), eight fēn (分) high,
decorated with gold and colorful patterns.
Flower carpets are spread all around inside the balustrade.
A cloud-dragon throne is in the center,
one chǐ (尺), three cùn (寸) high.
To the left, a bronze tripod is placed;
to the right, a ceremonial sword is erected.
There are four shafts.
The inner two shafts are three zhàng (丈), eight cùn (寸), five fēn (分) long.
The outer two shafts are two zhàng (丈), nine chǐ (尺) long.
Golden dragon heads and tails connect the two ends.
For ascending, a five-step nàbì (納陛) is used.
The left and right balustrades are all vermilion,
also decorated with gold and colorful patterns.
It is carried by thirty-six people.
The Golden Palanquin
has a round canopy and a square base.
It is one zhàng and five chì high.
The canopy is one chì and nine cùn high.
The canopy is decorated with four round gold plates set with niánjīn.
It is topped with a golden round finial.
The diameter of the eaves is seven chì and one cùn.
Two layers of yellow satin curtains hang down.
The posts are five chì high,
each spaced four chì and nine cùn apart.
The door is four chì, seven cùn, and five fēn high.
In winter, yellow felt door curtains are hung,
replaced in summer by crimson blinds,
edged with black satin,
three on each of the four sides.
The upper part of the seat is seven chì and three cùn square,
the lower part is seven chì and five cùn square,
encircled by a crimson railing,
one chì and three cùn high.
There are four shafts;
the inner two shafts are two zhàng, eight chì, and one cùn long,
the outer two shafts are two zhàng, six chì, and one cùn long.
It is borne by twenty-eight people.
The rest is in the style of the Jade Palanquin.
(According to the 13th year of Qiánlóng's reign,
the Cool Walking Palanquin was changed to the Golden Palanquin.
In its original form,
the Cool Walking Palanquin was one zhàng, one chì, and two cùn high,
with the seat two chì and five cùn high.
The palanquin seat was crimson,
the seat board and all four sides were crimson-framed,
with twenty carved wooden gold-leafed cloud panels,
and twelve panels above, decorated with gold ground and carved five-color cloud patterns,
with inverted and everted lotus bases.
There were four lower shafts,
the middle two shafts were two zhàng, eight chì, and five cùn long,
the left and right shafts were two chì shorter,
all crimson,
with gilded copper dragon heads and tails affixed at the front and back.
Eight round yellow cord ropes were used for pulling the shafts.
The palanquin pavilion was five chì, five cùn, and five fēn high,
four chì and eight cùn square,
crimson.
The door was four chì and seven cùn high
and two chì and two cùn wide.
The left and right doors were also of the same width.
On all four sides above were twelve agarwood-colored panels with painted gold auspicious plants,
with two latticed doors on the front and each side,
and three latticed doors at the back,
all with clear tenons,
all crimson,
woven with yellow cord ropes.
Flower carpets and straw mats were laid on the palanquin board,
along with red brocade cushions interwoven with gold.
There was one crimson gold-inlaid cloud-dragon seat chair,
with carved wooden agarwood-colored painted gold clouds around the base of the seat,
and above it, one carved agarwood-colored painted gold dragon on the backrest,
along with five-color clouds,
and below, one gold-leafed cloud panel,
one crimson "Fúshòu" panel,
and its cover.
Inside the pavilion, one carved wooden gold-leafed sword stand
and one footrest were placed,
all covered with yellow satin.
One copper brazier and one gilded copper brazier inlaid with precious stones were present.
Seat cushions, chair skirts, curtains, and the like
were all the same as for the large and small horse palanquins.
The palanquin roof was two chì and five cùn high,
with a gilded copper jeweled finial,
supported by an inverted and everted lotus base,
one chì, three cùn, and two fēn high,
with four yellow wool ropes hanging from the finial.
The roof was crimson,
covered with yellow felt,
with "rúyì" clouds at the four corners and along the edges,
also made of yellow felt.
Two layers of golden-yellow silk brocade drip-aprons surrounded it,
each layer with 124 pleats,
embroidered with cloud-dragons,
interspersed with five-color cloud patterns.
Sixteen walking dragons were embroidered on the waist.
Alternatively, a dark red silk gauze covered the top,
with "rúyì" cloud edges also made of red silk gauze.
Four gilded copper clouds were at the four corners.
Inside the pavilion, the precious canopy was embroidered with five dragons,
the top used a crimson wooden frame,
covered with yellow silk,
called the "Huángwū".
Around the center of the top, one cloud-dragon was embroidered on each side.
Four round yellow cord ropes extended from the four corners of the palanquin pavilion to the finial of the palanquin seat,
along with gold-leafed wooden fish.
The exterior of the pavilion was surrounded by a set of red felt covering, golden-yellow felt edging, and silk gauze felt cover.
Two turning corner railings at the front left and right of the palanquin pavilion,
and two straight and turning corner railings at the back,
all crimson,
with sixteen carved wooden exquisitely gold-grounded five-color auspicious cloud panels.
The four screens had a total of twelve posts,
the top decoration of each post was the same as the large carriage.
Flower carpets and straw mats were laid around inside the railing.
There was one stepping ladder,
wooden, crimson,
with six gold-leafed five-color cloud exquisitely carved panels,
and twelve painted gold water panels.
Four crouching dragons,
all with gold-painted copper carved leaf decorations.
Also four gilded copper hooks,
and golden-yellow round cord ropes,
the number of which was also the same.
Four red lacquered high stools,
two yellow felt footstools,
one golden-yellow cloth enclosed cover, and one golden-yellow oiled silk rain cover.
The Ritual Sedan
has a solid structure.
It is six chì and three cùn high.
Above it is a double-layered domed canopy,
one chì and three cùn high.
The upper layer is octagonal,
decorated with golden walking dragons.
The four lower corners
are decorated similarly.
It is topped with a golden round finial,
supported by openwork gilded hanging clouds,
inlaid with various precious stones.
The eaves are four chì and seven cùn long vertically
and three chì and five cùn wide horizontally.
Two layers of bright yellow satin curtains hang down,
embroidered with golden cloud-dragons.
The four posts are five chì high,
decorated with coiling dragons,
the door ends and the left and right railings are decorated with cloud-dragons,
all in openwork gold.
Inside, a golden dragon treasure seat is placed,
one chì and seven cùn high.
The curtains are made of bright yellow cloud satin and gauze felt,
each according to the season.
The left and right windows open,
using blue gauze in summer
and glass in winter.
There are two straight shafts,
one zhàng, seven chì, six cùn, and five fēn long.
Two large crossbars,
nine chì long.
Four small crossbars,
two chì, two cùn, and five fēn long.
Eight shoulder poles,
five chì and eight cùn long.
All are crimson,
painted with golden cloud-dragons.
They have transverse copper drills,
and longitudinal golden dragon heads and tails.
It is borne by sixteen people.
(According to the revised design, the Ritual Sedan was formerly the Grand Ceremonial Sedan.
In its original form,
the Grand Ceremonial Sedan was four chì, eight cùn, and five fēn high,
with a roof one chì and three cùn high
and two chì and eight cùn wide.
The roof was double-layered,
fully covered with gold leaf and carved with nine dragons,
cloud patterns and auspicious plant patterns,
with two layers of gold-embroidered dragon drip-aprons,
made of yellow silk damask.
Two straight golden poles,
with front and rear cross-poles of the same.
Four short carrying poles,
and double that number of shoulder carrying poles.
Two support poles.
Twelve crouching dragons on the sedan roof,
with a golden finial carved with dragon patterns,
inlaid with coral, lapis lazuli, pine nuts, and other stones.
The sedan poles were decorated with gilded copper dragon heads and tails.
One yellow cloth cover, one oiled silk rain cover, and one yellow felt roof.
The Qīngbùyú,
also carried by sixteen bearers,
was made of wood, painted vermilion,
and had no curtain.
The canopy was three chì four cùn high.
The backrest was one chì five cùn eight fēn high,
made of ivory.
The seat was one chì eight cùn two fēn high,
one chì eight cùn three fēn deep,
and two chì two cùn wide.
The footrest was three cùn high,
made of gold.
There were two straight shafts,
one zhàng five chì four cùn five fēn long,
with bronze dragon heads and tails attached.
There were two large horizontal poles,
nine chì one cùn long.
There were four small horizontal poles,
two chì eight cùn four fēn long.
There were eight shoulder poles,
five chì eight cùn five fēn long,
all drilled with bronze.
The rest of its design was the same as the Bùyú.
(Note: The term Qīngbùyú
was changed from Zhéhé Míngjiào.
Originally,
the Zhéhé Míngjiào
was golden-lacquered and carved with flowers, plants, and animal faces.
It was two chì two cùn wide
and three chì four cùn high.
The flat base was as wide as the轎 body.
The number of straight shafts below was also like the Dàyíjiào.
The decorations, curtains, and other designs were all the same as the Míngjiào.)
The
Bùyú,
also carried by sixteen bearers,
was made of wood coated in gold,
and had no curtain.
The canopy was three chì five cùn high.
The backrest was one chì six cùn five fēn high,
carved with floral patterns.
In the center was a coiled dragon seat,
the seat being one chì eight cùn five fēn high,
one chì eight cùn deep,
and two chì two cùn wide.
For the seating, purple sable was used in winter,
and bright yellow brocade satin in summer.
Its four feet were tiger claws with lí heads,
supported by round pearls,
and surrounded by painted clouds and dragons.
The footrest was three cùn one fēn high,
covered with yellow satin.
There were two straight shafts,
one zhàng five chì five cùn long.
There were two large horizontal poles,
seven chì six cùn long,
with two dragon heads facing each other in the middle.
There were four small horizontal poles,
two chì eight cùn long.
There were eight shoulder poles,
five chì six cùn long.
The rest was designed the same as the Lǐyú.
(Note: The Bùyú was the changed name for the Dàjiào.
Originally,
the Dàjiào had a single vermilion top,
was three chì wide,
and five chì high,
with gold leaf applied.
The top was eight cùn wider than the轿 body,
and eight cùn high.
There was a layer of gold-embossed dragons with flowing water patterns,
made of yellow silk twill.
It was decorated with four golden crouching dragons.
The number of straight shafts below was also like the Dàyíjiào.
The rest of the design below the golden top was identical.)
The
Empress's Fèngyú
was made of wood,
bright yellow,
and seven chì high.
It had a double arched canopy,
one chì five cùn five fēn high.
The upper part was octagonal,
the lower part had four corners,
all decorated with golden phoenixes.
It was crowned with a golden round top,
carved with cloud patterns,
inlaid with various treasures.
The eaves were five chì deep,
and three chì seven cùn six fēn wide,
with bright yellow satin curtains hanging down,
both upper and lower parts embossed with golden phoenixes.
The four pillars
were four chì seven cùn high,
all painted with golden phoenixes.
The four trellises could be opened,
netted with green cords.
In front were double doors,
two chì six cùn high;
when the doors were opened, the trellises were lifted and hung up,
and the interior was light red.
In the center was a vermilion seat,
one chì seven cùn high.
The backrest was one chì eight cùn high,
bright yellow,
painted with golden phoenixes.
The seating was bright yellow satin embroidered with colorful phoenixes.
In front was a handrest,
bright yellow with painted golden phoenixes, similar to the rest.
There were two straight shafts,
one zhàng seven chì two cùn five fēn long.
There were two large horizontal poles,
eight chì long,
with two iron-inlaid golden phoenixes facing each other in the middle.
There were four small horizontal poles,
three chì long.
There were eight shoulder poles,
five chì one cùn long.
All were bright yellow,
horizontally drilled with bronze,
and vertically adorned with bronze-inlaid golden phoenix heads and tails.
It was carried by sixteen bearers.
It was used by the Empress for the Sericulture Ceremony.
(Note: The regulations for empresses' and concubines' palanquins and carriages
were revised in the 14th year of Qiánlóng.
Originally,
besides the Fèngyú, there was also the Fèngniǎn.
Its pillars were three chì six cùn high,
and five chì two cùn wide.
The seat was one chì eight cùn high,
with surrounding balusters and rings carved with flowers,
painted vermilion with gold leaf decorations.
The imperial seat was in the center,
with an immortal bridge below,
and the seat was woven with rattan.
The window frames were woven with dark blue threads,
and the canopy cover was made of yellow knotted silk gauze.
There were two layers of gold-embossed phoenixes with flowing water patterns.
Yellow satin curtains.
Pearl curtains hung outside.
There were four straight poles,
with double the number of inner poles.
The number of short poles was the same as the inner poles.
All were vermilion.
The pure gold top was engraved with phoenix patterns,
inlaid with lapis lazuli, coral, pine nuts, and other stones.
The ends of the poles were adorned with golden phoenix heads and tails.
There were four red oil-painted stools.
Two support forks.
One yellow cloth curtain and one oil-silk raincoat each.
The Fèngyú measured three chì one cùn five fēn wide,
its pillars were three chì three cùn two fēn high,
the doors were two chì eight cùn high,
and the top was eight cùn wider than the front.
The top roof had six petals,
each petal one chì five cùn wide,
with a total height of one chì two cùn.
The shafts were one zhàng seven chì five cùn long,
and the wheels were five chì high,
all painted with yellow oil and adorned with golden phoenixes.
It had a pure gold top,
decorated with gilded leaves.
The cover was plain yellow silk twill,
with two layers of gold-embossed phoenixes with flowing water patterns on top.)
The Yíyú (ceremonial sedan chair)
is made of wood,
painted bright yellow.
Its height is one chi and one cun less than that of the Fèngyú.
Above is a domed canopy,
six cun and seven fen high.
It is crowned with a golden spherical finial,
and its eaves are gilded.
The vertical length is four chi and seven cun.
Yellow velvet ropes are tied at the four corners,
attached to the straight shafts.
Bright yellow satin valances hang down.
There are four pillars,
four chi and seven cun high.
The door curtains are red jiàn,
also made of bright yellow satin.
In the center is a vermilion seat,
one chi and five cun high,
with a bright yellow backrest,
one chi and six cun high,
painted with golden phoenixes.
The seat cushion is bright yellow satin,
embroidered with colorful phoenixes.
There are two straight shafts,
one zhang and five chi and five cun long.
There are two crossbars,
seven chi and seven cun long,
in the center of which are two iron-inlaid golden phoenixes facing each other.
There are four shoulder poles,
five chi and two cun long,
with bronze-inlaid gold at both ends.
It is carried by eight people.
(Initially,
the Yíyú was three chi and two cun wide,
its pillars were three chi and four cun high,
the width of its top was three cun wider than the front shaft,
its height was nine cun,
the shafts were the same length as the Fèngyú,
and its wheels were two cun lower.
All were coated with yellow lacquer.
It had a pure gold finial,
adorned with gilded leaf-shaped nails.
Its coverings were made of yellow cloud-patterned satin.
It had a double-eaved, drip-proof roof.
The curtains were red jiàn.
It came with one yellow cloth covering, one oil-silk raincoat, and one yellow felt top.
The Fèngchē (phoenix carriage)
is made of wood,
lacquered bright yellow,
nine chi and five cun high.
It has a double-layered domed canopy,
one chi and seven cun high,
with the Eight Treasures painted on the upper layer.
The eight corners are decorated with golden phoenixes,
and cloud patterns are painted on the lower layer.
The decorations at the four corners are similar.
It is crowned with a golden spherical finial,
carved with clouds,
inlaid with various jewels.
The vertical length of the eaves is four chi and nine cun,
and the horizontal length is four chi.
Bright yellow satin valances hang down,
and the canopy is covered with bright yellow netting.
Ropes are tied at the four corners,
made of bright yellow velvet,
attached to the axle supports (zhěn).
There are four pillars,
three chi and three cun high,
with golden phoenixes painted on the left, right, and rear sides.
Each side has a window frame (líng) in the middle,
netted with blue ropes.
The door is three chi high,
with carved golden phoenixes facing each other above.
It has bright yellow satin curtains
and yellow jiàn.
The seat cushion is also made of bright yellow satin,
embroidered with colorful phoenixes.
The wheels have a diameter of four chi and nine cun,
each with eighteen spokes.
There are two shafts,
one zhang and seven chi and five cun long,
with iron-inlaid gold at both ends.
The axle support (zhěn) is six chi and two cun long.
It is drawn by one horse.
The Yíchē (ceremonial carriage)
is made of wood,
bright yellow,
nine chi and five cun high.
It has a domed canopy,
round on top and square on the bottom,
nine cun high.
It is crowned with a silver spherical finial,
gilded.
The vertical length of the eaves is five chi and five cun,
and the horizontal length is four chi and one cun.
Ropes are tied at the four corners,
made of bright yellow velvet,
attached to the axle supports (zhěn).
Bright yellow satin valances hang down.
There are four pillars,
two chi and eight cun high,
without added paintings or decorations.
The jiàn are light red.
It has yellow jiàn and bright yellow satin curtains.
The seat cushion is also made of bright yellow satin,
embroidered with colorful phoenixes.
The wheels have a diameter of four chi,
each with eighteen spokes.
There are two shafts,
one zhang and five chi long,
inlaid with iron and silver.
The axle support (zhěn) is five chi and eight cun long.
It is drawn by one horse.
(Note: Initially, there was no Yíchē.
There was a Dàyíjiào (grand ceremonial palanquin),
two chi and nine cun wide,
four chi and eight cun high.
The top width was the same as the Yíyú.
The top structure had eight petals,
all coated with yellow lacquer.
It was adorned with gold-leafed cloud-and-phoenix tassels and rings,
inlaid with five-colored gemstones.
Its coverings were made of yellow patterned silk,
with two layers of gold-embroidered phoenix drip-proof roofs.
There were two straight poles and two cross-poles,
four short carrying poles,
twice as many shoulder poles,
and two support poles,
all vermilion.
The palanquin top was decorated with twelve golden phoenixes,
and the golden finial was engraved with seahorse patterns,
inlaid with blue, red, and indigo gemstones.
The palanquin poles were fitted with gilded bronze phoenix heads and tails.
The specifications for the coverings were the same as the Yíyú.
The regulations for the Huángtàihòu's (Empress Dowager's) palanquin and carriage
are the same as the Huánghòu's,
except that dragon motifs are added to the paintings and embroidery.
Therefore, their names are differentiated as Lóngyú (dragon palanquin) and Lóngfèngchē (dragon-phoenix carriage).
In the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng,
for the Huángtàihòu's sixtieth birthday,
the Emperor personally escorted the imperial palanquin from Chàngchūnyuán into the palace.
The Huángtàihòu rode in the Jīnniǎn (golden palanquin),
which was embroidered with the seal script character shòu (longevity) in bright yellow satin.
The palanquin was borne by twenty-eight people.
In the twenty-sixth and thirty-sixth years,
for the Huángtàihòu's seventieth and eightieth birthdays,
she also rode in this palanquin
from Chàngchūnyuán into the palace.
It was named the Wànshòuniǎn (longevity palanquin).
The Huángguìfēi's (Imperial Noble Consort's) Díyú (pheasant palanquin)
is made of wood,
bright yellow,
with all paintings and embroidery featuring golden dí (pheasants).
In the center of the crossbars are two iron-inlaid silver dí facing each other,
with the dí heads inlaid with gold.
All poles are fitted with bronze-inlaid golden dí heads and tails.
There are four shoulder poles.
It is carried by eight people.
The rest is the same as the Huánghòu's Fèngyú.

There were two straight poles
and two cross-poles.

The palanquin top was decorated with ten golden dí.

Among Manchu officials, only Qīn Wáng, Jùn Wáng, Dà Xué Shì, and Shàng Shū may ride in sedan chairs.
Bèi Lè, Bèi Zǐ, Gōng, Dū Tǒng, and civil officials of the second rank,
if not elderly, may not ride in sedan chairs.
The rest of the civil and military officials all ride horses.
In the Hàn Dynasty, officials of the third rank and above used silver for the top of their carriages and palanquins,
and black cloth for the curtains.
Within the capital, four bearers were used for palanquins;
outside the capital, eight bearers.
For civil officials of the fourth rank and below,
two bearers were used,
and the top of the palanquin was made of tin.
For provincial Dūfǔ,
eight bearers.
For Sī-Dào and below,
and above the teaching positions (Jiàozhí),
four bearers.
Miscellaneous officials (Zázhí) rode horses.
For Qīnchāiguān of the third rank and above,
eight bearers.
Military officials of the third rank were still not permitted to use palanquins.
All military officials rode horses.
Jiāngjūn, Tídū, and Zǒngbīngguān
who were over seventy years old and unable to ride horses
were to report it to the emperor and request an imperial decree.
(In the initial regulations,
all officials from Gōng, Hóu, Bó and below,
of the third rank and above,
rode in four-bearer enclosed palanquins,
with gilded ornamentation,
silver chí-dragons,
embroidered sashes,
and blue curtains.
For those of the fourth rank and below,
they rode in two-bearer enclosed palanquins,
or in carriages;
those who wished to ride horses were permitted.
Regarding the regulations for palanquins and carriages,
those of the fourth and fifth ranks had plain lions and embroidered sashes.
Those of the sixth rank and below
had plain cloud-heads and plain sashes,
with blue curtains.
Hàn military officials who used palanquins
were forbidden, as per the regulations.
In the fifteenth year of Qiánlóng, an imperial edict stated:
"According to the old regulations of Our Dynasty,
Manchu and Hàn civil and military high officials,
whenever attending court assemblies, all rode horses
and did not sit in palanquins.
Previously, some Manchu high officials sat in palanquins,
so an imperial decree was issued to prohibit military high officials from sitting in palanquins,
but civil high officials were not prohibited.
Now it is heard that civil high officials, seeking comfort,
even in places very close to the capital,
all sit in palanquins.
If it is argued that when traveling to ministries and courts one should sit in a palanquin,
then at the beginning of the dynasty, high officials of the ministries and courts never sat in palanquins.
This is due to a lack of diligent practice of their skills and professions,
and merely seeking comfort.
Manchu high officials should remember the old regulations of Our Dynasty
and comply accordingly.
Henceforth, among civil high officials, those who have reached sixty years of age and are truly unable to ride horses
are permitted to sit in palanquins as usual;
the rest are hereby prohibited."

Chapter 78: Carriages and Attire (2). Emperor's Crown and Robes. Empress's Crown and Robes (including Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager). Imperial Consorts (Huáng Guìfēi and below) Crown and Robes. Imperial Princes (Huángzǐ Qīnwáng and below) Crown and Robes. Wives of Imperial Princes (Huángzǐ Qīnwáng Fùjìn and below) Crown and Robes. Civil and Military Officials' Crown and Robes. Mìngfù's Crown and Robes. Scholars' and Commoners' Crown and Robes.
In the second year of Chóngdé,
an edict was issued to the various princes (zhū wáng) and bèilè, stating:
“In the past, Jīn Xīzōng and Jīn Zhǔ Liàng abolished the hats and robes of their ancestors’ time,
and adopted the clothing and headwear of the Hànrén.
It was not until Shìzōng
that the old system was restored.
Our nation takes horsemanship and archery as its profession.
If we now lightly follow the customs of the Hànrén
and neglect bows and arrows,
how can military preparedness be cultivated?
Hunting is
a method of martial practice;
dress regulations are
the foundational principles of the state.
Henceforth, for all military expeditions and hunting,
casual clothes (biànfú) may be worn;
for all other occasions, the regulations established at the founding of the state (guóchū dìngzhì) must be followed,
and court attire (cháoyī) must still be worn.
We also wish that future generations of descendants will not lightly alter or abandon ancestral systems (zǔzhì).”
In the thirty-seventh year of Qiánlóng,
the Sāntōng Guǎn presented the submitted “● Jiālǐ Kǎo”,
which was unclear regarding the systems of hats and robes for the Liáo, Jīn, and Yuán Dynasties.
An edict was received, stating:
“The clothing and headwear of Liáo, Jīn, and Yuán,
initially did not fail to follow their national customs,
but later they changed to the styles of Hàn and Táng Dynasties.
The sequence of these continuities and reforms
originally did not occur at a single time.
For example, regarding the court sacrifice attire of the Jīn Dynasty,
although embellishments were added earlier,
it did not reach the point of completely abandoning the old.
It was not until Zhāngzōng that a complete change of system was made.
This should be thoroughly investigated
to ascertain the reasons for discarding old institutions.
Clothing and headwear represent the illustrious system of an era;
the Xià Dynasty’s 'shōu' and the Yīn Dynasty’s 'xǔ' were
not inherited from each other.
Whatever was used by a dynasty
originally had its own regulations and procedures;
this is what is meant by ‘rites do not forget their origin.’
It was from the Běi Wèi Dynasty that the idea of changing attire began,
and extending to the rulers of Liáo, Jīn, and Yuán, they superficially admired reputation,
changing their clothing and headwear every generation or two,
completely abandoning their simple and unadorned customs.
Not long after this was transmitted,
the national power gradually weakened.
Moreover, considering those who advocated for change,
they merely said that imperial robes and crowns (gǔnmiǎn) were fully decorated
and the cultural artifacts (wénwù) were worth observing.
They were unaware that in adorning and decorating the body,
even if one takes their patterns,
why must one merely follow their style?
For example, the court sacrifice attire established by our dynasty,
with its mountains, dragons, algae, and fire
all brilliantly displayed,
are all based on the principles of the ritual classics;
so what is there to speak of regarding the tōngtiān jiàngshā? ”
Indeed, from the first year of Chóngdé, the Qīng Dynasty
had already clarified and established all systems of hats and robes for all ranks.
During the reign of Gāozōng,
the regulations and styles were made even more detailed,
yet he still earnestly admonished
against abandoning one’s origin and forgetting one’s ancestors.
He also deeply considered the fundamental and ultimate plan,
that old customs should not be lightly changed.
The established precedents of our ancestors are all in place,
and should be eternally upheld without transgression.
Herein, the regulations augmented and revised during the Qiánlóng reign
are categorized,
and those initially established are also appended to this chapter.
The Emperor’s Court Hat (huángdì cháoguān):
For winter, smoked sable (xūndiāo) is used;
from the first day of the eleventh month until the Shàngyuán Festival, black fox (hēihú) is used.
It is adorned with a vermilion velvet rim (zhūwèi) on top.
The finial (dǐng) has three layers,
each set with one Eastern pearl (dōngzhū),
all supported by four golden dragons (jīnlóng);
the remaining Eastern pearls are according to their designated number,
and a large pearl (zhēnzhū) is set on top.
For summer, it is woven from jade grass (yùcǎo) or rattan and bamboo threads (téngzhúsī),
edged with two layers of dark blue (shíqīng) gold thread (piànjīn),
and the lining (xià) is made of red gold thread (hóngpiànjīn) or red gauze (hóngshā).
It is adorned with a vermilion velvet rim (zhūwèi) on top,
with a golden Buddha (Jīnfó) at the front,
decorated with fifteen Eastern pearls (dōngzhū).
At the back, a Shèlín ornament is attached,
decorated with seven Eastern pearls (dōngzhū),
and the finial is as per the winter style.
Auspicious Attire Hat (jífúguān):
For winter, sea otter fur (hǎilóng), smoked sable (xūndiāo), or purple sable (zǐdiāo) is used depending on the season.
It is adorned with a vermilion velvet rim (zhūwèi) on top.
The finial is a full floral golden base,
with one large pearl (zhēnzhū) set on top.
For summer, it is woven from jade grass (yùcǎo) or rattan and bamboo threads (téngzhúsī),
with a red gauze (hóngshā) silk lining,
and edged with dark blue (shíqīng) gold thread (piànjīn).
It is adorned with a vermilion velvet rim (zhūwèi) on top.
The finial is as per the winter auspicious attire hat.
Everyday Attire Hat (chángfúguān):
The finial (dǐng) is a red velvet (hóngróng) knot,
without a ridge (liáng);
the rest is as per the auspicious attire hat.
Traveling Hat (xíngguān):
For winter, black fox (hēihú) or black lambskin (hēiyángpí) or dark blue velvet (qīngróng) is used;
the rest is as per the everyday attire hat.
For summer, it is woven from rattan and bamboo threads (téngzhúsī),
with a red gauze (hóngshā) lining.
It is adorned with a red yak hair tassel (zhūmáo) on top.
The finial (dǐng) and ridge (liáng) are all yellow,
with one pearl (zhēnzhū) attached at the front.
Duānzhào (formal jacket/robe):

From the first day of the eleventh month until the Shàngyuán Festival, black fox (hēihú) is used.
It has a bright yellow (mínghuáng) satin (duàn) lining.
Two hanging ribbons (chuídài) on the left and right,

the same color as the lining.
Imperial Dragon Robe (gǔnfú):
Dark blue (shíqīng) in color,

Its ornaments include the sun on the left and the moon on the right,

interspersed with five-colored clouds (wǔsèyún).
Padded (mián) for spring and autumn, lined (jiá) for spring and autumn,
fur-lined (qiú) for winter, and gauze (shā) for summer, depending on the season.
Court Robe (cháofú):
Bright yellow (mínghuáng) in color,

From the first day of the eleventh month until the Shàngyuán Festival,

The embroidery includes on both shoulders,

Displaying the Twelve Ornaments,
all on the upper garment,
interspersed with five-colored clouds (wǔsèyún).

Padded (mián), lined (jiá), gauze (shā), or fur-lined (qiú)

Court beads,

Bright yellow ribbons,

Ear ornaments,

arranged in three rows and three tiers.
In the middle, two gold-set lapis lazuli knots,
each adorned with six Eastern pearls and six pearls,
and coral attached at the ends.
Ear ornaments use second-grade Eastern pearls,
the rest are the same as the Empress's.
Court jackets, court robes, dragon jackets, dragon robes, ceremonial handkerchiefs, and court skirts are all the same as the Empress's.
The collar-necklace
is made of carved gold,
adorned with seven Eastern pearls,
interspersed with coral.
Two bright yellow cords hang from both ends,
with coral strung through the middle,
and two coral beads each at the ends.
For court attire, there are three strings of court beads,
one of amber (mì pò),
two of coral.
For festive attire, there is one string of court beads.
The cords are bright yellow.
The Noble Consort's (Guìfēi) crown, robes, and hanging cords are all golden yellow (jīn huáng sè);
the rest are the same as the Imperial Noble Consort's.
The Consort's (Fēi) court crown
has two layers at the top,
with one Eastern pearl each,
all supported by golden phoenixes,
adorned with nine Eastern pearls,
and seventeen pearls,
with a cat's eye stone set on top.
A crimson crown-base.
Five golden phoenixes are affixed around the top,
adorned with seven Eastern pearls,
and twenty-one pearls.
At the back, one golden pheasant,
adorned with one cat's eye stone,
and sixteen pearls;
the pheasant's tail has hanging pearls,
totaling one hundred eighty-eight pearls,
arranged in three rows and two tiers.
In the middle, a gold-set lapis lazuli knot,
adorned with four Eastern pearls and four pearls each,
and coral attached at the end.
Two golden yellow cords hang from the neck-guard at the back of the crown,
with precious stones attached at the ends.
The band is made of dark blue satin.
The festive attire crown top uses a green gemstone (bì yù).
The rest are the same as the Noble Consort's.
The *jīnyuē* (gold hair ornament)
has eleven gold-filigreed clouds,
each adorned with a *Dōngzhū* (Eastern Pearl),
interspersed with lapis lazuli,
and red gilded borders.
At the back, it is tied with a gold-set turquoise knot,
from which pearls hang down.
There are 197 pearls in total,
arranged in three rows and three tiers.
In the middle are two gold-set lapis lazuli knots,
each adorned with six *Dōngzhū* and six pearls,
ending with coral.
The earrings use third-grade *Dōngzhū*.
The rest is the same as for *Guìfēi* (Imperial Consort).

The *cháoguà* (ceremonial jacket), *cháopáo* (ceremonial robe), *lóngguà* (dragon jacket), *lóngpáo* (dragon robe), *lǐngyuē* (collar ornament), *cháoqún* (ceremonial skirt), and *cháozhū* (ceremonial beads) are all the same as for *Guìfēi*.
The *cǎishuì* (embroidered sash)
is embroidered with
"clouds and auspicious grasses."
The rest is the same as for *Guìfēi*.
For *Pín* (Consort), the *cháoguān* (ceremonial headdress)
has two layers at the top,
each threaded with a *Dōngzhū*,
all supported by a golden *dí* (pheasant),
adorned with nine *Dōngzhū*,
and seventeen pearls,
with a *quēzi* (plum blossom) at the top.
It has a vermilion tassel fringe.
Around the top are five golden *dí*,
adorned with five *Dōngzhū*,
and nineteen pearls.
At the back is one golden *dí*,
adorned with sixteen pearls,
and from the tail of the *dí* hang pearls,
a total of 172 pearls,
arranged in three rows and two tiers.
In the middle is one gold-set lapis lazuli knot,
adorned with three *Dōngzhū* and three pearls,
ending with coral.
At the back of the headdress, two golden-yellow tassels hang from the collar guard,
ending with gemstones.
The sash is made of blue satin.
The *jífúguān* (auspicious attire headdress) is the same as for *Fēi* (Consort).
The *jīnyuē*
has eight gold-filigreed clouds,
each adorned with a *Dōngzhū*,
interspersed with lapis lazuli,
and red gilded borders.
At the back, it is tied with a gold-set turquoise knot,
from which pearls hang down.
There are 177 pearls in total,
arranged in three rows and two tiers.
In the middle are two gold-set lapis lazuli knots,
each adorned with four *Dōngzhū* and four pearls,
ending with coral.
The earrings use fourth-grade *Dōngzhū*.
The rest is the same as for *Fēi*.
The *cháoguà*
is the same as for *Fēi*.
The *lóngguà*
is embroidered with one front-facing dragon on each shoulder, front and back,
and four *kuí* dragons on the lapel.
The rest is the same as *Fēi*'s regulations.
The *cháopáo* and *lóngpáo* both use incense yellow.
The rest is the same as for *Fēi*.
The *cháofú cháozhū* (ceremonial court beads) consist of three strands:
one of coral and two of amber.
The *jífú cháozhū* (auspicious attire court beads) consist of one strand.
The tassels are golden-yellow.
The *lǐngyuē* and *cháoqún* are all the same as for *Fēi*.
The *cǎishuì* is not embroidered with floral patterns.
The rest is the same as *Fēi*'s regulations.
(Originally,
for *Huáng Guìfēi* (Imperial Noble Consort), *Guìfēi*, *Fēi*, and *Pín*'s court attire,
for all major celebratory ceremonies,
*Huáng Guìfēi* and *Guìfēi*'s headdress tops used twelve *Dōngzhū*,
*Fēi*'s headdress top used eleven *Dōngzhū*.
The ceremonial robes used satin with phoenixes and *dí* birds,
five-clawed dragon satin, funeral satin, eight-round dragon satin, etc.
As for yellow and incense yellow,
from *Huáng Guìfēi* downwards,
they were generally not permitted to wear them.
*Pín*'s headdress top used ten *Dōngzhū*,
the ceremonial robes used satin with *dí* birds,
five-clawed dragon satin, funeral satin, four-round dragon satin, etc.)
The *Huángzǐ*'s (Imperial Prince's) *cháoguān*,
for winter, uses smoked sable or blue fox, depending on the season.
At the top is a vermilion tassel fringe.
The top has two layers of golden dragons,
adorned with ten *Dōngzhū*,
and a red gemstone at the mouth.
For summer, it is woven from jade grass or rattan and bamboo silk.
It has two layers of dark blue silk with gold threads at the edge,
and the border uses red gilded silk or red gauze.
At the top is a vermilion tassel fringe.
At the front is a *shělin* (shelin, or bead cluster),
adorned with five *Dōngzhū*.
At the back is a gold flower,
adorned with four *Dōngzhū*.
The top is like the winter *cháoguān*.
The *jífúguān* has a red velvet knot at the top.
The *duānzhào* (formal coat)
is made of purple sable,
with golden-yellow satin borders.
Two straps hang down on each side,
wider at the bottom and tapering,
the color matching the borders.
The *lóngguà*
is dark blue.
The front is embroidered with four roundels of five-clawed golden dragons,
one on each shoulder, front and back,
interspersed with five-colored clouds.
There are two types of *cháofú* (ceremonial court attire),
both golden-yellow: First,
the *pīlǐng* (collar cape) and skirt are both trimmed with purple sable.
The cuffs are smoked sable.
The embroidery has one front-facing dragon on each shoulder, front and back,
six walking dragons in the pleats,
interspersed with five-colored clouds.
Second,
the *pīlǐng* and sleeves are both dark blue,
with gilded edges,
with additional sea otter trim in winter.
The embroidery has one front-facing dragon on each shoulder, front and back,
four walking dragons on the waist panel,
eight walking dragons on the skirt,
two walking dragons on the *pīlǐng*,
and one front-facing dragon on each cuff.
The lower hem features eight treasures and flat water patterns.
The *mǎngpáo* (dragon robe) is also golden-yellow,
with gilded edges,
embroidered with nine *mǎng* (pythons),
with openings on the left and right sides of the hem.
*Dōngzhū* are not permitted for *cháozhū*,
the rest is as used,
and the tassels are all golden-yellow.
The *cháodài* (ceremonial court belt)
is golden-yellow,
with four gold-set jade square plaques,
each adorned with four *Dōngzhū*,
and one cat's-eye stone in the center,
with tassels on the left and right in the color of the belt.
The *jífúdài* (auspicious attire belt) is also golden-yellow,
with plaque decorations as appropriate,
and tassels in the color of the belt.
The *yǔguān* (rain hat), *yǔyī* (rain coat), and *yǔshang* (rain skirt)
are all red,
made of felt, wool gauze, or oiled silk,
depending on the season.
(Originally,
for *Huángzǐ*'s court attire,
for all major celebratory ceremonies,
the headdress used thirteen *Dōngzhū* for the top setting,
the ceremonial robes used colors such as incense yellow,
five-clawed and three-clawed dragon satin,
full jadeite eight-round dragon satin, etc.,
and a belt inlaid with gold, jade, and *Dōngzhū* was worn.)
The *Qīnwáng*'s (Prince of the First Rank's) *cháoguān*
is the same as for *Huángzǐ*.
The *jífúguān*,
for winter, uses sea otter, smoked sable, or purple sable, depending on the season.
For summer, it is woven from jade grass or rattan and bamboo silk.
It has red gauze borders.
It has dark blue gilded edges.
At the top is a vermilion tassel fringe.
The top uses a red gemstone;
if a red velvet knot was previously bestowed,
it may also be used.
The *duānzhào*
is made of blue fox,
with pale blue satin borders;
if a golden-yellow one was previously bestowed,
it may also be used.
The *bǔfú* (embroidered official robe) is dark blue,
embroidered with four roundels of five-clawed golden dragons,
front-facing dragons on the front and back,
and walking dragons on the shoulders.
The *cháofú* and *mǎngpáo* are blue or dark blue, depending on what is used;
if a golden-yellow one was previously bestowed,
it may also be used.
The rest is the same as for *Huángzǐ*.
Court beads, court sashes, auspicious attire sashes, rain hats, rain coats, and rain skirts,
are all the same as for imperial princes.
(In the 1st year of Chóngdé,
it was stipulated that a Qīnwáng’s crown finial has three layers,
adorned with a ruby on top,
and eight Dōngzhū in the middle.
The front shělín
is set with four Dōngzhū.
The rear jīnhuā
is set with three Dōngzhū.
The sash uses four pieces of gold-inlaid jade plaques,
set with four Dōngzhū.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that the crown finial should be set with ten Dōngzhū in total,
with the shělín and jīnhuā each increasing by one Dōngzhū.
The sash, with four pieces,
each piece set with four Dōngzhū.
The attire uses five-clawed, four-round dragon insignias, five-clawed dragon satin, and four full-embroidered insignias satin, etc.
For the crown of a Qīnwáng Shìzǐ,
the finial has two layers of golden dragons,
decorated with nine Dōngzhū,
and a ruby on top.
The summer court crown has a shělín attached to the front,
decorated with five Dōngzhū.
A jīnhuā is attached to the back,
decorated with four Dōngzhū.
The auspicious attire crown, duānzhào, official robe, court robe, python robe, and court beads are all the same as for a Qīnwáng.
The court sash
is golden yellow in color,
with four gold-inlaid jade square plaques,
each decorated with three Dōngzhū.
The tassels worn on the left and right are the same color as the sash.
The auspicious attire sash is the same as for a Qīnwáng.
(In the 9th year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that a Qīnwáng Shìzǐ’s crown finial has three layers,
set with nine Dōngzhū in total.
The sash uses four pieces of gold-inlaid jade plaques,
each piece set with three Dōngzhū.
The attire is the same as for a Qīnwáng.
For a Jùnwáng’s court crown,
the finial has two layers of golden dragons,
decorated with eight Dōngzhū,
and a ruby on top.
The summer court crown has a shělín attached to the front,
decorated with four Dōngzhū.
A jīnhuā is attached to the back,
decorated with three Dōngzhū.
The auspicious attire crown and duānzhào are both the same as for a Qīnwáng Shìzǐ.
The official robe
is made of dark blue stone color,
embroidered with four round five-clawed ascending dragons,
one on each shoulder, front and back.
The court robe, python robe, and court beads are all the same as for a Qīnwáng Shìzǐ.
The court sash
is golden yellow in color,
with four gold-inlaid jade square plaques,
each decorated with two Dōngzhū
and one cat's-eye stone.
The tassels are the same color as the sash.
The auspicious attire sash is the same as for a Qīnwáng Shìzǐ.
(In the 1st year of Chóngdé,
it was stipulated that a Jùnwáng’s crown finial has three layers,
adorned with a ruby on top,
and seven Dōngzhū in the middle.
The front shělín
is set with three Dōngzhū.
The rear jīnhuā
is set with two Dōngzhū.
The sash uses four pieces of gold-inlaid jade plaques,
set with four turquoise stones.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that the crown finial should be set with eight Dōngzhū in total,
with the shělín and jīnhuā each increasing by one Dōngzhū.
The sash, with four pieces,
each piece set with two Dōngzhū.
The attire is the same as for a Qīnwáng.
For a Bèilè’s court crown,
the finial has two layers of golden dragons,
decorated with seven Dōngzhū,
and a ruby on top.
The summer court crown has a shělín attached to the front,
decorated with three Dōngzhū.
A jīnhuā is attached to the back,
decorated with two Dōngzhū.
The auspicious attire crown and duānzhào are both the same as for a Jùnwáng.
The official robe
is made of dark blue stone color,
embroidered with one round four-clawed front-facing python on the front and back.
The court robe is fully embroidered with four-clawed python patterns,
and the python robe is also like this.
None should use golden yellow color;
other colors are at discretion.
The court bead tassels are dark blue stone color.
The rest are the same as for a Jùnwáng.
The court sash is golden yellow in color,
with four gold-inlaid jade square plaques,
each decorated with two Dōngzhū.
All tassels are dark blue stone color.
The auspicious attire sash is golden yellow in color,
and the plaque decorations are as appropriate.
All tassels are also dark blue stone color.
(In the 1st year of Chóngdé,
it was stipulated that a Bèilè’s crown finial has three layers,
adorned with a ruby on top,
and six Dōngzhū in the middle.
The front shělín
is adorned with two Dōngzhū.
The rear jīnhuā
is adorned with one Dōngzhū.
The sash uses four pieces of gold-inlaid jade plaques,
set with four gemstones.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that the crown finial should be set with seven Dōngzhū in total,
with the shělín and jīnhuā each increasing by one Dōngzhū.
The sash, with four pieces,
each piece set with two Dōngzhū.
The attire uses four-clawed two-round dragon insignias, and python satin, and "cāng" satin.
For a Bèizǐ’s court crown,
the finial has two layers of golden dragons,
decorated with six Dōngzhū,
and a ruby on top.
The summer court crown has a shělín attached to the front,
decorated with two Dōngzhū.
A jīnhuā is attached to the back,
decorated with one Dōngzhū.
The auspicious attire crown finial uses a ruby.
All wear three-eyed peacock feathers.
(Peacock feathers are divided into three-eyed, two-eyed, and single-eyed.
They may be worn when bestowed.
) The duānzhào is made in the same style as for a Bèilè.
The official robe is made of dark blue stone color,
embroidered with one round four-clawed ascending python on the front and back.
The court robe, python robe, and court beads are all the same as for a Bèilè.
The court sash
is golden yellow in color,
with four gold-inlaid jade square plaques,
each decorated with one Dōngzhū.
The auspicious attire sash is the same as for a Bèilè.
(In the 1st year of Chóngdé,
it was stipulated that a Bèizǐ’s crown finial has two layers.
Adorned with a ruby on top,
and five Dōngzhū in the middle.
The front shělín
and the rear jīnhuā
are each set with one Dōngzhū.
The sash uses four pieces of gold-inlaid jade plaques,
each piece set with one sapphire.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that the crown finial should be set with six Dōngzhū in total,
the shělín increasing by one Dōngzhū,
the rest remaining as before.
The sash, with four pieces,
each piece set with one Dōngzhū.
The attire is the same as for a Bèilè.
For a Zhèn’guógōng’s court crown,
the finial has two layers of golden dragons,
decorated with five Dōngzhū,
and a ruby on top.
The summer court crown has a shělín attached to the front,
decorated with one Dōngzhū.
A jīnhuā is attached to the back,
decorated with one turquoise stone.
For the auspicious attire crown,
those within the eight privileged ranks (rù bāfēngōng) use a ruby for the finial,
while those not within the eight privileged ranks (wèi rù bāfēngōng) use coral.
All wear two-eyed peacock feathers.
The duānzhào is made of purple sable,
lined with moon-white satin.
The official robe is embroidered with square insignias of four-clawed front-facing pythons on the front and back.
The court robe, python robe, and court beads are the same as for a Bèizǐ.
The court sash
has four gold-inlaid jade square plaques,
each decorated with one cat's-eye stone.
The auspicious attire sash is the same as for a Bèizǐ.
(In the 1st year of Chóngdé,
it was stipulated that a Zhèn’guógōng’s crown finial has two layers,
adorned with a ruby on top,
and four Dōngzhū in the middle.
The front shělín
is set with one Dōngzhū.
The rear jīnhuā
is set with one turquoise stone.
The sash is the same as for a Bèizǐ.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that the crown finial should be set with five Dōngzhū in total,
the rest remaining as before.
The sash, with four pieces,
each piece set with one cat's-eye stone.
The attire uses square insignias of four-clawed pythons.
The rest are the same as for a Bèilè.
The ceremonial hat of a Fǔguó Gōng
has a two-tiered golden dragon finial,
adorned with four Dōngzhū,
with a ruby at the top.
The rest are all as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Fǔguó Gōng’s hat finial should be two-tiered,
with a ruby at the top,
and three Dōngzhū embedded in the middle.
The front Shèlín
had one turquoise embedded.
The rear golden flower
had one gemstone embedded.
The belt was as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the hat finial should have a total of four Dōngzhū embedded,
and the Shèlín, golden flower, belt, and dress colors were all the same as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.)
The ceremonial hat of a Zhènnguó Jiāngjūn
has an openwork golden base finial,
adorned with one Dōngzhū in the middle,
with a ruby at the top.
The finial for the auspicious attire hat uses coral.
The front and back of the embroidered badge robe are embroidered with a Qílín.
The rest are all considered equivalent to a military first rank.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Zhènnguó Jiāngjūn’s hat finial should have a ruby at the top,
and the belt should use gold-mounted circular plaques,
embedded with four rubies.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the middle section of the hat finial should be embedded with Dōngzhū,
and the belt should use gold-mounted square jade plaques,
each embedded with one ruby.
The embroidered badge robe was embroidered with a Qílín,
and the rest were the same as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.)
The ceremonial hat of a Fǔguó Jiāngjūn
has an openwork golden base finial,
adorned with a small ruby in the middle,
with an openwork coral at the top.
The finial for the auspicious attire hat also uses openwork coral.
The front and back of the embroidered badge robe are embroidered with a lion.
The rest are all considered equivalent to a military second rank.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Fǔguó Jiāngjūn’s hat finial should have a sapphire at the top,
and the belt should use circular golden plaques.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the hat finial should be changed to have a ruby at the top,
and one small ruby embedded in the middle section.
The belt was as for a Zhènnguó Jiāngjūn.
The embroidered badge robe was embroidered with a lion.
The rest were the same as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.)
The ceremonial hat of a Fèngguó Jiāngjūn
has an openwork golden base finial,
adorned with one small ruby in the middle,
with a sapphire at the top.
The finial for the auspicious attire hat also uses sapphire.
The front and back of the embroidered badge robe are embroidered with a leopard.
The rest are all considered equivalent to a military third rank.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Fèngguó Jiāngjūn’s hat finial should have a crystal at the top,
and the belt should use ornate gold-mounted square iron plaques.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the hat finial should have a ruby at the top,
and one small sapphire embedded in the middle section.
The belt should use embossed circular golden plaques.
The embroidered badge robe was embroidered with a leopard.
The rest were the same as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.)
The ceremonial hat of a Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn
has an openwork golden base finial,
adorned with one small sapphire in the middle,
with a lapis lazuli at the top.
The front and back of the embroidered badge robe are embroidered with a tiger.
The rest are all considered equivalent to a military fourth rank,
except that the garment has four openings at the hem.
The belt uses a golden-yellow color,
all imperial clansmen use this,
while Juéluó use red.
(In the ninth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn’s hat finial should have a sapphire at the top,
and one small sapphire embedded in the middle section.
The belt should use embossed gold-mounted silver circular plaques.
The embroidered badge robe was embroidered with a tiger,
and the rest were the same as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.)
The auspicious attire hat of a Gùlún Èfù
has a ruby finial,
and a three-eyed peacock feather.
The auspicious attire belt uses a golden-yellow color.
The rest are the same as for a Bèizi.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Gùlún Èfù’s hat and attire were the same as for a Bèizi.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the hat finial should be embedded with six Dōngzhū.
The Shèlín was embedded with two Dōngzhū.
The golden flower was embedded with one Dōngzhū.
The belt used four gold-mounted jade circular plaques,
each embedded with one Dōngzhū.)
The auspicious attire hat of a Héshuò Èfù
has a coral finial,
and a two-eyed peacock feather.
The ceremonial belt color uses dark blue or blue,
with four gold-mounted jade circular plaques.
The rest are the same as for a Zhènnguó Gōng.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Héshuò Èfù’s hat and attire were the same as for a Chāopǐn Gōng.
If their peerage was above that of a Gōng,
they would still dress according to their original rank.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the hat finial should be embedded with four Dōngzhū,
and the Shèlín embedded with one Dōngzhū.
The golden flower was embedded with one turquoise.
The belt used four gold-mounted jade circular plaques,
each embedded with one cat's eye stone.)
The ceremonial belt of a Jùnjǔ Èfù
uses four openwork golden circular plaques,
each adorned with one turquoise.
The rest are considered equivalent to a military first rank.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Jùnjǔ Èfù’s hat finial should have a ruby at the top,
and one Dōngzhū embedded.
The belt used four circular golden plaques,
embedded with four turquoises.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì
it was stipulated that the hat and belt were the same as for a Hóu or Bó.
In the first year of Kāngxī
it was stipulated that a four-clawed python embroidered badge robe should be used.)
The hat and attire of a Xiànzhǔ Èfù
are considered equivalent to a military second rank.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Xiànzhǔ Èfù’s hat finial should have a ruby at the top.
The belt used four circular golden plaques,
each embedded with four rubies.)
The hat and attire of a Jùnjūn Èfù
are considered equivalent to a military third rank.
(In the first year of Chóngdé
it was stipulated that the Jùnjūn Èfù’s hat finial should be embedded with a sapphire.

all use blue.
As for bright yellow riding jackets (xíngguà),
the Commanders of the Imperial Bodyguards, Imperial Ministers, Captains of the Bodyguard, Commanders of the Guards, Wing Commanders of the Jiànruì Yíng, and all ministers who have been granted them,
may all use them.
Regarding belts,
from Qīnwáng down to Zōngshì,
all wear golden yellow belts.
Juéluó wear red belts.
Golden yellow belts and red belts,
if not bestowed by the Emperor,
may not be given to those of different surnames.
Regarding court beads,
from Wánggōng down,
civil officials of the fifth rank, military officials of the fourth rank and above, Hàn-Zhān, Kē-Dào, Imperial Bodyguards,
Princesses, Fùjìn and below,
and noblewomen of the fifth rank and above may all use them.
They are made of various precious stones and incenses.
However, for the Lǐbù Zhǔshì,
Tàicháng Sì Bóshì, Diǎnbù, Dúzhù Guān, Zànlǐ Láng,
Hónglú Sì Míngzàn,
Guānglù Sì Shǔzhèng, Shǔchéng, Diǎnbù,
Guózǐ Jiàn Jiānchéng, Bóshì, Zhùjiào, Xuézhèng, Xuélù,
except when performing duties at altars and temples or acting as ceremonial attendants in the palace, they are permitted to use them.
But for ordinary leisure and when in their official residences,
they are still not permitted to use them.
Regarding peacock feathers (kǒngquè líng),
those with three "eyes" at the tip of the feather
are worn by Bèizǐ.
Those with two "eyes"
are worn by Zhènguógōng, Fǔguógōng, and Héshuò Èfù.
Those with one "eye"
are worn by Nèidàchén,
Imperial Bodyguards of the first, second, third, and fourth ranks,
Commanders and Colonels of the Vanguards and Guards,
Vanguard Bodyguards,
Chief Secretaries of Princely Mansions,
Sǎnqí Láng,
and second-class Imperial Bodyguards;
all may wear them.
The base of the feather is also affixed with a blue feather (lánlíng).
The Master of Ceremonies of a Bèilè mansion,
and second and third-class Imperial Bodyguards and Vanguard, Imperial Guard, and Guard officers from Qīnwáng downwards,
all wear dyed blue feathers.
Regarding seat cushions,
Qīnwáng use sable in winter,
and red silk with dragon patterns in summer.
Shìzǐ and Jùnwáng use lynx and sable-trimmed cushions in winter,
and blue silk with python patterns in summer.
Bèilè use lynx in winter,
and blue silk with colorful embroidery in summer.
Bèizǐ use white leopard in winter,
and colorful silk edged with blue silk in summer.
All are backed with red and white felt.
Zhènguógōng use full red leopard skin in winter,
and blue-patterned red silk in summer.
Fǔguógōng use square red leopard skin in winter,
and red-patterned black silk in summer.
All are backed with red felt.
Zhènguó Jiāngjūn are treated as first rank,
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn as second rank,
Fèngguó Jiāngjūn as third rank,
and Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn as fourth rank.
Míngōng use full tiger skin in winter,
and black silk in summer.
Hóu and Bó both use square tiger skin in winter.
In summer, Hóu use black silk with an embroidered border.
Bó use blue cloud-patterned silk.
All are backed with red felt.
Zǐ and Nán follow their respective ranks.
Gǔlún Gōngzhǔ Èfù are treated as Bèizǐ.
Héshuò Gōngzhǔ Èfù are treated as Zhènguógōng.
Jùnjǔn Èfù use badger in winter,
and blackish-brown edged with reddish-brown in summer.
All are backed with red felt.
Jùnjūn Èfù are treated as third rank.
Xiànjūn Èfù are treated as fourth rank.
Xiāngjūn Èfù are treated as fifth rank.
Civil and military officials of the first rank use wolf in winter,
and reddish-brown in summer.
Second rank use badger in winter,
and reddish-brown edged with blackish-brown in summer.
Third rank use racoon dog (háo) in winter,
and blackish-brown edged with reddish-brown in summer.
Fourth rank use blue mountain goat in winter,
and blackish-brown cloth in summer.
All are backed with red felt.
Fifth rank use blue sheep in winter,
and blue cloth in summer.
Sixth rank use black sheep in winter,
and brownish cloth in summer.
Seventh rank use deer in winter,
and gray cloth in summer.
Eighth rank use [a type of animal, character missing] in winter,
and coarse earth-colored cloth in summer.
Ninth rank use otter in winter,
and the same as eighth rank in summer.
All are backed with white felt.
Regarding the seasonal change of caps and attire,
in spring, cool court caps and lined court robes are used.
In autumn, warm court caps and fur-trimmed court robes are used.
Within the third and ninth months,
on the fifth,
or the fifteenth,
or the twenty-fifth day,
one day is chosen as appropriate.
All requests are submitted by the Lǐbù one month in advance,
and upon receiving the imperial decree,
it is circulated to all yámen for uniform compliance.
Generally, the hat ornaments and belts of civil and military probationary officials and selected officials are all the same as those of incumbent officials.
(In the first year of Chóngdé,
it was stipulated that the hat ornaments of Dūtǒng and Shàngshū should be mounted with rubies on top.
Their belts used four round gold plaques,
inlaid with four rubies.
The hat ornaments of Nèidàchén, Dàxuéshì, Fùdūtǒng, Hùjūntǒnglǐng, Qiánfēngtǒnglǐng, and Shìláng were mounted with sapphires on top.
Their belts used four round gold plaques.
The hat ornaments of Yīděng Shìwèi, Hùwèi Cānlǐng, Xuéshì, Mǎn Qǐxīnláng, and Lángzhōng were mounted with crystals on top.
Their belts used four patterned gold-iron plaques.
Èrděng and Sānděng Shìwèi,
Hùwèi,
Zuǒlǐng,
Hàn Qǐxīnláng,
and Yuánwàiláng had hat ornaments with gold tops.
Their belts used four patterned gold-iron round plaques.
Hùjūnxiào and Zhǔshì had hat ornaments with gold tops.
Their belts used two patterned gold-iron round plaques.
In the second year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that First rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops,
mounted with rubies on top,
and inlaid with one Dōngzhū pearl in the center.
Their belts used four gold-mounted square jade plaques,
each piece inlaid with one ruby.
Second rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops,
mounted with rubies on top,
and inlaid with small rubies in the center.
Their belts used four embossed gold round plaques,
inlaid with one ruby.
Third rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops,
mounted with rubies on top,
and inlaid with small sapphires in the center.
Their belts used four embossed gold round plaques.
Fourth rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops,
mounted with sapphires on top,
and inlaid with small sapphires in the center.
Their belts used four embossed gold round plaques,
silver-edged.
Fifth rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops,
mounted with crystals on top,
and inlaid with small sapphires in the center.
Their belts used four plain gold round plaques,
silver-edged.
Sixth rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops,
mounted with crystals on top.
Their belts used four tortoise shell round plaques,
silver-edged.
Seventh rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops,
inlaid with small sapphires in the center.
Their belts used four plain silver round plaques.
Eighth rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed gold tops.
Their belts used four polished horn round plaques,
silver-edged.
Ninth rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed silver tops.
Their belts used four dark horn round plaques,
silver-edged.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì,
it was stipulated that the rank badges of military officials of First and Second ranks used lions,
Third rank used tigers,
and Fourth rank used leopards.
Moreover, in the fifth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was stipulated that Fèngguó Jiāngjūn and Third rank officials' hat ornaments used embossed coral tops.
Sixth rank officials' hat ornaments used crystal stone tops.
The court headdress of a First rank Mìngfù had a
carved gold base on top,
decorated with one Dōngzhū pearl in the center,
and mounted with a ruby on top.
All other aspects were as for a Míngōng Fūrén.
The court headdress of a Second rank Mìngfù had a
carved gold base on top,
decorated with one ruby in the center,
and mounted with carved coral on top.
The auspicious attire hat ornament also used carved coral.
All other aspects were as for a First rank Mìngfù.
The court headdress of a Third rank Mìngfù had a
carved gold base on top,
decorated with one ruby in the center,
and mounted with a sapphire on top.
The auspicious attire hat ornament also used a sapphire.
All other aspects were as for a Second rank Mìngfù.
The court headdress of a Fourth rank Mìngfù had a
carved gold base on top,
decorated with one small sapphire in the center,
and mounted with lapis lazuli on top.
The auspicious attire hat ornament also used lapis lazuli.
The court robe was gold-edged,
with two walking dragon embroidered patterns each on the front and back,
and no pleats in the middle.
A dark blue cord hung at the back,
with various ornaments as appropriate.
The mǎngpáo was entirely embroidered with eight four-clawed dragons.
The court skirt was gold-edged,
the upper part used green satin,
the lower part used dark blue satin with a "walking dragon" pattern,
all full width,
with pleats.
All other aspects were as for a Third rank Mìngfù.
The court headdress of a Fifth rank Mìngfù had a
carved gold base on top,
decorated with one small sapphire in the center,
and mounted with crystal on top.
The auspicious attire hat ornament also used crystal.
All other aspects were as for a Fourth rank Mìngfù.
The court headdress of a Sixth rank Mìngfù had a
carved gold base on top,
decorated with one small sapphire in the center,
and mounted with tridacna shell on top.
The auspicious attire hat ornament also used tridacna shell.
All other aspects were as for a Fifth rank Mìngfù.
The court headdress of a Seventh rank Mìngfù had a
carved gold base on top,
decorated with one small crystal in the center,
and mounted with plain gold on top.
The auspicious attire hat ornament also used plain gold.
The mǎngpáo was entirely embroidered with five dragons.
All other aspects were as for a Sixth rank Mìngfù.
(In the first year of Chóngdé,
it was stipulated that Mìngfù's headdresses and robes were each determined by their husband's official rank.
The headdresses of attendant ladies of the Huánghòu used gold tops,
mounted with rubies on top.
The headdresses of attendant ladies of the Guìfēi used gold tops,
mounted with crystals on top.
Attendant ladies of Qīn and Jùnwángfēi were the same as attendant ladies of a Fēi.
The headdresses of attendant ladies of a Bèilè Fūrén used gold tops.
The headdresses of attendant ladies of a Bèizi Fūrén did not use a top ornament.
Their head ornaments were inlaid with pearls, precious stones, and turquoise.
The court cap for tribute scholars who passed the metropolitan examination
had a top with an engraved gold base,
mounted with three golden branches and nine leaves.
For auspicious attire, the cap top used plain gold.
The *zhuàngyuán* had a gold top,
mounted with crystal.
After receiving appointments,
each observed their rank.
The official uniform cap for *jǔrén*
had a top with an engraved silver base,
mounted with a golden sparrow.
The official uniform robe
was made of blue silk with a blue trim.
The collar was in the same style as the robe.
The official uniform belt
was made like the court belt of an eighth-rank civil official.
The auspicious attire cap
had a silver base on top,
mounted with plain gold.
The auspicious attire cap for tribute students
had an engraved gold top.
The rest was the same as for *jǔrén*.
The auspicious attire cap for *jiānshēng*
had a plain silver top.
The rest was the same as for tribute students.
The cap for *shēngyuán*
had a top with an engraved silver base,
mounted with a silver sparrow.
The official uniform robe
was made of blue silk with a green trim.
The collar was in the same style as the robe.
The official uniform belt
was made like the court belt of a ninth-rank civil official.
The auspicious attire cap
had the same top as for *jiānshēng*.
*Wàiláng* and elders
had cap tops made of tin.
Officials overseeing farming
had robes made of blue velvet.
The top was the same as for eighth-rank officials.
The winter cap for civil dancers in sacrifices
was made of *sāoshǔ* fur,
with a top featuring an engraved copper base,
adorned in the center with a square copper piece
engraved with a sunflower,
and mounted with a copper triangle on top,
shaped like a flaming pearl.
The robe was made of silk;
its color was dark blue for the Southern Suburbs,
black for the Northern Suburbs,
red for all other altars and temples,
except for the Altar of the Setting Moon, which used moon white.
The front and back square panels were embellished with gold-threaded sunflowers.
The belt was made of green silk.
The cap top for martial dancers was mounted with a copper trident,
shaped like an ancient *jǐ*.
The robe was made of silk,
entirely embellished with gold-threaded sunflowers.
The rest was the same as for civil dancers.
Musicians of the music department
had caps with an engraved copper base on top,
mounted with a bright yellow feather.
Robes for the music department were made of red satin.
One type,
with embroidered yellow orioles on the front and back square panels,
was worn by musicians of the *Zhōnghé Sháoyuè* Department who held performing bamboo figures;
another type,
with small round sunflowers woven throughout,
was worn by musicians of the Grand *Dānbì* Music departments.
Belts were all made of green cloud-patterned satin.
The winter cap for *lǔbù* attendants
was made of leopard skin and black felt,
with an engraved copper base on top,
mounted with a bright yellow feather.
The robe was the same as for musicians of the Grand *Dānbì* Music departments.
The belt was the same as for civil dancers in sacrifices.
The robe for *lǔbù* guards was made of dark blue satin,
entirely woven with gold *shòu* characters,
and edged with gold thread.
The collar and sleeves were both woven with gold-threaded sunflowers.
The winter cap for *lǔbù* marshals
had a flat brim,
with a plain copper top,
mounted with a bright yellow feather.
The robe and belt were both the same as for *lǔbù* attendants.
(In the third year of *Shùnzhì*,
it was decreed that commoners were not permitted to wear satin or embroidered clothing.
The use of *máng* satin, funeral satin, or brocade clothing by household servants of Manchus
was strictly forbidden.
In the ninth year,
it was decreed that the round crown of cool hats and warm hats
should use red gold-threaded fabric only for officials,
while commoners should use red satin.
For Buddhist and Daoist robes,
excluding *jiāshā* and Daoist robes,
紬 (pongee), 絹 (thin silk), 紡 (spun silk), and plain gauze of various colors were permitted.
Cloth robes could use dull black or charcoal black.
In the first year of *Kāngxī*,

it was decreed that civilians and military personnel were forbidden to wear clothing or accessories made of *máng* satin, funeral satin, gold-flowered satin, gold-threaded Japanese satin, sable, fox fur, or lynx.
This was prohibited.
In the thirty-ninth year,
it was decreed that *Bāqí jǔrén*, official students, tribute students, *shēngyuán*, *jiānshēng*, guards, and foremen were permitted to wear ordinary satin and gauze.
*Tiānmǎ* (ermine) and silver fox fur were not allowed to be worn.
For Han *jǔrén*, official students, tribute students, *jiānshēng*, and *shēngyuán*,
the rule was the same, except for wolf fur.
Military and civilian clerks were not permitted to use wolf or fox fur.
Those who wore sable caps
were also prohibited.
Furthermore, saddles and bridles for military and civilian personnel were not allowed to be adorned with embroidery, Japanese satin, interwoven threads,鑲緣 (inlaid borders), or gilding.
In the first year of *Yōngzhèng*,
because officials did not follow regulations,
wearing rosaries,
hanging red tassels on horses' necks,
and having outriders leading their horses;
and some even overstepped their bounds,
using silk for their saddle blankets.
The *Bāqí* ministers, commanders' yamen, and the *Dùchá Yuàn* were ordered to strictly investigate,
and if ministers or others showed favoritism or negligence,
they would be equally punished.
Furthermore, when *zhūwáng* awarded rosaries or other items to their subordinates,
they were to formally report and record it in their respective banners' archives,
and submit a consolidated report annually.
In the second year,
the prohibition against officials with increased ranks from presumptuously using higher-grade cap ornaments, belts, official robes, and saddle blankets was reiterated.

Officials, military personnel, and commoners who used black fox fur, "autumn incense" color, "rice" color, "fragrance" color for their clothing, or "rice" color and "autumn incense" color for saddles and bridles,
beyond the stipulated regulations,
would be punished with additional penalties.
Supervising officials who failed to report such instances would also be similarly punished.

*Zhì* 79: Carriages and Attire 3: Imperial Seal of the Emperor, Golden Seal of the Empress (with Golden and Jade Seals of the Grand Empress Dowager and Empress Dowager appended), Seals and Stamps of Imperial Consorts and below, Seals and Stamps of Imperial Princes and below, Seals and Tallies of Civil and Military Officials.
In the early Qīng dynasty, the imperial seals (yùbǎo) were kept in the Jiāotài Diàn,
and the Shàngbǎo Sī was established.
Later, eunuchs (nèi jiān) were in charge of their safekeeping.
When needed, the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) would request their use.
In the eleventh year of Qiánlóng (1746),
the seal register (bǎopǔ) was compiled and finalized.
Twenty-five were stored in the Jiāotài Diàn,
and ten were stored in Shèngjīng.
Those stored in the Jiāotài Diàn are:
The "Dà Qīng Shòumìng Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Great Qīng's Mandate),
for proclaiming the imperial succession (huángxù).
Made of white jade,
it is four cǔn and four fēn square,
and one cǔn thick.
With a coiled dragon (pánlóng) knob,
it is two cǔn high.
The
"Huángdì Fèngtīan Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor's Obedience to Heaven),
for proclaiming reverence (fèngruò).
Made of jasper (bìyù),
it is four cǔn and four fēn square,
and one cǔn and one fēn thick.
With a coiled dragon knob,
it is three cǔn and five fēn high.
The
"Dà Qīng Sìtiānzǐ Bǎo" (Seal of the Great Qīng's Successor Emperor),
for proclaiming the continuation of lineage (jìshéng).
Made of gold,
it is two cǔn and four fēn square,
and eight fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons (jiāolóng) knob,
it is one cǔn and seven fēn high.
The
"Huángdì Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor),
for issuing edicts (zhàoshè) and pardons.
Made of celadon jade (qīngyù),
it is three cǔn and nine fēn square,
and one cǔn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn and one fēn high.
The
"Huángdì Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor),
for dignifying the imperial carriage (fǎjià).
Made of sandalwood (zhāntán xiāngmù),
it is four cǔn and eight fēn square,
and one cǔn and eight fēn thick.
With a coiled dragon knob,
it is three cǔn and five fēn high.
The
"Tiānzǐ Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Son of Heaven),
for sacrificing to all deities (bǎishén).
Made of white jade,
it is two cǔn and four fēn square,
and eight fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is one cǔn and three fēn high.
The
"Huángdì Zūnqīn Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor's Honoring of Relatives),
for presenting honorable titles (huīhào).
Made of white jade,
it is two cǔn and one fēn square,
and seven fēn thick.
With a coiled dragon knob,
it is one cǔn and three fēn high.
The
"Huángdì Qīnqīn Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor's Affection for Relatives),
for extending ancestral alliances (zōngméng).
Made of white jade,
it is two cǔn and two fēn square,
and one cǔn and two fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is one cǔn and two fēn high.
The
"Huángdì Xíng Bǎo" (Seal of the Emperor for Travel),
for bestowing gifts (bāncì lài).
Made of jasper,
it is four cǔn and eight fēn square,
and one cǔn and nine fēn thick.
With a squatting dragon (dūnlóng) knob,
it is two cǔn and five fēn high.
The
"Huángdì Xìnbǎo" (Seal of the Emperor's Credence),
for mobilizing military units (róngwǔ).
Made of white jade,
it is three cǔn and three fēn square,
and six fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is one cǔn and six fēn high.
The
"Tiānzǐ Xíng Bǎo" (Seal of the Son of Heaven for Travel),
for enfeoffing foreign tribes (wàimán).
Made of jasper,
it is four cǔn and eight fēn square,
and one cǔn and nine fēn thick.
With a squatting dragon knob,
it is two cǔn and three fēn high.
The
"Tiānzǐ Xìnbǎo" (Seal of the Son of Heaven's Credence),
for commanding distant lands (shūfāng).
Made of celadon jade,
it is three cǔn and eight fēn square,
and one cǔn and three fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is one cǔn and seven fēn high.
The
"Jìngtīan Qínmín Zhī Bǎo" (Seal of Reverence for Heaven and Diligence for the People),
for admonishing officials during audiences (jìn lì).
Made of white jade,
it is three cǔn and one fēn square,
and one cǔn and five fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is one cǔn and seven fēn high.
The
"Zhìgào Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Issuing Edicts),
for instructing officials (chénliáo).
Made of celadon jade,
it is four cǔn square,
and two cǔn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn and seven fēn high.
The
"Chìmìng Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Imperial Decrees),
for sealing imperial proclamations (gàochì).
Made of jasper,
it is three cǔn and five fēn square,
and one cǔn and three fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is one cǔn and eight fēn high.
The
"Chuíxùn Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Transmitting Instructions),
for promulgating national laws (guóxiàn).
Made of jasper,
it is four cǔn square,
and one cǔn and five fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn high.
The
"Mìngdé Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Bestowing Virtue),
for rewarding loyal and virtuous individuals (zhōngliáng).
Made of celadon jade,
it is four cǔn square,
and one cǔn and four fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn and one fēn high.
The
"Qīnwén Zhī Xǐ" (Seal for Reverence of Culture),
for emphasizing literary education (wénjiào).
Made of black jade (mòyù),
it is three cǔn and six fēn square,
and one cǔn and five fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is one cǔn and six fēn high.
The
"Biǎozhāng Jīngshǐ Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Commending Classics and Histories),
for upholding ancient teachings (gǔxùn).
Made of jasper,
it is four cǔn and seven fēn square,
and two cǔn and one fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn and two fēn high.
The
"Xúnshǒu Tiānxià Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Imperial Tours of the Realm),
for conducting inspections of regions (shěngfāng).
Made of celadon jade,
it is four cǔn and seven fēn square,
and two cǔn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn and five fēn high.
The
"Tǎozuì Ānmín Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Punishing Evildoers and Bringing Peace to the People),
for declaring punitive expeditions (zhēngfá).
Made of celadon jade,
it is four cǔn and eight fēn square,
and two cǔn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn and five fēn high.
The
"Zhìyù Liù Shī Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Commanding the Six Armies),
for organizing military operations (róngháng).
Made of black jade,
it is five cǔn and three fēn square,
and one cǔn and four fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn and two fēn high.
The
"Chìzhèng Wànbāng Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Imperially Rectifying All Nations),
for issuing proclamations to foreign countries (wàiguó).
Made of celadon jade,
it is three cǔn and eight fēn square,
and one cǔn and five fēn thick.
With a coiled dragon knob,
it is two cǔn and three fēn high.
The
"Chìzhèng Wànmín Zhī Bǎo" (Seal for Imperially Rectifying All People),
for issuing proclamations to the four quarters (sìfāng).
Made of celadon jade,
it is four cǔn and one fēn square,
and one cǔn and five fēn thick.
With an intertwined dragons knob,
it is two cǔn high.
