Gāozōng’s imperial compilation, Records of the Dynastic Transmitted Treasures, states:
“Our dynasty, having received the Mandate of Heaven,
adopted ancient systems to create seals.
They are managed by the Director of the Palace Hall Bureau,
stored in multiple layers of caskets,
placed on stands,
and set up in the Jiāotàidiàn.
They are arranged in order to the left and right.
When needed, the Nèigé requests permission to use them.
Their materials include jade, gold, and sandalwood.
The types of jade include white, green, and celadon.
The knobs include intertwined dragons, coiled dragons, and crouching dragons.
The inscriptions, from the time before Tàizōng Wénhuángdì,
exclusively used the national script.
Later, ancient seal script was also used.
Their sizes vary, from six inches square to two inches and one fen.
I once examined the Dàqīng Huìdiǎn,
which records twenty-nine imperial seals.
Currently, thirty-nine are stored in the Jiāotàidiàn.
The Huìdiǎn also says: ‘Six are stored within the palace,
and twenty-three are stored in the inner treasury.’
Now, all are stored in the Jiāotàidiàn,
so both the number and location are incorrect.
As for the statement that ‘Huángdì Fèngtiān Zhī Bǎo’
is the Chuán Guó Xǐ,
used for the two grand suburban sacrifices and for the ‘green petitions’ to Heaven in the palace on imperial birthdays,
this statement is especially absurd and erroneous.
For grand sacrifices, ancient rites are followed,
using a prayer tablet signed with a name but without a seal.
On imperial birthdays, there has never been a ceremony of petitioning Heaven in the palace.
Perhaps Dàolù Zhùlí ceremonies
are occasionally performed,
but they are merely an occasional preservation of their teachings,
and never involve commissioning literati for green petitions,
nor do they use a seal.
Furthermore, which of these seals is not transmitted and guarded through the generations?
To designate one specific seal as the Chuán Guó Xǐ
is also improper.
This is likely because the officials who compiled the Huìdiǎn lacked profound scholarship and acute insight,
and moreover never sought imperial instruction for judgment.
They merely followed the registers written by the palace eunuchs during the Míng dynasty,
passing on errors and perpetuating falsehoods,
which led to this situation.
How difficult indeed it is to record history accurately!
Furthermore, there is an additional seal not recorded in the Huìdiǎn,
namely ‘Shòumìng Yú Tiān Jì Shòu Yǒngchāng’.
I do not know when it was secretly stored in the hall,
and it is even placed in the very center.
Although its inscription resembles the ancient Qín seal,
its seal script is clumsy and vulgar,
clearly not the ancient Li Sī ‘insect-bird’ style.
Only the jade itself is lustrous and pure, like cut fat.
It measures four cún and four fēn on each side,
and its thickness is one-third of its side length.
It is indeed true that such fine jade is not easily obtained.
As for considering it a treasure,
regardless of whether it is not a Qín seal,
even if it were a true Qín seal,
how could it be particularly valuable?
In the third year of Qiánlóng,
Gāo Bīn, while supervising river works, presented a jade seal obtained by his subordinates when dredging the Báoyīng River.
It possessed an ancient luster and was charming.
It also closely matched the one recorded by Cài Zhōngpíng in the Chuògēnglù.
I stated that this was made by an enthusiast imitating an engraving.
It is stored in a separate hall
and regarded merely as an old curio.
The Qín seal was incinerated;
ancients have discussed this in detail.
Even if it still existed,
how could the artifact of Zhèng and Sī
be stored together with the dynastic transmitted treasures of our court?
It is inappropriate in principle.
Also, during the Yōngzhèng reign, the late Grand Secretary Gāo Qíwèi presented an uncarved celadon jade seal.
Since it had no inscription,
it was not yet a seal,
yet it was stored with the other seals.
This is also inappropriate.
I have often argued that
a ruler's position lies in virtue, not in treasures.
Although a treasure is important,
it is but an object.
What difference is there between it and carriages, banners, or official robes,
which distinguish ranks and serve as symbols of trust?
If virtue is insufficient,
then even formidable mountains and rivers,
or vast and wealthy territories,
will be handed over to others with folded hands.
No one has ever relied solely on this mere foot-sized piece of jade
to secure themselves.
If one can diligently cultivate noble virtue
and secure the hearts of the people,
then with commands transmitted and edicts widely proclaimed,
people will rush from thousands of miles away.
Even if the treasure is not the Hébì,
its form is not that of dragons or chī,
and its script is not that of Sī or Zhòu,
who would dare not respect, trust, and obey it,
revering it as divine?
Therefore, the artifact is not the treasure;
the treasure lies in having virtue.
In ancient times, when rulers obtained talismans and seals from previous dynasties,
their monarchs and ministers would change expression, boast, and flaunt them,
extolling them as auspicious omens.
When our Tàizōng Wénhuángdì
obtained the imperial seal of the Yuán dynasty transmitted by the Mongols,
he accepted and stored it,
but he never relied on it as a symbol of having received the Mandate.
Thinking about it now,
was Wénhuángdì’s subjugation of the entire realm
and his establishment of a lasting lineage for ten thousand generations
due to virtue
or due to a treasure?
One does not need to be wise to know the answer.
Well said were the words of Táng Liáng Sù: ‘
The lightness or heaviness of the tripod,
the coming or going of the seal,
depends on the height of virtue and the security of the position.’
Therefore, when a ruler inherits what was entrusted by ancestors,
and hopes to forever secure these treasures
and continue them without end,
it does not mean guarding them securely with multiple layers of covers.
It means constantly renewing one's virtue,
being mindful of danger in times of peace,
and firmly receiving the great and precious Mandate of August Heaven.
Then virtue will be worthy of the treasure,
and the treasure will become even more valued.
Since ancient times, there has been no fixed number of seals and jades.
Those currently stored in the Jiāotàidiàn
have been there for a long time,
and the records are inaccurate,
with some even being duplicates.
Therefore, I have re-examined and arranged them,
determining the number to be twenty-five,
to accord with the heavenly count.
Furthermore, a compendium has been written,
and its general purport is as stated above.”
The preface to the Sacred Imperial Seal Compendium stored in Shèngjīng also states:
“In the spring of the eleventh year of Qiánlóng,
I inspected the various seals stored in the Jiāotàidiàn.
After carefully determining their positions,
I composed an essay to record them.
Those that should be stored separately
were stored accordingly.
As for those whose inscriptions were duplicated,
or those used in the early days of the dynasty,
their total number was ten.
Although they are not the seals currently in use,
they cannot be categorized with ancient curios.
Recalling that Shèngjīng is the birthplace of our nation,
where the spirits of our ancestors
are truly depended upon,
and I have already had the Veritable Records of the Imperial Ancestors recopied,
sacredly preserved in the Fènghuánglóu,
to manifest their glorious achievements
and transmit them boundlessly;
I imagine that at the beginning of the founding of the dynasty,
when the imperial mandate was firmly received,
and the precious talismans shone brightly,
the six regions submitted to our model,
and these beautiful jades were cherished,
the traces of their hands still exist there.
Does the record not say,
‘display their ancestral vessels,’
referring to the grand jades and precious tablets
displayed in the western hall,
venerating their generational preservation?
Therefore, these ten seals
have been respectfully conveyed to Shèngjīng,
locked and stored there,
and the reason for this is as stated above.”
In the ninth month of the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the imperial seals were re-engraved,
and the Qīng seal script (清篆文) was first adopted.
The left side used the Qīng seal script (清篆),
and the right side used the Hàn seal script (漢篆).
Gāozōng (高宗) wrote after the preface to the Jiāotàidiàn Seal Registry (交泰殿寶譜序):
“The Seal Registry (寶譜) was completed in the eleventh year of Qiánlóng, the bǐngyín (丙寅) year.
Three years later, in the wùchén (戊辰) year,
I first instructed the Confucian ministers to write the various seal scripts in Mǎnchú (清文) characters.
I then considered that the former national seals
and official seals
used seal script for the Hàn text,
but the original characters for the Mǎnchú text,
because the Mǎnchú seal script (國書篆體) was not yet fully developed.
Now that the seal script method (篆法) has been established,
it should be applied to seals and stamps,
to ensure uniformity.
According to the registry, the ‘Emperor's Seal’ (皇帝之寶) of green jade
originally had Mǎnchú characters in seal script,
transmitted from the time of Tàizōng Wénhuángdì (太宗文皇帝).
From that point upwards, the four seals
were inherited from previous generations,
and passed down as family treasures,
which dared not be easily changed.
The sandalwood ‘Emperor's Seal’ (皇帝之寶)
and the twenty-one seals below it
were commonly used in court ceremonies and imperial edicts,
and should follow the new system.
Therefore, I commanded the relevant offices to uniformly re-engrave them,
to match the Hàn seal script (漢篆文),
and also recorded this after the preface to the Seal Registry (寶譜序).”
In the eighth month of the forty-fifth year of Qiánlóng,
for Gāozōng’s (高宗) seventieth sacred birthday,
the phrase from Dù Fǔ (杜甫) was engraved
as "Seal of the Son of Heaven of Ancient Rarity" (古稀天子之寶).
He also personally composed "A Discourse on Ancient Rarity" (古稀說),
and attached a poem to it.
In the first month of the forty-sixth year,
following the example of storing the
"Seal of Reverence for Heaven and Diligence for the People" (敬天勤民寶)
in the west warm chamber of the Qiánqīnggōng (乾清宮),
the
"Seal of the Son of Heaven of Ancient Rarity" (古稀天子之寶)
was stored in the east warm chamber.

One each of the Qīnglóng, Báihǔ, Zhūquè, and Shénwǔ banners;
four each of the Bàowěi fān and Lóngtóu gānfān.
Four golden staffs.
Twenty each of the xiāojīn lóngdú and xiāojīn lóng xiǎoqí.
Six golden yuè.
Ten horses.
Eight luánfèng shàn;
twelve dānlóng shàn;
twenty shuānglóng shàn.
Two fúzi;
six red dēng;
two each of the jīnxiānglú, jīnpíng, and jīnxiānghé;
one each of the jīntuòhú, jīnpén, jīnwū, jīn jiāoyǐ, and jīnjiǎotà.
Six yùzhàng;
six xīng.
Eight bìtóu.
Thirty zōngjiàn.
Thirty jìngbiān.
Seventy-two pǐnjí shān.
Two each of the Sùjìng qí, Jīngǔ qí, and Báizé qí;
eight ménqí;
one each of the rì, yuè, fēng, yún, léi, and yǔ qí;
five wǔwěi qí;
one each of the Èrshíbāxiù qí;
one Běidǒu qí;
five Wǔyuè qí;
four Sìdú qí;
one each of the Qīnglóng, Báihǔ, Zhūquè, Shénwǔ, Tiānlù, Tiānmǎ, Luánlín, and Xióngpí qí.
Six each of the lìguā, wòguā, and wúzhàng.
Twenty-four huàjiǎo;
forty-eight gǔ;
eight each of the dàtónghào and xiǎotónghào;
four each of the jīn, jīngzhēng, and zhànggǔ;
twelve lóngtóudí;
four strings of bǎn.
All these are used for suburban sacrifices,
the grand court assemblies on Wànshòu, Yuándàn, and Dōngzhì, and other ceremonies.
The fǎjià lǔbù
is the same as the dàjià lǔbù,
except that the latter uses ráo gē yuè,
while the former uses ráo gē gǔchuī.
Its instruments include eight dàtóngjiǎo,
eight xiǎotóngjiǎo,
four jīngzhēng,
twenty-four huàjiǎo,
twenty-four lónggǔ,
twelve lóngdí,
four pāibǎn,
four zhànggǔ,
two jīn,
twenty-four lónggǔ,
interspersed with six red dēng,
which is a reduction compared to the ráo gē yuè.
Additionally, the yùzhàng, wúzhàng, lìguā, wòguā, xīng, and yuè each number six;
twenty wǔsè jīnlóng xiǎoqí;
twenty wǔsè lóngdú;
ten jiǔlóng huánggài;
twenty bàowěiqiāng;
twenty gōngshǐ;
twenty yídāo.
Ten attendants carrying gōngshǐ;
the chì mǎn dānlóng tuánshàn, huáng mǎn shuānglóng tuánshàn, and wǔsè duànsǎn are all omitted,
also a reduction compared to the dàjià.
Furthermore, the yùniǎn is replaced by a jīnniǎn,
the rest being the same as the dàjià lǔbù.
These are displayed for sacrifices at various altars: Fāngzé, Tàimiào, Shèjì, Rìyuè, Xiānnóng;
and various temples: Lìdài Dìwáng, Xiānshī.
When it is a celebration or court audience,
it is displayed
in the courtyard of the Tàihédiàn.
Its arrangement is as follows:
The jiǔlóng qǔbǐng huáng huágài is placed in the center outside the gate of the Tàihédiàn.
Next, the fú, lú, hé, yú, pán, píng, yǐ, and jǐ are placed on the east and west sides of the diànyán.
Next, the yídāo, gōngshǐ, and bàowěiqiāng of the qīnjūn and hùjūn are arranged in ten alternating ranks,
along with the shūjǐ,
all on the east and west of the dānbì.
Next, the jiǔlóng qǔbǐng huánggài, cuìhuágài, zǐzhīgài, jiǔlóng huánggài, wǔsè jiǔlóngsǎn, and wǔsè huāsǎn,
from the dānbì, form three rows,
alternating up to both steps.
Below the steps, the jìngbiān and zhàngmǎ are arrayed on the east and west of the yǒngdào.
The zǐ and chì fāngsǎn and shàn,
chuáng, fān, jīng, jié, chǎng, huī, dú, qí, yuè, xīng, guā, and zhàng,
are arrayed on the east and west of the dānchí.
The yùniǎn and jīnniǎn are outside the Tàihémén;
the wǔlù are outside the Wǔmén;
the bǎoxiàng are south of the wǔlù;
the lǔbù yuè (i.e., ráo gē gǔchuī)
is south of the bǎoxiàng;
the cháoxiàng (i.e., dǎoxiàng)
is outside the Tiān'ānmén.
If a celebration ceremony is held at the Yuánmíngyuán,
it is displayed below the steps of the Zhèngdàguāngmíngdiàn,
extending to outside the Dàgōngmén,
but the niǎn, lù, and yíxiàng are not set up.
If the emperor ascends the tower to receive captives,
the jiǔlóng qǔbǐng huáng huágài is set up under the eaves of the tower;
the dānbì lǔbù is set up below the left and right guān outside the Wǔmén;
the dānchí lǔbù is set up from the left and right gates of the quē to north of the Duānmén;
the zhàngmǎ are set up in front of the two jiǎolóu;
the niǎn, lù, and yíxiàng are set up outside the Tiān'ānmén;
the jìngbiān are set up to the left and right of the yùdào between the two jiǎolóu;
the jīnggǔ ráo gē dàyuè (ráo gē gǔchuī displayed alongside the front section of the dàyuè,
called jīnggǔ ráo gē dàyuè)
is set up in front of the Wǔmén.
The dānbì dàyuè is set up at the end of the lǔbù;
its instruments are two yúnhuó,
two fāngxiǎng,
two xiāo,
four dí,
four tóuguǎn,
four shēng,
two dàgǔ,
one zhànggǔ,
and one pāibǎn.
The luánjià lǔbù
is displayed when the emperor travels within the Huángchéng.
Its arrangement is:
first, the dǎoyíng yuè,
starting with two xìzhú,
followed by six guǎn,
four dí,
two shēng,
two yúnhuó,
one dǎoyíng gǔ,
and one pāibǎn.
Next, four yùzhàng;
four wúzhàng;
four each of the lìguā, wòguā, xīng, and yuè.
Next, ten wǔsè jīnlóng xiǎoqí;
ten wǔsè lóngdú.
Next, ten shuānglóng huáng tuánshàn;
ten huáng jiǔlóngsǎn.
Next, one jiǔlóng qǔbǐng huáng huágài.
All these are in front of the emperor's bùniǎn.
Next, ten ministers with daos leading the procession;
two ministers with daos protecting the rear;
the bùniǎn in the middle.
Next, ten Bàowěibān imperial guards carrying spears;
ten carrying yídāo;
ten carrying gōngshǐ.
The procession is concluded with a huánglóng dàdú.
(Originally, for the xíngjià yízhàng,
ten xiāojīn jiǔlóngsǎn;
ten xiāojīn lóngdú;
ten xiāojīn lóng xiǎoqí;
ten shuānglóng shàn.
Four jīn yuè;
four xīng;
four yùzhàng;
four wúzhàng;
four each of the lìguā and wòguā.
Whenever the imperial carriage goes in or out,
the attendants are arrayed on horseback.)
The imperial procession and ceremonial guard,
when the emperor inspects various regions or conducts a grand review, are displayed.
Its system
first arrays the nāogē dàlè (grand ceremonial music).
Interspersed are nāogē qīnglè (ceremonial light music),
with instruments including eight large bronze horns,
eight small bronze horns,
eight gold-mouthed horns,
two yúnluó (cloud gongs),
two lóngdí (dragon flutes),
two píngdí (flat flutes),
two guǎn (oboes),
two shēng (mouth organs),
four bronze drums,
two jīn (bronze gongs),
two tóngdiǎn (bronze bell-chimes),
two tóngbó (bronze cymbals),
two xínggǔ (marching drums),
and two Ménggǔ jiǎo (Mongolian horns).
Next are six yùzhàng (imperial staffs),
six wúzhàng (ceremonial staffs),
and six each of lìguā (standing melons), wòguā (lying melons), xīng (stars), and yuè (axes).
Next are ten five-colored golden dragon small banners
and ten five-colored lóngdú (dragon banners).
Next are six single-dragon red round fans,
six double-dragon yellow round fans,
and ten five-colored floral umbrellas.
Next are ten bàowěi qiāng (leopard-tail spears),
ten bows and arrows,
and ten yídāo (ceremonial sabers).
Next is one nine-dragon curved-handle yellow huágài (canopy).
All of these are in front of the Huángdì's (Emperor's) light sedan chair;
if he rides a horse, they are in front of the horse.
Next, leading the procession, are ten ministers with佩刀 (sash sabers),
and two ministers with佩刀 (sash sabers) bringing up the rear,
with the light sedan chair in the middle.
Next are ten bàowěibān (leopard-tail guard) attendants carrying spears,
ten wearing yídāo (ceremonial sabers),
ten wearing bows and arrows,
and the procession concludes with a large yellow dragon dàdú (banner).
When the imperial retinue halts at the imperial camp,
the Ménggǔ jiǎo (Mongolian horns) are displayed in the morning,
and the nāogē yuè (ceremonial music) in the evening.
During a grand review, the lúbù (ceremonial guard) is displayed outside the temporary palace gate.
(Originally stipulated for imperial travel ceremonies,
ten satin umbrellas,
ten gold-embroidered lóngdú (dragon banners),
ten gold-embroidered dragon small banners.
Six double-dragon fans,
four single-dragon fans.
Ten bàowěi qiāng (leopard-tail spears),
ten dàdāo (large sabers),
ten bows and arrows.
Six jīn yuè (gold axes),
six xīng (stars),
and six each of yùzhàng (imperial staffs), wúzhàng (ceremonial staffs), lìguā (standing melons), and wòguā (lying melons).
Two jīn (bronze gongs),
two shēng (mouth organs),
two yúnluó (cloud gongs),
two guǎn (oboes),
four dí (flutes),
four jīnzhēng (gold gongs),
four tóngbó (bronze cymbals),
two gǔ (drums),
eight suǒnà (suonas),
two tóngdiǎn (bronze bell-chimes),
eight each of small and large hàos (trumpets),
and six Ménggǔ hào (Mongolian trumpets).
Whenever the imperial carriage travels,
the personnel line up on foot.)
For the Tàishàng Huáng's (Emperor Emeritus') lúbù (ceremonial guard),
there was originally no provision.
In the first year of Jiāqìng's (嘉慶) reign,
due to the completion of the abdication ceremony,
the Tàishàng Huáng's (Emperor Emeritus') lúbù (ceremonial guard) was displayed at Níngshòu Gōng (寧壽宮).
Its system includes
six yǐnzhàng (leading staffs),
sixteen yùzhàng (imperial staffs),
sixteen wúzhàng (ceremonial staffs),
sixteen each of lìguā (standing melons) and wòguā (lying melons),
sixteen each of xīng (stars) and yuè (axes),
two hundred twenty-four qí (flags) and dú (banners),
four each of huī (pennants), chǎng (feather banners), and jié (insignia),
sixteen jīng (streamers),
twelve fān (banners),
twenty chuáng (canopies),
eighty-six shàn (fans),
sixty-six sǎn (umbrellas),
four each of jí (halberds) and shū (pikes),
thirty each of bàowěi qiāng (leopard-tail spears), bows and arrows, and yídāo (ceremonial sabers),
one gold jiāoyǐ (folding chair) and one gold mǎwù (horse stool),
two fú (whisks),
eight gold vessels,
one silver water pot and one silver fire pot,
two rain umbrellas,
two coiled-wire lanterns,
and six red lanterns.
Musical instruments are fully equipped,
including two each of shēng (mouth organs), guǎn (oboes), yúnluó (cloud gongs), píngdí (flat flutes), bó (cymbals), and diǎngǔ (spot drums),
four each of jīn (bronze gongs) and jīnzhēng (gold gongs), tónggǔ (bronze drums), biǎngǔ (flat drums), and zhànggǔ (staff drums),
twelve each of jiàgǔ (frame drums) and jīnkuò jiǎo (gold-mouthed horns),
fourteen lóngdí (dragon flutes),
twenty-four each of large bronze horns, small bronze horns, and Ménggǔ huàjiǎo (Mongolian painted horns),
and forty-eight lónggǔ (dragon drums).
For the Huáng Tàizǐ's (Crown Prince's) ceremonial guard,
since the 52nd year of Kāngxī's (康熙) reign, no heir apparent was again established,
thus, although there were imperial crown prince's ceremonial guards in the early days of the dynasty,
they were almost an empty formality.
In the 60th year of Qiánlóng's (乾隆) reign,
as an abdication was to occur the following year,
in the ninth month,
it was decided that when the Huáng Tàizǐ (Crown Prince) entered and exited the Inner Court,
he would be accompanied by four dìcóng shìwèi (escorting guards)
and two Qiánqīng Mén shìwèi (guards of the Gate of Heavenly Purity).
If he went out to the Outer Court or inside and outside the city,
he would be accompanied by one sǎnzhí dàchén (minister without portfolio),
ten shìwèi (guards),
one lǐng shìwèi nèi dàchén (grand minister of the Imperial Bodyguard),
and four Qiánqīng Mén shìwèi (guards of the Gate of Heavenly Purity).
In front would be six hǔqiāng (tiger spears),
and at the rear eight bàowěi qiāng (leopard-tail spears).
In that year, an edict was again issued to the ministers of rites,
stating that since the ceremony for establishing the crown prince would not be held,
there was no need to separately prepare
any of the ceremonial items that would take time to manufacture.

four square umbrellas,
four double-dragon fans,
four peacock fans.

and two yíhuáng chǎng (ceremonial phoenix feather banners).
Ten gold-embroidered lóngdú (dragon banners),
ten gold-embroidered dragon small banners.
Ten bàowěi qiāng (leopard-tail spears),
ten bows and arrows,
ten dàdāo (large sabers),
eight horses,
four gold yuè (axes),
and four each of lìguā (standing melons), wòguā (lying melons), gǔduǒ (maces), and wúzhàng (ceremonial staffs).
Two fú (whisks).
Twelve huàjiǎo (painted horns),
twenty-four huākuāng gǔ (floral-frame drums),
eight large bronze hàos (trumpets),
two small bronze hàos (trumpets),
two each of jīn (bronze gongs), jīnzhēng (gold gongs), and zhànggǔ (staff drums),

two dàdáo,

Four leopard-tail spears,

Two red silk umbrellas and two fans.

Treatise 81: Selections (1)
Of the ancient methods for selecting officials,
none were as comprehensive as those of Chéng Zhōu,
and the abundance of talented individuals obtained
was also greatest in Chéng Zhōu.
After the Táng dynasty,
the system of elections was abolished,
and replaced with the examination system.
This was followed by successive dynasties.
The Míng dynasty exclusively used the Four Books and the Five Classics (Yì, Shū, Shī, Chūnqiū, Lǐjì) for examination topics to test scholars,
which was called 'composition according to standard' (zhìyì).
The Qīng dynasty completely adopted the Míng system.
For over two hundred years,
although there were those who entered through other paths,
they ultimately could not compare to those who gained official positions through the examination system.
During the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns,
special imperial examinations were instituted.
The 'Broad Scholars and Grand Literati' (bóxuéhóngcí) examinations
were lauded for attracting talented individuals.
However, what was tested was merely poetry, rhapsodies, and policy essays.
By the late period,
world changes became increasingly urgent.
Critics argued that the talent produced by the examination system was insufficient to meet the demands of the times,
and resolutely abolished the imperial examinations
to promote schools.
They adopted new educational systems from Eastern and Western countries,
transforming the established rules of selection since the Táng and Sòng dynasties.
The educational systems before and after
were distinctly two different matters.
Now, we will summarize the causes of the new and old differences and the evolution of their regulations and systems in this chapter.
Schools (1)
The Qīng dynasty schools
initially followed the Míng system.
The imperial capital's school was called Guóxué, and schools for the Eight Banners and imperial clan were also established.
In the provinces, there were prefecture, sub-prefecture, and county schools.
When Shìzǔ established the capital at Yānjīng,
he renovated and clarified the Northern Academy as the Tàixué.
In Shùnzhì first year (1644),
officials such as jìjiǔ, sīyè, jiāncéng, bóshì, zhùjiào, xuézhèng, xuélù, diǎnjí, and diǎnbù were appointed.
Six halls were set up for instruction and practice,
namely Shuàixìng, Xiūdào, Chéngxīn, Zhèngyì, Chóngzhì, and Guǎngyè,
all retaining the old Míng system.
Shàozhànshì Lǐ Ruòlín was first appointed jìjiǔ,
and requested to imitate the early Míng system
to widely recruit students.
Apart from those entering through hereditary privilege (ēn'yìn),
sons of officials of the seventh rank and above who were diligent and fond of learning,
and among commoners, apart from gòngshēng,
students who were lǐnshēng, zēngshēng, or fùshēng and excelled in literary composition
were all permitted to be selected by the tíxué and sent to the academy.
He also stated that the academy was named Guózǐ,
meaning that noble and distinguished sons of the state studied there.
In the previous dynasty, princes, marquises, earls, and imperial sons-in-law (fùmǎ) who were newly conferred titles
all entered the Guóxué to study.
Sons of Manchu meritorious officials who had aspirations for learning
were also requested to be sent to the academy for study.
An imperial edict approved the addition of Manchu sīyè, zhùjiào, and other officials,
marking the beginning of Eight Banners' sons entering the academy.
Subsequently, restrictions were set,
and regulations were revised multiple times,
becoming increasingly detailed and comprehensive.
Students studying in the academy
were either gòngshēng or jiānshēng.
There were six types of gòngshēng: suìgòng, ēgòng, bágòng, yōugòng, fùgòng, and lìgòng.
There were four types of jiānshēng: ēn jiān, yīn jiān, yōu jiān, and lì jiān.
There were two types of yīn jiān: ēn'yīn and nán'yīn.
They were collectively called Guózǐjiān shēng.
Students in the six halls
were divided into inner and outer classes.
Initially,
the inner class had 150 students,
25 per hall;
the outer class had 120 students,
20 per hall.
The Board of Revenue annually allocated silver from the treasury
to provide 'lamp-oil money' (gāohuǒ)
and varying rewards,
with the remainder reserved for relief.
In the early Qiánlóng period,
the inner class was changed to 30 students per hall,
with a total of 300 students for both inner and outer classes.
Later, the outer class of 120 students was abolished,
the gāohuǒ for the inner class was increased,
and 24 students from the inner class were assigned to be an 'outer class'.
In the early Jiāqìng period,
students from the Eight Banners and the two counties Dàxīng and Wànmíng who lived nearby,
and did not reside in the dormitories,
were not allowed to be assigned to the inner class.
At the beginning of class assignments,
students went to the academy for an examination,
called kǎodào.
Those ranked first or second were tested again,
called kǎoyàn.
Only gòngshēng ranked first or second,
and jiānshēng ranked first,
were permitted to study.
Returning to the academy after a leave was called fùbān.
Inner class students who wished to reside with relatives,
or Manchu, Mongol, or Han Banner ēn jiānshēng who were practicing translation or archery and horsemanship,
and could not attend school for a full month,
were changed to the outer class.
Missing one major lesson,
or unauthorized absence from school three times or more,
resulted in punishment by reassignment to the outer class.
A 'Record of Transgressions' (jíqiān cè) was kept
to deal with those who did not obey the teaching.
Entry and exit had to be recorded in a register,
managed by the jiāncéng.
Students visiting parents, getting married, observing mourning for parents, reporting illness, or observing mourning for an uncle or older brother without a son,
were granted leave to return to their hometown,
with a time limit for returning to the academy.
Delay resulted in punishment,
unauthorized departure resulted in dismissal,
and impersonation resulted in expulsion.
Regarding the method of teaching scholars,
on the first and fifteenth days of each month, after the ceremonies (shìdiàn) were completed,
the bóshì hall gathered all the students
to explain the classics.
In the first ten days of the month, the zhùjiào lectured on the meaning.
After the fifteenth,
the xuézhèng and xuélù each lectured on books once.
Joint lectures, review lectures, presenting books, and reciting from memory
occurred three times a month,
repeating in a cycle.
The books studied included the Four Books, Five Classics, Xìnglǐ, Tōngjiàn, and other works;
those who were also conversant with the Thirteen Classics, Twenty-One Histories,
and had extensively read numerous books
were allowed to proceed according to their aptitude and learning.
Daily, several hundred characters were copied from famous calligraphic models of the Jìn and Táng dynasties,
and a daily lesson book was established.
Every ten days, it was presented to the zhùjiào and others for critique,
and on the first and fifteenth, it was presented to the hall for inspection.
The jìjiǔ and sīyè alternately assigned a Four Books essay and a poem on the fifteenth of each month,
called 'major lessons'.
The jìjiǔ conducted quarterly examinations,
and the sīyè conducted monthly lessons,
all using essays from the Four Books and Five Classics,
as well as imperial edicts, proclamations, memorials, policy essays, and judgments.
On the first day of the month,
the bóshì hall assigned classical texts, classical commentaries, and policy essays.
On the third day of the month,
the zhùjiào assigned lessons,
and on the eighteenth,
the xuézhèng and xuélù assigned lessons,
each testing one Four Books essay, one poem, and one classical text or policy essay.
The method of integrating service for Imperial College students
was implemented in the early years of the dynasty.
When an Imperial College student's period of study at the Imperial College was full,
they would be assigned to various ministries and courts to practice governance.
Their diligence would be assessed after three months,
and after one year, they would be sent for the palace examination.
For those who were exempted from studying at the Imperial College,
or exempted from one or two months of service,
there were imperial edicts for this,
which were not standard practice.
In Shùnzhì three years (1646),
the Chancellor of the Imperial Academy, Xuē Suǒyùn, memorialized to establish the积分法 (Jīfēn Fǎ, point-based credit system) for Han Imperial College students.
In addition to the regular curriculum,
there would be a monthly test on classical exegesis and policy essays,
and those who met the standards would be promoted to the first rank.
Earning twelve first ranks in the annual examinations qualified one
for exemption from assignment to service,
and they would be sent directly to the palace examination for special selection.
In Shùnzhì fifteen years (1658),
the Chancellor of the Imperial Academy, Gù'ěrjiāhún, deliberated:
"When Imperial College students are examined,
those who are exceptionally outstanding shall be allowed to accumulate points;
those who are not,
upon completion of their term, shall be referred to the ministries for practical service.
The积分法 (Jīfēn Fǎ) is limited to one year.
In addition to the regular curriculum,
a first rank in the monthly test earns one point,
a second rank earns half a point,
and below second rank earns no points.
Those proficient in the Five Classics,
thoroughly familiar with all historical records,
or skilled in imitating the calligraphy of Zhōng and Wáng [Xīzhī and Xiànzhī]
shall also be given one point, even if their essays do not meet the standard.
Accumulating eight points qualifies one
for graduation, which does not exceed more than ten people annually.
The 恩贡 (Ēngòng), 拔贡 (Bágòng), 岁贡 (Suìgòng), and 副贡 (Fùgòng) [types of tribute students],
upon completion of their service referred by the ministries, shall be examined for official positions,
following the precedent of the teaching tribute students:
those in the 'superior-superior' category shall be appointed as tongpàn (通判, Assistant Prefect),
and those in the 'superior' category as zhīxiàn (知縣, County Magistrate).
Regular Imperial College students who complete their service and are examined for official positions
shall participate in the palace examination alongside tribute students who did not accumulate points.
For every hundred candidates, eight principal officials shall be selected,
and the rest shall serve as subordinate officials in prefectures and counties.
Those who do not accumulate enough points
but wish to be assigned to a ministry
shall be referred to the ministry but not granted preferential selection.
Those who wish to continue their studies until they accumulate the full points are permitted."
This was approved.
In the same year,
the Supervising Secretary Wáng Mìngyuè, citing the obstruction of the tribute student path,
requested a temporary suspension of the 恩贡 (Ēngòng), 拔贡 (Bágòng), and 岁贡 (Suìgòng) selections.
Consequently, fewer students attended the Imperial College,
making it difficult to compare scores.
In Shùnzhì seventeen years (1660),
Gù'ěrjiāhún memorialized to suspend the积分法 (Jīfēn Fǎ),
which was subsequently not reinstated.
In the early Kāngxī period,
the assignment to service was also suspended.
Upon completion of their term, students would be referred to the ministries for examination
and appointed as zhōutóng (州同, Assistant Subprefect), zhōupàn (州判, Subprefectural Judge), xiànchéng (縣丞, Assistant County Magistrate), zhǔbù (主簿, Registrar), or lìmù (吏目, Clerk).
From then on, there were no Imperial College students in the various departments of the ministries and courts.
Only those who were knowledgeable in literature and capable of writing in standard script
were selected for examination and sent to various writing bureaus
to have their years of service and merits assessed,
and then selected for appropriate official titles,
with superior ones sometimes receiving higher ranks.
The term of study at the Imperial College for students was:
恩贡 (Ēngòng) six months,
岁贡 (Suìgòng) eight months,
副贡 (Fùgòng) and lǐnshàn (廩膳) six months,
zēng (增) and fù (附) eight months,
拔贡 (Bágòng) and lǐnshàn (廩膳) fourteen months,
zēng (增) and fù (附) sixteen months,
恩廕 (Ēnyìn) twenty-four months,
難廕 (Nányìn) six months,
例贡 (Lìgòng) and lǐnshàn (廩膳) fourteen months,
zēng (增) and fù (附) sixteen months,
and Jùnxiù (俊秀) twenty-four months.
For 例监 (Lìjiān) [students who purchased their status], the donated months of study totaled thirty-six months.
In Yōngzhèng five years (1727),
regulations were established for calculating the term of study.
All Imperial College students' studies
generally used a term of three years, deducting intercalary months.
Leave of absence, mourning leave, poor performance, or demerits
would result in deductions of months and days.
If one returned to the Imperial College by the deadline after a leave of absence,
or exceeded the deadline but had a document from their local official,
the previous and subsequent periods would still be counted together.
According to the old system,
the Chancellor and Vice-Chancellor of the Imperial Academy jointly managed Imperial College affairs.
In Yōngzhèng three years (1725),
a Minister Overseeing Imperial College Affairs was first established.
In Qiánlóng two years (1737),
Sūn Jiāgàn, as the Minister of Punishments, managed Imperial College affairs.
Earlier, Sūn Jiāgàn served as Vice-Chancellor during Emperor Shìzōng's (Yōngzhèng's) reign,
and memorialized:
"The education in schools
should prioritize classical scholarship.
I request an imperial edict to all educational officials in the realm
to select and promote scholars to the Imperial College,
and that the Nine Ministers recommend scholars learned in classics and upright in conduct to serve as assistant teachers,
solely for cultivating scholars through classical scholarship.
After three years of assessment,
they should be recommended for use."
The proposal was not yet implemented
when he was promoted to Chancellor of the Imperial Academy,
where he reiterated his request,
and Emperor Shìzōng approved it.
Previously, Imperial College students, though nominally studying at the Imperial College,
usually rented lodgings and were scattered.
They would only gather temporarily for ritual ceremonies, hall gatherings, seasonal examinations, and monthly lessons.
The Imperial College originally had over five hundred residential cells,
but they were not repaired in a timely manner,
and with insufficient funds,
there was no way to house the students.
Sūn Jiāgàn said:
"Over three hundred 拔贡 (Bágòng) students from various provinces have gathered in the capital,
needing to reside at the Imperial College.
The six halls are only suitable for reading,
not for dwelling.
I beg for the official residences south of the Imperial College
to be given to the assistant teachers and students for their residence.
Six thousand taels of silver should be provided annually for lecture fees, meals, clothing, and relief."
This was granted.
This became the Nánxuè (南學, Southern School).
At this point,
he requested to emulate the ancient method of Sòng (宋) scholar Hú Yuàn, which divided classical exegesis and practical governance into separate academies.
Those who studied the classics
would specialize in one classic,
or simultaneously study other classics,
focusing on the 御纂折中 (Yùzuǎn Zhézhōng) and various traditional commentaries,
delving into their origins,
and elucidating the principles of human relations and daily life.
Those who studied practical governance
focused on topics such as historical rites, land tax and corvée, laws and statutes, border defense, water conservancy, astronomy, canals, and arithmetic.
They would specialize in one area,
or concurrently study several areas,
diligently researching their origins, merits, and drawbacks.
During examinations,
profound classical scholarship, thorough understanding of practical matters, and an appreciation for ancient history and love for the people were required.
Upon completion of the three-year term,
students would be categorized into different grades
to encourage and admonish.
This was approved.
Students were instructed that if they had insights or doubts,
they should note each point,
present it to the assistant teachers for critique,
and then present it to the hall regularly.
For seasonal examinations and monthly lessons,
one question from the Four Books,
one question on the commentary of each of the Five Classics,
and one policy question on practical governance were set.
At that time, Emperor Gāozōng (Qiánlóng) paid special attention to the Imperial College.
Sūn Jiāgàn strictly established the curriculum,
and his encouragement and inducement were thorough.
The lecturers of the six halls
were the best selections of the era.
Jǔrén (舉人) Wú Dǐng and Liáng Xīyú
were both recommended for their classical scholarship and appointed as Vice-Chancellors.
Jìnshì (進士) Zhuāng Hēngyáng;
Jǔrén (舉人) Pān Yǒngjì, Cài Déjùn, Qín Huìtián, Wú Nài;
Gòngshēng (貢生) Guān Xiànyáo, Wáng Wénzhèn;
and Jiānshēng (監生) Xià Zōnglán
were all recommended for their profound study of the classics
and successively appointed as officials of the Imperial College.
They were divided to lead the six halls,
each specializing in one classic,
and were
known as the "Four Worthies and Five Gentlemen."
Teachers and students, numerous and flourishing,
all strived to improve themselves
and diligently pursued practical learning.
Furthermore, the Chancellor of the Imperial Academy Zhào Guólín, in addition to classical exegesis and practical governance,
believed that contemporary essays should be taught and practiced,
and requested the imperial promulgation of the Imperially Sanctioned Four Books for recitation and study in the six halls.
This was also approved.
During the Qīng dynasty, the grand ceremony of the emperor inspecting the National Academy was of utmost importance.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì (1652),
Shìzǔ (Emperor Shùnzhì) personally presided over the inspection for the first time.
Prior to this, the Yǎnshèng Gōng and the Wǔjīng Bóshì were summoned to lead the descendants of the Kǒng clan and the various clans of the former sages to the capital to observe the ceremony.
After the emperor completed the memorial rites,
he proceeded to the Yílún Táng and sat in the lecture tent.
The Jìjiǔ lectured on the Fóur Shū (Four Books),
and the Sīyè lectured on the classics.
An imperial edict was proclaimed to encourage the students of the Grand Academy.
On the following day,
the Yǎnshèng Gōng was bestowed with robes and hats,
and officials of the Guózǐjiān (National Academy) received various rewards.
Descendants of the various clans were sent to the academy for study.
Thereafter, this was regularly performed by successive emperors.
In the forty-eighth year of Qiánlóng (1783), an imperial edict stated:
"Examining the ancient system of national education,
the emperor's academy was called Bìyōng,
where rites and music were performed, virtue and transformation promulgated, civilization manifested, and the benefits of education spread;
this was a matter of immense significance.
The national academy is a place where culture and talent converge,
and its regulations should be grand.
Regarding the establishment of Bìyōng,
since the Yuán and Míng dynasties,
the ceremony has been lacking,
and it should be expanded to achieve perfection."
He commanded Shàngshū Débǎo,
Shàngshū and concurrent Guózǐjiān administrator Liú Yǒng,
and Shìláng Déchéng,
to follow the old system of the Lǐjīng (Book of Rites)
and construct it south of the Yílún Táng.
The following year,
it was completed.
The year after that,
Gāozōng (Emperor Qiánlóng) personally visited Bìyōng to perform the lecturing ceremony.
He commanded Dàxuéshì and Bó Wǔmítài,
and Dàxuéshì and academy administrator Cài Xīn,
to lecture on the Sì Shū (Four Books).
Jìjiǔ Juéluó Jíshàn and Zōu Yìxiào
lectured on the Zhōu Yì (Book of Changes).
Two imperial treatises were promulgated,
expounding their profound meanings.
Princes, dukes, the Yǎnshèng Gōng, officials below the rank of Dàxuéshì,
as well as the 3,088 students
who were studying and observing the ceremony,
listened to the lecture around the bridge.
After the ceremony,
a banquet was bestowed upon the Lǐbù (Ministry of Rites),
with additional favors.
At this time, the Son of Heaven favored literary culture,
and all officials personally experienced a flourishing and enlightened era,
assisting in the promotion of culture,
which was truly reaching its peak.
After Jiāqìng,
the ceremony of inspecting the academy
was generally followed and not abolished.
In the early Xiánfēng period,
it was still held once.
At the end of Dàoguāng,
an edict was issued to rectify the southern academy;
over a hundred students resided there,
but the academy's regulations had been long neglected
and were difficult to revitalize.
During the Xiánfēng military campaigns,
annual stipends were disbursed in installments,
and regulations were frequently changed.
In the first year of Tóngzhì (1862),
considering that the national academy focused solely on literature and arts,
which was not beneficial for practical learning,
it was ordered to also teach essays and policy papers.
Topics were set using classics, histories, and neo-Confucian texts,
to encourage those who paid attention to current affairs.
The following year,
an additional three thousand taels were disbursed for annual expenses.
In the ninth year (1870),
the old quota was restored.
Forty students with excellent literary skills and conduct were selected to reside in the southern academy,
and generously provided with stipends,
whereupon the literary atmosphere gradually revived.
In the second year of Guāngxù (1876),
twenty more students were added.
In the eleventh year (1885),
Jǔrén from various provinces were allowed to enter the academy,
known as Jǔjiān.
Thereafter, regardless of whether they were Jǔrén or Gòngjiānshēng,
as long as they were not officially appointed officials who had not yet submitted their reports,
or Jǔrén and Gòngshēng who had not yet been summoned by an instructor,
they were allowed to enter the academy,
to broaden the scope of talent cultivation.
The various categories of Gòngjiānshēng mostly followed the Míng system.
For Suìgòng (annual tribute students),
those from prefectural, subprefectural, and county schools who had received stipends for many years were selected,
and promoted in sequence.
In the second year of Shùnzhì (1645),
it was ordered that Suìgòng scholars from directly administered provinces proceed to the capital.
One student annually from a prefectural school,
two students every three years from a subprefectural school,
and one student every two years from a county school,
with one main and two accompanying students.
The Xuézhèng (Education Commissioner) rigorously selected them,
and those improperly chosen were sent back to their original schools.
If there were five or more such cases,
the Xuézhèng was punished by deduction of salary.
In the fifteenth year (1658),
it was ordered that upon arrival at the ministry, a detailed inspection should be carried out,
and only those who were strong and vigorous
were allowed to be sent to the academy.
In the first year of Kāngxī (1662),
the Gòng quota was reduced:
two students every three years from a prefecture,
one student every two years from a subprefecture,
and one student every three years from a county.
In the eighth year (1669),
it reverted to the system of the second year of Shùnzhì.
In the twenty-sixth year (1687),
the court examination for Suìgòng was abolished.
Thereafter, they were merely examined and approved by the Xuézhèng in sequence and recommended to the ministry for appointment as local Xùndǎo (instructors).
After obtaining a position,
the Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor) would conduct another examination,
and fewer wished to enter the academy.
Ēngòng (grace tribute students),
following the Míng system,
were filled by those who would have been Gòng students
when the nation had auspicious ceremonies or an imperial ascension edict.
In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
an edict ordered that in prefectural, subprefectural, and county schools of directly administered provinces,
the regular Gòng of that year be designated Ēngòng,
and the next Gòng be designated Suìgòng.
Successive imperial edicts were all similar.
In the ninth year (1652),
fifteen students who were descendants of the Five Clans and observed the ceremony
were sent to the academy for study,
and allowed to be counted as Ēngòng.
After Qiánlóng,
it became customary for Lǐnshēng, Zēngshēng, and Fùshēng, who were descendants of sages and worthies, to be granted the favor of observing the ceremony at Bìyōng and entering the academy.
During the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns,
when the Son of Heaven made eastern tours
and personally visited Quèlǐ,
he selected students from the Five Clans and Thirteen Clans to be Gòng and enter Chéngjūn (the National Academy);
this was an act of special grace towards the descendants of sages,
and not a regular system.
Bágòng (selected tribute students),
based on the remnants of the Míng selection system,
were instituted in the first year of Shùnzhì (1644).
Six for Shùntiān (Prefecture),
two from each prefectural school in directly administered provinces,
and one from each subprefectural and county school.
In the tenth year of Kāngxī (1671),
the academic officials were ordered to select those with both excellent literary skills and conduct from among the first and second-class students examined
to be Gòng to the Grand Academy,
following the request of Jìjiǔ Zhā Lù.
The following year,
Baqí students were first selected:
two for Mǎnzhōu and Ménggǔ,
and one for Hànjūn.
At that time, many provincial selections for Gòng were fraudulent;
between the thirty-seventh and thirty-eighth years (1698-1699),
Jìjiǔ Tèmòdé and Sūn Yuèbān personally interviewed six selected students from Shānxī, including Zhāng Hànchōng,
four from Shǎnxī, including Lǚ Ěr,
and three from Guǎngdōng, including Chén Qíwěi.
All of them were found to be academically incompetent,
with erroneous handwriting and calligraphy.
Their original papers were rejected,
the academic officials were impeached and dealt with,
and thus the selection of Bágòng was suspended.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (1723),
Lǐbù Shàngshū Chén Yuánlóng memorialized to request strict regulations for study at Chéngjūn.
The ministry deliberated,
that students of the Grand Academy
were all admitted through donation,
and talented literary scholars were scarce,
so academic officials should be ordered to select and send students to the academy according to the old system.
This was approved.
In the fifth year (1727),
Shìzōng (Emperor Yōngzhèng), considering that Suìgòng were selected based on the duration of stipends,
and many were old and infirm,
wished to obtain talented individuals,
which necessitated selection.
He ordered that thereafter, selections be made once every six years.
The following year,
an edict further instructed that Xuézhèng in selecting Bágòng should not be restricted to first or second-class students,
but should test them with policy essays on current affairs,
and if they indeed possessed insight and ability,
their character should be investigated,
and even if they were not ranked in the excellent category,
they should still be allowed to be selected.
Therefore, during the Yōngzhèng and Qiánlóng reigns, the Bágòng system was the most flourishing for filling positions in the national academy.
In addition, there were schools for commoners,
which were the Eight Banners official schools.
In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
Ruòlín memorialized,
"Your servant's office is located in the northeast corner of the city,
which is inconvenient for Manchu officials' children to attend school.
It is proposed that academies be established in each of the Eight Gùshān (Banners) areas of Mǎnzhōu,
and that the two halls and six classrooms of the Guóxué's instructors be assigned to teach there,
attending examinations and evaluations periodically."
The proposal was submitted to the Board for discussion and implementation.
Thus, schoolhouses were built for each of the Eight Banners.
One official student was selected from each zuǒlǐng (company),
with ten studying Hànshū (Chinese classics),
and the rest studying Mǎnshū (Manchu classics).
In the second year (1645),
following Suǒyùn's suggestion,
two banners were combined into one school.
Each school had ten instructors,
who were chosen from students (shēngyuán) in the capital and provinces.
Later, the student quota was repeatedly increased or decreased,
and instructors were selected from students who had completed their studies at the Guóxué,
using only ēn gòngshēng, bá gòngshēng, fù gòngshēng, and suì gòngshēng.
If none such were available,
jìan shēng were also allowed to take the examination.
Jǔrén who wished to serve
were also selected by examination.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (1723),
from among the Mongolian Banner's hùjūn (guards) and lǐngcuī (corporals), and xiāoqí (cavalrymen),
sixteen individuals skilled in Guóyǔ (Manchu language) and Mongolian language were selected
to serve as Mongolian instructors.
Traditionally, official students were selected and sent by their zuǒlǐng.
In the fifth year (1727),
it was stipulated that each banner would have a quota of one hundred students:
sixty Mǎnzhōu,
with half studying Qīngshū (Manchu classics) and half Hànshū (Chinese classics).
Mongolian and Hànjūn (Chinese-Martial) each had twenty,
selected from the entire banner,
without regard to zuǒlǐng.
Younger students studied Qīngshū,
while older ones studied Hànwén (Chinese writing).
Thirty Mǎnzhōu and ten Mongolian and Hànjūn from the Eight Banners' soldiers designated for education and training
were allocated stipends for students.
It was stipulated that each banner should have five Hàn instructors.
In the early years of Qiánlóng,
it was stipulated that official students should study for a period of ten years.
Within three years, they would recite and expound on classics,
and supervising officials would test them.
Those with brilliant talent and strong scholarly resolve were selected
for the Hànwén class;
older students who wished to learn translation
were assigned to the Mǎnwén class.
After three years,
ministers appointed by imperial decree would test and select those proficient in Hànwén,
promote them to jìan shēng,
and advance them to the Tàixué.
They, along with Hàn gòngshēng and jìan shēng, would diligently study classics and manage affairs.
Upon completion of their term,
the best among them would be recommended,
examined, and appointed.
In the eighth year (1743),
it was stipulated that Hàn instructors, upon completing their three-year term,
would be granted an audience according to their ranking.
First-class instructors would be appointed as zhīxiàn (magistrates);
second-class instructors would be selected for appointments as zhīxiàn or educational officials.
First-class instructors who served another three years
and genuinely excelled in teaching
would be directly appointed as zhīxiàn.
Mongolian instructors who genuinely excelled in teaching after completing their five-year term
would be appointed as hùjūnxiào or xiāoqíxiào.
Each banner had two Manchu assistant instructors,
selected from Eight Banners literary jìnshì and jǔrén,
translation jìnshì and jǔrén,
ēn gòngshēng, bá gòngshēng, fù gòngshēng, suì gòngshēng,
literary shēngyuán,
translation shēngyuán,
dismissed officials,
and bǐtiēshì.
In the thirty-third year (1768),
ten additional students were added to each of the Lower Five Banners' bāoyī (bondservant companies).
Six Manchu,
two Mongolian, and two Hànjūn,
without stipends.
In the fifty-fourth year (1789),
ten students were cut from the hundred in each banner,
and twenty individuals proficient in classics and excellent in literary skills were selected
and given extra stipends as encouragement.
After the Jiāqìng and Dàoguāng eras,
the official schools gradually declined,
and Eight Banners' children relied solely on them for advancement.
The rule of appointing instructors upon completion of their term was suspended,
and monthly evaluations were merely a formality.
Although clear edicts repeatedly urged rectification,
it was difficult to revitalize them.
In the early years of Guāngxù,
efforts were made to reorganize them.
Each school had one Mǎn or Hàn imperial examination official as guǎnxuéguān (school superintendent),
specially responsible for evaluating students' coursework
and instructors' diligence or idleness.
Two high-ranking officials of Mǎn and Hàn jìnshì background were appointed by imperial decree as ministers overseeing the Eight Banners official schools.
One hànlín biān (compiler) or jiǎn (editor) was added to each school.
Monthly and quarterly examinations
were separately administered.
Spring and autumn joint examinations at the Guózi Jiān continued as before.
Between Tóngzhì and Guāngxù,
the Guóxué and official schools produced many talents for the imperial examinations,
and were quite flourishing.
However, they were constrained by "tīekuò" (stereotyped essays),
and the old system rarely adapted.
In the thirty-first year (1905),
the supervising minister memorialized to add a science curriculum to the Nánxué.
Soon after,
the Guózi Jiān was abolished,
and the Xúebù (Ministry of Education) was established.
The sacrifices at the Confucius Temple
were managed by one Guózi Chéng.
The Eight Banners official schools were reorganized and merged into Xúetáng (modern schools),
and the mathematics school was also renamed Qīntiānlǐan Tiānwén Suànxué (Imperial Astronomical Bureau School of Astronomy and Mathematics),
subordinated to the Qīntiānlǐan.
And thus, the Tàixué, along with the imperial examinations, was abolished.
The Zōngxué (Imperial Clan Schools) originated from Yú Tíng (the court of Emperor Shùn),
when Kuí was ordered to manage music,
teaching the imperial descendants.
During the Three Dynasties, there was no name "Zōngxué,"
but its meaning was already fulfilled.
After the Táng and Sòng dynasties,
the name existed, but the system was not detailed.
In the tenth year of Qīng Shùnzhì (1653),
each of the Eight Banners established Zōngxué,
selecting Mǎnzhōu shēngyuán as teachers.
All un-ennobled imperial clan members' children,
aged ten and above,
all entered to study Qīngshū.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng (1724), a system was established:
one Mǎn and one Hàn school were set up for both the Left and Right Wings.
Children of princes, dukes, generals, and unemployed imperial clan members, under eighteen years old,
entered to study Qīngshū and Hànshū separately,
along with archery and horsemanship.
One prince or duke was in charge of the overall administration.
General and deputy administrators were appointed,
chosen from the most respected and senior imperial clan members.
Two Qīngshū instructors were appointed,
selected from dismissed idle banner officials, and jìnshì, jǔrén, gòngshēng, and shēngyuán skilled in translation.
Two archery and horsemanship instructors were appointed,
selected from dismissed idle banner officials and hùjūnxiào skilled in archery.
For every ten students,
one Hànshū instructor was appointed,
selected by the Lǐbù (Board of Rites) from jǔrén and gòngshēng.
Upon completion of a three-year term,
they were recorded and appointed according to their rank.
In the eleventh year (1733),
two hànlín officials were appointed to each of the two schools to supervise the curriculum,
lecturing on classical exegesis and grammar on alternate days.
In the early years of Qiánlóng,
one Mǎn and one Hàn Jīngtáng (central government official) were appointed to oversee the school's curriculum,
with monthly examinations in classical exegesis, translation, and archery skills.
In the ninth year (1744),
it was stipulated that every five years,
ministers would be appointed by imperial decree to jointly examine students from both wings,
and their rankings would be imperially determined
and registered as having passed the huìshì (metropolitan examination).
In the year of the huìshì,
those who studied translation
would be granted an audience together with the Eight Banners' translation gòngshēng,
awarded the jìnshì degree,
and appointed as supernumerary zhǔshì (secretaries) in government offices.
Those who studied Hànwén
would take the diànshì (palace examination) together with all other gòngshì (tribute scholars),
awarded the jìnshì jiǎdì (first class jìnshì),
and appointed as officials in the hànlín academy or its subordinate offices.
In the tenth year (1745),
the examinations in Hànwén and translation yielded no excellent works.
An edict stated:
"Our dynasty values fundamental principles.
Children of the imperial clan should all study Qīngwén
and become proficient in archery and horsemanship.
I truly fear that studying Hànwén
will lead to the decadent practices of the Hàn people.
Shìzǔ (Emperor Shùnzhì) decreed the suspension of Hànshū study,
thereby strengthening the fundamentals and eliminating extravagance.
Henceforth, those imperial clan children who cannot study Hànwén
should all vigorously practice martial arts,
to be reserved as useful tools for the nation."
The following year (1746),
student quotas were set:
seventy for the Left Wing,
and sixty for the Right Wing.
In the twenty-first year (1756),
nine Hàn instructors were dismissed
and replaced with translation instructors.
Archery and horsemanship instructors were increased,
one for each wing.
In the early years of Jiāqìng,
the student quotas for both wings were standardized,
and the Right Wing's quota was increased by ten.
It was stipulated that each school would have three Mǎn instructors
and four Hàn instructors.
In the thirteenth year (1808),
each wing's quota was increased by thirty,
reaching one hundred students,
which became a permanent system.
The Jiàoluó School.
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1729),
an imperial decree ordered the establishment of one Manchu school and one Han school adjacent to the yámén of each of the Eight Banners.
Jiàoluó children aged eight to eighteen
were admitted to study and practice archery.
Its regulations were slightly similar to those of the Zōng School.
The supervising Princes and Dukes
conducted examinations in spring and autumn.
Every three years, specially appointed ministers, in conjunction with the Zōngrénfǔ, conducted examinations
and meted out rewards and punishments accordingly.
Upon completion of their studies,
they could participate in the Suì and Kē examinations, and the Xiāng and Huì examinations, along with other Banner people,
and also be examined for positions as Zhōngshū and Bǐtiěshì.
The student quotas were: sixty-one for the Bordered Yellow Banner,
thirty-six for the Plain Yellow Banner,
forty each for the Plain White Banner and the Plain Red Banner,
fifteen for the Bordered White Banner,
sixty-four for the Bordered Red Banner,
thirty-nine for the Plain Blue Banner,
and forty-five for the Bordered Blue Banner.
For Manchu and Han instructors,
there were two for each banner,
except for the Bordered White Banner, which had one of each.
The Jǐngshān Official School.
In the twenty-fourth year of Kāngxī's reign (1685),
an order was issued to establish an official school in the government offices on both sides of the Běishàngmén.
Three hundred and sixty young children were selected from the Zǔolǐng and Guǎnlǐng of the three Imperial Household Banners.
There were three Manchu language divisions,
each with three instructors.
There were three Han language divisions,
each with four instructors.
Initially,
Manchu instructors were chosen from experienced officials of the Imperial Household,
while Han instructors were selected through examinations by the Lǐbù from among talented Xiùcái.
Later, this was changed to selecting experienced Zhōngshū from the Nèigé skilled in calligraphy and archery to be Manchu instructors,
and experienced new Jìnshì to be Han instructors.
After Yōngzhèng's reign,
Han instructors were selected from Jǔrén and Gòngshēng through examination.
After serving for three years,
they were recommended to the board for employment.
Students who studied for three years,
if ranked in the first class, were employed as Bǐtiěshì;
if in the second class, as Kùshǐ or Kùshǒu.
In the forty-fourth year of Qiánlóng's reign (1779),
four students from the Huízǐ Zuǒlǐng were allowed to be selected and recruited.
During the Jiāqìng period,
the fixed quotas were one hundred and twenty-four each for the Bordered Yellow Banner and the Plain White Banner,
one hundred and forty for the Plain Yellow Banner,
and four for Hui children.
The Xián'āngōng Official School.
In the sixth year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1728),
an imperial decree ordered the selection of ninety gifted young children from the Zuǒlǐng and Guǎnlǐng of the three Imperial Household Banners and other talented individuals from the Eight Banners.
They were taught by Hànlín officials residing in the Xián'āngōng.
There were twelve Han language divisions
and three Manchu language divisions,
each with one instructor.
For archery and the national language,
there were three instructors each,
following the examination model of the Jǐngshān Official School.
Every five years, specially appointed ministers conducted examinations.
Those in the first and second classes were employed as seventh or eighth-rank Bǐtiěshì.
Han instructors served for three years, and Manchu language and archery instructors for five years,
with their employment discussed separately.
In the early Qiánlóng period,
it was stipulated that Han instructors be selected from new Jìnshì;
if there were not enough,
Jǔrén from the Míngtōng list were examined and appointed.
Upon completing their term,
Jìnshì were employed as Zhǔshì or Zhīxiàn,
and Jǔrén as Zhīxiàn or in educational positions.
After the twenty-third year (1758),
regardless of their year of entry,
students were allowed to take examinations for Fānyì Zhōngshū, Bǐtiěshì, and Kùshǐ.
The fixed number of instructors was nine for Han
and six for Manchu.
The Zōng School and the Jiàoluó School were subordinate to the Zōngrénfǔ,
while the Jǐngshān School and the Xián'āngōng School were subordinate to the Nèiwùfǔ.
The superintendents and instructors of these schools
often lacked comprehensive talent,
and the expenses were merely wasted.
In severe cases, the school buildings were empty,
and at the end of the term,
only a certain number of "achieving students" were routinely reported.
In the twenty-eighth year of Guāngxù's reign (1902),
Bǎoxī, a Shìdú of the Hànlínyuàn, memorialized to request, citing the precedent of the Tóngwénguǎn being merged into the Dàxué Táng,
that the imperial clan, Jiàoluó, Eight Banners, and other official schools be reorganized and merged into primary and secondary schools,
all to be managed by the ministers in charge of education.
This was approved.
Other schools, such as the Hereditary Official School,
the Eight Banners and Lǐbù Charity Schools,
and the Jiànruìyíng, Wàihuǒqìyíng, Yuánmíngyuán, and Hùjūnyíng Schools,
were all specially established during the Qīng dynasty
to teach Manchu and Mongolian languages and scripts.
The Fǔ, Zhōu, Xiàn, and Wèi Confucian schools
were well-established under the Míng system,
and the Qīng adopted them.
After Shìzǔ pacified the realm,
he ordered relief for poor students,
exempted currently enrolled students,
and provided government stipends.
In the seventh year of Shùnzhì's reign (1650),
the Nánjīng Guózǐjiān was renamed the Jiāngníngfǔ School.
Soon after, the Wòbēi text was promulgated
and carved on stone steles erected in the school temples of all provinces.
An edict to the Lǐbù stated:
"For emperors and kings to govern,
cultural education comes first.
For ministers and sons to serve their lord,
classical learning is fundamental.
Since the turmoil at the end of the Míng dynasty,
there have been daily conflicts,
and the way of scholarship
has been neglected and unaddressed.
Now that the realm is gradually settled,
We intend to promote cultural education
and revere classical learning
to usher in an era of great peace.
Your ministry shall transmit this edict to the education officials of the provinces,
instructing and supervising scholars,
that they must diligently research and thoroughly master all books on Neo-Confucianism, ethics, statecraft, and historical precedents.
Those who understand the essence will be true Confucians;
those who can apply it will be good officials.
If there are truly learned individuals,
We shall certainly promote them without regard to sequence
and give them important appointments."
Initially,
each province established a Dūxué Dào,
filled by Lángzhōng from various ministries who were Jìnshì.
Only Shùntiān, Jiāngnán, and Zhèjiāng had Tídū Xuézhèng,
using Hànlín officials.
Xuāndà, Sūsōng, Jiāng'ān, Huái Yáng, Zhào Gāo were initially separately established,
but later merged.
Shàngxiàjiāng and Húnánhán were divided again after being merged.
In the middle of Yōngzhèng's reign,
they were uniformly renamed Xuéyuàn,
with one person established per province.
Fèngtiān had the Fǔchéng, and Táiwān had the Táiwāndào concurrently hold the position.
Gānsù, after the division of examination halls,
first established a Xuézhèng.
For instructors in various schools,
a Jiàoshòu was set up for each Fǔ,
a Xuézhèng for each Zhōu,
and a Jiàoyù for each Xiàn,
each with one,
all assisted by a Xùndǎo.
Quotas for personnel were sometimes merged or reduced.
Categories of students (Shēngyuán)
were Lǐnshànshēng, Zēngguǎngshēng, and Fùshēng.
Those initially admitted were called Fùxué Shēngyuán.
Lǐn and Zēng had fixed quotas, supplemented by those with higher rankings in the Suì and Kē examinations.
The initial quota for Shēngyuán varied based on the population density,
divided into Dàxué, Zhōngxué, and Xiǎoxué.
Dàxué had forty students,
Zhōngxué thirty,
and Xiǎoxué twenty.
Subsequently, Fǔ was equated with Dàxué,
large Zhōu and Xiàn with half of Zhōngxué,
and Xiǎoxué with four or five students.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī's reign (1670),
large Fǔ, Zhōu, and Xiàn reverted to their old quotas,
while Zhōngxué was re-set to twelve students,
and Xiǎoxué to seven or eight students.
Later, there were several increases.
Children of Manchu, Mongolian, and Han Banner people
were initially admitted through examinations in Shùntiān.
There were one hundred and twenty each for Manchu and Han Banner,
and sixty for Mongolian.
In the middle of Kāngxī's reign, the quotas were reduced to forty each for Manchu and Mongolian,
and twenty for Han Banner.
Soon after, they were increased again to sixty each for Manchu and Mongolian,
and thirty for Han Banner.
The Xuézhèng served for three years.
There were the Suì and Kē examinations.
In the fifteenth year of Shùnzhì's reign (1658), the Kē examinations in the provinces were suspended,
and in the twelfth year of Kāngxī's reign (1673), they were reinstated.
For the examination for Confucian students entering school,
initially one essay on the Fóur Shū and one discourse on the Xiàojīng were used.
As there were few topics from the Xiàojīng,
they also set questions from the Xìnglǐ, Tàijí Túshuō, Tōngshū, Xīmíng, and Zhèngméng.
Later, it was stipulated that the main examination should consist of two essays on the Fóur Shū.
The re-examination consisted of one essay on the Fóur Shū and one discourse on the Xiǎoxué.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
scripture essays were added to the 科試 (kēshì).
In winter months, when daylight hours were short,
one Fóur Shū essay and one scripture essay were given.
Soon after, it was stipulated that in addition to the Fóur Shū and scripture essays for the kēshì,
a policy essay question was added,
still using the Xiàojīng.
In the early Qiánlóng reign,
the re-examination also included a Xiǎoxué discourse.
After the mid-reign,
the examination included one essay on book learning and one essay on scriptural learning.
A five-character, six-rhyme poem was added.
The Shèngzǔ (Kāngxī Emperor) successively promulgated the Shèngyù Guǎngxùn and the Xùnchì Shìzǐ Wén to the Confucian schools in the directly administered provinces.
During the Yōngzhèng period,
Grand Secretary Zhāng Zhào memorialized to order Confucian students to take re-examinations at the county and prefectural levels,
reciting one section of the Shèngyù Guǎngxùn from memory,
which was made into a regulation.
All newly admitted shēngyuán,
following the example of those studying at the Guózǐjiàn,
were required to study at the school,
completing their term when the next cohort of new students entered.
The method for instructional officials (jiàoguān) to examine and assess students
included monthly assignments and quarterly examinations.
In addition to Fóur Shū essays,
policy essays were also tested.
The next day, several key articles of the Dàqīng Lǜ concerning criminal law, money, and grain were lectured.
Monthly, all students gathered in the Mínglún Táng,
reciting the Xùnchì Shìzǐ Wén and various articles from the Wòbēi,
with the students listening in a circle.
Except for those in mourning, ill, studying abroad, or with other valid reasons,
those who failed to attend monthly assignments three times were admonished.
Those who failed to attend without reason for a whole year were expelled.
Examination papers were submitted to the Xuézhèng for review.
Towards the end of the Jiāqìng reign,
monthly assignments gradually ceased to be held.
Censor Xīn Cóngyì spoke about this,
and an imperial edict ordered rectification.
Thereafter, many jiàoguān were incompetent and unworthy of their positions,
having the name of teacher and student,
but lacking the substance of instruction.
The Xuézhèng assessed jiàoguān
based on their character, conduct, and diligence in instructing students,
recommending or dismissing them as appropriate.
During the Kāngxī reign,
governors were ordered to examine them.
Later, after instructional posts were selected by the Board,
they would proceed to the governor's yámen for examination.
Those in the fourth grade or above
were given credentials to take up their posts;
those in the fifth grade would study for three years and be re-examined;
those in the sixth grade were dismissed from office.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
it was stipulated that those in the fourth and fifth grades were both to be relieved of their posts for further study.
After six years of excellent performance and completion of their term,
if they had diligently instructed and the students had committed no transgressions,
the Dūdù (governor-general), Fǔtái (governor), and Xuézhèng would recommend them for promotion
to the position of Zhīxiàn.
When the Xuéchén (Educational Commissioner) arrived,
he would pay respects to the former teachers,
ascend the Mínglún Táng,
and officials and students would greet him in order.
Shēngyuán would draw lots to lecture on books,
each lecturing on three articles from the Dàqīng Lǜ,
standing facing west;
after lecturing,
they would stand facing east, awaiting rewards or punishments.
For the examination of shēngyuán,
the old regulation for both the Suìshì and Kēshì was two Fóur Shū essays and one scripture essay.
Since the prohibition on giving candles,
it was customary not to set scripture topics.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
scripture essays were added to the Kēshì,
with one Fóur Shū essay and one scripture essay in winter months.
In the sixth year,
it was revised to two Fóur Shū essays and one scripture essay for the Suìshì,
and one Fóur Shū essay and one scripture essay in winter months.
For the Kēshì, it was one Fóur Shū essay, one scripture essay, and one policy essay,
with the scripture essay reduced in winter months.
In the twenty-third year of Qiánlóng,
it was changed to one Fóur Shū essay and one scripture essay for the Suìshì,
and one Fóur Shū essay, one policy essay, and one poem for the Kēshì,
with the same for winter months.
Those who missed examinations
were given a deadline to make them up.
Three absences
resulted in expulsion.
Later, the rule was relaxed,
with expulsion only after five or more absences.
For examinations of the garrison troops,
in the early Qīng dynasty, it was stipulated
that sons of officers and soldiers of the garrisons in various provinces who could read
should go to the capital for examinations.
During the Qiánlóng era,
Cānlǐng Jīn Héng requested permission for the general to first examine their horsemanship and archery for the Suìshì and Kēshì,
and then send them to the prefectural yámen nearby for admission.
A severe imperial edict sternly rebuked him.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
Húnán Bùzhèngshǐ Tōng'ēn memorialized in agreement with Jīn Héng's suggestion,
and an imperial edict discussed its implementation.
For the child students taking the examination,
one out of five or six was admitted,
and the Zuǒlǐng would supervise them.
They were trained in Manchu language, horsemanship, and archery,
and the prefectural school taught literature and arts.
The following year, an edict stated:
"The foundation of our Mǎnzhōu [people]
is primarily horsemanship and archery.
If the sons of the Eight Banners exclusively consider reading and taking examinations as their ability,
lightly regarding archery and horsemanship,
and neglecting military preparedness,
it would greatly deviate from the state's intention in establishing garrisons.
Henceforth, sons of officials and soldiers of the garrisons in various provinces
must not neglect their primary profession
due to the existence of nearby examination regulations."
The establishment of lǐn and zēng quotas for the Hànjūn [Banner]
began in the ninth year of Shùnzhì.
In the tenth year of Kāngxī,
Mǎn and Méng also established lǐn and zēng quotas.
Initially, there were twenty for each,
later reduced to ten for the Hànjūn.
During the Yōngzhèng period, quotas were fixed:
sixty for Mǎn and Méng,
thirty for Hànjūn.
For directly administered provinces, the lǐn and zēng quotas were:
forty for prefectures,
thirty for zhōu,
twenty for xiàn,
and ten for wèi.
For newly established ones,
prefectural schools were treated like zhōu schools,
and zhōu schools like xiàn schools.
If one school was divided into two,
the quota was equally divided,
or distributed differentially.
The six-grade promotion and demotion system
was more intricate than that of the Míng dynasty.
If ranked first grade,
zēng, fù, qīng, and shè all filled lǐn vacancies.
If no lǐn vacancies,
fù, qīng, and shè filled zēng vacancies.
If no zēng vacancies,
qīng and shè reverted to fù,
each awaiting a lǐn position.
Original lǐn and zēng who were suspended or demoted were reinstated.
Second grade:
zēng filled lǐn vacancies,
fù, qīng, and shè filled zēng vacancies.
If no zēng vacancies,
qīng and shè reverted to fù.
Those whose lǐn status was suspended and demoted to zēng were reinstated to lǐn.
Those whose zēng status was demoted to fù were reinstated to zēng,
but not allowed to fill lǐn vacancies.
Third grade:
those whose lǐn status was suspended were reinstated to await lǐn.
Those who returned from mourning,
recovered from illness and were re-examined,
or were reinstated due to other matters,
and zēng demoted to fù were allowed to be reinstated.
Qīngyī sent to shè were reinstated to fù.
Lǐn demoted to zēng were not allowed to be reinstated.
Fourth grade:
lǐn were exempt from responsibility but had their stipends suspended,
not creating a vacancy,
and were given six months to study before being sent for examination.
Those who were suspended or demoted were not allowed to take this examination.
Zēng, fù, qīng, and shè were all punished with beating.
Fifth grade:
lǐn were suspended, creating a vacancy.
Those originally suspended from lǐn were demoted to zēng;
zēng demoted to fù;
fù demoted to qīngyī;
qīngyī sent to shè;
those originally sent to shè were expelled and became commoners.
Sixth grade:
lǐn who had received stipends for ten years or more were sent to shè.
Those with six years or more, along with zēng with ten years or more,
were sent to their local area to serve as clerks.
The rest were expelled and became commoners.
Those who had been admitted for less than six years were sent to shè.
First and second grades in the Kēshì were sent to the Xiāngshì,
and helped to fill lǐn and zēng vacancies.
As for the Suìshì, they were generally only ranked third grade.
Eight Banners shēngyuán were given money and grain.
Those ranked fourth grade or below had their stipends suspended.
If they ranked first, second, or third grade in the next examination, their stipends were restored.
Excellent grades filled lǐn and zēng vacancies.
Poor grades were demoted to qīng or shè,
like Hàn shēngyuán.
The Eight Banners always valued horsemanship and archery,
often not strictly demanding literary and artistic skills,
but merely placing them in lower grades.
The Shànghǎi Guǎngfāngyánguǎn (Shanghai Institute of Foreign Languages)
was founded in the second year of the Tóngzhì reign (1863).
Jiāngsū巡撫 Lǐ Hóngzhāng stated:
"The establishment of the Jīngshī Tóngwénguǎn (Peking Tongwen Guan)
is truly an excellent method.
However, the principal hubs for foreigners
are the two ports of Shànghǎi and Guǎngdōng.
It is proposed to imitate the example of the Tóngwénguǎn
and establish an institute for foreign languages and writing in Shànghǎi,
selecting literate youths from nearby prefectures, under fourteen years of age, with sharp intellect and calm, upright character,
to be taught by Western teachers,
