and also engaging jǔgòngshēngyuán (recommended scholars) from the interior who possess both excellent character and scholarship
to instruct them in the classics, history, and literature.
Upon completion of their studies, they would be sent to the provincial dūfǔ (governor-general and governor) for examination,
to be registered as fùxuésheng (attached students) of their respective counties.
As for probationary officials, assistant officials, and the like,
those who are young and intelligent
would be permitted to enter the institute for the same studies,
and upon completion, would be given appropriate promotion opportunities.
After three to five years,
with this kind of educated and enlightened individual,
fluent in foreign languages,
any yámén (government office) of commerce, dūfǔ, and maritime customs superintendents
that require translation officials to handle foreign affairs
could select and appoint them from the institute.
This would ensure the verification of customs duties and military provisions;
unruly interpreters
would also somewhat curb their activities.
Moreover, they would be able to read all Western specialized books not yet translated,
exploring profound mysteries,
and all ingenious techniques such as steamships and firearms
would gradually become understood,
providing no small benefit
to the path of self-strengthening."
The emperor decreed that the Guǎngzhōu Jiāngjūn (Guangzhou General) should follow this plan.
The Fújiàn Chuánchǎng (Fujian Shipyard)
was proposed and established in the fifth year of Tóngzhì (1866)
by Zuǒ Zōngtáng when he was the governor-general of Fújiàn,
with an associated school.
It was divided into two halls: a Front Hall and a Rear Hall.
The Front Hall studied French
and practiced shipbuilding techniques;
the Rear Hall studied English
and practiced navigation techniques.
In addition to the regular courses required for shipbuilding and navigation,
the curriculum also included policy essays,
and students were made to read the Shèngyù Guǎngxùn (Sacred Edict with Amplifications) and the Xiàojīng (Classic of Filial Piety) to understand moral principles.
The first director of the shipbuilding administration was Shěn Bǎozhēn,
whose plans were grand and far-reaching,
and who particularly emphasized the school.
In the twelfth year (1873),
he submitted a memorial on the follow-up matters for the shipyard workers:
"I request that students from the Front and Rear Halls be selected and dispatched to England and France
to learn methods of manufacturing and navigation,
as well as the principles of innovation and of training troops for victory.
Students with outstanding natural talent
who can study mining, chemistry, diplomacy, public law, and other subjects
may pursue these studies as appropriate."
Soon after, Bǎozhēn was appointed Nányáng Dàchén (Minister for Southern Ports).
In the second year of Guāngxù (1876),
he memorialized to appoint Chinese and foreign supervisors
and to establish regulations.
The talents produced by the Chuánzhèng Xuétáng (Naval Administration School)
were truly the pioneering figures of the Chinese navy.
The school was located in Mǎwěi,
hence during the late Qīng dynasty, naval commanders
were mostly from Fújiàn.
The Tiānjīn Shuǐshī Xuétáng (Tianjin Naval Academy)
was proposed and established in the eighth year of Guāngxù (1882)
by the Běiyáng Dàchén (Minister for Northern Ports), Lǐ Hóngzhāng.
Students were recruited the following year
to enter the academy for study.
It was divided into two departments: navigation and engine management.
Instruction was in English,
combined with drill practice
and courses in the classics and Chinese language.
Excellent students were sent abroad for further study
to deepen their expertise.
Subsequently, many naval generals graduated from this institution.
Hóngzhāng also proposed the establishment of the Tiānjīn Wǔbèi Xuétáng (Tianjin Military Academy) in the eleventh year of Guāngxù (1885),
the regulations of which generally imitated Western military academies.
Robust, intelligent officers and non-commissioned officers from the battalions, who had a basic understanding of literature, were selected
to enter the academy for study.
Civil officials willing to learn military affairs
were also admitted.
The curriculum involved, on one hand, researching new Western military methods,
such as various breech-loading rifles and cannons,
civil engineering and encampment, and various tactics for deployment, dispersion, attack, and defense.
On the other hand, they would go to the camps for practical training,
practicing rifle and cannon formations and constructing earthworks and fortifications.
However, since the students were selected officers and non-commissioned officers,
even though German instructors were employed,
they could not listen directly to lectures,
and still used interpreters,
making the teaching indirect,
which was different from the Naval Academy's emphasis on foreign languages.
Initially,
after one year of study,
students who passed the examinations
were sent back to their respective battalions,
where their commanders would assign them duties according to their abilities.
Later, the duration was gradually extended,
and young children from good families were recruited for study.
By the time of the Gēngzǐ Zhībiàn (Boxer Rebellion),
the academy happened to be in the war zone,
and the entire school was reduced to ashes.
In addition, the Guǎngdōng Shuǐlùshī Xuétáng (Guangdong Naval and Army Academy)
was proposed by the Yuè Dū (Governor-General of Guangdong and Guangxi), Zhāng Zhīdòng, in the thirteenth year of Guāngxù (1887).
When Zhīdòng was transferred to become the È Dū (Governor-General of Huguang),
he again proposed the establishment of the Húběi Wǔbèi Xuétáng (Hubei Military Academy) in the twenty-first year (1895).
Its methods and curriculum
for the navy were divided into engine management and navigation,
and for the army into cavalry and infantry,
rifles and cannons,
and engineering,
largely following the established practices of Běiyáng.
By the time the navy was established
and the new army was restructured,
such academies,
in Nányáng and various provinces, increased significantly,
and will not be detailed here.
As for the Húběi Zìqiáng Xuétáng (Hubei Self-Strengthening Academy),
it was also founded by Zhīdòng.
Initially, it was divided into four departments: foreign languages, science, mathematics, and commerce.
However, only the foreign language section
had residential study,
while the other three sections held monthly examinations.
Later, mathematics was transferred to the Liǎnghú Shūyuàn (Two Hu Academies) for instruction,
and science and commerce classes were suspended.
The main academy specialized in foreign languages,
serving as a stepping stone to Western learning.
The foreign language department was divided into English, French, German, and Russian,
and was similar to the Tóngwénguǎn schools.
Between the Bǐngshēn and Dīngyǒu years of Guāngxù (1896-1897),
as academies could not be universally established in the provinces,
many Chinese and foreign officials requested that shūyuàn (academies of classical learning) be reformed and reorganized.
An imperial edict ordered their reform,
and the Lǐbù (Board of Rites) approved regulations
for incorporating astronomy, mathematics, and science into the curriculum.
Provinces like Shǎnxī established Gézhì Shíxué Shūyuàn (Academies for Practical Science)
to compensate for the shortcomings of the academies.
Generally, the objective of establishing schools during this period
was solely focused on practicality.
This was because the motivation stemmed from foreign relations,
hence foreign languages and the army and navy received primary focus in education during this period,
with no systematic educational structure to speak of.
However, although the Nányáng Gōngxué (Nanyang Public School) also inherited the educational objectives of this period,
its educational system was divided into three grades,
already embodying the concept of general schools and preparatory education.
Earlier, in the twenty-first year of Guāngxù (1895),
the Jīnhǎiguāndào (Tianjin Customs Dao), Shèng Xuánhuái, founded first and second-grade schools in Tiānjīn.
The first-grade school had a four-year curriculum;
after completing the first year,
those wishing to specialize in one field
could have their aptitude assessed and determined accordingly.
There were five specializations: one, engineering;
two, electrical engineering;
three, mining;
four, mechanical engineering;
five, law.
The second-grade school had a four-year curriculum,
advancing by class,
and upon completion, students would advance to the first grade.
The intention was that the second grade resembled foreign primary schools,
and the first grade resembled foreign universities.
Due to its initial establishment,
a flexible and quick approach was adopted.
As teachers were scarce,
and students were difficult to select precisely,
there was little success.
In the twenty-third year (1897),
Xuánhuái again founded the Nányáng Gōngxué in Shànghǎi,
adapting and modifying the Tiānjīn system,
with funding provided by donations from the Zhāoshāngjú (China Merchants' Steam Navigation Company) and the Diànbàojú (Imperial Chinese Telegraph Administration).
It was memorialized and approved for operation,
hence named Gōngxué (Public School).
It was divided into four departments: Shīfànyuàn (Normal Department),
Wàiyuàn (External Department),
Zhōngyuàn (Middle Department),
and Shàngyuàn (Upper Department).
The Wàiyuàn was an affiliated primary school,
serving as a practice ground for normal students.
The Zhōngyuàn and Shàngyuàn were the second-grade and first-grade schools,
embodying the meaning of secondary school and higher school.
The curriculum was broadly divided into Chinese and English sections,
with an emphasis on political science, law, and economics.
Graduates of the Shàngyuàn,
especially the most outstanding, were recommended to study abroad
at universities in various countries.
The intention was that since a domestic university could not be established immediately,
the Gōngxué served as a preparatory school,
and foreign universities were considered the highest institutions of learning.
Commentators say that this marked the beginning of a systematic organization of Chinese education.
Later, it was transferred to the jurisdiction of the Yóuchuánbù (Ministry of Posts and Communications)
and renamed Gāoděng Shíyè Xuétáng (Higher Industrial School).
Its curriculum and nature
were no longer the same as its initial purpose.
This generally covers the first period of unsystematic education.
Since the Jǐnwǔ campaign,
the army was lost and the nation humiliated.
The great powers rose en masse,
scrambling for rights and seizing privileges,
and the nation's situation became even more precarious.
Patriots both in and out of government
suddenly realized that the previous reforms had not grasped the fundamental issues.
Vice Minister Lǐ Duānfēn, Director Kāng Yǒuwéi, and others
all submitted memorials proposing the widespread establishment of schools.
In the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù,
Emperor Dézōng decreed:
“Recently, several edicts have been issued,
establishing special imperial examinations,
reforming the military examination system,
and setting up universities and primary schools.
However, the prevailing customs have not yet fully opened up,
and discussions are far from reaching a consensus.
If the national situation is unstable,
then decrees will not be effective.
It is hereby clearly announced to both domestic and foreign audiences
that from princes and dukes to scholars and commoners,
all should strive diligently and with fervor,
to cultivate their foundation with the studies of sagely principles and righteousness,
broadly adopt Western learning relevant to current affairs,
and earnestly apply themselves to its study,
in order to remedy the shortcomings of superficiality and misguidedness.
The Capital University shall set an example for all provinces
and should be established first.
All Hanlin Academicians (biānxiū and jiǎnchá),
department and court officials,
palace guards from all gates,
expectant Dàotái,
officials below prefect, zhōu, and xiàn magistrates,
children of high officials,
hereditary officials of the Eight Banners,
and descendants of military officials from all provinces
are permitted to enroll and study,
with the aim of producing a multitude of talents
to jointly overcome the national difficulties.”
It was ordered that the Grand Councillors and the Princes and Ministers overseeing the Zǒnglǐ Gèguó Shìwù Yámén
should deliberate and report.
Soon after, a report was submitted proposing the establishment of the Jīngshī Dàxué Táng (Capital University).
Draft regulations outlined four main points: firstly, broadly raise funds;
secondly, extensively construct school buildings;
thirdly, carefully select the Minister of Education;
and fourthly, appoint a Chief Instructor.
The edict was issued as proposed.
Sūn Jiānài was appointed to manage the affairs of the university,
and funds were to be allocated by the Hùbù.
In the fifth month,
another edict was issued to the Governors-General and Governors of all provinces,
ordering that all large and small academies (shūyuàn) in the prefectures, departments (tīng), zhōu, and xiàn of their respective provinces
be uniformly converted into schools teaching both Chinese and Western subjects.
Regarding their hierarchy,
the large academies in provincial capitals were to be High Schools (gāoděng xué),
academies in prefectural cities Middle Schools (zhōngxué),
and academies in zhōu and xiàn Primary Schools (xiǎoxué).
The regulations for the Jīngshī Dàxué were promulgated,
ordering that they be followed.
All funds from the academies
were to be fully transferred for school expenses.
If gentry and commoners could donate to build schools,
or widely solicit contributions,
they were permitted to petition for awards.
Those who independently raised large sums of money
were to be given exceptional rewards.
Private ancestral temples not included in the official sacrificial canon
were to be uniformly converted into schools,
to save lavish expenses and promote education.
At this time, the authority of the Minister of Education
was not limited to managing the Jīngshī Dàxué Táng;
it also extended to supervising schools established in all provinces.
This position effectively held the powers of a university president concurrently with a national minister of education.
Furthermore, since the Tóngwén Guǎn and Běiyáng Xuétáng largely employed Westerners as chief instructors,
this inevitably led to a deficiency in Chinese studies.
Moreover, there was more than one foreign language,
and academic disciplines each had their specialties,
which no single Westerner could manage.
Therefore, it was necessary to select Chinese scholars
who were well-versed in both Chinese and Western learning
and could grasp the greater picture
to serve as chief instructors,
hiring them exceptionally
and granting them the power to select sectional instructors.
The reasoning was that the Minister of Education had to be a Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) or a President of a Board (Shàngshū),
while chief instructors were not restricted by qualifications,
thus allowing for the recruitment of new and emerging talents.
Students were divided into two classes:
those who had completed ordinary studies formed the first class,
and those currently pursuing ordinary studies formed the second class,
which was similar to the old system of the Nányáng Gōngxué.
The curriculum was divided into two categories: ordinary and specialized.
Ordinary studies
were compulsory for all students;
specialized studies
allowed each person to focus on one or two subjects.
Ordinary subjects included Classics (jīngxué),
Neo-Confucianism (lǐxué),
Institutional History (zhǎnggùxué),
Masters' Studies (zhūzǐxué),
elementary mathematics,
elementary physics,
elementary politics,
elementary geography,
literature,
gymnastics,
and linguistics.
Specialized subjects included advanced mathematics,
advanced physics,
advanced politics (including law),
advanced geography (including surveying),
agriculture,
mining,
engineering,
commerce,
military science,
and hygiene (including medicine).
Student assessment
used a points system.
Students received varying monthly stipends.
An editing and translation bureau was established in Shànghǎi,
and for all subjects except foreign languages,
translated textbooks were to be used.
This was the outline of the university establishment regulations.
Not long after,
the coup d'état of the eighth month occurred,
and the old party seized control of the court,
eventually leading to the disaster of Gēngzǐ.
It was not until the twenty-seventh year
that discussions for the revival of schools gradually emerged.
The primary proponent
was Yuán Shìkǎi, Governor of Shāndōng.
Initially,
Shìkǎi memorialized on the regulations for establishing universities in Shāndōng Province,
and an imperial edict instructed other provinces to follow suit,
ordering the Zhèngwù Chù to jointly deliberate with the Lǐbù on regulations for selection and encouragement.
Soon after, a discussion suggested:
“In Western and Eastern countries, schools
are progressively structured from primary to secondary to university,
and only after graduation are qualifications granted.
We propose to follow this method.
Primary school graduates who pass examinations
are selected for middle schools.
Middle school graduates who pass examinations
are then selected for universities.
University graduates who pass examinations
are issued certificates.
Governors-General, Governors, and Education Commissioners
shall rigorously conduct closed examinations
based on their coursework.
Outstanding candidates will be ranked
and recommended to the Jīngshī Dàxué Táng for a re-examination,
to be granted the status of Jǔrén or Gòngshēng.
Gòngshēng may sit for the next examination;
those wishing to take the xiāngshì are permitted.
When a sufficient number of Jǔrén accumulate,
the Jīngshī Dàxué Táng shall conduct rigorous examinations,
and outstanding candidates will be ranked
and recommended to the Lǐbù.
Ministers will be specially appointed to conduct examinations,
and upon imperial approval,
they will be designated as Jìnshì,
all of whom will participate in the diànshì,
and will be appropriately promoted and appointed,
with generous official ranks.
Regarding Shìkǎi’s approach,
since it was not possible to establish schools throughout the entire province at once,
schools were first established in the provincial capital,
divided into separate halls for instruction.
The ‘Ready Hall’ (bèizhāi) and ‘Main Hall’ (zhèngzhāi)
implicitly represented the regulations for primary and middle schools.
Since an edict has ordered all provinces to follow suit,
the future examination and promotion regulations should be considered
to provide encouragement.”
The report was approved.
The proposed integration of the imperial examination system and the school system into one,
called the “Regulations for School Examination and Encouragement,”
was mostly not implemented by the provinces before being abandoned.
On the *xīnchǒu* day,
the two imperial palaces returned.
Due to the deep pain of the wounds,
reforms were vigorously sought.
In the twelfth month,
an imperial edict stated:
“Establishing schools and nurturing talent
is indeed the most urgent task of the present time.
The capital, as the premier district,
should especially pay attention to cultivation
to set an example.
The university established previously
should be earnestly implemented.
Zhāng Bǎixī is appointed as Minister of Education,
charged with its management,
and must ensure its proper direction
and the cultivation of versatile talents.
He should draft the regulations
and submit them for imperial approval.”
Shortly thereafter, an edict ordered the Tongwén Guǎn to be merged into the university,
and no longer affiliated with the Ministry of Foreign Affairs.
In the first month of the twenty-eighth year,
Bǎixī submitted a memorial on the preparations for the university and a provisional plan,
stating:
“In the educational systems of various countries,
children enter primary school after graduating from elementary school;
after three years of primary school, they advance to middle school;
after another three years, they advance to higher education;
and after another three years, they advance to university.
Applying this to China,
primary schools are the county schools,
middle schools are the prefectural schools,
and higher education institutions are the provincial schools.
Currently, there are no students ready to enter university,
so as a flexible arrangement,
the only option is to temporarily not establish specialized departments,
but first establish a higher education institution as a preparatory course for the university.
It will be divided into two departments: politics and arts.
Classical studies, history, politics, law, commerce, finance, and other related matters will be under the political department,
while acoustics, optics, electricity, chemistry, agriculture, engineering, medicine, mathematics, and other related matters will be under the arts department.
Among the schools in the capital and provinces,
those that have achieved good results
are the Húběi Zìqiáng Xuétáng and Shànghǎi Nányáng Gōngxué.
In addition, schools like the Jīngshī Tóngwén Guǎn,
Shànghǎi Guǎngfāngyán Guǎn,
Guǎngdōng Shímǐn, and Zhèjiāng Qiúshì Xuétáng
have been established for several years
and are not lacking in qualified talents.
Furthermore, governors, viceroys, and education commissioners from various provinces shall select high-achieving students from prefectures, departments, and counties,
send them to the capital,
and if they pass the re-examination,
they will enter the school for studies.
After three years of study,
those who pass will advance to the regular university program.
Those who do not pass
will be transferred to study abroad or withdrawn.
The preparatory university students will be at the same level as graduates from provincial schools,
and after passing the examination administered by the Minister of Education,
an imperial decree will be requested to grant them the *Jǔrén* title.
After graduating from the regular program,
and passing the examination,
an imperial decree will be requested to grant them the *Jìnshì* title.
However, the state urgently needs talent,
and to achieve quick results and minimize the loss of talent,
there is a method for training teachers rapidly.
Outside the preparatory department, a crash course department will be established,
divided into two sections: the Shìxué Guǎn and the Shīfàn Guǎn.
All capital officials of rank five and below, but eight and above,
and provincial officials of the *dàoyuán* rank and below, but teaching positions and above,
are permitted to test into the Shìxué Guǎn.
*Jǔ*, *gòng*, *shēng*, and *jiàn* students
are all permitted to test into the Shīfàn Guǎn.
After three years of study in the Shìxué Guǎn,
the most outstanding will be selected and rewarded.
After three years of study in the Shīfàn Guǎn,
the most outstanding will be chosen and presented for imperial audience.
*Shēng* students will be permitted to become *gòngshēng*,
*gòngshēng* students will be permitted to become *jǔrén*,
and *jǔrén* students will be permitted to become *jìnshì*,
and will be granted diplomas allowing them to serve as primary or middle school teachers respectively.
For preparatory students, we must select those who are older and somewhat proficient in academics,
and with further training,
store them as truly qualified talents.
For crash course students, we select those with more experience and a strong will to advance,
taking advantage of their ability to quickly adapt.
As for constructing new school buildings,
establishing an affiliated translation bureau,
and purchasing a large number of books and instruments,
the most crucial foundation is to secure ample funding.
Funding will be divided into two categories: first,
the interest from the deposits in the Huá’é Dàoshèng Yínháng
will be entirely allocated to the university;
second,
an imperial order will be requested to instruct various provinces to contribute funds,
with large provinces contributing twenty thousand *jīn* annually,
medium provinces ten thousand *jīn*,
and small provinces five thousand *jīn*,
to be regularly remitted to the capital.”
This was approved.
In the seventh month,
Bǎixī, following the proposed regulations for schools,
memorialized:
“Ancient and modern, Chinese and foreign,
academic disciplines differ,
but their practical application is the same.
The current systems of Europe, America, and Japan
are quite similar to the excellent methods of China's prosperous ancient times.
The *Lǐ Jì* records that in a family there is a *shú*,
in a district there is a *xiáng*,
in a state there is an *xù*,
and in the capital there is a school.
Compared to other countries,
the capital school is the university,
and the family *shú*, district *xiáng*, and state *xù* are the elementary, primary, and middle schools.
The hierarchy is very clear.
Before the Zhōu dynasty, elections and schools were integrated;
after the Hàn dynasty, emphasis shifted to elections,
and since the establishment of the *Jìnshì* examination in the Suí dynasty,
scholars devoted all their energy to poetry, rhymed prose, policy essays, and treatises,
and the so-called schools
existed in name only.
Today, when discussing the revitalization of education,
the first priority must be to truly restore the former system of schools.
Although the political and educational customs of China and foreign countries originally differ,
their profound and unalterable structure and order
mean that while one need not cling to every detail,
one cannot but adopt their strengths.
Therefore, respectfully tracing back to ancient systems
and referring to various nations,
I have drafted the regulations for the Capital University and the provincial higher schools, middle schools, primary schools, and elementary schools.
These await imperial approval and promulgation to the provinces,
to be earnestly implemented.
All schools that exist in name but not in reality, and teachers who are incompetent and merely fill positions,
shall be strictly rectified.”
An imperial edict was issued to the governors and viceroys of various provinces,
ordering them to diligently carry out the regulations.
This marked the "Imperial Approved School Regulations."
The systematic nature of education began from this point.
The Jīngshī Dàxuétáng (京師大學堂) was divided into a Dàxuéyuàn (大學院), a Dàxué Zhuānmén Fēnkē (大學專門分科), and a Dàxué Yùbèikē (大學豫備科).
Attached institutions
were the Shìxué (仕學) and Shīfàn (師範) schools.
The Dàxuéyuàn primarily focused on research,
offering no lectures
and establishing no curricula.
There were seven specialized divisions:
Political Science,
Literature,
Science,
Agriculture,
Technology,
Commerce,
and Medicine.
The Political Science division had two categories:
Politics
and Law.
The Literature division had seven categories:
Classics,
History,
Philosophy,
Masters' Works,
Institutions and Antiquities,
Rhetoric and Belles-Lettres,
and Foreign Languages.
The Science division had six categories:
Astronomy,
Geology,
Advanced Mathematics,
Chemistry,
Physics,
and Zoology and Botany.
The Agriculture division had four categories:
Agronomy,
Agricultural Chemistry,
Forestry,
and Veterinary Medicine.
The Technology division had eight categories:
Civil Engineering,
Mechanical Engineering,
Shipbuilding,
Ordnance Manufacturing,
Electrical Engineering,
Architecture,
Applied Chemistry,
and Mining and Metallurgy.
The Commerce division had six categories:
Bookkeeping,
Industrial Manufacturing,
Commercial Languages,
Commercial Law,
Commercial History,
and Commercial Geography.
The Medicine division had two categories:
Medicine
and Pharmacy.
The Yùbèikē (豫備科) was divided into two sections: Political (政科) and Technical (藝科).
The Political Section curriculum included:
Ethics,
Classics,
Masters' Works,
Rhetoric and Belles-Lettres,
Mathematics,
Chinese and Foreign History,
Chinese and Foreign Geography,
Foreign Languages,
Physics,
Logic,
Law,
Public Finance,
and Gymnastics.
The Technical Section curriculum included:
Ethics,
Chinese and Foreign History,
Foreign Languages,
Mathematics,
Physics,
Chemistry,
Zoology and Botany,
Geology and Mineralogy,
Drawing,
and Gymnastics.
To facilitate entry into a specific specialized division,
some subjects could be added or removed.
All courses required three years to complete.
The Shìxuéguǎn (仕學館) curriculum included:
Mathematics,
Natural History,
Physics,
Foreign Languages,
Geography,
History,
Institutions and Antiquities,
Public Finance,
Diplomacy,
Law,
and Politics.
The Shīfànguǎn (師範館) curriculum included:
Ethics,
Classics,
Pedagogy,
Calligraphy,
Composition,
Mathematics,
Chinese and Foreign History,
Chinese and Foreign Geography,
Natural History,
Physics,
Chemistry,
Foreign Languages,
Drawing,
and Gymnastics.
Higher schools (Gāoděng Xuétáng 高等學堂) in each province served as a path for middle school graduates to advance,
and also as preparation for entry into the specialized divisions of the university.
They were divided into Political (政科) and Technical (藝科) sections.
The curriculum was the same as the university preparatory course.
Three years to graduate.
In addition to the higher schools,
higher vocational schools (Gāoděng Shíyè Xuétáng 高等實業學堂) for agriculture, engineering, commerce, and medicine could be established,
also for middle school graduates to enter.
Teaching employed a specialized faculty system,
with each teacher responsible for one subject.
Middle schools (Zhōngxuétáng 中學堂) served as a path for higher primary school graduates to advance,
and also as preparation for entry into higher schools.
The curriculum included:
Morality,
Classical Studies,
Mathematics,
Rhetoric and Belles-Lettres,
Chinese and Foreign History,
Chinese and Foreign Geography,
Foreign Languages,
Drawing,
Natural History,
Physics,
Chemistry,
and Gymnastics.
Four years to graduate.
In addition to middle schools,
secondary vocational schools (Zhōngděng Shíyè Xuétáng 中等實業學堂) for agriculture, engineering, and commerce could be established,
for higher primary school graduates who did not wish to pursue general studies.
Normal schools (Shīfàn Xuétáng 師範學堂) were also attached,
with a curriculum similar to middle schools,
but with a reduction in foreign languages
and the addition of pedagogy and teaching methods.
Two or three classes could be combined,
with two or three teachers each responsible for several subjects,
teaching them separately.
Primary schools (Xiǎoxuétáng 小學堂) were divided into higher and ordinary levels.
Children starting from six years old
received four years of basic education (méngxué 蒙學).
At ten years old, they entered ordinary primary school (xúncháng xiǎoxué 尋常小學),
studying for three years.
These seven years were designated as compulsory education.
At thirteen years old, they entered higher primary school (gāoděng xiǎoxué 高等小學),
graduating after three years.
Simple vocational schools (Jiǎnyì Shíyè Xuétáng 簡易實業學堂) for agriculture, engineering, and commerce could be attached,
for ordinary primary school graduates to enter.
The ordinary primary school curriculum included:
Morality,
Classical Studies,
Composition,
Calligraphy,
History,
Geography,
Arithmetic,
and Gymnastics.
The higher primary school curriculum
added the study of classical prose, science, and drawing,
with the rest being the same as ordinary primary school.
Teaching adopted the class teacher system.
In addition to regular teachers (zhèng jiàoxí 正教習),
assistant teachers (fù jiàoxí 副教習) could be appointed.
The basic education schools (Méngxuétáng 蒙學堂) belonged to compulsory education,
and should be established in prefectures (fǔ 府), sub-prefectures (tīng 廳), departments (zhōu 州), districts (xiàn 縣), cities (chéng 城), towns (zhèn 鎮), townships (xiāng 鄉), and market towns (jí 集).
All charity schools (yìjú 義塾) or private academies (jiājú 家塾)
should be reorganized according to the basic education curriculum.
The curriculum was the same as ordinary primary schools,
but composition was replaced by character lessons.
The purpose of basic education
was to reform private schools,
hence the regulations
Previously, Bǎi Xī 招致 [recruited] famous scholars from all over the country,
to serve in various positions in the Imperial University (Dàxué Táng).
Wú Rǔlún was the Chief Instructor (zǒng jiàoxí),
and went to Japan to observe schools.
At that time, students studying in Japan frequently stirred up trouble,
rumors were rife,
and partisan disputes grew increasingly intense.
In the first month of the twenty-ninth year
Róng Qìng was ordered to jointly manage the affairs of the Imperial University with Bǎi Xī.
Their academic thoughts
were already different,
and their opinions on personnel appointments and administration
were even more divergent.
At this time, the Governor of Húběi, Zhāng Zhīdòng, came to the capital for an audience.
Zhīdòng enjoyed great prestige throughout the country,
and in Sìchuān, Jìn, Yuè, and È (Guǎngdōng and Húběi),
he had established academies (shūyuàn) and schools (xuétáng).
His work "Quànxué Piān" (Exhortation to Study)
was widely read for a time;
he particularly harbored a long-standing ambition to rectify educational affairs.
In the intercalary fifth month,
Róng Qìng, together with Bǎi Xī, submitted a memorial requesting the additional appointment of Zhīdòng to jointly discuss educational affairs.
An imperial edict ordered Zhīdòng to collaborate with the Ministers of Education (guǎnxué dàchén) to define all school regulations,
so as to ensure their implementation without irregularities.
In the eleventh month,
Bǎi Xī, Róng Qìng, and Zhīdòng jointly submitted a memorial to revise the school regulations,
stating:
"When various provinces first establish schools,
it is difficult to find people deeply versed in educational principles and methods.
Students are mostly drawn from those originally pursuing the imperial examinations,
having not been refined by primary education,
their speech and conduct
inevitably exceed proper bounds.
This time, having received the imperial command to jointly discuss and define,
we have meticulously considered
and exercised extreme caution.
We have extensively examined the curricula and subjects of various foreign schools,
adapted and modified them with discretion,
using those that are suitable,
omitting those unsuitable for China,
changing subject names that are incomprehensible,
and reducing those that are overly burdensome.
Regardless of the type of school,
all shall take loyalty and filial piety as their foundation,
and the study of Chinese classics and history as their base,
so that students' moral character (xīnshù) will be entirely pure and upright.
Thereafter, Western learning shall be used to cultivate their knowledge
and train their skills,
with the aim that in the future they will become talented individuals,
each serving practical use.
We have drafted regulations for elementary primary schools (chūděng xiǎoxué), higher primary schools (gāoděng xiǎoxué), middle schools (zhōngxué), and higher education (gāoděng xué),
as well as regulations for the Imperial University (dàxué) with its attached Academy for General Scholars (tōngrú yuàn).
The original regulations contained the category of 'Měngxué' (children's education),
which in reality listed matters pertaining to foreign elementary primary schools.
Foreign nurseries (měngyǎngyuàn),
also known as kindergartens (yòuzhìyuán),
have been considered,
and regulations for nurseries and methods for family education have been drafted.
These were present in the original regulations,
but their omissions have been supplemented.
In managing schools,
the first priority is teacher training.
The originally drafted regulations for Normal Schools (shīfàn guǎn)
were only tentatively implemented based on the situation in the capital,
and were still rudimentary.
Separate regulations have been drafted for junior (chūjí) and senior (yōují) normal schools,
as well as regulations for the appointment of teachers.
The Normal School in the capital shall be reformed to operate according to the senior normal school model.
Furthermore, the Academy for Officials (shìxué guǎn) is temporarily established
and is not within the general system of schools;
its original regulations should temporarily remain as they are.
The Translation Academy (yìxué guǎn) is the same as the School of Foreign Languages (fāngyán xuétáng);
the Jinshi Academy (jìnshì guǎn) was established by special imperial decree,
ordering all new jinshì to enter the academy for study.
Its curriculum differs from other schools,
and its regulations and curriculum have also been appropriately defined.
Moreover, for the livelihood of the people and the nation,
nothing is more essential than agriculture, industry, and commerce (nóng, gōng, shāng shíyè).
Establishing practical industry schools (shíyè xuétáng)
brings a hundred benefits and no harm.
Separate regulations have been drafted for elementary, middle, and higher agricultural, industrial, and commercial practical industry schools,

along with regulations for practical industry supplementary general schools (shíyè bǔxí pǔtōng xuétáng), apprentice schools (yìtú xuétáng), and practical industry teacher training institutes (shíyè jiàoyuán jiǎngxí suǒ).
These were not covered in the original regulations,
but have been separately compiled.
Furthermore, China's rites, ethics, politics, and customs differ from those of other countries.
Young students, upon initial learning,
lack established discernment,
and are prone to confusion and superficiality,
which is unavoidable.
Discipline must be strict,
and supervision must be rigorous.
Specific rules have been established,
and prohibitions clarified,
to serve as general guidelines for school management.
The aims of establishing schools and the key principles of legislation
have also been summarized and elucidated,
to serve as the纲要 (gāngyào) [main points/program] for educational affairs.
If these newly defined regulations can be seriously implemented,
the intelligence of the people can be enlightened,
the nation's strength can be enriched,
and talents can be nurtured,
without giving rise to other malpractices.
As for student graduation examinations,
promotion and entrance examinations, and methods of reward and employment,
special chapters have also been meticulously drafted,
awaiting imperial decision."
They also reported:
"By imperial decree, the establishment of schools began
more than two years ago.
To this day, the reason why many provinces have not been able to establish more
is the difficulty in raising funds.
The reason funds cannot be collected
is that the imperial examinations have not been abolished.
The literati of the realm believe that the court does not attach sole importance to schools.
If the imperial examinations are not reformed and reduced,
human nature will inevitably lead to a wait-and-see attitude.
Which gentry and wealthy would be willing to contribute funds?
Funds certainly cannot be raised,
and schools certainly cannot be numerous.
Those who enter schools
rely on the imperial examinations as a fallback,
are unwilling to devote themselves to learning,
and are unwilling to strictly adhere to school regulations.
Moreover, imperial examination essays often involve plagiarism,
while schoolwork emphasizes practical cultivation;
the imperial examinations depend solely on a single day's performance,
while schools require years of research;
the imperial examinations only value literary talent,
while schools also emphasize conduct.
Comparing the two,
the difficulty levels are different.
Human nature always avoids difficulty and seeks ease.
At this critical juncture,
apart from establishing schools,
there is no other way to cultivate talent and save the times.
Some worry that if the imperial examinations are abolished,
scholars will compete to study Western learning,
and no one will be willing to teach Chinese learning.
The regulations currently proposed
place even greater emphasis on Chinese learning.
All traditional Chinese studies, such as classics (jīngxué), history (shǐxué), literature (wénxué), and philosophy (lǐxué),
are comprehensively included without omission.
Whatever is taught in the imperial examinations,
schools excel in;
whatever schools also encompass,
the imperial examinations lack.
Therefore, drawing talent from the imperial examinations
is not as good as drawing talent from schools;
this is evident.
Others worry that although schools emphasize a system of grading,
the scores are determined by the teachers,
and there is no guarantee against arbitrary increases or decreases based on personal likes and dislikes.
They do not know that the quality of schoolwork
is tested on the spot in class.
Even if a teacher wished to disregard public opinion and act selfishly,
public consensus can be relied upon,
making it impossible to conceal.
We (ministers) are still concerned that such abuses might occasionally occur,
so for Chinese learning examinations,
they are presided over by the education commissioner (xuězhèng),
who supervises the prefects (dào) and sub-prefects (fǔ) in their handling.
For higher-level school graduates,
we request the appointment of chief examiners (zhǔkǎo)
to jointly examine with the governors-general (dū), governors (fǔ), and education commissioners.
For university graduates,
we request the appointment of general directors (zǒngcái)
to jointly examine with the ministers of education affairs (xuéwù dàchén).
This does not rely solely on the scores determined by the school itself.
All methods of selecting talent through the imperial examinations
are already encompassed within the encouragement system of schools,
effectively merging the imperial examinations and schools into one.
Logically speaking,
the imperial examinations must be immediately abolished
for the school system to show improvement,
and only then can funds be raised.
However, at this time, schools in various provinces
have not been universally established,
and existing schools
have not been managed entirely according to regulations.
Therefore, we do not wish to rashly discuss the abolition of the imperial examinations.
But if no action is taken,
the world will not see a clear imperial decree from the court regarding a gradual reduction leading to abolition,
which is insufficient to inspire the literati and common people nationwide
and achieve the effect of invigorating schools.
We request that you refer to the original memorial by Wén Zhī-dòng and Yuán Shì-kǎi regarding the method of gradual reduction by subject,
issue a clear imperial edict,
and starting from the next Bǐng-wǔ (丙午) examination,
reduce the quota for central degrees by one-third for each examination.
At the same time, according to the currently established school regulations,
starting with normal schools,
instruct each province to earnestly implement them,
until the third Rén-zǐ (壬子) examination when the reduction should be complete,
which is still ten years away.
It is estimated that by then, schools established in the capital and provinces
will have been operating for more than ten years,
and talent should have emerged in great numbers.
The hearts of scholars nationwide will be solely focused on schools,
and the raising of funds will surely be seen to surge.
Everyone will strive to improve themselves,
flocking to schools
to seek practical and useful knowledge.
The atmosphere will be renewed,
and talent will naturally flourish.
Turning weakness into strength
is truly based on this."
The emperor approved everything as requested.
This was the time when the memorialized and approved regulations were promulgated,
though the imperial examinations were not yet completely abolished.
Then, in the 31st year [of Guāngxù, 1905],
Shì-kǎi and Zhī-dòng jointly memorialized:
"As long as the imperial examinations are not abolished,
scholars will harbor the hope of luckily passing,
thereby diverting their resolve for earnest cultivation and practical study.
The common people will generally adopt a wait-and-see attitude,
and very few private schools will be established.
If the abolition of the imperial examinations is delayed for another ten years,
schools will be prone to procrastination,
and talent will not be found quickly.
It will require more than twenty years
to gain the service of many scholars.
We propose that Your Majesty make an independent decision
and immediately abolish the imperial examinations.
Instruct the governors-general (dū), governors (fǔ), and education commissioners (xuězhèng) of each province:
for provinces where schools have not yet been established,
promote them expeditiously;
for those where schools have been established,
expand them vigorously.
The quality of students,
and the merits and demerits of school administrators,
must be thoroughly investigated,
and they must not shirk their responsibilities."
An imperial edict was then issued, stating that starting from the Bǐng-wǔ (丙午) examination,
the provincial (xiāng) and metropolitan (huì) examinations, as well as the annual (suì) and departmental (kē) examinations in all provinces, would be abolished.
Soon after, an edict instructed the education commissioners of each province to specialize in examining and supervising school affairs.
Thus, the imperial examination system, which had been inherited for over a thousand years,
was fundamentally eradicated.
Thereafter, schools gradually expanded,
and academic thought consequently underwent changes;
this was a major turning point.
At that time, the organization of education affairs
underwent another important change:
the exclusive establishment of the Minister for General Control of Education Affairs (Zǒnglǐ Xuéwù Dàchén).
In the 29th year [of Guāngxù, 1903],
Zhī-dòng stated:
"The Minister in Charge of Education (Guǎn Xué Dàchén) supervises both the Imperial University (Dàxué Táng) in the capital
and the various schools in the outer provinces.
At this time of initiation and planning,
with countless threads of affairs,
a dedicated official is still concerned about being insufficient,
and a concurrent official would be even more difficult to manage comprehensively.
We request the exclusive establishment of a Minister for General Control of Education Affairs (Zǒnglǐ Xuéwù Dàchén) in the capital,
to oversee all educational affairs nationwide.
Furthermore, establish one General Superintendent (Zǒng Jiāndū)
to specifically manage the affairs of the Imperial University (Jīngshī Dàxué Táng),
subject to the control and assessment of the Minister for General Control of Education Affairs,
so that there is specialized responsibility."
The emperor granted the request to rename the Minister in Charge of Education as Minister of Education Affairs (Xuéwù Dàchén),
and additionally appointed Sūn Jiā-nài as Minister of Education Affairs,
ordering Zhāng Hēng-jiā, the Junior Court Proctor (Dàlǐ Sì Shǎoqīng), to serve as General Superintendent of the Imperial University.
The approved regulations
specified the school system,
sufficiently supplementing what was incomplete in the Imperially Sanctioned Regulations (Qīndìng Zhāngchéng).
The division of subjects and curriculum
also had many changes compared to the old regulations.
The university established a College of Classical Scholars (Tōngrú Yuàn) and university undergraduate programs (dàxué běnkē).
The College of Classical Scholars did not offer instruction
and had no prescribed curriculum.
University undergraduate programs were divided into eight subjects.
These were: Classics (jīngxué) subject,
divided into eleven fields: Zhōu Yì, Shàng Shū, Máoshī, Chūnqiū Zuǒzhuàn, Chūnqiū Sānzhuàn, Zhōu Lǐ, Yílǐ, Lǐ Jì, Lúnyǔ, Mèngzǐ,
with philosophy (lǐxué) appended.
Political Science and Law (zhèngfǎ) subject,
divided into two fields: politics and law.
Literature (wénxué) subject,

divided into nine fields: Chinese history, world history, Chinese and foreign geography, Chinese literature, English literature, French literature, Russian literature, German literature, Japanese literature.
Medicine (yīkē) subject,
divided into two fields: medicine and pharmacy.
Science (gézhì) subject,
divided into six fields: mathematics, astronomy, physics, chemistry, botany and zoology, geology.
Agriculture (nóngkē) subject,
divided into four fields: agriculture, agricultural chemistry, forestry, veterinary medicine.
Engineering (gōngkē) subject,
divided into nine fields: civil engineering, machinery, shipbuilding, armaments manufacturing, electrical engineering, architecture, applied chemistry, explosives, mining and metallurgy.
Business (shāngkē) subject,
divided into three fields: banking and insurance, trade and transportation, customs duties.
Each specialized in one field.
Those in the Classics (jīngxué) who wished to also study one or two other classics were permitted.
Each academic subject was divided into core courses and supplementary courses.
Graduation took three years.
Only Political Science and Medicine required four years to graduate.
Gaoděng Xuéyù (Higher Education) had the same nature as university preparatory courses.
The curriculum was divided into three categories: the first category was for those preparing to enter universities specializing in Classics, Political Science and Law, Literature, Business, etc.;
the second category was for those preparing to enter universities specializing in Natural Sciences, Agriculture, Engineering, etc.;
the third category was for those preparing to enter medical universities.

Aside from ethics and morals (rénlún dáodé), the general meaning of the Classics (jīngxué dàyì), Chinese literature (Zhōngguó wénxué), foreign languages (wàiguóyǔ), and gymnastics (tǐcāo), which were common to all categories,
the first category taught history, geography, dialectics, law, and economics.
The second category taught mathematics, physics, chemistry, geology, mineralogy, and drawing.
The third category taught Latin, mathematics, physics, chemistry, zoology, and botany.
Those who aspired to a particular field or subject
could omit subjects or add other subjects,
divided into general study and principal subjects.
Graduation was after three years.

The curriculum for Zhōngxué (Middle School) included: self-cultivation (xiūshēn), reading the classics (dújīng), expounding on the classics (jiǎngjīng), Chinese literature, foreign languages, history, geography, mathematics, natural history (bówù), physics and chemistry, law and economics, drawing, and gymnastics.
Graduation was after five years.

The curriculum for Gāoděng Xiǎoxué (Higher Primary School) included: self-cultivation, reading the classics, expounding on the classics, Chinese literature, arithmetic, Chinese history, geography, natural sciences (gézhì), drawing, and gymnastics.
Depending on local conditions,
additional subjects such as handicraft, agriculture, or commerce could be taught.
Graduation was after four years.

The curriculum for Chūdeng Xiǎoxué (Lower Primary School) included: self-cultivation, reading the classics, expounding on the classics, Chinese literature, arithmetic, history, geography, natural sciences, and gymnastics,
constituting a complete course.
Depending on local conditions,
one or two additional subjects such as drawing or handicraft could be taught.
In poor and sparsely populated rural areas lacking teachers and scholars (shīrú),
a simplified curriculum could be adopted:
self-cultivation and reading the classics were combined into one subject;
Chinese literature;
history, geography, and natural sciences were combined into one subject;
arithmetic and gymnastics,
forming a simplified course.
Graduation was after five years.
The subjects for middle and primary schools
were essentially subjects of general education.
The distinctive feature
was the subject of reading the classics and expounding on the classics.
The "Outline of Educational Affairs" (Xuéwù Gāngyào) stated that middle and primary schools should pay attention to reading the classics to preserve the sacred teachings (shèngjiào),
saying:
"Foreign schools have a religious subject;
Chinese classics are China's religion.
If schools do not read the classics,
then the Way of Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, Tāng, Wén, Wǔ, Zhōugōng, and Kǒngzǐ,
the so-called Three Cardinal Guides and Five Constant Virtues (sāngāng wǔcháng),
will be entirely abolished,
and China will surely be unable to establish itself as a nation.
Regardless of what profession students will pursue in the future,
even those who change professions after primary school
must have recited the essential words of the classics
and heard briefly the essential meaning of the sacred teachings,
to settle their character (xīn xìng)
and rectify their origin.
However, as school curricula are rather extensive
and time is limited,
requiring complete reading of the Thirteen Classics (Shísān Jīng)
would certainly not provide enough energy or daily time.
Therefore, essential classics are selected
and distributed among middle and primary schools.
For lengthy works like the Lǐjì and Zhōulǐ,
only abridged versions by accomplished scholars (tōngrú jiéběn) will be selected for reading;
for the Yílǐ, only the most essential chapter will be selected for reading.
From the first year of lower primary school, students will read approximately forty characters daily,
up to middle school where they will read approximately two hundred characters daily.
Generally, primary schools will dedicate one hour daily to reading classics
and one hour to reciting from memory and shallow explanation.
Middle schools will dedicate six hours weekly to reading classics
and three hours to reciting from memory and explanation.
Reviewing classics will be for half an hour daily,
supervised during self-study.
Students will not be excessively burdened,
nor will it interfere with the daily time for studying Western knowledge.
It is estimated that by middle school graduation,
students will have read the Xiàojīng, the Four Books (Sìshū), Yì, Shū, Shī, Zuǒzhuàn, and abridged versions of the Lǐjì, Zhōulǐ, and Yílǐ—ten classics in total—
and understood their general meanings.
Compared to what was read and understood in traditional private schools (shūshú) and academies (shūyuàn),
this is an increase.
Not only will the sacred scriptures not fall into disuse,
but classical studies will henceforth flourish even more."
Its argument was very sound,
which reveals the prevailing atmosphere of the time.
The Méngyǎng Yuàn (Kindergarten) aimed to combine preschool education and home education,
assisting family education,
and also included education for girls.
In addition to the regular schools,
detailed regulations were also established for normal schools (shīfàn xuétáng) and vocational schools (shíyè xuétáng).
A significant difference from the old regulations
was the Yōují Shīfàn Xuétáng (Higher Normal School).
Its curriculum was divided into three sections: one was the general subjects (gōnggòng kē),
to supplement the deficiencies of middle school and serve as preparation for the main course.
Subjects: ethics and morals, origins and development of the various classics (qúnjīng yuánliú), Chinese literature, East Asian languages (dōngyǔ), English, dialectics, mathematics, and gymnastics.
Graduation was after one year.
The second was the specialized subjects (fēnlèi kē),
with four categories: the first category focused on Chinese literature and foreign languages.
The second category focused on geography and history.
The third category focused on mathematics, physics, and chemistry.
The fourth category focused on zoology, botany, and physiology.
Aside from ethics and morals, the general meaning of the classics, Chinese literature, educational psychology, and gymnastics, which were common to all categories,
the first category taught pre-Qín masters (Zhōu Qín zhūzǐ), English, German or French, dialectics, biology, and physiology.
The second category taught geography, history, legal systems, economics, English, and biology.
The third category taught mathematics, physics, chemistry, English, drawing, and handicraft.
The fourth category taught botany, zoology, physiology, mineralogy, geology, agriculture, English, and drawing.
Divided into general study and principal subjects,
all with three years to graduation.
The third was the advanced study subjects (jiāxí kē),
after graduating from the specialized subjects,
selecting several important educational fields
for an additional year of study
to deepen one's expertise.

Subjects: ethics and morals, pedagogy, educational systems, educational administrative bodies, aesthetics, experimental psychology, school hygiene, specialized education, child study, and educational practice.
Also added was practical teaching practice.
Higher Normal Schools had affiliated middle schools and primary schools.
The level of the curriculum for Chūjí Shīfàn (Junior Normal Schools)
was similar to that of middle schools.
For the complete course,
in addition to middle school subjects,
pedagogy and calligraphy were added.
Depending on local conditions,
a foreign language,
handicraft,
or one or more subjects from agriculture or industry could be added.
Graduation was after five years.
Junior Normal Schools had affiliated primary schools.
The types of vocational schools included:
vocational teacher training institutes (shíyè jiàoyuán jiǎngxísuǒ),
higher agricultural, engineering, and commercial vocational schools (gāoděng nóng, gōng, shāng shíyè xuétáng),
secondary agricultural, engineering, and commercial vocational schools (zhōngděng nóng, gōng, shāng shíyè xuétáng),
lower agricultural, engineering, and commercial vocational schools (chūdeng nóng, gōng, shāng shíyè xuétáng),
as well as higher, secondary, and lower merchant marine schools (shāngchuán xuétáng),
vocational supplementary general schools (shíyè bǔxí pǔtōng xuétáng),
and apprentice schools (yìtú xuétáng).
Vocational teacher training institutes
were for training teachers for various vocational schools.
They were divided into three types: agriculture, commerce, and engineering.
For agricultural and commercial teacher training institutes,
in addition to ethics and morals, English, education, teaching methods, and gymnastics being common subjects,

agriculture subjects included: mathematics and surveying meteorology, general agriculture, agricultural chemistry, farm implements, soil, fertilizer, cultivation, animal husbandry, horticulture, entomology, veterinary medicine, aquaculture, forestry, agricultural product manufacturing, and agricultural financial practice.

Commercial subjects included: applied chemistry, applied physics, commercial composition, commercial arithmetic, commercial geography, commercial history, bookkeeping, commodities, commercial finance, and commercial practice.
All graduated after two years.
Engineering teacher training institutes
offered both complete and simplified courses.

The complete course had six types: metallurgy (jīngōng kē), carpentry (mùgōng kē), dyeing and weaving (rǎnzhī kē), ceramics (yáoyè kē), applied chemistry (yìngyòng huàxué kē), and industrial drawing (gōngyè túyàng kē).

In addition to ethics and morals, mathematics, physics, chemistry, drawing, industrial finance, industrial hygiene, machine drawing practice, English, education, teaching methods, and gymnastics being common subjects,
metallurgy subjects included: inorganic chemistry, applied mechanics, workshop tools and manufacturing methods, general principles of electrical engineering, and engines.

Carpentry subjects included: inorganic chemistry, applied mechanics, workshop tools and manufacturing methods, construction materials, furniture and architectural styles, house construction, hygiene, architectural drawing and design.
Dyeing and weaving subjects included: all aspects of applied chemistry, applied machinery, qualitative analysis, industrial analysis, dyeing and color matching, weaving and design.
Ceramics subjects included: all aspects of applied chemistry, applied machinery, qualitative analysis, industrial analysis, and ceramic product manufacturing.
Applied chemistry subjects included: all aspects of applied chemistry, machinery, electroplating, and electrometallurgy.
Industrial drawing subjects included: drawing and materials.
All graduated after three years.
The simplified course was divided into six subjects: metallurgy, carpentry, dyeing, weaving, pottery, and lacquerware.
The subjects were more abbreviated.
Graduation was after one year.
Higher vocational schools were equivalent in level to higher schools,
divided into preparatory and main courses.
The preparatory course provided general basic lessons for various subjects.
Graduation was after one year.
The higher agricultural main course had three types: agronomy (nóngxué kē),
forestry (línxué kē),
and veterinary medicine (shòuyī xué kē).
Higher industrial schools were divided into thirteen specialized subjects: applied chemistry,
dyeing,
weaving,
architecture,
ceramics,
machinery,
electrical engineering,
electrochemistry,
civil engineering (tǔmù kē),
mining (kuàngyè kē),
shipbuilding (zàochuán kē),
lacquerware (qī gōng kē),
and drawing and design (túgǎo huìhuà kē).
Each taught the principles, theories, application methods, and auxiliary subjects for its main course,
some having more than thirty subjects.
Appropriate subjects could be selected and offered based on local conditions.
All graduated after three years.
Secondary vocational schools were equivalent in level to middle schools,
also divided into preparatory and main courses,
with subjects more abbreviated than those of higher schools.
Lower vocational schools were equivalent in level to higher primary schools,
divided into general and practical subjects.
All graduated after three years.
Merchant marine schools were also divided into three levels,
to teach navigation and machinery knowledge and the skills for piloting merchant ships.
Graduation was after five or three years.
Vocational supplementary general schools
provided essential vocational knowledge and skills using simplified teaching methods,
and also supplemented primary school subjects.
Apprentice schools
taught engineering and construction techniques of an equivalent level
to produce skilled craftsmen,
and could all be conveniently affiliated with middle and primary schools.
Those not within the school system
were called Yìxuéguǎn (譯學館)
and Jìnshìguǎn (進士館).
Previously, the Tóngwénguǎn (同文館) was merged into the Dàxúetáng (大學堂),
establishing specialized language programs in English, French, Russian, German, and Japanese.
Later, it separated from the Dàxúetáng
and was named Yìxuéguǎn (譯學館).
It still offered one program each for English, French, Russian, German, and Japanese.
Regardless of the language studied,
all students had to study both general and specialized subjects.
General subjects: ethics and morals, Chinese literature, history, geography, mathematics, natural history, physics and chemistry, drawing, and gymnastics.
Specialized subjects: diplomacy, finance, and education.
Graduation was after five years.
The Jìnshìguǎn (進士館) mandated that newly successful candidates in the imperial examinations (jìnshì) who served as subordinates in the Hánlín (翰林) Academy or as secretaries
enter the institution for study,
focusing on practical knowledge.

Curriculum: history, geography, education, law, finance, diplomacy, military administration, agricultural administration, industrial administration, commercial administration, and scientific inquiry (gézì).
Students could choose to study one or two subjects from agriculture, industry, commerce, or military affairs.
Western languages, Eastern languages, mathematics, and gymnastics were elective subjects.
Graduation was after three years.
The general regulations for managing all schools
were largely consistent with previous rules.
On the first day of each month,
the superintendent and teachers would gather all students in the assembly hall
to recite one article from the Shèngyù Guǎngxùn (聖諭廣訓).
On the birthdays of the Empress Dowager and the Emperor,
and the birthday of the Most Holy Sage and First Teacher Kǒngzǐ (孔子),
as well as the spring and autumn Shàngdīng (上丁) sacrifices,
were designated as celebration days.
All staff in the school would lead students to perform the three kneelings and nine kowtows before the Wànsuì (萬歲) tablet or the sage's memorial tablet.
Afterward,
all staff would stand facing west,
and students would perform three bows to the staff
before withdrawing.
At the beginning or end of a term, or upon graduation,
students were led to perform the same rites before the Wànsuì (萬歲) tablet or the sage's memorial tablet.
Students would perform one kneeling and three kowtows to the superintendent and teachers.
After the superintendent and others gave their instructions,
they would disperse.
On the first day of each month,
students were led to perform rites before the sage's memorial tablet as usual.
Daily classroom instruction
should not exceed six hours.
The days of Fáng (房), Xū (虛), Xīng (星), and Mǎo (昴) were regular rest days.
Celebration days, the Duānwǔ (端午) Festival, and the Zhōngqiū (中秋) Festival each had one day off.
Each year, the term began on the twentieth day of the first lunar month
and ended at the Xiǎoshǔ (小暑) solar term,
constituting the first semester.
The second semester began six days after the Lìqiū (立秋) solar term
and ended on the fifteenth day of the twelfth lunar month,
constituting the second semester.
Student awards and punishments
were proposed by teachers and academic supervisors and
approved by the superintendent.
There were three types of awards:
verbal encouragement,
honorary awards,
and material rewards.
There were three types of punishments:
recording a demerit,
restricting leave, and expulsion from school.
Students considered integrity and proper conduct as the primary essential meaning.
Superintendents, academic supervisors, and teachers would periodically inspect this,
assigning detailed scores which were then combined with academic scores.
School examinations were divided into five types:
ad hoc examinations,
semester examinations,
year-end examinations,
graduation examinations,
and entrance examinations for higher education.
Ad hoc examinations had no fixed schedule, while semester, year-end, and graduation examination scores were averaged with daily scores.
Those who passed the annual examination were promoted one level.
Those who failed remained at their original level for remedial study
and retested in the next session.
If they still failed, they were expelled.
In evaluating scores,
one hundred percent was considered full marks.
Eighty percent or above was considered excellent,
sixty percent or above was good,
forty percent or above was average,
and twenty percent or above was substandard,
which was considered passing.
Below twenty percent was considered the lowest grade
and warranted expulsion.
The graduation examination was the most important.
Depending on the school's level,
local officials would collaborate with the superintendent and teachers to personally oversee it,
following the precedents of the xiānghuì (鄉會) examinations.
For graduation from higher education (gāoděngxué),
chief examiners would be specially appointed
to conduct the examination in collaboration with the governor-general (dū), provincial governor (fǔ), and education commissioner (xuézhèng).
For graduation from specialized programs at the university (dàxué),
presidents would be specially appointed
to conduct the examination in collaboration with the Minister of Education (xuéwù dàchén).
It was divided into two parts: an external examination
held at the school.
One or two key points from the lecture notes of each subject were selected and asked,
and students were required to answer.
The internal examination
was held in a secluded location.
It was divided into two sessions: the first session featured topics from Chinese studies (zhōngxué),
one from the classics (jīng) and one from history (shǐ).
For the classics, essays (lùn) were used;
for history, policy questions (cè) were used.
The second session featured topics from Western studies (xīxué),
one from politics (zhèng) and one from arts/sciences (yì).
For Western politics, examinations (kǎo) were used;
for Western arts/sciences, explanations (shuō) were used.
For graduation from the Tōngrúyuàn (通儒院),
no examiners were dispatched.
Instead, various works and writings produced from their usual research
were evaluated and graded,
and submitted to the throne
for imperial approval.
The regulations for awards
were modeled after the awards for students studying abroad in Japan.
Graduates of the Tōngrúyuàn (通儒院)
were elevated in rank in the Hánlín (翰林) Academy
or appointed to superior official positions in the capital or provinces.
Graduates of specialized university (dàxué) programs who were in the excellent grade
were given the status of a jìnshì (進士),
appointed as compiler (biānxiū) or reviser (jiǎntǎo) in the Hánlín (翰lín) Academy.
Those in the good and average grades were also given the status of jìnshì (進士),
appointed as bachelor (shùjíshì) in the Hánlín (翰lín) Academy or principal (zhǔshì) in various ministries, respectively.
University (dàxué) elective program graduates
received awards according to a lower grade compared to specialized university (dàxué) programs.
Graduates of university (dàxué) preparatory programs and provincial higher schools (gāoděngxué)
who were in the excellent grade were given the status of a jǔrén (舉人),
appointed as a secretary (zhōngshū) in the Grand Secretariat or prefect (zhīzhōu).
Those in the good and average grades were also given the status of jǔrén (舉人),
appointed as a secretary (zhōngshū) in the Secretariat of the Grand Secretariat, department secretary (bùsīwù), county magistrate (zhīxiàn), or assistant prefect (tōngpàn).
Graduates of middle schools (zhōngxué)
were awarded with bá gòng (拔貢), yōu gòng (優貢), or suì gòng (歲貢) respectively.
Graduates of higher primary schools (gāoděng xiǎoxué)
were awarded with lǐn (廩), zēng (增), or fùshēng (附生) respectively.
Elementary primary education (chūděng xiǎoxué) was compulsory education,
and no awards were given.
Graduates of superior normal schools (yōují shīfàn)
in the excellent, good, and average grades were all given the status of jǔrén (舉人),
appointed as academician (bóshì), assistant lecturer (zhùjiào), or academic instructor (xuézhèng) in the Guózǐjiān (國子監) respectively.
Graduates of elementary normal schools (chūjí shīfàn)
were awarded with bá gòng (拔貢), yōu gòng (優貢), or suì gòng (歲貢) respectively,
appointed as professor (jiàoshòu), instructor (jiàoyù), or educational supervisor (xùndǎo).
Graduates of higher vocational schools (gāoděng shíyè xuétáng)
in the excellent, good, and average grades were all given the status of jǔrén (舉人),
appointed as prefect (zhīzhōu), county magistrate (zhīxiàn), or assistant prefectural magistrate (zhōutóng) respectively.
Graduates of middle vocational schools (zhōngděng shíyè xuétáng)
received awards similar to middle school (zhōngxué) graduates.
Such was the outline of the approved regulations.
The Qīng dynasty selected scholars through the imperial examination system,
continuing the Míng dynasty's use of eight-legged essays.
Topics were drawn from the Four Books and the Five Classics (Yì, Shū, Shī, Chūnqiū, Lǐjì),
known as zhìyì.
The grand triennial examination,
called xiāngshì, tested xiùcái in the various provinces.
Those who passed were called jǔrén.
The following year, jǔrén were tested in the capital
in the huìshì.
Those who passed were called gòngshì.
The emperor personally presided over a policy question examination in the palace,
called diànshì.
The successful candidates were ranked into three classes: First, Second, and Third.
The First Class had three candidates,
called zhuàngyuán, bǎngyǎn, and tànhuā,
and were granted the title of Jìnshì Jíyǐ.
The Second Class had a certain number of candidates
and were granted the title of Jìnshì Chūshēn.
The Third Class had a certain number of candidates
and were granted the title of Tóng Jìnshì Chūshēn.
The first in the xiāngshì was called jièyuán;
the first in the huìshì was called huìyuán;
the first in the Second Class was called chuánlú.
These were all old Míng dynasty titles.
When Shìzǔ unified China,
in Shùnzhì first year (1644),
it was decided that xiāngshì would be held in the years of Zǐ, Wǔ, Mǎo, Yǒu,
and huìshì in the years of Chén, Xū, Chǒu, Wèi.
Xiāngshì were in the eighth month,
and huìshì in the second month.
Both had their first session on the ninth day,
second session on the twelfth day,
and third session on the fifteenth day.
Diànshì were in the third month.
In the second year (1645),
regulations for the examination halls were promulgated.
Upon deliberation by the Lǐbù,
Gōng Dǐngzī, a Gěishìzhōng, submitted a memorial stating:
"The old system of the former Míng dynasty
required seven shísìwén essays in the first session,
one lùn and one biǎo in the second session,
five pàn,
and five cè in the third session.
It should be as requested by the various officials,
reducing shísìwén by two essays,
adding poetry in addition to lùn, biǎo, and pàn,
and replacing cè with zòusū."
The emperor did not approve.
He ordered adherence to the old regulations.
The first session had three topics from the Four Books
and four topics from each of the Five Classics,
with each scholar specializing in one Classic.
For the Four Books, Zhū Zǐ Jízhù was primary;
for the Yì, Chéngchuán and Zhū Zǐ Běnyì;
for the Shū, Cài Chuán;
for the Shī, Zhū Zǐ Jízhuàn;
for the Chūnqiū, Hú Ānguó Chuán;
for the Lǐjì, Chén Hào Jíshuō.
Later, Hú Chuán was not used for the Chūnqiū;
instead, essays were based on Zuǒ Chuán,
with reference to Gōngyáng and Gǔliáng.
The second session had one lùn,
five pàn,
and one section from zhào, gào, or biǎo.
The third session had five cè on current affairs concerning the Classics and histories.
This applied to both xiāngshì and huìshì.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
the huìshì was changed to the third month,
and the diànshì to the fourth month,
which became a permanent system.
For the xiāngshì,
students and scholars who had thoroughly mastered all three sessions were examined and recommended by the Tíxué in advance,
to prevent unqualified entries.
Gòngshēng and jiànshēng enrolled in the guózijìan were examined and recommended by their supervising officials.
Families of entertainers, servants, and slaves,
and those in mourning for their parents,
were not allowed to take the examination.
The front of the examination paper listed the name, place of origin, age, appearance, background (three generations), and the Classic studied.
Examination papers with disorganized writing,
incomplete true or cursive script,
exceeding the margins, leaving too much blank space,
excessive smudging or defilement,
or where the opening and closing particles of the seven essays in the first session were identical,
or the biǎo in the second session lacked the reign title,
or the cè questions in the third session were mistakenly written,
as well as writing that failed to avoid imperial taboos, the emperor's personal name, or the name of the Most Holy (Confucius),
were considered non-compliant
and publicly posted as such.
Scholars used black ink,
and their papers were called mòjuàn.
Transcribers used red ink,
and their copies were called zhūjuàn.
The chief examiner used a black pen,
and co-examiners used blue pens.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
co-examiners changed to purple pens.
Soon after,
they reverted to blue.
The place where scholars were tested was called gòngyuàn.
The scholars' cubicles were called hàofáng.
The soldiers assigned to guard them were called hàojūn.
Examiners entered the examination hall, which was then sealed and locked.
The inner and outer doors were separated by a screen.
Officials outside, such as the Tídiào and Jiānshì, were called wàilián guān.
Officials inside, the chief examiner and co-examiners, were called nèilián guān.
There were also nèijiānshì,
who were responsible for supervision and correction,
but not for evaluating essays.
Senior officials were appointed to oversee the entire examination process.
For xiāngshì, this official was called jiānlín.
For Shùntiān prefecture, it was the Fǔyǐn;
for other provinces, initially the Xún'àn Yùshǐ.
When the Xún'àn position was abolished,
the Xúnfǔ took over.
For huìshì, the official was called Zhī Gòngjǔ,
and it was typically held by a Lǐbù Shìláng.
For Shùntiān, the Tídiào was the Fǔchéng,
and the Jiānshì was a Yùshǐ.
Initially,
for other provinces, the Tídiào was the Bùzhèngshǐ,
the Jiānshì was the Àncháshǐ,
and their deputies were Dàoyuán.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
since the Fān and Niè two commissioners oversaw all provincial financial and judicial matters,
and staying in the examination hall for over a month
might cause delays,
the Tídiào and Jiānshì duties
were solely entrusted to two Dàoyuán.
For huìshì, the Jiānshì was a Yùshǐ.
For the diànshì, the emperor personally posed the questions from the imperial platform.
Officials who had attained jìnshì status were appointed as Dújuǎnguān,
who proposed the rankings and submitted them to the emperor,
which might be approved as proposed,
or might be altered.
The zhuàngyuán of the First Class was appointed Xiūzhuàn; the bǎngyǎn and tànhuā were appointed Biānxiū.
Jìnshì of the Second and Third Classes were appointed to various offices such as Shùjíshì, Zhǔshì, Zhōngshū, Xíngrén, Píngshì, Bóshì, Tuīguān, Zhīzhōu, or Zhīxiàn.
The Qīng dynasty considered the imperial examination a grand ceremony for selecting talent.
Although its initial system largely followed the old Míng one,
it meticulously emphasized examination reputations and
strictly guarded against malpractices,
making its legislation comprehensive
and its selection of talent abundant,
far surpassing previous dynasties.
The modifications to its regulations,
and the changes in social trends,
were linked to the rise and fall of talent
and the successes and failures of the imperial government.
To narrate the major aspects
is essential.
The first session of the xiāngshì and huìshì used eight-legged essays.
In Kāngxī second year (1663),
the zhìyì system was abolished.
The five cè questions of the third session were moved to the first session,
one lùn was added to the second session,
and biǎo and pàn remained as before.
This was implemented for only two examinations and then ceased.
In the fourth year (1665),
Huáng Jī, a Lǐbù Shìláng, stated:
"The examination system traditionally consisted of three sessions.
The first used the Classics,
to enable the elucidation of the subtle meaning of the sages,
thereby observing their character.
The next used policy questions and essays,
to enable understanding of ancient and modern affairs,
thereby assessing their talent.
Now, only policy questions and essays are used,
and one session is removed,
which seems too simple.
Furthermore, without using the Classics for essays,
people will neglect the learning of the sages.
I request the restoration of the old three-session system."
This was approved.
In the seventh year (1668),
the original system was restored,
and eight-legged essays were used again.
In the twenty-fourth year (1685),
upon the request of Gěishìzhōng Yáng Ěrshú,
all Four Books topics for the Lǐwéi (huìshì) and Shùntiān examinations were imperially designated.
At that time, candidates typically did not write on zhào and gào topics.
Essays, treatises, memorials, judgments, and policy questions were often repetitive and plagiarized.
While nominally three sessions were tested,
the first session was in fact the most important.
And within the first session, the Four Books essays were the most important.
