In the twenty-sixth year (1687), zhào and gào were abolished.
Later, candidates were required to write on both Five Classics and other topics.
Lùn topics were formerly drawn from the Xiàojīng.
In Kāngxī twenty-ninth year (1690),
Xìnglǐ, Tàijítú Shuō, Tōngshū, Xīmíng, and Zhèngméng were also used.
In the fifty-seventh year (1718),
lùn topics exclusively used Xìnglǐ.
In Shìzōng's first year (1723),
an edict declared the Xiàojīng as important as the Five Classics,
being the foundation for civilizing people and establishing customs.
Although Sòng dynasty scholars' books were sufficient to assist the Classics,
they were not as vast as the words of the sages.
Thus, lùn topics continued to use the Xiàojīng.
In the third year of Qiánlóng’s reign (1738),
Shūhèdé, an Assistant Minister of War, stated:
“The examination system,
which selects candidates based on their essays
and appoints officials based on their adherence to fixed formats,
is no longer a good method.
Moreover, its accumulated弊 (bì) are deepening daily,
and those relying on luck are becoming more numerous.
The ancients inquired into affairs and examined speeches;
what they spoke of
were precisely the duties they were expected to perform in office.
Contemporary essays are mere empty words,
unsuitable for practical use.
The practice of 'dark examination papers' (mòjuàn fángxíng)
involves widespread plagiarism,
superficial rhetoric, and specious arguments,
spreading endlessly and disjointedly,
only for the sake of passing the examinations.
Each scholar specializes in one classic;
for each classic, the topics proposed
can be over a hundred for some,
and dozens for others.
The ancients spent their entire lives studying them and still found it insufficient,
but now, people master them in a few months with time to spare.
Memorials (biǎo) and judgments (pàn) can be prepared in advance,
while policy essays (cè) are merely perfunctory responses to topics,
without any original insights.
These are truly insufficient for selecting talent.
The examination regulations [should be] revised and reformed,
and a different method for selecting genuinely talented and learned individuals should be sought.”
This memorial was sent down to the Ministry of Rites,
which reported back:
“The method of selecting scholars
in the Three Dynasties and earlier came from schools;
after the Hàn dynasty, it came from local officials in commanderies and counties;
after the Wèi and Jìn dynasties, it came from the Nine-rank System (jiǔpǐn zhōngzhèng);
from the Suí and Táng dynasties to the present,
it has come from the imperial examinations.
Although the methods of the imperial examinations have varied,
from the Míng dynasty to the present,
they have all originated from 'timely essays' (shíyì).
Regarding the弊 (bì) of the imperial examinations,
poetry and prose merely emphasize superficiality
without any practical utility.
The 'enlightenment of the classics' (míngjīng) is solely about memorization
without understanding the meaning of the text.
What Zhào Kuāng of the Táng dynasty called 'learning what is not used,
and using what is not learned'
is precisely this.
The弊 (bì) of 'timely essays' are
what the said Assistant Minister has now presented.
Sages cannot legislate without弊 (bì);
it is about remedying them as times change.
Sū Shì (Sū Dōngpō) once said: ‘The way to acquire talent
lies in knowing people.
The way to know people
lies in demanding substance.’
If substance can be demanded,
even by following the current path,
by invigorating and encouraging,
talent will naturally emerge with enthusiasm.
If one merely seeks fame,
even if grand words are spoken about restoring ancient ways,
problems will arise as soon as laws are established,
and it will ultimately be of no benefit to cultivating scholars.
To now say that 'timely essays,' 'classic interpretations' (jīngyì), and memorials (biǎo), judgments (pàn), and policy essays (cè lùn) are all empty words, plagiarized and useless,
this is precisely the fault of not demanding substance.
Anything that is uttered aloud
or written down
is empty words;
why are only today's 'timely essays' considered so?
'Timely essays' discuss
the subtle words and
profound principles of Kǒngzǐ and Mèngzǐ.
They are supplemented by the classics, histories, philosophers, and collected works
to reveal their brilliance;
they are constrained by rules and standards
to make their regulations precise.
Although considered minor skills,
talents for both civil and military administration, capable individuals, and outstanding personalities
have never failed to emerge from within them.
Not thinking of strenuously rectifying the current decline,
but instead blaming the inadequacy of the established method,
is this not excessive?
Even for classic interpretations (jīngyì), memorials (biǎo), judgments (pàn), and policy essays (lùn cè),
if substance is genuinely sought,
how could they be easily matched?
Although classic texts are as important as the Four Books,
due to ingrained habits,
scholars do not concentrate on studying them.
If they were stipulated as strict regulations,
only those who excelled would be recorded.
Memorials (biǎo), judgments (pàn), and policy essays (lùn cè)
should all undergo rigorous review.
Only those well-versed in rhetoric and thoroughly familiar with laws and statutes
can produce memorials and judgments.
Those with insight into ancient affairs,
talent for decision-making,
thorough understanding of past and present,
and clear grasp of current affairs
can then produce policy essays.
How can any of these not be implemented
and be pertinent to practical use?
If we must change the current method
and adopt ancient systems,
we would then have to build palaces, support wandering scholars,
establish officials and teachers
within a hundred li radius,
where lawsuits would be heard
and military matters planned.
We would also have to select those who do not follow instructions
and banish them to distant lands,
disgraced for life.
Would this not be chaotic and impracticable?
Moreover, human hearts are not as they were in antiquity;
the superiors seek substance,
but the inferiors respond with fame.
Promote filial piety, and there will be those who cut their flesh or build huts by graves to seek fame.
Promote integrity, and there will be those who wear shabby clothes, eat meager food, and use worn-out carriages with emaciated horses to feign virtue.
They would collectively engage in deceit,
using empty fame to gain advancement.
And after assuming office,
they would completely reverse their behavior,
becoming worse than ordinary people.
This is especially evident in the recently selected 'filial and incorrupt' (xiàolián) and 'upright and honest' (fāngzhèng) individuals,
so what benefit is there?
If those responsible for overseeing literary examinations and assessing scholars
could truly comprehend the imperial edict,
demand substance behind titles,
strenuously eliminate ingrained habits,
and prevent reliance on luck,
literary styles would flourish daily,
and true talent would naturally emerge.
There would be no need to reform the established system.”
Consequently, the proposal was shelved.
At that time, Grand Secretary È'ěrtài was in power,
and he strongly advocated for rejecting the proposal,
thus ensuring that the classical prose of the examination system was not abolished.
In the twenty-second year (1757),
an edict ordered the elimination of old habits and the pursuit of practical results.
Classic texts (jīngwén) were moved to the second session,
while policy essays (lùn), memorials (biǎo), and judgments (pàn) were abolished,
and five-character, eight-rhyme regulated verse (wǔyán bārùn lǜshī) was added.
The following year (1758),
discussions on Neo-Confucianism (xìnglǐ lùn) were added to the first session.
Censor Yáng Fānglì memorialized, requesting that topics from the two classics, Zhōulǐ and Yílǐ, be added to the provincial and metropolitan examinations.
The Emperor, believing that the meanings of these two rituals were already contained in the Dàijì (Lǐjì),
did not approve.
In the forty-seventh year (1782),
regulated verse (lǜshī) was moved to after the examination essays (shìyì) in the first session,
and discussions on Neo-Confucianism (xìnglǐ lùn) were moved to after the classic texts (jīngwén) in the second session.
In the fifty-second year (1787),
Gāozōng believed that having separate examiners for each classic
easily led to abuses.
Moreover, scholars specializing in one classic
did not extensively study other classics,
which was not the way to promote practical learning.
He decreed that starting from the Xīnshen provincial examination the following year (1788),
within five provincial and metropolitan examination cycles,
one classic would be examined in rotation each year.
After this was completed,
the policy essay (lùntí) would be abolished in both the provincial and metropolitan examinations,
and topics from the Five Classics would be set and examined simultaneously.
This was to be permanently established as a regulation.
The formulation of topics for the imperial examinations was of utmost importance.
In the 52nd year of Kāngxī (1713),
it was observed that the chief examiners, when formulating topics,
often selected auspicious phrases and platitudes from the Four Books and Five Classics,
which led to many candidates succeeding through pre-prepared essays.
An imperial decree therefore mandated that thereafter, no taboos should be observed.
Previously, it was forbidden for examiners to set topics on which they themselves had passed the examinations;
at this point, the prohibition was relaxed.
Throughout the various examination sessions,
many examiners were censured for errors in setting topics.
Earlier, in the 56th year of Kāngxī (1717),
following the advice of Shìláng Wáng Yìqīng,
in the seven sections of the examination essays,
the introductory phrases (pò, chéng, kāijiǎng)
were not to be transcribed,
to prevent collusion.
In the 47th year of Qiánlóng (1782),
examiners were ordered to pre-draft the introductory phrases (pò, chéng, kāijiǎng)
and issue them with the topic papers for candidates to follow.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng (1799),
this practice was abolished
as it was deemed to have no connection to malpractice.
The practice of using a grand conclusion (dàjié) at the end of the examination essay
in the mid-Míng dynasty
was often used for collusion.
In the late Kāngxī era,
it was expressly prohibited.
In the 12th year of Qiánlóng (1747),
Biānxiū Yáng Shùzēng requested its reintroduction,
but Dàxuéshì Zhāng Tíngyù and others deemed it useless and likely to lead to more malpractice,
and memorialized against it, rejecting the proposal.
Originally, essays for the first session were limited to 550 characters per essay;
in the 20th year of Kāngxī (1681), 100 characters were added.
In the 54th year (1715),
Huìyuán Shàng Jūyì was dismissed
because his main essay exceeded 1200 characters.
In the 43rd year of Qiánlóng (1778),
it was first stipulated that each essay for the xiāngshì and huìshì should be limited to 700 characters,
and those who violated this would not be recorded.
Thereafter, this was strictly followed.
For the policy questions (cètí) in the third session,
it was originally stipulated that they should not exceed 300 characters.
In the 1st year of Qiánlóng (1736),
candidates were forbidden from merely listing categories
and perfunctorily completing the task.
Subsequently, the topics formulated by examiners
sometimes amounted to five or six hundred characters per question,
and those who were superficial often merely rearranged the words from the question,
editing and patching them into an essay.
In the 36th year (1771),
Zuǒ Dōu Yùshǐ Zhāng Ruòjì memorialized about this,
and an imperial decree reaffirmed the standing regulations.
In the 51st year (1786),
it was stipulated that answers to policy questions under 300 characters
would be penalized with a suspension from examinations according to the "error in writing" regulation.
However, both examiners and candidates still prioritized the first session
and slighted the third,
a deeply entrenched habit difficult to change.
The style of the examination essay (zhìyì)
emphasized clear expression and pure reasoning.
In the 9th year of Shùnzhì (1652),
Chéng Kězē, who ranked first in the huìshì, was stripped of his name for contradicting the meaning of the classics.
Examiners Xuéshì Hú Tǒngyú and others were also punished.
Shìzōng repeatedly admonished examiners to maintain a clear, authentic, elegant, and upright style.
In the 1st year of Qiánlóng (1736),
Gāozōng issued an imperial decree stating:
"The state selects scholars based on their understanding of the classics
to gauge the depth of their scholarship
and the purity or superficiality of their character and insight.
The prevailing trends
are related to the national destiny.
The signs of human hearts and scholarly habits
are very subtle in their manifestation,
but their implications are profound.
We must clearly indicate the standard
so that scholars know what to choose."
Thereupon, Xuéshì Fāng Bāo was commanded to compile and select 41 volumes of contemporary essays by various prominent Míng and Qīng masters,
titled "Qīndìng Sìshū Wén,"
which were promulgated as a model.
After this had been practiced for a long time,
those who wrote examination essays
sometimes plagiarized empty rhetoric,
ignorant of the fundamentals.
Yáng Shùzēng even requested the abolition of zhìyì to remedy its弊.
In the 45th year (1780),
Dèng Cháojìn, the third-place finisher in the huìshì, had crude and muddled language in his main essay,
and Gù Wèn, the jièyuán from Jiāngnán, used exclusively parallel couplets in his Four Books essays.
The examiners were both censured.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
candidates began to extract obscure phrases and words from abstruse books,
competing to show off novelty in their essays.
Yùshǐ Xīn Cóngyì argued against this malpractice.
An imperial decree stated:
"Recently, scholars have been hunting for bizarre and strange phrases,
using abstruse language to cover up their superficiality,
which greatly deviates from proper literary style.
Examiners must discern and reject spurious styles.
Disjointed and grotesque essays
must not be selected."
Throughout the dynasties, examiners were often charged with rectifying literary styles,
but there was never any real effect.
Commentators believed that literary trends were related to national destiny.
Many famous ministers of the Qīng dynasty rose through the imperial examinations,
and all were skilled in zhìyì.
In the early days of the dynasty,
figures like Xióng Bólóng, Liú Zǐzhuàng, and Zhāng Yùshū,
wrote essays that were grand and profound,
reversing decline and restoring vitality.
After Kāngxī, it became even more aligned with the correct path,
with Lǐ Guāngdì and Hán Tǎn as its exemplars.
Fāng Bāo of Tóngchéng adapted ancient prose for contemporary essays,
truly reaching the utmost standard.
During the Yōngzhèng and Qiánlóng eras,
authors emerged in great numbers,
with increasingly refined rules and comprehensive methods.
Its decline began in the Jiāqìng and Dàoguāng eras,
as the national destiny gradually weakened,
scholarly habits became increasingly lax,
and literary style also grew increasingly poor and superficial.
By the end of the dynasty, essays were plagiarized and mediocre,
and zhìyì thus became a subject of criticism.
In the 24th year of Guāngxù (1898),
Húguǎng Zǒngdū Zhāng Zhīdòng memorialized for reforms to the imperial examination system.
In the 27th year (1901),
the first session of the xiāngshì and huìshì was changed to five essays on Chinese political history,
the second session to five policy questions on the politics, arts, and learning of various countries,
and the third session to two essays on the meaning of the Four Books and one essay on the meaning of the Five Classics.
Other examinations followed this example.
This was based on Zhāng Zhīdòng’s proposal.
It was implemented until the abolition of the imperial examination system.
For xiāngshì and huìshì examiners,
under the initial system,
the chief examiners and deputy chief examiners for Shùntiān and Jiāngnán,
and the chief examiners for Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and Fújiàn,
were appointed from eight Hànlín officials.
Other provinces used Gěishìzhōng, Guānglùsì Shàoqīng, Six Boards Sīguān, Xíngrén, Zhōngshū, and Píngshì.
Which official was sent to which province
was fixed.
In the 3rd year of Kāngxī (1664), this regulation was abolished.
Shùntiān initially followed other provinces,
appointing two officials as chief and deputy.
In the mid-Qiánlóng era, this increased to three,
selected from officials of Xiébàn Dàxuéshì, Shàngshū and below,
and Fù Dōu Yùshǐ and above,
with Biānxiū and Jiǎntǎo no longer participating.
During Dàoguāng,
three or four were selected.
After Tóngzhì,
four were regularly selected.
Initially,
examiners were not limited by their origin.
In the early Kāngxī era,
Zhǔshì Cài Zōu and Cáo Shǒuwàng both served as examiners despite being bàgòng (special graduates).
In the 10th year (1671),
following the request of Yùshǐ Hé Yuányīng,
examiners were exclusively selected from jìnshì graduates.
However, those from jǔrén backgrounds sometimes also participated.
In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng (1725),
examination regulations were promulgated,
finally limiting appointments to Hànlín and jìnshì-educated officials of the Boards and Courts,
while still incorporating the recommendation system.
In the 9th year of Qiánlóng (1744),
Yùshǐ Lǐ Qīngfāng stated:
"Among the 49 chief examiners recommended by high officials for appointment,
four are Manchus,
16 are from various direct provinces,
and the rest are all from Jiāngnán and Zhèjiāng.
Those who recommend are mostly people with whom they have daily dealings and who are familiar with each other,
rich in wealth and influential in power.
As for those who uphold integrity and are not swayed,
they are unwilling to attend at the gates of dukes and ministers.
Scholars from remote areas,
whose voices are not heard
and whose social circles are not broad,
have no one to recommend them.
I request that all eligible personnel be universally examined."
The emperor suspected Lǐ Qīngfāng had not been recommended
and was provoked to say this,
so he did not grant the request,
and both examination and recommendation continued to be practiced.
After the 36th year (1771),
examination became a fixed regulation.
Initially, the lists of successful candidates from imperial examinations were all published.
Later, the rankings were secretly determined
and no longer publicly announced.
After Jiāqìng,
there was an additional special examination for officials like Shìláng, Géxué, and third-rank capital officials,
called the "Dàkǎo Chā."
For the chief examiners of the huìshì,
initially four or six high-ranking officials from the Grand Secretariat and Boards were used,
sometimes up to seven.
Subsequently, two, three, or four or five were selected.
After Xiánfēng,
four were regularly selected
as the standard.
Examiners.
Initially,
for the Shùntiān examinations for metropolitan candidates,
investigating officials (Tuīguān) and magistrates (Zhīxiàn) were used concurrently.
For each province, officials of the first degree (Jiǎkē) and their subordinates, as well as Jiǎkē Tuīguān and Zhīxiàn from neighboring provinces, were employed.
Sometimes, instructors (Jiàoguān) of the provincial examination (Xiāngkē) were used.
The number of examination rooms was not fixed.
For the metropolitan examination (Huìshì), initially twenty people were used:
twelve from the Hànlín Academy,
four from the Six Offices of Scrutiny (Liùkē),
one each from the Ministries of Personnel (Lìbù), Rites (Lǐbù), and War (Bīngbù),
and one from the Ministries of Revenue (Hùbù), Punishments (Xíngbù), and Works (Gōngbù) rotated in turn for each examination.
Later, the quota was set at eighteen people,
and the same applied to the Shùntiān examinations.
In the 54th year of Kāngxī's reign (1715),
it was mandated that two examiners from different provinces should jointly review the papers
to mutually supervise each other,
using thirty-six people.
However, this was abolished shortly after.
During the Kāngxī and Yōngzhèng periods,
the use of metropolitan officials for Shùntiān examination room examiners was discontinued.
Only qualified Zhílí magistrates who had passed the imperial examinations were used.
For other provinces, the use of incumbent Zhīxiàn from their own province was stopped,
and instead, candidates for appointment (Hòuxuǎn) who were residing in neighboring provinces (Jìnshì or Jǔrén) were specially assigned.
Large provinces had eighteen,
medium provinces fourteen,
and small provinces twelve down to ten,
all equally divided for review and correction.
Subsequently, there were various increases and decreases,
with small provinces reducing to eight people.
During the Qiánlóng period,
the Lǐwéi (examination of the Ministry of Rites) and Shùntiān assistant examiners
began to be personally appointed from metropolitan officials.
Each province resumed using its own Jiǎkē subordinate officials.
In the 42nd year (1777),
the rule of dividing examination rooms by the Five Classics was abolished.
Regarding the Shùntiān examination room examiners,
people from the southern and northern provinces avoided reviewing papers from the southern and northern regions,
and people from border provinces avoided reviewing papers from the central regions.
For the Huìshì examination rooms, people from the same province avoided each other.
The chief examiners (Kǎoguān) were responsible for overall evaluation,
while the examination room examiners (Fángkǎo) undertook the task of detailed grading.
Throughout the dynasties, their selection was considered extremely important.
During the Kāngxī period,
Zhèng Jiāng, a Shùjǐshì and assistant examiner for the Shùntiān examination, was granted the position of Jiǎntǎo
for his fair and appropriate review.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1723),
Zhū Shì and Zhāng Tíngyù, the chief examiners for the Huìshì, selected candidates justly and impartially.
The emperor praised them
and granted them the titles of Tàifù and Tàibǎo respectively, with differing ranks.
As for those who were unfair in their judgment or acted carelessly,
punishments were not spared.
Those who engaged in bribery through illicit connections
were deemed to have even more serious offenses.
In the 14th year of Shùnzhì's reign, Dīngyǒu (1657),

Lǐ Zhènyè and Zhāng Wǒpǔ, assistant examiners for the Shùntiān examination, accepted bribes from the scrutiny official (Kēchén) Lù Yíjí, the Academician (Bóshì) Cài Yuánxǐ, and the Jìnshì Xiàng Shàofāng.
They passed Tián Sì and Wū Zuòlín as Jǔrén.
The Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Rèn Kèpǔ impeached them,
and the facts were confirmed through interrogation.
An imperial edict ordered the public execution of the seven people,
the confiscation of their family property,
and the banishment of their parents, brothers, wives, and children to the frontier.
Cáo Běnrong, a Shùzǐ, and Sòng Zhīshéng, a Zhōngyǔn, both examiners, were demoted for negligence.
Fāng Yóu, a Shìjiǎng and chief examiner for Jiāngnán, and Qián Kāizōng, a Jiǎntǎo,
bribed to establish illicit connections.
A bookstore in Jiāngníng published the "Wànjīn Chuánqí Jì" (Record of Ten Thousand Gold Legends) slandering them.
Censorate officials submitted memorials one after another to impeach them,
and the Ministry of Punishments confirmed the facts.
Shìzǔ was furious.
Yóu, Kāizōng, and seventeen other people, including the assistant examiner Yè Chǔhuái, were all executed in the marketplace,
and their wives, children, and family property were confiscated.
For a time, people's hearts were greatly shaken,
and the malpractices in the imperial examinations were cleared up for several decades.
In the 50th year of Kāngxī's reign, Xīnmǎo (1711),
Wú Bì and Chéng Guāngkuí, scholars from Jiāngnán, bribed the deputy examiner, editor (Biānxīu) Zhào Jìn, to pass the examination.
Neither of them was known for their literary talent,
and public opinion was in an uproar.
When the matter was reported,
the Minister (Shàngshū) Zhāng Pénghé was ordered to work with the Governor-General (Dūdú) and Governor (Fǔ) of Jiāngnán to conduct a strict investigation.
The Governor of Sūzhōu (Sūfǔ) Zhāng Bóxíng impeached Governor-General Gá Lǐ for bribery and favoritism,
while Gá Lǐ also impeached Bóxíng for other crimes.
An imperial edict ordered both to be dismissed from their posts.
Pénghé was instructed to work with the Grand Canal Administrator (Zǒngcáo) Hè Shòu for a thorough investigation.
They reported back, requesting Gá Lǐ's demotion
and Bóxíng's dismissal.
The emperor was angered by their cover-up and compromise.
He then dispatched Ministers Mù Hélún and Zhāng Tíngshū to conduct another investigation,
and their report was largely consistent with Pénghé's findings.
The Ministry's deliberation was that
mutual accusations went against the decorum of high officials
and both should be stripped of their posts.
The emperor ultimately stripped Gá Lǐ of his post.
As Bóxíng's reputation for integrity was well-known,
he was stripped of his post but allowed to remain in office.
Jìn and the assistant examiners Wáng Yuēyú and Fāng Míng were sentenced to capital punishment.
The chief examiner Zuǒ Bìfān was stripped of his official rank for negligence.
In the same year, Wú Zhàozhōng, a Fángkǎo in Fújiàn, was also executed for bribery.
The examiner, Jiǎntǎo Jiè Xiàomó, and the Secretariat Official (Zhǔshì) Liú Yǎn were stripped of their posts for negligence.
In the 8th year of Xiánfēng's reign, Wùwǔ (1858),
Píng Líng, a Jǔrén from Shùntiān, had discrepancies between his final and draft examination papers,
causing public outrage.
The Censor (Yùshǐ) Mèng Chuánjīn exposed the matter.
Princes and high officials such as Zài Yuán investigated and found that the chief examiner, Grand Secretary Bǎi Jùn, had shown favoritism at the request of his servant Jìn Xiáng.
He passed Luó Hóngyì's paper, which had been reviewed by the assistant examiner and editor Pǔ Ān.
In accordance with the regulations for illicit connections, solicitations, and bribery,
Bǎi Jùn and Pǔ Ān were executed in the marketplace.
Tens of others were punished with military service, exile, demotion, or dismissal.
Chéng Tíngguì, the deputy chief examiner and Deputy Censor-in-Chief on the Left, and his son Chéng Bǐngcǎi, a Langzhong,
were executed for receiving illicit connections.
Tíngguì was banished to the frontier.
It is said that Zài Yuán, Duān Huá, and Sù Shùn, the Minister who presided over the joint trial, had always disliked the examination system
and had a grudge against Bǎi Jùn.
Thus, they orchestrated a major case
and sentenced Bǎi Jùn to death.
Commentators believed that since Jìn Xiáng was already dead,
the judgment was not entirely trustworthy.
However, since the Jiāqìng and Dàoguāng eras,
the children of high-ranking officials and nobles regarded success in the imperial examination as a birthright.
With this case,
the entrenched malpractices in the northern examination hall changed dramatically.
In the 19th year of Guāngxù's reign (1893),
the editor Dīng Wéizhī presided over the Shǎnxī provincial examination.
His friend from the same examination year, Ráo Shìténg, had previously arranged for illicit connections on his behalf.
When the matter was discovered,
both were arrested and interrogated.
Shìténg committed suicide
and was subsequently stripped of his post.
Were there any who were punished without involving illicit connections or bribery?
In the 38th year of Kāngxī's reign, Jǐmǎo (1699),
the Censor Lù Yòu impeached the Shùntiān examination for unfairness.
Lǐ Pán, the chief examiner and Compiler (Xiūzhuàn), was banished to the frontier.
Jiāng Chényīng, the deputy chief examiner and Biānxīu, was implicated and imprisoned.
He was not brought to trial
and died in prison.
Chényīng was a famous scholar from Zhèjiāng,
skilled in ancient prose.
The entire court knew he was innocent,
and everyone lamented his fate.
In the 44th year, Yǐyǒu (1705),
Wāng Bīn, a Shìláng and chief examiner for Shùntiān, and Yáo Shìlěi, a Zànshàn, were negligent in their review,
leaving many rejected papers unchecked.
Those who failed tied straw figures resembling people
and went to their gates to 'execute' them.
When the matter was reported,
they were stripped of their posts.
In the 60th year, Xīnchǒu (1721),
Lǐ Fú, the deputy chief examiner for the Huìshì and Deputy Censor-in-Chief on the Left, used the Táng dynasty method of open ranking,
selecting famous scholars.
Those who failed created a commotion at his gate.
He was impeached and stripped of his post,
and sent to perform forced labor at the Yǒngdìng River.
However, that examination successfully brought almost all notable scholars of the time into the fold,
and was quite praised by contemporary opinion.
Other instances of bribery through illicit connections that were not exposed,
and those who were condemned for minor errors,
were subject to a variety of different regulations.
For the quota of successful candidates in the provincial examinations (Xiāngshì),
in the early Shuìzhì reign, the quota was set generously.
Shùntiān and Jiāngnán both had over 160 successful candidates.
Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and Fújiàn all had over 100 successful candidates.
Hénán, Shāndōng, Guǎngdōng, Sìchuān, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Guǎngxī, and Yúnnán gradually decreased from over 90 successful candidates,
down to Guìzhōu which had 40, the fewest.
All were divided by classic (Jīng) for selection.
In the Shùntiān examination, students from Zhílì (Shēngyuán Bèizìhào) accounted for about seven-tenths of the quota,
students from the Northern Imperial Academy (Běijiānshēng Mǐnzìhào) three-tenths,
while Xuānhuà (Dànzì) and Fèngtiān (Jiázì) had only two or three successful candidates.
In the Jiāngnán examination, students from the Southern Imperial Academy (Nánjiānshēng Mǐnzìhào) accounted for about two-tenths,
the rest being the combined quota for students from Jiāngsū and Ānhuī in the same examination hall.
When the Southern Imperial Academy (Nányōng) was abolished,
its quota for successful candidates was merged into that of the Northern Imperial Academy.
In the fourteenth year [of Shùnzhì],
students from the Imperial Academy were divided into Southern and Northern rolls.
The eight prefectures of Zhílì,
the two sub-prefectures of Yánqìng and Bǎo'ān,
Liáodōng, Xuānfǔ, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, Shǎnxī, Sìchuān, and Guǎngxī were for the Northern roll (Běimǐn).
Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Húguǎng, and Guǎngdōng were for the Southern roll (Nánmǐn).
The quota of successful candidates was determined by the number of participants.
In the seventeenth year,
the quota for successful candidates in various provinces directly administered was halved.
During the Kāngxī reign,
the quota for successful candidates in provinces directly administered was expanded multiple times.
In the fiftieth year,
an additional one-fifth was added to each.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
Húnán and Húběi held separate examinations,
with their quotas for successful candidates divided according to the old quotas.
There were slight increases and decreases in other provinces.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
the Mǐnzìhào for Shùntiān was divided into Southern, Northern, and Central rolls.
Fèngtiān, Zhílì, Shāndōng, Hénán, Shānxī, and Shǎnxī were for the Northern roll (Běimǐn).
Jiāngnán, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, Húguǎng, and Guǎngdōng were for the Southern roll (Nánmǐn).
Each had a quota of thirty-nine successful candidates.
Sìchuān, Guǎngxī, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu were separately compiled into the Central roll (Zhōngmǐn),
with one successful candidate chosen for every fifteen.
Jiāngnán was divided into Upper Jiāng and Lower Jiāng.
Lower Jiāng (Jiāngsū) had six-tenths of the successful candidates,
and Upper Jiāng (Ānhuī) had four-tenths.
In the ninth year,
strict rules for searching and inspection were established.
In the Northern examination, over forty people were exposed for bringing in cheat sheets,
3,800 to several tens of people left prematurely,
and several hundred more either submitted blank papers, unfinished essays, or essays not relevant to the topic.
The Emperor then punished the Superintendent of Education (Xuézhèng) and the Chancellor of the Imperial Academy (Jìjiǔ) for their negligence.
An imperial edict reduced the quota for successful candidates in each directly administered province by one-tenth.
Thus, the quotas were set: Shùntiān's Southern (Nánmǐn) and Northern (Běimǐn) rolls each had thirty-six;
the Central roll (Zhōngmǐn) was changed to one successful candidate for every twenty;
Bèizìhào had 102;
Jiázì and Dànzì each had four.
Jiāngnán's Upper Jiāng had forty-five;
Lower Jiāng had sixty-nine;
Zhèjiāng and Jiāngxī each had ninety-four;
Fújiàn had eighty-five;
Guǎngdōng had seventy-two;
Hénán had seventy-one;
Shāndōng had sixty-nine;
Shǎnxī had sixty-one;
Shānxī and Sìchuān each had sixty;
Yúnnán had fifty-four;
Húběi had forty-eight;
Húnán and Guǎngxī each had forty-five;
Guìzhōu had thirty-six.
From then on, these regulations were strictly followed without deviation.
In the first year of Guāngxù,
Shǎn and Gān held separate examinations.
Shǎnxī had forty-one successful candidates,
and Gānsù had thirty.
During the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns,
various provinces often contributed several million [taels of silver] in taxes,
and the quotas for successful candidates were expanded multiple times.
Sìchuān had twenty;
Jiāngsū eighteen;
Guǎngdōng fourteen;
Fújiàn and Táiwān thirteen;
Zhèjiāng, Húnán, Húběi, Jiāngxī, Shānxī, Ānhuī, Gānsù, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu each had ten;
Shǎnxī nine;
Hénán and Guǎngxī each eight;
Zhílì and Shāndōng each two.
This was even more than the initially set quotas.
There was no fixed quota for the metropolitan examinations (Huìshì).
In the third and ninth years of Shùnzhì, there were both four hundred successful candidates.
They were divided into Southern, Northern, and Central rolls.
The five provinces of Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Húguǎng, and Guǎngdōng,
the eleven prefectures of Jiāngníng, Sū, Sōng, Cháng, Zhèn, Huái, Yáng, Huī, Níng, Chí, and Tài,
and the one sub-prefecture of Guǎngdé constituted the Southern roll,
with 233 successful candidates.
The four provinces of Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, and Shǎnxī,
the eight prefectures of Shùntiān, Yǒngpíng, Báodìng, Héjiān, Zhēndìng, Shùndé, Guǎngpíng, and Dàmíng,
the two sub-prefectures of Yánqìng and Bǎo'ān,
and the various places of Fèngtiān, Liáodōng, Dàníng, and Wànquán constituted the Northern roll,
with 153 successful candidates.
The four provinces of Sìchuān, Guǎngxī, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu,
and the prefectures and sub-prefectures of Ān, Lú, Fèng, Chú, Xú, and Hé constituted the Central roll,
with fourteen successful candidates.
In the twelfth year,
the Central roll was merged into the Southern and Northern rolls.
Thereafter, the Central roll was repeatedly divided and merged,
or further divided from the Southern, Northern, and Central rolls into Left and Right rolls.
Sometimes, successful candidates were exclusively chosen from the four provinces of Sìchuān, Guǎng, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu,
each assigned specific character numbers,
and separately ranked as first, second, and third.
In the fifty-first year,
due to the uneven number of successful candidates chosen from various provinces,
and the possibility of neglecting border provinces,
the Southern and Northern official and commoner character numbers were abolished,
and successful candidates were chosen by province.
The quota of successful candidates was imperially set
according to the number of examinees.
Historically, there were generally several hundreds of successful candidates,
sometimes as few as one hundred or so,
with the most being 406 in the Gēngxū year of Yōngzhèng,
and the fewest being 96 in the Jǐyǒu year of Qiánlóng.
The system of "Five Classics successful candidates" (Wǔjīng Zhōngshì)
was imitated from the Míng dynasty.
In the first session, three essays on literary composition (Shūyì) and
four essays on classical exegesis (Jīngyì) were tested.
Those who excelled in writing on the Five Classics [in their combined rolls]
were known as
"Twenty-three Essays" (Èrshísānpìan)
candidates.
In the Yǐyǒu year of Shùnzhì,
during the Shāndōng provincial examination,
Fǎ Ruòzhēn, for his complete essays on the Five Classics, was granted the title of Grand Secretariat Secretary (Nèigé Zhōngshū)
and allowed to participate in the metropolitan examination directly.
In the Dīngmǎo year of Kāngxī, during the Shùntiān provincial examination,
Zhā Shìhán, a student from Zhèjiāng Imperial Academy (Jiānshēng), and Lín Wényīng, a tribute student (Gòngshēng) from Fújiàn,
and in the Rénwǔ year, Zhuāng Lìngyú and Yú Chángcè, students from the Shùntiān Southern Imperial Academy (Nánmǐn Jiānshēng),
were reported for violating regulations by submitting twenty-three essays that combined the Four Books and Five Classics.
Upon imperial report,
they were all granted the title of Jǔrén.
An edict later declared that there was no need to prohibit this in the future,
and this was soon made into a standing regulation.
For the Five Classics rolls in the provincial and metropolitan examinations,
three additional successful candidates were chosen beyond the regular quota.
In the second session, one imperial edict (Zhào) and one imperial mandate (Gào) were added to the examination.
Consequently, more people studied them.
In provinces like Zhílì and Shǎnxī, there were even those who became top scorers (Lún Yuán) through the Five Classics rolls.
In the fiftieth year,
one successful candidate was added to the provincial examination for each province,
and two for Shùntiān,
and three for the metropolitan examination.
In the fifty-sixth year,
the examination of the Five Classics was suspended.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
the system was restored.
Four successful candidates were chosen for the Shùntiān Mǐnzìhào,
and one additional successful candidate was added for every nine in each province's quota.
In large provinces with many talented individuals and excellent essays,
three or four "deputy roll" (Fùbǎng) candidates were additionally chosen.
In the fourth year, Bǐngwǔ,
an edict permitted those who became Fùbǎng candidates through the Five Classics in that examination session
to be treated as Jǔrén,
and participate in the metropolitan examination directly,
which was particularly exceptional.
In the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the practice of selecting successful candidates based on the Five Classics was finally abolished.
As for subsequent imperial visits to the Imperial Academy (Línyōng),
the increase in the quota for successful candidates from the Northern Imperial Academy (Běiwéi Jiānshēng),
and imperial decrees expanding the quotas for successful candidates in the provincial and metropolitan examinations,
these were all beyond the regular quotas.
Beyond the main list (Zhèngbǎng) in the provincial and metropolitan examinations, deputy roll (Fùbǎng) candidates were also selected.
Metropolitan examination Fùbǎng candidates were exempted from the palace examination (Tíngshì)
and appointed to positions by the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù).
This was abolished in the third year of Kāngxī.
The original quota for provincial examination Fùbǎng candidates was twenty for Shùntiān,
twelve for Jiāngnán,
eleven for Jiāngxī,
ten each for Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, and Húguǎng,
nine each for Shāndōng and Hénán,
eight each for Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Sìchuān, and Guǎngdōng,
and six for Guǎngxī.
Those with superior literary ability were chosen,
regardless of their classical school (Jīngfáng).
The selection was suspended in the first year of Kāngxī.
In the eleventh year,
selection resumed according to the old rules.
Five were added for Yúnnán,
and four for Guìzhōu.
Thereafter, each directly administered province generally had one Fùbǎng candidate for every five Zhèngbǎng candidates,
except for the expanded quotas during imperial grace examinations (Ēnkē).
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
those who were selected as Fùbǎng candidates for a second time in that examination session were permitted to be treated as Jǔrén,
which was an extraordinary exception.
In the fifth year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1727),
the governors-general, governors, and education superintendents of each province were ordered to screen elderly teaching officials for retirement vacancies.
These positions were then filled by *jǔrén* (provincial graduates) whose examination papers for that year's metropolitan examination were well-structured and fluent.
During the Qiánlóng era,
selection was repeatedly carried out according to this precedent,
with several tens of names from large, medium, and small provinces respectively.
*Míngtōng* (those who passed the special examination for capable officials) formed a separate list.
In the twenty-sixth year (1761),
the court deliberated and decided to select forty *zhōngshū* (secretaries) from outside the *míngtōng* list.
As for others who were advanced in years, mature, and suitable for teaching scholars,
several *xuézhèng* (directors of studies) and *xuélù* (assistant directors of studies) were separately selected and appointed.
This was approved.
In the fifty-fifth year (1790), it was all abolished.
Thereafter, those who failed the examinations
were selected as copyists from outside the main list,
several hundred or one hundred-odd names in the northern examination.
The quota for the metropolitan examination was fixed at forty names,
to be reserved for writing in various academies,
and accumulating merit could lead to consideration for appointment.
This was to broadly gather and select talents, enabling humble scholars to gain more avenues for advancement.
For the Eight Banners, cavalry and archery were fundamental,
prioritizing military arts over civil studies.
When Shìzǔ (Emperor Shùnzhì) ascended the throne,
an edict was issued to open the imperial examinations,
but Eight Banners individuals were not included.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì (1651),
the Ministry of Personnel memorialized, saying:
"Many Eight Banners youths are talented
and suitable for selection as virtuous officials.
It is fitting to follow established precedent and open the examinations,
appointing the outstanding ones from the provincial and metropolitan examinations."
This was approved.
The Eight Banners provincial and metropolitan examinations began in that year.
At that time, for Eight Banners youths,
there was a fixed quota for those under each *niúrù* (company) who studied Manchu and Han books.
Those taking examinations and those appointed to various yamen
were all drawn from this pool,
and those outside the quota were not allowed to study.
Often, there were not enough to meet the selection.
Therefore, from the fourteenth year (1657) to the fifteenth year of Kāngxī (1676),
Eight Banners examinations
were sometimes held and sometimes suspended.
Previously, for the provincial, metropolitan,
and palace examinations,
Manchus and Mongols formed one list,
while Han Bannermen and Han Chinese formed another list.
In the twenty-sixth year of Kāngxī (1687),
an edict decreed that they should all take the examination together with the Han Chinese.
Soon after, a system was established:
in the provincial and metropolitan examination halls, cavalry and archery were tested first.
Only those who passed the riding and archery tests
were allowed to take the civil examinations.
This ensured that civil pursuits did not hinder military preparedness,
and it became a permanent institution.
Initially, for the Eight Banners provincial examination,
only one essay in Manchu or Mongolian was tested.
The metropolitan examination had double that.
Han Bannermen tested two essays on calligraphy and one on classical scholarship.
Those unfamiliar with the classics
would have an additional calligraphy essay.
The second and third rounds tested one discourse and one policy question each.
Gradually increasing with each examination,
from the time they began to be tested together with the Han Chinese,
it was no longer as simple as before.
For the provincial examination quota,
in the eighth year of Shùnzhì (1651),
it was set at fifty each for Manchus and Han Bannermen,
and twenty for Mongols.
Later, the quotas for Manchus and Han Bannermen were reduced by one-fifth each,
and for Mongols by one-fourth.
In the eighth year of Kāngxī (1669),
Manchus and Mongols were grouped under the 'Mǎn' (Manchu) designation,
and Han Bannermen under the 'Hé' (Combined) designation,
each selecting ten names.
In the twenty-sixth year (1687),
the Han Bannermen quota was further reduced by five names.
Later, it was gradually increased again.
In the ninth year of Qiánlóng (1744),
an edict decreed a reduction of one-tenth for each,
fixing the quotas at twenty-seven for Manchus and Mongols,
and twelve for Han Bannermen.
During the Tóngzhì era,
due to contributions of grain, six names were added for Manchus and Mongols,
and four for Han Bannermen.
Initially, garrison troops in various provinces
also took the Shùntiān (Beijing) examination.
In the eighteenth year of Jiāqìng (1813),
they began to be examined in their respective garrison provinces.
One in ten passed,
usually not exceeding three names,
with *fùbǎng* (supplementary list) as per usual.
The initial system for the metropolitan examination was,
twenty-five *jìnshì* (metropolitan graduates) each for Manchus and Han Bannermen,
and ten for Mongols.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī (1670),
the 'Mǎn' and 'Hé' designations were established,
following the provincial examination precedent,
each selecting four names.
Thereafter, imperial decrees were sought on a case-by-case basis,
with no fixed quota.
Imperial clan members were not allowed to take the provincial and metropolitan examinations;
Shèngzǔ (Emperor Kāngxī) and Shìzōng (Emperor Yōngzhèng) had issued clear edicts on this.
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng (1743),
the Imperial Clan Court examined the Imperial Clan School students,
selecting outstanding individuals such as Yùdǐngzhù as *jìnshì*,
who then participated in the palace examination as a group.
This marked the beginning of metropolitan examinations for imperial clan members.
It was suspended not long after.
In the sixth year of Jiāqìng (1801),
it was finally mandated that imperial clan members could take the provincial and metropolitan examinations.
Prior to this, the Imperial Clan Court or the Imperial Clan School in Fèngtiān (Shenyang) conducted cavalry and archery examinations as per precedent.
The examination period was either before the civil provincial and metropolitan examination,
or after it,
or on the same day.
One essay on policy and one regulated verse poem were tested,
completed in one day.
For the provincial examination, one in nine passed.
For the metropolitan examination,
the examiners would select a few papers for imperial review,
forming a separate list.
For the palace examination and court examination,
Manchus and Han Chinese were treated equally,
except for differences in official positions like *shùjíshì* (bachelor of the Hanlin Academy).
In the fifteenth year of Shùnzhì,
the Emperor, seeing that the examiners for Shùntiān and Jiāngnán had both been dismissed for bribery,
personally re-examined the *jǔrén* from both examination bureaus.
This marked the beginning of re-examinations for the provincial examinations.
Mi Hànwén and 181 others from Shùntiān were selected,
and permitted to take the metropolitan examination.
Wāng Pǔxūn and 97 others from Jiāngnán were
permitted to be *jǔrén*.
Twenty-two individuals were penalized by being suspended from the metropolitan examination or having their names removed.
Only Wú Kēmíng, whose essays from three examinations were exceptionally well-written,
was specially permitted to participate in the palace examination as usual;
this was an unusual exception.
In the thirty-eighth year of Kāngxī,
the Emperor, finding the selection of scholars in the northern examination unfair,
ordered a re-examination within the imperial court.
Those ranked third class or above were allowed to take the metropolitan examination;
those in the fourth class were dismissed.
In the fifty-first year, *rénchén*,
Zhā Wéirén, the *jièyuán* from Shùntiān, fled after his involvement in transmitting answers was discovered.
The Emperor suspected that some new *jìnshì* had hired others to take the examination for them,
and personally conducted a re-examination at Chàngchūnyuán,
dismissing five people.
Re-examinations for the metropolitan examination began from this point.
During the Qiánlóng era,
sometimes the governors, governors-general, and education superintendents of each province were ordered to conduct re-examinations after the provincial examination results were announced;
sometimes only the "outstanding" *gòngjiàn* who had passed the examinations in the three *bǐngwǔ* cohorts from Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, Guǎngdōng, and Shānxī provinces were re-examined;
sometimes only the successful *jìnshì* were re-examined;
or sometimes the *jǔrén* from the northern examination were re-examined.
An imperial decree was issued at the time,
with no fixed rule.
In the fifty-fourth year,
Gòngshì Shàn Kěhóng's re-examination poem was out of tune and erroneous,
not matching his original examination paper,
and his name was removed.
The imperial decree was stern,
stating,
"Unless the Ministry of Rites conducts strict re-examinations,
it will be insufficient to select true talents and punish those who advance by luck."
By the early Jiāqìng reign,
this was formally established as a regulation.
In the twenty-third year of Dàoguāng,
a system was established
where all provincial *jǔrén*
were uniformly required to come to the capital for re-examination;
without undergoing re-examination,
they were not permitted to take the metropolitan examination.
If delayed due to circumstances,
they would participate in the next three cohorts.
Except for those taking leave due to mourning,
those who failed to appear under false pretenses
were considered to be evading the examination,
and permanently barred from the metropolitan examination and selection by the Ministry of Personnel.
The re-examination period was in the second month of the metropolitan examination year.
During the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns,
due to military uprisings obstructing roads,
and in the final years of Guāngxù,
due to the Xīncǒu Treaty,
examinations were suspended in the capital,
and held in Hénán;
in these cases, metropolitan examinations could be taken first, followed by re-examinations,
which was not the usual system.
If re-examination essays or poems contained flaws,
such as a poem being out of tune,
mistakes in transcription,
or failure to avoid imperial names, temple names, or the name of the Most Sacred Sage,
the penalty was suspension from the metropolitan and palace examinations for one or more cohorts.
Those whose writing was incoherent,
or whose writing style or handwriting did not match their original examination paper, were dismissed.
In the fifty-eighth year of Qiánlóng,
eight successful *jǔrén*, including Dèng Fēnchūn, underwent supplementary re-examination;
five were suspended for one cohort,
two were dismissed,
and the supervising officials were all reprimanded.
In various cohorts, there were those who were dismissed or punished for similar reasons.
However, by the late period, the trend became increasingly lenient.
In the nineteenth year of Guāngxù,
tens of people in the northern examination were found to have hired others to write for them or to have impersonated others to pass.
Censors impeached six *jǔrén*: Zhōu Xuéxī, Tāng Bǎolín, Cài Xuéyuān, Chén Bùluán, Huáng Shùshēng, and Wàn Háng.
The relevant authorities were ordered to identify those whose recorded examination papers did not match their originals.
Xuéyuān, Shùshēng, and Háng were all dismissed;
none of the others were dismissed after re-examination,
and the supervising officials were exempted from discussion,
leading to a proliferation of those who relied on luck.
According to established regulations, after the results of provincial examinations in each province were announced,
the examination papers were to be submitted to the Ministry for scrutiny within a specified timeframe;
delays were penalized.
This was to prevent examiners from altering examination papers after the examination to avoid official censure.
Scrutiny primarily focused on eliminating fraud,
and secondarily on identifying flaws.
Minor textual flaws were forgiven.
If words or phrases were suspicious,
or the writing style was incorrect,
the *jǔrén* was removed from the list.
If there were a certain number of such papers or more,
the chief examiner and assistant examiners were dismissed or arrested for questioning.
If fewer than a certain number of papers,
their salary was docked or they were demoted.
If the review was careless,
producing similar or poor quality work,
with various problems appearing together,
or if examination papers showed unfamiliarity with prohibitions,
contained obscure, erroneous, or flawed words and phrases,
had incorrect characters in the title,
lacked completeness in regular or cursive script,
or had transcription errors,
the officials of the inner and outer examination bureaus and the examinees were penalized differently.
The strictness of these prohibitions
was unprecedented.
Initially, the Ministry of Rites and the Department of Rites were responsible for scrutiny.
During the Kāngxī reign,
ministers were specially appointed by imperial decree to oversee this task.
As the number of successful candidates gradually increased,
and the number of examination papers grew,
the Nine Chief Ministers were then ordered to jointly conduct the scrutiny.
The officials of the Six Ministries, constrained by their regular duties,
used their spare time for examination and scrutiny,
often merely going through the motions.
In the early Qiánlóng reign,
this responsibility was changed to officials from the Censorate, specifically departments and circuits, of fifth rank or higher,
and Hanlin and Grand Secretariat officials, such as *kējǐa Jīngtáng* and *zhōngzàn* or higher,
who would gather in the imperial antechamber for scrutiny.
Later, *biānxiū* and *jiǎnshì* were added.
The fixed number was forty people,
to ensure focused responsibility.
Previously, examination papers under scrutiny were not signed,
nor were there rules for merits or demerits.
Those involved in this task
often claimed generosity,
unwilling to thoroughly investigate.
In the twenty-first year of Qiánlóng,
scrutiny officials were first required to fill in their titles and names.
In the twenty-fifth year,
a regulation for re-scrutiny by high officials was added,
with separate provisions for discussion and punishment,
making the regulations truly strict.
That year, Qín Huìtián, Guānbǎo, and Qián Rǔchéng were specially appointed as re-scrutiny ministers.
After the matter was concluded,
the original scrutiny official, Censor Zhū Pīliè, impeached them for favoritism.
The matter was sent to the Grand Councilors for review.
Huìtián and others indeed had errors in rejecting papers and omissions,
and Pīliè was also penalized for making unsubstantiated accusations;
both cases were sent to the Ministry for deliberation.
At that time, all the scrutiny officials handled matters with great care,
without showing any leniency,
completely changing the old habit of following convention and being perfunctory.
Gōng Huànwén, Grand Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud; Yán Xúnqí, Zhū Jī, and Zhū Pīliè, Censors;
and Xīn Cóngyì, Censor in the early Jiāqìng reign,
were all known at the time for their discerning and meticulous investigations.
In various cohorts, there were many examination officials and examinees who were reprimanded or dismissed because of this,
but there were also instances of using this as an excuse for retaliation.
In the sixtieth year of Qiánlóng, *yǐmǎo*,
the *huìyuán* was Wáng Yǐwǔ from Zhèjiāng,
and the second place was his younger brother Yǐxián.
The Emperor found this unusual.
The chief examiner, Assistant Minister Dòu Guāngnài, had always been at odds with Héshēn,
and had also offended his colleagues by criticizing junior scholars;
both wanted to use this to bring him down.
They then picked out the phrase
"the kingly way is rooted in human nature"
which appeared in both brothers' examination papers,
claiming it indicated collusion.
Consequently, Yǐwǔ was placed at the very end of the list and
his palace examination was suspended. Guāngnài was demoted to fourth rank and retired,
and Assistant Minister Liú Yuèyún, a vice-examiner, and Jìjiǔ Hútúllǐ were both demoted four ranks.
When the palace examination results were announced,
Yǐxián was first,
and the Emperor's mind was at ease.
He instructed his court officials, saying,
"Could this also be my collusion?"
Yǐwǔ later also entered the Hanlin Academy.
In the fifth year of Jiāqìng,
scrutiny officials Xīn Cóngyì and Dài Lù spared no effort in identifying flaws in the policy questions and examination papers of the northern examination.
Cóngyì, a native of Jiāngxī,
was known for his strict scrutiny.
In this cohort, only one person from Jiāngxī passed,
and Lù's son failed.
People said that this led to excessive fault-finding.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor
ordered both men to withdraw from the scrutiny panel.
During the Tóngzhì reign,
Liáng Sēngbǎo, Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices, was again feared for his overly strict scrutiny.
Indeed, since the implementation of scrutiny regulations,
it had been instrumental in correcting writing styles,
uncovering abuses,
and benefiting the examination system,
which was by no means insignificant.
The circumstances of various examination sessions were slightly different.
In the third year of Shùnzhì,
following the request of Grand Secretary Gānglín,
because the empire had just been settled
and talent was to be widely recruited,
the Xiāngshì and Huìshì were held again.
In the sixteenth year,
because Yúnnán and Guìzhōu had newly submitted
and personnel were needed for pacification and consolidation,
the Lǐbùshì was held again.
Neither of these followed the old Zi-Chǒu year cycle pattern.
In the sixteenth year of Kāngxī,
for the Xiāngshì in Shùntiān, special officials were dispatched;
Shāndōng, Shānxī, and Shǎnxī were combined with Hénán Province;
Húguǎng and Jiāngxī were combined with Jiāngnán Province;
and Fújiàn was combined with Zhèjiāng Province for the examinations.
The examination period was in the ninth month,
one in fifteen candidates passed,
no Fùbǎng (supplementary list) candidates were selected,
and there was no Huìshì.
In the Jiāngnán list of successful candidates, Jiāngxī had no successful candidates.
During the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns, military uprisings occurred,
and various Zhíshěng (provinces directly under the central government) either did not hold examinations for several sessions,
or combined several sessions into one examination,
selecting double the quota of candidates.
Alternatively, a province might only hold examinations in a few Fǔ (prefectures), Zhōu (departments), or Xiàn (counties),
selecting a reduced quota of candidates.
The examination period was sometimes delayed until October or November,
not adhering to established precedents.
The chief examiner of Shùntiān
was initially always an official dispatched from the Hànlín Academy.
In the early Kāngxī reign,
following the Míng system,
the Zhuàngyuán (first rank, first place) of the previous session served in this capacity.
Scholars hoping for illicit encounters
could communicate connections in advance.
In the twentieth year,
the Xiūzhuàn Guī Yǔnsù presided over the Shùntiān examination,
writing an essay swearing to strenuously eliminate accumulated malpractices
and avoid backdoor dealings.
After the results were posted, those who failed clamored loudly,
hoping to instigate a major legal case.
Wèi Xiàngshū, the Minister of the Board of Punishments, exposed the matter,
and the groundless speculations finally subsided.
The system was also soon abolished.
In the second year,
for a Chūnqiū Tí (Spring and Autumn Annals question) in Shùntiān,
"Zhūzǐ"
was erroneously written as
"Zhūrén."
The examiners Bái Nǎizhēn and others were dismissed from their posts.
Scholars who had written the character '子' and displayed their papers
had them re-examined by officials of the Hóngwén Academy;
the excellent ones were permitted to be Jǔrén,
but there were no successful candidates (among those who correctly wrote '子' in the initial grading).
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
after the Shùntiān results were posted,
Grand Secretary Wáng Xùlíng and others, together with Hànlín officials from the Nánshūfáng (Southern Study), were ordered to review the failed examination papers,
and two people were selected.
That year, the Huìshì failed papers were re-examined as before,
and seventy-eight people were selected from them.
In the second year,
seventy-seven people were selected.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
thirty-eight people were selected.
Afterwards, this practice was no longer carried out.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
because Zhā Sìtíng and Wāng Jǐngqí, both from Zhèjiāng, authored rebellious books,
and after they had been investigated and dealt with,
the Zhèjiāng Xiāngshì and Huìshì were suspended.
Not long after,
due to requests from Lǐ Wèi and others,
the prohibition was relaxed.
In the seventh year,
Zhū Zhènjī, the Zhīzhōu of Liánzhōu in Guǎngdōng, privately worshipped Lǚ Liúliáng.
Shēngyuán Chén Xī was the first to report this,
and the emperor praised him.
He ordered that four excellent and proficient candidates from this session's examination in Liánzhōu
be selected by the Xuézhèng (Education Commissioner) and awarded Jǔrén status.
In the Xīnchǒu Huìshì of the forty-sixth year of Qiánlóng,

Qián Qǐ, the Jièyuán (first-place graduate in the provincial examination) from Jiāngnán, obtained both the Huìyuán (first-place in the metropolitan examination) and Zhuàngyuán (overall chief graduate) in that session.
In the Gēngchén Huìshì of the twenty-fifth year of Jiāqìng,
Chén Jìchāng, the Jièyuán from Guǎngxī, also obtained both the Huìyuán and Zhuàngyuán in that session.
Scholars admiringly called this
"Sānyuán" (Triple First).
Throughout the Qīng dynasty,
there were only two such individuals.
The Bāqí (Eight Banners) and Hànrén (Han Chinese) examined together,
but since the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns,
none from the Banners had attained the Dǐngjiǎ (top three graduates).
In the fourth year of Tóngzhì,
Chóngqǐ, a Mongol, achieved the Yījiǎ Yīmíng (first rank, first place, Zhuàngyuán).
In the ninth year of Guāngxù,
Shòuqí, an Imperial Clansman, achieved the Yījiǎ Èrmíng (first rank, second place, Bàngyǎn).
The Hànjūn (Han Banners) had even more Dǐngjiǎ recipients.
As for the system throughout the dynasty of awarding Jǔrén status for donations to military provisions, disaster relief, or garden and palace construction projects,
or for capturing rebels and bandits, or achieving merit by killing enemies,
there were precedents of Gòngjiān (Imperial College students) being granted Jǔrén status, and Jǔrén being granted Jìnshì status.
These were, however, temporary expedient measures.
Initially,
Tàizōng, in addition to the Mongolian script,
created the Qīng script.
In the eighth year of Tiāncōng,
he ordered the Lǐbù to examine scholars,
and selected Gānglín and one other person,
and from those proficient in the Mongolian script, Ébótè and two others.
All were granted the title of Jǔrén.
Later, they were re-examined.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì,
the Bāqí xiāngshì was held.
Those unable to write in Chinese were tested on one Qīng script essay,
and then it was held once more and ceased.
In the early Kāngxī period,
the fānyì xiāngshì was reinstated.
From the system of joint Manchu and Han examinations for official positions,
the fānyì division was abolished.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
an imperial edict stipulated that in addition to the examinations for Hanzi Shēngyuán, Jǔrén, and Jìnshì for Manchu Bāqí,
a separate fānyì examination should be held.
The court deliberated that all three rounds should be tested concurrently,
with two chief examiners and two deputy examiners each for Manchu and Han,
and four assistant examiners for Manchu.
The imperial edict stipulated that the xiāngshì should only test one round,
either one memorial or report,
or one topic drawn from the Sìshū Wǔjīng,
eliminating Han examiners,
increasing transcribers,
with other regulations following the literary examination precedents.
Subsequently, for fānyì imperial edicts,
or for Xìnglǐ Jīngyì and Xiǎoxué,
topics were assigned with a limit of three hundred characters.
In the third year of Qiánlóng,
it was ordered to write one Qīng script essay in addition to the fānyì topic.
In the seventh year,
it was decided that the first round of the huìshì would test Qīng script essays on the Sìshū,
and one essay each on the Xiàojīng and Xìnglǐ Lùn.
The second round would test fānyì.
All Manchus, Hanjun Manchu, Hanzi Gòng, Jiànshēngyuán, and Bǐtiēshì
were eligible for the xiāngshì.
Literary Jǔrén and military officers capable of fānyì
were permitted to take the huìshì.
Riding and archery were tested first as per regulations.
For the Mongolian fānyì division,
in the ninth year of Yōngzhèng,
an imperial edict ordered one chief examiner for Mongolian,
with assistant examiners numbering twice that.
Initially, for the xiāngshì and huìshì topics,
one Mongolian translation of a Qīng script Sìshū essay and one memorial were required.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
this was changed to translating Qīng script Xìnglǐ Xiǎoxué,
tested concurrently with the Manchu fānyì,
but with a separate list of successful candidates.
At that time, for the Qīng script xiāngshì,
typically five or six hundred candidates competed for thirty-three positions.
For the Mongolian script xiāngshì,
typically fifty or sixty candidates competed for six positions.
It was originally stipulated that the fānyì xiāngshì and huìshì be held once every three years,
but the huìshì was never held after its initial instance.
In the fourth year of Qiánlóng,
as the xiāngshì had been held for six cycles,
the huìshì finally took place in the eighth month.
Twenty Manchus and
two Mongols passed.
Because the number of participants was not large,
an imperial edict exempted them from the diànshì,
and all were granted the status of Jìnshì,
with the best appointed as Lìubù Zhǔshì.
In the twenty-second year,
because the fānyì division generally involved merely quoting passages and sentences,
irrelevant to the true meaning of fānyì,
an imperial edict suspended it.
In the forty-third year,
the xiāngshì was reinstated,
and the copying and proofreading were abolished.
The next year's huìshì,
which normally required sixty participants,
had only forty-seven for this session,
so special permission was granted for a conference,
and the tíngshì was waived,
as in the fourth year's precedent.
From then on, every three years,
whether to hold the examination was decided by imperial decree.
In the fifty-second year,
it was revised to hold the xiāngshì and huìshì once every five years.
However, from the fifty-third year of the huìwéi until the eighth year of Jiāqìng,
it was held only once,
still falling short of the stipulated sixty candidates.
Furthermore, proxy examination and impersonation
were rampant and beyond investigation.
The Mongolian examination was often suspended due to fewer than seven or eight candidates.
Although imperial edicts repeatedly urged the importance of the national language and riding and archery as the foundation for banner people,
the number of candidates remained sparse.
In the eighth year [of Jiāqìng],
following the request of Shìláng Gēngyīn,
the old system of holding it once every three years as a regular practice was restored.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the xiāngshì and fùshì were determined to follow the rules of the wénwéi.
In the eighth year of Dàoguāng,
the fānyì assistant examiners were abolished,
and only at the end of this year were Shùjíshì employed.
Initially, the Bāqí garrisons in various provinces
only took the Hanzi xiāngshì and huìshì.
In the twenty-third year of Dàoguāng,
it was changed to the fānyì examination,
with one in ten passing,
and three positions as the quota.
The Imperial Clan's participation in the fānyì examination
began during the Qiánlóng era.
A separate topic was set,
and the quota for successful candidates was personally fixed by the emperor.
For military examinations (Wǔkē),
since the first year of Shìzǔ's reign, an imperial edict was issued to hold them.
The xiāngshì was in the Zǐ, Wǔ, Mǎo, Yǒu years,
and the huìshì in the Chén, Xū, Chǒu, Wèi years,
following the system of the literary examinations (Wénkē).
The xiāngshì was held in the tenth month.
In Zhílì and Fèngtiān, it was at Shùntiānfǔ;
in other provinces, at Bùzhèngsī.
Those who passed were called Wǔjǔrén.
The next year, in the ninth month, the huìshì was held in Jīngshī.
Those who passed were called Wǔjìnshì.
All xiāngshì and huìshì were divided into three inner and outer rounds.
The first round was mounted archery,
the second round was foot archery and martial skills,
forming the outer rounds.
The third round involved two policy questions and one essay,
forming the inner round.
For the outer rounds' examiners,
at Shùntiān and the huìwéi, four Dàchén, Dàxuéshì, or Dūtǒng served.
For the inner rounds' examiners,
at Shùntiān, two Hánlín officials served;
at the huìwéi, two Gébù, Dūcháyuan, Hàn, Zhāntáng officials served.
For assistant examiners, at Shùntiān, four capital officials with examination backgrounds served;
at the huìwéi, four Gébù, Kēbù officials with examination backgrounds served.
The Zhīwǔjǔ for the huìshì
was served by the Bīngbù Shìláng.
In various Zhílì provinces, the Zǒngdū and Xúnfǔ served as Jiānlín and Zhǔkǎoguān.
Four Tóngzhī and Zhīxiàn with examination backgrounds served as assistant examiners.
Outer rounds were assisted by high-ranking Tí and Zhèn officials.
As for the Tídiào, Jiānshè, Jiānshì, Shòujuàn, Mífēng, Jiānmén, Xúnchuò, Sōujiǎn, and Gōngjǐ, all had fixed personnel,
generally reduced in number compared to the wénwéi.
For the diànshì, four court officials were selected as Dújuan Guān,
who personally reviewed riding, archery, and martial skills,
and then tested policy essays.
From the imperial presence, the names of Zhuàngyuán, Bǎngyǎn, and Tànhuā were announced,
just like in the wénkē.
In the initial system,
first-class Jìnshì were appointed as Fùjiàng, Cānjìang, Yóují, or Dūsī;
second and third-class Jìnshì were appointed as Shǒubèi or acting Shǒubèi.
Later, the first-place candidate of the first class was appointed as Yīděng Shìwèi,
the second and third-place candidates as Èrděng Shìwèi.
Second and third-class Jìnshì were appointed as Sānděng and Lánlíng Shìwèi,
with variations for Yíng and Wèi Shǒubèi.
All Wǔshēng from various provinces and Lǜyíng soldiers were eligible for the xiāngshì.
Wǔjǔ, incumbent Yíng Qiān, Bǎzǒng,
Mén, Wèi, Suǒ Qiānzǒng,
and Qiānzǒng who had reached the required age,
and understood literary meaning,
were all eligible for the huìshì.
However, those over sixty years old
were not allowed to take the examination.
Subsequently, for military officers' huìshì,
only those with Wǔjǔ backgrounds were permitted.
During the Kāngxī era,
desiring to gather talent proficient in both civil and military arts,
it was once permitted for literary Shēngyuán to take the military xiāngshì,
and literary Jǔrén to take the military huìshì,
which led to considerable abuses in the examination halls.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng,
following the advice of Yùshǐ Chén Dàjiè,
the mutual examination system for civil and military candidates was abolished.
When the examination system was first established,
the first round involved mounted archery, shooting at felt targets.
The second round involved foot archery, shooting at cloth targets.
Both required firing nine arrows.
Hitting two in mounted archery
and three in foot archery constituted passing.
Then, tests of strength and courage were conducted by drawing a bow, wielding a saber, and lifting a stone.
In the 17th year of Shùnzhì,
the strength and courage tests were suspended.
They were reinstated in the 13th year of Kāngxī.
The mounted archery target distance was changed to thirty-five paces,
and hitting three arrows constituted passing.
Those who did not pass could not proceed to the second round.
The foot archery distance was eighty paces,
and hitting two arrows constituted passing.
Then, candidates were tested with bows of eight, ten, and twelve strengths,
sabers of eighty, one hundred, and one hundred twenty *jīn*,
and stones of two hundred, two hundred fifty, and three hundred *jīn*.
Drawing the bow fully,
wielding the saber skillfully,
and lifting the stone one *chǐ* off the ground –
those who could perform one or two of these three items constituted passing.
Those who did not pass could not proceed to the third round.
Those who passed had a mark imprinted on their cheek,
which was later changed to the forearm
to prevent impersonation.
In the 32nd year,
the foot archery target distance was changed to fifty paces, with hitting two arrows constituting passing.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
it was again changed to shooting six arrows at thirty paces, with hitting two constituting passing.
Ground ball shooting was added to mounted archery,
and for the three strength and courage items—bow, saber, and stone—
at least one item had to be of the first or second grade
to qualify as passing.
This then became the permanent system.
For the inner examination questions,
the Seven Military Classics (*Wǔjīng Qīshū*) were traditionally used.
Because the texts were diverse and complex,
Shèngzǔ decreed the addition of the *Lúnyǔ* and *Mèngzǐ*.
Consequently, the number of discussion questions was changed to two:
the first question used the *Lúnyǔ* and *Mèngzǐ*,
and the second used the *Sūnzǐ*, *Wúzǐ*, and *Sīmǎ Fǎ*.
The quota for successful candidates in the provincial examinations (*xiāngshì*),
established in the 26th year of Kāngxī,
was roughly half that of the civil examinations (*wénwéi*) in each province.
During the Yōngzhèng reign, there were minor adjustments.
However, for Shǎnxī and Gānsù, due to the robust physique of their talent
and their proficiency in archery and horsemanship,
from Kāngxī to Qiánlóng,
an additional thirty successful candidates were added for each province at different times.
During the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns,
each province had expanded quotas for contributing funds, similar to the civil examinations.
In total, Shùntiān had a quota of one hundred ten,
Hànjūn forty,
Fèngtiān and Jǐnzhōu three,
Jiāngnán eighty-one,
Fújiàn sixty-three,
Zhèjiāng and Sìchuān sixty each,
Shǎnxī fifty-nine,
Hénán fifty-five,
Jiāngxī, Guǎngdōng, and Gānsù fifty-four each,
Shānxī fifty,
Shāndōng forty-eight,
Yúnnán forty-two,
Guǎngxī thirty-six,
Húběi thirty-five,
Húnán thirty-four,
and Guìzhōu twenty-five.
The metropolitan examination (*huìshì*) quota was often three hundred,
and at least one hundred.
During the Kāngxī reign,
the inner examination was divided into Southern and Northern scrolls,
with fifty successful candidates from each.
In the 52nd year,
selection by province began,
with the number of passing candidates from the outer examination being reported to the emperor for final decision.
In the 6th year of Jiāqìng,
Rénzōng, considering the equal importance of civil and military examinations,
noted that civil examination regulations were very strict,
with thorough measures against malpractice,
while military examination officials decided pass/fail on the spot,
which was more prone to abuses.
He ordered that, in accordance with the civil examination review system,
the names of successful military students in the provincial examination (*xiāngshì*), along with their mounted archery, foot archery, and strength and courage scores, be detailed and submitted.
Each province submitted these to the Ministry of War (*Bīngbù*);
Shùntiān separately appointed review officials for verification.
Those who were unjustly passed or whose scores were exaggerated were punished without leniency.
The re-examination (*fùshì*) began during the Qiánlóng era.
The initial regulations were strict,
applied only to the metropolitan examination.
Those who failed were penalized by suspension from further examinations,
and the examiners were subject to disciplinary action.
Those who failed three re-examinations
were dismissed.
In the 15th year of Dàoguāng,
the re-examination for Shùntiān military *jǔrén* began, following the metropolitan examination precedent.
In the 7th year of Xiánfēng,
re-examinations for military *jǔrén* in all provinces followed the Shùntiān precedent,
though with a slightly more lenient approach.
Initially,
the outer examination only had one passing standard,
with no distinction made for the quality of archery and horsemanship
or the strength and weakness of martial skills.
The inner examination selected candidates based solely on their essays,
which meant that those skilled in horsemanship and archery or proficient in field arts
might be overlooked.
In the 52nd year of Kāngxī,
it was ordered that in the metropolitan examination's outer round, those with notable talent in mounted archery, foot archery, and martial skills
be designated
"good"
candidates with a special mark
and secretly passed to the inner examination.
The inner examination officials would first select those with clear reasoning
from the "good" scrolls.
If insufficient,
they would then select from the general passing scrolls.
In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng,
following the advice of Vice Minister Shǐ Yízhí,
all provincial examinations' outer rounds also adopted the "good" designation.
Later, "good" candidates were further divided into "double good" and "single good."
The inner examination first selected "double good" candidates,
then "single good."
However, the general passing scrolls often numbered over a thousand candidates,
with only a few selected,
leading to various abuses in the inner examination, such as proxy examination and impersonation.
In the 24th year of Qiánlóng,
Censor Gē Tāo impeached these abuses,
whereupon the outer examination strictly enforced passing standards,
and the inner examination abolished the Four Books essays.
Only a basic understanding of logic was required,
and the importance of writing gradually diminished.
In the 12th year of Jiāqìng,
the policy questions in the provincial and metropolitan inner examinations were changed to memorizing and writing over a hundred characters from the military classics,
with no errors constituting passing.
Co-examiners were abolished,
and hence, mounted archery and martial skills became paramount,
rendering the inner examination virtually nominal.
This system was followed through successive generations,
without change.
In the 24th year of Guāngxù,
officials both inside and outside the court requested changes to the old military examination system,
abolishing bows, arrows, sabers, and stones,
and testing with rifles and cannons.
This was not permitted.
In the 27th year,
it was finally abolished because the hard bows, sabers, stones, and mounted and foot archery practiced in the military examinations
had no relevance to military affairs.
Mǎnzhōu began participating in the military examinations in the 1st year of Yōngzhèng.
Twenty candidates passed the provincial examination,
and four passed the metropolitan examination.
In the 12th year,
this was decreed to stop,
and it was not resumed for several decades.
In the 18th year of Jiāqìng,
the old system was reinstated.
Thirteen Mǎnzhōu and Ménggǔ candidates passed the provincial examination.
