Those stationed in various provinces took the examination in their respective provinces,
typically one out of ten passing,
with a maximum of ten
and a minimum of one.
There was no fixed quota for the metropolitan examination.
All *xiāojí xiào*,
*chéngmén lì*,
*lánlíng zhǎng*,
*bàitáng ā*,
*ēnqíwèi*,
*qīnjūn qiánfēng*,
*hùjūn*,
*lǐngcuī*,
*mǎjiǎ*,
*xúnpǔyíng qiānzǒng* and *bǎzǒng*, as well as civil officials like *zhōngshū*,
seventh- and eighth-rank *bǐtiēshì*,
and *yìnshēng*,
were all permitted to take the provincial examination alongside military students.
The provincial and metropolitan inner and outer examinations were conducted identically for Mǎnzhōu, Ménggǔ, and Hàn people.
Record Eighty-four: Selection Four: Special Examinations and Recommendations.
Special examinations (*zhìkē*)
were personally decreed by the Son of Heaven to await exceptionally talented individuals.
The Táng and Sòng dynasties established the most such examinations,
considering them a superior method of selection.
The Qing dynasty's examination system for selecting scholars
became a fixed institution.
Those specifically decreed were called the *Bóxué Hóngcí Kē*, *Jīngjì Tèkē*, and *Xiàolián Fāngzhèng Kē*.
As for classical studies (*jīngxué*)
or examinations summoned during imperial tours,
although not formally established as special examinations,
they can be included here.
Shèngzǔ emphasized practical learning,
and in the *Jiǎchén* and *Dīngwèi* examinations of Kāngxī,
the essays were changed to policy questions.
However, court officials argued that ancient learning could not be mastered quickly
and requested a return to the old system.
In the seventeenth year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Since ancient times, every flourishing dynasty
has always had erudite and distinguished scholars
chosen for consultation and literary work.
Since Our dynasty was established,
We have revered scholars and valued the Way,
cultivating talent.
With the vastness of the Four Seas,
how could there be no extraordinary talents and eminent individuals, profound in learning, splendid in literary expression, who emulate the sages of the past?
Anyone with both excellent scholarship and conduct, and outstanding literary skill,
regardless of whether they are already in office or not,
the officials in the capital of the third rank and above, as well as those in the various departments and the Censorate,
and the Governors-General, Governors, Provincial Administration Commissioners, and Provincial Judicial Commissioners in the provinces,
should each recommend those they know.
We will personally test and appoint them.
As for all officials, both in the capital and the provinces,
if they genuinely have insightful knowledge,
those in the capital should submit their recommendations to the Lìbù,
and those in the provinces should report to the Governors-General and Governors,
who will then recommend them on their behalf."
When the recommended personnel subsequently arrived in the capital,
an edict ordered the Hùbù to provide them with monthly stipends.
In March of the following year,
they were summoned for examination in the Tǐrén Gé.
A total of one hundred and forty-three individuals
were granted a banquet,
and tested on one fu and one poem.
The Emperor personally reviewed the examination papers,

and selected twenty individuals for the first class: Péng Sūnyù, Ní Càn, Zhāng Liè, Wāng Yǔ, Qiáo Lái, Wáng Xùlíng, Lǐ Yīndǔ, Qín Sōnglíng, Zhōu Qīngyuán, Chén Wéisōng, Xú Jiāyán, Lù Róu, Féng Xù, Qián Zhōngxié, Wāng Jí, Yuán Yòu, Zhū Yízūn, Tāng Bīn, Wāng Wǎn, and Qiū Xiàngsuí.

Thirty individuals were selected for the second class: Lǐ Láitài, Pān Lèi, Shěn Héng, Shī Rùnzhāng, Mǐ Hànwén, Huáng Yǔjiān, Lǐ Kǎi, Xú Zhāo, Shěn Jūn, Zhōu Qìngzēng, Yóu Tóng, Fàn Bìyīng, Cuī Rúyuè, Zhāng Hóngliè, Fāng Xiàngyīng, Lǐ Chéngzhōng, Wú Yuánlóng, Páng Kǎi, Máo Qílíng, Qián Jīnfǔ, Wú Rènchén, Chén Hóngjì, Cáo Yípǔ, Máo Shēngfāng, Cáo Hé, Lí Qiān, Gāo Yǒng, Lóng Xiè, Shào Wúyuǎn, and Yán Shéngsūn.
The third and fourth classes were all rejected.
The Grand Secretaries were ordered to consult the precedents of previous dynasties' special examinations
to deliberate on their appointments.
Subsequently, they deliberated:
"During the Two Hàn dynasties, appointments had no fixed positions.
In the Jìn dynasty, those in the highest class were appointed as Shàngshū Láng.
Under the Táng system, those with high marks in the policy examination were specially appointed to prestigious offices,
while those with secondary marks were granted official eligibility,
hence the terms 'Jídì' and 'Chūshēn'.
The Sòng dynasty divided them into five classes: the first and second classes were all promoted without delay;
the third class was considered superior,
and its favors were comparable to the first person in the imperial examination;
the fourth class was considered medium,
comparable to the third person in the imperial examination;
all of these were granted the 'Zhìkē chūshēn' status.
The fifth class was considered inferior,
and was granted the 'Jìnshì chūshēn' status."
An imperial decree was issued,
appointing all of them as Hàlín officials.
Shào Wúyuǎn, who was a Guānglù Shàogīng, was appointed as a Shìdú.
Tāng Bīn and three other Dao officials and Langzhōng were appointed as Shìjiǎng.
Eighteen individuals, including Péng Sūnyù, who were Zhǔshì with Jìnshì Chūshēn, Zhong, Xíng, Píng, Bó, Neigé Diǎnjí, Zhìxiàn, and those not yet in office, were appointed as Biānxiū.

Twenty-seven individuals, including Ní Càn, who were Tuī or Zhī with Jǔ or Gòng Chūshēn, Jiaozhí, Jianntǎo or Zhìxiàn who had been dismissed from office, and those not yet in office from the ranks of Jǔ, Gòng, Yìn, Jiān, and commoners, were appointed as Jiǎntǎo.
All entered the Imperial Historiography Academy
to compile the History of the Míng Dynasty.
At that time, Lǐ Yīndǔ from Fùpíng, Féng Xù from Chángzhōu, Zhū Yízūn from Xiùshuǐ, Pān Lèi from Wújiāng, and Yán Shéngsūn from Wúxī,
all entered the selection as commoners,
which brought them glory throughout the realm.
As for Dù Yuè, Fù Shān, Wáng Fānggǔ, and others who were elderly and did not participate in the examination,
and whose literary achievements were long-standing,
all were appointed as Neigé Zhōngshū,
and permitted to return to their hometowns.
In the eleventh year of Yōngzhèng,
an imperial edict stated:
"The 'Bóxué Hóngcí' examination
is for outstanding and profoundly learned scholars.
In the seventeenth year of Kāngxī,
a special edict called for recommendations,
and examinations were held to confer offices,
resulting in a great number of talented individuals.
For several decades since then,
there has not been extensive recruitment.
We are earnest in seeking out talent,
and there should be those who diligently study the classics and histories, possess extensive knowledge, and are worthy of being selected as 'Hóngbó'.
Therefore, a special grand ceremony should be revived,
and We commend extensive search.
All Mǎn and Hàn officials of the third rank and above in the capital,
and Governors-General, Governors, and Education Superintendents in the provinces,
should diligently investigate and ascertain,
and recommend them to the board.
We will personally conduct the examination in the imperial hall,
and grant them preferential appointments."
When the imperial edict was first issued,
the high officials, both in the capital and the provinces,
hesitated and looked at each other,
as the matter concerned a grand, rare event.
More than a year later,
only the Governor-General of Hédōng recommended one person,
and the Governor-General of Zhílì recommended two people;
other provinces had no applicants.
An edict reprimanded the officials for their wait-and-see attitude.
Upon the accession of Gāozōng,
another edict urged them.
The deadline was set for one year for all to gather at the imperial court,
and those who arrived first would receive monthly stipends.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
Imperial Censor Wú Yuán'ān said:
"The recommendation of 'Bóxué Hóngcí'
originally aimed to obtain scholars who were profound in classical studies and cultivated practical learning.
While poetry and fu were also valued,
classics and history were especially fundamental.
If one merely strings together ornate phrases
and meticulously polishes rhythm,
even if their literary adornment is admirable,
it will ultimately feel that the name does not match the reality."
This was submitted to the Lìbù for deliberation,
and it was decided to have two sessions,
adding essays and policy questions in addition to fu and poetry.
In September,
one hundred and seventy-six individuals were summoned for examination in the Bǎohé Diàn,
and granted a banquet as per custom.
The examination questions for the first session included one fu, one poem, and one essay each;
the second session included two policy questions.
Five individuals were selected for the first class: Liú Lún, Pān Ānlǐ, Zhū Jǐn, Yú Zhèn, and Háng Shìjùn,
and appointed as Biānxiū.
Ten individuals were selected for the second class:
Chén Zhàolún, Liú Zǎo, Xià Zhīróng, Zhōu Chángfā, and Chéng Xún,
appointed as Jiǎntǎo;
Yáng Dùwāng, Shěn Tíngfāng, Wāng Shìhuáng, Chén Shìfán, and Qí Zhàonán,
appointed as Shùjíshì.
In the second year,
a supplementary examination was held in the Tǐrén Gé.
The first session included two policy questions;
the second session included one fu, one poem, and one essay each.
Wàn Sōnglíng was selected for the first class,
and appointed as Jiǎntǎo.
Zhāng Hàn was selected for the second class,
and appointed as Jiǎntǎo;
Zhū Quán and Hóng Shìzé
were appointed as Shùjíshì.
From the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns,
the 'Cíkē' examination was held twice,
and among those selected,
the number of reclusive scholars
was greater than that of gentry,
a flourishing of literary patronage
rarely heard of in ancient times.
At that time, with successive generations of peace,
many scholars throughout the realm dedicated themselves to fundamental learning.
The Son of Heaven also promoted the overlooked and talented,
to serve as an encouragement and inspiration.
Hence, a system for recommending classical scholars was established.
In the fourteenth year of Qiánlóng,
an imperial edict stated:
"Venerating classical learning
is related to the moral state of the world and people's minds.
Now, with peace throughout the land,
there must be no lack of scholars and officials who diligently study their primary fields,
toiling year after year,
and revering Confucian predecessors.
The Grand Secretaries, Nine Ministers, Governors-General, and Governors
should publicly recommend those they know,
without restriction to Jìnshì, Jǔrén, or Zhūshēng, or retired and unemployed personnel,
who can wholeheartedly delve into classical studies.
They must be carefully selected without abuse."
Subsequently, over forty individuals were recommended by officials in the capital and provinces.
To prevent opportunistic advancements, the Emperor
ordered the court officials to review and verify them,
resulting in four individuals: Chén Zǔfàn, Wú Dǐng, Liáng Xīyú, and Gù Dònggāo.
They were ordered to submit their writings for imperial review,
and Hàlín and Zhōngshū officials were dispatched to Wǔyīng Diàn to transcribe one copy of each.
Subsequently, Wú Dǐng and Liáng Xīyú were appointed as Guózǐjiān Sīyè,
and summoned for an audience in Qínzhèng Diàn.
Chén Zǔfàn and Gù Dònggāo, due to their advanced age and inability to perform official duties,
were both granted the title of Sīyè.
Afterwards, this was not held again.
When the imperial chariot arrived for the emperor's visit,
he greatly encouraged the literati.
In the 42nd and 44th years of the Kāngxī reign,
Shèngzǔ made imperial tours to Jiāngnán and Zhèjiāng,
summoning scholars for examinations.
Those who were selected were bestowed with silver,
and were summoned to the capital for employment with varying distinctions.
Gāozōng made six imperial tours to Jiāngnán and Zhèjiāng,
three to Shāndōng,
and four to Tiānjīn.
All scholars who presented poems and rhapsodies
were summoned for examinations at the imperial residence.
Those of superior grade were granted official status
and appointed as Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé Zhōngshū);
those of secondary grade were bestowed with bundles of silk.
Rénzōng's eastern tour to Jīn and Diàn,
and western tour to Wǔtái,
also followed the previous precedents
for summoning for examinations.
After the Dàoguāng reign,
the imperial examinations increasingly emphasized "eight-legged essays" (shíwén).
After this custom had been practiced for a long time,
it became mediocre, superficial, and specious,
gradually losing its true essence.
In the 30th year [of the Dàoguāng reign],
Zhāng Xī-gēng, a prospective京堂 (Jīngtáng) official, requested the re-establishment of the Bóxué Hóngcí (Erudite Scholars and Great Writers) examination
to cultivate talent.
The Board of Rites (Lǐbù) deliberated that it was not an urgent matter,
and thus it was dropped.
By the middle of the Guāngxù reign,
foreign aggressions were severe,
and the empire was in turmoil,
leading to widespread calls for reform.
In the 24th year,
Yán Xiū, the Educational Commissioner (Xuézhèng) of Guìzhōu, requested the establishment of a special examination for statecraft (Jīngjì Tèkē).
This was submitted to the Zǒnglǐ Gèguó Shìwù Yámén (Office for General Management of Affairs with Foreign Nations) for joint deliberation with the Board of Rites.
In the eighth month,
Cíxǐ Huángtàihòu assumed regency and exercised governmental power.
Citing that the Jīngjì Tèkē might easily lead to abuses,
she abolished it.
In the Gēngzǐ year (1900),
the capital was embroiled in chaos,
and the imperial carriage fled.
The two empresses, distressed by the perilous situation,
urgently sought to recruit exceptional talent
to aid in governance.
In the 27th year,
the Empress Dowager issued an edict to revive the Jīngjì Tèkē.

She commanded officials of the various Boards and Courts (Bù, Yuàn Tángguān) in the capital, and Governors-General, Governors, and Educational Commissioners (Dū, Fǔ, Xuézhèng) in the provinces to recommend candidates.
Those with loyal and pure intentions, grand and far-reaching vision, extensive and profound learning, and a thorough understanding of domestic and foreign current affairs,
were to be carefully sought out.
Furthermore, the Ministers of State Affairs (Zhèngwù Dàchén) were ordered to draft examination regulations.
Cén Bǐngsōng, a Censor (Yùshǐ), memorialized requesting the vigorous elimination of entrenched practices of favoritism and corruption.
An edict was issued instructing all officials to act with utmost impartiality.
When various capital officials of the third rank and below began to recommend candidates in large numbers,
the Emperor perceived it as excessive and indiscriminate.
Coincidentally, Lóng'ēn, a Junior Supervisor of the Court of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Shàokīng), submitted a memorial of recommendation,
but the Emperor ultimately dismissed it
and also ordered the withdrawal of all candidates previously recommended by Lǐ Zhuóyīng, a Junior Supervisor of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Shàokīng).
In the 29th year,
the Zhèngwù Chù (Office of State Affairs) deliberated and decided on the examination system,
which, like the palace examination (tíngshì),
would have the Son of Heaven personally set the policy questions in the Bǎohé Diàn.
The examination lasted two days.
Those selected in the first round
were permitted to take the second examination,
both consisting of one essay (lùn) and one policy question (cè).
Senior ministers were appointed to review the papers.
Nine candidates were selected for the first class: Yuán Jiāgǔ, Zhāng Yīlín, Fāng Lǚzhōng, Táo Jiǒngzhào, Xú Yuán, Hú Yùjìn, Qín Xīzhèn, Yú Bìyún, and Yuán Lìzhǔn.

Eighteen candidates were selected for the second class: Féng Shànzhēng, Luó Liángjiàn, Qín Shùshēng, Wèi Jiāhuá, Wú Zhōngshàn, Qián Hóng, Xiāo Yìngchūn, Liáng Huànkuí, Cài Bǎoshàn, Zhāng Xiàoqiān, Duān Xù, Mài Hóngjūn, Xǔ Yuèzhōng, Zhāng Tōngmó, Yáng Dàolín, Zhāng Zǔlián, Wú Liè, and Chén Zēngshòu.
When the imperial decrees for appointments were issued,
for capital posts and provincial assignments,
they were merely given a slight promotion from their original ranks.
Those who were Jǔrén or Gòngshēng were appointed as county magistrates (zhīxiàn) or sub-prefectural assistants (zhōuzuǒ).
Compared to the generous treatment of literary examination candidates during the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng eras,
this was indeed inferior.
In the 34th year,
Bǐ Shòu, a Censor, requested the special establishment of the Zhìkē (Special Branch Examination).
The ministers of the Zhèngwù Chù deliberated, stating that
"The Xiàolián Fāngzhèng (Filial, Incorruptible, Upright) and Zhíyán Jíjiàn (Speaking Frankly and Offering Bold Admonition) examinations
both lack practical utility.
Only the Bóxué Hóngcí examination,
held twice during the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns,
successfully attracted many talented individuals.
At this time, when literature is gradually declining,
preserving national essence
is truly an urgent matter today.
It should be sent to the Xuébù (Ministry of Education) for deliberation."
At that time, an edict was issued to the provinces to recruit eminent scholars and venerable literati.
Wáng Kǎiyùn, a Jǔrén from Húnán, was recommended
and appointed as a Compiler of the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Jiǎntǎo).
Jiāngnán and Ānhuī successively recommended Wáng Gēngxīn, Sūn Bǎotián, Chéng Cháoyí, Wú Chuánqǐ, Yáo Yǒngpú, Yáo Yǒnggài, Féng Chéng, and others.
The Ministry deliberated that these individuals had profound research in classics and history,
making them suitable for selection through a literary examination.
Once the regulations were finalized,
a memorial would be submitted to request its implementation.
Soon after,
Dézōng died,
and thus it was dropped.
The Xiàolián Fāngzhèng examination
began in the 61st year of Kāngxī.
When Shìzōng ascended the throne,
he issued an edict for prefectures, departments, counties, and garrisons (fǔ, zhōu, xiàn, wèi) in all provinces to recommend Xiàolián Fāngzhèng candidates.
They were granted six-rank official attire,
to be held in reserve for appointment.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
an edict stated:
"The state, in its endeavor to uphold upright customs,
places paramount importance on the virtuous and capable.
A previous edict called for the recommendation of Xiàolián Fāngzhèng;
several months have passed since then,
but no memorials have been heard.
I fear that officials are negligent in their investigations,
and thus those with truly upright character have no means to be brought forth.
All Governors-General and Governors must promptly comply with the previous edict,
carefully investigate and memorialize recommendations."
Subsequently, Zhèjiāng, Zhílì, Fújiàn, and Guǎngxī each recommended two officials,
who were appointed as county magistrates (zhīxiàn);
those aged fifty-five and above
were appointed as department magistrates (zhīzhōu).
Thereafter, with each succession to the throne,
imperial edicts for such recommendations became customary.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
Lì Zōngwàn, a Vice Minister of the Board of Punishments (Xíngbù Shìláng), stated:
"The system of recommending Xiàolián Fāngzhèng,
if there is even slight fraudulent or indiscriminate behavior,
will result in injustice and suppression.
Previous officials responsible for selections
rarely acted with public impartiality.
They were either powerful and wealthy gentry from their local areas
or renowned scholarly bullies within official circles.
After entering office,
the mediocre might be dismissed for incompetence,
and the cunning might be disgraced for corruption.
I request careful selection
to uphold the integrity of official positions."
The Board of Civil Office (Lìbù) approved that for the recommendation of Xiàolián Fāngzhèng by prefectures, departments, counties, and garrisons,
it should be a public recommendation jointly made by local gentry and village elders (shēnshì lǐdǎng).
Department and county officials should investigate and gather public opinion,
thoroughly examining the facts.
If the recommended person was a scholar (shēngyuán),
the educational officials would jointly examine and verify them,
sending them to the high officials (dàlì) for further verification and memorialization.
They would be granted six-rank official attire as an honor.
If there truly were individuals excellent in both virtue and talent,
the Governors-General and Governors could make exceptional recommendations to the Board.
The Nine Chief Ministers (Jiǔqīng), officials of the Hanlin Academy (Hàn, Zhān), Censors (Kē), and Circuit Censors (Dào) would jointly examine them
and await an imperial decree for promotion and appointment.
Those who made indiscriminate recommendations would be punished.
In the fifth year,
examination regulations were established.
Except for those who were simple, cautious, lacked other skills, and were unable to take the examination,
who were granted official hats (dǐngdài) as per regulation and not sent to the Board,
those recommended and sent to the Board,
after examination,
would be tested inside the gate of the Tàihé Diàn with one policy question on current affairs, one memorial (jiān), and one petition (zòu).
During the Dàoguāng reign,
this was changed to the Bǎohé Diàn,
similar to the examination for Censors.
In the early years of Tóngzhì,
a clear edict was issued for selections,
and furthermore, based on the memorial by Lǐ Shùchāng, a County Magistrate,
it was decreed that officials of the fourth rank and above in the capital,
and Governors-General, Governors, and Educational Commissioners in the provinces,
should each recommend those they knew,
without limitation to gentry or commoners.
Practical conduct should be prioritized,
and flowery literary style should not be exclusively sought,
to avoid indiscriminately bestowing this grand ceremony.
For those who were elderly (dēng máotié),
or sincerely simple and unadorned,
who served as models for their communities,
and were unwilling to come to the capital,
county officials were to visit and inquire about them seasonally,
bestowing wine and rice.
In the sixth year of Guāngxù,
it was stipulated that from the date of the imperial edict,
a limit of eight years was given
for the recommended individuals to arrive at the Ministry.
Annually in February and August,
they would be jointly examined and assessed once.
Those who exceeded the deadline
would only be allowed the honor of official attire,
but not permitted to take the examination.
Initially, appointments to office were made for Zhīzhōu and Zhīxiàn.
Subsequently, as the number of recommended individuals grew,
the scope of their use was broadened.
They were specifically used for such officials as Zhīxiàn, Zhílìzhōu Zhōutóng, Zhōupàn, Zuózá, and also for teaching positions.
Vacancies for Zhīxiàn were filled by those selected as Bágòng;
teaching positions by those selected as Dàtiāo Èrděng Jǔrén;
the rest were assigned province by province according to the order of their trial appointments.
Throughout successive dynasties,
officials simply followed
established practices.
The abuses of favoritism and unwarranted promotions
were repeatedly reported to the emperor by the Táijiàn.
However, during the Jiāqìng reign, Yán Rúyù from Húnán, who ranked first in the policy examination,
was granted an audience and appointed Zhīxiàn.
During the Xiánfēng reign, Luó Zénán from Húnán, a scholar, led the Xiāngyǒng across the border to suppress bandits.
Both were renowned at the time for their meritorious achievements.
In the early Xuāntǒng era,
the number of individuals recommended by each province often reached one hundred or more,
and rarely fewer than several dozen.
An imperial edict ordered strict scrutiny and verification.
The practice of selection
had become excessive by this point.
Beyond the civil service examinations for selecting scholars in the Qīng dynasty,
talented individuals were also sought from recluses,
promoted based on integrity and competence,
recommended for their literary accomplishments,
selected from military service,
or appointed to staff positions.
The path of recommendation and promotion
was highly successful in acquiring talent,
and is worth mentioning.
Tàizǔ, rising in the eastern lands,
selected heroes to assist in his great endeavor.
Scholars who offered counsel were all promoted and employed,
either invited to the Wénguǎn
or retained for strategic planning.
In the eleventh month of the Yǐmǎo year,
he instructed his officials, saying:
"State affairs are numerous and complex;
we must acquire many talented individuals
and assign them positions according to their abilities.
Those brave and skilled in combat
should manage the military;
those with superior economic talents
should govern the state;
those broadly versed in precedents
should be consulted on gains and losses;
those proficient in ritual and ceremony
should assist with state rites.
We must widely seek them out everywhere,
to fill various official posts."
At that time, various states had been pacified,
and the Eight Banners system established,
so there was an urgent need for talent.
Upon Tàizōng's ascension,
he first appointed the Confucian minister Fàn Wénchéng to lead important matters of the Shūmì.
In the eighth year of Tiāncōng,
Jiǎlā Zhāngjīng Zhū Jìwén's son, Yánqìng, submitted a memorial,
stating:
"In our dynasty, there is no shortage of those who attack cities, defeat enemies, and cut down generals and seize banners,
but those who guard borders, govern the people, secure the interior, and repel external threats are not often seen."
He therefore recommended the Hàn Chinese Chén Jíxīn and Xíngbù Qǐxīnláng Shēn Cháojì,
who were fully capable of being entrusted with duties.
The emperor summoned Yánqìng and others before him,
and kindly praised them.
He ordered Yánqìng and Jíxīn
to be employed in the Wénguǎn;
Cháojì remained in his departmental post.
In the ninth year,
an edict instructed all Mǎn, Hàn, and Měnggǔ officials
to recommend talented individuals,
without restriction as to whether they were already in office or not,
and to submit their names to the Lì and Lǐ ministries,
with their names explicitly stated.
Zhí Wénguǎn Níng Wánwǒ said:
"In ancient times, the system of recommendation
involved joint responsibility for merits and faults,
thus preventing abuses and unwarranted promotions.
I request that from now on, for anyone recommended,
whether they achieve merit or commit a fault,
the recommender shall share in it.
If such a person maintains integrity at first,
but changes their principles later,
the recommender shall be permitted to report them at any time,
to avoid joint responsibility."
The emperor graciously accepted this.
Shìzǔ established his capital in the Central Plains.
In the early Shuànzhì reign,
officials were dispatched to seek out forgotten worthies,
and their carriages were continuous.
The Lìbù meticulously examined their backgrounds,
and rigorously verified their talents and character,
urging them to come to the capital.
They also instructed the Fǔ and Àn officials
to proactively recommend hidden talents and worthy individuals within their jurisdictions,
one by one,
for recruitment and promotion.
Shùntiān Xúnfǔ Sòng Quán presented three strategies for governance,
the first being to widely gather talented individuals to assist the emperor,
and recommended former Míng Jìliáo Zǒngdū Wáng Yǒngjí and others.
An edict commanded court officials to each recommend those they knew.
At that time, former officials from the late Míng period, such as Xiè Shēng, Féng Quán, Dǎng Chóngyǎ, etc.,
were successively promoted.
The number of officials, both inside and outside the court, who were appointed to office through recommendation
was countless.
Subsequently, because those recommended by court officials
were mostly former and dismissed officials from the late Míng period,
and not truly reclusive and distinguished individuals who shunned fame,
an edict was issued strictly holding recommenders accountable.
Those who successfully found talent would be generously rewarded for advancing worthies,
while those who erred would be severely punished with joint responsibility.
Recommendation memorials were to report only their backgrounds,
leaving their suitability in terms of talent and character
to the court's discretion.
If individuals like Zīláng or miscellaneous officials, or dismissed scholars and unemployed military officers,
were falsely presented as recluses,
the blame would be assigned.
However, if officials feared joint responsibility
and remained silent, failing to recommend,
they would be punished for the crime of concealing worthies.
In the second year,
after Shǎnxī and Jiāngnán were pacified,
an edict summoned recluses from mountains and forests,
as well as former Míng civil and military Jìnshì and Jǔrén.
Shāndōng Xúnfǔ Lǐ Zhīqí was sharply reproved by imperial edict
for recommending inappropriately, extending to Zīláng.
In the thirteenth year,
Jiāngnán Xúnfǔ Zhāng Zhōngyuán recommended former Míng Jìnshì Lù Yíjí and Yú Zhǐ,
whom the emperor personally tested.
That same year, an edict again instructed all provinces to recommend local talents.
Gěishìzhōng Liáng Hóng said:
"Your Majesty earnestly seeks talent day and night,
and has issued edicts to recommend recluses from mountains and forests,
so there is no shortage of individuals who should accept the invitation.
However, the investigations are not accurate,
which undermines this grand initiative.
For example, Lǚ Yáng from Jiāngnán was recommended
and appointed Jiānsī,
but not long after, he failed due to corruption.
Wáng Yùnxī from Shāndōng was recommended
and appointed Kēyuán,
but showed no significant achievements
and was removed during the triennial evaluation.
How could Lǚ Yáng and others truly possess talents for national salvation?
They were merely means to personal advancement.
What are 'mountains and forests'?
They refer to being far from the court and city.
What are 'recluses'?
They refer to being different from those who seek competition.
Only by finding the right person
can they be suited for their position.
I request that detailed investigations be ordered."
The memorial was submitted,
and reported.
Between the Shùnzhì and Kāngxī reigns,
great masters and venerable scholars throughout the realm
valued their integrity above all else.
Some were jointly recommended by court officials in memorials,
or earnestly urged by frontier officials with full courtesy,
yet they remained resolutely retired.
Such as Sūn Qífēng, Lǐ Yǒng, and Huáng Zōngxī,
the emperor knew they could not be compelled,
and could only sigh deeply.
He merely ordered governors-general and governors
to copy their writings and send them to the capital.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī,
after the ritual of enthroning Empress Xiàokāng was completed,
an edict was promulgated throughout the empire,
commanding officials to recommend individuals of superior talent and character, and recluses from mountains and forests.
Subsequently, although such acts of imperial grace in successive reigns
were carried out as a matter of routine,
few actually responded.
Initially,
when Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) were promoted, transferred, or left office,
they would recommend talent once.
Later, an order was issued for recommendations to be made annually.
The Bù (部) deliberated that large provinces were limited to ten people,
and small provinces to three or four people.
Later, it was changed again to recommendations once every two years.
From Shùnzhì (順治) eighteen years, the dispatch of Xún'àn (巡按) was suspended,
and it was then decided that each province's Xúnfǔ (巡撫) should recommend officials of Fāngmiàn (方面), Yǒusī (有司), Zuǒ'èr (佐貳), and Jiàoguān (教官) based on quotas.
Zǒngcáo (總漕) and Zǒnghé (總河) should recommend officials of Fāngmiàn (方面), Yǒusī (有司), and Zuǒ'èr (佐貳) based on quotas,
which also became a rule.
In Kāngxī (康熙) two years,
Yùshǐ (御史) Zhāng Jíwǔ (張吉午) memorialized:
"The method of 'three-year evaluation for full term' (sānnián kǎomǎn zhīfǎ),
where those rated first or second class as 'competent' (chēngzhí)
are already considered recommendations,
requests the abolition of the Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) two-year recommendation rule."
This was followed.
In six years,
the evaluation for full term was suspended.
Based on the words of Gěishìzhōng (給事中) Lǐ Zōngkǒng (李宗孔), recommendations were reinstated,
to be implemented alongside Zhuóyì (卓異).
Previously, the recommendation rule for Cáo (漕) and Hé (河) had been suspended.
In twelve years,
Cáodū (漕督) Shuài Yánbǎo (帥顏保) requested the restoration of the old rule,
allowing him to recommend or impeach subordinate officials annually to demonstrate encouragement and punishment.
The Bù (部) deliberated and approved it.
Consequently, he memorialized to recommend Liángdào (糧道) Fàn Zhōu (范周), Chí Rìxùn (遲日巽), and Zhīxiàn (知縣) Wú Xīngzuò (吳興祚).
An imperial edict promoted Xīngzuò (興祚) to Fújiàn Ànchásǐ (福建按察使).
When Shèngzǔ (聖祖) personally governed,
he was determined to rectify official administration,
repeatedly issuing edicts for his ministers to recommend honest and capable officials throughout the realm.
In eighteen years,
Zuǒdūyùshǐ (左都御史) Wèi Xiàngshū (魏象樞) memorialized to recommend ten honest and clean officials:
former Shìláng (侍郎) Gāo Héng (高珩), Dáhātǎ (達哈塔), Léi Hǔ (雷虎), Bāndí (班迪);
Dàlǐqīng (大理卿) Húmìsè (瑚密色);
Shìdú (侍讀) Xiāo Wéiyù (蕭維豫);
Lángzhōng (郎中) Sòng Wènyùn (宋文運);
Bùzhèngshǐ (布政使) Bì Zhènjī (畢振姬);
Zhīxiàn (知縣) Zhāng Mù (張沐), Lù Lóngqí (陸隴其), and others.
An imperial decree ordered their respective employment.
It also instructed that Lù Lóngqí (陸隴qí), as an honest and capable official,
should be appointed to demanding posts,
such as Qīngyuàn (清苑) county in Zhílì (直隸) or Wúxī (無錫) county in Jiāngsū (江蘇),
so that his talent could be demonstrated.
In nineteen years,
Fújiàn Xúnfǔ (福建巡撫) Wú Xīngzuò (吳興祚) recommended Ànchásǐ (按察使) Yú Chénglóng (于成龍) as the foremost honest and capable official in the realm,
who was promoted to Bùzhèngshǐ (布政使),
and soon after, to Zhílì Xúnfǔ (直隸巡撫).
In twenty years, upon his audience,
the Emperor graciously praised him.
He asked if there were also honest and clean officials among his subordinates.
Chénglóng (成龍) replied with Zhīxiàn (知縣) Xiè Xīwèi (謝錫袞), Tóngzhī (同知) Hé Rúyù (何如玉), and Luó Jīng (羅京).
Not long after,
Chénglóng (成龍) was transferred to be Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū (兩江總督).
Before departing,

he memorialized to recommend Zhílì Shǒudào (直隸守道) Dǒng Bǐngzhōng (董秉忠), Tōngzhōu Zhīzhōu (通州知州) Yú Chénglóng (于成龍), Nánlù Tōngpàn (南路通判) Chén Dàdòng (陳大棟), Bǎixiāng Zhīxiàn (柏鄉知縣) Shào Sìyáo (邵嗣堯), Fùchéng Zhīxiàn (阜城知縣) Wáng Xiè (王燮), Gāoyáng Zhīxiàn (高陽知縣) Sūn Hóngyè (孫宏業), and Bàzhōu Zhōupàn (霸州州判) Wèi Jìxián (衞濟賢),
all of whom were suitable for important appointments.
At the time, there was a vacancy for the Jiāngníng Zhīfǔ (江寧知府),
and an imperial edict immediately promoted Tōngzhōu Zhīzhōu (通州知州) Yú Chénglóng (于成龍) to fill it.
Within a few years,
he was promoted to Zhílì Xúnfǔ (直隸巡撫).
At the same time, there were two Yú Chénglóngs (于成龍),
who were successively promoted,
and both were especially favored by the Emperor for their integrity,
praised by contemporary opinion.
In twenty-three years,
an imperial edict instructed the Bù (部) ministers to recommend candidates for vacant customs posts.
They all responded,
"There is no shortage of talented and cautious people,
but integrity is truly hard to know."
The Emperor said:
"How can integrity be discarded?
For example, Hǎo Yù (郝浴) was an excellent official,
yet still embezzled funds and provisions.
Wèi Xiàngshū (魏象樞) once recommended Hǎo Yù (郝浴);
how could this have been known in advance?
I trust the integrity of the Bùyuàn Tángguān (部院堂官) and appoint them;
Tángguān (堂官) also trust and appoint Sīguān (司官).
Just recommend people of integrity,
and those recommended will naturally serve effectively."
That year, the Jiǔqīng (九卿), Zhànshì (詹事), Kē (科), and Dào (道) followed the imperial decree to memorialize and recommend honest and clean officials: Zhílì Xúnfǔ (直隸巡撫) Gé'ěrgǔdé (格爾古德);
Lìbù Lángzhōng (吏部郎中) Sūhè (蘇赫), Fàn Chéngxūn (范承勳);
Jiāngnán Xuédào (江南學道) Zhào Lún (趙崙);
Yángzhōu Zhīfǔ (揚州知府) Cuī Huá (崔華);
Yǎnzhōu Zhīfǔ (兗州知府) Zhāng Pénghé (張鵬翮);
Língshòu Zhīxiàn (靈壽知縣) Lù Lóngqí (陸隴其), and others.
In twenty-six years,
the Emperor commended Zhílì Xúnfǔ (直隸巡撫) Yú Chénglóng (于成龍) for his honesty and integrity,
ordering each of the Jiǔqīng (九卿) to recommend honest officials like Chénglóng (成龍).
The Dàxuéshì (大學士) and others recommended Yún-Guì Zǒngdū (雲貴總督) Fàn Chéngxūn (范承勳), Shānxī Xúnfǔ (山西巡撫) Mǎ Qí (馬齊), and Sìchuān Xúnfǔ (四川巡撫) Yáo Dìyú (姚締虞).
The Emperor said that Chéngxūn (承勳) and the others were all excellent officials,
but still had some reluctance.
Chénglóng (成龍), however, acted out of sincerity,
without any hesitation or reservation.
He ordered Chénglóng (成龍) to be given the title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (太子少保),
to encourage honesty and capability.
In forty years,
an imperial decree ordered Zǒngdū (總督) Guō Xiù (郭琇), Zhāng Pénghé (張鵬翮), Sāng'é (桑額), Huá Xiǎn (華顯),
and Xúnfǔ (巡撫) Péng Péng (彭鵬), Lǐ Guāngdì (李光地), Xú Cháo (徐潮) to recommend officials from Dào (道) and Fǔ (府) downwards,
and from Zhīxiàn (知縣) upwards,
who were honest and loved the people.
They were not to consider past errors, demotions, or punishments,
nor be confined to their own province or neighboring jurisdictions,
but to submit their names.
At that time, the Emperor extensively promoted moral integrity,
and all scholars emulated him,
leading to a significant transformation in official administration.
Upright officials who were recommended and received prominent promotions
succeeded one another.
Previously, when court ministers jointly nominated for the vacant Guǎngxī Ànchásǐ (廣西按察使) position,
Lìbù Shìláng (吏部侍郎) Hú Jiǎnjìng (胡簡敬),
a native of Huái'ān (淮安),
was condemned for recommending Huái-Yáng Dào (淮揚道) Gāo Chéngměi (高成美) in violation of regulations.
It was then strictly forbidden for Jiǔqīng (九卿) to recommend fellow townsmen or officials from their own province.
Furthermore, each person was limited to recommending no more than ten people per year.
In fifty-three years,
Shàngshū (尚書) Zhào Shēnjiáo (趙申喬) recommended Cháozhōu Zhīfǔ (潮州知府) Zhāng Yìngzhào (張應詔) as being capable of enduring poverty,
and suitable for Yìngzhào (張應詔) as Liǎnghuái Yùnsǐ (兩淮運使).
The Emperor said:
"Being an honest official is not about being rich or poor.
Zhāng Bóxíng's (張伯行) family was quite wealthy,
and his daily expenses in office were all taken from his household;
can he be considered not honest?
One who wholeheartedly serves the country is a good official.
If one's integrity is clean,
but one cannot manage affairs,
what benefit is that to the country?"
In sixty-one years,
Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne.
He issued an edict saying:
"Knowing people is wisdom,
which has always been difficult.
At the beginning of my reign,
when selecting and employing talent,
whether they have upright character,
or clean integrity,
or acute abilities,
all ministers shall secretly memorialize what they know.
Do not avoid suspicion or act on favoritism,
or seek fame or curry favor,
and thus fail my inquiry."
He also decreed that Dào (道), Fǔ (府), Zhōu (州), and Xiàn (縣),
being crucial positions for directly serving the people,
Zǒngdū (總督) should recommend three officials,
Xúnfǔ (巡撫) two officials,
Bù (布) and Àn (按) one official each,
and Jiāngjūn (將軍) and Tídū (提督) could also recommend one official,
to be sealed and submitted in a memorial.
In Yōngzhèng (雍正) four years,
as the recommendations from various provinces failed to meet his satisfaction,
an imperial edict sternly criticized them.
He ordered each to clearly recommend one person,
without identical recommendations.
At that time,
imperial edicts recommending worthy individuals were repeatedly issued,
and the Emperor reviewed the names and their actual merits,
ensuring rewards and punishments were carried out.
In seven years,
considering Dū (督), Fǔ (撫), Bù (布), and Àn (按) as role models for the entire province,
he ordered Jingguān (京官) of Xuéshì (學士) and Shìláng (侍郎) rank and above,
and Wàiguān (外官) of Fān (藩) and Niè (臬) rank and above,
each to secretly recommend one person,
without distinction of Mǎn (滿) or Hàn (漢),
or limitation of qualifications.
Even if there were officials at the Fǔ (府) or Xiàn (縣) level whom they believed could be entrusted with the important posts of Fēngjiāng Dàliáo (封疆大僚),
they were permitted to include them in their recommendations.
Gāozōng attached great importance to officials who were close to the people.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
an edict was issued to imitate the precedent of the Yōngzhèng era,
where Dū, Fǔ, Bù, and Àn officials
each secretly recommended one or two individuals.
The following year,
the Grand Secretaries and Nine Ministers were again ordered to recommend suitable Dào and Fǔ personnel,
submitting their recommendations openly in memorials.
In the eighth year,
an imperial edict instructed the Grand Secretaries to recommend compilers and revisers capable of serving as Zhīfǔ.
In the fourteenth year,
officials from Shìláng upwards were ordered to recommend those capable of serving as third-rank Jīngtáng officials,
and officials from Shàngshū upwards were ordered to recommend those capable of serving as Shìláng.
During this time, both open recommendations (míngyáng) and secret recommendations (mìbǎo)
were practiced without being abolished.
As for selection by examination for the Kē and Dào circuits,
the old system was restored in the seventh year of Kāngxī.
An edict commanded Dū and Fǔ officials to recommend officials who were close to the people,
those who were virtuous, capable, and already renowned,
for direct selection and appointment.
In the twenty-ninth year,
an edict ordered each of the Nine Ministers to recommend those they knew.
Shàngshū Wáng Zhì recommended Shào Sìyáo, the Zhīxiàn of Qīngyuàn;
Lǐ Tiānfù recommended Péng Péng, the Zhīxiàn of Sānhé, and Lù Lóngqí, the Zhīxiàn of Língshòu;
Xú Yuánwén recommended Zhào Cāngbì, the Zhīxiàn of Máchéng.
When the court discussion (Tíngtuī) took place,
the Emperor again asked Zuǒ Dūyùshǐ Chén Tíngjìng,
"Who among them is incorruptible?"
Chén Tíngjìng also spoke of Lóngqí and Sìyáo as the most upright officials under heaven.
At that time, twelve individuals were jointly recommended,
all of whom were employed in Kē and Dào positions.
This was a time when talent was acquired most effectively.
In the fourth year of Qiánlóng,
the Lìbù memorialized requesting the practice of selection by examination.
Gāozōng ordered the Shàngshū, Dūyùshǐ, and Shìláng to impartially recommend individuals from their respective ministries' subordinates,
and from within the Zhōu and Xiàn,
following the precedent of the twenty-ninth year of Kāngxī.
The following year,
an edict stated:
"In the time of Shèngzǔ, individuals like Tāng Bīn and Lù Lóngqí possessed pure scholarship,
with their words matching their deeds; Chén Bīn and Péng Péng were incorruptible in their conduct,
and outstanding in their governance.
In a vast realm,
with such a multitude of talents,
how could there not be those who can rival these few individuals?
The Grand Secretaries and Nine Ministers should publicly recommend them for selection."
In the seventh year,
the Emperor, thinking of forthright and unpretentious scholars,
such as the ancient Mǎ Zhōu and Yáng Chéng who rose from commoners to become Censor,
issued an edict to the Grand Secretaries, Nine Ministers, and Dū and Fǔ officials,
to recommend individuals without regard to their qualifications,
submitting their names in a memorial.
Subsequently, the memorials submitted by the various officials
were sent to the Lìbù to set a date for examinations.
In the second month of the following year,
Censors were selected through examination,
with a policy essay on current affairs as the test.
The Emperor personally selected Hú Bǎochuán, a Zhōngshū, as first.
During the imperial audience,
Bǎochuán, Tú Féngzhèn, and ten others were appointed as Censors,
while Shěn Lán was assigned to Jīangnán for later use.
Afterwards, following the memorial of Censor Lǐ Qīngfāng,
it was decided that for the selection of Censors,
the Lìbù should memorialize requesting examinations for eligible personnel.
Thus, the practice of recommending Censors was abolished.
The Qīng dynasty did not establish a special section for outspoken remonstrance,
yet the selection of censorial officials was extremely cautious,
greatly benefiting governance;
this was by no means insignificant.
From the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns,
practical learning was highly esteemed.
At that time, it is particularly difficult to enumerate
the numerous renowned scholars and eminent figures
who were recommended and promoted.
In the seventeenth year of Kāngxī,
Shèngzǔ asked the Grand Secretaries,
"Among those in court, who is the most learned and skilled in poetry and prose?"
Lǐ Wèi, Féng Pǔ, Chén Tíngjìng, and Zhāng Yīng all recommended Wáng Shìzhēn, a Lángzhōng of the Hùbù.
He was summoned for an imperial audience in the Màosì Hall,
composed a poem that pleased the Emperor,
and was appointed Shìjiǎng of the Hànlín Yuàn.
The change from a departmental official to a literary official
began with Shìzhēn.
In the thirty-third year,
an edict ordered the Grand Secretaries to recommend those skilled in literature.
Wáng Xī and Zhāng Yùshū memorialized recommending the retired Shàngshū Xú Qiánxué, Zuǒ Dūyùshǐ Wáng Hóngxù, and Shào Zhānshì Gāo Shìqí.
They were summoned to the capital to revise books.
Qiánxué died before hearing the command;
an edict ordered his posthumous works to be presented,
and also summoned his brother Bǐngyì to the capital.
In the forty-fifth year,
Grand Secretary Lǐ Guāngdì recommended Wáng Lánshēng, a Shēngyuán from Zhílì, to serve in the imperial palace.
Soon after, he was granted the titles of Jǔrén and Jìnshì,
appointed Biānxiū,
and gradually rose to become a Qīng and Èr (high-ranking official).
Throughout the Kāngxī, Yōngzhèng, and Qiánlóng reigns,
he was involved in the collation
of all the secretarial works of Tiānlù.
At the same time, Hé Zhuó from Jiāngnán
also, as a humble scholar, was granted the titles of Jǔrén and Jìnshì,
served directly in the Nán Shūfáng,
and was appointed Biānxiū.
Impeached and dismissed from office,
he continued to serve directly in the editorial bureau.
He was also recommended by Guāngdì.
In the middle of Yōngzhèng's reign,
Shìláng and Jijìu Sūn Jiāgàn recommended the Jǔrén Léi Hóng for his scholarship and conduct,
appointing him Xuézhèng of the Guózǐjiān.
In the early Qiánlóng reign,
Shàngshū and Guǎnjiānsì Yáng Míngshí recommended the Jìnshì Zhuāng Hēngyáng, Jǔrén Pān Yǒngjì, Cài Déjùn, Qín Huìtián, Wú Nài,
Gòngshēng Guān Xiànyáo, Wáng Wénzhèn,
and Jiānshēng Xià Zōnglán, among others,
who were devoted to classical studies,
and all served as subordinate officials in the Guózǐjiān.
In the thirty-eighth year,
an edict was issued to establish the Sīkù Quánshū bureau.
Scholars were invited to serve.
As the Hànlín officials were insufficient for compilation,
Grand Secretary Liú Tǒngxūn recommended Jìnshì Shào Jìnhán and Zhōu Yǒngnián;
Shàngshū Qiú Yuēxiū recommended Jìnshì Yú Jí and Jǔrén Dài Zhèn;
Shàngshū Wáng Jìhuá recommended Jǔrén Yáng Chānglín,
to jointly manage the secret texts.
Later, they were all transferred to the Hànlín Academy,
and were then known as
the "Five Zhēngjūn (Recalled Gentlemen)."
These are the most notable examples.
In the early Jiāqìng reign,
when Héshēn was defeated,
Rénzōng issued an edict seeking talented individuals.
He commanded Manchu and Han ministers
to secretly recommend those with upright conduct, capable management, and verifiable records in office.
An imperial decree was issued to highly commend the incorruptible official Liú Qīng,
thereby setting a strong example for the entire realm.
In the nineteenth year,
Censor Zhuó Bǐngtián requested a strict prohibition on excessive and unwarranted recommendations,
and the Emperor approved.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
Shàngshū Liú Huánzhī recommended the renowned scholar Táng Jiàn,
who was appointed Zhīfǔ of Guǎngxī.
Jiǎng Yōuxiān, Governor-General of Sìchuān, recommended Táo Shù, the Dào of Chuāndōng, for his outstanding governance,
and he was promoted to Ànchásǐ.
Shù enjoyed evaluating people;
when he opened his administration in Wǎnzhōng (Ānhuī),
he came to the capital for an audience and presented memorials,
speaking frankly and making many recommendations and impeachments.
Xuānzōng was suspicious of him.
He secretly ordered Governor Sūn Ěrzhǔn to investigate his character.
Ěrzhǔn listed his good policies
and secretly memorialized recommending him.
Consequently, Táo Shù was greatly employed,
and promoted to Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng.
Before his death, he left a memorial recommending Lín Zéxú, the Governor of Yuè (Guǎngdōng), to succeed him.
Shù was known for his ability to discern people,
and many of the renowned ministers who brought about the revival in the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì eras
were recognized and promoted by him.
Upon Wénzōng's succession,
an edict was issued seeking candid advice.
Shìláng Zēng Guófān memorialized, stating:
"The fundamental and ultimate plan
lies in the selection of personnel.
There are ways to cultivate talent,
methods of nurturing,
and means of evaluation."
The Emperor praised and accepted this.
An edict ordered ministers both within and outside the capital to recommend talented individuals.
Grand Secretary Mùzhāng'ā memorialized recommending the imperial clan members Wéncǎi
and Niè Yún.
A special imperial decree appointed them as Jīngtáng officials.
Grand Secretary Pān Shì'ēn memorialized recommending the former Governor-General Lín Zéxú, Ànchásǐ Yáo Yíng, Yuánwàiláng Shào Yìchén, and Zhōngyǔn Féng Guìfēn.
Shàngshū Dù Shòutián first recommended Zéxú and the former Grain Transport Governor Zhōu Tiānjué.
An edict ordered Zéxú to lead troops,
and Tiānjué to be Governor of Guǎngxī.
Shìláng Zēng Guófān recommended Tài Cháng Shàocīng Lǐ Tángjiē, Lángzhōng Wú Tíngdòng, Tōngzhèng Fùshǐ Wáng Qìngyún, Jiāngsū Huáiyáng Dào Yán Zhèngjī, and Zhīxiàn of Zhèjiāng Jiāng Zhōngyuán.
Shàngshū Zhōu Zǔpéi also recommended Tángjiē, Tíngdòng, and Lángzhōng Yì Táng, among others,
many of whom received promotions.
Wú Wénróng, Governor-General of Yún-Guì, and Qiáo Yòngqiān, Governor of Guìzhōu, recommended Zhīfǔ Hú Línyì,
who was promoted to Dàoyuán.
In the fifth year of Xiánfēng,
due to military campaigns in various provinces,
an imperial edict was issued to seek out individuals combining both civil and military talent, and possessing outstanding courage and discernment.
Censor Zōng Jìchén memorialized to recommend Zuǒ Zōngtáng from Húnán,
Yáo Chéngyú from Zhèjiāng,
Zhōu Ténghǔ and Guǎn Yàn from Jiāngsū,
and Táng Qǐhuá from Guǎngxī.
An order was issued for various governors-general and governors to investigate them
and send them to the capital for an audience.
At this time, the country faced many challenges,
with the Cantonese rebels rampant.
Wénqìng, as a Grand Secretary, served directly in the Grand Council.
He repeatedly made secret pleas to break down the barriers between Manchus and Han Chinese,
and to employ people without regard to their background or origin.
He stated that Han Chinese came from the fields,
understood the people's suffering,
and were well-versed in human nature and deceit.
Therefore, Han Chinese should be heavily relied upon in dealing with rebels.
Guófān had raised local militia to fight the rebels,
but suffered defeats,
leading to a proliferation of criticism and slander.
Wénqìng alone maintained that Guófān was loyal, sincere, and enjoyed the current trust,
and would ultimately achieve extraordinary accomplishments,
and should be given full authority to suppress the rebels.
He also once admired Lín Yì's talent and strategy.
Lín Yì, as a Guìzhōu circuit director, remained in Chǔ leading troops to suppress rebels.
Guófān recommended that his talent was fit for great use,
ten times superior to his own.
Within a year, he was promoted to Húběi Provincial Governor,
with Wénqìng truly being the main proponent behind it.
Yuán Jiǎsān commanded the army along the Huái River,
and Luò Bǐngzhāng was Provincial Governor of Húnán.
Wénqìng recommended their talent,
requesting that they not be transferred elsewhere,
so that their achievements could be observed.
Contemporary opinion praised this.
In the seventh year,
Lín Yì memorialized about Wàn Húquán, a hermit from Xìngguó, and his disciples Sòng Dǐng and Zōu Jīnsù,
who maintained integrity and honesty,
and did not seek official advancement.
He requested that they be commended.
An imperial edict awarded Húquán and others seventh-rank official attire with distinctions.
At that time, military affairs were pressing,
and repeated orders were issued to frontier officials and commanding generals of various routes to recommend military talents.
Lín Yì recommended Zuǒ Zōngtáng,
who was granted a fourth-rank京堂 (Jīngtáng) position,
to assist Guófān with military affairs.
Shěn Bǎozhēn, Liú Róng, and Zhāng Yùnlán
were ordered to be deployed by Guófān and Lín Yì.
Others such as Tǎ Qíbù, Luó Zénán, Lǐ Xùbīn, Lǐ Xùyí, Péng Yùlín, Yáng Yuèbīn, etc.,
all started as low-ranking officers or scholars,
were promoted from military service,
and achieved brilliant reputations.
Zēng and Hú knew people well and were skilled at employing them,
recommending worthy individuals throughout the country,
ultimately achieving the success of the restoration.
When Mùzōng ascended the throne,
seeing the decline of governance after the military campaigns,
he specifically promoted Shí Zànqīng, Prefect of Tiānjīn, to Prefect of Shùntiān Prefecture,
and issued an edict to all provinces to seek out honest and upright officials.
He also called for officials to investigate those dwelling in mountains and forests, possessing pure virtue, profound learning,
and for governors-general, governors, and education commissioners to truthfully report them.
Soon, Guófān memorialized that the gentry and common people of Chángzhōu upheld integrity and righteousness,
and resisted the rebels after the city fell.
Many of its scholars were well-read and studied antiquity.
Such as the expectant Assistant Prefect Liú Hànqīng,
Imperial College Students Zhào Lièwén, Fāng Jùnmó, Huá Héngfāng,
and Ninth-Rank Official Xú Shòu, etc.,
if allowed to gain military experience,
broaden their horizons,
they could be beneficial to military strategy.
An imperial edict ordered Tán Tíngxiāng, Yán Shùsēn, Zuǒ Zōngtáng, and Xuē Huàn to seek them out,
and send them to Guófān's military camp for employment.
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
an edict was issued to court officials, saying:
"Last year, several imperial decrees were issued to recommend talented individuals,
and various governors-general and governors have already listed those with outstanding political achievements in their recommendations.
In the capital, such as Grand Secretary Zhōu Zǔpéi,
Grand Secretary designate Qí Jùnzǎo and Wēng Xīncún,
Assistant Grand Secretary Wō Rén,
Vice Ministers Sòng Jìn and Wáng Màoyìn,
and Censors Gāo Yánhù, Xuē Chūnlí, Guō Xiángruì, etc.,
each have made recommendations.
As ministers, you serve the monarch with human affairs;
you need not wait for a clear imperial decree
before you can present your views.
Each of you should enumerate facts
and make recommendations fairly."
Repeated edicts further urged Guófān to recommend high-ranking governors-general and governors.
Guófān stated:
"Frontier generals and commanders
are appointed solely by the Son of Heaven.
With many troubles in the four directions,
since frontier ministers already possess the authority to campaign,
they should not further be given the power of dismissal and promotion,
to prevent the gradual trend of the periphery becoming stronger than the center,
and also to prevent the beginnings of forming factions for personal gain."
The Emperor issued a gracious edict in praise and response.
In the second year,
Jǐng Qíjùn, the Hénán Education Commissioner, memorialized about the scholarship and conduct of Assistant Tribute Student Sū Yuánshēng and others,
who were appointed as provincial instructors.
An order was issued for all education officials to seek out scholars with profound knowledge and excellent conduct,
and to recommend a few,
without making it a permanent system.
In the ninth year,
Xú Shùmíng, the Zhèjiāng Education Commissioner,
in seeking out refined scholars,
memorialized to recommend Yú Yuè, a formerly dismissed Hanlin Compiler,
requesting that his original title be restored
and that he be sent to the Board for an audience;
and Tán Tíngxiàn, an instructor from Xiùshuǐ, the *jǔrén* Zhào Míng, the *bágòng* Yáng Xīmǐn from Jiāngxī, etc.,
be granted a court examination,
following the precedent of summoning scholars for the *Bóxué Hóngcí* examination.
The Emperor, deeming Shùmíng to be acting on private motives,
sent the matter to the Board for severe deliberation,
and he was demoted four grades.
This instance of being condemned for making recommendations
was a change from the norm.
In the seventh year of Guāngxù,
Zhāng Shùshēng, Governor-General of Liǎngguǎng, and Yù Kuān, Governor,
recommended the gentry scholar residing at home, Zhū Cìqí, a *jìnshì* from Nánhǎi and former magistrate of Xiānglíng, Shānxī;
and Chén Lǐ, a *jǔrén* from Pānyú with the title of Guózǐjiàn Diǎnjí, for their upright conduct.
An imperial edict granted them fifth-rank minister titles
to encourage scholarly achievement.
In the tenth year,
due to repeated foreign provocations,
the times became increasingly difficult.
An edict was issued to Grand Secretaries, the Six Boards, the Nine Ministers, generals of directly-governed provinces, governors-general, and governors:
"Regardless of civil or military paths,
those who possess both fundamental principles and practical application,
are excellent in both strategy and courage,
or are skilled in governance and military affairs,
familiar with domestic and foreign relations,
or are good at manufacturing ships and weapons,
proficient in mathematics,
or are resourceful and ingenious,
brave and skilled in combat,
or are knowledgeable about naval matters and coastal conditions,
should be widely sought out
and truthfully reported."
In the twenty-first year,
a search was made for extraordinary talents and unusual abilities,
specializing in astronomy, geography, mathematics, natural science, and manufacturing.
In the twenty-fourth year,

Xú Zhìjìng, a Hanlin Academy Reader-Scholar, memorialized to recommend Kāng Yǒuwéi, a Secretary in the Board of Works; Zhāng Yuánjì, a Secretary in the Board of Punishments; Huáng Zūnxiàn, Salt Controller for Chángbǎo Circuit in Húnán; Tán Sìtóng, Prefect of Jiāngsū; and Liáng Qǐchāo, a *jǔrén* from Guǎngdōng.
They were specially granted an imperial audience.
Zūnxiàn and Sìtóng were summoned to the capital;
Qǐchāo was granted a sixth-rank title
and appointed to the Translation Bureau.
At this time, Dèzōng was in personal charge of government,
spurred by external pressures,
and urgently sought to strengthen the nation.
Edicts were issued seeking talented individuals who understood current affairs,
and both central and local officials enthusiastically made recommendations.
However, new ministers from the grassroots
were eager to pursue novelty
and loudly advocated for reforms.
Not long after, party strife erupted,
and Empress Dowager Cíxǐ resumed regency.
Yǒuwéi fled overseas;
his brother Guǎngrén, together with Censor Yáng Shēnxiù, Grand Council Secretaries Tán Sìtóng, Lín Xù, Yáng Ruì, and Liú Guāngdì, were executed in the marketplace.
Zhìjìng was imprisoned for being a partisan follower;
furthermore, the crimes of the original recommending ministers were re-investigated.
Censor Sòng Bólǔ and Húnán Governor Chén Bǎozhēn,
along with Wēng Tónghé, who had been removed from his post as President of the Board of Revenue and Assistant Grand Secretary,
all had their official ranks stripped and were never to be employed again.
Lǐ Duānfēn, President of the Board of Rites, was exiled to the frontier;
Zhāng Bǎixī, Grand Secretary of the Grand Secretariat, was sent to the Board for deliberation on punishment.
Other proponents of new policies were almost entirely dismissed and banished.
When the Gēngzǐ incident plunged the capital into chaos,
the peace treaty was concluded the following year.
The two empresses returned to the capital from their western journey,
and the political situation became more critical daily.
In the thirty-third year of the Guāngxù reign,
an imperial edict was issued to ministers inside and outside the court to seek out talent,
regardless of official rank,
or whether they held any office.
Those truly capable of great service
and those with specialized skills
were to be earnestly recommended.
Princes and ministers were dispatched to investigate and inquire,
to provide evaluations,
and to grant audiences.
At that time, recommended personnel
traveled to the capital in groups.
Those who were appointed to office
were still being selected even into the Xuāntǒng reign.
However, from the late Guāngxù period,
the official system was revised,
new government offices were added,
and new positions created.
Personnel appointed exceptionally often numbered in the thousands,
and recommendations and promotions became too indiscriminate.
In the first year of the Xuāntǒng reign,
Censor Xiè Yuǎnhán stated:
“Since the reforms began,
high officials only recommend old acquaintances,
and scholars do not shy away from intrigue.
I request a strict set of regulations be established,
so that those known for greed and incompetence,
their recommender shall be held responsible,
and punished.”
The memorial was sent to the relevant departments, and that was all.
Recommendations were not restricted by social standing.
Among talented officials of the Qīng dynasty,
those who rose from the ranks of subordinate officials to become provincial governors
include Lǐ Wèi and Tián Wénjìng during the Yōngzhèng reign,
and Yáng Jǐngsù and Lǐ Shìjié during the Qiánlóng reign,
whose administrative achievements were most notable.
Later, the practice of purchasing official titles became widespread,
and countless individuals from miscellaneous backgrounds
received prominent promotions.
Most of these individuals were quite capable and effective,
especially compared to those who advanced based on examination degrees and seniority,
attaining high positions purely by virtue of their qualifications.
The two groups were indeed incomparable.
Even more unusual examples of recommendation include:
In the early Kāngxī reign,
Shǎnxī Provincial Military Commander Wáng Jìnbǎo
recommended his son, saying he was brave and capable enough to serve as a Brigadier General.
Later, he was promoted to Commander-in-Chief for his achievements,
and father and son jointly received high military honors.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
Yúnnán Commander-in-Chief Zhào Kūn was promoted to Guìzhōu Provincial Military Commander.
He requested his son, Bǐngduó, be appointed as Guìzhōu Provincial Brigade Colonel.
The Emperor granted the request.
Sūn Jiāgàn, serving as Chancellor of the Imperial Academy,
recommended his younger brother, Yánggàn, as Academician of the Imperial Academy.
Wāng Shěn, the Circuit Intendant of Héngyǒngchēnguì in Húnán,
even recommended his father, Yún, a former official in the Board of Punishments, for his profound scholarship
and experienced handling of state affairs.
He was appointed as Zhīfǔ of Sìchuān.
These instances show that recommendations were not avoided for relatives,
thus breaking established precedents.
Regarding the recruitment of private secretaries (mùliáo):
In the first year of Yōngzhèng, an edict was issued to the Board of Civil Office,
stating that henceforth, the names of private secretaries employed by Governors-General and Governors
should be reported to the throne.
Those found competent would be deliberated by the Board
and appointed to official positions,
as an encouragement.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
Vice Minister Wú Yìngfēn, to encourage talented individuals,
requested the establishment of a system of rewards and punishments.
By the Dàoguāng reign,
private secretaries indiscriminately sought selection and appointment,
and the censors repeatedly raised concerns.
An edict was issued to Governors-General, Governors, and Salt Commissioners
that in all deliberations,
private secretaries were not allowed to be included in recommendations,
and it strictly prohibited subordinate officials of the province from being indiscriminately appointed.
Violators would be investigated by the Board of Civil Office and dealt with.
However, in the Kāngxī era,
the commoner Chén Huáng assisted Jìn Fǔ in river conservancy and
was specially granted the title of Qianshi Dàoxian.
In the Yōngzhèng era,
Fāng Guānchéng served as a secretary to Prince Píng, the Generalissimo of the Pacification of the Border.
As a commoner, he was granted an imperial audience
and bestowed with the title of Zhongshu.
During the Qiánlóng and Jiāqìng reigns,
famous officials such as Wáng Jié, Yán Rúyù, and Lín Zéxú
all first served as private secretaries before entering officialdom.
By the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì military campaigns,
Zuǒ Zōngtáng, Lǐ Hóngzhāng, Liú Róng, and others
mostly served as private secretaries, assisting in military affairs
and accomplishing the work of restoration.
Zēng Guófān, who commanded the military affairs,
had a private secretariat known for its many talents,
and his retainers were the best selection of their time,
which is particularly noteworthy.
Volume 85: Elections 5 – Enfeoffment and蔭 (Hereditary Privilege) / Recommendation
The system of enfeoffment and bestowal of titles,
for civil officials, belonged to the Board of Civil Office;
for military officials of the Eight Banners and Green Standard Army, it belonged to the Board of War.
During the Shùnzhì reign,
both general grace and completion of three-year terms
were grounds for enfeoffment and bestowal.
In the early Kāngxī reign,
the enfeoffment and bestowal for civil and military officials upon completion of terms were abolished.
The ranks for enfeoffment and bestowal of civil officials were initially
Principal First Rank: Tèjìn Guānglù Dàfū,
later changed to Guānglù Dàfū.
A1st Rank: Guānglù Dàfū,
later changed to Rónglù Dàfū.
Principal Second Rank: Zīzhèng Dàfū.
A2nd Rank: Tōngfèng Dàfū.
Principal Third Rank: Tōngyì Dàfū.
A3rd Rank: Zhōngyì Dàfū.
Principal Fourth Rank: Zhōngxiàn Dàfū.
A4th Rank: Cháoyì Dàfū.
Principal Fifth Rank: Fèngzhèng Dàfū.
A5th Rank: Fèngzhí Dàfū.
Principal Sixth Rank: Chéngdé Láng.
A6th Rank: Rúlín Láng;
those from clerical backgrounds: Xuāndé Láng.
Principal Seventh Rank: Wénlín Láng;
those from clerical backgrounds: Xuānyì Láng.
A7th Rank: Zhēngshì Láng.
Principal Eighth Rank: Xiūzhí Láng.
A8th Rank: Xiūzhí Zuǒláng.
Principal Ninth Rank: Dēngshì Láng.
A9th Rank: Dēngshì Zuǒláng.
The ranks of enfeoffment and bestowal for military officials
were initially divided into three systems.
Firstly, Manchu and Han Dukes, Marquises, and Earls were enfeoffed as Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫),
later changed to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍).
Secondly, the Eight Banners.
First rank: Guānglù Dàfū (光祿大夫).
Second rank: Zīzhèng Dàfū (資政大夫).
Third rank: Tōngyì Dàfū (通議大夫).
Fourth rank: Zhōngxiàn Dàfū (中憲大夫).
Fifth rank: Fèngzhèng Dàfū (奉政大夫).
Sixth rank: Chéngdé Láng (承德郎),
later changed to Wǔxìn Láng (武信郎).
Seventh rank: Wénlín Láng (文林郎),
later changed to Fènwǔ Láng (奮武郎).
Eighth rank: Xiūzhí Láng (修職郎).
Ninth rank: Dēngshì Láng (登仕郎).
In the 32nd year of Qiánlóng (乾隆)
this was changed to be the same as the Green Standard Army.
Thirdly, the Green Standard Army (Lǜqí Yíng 綠旗營).
The official ranks of enfeoffment and bestowal changed frequently.
The initial system had Principal and Auxiliary First Ranks as Rónglù Dàfū (榮祿大夫).
Principal Second Rank: Piàojí Jiāngjūn (驃騎將軍).
Auxiliary Second Rank: Xiāojí Jiāngjūn (驍騎將軍).
Principal Third Rank: Zhāoyǒng Jiāngjūn (昭勇將軍).
Auxiliary Third Rank: Huáiyuǎn Jiāngjūn (懷遠將軍).
Principal Fourth Rank: Míngwēi Jiāngjūn (明威將軍).
Auxiliary Fourth Rank: Xuānwǔ Jiāngjūn (宣武將軍).
Principal Fifth Rank: Wǔdé Jiāngjūn (武德將軍).
Auxiliary Fifth Rank: Wǔlüè Jiāngjūn (武略將軍).
Principal Sixth Rank: Zhāoxìn Xiàowèi (昭信校尉).
Auxiliary Sixth Rank: Zhōngxiǎn Xiàowèi (忠顯校尉).
Later, Principal Seventh Rank Fènyǒng Xiàowèi (奮勇校尉) was added.
In the 20th year of Qiánlóng (乾隆),
the Principal Second Rank was changed to Wǔxiǎn Dàfū (武顯大夫).
Auxiliary Second Rank: Wǔgōng Dàfū (武功大夫).
Principal Third Rank: Wǔyì Dàfū (武義大夫).
Auxiliary Third Rank: Wǔyì Dàfū (武翼大夫).
Principal Fourth Rank: Zhāowǔ Dàfū (昭武大夫).
Auxiliary Fourth Rank: Xuānwǔ Dàfū (宣武大夫).
Principal Fifth Rank: Wǔdé Láng (武德郎).
Auxiliary Fifth Rank: Wǔlüè Láng (武略郎).
Principal Sixth Rank: Wǔxìn Láng (武信郎).
Auxiliary Sixth Rank: Wǔxìn Zuǒláng (武信佐郎).
Principal Seventh Rank: Fènwǔ Láng (奮武郎).
In the 32nd year,
Principal First Rank was changed to Jiànwēi Dàfū (建威大夫).
Auxiliary First Rank: Zhènwēi Dàfū (振威大夫).
Auxiliary Seventh Rank Fènwǔ Zuǒláng (奮武佐郎) was added.
Principal Eighth Rank: Xiūwǔ Láng (修武郎).
Auxiliary Eighth Rank: Xiūwǔ Zuǒláng (修武佐郎).
The systems for the Eight Banners and Green Standard Army thus became unified.
In the 51st year,
Principal First Rank was changed to Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn (建威將軍).
Auxiliary First Rank: Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn (振威將軍).
Principal Second Rank: Wǔxiǎn Jiāngjūn (武顯將軍).
Auxiliary Second Rank: Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn (武功將軍).
Principal Third Rank: Wǔyì Dūwèi (武義都尉).
Auxiliary Third Rank: Wǔyì Dūwèi (武翼都尉).
Principal Fourth Rank: Zhāowǔ Dūwèi (昭武都尉).
Auxiliary Fourth Rank: Xuānwǔ Dūwèi (宣武都尉).
Principal Fifth Rank: Wǔdé Jíwèi (武德騎尉).
Auxiliary Fifth Rank: Wǔdé Zuǒjíwèi (武德佐騎尉).
Principal Sixth Rank: Wǔlüè Jíwèi (武略騎尉).
Auxiliary Sixth Rank: Wǔlüè Zuǒjíwèi (武略佐騎尉).
Principal Seventh Rank: Wǔxìn Jíwèi (武信騎尉).
Auxiliary Seventh Rank: Wǔxìn Zuǒjíwèi (武信佐騎尉).
Principal Eighth Rank: Fènwǔ Xiàowèi (奮武校尉).
Auxiliary Eighth Rank: Fènwǔ Zuǒxiàowèi (奮武佐校尉).
Principal Ninth Rank Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi (修武校尉) was added.
Auxiliary Ninth Rank: Xiūwǔ Zuǒxiàowèi (修武佐校尉).
Thus, the civil and military official ranks became commensurate.
The wives of civil and military officials of Principal and Auxiliary First Ranks were enfeoffed as Yīpǐn Fūrén (一品夫人).
The wives of Manchu and Han Dukes were Gōngqī Yīpǐn Fūrén (公妻一品夫人).
The wives of Marquises were Hóuqī Yīpǐn Fūrén (侯妻一品夫人).
The wives of Earls were Bóqī Yīpǐn Fūrén (伯妻一品夫人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Second Ranks were Fūrén (夫人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Third Ranks were Shūrén (淑人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Fourth Ranks were Gōngrén (恭人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Fifth Ranks were Yírén (宜人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Sixth Ranks were Ānrén (安人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Seventh Ranks were Rúrén (孺人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Eighth Ranks were Bāpǐn Rúrén (八品孺人).
Wives of Principal and Auxiliary Ninth Ranks were Jiǔpǐn Rúrén (九品孺人).
The wives of military officials of the Eight Banners below the Eighth Rank, and of the Green Standard Army below the Seventh Rank, received no enfeoffment.
Later, the wives of Green Standard Army officials of Principal Seventh Rank were enfeoffed as Rúrén (孺人).
In the 5th year of Shùnzhì (順治),
a system was established:
whenever there was an imperial edict of grace,
First Rank officials would have three generations enfeoffed and bestowed,
with four scrolls of imperial patents (gàomìng 誥命).
Second and Third Rank officials would have two generations enfeoffed and bestowed,
with three scrolls of imperial patents.
Fourth and Fifth Rank officials would have one generation enfeoffed and bestowed,
with two scrolls of imperial patents.
Sixth and Seventh Rank officials would have one generation enfeoffed and bestowed,
with two scrolls of imperial decrees (chìmìng 敕命).
Eighth and Ninth Rank officials would only have themselves enfeoffed and bestowed,
with one scroll of imperial decree.
For the shaft ends, First Rank used jade,
Second Rank used rhinoceros horn,
Third and Fourth Ranks used gold-wrapped,
and Fifth Rank and below used horn.
Regarding the rules for posthumous enfeoffment:
the initial system of Shùnzhì (順治) stated that
if a father or grandfather was currently in office,
they could not receive enfeoffment from their descendants.
Those who had retired or passed away were permitted,
and those who wished to resign their office to accept enfeoffment were allowed.
If two sons both held office,
their parents would receive enfeoffment
according to the higher rank among the sons.
If a woman received enfeoffment due to her son,
and both her husband and son held office,
it would also follow the higher rank.
If the father's office was higher than the son's,
the principal wife followed the father's office,
and the birth mother followed the son's office.
For those adopted as heirs,
if their adoptive grandparents and parents had already been enfeoffed and bestowed,
and they requested to transfer their own wife's enfeoffment honor to their birth grandparents and parents,
such transfer was permitted.
In the 5th year of Kāngxī (康熙),
it was decreed that if the father's office was higher than the son's,
enfeoffment and bestowal would follow the father's original rank.
If the office was lower than the son's,
enfeoffment and bestowal would follow the son's office.
If a son of a military official held a civil office,
enfeoffment and bestowal would follow the civil official rules.
In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng (雍正),
it was decreed that officials from Fourth to Seventh Rank who wished to transfer their own wife's enfeoffment honor to their grandparents,
and officials of Eighth and Ninth Ranks who wished to transfer it to their parents,
were all permitted such transfer.
For officials of Third Rank and above who wished to transfer to their great-grandparents,
an imperial edict was required for decision.
During the Qiánlóng (乾隆) era,
the ritual system was adjusted,
and many changes were made.
An imperial edict of the 27th year stated:
"If the official rank of the grandson is not as high as that of the grandfather or father,
then the father is a grand master and the son is a scholar,
as clearly stated in records.
The old practice of enfeoffing and bestowing according to the grandfather's or father's original rank
is truly inappropriate;
let it be discussed and changed."
The Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù 吏部) decided that if the official rank of a civil or military official's son or grandson was higher,
and the grandfather's or father's rank was lower,
enfeoffment and bestowal would follow the son's or grandson's official rank.
If the grandfather's or father's rank was higher,
and the son's or grandson's rank was lower,
enfeoffment and bestowal could not follow the grandfather's or father's original rank.
If the father's office was higher than the son's,
the birth mother would receive enfeoffment and bestowal according to the son's office,
while the principal wife and stepmother could not request enfeoffment according to the father's office;
if they wished to receive enfeoffment according to the son's office, it was permitted.
This also applied to sons of military officials who held civil office.
In the 50th year,
it was decreed that officials of First to Third Ranks could not transfer enfeoffment to their great-great-grandparents,
officials of Fourth to Seventh Ranks could not transfer to their great-grandparents,
and officials of Eighth Rank and below could not transfer to their grandparents.
After the Dàoguāng 帝 era,
the system of purchasing titles (juānfēng lìkāi 捐封例開) was introduced.
In the 23rd year [of Dàoguāng (1843)],
officials of the third rank and above who wished to purchase enfeoffment for their biological great-grandfathers and great-grandmothers [of their birth family]
were permitted to report the donation according to the regulations for extended enfeoffment (yí fēng 貤封) of great-grandfathers and great-grandmothers.
In the 28th year [of Dàoguāng (1848)],
officials from the fourth to the seventh rank were permitted to purchase extended enfeoffment for their great-grandfathers and great-grandmothers,
and officials of the eighth rank and below were permitted to purchase extended enfeoffment for their grandfathers and grandmothers.
All of them were to report donations at double the usual rate.
Thus, the restrictions were finally abolished.
According to old regulations, officials of the eighth and ninth ranks were allowed to enfeoff their fathers and mothers,
but not their own wives.
For those whose wives were to be enfeoffed,
only one principal wife (zhèngqī 正妻) could be enfeoffed.
If the principal wife died before being enfeoffed,
and a secondary wife (jìshì 繼室) was eligible for enfeoffment,
the principal wife could also be posthumously granted a title.
Further secondary wives (zàijì 再繼) were not permitted to be granted titles.
In the 23rd year of Dàoguāng (1843),
personnel of the eighth rank and below who purchased enfeoffment and wished to include their wives
were to report donations at double the rate.
In the second year of Xiánfēng (1852),
civil officials in the capital and provinces, as well as those who purchased their positions, were permitted to first enfeoff themselves and their principal and first secondary wives.
Then, according to their own rank, they could purchase enfeoffment for their third secondary wife.
In the fourth year [of Xiánfēng (1854)],
following the Ministry's deliberation,
after the third secondary wife,
successive wives were considered equal in status,
and were also permitted to be successively enfeoffed by donation.
According to old regulations, if an official reached the third rank,
and had been raised in childhood by his maternal grandfather and grandmother,
and his maternal grandfather and grandmother died without heirs,
he was permitted to grant them extended enfeoffment according to his official rank.
Other maternal relatives were not allowed extended enfeoffment.
In the 23rd year of Dàoguāng (1843),

personnel who purchased enfeoffment were permitted to purchase extended enfeoffment for their maternal uncles (mǔjiù 母舅), maternal aunts (jiùmu 舅母), paternal aunts' husbands (gūfu 姑夫), paternal aunts (gūmǔ 姑母), maternal aunts' husbands (yífu 姨夫), maternal aunts (yímǔ 姨母), fathers-in-law (qīfù 妻父), and mothers-in-law (qīmǔ 妻母), who had nurtured them, following the precedent of extended enfeoffment for maternal grandfathers and grandmothers.
This was done through donation.
In the third year of Xiánfēng (1853),
it was also permitted to purchase extended enfeoffment for great-grandfathers and great-grandmothers,
grandfathers' elder brothers (bóshū zǔfù 伯叔祖父) and their wives (bóshū zǔmǔ 伯叔祖母),
father's elder brothers (bóshū fùmǔ 伯叔父母) and their wives,
stepmothers (shùmǔ 庶母),
elder brothers and their wives (xiōngsǎo 兄嫂), as well as paternal grand-uncles (dí táng bóshū zǔfù 嫡堂伯叔祖父) and their wives (dí táng bóshū zǔmǔ 嫡堂伯叔祖母),
paternal uncles (dí táng bóshū fù 嫡堂伯叔父) and their wives (dí táng bóshū mǔ 嫡堂伯叔母),
paternal cousins (dí táng xiōng 嫡堂兄) and their wives (dí táng sǎo 嫡堂嫂),
cousins of the second (cóng táng 從堂) and third degree (zàicóng táng 再從堂) in the elder generation, as well as maternal great-grandfathers and great-grandmothers,
maternal grandfathers and grandmothers,
and wives' grandfathers and grandmothers.
According to the established regulations for rank,
all could be requested through donation.
Furthermore, it was permitted for women
to purchase positions and enfeoffment for their deceased husbands' grandfathers or fathers.
Those adopted as heirs
could purchase extended enfeoffment for their ancestors through their grandfathers or fathers.
This proliferation [of regulations]
completely eroded the established system.
