The system of requesting enfeoffment by promotion (jiājí qǐngfēng 加級請封)
was initially also strictly restricted.
In the early years of Shùnzhì 順治 帝,
for all who were promoted by imperial grace,
enfeoffment was granted according to the newly added rank.
In the 52nd year of Kāngxī 康熙 帝 (1713),
a regulation was established that for those of the seventh rank and below requesting enfeoffment by promotion,
it could not exceed the fifth rank;
for those of the fifth and sixth ranks, it could not exceed the fourth rank;
for those of the third and fourth ranks, it could not exceed the second rank.
Purchased ranks (juānjí 捐級) were not to be counted.
During the Qiánlóng 乾隆 帝 era,
for provincial officials, regardless of whether their promotion was new or old,
they could not request enfeoffment based on the promoted rank.
In the 50th year [of Qiánlóng (1785)],
the Ministry deliberated that for capital officials of the eighth rank and below,
they could request enfeoffment up to the fifth rank.
This was not only an excessive privilege
but also felt too lenient.
Subsequently, those of the eighth rank and below could not exceed the seventh rank,
and those without official rank in the provinces were not to be granted enfeoffment.
However, those who wished to purchase honors for their relatives
were permitted to purchase enfeoffment.
This was adopted.
After the Jiāqìng 嘉慶 帝 era,
restrictions gradually relaxed.
Capital and provincial officials who encountered imperial grace
were permitted to report donations for new ranks to request enfeoffment.
It was deliberated that personnel with official titles of the third and fourth ranks,
who purchased enfeoffment of the second rank by promotion,
were permitted to pay double the silver,
and enfeoffment was granted according to the regulations for current, expectant, and candidate officials.
In the early Xiánfēng 咸豐 帝 era,
following the regulations for donations in Guǎngdōng 廣東 (fǔguǎng juānlì 撫廣捐例),
for all capital and provincial officials and those who purchased their positions,
who requested enfeoffment through promoted or additionally purchased ranks:
current, expectant, and candidate officials of the third and fourth ranks
were permitted to purchase up to the second rank.
For those of the fifth and sixth ranks who purchased enfeoffment of the third rank by promotion,
they were to report donations at double the usual rate.
For those who purchased enfeoffment up to the second rank by promotion,
following the precedent that officials of the fourth rank could purchase enfeoffment of the second rank,
they were to report donations at one and a half times the double rate.
For those of the seventh rank who purchased enfeoffment of the third or fourth rank by promotion,
and those of the eighth rank and below who purchased enfeoffment of the fifth or sixth rank by promotion,
all were to follow the usual regulations,
reporting donations at double the rate according to their respective ranks.
In the tenth year [of Xiánfēng (1860)],
it was stipulated that for third-rank personnel who purchased enfeoffment by promotion,
they were permitted to be granted enfeoffment of the junior first rank (cóngyīpǐn 從一品),
paying double the silver amount for first-rank personnel.
For personnel with nominal titles of the second and third ranks who purchased enfeoffment of the junior first rank,
they should report donations at an increased rate or double the silver amount for actual officials of the second and third ranks.
For those who purchased enfeoffment of the junior first rank for maternal relatives,
they were each permitted to report donations at an additionally increased rate,
based on the silver amounts for actual officials or nominal titles of the second and third ranks.
As this decline continued until the mid-Guāngxù 光緒 帝 era,
Censor Lǐ Címíng 李慈銘 submitted a memorial stating:
"The essence of governing a nation
lies solely in rewards and punishments.
While punishments must not be slightly exceeded,
how can rewards be indiscriminately bestowed?
During the Kāngxī and Qiánlóng reigns,
the empire enjoyed longevity,
and the celebratory ceremonies and military achievements
were too numerous to count.
During that time, officials both inside and outside the court
frequently encountered imperial grace,
and rewards were dispensed based on merit,
with ranks and order well-defined,
never exceeding their proper grades.
Now, many provincial officials (dàoyuán 道員) have reached the second rank,
and their enfeoffments all reach the first rank.
Many prefects (zhīfǔ 知府) and assistant prefects (tóngzhī 同知) are promoted to the third rank,
and their enfeoffments all reach the second rank.
Most magistrates (mùlìng 牧令) are of the fourth rank,
and most registrars (bù 簿) and jail wardens (wèi 尉) are of the fifth or sixth rank,
yet their enfeoffments frequently reach the third or fourth rank.
Indeed, titles and rewards
are how the sovereign promotes the worthy and demotes the foolish,
and how court officials motivate their subordinates.
If they are obtained too easily,
people will not appreciate the grace.
If they are bestowed too hastily,
officials will have no incentive to exert themselves.
When the superior and inferior are indistinguishable,
and the ranks are unclear,
it encourages the arrogance of false scholars
and confuses the public,
which is not the way to uphold the court's dignity or purify the official class."
The memorial was presented,
but no reduction was made.
Subsequently, foreign troubles were frequent,
and talent was scarce.
In the 26th year [of Guāngxù (1900)],
an imperial edict halted the purchase of actual official positions (shíguān 實官),
but the purchase of nominal titles (xūxián 虛銜) and enfeoffment continued as before.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng 宣統 帝 (1909),
the Ministry of Personnel deliberated and set out regulations:
capital officials were to request enfeoffment based on their promoted ranks, and provincial officials based on their actual positions.
There was a strong desire to restore the old system,
but it could not be implemented.
The following year,
it was revised that capital officials were to be based on their promoted ranks,
and provincial officials on their additional titles (jiāxián 加銜).
Personnel of the fifth rank were permitted to request enfeoffment up to the third rank,
and personnel of the eighth rank were permitted to request enfeoffment up to the sixth rank.
Although there was a desire to make some remedies,
the deeply ingrained problem was difficult to reverse.
The system of imperial patronage (yìn 廕)
included: grace patronage (ēnyìn 恩廕),
hardship patronage (nányìn 難廕),
and special patronage (tèyìn 特廕).
Grace patronage began in the 18th year of Shùnzhì (1661).
By imperial grace, Manchu and Han civil officials of the fourth rank and above in the capital, and third rank and above in the provinces,
and military officials of the second rank and above in the capital and provinces,
each sent one son to the Imperial Academy (jiàn 監).

Sons of Hulunjīngtǒnglǐng 護軍統領 (Commandants of the Imperial Guards), Fùdūtǒnglǐng 副都統 (Deputy Lieutenant-Generals), Āsīhānīhāfān 阿思哈尼哈番 (a type of noble title), Shìláng 侍郎 (Vice-Ministers), Xuéshì 學士 (Academicians) and above became senior Imperial Academy students (yìngshēng 廕生),
while the rest became ordinary Imperial Academy students (jiànshēng 監生).
The initial system stipulated that
Gōng 公 (Dukes), Hóu 侯 (Marquises), and Bó 伯 (Counts) were granted first-rank patronage.
Zǐ 子 (Viscounts) and Nán 男 (Barons) were granted patronage separately.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng 雍正 帝 (1724), this was changed so that all hereditary positions were granted third-rank patronage.
In the 34th year of Qiánlóng (1769),
it was stipulated that Gōng, Hóu, and Bó were granted first-rank patronage,
Zǐ were granted second-rank patronage,
and Nán were granted third-rank patronage.
In the early Yōngzhèng era,
it was stipulated that those among the yìngshēng and jiànshēng who were proficient in literature and principles
were to be assigned by the Ministry of Personnel to various ministries and courts for examination and practical training.
Those aged 15 and above who were sent to the Imperial Academy for study,
upon reaching adulthood and completing their studies,
were to be reported to the Ministry and memorialized to the throne,
and then assigned to various ministries and courts for practical training.
It was also ordered that civil and military yìngshēng and jiànshēng who were proficient in literary principles
were to undergo examinations according to regulations
and be employed in civil service positions.
Those who had studied martial arts in their youth,
were physically strong and talented,
and wished to switch to military positions,
were to clearly present their case to the Ministry of Personnel,
which would then transfer them to the Ministry of War to change their patronage.
Regarding the methods of examination:
In the third year of Yōngzhèng,
it was decreed that Yìnshēng aged twenty and above who had reported to the ministry
should be presented for examination and imperial audience by memorial.
In the eleventh year of Qiánlóng,
it was established that examinations would consist of an essay on ancient topics and a policy question on current affairs.
Specially appointed ministers would review the papers,
classify them as A or B,
and present them for imperial perusal.
Those whose literary skills and reasoning were excellent
would be handed over to the ministry for imperial audience.
Those who were absurd
would be sent back to their native places to study,
to be re-examined three years later.
This was followed according to precedent throughout successive generations.
In the thirty-first year of Guāngxù,
Han Yìnshēng were exempted from examination, following the precedent for Manchu officials.
Regarding methods of appointment:
Han Yìnshēng had three avenues: internal appointments, external appointments, and conversion to military posts.
For internal appointments:
In the first year of Yōngzhèng, it was decreed that
a Shàngshū of the first rank would appoint a Yuánwàiláng,
a Shìláng of the second rank would appoint a Zhǔshì,
a Zǒngdū would be equivalent to a Shàngshū,
and a Xúnfǔ to a Shìláng.
In the seventh year,
it was revised that a Zheng-yīpǐn official would appoint a Yuánwàiláng or Zhìzhōng;
a Cóng-yīpǐn official would appoint a Zhǔshì;
a Zheng-èrpǐn official would appoint a Zhǔshì, Dūcháyuàn Jīnglì, or Jīngfǔ Tōngpàn;
a Cóng-èrpǐn official would appoint a Guānglùsì Shǔzhèng or Dàlǐsì Sìfù;
a Zheng-sānpǐn official would appoint a Tōngzhèngshǐsī Jīnglì, Tàichángsì Diǎnbù, Zhōng, Xíng, Píng, or Bó;
a Cóng-sānpǐn official would appoint a Guānglùsì Diǎnbù, Luányíwèi Jīnglì, Zhānshìfǔ Zhǔbù, or Jīngfǔ Jīnglì.
Fourth-rank Yìnshēng were treated the same as those who had obtained qualifications through donation (Jùn nà) or were Gòngjiàn scholars qualifying for office by examination,
and were selected in rotation.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that a Zuǒdūyùshǐ's Yìn privileges were equivalent to those of a Shàngshū.
In the tenth year of Tóngzhì,
it was decreed that a Hédàozǒngdū could appoint a Yuánwàiláng or Zhǔshì through Yìn privileges.
During the Xuāntǒng period,
the official system was reformed,
various offices were abolished,
and appointments were made to equivalent ranks.
For external appointments:
During the Qiánlóng period, it was decreed that
a Zheng-yīpǐn official would appoint a Fǔtóngzhī;
a Cóng-yīpǐn official would appoint a Zhīzhōu;
a second-rank official would appoint a Tōngpàn;
a third-rank official would appoint a Zhīxiàn;
and a Han nobleman with the title Zǐjué would appoint a Zhīxiàn.
This remained unchanged throughout the Qīng dynasty.
For conversion to military posts:
During the Yōngzhèng period, it was decreed that
for Beijing-based officials of the first rank, such as Shàngshū,
and external officials like Zǒngdū and Jiāngjūn,
Yìnshēng would be appointed with the title of Dū sī and manage as Dū sī.
For officials of the second rank, such as Shìláng,
and Xúnfǔ and Tídū,
they would be appointed with the acting title of Dū sī and manage as Dū sī.
For officials of the third rank, such as Fùdūyùshǐ,
and Bùzhèngshǐ and Zǒngbīngguān,
they would be appointed with the title of Shǒubèi and manage as Shǒubèi.
For Ànchásǐ and Fùjiàng with an added first-rank title,
they would be appointed with the acting title of Shǒubèi and manage as Shǒubèi.
For Fùjiàng with a second-rank title,
they would be appointed as a Shǒuyùsuǒ Qiānzǒng.
During the Qiánlóng period, it was decreed that a Han Zǐjué of the third rank would appoint a Qiānzǒng,
and a Nánjué of the fourth rank would appoint a Bǎzǒng.
For the appointment of Han Banner members:
In the twelfth year of Kāngxī, it was originally decreed that a first-rank official would appoint a Yuánwàiláng,
and a second-rank official would appoint a Dàlǐsì Sìzhèng or Zhīzhōu.
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng,
those appointed as Zhīzhōu were re-designated as Zhǔshì.
In the fifth year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that a third-rank official would appoint a seventh-rank Bǐtiēshì,
and a fourth-rank official would appoint an eighth-rank Bǐtiēshì.
In the first year of Xuāntǒǒng,
the Lìbù memorialized:
"For Han civil and military officials' Yìnshēng,
appointments are made according to their exact (zhèng) and approximate (cóng) ranks,
but for Manchu Yìnshēng, there is no distinction between exact and approximate ranks.
When Han Yìnshēng are presented for imperial audience,
edicts are drafted proposing internal or external appointments;
for Manchu Yìnshēng, edicts are drafted proposing civil posts, imperial guards, or banner officers.
However, after the thirty-second year of Guāngxù,
Han officials were uniformly selected,
and if current Dūtǒng or Fùdūtǒng were to grant Yìn privileges according to Manchu regulations,
it would cause difficulties.
It is proposed that
for those originally Shàngshū or Shìláng who were reappointed or promoted,
Dūtǒng should follow the precedent for Han Shàngshū,
Fùdūtǒng should follow the precedent for Han Shìláng,
and Fùdūtǒng promoted from third-rank and below Beijing departments or supervisory officials
should follow the precedent for Han Zheng-èrpǐn officials,
with edicts still proposing internal or external appointments."
This was granted.
Originally,
only incumbent officials could grant Yìn privileges,
and officials below Zuǒlǐng in the Nèiwùfǔ were not granted Yìn.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī,
it was decreed that all officials, regardless of rank or title,
should grant Yìn privileges to their sons based on their actual emoluments.
From this year onwards, the sons of officials below Zuǒlǐng in the Nèiwùfǔ were permitted to receive Yìn.
In the twelfth year,
those who had resigned from their original posts but were still receiving stipends were also permitted to grant Yìn.
Earlier, in the third year of Kāngxī, it was decreed that Yìn scholars and Jiànshēng who had already obtained official posts or passed civil service examinations
could not receive Yìn appointments.
In the forty-fifth year of Qiánlóng, it was revised that if the eldest legitimate son or grandson had passed examinations but not yet been appointed,
or if they held an official title and wished to inherit Yìn,
they were permitted to receive Yìn appointments.
After Dàoguāng,
the system of official donations (Jùn lì) was widely opened,
and even those who had already obtained official posts
were still permitted to receive Yìn appointments.
The selection process became confused,
and opportunistic advancements became numerous.
In the twenty-second year of Guāngxù,
Censor Xīlín memorialized:
"In the selection process of the Lìbù,
personnel appointed by special imperial decree are uniformly given precedence over all other categories.
However, for Yìnshēng and those presented for audience upon reaching the required age,
if they had previously purchased the rank of Dàofǔ,
and upon audience received an imperial edict to be selected as Dàofǔ,
they are essentially from the donation category,
yet ministerial regulations classify them under the special imperial decree category for selection.
In recent years,
this has often been exploited for personal gain and opportunism,
by prematurely purchasing the rank of Dàofǔ
to secure a future position for obtaining special imperial decrees and precedence over other categories.
This leads to a situation where, for the same Yìnshēng and age-qualified personnel,
the descendants of honest officials
sigh over their limited opportunities,
while the sons of wealthy idlers
freely pursue connections,
which greatly impacts
public morality and sentiment.
It is requested that such personnel who have additionally purchased the rank of Dào or Fǔ
be selected in the same category as those who obtained office through donation."
This was referred to the ministry for deliberation and implementation.
Regarding difficult Yìn cases:
In the third year of Shùnzhì, it was decreed that
officials who died in the service of the state
would be posthumously granted the title of their deserved promotion in rank,
and one son would be appointed as a Jiànshēng to study,
and after the term, await selection.
In the eighteenth year of Kāngxī, it was decreed that officials who died for the country would grant Yìn privileges to their sons according to their actual rank,
not their posthumously granted rank.
In the twelfth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was memorialized and decreed that officials on official assignments,
who perished by being swept away by storms in the open ocean, great rivers, the Yellow River,
or lakes like Dòngtíng and Hóngzé,
would be granted Yìn and posthumous titles according to their deserved promotion in rank.
Those who perished by being swept away in inland waters or rivers
would receive reduced Yìn and posthumous titles;
officials of the eighth rank and below
would receive posthumous titles but no Yìn.
In the sixtieth year of Qiánlóng, it was decreed that officials serving in military camps,
who exerted themselves in urging supplies,
and died of illness,
would receive Yìn and posthumous titles according to the precedent for those swept away in inland waters or rivers.
In the twenty-third year of Dàoguāng,
officials of the eighth rank and below who perished on duty by being swept away or died of illness in military camps
were permitted posthumous titles,
and one son would be appointed as a Jiànshēng,
allowed to take examinations,
but not to be selected for office.
In the second year of Guāngxù, it was memorialized and decreed that incumbent officials who died in the line of duty against rebels or died of illness in military camps,
if they were promoted, appointed, or immediately appointed to certain official ranks, or had purchased promotional titles,
would receive Yìn according to their promoted rank, promotional title, or posthumous title,
and Yìn based on their actual official rank.
Those awaiting appointment or selection
would receive Yìn and posthumous titles as incumbent officials.
Those who had retired or taken sick leave
would receive Yìn and posthumous titles according to their original official rank.
Those who had been demoted or transferred
would receive Yìn and posthumous titles according to their demoted rank.
Already selected Jǔrén,
Èn, Bá, Fù, Suì, Yōu Gòngshēng who had taken up office or teaching positions,
and Gòngjiànshēng who had obtained official titles through donation and examination,
would each receive Yìn and posthumous titles according to their rank and as incumbent officials.
Jǔrén not yet selected
would follow the precedent of a seventh-rank official.
Èn, Bá, Fù, Suì, Yōu Gòngshēng would follow the precedent of an eighth-rank official.
Lǐn, Zēng, Fù Wénshēngyuán would receive Yìn and posthumous titles according to the precedent of a ninth-rank official.
Personnel with honorary titles or official caps
would only receive posthumous titles,
but no Yìn.
Prior to the reign of Qiánlóng Emperor,
Banner System officials who served in the military
and achieved distinguished merits,
as well as those who died in battle,
their descendants were entitled to hereditary posts by custom.
If a person was not yet of age
but had already inherited a post without yet serving in it,
they were granted half pay.
For Green Standard Army officers who died in battle, the protocol for posthumous honors and pensions
only extended to special hereditary appointments.
In the forty-ninth year of Qiánlóng (1784), an imperial edict stated:
"Both Banner System officials and Green Standard Army personnel,
who lay down their lives on the battlefield,
equally demonstrate loyalty and die in service;
how can we bear to maintain any discrimination?
Henceforth, for Green Standard Army officers' military achievements and posthumous honors,
the old regulations shall be followed.
For personnel who die in battle,
regardless of whether they are Hàn people or Banner people,
if they served in the Green Standard Army,
they shall all be granted hereditary posts.
When the succession order is exhausted,
an恩騎尉 (ēn qíwèi) shall be appropriately granted according to regulations,
so that the reward may extend through the generations."
From then on, many Hàn officials who died in hardship
also received hereditary posts.
For all those who died for the country and were granted posthumous titles:
A Zǒngdū (Governor-General) with an added Shàngshū (Minister) title
was posthumously granted the title of Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (Junior Guardian of the Heir Apparent).
A Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor) with an added Fù Dū Yùshǐ (Vice Censor-in-Chief) title
was posthumously granted the title of Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ (Left Censor-in-Chief).
A Bùzhèngshǐ (Provincial Administration Commissioner) was posthumously granted the title of Nèigé Xuéshì (Grand Secretary of the Cabinet).
An Ànchásǐ (Provincial Surveillance Commissioner) or Yányùnshǐ (Salt Commissioner) was posthumously granted the title of Tàichángsì Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices).
A Dàoyuán (Circuit Intendant) was posthumously granted the title of Guānglùsì Qīng (Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments).
A Zhīfǔ (Prefect) was posthumously granted the title of Tàipúsì Qīng (Minister of the Court of the Imperial Stud).
A Tóngzhī (Assistant Prefect), Zhīzhōu (Department Magistrate), or Tōngpàn (Sub-Prefect) was posthumously granted the title of Dàoyuán (Circuit Intendant).
A Zhīxiàn (County Magistrate) was posthumously granted the title of Zhīfǔ (Prefect).
A Jiàoyù (Instructor) or Xùndǎo (Director of Studies) was posthumously granted the title of Guózǐjiān Zhùjiào (Assistant Instructor of the Imperial Academy) or Xuélù (Registrar).
For other officials,
posthumous titles were added proportionally according to their rank.
In the second year of Guāngxù (1876),
it was stipulated that those who perished by drowning in inland waters or rivers, or died of illness in military camps,
would receive posthumous titles of a reduced grade.
However, Zǒngdū, Xúnfǔ, and Bùzhèngshǐ
were not subject to reduction in their posthumous titles,
though their hereditary appointments were still reduced in grade.
Regarding hereditary appointments,
it was customary during the Kāngxī reign
that officials of the third rank and above could appoint a Zhīzhōu;
those from the fourth rank down to Tōngpàn could appoint a Zhīxiàn;

the principal officials of the three departments of Bùzhèngsǐ, Ànchásǐ, and Dūzhuǎn Yányùnsǐ, as well as Zhōu and Xiàn subordinate officials of the sixth and seventh ranks, could appoint a Xiànchéng (Assistant County Magistrate);
officials of the eighth and ninth ranks could appoint a Xiàn Zhǔbù (County Registrar);
and those not in the official stream could appoint a Zhōulìmù (Department Clerk).
In the second year of Guāngxù (1876),
it was stipulated that officials who died for the country during banditry would receive hereditary appointments according to the old Kāngxī regulations.
However, a Zhīxiàn would appoint a Zhōupàn (Department Judge),
and those who died of illness in military camps or drowned due to official duties
would have their sons appointed to a reduced grade.
For military hereditary appointments,
there were Dūsī (Company Commander), Shǒubèi (Garrison Commander), Qiānzǒng (Lieutenant), and Bǎzǒng (Sergeant),
which were equivalent to those obtained through imperial grace and then converted to military posts.
Regarding the granting of hereditary posts:
A Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief) who died in battle,
according to the regulations for Cānzàn (Counsellor) and Dūtǒng (Brigade-General),
was granted a Qí Dūwèi (Light Cavalry Captain) concurrently with a Yún Qíwèi (Cloud Cavalry Captain).
A Zǒngbīngguān (Brigade General), according to the regulations for Fù Dūtǒng (Deputy Brigade-General),
was granted a Qí Dūwèi.
From Fùjiàng (Vice General) downwards,
and from Bǎzǒng (Sergeant), Jīngzhì (Regular Officer), Wàiwěi (Unranked Officer) upwards,
according to the regulations for Cānlǐng (Brigade Commander) downwards and officials with official hats upwards,
all were granted a Yún Qíwèi.
Personnel eligible for succession who were eighteen years old
were sent to the ministry for imperial audience
and then assigned to the military for training.
Those not yet of age were given half pay,
and upon reaching age, were sent for imperial audience.
During the Guāngxù reign,
ministerial regulations permitted hereditary appointments by imperial grace to be assigned to various departments,
but special hereditary appointments for those who died in service were not allowed to follow this precedent.
In the twenty-second year of Guāngxù (1896),
Xīlín memorialized, stating:
"Hereditary appointments by imperial grace are already treated favorably by being assigned to both internal departments and external posts.
They are already treated generously,
and furthermore are allowed to be assigned to various posts.
Special hereditary appointments for those who died in service are solely for external posts,
already treated deficiently,
and are not allowed to be assigned to various posts,
which is utterly unfair.
The current times are fraught with difficulties,
and people are desperately needed.
We rely on inspiring the spirit of loyalty and righteousness throughout the land,
so that people will not act negligently in times of difficulty.
However, hereditary appointments by imperial grace expand the path to fame and achievement for the sons and grandsons of prominent officials,
while hereditary appointments for those who died in service do not open a glimmer of hope for the descendants of loyal ministers.
This causes the national martyrs to harbor resentment in the underworld,
and loyalty and righteousness to be disheartened in times of need.
I request that the ministers of the board be ordered to follow the precedent of hereditary appointments by imperial grace for external postings,
and uniformly allow them to be assigned for appointment."
This was submitted to the ministry for deliberation and implementation.
Regarding special hereditary appointments:
In the third year of Qiánlóng (1738), an imperial edict stated:
"My imperial father, in rewarding and remembering old merits,
established the Xiánliáng Cí (Shrine of Worthies) in the capital.
All ministers of our dynasty who labored for the state, assisted in governance, and preserved their complete integrity,
shall forever enjoy sacrificial veneration
and infinite renown.
While many of their descendants have entered officialdom,
some may be unable to uplift themselves and gradually fall into destitution.
I deeply pity them.
Therefore, let the Dūtǒng, Dū, and Fǔ (Brigade-Generals, Governors-General, and Provincial Governors)
seek out the descendants of these worthies who have no official positions,
or whose ranks are low,
select their direct descendants
who possess good character and talent that can be nurtured,
and send them to the ministry for imperial audience and special grace."
In the forty-seventh year of Qiánlóng (1782),
Shìhǎi and others, great-grandsons of the former Guǎngxī Xúnfǔ (Guangxi Provincial Governor) and Mièkòu Jiāngjūn (General for Suppressing Bandits) Fù Hóngliè,
received an imperial decree for their employment.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng (1799),
the deceased Yùshǐ (Censor) Cáo Xībǎo was posthumously granted the title of Fù Dū Yùshǐ,
and his son was granted a Yìnshēng (hereditary student) status according to the posthumous title.
Throughout the dynasties, the descendants of meritorious officials were remembered with favor,
and imperial decrees of grace were frequently issued.
In the last years of Guāngxù,
there were many troubles within the empire.
Considering the meritorious generals and officials,
an imperial edict stated:
"Since the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns,
the Fà (Taiping), Niǎn (Nian), and Huí (Muslim) bandits
have been successively suppressed.
Many civil and military high officials
achieved outstanding merits.
More than fifty years have passed
since the lavish rewards and remunerations.
Among the descendants of these meritorious officials,
there is no shortage of those who are prominent in name and position;
however,
those who remain in humble positions
or live in obscurity in their hometowns
are also numerous."
Therefore, all Dū, Fǔ, and Dūtǒng were ordered to thoroughly investigate the descendants of meritorious officials,
ascertaining their official positions or lack thereof,
and compile a report for imperial review.
The Jūnjī Dàchén (Grand Councilors) prepared a list for presentation.
The second grandson of the former Xī'ān Jiāngjūn (General of Xi'an) Duōlóng'ā, Shòuqìng, and his great-grandson Kuíbì;
the great-grandsons of Húběi Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Hubei) Xiàng Róng, Kǎi and Nǎiquán;
the grandson of Ānhuī Xúnfǔ (Anhui Provincial Governor) Jiāng Zhōngyuán, Shènxūn, and his great-grandson Qínpéi;

the grandson of Bùzhèngshǐ銜 (Provincial Administration Commissioner title) and Zhèjiāng Níngshàotái Dào (Circuit Intendant of Ningbo, Shaoxing, and Taizhou in Zhejiang) Luó Zénán, Chánggěng, and his great-grandson Yánzuò;
the grandson of Xié bàn Dàxuéshì (Associate Grand Secretary) and Sìchuān Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Sichuan) Luò Bǐngzhāng, Màoxūn, and his great-grandson Yùshū;
the grandsons of Jiāngnán Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Jiangnan) Zhāng Guóliáng, Shéngzǔ and Jìzǔ;
the grandson of Xúnfǔ銜 (Provincial Governor title) and Zhèjiāng Bùzhèngshǐ (Zhejiang Provincial Administration Commissioner) Lǐ Xùbīn, Qiánpǔ, and his great-grandson Zhèngshéng;
the second grandson of Bīngbù Shàngshū (Minister of War) Péng Yùlín, Jiànsuí, and his great-grandson Wànchéng;
the son of Shǎnxī-Gānsù Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Shaanxi and Gansu) Yáng Yuèbīn, Zhèngyí, and his grandson Dàochéng;
the second son of Sìchuān Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Sichuan) Bào Chāo, Zǔ'ēn, and his grandson Shìjué;
the grandsons of Shǔ Ānhuī Xúnfǔ (Acting Anhui Provincial Governor) and Bùzhèngshǐ (Provincial Administration Commissioner) Lǐ Mèngqún, Xīngrén and Xīngxiào;
the adopted son of Jiāngxī Nángàn Zhèn Zǒngbīng (Brigade General of Nangan Garrison in Jiangxi) Chéng Xuéqǐ, Jiànxūn;
the grandson of Guǎngdōng Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Guangdong) Liú Sōngshān, Guó'ān, and his great-grandson Jiākūn;
the second son of Guìzhōu Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Guizhou) Féng Zǐcái, Xiānghuá, and his grandson Chéngfèng, etc.,
were all ordered to be promoted according to their official ranks.
For Húnán Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Hunan) Tǎ Qíbù,
it was ordered to investigate and confirm his adopted successor,
and then memorialize for imperial grace.
The following year,
another edict listed the most distinguished meritorious officials:
the former Yúnnán-Guìzhōu Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Yunnan and Guizhou) Liú Chángyòu;
Táiwān Xúnfǔ (Taiwan Provincial Governor) and Yīděng Nán (First-Class Baron) Liú Míngchuán;
posthumously granted Bùzhèngshǐ and Dàoyuán Wáng Zhēn;
Suíyuǎncchéng Jiāngjūn (General of Suiyuan City) Fú Xīng;
Fújiàn Lùlù Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Land Forces in Fujian) and Yīděng Nán Xiāo Fúsì;
recorded Tídū, Yīděng Zǐ (First-Class Viscount), and Hénán Guīdé Zhèn Zǒngbīng (Brigade General of Guide Garrison in Henan) Lǐ Chéndiǎn;
Zhèjiāng Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief of Zhejiang) Dèng Shàoliáng;
Dūtǒng銜 (Brigade-General title) and Guǎngdōng Fù Dūtǒng (Deputy Brigade-General of Guangdong) Wū Lántài;
acting Guǎngxī Tídū (Guangxi Provincial Commander-in-Chief) and Gānsù Sùzhōu Zhèn Zǒngbīng (Brigade General of Suzhou Garrison in Gansu) Zhāng Yùliáng;
Gōngbù Zuǒ Shìláng (Junior Vice Minister of the Board of Works) Lǚ Xiánjī;
Cáoyùn Zǒngdū (Grand Canal Governor) Yuán Jiǎsān;
Dūcháyuàn Fù Dū Yùshǐ (Vice Censor-in-Chief of the Censorate) and Jiāngxī Xúnfǔ (Jiangxi Provincial Governor) Zhāng Fèi;
acting Guìzhōu Xúnfǔ (Guizhou Provincial Governor) Hán Chāo;
Bùzhèngshǐ銜 (Provincial Administration Commissioner title)
and Fújiàn Dūliáng Dào (Grain Intendant of Fujian) Zhào Jǐngxián;
Yúnnán Hèlì Zhèn Zǒngbīng (Brigade General of Heli Garrison in Yunnan) Zhū Hóngzhāng;
Zhílì Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Zhili) Guō Sōnglín;
Guǎngdōng Děng Shěng Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor of Guangdong and other provinces) Jiǎng Yìlǐ;
Bùzhèngshǐ銜 (Provincial Administration Commissioner title) and Jiāngnán Dàoyuán (Circuit Intendant of Jiangnan) Wēn Shàoyuán;
acting Ānhuī Lúfèngyǐng Dào (Circuit Intendant of Lufu and Ying in Anhui) Jīn Guāngjīn;
Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng (Commander of the Vanguard Division) Héng Líng;
Xīnjiāng Xúnfǔ (Xinjiang Provincial Governor) and Yīděng Nán Liú Jǐntáng;
recorded Tídū and Guǎngxī Yòujiāng Zhèn Zǒngbīng (Brigade General of Youjiang Garrison in Guangxi) Zhāng Shùshān;
posthumously granted Bùzhèngshǐ銜, promoted Zhīfǔ, and Tiānjīn Zhīxiàn (Tianjin County Magistrate) Xiè Zǐchéng;
ordering all Dūtǒng, Dū, and Fǔ to investigate and confirm if they had any descendants,
what official positions they held,
and then request imperial decrees to bestow grace.
As for the imperial grace in the forty-eighth year of Qiánlóng (1783) that employed
the fifth-generation grandson of the Míng dynasty minister-strategist Xióng Tíngbì, Shìxiān,
and the fifth-generation grandson of the Míng dynasty military commander Yuán Chónghuàn, Bǐng,
these were even more extraordinary precedents for extending imperial favor and special hereditary appointments to the descendants of loyal ministers of previous dynasties.
The method of appointing officials,
for civil positions, the Lìbù (Board of Civil Office) was in charge of selection;
for military positions, the Bīngbù (Board of War) was in charge of selection.
Within the Lìbù were four bureaus (sī):
the Xuǎnsī (Bureau of Selection) managed recommendations and selections,
a particularly crucial responsibility.
All Manchu and Han individuals entering officialdom

could do so via various paths: Kējǐa (degree holders), Gòngshēng (tribute students), Jiānshēng (imperial academy students), Yìnshēng (hereditary privilege students), Yì (recommendation), Záliú (miscellaneous streams), Juānnà (purchase of office), Guān xuéshēng (official students), Jùnxiù (talented individuals).

By established regulations, those who originated from Kējǐa, as well as Ēn (grace), Bá (selected), Fù (assistant), Suì (annual), Yōu (excellent) Gòngshēng, and Yìnshēng were considered to be from the Zhèngtú (orthodox path).
The rest were from the Yìtú (heterodox path).
If those from the Yìtú were recommended,
they would also be treated like those from the Zhèngtú,
but they could not be examined for selection to the Kē (Censorate) or Dào (Circuit).
Those not from the Kējǐa Zhèngtú
could not become officials in the Hàn (Hanlin Academy), Zhān (Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction), or the Lìbù and Lǐbù (Board of Rites).
However, banner officers (Qíyuán) were exempt from this rule.
All officials and clerks were limited to those with a clear family background;
individuals from Eight Banners households (Bāqí hùxià rén),
Han family bondservants (Hànrén jiānú), and personal attendants (chángsuí)
were not allowed to enter official ranks indiscriminately.
Among those who entered officialdom through various paths,

within the capital were Xiūzhuàn (compiler), Biān (editor), Jiǎn (reviser), Shùjíshì (probationary bachelor), Zhǔshì (section chief), Zhōngshū (secretary), Xíngrén (messenger), Píngshì (evaluator), Bóshì (erudite);
outside the capital were Zhīzhōu (prefect), Tuīguān (judicial subprefect), Zhōuxiàn Jiàoshòu (prefectural and county instructors).
These were appointed from Jìnshì (metropolitan graduates).
Nèigé Zhōngshū (Grand Secretariat secretaries), Guózǐjiān Xuézhèng (National Academy academicians), Xuélù (academic recorders), Zhīxiàn (county magistrates), Xuézhèng (academic instructors)
were examined and appointed from Jǔrén (provincial graduates) or selected through Dàtiāo (grand selection).
Xiǎo Jīngguān (minor Beijing officials), Zhīxiàn, Jiàozhí (educational officials), Zhōupàn (subprefectural judges)
were recruited from Yōu and Bá Gòngshēng.
Yuánwàiláng (assistant director), Zhǔshì, Zhìzhōng (assistant prefect), Zhīzhōu, Tōngpàn (assistant subprefect)
were examined and appointed from first and second-rank Yìnshēng.
In addition, Gòng and Jiānshēng who passed examinations for office

were appointed as Zhōupàn, Zhōutóng (subprefectural second-class assistant), Xiànchéng (county assistant magistrate), Zhǔbù (chief registrar), Lìmù (clerk), Jīngtōngcāngshū (Beijing and Tongzhou granary clerks), and clerks (shūlì) and attendants (gōngshì) in various Yámén (offices) such as the Nèigé (Grand Secretariat) and the Six Boards.
After five years of service,
they were appointed to the rank of Cóng Jiǔpǐn wèirùliú (unranked, ninth-class).
Rúshì (Confucian scholars) in the Lǐbù (Board of Rites) who received stipends for three years
were appointed as Fǔjiǎnjiào (prefectural inspectors) and Diǎnshǐ (judicial clerks).
Lìyuán (clerks) who passed examinations for office:
first class were appointed as Zhèng Bāpǐn Jīnglì (eighth-rank administrators);
second class as Zhèng Jiǔpǐn Zhǔbù (ninth-rank chief registrars);
third and fourth classes as Cóng Jiǔpǐn wèirùliú.
Guān xuéshēng who passed examinations
were appointed as Cóng Jiǔpǐn Bǐtiēshì (scribes), Kùshǐ (treasury custodians), Wàiláng (external directors).
Jùnxiù who knew Manchu and Han characters were examined for translation,
and the excellent ones were appointed as Bāpǐn Bǐtiēshì.
Later, the official system changed,
with slight variations.
For those from heterodox paths,
Han Chinese not recommended, and Han Banners (Hànjūn) not examined,
were not appointed as capital officials (Jīngguān) or principal officials (Zhèngyìngguān),
this was to distinguish their social standing
and strictly control their advancement.
All internal and external official positions were divided into Manchu vacancies, Mongol vacancies, Han Banner vacancies, and Han vacancies.
Manchu also had vacancies for Zōngshì (imperial clan members) and Nèiwùfǔ Báoyī (Imperial Household Department bondservants).
Those exclusively designated
included vacancies for the Fǔyǐn (prefect) of Fèngtiān Fǔ, and for various Dào (circuits) such as Fèngjǐn, Shānhǎi, Jílín, Rèhé, Kǒuběi, Shānxī, and Guīsuī.
Garrison officers (Zhùfángguān), Lǐshì (managers), Tóngzhī (second-class assistant prefects), and Tōngpàn in various provinces were Manchu vacancies.
Tánggǔtè Sīyè (Tangut instructors), Zhùjiào (assistant instructors), Zhōngshū, Yóumù Yuánwàiláng (nomadic assistant directors), and Zhǔshì were Mongol vacancies.
The Cóng Liùpǐn Qiūguānzhèng (sixth-rank astronomical officer) of the Qīntiānjīan (Imperial Observatory) was a Han Banner vacancy.
Officials of the Zōngrénfǔ (Imperial Clan Court) were Zōngshì vacancies.
Officials of the Nèiwùfǔ were Nèiwùfǔ Báoyī vacancies.
In addition, quota vacancies (Équē) were set in various capital Yámén, imperial tomb Yámén, the five boards of Shèngjīng, and local Yámén in various provinces.
Manchu vacancies above Jīngtáng (capital minister rank)
could be mutually filled by Zōngshì and Han Banners.
Han vacancies above Sīguān (bureau official rank)
could be mutually filled by Han Banners.
For external officials, Mongols could fill Manchu vacancies,
and both Manchu and Mongol Báoyī could fill Han vacancies.
However, the Fǔyǐn and Fǔchéng (assistant prefect) of Shùntiān Fǔ,
the Fǔchéng of Fèngtiān Fǔ,
officials of capital prefectures and counties (Jīngfǔ, Jīngxiàn),
and Sī, Fāngguān (bureau, ward officials) were not appointed to Manchus.
Sīguān of the Xíngbù (Board of Punishments) were not appointed to Han Banners.
External officials of Cóng Liùpǐn Shǒulǐng (sixth-rank chiefs)
and those below Zuǒèr (assistant officials) were not appointed to Manchus or Mongols.
Those below Dàoyuán (circuit intendant) were not appointed to Zōngshì.
These were the general rules.
The promotion of officials and clerks based on their emolument seniority was called Tuīshēng (recommended promotion);
promotion without waiting for the full term of emolument was called Jíshēng (immediate promotion).
Internally, from Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretary) to Jīngtáng,
and externally, from Dū (governor-general), Fǔ (governor), Fān (provincial treasurer), Niè (provincial judicial commissioner),
initially followed the Ming system of joint recommendation by court officials.
Later, joint recommendation was suspended,
and proposals were listed for imperial request.
Tàicháng (Court of Imperial Sacrifices), Hónglú (Court of State Ceremonial), and Manchu Shà qīng (vice minister)
were listed and granted imperial audience.
If not listed,
eligible officials were nominated as principal and accompanying candidates for imperial audience and appointment, which was called Jiǎnshòu (selected appointment).
Twenty officials were recommended based on emolument seniority for imperial audience and appointment, which was called Tuīshòu (recommended appointment).
Jīng Sīguān (capital bureau officials), Xiǎo Jīngguān, Bǐtiēshì
were categorized as Liúshòu (retained appointment), Diàoshòu (transferred appointment), Jiǎnshòu, Kǎoshòu (examined appointment),
all awaiting imperial audience and decree;
the rest were selected.
For external officials, Bùzhèngshǐ (provincial treasurer) and Ànchásǐ (provincial judicial commissioner) were listed,
while Yùnshǐ (salt commissioner) required an imperial decree.
Dào (circuit) and Fǔ (prefecture) vacancies had different methods: Qǐngzhǐ (imperial request), Jiǎnshòu, Tíshòu (nominated appointment), Diàoshòu, Liúshòu;
the rest were selected.
Tīng (department), Zhōu (subprefecture), and Xiàn (county) vacancies were similar to Dào and Fǔ,
but without Qǐngzhǐ.
Zuǒzá (assistant and miscellaneous officials), Jiàozhí (educational officials), Yánguān (salt officials):
crucial vacancies were retained (liú),
others were either consulted (zī) or selected (xuǎn).
Initially, for Jīng Sīguān vacancies,
there was no fixed rule for nomination (tí) or selection (xuǎn);
the senior officials decided promotions and demotions at will.
After a long time,
most vacancies were filled by nomination,
which led to many eligible for promotion, appointment, or selection becoming stagnant.
In the ninth year of Qiánlóng (1744),
an imperial edict mandated that nominated vacancies (Tíquē) from various bureaus be reported to the Board for registration,
while other vacancies were to be filled by selection,
without mixing them.
Thus, it was stipulated how many Han Lángzhōng (director), Yuánwàiláng, and Zhǔshì positions in each board and bureau were to be filled by nomination,
and how many remaining vacancies were to be filled by selection.
During the Dàoguāng (reign) period,
the quotas for nominated appointments were further revised,
and later, various boards occasionally increased them.
In the twelfth year of Shùnzhì (1655),
an imperial edict ordered the Lìbù to meticulously examine old precedents,
consider current circumstances,
and categorize Zhōu and Xiàn vacancies into three grades.
Candidates were assessed on their physical appearance (shēn), speech (yán), calligraphy (shū), and judgment (pàn),
also divided into three grades,
and appointments were made accordingly.
Subsequently, the urgency of vacancies was determined by four factors: Chōng (strategic), Fán (busy), Pí (exhausting), Nán (difficult).
Those combining all four factors were the most crucial;
three factors were next;
two or one factor were less crucial.
Consequently, vacancies for Zhīfǔ (prefect), Tóng (assistant prefect), Tōng (assistant subprefect), Zhōu, and Xiàn
had different methods such as Qǐngzhǐ Diàobǔ (imperial decree transfer and appointment) and Bùxuǎn (Board selection).
All selections for vacancies are classified as immediate selection, regular selection, supplementary selection, combined selection, offsetting selection, and waiting selection.
For each, it is distinguished whether there are accumulated vacancies or not.
Those who arrive at their post are selected.

Selection categories include those whose terms are full, leaves are full, salaries are full, those who are reinstated, those due for appointments, those demoted for appointments, scattered Hánlín Shùjíshì, Jìnshì, Jǔrén, Gòngshēng, Yìnshēng, those recommended through deliberation, those who purchased offices through donation, and those promoted.
Grand selections are held in even-numbered months,
and urgent selections in odd-numbered months.
Mǎn, Méng, and Hànjūn are in the first ten days of the month,
Hàn officials in the last ten days,
and Bǐtiēshì in the middle ten days.
In the early system,
candidates for selection all reported to the ministry for registration and roll call.
Later, this practice was suspended by regulation,
allowing them to return to their hometowns.
The ministry would investigate the chronological order and draw lots for selection,
then send credentials for them to proceed to their posts.
In the second year of Kāngxī
Censorial Official Yú Kětuō [于可託] stated:
"Since sending credentials invites the risk of impersonation,
candidates from distant provinces often take a year to travel back and forth.
Should any incident occur,
returning the credentials for re-selection
also takes time.
Vacancies remain unfilled for extended periods,
and acting officials are impeached for corruption,
while demands for new appointees to arrive quickly
are constantly reported.
It would be better to revert to requiring candidates to report to the ministry in person,
and conduct selections in sequence."
In the eighth year
Censor Gē Yīng [戈英] reiterated this point.
The proposal was adopted.
From then on, all candidates for selection reported to the ministry for registration and roll call,
establishing a permanent system.
Emperor Shèngzǔ [聖祖], mindful that candidates could not immediately obtain office,
often suffered from hunger and cold in their lodgings,
ordered the Ministry of Personnel to retain a year's worth of candidates in the capital,
while allowing others to return home.
Censor Tián Liùshàn [田六善] said:
"For the past half-year,

among retained candidates, eighty were for judicial commissioner (Tuīguān) but only one was selected; for county magistrates (Zhīxiàn), three hundred were for selection, but only thirty-one were selected.
The rest have to wait three or four years.
Drawing empty lots as companions,
the selection period is unpredictable.
We should draw actual lots according to name in order,
with candidates reporting two months before the selection."
This was submitted to the ministry for deliberation,
which abolished the monthly roll call and the drawing of empty lots,
and an imperial edict reduced the number of retained candidates by half.
Candidates reported for selection,
initially on the fifteenth day of the month preceding the selection.
Being close to the selection date,
the quality of vacancies easily led to abuses.
Later, it was changed to reporting on the first day of each month,
with selections and appointments occurring every other selection period,
which became a regulation.
When candidates obtained a vacancy,
they were initially tested on eight-legged essays,
but this was soon abolished.
It was changed to writing a three-hundred-character biography,
listing methods for governing the people, fostering good customs, urging tax collection and caring for the populace, and judging lawsuits,
called "memorials of methods" (tiáochén).
For appointments and promotions,
one also had to present the advantages and disadvantages of the previous post's locality.
However, these "memorials of methods" were often ghostwritten,
or merely consisted of praises for the emperor,
and this system was also abandoned not long after.
Candidates were customarily inspected by the Ministry of Personnel in conjunction with the Nine Chief Ministers.
Later, officials from the Six Departments (Kē), Circuit Censors (Dào), and officials of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Zhānshì) were added.
In the twenty-seventh year of Kāngxī
following the suggestion of Censor Jīng Yuánshí [荊元實],
officials such as Zhōu, Xiàn, Tóng, Tōng, etc., after drawing lots for vacancies,
were all to be granted imperial audience with their memorials,
a practice continued by later generations.
Historically,
when ministers inspected monthly officials,
they would report those found to have improper conduct, illegitimate origins, grandfathers or fathers with arrears in land tax, or whose personal qualities did not match the vacant position.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
when monthly officials had unsuitable personal qualities,
the Emperor would personally reassign them during the imperial audience,
which greatly helped to remedy the shortcomings of the selection system.
In the tenth year
when monthly officials were granted audience,
the Emperor deemed four individuals, including Magistrate Zhōu Zhòng [周仲], to be infirm,
and specifically demoted them to educational posts.
In the twelfth year
he personally again dismissed four infirm and incompetent magistrates,
and severely reprimanded the inspecting officials for not impeaching them.
Subsequently, Zhōu, Xiàn, Tóng, Tōng officials assigned, awaiting appointment, or on probation,
were also all granted imperial audience,
not limited to substantive officials.
Over time,
Zhōu, Xiàn, Tóng, Tōng officials appointed to external posts,
as well as miscellaneous officials assigned,
were able to cite precedent to be exempted from imperial audience through donation,
and inspection was increasingly viewed as a mere formality,
of little significance.
The interchangeability of internal and external officials
already had established precedents.
Initially, a system of internal promotion and external transfer was implemented.
Within the capital, officials from the four yamens of Hánlín, Zhānshì, Kē, and Dào were considered the most reputable and upright,
and their promotions and transfers were distinct from other officials.
Compilers (Biānxiū) and Revisers (Jiǎnǎo) promoted to Grand Secretaries (Zhōngyǔn) and Sub-Grand Secretaries (Zànshàn) were called "opening the memorial archway" (kāifāng).
Other officials, such as those from Hánlín, Zhānshì, Fāng, Jú, officials of the Guózǐjiān (Imperial Academy), and capital-based officials (Jīngtáng),
were all eligible for promotion and transfer.
Those who excelled in the grand examination
were promoted without regard to usual sequence.
External transfers began in the tenth year of Shùnzhì

when an imperial edict stipulated that twenty-one officials from Assistant Supervisor of Instruction (Shǎozhānshì) downwards be employed as provincial administrators (Sī) and circuit intendants (Dào).
Those with excellent administrative records
were promoted internally to capital-based officials.
Soon after, it was further stipulated that Supervisors of Instruction (Zhānshì) and Assistant Supervisors of Instruction be used as Provincial Administrative Commissioners (Bùzhèng);
Academicians of the Imperial Academy (Shìdú Xuéshì) as Provincial Judicial Commissioners (Ànchá);
Grand Secretaries as Provincial Administration Vice Commissioners (Cānzhèng);
and Compilers and Revisers as Provincial Surveillance Vice Commissioners (Fùshǐ).
In the eighteenth year
it was again stipulated that one official from Academician of the Imperial Academy downwards be transferred externally each spring and autumn.
Academicians (Dú) and Lecturers (Jiǎng) were used as Provincial Administration Vice Commissioners,
Editors (Xiūzhuàn) as Provincial Surveillance Vice Commissioners,
and Compilers and Revisers as Provincial Administration Counselors (Cānyì).
This practice was suspended not long after.
In the twenty-fifth year of Kāngxī
ordinary Hánlín officials were evaluated
and appointed externally as Prefectural Sub-magistrates (Tóngzhī), Assistant Salt Commissioners (Yùnfù), or Assistant Prefects (Tíjǔ Tōngpàn).
In the twenty-eighth year
Compiler Lǐ Tāo [李濤] was exceptionally appointed as a Prefect (Zhīfǔ).
The appointment of Hánlín officials as Prefects began with Lǐ Tāo.
In the thirty-seventh year
Assistant Censor-in-Chief Wú Hán [吳涵] stated that the promotions and transfers of Compilers and Revisers were slow,
and requested their exceptional external appointment.
He suggested that, following the precedent of Compiler Lǐ Tāo and Reviser Wāng Jí [汪楫],
one or two be appointed as Prefects.
If exceptional reassignments were made,
he requested that, following the precedent of Assistant Supervisor of Instruction Wáng Shìzhēn [王士禎] and Xú Cháo [徐潮],
Academician Gù Zǎo [顧藻],
and Compiler Wáng Jiǔlíng [王九齡],
they be appointed as Vice Censor-in-Chief (Fùdū Yùshǐ) or Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tōngzhèngshǐ).
The Emperor accepted his suggestion,
and appointed Reviser Liú Hán [劉涵] as Prefect.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
due to the large number of Compilers, Revisers, and Hánlín Shùjíshì,
they were appointed internally to the Six Departments, Circuit Censors, and Ministry of Personnel,
and externally to Circuit Intendants, Prefects, Zhōu and Xiàn,
to ease the congestion.
Thereafter, Compilers and Revisers were often promoted internally to the Fāng vacancies,
appointed as Six Departments officials or Circuit Censors,
and externally as Circuit Intendants or Prefects,
which became the norm.
The Ministry of Personnel was the chief of the Six Ministries.
Initially, it was stipulated that one departmental official (Sīguān) would be promoted internally and one transferred externally each year.
Later,
this system was abolished.
In the eighth year of Kāngxī
it was reinstated based on the suggestion of Censor Yú Jìn [余縉].
In the fortieth year
the practice was again suspended,
and they were subject to salary comparisons like officials of other ministries.
Censorial Officials (Gěishìzhōng) were promoted and transferred once a year,
and Censors (Yùshǐ) twice.
They were exceptionally appointed externally as Circuit Intendants or Prefects,
and promoted internally to capital-based officials.
In the fifty-ninth year
an imperial edict established the salary-period system:
for those appointed from Compilers, Revisers, or Department Directors (Lángzhōng), the limit was two years;
for those appointed from Assistant Department Directors (Yuánwàiláng) or Secretaries (Zhǔshì), it increased by one year successively.
In the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng
it was stipulated that Six Departments officials and Circuit Censors be promoted and transferred once every three years.
In the fifty-fifth year
Internal officials appointed externally,
besides the Capital Grand Review (Jīngchá), had the system of "selected for recommendation" (jiéqǔ bǎosòng),
all awaiting completion of their salary term for recommendation.
For selected for recommendation and assignment,
the choice of busy or simple posts
was determined by the chief official.
Prefects, Magistrates, County Magistrates, Assistant Magistrates, and Assistant Prefects could all change to external posts according to their seniority.
External officials promoted internally,
initially limited to three Sī and Dào officials annually.
Hàn Chinese were limited to those from the examination system, and also those highly distinguished and exceptionally recommended after their salary term.
The system of selecting prefecture magistrates (zhīxiàn) for promotion
was modeled after the Míng dynasty system.
Initially, officials recommended or known to be competent were eligible to be considered for selection as censors (kē) or circuit intendants (dào).
During the Kāngxī reign, several imperial edicts ordered the ministers of the Board (bùchén) to select able and virtuous individuals
for internal appointments as censors (kē) or circuit intendants (dào).

Guō Xiù, the prefecture magistrate (zhīxiàn) of Wújiāng; Shào Sìyáo, the prefecture magistrate (zhīxiàn) of Qīngyuàn; Péng Péng, the prefecture magistrate (zhīxiàn) of Sānhé; Lù Lóngqí, the prefecture magistrate (zhīxiàn) of Língshòu; and Zhào Cāngbì, the prefecture magistrate (zhīxiàn) of Máchéng,
were all recommended by high officials
and selected for promotion to the post of Imperial Censor (yùshǐ),
and were considered excellent appointments.
In the forty-third year [of Kāngxī],
the Governor (chuānfǔ) Néng Tài requested to abolish the system of recommendation by governors-general (dū) and governors (fǔ),
and the Emperor approved it.
An edict then stipulated that henceforth, prefecture magistrates (zhīxiàn) without outstanding tax (qiánliáng) or banditry (dào'àn) cases
would be selected for promotion in numbers of three or four per province (shěng).
The following year,
Imperial Censor (yùshǐ) Huáng Bǐngzhōng stated that selecting prefecture magistrates (zhīxiàn) for promotion to censor (kē) or circuit intendant (dào)
felt too abrupt.
The court deliberated and decided to halt it.
Soon after, it was stipulated that selections for promotion would occur once every three years,
with five officials from Zhílì, Jiāngnán, Húguǎng, and Shǎnxī each,
and varying numbers of three or one from other provinces (yúshěng),
to be appointed as secretaries (zhǔshì).
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
the Minister of Justice (xíngbù shàngshū) Xú Běn requested the restoration of the old system of selecting Imperial Censors (yùshǐ) for promotion,
but it was obstructed by the Board's deliberations.
Officials selected for promotion and appointed as secretaries (zhǔshì)
were initially easy to select and fill,
but later, with the interposition of purchased appointments,
it became severely congested.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
an order was issued to follow the precedent of military officers recommended and registered,
allowing them to remain in their original posts.
Those who had already gone to the capital (jīng)
were permitted to be appointed externally as assistant prefects (tóngzhī).
At that time, various provinces (gèshěng) regarded these selections for promotion as mere formalities,
typically choosing officials from lower-grade prefectures (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) who had no reprimands or penalties.
In the sixteenth year, this system was abolished.
By the late Guāngxù reign,
officials holding substantive posts (shíguān) at or above the prefecture (zhōu) and county (xiàn) level, as well as those who had previously acted in vacant posts,
were uniformly examined for the position of Imperial Censor (yùshǐ).
This was no longer the original intention of selecting for promotion,
and it was also abandoned after a short period.
Appointments and selections (quánxuǎn) were made according to prescribed regulations and proposed recommendations,
with vacancies filled by drawing lots,
constrained by established precedents.
Throughout the dynasties, a system of recommendation (bǎojiàn zhì) was occasionally implemented
to compensate for the shortcomings of the regular appointment system.
In the early Shùnzhì reign,
the system of joint responsibility for recommendations was established.
In the twelfth year,
due to the strategic importance of thirty prefectures (fǔ), including Bǎodìng and Héjiān in Zhílì;
Jiāngníng, Huái, Yáng, Sū, Sōng, Cháng, and Zhèn in Jiāngnán;
and Háng, Jiā, Hú, and Shào in Zhèjiāng,
an edict ordered high officials (tángguān) in the capital (jīng) and provinces (wài), governors-general (dū), and governors (fǔ) to each recommend one person for imperial selection (bèijiǎn),
to be promoted without regard to seniority.
Later,
some failed due to corruption and incompetence.
The Supervising Secretary (gěishìzhōng) Rèn Kèpǔ stated:
"The Emperor has identified thirty prefectures (zhīfǔ) among all in the empire as the most complex and difficult to govern,
allowing officials of the second rank (èrpǐn) and above to recommend candidates,
to be appointed outside the usual rules.
But in a short time,
several have been impeached and dismissed for corruption and inferiority.
These ministers have failed to align with the Emperor's sagely intention
and select impartially and carefully.
I request that they be subjected to official deliberation (lìyì)."
This was adopted.
In the seventh year of Kāngxī,
an edict stipulated that talented and outstanding Manchu and Han officials of the Boards (bù) and Censorate (yuàn)
were permitted to be appointed without considering their seniority (zī).
The following year,
the Board of Civil Office (lìbù) requested to abolish recommendations,
and instead follow promotion based on salary seniority,
to prevent illicit maneuvering and bribery.
This was approved.
In the fortieth year,
governors-general (zǒngdū) Guō Xiù and Zhāng Pénghé,
and governors (xúnfǔ) Péng Péng and Lǐ Guāngdì,
were ordered to each recommend benevolent and incorruptible circuit intendants (dào), prefects (fǔ), prefecture magistrates (zhōu), and county magistrates (xiàn).
Upon the enthronement of Shìzōng [Yōngzhèng Emperor],

he repeatedly ordered high officials in the capital (jīng) and provinces (wài) to recommend circuit intendants (dào), prefects (fǔ), assistant prefects (tóng), sub-prefectural magistrates (tōng), prefecture magistrates (zhōu), and county magistrates (xiàn).
Those who recommended unsuitable individuals
often faced severe reprimands.
The Minister of Revenue (hùbù shàngshū) Shǐ Yízhí stated:
"Promotions (qiāndié) should follow qualifications (zīgé).
While qualifications may not produce exceptional talents,
they can cultivate mediocre ones.
Abandoning seniority and ranks,
the opportunistically advanced do not regard it as fair encouragement,
but secretly rejoice in their unique skill at advancement;
the stagnated do not blame their own lack of talent,
but merely resent the absence of a path to promotion.
I request to follow the old system,
advancing step by step, rank by rank,
with appointments in sequence.
If there are indeed outstanding talents
and excellent administrative achievements,
they may still be recommended for promotion outside the usual rules."
This was adopted.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
the system of recommendation (bǎojiàn) was strictly enforced,
and many circuit intendants (sī), prefects (dào), and commanders of garrisons (jùnshǒu)
were selected through this method.
In the first year of Xuānzōng [Dàoguāng Emperor],
Director (lángzhōng) Zhèng Yù, Prefect (zhīfǔ) Ā Lín, and Táng Zhòngmiǎn
were all promoted by high officials
to provincial positions (fāngmiàn) and key regional posts (jiāngqí).
This practice continued through the dynasties,
generally tasking officials with recommending virtuous and capable individuals,
and occasionally appointing them outside the usual rules.
Initially, capital (jīng) officials were selected as circuit intendants (dào) and prefects (fǔ).
If provincial authorities (jiānglì) found their abilities insufficient for the post,
they would memorialize to request their transfer back to capital (jīng) appointments,
and often this was granted.
In the early Qiánlóng reign,
court officials (tíngchén) stated that senile and incompetent individuals should not be allowed to defile official positions (cáosī),
and an edict strictly prohibited this.
Thereafter, external officials whose abilities were lacking
were only eligible for retirement or demotion and reassignment,
and no longer for internal appointments.
Official promotions were based on salary,
but external officials' promotions were determined by years of service and merit (niánláo wéi chà),
differing from capital (jīng) ranks.
External officials had frontier salaries (biānfèng) and inner salaries (fùfèng).
For those with inner salaries (fùfèng), circuit intendants (dào), prefects (fǔ), prefecture magistrates (zhōu), assistant county magistrates (xiàn zuò'èr), and heads of departments (shǒulǐngguān),
if they had no faults for five years,
they were typically eligible for promotion.
Frontier salaries (biānfèng) differed.
Counties (xiàn) like Yázhōu, Gǎn'ēn, Chānghuà, and Língshuǐ in Guǎngdōng;

prefectures (fǔ), sub-prefectures (tīng), departments (zhōu), and counties (xiàn) like Bǎisè, Tàipíng, Níngmíng, Míngjiāng, Zhèn'ān, Sìchéng, Língyún, Xīlóng, and Xīlín in Guǎngxī, as well as dozens of miscellaneous posts (zázhí) like Zhōngzhōu and Héchí,
were considered miasmatic (yānzhàng) posts.
Sub-prefectural magistrates (tōngpàn) and assistant prefects (tóngzhī) of prefectures (fǔ) like Yuánjiāng, Hèqìng, Guǎngnán, Pǔ'ěr, Zhāotōng, and Zhènbiān in Yúnnán;
and departments (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) like Zhènxíóng, Ēnlè, Ēn'ān, Yǒngshàn, Níng'ěr, and Bǎoníng;
the military readiness circuit intendant (bīngbèidào) of Gǔzhōu in Guìzhōu;
assistant prefects (tóngzhī) of prefectures (fǔ) like Lípíng, Zhènyuǎn, Dūyún, and Tóngrén;
sub-prefectural magistrates (tōngpàn) of Qīngjiāng, Dūjiāng, and Dānjiāng;
prefecture magistrate (zhīzhōu) of Yǒngfēng;
county magistrate (zhīxiàn) of Lìbō;
and assistant prefects (tóngzhī) of Mǎbiān and Yuèxí in Sìchuān,
were considered Miaoland (miáojiāng) posts.
All these, upon completing three years of service with their full salary,
if they had administrative achievements and no major faults,
were typically promoted.
Ten counties (xiàn) like Tàicāng and Shànghǎi in Jiāngsū;
seventeen counties (xiàn) like Rénhé and Hǎiníng in Zhèjiāng;
seven departments (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) like Zhūchéng and Jiāozhōu in Shāndōng;
thirteen counties (xiàn) like Dōngguǎn and Xiāngshān in Guǎngdōng;
and nine counties (xiàn) like Mǐnhóu in Fújiàn,
were considered coastal (yánhǎi) posts.
Twelve departments (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) like Liángxiāng and Tōngzhōu in Zhílì;
eleven departments (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) like Xiángfú and Zhèngzhōu in Hénán;
thirteen departments (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) like Dézhōu and Dōngpíng in Shāndōng;
and thirteen departments (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) like Shānyáng and Pízhōu in Jiāngnán,
were considered riverside (yánhé) posts.
Promotions based on service in these posts
were similar to those with frontier salaries (biānfèng).
In frontier regions (biānjiāng) with harsh climates and environments,
promotions might occur even before three years.
For areas where the climate was not extremely harsh,
and Miaoland (miáojiāng) was not extremely critical,
promotions might be similar to those with inner salaries (fùfèng).
During the Qiánlóng reign,
regulations were established for long-term service in frontier (biānquè), barbarian (yíjiāng), and maritime (hǎijiāng) posts,
where promotions required eight or six full years,
thus selecting people for specific places,
without being constrained by ordinary rules.
Recommendation for promotion was a system of national reward,
intended to encourage diligence and acknowledge merit.
Successive dynasties compiled Veritable Records (Shílù),
and various bureaus were commanded to compile books.
Rewards were also given to those who distinguished themselves in military camps, river conservancy, tax collection, and bandit suppression in various provinces.
In the eleventh year of Kāngxī, when the Shìzǔ Shílù was completed,
and in the forty-ninth year, when the Píngdìng Shuòmò Fānglüè was completed,
officials from vice-presidents (fùzǒngcái) downwards were merely rewarded with a raise in rank.
In the sixty-first year, when the Suànfǎ (Mathematical Methods) was completed,
it was first proposed to grant third-class merits,
rewarding those due for promotion (yìngshēng), those due for a raise in rank (jiāděng), or those for immediate appointment (jíyòng) with distinctions.
When the Shílù of the Kāngxī and Yōngzhèng reigns were completed,
the request from the presidents (zǒngcái) was followed,
with no further deliberation.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
officials of the Imperial Historiography Institute (Xiūshūguǎn) requested extraordinary first or second-class commendations,
but the emperor disallowed it.
Soon after, it was decreed that officials not specially appointed by imperial edict
should not be considered for promotion or appointment,
a rule that was followed by subsequent generations.
In cases of rewards for military camps, river conservancy, etc.,
they initially did not exceed a raise in rank,
or promotion without waiting for the full term of service,
as official positions and honors (míngqì) were not to be obtained by chance.
However, in later times, recommendations became a shortcut,
and reward cases in the capital and provinces
often abused the system and disregarded established precedents.
In the first year of Guāngxù,
Censor Wáng Róngguǎn requested a ban on promotions skipping ranks.
The emperor approved.
In the third year,
as the compilation of the Mùzōng Shílù was more than halfway complete,
all participating officials were promoted and granted additional titles,
receiving exceptionally high commendations.
In the tenth year,
the Board (bù) deliberated on restricting recommendations,
stating that five- or six-rank officials in Beijing (Jīngtáng), Hanlin (Hàn), and Zhan事 (Zhànshì) academies,
as well as those filling vacancies through imperial audience (yùquētízòu),
were not to be recommended arbitrarily.
Not long after,
there were still cases of candidates for Langzhong (lángzhōng) being recommended for Jīngtáng,
or compilers (biān), proofreaders (jiǎn) for four or five-rank academy positions,
and those due for promotion being listed at the forefront.
During the military campaigns of Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì,
recommendation cases surged.
The Board of Civil Office (Lìbù) established a special department within the Department of Selection (Wénxuǎnsī) to oversee audits,
the complexity of which
was comparable to that of an entire department.
In the twelfth year of Tóngzhì,
Fujian Governor (Mǐnfǔ) Wáng Kǎitài said:
"Since the outbreak of military campaigns,
recommendation cases have accumulated, and
after the opening of donation systems (kāijuān), schemes have become numerous.
Military camp recommendations
used various schemes to vie for precedence, and
other types of recommendations
also adopted military camp names, arriving in droves.
The abuse of official positions and honors (míngqì)
has reached its extreme.
Thousands upon hundreds
merely add to the redundancy.
I request an imperial edict instructing the Board to examine and verify personnel in all ranks, both in the capital and provinces,
retaining two or three tenths,
and ordering the rest to return home to await further notice."
This was sent to the relevant department for review and deliberation.
Aside from military merits,
those widely considered redundant and abusive
were river conservancy recommendations.
In the twentieth year of Guāngxù,
Censor Zhāng Zhòngxīn said:
"Shāndōng river conservancy recommendations
have recently amounted to five or six hundred people.
The Board stipulates that for one breach,
six people are rewarded as extraordinary or ordinary.
The number of breaches reported by that province
is often measured by the number of people recommended.
Those seeking recommendations use Shāndōng as a shortcut.
Donating for a county assistant (xiànchéng) or miscellaneous clerk (zuǒzá),
they become a proper magistrate (zhèngyìn) in just a few months.
I request that the relevant department be ordered to strictly set regulations."
The emperor approved his request.
In the thirty-second year,
Censor Liú Rǔjì again said:
"Among the maladies of governance,
none is worse than the path of recommendation.
Those who deceive superiors for private gain
are, firstly, from river conservancy.
The state spends hundreds of thousands of taels (tángjīn) annually to strengthen river defenses,
but frontier governors (fēngjiāng dàlì) use this as a means to adjust their subordinates.
If fortunately nothing happens,
county assistants (chéng), sub-magistrates (cuì) are recommended as magistrates (zhōu), counties (xiàn);
department administrators (tóng), prefectural assistants (tōng) are recommended as prefects (fǔ), circuits (dào).
Secondly, military merits.
The clamor of factories
or the gathering of hungry people
are often exaggerated as 'great punitive expeditions.'
Those who have never heard a drum
nor set foot on a battlefield,
but falsely claim to have killed enemies and achieved results,
or to have personally experienced a hundred battles,
are ubiquitous.
Thirdly, encouraging donations (quànjuān).
The Shùntiān famine relief donation case
saw over 1,300 people recommended;
Shāndōng labor relief (gōngzhèn) saw over 500 people recommended;
other provinces annually accounted for no fewer than a thousand people.
I request a strict prohibition against favoritism and indiscriminate recommendations
to prevent undeserved advancement."
This was sent to the relevant department to deliberate on methods of restriction.
At that time, the Board of Civil Office received four or five hundred applications (tóugōng) monthly,
and three or four hundred appointments (fēnfā).
The original selection department (Xuǎnsī) had a dedicated assignment office (Pàibànchù),
with over ten people managing its affairs,
yet it still feared inadequacy.
In its final years, it resolutely abolished donation for office (juānnà)
and suspended Board selection (bùxuǎn),
as a plan to unblock official careers
and carefully select magistrates (zhōu), counties (xiàn).
However, although the donation system was suspended,
old donation-based rewards
continued to emerge endlessly.
Furthermore, after the abolition of the imperial examination system (kējǔ),
graduates of modern schools
were directly rewarded with official positions.
The number of recommended candidates (jǔ), tribute students (gòng), and regular students (shēngyuán) taking examinations for official positions
greatly exceeded the usual quota.
Moreover, descendants of meritorious officials
were all granted official ranks,
and newly appointed personnel
were granted nominal titles and transferred by imperial rescript.
The resulting confusion and complexity
made it even harder to manage.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng,
the Board of Civil Office was abolished,
and a Ministry of Civil Appointments (Quánjú) was established.
Although there was an opportunity to refresh political administration,
the civil appointment system of that era
ultimately could not be purified.
Military officials were subordinate to the Board of War (Bīngbù).
The selection and appointment of Eight Banners (Bāqí) and camp (yíng), guard (wèi) officials
were managed by the Department of Military Selection (Wǔxuǎnsī).
Internally, the various camps of Valiant Cavalry (Xiāoqí), Vanguard (Qiánfēng), Elite Guard (Hùjūn), Infantry (Bùjūn), Firearms (Huǒqì), Agile Braves (Jiànruì), and Tiger Spear (Hǔqiāng);

externally, the posts at imperial tombs (língqǐn), hunting grounds (wéichǎng), Rèhé, Ūliyasutai, Kēbùduō, Ā'ěrtài, Ūliánghǎi, Xīníng, Xīzàng, Tǎ'ěrbāhātái nomadic areas, Cháhā'ěr, Suīyuǎnchéng, and garrisons in various provinces,
were all Banner (qí) vacancies,
belonging to the Eight Banners.
Gate Commander (Ménqiānzǒng) was a gate (mén) vacancy,
belonging to the Han Banners (Hànjūn).
River camps (héyíng), land forces (lùlù), and naval forces (shuǐshī) were all camp (yíng) vacancies,
divided between Manchu and Han.
Grain transport (cáoyùn) was a guard (wèi) vacancy,
which could be filled by both Han Banners and Han people.
For Banner vacancies, positions of Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) and above were listed,
while others were selected.
Fifth rank and above were submitted for appointment (tíbǔ),
sixth rank and below were recommended for appointment (zīmǔ).
For Green Standard Army (Lǜqí) General-in-chief (zǒngbīng) and above,
initially a joint recommendation (huìtuī) was used,
but this rule was later abolished,
and they were listed and submitted.
Brigade-General (fùjiàng) candidates were presented for imperial audience (yǐnjiàn),
and some were also listed.
Important vacancies were submitted (tí),
lesser ones were recommended (tuī),
and battalion commanders (bǎzǒng) were appointed by selection (bábǔ).
This is a general outline.
Generally, for Manchus and Han Chinese entering officialdom,
there were hereditary posts, *yǐnshēng* (privileges for sons of officials), and military *kēkǎo* (examinations).
For Eight Banners hereditary posts,
Gōng, Hóu, Bó, Zǐ, Nán were appointed as Fùdūtǒng.
Qīngchē Dūwèi and Qí Dūwèi were appointed as Zuǒlǐng.
Yúnqí Wèi were appointed as Fángyù.
Ēnqí Wèi were appointed as Xiāoqí Xiào.
For Han Chinese, Bó, Zǐ, Nán were appointed as Fùjiàng.
Qīngchē Dūwèi were appointed as Cānjiàng.
Qí Dūwèi were appointed as Yóují or Dūsī.
Yúnqí Wèi were appointed as Shǒubèi.
For officials from Shàngshū down to Fùdū Yùshǐ,
and *yǐnshēng* of Zǒngdū, Jiāngjūn down to second-rank Fùjiàng who switched to military service,
they were appointed as Dūsī, Shǒubèi, Shǒuyùsuǒ Qiānzǒng, Wèi Qiānzǒng.
For military *jìnshì* (first-degree graduates), the first-rank number one was appointed as Touděng Shìwèi.
Numbers two and three were appointed as Èrděng Shìwèi.
From the second and third ranks, ten were selected and appointed as Sānděng Shìwèi.
Sixteen were appointed as Lánlíng Shìwèi.
The rest were appointed to fill vacancies as Yíng Wèi Shǒubèi.
For Han Chinese military *jǔrén* (second-degree graduates) and Han Banner military *jǔrén*, those selected for the first and second ranks were appointed as Mén Qiānzǒng and Yíng Qiānzǒng.
Those of the third rank were appointed as Wèi Qiānzǒng.
For those promoted based on seniority and merit,
such as Yíngwǔ chāi guān,
Títáng,
Suíbāng,
Suíyíng Chāicāo,
Jīngzhì and Wàiwěi,
Qiānzǒng, Bǎzǒng, and officials without responsibility who achieved merit,
those promoted with titles from Dūdū down to Fùjiàng for their accomplishments were appointed as Yóují.
Those promoted with titles of Cānjiàng or Yóují were appointed as Dūsī.
Those promoted with titles of Dūsī or Shǒubèi were appointed as Shǒubèi.
Those promoted with the title of Qiānzǒng were promoted to Bǎzǒng.
Military *jìnshì* and military *jǔrén* serving as Títáng chāi guān for three full years,
after being examined by the Board in archery and horsemanship,
the excellent ones were appointed as Yíng Wèi Shǒubèi.
The next best military *jǔrén* were appointed as Fángyùsuǒ Qiānzǒng.
Military *jǔrén* serving in Suíyíng Chāicāo for three full years
were promoted to Yíng Qiānzǒng.
Those serving in Suíbāng for three full terms
were appointed as Wèi Qiānzǒng.
For vacancies recommended by the Board,
in the second month of the year,
for Cānjiàng and Yóují vacancies,
one Han Chinese First or Second Rank Shìwèi was appointed.
In the fourth, sixth, and eighth months, for Yóují and Dūsī vacancies,
three Han Chinese Third Rank Shìwèi were appointed.
In the first, third, fifth, seventh, and ninth months, for Dūsī vacancies,
five Lánlíng Shìwèi were appointed.
In the first and seventh months, for Yíng Shǒubèi vacancies,
Mén Qiānzǒng and Wèi Qiānzǒng were promoted.
For other odd-month vacancies, there were seven rotation groups for appointments.
For even-month vacancies, there were twelve rotation groups for appointments.
For Wèi Shǒubèi odd-month vacancies, there were eleven rotation groups for appointments.
For even-month vacancies, there were six rotation groups for appointments.
For Shǒuyùsuǒ Qiānzǒng and Wèi Qiānzǒng vacancies,
appointments were made regardless of odd or even months.
