However, Mén Qiānzǒng were exclusively selected in even months.
Manchus entering officialdom,
especially those from prominent families,
often started as Shìwèi or Bàitáng'ā.
Traditionally,
sons of Manchu ministers, both central and local,
were selected as Shìwèi or Bàitáng'ā once every five years.
As a result, idle personnel,
and members of old noble families,
once selected,
served in the imperial guard,
and were subsequently appointed to important external positions.
It was common
for them to achieve prominent offices within a few years.
For the Green Standard military officers,
there were even more vacancies.
According to old regulations, for Fùjiàng, Cānjiàng, Yóují, Dūsī, and Shǒubèi vacancies from Shānhǎiguān to Shāhǔkǒu and Báodézhōu,
Green Standard officers filled three-tenths,
while Manchu officers filled seven-tenths.
For the two garrisons of Mǎlán and Tàiníng,
and Fùjiàng, Cānjiàng, Yóují, Dūsī, and Shǒubèi vacancies along the borders of Zhílì and Shānxī,
Manchu and Han Chinese each filled one part.
In the sixth year of Yōngzhèng,
Fùdūtǒng Zōngshì Mǎnzhūxīlǐ argued that from Cānjiàng down to Qiānzǒng in the capital garrisons,
it was inappropriate to exclusively use Han Chinese.
An imperial edict was issued:
"The number of Manchus is inherently small.
Appointing them to important central and external positions is sufficient.
If all positions from Cānjiàng downwards in the capital garrisons were filled by Manchus,
then the numbers would be insufficient,
and there would inevitably be vacancies without personnel to fill them."
During the Qiánlóng reign,
Manchus were often selected for military positions in various provinces.
The Emperor said:
"For Green Standard generals,
Manchus and Han Chinese should be employed together.
The number of personnel and vacancies must be appropriately balanced
to conform to the system.
If Manchu officers are generally selected,
over time,
the Green Standard will become entirely Manchu vacancies,
which is not conducive to broadening selection and encouraging talent."
He ordered the relevant department to deliberate on a method for alternating Manchu and Han Chinese appointments.
The Board of War submitted its deliberation:
All Han Chinese Shìwèi who had served for two full years,
and Manchu and Mongol personnel of the Eight Banners in the Xúnbǔyíng,
were to be recommended and registered by their respective supervising ministers.
During selection,
they, along with those awaiting appointment or recommendation in the Board,
were to be presented for imperial audience, divided by Manchu and Han Chinese.
This was implemented as deliberated.
In the thirty-eighth year,
the Board of War again memorialized:
"In the five provinces of Zhílì, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Gānsù, and Sìchuān,
from Fùjiàng to Shǒubèi, there are 647 Manchu vacancies.
In each province, from Fùjiàng to Shǒubèi,
there are 1,179 vacancies
traditionally filled by Green Standard personnel.
Currently, the number of Manchu and Mongol personnel in the Green Standard exceeds the original quota by more than double.
This is truly because when provinces request personnel,
they mostly select Manchu officers.
We request that, from now on, besides provinces that originally used Manchu officers,
for provinces in the heartland like Hénán, Shāndōng, Jiāngnán, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and coastal and malarial provinces like Mǐn, Zhè, and Liǎngguǎng,
when requesting personnel for selection,
they should select from Green Standard personnel awaiting appointment or recommendation,
and recommended personnel,
as well as First, Second, and Third Rank Shìwèi and Lánlíng Shìwèi who have served for the required number of years,
all together."
This was approved.
From then on, the balance of Manchu and Han Chinese vacancies in the Green Standard began to stabilize slightly,
no longer being as unrestricted as before.
Military officers from the ranks (*hángwǔ*) were considered the proper path,
while those from the *kēmù* (examination system) were secondary.
Traditionally,
those among the personnel recommended by the Board who were found to be old, infirm, or disabled were
ordered to retire.
However, those with military injuries,
even if old, were still recommended for appointments.
Fùjiàng and Cānjiàng were usually appointed by promotion from Cānjiàng and Yóují based on seniority in their stipends.
However, if there was a recommendation for military merit,
even those with less seniority in stipends could be included.
The *kēmù* system suffered from stagnation from the early Kāngxī reign.
Censor Zhū Fěi memorialized, requesting a system of separate vacancies for *kēmù* and *hángwǔ*.
Comparing the numbers of Wàiwěi and those with effective service to military *jìnshì* and military *jǔrén*,
he suggested a two-to-eight split of vacancies,
prioritizing the selection of *kēmù* personnel.
As for the various Wàiwěi officers,
they must have actual military achievements and records of suppressing banditry,
and not merely be selected based on referrals.
This was sent to the relevant department for deliberation and implementation.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
court officials proposed merging the various *wèi* and *suǒ* with the *zhōu* and *xiàn*.
The Board deliberated:
"Personnel from the *kējiǎ* (examination system) are specifically selected for Wèi Suǒ Shǒubèi and Qiānzǒng.
If all *wèi* and *suǒ* are abolished,
it will inevitably lead to stagnation in the selection process,
which is not feasible."
The Emperor disallowed it.
Instead, he decided to increase the use of Yíng Shǒubèi for newly successful *jìnshì* to adjust the balance.
In the fifteenth year of Qiánlóng,
Grand Secretary Yáng Èryǒu said:
"There are thirty-nine vacancies for provincial and *wèi* Shǒubèi selected by the Board.
Currently, military *jìnshì* designated for *wèi* positions have accumulated to several hundred people.
Títáng chāi guān and those who have completed their effective service and returned to the selection queue also number several tens.
Adding to this, the new system allows for faster appointments to bypass the queue,
resulting in fewer vacancies and more candidates,
with no fixed date for selection.
I request that, in accordance with the regulation of the first year of Qiánlóng,
Third Rank military *jìnshì* be re-selected.
First and Second Ranks be designated for *yíng* positions,
and Third Ranks still for *wèi* positions."
This was approved.
Traditionally, military *jìnshì* selected for *yíng* positions
found vacancies more easily,
while those designated for *wèi* positions often stagnated and could not obtain office.
By the Dàoguāng reign,
military *jìnshì* designated for *wèi* positions were allowed to donate money to change to *yíng* positions.
And the abolished Wèi Shǒubèi, Wèi Qiānzǒng, and Shǒuyùsuǒ Qiānzǒng vacancies
were all permitted to be reclassified under the Green Standard.
Officials from Yíng Shǒubèi upwards
were also allowed to donate money for appointments.
Consequently, both Board recommendations and external appointments
suffered the same stagnation,
and not just those from the *kēmù* system.
All vacancies not subject to departmental recommendation
were to be filled first by those registered as *yùbǎo*.
It was a standing rule that vacancies for naval officers in border regions, inland rivers, and the open sea, as well as crucial positions in the land forces, could be filled by *yùbǎo*.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī's reign (1670),
the Ministry of War submitted a memorial stating:
“When a Governor-General (*zǒngdū*), Provincial Commander-in-Chief (*tí*), or Brigade-General (*zhèn*) encounters vacancies for banner (*biāo*) or battalion (*yíng*) officers,
regardless of the urgency of the locality,
if the rank and vacancy are suitable,
they often directly nominate banner officers by name to fill them,
causing many experienced officers who should be promoted to be obstructed.
We request a regulation that when vacancies arise for officers from Vice-General (*fùjiàng*) down to Company Commander (*shǒubèi*) up,
only those who are truly suitable for coastal, border, or mountainous regions
be considered for nomination and appointment.
Others should not be hastily nominated and requested.”
This was adopted.
In the fifth year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1727),

an edict ordered that vacancies subject to departmental recommendation be nominated and held in reserve by the various Governors-General (*dū*), Governors (*fǔ*), Provincial Commanders-in-Chief (*tí*), and Brigade-Generals (*zhèn*).
In the early years of Qiánlóng's reign,
the *yùbǎo* system for land forces in provinces near the capital was abolished.
In the tenth year (1745),
Yǐn Jìshàn, the Governor-General of Jiāngnán, stated:
“The *yùbǎo* system for military officials,
where one registers with the ministry
and is drawn to fill a vacancy,
is indeed an excellent method for handling important positions with caution.
However, sometimes at the beginning of *yùbǎo*,
one's vigor is strong,
but after several years, one gradually becomes old and infirm,
loses proficiency in riding and archery,
and becomes lax in military discipline.
I request that those who have been *yùbǎo* for three full years and have not yet obtained a vacancy
be re-evaluated by the respective Provincial Commanders-in-Chief.
If they are indeed suitable for promotion,
a performance review should be issued and submitted to the ministry;
otherwise, they should be struck off the register.”
This was approved.
At that time, recommendations were divided into three grades,
with a limit of five years.

Particular care was taken in selecting Vice-Generals (*fùjiàng*) suitable for promotion to Commander-in-Chief (*zǒngbīng*), and Colonels (*cānjīàng*) suitable for promotion to Vice-General (*fùjiàng*).
Once recommended,
they were immediately promoted.
By the time of the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì military campaigns,
the old system of recommendation for over ten years was no longer practiced.
The only means of encouraging talent
was through recommendations for military merit (*jūngōng bǎojǔ*).
Cases of commendation
were endless.
The number of common soldiers who, through accumulated merit, were nominated for promotion to Provincial Commander-in-Chief (*tí*) or Brigade-General (*zhèn*)
is almost incalculable.
In the fifth year of Tóngzhì's reign (1866),
an edict ordered that those nominated as Provincial Commander-in-Chief (*tí*) or Brigade-General (*zhèn*) who had no banner or battalion to return to
be dispatched to various provinces for temporary assignments in various camps.
Among those waiting for appointments in various provincial banners,
the Provincial Commanders-in-Chief (*tí*) and Brigade-Generals (*zhèn*) numbered in the tens,
and Vice-Generals (*fù*), Colonels (*cān*), and below numbered in the hundreds.
To be appointed to one's original rank
became a lifelong impossibility.
Thus, the system of temporary appointments (*jièbǔ*) was established.
Provincial Commanders-in-Chief (*tí*) and Brigade-Generals (*zhèn*) were allowed to temporarily fill vacancies of Vice-Generals (*fù*), Colonels (*cān*), or Major-Generals (*yóu*).
Vice-Generals (*fù*), Colonels (*cān*), and Major-Generals (*yóu*) were allowed to temporarily fill vacancies of Regional Commanders (*dū*) or Company Commanders (*shǒubèi*).
Regional Commanders (*dū*) and Company Commanders (*shǒubèi*) were allowed to temporarily fill vacancies of Commanders (*qiān*) or Lieutenants (*bǎzǒng*).
Although departmental recommendations were internally suspended,
and priority appointments externally suspended,
these measures were still insufficient to alleviate the stagnation caused by overstaffing.
In the final years of Guāngxù's reign,
an edict ordered the abolition of the Green Standard Army (*Lùyíng*),
the training of new armies,
the cessation of military examinations (*wǔkē*),
and the establishment of military academies (*wǔbèi xuéxiào*).
At that time, generals and officers of the new army,
as well as those who received official appointments after completing their studies,
were given special preferential treatment.
The intention of past dynasties to respect military officials who rose through the ranks
was completely lost.
Although Green Standard Army military officials were not entirely abolished,
there was virtually no system of selection to speak of.
Volume 86: Elections 6: Performance Review
The method of three-year performance reviews
originated in the Táng and Yú periods.
The Qīng Dynasty followed the Míng system,
but with slightly different classifications and forms.

Metropolitan officials underwent the *Jīngchá* (Metropolitan Review), while provincial officials underwent the *Dàjì* (Grand Review), both managed by the Bureau of Merits (*Kǎogōng Sī*) of the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*).
The *Jīngchá* was conducted in the *zǐ, mǎo, wǔ, yǒu* years,
where officials of ministries, courts, and bureaus were reviewed by their superiors,
evaluated according to four criteria,
with "talent, integrity, governance, and age"
as the benchmarks.
They were divided into three grades: competent (*chēngzhí*), diligent (*qínzhí*), and serving (*gōngzhí*).
Those ranked in the first grade
received a promotion in rank and a commendation,
and were additionally summoned for an audience to be considered for external appointments.
Six rules were used for impeachment:
the indiscreet and weak were dismissed,
the impetuous and incompetent were demoted,
the aged and infirm were retired,
and their reviews were sent to the ministry.
Except for the Hànglín Academy, Grand Secretariat, supervising censors, and circuit censors,
all others were reviewed in order.
For third-rank metropolitan officials, the ministry would list their factual conduct;
for fourth and fifth-rank officials, princes and grand ministers would classify them by grade,
and memorialize the emperor for an audience to receive the imperial decision.
The *Dàjì* was conducted in the *yín, sì, shēn, hài* years.
Beforehand, the Provincial Treasurer (*fān*), Provincial Judicial Commissioner (*niè*), Intendant (*dào*), and Prefect (*fǔ*) would successively examine the worthiness of their subordinates,
reporting to the Governor-General (*dū*) and Governor (*fǔ*).
The Governor-General (*dū*) and Governor (*fǔ*) would review their conduct,
record their evaluations, compile a roster, and send it to the ministry for re-examination.
Those excellent in both talent and integrity
were recommended as outstanding (*zhuóyì*).
Those who were inferior
were impeached according to the six rules.
Those not subject to recommendation or impeachment were classified as ordinary (*píngděng*).
Outstanding officials from District Magistrate (*zhīxiàn*) upwards
were all granted an audience to await the imperial decree.
Disciplinary actions based on the six rules were similar to the *Jīngchá*;
the corrupt and cruel were specifically impeached.
There was a fixed quota for *Jīngchá* first grade and *Dàjì* outstanding officials:
one in seven for metropolitan officials,
one in eight for *bǐtiēshì*,
one in fifteen for Intendants (*dào*), Prefects (*fǔ*), Sub-Prefects (*tīng*), Departments (*zhōu*), and Districts (*xiàn*),
and one in one hundred thirty for minor officials (*zuǒzá*) and education officials (*jiàoguān*).
This was the general rule.
Those who had not completed their full term of service,
or had not reached the age limit,
or were dismissed but retained in office, or had outstanding tax arrears,
or Manchu officials who could not shoot a target or did not understand Manchu language,
were all ineligible for top evaluations.
These were the main provisions.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì's reign (1651),
the *Jīngchá* was first established as a regulation,
set for a six-year cycle.
In the thirteenth year (1656),
the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*) memorialized to establish the regulations:
officials of the third rank and above submitted self-assessments;
for officials of the fourth rank and below, the Ministry of Personnel (*Lìbù*) and the Censorate (*Dūcháyuàn*) conducted reviews and proposed recommendations,
with the emperor personally deciding their retention or dismissal.
*Bǐtiēshì* were reviewed in the same manner as other officials.
During the *Jīngchá*,
all official promotions and transfers were temporarily suspended.
Soon after, a regulation for reviews upon completion of term (*kǎomǎn*) was established,
with the three-year *kǎomǎn* and the six-year *Jīngchá* operating concurrently.
In the seventeenth year (1660),
following the request of Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ Wèi Yìjiè,
the method of impeachment and dismissal (*jiūshí*) was implemented,
to supplement what the evaluations might miss.
In the first year of Kāngxī's reign (1662), the *Jīngchá* was abolished,
and only the three-year *kǎomǎn* system was used.
Officials of the third rank and above still submitted self-assessments.
Other officials were divided into five grades: first grade competent (*chēngzhí*) were recorded,
second grade competent were rewarded,
ordinary were retained,
inferior were demoted,
and incompetent were dismissed.
In the third year (1664),
Censor Jì Zhènyí submitted three memorials requesting the abolition of the *kǎomǎn* system,
arguing vehemently that it led to favoritism and corrupt practices,
and resulted in cumbersome memorials
without aiding in encouragement or punishment.
Consequently, the *kǎomǎn* self-assessment system was suspended.
In the sixth year (1667),
the *Jīngchá* was reinstated.
The following year (1668),
thirty-seven officials were dismissed through evaluation.
Subsequently, as the evaluation of officials in various ministries and courts
often concerned minor positions,
in the twenty-third year (1684),
a strict edict ordered direct impeachment by name,
and an additional thirty-six individuals, including Wáng Sānshěng, were dismissed.
The following year (1685),
the *Jīngchá* was again suspended.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1723), it was reinstated,
changed to a three-year cycle,
and from then on became a fixed system.
Initially,
there was no fixed quota for the first class of the Jīngchá.
In the third year of Kāngxī,
Censor Zhāng Chōngyì submitted a memorial requesting that the number of first and second class officials be determined by the number of officials in the ministries and courts,
in order to curb contention for advancement.
This was approved.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
when ministries and courts recommended officials for the first class,
sometimes the number exceeded the old quota.
An edict was issued to suspend their concurrent service in ministries,
and they were to return to their original yamens for separate reviews.
Furthermore, those who had not served for a full half-year upon arrival
were still to be evaluated by their original yamens.
The practice of recommending unsalaried Shùjíshì for the first class was also abolished,
to show restraint.
In the forty-second year,
it was ordered that the number of first-class officials recommended by ministries and courts
should not rigidly adhere to the precedents of previous terms,
but should be gradually reduced
to prevent exceeding the quota.
The numbers from the previous two occasions should be compared,
and a moderate system established.
This would prevent both indiscriminate recommendations
and the suppression of talent.
In the fiftieth year,
it was stipulated that the number of recommended first-class officials
should not exceed the original quota of the forty-eighth year.
This was followed in later generations,
with occasional increases or decreases,
but no significant disparities.
Traditionally, officials of the ministries and courts were examined by the Lìbù and Dūcháyuan.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was ordered that Grand Secretaries of the Nèigé should also review them.
In the ninth year of Qiánlóng,
the Emperor, concerned that principal officials of ministries and courts might show favoritism in listing officials for the first class,
decreed that Grand Secretaries should inspect them,
carefully distinguish,
and dismiss those not worthy of the first class.
In the eleventh year, an edict stated:
"My previous order for Grand Secretaries to differentiate and decide on retention or dismissal
was also a temporary measure.
In evaluating division officials,
the principal officials are most familiar with them.
The key is to pay attention and observe carefully in everyday work,
and to act fairly at the time of evaluation.
For example, those who were designated first class last time,
but whose performance was ordinary over the past three years,
should be reclassified as second or third class.
Those who were originally listed as second or third class last time,
but showed diligence over the past three years,
should be reclassified as first class.
This way, the evaluation system will be strict, and people will know about encouragement and punishment."
Thereafter, the power and responsibility for evaluations
fully belonged to the Lìbù,
and the inspection by Grand Secretaries merely followed established practice.
Ministers routinely submitted self-impeachment memorials requesting dismissal,
and awaited imperial edicts to resume their original duties.
This had been practiced since the early days of the dynasty.
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng,
an edict instructed ministers who impeached themselves for dismissal to recommend worthy replacements.
However, since the recommended individuals were often unsuitable,
or formed factions for personal gain,
the practice was soon abolished.
In the seventeenth year,
the Emperor stated,
"I personally select and promote both inner and outer ministers,
and can dismiss or promote them at any time.
Why wait three years?
The self-impeachment is a superfluous formality,
everyone feigns it,
which is utterly meaningless."
An edict was issued to abolish this practice.
Previously, there was no selection process for Jīngtáng officials.
In the fifteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the Emperor noted that principal officials of third rank and above
submitted memorials of self-impeachment,
and division officials of ministries and courts
were all granted imperial audiences,
but Jīngtáng officials of fourth and fifth rank were neither included in self-impeachment
nor granted imperial audiences.
The evaluations by the Lìbù and Dūcháyuan lacked substance,
allowing incompetent and mediocre individuals to be tolerated,
while talented individuals had no means to be recognized.
Therefore, princes and ministers were specially dispatched to categorize them,
report to the throne, and grant imperial audiences.
In the eighteenth year,
the Lìbù was ordered to list the facts regarding third-rank Jīngtáng officials,
and the Emperor personally made decisions.
In the forty-eighth year,
since it was inconvenient for ministers to inspect third-rank Jīngtáng officials,
the Lìbù was instructed to bring them for imperial audience in groups.
In the twelfth year of Jiāqìng,
it was noted that for third and fourth-rank Jīngtáng officials,
the Jīngchá had only involved demotion or dismissal, but no selection.
This was inconsistent with how inner and outer ministers were handled,
and they also did not receive promotions like division officials of ministries and courts.
Therefore, a proposal from Tàicháng Shàocīng Sèkèjīng'é and others was accepted,
and Chén Zhōngchēn and others were allowed to retire.
From then on, the practice of selection for Jīngtáng officials below the third rank began.
Retirement due to old age
was clearly stipulated by regulation.
In the twenty-second year of Qiánlóng,
it was stipulated that for officials of ministries and courts aged fifty-five and above,
the principal officials should carefully evaluate them.
In the thirty-third year,
it was revised that all officials retained in the second and third classes of the Jīngchá,
aged sixty-five and above, should be granted imperial audiences.
In the third year of Jiāqìng,
it was ordered that officials in the second and third classes of the Jīngchá should be granted imperial audiences,
with an age limit of seventy.
Soon after, the old practice was restored.
The six methods of disciplinary action were extremely strict,
but senior officials often sought a reputation for leniency.
At each Jīngchá,
only a few people were dismissed,
merely going through the motions,
while others were generally tolerated,
and those who were impeached were inevitably wronged.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
Wāng Jǐngqí, Zhā Sìtíng, and their like commented on contemporary governance,
mentioning the stagnation of ministry officials,
with phrases like
"ten years without transfer, white-haired as a Láng."
The Emperor accused them of resentment and slander,
but the facts could not be called false.
Indeed, the redundancy of ministry officials
was already present during the Kāngxī and Yōngzhèng eras.
In the third year of Qiánlóng,
Hónglú Shàocīng Zhā Sìhǎi memorialized, saying:
"When a Jīngguān is impeached,
it is not uncommon for personal animosity to influence official deliberations.
Officials subject to the six methods of the Jīngchá
should be sent to the ministry for imperial audience, following the precedent of Dàjì."
This was approved.
Towards the end of Qiánlóng,
scholars had become accustomed to flattery,
and principal officials, in selecting division officials,
often considered those who were adept at ingratiation as knowledgeable,
leading to laxity in the evaluation system.
In the early years of Rénzōng,
he was keen on seeking good governance,
and quite inclined to value substance over superficiality,
and encourage integrity,
setting an example for the empire.
In the fifth year of Jiāqìng,
an edict ordered principal officials of ministries and courts to carefully select,
recommending first those who excelled in both conduct and integrity.
For others, it was preferable to choose officials with longer qualifications, who were cautious, sincere, and practical.
As for those who were young, frivolous, and overly showy with their talents,
they should be made to gain deeper experience,
and be listed for recommendation in the next term.
Each Shàngshū and Shìláng should prepare a confidential register noting the worthy and unworthy,
and review it together in public discussion.
In the eleventh year,
Grand Secretaries and Shàngshū submitted a memorial discussing Jīngchá matters:
"For officials who acquired their positions through purchase of rank,
limits should be placed based on years of service.
Only those Sīyuán of the Jūnjīchù who are capable of handling concurrent ministerial duties
should be listed as excellent;
indiscriminate recommendations to fill quotas are not allowed."
This was approved.
In the fourth year of the Dàoguāng reign,
regarding the case of Hòu Jìqīng's malpractices in atoning for his sins,
the Ministry of Punishments officials Ēndé and others conspired to deceive the ministerial presidents,
by erroneously listing him in the recommendation document,
ensuring he was ranked in the first class.
The case was referred to the appropriate ministry for deliberation and punishment.
An imperial edict was issued stating that thereafter, officials found guilty of fraud or favoritism in the Capital Review (Jīngchá) would be punished by association.
In the seventh year,
Supervising Censor Wú Jié submitted a memorial, stating:
"Both the Grand Review (Dàjì) and military evaluations
involve both recommendations and impeachments.
In recent years, when the Six Ministries conducted the Capital Review,
apart from those recommended to the first class,
regardless of their virtue or lack thereof,
all were generally listed in the second class.
Occasionally, a few individuals were in the third class,
but they were still allowed to retain their posts.
The six disciplinary methods were not applied;
there was encouragement but no punishment.
The old regulations should be reiterated,
with both recommendations and impeachments being used."
The Emperor approved his words
and issued an edict to enforce them.
In the fifteenth year,
an order was given to conduct investigations and impeachments at any time, in addition to the Capital Review,
as a corrective measure.
In the tenth year of the Xiánfēng reign,
the Ministry of Punishments' ministerial presidents indiscriminately recommended officials who were unfamiliar with legal precedents.
The imperial court, consistently inclined towards leniency,
often considered this a prevailing custom,
not unique to the Ministry of Punishments,
and largely pardoned such offenses.
Grand Secretary Guìliáng and others were merely demoted but retained their posts,
and examining ministerial presidents were fined salaries.
Upon Emperor Mùzōng's ascension,
with great difficulties yet unsettled,
he dedicated himself to rectification.
In the fifth year of the Tóngzhì reign,

an imperial edict commanded ministerial presidents of the ministries and Censorate to strictly adhere to the Jiāqìng fifth-year edict, which required keeping confidential records of officials' virtue and lack thereof, and jointly reviewing them publicly,
and also to regularly attend their offices
to discuss official matters with their subordinates,
thereby observing their subordinates' virtue or lack thereof.
In the eighth year,
another edict stated that the Capital Review should not have recommendations without impeachments,
hoping to cleanse old habits
and refresh all administrative affairs.
However, the momentum of deep-seated issues
could not be reversed.
In the seventh year of the Guāngxù reign,
Vice Minister of Rites Bǎotíng memorialized about the chronic abuses of the Capital Review,
speaking with profound anguish,
saying:
"The abuse of deferring to personal connections
is not confined to the ministerial presidents of the ministries and Censorate.
The Grand Councilors (shūchén) should be held responsible for investigations,
which must be fair and strict.
If the Grand Councilors are truly pure-hearted
and disregard personal connections,
they can not only investigate the virtue or lack thereof of the officials of the ministries and Censorate,
but also investigate the virtue or lack thereof of high-ranking officials both within and outside the capital.
And the evaluation of the merits and demerits of the Grand Councilors
rests with the sagacious Emperor's sole judgment.
If the imperial court first treats the Capital Review as a mere formality,
how can one hold the Grand Councilors responsible,
much less the ministerial presidents of the ministries and Censorate!"
Though his arguments were incisive, they were difficult to implement,
merely empty words.
In the second year of the Xuāntǒng reign,
the Ministry of Personnel established the Constitutional Preparation Office,
changing the Department of Merits and Demerits to the Performance Evaluation Section,
to manage matters related to the evaluation of civil officials' merits and demerits that required changes.
At that time, various superficial opinions abounded,
mixing old and new,
making the Ministry of Personnel like a superfluous appendage.
The Grand Review began in the second year of the Shùnzhì reign,
when Censor Zhāng Hù memorialized that for officials' evaluations,
those who were self-disciplined, upright, and genuinely loved the people should be considered superior.
The ministry's reply agreed with the proposal.
The following year,
the court audience evaluation was established,
and five-color rosters were issued,
ordering governors and governors-general to record evaluations in four categories.
According to custom,
in addition to the Grand Review,
the Censorate and provinces typically conducted "correction of oversights" (shíyí).
That year, when evaluating all officials,
only the reports submitted by the governors and investigating censors were used for promotion and demotion.
The Censorate and provinces intended to follow the old custom,
but the Grand Secretaries (nèidàchén) disliked it.
Grand Secretary Chén Míngxià strongly advocated for it,
and Supervising Censor Wèi Xiàngshū also made a request.
An imperial decree was issued, stating that
officials who made false accusations out of personal spite during "correction of oversights" would be punished according to the rules of the Grand Review.
Thereafter, the Censorate and provinces became hesitant,
and few made "correction of oversights."
Soon after,
it was abolished,
and the power of governors and governors-general grew daily.
In the fourth year,
it was decided that the Grand Review would be held every three years,
and officials punished by the Grand Review were not allowed to return to their posts.
An edict was issued to officials attending the court audience:
"The corrupt and cruel shall be severely punished;
the incompetent shall not be pardoned.
You who are temporarily permitted to retain your posts
must reflect on cleansing past transgressions
and strive for future effectiveness."
Thereafter, whenever it was the year for court audiences,
strict admonitions were invariably given as a routine.
According to old regulations for court audiences and the Grand Review,
chief officials of financial commissioners (fān), judicial commissioners (niè), prefects (fǔ), sub-prefectures (zhōu), and counties (xiàn) all had to attend.
In the ninth year of the Shùnzhì reign,
only one financial commissioner, one judicial commissioner, and one assistant prefect from each prefecture were allowed to attend as representatives.
In the eighteenth year,
Supervising Censor Léi Yīlóng memorialized:
"During the triennial Grand Review,
one must not overlook high officials while singling out minor ones,
nor punish those who have left office while being lenient with those currently in office.
I request that financial and judicial commissioners report to the ministry,
to jointly and accurately identify facts face-to-face,
and meticulously examine them according to the rosters."
This was submitted to the ministry for deliberation and implementation.
In the first year of the Kāngxī reign,
the attendance of financial and judicial commissioners at court audiences was suspended,
with officials like administration commissioners and surveillance vice commissioners attending instead.
In the twelfth year,
financial and judicial commissioners were again ordered to attend.
In the twenty-fifth year,
because court audiences were used as an excuse for harsh levies,
leading to the proliferation of corrupt practices,
the practice of financial commissioners, judicial commissioners, and assistant prefects attending court audiences was completely abolished.
The retention or dismissal of officials, based on their virtue or lack thereof,
relied on the records of governors and governors-general,
and the registers of the two financial and judicial commissions were entirely suspended.
In the early Qing dynasty, the Grand Review and "full-term evaluation" (kǎomǎn) were conducted concurrently.
In the first year of the Kāngxī reign,
the Grand Review was abolished,
and only "full-term evaluation" was carried out.
Department and circuit officials served two years in the interior or one and a half years in border areas;
county magistrates served two years in border areas or three years in the interior.
Those who had fully settled all taxes and grain contributions were allowed to undergo "full-term evaluation."
Localities were categorized as barren/ruined, crucial/exhausted, well-supplied/thriving, or simple/easy, and recorded accordingly,
with grades determined based on the quantity of administrative achievements.
In the fourth year,
"full-term evaluation" was suspended,
and the Grand Review was reinstated
as a permanent system.
For the Grand Review's recommendations, impeachments, and evaluations,
chief officials of sub-prefectures and counties would customarily submit them to their respective prefectures and circuits for review;
educational officials would be reviewed by educational commissioners, and salt administration officials by their respective chief officials;
then forwarded to the financial and judicial commissioners for re-review;
then approved by governors and governors-general,
and finally reported to the ministries and Censorate.
For river officials who also had responsibilities for criminal cases and financial matters,
the Director-General of Rivers, governors-general, and governors would each conduct reviews.
Those solely in charge of river affairs
would be reviewed and memorialized by the Director-General of Rivers himself.
In the twenty-third year of Kāngxī's reign,
due to the close ties between Fān (藩) and Niè (臬) officials and Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials,
their Zhuóyì (卓異) recommendations were suspended.
Officials recommended as Zhuóyì (卓異) were immediately recorded and promoted,
without following the usual sequence.
Successive dynasties greatly emphasized their selection,
and those who made fraudulent recommendations out of personal favoritism were punished.
At the beginning of Kāngxī's reign,
Censor Zhāng Chōngyì (張沖翼) requested stricter enforcement of the fixed quotas for Zhuóyì (卓異) recommendations,
emphasizing the need for detailed verification of achievements
to ensure that reputation matched reality.
This was submitted to the ministry for deliberation.
In the sixth year,
following the request of Censor Tián Liùshàn (田六善),
Zhuóyì (卓異) officials were to be based on integrity and honesty.
Sī (司) and Dào (道) officials and the like must have it explicitly noted that they did not demand festive gifts or solicit bribes,

while Zhōu (州) and Xiàn (縣) officials and the like must have it explicitly noted that they did not impose miscellaneous levies, heavy fire-loss fees, cause losses to merchants, or forcibly lend to the wealthy.
The presence or absence of honest officials
would determine the worthiness or unworthiness of Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials.
At that time, honest officials emerged in great numbers,
such as Lù Lǒngqí (陸隴其), magistrate of Língshòu (靈壽), who was promoted to the Censorate.
Governance thrived,
and it was praised as a period of great prosperity.
In the forty-fourth year,
an imperial edict called for Zhuóyì (卓異) recommendations,
insisting that there be no additional levies,
no excessive punishments,
no theft cases,
no prolonged arrears in grain taxes or deficits in granaries,
that the populace should find their livelihoods,
and that local conditions should improve daily.
Other mere formalities
were not to be listed.
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng's reign,
Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials were ordered to scrutinize their subordinates based on the fundamental principle of promoting agriculture.
Commentators said that making the encouragement of agriculture central to encouraging officials
was a profound grasp of fundamental governance,
akin to the edicts of the Hàn (漢) dynasty.
Previously, in the sixth year of Yōngzhèng's reign,
regulations were established for punishments for inaccurate Zhuóyì (卓異) recommendations,
but those who reported themselves were exempted.
If a Zhuóyì (卓ò異) official was found to be corrupt, cruel, or unlawful,
or had outstanding arrears in grain taxes or unsolved theft cases,
the original recommending Dū (督) or Fǔ (撫) official
would receive a lighter punishment than Sī (司), Dào (道), or Fǔ (府) officials.
In the forty-eighth year of Qiánlóng's reign,
it was revised that if a Zhuóyì (卓異) official committed embezzlement,
the year and month would be investigated to determine whether it occurred before or after the departure of the original recommending superior,
and punishment would be determined accordingly.
Nièsī (臬司), Dào (道), and Fǔ (府) officials would receive one grade lighter punishment than Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials,
while Fānsī (藩司) officials would follow the precedent of Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials,
as Dào (道) and Fǔ (府) officials would, by regulation, report details to Dū (督), Fǔ (撫), and Fānsī (藩司) officials for personal verification and decision.
In the fiftieth year,
the emperor observed that recommendations for Zhuóyì (卓異)
were traditionally divided into principal and supplementary,
without clear limitations,
which easily led to opportunism.
He instructed the ministry to thoroughly investigate the size of each province and the number of vacancies,
and to establish appropriate regulations,
eliminating the category of supplementary recommendations.
Consequently, there were fixed quotas for Zhuóyì (卓異) officials in each province,
and there were no major changes throughout the Qīng (清) dynasty.
The Bāfǎ (八法) disciplinary system,
having been in practice for a long time,
was sometimes treated as a mere formality by senior officials,
who often filled it with trivial matters concerning minor officials
to shirk responsibility.
Successive dynasties issued repeated instructions,
forcefully warning against favoritism,
still guarding against grievances.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng's reign,
an edict stated that officials downgraded or fined in the Grand Review (Dàjì, 大計)
were generally not allowed Zhuóyì (卓異) status,
but if there were honest and capable officials who erred due to public duty,
they would be permitted Zhuóyì (卓異) status.
It was also noted that the Bāfǎ (八法) for Zhuóyì (卓異) only nominated a few dozen individuals.
For other equal-ranking officials not included in the nominations,
from Zhīxiàn (知縣) upwards,
Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials were ordered to submit their performance evaluations
to the ministry for review.
In the fourth year,
an edict stated that there might be grievances or evasions of serious charges by those impeached.
Except for corrupt and cruel officials, who did not need an imperial audience,
impeached officials categorized as careless, impetuous, or inadequate
were to be issued a dispatch by Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials and sent to the ministry for an imperial audience.
In the twenty-fourth year of Qiánlóng's reign,
the emperor observed that the Bāfǎ (八法) impeachment memorials regarding careless and impetuous officials
did not specify what actions were careless or what actions were impetuous.
Perhaps public affairs were not mishandled, but there were minor omissions,
or perhaps they were talented and capable but rough in temperament.
If a superior, due to differing opinions,
simply included them in the "white memorial" (dismissal list),
it would be regrettable.
Or perhaps they had a flawed character and exceeded proper bounds,
but were merely given a light charge instead of a serious one.
Neither of these situations aligned with the intent of rectifying official conduct.
He ordered detailed annotations of actual deeds
and forbade vague impeachments.
In the eighth year of Jiāqìng's reign,
it was stipulated that Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials could impeach incompetent and mediocre officials at any time,
even if their positive achievements were not yet recorded.
Impeached officials who wished to appear for an imperial audience at the ministry
could invoke the precedent of the Dàjì Liùfǎ (大計六法).
This demonstrated that evaluations could not be too detailed and meticulous,
in hopes of finding hidden talents,
supplementing the shortcomings of the Dàjì (大計) system.
After the Jiā (嘉) and Dào (道) reigns,
the Dàjì (大計) system largely followed old precedents,
and Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials merely went through the motions,
rarely making vigorous efforts.
In the eighth year of Dàoguāng's reign,
in the Shāndōng (山東) Dàjì (大計) Zhuóyì (卓異) recommendations,
acting Fǔ (撫) Hè Chánglíng (賀長齡) originally noted that Róng Bǐng (容昺), the magistrate of Xīnchéng (新城), was "sincere and benevolent,"
but an imperial edict stated that "generosity and mildness are difficult to qualify for a top evaluation,"
ordering all provinces to recommend officials who possessed both ability and virtue, and were skilled in governance.
During the Xián (咸) and Tóng (同) military uprisings,
sometimes localities had just been recovered and needed appeasement,
or borders were threatened by rebels
and needed urgent defense.
Edicts instructed Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials to diligently record honest and capable members
for top evaluations,
to be prepared for promotion.
At that time, Dū (督) and Fǔ (撫) officials acted expediently,
employing people regardless of their official qualifications,
making decisions as circumstances demanded.
Thus, they could not be bound by the usual regulations of the Dàjì (大計) system afterwards.
During the Guāngxù (光緒) period,
commentators often memorialized about the accumulated abuses of the Dàjì (大計) system,
requesting that border officials be ordered to conduct serious investigations.
Repeated edicts admonished them.
However, as talent declined
and official governance deteriorated daily,
mere laws ultimately could not be enforced.
In the twenty-eighth year,
an edict ordered each province to establish Kèlǐguǎn (課吏館) (official training halls),
and to submit a memorial once every six months.
In the thirty-first year,
regulations were established for evaluating the actual performance of Zhōu (州) and Xiàn (縣) officials,
divided into four grades: "most excellent," "excellent," "average," and "inferior."
However, the Kèlǐ (課吏) relied only on one day's written work,
and the evaluations were based on only one year's performance.
To expect impartiality
was indeed difficult.
In the second year of Xuāntǒng's reign,
the Xiànzhèng Biāncháguǎn (憲政編查館) (Bureau for Constitutional Revision and Investigation) memorialized to evaluate Zhōu (州) and Xiàn (縣) officials,
distinguishing their performance in areas such as schools, police, industry, agriculture, homicides and robberies, lawsuits, imprisonment, and grain taxes,
to determine their merits and demerits.
The responsible governmental agencies were to formulate separate evaluation regulations.
With numerous categories
and fabricated reports,
it merely served to impress superficially,
and was not effective in encouraging or deterring.
As for the old system of the Grand Review for Hàn (翰) and Zhān (詹) officials,
which distinguished between superior and inferior,
leading to promotions, transfers, demotions, or dismissals,
it was a method of special performance review.
For Sī (司) and Dào (道) officials in the provinces,
there was a secret review at the end of the year.
Zhōu (州) and Xiàn (縣) officials, upon completing one year,
and Jiào (教) and Zuǒ (佐) officials, upon completing six years of salary,
all underwent selection.
These were methods of ongoing assessment,
not belonging to the Chá (察) or Jì (計) canons.
Military reviews (Jūngzhèng, 軍政),
like civilian evaluations,
were managed by the Zhí Fāng Sī (職方司) of the Bīngbù (兵部).
Internal and external Wèi (衞) and Suǒ (所) (military garrisons)
were under the Wǔxuǎnsī (武選司).
Military officials in the capital
were reviewed and memorialized by the banner commanders and the ministries/courts;
those in the provinces were evaluated by the commanding generals.
For Qiānzǒng (千總) and above in the capital garrisons,
and Shǒubèi (守備) and above in the Green Standard Army in the provinces,
each was evaluated by their superior officers,
categorized into four aspects: conduct, ability, horsemanship and archery, and age.
Recommendations and impeachments were the same as for civilian officials.
Officials of the third rank and above submitted self-reports,
which were submitted by the ministry for imperial instruction.
For hereditary nobles of the Eight Banners,
their advancement or demotion was based on their martial arts proficiency.
For the Green Standard Army, recommendations and impeachments
were usually conducted one and a half years after the Jūngzhèng (軍政) review.
One or two individuals were nominated for promotion and entered the recommended promotion list,
while those impeached were disciplined according to the Jūngzhèng (軍政) regulations.
This is the general outline.
In the early days of the dynasty, no restrictions were established.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì,
it was decided that an assessment would be held every six years.
This marked the beginning of the military performance review (jūnzhèng kǎohé).
In the eleventh year,
the term was changed to five years.
In the thirteenth year,
following the request of Grand Secretary (gěishìzhōng) Zhāng Wénguāng,
those with exceptional military performance
were to be granted official robes and commendations, similar to civil officials.
Later, this was changed to a promotion of one rank.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
the military performance review was suspended,
and only the full term review (kǎomǎn) was conducted.
Soon after, the Ministry of War (Bīngbù) submitted a memorial requesting that military officials in the direct provinces should follow the precedent of civil officials,
and be impeached or commended annually by the governor-general (zǒngdū) and commander-in-chief (tídū) jointly.
Censor (Yùshǐ) Jì Zhènyí submitted a memorial stating:
"During the full term review of military officials,
if they focus on personal gain and excellent performance,
they might embezzle military provisions
and jeopardize the frontier.
I request that promotions be based on their past service and merits."
Thus, in the sixth year, regulations for conducting the military performance review were established.
Metropolitan and provincial military chief officials
were to be categorized into four grades,
with detailed accounts of their conduct and military achievements,
and decisions on their retention or dismissal
were to be reported to the ministry.

It was mandatory to include evaluative comments such as "upright conduct," "skilled in archery and horsemanship," "strict in command," "diligent and cautious in duty," and "does not harass the locality"
before recommending them.
Only if there were concrete instances conforming to the "Eight Laws" (bāfǎ) and other regulations
would an impeachment be initiated.
Furthermore, commanders-in-chief and brigade-generals (zǒngbīngguān) were ordered to make self-declarations.
Commanders-in-chief were reviewed by governors-general,
and brigade-generals by governors-general and commanders-in-chief.
In provinces without a governor-general,
the provincial governor (xúnfǔ) conducted the review.
Subsequently, due to military campaigns in the Diān Province,
the entire country was in turmoil,
and urgent military dispatches were frequent.
The military performance review was suspended for ten years.
By the twenty-first year,
the Diān rebellion was pacified.
Following the request of Grand Secretary Shuòmùkē,
the grand ceremony of military performance review was conducted,
with officials' actual conduct and performance
recorded starting from the military review after the eleventh year of Kāngxī.
Battalion commanders (qiānzǒng) of the Nine Gates (Jiǔmén) were reviewed by the Commander of the Nine Gates (Jiǔmén Tídū).
Candidate brigade-generals (hòubǔ zǒngbīngguān) were also required to make self-declarations.
Those below vice-general (fùjiàng) who were awaiting appointment
were inspected according to old regulations.
In the sixty-first year,
it was decreed that metropolitan military officials such as Guards Commanders (lǐng shìwèi nèidàchén),
Commanders of the Eight Banners (Bāqí Dūtǒng),
Commanders of the Vanguard and Guards (qiánfēng hùjūn bùjūn tǒnglǐng),
and Deputy Commanders (fùdūtǒng)
were exempt from self-declaration.
During the selection for military performance review,
subordinate officials' reviews
followed the procedures for impeachment and commendation in the provinces.
Generals (jiāngjūn) and deputy commanders stationed in various provinces
made self-declarations according to the regulations for commanders-in-chief and brigade-generals.
Subordinate officials followed the regulations for the capital.
For garrison commanders (chéngshǒuwèi) and associate commanders (xiélǐng) in places like Dézhōu,
ministers were dispatched to conduct reviews,
jointly inspecting their subordinates,
and reporting their findings.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
it was decreed that officials from Battalion Commander (shǒubèi) level and above
were to be reviewed by governors-general, provincial governors, commanders-in-chief, and brigade-generals.
That winter,
an edict stated:
"For the initial military performance review,
those who have rendered meritorious service in battle, are old and have long service, but are still capable of managing affairs,
shall remain in office.
Those unsuitable for retention
shall be specially reported for imperial favor.
Or, even if they have not performed service in the field,
but have served for many years,
attention should still be paid to evaluating them."
This was an act of benevolent consideration for experience and diligence,
a special broad leniency,
not a regular precedent.
In the second year,
an edict instructed that vice-generals, colonels (cāntuán), and lieutenant-colonels (yóujī) recommended by various provinces
were to be presented for imperial audience in rotation,
to assess their talent in personnel and martial skills.
Governors-general, provincial governors, commanders-in-chief, and brigade-generals were to secretly report their conduct and training,
categorizing them into different grades.
In the sixth year,
Yuán Lìsōng, the Brigade-General of Tàiyuán, Shānxī, memorialized that Liáng Yù, a Battalion Commander of the Píngyuán Battalion, was honest and competent,
but due to old age was subjected to impeachment.
The emperor, considering that experienced talent was rare,
ordered him to be appointed as a lieutenant-colonel as appropriate,
which was an extraordinary favor.
In this year, it was stipulated that if an official with excellent performance had previously been corrupt or lawless,
or if after being promoted or transferred to another province,
committed another crime of corruption,
the recommending superior official
would be punished accordingly.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
the Ministry (Bù) deliberated that personnel who had rendered meritorious service in battle and were old and retired,
should have one son enter military service to receive provisions.
If they had no sons, they would also be given provisions for their support.
This was adopted.
At that time, officials recommended from the direct provinces
were often praised for being clear-headed, diligent, and capable of handling affairs, thus making it to the top selection.
In the eleventh year,
an edict stated that henceforth, recommendations
must heavily emphasize archery and horsemanship.
In the fifteenth year,
finding that the brigade-generals recommended by various provinces were rarely satisfactory,
the emperor decreed:
"The category of battalion commanders who have completed their term
are mostly mediocre.
For the state to employ military officials,
the military camps are the proper path.
When promoting and appointing generals and officers,
such individuals must be selected.
Promotions through the ranks
all begin with battalion commanders who have completed their term.
The use of them for breaking enemy formations and resisting aggression
must be planned in advance during times of peace and tranquility;
it cannot be regarded as a deferred plan."
In the twenty-fourth year,
since the practice of ministers' self-declaration was abolished,
the Ministry of War was commanded, during the year of military performance review,
to prepare three separate memorials for
metropolitan commanders and deputy commanders,
garrisoned generals, commanders, and deputy commanders in the provinces,
and commanders-in-chief and brigade-generals in various provinces,
listing their actual performance for imperial scrutiny and decision,
to emphasize the performance review.
In the forty-second year,
it was stipulated that if Green Standard Army (Lǜyíng) military officials from garrisons (wèi) and posts (suǒ) who were recommended for excellent performance had not yet been promoted,
and then encountered another military performance review where they were rated as ordinary,
their previous excellent performance would be nullified.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
it was stipulated for the review of Imperial Guards (shìwèi) that
as per custom, during the year of military review,
one was not allowed to claim illness or request retirement,
to prevent evasion.
In the eighth year,
it was reiterated that during the year of inspecting military camps,
which concerned performance reviews,
one was not allowed to claim illness or request retirement,
following the military review regulations.
During the military campaigns of Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì,
many regulations were relaxed.
However, the grand ceremony of military performance review
continued without cessation.
In the second year of Xiánfēng,
Yīnglóng, the General of Hēilóngjiāng, facing Russian troops' encroachment,
dispatched officers to guard strategic passes,
and memorialized to postpone that year's military review.
This was not granted.
Subsequently, Chéng Yùcǎi, Governor-General of Húguǎng, and others, due to unfinished military affairs,
memorialized for postponement,
requesting a supplementary review after the victorious withdrawal.
It was also decreed that those who were old and infirm
should be impeached and dealt with at any time.
This continued until the reign of Dézōng,
who, though earnestly trying to revitalize and rectify,
was at the end of his tether.
The postponement of reviews
was frequently recorded in history.
In the fourteenth year of Guāngxù,
the Běiyáng Navy (Běiyáng Hǎijūn) was established,
and its promotions and demotions were managed by the Naval Yámen (Hǎijūn Yámén).
After the Jiǎwǔ War,
learning from past mistakes,
the Green Standard Army was abolished,
new armies were trained,
and separate performance review regulations were established.
In the thirty-second year,
the Ministry of War was reorganized into the Ministry of the Army (Lùjūn Bù),
and its performance reviews were under the Department of Military Control (Jūnhéng Sī).
In the second year of Xuāntǒng,
the Ministry of the Navy (Hǎijūn Bù) was established,
and its performance reviews were under the Department of Military Regulations (Jūnzhì Sī).
The imperial court was keen on reform,
and military discipline should have been somewhat revitalized.
However, old habits were deeply ingrained,
and the times became increasingly difficult,
ultimately to no avail.
Record Eighty-Seven, Elections Seven, Donations
Under the [Qīng] system,
entry into officialdom highly valued the regular path.
Since the opening of the donation system,
officials and clerks could advance through wealth.
Initially, this was indeed to recruit talented individuals from alternative paths,
complementing those not covered by the examination system.
However, from the mid-period onwards,
the dignity of official titles declined,
and promotions became indiscriminate,
leading to the confusion of official careers.
Donation cases were primarily for famine relief, river works, and military expenses.
These were called "temporary cases,"
to be halted upon expiration or completion of the task,
but "current cases" were not.
Through donation, civil officials could rise from minor capital officials to department directors (lángzhōng),
and from unranked to provincial administrators (dàoyuán);
military officials from captains (qiānbǎzǒng) to brigadier generals (cāncānjìang).
Incumbent officials could also donate for promotion,
to change their donation category,
to lower their donation amount,
to secure various ranks for selection and appointment, provincial assignments,翎銜 (língxián), enfeoffments (fēngdiǎn), seniority increments (jiājí), and merit records (jìlù).
Furthermore, those demoted, dismissed, or who had left office
could donate to restore their original rank, original seniority, or original 翎銜 (língxián),
and fill their original vacancies.

Probationary salaries (shìfèng), cumulative salaries (lìfèng), substantive appointments (shíshòu), recommendations (bǎojǔ), probationary service (shìyòng), audiences upon leaving office (lírrènyǐnjàn), submission of credentials (tóugòng), inspections (yànkàn), and recusals (huíbì) could be exempted through donation.
Commoners could donate to become gòngjiān (gòngshēng and jiànshēng), receive enfeoffments, and official titles.
Generally, gòngjiān, titles and enfeoffments, seniority increments, and merit records, which were not related to the civil service examination system,
belonged to "current cases";
the rest belonged to "temporary cases."
Donation regulations throughout the dynasties
changed from time to time,
but it was stipulated that donated officials could not be assigned to the Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) or the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù),
and that dàoyuán and fǔ (prefects), unless they had previously served as substantive principal officials,
would only be granted minor positions through donation,
which became a fixed rule.
For appointments, new donation ranks were considered superior to older ones;
this was a general rule.
Donation matters were managed by the Donation Office (Juānnàfáng) of the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù).
Donations could be collected from outer provinces,
from the Ministry's treasury,
or reported simultaneously to both provincial and ministerial authorities.
After the [Xiánfēng] reign,
they were also handled by the Beijing Copper Bureau (Jīngtóngjú).
Those who reported donations were called "official students" (guānsheng);
the Ministry issued them credentials,
called "permits" (zhízhào).
Gòngjiān also received certificates from the Imperial Academy (Guózǐjiān).
For promising individuals who donated to become gòngjiān or acquire official titles,
and for gòngjiān who acquired official titles,
local officials from their native places were to investigate and compile a roster of their pure family backgrounds,
reporting quarterly or annually.
For those donating for official positions,
it was required to verify any disqualifications,
obtain a bond from their clansmen and neighbors (zúlín gānjié),
and report within the deadline.
Late reporting or inaccurate reporting
resulted in punishment.
This outlines the general procedures.
Civil official donations began in the thirteenth year of [Kāngxī] (1674),
due to the campaign against the Three Feudatories (Sānfān),
when military expenses were extremely urgent,
and temporary cases were opened.
In the sixteenth year (1677),
the Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ) [Sòng Déyí] said:
"Three years have passed since the opening of the system,
and over five hundred county magistrates (zhīxiàn) have donated.
Initially, as there were many vacancies and it was easy to obtain them,
people eagerly rushed to apply.
Now, seeing that it takes several years to be selected and appointed,
they hesitate and observe.
It is advisable to set a deadline to stop it,
so that those who wish to donate will do so before it's too late.
This will both aid military expenses
and treat official titles with solemnity."
The Emperor accepted his words.
After the recapture of [Diānnán] (Yunnan),
the donation system was suspended.
Later, due to famine in [Xī'ān] and [Dàtóng],
and also river works on the [Yǒngdìng Hé],
the system was reopened.
In the fifty-first year (1712),
when the [Tōngzhōu] granaries were expanded,
a censorial official requested the opening of donations,
and the court deliberated and approved the request.
Vice Minister (Shìláng) [Wáng Yàn] strongly argued in a memorial:
"Naive villagers,
once they donate funds,
suddenly become superiors to the people.
Some may take charge of a county,
others may hold the insignia of a circuit.
This not only indiscriminately demeans official titles
but also burdens the locality.
It should be prohibited
to block the path of opportunism
and close the door to profiteering."
The Emperor approved his words,
and ordered the Nine Ministers (Jiǔqīng) to deliberate again.
During the campaign in [Qīnghǎi],
military provisions were insufficient.
The Grand Ministers (Nèi Dàchén) debated suspending the waiting periods for appointments and promotions for all paths,
and exclusively using those who donated funds for provisions.
Minister of Justice (Xíngbù Shàngshū) [Zhāng Tíngshū] said:
"Only vacancies designated for donation can be filled by donated officials;
those from the regular path and for promotions should remain as before."
This was adopted.
In the second year of [Yōngzhèng] (1724),
the case for transporting rice to [Ā'ěrtái] was opened.
In the fifth year (1727),
due to floods in [Zhílì],
the establishment of military farms (yíngtián) was proposed.
Following the request of Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) [Zhū Shì],
the military farm donation case was opened.
Governor-General of [Yún Guì] (Yunnan and Guizhou) [È'ěrtài], seeing that funds were lacking for land reclamation in [Diān] (Yunnan) and [Qián] (Guizhou),
requested the opening of donations similar to the military farm case.
The Emperor said:
"The land reclamation donation case
is beneficial to the localities.
Previously, due to the large number of people from various donation cases,
it was difficult to select officials,
so a decree was issued to stop it.
In recent years, the available donated personnel
are almost used up.
After a few more years,
there will certainly be no donated personnel,
and only examination graduates will be used.
The terms for donation should be appropriately increased.
Excluding dàoyuán, fǔ (prefects), and tóngzhī (assistant prefects), who are not allowed to donate,
commissaries (tōngpàn), zhìzhōu (prefectural magistrates), zhīxiàn (county magistrates), and zhōutóng (assistant prefectural magistrates), xiànchéng (assistant county magistrates), etc.,
should be deliberated upon and allowed to donate."
This was submitted to the Nine Ministers for discussion and implementation.
In the twelfth year (1734),
the case for pre-planning grain transport was opened.
Earlier, promising individuals with [Huái] gòngshēng status could donate funds to become educational officials (jiàozhí).
Subsequently,
concerned that personnel from alternative paths might not be competent for the responsibility of teaching and setting examples,
in the thirty-third year of [Kāngxī] (1694),
it was ordered that promising gòngshēng who donated to become xúezhèng (directors of studies) or jiàoyù (instructors) should be reclassified as xiànchéng,
and xùndǎo (sub-instructors) as zhǔbù (clerks).
In the first year of [Yōngzhèng] (1723),
an edict stated:
"Many who donate for educational posts
are young people not versed in literature.
Is it appropriate to make them teachers of those who excel in scholarship and are advanced in years?"
It was decreed to revert to the former regulations for their use.
In the early years of [Gāozōng]'s reign (1736-1738),
an edict ordered the suspension of donation cases in both the capital and the provinces.
In the seventh year of [Qiánlóng] (1742),
due to floods in the upper and lower [Jiāng] (Yangzi River) regions,
Minister of Justice [Zhōu Xúejàn] and Governor-General of [Zhílì] [Gāo Bīn] were ordered to work with the governors-general and governors to handle the situation.
Soon, they jointly memorialized that relief and hydraulic works required vast expenses,
and requested to follow the precedent of "charitable donors" (Lèshànhàoshī lì),
where those who contributed funds and effort would be granted official ranks according to the amount.
An edict stated that for capital officials below zhòng, háng, píng, bó,
and provincial officials below tóngzhī and tōngpàn,
it would not impede the regular path,
and their request was granted.
Subsequently, the upper and lower [Jiāng], [Zhílì], [Shāndōng], and [Hénán] regions repeatedly reported disasters,
and the Emperor often acceded to the requests of his officials
to allow the opening of donation cases.
In the thirteenth year (1748),
during the advance on [Dà Jīnchuān],
Governor of [Sìchuān] [Jì Shān] memorialized for the implementation of the rice transport donation case.
The Ministry deliberated that one shi of transported rice would be equivalent to twenty-five taels of donated silver,
and officials were appointed accordingly.
Governor-General of [Chuān Shǎan] (Sichuan and Shaanxi) [Zhāng Guǎngsì] said:
"Military rations at the front are issued in cash equivalents,
with each shi valued at five or six taels of silver.
Now that the donation case is open,
various officials use stored rice for donation,
calculating that immediate-appointment tóngzhī through gòngjiān status cost no more than a thousand taels of gold,
and immediate-appointment minor capital officials no more than several hundred taels of gold.
I request that they be required to pay the full amount in silver
to prevent abuses."
The report was approved.
In the thirty-ninth year (1774),
during the second campaign against [Jīnchuān],
the [Sìchuān] transport donation case was reopened.
However, positions like copyists (ténglù) and deliberators (yì) for the [Sìkù Quánshū] (Imperial Library)
were largely reserved and not open to donation,
while others could be reported for donation as a whole.
The donation for dàoyuán and fǔ by gòngjiān,
which had not been implemented for decades after the fifth year of [Yōngzhèng] (1727),
was revived at this time.
In the fifty-eighth year,
an imperial edict stated:
“Previously, due to military expenditures and river works,
the outlays were enormous,
and special contributions were temporarily opened.
This was merely a temporary expedient.
Now, after more than twenty years,
the imperial treasuries are full,
and not the slightest shortage has occurred due to the cessation of contributions.
It is evident that the system of contributions is indeed unnecessary.
This not only demonstrates carefulness with official appointments
but also bestows grace upon the literati.
My descendants shall forever take this as a rule.
If anyone requests to open contributions,
they shall be considered a minister who seeks profit,
and shall be reprimanded and not employed.”
In the third year of Jiāqìng,
following the request of Hùbù Shìláng Jiǎng Cìqǐ,
the special contributions for the rehabilitation of Chuān and Chǔ were opened.
The Emperor feared that this would impede the regular career path,
and ordered a thorough discussion of the regulations.
Soon after, it was deliberated:
“For capital officials such as Lángzhōng and Yuánwàiláng,
and for provincial officials such as Dào and Fǔ,
who have the responsibility of managing affairs and governing the people,
it is inappropriate to allow indiscriminate advancement.
Only Jìnshì,
Jǔrén,
and those who have obtained ēn, bá, fù, yōu, or suì gòng degrees
are permitted to make contributions.
Non-regular path candidates for appointment or election to principal positions
may also contribute by advancement.
Current officials, those awaiting appointment, and candidates for junior capital officials and subordinate positions
are only permitted to contribute for promotion to their respective ranks.”
This was adopted.
Subsequently, due to repeated river breaches,
further contributions were opened for Hénggōng, Yùdōng, Wǔzhì, and other projects.
In the eleventh year,
it was stipulated that those contributing for Dào and Fǔ positions
must be former Zhīfǔ, Tóngzhī, Zhílì Zhōu Zhīzhōu, and other principal officials of zhōu and xiàn who have contributed extra,
as well as current capital officials
who are capable of handling demanding posts.
They were permitted to be selected for various posts, both demanding and simple.
As for those who were Gòngshēng or Jiànshēng making their initial contributions,
and current capital officials only suitable for simple posts,
as well as subordinate officials in the provinces contributing by advancement,
they were to be exclusively selected for simple posts.
At the beginning of the reigns of Xuānzōng and Wénzōng,
the system of contributions was first suspended,
which was considered an excellent measure at the time.
From the seventh year of Dàoguāng, regular contributions were opened for discretionary increases,
and for raising funds,
Yùgōng contributions were followed,
and new contributions in Shùntiān, Liǎngguǎng, and the three provinces
were successively deliberated and implemented.
At that time, most contribution rules followed old customs,
except that in the expansion of contributions, Gòngshēng were allowed to contribute for Zhōngshū,
and in the Yùgōng rules, Zēngshēng and Fùshēng were allowed to contribute for teaching positions.
In the first year of Xiánfēng,
following the words of Gěishìzhōng Wāng Yuánfāng,
the contributions for Zēngshēng and Fùshēng to teaching positions were abolished,
and those who had already been selected and appointed
were not allowed to be indiscriminately recommended.
In that year, special contributions for raising military provisions were opened;
the following year,
regulations for broadly raising military provisions were further promulgated.
In the ninth year,
the system of contributions was again expanded.
At that time, military campaigns led to a shortage of provisions,
and contributions became numerous,
without further restrictions,
and the officialdom became increasingly chaotic.
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
Yùshǐ Qiú Déjùn requested that merchants not be allowed to contribute for principal substantive official positions,
but be limited to honorary titles and miscellaneous posts.
This was sent to the board for deliberation and implementation.
Soon, the board ministers stated that contributors were hesitant,
which hindered military provisions,
so an imperial edict restored the old system.
In the fourth year,
Shāndōng Xúnfǔ Yán Jìngmíng stated:
“The discounted contributions from various provinces,
according to the established rules for raising military provisions,
do not amount to three-tenths of the full sum.
Those people treat official positions as a trade,
and a slight embezzlement of money and grain
already exceeds their original contribution.
They contribute openly,
but secretly deplete the treasury.
I request that Dào, Fǔ, Zhōu, and Xiàn positions be discounted by two-tenths according to the military provision rules,
and be exclusively contributed through the Jīngtóng Bureau.”
This was adopted.
At that time, internally there was the Jīngjuān Bureau,
and externally there were Gānjuan, Wǎnjuan, Qiánjuan,
with bureaus established throughout the various provinces.
Embezzlement, forced levies, and private discounts
all occurred.
In the early years of Guāngxù,
commentators said that the regular contributions during the Qiánlóng era,
including Gòngshēng, Jiànshēng, honorary titles, and miscellaneous posts, amounted to about three million per year.
Now, with the discounted contributions,
the annual income is less than one and a half million.
If official appointments are valued,
even honorary titles feel honorable,
and people spend much without regret.
If official appointments are undervalued,
then substantive posts are easily obtained,
and people are not necessarily happy to contribute
even with a reduced amount.
The gain is minimal,
while the damage is substantial.
Stopping contributions would be better.
At that time, there were also those who said that contributing officials should be tested,
and contributions for huālíng and those for incumbent or candidate positions should be stopped.
These were always sent to the board for deliberation.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor, believing that contributions were unhelpful for military provisions
and truly harmed the integrity of officialdom,
issued a clear edict to stop them.
Not long after,
there were many troubles on the maritime frontiers,
and in the tenth year,
maritime defense contributions were opened,
similar to the military provision rules,
with a two-tenths discount for collection,
and regular contributions were also discounted.
At this time, Táiwān first opened contributions for substantive official positions.
Other contributions, such as Sìchuān’s contributions for grain subsidies,
the various relief contributions in Shùntiān, Zhílì, Hénán, Zhèjiāng, Ānhuī, and Húběi,
Hùbù’s contributions for military supplies in Guǎngdōng,
Fújiàn’s contributions for foreign opium and tea,
and Yúnnán’s contributions for rice,
were all implemented after the maritime defense contributions.
However, the Chuān contributions remained as before,
while the others were either merged or abolished.
In the thirteenth year,
in Wǔzhì, Hénán,
the Qìn and Huáng rivers in Zhèngzhōu breached their banks.
Yùshǐ Zhōu Tiānlín and Lǐ Shìkūn successively requested the opening of Zhènggōng contributions
to aid essential projects.
The board deliberated to stop maritime defense contributions
and open Zhènggōng contributions.
In the fifteenth year,
for the establishment of the navy,
Zhènggōng contributions were again abolished,
and new maritime defense contributions were opened.
The new contributions were repeatedly extended
and remained in effect for more than ten years.
Between the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh years,
fundraising in Jiāngníng,
substantive official contributions in Qín and Jìn,
and relief contributions for post-disaster rehabilitation in Shùnzhí
were successively launched.
The Jiāngníng and Shùnzhí contributions followed the new maritime defense rules,
while the Qín and Jìn contributions only rewarded substantive official positions below the fifth rank.
After the Gēngzǐ Incident,
the Emperor was determined to govern effectively,
and many said that contributions were not good governance,
so an edict immediately stopped them.
However, those who contributed for service,
and old contributions designated for rewards,
continued to be implemented.
There was only the name of stopping contributions.
Donations for military posts.
In the early years of the Yōngzhèng reign, only Nàqiān and Bǎzǒng positions could be obtained through donation.
In the ninth year of Qiánlóng,
for direct relief donations, there were those who donated for Wèishǒubèi.
In the thirty-ninth year,
following the Chuān Yùn regulations,
Cān, Yóu, Dū, and Shǒu positions could begin to be obtained through successive donations.
However, for Wǔshēng and Jiāshēng, donations stopped at the Dūsī level.
In the third year of Jiāqìng,
the Chuānchǔ Shànhòu regulations were established,
where donations for military camps
were roughly similar to those for Chuān Yùn.
In the fifth year of Tóngzhì,
Zuo Zōngtáng, the Governor-General of Mǐnzhè, stated:
“There are too many donation ranks for military camps in Mǐn province,
and they should be strictly differentiated
to discipline the military administration.”
He also requested the abolition of military post donations,
which was granted.
In the twenty-first year of Guāngxù,
the new Hǎifáng regulations extended the deadline,
and an increase in military post donations was proposed.
A separate class was established apart from those selected for appointments,
to encourage enthusiastic contributions.
In the thirty-first year,
the Ministry of War reported:
“After ten years of opening donations,
the revenue collected is only a little over 100,000,
which does not benefit the national treasury
and hinders military organization.
We request that donations for actual official posts and honorary titles, as well as plume distinctions and imperial commendations, be entirely abolished.”
This was approved.
When the donation regulations were first opened,
fearing their abuses,
restrictions were often established,
but these methods often broke down before long.
In the eighteenth year of Kāngxī,
it was stipulated that officials who obtained their positions through donation, if competent after three years in office,
should be recommended for promotion;
if incompetent, they should be impeached.
However, frontier officials rarely reported incompetence.
Later,
it was ordered that those below Dào and Fǔ who donated silver were exempt from being recommended,
and were promoted as usual.
Xú Yuánwén, the Left Censor-in-Chief, stated:
“What is crucial for the overall national system
is only the distinction between the worthy and the unworthy.
The three-year recommendation was
intended to encourage the worthy
and deter the unworthy.
To be exempt from recommendation by donating silver
is to equate those with much money with those who are competent.
What would such individuals not do, using their current official positions to scheme for input [of funds]?
