It should be stopped immediately.”
During the Shùnzhì reign,
officials from Gòng and Lìjiān backgrounds were not allowed to be promoted to Zheng Yìn positions.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī,
a system of recommendation was established,
where officials from various paths,
if recommended as competent by the relevant minister and by the Governor-General or Governor,
were promoted to metropolitan officials and Zheng Yìn.
Those without recommendation
were promoted to Zuǒ'èr and Zázhí.
In the thirtieth year,
when the large army was campaigning against Gá'ěrdān,
the Ministry of Revenue proposed implementing regulations for transporting fodder and beans,
allowing personnel from alternative paths to donate for exemption from recommendation.
Yùshǐ Lù Lǒngqí stated:
“The matter of donations
was opened temporarily out of necessity.
Allowing donations for exemption from recommendation
makes them no different from the regular path.
Moreover, those recommended by Governors-General and Governors
must be honest and incorruptible to conform to the regulations.
If recommendation can be exempted by donation,
then honesty and incorruptibility can be obtained by paying money.”
He also stated:
“Governors-General and Governors, regarding donated personnel,
sometimes delay recommending them for several years, without also impeaching them.
I beg that the Ministry be ordered to thoroughly investigate donated officials who have been in office for three years without recommendation,
and dismiss them from their posts.”
The memorial was sent down to the Nine Ministers,
who deliberated:
“Donating for exemption from recommendation
does not hinder the regular path.
If being without recommendation for three years immediately leads to dismissal,
then the pursuit of recommendations will become even more intense,
and this should not be deliberated.”
Lù Lǒngqí held his ground even more firmly.
The court deliberated that Lù Lǒngqí did not consider urgency, importance, or triviality,
and used flowery rhetoric to embellish,
causing donation students to hesitate,
and delaying military affairs,
and proposed his dismissal from office.
The Emperor specially pardoned him.
From then on, those from Lìyuán and Lìjiān backgrounds,
who wished to be promoted or to donate for metropolitan or external Zhèng Yìn positions, had to first donate for exemption from recommendation,
with only Zhǔngòng being an exception.
Initially,
those who paid Suìgòng were treated the same as the regular path.
Therefore, when the regulation for donating for exemption from recommendation was established,
although Gòng and Jiān were both donation paths,
there was a significant difference in status.
In the twenty-sixth year of Qiánlóng,
the Ministry deliberated on the memorial by Yùshǐ Wáng Qǐxù regarding the Yùgōng regulations,
stating that Gòng who donated for metropolitan or external Zhèng Yìn positions,
and donated for exemption from recommendation,
should follow the Lìjiān example.
Those who had already obtained positions through donation
should retroactively make up the donation for exemption.
Those unwilling
were to be reassigned as Zuǒ'èr.
This was a change to the established regulations.
Donated officials from the Hànjūn,
unless they passed examinations,
were not allowed to be selected for appointments,
following the example of Hàn officials requiring recommendation.
During the Kāngxī reign,
exemption by donation was also permitted.
In the sixty-first year,
the Emperor, noting that Ministry officials who obtained posts through donation were promoted from Zhǔshì to Yuánláng very quickly,
and the same applied to external officials at Dào and Fǔ levels,
ordered deliberations on a system of probationary salaries.
Subsequently, it was decided that for those from Lángzhōng, Dào, and Fǔ levels downwards,
and from Xiǎojīngguān, Zuǒzá levels upwards,
they would serve a three-year probationary period in their current positions,
and only after official confirmation through recommendation or consultation
were they permitted to be promoted,
which was approved.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
the probationary salary could again be exempted by donation.
In the forty-first year,
the Ministry of Revenue requested that regulations for recommendation, examination, probationary salary, and donation for exemption
be included in regular donations.
By this point,
all restrictive measures had been relaxed.

That month, the Xiànzhèng Biānchá Guǎn (Bureau for Constitutional Reform and Compilation) and the Zīzhèng Yuàn (Advisory Council) jointly drafted the regulations for provincial Zīyì Jú (Provincial Advisory Bureaus),
as well as the regulations for the election of their members.
A memorial was submitted, stating:
“The essential meaning of a constitutional government
lies in granting the people the right to participate in government affairs
and to act as supervisors of administrative officials.
In constitutional countries of the East and West,
although their state systems differ
and their legal systems vary,
without exception, they establish parliaments
and enable the people to elect members
to represent public opinion.
This ensures that the sentiments of superiors and subordinates are communicated,
and the drawbacks of isolation are minimized.
China traditionally had no concept of a parliament,
and now that its establishment is proposed,
many regard it as a pioneering endeavor.
Yet, they are unaware that the clear-sightedness and sharp hearing of Yú Tíng (the court of Emperor Shùn),
the building of the táodú (drums and bells for expressing opinions) by Dà Yǔ (Yu the Great),
the consultation with the common people in the Hóngfàn (Great Plan),
and the inquiry to the Outer Court in Zhōuguān (Rites of Zhou)
all illustrate that in ancient times of prosperity,
public opinion was widely collected
to serve as the criterion for administration.
It was simply that the system of a parliament did not exist.
Now that a parliament is to be established,
if strict rules are not set,
measures for each matter are not instituted,
and precautions are not meticulously taken,
the resulting harms will be immeasurable.
China is vast and populous,
governed by provinces.
The administration of each province
is overseen by Dūfǔ (Governors-General and Governors),
which differs from the local governance of other countries that is directly connected to the national capital.
Moreover, the system of Jùnxiàn (commanderies and counties)
differs from feudalism,
as Dūfǔ receive all orders from the imperial court,
which is also unlike the federal states of other countries, each having its own legal system.
The Zīyì Jú serve as a pivot between local self-governance and central authority.
They must be able to gather the public opinion of a province below
while still not obstructing the state's paramount authority for national unity above.
The current methods for provincial Zīyì Jú
must complement and not contradict the future methods for the Jīngshī Yìyuàn (Capital Parliament).
We respectfully embody the sacred instructions,
extensively research the legislative intentions of various countries,
adopt the regulations drafted by other provinces,
and, through careful deliberation and compromise,
have drafted the regulations for provincial Zīyì Jú,
and separately, one hundred and fifteen articles for election regulations,
awaiting imperial approval and promulgation.”
An imperial edict ordered all Dūfǔ to swiftly implement these measures,
earnestly carry them out,
and complete them uniformly within one year.
The edict further stated:
“The imperial court, mindful of the people’s reliance,
will allow the populace to participate in government affairs.
First, Zīyì Jú will be established in each province
to gain experience.
All our officials and common people
must collectively understand the difficulties of the time
and together express loyalty and patriotism.
Regarding the benefits and harms in their localities that should be promoted or abolished,
they should truthfully point them out.
Regarding the duties that citizens should fulfill
and the order that should be followed,
they should earnestly adhere to them.
All Dūfǔ must act with a spirit of pooling wisdom and broadening benefits,
and govern with preferences aligned with the people,
humbly and carefully examine,
and only follow what is good.
Regarding the election of members,
they must particularly supervise officials,
seriously oversee,
and carefully select.
The Xiànzhèng Biānchá Guǎn and Zīzhèng Yuàn must swiftly compile the outline of a constitutional monarchy,
as well as various laws for parliamentary elections,
selecting the essential points.
They must also draft and submit for imperial approval various matters to be prepared before the parliament opens,
divided into phases.
After imperial approval,
the timeframe for opening the parliament
will be imperially determined and announced.”
In August,
the Xiànzhèng Biānchá Guǎn and Zīzhèng Yuàn jointly memorialized, reporting the draft outline of the constitution and parliamentary election law,
as well as the yearly preparatory matters before the parliament opens.
Starting from this year,
preparations would be divided into nine years.
Regarding the election of members,
in the first year, provinces would prepare the Zīyì Jú;
in the second year, Zīyì Jú elections would be held,
and all provinces would establish them uniformly,
the regulations for the Zīzhèng Yuàn would be promulgated,
and Zīzhèng Yuàn elections would be held.
In the third year, Zīzhèng Yuàn members would be convened for the opening session.
In the ninth year, the constitution would finally be announced,
parliamentary laws promulgated,
along with the election laws for members of the upper and lower houses,
and elections for members of the upper and lower houses would be held.
An imperial order instructed all central and local government offices to proceed within the deadlines.
Previously, the Zīzhèng Yuàn had submitted a draft table of contents for its regulations,
with Chapter Two being “Elections.”
In July of Xuāntǒng (Xuantong) 1 (1909),
the Zīzhèng Yuàn submitted further draft regulations,
revising the title of Chapter Two to “Members,”
detailing specifically the qualifications, number, categories, and term of office for members,
and separately establishing detailed election regulations
to avoid confusion,
which was approved.
The regulations stipulated the qualifications for Zīzhèng Yuàn members,
who would be selected from the following categories of individuals aged thirty years or older:
Imperial clan princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
Manchu and Han hereditary nobles;
Outer vassal princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
Imperial clan members (Zōngshì) and collateral imperial relatives (Juéluó);
Officials from various ministries and courts holding ranks from the fourth to seventh grade,
excluding judicial, prosecutorial, and police officers;
Scholars of profound learning and broad knowledge;
High taxpayers;
Members of provincial Zīyì Jú.
The fixed quotas were: sixteen for imperial clan princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
twelve for Manchu and Han hereditary nobles;
fourteen for outer vassal princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
six for Zōngshì and Juéluó;
thirty-two for officials from various ministries and courts;
ten for scholars of profound learning and broad knowledge;
ten for high taxpayers.
One hundred for members of provincial Zīyì Jú.
Categories of selection were imperial appointment (qīnxuǎn) and mutual election (hùxuǎn).
Imperial clan princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
Manchu and Han hereditary nobles;
outer vassal princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
Zōngshì and Juéluó;
officials from various ministries and courts;
scholars of profound learning and broad knowledge;
and high taxpayers
were imperially appointed.
Members of provincial Zīyì Jú were mutually elected.
The term of office was three years,
after which all were subject to re-election.
In the ninth month,
the Zīzhèngyuàn (資政院) submitted a memorial on the regulations for the election of Zīzhèngyuàn members,
stating:
“The methods for selecting and appointing Zīzhèngyuàn members
are broadly divided into two categories: imperial selection (qīn xuǎn, 欽選) and mutual election (hù xuǎn, 互選),
each having its own rationale.
For imperially selected members, there are differences in status,
and variations in numbers.
Arrangements should be made according to what is appropriate
to facilitate implementation.
For members of the imperial clan (Zōngshì, 宗室) who are princes (wáng, 王) and dukes (gōng, 公) with hereditary titles (shìjué, 世爵),
Manchu and Han hereditary nobles, and princes and dukes from outer vassal states (wàifān, 外藩) with hereditary titles,
their ranks are already high,
and their numbers relatively small.
A complete list should be compiled
for imperial appointment.
For other members of the imperial clan (Zōngshì, 宗室) and collateral imperial relatives (Juéluó, 覺羅),
officials from various boards (bù, 部) and courts (yuàn, 院), and those who pay large amounts of taxes,
the number of qualified individuals
and the fixed quota of members
show a significant disparity.
Considering the foreign system of an upper house,
many appointed members are selected through mutual election.
We propose to slightly adapt this idea
by holding a mutual election
before the imperial selection.
According to the fixed quota,
an additional number of candidates will be listed.
While popular sentiment will indicate preferences,
the final decision on appointment or rejection will still rest with the emperor (chén duàn, 宸斷).
For accomplished scholars and profound Confucians (shuòxué tōngrú, 碩學通儒),
whose qualifications are more difficult to ascertain
and whose numbers are hard to survey,
mutual election is practically unfeasible.
We propose to slightly emulate the previous system of recommending exceptional talents (hóngbó, 鴻博),
by casting a wide net but being strict in selection.
The task of surveying and collecting candidates
will be entrusted to various officials.
The power of selection
will be vested in the Board of Education (Xuébù, 學部).
A generous number of candidates will still be listed,
hoping not to lose the original intent of imperial selection.
The above items
roughly adopt the methods of upper houses in various countries,
serving as the foundation for establishing an upper house.
However, the Zīzhèngyuàn also possesses characteristics of a lower house,
and therefore cannot be without popularly elected members
to counterbalance the imperially selected members.
Specifically, the Zīyìjú (諮議局) will serve as the mutual election body for half of the Zīzhèngyuàn members.
Since Zīyìjú members are originally re-elected by qualified gentry and commoners from each province,
then the Zīzhèngyuàn members promoted through public recommendation by the Zīyìjú
are virtually indirectly elected by the people.
The standard for public recommendation and promotion
must be based on the number of votes received.
However, the power of supervision belongs to the governors-general (dū, 督) and governors (fǔ, 撫),
and without their final approval,
one may not immediately assume the election.
This shows a distinction from the imperial selection power
and is thus not contrary to the essential principles of a lower house.”
An edict was issued to implement the proposal.
The regulations for the election of Zīzhèngyuàn members stipulate that
for members of the imperial clan who are princes and dukes with hereditary titles,
there are twelve ranks of nobility: 1.
Héshuò Qīnwáng (和碩親王);
Duōluó Jùnwáng (多羅郡王);
Duōluó Bèilè (多羅貝勒);
Gùshān Bèizǐ (固山貝子);
Fèng'ēn Zhènguó Gōng (奉恩鎮國公);
Fèng'ēn Fǔguó Gōng (奉恩輔國公);
Bùrù Bāfēn Zhènguó Gōng (不入八分鎮國公);
Bùrù Bāfēn Fǔguó Gōng (不入八分輔國公);
Zhènguó Jiāngjūn (鎮國將軍);
10. Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍);
Fèngguó Jiāngjūn (奉國將軍);
Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn (奉恩將軍).
According to the fixed quota allocation in the Zīzhèngyuàn regulations,
from Héshuò Qīnwáng to Fèng'ēn Fǔguó Gōng, ten persons;
from Bùrù Bāfēn Zhènguó Gōng to Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn, six persons.
For Manchu and Han hereditary nobles, limited to ranks of third-class marquis (sānděng hóu, 三等侯) and above for Manchu, Mongol, and Han Banner (qíyuán, 旗員) officers, and Han officials,
they are allocated according to the fixed quota.
Eight persons for first-class marquis (yīdèng hóu, 一等侯) and above;
four persons for first-class earl (yīdèng bó, 一等伯) to third-class baron (sānděng nán, 三等男).
For hereditary nobles of outer vassal princes and dukes,
including all the following Mongolian, Hui (Huíbù, 回部), and Tibetan (Xīzàng, 西藏) noble ranks: 1.
Khan (hán, 汗);
Qīnwáng (親王);
Jùnwáng (郡王);
Bèilè (貝勒);
Bèizǐ (貝子);
Zhènguó Gōng (鎮國公);
Fǔguó Gōng (輔國公).
They are allocated according to the fixed quota.
From the six leagues (méng, 盟) of Inner Mongolia (Nèiménggǔ, 內蒙古),
one person from each league;
from the four leagues of Outer Mongolia (Wàiménggǔ, 外蒙古),
one person from each league;
one person from the various Mongol banners belonging to Kobdo (Kēbùduō, 科布多) and Xinjiang (Xīnjiāng);
one person from the various Mongol banners belonging to Qinghai (Qīnghǎi);
one person from the Hui部;
one person from Tibet.
All hereditary nobles of the above categories who are thirty years of age or older,
who have not been specially ordered to cease their official duties or emoluments,
and who have not requested to be relieved of all duties due to illness or incident,
are eligible to be selected as Zīzhèngyuàn members.
For each election,
the Zīzhèngyuàn shall, in September of the preceding year, notify the Zōngrénfǔ (宗人府),
the respective governing yamen (yámén, 衙門), and the Lǐfānbù (理藩部),
who shall separately verify qualified individuals,
compile a clear roster,
and submit it to the Zīzhèngyuàn
before February of the election year.
The Zīzhèngyuàn shall then separately list the candidates
and request imperial selection according to the quota
before March.
Princes and dukes of the imperial clan,
Manchu and Han hereditary nobles,
incumbent Grand Councillors (Jūnjī Dàchén, 軍機大臣),
ministers assisting in government affairs (Cānyù Zhèngwù Dàchén, 參豫政務大臣),
and the President (zǒngcái, 總裁) and Vice-President (fùzǒngcái, 副總裁) of the Zīzhèngyuàn
do not need to be selected for appointment.
Should there be vacancies,
the Zīzhèngyuàn shall promptly notify the respective yamen
to amend the roster.
Those who should be selected according to their noble rank or tribe
shall be submitted for imperial selection to fill the vacancies.
Members of the Imperial Clan (Zōngshì) and Imperial Lineage (Juéluó),
any male aged thirty or above,
who does not have any of the following conditions,
may be selected as a member of the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn): 1.
Those who have been imprisoned (quānjìn) or exiled;
Those who have lost credit concerning their property, have been accused of it, and have not yet settled the matter;
Those who smoke opium;
Those with heart disease;
Those who are illiterate.
Current officials of the third rank (sānpǐn) or above,
judicial, procuratorial, and police officers,
and active military personnel of the army and navy
need not be selected.
According to the prescribed quota,
four members from the Imperial Clan (Zōngshì)
and two from the Imperial Lineage (Juéluó)
shall first be mutually elected by the eligible individuals concerned.
This shall take place on the first day of the second month of the election year,
in the capital (Jīngshī) and Fengtian Prefecture (Fèngtiān Fǔ).
In the capital (Jīngshī), the presiding officials (tángguān) of the Imperial Clan Court (Zōngrénfǔ) shall serve as supervisors.
In Fengtian (Fèngtiān), the Governor-General of the Three Eastern Provinces (Dōngsānsheng Zǒngdū) shall serve as supervisor.
For each mutual election,
the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn) shall inform the mutual election supervisors in September of the preceding year,
who shall conduct it according to regulations.
Mutual election administrators shall be appointed
to be responsible for investigating eligible voters (hùxuǎnrén),
and managing voting, vote counting, ballot inspection, and other related matters.
The mutual election administrators shall verify the eligible personnel,
compile a roster of eligible voters (hùxuǎnrén míngcè),
and present it in advance to the mutual election supervisor for public proclamation.
If any individual believes there is an error or omission,
they may, within the proclamation period,
petition the mutual election supervisor for correction or inclusion.
Those whose petitions have been rejected
shall not re-petition frivolously.
Both the electors and candidates in the mutual election
are limited to those listed in the roster of eligible voters (hùxuǎnrén míngcè).
When the time comes, the mutual election supervisor shall personally attend the polling station,
or dispatch an officer to oversee it.
Eligible voters shall personally go to the polling station to cast their votes,
using a signed single-vote method (jì míngdān jìfǎ).
If an eligible voter is unable to personally attend the polling station due to official duties, illness, or an accident,
they may entrust another eligible voter to cast their vote on their behalf.
This must be personally handwritten by the individual, sealed, signed, and fingerprinted,
and together with the letter of authorization (wěituō píngzhèng),
sent to the authorized person.
The authorized person shall present the sealed document and letter of authorization to the mutual election supervisor for verification at the time
before being permitted to cast the vote on their behalf.
Those who receive the most votes shall be elected.
The number of successful candidates in the mutual election
shall be ten times the prescribed quota for members.
Upon completion of the mutual election,
the mutual election supervisor shall immediately post the list of successful candidates at the polling station.
Those who do not wish to be selected
may present a petition to the mutual election supervisor within three days to withdraw,
and the candidate with the next highest number of votes shall fill the vacancy.
The mutual election administrators shall compile a roster of successful candidates,
together with the ballots,
and present it to the mutual election supervisor, who shall forward it to the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn).
The Assembly shall then prepare a list of the names of the successful candidates and their vote counts,
and before March of the election year,
submit a memorial to the throne for imperial selection (qīnxuǎn) according to the quota.
If there is a vacancy,
the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn) shall at any time submit a list of the current successful candidates and memorialize for imperial selection (qīnxuǎn) to fill it.
If the number of current successful candidates is less than three times the vacant seats for members,
a provisional mutual election shall be held,
and all procedures shall follow those of a regular mutual election.
Officials from various ministries (bù) and courts (yuàn)
are limited to the following: 1.
Those from the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) from Reader-in-waiting (shìdú xuéshì) downwards,
and from Middle-ranking Secretariat Official (zhōngshū) upwards;
Those from the Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn) from Reader-in-waiting (shìdú xuéshì) downwards,
and from Imperial Compiler (shùjíshì) upwards;
Those from various ministries (bù) from Left and Right Vice Minister (zuǒ yòu cānyì) downwards,
and from Seventh-rank minor capital official (qīpǐn xiǎo Jīngguān) upwards;
Bearer of the Seal, Remonstrance Official (gěishìzhōng), and Censor (jiānchá yùshǐ).
All officials aged thirty or above,
possessing one of the following qualifications,
may be selected as members of the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn): 1.
Those currently holding substantive posts;
Those who previously held substantive posts and have not retired or been dismissed;
Those who have been appointed acting (shǔlǐ) or provisionally appointed (zòushǔ) by imperial decree;
Those who have been designated for appointment (hòubǔ), appointed for service (bǔyòng), selected for appointment (xuǎnyòng), or undergoing probation (xuéxí xíngzǒu) by imperial decree;
Other candidates who have completed three years or more of waiting for appointment.
They shall first be mutually elected by eligible individuals,
which shall take place on the first day of the second month of the election year in the capital (Jīngshī),
with the presiding officials (tángguān) of the Censorate (Dūcháyùn) as supervisors.
The number of successful candidates in the mutual election
shall be five times the prescribed quota for members.
Officials from various ministries (bù) and courts (yuàn) selected as members of the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn),
regarding their functions and powers within the Assembly,
their superior officials in their own government offices (yámén) shall not interfere.
Those who lose their original qualifications due to promotion, transfer, demotion, or reassignment
shall simultaneously lose their qualifications as members of the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn).
All regulations concerning the conduct of mutual elections, memorializing for imperial selection (qīnxuǎn), and filling vacancies
shall be the same as those for the Imperial Clan (Zōngshì) and Imperial Lineage (Juéluó) elections.
There are four qualifications for eminent scholars and learned Confucians (shuòxué tōngrú): 1.
Those who have been granted clean (qīngzhì) ranks by special imperial decree without examination;
Those whose writings have contributed to politics or academia;
Those who possess the qualifications to enter the Academy of Learned Confucians (Tōngrúyuàn);
Those who have served as instructors of major subjects in higher and specialized schools for five years or more and have achieved notable results.
Any male aged thirty or above,
possessing one of the aforementioned qualifications,
may be selected as a member of the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn).
For each election,
the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn) shall inform the Ministry of Education (Xuébù) in September of the preceding year.

The Ministry shall then notify officials of the capital (Jīngtáng) rank or above, Hanlin academicians (Hànlín), Remonstrance Officials (gěishìzhōng), Censors (yùshǐ), Governors-General (dū) and Governors (fǔ) of various provinces, Education Commissioners (tíxuéshǐ), and Ministers to various countries,
each to seek out one or two individuals,
state the facts,
and recommend them to the Ministry of Education (Xuébù) for review.
Thirty individuals who are deemed qualified and have received the most recommendations shall be selected
as candidates for eminent scholars and learned Confucians (shuòxué tōngrú) members.
Before February of the election year,
their names shall be forwarded to the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn).
The Assembly shall then prepare a list of the names of the candidates and the names and official titles of their original recommenders,
and before March,
submit a memorial to the throne for imperial selection (qīnxuǎn) according to the quota.
If there is a vacancy,
the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn) shall at any time submit a list of the current candidates and memorialize for imperial selection (qīnxuǎn) according to regulations to fill it.
If the number of current candidates is less than three times the vacant seats for members,
additional recommendations shall be sought.
Taxpayers with large contributions
are limited to the following qualifications: 1.
Males who possess voting rights according to local autonomy regulations;
Those who annually pay a relatively large amount of regular tax or local public welfare contributions
in their resident province.
Any individual possessing these qualifications,
aged thirty or above,
may be selected as a member of the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn).
They shall first be mutually elected by eligible individuals,
which shall take place on the first day of the second month of the election year in the provincial capitals (shěngchéng) of various provinces,
with the Provincial Administration Commissioner (Bùzhèngshǐ) or Civil Administration Commissioner (Mínzhèngshǐ) as supervisor.
For each mutual election,
the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn) shall inform the Governors-General (dū) and Governors (fǔ) of various provinces in September of the preceding year,
who shall conduct it according to regulations.
The mutual election supervisor, in conjunction with the President and Vice President of the General Chamber of Commerce (Shāngwù Zǒnghuì Zǒnglǐ, Xiélǐ),
shall appoint mutual election administrators.
The mutual election procedures shall be the same as those for ordinary mutual elections.
The number of eligible voters (hùxuǎnrén).
Each province shall be limited to twenty individuals.
Voting shall use a signed cumulative vote method (jìmíng liánjìfǎ),
and those who receive more than one-third of the votes from the eligible voters shall be elected.
The number of successful candidates in the mutual election
shall be one-tenth of the number of eligible voters (hùxuǎnrén).
If the number of successful candidates is less than the prescribed quota,
the eligible voters shall cast their votes again for those with more votes,
until the quota is met.
Those who meet the vote threshold but are not elected due to the quota being filled
shall serve as alternate successful candidates.
If a successful candidate does not wish to be selected,
they may petition the mutual election supervisor to withdraw,
and the alternate successful candidates shall fill the vacancy in sequence.
The mutual election administrators shall compile a roster of successful candidates and alternate successful candidates,
together with the ballots,
and present it to the mutual election supervisor, who shall submit it to the Governor-General (dū) or Governor (fǔ) of the respective province.
Each Governor-General (dū) or Governor (fǔ) shall then forward the names of the successful candidates and their vote counts to the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn).
The Assembly shall prepare a list,
and before March,
submit a memorial to the throne for imperial selection (qīnxuǎn) according to the quota.
If there is a vacancy,
the Consultative Assembly (Zīzhèngyuàn) shall at any time submit a list of the current successful candidates and memorialize for imperial selection (qīnxuǎn) to fill it.
If the number of current successful candidates is less than three times the vacant seats for members,
the alternate successful candidates shall fill the vacancy.
If the number of alternate successful candidates is insufficient,
a provisional mutual election shall be held.
Tài-zǔ (太祖) laid the foundation in the Eastern Lands.
The national customs were pure and unified.
Affairs were simple, and duties specialized.
Eight Grand Ministers of the Banner Corps (bāqí zǒngguǎn dàchén 八旗總管大臣) and Assistant Grand Ministers (zuǒguǎn dàchén 佐管大臣) were appointed to oversee military affairs.
Five Grand Deliberative Ministers (yìzhèng wǔ dàchén 議政五大臣) and ten Grand Executive Ministers (lǐshì shí dàchén 理事十大臣) were appointed to manage governance and justice.
Only a few close relatives and noble subjects were employed.
Offices were named according to their functions,
and officials were appointed according to their offices.
It flourished vigorously.
Tài-zōng (太宗) diligently managed the state.
He established the Three Institutes (sānguǎn 三館)
and appointed eight Chief Secretaries (bā chéngzhèng 八承政).
He assessed merits and evaluated diligence,
leading to a universally well-governed state.
Shì-zǔ (世祖) entered the Pass.
Building upon the inherited Ming (明) system,
from the Grand Secretariat (gē 閣) and Six Boards (bù 部) down to the various庶司 [shùsī],
adjustments were made with substance.
The Court of Colonial Affairs (fānbù 藩部) was newly established,
its name ranking alongside the Seven Ministers (qīqīng 七卿).
Externally, Governors-General (dūdǎo 督撫) were appointed
to prevent frequent changes,
which were enshrined in regulations.
For the Green Standard Army (lǜyíng 綠營), from Commanders (tízhèn 提鎮) downwards,
all appointments were changed from temporary assignments to permanent official positions.
For the Banner Army (qíyíng 旗營) Imperial Guards (yùqián lǐngwèi 御前領衞),
length of service meant high rank,
and they were trusted with important, confidential matters.
Commandants-General (dūtǒng 都統) and Banner Chiefs (qízhǎng 旗長)
jointly governed military and civilian affairs.
Their duties were specific to their garrisons in the specialized regions,
distinguishing them from the Hanlin Academy (hànlín 翰林) outside the capital area,
thereby regulating the capital's system.
In the northwest frontiers,
they were guarded by high-ranking officials.
They pacified the Mongols (méng 蒙) and Tibetans (fān 番),
their functions paralleling the Protectorates (dūhù 都護).
All these were adaptations to local customs,
finding what was appropriate.
Shì-zōng (世宗) comprehensively reviewed the system,
abolishing positions like Supervisor of Imperial Seals (shàngbǎo 尚寶), Director of the Court of State Ceremonial (xíngrén 行人), and Vice Censors-in-Chief (qiāndū 僉都).
Gāo-zōng (高宗) was enlightened and wise,
reducing titles such as Policy Advisors (cāncè 參政), Counselors (cānyì 參議), Vice Envoys (fùshǐ 副使), and Investigation Censors (qiānshì 僉事).
He eliminated redundant positions,
and officials performed their duties with solemnity.
After Jiā-qìng (嘉慶) and Dào-guāng (道光),
the system was reformed as before.
With the passage of time, decay and slackness set in,
and the original spirit gradually disappeared.
With daily and monthly changes,
a hundred offices encroached upon one another.
Gūang-xù (光緒) initiated reforms,
and Xuān-tǒng (宣統) deliberated on the system.
The categories were elaborate and confused,
and responsibilities were disordered.
Intending to bring peace to the nation,
did it not instead increase chaos?
The authority of a nation's affairs
was wielded by the Grand Council (shūyuán 樞垣),
converged at the Six Boards (liùcáo 六曹),
and distributed among the provincial governors (jiānglì 疆吏).
From the transformation of the Inner Three Courts (nèi sān yuàn 內三院) into the Grand Secretariat (nèi gé 內閣),
the Grand Secretaries (tái fǔ 台輔) stood idly by.
When the Grand Council (jūnjī chù 軍機處) was established,
memorial papers were abolished,
and the Grand Secretariat became even more like a superfluous office.
The chief officials of the Six Boards numbered three or four,
each without specialized duties.
Sometimes, one might hold the power of appointment in the morning,
and oversee expenditures in the evening;
having just led military affairs,
they would then take charge of judicial matters.
One position had several officials,
and one official held several positions.
With constant reporting and deferring,
how could any achievements be made?
At that time, the power of the Grand Council
stood uniquely above all else.
When the state undertook major military campaigns,
Grand Ministers Overseeing Military Affairs (jīnglüè dàchén 經略大臣) and Assistant Grand Ministers (cānzàn dàchén 參贊大臣) were specially appointed,
personally entrusted with vital military matters.
The Ministry of Personnel (lìbù 吏部) assisted in deploying personnel,
and the Ministry of Revenue (hùbù 戶部) provided vast provisions.
It was through the leverage of these powerful positions
that they achieved great successes.
From then on, power shifted again to the Grand Ministers Overseeing Military Affairs.
Although Governors-General (dūdǎo 督撫) were ostensibly of equal rank,
they merely carried out orders and prepared for contingencies.
Later, when conflicts arose along the maritime borders,
the talent and prestige of the Grand Ministers Overseeing Military Affairs waned slightly,
and their power gradually diminished.
During the disturbances in Guǎngdōng (廣東),
the Prime Minister (xiàngshǒu 首相) commanded the army,
repeatedly failing in their endeavors.
The court occasionally used Governors-General to lead military affairs,
and most did not disgrace their orders.
Moreover, they were not constrained by bureaucratic formalities,
thus able to exert their full strength.
From then on, power shifted again to the Governors-General.
The Tóng-zhì (同治) Restoration and
Gūang-xù's (光緒) return to the capital
were all due to their efforts.
By the late period,
close relatives held sway,
power was diminished in the periphery,
and heavily concentrated at the center,
leading to the collapse of frontier affairs.
In the initial system, internal and external officials
were jointly appointed from Manchu (mǎnhàn 滿漢),
Mongolian (ménggǔ 蒙古), and Han (hànjūn 漢軍) Banners,
distributed in sequence.
During the Kāng-xī (康熙) and Yōng-zhèng (雍正) reigns,
the positions of Governors-General in the northwest
were designated for Manchus.
Leaders (lǐngduì 領隊) and Executive Ministers (bànshì dàchén 辦事大臣)
were exclusively appointed from Manchu officials.
Throughout various dynasties, those who held important military commands outside the capital
were mostly Manchu officials.
However, during Wén-zōng's (文宗) reign, Han people were also used,
and their meritorious achievements became notable.
Generally, before the mid-period,
the expansion of territory
was largely accomplished by Manchus.
After the mid-period,
the resolution of severe crises and restoration of order
were largely accomplished by Han people.
In the final era, when the official system was regulated,
it was initially hoped to blend the boundaries
to solidify the foundation.
But the corrupt practices persisted,
each entity acting as its own master,
merely causing suspicion and fear.
Even the policies of decline and peril,
though not central to important records,
must also be compiled and listed
to illustrate the historical facts of the time.
The traces of order and chaos
will then be clear as if observed.

Court of the Imperial Clan (zōngrén fǔ 宗人府); Grand Tutors and Protectors (shīfù bǎobǎo 師傅保); Grand Secretariat (nèi gé 內閣) (Office for Investigating and Reviewing Imperial Edicts, jīchá qīnfèng shàngyù shìjiàn chù 稽查欽奉上諭事件處; Grand Secretariat Drafting Office, zhōngshū kē 中書科); Grand Council (jūnjī chù 軍機處) (Inner Translation Bureau, nèi fānshū fáng 內繙書房; Strategic Archives, fānglüè guǎn 方略館); Ministry of Personnel (lìbù 吏部); Ministry of Revenue (hùbù 戶部) (Three Imperial Treasuries, sānkù 三庫; Granaries and Canal Transport, cāngchǎng 倉場; Customs and Taxes, guānshuì gè chā 關稅各差); Ministry of Rites (lǐbù 禮部) (Court of State Ceremonial and Four Interpreters, huìtóng sìyì guǎn 會同四譯館; Imperial Music Department, yuèbù 樂部); Ministry of War (bīngbù 兵部); Ministry of Justice (xíngbù 刑部); Ministry of Works (gōngbù 工部) (Gunpowder Bureau, huǒyào jú 火藥局; River Conservancy and Canals, hédào gōuqú 河道溝渠); Five Boards of Shèngjīng (shèngjīng wǔbù 盛京五部).
Court of the Imperial Clan (zōngrén fǔ 宗人府): Imperial Clan Director (zōnglìng 宗令),
one Left and one Right Imperial Clan Chief (zuǒ yòu zōngzhèng 左右宗正),
one Left and one Right Imperial Clan Member (zuǒ yòu zōngrén 左右宗人),
all each one person.
(These positions were held by Imperial Clan princes and nobles.)
Vice Director (fǔchéng 府丞),
one Han (hàn 漢) official.
(Rank 3a.)
Its subordinates: Department Director (táng zhǔshì 堂主事),
Han Department Director (hàn zhǔshì 漢主事),
Director of the Registry (jīnglì sī jīnglì 經歷司經歷),
(all Rank 6a.)
Left and Right Department Executive Officers (zuǒ yòu èr sī lǐshì guān 左右二司理事官),
(Rank 5a.)
Assistant Executive Officers (fù lǐshì guān 副理事官),
(Rank 5b.)
Department Directors (zhǔshì 主事),
Acting Department Directors (wěishǔ zhǔshì 委署主事),
all each two persons;
Secretaries (bǐtiēshì 筆帖式),
Probationary Secretaries (xiàolì bǐtiēshì 効力筆帖式),
each twenty-four persons.
(All these were held by Imperial Clan members.)
The Zōnglìng (宗令) was in charge of the imperial clan's registry.
(The main lineage of Xiǎnzǔ Xuān Huángdì (顯祖宣皇帝) was the Zōngshì (宗室),
who wore a golden-yellow sash.
Collateral branches were called Juéluó (覺羅),
who wore a red sash.
Those stripped of their status
wore a purple sash.) He was to revise and compile the Yùdié (玉牒) periodically,
establish the generational order (zhāomù),
and arrange ranks and stipends.
(There were twelve ranks of enfeoffment for Zōngshì (宗室):
Hèshuò Qīnwáng (和碩親王),
Duōluó Jùnwáng (多羅郡王),
Duōluó Bèilè (多羅貝勒),
Gùshān Bèizǐ (固山貝子),
Fèng'ēn Zhènguógōng (奉恩鎮國公),
Fèng'ēn Fǔguógōng (奉恩輔國公),
Bùrù Bāfēn Zhènguógōng (不入八分鎮國公),
Bùrù Bāfēn Fǔguógōng (不入八分輔國公),
Zhènguó Jiāngjūn (鎮國將軍),
Fǔguó Jiāngjūn (輔國將軍),
Fèngguó Jiāngjūn (奉國將軍),
Fèng'ēn Jiāngjūn (奉恩將軍).
There were two titles for嫡子 (dìzǐ) receiving enfeoffment:
Shìzǐ (世子) and Chángzǐ (長子).
The titles of Fújìn (福晉) and Fūrén (夫人) varied
according to their husbands' ranks.
There were two ranks of Gōngzhǔ (公主):
Gùlún Gōngzhǔ (固倫公主) and Hèshuò Gōngzhǔ (和碩公主).
There were five ranks of Gégé (格格):
Jùnzhǔ (郡主),
Xiànzhǔ (縣主),
Jùnjūn (郡君),
Xiànjūn (縣君), and Xiāngjūn (鄉君).
Those not included in the five ranks were called Zōngnǚ (宗女).
The ranks of Éfù (額駙) varied
according to the ranks of the Gōngzhǔ (公主) and Gégé (格格).
He also arranged the lineage divisions,
issued admonitions and instructions,
deliberated on rewards and punishments,
and superintended the ancestral temple sacrifices.
The Zōngzhèng (宗正) and Zōngrén (宗人) assisted him.
The Fǔchéng (府丞) was in charge of proofreading Chinese records.
The two departments of Zuǒ (左) and Yòu (右) separately managed the genealogies of the Zōngshì (宗室) and Juéluó (覺羅) of the left and right wings,
recording the births, deaths, marriages,
official ranks, and posthumous titles of their sons and daughters, legitimate and illegitimate;
they also verified the order of succession,
salary grades,
and matters of support and pensions.
The Tángzhǔshì (堂主事) was in charge of Manchu memorials.
The Hànzhǔshì (漢主事) was in charge of Chinese documents.
The Jīnglì (經歷) was in charge of receiving and issuing dispatches.
The Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式) was in charge of translating documents.
(This applied to all departments.
Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式) was a stepping stone for Manchu officials.
In the early years of the dynasty,
Grand Secretaries Dáhǎi (達海), Érdéní (額爾德尼), Suǒní (索尼), and others
started their careers as military officials.
Because of their proficiency in the national language,
they were specially granted the title "Bākèshí" (巴克什),
which was the forerunner of the later Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式).
Subsequently, the number of candidates for various posts became innumerable.)
Those concurrently holding positions were: two Wáng (王) as General Managers of Scholastic Affairs for the Left and Right Wing Zōngxué (宗學),
three Jīngtángguān (京堂官) as Investigators of Scholastic Affairs,
(all appointed by imperial decree),
four General Supervisors,
(receiving a seventh-rank stipend),
sixteen Assistant Supervisors,
(receiving an eighth-rank stipend),
(all appointed by imperial audience from among the respected elders of the Zōngshì (宗室)),
six Manchu language instructors and six archery instructors,
and eight Chinese language instructors.
The subordinate Silver Treasury
was managed by one Tángguān (堂官) from this yámen and one Manchu grandee,
(appointed by imperial decree),
two司官 (sīguān),
(appointed by imperial audience from this yámen),
and four Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式).
The Kōngfáng (空房)
had the same number of Sīguān (司官) and Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式).
The Huángdàngfáng (黃檔房)
had no fixed limit on the number of Sīguān (司官) and Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式).
In the initial system,
the offices were located in front of the Dǔgōngdiàn (篤恭殿),
where eight Hèshuò Bèilè (和碩貝勒) jointly deliberated on state affairs,
each with their own officials.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì (順治) (1652),
the Zōngrénfǔ (宗人府) was established,
with one Zōnglìng (宗令);
(held by Qīnwáng (親王) or Jùnwáng (郡王));
two Zuǒ Zōngzhèng (左宗正) and Yòu Zōngzhèng (右宗正),
(concurrently held by Bèilè (貝勒) or Bèizǐ (貝子));
and two Zōngrén (宗人),
(concurrently held by Zhènguógōng (鎮國公), Fǔguógōng (輔國公), or Jiāngjūn (將軍).
Later, worthy individuals were selected,
not limited by rank.)
There was one Qǐxīnláng (啟心郎) from the Juéluó (覺羅) and two from the Hànjūn (漢軍).
(Initially, their rank was equivalent to that of Lǐshìguān (理事官).
In the ninth year,
it was changed to be equivalent to Shìláng (侍郎).
Initially, because Manchu officials were not fluent in Chinese,
they were seated among the deliberators.
Later, many took advantage of this to commit malpractice,
and the position was abolished in the twelfth year of Kāngxī (康熙) (1673).)
These, along with the Fǔchéng (府丞), were principal officials.
There were six Lángzhōng (郎中),
(two were abolished in the thirty-eighth year of Kāngxī (1699)),
four Yuánwàiláng (員外郎),
and three Zhǔshì (主事),
held by Juéluó (覺羅).
Later, it was changed to be filled by Juéluó (覺羅) and Manchu officials concurrently.
There were two Tángzhǔshì (堂主事),
three Jīnglì (經歷),
(two Zōngshì (宗室) or Manchu, one Han.
The Han vacancy was abolished in the thirty-eighth year of Kāngxī (1699).
In the twenty-ninth year of Qiánlóng (1764), it was changed to be filled by Zōngshì (宗室)).
There were twenty-four Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式).
(Later, the number fluctuated.
Initially, they were Tāchì Hāfān (他赤哈哈番) and Bǐtiēshì Hāfān (筆帖式哈番).
Soon after, they were changed to sixth, seventh, eighth rank, and untitled Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式).
This applied to all departments.)
In the twelfth year of Kāngxī (1673),
the Qǐxīnláng (啟心郎) position was abolished,
and one Manchu Zhǔshì (主事) was added,
assigned to the Left and Right Departments.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (雍正) (1723),
two Han Zhǔshì (主事) were added.
(Filled by those with a Jìnshì (進士) degree.)
The following year,
Lángzhōng (郎中) was changed to Lǐshìguān (理事官),
and Yuánwàiláng (員外郎) to Fùlǐshìguān (副理事官),
and it was stipulated that they should be filled by Zōngshì (宗室) and Manchu officials concurrently.
In the twenty-ninth year of Qiánlóng (1764),
upon the memorial of Fǔchéng (府丞) Chǔ Línzhǐ (儲麟趾),
it was finally stipulated that only Zōngshì (宗shì) personnel should be employed.
In the fifty-third year (1788),
four Wěishǔ Zhǔshì (委署主事) were added.
(Changed from Bǐtiēshì (筆帖式).)
The Tàishī (太師), Tàifù (太傅), and Tàibǎo (太保) were the Three Grandees (Sāngōng).
(Senior First Rank.)
The Shàoshī (少師), Shàofù (少傅), and Shàobǎo (少保) were the Three Minor Grandees (Sāngū).
(Junior First Rank.)
The Tàizǐ Tàishī (太子太師), Tàizǐ Tàifù (太子太傅), and Tàizǐ Tàibǎo (太子太保),
(Junior First Rank),
and Tàizǐ Shàoshī (太子少師), Tàizǐ Shàofù (太子少傅), and Tàizǐ Shàobǎo (太子少保),
(Senior Second Rank),
were all Eastern Palace ministers,
with no fixed number
and not specially appointed.
Initially, following the Ming system,
ministers were granted the titles of Gōng (公) or Gū (孤).
Later, these were designated as concurrent, added, or posthumous titles.

two Manchu and two Han.

Han officials Grade 2.

forty Manchu,

The Grand Secretaries were in charge of governing the nation,
assisting with imperial edicts,
clarifying constitutional statutes,
deliberating on major rites and policies,
and deciding on the appropriateness of reporting to the emperor.
The Assistant Grand Secretaries assisted them.
(They served as the supervisors and chief compilers
for the compilation of the Veritable Records (Shílù), histories (Shǐ), and gazetteers (Zhì).
They led the lecturers in imperial lectures (Jīngyán).
They served as examiners for the metropolitan examinations (Huìshì).
They served as readers of examination papers for the palace examinations (Diànshì).
During the spring and autumn ceremonies for Confucius (Shìdiàn),
they acted on behalf of the emperor in performing the sacrifices.
)The Academicians were in charge of memorials and reports.
The Readers were in charge of collation and proofreading.
The Shìdú were in charge of verification and comparison.
The Registrars were in charge of the receipt and dispatch of documents.
(The Grand Secretariat (Nèigé) was the place for managing imperial edicts;
from the Grand Secretaries downwards,
none held seals,
only the Registrars held them
for stamping incoming and outgoing documents.
)The Secretaries were in charge of drafting and translation.
There were five divisions for handling memorials: the Manchu Memorial Office (Mǎnběnfáng),
the Han Memorial Office (Hànběnfáng),
the Mongol Memorial Office (Ménggǔběnfáng),
the Manchu Edict-Drafting Office (Mǎnqiānrpiàochù),
and the Han Edict-Drafting Office (Hànqiānrpiàochù).
Additionally, there were the Patent-Granting Office (Gàochìfáng),
the Audit Office (Jīcháfáng),
the Office for Receipt and Dispatch of Red Memorials and Copies (Shōufà Hóngběn Fùběnchù),
and the Silver Ration Treasury (Fànyínkù),
all of which were overseen by officials from the Shìdú and below, as appointed by the Grand Secretaries.
However, the Memorial Review Office (Pībĕnchù) was specifically staffed with one Manchu Hanlin official
(appointed by imperial decree)
and seven Secretaries.
(Appointed from among Manchu Secretaries.
Initially,
in the second year of Tiāncōng,
the Wénguǎn (Literary Hall) was established,
and Confucian ministers were ordered to serve there.
In the tenth year,
it was renamed the Nèi Sān Yuàn (Three Inner Courts).
(Namely, the Guóshǐ Yuàn (National History Court),
the Mìshū Yuàn (Secretariat Court),
and the Hóngwén Yuàn (Grand Literary Court).
)Initially, they also adopted the title of Chéngzhèng (Administrators),

In the first year of Shùnzhì,
Manchu and Han Grand Secretaries were appointed,
without a fixed number,
and concurrently held the titles of Ministers of various Boards.

In the tenth year,
two Han Grand Secretaries were appointed for each of the Three Courts.
In the fifteenth year,
it was renamed the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé),
and separate Hanlin Academy (Hànlín Yuàn) officials were established,
with Grand Secretaries concurrently holding these posts.
The palace halls were the Zhōnghé Diàn, Bǎohé Diàn, Wénhuá Diàn, Wǔyīng Diàn, Wényuān Gé, and Dōng Gé.
All Grand Secretaries still concurrently held the title of Minister (Shàngshū),
and Academicians did likewise.
In the eighteenth year,
the old system of the Three Courts was reinstated.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī,
the Hanlin Academy was again separately established,
the Three Courts were renamed the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé),
and four Manchu and Han Grand Secretaries were appointed.
In the ninth year of Yōngzhèng,
Chén Yuánlóng, Minister of Rites, and Yǐn Tà, Left Censor-in-Chief (Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ), were specially appointed as additional Grand Secretaries.
The establishment of Assistant Grand Secretaries began from this point.
Thereafter, there were often as many as six,
or as few as one or two.
In the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the number of Grand Secretaries and Assistant Grand Secretaries was finally fixed,
the Zhōnghé Diàn was abolished,
and the Tǐrén Gé was added,
making the Three Halls and Three Pavilions (Sān Diàn, Sān Gé) the standard system.
However, the Bǎohé Diàn was not always staffed.
(Thereafter, Fù Héng was the only one granted the title associated with Bǎohé Diàn.
During imperial audiences and celebrations on New Year's Day and other festivals,
Han officials were ranked below Manchu officials.
However, from the Guāngxù reign, when Lǐ Hóngzhāng held the title of Wénhuá Diàn (Hall of Literary Glory),
and Bǎo Yún held the title of Wǔyīng Diàn (Hall of Martial Valour),
their position in the official ranking shifted to the right of the Manchu Grand Secretaries.)
In the fifty-eighth year,
the concurrent title of Minister (Shàngshū) was abolished.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng,
the Grand Secretariat was reorganized,
and Grand Secretaries were separately ordered to be ranked in the Hanlin Academy.
Previously, when Shìzǔ personally handled government affairs,
he went to the Memorial Review Office (Piàoběnfáng daily),
and the Grand Secretaries were in charge of drafting memoranda,
holding significant and confidential power.
During Kāngxī's reign,
the Grand Secretariat was reorganized,
and its functions were divided by establishing the Hanlin Academy.
During Yōngzhèng's reign,
with the Qinghai emergency,
its functions were again divided by establishing the Grand Council (Jūnjīchù),
which some debated was no different from the Nèi Sān Yuàn.
However, although the Hanlin officials in the Nánshūfáng (Southern Study) managed imperial edicts,
the overall military and state secrets still belonged to the Grand Secretariat,
making it a crucial responsibility.
Once memorials were submitted to the Grand Secretariat,
and major policies were executed by the Grand Councilors (Shūchén) by imperial order,
its power gradually diminished.
The Office for Investigating and Auditing Edicts.
The concurrently serving ministers have no fixed number.
(Specially appointed from among Manchu and Han Grand Secretaries, Presidents of Boards, and Censor-in-Chiefs.)
They are responsible for investigating special cases handed down by imperial edicts to various departments,
and overseeing them within prescribed time limits.

one Manchu.

four Han.

Secretaries (Bǐtiēshì): forty.

Eight Han Secretarial Department Drafters.

In Shùnzhì 9th year,
Manchu Record-keeping Officials (Jìshì Guān) were established,

In Kāngxī 9th year,
the Record-keeping Officials were changed to Secretarial Department Drafters.
In Qiánlóng 36th year,
one Han Grand Secretary (Nèigé Xuéshì) to manage the Secretarial Department was established.
The following year,
the "managing departmental affairs" was changed to "investigating departmental affairs";
one Manchu Grand Secretary was added;
the Secretarial Department Drafters were changed to the Secretarial Department (Zhōngshū Kē),
and Seal-holding Secretaries were established,
one Manchu, one Han.
Abolished in Xuāntǒng 3rd year.
The Grand Council (Jūnjī Chù). Grand Councilors (Jūnjī Dàchén):
(no fixed number,
specially summoned by imperial decree from among Grand Secretaries, Presidents and Vice-Presidents of Boards.
They are distinguished by the titles "Dàchén" or "Dàchén shàng xíngzǒu".
Those newly appointed are given
the prefix
"xuéxí"
“Trainee”.)
They are responsible for major military and state affairs,
assisting with urgent matters of state.
They are on duty daily,
responding and offering counsel,
and likewise during imperial tours.
(Edicts are issued publicly,
then conveyed to the Grand Secretariat.
Those edicts to be executed by this office
are sealed and sent to the relevant departments.
Personnel are also registered and recorded in ledgers,
to be reported when due.)
Its subordinates are called Secretaries (Zhāngjīng):
sixteen Manchu,
twenty Han.
(They are called "xíngzǒu",
divided into first and second shifts.
Initially, there was no fixed quota,

Later, additions and reductions were irregular.
In Guāngxù 32nd year, thirty-six were fixed,
and it was further stipulated that leading secretaries (lǐngbān) ranked as third-grade officials,
assistant leading secretaries (bānglǐngbān) as fourth-grade officials,
while others served in their original official capacities.
In 34th year,
leading secretaries were changed to junior third-grade,
and assistant leading secretaries to junior fourth-grade.)
They are separately responsible for Manchu and Chinese texts.
Initially, the Council of Deliberative Princes and Ministers (Yìzhèng Chù) was established,
with Gǒng'ādài (鞏阿岱) and others appointed as Deliberative Ministers,
to participate in important military discussions.
In Yōngzhèng 10th year,
during the military campaign in the Northwest,
fearing that those on duty might leak secrets,
the Grand Council Office (Jūnjī Fáng) was first established,
later renamed the Grand Council (Jūnjī Chù).
However, Manchu Grand Secretaries still held the title of Deliberative Minister.
(Abolished in Qiánlóng 56th year.)
When Gāozōng (高宗) took office,
it was renamed the Office of General Management (Zǒnglǐ Chù),
but soon reverted to its original name.
At that time, those who served on duty were all important ministers.
Traditionally,
princes were not given real power.
However, in Jiāqìng 4th year,
Chéng Qīnwáng (成親王) was first ordered to serve on duty,
but was soon removed.
During the Xiánfēng (咸豐) era,
Gōng Qīnwáng (恭親王) was again ordered to serve on duty,
leading the council for three reigns as before.
Thereafter, Chúnxián Qīnwáng (醇賢親王), Lǐ Qīnwáng (禮親王), Qìng Qīnwáng (慶親王), and others followed.
In Guāngxù 27th year,

The Shàngshū manages the selection and overall administration,
thereby distributing state offices.
The Shìláng assist him.
The Táng Zhǔshì manage documents and memorials.
The Sīwù manage the receipt and dispatch of official correspondence.
(These two officials are the same for all Boards.)
Wénxuǎn manages official ranks, promotions, and demotions,
and ensures fairness in selection methods.
Officials are divided into nine ranks,
each categorized as Zheng [正] or Cóng [從],
making eighteen grades.
Below the ninth rank is called Wèirùliú [未入流].
Candidates are entered into the merit register,
and promoted according to their category,
following the sequence of old records.
Kǎogōng manages evaluations and assessments,
conducting performance reviews every three years.
Jīngchá [京察] and Dàjì [大計] are both subject to inspection by the chief official,
and records are kept.
All impeachments, exonerations, retirements due to age, or claims of illness,
as well as reviews of merits, demerits, and disciplinary actions, are processed here.
For matters referred for deliberation,
it distinguishes between public and private, minor and major,
and submits proposals.
Jīxūn manages meritorious ranks, personnel registers, mourning and support;
it also audits the stipends of capital and court officials,
(Jīfèng Tīng [稽俸廳] is subordinate to it.)
the number of Hàn Sī officials,
and the hereditary succession of Eight Banners' hereditary posts.
Yànfēng manages Yīn [廕] (hereditary privilege), (A Zheng-Yī-Pǐn [正一品] official's son is Zheng-Wǔ-Pǐn [正五品];
a Cóng-Yī-Pǐn [從一品] official's son is Cóng-Wǔ-Pǐn [從五品];
the rest are differentiated accordingly.)
Fēngzèng [封贈] (posthumous honors), (There are eighteen ranks for Fēngzèng:
Zheng-Yī-Pǐn [正一品] is granted Guānglù Dàfū [光祿大夫],
Cóng-Yī-Pǐn [從一品] is granted Rónglù Dàfū [榮祿大夫],
Zheng-Èr-Pǐn [正二品] is granted Zīzhèng Dàfū [資政大夫],
Cóng-Èr-Pǐn [從二品] is granted Fèngzhèng Dàfū [奉政大夫],
Zheng-Sān-Pǐn [正三品] is granted Tōngyì Dàfū [通議大夫],
Cóng-Sān-Pǐn [從三品] is granted Zhōngyì Dàfū [中議大夫],
Zheng-Sì-Pǐn [正四品] is granted Zhōngxiàn Dàfū [中憲大夫],
Cóng-Sì-Pǐn [從四品] is granted Cháoyì Dàfū [朝議大夫],
Zheng-Wǔ-Pǐn [正五品] is granted Fèngzhèng Dàfū [奉政大夫],
Cóng-Wǔ-Pǐn [從五品] is granted Fèngzhí Dàfū [奉直大夫].
All are granted Gàomìng [誥命].
Zheng-Liù-Pǐn [正六品] is granted Chéngdé Láng [承德郎],
Cóng-Liù-Pǐn [從六品] is granted Rúlín Láng [儒林郎],
those from clerical background are Xuāndé Láng [宣德郎],
Zheng-Qī-Pǐn [正七品] is granted Wénlín Láng [文林郎],
those from clerical background are Xuānyì Láng [宣義郎],
Cóng-Qī-Pǐn [從七品] is granted Zhēngshì Láng [徵仕郎],
Zheng-Bā-Pǐn [正八品] is granted Xiūzhí Láng [修職郎],
Cóng-Bā-Pǐn [從八品] is granted Xiūzhí Zuǒláng [修職佐郎],
Zheng-Jiǔ-Pǐn [正九品] is granted Dēngshì Láng [登仕郎],
Cóng-Jiǔ-Pǐn [從九品] is granted Dēngshì Zuǒláng [登仕佐郎].
All are granted Chìmìng [敕命].
There are nine titles for official wives:
First Rank is Yīpǐn Fūrén [一品夫人],
Second Rank is also Fūrén,
Third Rank is Shūrén [淑人],
Fourth Rank is Gōngrén [恭人],
Fifth Rank is Yírén [宜人],
Sixth Rank is Ānrén [安人],
Seventh Rank is Rúrén [孺人],
Eighth Rank is Bāpǐn Rúrén [八品孺人],
Ninth Rank is Jiǔpǐn Rúrén [九品孺人].
There is no distinction between Zheng and Cóng.
If granted due to their sons and grandsons, the character
"Tài" [太] is added;
if the husband is alive, it is not.
First Rank grants three generations,
Second and Third Ranks two generations,
Fourth to Seventh Ranks one generation.
Below that, only the individual himself is granted.
First Rank uses four jade axes for the patent,
Second Rank uses three rhino horn axes,
Third Rank uses three gilt axes, Fourth Rank two gilt axes,
Fifth Rank and below use two horn axes.
If the principal mother is alive,
the birth mother cannot be simultaneously granted.
If two sons are eligible for granting,
the one with the higher rank is chosen.)
and酬庸 (rewards for merit) and Jiǎngzhōng (commendations for loyalty).
It verifies the appropriateness of grants and Yīn (for deceased officials,
there are grants and Yīn).
For hereditary enfeoffment, it distinguishes between merging and separating,
and differentiates collateral branches.
For hereditary ranks, demotions, and removals,
and for verifying Tǔguān [土官] hereditary posts,
it sends documents to Wénxuǎn Sī for recommendation.
Extending imperial favor to maternal relatives,
honoring the descendants of sages,
and providing special care for the descendants of former dynasties,
are all reported to the throne according to regulations.
A separate Dūcuī Suǒ [督催所] is established
to urge the various Sī to submit deliberated matters,
enforcing the prescribed deadlines.
For matters to be processed within the current month,
it oversees the receipt and distribution of tasks,
and supervises the hall seal.
(Officials are selected from the Sī and assigned to this office.
The same applies to all Boards.)
Initially,
in the fifth year of Tiāncōng (1631),
an imperial edict commanded officials to deliberate and establish an official system.
Six Boards were created,
each led by one BèiLè.
(This was abolished in the first year of Shùnzhì (1644).
In the eighth year (1651), it was restored for QīnWáng and JùnWáng to concurrently hold,
and abolished again in the ninth year (1652).)
Four ChéngZhèng were appointed,
(two Manchu,
one Mongol, and one Han.
Only the Board of Works had one Manchu
and two Han.)
Eight CānZhèng were appointed,
(only the Board of Works had two Mongols and two Han,
totaling twelve.)
One QǐXīnLáng was appointed.
(The Board of Works had two Han.
In the ninth year of Shùnzhì (1652), their rank was set to be equivalent to ShìLáng.)
In the third year of Chóngdé (1638),
the Six Boards were reorganized to have one ChéngZhèng,
two ZǔoCānZhèng,
three YòoCānZhèng,
(the Board of Revenue had four.)
three QǐXīnLáng,
(one Manchu,
two Han.)
Forty-three LǐShìGuān,
(the Boards of Civil Office and Rites each had four,
the Boards of Revenue and War each had ten,
the Board of Punishments had six,
the Board of Works had nine.)
Sixty-five FùLǐShìGuān,
(the Board of Civil Office had six,
the Boards of Revenue and War each had sixteen,
the Board of Rites had seven,
the Board of Punishments had eight,
the Board of Works had twelve.)
Two ÉZhéKù.
In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
ChéngZhèng were renamed ShàngShū,
CānZhèng were renamed ShìLáng,
LǐShìGuān were renamed LángZhōng,
FùLǐShìGuān were renamed YuánWàiLáng,
and ÉZhéKù were renamed ZhǔShì.
Initially, the establishment numbers fluctuated without fixed limits.
At that time, Manchu ShàngShū,
and Manchu and Han Zǔo and YòoShìLáng,
also had no specific quotas.
The Han YòoShìLáng concurrently held the title of HàLínYuàn XuéShì.
(Those not from the Hanlin background did not hold this concurrently.
This was soon abolished.)
Within this Board (of Civil Office), there were four Manchu LángZhōng,
(four more were added in the twelfth year (1655).
In the thirteenth year of GuāngXù (1887), one for WénXuǎn was added.)
Two HánJūn (Manchu-Chinese Banner) LángZhōng,
(abolished in the fifth year of YōngZhèng (1727).)
Eight Manchu and Mongol YuánWàiLáng,
(the Mongol quota was removed in the twelfth year (1655).
In the eighteenth year (1661), eight Mongols were reinstated,
removed in the first year of KāngXī (1662),
and one was reinstated in the fifty-seventh year (1718).)
Six HánJūn YuánWàiLáng.
(Four were removed in the thirty-eighth year of KāngXī (1699).
All were removed in the fifth year of YōngZhèng (1727).)
Manchu TángZhǔShì (two each for pure Manchu and Manchu-Chinese script),
and Manchu SīZhǔShì (in the thirteenth year of GuāngXù (1887), one for WénXuǎn was added)
each had four;
one HánJūn ZhǔShì;
two Han SīWù.
(One was removed in the fourth year (1647).
In the fifteenth year (1658), it was set at one Manchu and one Han.
The same applied to other Boards.)
In the WénXuǎn Division,
there was one Han LángZhōng and one YuánWàiLáng,
(one YuánWàiLáng was added in the fifth year of YōngZhèng (1727).
In the thirteenth year of GuāngXù (1887), one each was added.)
Two ZhǔShì.
(One was added in the thirteenth year of GuāngXù (1887).)
In the KǎoGōng, JīXūn, and YànFēng three divisions,
there was one Han LángZhōng, one YuánWàiLáng, and one ZhǔShì each.
(One KǎoGōng ZhǔShì was added in the fifth year of YōngZhèng (1727).)
Also appointed were BǐTiēShì,
assigned to various Táng and Sī.
(The same applied to other Boards.)
In the fifth year (1648),
it was decided to have one Manchu and one Han ShàngShū each.
(One Manchu was added in the seventh year (1650),
and removed in the tenth year (1653).)
In the fifteenth year (1658),
QǐXīnLáng were abolished,
and it was decided to have one Manchu and one Han Zǔo and YòoShìLáng each.
In the fifty-seventh year of KāngXī (1718),
one Mongol LángZhōng and one Mongol ZhǔShì were added.
In the first year of YōngZhèng (1723),
DàXuéShì were appointed to lead the Board's affairs.
In the fourth year of JiāQìng (1799),
it was further ordered that QīnWáng oversee it,
(this was soon abolished.)
One Manchu YuánWàiLáng and one ZhǔShì were changed to imperial clan member quotas.
In the sixth year (1801),
DàXuéShì were again put in charge of the Board,
and this became the fixed system thereafter.
In the twenty-third year of GuāngXù (1897),
clerical staff were purged and streamlined,
and one LángZhōng, YuánWàiLáng, and ZhǔShì each were added to the WénXuǎn and KǎoGōng divisions.
(Manchu and Han officials were used interchangeably.)
In the thirty-second year (1906),
the positions of ShàngShū,
Zǔo and YòoShìLáng,
and Zǔo and YòoCéng and Cān were each fixed at one.
(The ranks of Céng and Cān
are detailed under the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the new official system.)
Under the initial system,
Manchu, Mongol, and HánJūn SīGuān
had their numbers determined for the Six Boards collectively,
without specific departments,
later they were separated into divisions and their ranks were set like those of Han officials.
In the final years of the dynasty, edicts erased the distinctions between Manchu and Han,
and officials of various backgrounds were again used interchangeably in each Board.
The Board of Civil Office's rank was formerly above the other Five Boards.
LángGuān of various divisions,
if not from the KēJiǎ (Imperial Examination) background,
could not be appointed.
(The same applied to ZhǔShì of the Board of Rites, ZōngRénFǔ, and QǐJūZhù.)
Since the establishment of the Ministry of Foreign Affairs,
its ranking position was slightly altered;
with the reorganization of the Grand Secretariat and the establishment of bureaus like Quán and ZhìGào,
the Board of Civil Office was eventually abolished.
Board of Revenue: ShàngShū,
Zǔo and YòoShìLáng,
both one Manchu and one Han.

two Manchu for the Southern Archives,

SīWù in the SīWùTīng,

The Shàngshū of the Hùbù was in charge of military and national financial plans,
to ensure sufficiency for national expenditures.
The Shìláng served as his deputy.
The Yòu Shìláng concurrently managed the minting operations of the Bǎoquán Jú.
The fourteen divisions,
each managed their respective provincial civil revenues,
and the salaries and provisions of various Yāmén under the Eight Banners,
military rations,
various granaries,
salt taxes,
customs duties,
and miscellaneous taxes.
(The Jiāngnán Sī concurrently oversaw the expenditures of the Jiāngníng and Sūzhōu textile manufactories,
the salaries and provisions of the garrisons in Jiāngníng and Jīngkǒu,
and cases of land and poll taxes in various provinces that exceeded the deadline and remained unsettled.
The Jiāngxī Sī concurrently oversaw the contributions from various provinces.
The Zhèjiāng Sī concurrently oversaw the expenditures of the Hángzhōu textile manufactory,
the salaries and provisions of the Hángzhōu and Zhàpǔ garrisons,
and the population and grain figures of various provinces.
The Fújiàn Sī concurrently oversaw the civil revenues of Zhílì,
the maritime customs duties of Tiānjīn,
the salaries and provisions of the garrisons in Dōng Xī Líng, Rèhé, and Mìyún,
the administration of dairy cattle and horse pastures,
the expenses for the civil and military provincial and metropolitan examinations,
and the distribution of grain for relief in the Five Cities.
The Húguǎng Sī concurrently oversaw the factory taxes of Fèngshěng,
the salaries and provisions of the Jīngzhōu garrison,
and the figures for land and poll tax surcharges in various provinces.
The Hénán Sī concurrently oversaw the salaries and provisions of the Kāifēng garrison,
the salaries and provisions of Cháhā'ěr,
and outstanding unreconciled accounts.
The Shāndōng Sī concurrently oversaw the salaries and provisions of the Qīngzhōu and Dézhōu garrisons,
the receipts and disbursements of military provisions in the Three Eastern Provinces,
the ●ticket livestock tax,
and inspected the issuance of integrity allowances to Eight Banner officials,
and salt taxes in Chánglú and other places.
The Shānxī Sī concurrently oversaw the lands of nomadic Cháhā'ěr,
the land and grain taxes of Tǔmòtè,
the official staff of the Dìngbiān Zuǒ Fùjiāngjūn in Khalkha and Huíbù,
the salaries and provisions of the post stations in Zhāngjiākǒu and Sài'ěrwūsūtái,
the rotation of military colonists and soldiers in Wūlǐyàsūtái and Kēbùduō,
and the annual revenue and expenditure figures of various provinces.
The Shǎnxī Sī concurrently oversaw the civil revenues of Gānsù,
the circulation of salt warrants,
the salaries and provisions of the garrisons in Xī'ān, Níngxià, Liángzhōu, and Zhuānglàng,
and compiled and verified the disbursements in the capital,
and expenses in Xīnjiāng.
The Sìchuān Sī concurrently oversaw the customs duties of its province,
the military colonies in the two Jīnchuān areas and Xīnjiāng,
the salaries and provisions of the Chéngdū garrison,
and the receipts and disbursements of the straw factories in the capital,
the expenses for paper and vermillion ink for various ministries and courts,
households whose property escheated to the government,
and fines and confiscations of silver.
It also annually reported the figures for good or bad harvests, floods or droughts in all provinces, prefectures, and counties.
The Guǎngdōng Sī concurrently oversaw the salaries and provisions of the Guǎngzhōu garrison,
the succession and change of ownership of properties for Eight Banner heir households,
and provided archways for those designated as centenarians, filial sons, or chaste women.
The Guǎngxī Sī concurrently oversaw the mining administration and factory taxes of its province,
and the coinage regulations in the capital and provinces,
and the receipts and disbursements of the internal granaries.
The Yúnnán Sī concurrently oversaw the factory taxes of its province,
the grain transport administration of Shāndōng, Hénán, Jiāngnán, Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, and Húguǎng,
the granary stores in the capital and Tōngzhōu,
and the auditing of the six waterborne granaries in Jiāngníng.
The Guìzhōu Sī concurrently oversaw various customs duties and taxes,
and audited the sable tribute.

was in charge of land transport at Dàtōng.
The Supervisors of the Eleven Granaries (十一倉監督)
(namely Lùmǐ (祿米), Nánxīn (南新), Jiùtài (舊太), Fùxīn (富新), Xīngpíng (興平), Hǎiyùn (海運), Běixīn (北新), Tàipíng (太平),
all established in the early Qīng dynasty;
Běnyù (本裕),
established in the 45th year of Kāngxī (康熙);
Chúkǎi (儲濟),
established in the 6th year of Yōngzhèng (雍正);
Fēngyì (豐益),
established in the 7th year of Yōngzhèng.
There were formerly Wàn'ān (萬安) and Yùfēng (裕豐),
which were later abolished.
The Ēnfēng Cāng (恩豐倉),
established in the 26th year of Qiánlóng (乾隆),
belonged to the Imperial Household Department (內府).)
All comprised one Manchu and one Han,
(recommended by various Boards and Courts for appointment),
and managed the capital granaries (京倉) separately.
The Supervisors of the Central (中) and Western (西) Two Granaries (二倉監督),
(established following the Míng (明) system.
There was formerly a Southern Granary (南倉),
which was later abolished.),
one Manchu and one Han,
(transferred from among the supervisors of the Eleven Granaries),
managed the Tōngzhōu granaries (通倉) separately.
In the 1st year of Shùnzhì (順治),
a Han Assistant Minister (侍郎) was appointed.
(Abolished in the 8th year of Kāngxī,
restored in the 18th year.)
The capital and Tōngzhōu granaries
were administered separately by officials from the Board of Revenue (戶部).
The Tōngzhōu Zùliángtīng (通州坐糧廳),
(the Jīngliángtīng (京糧廳) was established in the 12th year [of Shùnzhì].
In the 15th year, it was merged into Dàtōngqiáo (大通橋).
In the 2nd year of Kāngxī, one Manchu and one Han supervisor were appointed,
but soon abolished.
Restored in the 47th year.),
was managed by one official from the Board of Revenue.
In the 9th year [of Shùnzhì],
one Manchu (滿洲) and one Han Bordered Yellow Banner (漢軍) Assistant Minister were appointed.
(The position for the Han Bordered Yellow Banner was soon abolished.
In the 15th year,
it was set as one Manchu and one Han.)
In the 50th year of Kāngxī,
it was decreed that the supervisors of the capital and Tōngzhōu granaries should be one Manchu and one Han.
(In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng, deputy supervisors were appointed,
but soon abolished.
Their positions were filled by alternate selection from among Cabinet (內閣) secretaries (中書) and directors (監寺官) of Boards and Courts.)
Initially, there was also a Superintendent (總理),
a Manchu Assistant Minister,
who jointly managed river transport (漕務) with the Governor-General of Grand Canal (總漕).
Abolished in the 8th year of Shùnzhì,
restored in the 12th year,
and again abolished in the 18th year.
At the Chóngwénmén (崇文門) in the capital,
there were a Chief Supervisor (正監督), Deputy Supervisor (副監督),
and one each for the Left Wing (左翼) and Right Wing (右翼).
(Ministers of the Imperial Household Department (內府大臣) and Presidents/Vice Presidents (尚書侍郎) of Boards concurrently held these posts.
For other regular customs barriers (常關),
either Board Ministers (部臣) would specially recommend appointments,
or Board and Department (部司) officials would be drawn by lot from the capital,
or outer officials (外官) would be concurrently assigned.
The Tiānjīn Customs (天津關)
was concurrently managed by the Chánglú Salt Commissioner (長蘆鹽政).
Tōngzhōu (通州)
was concurrently managed by the Zùliángtīng.
Zhāngjiākǒu (張家口) and Shāhǔkǒu (殺虎口)
were concurrently held by Board and Court (部院) department officials (司員).
Pántáokǒu (潘桃口)
was concurrently managed by the Duōlúnnuò'ěr Assistant Prefect (多倫諾爾同知).
Lóngquán (龍泉), Zǐjīng (紫荊), Xǐfēng (喜峯), Wǔhǔ (五虎), Gùguān (固關), Báishí (白石), Dàomǎ (倒馬), Cígōu (茨溝), Chājiànlǐng (插箭嶺), Mǎshuǐkǒu (馬水口)
were concurrently managed by the Commander-in-Chief (提督),
who delegated a Colonel (參將), Regional Commander (都司), Garrison Commander (守備), or Company Commander (把總) to supervise collections.
Sānzuòtǎ (三座塔), Bāgōu (八溝), Wūlánhādá (烏蘭哈達)
were concurrently held by department officials of the Court of Colonial Affairs.
The Fèngtiān (奉天) cattle and horse tax
was concurrently held by Board and Court department officials.
Zhōngjiāng (中江)
was alternately selected from among officers (章京) of the Shèngjīng General's (盛京將軍) yamen (衙門) and department officials of the Five Boards,
later transferred to be concurrently managed by the Xīngfèng Circuit Intendant (興鳳道).
Línqīng (臨清)
was concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor (巡撫),
who delegated a Sub-prefect (知州) to supervise collections.
Guīhuàchéng (歸化城)
was concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor,
who delegated a Circuit Intendant (道員) to supervise collections.
Tóngguān (潼關)
was concurrently managed by a Circuit Intendant.
Hǔxùguān (滸墅關)
was supervised by the Sūzhōu Textile Commissioner (蘇州織造).
Huái'ān Customs (淮安關) and Miàowānkǒu (廟灣口)
were concurrently held by department officials of the Imperial Household Department.
Yáng Customs (揚關)
was concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor,
who delegated the Huái-Yáng Maritime Circuit Intendant (淮揚海道) to supervise collections.
Xīxīnguān (西新關)
was concurrently managed by the Jiāngníng Textile Commissioner (江寧織造),
later transferred to the Provincial Governor.
Fèngyáng Customs (鳳陽關)
was concurrently managed by the Wǎnběi Circuit Intendant (皖北道).
Gàn Customs (贛關)
was concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor,
who delegated the Jínángànníng Circuit Intendant (吉南贛寧道) to supervise collections.
Mǐn'ān Customs (閩安關)
was concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor,
later transferred to the Governor-General (總督),
who delegated a Fúzhōu (福州) Sub-prefect (同知) to supervise collections.
Běixīnguān (北新關)
was concurrently managed by the Hángzhōu Textile Commissioner (杭州織造),
later transferred to the Provincial Governor.
Wǔchāngchǎng (武昌廠) and Jīng Customs (荊關)
were concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor,
later transferred to the Governor-General, who delegated an official to supervise collections.
Kuí Customs (夔關)
was concurrently managed by the Governor-General,
who delegated a Prefect (知府) to supervise collections.
Dǎjiànlú (打箭爐)
was concurrently managed by an Assistant Prefect.
Tàipíng Customs (太平關)
was concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor,
who delegated the Nánsháolián Circuit Intendant (南韶連道) to supervise collections.
Wúchǎng (梧廠) and Xúnchǎng (潯廠)
were concurrently managed by the Provincial Governor,
who delegated the two Prefects of Wú and Xún (梧、潯二知府) to supervise collections.)
Initially,
those who levied duties on all goods were called Household Customs (戶關),
and those who levied duties on bamboo, timber, and boat taxes were called Works Customs (工關).
They were administered separately by departments of the Board of Revenue and the Board of Works (工部).
Later, the current system was adopted.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng (宣統),
many Works Customs were renamed Regular Customs (常關),
(only in Zhílì (直隸) and other provinces did the names remain as before),
and all were subordinate to the Ministry of Finance (度支部).
In the past, officials of the Imperial Household Department were appointed.
During the Qiánlóng (乾隆) era,
it was changed to Ministers of the Imperial Household Department.
Later, Ministers of Boards and Courts were also eligible for appointment,
and it was set as a Manchu official position.
