The Shàngshū (Minister) was in charge of the five rites and their order,
presiding over schools and tribute examinations,
thereby disseminating state education.
The Shìláng (Vice Minister) was his deputy.
The Diǎnzhì (Director of Ceremonial Regulations) was in charge of auspicious rites and military rites.
They audited traditional regulations,
distinguished names and numbers,
and promulgated standards to various offices.
Every three years, for the grand triennial examination,
they managed its registers.
For loyalty, filial piety, chastity, and righteousness from all four directions,
they sought out and honored those of great merit.
The Cízhài (Director of Sacrifices) was in charge of auspicious rites and inauspicious rites.
For all grand sacrifices, medium sacrifices, and group sacrifices,
they determined the sequence of events and the equivalence of their uses according to the season.
During solar and lunar eclipses,
all internal and external offices carried out rescue measures;
if there were disasters or anomalies, they immediately reported them.
For all funerals and sacrifices,
there were different grades for the noble and the humble,
all of which were standardized and promulgated.
Requests from meritorious relatives, high-ranking civil and military officials for funerals, sacrifices, posthumous honors, and谥 (shì, posthumous names)
had to be transferred to the relevant office for verification and implementation.
They also registered and supervised historians, ritual officiants, doctors, shamans, musicians, Buddhist monks, and Daoist priests,
enforcing prohibitions among them;
those guilty of sorcery or deception were punished without mercy.
The Zhǔkè (Director of Guests) was in charge of guest rites.
For all tributary missions from foreign states,
their lodging, provisions, and赐予 (cìyǔ, bestowals)
were determined by distinguishing the distance of their tribute route, the number of envoys, and the abundance or scarcity of their tribute goods.
They promulgated the "Veritable Records" and the "Jade Genealogy" upon their completion, and awarded commendations.
They audited the annual quota of Huòchá.
The Jīngshàn (Director of Refined Provisions) was in charge of the five rites of banquets and their sacrificial animals.
When bestowing ritual food upon all officials,
it was differentiated according to their rank.
The Guānglù (Court of Imperial Entertainments) provided the delicacies,
while the Jìhuì (Accountant) tallied their numbers and managed their receipts and disbursements,
consolidating the accounts of each office.
The Zhùyìnjú (Bureau for Casting Seals) was responsible for engraving, melting, and casting seals.
They were in charge of casting the imperial seals.
All seals and credentials of internal and external offices
were cast by them.

there was one Mǎnzhōu Yuánwàiláng,

and one Hàn Dàshǐ (Ambassador).
In the 5th year,
it was decided that there would be one Mǎnzhōu and one Hàn Shàngshū each.
In the 57th year of Kāngxī,
one Ménggǔ Lángzhōng (for the Zhǔkè Sī),
one Yuánwàiláng (for the Cíji Sī),
and one Zhǔshì (for the Jīngshàn Sī)
were added.
In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng,
Qīnwáng (Princes of the First Rank), Jùnwáng (Princes of the Second Rank), and Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretaries) were appointed to lead the Board,
appointed as needed and
not as permanent officials.
In the 3rd year of Qiánlóng,
one Hàn Yuánwàiláng, Bǐtiēshì (Clerk), and provisional Zhǔshì each were added for the Zhùyì Jú.
In the 13th year,
the Xíngrén Sī (Court of State Ceremonial) was abolished and merged into it.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng,
one Mǎnzhōu Yuánwàiláng and one Zhǔshì each were changed to宗shì (Imperial Clansmen) positions.
In the 24th year of Guāngxù,
the Guānglù Sì (Court of Imperial Entertainments) and Hónglú Sì (Court of State Ceremonial) were abolished and merged into it,
but soon restored to their former status.
In the 31st year,
an imperial edict abolished the imperial examinations.
The Xuézhèng (Education Commissioners) of the various provinces were transferred to the Xúewù Dàchén (Minister of Education).
From then on, the responsibility for correcting the士fēng (moral conduct of scholars)
no longer belonged to this Board.
In the 32nd year,
the Guānglù Sì, Tàicháng Sì, and Hónglú Sì were designated as Zhílǐguān (Officers of Ceremony)
and again merged into the Board.
The Jīngshàn Sī was renamed Guānglù,
and the Zhǔkè Sī was renamed Tàicháng.
Each was assigned one Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, and Zhǔshì.
The duties of Hónglú were relatively simple,
so it was incorporated into the Diǎnzì Sī,
with one Yuánwàiláng added,
and Mǎnzhōu and Hàn officials used interchangeably.
In this year, the establishment of Shàngshū,
Shìláng,
Zuǒ and Yòu Chéng (Left and Right Grand Masters of Ceremonies), and Cān (Councilors) was set
to be the same as the Lìbù (Board of Civil Office).
A Lǐqì Kù (Ritual Implement Depot) was established,
with one Lángzhōng and one Yuánwàiláng each, and one Zànlǐguān (Ceremonial Master) and one Dúzhùguān (Prayer Reader) each.
(All were of rank 6.
The Tàicháng Sì Chéng were reassigned to these posts.)
Four Bùzhèng (Chief Clerks)
(reassigned from Guānglù Sì Shǔzhèng),
and four Diǎnbù (Archivists) (three reassigned from Tàicháng Sì Bóshì,
one reassigned from Guānglù Sì Diǎnbù).
Two Sīkù (Storehouse Keepers),
(reassigned from the Sīkù of Tàicháng Sì and Guānglù Sì.
The ranks of the above officials remained as before.)
There were fourteen Bǐtiēshì.
(Selected and retained from the three courts.)
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng,
to avoid the emperor's given name,
the Yízhì Sī was renamed Diǎnzì.
In the initial system,
the Lǐbù established a Mǎguǎn (Horse Stable),
with one Zhèng Jiāndū (Chief Supervisor) and one Fù Jiāndū (Deputy Supervisor).
(The Zhèng Jiāndū
was filled by a Sīyuán of this Board.
The Fù Jiāndū
was filled by a Sīyuán of the Lǐfān Yuàn.)
In the 27th year of Qiánlóng,
it was abolished and merged into the Lǐfān Yuàn.
Initially, four Mǎnzhōu Xuānbiǎoguān (Proclamatory Officers) were established,
later reduced to two,
and soon merged into the Tàicháng Sì.
For the Huìtóng Sìyì Guǎn (Joint Four Interpreters' Bureau),
there were two Mǎnzhōu Jīchá Dàchén (Inspectors General),
(appointed from the Tángguān of Boards, Courts, and Temples.)
One Tídú Guǎnshì (Superintendent of the Bureau) concurrently serving as Hónglú Sì Shà qīng (Junior Vice-President of the Court of State Ceremonial),
(selected from the Lángzhōng of the Lǐbù.)
They were in charge of entertaining guests
and translating languages.
One Hàn Dàshǐ,
(rank 9a).
Two Hàn Zhèngjiào (Chief Teachers) and Xùbān (Ceremonial Officers).
Eight Cháoxiǎn Tōngshìguān (Korean Interpreters).
(Two of rank 6, two of rank 7,
and four of rank 8.)
In the 1st year of Shùnzhì,
the Huìtóng Sìyì Guǎn was divided into two separate Bureaus.
The Huìtóng Guǎn was subordinate to the Lǐbù,
superintended by one Mǎnzhōu and one Hàn Zhǔshì from the Zhǔkè Sī.
The Sìyì Guǎn was subordinate to the Hànlín Yuàn,
superintended by one Hàn Shà qīng from the Tàicháng Sì.
Eight bureaus were established: Huíhuí (Muslim), Miǎndiàn (Burmese), Bǎiyí (Tai), Xīfān (Tibetan), Gāochāng (Kao-chang), Xītiān (Indian), Bābǎi (Siamese), and Xiānlúo (Siamese),
for translating tributary documents from distant lands.
Twenty Xùbān were established,
(in the 15th year, eight Zhèngjiào and eight Xiéjiào were stipulated.
During Kāngxī's reign, they were reduced to nine,
with one managing the Diǎnwù Tīngshì.
In the 13th year of Qiánlóng,
one Diǎnwù official and six Xùbān were abolished,
leaving two as the fixed quota.)
Six Cháoxiǎn Tōngshìguān.
(Later increased by ten.
Totaling ten of rank 6 and six of rank 7.
In the 23rd year of Qiánlóng, four of rank 6 and two of rank 7 were abolished,
and two of rank 8 were added.
Later all were abolished.)
In the 14th year,
one Tōngshì of Yuánwàiláng rank was established,
in charge of the Huìtóng Guǎn seal.
(Soon abolished.)
In the 13th year of Qiánlóng,
the Sìyì Guǎn was abolished and merged into the Lǐbù,
renamed Huìtóng Sìyì Guǎn.
The eight bureaus were reorganized into two,
called Xīyù (Western Regions)
and Bǎiyí,
overseen by one Lángzhōng of the Lǐbù concurrently holding the title of Hónglú Sì Shà qīng.
It was abolished in the 29th year of Guāngxù.
For the Yuèbù (Music Department),
there was no limit to the number of Diǎnyuè Dàchén (Ministers of Music),
(one Mǎnzhōu Shàngshū of the Lǐbù concurrently held the post.
Later, Shìláng from various boards and Dàchén from the Nèiwùfǔ concurrently managed it.
Also, Mǎnzhōu Wáng and Dàchén who understood music
were also called Guǎnlǐ Dàchén.)
They were in charge of examining musical scales, pitches, and tempos,
harmonizing them with vocal music,
and conveying them with instruments.
They differentiated their use for sacrifices, court assemblies, and banquets,
to move both the seen and unseen,
and bring harmony between superiors and inferiors.
For the Shénlè Shǔ (Divine Music Office),
there was one Shǔzhèng (Director),
(rank 6a).
One Zuǒ Shǔchéng (Left Assistant Director) and one Yòu Shǔchéng (Right Assistant Director) each,
(rank 8b).
Five Xiélǜ Láng (Harmonists),
(rank 8a).
Twenty-five Sīyuè (Musicians).
(rank 9a).
One hundred eighty Yuèsheng (Musical Performers) and three hundred Wǔsheng (Dancers) belonged to it.
All were Hàn officials,
also subordinate to the Tàicháng Sì,
and in charge of music for suburban altars, ancestral temples, and sacrificial rites.
For the Héshēng Shǔ (Harmonious Music Office),
there was one Shǔzhèng and one Shǔchéng each,
for both Mǎnzhōu and Hàn.
(Mǎnzhōu officials
concurrently served as Lángzhōng and Yuánwàiláng of the Nèiwùfǔ.
Hàn officials
concurrently served as Lángzhōng and Yuánwàiláng of the Lǐbù.)
There were thirty Gōngyòngguān (Service Officers),
(eight from this office.
Two Bǐtiēshì from the Lǐbù concurrently served,
six Zànlǐ Láng from the Nèiwùfǔ concurrently served,
twelve Bǐtiēshì and other ranked officials concurrently served,
two Míngzànguān from the Hónglú Sì concurrently served.)
Sixteen Shǔshǐzhǎng (Chief Clerks),
and one hundred forty-eight Shǔshǐ (Clerks) belonged to it.
They were in charge of music for palace and court assemblies and banquets.
As for court music,
it was overseen by the Zhōnghé Yuèchù of the Nèiwùfǔ's Zhǎnglǐ Sī.
The music for the imperial procession
was managed by the校wèi (Guards) of the Luányú Wèi (Imperial Carriage Guard) and Qíshǒu Wèi (Standard-Bearer Guard).
All were subordinate to the Board.
elsewhere,
one Duō'ěrqìdá;
(concurrently three third-rank guards)
two holding sixth-rank titles and two holding seventh-rank titles.
Sixty Bàitáng'ā
(concurrently attached to the Imperial Bodyguard Office)
were in charge of performing the Duō'ěrmì music
for banquets.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
the Jiàofāngsī was established,
with one Fèngluán,
one Left Sháowǔ, one Right Sháowǔ,
one Left Sīyuè, one Right Sīyuè,
and ten Xiétóng.
(All of the above were of 正九品 (rank 9a).)
There was no fixed number of Páizhǎng.
(Unranked.)
In the Shénlèguān of the Tàichángsì,
there was one Hàn Típiǎnddiǎn,
(正六品 (rank 6a))
one Left Zhīguān, one Right Zhīguān,
(正八品 (rank 8a))
and five Hàn Xiélǜláng.
(Abolished in the 38th year of Kāngxī.
Restored in the first year of Yōngzhèng.
Three added in the second year of Qiánlóng.
Six abolished in the ninth year.
Two added in the fourth year of Jiāqìng.
Two added in the first year of Dàoguāng.
Two added in the second year of Xiánfēng.)
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng,
the Jiàofāngsī was changed to Hélèshǔ,
and the Fèngluán and other officials were abolished.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng,
the Yuèbù was established,
with a Jiǎndiǎnyuè Dàchén appointed to lead it.
Officials of the Héshēngshǔ were established,
with concurrent appointments from officials of the Nèifǔ, Tàicháng, and Hónglú.
(Shìcóng and Dàizhào were honorary titles.)
An imperial edict also prohibited Tàicháng music officials from practicing Daoism,
and those unwilling to change professions were struck from the register.
(Previously, in accordance with the Míng system,
all music officials and sacrificial assistants were Daoists.)
The following year,
the Shénlèguān was changed to Shénlèsuǒ,
and Zhīguān was changed to Zhīsuǒ.
In the 13th year,
the Shénlèsuǒ was again changed to Shénlèshǔ,
and Típiǎnddiǎn was renamed Shǔzhèng,
while Zhīsuǒ was renamed Shǔchéng.
The Bīngbù had a Shàngshū,
and Left and Right Shìláng,
each with one Manchu and one Han.
Its subordinates included: Tángzhǔshì,
two Manchus in the Qīngdàngfáng,
two Manchus in the Hànběnfáng,
and one Han bannerman.
In the Sīwùtīng, there was one Manchu and one Han Sīwù.
There were fifteen Shànběnbǐtiěshì.
The four Qīnglìsī of Wǔxuǎn, Chējià, Zhífāng, and Wǔkù: Lángzhōng,
one Zōngshì
(appointed in the Chējiàsī),
eleven Manchus
(three in Wǔxuǎn,
five in Zhífāng,
one in Chējià,
two in Wǔkù),
one Mongol
(appointed in the Wǔxuǎnsī),
and five Hans
(two in Zhífāng,
and one each in the others).
Yuánwàiláng,
one Zōngshì
(appointed in the Chējiàsī),
nine Manchus
(four in Wǔxuǎn,
two each in Zhífāng and Chējià,
one in Wǔkù),
three Mongols
(one each in Zhífāng, Chējià, and Wǔkù),
and four Hans
(two each in Wǔxuǎn and Zhífāng).
Zhǔshì,
four Manchus and four Hans.
(One in each Sī.)
Bǐtiěshì,
one Zōngshì,
sixty-two Manchus,
and eight Mongols and Han bannermen each.
The Shàngshū was in charge of managing military affairs
and reviewing military supplies
to strengthen the nation's core.
The Shìláng assisted him.
Wǔxuǎn was in charge of the selection and appointment of military officials, their ranks,
(eighteen grades: 正一品 (rank 1a) awarded the title Jiànwēi Jiāngjūn,
with Gōng, Hóu, Bó being equivalent;
從一品 (rank 1b) awarded Zhènwēi Jiāngjūn;
正二品 (rank 2a) awarded Wǔxiǎn Jiāngjūn;
從二品 (rank 2b) awarded Wǔgōng Jiāngjūn;
正三品 (rank 3a) awarded Wǔyì Dūwèi;
從三品 (rank 3b) awarded Wǔyì Dūwèi;
正四品 (rank 4a) awarded Zhāowǔ Dūwèi;
從四品 (rank 4b) awarded Xuānwǔ Dūwèi;
正五品 (rank 5a) awarded Wǔdé Qíwèi;
從五品 (rank 5b) awarded Wǔdé Zuǒqíwèi;
正六品 (rank 6a) awarded Wǔlüè Qíwèi;
從六品 (rank 6b) awarded Wǔlüè Zuǒqíwèi;
正七品 (rank 7a) awarded Wǔxìn Qíwèi;
從七品 (rank 7b) awarded Wǔxìn Zuǒqíwèi;
正八品 (rank 8a) awarded Fènwǔ Xiàowèi;
從八品 (rank 8b) awarded Fènwǔ Zuǒxiàowèi;
正九品 (rank 9a) awarded Xiūwǔ Xiàowèi;
從九品 (rank 9b) awarded Xiūwǔ Zuǒxiàowèi.
High and low ranks were according to their grade.
The titles for noblewomen corresponded to civil officials.)
enfeoffment, and hereditary privileges.
(All were the same as for civil officials.)
It also governed the military system
and the administration of the Indigenous Chieftains (Tǔsī).
Zhífāng was in charge of maps of all provinces.
Green Standard Army officers were evaluated every three years for age,
and every five years for military performance,
with merits and demerits reviewed for rewards, punishments, dismissals, and promotions.
It also handled disciplinary actions, relief, border controls, and maritime prohibitions.
Chējià was in charge of regulations for horse pasturage
to ensure military readiness.
All postal establishments, called yì, zhàn, táng, tái, suǒ, or pù,
were to verify official travel tallies for those using them,
and those who concealed or delayed them were to be punished according to the law.
Wǔkù was in charge of military registers, weapons,
provincial and metropolitan military examinations,
and matters related to conscription and garrisoned troops.
In case of military campaigns,
the Gōngbù provided weapons and kept records of their numbers.
Imperial edicts for conscription in various border regions,
or for personnel exiting the pass,
required verification of official documents.
For concurrent appointments,
one Shìláng from the Huìtóngguǎn managed the Guǎnsuǒ,
(this Shìláng was selected from the department itself)
and one Manchu and one Han superintendent
(appointed from within the staff)
were in charge of the capital's postal service
for imperial envoys.
There was no fixed quota for Sīguān in the Jiébàochù.
There were sixteen Zhùjīng Títángguān.
(One each for Zhílì, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, Húběi, Húnán, Sìchuān, Guǎngdōng;
one for Shǎnxī-Gānsù and Xīnjiāng;
one for Yúnnán and Guìzhōu;
one for Cáohé.
They were recommended by Governors-General and Governors from provincial military graduates, provincial graduates, and garrison commanders, then appointed.
Later, it was transferred to the Yóuchuánbù.)
Initially,
in the fifth year of Tiāncōng,
the Bīngbù was established.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
the Shàngshū and Shìláng and other officials were established.
Lángzhōng:
eight Manchus
(three added in the 12th year;
one added in the fifth year of Yōngzhèng),
four Mongols
(abolished in the 38th year of Kāngxī;
one restored in the 57th year),
two Han bannermen
(abolished in the fifth year of Yōngzhèng),
and four Hans
(one added in the fifth year of Yōngzhèng).
Yuánwàiláng:
eight Manchus
(five added in the 12th year;
three abolished in the 38th year of Kāngxī),
four Mongols
(abolished in the 38th year of Kāngxī;
three restored in the 57th year),
six Han bannermen
(four abolished in the 38th year of Kāngxī;
all abolished in the fifth year of Yōngzhèng),
and four Hans
(two abolished in the 11th year;
one added in the fifth year of Yōngzhèng).
Tángzhǔshì and Sīzhǔshì,
both with four Manchus;
one Han bannerman Tángzhǔshì;
five Han Zhǔshì.
One Huìtóngguǎn Dàshǐ.
(Abolished in the 38th year of Kāngxī.)
In the fifth year,
it was decreed that there would be one Manchu and one Han Shàngshū each.
In the eighth year,
various princes and Bèilè concurrently managed departmental affairs.
(Soon abolished.)
In the eleventh year,
an additional Supervising and Arresting Department (dūbǔ) was established.
There was one Manchu Zǔo Shìláng and one Han Yòo Shìláng.
There were two Han officials assisting in supervising and arresting (xiélǐ dūbǔ) and serving as Lesser Ministers of the Court of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Sì Shàoqīng).
(These were) two persons.
(Later changed.)
There was one Manchu and one Han Banner (Hànjūn)
left and right director (lǐshìguān).
(Later changed to one Manchu and one Han.)
There was one Manchu and one Han Department Director (Lángzhōng).
There were supernumerary secretaries (Yuánwàiláng):
seven Manchus, eight Han Banner (Hànjūn)
and one Han.
There were Department Secretaries (Táng Zhǔshì):
three Manchus,
one section secretary (Sī Zhǔshì)
(one added in the fourteenth year),
six Han secretaries (Hàn Zhǔshì),
and two prison wardens (Sīyù).
(Below the rank of Department Director (Lángzhōng), some also held the title of Supervisor of Arrests (dūbǔ xián).)
They were divided into eight sections (sī) responsible for arrest administration.
(The officers and soldiers of the three garrisons (sānyíng) were subordinate to them.)
In the twelfth year,
eight additional supernumerary secretaries (Yuánwàiláng) for supervising and arresting were established.
(One for each banner (qí).)
At that time, the selection, appointment, and disciplinary actions for military officials of the Eight Banners (Bāqí)
were all under the Board of Civil Office (Quáncáo).
They began to be subordinate to this department in the second year of Kāngxī.
In the thirty-eighth year,
the Supervising and Arresting Minister (dūbǔ shìláng) and other officials were abolished
and merged into the Board of Punishments (Xíngbù).
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
it was decreed that a Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) should manage the board,
and this became a permanent practice thereafter.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
one Manchu Department Director (Lángzhōng) and one supernumerary secretary (Yuánwàiláng) were abolished
to create vacancies for imperial clan members (zōngshì).
In the thirty-second year of Guāngxù,
its name was changed to the Board of the Army (Lùjūnbù).
Board of Punishments (Xíngbù):
There was one Minister (Shàngshū), one Left Minister (Zǔo Shìláng), and one Right Minister (Yòo Shìláng),
all with one Manchu and one Han.
Its subordinates: Department Secretaries (Táng Zhǔshì):
two Manchus in the Manchu Archives Office (Qīngdàngfáng),
three Manchus in the Han Memorials Office (Hànběnfáng),
one Han Banner (Hànjūn).
Service Hall Archivists (Sīwùtīng Sīwù):
one Manchu and one Han.
Forty copyists (shànběn bǐtiēshì).

Seventeen Clerical Bureaus (Qīnglì Sī) for Zhílì, Fèngtiān, Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, Húguǎng, Hénán, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Sìchuān, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu: Department Directors (Lángzhōng):

Supervising and Arresting Clerical Bureau (Dūbǔ Qīnglì Sī): Department Directors (Lángzhōng):

Supernumerary Secretaries (Yuánwàiláng):
one Manchu.
Secretaries (Zhǔshì):

Clerks (Bǐtiēshì):

Prison Hall Secretaries (Tíláo Tīng Zhǔshì):

The Shàngshū 尚書 (President) was in charge of trying cases and reviewing punishments.
They scrutinized laws and regulations,
and for doubtful cases submitted by the provinces,
they would make appropriate decisions and report them
to maintain the order of the state.
The Shìláng 侍郎 (Vice-President) assisted them.
The seventeen Departments each managed the criminal cases belonging to their respective provincial jurisdictions.
(The Zhílì Sī 直隸司 (Department of Zhílì) also managed cases related to the Eight Banners' nomadic pastures and the Cháhā'ěr Zuǒyì 察哈爾左翼 (Chahar Left Wing) territories.

It also handled official documents from the Jīngjī Dào Yùshǐ 京畿道御史 (Censor of the Metropolitan Region), the Shùntiān Fǔ 順天府 (Prefecture of Shùntiān), the Dōngxī Líng 東西陵 (Eastern and Western Tombs), the Rèhé Dūtǒng 熱河都統 (Military Governor of Rèhé), the Wéichǎng Zǒngguǎn 圍場總管 (Director-General of the Imperial Hunting Grounds), the Mìyún Fùdūtǒng 密雲副都統 (Deputy Military Governor of Mìyún), the Shānhǎiguān Fùdūtǒng 山海關副都統 (Deputy Military Governor of Shānhǎiguān), Gǔběikǒu 古北口, Zhāngjiākǒu 張家口, Dúshíkǒu 獨石口, Xīfēngkǒu 喜峯口, Lúfēngkǒu 蘆峯口, Tǎzigōu 塔子溝, Sānzuò Tǎ 三座塔, Bāgōu 八溝, Wūlánhādá 烏蘭哈達, Kālāhétún 喀拉河屯, and Duōlúnnuò'ěr 多倫諾爾.
The Fèngtiān Sī 奉天司 (Department of Fèngtiān) also managed cases related to Jílín 吉林 and Hēilóngjiāng 黑龍江.
It also handled official documents from the Zōngrén Fǔ 宗人府 (Imperial Clan Court) and the Lǐfān Yuàn 理藩院 (Court of Colonial Affairs).
The Jiāngsū Sī 江蘇司 (Department of Jiāngsū) also managed cases of sentence reduction or exemption from all provinces.
Whenever an amnesty was granted,
it would review the details and report to the throne.

It also handled official documents from the Jiāngnán Dào Yùshǐ 江南道御史 (Censor of the Jiāngnán Circuit), the Jiāngníng Jiāngjūn 江寧將軍 (General of Jiāngníng), the Jīngkǒu Fùdūtǒng 京口副都統 (Deputy Military Governor of Jīngkǒu), the Cáoyùn Zǒngdū 漕運總督 (Governor-General of Grain Transport), and the Nánhé Zǒngdū 南河總督 (Governor-General of the Southern River).
The Ānhuī Sī 安徽司 (Department of Ānhuī) also handled official documents from the Xiānghóng Qí 鑲紅旗 (Bordered Red Banner) and Xuānwǔmén 宣武門.

The Jiāngxī Sī 江西司 (Department of Jiāngxī) also handled official documents from the Jiāngxī Dào Yùshǐ 江西道御史 (Censor of the Jiāngxī Circuit), the Zhōngchéng Yùshǐ 中城御史 (Censor of the Central City), the Zhènghuáng Qí 正黃旗 (Plain Yellow Banner), and Xīzhímén 西直門.

The Zhèjiāng Sī 浙江司 (Department of Zhèjiāng) also handled official documents from the Dūcháyuan Xíngkē 都察院刑科 (Censorate's Department of Punishment), the Zhèjiāng Dào Yùshǐ 浙江道御史 (Censor of the Zhèjiāng Circuit), the Nánchéng Yùshǐ 南城御史 (Censor of the Southern City), the Hángzhōu Jiāngjūn 杭州將軍 (General of Hángzhōu), and the Zhàpǔ Fùdūtǒng 乍浦副都統 (Deputy Military Governor of Zhàpǔ).
It also managed the compilation and submission of memorials with suggestions,
and for all case records from other departments that were rejected or rectified,
it would compile their final versions
and submit them to the throne annually.

The Fújiàn Sī 福建司 (Department of Fújiàn) also handled official documents from the Dūcháyuan Hùkē 都察院戶科 (Censorate's Department of Revenue), the Cāngchǎng Yámén 倉場衙門 (Granaries and Stores Office), the Zuǒyòu Liǎngyì Jiāndū 左右兩翼監督 (Superintendents of the Left and Right Wings), the Xiānglán Qí 鑲藍旗 (Bordered Blue Banner), Fùchéngmén 阜成門, and the Fúzhōu Jiāngjūn 福州將軍 (General of Fúzhōu).
The Húguǎng Sī 湖廣司 (Department of Húguǎng) also managed cases related to Húběi 湖北 and Húnán 湖南.
It also handled official documents from the Húguǎng Dào Yùshǐ 湖廣道御史 (Censor of the Húguǎng Circuit) and the Jīngzhōu Jiāngjūn 荊州將軍 (General of Jīngzhōu).

The Hénán Sī 河南司 (Department of Hénán) also handled official documents from the Lǐbù 禮部 (Board of Rites), the Dūcháyuan Lǐkē 都察院禮科 (Censorate's Department of Rites), the Hénán Dào Yùshǐ 河南道御史 (Censor of the Hénán Circuit), the Tàicháng Sì 太常寺 (Court of Imperial Sacrifices), the Guānglù Sì 光祿寺 (Court of Imperial Entertainments), the Guózǐjiān 國子監 (Imperial Academy), the Hónglú Sì 鴻臚寺 (Court of State Ceremonial), the Qīntiān Jiān 欽天監 (Imperial Astronomical Bureau), the Tàiyī Yuàn 太醫院 (Imperial Academy of Medicine), the Dōngchéng Yùshǐ 東城御史 (Censor of the Eastern City), the Zhènghóng Qí 正紅旗 (Plain Red Banner), and Déshèngmén 德勝門.
During the summer heat, cases were reviewed (rèshěn 熱審),
and imperial pardons were issued to all provinces according to the regulations.

The Shāndōng Sī 山東司 (Department of Shāndōng) also handled official documents from the Bīngbù 兵部 (Board of War), the Dūcháyuan Bīngkē 都察院兵科 (Censorate's Department of War), the Shāndōng Dào Yùshǐ 山東道御史 (Censor of the Shāndōng Circuit), the Tàipú Sì 太僕寺 (Court of the Imperial Stud), the Qīngzhōu Fùdūtǒng 青州副都統 (Deputy Military Governor of Qīngzhōu), and the Dōnghé Zǒngdū 東河總督 (Governor-General of the Eastern River).
For all bandits caught by the infantry battalions,
their numbers were reported annually and submitted for approval.

The Shānxī Sī 山西司 (Department of Shānxī) also managed cases related to Cháhā'ěr Yòuyì 察哈爾右翼 (Chahar Right Wing), the Suíyuǎnchéng Jiāngjūn 綏遠城將軍 (General of Suíyuǎnchéng), the Guīhuàchéng Fùdūtǒng 歸化城副都統 (Deputy Military Governor of Guīhuàchéng), the Dìngbiān Zuǒfù Jiāngjūn 定邊左副將軍 (Assistant General of the Left Flank at Dìngbiān), the Kēbùduō Cānzàn Dàchén 科布多參贊大臣 (Assistant Amban in Kobdo), and the Kùlún Bànshì Dàchén 庫倫辦事大臣 (Resident Amban in Urga).

It also handled official documents from the Jūnjī Chù 軍機處 (Grand Council), the Nèigé 內閣 (Grand Secretariat), the Hànlín Yuàn 翰林院 (Hanlin Academy), the Zhānshì Fǔ 詹事府 (Supervisorate of Imperial Instruction), the Qǐjūzhù 起居注 (Diaries of Activity and Repose), the Zhōngshūkē 中書科 (Secretariat Department), the Nèitíng Gèguǎn 內廷各館 (various Imperial Household Departments), the Nèiwù Fǔ 內務府 (Imperial Household Department), the Shānxī Dào Yùshǐ 山西道御史 (Censor of the Shānxī Circuit), the Běichéng Yùshǐ 北城御史 (Censor of the Northern City), the Xiāngbái Qí 鑲白旗 (Bordered White Banner), and Chóngwénmén 崇文門.
It also handled cases reported annually by all provinces.

The Shǎnxī Sī 陝西司 (Department of Shǎnxī) also managed cases related to Gānsù 甘肅, Yīlí 伊犂, Wūlǔmùqí 烏魯木齊, Tǎ'ěrbāhātái 塔爾巴哈台, Yè'ěrqiāng 葉爾羌, Kāshígá'ěr 喀什噶爾, Wūshí 烏什, Ākèsū 阿克蘇, Kùchē 庫車, Tǔlǔfān 吐魯番, Hāláshā'ěr 哈喇沙爾, Hétián 和闐, and Hāmì 哈密.

It also handled official documents from the Shǎnxī Dào Yùshǐ 陝西道御史 (Censor of the Shǎnxī Circuit), the Dàlǐ Sì 大理寺 (Grand Court of Revision), the Xīchéng Yùshǐ 西城御史 (Censor of the Western City), the Xī'ān Jiāngjūn 西安將軍 (General of Xī'ān), the Níngxià Jiāngjūn 寧夏將軍 (General of Níngxià), the Liángzhōu Fùdūtǒng 涼州副都統 (Deputy Military Governor of Liángzhōu), and the Yīlí Jiāngjūn 伊犂將軍 (General of Yīlí).
Prisoners' rations were distributed in a timely manner.

The Sìchuān Sī 四川司 (Department of Sìchuān) also handled official documents from the Gōngbù 工部 (Board of Works), the Dūcháyuan Gōngkē 都察院工科 (Censorate's Department of Works), the Sìchuān Dào Yùshǐ 四川道御史 (Censor of the Sìchuān Circuit), and the Chéngdū Jiāngjūn 成都將軍 (General of Chéngdū).
During the Autumn Assizes (qiūshěn 秋審),
the Jiǔqīng 九卿 (Nine Chief Ministers) and Zhānshì 詹事 (Supervisor of Imperial Instruction) would meet in the imperial office to finalize the case records.
It also handled the collection and distribution of torture instruments.

The Guǎngdōng Sī 廣東司 (Department of Guǎngdōng) also handled official documents from the Luányú Wèi 鑾輿衞 (Imperial Guards of the Emperor's Sedan), the Zhèngbái Qí 正白旗 (Plain White Banner), the Guǎngdōng Dào Yùshǐ 廣東道御史 (Censor of the Guǎngdōng Circuit), and Āndìngmén 安定門,
and the Guǎngzhōu Jiāngjūn 廣州將軍 (General of Guǎngzhōu).
The Guǎngxī Sī 廣西司 (Department of Guǎngxī) also handled official documents from the Tōngzhèng Sī 通政司 (Office of Transmission) and the Guǎngxī Dào Yùshǐ 廣西道御史 (Censor of the Guǎngxī Circuit).
During the Court Assizes (cháoshěn 朝審),
draft memorials were prepared,
and prisoners' clothes were distributed in a timely manner.
The Yúnnán Sī 雲南司 (Department of Yúnnán) also handled official documents from the Xiānghuáng Qí 鑲黃旗 (Bordered Yellow Banner), the Yúnnán Dào Yùshǐ 雲南道御史 (Censor of the Yúnnán Circuit),
and Dōngzhímén 東直門.
It also managed the department's seal and the sealing and opening of documents.

The Guìzhōu Sī 貴州司 (Department of Guìzhōu) also handled official documents from the Lìbù 吏部 (Board of Civil Office), the Dūcháyuan Lìkē 都察院吏科 (Censorate's Department of Civil Office), the Zhènglán Qí 正藍旗 (Plain Blue Banner), the Guìzhōu Dào Yùshǐ 貴州道御史 (Censor of the Guìzhōu Circuit), and Cháoyángmén 朝陽門.
It also determined the promotions and appointments of Han officials in each department.
The Dūbǔ Sī 督捕司 (Department of Supervision and Apprehension) was in charge of runaways from the Eight Banners and all provinces.
The Tíláo Tīng 提牢廳 (Prison Supervision Office) was in charge of inspecting prisons.
The Sīyù 司獄 (Prison Warden) was in charge of supervising prison guards.
The Zāngfá Kù 贓罰庫 (Treasury for Illicit Gains and Fines) was in charge of storing confiscated funds from ongoing cases,
and would account for them and send them to the Hùbù 戶部 (Board of Revenue).
Separately, a Lǜlì Guǎn 律例館 (Bureau for Laws and Regulations) was established,
with a Shàngshū 尚書 or Shìláng 侍郎 serving as Zǒngcái 總裁 (Director-General).
There was one Tídiào 提調 (Coordinator),
four Zuǎnxiū 纂修 (Compilers),
(who were concurrently serving department officials).
There were four Jiàoduì 校對 (Proofreaders),
two Shōuzhǎng 收掌 (Custodians),
and four Fānyì 翻譯 (Translators) and Ténglù 謄錄 (Transcribers) each.
(These were concurrently serving department officials and Bǐtiěshì 筆帖式 (Secretaries)).
They were in charge of revising the laws and regulations.
Every five years, a compilation was made for a "minor revision" (xiǎoxiū 小修),
and every ten years, a complete re-editing was done for a "major revision" (dàxiū 大修).
The Qiūshěn Chù 秋審處 (Autumn Assizes Office)
was primarily responsible for reviewing the major records of the Autumn Assizes.
(Initially, the Sìchuān 四川 and Guǎngxī 廣西 Departments divided this responsibility.
In Yōngzhèng 雍正 12th year (1734),
two Manchu and two Han officials were specially dispatched
to be called the Zǒngbàn Qiūshěn Chù 總辦秋審處 (Director-General of the Autumn Assizes Office).
Later, four Xiébàn 協辦 (Assistant Directors) were added.)
The review of prisoners from all provinces
was called the Autumn Assizes;
the review of prisoners from the Ministry itself
was called the Court Assizes.
In the eighth month of each year,
the Jiǔqīng 九卿 (Nine Chief Ministers), Zhānshì 詹事 (Supervisor of Imperial Instruction), and Kēdào 科道 (Censors of the Surveillance Bureau) would jointly review the case records
to verify the facts.
For all capital crimes,
Censors (Yùshǐ 御史) and officials of the Dàlǐ Sì 大理寺 (Grand Court of Revision) would jointly interrogate the accused with the Xíngsī 刑司 (Department of Punishment),
and the verdict would be immediately delivered according to law.
This was called the "minor three judicial offices joint trial" (huìxiǎo sānfǎsī 會小三法司).
After the interrogation,
it would be reported to the senior officials.
The Dūyùshǐ 都御史 (Censor-in-Chief) and Dàlǐ Qīng 大理卿 (Minister of the Grand Court of Revision) would go to the Ministry and, together with the Shàngshū 尚書 and Shìláng 侍郎, would conduct a joint trial.
Each would discuss the case according to the law.
This was called the "major three judicial offices joint trial" (huìdà sānfǎsī 會大三法司).
After the verdict was submitted,
ministers would again be summoned to review and re-examine it,
only then would the capital punishment be carried out.
(Initially,
the Xíngbù 刑部 (Board of Punishments) would jointly deliberate on cases for the Court Assizes,
which were all cases from the Ministry itself.
For cases from outside the capital,
it was only in Kāngxī 康熙 16th year (1677) that the Xíngbù 刑部 was ordered to review and re-examine them,
and the Jiǔqīng 九卿 would hold a joint conference.)
Initially,
in Tiāncōng 天聰 5th year (1631),
the Xíngbù 刑部 was established.
In Shùnzhì 順治 1st year (1644),
officials such as Shàngshū 尚書 and Shìláng 侍郎 were appointed.

Fourteen Departments were established: Jiāngnán 江南, Zhèjiāng 浙江, Fújiàn 福建, Sìchuān 四川, Húguǎng 湖廣, Shǎnxī 陝西, Hénán 河南, Jiāngxī 江西, Shāndōng 山東, Shānxī 山西, Guǎngdōng 廣東, Guǎngxī 廣西, Yúnnán 雲南, and Guìzhōu 貴州.
Six Manchu Lángzhōng 郎中 (Secretaries) were appointed,
(increased to eight in the 5th year).
Eight Yuánwàiláng 員外郎 (Assistant Secretaries),
(increased to ten in the 5th year).
Five Táng Zhǔshì 堂主事 (Chief Clerks of the Ministry),
and fourteen Sī Zhǔshì 司主事 (Department Clerks).
Four Han-military Lángzhōng 郎中,
(abolished in Yōngzhèng 雍正 5th year).
Twelve Yuánwàiláng 員外郎,
(eight abolished in Kāngxī 康熙 38th year,
all abolished in Yōngzhèng 雍正 5th year).
One Táng Zhǔshì 堂主事.
Han Lángzhōng,
(in Yōngzhèng 雍正 5th year, one each was added to the Jiāngnán 江南, Húguǎng 湖廣, and Shǎnxī 陝西 Departments).
Yuánwàiláng,
(in the 15th year, one each was abolished from the Húguǎng 湖廣, Guǎngxī 廣西, Yúnnán 雲南, and Guǎngdōng 廣東 Departments.
In Yōngzhèng 雍正 3rd year, they were restored to their original number,
and one was added to the Sìchuān 四川 Department.
In the 5th year, one each was added to the Zhèjiāng 浙江 and Shāndōng 山東 Departments).
and Zhǔshì,
(in the 15th year, one each was abolished from the Hénán 河南, Sìchuān 四chuān, Shǎnxī 陝西, and Guìzhōu 貴州 Departments.
In Yōngzhèng 雍正 3rd year, they were restored to their original number).
There were fourteen of each. One Manchu Sīkù 司庫 (Department Treasurer),
and four Han Sīyù 司獄 (Prison Wardens).
(In Kāngxī 康熙 51st year, four Manchu ones were added.
In Qiánlóng 乾隆 6th year, it was set at two Han-military and two Han each.)
In the 5th year,
it was decided to have one Manchu and one Han Shàngshū 尚書 each.
(In the 7th year, one Manchu was added,
but abolished in the 10th year.)
In the 18th year,
eight Mongol Yuánwàiláng 員外郎 were appointed.
(Abolished in Kāngxī 康熙 1st year.)
In Kāngxī 康xī 38th year,
the Dūbǔ Qián Sī 督捕前司 (Former Department of Supervision and Apprehension) and Hòu Sī 後司 (Later Department of Supervision and Apprehension) were added,
making sixteen Departments.
(Merged from the Bīngbù 兵部.)
In the 57th year,
one Mongol Lángzhōng 郎中, Yuánwàiláng 員外郎, and Zhǔshì 主事 each were added.
In Yōngzhèng 雍正 1st year,
the Xiànshěn Zuǒ Sī 現審左司 (Left Department of Current Trials) and Yòu Sī 右司 (Right Department of Current Trials) were established,
in charge of interrogation, trial, and detention of prisoners.
In the 12th year,
the Jiāngnán Sī 江南司 was divided into the Jiāngsū Sī 江蘇司 and Ānhuī Sī 安徽司.
It was decided to have one Manchu and one Han Lángzhōng each.
Three Manchu Yuánwàiláng,
(two for the Jiāngsū Sī,
one for the Ānhuī Sī).
Two Han Yuánwàiláng.
One Manchu and one Han Zhǔshì each for the Departments.
The Dūbǔ Qián Sī and Hòu Sī were merged into one.
From that time onward,
Princes and Commandery Princes were appointed to manage the Ministry,
but without permanent members.
In Qiánlóng 乾隆 6th year,
the Xiànshěn Zuǒ Sī was renamed Fèngtiān Sī 奉天司,
and the Yòu Sī was renamed Zhílì Sī 直隸司.
It was decided to have one Manchu
(appointed in the Zhílì Sī)
and one Mongol (appointed in the Fèngtiān Sī) Lángzhōng each.
One Han Lángzhōng each.
Two Manchu Yuánwàiláng.
One Mongol,
(appointed in the Zhílì Sī).
Three Han,
(one for the Fèngtiān Sī,
two for the Zhílì Sī).
One Manchu and one Han Zhǔshì each.
This made a total of seventeen Departments.
In Jiāqìng 嘉慶 4th year,
a Dàxuéshì 大學士 (Grand Secretary) was appointed to lead the Ministry's affairs,
and one Manchu Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, and Zhǔshì each were changed to宗室 (Imperial Clan) vacancies.
In Guāngxù 光緒 6th year,
one Zōngshì Yuánwàiláng 宗室員外郎 (Imperial Clan Assistant Secretary) was added to the Yúnnán Sī 雲南司.
In the 32nd year,
it was renamed Fǎbù 法部 (Ministry of Justice).
Gōngbù Shàngshū,
Zuǒ and Yòushìláng,
each with one Manchu and one Han appointee.
Its subordinates: Tángzhǔshì,
three Manchus in the Qīngdǎngfáng,
one Manchu and one Han Bannerman in the Hànběnfáng.
Sīwù in the Sīwùtīng,
one Manchu and one Han.
Shànběnbǐtiēshì,
one imperial kinsman,
ten Manchus.
Yíngshàn, Yúhéng, Dūshuǐ, and Túntián, four Qīnglìsī: Lángzhōng,
one imperial kinsman,
(stationed in Túntiánsī.)
sixteen Manchus,
(four each in Yíngshàn and Yúhéng,
five in Dūshuǐ,
three in Túntián.)
one Mongol,
(stationed in Yíngshànsī.)
four Han.
(one in each Sī.)
Yuánwàiláng,
one imperial kinsman,
(stationed in Yúhéngsī.)
sixteen Manchus,
(four each in Yíngshàn and Yúhéng,
five in Dūshuǐ,
three in Túntián.)
one Mongol,
(stationed in Yíngshànsī.)
four Han.
(one in each Sī.)
Zhǔshì,
one imperial kinsman,
(stationed in Túntiánsī.)
eleven Manchus,
(two each in Yíngshàn and Túntián,
three in Yúhéng,
four in Dūshuǐ.)
one Mongol,
(stationed in Yíngshànsī.)
six Han.
(two each in Yíngshàn and Dūshuǐ,
one each in Yúhéng and Túntián.)
Bǐtiēshì,
one imperial kinsman,
eighty-five Manchus,
two Mongols,
ten Han Bannermen.
Zhìzàokù,
Lángzhōng,
two Manchus,
one Han;
Sīkù (regular seventh rank),
Sījiàng,
(initially seventh rank,
fixed as concurrent ninth rank in the ninth year of Kāngxī.)
both with two Manchus;
Kùshǐ,
(unranked.)
twenty-one Manchus.
Jiéshènkù,
one Manchu Lángzhōng and one Yuánwàiláng each,
two Sīkù,
twelve Kùshǐ.
Xiāohuángkù and Qiānzǐkù,
one Manchu Yuánwàiláng and one Zhǔshì each.
The Shàngshū manages works, military provisions and implements, discerning materials and preparing resources,
to regulate state affairs.
The Shìláng assists in this.
The Yòushìláng concurrently manages the casting of coins in the Bǎoyuánjú.
Yíngshàn manages construction projects,
including altars and temples, palaces and yamen, city walls, granaries, offices, and military barracks,
mobilizing labor and gathering materials,
and also supervises the labor registry,
and checks and collects timber tax and reed tax.
Yúhéng manages mountain and marsh hunting and fishing,
and the smelting and manufacturing of implements.
All military equipment and munitions,
according to the established quotas and prices of each battalion,
are accounted for, audited, and written off;
for the capital garrisons, they are supplied by the board.
It issues standard weights and measures,
and categorizes eastern pearls.
Dūshuǐ manages rivers, canals, and boats,
roads, passes, and bridges,
and all public and private water affairs.
In the twelfth month of the year,
it harvests ice and stores it in cellars,
distributing it in mid-summer;
and also manages the implements for altars, temples, and palace halls.
Túntián manages major construction projects for imperial tombs,

The Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ is in charge of scrutinizing official conduct
and upholding discipline.
They lead the Kē Dào officials in speaking their minds truthfully about their duties,
and lead the Jīngjī Dào in investigating negligence and corruption,
and also participate in major court deliberations.
In all capital punishment cases,
they convene with the Xíngbù and Dàlǐ Sì to finalize the verdict.
During sacrifices, court assemblies, Jīngyán lectures, and Lín Yōng ceremonies,
they enforce the law and correct those who do not comply with the rites.
The Zuǒ Fù Dū Yùshǐ assists them.
The fifteen Dào are responsible for impeaching corrupt officials,
submitting proposals on governance,
and each scrutinizes criminal cases in their respective provinces.
(Jīngjī Dào manages the affairs of the court,
as well as criminal cases in Zhílì and Shèngjīng,
and inspects the Nèigé, Shùntiān Fǔ, and the two counties of Dàxīng and Wǎnpíng.
Hénán Dào reviews the documents and archives of various departments and courts,
and inspects the Lìbù, Zhānshì Fǔ, Bùjūn Tǒnglǐng, and the Five Cities.
Jiāngnán Dào inspects the Hùbù, Bǎoquán Jú, left and right wing supervisors, capital granaries, and the Grand Coordinator of Grain Transport,
and examines the accounts of the Three Treasuries.
Zhèjiāng Dào inspects the Lǐbù and this court.
Shānxī Dào inspects the Bīngbù, Hànlín Yuàn, Six Kē, Zhōngshū Kē, Grand Coordinator of Granaries, Zuòliáng Tīng, Dàtōng Qiáo Supervisor, and the two granaries in Tōngzhōu.
Shāndōng Dào inspects the Xíngbù, Tàiyī Yuàn, and the Grand Coordinator of Waterways,
and urges the comparison of records for murder and robbery cases in the Five Cities and the apprehension of criminals.
Shǎnxī Dào inspects the Gōngbù, Bǎoyuán Jú,
and re-examines engineering projects in the capital.
Húguǎng Dào inspects the Tōngzhèngshǐ Sī and Guózǐ Jiān.

In the twentieth year (1755),
Jīngjīdào was again ordered to be listed before Hénándào,
The responsibilities of the various circuit censors were interchanged,
and thus the Jīngjī Dào became an important post.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
one Dū Yùshǐ and two Fù Dū Yùshǐ were appointed,
with circuits divided by province.
The Liáoshěn Dào was added,
following the precedent of the Jīngjī Dào,
with two Zhǎng Dào and two Xié Dào each.
Jiāngnán was split into Jiāngsū and Ānhuī Dào,
Húguǎng into Húběi and Húnán Dào;
Gānsù and Xīnjiāng Dào were also added,
each with one Mǎn and one Hàn Yùshǐ.
This made for twenty circuits.
They were ordered to investigate advantages and disadvantages,
and specifically charged with inspection and impeachment.
(However, many matters concerning the later-established departments of Wàiwù, Nónggōngshāng, and Mínzhèng
were not reported to them.
According to the old system,
various departments and yamens were inspected by circuit censors,
but this practice ceased at this time.)
The system had already become quite different from the old one.
In the early years of Shùnzhì,
there were also Xún'àn Yùshǐ,
one for each province.
(Abolished in the 17th year.)
Xúnyán Yùshǐ,
one each for Liǎnghuái, Liǎngzhè, Chánglú, and Hédōng.
(Suspended in the 10th year,
restored in the 12th year.
Suspended in the 11th year of Kāngxī,
soon restored.
In the 30th year, one each was again assigned to Fújiàn and Liǎngguǎng.
In the 59th year, the Liǎngguǎng salt commissioner was suspended.
In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng, the Fújiàn salt commissioner was suspended.
The following year, the Chánglú and Hédōng salt commissioners were suspended.
In the 4th year, the Liǎngzhè salt commissioner was suspended.)
Xúncáo Yùshǐ, one.
(Suspended in the 14th year.
In the 7th year of Yōngzhèng, two each were assigned to Huái'ān and Tōngzhōu.
In the 20th year of Qiánlóng, this was changed to one each for Huái'ān, Jìníng, Tiānjīn, and Tōngzhōu.
In the 17th year, four more were assigned to Tōngzhōu.
In the 23rd year, the one assigned to Tiānjīn was suspended.
In the 26th year, one was again assigned to Tiānjīn.
In the 13th year of Jiāqìng, it was stipulated that Kē and Dào officials were to be assigned concurrently.
In the 2nd year of Dàoguāng, all were suspended.)
Xúnshì Jīngtōng Gè Cāng Yùshǐ, one.
(Suspended in the 7th year,
restored in the 8th year.
Suspended again in the 7th year of Kāngxī.
In the 20th year, it was stipulated that one Mǎn and one Hàn official were to be assigned,
and suspended again in the 26th year.
In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng, one Xúnchá Yùshǐ was established
to generally investigate granary abuses.
In the 5th year, this was changed to one official each for Jīng Cāng and Tōng Cāng.
In the 17th year of Qiánlóng, it was stipulated that Kē and Dào officials were to be assigned concurrently.
In the 43rd year, one more for Nèicāng was added.
In the 59th year, it was changed to Kē and Dào officials supervising disbursements,
and the granary inspection official was suspended.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng, it was restored.
Suspended again in the 28th year of Guāngxù.)
Xúnshì Jiāngnán Shàngxià Liǎng Jiāng Yùshǐ, two.
(Abolished in the 6th year.)
Xúnshì Túntián Yùshǐ, one.
(Abolished in the 4th year.)
Dūlǐ Shǎnxī Gānsù Táoxuān Děng Chù Chámǎ Yùshǐ, one.
(Abolished in the 7th year of Kāngxī,
restored in the 34th year,
and abolished again in the 42nd year.)
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
Xúnchá Gè Shěng Yùshǐ were established:
one for Jiāngníng and Ānhuī,
one for Húběi and Húnán,
one for Shāndōng and Hénán.
Xúnshì Jílín Hēilóngjiāng Kē Dào,
two Mǎnzhōu.
Jīchá Fèngtiān Wǔnwǔ Yámén Yùshǐ, one.
Xúnshì Shāndōng Hénán Gōngwù Yùshǐ, one.
Zhílì Xúnchá Yùshǐ: two for Shùntiān, Yǒngpíng, Xuānhuà;
two for Bǎodìng, Zhèngdìng, Héjiān;
two for Shùndé, Guǎngpíng, Dàmíng.
Xúnnóng Yùshǐ, one.
All were subsequently abolished.
The Six Kē Gěishìzhōng:
Zhǎngyìn Gěishìzhōng for Lì, Hù, Lǐ, Bīng, Xíng, Gōng Kē,
one Mǎn and one Hàn each.
(Initial system:
Mǎn official fourth rank,
Hàn official seventh rank.
In the 2nd year of Kāngxī, Mǎn official changed to seventh rank,
restored to fourth rank in the 6th year.
All fixed at seventh rank in the 9th year.
Promoted to principal fifth rank in the 7th year of Yōngzhèng.
Promoted to principal fourth rank in the 32nd year of Guāngxù.)
Gěishìzhōng,
one Mǎn and one Hàn each.
(Initial system: seventh rank.
Promoted to principal fifth rank in the 7th year of Yōngzhèng.)
Bǐtiēshì, eighty persons.
(Fifteen each for Lì, Hù, Bīng, Xíng;
ten each for Lǐ, Gōng.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù, thirty were selectively retained.)
They were responsible for speech and remonstrance,
transmitting imperial decrees,
examining and adjudicating official public documents,
and canceling documents.
(The Lì Kē was responsible for personnel assessment,
and canceling documents from the Lìbù and Shùntiān Fǔ.
The Hù Kē was responsible for finance and revenue,
and canceling documents from the Hùbù.
The Lǐ Kē was responsible for rites and ceremonies,
and canceling documents from the Lǐbù, Zōngrén Fǔ, Lǐfānyuàn, Tàicháng Sì, Guānglù Sì, Hónglú Sì, Guózǐ Jiān, and Qīntiān Jiān.
The Bīng Kē was responsible for military administration,
and canceling documents from the Bīngbù, Luányú Wèi, and Tàipú Sì.
The Xíng Kē was responsible for penal law,
and canceling documents from the Xíngbù.
The Gōng Kē was responsible for public works,
and canceling documents from the Gōngbù.)
Any instance of sealing and rejection was immediately reported.
Initially following the Míng system,
the Six Kē were a separate office,
with no limit on the number of Gěishìzhōng,
and Hànjūn Fù Lǐshìguān were also appointed.
In the 18th year of Shùnzhì,
one Mǎn and one Hàn Dū Gěishìzhōng,
and one Zuǒ and one Yòu Gěishìzhōng were stipulated,
each one person.
(The Dū Gěishìzhōng was transferred from Zuǒ Gěishìzhōng,
and Zuǒ Gěishìzhōng from Yòu Gěishìzhōng.)
Two Hàn Gěishìzhōng were appointed,
and Fù Lǐshìguān were abolished.
In the 3rd year of Kāngxī,
only one Mǎn and one Hàn official were retained in the Six Kē.
In the 5th year,
Dū Gěishìzhōng was changed to Zhǎngyìn.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign,
due to internal promotions and external transfers within the Six Kē,
they first came under the jurisdiction of the Dūcháyuàn.
Whenever Censors were dispatched concurrently for cities, granaries, grain transport, or salt,
from this point onward, the Censorate and the Six Kē became one.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
the name "Six Kē" was abolished,
a separate Gěishìzhōng seal was cast,
and the quota was set at twenty persons.
Tōngzhèngshǐ Sì: Tōngzhèngshǐ,
(Initial system:
Mǎn official second rank,
Hàn official third rank.
In the 16th year of Shùnzhì, both were fixed at third rank.
Restored in the 6th year of Kāngxī.
Changed back to principal third rank in the 9th year.)
Fùshǐ,
(Initial system:
Mǎn official third rank,
Hàn official fourth rank.
In the 16th year of Shùnzhì, both were fixed at fourth rank,
restored in the 6th year of Kāngxī,
changed back to principal fourth rank in the 9th year.)
Cānyì,
(Initial system:
Mǎn official fourth rank,
Hàn official fifth rank.
In the 16th year of Shùnzhì, both were fixed at principal fifth rank.)
All one Mǎn and one Hàn each.
Its subordinates: Jīnglì Sì Jīnglì, (principal seventh rank.)
Zhīshì,
(Initial system: fourth rank,
later changed to principal seventh rank.)
one Mǎn and one Hàn each.
Bǐtiēshì,
six Mǎnzhōu,
two Hànjūn.
The Tōngzhèngshǐ was responsible for receiving memorials from various provinces,
reviewing and forwarding them to the Grand Secretariat,
and checking deadlines;
those that violated the format were impeached.
In cases of major injustice or difficult lawsuits,
they participated in preliminary discussions with the various Boards and the Censorate.
The Fùshǐ and Cānyì assisted them.
Jīnglì and Zhīshì
were separately responsible for managing the receipt and dispatch of documents.
Those with concurrent duties included: Dēngwéngǔ Tīng,
(one Cānyì on duty,
a Zhīshì leading the patrol.)
Bǐtiēshì,
one Mǎnzhōu and one Hànjūn each,
responsible for redressing grievances,
and those who made false accusations or illegal appeals were punished according to law.
Initially,
in the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
an edict stated:
"From now on, all internal and external memorials
shall be sealed and submitted through the Tōngzhèng Sī."
One Mǎn and one Hàn Tōngzhèng Shǐ were established,
and one Zuǒ Tōngzhèng Shǐ.
Two Hàn Yòu Tōngzhèng Shǐ.
(One was abolished in the tenth year of Qiánlóng,
and both were abolished in the thirteenth year.)
Two Zuǒ Cānyì,
one Mǎn and one Hàn.
(One Hàn was abolished in the fifty-third year of Kāngxī.
One of each was abolished in the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng.)
Two Yòu Cānyì,
both Hàn.
(One was abolished in the thirty-eighth year of Kāngxī.
Both were abolished in the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng.)
One Mǎn and one Hàn Sīwù.
(Later changed to Jīnglì.)
Zhīshì:
Two Mǎnzhōu and one Hànjūn.
(In the seventeenth year of Qiánlóng, this was changed to one Mǎn and one Hàn.)
In the sixty-first year of Kāngxī,
the Bǐtiēshì from the Dēngwéngǔ Tīng were transferred to its jurisdiction.
According to old practice,
petition memorials (memorials from the Tōngzhèng Sī)
and drum memorials (memorials from the Dēngwényuàn)
caused endless disputes.
Those who lodged complaints went to the Dūcháyuan,
where one Jǐshìzhōng or Yùshǐ was in charge of receiving lawsuits.
At this point, the assignments of Kē and Dào officials were stopped,
and they were reassigned to this department.
In the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the Zuǒ Tōngzhèng Shǐ was changed to Fùshǐ,
and the titles Zuǒ and Yòu were removed;
the Cānyì were also treated similarly.
In the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù,
it was abolished and merged into the Nèigé,
but soon restored.
In the twenty-eighth year,
as memorials were changed to "zòu" (reports) and not "tí" (proposals),
its office had no exclusive duties,
so it was again abolished.
Dàlǐ Sì Qīng:
(Initially,
Mǎn officials were second rank,
Hàn officials third rank.
In the sixteenth year of Shùnzhì, both were set at third rank.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī, it reverted to the old system,
then in the ninth year it was again fixed as Zheng third rank.)
Shǎoqīng:
(Initially,
Mǎn officials were third rank,
Hàn officials fourth rank.
In the sixteenth year of Shùnzhì, both were set at fourth rank.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī, it reverted to the old system,
then in the ninth year it was again fixed as Zheng fourth rank.)
One Mǎn and one Hàn for each.
Its subordinates included: Táng Píngshì,
(Initially fourth rank.
In the sixteenth year of Shùnzhì, changed to seventh rank.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī, promoted to fifth rank,
then in the ninth year fixed as Zheng seventh rank.)
One Mǎnzhōu.
Sīwù Tīng Sīwù:
One Mǎn and one Hàn.
Zuǒ and Yòu Sìchéng:
(Initially,
Mǎn officials were fourth rank,
Hàn officials sixth rank.
In the sixteenth year of Shùnzhì, both were set at sixth rank.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī, promoted to fifth rank.
Then in the ninth year it was again fixed as Zheng sixth rank.)
One Mǎnzhōu, one Hànjūn, and one Hàn.
Zuǒ and Yòu Píngshì:
One Hàn each.
Bǐtiēshì:
Forty Mǎnzhōu,
two Hànjūn.
The Qīng presided over the reversal of grave sentences
and assisted in national justice.
Together with the Xíngbù and Dūcháyuan, they were called the Sānfǎ Sī.
For all reviews,
the Xíngbù determined doubtful verdicts,
and the Dūcháyuan examined them.
When a case was complete,
it was sent to the Sì for final judgment.
If there was disagreement,
it was allowed to be deliberated by both,
and a memorial was submitted for a decision.
They also participated in major court policies.
The Shǎoqīng assisted them.
The Sìchéng were in charge of examining internal and external criminal cases,
reporting to their superiors,
and correcting departmental verdicts.
The Píngshì were in charge of drafting memorials for the two Zuǒ and Yòu Sì.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
it was decreed that there would be one Mǎn and one Hàn Qīng.
One Mǎnzhōu Shǎoqīng and two Hàn.
(One was abolished in the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng.)
One Mǎn Sìchéng.
(Zheng fifth rank.
Abolished in the thirty-eighth year of Kāngxī.)
Two Hàn Sīwù.
(In the fifteenth year, one Mǎn and one Hàn were designated.)
Zuǒ and Yòu Sìzhèng:
(Zheng sixth rank.)
One Mǎnzhōu, one Hànjūn, and one Hàn.
Zuǒ and Yòu Sìfù:
(Cóng sixth rank.)
One Hàn each.
(Abolished in the thirty-eighth year of Kāngxī.)
Táng Píngshì:
One Mǎn and one Hàn.
(One Hànjūn was abolished in the thirty-eighth year of Kāngxī.)
Zuǒ and Yòu Píngshì:
One Hàn each.
In the eleventh year,
one Sìzhèng and one Sìfù were dispatched to each province as Xùxíngguān.
(The Xíngbù dispatched thirteen Lángzhōng and Yuánwàiláng.
Soon abolished.)
In the seventeenth year of Qiánlóng,
the Zuǒ and Yòu Sìzhèng were changed to Sìchéng.
In the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù,
it was abolished and merged into the Xíngbù,
but soon restored.
In the thirty-second year,
the "Sì" (court) was changed to "Yuàn" (grand court).
Hànlín Yuàn Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì:
(Initially Zheng fifth rank.
In the first year of Shùnzhì, promoted to Zheng third rank.
In the eighth year of Yōngzhèng, promoted to Cóng second rank.
Specially appointed from amongst Grand Secretaries or Ministers of the Six Boards.)
One Mǎn and one Hàn.
Shìdú Xuéshì (Initially Cóng fourth rank.
In the twenty-ninth year of Guāngxù, promoted to Zheng fourth rank.)
and Shìjiǎng Xuéshì:
(Initially Cóng fourth rank.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng, promoted to Zheng fourth rank.)
Two Mǎnzhōu each,
three Hàn each.
Shìdú (Initially Zheng sixth rank.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng, promoted to Cóng fifth rank.
In the twenty-ninth year of Guāngxù, promoted to Zheng fifth rank.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng, promoted to Cóng fourth rank.)
and Shìjiǎng:
(Initially Zheng sixth rank.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng, promoted to Cóng fifth rank.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng, promoted to Cóng fourth rank.)
Three Mǎnzhōu each,
four Hàn each.
Xiūzhuàn (Initially Cóng sixth rank.)
Biānxiū (Initially Zheng seventh rank.)
Jiǎntǎo:
(Initially Cóng seventh rank.
From Xiūzhuàn downwards, in the first year of Xuāntǒng, all were changed to Cóng fifth rank.)
Shùjíshì:
(Appointed from new Jinshì graduates.
Those who passed the Bóxué Hóngcí examination,
or were specially ordered by imperial decree to be assigned to the academy,
were occasionally appointed.
At the end of Guāngxù, the imperial examination system was abolished,
and those who graduated from foreign universities or domestic universities,
after a court examination, were appointed,
receiving a seventh-rank salary.
Some were directly appointed Biānxiū or Jiǎntǎo,
which differed from the old system.)
All had no fixed number.
Its subordinates included: Zhǔshì:
Two Mǎnzhōu,
one Hànjūn.
Diǎnbù Tīng Diǎnbù (Cóng eighth rank.)
and Kǒngmù:
(Mǎn officials Cóng ninth rank,
Hàn officials unranked.)
One Mǎn and one Hàn for each.
Dàizhào Tīng Dàizhào:
(Cóng ninth rank.)
Two Mǎn and two Hàn.
Bǐtiēshì:
Forty Mǎnzhōu,
four Hànjūn.
The Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy (Zhǎngyuàn) was in charge of the imperial history and literary affairs,
serving as a consultant to the emperor.
Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú Xuéshì) and below were responsible for composing and recording.
When making sacrifices and announcements to the gods of the suburban altars and ancestral temples (Jiāomiào Shénqí),
they drafted the sacrificial prayers (Zhùwén).
When respectfully bestowing honorific titles (Huīhào), establishing empresses or crown princes (Cèlì), and enfeoffing (Cèfēng),
they drafted the edicts of investiture (Cèwén) and imperial seals (Bǎowén),
as well as sacrificial texts (Jìwén) and monumental inscriptions (Bēiwén) bestowed upon civil and military officials, both inside and outside the court.
Serving on duty in the Southern Study (Nánshūfáng Shìzhí)
and as instructors in the Imperial Study (Shàngshūfáng Jiàoxí)
were all within their selection.
For compiling the Veritable Records (Shílù), histories (Shǐ), and treatises (Zhì),
they served as directors (Tídiào), chief compilers (Zǒngzuǎn), compilers (Zuǎnxiū), assistant compilers (Xiéxiū), and other such officials.
When probationary bachelors (Shùjíshì) entered the academy,
they were assigned to study both Manchu (Qīng) and Chinese (Hàn) scripts.
The Ministry of Personnel (Lìbù) memorialized to request the selection and appointment of two high officials to lead the instruction.
(Initially, Academicians of the Inner Court (Nèiyuàn Xuéshì) held this position,
and scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú) and other officials also occasionally participated.
Later, the Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy (Zhǎngyuàn) was ordered to concurrently hold this post.
In the 6th year of Kāngxī (1667),
Chén Yuánlóng, a Minister of Works (Gōngbù Shàngshū), first assumed leadership,
and thereafter Ministers (Shàngshū), Vice Ministers (Shìláng), and Grand Secretaries of the Grand Secretariat (Nèigé Xuéshì) could all hold this position.
These were the Grand Instructors (Dàjiàoxí).
The Junior Instructors (Xiǎojiàoxí) were selected and dispatched by the Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy (Zhǎngyuàn),
starting in the 33rd year of Kāngxī (1694).
It was suspended during the Yōngzhèng reign,
but Gāozōng restored the old system.)
Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú) and lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng) were responsible for teaching and tutoring.
Two compilers (Biān) and revisers (Jiǎn) were dispatched to oversee the academy's provisions (Guǎnxì).
After three years, an examination was held,
and they were dispersed or retained accordingly.
There were two managing Hanlin officials (Bànshì Hànlín) each for Manchu and Chinese.
(In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng (1723),
it was ordered that compilers (Biān) and revisers (Jiǎn) with lower stipends should preside over the final draft discussions (Dìnggǎo Shuōtáng).
This marked the beginning of the managing Hanlin officials (Bànshì Hànlín) of the Qing Secret Hall (Qīngmìtáng).
Later, the number of people slightly increased,
with titles such as "memorializing official" (Zòubàn) and "assisting official" (Xiébàn).
Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú) and lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng) also occasionally held these roles.)
They were in charge of the administration of the main hall (Shuàitīng) officials.
Directors (Zhǔshì), record keepers (Diǎnbù), and chief clerks (Kǒngmù)
managed memorials and documents,
and supervised the academy clerks (Lìyì).
Attendants (Dàizhào) were in charge of transcription and proofreading.
Initially,
the positions of the Hanlin Academy were subordinate to the Three Inner Academies (Nèisānyuàn).
In the 1st year of Shùnzhì (1644),
the Hanlin Academy (Hànlínyuàn) was established,
and the Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy (Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì) was designated as a dedicated official.
One Han Chinese official (Hànyuán) was appointed,
concurrently holding the title of Vice Minister of Rites (Lǐbù Shìláng).
There were two Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú Xuéshì) and two Lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì) each.
(In the 15th year, two were added to each.)
There were two Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú) and two Lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng) each.
(In the 15th year, one was added to each.)
There were no fixed numbers for Revisers (Xiūzhuàn), Compilers (Biānxiū), Recommenders (Jiǎntǎo), and Probationary Bachelors (Shùjíshì).
Two record keepers (Diǎnbù).
(In the 15th year, one was changed to a Manchu vacancy.)
One chief clerk (Kǒngmù).
(In the 15th year, one Manchu was added.)
All were held by Han Chinese.
The following year,
it was merged into the Three Inner Academies (Nèisānyuàn).
In the 15th year (1658),
the old system was restored,
and one Manchu Chancellor of the Hanlin Academy (Mǎnzhōu Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì) was added,
with concurrent titles as before.
(It was abolished in the 58th year of Qiánlóng (1793).)
Six attendants (Dàizhào) were appointed.
(Four Manchu officials,
two Han Chinese officials.)
In the 18th year (1661),
it was again merged into the Three Inner Academies (Nèisānyuàn).
In the 9th year of Kāngxī (1670),
the numbers were set: three Manchu and Han Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú Xuéshì), Lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì), Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú), and Lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng) each;
(In the 50th year of Qiánlóng (1785), one Manchu was removed from each.
In the 29th year of Guāngxù (1903), two Manchu and Han Scholars-in-waiting (Shìdú) and Lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng) were added to each.)
one record keeper (Diǎnbù) and one chief clerk (Kǒngmù) each,
and two attendants (Dàizhào) each.
(In the 9th year of Kāngxī, it was set to one Manchu and one Han each.)
In the 16th year (1677),
Lecturer-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì) Zhāng Yīng and others were ordered to serve on duty in the Southern Study (Nánshūfáng).
Previously, imperial edicts, decrees, and literary compositions were often drafted by the academy.
From this point on, it became a specialized duty of the Western Study (Xīqīng).
(Later, it was transferred to the Grand Council (Jūnjīchù).)
In the 28th year (1689),
due to the decline of academy affairs,
Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì) Xú Yuánwén was ordered to concurrently manage the academy.
The practice of high officials concurrently holding this position began from this time.
(The following year, it was stipulated that Ministers (Shàngshū), Vice Ministers (Shìláng), and Censor-in-chief of the Left (Zuǒ Dū Yùshǐ) could all concurrently hold it.)
In the 29th year of Guāngxù (1903),
additional directors (Táng Zhǔshì) were appointed:
two Manchu and one Han Chinese.
That year, the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Zhānshì Fǔ) was abolished,
and because literary officials had no path for promotion,
one Manchu and one Han Academician (Xuéshì) (Rank 3a)
each, and two Manchu and Han drafters (Zhuànwén) (Rank 6a.
Promoted to Rank 5a in the 1st year of Xuāntǒng)
each were added.
In the 33rd year (1907),
additional secretaries (Mìshūláng) were appointed,
(Rank 6b.
Promoted to Rank 5a in the 1st year of Xuāntǒng)

A lecture and practice hall (Jiǎngxí Guǎn) was also established,

In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
the ranks of Lecturers-in-waiting (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì) and below were once again elevated,
and promotion from external positions was halted.
(In the initial system, when there were vacancies in the Hanlin Academy (Hàn) and the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Zhān),
and there were not enough compilers (Biān) and revisers (Jiǎn) for promotion,
officials from other ministries and departments (Bù Yuàn) who had passed the imperial examinations (Kējǐa) were promoted,
and these were known as external positions (Wàibān).)
In the initial system,
successful imperial examination candidates (Jìnshì) were classified by their grades,
and Revisers (Xiūzhuàn), Compilers (Biānxiū), and Recommenders (Jiǎntǎo) were not distinguished by promotion or demotion.
(During the Shùnzhì reign,
Compilers (Biānxiū) Chéng Fāngcháo and others were appointed as Revisers (Xiūzhuàn),
Recommenders (Jiǎntǎo) Lǐ Wèi and others as Compilers (Biānxiū),
and Jiāng Yuánhéng was demoted from Compiler (Biānxiū) to Recommender (Jiǎntǎo),
but this was not a fixed system.
Also, officials such as compilers (Biānxiū) in the Three Inner Academies (Nèisānyuàn) did not necessarily all come from the imperial examination system.
Jìn Fǔ, Liú Zhàolín, and others were appointed as compilers (Biānxiū) as imperial students (Guānxuéshēng),
which was also an innovative move.)
Probationary bachelors (Shùjíshì) were originally subordinate to the Inner Academy for the Propagation of Culture (Nèi Hóngwényuàn).
Later, when this academy (Běnyuàn) was established,
they came under its jurisdiction.
In the 13th year of Yōngzhèng (1735),
the Academy for Probationary Bachelors (Shùchángguǎn) was built.
According to custom,
officials were only appointed after completing their probationary period (Sàn guǎn).
However, there were also those who were appointed immediately without being selected as probationary bachelors (Shùcháng),
all of which were special exceptions.

responsible for custodianship, collation, and compilation.

In the initial system,
Grand Secretaries (Dàxuéshì) were in charge of the imperial lectures (Jīngyán).
Later, it was stipulated that there would be six lecturers for the imperial lectures (Jīngyán Jiǎngguān) each for Manchu and Han,
and cabinet ministers (Géc chén) no longer lectured.
From the time Xú Yuánwén and Xióng Cìlǚ and others were successively promoted from Minister (Shàngshū) to Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì),
they continued to concurrently hold the position,
and this became customary thereafter.
In the early Xuāntǒng period,
department vice ministers (Chéng) and counselors (Cān) also occasionally participated.
The Grand Secretariat's Office of the Diaries of Activity and Repose;
The Officials of the Daily Lectures and Diaries of Activity and Repose.
Ten Manchu individuals,

The Daily Lecturers were in charge of attending to the Emperor's daily life,
recording his words and actions.
During the Jīngyán lectures, ceremonies at the Línyōng Hall,
imperial audiences at the Wǔmén Gate,
sacrifices, ritual plowing,
court assemblies, banquets,
and the final review of death sentences,
two officials would attend.
Whenever the Emperor visited imperial tombs, went on hunting expeditions, or toured the provincial capitals,
they would request imperial instructions, follow the retinue, and attend to their duties,
reverently listening to the imperial pronouncements,
and then retire to meticulously record them.
Monthly summaries and annual compilations
were stored in an iron casket
and sent to the Nèigé for esteemed safekeeping.
The Supervisors were in charge of handling documents
and proofreading classics.
Initially,
in the second year of Tiāncōng,
scholarly officials were ordered to divide into two shifts:
Bākèshí Dáhǎi and others translated Han Chinese texts,
which was the origin of the daily lectures;
Bākèshí Kù'ěrzhú and others recorded government affairs,
which was the origin of the Officials of the Diaries of Activity and Repose.
In the twelfth year of Shùnzhì,
Daily Lecturers were first established.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī,
the Office of the Diaries of Activity and Repose was first established,
(located in the west wing of the Tàihé Mén.)
Four Manchu officials for recording and annotation were appointed,
and eight Han officials,
with Daily Lecturers concurrently holding these positions.
(In the twelfth year, one Manchu official and
two Han officials were added.
In the sixteenth year, one more Manchu official was added.
In the twentieth year, eight Han officials were added.
In the thirtieth year, the number of Han officials was fixed at twelve.)
At that time, the Daily Lectures and the Diaries of Activity and Repose were separate functions.
Two Manchu Supervisors were also appointed,
and one Han Banner individual.
(Abolished in the fifty-seventh year.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng, two Manchu individuals were appointed.
In the twelfth year, one Han individual was added.)
In the twenty-fifth year, the Daily Lectures were suspended,
but the Officials of the Diaries of Activity and Repose retained the title
"Daily Lecturer".
In the fifty-seventh year,
the Office of the Diaries of Activity and Repose was abolished
and reorganized under the Nèigé.
On days when affairs were handled,
five Hànlín officials attended.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
the Daily Lectures and Diaries of Activity and Repose were re-established:
six Manchu individuals,
twelve Han individuals.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
two Manchu officials were added.
In the eighth year of Jiāqìng,
two more Manchu officials were added.
Thus, the Daily Lectures and Diaries of Activity and Repose were merged into one.

The Qīng is in charge of managing and guarding the altars, shrines, and ancestral temples,
conducting seasonal sacrifices,
proclaiming ritual protocols,
supplying offerings,
and identifying types of vessels.
Before the appointed date, they present the prayer tablets,
inspect the fasting of all officials,
and on the day of the sacrifice, lead their subordinates to perform their duties.
The Shàoqīng assists them.
The Tàicháng Sì Chéng is in charge of the forms and types of sacrificial offerings,
distinguishing duties to instruct the relevant officials,
and also selecting and supplementing staff,
and checking and auditing the sacrificial animals and provisions.
The Zànlǐ Láng and Dúzhù Guān are separately in charge of guiding the ceremonies and arranging affairs,
preparing articles and purifying vessels,
and also practicing ritual movements and reciting prayers,
each performing their assigned duties during sacrifices.
The Bóshì examines prayer texts and ritual protocols,
registers them as models,
and after the altars and temples are arranged,
escorts the Lǐbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of the Board of Rites) to inspect the fasting,
and also annually reviews sacrificial levies.
The Diǎnbù is in charge of inspecting sacrificial offerings,
arranging sacrificial animals,
and managing clerical staff.
The Kùshǐ is in charge of guarding the treasury.
In the 1st year of Shùnzhì (1644),

The Qīng manages the imperial banquets, labor, recommendations, and offerings;
differentiates between grades and styles;
and audits expenses.
For all sacrifices,
he meets with the Tàicháng Qīng to inspect the sacrificial animals.
After the ritual is complete,
he presents the sacrificial meat to the Tiānzǐ,
and distributes it to all officials.
For barbarian envoys and provisions,
he provides according to their ranks.
The Shǎoqīng assists him.
The Dàguān manages the supply of pork,
prepares utensils,
audits market prices,
and collects taxes from vegetable fields and delivers them to the treasury.
The Zhēnxiū manages the supply of poultry, rabbits, and fish;
for major sacrifices, it supplies "dragon pots" (lónghú) and "dragon goblets" (lóngjué);
and differentiates between grades of banquets and feasts.
The Liángyùn manages the supply of wines and sweet wines,
distinguishes water sources,
measures [màiqū] and sprouts,

The Yǎnshèng Gōng [衍聖公] was in charge of presiding over the sacrifices at the Zhìshèng Quèlǐ Miào [至聖闕里廟] (Temple of the Foremost Sage at Quèlǐ).
The Hàn Bó [翰博] (Erudites of the Hànlín Academy) of the descendants of sages and worthies each presided over the sacrificial rites of their ancestors.
The Tàicháng Bóshì [太常博士] (Erudite of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices) of the sacred lineage presided over the sacrifices at the Shèngzé Shūyuàn [聖澤書院] (Holy Grace Academy).
The Guózǐjiān Xuézhèng [國子監學正] (Director of Studies of the Imperial Academy) presided over the sacrifices at the Yífēng Shèngmiào [儀封聖廟] (Sacred Temple of Yífēng).
The Xuélù [學錄] (Registrars) were responsible for the sacrifices at the two academies of Níshān [尼山] and Zhūsì [洙泗].
The hereditary Sixth Grade official was in charge of the supplementary sacrifices at the Chóngshèng Cí [崇聖祠] (Ancestral Temple for the Veneration of Sages).
The Professors and Xuélù [學錄] of the four clans were in charge of instructing the students of the four clans.
The Zhíshìguān [執事官] (Officials in Charge) managed the sacrificial offerings and supplementary sacrifices,
and also oversaw the sacrificial wine, silk, incense, and invocations.
The Sīyuè [司樂] (Director of Music) managed the musical scores and instruments.
The Diǎnjí [典籍] (Archivist) managed the books and ritual performers.
The Guǎngōu [管勾] (Overseer) managed the income and expenditure of sacrificial land, money, and grain.
The Bǎihù [百戶] (Battalion Commander) managed the household registration of the imperial mausoleum and temple,
was responsible for the safekeeping of musical instruments,
and during sacrifices, oversaw the purification and washing.
The Zhīyìn [知印] (Seal Keeper), Zhǎngshū [掌書] (Scribe), and Shūxiě [書寫] (Clerk) managed documents and seals.
The Zòuchāi [奏差] (Memorial Dispatcher) was in charge of delivering memorials, petitions, and reports.
The Suícháo Bànguān [隨朝伴官] (Attendant Officials) were in charge of accompanying during imperial audiences and handling affairs.
