Salaried Yin-Yang Students (Shíliáng Yīnyángshēng),
ten Han.
(All were granted ninth-rank hats and sashes.)
One Assistant Instructor (Zhùjiào) of the Assistant Instructor Office (Zhùjiào Tīng),
and two Teaching Assistants (Jiàoxí).
The Director manages the techniques of calculation
and the positions of constellations without error.
At the end of the year, he presents the new calendar
to the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù) for promulgation.
The Deputy Directors assist him.
The Department of Seasonal Rites is in charge of calculating the movements of the heavens,
verifying the precession of the equinoxes to adjust the solar terms,
and compiling the seasonal calendar.
(Those translated and disseminated in the national language and Mongolian script
are overseen by the Manchu and Mongol Five Bureau Directors.
Calculations for solar and lunar eclipses, the distances between the Seven Luminaries, retrogrades, stations, hidden phases, conjunctions, and shared degrees
are overseen by the Han Five Bureau Directors.)
It is promulgated throughout the four directions.
The Department of Astronomy is in charge of observing celestial phenomena,
recording auspicious and inauspicious signs from clouds and other objects;
leading astronomical students to ascend the observatory,
and recording all clear and rainy days, wind and thunder, clouds and rainbows, halos and parhelia, meteors, and unusual stars
into ledgers.
Matters requiring memorialization are sent to the Directorate,
and then secretly submitted to the emperor.
The Department of Clepsydra is in charge of adjusting clepsydras,
measuring the culminating stars,
and determining latitudes;
for sacrifices, court audiences, and construction,
it selects auspicious days
and identifies taboos.
The Principal Clerk is in charge of memorials, official documents,
registers, and personnel numbers.
Astronomical Students are assigned to the three departments
and are in charge of observation, waiting, and calculation.
Yin-Yang Students belong to the Department of Clepsydra
and are in charge of the watchtower and night watches.
The Directorate officials regularly examine their skills and conduct promotions and demotions accordingly.
The Assistant Instructor is in charge of teaching mathematics to various students.
Initially,
the Qīntiānjiān was established in the 1st year of Shùnzhì,
divided into four departments: Astronomy, Seasonal Rites, Clepsydra, and Muslim Astronomy (Huíhuí).

Officials such as Director, Deputy Director, Five Bureau Directors, Protectors of Calendrical Matters (Bǎozhāngzhèng), Clepsydra Officers, Observatory Administrators, Observational Clerks, Time Keepers, Scribal Clerks, Academicians, and Principal Clerks were appointed,
all filled by Han people.
Official communications and memorials were submitted to the Ministry of Rites.
In the middle autumn new moon of that year, there was a solar eclipse.
As the calculations by the Westerner Tāng Ruòwàng were precise and accurate,
(the Dàtǒng and Huíhuí methods both had errors in time.)
he was ordered to revise the seasonal calendar
and take charge of Directorate affairs.
In the 14th year,
the Huíhuí Department was abolished,
and its duties were transferred to the Autumn Bureau Director.
Soon after, the old system was restored.
In the 15th year,
its responsibilities were formally separated from those of the Ministry of Rites.
In the 2nd year of Kāngxī,
it was again subordinate to the Ministry of Rites.
The following year,
five Manchu officials were added to the Department of Astronomy,
marking the beginning of Manchu officials entering the Directorate.
The year after that,
it was decided to have one Manchu and one Han Director,
two Left and Right Deputy Directors each,
one Principal Clerk each,
and two Manchu and two Mongol Five Bureau Directors each.
The Academicians of the abolished Huíhuí Department were still subordinate to the Autumn Bureau Director.
One Han bannerman Autumn Bureau Director was established,
and one Han each for the Spring, Summer, Central, Autumn, and Winter Five Bureau Directors.
Three Manchu Observatory Administrators,
(In the 47th year of Qiánlóng, one was changed to a Mongol vacancy.)
one Han bannerman,
and four Han.
Two Manchu Clepsydra Officers,
(In the 47th year of Qiánlóng, one was changed to a Mongol vacancy.)
and two Han.
One Han Observational Clerk,
two Protectors of Calendrical Matters,
(Principal eighth rank.
Abolished in the 14th year.)
two Scribal Clerks.
(One was abolished in the 14th year.)
One Han bannerman Time Keeper,
and one Han.
(Abolished in the 14th year.)
Six Manchu Academicians,
(In the 47th year of Qiánlóng, one was changed to a Mongol vacancy.)
two Han bannermen,
and thirty-six Han.
(Soon after, fourteen were abolished,
and two were re-established in the 5th year,
making a total of twenty-four with the old ones.)
It was also decreed that Directorate officials' promotions and transfers would not move them from their original agency,
and that accumulated service would only lead to honorary title promotions,
setting this as a precedent.
Previously, Yáng Guāngxiān, a student official from Xīn'ān Guard, had requested the execution of heretical religions
and the dismissal of Ruòwàng's position.
Consequently, Guāngxiān was made Deputy Director,
and soon promoted to Director,
still using the Huíhuí method.
Nán Huáirén submitted a memorial to redress the injustice.
In the 8th year,
Guāngxiān was again dismissed,
and Nán Huáirén was appointed Han Director,
his title changed to Supervising Compiler (Jiānxiū),
and the Western method was used as before.
In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng,
the Westerner Dài Jìnxián was formally appointed Director,
and the title Supervising Compiler was removed.
In the 8th year,
one Western Deputy Director was added.
In the 4th year of Qiánlóng,
one Han Assistant Instructor of Mathematics was established,
subordinate to the Guózǐjiān.
In the 10th year,
it was decided that Deputy Directors would be appointed separately from Manchu, Han, and Western backgrounds.
(In the 18th year, one Manchu and one Han were abolished,
and two Westerners were added,
divided into Left and Right.)
In the 44th year,
it was further decreed that a Prince (Qīnwáng) should lead it.
In the 6th year of Dàoguāng,
it was again decided to have one Manchu and one Han Director,
and two Left and Right Deputy Directors each.
At this time, Westerners like Gāo Gǒngchén had either returned or died,
and the Directorate itself was already familiar with Western methods,
so the entry of foreigners into official positions was stopped.
In the 31st year of Guāngxù,
the Assistant Instructors from the Guózǐjiān began to be subordinate to it after a reform.
Tài-yī-yuàn 太醫院 (Imperial Academy of Medicine): One Grand Minister (Wáng Dà-chén 王大臣) for managing academy affairs.
(Specially appointed.)
One Yuàn-shǐ 院使 (Academician Director).
(Originally a senior fifth-grade official.
Promoted to senior fourth-grade in the first year of Xuān-tǒng 宣統.)
One Zǔo Yuàn-pàn 左院判 (Left Academician Judge) and one Yòu Yuàn-pàn 右院判.
(Originally senior sixth-grade officials.
Promoted to senior fifth-grade in the first year of Xuān-tǒng 宣統.)
All of these are Han officials.
Its subordinates: Thirteen Yù-yī 御醫 (Imperial Physicians).
(Two concurrently serving as Shǒu-lǐng Tīng-shì 首領廳事 (Head of Hall Affairs).
Originally senior eighth-grade officials.
Promoted to seventh-grade in the seventh year of Yōng-zhèng 雍正,
and granted sixth-grade hat and belt.
Promoted to senior sixth-grade in the first year of Xuān-tǒng 宣統.)
Twenty-six Lì-mù 吏目 (Clerical Officers).
(One concurrently serving as Shǒu-lǐng Tīng-shì 首領廳事.
Originally thirteen of eighth-grade and thirteen of ninth-grade.
In the first year of Xuān-tǒng 宣統,
eighth-grade was changed to seventh-grade,
and ninth-grade to eighth-grade.)
Twenty Yī-shì 醫士 (Medical Scholars).
(One concurrently serving as Shǒu-lǐng Tīng-shì 首領廳事,
and granted a junior ninth-grade hat and belt.)
Thirty Yī-shēng 醫生 (Doctors).
The Yuàn-shǐ 院使 and Yuàn-pàn 院判 are in charge of examining the methods of the nine specialties,
and leading their subordinates to perform medical duties.
The Yù-yī 御醫, Lì-mù 吏目, and Yī-shì 醫士 each specialize in one branch,

namely: Dà-fāng-mài 大方脈 (Internal Medicine for Adults), Xiǎo-fāng-mài 小方脈 (Pediatrics), Shāng-hán-kē 傷寒科 (Typhoid and Febrile Diseases), Fù-rén-kē 婦人科 (Gynecology), Chuāng-yáng-kē 瘡瘍科 (Surgery for Sores and Ulcers), Zhēn-jiǔ-kē 鍼灸科 (Acupuncture and Moxibustion), Yǎn-kē 眼科 (Ophthalmology), Yān-hóu-kē 咽喉科 (Otolaryngology), Zhèng-gǔ-kē 正骨科 (Orthopedics).
These constitute the nine specialties.
(Originally eleven specialties were established.
Later, the Dòu-zhěn-kē 痘疹科 (Smallpox and Measles) was merged into Xiǎo-fāng-mài 小方脈,
and Yān-hóu-kē 咽喉科 and Kǒu-chǐ-kē 口齒科 (Dentistry) were combined into one specialty.)
They are responsible for assigning shifts to attend duty.
Those serving in the palace are called Gōng-zhí 宮直 (Palace Attendants);
those serving in the outer court are called Liù-zhí 六直 (Six Attendants).
Two officials from this academy are on duty overnight at the Shòu-lè-fáng 壽樂房 in Xī-yuàn 西苑.
In the first year of Shùn-zhì 順治,
one Yuàn-shǐ 院使,
one Zǔo Yuàn-pàn 左院判 and one Yòu Yuàn-pàn 右院判 were established,
along with thirty Lì-mù 吏目.
(Twenty were removed in the eighteenth year,
then restored in the ninth year of Kāng-xī 康熙.
Ten were removed in the fourteenth year,
and restored again in the first year of Yōng-zhèng 雍正.)
Ten Yù-shòu Lì-mù 豫授吏目 (Provisional Clerical Officers).
(Removed in the eighteenth year.
Restored in the ninth year of Kāng-xī 康熙,
then removed again in the thirty-first year.)
Ten Yù-yī 御醫.
(Two were removed in the fifty-third year of Kāng-xī 康熙.
Restored in the first year of Yōng-zhèng 雍正,
and five were added in the seventh year.
Two were removed in the twenty-third year of Dào-guāng 道光.)
Twenty Yī-shì 醫士.
(Twenty were removed in the eighteenth year.
Restored in the ninth year of Kāng-xī 康熙,
then ten were removed in the fourteenth year.
Twenty were added in the first year of Yōng-zhèng 雍正.)
All entry and exit of medicinal materials were subordinate to the Lǐ-bù 禮部 (Board of Rites).
In the sixteenth year,
it was transferred back to this academy.
In the eighteenth year,
the Shēng-yào-kù 生藥庫 (Raw Medicinal Material Depot) was again subordinate to the Lǐ-bù 禮部.
In the third year of Kāng-xī 康熙,
it was decreed that medicinal materials from the provinces,
along with payments in lieu of grain,
be collected, stored, and disbursed by the Hù-bù 戶部 (Board of Revenue).
In the seventh year of Yōng-zhèng 雍正,
it was decreed there be ten eighth-grade Lì-mù 吏目
and twenty ninth-grade.
(Later, thirteen of each were established.)
In the fifty-eighth year of Qián-lóng 乾隆,
Ministers of the Nèi-fǔ 內府 (Imperial Household Department) were ordered to lead the academy's affairs.
In the first year of Xuān-tǒng 宣統,
Yuàn-shǐ Zhāng Zhòng-yuán 張仲元 memorialized to reform the old system,
specifically raising the official ranks of the Yuàn-shǐ 院使 and subsequent officials.
According to the original system,
those entering the academy for study
and passing examinations for "grace rations"
took a very long time,
and Yī-shì 醫士 for military camps and prisons were all selected from the academy.
Towards the end of Guāng-xù 光緒,
the Yī-guān 醫官 (Medical Officials) of the Mín-zhèng-bù 民政部 (Ministry of Civil Affairs)
and the Jūn-yī Sī-zhǎng 軍醫司長 (Director of the Military Medical Department) of the Lù-jūn-bù 陸軍部 (Ministry of War)
held the same rank as the Yuàn-shǐ 院使 and Yuàn-pàn 院判.
Therefore, regulations were established
to elevate the status of the imperial court system.
Furthermore, it was decreed that
academy officials' transfers should not leave their current department.
During the Tóng-zhì 同治 reign,
it was once proposed that Lì-mù 吏目, after six years of salary,
be promoted to Àn-chá-sī Jīng-lì 按察司經歷 (Experience Officer of the Provincial Judicial Commissioner) or Zhōu-pàn 州判 (Assistant Prefect).
Later, as this was contrary to their usual duties,
it was abandoned.

Eight Tiān-tán-wèi 天壇尉 (Heavenly Altar Commanders)
and eight Dì-tán-wèi 地壇尉 (Earthly Altar Commanders).
(One fifth-grade,
seven sixth-grade.)

(Two fourth-grade,
eight fifth-grade.)

(One fifth-grade,
four sixth-grade,
all subordinate to the Tài-cháng-sì 太常寺 (Court of Imperial Sacrifices).)
Eight Táng-zi-wèi 堂子尉 (Táng-zi Commanders).
(Two seventh-grade,
six eighth-grade,
subordinate to the Lǐ-bù 禮部.)
All are Manchu officials.
They are responsible for managing keys,
guarding and standing watch overnight,
and presenting incense on the first and fifteenth of each month for ceremonies.
One Fèng-sì 奉祀 (Sacrificial Administrator) (junior seventh-grade)
and one Sì-chéng 祀丞 (Assistant Sacrificial Administrator) (junior eighth-grade)
each for the Cí-jì-shǔ 祠祭署 (Bureau of Sacrificial Rites) of the Tiān-tán 天壇, Dì-tán 地壇, Cháo-rì-tán 朝日壇, Xī-yuè-tán 夕月壇, and Xiān-nóng-tán 先農壇.
(The Sì-chéng 祀丞 for the Rì 日 (Sun) and Yuè 月 (Moon) Altars were later removed.)
The Dì-wáng-miào Cí-jì-shǔ 帝王廟祠祭署 (Bureau of Sacrificial Rites for the Temple of Emperors and Kings) has no dedicated officials.
(One Han Zàn-lǐ-láng 贊禮郎 (Ceremonial Officer) or Sī-yuè 司樂 (Music Master) is appointed to fill the position,
all subordinate to the Yuè-bù 樂部 (Board of Music).)
All are Han officials.
They are responsible for guarding the sacred treasury,
inspecting it at appointed times,
and supervising workers in cleaning and sweeping;
as well as renovating walls and buildings, planting trees,
and respectfully attending to these duties.
(Fourth-grade Wèi 尉 are promoted from fifth-grade,
and lower ranks follow this pattern.
However, Tài-miào-wèi 太廟尉 are selected from sixth-grade Wèi 尉 of various altars and retired Láng-yuán 郎員 (Secretaries) from various boards and departments.
Sixth-grade and other Wèi 尉 are appointed by the Lì-bù 吏部 (Board of Civil Office) through a roster of the Eight Banners.
Fèng-sì 奉祀 are promoted from Sì-chéng 祀丞,
and Sì-chéng 祀丞 are selected from Zhù-bǎn-shēng 祝版生 (Writers of Prayer Tablets).)
Líng-qǐn-guān 陵寢官 (Officials of Imperial Tombs):
One Sān-líng Zǒng-lǐ Shì-wù Dà-chén 三陵總理事務大臣 (Grand Minister Overseeing Affairs of the Three Tombs).
(Concurrently held by the Shèng-jīng Jiāng-jūn 盛京將軍 (General of Shèng-jīng).
In the thirtieth year of Guāng-xù 光緒, it was transferred to the Zǒng-dū 總督 (Governor-General) of the three eastern provinces.)

(In the thirty-first year of Guāng-xù 光緒, this was established by modifying the Shèng-jīng Shǒu-hù Dà-chén 盛京守護大臣 (Grand Minister Guarding Shèng-jīng).)

One sixth- or seventh-grade official from the Lǐ-bù 禮部 (Board of Rites),

Additionally, twenty Wài-láng 外郎 from the Hù-bù 戶部, Lǐ-bù 禮部, and Gōng-bù 工部 were appointed.
In the thirty-first year of Guāng-xù 光緒,
eleven Wài-láng 外郎 were removed.
From the Dú-zhù-guān 讀祝官 downwards,

The Zǒngguǎn Dàchén was in charge of supervising officers and soldiers for patrols and inspections
to protect the imperial tombs.
Officials of the Nèiwùfǔ were in charge of ritual offerings and sacrifices,
and managing cleaning and opening/closing.
Officials of the Lǐbù were in charge of reviewing and endorsing documents,
supervising ceremonies,
and providing annual tribute items
to arrange sacrificial matters.
Officials of the Gōngbù were in charge of repairs and maintenance,
and providing paper money for all sacrifices.
In Shùnzhì thirteen years (1656),
officials such as Zhǎngguānfáng were established for the Fúlíng and Zhāolíng.
In Kāngxī two years (1663),
officials of the Nèifǔ, Lǐbù, and Gōngbù were re-established for each imperial tomb.
In Guāngxù thirty-one years (1905),
the imperial tomb officials of the Hùbù, Lǐbù, and Gōngbù in Shèngjīng were transferred to the Zǒnglǐ Sānlíng Shìwù Yámén.
In Xuāntǒng three years (1911),
all vacant posts of Láng, Yuán, and Zhǔ for the imperial tombs were transferred to the Nèiwùfǔ,
retaining their Lǐbù and Gōngbù titles as before.

Initially,
in the sixth year of Tiāncōng,
it was decreed that monks and Daoists of various temples should be managed by the Saṅglùsī and Dàolùsī.
All who understood the scriptures and observed the monastic rules
were granted ordination certificates.
In the second year of Shùnzhì,
the practice of paying silver for ordination certificates was abolished.
In the eighth year,
Zhāng Yìngjīng was appointed Zhèngyī Sìjiào Dàzhēnrén,
in charge of Daoism.
In the thirteenth year of Kāngxī,
the vacancies for officials in the Saṅglùsī and Dàolùsī were determined,
as well as the method for successive appointments.
In the sixteenth year,
an imperial decree ordered the Saṅglùsī and Dàolùsī to investigate the establishment of religious teachings and gatherings,
and severe punishments were prescribed.
In the ninth year of Yōngzhèng,
Fǎguān Lóu Jìnyuán was commended for his loyalty,
appointed as a Fourth-Rank Tídiǎn,
and later enfeoffed as Miàozhèng Zhēnrén.
In the tenth year,
vacancies for officials from Tídiǎn downwards were determined.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
ordination certificates were tentatively reinstated,
and the Zhèngyī Zhēnrén was granted the title of Guānglù Dàfū,
and the Miàozhèng Zhēnrén was granted Tōngyì Dàfū.
In the fifth year,
the Zhèngyī Zhēnrén went to the capital to offer birthday felicitations,
and Hónglúsì Qīng Méi Juéchéng memorialized, saying:
"Daoists are lowly and should not presume to participate in court ceremonies."
Consequently, the court audience and banquet practice was suspended.
In the seventeenth year,
the Zhèngyī Zhēnrén was reclassified as Principal Fifth Rank,
and was not allowed to claim enfeoffment by precedent.
In the thirty-first year,
due to the higher official rank of Fǎguān,
the Zhèngyī Zhēnrén was reinstated to Principal Third Rank.
In the thirty-ninth year,
Zhāng Kèchéng of the Zhēnrén Fǔ Jiānjìsī remained in the capital,
and two Xiéli Tídiǎn were established.
In the forty-second year,
Kèchéng was appointed Tídiǎn,
concurrently serving as Jīngjī Dàolùsī,
and the Xiéli were abolished.

The Yǐn is in charge of purifying and regulating the imperial domain,
administering the four routes,
and leading the capital counties in issuing government decrees and regulations.
Annually, at the beginning of spring,
he welcomes spring in the eastern suburbs.
When the Son of Heaven plows the ceremonial field,
he provides the plows, spades, and silk whips,
presents the blue box for sowing seeds,
and after the ceremony,
leads the common people to finish the field.
The collection and disbursement of land taxes
are checked at appropriate times,
and the essentials are reported to the Hùbù.
He manages the rituals of the rural drinking ceremony.
He serves as the Imperial Examiner for the provincial examinations.
The Céng is in charge of educational policies and decrees,
and serves as the Director for the provincial examinations.
The Zhìzhōng is in charge of assisting in governmental affairs,
organizing various duties,
and concurrently managing the examination venues for provincial and metropolitan examinations.
The Tōngpàn is in charge of collecting market taxes,
and suppressing disputes and fraud.
The Jīnglì and Zhàomó are in charge of documenting receipts and disbursements.
The Sījù is in charge of registering and recording prisoners.
The Rúxué is in charge of schools in the imperial domain,
assessing the arts and archery skills of civil and military students monthly,
admonishing those who do not follow instructions,
and reporting their performance to the Xuézhèng every three years.
The two counties of Dàxīng and Wǎnpíng each manage the government affairs of their respective counties,
sharing jurisdiction with the Wǔchéng Bīngmǎsī,
and their official ranks and insignia are one grade higher than those of external counties.

Shìzǔ (世祖) established his capital in Yānjīng (燕京),
founding Shùntiān Fǔ (順天府).

(In Qiánlóng (乾隆) 58th year, this was abolished.

The Yǐn (尹) was in charge of governing and transforming the subordinate capital and its prohibitions,
deciding minor matters,
and reporting major matters.
The Chéng (丞) was in charge of schools,
concurrently overseeing the schools for imperial relatives and collateral imperial relatives, and charity schools.
The duties of Zhìzhōng (治中) and other subordinate officials were similar to those in Shùntiān Fǔ (順天府).

in Shùnzhì (順治) 10th year,

In Qiánlóng (乾隆) 27th year,
an imperial edict stated that the Fǔyǐn (府尹) was to be subject to the Jiāngjūn (將軍)'s command.
The following year,
one Xīngjīng Lǐshìtīng Tōngpàn (興京理事廳通判) was added.
(Abolished in Guāngxù (光緒) 2nd year.)
In the 30th year,
a Shìláng (侍郎) was first appointed as concurrent Yǐn (尹),
and this was established as a regulation.
In Guāngxù (光緒) 2nd year,
Zhìzhōng (治中) was abolished,
(a separate Yìxúndào (驛巡道) was established.)
and the Jiāngjūn (將軍) was re-appointed to manage concurrently;
the concurrent Yǐn (尹) was given the title of Zǒngdū (總督),
and the Fǔyǐn (府尹) was given the rank of 2nd grade,
with the Bīngbù Shìláng (兵部侍郎) and Yòufùdūyùshǐ (右副都御史) acting as Xúnfǔ (巡撫).
In the 31st year,
it was reorganized into a province,
the Yǐn (尹) and Chéng (丞) were abolished,
and Zhīfǔ (知府) was appointed.
In Xuāntǒng (宣統) 1st year,
all teaching assistant officials were abolished.
The following year,
Chéngdé Xiàn (承德縣) was abolished.
The Zǒngdū (總督) (from rank 1)
was in charge of managing military and civilian affairs,
comprehensively controlling civil and military officials,
inspecting and recommending officials,
and maintaining and reinforcing border defenses.
Under his banner were officials such as Fùjiàng (副將) and Cānjìàng (參將).
The Xúnfǔ (巡撫) (from rank 2)
was in charge of proclaiming the emperor's benevolence,
pacifying the common people,
rectifying and clarifying administration and laws,
promoting beneficial changes and abolishing harmful practices,
evaluating all officials,
and consulting with the Zǒngdū (總督) to recommend abolitions or appointments to the emperor.
Under his banner were officials such as Cānjìàng (參將) and Yóujī (游擊).
In the triennial grand examinations, they served as chief supervisors,
and in the military examinations, they served as chief examiners.
This applied to both the Zǒngdū (總督) and the Xúnfǔ (巡撫).
Initially, following the Míng system,
Dūdù (Governors-general) and Fǔ (Governors) held the titles of Yòu Dū Yùshǐ, Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ, and Yòu Qiān Dū Yùshǐ.
There was no fixed quota.
In Shùnzhì year 10 (1653),
an edict ordered the joint recommendation of Dūdù and Fǔ,
without regard to rank,
selecting the virtuous and capable for memorialization.
In Kāngxī year 1 (1662),
the additional title of Gōngbù (Ministry of Public Works) for Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governors) who concurrently managed military affairs was abolished.
(In provinces where no Zǒngdū (Governor-general) was established,
they concurrently supervised officials below Fùjiàng (Brigade-general) rank.)
In year 12 (1673), the old system was restored,
and the Fǔbiāo Zuǒ and Yòu Èr Yíng (Two Governor's Standard Left and Right Battalions) were established.
In year 31 (1692),
the system for additional titles for Zǒngdū was formalized.
(Those appointed from among the Zuǒ and Yòu Shìláng of various ministries
were changed to Bīngbù Zuǒ and Yòu Shìláng (Left and Right Vice Ministers of War);
those appointed from among Xúnfǔ
were promoted to Bīngbù Yòu Shìláng (Right Vice Minister of War) concurrently with Dūcháyuan Yòu Fù Dū Yùshǐ (Right Vice Censor-in-chief of the Censorate).
In Qiánlóng year 13 (1748),
it was stipulated that Dàxuéshì (Grand Secretaries) who concurrently managed Zǒngdū affairs would retain their original titles.
The following year,
they were granted the title of Yòu Dū Yùshǐ;
their Bīngbù Shàngshū (Minister of War) title was to be determined by a memorial from the Lìbù (Ministry of Personnel).
In Jiāqìng year 14 (1809),
it was decided that those appointed with a second-rank button would concurrently hold the Bīngbù Shìláng (Vice Minister of War) title,

Initially,
provinces like Hénán, Shāndōng, and Shānxī had dedicated Xúnfǔ,

and the Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-chief) was a concurrent title.
Provinces like Zhílì, Sìchuān, and Gānsù had dedicated Zǒngdū,
who were responsible for evaluating official conduct,
and Xúnfǔ was a concurrent title.
However, Xúnfǔ were customarily subject to the Zǒngdū's command,
gradually leading to Xúnfǔ in the same city holding only nominal authority.
Even those in separate provinces,
their military and civil affairs were also largely decided by the Zǒngdū.
When Wénzōng (Emperor Xiánfēng) took power,
he ordered the Xúnfǔ of Zhèjiāng, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Shǎnxī, Húnán, Guǎngxī, and Guìzhōu to command Zhèn (garrisons) and Xié (sub-garrisons) military officials;
for provinces concurrently administered by a Zǒngdū,
the Xúnfǔ would draft memorials for review and recommendation,
and inspect and manage defense and suppression,
making it a dedicated responsibility,
thus their authority gradually increased.
In the last years of Guāngxù,
the concurrent Xúnfǔ in the same city were abolished;
for those in separate provinces,
their authority was nearly equal to that of the Zǒngdū;
the so-called concurrent administration
was merely for transmitting documents.
During the Xuāntǒng era,
military and salt administration were largely centralized,

provinces were established,

One Provincial Governor of Hénán and other areas, overseeing military affairs, grain supply, and concurrently managing riverways and garrison farms.
Established in the 1st year of Shùnzhì (1644),
residing in Kāifēng.
In the 17th year of Kāngxī (1678),
it was decreed that he manage Hénán's annual repair projects.
In the 4th year of Yōngzhèng (1726),
the title of Grand Coordinator was added,
but this was not a precedent.
Soon after, it was abolished.
Re-established in the 13th year (1735).
In the 5th year of Qiánlóng (1740),
due to bandit alerts,
the title of Tiándū was added.
One Provincial Governor of Shǎnxī and other areas, overseeing military affairs, commanding various garrisons, and concurrently managing grain supply.
Established in the 1st year of Shùnzhì (1644),
residing in Xī'ān,
designated as a Manchu-only post.
In the 9th year of Yōngzhèng (1731),
Shǐ Yízhí, Minister of War, acting as Provincial Governor,
the practice of appointing Han Chinese began from this point.
One Provincial Governor of Xīnjiāng and other areas, overseeing military affairs and concurrently managing grain supply.
In the 1st year of Shùnzhì (1644),
a Provincial Governor of Gānsù was established,
residing in Gānzhōuwèi.
(In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng (1724), Wèi was changed to Fǔ.)
In the 5th year (1648),
it moved to Lánzhōu.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī (1662),
it moved its residence to Liángzhōuwèi.
(Later also changed to Fǔ.)
In the 5th year (1666),
it returned to reside in Lánzhōu,
and soon after moved to Gǒngchāng.
In the 19th year (1680),
it returned to Lánzhōu.
In the 44th year (1705),
he concurrently managed tea and horse affairs.
Abolished in the 19th year of Qiánlóng (1754),
and the Grand Coordinator of Shǎn-Gān moved to reside there,
concurrently serving as Provincial Governor.
In the 10th year of Guāngxù (1884),
Xīnjiāng was established as a province,
and a Provincial Governor of Gānsù and Xīnjiāng was established,
residing in Wūlǔmùqí.
(Initially, there were one Provincial Governor of Yánsuī and one Provincial Governor of Níngxià,
both abolished during the Kāngxī era.)
One Grand Coordinator of Zhèjiāng and other areas, responsible for military affairs, controlling all land and naval garrisons, and managing grain supply.
Established in the first year of Shùnzhì.
Stationed in Hángzhōu.
In the fifth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was changed to Governor-General.
In the thirteenth year,
it reverted to Grand Coordinator,
also holding the title of Governor-General.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
a Governor-General was re-established.
In the third year, it returned to its former status.
One Grand Coordinator of Jiāngxī and other areas, responsible for military affairs, controlling all garrisons, and managing grain supply.
Established in the first year of Shùnzhì.
Stationed in Nánchāng,
with jurisdiction over eleven prefectures.
In the third year of Kāngxī,
it also governed Nán'ān and Gànzhōu.
(Initially, a Grand Coordinator of Nán-Gàn was established,
but was abolished and incorporated here.)
In the fourteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the title of Provincial Commander-in-Chief was added.
One Grand Coordinator of Húnán and other areas, responsible for military affairs, controlling all garrisons, and managing grain supply.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
a Grand Coordinator of Piān-Yuán was established,
stationed at Piānqiáo Zhèn.
(At the same time, a Censor-in-Chief overseeing Yúnxiáng was established,
stationed in Yuánzhōu,
to control the border areas of Xiāng, Shǔ, Yù, and Jìn;
it was abolished in the eighteenth year.
In the fifteenth year of Kāngxī,
it was re-established due to bandit alerts.
It was abolished again in the nineteenth year.)
In the third year of Kāngxī,
Húnán became a separate province,
and the Grand Coordinator relocated to Chángshā.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
the title was changed to Grand Coordinator of Húnán,
with orders to control all garrisons.
One Grand Coordinator of Húběi and other areas, responsible for military affairs and managing grain supply.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
a Grand Coordinator of Húguǎng was established,
stationed in Wǔchāng.
In the third year of Kāngxī,
the title was changed to Grand Coordinator of Húběi.
It was abolished in the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù,
and soon re-established.
It was abolished again in the thirty-second year.
One Grand Coordinator of Guǎngdōng and other areas, responsible for military affairs and managing grain supply.
Established in the first year of Shùnzhì.
Stationed in Guǎngzhōu.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
it also managed customs at Tàipíng Pass.
It was abolished in the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù,
and soon re-established.
In the thirty-first year,
with the pacification of military affairs in Guǎngxī,
it was again abolished.
One Grand Coordinator of Guǎngxī and other areas, responsible for military affairs, managing grain supply, and holding the title of controlling all provincial troops.
Established in the first year of Shùnzhì.
Stationed in Guìlín.
In the sixth year,
the standard troops of the Grand Coordinator of Fèngyáng were abolished and transferred to this post.
In the ninth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was ordered to control all provincial troops.
One Grand Coordinator of Yúnnán and other areas, responsible for military affairs and managing grain supply.
Established in the first year of Shùnzhì.
Stationed in Yúnnán Fǔ.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
È'ěrtài, the Financial Commissioner of Jiāngsū, was appointed Grand Coordinator,
also acting as Governor-General.
In the tenth year,
he was promoted to Governor-General,
also acting as Grand Coordinator.
Zhāng Guǎngsì succeeded him,
also acting as Grand Coordinator.
In the twelfth year of Qiánlóng,
Tú'ěrbǐng'ā was first appointed Grand Coordinator.
It was abolished in the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù,
and soon re-established.
It was abolished again in the thirtieth year.
One Grand Coordinator of Guìzhōu and other areas, responsible for military affairs, managing grain supply, and holding the title of controlling all provincial troops.
Established in the fifteenth year of Shùnzhì.
In the eighteenth year,
the responsibility for military affairs was discontinued.
In the twelfth year of Qiánlóng,
it was reinstated due to Miao unrest.
The following year,
Àibìdá was given the title of controlling all provincial troops.
In the eighteenth year,
this became a standard practice.
One Grand Coordinator of Táiwān and other areas, responsible for military affairs and managing grain supply.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
a Grand Coordinator of Fújiàn was established,
stationed in Fúzhōu.
In the first year of Guāngxù,
it was relocated to Táiběi.
In the eleventh year,
Táiwān was made a province,
and the Grand Coordinator of Fújiàn was renamed Grand Coordinator of Táiwān,
also managing educational affairs;
the affairs of the Grand Coordinator of Fújiàn were concurrently managed by the Governor-General of Mǐnzhè.
In the twenty-first year,
Táiwān was ceded,
and the Grand Coordinator was abolished.
One Provincial Education Commissioner for each province.

(Selected from officials with a *jìnshì* degree, such as Vice Ministers, Metropolitan Officials, Hanlin Academicians, Grand Secretariat officials, Supervising Censors, Circuit officials, and departmental subordinates.
Each retained their original titles and ranks.)
They managed educational policies and regulations,
conducting the annual and triennial examinations.
Wherever they toured,
they investigated the performance of teachers and scholars,
and the diligence or idleness of *shēngyuán*,
promoting the virtuous and capable,
and dismissing those who failed to follow instruction.
Any reforms or changes
were implemented jointly with the Governor-General and Grand Coordinator.
Originally,
each province also had an Education Intendant,
holding the title of Surveillance Commissioner Assistant.
(Selected from *jìnshì* degree holders who were department directors.)
Only Zhílì had one Supervising Censor for education,
(later known as Shùntiān Education Commissioner.
In the tenth year of Shùnzhì, Hanlin Academicians, such as compilers, revisers, and lecturers, were appointed.
Since Qiánlóng, senior officials were often appointed.)
Jiāngnán and Jiāngběi had two each,
(In the tenth year of Shùnzhì, Hanlin officials were appointed;
the following year, Surveillance Commissioner Assistants were again used.
In the first year of Kāngxī, they were merged into one;
in the twenty-fourth year, Hanlin officials were again appointed.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng,
they were separated into one each for Jiāngsū and Ānhuī.)
Called Academic Commissioner.
In the seventh year of Shùnzhì,
a system was established for selecting departmental subordinates as Education Intendants.
(Selected by the Grand Secretariat in conjunction with the Boards of Civil Office and Rites;
two from the Board of Rites,
and one each from the Boards of Revenue, War, Punishments, and Works.
This was discontinued in the sixteenth year.)
In the fifteenth year,
the Xuān-Dà Education Commissioner was abolished and its duties were concurrently managed by the Shānxī Education Intendant.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
the Húběi and Húnán Education Intendants were merged into one,
and renamed Húguǎng Education Intendant.
(They were separated again in the second year of Yōngzhèng.)
The following year,
the Vice Prefect of Fèngtiān Fǔ was ordered to preside over examination affairs,
and the Shǎnxī Língōng Education Commissioner was abolished and its duties concurrently managed by the Xī'ān Education Intendant.
In the twenty-third year,
the practice of appointing Education Supervising Censors based on salary was discontinued,
and it was decided that Zhèjiāng would use Hanlin officials,
and like Shùntiān and Jiāngnán/Jiāngběi, be called Academic Commissioner.
For other provinces where departmental subordinates, circuit officials, or prefectural officials served,
they remained Education Intendants.
In the thirty-ninth year,
it was decided that Hanlin officials and departmental subordinates would be appointed concurrently.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
all provincial Education Supervising Censors were renamed Academic Commissioner.
All who served as departmental subordinates
were given the titles of compiler and reviser.
From then on, Education Commissioners no longer held the title of Intendant.
The following year,
the Inspecting Censor was ordered to concurrently manage Táiwān educational affairs.
(In the seventeenth year of Qiánlóng, the Táiwān Circuit Intendant was changed to concurrently manage it.
In the twelfth year of Guāngxù,
the Grand Coordinator concurrently managed educational affairs.)
In the seventh year,
the Guǎngdōng Academic Commissioner was renamed Guǎng-Sháo Academic Commissioner,
and an additional Zhào-Gāo Academic Commissioner was established.
In the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng,
they were again merged into one.
In the second year of Guāngxù,
an additional Gānsù Academic Commissioner was established.
(Previously, Gānsù's annual and triennial examinations were concurrently managed by the Shǎnxī Academic Commissioner;
it was only then that a separate one was established.)
In the thirty-first year,
the Vice Prefect of Fèngtiān Fǔ was abolished,
and an additional Academic Commissioner for the Three Eastern Provinces was established.
That year, the imperial examination system was abolished,
and schools were promoted,
changing the Academic Commissioner to Education Commissioner.
(Details in the New Official System.)
Initially,
there was an Education Commissioner for Manchu and Mongolian Translators,
filled by Manchu Lecturers and Expositors.
It was abolished in the first year of Yōngzhèng.
The **Chéngxuān Bùzhèngshǐ Sī** (Provincial Administration Commission) had one **Bùzhèngshǐ** (Provincial Administration Commissioner)
per province.
(Rank 2b.)
Its subordinates included: one **Jīnglìsī Jīnglì** (Registrar in the Registry Office)
(Rank 6a);
one **Dūshì** (Secretary)
(Rank 7b);
one **Zhàomósuǒ Zhàomó** (Document Scrutinizer in the Document Scrutiny Office)
(Rank 8b);
one **Lǐwènsuǒ Lǐwèn** (Inquirer in the Inquiry Office)
(Rank 6b);
one **Kù Dàshǐ** (Treasurer in charge of the Treasury)
(Rank 8a);
and one **Cāng Dàshǐ** (Grain Supervisor in charge of Granaries),
(Rank 9b)
each person.
The **Bùzhèngshǐ** was responsible for promoting imperial decrees and carrying out instructions,
leading officials of prefectures, departments, and counties,
inspecting their performance and capabilities,
and submitting their evaluations
to the **Dū-fǔ** (Governors-general and Governors) for transmission to the **Lìbù** (Ministry of Personnel).
Every three years during the **bīnxīng** (provincial examinations),
they supervised the examinations,
promoted the worthy and capable,
and reported to the **Lǐbù** (Ministry of Rites).
Every ten years, they compiled household registers,
equalized taxes and corvée,
recorded population and cultivated land figures,
and reported to the **Hùbù** (Ministry of Revenue).
All other administrative matters
were discussed and implemented in conjunction with the **Dū-fǔ**.
The **Jīnglì** and **Dūshì** managed the handling of documents and dispatches.
The **Zhàomó** was in charge of checking and verifying dossiers.
The **Lǐwèn** was in charge of investigating criminal cases.
The **Kù Dàshǐ** was in charge of treasury accounts.
The **Cāng Dàshǐ** was in charge of inspecting granaries.
Initially,
**Zhílì** (Directly Ruled Area) did not have a **Bùzhèngshǐ**.
Instead, one **Kǒuběi Dào** (Circuit Intendant of Koubei) was appointed to oversee finance,
concurrently holding the title of **Shānxī Bùzhèngshǐ**.
(In the 2nd year of **Yōngzhèng**
this was changed to concurrently holding the title of **Zhílì Bùzhèngshǐ**.)
Each province had one **Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ** (Left Provincial Administration Commissioner) and one **Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ** (Right Provincial Administration Commissioner).
(**Guìzhōu**, having fewer affairs,
did not have a **Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ**.)
**Zuǒ Cānzhèng** (Left Policy Advisor), **Yòu Cānzhèng** (Right Policy Advisor), and **Cānyì** (Advisor)
were appointed as needed.
**Shǒudào** (Circuit Intendants) also concurrently held the titles of **Cānzhèng** and **Cānyì**.
Subordinates included **Jīnglì**,
(**Jiāngníng**, **Sūzhōu**, **Húnán**, and **Gānsù** did not have them.)
**Dūshì**,
(**Fújiàn** and **Hénán** each had one.)
**Zhàomó**,
(**Zhèjiāng**, **Fújiàn**, **Húběi**, **Shānxī**, **Sìchuān**, and **Gānsù** each had one.)
**Jiǎnjiào** (Proofreader),
(Rank 9a.
Abolished in the 2nd year of **Yōngzhèng**.)
**Lǐwèn**,
**Fù Lǐwèn** (Assistant Inquirer),
(Rank 7b.
Abolished in the 38th year of **Kāngxī**.)
**Kù Dàshǐ**,
**Cāng Dàshǐ**,
and **Bǎoyuán Jú Dàshǐ** (Supervisor of the Baoyuan Mint),
(Rank 9a.
Abolished in the 38th year of **Kāngxī**.)
Their establishment or abolition
varied by time and place.
In the 3rd year of **Shùnzhì**
the old **Bùyuàn** (Ministries and Censorate) and dispatched **Shìláng** (Vice Ministers) from **Nán Zhílì** (Southern Directly Ruled Area) were abolished.
One Manchu and one Han **Shìláng**
were stationed in **Jiāngníng** to manage affairs.
At this point, these were abolished,
and it was decided to establish one **Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ** and one **Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ** each.
In the 18th year
**Jiāngnán** (Jiangnan province) was divided.
The **Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ** moved to **Sūzhōu**,
while the **Zuǒ** remained stationed in **Jiāngníng**.
In the 2nd year of **Kāngxī**
**Shǎnxī** (Shaanxi province) was divided.
The **Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ** moved to **Gǒngchāng**,
administering **Gānsù**.
The next year
**Húguǎng** (Huguan province) was divided.
The **Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ** moved to **Chángshā**,
administering **Húnán**.
In the 6th year
the **Jiāngnán Yòu Bùzhèngshǐ** was renamed **Jiāngsū Bùzhèngshǐ**,
and the **Zuǒ** was renamed **Ānhuī Bùzhèngshǐ**;
the **Shǎnxī Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ** was renamed **Xī’ān Bùzhèngshǐ**,
and the **Yòu** was renamed **Gǒngchāng Bùzhèngshǐ**;
the **Húguǎng Zuǒ Bùzhèngshǐ** was renamed **Húběi Bùzhèngshǐ**,
and the **Yòu** was renamed **Húnán Bùzhèngshǐ**.

It was also decided that **Shāndōng**, **Shānxī**, **Hénán**, **Jiāngsū**, **Ānhuī**, **Jiāngxī**, **Fújiàn**, **Zhèjiāng**, **Húběi**, **Húnán**, **Sìchuān**, **Guǎngdōng**, **Guǎngxī**, **Yúnnán**, and **Guìzhōu** each had one **Bùzhèngshǐ**,
**Shǎnxī** had two.
The titles of **Zuǒ** and **Yòu** were abolished,
and they were named **Shǒudào**.
In the 7th year
it was decided that **Shānxī**, **Shǎnxī**, and **Gānsù** were Manchu-only posts.
(In the 1st year of **Yōngzhèng**
**Hú Qíhéng** was appointed **Shǎnxī Bùzhèngshǐ**.
The next year
**Gāo Chénglíng** was appointed **Shānxī Bùzhèngshǐ**.
The year after that
**Kǒng Yùpú** was appointed **Gānsù Bùzhèngshǐ**.
The use of Han officials began from this point.)
In the 8th year
one **Zhílì Shǒudào** was established,
to oversee finance;
the **Xī’ān Bùzhèngshǐ** was renamed **Shǎnxī Bùzhèngshǐ**;
and the **Gǒngchāng Bùzhèngshǐ** moved to **Lánzhōu**,
becoming the **Gānsù Bùzhèngshǐ**.
In the 2nd year of **Yōngzhèng**
the **Zhílì Shǒudào** was renamed **Bùzhèngshǐ**.
In the 18th year of **Qiánlóng**
the concurrent titles of **Bùzhèngshǐ**, **Cānzhèng**, and **Cānyì** for provincial **Shǒudào** were abolished.
In the 25th year
due to the heavy financial and grain administration in **Jiāngníng**,
an additional **Bùzhèngshǐ** was established,
and the six prefectures/departments of **Jiāng**, **Huái**, **Yáng**, **Xú**, **Tōng**, and **Hǎi** were placed under his jurisdiction;
the five prefectures of **Sū**, **Sōng**, **Cháng**, **Zhèn**, and **Tài** remained under the **Sūzhōu Bùzhèngshǐ**;
and the **Ānhuī Bùzhèngshǐ** returned to govern from **Ānqìng**.
In the 10th year of **Guāngxù**
**Xīnjiāng** was established as a province,
and one **Gānsù Xīnjiāng** **Bùzhèngshǐ** was added,
stationed in **Wūlǔmùqí**.
In the 13th year
**Táiwān** was established as a province,
and one **Fújiàn Táiwān Bùzhèngshǐ** was added,
stationed in **Táiběi**.
(In the 21st year
and this position was consequently abolished.)
In the 30th year
the **Jiāngníng Bùzhèngshǐ** was ordered to concurrently manage the affairs of the **Jiānghuái Bùzhèngshǐ**,
but this was soon abolished.
In the 2nd year of **Xuāntǒng**
Financial Public Offices were established in each province,
(or sometimes named Budget Public Offices)
dividing responsibilities by department,
with the **Bùzhèngshǐ** responsible for their overall success,
and the positions of **Jīnglì** and other officials were sometimes abolished.
The **Tíxíng Ànchásǐ Sī Àncháshǐ** (Provincial Judicial Commissioner in the Provincial Surveillance Commission)
was one per province.
(Rank 3a.)
Its subordinates included: one **Jīnglìsī Jīnglì** (Registrar in the Registry Office)
(Rank 7a);
one **Zhīshì** (Secretary)
(Rank 8a);
one **Zhàomósuǒ Zhàomó** (Document Scrutinizer in the Document Scrutiny Office)
(Rank 9a);
and one **Sīyùsī Sīyù** (Warden in the Prison Office),
(Rank 9b)
each person.
The **Àncháshǐ** was responsible for upholding moral discipline
and purifying the administration.
Wherever they went, they registered prisoners,
examined confessions,
and for major cases, they convened a discussion with the **Fānsī** (Provincial Administration Commission)
for approval by the **Bù-yuàn** (Ministries and Censorate).
They also concurrently managed all provincial post stations.
Every three years, they served as chief examiners for the major examinations (**dàbǐ**),
as evaluators for the major review of officials (**dàjì**),
and as chief drafters for the autumn assizes (**qiūshěn**).
The **Zhīshì** was responsible for investigating criminal cases.
The **Sīyù** was responsible for inspecting prisoners.
The **Jīnglì** and **Zhàomó** performed duties similar to those in the Provincial Administration Office.
Initially,
Zhílì did not establish an Ànchásǐ.
Instead, it established a Dàmíng Xúndào concurrently holding the title of Hénán Ànchásǐ,
a Tōngyǒng Tiānjīn Xúndào concurrently holding the title of Shāndōng Ànchásǐ,
and a Bàchāng Jǐngxíng Xúndào concurrently holding the title of Shānxī Ànchásǐ.
(In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng, this was changed to Zhílì Ànchásǐ titles.)
Each province established one Ànchásǐ.
Fùshǐ and Qiānshì
were established as needed, at discretion.
Xúndào also concurrently held the titles of Fùshǐ and Qiānshì.
Subordinate Jīnglì (Ānhuī, Húnán, Gānsù, Guìzhōu did not establish these),
Zhìshì (Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Shānxī, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī each had one),
Zhàomó (Ānhuī, Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, Húnán, Gānsù, Guìzhōu each had one),
Jiǎnjiào (established in the 6th year of Kāngxī, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Shānxī, Shǎnxī each had one;
abolished in the 39th year),
Sīyù,
their establishment or abolition varied
with time and place, without fixed rules.
In the 3rd year of Shùnzhì,
one Jiāngníng Ànchásǐ was added.
In the 3rd year of Kāngxī,
Jiāngběi Ànchásǐ was added,
stationed at Sīzhōu;
Húguǎng Ànchásǐ,
stationed at Chángshā;
Gānsù Ànchásǐ,
stationed at Gǒngchāng.
In the 6th year,
it was stipulated that Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Húběi, Húnán, Shǎnxī, Gānsù, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, Sìchuān, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Yúnnán, Guìzhōu each had one
known as Xúndào.
The Ānhuī Ànchásǐ was moved to Ānqìng.
In the 7th year,
Shānxī, Shǎnxī, and Gānsù were designated as Manchu vacancies.
(In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng,
Gāo Chénglíng was appointed Shānxī Ànchásǐ.
In the 2nd year,
Fèi Jīnwú was appointed Shǎnxī Ànchásǐ,
and Zhāng Shì Gānsù Ànchásǐ.
The use of Han people began from this point.)
In the 8th year,
one Zhílì Xúndào was added,
responsible for criminal cases.
The Gānsù Ànchásǐ was moved to Lánzhōu.
In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng,
the Zhílì Xúndào was changed to Ànchásǐ.
In the 8th year,
the Jiāngsū Ànchásǐ moved to Sūzhōu.
(Jiāngsū was subordinate to this.)
In the 18th year of Qiánlóng,
the concurrent titles of Ànchásǐ Fùshǐ and Qiānshì for provincial Xúndào were abolished.
In the 3rd year of Xiánfēng,
the Ānhuī Huīníngchítàiguǎng Dào was given the additional title of Ànchásǐ.
(Later changed to Wǎnnán Dào.)
In the 5th year of Tóngzhì,
the Fèngtiān Fèngjǐnshānhǎi Dào was given the additional title of Ànchásǐ.
(Later changed to Jǐnxīnyíngkǒu Dào.)
In the 13th year of Guāngxù,
the Fújiàn Táiwān Dào and Gānsù Xīnjiāng Dào were both given the additional title of Ànchásǐ.
In the 30th year,
the Jiāngsū Huáiyáng Hǎidào was given the additional title of Ànchásǐ.
(The Fújiàn Táiwān Dào was later abolished,
the rest were changed to Tífǎshǐ titles.)
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
the name was changed to Tífǎshǐ,
and some Jīnglì and other officials were abolished.
Dūzhuǎn Yányùnsǐ Yányùnshǐ,
(ranked 3a)
Fèngtiān, Zhílì, Shāndōng, Liǎnghuái, Liǎngzhè, Guǎngdōng, Sìchuān each had one.
Yánfǎdào,

The Yùnshǐ was in charge of supervising the livelihoods of salt field residents,
the comings and goings of merchants,
water and land transport,
calculating distances,
regulating prices,
and reporting to the Yánzhèng.
(Chánglú and Liǎnghuái each had one.
In Fújiàn, Sìchuān, Guǎngdōng,
the Zǒngdū concurrently held the position.
In Liǎngzhè, Shānxī, Yúnnán,
the Xúnfǔ concurrently held the position.
Developments are detailed below.)
The Yánfǎdào also did likewise.
The Yùntóng,
Yùnfù,
and Yùnpàn
were in charge of the Fēnsī salt production areas,
assisting the Yùnshǐ and Yándào in managing their affairs.
The Tóngzhī was in charge of controlling salt regulations.
The Tíjǔ managed affairs like the Fēnsī.
The Chǎng Dàshǐ was in charge of managing salt fields, ponds, and wells,
subordinate to the Yùntóng and Yùnpàn,
and generally supervised by the Yùnshǐ or Yánfǎdào.
Initially, censors (yùshǐ) were dispatched to inspect the salt tax (yánkè).
One for Chánglú, (In the 10th year of Xiánfēng, it was assigned to the direct jurisdiction of the Zhílì Governor-General.)
one for Hédōng, (In the 2nd year of Yōngzhèng, it was assigned to the direct jurisdiction of the Chuānshǎn Governor-General,
and restored to its former status the following year.
In the 43rd year of Qiánlóng, it was assigned to the direct jurisdiction of the Shānxī Governor.
In the 12th year of Jiāqìng, it was transferred to the Hédōng Circuit.)
one for Liǎnghuái, (In the 11th year of Dàoguāng, it was assigned to the direct jurisdiction of the Liǎngjiāng Governor-General.)
and one for Liǎngzhè (In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng, it was assigned to the direct jurisdiction of the Zhèjiāng Governor.
In the 58th year of Qiánlóng, the weaving commissioner (zhīzào) was changed to the salt commissioner (yánzhèng).
In the 25th year of Jiāqìng, it reverted to the governor.)
each.
(In the 10th year, the dispatch of salt inspection censors was halted.
In the 12th year, it was restored.
In the 6th year of Kāngxī,
it was stipulated that one Manchu and one Han official from each department (lángyuán) would be dispatched upon completion of their terms.
In the 8th year, it was again changed back to censors.
In the 10th year, it was set that one person would be dispatched.
In the 11th year, all were assigned to the direct jurisdiction of the provincial governors.
In the 12th year, they were again dispatched.
Later, internal court officials were concurrently dispatched.
They were all referred to as salt commissioners.)
A Commissioner of Salt Administration (dūzhuǎn yányùnshǐ) was established.
One for Chánglú, Shāndōng, Hédōng, (Abolished in the 57th year of Qiánlóng.)
Liǎnghuái, Liǎngzhè, (Changed to Courier and Salt Circuit (yìyándào) in the 49th year of Kāngxī.
Restored to its former status in the 58th year of Qiánlóng.)
Fújiàn, (Changed to Courier and Salt Circuit in the 4th year of Yōngzhèng.
Renamed Salt Law (yánfǎ) in the 12th year.)
and Liǎngguǎng (Soon changed to Courier and Salt Circuit.
Restored to its former status in the 32nd year of Kāngxī.)
each,
and one Salt Law Circuit (yánfǎdào) for Yúnnán.
The marketing affairs in each province,
as well as the守巡道 (shǒuxúndào), were also handled concurrently.
Assistant Commissioners (yùntóng).
One for Chánglú, Shāndōng, (Both abolished in the 16th year of Kāngxī,
and re-established the following year.)
one for Liǎnghuái, (Abolished in the 60th year of Kāngxī.)
one for Liǎngzhè (Abolished in the 16th year of Kāngxī.

one for Hédōng, (Abolished in the 16th year of Kāngxī.

and one for Liǎngzhè (Abolished in the 16th year of Kāngxī.

each.

Secretaries (jīnglì),
registrars (zhīshì),

one Courier and Salt Circuit for Húběi was established.

re-established in the 13th year.
Again abolished in the 58th year.
Re-established in the 1st year of Yōngzhèng.
In the 44th year of Qiánlóng, it was changed to the Salt Law Circuit for Wǔchāng, responsible for defense.)
The following year,
one Assistant Prefect for Salt Tax in Qìngyáng, Gānsù, was established.

one Courier and Salt Circuit for Jiāngxī was established.

one Assistant Commissioner for Fújiàn was established.
(Abolished in the 43rd year.)
In the 30th year,
salt inspection censors were dispatched.

In the 12th year, it was transferred to the Salt Law Circuit.)
each.

one Assistant Prefect for Salt and Bandit Suppression in Shānxī was established.
(Abolished in the 12th year of Jiāqìng.)
The following year,
one Courier and Salt Circuit for Sìchuān was established.
(Previously, it was concurrently handled by the Grain Circuit.
In the 25th year, it specialized in salt and tea.)
In the 11th year,
one Salt Affairs Inspection Circuit for Jiāngsū,
(Abolished in the 6th year of Qiánlóng.)
and one Judicial Officer for Liǎngguǎng,
(Abolished in the 7th year of Qiánlóng.)

In the 12th year,
the Courier Circuit of Shǎnxī was changed to Courier and Salt,
specializing in salt law.
(In the 59th year of Qiánlóng, it was changed to the Fèngbīn Patrol Circuit.)
And one Courier and Salt Circuit for Húnán was also established.
(Concurrently administered Chángdé and Báoyìng.)
In the 13th year,
the Kāiguī Circuit of Hénán was changed to the Grain, Courier, and Salt Circuit responsible for defense.
(Previously, it was concurrently handled by the Dàliáng Circuit.)
In the 1st year of Qiánlóng,
one Assistant Commissioner for Wúzhōu, Guǎngxī, was established.
(Abolished in the 7th year.)
In the 24th year,
two Assistant Prefects for Supervising Salt Production in Huáinán and Huáiběi were designated.
(Selected officials were concurrently appointed.
The following year, it was designated as a fixed position.)
In the 11th year of Jiāqìng,
the Fèngbīn Circuit of Shǎnxī, (In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng, it was assigned to the direct jurisdiction of the Police Circuit.)
and the Níngxià Circuit of Gānsù were designated to concurrently handle salt law.
The following year,
the Salt Bureau of Shānxī was re-established,
with the Hédōng Circuit concurrently handling salt law,
and one Assistant Prefect for Supervising Salt Production was established.
In the 2nd year of Xuāntǒng,
one Commissioner for Fèngtiān was added,
and the Salt and Tea Circuit of Sìchuān was again changed to Commissioner.
The following year,
the Commissioners of each province were changed to Chief Salt Supervisors (yánwù zhèngjiāndū),
(Adding one each for Fújiàn, Yúnnán, Shāndōng, and Hédōng.)
the Salt Law Circuits were abolished,
and Deputy Supervisors (fùjiāndū) were established,
(Designated one each for Huáinán, Jiāng'àn, Wǎn'àn, Xī'àn, È'àn, Xiāng'àn, Huáiběi, Sìchuān, Diānqiánbiānjì, Jìchǔ, Guǎngxī, and Gānsù.)
each,
under the unified administration of the Minister of Salt Administration (yánzhèng dàchén).
