In Sìchuān: Chéngmián Lóngmào Dào
(also overseeing water conservancy
and stationed in the provincial capital
and abolished in the 34th year of Guāngxù);
Jiànchāng Shàngnán Dào
(also overseeing postal relays
and pacifying Tǔsī
and stationed in Yǎzhōu);
Chuāndōng Dào
(also overseeing postal relays
and stationed in Chóngqìng);
Chuānběi Dào
(stationed in Bǎoníng);
Kāng'ān Dào
(stationed in Bā'ān
and granted the title of Judicial Commissioner);
(stationed in Dēngkē
—the above two officials
were established in the 2nd year of Xuāntǒng
and subordinate to the Minister of Sichuan-Yunnan Border Affairs).
In Guǎngdōng: Nánsháo Lián Dào
(also overseeing water conservancy
and stationed in Sháozhōu);
Huìcháo Jiā Dào
(stationed in Huìzhōu);
Liánqīn Dào
(stationed in Qīnzhōu);
Gāoléiyáng Dào
(stationed in Gāozhōu);
Qióngyá Dào
(stationed in Qióngzhōu).
In Guǎngxī: Zuǒjiāng Dào
(stationed in Nánníng);
Yòujiāng Dào
(stationed in Liǔzhōu);
Tàipíng Sīshùn Dào
(stationed in Lóngzhōu
—the above two officials
also controlled both Hàn and indigenous populations).
In Yúnnán: Yǐdōng Dào
(also overseeing postal relays
and stationed in Qǔjìng);
Yǐxī Dào
(also overseeing postal relays and customs
and stationed in Dàlǐ);
Yǐnán Dào
(also overseeing postal relays
and stationed in Pǔ'ěr).
In Guìzhōu: Guìdōng Dào
(also overseeing postal relays
and guarding the Miáojiāng
and stationed in Gǔzhōu);
Guìxī Dào
(stationed in Ānshùn
and abolished in the 2nd year of Xuāntǒng).
The Zhěngchì Bīngbèi Dào (Intendant of Military Preparedness and Rectification):
In Zhílì: Rèhé Dào
(granted the title of Judicial Commissioner
and stationed in the provincial capital).
In Jiāngnán: Jiāngníng Dào
(also overseeing salt administration
and water conservancy
and stationed in the provincial capital).
In Shāndōng: Dēngláiqīng Dào
(also overseeing maritime defense and water conservancy
and stationed in Dēngzhōu).
In Shǎnxī: Yányúsuí Dào
(also overseeing salt and tea
and stationed in Yúlín).
In Gānsù: Níngxià Dào
(also overseeing salt administration and water conservancy
and stationed in Níngxià);
Gǒngqínjiē Dào
(also overseeing tea and horses, and military colonies
and stationed in Qínzhōu).
In Xīnjiāng: Zhèndí Dào
(also overseeing postal relays
and granted the title of Judicial Commissioner
and stationed in the provincial capital);
Yītǎ Dào
(also overseeing water conservancy and military colonies
and inspecting border posts
and stationed in Níngyuǎn).
The Fǔzhì Bīngbèi Dào (Intendant of Military Preparedness and Pacification):
In Gānsù: Xīníng Dào
(also administering affairs for Mongol and Tibetan populations
and stationed in Xīníng
—established as a Manchu-Mongol post during the Qiánlóng era
and later sometimes filled by Hàn Chinese;
the old system was restored during the Jiāqìng era
but later still sometimes filled by Hàn Chinese);
Ānsù Dào
(also overseeing military colonies
and stationed in Sùzhōu).
Each administered their respective jurisdictions as circuit intendants (fēnshǒu, fēnxún),
and handled rivers, grain, salt, and tea,
or also water conservancy and postal relays,
or also customs and military colonies.
They also assisted the Provincial Administration Commissioners (Fān) and Provincial Surveillance Commissioners (Niè) in reviewing officials,
assessing agriculture and sericulture,
promoting worthy and capable individuals,
improving local customs,
inspecting military provisions,
and securing their borders,
thereby leading their subordinates and inspecting their governance.
Among the miscellaneous officials were the Kù Dàshǐ (Storehouse Supervisor)
(of rank 9b),
the Cāng Dàshǐ (Granary Supervisor),
and the Guān Dàshǐ (Customs Supervisor)
(all unranked,
detailed later under miscellaneous officials).
These were established according to local needs
and not uniformly set up.
The Provincial Administration Commissioner and Provincial Surveillance Commissioner offices had a chief and a deputy.
Later, these were changed to Left and Right Counselor (Cānyì) for the Provincial Administration Commissioner,
which became the Shǒudào (Defense Intendant);
and Deputy Commissioner (Fùshǐ) and Clerk (Qiānshì) for the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner,
which became the Xúndào (Patrol Intendant).
At that time, a Dàoyuán (Circuit Intendant) only governed one prefecture,
or sometimes several Dàos jointly governed one prefecture.
In the 16th year of Shùnzhì,
an imperial decree ordered all Dàos to concurrently hold titles from both the Provincial Administration Commissioner and Provincial Surveillance Commissioner offices,
establishing this as a precedent.
In the 6th year of Kāngxī,
one hundred and eight Shǒudào and Xúndào were abolished.
Subsequently, they were gradually re-established;
some had jurisdiction over an entire province,
while others administered three or four prefectures and departments.
The number of establishments in each province was not constant,
and their assigned ranks were not fixed,
all depending on their promotion or appointment to their main post.
(For example, those appointed from metropolitan officials (Jīngtáng) were Cānzhèng Dào;
those appointed from Grand Secretary supervising seals (Zhǎngyìn Gěishìzhōng) or Prefects (Zhīfǔ) were Fùshǐ Dào;
those appointed from Supervising Censor (Kēdào) were Cānyì Dào;
those appointed from Director (Lángzhōng), Assistant Director (Yuánwàiláng), Secretary (Zhǔshì), or Sub-prefect (Tóngzhī) were Qiānshì Dào;
this applied to both Shǒu and Xún Dào).
In the 18th year of Qiánlóng,
the titles of Cānzhèng, Cānyì, Fùshǐ, and Qiānshì were abolished,
and their official ranks were specifically elevated.
(Initially,
Cānzhèng Dào was 3b,
Fùshǐ Dào was 4a,
Cānyì Dào was 4b,
and Qiānshì Dào was 5a.
By this time, all were fixed at 4a).
Subsequently, over eighty Shǒudào and Xúndào were successively granted additional Bīngbèi (military preparedness) duties.
In the 41st year,
an imperial edict permitted Dàoyuán concurrently holding posts of Provincial Administration Commissioner or Provincial Surveillance Commissioner
to submit memorials directly to the emperor.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng,
considering the Dàoyuán's function of inspection and supervision,
an imperial edict restored the old system from the Yōngzhèng era,
allowing them to express opinions on state affairs.
From Dèzōng (Guāngxù Emperor) onwards,
separate巡警 Xúnpǐng (Police and Security) and Quànyè (Industrial Promotion) Dàos were established in provincial capitals,
with duties divided by department.
There was a proposal to abolish Shǒudào and Xúndào in the provinces,
keeping only one or two with Bīngbèi duties,
but this was not realized.
(Also, initially, there were Xīngtún Dào (Military Colony Promotion Intendants) in Shāndōng, Ānhuī, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húběi, and Húnán;
Hǎifáng Dào (Maritime Defense Intendants) in Zhèjiāng and Jiāngsū;
Xúnhǎi Dào (Maritime Patrol Intendant) in Fújiàn;
Jiāngfáng Dào (River Defense Intendant) in Jiāngsū;
and Mǎzhèng Dào (Horse Administration Intendant);
all were later abolished.)
府 Fǔ: The Prefect. One zhīfǔ 知府.
(Initially, zèngsìpǐn 正四品.
In the 18th year of Qiánlóng 乾隆, changed to cóngsìpǐn 從四品.) Tóngzhī 同知,
(zèngwǔpǐn 正五品.) Tōngpàn 通判,
(zèngliùpǐn 正六pǐn.) with no fixed number of appointees.
Its subordinates: Jīnglì Sī Jīnglì 經歷司經歷,
(zèngbāpǐn 正八品.) Zhīshì 知事,
(zèngjiǔpǐn 正九品.) Zhàomó Suǒ Zhàomó 照磨所照磨,
(cóngjiǔpǐn 從九品.) Sīyù Sī Sīyù 司獄司司獄,
(cóngjiǔpǐn 從九品.) one of each.
(Additionally, Jiāngsū Jiǎnjiào 江蘇檢校 and Guìzhōu Chángguān Sī Lìmù 貴州長官司吏目,
two of each.)
The zhīfǔ 知府 was in overall charge of the subordinate xiàn 縣,
announcing regulations and teachings,
promoting benefits and eliminating harms,
and judging lawsuits and investigating wrongdoing.
Every three years, they would assess the competence of subordinate officials,
the performance or neglect of their duties,
and report recommendations or criticisms upwards.
Important local policies were reported to the Dūdū 督 and Fǔfǔ 撫,
and acted upon only after approval.
The tóngzhī 同知 and tōngpàn 通判
were separately in charge of grain and salt, supervision of capture,
river and sea defenses,
river conservancy and waterworks,
managing the Qing army,
and pacifying the populace and barbarians, among other important duties.
Those under the direct jurisdiction of the Bùzhèngshǐ 布政使
numbered twenty-two nationwide.
Their system was the same as zhílì zhōu 直隸州,
or they were subordinate to a Jiāngjūn 將軍 or Dàoyuán 道員,
each established as appropriate to the locality.
The jīnglì 經歷, zhīshì 知事, zhàomó 照磨, and sīyù 司獄
held responsibilities similar to the chief officials of the two departments.
From the tóngzhī 同知 downwards,
those whose duties were simple were not always appointed.
Initially,
the zhīfǔ 知府 ranked zèngsìpǐn 正四品,
divided into three classes,
mostly staffed by Hàn 漢 officials.
(At that time, Mǎnzhōu láng 滿洲郎 and yuánwài 員外 transferred to bù 佈 and àn 按 did not occupy fǔ 府 positions.
They began to be employed in the early Kāngxī 康熙 period.)
Also, tuīguān 推官 (abolished in the 6th year of Kāngxī 康熙)
and guàxián tuīguān 掛銜推官
(abolished in the 3rd year of Shùnzhì 順治) were established.
One Dūbǔ Zuǒlǐshìguān 督捕左理事官 and one Yòulǐshìguān 右理事官 (abolished in the 38th year of Kāngxī 康熙)
each.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī 康熙,
the responsibility for temporary appointments to zhōu 州 and xiàn 縣 was exclusively entrusted to the zhīfǔ 知fǔ,
and the system of recommendation and collective responsibility was implemented.
In the 51st year,
approving Yùshǐ Xú Shùyōng's 御史徐樹庸 request,
specially recommended personnel by Dūdū 督 and Fǔfǔ 撫 were granted audiences.
From then on, when zhīfǔ 知fǔ were appointed,
their petitions were observed during audiences,
and their administrative achievements were assessed when reporting their best work,
which was established as a rule.
In the 1st year of Yōngzhèng 雍正,
an imperial edict instructed the Dūdū 督 and Fǔfǔ 撫 to select and evaluate zhīfǔ 知fǔ.
Later, fǔ 府 and tóngzhī 同知 were even allowed to speak on matters.
(Later discontinued.)
In the 12th year,
recognizing the importance of the fǔ 府 position,
and citing ancient principles,
there was a desire to restore the system of long-term tenure.
The Ministry deliberated on promotion as encouragement,
but limited it to promotion or transfer after a set number of years.
When Rénzōng 仁宗 personally governed,
he regarded the zhīfǔ 知fǔ as a crucial link between superiors and subordinates,
and strictly ordered all Dūdū 督 and Fǔfǔ 撫 to rigorously examine them.
This continued during Xuānzōng's 宣宗 time.
From Wénzōng 文宗 and Mùzōng 穆宗 onwards,
the ancient path gradually drifted away.
In the final years of Xuāntǒng 宣統,
the xiàn 縣 attached to the fǔ 府 were abolished,
and the zhīfǔ 知fǔ took charge of their affairs.
Since Jiāngnán 江南, Shǎnxī 陝西, Húguǎng 湖廣 were divided into provinces,
Fèngtiān 奉天, Jílín 吉林, Hēilóngjiāng 黑龍江, and Xīnjiāng 新疆 were established as provinces,
and Sìchuān 四川 and Yúnnán 雲南 had their tǔguān 土官 system replaced by liúguān 流官,
each fǔ 府 was subordinated to them.
The total number of fǔ 府 nationwide was two hundred fifteen.
州 Zhōu: The Department Magistrate. One zhīzhōu 知州.
(Initially, cóngwǔpǐn 從五品.
In the 35th year of Qiánlóng 乾隆, zhílì zhōu zhīzhōu 直隸州知州 was changed to zèngwǔpǐn 正五品.) Zhōutóng 州同,
(cóngliùpǐn 從六品.) Zhōupàn 州判,
(cóngqīpǐn 從七品.) with no fixed number of appointees.
Its subordinate: one Lìmù 吏目.
(cóngjiǔpǐn 從九品.)
The zhīzhōu 知zhōu was in charge of the governance of a zhōu 州.
Subordinate zhōu 州 were treated like xiàn 縣,
and zhílì zhōu 直隸州 like fǔ 府.
(Except that there were no attached xiàn 縣.)
The zhōutóng 州同 and zhōupàn 州判
were separately in charge of grain affairs, water conservancy, coastal defense, and river management, among other duties.
The lìmù 吏目 was in charge of investigating fraud and theft, inspecting prisoners, and managing records.
Initially,
one zhīzhōu 知zhōu was established for each zhōu 州.
Subsequently, as local conditions dictated,
abolitions, divisions, and mergers were made as needed,
and the same applied to assistant officials.
The total number of zhílì zhōu 直隸州 nationwide was seventy-six,
and subordinate zhōu 州 forty-eight.
縣 Xiàn: The District Magistrate. One zhīxiàn 知縣.
(zèngqīpǐn 正七品.) One xiànchéng 縣丞.
(zèngbāpǐn 正八品.) Bùzhǔ 簿主 with no fixed number of appointees.
(zèngjiǔpǐn 正九品.) One diǎnshǐ 典史.
(Not officially ranked.)
The zhīxiàn 知xiàn was in charge of the governance of a xiàn 縣,
judging lawsuits and pronouncing sentences,
encouraging agriculture and relieving poverty,
suppressing scoundrels and eliminating evildoers,
and promoting welfare and establishing education.
Everything from recommending scholars, interpreting laws, caring for the elderly, and sacrificing to gods,
was within their purview.
The xiànchéng 縣丞 and bùzhǔ 簿主
were separately in charge of grain and horses, taxation, household registration, and apprehending criminals, among other duties.
The diǎnshǐ 典史 was in charge of inspecting prisoners.
(If there was no chéng 丞 or bù 簿,
they would also take on those duties.)
Initially,
one zhīxiàn 知xiàn was established for each xiàn 縣.
In the 12th year of Shùnzhì 順治,
an imperial edict instructed the Lìbù 吏部 to consider the systems of zhōu 州 and xiàn 縣,
and divide them into three classes.
Previously, when the táijiàn 臺諫 needed personnel,
following the Ming 明 dynasty precedent,
zhīxiàn 知xiàn were recruited.
When Shèngzǔ 聖祖 personally governed,
recognizing that officials close to the people needed to understand advantages and disadvantages,
he ordered Dūdū 督 and Fǔfǔ 撫 to recommend virtuous and capable individuals.
In the 29th year of Kāngxī 康熙,
he again issued an edict to the Jiǔqīng 九卿 to identify honest officials.
Twelve individuals, including Qīngyuàn Zhīxiàn Shào Sìyáo 清苑知縣邵嗣堯, were promoted to the xiànfǔ 憲府,
making a remarkable name for themselves.
Gāozōng 高宗 still frequently praised them.
However, after the Ministry deliberated on preventing too rapid advancement,
allowing them to circulate among various offices,
their path became somewhat more circuitous.
In the 16th year of Qiánlóng 乾隆,
the practice of recruiting officials to be promoted to Ministry officials was stopped,
but virtuous and capable individuals could still be nominated for promotion.
In the 15th year of Jiāqìng 嘉慶,
the book Qīndìng Xùnshì Zhōuxiàn Guītiáo 欽定訓飭州縣規條 was published,
and distributed to all provinces.
During Wénzōng's 文宗 time,
military dispatches were frequent,
and people's livelihoods were in decline.
He repeatedly ordered Dūdū 督 and Fǔfǔ 撫 to strictly investigate at all times.
However, at that time, various irregular officials competed for advancement,
and honest and capable ones were few.
Mùzōng 穆宗 exerted himself to govern well,
ordering all provinces to evaluate officials who gained office through donation or military merit.
Soon after, he assessed their performance in attracting vagrants and reclaiming land.
In the 7th year of Tóngzhì 同治,
he again ordered the establishment of bureaus to publish various books for local officials,
still retaining the utmost intention of revitalization.
During the Guāngxù 光緒 era,
Dūdū 督 and Fǔfǔ 撫 irregularly transferred zhōu 州 and xiàn 縣 officials,
treating them like temporary lodgings.
In the 24th year,
the restoration of the long-term tenure system was discussed.
In the 31st year,
regulations for evaluating zhōu 州 and xiàn 縣 officials were established,
(detailed in 'Evaluation of Merit'.)
and the system became somewhat more rigorous.
The total number of xiàn 縣 nationwide was one thousand three hundred fifty-eight.
Confucians: Professors (府教授, fǔ jiàoshòu), (rank 7a.
) Instructors (訓導, xùndǎo),
(rank 8b.
) Prefecture School Masters (州學正, zhōu xuézhèng), (rank 8a.
) Instructors (訓導, xùndǎo),
District School Masters (縣教諭, xiàn jiàoyù), (rank 8a.
) Instructors (訓導, xùndǎo),
all one person each.
Professors (教授, jiàoshòu), School Masters (學正, xuézhèng), and District School Masters (教諭, jiàoyù)
were in charge of instructing and guiding school students,
assessing their academic performance and diligence,
and evaluating the merits and demerits of their conduct,
to be reported to the Education Superintendent (學政, xuézhèng).
Instructors (訓導, xùndǎo) assisted them.
(Normally, people from the local province were employed.
Not applicable to those from the same prefecture or subprefecture.
Applies to both Jiāngsū and Ānhuī provinces.
) Initially, following the Míng dynasty system,
educational officials were established in prefectures (府, fǔ), departments (廳, tīng), subprefectures (州, zhōu), districts (縣, xiàn), and all military garrisons (衞, wèi).
In the third year of Kāngxī (1664),
instructors (訓導, xùndǎo) were abolished in prefectures (府, fǔ), subprefectures (州, zhōu), and large districts (大縣, dàxiàn);
district school masters (教諭, jiàoyù) were abolished in small districts (小縣, xiǎo xiàn).
They were reinstated in the fifteenth year (1676),
and from then on, teaching positions were divided and restored.
Subsequently, a precedent was established for outstanding imperial students (監生, jiànshenɡ) to donate for teaching positions.
In the thirtieth year (1691),
the request of Xǔ Rǔlín (許汝霖), the Education Superintendent (學政, xuézhèng) of Jiāngnán, was granted:
those who donated for the positions of School Master (學正, xuézhèng) and District School Master (教諭, jiàoyù) were changed to District Assistant Magistrates (縣丞, xiànchéng);
Instructors (訓導, xùndǎo) were changed to Chief Clerks (主簿, zhǔbù).
From then on, only licentiates (生員, shengyuán) could contribute funds,
and Professors (教授, jiàoshòu) had to be appointed through the imperial examination system.
In the thirty-second year (1693),
Instructors (訓導, xùndǎo) in all military garrisons (衞武學, wèi wǔxué) were abolished.
In the thirty-ninth year (1700),
the sixteen edicts of the Sacred Edict (聖諭, shèngyù) were promulgated for Confucian temples (學宮, xuégōng),
and every first and fifteenth day of the month, Confucian officials (儒學官, rúxuéguān) were ordered to gather students (諸生, zhūshēng) to read them aloud.
In the forty-first year (1702),
the Imperial Edict for Admonishing Scholars (御製訓飭士子文, yùzhì xùnshì shǐzǐ wén) was promulgated,
and Confucian temples (學宮, xuégōng) were ordered to engrave it on stone.
In the forty-second year (1703),
teaching positions were established,
with two for each school.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (1723),

permission was granted to establish charity schools (義學, yìxué) in Yúnnán (雲南) for indigenous people (土人, tǔrén), in Jiànchāng (建昌), Sìchuān (四川) for barbarian tribes (番夷, fānyí), and in Yǒngsuí (永綏), Húnán (湖南) and other places.
Thereafter, with the policy of "gai tu gui liu" (改土歸流, replacing hereditary native chieftains with appointed officials),
Confucian schools (儒學, rúxué) were gradually established in the desolate frontier areas beyond the Great Wall.
The following year (1724),
an Instructor (訓導, xùndǎo) was established for the well-school (井學, jǐngxué) in Yúnnán (雲南),
marking the beginning of well-schools (井學, jǐngxué).
The year after that (1725),
the Confucian schools (儒學, rúxué) of the provincial military commands (都司, dūsi) and the Professors (教授, jiàoshòu) of the Capital Guards military schools (京衞武學, jīngwèi wǔxué) were abolished,
and Manchu students (滿洲生員, Mǎnzhōu shengyuán) were also assigned to the monthly lessons of Han officials.
In the thirteenth year (1735),
the ranks of Confucian officials (儒學官, rúxuéguān) in prefectures (府, fǔ), subprefectures (州, zhōu), and districts (縣, xiàn) were set.
(As listed above.
) After the thirtieth year of Guāngxù (1904),
as the imperial examination system was abolished,
vacancies in teaching positions in various provinces were not filled.
At the time, there was a proposal to establish officials for the Confucius temples (文廟官, wénmiào guān),
but it was not carried out.
Patrol Inspectors (巡檢, xúnjiǎn) of the Patrol Divisions (巡檢司, xúnjiǎnsī),
(rank 9b.
) were in charge of arresting bandits and thieves,
and investigating traitors and evildoers.
They were established in strategic locations, important passes, and dangerous areas of subprefectures and districts.
Those under the jurisdiction of a subprefecture (州, zhōu) or department (廳, tīng)
were specifically responsible for river defense.
Post Stations: Post Station Masters (驛丞, yìchéng),
(unranked.
) were in charge of postal transport, receiving, and sending.
They managed boats, carts, laborers, and horses,
and provided provisions, food, and meals,
according to the rank of the envoy.
Costs were paid by the prefecture (府, fǔ), subprefecture (州, zhōu), or district (縣, xiàn),
and their income and expenditure were recorded.
In the sixth year of Yōngzhèng (1728),
it was stipulated that Manchus could not serve as Post Station Masters (驛丞, yìchéng).
Assistant Magistrates (典史, diǎnshǐ) were subject to the same rule.
Treasury Keeper (庫大使, kù dàshǐ), one person.
(Those under the Financial Commissioner (布政使, bùzhèngshǐ) were rank 8a;
those under the Salt Commissioner (運使, yùnshǐ), Salt and Customs Intendant (鹽法道, yánfǎdào), and various intendants (道, dào) were rank 9b;
those under the Salt and Tea Intendant (鹽茶道, yánchádào) and various bureaus (所, suǒ) were unranked.
) They were in charge of managing the treasury.
Granary Keeper (倉大使, cāng dàshǐ), one person.
(Those under the Financial Commissioner (布政使, bùzhèngshǐ) and various prefectures (府, fǔ) were rank 9b.
Those in subprefectures (州, zhōu) and districts (縣, xiàn) were unranked.
) They were in charge of managing granaries.
Tax Collection Director (稅課司大使, shuìkèsī dàshǐ), one person.
(Those under intendants (道, dào) or prefectures (府, fǔ) were rank 9b.
Those in subprefectures (州, zhōu) and districts (縣, xiàn) were unranked.
) They were in charge of tax matters.
All merchants, brokers, butchers, and miscellaneous markets had regular levies,
which were collected periodically,
and paid to the intendant (道, dào), prefecture (府, fǔ), or district (縣, xiàn).
Sluice Gate Officer (牐官, zhágērn), one person.
(Unranked.
) They were in charge of water storage and release, opening and closing sluices.
Fishery Tax Collection Director (河泊所大使, hébósuǒ dàshǐ), one person.
(Unranked.
) They were in charge of collecting fish taxes.
Medical Studies: Prefecture Chief Physician (府正科, fǔ zhèngkē),
Subprefecture Medical Officer (州典科, zhōu diǎnkē),
District Medical Officer (縣訓科, xiàn xùnkē),
one person each.
(All unranked.
) Those proficient in medical principles were selected by the local authorities under their jurisdiction
and reported to the Ministry for appointment certificates.
(In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
after the Féngtiān (奉天) Model Prison was completed,
a Director of the Medical Office (醫務所所長, yīwùsuǒ suǒzhǎng) was established,
and the Prefecture Chief Physician (府正科, fǔ zhèngkē) was abolished.
Astronomy and Divination Studies: Prefecture Chief Astrologer (府正術, fǔ zhèngshù),
Subprefecture Astrologer (州典術, zhōu diǎnshù),
District Astrologer (縣訓術, xiàn xùnshù),
one person each.
(All unranked.
) Those with upright conduct were selected by the local authorities under their jurisdiction
and reported to the Ministry for appointment certificates.
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng (1729),
they were ordered to concurrently manage astronomy.
Prefecture Buddhist Registry: Chief Monk (都綱, dūgāng), Deputy Chief Monk (副都綱, fùdūgāng),
Subprefecture Buddhist Registry: Buddhist Rector (僧正, sēngzhèng),
District Buddhist Registry: Buddhist Registrar (僧會, sēnghuì),
one person each.
Prefecture Daoist Registry: Chief Daoist (都紀, dūjì), Deputy Chief Daoist (副都紀, fùdūjì),
Subprefecture Daoist Registry: Daoist Rector (道正, dàozhèng),
District Daoist Registry: Daoist Registrar (道會, dàohuì),
one person each.
(All unranked.
) Those who were knowledgeable in Buddhist or Daoist scriptures and strictly observed the precepts
were granted ordination certificates.

Volume 92: Officials, Part 4 (Military Officials; Officials of the Tributary Tribes and Tusi) Dukes, Marquises, Earls, Viscounts, Barons; Imperial Sons-in-Law (額駙, éfù); Imperial Bodyguard Department (侍衞處, shìwèichù); Imperial Guard (鑾輿衞, luányúwèi); Commanders-in-Chief of the Eight Banners Elite Cavalry (驍騎營八旗都統, xiāoqíyíng Bāqí Dūtǒng); Commanders of the Vanguard and Palace Guard Battalions (前鋒營護軍營統領, qiánfēngyíng hùjūnyíng tǒnglǐng) (on duty at Jǐngyùnmén); Commanders of the Imperial Household Department's Three Banners Palace Guard Battalions (八旗內務府三旗護軍營總統, Bāqí Nèiwùfǔ Sānqí Hùjūnyíng Zǒngtǒng) (Three Banners Bondservant Elite Cavalry; Three Banners Bondservant Palace Guard Battalions); Infantry Commander (步軍統領, bùjūn tǒnglǐng); Artillery, Elite and Valiant, Divine Machine, Tiger Musket Battalions (火器健銳神機虎鎗諸營, huǒqì jiànruì shénjī hǔqiāng zhūyíng) (Guide Office; Imperial Hunting Reserve Office; Wrestling Camp); Officials of Princely Mansions (王公府屬各官, wánggōng fǔshǔ gèguān) (Princess's Household Administrator); Officials of Mausoleum Garrisons; Generals and other officials stationed in various provinces; Admirals and other officials; Ministers stationed in various places; Officials of Huí (Muslim) Tribes; Officials of Tributary Tribes; Officials of Tusi (Native Chieftain) Territories; Tibetan Buddhist Officials.
Duke (公, gōng), Marquis (侯, hóu), Earl (伯, bó), (super-rank.
) Viscount (子, zǐ), (rank 1a.
) Baron (男, nán), (rank 2a.
) Light Chariot Captain (輕車都尉, qīngchē dūwèi), (rank 3a.
The above are all divided into three classes.
) Cavalry Captain (騎都尉, jídūwèi), (rank 4a.
) Cloud Cavalry Captain (雲騎尉, yúnqíwèi), (rank 5a.
) Grace Cavalry Captain (恩騎尉, ēnqíwèi),
(rank 7a.
) A total of nine ranks,
conferred upon meritorious ministers and imperial relatives.
Initially,
in the fifth year of Tiānmìng,
ranks of five noble titles were established based on merit,
and the zǒngbīng were divided into three grades.
Fùjiàng, cānjíang, and yóují were likewise graded.
The niúlù èzhēn were called bèiyù.
In the eighth year of Tiāncōng,
the first-grade gōng was first established,
(who was the zǒngbīng of the five bèiyù.)
as well as first, second, and third-grade Ángbāng Zhāngjīng
(who were zǒngbīng),
Méilè Zhāngjīng
(who were fùjiàng),
Zālán Zhāngjīng
(first and second-grade were cānjíang,
third-grade were yóují),
and Niúlù Zhāngjīng
(who were bèiyù).
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
meritorious officials were enfeoffed as hereditary gōng, hóu, and bó,
and bestowed with imperial edicts and warrants.
At that time, there were no zǐ or nán below gōng, hóu, and bó;
fù and cān were their titles.
In the fourth year,
Ángbāng Zhāngjīng was changed to Jīngqíníhāfān,
Méilè Zhāngjīng to Āsīhānīhāfān,
Zālán Zhāngjīng to Ādáhāhāfān,
and Niúlù Zhāngjīng to Bàitālabùlèhāfān.
The conferment of titles began with Tuōshālàhāfān,
(formerly "half a career,"
called wàisuǒ qiānzǒng in Han,
of 正五品, rank 5a.)
then progressed upwards to Bàitālabùlèhāfān,
(called wàiwèi zhǐhuī fùqiānshì in Han,
of 從四品, rank 4b.
Another Tuōshālàhāfān
was called wàiwèi zhǐhuī qiānshì,
of 正四品, rank 4a.)
Ādáhāhāfān,
(third-grade was called wàiwèi fùtóngzhī,
second-grade was called wàiwèi zhǐhuī tóngzhī,
both of 從三品, rank 3b.
First-grade was called wàiwèi zhǐhuī fùshǐ,
another Tuōshālàhāfān
was called wàiwèi zhǐhuī shǐ,
of 正三品, rank 3a.)
Āsīhānīhāfān,
(third-grade was called wàiwèi dūzhǐhuī fùtóngzhī,
second-grade was called wàiwèi dūzhǐhuī tóngzhī,
both of 從二品, rank 2b.
First-grade was called wàiwèi dūzhǐhuī fùshǐ,
another Tuōshālàhāfān
was called wàiwèi dūzhǐhuī shǐ,
both of 正二品, rank 2a.)
Jīngqíníhāfān.
(Second-grade was called luányíwèi dūzhǐhuī tóngzhī,
of 從一品, rank 1b.
First-grade was called luányíwèi dūzhǐhuī shǐ,
of 正一品, rank 1a.)
Twenty-six accumulated Tuōshālàhāfān
made a first-grade gōng.
In the eighth year,
the system of hereditary succession without diminishment (shìxí wǎngdì) was established.
In the eighteenth year,
the system of combined inheritance (hébìng chéngxí) was established.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
for hereditary titles that had been combined up to gōng, hóu, or bó,
separate inheritance was still permitted.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
Zhū Zhīlián, a descendant of the Míng dynasty, was granted the title of first-grade hóu.
(In the fourteenth year of Qiánlóng,
the title was bestowed with the name Yán'ēn.)
In the eighth year,
Grand Secretary Zhāng Tíngyù and others were commended for their diligent assistance,
and granted the hereditary title of first-grade Ādáhāhāfān.
This marked the beginning of hereditary official positions for Han officials.
The next year,
gōng titles were given honorific names.
(Such as Bāojì, Zhōngdá, and similar types.)
Imperial relatives by marriage were made Chéng'ēn Gōng.
(The old system was first-grade gōng.
In the forty-third year of Qiánlóng, this was changed to third-grade.)
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
the Han Chinese character for Jīngqíníhāfān was set as zǐ,
Āsīhānīhāfān as nán,
Ādáhāhāfān as qīngchē dūwèi,
Bàitālabùlèhāfān as qí dūwèi,
and Tuōshālàhāfān as yún qíwèi.
The Manchu script remained unchanged.
In the thirteenth year,
the table of titles for gōng, hóu, and bó and their subordinates was established.
(First-grade gōng inherited twenty-six times;
first-grade hóu plus one yún qíwèi inherited twenty-three times;
first-grade bó plus one yún qíwèi nineteen times;
first-grade nán plus one yún qíwèi eleven times.
From gōng to nán,
first, second, and third-grades successively decreased.)
In the fourteenth year,
honorific names were retroactively bestowed upon hóu and bó.
(Such as Fèngyì Hóu, Dūnhuì Bó, and similar types.)
From then on, this became a permanent system.
In the sixteenth year,
the hereditary seventh-rank official was designated Ēnqíwèi,
making it the ninth grade.
In the thirty-second year,
Huáng Fāngdù's meritorious service was commended,
and he was granted a gōng title for twelve generations,
and additionally, following the Eight Banners' precedent,
was granted Ēnqíwèi,
providing generous support indefinitely.
At this time, General Zhāng Yǒng and others,
Admiral Sūn Sīkè and others,
also received this grace,
and thus Han officials also had the precedent of hereditary succession without diminishment.
During the Tóngzhì Restoration,
those who received symbols of authority (pǒufú xīguī)
were mostly Han officials,
similar to the ancient martial merit titles.
In the thirty-third year of Guāngxù,
a system was established to grant zǐ or nán titles to those who initiated great enterprises,
called "commercial titles" (shāngjué),
which introduced a slight variation to the system of bestowing titles.
Princesses and their consorts (éfù)
ranked above hóu and bó.
The consort of a Gùlún Gōngzhǔ (a daughter born to the empress)
was called a Gùlún Éfù,
whose rank was equivalent to a Gùshān Bèizǐ;
the consort of a Héshuò Gōngzhǔ (a daughter born to a concubine or adopted by the empress)
was called a Héshuò Éfù,
whose rank was equivalent to an extraordinary-grade gōng.
(A Qīnwáng's daughter was a Jùnzhǔ,
her consort's rank was equivalent to a first-rank military official.
A Shìzǐ or Jùnwáng's daughter was a Xiànzhǔ,
her consort's rank was equivalent to a second-rank official.
A Bèilè's daughter was a Jùnjūn,
her consort's rank was equivalent to a third-rank official.
A Bèizǐ's daughter was a Xiànjūn,
her consort's rank was equivalent to a fourth-rank official.
A daughter of an "Eight Divisions" Zhèn Guógōng or Fǔ Guógōng was a Xiāngjūn,
her consort's rank was equivalent to a fifth-rank official.
Close relatives (Jìnzhī Gégé) were given annual stipends;
distant relatives were only given honorary titles.)
Those married into Mongolian banners were treated similarly.
Their sons
were each given their father's rank.
Initially,
during the reign of Tàizǔ,
Éfù Hé Hélǐ was appointed Dūtǒng,
and Dá'ěrhàn succeeded him.
During the reign of Tàizōng,
Bāyǎsīhúláng was appointed Dūtǒng,
and Lāhā succeeded him.
From then on, the ministers of the imperial bodyguards (yùqián shìwèi dàchén) and commanders of the vanguard and infantry (hùjūn qiánfēng tǒnglǐng)
became specialized positions.
There were also those who only received annual stipends,
but were commissioned to serve as escorts and accompany military campaigns.
As for those appointed to govern the northwest,
it began with Cèlíng, the Deputy General of the Left for the Pacification of the Border.
Those who followed him were,
during the reign of Shìzōng,
Guānyīnbǎo as leader of the contingent (lǐngduì dàchén),
and during the reign of Gāozōng,
Sèbùténgbālèzhū'ěr as consultant minister (cānzàn dàchén).
As for those appointed to civil positions,
there were only Sūnài during the Tiānmìng era and Fúlóng'ān during the Qiánlóng era, both as Shàngshū.
Shìwèi Chù (Imperial Bodyguard Department) Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén (Minister of the Imperial Bodyguard),
(first rank, principal.

Total of five hundred and seventy persons across the three banners.
Thirty-four of whom were attached to Niángān Chù,
twenty-four to Shàngsì Yuàn,
and thirty-six to Shàngyú Bèiyòng Chù.
Shànpū Yíng and Wǔbèi Yuàn had no fixed quotas.
) Sìděng Shìwèi (Fourth-class Bodyguard), Hàn Shìwèi (Han Bodyguard),

Qīnjūn Xiào (Imperial Guard Officer),
(sixth rank, principal.
) Shǔ Qīnjūn Xiào (Acting Imperial Guard Officer),
(initially without rank.
In Qiánlóng 51, fixed as eighth rank, secondary.
) Seventy-seven of each.
Lǐng Shìwèi was in charge of commanding and deploying the imperial bodyguards and imperial guards,
and together with the Nèi Dàchén and Sànzhì Dàchén, provided escort and protection.
Xiélǐ, Zhǔshì, and Bǐtiěshì
were responsible for memorials and official dispatches.
The Shìwèi (Bodyguards) were in charge of patrolling the encampments and guarding the imperial residences,
taking turns on duty.
(Divided into two wings for night watch.
The Qiánqīng Mén, Nèi Yòumén, Shénwǔ Mén, and Níngshòu Mén constituted the inner watch,
while the Tàihé Mén was the outer watch.
) When the emperor traveled or stayed elsewhere, the system for the palace interior was followed.
During court assemblies, rituals, and imperial comings and goings,
the guard officials filled the streets,
and cavalry blocked the roads.
The Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén and Shìwèi Bānlǐng
commanded the Leopard Tail Brigade Bodyguards.
The Sànzhì Dàchén and Shìwèi Shízhǎng
held banners and led imperial guards for escort,
and during grand reviews, they encircled the area in formation.
Qīnjūn Xiào were in charge of distributing and managing the troops.
Those regularly on duty were:
Yùqián Dàchén (Ministers before the Emperor), (concurrently held by princely ministers.
) Yùqián Shìwèi (Bodyguards before the Emperor), Yùqián Xíngzǒu (Walking before the Emperor), Qiánqīng Mén Xíngzǒu (Walking at the Qiánqīng Gate).
(All were specially selected from among the bodyguards.
) There were no fixed numbers.
(According to precedent,
of all officials on night watch,
only Manchu officials were appointed as Qiánqīng Mén Shìwèi,
and those particularly esteemed due to noble relatives or exceptional talent
were promoted to serve before the Emperor.
Han officials were often appointed as guards for the main gates (Dàmén Shàng Shìwèi),
under the jurisdiction of the Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén.
Those promoted to serve at the Qiánqīng Mén due to their talent and bravery
held extremely high ranks.
However, during the Jiāqìng reign, Yáng Fāng was specially appointed as Guóshíhā Xiá,
a Han Guóshíhā Nèi Dàchén,
which was considered unprecedented.
) Those escorting the emperor on his outings were:
Hòuhù Dàchén (Ministers of Rear Escort) two persons,
(concurrently held by Yùqián Dàchén and Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén.
) Qiányǐn Dàchén (Ministers of Front Escort) ten persons.
(concurrently held by Nèi Dàchén, Sànzhì Dàchén, Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng, Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng, and Fù Dūtǒng.
) Under their jurisdiction was the Zòushì Chù (Memorial Reporting Office),
(managed concurrently by Yùqián Dàchén.
) Shìwèi one person,
(specially selected from Yùqián Shìwèi or Qiánqīng Mén Shìwèi.
) Zhāngjīng (Secretaries) six persons,
(four officials from the Nèifǔ,
two officials from various ministries and courts.
) Bǐtiěshì two persons,
(concurrently filled by Nèifǔ Bǐtiěshì.
) Shìwèi for reporting on Mongolian affairs six persons.
(concurrently filled by Qiánqīng Mén or Dàmén Shìwèi.
Initially,
Tàizǔ (Nurhaci) established the Eight Banners imperial army to pacify the land.
The Bordered Yellow, Plain Yellow, and Plain White Banners were all commanded by himself.
He then selected their sons and younger brothers,
naming them Shìwèi.
Occasionally, he also included talented members of the imperial clan (Zōngshì Xiùyàn) and princely attendants from outer domains (Wàifān Shìzǐ),
unifying them under meritorious relatives,
to serve as constant guards.
In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
the number of officials in the Shìwèi Chù was fixed.
(As listed previously.
At that time, Han Yìnshēng were also selected,
but this was soon abolished.
) In the 29th year of Kāngxī (1690),
martial scholars (Wǔ Jìnshì) skilled in horsemanship and archery were promoted to Shìwèi,
attached to the Three Banners.
In the 37th year (1698),
Zōngshì Shìwèi (Imperial Clan Bodyguards) were increased,
without a fixed number.
(In Yōngzhèng 7 (1729), the number was fixed at ninety.
) In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng (1725),
Lánlíng Shìwèi (Blue-feathered Bodyguards) of strong physique and talent were selected and placed in the fourth class.
(Later, it reverted to the original system.
) The following year (1726),
it was decreed that the first-place candidate in the first rank of Wǔ Jìnshì be appointed Yīděng Shìwèi (First-class Bodyguard),
the second and third-place candidates be appointed Èrděng (Second-class),
those selected from the second rank be Sānděng (Third-class),
and those selected from the third rank be Lánlíng (Blue-feathered).
One Manchu Zhǔshì (Secretary) was established.
In the 36th year of Qiánlóng (1771),
the Xiélǐ Shìwù Shìwèi Bānlǐng (Bodyguard Captain Assisting with Affairs) who carried seals were made first class,
and Shìwèi Bānlǐng (Bodyguard Captains) were made second class.
For every ten persons, one leader was appointed.
There were sixty Shízhǎng (Decurions) from the three banners,
and nine from the imperial clan.
In the 40th year (1775),
seventy-seven acting Qīnjūn Xiào (Imperial Guard Officers) were added.
In the 19th year of Jiāqìng (1814),
due to Sànzhì Dàchén (Ministers Without Portfolio) having no administrative responsibilities,
an edict was issued that those promoted to Dūtǒng (Generals) should cease holding concurrent posts.
Luányúwèi (Imperial Carriages and Guards)
— It is headed by one Dàchén (Minister)
(of Zheng Yīpǐn rank.
There is no dedicated appointee;
Mongolian and Manchu princes, dukes, and ministers concurrently hold this post.)
Luányúshǐ (Director of Imperial Carriages)
(initially of Zheng Èrpǐn rank.
In the second year of Kāngxī, it was changed to Zheng Sānpǐn,
and in the seventh year, it reverted to its former rank.)
Two Manchus
(all Manchu vacancies can also be filled by Mongols concurrently),
and one Han bannerman
(all Han bannerman vacancies can also be filled by Han Chinese concurrently).
Its subordinates include: one Tángzhǔshì (Department Director),
a Manchu.
One Jīnglì (Registrar) of the Jīnglìtīng (Registry Office),
a Han Chinese.
Bǐtiěshì (Scribes):
seven Manchus,
and three Han bannermen.
There are also six Suǒ (Stations) and one Wèi (Guard): namely Zuǒsuǒ (Left Station),
Yòusuǒ (Right Station),
Zhōngsuǒ (Middle Station),
Qiánsuǒ (Front Station),
Hòusuǒ (Rear Station),
Xùnxàngsuǒ (Elephant Training Station),
and Qíshǒuwèi (Banner Guard).
Guānjūnshǐ (Chief of the Vanguard)
(initially of Zheng Sānpǐn rank.
In the second year of Kāngxī, it was changed to Zheng Sìpǐn,
and in the seventh year, it reverted to its former rank):
one Zōngshì (Imperial Clansman),
seven Manchus and Han bannermen.
Yúnhuīshǐ (Commander of the Cloud Banners)
(initially of Zheng Sìpǐn rank.
In the second year of Kāngxī, it was changed to Zheng Wǔpǐn,
and in the seventh year, it reverted to its former rank):
two Zōngshì,
eighteen Manchus and Han bannermen.
Zhìyízhèng (Director of Ceremonies)
(initially of Zheng Wǔpǐn rank.
In the second year of Kāngxī, it was changed to Zheng Liùpǐn,
and in the seventh year, it reverted to its former rank):
three Zōngshì,
twenty-nine Manchus and Han bannermen.
Zhěngyíwèi (Assistant Director of Ceremonies)
(initially of Zheng Liùpǐn rank.
In the second year of Kāngxī, it was changed to Cóng Liùpǐn,
and in the seventh year, it reverted to its former rank.
In the tenth year of Yōngzhèng, it was promoted to Zheng Wǔpǐn,
but later changed back to Cóng Liùpǐn):
three Zōngshì,
twenty-three Manchus and Han bannermen.
Míngzànbīangūan (Announcing Whip Officers)
(appointed on the recommendation of the Zànlǐláng and Míngzànguān of the Tàichángsì and Hónglúsì):
four Manchus,
and two trainees.
The Luányúshǐ is in charge of presenting the imperial carriage, maintaining order, and managing the ceremonial retinue,
identifying its names and objects, and its ranks.
For all sacrifices, court assemblies, imperial tours, and grand reviews,
they lead their subordinates to attend to these matters.
The Zuǒsuǒ is in charge of imperial carriages, palanquins, and sedan chairs;
the Yòusuǒ is in charge of parasols, canopies, swords, halberds, bows, arrows, spears, and lances;
the Zhōngsuǒ is in charge of banners, cloaks, pennants, streamers, standards, axes, staffs, and saddled horses;
the Qiánsuǒ is in charge of fans, censers, vases, bowls, stools, chairs, fly whisks, imperial staffs, palm mats, silent whips, and rank markers;
the Hòusuǒ is in charge of flag bearers and imperial staffs;
the Xùnxàngsuǒ is in charge of ceremonial elephants, riding gear, ceremonial retinues, and the grand music of the front guard;
the Qíshǒuwèi is in charge of gongs, drums, horns, cymbals, and grand music,
and concurrently manages the bell at the Wǔmén Gate
and the clock and drum towers at Shénwǔmén Gate for nightly watches.
The Zhǔshì is in charge of memorials.
The Jīnglì is in charge of official documents.
As for separate establishments:
In the old system, there was one Bùniǎn Yúnhuīshǐ (Commander of Palanquin Cloud Banners),
three Zhìyízhèng,
and two Jiàkù Guǎnlǐ Zhěngyíwèi (Assistant Directors of Ceremonies for Carriage Depot Management),
all held by Han bannermen.
Later, the five types of carriages (gold, jade, ivory, leather, and wood) were divided,
and the management of kneeling mats, palm blankets, combs, pavilion seats, and carriage coverings
was assigned to Guānjūnshǐ and other officers concurrently,
with Manchu officers also participating.
In the first year of Shùnzhì,
the Jǐnyīwèi was established,
with Zhǐhuī and other officers.
The following year,
its name was changed to Luányíwèi,
and the ranks of various officers were stipulated.
At that time, there were five Suǒ in total,
but each Suǒ retained only one Sī (Department).
In the fourth year,
the Zhǐhuīshǐ was abolished,
and Luányíshǐ and other officers were established.
The following year,
the Fùguān (Deputy Officers) and 114 Wèiguān (Guard Officers) were abolished.
In the sixth year,
two Han Èrpǐn Luányíshǐ,
two Sānpǐn Guānjūnshǐ,
two Sìpǐn Yúnhuīshǐ,
and two Wǔpǐn Zhìyízhèng
were added under the Regent Prince;
and three Zhěngyíwèi.
(All were later abolished.)
In the ninth year,
Nèidàchén (Grand Ministers of the Interior) began to manage the affairs of the Guard.
(In the ninth year of Qiánlóng, one concurrent Weiguanshi was established.
It was abolished in the fourteenth year,
re-established in the twenty-sixth year as one Zǒnglǐ Wèishì Nèidàchén (Grand Minister of the Interior in Charge of Guard Affairs),
and abolished again in the thirtieth year.)
In the eleventh year,
the number of Luányíshǐ was set at two Manchus and two Han Chinese.
(In the thirty-first year of Kāngxī, one Han appointee was abolished.
In the fiftieth year of Qiánlóng, the Manchu envoys were divided into left and right.
In the fifty-seventh year, the old system was restored.)
Two Han Pèisì Guānjūnshǐ (Guānjūnshǐ for Sacrificial Attendance).
(In the twenty-third year of Kāngxī,
they managed palanquin affairs.
In the thirty-seventh year,
one person was in charge of storehouse affairs.
Both were abolished in the forty-eighth year.)
Five Suǒ were established: Zuǒ, Yòu, Zhōng, Qián, and Hòu.

Ten Sī were established: Luányú (Imperial Carriages), Xùnmǎ (Horse Training), Qínggài (Canopy Bearing), Gōngshǐ (Bows and Arrows), Jīngjié (Banners and Staffs), Fānchuáng (Pennants and Streamers), Shànshǒu (Fan Bearers), Fǔyuè (Axes), Gējǐ (Halberds), and Bānjiàn (Ceremonial Swords).
One Xùnxàngsuǒ was established,
divided into two Sī: Dōng (East) and Xī (West).
One Qíshǒuwèi was established,
divided into two Sī: Zuǒ and Yòu.
The number of Guānjūnshǐ was set at ten
(one Zōngshì,
seven Manchus,
and two Han bannermen).
Twenty-two Yúnhuīshǐ
(two Zōngshì,
twelve Manchus,
and eight Han bannermen),
and six Xiánsǎn (Supernumeraries)
(Manchu vacancies).
Twenty-four Zhìyízhèng
(four Zōngshì,
and twenty Han bannermen),
and eighteen Xiánsǎn
(Manchu vacancies).
Twenty-nine Zhěngyíwèi
(four Zōngshì,
fifteen Manchus,
and ten Han bannermen).
In the fifteenth year,
one Manchu Jīnglì was abolished.
In the sixteenth year of Kāngxī,
the Jīnglì position was changed to a Han vacancy,
and one Manchu Zhǔshì was added.
In the thirty-seventh year of Qiánlóng,
four Míngzànbīangūan were added.
(In the thirteenth year of Jiāqìng, two trainees were added.)
In the forty-eighth year,
one Zǒngbàn (General Manager), one Xiébàn (Assistant Manager), one Tángwù (Department Affairs Officer), and one Guānjūnshǐ
were established.
(The Guānjūnshǐ of the Suǒ and Wèi concurrently held these positions.
In the sixth year of Jiāqìng, the name was changed to Zōnglǐ Qīsuǒ Shìwù Guānjūnshǐ (Guānjūnshǐ in Overall Charge of Affairs of the Seven Stations),
and two Yúnhuīshǐ were assigned to assist.)
In the thirty-third year of Guāngxù,
two Guānjūnshǐ,
eight Yúnhuīshǐ,
ten Zhìyízhèng,
and four Zhěngyíwèi were abolished.
The quota for Zōngshì was set
(as previously listed),
and the rest were filled by both Manchus and Han Chinese.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
to avoid the emperor's taboo name,
Luányíshǐ was changed to Luányúshǐ,
and the character
"yí" (儀)
in Zhìyízhèng and Zhěngyíwèi
was replaced with "yí" (宜).
The Command of the Vanguard. The Eight Banners' Dūtǒng,
(originally a Grade 1a official,
later changed to Grade 1b.)
One for each of the Mǎn, Méng, and Hànjūn Banners.
Fùdūtǒng,
(Grade 2a.)
Two for each Banner.
Cānlǐng,
(Grade 3a.)
Fùcānlǐng,
(Grade 4a.)
In total, ninety-six officials.
(Forty for each of the Mǎnzhōu and Hànjūn,
sixteen for Ménggǔ.)
Zuǒlǐng,
(Grade 4a.)
Xiāoqíjiao,
(Grade 6a.)
In total, one thousand one hundred and fifty-one officials.
(Six hundred and eighty-one for each of the Mǎnzhōu,
two hundred and four for each of the Ménggǔ,
two hundred and sixty-six for each of the Hànjūn.)
Forty Xiélǐ Shìwù Cānlǐng.
(Sixteen for each of the Mǎnzhōu and Hànjūn,
eight for Ménggǔ.
Appointed from the Cānlǐng of their respective Banners.)
Zhāngjīng,
Bǐtiěshì,
In total, one hundred and forty-four officials.
(Sixty-four for each of the Mǎnzhōu,
thirty-two for each of the Ménggǔ,
forty-eight for each of the Hànjūn.)
Suí Yìnfáng Xíngzǒu Sànzhíguān had no fixed number.
The Dūtǒng
and Fùdūtǒng were in charge of the Eight Banners' administration and decrees,
disseminating instruction and nurturing,
clarifying and investigating military affairs,
to assist in Banner matters.
Cānlǐng and Fùcānlǐng were in charge of receiving and assigning tasks to reach the Zuǒlǐng.
Zuǒlǐng were in charge of auditing the households, fields, residences, and military registers under their jurisdiction,
and at seasonal intervals issuing instructions and warnings.
The Xiélǐ officials were in charge of memorials and documents,
and accounting for income and expenditure.
(The same applies to all commands.)
Those specially appointed: Eight Zhínián Qí Dàchén;
(Their subordinates included Cānlǐng,
Zhāngjīng,
and Bǐtiěshì.
Appointed from Banner officials.)
One Guǎnlǐ Jiù Yíngfáng Dàchén for Mǎn and Méng each;
(Their subordinates included Yíngzǒng Zhāngjīng
and Xiāoqíjiao.)
Xīn Yíngfáng Dàchén,
Guānfáng Dàchén,
Eight for each of Mǎn, Méng, and Hànjūn;
(Their subordinates were the same as those of the Jiù Yíngfáng.)
Zuǒ, Yòu Yì Tiějiàng Jú Fùdūtǒng;
(Their subordinates included Cānlǐng,
Sànzhíguān,
and Xiāoqíjiao.)
Two Jīchá Báodǐ Děngchù Zhùfáng Dàchén each;
Ten Zuǒ, Yòu Yì Shìzhí Guānxué Zǒnglǐ Dàchén;
(Their subordinates included Cānlǐng Zhāngjīng,
Qīngyǔ and Qíshè Jiàoxí.)
Shíwǔ Shànshè Chù Guǎnlǐ Dàchén,
One for each wing;
Eight Hànjūn Qīngwén Yìxué Jīchá Xuéwù Cānlǐng.
Those appointed concurrently: Fènglǎng Chù, Mǎcè Fáng, Guǎnlǐ Mǎjuàn, Téngpái Yíng Cānlǐng and other officials,
Hànjūn Niǎoqiāng Yíng Lǐngcuī and other officials,
Chéngmén Piānjí Zhāngjīng Xiāoqíjiao,
all selected from Banner officials.
Initially,
in the Xīnchǒu year of Tàizǔ's reign,
three hundred men were first organized into one Níulù,
and one Ézhēn was appointed.
(Before this, when dispatching troops for hunting,
each man took an arrow,
and one chief led them,
called Níulù.
From this point, it became the name of an official.
In the first year of Tiānmìng, the Mǎnzhōu Níulù were organized.
In the eighth year, Ménggǔ Níulù were added.
In the fourth year of Tiāncōng,
the Hànjūn Níulù were established.)
They were first divided into four Banners,
and soon increased to eight Banners.
In the Yǐmǎo year,
it was decreed that five Níulù formed one Zhālán Ézhēn,
and five Zhālán formed one Gùshān Ézhēn,
assisted by the Zuǒ, Yòu Méilè Ézhēn.
When Tàizōng ascended the throne,
eight Zǒngguǎn Qíwù Dàchén were appointed,
to manage government affairs;
(These were the Gùshān Ézhēn concurrently serving as Yìzhèng Dàchén.)
Sixteen Zuǒguǎn Dàchén were appointed,
to manage administrative matters and hear lawsuits.
(These were the Méilè Ézhēn concurrently serving as Lǐshì Dàchén.)
In the eighth year of Tiāncōng,
Ézhēn was changed to Zhāngjīng,
but Gùshān Ézhēn remained as before.
(Those who managed Méilè were called Méilè Zhāngjīng,
those who managed Zhālán were called Zhālán Zhāngjīng,
those who managed Níulù were called Níulù Zhāngjīng.)
The cavalry soldiers accompanying the camps were called Ālǐhā Chāohā.
This was the beginning of the Xiāoqíyíng,
but it still united Mǎn, Méng, and Hànjūn as one.
In the ninth year,
the Ménggǔ Eight Banners were first separately established.
In the seventh year of Chóngdé,
the Hànjūn Eight Banners were again separately established.
(Prior to this, in the second year, two Banners were established,
and in the fourth year, they were divided into four.)
The system of twenty-four Banners was thus complete.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì,
Zhālán Zhāngjīng was formally referred to by its Chinese name Cānlǐng.
In the seventeenth year,
Gùshān Ézhēn was formally referred to by its Chinese name Dūtǒng,
(in the first year of Yōngzhèng, the Manchu Gùshān Ézhēn was changed to Gùshān Ángbāng.)
Méilè Zhāngjīng was called Fùdūtǒng,
Níulù Zhāngjīng was called Zuǒlǐng,
Fēndé Bōshíkù was called Xiāoqíjiao,
and the fixed number of Dūtǒng and Fùdūtǒng was established.
(As listed previously.)
Cānlǐng,
five for each of the Mǎnzhōu and Hànjūn Banners,
three for each of the Ménggǔ.
(Soon after, one was added to each.)
The number of Zuǒlǐng varied according to actual duties.
(Divided into four grades:
tribal chiefs who led their subordinates to surrender,
and their descendants, were called Xūnjiù Zuǒlǐng;
those whose merits were celebrated,
and who were granted households,
were called Yōuyì Shìguǎn Zuǒlǐng;
those who returned with only their brothers and clansmen,
and whose positions were hereditary,
were called Shìguǎn Zuǒlǐng;
those with few households,
where several surnames were combined,
and who took turns holding the office,
were called Hùguǎn Zuǒlǐng.
In the thirteenth year of Kāngxī, additional Gōngzhōng Zuǒlǐng were established from the surplus men of various Zuǒlǐng.)
The number of Xiāoqíjiao was the same as Cānlǐng.
In the thirty-fourth year of Kāngxī,
Wěishǔ Cānlǐng were added,
with their number based on the Zhālán.
(In the first year of Yōngzhèng, they were renamed Fù Xiāoqí Cānlǐng,
with five for each of the Mǎnzhōu and Hànjūn Banners,
and three for each of the Ménggǔ.)
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng,
Zuǒ, Yòu Sī Zhǎng Guānfáng Cānlǐng and other officials like Sīwù were added.
(Two for each Banner.
All were abolished in the thirteenth year.)
The following year,
the Hànjūn Upper Three Banners were set at forty Zuǒlǐng,
(in the thirty-ninth year of Qiánlóng, one was added to Xiānghuáng Qí.
In the fortieth year, another was added.
In the fifty-fifth year, yet another was added.
In the ninth year of Jiāqìng, one was abolished.)
The Lower Five Banners were set at thirty Zuǒlǐng,
(in the twenty-first year of Qiánlóng, two were abolished from Zhènghóng and Xiānghóng Qí respectively,
and one from Xiānglán Qí.
In the thirty-ninth year, one was abolished from Zhènglàn Qí.)
And the number of officials for Mǎnzhōu,
(eighty-six each for Xiānghuáng, Zhèngbái, and Xiānghóng Qí,
eighty-four each for Xiāngbái Qí and Zhènglàn Qí,
ninety-three for Zhènghuáng Qí,
seventy-four for Zhènghóng Qí,
eighty-six for Xiānghóng Qí.)
and Ménggǔ
(twenty-four each for Zhènghuáng and Xiāngbái Qí,
twenty-two each for Zhènghóng and Xiānghóng Qí,
twenty-eight for Xiānghuáng Qí,
twenty-nine for Zhèngbái Qí,
thirty for Zhènglàn Qí,
twenty-five for Xiānglán Qí.)
In the first year of Qiánlóng, Yìnwù Cānlǐng and Zhāngjīng were added.
Qiánfēng Yíng (Vanguard Camp) Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng (Vanguard Commander),
(Principal second rank.
Princes, dukes, and grand ministers concurrently hold this post.)
One for the Left Wing and one for the Right Wing.
(From the Tǒnglǐng downwards,
all are filled by Manchus and Mongols.
The Hùjūn, Huǒqì, and Jiànruì camps are the same.) Cānlǐng (Commandant),
(Principal third rank.)
eight in total. Shìwèi (Imperial Bodyguard),
(Originally principal fifth rank.
In the first year of Qiánlóng, promoted to principal fourth rank.)
eight in total. Wěishǔ Shìwèi (Acting Imperial Bodyguard),
(Given the fifth-rank button,
still drawing the monthly stipend of a Qiánfēng Xiào.)
four in total. Qiánfēng Xiào (Vanguard Officer),
(Principal sixth rank.)
forty-four in total. Xiélǐ Shìwù Cānlǐng (Assistant Commandant for Affairs)
and Shìwèi (Imperial Bodyguard),
one each.
(Appointed from among the Cānlǐng and Shìwèi of their respective wings.)
Qiánfēng Xiào (Vanguard Officer),
two each.
(Appointed at discretion from among the Qiánfēng Xiào of their respective wings.) Bǐtiěshì (Secretary),
four in total. The Tǒnglǐng commands the political and military affairs of the Vanguard,
selecting elite Manchu and Mongol soldiers,
and training them in their skills in due course.
The Cānlǐng and Shìwèi are responsible for supervising the Vanguard,
providing security during imperial processions and acting as palace guards.
In the eighth year of Tiāncōng,
the vanguard soldiers of the Bāyālǎ Camp were designated Gábùshíxián Chāohā.
In the seventeenth year of Shùnzhì,
the Manchu term Gábùshíxián Gálóuyī Ángbāng was officially translated into Chinese characters as Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng,
and its Zhāngjīng as Cānlǐng;
positions for Qiánfēng Shìwèi and Qiánfēng Xiào were established,
and their numbers fixed.
(As listed above.) In the third year of Yōngzhèng,
one suíyìn Xiélǐ Shìwù Cānlǐng and Shìwèi each for the Left and Right Wings were established,
and two Qiánfēng Xiào each.
In the seventeenth year of Qiánlóng,
Wěishǔ Qiánfēng Shìwèi were added,
one for each banner.
In the fifty-fourth year,
ten Bìshǔ Shānzhuāng Dàilíng Qiánfēng Xiào were established.
(These were still counted within the regular number of Qiánfēng Xiào.)
Hùjūn Yíng (Guards Camp) Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng (Guards Commander),
(Principal second rank.)
eight in total. Cānlǐng (Commandant),
(Principal third rank.)
and Fù Cānlǐng (Assistant Commandant),
(Originally principal fifth rank.
In the twelfth year of Yōngzhèng, promoted to principal fourth rank.)
one hundred twelve in total.
(Eighty for each Manchu banner,
thirty-two for each Mongol banner.) Wěishǔ Cānlǐng (Acting Commandant),
(Given the fifth-rank button,
selected from among the Hùjūn Xiào.)
fifty-six in total. Hùjūn Xiào (Guards Officer),
(Principal sixth rank.)
eight hundred eighty-five in total.
(Six hundred eighty-one Manchu,
two hundred four Mongol.) Wěishǔ Hùjūn Xiào (Acting Guards Officer), (Given a golden-button honorary title,
drawing the monthly stipend of a Hùjūn.)
same number as Acting Commandants. Xiélǐ Shìwù Cānlǐng (Assistant Commandant for Affairs)
and Fù Cānlǐng (Assistant Commandant),
eight each.
(Selected from among the Cānlǐng and Fù Cānlǐng of their respective banners.)
Hùjūn Xiào (Guards Officer),
(Appointed at discretion from their respective banners.)
Bǐtiěshì (Secretary),
sixteen each. The Tǒnglǐng commands the political and military affairs of the Guards,
selecting elite Manchu and Mongol soldiers,
and training them in their skills in due course.
During grand reviews, they form the leading contingent,
arrayed flanking the Vanguard.
Whenever there are imperial audiences,
they may report illegal activities.
The Cānlǐng and Fù Cānlǐng are responsible for supervising the Guards.
When the emperor travels, they ride flanking the imperial carriage;
when in residence, they stand guard at the palace gates.
Initially,
the Bāyālǎ Camp was established,
commanded by a Bāyālǎ Dàozhāngjīng,
with Jiǎlǎ Zhāngjīng as subordinate commanders.
In the seventeenth year of Shùnzhì,
the Manchu term Bāyālǎ Dàozhāngjīng was officially translated into Chinese characters as Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng,
one for each banner;
the Jiǎlǎ Zhāngjīng became Hùjūn Cānlǐng,
fourteen for each banner.
The establishment of Hùjūn Xiào followed the model of Zuǒlǐng.
(In the thirty-third year of Qiánlóng, two hundred fourteen were added.)
An quota for Acting Hùjūn Cānlǐng was also established.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
Acting Cānlǐng were changed to Fù Cānlǐng,
fourteen for each banner.
(In the thirty-third year of Qiánlóng, sixteen were added.)
In the third year,
positions such as suíyìn Hùjūn Cānlǐng, Fù Cānlǐng, and Hùjūn Xiào were established.
In the seventeenth year of Qiánlóng,
Wěishǔ Hùjūn Cānlǐng were added,
seven for each banner.
(In the thirty-third year, thirty-two were added.)
In the forty-first year,
seventy-seven Hùjūn of superior strength and ability were selected
to be Wěishǔ Hùjūn Xiào.
Jǐngyùnmén Zhíbān Dàchén (Grand Minister on Duty at Jǐngyùn Gate),
one. (The Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng and Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng take turns on duty.)
Yìnwù Zhāngjīng (Seal Affairs Officer),
(Ten Seal Affairs Cānlǐng from the Vanguard and Guards take turns on duty.)
Shàngsān Qí and Xiàwǔ Qí Gè Sīyào Zhāngjīng (Gate Key Officers for each of the Upper Three Banners and Lower Five Banners),
(Hùjūn Cānlǐng of their respective banners take turns for imperial appointment.)
one each. Zhíbān Qiánfēng Cānlǐng (Vanguard Commandant on Duty)
and Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Guards Commandant on Duty),
twenty-nine in total.

twenty-seven Guards.)
Bākèshén Hùjūn (Bākèshén Guards) equal to the number of Cānlǐng.
Qiánfēng Xiào (Vanguard Officer)
and Hùjūn Xiào (Guards Officer),

ninety-one Guards.)

one. (One Zhǔshì and Acting Zhǔshì each from the Shàngsān Qí take turns on duty.)
Mén Bǐtiěshì (Gate Secretary),
five. (Ten from the Shàngsān Qí,

Yuánmíngyuán Bāqí, Nèiwùfǔ Sānqí Hùjūn Yíng Zhǎngyìn Zǒngtǒng Dàchén (Grand Minister Commander in Charge of Seals for the Yuánmíngyuán Eight Banners and Nèiwùfǔ Three Banners Guards Camp),
one. (Specially appointed from among the Zǒngtǒng Dàchén of this camp.
Same for other camps.)
Zǒngtǒng Dàchén (Commander in Chief), unlimited number.
(Princes, dukes, and grand ministers hold concurrent posts.)
Bāqí Yíngzǒng Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Guards Commandant of the Eight Banners Camp),
eight each,
(All principal third rank.)
Fù Cānlǐng (Assistant Commandant), double that number.

In the tenth year of Yōngzhèng, promoted to principal fourth rank.)
Shǔ Cānlǐng (Acting Commandant), double that again.
(Originally sixth rank.
In the tenth year of Yōngzhèng, promoted to principal fifth rank.)
Hùjūn Xiào (Guards Officer),
(Principal sixth rank.)
Fù Hùjūn Xiào (Assistant Guards Officer),
(From eighth rank.)
one hundred twenty-eight each. Xiélǐ Shìwù Yíngzǒng Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Assistant Commandant for Affairs of the Guards Camp),
two each,
Hùjūn Xiào (Guards Officer), four.
Bǐtiěshì (Secretary), thirty-two.
Sānqí Yíngzǒng (Commander of the Three Banners Camp),
one. (Originally fourth rank.

Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Guards Commandant),

Fù Cānlǐng (Assistant Commandant),

Wěishǔ Cānlǐng (Acting Commandant),

three each. Hùjūn Xiào (Guards Officer), nine.
Fù Hùjūn Xiào (Assistant Guards Officer), three.
Bǐtiěshì (Secretary), four.
The Zǒngtǒng (President) was in charge of the administration of the Yìwèi (Palace Guard) of Yuánmíngyuán.
When the imperial carriage entered or exited, there would be a警蹕 (jingbi - imperial clear-the-way announcement).
They oversaw the guard posts at the gates surrounding the garden,
supervising and controlling the security.
The Yíngzǒng (Battalion Commander) and below were responsible for commanding the troops, patrolling at night and during the day.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1724),
the Yuánmíngyuán Hùjūnyíng (Guard Battalion) was established,
with eight Bāqí Yíngzǒng (Eight Banners Battalion Commanders),
sixteen Fù Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Deputy Guard Commanders),
thirty-two Shǔ Fù Cānlǐng (Acting Deputy Commanders),
and eighty Hùjūnxiào (Guard Captains).
(In the tenth year, thirty-three were added.

Also established were the Nèi Wù Fǔ Sānqí Hùjūnyíng (Imperial Household Department Three Banners Guard Battalions),
with Cānlǐng (Commanders), Shìwèi (Imperial Bodyguards), Wěishǔ Cānlǐng (Acting Commanders) (later changed to Fù Cānlǐng - Deputy Commanders),

One Wěishǔ Hùjūnxiào (Acting Guard Captain) for each.
(Later changed to Fù Hùjūnxiào - Deputy Guard Captains.)
A Jiǎn Zǒngtǒng Dàchén (Minister of General Command by Selection) was appointed to lead them.
In the seventh year,
seventy-two Hùjūnxiào (Guard Captains) were appointed in the Bāqí (Eight Banners).
(In the tenth year, forty were added.
In the twelfth year of Qiánlóng's reign, sixteen were added.)
In the tenth year,
one Yíngzǒng (Battalion Commander) was appointed for the Sānqí (Three Banners),
and one Bāqí Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Eight Banners Guard Commander) for each.
In the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng's reign (1751),
the Suíyìn Xiélǐ Shìwù Yíngzǒng (Battalion Commander Assisting Affairs with Seal) and other officials were appointed.

The Xiāoqíyíng Cānlǐng (Light Cavalry Battalion Commanders) and Fù Cānlǐng (Deputy Commanders) were in charge of guarding the forbidden city,
and concurrently managed succession to office, archery examinations, and selection of armor.
The Zuǒlǐng (Company Commanders) and below were in charge of commanding the banner troops,
auditing households, salaries, and provisions,
and registering them with the Cānlǐng (Commanders).
The Hùjūnyíng (Guard Battalions) were in charge of guarding the imperial palace,
leading and escorting.
The Qiánfēngyíng (Vanguard Battalions) were in charge of practicing unbridling horses and "flower horse" archery.
Initially, the Nèi Wù Fǔ (Imperial Household Department) was established,
with four Nèi Guǎnlǐng (Palace Servants Supervisors).
(In the third and sixth years of Shùnzhì's reign, four were added in each;
in the eleventh year, eight were added;
in the twenty-fourth year of Kāngxī's reign, another four were added;
in the thirtieth year, six were added.)
In the first year of Shùnzhì's reign (1644),
nine Nèifǔ Sānqí Mǎnzhōu Zuǒlǐng (Imperial Household Department Three Banners Manchu Company Commanders) were appointed,
twelve Qígǔ Zuǒlǐng (Banner and Drum Company Commanders)
(in the thirty-fourth year of Kāngxī's reign, two were added to each banner),
one Cháoxiān Zuǒlǐng (Korean Company Commander)
(in the thirty-fourth year of Kāngxī's reign, one was added;
in the tenth year of Yōngzhèng's reign, changed to Shìguǎn Zuǒlǐng - Hereditary Company Commander),
subordinate to the Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén (Minister Overseeing Imperial Bodyguards).
In the eighteenth year,
two Hùjūnxiào (Guard Captains) were appointed under each Mǎnzhōu Zuǒlǐng (Manchu Company Commander),
and one Nèi Guǎnlǐng Hùjūnxiào (Palace Servants Supervisor Guard Captain) under each Qígǔ Zuǒlǐng (Banner and Drum Company Commander).
(In the twenty-third year of Kāngxī's reign, twelve were abolished.
In the ninth year of Yōngzhèng's reign, fifteen were added.)
In the thirteenth year of Kāngxī's reign (1674),
they were transferred to the Nèi Wù Fǔ (Imperial Household Department).
In the sixteenth year,
it was stipulated that each of the Sānqí (Three Banners) should be organized into five Cānlǐng (Commanders),
appointing Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Guard Commanders) and Xiāoqí Cānlǐng (Light Cavalry Commanders)
(in the sixteenth year of Qiánlóng's reign, five Sīguān (department officials) from the Fǔ (Department) were selected to manage the seal).
The old Cānlǐng (Commanders) were changed to Fù Cānlǐng (Deputy Commanders)
in the same number.
The establishment of Xiāoqíxiào (Light Cavalry Captains) was based on the Zuǒlǐng (Company Commanders).
(In the thirty-fourth year of Kāngxī's reign, thirty-three Zuǒlǐng (Company Commanders) were added,
and the same number of Xiāoqíxiào (Light Cavalry Captains)).
In the twentieth year,
Wěishǔ Hùjūn Cānlǐng (Acting Guard Commanders) were appointed
(in the ninth year of Yōngzhèng's reign, five were added to each banner;
in the twelfth year, five were abolished from each).
Wěishǔ Hùjūnxiào (Acting Guard Captains)
(in the third year of Yōngzhèng's reign, changed to Fù Hùjūnxiào - Deputy Guard Captains).
In the ninth year,
five were added to each banner.
In the thirteenth year, they were abolished.
Five for each banner.
In the twenty-third year,
one Fù Nèi Guǎnlǐng (Deputy Palace Servants Supervisor) was added.
(In the twenty-fourth year, four were added.
In the thirtieth and thirty-fourth years, three were added in each).
In the thirty-fourth year,
the Hùjūn (Guards) remained subordinate to the Shìwèichù (Imperial Bodyguard Department).
In the thirty-sixth year,
Shìwèi (Imperial Bodyguards) and Wěishǔ Cānlǐng (Acting Commanders) were added,
three for each banner.
(In the ninth year of Yōngzhèng's reign, two were added to each.
In the thirtieth year of Qiánlóng's reign, one was added,
in charge of the Qiánfēngyíng - Vanguard Battalion).
In the forty-third year,
Fù Xiāoqíyíng Cānlǐng (Deputy Light Cavalry Battalion Commanders) were added in the same number as Cānlǐng (Commanders).
(In the thirteenth year of Yōngzhèng's reign, they were abolished).
In the first year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1723),
Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng (Guard Commandants) were added,
one for each banner,
and again transferred to the Nèifǔ (Imperial Household Department).
In the fourth year,
Wěishǔ Fù Xiāoqíxiào (Acting Deputy Light Cavalry Captains) were appointed in the same number as Zuǒlǐng (Company Commanders).
(In the thirteenth year, they were abolished).
In the thirteenth year of Qiánlóng's reign (1748),
the Qiánfēngyíng (Vanguard Battalion) was first established,
with two Cānlǐng (Commanders), Wěishǔ Cānlǐng (Acting Commanders), and Qiánfēngxiào (Vanguard Captains) each,
commanded by the Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng (Guard Commandants).
In the fifteenth year,
two Wěishǔ Qiánfēngxiào (Acting Vanguard Captains) were added.
(Selected from guards).
In the twenty-fifth year,
one Huízǐ Zuǒlǐng (Hui Company Commander) and one Xiāoqíxiào (Light Cavalry Captain) were appointed.
In the thirty-second year,
five Hùjūn Lánlíngzhǎng (Guard Blue Feather Chiefs) were added.
In the forty-seventh year,
two Xiàowèizhǎng Xiāoqíxiào (Chief of Patrol Light Cavalry Captains) were added.
In the seventh year of Jiāqìng's reign (1802),
four Qiánfēngyíng Lánlíngzhǎng (Vanguard Battalion Blue Feather Chiefs) were added.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng's reign (1911),
they were transferred to the Qiánfēng Hùjūn Děngyíng Shìwùchù (Vanguard and Guard Battalions Affairs Office).
Xiàngdǎo Chù: One Zhǎngyìn Zǒngtǒng Dàchén.
(The Zǒngtǒng Dàchén are specially appointed.)
There is no limit to the number of Zǒngtǒng Dàchén.

Thirty-two Zhāngjīng,

Four Lánlíngzhǎng.

Whenever there is an imperial inspection or provincial tour,

Six Bǐtiēshì.
This battalion is in charge of selecting brave warriors from the Eight Banners to practice wrestling,
and for imperial escort and guard duties.

In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
the number of Hùwèi for all Wáng, Bèilè, Bèizǐ, and Gōng was fixed: Thirty for the Shèzhèng Wáng,

In the eighth year (1651),
the system of military officials for princely mansions was established,
creating posts such as Chángshǐ, Sīyízhǎng, Sǎnqíráng, Hùwèi, and Diǎnyí,
and establishing varying numbers of Xiāoqíjiao under each Zuǒlǐng.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng (1726),
the number of Sǎnqíráng for princely mansions was fixed,
and the posts for Bèizǐ and below were abolished.
In the nineteenth year of Qiánlóng (1754),
it was decreed that Wáng and Gōng's Hùwèi, Diǎnyí and other officials,
were all to be of junior ranks.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
to avoid the Emperor's taboo name,
Sīyízhǎng was changed to Sīlǐzhǎng,
and Diǎnyí was changed to Diǎnwèi.
(The Princess's mansions were the same.)
Previously, Yíxián Qīnwáng assisted Shìzōng,
and Zhuāngkè Qīnwáng aided Gāozōng;
both were granted the title of Double Qīnwáng,
and their Hùwèi were doubled.
In the early Jiāqìng reign,
the two Wáng, Yí and Chéng, each had two First, Second, and Third Class Hùwèi added;
Dìng Qīnwáng and Qìng Jùnwáng had one First Class Hùwèi added,
and two each for Second and Third Class.
Upon Xuāntǒng's accession,
the official system for the Jiānguó Shèzhèng Wáng was deliberated and fixed,
which was double that of a Qīnwáng.
These were all exceptional precedents.
Gùlún Gōngzhǔ Mansion: Chángshǐ,
one First Class Hùwèi,
one each;
two each for Second and Third Class;
two Diǎnwèi.
Héshuò Gōngzhǔ Mansion: One Sīlǐzhǎng;
two Second Class Hùwèi,
one Third Class;
one each of sixth and seventh rank Diǎnwèi.
In the fifty-first year of Qiánlóng (1786),
the number of subordinate officials for Princess's mansions was first fixed.

Dīngyù and Xiāoqíxiào were specially established,
with quotas as follows.)
One Sīgōngjiàng for each.

All officials from Yìzhǎng downwards were subordinate to him,
and received orders from the Fù Dūtǒng.
Initially,
in the 8th year of Tiāncōng,
a Sànzhì Rank 5 official for brick and tile firing was established at Yǒnglíng.
(In the 5th year of Shùnzhì, one more was added for Fúlǐng and Zhāolíng respectively.

In the 2nd year of Shùnzhì,
one Fángyù was established for Fúlǐng.

Zǒngguǎn, Yìlǐng (changed to Yìzhǎng in the 59th year of Qiánlóng),

In the 2nd year of Qiánlóng,
two Xiāoqíxiào were established for each mausoleum,
and this became the established system thereafter.
In the 1st year of Guāngxù,
the Fù Dūtǒng of Xīngjīng was first established.

Initially, seals for Dàjiāngjūn and Jiāngjūn were cast.
(Over a hundred seals for Jīnglüè, Dàjiāngjūn, and Jiāngjūn were stored in the treasury,
and were destroyed starting from the 14th year of Qiánlóng.)
Seven Dàjiāngjūn seals: Fǔyuǎn, Níngyuǎn, Āndōng, Zhēngnán, Píngxī, Píngběi;
Seven Jiāngjūn seals: Zhènhǎi, Yángwēi, Jìngnì, Jìngdōng, Zhēngnán, Dìngxī, Dìngběi,
were stored in the Huángshǐchéng.
When commanding an army to go on an expedition,
a memorial was submitted to request their issuance.
During the Kāngxī and Yōngzhèng reigns,
there were titles such as Jìngkòu, Ānyuǎn, Fèngmìng, Píngnì, Píngkòu, Jiànwǔ, Tàonì, Níngyuǎn, Jìngbiān, Dìngbiān, Suíyuǎn, Zhènwǔ, Jìngnì, Dàngkòu;
during the Qiánlóng reign, Níngyuǎn, Jìngbiān, Fènwēi, Jìngnì;
during the Jiāqìng reign, Dìngxī;
during the Dàoguāng reign, Yángwēi;
all were issued with seals of office.
Their ranks followed their original official positions.
Previously, Jīnglüè Dàchén, Dàjiāngjūn, and Jiāngjūn were
selected from princes, Bèilè, Bèizǐ, Gōng, or Dūtǒng, and trusted ministers.
They were appointed for major campaigns and disbanded afterward.
When the Eight Banners were established,
garrisons were commanded by selected Jiāngjūn and Dūtǒng.
Jiāngjūn became exclusively Manchu officials.
Ministers in the northwest frontier and various Chéngshǒuwèi officials
were also generally designated as Manchu positions.
From the capital region to various provinces,
to the east were Fèngtiān, Jílín, Hēilóngjiāng;
to the west Huíjiāng, Zàngdì;
to the north included Inner and Outer Měnggǔ.
Jiāngjūn, Dūtǒng, and ministers were stationed to govern them.
A summary is given
in the left column.
One Jiāngjūn stationed in Shèngjīng.
(His subordinates included Zhǔshì, Bǐtiēshì, and other officials.
The same applied to Jílín and Hēilóngjiāng.)
Initially, one Nèi Dàchén served as the Liúshǒu.
In the 3rd year of Shùnzhì,
it was changed to Ángbāngzhāngjīng.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī, it was moved to Liáodōng,
and called Liáodōng Jiāngjūn.

Tídū and other officials: Tídū Jūnwù Zǒngbīngguān,
(First rank, junior.)
managed the consolidation and protection of borders,
commanded troops,
exercised jurisdiction over Zhèn, Xié, Yíng, and Xùn,
assessed merits and demerits,
and reported to the Zǒngdū.
Zhènshǒu Zǒngbīngguān,
(Second rank, senior.)
managed the military administration of a Zhèn,
commanded the officers and soldiers of his own battalion,
and deployed generals and officials for defense,
and reported to the Tídū.
Fùjiàng,
(Second rank, junior.)
served as Tíbiāo when Tídū and Zhèn guarded strategic posts,
served as Dūbiāo Zhōngjūn when the Zǒngdū generally managed military affairs;
Jiāngjūnbiao, Hébiāo, and Cáobiāo were also similar.
Cānjiàng,
(Third rank, senior.)
Yóují,
(Initially third rank, senior.
In the 10th year of Shùnzhì, changed to junior.
) managed military administration for defense posts,
and served as Zhōngjūnguān in various Zhèn.
Dūsī,
(Initially third rank, senior.
In the 10th year of Shùnzhì, changed to junior.
In the 18th year, changed to fourth rank, senior.
In the 9th year of Kāngxī, restored to former rank.
In the 24th year, fixed as fourth rank, senior.
) managed affairs similar to Cān and Yóu,
and served as Fùjiàng Zhōngjūnguān.
Shǒubèi,
(Initially fourth rank, senior.
In the 34th year of Kāngxī, fixed as fifth rank, senior.
) managed camp affairs and provisions,
and served as Cān and Yóu Zhōngjūnguān.
Qiānzǒng,
(Initially sixth rank, senior.
In the 34th year of Kāngxī, Yíng Qiānzǒng was changed to sixth rank, junior.
In the 58th year, restored to former rank.)
Bǎzǒng,
(Seventh rank, senior.)
Wàiwěi Bǎzǒng,
(Ninth rank, senior.)
Éwài Wàiwěi,
(Ninth rank, junior.)
each managed camp, patrol, and garrison areas.
Initially,
Tídū and Zǒngbīng had no fixed ranks,
but held titles such as Zuǒyòu Dūdū, Dūdū, Tóngzhī, and Qiānshì.
(Abolished in the 18th year of Qiánlóng.
Ranks were then fixed.)
Tídū commanded troops,
from the coastal areas of the imperial domain to the snowy mountains and burning frontiers,
spread out like stars.
In the interior, they also served as Xúnfǔ,
followed by Zǒngbīng.
Below Fùjiàng,
the ranks were numerous and distinct;
in times of need, they served as officials with Tí and Zhèn,
(such as those accompanying expeditions, reinforcing camps, or suppressing bandit camps.)
and were abolished after the completion of affairs.
Since the Revolt of the Three Feudatories,
many Tí and Zhèn were effective.
During the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns,
when the Fà and Niǎn rebellions were pacified,
many soldiers from Xiāng, Huái, and Chǔ battalions,
who rose from humble origins,
were promoted to Tí and Zhèn,
and officials below Cān and Yóu
became even more numerous,
with recommendations becoming redundant and excessive.
Often, Tí and Zhèn were registered by name,
demoted to junior officers,
or designated as probationary Qiān and Bǎ,
suddenly rising to command generals.
The disparity in official positions
reached its extreme at this point.
During the Guāngxù reign,
the navy was established,
and Tí and Zhèn were also appointed,
but dismissed if they showed no merit.
Afterwards, the army's official system was revised,
and the Hé and Cáo banner battalions
were successively abolished.
The Green Standard Army saw annual reductions and reforms,
which were rigorously implemented in Zhèjiāng,
followed by Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Húnán, and Húběi;
only verifiable records are presented in this chapter.

In the thirty-fourth year,
after the pacification of the western frontier,
due to their old names,
officials such as Bókè were established.
At that time, those who rendered meritorious service in the expedition
were all enfeoffed as third-rank Āqímù,
with Yè'ěrqiāng granted to Èduì,
Kāshígá'ěr to Sètíbā'ěrdì,
Kùchē to Èsīmàn,
Hétián to Hànzā'ěrbā,
Ākèsū to Dámòtè,
and Wūshí to Ābùdùlā.
These were the Bókè of the six major cities,
ranging from third-rank to seventh-rank,
each differentiated by the territory granted.
(Third-rank was granted 200 pǎzǐtèmǎ pǎ of land,
and 100 cultivators.
Fourth-rank 150 mu,
50 persons.

30 persons.

by rule were not given additional land,
but each had 5 cultivators.
)Huí people from Ākèsū were relocated to station in Yīlí,
and Màosà (Èmǐnhézhuō's second son)
was granted the title of Āqímù.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Níngyuǎn Chéng was built in Yīlí,
and Huí people from Wūshí, Yè'ěrqiāng, Hétián, Hāmì, and Túlǔfān were again relocated to station there,
and various Bókè, large and small, were established.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the promotion and appointment system was finalized.
In the thirty-first year,
Huí people from Kālāshā'ěr and Kù'ěrlè were relocated to station in Kùchè Mā,
one sixth-rank Hāzī was abolished,
one fourth-rank Āqímù was added,
who, along with the fifth-rank Gázálāqí and seventh-rank Yùzī Bókè,
were all stationed in that place.
In the thirty-eighth year,
they returned to station in Kù'ěrlè,
and the old system was restored.
In the ninth year of Jiāqìng,
following the example of Kāshígá'ěr and Yè'ěrqiāng,
one sixth-rank Bājíjír and one seventh-rank Sèdí'ěr were added to Yīlí.
In the eighth year of Dàoguāng,
it was stipulated that Bókè of third- to fifth-rank were to be filled and implemented by the minister of the local city,
who would submit a report to the Kāshígá'ěr Cānzàn Dàchén for review and forwarding to the emperor,
while sixth- and seventh-rank Bókè were directly submitted for verification and release.
According to custom,
senior Bókè avoided their hometowns,
and junior Bókè avoided their own villages.
This prohibition was strictly enforced,
(Sèlèkù'ěr, a dependent of Yè'ěrqiāng, was far from the karun,
and was not subject to this rule.)
Additionally, three fifth-rank Nèkèbù, Mìtúwǎlì, and Mòtìsèbùyī from Kāshígá'ěr were relocated to station in Hǎn'àilǐkè,
and given the official title of fifth-rank Āqímù,
while a sixth-rank Hāzī was stationed in Chálāgēn
to primarily manage agricultural land.
Two seventh-rank Míng Bókè from Āsītú'ā'ěrtúshí were abolished,
one was relocated to assist in Chálāgēn,
and another was moved to Ā'ěrhú to fill the position of Hāzī.
That year, due to the serious incident at Yīngjíshā'ěr,
he was awarded the sixth-grade Hāzī Yīshíhǎn title,
to assist the Āqímù in governing affairs.
In the tenth year of Guāngxù
when the system of prefectures and counties was reformed,
all were abolished.
Since the positions of Āqímù and Yīshíhǎn had relatively high ranks,
they retained their original titles
to distinguish them from ordinary people.

each banner had one person.
(Inside the great desert, there were twenty-four tribes such as Kē'ěrqìn,

Outside the great desert, there were four tribes of Kākěrkā,
with eighty-six banners.
In Qīnghǎi, there were five tribes,

In the Western Bend, there were ten tribes in total, namely Élǔtè, Éjìnà Tǔ'ěrhùtè, Dǔ'ěrbótè, Tǔ'ěrhùtè, and Héshuòtè,
with thirty-four banners.
Kings (Wáng), Bèilè, Bèizǐ, Gōng, Táijí, and Tābùnáng served in these roles.
Those who did not have a Zāfúkè
were subordinate to generals (Jiāngjūn), military governors (Dūtǒng), and ministers (Dàchén).

Initially, the Zāfúkè was established to comprehensively manage banner affairs,
