and they were given eighth-rank official titles.
(In the twenty-sixth year of Qiánlóng,
the quota for Wénhuá Hall was abolished.
In the forty-seventh year,
all the straight-hall tài​jiàn of the Three Great Halls were abolished.) In the sixty-first year,
one fifth-rank zǒng​guǎn was appointed,
three fifth-rank tài​jiàn,
and two sixth-rank tài​jiàn.
This marked the beginning of tài​jiàn being granted official positions.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
the zǒng​guǎn was given a fourth-rank emolument,
the fù​zǒng​guǎn a sixth-rank,
the suí​shì shǒu​lǐng a seventh-rank,
and the gōng​diàn shǒu​lǐng an eighth-rank.
In the fourth year,
the fourth-rank zǒng​guǎn of the Jìng​shì​fáng was designated the gōng​diàn jiān​dū lǐng​shì xián,
the concurrently fourth-rank fù​zǒng​guǎn was designated the gōng​diàn jiān zhèng​shì xián,
(later changed to fifth-rank.)
The sixth-rank fù​zǒng​guǎn was designated the gōng​diàn jiān fù​shì xián,
the seventh-rank shǒu​lǐng was designated the zhí​shǒu​shì xián,
and the eighth-rank shǒu​lǐng was designated the shì​jiān xián.
In the eighth year,
it was again stipulated that ranks from fourth to eighth
were not divided into principal and concurrent.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that the system of granting noble ranks to inner palace officials should not be exceeded.
According to precedent,
eunuchs did not exceed the fourth rank,
and this was now compiled into a legal code.
In the fifty-first year,
the numbers of leading tài​jiàn for qīn​wáng, jùn​wáng, and gōng​zhǔ were set,
and they were all given eighth-rank titles.
(During the Jiāqìng period, the emolument of qīn​wáng shǒu​lǐng was increased to seventh-rank.)
In the sixth year of Jiāqìng,
Qìng​jùn​wáng was granted three seventh-rank tài​jiàn,
and Yí​qīn​wáng, Chéng​qīn​wáng, and Dìng​qīn​wáng each had one eighth-rank tài​jiàn added,
but this was not made a permanent system.
Tài​zǔ and Tài​zōng, learning from the past, changed the system
and did not appoint eunuchs.
When Shì​zǔ entered the pass,
he adopted the old system of the Míng imperial palace
and set the quotas,
numbering just over a thousand.
He issued an edict saying:
"I have examined the official system,
and in the Táng, Yú, Xià, and Shāng dynasties, eunuchs were not used.
It was in the Zhōu dynasty that their duties began to be defined.
After the Qín and Hàn dynasties,
they meddled in military and political affairs,
causing endless disasters."
Officials were strictly ordered not to associate with inner palace officials.
Furthermore, an iron stele was cast in the Jiāotài Hall,
with an inscription stating:
"Henceforth, anyone who breaks the law and interferes in politics,
usurps power and accepts bribes,
entrusts matters to inner and outer yámén,
colludes with Mǎn and Hàn officials,
exceeds their authority by memorializing on external affairs,
or comments on the merits of officials,
shall be executed by slow slicing."
Not long after,
individuals like Wú Liáng​fǔ incited the establishment of the Thirteen Yámén,
usurping authority and acting arbitrarily.
Shì​zǔ's dying edict exposed their wickedness.
Shèng​zǔ succeeded to the throne
and exterminated these great villains.
At that time, some Míng dynasty inner palace eunuchs were still serving in the palace,
and discipline was strict.
During the Yōngzhèng period,
measures were taken to prevent inner palace eunuchs' families from causing trouble,
and inner officials were ordered to exercise restraint,
with the Zhí​dū submitting memorials.
Gāo​zōng's laws were severe.
When the tài​jiàn Gāo Yún​cóng slightly dabbled in external affairs,
and Zhāng Fèng stole and destroyed a golden imperial decree,
both were punished according to the law.
When the imperial carriage visited Luányáng,
the xún​jiǎn Zhāng Ruò​yíng flogged unruly inner palace eunuchs,
and was specially promoted seven ranks,
and regulations were promulgated
to be observed forever.
He also issued an edict saying:
"In the Míng dynasty, inner palace eunuchs numbered tens of thousands,
and imperial robes were excessively granted.
Now, the system for the palace and imperial gardens
totals no more than three thousand."
At that time, they were all subordinate to the Nèi​fǔ,
which still embodied the meaning of a chief minister overseeing eunuchs.
However, their numbers had already doubled compared to Shì​zǔ's time.
Regarding the "Jiào" character being stopped for dispatching Hàn officials,
reports of recruitment not going through the Lǐ​bù,
and the changing of surnames for memorializing,
measures were repeatedly taken to curtail them
to purify conduct.
Therefore, throughout Gāo​zōng's sixty-plus years,
eunuchs dared not commit evil.
In the early years of Jiāqìng,
due to collusion between inside and outside,
Wú Tiān​chéng was demoted to seventh-rank zǒng​guǎn.
Then, because Cháng Yǒng​guì was arrogant and lawless,
his sixth-rank zǒng​guǎn position was revoked.
Xiāo Dé​lù was punished for abusive endorsement,
and his dú​lǐng​shì position was also revoked.
Later, individuals like Liú Dé​cái and Liú Jīn believed in邪教,
and conspired to harbor rebels,
leading to the great upheaval of Lín Qīng.
Their wickedness grew considerably.
Afterwards, Cáo Jìn​xǐ demanded a list of official names from the Lì​bīng​cáo zhǎng,
Mǎ Cháng​xǐ misused official titles,
Cáo Dé​yīng privately released fowling pieces,
and Zhāng Fǔ even privately stored weapons.
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
the Yù​shǐ Jiǎ Duó memorialized about inner palace eunuchs performing plays,
cutting gòng​duàn to make costumes,
but no punishment was heard of.
In the eighth year,
there was then Ān Dé​hǎi who falsely claimed to be an imperial envoy,
arranged the weaving of imperial robes,
and sailed with fluttering banners,
terrifying the residents.
Other transgressions included keeping actors,
galloping horses and causing disruptions,
repeatedly corrupting the laws,
which cannot be fully enumerated.
In the twelfth year of Guāngxù,
the Yù​shǐ Zhū Yī​xīn memorialized that Lǐ Lián​yīng accompanying Chún​qīn​wáng on an inspection of the seaports
easily risked repeating the mistakes of the Táng dynasty,
and an edict demoted him to zhǔ​shì.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Zǒng​dū Táo Mó memorialized that the recent affairs of eunuchs, though minor, caused severe harm,
and corrupt practices should be eliminated,
but the memorial received no reply.
Thus, eunuchs ended their existence with the state.

Gazetteer ninety-four: Official System Six (New Official System) Nèi​gè, Wài​wù​bù (Chū​shǐ​dà​chén, Shuì​wù​chù), Mín​zhèng​bù (Nèi​wài​xún​jǐng​zǒng​tīng), Dù​zhī​bù (Qīng​lǐ​cái​zhèng​chù, Dà​qīng​yín​háng​zào​bì​zǒng​chǎng), Xué​bù (Guó​zǐ​jiān, Dà​xué​táng), Lù​jūn​bù, Hǎi​jūn​bù, Fǎ​bù (Xiū​dìng​fǎ​lǜ​guǎn, Dà​lǐ​yuàn, Jīng​shī​gè​jí​shěn​jiǎn​tīng), Nóng​gōng​shāng​bù, Yóu​chuán​bù, Jūn​zī​fǔ, Bì​dé​yuàn, Zī​zhèng​yuàn, Yán​zhèng​yuàn, Diǎn​lǐ​yuàn (Lǐ​xué​guǎn), Tí​xué​shǐ, Tí​fǎ​shǐ (Wài​shěng​gè​jí​shěn​jiǎn​tīng), Dōng​sān​shěng​gè​sī, Jìn​wèi​jūn​dū​liàn​gōng​suǒ, Jūn​zhì, Zhèn​zhì (Lù​jūn​zhèn​jiān), Xún​fáng​duì, Hǎi​jūn​jiàn​zhì.
In the early Qīng dynasty, the official system was set,
and the framework of offices was roughly complete.
It underwent six or seven iterations in the middle,
with some preserved and others changed,
making each era different.
Extending to Dé​zōng's reign,
as foreign troubles followed,
the Yì​shǔ was first established.
It was later changed to a specialized ministry,
and the ministries of commerce, police, and education were established one after another,
while some fǔ and sì were abolished,
and then divided into ten ministries.
Later, when a constitution was proposed,
the Lǐ​fān​yuàn was changed to a ministry,
the Jūn​zī​chù was established,
and Xún​jǐng was again changed to Mín​zhèng,
Hù​bù to Dù​zhī​bù,
Shāng​bù to Nóng​gōng​shāng​bù,
Bīng​bù to Lù​jūn​bù,
with a Hǎi​jūn​chù additionally established,
Xíng​bù to Fǎ​bù,
with a Dà​lǐ​yuàn separately established.
Furthermore, the duties of the Gōng​bù concerning roads, railways, post, and telegraph were spun off to create the Yóu​chuán​bù.
Comparing the present to the past,
it is indeed a multitude of systems.
Xuāntǒng succeeded,
centralizing power in the cabinet,
adding the Hǎi​jūn​bù,
abolishing the Lì​bù,
and changing the Lǐ​bù to the Diǎn​lǐ​yuàn,
and the Yán​zhèng​chù to the Yán​zhèng​yuàn.
Still concerned that the cabinet's power was too great,
the Bì​dé​yuàn was established to maintain checks and balances,
and the Zī​zhèng​yuàn to act as oversight.
Compared to previous affairs,
they adopted standards from different regions,
created names according to circumstances,
resulting in redundant officials and mixed duties,
with ranks and official positions
not yet clearly delineated.
The simplified memorials, consultations, and appointments
are still extant.
Compiled and preserved,
they are fully recorded in the subsequent brief,
also serving as a record of gains and losses.
Nèigé: Zǒnglǐ Dàchén,
Xiélǐ Dàchén,
one of each.
(Specially appointed.)
Shí Guówù Dàchén.
(Also serving as ministers of various departments.)
One Chéng.
Chéngxūantīng Tīngzhǎng,
Fùtīngzhǎng,
one of each.
Zhìzī, Guān, Tǒngjì, Yìnzhù four bureaus,
one Júzhang each.
(From Chéng downwards, all are appointed by request.)
Its subordinates include: Qiānshì,
Yìnzhù Yìshī,
(all appointed by memorial.)
Yìshì,
Lùshì (all appointed by official correspondence.)
Various officials.
Under its jurisdiction: Fǎzhìyuàn,
Yuànzhǎng,
Fùyuànzhǎng,
one of each.
Sì Cānyì.
(All appointed by request.)
Cānshì,
(appointed by memorial.)
Qiānshì,
Lùshì,
their numbers are determined by the complexity of affairs.
The Zǒnglǐ is in charge of participating in critical confidential matters
and managing current affairs.
For laws, edicts, and decrees,
they are jointly signed by the Guówù Dàchén.
(If a matter involves one or several departments,
it is signed by the ministers in charge.)
During meetings, they serve as the presiding officer,
assisted by the Xiélǐ.
The Chéng manages cabinet affairs,
oversees all bureaus,
and sets the standard for various chiefs.
The Chéngxūan is in charge of promulgating imperial decrees,
upholding legal codes,
and managing documents and maps.
The Zhìgào is in charge of imperial edicts and decrees,
sealed letters and enfeoffments,
drafting and submitting proposals,
auditing the issuance of precious star medals,
and administering fiefdoms and noble ranks.
The Guān is in charge of evaluating performance and setting assessments,
and compiling and verifying implementation.
The Tǒngjì is in charge of unifying statistical tables
and publishing yearbooks.
The Yìnzhù is in charge of editing official gazettes.
The rest follow the old system.
(Detailed in Lǐbù.)
The Fǎzhìyuàn is in charge of compiling regulations,
revising laws and decrees,
and submitting proposals for approval.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
the Nèigé was reorganized,
and a Huìyì Zhèngwùchù was established,
with the various Bù Shàngshū serving as Nèigé Zhèngwù Dàchén.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
it was reorganized into a Zérèn Nèigé,
with the Jūnjī Dàchén serving as the Zǒnglǐ and Xiélǐ Dàchén,
and the system for Nèigé subordinate officials was established.
(As listed previously.)
Wàiwùbù: Wàiwù Dàchén,
Fùdàchén,
one of each.
(Specially appointed.)
Chéngzhèngtīng Zuǒ, Yòuchéng,
Cānyìtīng Zuǒ, Yòucānyì,
one of each.
(All appointed by request.)
Sì Cānshì.
(Appointed by memorial.)
Its subordinates: Sìwùtīng Sìwù, two persons.
(Appointed by official correspondence.)
Héhuì, Kǎogōng, Quèsuàn, Shùwù four divisions,
Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, Zhǔshì, two of each.
(All appointed by memorial.
The same applies to the above departments.)
The Dàchén is in charge of foreign negotiations,
proclaiming virtue and trustworthiness,
protecting overseas Chinese and foreign employees,
to ensure careful diplomatic relations.
The Fùdàchén assists them.
The Chéng is in charge of confidential documents
and oversees various affairs.
The Cānyì is in charge of reviewing laws and decrees,
assisted by the Cānshì.
(The same applies to all departments.)
The Héhuì is in charge of receiving envoys in audience,
treaties and rewards,
and also manages the rotation of consuls
and the transfer of officials.
The Kǎogōng is in charge of railways, mineral production, telegraph lines, and naval affairs;
all matters concerning the manufacturing of firearms,
the employment of foreign advisors,
recruiting laborers, and overseas study,
each performing their respective duties.
The Quèsuàn is in charge of foreign goods, maritime trade and taxation,
overseeing national debt and postal services,
and auditing the expenditures of this department and foreign missions.
The Dùwù is in charge of river and sea defenses,
territorial boundaries;
all matters concerning missionary work, travel,
rewards and relief, prohibitions,
and judicial cases,
are handled according to treaties.
There are Chéng and Cān on active duty,
supernumerary officials,
and seventh-rank minor capital officials.
(The quotas for minor capital officials in Mínzhèng, Yóuchuán, and Fǎbù are fixed.)
Under its jurisdiction: Chúcáiguǎn,
Tídiào, Bāngtídiào, one of each.
(Selected from the department's officials.)
Wén'àn, Zhīyìng, Shùwù, all dispatched officials to manage their respective affairs.
In the 5th year of Yōngzhèng,
the Qiàkètú trade agreement was established,
and a Bànlǐ Éshì Dàchén was appointed,
(see item 5.)
It was not a permanent position.
In the 1st year of Xiánfēng,
it was transferred to the Lǐfānyuàn.
In the 10th year,
Wénzōng fled north,
and a special official was appointed to manage peace negotiations.
In that winter,
the Zǒnglǐ Gèguó Shìwù Yámén was established,
and Gōngqīnwáng Yìxīn was appointed to lead it.
The officials were collectively called Zhāngjīng,
with eight Manchu and eight Han.
At that time, the system of governing by separate offices was in place.
(Hùbù officials audited customs duties,
Lǐfānbù officials managed documents,
Bīngbù officials managed relay stations and post services,
Nèigé personnel managed confidential matters,
all subordinate to the Zǒngbàn and Bāngbàn.)
In the 3rd year,
it was reorganized into four sections: England, France, Russia, and America.
In the 9th year,
a naval defense section was added.
Later it was changed to five sections: Russia, Germany, England, France, and Japan.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng,
Russia and Germany were combined into one,
and two new sections, Mìshū and Jīyào, were added.
The following year,
four Zǒngbàn were appointed,
called Zǒngbàn Zhāngjīng.
In the 1st year of Tóngzhì,
supernumerary Zhāngjīng were added,
two Manchu and two Han.
(In the 2nd year, six were added to each;
in the 9th year of Guāngxù, four were added to each;
in the 10th year, four were reduced from each;
in the 23rd year, two were added to each.)
In the 3rd year,
a Sìwùtīng was established,
with two Sìwù.
In the 27th year of Guāngxù,
after the Xīnchǒu Treaty was concluded,
its name was changed to Wàiwùbù,
ranking above all other departments.
A Zǒnglǐ Qīnwáng was appointed,
a Huìbàn Shàngshū,
and concurrently a Huìbàn Zuǒ, Yòushìláng,
one of each;
the Zǒngbàn were renamed Zuǒ, Yòuchéng,
and one Zuǒ, Yòucānyì each.
Also appointed were Lángzhōng and other officials,
without distinction between Manchu and Han.
(In the 32nd year, the official system was revised
with the intention of combining Manchu and Han,
but the Hánlín and Dūchá two academies still followed the old system.)
In that year, fifteen additional Fānyìguān were appointed.
(Five of the 7th, 8th, and 9th ranks each,
divided into sections to manage affairs.)
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
when the new Nèigé was formed,
the concurrent positions of Zǒnglǐ and Huìbàn were abolished,
Shàngshū was changed to Dàchén,
and Shìláng to Fùdàchén.
(One Shìláng position was abolished,
the same for all departments.)
The system of supervising ministers
was thus abolished.
First-class Envoys Plenipotentiary
(First Rank,
specially appointed)
Councillors
(Third Rank)
and Interpreters
(Fifth Rank)
are all appointed by memorial.
There is no fixed number
and they are appointed as needed,
then dismissed when the task is complete.
Second-class Envoys Plenipotentiary
(Second Rank,
specially appointed)
and Councillors
(initially Fourth Rank,
later changed to From Fourth Rank)
are appointed by memorial,
one for each.
(One each for Great Britain, Russia, Germany, Japan, Austria-Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium.
One each for France, Japan, and Portugal.
One each for the United States, Mexico, Peru, and Cuba.)
Two second-class Councillors serve as acting envoys in branch legations.
(One for Spain.
One for Portugal.)
Three second-class Councillors concurrently serve as Consuls-General.
(One for Mexico.
One for Peru.
One for Cuba.)
There are eight third-class Councillors.
(Initially Fifth Rank,
later changed to Correct Fifth Rank.
Appointed by memorial.
One each for Great Britain, France, Germany, and Russia.
Two each for the United States and Japan.)
Second and third-class Interpreters
(Second-class From Fifth Rank;
Third-class From Sixth Rank,
appointed by memorial)
and first and second-class Secretaries
(First-class From Fifth Rank;
Second-class From Sixth Rank,
appointed by memorial).
Commercial Commissioners
(Fifth Rank,
appointed by memorial)
and Military Attachés,
one for each legation.
(However, Austria-Hungary, Italy, the Netherlands, and Belgium do not have third-class interpreters or military attachés.)
Branch legations have one second-class Interpreter and one Secretary each.
There are thirteen Consuls-General
(From Fourth Rank,
appointed by memorial).
(One each for Singapore, Australia, South Africa, and Canada,
subordinate to the British envoy.
One for Vladivostok,
subordinate to the Russian envoy.
One each for Mexico, Cuba, San Francisco, Manila, Melbourne, and Panama,
subordinate to the American envoy.
One each for Yokohama and Joseon,
subordinate to the Japanese envoy.
One for Java,
subordinate to the Dutch envoy.)
There are fourteen Consuls
(Fifth Rank,
appointed by memorial).
(One each for Penang, New Zealand, Rangoon, and Vancouver,
subordinate to the British envoy.
One each for Honolulu and Calcutta,
subordinate to the American envoy.
One for Samoa,
subordinate to the German envoy.
One each for Kōbe, Nagasaki, Incheon, Busan, and Sinuiju,
subordinate to the Japanese envoy.
One each for Surabaya and Padang,
subordinate to the Dutch envoy.)
There are two Vice-Consuls
(From Fifth Rank,
appointed by memorial).
(One each for Wŏnsan and Chinnampo,
subordinate to the Japanese envoy.)
There are also foreigners serving as honorary consuls.
(France:
Marseille;
Italy:
Milan, Naples;
United States:
Boston, Philadelphia, and other places.)
Envoys manage international negotiations.
Councillors assist them.
Consuls are in charge of protecting overseas Chinese.
In the early reign of Kāngxī,
Russia sent an envoy,
but no system was established.
In the sixth year of Tóngzhì (1867),
envoys were first dispatched to handle negotiations,
with Dàoyuán Zhìgāng and others, as well as the American envoy Pǔ'ānchén (Anson Burlingame), selected for the task.
In the first year of Guāngxù (1875),
the system for dispatching envoys was established.
Shìláng Guō Sōngtāo was ordered to serve as envoy to Great Britain,
Hànlín Yuàn Shìjiǎng Hé Rúzhāng to Japan,
and Jīngqīng Chén Lánbīn to the United States, Japan, and Peru.
All were appointed with deputy envoys.
Separate branch legations were set up for Peru and Japan,
and Consuls-General were appointed for San Francisco, Calcutta, and Cuba.
(Later, these became independent countries,
and ministers plenipotentiary were dispatched instead.)
In the second year (1876),
it was stipulated that legations should have two Councillors
and four Translators.
(In the fourteenth year (1888),
it was again stipulated that there should be two or three Translators and Attachés.
Branch legations should have one Councillor concurrently serving as Consul,
one Translator, and one Attaché,
with the number of Councillors remaining as before.
In the thirty-second year (1906),
the quotas for Councillors and other officials were set
as listed above.)
Thereafter, envoys were dispatched one after another.
The British envoy concurrently led Italy and Belgium.
The Russian envoy was concurrently stationed in Germany,
with Austria-Hungary and the Netherlands subordinate to him.
In the fourth year (1878),
a Consul for Singapore was appointed
(later changed to Consul-General),
and Administrators for various Japanese ports.
(Later changed to Consuls.)
The following year (1879),
the post of deputy envoy was abolished,
and a Consul for Honolulu was appointed.
In the eighth year (1882),
a Consul for New York was appointed.
In the thirteenth year (1887),
a Consul-General for Manila,
a Consul for Rangoon,
and a Vice-Consul for Penang were appointed.
(Later changed to Consul.)
In the seventeenth year (1891),
Consuls for various islands in the South Seas were appointed.
In the twenty-first year (1895),
a special envoy for France was appointed.
In the twenty-third year (1897),
a special envoy for Germany was appointed,
and the Netherlands became subordinate to him.
Consuls for Korea were also added.
(Withdrawn in the thirty-third year (1907),
and changed to Consuls-General.)
In the twenty-sixth year (1900),
Consuls for various ports in Korea
and a Commercial Commissioner for Vladivostok were appointed.
(Later changed to Consul-General.)
In the twenty-eighth year (1902),
the envoy to France was changed to concurrently serve as envoy to Japan,
and the envoy to the United States to concurrently serve as envoy to Cuba.
Separate branch legations were established,
and special envoys for Austria-Hungary, Italy, and Belgium were appointed.
The following year (1903),
a branch legation for Mexico was established.
In the thirtieth year (1904),
a Consul-General for South Africa was appointed.
In the thirty-first year (1905),
a special envoy for the Netherlands was appointed to concurrently manage the matters of the Peace Conference,
and the French and Japanese envoys were made to concurrently lead the Portuguese envoy.
Soon after, a Portuguese branch legation was established.
In the thirty-fourth year (1908),
envoys were designated as Second Rank special officials,
along with the ranks of Councillors and other officials.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
Consuls-General for Melbourne, Canada, and Panama were appointed.
Thereafter, Consuls for Australia, Vancouver, Samoa, and New Zealand followed consecutively.
In the third year (1911),
a Consul-General for Java,
and Consuls for Surabaya and Padang were appointed.
That autumn, a Consul for Sinuiju, Joseon, was appointed.
Third-class Envoys Plenipotentiary
(Third Rank,
specially appointed),
Councillors,
and Interpreters
have no fixed number
and are not permanently established.
One special envoy for the Peace Conference
(Second Rank,
specially appointed).
One Army Representative
(filled by military officers proficient in Western languages).
In the thirty-third year of Guāngxù (1907),
the concurrent post of Dutch envoy was abolished and a new position was created.
Dūbàn Shuìwù Dàchén (Minister Overseeing Taxation),
Bāngbàn Dàchén (Assistant Minister),
one of each.
(Filled by Dàxuéshì, Shàngshū, Shìláng.
Later changed to Dàchén, Fù Dàchén.)
They were in charge of customs duties
and overseeing customs officials.
Tídiào (Superintendent),
Bāng Tídiào (Assistant Superintendent),
Fènggǔ Zǒngbàn (Section Chief),
Bāngbàn (Assistant),
one of each.
(Filled concurrently by Wàiwù Bù and Dùzhī Bù Céng, Cān.)
Under their jurisdiction: Zǒng Shuìwù Sī (Inspector General of Customs),
Fù Zǒng Shuìwù Sī (Deputy Inspector General of Customs),
one of each.
Shuìwù Sī (Customs Commissioners) four people,
Fù Shuìwù Sī (Deputy Customs Commissioners) six people,
Customs Commissioners for each customhouse fifty-nine people.
(Cháohǎi five people.
Yuèhǎi, Yuèzhōu, Běihǎi three people each.
Jiāohǎi, Zhènjiāng, Dōnghǎi, Mǐnhǎi, Jīnhǎi, Jīnlíng, Sūzhōu, Jílín two people each.

Jiānghǎi, Wúzhōu, Gǒngběi, Hā'ěrbīn, Shānhǎi, Zhèhǎi, Xiàmén, Jiǔlóng, Jiǔjiāng, Yàdōng, Chángshā, Dàlián, Ōuhǎi, Fúhǎi, Sānshuǐ, Lóngzhōu, Hángzhōu, Āndōng, Shāshì, Chóngqìng, Jiāngmén, Nánníng, Qiónghǎi, Yíchāng, Fèngtiān, Téngyuè, Sīmáo, Méngzì one person each.)
Deputy Customs Commissioners thirty-seven people.
(Jiānghàn, Yuèhǎi, Jiānghǎi, Sānshuǐ, Jīnhǎi, Húnchūn three people each.
Dàlián, Cháohǎi, Qiónghǎi, Jiǔlóng two people each.
Sūzhōu, Nánníng, Lóngzhōu, Chóngqìng, Fèngtiān, Hángzhōu, Xiàmén, Mǐnhǎi, Hā'ěrbīn, Wúhú, Dàtōng Líjú one person each.)
(All of the above were foreigners.)
Initially,
the customs set up Jiāndū (Supervisors).
(Filled by senior departmental officials with long service.)
Soon, supervision was reverted to Dū and Fǔ,
merely in name.
Since the Dàoguāng reign,
as the maritime frontier expanded daily,
Běiyáng and Nányáng Tōngshāng Dàchén (Ministers for Northern and Southern Ports) were first established,
and the Guāndào and Jiāndū were subordinate to them.
Some generals also managed these concurrently.
(Jīnhǎi was managed by the Zhílì Jīnhǎi Dào,
Shānhǎi by the Fèngtiān Fèngjǐn Shānhǎi Dào,
Dōnghǎi by the Shāndōng Dēngláiqīng Dào,
all subordinate to Běiyáng.
Zhènjiāng was managed by the Jiāngsū Chángzhèn Tōngdào,
Jiānghǎi by the Jiāngsū Sūsōngtài Dào,
Wúhú by the Ānhuī Wǎnnán Dào,
Zhèhǎi by the Zhèjiāng Níngshàotái Dào,
Ōuhǎi by the Zhèjiāng Wēnchù Dào,
Jiānghàn by the Húběi Hànghuángdé Dào,
Yíchāng by the Húběi Jīngyíshī Dào,
Chóngqìng by the Sìchuān Chuāndōng Dào,
all subordinate to Nányáng.
Mǐnhǎi was managed by the Fúzhōu Jiāngjūn.
Yuèhǎi, Cháohǎi, Běihǎi, Qiónghǎi, Jiǔlóng, Gǒngběi,
each had one Jiāndū.
Jiāyù was managed by the Gānsù Ānsù Dào,
Lóngzhōu by the Guǎngxī Tàipíng Sīshùn Dào,
Méngzì by the Yúnnán Lín'ān Kāiguǎng Dào,
all subordinate to their respective provincial Dū or Fǔ.)
After Xiánfēng,
the Englishman Wēituǒmǎ (Wade) and the American Sīmìsī (Smith) were hired to assist with tax affairs,
followed by Lǐ Tàiguó (Robert Hart).
He was appointed Zǒng Shuìwù Sī (Inspector General of Customs);
all customhouses were staffed with Shuìwù Sī and Fù Shuìwù Sī.
(Later, various ports along the river,
and newly opened land border ports in the interior,
were also brought under customs jurisdiction.)
This marked the beginning of hiring foreign experts for the customs service.
At that time, the authority of jurisdiction belonged to the Zǒnglǐ Yámén.
In the twenty-third year of Guāngxù (1897),
the Shuìwù Chù (Customs Office) was established,
and the Zǒng Shuìwù Sī and all subordinate officials were subject to its direction.
Before this, the Hùguān (Household Customs) and Gōngguān (Works Customs) were subordinate to the Hù and Gōng ministries respectively;
at this point, they began to be designated as Chángguān (Regular Customs).
Subsequently, the Wàibù (Ministry of Foreign Affairs) and this office determined that separate tax bureaus should be established for Chángguān;
those more than fifty *lǐ* away were under the Jiāndū,
while those within fifty *lǐ* were under the Shuìwù Sī.
This is the origin of the names Nèi (Internal) and Wài (External) Chángguān.
Mínzhèng Bù (Ministry of Civil Affairs): Mínzhèng Dàchén (Minister of Civil Affairs),
Fù Dàchén (Vice Minister),
Zuǒ, Yòu Céng (Left and Right Secretary),
Zuǒ, Yòu Cānyì (Left and Right Counselors),
one of each.
Chéngzhèng Tīng Yuánwàiláng (Director of Administration, Bureau of Political Affairs),
Zhǔshì (Secretary),
Xiǎojīngguān (Junior Officials),
four of each.
Cānyì Tīng Cānshì (Counselors, Bureau of Counsel) two people.
Mínzhì, Jǐngzhèng, Jiānglǐ, Yíngshàn, Wèishēng Wǔ Sī (Five Bureaus of Civil Administration, Police Administration, Territory Management, Public Works, and Hygiene),
Lángzhōng (Director) eight people,
(Mínzhì,
Jǐngzhèng, Jiānglǐ two people each,
the rest one person each.)
Yuánwàiláng sixteen people,
(Mínzhì, Jǐngzhèng, Yíngshàn four people each,
the rest two people each.)
Zhǔshì eighteen people,
(Mínzhì, Jǐngzhèng five people each,
Yíngshàn four people,
the rest two people each.)
Xiǎojīngguān one person each.
Xíyì Suǒ Yuánwàiláng (Director of the Skills Training Institute) one person,
(also concurrently General Manager of the Fire Brigade.)
Zhǔshì two people,
Wǔ Pǐn Jǐngguān (Fifth-Rank Police Officers) five people,
(Fire Brigade three people.
Xíyì Suǒ two people.)
Liù, Qī Pǐn Jǐngguān (Sixth and Seventh-Rank Police Officers) nine people each,
(Fire Brigade six people each.
Xíyì Suǒ three people each.)
Bā, Jiǔ Pǐn Jǐngguān (Eighth and Ninth-Rank Police Officers) twelve people each.
(Fire Brigade eight people each.
Xíyì Suǒ four people each.
All of the above were subordinate to the Jǐngzhèng Sī.)
Liù, Qī Pǐn Yìshī (Sixth and Seventh-Rank Artisans) one person each.
(Subordinate to the Yíngshàn Sī.)
Liù, Qī Pǐn Yīguān (Sixth and Seventh-Rank Medical Officers) one person each.
(Subordinate to the Wèishēng Sī.
From police officers downwards, all were appointed by memorial.)
Bā Pǐn Lùshì (Eighth-Rank Clerks) twenty people,
Jiǔ Pǐn Lùshì (Ninth-Rank Clerks) thirty-two people.
(All appointed by consultation.)
The Dàchén (Minister) was in charge of household registers,
rectifying customs and education,
pacifying the populace,
to establish national governance.
The Fù Dàchén (Vice Minister) assisted.
Mínzhì (Civil Administration) was in charge of compiling and reviewing household registrations,
and also managed welfare and local administration.
Jǐngzhèng (Police Administration) was in charge of patrols and prohibitions,
and separately administered executive and judicial affairs.
Jiānglǐ (Territory Management) was in charge of territorial maps and gazetteers,
and examining land owned by officials and commoners.
Yíngshàn (Public Works) was in charge of imperial tomb projects,
repairing roads,
and preserving ancient relics and ancestral temples.
Wèishēng (Hygiene) was in charge of medical inspections and epidemic prevention,
and establishing hospitals.
Under its jurisdiction: Yùshěn Suǒ (Preliminary Review Office),
(later subordinate to the Dàlǐ Yuàn.)
Lùgōng Jú (Road Works Bureau),
Jiàoyǎng Jú (Education and Relief Bureau),
all managed by appointed officials.
In the thirtieth year of Guāngxù (1904),
the Xúnjǐng Bù (Ministry of Police) was established,
with a Shàngshū (Minister),
Zuǒ, Yòu Shìláng (Left and Right Vice Ministers),
Zuǒ, Yòu Céng (Left and Right Secretaries),
Cānyì (Counselor),
one of each.
Jǐngzhèng, Jǐngfǎ, Jǐngbǎo, Jǐngxué, Jǐngwù Wǔ Sī (Five Bureaus of Police Administration, Police Law, Police Security, Police Education, and Police Affairs),
Lángzhōng (Director) five people,
(two added in the thirty-second year.)
Yuánwàiláng and Zhǔshì sixteen people each,
(two Yuánwàiláng and four Zhǔshì added in the thirty-second year.
One Yíngshàn Sī added in the thirty-fourth year.)
Xiǎojīngguān four people,
(five added in the thirty-second year.)
Yī, Èr, Sān Děng Shūjìguān (First, Second, and Third Class Secretaries) ten people each.
(Modeled after the old system of Qī, Bā, Jiǔ Pǐn Bǐtiěshì.
Changed to Bā, Jiǔ Pǐn Lùshì in the thirty-second year.)
Xíyì Suǒ Yuánwàiláng (Director of the Skills Training Institute) one person,
Zhǔshì two people.
In the thirty-second year (1906),
it was renamed Mínzhèng Bù (Ministry of Civil Affairs).
Two bureaus, Chéngzhèng and Cānyì, were established,
and two Cānshì (Counselors) were appointed.
The Mínzhì, Jiānglǐ, Yíngshàn, and Wèishēng bureaus were re-established,
Jǐngzhèng remained as before.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
the quotas for the Xíyì Suǒ and Fire Brigade were set.
(As listed above.)
In the third year (1911),
Shàngshū was changed to Dàchén,
and Shìláng to Fù Dàchén.
The General Administrations of Patrol and Police for the Inner and Outer Cities,
each with one Tīngchéng.
(Initially of junior fourth rank.
In the 33rd year of Guāngxù, promoted to senior third rank.
Appointed by imperial selection.)
They were responsible for patrolling the wards and districts,
and also for guarding imperial routes.
The General Affairs Department had one Zǒngqiānshì each.
(Of senior fourth rank.
Appointed by memorial.)
The Administrative, Judicial, and Health Departments each had three Qiānshì.
(Of junior fifth rank.
All appointed by memorial.)
Four fifth-rank police officers.
Nineteen sixth-rank police officers.
(Ten in the Inner City.
Nine in the Outer City.)
Twenty seventh-rank police officers.
(Eleven in the Inner City.
Nine in the Outer City.)
Twenty-seven eighth-rank police officers.
(Fourteen in the Inner City.
Thirteen in the Outer City.)
Twenty-eight ninth-rank police officers.
(Fifteen in the Inner City.
Thirteen in the Outer City.
Seventh rank and above were appointed by memorial.
Eighth rank and below were appointed by official communication.)
Four record keepers each of eighth and ninth rank.
(Appointed by commission.)
In the 30th year of Guāngxù,
the General Administrations of Patrol and Police for the Inner and Outer Cities of the capital were established,
each with one Tīngchéng.
Three departments were established: General Affairs, Police Affairs, and Health,
each with one Cānshì.
(Of junior fifth rank.
In the 33rd year, changed to Qiānshì.)
The Inner City had five sub-administrations,
the Outer City had four sub-administrations,
with nine Zhīshì.
(Of junior fifth rank.)
In the 32nd year,
a Judicial Department was added.
Police Affairs was renamed Administration.
The rank of Qiānshì in the General Affairs Department was raised to that of a leading official among subordinates.
Police officers of fifth rank and below were appointed,
with no fixed number.
Four record keepers each of eighth and ninth rank.
The five Inner City sub-administrations were merged into three: Central, Left, and Right.
The four Outer City sub-administrations were merged into two: Left and Right,
reducing four Zhīshì.
Twenty-six districts were established in the Inner City,
and twenty in the Outer City,
each with one Qūguān (filled by sixth- and seventh-rank police officers,
later changed to Qūzhǎng)
and one Qūfù (filled by eighth- and ninth-rank police officers,
later changed to Qūyuán).
In the 34th year,
the number of Inner and Outer City districts was halved.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng,
the sub-administrations were abolished,
and the Zhīshì were reduced.
The Ministry of Finance (Dùzhībù):
One Dùzhīdàchén,
and one Fùdàchén.
One Zuǒchéng and one Yòuchéng.
One Zuǒcānyì and one Yòucānyì.
Both the Chéngzhèng and Cānyì Departments
each had three Lángzhōng,
four Yuánwàiláng,
and three Zhǔshì.

The ten Bureaus of Land Tax (Tiánfù), Grain Transport and Granaries (Cáocāng), Taxation (Shuìkè), Monopolies and Duties (Guǎnquè), Currency and Finance (Tōngfù), Treasury (Kùcáng), Salaries and Stipends (Liánfèng), Military Provisions (Jūnsiǎng), Expenditures (Zhìyòng), and Accounting (Kuàijì),
had thirty-one Lángzhōng,
(four for Zhìyòng,
three for each of the others.)
Forty-four Yuánwàiláng,
(six for Zhìyòng,
five each for Tiánfù and Kùcáng,
four for each of the others.)
Thirty-five Zhǔshì.
(Four each for Tiánfù, Guǎnquè, Tōngfù, Liánfèng, and Kuàijì,
three for each of the others.)
The Gold and Silver Treasury (Jīnyínkù),
had one Lángzhōng,
four Yuánwàiláng,
and two Zhǔshì.
The Receipt, Dispatch, and Audit Office (Shōufā Jīcháchù),
(renamed from the Supervisory and Urging Office,)
had one Yuánwàiláng,
and two Zhǔshì.
The Dàchén was responsible for overseeing calculations,
coordinating with banks and mints,
and the unified tax on native opium,
to manage national expenditures.
The Fùdàchén assisted.
Tiánfù was in charge of land and fiscal revenue,
and auditing the Zhuangtian (estate land) and acreage of the Eight Banners and Imperial Household.
Cáocāng was in charge of auditing and liquidating grain transport,
accumulating granary grain,
and the amount of military rice and grain in each province,
compiling these accounts for reporting.
Shuìkè was in charge of the unified tax on commercial goods,
comparing the surplus and deficit of Maritime and Regular Customs.
Guǎnquè was in charge of salt administration and miscellaneous taxes,
including inspecting transport routes,
various treasury collections and disbursements,
and the unified tax on native opium,
and verifying their actual figures.
Tōngfù was in charge of mining administration and currency system,
and inspecting documents from banks and mints.
Kùcáng was in charge of national treasury storage,
and guarding the two treasuries of pigments and silks.
Liánféng was in charge of auditing and issuing official salaries,
and reviewing the official stipends and meal allowances of all bureaus.
Jūnsiǎng was in charge of auditing and issuing military provisions,
and examining the provincial reports of remitted aid funds.
Zhìyòng was in charge of auditing construction funds,
planning various funds for the capital and provinces,
and also overseeing miscellaneous and customary expenditures.
Kuàijì was in charge of national income and expenditure,
auditing public debt and foreign loans,
and compiling income and expenditure statements.
Jīnyínkù was in charge of gold, silver, and regular financial meetings.
Shōufā Jīcháchù was in charge of receiving and dispatching affairs for all bureaus.
Under its jurisdiction: the Currency System Bureau (Bìzhìsī),
with one Tídiào,
and two Bāngtídiào.
(Concurrently held by the Chéng and Cān of this ministry.)
The General Affairs Office (Shùwùchù),
with various sections for investigation, planning, auditing, and compilation,
with designated personnel assigned to manage their respective tasks.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù,
it was reorganized from the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù),
incorporating the Department of Finance (Cáizhèngchù).
A Shàngshū,
a Zuǒshìláng and a Yòushìláng,
a Zuǒchéng and a Yòuchéng,
and a Cānyì,
each with one incumbent, were appointed.
The fourteen bureaus were combined into ten,
and officials from Lángzhōng downwards were reappointed.
(As listed previously.)
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
Shàngshū was renamed Dàchén,
and Shìláng was renamed Fùdàchén.
The Financial Review Office (Qīnglǐ Cáizhèngchù),
had two Tídiào,
and two Bāngtídiào.
(Concurrently held by the Chéng and Cān of this ministry.)
One Zǒngbàn,
and one Bāngzǒngbàn.
The number of Zǒnghézuòbàn Kēyuán was not fixed.
Twenty Chief Financial Supervisors (Qīnglǐ Cáizhèng Zhèngjiānlǐguān) in various provinces,
(given the honorary title of junior third or junior fourth rank Qing,
one each for Fèngtiān, Zhílì, Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, Shǎnxī, Gānsù, Xīnjiāng, Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húběi, Húnán, Sìchuān, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxi, Yúnnán, Guìzhōu.)
Twenty-four Deputy Financial Supervisors (Fùjiānlǐguān).
(Appointed by memorial, one each for Jílín, Hēilóngjiāng, Jiāngníng, and Liǎnghuái,
the rest corresponding to the Chief Financial Supervisors.)
Established in the 1st year of Xuāntǒng.
The Dàqīng Bank (Dàqīng Yínháng),
had one Chief Supervisor (Zhèngjiāndū),
(of junior third rank.
Appointed by imperial selection.)
And one Deputy Supervisor (Fùjiāndū).
The Savings Bank had one Zǒngbàn.
Branch banks had twenty Zǒngbàn.

(One each for Jīn [Tiānjīn], Hù [Shànghǎi], Hàn [Hànkǒu], Jì [Jǐnán], Fèng [Fèngtiān], Yíng [Yíngkǒu], Kù [Kùlún], Chóng [Chóngqìng], Guǎng [Guǎngzhōu], Gàn [Gànzhōu], Jìn [Tàiyuán], Biàn [Kāifēng], Zhè [Hángzhōu], Mǐn [Fúzhōu], Jí [Jílín], Qín [Xī'ān], Wǎn [Ānqìng], Xiāng [Chángshā], Diān [Kūnmíng], Níng [Nánjīng].)
(The above were appointed by memorial by the Dàchén.)
In the 33rd year of Guāngxù,
the Hùbù Bank was established,
with a Zǒngjiāndū,
whose rank was equivalent to that of Zuǒchéng.
It was later renamed Zhèngjiāndū.
The following year, it was renamed Dàqīng Yínháng.
The General Mint (Zàobì Zǒngchǎng),
had one Chief Supervisor (Zhèngjiāndū),
(of junior third rank.
Appointed by imperial selection.)
And two Deputy Supervisors (Fùjiāndū).
Branch mints (Fēnchǎng),
had five Zǒngbàn (Fèngtiān, Jiāngníng, Guǎngzhōu, Sìchuān, Yúnnán,
concurrently held by the Chief Financial Supervisors),
and five Bāngbàn (Jiāngníng, Wǔchāng, Guǎngzhōu, Sìchuān, Yúnnán,
concurrently held by the Deputy Financial Supervisors).
Established in the 33rd year of Guāngxù.
Xuébù:
Xuéfù Dàchén,
Fù Dàchén, each one person.
Zuǒ Chéng, Yòu Chéng,
Zuǒ Cānyì, Yòu Cānyì,
each one person.
Cānshì Tīng cānshì four people.
Sīwù Tīng sīwù two people.
Zǒngwù, Zhuānmén, Pǔtōng, Shíyè, Kuàijì five Sī.
Lángzhōng each two people,
Yuánwàiláng fifteen people.
(Zǒngwù five people,
Pǔtōng four people,
the rest each two people.)
Zhǔshì eighteen people.
(Zǒngwù and Pǔtōng each six people,
the rest each two people.)
Yīděng Shūjìguān (Rank 7a.
Appointed by imperial decree.)
eleven people,
Èrděng (Rank 8a.)
seventeen people,
Sānděng (Rank 9a.)
fifteen people.
(Èr and Sān Děng were all appointed by recommendation.)
The Dàchén was in charge of promoting learning and cultivating talent,
and inspecting and promulgating various school policies and decrees,
to enlighten the people's intellect.
The Fù Dàchén assisted him.
The Zǒngwù was in charge of confidential documents and dispatches,
and reviewing books and classics.
The Zhuānmén was in charge of Dàxué and Gāoděng Xuéxiào,
and all professional programs in politics and arts were under its comprehensive leadership.
The Pǔtōng was in charge of Shīfàn, Zhōng, and Xiǎo Xuéxiào,
each inspecting and supervising curricula according to their statutory regulations.
The Shíyè was in charge of Nóng, Gōng, and Shāng Xuéxiào,
and also reviewed various industries in the provinces,
to create benefits for the people.
The Kuàijì was in charge of managing income and expenditure,
taking custody of instruments and materials,
and educational grants.
Those concurrently managed included:
Bāqí Xuéwù Chù Zǒnglǐ,
Xiélǐ,
Dūxué,
Diàochá Túshū Gè Júzhǎng,
Júyuán,
Biāndìng Míngcí Guǎn Zǒngzuǎn,
Túshūguǎn Zhèng Fù Jiāndū, and subsequent various officials.
These were all chosen for appointment
and no special official positions were established.
In Guāngxù twenty-second year,
a Guǎnlǐ Guānshū Jú Dàchén was established.
(Previously, a Qiángxué Shūjú was established in the capital,
to thoroughly study current affairs.
At this time, it was converted to official management.)
In the twenty-seventh year,
Shàngshū Zhāng Bǎixī was further appointed as Guǎnxué Dàchén,
to manage the Dàxué Táng.
In the twenty-ninth year,
it was changed to Xuéwù Dàchén.
In the thirty-second year,
the Xuébù was finally established,
with a Shàngshū,
Shìláng,
Zuǒ Chéng, Yòu Chéng,
Cānyì,
each one person;
Lángzhōng of the five Sī each one person,
Yuánwàiláng twelve people,
Zhǔshì fifteen people,
and the Shìxuéguān had no fixed quota.
(Designated Rank 5a.
Temporarily filled by Sī Yuán.)
The following year,
Grand Secretary Zhāng Zhīdòng was ordered to lead the department,
which was not a permanent system.
In Xuāntǒng first year,
Shìxuéguān was changed to a temporary assignment,
and five Lángzhōng, four Yuánwàiláng, and three Zhǔshì were added.
In the third year,
Shàngshū was changed to Dàchén,
and Shìláng to Fù Dàchén.
Guózǐjiān:
Chéng one person.
(Rank 4a.
Requested for selection.)
In charge of the ceremonies of the Wénmiào and Pìyōng.
Diǎnbù (Rank 7a.
Appointed by imperial decree.)
four people,
in charge of sacrificial rites and temple households.
Diǎnjí (Rank 8a.
Appointed by recommendation.)
four people,
in charge of sacrificial vessels and musical instruments.
Wénmiào Rank 7, 8, and 9 Fèngsìguān each two people.
(Appointed by recommendation.)
Zhèng Tōngzànguān (Rank 6b.
Appointed by imperial decree.)
and Fù Tōngzànguān (Rank 8b.
Appointed by recommendation.)
each two people.
Èr and Sān Děng Shūjìguān each three people.
Established in Guāngxù thirty-second year.
Dàxué Táng:
Zǒng Jiāndū one person.
(Rank 3a.
Requested for selection.)
Jīng, Fǎ, Wén, Gōng, Shāng five sections' Jiāndū each one person.
(Appointed by imperial command.)
Jiàowù, Shùwù, Zhāiwù Tídiào,
were all invited to serve by those familiar with educational affairs.
In Guāngxù twenty-fifth year,
the Jīngshī Dàxué Táng was founded,
and Grand Secretary Sūn Jiānài was ordered to lead it.
In the thirty-second year,
Zǒng Jiāndū was designated as a special official.
Lùjūnbù (Ministry of the Army) Lùjūn Dàchén (Minister of the Army),

Tèjiǎn.) one person each.

The Dàchén (Minister) is in charge of the army,
responsible for inspecting and issuing regulations for barracks, provisions, and chapters,
to consolidate land defense.
The Fù Dàchén (Vice Minister) assists him.
The Cānshì (Counselor) is in charge of laws and regulations.
The Jiǎncháguān (Inspector General) is in charge of inspecting the army, schools, bureaus, and factories.
The Bù Fùguān (Department Adjutant) is in charge of transmitting orders.
The Chéngzhèng (Secretary) is in charge of handling incoming and outgoing documents,
and distinguishing between the merits and demerits of officials and staff.
The Jūnzhì (Military Organization Bureau) is in charge of organization, conscription, and deployment,
as well as the manufacturing of all military equipment,
communication infrastructure,
and the examination and verification of legal standards.
The Jūnhéng (Military Ranks Bureau) is in charge of official ranks,
grades (Dàjiāngjūn (Grand General) and Jiāngjūn (General) are Zheng Yīpǐn (Senior First Rank),
filled by Zhèng Dūtǒng (General Commandant) with accumulated merits.
Zhèng Dūtǒng is Cóng Yīpǐn (Junior First Rank),
Fù Dūtǒng (Deputy Commandant) is Zhèng Èrpǐn (Senior Second Rank),
Xié Dūtǒng (Assistant Commandant) is Cóng Èrpǐn (Junior Second Rank),
Zhèng Cānlǐng (Senior Captain) is Zhèng Sānpǐn (Senior Third Rank),
Fù Cānlǐng (Deputy Captain) is Cóng Sānpǐn (Junior Third Rank),
Xié Cānlǐng (Assistant Captain) is Zhèng Sìpǐn (Senior Fourth Rank),
Zhèng Jūnxiào (Senior Officer Cadet) is Zhèng Wǔpǐn (Senior Fifth Rank),
Fù Jūnxiào (Deputy Officer Cadet) is Zhèng Liùpǐn (Senior Sixth Rank),
Xié Jūnxiào (Assistant Officer Cadet) is Zhèng Qīpǐn (Senior Seventh Rank),
Sīwùzhǎng (Chief Steward) and Jìshìzhǎng (Chief Technician) are Zhèng Bāpǐn (Senior Eighth Rank),
Shàngshì (Sergeant First Class) is Cóng Bāpǐn (Junior Eighth Rank),
Zhōngshì (Sergeant) is Zhèng Jiǔpǐn (Senior Ninth Rank),
Xiàshì (Corporal) is Cóng Jiǔpǐn (Junior Ninth Rank).
There are fourteen grades),
and honorary titles (a total of three ranks and nine grades: the first grade of the upper rank is the position of Zhèng Dūtǒng,
serving as Zǒngtǒngguān (Presidential Officer),
with a rank equivalent to Tídū (Provincial Commander-in-Chief).
The second grade is the position of Fù Dūtǒng,
serving as Tǒngzhìguān (Commander),
with a rank equivalent to Zǒngbīng (Brigade General).
The third grade is the position of Xié Dūtǒng,
serving as Tǒnglǐngguān (Battalion Commander),
with a rank equivalent to Fùjiàng (Deputy General).
The first grade of the middle rank is the position of Zhèng Cānlǐng,
serving as Tǒngzhìguān (Commander),
Zhèng Cānmóuguān (Senior Staff Officer),
Gōngduì Cānlǐngguān (Engineer Corps Captain),
Zǒng Jūnjièguān (Chief Ordnance Officer),
Hùjūnguān (Guard Officer);
those with the same position as Zhèng Cānlǐng serve as
Zǒng Jūnxūguān (Chief Quartermaster),
Zǒnglǐ Yīguān (Chief Medical Officer),
Zǒng Zhífǎguān (Chief Legal Officer),
with a rank equivalent to Cānjiàng (Colonel).
The second grade is the position of Fù Cānlǐng,
serving as Jiàoliànguān (Training Officer),
Yīděng Cānmóuguān (First-Class Staff Officer),
Zhèng Jūnjièguān (Senior Ordnance Officer),
Zhōngjūnguān (Headquarters Officer);
those with the same position as Fù Cānlǐng serve as
Zhèng Jūnxūguān (Senior Quartermaster),
Zhèng Jūnyīguān (Senior Medical Officer),
Zhèng Zhífǎguān (Senior Legal Officer),
Zǒng Mǎyīguān (Chief Veterinary Officer),
Yīděng Shūjìguān (First-Class Secretary),
with a rank equivalent to Yóují (Major).
The third grade is the position of Xié Cānlǐng,
serving as Guǎndàiguān (Company Commander),
Èrděng Cānmóuguān (Second-Class Staff Officer),
Fù Jūnjièguān (Deputy Ordnance Officer),
Cānjūnguān (Adjutant);
those with the same position as Xié Cānlǐng serve as
Fù Jūnxūguān (Deputy Quartermaster),
Fù Jūnyīguān (Deputy Medical Officer),
Zhèng Mǎyīguān (Senior Veterinary Officer),
Èrděng Shūjìguān (Second-Class Secretary),
with a rank equivalent to Dūsī (Captain).
The first grade of the lower rank is the position of Zhèng Jūnxiào,
serving as Dūdùiguān (Platoon Commander),
Duìguān (Team Leader),
Sānděng Cānmóuguān (Third-Class Staff Officer),
Chámǎzhǎng (Chief Horse Inspector),
Jūnjièzhǎng (Chief Armorer),
Zhíshìguān (Duty Officer);
those with the same position as Zhèng Jūnxiào serve as
Jūnxūzhǎng (Quartermaster Sergeant),
Jūnyīzhǎng (Medical Sergeant),
Jīcháguān (Investigator),
Jūnyuèduìguān (Military Band Officer),
Fù Mǎyīguān (Deputy Veterinary Officer),
Sānděng Shūjìguān (Third-Class Secretary),
with a rank equivalent to Shǒubèi (Lieutenant).
The second grade is the position of Fù Jūnxiào,
serving as Páizhǎng (Squad Leader),
Zhǎngqíguān (Flag Bearer);
those with the same position as Fù Jūnxiào serve as
Sīshìshēng (Clerk),
Yīshēng (Doctor),
Sīhàoguān (Signal Officer),
Jūnyuèpáizhǎng (Military Band Squad Leader),
Mǎyīzhǎng (Veterinary Sergeant),
Shūjìzhǎng (Chief Clerk),
with a rank equivalent to Qiānzǒng (Lieutenant);
those with the same position as Xié Jūnxiào serve as
Sīhàozhǎng (Chief Signalman),
Yīshēng (Doctor),
Sīshūshēng (Scribe),
with a rank equivalent to Bǎzǒng (Sergeant Major)).
Also in charge of enfeoffment, bestowal, and hereditary privilege, as well as the registration of all military officers and auxiliary staff.
The Jūnxū (Military Provisions Bureau) is in charge of rations, provisions, weapons, and fodder,
and also oversees the training of quartermaster personnel.
The Jūnyī (Military Medical Bureau) is in charge of disease prevention and treatment,
and also oversees the promotion and training of medical personnel.
The Jūnfǎ (Military Law Bureau) is in charge of trials and prisons,
and reviewing military treaties.
The Jūnshísuǒ (Military Materiel Office) is in charge of matters
equivalent to the former Wǔkùsī (Armory Department).
The Jūnmùsuǒ (Military Horsemanship Office) is in charge of matters
equivalent to the former Tàipúsì (Court of the Imperial Stud).
The Jūnxué (Military Education Bureau) is in charge of school education
and troop drills.
The Shěnjì (Auditing Bureau) is in charge of budgets and final accounts,
and auditing expenditures.
Under its jurisdiction are: the Xiànzhèng Chóubèichù (Constitutional Preparatory Office),
Yínkù (Treasury),
Jiébàochù (Intelligence Office),
Mǎguǎn (Horse Stables),
with personnel assigned to manage their respective affairs.
In the 32nd year of the Guāngxù reign (1906), the Bīngbù (Ministry of War) was reorganized and established.
The Liànbīngchù (Army Reorganization and Training Bureau) was merged into it.
(Previously, a Zǒnglǐ Qīnwáng (Chief Prince) was appointed,
along with one Huìbàn (Associate Director), one Xiāngbàn (Assistant Director), and one Tídiào (Superintendent).
There were also one Chief and one Deputy for each of the three departments: Jūngzhèng (Military Administration), Jūnnglìng (Military Command), and Jūnxué (Military Education).
From the Qīnwáng downwards, all were appointed by imperial decree.
Personnel evaluation, procurement of provisions and fodder,
medical affairs, law, and ordnance were subordinate to Jūngzhèng.
Strategy, guidance, surveying and mapping, and talent reserves were subordinate to Jūnnglìng.
Translation, training, education, and naval affairs were subordinate to Jūnxué.
There was one Supervisor for each of the fourteen sections,
all selected and appointed by the Zǒnglǐ.
) A Shàngshū (Minister) was appointed,
along with a Zuǒ Shìláng (Senior Vice Minister) and a Yòu Shìláng (Junior Vice Minister),
one of each.
Two offices, Chéngzhèng (Administration) and Cānyì (Deliberation), were established,
with one Zuǒ Chéng (Left Administrator), one Yòu Chéng (Right Administrator),
and one Cānyì (Councillor)
each.
There were also First, Second, and Third Class Zīyìguān (Advisory Officers) and Jiǎncáchuān (Inspectors),
(talented civil and military officials were selected to fill these roles.)
and Chief and Deputy Cóngshìguān (Executive Officers),
(filled by Fùxiécānlǐng (Associate Junior Captains).)
without a fixed number.

Ten departments were established: Jūnhéng (Military Assessment), Jūnchéng (Military Transport), Jūnjì (Military Accounting), Jūnshí (Military Materiel), Jūnzhì (Military System), Jūnxū (Military Provisions), Jūnxué (Military Education), Jūnyī (Military Medical), Jūnfǎ (Military Law), and Jūnmù (Military Animal Husbandry).
Each department was staffed with one Sīzhǎng (Department Head),
thirty-three Kēzhǎng (Section Chiefs),
two hundred and five First, Second, and Third Class Kēyuán (Clerks),
twelve Chéngfāguān (Dispatch Officers),
(two for Chéngzhèng,
and one for each of the others.
Jūnfǎ had none yet.)
five Yìyuán (Translators),
two Huìtúyuán (Draftsmen), two Yìshī (Artisans), and two Yìshì (Technicians) each,
and one hundred and sixteen Lùshì (Recorders).
Sixteen Lángzhōng (Secretaries) were appointed,
eighteen Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Secretaries),
twenty-two Zhǔshì (Clerks),
and one hundred and ten Bǐtiēshì (Copyists).
(These collectively formed the staff quota of the Ministry,
and were not assigned to specific departments.)
Eight Zhèngcānlǐng (Senior Captains),
four Tóngzhèngcānlǐng (Concurrent Senior Captains).
Twelve Fùcānlǐng (Associate Captains),
six Tóngfùcānlǐng (Concurrent Associate Captains).
Eighteen Xiécānlǐng (Junior Captains),
eight Tóngxiécānlǐng (Concurrent Junior Captains).
(These quotas were equivalent to Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, and Zhǔshì respectively.)
Eighteen Zhèngjūnxiào (Senior Cadets),
eight Tóngzhèngjūnxiào (Concurrent Senior Cadets).
Twenty-four Fùjūnxiào (Associate Cadets),
twelve Tóngfùjūnxiào (Concurrent Associate Cadets).
Thirty-two Xiéjūnxiào (Junior Cadets),
sixteen Tóngxiéjūnxiào (Concurrent Junior Cadets).
(These quotas were equivalent to ranks 7, 8, and 9 Bǐtiēshì respectively.)
Officials were assigned to various posts based on their ranks.
In the 33rd year (1907),
Qìng Qīnwáng Yìkuāng was ordered to lead the Ministry,
which was an irregular arrangement.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
the army officer system was revised.
From Zhèngcānlǐng downwards for military officers,
and from Fùdūtǒng downwards for military aides,
all were named according to their specialized subjects
and prefixed with their respective corps (such as cavalry, infantry, artillery, engineering, transport, and police corps,
including Zhèng, Fù, Xiécānlǐng,
Zhèng, Fù, Xiéjūnxiào,
Sīwùzhǎng (Quartermasters),
and the ranks of Shangshì (Master Sergeant), Zhōngshì (Sergeant), Xiàshì (Corporal), etc.).
Specialized titles (such as Jūnxū, Jūnyī, Zhìxiè Fùxiédūtǒng (Associate Junior Commanders for Provisions, Medical, Ordnance),
Zhèng, Fù, Xiédūtǒng (Senior, Associate, Junior Commanders),
Zhèng, Fù, Xiéjūnxiào (Senior, Associate, Junior Cadets),
Mǎyī (Veterinarian), Cèhuì (Surveying and Mapping) Zhèng, Fù, Xiécānlǐng (Senior, Associate, Junior Captains),
Zhèng, Fù, Xiéjūnxiào (Senior, Associate, Junior Cadets),
Jūnyuè Xiéjūnxiào (Junior Military Band Cadet),
Cèhuì (Surveying and Mapping), Jūnyuè (Military Band) Sīwùzhǎng (Quartermasters),
and Shang, Zhōng, Xià Shì (Master Sergeants, Sergeants, Corporals),
Kuàijì (Accounting), Tiáohù (Nursing) Shang, Zhōng, Xià Shì (Master Sergeants, Sergeants, Corporals)
) had the character "Tóng" (concurrent) removed.
In the 2nd year (1910),
Shàngshū was changed to Dàchén (Minister),
and Shìláng to Fùdàchén (Vice Minister).
The positions of Zuǒ, Yòu Chéng,
Cānyì,
Zīyì,
and Chéngfā officers were abolished.
The two offices and ten departments were merged into eight departments.
(An additional Chéngzhèng department was added,
while Jūnchéng, Jūnjì, and Jūnxué departments were abolished.)
Jūnxué (Military Education) and Shěnjì (Audit) Bureaus were established.
The following year (1911),
the system for supplementary army officers and aides was finalized.
Ministry Fùguān (Adjutants) and Diàocháyuán (Investigators) were appointed.
The Jūnshí (Military Materiel) Department was merged into Jūnzhì (Military System).
The Jūnmù (Military Animal Husbandry) Department and Jūnxué (Military Education) Bureau were temporarily established,
with the hope of laying the foundation for a Jūnmǎ Zǒngjiān (Inspector General of Military Horses) and a Jūnxiéyuàn (Military Academy).
In the 3rd year (1911),
the system for appointment of army officers and aides was re-established,
(as previously listed.)
and still intertwined with the former departmental staff.
Hǎijūnbù (Ministry of Navy): Hǎijūn Dàchén (Minister of Navy),
(Zhèngdūtǒng (Senior Commander) rank.)
Fùdàchén (Vice Minister),

one of each.
Two First-Class Cānmóuguān (Staff Officers),
four Second-Class.

Two Cānshìguān (Counsellors).

Sīdiànyuán (Telegraphers),
Yìshī (Artisans),
Yìshì (Technicians),

Lùshì (Recorders),
