without a fixed quota.

Seven departments: Jūnzhì (Military System), Jūngzhèng (Military Administration), Jūnxué (Military Education), Jūnshū (Military Secretariat), Jūnchú (Military Logistics), Jūnfǎ (Military Law), and Jūnyī (Military Medical).
One Sīzhǎng (Department Head) for each department.
(Filled by Xiédūtǒng (Junior Commanders) or Zhèngcānlǐng (Senior Captains).)
Twenty-one Kēzhǎng (Section Chiefs).
(Jūnzhì had five sections: Zhìdù (Regulations),
Kǎohé (Review),
Quánhéng (Assessment),
Jiàshǐ (Navigation),
Lúnjī (Machinery).
Jūngzhèng had three sections: Zhìzào (Manufacturing),
Jiànzhú (Construction),
Qìxiè (Ordnance).
Jūnxué had five sections: Jiàoyù (Education),
Xùnliàn (Training),
Móulüè (Strategy),
Zhēncè (Reconnaissance),
Biānyì (Compilation and Translation).
Jūnshū had three sections: Zòuzī (Memorials and Communications),
Diǎnzhāng (Regulations),
Chéngfā (Dispatch).
Jūnchú had three sections: Shōuzhī (Income and Expenditure),
Chúbèi (Reserves),
Shùwù (General Affairs).
Jūnyī had two sections: Yīwù (Medical Affairs),
Wèishēng (Hygiene).
One Kēzhǎng for each section.
Filled by Zhèng, Fù Cānlǐng (Senior and Associate Captains).
Same applies below.
) Sixty First, Second, and Third Class Kēyuán (Clerks).
(Jūnzhì and Jūnxué each had fourteen.
Jūnshū and Jūnchú each had ten.
Jūngzhèng had eight.
Jūnyī had four.
Appointments were similar to the Ministry of Army.)
Two First-Class Sīfǎguān (Judicial Officers),
Second and Third Class Sīfǎguān,
and eight Xuéxísīfǎguān (Probationary Judicial Officers).
(Filled by military officers who studied law.)
One Jìzhǎng (Chief Accountant) for the Zhǔjìchù (Accounting Bureau).
(Filled by Zhèngcānlǐng (Senior Captains).)
Two Kēzhǎng (Section Chiefs).
(One for Kuàijì (Accounting) and one for Tǒngjì (Statistics).)
Forty-eight Lùshì (Recorders) for all departments and bureaus.
The Dàchén (Minister) was responsible for leading the navy,
inspecting naval forces and headquarters,
to secure the maritime borders.
The Fùdàchén (Vice Minister) assisted him.
Cānmóu (Staff Officers) were responsible for participating in reforms.
Cānshì (Counsellors) were responsible for laws and regulations.
Mìshū (Secretaries) were responsible for confidential documents.
Jūnzhì (Military System) was responsible for regulations and assessment laws,
distinguishing naval personnel,
and managing merits, demerits, imperial patronage, rewards, and pensions.
Jūngzhèng (Military Administration) was responsible for building ships,
inspecting ordnance,
and also managing naval port engineering.
Jūnxué (Military Education) was responsible for school education
and fleet training.
Jūnshū (Military Secretariat) was responsible for documents and regulations,
and compiling records of staff meetings and official papers.
Jūnchú (Military Logistics) was responsible for managing expenditures,
and inspecting provisions, uniforms, and other materiel.
The duties of Jūnfǎ (Military Law), Jūnyī (Military Medical), and Zhǔjì (Accounting) were similar to those of the Ministry of Army.
In the eleventh year of Guāngxù
an imperial edict established the Hǎijūn Yámén (Naval Office).
Following the precedent of the Jūnjī Zǒngshǔ (Grand Council),
Yīxīn, Prince Chún, was ordered to oversee it,
and Grand Secretary Lǐ Hóngzhāng was specifically tasked with its planning and establishment.
In the thirteenth year
the Běiyáng Navy was formed,
with the posts of Tídū (Admiral), Zǒngbīng (Commander-in-Chief), and other officers.
In the Jiǎwǔ year
Not until the thirty-third year
was its restoration first proposed,
and the Hǎijūn Chù (Naval Department) was established,
temporarily subordinated to the Lùjūn Bù (Ministry of the Army).
One Zhèngshǐ (Chief Commissioner) was appointed,
(ranking as Xiédūtǒng,
or Associate Commander-in-Chief.) One Fùshǐ (Deputy Commissioner) was appointed,
(ranking as Zhèngcānlǐng,
or Senior Adjutant.)
Two Chéngfā Guān (Receiving and Dispatching Officers),
and four Lùshì (Clerks).
Three Divisions were established: Jīyào (Confidential Affairs), Chuánzhèng (Naval Administration), and Yùnchóu (Strategy),
with one Sīzhǎng (Division Chief) and one Fùguān (Adjutant) each.
Seven Kēzhǎng (Section Chiefs) were appointed,
(four in the Jīyào Section: namely Zhìdù (Regulations),
Chóuxiè (Armament Planning),
Jiàyù (Command),
and Lúnjī (Engine Machinery).
Three in the Yùnchóu Section: namely Móulüè (Tactics),
Jiàowù (Training Affairs),
and Cèhǎi (Hydrography).
One person for each section.
The Chuánzhèng Section was not divided into sub-sections.)
Three Chéngfā Guān (Receiving and Dispatching Officers),
(one for each division.)
Eighteen Yī Èr Sān Děng Kēyuán (First, Second, and Third Class Section Members).
(Twelve in Jīyào,
six in Yùnchóu.)
Five Kǎogōng Guān (Inspectors of Works),
(appointed by the Chuánzhèng Division.)
Three Yìshī (Artisans),
(one in Chuánzhèng,
two in Yùnchóu.)
Four Yìshì (Technicians).
(Two each in Chuánzhèng and Yùnchóu.)
Gǔzhǎng (Squad Leaders) and Gǔyuán (Squad Members)
were appointed according to the urgency of tasks.
Eighteen Lùshì (Clerks).
The following year
it was reorganized into six divisions: Hǎizhèng (Naval Affairs), Chuánzhèng (Naval Administration), Chóubèi (Preparation), Chúxù (Logistics), Yīwù (Medical Affairs), and Fǎwù (Legal Affairs).
Soon after, a Zhǔjì Chù (Accounting Office) was established,
with one Jìzhǎng (Accountant-in-Chief) and one Fùzhǎng (Deputy Accountant-in-Chief).
In the first year of Xuāntǒng
Shànqí, Prince Sù, and others were ordered to prepare for the navy,
and a Cānzàn Tīng (Advisory Council) was established,
divided into two divisions: Mìshū (Secretarial) and Shùwù (General Affairs),
with First, Second, and Third Class Cānmóu Guān (Staff Officers).
Additionally, the First, Second, Third, and Fourth Divisions were established,
with Sīzhǎng (Division Chiefs) and other positions.
That summer,
Bèilè Zǎitāo and others were again appointed as Chóubàn Hǎijūn Dàchén (Ministers for Naval Preparation),
and an Yīwù Sī (Medical Affairs Division) was added.
In the second year
the provisional naval official system was enacted,
renaming the First Division to Jūnzhì (Military System),
the Second Division to Jūnzhèng (Military Administration),
the Third Division to Jūnxué (Military Education),
the Fourth to Jūnfáng (Military Defense),
the Yīwù Sī to Jūnyī (Military Medical),
the Mìshū Sī to Jūnshū (Military Secretariat),
and the Shùwù Sī to Jūnchǔ (Military Supply);
a separate Jūnfǎ Sī (Military Law Division) was established,
making a total of eight divisions.
The positions in the Cānzàn Tīng were abolished.
Soon after, the Chù (Department) was reorganized into a Bù (Ministry),
the Jūnfáng Sī was abolished,
and one Dàchén (Minister) and one Fùdàchén (Vice Minister) were appointed.
Fǎ Bù (Ministry of Justice) – one Sīfǎ Dàchén (Minister of Justice),
one Fùdàchén (Vice Minister).
One Zuǒ Chéng (Left Chancellor), one Yòu Chéng (Right Chancellor),
one Cānyì (Councillor).
Four Cānshì (Advisers).

Eight Divisions: Shěnlù (Review of Cases), Zhìkān (Sentencing and Inspection), Biānzhì (Exile and Placement), Yòuxù (Clemency), Jǔ (Appointments), Diǎnyù (Prison Administration), Kuàijì (Accounting), and Dūshì (General Affairs).
Twenty-five Lángzhōng (Director).
(Four in Shěnlù,
including one position reserved for an Imperial Clan member.
Three in each of the others.)
Thirty-four Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Director).
(Five each in Zhìkān and Biānzhì,
including one position reserved for an Imperial Clan member in each.
Four in each of the others.)
Thirty-three Zhǔshì (Secretary).
(Five in Yòuxù,
including one position reserved for an Imperial Clan member.
Four in each of the others.)
Two Yuánwàiláng and two Zhǔshì in the Shōufā Suǒ (Reception and Dispatch Office).
Twenty-six Qīpǐn Xiǎo Jīngguān (Seventh Rank Junior Officials).
(Including two positions reserved for Imperial Clan members.)
Fifty-three Bāpǐn Lùshì (Eighth Rank Clerks),
and thirty Jiǔpǐn (Ninth Rank Clerks).
(Including two positions reserved for Imperial Clan members in each.)
The Dàchén was in charge of legal functions,
supervising the Dàlǐ Yuàn (Grand Court of Revision) and judicial and procuratorial affairs in the capital and provinces,
to maintain the rule of law.
The Fùdàchén assisted him.
Shěnlù was in charge of reviewing and recording prisoners for imperial review,
and re-examining criminal cases from the Dàlǐ Yuàn and trial courts.
(Also responsible for inspecting cases from Yúnnán, Guìzhōu, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, and the Left Wing of Cháhā'ěr.)
Zhìkān was in charge of recording the actual deferments of autumn executions
and determining sentences and prohibitions.
(Also responsible for inspecting cases from Sìchuān, Hénán, Shǎnxī, Gānsù, Xīnjiāng, Wūlǐyàsūtái, and Kēbùduō.)
Biānzhì was in charge of reducing sentences for robbers
and determining locations for exile.
(Also responsible for inspecting cases from Fèngtiān, Jílín, Hēilóngjiāng, Shāndōng, Shānxī, the Right Wing of Cháhā'ěr, Suīyuǎn Chéng, and Guīhuà Chéng.)
Yòuxù was in charge of imperial edicts of clemency,
and clearing up miscellaneous prison cases.
(Also responsible for inspecting cases from Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, Húběi, and Húnán.)
Jǔ was in charge of promotions, transfers, and appointments,
registering merits and demerits,
and recruiting and examining judicial officials, lawyers, and clerks.
Diǎnyù was in charge of repairing prisons,
securing locks,
and managing records of captives and forced laborers in art training workshops.
Kuàijì was in charge of financial receipts and disbursements,
and verifying fines and precious metals.
Dūshì was in charge of translating memorials,
and receiving and dispatching documents concerning prisoners.
Under its jurisdiction: two Sīyù Zǒngguǎn Shǒuzhǎng (Chief Wardens of Prisons) and two Zhèngguǎn Shǒuzhǎng (Wardens),
six Fùguǎn Shǒuzhǎng (Deputy Wardens),
one Jiānyī Zhèng (Senior Prison Doctor) (ranking as Zhèng Bāpǐn),
and one Jiānyī Fù (Junior Prison Doctor) (ranking as Zhèng Jiǔpǐn).
Established in the thirty-second year of Guāngxù
with a Shàngshū (President),
Shìláng (Vice President),
Zuǒ Chéng (Left Chancellor), Yòu Chéng (Right Chancellor), Cān (Councillor), and other subordinate officials.
The seventeen divisions were consolidated into eight divisions.
A Shōufā Suǒ (Reception and Dispatch Office) was established.
Yuánwàiláng and Zhǔshì and other officials were appointed.
The following year
one Zōngshì Lángzhōng (Imperial Clan Director) and one Zhǔshì (Secretary) were added;
two Yuánwàiláng (Assistant Directors),
two Xiǎo Jīngguān (Junior Officials),
and two Bā Jiǔ Pǐn Lùshì (Eighth and Ninth Rank Clerks) were added.
The Sīwù (Executive Secretary) was merged into the Dūshì Sī,
and the Sīkù (Treasurer) into the Kuàijì Sī.
The position of Sīyù (Prison Superintendent)
was redesignated for a Xiǎo Jīngguān of the Diǎnyù Sī to concurrently hold,
known as Zhèngguǎn Shǒuzhǎng;
and for Bā Jiǔ Pǐn Lùshì to concurrently hold,
known as Fùguǎn Shǒuzhǎng.
The previously established Tíláo Tīng (Prison Bureau)
had its Yuánwàiláng and Zhǔshì from the Diǎnyù Sī concurrently serving,
known as Zǒngguǎn Shǒuzhǎng.
In the thirty-fourth year
based on the old system of Sīyù in the Tíláo Tīng,
it was still designated as a concurrent position.
Soon after, one Jiānyī Zhèng (Senior Prison Doctor) and one Jiānyī Fù (Junior Prison Doctor) were appointed.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng
the Shàngshū was changed to Dàchén (Minister),
and the Shìláng to Fùdàchén (Vice Minister).
Xiūdìng Fǎlǜ Guǎn Dàchén (Minister for the Law Revision Bureau) had no fixed number of members.
(Specifically appointed concurrently.)
Two Tídiao (Supervisors).
Four Zǒngzuǎn (Chief Compilers),
six Zuǎnxiū (Compilers), and six Xiéxiū (Assistant Compilers).
One Zǒngbàn (Director-General) of the Shùwù Chù (General Affairs Office).
Translators and Commissioners had no fixed quota.
(And were filled by personnel familiar with law.)
Established in the thirty-third year of Guāngxù
Dàlǐ Yuàn (Grand Court of Revision): one Zhèngqīng (Chief Justice),
(ranking as Zhèng Èrpǐn,
Second Rank Proper.)
One Shǎoqīng (Associate Chief Justice),
(ranking as Zhèng Sānpǐn,
Third Rank Proper. Both specially appointed.)
One Xíngkē Tuīchéng (Procurator for Criminal Cases) and one Mínkē Tuīchéng (Procurator for Civil Cases).
(Ranking as Zhèng Sìpǐn,
Fourth Rank Proper. Subject to imperial approval.)
Twenty-eight Tuīshì (Judges).
(Ranking as Zhèng Wǔpǐn,
Fifth Rank Proper. Four each in the First Chambers of both Criminal and Civil Divisions,
and five each in the Second and Third Chambers of both.)
Diǎnbù Tīng (Archival Bureau): one Dūdiǎnbù (Chief Archivist),
(ranking as Cóng Wǔpǐn,
Fifth Rank Subsidiary.)
Four Diǎnbù (Archivists).
(Ranking as Cóng Liùpǐn,
Sixth Rank Subsidiary.)
Six Zhǔbù (Registrars),
(ranking as Zhèng Qīpǐn,
Seventh Rank Proper. All above positions subject to memorialized appointment.)
Thirty Bā Jiǔ Pǐn Lùshì (Eighth and Ninth Rank Clerks). (Subject to consultation for appointment.)
The Zhèngqīng 掌 (zhǎng) oversaw the redress of wrongs and the review of cases,
interpreted laws,
supervised judicial proceedings at all levels,
and unified judicial authority.
The Shàoqīng 佐 (zuǒ) assisted him.
The Tuīchéng 分 (fēn) were responsible for civil and criminal cases [⿰⺨發],
and deliberated on difficult cases.
The Xíngkē 掌 (zhǎng) was responsible for interrogating imperial clan members and officials involved in crimes by imperial decree,
and reviewing and detailing criminal appeals and legal petitions submitted to the capital.
The Mínkē 掌 (zhǎng) was responsible for disputes involving imperial clan members,
and reviewing and detailing civil appeals and legal petitions submitted to the capital.
The Dūdìanbù 掌 (zhǎng) managed ledgers and prisoners.
The Diǎnbù 掌 (zhǎng) managed the issuance and receipt of documents.
The Dàlǐ 大理 (dàlǐ) served as the court of final appeal for serious crimes.
For all court trials,
five Tuīshì 審 (shěn) would jointly interrogate,
which constituted a collegial system.
A General Procuratorate was also established,
responsible for overseeing all prosecutorial affairs within Dàlǐ civil and criminal cases,
supervising procuratorates at all levels,
and deploying judicial police officers.
One Tīngchéng 廳丞,
(rank from third grade.
Appointed by imperial selection.) six Jiǎncháguān 檢察官,
(rank regular fifth grade.
Appointed by memorial.) two Zhǔbù 主簿,
and four Lùshì 錄事 of eighth and ninth grade.
One Kānshǒusuǒ Suǒzhǎng 看守所所長,
(rank from fifth grade.
Appointed by memorial.) four Suǒguān 所官,
(rank regular eighth grade.
Appointed by memorial.) and two Lùshì 錄事 of ninth grade.
In the 32nd year of Guāngxù 光緒 (guāngxù)
the Dàlísì 大理寺 (dàlísì) was reformed and established,
with one Zhèngqīng 正卿 and one Shàoqīng 少卿,
and two Tuīchéng 推丞.
There were four Xíngshì Tíng 刑事庭,
with nineteen Tuīshì 推事.
Two Mínshì Tíng 民事庭,
with nine Tuīshì 推事.
The Diǎnbù Tīng 典簿廳 and other various officials were also established.
In addition, the General Procuratorate had one Tīngchéng 廳丞,
six Jiǎncháguān 檢察官,
one Zhǔbù 主簿,
and four Lùshì 錄事.
A Kānshǒusuǒ 看守所 was established,
with its Suǒzhǎng 所長 and other officials.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng 宣統 (xuāntǒng)
the four Xíngkē Tíng 刑科庭 were changed to three Mínkē Tíng 民科庭,
with fourteen Tuīshì 推事 each.
In the 3rd year
one Diǎnbù 典簿 was added to the General Procuratorate,
and the Lùshì 錄事 were changed to two each of eighth and ninth grade.
The Jīngshī Gāoděng Shěnpàntīng 京師高等審判廳,
had one Tīngchéng 廳丞,
(rank regular fourth grade.
Appointed by imperial selection.) responsible for managing the affairs of the court,
and supervising lower-level trial courts.
(The same below.)
There were twelve Tuīshì 推事 for Xíngkē 刑科 and Mínkē 民科.
(rank from fifth grade.
The first and second tribunals of Xíngkē 刑科 and Mínkē 民科 each had three.)
Two Diǎnbù 典簿 for the Diǎnbù Tīng 典簿廳,
(rank regular seventh grade.)
four Zhǔbù 主簿,
(rank from seventh grade.
All above appointed by memorial.)
and six Lùshì 錄事 of ninth grade.
It served as the second instance for serious crimes,
and the final instance for minor crimes.
Trial by joint interrogation was modeled after the Dàlǐ 大理.
The Jiǎnchátīng 檢察廳 had one Jiǎncházhǎng 檢察長,
(rank regular fourth grade.
Appointed by imperial selection.) responsible for correcting judgments of courts at the same level,
and supervising lower-level procuratorates.
(The same below.)
Four Jiǎncháguān 檢察官,
(rank from fifth grade.
Appointed by memorial.)
one Diǎnbù 典簿 and one Zhǔbù 主簿 each,
and two Lùshì 錄事 of ninth grade.
One Kānshǒusuǒ Suǒzhǎng 看守所所長,
(rank regular sixth grade.
Appointed by memorial.) and one Suǒguān 所官 each,
(rank from eighth grade.
Appointed by recommendation.)
and six Lùshì 錄事.
Established in the 33rd year of Guāngxù 光緒 (guāngxù)
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng 宣統 (xuāntǒng)
one Diǎnbù 典簿 and one Zhǔbù 主簿 were added to the Jiǎnchátīng 檢察廳,
and various officials were also appointed to the Kānshǒusuǒ 所長.
The Jīngshī Dìfāng Shěnpàntīng 京師地方審判廳,
had one Tīngchéng 廳丞.
(rank from fourth grade.
Appointed by imperial selection.)
Thirty Tuīshì 推事 for Xíngkē 刑科 and Mínkē 民科.
(rank from fifth grade.
The first and second tribunals of Mín 民 and Xíng 刑 each had six,
and the third tribunals each had three.)
Two Diǎnbù 典簿,
(rank regular seventh grade.)
two Zhǔbù 主簿,
(rank regular eighth grade.
All above appointed by memorial.)
and fourteen Lùshì 錄事.
It served as the first instance for serious crimes,
and the second instance for minor crimes.
Three Tuīshì 推事 would jointly interrogate,
which was also a collegial system.
The Jiǎnchátīng 檢察廳 had one Jiǎncházhǎng 檢察長,
(rank regular fifth grade.
Appointed by memorial.)
five Jiǎncháguān 檢察官,
(rank regular sixth grade.
Appointed by memorial.)
and two each of Diǎnbù 典簿,
(rank from seventh grade.)
Zhǔbù 主簿,
(rank from eighth grade.)
and Lùshì 錄事.
One Kānshǒusuǒ Suǒzhǎng 看守所所長,
(rank from sixth grade.
Appointed by memorial.)
and two Suǒguān 所官.
Established in the 33rd year of Guāngxù 光緒 (guāngxù)
Previously, Yùshěntīng 豫審廳 had been established inside and outside the capital,
responsible for presiding over disputes,
and subordinate to the Mínzhèngbù 民政部.
At this time, it was merged,
and one Tīngchéng 廳丞 was appointed.
Two civil and two criminal tribunals were established,
with twenty-four Tuīshì 推事.
Two Diǎnbù 典簿 and two Zhǔbù 主簿 each,
and ten Lùshì 錄事.
The Jiǎnchátīng 檢察廳 had one Jiǎncházhǎng 檢察長,
four Jiǎncháguān 檢察官,
and one Diǎnbù 典簿 and one Zhǔbù 主簿 each.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng 宣統 (xuāntǒng)
due to the proliferation of lawsuits,
one civil and one criminal tribunal were added,
with three Tuīshì 推事 each,
and four Lùshì 錄事.
One Jiǎncháguān 檢察官 was added to the Jiǎnchátīng 檢察廳.
In the 3rd year
one Diǎnbù 典簿 and one Zhǔbù 主簿 were added to the Jiǎnchátīng 檢察廳.
The Jīngshī Chūjí Shěnpàntīng 京師初級審判廳,
(divided into five districts.)
had one Tuīshì 推事 each for Xíngkē 刑科 and Mínkē 民科.
(rank from sixth grade.
Appointed by memorial.)
Two Lùshì 錄事.
It served as the first instance for minor crimes,
with one Tuīshì 推事 hearing and deciding cases,
which constituted a sole judge system.
The Jiǎnchátīng 檢察廳 had two Jiǎncháguān 檢察官,
(rank from sixth grade.
Appointed by memorial.)
and one Lùshì 錄事.
(Junior courts generally did not have a chief official;
one experienced person was selected by the ministry to serve as supervisor.)
The Nónggōngshāngbù 農工商部:
One Nónggōngshāng Dàchén 農工商大臣,
one Fù Dàchén 副大臣,
one Zuǒchéng 左丞 and one Yòuchéng 右丞 each,
one Zuǒ Cānyì 左參議 and one Yòu Cānyì 右參議 each.
The four Sī 司 of Nóngwù 農務 (Agriculture), Gōngwù 工務 (Industry), Shāngwù 商務 (Commerce), and Shùwù 庶務 (General Affairs).
Twelve Lángzhōng 郎中,
(three per Sī 司.)
sixteen Yuánwàiláng 員外郎,
(four per Sī 司.)
eighteen Zhǔshì 主事.
(six for Shùwù 庶務,
four for the rest.)
Two each of first and second class Yìshī 藝師,
(first class regular sixth grade,
second class regular seventh grade.
Appointed by memorial.)
and Yìshì 藝士,
(first class regular eighth grade,
second class regular ninth grade.
Appointed by recommendation.)
each.
The Dàchén was in charge of the regulations for agriculture, industry, and commerce,
specializing in the promotion of practical enterprises,
to enrich the lives of the people.
The Fùdàchén served as their deputy.
The Nóngwù was in charge of agriculture, sericulture, and reclamation,
including arboriculture and animal husbandry.
They also oversaw water conservancy across the provinces,
and compiled and reviewed expenditures.
The Gōngwù was in charge of supervising various tasks and training workers,
manufacturing instruments based on models,
and surveying and appraising mineral resources in various provinces,
devising methods for their profitable exploitation.
The Shāngwù was in charge of the administration and education of ports and markets,
encouraging people to trade goods,
revising patent and insurance agreements,
and inspecting, issuing, and prohibiting protective lawsuits.
The Shùwù was in charge of memorials to the throne and official dispatches,
accounting for the receipts and expenditures of the ministry,
and recording the appointments and transfers of officials and clerks.
Yìshī and Yìshì were in charge of specialized professions.
Their subordinate offices included: agricultural experiment stations,
bureaus of craftsmanship,
industrial promotion exhibition halls,
mineral analysis institutes,
bureaus of weights and measures,
trademark bureaus,
and commercial law institutes.
These were all managed by carefully selected specialists.
In Guāngxù twenty-fourth year (1898),
the Kuàngwù Tiělù Zǒngjú was established.
Soon after, the Nónggōngshāng Zǒngjú was re-established,
with the Dàchén in overall charge.
(It was soon abolished.)
In the twenty-ninth year (1903),
the Shāngbù was established,
and the Tiělù Kuàngwù Zǒngjú was merged into it.
It had a Shàngshū,
a Zuǒ Shìláng and a Yòu Shìláng,
a Zuǒ Chéng and a Yòu Chéng,
and a Cānyì,
each one person.
There were two Sīwù in the Sīwùsuǒ.
In the thirty-second year (1906),
its name was changed to Nónggōngshāng Bù.
The Píngjūn Sī was renamed Nóngwù,
(and the affairs of agriculture and sericulture from the Hùbù were assigned to it.)
The Tōngyì Sī was renamed Gōngwù,
(while railway affairs, etc., were transferred to the Yóuchuán Bù.)
The Bǎohuì Sī was renamed Shāngwù.
One Lángzhōng,
two Yuánwàiláng, and two Zhǔshì were added for each division.
The Sīwùtīng and Kuàijì Sī were merged into Shùwù,
reducing two Sīwù,
and adding one Lángzhōng,
two Yuánwàiláng,
and four Zhǔshì.
In Xuāntǒng third year (1911),
the Shàngshū was renamed Dàchén,
and the Shìláng was renamed Fùdàchén.
Yóuchuán Bù: one Yóuchuán Dàchén,
one Fùdàchén.
Each one person.
One Zuǒ Chéng and one Yòu Chéng,
one Zuǒ Cānyì and one Yòu Cānyì,
each one person.
Two Qiānshì for the Chéngzhèng and Cānyì halls,
(rank five,
appointed by memorial.)
Two Yuánwàiláng,
two Zhǔshì,
and two Xiǎojīngguān,
each two persons.
For the four divisions of Chuánzhèng, Lùzhèng, Diànzhèng, and Yóuzhèng,
each two Lángzhōng,
ten Yuánwàiláng,
(two for Chuánzhèng and Yóuzhèng each;
three for Lùzhèng and Diànzhèng each.)
Twenty Zhǔshì,
(four for Chuánzhèng and Yóuzhèng each;
six for Lùzhèng and Diànzhèng each.)
Each two Xiǎojīngguān.
The number of Lùshì of ranks eight and nine was not fixed.
The Dàchén was in charge of the regulations for transportation and communication,
overseeing steamships and vehicles,
and transmitting messages by telegraph,
encompassing all aspects
to benefit the people's use.
The Fùdàchén served as their deputy.
The Chuánzhèng was in charge of deliberating on maritime laws,
and also managed the construction of factories and docks,
and the surveying of sandbars.
The Lùzhèng was in charge of deliberating on railway laws,
and also managed the standardization of track gauges,
and the planning of railway lines.
The Diànzhèng was in charge of deliberating on telegraph laws,
and also managed the regulations for official and commercial bureaus,
and the rules for land and submarine cables.
The Yóuzhèng was in charge of deliberating on postal laws,
and also managed postal remittances,
and postal union treaties.
Their subordinate offices included: one director of the Yóuzhèng Zǒngjú,
(also held by the Fùdàchén.)
One Zǒngbàn,
(filled by a Frenchman.)
Each one person.
Two Tídiào for the Tiělù Zǒngjú.
One Zǒngbàn and one Tídiào for the Jīnghàn Lùjú;
one Huìbàn for the Nánjú and Jīngjú respectively.
Two Zǒngbàn for the Jīngfèng Lùjú,
each one Tídiào.
One Zǒngbàn and one Huìbàn for the Jīngzhāng Tiělù,
each one person.
One Zǒngbàn for the Hùníng Lùjú.
For the Jícháng Lùjú and Guǎngjiǔ Lùjú,
each one Zǒngbàn and one Tídiào.
One Zǒngbàn and one Huìbàn for the Zhāngsuī Tiělù.
For the Píngzhū Tiělù, Zhèngtài Lùjú, Biànluò Lùjú, and Dàoqīng Lùjú,
each one Zǒngbàn.
One Director for the Diànzhèng Zǒngjú,
and two Tídiào.
One Zǒngbàn, one Bāngbàn, and one Tídiào for each branch bureau.
One Zǒngbàn for each provincial branch bureau.
One Zǒngbàn and one Huìbàn for each Diànhuà Jú.
One Zǒngbàn for Tiānjīn, Guǎngzhōu, Tàiyuán, and Yāntái respectively.
One Zǒnglǐ and one Bānglǐ for the Jiāotōng Yínháng.
For the Běijīng Zǒngyínháng,
and the branch banks in Shànghǎi, Hànkǒu, and Guǎngzhōu,
each one Zǒngbàn.
One Guǎnlǐ for Tiānjīn and Yíngkǒu respectively.
Thirty-four Chāoguān.
Thirteen Títángguān.
(Formerly subordinate to the Bīngbù.)
All affairs were managed by specially selected officials.
Established in Guāngxù thirty-third year (1907).
Previously, the Chuánzhèng Zhāoshāngjú was subordinate to the Běiyáng Dàchén,
domestic merchant ships were subordinate to the Gōngbù,
the postal service was subordinate to the Zǒng Shuìwù Sī,
and separate Dàchén were appointed to lead railway and telegraph affairs.
By this time, all were merged.
It established a Shàngshū,
a Zuǒ Shìláng and a Yòu Shìláng,
a Zuǒ Chéng and a Yòu Chéng,
and a Cānyì,
each one person,
as well as Qiānshì and other officials for the Chéngzhèng and Cānyì halls.
Five divisions were established: Chuánzhèng, Lùzhèng, Diànzhèng, Yóuzhèng, and Shùwù.
It had ten Lángzhōng,
twelve Yuánwàiláng,
twenty-four Zhǔshì,
and fourteen Xiǎojīngguān.
In Xuāntǒng first year (1909),
the Shùwù Sī's Lángzhōng, Yuánwàiláng, and Xiǎojīngguān were reduced by two each,
and Zhǔshì by four.
Two Yuánwàiláng and two Zhǔshì were added to both the Chéngzhèng and Cānyì halls.
In the third year (1911),
the Shàngshū was renamed Dàchén,
and the Shìláng was renamed Fùdàchén.
Jūnzī Fǔ (Council of Military Affairs) Two Jūnzī Dàchén (Ministers of Military Affairs),
(specially appointed).
They were in charge of receiving imperial edicts
and assisting in military planning.
Two Jūnzī Shǐ (Military Councillors) for the Zǒngwù Tīng (General Affairs Department),

Zhèng and Fù Jūnxiào.

One Dìshì Zhǎng (Head of Secretariat),

Three Sīwù (Clerks).
Three divisions: Sānjiǎo (Triangulation), Dìxíng (Topography), and Zhìtú (Cartography),

Bānzhǎng (Squad Leaders),
Bānyuán (Squad Members),
Kēyuán of the Yìnshuā Suǒ (Printing Office),
Yìshì (Artisans),
Sīwù,

Jūnshì Guānbào Jú (Military Gazette Bureau):
one Zhèng Júzhang (Director) and one Fù Júzhang (Deputy Director).
Shùwù (General Affairs),
Wéndú (Documentation),
Shōuzhī (Revenue and Expenditure),
Biānzuǎn (Compilation),
Yìshù (Translation),
Jiàoduì (Proofreading),

and one Yìshù (Translator)).
Sixty-three Lùshì (Scribes).
(Filled by extra army officers, sergeants, and corporals).
Fifteen Jūnshì Cānyì Guān (Military Advisory Officials).
(One each for Zhílì, Jiāngníng, Jiāngsū, Jiāngběi, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Hénán, Húběi, Húnán, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, Zhèjiāng, Shǎnxī.
Filled by Xié Dūtǒng,
Zhèng and Fù Xié Cānlǐng).
In the 33rd year of Guāngxù (1907),
the Jūnzī Chù (Military Advisory Office) was established.
One Xié Dūtǒng was appointed as Zhèngshǐ (Chief Commissioner),
one Zhèng Cānlǐng as Fùshǐ (Deputy Commissioner),
six Fù Cānlǐng,
one Tóng Fù Cānlǐng,
ten Xié Cānlǐng,
two Tóng Xié Cānlǐng,
ten Zhèng Jūnxiào,

and first, second, and third-class Kēyuán.
(The First and Second Divisions
were filled by Xié and Fù Cānlǐng.
The Cèdì Sī (Surveying Division)
was filled by Tóng Zhèng and Fù Cānlǐng.
There were eighteen Kēzhǎng, one for each section,
filled by Fù Cānlǐng for the First and Second Divisions.
The Cèdì Sī
was filled by Tóng Fù and Xié Cānlǐng.
There were sixteen Kēyuán in the First Division,
four in the Second Division,
filled by Zhèng and Fù Xié Jūnxiào.
Six in the Cèdì Sī,
filled by Tóng Zhèng and Fù Xié Jūnxiào).
There was one Chéngfā Guān (Disbursement Officer) for each division,
five Yìyuán (Translators),
(belonging to the First Division).
Four Yìshī (Art Masters),
six Yìshì (Artisans),
(belonging to the Cèdì Sī).
All were filled by army officers or students.
Subordinate to the Lùjūn Bù (Ministry of the Army).
In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
according to the Constitutional Outline which stated that the Emperor commanded the army and navy,
a separate Jūnzī Chù was established,
led by Bèilè Zàitāo and others.
A Zǒngwù Tīng was established,
with two Jūnzī Shǐ.
Four departments were separately established,
each with one Tīngzhǎng (Department Head),
sixteen Kēzhǎng,
and no fixed quota for Kēyuán.
A system for supplementing civilian officials was also established.
(As listed previously).
Soon, the character "Tóng" was removed.
(Details can be found in the Lùjūn Bù above).
The following year,
the Jūnshì Huìyì Chù (Military Conference Office) was established.
In the third year,
it was renamed Fǔ,
and the Lùjūn Dàchén was ordered to lead its affairs.
Bìdé Yuàn (Council of Counselors) One Yuànzhǎng (President)
and one Fù Yuànzhǎng (Vice President),
each had one person.
(Specially appointed concurrently).
Thirty-two Gùwèn Dàchén (Advisory Ministers).
(Specially appointed concurrently).
They were in charge of participating in confidential matters,
discussing and reflecting day and night,
and deliberating on major policies and difficult issues.
Ten Cānyì (Councillors),
(appointed by request).
They were in charge of drafting regulations and systems.
One Mìshū Tīng Mìshūzhǎng (Secretary-General of the Secretariat),
(appointed by request).
Three first-class Mìshū Guān (Secretaries), three second-class,
and six third-class,
(all appointed by memorial).
They were separately in charge of general affairs.
Established in the third year of Xuāntǒng.
Zīzhèng Yuàn (Advisory Council) One Zǒngcái (President),
(specially appointed from among princes, dukes, and ministers).
One Fù Zǒngcái (Vice President),
(appointed from among ministers of the third rank or above).
Each had one person.
They were in charge of determining public opinion.
All annual revenues and expenditures,
legal codes and court regulations,
public debt and tax rates,
and matters referred for consultation by imperial decree,
after being deliberated and resolved by the Yìyuán (Members),
were submitted to the Guówù Dàchén (State Ministers) for imperial decision.
One Mìshū Tīng Mìshūzhǎng (Secretary-General of the Secretariat),
(appointed by request).
Four first-class Mìshū Guān, four second-class, and four third-class,
(appointed by memorial).
They were in charge of accounting and documentation.
Yìyuán:
sixteen Zōngshì (Imperial Clansmen) princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
twelve Mǎn and Hàn hereditary nobles;
fourteen Wàifān (Outer Vassal) princes, dukes, and hereditary nobles;
six Zōngshì and Juéluó (Imperial Lineage members);
thirty-two officials from various ministries and courts;
ten each of highly learned scholars and high taxpayers.
(All imperially selected).
Six from each provincial Zīyì Jú (Provincial Advisory Bureau).
(Elected by the people).
Established in the 33rd year of Guāngxù,
with two Zǒngcái.
Soon, four Xiélǐ (Assistants) were added.
The following year,
three Bāngbàn (Assistant Managers) and three Cānyì (Councillors) were again appointed.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
the official system for the Mìshū Tīng was established.
In the second year,
it was stipulated that there would be one Zǒngcái and one Fù Zǒngcái.
Yánzhèng Yuàn (Salt Administration Council) One Yánzhèng Dàchén (Minister of Salt Administration)
(specially appointed concurrently from among State Ministers).
One Chéng (Assistant Minister).
One Tīngzhǎng for the Zǒngwù Tīng (General Affairs Department),
one Cānyì (Councillor),
one Tīngzhǎng for the Nányán Tīng (Southern Salt Department),
one Tīngzhǎng for the Běiyán Tīng (Northern Salt Department),
each had one person.
(The above were all appointed by request).
Two Cānshì (Advisors),
first, second, third, and fourth-class Qiānshì (Junior Officials),
(all appointed by memorial).
First, second, and third-class Lùshì (Scribes),
(appointed by consultation).
Their numbers were determined based on the workload.
The Grand Minister (Dàchén) was in charge of the salt administration.
The Vice Minister (Chéng) assisted in managing the salt policy (cuógāng).
The Director of General Affairs (Zǒngwù) was in charge of overseeing various general matters,
and safeguarding confidential information.
The Councilor (Cānyì) was in charge of drafting laws and regulations,
assisted by the Attendant (Qiānshì).
The Southern Salt Bureau (Nányán Tīng) was in charge of salt affairs in Huái, Zhè, Mǐn, and Yuè.
The Northern Salt Bureau (Běiyán Tīng) was in charge of salt affairs in Fèng, Zhí, Lù, and Dōng.
Initially, following the Míng dynasty system,
Censors (Yùshǐ) were dispatched to inspect salt taxes (yánkè).
Later, this was changed to Salt Commissioner (Yánzhèng).
(Specially appointed concurrently.
) Those dispatched by the Grand Court of Revision (Dūcháyuan) were also named Salt Commissioner (Yánzhèng).
(Those appointed from officials of the Ministry of Internal Affairs (Nèiwùsī) still held the title of Censor (Yùshǐ).
) For each province, those who oversaw these matters were the Governor-General (Dūdū) and the Provincial Governor (Fǔ),
and the system was adapted to local conditions
and established as a permanent regulation.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
an Office of Salt Administration (Dūbàn Yánzhèng Chǔ) was established,
and Prince Zhenguo (Zhènguógōng) Zàizé was appointed Minister Director (Dūbàn Dàchén).
The Governor-Generals (Dūdū) and Provincial Governors (Fǔ) of all provinces producing and distributing salt
were all appointed Associate Directors (Huìbàn).
In the third year (1911),
to reorganize national taxation,
the Office (Chǔ) was changed to a Board (Yuàn),
and special officials for salt administration were appointed.
The Board of Rites (Diǎnlǐ Yuàn): Grand Academician (Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì),
Vice Grand Academician (Fù Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì),
one of each.
(Specially appointed.
) Academicians (Xuéshì),
and Direct Academicians (Zhí Xuéshì),
eight of each.
(By imperial nomination.
) Director of General Affairs (Zǒngwù Tīng Tīngzhǎng), one person.
Registrar (Bùzhèng), Recorder (Diǎnbù), Treasurer (Sīkù),
(All by imperial nomination.
) with no fixed number.
Directors of the four bureaus: Bureau of Rites (Lǐzhì), Bureau of Sacrifices (Cí jì), Bureau of Protocols (Fèngcháng), and Bureau of Imperial Cuisine (Jīngshàn), one of each.
Attendants (Qiānshì) of the first, second, and third ranks,
Ushers (Míngzàn),
(All by imperial nomination.
) Master of Ceremonies (Xùbān),
Scribes (Lùshì),
(By recommendation.
) appointed according to the busyness or idleness of affairs.
The Officials for Reading Prayers (Dúzhù Guān), Officials for Supervising Rites (Zànlǐ Láng), and various officials of the imperial tombs (Língqǐn) remained as before.
The Grand Academician (Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì) was in charge of refining rites and music,
presiding over court assemblies,
and solemnly conducting major sacrifices.
The Vice Grand Academician (Fù Zhǎngyuàn Xuéshì) assisted him.
Academicians (Xuéshì) and Direct Academicians (Zhí Xuéshì) were in charge of discussion and review.
The Director of General Affairs (Zǒngwù) was in charge of overseeing all general matters.
The Registrar (Bùzhèng) was in charge of the receipt and dispatch of treasury stores,
and their arrangement,
as well as overseeing prison matters.
The Recorder (Diǎnbù) was in charge of keeping records of treasury stores,
and also auditing income and expenditure.
The Treasurer (Sīkù) was in charge of guarding various treasuries,
and supervising treasury clerks,
and inspecting treasury guards.
The Bureau of Rites (Lǐzhì) was in charge of court assemblies and celebrations.
The Bureau of Sacrifices (Cíjì) was in charge of altars, temples, and imperial tombs.
The Bureau of Protocols (Fèngcháng) was in charge of ushering and guiding.
The Bureau of Imperial Cuisine (Jīngshàn) was in charge of banquets and sacrificial offerings.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng (1911), it was reformed from the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù).
All administrative matters
were transferred to various ministries.
The provincial official system
underwent relatively few changes;
only the provincial capital, judicial circuits (sī dào) were given new names,
(details of the Patrol and Police Circuit (Xúnjǐng Dào) and Industrial Promotion Circuit (Quànyè Dào) are given earlier)
and the number of officials increased further.
The Education Commissioner (Xuézhèng) was changed to Education Administrator (Tíxuéshǐ).
The Provincial Judicial Commissioner (Ànchásǐ) was changed to Judicial Administrator (Tífǎshǐ),
and various levels of judicial and procuratorial courts were subordinate to them.
According to custom,
whenever important local political matters arose,
the financial and judicial commissioners (Fān, Niè liǎng sī) could discuss with the Governor-General (Dūdū) or Provincial Governor (Fǔ),
and after deliberation, report for implementation.
In matters of promotion, transfer, or appointment of officials,
they would also jointly report in detail.
At this point,
they were referred to as the Three Commissioners (Sānsī).
The Office of the Education Administrator (Tíxuéshǐ Sī): One Education Administrator (Tíxuéshǐ),
(Rank 3a).
In charge of education administration,
auditing school regulations,
and examining arts and teacher training.
The office established six sections: General Affairs (Zǒngwù),
Specialized Education (Zhuānmén),
General Education (Pǔtōng),
Industrial Education (Shíyè),
Libraries (Túshū),
and Accounting (Kuàijì).
Section Chiefs (Kēzhǎng) and Section Members (Kēyuán) were in charge of their respective duties.
(Selected from those familiar with educational affairs.
) A separate Education Affairs Public Office (Xuéwù Gōngsuǒ) was established,
with a President (Yìzhǎng) and Gentry Councillors (Yìshēn) to discuss matters.
(Appointed by imperial nomination.
) Established in the 31st year of Guāngxù (1905).
One each was added for Jílín, Hēilóngjiāng, Jiāngníng, Jiāngsū,
(Previously, a Jiāngnán Education Commissioner (Jiāngnán Xuézhèng) was established)
and Xīnjiāng, while the rest maintained the original quota of Education Commissioners (Xuézhèng).
The Office of the Judicial Administrator (Tífǎshǐ Sī): One Judicial Administrator (Tífǎshǐ),
(Rank 3a).
In charge of judicial administration,
supervising various levels of trial courts,
and managing procuratorial affairs.
The office established three sections: General Affairs (Zǒngwù),
Civil and Criminal Affairs (Mínxíng),
and Prison Administration (Diǎnyù).
One Section Chief (Kēzhǎng) for each section,
(Rank 5a).
One First-Class Section Member (Yīděng Kēyuán) for each,
(Rank 6a).
Second-Class Section Members (Èrděng Kēyuán) (Rank 7a)
had no fixed number.
(Only Fèngtiān had Attendant Section Members (Qiānshì Kēyuán).
There were also Principal Clerks (Zhèng Sīshū),
Rank 8a;
and Assistant Clerks (Fù Sīshū),
Rank 9a.
) In the 33rd year of Guāngxù (1907), one Judicial Administrator (Tífǎshǐ) was established in each of the Three Eastern Provinces (Dōngsānsěng).
In the second year of Xuāntǒng (1910),
the Provincial Judicial Commissioners (Ànchásǐ) of all provinces were changed to Judicial Administrators (Tífǎshǐ),
and their jurisdiction over post stations (yìchuán) was abolished.
High Court of Justice (Gāoděng Shěnpàntīng): One Chief Clerk (Tīngchéng),
(Rank 4b).
(In branch courts in treaty ports (shāngbù), the Chief Judge (Tuīshìzhǎng) acted in his place).
Six Judges (Tuīshì) for the Criminal Division (Xíngkē) and Civil Division (Mínkē).
(Rank 6a).
One Recorder (Diǎnbù).
(Rank 7a).
Two Clerks (Zhǔbù),
(Rank 8a).
Scribes (Lùshì) had no fixed number.
(Rank 9b).
Procuratorate (Jiǎnchátīng): One Chief Procurator (Jiǎncházhǎng),
(Rank 4b).
One Procurator (Jiǎncháguān),
(Rank 6a).
Two Scribes (Lùshì).
Local Court of Justice (Dìfāng Shěnpàntīng): One Chief Judge (Tuīshìzhǎng),
(Rank 5b).
Six Judges (Tuīshì) for the Criminal Division (Xíngkē) and Civil Division (Mínkē).
(Rank 6b).
One Recorder (Diǎnbù), (Rank 7b);
and one Clerk (Zhǔbù) (Rank 8b;
possibly two if busy,
none if simple).
Scribes (Lùshì) had no fixed number.
Procuratorate (Jiǎnchátīng): One Chief Procurator (Jiǎncházhǎng),
(Rank 5b).
One Procurator (Jiǎncháguān),
(Rank 6b).
Two Scribes (Lùshì).
Detention Center (Kànshǒusuǒ): One Officer (Suǒguān),
(Rank 9a).
Scribes (Lùshì) had no fixed number.
Primary Court of Justice (Chūjí Shěnpàntīng): Two Judges (Tuīshì),
(Rank 7a).
(Possibly three or four if busy).
Scribes (Lùshì) had no fixed number.
Procuratorate (Jiǎnchátīng): One Procurator (Jiǎncháguān),
(Rank 7a).
Two Scribes (Lùshì).
Detention Center (Kànshǒusuǒ): One Officer (Suǒguān).
One Prison Governor (Guǎnyùguān),
(Rank 5b).
One Deputy Prison Governor (Fù Guǎnyùguān).
(Rank 6b).
Three Section Chiefs (Kèzhǎng).
(Rank 8a.
One each for Documents (Wéndú), Security (Shǒuwèi), and General Affairs (Shùwù)).
Two Wardens (Suǒzhǎng).
(Rank 9a.
One each for Instruction (Jiàohuì) and Medical Affairs (Yīwù)).
One Prefectural Prison Governor (Fǔ Guǎnyùguān).
(Rank 7b).
One Subprefectural/County Deputy Prison Governor (Zhōu, Xiàn Fù Guǎnyùguān).
(Rank 8b).
In the 34th year of Guāngxù (1908),
a model prison was established in Fèngtiān,
with a Principal Prison Governor (Zhèng Guǎnyùguān),
Provincial and Prefectural Prison Wardens (Shěngfǔ Sīyù), and County Clerks (Xiàn Diǎnshǐ).
In the second year of Xuāntǒng (1910),
a Deputy Prison Governor (Fù Guǎnyùguān) was added.
Subsequently, various prefectures (fǔ), departments (tīng), subprefectures (zhōu), and counties (xiàn) imitated and implemented this system.
(At the time, prisons in Tiānjīn, Bǎodìng, and Húběi were completed,
but no special officials were appointed).
The Three Eastern Provinces (Dōngsānshěng) are strategically located.
Since their reorganization into provinces,
the regular regulations have been modified,
and additional judicial and administrative posts (Sī Dào) have been established.
The Education Commissioner (Tíxué) and Judicial Commissioner (Tífǎ) posts
are common to all provinces
and need no further elaboration.
A summary of the newly established offices is detailed below.
(When the provinces were first established,
the Governor-General's (Dūdū) office had two departments, Chenggxuān and Zīyì,
and one Left Assistant (Zuǒ Cānzàn) and one Right Assistant (Yòu Cānzàn) were appointed,
of rank From the Second Grade.
One Attendant Official (Qiānshì),
and first, second, and third-class clerks assisted them.
They were soon abolished.)
Civil Affairs Department (Mínzhèng Shǐ Sī): One Civil Affairs Commissioner (Mínzhèng Shǐ)
(From the Second Grade).
Manages household registration.
Attendant Officials (Qiānshì)
(From the Fourth Grade),
and clerks (Kēyuán)
(First class: From the Fifth Grade;
Second class: Regular Sixth Grade;
Third class: Regular Seventh Grade.
The same applies to all departments.)
Each has permanent duties.
There is no fixed number of first and second-class medical officers (Yīguān)
(First class: Regular Sixth Grade;
Second class: Regular Seventh Grade).
Established in the 33rd year of Guāngxù (1907),
with a rank of Regular Third Grade.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
following the precedent of the Provincial Administration Commissioner (Bùzhèngshǐ),
it was promoted to From the Second Grade,
in charge of the promotion, transfer, and appointment of subordinate officials.
Foreign Affairs Department (Jiāoshè Shǐ Sī): One Foreign Affairs Commissioner (Jiāoshè Shǐ)
(Regular Third Grade).
Manages foreign relations.
Assisted by Attendant Officials (Qiānshì),
clerks (Kēyuán),
and first and second-class interpreters (Yìguān)
(First class: Regular Sixth Grade;
Second class: Regular Seventh Grade).
In the 33rd year of Guāngxù (1907),
one was established in Fèngtiān and Jílín respectively.
In the 2nd year of Xuāntǒng (1910),
Zhílì, Jiāngsū, Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Húběi, Guǎngdōng, and Yúnnán
followed Fèngtiān's example and established similar posts.
Finance Department (Dùzhī Shǐ Sī): One Finance Commissioner (Dùzhī Shǐ)
(Regular Third Grade).
Manages finance and taxation.
Assisted by Attendant Officials (Qiānshì),
clerks (Kēyuán),
and first and second-class treasury officials (Kùguān)
(First class: Regular Sixth Grade;
Second class: Regular Seventh Grade).
In the 33rd year of Guāngxù (1907),
one was established in each of the three provinces.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒnt (1909),
the one in Hēilóngjiāng was abolished,
its duties falling under the purview of the Civil Affairs Department.
(In the 33rd year of Guāngxù (1907),
Fèngtiān also established one Banner Affairs Department (Qíwù Shǐ Sī) with one Commissioner.
Attendant Officials and clerks were the same as in other departments.
Abolished in the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909).)
After the defeat in the First Sino-Japanese War (Jiǎwǔ bù jìng),
the officials concerned, realizing the inadequacy of military administration,
took the strong nations as their model.
From the Imperial Guard (Jìnwèi Jūn) internally,
to the Commander-in-Chief's Training Office (Dūliàn Gōngsuǒ) externally,
they gradually implemented
the newly established regulations and systems.
However, just as the three armies and two divisions (Sānjūn Liǎngxié) were completed,
a great change occurred.
Therefore, what can be verified is recorded in this chapter.
Imperial Guard (Jìnwèi Jūn): Three Training Ministers (Xùnliàn Dàchén)
(concurrently held by Imperial Princes and Ministers (Wáng Dàchén)).
In charge of all military administration and orders.
Six Military Counselors (Jūnzīguān) and
ten Executive Officers (Zhíshìyuán)
handle memorials and official documents,
and also oversee the four sections.
Assisted by executive officers from divisions (Xié), brigades (Biāo), battalions (Yíng), and companies (Duì).
Five Scribes (Shūjìyuán)
(one first-class,
two second-class, and two third-class).
Two Cartographers (Huìtúyuán).
One each for Printing (Yìnshuā), Revenue and Expenditure (Shōuzhī), General Affairs (Shùwù), and Dispatch (Dìshì).
One Superintendent (Jiāndū) each for the four sections: Ordnance (Jūnxiè), Military Law (Jūnfǎ), Military Logistics (Jūnxū), and Military Medical (Jūnyī).
Fifteen section clerks (Kēyuán)
(four for Ordnance,
five for Military Logistics,
and two for each of the others).
All selected officials were appointed to manage their respective duties.
Divisional Command Headquarters (Xié Sīlìng Chù): One Commander (Tǒnglǐngguān)
(held by a Divisional Commander-in-chief (Xié Dūtǒng)).
In charge of commanding the entire division.
One Adjutant (Cānjūnguān) (held by a Divisional Battalion Commander (Xié Cānlǐng)),
in charge of strategic planning;
one Aide-de-camp (Fùguān) (held by a Senior Military Officer (Zhèng Jūnxiào)),
in charge of overall administration;
each has one person.
One Chief Bugler (Sīhàozhǎng)
(held by a Junior Military Officer (Xié Jūnxiào)).
Two Scribes (Sīshūshēng)
(same as above).
Brigade Headquarters (Biāo Běnshǔ): One Brigade Commander (Tǒngdàiguān)
(held by a Senior Battalion Commander (Zhèng Cānlǐng)).
In charge of commanding the entire brigade.
One Training Officer (Jiàoliànguān)
(held by a Deputy Battalion Commander (Fù Cānlǐng)),
one Aide-de-camp (Fùguān),
one Flag Officer (Zhǎngqíguān)
(all held by Deputy Military Officers (Fù Jūnxiào)).
One Deputy Ordnance Officer (Fù Jūnxièguān),
one Deputy Logistics Officer (Fù Jūnxūguān),
one Deputy Medical Officer (Fù Jūnyīguān)
(all held by Divisional Battalion Commanders (Xié Cānlǐng)).
One Deputy Veterinary Officer (Fù Mǎyīguān)
(held by a Senior Military Officer (Zhèng Jūnxiào)).
One Chief Bugler (Sīhàozhǎng).
Each has one person.
Two Scribes (Sīshūshēng).

Company Commanders (Guǎndàiguān) for Infantry (Bù), Cavalry (Mǎ), Engineering (Gōngchéng), Transport (Zīzhòng), Communications (Jiāotōng), Field Artillery (Lùlù Pào), Machine Gun (Jīguān Pào), and Police (Jǐngchá) Companies
(held by Divisional Battalion Commanders (Xié Cānlǐng));
one Aide-de-camp (Fùguān),
one Logistics Chief (Jūnxūzhǎng),
one Medical Chief (Jūnyīzhǎng)
(all held by Senior Military Officers (Zhèng Jūnxiào)).
Each has one person.
Four Company Officers (Duìguān)
(held by Senior Military Officers (Zhèng Jūnxiào))
each. Three Platoon Leaders (Páizhǎng)
(one Deputy Military Officer (Fù Jūnxiào),
two Junior Military Officers (Xié Jūnxiào)).
(Originally, there were twelve each for Infantry and Machine Gun Companies,
eight for Cavalry Companies,
nine for Field Artillery Companies,
and six each for Engineering, Transport, Communications, and Police Companies.
The current system was revised in the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng (1911).)
Seventy-nine Quartermasters (Sìwùzhǎng)
(four each for Cavalry, Infantry, and Machine Gun Companies;
three for Field Artillery Companies;
and two each for Engineering, Transport, and Communications Companies.
Initially held by Junior Military Officers (Xié Jūnxiào).
Revised to be appointed by special order in the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909).)
Four Ordnance Chiefs (Jūnxièzhǎng)
(held by Senior Military Officers (Zhèng Jūnxiào))
(one each for Engineering, Communications, Field Artillery, and Machine Gun Companies).
Three Horse Inspectors (Chámǎzhǎng)
(held by Senior Military Officers (Zhèng Jūnxiào))
and three Veterinary Chiefs (Mǎyīzhǎng)
(held by Deputy Military Officers (Fù Jūnxiào)).
Each has three persons.
Thirty-five Scribes (Sīshūshēng)
(six each for Cavalry, Infantry, and Machine Gun Companies;
five for Field Artillery Companies;
and four each for Engineering, Transport, and Communications Companies).
Three Technical Masters (Yìshī)
(subordinate to the Communications Company).
One Military Band Officer (Jūnyuè Duìguān)
and one Platoon Leader (Páizhǎng).
Each has one person.
In the 34th year of Guāngxù (1908),
the Imperial Guard (Jìnwèi Jūn) was established,
personally led by the Regent Prince (Jiānguó Shèzhèngwáng).
Bèilè Zàitāo and others were in charge of training.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
the number of Training Ministers (Xùnliàn Dàchén) was set at three,
and the quotas for Military Counselors (Jūnzīguān) and other subordinate officers were fixed.
Previously, executive officers and supervisory officers were appointed for each division (Xié), brigade (Biāo), and battalion (Yíng);
these were all changed to aides-de-camp (Fùguān).
The second-class scribes (Shūjìguān) for divisions and brigades, and the Chief Scribe (Shūjìzhǎng) for the entire division, were abolished.
Dūliàn Gōngsuǒ (Bureau for Supervising and Training)
The Dūbàn (Superintendent-General) is one person,
(appointed by the Dū, Fǔ, Jiāngjūn, or Dū Tǒnglǐng)
in charge of reorganizing the new and old military camps throughout the province.
The Jūnshì Cānyìguān (Military Counselor) is one person,
(appointed by Xiédū Tǒngtǒng or Zhèng Cānlǐng)
in charge of overseeing the sections and bureaus.
The Yīděng Fùguān (First-Class Adjutant) is one person,
(appointed by Xié Cānlǐng)
the Èrděng Fùguān (Second-Class Adjutant) are two people,
(appointed by Zhèng Jūnxiào)
separately managing documents and various affairs.
The Yī, Èr, Sān děng Shūjìguān (First, Second, Third Class Secretaries) are five people,
(appointed by fifth, sixth, and seventh rank civil officials)
and the Sīshūshēng (Clerks) are sixteen people.
(appointed by eighth and ninth rank civil officials)
There are two sections: Chóubèi (Preparation) and Liángxiǎng (Provisions).
Each section has one Kēzhǎng (Section Chief),
separately managing the organization and training of new armies,
the reduction and elimination of old camps,
accounting and disbursement,
and uniforms and supplies.
The Jūnxiè Jú (Armaments Bureau) has one Júzhǎng (Bureau Chief),
in charge of new and old military firearms, cannons, and ammunition.
(All of the above are appointed by Fù Jūnxiào)
There are five Yīděng Kēyuán (First-Class Section Members),
(two each for the Chóubèi and Liángxiǎng Sections,
one for Jūnxiè)
(appointed by Xié Cānlǐng).
There are eleven Èrděng Kēyuán (Second-Class Section Members),
(four for Chóubèi,
five for Liángxiǎng,
two for Jūnxiè)
(appointed by Zhèng Jūnxiào).
There are twelve Sānděng Kēyuán (Third-Class Section Members).
(five for Chóubèi,
four for Liángxiǎng,
three for Jūnxiè)
(appointed by Xié Jūnxiào).
The Cèdì Fēnjú (Topographical Survey Sub-Bureau)
has vacant positions.
In the 30th year of Guāngxù
(1904), Dūliàn Gōngsuǒ were established in each province,
divided into three departments: Bīngbèi (Military Preparedness), Cānmóu (Staff), and Jiàoliàn (Training),
with positions such as Zǒngbàn (General Manager), Bāngbàn (Assistant Manager), and Tídiào (Supervisor).
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng
(1911), they were reorganized into sections and bureaus,
imitating the new army system,
appointing officials and assigning duties.
(As listed above).
Jūnzhì (Army System)
The Zǒngtǒng (Commander-in-Chief) is one person,
(appointed by Zhèng Dūtǒng)
in charge of all military administration and orders.
The Zǒng Cānmóuguān (Chief of Staff),
(appointed by Xiédū Tǒngtǒng)
Yīděng Cānmóuguān (First-Class Staff Officer),
(appointed by Zhèng Cānlǐng)
Èrděng Cānmóuguān (Second-Class Staff Officer),
(appointed by Xié Cānlǐng)
are in charge of assisting in issuing orders and planning strategies.
The first and second class officers assist them.
The Gōngchéngduì Cānlǐngguān (Engineering Corps Staff Officer)
is in charge of assisting with the affairs of the corps.
The Hùjūnguān (Guards Officer) manages miscellaneous affairs,
commanding officers and soldiers.
The Pàoduì Xiélǐngguān (Artillery Corps Sub-Commander) has the same duties as the Gōngchéngduì.
The Zǒng Jūnxièguān (Chief Armaments Officer),
Zǒng Zhífǎguān (Chief Law Enforcement Officer),
Zǒng Jūnxūguān (Chief Quartermaster),
Zǒng Jūnyīguān (Chief Medical Officer),
(details in Jìnwèijūn)
(from the Engineering Corps downwards,
all appointed by Zhèng Cānlǐng)
and the Zǒng Mǎyīguān (Chief Veterinary Officer),
(appointed by Fù Cānlǐng)
are each one person.
The Sīshūshēng (Clerks) are fifteen people.
(appointed by Fù Xié Jūnxiào)
Initially,
Jūn, Zhèn, Xié, and Biāo all had Sīshì (Administrators) positions,
but these were later abolished.
Zhènzhì (Division System)
The Tǒngzhìguān (Divisional Commander) is one person,
(appointed by Fù Dūtǒng)
in charge of commanding the entire division.
The Zhèng Cānmóuguān (Chief Staff Officer),
(appointed by Zhèng Cānlǐng)
Èr, Sān děng Cānmóuguān (Second and Third Class Staff Officers)
have the same duties as in the Jūnzhì.
The Zhíshìguān (Executive Officer),
(all appointed by Zhèng Jūnxiào)
and the Zhōngjūnguān (Aide-de-Camp),
(appointed by Fù Xié Cānlǐng)
are in charge of miscellaneous affairs.
The Zhèng Jūnxièguān (Chief Armaments Officer),
Zhèng Zhífǎguān (Chief Law Enforcement Officer),
Zhèng Jūnxūguān (Chief Quartermaster),
Zhèng Jūnyīguān (Chief Medical Officer),
(all appointed by Fù Xié Cānlǐng)
and the Zhèng Mǎyīguān (Chief Veterinary Officer),
(appointed by Xié Cānlǐng)
and the Sīhàozhǎng (Chief Bugler),
(appointed by Fù Jūnxiào)
are each one person.
The Sīshūshēng (Clerks) are fifteen people.
The Xié, Biāo, and Yíng systems are similar to the Jìnwèijūn (Imperial Guard).
In the 30th year of Guāngxù (1904),
the new army was reorganized
and divided into thirty-six Zhèn (Divisions),
establishing the official system for Zhèn, Xié, Biāo, and Yíng.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
various provinces successively organized Hùnchéng děng Xié (mixed brigades, etc.),
temporarily appointing one Zhífǎguān (Law Enforcement Officer) and one Sīshìshēng (Clerk) each,
but these were later abolished.
In the 3rd year (1911),
twenty-six Zhèn were reported as fully formed,
with one Zǒngtǒng (Commander-in-Chief) appointed.
Positions below Zǒng Cānmóu (Chief of Staff) were vacant.
The remaining units were either organized into two Xié,
or one Xié and one Biāo,
so the full number of Zhèn was not yet complete.
Lùjūn Zhènjiān (Army Division Prisons)
The Jiānzhǎng (Prison Warden)
(appointed by Xié Cānlǐng or Zhèng Jūnxiào)
and Jiānfù (Deputy Warden),
(appointed by Zhèng or Fù Jūnxiào)
are each one person.
The Sīshūshēng (Clerks) are two people.
In the 34th year of Guāngxù (1908),
the prison staff establishment was finalized.
Xúnfángduì Fēnlù Tǒnglǐngguān (Route Commander of the Patrol and Defense Corps)
(position was simplified and delayed)
Bāngtǒngguān (Assistant Commander),
Shūjìguān (Secretary),
Kuàijìguān (Accountant),
and Zhíshìguān (Executive Officer)
are each one person.
The Mǎ, Bùduì Guǎndàiguān (Cavalry and Infantry Commander) is one person.
The Shàoguān (Platoon Leader) and Shàozhǎng (Platoon Chief) are each three people.
The Shūjìzhǎng (Chief Secretary) is one person.
(All the above officers
were concurrently held by officers of the Lǜyíng (Green Standard Army)).
In the 33rd year of Guāngxù (1907),
due to the inconsistent organization of the various old patrol and training units,
the system of Tǒnglǐng (Commander) and other positions was established,
following the new army's successful methods.
Hǎijūn Jiànzhì (Naval Ship System)
The Xúnyáng Chángjiāng Jiànduì Tǒngzhì (Commander of the Cruiser Yangtze Fleet) is one person,
(Fù Dūtǒng with the rank of Zhèng Dūtǒng).
The Tǒnglǐng (Commanders) are two people,
(Xiédū Tǒngtǒng).
The Hǎiqí Xúnyángjiàn Guǎndài (Captain of the cruiser Hǎiqí),
Zǒng Guǎnlún (Chief Engineer),
(Zhèng Cānlǐng)
and Yīděng Cānmóuguān (First-Class Staff Officer),
as well as the various Guǎndài (Captains) of the Hǎichóu, Hǎichēn, Hǎiróng Xúnyángjiàn (cruisers Hǎichóu, Hǎichēn, Hǎiróng),
Nánchēn, Jìngqīng, Tōngjì Liànchuán (training ships Nánchēn, Jìngqīng, Tōngjì),
Jiāngyuán, Jiānglì, Chǔtóng, Chǔtài, Chǔyǒu, Jiāngyuán Pàochuán (gunboats Jiāngyuán, Jiānglì, Chǔtóng, Chǔtài, Chǔyǒu, Jiāngyuán),
Bǎomín Yùnchuán (transport ship Bǎomín),
(Fù Cānlǐng)
the various Guǎndài (Captains) of the Fēiyīng Yúléilièchuán (torpedo boat Fēiyīng),
Jiànwēi, Jiàn’ān Yúléipàochuán (torpedo gunboats Jiànwēi, Jiàn’ān),
Jiānghēng, Chǔqiān, Chǔyù, Liánjīng, Chǔguān, Wǔfèng Pàochuán (gunboats Jiānghēng, Chǔqiān, Chǔyù, Liánjīng, Chǔguān, Wǔfèng),
(Xié Cānlǐng)
and the Jiānzàoyuán (Supervising Engineers) at Vickers and Armstrong shipyards in England,
(Zhèng Cānlǐng)
are each one person.
The rest were not yet appointed.
In the 13th year of Tóngzhì (1874),
the court deliberated on coastal defense
and purchased a total of twenty warships.
In the 10th year of Guāngxù (1884),
the French military provoked conflict,
annihilating all of them.
Three years later,
the navy was established as a regular force,
divided into four fleets,
with one Tídū (Admiral) as the Left Wing
and two Zǒngbīng (Commander-in-Chiefs) as the Right Wing.
Additionally, five Fùjiàng (Brigadier-Generals),
four Cānlǐng (Colonels),
nine Yóují (Majors),
twenty-seven Dūsī (Captains),
sixty Shǒubèi (Lieutenants),
sixty-five Qiānzǒng (Ensigns),
and ninety-nine Bǎzǒng (Sergeants) were appointed.
By this time, the army was re-established.
During the Jiǎwǔ War (1894-1895), it was annihilated again.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
a Chóubèichù (Preparatory Office) was established,
and a Hǎijūn Tídū (Naval Admiral) was reappointed.
Imitating the army's ranks,
the naval official system was stipulated.
In the 3rd year (1911), the department was formed, and appointments were made as specified above.
In the late Míng dynasty,
oppressive policies proliferated,
fundraising and increased military provisions were levied,
the people were impoverished, and the national treasury was drained.
When the Qīng entered and took control of Zhōngguó,
they generally abolished these burdens,
and began anew with the people.
By the reigns of Kāngxī and Qiánlóng,
the nation was prosperous and the people were affluent.
All increases in population
were permanently exempt from additional taxes,
and universal exemptions from national rent and taxes were granted,
again and again.
Alas,
this was unprecedented in ancient times.
From the Dàoguāng and Xiánfēng reigns onward,
the maritime prohibitions were largely lifted,
and the nation faced many difficulties.
The avenues for squandering wealth expanded,
while the means of generating wealth stagnated.
Those in power were ignorant of the broader situation in Zhōngguó and abroad,
bringing about disaster and war,
and the stores of the national treasury and granaries
were suddenly depleted.
War indemnities and expenses amounted to over four hundred million.
Zhōngguó's entire assets were pledged for foreign loans,
accumulating debts that could not be repaid for decades.
Apportionments and additional levies
burdened both the higher and lower classes.
Thus, sea transport was adopted to save on grain transport costs,
the currency system was reformed to implement national currency,
salt administration was discussed to increase annual revenue,
and mineral production was opened to expand financial sources.
This included the creation of railways,
reform of postal services,
establishment of telegraph offices,
and opening of maritime shipping.
New policies flourished,
diligently seeking profit,
yet they were ignorant of and failed to discuss the ancient sagely kings' way of providing for the many with few resources, and alleviating suffering.
Indeed,
even during the peaceful reigns of Táng and Yú,
their admonishments to Shùn and Yǔ
earnestly cautioned them with
"if the four seas are in distress and poverty,
the Heavenly mandate will forever end."
How could those who govern a nation neglect this!
Herein, the history of Qīng dynasty financial administration
is presented in chapters.
Households and Land System
Households: Regarding the population of the Qīng,
only the registers of household and adult males belonging to the Zhāsàkè of the outer dependencies were managed by the Lǐfānyuàn.
As for the various types of households in each province,
their local officials compiled registers in the tenth month,
and were required to send them to the Hùbù by the eighth month of the following year,
where the Zhèjiāng Qīnglìsī managed them.
However, the registers of Mǎnzhōu, Ménggǔ, and Hànjūn adult males were managed by the Hùbù Bāqí Fèngxiǎng Chù.
At the end of the year,
the population figures were compiled into the "Yellow Registers" and reported.
The categories of households
were: military,
civilian,
artisan,
and salt-producing households.
Additionally, groups such as Huí, Fān, Qiāng, Miáo, Yáo, Lí, and Yí households
were all subordinate to their respective fǔ, tīng, zhōu, and xiàn.
Among the common people,
males were called dīng (adult males),
and females were called kǒu (mouths/persons).
A male aged sixteen was considered an adult male (chéngdīng);
those not yet adult males were also called kǒu.
Dīng and kǒu were attached to households.
The population of inner provinces was counted by dīng and kǒu;
border residents were counted by households.
This is because indigenous peoples such as Fān, Huí, Lí, Miáo, Yáo, and Yí,
having long been assimilated,
were all counted as part of the civilian population based on dīng and kǒu.
Those counted by household
included groups such as the Hèzhé, Fèiyākā, Qílèér, Kùyè, Èlúnchūn, and Hākèlā of the fifty-six clans belonging to Sānxìng,
various native chiefs (tǔsī) in Gānsù,
and the Fānzǐ belonging to Zhuānglàng Tīng,
the thirty-nine tribes belonging to various tǔsī in Xīzàng,
the families in Tángnǔ Wūliánghǎi under Wūliáyāsītái who paid sable tribute,
the families in Āěrtài Wūliánghǎi under Kēbùduō who paid sable tribute, and those who paid fox fur tribute,
and the families in Āěrtài Nuòér Wūliánghǎi who paid sable tribute and those who paid gray squirrel fur tribute;
these are all examples.
As for the Fān and Yí peoples belonging to the tǔsī,
only the number of villages and tribes was reported,
and those not counted by household were excluded from the figures.
Regarding the registration of common people,
there were four distinctions: civilian registration (mínjí);
military registration (jūnjí), also known as wèijí;
merchant registration (shāngjí);
and salt-producer registration (zàojí).
When managing these,
one must investigate their ancestral registration.
For example, if a household has established graves and residences in a place of temporary residence for over twenty years,
they are permitted to register and enter official service,
but must declare their ancestral registration to avoid conflicts of interest.
If the person themselves has passed away,
and their descendants have land, adult males, and grain in another province,
and wish to be included in that registration,
it is allowed.
Descendants of military exiles and other similar persons who are registered with their spouses
are permitted to take examinations.
Furthermore, their lineage must be distinguished.
For example, if a commoner has no son,
they are permitted to adopt a male from the same clan and appropriate generation as heir.
However, sons-in-law, adopted sons, and children adopted under the age of three,
who are given property according to discretion,
cannot automatically be considered heirs.
Moreover, the respectable and the humble must be differentiated.
For example, the four classes of people were considered respectable,
while servants, prostitutes, and actors were considered humble.

All yamen runners, such as zàolì (attendants), mǎkuài (horse-riding constables), bùkuài (foot constables), xiǎomǎ (junior horsemen), jìnzú (jailers), ménzǐ (gatekeepers), gōngbīng (bowmen), wǔzuò (coroner's assistants), liángchāi (grain tax collectors), and patrol camp police (fānyì),
were all considered humble occupations,
as were long-term retainers and servants.
False registration, multi-jurisdictional registration, cross-border registration, and temporary residence registration were all prohibited.
When Shìzǔ entered the pass,
there was an order to organize households into pái-jiǎ (ward and tithing) units.
The method was as follows:
in the cities and rural areas of each zhōu and xiàn, ten households formed one pái-zhǎng (ward head),
ten pái formed one jiǎ-zhǎng (tithing head),
and ten jiǎ formed one bǎo-zhǎng (district head).
Each household was issued an imprinted plaque,
on which their names and the number of dīng (adult males) were written.
When going out, their destination was noted;
when coming in, their origin was checked.
Temples and monasteries were also uniformly issued these plaques,
to monitor the comings and goings of monks and Daoists.
Inns were ordered to keep a ledger,
recording the names and belongings of their guests,
for ease of inspection.
In the 22nd year of Qiánlóng,
fifteen articles were revised and enacted: One,
every household in the directly administered provinces was to be issued a ménpái (door plaque) annually.
Pái-zhǎng and jiǎ-zhǎng were to be replaced every three years,
and bǎo-zhǎng every year.

If there were incidents of theft, heterodox sects, gambling, gambling tools, harboring fugitives, abduction and trafficking, private minting, private sales, private salt, stepping on or selling opium, selling saltpeter and sulfur,
and privately establishing names for fundraising gatherings,
as well as unfamiliar and suspicious individuals,
the responsible specialized official was ordered to investigate and report.
Changes in household registration due to migration or attrition
were to be reported promptly,
and the ménpái was to be revised and reissued accordingly.
One,
the households of gentry and scholars
were to be organized in the same manner as commoners.
One,
in villages where Banner people and commoners lived intermingled,
they were to be organized together.
If Banner people or commoners committed offenses,
the local official was to handle it jointly with the lǐshì tóngzhī (Assistant Department Magistrate for Affairs).
As for merchants and commoners trading and residing within the駐防營 (garrison camps) in various provinces,
and officials hiring servants,
separate plaque registers were to be compiled,
and reported to the lǐshì tīng (Department for Affairs) for verification.
One,
for commoners farming in the Měnggǔ (Mongolian) areas beyond the frontier,
pái-tóu (plaque heads), zǒng-jiǎ (chief tithing heads), and shí-jiā-zhǎng (ten-household heads) were to be established.
If there were cases of theft, banditry,
or harboring fugitives,
they were ordered to investigate and report.
One,
all guest commoners trading in the interior,
or those who owned property,
were to be organized similarly to local residents.
One,
salt fields and well furnaces
were to have separate pái-jiǎ organizations.
Hired workers
were to be registered with the furnace households.
One,
for mining households,
factory officials were to supervise factory owners, kè-zhǎng (tax managers), dòng-zhǎng (cave heads), lú-tóu (furnace masters), etc., in compiling and checking.
Coal mine employers in various locations
were to register their hired workers with the local authorities for verification.
One,
for shān-jū péng-mín (shed-dwelling people in mountainous areas) in various provinces,
household registers were to be compiled,
and the landlord and bǎo-jiǎ were to jointly report.
For Liáomín (Liao people) in Guǎngdōng,
each liáo (dwelling) was to be given a plaque,
and they were to provide mutual guarantees.
One,
for merchant and fishing vessels in coastal provinces,
guarantees were to be obtained from ào-jiǎ (harbor tithing heads) and neighboring relatives,
reported to the officials, and a permit issued.
For merchant ships, the name, age, origin of the shipowner, helmsman, and sailors were to be filled in the permit.
When sailing offshore,
mutual guarantees were to be obtained from other ships,
and verified at the xùn-kǒu (patrol station) before being allowed to proceed.
Fishing vessels only needed to fill in the shipowner's name, age, and origin.
For small boats engaged in fishing and harvesting in inland waters,
the ào-jiǎ were ordered to inspect them.
As for inland river vessels,
a white plaque was to be set up at the stern,
and the bù-tóu (wharf heads) were ordered to inspect them.
Fishing boat households and people living in temporary sheds by the water for a living
were all to be managed by the nearest bǎo-jiǎ.
One,
for Miáo (Miao) people who had settled in the interior
and had long been registered as commoners,
they were to be investigated and registered in the same way as commoners.
The remaining Miáo and Yáo (Yao) people in other areas
were to be inspected and restrained by their qiān-bǎi-hù (thousand and hundred household heads), tóu-rén (chiefs), and dòng-zhǎng.
One,
in Yúnnán, where Yí (Yi) and commoners lived intermingled,
they were to be uniformly organized into bǎo-jiǎ.
For those who formed their own villages by mountains and rivers,
the guǎn-shì tóu-mù (managing headmen) were ordered to compile registers and inspect them.
One,
guest commoners in Sìchuān province
were to be investigated and registered in the same way as local residents.
One,
for Fānzi (Tibetan) indigenous people in Gānsù,
the tǔ-sī (native chieftains) were made responsible for investigation.
For those under the jurisdiction of local officials,
the responsible headmen were ordered to compile and check,
and the local officials were to issue plaques and report.
For various Fān (Tibetan) villages in Sìchuān where the tǔ-sī system was abolished and replaced with regular administration,
xiāng-yuē (village compacts) and jiǎ-zhǎng were ordered to inspect them,
all subject to the management of the fǔ-yí zhǎng-bǎo (intendant of native affairs and fort commander).
One,
for monks and Daoists in temples and monasteries,
the sēng-gāng (monastic superintendents) and dào-jì (Daoist registrars) were ordered to report quarterly.
For Huímín (Hui people) in various provinces,
the zhǎng-jiào (imams) of the mosques were ordered to inspect them.
One,
for foreign transient beggars,
the bǎo-zhèng (head of a bǎo) was to supervise the gài-tóu (beggar chiefs) in investigating them.
The young and strong were to be sent back to their native places for resettlement,
while the rest were to be managed by facilities like the qī-liú suǒ (shelter for vagrants).
From then on, the laws became even more stringent.
At that time, Fān and Miáo people in various provinces often had language barriers with commoners in the interior,
leading to frequent conflicts.
In the 24th year,
regulations were established for defining the Fān boundary and prohibiting entry into Miáo territory.
Taiwanese commoners and Fān were not allowed to intermarry;
violators would be divorced.
Commoners from various provinces who entered Miáo land without reason,
and Miáo people who entered commoner land without reason,
were all to be punished according to regulations.
If they wished to travel for trade,
they must obtain guarantees from their business associates and neighbors,
report to officials for a permit,
and only proceed after verification and release by the táng-xùn (patrol stations).
The term "棚民" (péngmín)
originated in the three provinces of Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, and Fújiàn.
Within various mountain counties,
there have long been people who built sheds (棚) to live in,
engaging in cultivation of hemp and bamboo,
opening furnaces and smelting iron,
and making paper and cultivating mushrooms as their livelihoods.
As for the poor people of Guǎngdōng who entered the mountains to build huts (寮)
to extract fragrant wood and pound it into powder, or chop firewood and burn charcoal as their livelihoods,
they were called "寮民" (liáomín).
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
it was decreed that they should all be registered and investigated according to the bǎojiǎ system.
In the twenty-eighth year of Qiánlóng,
it was stipulated that péngmín in various provinces who rented land as single individuals
should be required to obtain an official ticket (印票) from their native prefecture or county,
and also have relatives to vouch for them,
before being permitted to rent land and settle.
Should their origins be unclear,
the guarantor would be held strictly responsible for investigation, reporting, and prosecution.
In the fifty-fifth year,
an edict stated:
"The Governor-General of Guǎngdōng reported,
requesting the demolition of liáofáng (huts) in Wēizhōu, on the sea border of Léi and Lián, and in Xiáyáng, east of there,
and their occupants be sent back to their native places,
to prevent collusion with foreign pirates and causing trouble.
And also to destroy liáofáng in thirty-two places, including Jiàoyǐwān, totaling one hundred and sixty-two households,
and provide alternative relief and resettlement.
Many islands belonging to coastal provinces
have inland people living and working peacefully.
If they are suddenly ordered to relocate,
causing hundreds of thousands of lives to be displaced,
how can the heart bear it?
Furthermore, there is a fear that if handled improperly,
good people might turn into bandits.
Therefore, concerning all islands in various provinces,
except for those that are by law to be sealed off,
the rest shall remain as they are.
As for scattered individuals,
they are all poor people,
and it is especially unacceptable to leave them isolated.
And fishermen who go out to sea for fishing and hunting,
temporarily building huts on islands to stay,
should not be entirely prohibited.
Moreover, as the population is small,
investigation is not difficult;
it is only up to the various governors-general and governors to strictly instruct civil and military officials to establish the bǎojiǎ system.
If any bandits are mixed in,
or if anyone harbors bandits,
once discovered,
their dwelling huts shall all be burned down,
so they know to be fearful and cautious.
As for fishing boats entering and exiting ports,
it is imperative that they obtain guarantees and permits,
with names registered.
If, upon entry, they hide goods
and appear suspicious,
a strict interrogation should be conducted,
and they will not be difficult to apprehend immediately."
In the fifty-seventh year,
an edict stated:
"According to what Fúníng reported,
there are over twenty thousand residents on the islands of Shāndōng province,
and there must also be many on the islands of other provinces.
We should comply with previous directives,
prohibiting the construction of additional houses,
to prevent the population from growing daily.
Vigilant investigation should still be maintained,
to prevent them from colluding with bandits
and causing incidents."
In the first year of Xiánfēng,
Cháng Dàchún, the Governor of Zhèjiāng, reported:
"The péngmín of Zhèjiāng have opened up too many mountains,
leading to silt accumulation and soil blockage,
obstructing waterways and fields.
I request measures to be established for registration, investigation, and resettlement,
distinguishing between those to stay and those to leave."
This was acted upon as proposed.
After the chaos of Zhāng Xiànzhōng in Sìchuān,
only one or two out of a hundred survived,
and all cultivation was done by people from the Three Rivers and Húguǎng who had migrated there.
In the fifth year of Yōngzhèng,
the number of those who arrived due to famine increased.
An edict ordered the prefectures and counties of Sìchuān to meticulously investigate the names and native places of each household.
If they were indeed poor people without means,
then according to the size of their labor force,
they were to be granted fifty or sixty mù, or thirty or forty mù of barren land,
for them to cultivate.
As for the areas of Jílín, Nínggǔtǎ, Bódōunà, Àlèchǔkā, Lāllín, and so forth,
a decree in the twenty-seventh year of Qiánlóng prohibited unregistered vagrants from residing there.
By the thirty-fourth year,
Fùliáng, the General of Jílín, reported:
"There are two hundred and forty-two households of vagrants in the Àlèchǔkā and Lāllín areas,
and I request that they be completely expelled within one year."
The Emperor said:
"Since the migrants arrived before the fixed regulation,
they should be permitted to register and cultivate land,
and be resettled uniformly,
so that none are left homeless."
In the middle of Jiāqìng,
Guō'ěrluósī again had two thousand three hundred and thirty households of new migrants from inland areas;
Jílín Tīng had one thousand four hundred and fifty-nine households;
Chángchūn Tīng had six thousand nine hundred and fifty-three households.
All were reported by the General and ordered to be registered and settled.
As for the people of Shāndōng who migrated beyond the pass,
in the fifty-first year of Kāngxī, there were already over one hundred thousand people.
Shèngzǔ issued an edict:
"Henceforth, for people from Shāndōng who go beyond the pass, or return to Shāndōng from beyond the pass,
their age, appearance, and native place should be investigated,
and a register compiled for scrutiny,
cross-referenced with each other."
Later, many people from Zhílì and Shānxī also went beyond the pass.
In the early Yōngzhèng era,
due to the successive establishment of three assistant magistrates (tóngzhī) at Gǔběikǒu, Zhāngjiākǒu, and Guīhuàchéng for administration,
the county sub-magistrate (xiànchéng) of Wànquán Xiàn was subsequently moved to Zhāngjiākǒu.
At Gǔběikǒu, one patrol inspector (xúnjiǎn) was added;
at Guīhuàchéng, four assistant sub-prefects (tōngpàn) and one patrol inspector were added.
Each, according to the people under their jurisdiction,
following the bǎojiǎ system,
registered their names and native places,
and annually submitted them to the Board for verification.
Whenever people entered or exited the passes,
their native prefecture or county issued an official ticket for verification and release.
All issued tickets
were compiled into a register and reported to the Board.
