The people of Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng who migrated to Táiwān were particularly numerous.
In the fifteenth year of Jiāqìng,
Fāng Wéidiàn, the Governor-General of Zhè and Mǐn, reported:
"The land in Gámǎlán is fertile,
and many inland people have migrated there.
Current household registration checks show
forty-two thousand five hundred odd adult males from Zhāngzhōu,
two hundred and fifty odd adult males from Quánzhōu,
and one hundred and forty odd adult males from Yuèdōng,
living interspersed with various 'cooked' and 'raw' Fān (aborigines).
There must be some control over them."
Therefore, it was decided to add one assistant sub-prefect for Gámǎlán.
Furthermore, in counties like Tóng and Pèi in Jiāngsū,
after the Yellow River receded,
it became barren land.
People from Shāndōng's Cáo, Jì, and other prefectures continuously moved there,
establishing "lake societies" (hútuan)
and collectively cultivating the land.
The native people of Tóng and Pèi, due to the occupation of land by "guest people" (kèmín),
constantly sued and fought each other.
In the fifth year of Tóngzhì,
the Board of Revenue reported:
"Having investigated and confirmed the Diāo and Wáng tuán (societies) that harbored Nian bandits,
they are to be driven back to their native places.
The law-abiding good tuán are to be allowed to continue their peaceful livelihoods."
In all these cases of intermingling between Yí (non-Han) and Hàn,
and mutual suspicion between natives and guests,
when there was a concern about trouble,
strict prevention measures were taken;
when pity was felt for the homeless,
generous provisions were made for them.
The key to all these was the bǎojiǎ system.
However, the bǎo jiǎ (保甲) system operated in peacetime,
while biān shěn (編審) was the origin of the dīng fù (丁賦), or poll tax.
The system of biān shěn mandated that
prefectural and county officials create registers and submit them to the fǔ (府, prefecture);
the fǔ, in turn, would create a consolidated register and submit it to the Bùzhèng Sī (布政司, Provincial Administration Commission).
There were four registers: military, civilian, artisan, and salt-worker,
each divided into three grades: upper, middle, and lower.
There were also various types of dīng (丁, adult males): civilian dīng, station dīng, indigenous military dīng, guard dīng, and garrison dīng.
The total number of dīng was recorded in the Huáng Cè (黃冊, Yellow Register).
Governors-general and governors would report the records from the Bùzhèng Sī to the Hù Bù (戶部, Board of Revenue),
compiling memorials to inform the emperor.
In Shùnzhì (順治) 14th year (1657),
an order was issued for prefectural and county officials to conduct a biān shěn of households and population.
Those who increased the dīng count by more than 2,000 individuals
were to be given a commendation.
In Kāngxī (康熙) 51st year (1712),
an edict was issued stating:
“Newly added dīng shall never be subject to additional tax.”
From then on, this benevolent policy of the Shèngzǔ (聖祖, Kāngxī Emperor)
continued throughout the dynasty.
However, when dīng were removed (from the registers),
it was impossible to avoid filling the vacancies.
Thus, in Kāngxī 55th year (1716),
the Hù Bù requested that
the newly added dīng from biān shěn be used to make up for the old shortfalls.
If there were surplus dīng,
they were to be recorded in the Zīshēng Cè (滋生冊, Register of Natural Increase) and reported,
which was approved.
Gāozōng (高宗, Qiánlóng Emperor) instructed the Nèigé (內閣, Grand Secretariat), saying:
“I have examined the population figures reported by the various provinces last year;
compared to the Kāngxī (康熙) period,
they have increased by more than ten times.
With prolonged peace,
the population grows daily,
and resources naturally cannot be as abundant as before.
Furthermore, the land occupied by dwellings
has more than quintupled.
Those who produce are few,
and those who consume are many.
I am greatly concerned about this.
Fortunately, since my ascension to the throne,
I have expanded our territory and frontiers,
and the domain has daily broadened.
The common people have all been able to reclaim land outside the borders,
thereby temporarily securing food and clothing.
However, for a long-term plan,
unless there is no wasteland in the wilderness
and every household has surplus grain,
it will not be easy to enjoy the blessings of peace.
Governors-general and governors of all provinces, and those responsible for governing the people,
must at all times exhort and instruct them
to cultivate frugality as a custom,
to cherish resources and fully utilize the land.
They must not compete in extravagance
or fall into idleness.
At this time, the biān shěn system had already been discontinued.
The population figures reported by the directly governed provinces
were mostly based on the annual Yānhù Cè (煙戶冊, Household Register).
Over time,
officials regarded it as a mere formality,
and their reports were often not thoroughly checked.
How can this fulfill my desire to know the number of people in the entire realm?”
He further decreed:
“According to Zhèng Huīzǔ (鄭輝祖),
the previously compiled population registers showed
the annual increase in population
to be uniformly identical.
Such a perfunctory continuation of practice—
what kind of system is this!
All population registers that should be submitted by the various provinces this year
are extended until the end of next year.
Should there be any further errors or omissions,
punishment will definitely be administered.”
At that time, the population registers were probably not immune to the abuse of arbitrary filling.
However, since the Shèngzǔ (Kāngxī Emperor),
after more than a hundred years of recuperation and growth,
the people living during that time,
from youth to old age,
did not know the suffering of war.
Moreover, with abundant harvests and happy people,
without premature deaths, diseases, or plagues,
or those forced to move and fall into destitution leading to depopulation,
their household and population proliferation
cannot be said to be entirely fictitious.
As for the discontinuation of biān shěn,
it began in Yōngzhèng (雍正) 4th year (1726).
Lǐ Fú (李紱), the Governor-general of Zhílì (直隸), submitted a memorial proposing to replace biān shěn with bǎo jiǎ, which roughly stated:
“Biān shěn is conducted once every five years.
Although its intention is to clarify household registration,
it is not as detailed and precise as bǎo jiǎ,
which can both investigate transient populations
and eliminate the need for separate household inquiries.
I request that from now on, strict orders be given to arrange the dīng,
ensuring that no one aged sixteen or above
is omitted.
At year-end, registers should be compiled,
and the Bùzhèng Sī (布政司) should consolidate them,
creating a separate comprehensive register for presentation.
This register should only include the actual number of dīng in the villages and households,
omitting ‘flower households’ (fictitious or empty households),
thereby simplifying the records while ensuring a complete dīng count.”
In Qiánlóng (乾隆) 5th year (1740),
the Hù Bù again requested that the governors-general and governors
report the household and population figures along with grain figures every November;
this exception did not apply to barbarian (Fān) and Miao (Miáo) border regions not included in biān shěn.
This was approved.
In the 37th year (1772),
following Lǐ Hàn’s (李瀚) request,
biān shěn was permanently discontinued.
Thereafter, only the transport dīng were subjected to biān shěn every four years.
The Qīng (清) dynasty inherited the chaos and devastation of the late Míng (明) dynasty,
with a depleted population.
Through successive reigns of recuperation and growth,
the population figures
increased annually.
To summarize: In Shùnzhì 18th year (1661),
the total population of the empire was calculated at
19,203,233 individuals.
In Kāngxī 50th year (1711),
it was 24,621,324 individuals.
In the 60th year (1721),
it was 29,148,359 individuals,
plus 467,850 naturally increasing dīng.
In Yōngzhèng 12th year (1734),
it was 26,417,932 individuals,
plus 937,530 naturally increasing dīng.
In Qiánlóng 29th year (1764),
it was 205,591,017 individuals.
In the 60th year (1795),
it was 296,960,545 individuals.
In Jiāqìng (嘉慶) 24th year (1819),
it was 301,260,545 individuals.
In Dàoguāng (道光) 29th year (1849),
it was 412,986,649 individuals.
During the Xiánfēng (咸豐) and Tóngzhì (同治) periods,
wars erupted everywhere,
and reports from several provinces were often missing.
The verifiable figures
ranged from 200 to 300 million individuals.
In Guāngxù (光緒) 1st year (1875),
it was 322,655,781 individuals.
In the 32nd year (1906),
the official system was reformed.
The Hù Bù was renamed the Dùzhī Bù (度支部, Board of Finance),
and the previously established Xúnjǐng Bù (巡警部, Ministry of Police) was changed to the Mínzhèng Bù (民政部, Ministry of Civil Affairs).
The investigation of population
became its responsibility,
with Xúnjǐng Dào (巡警道, Police Intendants) in each province specifically managing this task.
The following year (1907),
an edict was issued to the directly governed provinces to report population figures,
emphasizing that accurate numbers must be verified
to serve as the foundation for all government affairs.
The Mínzhèng Bù memorialized, stating:
“Upon review, the dīng registers for Hēilóngjiāng (黑龍江), Ānhuī (安徽), Jiāngsū (江蘇), Fújiàn (福建), Gānsù (甘肅), Guǎngxī (廣西), and Yúnnán (雲南) in the 32nd year,
as well as the dīng registers for the 31st year,
were not completed.
Although the various governors-general and governors clearly knew they had exceeded the deadline
and should have been impeached according to regulations,
old habits are difficult to change.
Upon taking over, our ministry
planned practical measures.
We propose to request an imperial edict to the various governors-general and governors,
tasking prefectures, sub-prefectures, departments, and counties
to investigate the accurate number of dīng and households by dividing their areas into townships and districts.
These figures should be tallied at the end of December each year
to clarify the boundaries.
They should still be submitted to the ministry for compilation and memorialization by October of the following year.”
The decree was approved.
In Xuāntǒng (宣統) 1st year (1909),
the format for household registration was re-issued.
It ordered an initial count of households and population,
to be reported by October of the following year.
A subsequent count of individuals was to be reported
by October of Xuāntǒng 4th year (1912).
By October of the 3rd year (1911),

according to reports from the inner and outer cities of Jīngshī (京師, Beijing), Shùntiān Fǔ (順天府), various directly governed provinces, various banner garrisons, various stationed garrisons, and various Mongolian banners,
excluding the provinces of Xīnjiāng (新疆), Húběi (湖北), Guǎngdōng (廣東), Guǎngxī (廣西);
the garrisons of Jiāngníng (江寧), Qīngzhōu (青州), Xī'ān (西安), Liángzhōu (涼州), Yīlí (伊犁), Guìzhōu (貴州), Xīníng (西寧);
the Tàiníng Zhèn (泰寧鎮) and the Mongolian banners of Rèhé (熱河);
and the border affairs of Chuān (川, Sìchuān) and Diān (滇, Yúnnán),
which had not yet submitted their registers to the ministry,
there were 54,668,004 principal households,
14,578,370 dependent households,
totaling 69,246,374 households.
The number of males was 139,662,410,
totaling 239,594,668 individuals.
Since the thirteenth year of Yōngzhèng, the Ministry of Revenue approved a memorial,
stating that one hundred and ninety-nine aboriginals (shēngfān) from Táiwān Fǔ, Fújiàn,
were registered in Zhānghuà;
and one hundred and seventy-nine assimilated indigenous people (guīliú tǔmín) from Qìngyuǎn Fǔ, Guǎngxī,
were registered in Yíshān.
Subsequently, many Táiwān shēngfān, Sìchuān shēngfān, and Língyí assimilated.
Regulations were established for specialized officials to organize them into bǎojiǎ units
to investigate and arrest bandits,
and to regularly lecture on imperial edicts on the full moon day
to promote civilization.
From then on, the clothing, caps, and language of these indigenous people were no different from those of the local populace,
and some even studied and took imperial examinations.
During the reigns of Tóngzhì and Guāngxù,
communication became increasingly widespread,
and our nation's people engaged in farming, trade, and migration,
spreading across the vast oceans.
There were also cases of them changing their nationality to that of other countries.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs, in collaboration with the Minister for Revising Laws, drafted nationality regulations.
Because national nationality laws include both the principle of territory (dìmàixì) and the principle of blood (xuèmàixì),
that is, the two meanings of jus soli and jus sanguinis,
these two meanings, when in conflict,
inevitably lead to contradictions.
Therefore, a compromise system was adopted,
divided into four chapters: inherent nationality, naturalization, expatriation, and re-naturalization,
with an emphasis on the principle of blood (xuèmàixì).
The Constitutional Compiling and Investigation Bureau (Xiànzhèng Biānchá Guǎn) further divided these four chapters into twenty-four articles.
The chapter on inherent nationality states:
First,
regardless of whether one is born in China,
those who possess Chinese nationality are of three types: one,
those whose father is Chinese at birth;
two,
those born after their father's death, where the father was Chinese at the time of death;
three,
those whose mother is Chinese and whose father is unascertainable
or stateless.
Second,
if both parents are unascertainable
or stateless,
but the person is born in Chinese territory,
they also possess Chinese nationality.
The same applies to abandoned children whose place of birth is unascertainable but who are found in Chinese territory.
The chapter on naturalization states:
Third,
all foreigners who wish to acquire Chinese nationality
may petition for naturalization.
The five essential conditions are: one,
having continuously resided in China for ten years or more;
two,
being twenty years of age or older and considered capable according to their national laws;
three,
having good conduct;
four,
possessing sufficient assets or skills
to be self-reliant;
five,
being able to renounce their original nationality upon naturalization, according to their national laws.
For stateless persons wishing to acquire Chinese nationality,
they must be twenty years of age or older
and fulfill conditions one, three, and four of the preceding paragraph.
Fourth,
any foreigner or stateless person who has rendered exceptional service to China,
even if not meeting conditions one to four,
may be specially permitted to naturalize upon a joint memorial from the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and the Ministry of Civil Affairs, requesting an imperial decree.
Fifth,
any foreign or stateless woman who marries a Chinese man;
or who lives with a Chinese man as a step-parent;
or an illegitimate child whose
father is Chinese and who is acknowledged by the father;
or an illegitimate child whose
mother is Chinese and whose
father is unwilling to acknowledge, but is acknowledged by the mother.
If any of these circumstances exist,
they shall be considered naturalized.
However, for women marrying Chinese men,
this is limited to those whose official marriage has been duly registered.
Other provisions are limited to those who are not yet adults or not yet married women according to their national laws.
Sixth,
when a man is naturalized,
his wife and minor children should also be naturalized.
However, this does not apply to those whose original nationality is not simultaneously renounced according to their national laws.
If his wife voluntarily wishes to naturalize,
or if the naturalized person voluntarily wishes his minor children to naturalize,
even if they do not meet conditions one to four of Article Three,
their petition for naturalization shall be approved.
Seventh,
adult children of a naturalized person who currently reside in China,
even if not meeting conditions one to four of Article Three,
may also petition for naturalization.
Eighth,
naturalized persons may not hold the following official positions: one,
all officials of the Grand Council (Jūnjī Chù) and the Imperial Household Department (Nèi Wù Fǔ), and civil officials of the fourth rank or higher in the capital and provinces;
two,
all military officers and soldiers;
three,
members of both houses of parliament and provincial advisory councils (zīyì jú).
These restrictions,
for specially naturalized persons, may be waived by imperial decree upon request from the Ministry of Civil Affairs after ten years; and for other naturalized persons, after twenty years.
Ninth,
all petitioners for naturalization
must declare that they will abide by Chinese laws after naturalization
and renounce their original national rights,
submit a written pledge to that effect,
and also have two impartial local gentry members each provide a guarantee.
Tenth,
all petitioners for naturalization
should submit their petition to the local official where they reside,
who shall detail the request to the supervising superior for a memorial to the Ministry of Civil Affairs for approval and public announcement,
and issue a certificate as proof.
For those abroad,
they should submit their petition to the consul,
who will forward it through the Minister Plenipotentiary (chūshǐ dàchén),
or directly submit it to the Minister Plenipotentiary for memorial to the Ministry for record.
The chapter on expatriation states:
Eleventh,
all Chinese citizens wishing to acquire foreign nationality
must first petition for expatriation.
Twelfth,
Chinese citizens may be permitted to expatriate if they meet four conditions: one,
having no pending criminal or civil lawsuits;
two,
having no military service obligations;
three,
having no overdue taxes;
four,
holding no official rank or status.
Thirteenth,
any Chinese woman who marries a foreigner;
or who lives with a foreigner as a step-parent;
or an illegitimate child whose
father is a foreigner and who is acknowledged by the father;
or an illegitimate child whose
mother is a foreigner and whose
father is unwilling to acknowledge, but is acknowledged by the mother.
If any of these circumstances exist,
they shall be considered expatriated.
However, for women marrying foreigners,
this is limited to those whose official marriage has been duly registered.
Other provisions are limited to those who are not yet adults or not yet married women according to Chinese laws.
Fourteenth,
when a man expatriates,
his wife and minor children shall also be expatriated.
If the wife voluntarily wishes to retain her nationality,
or if the expatriated person wishes his minor children to retain their nationality,
their declaration shall be approved,
and they shall remain of Chinese nationality.
Fifteenth,
a married woman
may not independently petition for expatriation.
Those who are not yet adults or are incapacitated according to Chinese laws
are also not permitted to independently petition for expatriation.
Sixteenth,
all Chinese citizens who expatriate
shall not enjoy
any special benefits they might have had in the interior.
Seventeenth,
all petitioners for expatriation
must personally submit a written pledge,
declaring that they do not have any of the conditions listed in Article Twelve or undiscovered criminal offenses.
Eighteenth,
all petitioners for expatriation
should submit their petition to the local official of their place of origin,
who shall detail the request to the supervising superior for a memorial to the Ministry of Civil Affairs for approval and public announcement.
For those abroad,
they should submit their petition to the consul,
who will forward it through the Minister Plenipotentiary,
or directly submit it to the Minister Plenipotentiary for memorial to the Ministry.
If not petitioned and approved,
regardless of the circumstances,
they shall still be of Chinese nationality.
Regulations for Re-registration
Article 19:
Those who lost their registration due to marrying a foreigner
may, if divorced or widowed,
apply for re-registration.
Article 20:
The wives of those whose registration was annulled,
after divorce or the death of their husband,
and their minor sons after reaching adulthood,
may all apply for re-registration.
Article 21:
If, after approval for annulment of registration,
one continues to reside in Zhōngguó for three years or more,
and meets the conditions of Article 3, paragraphs 3 and 4,
they may apply for re-registration.
This limit does not apply
to foreigners who acquired registration and then renounced it.
Article 22:
For any application for re-registration,
two impartial gentry or merchants from the applicant's original province must provide a guarantee,
and submit it to the local official,
who will then request the superior officer to memorialize the Mínzhèngbù for approval and public announcement.
Article 23:
Those who are re-registered
may not hold official positions listed in Article 8
until five years have passed.
Article 24:
These regulations shall take effect immediately
after they are memorialized and approved by imperial decree.
Additionally, the Qīng dynasty had benevolent policies
regarding changing status to commoner.
In provinces like Shānxī, there were musical households (yuèhù).
Their ancestors were registered as yuèjí (musical households) because they did not support the Yān troops at the end of the Jiànwén reign of the Míng dynasty.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
an order was issued to prohibit and abolish them in all jurisdictions,
allowing them to change their profession and become commoners.
It also decreed that the duòmín of Zhèjiāng
and the gàihù of Sūzhōu,
whose occupations were no different from yuèjí,
should also have their registration abolished.
In the fifth year,
it was noted that in Huīzhōu, Jiāngnán, there were bàndāng,
and in Níngguó, there were shìpú (hereditary servants).
Locals called them
"xìmín" (inferior people);
there were even villages where the populations of two families were equal,
yet one family served the other,
like slaves.
It was also decreed that they be emancipated.
In the seventh year,
it was decreed that Guǎngdōng dàn hù (boat people) who fished from boats
and were not allowed to come ashore by the Yuè people
should be specifically prohibited from this restriction.
They were permitted to reside in waterside villages
and be incorporated into the bǎojiǎ system like ordinary commoners.
In the thirty-sixth year of Qiánlóng,
Liú Zūn, the education commissioner of Shǎnxī, memorialized that rules should be established to prohibit yuèhù and gàihù in Shān-Shǎn.
The Bù (Board) deliberated that after reporting to officials and changing their profession,
four generations must pass,
and all direct relatives of the clan must be of clear and upright conduct,
before they could apply for donations and examinations.
The dàn hù of Guǎngdōng,
the jiǔxìng yúchuán of Zhèjiāng,
and all similar cases
should be handled according to this.
In the fourteenth year of Jiāqìng,
it was again noted that shìpú from the three prefectures of Huīzhōu, Níngguó, and Chízhōu who donated to become gōngshēng (imperial students) and took examinations
were often denounced and impeached by locals.
An imperial edict stated:
"Such statuses
should always be determined by whether they are currently in service.
If the years are distant and written contracts are untraceable,
they shall be immediately emancipated."
For the Eight Banners population,
a review was stipulated every three years,
ordering each zuǒlǐng to inspect those who had reached adulthood
and add them to the population register.
If able-bodied men were concealed for official positions,
their master, zuǒlǐng, and lǐngcuī would all be punished differently.
Initially, three hundred able-bodied men constituted one zuǒlǐng;
later, it was revised to two hundred.
In the fourth year of Kāngxī,
it was decreed that if the surplus population within the Mǎnzhōu and Ménggǔ zuǒlǐng reached over one hundred,
those who wished to be divided into two zuǒlǐngs
were permitted to do so.
In the fourth year of Yōngzhèng,
an edict was issued to the Eight Banners dùtǒng and the resident dùtǒng and jiāngjūn in the provinces,
instructing them to hand over to the zuǒlǐng, xiāoqíjào, and lǐngcuī
the task of clearly listing new and old able-bodied men household by household,
and submitting the names of the reviewing officials,
with guarantees, to the Bù.
Those who had not reached adulthood,
those who were not legitimate children of respectable families,
and those whose registration should be removed
were to be verified and removed.
In the fifth year,
it was decreed that for all population registers,
each household should write "such-and-such person, such-and-such official" for separate households,
or "idle such-and-such" if without office;
the official titles and names of fathers and elder brothers should be written above,
and the children, sons of brothers,
and the number of people under the household should be written beside.
Whether residing at home
or elsewhere,
all should be fully recorded.
For banner members and soldiers stationed in various provinces,
and the children and family members of civil and military officials serving outside the capital,
the respective jiāngjūn, dūdū, and fǔ (governors) were ordered to compile registers and send them to the relevant banners.
In the sixth year of Qiánlóng,
it was decreed that for the Eight Banners, all those who had reached adulthood or were underage but receiving stipends under each zuǒlǐng
should be entered into the population register,
distinguishing between principal households and opening separate accounts,
and for each name under the household, three generations of ancestors' records should be written.
For people under a household whose ancestors were either purchased by contract,
or brought from Shèngjīng,
or defected with their land,
these distinctions should be noted.
The children of principal households
were all to be registered as having principal status.
In the seventh year,
an edict stated:
"The Eight Banners Hànjūn
were originally Hàn people.
Some followed the dragon into the pass,
some submitted after the establishment of the capital,
some entered the banners due to offenses, or were transferred from the households of the Three Feudatories,
some were transferred from the Nèiwùfǔ or princely baōyī (bondservants),
as well as recruited artillerymen,
adopted individuals of different surnames,
and those who joined with their mothers due to kinship, etc.
They joined the banners at different times
and under varied circumstances.
Among them, only the descendants of those who followed the dragon
all possess old merits
and require no separate discussion or change.
As for all other categories of people,
I wish to broaden their paths to livelihood.
If they wish to return to their original registered places,
they shall be uniformly incorporated into the bǎojiǎ system.
Those who wish to reside in other provinces
are also permitted to go.
If any among them hold hereditary official positions,
they are still allowed to inherit them.
Those who do not wish to leave the banners
may remain."
In the eighth year,
another edict stated:
"The previous imperial decree
primarily referred to those who had not yet entered officialdom or were of low rank.
As for those who have served in office for a long time
and have continuously received national favor,
they themselves and their children
are not permitted to apply to leave the banners."
In the twelfth year,
another edict stated:
"Those listed in separate registers of the Eight Banners
were originally household slaves who fraudulently entered principal households,
and later voluntarily confessed;
and banner people who adopted commoners as sons.
For those who wish to leave the banners and become commoners,
where they register is entirely up to them.
Their own land and property
are also permitted to be taken with them."
In the twenty-sixth year,
it was stipulated that Hànjūn currently serving outside the capital as tóngzhī, shǒubèi and above,
capital officials as zhǔshì and above,
and banner officials as fifth rank and above,
were all not permitted to change to commoner status.
The rest in the capital were to report to their respective banners, which would consult the Bù and circulate the order to various provinces;
those outside the capital were to report to the dūdū and fǔ, who would consult the Bù and banners,
to be incorporated into commoner registration,
and were also permitted to take examinations uniformly.
Generally, the Qīng dynasty supported all Eight Banners members with national resources.
However, as their numbers proliferated later,
even though several million taels were spent annually,
it was still insufficient,
and the prohibition on escapees became strict again.
Banner members and commoners consequently grew increasingly impoverished.
In the early Qiánlóng period,
censors Shū Hèdé, Fàn Xián, Hè Tài,
and Vice Minister of the Hùbù Liáng Shīzhèng, among others,
successively memorialized for a clear-up of uncultivated land in the Three Eastern Provinces,
to allow relocation and reclamation
for self-sufficiency.
Although repeated imperial decrees were issued and discussed for implementation,
they ultimately failed to be effectively carried out.
As for the opening of separate households for people under the Eight Banners,
this required military merit or exceptional skill;
sometimes, the master, recalling generations of diligent service,
would permit a separate household
or release them to become commoners.
There were also cases where release as commoners was not permitted,
but only the opening of a separate household was allowed;
these regulations again differed.
Land System: Refers to official land.
Initially, official estates (guānzhuāng) were established,
with commoners from the capital region who submitted themselves becoming estate heads (zhuāngtóu),
granted "rope land" (shéngdì).
One "rope" was forty-two *mǔ*.
Subsequently, the fields and lands of the various estate heads were registered and categorized into four grades,
and revised every ten years.
Grain estates (liángzhuāng) were established,
each estate being granted three hundred *shǎng* of land,
with one *shǎng* being approximately six *mǔ*.
The estate lands were located in various prefectures belonging to Shùn, Bǎo, Yǒng, and Xuān,
and were also established in Fèngtiān, Shānhǎiguān, Gǔběikǒu, and Xǐfēngkǒu.
All were administered by the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ).
Additionally, there were ministry and temple official estates (bù sì guānzhuāng),
separately administered by the Board of Rites (Lǐbù) and the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Sì).
Garden lands (yuándì) were also established
for planting melons, fruits, and vegetables,
with strong men selected to be garden heads (yuántóu).
In the early reign of Shìzōng,
a Director-General (Zǒnglǐ Zhuān Guān) was appointed
to manage the reporting of grain and the auditing of land outside the passes.
Nányuàn was originally a military training ground,
and by regulation, cultivation was prohibited.
Xuānzōng once decreed that any land previously opened for cultivation must be abandoned.
However, between the Xiánfēng and Tóngzhì reigns,
Sōnglíng, Dékuí, Liú Yǒumíng, and Tiěqí successively submitted memorials proposing the opening up of land,
but all were severely rebuked by imperial decree.
Nevertheless, by the final years of the Guāngxù reign,
it was still leased to the common people.
Thereafter, those who held the land followed one after another.
Upon examination, the estates and fields (zhuāngtián) of the various Manchu banners, princes (wáng), dukes (gōng), and imperial clan members (zōngshì)
totaled more than 13,300 *qǐng*.
The land allocated to the officers and soldiers of the various banners
totaled more than 140,900 *qǐng*.
All close relatives of princes and dukes
were separately granted land.
Large estates were granted 420 to 720 *mǔ* of land,
half-estates 240 to 360 *mǔ*,
gardens 60 to 120 or 180 *mǔ*.
Those under the administration of princely mansions (wángfǔ guǎnlǐng) and officers' attendants (guānshǔ zhuàngdīng) were granted 36 *mǔ* per person,
and did not receive grain stipends.
All land allocations were based on the current situation.
Subsequent increases in population did not lead to additional land,
nor did population decreases lead to land reclamation.
In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
it was decreed that barren lands near the capital and ownerless estates and fields from the former Míng dynasty
should be allocated to the officers and soldiers who had come from the east.
The "land enclosure" (quāndì) discussions began from this point.
Consequently, Supervising Censor (xún'àn yùshǐ) Liǔ Yīndōng submitted a memorial on the "five conveniences" of separate residences for Manchus and Han.
The Board deliberated and implemented it.
In the second year (1645),
it was ordered that for commoners' land that had been designated for enclosure,
compensation should be swiftly provided,
ensuring equal quality.
In the fourth year (1647),
over 1,090,000 *shǎng* of land in the various prefectures and counties of Shùnzhí (Zhílì) was enclosed
and granted to the Manchus as estates and settlements (zhuāngtún).
In the eighth year (1651),
the emperor, considering that land enclosure harmed the common people,
decreed that all previously enclosed land should be returned.
In the tenth year (1653),
he again ordered a halt to enclosure and allocation.
However, when banner-land fell into disuse
and nomadic people submitted themselves,
enclosure for compensation was resumed.
There were also instances where adjacent commoners' land was enclosed alongside land designated for compensation.
In the early Kāngxī reign (1662-1722),
Áobài monopolized power,
intending to give the settlements of the Bordered White Banner (Zhèngbái Qí) to the Bordered Yellow Banner (Xiānghuáng Qí),
and then enclose commoners' land as compensation.
Minister of the Board of Revenue (Hùbù Shàngshū) Sūnàhǎi, Governor-General (Zǒngdū) Zhū Chāngzuò, and Provincial Governor (Xúnfǔ) Wáng Dēnglián all deemed this inappropriate,
and were sentenced to death.
When the Holy Ancestor (Shèngzǔ, i.e., Kāngxī Emperor) began his personal rule (1669),
he decreed a halt to land enclosure.
All houses and land enclosed that year were returned.
Furthermore, vacant land in places like Zhāngjiākǒu and Shānhǎiguān was exchanged and allocated to various regions,
and new Manchus were ordered to be allocated surplus land from official estates.
The land that had been designated for enclosure was returned to the common people.
This constituted the return of banner-land.
All official land
was, by regulation, forbidden from being traded with commoners.
However, as banner people were unaccustomed to farming
and their population grew daily,
private mortgaging and selling were inevitable.
In the early Yōngzhèng reign (1723-1735),
banner-land was cleaned up,
and it was ordered that funds be issued for its redemption.
All who failed to report themselves, or privately engaged in transactions,
were to have their land confiscated by the government as public property.

For banner-land, the Imperial Clan Court (Zōngrénfǔ) and the Eight Banners under the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ Bā Qí) were ordered to detail the location and four boundaries of all types of land,
and compile a clear register,
known as the "Red Register" (Hóngcè),
for reviewing and adjudicating disputes between banner people and commoners over fields and land.
In the early Qiánlóng reign (1736-1795),
it was stipulated that redeemed banner-land should still be cultivated by its original tenants,
and powerful estate heads who competed for it would be punished.
All land redeemed by the government, as well as land confiscated to offset funds or seized,
was subject to rent,
known as "banner rent" (qí zū).
Previously, fixed rents for confiscated land were inspected
and managed by banner officials.
In the 34th year (1769),
based on the words of the Governor-General of Zhílì, Yáng Tíngzhāng,
this practice was abolished.
Commoners leasing banner-land
were originally limited to three years.
If private long-term leases were made,
both the owner and the tenant would be punished under the law against prohibitions.
Banner landlords had long been forbidden from dispossessing tenants or increasing rent.
When Héshēn took charge of agricultural affairs,
he proposed changes to the former regulations.
Consequently, banner people and estate heads of princely mansions frequently withdrew land from tenants and leased it to others,
leading to many poor people losing their livelihoods.
In the fifth year of Jiāqìng (1800),
the ministers of the Boards requested that the previous prohibitions be reaffirmed.
An imperial edict ordered it to be compiled into the established regulations for general circulation.
In the first year of Xiánfēng (1851),
another order reaffirmed that rent should be levied at the fixed rate,
and neither landlord nor tenant should arbitrarily increase or decrease it.
If banner-land was mortgaged or sold,
it was treated as "illicit sale of official land" (dàomài guāndì),
with both parties to the transaction being punished.
However, as time passed and the law slackened,
sometimes land was used as collateral for loans,
or long-term rents were advanced.
Outward compliance and inward defiance became common,
and corrupt clerks and yamen runners conspired to extort,
leading to numerous abuses.
Although warnings were repeatedly issued,
due to other circumstances,
the prohibitions often slackened inconsistently.
By the middle of the Guāngxù reign (1875-1908),
it was finally stipulated that this property, whether previously enclosed or privately acquired,
was generally not allowed to be sold to commoners.
However, for land previously purchased by commoners and subject to taxation,
they were still permitted to hold the property.
For the official estates of Shèngjīng,
the boundaries for the Eight Banners' settlements were set in the early Shùnzhì reign.
Soon after, it was decreed that within the area beyond the Shāhé River and within Jǐnzhōu,
land should be granted to banner officials' household retainers (jiādīng),
36 *mǔ* per person.
In the Kāngxī reign,
it was decreed that land belonging to Fèngtiān should be granted to new Manchus who had relocated there.
The surveyed land totaled over 329,000 *qǐng*,
of which over 276,300 *qǐng* became banner-land,
with boundaries divided by banner.
Additionally, official estates and settlements were established for officials of the various banners,
and soldiers in various cities
were granted land commensurate with their posts.
Soon after, Sōluón and Dáhú'ěr officers and soldiers were ordered to cultivate the land of Mò'ěrgēn,
and Fèngtiān officers and soldiers were ordered to cultivate the land of Hēilóngjiāng.
In the early Qiánlóng reign,
Hēilóngjiāng settlements were established.
Forty estates were established in Hūlán,
with selected Shèngjīng banner soldiers and their families sent there.
The government provided funds for equipment, built houses, and supplied tools.
Each soldier was granted 60 *mǔ* of land,
with ten soldiers forming one estate.
For every six *mǔ*, two *dǒu* of seeds were provided.
Each estate was given six oxen,
and rations were also provided.
Wēndéhēng and Dū'ěrtú also followed this system.
All official land attached to official posts was to be registered under the banners,
and officials were prohibited from encroaching upon it.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
it was decreed that confiscated land in Shèngjīng
should be offered for rent to landless poor commoners,
and children of officials were not allowed to cultivate it.
Officials in charge of specific areas
were also prohibited from acquiring houses or land in their jurisdiction under their children's names.
During the Dàoguāng reign,
the official estates of Nínggǔtǎ, Bódūnnà, Sānxìng, Ālèchǔkā, and Lālín
collectively totaled an original quota of 10,200 *shǎng* of land.
The Eight Banners of Jílín and banner-land in various other places, as well as the land of the Wūlā Banner,
totaled 365,092 *shǎng*.
In the early Guāngxù reign,
barren land in Sānxìng was allocated as land for officers and soldiers commensurate with their posts,
amounting to over 29,000 *shǎng*.
During the Xuāntǒng reign,
due to widespread abuses of illicit mortgaging and secret occupation of banner-land in Fèng Province,
it was ordered that thorough investigations and precise verifications be conducted,
without confusion with the clear land tax.
First, urban banners,
then outer city areas,
were progressively delineated.
These are the official estates belonging to the Three Eastern Provinces (Dōngsānsěng).
Each province established garrison Manchu banner troops,
and set up agricultural estates in their stationed locations,
giving each farmer three *mǔ* of land.
For those who brought their entire families,
the land previously granted in the capital was withdrawn and returned.
Banner officials were allotted garden plots;
the most received two hundred forty *mǔ*,
the least sixty *mǔ*,
and the arrangements varied across provinces.
However, the garrisons in Zhèjiāng had no land
and instead received stipends and rations.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
the ban on garrison soldiers acquiring property was relaxed,
but the ban on Eight Banners officials remained as before.
Towards the end of the Guāngxù reign,
an edict stated:
"Inspect the number of banner households in each locality,
and, utilizing the existing horse ranches and agricultural estates,
divide the land among them by household
and hold them responsible for farming.
For those who originally had no ranches or estates,
or whose holdings were insufficient,
the responsible authorities shall purchase civilian land nearby and distribute it to them
as a hereditary enterprise.
This shall be gradually expanded,
allowing banner households to return to agriculture,
be governed by the prefectures and counties,
and be no different from ordinary civilians."
This was not implemented.
The Mongols were initially divided into five ranks.
The first and second ranks were provided with agricultural estates and garden plots.
Those from the third rank downwards
were only given agricultural estates.
Each was to guard their own territory,
and not cross borders.
Later, civilians gradually began to acquire Mongol land at low prices.
In the mid-Qiánlóng reign, it was decreed:
"Those who mortgage or sell land shall be severely punished,
and this shall be established as a permanent regulation."
The distribution of official land to outer vassals was generally as described.
Thus, the agricultural estates of the Ming internal eunuchs
were under the overall administration of the Hùbù.
The stipendiary lands of the imperial clan members scattered across various provinces
were all subject to taxation like civilian land.
Previously,
two hundred ten *qǐng* of official land in Xīnchéng and Gù'ān were converted into a well-field system,
and one hundred banner and civilian households were selected,
each granted one hundred *mǔ*,
with one hundred *mǔ* designated as public land.
All households jointly cultivated the public land.
Subsequently, this was replicated in Bàzhōu and Yǒngqīng,
but with little success.
In the early Qiánlóng reign,
it was changed to military farm-settlements.
Diligent and astute individuals were chosen as military farmers,
and grain taxes were levied based on the *mǔ*.
This was the conversion of well-fields into military farm-settlement land.
All official lands for altars and mounds in the capital,
as well as the public lands for altars to the gods of earth and grain, mountains and rivers, pestilence, Confucius temples, ancestral halls, tombs, monasteries, and temples across the empire,
were entirely exempt from levies.
In the early days of the dynasty's founding,
sacrificial lands were bestowed upon the descendants of sages.
The lands of Kǒnglín, the school lands of the Four Sages' academies, cemetery lands, and grave lands
were all exempt from rent and taxes.
School lands
were specifically designated for establishing schools and supporting impoverished scholars;
tenants cultivated them for rent, but the rent rates were inconsistent,
and there was no fixed quota in the past.
In the mid-Qiánlóng reign,
the total school land in the empire amounted to over eleven thousand five hundred eighty *qǐng*.
During the Guāngxù reforms,
schools proliferated across the provinces,
and expenses were boundless.
Therefore, available wasteland in various localities was allocated,
designated as school land to supplement funding.
The ceremonial plowing field (jìtián) was located at the Xiānnóngtán in the capital.
The altar's land totaled one thousand seven hundred *mǔ*.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
provincial governors were ordered to instruct their subordinates to establish ceremonial plowing fields.
Within the red stakes of the Eastern and Western Mausoleum lands, cultivation and woodcutting were forbidden by regulation.
Beyond the white stake boundaries of the Eastern Mausoleum, civilian cultivation was initially permitted.
During the Dàoguāng reign, the prohibition was strictly enforced.
Beyond the green stakes,
within the boundaries of Zūn, Jì, Mì, and Chéng, soldiers and civilians privately reclaimed land,
amounting to over ten thousand plots,
which steadily expanded over time.
At the end of the Guāngxù reign,
it was decided to survey and measure these plots by area,
assess taxes on the cultivated land,
and reserve the proceeds for school use.
As for horse pastures and grasslands in the Gīfǔ area,
in the second year of Shùnzhì (1645),
available wasteland near the capital was designated as pastures.
These were established in various prefectures of Shùntiān, Jīn, and Bǎo according to banner divisions.
From the Yùmǎchǎng downwards,
each banner grazed horses on its own land.
Princely lands were two *lǐ* square,
princely lands one *lǐ* square;
these were also enclosed lands.
This was called military land reclamation.
During the Kāngxī reign,
reclamation of pastures in the two wings of Tiānjīn was encouraged,
totaling over twenty-one thousand five hundred *mǔ*.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
horse ranch lands in Zhílì were surveyed and distributed to impoverished commoners to establish livelihoods,
designated as "grace-bestowed official land."
In Shèngjīng,
the military farm-settlements and guard lands in Fèngtiān
were divided among the Eight Banners as pastures.
From east to west,
civilian reclamation was originally prohibited,
and restricted by mounds built at the defined boundaries.
However, the over three hundred eleven thousand eight hundred *mǔ* of wasteland in the Dàlínghé Eastern and Western Ranches,
and over fourteen thousand six hundred *shǎng* of surplus land from the Yǎngxī pastures,
were successively opened for reclamation during the Qiánlóng and Jiāqìng reigns.
Later, over three hundred eighty-nine thousand *mǔ* of reclaimable land in the horse ranches of various city banners were consolidated,
all assigned to city banners for cultivation.
Furthermore, Eight Banners princes, dukes, and idle imperial clan members
who wished to reclaim their allotted pastures
were permitted to apply.
However, Sōngyún's proposal to resettle banner people in the idle lands of Yǎngxī was abandoned due to lack of funds.
In the Xiánfēng reign,
reclamation on the west bank of Dàlíng was deemed detrimental to horse administration,
and the previous ban was re-imposed.
Yet, in the second year of Tóngzhì (1863),
the wasteland of Jǐnzhōu, Guǎngníng, and Yìzhōu Ranches was flexibly managed:
the Western Ranch was reserved for grazing,
while the Eastern Ranch recruited tenants.
The Gāoshānzi land of several tens of thousands of *mǔ* in its northeast corner,
and the idle land of over ten thousand *mǔ* in the Yìzhōu drill ground,
were also rented out
to serve as military fields for city soldiers.
However, at that time, the Western Ranch had old lands claimed by banners
which were gradually encroached upon and interfered with grazing.
In the eighth year (1869),
an order was given to clear them.
Thus, the proposal for Dàlínghé reclamation was thwarted.
Meanwhile, the barren mountains of Jí, Hēi had many pastures and hunting grounds,
and the prohibition against treacherous civilians seizing and selling them was strictly enforced.
The Yǎngxī pastures,
when first opened, were divided by eastern and western boundaries,
and special officials were appointed to manage their rental income.
Zhāngwǔ was originally official pasture land,
but was soon also encouraged for reclamation and taxation was proposed.
Consequently, a total of over six hundred eighteen thousand eight hundred *mǔ* of cultivated and uncultivated Yǎngxī pastures were opened,
with over eighty-nine thousand six hundred *mǔ* of remaining wasteland,
and over thirty-five thousand three hundred *mǔ* of residual land
designated for mixed Mongol and Han settlement and tenancy,
concurrently supporting impoverished people.
In Wūlā, Jílín,
during the Kāngxī reign,
farm-settler lands were divided among the five military farm-settlements,
becoming five official pastures,
possessing considerable scattered wasteland.
During the Xuāntǒng reign,
it was allocated as school land,
and over two thousand three hundred *shǎng* of actual land were opened for reclamation.
All garrison camps established horse ranches,
and the surplus lands adjacent to their pastures and estates
were invariably opened for reclamation.
As for the cultivated land of the Jīngfáng Horse Ranch,
it was long ago granted to the people.
In Shíshǒu and Jiānlì,
towards the end of Guāngxù, over twenty thousand *mǔ* of ranch land were demarcated
and all opened for tenant recruitment,
with rental income used to fund police administration and primary schools.
In the early Xuāntǒng reign,
in the surplus boundaries of the Níngxià Manchu camp pastures,
canals were dug and land was reclaimed,
amounting to two hundred ten thousand *mǔ*,
equally divided between banners and civilians.
Civilian claims required payment as capital for banner soldiers' reclamation.
In the third year (1911),
the Wànqǐnghú pasture in Ānhuī
was converted into over eighty-two thousand seven hundred *mǔ* of reclaimed land,
with migrant cultivators and private reclaimers of wasteland
all designated as tenant farmers.
Twenty thousand *mǔ* of land reserved for banner households
also recruited civilian tenants,
who annually paid grain and wheat,
becoming official tenants.
By this time, due to rent disputes,
it was decided that civilian tenants would rent the land,
and companies would compensate for and acquire the property,
to provide for the livelihood of the Eight Banners.
Outside the passes, the pastures
subordinate to Dúshí were the Imperial Horse Pastures.
Beyond these, the Ministry of Rites (Lǐbù), the Court of the Imperial Stud (Tàipú Sì), the Left and Right Wings (Zuǒ Yì, Yòu Yì), and the Eight Banners (Bāqí)
all had pastures outside Zhāngjiākǒu.
Regarding the proposed mu-rent at Shāhǔkǒu,
the suppression of private reclamation in Cháhā'ěr territory,
the broad exemption of commoners' occupation at Dàqīng Shān,
and the invitation of merchants to cultivate land at Yìxīng Dì,
successive dynasties adapted to the times,
not being bound by precedents.
Later, Mìyún and Rèhé simultaneously opened up wasteland.
Rèhé was vast,
and besides retaining pastures, it gained one thousand four to five hundred qǐng of land.
Moreover, one-third was kept for grazing,
and the rest was all offered for reclamation.
The land was developed, and farming and grazing did not interfere with each other,
which was an excellent policy.
The Míng dynasty's establishment of the Wèi system
was to support the military through agricultural colonies (tún),
and to subordinate the military to the Wèi.
When military administration was abolished and civilian militias were recruited,
the tún soldiers began to specialize in grain transport (cáoyùn),
and those without transport duties suffered endless labor,
greatly distressing the tún households.
The Qīng dynasty inherited the Míng system,
assigning Wèi tún lands to soldiers for tenancy,
and abolishing their miscellaneous corvées.
In the first year of Shùnzhì (1644),
imperial censors (yùshǐ) were dispatched to inspect the tún fields.
In the third year (1646),
the official system for tún fields was established.
Each Wèi was to have one defense commander (shǒubèi),
who also managed the tún fields.
Additionally, there were company commanders (qiānzǒng) and platoon commanders (bǎizǒng)
to manage Wèi affairs separately.
The Wèi soldiers were renamed tún dīng (tún laborers).
In the sixth year (1649),
regulations for land rent in Zhílì tún fields were established.
At that time, the tún field imperial censors were abolished,
followed by the abolition of inspecting censors (xún'àn),
with administration falling to the provincial governors (xúnfǔ).
In the thirteenth year (1656),
regulations for tún soldiers' transport subsidies were established.
In various Wèi of Zhèjiāng province, whether they had tún but no transport duties, or no tún but transport duties,
they were all levied and allocated subsidies,
and the plight of the tún households began to ease slightly.
In the fifteenth year of Kāngxī (1676),
as various Wèi's desolate lands were within the jurisdiction of prefectures and counties,
and there was much surreptitious appropriation of military land as civilian land,
an order was issued to the relevant authorities to investigate and clarify.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng (1724),
following the request of court officials,
the tún Wèi in the interior were merged into the prefectures and counties,
and officials below the regional military commissioner (dūwèi) were abolished.
Only those tún with transport duties,
and border Wèi without prefectures or counties to be subordinate to,
remained as before.
In the ninth year (1731),
it was ordered that tún Wèi land could be mortgaged to military households,
but not privately to commoners.
In the first year of Qiánlóng (1736),
the surplus tún field taxes in Guǎngdōng were exempted,
and consequently, the system of extra levies on military fields in other provinces was abolished.
Previously, when tún dīng sold property,
officials profited from the tax revenue,
issuing deeds and allowing the transactions.
At this point, it was again ordered that transport lands should revert to the boatmen,
and mortgaging by soldiers and commoners was prohibited.
In reality, mortgaging of tún lands to commoners occurred
everywhere in the provinces.
In the sixth year (1741),
a one-year limit was set for tún fields.
Regardless of whether they were held by soldiers or commoners,
they were all to be cleared and returned to the dīng for transport duties.
In the twelfth year (1747),
the grain transport supervisor (cáodū) Gù Cóng requested that fields already mortgaged to commoners
be redeemed by Banner dīng.
However, commoners had long held the property,
and the dīng were poor and unable to redeem them.
Following Āsīhā's suggestion,
the dīng fields in Jiāngxī were clarified:
those held by soldiers belonged to soldiers,
and those held by commoners would have increased rent paid to the dīng,
established as a permanent system.
In the thirty-seventh year (1772),
again based on the memorial of grain transport supervisor Jiāmó,
an order was issued to investigate and clarify the tún fields in Húguǎng, Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, Shāndōng, and other provinces.
The following year (1773),
Péi Zōngxī then memorialized about the Wèi tún fields in the Two Jiāng provinces, which had never been used for transport duties,
proposing an additional levy for transport expenses.
The Emperor, considering it burdensome to the common people,
disallowed it.
In the fortieth year (1775),
the Húběi governor Chén Huīzǔ memorialized:
"The various Wèi in Wǔchāng have cleared out the mortgaged and sold tún fields.
I request to add a subsidy for transport support."
The Board (Bù) deliberated:
"If this is done, those who privately transfer ownership will be deterred,
and yet will not suffer loss of livelihood.
Perhaps the abuses of mortgaging and selling will gradually be eliminated."
In the fiftieth year (1785),
due to the confusion surrounding the resale of original officers' fields in Chángshā and Lǐzhōu,
an order was issued to remove the name of officers' fields,
and allow them to be transferred as civilian property.
In the fifty-fourth year (1789),
Bì Yuán and others memorialized that
the tún dīng in each province were audited every four years,
but only the number of households was checked.
Their land property might have omissions or concealments,
and should be verified in due course.
Over a hundred years,
the benefits and problems of tún fields
were inextricably linked with grain transport.
When grain transport from the south was shifted to sea transport,
the concealment of tún Wèi became difficult to ascertain,
leading to a major change.
In the twenty-fourth year of Guāngxù (1898),
the Grand Minister of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Tàicháng Qīng) Yuán Chǎng memorialized to rectify tún fields,
which led to an edict to change Wèi to tún,
ordering all under heaven to verify the number of Wèi fields,
and to precisely determine rent regulations.
However, Jiāngxī, where all rents were used for military provisions,
differed from other provinces where they supported transport,
and petitioned to revert to the old practice.
In the twenty-seventh year (1901),
Liú Kūnyī and Zhāng Zhīdòng memorialized that tún Wèi should be abolished.
They briefly stated:
"The transport soldiers have long been non-existent,
and the Wèi officials are idle.
The tún fields belonging to a Wèi
might span across prefectures
or provinces.
Everything is handled by clerks,
and the abuses in land and provisions
are inexhaustible."
The following year (1902),
an edict was issued to verify tún lands in each province,
ordering tún households to pay deed tax and register their property,
changing tún provisions to dīng grain,
to be collected and remitted by prefectures and counties.
The titles of tún dīng and transport soldiers were abolished,
and Wèi officials were dismissed.
At this time, the total tún fields in the provinces amounted to over 250,000 qǐng,
but many were mixed with civilian land.
Moreover, various dīng had privately mortgaged and sold them,
long losing their original status.
Compounded by the complete loss of registers after the wars,
it was impossible to trace land production.
The grain transport supervisor Chén Kuílong presented three main points:
first, to distinguish between dīng property and civilian property;
second, that current levies should not pursue the original quotas;
third, that the supplementary payment for land value should be light.
And in Jiāngnán, Ānhuī, and the Two Zhè provinces, a compromise was reached to establish regulations,
separately paying land value and taxes.
For example, in the four Wèi of Huái'ān, Yángzhōu, and Xúzhōu,
the rates were set at three liǎng for upper grade, two liǎng for middle, and one liǎng for lower.
The tún tax was three fēn per liǎng,
with other variations.
Only Shāndōng requested exemption due to hardship and famine.
The Húběi governor Zhāng Zhīdòng, however, stated that Húběi Wèi fields
were relied upon by military households for sustenance.
Even if commoners had falsely claimed them,
they were generally not wealthy,
and it was difficult to require them to present payment for the land.
Only a deed tax was levied.
Its tax rate was comparable to civilian land.
By the thirty-first year (1905),
a dispute erupted over tún land in Yíchéng,
as the Wèi field system was inconvenient.
Zhāng Zhīdòng devised eight simplified methods,
the main gist being to abolish the original principles,
reduce taxes and remit levies over several years,
and abolish miscellaneous duties.
However, contributions for schools were the same as for civilian land,
in preparation for converting tún land to civilian land.
Those who complied were given official certificates.
Subsequently, Húnán province also followed this practice.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
the Zhèjiāng governor Zēng Yùn further requested that those who held the land merely report it by a deadline,
and uniformly not pay for the land.
The Board deliberated and immediately allowed occupation,
but advised that a moderate amount of tún land value could still be collected.
This was because the transformation of tún Wèi
was dictated by the circumstances of the time.
From the Qing's Qīng's initial founding,
able-bodied men were dispatched to uncultivated lands for military-agricultural colonies (túntián 屯田).
Furthermore, near the túntián 屯田 settlements,
cities were built and soldiers stationed to protect the farmers.
When Shìzǔ 世祖 first entered the pass,
he established a decree for reclaiming wasteland and promoting túntián 屯田.
All masterless barren lands in zhōu 州, xiàn 縣, and wèi 衛
were distributed to migrants and military personnel for cultivation.
If they lacked the ability to cultivate,
the officials would provide cattle, tools, and seeds,
or appropriate túntián 屯田 capital.
Half was paid the following year,
and the full amount in the third year.
Grand Secretary Fàn Wénchéng 范文程 submitted four matters concerning túntián 屯田: one,
selecting the right people;
one,
appropriate harvesting;
one,
effective transportation;
one,
reliable rewards and punishments.
The Emperor approved of these.
It was decreed that all who surrendered and pledged allegiance
would be granted barren land as permanent property.
Wèi Yìjiè 魏裔介 also requested that famine victims be relocated,
allowing them to register and occupy land.
Criminals sentenced to exile
were limited to a certain number of years for túntián 屯田 cultivation,
after which they would be released.
Those who wished to stay and occupy the land
were permitted.
Regarding túntián 屯田 in the zhíshěng 直省 (directly administered provinces),
for those who received official assistance with cattle and seeds,
one-third of the harvested grain was taken;
for those who provided their own,
one-tenth was taken in the current year,
and one-third in the second and third years.
Initially, regulations for encouragement and discouragement were established,
and the time limit system was very strict.
In the early Kāngxī 康熙 period,
fearing false reporting and arbitrary levies by officials,
the time limit decree was suspended.
Soon after, Censor Xú Xùlín 徐旭林 discussed three disadvantages of land reclamation,
his words being very incisive;
however, the time limit remained impracticable.
Subsequently, it was decreed that scholars and commoners who reclaimed twenty qǐng 頃 of land,
and whose literary talent excelled when tested,
would be appointed as xiànchéng 縣丞 (county magistrates);
one hundred qǐng 頃 would qualify them as zhīxiàn 知縣 (county magistrates).
For all newly reclaimed land,
it was initially decreed that taxes would begin after three years.
Later, this was extended to after six years.
Soon it was decreed to calculate a total of ten years.
Eventually, the six-year rule was still used,
though some followed the old three-year system.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng 雍正,
an edict specified the tax collection limit.
Six years for paddy fields,
ten years for dry fields,
were established as the rule.
During the Shùnzhì 順治 and Kāngxī 康熙 periods,
high officials in the zhíshěng 直省 regarded land expansion as an achievement,
and the total reported area of reclaimed land
was, for some, like Hénán 河南,
as much as nineteen thousand three hundred sixty-one qǐng 頃;
for others, like Shāndōng 山東,
a little over one hundred twenty qǐng 頃.
In the last years of Shìzōng 世宗,
because many figures were inaccurate,
strict warnings were issued for review and verification.
Any embellishment
would be punished according to the law.
The method of deliberation was established.
For officials who recruited tenants to invest in cultivation,
it was carried out according to the number of households;
for military and civilian personnel who self-funded their labor,
it was carried out according to the number of mù 畝 (mu).
During the Qiánlóng 乾隆 era,
it was decreed that for official mountains and official lands,
regardless of whether they were natives or migrants,
they would be granted for cultivation based on the order of reporting.
Private land was to be reported first by the owner.
If the owner lacked sufficient capability,
others could then take it over.
For túnhù 屯戶 (túntián households) who cultivated additional land,
all were ordered to convert their túntián 屯田 status and have taxes levied.
It was also decreed that already cultivated land
should be carefully protected.
For all official and private lands,
where they related to watercourse storage and drainage,
cultivation was not to be undertaken without authorization.
If one falsely claimed ownership
and privately cultivated ponds, weirs, or swamps for fields,
they would be immediately punished.
Now, examining the túntián 屯田 and reclamation policies of successive dynasties,
first are the túntián 屯田 of the zhíshěng 直省,
then the túntián 屯田 of Xīnjiāng 新疆,
then the reclamation of the Dōng Sānshěng 東三省 (Three Eastern Provinces),
then the reclamation of Měnggǔ 蒙古 (Mongolia),
and the reclamation efforts in places like Qīnghǎi 青海 and Rèhé 熱河,
all are detailed in this chapter.
In the first year of Shùnzhì 順治,
it was decreed that newly reclaimed land in Shānxī 山西 would be exempt from rent and tax for one year;
and for over ninety-four thousand five hundred qǐng 頃 of barren land in northern Hénán 河南,
Governor Luó Xiùjǐn's 羅繡錦's proposal was approved,
allowing soldiers to cultivate it.
In the second year,
Shùntiān 順天 implemented the method of counting soldiers and granting land,
giving each garrison soldier ten mù 畝 of arable land,
with cattle, tools, and seeds funded by the officials.
Also, in Zhílì 直隸, Shāndōng 山東, Jiāngběi 江北, and Shānxī 山西,
wherever Manchu soldiers were stationed,
masterless land was given to them for cultivation.
In the fourth year,
Grand Secretary Liáng Wéiběn 梁維本 requested the opening of barren lands in Qín 秦 (Shaanxi), Yù 豫 (Henan), as well as Lú 廬 (Luzhou) and Fèng 鳳 (Fengyang).
In the sixth year,
it was decreed that all provinces should also recruit migrants,
register them, issue permits,
and have them reclaim wasteland as their occupation,
without unauthorized levies or private apportionments;
after six years, grain taxes would be collected according to the cultivated land.
In the tenth year,
it was decided that barren land in Sìchuān 四川 would be open for civilian reclamation.
For barren land in Shǎnxī 陝西, infantry would be appropriately dispatched,
with officials providing cattle and grain.
In the sixth year of Kāngxī 康熙,
it was decreed that túntián 屯田 settlements for surrendered military personnel would be established in provinces like Jiāngsū 江蘇 and Zhèjiāng 浙江,
each person being given fifty mù 畝 of barren land,
and eligible for a stipend.
For those with large families,
the amount of land would be increased according to the number of mouths to feed.
Fújiàn 福建 had no barren land,
so they were stationed in túntián 屯田 provinces.
In the seventh year,
Censor Xiāo Zhèn 蕭震 memorialized, saying:
"Of the state's annual expenditures,
military pay accounts for eight-tenths,
and of that, the Green Standard Army's pay accounts for eight-tenths.
If we sincerely establish túntián 屯田 in Qián 黔 (Guizhou) and Shǔ 蜀 (Sichuan),
and have the soldiers stationed in counties
cultivate the land in those counties,
then expenses will be saved and barren lands gradually opened."
This was submitted to the ministries for deliberation and implementation.
At that time, Zhílì 直隸, Shǎnxī 陝西, Yuè 粵 (Guangdong), and Mǐn 閩 (Fujian) successively established regulations for wasteland reclamation,
and Sìchuān 四chuān even created special regulations,
allowing officials to be rewarded for their merits.
Consequently, barren lands in provinces like Xiāng 湘 (Hunan), È 鄂 (Hubei), Mǐn 閩 (Fujian), Lǔ 魯 (Shandong), Jìn 晉 (Shanxi), and Yù 豫 (Henan) were open for civilian planting,
with a time limit for complete cultivation.
In the fourth year of Yǒngzhèng,
the flat and expansive land of Chāhàn and Tuōhuī in Gānsù and Níngxià,
could be cultivated for over six hundred thousand mù.
Households were invited to claim it,
each household receiving one hundred mù.
In the fifth year,
the governor of Yuè, Ākèdūn, reported four common problems with land reclamation in Yuèdōng in recent years: one,
occupation and seizure by powerful gentry;
one,
extortion by yamen clerks;
one,
insufficient capital;
and one,
barren land feared to incur tax burdens.
He proposed five methods for encouragement: settling boundaries,
preventing harsh exactions,
lending seeds,
lightening tax quotas,
and widely attracting settlers.
Thereafter, impoverished people from Huì and Cháo cultivated land in the Zhaòqìng area,
and the barren and infertile mountainous regions of Gāo, Lián, and Léi,
were all provided with funds to attract settlers,
and were also exempted from increased taxation.
Subsequently, Qióngzhōu also followed suit.
The land reclamation plans for Diān and Qián were also expanded,
with soldiers and commoners in Wūméng both undertaking cultivation,
each household not exceeding two qǐng.
For commoners from other provinces settling in Shǔ,
each household was given thirty mù of paddy field
and fifty mù of dry land.
In Ānxī, Gānsù, military colonization had long been practiced,
with families relocated to garrison the area,
sharing this with the two garrisons of Liáng and Sù.
Many garrison soldiers were poor,
so all reclamation funds were lent by the government.
Furthermore, in border provinces and inland areas where scattered land could be reclaimed,
commoners and indigenous people were allowed to cultivate it;
and for newly reclaimed barren land in Shānxī,
ten mù or less,
and in Shǎnxī, odd parcels of five mù or less,
all were exempted from increased taxation.
All vacant land, land impacted by floods with sand and杂,
and fields less than one mù,
as well as open land at the foot of mountains and along riverbanks in border provinces,
were permanently exempted from taxation.
For new silted land in Zhèjiāng,
both commoners and salt households claimed it,
one hundred mù forming a hào,
ten hào forming a jiǎ,
and ten jiǎ guided by experienced farmers.
Later, when new land emerged,
people all benefited from it.
Subsequently, there was a ban on encroaching and cultivating Xīhú.
In the fifty-ninth year of Qiánlóng,
Governor Jíqìng stated
that coastal sandbanks and silted land constantly changed,
approximately one hundred thirty-three thousand mù,
all of which should be appropriated by the government,
and handed over to the original tenants for cultivation and rent payment,
to be established as a permanent rule.
For all newly reclaimed barren fields and land in prefectures and counties across the provinces each year,
as well as marshland and lake silt,
governors and provincial governors were to report them promptly for increased taxation.
Indeed, since Yōngzhèng and Qiánlóng,
military settlements and civilian reclamation in all provinces
were considered to have reached their peak.
In Fújiàn, the vast lands of indigenous deer grounds
were customarily allowed to be rented to commoners for cultivation.
However, in Táiwān, since successive garrison commanders established estates and attracted tenants,
they often encroached upon the land of commoners and indigenous people.
During the Qiánlóng era,
an edict prohibited military officers from reclaiming barren land.
Subsequently, indigenous people were forbidden from privately purchasing indigenous land.
In the fifty-third year,
Fúkāng'ān requested that surplus land be allocated to indigenous people and commoners for self-cultivation,
and that strong and healthy individuals be selected as military colonists.
Over eight thousand eight hundred jiǎ of uncultivated land in the inner mountains and abandoned government-owned wasteland,
each jiǎ allowing eleven mù and some零 of commoner land,
totaling four thousand military colonists,
were allotted land for cultivation,
exempt from taxes but not given stipends,
which was approved.
During the Jiāqìng era,
seven thousand fifty jiǎ and odd of fields were opened in Gámǎlán.
In the early Dàoguāng era,
uncultivated barren plains of the Dìngfān community were distributed to commoners for rent collection.
In Yuèxī, indigenous soldiers and Láng soldiers were established,
all given military land.
In Yuèdōng, there was Láng land and Yáo land,
which were still used to provide soldiers according to the fields,
and this land was forbidden for commoners to mortgage.
The indigenous land in Táiwān was similar.
However, in Yǒngběi, Dàyáo, and other places in Yúnnán,
Han people mortgaging indigenous land
had accumulated disputes for several decades.
In the first year of Dàoguāng,
the arrangements were somewhat settled.
In the thirteenth year,
a conflict again arose in Sìchuān over Han people cultivating indigenous land,
so boundaries were demarcated,
prohibiting Han and indigenous people from occupying each other's land.
Following the proposal of the governor of Diān, Ruǎn Yuán,
roaming commoners were forbidden from privately renting Miáo land,
and neighboring Miáo tenant households were forbidden from mortgaging or selling Miáo property.
In the sixteenth year,
because Kāihuà, Guǎngnán, and Pǔ'ěr had much vacant land,
roaming commoners built temporary shelters and started cultivation,
leading to discussions about registering them in household registers.
Censor Táo Shìlín argued that this harmed farmers and harbored villains,
and it was banned.
Earlier, silted land in Jiāngsū,
suffered increasingly from unauthorized reclamation,
until the eighth year of Dàoguāng,
when it was finally designated as public property.
However, disputes over official property and private ownership
were intertwined.
Therefore, the governor of Jiāng, Táo Shù, proposed allowing commoners to purchase it.
The Board argued that rivers should not be exploited for reclamation,
and thus sandbars should not be occupied and sold to commoners.
Instead, all should be appropriated by the government for disposal.
Soon after, Qíyīng stated,
“If commoners purchase and build with their own funds,
to suddenly reclaim it
would appear to be contending for profit.
I request leniency for past actions and prohibition for future ones.”
This was approved.
In the twenty-third year,
Qíxì requested the repair of Hǔmén and other fortresses,
which required military colonies for protection.
The following year,
Chéng Yǔcǎi recruited two thousand laborers to try it out.
The Emperor said:
“For local people to cultivate local land,
defending strategic passes means defending their homes and families,
which is indeed a long-term plan.”
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
due to urgent military provisions,
an edict ordered garrison soldiers in Fèng, Yǐng, and other areas to reclaim nearby abandoned land,
gradually extending this to all prefectures.
Shāndōng suffered from the Nian Rebellion,
and the fields and villages of Zōu and Téng counties became desolate.
In the third year,
a policy of relocating settlers was decided upon,
and the property of rebels and land of extinct households in Dōngchāng, Línqīng, Yǎn, and Cáo areas
were all confiscated by the government.
In the fifth year,
an edict was issued concerning the management of lake settlements (hútuán).
Hútuán referred to
migrants from Cáo and Jǐ cultivating lake land in Tóng and Pèi on the border of Sū and Qí,
forming settlements by gathering families.
Subsequently, when indigenous residents returned to their homes,
there were endless disputes.
However, the migrant cultivation was organized by the government,
and there was no shortage of government-owned wasteland,
the occupied land was not very extensive,
and the litigants were not actual land-owning households.
Thereupon, Zēng Guófān investigated the situation,
expelled the unruly households,
retained the good settlements,
and allowed each to settle into their occupation.
Regarding abandoned property due to rebellion in Shǎnxī,
an edict the previous year had ordered preparations for establishing military colonies.
Governor Liú Róng stated that as military affairs were urgent,
attracting settlers was more convenient than military colonization.
The Board agreed with his proposal.
Thus, four new regulations for attracting settlers were established: namely, rectifying boundaries,
setting limits,
deferring money and grain taxes,
and fixing rent in grain.
For coastal sandbanks in Guǎngdōng,
a standing rule was that when the water receded, an inspection should be reported,
and those undertaking cultivation should not exceed one qǐng per person;
after three years of maturation,
taxes would be levied according to paddy fields.
Later, when gentry and officials monopolized and exploited,
an order was issued to investigate and prohibit such actions.
At this time,
following the ravages of war in the southeast,
farmers had long been out of work.
Zhèng Xīyíng (鄭錫瀛), Assistant Minister of the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglù Shǎoqīng), stated that the annual national revenue was approximately forty-four million taels,
and half of it was consumed by military provisions and pay.
It would be advisable to expand military colonies (túntián) to support soldiers and reduce expenses.
Soon after, Censor Wāng Cháojǐ (汪朝棨) asserted that the newly recovered territories in various provinces
should be urgently reclaimed.
Xú Jǐngshì (徐景軾) also spoke of improving agriculture and settling displaced people.
Consequently, Zēng Guófān (曾國藩) in Ān (皖),
and Yáng Chāngjùn (楊昌濬) in Zhè (浙),
both differentiated between locals and immigrants,
and deployed forces to open up wasteland.
Mǎ Xīnyí (馬新貽) in Sū (蘇)
and Liú Diǎn (劉典) in Shǎn (陝)
were also diligently supervising and encouraging this effort.
Zēng Bìguāng (曾璧光) and Lí Péijìng (黎培敬) successively implemented túntián policies in Qián (黔).
In the eighth month,
acting on Sū Tíngkuí’s (蘇廷魁) suggestion,
plans were made to reclaim the dry riverbeds below Lányí (蘭儀).
In the eleventh year,
an imperial decree was issued to the Yán (延) and Yú (榆) prefectures of Shǎnxī (陝西), stating that
the land was barren and the people impoverished,
so reclamation should be expedited,
and the performance assessments of zhōu (州) and xiàn (縣) officials should be strict.
This was at a time when the Huí (回) communities had just submitted to pacification.
Earlier, Censor Huáng Xītóng (黃錫彤) had requested the establishment of túntián garrisons in Sū (蘇) and Wǎn (皖),
selecting scattered soldiers from Xiāng (湘) and Huái (淮) to reclaim land along the river.
In the second year of Guāngxù (光緒),
Zhū Yǐzēng (朱以增) also stated:
"Some say that the túntián policy is suitable for the frontier but not for the interior.
They do not realize that if there is wasteland to reclaim,
why can't soldiers farm,
and why can't land be made into túntián?
Simply transfer a few battalions,
gradually initiating the effort,
and in the future, turning soldiers into farmers will
greatly benefit the country."
At that time, the reclamation efforts by the Tiānjīn (津) coastal defense garrisons were effective,
hence the statement.
Zēng Guófān (曾國藩) once said:
"Only by obtaining a thousand acres of ownerless land,
not mixed with common people's land,
can soldiers be settled in túntián."
Lǐ Hóngzhāng (李鴻章) also believed that mixed residency of soldiers and civilians
was not suitable for the interior.
The proposal was thus shelved.
Initially, Guìzhōu (貴州) stationed túntián troops in the five sub-prefectures of Gǔzhōu (古州), Bāzhài (八寨), Táigǒng (台拱), Dānjiāng (丹江), and Qīngjiāng (清江),
establishing one hundred and twenty fortified villages (bǎo),
