forming eight thousand nine hundred and thirty-nine túntián households.
Each household was given six *mǔ* (畝) of superior land,
eight *mǔ* of medium land,
ten *mǔ* of inferior land,
with no limit on nearby mountain land.
By the mid-Qiánlóng (乾隆) period,
túntián soldiers were prohibited from privately leasing or selling their assigned land.
In the early Jiāqìng (嘉慶) period,
blockhouses were built in the Miáo (苗) territories of Tóngrén (銅仁) and Shíxiàn (石峴),
and túntián troops were stationed.
For every hundred soldiers,
one *bǎihù* (百戶) and
two *zǒngqí* (總旗) were appointed.
Each soldier was given four *mǔ* of paddy field,
a *bǎihù* six *mǔ*,
and a *zǒngqí* five *mǔ*,
all exempt from rent.
By the early Tóngzhì (同治) period,
the Líyáng (黎平) túntián regulations were revised.
At this time,
Luó Yīngliú (羅應旒) stated:
"The túntián established among the Qián Miáo (黔苗) have long been nominal with little substance.
It would be better to discard the name of 'soldier'
and focus on the reality of 'farmer'."
At that time, there were ten *wèi* (衞) of túntián troops in total.
Subsequently, it was decided by imperial decree to divide them into two shifts,
like regular garrison soldiers,
with fixed quotas for drills, defense, and levies,
and officials such as *bǎihù* and *zǒngqí* appointed in the túntián.
Those who were not diligent
were immediately dismissed and replaced.
Earlier, Shěn Guìfēn (沈桂芬) had submitted a memorial proposing the settlement of Banner People (qírén) in various provinces.
Censor Huáng Yuánshàn (黃元善) also stated that when reclaiming wasteland in provinces like Shānxī (山西) and Jiāngsū (江蘇),
the old regulations of Shuāngchéngbǎo (雙城堡) should be imitated,
ordering Banner People and civilians to migrate and reclaim land.
However, due to the difficulty and magnitude of the undertaking,
it was not fully implemented.
In the twelfth year,
Liú Míngchuán (劉銘chuán), the Governor of Táiwān (台灣), planned to reclaim the indigenous wasteland in the interior mountains,
selling timber for value
to fund pacification and relief.
In the sixteenth year,
new silted land formed in Dòngtíng (洞庭) Lake in Húnán (湖南),
and the Nánzhōu (南洲) prefecture was established.
Rents from private land were collected by the government,
and a total of over one hundred and thirty thousand *mǔ* of verified private land
and eighty-nine thousand two hundred *mǔ* of official land were surveyed.
In the twenty-second year,
Shǐ Niànzǔ (史念祖), the Governor of Guì (桂), stated that
the official and private wasteland in various prefectures of Yuèxī (粵西) could be reclaimed.
He ordered officials to take the lead vigorously,
appropriately select túntián soldiers,
oversee the cultivation of the land,
allow common people to lease and farm it,
and determine taxes based on the fertility of the land.
A total of over fourteen thousand three hundred *mǔ* of wasteland was reclaimed across the various prefectures.
At this time, Shǎnxī (陝西) was vigorously clearing wasteland.
Governor Zhāng Rǔméi (張汝梅) stated:
"In Shǎn (陝) land, war and calamity are intertwined,
and the common people are scattered.
The climate in the northern mountains
is cold in summer and experiences early frosts,
making harvests unreliable.
Moreover, labor is scarce and grain prices are low,
resulting in more loss than gain.
Not only do immigrant people come and go without fixed abode,
even native people frequently abandon their work.
To prevent the land from becoming barren again,
the only way is to extend the initial reclamation period
and relax the responsibility placed on local officials.
Then, fewer people will flee,
officials will have fewer worries,
and both public and private interests will benefit."
In the twenty-fifth year,
it was decided that the approximately one hundred thousand *mǔ* of barren land in Xīnyáng (新陽)
that was ownerless would be designated as official land available for claiming.
A fee, known as *xìjiǎoxián* (繫腳錢),
was to be paid in three grades: field, land, and yard.
Land with owners was given a deadline for reporting reclamation,
and if the deadline was missed, it would revert to official land.
This was done at the request of Liú Kūnyī (劉坤一), Governor-General of Jiāng (江).
In the twenty-eighth year,
Shēng Yǔn (升允), the Governor of Shǎn (陝), stated:
"At the various barren lands of the Xī'ān (西安) horse farm,
trial cultivation of irrigated and dry fields should be carried out,
and túntián implemented.
Officers of battalions and patrols (yíngshào guān) would be allocated sixty *mǔ* or less,
and túntián soldiers ten *mǔ* per person.
For every hundred *mǔ*, two government oxen and three *shí* (石) of seeds would be lent.
The government would provide farm implements.
The oxen were to be returned in one year,
and all loans repaid in two years.
It was also proposed to cut their military pay incrementally over the years.
At the beginning of túntián establishment,
full pay would be issued annually.
In the second year, half would be cut,
and in the third year, all pay would be cut."
Subsequently, the land was damaged by floods and hail,
and harvests were not abundant.
Thus, he submitted another memorial:
"Forcing soldiers without pay
to support themselves
will inevitably cause their ambition to wane in the fields
and their elite strength to be eroded by farming.
There would be túntián but no real soldiers,
and soldiers but they would be useless.
This would contradict the original intention of establishing túntián.
It would be better not to cut their pay,
and instead, all túntián profits should go to the public,
with two or three tenths of the annual harvest then distributed as rewards.
This is what is meant by 'benefiting both'."
Xinjiāng’s jūn tún (military colonies) were divided into shares.
Each person harvested fifteen to eighteen dàn of fine grain.
By official decree,
soldiers were rewarded with one month's salt and vegetable allowance (yán cài yín).
Those who harvested twenty-five dàn received double that.
For those with twelve dàn or more,
half of the merit or demerit applied.
If they harvested less,
they were subject to official punishment.
Soldiers were heavily reprimanded and kept in the tún (colony).
They were reinstated the following year if they made up the full harvest.
In Wūlǔmùqí, a reward was given for a harvest of eleven dàn or more.
Tǎlè'nàqìn was particularly barren and infertile,
so rewards and punishments were progressively reduced there.
If there was no salt and vegetables, rations (kǒu liáng) were provided.
For Āqímù Bókè and others, bolts of silk (duàn pǐ) were awarded.
However, Yīlí suffered greatly from these burdens,
which Fúkāng'ān often spoke against.
Finally, General Chánggēng requested that the Wūlǔmùqí precedent be followed,
but the board’s deliberation still did not include a reduction.
According to previous regulations, banished offenders were allowed to establish new fields.
The various districts of Hāmì intercepted banished offenders from Yīlí and Wūlǔmùqí for reclamation and cultivation.
Only after their term was complete were they sent to their respective destinations.
Those with serious crimes were not allowed to stay.
Furthermore, as this was insufficient for agricultural work,
it was limited to stopping foreign bandits.
Later, those whose crimes were light were allowed to convert their guard duty into family settlements,
to retain them through a conciliatory policy (jī mí zhī).
For banished offenders who achieved the soldier's harvest quota,
their rewards and other matters followed the original regulations.
In the thirteenth year of Jiāqìng,
soldiers from Tǎ'ěrbāhātái were allocated to Yīlí to cultivate fields.
During agricultural slack periods, they underwent drill and training,
and military officers were appointed to lead them.
These officers were rotated every three years.
The original plan for Yīlí was to have three thousand tún (colony) soldiers.
Each year, for cultivation,
a certain number were selected
to practice military readiness.
This number varied from year to year,
depending on the circumstances.
The eighteen already cultivated tún (colonies)
were rotated for fallow periods,
to allow the land to recover its fertility.
It was subsequently decided that starting from the twentieth year,
two additional tún (colonies) would be planted each year.
Initially,
Yīlí had much arable land.
Huìyuǎn and Huìníng, two Manchu cities, were ordered to assign idle Banner people to try planting in divided lands.
Cattle and tools were lent to them, and the results were clear.
In the ninth year,
Sōngyún suggested that, following the example of the Xībó camp's tún (colony) cultivation,
land should be distributed to Banner soldiers,
allowing each to cultivate their own,
to be their perpetual family property.
However, this was deemed to interfere with military drills,
so it was only allowed for idle Banner people to transfer it for others to cultivate on their behalf.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Manchu camps were ordered to also plant various grains.
They successively divided over forty-four thousand mu of land,
assigning it to the idle Eight Banners for self-cultivation.
However, they were forbidden from illegally leasing or privately mortgaging and selling the land.
In the early years of Dàoguāng,
after Zhānggé'ěr was suppressed,
Uyghur soldiers were ordered to try reclaiming Dàhé Guǎi.
To increase the quota, poor Uyghurs were recruited.
Consequently, in Wūshí, Ākèsū, and Hétián, Uyghur households were scattered for cultivation.
In Fùkāng, Qítái, and Tǔlǔfān, under Wūlǔmùqí,
civilian households were recruited.
East of Huìyuǎn city in Yīlí,
local residents were also selected.
For the barren Ābólèsī,
Uyghur households were allocated.
Five zhuāng (villages) were established,
with one hundred households per zhuāng.
Each household received two hundred mu of land.
In Kālāshā'ěr, tún (colonies) were abolished and households settled.
The barren land in Kùchē
was also given to unemployed Uyghurs.
Bā'ěrchǔkā, under Yè'ěrqiāng, had much vacant land,
so many family settlers were extensively recruited.
The new fields in Huò'ěrhǎn
were distributed to Uyghur households.
When Kāshígá'ěr was first opened up,
the land was divided on the east and west sides of the river.
The east was given to Uyghurs,
and the west recruited civilian households.
Some areas were exclusively designated,
while others involved mixed recruitment,
all with the hope of achieving harmony.
For all civilians going to Huíjiāng to claim land,
officials issued printed vouchers.
They carried these themselves when traveling.
The grain tax was as high as two dòu, four shēng per mu,
next was eight shēng of wheat,
next six shēng, five hé,
and the least was three shēng.
This was generally determined by the fertility or barrenness of the soil.
Ābólèsī submitted sixteen dàn of three-color grains.
The training stipends for the Manchu camp's cavalry were drawn from this.
Since the Jiāqìng and Dàoguāng eras,
over several decades,
the pioneers in Yīlí’s túnkěn (colony reclamation)
included Generals Sōngyún, Nàyànchéng, and Bùyàntài.
When Lín Zéxú was banished to the frontier,
he personally surveyed various areas
and also initiated water conservancy projects in Yīlālǐkè,
achieving particularly great results.
In the second year of Tóngzhì,
Dūtǒng Píngruì reported that
the idle vastness of Wūlǔmùqí was generating horse pastures.
He proposed recruiting merchant households for relocation and reclamation,
and also requested that in the various cities of Yīlí,
a uniform plan be implemented to divide tún (colony) land among the tún (colony) soldiers.
The imperial order was to gradually implement this.
In the third year,
Hāmì was ordered to expand its original tún (colony).
In the third year of Guāngxù,
Shìdú Zhāng Pèilún requested to conscript Banner men for tún (colonies) in Xīnjiāng.
Shǎnxī Gānsù Zǒngdū Zuǒ Zōngtáng stated that there were six obstacles and doubts,
and so the proposal was shelved.
At that time, the southern route (Nánlù) of Chán and civilians were prosperous,
and barren wilderness was still rare.
In the northern route (Běilù), the various districts of Zhèn and Dí,
only twelve or thirteen percent of the land was cultivated.
Taxes were deficient,
and the communities were impoverished.
Later, the Xīnjiāng province was established.
In the thirteenth year,
Xúnfǔ Liú Jǐntáng further deliberated and set new regulations.
Each household was given sixty mu of land,
officials lent two dàn of seeds and grain,
six liǎng of silver for farm tools,
eight liǎng of silver for housing repairs,
and two oxen.
Two people constituted one household.
Monthly salt, vegetable, and grain rations were provided.
A deadline was set: half was to be repaid in the first year,
and the full amount in the second year.
After repayment,
taxes were levied by the mu.
Half was levied in the third year,
and the full amount in the following year.
The營田 (yíng tián - military farming system) was still emulated.
Ten households formed a túnzhǎng (colony head),
fifty households formed a túnzhèng (colony chief).
For every five túnzhèng,
a guǎnlǐng zhuānyuán (special commissioner for management) was established.
Túnzhèng and túnzhǎng received land and loans,
just like ordinary households.
In total, one thousand ninety native and settler households were settled,
and the system was progressively extended.
For the new reclaimed land of over nineteen thousand mu in the southern route (Nánlù) districts,
taxes were levied in stages over the years,
and no reclamation fees were received.
The northern and southern routes were surveyed, showing over eleven million four hundred eighty thousand mu of barren and cultivated land.
The various city bókè (beys) previously had yǎnglián dì (integrity-fostering land).
Since the conversion to jun (commanderies) and xiàn (counties),
the bókè’s integrity land was uniformly confiscated and leased by the government.
In the seventeenth year,
Wèi Guāngtáo divided the lands of Yīlí, assigning over sixty thousand mu each to banner tún (colonies) and civilian tún (colonies),
making them self-sufficient.
Thereafter, the native and settler populations thrived and multiplied.
There were repeated good harvests each year.
Han and Hui people from within the passes (guān nèi) brought their families to undertake reclamation,
arriving in continuous streams.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng,
Xúnfǔ Yuán Dàhuà said:
“Xīnjiāng has long been known as an agricultural and pastoral country.
Today’s poverty
stems from vast land and sparse population.
From Díhuà westward
to Jīnghé eastward,
the land is filled with government fallows,
grassy lakes, and reed marshes,
amounting to tens of millions of qǐng.
The eastern route of Nánjiāng is similarly vast and desolate.
Proposing to gather overseas Chinese to establish companies
for rapid results is not easy.
Now, all existing officials in Xīnjiāng
who independently or jointly invest in reclaiming barren land with clear and outstanding results
shall be separately reported for imperial commendation,
as an encouragement.”
The proposal was approved and implemented.
Jīnchuān was pacified by military conquest in the 40th year of Qiánlóng.
Initially, following the suggestion of General Dìngxī Āguì,
military colonies were established near Cuánlā in Xīchuān,
in places like Měinuò and Dǐmùdá.
Troops were ordered to be stationed there, granted land, and taught to farm.
Biesīmǎn and other areas in sequence had their indigenous administrations changed to military colonies.
Each was provided with屯弁 (túnbàn, military colony officials) to manage affairs.
Furthermore, surrendered indigenous peoples from Bógá'ěr, Jiǎojiáo, and other places
were all treated according to the regulations for military colonists,
generally provided with cattle, tools, seeds, and grain.
Households of indigenous people with many members received thirty to forty units of land,
while those with fewer received ten to twenty.
Initially, they were exempt from taxes during reclamation,
and after three years, they began to pay grain.
Soon, the stationed troops were ordered to bring their families and move forward.
As the population increased daily,
an additional thirty *mǔ* of land were allocated per household,
so they could cultivate more and become self-sufficient.
The land's productivity gradually expanded.
Consequently, the five military colonies of Màogōng in Sìchuān,
where surrendered indigenous people were settled,
also allocated thirty *mǔ* of land per household.
A thousand able-bodied men were selected,
half to serve as salaried military colonists,
and half as additional non-salaried laborers.
Later, uncultivated wasteland was surveyed,
and also distributed in varying grades.
The fertile regions of Bātáng and Lìtáng were not lacking.
By the 33rd year of Guāngxù,
the Governor of Chuān, Zhào Ěrfēng, proposed a memorial for a reclamation plan,
recruiting farmers from the interior, with the government funding their resettlement.
Outside the passes, land was vast and sparsely populated,
especially the extensive Mongolian territories,
which were suitable for military colonization.
In the early Qīng dynasty, banner divisions had fixed boundaries.
Later, due to barren land and grain shortages within the borders,
the frontiers were expanded for migration and cultivation.
In the Tiāncōng era,
each *niúlù* (company) was ordered to choose suitable areas for cultivation
near their respective colonies.
Following Shěn Pèiruì's suggestion,
strong farmers were selected from east and west Guǎngníng and Lǘyáng Yì
to serve as infantry and military colonists,
divided into eight *gùshān* (banners).
The *niúlù* were classified into two grades,
provided with cattle, seeds, and farm tools,
and capable individuals were ordered to lead the military colonists to farm.
In the 5th year of Chóngdé,
government troops built a city and established a military colony in Yìzhōu.
In the 25th year of Kāngxī,
eight areas of wasteland, including Jǐnzhōu and Fènghuángchéng, were distributed to banner people for cultivation.
Convicts were also sent to cultivate idle land in Shèngjīng.
In the 28th year,
it was stipulated that banner people and commoners in Fèngtiān and other places must each keep to their own land boundaries,
and not encroach upon each other.
In the 5th year of Qiánlóng,
Assistant Minister Liáng Shīzhèng requested that idle Eight Banner members be settled on the frontier for cultivation
to expand their livelihoods.
Ālǐgǔn was ordered to Fèngtiān to survey suitable land.
At that time, Jílín, Nínggǔtǎ, Bódū'nà, Ālèchǔkā, Sānxìng, Húnchūn, and Chángchūn
were all engaged in cultivation.
For the poor and those lacking means,
government funds were loaned.
In the 40th year,
exiles were illicitly cultivating land in the Xiùyán pastures.
Consequently, a regulation was established to incorporate them into the official system and collect rent.
In the 42nd year,
due to the rich and fertile land northwest of Dàlínghé, namely Xìngshān and Sōngshān,
idle imperial clan members were relocated,
provided with three *qǐng* of land,
half for official cultivation,
half for self-cultivation.
Houses were built and military colonies organized,
and they were assisted with seeds and tools.
In the 55th year,
it was ordered that from Yīng'é to the border of Àiyáng in Fèngtiān,
wasteland be measured and distributed to landless city-banner people.
Except for reserved hunting grounds and ginseng mountains,
the rest was allocated based on fertility.
Vagrants were prohibited from crossing the border for private cultivation,
but those who had accumulated long-term settlements were still registered as households.
In the 16th year of Jiāqìng,
all passes were ordered to inspect and prohibit this.
Initially, due to the large population of the Eight Banners,
land in Lālín was allocated for them to open fields and cultivate.
In the 17th year,
Sàichōng'ā stated,
"There are over 25,000 *shǎng* of idle wasteland near Lālín that can be cultivated,
and much land in Sāndàokǎ, Sàlí, and other places is uncultivated.
I request that banner people be relocated there."
Soon, Fùjùn requested that a thousand *túndīng* (military colonists) be selected,
allocated thirty *shǎng* of wasteland,
given twenty-five *liǎng* of silver,
and two *shí* of seeds and grain.
They were to cultivate twenty *shǎng*,
leaving ten *shǎng* fallow.
After three years of trial cultivation,
grain payments would begin in the fourth year.
Upon the relocation of imperial banner members, they would be allocated fifteen *shǎng* of cultivated land and five *shǎng* of wasteland.
The remaining five *shǎng* of wasteland and five *shǎng* of cultivated land
would be given to the original *túndīng* as their property, and they would be exempt from military grain.
Afterward,
Fùjùn further suggested establishing a military colony at Shuāngchéngbǎo, northwest of Lālín,
relocating idle imperial banner members.
This involved over ninety thousand *shǎng* of land,
and three thousand households to be relocated,
two hundred households per year.
Land was demarcated per household,
with all expenses covered by the government.
The area was divided into three colonies: Central, Left, and Right.
Each colony dug two wells.
*Túndīng* were selected and granted land,
following the same regulations as Lālín.
Imperial banner members, after holding land for five years,
would pay twenty *shí* of grain.
Each large colony accommodated forty sub-colonies.
Each banner had five sub-colonies.
Eight chief and deputy *túndá* (colony headmen) were appointed.
Each sub-colony had thirty households of *túndīng* from the imperial banners.
Two or more individuals were considered a household.
Each of the three main colonies established a charitable school for young men.
In the 5th year of Dàoguāng,
seventy-seven households were relocated,
cultivating over 33,100 *shǎng* of land.
Since Fùjùn and Sōngyún oversaw this endeavor from beginning to end,
its effects were very notable.
Afterward, those in charge gradually slackened,
and furthermore, the area experienced early frosts and cold weather,
so few were willing to relocate.
Consequently, Bóqǐtú reduced the number of relocated households to one thousand.
Using the remaining land,
each household gained an additional fifteen *shǎng*.
Idle banner members, being unfit for farming,
could hire servants or laborers to assist.
Yīnghé once memorialized that this success should be expanded,
but the plan was never fully realized.
The vacant hunting grounds of Bódū'nà spanned over 200,000 *shǎng*,
long fallow and fertile.
Cultivating it would yield twice the results with half the effort compared to Shuāngchéngbǎo.
Fùjùn requested that it be divided into colonies and boundaries drawn,
roughly following previous regulations.
The area was named Xīnchéng,
and household numbers were assigned in sequence,
totaling 120 colonies.
His memorials were submitted six or seven times.
However, the court soon deliberated that the Shuāngchéngbǎo affair was not yet fully settled,
and funds were insufficient.
The matter was eventually dropped.
In the 28th year,
for privately cultivated land on the border of Fènghuángchéng,
both cultivated and partially cultivated areas,
tenants were recruited and rent collected.
Before long,
banner people and commoners reported cultivating up to 240,000 *mǔ*.
In the 4th year of Xiánfēng,
wasteland in Wǔchángbǎo, Jílín, was opened.
Earlier, official military colonies were established in Qíqíhā'ěr,
where convicts and banner slaves were ordered to farm.
Soon, idlers were dismissed,
and able-bodied men were selected to replace them.
Afterward, Censor Wú Zhuó stated that the wasteland of Hūlán Ménggǔ'ěr Shān was suitable for cultivation.
Soon, due to its status as a prohibited area for ginseng collection
and its interference with border affairs,
the plan was ultimately not implemented.
During the Tóngzhì era,
Pánshé Yì, south of Guǎngníng,
was proposed to release a million *mǔ* of land,
and commoners claimed up to half of it.
Afterward, frequent floods occurred,
and it was not until the end of Guāngxù
that the opening was completed.
At this time, vagrants from gold mines lost their livelihoods.
Following Fù Míng'ā's suggestion,
official wasteland in various rivers like Cángshā and places like Huàpídìanzi was allocated for cultivation,
exempting deposit fees.
Meanwhile, in Fǎkùmén and Àijiāng, there were often vagrants illicitly cultivating land.
When Dūxīng'ā conducted a thorough investigation,
the west bank of Àijiāng, being close to Cháoxiǎn (Korea),
was difficult to settle.
Only strict prohibition of crossing was enforced
to maintain border security.
Those who secretly cultivated along the river and disturbed the border areas
were immediately arrested and penalized.
In the 9th year,
ninety-one areas of wasteland along the border from Àiyángmén to Fènghuángmén
were surveyed and their boundaries expanded,
to settle impoverished commoners.
However, private cultivation continued to fill the border regions as before.
In the seventh year of Guāngxù
Wú Dàchéng submitted a memorial, stating:
“The Sānchākǒu of Nínggǔtǎ has fertile land suitable for cultivation.
Farmers willing to emigrate from Qí and Lǔ [Shāndōng]
can be recruited to form one military-agricultural colony [tún],
to fortify the frontier.”
In the fourteenth year
General Xīyuán first established a bureau and regulations.
Because the frontier land was barren and yielded meager harvests,
he stipulated that taxes would be levied after ten years.
Soon, five communities [shè] were established,
cultivating over 13,400 shǎng of land.
In the twenty-second year
Yánmào re-memorialized on the cultivation of Jílín, stating that
it was initially hampered by discord between banner people and commoners,
and subsequently by the self-interest of the commissioners.
Sixteen years after the bureau was established,
the losses outweighed the gains.
The Board then decided to distinguish and either abolish or retain [the projects].
Thus, the rivers of Fāngzhèng Pào, Duìlí Chǎng, Èrdào Piāohé, Tóu'èrdào Jiāng, Mǎyán Hé, Dàshājídòng, etc.,
were urgently dedicated to expanding land and settling people.
Originally,
in Jílín, land was granted to "攬頭 (lǎntóu)" [contractors] for reclamation.
Although the desolate areas stretched far and wide,
work was often initiated at specified times.
However, the abuses exceeded the benefits,
and this was finally reformed.
Additionally, various tún in the interior that had appended wasteland,
varying in amount,
were all very fertile.
Those who sought to claim them swarmed in,
and lots were drawn to decide.
Earlier, in the twelfth year
Hēilóngjiāng General Gōngtáng requested to open up the wasteland of Tōngkěn, subordinate to Hūlán,
outlining ten benefits in his memorial.
This was subsequently decided upon and implemented.
By the twenty-fourth year
the wasteland affairs of Yíng Tōngkěn Kèyīn were managed,
tún were demarcated and wells dug,
and commoners were recruited as tenant farmers.
Commoners paid land taxes,
banner people provided regular tribute,
and officials provided contracts,
without seizing tenancy profits or rent.
In the twenty-fifth year
approximately 400,000 shǎng of idle wasteland along the Nàmó'ěr Hé in Bùtèhā were reclaimed.
Banner people and commoners leased the land,
incurring expenses but being exempt from rent,
following Ēnzé's request.
Eight years later
over 375,100 shǎng south of Nèhé were opened for reclamation.
In the twenty-eighth year
Jílín established a bureau to clear up land taxes [Qīng Fù]
and simultaneously release scattered wasteland.
Households of banner people in various subordinate areas originally had no fixed grain quotas,
but reports were gathered from various places for tax assessment.
However, at that time, land boundaries were already confused,
and fraudulent concealed claims [bāo tào guǐ jì] were
tangled like a mess of threads.
Soon, the Japanese and Russian conflict erupted,
making matters even more difficult.
General Dáguì and Governor Chén Zhāocháng successively carried out investigations.
By the beginning of Xuāntǒng
the total original land in Jílín subject to large rents was over 1,183,100 shǎng,
with an excess of over 284,800 shǎng.
The following year
after the examination and release of civilian land, banner land, and scattered wasteland in the entire Jí province were completed,
another over 793,300 shǎng were identified as excess.
For land with excess area,
such as square terrain or land long east-west,
the west was generally considered the excess.
For land long north-south, it was the north.
If there were graves in the northwest, it was the southeast.
If one piece of land had two rules applying,
the secondary rule determined the excess.
Fèngtiān's Great Hunting Grounds [Dàwéichǎng] were divided into eastern and western streams [liú],
and this wilderness was reserved from the beginning of the dynasty.
There were fifteen "fresh enclosures" [xiān wéi] for hunting game,
and ninety "great enclosures" [dà wéi] for military training.
Over time, defenses slackened,
and migrants privately reclaimed land for years.
In the early Guāngxù period [1875-1908],
General Qíyuán memorialized to add twenty enclosures to Hǎilóng Jurisdiction,
assessing taxes on the spot.
By the thirtieth year
those who paid taxes on the two wings of Hǎilóng
had reached over 1,290,800 mù.
The remaining eighty-five enclosures:
The western forty-five enclosures
were scheduled for reclamation in the twenty-second year
and completed by the thirtieth year
amounting to over 3,022,000 mù of regular and scattered mountain wilderness, forests, rivers, and meadows.
The price for this wasteland was one liǎng and two qián of silver per mù;
for cultivated mountain land, six qián;
for uncultivated land, three qián;
and for urban base land, twenty liǎng per mù.
For land privately cultivated for many years, double the price was paid, i.e., two liǎng and four qián,
with appropriate reductions for medium and lower grades.
The original households were allowed to reclaim it,
otherwise it was withdrawn and released.
The eastern forty enclosures
were used to resettle households displaced from Jīnzhōu,
opening up and allocating wasteland.
By the thirty-first year
a total of over 1,127,200 mù had been released.
Urban land was twenty-five liǎng per mù for superior grade,
twenty liǎng for medium,
and fifteen liǎng for inferior.
Wasteland paid a regular tax of two fēn per mù,
and ten fēn for wear and tear.
Initially, people were allowed to choose wasteland in the two stream enclosures,
but the remaining interspersed wasteland
was often encroached upon and cultivated,
leading to corruption by officials.
Since Tíngjié re-surveyed it,
accumulated abuses were clarified.
The eastern stream enclosure, which was the entire territory of Dōngpíng,
was secretly merged and almost surpassed the western stream,
leading to numerous disputes and litigations.
In the thirty-second year
the mountain wasteland of both streams was re-measured,
with every ten mù recorded as seven mù.
For the excess land for which the price had already been paid,
but not yet adjusted,
it was stipulated that taxes would be levied after eight years,
to achieve fairness.
Generally, cultivated land began taxation in the current year,
while wasteland had a four-year limit.
At that time, with the Japanese and Russians engaged in war,
Fèng Province's taxes were stagnant and its treasury empty.
Therefore, the remaining privately cultivated wasteland in various subordinate areas of Dōngbiān Hǎilóng was again investigated,
and its value collected to raise funds,
thereby maintaining the new policies.
Additionally, the land reclaimed from the sea, river silt, and various spontaneously generated lands in thirty-two locations within Jǐnzhōu Prefecture were measured and released.
As for Hēilóngjiāng land,
in the eighteenth year of Guāngxù
1,200 banner households for military-agricultural colonies were established at Běituánlínzi in Suíhuà,
and over 600 households in the mountains and forests of Bālānsūsū.
Land was allotted according to households,
forty-five shǎng per household,
of which fifteen shǎng were permanent holdings for the tún soldiers,
and thirty shǎng were subject to taxation.
When the Boxer Rebellion broke out,
there were frequent migrations for years.
Later, households were recruited at Tiěshānbāo,
and various tún in Àihún were appeased,
and it gradually returned to its former state.
However, at that time, east of Jiāng Province,
the number of civilian households increased daily,
and much land was plundered and discarded,
with only two or three tenths remaining.
Wealthy magnates monopolized and hoarded land,
and small households were unable to afford their share.
Wasteland was released quickly, but collection of prices was slow;
much land was claimed, but little was cultivated.
In the thirty-third year
a change was proposed,
allowing idle retired soldiers and willing farmers
to be granted land for cultivation over several years,
integrating settlement into military-agricultural colonies.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng
it was further ordered to widely attract people,
establish commendations,
prevent monopolistic contracting,
and reward with expenses.
Each household still received fifteen shǎng of land,
with a public fee of four qián per shǎng.
Generally, the price of wasteland was graded according to the land.
Mùlán and Suíhuà collected seven qián of silver per shǎng,
Tōngkěn two liǎng and one qián,
while Hūlán and Mò'ěrgēn collected a deposit of one liǎng and four qián.
The amounts varied,
and an additional fifteen percent for expenses was uniformly levied;
this was the general principle.
At that time, the unreleased wasteland west of Nènjiāng was also reserved as a livelihood for landless officials and soldiers.
The policy of allocating soldiers to assist military-agricultural colonies [tún]
was first experimented with at Hālāhuǒshāo.
However, the land was rarely fertile,
and soldiers were lazy and unwilling to cultivate.
Each mù yielded only a dòu of grain,
and sometimes there was no harvest at all.
Their food still depended on government supply,
so the policy was again proposed to be suspended.
In the second year
it was changed back to recruiting civilian tenant farmers.
Initially,
Fèngshěng rigorously implemented the qīngfù,
mandating that all excess land be declared by households as truly owned,
and that taxes be levied upon payment for it.
After more than three years,
only over 800,000 *mǔ* of fallow and cultivated land were obtained.
Subsequently, a council was established,
and the method of annual price exemption was adopted.
The Governor-General of the East, Xīliáng, reported:
"The qīngfù emphasizes increasing tax assessments, not collecting land prices,
and the long-term and short-term benefits differ greatly.
Furthermore, the eastern provinces are the foundation of the Bāqí,
where both Banner people and commoners live mixed together as indigenous inhabitants,
different from the garrisons in other provinces.
The Banner people in the inner and outer cities received land according to their vacancies in military ranks,
and there has always been a fixed quota,
which is the lingering intent of 'allotting land according to population.'
Over several centuries,
the population has increased while land has become insufficient.
The 'allotting land according to population' system is too complex to implement,
but reclamation and cultivation are easy to carry out.
Now that Chángbái has newly established administration,
relocation and settlement are most suitable.
If we adopt a strategy to strengthen the border
and provide resources for the people's livelihood,
it will be 'beneficial to both,' as it is said.
Indeed, we must first eliminate their habit of relying on others for food,
and then gradually devise plans for people to support themselves.
Giving land will encourage them to farm diligently,
and relocating them will eliminate their dependence.
For the sake of the Bāqí,
nothing is more crucial than this."
Three years later,
Fèngtiān's various prefectures widely released fallow land to commoners,
totaling 120,000 *mǔ*.
Since the Shùnzhì reign,
it was ordered that vacant land within the various border passes be open for soldiers to cultivate,
but they were not allowed to go and reclaim grazing land outside the passes.
Considering that the land was fertile and suitable for farming,
in the early Yōngzhèng reign,
800 Beijing soldiers were sent to three locations in Hālāhétún, Rèhé, to establish reclamation,
and various superintendents were appointed.
Soon after, a Sub-Prefect was appointed for Zhāngjiākǒu,
dividing its land into ten parts.
Annually, those who cultivated more than their share were rewarded,
and those who cultivated less than five parts were punished.
By the early Qiánlóng reign,
the eastern and western parts of Rèhé had a total of about 20,000 *qǐng* of Banner land demarcated.
From Gǔběikǒu to Wéichǎng, there was previously no civilian land,
but over the years, civilian reclamation increased, leading to disputes,
so it was ordered to allocate land to Banner households.
Not long after,
Gāo Bīn requested the restoration of the old system,
which was granted.
After Rèhé was reorganized into prefectures and counties,
both mountainous areas and plains were subjected to reclamation and cultivation,
with all taxes paid to the Ménggǔ,
a practice that had long been followed.
The Wéichǎng spanned over a thousand *lǐ*,
comprising seventy-two hunting enclosures,
with one superintendent appointed,
and a thousand Banner soldiers stationed there.
During the Tóngzhì reign,
following the advice of the Military Governor Ruìlín,
fallow land was expanded for cultivation
to provide for military provisions.
Wealthy households were ordered to take charge of the reclamation,
and the occupation of adjacent civilian land was prohibited.
Boundaries were established with guard posts (*kǎlún*) outside the red stakes.
Soon after, Assistant Commanders Guìshān and others were punished for obstruction.
At that time, half of the entire hunting ground had already been released.
Those who received fallow land gradually encroached upon the main hunting ground.
Therefore, an edict was issued to uniformly seal off and prohibit all tenant-cultivated and secretly cultivated land east and west of the river,
and to expel all households engaged in private reclamation.
Those who encroached upon mountain slopes and ravines,
or reported receiving more land but concealed the true amount,
were severely punished.
Later, Kùkèjítài was assigned to manage this matter.
He allocated hidden land outside the Banner tenants' enclosure
to compensate civilian tenants within the enclosure,
so they could relocate and settle,
thereby clarifying the enclosure boundaries.
However, the commissioner's measures were inappropriate,
and treacherous tenants resisted and caused disturbances.
Chóngshí subsequently conducted another survey and measurement,
and further stipulated that the main hunting ground, which had already been cleared, should be permanently prohibited according to the records.
Ruìlín succeeded him,
but still found no effective solution.
In the early Guāngxù reign,
Censor Dèng Qìnglín listed the accumulated abuses.
Subsequently, it was decided to organize the relocation of Jīngqí households to open up agricultural colonies.
Later, a precise survey of the amount of fallow land in Rèhé's five river valleys confirmed
a total of over 2,300 *qǐng*,
with plains land being only about half of that.
Reclamation was immediately invited,
using the fallow land as collateral for military pay.
In the final years,
Military Governor Xīliáng discussed ten matters concerning the opening of the Wéichǎng fallow land.
The main points were to retain the original hunting ground sites,
assign serial numbers,
increase the price of fallow land,
and prevent speculative resales.
All these matters were approved for implementation.
During the Kāngxī reign, for the lands of the Kālāqìn and other banners,
because civilian cultivation benefited from the income,
people often cheaply recruited (Ménggǔ for cultivation),
thus impeding nomadic grazing.
In the early Qiánlóng reign,
it was also ordered for the Ménggǔ and commoners in Cháhāěr to relocate easily.
However, they had lived mixed for years,
households were numerous, and cultivation was widespread,
making it difficult to force relocation without easily causing conflicts.
Debaters often cited the convenience of expulsion.
By the early Jiāqìng reign,
the lands of the Tǔxiètúhán and other banners
often had vagrants residing there.
When Ménggǔ people incurred civilian debts they could not repay,
and poor commoners again suffered from having no place to return to,
boundaries and limits were clearly set for them.
Past transgressions were not blamed.
If, in the future, even one furrow was privately opened
or one more person moved in,
the supervising league chiefs and others would be punished.
Officials were not to inquire about the rent and taxes;
each Zāsàkè was to levy them themselves.
At that time, Guōěrluósī had over 265,000 *mǔ* of cultivated land,
with a fixed tax rate of four *shēng* of grain per *mǔ*.
By the eleventh year,
reclaimers followed one another,
so border prohibitions were extended,
and an edict was issued to prohibit private transactions between commoners.
Violators, including the Táijí, would be held jointly accountable.
However, private cultivation by itinerants became a habit,
which could not be stopped.
Initially, people cultivating land in Guīhuà were ordered to be registered according to the *jiǎ* system,
and their census was submitted annually.
However, in places like Suīyuǎn outside the passes,
only single merchants were allowed to travel,
and those who brought their families were prohibited.
Later, the households recruited for cultivation by the Dáěrhàn and Bīntú Two Princely Banners,
and the Zhuólǐkètú and Bīngtú Two Banners, all belonging to Kēěrqìn,
were also organized into *jiǎ* communities,
and village chiefs were appointed.
In the twelfth year of Dàoguāng,
Shèngjīng Jiāngjūn Yùtài submitted eight regulations for Kēěrqìn reclamation: whoever registers land must use their own name,
and it should not exceed five *qǐng*;
if one plot is registered by multiple parties,
the later household and the earlier household shall share it equally;
if a village or hamlet is mortgaged to commoners,
the contract shall be redeemed and compensation paid;
if the landowner is unable to redeem it,
commoners may cultivate it again,
with a time limit for repayment;
upon expiration, only self-cultivation is allowed,
or leasing to the original tenant,
but no re-mortgaging or recruitment of new people;
after commoner households surrender land,
they may themselves explore and cultivate fallow land,
with official permission to undertake cultivation;
Ménggǔ-cultivated land
is not allowed to be leased to others;
and those cultivated by commoners outside the boundary are also not allowed to be misrepresented.
All were implemented as proposed.
The Tǔmòtè pastures
were previously cultivated at will.
Later, surplus land was distributed to Ménggǔ people,
at a rate of one *qǐng* per person,
but many were tenants or commoner cultivators.
By the seventeenth year,
it was ordered to collect mortgage rent from Ménggǔ,
with one-fourth used for official expenses,
one-fourth of the rent and interest given to unemployed Ménggǔ people,
and the public treasury and the Bèilè of the banner each receiving one-third.
In the seventh year of Tóngzhì,
households from Kālāqìn who had over-reclaimed land were relocated and reassigned to various banners.
In the seventh year of Guāngxù
ten *qǐng* and sixty *mǔ* of land in Wūlǐyǎsūtái were established as a *tún* (military-agricultural colony),
with a total of seven such *tún*.
Expenses for digging canals, constructing dwellings, cattle, and seeds,
were also subsidized by the government.
In the eighth year
indigenous inhabitants of Kùlún were selected to establish experimental *túnkěn* (reclamation colonies) in the western tribal areas of Túshén and Chēchén,
at the request of Xǐchāng.
When the Měnggǔ population was steadily increasing,
land that did not impede pasturage was reclaimed.
This was called pastoral land (*mùdì*).
There were also rented lands (*zūdì*), sustenance lands (*yǎngshàndì*), and incense lands (*xiānghuǒdì*),
all self-cultivated or self-rented.
In the ninth year
Zhāng Zhīdòng, the Governor of Shānxī, stated,
"The two sub-prefectures of Fēng and Níng, and the five sub-prefectures of Guīsuī,
have seen their households grow daily since they began to recruit settlers for Měnggǔ wasteland.
Any remaining wasteland in these areas
is also given to unemployed tenant farmers for rent and cultivation.
The income from this rent,
apart from the portion conventionally given to the Měngqí (Mongol banners),
covers all basic salaries, public annual expenses, and all other necessities for opening up land.
All these are provided from it,
and the benefit is considerable."
In the twenty-first year
Zēng Qí, the General of Fèngtiān, requested the surveying and release of various Měnggǔ wastelands.
Deputy Commandant Shòu Shān also spoke on this matter.
Huáng Sīyǒng, the Director of the Guózǐ (Imperial Academy), requested the reclamation of pastoral lands in the two leagues of Yīkèzhāo and Wūlánchábù in Nèiméng (Inner Mongolia).
The league chiefs claimed this would hinder the livelihoods of their people,
so it could not be implemented.
At this time, the number of settlers in Fēngzhèn and Níngyuǎn on the Jìn border had accumulated to tens of thousands of households.
Moreover, Zhālài, Dù'ěrbótè, and Guōluósī successively reported land for reclamation,
and people flocked to them.
Although private reclamation of Cháhā'ěr banner pastures and grasslands was prohibited,
since the relaxation of restrictions on horse ranches in the middle of Xiánfēng's reign,
unauthorized occupation became rampant in recent years.
Settlers and banner members
were embroiled in endless lawsuits.
In the twenty-fourth year
Commandant Xiáng Lín therefore stated,
"To prevent unauthorized reclamation of Měnggǔ land,
severe penalties must be imposed.
To prevent unauthorized release of land by Měnggǔ officials,
unscrupulous merchants must be punished."
In the twenty-eighth year
Attendant Minister Yí Gǔ was ordered to oversee reclamation affairs
and plan for Cháhā'ěr.
He proposed several measures for expansion and adaptation,
the main thrust of which was
"to clarify previously reclaimed land,
and recruit new settlers.
The livelihood of the Měngqí depends on cultivation, not pasturage.
Regarding Měnggǔ land rents,
some are used for compensation,
some are privately embezzled,
or one piece of land has multiple owners,
and even multiple rents,
with cunning merchants exploiting these gaps to monopolize.
It is advisable for the general managers of each banner to report in detail,
hand over land for release,
completely eliminate the former names of landlords and chief merchants,
establish land reclamation companies in both wings,
with each banner trying it out successively.
Banners and leagues that comply with the order immediately will be rewarded,
and those that resist or delay will be punished."
Consequently, the princely banners of Yīkèzhāo League
and Zhǔngá'ěr,
successively reported their land.
Hángjǐn and Wūshěn were somewhat indecisive,
and Wūlánchábù also had doubts,
but all had gone to the discussion.
For the reclaimed and unreclaimed land in Suīyuǎn,
there was no accurate figure even in the early years of Qiánlóng.
To this day, the eight banner horse ranches
have land mixed with sand and stone,
with few being cultivated,
and the people are hesitant.
Therefore, it was proposed that everyone from the General downwards should identify land,
to guide merchants and common people.
Soon, due to insufficient funds,
a cattle tax (*niújūan*) was initiated,
followed by the expansion of the *tún* tax (*túnjūan*).
When surveying Měnggǔ land,
five *chǐ* made a *gōng*,
two hundred forty *gōng* made a *mǔ*,
one hundred *mǔ* made a *qǐng*,
and *qǐng* were numbered.
In the two wings of Cháhā'ěr,
a *mǔ* was three hundred sixty *gōng*,
and numbers were assigned by five *qǐng*.
For Zhāsàkètú, a *mǔ* was two hundred eighty-eight *gōng*,
ten *mǔ* made a *shǎng*,
and forty-five *shǎng* made a *fāng*.
For Měngqí wasteland prices,
half went to the state,
and half to the Měngqí.
Of the portion going to the Měngqí,
from princes, dukes, and *tàijí* down to common men and lamas,
the grades were clarified,
and each had a designated share.
Lands that were formally designated were "arranged lands" (*páidì*),
which were exempt from advance rent (*yāzū*).
For raw land (*shēngdì mǔ*), an advance rent of three *qián* and three *fēn* was collected,
and for cultivated land (*zīshēngdì*), it was double.
Yí Gǔ, out of concern for the difficulties of the Měnggǔ,
therefore collected only two *qián* per *mǔ* for wasteland in advance,
with only an additional one *qián*.
Of this, six parts went to the bureau,
and four parts to the banner itself.
For Hángjǐn, in the downstream area near the irrigation canals,
the advance wasteland price for superior land was eight *qián* per *mǔ*,
seven *qián* for medium,
and six *qián* for inferior.
He also stated that too much rent burdens the people,
and too little burdens the Měnggǔ.
It was difficult to impose the same terms on different banners,
and the rules for Outer Měnggǔ and Inner Měnggǔ were not uniform.
Therefore, the wasteland prices for the three banners of Wūshěn, Zhāsàkè, and Jùnwáng were set:
three *qián* for superior,
two *qián* for medium,
and one *qián* for inferior.
The regions of the two banners Ètuōkè and Zhǔngá'ěr were divided into four grades.
A separate rule was established for medium and inferior.
For Ètuōkè banner, superior was four *qián*,
and for Zhǔngá'ěr banner, superior was six *qián*,
medium four *qián*,
with subsequent grades decreasing in difference.
The four banners of Wūlán League: Sīzǐwáng, Dá'ěrhàn, Màomíng'ān, and Wūlātè Hòuqí, all had dry land.
All followed the previous regulations.
In the thirty-fourth year
Wénzhéhuī impeached Yí Gǔ for ruining the border administration.
Lù Chuánlín, the minister investigating the case, criticized his handling of reclamation with two errors and four crimes,
and then proposed four measures for improvement.
He said,
"If wasteland prices and surveying measurements are lenient,
then surveying and releasing land will be easy.
To collect more land prices,
original tenants should first be allowed to continue cultivation.
Reduce annual rent but increase canal rent,
to use that rent to cover canal expenses.
When canals increase, land increases;
when land increases, rent increases.
Over time, even saline-alkali land will become fertile."
After Yí Gǔ was arrested and imprisoned,
Xìn Qín succeeded him.
He reduced Hángjǐn's wasteland prices:
superior land was ninety *liǎng* per *qǐng*,
subsequent grades decreasing by five,
with the lowest being seventy *liǎng*.
Wūlātè land was divided into three public areas: east, west, and central.
Dry land advance wasteland prices were divided into six grades:
superior land was one hundred forty *liǎng* per *qǐng*,
next one hundred,
medium seventy,
medium-lower forty,
lower twenty,
and lowest ten *liǎng*.
Three-tenths of this was first allocated as public funds,
and the remainder was half for the Měnggǔ and half for public funds,
all according to regulations.
The land rents accruing to the Měnggǔ were also divided into four grades.
Canal land was subject to an annual canal rent of four *fēn* and five *lí* per *mǔ*.
The experimental settlement and reclamation in Kēbùduō and Wūlángǔmù
began in the late Kāngxī period.
At that time, Advisor Lián Kuí presented a new policy for the Kēbùduō region,
stating,
"Wūlángǔmù and Bāyǎtè are both pasturelands of the Dù'ěrbótè tribe in Kēbùduō.
It is advisable to greatly expand reclamation efforts.
Although the Kēbùduō region is mostly desert,
the Zháhāqìn Banner, the Left and Right Wings of the Míng'ātè Banner, and the Èlútè Banner
are all adjacent to their respective rivers and lakes.
There are many cultivable fields along the rivers.
Promoting reclamation and strengthening the frontier
depends on this."
The imperial court deliberated and approved it.
As for the Bùléntuō Hǎi Mongol land belonging to the Wūliánghǎi,
reclamation began during the Tóngzhì era,
and one hundred thousand ounces of silver were disbursed.
Subsequently, Lǐ Yúnlín’s overly harsh measures incited a mutiny,
and the reclamation work was suspended.
By this time, the repair of the irrigation canal was completed,
merging the soldiers of the upper canal settlement with those of the lower canal,
for their convenience.
The Ā'ěrtài Banner is high, cold, and sparsely watered;
only four official settlements and one civilian settlement were established, it is said.
For the wasteland of the Zhásàkètú princely banner,
for each shǎng, the top grade was four liǎng and four qián,
the middle grade two liǎng and four,
and the bottom grade one liǎng and four,
all subject to a one-fifth charge for expenses.
Generally, land was claimed in sequence;
for every hundred shǎng of cultivated land,
two hundred shǎng of uncultivated wasteland had to be taken as well.
The princely banner's land distribution was completed by the eleventh year,
totaling over 625,000 shǎng.
The following year,
the remaining wasteland in the banner's mountain borders was continuously distributed,
and two subordinate counties were established in Táonán.
Households recruited by the public banner were called 'red households' (hónghù),
while those privately recruited by Tàijí and able-bodied men were called 'black households' (hēihù).
After the Táonán section of wasteland was fully distributed,
the wasteland north of the river,
by the first year of Xuāntǒng,
totaled over 194,000 shǎng after measurement.
The Túshìyètú Mongol wasteland
also followed the precedent of the Zhásàkètú case.
For the Rèhé Mongol wasteland,
the eastern banner of Kālāqìn had already become fertile,
the Àohàn was half barren,
and Bālín was relatively rich.
Dūtǒng Tíng Jié proposed eight recommendations,
to be gradually implemented.
As for the Mongol banner wasteland belonging to the Fèngtiān jurisdiction,
approximately over 89,000 shǎng were distributed,
while the cultivable land in the Ālǔkē'ěrqìn and the East and West Zālǔtè Banners of the Zhāo'ūdá League
totaled eight thousand qǐng.
The price per qǐng for top-grade land was seventy liǎng,
middle-grade fifty,
and bottom-grade thirty.
The new and old distributions of the Zhālàitè Mongol Banner totaled sixty to seventy thousand shǎng,
and Dàlài Tīng was established.
Forty-seven Mongol settlements within the banner were surveyed,
and fifty-nine settlements from outside banners.
For the remaining nearby wasteland,
a rent of one liǎng and four qián per shǎng was collected as a deposit.
At this time, the Kē'ěrqìn public banner land, totaling over 241,400 shǎng, was re-measured.
The land along the river in the Hòu banner of Guō'ěrluósī was desolate but actually fertile.
An additional thirty liǎng per shǎng was collected for public expenses,
to be divided equally between Mongol land matters and educational affairs.
By this time, nothing remained to be opened.
The following year,
the remaining wasteland in Chéngdiàn was also fully distributed.
Chángchūn was originally Mongol land of the former banner,
totaling over 419,000 shǎng.
In the second year of Xuāntǒng,
new wasteland was again distributed,
using public funds to finance judicial administration in the prefectural jurisdiction,
expanding reclamation efforts to aid the new policies.
The wasteland prices for Bālín were revised:
top-grade qǐng seventy liǎng,
middle-grade fifty,
bottom-grade thirty.
The Dá'ěrhàn princely banner's Cǎihā Xīndiàn wasteland was divided into three grades:
top-grade six liǎng per shǎng,
middle-grade four liǎng,
bottom-grade two liǎng.
A total of 60,200 shǎng of actual wasteland was distributed.
In the third year,
the Dá'ěrhàn Táo and Liáo station wasteland was again distributed,
to be used for establishing postal routes.
Qīnghǎi had long been a pastureland for Mongols and Tibetans,
and Han and Hui people were long forbidden from cultivating fields,
yet there was considerable fertile land suitable for cultivation.
Níng Gēngyáo had previously decided to open settlements,
sending convicts from the five northern provinces who could farm to Bùlóngjílér for reclamation.
Finally, Qìng Shù presided over the matter,
pointing out that due to the mixed habitation of Tibetan tribes,
it differed greatly from purely Mongol lands,
and he strongly articulated five concerns.
Subsequently, he further persuaded Mongol and Tibetan tribes to cede land
for development,
allowing Han civilians, regardless of distance, to claim it,
but completely excluding Hui people
to prevent disturbances.
Thus, an office was established for wasteland distribution.
South of the Yellow River, over ten thousand mù of wasteland were released,
and northward, up to over fifty thousand mù.
Fearing their potential resurgence,
additional soldiers were recruited
and stationed to suppress them.
Tibetan lands were remote,
with steep and cold mountains;
only oats and rapeseed were grown.
Even in bumper harvest years,
the yield per mù was no more than four or five shēng.
Taxes were kept light,
to be progressively implemented.
In nearby areas, starting around the Guāngxù and Xuāntǒng eras,
the discussion of wasteland reclamation was particularly urgent,
given the difficulty of material resources
and the absence of opportunities for major initiatives.
It was hoped that the land would not have its benefits abandoned,
and people would not have surplus labor,
but there was still much to be done.
The re-measurement of reed marsh fields:
the reed lands along the Jiǔjiāng riverbank, which had previously been approved for implementation,
were originally set to be taxed at the lowest rate.
Subsequently, the grain levy on reed marshes
was generally set at a rate of one percent or less.
Reclamation of marshland in the Guǎngníng area of Fèngtiān had a long history.
Later, following the words of General Hóng Shǎng,
over 382,000 qǐng of marshland along the Yào and Yīng rivers were opened,
to be taxed after three years
and measured after five years.
As for the reed beds in Niúzhuāng and other places,
river changes in recent years had exposed wasteland.
Most reed merchants secretly reclaimed it,
often leading to disputes.
Successive flexible regulations were established,
distinct from old wasteland precedents.
Soon, reed beds in Fènghuáng, Xiùyán, and Āndōng, totaling about over one hundred thousand mù, were measured and released.
They were numbered according to their location
and recorded in 'fish-scale' cadastral maps.
This occurred in the late Guāngxù era.
The reed camps and grasslands of Jiāngnán
had long been leased for cultivation and rent collection by the Dàhé Wèizǐ.
However, in Jiāngběi, woodcutter soldiers were stationed to manage river affairs,
with two camps, left and right,
located between Háizhōu and Fùníng,
totaling over 8,500 qǐng of land,
not including newly dried or expanded areas.
After the river channel changed, the woodcutter soldiers became superfluous.
During the Xuāntǒng era, the Ministry proposed their disbandment
and converting the land to wasteland for distribution,
allowing people to invest and undertake cultivation, it is said.
From the mid-Guāngxù period,
Cén Zhōngyàn, an Imperial Censor, memorialized to promote agricultural studies,
leading to the special establishment of the Ministry of Agriculture, Industry, and Commerce,
with its dedicated functions.
Several imperial edicts instructed officials throughout the realm
to diligently study and reform wasteland production
as a means of revitalization.
In the early Xuāntǒng era,
the Ministry presented twenty-two items for agricultural and forestry promotion,
starting with the planning and management of wasteland.
Flat areas were suitable for opening fields,
while mountain ridges and scattered borderlands were suitable for forests.
Officials were tasked with surveying climate and soil properties within their jurisdictions,
charting and mapping them.
The exemption or non-exemption of wasteland prices
and the urgency or delay of taxation
were to be differentiated by grade.
Officials' performance was to be assessed based on reported results
to implement rewards and punishments.
Special regulations for planting trees and managing waterways were also established.
By the time the revolution was taking shape,
many matters that had not been fully implemented
still remained.
Concerning agricultural land and water conservancy.
During the reign of
Shèngzǔ, ten thousand *mǔ* of wasteland in Tiānjīn were reclaimed to become paddy fields.
Shìzōng established agricultural fields in Luán and Jì,
and set up the Yíngtián Shuǐlì Fǔ (Bureau of Agricultural Land and Water Conservancy),
appointing Yí Qīnwáng to oversee its affairs.
The Prince and Grand Secretary Zhū Shì compiled and submitted four precedents.
Soon after, four agricultural bureaus were established in Tiānjīn and other prefectures,
each led by a dedicated official.
Depending on the terrain, channels were dredged and dikes were built,
and gates were constructed and canals opened.
For those common people willing to cultivate,
the officials provided capital and labor.
Experienced farmers from Jiāng and Zhè were recruited,
given monthly stipends,
and taught how to cultivate and harvest.
The following year,
over 150 *qǐng* of cultivated land were obtained.
By the seventh year of Yōngzhèng,
over 6,000 *qǐng* of paddy fields had been developed.
Although the expenditure was considerable,
the endeavor proved effective.
Unfortunately, the work was not completed,
and it gradually fell into disuse later.
Only the irrigation system in Cízhōu remained as before,
enjoying constant abundant harvests year after year.
Gāozōng instructed the Zhílì governor-general Lǐ Wèi to repair and manage the paddy fields,
and further dispatched Dàlǐ Qīng Wāng Méng to oversee water conservancy projects in Jiāngnán,
with efforts made in both the north and south.
Later, Gāo Bīn suggested that large canals could be opened on both banks of the Sānggān Hé
to draw water for cultivating rice fields,
which was approved.
Towards the end of Jiāqìng's reign,
Fāng Shòuchóu was ordered to plan water conservancy in Zhílì province,
and also enjoined Lǔ, Jìn, and Yù to devise their own schemes within their respective territories.
However, there were still those who claimed that paddy cultivation was difficult to implement in Zhílì.
Over the past century,
Lǐ Guāngdì, Lù Lóngqí, Zhū Shì, and others had all elaborated on the benefits of paddy fields in Zhílì.
Lín Zéxú's memorial proposing the opening of paddy fields near the capital was particularly incisive.
Due to financial constraints and discouraging discussions,
it was never widely implemented.
Thereafter, Sēnggélínqìn donated to initiate water conservancy projects in the Dàgūkǒu area,
resulting in over 4,200 *mǔ* of rice fields.
Chóng Hòu continued this effort,
and frequent encouragement of reclamation in Yánshuǐgū also yielded considerable results.
Subsequently, Zhōu Shèngchuán garrisoned Tiānjīn,
repaired water conservancy systems,
and created over 60,000 *qǐng* of rice fields.
The soil became fertile and harvests abundant,
benefiting the region to this day.
During the Tóngzhì era,
bureaus were established in Xī'ān, Tóngzhōu, and other prefectures in Shǎnxī to assess barren land
and promote agricultural development.
By the mid-Guāngxù period,
reclamation gradually reached over 34,000 *mǔ*.
The bureaus were converted into offices,
with prefectures and counties taking charge.
At this time, half of Zhílì's agricultural fields lay fallow.
Jìn suffered repeated disasters.
Court officials Xià Xiànxīn, Táng Shùnán, Péng Shìchāng, Liú Ruìqí, and others successively memorialized on water conservancy.
Huá Huī also presented eight proposals.
The Zhílì governor-general Wáng Wénsháo stated
that "lightening rent prices to relieve the people's hardship and dredging canals to improve waterways
would encourage more people to cultivate."
Consequently, rent was levied on over 40,900 *mǔ* of agricultural land in Tiānjīn.
Shāndōng governor Zhāng Rǔméi also requested the dredging of rivers
and canals
to make water conservancy the foundation of agricultural policy.
Shǎnxī Gānsù governor-general Shēng Yǔn, on the other hand, requested the recruitment of two banners of new water conservancy troops in Shǎnxī,
who would eventually be assigned to military farms,
granted land to cultivate,
and thus expand military agricultural policy.
Thereafter, Fèngtiān, due to the lack of any water conservancy along the Dōngxī Liáohé and Dàlínghé rivers,
also memorialized and established methods for drawing water from inland channels to irrigate land,
first attempting to dig channels from branches of small rivers.
Gazetteer 96, Food and Money 2, Taxes and Corvée, Granaries
Taxes and Corvée, Part 1: Tax Regulations.
At the beginning of the Qīng dynasty, upon entering the passes,
the first action was to abolish the three additional levies from the late Míng dynasty.
At that time, many tax registers and land records had been destroyed by roving bandits.
In the third year of Shùnzhì,
an imperial edict instructed the Hùbù (Board of Revenue) to investigate the original quotas of money and grain
and compile them into a comprehensive tax and corvée register,
fully restoring the old system from the Wànlì era of the Míng dynasty.
Counting the empire's financial resources,
Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, and Jiāngxī were the most important,
and among these three provinces, the prefectures of Sū, Sōng, Jiā, and Hú were the most significant.
In the sixth year,
Dǒng Dúxíng, a Right Remonstrance Official of the Household Affairs Section, requested the promulgation of easily understandable tax slips.
In the eighth year,
Shìzǔ began to govern personally,
and successively dispatched censors to tour the provinces
to investigate the people's advantages and disadvantages.
Qín Shìzhēn, the Circuit Censor of Sūsōng, submitted a memorial with eight proposals:
First, that landowners themselves measure their land
and clearly record it in registers;
Second, that fixed money and grain taxes
be filled in on easily understandable tax slips,
and if there were any increases or decreases,
separate small slips be issued
to prevent corrupt clerks from taking advantage;
Third, that the tax slips detail the total and distributed amounts,
along with the names of the households,
for easy verification;
Fourth, that rolling registers be established
to sequentially track and collect arrears;
Fifth, that households be allowed to personally submit grain to the granary,
with the seal of the司府 (local government office) stamped on it;
Sixth, that tax exemptions prioritize the urgent over the less urgent,
with deadlines for cancellation;
Seventh, that commoner corvée service for land inspection be equally distributed
and verified against household registers;
Eighth, that reserve silver
not be overdrawn beyond the quota,
and that silver collection and remittance registers
be extracted quarterly by the Bùzhèng Sī (Provincial Administration Commission)
and reported to the Board at year-end.
Thereafter, the long-standing abuses in money and grain collection were gradually rectified and clarified.
In the eleventh year,
Right Vice-Minister Wáng Hóngzuò was ordered to revise the comprehensive tax and corvée register,
first listing the original land and poll tax quotas,
then wasteland and losses,
then actual collections,
and then transportation and retention.
Transportation was distinguished by Board, temple, and granary,
and retention detailed the numerous expenditure items.
Newly reclaimed land and recruited households
were subsequently added to the end of the register.
Each prefecture and county received two copies,
one for the local official,
and one for the academy.
Tax registers included the land measurement register,
also known as the *yúlín cè* (fish-scale register),
which detailed the tax rates for superior, medium, and inferior fields.
There was also the *huáng cè* (yellow register),
which annually recorded household changes,
and corresponded with the comprehensive tax and corvée register.
There was the *chì lì* (red calendar),
where common people recorded their own payment amounts,
which was submitted to the Bùzhèng Sī,
and verified at year-end.
There was also the *kuàijì cè* (accounting register),
which fully recorded the regular and supplementary money and grain taxes of prefectures and counties,
noting the year and month of remittance to the Board.
The "Single-Whip Method" of the Míng Wànlì era was also adopted.
The Single-Whip Method
combined the annual quotas for summer tax, autumn grain, retention, and transportation for prefectures, departments, and counties,
along with the quotas for corvée, *lijia* (local self-governance system), local tribute, hired labor, and additional silver,
into a single item,
which was collectively collected and evenly disbursed.
As for transportation and payment of hired labor,
these were all handled by officials,
and the common people were not involved.
Easily understandable tax slips were issued to all taxpaying households.
The format of the tax slips
listed superior, medium, and inferior tax rates for each prefecture and county,
regular and miscellaneous money and grain taxes (original and discounted),
with a total appended at the end,
and were issued one month before collection began.
This was supplemented by *jiépiào* (cut tickets), *yìnbù* (printed ledgers), *xúnhuánbù* (circulation ledgers), as well as grain registers and audit registers.
The *jiépiào*
listed the actual amount of land and poll tax,
divided into ten installments,
with one-tenth paid monthly.
Upon completion, it was cut,
and a seal was stamped on the ticket's face,
divided in the middle of the printed characters.
Officials and common people each held half,
which was also known as *chuàntpiào*.
The *yìnbù*
was issued by the Bùzhèng Sī,
requiring prefecture and county taxpayers to personally fill it in,
and submit it to the Commission and report to the Board in the last month of winter.
The *xúnhuánbù*
followed the expenditure items in the comprehensive tax and corvée register,
prioritizing them by urgency,
and collected taxes on a monthly rotating basis.
The grain registers
recorded the detailed names and numbers of taxpayers in each district,
matching the total amount for each *jia* (group of households).
The audit registers
compiled a clear register of all tax collections, arrears, disbursements, and retentions for the entire province,
which was reported to the Board for audit at year-end.
The established system could be described as thorough and comprehensive.
In the fifteenth year,
Xǔ Zhījiàn, the Imperial Censor of Jiāngxī, stated:
"The greatest harm to revenue and taxation
is nothing like the predatory yáoyì (corvée labor).
Officials are dismissed due to penalties,
but these predatory yáoyì remain entrenched as before.
I request that the fǔ (governors) and àn (inspectors) be ordered to conduct a thorough investigation,
and those who are most egregious should be punished with the death penalty,
so that accumulated abuses may hopefully be cleared away."
Shǐ Biāogǔ, a Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Public Works, requested a strict prohibition on additional levies outside of the regular tribute,
and that the imperial edict admonishing private levies be published in the 'Yì zhī yóu dān' (Easy-to-understand tax receipts),
so that the people might all know.
The emperor deemed all these memorials to be incisive and pertinent to contemporary abuses,
and sent them to the relevant departments for detailed deliberation and report.
Upon the accession of Shèngzǔ,
strict prohibitions were reiterated against zhōuxiàn (county) officials concealing land, not paying taxes, and falsely reporting newly reclaimed land.
The regulations for punishing officials responsible for催徵 (cūizhēng, pressing for payment), 議經徵 (yìjīngzhēng, deliberating on collection), and 督催 (dūcuī, supervising collection) were revised.
Zhōuxiàn officials who misappropriated regular fā (taxes), falsely claimed that the people owed arrears,
or imposed additional levies and private collections,
were punished.
The emperor, finding the items on the yóu dān (tax receipts) to be numerous,
and not easily understood by the people,
ordered that the actual silver and grain amounts to be collected per亩 (mǔ) for land of upper, middle, and lower grades be listed on the receipts.
The yóu dān (tax receipts) were to be reported to the Ministry;
those who exceeded the eight-month deadline
were to be punished: zhōuxiàn (county) officials, wèisuǒ (guard stations), and transferring officials.
Supervising Secretary Yáo Wénrán memorialized:
"For calamity remissions,
there are instances where collection is completed before the order is issued.
In such cases, the taxes to be remitted for the current year are offset against the regular tribute payable in the following year,
called 'liú dǐ' (flowing offset).
This should naturally be entered into the yóu dān (tax receipts)
so that the people receive actual benefit.
However, the Ministry-approved fixed-quota yóu dān (tax receipts)
are issued to the zhōuxiàn (counties) in the eleventh month of the previous year.
The calculation and compilation
must take place between the ninth and tenth months.
Whereas, reports of calamities from various provinces,
summer calamities in the sixth month
and autumn calamities in the ninth month,
require the Ministry to conduct investigations, report back to the emperor,
and issue dispatches to the fǔchén (governors),
who then instruct local officials.
This protracted process
means it will already be after the yóu dān (tax receipts) have been issued,
making it impossible to enter the information.
Therefore, it should be requested that it be entered into the yóu dān (tax receipts) in the year following the liú dǐ (offset)
to prevent this abuse."
This was sent to the Ministry for deliberation and implementation.
For the collection of qiánliáng (money and grain) in the zhíshěng (direct provinces),
summer taxes were in the fifth and sixth months,
and autumn grain in the ninth and tenth months.
The numbers reported to the Ministry
were to be meticulously scrutinized by the various司 (sī, departments) during the financial review,
and submitted annually to the Jīngjī Dào (Capital Circuit) for auditing.
Since Shìzǔ established the system of taxation,
the regular and miscellaneous fā (taxes) were numerous and complex.
Discrepancies in memorials and reports
led to rejections and orders for re-investigation.
Officials in charge of seals then exploited the name of Ministry rejection
to unilaterally impose private levies.
While the regular qiánliáng (money and grain) had fixed quotas,
local officials, whenever there was a need for other expenses,
would immediately find ways
that were no different from imposing additional levies.
At this point, an order was issued for strict prohibition,
and the system of zhōuxiàn (county) officials owing grain, remaining in office pending a replacement, and complete exoneration was abolished.
In the seventh year,
because the deadlines for summer and autumn taxes were slightly delayed,
fearing it might affect the military provisions,
the old system was reinstated,
where after zhōuxiàn (counties) began collection, it was immediately collected and remitted.
For all dìdīng qiánliáng (land and poll taxes) in the various provinces,
the Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor) would conduct a financial review at the end of the year,
detailing the total amount of qiánliáng (money and grain) transported, retained, allocated for military provisions, purchased for pigments, and the surplus,
and submit a detailed roster.
The huángcè (Yellow Registers) and huìjìcè (Accounting Registers), being complex and uselessly expensive,
were all abolished.
In the fifteenth year,
penalties for officials and commoners concealing land were strictly defined.
Officials who discovered concealed land
were to be deliberated upon separately.
If commoners reported concealed land exceeding ten qǐng,
the land would be given to them.
In the eighteenth year,
zhōuxiàn (counties) were ordered to submit their daily qiánliáng (money and grain) running accounts to the司 (sī, departments) for auditing,
and the chìlì (red calendars) were abolished.
Since the revision of the 'Fùyì Quánshū' (Complete Book of Taxation and Corvée) during the Shùnzhì reign,
over twenty years had passed by this point.
The population and cultivated land
had increased compared to the past.
Corvée duties were increased according to households,
and taxes were added based on land.
The items were numerous and complex,
easily leading to confusion.
In the twenty-fourth year,
an order was issued for a major revision.
Only essential fā (tax) items such as those for transport, retention, grain transport, and river works were included,
and fractional tails below 'sī' and 'miǎo' were removed.
It was named 'Jiǎnmíng Fùyì Quánshū' (Simplified Complete Book of Taxation and Corvée).
The book was completed in the twenty-sixth year.
The court deliberated that the old book had been in use for a long time,
and the annual increases and decreases in dìdīng yínmǐ (land and poll tax silver and grain)
were all verifiable through recorded registers.
Thus, the new book was ultimately not promulgated.
That year, an edict was issued for all provinces to be exempted from printing yóu dān (tax receipts)
to prevent the abuses of levying fees and disturbing the people.
In the twenty-eighth year,
all Provincial Governors were ordered to inspect the qiánliáng (money and grain) in the司 (sī, department) treasuries during their annual financial reviews.
Previously, zhōuxiàn (counties) used two-part serial tickets for collection,
with one for officials and one for commoners.
Dishonest officials colluded with corrupt yáoxū (clerks),
treating paid amounts as unpaid,
and over-collected amounts as under-collected,
leading to daily increasing abuses.
At this point, the three-part serial ticket system was deliberated and implemented:
one for the officials,
one for the yáoyì (corvée laborers) to compare,
and one for the commoners as a receipt.
Later, four-part serial tickets were printed:
one sent to the fǔ (prefecture),
one retained as a stub,
one given to the taxpayers,
and one for the taxpayers to submit to a separate counter when paying taxes to clear their arrears.
Not long after,
the system reverted to the three-part serial ticket.
Gentry and scholars in various provinces originally had the privilege of tax exemption for dìngyín (poll tax silver).
However, powerful local magnates
often fraudulently registered (land under others' names) and abused exemptions.
Furthermore, gentry and scholars monopolized qiánliáng (money and grain) and fees,
all enriching their private coffers,
burdening both officials and commoners.
An imperial edict stated
that fraudulently registered land
should all be returned to the original owners.
In the thirtieth year,
since the yóu dān (tax receipts) had been discontinued,

zhōuxiàn (counties) and wèisuǒ (guard stations) in the zhíshěng (direct provinces) were ordered to engrave on stone tablets outside their gates the assessed amounts for payment according to the 'Fùyì Quánshū' (Complete Book of Taxation and Corvée).
Furthermore, an edict allowed commoners who concealed land
a two-year period to self-report,
which was later extended by another two years.
An edict instructed Fújiàn to survey coastal land,
and define boundaries.
For Húnán, with its vast territory,
people were first ordered to survey their land themselves,
and then officials would conduct sample surveys.
