Those who concealed or omitted land were punished.
At this time, officials often privately imposed various levies during qiánliáng (money and grain) collection,
which had different names.
When an entire township or village jointly shared and paid,
it was called 'ruǎnài' (soft imposition).
When each village or jiǎ (tithing unit) took turns bearing the burden alone,
it was called 'yìngtuó' (hard burden).
Thus, 'gǔndān' (rolling receipts) were introduced to prevent these abuses.
The method involved, within each lǐ (village unit),
grouping five or ten households per receipt.
It would specify under whose name how much land, how much silver and grain, and how much was due in spring and autumn respectively.
Divided into ten installments,
it was issued to the jiǎshǒu (head of the jiǎ unit),
who would sequentially urge payment
and personally deliver it to the counter.
Once one installment was set,
the second installment would be urged in sequence.
Those who delayed, failed to complete payment, or failed to submit were severely punished,
which the people found convenient.
In Zhèjiāng, Húběi, Shāndōng, and other provinces, jiàngbānyín (artisan-service silver)
was all incorporated into dìdīng (land and poll tax) collection.
In the forty-fifth year,
the Jiǔjiāng Fǔ (prefecture) surveyed over three thousand qǐng of reed marshland along the river,
all of which were assessed for taxation at the lowest rate.
In the 51st year,
the Governor of Sìchuān, Nián Gēngyáo, reported:
“The original quota for taxes and grain in Sìchuān was 1,610,000 taels and some extra.
Currently, only one-tenth is being collected.
It is advisable to establish a system of rewards and punishments.
Those who increase collections by four or five tenths of the original quota within five years shall be promoted.
Those who fail to reach two tenths shall have their promotion suspended.
Those who fail to reach one tenth shall be demoted.
Those with no increase shall be dismissed from their posts.”
Censor Duàn Xī submitted a memorial refuting this,
briefly stating:
“Since the turmoil of the late Míng dynasty,
Sìchuān province has been vast in land but sparse in population.
After our dynasty pacified the region,
even after subsequent cleanups,
the reported increase barely reached one-tenth of the original quota.
Recently, the governor has diligently urged investigations,
resulting in an increase of over 26,000 taels.
Now, to expect an increase of two-tenths or even four or five tenths of the original quota within five years
means increasing the current collections by three or four times.
Competent officials
will inevitably face impeachment for failing to meet the quotas,
while corrupt officials will exploit and extort,
leading to endless disturbances.
I request that concealed and leaked taxes and grain in Sìchuān province
be thoroughly investigated,
without needing to establish a separate system of rewards and punishments.”
This was adopted.
In the 59th year,
an edict stated:
“Henceforth, taxes and grain from all prefectures and counties
shall be remitted as soon as they are collected.
If, after a prefecture or county approves remittance,
the Provincial Administration Commissioner’s Office diverts it for miscellaneous expenses
and withholds approval,
the prefecture or county may report directly to the governor-general or governor.”
The following year,
it was also ordered that all governors-general and governors make up for shortfalls in granary grain
within a three-year limit.
During Shèngzǔ’s 60-year reign,
government affairs were generally lenient.
Corrupt officials
often relied on this leniency,
arbitrarily creating shortfalls,
and superior officials also covertly tolerated them,
setting deadlines for recovery,
treating it as routine.
When Shìzōng was in the imperial household,
he was already well aware of these abuses.
After his ascension,
he instructed the Boards of Revenue and Works
that henceforth, when reporting on taxes, grain, stone, prices, and labor and materials,
they must meticulously investigate and verify them,
and prepare registers for imperial submission.
Those who inflate small amounts to large, cheap items to expensive, whose figures do not match, or whose valuations are not accurate,
shall be punished.
He also ordered all governors-general and governors to strictly audit shortfalls in taxes and grain under their jurisdiction,
requiring them to be made up within three years,
without using pretexts to cover them up
or imposing harsh levies on the populace.
Failure to make up within the deadline
would result in severe punishment.
For land along rivers and coasts,
it was customary to conduct a land survey every ten years.
In Yōngzhèng’s first year,
an edict ordered immediate surveys,
exempting collapsed land and
taxing newly formed land.
In the second year,
following the request of Nánmǐn, Governor of Shānxī, and Gāo Chénglíng, Provincial Administration Commissioner, to remit the "fire consumption" (huǒ hào) surcharges to the public treasury,
to be distributed to officials as integrity allowances (yǎng lián) and for other public uses.
Huǒ hào referred to
surcharges added beyond the official tax quota.
This was because converting grain to silver
inevitably involved loss during smelting,
and transportation back and forth
required various expenses.
Prefectures and counties, in their collection,
could not but take a small surplus to cover these losses,
ranging from several qián for heavy items to over one qián for light ones.
After being practiced for a long time,
prefectures and counties heavily taxed the people,
and superior authorities harshly extorted prefectures and counties.
Whenever public business arose,
additional levies and private collections were imposed,
under numerous pretexts,
and not limited to just the huǒ hào.
In the final years of Kāngxī,
Nián Gēngyáo, Governor-General of Shǎnxī and Gānsù, requested to retain a portion of the huǒ hào in Qín province for officials’ expenses,
donating the remainder to make up for shortfalls,
but Shèngzǔ did not permit it.
Now, Nánmǐn and others raised the issue again.
An imperial edict granted their request.
Nánmǐn further requested to set a fixed percentage.
The Emperor said:
“If a percentage is set,
it will become a fixed regulation in the future,
which will inevitably lead to increases without reductions.
Currently, if huǒ hào is remitted along with the main tax,
prefectures and counties will know that excessive huǒ hào is not beneficial to themselves,
so who would dare to collect more?
If the due amount is withheld,
they will inevitably take an extra surplus,
exceeding the amount they should receive.”
Thus, the system of official integrity allowances was established.
Shí Wénzhuó, Governor of Hénán, requested to make the huǒ hào from grain donations public,
and the Emperor said:
“The huǒ hào retained in the treasury
is for local public use.
National expenditures
have their own regular quotas.
How can huǒ hào be incorporated into the main tax
and thereby lead to other abuses of separate appropriation and diversion!”
He also instructed the Board of Revenue, saying:
“Regarding shortfalls in taxes and grain in prefectures and counties,
where the entire populace of the jurisdiction contributes to repay them,
though called ‘voluntary contributions’ (lè juān),
it is in reality no different from forced levies.
This should be ordered to be prohibited.”
As Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng had more excessive levies than other provinces,
an edict remitted 300,000 taels from Sūzhōu’s quota
and 150,000 taels from Sōngjiāng,
to be permanently set as a precedent.
Zhāng Kǎi, Governor of Jiāngsū, memorialized, stating:
“The annual quota for Jiāngsū,
after remitting excessive levies,
should be 3,500,000 taels and some extra.
Accumulated arrears over the years amount to 8,810,000 taels and some extra,
totaling over 12,000,000.
To exhaust a small commoner’s annual harvest
makes it impossible to collect in full.
The current method for collection being devised is:
this year’s new grain
is to be collected in full;
old arrears are to be divided into ten parts.
Starting next year,
one-tenth will be collected annually,
completing in ten years.
When reporting annual accounts,
a separate register will be submitted.
Jiādìng county alone has accumulated over 1,400,000 in arrears,
so I request that it be divided into fifteen parts for collection.
Shànghǎi, Kūnshān, Chángshú, Huátíng, Yíxīng, Wújiāng, Wǔjìn, Lóu, and Chángzhōu nine counties all have accumulated over 400,000,
so they should be divided into twelve parts for collection,
to alleviate the burden on the people.”
The Emperor deeply accepted this.
Among the provinces with heavy taxes,
besides Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
Jiāxìng and Húzhōu prefectures in Zhèjiāng were the most burdened.
In the fifth year,
an edict reduced their taxes by one-tenth,
totaling over 80,000 taels.
It was also ordered that for Nánqiū and other rice taxes in Zhèjiāng province,
the annual quota be calculated as ten parts,
and a separate memorial be submitted for cancellation.
If remittance was incomplete,
the responsible officials would be punished.
Regarding the detailed figures of tax collections and arrears in various provinces,
officials often did not disclose them,
and petty clerks took advantage to engage in malpractices,
treating shortfalls and arrears as commonplace.

Edicts ordered all governors-general, governors, and provincial administration commissioners to instruct prefecture and county officials to annually submit the figures of collections and arrears for each village and locality,
for verification and approval,
and to post them in their respective localities,
so that the people would be aware.
If there was embezzlement,
the people were permitted to present their receipts and lodge complaints.
For items collected in installments over multiple years,
the amount due annually from each household
should also be explicitly listed and posted,
to prevent excessive or additional levies.
In the seventh year,
three-tenths of Zhèjiāng’s quota were remitted,
totaling 100,000 taels.
As for Jiāngsū’s overdue taxes,
starting from the Rénzǐ year,
items involving embezzlement and private appropriation
were to be collected in installments over ten years.
Items genuinely owed by the people
were to be collected in installments over twenty years.
Whatever amount was collected this year,
the same amount of the quota would be remitted the following year.
If more than the quota was collected,
the excess amount would also be remitted the following year.
In the eleventh year,
Xú Běntiáo, the Governor of Ānhuī, presented a memorial on matters of grain collection: first,
regarding the grain chests collected by zhōuxiàn (prefectures and counties),
he requested that zhōuxiàn seals be used directly;
second,
when common households paid their grain tax,
the triple-part receipt should still be used;
third,
for small amounts of money and grain from ordinary people,
if less than one qián,
they should be permitted to pay in token coinage by variation.
This was approved.
In the twelfth year,
the Fùyì Quánshū (Complete Book of Taxes and Services) was revised.
For the regularly levied land and poll taxes, commercial and pawnshop duties,
as well as the expenses for official salaries, labor, courier stations, and supplies,
and also items to be remitted such as raw and refined silk, cloth, dyes, cinnabar, copper, tin, tea, and wax,
the original quotas, newly levied amounts, and total scattered figures were to be clearly analyzed,
ensuring accuracy and meticulousness.
Thereafter, it was to be revised every ten years.
In provinces like Jiāngnán and Húguǎng,
the collapse and accretion of reed shoals were not fixed,
and it was customary to conduct a land survey every five years.
Dishonest officials
often used this as an opportunity for bribery and malpractice.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
an imperial edict was issued to investigate this.
It also prohibited provinces from falsely reporting land reclamation.
Grand Secretary Zhū Shì requested a ban on private land surveys initiated and reported by commoners.
Censor Jiǎng Bǐng memorialized on three abuses in zhōuxiàn grain collection: first,
the differing tax rates for fields,
requesting that the annual quota issued by the Board be
verified and publicly displayed;
second,
if there was a shortage or discrepancy when a zhōuxiàn broke a seal,
the amount should be noted on the bag,
and the household instructed to make up the difference themselves;
third,
zhōuxiàn had established official artisans
for melting down silver,
extorting fixed payments,
and profiting excessively.
Henceforth, households would be allowed to melt down silver anywhere,
and official artisans were permanently prohibited.
All these proposals were adopted.
An edict ordered the reduction of 120,000 shí of "white grain" in Jiāngnán and Zhèjiāng,
and exempted Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng from 200,000 shí of "floating grain" in silver.
Since the remittance of "fire loss" from Shānxī,
other provinces had gradually implemented it.
Later, a proportional system was further established,
with over 2.8 million liǎng for the integrity allowances of civil officials in various provinces,
and various public expenses,
all sourced from this.
When the Emperor ascended the throne,
many court officials spoke of its inconvenience.
The Emperor also worried about burdening the people excessively.
When examining scholars from the imperial platform,
he immediately posed this question,
and further ordered court officials and governors-general to express their views.
Grand Secretary È'ěrtài, Vice Minister of Justice Qián Chénqún, and Governor-General of Húguǎng Sūn Jiāgàn all stated:
"The system of 'loss and wastage'
has been in place for a long time.
The collection is fixed,
and officials do not dare to take more.
The calculated fixed amount,
compared to before it was fixed,
is still less than half.
This appears to be an increased tax but is actually a reduced collection.
Moreover, with 'fire loss' going to the public,
all corrupt practices have been eliminated.
Superior officials have no abuses of extortion,
zhōuxiàn have no pretexts for arbitrary levies,
and ordinary people are not burdened by heavy losses.
The law is good and the intention excellent;
it can endure for a long time."
Censor Zhào Qīnglí also said:
"With 'loss and wastage' going to the public,
it pools the excess to benefit the scarce,
and a relaxation of one fen brings a benefit of one fen.
Furthermore, since the name of 'loss and wastage' exists,
one should not seek more beyond the regular quota.
Please do not lightly discuss changes."
Only Censor Chái Cháoshēng believed that 'loss and wastage' was a major abuse today.
An edict adopted the proposal of È'ěrtài and other officials.
Previously, when provinces remitted imperial funds to the capital,
there was a customary practice of "accompanying silver."
In the early Yōngzhèng period,
there had been an edict prohibiting it.
Later, due to the investigation of a deficit of over 2.5 million in the Board's treasury,
Prince Yí proposed using the "accompanying silver" from imperial funds to make up the difference.
For every thousand liǎng of imperial silver,
twenty-five liǎng of "accompanying silver" were collected,
all drawn from the "loss and wastage" and remitted.
This was already a significant reduction compared to previous informal practices.
Soon after the deficit was made up,
the collection was halved.
At this point, remittances to the Board were stopped,
and the funds were stored in the provincial treasury
to be used for disaster relief in the province and for benefiting the people's livelihoods.
Since the Míng dynasty,
in Jiāngnán, besides the annual quotas for money and grain, land and poll taxes, canal transport fees, reed taxes, and miscellaneous duties,
there was also what was called "miscellaneous handling" (zábàn).
There were many categories,
all aggregated into the land and poll tax for reporting.
When the Fùyì Quánshū was compiled,
it only recorded the categories to be remitted,
but did not list the origins of zábàn.
Now, regulations were properly established
to prevent excessive collection.
Actual shortages that burdened officials and commoners were exempted,
and zhōuxiàn were prohibited from collecting excessive fractional amounts of grain.
In the twelfth year,
Grand Secretary Nàqīn and others proposed that the arrears of money and grain in Jiāngsū amounted to over 2 million,
inevitably involving embezzlement by clerks and yamen runners.
Regulations for self-reporting and reduction/exemption were formulated.
An edict further instructed Huáng Tíngguì and others to rectify various abuses in Jiāngsū's tax collection.
Accumulated arrears of money and grain in various provinces
were reported at the end of the year,
but the actual completed or outstanding amounts could only be determined after the accounts were finalized in the fifth month of the following year.
The edict stated:
"Henceforth, for the annual completion or arrears of money and grain in each province,
a verified report shall be submitted with the account finalization,
without following the precedent of reporting at year-end."
In the twenty-second year,
arrears of canal transport fees, silver, rice, land value, and "loss and wastage" in Jiāngnán from before the tenth year of Qiánlóng were remitted.
Chén Hóngmóu, the Governor of Jiāngsū, memorialized:
"The money and grain in Jiāngsū have accumulated arrears for years
because zhōuxiàn case files
were taken and stored in private rooms by clerks,
leading to incompleteness and inability to查考 (investigate).
It should be strictly ordered that all zhōuxiàn bind and seal their files,
storing them properly in the yamen.
As for the numerous expenditures in Jiāngsū province,
zhōuxiàn inevitably advance funds.
Henceforth, they should still be allowed to detail their requests for offsetting payments at any time.
If not reported in detail within four months,
and the amount reaches over 500 liǎng,
they shall be impeached;
if delayed by a year,
the prefecture and zhōuxiàn shall also be jointly impeached."
All were carried out as proposed.
In the thirtieth year,
an edict stated:
"The account finalization ledger's front lists mountain lands, fields, ponds, desolate and newly reclaimed lands,
followed by the three gates and nine categories of fixed levy, original and revised land and poll taxes, remittances and retentions,
which is very clear.
Let the Fùyì Quánshū be printed henceforth,
using the account finalization articles as a model,
only adding new collapses and new reclamations within the past ten years,
and deleting trivial, unsanctioned categories."
The Board of Revenue deliberated and decided on the collection of money and grain in various provinces,
and all matters of account finalization and disbursement.
All silver was to be calculated to the lí,
and amounts less than a lí were to be rounded down.
Grain was to be calculated to the sháo,
and odd amounts of five miǎo or more were counted as one sháo,
while less than five miǎo were removed.
Payments of salaries and stipends in token coinage were stopped at one wén,
and any minute or negligible fictitious numbers in the ledger
were to be deleted simultaneously.
As for the silver to be collected by various zhōuxiàn and guards (wèisuǒ),
all fractional amounts below the total on the general receipt were to be rounded down,
while the detailed figures listed within the receipt
were to retain their original form,
so as to match the figures in the Fùyì Quánshū and the Yúlín Cè (Fish-Scale Registers).
In the thirty-third year,
an edict ordered that meritorious lands (xūntián) in the directly governed provinces
be reported by common households
and taxed uniformly.
In the 36th year [of the reign],
due to the annual remission of taxes on money and grain throughout the empire,
the people's strength and resources were abundant.
Orders were given to all governors-general and governors that during the year of remission,
all arrears in payments
must be diligently collected and submitted,
so as to avoid the burden of collecting both old and new taxes in the following year.
In the 47th year,
Censor Zhèng Chéng requested that governors-general and governors be ordered to thoroughly inspect granaries and treasuries.
If any deficiencies were found,
the responsible official would be punished and made to compensate.
Governors-general and governors would be severely penalized
and made to pay double the share.
Furthermore, all prefectures and counties were ordered to report the actual amount stored in their granaries and treasuries
every three months,
and governors-general and governors would supervise and verify this at all times.
In Shāndōng, prefectures and counties often suffered from the malpractice of embezzlement and misappropriation of treasury funds.
There were also cases where there was no actual shortage,
but upon leaving office, officials would falsely claim a deficit,
secretly establish a debt agreement,
and hand it over to their successor,
as a means of enriching themselves.
A request was made to instruct all governors-general and governors
that if a former official's deficit was found, and the successor had a verifiable debt agreement,
in addition to holding the successor responsible for making up the deficit,
the former official should still be ordered to recover the amount and pay it to the government,
to prevent the malpractice of short deliveries and indiscriminate acceptance.
The Emperor graciously accepted this.
it was again ordered that when local officials transferred duties,
if they could not settle their accounts within the deadline,
the official concerned should be detained
until the funds were settled,
only then would they be allowed to proceed to their new post or return home.
The practice of secretly establishing agreements was also prohibited.
From then on,
the prohibitions became even stricter.
Censor Péng Xīluò reported that many provinces had the malpractice of overcharging for money and grain taxes.
An edict was issued that henceforth, all governors-general and governors must, before collection began,
verify the actual amount to be converted into silver and paid into the treasury according to market prices,
post it on public thoroughfares,
and allow the people to pay in silver or convert it into cash
as they pleased.
At that time, local officials in various provinces
often shifted new and old accounts
regarding the taxes on money and grain to be collected,
treating collected amounts as arrears.
For three or four years,
accumulated arrears amounted to over 20 million taels.
An imperial edict ordered a thorough investigation of all accumulated arrears in the provinces over the years,
whether owed by the people or by officials,
all were to be investigated uniformly.
Some were to be stored,
others disbursed.
Violators would be punished.
The Board of Revenue reported:
"In the past five years, various provinces have borrowed from their surplus 'loss and wastage' funds.
We request that governors-general and governors be held responsible for investigating and returning these to the original funds,
and for appropriately reducing the 'loss and wastage' funds that have been expended.
All idle funds stored
should also be reported in detail."
In Zhílì, the accumulated deficits of various prefectures over the years amounted to millions.
Ānhuī's granaries and treasuries had a deficit of over 1.8 million taels of silver.
The Emperor ordered newly deficient officials
to complete the payment of old deficits within four years, starting from the current year.
For those who failed to complete payments,
95% of the annual 'integrity allowance' of judicial commissioners, intendants, prefects, sub-prefects, and county magistrates would be deducted and stored in the treasury to cover the arrears.
The Board reported that in Zhílì and fifteen other provinces,
excluding deferred and supplementary collections,
the unpaid land and poll tax still amounted to over 8.7 million taels,
and in the 12th year, an additional unpaid land and poll tax of over 2.9 million taels accrued.
The Emperor observed that senior officials, when an official responsible for collection
was nearing the end of their term,
would arrange for their transfer to an acting position,
so that the incoming acting official would start a new term limit,
which county magistrates used as a means of evasion.
He ordered that henceforth, when county magistrates were transferred to acting positions,
it must first be verified whether there were indeed no uncollected taxes or grain owed during their tenure,
and this should be reported to the Board for verification.
They should not be transferred to an acting position in violation of regulations
when their term limit was about to expire.
Remonstrance Official Zhào Pèi-xiāng reported:
"Deficits in various provinces,
when repeatedly investigated,
often lead to protracted delays in counties.
We request a strict prohibition."
Previously, in Zhílì, due to county magistrates' deficits in granaries and treasuries,
high officials were secretly ordered to investigate
and pursue compensation separately.
Subsequently, other provinces followed suit,
requesting the establishment of bureaus for investigation.
This led to shifting new debts to cover old ones,
and malpractices secretly proliferated.
There were even those who borrowed the name of compensation
to secretly extort.
Therefore, Pèi-xiāng raised this issue.
The Emperor ordered that all outstanding payments from the three investigations in Zhílì
be collected in installments,
and if they were not completed by the deadline,
the supervising official would be held responsible for sharing the compensation.
Thereafter, thorough investigations would be permanently abolished,
and those who improperly requested them would be punished.
In the 17th year,
the Board of Revenue compiled the accumulated arrears of money and grain taxes, as well as the 'loss and wastage' and miscellaneous funds, for various provinces.
Ānhuī and Shāndōng each owed over 4 million,
Jiāngníng and Jiāngsū each over 2 million,
Fújiàn, Zhílì, Guǎngdōng, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Gānsù, Hénán, Shǎnxī, Húnán, and Húběi accumulated arrears of over 1 million, hundreds of thousands, and tens of thousands, respectively.
The Emperor severely reprimanded the high officials for their ineffective supervision of collection,
and ordered the Board of Revenue to report in detail at year-end
the original, completed, and outstanding amounts for each province.
Among the provinces, Jiāngsū had the most unpaid taxes.
Governor Zhū Lǐ proposed a system for collection and compensation,
to be completed over several years,
to prevent new deficits.
However, subordinate officials continued to cover up and delay as before.
From the 2nd to the 18th year, Zhílì
accumulated arrears of over 3.4 million taels of silver
and over 140,000 shí of grain and other items.
Governor-General Nà Yàn-chéng memorialized requesting appropriate remission,
but an imperial edict severely rebuked him.
In Shāndōng, prefectures and counties owed over 6 million taels in new and old deficits.
One county alone had a deficit of over 60,000 taels.
Strict regulations were then established:
those with deficits of 10,000 taels would be sentenced to death with a reprieve,
and those with 20,000 taels or more would be immediately executed.
The deficient amount
was to be collected within a set deadline while under supervision.
Complete payment within the deadline would grant a commutation of the death sentence,
but they would be permanently disqualified from office.
Failure to complete payment by the deadline would result in execution without pardon.
Censor Yè Zhōng-wàn requested a clear arrangement of borrowings from provincial treasuries.
Hú Chéng-gǒng requested a rectification of various malpractices regarding deficits in Zhílì.
At that time, provincial treasuries,
due to urgent needs in prefectures and counties,
often made excessive borrowings.
These were not repaid for a long time,
leading to constant shifts and offsets,
and various malpractices arose.
Moreover, the names for shared contributions and allowances
increased daily,
and the burden on prefectures and counties became excessive.
Officials struggled to carry out their duties,
and deficits in regular revenues were inevitable,
which could not be prohibited even by severe laws and harsh penalties.
In the late years of Qiánlóng,
the empire was peaceful,
and public affairs were prosperous.
The funds in the Board's treasury
accumulated to over 70 million taels.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
wars were waged in Sìchuān and Húběi,
the Yellow River overflowed,
and major public works were frequently undertaken,
resulting in immense expenses.
Meanwhile, unpaid taxes increased monthly and annually,
and the stored reserves in granaries and treasuries
gradually depleted.
In the second year of Dàoguāng (1822),
Censor Luó Chén (羅宸) submitted a memorial on the collection of money and grain taxes in the directly-governed provinces.
He proposed imitating the system of salt and tea permits
to prevent embezzlement by officials.
The Emperor, deeming it troublesome,
did not permit it.
The positions of grain superintendent (liángzǒng) and treasury superintendent (kùzǒng) in zhōu and xiàn were abolished,
following the request of Censor Yú Wénquán (余文銓).
In the early years of Qiánlóng (1736-1795),
when zhōu and xiàn collected money and grain taxes,
the malpractice of excessive collection (fúshōu) was still rare.
Later, various abuses proliferated.
Initially, this was merely over-collection based on the measuring container (húmiàn),
but soon,
the practice of "discounting" (zhékòu) emerged.
For every dàn (石) of grain, several shēng (升) were deducted for spoilage,
gradually increasing to a five-tenths or six-tenths discount (wǔzhé liùzhé).
Eventually, only two dòu (斗) and five shēng (升) of the remaining grain were collected,
which afflicted the common people.
The court debated collecting at an eight-tenths discount (bāzhé zhēngshōu),
considering it a measure to limit excessive collection.
Grand Secretary Tāng Jīnzhāo (湯金zhāo) rebutted this in a memorial.
Censor Wáng Jiāxiàng (王家相) also stated,
"The proposal of an eight-tenths discount,
if implemented in the prefectures of Chángzhōu (常州), Zhènjiāng (鎮江), Jiāngníng (江寧), Huái'ān (淮安), Yángzhōu (揚州), Xúzhōu (徐州), etc.,
might be worth trying,
but in the heavy grain tax regions of Sūzhōu (蘇州) and Sōngjiāng (松江),
there would be numerous obstacles."
The discussion was thus dropped.
At that time, the wealthy southeastern regions
were half-ravaged.
Zhōu and xiàn not affected by warfare
also suffered from greedy officials who over-collected and forcibly discounted (fúshōu lèzhé),
leading to widespread popular resentment,
and frequent incidents of crowds attacking officials.
Zhōu and xiàn officials often used "resisting grain tax" (kàngliáng) as a pretext
to conceal their own malpractices of over-collection and forced discounts.
In areas like Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng in Jiāngsū (江蘇),
whenever tax exemptions or deferments (juānhuǎn) occurred,
clerks (shūlì) would often demand money from landowners,
calling it "selling barren land" (màihuāng).
Those who paid the money,
even with a bumper harvest, could still defer payment;
those who did not pay,
even in times of famine and poor harvest, would not be investigated.
An imperial edict prohibited both practices.
In Húběi (湖北), long-standing malpractices plagued the grain tribute (cáoyùn) system.
Governor Hú Línyì (胡林翼) submitted a memorial requesting the conversion of grain tribute to money payments and the abolition of customary fees (guīfèi).
This reduced the burden on the people by over 1.4 million qián (錢) and wén (文),
increased the national treasury's silver by over 400,000 liǎng (兩),
and saved over 300,000 liǎng (兩) in deposited silver.
An imperial edict commended him.
After the military campaigns (jūnxīng),
provinces like Sìchuān (四川)
implemented "borrowed collection" (jièzhēng)
to fund military expenses.
Yù Ruì (裕瑞) memorialized, requesting to persuade gentry and commoners
to pay a grain subsidy (liángjīntiē) and abolish borrowed collection.
Yīng Guì (英桂) memorialized:
"The system of paying money and grain taxes half in silver and half in copper cash (qián),
where officials still collected silver from the people,
with 2,000 copper cash counted as one liǎng (兩) of silver,
resulted in no silver being remitted for spoilage (hàoyín).
I request that for dìdīng (地丁) taxes that should be allocated,
official notes (guānbiao) be accepted,
but for hao xian (耗羨) surcharges not allocated,
actual silver still be collected."
The Board ministers (bùchén) found the method ambiguous
and requested adherence to the original regulations,
where both principal and miscellaneous money and grain taxes
would uniformly accept official notes.
However, local officials still collected actual silver
and remitted cheap notes to the provincial treasury (fānkù).
The Emperor ordered strict prohibition.
In the first year of Tóngzhì (1862),
a thorough investigation of money and grain taxes in the directly-governed provinces was conducted.
In the second year,
the Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng (兩江), Zēng Guófān (曾國藩), and the Governor of Jiāngsū, Lǐ Hóngzhāng (李鴻章), memorialized, stating:
"The excessive taxes in Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Tàicāng (太倉),
looking back,
were three times higher than in the Yuán (元) Dynasty,
and seven times higher than in the Sòng (宋) Dynasty.
Comparing them laterally,
they were three times higher than the adjacent Chángzhōu Prefecture,
four or five times higher than Zhènjiāng Prefecture and other prefectures in the same province,
and anywhere from ten to twenty times higher than in other provinces.
This malpractice stemmed from inheriting the official land (guāntián) rent quotas of previous dynasties,
leading to an uneven tax burden.
Since the early years of the dynasty,
after a long period of peace,
the country was prosperous,
which was rare in ancient times.
Therefore, after the middle years of Qiánlóng,
the system of full grain tribute (quáncáo) was maintained for several decades,
for no other reason
than the wealth of the people.
Then came the great flood in Dàoguāng guǐwèi (1823),
which severely depleted the vital essence of the land.
Yet, it barely held on for ten years.
After the great flood in guǐsì (1833),
no year was without famine,
and no xiàn was without deferment (huǎn).
The state's extraordinary acts of exemption and reduction (juānjiǎn kuàngdiǎn)
thus became an annual practice.
Board ministers, whose duty was to uphold the law,
naturally insisted on maintaining the official quota without reduction.
Frontier officials, whose duty was to pacify the people,
could not but resort to methods of covert reduction.
The first to implement this
were the former Governor-General Táo Shù (陶澍) and former Governor Lín Zéxú (林則徐).
Furthermore, the practice of officials advancing payments for outstanding popular debts (guāndiàn mínqiàn)
was merely shifting miscellaneous funds to regular funds,
shifting deferred payments to urgent ones,
shifting new debts to old ones,
or shifting silver to grain.
It was using official funds to complete official grain payments,
which would eventually either be exempted
or spread out among others,
all leading to irretrievable losses.
Therefore, past grain registers
must have the fictitious figures of advanced and outstanding payments removed
to obtain the actual collected amount.
The full grain tribute (quáncáo) for Sūzhōu was 1.6 million (dàn),
but it gradually decreased thereafter.
In the ten years after Dàoguāng xīnmǎo (1831),
after deducting official advances for popular debts,
seven or eight-tenths of the full quota was collected;
in the ten years after xī丑 (1841),
after deducting advanced and outstanding payments,
five or six-tenths of the full quota was collected;
in the ten years of Xiánfēng xīnhài (1851-1861),
after deducting advanced and outstanding payments,
only four-tenths of the full quota was collected.
Since the Taiping rebels (Yuè Nì) invaded Sūzhōu and Chángzhōu,
burning, killing, and looting,
the misery is indescribable.
Your humble servants have personally visited the newly recovered zhōu and xiàn,
where markets and towns are ruins,
and human habitation is sparse.
If the recovered areas are like this,
what about those not yet recovered?
To still demand a tax burden several times heavier than elsewhere,
even the previously rapacious officials
would find nothing left to exploit.
Upon careful examination of the annual grain figures,
in the ten years of Xiánfēng,
there was only one year with over one million (dàn),
and six years with over 800,000 (dàn),
all of which included over 100,000 (dàn) of official advances for popular debts.
Thus, in the year with the highest collection,
the actual amount paid by the people was no more than 900,000 (dàn).
The established facts are thus,
and the people's capacity is thus.
We only implore permission to reduce the grain quotas for the three regions of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Tàicāng.
Taking the seven years with relatively higher collections during Xiánfēng as a standard,
a compromise figure should be set.
The aim is to reconcile and recalculate it with the original quotas of the neighboring Chángzhōu and Zhènjiāng regions,
establishing a fixed quota.
Starting from the year of subsequent collection,
this should be permanently observed,
and no more advanced payments for popular debts should be allowed.
Henceforth, no false disasters should be fabricated if there are no floods or droughts,
to eliminate useless empty pretexts
and seek actual collection that is viable.
As for the reduction of the grain tribute in Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
it must begin by abolishing the distinctions of 'large household' and 'small household' (dàxiǎohù) as the root cause of clearing excessive collection,
and by reducing corrupt practices (lòuguī) as the means to prohibit excessive collection."
The decree was approved.
Earlier, Taicháng Qīng Pān Zǔyìn (潘祖蔭) and Censor Dīng Shòuchāng (丁壽昌) had jointly memorialized on tax reduction,
and both were sent to the Board for deliberation.
The reply approved a one-third reduction for Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
and a one-tenth reduction for Chángzhōu and Zhènjiāng.
Generally, the tax per mù (畝) in Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Tàicāng,
for the heaviest rates, was almost two dòu (斗),
and for the lighter rates, still one dòu (斗).
Successive dynasties repeatedly debated reviewing and reducing these,
but were often blocked by Board deliberations.
During Yōngzhèng (1723-1735),
following the request of Yī Qīnwáng (怡親王),
the full silver tax for Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng prefectures was exempted.
During Qiánlóng,
the excessive grain tax in Jiāngsū Province was again reduced,
but these reductions were in silver and did not affect grain.
Upon the issuance of this edict,
all the common people celebrated.
In the third year,
acting on the request of the Fújiàn-Zhèjiāng viceroy, Zuǒ Zōngtáng,
an imperial edict was issued for the eight counties and six markets of Shàoxīng Prefecture,
stating that regular and miscellaneous taxes
should all be levied and remitted according to their silver value,
and that all forms of apportioned donations and illicit fees be abolished.
It was calculated that the excessive collection of money was reduced by over 220,000 [qián],
and rice by over 360 dàn.
For the one subprefecture, five counties, and six markets of Níngbō Prefecture,
the excessive collection of money was reduced by over 104,000 [qián],
and rice by over 800 dàn.
In the fourth year,
the Zhèjiāng provincial governor, Mǎ Xīnyí, requested the elimination of excessive collections in Jīnhuá: over 150,000 strings of money,
and over 500 dàn of rice;
in Qúzhōu: over 100,000 strings of money,
and over 60 dàn of rice;
in Yánzhōu: over 60,000 strings of money,
and over 6,000 dàn of rice,
and over 80 foreign silver dollars,
and over 100 dàn of rice.
This was approved.
That year, Zuǒ Zōngtáng captured Húzhōu,
and in a memorial stated that the excessive collection of grain tax in the south was too high,
requesting a drastic reduction.
The matter was referred to the Board for deliberation.
A memorial in reply suggested that for the grain tax in Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Húzhōu,
the Jiangsu precedent be followed,
reducing the original quota by eight-thirtieths,
and also that the land tax regulations be thoroughly investigated,
with reductions made based on the severity of the burden.
All excessive collections and illicit fees
were to be abolished.
The rice and stone of the southern artisans
were not to be considered for reduction.
It was calculated that the original quota of white tribute rice, transit rice, and other monthly rice for the three prefectures was over one million dàn.
According to the eight-thirtieths reduction,
a total of over 266,000 dàn of rice would be reduced.
Guófān requested that the land and grain taxes in Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and other affiliated areas also be appropriately reduced uniformly,
but this was not permitted.
Since the Qiánlóng and Jiāqìng reigns,
prefectures and counties, when collecting money and grain,
often privately converted prices,
with one dàn sometimes converted to as much as twenty thousand qián.
During the Xiánfēng period,
Hú Línyì first set the standard for collecting grain tax:
each dàn was not to exceed six thousand qián.
Later, Shāndōng also set the collection at six thousand qián per dàn.
Jiāngsū set it at four thousand five hundred qián for those who paid within the year,
and five thousand qián for those who paid outside the year.
Jiāngxī collected three thousand four hundred qián.
Hénán converted each dàn to three liǎng of silver.
Ānhuī to two liǎng and two qián.
Excessive collection of grain tax
had a long history.
Both river transport and sea transport
had allowances.
In Jiāxīng Prefecture,
for one dàn of grain collected,
there were allowances exceeding seven qián.
Furthermore, when collecting grain tax,
there was customarily a "grain surplus,"
the amount of which varied,
largely depending on the wealth or poverty of the district.
Historically, both actual grain and converted currency were collected,
but the excessive collection in converted currency
was even more severe than that in actual grain.
Since the official quotas were reduced and the converted prices fixed,
the problem of excessive collection gradually lessened.
Zhílì and Fèngtiān had many areas without registered grain,
known as "black land,"
which were either former Banner lands lost over time,
or newly reclaimed fields in mountainous corners or along the sea.
In the last years of Xiánfēng,
Bǎo Yún and others discovered over four hundred and forty qǐng of black land in Chāngpíng,
and initiated the trial of registering them for tax.
An imperial edict ordered the Zhílì viceroy, the Shèngjīng general, and the prefectural magistrates of Shùntiān and Fèngtiān to handle the matter uniformly.
In the early years of Tóngzhì,
landowners of black land were ordered to report to their respective government offices for tax registration,
and were allowed to own the land permanently.
Censor Chén Jùn memorialized:
“Apart from Chāngpíng in Zhílì and Fèngtiān,
those reporting for tax registration were few,
because local officials appropriated the collections for themselves,
delaying reporting,
and even resorted to suppressing and torturing those who reported their land.”
The Emperor dispatched high officials to investigate separately.
Grand Secretary Wō Rén memorialized on the black land tax registration,
stating that prefectures and counties feared the difficulty and sought temporary comfort,
requesting a clear declaration of rewards and punishments.
Soon, it was stipulated that if prefectures and counties discovered over twenty qǐng of hidden land, it would be considered excellent;
those who registered more land for tax would be rewarded.
Those who condoned hidden reclamation, or clerks and yamen runners who extorted bribes,
would be treated as derelict in duty.
Those scoundrels who falsely claimed to be commissioners
and extorted money
would be severely punished according to regulations.
At the beginning of Dézōng’s reign,
Xīnjiāng was recovered,
and coastal defenses were strengthened.
National expenditures increased daily.
The Board of Revenue presented a policy for rectifying money and grain,
which generally stated:
“Tracing back to the suppression of the long-haired rebels,
nearly twenty years have passed,
and regular and miscellaneous money and grain
should gradually return to their original quotas.
However, an examination of the total amount of regular and miscellaneous taxes levied
shows an annual total of over 34 million liǎng,
while the actual collection is only 1.45 million liǎng.
Such is the deficit in taxes.
Wealth is neither with the state
nor with the people,
but largely embezzled by corrupt officials and venal clerks.
In summary,
there are five abuses: first, inaccurate reporting of wasteland;
second, inaccurate reporting of disasters;
third, fabricating collection and arrears;
fourth, collecting and not remitting;
fifth, delaying transfers.
It is calculated that in recent years, the shortfall in tax collection
is highest in Ānhuī and Jiāngníng in Jiāngsū,
followed by Sūzhōu and Jiāngxī,
and then Hénán.
In many cases, less than five-tenths of the expected amount is collected,
and even in the lesser cases, there is a deficit of one to two-tenths.
It is requested that all viceroys, governors, and provincial administration commissioners be ordered to earnestly rectify these issues
to enrich state revenues.”
An imperial edict approved the request.
However, throughout the Qīng dynasty,
these abuses could never be entirely eradicated.
In the twentieth year,
the war between China and Japan
resulted in an indemnity of 200 million [liǎng] for military expenses.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Boxer Rebellion caused disaster,
and another 450 million [liǎng] was paid to various nations for military expenses.
Subsequently, training new armies,
promoting education,
and establishing police forces
required even more funds,
mostly raised locally.
Sìchuān, due to remitting indemnities,
levied additional donations based on land tax,
and also had new indemnity donations.
The Two Jiāngs, Fújiàn, Zhèjiāng, Húběi, Hénán, Shǎnxī, and Xīnjiāng, in addition to the customary land and grain taxes,
had "indemnity donations,"
“restoration of money value,”
“restoration of corvée services,”
and “increased collection of wastage fees.”
Although the names differed,
they were in fact not much different from increased taxation.
In total, the national tax quotas that can be verified were: at the end of Shùnzhì's reign,
an annual collection of over 21.5 million liǎng of silver
and over 6.4 million dàn of grain;
in the middle of Kāngxī's reign,
an annual collection of over 24.4 million liǎng of silver
and over 4.3 million dàn of grain;
at the beginning of Yōngzhèng's reign,
an annual collection of over 26.3 million liǎng of silver
and over 4.7 million dàn of grain;
at the end of Gāozōng's reign,
an annual collection of over 29.9 million liǎng of silver
and over 8.3 million dàn of grain,
which was considered the peak.
Second is the corvée system.
Initially, it followed the old Míng system,
assigning corvée based on the number of able-bodied men (dīng),
with a review every three years,
later changed to five years.
Each lǐ consisted of one hundred and ten households,
from which ten men with many dīng were chosen as chiefs (zhǎng),
and the remaining one hundred households were divided into ten jiǎ,
with ten men per jiǎ.
Each year, one lǐzhǎng was removed,
who managed the affairs of one lǐ.
In the city, it was called fāng;
near the city, it was called xiāng;
in the countryside, it was called lǐ.
The ten lǐzhǎng took turns fulfilling their duties,
urging payment of money and grain,
and handling public affairs,
completing a cycle in ten years,
with the order determined by the number of dīng,
and instructed to press for payment of money and grain from each household,
without burdening them with corvée.
The system of review
verified the actual number of dīng in the empire,
which was fully recorded in the registers.
Those aged sixty and above were removed,
and those sixteen and above were added.
As the number of dīng increased,
the taxes followed.
There were divisions of urban residents, rural residents, wealthy residents, tenant farmers, and sojourners.
Besides civilian dīng, there were also categories such as military, artisan, salt-boiler, tún field, relay station, and indigenous dīng.
In the directly governed provinces, the *dìngyáo* (poll tax and labor service)
had methods of division into three grades and nine categories,
the *yītiáobiān* (single-whip) system of collection,
the system where *dìng* (adult male units) were assigned according to land,
and the system where *dìng* were assigned according to other *dìng*.
Later, the system of assigning *dìng* according to land was adopted,
accounting for seven tenths of the total.
Across all directly governed provinces, the *yáolǐ yín* (labor service and *lǐ* system silver) amounted to over three million *liǎng*,
with occasional collection of rice and beans.
The lightest rate was 1 *fēn* 5 *lí* per *dìng*,
while the heaviest reached over 1 *liǎng*.
In Shānxī, it could be over 4 *liǎng*,
and in Gǒngchāng, up to 8 or 9 *liǎng*.
This was adapted to local conditions
and did not need to be entirely uniform.
The method of three grades and nine categories
originated from the previous Míng dynasty,
as did the *yītiáobiān*.
This method combined various silver payments, such as *jūnyáo* (equalized labor service) and *jūnfèi* (equalized expenses),
without distinguishing between silver or labor services,
and handled them all under the *yītiáobiān*.
All *dìng* and grain for ten *jiǎ* (tithings)
were aggregated in one *lǐ* (village unit),
and the *dìng* and grain of each *lǐ*
were aggregated in one *zhōuxiàn* (prefecture/county),
then to the *fǔ* (prefecture),
and then to the *Bùzhèng Sī* (Provincial Administration Commission).
The total *dìng* and grain of a province
were equally distributed for the province's labor services.
The *lǐjiǎ* (community self-governance) system was combined with the *liǎngshuì* (two-tax) system.
All *dìng* silver of a *zhōuxiàn* was remitted to the officials,
who would then recruit
to fulfill the year's labor services.
The people were not disturbed, and the tasks were easily completed.
Fixed quotas were established for clerks and yamen runners in various inner and outer government offices,
to be filled by good citizens.
Clerks and scribes were selected and assigned from various places,
later changed to selection through examination,
or through recruitment by public invitation.
Service terms were set at five years,
and those who did not retire were dismissed.
The *fǔ*, *zhōu*, and *xiàn* were allotted *zhīhòu* (attendants), *jìnzi* (gaolers), and *gōngbīng* (archers),
who were exempt from miscellaneous levies for corvée duties.
There were also *kuàishǒu* (fast runners), *zàolì* (yamen runners), *ménzú* (gate guards), and *kùzi* (treasury custodians),
all recruited according to established quotas.
Those who filled positions beyond the quota were called *báiyì* (unofficial runners),
and *báiyì* were prohibited.
However, as *zhōuxiàn* affairs were arduous and service needs numerous,
their assistance was essential,
and they could not be entirely abolished.
Regulations were also established for *zhōuxiàn* courier stations and bowmen,
and private conscription was prohibited.
People were forbidden from privately serving as brokers or wharf managers.
In areas along rivers,
it was customary to have labor conscription for protection.
In the 4th year of Shùnzhì (1647),
following the suggestion of Censor Tóng Fèngcǎi,
river embankment laborers were established in Zhílì.
In the 9th year (1652),
the river breached at Fēngqiū,
mobilizing tens of thousands of *dìngfū* (adult male laborers) from Dàmíng, Dōngchāng, Yǎnzhōu, and Hénán to stop it.
In the 12th year (1655),
river laborers were given increased wages and rations.
There were two systems for employing people in river works: one called *qiānpài* (assigned conscription),
the other called *zhàomù* (recruitment).
*Qiānpài* assigned laborers according to land holdings,
while *zhàomù* paid a certain wage.
Later, all established laborers
were given wages and rations,
changing from assigned conscription to recruitment.
Paying the recruited people
was an improvement over the ancient system.
In the 17th year (1660),
the abuses of *zhōuxiàn* privately assigning *lǐjiǎ* were prohibited.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī (1662),
the *jūntián jūnyì* (equal land, equal service) method was ordered for the *Sū* and *Sōng* prefectures in Jiāngnán.
Kē Sǒng, a supervising secretary of the Ministry of Revenue, stated:
"To levy taxes according to land
and assign service based on fields
is a constant and unchangeable law of all times.
However, as household populations grow and shrink differently,
and land acreage also varies,
the method of ten-year cadastral reviews was established,
where service shifts with land,
and registers change with the times,
so that the wealthy do not escape their duties,
and the poor are not burdened beyond their means.
I often observe the exploitation by officials
and the heavy burden of corvée,
the source of which is always unfair selection,
and accumulated abuses that have not been eradicated.
Inquiring into the land quota of a county,
and the number of *lǐzhǎng* (village chiefs) to be reviewed,
each *lǐ* having ten *jiǎ*,
each *jiǎ* having a certain amount of land—
those with much land alone fulfill one position,
those with less land jointly fulfill one position,
and the most scattered households are appended to the end of a *jiǎ*,
named 'flower households' (*huāhù*)—
this is the established rule.
All various labor services
are taken up by *lǐzhǎng* in rotation by *jiǎ*,
thus labor is not exhaustive and tasks are easily completed.
But in the *Sū* and *Sōng* prefectures alone,
though named 'selection of the affluent',
no investigation of land is conducted.
There are cases of those who have sold all their land being assigned *lǐyì* (village labor service),
and those with vast fields who are not assigned service at all.
Annual minor reviews
involve shifts and replacements,
leading to numerous abuses.
Land goes to households without service,
while service burdens households without land,
causing the poor to struggle to their bones and collapse,
and flee to other jurisdictions.
Now is the year for a major new census;
I request that the provincial governor be instructed to universally inform both prefectures
to assign service according to land,
and not to arbitrarily select based on empty reports,
to prevent the abuses of selling off the rich and burdening the poor.
Other abuses such as 'flower households' splitting accounts, fraudulent registration for exemptions, establishing households in other jurisdictions, and buying positions as scribes,
should be strictly prohibited and abolished."
This was submitted to the Ministry for deliberation and implementation.
In the 6th year (1667),
the burdening of people by *tíjiǎ* (conscription by tithing) in Jiāngxī was strictly prohibited.
The concept of *tíjiǎ*
was called *tíbiān* (repeated conscription) in the Míng dynasty:
after current year's collections were completed,
the next *jiǎ* would be conscripted
and held responsible for preparations.
In the prefectures of Guǎngxìn and others,
there were cases of repeated conscription of several *jiǎ*,
which was no different from an additional levy.
Based on the suggestion of Censor Gē Yīng,
it was abolished.
In the 7th year (1668),
regulations for providing laborers for post stations were established.
Wherever there was a post station,
laborers were established to provide transportation.
The quota was determined by whether the road was busy or remote,
and daily wages and rations were provided,
all included in the regular tax collection.
These laborers
were mostly recruited from the populace.
If the service demands were slightly heavy,
additional temporary hires were made.
Water post stations were similar.
In the 12th year (1673),
assigned conscription of river laborers in Hénán was suspended,
and silver was collected according to *mǔ* (mu, a unit of area)
to cover hiring costs.
In the 16th year (1677),
Jìn Fǔ, the Governor-General of River Conservancy, reported:
"When river projects were undertaken,
it was customary for *zhōuxiàn* to be compelled to assign and hire villagers,
where one unit of expense incurred ten.
Now that both rivers are being worked on,
requiring over 100,000 laborers daily,
assigned conscription was changed to recruitment,
and with much encouragement,
the work was completed in a few months."
Large-scale projects using recruited labor began with Jìn Fǔ.
In this year, local officials were prohibited from levying fines on the common people to repair city walls and moats.
In the 29th year (1690),
following the suggestion of Fó Lún, the Governor of Shāndōng,
it was ordered that the land of gentry and scholars in the directly governed provinces should be subject to the same labor service as the common people.
In the 51st year (1712),
an edict stated:
"The empire has enjoyed long peace,
and the population has increased daily,
but the land has not expanded.
The current *dìng* registers should be set as a permanent quota.
From now on, newly born individuals
will not be subject to money or grain taxes.
During cadastral reviews,
only the actual numbers will be checked and reported."
The court deliberated:
"After the 50th year,
newly born individuals in what is called a 'prosperous age'
shall never have their taxes increased.
Reviews shall still be conducted every five years."
The Ministry of Revenue deliberated:
"Deficient *dìng* numbers
will be replenished by newly added individuals in the same household;
if insufficient,
by relatives with a surplus of *dìng*;
if still insufficient,
by *dìng* from the same *jiǎ* with more grain tax liability."
In the early years of the Yōngzhèng reign,
an order was issued to the provinces to
incorporate the poll tax (dīngkǒu zhī fù) into the land tax (dìmǔ shūnà zhēngjiě),
which was collectively known as
"Dìdīng" (land-poll tax).
Earlier, in the final years of the Kāngxī reign,
Sìchuān and Guǎngdōng provinces had already implemented this system.
Now, approval was given to the request of the Zhílì Governor, Lǐ Wéijūn,
to collect the poll silver (dīngyín) along with the land tax.
For every tael of land tax,
two mace and two fen of poll silver were apportioned.
Thereafter, this was uniformly adopted across the directly governed provinces.
Thus, for every tael of land tax,
Fújiàn apportioned dīngyín ranging from five fen, two lí, seven háo to three qián, one fen, two lí;
Shāndōng apportioned one qián, one fen, five lí;
Hénán apportioned from one fen, one lí, seven háo to two qián, seven lí;
Gānsù,
Hédōng (east of the river) apportioned one qián, five fen, nine lí, three háo,
Héxī (west of the river) apportioned one fen, six háo;
Jiāngxī apportioned one qián, five lí, six háo;
Guǎngxī apportioned one qián, three fen, six lí;
Húběi apportioned one qián, two fen, nine lí, six háo;
Jiāngsū and Ānhuī apportioned from one lí, one háo to two fen, two lí, nine háo per acre;
Húnán apportioned from one háo to eight qián, six fen, one lí for every picul of land grain.
Thereafter, the poll service (dīngyáo) and the land tax became one.
After paying the Dìdīng,
the people had no other corvée duties.
However, in Fèngtiān and Guìzhōu, as the household registration was not yet settled,
the poll tax and land tax were still collected separately.
Furthermore, in Yángqǔ and forty-two other zhou and xian in Shānxī,
dīngyín was also separately assessed.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
Jiāngxī Governor Péi Wěidù memorialized to abolish the office of lìzhǎng (head of the li).
At that time, court officials remarked that in large and small yámens,
when official matters required items,
they would arbitrarily impose levies.
The zǒngjiǎ (head of the jia) would collude with corrupt clerks (jiān xū),
profiting from it.
All workers and artisans
were assigned zǒngjiǎ,
who designated those to serve officially
and rotated them in turn.
They also created a category called tiē chāi (substitute service),
where those unwilling to serve in official duties
were forced to pay silver,
which greatly harmed the people.
An imperial edict prohibited these practices.
However, with the passage of time, laxity arose,
and disturbances became even worse.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
another edict was issued to reiterate the prohibition.
It was also decreed that all annual repair projects,
such as the Grand Canal in Zhílì and Shāndōng,
the sea walls in Jiāngnán,
the dikes and weirs in Sìchuān,
and the Qìn River and Xiǎojīndī in Mèngxiàn, Hénán,
which were previously funded by donations levied on people's fields based on acreage,
and managed by lìjiǎ,
were not free from harsh exactions.
Henceforth, these levies were to be permanently stopped.
All construction work
was to be funded by government treasury (tángjīn).
In the tenth year,
Chuānshǎn Governor-General Qìngfù memorialized to repair the city walls of various prefectures,
requesting that zhou and xian officials donate from their integrity allowance (lián),
to jointly assist in the matter.
The emperor said:
"Officials' integrity allowances
may not necessarily be more than enough.
Though nominally aiding repairs,
it is in reality a levy on the common people,
which is an even greater abuse."
This was not permitted.
It was then decreed that for city projects in various provinces costing less than a thousand taels,
repairs should be carried out over several years.
For earthworks and small tasks,
civilian labor could be appropriately utilized,
while the rest would be paid for from public funds.
In the twenty-second year,
the method for corvée labor for dike repairs in Jiāngxī was revised.
For all earth dike construction,
the entire district would share the cost.
Laborers would be conscripted based on grain tax,
and officials would apportion them according to the dikes,
hiring workers for construction.
This was in accordance with the request of Governor Hú Bǎoxún.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Censor Dīng Tiánshù stated:
"Since the poll tax (dīngliáng) was merged with the land tax (dìmǔ),
all corvée services (chāiyáo) and military provisions
and there is no such thing as conscripted labor (lìyì zhī zhēng).
Recently, zhou and xian officials, for the reception of superiors
or the visits of colleagues,
often arbitrarily commandeered carts and boats.
Corrupt yámén runners (jiān yì) would use tickets to extort levies.
The official price issued
was less than half of the market price,
must be paid for at a fixed rate,
was completely ignored.
This resulted in merchants halting their travels
and commodity prices soaring.
Henceforth, unless handling major official assignments
or commissioned to transport official goods,
official prices shall not be reduced,
nor tickets issued for commandeering.
Violators shall be severely impeached and punished."
An imperial decree granted approval for this.
In the thirty-second year,
due to the war with Miǎndiàn (Burma),
and the transit through various regions,
the transport of men and horses
greatly relied on civilian labor.
A special grant of imperial silver was issued,
one hundred thousand taels per province,
to be distributed among the people.
The land tax and service duties
originally had established regulations.
Generally, the southeastern provinces
had heavy taxes and light labor,
while the northwestern provinces had light taxes and heavy labor.
In Zhílì, the imposition of corvée labor
was sometimes based on cattle and donkeys,
sometimes on villages,
and sometimes on household registers (páijiǎ hùkǒu).
Occasionally, it was also based on acreage.
However, the wealthy, having much land, could conceal it,
while the poor were levied on every fraction of an acre.
This was chaotic and disorderly,
uneven and unjust.
The most egregious among these
was the dichotomy between gentry and commoners.
Sometimes the gentry paid three parts and the commoners seven parts;
sometimes the gentry paid nothing and the commoners paid alone.
The common people suffered greatly and were displaced,
with no one to complain to.
At that time, there was a proposal to emulate the system of apportioning the poll tax to land,
reducing and equalizing corvée duties,
by levying one fen per mu of land,
equally shared regardless of whether one was gentry or commoner.
Zhílì Governor-General Yán Jiǎn strongly argued against it,
stating:
"As the proponents suggest,
to levy one fen of service silver (chāiyín) per mu of land,
the intention is to use the tax to achieve the actual effect of reducing corvée.
However, they do not realize that it merely adds a nominal tax burden through the corvée,
harming officials and afflicting the people,
and the abuses would still not be avoided."
Upon the submission of his memorial,
the proposal was dropped.
During the Xiánfēng era,
due to uprisings in Yuèxī (Western Guǎngdōng),
conscriptions and levies were frequent,
and reliance on civilian labor was unavoidable.
For every tael of grain tax,
service silver was levied at several times that amount, varying.
After the conflict settled,
the corvée duties remained heavy as before.
Moreover, while grain taxes might be remitted or deferred,
service silver was still collected even in lean years.
In the 4th year of Guangxù,
Zēng Guóquán, the Governor of Shānxī, memorialized that the devastation in Shānxī Province was difficult to recover from.
He requested a uniform reduction in corvée and levies to alleviate the people's hardship.
His memorial roughly stated:
"Shānxī Province, the right flank of the capital region,
communicates with Qín and Shǔ to the west.
Military levies, provisions levies, and tribute levies
travel in an endless stream on the roads.
The burden of supply and provision on the prefectures and counties
is such that they are almost always busy.
While carts and horses are provided by the common people,
the laborers are also demanded from the *lǐjiǎ* (neighborhood and hundred-household units).
However, the way it is handled varies among the different jurisdictions.
Some have the *lǐjiǎ* of an entire district annually share the burden,
drawing on collective strength to fulfill the service,
a method which is still fair.
Others divide the *lǐ* and *jiǎ* to take turns annually.
In the first year, it is allocated to the first *jiǎ* and first *lǐ*;
in the next year, to the second *jiǎ* and second *lǐ*.
The amount of corvée and levies varies from year to year,
which means the *lǐjiǎ* bear uneven shares of hardship and ease.
The powerful and cunning exploit the abuses of 'one *jiǎ* burdening another *jiǎ*, and one household burdening another household,'
selling their land at high prices
and verbally declaring their grain payments.
After three to five years,
they abscond opportunistically.
Consequently, their own *jiǎ* not only compensates for the ownerless grain
but also assumes the ownerless corvée,
causing endless harm.
The only solution is to reduce and equalize the corvée and levies,
which might offer some slight remedy.
Except for major levies requiring official passes and documents,
which are to be handled as per usual,
other instances are not permitted to impose arbitrary demands.
Should anyone extort carts and horses without authorization,
they shall be punished with their due crime."
This was approved.
In the 5th year,
Yán Jìngmíng again memorialized eight points: 1.
Reduce customary and borrowed levies;
The Judicial Commissioner (*Niè Sī*) should issue cart and horse tickets;
The comings and goings of lamas
must have a fixed schedule;
Ministers on imperial missions
should be prohibited from making excessive demands;
Strictly eradicate corrupt yamen runners and local ruffians;
Allow the common people to pay corvée money in lieu of service,
to be managed by the yamen itself;
Strictly ensure that post horses are adequately stocked and ready for use;
The provincial troops for campaigns and defense
should be given long wagons,
to be managed by the barracks themselves.
This was sent to the relevant departments for deliberation and implementation.
In the 8th year,
Zhāng Zhīdòng assumed the post of Governor of Shānxī,
and again stated:
"The policies that oppress the people in Shānxī Province
are not in taxation but in corvée.
According to precedent, the corvée money levied on each county,
for large counties, amounted to fifty to sixty thousand *mín* of copper cash,
and for small counties, at least ten thousand *mín*.
This was allocated according to land tax,
and officials colluded to share it.
In counties along busy routes,
'cart depots' (*chēguì*) were established,
where livestock from the four rural areas were rounded up,
and travelers' carts and horses were detained.
Sometimes a fee was collected year-round,
sometimes prices were extorted on the spot,
afflicting both residents and travelers.
It is now proposed to raise funds
and for the government to establish corvée bureaus,
strictly defining the regulations for corvée service
and prohibiting unauthorized expenditures by corvée officers."
The corrupt practice of *chēguì* was subsequently abolished.
Previously, ancestral imperial tombs
all had tomb households responsible for inspection, sweeping, and cleaning,
and were exempt from corvée as a matter of custom.
Also, for various temples dedicated to past worthies,
if they had sacrificial land,
their household and poll taxes were exempted.
For soldiers and civilians aged seventy or above,
one son was permitted to serve as an attendant,
exempting him from miscellaneous corvée duties.
In the 2nd year of Shùnzhì,
the fee for imperial artisan classes in the direct provinces was abolished,
and their artisan registration was also removed.
Regulations for gentry and scholars' exemptions were established.
First-rank internal officials were exempted from 30 *dàn* of grain tax and 30 poll taxes;
second-rank from 24 *dàn* of grain tax and 24 poll taxes;
those below them had their exemptions progressively reduced;
external officials had their exemptions halved.
In the 14th year,
the Board discussed and decided that exemption from poll tax
applied only to the individual himself.
In the 4th year of Yōngzhèng,
Luó Yīntài, the Governor of Sìchuān, stated that
in the various jurisdictions of Sìchuān Province,
poll tax was tied to land tax,
and requested the prohibition of gentry, *gòngshēng*, and *jiānshēng*'s exemption privileges.
The Board rejected this proposal.
It was then sent to the Nine Ministers for deliberation,
who decided that gentry and scholars were only exempted in person;
their sons, grandsons, and relatives who falsely claimed exemptions,
as well as those who privately established "scholar households" or "official households,"
were to be punished.
In the 1st year of Qiánlóng,
the order exempting *jǔrén*, *gòngshēng*, and *jiānshēng* from miscellaneous levies was reissued.
In the 37th year,
the quinquennial census and register compilation were suspended.
At that time, the poll silver was already incorporated into the land tax,
and newly born individuals were not subject to additional taxes.
The quinquennial census was merely a continuation of empty formalities,
without any benefit to actual governance.
At this point, based on Lǐ Hàn's suggestion,
it was thus abolished.
The following year,
Chén Huīzǔ requested that the poll silver from newly reclaimed civilian farmland be levied annually.
The Emperor deemed the memorial to be haggling over trifles with the common people,
not the way of beneficence and compassion for the people,
and decreed that henceforth, the management of poll tax and land tax in all provinces
should follow the old system,
and no changes should be rashly proposed.
First, the remission of taxes.
There were two types of remission:
gracious remission and disaster remission.
Gracious remission occurred
when there were national celebrations,
or imperial tours,
or military campaigns,
whereupon land tax was often remitted.
When Shìzǔ entered the pass,
he first exempted residents of the capital who had suffered from warfare from taxes and corvée for three years.
In the 2nd year of Shùnzhì,
because Shānxī had just been recovered,
half of that year's land rent was remitted.
In the 3rd year,
after Jiangnán was taken,
one-third of the tribute grain was remitted.
In the 8th year,
Shìzǔ began to rule personally,
restoring the extra levies imposed on nine provinces,
and remitting the fixed grain tax on 15,000 *qǐng* of wasteland in Shānxī,
as well as the fixed taxes on devastated land in Zhílì, Shāndōng, Hénán, and Shǎnxī.
Edicts of gracious and disaster remissions
were issued four times a year.
In the 10th year of Kāngxī, during his eastern tour,
he remitted that year's rent for areas along the imperial route.
In the 13th year,
outstanding accumulated land and poll taxes for the 8th and 9th years that were still owed by the people in various provinces were remitted.
At this time, the empire was largely pacified,
and an edict was issued remitting all accumulated taxes owed since the military campaigns.
In the 27th year, during his southern tour,
he remitted accumulated land and poll taxes in Jiangnán,
as well as military farm grain, reed taxes, rice, wheat, beans, and miscellaneous taxes.
In the 33rd year,
he remitted the land and poll silver and grain to be collected in the four provinces of Guǎngxī, Sìchuān, Guìzhōu, and Yúnnán.
In the 45th year,
he remitted the current year's accumulated taxes in Zhílì and Shāndōng.
For Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Gānsù, Jiāngsū, Zhèjiāng, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Húběi, Húnán, Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, and Guǎngxī provinces,
all outstanding land and poll silver from before the 43rd year of Kāngxī,
amounting to over 2.12 million,
and grain amounting to over 105,000 *dàn*,
were entirely remitted.
With a long period of peace,
the population gradually increased,
but land did not,
leading to concerns about people's livelihoods.
An edict declared that from the 50th year, the direct provinces
would have their taxes remitted in rotation over three years, completing one cycle.
Over these three years, an estimated 38 million *dàn* of land and poll taxes were remitted nationwide.
In the 56th year,
he remitted over 2.39 million taels of land, poll, military farm, and garrison silver collected in Zhílì, Ānhuī, Jiāngsū, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, Xī'ān, and Gānsù.
Of the tribute grain silver, over 490,000 taels,
and over 140,000 *dàn* of rice, wheat, and beans collected in Ānhuī and Jiāngsū,
half was remitted.
In the 57th year,
due to the campaign against Cèwàng Ālābùdān,
over 1.8 million taels of land and poll tax for the following year in Shǎnxī and Gān were remitted.
Shèngzǔ once read Emperor Wén of Hàn's edict on remitting land rent for the people,
and sighed:
"Remitting rent is the foremost benevolent policy of all time,
bringing real benefit even to remote valleys and desolate corners.
However,
unless the imperial court itself strongly promotes frugality,
this cannot be done."
Thus, during his sixty-year reign,
he repeatedly issued gracious edicts.
In some years, several provinces received remissions;
in some provinces, remissions were granted for several consecutive years.
The total amount remitted,
front and back, exceeded 100 million.
Cāngkù
The granaries,
in Jīngshī, there are fifteen.
Those belonging to the Hùbù and the Nèiwùfǔ
are called Nèicāng,
and Ēnfēng;
besides these, there are Lù Mǐ,
Nánxīn,
Jiù Tài,
Fùxīn,
Xīngpíng,
Hǎiyùn,
Běixīn,
Tàipíng,
Běnyù,
Wàn'ān,
Chújí,
Yùfēng,
and Fēngyì.
Those in Tōngzhōu
are called Xīcāng
and Zhōngcāng.
The grain transported by the various provinces
is stored here.
The zhíshěng have seven Shuǐcì Cāng:
Dézhōu,
Línqīng,
Huái'ān,
Xúzhōu,
Jiāngníng, each with one;
only Fèngyáng has two.
These are for issuing monthly rations to transport soldiers and for the provisions of resident and passing officers and soldiers.
From the provincial capitals to the fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn,
Chángpíng Cāng are built,
or sometimes Yùbèi Cāng are also established.
Shècāng are established in villages,
Yìcāng in market towns,
Qícāng in the Dōng Sānshěng,
Yíngcāng near the borders,
and Yányìcāng along the coast,
either for the convenience of the people
or for supplying the military.
Generally, the rice distributed from the Jīng and Tōng granaries
is called guānfèng
or guānliáng,
also known as Jiǎmǐ;
these two account for six-tenths of the total漕运 (cáoyùn).
One-tenth
feeds artisans,
and is called Jiàngmǐ.
One-tenth
was for the nine princes:
when the dynasty was established, six imperial kinsmen were enfeoffed as qīnwáng,
two were enfeoffed as jùnwáng,
and one qīnwáng was enfeoffed for Shìzōng's younger brother.
The descendants of these nine princes,
even those beyond the direct line,
also received noble titles,
which descended through generations.
This is collectively called Ēnmǐ.
These two account for one-hundredth of the Jīng granaries.
Thus, before Yōngzhèng,
the grain in the Tàicāng often had a surplus.
In the 28th year of Qiánlóng,
Hùbù Shìláng Yīnglián memorialized, saying:
"In recent years, due to frequent relief efforts, grain transport has been repeatedly intercepted.
When grain prices in Jīngshī were high,
inner granary rice was again released for sale at stable prices,
and reserves gradually dwindled.
I request to open up donations for gòngjiān (tribute students) in the rice-producing regions of Húguǎng, Jiāngxī, Jiāngnán, and Zhèjiāng,
to collect actual grain,
and store it separately once enough is collected.
In years when grain transport is intercepted,
the same amount should be transported to the Jīng granaries in the following year as replenishment."
The Jiǔ Qīng deliberated and approved it,
but it was soon stopped again.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
bandits rose in Chuān and Chǔ,
and floods and droughts occurred alternately.
Artisans were twice as numerous as before,
and the descendants of the Nine Princes also multiplied.
After Xiánfēng,
there was again the rebellion of the Yuèkòu,
and transport routes were blocked,
further depleting granary reserves.
After the rebellion was quelled, the old system was somewhat restored.
For selling grain at stable prices in Jīngshī,
there were the Wǔchéng Mǐjú
and Bāqí Mǐjú.
The Wǔchéng Mǐjú began in Kāngxī.
In the 4th year of Yōngzhèng,
factories were added in the inner city,
and one factory each was added to Wǔchéng and Tōngzhōu.
In the 2nd year of Qiánlóng,
Wǔchéng was increased to ten factories,
and soon eight more factories were added in the four suburbs.
In the 9th year,
four factories were established under the four-route tóngzhī.
There were twenty-four Bāqí Mǐjú,
plus two bureaus in the left and right wings of Tōngzhōu,
all established in the 6th year of Yōngzhèng.
In the 1st year of Qiánlóng,
they were merged into eight bureaus,
but soon reverted to the old system.
In the 15th year,
it was ordered that the twenty-four bureaus handle affairs in left and right wings,
regardless of banner affiliation.
In the 17th year,
as rice prices had not stabilized
and there was the problem of forced purchases,
an edict ordered the two Tōngzhōu bureaus to be stopped.
Regarding the Chángpíng and Yùbèi granaries in the zhíshěng,
in the 11th year of Shùnzhì,
it was ordered that each dàoyuán manage them exclusively,
and submit a ledger to the board annually.
In the 17th year,
the Hùbù deliberated and stipulated that Chángpíng granary grain
should be sold in spring and summer,
and repurchased in autumn and winter,
generating interest at stable prices,
and distributed to poor households according to quantity in famine years.
In the 6th year of Kāngxī,
