Gānsù Xúnfǔ Liú Dǒu memorialized, saying:
"Stored rice may rot after many years;
I request to sell it and purchase new grain."
This was approved.
In the 7th year,
Shǎnxī Xúnfǔ Jiǎ Hàn again requested to sell stored grain for interest.
The Emperor decreed that "selling old and buying new was originally for the benefit of the people;
if interest is reported to the board,
it will instead burden the people,"
and ordered to stop generating interest.
In the 19th year,
an edict ordered Chángpíng granaries to reserve grain for relief in their respective zhōu and xiàn,
and Yìcāng and Shècāng to reserve grain for relief in their respective villages and towns.
In the 30th year,
the Hùbù deliberated and ordered that for donated rice in Zhílì,
large xiàn should store 5,000 shí,
medium xiàn 4,000,
and small xiàn 3,000;
later, it was ordered to double this storage.
In the 31st year,
it was stipulated that zhōu and xiàn stored grain
should be accounted for like regular money and provisions;
shortages would be treated as embezzlement.
In the 34th year,
it was stipulated for stored grain in Jiāngnán
that seven-tenths should be stored in the granary annually,
and three-tenths released for sale,
and this was to become a general rule.
In the 43rd year,
it was stipulated that officials whose zhōu and xiàn granary grain molded or rotted
should be dismissed but retained in office,
with a one-year limit to repay in full and be reinstated;
if not repaid within the year,
they would be relieved of office;
if not repaid beyond three years,
they would be convicted,
and their family property seized for compensation.
At this time, the amount of grain stored in zhōu and xiàn across the provinces was:
for large zhōu and xiàn in Shāndōng and Shānxī, 20,000 shí;
medium zhōu and xiàn, 16,000 shí;
small zhōu and xiàn, 12,000 shí;
for large zhōu and xiàn in Jiāngxī, 12,000 shí;
Jiāngsū and Sìchuān generally did not exceed 5,000 or 6,000 shí;
while Fújiàn currently had 270,000 shí of donated grain,
and Chángpíng stored another 560,000 shí;
Táiwān had the most donated grain and Chángpíng grain,
totaling over 800,000 shí.
It was ordered to reserve enough for three years of military needs,
and sell the rest for military pay.
In the 47th year,
it was stipulated that zhōu and xiàn officials who purchased and stored additional grain beyond the quota
would be allowed to do so.
However, if donated grain was underreported,
or existing stored rice was falsely claimed as donations,
and discovered later,
in addition to compensation from the supervising zhīfǔ,
the original reporting dūfǔ would also be jointly punished.
If an official privately lent granary grain to the people,
the amount embezzled would be treated as embezzlement by a custodian,
and the grain (shí) would be fully recovered.
In the 54th year,
it was stipulated that for gentry and commoners who donated grain,
according to the amount donated,
dūfǔ, dàofǔ, zhōuxiàn would separately award plaques,
and they would be permanently exempt from corvée labor.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng's reign,
due to the dampness in the south,
an order was given to change the storage ratio to one dān of rice for two dān of grain.
In the fourth year,
Gāo Qízhuō, the Governor-General of Zhè-Mǐn, submitted a memorial stating:
"The ever-normal granary system in Fújiàn province suffers from two major problems: First,
the transfer of accounts is unclear.
When officials hand over and receive,
it is all about the price without the actual grain,
and the price is not enough to cover purchases and replenishments.
Second,
the price for ever-normal sales is too low,
with each dān discounted by as much as one liǎng,
and some even less than one liǎng.
Although various prefectures and counties wish to buy and replenish,
they are helpless due to the insufficient price.
Cunning people seize this opportunity to profit,
often using high prices
to incite the poor,
desiring that the period for ever-normal sales
be earlier each year,
and the price for ever-normal sales
be lower each year.
I request that from now on, based on the market price of rice,
each dān be set at one liǎng two qián or one liǎng three qián;
for grain, it should be set at six qián five fēn or six qián.
The standard should generally be the ever-normal price after the autumn harvest."
The Emperor approved his words.
Soon after, it was stipulated that officials responsible for damaged rice and grain in unrepaired granaries of zhoū and xiàn
should be punished as if they had embezzled it,
and those from zhoū and xiàn with deficits should be dismissed from their posts.
They were ordered to personally recover the grain
within one year,
and those who exceeded the limit would be prosecuted.
In the fifth year,
it was decided that ever-normal granaries in each province
should be inspected by their respective fǔ and zhoū at the end of each year.
If spring loans were not repaid by October,
or if false reports were made,
they would all be impeached and punished,
and the full amount would be recovered.
Also, because in Fújiàn's ever-normal granaries, some prefectures and counties had both empty silver and grain stores,
and some had no grain but only the price remaining,
upon verification,
the officials of the deficient zhoū and xiàn would be replaced.
In the thirteenth year,
Fāng Bāo, a Grand Secretary of the Grand Secretariat, presented three proposals concerning ever-normal sales of granary grain:
"First,
for granary grain, seven parts should be stored and three parts sold annually.
If prices are high,
it requires detailed reporting and price setting,
meaning the poor cannot immediately benefit.
I request that each zhoū and xiàn be allowed to determine an official price at their discretion,
commence sales immediately,
and report the details afterwards.
Second,
south of the Jiāng-Huái region, the climate is low-lying and humid.
If the general rule of storing seven and selling three is followed,
it is feared that after several years of accumulation,
there will inevitably be several million dān of moldy and rotten grain.
Officials, fearing punishment,
often compel local households to accept spoiled grain.
I request that the Governors-General and Governors of the southern provinces be instructed
to inspect the quality of the stored grain,
and, according to local conditions and annual variations,
discretionarily determine the proportions for storage and sale.
In the five provinces north of the Yellow River,
if there is a poor harvest,
they should also not be restricted by the three-seven rule.
Third,
stored grain is subject to rat damage,
inventory checking incurs reductions,
movement incurs transport costs,
and sales and purchases at granaries require labor costs and consumption.
Even if there is a slight surplus from spring sales,
it is only enough to cover these expenses.
I request that Surveillance Commissioners and Prefects be instructed to inspect at year-end,
and as long as the quantity is not deficient,
they should not use it as an excuse to extort.
If the autumn purchase price is low,
and after deducting all expenses,
there is indeed a surplus,
it should be clearly reported to the superior authorities and stored separately
for use in lean years."
The proposals were sent to the board for deliberation and implementation.
In the third year of Qiánlóng's reign,
Nàsūtú, the Governor-General of Liǎng-Jiāng, memorialized regarding ever-normal sales, stating that the price only needed to be reduced by one or two fēn compared to the market price.
Èmǐdá, the Governor-General of Liǎng-Guǎng, also stated:
"The price for ever-normal sales
should not be drastically reduced.
For common people, every tiny bit matters.
If, during ever-normal sales, the official price differs greatly from the market price,
then unscrupulous merchants will certainly hoard in anticipation of higher prices,
and those common people who rely on it for daily sustenance
will all depend on official grain.
Granary reserves are limited,
and merchants will instead be able to manipulate the market,
which means the intention was to stabilize prices, but prices remain unstable.
It has always been the case that when goods accumulate, prices fall.
Since common people can buy official grain,
they do not entirely rely on merchants' rice.
Merchants, seeing that the official grain's discount is limited,
will also slightly lower their prices to encourage circulation.
I request that the price be reduced by only one-tenth of the market price,
then gradually reduced further,
stopping after a year.
This way, merchants will have no power to manipulate,
and the official grain will not be at risk of depletion."
Both proposals were approved.
In the seventh year,
an imperial edict stated:
"Previously, Zhāng Qú requested to sell grain at reduced prices.
In years of good harvest,
each dān was to be reduced by five fēn from the market price,
and in years of high rice prices, by one qián.
However, I consider that a reduction of only one qián in lean years
still makes it difficult for the poor to obtain rice.
Henceforth, Governors-General and Governors are to determine the appropriate reduction temporarily
and memorialize for an imperial decree.
If there are unscrupulous people buying cheaply and selling expensively,
they should be strictly arrested and prosecuted."
In the thirteenth year,
Gāozōng instructed the Grand Secretaries and the Ministry of Revenue:
"Recently, the quotas for ever-normal granaries have been increasing daily,
which hinders the people's livelihood.
Henceforth, the old quotas from the Yōngzhèng era should be adopted as the standard."
Soon after, it was deliberated that Yúnnán was not near waterways,
and Shǎn-Gān also served military purposes,
having no fixed quota previously.
It was requested that the current quotas be used as the standard:
Yúnnán 700,000 dān,
Gānsù 3,700,000 dān,
each with some excess.
Also, Fújiàn is surrounded by mountains and sea,
with difficult commercial transport;
Guǎngdōng has intertwined mountains and seas,
producing little grain;
Guìzhōu has no navigable waterways.
Storage should be abundant in all these regions,
so the current quotas were to be used as the standard:
Fújiàn over 2,500,000 dān,
Guǎngdōng over 2,900,000 dān,
Guìzhōu 500,000 dān.
For the rest, the old quotas from the Yōngzhèng era were to be followed:
Zhílì 2,100,000 dān,
Fèngtiān 1,200,000 dān,
Shāndōng 2,900,000 dān,
Shānxī 1,300,000 dān,
Hénán 2,300,000 dān,
Jiāngsū 1,500,000 dān,
Ānhuī 1,800,000 dān,
Jiāngxī 1,300,000 dān,
Zhèjiāng 2,800,000 dān,
Húběi 500,000 dān,
Húnán 700,000 dān,
Sìchuān 1,000,000 dān,
Guǎngxī 200,000 dān,
each with some excess.
The total accumulated grain in the nineteen provinces was over 33,700,000 dān.
Compared to the old quota of over 44,000,000 dān,
this meant a reduction in storage of over 14,000,000 dān.
From then on, the quotas in some provinces were not replenished when deficient.
In the twenty-third year,
a special edict ordered purchases to replenish the granaries.
In the thirty-first year,
when various provinces submitted their accounts,
reporting actual stored grain quantities,
only Jiāngxī, Hénán, and Guǎngdōng matched the quotas set in the thirteenth year.
Those that increased compared to the old quota were:
Húnán 1,430,000 dān,
Shānxī 2,300,000 dān,
Sìchuān 1,850,000 dān,
Guǎngxī 1,830,000 dān,
and Yúnnán and Guìzhōu both over 800,000 dān.
However, Zhèjiāng decreased by 2,200,000 dān compared to the old quota,
Fèngtiān by 1,000,000,
Gānsù by 1,400,000;
while Zhílì, Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Fújiàn, Húběi, Shāndōng, and Shǎnxī decreased by 200,000 or by 500,000-600,000 dān.
In the early years of the Jiāqìng reign,
Rénzōng repeatedly issued orders for procurement and replenishment.
In the fourth year,
an edict stated:
"The state established ever-normal granaries.
If they are not stored according to the quota,
and merely grain prices are kept in the treasury,
when there is a sudden need for rice,
how can silver meet the demand? "
He ordered all provinces to purchase and return grain to the granaries.
In the seventeenth year,
the number of ever-normal granary grains stored by the Zhèjiāng Division of the Ministry of Revenue totaled 33,508,575 *shí* and odd,
which was not far from the quota set in the mid-Qiánlóng period.
By the eleventh year of Dàoguāng,
Vice Censor-in-Chief Liú Zhònglín and Censor Biàn Shìyún successively memorialized, stating
that most prefectures and counties in the provinces only had the value of ever-normal granary grain, not the grain itself,
and even this value was inevitably misappropriated.
The Emperor ordered the Governors-General and Governors to investigate and deal with this strictly.
However, according to a memorial from the Ministry of Revenue in the fifteenth year,
the actual number of ever-normal granary grains in the various provinces
was still only over 24 million *shí*,
which was incomparable to the Jiāqìng period,
let alone the chaotic times during the Xiánfēng reign.
In the third year of Tóngzhì, an edict stated:
"In recent times, military affairs have been bustling,
and bandits have risen everywhere.
The places they reach are often captured due to exhausted provisions.
The reason for this is that various prefectures and counties arbitrarily misappropriated funds,
leaving nothing to rely on in times of crisis.
Henceforth, the ever-normal granaries in all provinces
will be the responsibility of the Governors-General and Governors to seriously rectify. "
By the early Guāngxù reign,
Zhílì, Hénán, Shǎnxī, and Shānxī suffered successive droughts,
and the number of famine victims dying daily approached ten thousand.
In the fourth year,
Censor Cuī Mùzhī,
and in the eighth year,
Censor Wū Chúnhé,
again successively requested the planning and management of granary grains,
whereupon the various Governors-General and Governors began to pay slightly more attention.
The community granaries (*shècāng*) and benevolent granaries (*yìcāng*)
originated in the eighteenth year of Kāngxī.
The Ministry of Revenue approved the establishment of community granaries in villages
and benevolent granaries in market towns,
with locals publicly elected
to replace old grain with new.
Loans were made in spring,
and repaid after the autumn harvest,
with an interest of one *dǒu* per *shí* of grain.
At the end of the year, prefectures and counties would report the accounts to their superiors and then to the Ministry.
In the sixtieth year,
Zhū Shì, dispatched as the Left Censor-in-Chief of Shānxī, memorialized requesting the establishment of community granaries in Shānxī.
An edict stated:
"Previously, Lǐ Guāngdì memorialized concerning community granaries,
and I issued an edict saying that it was easier said than done.
After a few years of implementation,
it indeed bore no results.
Zhāng Bóxíng also memorialized about the benefits of community granaries,
and I ordered him to temporarily implement it in Yǒngpíng.
Whether it was effective or not
has not been reported to this day.
For the establishment of community granaries,
it is essential to select solid and reliable local people to oversee the affairs.
Since these individuals are not officials,
who will be dispatched to urge repayment
when the borrowed rice is due for return?
Even in years of abundant harvest,
repayment is difficult,
let alone in lean years?
Initially, the grain of the common people is deducted and stored,
with no one guarding it.
When the stored rice becomes depleted,
those in charge will inevitably have to compensate,
thus rendering the common people's rice useless,
and the person in charge is unjustly ruined and made to compensate.
The method of community granaries
is only suitable for small towns and villages.
If implemented by officials,
it will be of no benefit to the people.
Now Zhū Shì again requests this;
let him reside in Shānxī for a long time
and encourage its trial implementation. "
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
an edict was issued to Grand Coordinator Yáng Zōngrén of Húguǎng, Governor Nàqíka of Húběi, Governor Wèi Tíngzhēn of Húnán, and others:
"The previous order to establish community granaries
was fundamentally for the people's benefit.
Soliciting donations must await a prosperous year;
if it is a lean year,
the deadline should be extended.
All regulations
should not involve officials,
so that community granaries do not immediately become official granaries.
Yet now, each prefecture and county is ordered that for every *liǎng* of regular tax due,
one *shí* of community granary grain must be added.
It is heard that the current market price of grain in Chǔ province varies from four to five *qián*.
How is this different from adding four or five *qián* of 'fire loss' tax on top of one *liǎng* of regular tax? "
Soon it was deliberated and decided: Prefectural and county officials were only to supervise.
Methods of encouraging and rewarding donations
ranged from red envelopes and successively increasing plaques to being decorated as an eighth-rank official.
If the chief and deputy directors managed for ten years without fault,
they would also be granted the decoration of an eighth-rank official.
Regarding the method of collecting interest:
For every *shí* of original grain borrowed,
two *dǒu* of interest would be collected in winter.
For minor shortfalls, it would be halved;
for major shortfalls, it would be entirely waived,
only the original grain being collected.
After ten years,
if the interest doubled the principal,
only one additional interest would be collected.
In the third year,
following the request of Governor Hé Tiānpéi of Jiāngsū,
only five matters concerning community granaries were promulgated: One,
relief loans should all be recorded in pre-compiled household registers;
two,
besides the chief and deputy directors, another substantial person should be elected to generally manage the affairs;
three,
prefectural and county officials were not allowed to interfere with receipts and disbursements;
four,
the necessary paper and brushes
must be solicited through voluntary contributions,
or officials could allocate penalty funds for use;
five,
when stored grain accumulated sufficiently,
it should be sold at a reduced price between summer and autumn,
and replenished at market price after the autumn harvest.
In the fifth year,
due to deficits in the Húguǎng community granaries,
an edict stated:
"In recent years, among the Governors-General and Governors who exerted the most effort in managing community granaries,
was only Grand Coordinator Yáng Zōngrén of Húguǎng.
Now, according to Fúmǐn's audit,
it is only known that the original reported amount was very large,
but what is currently stored is meager.
I believe implementing this method is truly difficult.
My Holy Ancestor Rén-dì deeply understood this,
which is why Lǐ Guāngdì's request was not granted,
and Zhāng Bóxíng's temporary implementation was immediately halted.
For the wealthy people have no need of granaries,
thus they are reluctant to contribute,
while the poor have no surplus grain to contribute.
As for prefectural and county officials,
how many can be truly dedicated?
If the deficit in Húguǎng
was due to private use by prefectural and county officials,
they must be strictly pursued and made to compensate.
If the people originally did not hand over grain to the granaries,
or if the amount handed over did not match the original report,
ordering them to fully pay the amount
might be beyond their capacity,
so it needs to be handled with discretion. "
In the sixth year,
Shìzōng issued an edict stating:
"Previously, Yuè Zhōngqí requested to reduce five *fēn* per *liǎng* from the additional two *fēn* 'fire loss' tax collected throughout the province.
This amount was to be temporarily collected
and issued to the people to buy grain,
which would be stored in community granaries.
Once the amount was sufficient, the reduction would be implemented.
This was a method of encouraging contributions implicitly embedded within the temporary collection of 'fire loss' taxes that needed to be deliberated.
In reality, the 'fire loss' tax that should be deliberated
is the direct wealth of the common people,
and the granary storage bought and stored on behalf of the people
is the accumulation contributed by the common people themselves.
However, the officials of Shǎnxī province believed that what was stored by the officials
was official property,
and thus the clerks managing its receipts and disbursements
engaged in abuses of forced purchase and forced lending.
Now, it is specifically announced
and engraved on stone for promulgation:
If any local official acts as before,
they shall be punished for disrupting state governance and harming the people's livelihood. "
In the 4th year of Qiánlóng,
the Ministry of Revenue approved the memorial by Zhāng Kǎi, the巡撫 of Shǎnxī, establishing regulations for community granaries (shècāng): First,
the community head (shèzhǎng) was to be replaced every three years.
Second,
when lending in spring, half the grain should be reserved,
to guard against autumn shortages.
Third,
repayment was limited to within the same year.
Fourth,
the names and grain amounts of borrowing households were to be publicized.
Fifth,
local officials were ordered to inspect and be accountable for shared compensation.
In the 5th year,
it was decided that for community grain in Shǎnxī and Gānsù that belonged to the populace,
the people could choose their own chief and deputy granary managers.
For grain that was part of the five fen retained from the additional two hao tax as community grain,
local officials were held responsible for its management,
and it was included in their accounts.
From then on,
prefectural and county officials regarded it as government property.
Whenever grain was to be lent out,
detailed reports had to be submitted layer by layer.
Even during critical periods before the new harvest,
if the superior's approval had not yet arrived,
the common people had no way to borrow and receive it.
Therefore, it was subsequently requested that prefectural and county officials, after the seal was closed each year,
determine appropriate lending periods.
They should simultaneously report it and
begin lending,
with the timing adjusted according to the early or late cultivation schedule.
The emperor granted approval.
In the 18th year,
Fāng Guānchéng, the總督 of Zhílì, memorialized, saying:
“Charity granaries (yìcāng) began with Chángsūn Píng in the Suí dynasty,
and by Zhū Zǐ in the Sòng dynasty, the plans were detailed and complete.
Although named ‘community’ (shè),
they are practically equivalent to ‘charity’ (yì).
The key is that the location is close to the people,
the people are familiar with the matter,
and what officials plan for the people
is not as good as what the people plan for themselves.
Therefore, they are managed by the people, not by officials;
preparation concentrated in cities
is not as good as widespread preparation in the countryside.
Therefore, they are stored in the countryside, not in cities.
Now, let all magistrates appropriately establish them in the four countryside areas,
using millet or sorghum as convenient,
and select chief and deputy granary managers,
without allowing yamen clerks to interfere.
Currently, the reported amount of donated grain totals over 285,300 dàn,
covering 144 prefectures, counties, and garrisons,
a total of 35,210 villages,
with 1,005 granaries.”
The emperor praised this.
In the 37th year,
the Ministry of Revenue deliberated and approved that
community granaries (shècāng) should still be managed by officials for receipts and disbursements.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng,
it was again approved that for receipts and disbursements of community and charity granaries (shè yì gè cāng),
they would be managed by the chief and deputy heads,
only reporting to officials for registration.
In the 5th year of Dàoguāng,
Táo Shù, the巡撫 of Ānhuī, memorialized, saying:
“If charity granaries (yìcāng) are to be free from abuses,
the only way is to allow the populace, after the autumn harvest, to donate according to their means,
to choose experienced individuals to manage them,
not to reduce sales,
not to exchange,
not to lend,
but to focus solely on storage,
to await famine relief distribution.”
This was implemented as proposed.
Later, during military campaigns,
all provinces abolished them.
In the 6th year of Tóngzhì,
a special imperial edict ordered their revival.
During the Guāngxù reign,
only those planned and built by Fēng Yùjì, the巡撫 of Shǎnxī, numbering over 1,600, were the most numerous.
As for banner granaries (qí cāng) in the Three Eastern Provinces (dōng sān shěng),
initially all stored 20 million dàn of rice.
Garrison granaries (yíng cāng) began in the 22nd year of Kāngxī.
At that time, granaries were built at various passes of Shānhǎiguān,
extending to Mò'ěrgēn in Hēilóngjiāng.
In the 30th year,
Jiāngníng, Jīngkǒu, and other places were ordered to each retain 100,000 dàn of tribute grain for storage.
In the 36th year,
an edict ordered that border garrisons and forts like Yúlín and other places all store grain.
In the 49th year,
as Zhènggān, Húnán, was changed from a battalion to a division,
3,000 liǎng of silver from the imperial treasury was allocated
to purchase grain for storage in granaries.
In the 54th year,
it was ordered that rice be stored in Mìyún and Gǔběikǒu.
In the 3rd year of Yōngzhèng,
grain was stored in Tuōlākù in Guīhuàchéng.
In the 47th year,
Guǎngdōng Tíbiāo various battalions and all divisions and brigades were successively ordered to store grain,
and subsequently, this was extended to Guìzhōu, Sìchuān, Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, and Hénán.
In the 11th year,
it was ordered that grain be stored in Xǐfēngkǒu.
In the 1st year of Qiánlóng,
river fleet (hébiāo) garrison granaries were established.
In the 11th year,
it was again ordered that Shāndōng river fleet establish them.
Salt charity granaries (yán yìcāng)
began in the 4th year of Yōngzhèng.
At that time, various merchants of Liǎnghuái donated 240,000 liǎng of silver
for purchasing grain and building granaries in Jiāngnán.
The Salt Censor Gá'ěrtài reported this,
and also submitted 80,000 liǎng of public affairs silver,
totaling 320,000 liǎng.
An edict awarded 30,000 liǎng to Gá'ěrtài,
and the rest was handled as requested,
bestowing the name
“Yán Yì” (Salt Charity).
Soon after, various merchants in Zhèjiāng also donated 100,000 liǎng of silver,
and the巡撫 Lǐ Wèi was ordered to build granaries in Hángzhōu.
In the 9th year of Qiánlóng,
Shāndōng ticket merchants were also permitted to follow suit.
Of the treasuries in the capital belonging to the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ),
the Directorate of Imperial Manufactories (Yùyòngjiān) managed them.
In the 16th year of Shùnzhì, it was reformed into Guǎngchúsī.
In the 18th year,
the Satin Treasury (duànkù), Silver Treasury (yínkù), Fur Treasury (píkù), and Clothing Treasury (yīkù) were separately established.
In the 18th year of Kāngxī,
the Tea Treasury (chákù) and Porcelain Treasury (cíkù) were added,
making a total of six.
Those belonging to the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù)
were the Silver Treasury (yínkù), Satin Treasury (duànkù), and Pigment Treasury (yánliàokù),
making a total of three.
Furthermore, the Ministry of Revenue Silver Treasury in Shèngjīng
stored gold, silver, currency, silk, pigments, and other items,
for offerings at the two imperial tombs,
and for salaries, provisions, and rewards for officials and soldiers in the Three Eastern Provinces (dōng sān shěng).
The treasuries of generals (jiāngjūn), deputy lieutenant-generals (fù dū tǒng), and city commandants (chéngshǒuwèi) in various provinces
each stored salaries and provisions for officials and soldiers,
and prices for grain sold from miscellaneous taxes and government estates.
The treasuries of the Provincial Administration Commission (Bùzhèngshǐsī)
stored silver from annual land taxes and miscellaneous taxes collected from various prefectures and counties.
The treasuries of the Provincial Surveillance Commission (Ànchásī)
stored silver and cash from fines for illicit gains.
The treasuries of the Grain Intendant (Liángdào)
stored silver from grain taxes and funds for post-station porters and materials.
The treasuries of the River Intendant (Hédào)
stored river conservancy funds.
The treasuries of the Military Preparedness Intendant (Bīngbèidào)
stored military funds.
For salt duties and various taxes managed by the Salt Commissioner (Yányùnshǐsī) via ministry envoys,
there were Supervisor's Treasuries (jiāndūkù).
For officials like Dao, Fu, Ting, Zhou, and Xian who concurrently managed such affairs,
there were Concurrently Managed Official Treasuries (jiān lǐ guān kù),
all storing treasury notes.

For treasuries of circuit intendants (fēnxún dào kù), prefectures (fǔ kù), independent subprefectures (zhílì zhōu kù) in strategically important locations, and subprefects (tóngzhī), assistant magistrates (tōngpàn) stationed in Miao territories,
the Provincial Administration Commission's silver was allocated and stored,
with the amount adjusted according to the size of the locality
and its distance from the provincial capital.
The treasuries of subprefectures (zhōu), counties (xiàn), and garrisons (wèisuǒ)
stored silver from principal and miscellaneous taxes in kind.
Retained amounts were disbursed as needed,
while transported amounts were sent to the Provincial Administration Commission's treasury.
For all treasuries, the annual figures for receipts and disbursements
are all compiled into registers and sent to the Hùbù to be inspected and verified.
The only exceptions are fines and confiscated goods, which are paid to the Xíngbù;
and funds for river works and military provisions, which are also managed by both the Bīngbù and Gōngbù.
Regarding the Hùbù's oversight of provincial treasury reserves,
there are five distinct categories.
The first is sealed reserves (fēngchǔ).
For example, the silver allocated to each Bùzhèngsī
is jointly sealed and stored by the Dūfǔ.
In urgent need,
a memorial must be submitted to request its use;
unauthorized use is punishable by beheading.
This regulation was established in Yōngzhèng’s fifth year.
Because Zhílì was near the capital,
it alone had no reserved storage.
For other provinces, the amounts ranged from 300,000 to 100,000,
divided into three grades.
Later, Zhílì also had such reserves.
However, for the Shèngjīng Hùbù Silver Treasury,
starting from Qiánlóng’s forty-second year, a sum of ten million was allocated from the capital
to be permanently stored.
In the forty-third year,
it was again ordered that the general concurrently manage it.
The second is divided reserves (fēnchǔ).
For example, the silver sealed and stored in provincial dàokù and fǔkù
is immediately issued when a zhōuxiàn has urgent needs.
At the same time, detailed reports are submitted to the Fānsī and Dūfǔ,
and each zhōuxiàn is still required to provide detailed reports on their expenditures
with the relevant cases for verification.
Later, for busy and complex zhōuxiàn,
funds were also allocated for storage according to the precedent of capital zhōuxiàn,
but without a fixed quota.
By Yōngzhèng’s eighth year,
the quotas for divided storage in provincial dào, fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn
were set, ranging from 300,000 to 100,000,
divided into four grades.
The third is retained reserves (liúchǔ).
For example, the silver retained in subordinate treasuries for direct expenditure,
when funds are allocated and issued,
is exempted by rule from being remitted to the Sī.
The fourth is remitted reserves (jiěchǔ).
For example, the Bùzhèngshǐsī treasury
stores the primary and miscellaneous tax silver remitted by fǔ, zhōu, xiàn, and wèi;
the Ànchásī treasury
receives fines and confiscated silver;
and the treasuries of the Jiāngjūn, Fùdūtǒng, and Chéngshǒuwèi,
and the Liángdàokù
receive silver for officials' salaries, military pay, and grain transport from various places.
The fifth is allocated reserves (bōchǔ).
For example, the Bīngbèidàokù in each province
annually stores silver for soldiers and officers allocated from the Bùzhèngsī or neighboring provinces;
the Hédàokù
annually stores salaries and provisions for soldiers and officers allocated from its own province and neighboring provinces,
as well as funds for annual repairs and emergency repairs;
and the annual required salaries and provisions for Yīlí,
the annual required new provisions for Tǎěrbāhātái,
the annual required station fees for Xīzàng,
the annual required copper capital for Yúnnán,
and the annual required lead capital for Guìzhōu
are all allocated from various provinces.
The Hùbù generally oversees these,
to ensure careful receipts and disbursements.
It orders each province to remit Dìdīng taxes to the department,
melting full-purity silver into yuánbǎo,
conforming to the standard weight (fǎmǎ) issued by the department.
Each ingot should be fifty liǎng,
without adding extra small drops of silver.
For all remitted provision silver,
the Bùzhèngshǐ personally, with the remitting official, weighs, seals, and signs it,
and instructs the treasury official to affix the seal.
It is packed into scabbards in the hall
and military tallies are issued.
Furthermore, for the handover of official funds and grain by zhōuxiàn officials,
the succeeding official compiles a receipt register and report,
which, along with the verifying official's sealed report,
is sent to the superior office with an added report,
and detailed requests are submitted to the department,
without exceeding the deadline.
When a Bùzhèngshǐ is promoted or leaves office,
a memorial is submitted stating that there are no deficits or misappropriations in the treasury reserves and grain.
The new appointee's receipt of these
is also reported in a memorial,
and a detailed report must be submitted within the prescribed period as usual.
For the handover by an Ànchásǐ,
the Xúnfǔ, in conjunction with the Fānsī, investigates, verifies, and submits a detailed memorial.
They also conduct periodic inspections,
requiring each Dūfǔ to personally inspect
the treasury funds and grain of the Bùzhèngsǐsī when they are reported and handed over,
and submit a sealed report.
The same applies to newly appointed Dūfǔ.
When the fǔ, zhōu, and xiàn treasury reserves and grain are reported,
the supervising dàodao and fǔ must personally inspect and report,
and are not allowed to delegate the inspection and merely obtain a report,
or to give advance notice of the date,
allowing for concealment.
As for the Hùbù Silver Treasury,
in Kāngxī’s forty-fifth year,
due to the large amount of silver stored,
an edict ordered that newly received silver each year be stored separately,
and when silver was needed,
the old silver was to be used in sequence.
In Qiánlóng’s forty-first year,
the Hùbù memorialized and obtained approval that for silver remitted to the capital from various provinces,
regardless of whether it was yuánbǎo or small ingots,
the zhōuxiàn, date, and silversmith's name must be engraved.
In Jiāqìng’s nineteenth year,
it was ordered that provincial silver remitted to the department
be handed over upon arrival.
In Dàoguāng’s twelfth year,
it was again ordered that officials remit to officials.
This was because previously, capital provisions and donated funds
were all delivered to the treasury by silver shops,
but this abuse was not easily eradicated.
In Tóngzhì’s third year,
the Hùbù memorialized and obtained approval that all silver delivered to the treasury by silver shops
must be full-purity silver,
with the silver shop's name clearly engraved on the ingot face.
If any malpractice occurred,
the shop would be fined ten times the original amount.
In Guāngxù’s fourth year,
it was again memorialized and approved that henceforth, Dūfǔ of various provinces and commanding ministers of various routes who come to the department to claim provisions
must follow regulations and submit a sealed voucher for collection,
which was to emphasize the importance of treasury reserves and prevent malpractices.
Record Ninety-Seven, Food and Money III, Grain Transport (Cáoyùn)
In the early Qīng dynasty,
grain transport policy continued the Míng system,
using tūndīng for long-distance transport.
Long-distance transport meant
that guā and huái transport soldiers' boats were ordered to go to various zhōuxiàn waterways to receive and exchange grain from the populace,
with an added cross-river consumption fee,
varying by distance.
The four granaries of Huái, Xú, Lín, and Dé still received grain transported by the populace,
as well as grain from transport soldiers' boats,
which was called "changing to exchange transport."
By the middle period,
the Huìtōnghé became blocked,
and the old Jiāolái waterway could not be quickly restored.
Various methods of using the Huánghé for transshipment were implemented, but not without problems.
Therefore, Xuānzōng adopted the proposals of ministers like Yīnghé, Táoshù, and Hè Chánglíng to revive sea transport.
Officials were selected to gather grain,
and merchant ships were hired from Shànghǎi to transship the grain to Jīngshī.
The people all praised its convenience.
River transport was thus abandoned.
River transport had costs for dredging,
costs for passing locks and crossing the Huái River,
and costs for expediting and warehouse transfer.
The emperor paid over a million in grain transport fees,
and the people below paid over a million in auxiliary fees.
The people's livelihood became increasingly difficult,
and the national economy grew poorer.
Sea transport, however, did not pass through the interior,
did not enrich many,
had no troubles of shipbuilding,
and no disturbances of recruiting laborers.
It benefited the nation and facilitated the people,
with no better plan than this.
When the maritime prohibition was lifted and
steamships became common,
grain from the southeast arrived continuously,
without waiting for official transport.
Consequently, grain transport was completely abolished,
and collection was converted to cash payments for grain (zhécáo),
which became an unchangeable policy.
This section on grain transport
begins with grain rations (cáoliáng),
followed by unhusked rice (báiliáng),
then superintendence of transport (dūyùn),
then grain boats (cáochuán),
then funds and grain (qiánliáng),
then performance evaluation (kǎochéng),
then rewards and relief (shǎngxù),
and concludes with sea transport (hǎiyùn).
At first, the grain tribute transportation (Cáoyùn) mostly followed the old system of the Míng dynasty.
There were Zhèngduì, Gǎiduì, Gǎizhēng, and Zhézhēng.
These four [categories]
formed the general principles of the grain tribute transportation, whether in kind or commuted to silver.
In the second year of Shùnzhì (1645),
the Ministry of Revenue (Hùbù) memorialized and fixed the annual grain tribute quota at four million dàn.
That which was transported to the capital granaries (Jīngcāng) was called Zhèngduì Rice,
with an original quota of 3.3 million dàn: Jiāngnán 1.5 million,
Zhèjiāng 600,000,
Jiāngxī 400,000,
Húguǎng 250,000,
Shāndōng 200,000,
That which was transported to Tōngzhōu was called Gǎiduì Rice,
with an original quota of 700,000 dàn: Jiāngnán 294,400,
Zhèjiāng 30,000,
Jiāngxī 170,000,
Shāndōng 95,600,
Afterwards, there were quite a few changes to commutation.
By the eighteenth year of Qiánlóng (1753),
the actual collection of Zhèngduì Rice was over 2.75 million dàn,
and Gǎiduì Rice was over 500,000 dàn.
Those amounts temporarily withheld, remitted, or deferred were not included in these figures.
Besides grain tribute from Shāndōng and Hénán, there were also wheat (xiǎomài) and black beans (hēidòu).
Both provinces generally collected Zhèngduì.
The commuted-for-loss wheat (gǎihàomài) was 69,561 dàn, 8 dòu, 4 shēng and odd,
and beans were 208,199 dàn, 3 dòu, 1 shēng and odd,
all transported to the capital granaries.
Black beans were collected by commutation from millet (sùmǐ),
with no fixed quota.
All Gǎizhēng required a special imperial edict;
there was no standing rule.
There were four categories of Zhézhēng: called Yǒngzhé,
called Huīshímǐzhé,
called Jiǎnzhēng,
and called Mínzhéguānbàn.
For permanently commuted grain tribute (Yǒngzhé Cáoliáng),
Shāndōng and Hénán each had 70,000 dàn,
commuted at a rate of six qián to eight qián of silver per dàn, varying;
Jiāngsū had over 106,492 dàn,
commuted at a rate of six qián of silver per dàn, varying;
Ānhuī had over 75,961 dàn,
commuted at a rate of five qián to seven qián of silver per dàn, varying;
Húběi had 32,520 dàn,
Húnán had over 5,212 dàn each,
with each dàn commuted at seven qián of silver.
The silver equivalent was all reported to the Ministry of Revenue under the category of land tax (Dìdīng).
For commuted ash and stone (Huīshí Gǎizhé),
Jiāngsū had 29,424 dàn,
Zhèjiāng had 18,653 dàn.
In intercalary years, an additional 4,015 dàn were commuted,
at one liǎng and six qián of silver per dàn,
to be used by the Ministry of Public Works (Gōngbù) for procuring ash and stone.
This began in the seventeenth year of Shùnzhì (1660).
The following year,
the senior officials of the three provinces of Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, and Jiāngxī were ordered
that all commuted payments (gǎizhé) were only allowed to be collected at the market price.
If anyone used the pretext of grain tribute collection
to extort excessively,
they would be investigated and impeached.
Moreover, due to the heavy labor service and taxes (chāifù) in the four prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, Chángzhōu, and Zhènjiāng,
each dàn of grain tribute was commuted to one liǎng of silver.
The various additional charges that accompanied the grain tribute, such as those for mats, timber, and the like (qīngjī xímù zèngjié děng yín),
were still collected as commuted-for-loss rice (hàomǐ),
and the rice provided for military travel allowances (jūnxíng yuèzèng hào děng mǐ)
was also commuted at the prevailing market price.
In the eighth year of Kāngxī (1669),
it was stipulated that Hénán's grain tribute should be commuted at eight qián of silver per dàn.
In the ninth year (1670),
due to disasters in the two prefectures of Jiāxīng and Húzhōu in Zhèjiāng,
each dàn was commuted at one liǎng.
In the fifty-eighth year (1719),
it was re-approved that for prefectures and counties in Hénán near waterways,
out of the eight qián of silver per dàn for the fixed grain tribute,
one qián and five fēn would be saved,
still to be paid by the common people.
The remaining six qián and five fēn
were to be collected in kind and transported.
As for prefectures and counties farther from or not near waterways,
the fixed grain dàn
would still be collected at eight qián of silver according to the old rule,
with one qián and five fēn remitted to the Ministry,
and the remainder handed over to the Grain Intendant (Liángdào) for purchasing grain in kind.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng (1723),
due to disasters in the prefectures and counties belonging to Jiāxīng and Húzhōu,
an edict ordered that grain tribute be collected half in kind and half commuted,
with the commuted price following the example of the ninth year of Kāngxī.
In the sixth year (1728),
it was decided that prefectures and counties in Hénán somewhat distant from waterways
should all collect in kind.
However, for the prefectures of Nányáng and Rǔníng,
the three counties of Lúshì, Sōng, and Yǒngníng in Hénán Prefecture, and the two prefectures of Guāngzhōu and Rǔzhōu and their subordinate counties,
as well as Língbǎo and Wénsī, which were farthest from waterways,
due to their long distance and difficult transport,
a total of over 15,062 dàn of rice was proportionally reduced,
exempting them from handling and transporting it.
This amount was allocated to the five counties of Nèihuáng, Jùn, Huá, Yífēng, and Kǎochéng to assist in the payment,
and deducted from the Dìdīng silver of these five counties to complete the grain tribute payment.
According to the Ministry's price of eight qián per dàn,
six qián and five fēn were used for transportation,
and the saved one qián and five fēn
were collected and remitted to the Grain Intendant as a supplementary fund.
For the prefectures of Nányáng and Rǔníng and their subordinate areas,
eight qián of silver per dàn were remitted to the Provincial Treasurer (Bùzhèngsī)
to offset the Dìdīng silver amount of the five counties of Jùn, Huá, etc.
This is what was called Jiǎnzhēng (reduced collection).
In the second year of Qiánlóng (1737),
due to the large-scale dredging of the Grand Canal,
the grain tribute of the counties of Shānyáng, Yánchéng, Fùníng in Huái'ān Prefecture,
and Jiāngdū, Gānquán, Gāoyóu, Bǎoyīng in Yángzhōu Prefecture in Jiāngsū,
was commuted to one liǎng of silver per dàn.
Later, the two counties of Hǎizhōu and Gànyú also followed suit.
The black beans that Shāndōng and Hénán had previously commuted to collect
were insufficient for supply,
so Hénán commuted an additional 20,000 dàn,
and Shāndōng an additional 40,000 dàn.
In the third year (1738),
the Governor-General (Zǒngdū) of Húguǎng, Dépèi, stated that Píngjiāng in Húnán was over five hundred lǐ from a waterway,
and requested that it be commuted to silver.
He proposed allocating the responsibility to Héngyáng and Xiāngtán to purchase and transport on its behalf,
which was approved.
In the seventh year (1742),
as the commuted price of eight qián for Lúxī in Jiāngxī was insufficient for purchase,
it was decided that from then on, in August of each year, silver would be borrowed from the Provincial Treasurer's (Sīkù) treasury and allocated to the county for purchase,
and silver would be collected at the purchase price for repayment.
Later, Jiādìng, Bǎoshān, Hǎizhōu, Gànyú in Jiāngsū,
Níngguó, Jīngdé, Tàipíng, Yīngshān in Ānhuī,
and Tōngshān, Dāngyáng and other prefectures and counties in Húběi
all followed this precedent.
In the eleventh year (1746),
it was stipulated that for the fixed millet collection in Xiángfú and other forty prefectures and counties in Hénán,
10,000 dàn of wheat would be commuted annually,
and collected and transported to Tōngzhōu along with the grain tribute rice and black beans.
In the sixteenth year (1751),
since the imperial army (jīngshī guānbīng) raised horses and camels,
black beans were needed.
From the tenth year of Yōngzhèng (1732), the two provinces of Hénán (Yù) and Shāndōng (Dōng)
had successively commuted and collected [black beans] from the grain tribute millet.
The annual quota of black beans to be remitted was over 209,000 dàn.
Each province was to consider and commute an additional 10,000 to 20,000 dàn of black beans.
It was then decided that Shāndōng would collect 30,000 dàn,
and Hénán 20,000 dàn,
from their fixed millet collection.
The corresponding amount would be deducted.
The one qián and five fēn of silver saved for transport expenses would also be collected.
In the eighteenth year (1753),
the Vice Minister of Granaries (Cāngchǎng Shìláng), Hènián, stated:
"Currently, there are over 600,000 dàn of black beans in the capital granaries,
sufficient for three years' supply.
I request that starting from next year,
of the black beans to be transported by Hénán and Shāndōng,
half be commuted to millet as appropriate,
and stored separately in the capital and Tōngzhōu granaries.
This way, there will be no risk of the beans becoming damp or moldy,
and the price of millet will also stabilize."
This was approved.
In the twenty-sixth year (1761),
since Qīnghé, Táoyuán, Sùqiān, and Shùyáng in Jiāngsū did not produce rice or millet,
it was ordered that from then on, silver from the Provincial Treasurer's treasury would first be used,
to purchase [grain] at market price,
and the people would pay silver to reimburse the funds.
This was called Mínzhéguānbàn (people commute, officials handle).
Later, Fùníng, Jīngdé, Tàixīng, Níngguó, Tàipíng, and Yīngshān counties all followed suit.
An edict in the twenty-first year (1756) stated:
"Grain tribute is annually delivered to the imperial granary (Tiānyǔ),
and traditionally collected in kind.
Forcibly collecting commuted silver
has always been strictly prohibited.
Currently, with a year of abundant harvest and cheap grain,
if the common people are made to sell their grain at low prices
to pay commuted silver,
then the people's year-long toil
will result in their meager gains
largely being sold to pay the government.
Their limited reserves
will be subject to endless exploitation,
which truly harms the people greatly.
Therefore, it is ordered that senior officials in provinces with grain tribute
instruct their subordinates to collect grain and rice
entirely in kind,
and not to allow forced commutation to create abuses.
If there are those who seek personal profit and oppress the people,
they shall be severely impeached based on the facts."
However, prefectures and counties often still used the pretext of commutation to overcharge.
Although there were clear decrees, it was impossible to prohibit it.
Initially,
the grain tribute (cáoliáng) from each province was changed to official collection and official exchange.
The supplementary allowances had different names:
in Shāndōng and Hénán it was called rùnhào,
in Jiāngsū and Ānhuī it was called cáotiē,
in Zhèjiāng it was called cáojié,
in Jiāngxī and the two Hú provinces it was called tiēyùn.
The amounts varied,
and were levied along with the grain.
They were all listed on easy-to-understand forms (yìzhī yóudān),
and those who privately appropriated or diverted them were punished.
Later, in Jiāngnán, for every hundred shí of grain,
more than one hundred liǎng were privately withheld,
and in Zhèjiāng, up to thirty-odd liǎng.
Liú Cháojùn, the Grain Intendant (Liángdào), was impeached for embezzling over twelve thousand liǎng in cáotiē,
and the Supervising Secretary (Gěishìzhōng) Xú Xùlíng also memorialized about the abuses of the zènghào.
However, corrupt officials (tānguān wūlì),
following entrenched practices,
could not be restrained.
In the tenth year of Kāngxī's reign,
it was deliberated and decided that the starting transport waste rice (hàomǐ) and regular grain (zhèliáng) for Jiāngníng and other prefectures would all be given a uniform allowance (tiēzèng).
The three prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Chángzhōu would convert (gǎizhé) to ash-colored rice (huīshí),
and all silver for allowances such as bāngtiē and cáozhé would be waived.
In the twenty-fourth year,
an order was issued for the cáojié silver from each province to be exempted from remittance to the Daoku (Dàokù),
and instead to be directly disbursed by the zhōuxiàn.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng's reign,
it was decreed that the zènghào for Jiāngnán's tribute grain (cáomǐ) would be permanently exempt from the rule of suspension.
Zhōuxiàn that collected tribute grain in the various provinces,
besides the regular waste rice (zhèng hàomǐ) and the transport soldiers' monthly provisions (yùnjūn xíngyuèliáng), original and converted allowances (běnzhé cáozèng), and other items,
also collected cáohào silver and rice.
The amounts also varied.
This rice, in addition to the waste (hàowài zhī mǐ),
was all for the miscellaneous expenses of officials and soldiers (guānjūn) exchanging tribute grain and for the zhōuxiàn's operational use.
The light transport silver (qīngzījīn)
began in the mid-Míng dynasty.
As grain was exchanged and transported from various granaries,
travel expenses had to be provided.
Waste rice was levied.
The exchanged and transported rice was of two types: plain (píng) and surplus (ruì).
The surplus rice (ruìmǐ) was measured and taken as waste on board the ships,
and the rest was converted into silver (zhéyín),
called qīngzī.
The Qīng dynasty followed this practice.
For every shí of regular exchanged rice annually,
Jiāngxī, the two Hú provinces, and other provinces added waste of four dòu six shēng or six dòu six shēng.
The surplus rice was all one dòu.
For those with an added waste of four dòu six shēng,
three dòu were used as waste on board the ships,
and the combined surplus of two dòu six shēng was converted into silver of one qián three fēn.
For those with an added waste of six dòu six shēng,
four dòu were used as waste on board the ships,
and the combined surplus of three dòu six shēng was converted into silver of one qián eight fēn,
called the sānliù qīngzī.
Jiāngsū and Ānhuī added waste of five dòu six shēng per shí,
and one dòu of surplus rice.
Excluding four dòu used as waste on board the ships,
the remaining two dòu six shēng of rice were converted into silver of one qián three fēn,
called the èrliù qīngzī.
Shāndōng and Hénán added waste of three shēng per shí,
and one dòu of surplus rice.
Excluding two dòu five shēng used as waste on board the ships,
the remaining one dòu six shēng of rice were converted into silver of eight fēn,
called the yīliù qīngzī.
For those converted exchanges that only had waste rice (hàomǐ),
ranging from three dòu two shēng to one dòu seven shēng,
only the actual grain was provided as waste on board the ships,
and the remaining two shēng of rice were exchanged for one fēn of silver,
called the zhéyì qīngzī.
All were levied at five lí of silver per shēng,
and remitted to the Tōngjì Kù of the Cāngchǎng.
In the forty-seventh year of Kāngxī's reign,
it was ordered that Jiāngnán and other provinces annually remit a quota of three hundred eighty-four thousand liǎng of qīngzī silver.
Of this, the quota of two hundred forty-six thousand nine hundred-odd liǎng from Shāndōng, Hénán, Húguǎng, Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngnán, and other provinces
was still retained in the Tōngjì Kù for use.
The quota of one hundred thirty-seven thousand-odd liǎng from the Sūzōng Liángdào's jurisdiction
was remitted directly to the Hùbù.
If the Cāngchǎng's funds were insufficient,
a memorial could be sent to the Hùbù for disbursement.
Subsequently, fifty thousand liǎng of the qīngzī silver quota belonging to the Sūzōng Liángdào were allocated to the Tōngjì Kù for reserve.
This qīngzī silver,
by regulation, should be used for exchanging tribute grain to facilitate transport operations.
In addition, there were mats, wood, bamboo boards, etc.,
which were all submitted along with the tribute grain.
Their dimensions (length, width, thickness)
all had fixed regulations.
In the twenty-ninth year of Dàoguāng's reign,
Lǐ Xīngyuán, the Governor-General of the Two Jiāngs (Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū), memorialized that the Hùbù's fixed price for the conversion of Southern tribute grain (Náncáo) was too low,
creating an opening for unscrupulous zhōuxiàn to extort excessively.
Lù Jiànyíng, the Governor of Jiāngsū (Jiāngsū Xúnfǔ), also spoke of its inconvenience.
Consequently, the conversion to levied silver (zhésè) was abolished.
In the fourth year of Tóngzhì's reign,
Zēng Guófān and Lǐ Hóngzhāng requested to convert the tribute grain of Zhènyáng and Tàicāng zhōuxiàn in Jiāngsū to levied silver (zhésè),
but it was not permitted.
In the tenth year of Guāngxù's reign,

Wáng Bāngxǐ, a Reader in the Hànlín Yuàn (Hànlínyuàn Shìdú), memorialized on five abuses, three difficulties, five advisabilities, and three inadvisabilities regarding the poll tax and tribute grain (Dīngcáo).
At this time, there were frequent accumulated arrears in Dīngcáo in the directly administered provinces (Zhíshěng),
hence Bāngxǐ spoke about it.
In the twenty-third year,
Ruìxún, a Senior Compiler in the Hànlín Yuàn (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì), stated that the conversion of Southern tribute grain (Náncáo) would be beneficial and without harm.
Previously, of the tribute grain from Jiāngsū and Zhèjiāng,
besides one hundred twenty to one hundred thirty thousand shí transported by river,
approximately one million two hundred thousand-odd shí were transported by sea annually.
In the twentieth year,
when managing coastal defense,
Jiāngsū and Zhèjiāng provinces each converted five or six tenths of their grain.
The following year,
Zhāng Zhīdòng, the Governor-General of the Two Jiāngs (Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū), proposed that the zhōuxiàn in Sūshěng (Jiāngsū Province) continue to collect converted or original grain as before,
but that the officials would convert and remit it entirely.
The Hùbù ordered that the original grain (běnsè) still be transported.
Zhāng Zhīdòng again memorialized,
stating that if Sūzhōu's tribute grain was entirely converted,
eight hundred thousand (liǎng) in transport costs could be saved annually.
If Zhèjiāng's grain was entirely converted,
and the procurement from the two Hú provinces completely stopped,
and various expenses for stripped boats (bōchuán) and river digging, and various items for tribute grain officials (cáozhí) and guards (wèiguān)
could all be appropriately reduced,
one million five hundred thousand (liǎng) could be saved annually.
Subsequently, the Hùbù, due to dwindling treasury reserves,
requested to temporarily reduce the sea transport of Jiāngsū's tribute grain by three hundred thousand shí,
obtaining over nine hundred eighty thousand liǎng of silver.
Yīkuāng and others memorialized:
“The Southern tribute grain (Náncáo) has a fixed annual quota,
which concerns the livelihoods of soldiers and common people.
The capital (Jīngshī) is a critical fundamental area,
and even more so requires ample reserves.
Those who speak of converting tribute grain often claim five or six million (liǎng) annually,
but in reality, it is merely a little over one million.
It seems inappropriate to lightly discuss changes.”
This was followed.
In addition to the tribute grain (cáoliáng),
the three prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Chángzhōu in Jiāngsū,
and Tàicāng prefecture (yī zhōu),
and the two prefectures of Jiāxīng and Húzhōu in Zhèjiāng,
annually supplied glutinous rice to the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ),
for the Emperor's use and the stipends of officials,
called white grain (báiláng).
The original quota of regular rice was over two hundred seventeen thousand four hundred seventy-two shí.
For waste rice (hàomǐ),
the three prefectures of Sūzhōu, Sōngjiāng, and Chángzhōu,
and Tàicāng prefecture added waste of three dòu per shí.
Five shēng or three shēng were submitted along with the regular rice,
and the rest was used as waste on board the ships,
totaling over twenty thousand seven hundred seven shí.
The two prefectures of Jiāxīng and Húzhōu added waste of four dòu per shí.
Five shēng or three shēng were submitted along with the regular rice,
and the rest was used as waste on board the ships,
totaling over thirteen thousand four hundred eighty-eight shí.
In the early Kāngxī period,
it was decreed that white grain be uniformly collected in actual grain (běnsè),
except for thirty thousand shí for the Court of Imperial Entertainments (Guānglùsì), which was converted,
with one liǎng five qián of silver levied per shí.
In the fourteenth year,
it was deliberated and decided that Jiāngnán's white grain would follow the example of Zhèshěng (Zhèjiāng Province),
using selected tribute grain ships for transport.
Each ship was to be given sixty-nine shí three dòu of monthly provision rice (xíngyuèliángmǐ),
and fifty-six liǎng seven qián six fēn of silver.
For administrative expenses (jīngfèiyín),
the old Zhèjiāng regulation was four hundred fifty-seven liǎng one qián one lí.
It was deliberated to reduce one hundred twenty-six liǎng two qián four fēn of silver and twenty-eight shí of rice.
Subsequently, as the transport of tribute grain and white grain were considered the same,
the administrative expenses for Jiāngnán and Zhèjiāng's white grain were abolished.
Following the example of tribute grain,
travel allowances (xíngzèng yínliǎng) were disbursed.
As for white grain, it was entirely transported in packages (bāomǐ),
without any conversion or waste (zhéhào).
Upon arrival at Tōngzhōu, it would be received according to regulations.
Previously, Jiāng and Zhèjiāng supplied over 220,000 *shí* of white grain.
The Taìchángsì and Guānglùsì guest houses each required over 2,000 *shí*.
The stipends for princes, dukes, and officials required approximately 150,000 to 160,000 *shí*.
The Household Department, Forbidden City soldiers, and eunuchs needed 10,000 *shí* for consumption.
There were still 50,000 *shí* remaining.
In the second year of Qiánlóng (1737),
Gāozōng said:
"The revenues and expenditures of the Guānglùsì and other such places
are originally for sacrificial ceremonies and the use of guest houses,
which are indispensable.
As for the stipend rice for princes, dukes, and officials,
half of the white grain should be appropriately reduced
and replaced with polished non-glutinous rice.
As for the rice given as rewards to Forbidden City soldiers and eunuchs,
the white grain should be replaced with polished non-glutinous rice
to ease the burden on the people."
From then on, the actual levy of white glutinous rice was no more than 100,000 *shí* with a surplus.
Furthermore, Sōngjiāng and Taìcāng's fixed levy of white glutinous rice was permitted
to be converted to grain for tribute transport.
This was to be managed by adjusting the assigned 100,000 *shí* of white rice
to equalize the amounts that should be reduced and transported.
Zhèjiāng traditionally did not produce glutinous rice.
The glutinous rice item within the white grain
was uniformly levied as rough polished non-glutinous rice along with the tribute grain.
Officials would then exchange it for glutinous rice for transport.
The white grain expenses for both provinces had been previously proposed for reduction,
but at this point, they were reinstated according to old precedents.
Jiāngsū levied over 186,985 *liǎng* of silver,
over 18,889 *shí* of rice,
and over 21,399 *shí* of hulled and prepared rice.
Zhèjiāng levied over 45,075 *liǎng* of silver,
3,969 *shí* of rice,
and over 13,290 *shí* of hulled and prepared rice.
The total actual levy was 232,061 *liǎng* of silver
and over 55,748 *shí* of rice.
After deducting amounts given to transport officers and soldiers, and remitting to the Tōngjìkù for the transportation fees to various granaries in Jīng and Tōng,
the remaining silver and its rice equivalent
were all cataloged and sent to the Board for allocation.
By the mid-Jiāqìng reign,
the white grain expenses for
Jiāngsū levied over 60,000 *liǎng* of silver,
and over 10,000 *shí* each of rice and hulled and prepared rice.
Zhèjiāng levied over 50,000 *liǎng* of silver,
over 3,000 *shí* of rice,
and over 10,000 *shí* of hulled and prepared rice.
The total actual levy was over 114,518 *liǎng* of silver
and over 53,729 *shí* of rice.
Compared to the expenses in silver during the Qiánlóng era, this was more than halved.
The transport of white grain by Jiāng and Zhèjiāng
initially followed the Ming dynasty system of civilian transport.
Subsequently, due to the last-minute hiring of civilian boats
which caused delays,
it was changed to official transport.
This still inconvenienced the people,
so orders were given for tribute grain boats to carry it as a side duty,
to relieve both officials and commoners of burdens.
In the third year of Kāngxī (1664),
the method of carrying tribute by Zhèjiāng was established.
It required 126 boats.
62 boats were selected from the tribute transport groups for loading and transport,
and 64 new boats were built and incorporated into the selection for transport.
Later, Jiāngsū also followed this practice.
Each boat transported 500 *shí*,
and sturdy and reliable military boats were chosen for transport.
They were replaced every five years.
It was stipulated that before the annual exchange,
the grain *dào* was responsible for conducting inspections.
If transport soldiers were fatigued or boats were not sturdy,
other reliable soldiers were to be selected to compensate for the transport.
In the sixteenth year (1677),
the Governor-General of Grain Transport, Húbǎo, memorialized:
"Jiāngsū white grain transport boats were previously rotated every five years.
However, this period is too long.
I request that, in accordance with the precedent of rotating tribute boats every three years,
it be stipulated that white grain transport boats be reselected every three years."
This was approved.
The white grain transport boats of Jiāng and Zhèjiāng provinces
were originally organized with Sūzhōu and Taìcāng as one group,
Sōngjiāng and Chángzhōu each as one group,
and Jiāxīng and Húzhōu each as one group.
Each group had two transport *qiānzǒng* [captains]
and one accompanying military *jǔrén*.
After official transport was implemented,
the prefectural *tōngpàn* served as the general director,
the county *chéng* and *diǎnshǐ* as assistant directors,
and clerks (*lìdiǎn*) as escorts.
Soon, the escorts were abolished.
Later, when white grain was changed to be transported by tribute grain boats,
the general and assistant director positions were also abolished.
Sū, Sōng, and Cháng prefectures each added two *qiānzǒng*,
who rotated in taking charge of transport.
Each group had one accompanying *bǎizǒng* [centurion]
to supervise the return of empty boats.
Zhèjiāng added four *qiānzǒng* and two accompanying officers.
Sūzhōu and Taìcāng's granary transport white grain boats
were originally set at 118 vessels.
With many boats and numerous soldiers,
they were divided into front and rear groups,
and two *qiānzǒng* and one accompanying officer were added.
After the white grain levy was reduced,
the two groups were merged into one,
and all their *qiānzǒng* and accompanying officers were cut.
In the early Qīng dynasty,
officials supervising the transport of tribute grain
adopted the Ming system with adjustments.
The overall manager of grain transport was the Governor-General of Grain Transport (*Cáoyùn Zǒngdū*).
Subordinate jurisdictions included the Grain Provision *Dào* (*Liángchú Dào*).
Supervisors of exchange and escorts included *Tóngzhī* and *Tōngpàn*.
Expeditors included generals and other officials along the river.
The Governor-General of Grain Transport resided in Huaínán,

responsible for selecting transport officers, building and repairing tribute boats, allocating manifests, organizing exchanges and departures, inspecting and controlling passage across the Huái River, urging and accelerating heavy transport, inspecting return empty boats, verifying losses and damages, and pressing for overdue tribute.
All civil and military officials in the seven provinces of Zhílì, Shāndōng, Hénán, Jiāngxī, Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, and Húguǎng who managed grain transport affairs were under his command.
There was one Grain *Dào*
each in Shāndōng, Jiāng'ān, Sūsōng, Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, Húběi, and Húnán.
In Hénán, the Kaīguī Salt and Courier *Dào* concurrently managed it.
The Grain *Dào* managed the grain provisions of the entire province,
overseeing local officials and military garrisons,
selecting and appointing various officers to lead transport and accompany groups,
and instructing prefectural *qīngjūn* officials to, in conjunction with transport officers, select transport soldiers.
Upon completion of the exchange,
they personally supervised the journey to the Huái River,
not allowing assistants to act as escorts.
If there were urgent military supply matters,
they had to report clearly to the Governor-General, Governor, and Grain Transport Minister,
before allowing a commissioner to take over their duties.
The supervision of exchange
was formerly handled by the *Tuīguān*.
When the *Tuīguān* position was abolished,
*Tóngzhī* and *Tōngpàn* were appointed instead.
In Shāndōng, there were the Wǔdìng *Tóngzhī*,
Dōngchāng *Qīngjūn Tóngzhī*,
four *Tōngpàn* from Jǐnán, Yǎnzhōu, Taì'ān, and Cáozhōu,
and two *Tóng* from the directly administered departments of Jìníng and Línqīng.
In Hénán, there were three *Tōngpàn* from Guīdé, Weìhuī, and Huaíqìng.
In Jiāngnán, there were the Jiāngníng and Sūzhōu Grain Supervising *Tóngzhī*,
Sōngjiāng Tribute Supervising *Tóngzhī*,
Fèngyáng *Tóngzhī*,
eight grain managing *Tōngpàn* from Sūzhōu, Yángzhōu, Lúzhōu, Taìpíng, Chízhōu, Níngguó, Ānqìng, and Chángzhōu,
and one assistant official (*chéngcuì*) temporarily appointed in Taìcāngzhōu.
In Zhèjiāng, there were the Húzhōu *Tóngzhī*,
Hángzhōu Bureau Grain *Tōngpàn*,
and Jiāxīng *Tōngpàn*.
In Jiāngxī, there were three *Tōngpàn* from Nánchāng, Jí'ān, and Línjiāng.
In Huaíběi and Xiāngnán, three officials were annually appointed from across the province's *Tóngzhī* and *Tōngpàn*
to supervise the exchange.
The officials in Jiāngxī, Húguǎng, and Ānhuī responsible for supervising exchange and escorting to the Huái River were later abolished.
For all exchanges,
the supervising official had to sit by the waterside,
ensuring that the main grain, spoilage, and monthly transported rice
were fully exchanged for each boat.
They verified the purity of the rice color
and personally handed it over to the escort official.
When the grain boats departed, they still personally supervised them to the Huái River,
where they were inspected by the Governor-General of Grain Transport.
If the grain quantity was insufficient or the rice color impure,
they would be punished.
If *Dào*, prefectural, or departmental officials failed to report it,
they would be disciplined according to the regulations for failing to investigate.
If there was an intention to cover up,
they would be disciplined according to the regulations for favoritism.
Escorting was originally the duty of the Grain *Dào*,
but the Grain *Dào* managed transport affairs in the south,
with no time to attend to both.
The Grain *Dào*s of Jiāng and Zhèjiāng
were only ordered to supervise and escort to the Huái River for inspection,
then return to their posts.
The Governor-General of Grain Transport, in conjunction with the Governor, selected one grain managing *Tōngpàn*
to specialize in supervising and escorting,
restraining transport soldiers,
and preventing abuses such as embezzlement and adulteration.
There was one *Tōngpàn* each in Shāndōng and Hénán,
seven in Jiāngnán,
three in Zhèjiāng,
two in Jiāngxī,
and one each in Húběi and Húnán.
Later, because the *Tōngpàn*'s rank was low and duties minor,
the Grain *Dào* was again ordered to escort.
As for the return of empty tribute boats,
the *Tōngpàn* was still ordered to manage the escort.
Passage across the Huái River had to be within the set deadline.
Any delays
would be disciplined according to the regulations for heavy transport exceeding the deadline.
Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, and Jiāngxī soon reinstated the system of *Tōngpàn* escorts.
After the escorting *Tóngzhī* and *Tōngpàn* arrived in Tōng,
they issued stamped certificates confirming no loss of grain,
which were sent by the Vice Minister of Granaries and Grain Transport to the Board for an audience.
A Grain *Dào* who escorted three times
was also permitted for the Governor-General or Governor to recommend to the Vice Minister of Granaries and Grain Transport for an audience with the Board.
As for officers, gentry, and directors who accompanied the escort to Tōng,
they were also permitted to be selectively commended and rewarded,
to encourage and inspire.
Subsequently, high officials in various provinces often used grain transport to promote their private connections,
and the imperial court had no way to investigate.
The generals of the towns and posts along the Huái-Běi and Huái-Nán rivers,
when encountering grain tribute boats entering their jurisdiction,
were each to supervise their passage according to their designated patrol areas.
If they failed to exert sufficient effort in urging the boats onward,
they would be subject to impeachment and discipline by the provincial governors and governors-general of the locality.
At Jiāng-Nán's Jīng-Kǒu and Guā-Zhōu, opposite each other across the river,
the Zhèn-Jiāng Circuit Intendant was ordered to supervise civil and military officials in urging the boats,
and the Commander-in-Chief (zǒng-bīng-guān) was also ordered to inspect the riverbanks
and assist in urging them across the river.
When the Commander-in-Chief position was abolished,
it was replaced by a Brigade-General (fù-jiāng) to manage.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng,
the Inspector of Grain Tribute (xún-cáo-yù-shǐ) Zhāng Tǎnlín memorialized on matters concerning the Northern Grain Tribute. Firstly,
from Tōng to Jīn,
the old patrol areas along the river were too far apart.
He requested that, following the example of dry patrol areas being five *lǐ* apart,
if a grain tribute boat arrived at a patrol area,
and the officials supervising the grain tribute sat by and watched it obstructed without reporting,
they should be punished according to the precedent for failing to exert sufficient effort in urging the boats.
Secondly,
there were about thirteen or fourteen shallow spots along the route.
The Granary Affairs Vice Minister (zuò-liáng-tīng) found it difficult to oversee these concurrently.
He requested that these be handed over to the patrol officers and their assistants to dredge and clear.
The expenses incurred
would still be managed by the Granary Affairs Vice Minister.
This was approved.
The Inspector of Grain Tribute Yīlāqí memorialized to impeach the abuses of the Hénán Grain Intendant (liáng-dào) in urging the grain.

The Provincial Governor (xún-fǔ) Yǐn Jìshàn also memorialized to request the abolition of the petty fees collected by various prefectures and counties from officials and yamen runners supervising and escorting grain.
When tribute grain boats returned empty to the province,
before they began unloading,
the provincial governor and grain intendant were held responsible.
Once they began unloading and left the province,
the Grain Tribute Governor-General (cáo-dū) and the civil and military officials along the route were held responsible.
Upon reaching Jīn,
the Vice Minister of Granaries (cāng-chǎng-shì-láng), the Granary Affairs Vice Minister, the Tiān-Jīn Commander-in-Chief, and the Tōng-Zhōu Brigade-General were held responsible
for strict inspection.
Those who violated regulations
would be apprehended and punished.
In the forty-eighth year,
the Grain Tribute Governor-General Yùqí said:
"Among the escorts from various provinces,
only the Shān-Dōng Grain Intendant (liáng-dào) escorts the grain to Tōng.
The others only escort it to Huái-Ān.
Henceforth, for heavy transport from all provinces,
all grain intendants are to escort their respective convoys to Lín-Qīng,
issue a sealed certificate confirming no loss of grain,
and then return to their posts.
For the section from Lín-Qīng to Tōng,
the Shān-Dōng Grain Intendant will generally be responsible for urging the boats onward and back.
The Shān-Dōng Grand Canal
closes its dams and dredges shallows on the first day of the eleventh month each year.
On the day the dams are opened,
it shall be based on the arrival of the southern provincial grain boats at Tái-Zhuāng.
Lake Wēi-Shān and others collect numerous springs,
serving as the water reservoir for grain transport in the eastern province.
Private interception of water sources by commoners is not permitted.
When water is low in spring and summer at the locks (zhá-hé),
the opening and closing must strictly adhere to grain transport regulations.
When a grain boat arrives at a lock,
both the upstream and downstream passes must be present
before the gates are opened.
If river water is ample,
opening and closing should be done judiciously
to speed up grain transport,
but the two locks must not be opened simultaneously
to avoid excessive water discharge.
If a boat encounters a strong wind in the river,
it is originally permissible to anchor and wait.
However, officials supervising the grain only know to press urgently,
causing military boats to proceed dangerously,
often risking being swept away and lost.
For empty return boats,
the transport officials and boatmen often act negligently,
or, out of reluctance to pay hiring fees,
dismiss experienced boatmen,
retaining those unfamiliar with handling boats.
And the escorting officials often return to their offices first,
not personally supervising on the boats,
often leading to incidents of transport boats being lost in storms."
An imperial edict instructed:
"Officials along the route urging the boats
should observe wind conditions and water levels,
and not be overly hasty
to the point of risking incidents.
Nor should they, because of this edict, arbitrarily delay
and exceed the set deadline."
Initially,
copper and lead boats and timber rafts in the Grand Canal
often moved recklessly,
and merchant boats mostly feared them and yielded.
Grain boats heading north were also obstructed by them.
At this time, the Inspector of Grain Tribute was ordered to transmit instructions to civil and military officials along the route
to urge the grain transport boats to proceed first,
with other boats following behind
and advancing in sequence.
Those who relied on their strength to rush ahead or disobeyed orders
would be punished.
For officials leading transport,
grain boats from each province were divided into convoys.
Each convoy was led by one or two Battalion Commanders (qiān-zǒng) from a military guard unit,
with one military *jǔ-rén* assisting the convoy.
In the sixth year of Shùnzhì,
it was decided to select those with outstanding talent from the military guard units involved in grain transport and appoint them as Battalion Commanders,
charging them with escorting the grain.
They would be promoted based on merit
and those with arrears would be punished and made to compensate.
Subsequently, the "Outer Commanders of Military Guard Units" (wài-wěi-bǎi-zǒng) were abolished
and replaced by "convoy officials" (suí-bāng-guān).
In the fifty-first year of Kāngxī,
thirty candidate Battalion Commanders were selected
and sent to serve in the Southern Grain Tribute Corps (nán-cáo-biāo).
If there was a vacancy for a Battalion Commander leading transport,
the Grain Tribute Governor-General (zǒng-cáo) could appoint someone to act as escort.
If they could complete the journey to Tōng intact,
the Governor-General of Granaries and Fields (cāng-chǎng-zǒng-dū) would memorialize the Ministry of War,
allowing them to be immediately appointed.
For selected military *jǔ-rén*,
if there were those waiting for appointment as Battalion Commander of a guard unit who wished to serve as a convoy assistant,
they could report to the Governor-General's office.
Upon a vacancy, they would be permitted to fill it.
If they performed without error for three years,
they would be recommended for appointment as a Battalion Commander of a guard unit.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng,
Grain Tribute Governor-General Zhāng Dàyǒu memorialized that Shān-Dōng and Hénán rotated in transporting grain for officers and soldiers in Jì-Zhōu, Zūn-Huà, and Fēng-Rùn.
The escorting along the route and urging of empty return boats
were, by regulation, the responsibility of the Assistant Prefect (tōng-pàn) escorting the grain.
He requested the addition of two Jì-Liáng Battalion Commanders (jì-liáng-qiān-zǒng)
to take turns leading the transport.
This was approved.
Although each guard unit had Battalion Commanders to lead transport,
the Grain Tribute Minister (cáo-chén) annually appointed additional escorting convoy officials,
dividing them into those escorting full boats and those escorting empty boats.
The cost for one full transport was two or three thousand gold,
and the cost for one empty transport exceeded a thousand gold.
The boatmen's savings were exhausted,
and the abuses of excessive collection grew daily.
In the twelfth year of Jiāqìng,
an edict prohibited the Grain Tribute Governor-General from dispatching too many officials
and forbade transport officials from accepting gifts.
In the fourteenth year,
the Inspector of Grain Tribute again requested a substantial reduction.
Since the third year of Xiánfēng,
river transport ceased,
boats no longer existed,
and the title of "leading transport" was also abolished.
The position of Inspector of Grain Tribute was initially abolished in the early Shùnzhì period.
In the seventh year of Yōngzhèng,
due to numerous illicit practices with grain boats crossing the Huái River
and the smuggling of prohibited goods,
two Censors (yù-shǐ) were dispatched
