to Huái-Ān to specialize in inspection.
Two Censors also inspected grain boats upon their arrival at Tōng.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
four Inspectors of Grain Tribute were established:
one stationed at Huái-Ān,
inspecting from Jiāng-Nán's river mouth to the Shān-Dōng border;
one stationed at Jì-Níng,
inspecting from Shān-Dōng's Tái-Zhuāng to the Zhí-Lì border;
one stationed at Tiān-Jīn,
inspecting to the Shān-Dōng border;
and one stationed at Tōng-Zhōu,
inspecting to Tiān-Jīn.
For the collection of tribute grain,
it was stipulated that granaries would open in the tenth month
and unloading would be completed by the twelfth month.
However, for boats inside the Lín-Qīng locks in Shān-Dōng,
unloading was changed to the second month of the following year,
arriving at Tōng on schedule.
Boats outside the locks
still unloaded and departed in winter.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
both boats inside and outside the locks were ordered to unload and depart in spring,
following the request of Grain Tribute Governor-General Yáng Xīfú.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
an edict stated:
"Unloading and departing in winter
makes the period too rushed.
Hereafter, for the eastern province's tribute grain,
collection will still follow the old regulations,
transported to the waterside.
Unloading and departure of convoys will be completed after the Start of Spring.
The following year will change to winter unloading and spring departure."
In the fifteenth year,
it was ordered that convoys both inside and outside the locks
should follow the precedent of spring unloading and spring departure.
For the northern Jiāng grain tribute in winter,
it was stipulated to begin unloading on the first day of the twelfth month,
with a deadline for completion and departure in the second month of the following year.
In all grain transport and exchange,
the quality of the rice is paramount.
If storehouse clerks commit fraud,
mixing in impurities to cause harm,
or if there is dampness and mildew,
before the exchange is accepted,
the responsibility rests with the zhōu xiàn.
Once the exchange is accepted,
the responsibility lies with the biàn jūn.
The duty of verification
falls to the jiān duì guān.
If a xiàn wèi disputes the rice quality,
the current exchange rice is to be sealed
and sent to the zǒng cáo xún fǔ for inspection.
If it is indeed damp and mixed with impurities,
they are all ordered to compensate with replacement, sifting, and winnowing.
Then a sample of the rice is sealed and sent to the zǒng cáo,
and after it passes Huái,
it will be checked and compared,
and individuals will be impeached accordingly.
However, the yùn jūn extort the zhōu xiàn,
often using rice quality as a pretext.
When the zhōu xiàn open their granaries for ten days,
there is abundant rice but limited storage space,
necessitating an early exchange.
The yùn jūn selectively pick at each boat,
unwilling to accept the exchange,
causing grain households to lack storage for delivery,
thereby creating disturbances.
The yùn jūn seize the opportunity to demand excessively,
or if their demands are not met,
the boats simply depart,
burdening the zhōu xiàn with the difficulty of exchanging with the next convoy.
When the grain exchange is completed,
the yùn biàn should issue a tōng guān.
The tōng guān originates from the jiān dīng.
The jiān dīng
are transport dīng who have handled affairs for many years;
other yùn dīng and yùn biàn all obey their command.
If a jiān dīng demands fees from the zhōu xiàn
and his desires are not met,
he will withhold the tōng guān,
causing the zhōu xiàn to unjustly suffer delayed punishment.
The yùn jūn and yùn biàn conspire together,
and the zhōu xiàn, fearing delayed exchange,
are forced to overcharge and extort discounts to satisfy their demands.
Although superior officials are well aware of these abuses,
they are reluctant to make changes.
Furthermore, they worry that abolishing the yùn jūn
would impede grain transport.
Thus, they condone and tolerate,
without prohibiting or interrogating them.
Since the zhōu xiàn overcharge extensively,
it is difficult to select fine quality rice.
Since the yùn jūn receive additional fees,
they no longer meticulously inspect the exchange.
Upon arrival at Tōngzhōu,
they bribe warehouse clerks and brokers,
manipulating the handover.
The abuses of damp and impure rice quality
are mostly due to this.
The accumulated problems are too deep-seated to reverse,
and the grain transport administration deteriorates daily.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
Cáoyùn Zǒngdū Gù Cóng submitted seven proposals for managing grain transport: First,
zhōu xiàn should personally collect the grain to prevent clerks and sub-officials from taking advantage of and harming the people.
Second,
to eliminate the abuse of wealthy individuals secretly hiring poor dīng to act as carriers.
Third,
to urge ships of unstarted convoys to depart quickly.
Fourth,
after grain ships pass Huái,
officials should be dispatched to urge them forward
to expedite grain transport.
Fifth,
any existing shallow spots in the river channels
should be dredged in advance
to prevent obstructions.
Sixth,
all gates should be opened and closed in accordance with grain transport regulations
at all times.
Jiāng and Guǎng grain ships carrying bamboo and wood
must unload them at designated locations.
Seventh,
the three shēng and five gé of surplus rice from empty return trips
should be quickly distributed to the副dīng
to assist with their food during the return journey.
An imperial edict approved his recommendations.
For grain from various provinces passing Huái,
in the early Shùnzhì reign,
it was stipulated that those from jiāng běi prefectures, zhōu, and xiàn must depart within the twelfth month;
those from jiāng nán's Jiāngníng, Sū, Sōng, and other areas within the first month;
those from Jiāngxī and Zhèjiāng within the second month;
and those from Shāndōng and Hénán must all depart within the first month.
If there were delays after passing Huái,
the dú fǔ, liáng dào, and jiān duì tuī guān would be downgraded or punished
according to the length of the delay.
Officers in charge of transport, such as lǐng yùn,
would be flogged and dismissed from office,
and would supervise under penalty.
The usual deadlines for arrival at Tōng were:
Shāndōng and Hénán by the first day of the third month;
jiāng běi by the first day of the fourth month;
jiāng nán by the first day of the fifth month;
Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, and Húguǎng by the first day of the sixth month.
Grain ships from all provinces arriving at Tōng
were limited to completing grain delivery within three months
and returning empty within ten days.
The Cāngchǎng established deadlines
and held the yā bāng guān responsible for arriving at Huái by the deadline.
If they failed to arrive at the destination by the deadline,
they would be impeached according to regulations.
As peace endured,
grain transport abuses proliferated daily.
The people of the southeast involved in grain transport
suffered from the yùn biàn and qí dīng,
being exploited to the bone,
with no avenue for complaint.
Yet, the yùn biàn and qí dīng were also compelled by external pressures.
For instance, when grain ships arrived at Tōng,
to submit documents at Cāngyuàn, Liángtīng, Hùbù Yúnnán Sī, and other offices,
each ship required a fee of ten jīn,
which was arranged and delivered by the bǎo jiā.
The bǎo jiā separately demanded three jīn.
There were also "zǒu bù"
who collected funds on their behalf.
As for passing the dams,
there were traditional fees for appointed commissioners
and regular charges for wǔ zhǎng,
as well as "shàng hú xià dàng" and other expenses,
each ship again requiring over ten jīn.
Upon delivery to the granary,
there were regular fees for the cāng guān,
and various demands from officials and scribes of the grain collection yámén,
costing another several dozen jīn.
These were the hardships of arriving at Tōng.
Furthermore, after grain ships passed Huái,
there were also accumulated fees for "jī xiē tān pài lì shū lòu guī"
and various expenses for submitting documents and passing through halls.
In total, each convoy of grain required five or six hundred jīn, or even a thousand jīn.
These were the hardships of passing Huái.
Previously, when the transport routes were deep,
officials supervising grain transport only sought to ensure heavy shipments arrived at Tōng on schedule,
without strict inspections.
At the start of transport, dīng would carry southern goods,
selling them upon arrival at Tōng
to earn a small profit.
After the fiftieth year of Qiánlóng,
the Yellow River was repeatedly opened for irrigation,
and the transport routes became increasingly silted.
Grain transport officials, fearing that heavily laden ships would be difficult to navigate,
strictly prohibited dīng from carrying excess goods.
Consequently, the dīng's means of livelihood were reduced.
As the transport routes became shallower,
the cost of dredging them actually increased.
At important gates and dams,
towing often required hundreds of people.
With long distances
and tight deadlines,
the exhaustion of the dīng's labor
was indeed due to this.
Although dú fǔ high officials painstakingly made adjustments,
the entrenched abuses were too deep,
and no substantial results were ever achieved.
The grain transport boats of each province
originally numbered 10,455.
In the 14th year of Jiāqìng (1809),
after deducting those converted to monetary payment, those reassigned for escort, and those reduced due to collapsed and abandoned fields,
there remained 6,242 vessels.
Every eleven years, when they were repaired and built,
it was called "annual construction."
Those that were lost due to changes in land tax categories, accumulated deficiencies, or sinking,
were called "supplementary repair and reconstruction,"
with a ten-year limit.
The amount of payment given
depended on the duration of use, whether it was old or new, and the distance of the location.
The cost of shipbuilding
was initially levied at seven-tenths from civilian land
and three-tenths from military land,
to cover the cost of materials.
If insufficient,
then a levy was collected from military guard families' fields to subsidize the construction of grain transport boats.
When the ten-year limit expired,
the Supervisor-General of Grain Transport (Zǒngcáo) would personally inspect them.
Only if they were truly unfit for transport
could they be rebuilt.
If some could be repaired and reused for transport,
a proportionate amount of silver for repair was given,
and they were still ordered to be reused for transport.
Calculated annually,
if old boats were still usable,
but were not inspected and operated for transport,
the Governor-General (Dūfǔ) would investigate and impeach those responsible.
Officials in charge of building and repairing grain transport boats,
who either falsely claimed they were dilapidated,
or claimed completion when repair was unfinished,
or concealed dilapidated boats in their reports,
or, as contractors, procrastinated and failed to complete work by the deadline,
or whose supervising officials were ineffective in urging completion,
or failed to appraise and report dilapidated boats,
were all subject to varying degrees of demotion or punishment.
Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Fèngyáng did not produce timber,
so factories were established at Qīngjiāng Customs (Qīngjiāng Guān),
with the Boat Administration Sub-Prefect (Chuánzhèng Tóngzhī) supervising construction.
The various brigades of Jiāngníng, totaling over 1,200 boats,
were also constructed in Qīngjiāng.
From Yízhēng upstream to Huái'ān,
a distance of over four hundred *lǐ*,
human labor was required along the way for towing.
After the boats were built, they had to cross the Great River again,
traveling a thousand *lǐ* (li)
to reach their destination, causing delays.
County officials were eager for good performance evaluations,
and banner soldiers (qídīng) profited from extortion.
Boats were handed over and exchanged before arrival,
a practice called "transfer to storage" (zhuǎn'áo).
Consequently, various abuses such as excessive consumption, expenses, compensation, and harsh exactions increased daily,
causing hardship for the transport soldiers.
Later, the Boat Administration Sub-Prefect (Chuánzhèng Tóngzhī) was abolished,
and all management was transferred to the Grain Intendant (Liángdào).
The transport soldiers were ordered to collect material payments and go to the factories for construction.
If insufficient,
funds were drawn from the grain transport silver reserves in the Intendant's (dào) treasury.
The grain transport boats of Xúzhōu Guard (Xúzhōu Wèi) and Hénán Rear Brigade (Hénán Hòubāng)
were also historically built at the Qīngjiāng shipyard.
They were then sailed to the Hénán riverside to exchange grain,
a distant journey
that easily caused delays in the exchange deadline.
Later, construction was changed to a factory established in Línqīng, Shāndōng.
In years when the full quota was due,
the soldiers were ordered to collect payments from the Jiāng and Ān (Jiāng'ān) Dao treasuries for construction.
The Jǐnán Front Brigade (Jǐnán Qiánbāng)
was built at Xiàchéngzhèn in Jiāngnán.
Later, this was also changed to a factory at Hújiāwān in Línqīng.
There were nine methods for inspecting completed boats: one, inspect the wood;
two, inspect the planks;
three, inspect the bottom;
four, inspect the beams;
five, inspect the deck;
six, inspect the nails;
seven, inspect the seams;
eight, inspect the holds;
nine, inspect the bow and stern of the holds.
In addition to the regular quota of grain transport boats, the various brigades of Shāndōng
historically maintained thirty "reserve boats" (liángcún chuán).
Yángzhōu, Jiāngsū, also had twenty-four reserve boats.
These were successively proposed for reduction,
and the boats of Yángzhōu Guard (Yángzhōu Wèi) designated for reduction
were used to compensate and replace the poor and worn-out military boats of the Jiāng and Xìng (Jiāngxìng) Guards.
In the 8th year of Qiánlóng (1743),
the Governor-General of Grain Transport (Cáoyùn Zǒngdū), Gù Cóng, submitted proposals for adapting grain transport boat matters: One,
in years when grain transport boats were due for major construction,
if there was a reduction in service,
construction would be suspended for one year,
making the age limits of these boats differ from those previously transported,
so that future construction would not need to be synchronized;
Two,
boats built for compensation had been used for transport multiple times
and were consistently less sturdy.
Henceforth, boats built for compensation would be counted as the original boats.
If they could still be used for transport after ten years,
they would be allowed to be sold in Tōng.
Three,
boats reaching their full age limit
were usually scheduled for construction in different years.
Among them, the sturdy ones
would be selected by the Supervisor-General of Grain Transport (Zǒngcáo) for additional repairs,
used for one more transport,
and then permitted to be freely sold.
This was approved.
In the 29th year (1764),
the Grain Transport Governor (Cáodū), Yáng Xíyàn, stated:
"In years when grain transport boats of various provinces reach their ten-year transport limit and are due for construction,
if the grain is transported to Tōng,
they shall be allowed to be sold for value in Tōng.
Furthermore, if boats bought as replacements have not completed their full transport service,
or unexpectedly encounter wind or fire accidents en route,
permission should be granted to sell them for value on the spot."
The emperor decreed to follow his proposal.
Grain transport boats of the Dàhé and Huái'ān brigades
often suffered from sinking due to storms.
Ā Guì (Āguì) reported
that this was due to the boats being too tall and large, making them difficult to steer and tow.
He requested a proportional reduction in size compared to the original specifications.
In the 15th year of Jiāqìng (1810),
the dimensions of grain transport boats for the Jiāng and Guǎng (Jiāngguǎng) provinces were further reduced.
Transport soldiers profited from carrying passengers and cargo,
insisting on large boat bodies,
unaware that heavy loads caused slow travel,
slow travel caused congestion,
impeding civilian boats.
Some even had to wait for tens of *zhàng* for ten days.
In addition, there were forced requisitions for loading and unloading,
accompanied by beatings,
causing widespread complaints.
This was not merely a concern of capsizing due to storms.
In the 17th year (1812),
due to increasing burdens from building grain transport boats in Zhèjiāng province,
in addition to the regular allowance of 208 *liǎng* per boat,
an additional 590-odd *liǎng* of silver was given
to relieve the burden on the soldiers.
The construction and repair of grain transport boats
involved regular and
extraordinary expenses,
costing millions of *kuàntàng* (kuòtáng) annually from the national treasury.
When they set out for transport,
extortion from local prefectures and counties also amounted to millions.
Rushing to deliver and escort,
they toiled year-round.
Smuggling became increasingly rampant.
Even in the inland rivers of Sūzhōu and Sōngjiāng,
there was no year without forced loading and unloading.
Forced loading and unloading still demanded boats from along the route,
even to the extent of blocking rivers to demand fees,
seizing boats, and destroying equipment,
causing distress to merchants and common people,
and defying officials.
Using the "heavenly granary" (tiānyǔ) as a pretext
and citing the Grain Transport Governor (Cáodū) as a shield,
civil and military officials and scholars
feared their influence
and dared not investigate.
All grain transport boats carrying rice
were not allowed to exceed 500 *shí*.
In addition to the standard and loss allowance rice,
it was customary to carry sixty *shí* of local produce.
In the 7th year of Yōngzhèng (1729),
this was increased by forty,
making a total of one hundred *shí*,
established as a permanent rule.
Subsequently, each boat's headman, artisan, and helmsman were permitted to carry three *shí* of local produce,
and each boat's crew (shuǐshǒu) was permitted to carry twenty *shí* of local produce.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng (1799),
it was stipulated that each boat could carry an additional twenty-four *shí* of local produce.
Garrison soldiers (túnyíng) transporting grain
departed in winter and returned in winter,
enduring extreme hardship.
Their daily expenses were also many times higher than at home,
leading to the malpractice of smuggling private goods.
Upon the arrival of grain transport boats at the waterways,
brokers would intercede,
arranging for passengers and cargo.
They would also linger and delay in places where city goods converged,
hoping to take on more cargo
to gain small profits.
Transport officials (yùnguān) profited from their bribes,
and unscrupulous merchants sneaked onto grain boats
to avoid national taxes.
Initially, when the transport route was smooth,
officials supervising grain transport were not overly strict in their inspections.
However, when the Yellow River (Huánghé) repeatedly flooded,
and the transport route became shallow,
the grain transport officials strictly enforced the ban on smuggling,
further burdening the soldiers.
When merchant power was abundant,
military ships returning empty over the Huái River
often privately carried salt.
Cáoyùn Zǒngdū Zhāng Dàyǒu submitted a memorial detailing six matters: First,
in the salt-producing areas of Chánglú and Liǎnghuái,
wicked civilians collude with kiln workers
to privately sell and trade salt.
Waiting for empty grain boats to pass,
they then load it onto the ships.
It is requested that this be strictly prohibited,
and violators be punished according to the private salt regulations;
Second,
when grain boats return empty,
it is requested that Guāzhōu Camp, in cooperation with department officials, search them at Guāzhōu and the river mouth;
Third,
regarding salt caught by Transport Commissioners and other officials,
it is requested that they be deliberated according to the regulations for officials with specialized and concurrent jurisdiction;
Fourth,
officials accompanying the convoy are specially tasked with overseeing empty returns.
Those who catch private salt three times, or whose convoy ships return empty three times without any private salt,
shall be promoted to Qiānzǒng;
Fifth,
each ship is allowed to carry 40 catties of table salt.
Those carrying more shall be punished according to the private salt regulations;
Sixth,
aside from the permitted local produce,
those who engage in contracting merchant ships and rafts
shall be punished according to the tax evasion regulations,
and their goods confiscated.
From then on, the prohibition network became tighter.
As the convoy workers suffered hardships,
a proposal for subsidies was made.
Among the Cáo transport ships in Jiāngsū,
the convoy workers from Sōngjiāng were the most exhausted.
It was stipulated that each ship from Sōng, Tài, and other prefectures would receive a subsidy of 300 taels of silver,
which was later increased to 500 taels.
The convoy workers regarded this as a fixed allowance,
but still desired further discussion on subsidies,
delaying the departure of ships.
Fearing that this would cause delay and lead to reprimand,
the zhōuxiàn officials often secretly bribed them,
which led to daily increases in subsidies,
a never-ending malpractice.
When the Cáo transport reached Tōng or encountered shallows,
peeling boats were required.
In the early Qīng dynasty, 600 red peeling boats were established.
Each boat was given 40 qīng of land,
the rent from which was used to support the boat,
and they were exempt from taxes.
Zhōuxiàn near the capital were far from the river,
and often hired civilian boats.
Vagrants by the river used this to their advantage,
and when transporting Cáo grain,
often engaged in the malpractice of illicitly selling and adulterating it.
Some even sold almost all of it,
then deliberately capsized their boats.
When transport officials investigated,
the local households were still held responsible for compensation,
leading to financial ruin.
Moreover, boat owners leading ships were ordinarily under the jurisdiction of the Tiānjīn Chāoguān Department.
Each year, on days before the river ice thawed,
department officials would urge them to appear in court and wait,
which invariably incurred expenses,
causing considerable hardship.
In the 39th year,
the red peeling boats were abolished.
The original rent income was distributed among the provinces,
collected under the Cáo grain item,
and remitted to the Liángdào Treasury for disbursement.
In the 2nd year of Qiánlóng,
it was stipulated that each boat be given two taels of red peeling silver,
to be disbursed by the accompanying Qiānzǒng.
If Cáo ships encountered shallows,
the transport soldiers would hire civilian boats themselves,
with the Zuòliáng Tīng determining the hire price.
In the 13th year,
an additional 60 boats were established.
The cost of building the boats, equipment, laborers, and wages
were all paid from the red peeling silver,
with the remainder distributed among the transport soldiers.
After the southern grain entered the northern river,
officials would hire boats for peeling and transport.
Before the grain ships arrived,
the peeling boats were prepared in advance,
waiting for many days,
and also hindering the transport of commercial salt.
In the 50th year,
an edict ordered the construction of additional peeling boats.
When southern grain reached the northern river,
it would be peeled and transported immediately to Tōng.
Henceforth, civilian boats should not be sealed,
to avoid causing disturbance and hardship.
Violators would be punished.
Subsequently, it was decided that officials would provide 1,200 peeling boats,
to be handed over to the eighteen zhōuxiàn near the river, such as Tiānjīn, for custody.
If there were merchant goods or salt,
they were permitted to transport them.
After the fourth month,
they would be dispatched to the water's edge,
and not allowed to travel far.
The following year, an additional 300 boats were built,
constructed in Jiāngxī and Húguǎng,
and transported to Tiānjīn,
to take turns with the original peeling boats at Yángcūn.
Due to shallow waters causing delays in Hè and Dōng provinces,
it was decided to build 300 peeling boats,
to be managed by the five zhōuxiàn of Dézhōu, Ēn, Wǔchéng, Xiàjīn, and Línqīng.
In the early Qīng dynasty, following the Míng Wèisuǒ system,
tuntian land was distributed to soldiers for tenancy,
and miscellaneous corvée was abolished.
Later, Wèi soldiers were changed to túndīng,
who were not allowed to enter civilian registers.
An audit was conducted every five years,
managed by the Liángdào.
In the early Kāngxī period,
it was stipulated that each Wèisuǒ in the provinces be allocated ten transport workers.
In the 35th year,
it was stipulated that when Cáo ships set sail,
one worker would be selected for each ship,
and the remaining nine would be filled by experienced boatmen.
The responsibility for selecting transport workers
rested with the Liángdào,
for reporting with the Wèi Shǒubèi,
for employment or dismissal with the Yùnbiàn,
and for guarantees with all convoy workers.
Later, one son of a regular soldier was selected as a vice-soldier.
In the early Yōngzhèng period,
literary students were exempted from transport selection.
Previously, Jiāngsū Ànchásǐ Hú Wénbó noted that the ten Wèi of Jiāng and Ān were far from the Sū and Sōng waterways.
When there were workers to be replaced,
transport officials had to go to the Wèi to select them,
which took a long time for the round trip.
He requested that reserve workers be selected in advance,
a roster compiled and sent to the Liángdào,
and then forwarded to the Zǒngcáo for record.
This was approved by the Hùbù.
Cáodū Yáng Xíyù memorialized against it,
briefly stating:
"There are two reasons why selecting idle workers in advance is unnecessary,
and two reasons why it is inconvenient.
The Wèi convoys in each province
vary in wealth.
Wealthy convoys
do not need idle workers prepared in advance;
poor convoys,
when workers need to be replaced,
search in every possible way
and still cannot find one or two wealthy workers.
How can there be dozens of idle workers available for advance preparation?
That is the first reason it is unnecessary.
Furthermore, prosperous military workers,
whose livelihoods are generally sufficient,
may suddenly become poor due to a bad harvest in one or two years.
If they are already selected and registered,
and when needed,
they are already impoverished,
this still means selecting exhausted workers.
That is the second reason it is unnecessary.
As for sending them to the Liángdào for inspection,
the arduous journey
wastes time and causes loss of livelihood.
That is the first inconvenience.
The clerks of the Wèisuǒ and zhōuxiàn,
who thrive on such matters,
will allow the wealthy to bribe their way out,
and the poor to be selected.
That is the second inconvenience.
I request that the advance selection and registration of idle workers be stopped."
It was granted.
In the ninth year,
Yáng Chāngjùn, the Governor of Zhèjiāng, memorialized:
“For the new grain tribute of Zhèjiāng province next year,
I propose fourteen articles for the sea transport regulations: One,
commissioners shall be appointed to manage the distribution,
to ensure individual responsibility;
One,
the new grain tribute shall still be received and dispatched from Shànghǎi,
the white grain shall still be packed in gunny sacks as per precedent,
and first transported to Hù;
One,
a wide provision of merchant ships for sea transport should be made,
and a greater number of shallow-draft ships should be dispatched from Sū province,
to be transferred to Zhè for use;
One,
the grain for transit losses and other expenses
shall still be disbursed in full,
while the merchant's loss allowance shall be ordered to carry actual grain and surplus coarse grain to be delivered to the granary;
One,
the allowance for Tianjin lighterage ships shall be increased,
to cover deficits;
One,
the expenses for Jīn and Tōng shall
be carried as per precedent,
while the surplus funds and other items
shall still be remitted in full;
One,
merchant ships shall be permitted to carry cannons and weapons,
and be escorted by merchant-donated steamships,
while the coastal naval forces shall still be held responsible for effective patrolling and defense;
One,
after the grain delivery at Tiānjīn,
the brokers shall still be held responsible as before;
subsequently arriving ships
shall still be inspected and received by the Tiānjīn Dào;
One,
the sea transport expenses shall be increased as per precedent;
One,
when grain ships arrive at Jīn,
more berths should be added,
and sufficient lighterage ships prepared;
One,
the freight charges and other items for merchant ships
shall be approved and disbursed as per precedent,
and 20% exemption from duties granted,
with rewards and penalties determined accordingly;
One,
the 20% duty-free goods carried by merchant ships
shall still be calculated by weight based on the grain *shí*,
and the bamboo and wood carried
shall be duty-free as per precedent;
One,
merchant ships returning empty and carrying goods
shall be duty-free according to past regulations;
One,
when grain ships arrive at Jīn for unloading,
brokers, stevedores, and lighterage ships are strictly forbidden from extorting excessive fees.”
The proposal was submitted to the Board for deliberation and implementation.
In the tenth year,
Hóngzhāng stated:
“Lighterage ships endure hardship and fatigue while waiting.
For every hundred *shí* of grain transported,
I request an additional freight charge of five *liǎng* of silver,
and a separate allocation of twelve thousand *liǎng* of silver for rations for the civilian ships transporting white grain during their wait,
to be disbursed from the grain tribute funds in the Sū and Zhè grain *dào* treasuries;
if insufficient,
it shall be borrowed from the provincial treasury.”
In the eleventh year,
Chāngjùn requested to use steamships for grain transport,
which was approved.
For the recruitment of steamships for merchant transport,
merchants borrowed two hundred thousand *chuàn* as capital for establishing the bureau,
with all profits and losses borne by the merchants.
Three sturdy and swift steamships were purchased,
and two hundred thousand *shí* of sea-transported grain tribute were allocated annually,
to be transported to Jīn by the merchant steamships.
Their freight charges, loss allowances, and other items
were still handled according to previous regulations.
When steamships arrived at Jīn,
the Governor-General of Zhí was ordered to prepare lighterage ships for transshipment,
and to jointly inspect them at the warehouses with the Assistant Minister of the Granaries.
Following the precedent of white grain,
the grain was to be transported and delivered by the Jiāng and Zhè governors and *dào* to Tōng,
to prevent losses and smuggling.
For steamships assisting in the transport of Jiāng and Zhè grain tribute,
the words indicating the province, "grain tribute," and "white grain" were to be clearly marked on the grain sacks.
When the grain was loaded onto the warehouses,
officials dispatched by the Hù bureau supervised the exchange;
upon completion of the exchange,
the steamship merchant bureau immediately issued a receipt for the grain.
Thereafter, the loading and departure of ships
were all managed by the merchant bureau,
and the Hù bureau no longer participated.
The warehouse fees and labor
were also borne by the merchant bureau.
For all grain tribute allocated to steamships,
the steamship merchant bureau judiciously appointed personnel
to conduct detailed inspections jointly with the Hù bureau.
Only if the grain was clean and dry
was it accepted for exchange,
and handed over to the steamship bureau to be escorted to the Eastern Warehouse at Pǔjiāng for measurement and receipt.
Upon arrival at Jīn,
the officials and directors of the Jīn bureau were ordered to inspect and receive it in advance,
to avoid congestion.
Each steamship carried three thousand *shí* of grain,
and a complete manifest was issued,
to be audited by the Jīn bureau;
all receipts for silver, grain, and other settlements were abolished.
For grain transported by steamship,
the Shànghǎi Dào issued a duty-free certificate,
and following precedent, 20% of goods could be carried.
However, foreign opium and goods carried beyond the 20% allowance
still required payment of duties.
Qiáo Sōngnián memorialized that the Yellow River in Shāndōng was increasingly overflowing,
and the Grand Canal was silted up.
He proposed to guide the flow according to the situation,
so that the Yellow River water would first be directed to Zhāngqiū.
North and south of Zhāngqiū,
dredging would be carried out universally,
and sluices and dams constructed to facilitate grain transport.
Dīng Bǎozhēn and Wénbīn memorialized to restore the old course of the Huái and Xú rivers.
The matter was submitted to court officials for a joint deliberation.
They reported that after the breach at Tóngwǎxiāng,
the old riverbed was too high due to siltation,
making it impossible to restore the old course of the Huái and Xú rivers.
As for borrowing Yellow River water to aid transport,
and building dikes to confine the water,
it was as difficult as the method of guiding the Wèi River for transport.
Hóngzhāng memorialized to continue using sea transport,
ordering each province to allocate a certain amount of actual grain to be transported to Hù,
and then by sea to Jīn,
while the remainder would be commuted according to regulations,
to save transport costs.
He also proposed to allocate grain tribute commutation silver at any time for procurement and replenishment,
and requested to stop river transport and procurement of grain,
and promote sea transport.
This was again submitted to the Board for deliberation.
Previously, the grain tribute from Jiāngběi
was transported via the river to Tōng;
now, sea transport was also tried.
In the thirteenth year,
it was approved that Jiāngxī would procure eighty thousand *shí* of grain tribute in Hù,
to be transported by the merchant bureau by sea to Jīn,
at a freight charge of two *liǎng* and seven *qián* of silver per *shí*.
In the first year of Guāngxù,
Húnán procured twenty thousand three hundred forty-five *shí* of main and loss-allowance grain tribute,
and Húběi procured thirty thousand *shí*,
all handed over to the merchant bureau for sea transport to Jīn.
Jiāngxī and Húnán later ceased this practice.
Bǎo Zhēn奏ed that the Grand Canal had fallen into disrepair,
which was undoubtedly caused by the Yellow River’s waters.
To manage the Grand Canal, one must first manage the Yellow River.
The double sluices at Wēishān Hú lake outlet and all other relief sluices
should be quickly repaired,
and water should be stored in a timely manner
to protect the lake’s storage.
The main course of the Grand Canal also needed to be dredged as appropriate.
Subsequently, Guì Qīng, Bì Dào Yuǎn, Guǎng Shòu, Hé Shòu Cí, and others also requested fundraising for the restoration of the Grand Canal.
Huáng Yuán Shàn further stated:
“Since the Yellow River shifted north,
the Grand Canal has been obstructed,
and shipping by sea
was originally a provisional measure.
At that time, it was decreed that Jiangsu’s grain tribute quota
would use the canal transport funds for sea transport expenses,
not exceeding seven qián per shí.
Later, due to insufficient funds,
requests for increases were made repeatedly.
The increase for Jiangsu
was not far from one liǎng,
while Zhejiang had already increased to one liǎng,
which is a stark contrast to the Dàoguāng 28th year and Xiánfēng 2nd year when sea transport funds still had surpluses returned to the public coffers.
Moreover, sea transport involves crossing vast oceans,
where storms are unpredictable,
and unforeseen circumstances
are a matter of no small consequence.
Although canal transport is circuitous,
it is stable along the way,
and expenses are consistent.
From the various provinces to the capital granaries,
the number of people who rely on it for their livelihood
is countless.
To enrich the nation and benefit the people,
no better plan exists.
Currently, the cessation of transport has not been long;
timely restoration
is still not too late.
If delayed for several more years,
the waterways will become increasingly silted,
requiring even greater expenditure.
Your servant believes that canal transport is circuitous but safe,
while sea transport is convenient but perilous.
For the sake of utmost safety,
resumption of canal transport is imperative.”
The Emperor ordered the River Governor, Grain Tribute Governor, and all governors and viceroys along the river to plan and report.

Shěn Bǎo Zhēn submitted a memorial refuting Guì Qīng, Bì Dào Yuǎn, and others’ proposal to appropriate a portion of the grain tribute funds from the grain tribute provinces and to divert ten to hundreds of thousands of shí of sea-borne grain back to canal transport,
and he emphatically stated
that “canal transport absolutely cannot be restored.
The canal is dredged only to be re-silted,
transport regulations are set only for the river to suddenly change its course,
and river flows constantly shift,
requiring the grain tribute route to also shift accordingly.
Moreover, using the Yellow River to feed the canal is
even more disastrous.
Before the previous silting is cleared,
the next season’s transport ships arrive, stern to bow,
with great differences in elevation,
making it impossible to cross.
Thus, a hundred schemes are employed to defy the nature of the water,
forcing it into our confines,
leading to all previous repair funds being wasted,
and the current season’s silt accumulating again.
Should the flow be diverted for the sake of canal transport,
if it flows north, the Gīfǔ region suffers;
if it flows south, the Huái and Xú regions suffer.
Millions of lives
will lament being ‘food for fish,’
which is more than just wasting vast sums without benefiting grain transport.”
In the 7th year,
an order was issued to the Zhí Governor to instruct the Merchants’ Steamship Navigation Company that when assisting in grain tribute transport,
a Dàoyuán should be stationed in Tiānjīn to inspect and check the grain,
and the Grain Intendant was charged with strictly supervising personnel involved in grain tribute management,
to meticulously inspect when weighing the rice.
This was due to various malpractices, such as adulteration and breakage,
when the Merchants’ Steamship Navigation Company assisted in transporting Jiangsu and Zhejiang grain tribute.
In the 10th year,
the French instigated hostilities,
and sea transport was obstructed.
Tài Cháng Qīng Xú Shù Míng said:
“Grain tribute should entirely revert to canal transport.
I request that rivers along the canal route be dredged,
sluices and dams be repaired,
and civilian boats be selected and hired to aid transport.”
The next year,
Zēng Guó Quán said:
“Next year, an additional 50,000 shí of Jiangsu grain tribute will be allocated for canal transport,
and the silted and shallow sections of the Pī and Sù waterways
will be estimated and dredged.”
This was approved.
Lú Shì Jié said:
“The Yellow River burst its banks and diverted its flow at Zhèngzhōu,
and outside the Shílǐbǎo Gate of the Shandong Grand Canal, the silt accumulation has widened daily,
preventing returning empty grain boats
from reaching the gate.
Currently, the new grain tribute from Níng and Sū awaits ships for loading.
Dredging silt and building dams in Pī and Sù
must await the passage of all empty ships
before construction can begin.”
The Emperor ordered the swift dredging of accumulated silt
to enable grain boats to travel south early.
In the 15th year,
following the request of Shandong巡撫Zhāng Yào,
200,000 shí of sea-borne grain tribute were re-allocated to canal transport.
Zēng Guó Quán and Huáng Péng Nián memorialized:
“The grain transported by canal from Jiāng and Ān
has already been diverted for disaster relief.
The 100,000 shí of grain tribute from the Sū prefecture transported by canal
was previously switched to sea transport.
The shipments from various prefectures and counties
have all arrived in Hù,
and a sudden switch back to canal transport
is difficult and impractical.
Moreover, hiring nearly a thousand ships
cannot be achieved overnight.
We request to wait until this year’s winter grain tribute
before complying with the imperial decree to advance canal transport,
in order to restore the old system.”
The edict was approved.
In the 19th year,
the Cháo and Bái rivers and other upstream rivers of the Northern Grand Canal rose dramatically,
with water levels several feet higher than the dikes.
The originally constructed upstream weir
was completely submerged.
There were over seventy major and minor breaches in the Grand Canal due to floods and droughts.
Thousands of shi of rice, wheat, and miscellaneous grains transported from Jīn to Jīng
were stranded in Yáng Cūn due to shallow water.
Lǐ Hóng Zhāng was ordered to block all breached outlets,
dredge the river course,
and retain water
to facilitate boat passage.
In the 22nd year,
Wáng Wén Sháo memorialized:
“The southern grain tribute has been switched to sea transport,
but the grain tribute from north of the Jiāng River still uses canal transport.
An additional 100,000 shí of rice from the Sū and Sōng quotas has been allocated for canal transport.
With many boats and long distances,
from the Yellow River into the Canal,
and from the Canal into the Wèi River,
obstructions occur at every stage.
Boatmen are too poor to recover,
stealing rice and adulterating it with water,
leading to numerous malpractices.
This year, the grain boats arrived in Jīn
two or three months later than usual,
and I truly fear they will miss the return trip.
Orders have been given to expedite the journey and urge quick action,
and to complete collection by a set date.
However, the 50,000 shí of Jiāngběi grain tribute diverted this time
is of good quality.
The 50,000 shí from Jiangsu
varies in rice quality,
some even steamed and spoiled.
Sorting and airing it
has been quite troublesome,
because canal transport suffers from the Yellow River’s maladies,
which can no longer be remedied by human effort.
I propose that starting from this year,
the 100,000 shí of Jiangsu grain tribute be entirely switched to sea transport.
As for Jiangsu’s winter grain tribute, it should still be managed by canal transport
to preserve the transport route.”
This was sent to the relevant board for discussion and implementation.
Censor Qín Kuí Yáng, citing the excessive labor and expense of canal transport north of the Jiāng River,
memorialized to cease it
and instead convert it to silver for remittance to the board.
The board deliberated that grain tribute concerns the storage in the capital granaries
and it would be inconvenient to abruptly change the old system.
In the twenty-sixth year,
as war had already broken out,
following Chén Bì's (陳璧) request,
the General Bureau of Grand Canal Transport was established in Qīngjiāngpǔ (清江浦).
When the imperial carriage moved west,
the Transit Bureau moved to Hànkǒu (漢口),
and a sub-bureau was established in Qīngjiāng (清江).
That year, the southern tribute grain was transported to the capital by train from Jīn (津).
In the twenty-seventh year,
due to a shortage of funds,
an edict was issued:
"From this year forward,
all river and sea transport in the direct provinces
shall uniformly be paid in silver equivalent.
The high officials of each province are to be held responsible for clarifying and rectifying the system,
saving bureau and transport expenses,
and investigating and verifying instances where various prefectures and counties have collected excessive fees,
compelling their surrender to the public treasury,
in order to accumulate a large sum."
Yìkuāng (奕劻) requested that, in addition to the white grain that must be handled,
one million shí (石) of tribute grain be purchased annually,
consisting purely of polished rice,
and that no arbitrary requests for retention be made.
This was approved.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the Board deliberated that the tribute grain from Jiāng (江) and Zhè (浙) this year
should be entirely handled by the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company's (招商局) steamships,
and expenses should be reduced as much as possible.
Shèng Xuānhuái (盛宣懷) memorialized:
"In recent years, the Shanghai Bureau's (滬局) steamships,
due to delays in dispatch for various reasons,
incurred significant storage losses.
Upon arrival at Tánggū (塘沽),
the allied forces had not yet withdrawn,
and expenses were double the usual.
In the twenty-sixth and twenty-seventh years,
the freight charges received by the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company
were genuinely insufficient to cover expenditures.
This year, the Taikoo (太古) foreign firm is willing to reduce prices for chartering.
England and Japan, in negotiating commercial treaties,
both wished to include grain transport in the articles.
Your ministers strongly resisted this.
This is because the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company is a Chinese company,
and Lǐ Hóngzhāng (李鴻zhāng) previously memorialized for approval that all tribute rice and military rice be transported by the China Merchants Steam Navigation Company,
which indeed harbored a deep intention.
After thoroughly observing the domestic and foreign situation this time,
it is proposed that starting from the winter grain transport of the twenty-eighth year,
five fen (分) be deducted from the customary three qián (錢) eight fēn (分) eight lí (釐) one háo (毫) of silver per shí (石) for steamship freight and insurance of tribute rice,
to become a permanent regulation."
This was approved.
Tribute grain from Jiāng (江) and Zhè (浙), transported by sea to Jīn (津),
was customarily carried by lighters to the public granaries (Tōngcāng - 通倉).
For each shí (石), one shēng (升) one gé (合) five sháo (勺) of loss-allowance rice was paid,
known as
"Jīn Bō Shí Hào" (津剝食耗).
Since the southern grain transport was changed to rail to the capital,
this loss-allowance rice
was instead ordered to be handed over to the granary along with the main delivery.
Later, due to completion of the rice transport,
losses often occurred,
so the former allowance was permitted to be issued again
to offset the losses from rail transport.
Gazetteer 98, Economy and Finance 4, Salt Administration.
The Qīng (清) salt administration
was largely based on the Míng (明) system, with additions and deletions.
Mongolia and Xīnjiāng (新疆) have many salt-producing areas,
but the eleven inland districts
were particularly beneficial to the national economy.
These eleven districts are: Chánglú (長蘆),
Fèngtiān (奉天),
Shāndōng (山東),
Liǎnghuái (兩淮),
Zhèjiāng (浙江),
Fújiàn (福建),
Guǎngdōng (廣東),
Sìchuān (四川),
Yúnnán (雲南),
Hédōng (河東),
Shǎnxī-Gānsù (陝甘).
Chánglú (長蘆) formerly had twenty salt fields,
later reduced to eight,
marketing to the provinces of Zhílì (直隸) and Hénán (河南).
Fèngtiān (奉天) formerly had twenty salt fields,
later divided into nine,
and when Japan occupied the Jīnchuāntān (金川灘) area,
eight fields remained,
marketing to the three provinces of Fèngtiān (奉天), Jílín (吉林), and Hēilóngjiāng (黑龍江).
Shāndōng (山東) formerly had nineteen salt fields,
later reduced to eight,
marketing to the four provinces of Shāndōng (山東), Hénán (河南), Jiāngsū (江蘇), and Ānhuī (安徽).
Liǎnghuái (兩淮) formerly had thirty salt fields,
later reduced to twenty-three,
marketing to the six provinces of Jiāngsū (江蘇), Ānhuī (安徽), Jiāngxī (江西), Húběi (湖北), Húnán (湖南), and Hénán (河南).
Zhèjiāng (浙江) had thirty-two salt fields,
whose territories were administered by Zhèjiāng (浙江) and Jiāngsū (江蘇),
marketing to the four provinces of Zhèjiāng (浙江), Jiāngsū (江蘇), Ānhuī (安徽), and Jiāngxī (江西).
Fújiàn (福建) had sixteen salt fields,
marketing to the two provinces of Fújiàn (福建) and Zhèjiāng (浙江).
Those in Táiwān (臺灣)
still had five fields,
marketing to that prefecture,
later absorbed by Japan.
Guǎngdōng (廣東) had twenty-seven salt fields,
marketing to the seven provinces of Guǎngdōng (廣東), Guǎngxī (廣西), Fújiàn (福建), Jiāngxī (江西), Húnán (湖南), Yúnnán (雲南), and Guìzhōu (貴州).
Sìchuān (四川) salt wells, where production was abundant,
were found in twenty-four prefectures and counties,
marketing to Xīzàng (西藏) and the six provinces of Sìchuān (四川), Húnán (湖南), Húběi (湖北), Guìzhōu (貴州), Yúnnán (雲南), and Gānsù (甘肅).
Yúnnán (雲南) had twenty-six most notable salt wells,
marketing to its own province.
Hédōng (河東) salt lakes were divided into three fields: eastern, central, and western,
marketing to the three provinces of Shānxī (山西), Hénán (河南), and Shǎnxī (陝西).
The most notable salt lakes in Shǎnxī-Gānsù (陝甘)
were called Huāmǎ Dàchí (花馬大池),
located in Língzhōu (靈州), Gānsù (甘肅),
marketing to the two provinces of Shǎnxī (陝西) and Gānsù (甘肅).
The salt of Chánglú (長蘆), Fèngtiān (奉天), Shāndōng (山東), Liǎnghuái (兩淮), Zhèjiāng (浙江), Fújiàn (福建), and Guǎngdōng (廣東) came from the sea;
Sìchuān (四川) and Yúnnán (雲南) from wells;
Hédōng (河東) and Shǎnxī-Gānsù (陝甘) from lakes.
Regarding the production methods,
sea salt involved boiling (jiān - 煎) or sun-drying (shài - 曬);
lake salt was all sun-dried;
well salt was all boiled.
In terms of quality and taste,
sea salt was superior,
followed by lake salt and well salt.
Among sea salts,
beach-dried (tānshài - 灘曬) was best,
board-dried (bǎnshài - 板曬) was next,
and boiled (jiān - 煎) was third.
In terms of cost,
sun-drying (shài - 曬) was cheapest,
boiling using reeds (dàngcǎo - 蕩草) was next,
coal fire (méihuǒ - 煤火) was third,
and wood (mù - 木) made the labor costs even heavier.
This is the general outline.
Initially,
salt administration belonged to the Shāndōng (山東) Department of the Board of Revenue.
In the second year of Xuāntǒng (宣統),
the Minister of the Board of Revenue was appointed concurrently as Supervisor-General of Salt Administration,
and Censors (Yùshǐ - 御史) were dispatched externally to inspect.
Later, it was returned to the management of Governors-General (Zǒngdū - 總督) and Provincial Governors (Xúnfǔ - 巡撫).
The dedicated office was called the Provincial Salt Commissioner's Office (Dū Zhuǎnyùn Shǐ Sī - 都轉運使司).
In provinces without a Transport Commissioner's Office (Yùn Sī - 運司),

it was sometimes concurrently managed by the Salt Administration Intendant (Yánfǎ Dào - 鹽法道), Salt and Grain Intendant (Yánliáng Dào - 鹽糧道), Post Station and Salt Intendant (Yìyán Dào - 驛鹽道), or Tea and Salt Intendant (Cháyán Dào - 茶鹽道).
There were seven methods of salt distribution:
government supervision, merchant sale (guāndū shāngxiāo - 官督商銷);
government transport, merchant sale (guānyùn shāngxiāo - 官運商銷);
merchant transport, merchant sale (shāngyùn shāngxiāo - 商運商銷);
merchant transport, civilian sale (shāngyùn mínxiāo - 商運民銷);
civilian transport, civilian sale (mínyùn mínxiāo - 民運民銷);
government supervision, civilian sale (guāndū mínxiāo - 官督民銷).
However, government supervision, merchant sale (guāndū shāngxiāo - 官督商銷) was the most widespread and long-lasting.
Merchants were of two kinds:
field merchants (chǎngshāng - 場商), who were responsible for collecting salt;
and transport merchants (yùnshāng - 運商), who were responsible for distributing salt.
Those who oversaw them all were called general merchants (zǒngshāng - 總商),
responsible for collecting taxes from scattered merchants.
Later, many abuses of exploitation and embezzlement arose.
During the reigns of Kāngxī (康熙) and Qiánlóng (乾隆),
attempts were made to abolish them but failed.
Only in Liǎnghuái (兩淮), during the Dàoguāng (道光) era, did Táo Shù (陶澍) reform the system,
memorializing to abolish the salt certificates (yǐnmù - 引目),
which were then printed on copper plates cast by the Board of Revenue's Bǎoquán (寶泉) Bureau.
In the third year of Shùnzhì (順治),
because the collection of salt certificates for Huái (淮) and Zhè (浙) was far from the capital,
an official was established to manage salt certificate affairs (dūlǐ yǐnwù guān - 都理引務官) stationed in Yángzhōu (揚州),
but it was abolished in the seventh year.
In the fifteenth year,
salt certificates were issued to the Transport Commissioner's Office,
but soon after, the Transport Commissioner was ordered to continue dispatching officials to the Board to collect them,
and tickets were also collected from the Board.
When merchants purchased salt,
they had to request a voucher (zhīdān - 支單) from the Transport Commissioner's Office,
also called a permit (zhàodān - 照單), a quota voucher (xiàndān - 限單), or a leather ticket (pípiào - 皮票),
which they held to purchase from the fields.
Upon obtaining salt, it was stored in government-designated areas.
In Fèngtiān (奉天), this was called a granary (cāng - 倉);
in Chánglú (長蘆), it was called a mound (tuó - 坨).
Uninspected salt was called raw salt (shēngyán - 生鹽);
inspected salt was mature salt (shúyán - 熟鹽).
Only mature salt could be sold.
The main depots in Liǎnghuái (兩淮) were initially run by merchants,
but later converted to government depots.
In Sìchuān (四川), those marketing to Qián (黔) and Diān (滇) were considered "border ports" (biān'àn - 邊岸);
those for the province itself and Húběi (湖北) were "accounting ports" (jì'àn - 計岸);
Tóngchuān (潼川) Prefecture was the "Tóng Port" (Tóng'àn - 潼岸).
The general depot (zǒng'àn - 總岸) for Hédōng (河東) was established in the early Xiánfēng (咸豐) reign.
For distribution to Shǎnxī (陝西),
Sānhékǒu (三河口) served as the collection point.
For distribution to Hénán (河南),
Huìxīngzhèn (會興鎮) served as the collection point.
In Shānxī (山西), Pú (蒲) and Jiě (解)
had depots established in Ānyì (安邑) and Yùnchéng (運城),
while Zé (澤) and Lù (潞) and other places also had separate establishments.
Generally, for areas where salt sales are slow outside of brisk-selling markets,
either the time limit for sales is extended,
or the number of *yǐn* (salt permits) is reduced,
or shipments are suspended,
or various methods such as *bìngyǐn fùxiāo*, *tǒngxiāo*, and *róngxiāo* are employed.
*Bìngyǐn fùxiāo* means
attaching accumulated salt
to sell one *yǐn* for every three *yǐn*s.
It also means paying the tax for one and a half *yǐn*s to sell the salt of one *yǐn*,
or paying the tax for three *yǐn*s to sell the salt of two *yǐn*s.
*Tǒngxiāo* means
burning all accumulated *yǐn*s (permits),
with merchants required to pay the principal and miscellaneous taxes and provisions in installments over several years.
*Róngxiāo* means
using brisk-selling areas to alleviate areas where sales are slow.
All *yǐn*s include *dàyǐn*,
which originated in the Míng dynasty,
with some weighing over two thousand several hundred *jīn* (catties).
*Xiǎoyǐn* (small permits)
were created by splitting the *yǐn*s issued during the Míng dynasty into two,
or even up to ten.

There were *zhèngyǐn* (regular permits), *gǎiyǐn* (revised permits), *yúyǐn* (surplus permits), *gāngyǐn* (quota permits), *shíyǐn* (consumption permits), *lùyǐn* (land permits), and *shuǐyǐn* (water permits).
In Zhèjiāng, in addition to *gāngyǐn*,
there were also *jiānyǐn* (shoulder permits) and *zhùyǐn* (residence permits).
Regarding the distinction between *yǐn* and *piào* (tickets),
*yǐn* merchants had exclusive sales territories,
called *yǐndì*.
The initial recognition required immense expenses,
hence it became a hereditary business,
known as *yǐnwō*.
Later, it was sometimes sold to carriers.
The purchase receipt was called a *wōdān*,
and the price was called *wōjià*.
In the tenth year of Dàoguāng (1830),
when Táo Shù was in Liǎnghuái,
he, considering its exorbitant price,
memorialized to request a limit of one *qián* two *fēn* per *yǐn*,
but it was soon prohibited.
*Piào* had no fixed territory but also had a price.
During the Dàoguāng and Xiánfēng periods,
each *piào* in Liǎnghuái was only five hundred *liǎng* of silver.
Later, officials and merchants competed to buy them,
and by the Guāngxù period,
they reached over ten thousand *jīn* (gold, here meaning taels of silver).
Furthermore, the sales quota for *yǐn* was determined by the size and breadth of the *yǐndì*,
while for *piào*, the sales quota was the same
for the same salt-selling territory.
Before Jiāqìng,
there were many *yǐn*s and few *piào*s;
later, there were few *yǐn*s and many *piào*s,
which demonstrates how laws change with the times.
As for annual revenue,
before Dàoguāng,
there was only salt tax (*yánkè*).
When the Xiánfēng military campaigns began,
salt *lí* (likin) was created.
Salt tax was divided into two categories: *chángkè* (field tax)
and *yǐnkè* (permit tax).
*Chángkè* was divided into *tānkè* (beach tax), *zàokè* (salt pan tax), *guōkè* (pot tax), and *jǐngkè* (well tax).
Chánglú had *biānbù*,
and Fújiàn had *qiūzhé*.
*Biānbù* means
that during the Míng dynasty, salt households were taxed according to the number of adult males (*dīng*),
and merchants paid grain at the frontier (*biān*),
receiving silver for disbursements,
which was called *biānyán*.
If a salt field was remote and had no merchants to purchase its salt,
they were required to pay three *zhàng* two *chǐ* of cloth for eight hundred *jīn* of salt.
Later, this was changed to a silver tax of three *qián*,
which was called *bùyán*.
*Zàokè* was traditionally divided into land tax (*dìkè*) and *dīng* tax.
However, not all *dīng* owned land.
During the Yōngzhèng reign,
following the suggestion of Zhèng Chánbǎo, the Salt Censor of Chánglú,
the *dīng* silver tax was apportioned and levied on land,
and thereafter, all provinces implemented this as memorialized.
However, the name *Chánglú biānbù* remained.
*Qiūzhé* refers to
the taxes and provisions paid by salt fields,
called *zhéjià*.
The taxes and provisions paid by the process of manufacture
were called *yánqiū*.
The supply of salt to the Imperial Household Department, the capital, and various government offices in Shèngjīng
was entirely abolished during the Kāngxī reign.
Only two hundred thousand *jīn* were supplied to the Imperial Household Department and the Guānglùsì (Court of Imperial Entertainments),
converted to silver and remitted to the Board for payment.
*Yǐnkè* included *zhèngkè* (regular tax), *bāokè* (contract tax), and *zákè* (miscellaneous tax).
Salt *lí* was divided into exit tax, entry tax, and land tax.
By the late period,
the method of price increases emerged,
whereupon the salt tax revenue equaled that of land tax and national taxes.
Thus, in the early Shùnzhì reign, when 1.7 million *yǐn*s of salt were circulated,
more than 560,000 *liǎng* of silver in tax were collected.
Later, with the unification of the country,
the number of *yǐn*s increased daily, and the tax also flourished daily.
In the eighteenth year of Qiánlóng (1753),
it amounted to more than 7,014,941 *liǎng*.
In the fifth year of Jiāqìng (1800),
it was more than 6,081,517 *liǎng*.
In the twenty-seventh year of Dàoguāng (1847),
it was more than 7,502,579 *liǎng*.
By the end of Guāngxù,
the total of tax and *lí* amounted to more than 24 million.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng (1911),
the Ministry of Finance's budget
estimated annual salt tax revenue at approximately 45 million.
Indeed, taxes increased with the times in this manner.
In the second year of Shùnzhì (1645),
an imperial decree was issued to all Salt Administrations, stating that
from the first day of the sixth month,
all salt would be taxed according to the original amount recorded in the previous dynasty's accounting records.
Soon after, new levies, training levies, and various additional assessments from the late Míng dynasty were exempted.
In the sixteenth year (1659),
the Board of Revenue approved that merchants' salt boats be branded with a hot iron on the bow,
and arbitrary seizures were forbidden.
When passing through customs, only boat fees were to be paid.
If officials exploited this to make excessive demands,
they would be prosecuted for violating the law.
In the seventeenth year (1660),
following the suggestion of Lǐ Zànyuán, the Salt Censor of Liǎnghuái,
empty grain boats returning were prohibited from being searched for smuggling private salt.
In the ninth year of Kāngxī (1670),
Xí Tèná and Xú Xùlíng, the Salt Censors of Liǎnghuái, stated:
"The accumulated abuses in Liǎnghuái cause six great hardships: first,
the hardship of payment and remittance;
second,
the hardship of passing bridges;
third,
the hardship of passing checkpoints;
fourth,
the hardship of opening rivers;
fifth,
the hardship of customs barriers;
sixth,
the hardship of ports.
In total, these six [hardships]
cost tens of thousands of *jīn* each year for each [merchant],
and we request their abolition.
Furthermore, there are three major abuses in weighing: first,
the abuse of adding *tuó* (weights);
second,
the abuse of 'sitting on the *jīn*' (false weighing);
third,
the abuse of manipulating and altering *jīn*s.
For these three abuses,
the only solution is strict prohibition of manipulating weights.
We humbly request this be submitted to the Board for deliberation."
It was decreed that
for all weighings at bridges and checkpoints,
any excess weight would be confiscated.
Shortages were three or four *jīn*, sometimes as many as seven or eight *jīn*,
and the limit must not be exceeded.
If excessive smuggling was found,
and the official in charge of weighing falsely declared too heavy a weight,
the merchant would be punished according to the number of *yǐn*s,
and the official would be charged with embezzlement based on the *jīn*s.
This way, weighing would be fair and national laws would be trusted.
The Emperor ordered a strict prohibition to be engraved on stone,
to be erected at bridges, checkpoints, and ports.
Xí Tèná also stated:
"Since the seventh year of Kāngxī (1668),
the assignment of salt officials has been somewhat delayed.
The previous salt official, in addition to collecting the current year's tax silver,
also heavily levied new salt.
Not a single *yǐn* of salt had been sold,
yet over 200,000 [silver *liǎng*] in tax had already been collected.
For such funds,
merchants faced desperate demands,
either borrowing at high interest
or pawning their assets to meet the deadline.
This practice should be stopped."
The request was granted.
In the sixteenth year (1677),
following the suggestion of Yú Guózhù, a Supervising Censor of the Ministry of Revenue,
it was decreed that the practice of adding twenty-five *jīn* to each *yǐn*
and an additional tax of two *qián* five *fēn* during the inspection of merchants' salt
be permanently abolished
and established as a precedent.
In the twentieth year (1681),
it was ordered to abolish the arbitrary salt tax levies of the Three Feudatories.
Since the reports of upheaval in Diān and Qián,
where people rose in revolt everywhere,
salt had no market,
and merchants all halted, unwilling to advance.
It reached a point where ruined villages were everywhere,
and there was no place to sell.
The Minister of Revenue, relying on military provisions,
issued urgent dispatches to press for payment of taxes,
which were as swift as shooting stars.
Merchants were consequently in great distress.
At that time, the salt tax throughout the empire was highest in Liǎnghuái,
and the distress was also most severe.
Thanks to the Salt Censors Liú Xī and Wèi Shuāngfèng, who provided widespread relief,
payment and collection continued tirelessly.
By this time, the country was prosperous,
and the prefectures of Níngguó, Tàipíng, and Chízhōu in Huáinán,
as well as Liǎngzhè, Shāndōng, Guǎngdōng, and Fújiàn,
successively increased their salt quotas,
gaining three times the profit.
Not only were additional quotas sold as before,
but they also willingly offered to pay the salt tax in advance,
requesting that previously suspended quotas be compensated.
Sìchuān, after the chaos of the late Míng dynasty,
saw people from Jiāng and Chǔ migrate to its territory,
increasing salt consumption daily.
The requested quotas were several times those of the past.
The wells that were opened
provided resources for Diān and Qián,
with smooth transportation by land and water.
Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, and Liǎngzhè recruited salt workers,
reclaimed salt fields and salt mounds,
and reported increases in taxes to the Board continuously.
Furthermore, various salt fields in Liǎngzhè reclaimed and developed over 22,700 *mǔ* of land.
In various ports of Guǎngdōng, seventy *jīn* were added per *jīn*.
For the salt quotas of Nán and Gàn prefectures in Jiāngxī,
by the thirty-sixth year,
the increase in *jīn* and allocation of taxes were likewise.
The emperor, seeing the world at peace,
remitted half of the silver for the increased *jīn* in Zhèjiāng,
totaling over 313.8 million.
In the thirty-eighth year, during his southern tour,
he again decreed to all salt officials:
"Previously, due to military expenses,
you collected private surplus profits in addition to the regular quotas.
This item is to be abolished.
As for the salt tax of Liǎnghuái,
it was previously increased by 400,000.
This is to be reduced by half."
In the forty-third year,
acting on the advice of the Governor-General of Jiāngnán, Āshān,
several hundred thousand in superfluous expenses in Liǎnghuái were eliminated,
and this was engraved in stone for perpetual prohibition.
In the fifty-sixth year,
Tián Wénjìng, the Salt Censor of Chánglú, requested that the salt quotas cut in Shāndōng be fully restored for tax collection.
The Board deliberated and approved.
The emperor, deeming that increasing quotas and taxes was unbeneficial,
disallowed it.
Prior to this, in the second year of Shùnzhì,
Shìzǔ established the system of imperial censors to inspect salt administration in Chánglú, Liǎnghuái, Liǎngzhè, and Hédōng,
assigning one supervising censor for each,
to be replaced annually.
Shāndōng salt affairs were concurrently managed by Chánglú,
and Shǎnxī by Hédōng.
In the tenth year, this system was suspended,
and salt affairs were solely entrusted to the Salt Distribution Commissioners.
Soon after, due to the limited authority of the Salt Distribution Commissioners,
censors were again ordered to inspect.
In the eleventh year of Kāngxī,
the salt inspection system was suspended again.
The following year,
Governor Jīn Shìdé, citing the numerous responsibilities in Zhílì,
requested that censors be dispatched again.
Consequently, the old system was restored in Liǎnghuái, Liǎngzhè, and Hédōng.
Later, Salt Censors were also established in Liǎngguǎng and Fújiàn.
In the fifty-ninth year,
it was again handed over to the Governors-General and Governors for management.
At that time, only Guǎngdōng and Yúnnán consistently had salt tax deficits.
This was because in the early Kāngxī period, Yuè merchants were reported to fill quotas from within villages,
with a change every three years,
known as "ranking merchants,"
leading to countless malpractices.
Subsequently, the "ranking merchant" fee of over 10,000 *liǎng* was included in the regular tax,
and prosperous households were recommended to serve as chief merchants for various salt fields and ports.
However, the salt field merchants had limited capital
and could not purchase all the salt,
leading to widespread private sales in the fields.
In the fifty-seventh year, the salt field merchants were abolished.
The Salt Distribution Treasury raised 360,000 *liǎng* as capital
and distributed it to field officials for purchasing salt.
Additionally, flat-bottomed boats were provided with transport fees,
shipping the salt to Dōngguān Cháoliáo,
where it was stored awaiting allocation.
Port merchants, upon allocating salt,
paid per package
and gained a surplus,
known as "field surplus."
The remaining salt *jīn* after brine loss and residual collection
were additional salt collected beyond the quota,
issued to merchants for transport.
There were also names like "subsidiary salt," "capital surplus," "residual salt," and "surplus silver."
Later, residual salt was converted into quotas,
and residual surplus was incorporated into the regular tax,
leading to the "managing surplus" practice in Yuè salt.
Later, Yuè merchants defaulted and ceased operations in over fifty ports.
Yúnnán salt was transported by merchants with tickets,
but the land lacked boats and carts,
relying entirely on human labor.
There was no coal or grass for boiling,
relying entirely on firewood.
Thus, transport costs and labor were both heavy,
and the salt tax rate was one part,
which was also heavier than other provinces.
Wealthy merchants abandoned it,
and villagers were forcibly assigned to undertake it.
When they defaulted and ceased operations, there was no way to recover payments,
so the responsibility was shifted to villages to levy it by household.
By the time of Qiánlóng,
it never recovered,
so the Governors-General and Governors of successive years were ordered to compensate.
In the early years of Shìzōng,
the Salt Censors of Fújiàn and Zhèjiāng were abolished.
At that time, the emperor paid considerable attention to salt administration.
The Hédōng salt lake was low-lying,
repeatedly flooded by mountain waters.
According to old regulations, building walls and dams
was assigned to the people of Pú and Xiè's thirteen prefectures and counties to undertake the labor.
Following the advice of Salt Censor Shuòsè,
6,000 *liǎng* of silver were allocated annually,
with 3,000 for annual repairs
and 3,000 stored in the Salt Distribution Treasury for major repairs,
thereby relieving the burden on the people.
He also believed that nothing was more urgent in salt law than apprehending smugglers,
but there were field smugglers, merchant smugglers, and powerful smugglers,
with neighboring smugglers and official smugglers causing even greater harm.
To apprehend field smugglers,
it was essential to empathize with salt producers and strictly enforce prohibitions.
Therefore, in the second year of Yōngzhèng, when the Fàn Embankment in Liǎnghuái breached,
and twenty-nine coastal salt fields were submerged by tides,
special funds were issued for relief.
In the fifth year,
as Huái merchants donated silver to build salt granaries for grain storage,
an edict was issued to build several more granaries near salt production areas,
to meet the urgent needs of salt households.
This policy was aimed at sympathizing with salt producers.
In the sixth year,
Fàn Shíyì, the Governor-General of Jiāngnán, stated:
"For salt production by salt households in Liǎnghuái,
merchants should be ordered to select several capable individuals,
and also establish salt field heads and inspectors
to check the amount of salt
and transport it into merchant compounds
to prevent private sales."
Dài Yīnbǎo, the Salt Censor of Liǎnghuái, stated:
"The equipment for boiling salt in the fields,
the deep ones are *pán* (pans),
the shallow ones are *hè* (trays).
There is a fixed number,
and boiling salt takes one day and night as a 'fire period,'
with inspections for private boiling after the fire is extinguished.
Recently, some salt households privately acquired salt *hè*,
and the 'fire periods' were not inspected,
leading to many excess quantities.
I request that salt officials be ordered to strictly enforce old laws.
As for sun-dried salt in Huáinán,
only merchants purchase and transport it,
and the quota tax should be appropriately increased."
Both were ordered to be made into regulations.
This was to strictly enforce prohibitions.
To apprehend merchant smugglers,
it was essential to empathize with merchants and strictly enforce prohibitions.
Therefore, in the second year, various salt fields in Liǎnghuái,
due to disaster and insufficient salt production by salt producers,
saw merchant capital double.
Following the advice of Salt Censor Gá'ěrtài,
it was ordered that the cost of production for the current year,
combined with transportation costs for distant and near places,
be used to determine appropriate market prices for buying and selling.
In places where salt was difficult to sell,
if the designated marketing areas were insufficient,
reallocation was also permitted.
Lú Xún, Minister of War, requested to increase quotas and remit taxes,
to reduce prices and counter smuggling.
It was ordered that Chánglú and Liǎnghuái add fifty *jīn* per quota
and be exempted from paying the tax silver.
This policy was aimed at sympathizing with merchants.
In the eleventh year,
following the advice of Yǐn Jìshàn, the Governor-General of Jiāngnán,
the Huáinán Surveillance Circuit was reorganized
to supervise salt affairs in Yángzhōu, Tōngzhōu, and other places,
and a special office for apprehending smugglers was established at Qīngshāntóu in Yízhēng.
As for the verification of official and private accounts,
since the Míng dynasty,
those who were assigned salt commissions,
upon returning to the capital, customarily presented gifts.
After the emperor strictly prohibited this,
they all began to report and hand over their income.
Only in Fújiàn, more than eighty thousand taels were discovered by Grand Governor Mǎn Bǎo.
Consequently, salt officials were abolished,
and salt merchants were ordered to have their salt fields supervised by zhōu and xiàn officials.
Later, Grand Governor Yáng Lín of Guǎngdōng said:
"When local officials collect taxes,
they must entrust the task to their household retainers and yámén runners.
If they don't set up stalls to sell and embezzle,
they will go to various places and impose levies.
Furthermore, fearing insufficient capital,
they might divert land and poll tax revenues.
Therefore, the field merchants should be abolished,
and the treasury should dispatch officials to supervise collection.
The port merchants should remain to transport, sell, and pay taxes."
This was adopted.
At that time, the emperor highly valued Lǐ Wèi among the salt officials.
What Lǐ Wèi could be praised for in Zhèjiāng,
none was better than managing the treasury salt.
Treasury salt refers to
the prosperous salt production in the three prefectures of Sōngjiāng, Táizhōu, and Wēnzhōu,
where many salt-makers secretly leaked salt.
Wèi requested that eighty thousand taels of treasury silver be issued
to field officials for purchase.
He further memorialized for the establishment of a Tóngzhī for Yùhuán,
to manage the salt collection.
Moreover, Guānlǐ officials were appointed for the inner and outer seas of Zhōushān, Xiùshān Chángtú near Dàishān, and Féicáo within Píngyáng Xiàn,
to manage collection and distribution.
For the salt fields of Chóngmíng,
the Zhīxiàn was ordered to take charge.
The collected treasury salt
was entirely sold to local fishermen and jellyfishermen.
Fishery salt was also permitted for permit merchants and treasury merchants to transport to other places for sale.
In addition to paying taxes according to the regulations,
they also paid an operational fee of one, two, or three qián of silver, varying.
After deducting the capital and operational expenses for the treasury,
the remaining silver was counted as surplus.
As a result, private sales were eliminated, official channels flourished,
and annually, the existing permits were insufficient for transport,
so an additional 150,000 surplus permits were issued.
For all surplus permits transported by merchants,
a rent of four fēn of silver per permit was paid.
The collected tax silver,
along with the treasury salt surplus,
was reported together in a single memorial,
amounting to approximately one hundred thousand taels of silver annually.
Since the emperor rectified salt administration,
accumulated malpractices were thoroughly cleansed.
However, after abolishing corrupt practices
and incorporating them into regular items,
the emperor also issued an edict:
"If the 'allowance for wastage' is included in the regular quota,
I fear there will be 'allowance for wastage' outside the regular quota again.
How can merchants bear it?"
This shows that he already knew of its abuses.
In the thirteenth year,
Acting Vice Censor-in-Chief Chén Shìguān said:
"The salt tax permits have a fixed quota,
and the catty amount has a fixed number.
Collecting taxes according to permits may not necessarily yield extraordinary profits,
and even if a small profit is made,
why not leave it to the merchants
to enrich their capital?
However, in recent years, many cases have emerged where 'profits are turned over to the public,'
but in reality, this is secretly coercing merchants to pay more.
Thus, an extra portion 'turned over to the public' for officials
means an extra portion of extortion for merchants.
This is what merchants suffer from.
Furthermore, those who propose 'donations' are considered 'public-spirited,'
but this also secretly coerces merchants into collective contributions.
When there is no source for the funds,
it leads to arrears in permit payments
or secretly increasing the catty weight per permit,
or excessively raising salt prices.
This is what both the state and the people suffer from.
I request that hereafter, taxes be collected strictly according to permits,
and all categories such as 'turning over to the public' and 'donations'
should be permanently stopped."
The emperor ordered Prince Zhuāng to deliberate on this.
Soon after, it was reported and enacted as requested.
At that time, Shěn Qǐyuán, the Salt Commissioner of Jiāngxī,
also wrote to Grand Governor Zhào Hóng'ēn of Jiāngnán,
saying,
"In former years, corrupt practices
were not all collected.
Now, the private gains of corrupt officials are reported as official revenue to the board.
High officials naturally have no reason to collect again,
but how can their subordinates avoid other social expenses?
This greatly burdens the merchants."
Later, something was heard by Gāozōng,
who then abolished the public expenses of the Liǎnghuái Salt Administration, the salaries of the Salt Commissioners,
and the customary silver for the black, white, and Láng wells in Yúnnán.
Initially,
Shìzōng, following Hóng'ēn's suggestion,
ordered the issuance of circulating tallies to poor people,
allowing them to carry and sell up to forty catties to make a living.
At the beginning of the Qiánlóng reign,
the Board of Revenue memorialized and approved that those aged sixty and above, or fifteen and below, or young adults with disabilities, or elderly women without support,
could report to their respective xiàn,
be issued engraved waist plaques and wooden tallies,
and go to the salt field once a day to buy salt.
Subsequently, Yǐn Huìyī, Salt Censor of Liǎnghuái, and Èmídá, Grand Governor of Liǎngguǎng, successively memorialized, saying:
"Crafty people use the pretext of poverty
to form gangs and smuggle salt.
Repeated investigations by soldiers and yámen runners
make it inconvenient to withdraw them completely."
Later, due to the excessive number of poor people,
plaque salt was suspended,
and each person was given ten to twenty-four wén of cash daily.
Soon, the Governor of Zhèjiāng was changed to Grand Governor,
concurrently managing salt administration,
and an edict was issued to appropriately determine the method of increasing catties and changing permits,
for the salt permits of Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Shàoxīng prefectures.
Following the old quota of Liǎnghuái,
fifty catties were added per permit.
For Sōngjiāng prefecture, following the example of Wēnzhōu and Táizhōu,
more than ninety thousand ticket permits were issued,
each giving four hundred catties,
with no additional tax,
in order to restore the old system.
Another edict ordered the reduction of the surplus in Yúnnán,
with prices reduced to below three taels.
Guǎngxī also had a further reduction of two lí,
and the tax on every thousand catties of salt in Liǎngguǎng was exempted from twenty-five taels of píngyín.
In the third year,
the Grand Governor of Zhèjiāng was again changed to Governor,
concurrently managing salt administration.
In the sixth year,
due to significant spoilage of Huáinán salt field salt in summer months,
it was ordered that in May and June, fifteen catties of spoilage allowance be added per permit,
