and in July and August, it be progressively reduced by five catties.
By the thirteenth year,
Huáiběi also followed suit.
It was also ordered that Liǎnghuái add ten catties per permit
beyond the fixed quota.
In the sixteenth year,
as the emperor was on an inspection tour,
an edict was issued to Liǎnghuái to add ten catties per permit to the salt permits for both commercial and edible salt, beyond the fixed quota.
Previously, at the beginning of Yōngzhèng's reign,
due to significant accumulated arrears in Chánglú,
fifty catties were added per permit.
Subsequently, the Board reported that after calculating the added catties,
the annual increase in tax revenue should be more than eighty-six thousand taels of silver.
Gāozōng, mindful of the merchants' difficulties,
ordered the tax to be halved.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the operating expenses of transporting merchants were abolished.
Following the suggestion of Liú Zǎo, Governor of Yúnnán,
additional capital silver for the black and white wells was granted.
In the forty-second year,
due to losses from land transport of Hédōng salt,
an allowance of five catties per catty was ordered.
At that time, prices were stable and sales were quick,
so Liǎnghuái requested to pre-withdraw permits from future quotas,
with annual revenue reaching five to six million.
However, due to repeated imperial tours,
with Tiānjīn as the primary stopping place,
the expenses for Lú merchants were immense,
not to mention Liǎnghuái.
Or, in times of military need,
the practice of various merchants making contributions
originated in the Yōngzhèng era,
when Lú merchants donated one hundred thousand taels of silver.
Subsequently, during the two Jīnchuān campaigns in the mid-Qiánlóng period,
the pacification of the Western Regions,
the establishment of military agricultural colonies in Yīlí,
the suppression of Taiwan rebels,
the military campaign in Hòuzàng,
and the rebellions in Chuān and Chǔ at the beginning of Jiāqìng's reign,
the donations from merchants of Huái, Zhè, Lú, and Dōng
ranged from hundreds of thousands, a million, up to eight million,
totaling no less than thirty million.
Their donations for other matters,
up to the Guāngxù and Xuāntǒng periods,
are countless.
Salt merchants often received imperial favor,
sometimes granted audiences,
sometimes awarded banquets,
with generous rewards,
comparable to high officials;
and the habit of luxury
also deepened from this.
In emergencies,
the imperial household also lent out several million to facilitate circulation.
In addition to the treasury principal, interest silver was also collected,
called treasury interest,
amounting annually to hundreds of thousands, tens of thousands, or over ten thousand, varying.
Merchant strength was consequently exhausted,
especially in Liǎnghuái and Hédōng.
In the 51st year,
due to Lǎnghuái’s salt taxes not having been prepaid for four consecutive years,
the Governor-general of Jiāngnán was ordered to investigate and report.
Soon after, a request was made that henceforth, the salt taxes be prepaid once every other *gāng*.
The Emperor decreed that the main priority was the smooth sale of the regular salt certificates,
and there was no need to adhere rigidly to specific time limits.
Subsequently, this was implemented only once in the 57th year and once in the 5th year of Jiāqìng.
Moreover, since the 33rd year, because merchants had not paid interest on the outstanding salt certificates, amounting to over 100,000 *liǎng*,
the Jiangsu Provincial Governor Zhāngbǎo was ordered to investigate and handle the matter.
The Salt Commissioner Gāo Héng and Pǔ Fú,
and the Salt Transport Commissioner Lú Jiànzēng were all severely punished,
and merchants were compelled to make up the losses.
By the 47th and 49th years,
a total of 3,632,700 *liǎng* and some odd amount had been successively remitted.
Later, when major expenditures arose,
merchants merely used the pretext of contributing funds,
and paid in installments.
After the first or second installment,
most would fall into arrears.
In the 56th year,
Jiangxi Provincial Governor Yáo Fēn reported:
“Jiànchāng Fǔ borders Fújiàn Province,
and there are many routes.
It is necessary to add anti-smuggling checkpoints and patrols
to achieve practical results.”
The Emperor said:
“The division of salt distribution areas
must ensure that the people do not have to abandon nearby sources for distant ones, or cheaper salt for more expensive salt.
Since Jiànchāng is close to Fújiàn,
the price of salt there must be lower.
Why is it not sold locally?
If the salt taxes and *yánkè* were appropriately adjusted and transferred for payment to that area,
not only would it benefit the people,
but even private smuggling would cease on its own without prohibition.”
Immediately, Jiāngnán and Jiāngxī Governor-general Juéluó Chánglín, Húguǎng Governor-general Bì Yuán, and others reported:
“The common people are solely driven by profit,
often wanting an inch after getting an *cùn* (foot).
If Jiànchāng were re-designated to Fújiàn Province,
then smugglers could easily cross into Fǔzhōu,
which would significantly affect the overall situation.”
Thus, it was ordered to remain as before.
Subsequently, Chánglín requested the establishment of a main shop in Jiànchāng
and branch shops in its subordinate counties,
to distribute taxed salt certificates.
The price would be reduced by two *wén* per *jīn* compared to Fújiàn Province’s current price to combat smuggling,
and strict patrols would be implemented at various key passes.
The Emperor’s decree ordered prompt action.
For Hédōng, since the 10th year, Zòngshénbǎo had fixed the current low price
as a permanent quota,
which subsequently caused hardship for merchants.
Later, due to poor harvests of pond salt,
salt from Lú, Méng, and Huāmǎchí was borrowed to make up the deficit,
and a small pond 60 *lǐ* west of Yúnchéng was also opened.
At that time, the people lacked food,
and no merchants were willing to undertake the business.
It was then ordered that withdrawing merchants report defaulting merchants,
with a change every five years,
but wealthy households evaded the responsibility due to cumulative burdens.
In the 47th year,
Provincial Governor Nóng Qǐ’s request was approved
to reinstate permanent merchants,
and the salt certificate territories were evenly distributed into three grades.
He further requested a price increase of two *lí*,
to be tried for three years before final determination.
Subsequently, the Ministry’s deliberation rejected it,
but the Emperor’s decree granted its implementation.
After a long time,
their strength remained exhausted.
In the 56th year,
Féng Guāngxióng was appointed Provincial Governor of Shānxī,
and Gānsu Administrative Commissioner Jiǎng Zhàokuí was transferred to be Shānxī Administrative Commissioner.
Initially,
Zhàokuí was received in audience as Hédōng Salt Transport Commissioner.
The Emperor asked about his strategy for managing Lù salt,
and he replied that the taxes should be incorporated into the land and poll tax (*dìdīng*).
When Guāngxióng arrived in the capital,
he was ordered to discuss it with the Grand Councilors.
Before a decision was made,
a memorial arrived from Zhèng Yuánshú, acting Provincial Governor and Administrative Commissioner of Shānxī,
strongly arguing against its convenience.
The Emperor said:
“Regarding the incorporation of taxes into *dìdīng*,
I had long anticipated that local officials, having received salt fees,
would surely raise objections.
Now Zhèng Yuánshú proves it.
He has been transferred to Hénán,
and Hénán also has areas where Hédōng salt is sold.
If he obstructs this from the middle,
he will be severely punished.”
In the eighth month,
Guāngxióng stated:
“The Hédōng salt administration is exhausted from accumulated fatigue.
The only solution is to incorporate the taxes into *dìdīng* and allow the people to transport salt themselves.
With no official taxes or miscellaneous fees,
and no military or police interrogations or customs detentions,
there is no reason it would not advance.
I request that starting from the 57th year of Qiánlóng,
all *yánkè* quotas for Shānxī, Shǎnxī, and Hénán
be levied under the *dìdīng* item across 172 subordinate districts within the three provinces’ salt certificate territories.”
Consequently, Shānxī was apportioned 281,102 *liǎng*, Shǎnxī 146,037 *liǎng*, and Hénán 86,633 *liǎng*, each with some odd amount.
Additionally, ten regulations were proposed: 1.
The tax silver shall be remitted to the respective provincial treasuries.
Even in years when *dìdīng* is remitted, this cannot be remitted.
The Ministry’s salt certificates shall cease to be issued,
and the fees for paper and vermilion ink shall be waived.
Local officials are not permitted to privately collect taxes or fees.
All officials below the Salt Commissioner and Salt Transport Commissioner shall be eliminated.
The Hédōng Circuit shall be relocated to Yúnchéng,
managing the three salt fields.
The salt ponds shall be maintained annually as before.
Official scales and brokers shall still be established in the three salt fields.
Within the tax items, there are accumulated surplus funds and other silver,
which should be separately apportioned for remission.
The grain and rice in the Yùnfù and Yùnchú granaries
should be merged and stored for borrowing separately.
All expenditures for the Salt Administration
shall be drawn from the nearest provincial treasury.
This was followed.
In the 57th year,
the Emperor visited Wǔtái,
and Guāngxióng and Zhàokuí reported
that since the relaxation of salt prohibitions,
the people had been freed from the hardship of apportioned taxes
and benefited from cheaper salt.
Shǎnxī Provincial Governor Qín Zōng’ēn and Hénán Provincial Governor Mù Hélín also reported that salt was plentiful and prices had decreased.
The Emperor was very pleased.
The Gānsù salt tax
had been incorporated into *dìdīng* in the 1st year of Yōngzhèng,
but merchants were recruited again in the 9th year.
At this time, the former method was resumed.
Furthermore, those in the prefectures of Hànzhōng and Yán’ān in Shǎnxī,
and various districts of Fūzhōu,
who consumed Huāmǎchí salt,
also had their salt taxes incorporated into *dìdīng*.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng,
an order was issued to cease the offering of tribute goods at the Mid-Autumn Festival by salt administrations in all provinces.
In the 5th year,
as Yúnnán's tax quota was consistently in deficit,
following the suggestion of Governor Chū Pénglíng,
it was changed to "竈煎竈賣" (stove-boiled, stove-sold),
and "民運民銷" (people transport, people sell).
This method allowed anyone, merchant or commoner,
to obtain a permit.
The transport of salt was not restricted to any specific well,
nor was the sale of salt restricted to any specific location.
After paying the tax, they were free to go wherever they wished.
Based on the actual amount boiled at various wells,
the fixed quota was evenly distributed for collection,
with any surplus treated as extra tax,
to be fully collected and remitted.
All matters concerning the issuance of permits and collection of taxes
were to be managed by well officials.
By the 8th year,
this was established as a fixed regulation.
In the 10th year,
an imperial edict instructed that each salt certificate for Liǎnghuái salt should be increased by ten catties,
which would not be included in the cost,
to cover deficits.
Previously, Àlāshàn Wang of Měnggǔ possessed the Jílāntài Salt Lake,
and commoners were permitted to purchase salt from there and transport it to Tuōkètuōchéng,
for distribution in areas of Shānxī that consumed local salt,
but it was not allowed to be transported downstream.
Subsequently, vigilance gradually slackened,
and it began to flow downstream,
not only monopolizing the lake salt but also
encroaching upon Chánglú and Liǎnghuái.
In the 14th year,
Shǎnxī-Gānsù Governor-General Nà Yànchéng memorialized about dealing with illicit merchants selling salt,
requesting that Àlāshàn Wang be ordered to hand over the treacherous Hàn and Huí commoners he was sheltering.
The King, in fear,
offered the salt lake,
and was ordered to be awarded the annual income of 8,000 taels of silver in full.
Soon, Vice Minister of Revenue Yīng Hé, along with the governors and governor-generals of Shānxī and Shǎnxī-Gānsù, jointly memorialized:
"Lù merchants are suffering losses
because a cheap price has been fixed as the regular quota.
We request that, in accordance with the precedent before the 10th year of Qiánlóng,
the price be set according to the current year's market.
As for the Jílāntài Lake,
Lù merchants find it difficult to manage both.
We request that other merchants be recruited."
In the 15th year,
due to the new merchants' deficits,
it was changed to government transport.
Vice Minister of Works Ruǎn Yuán said:
"Government transport is not difficult;
government sale is.
If the tax quota is in deficit,
it will inevitably be assigned to departments and districts,
which will either lead to the misappropriation of treasury funds
or the forced imposition on the common people.
This means the harm of being able to sell is even greater than not selling at all."
Thereupon, the ministry deliberated on the Jílāntài salt certificates,
requesting that they be returned to Àlāshàn Wang,
and the award payment be ceased.
The originally fixed quota certificates
were changed to Lù salt,
and the remaining certificates were named Jílāntài "活引" (floating certificates).
In Guǎngdōng-Guǎngxī, since the Kāngxī era, the treasury had issued funds to purchase salt,
and taxes were collected only after sale and distribution.
In the 53rd year of Qiánlóng,
Governor-General Sūn Shìyì, seeing that merchant debts had accumulated to over 698,000 taels,
requested to stop issuing treasury capital,
and instead ordered each to contribute their own funds,
setting up a bureau on the provincial river for management.
In the 54th year,
the newly appointed Governor-General Fúkāng'ān, together with Shìyì, drafted regulations,
combining the 150 ports of the two Guǎng provinces into one bureau,
appointing ten people as bureau merchants.
Externally, six sub-bureaus were established,
entrusting the bureau merchants to distribute and allocate salt to each sub-bureau
according to the fixed quota, taking into account the difficulty of sale in various areas.
All originally established port areas
were to recruit transport merchants,
allowing them to go to the bureau and sub-bureaus nearby to receive and sell salt,
and after paying taxes, 29 ports would be supplied with salt as before.
This was known as "改埠歸綱" (changing ports to a single network).
After being implemented for over twenty years,
the bureau merchants, lacking designated sales ports,
discriminated against port merchants.
Initially, bureau merchants were permitted to bundle and transport surplus salt
to make up for treasury interest.
Later, however, regardless of whether the main certificates were fulfilled,
they became greedy for selling surplus salt,
which in turn hindered the main certificates.
For stagnant ports with outstanding payments,
salt capital was often used to cover them,
and over time, losses accumulated significantly.
Although bureau merchants acknowledged and completed the payments,
port merchants still contributed according to their certificates,
but these ten individuals had already died,
and their family fortunes were ruined.
In the 11th year of Jiāqìng,
Governor-General Jiǎng Yōuxiān reported this,
and the bureau merchants were abolished,
changing the public bureau to a public office.
Six port merchants were selected to manage the six sub-bureaus,
each with their own port areas,
relying on their own funds,
thus avoiding misuse.
Furthermore, a three-year rotation was set
to prevent monopolization,
which was called "改綱歸所" (changing the network to offices).
In the 25th year,
an order was issued to cease the valuation and payment in silver for the jade tribute from Liǎnghuái.
In the 1st year of Dàoguāng,
Liǎngjiāng Governor-General Sūn Yùtíng stated that
there was no precedent for "封輪" (sealed shipment) for Huái salt reaching the Chǔ River banks,
but Salt Censor Quándé had initiated it,
and requested that scattered sales would be more convenient.
Húguǎng Governor-General Chén Ruòlín reported that a large amount of salt had accumulated,
and if fully opened for sale,
there was a risk that sales would not keep up,
leading to salt merchants and water peddlers undercutting prices and selling on credit.
An edict was issued to wait until the accumulated salt was sold out,
and then sell as it arrived.
In the 2nd year,
Liǎnghuái Salt Imperial Censor Zēng Yù reported that after the "輪規" (shipment rotation rule) was discontinued,
merchants rushed to sell, lowering prices,
which caused losses to their capital.
Yùtíng memorialized that this was not true.
Ruòlín stated that sales this year actually exceeded the previous year by over 260,000 certificates.
Thereupon, it was decided to open the shipments.
Later,
Húguǎng Governor-General Lǐ Hóngbǎo again stated that price-cutting was unavoidable,
and in the 8th year, "封輪" (sealed shipment) was reinstated.
At that time, private salt smugglers in Liǎnghuái grew daily,
and the salt administration deteriorated daily.
In Liǎnghuái,
the annual required quota of gāngyán was over 1.6 million yǐn.
By the tenth year,
Huáinán had sold only 500,000 yǐn,
resulting in a deficit of 57 million in accumulated tax silver over the years.
Huáiběi sold 20,000 yǐn,
with a deficit of 6 million in silver.
The emperor summoned Yōu Xiān back to the capital
and replaced him with Táo Shù, the Governor of Jiāngsū.
Soon after, he dispatched Wáng Dǐng, Minister of the Board of Revenue, and Shìláng Bǎo Xīng to investigate.
Shù reported, saying:
"The malpractices stem partly from the gradual accumulation of production costs
and partly from excessive private dealings conducted under official pretexts.
The only way is to greatly reduce superfluous expenses,
curtail miscellaneous levies,
and allow merchants to sell freely.
This would ensure smooth sales and stable prices,
and private salt smuggling would naturally cease."
An imperial order abolished the Salt Censor (Xún Yán Yùshǐ) position
and placed its functions under the overall management of the Governor-General (Zǒngdū).
After the ninth year,
Yùshǐ Wáng Zèngfāng, Shìjiǎng Xuéshì Gù Chún, and Guānglù Qīng Liáng Zhōngjìng all requested that taxes be set at the production sites (chǎngzào).
Tàipú Shà qīng Zhuó Bǐngtián further proposed imitating Wáng Shǒurén's method of establishing factories and levying taxes at Gàn Guān.
This was submitted to Shù for deliberation.
Shù consulted with Transport Commissioner Yú Déyuān,
who deemed it difficult to implement.
Consequently, Shù reported back, stating:
"There are three difficulties in assigning tax collection to the production sites.
First, collecting taxes from the salt workers (zàodīng).
Huáinán boils salt using a particular method,
while Huáiběi sun-dries salt in ponds,
with an approximate tax levy of over a hundred liǎng of silver.
The salt workers are all impoverished.
If taxes are collected before salt is produced,
they lack the means;
if salt is produced before taxes are collected,
should there be a poor harvest,
taxes will certainly be deferred and workers will flee.
This is the difficulty of collecting taxes from salt workers.
Second, collecting taxes from the merchants (yuánshāng).
This method, integrating scattered production into a unified system, seems more crucial.
However, salt workers, whose livelihood depends on their own efforts,
would certainly be unwilling to take orders from merchants.
Moreover, merchants are solely motivated by profit;
they would impose heavy weights when purchasing
and demand high interest on loans.
If salt workers are unwilling to sell their salt to merchants,
merchants will also lack the funds to pay the taxes.
This is also the difficulty of collecting taxes from merchants.
Third, government officials (chǎngguān) purchasing salt.
Levying taxes based on the established quota of salt certificates (yǐnyì) produced at each site
also seems practical.
However, the Huái tax amount is enormous;
how can minor officials be entrusted with it?
If they are allowed to collect and remit freely,
it's difficult to guarantee that they won't conceal reports or embezzle.
This is also the difficulty of government officials collecting taxes at the sites."
He further stated:
"Salt at the production sites
is worth only one or two wén per jīn.
If taxes are collected there,
the price will increase with the tax,
and many will compete for the profit.
In coastal areas where commoners and salt works are intermingled,
illicit boiling is very easy.
This will lead to widespread private production,
and the tax revenue will become even more deficient.
As for establishing factories to levy taxes,
it might be tried in one small area.
But do all provinces have strategic passes to defend?
Smuggling will certainly be worse than at the production sites.
In short, without officials or private dealings,
there must be no duties or taxes.
If there are already duties and taxes,
then there are officials and private dealings.
To say that returning to the production sites or establishing salt factories
can transform smugglers into law-abiding citizens,
I fear this is not possible."
The emperor approved of this.
The following year,
Shù traveled through various production sites
and proposed implementing the piàoyán (ticket salt) method in Huáiběi,
submitting ten articles of regulations.
One:
The Transport Commissioner (Yùnsī) shall print three-part tickets (piào),
one to be kept as a stub,
one to be stored by the sub-commissioner,
and one to be given to common vendors for transport.
A deadline for arrival at the destination (àndàn) shall be set,
and separation of ticketed salt or exceeding the designated destination shall not be permitted.
Two:
Every 400 jīn of salt shall constitute one yǐn,
amounting to six qián and four fēn of silver,
plus various miscellaneous fees,
totaling one liǎng, eight qián, and eight fēn.
Three:
Common vendors from various prefectures and counties
shall obtain permits from their respective prefectures and counties to purchase salt at the production sites.
Those near Hǎizhōu
shall apply and receive permits in Hǎizhōu.
Four:
Agencies and factories (júchǎng) shall be established at suitable locations within each production site
to facilitate salt delivery by salt workers
and tax payment by common vendors.
Five:
When common vendors purchase salt and leave the production site,
card inspectors (kǎyuán) shall verify it,
and then they shall proceed to their designated sales ports.
Six:
Commissioners shall be stationed at Qīngkǒu.
Seven:
Strict orders shall be given to civil and military officials to apprehend lawless elements.
Eight:
River defense.
Nine:
Establish a system for transport merchants to acknowledge sales
to ensure smooth market access.
Ten:
Abolish corrupt practices (lòuguī).
At that time, corrupt officials and clerks who profited from salt were clamorous in discussing its inconvenience,
but Shù was unmoved.
He appointed commissioners to lead and promote the transport.
Soon, people recognized its benefits,
and merchants converged from near and far,
with salt boats arriving one after another,
a sight not seen in decades.
In less than four months,
the salt requested for transport
had already exceeded 300,000 yǐn.
That year, Hǎizhōu suffered a great disaster,
and the famine victims relied on this system for transfer wages,
saving countless lives.
This method had low costs,
pure salt quality,
and cheap selling prices,
making private smuggling unprofitable,
so all switched to using ticket salt.
However, the trial implementation
was only for areas with stagnant lake transport,
including Fèngyáng, Huáiyuǎn, Fèng tái, Língbì, Fùyáng, Yǐngshàng, Xiāo Zhōu, Tàihé, Méngchéng, Yīngshān, Sìzhōu, Xūyí, Wǔhé in Ān,
Rǔyáng, Zhèngyáng, Shàngcài, Xīncài, Xīpíng, Suípíng, Xīxiàn, Quèshān in Yù,
and the 31 prefectures and counties within Jiāngsū province that were designated sales areas, namely Shānyáng, Qīnghé, Táoyuán, Pīzhōu, Suīníng, Sùqiān, Gànyú, Shúyáng, Āndōng, Hǎizhōu.
However, Shòuzhōu, Dìngyuǎn, Huòshān, Huòqiū, Liù'ān in Ān,
and Xìnyáng, Luóshān, Guāngzhōu, Guāngshān, Gùshǐ, Shāngchéng in Yù,
the 11 prefectures and counties that were previously designated as smoothly operating sales areas,
still followed the old system.
In the thirteenth year,
all were uniformly converted to the ticket system,
but the previous proposed tax rate was lower than the original quota.
It was then reverted to the original quota, with a levy of one liǎng, five fēn, and one lí per yǐn,
plus various fees,
setting the silver at two liǎng, five fēn, and one lí,
never to be increased.
Thus, the only areas not yet converted
were Tóngchéng, Shūchéng, Wúwéi, Héféi, Lújiāng, Cháoxiàn, Chúzhōu, Lái'ān, which traditionally relied on river transport from the Jiāng,
and Tiāncháng, which relied on transport from Gāoyóu Hú, a total of nine prefectures and counties.
These areas were intermingled with Huáinán
and were deemed unsuitable for attracting vendors,
lest it lead to the infiltration of private salt.
The legislation focused on changing the route, not the packaging (kǔn).
Although the old quota for Huáiběi was not light,
the cost per yǐn, transported smoothly to the destination,
already reached over ten liǎng.
The price could not cover the cost,
thus official salt could not compete with private salt.
Now, ticket salt does not follow the old route through Gàngbà Huái,
but instead changes course from Wángyíng Jiǎnbà, crossing the river into the lake.
Moreover, each package of 100 jīn,
upon leaving the production site, is not repackaged,
but goes directly to the destination.
Apart from the salt price and grain tax,
only one liǎng in transport fees
and one liǎng in river and lake boat fees are added.
Each yǐn costs a little over five liǎng,
which is more than half less than gāngyán.
The several tens of thousands of yǐn transported by river also followed this example.
Since the reform,
not only have taxes been fully collected with a surplus, not a deficit,
but also canal dredging, donation of public welfare factories, and repair of examination halls have been undertaken.
A hundred neglected affairs were revitalized,
because only by light taxation could private salt be combated,
and by smooth sales could quotas be exceeded.
Thus, the salt of two gāngs was sold with the effort of one gāng,
and the taxes of two gāngs were collected with the effort of one gāng.
At that time, there was a strong desire to extend this to Huáinán,
but it was not realized.

a great fire broke out at Tángjiǎo塘角 in Wǔchāng武昌, Húběi湖北,

More than five million in money, provisions, and capital were lost,

and requested that the ticketing system in Huáinán淮南 be reformed,

Category B salt referred to

200 jīn斤 of category B salt would be carried.

With the abolition of excessive fees

Thus, within a few months of implementation,

Salt prices in various districts of western Chǔ楚 plummeted,

In that year, the Liǎnghuái兩淮 region actually collected five million liǎng of silver.
Although after two convoys, permits again became stagnant and taxes were deficient,

Shù澍 first implemented this in Huáiběi,

Three years later,

In the six districts of Jì薊 and Zūn遵,

and the complete abandonment of廣西 (Guǎngxī)'s淮鹽 (Huáiyán) in the fields,
廣東 (Guǎngdōng)'s taxes still retained eighty to ninety percent.
In四川 (Sìchuān),
initially,鹽 (yán) production in射洪 (Shèhóng) and蓬溪 (Péngxī) of潼川府 (Tóngchuānfǔ) was robust,
followed by犍為 (Qiánwéi),樂山 (Lèshān),榮縣 (Róngxiàn) of嘉定府 (Jiādìngfǔ),
and then富順 (Fùshùn) of川府 (Chuānfǔ).
In a few years,
the saltworks of射洪 (Shèhóng) and蓬溪 (Péngxī) became inferior to those of犍 (Qián),樂 (Lè),富 (Fù), and榮 (Róng).
In the forty-ninth year of Qiánlóng,
salt wells everywhere were in decline.
林俊 (Lín Jùn),
who was the官鹽茶道 (guānyánchádào),
allowed the people to dig wells without increasing taxes,
and蜀鹽 (Shǔyán) then began to flourish.
However,潼川 (Tóngchuān) could not return to its former state.
Moreover, it produced more鹽花 (yánhuā) and less巴 (bā),
and boiling salt required grass and labor, leading to arrears of 70,000 in taxes.
It was then proposed to cooperate with犍 (Qián) merchants,
with a twelve-year limit,
to clear accumulated arrears by the deadline.
It was then requested to extend the cooperation for another twelve years,
and manage it independently when that term expired.
After just one year, it was already 20,000 overdue,
so another extension was requested.
By the eighth year of Dàoguāng,
three terms had expired,
but its saltworks produced even less salt.
Each year, only the regular tax was paid,
not the羨截 (xiànjié).
羨 (xiàn) refers to surplus.
截 (jié) refers to
payment made when the tax receipt was cut.

At that time, in漢州 (Hànzhōu),茂州 (Màozhōu),巴州 (Bāzhōu),劍州 (Jiànzhōu),蓬州 (Péngzhōu),什邡 (Shífāng),射洪 (Shèhóng),鹽亭 (Yántíng),平武 (Píngwǔ),江油 (Jiāngyóu),彰明 (Zhāngmíng),石泉 (Shíquán),營山 (Yíngshān),儀隴 (Yílǒng),新寧 (Xīnníng),閬中 (Lángzhōng),通江 (Tōngjiāng),安岳 (Ānyuè),羅江 (Luójiāng),安縣 (Ānxiàn),綿竹 (Miánzhú),德陽 (Déyáng),梓潼 (Zǐtóng),南江 (Nánjiāng),西充 (Xīchōng),井研 (Jǐngyán),銅梁 (Tóngliáng),大足 (Dàzú),定遠 (Dìngyuǎn),榮昌 (Róngchāng),隆昌 (Lóngchāng)—thirty-one prefectures and counties—
due to declining brine and stagnant sales,
merchants went bankrupt and depots were depleted.
People bought salt from nearby factories for consumption,
and regular and miscellaneous tax silver was included in the地丁 (dìdīng) levy.
This was because salt merchants were extravagant,
and their family fortunes declined daily.
They then sought wealthy households to rent out to permit merchants,
known as
"號商 (hàoshāng)."
The taxes and surplus paid
had to be submitted by the permit merchants for sealing,
and the permit merchants often misappropriated funds,
and officials sometimes colluded with them.
By the thirtieth year,
the entire system was in decay.
徐澤醇 (Xú Zéchún) became Governor-General,
and investigated accumulated arrears and surplus taxes totaling over 237,000兩 (liǎng),
and 228,581 unpaid remaining permits.
Therefore, he allocated temporary sales,
registered the names of號商 (hàoshāng),
and held them responsible for sealing their own boxes.
At that time, only the border merchants of犍 (Qián) and富 (Fù), and the 計商 (jìshāng) of成都 (Chéngdū) and華陽 (Huáyáng) were relatively prosperous,
and their sales outlets were also active.
The rest were sluggish,
with潼商 (Tóngshāng) being the worst.
So, the water permits used in黔邊 (Qiánbiān) were withdrawn
and handed over to the two merchants of犍 (Qián) and富 (Fù) for management.
In雲南 (Yúnnán),
after the reforms,
private salt became even more rampant,
and various wells often had deficits,
especially in迤西 (Yíxī) and迤南 (Yínán).
Its northeast corner consumed川鹽 (Chuānyán),
and its southeast corner consumed粵鹽 (Yuèyán),
making it very difficult to meet deadlines.
In the sixth year of Dàoguāng,
Governor-General趙慎畛 (Zhào Shènzhěn) memorialized, requesting that the amount of salt be inspected at the wells,
and sales areas be designated.
御史 (Yùshǐ)廖敦行 (Liáo Dūnxíng) also said that dividing sales areas
was not as good as widely seeking subsidiary wells.
The Emperor ordered the new Governor-General阮元 (Ruǎn Yuán) to implement it experimentally.
Later, when many large wells were flooded and abandoned,
it was still reliant on the subsidiary wells for replenishment,
and thus it recovered.
Guó Fān (曾國藩) reformed the salt administration.
What differed from Táo Shù (陶澍) was that
Shù's (澍) intention was to sell salt in scattered batches (散輪),
aligning with Yù Tíng (玉庭) and Ruò Lín (若霖).
Guó Fān's (國藩) intention was to sell in whole batches (整輪),
aligning with Quán Dé (全德) and Zēng Yù (曾燠).
However, when Yù Tíng (玉庭) and Ruò Lín (若霖) planned to sell in scattered batches,
they would first sell all the batches from the previous two months,
then open the batches that arrived in the next two months.
This was not without combining scattered sales with whole batches,
and Shù (澍) actually learned from their idea.
Therefore, Guó Fān (國藩), observing the drawbacks of抢售 (qiǎngshòu) (搶售,搶售) (搶售,搶售) (rush sales), advocated for whole batches,
thus establishing the General Depot for Supervised Sales (總棧督銷).
This was to protect both the field price (場價)
and the shore price (岸價).
The General Depot was initially
established in Guā Zhōu (瓜洲) because Yí Zhēng (儀徵) was not easily restored.
Later, the shore was eroded and collapsed by water,
so it was moved back to Yí Zhēng (儀徵).
The Office of Supervised Sales (督銷局) was located in Hàn Kǒu (漢口) for the Hú Běi (鄂) shore,
in Cháng Shā (長沙) for the Hú Nán (湘) shore,
in Nán Chāng (南昌) for the Jiāng Xī (西) shore,
and in Dà Tōng (大通) for the Ān Huī (皖) shore.
Not long after,
Guó Fān (國藩) was transferred to supervise Zhí Lì (直隸),
and Lǐ Hóng Zhāng (李鴻章) succeeded him.
Among the additional taxes,
the most important was the "循環給運" (xún huán gěi yùn) (cyclic allocation and transport) system.
This method integrated the issuance of permits (認引) with supervised sales,
allowing merchants to apply for permits for the next batch
immediately after selling the current batch of salt.
It was first implemented in Huái Nán (淮南),
and later extended to Huái Běi (淮北).
This essentially incorporated the gāng fǎ (綱法) (纲法) (綱法,纲法) (gāng fǎ) (gang system) into the piào fǎ (票法) (票法) (票法,票法) (ticket system),
maintaining existing merchants as primary distributors and not easily replacing them with new ones.
When merchants had generational businesses,
officials had assigned responsibilities,
which was seen as having fewer malpractices than the previous system of verifying assets and drawing lots.
From then on, successive officials followed this.
It was not until the fifth year of Guāng Xù (光緒) (1879) that the idea of increasing permits arose.
"Increasing permits" meant that
the Board advised an increase of 80,000 permits for Huái Běi (淮北).
At that time, Governor-General Shěn Bǎo Zhēn (沈葆楨) submitted a memorial stating:
"In recent years, salt merchants, due to high ticket prices,
have coveted an increase in permits.
Among past salt officials, none were more proficient in salt administration than Zēng Guó Fān (曾國藩).
Whenever he settled on a method,
he would consider the advantages and disadvantages over several decades,
as if personally involved,
and plan comprehensively.
However, the permit quota for Huái Běi (淮北)
was only set at just over 290,000.
How could he have disregarded state finance and commercial sentiment?
The deterioration of salt administration was primarily due to the quota exceeding sales.
Initially, it barely met the reporting limits,
but over time, it became unmanageable.
Consequently, old and new tickets were bundled together,
then soon followed by unified sales and melting sales,
and shortly after, by concurrent levies and suspension of transport.
Only when quotas are small will there be fewer merchants;
fewer merchants make it easier to eliminate malpractices
and also easier to facilitate sales."
In the eighth year (1882),
Zuǒ Zōng Táng (左宗棠) supervised the Liǎng Jiāng (兩江) region
and requested an increase in permits:
160,000 for Huái Běi (淮北),
110,000 for the Hú Běi (鄂) shore of Huái Nán (淮南), 40,000 for the Hú Nán (湘) shore, and over 42,000 for the Ān Huī (皖) shore.
The Board deliberated and approved the increase for Huái Běi (淮北),
but only 30,000 for the Hú Běi (鄂) shore, 10,000 for the Hú Nán (湘) shore, and over 17,000 for the Ān Huī (皖) shore.
When Zēng Guó Quán (曾國荃) took office,
he petitioned to revoke the additional permits for Huái Běi (淮北).
This was because the main tax (正課) from the Liǎng Huái (兩淮) region
initially, including various levies for weaving, river works, and copper,
totaled only over 1.8 million.
Each permit was taxed at just over one liǎng of silver.
The levies for weaving, river works, and copper
were due to the generous integrity-fostering allowance (養廉) for salt administration officials and transport commissioners,
and also many illicit fees.
Annually, 220,000 liǎng of silver were remitted for weaving,
and 50,000 liǎng were donated for river works.
During the Revolt of the Three Feudatories (三藩之變),
the supply of copper from Yún Nán (滇) was obstructed,
so various salt officials were assigned to purchase and contribute,
incurring another 50,000 liǎng for shipping costs.
By the middle of the Yōng Zhèng (雍正) reign (1723-1735),
the integrity-fostering allowance and illicit fees were reduced to become part of the main tax,
and subsequently other items were added.
Consequently, the total internal and external expenditures, both regular and miscellaneous, became enormous,
increasing to six or seven liǎng per permit,
only becoming lighter after the reform to tickets.
In the Tóng Zhì (同治) reign (1862-1875),
the permit territories had not yet recovered,
but the duty was effectively supplemented by likin (釐金),
so there was no need to increase permits.
Regarding the sales volume of southern salt,
the Hú Běi (鄂) shore traditionally accounted for the largest share.
When it was seized by Sì Chuān (川) salt,
in the seventh year of Tóng Zhì (同治) (1868),
Guó Fān (國藩) requested the restoration of permit territories.
The Board deliberated and ordered Sì Chuān (川) salt to cease distribution in Hú Běi (楚).
Governor-General Lǐ Hàn Zhāng (李瀚章) of Hú Guǎng (湖廣) memorialized that it should not be stopped,
but rather a bureau should be established in Shā Shì (沙市)
to distribute Sì Chuān (川) salt at 80% and Huái (淮) salt at 20%.
Later, calculated by package,
Huái (淮) salt weighed less per package than Sì Chuān (川) salt,
so the named 20% was actually less than 10%.
In the tenth year (1871),
Guó Fān (國藩) reiterated:
"Sì Chuān (川) encroaching on Huái (淮) territory
should lead to Huái (淮) salt being 80% and Sì Chuān (川) salt 20%,
or Huái (淮) 70% and Sì Chuān (川) 30%.
Currently, the Hú Běi (楚) Governor, due to the large Hú Běi (鄂) military expenditure,
fears that if Sì Chuān (川) salt sales are not smooth,
the revenue will sharply decrease.
What I seek is
that Huái (淮) salt can be sold on the Hú Běi (楚) shore,
which would revive merchant vitality.
I am willing to allocate a larger percentage or the entire amount of the likin (釐銀) due to Hú Běi (鄂)."
The Emperor ordered the Governors and Governors-General of Sì Chuān (川) and Hú Běi (楚) to convene and discuss.
Guó Fān (國藩) and others memorialized that
"the four prefectures of Wǔ Chāng (武昌), Hàn Yáng (漢陽), Huáng Zhōu (黃州), and Dé Ān (德安) be returned to Huái Nán (淮南);
the five prefectures of Ān Lù (安陸), Xiāng Yáng (襄陽), Yún Yáng (鄖陽), Jīng Zhōu (荊州), and Yí Chāng (宜昌),
and Jīng Mén Zhōu (荊門州), still permit Sì Chuān (川) salt for interim sales;
Hú Nán (湖南) allows Sì Chuān (川) salt to be sold only in the three prefectures of Yuè (岳), Cháng (常), and Lǐ (澧);
Yuè Zhōu (岳州) and Cháng Dé (常德) should also revert to Huái (淮),
while Lǐ Zhōu (澧州) temporarily sells Sì Chuān (川) salt."
The Board deliberated and approved this.
In the second year of Guāng Xù (光緒) (1876),
Guì Zhōu (貴州) was pacified,
and Censor Zhōu Shēng Shù (周聲澍) memorialized that the Sì Chuān (川) salt permit territories had been restored,
requesting that all prefectures and sub-prefectures in northern Hú Nán (湖南) be fully assigned to Huái Nán (淮南).
The Board deliberated and approved his request.
Thereupon, Bǎo Zhēn (葆楨) reported that the Sì Chuān (川) likin (釐) from Hú Běi (湖北)
annually reported to the Board amounted to over 1.5 million strings,
totaling less than 900,000 liǎng of silver,
requesting that Huái (淮) merchants undertake its complete payment.
However, the Governors and Governors-General of Hú Guǎng (湖廣), fearing that the fixed Sì Chuān (川) likin (釐)
would make contracted payments unreliable,
jointly sided with Sì Chuān (川) and rejected Huái (淮).
By the eighth year (1882),
Zōng Táng (宗棠) again exchanged letters to discuss the matter,
but it was never carried out.
Since the early Shùn Zhì (順治) reign (1644-1661), Cháng Lú (長蘆) only levied a tax of just over 202,000.
In the twelfth year (1655),
according to the Míng (明) system, deficiencies in the Níng (寧) military provisions and merchant "dripping pearl" payments were identified,
and continued to be collected and remitted as before.
In the Kāng Xī (康熙) reign (1662-1722),
taxes and permits were again increased,
reaching just over 426,000.
In the final years of Qián Lóng (乾隆) (late 18th century),
due to annual miscalculations in taxes,
many were impeached and dismissed.
Consequently, all merchants collectively agreed
to donate two qián of silver per permit in addition to the regular tax,
to serve as a compensatory fund,
named "參課" (cān kè) (participatory tax).
By the end of the Dào Guāng (道光) reign (1820-1850),
the tax quota became even heavier,
and "shore outstanding" amounts increased.
Thus, an additional "shore outstanding tax" was added,
requiring four fēn of silver per permit,
but it was still insufficient.
At this point, Guó Fān (國藩) supervised Zhí Lì (直隸)
and memorialized:
"Since the registered merchants (認商) have already remitted over a thousand liǎng of silver to the treasury,
a three-year limit should be set for the guaranteeing merchants (保商).
Any arrears within this limit
shall be recovered at 20% from the principal merchant.
The remaining 10% shall be jointly compensated by the gāng zǒng (綱總) (gang head) and the scattered merchants who issued the bond.
After the limit, they shall not be involved,
to avoid evasion."
This was adopted.
At that time, among the salt officials, besides Guó Fān, Hóng Zhāng, and Bǎo Zhēn,
only Zōng Táng and Dīng Bǎo Zhēn were renowned for their ability.
In the early Tóngzhì reign,
Zōng Táng was the Governor of Zhèjiāng.
He memorialized, saying:
"Since the fall of Jīnlíng,
Huái salt has inundated Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, and Sōngjiāng.
Only Shàoxīng has managed to hold its own with great effort.
Later, many salt distribution areas were lost,
and Zhèjiāng province also fell.
When eastern Zhèjiāng was recovered,
an order was first given to Shàoxīng to temporarily manage 'ticket salt' (piào yán).
The provincial capital, along with Jiāxīng and Húzhōu, were subsequently pacified,
but the old merchants lacked the strength to transport and sell.
I request that all four areas be universally converted to ticket salt,
and that a bureau be established to inspect sales figures."
The Ministry deliberated and approved.
In the tenth year,
Censor Qí Chén memorialized, saying:
"The prefectural bureaus in eastern Zhèjiāng,
when merchants bring salt,
often lower its price
to facilitate purchase by salt agencies,
then immediately raise its price again
for resale,
with the profits going to private pockets.
It should be abolished."
The Ministry deliberated and issued an imperial edict to Governor Yáng Chāngjùn to investigate and report.
Soon, he reported, stating:
"The two Zhèjiāng circuits originally collected taxes first, then salt.
Since the conversion to ticket transport,
due to the merchants' limited capital,
only half the tax was paid,
with the other half to be completed after sales.
It is proposed to abolish the salt agencies
but retain the prefectural bureaus
to supervise the collection of the latter half of the tax silver."
This was approved.
In Fújiàn during the Qiánlóng reign,
the fifteen zhou and xian subordinate to the three prefectures of Yánpíng, Jiànníng, and Shàowǔ in the western route,
the five zhou and xian subordinate to Fúníng prefecture in the eastern route,
and the two xian of Mǐnhóu in the southern route,
were managed by merchants,
known as
the "merchant guild" (shāng bāng).
The twenty-one ting, zhou, and xian subordinate to the four prefectures of Fúzhōu, Xīnghuà, Zhāngzhōu, and Quánzhōu in the southern route
were managed by officials,
known as
the "official guild" (guān bāng),
also called
the "xiàn ào official guild" (xiàn ào guān bāng),
which was contracted out to merchants,
named
"pò hù."
Afterwards, it was evenly distributed among the various merchants in the western route for代理銷售 (dài xiāo),
hence the name
"dai’é" (代額).
The merchant guild, finding the tax light,
was happy to undertake transport,
but then fell into arrears on the principal tax.
In the early Jiāqìng reign,
the system of "additional collection" (dài zhēng) and "reduced salt permits" (jiǎn yǐn) was implemented.
Subsequently, the dai’é system was abolished,
and after a long time, bankruptcies followed one another.
In the first year of Dàoguāng,
it was changed to "signed merchants" (qiān shāng).
At that time, all old debts were priced to new merchants,
coupled with the neglect of salt field affairs.
Officials residing in the provincial capital
allowed sea vessels to load salt
and engage in private trading,
called
"convenient sea" (biàn hǎi),
which led to numerous abuses.
By the twenty-ninth year, bankruptcies recurred,
so it was changed to official transport,
but those undertaking the transport pocketed half of the transport funds.
Indeed, in Fújiàn province, salt sales
in the Qiánlóng reign used "tuan cheng" (團秤) scales;
for every hundred catties, it was equivalent to one hundred sixty catties on a "shēn fǎ chèng" (申砝秤),
with thirty catties used to compensate for shrinkage.
In the middle of the Jiāqìng reign,
"bù fǎ chèng" (部砝秤) scales were adopted,
and no compensation salt was given.
The salt permit for each hundred catties of "dān yǐn" (擔引) or "péng yǐn" (篷引) only granted forty-two catties,
ordered to be sold as one hundred catties,
while completing the tax for one hundred catties of dai’é,
which led to increasingly severe losses.
Thereafter, the system became progressively worse.
In the fourth year of Tóngzhì,
Zōng Táng became the Governor-General of Mǐn,
and requested a change to ticket transport,
ordering officials of each salt field to reside there.
In the western route, "yǐn shāng" (引商) became "piào shāng" (票商);
in xiàn ào, "pò hù" became "fàn hù" (販戶);
"yán dào piào" (鹽道票) was used to replace the salt permit,
named
"fàn dān" (販單).
In the western route, thirty permits initiated a ticket;
in the eastern and southern routes and xiàn ào, one hundred permits initiated a ticket.
This was because each permit in the western route was six hundred seventy-five catties,
while each permit in the eastern and southern routes and xiàn ào was one hundred catties.
Miscellaneous taxes were abolished,
and a surcharge of one qián was added to each liǎng of the regular tax,
to be paid when collecting the ticket.
An additional five qián in likin (lí) was levied,
collected by bureaus established in various salt distribution areas.
In total, the western route collected four liǎng five qián and some fen of silver per permit,
while the eastern and southern routes and xiàn ào collected four qián four fen and some li.
Later, finding the western route's tax heavy,
he memorialized to reduce the likin collected with each liǎng of tax by four qián.
All old arrears were pardoned.
While the interest on the treasury funds was waived,
the principal was mandated to be gradually repaid.
In that year, over four hundred thousand liǎng of tax, shrinkage, and likin silver were collected,
along with over one hundred ninety thousand liǎng of old arrears.
The four hundred thousand liǎng were then set as the regular quota.
After several years of implementation,
merchants were greatly pleased, and
private smuggling disappeared.
The Huāmǎchí salt tax in Shǎnxī
was traditionally collected by the Provincial Administration Commissioner.
In the twelfth year of Tóngzhì,
Zōng Táng, as the Governor-General of Shǎnxī and Gānsù,
due to military campaigns in the western frontier,
changed the tax to likin,
establishing a bureau in Dìngbiān to collect it,
named Huādìng Yánlí.
Thus, the salt profits of Shǎnxī reverted to Gānsù province.
Initially, Chuān salt used Yúnnán and Guìzhōu as its border markets.
And the Guìzhōu market was further divided into four routes:
the route from Yǒngníng was called Yǒng'àn (永岸);
the route from Héjiāng reaching Rénhuái in Guìzhōu was called Rén'àn (仁岸);
the route from Fúzhōu was called Fú'àn (涪岸);
and the route from Qíjiāng was called Qí'àn (綦岸).
By this time, transport merchants were exhausted and impoverished,
relying solely on
"relieving Chǔ" (jì Chǔ) as a strategy for smooth sales.
When the Huáinán territory was recovered and its permits reinstated,
stagnant permits accumulated to over eighty thousand,
and accumulated arrears and surplus deductions amounted to over a million gold.
In the early Guāngxù reign,
Bǎo Zhēn, as Governor-General of Chuān,
set up official transport and merchant sales,
starting with the Guìzhōu market,
formulating fifteen regulations: namely, reducing excessive fees,
clarifying accumulated permits,
reviewing sales on commission,
bureau transport and merchant sales,
concurrently managing the Jì'àn (計岸),
permits allocated by bureaus,
extending the time limit for reporting sales,
strictly setting overhauls,
prudent handling of receipts and disbursements,
earnest collection of Guìzhōu likin,
actual payment of boat fares,
deleting "yǐn dǐ" (引底) (yǐn dǐ refers to
transport merchants renting permits from resident merchants to distribute salt,
paying over twenty liǎng of silver per permit,
collected by the merchant chief
as tax and surplus deduction,
for payment of permit fees,
and official and commissioner's collection fees,
and merchant bureau public expenses,
with the remaining two liǎng
distributed among the resident merchants.
By this time, the accumulated surplus deductions over the years
had already been paid by the transport merchants,
and should have been entirely abolished.
However, due to its long history,
it was provisionally allowed to remain at one liǎng),
adding ticket processing,
judiciously retaining subsidies,
and offering appropriate rewards.
A general bureau was established in Lúzhōu,
with branch bureaus in each of the four markets,
and Dàoyuán Táng Jiǒng was dispatched to supervise its operation.
Afterwards, the Yúnnán market was taken over.
Chuān salt distributed in Yúnnán
only had the Zhāngwō and Nánguǎng bureaus in Zhaotōng and Dōngchuān prefectures,
known as Dàdiānbian (大滇邊) and Xiǎodiānbian (小滇邊).
The management there was more difficult than in the Guìzhōu market,
because Yúnnán had its own salt,
making encroachment very easy.
Bǎo Zhēn devised methods to block and curb it,
and finally opened transport in the fifth year.
Since official transport and merchant sales began,
it is estimated that in the current year, all quotas for border regions and various other areas were completely cleared,
and in addition, over ten thousand accumulated *yǐn* were also sold.
The collected taxes, extra levies, tariffs, and various other revenues amounted to over a million more,
but treacherous commoners found it inconvenient.
The court sent Ēnchéng and Tónghuá to investigate other banks,
and when they reached Chuān,
Wáng Yúzhào, a prominent gentry member from Fùshùn, used the guise of salt-well households to present a complaint,
requesting a change to official supervision and merchant sales.
An imperial edict was issued seeking opinions.
Bǎozhēn memorialized, saying:
"Official supervision and merchant sales
mean profits go to officials and merchants.
Official transport and official sales
mean all power belongs to officials.
Both have great drawbacks.
Only with official transport and merchant sales
can officials and merchants mutually restrain each other."
Soon after, the complaint case was investigated and clarified,
and a memorial was presented requesting its handling.
By the end of the Guāngxù reign,
many of the various allocated areas also changed to official transport.
Beyond this, in areas like Fèngtiān, the system changed from taxation to salt permits (*yǐn*),
which ceased in the middle of the Kāngxī reign,
with no levies for over one hundred seventy years.
In the sixth year of Tóngzhì (1867),
General Dūxīng Ā memorialized and was granted approval to implement the *quèlí* (monopoly levy) method,
where each *què* of salt was subject to a thousand *dōngqián*,
to be used for local military expenses.
In the third year of Guāngxù (1877),
General Chónghòu requested an increase to two thousand four hundred *wén*.
In the eighth year (1882),
General Chóngqǐ again requested an increase of two thousand four hundred *wén*,
named the "four-eight salt *lí*",
which was a revenue source for training troops.
In the seventeenth year (1891),
the Hùbù (Board of Revenue) raised an additional two thousand four hundred *wén* for military provisions,
named the "two-four salt *lí*",
which was a revenue source to be remitted to the Board.
In the twenty-fourth year (1898),
General Yīkètáng'ā added one thousand two hundred *wén*,
named the "one-two salt *lí*",
which was a revenue source for promoting education.
These three items were collectively called the "eight-four salt *lí*".
In the twenty-eighth year (1902),
General Zēngqí again memorialized to establish a Dūxiāojú (Supervisory Sales Bureau),
adding four *zhìqián* per *jīn*,
called a "price increase,"
to serve as official capital.
However, the original proposal was for the government to set up a bureau to purchase,
establish warehouses, and transport for sale,
named "supervisory sales,"
but in reality, it was official transport.
When the Japan-Russia War broke out,
it was not implemented.
In the thirty-second year (1906),
General Zhào Ěrxùn requested to abolish the name "supervisory sales,"
establishing a Guānyán Zǒngjú (General Official Salt Bureau) in Fèngtiān,
with branches in Jílín and Hēilóngjiāng,
allowing merchants to pay tax and transport for sale directly at the salt pans.
In the thirty-third year (1907),
the Dōng Sānsěng (Three Eastern Provinces) were established as provinces,
and Governor-General Xú Shìchāng changed the Guānyán Zǒngjú to the Dōng Sānsěng Yánwù Zǒngjú (General Salt Affairs Bureau of the Three Eastern Provinces),
whereupon Jílín and Hēilóngjiāng began implementing official transport.
Initially, annual taxes collected were two hundred forty thousand or four hundred thousand *liǎng* of silver,
and when Ěrxùn arrived,
it reached over one million,
and later one million four hundred thousand.
Mongolian salt had always been managed by the Fānbù (Lifan Yuan).
For its sale in Shǎnxī and Gānsù,
the Jílāntài salt lake of the Ālāshàn Banner was the major source,
commonly known as "red salt."
Before Dàoguāng,
people were allowed to transport and sell it.
In the eighth year of Xiánfēng (1858),
merchants were first recruited to undertake transport,
paying eight *liǎng* of silver per hundred *jīn*.
During the Tóngzhì period,
it suffered from the Muslim rebellions,
merchants were distressed, and taxes were in arrears.
Zōngtáng reformed the tax into a *lí*,
adding five *zhìqián* per *jīn*.
In Shānxī,
red salt was also the most prevalent.
In the early Jiāqìng reign,
the Ālāshàn King presented the Jílāntài salt lake,
and the government recruited merchants to manage its transport,
designating the various departments outside the pass,
the two prefectures of Dàtóng and Shuòpíng,
and the districts formerly consuming local salt in Tàiyuán and Fénzhōu, etc.,
as the sales area for Jí salt permits.
This was abolished in the seventeenth year (1812).
For all salt entering the pass,
tax was collected at Shāhǔkǒu,
one *fēn* five *lí* per *jīn*.
In addition, there were three other types:
Ō'ěrdōusī Banner salt,
Sūnítè Banner salt,
commonly known as "white salt,"
and Wūzhūmùqìn Banner salt,
known as "green salt."
Initially, following the old and young salt regulations,
it was sold within the pass.
Tax was paid at the end of Jiāqìng.
By the Guāngxù reign,
all adopted the *chōulí* (levy collection) method.
In Zhílì,
the green salt and white salt
were subjected to a *chōulí* request by the Cháhā'ěr Dūshǒng in the twenty-eighth year of Guāngxù (1902),
four *zhìqián* per *jīn*,
yielding approximately over one hundred twenty thousand *liǎng* of silver annually.
The following year,
the Rèhé Dūshǒng also collected a similar levy,
five *wén* per *jīn*.
In the same year, the Zhílì Governor-General also requested to establish a Dūxiāojú in Zhāngjiākǒu,
setting up factories outside the pass to collect salt,
recruiting merchants to undertake the business,
paying a package tax of two *liǎng* of silver per thousand *jīn*,
yielding approximately over thirty thousand annually.
In the thirty-third year (1907),
Rèhé also established a bureau,
collecting four *qián* of silver per hundred *jīn*.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng (1909),
it was reduced to two *qián* five *fēn*,
yielding approximately over sixty thousand annually.
Xīnjiāng traditionally allowed people to transport and sell salt.
After the thirty-fourth year of Guāngxù (1908),
tax was first collected at the Jīnghé salt lake (fourteen thousand four hundred *liǎng*),
Díhuà (five thousand one hundred *liǎng*),
Shànshàn (two thousand four hundred *liǎng*),
while the rest remained untaxed.
Initially,
the salt *lí* was created in the north and south of Liǎnghuái,
and the amounts were heavy.
After Guófān's rectification,
it was slightly reduced.
Subsequently, to restore the Huái system,
it was also proposed to heavily collect the Chuān *lí*.
In the fifth year of Xiánfēng (1855),
it was set that for *huāyán*, eight *liǎng* of *lí* would be collected per *yǐn* of ten thousand *jīn*.
Later, due to merchants privately adding up to seventeen thousand *jīn*,
the Chuān Governor-General Luò Bǐngzhāng requested to add seventeen *liǎng* of *lí* per *yǐn* based on the added *jīn*,
making a total of twenty-five *liǎng* of regular *lí*.
Later, all provinces added similar levies.
By the Guāngxù reign, when copper coins were circulated,
salt prices had already secretly increased,
and beyond the *líjīn*, further price increases were proposed.
This matter originated during the Yōngzhèng period.
The price of Chánglú salt,
since the twenty-seventh year of Kāngxī (1688), ranged from one *fēn* four *háo* to one *fēn* two *lí* six *háo* of silver per *jīn*.
In the sixth year of Yōngzhèng (1728),
the Salt Inspector Censor Zhèng Chánbǎo memorialized, stating
"Merchants use silver for payments,
while commoners buy salt with copper coins.
In the Kāngxī era,
one *liǎng* of silver exchanged for one thousand four to five hundred *zhìqián*,
so one *jīn* of salt cost
sixteen *wén*.
Now, one *liǎng* of silver equals two thousand *qián*,
but the salt price remains the same,
or even drops to thirteen or fourteen *wén*.
Exchanging copper coins for silver
does not cover the original amount.
It should be requested that the ministerial officials consult with the governor-general to deliberate in detail."
By the tenth year (1732),
it was approved to add one *lí* of silver per *jīn*.
After Qiánlóng, this was extended to other provinces,
but the intention was only to assist merchants.
In the fifth year of Jiāqìng (1800),
the Chánglú Salt Inspector Censor Guān Yù, due to unrest in Chuān and Chǔ,
memorialized to request a price increase for urgent expenses.
Rénzōng decreed:
"To disturb the populace for military provisions,
I will not do it.
Currently, those who consume salt spend only one or two *wén* daily.
If the price is increased, everyone will suffer.
Moreover, private smuggling will surely arise due to excessively high salt prices."
Later, due to the expenses for river works,
there were still many price increases after Dàoguāng.
By the second year of Guāngxù (1876),
to manage the Western expedition's grain supply,
Assistant Minister of the Hùbù Yuán Bǎohéng memorialized to request a uniform increase of two *wén* in all provinces,
but it was shelved due to the strong objection of the Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, Shěn Bǎozhēn.
Since then, the Xīn Zhèng were implemented,
all of which drew upon the profits from salt.
For instance, in the 20th year [of Guāngxù's reign], due to provocation from Rìběn and the establishment of defenses,
the Board notified various provinces to collect an additional two *wén* per *jīn*.
In the 27th year, due to the need to raise indemnity funds for repayment,
an additional four *wén* were collected.
In the 34th year,
due to offsetting pharmaceutical taxes,
another four *wén* were added,
half for offsetting military training expenses,
and half allocated for use by salt-producing provinces;
these were the most notable instances.
At the time, frontier officials convened merchants for a meeting,
all expressing concern over stagnant sales,
but the situation could not be stopped;
since then, the income had increased several times compared to before the Dàoguāng reign.
However, Chánglú suffered disruptions from the Quánfěi,
merchants lost capital,
even resorting to foreign loans.
In various places where salt vouchers were issued in Shāndōng,
since the 6th year of Tóngzhì when it was decided to return to government management,
there have been many irregularities.
Hédōng still returned to joint government and private transport,
but sales were not brisk.
The same was true for voucher transport in Fújiàn and government transport in Sìchuān.
Guǎngdōng's Cháoqiáo,
formerly managed by government transport,
was then, along with the Liùguì, entirely transferred to merchant management,
but its effectiveness was also limited.
In Yúnnán's Zǐjǐng,
very few remained.
However, the decline in Huái and Zhè was particularly severe.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng,
Dùzhī Bù Shàngshū Zài Zé memorialized, saying:
"In Huáinán, due to the eastward shift of the sea,
the brine concentration gradually weakened,
salt production at fields like Shígǎng and Liúzhuāng decreased,
and Jīnshāchǎng even stopped producing salt.
As for the three fields in Huáiběi,
being close to the sea,
the brine concentration was still strong;
however, sun-dried salt was produced in brick ponds,
and by regulation, vouchers had to be issued according to the number of ponds.
Recently, beyond the brick ponds,
pond bases were extensively opened,
even leading to an increase in new bases,
while old beaches were not leveled,
resulting in an even more unlimited production quota.
Furthermore, the Southern merchants of Tóngdéchāng established ponds in Huáiběi,
which Northern merchants found particularly inconvenient.
Among the flourishing salt production areas in Liǎngzhè,
Yúyáo and Dàishān were foremost,
followed by Yuánpǔ, Qīngcūn, Héngpǔ, and other fields in Sōngjiāng;
all of these produced sun-dried salt on boards.
The various boiling salt fields belonging to Háng, Jiā, Níng, and Shào,
also purchased brine from Yúyáo.
In recent years, with expensive brine and high firewood costs,
the cost increased;
merchants abandoned boiling in favor of sun-drying,
and salt-boiling households also abandoned their furnaces and stopped boiling.
The number of boiling days became fewer,
so fields like Lóngtóu, Chángtíng, and Chánglín have long been lacking,
and the focus has shifted to Yú and Dài.
Yúyáo's beaches were far from the fields,
Dàishān was isolated overseas,
and traditionally no fields were set up there;
although bureaus were established and salt sheds built,
official collection was limited,
while private sun-drying was endless.
This was the situation in the various salt-producing areas.
Huái and Zhè salt sales
each had their own designated sales areas,
but Xīpíng and Suìpíng in Yù [Henan]
had long become defunct sales territories;
the three prefectures of Héng, Yǒng, Bǎo, and Jìngzhōu in Xiāng [Hunan],
originally part of the Huái jurisdiction, sold Yuè [Guangdong] salt;
the five prefectures of Ān, Xiāng, Yún, Jīng, Yí, and Jīngmén Zhōu in È [Hubei],
originally part of the Huái jurisdiction, sold Chuān [Sichuan] salt;
and places like Wēn, Tái, Níng, Chǔ in Zhè [Zhejiang],
only collected *lí* (likin) but had not yet implemented the voucher system.
Looking at the current situation,
Huáiběi relied on three-tier merchant transport,
which often led to disconnection regarding the conditions in the sales territories;
therefore, voucher merchants did not inquire about customs sales,
and Yù merchants often blamed Hú merchants;
this ailment lay in the lack of connection between merchant interests,
and the taxation by various provinces
was also sufficient to harm merchants.
Huáinán had four Dūxiāo,
with powers equivalent to a Yùnsī;
thus, the Yùnsī could not control the Dūxiāo,
and the sub-distributors were not entirely subject to the Dūxiāo's jurisdiction;
this ailment lay in the lack of unified government authority,
and the scattering of merchant interests
was also sufficient to harm itself.
For Zhè fields, those close to the fields
had a distinction between Jiānyǐn and Zhùyǐn.
Those far from the fields
had a distinction between Gāngdì and Yǐndì.
Furthermore, with government-managed and merchant-contracted systems,
the methods were not uniform,
leading to confusion and fragmentation,
with each section patched up.
As for salt bundles leaving the fields,
the difficulties caused by bureaus and checkpoints along the way,
and the smuggling by boatmen,
all these were unavoidable.
This was the situation in the various salt-selling areas.
Huái salt was sold in Sū and Wǎn,
bordering Zhè salt and Dōng salt sales areas;
sold in Yù'àn,
bordering Dōng salt and Lú salt sales areas;
sold in Xī'àn,
bordering Zhè, Mǐn, and Yuè salt sales areas;
sold in Xiāng and È's two sales territories,
bordering Chuān salt and È salt sales areas.
Furthermore, Xiāng and Fán in È [Hubei]
were infiltrated by Lúsī and Lùsī;
Héng, Yǒng, and Bǎo in Xiāng [Hunan]
were occupied by Yuèsī;
the designated sales areas of Liǎngzhè,
with Sū, Wǎn, and the three western territories all bordering Huái,
even places like Wēn and Tái within its own province,
were encroached upon by Mǐnsī;
these areas interlocked like a dog's teeth,
constantly giving rise to disputes.
In recent years, with the opening of the Jīnghàn Tiělù,
extending through Yù Shěng southwards,
the competition between Huái and Lú salts became even fiercer.
In the future, when railways like the Jīnpǔ and Yuèhàn are completed,
the Huái jurisdiction will face enemies on all four sides;
however, this only speaks of neighboring illicit trade.
What was even worse,
Wǎn [Anhui] and Yù [Henan] were both within the Huái jurisdiction,
but Yǐngzhōu in Wǎn, bordering Rǔ and Guāng,
encroached upon the Yù'àn because of slightly lower prices;
Tái and Chǔ were both within Zhè territory,
but Jìnyún in Chǔ was operated by Tái merchants,
and it encroached upon Chǔjùn again due to slightly lower contracted likin fees.
Jiāngxī's Jiànchāng had long been a defunct sales territory,
and recently a government transport bureau was established to attempt restoration,
but it had to lower prices to compete with illicit trade.
Fǔzhōu was already at risk of being inundated;
the foreign concessions in Shànghǎi had always been a haven for illicit trade,
and recently an office was established to plan for official sales,
but it transported salt across borders,
leading to frequent complaints from Sūshǔ;
this was Huái encroaching upon Huái, and Zhè encroaching upon Zhè.
Generally, where there is profit,
people flock to it,
and it is indeed not easy to stop;
the only reliance is strict anti-smuggling efforts.
However, the police and soldiers were corrupt and incompetent,
unable to control the powerful smugglers,
but instead harassed ordinary people.
Local officials, too, considering the Gāngfǎ had long been abolished,
did not take responsibility for success,
and intended to turn a blind eye.
This was the situation in the various areas where sales territories bordered each other.
Recently, when raising funds,
salt was considered a major source,
and Huái and Zhè, being at the center of the empire,
were especially crucial for the overall situation.
For the sake of rectification,
it was imperative to unify authority over affairs.
I propose that salt administration be placed under the overall management of my Ministry,
and the salt-producing provinces'
Governors-General and Governors shall serve as concurrent Huìbàn Yánzhèng Dàchén,
while the salt-selling provinces
shall all concurrently hold the title of Huìbàn Yánzhèng Dàchén."
An imperial edict replied, "Approved."
Regarding the mention of Southern merchants establishing ponds,
this was because in the 33rd year of Guāngxù,
due to insufficient salt sales in Huáinán,
new ponds were established in the reed marshes of Lèzikǒu, Zuǒyíng, in Huáiběi,
which were called the Jǐnán Yánchí.
In the 34th year,
Northern merchants claimed this obstructed sales from the old ponds,
and through Jiāngdū Zhāng Rénjùn, an order was given to set a quota based on Huáinán's deficit,
using 100,000 *yǐn* as the standard.
As for the three-tier merchant transport,
Huáiběi voucher salt
was formerly transported by voucher merchants from Yuán to Xībà,
sold to Hú merchants,
then transported by Hú merchants to Zhèngyángguān,
and sold in turns to Àn merchants.
Zài Zé, having received the imperial decree to supervise salt administration,
thereupon established the Salt Administration Bureau.
It was divided into eight departments according to various districts,
first making preparations for Huái běi.
There were four regulations: one was to restore the abandoned embankment at Xī Suì,
one was to remove the reed shops along theái,
one was to show sympathy for merchants burdened by road taxes,
and one was to collect the Lǐ price for Yù shěng as a lump sum.
He consulted with Wú Chóngxī, the巡撫 of Hénán,
but the latter insisted on retaining the old system for the last item.
Zài Zé also memorialized and decided to establish a General Salt Lǐ Bureau at Xī bà,
and an Inspection Bureau at Lín huái guān.
All other bureaus and checkpoints were to be abolished.
The three types of peddlers were uniformly changed to shore peddlers.
They were permitted to pay the Lǐ jīn additional price directly at the General Bureau,
set at two yuan and two jiǎo in silver currency per permit,
converting to one liǎng, six qián, and some零 of treasury silver.
All were to be collected in a single payment.
For areas where salt was sold locally with permits,
the amount was reduced by four jiǎo in silver currency,
converting to one liǎng and two qián,
which was thirty percent less than the original quota.
This happened in the seventh month of the second year.
In the various salt fields outside Zhāngjiākǒu in Zhílì, where Měng salt was collected,
it had always been managed by merchants.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
it was reorganized into a company.
By this time, it was again changed to government-run warehouses,
with various厅, zhōu, and xiàn serving as permit offices,
and merchants handling the permits in a lump sum.
Annually, two萬 (permits) were issued,
collecting one hundred and fifty-seven thousand silver.
In Sìchuān, for areas that reverted to Dīng for transportation by票,
after Xiánfēng, they increased to sixty-eight厅, zhōu, and xiàn.
Government transportation was often hindered by this.
At this time, it was memorialized to investigate salt wells and kilns, taking the existing ones as the quota,
strictly prohibiting illicit sales
to prevent private票.
In the third year,
seven million was issued by the Dàqīng Bank and six hundred thousand by the Zhílì Bank to compensate reed merchants for foreign debts.
Thirty-six permit areas were taken over for government management,
and a bureau was established in Tiānjīn.
For the seven districts of Yǒngpíng,
during the Dàoguāng era, it was managed by zhōu and xiàn for taxation.
In the twenty-ninth year of Guāngxù,
it was changed to a government transport bureau.
At this time, those in Xīnhé and Píngxiāng counties for which no merchants had taken responsibility,
were all managed by the Tiānjīn Bureau.
Initially, when trade commenced with various countries,
prohibited goods
were not allowed to be imported or exported,
and salt was one of them.
However, Dàlián and Lǚshùn in Fèngtiān,
Chángchūn in Jílín,
had Japanese salt;
Húnchūn and Yánjí in Jílín had Korean salt;
Mǎnzhōulǐ and Hēihé in Hēilóngjiāng,
Dōngníng in Jílín,
had Russian salt;
Zhènnánguān in Guǎngxī,
Méngzì in Yúnnán,
had French salt;
Hong Kong and Macao were places of infiltration and encroachment.
As for Jiāozhōu wān in Shāndōng, leased to Germany,
it encroached upon the Jìmò salt fields;
Liáodōng bàndǎo in Fèngtiān, leased to Russia,
then transferred to Japan,
occupied the Jīnzhōu salt flats;
and regarding the two islands of Jiāoliú and Fèngmíng in Fùzhōu,
there were proposals for both purchasing surplus salt and dispatching officers to suppress smuggling.
Later, the policy of suppressing smuggling was implemented,
but the purchase of salt was not carried out.
Guǎngzhōu wān in Guǎngdōng, leased to France,
had the Màohuí field of Wúchuān occupied.
Salt was transported to Hong Kong and Vietnam for sale,
then entered the interior,
all of which truly disrupted the salt laws.
Those who administered salt policy should have found a good way to manage it afterwards.
Scroll Ninety-Nine: Food and Goods V: Coinage Law, Tea Law, Mining Administration
Coinage Law: Tàizǔ first minted
the "Tiānmìng Tōngbǎo"
coin.
It was distinguished into two types by Mǎn and Hàn scripts.
The Mǎn script type was larger in coin quality than the Hàn script type.
Tiāncōng followed this.
Shìzǔ established his capital in Yānjīng,
extensively opened minting bureaus,
and first standardized one type.
The Bǎoquán Bureau was established in the Ministry of Revenue,
and the Bǎoyuán Bureau in the Ministry of Works.
The "Shùnzhì Tōngbǎo"
coin
was officially stipulated to be cast with seventy percent red copper and thirty percent white copper.
One thousand coins constituted one wàn,
two thousand strings formed one mǎo,
and thirty mǎo were cast annually.
Each coin weighed one qián.
In the second year,
its weight was increased by two fēn.
It was stipulated that seven coins were equivalent to one fēn of silver,
with old coins being double this value.
The people greatly complained about the high price of coins,
so it was changed to ten coins equivalent to one fēn.
Various provinces and garrisons followed this pattern to open mints,

establishing minting bureaus successively in Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Mìyún, Jì, Xuān, Dàtóng, Yánsuí, Línqīng, Shèngjīng, Jiāngxī, Hénán, Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Shāndōng, Húguǎng, and the three prefectures of Jīngzhōu, Chángdé, and Jiāngníng.
In the fifth year,
the Shèngjīng and Yánsuí bureaus were suspended.
In the sixth year,
the Dàtóng bureau was moved to Yánghé.
In the seventh year,
minting bureaus were opened in Xiāngyáng and Yúnyáng prefectures.
In the eighth year,
minting in all prefectures and garrisons was suspended.
In the tenth year,
the Mìyún, Jì, Xuān, Yánghé, and Línqīng minting bureaus were reopened.
Initially, the Ministry of Revenue, deeming the newly minted coins sufficient,
allowed only Chóngzhēn coins from previous dynasties to be temporarily in circulation,
while others were to be surrendered to the government as scrap copper,
compensated at their value.
Private minting, small coins, and counterfeit coins were also prohibited,
and the ban on old coins was re-emphasized.
Subsequently, as the surrender to the government took a long time to complete,
a general order was issued throughout the land,
setting a three-month deadline for completion of surrender.
Anyone using them after the deadline
would be punished.
In this year, the court deliberated on easing the coinage law,
setting the weight increase of one qián, two fēn, and five lí from the eighth year as the standard.
On the left side, the Hàn script characters
"yī lí"
were inscribed.
On the right, the Bǎoquán mint inscribed one character, saying
"hù,"
and Bǎoyuán said
"gōng."
Various provinces and garrisons also minted one character of their place names,
such as Tài yuán adding the character
"yuán,"
and Xuānfǔ adding the character
"xuān,"
and so on.
One thousand coins were equivalent to one liǎng of silver,
establishing a unified system for circulation.
Private minting bureaus were prohibited;
offenders were to be judged for perversion of justice and embezzlement.
At that time, government coins were stagnant,
so the method of collection and dispersion was adopted,
appropriately distributing coins from the capital and provincial bureaus
to match stipends and salaries.
The old system of collecting seven qián and three fēn of silver for grain taxes
was all stipulated as law.
However, the coins from the provincial bureaus were not refined,
and private minting took advantage of this,
eventually leading to stagnation and non-circulation.
All minting was abolished,
and reliance was placed solely on Bǎoquán and Bǎoyuán
to meticulously produce coins weighing one qián and four fēn,
using Mǎn script for the inscription
to make counterfeiting difficult for private mints.
Existing coins were to be melted down within three months.
The law for private minting was revised:
the ringleader and artisans were to be beheaded,
their property confiscated by the government;
accomplices, those who knowingly purchased and used them,
heads of ten-household groups (zǒngjiǎ) who knew but did not report,
and local officials who knew
were to be beheaded or strangled as appropriate.
Informers were rewarded fifty liǎng of silver.
In the seventeenth year,
minting in the provinces was resumed,
ordering compliance with the heavy coin standard,
with both Mǎn and Hàn scripts used for the inscription.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
regnal year coins were minted.
Thereafter, whenever a new emperor ascended the throne and changed the regnal year,
coins were minted according to this precedent.
Gāozōng abdicated internally,
minting twelve Qiánlóng coins
and eighteen Jiāqìng coins,
which was an unusual exception.
Since the recasting of one qián, four fēn coins,
unscrupulous people often privately melted them down,
so a law was enacted to punish this as equivalent to private minting.
Thus, the manufacture of bronze vessels was prohibited
due to private melting.
In the eighteenth year,
the prohibition was strictly re-emphasized,
allowing the manufacture and use of military and musical instruments weighing less than five jīn.
At that time, the heavy coins were increasingly melted down,
making their value prohibitively high.
In the twenty-third year,
the proposal of Chén Tíngjìng, a sub-chancellor of the Coinage Law, to revert to the old standard of one qián
was approved.
After a long time,
the coins remained expensive as before,
so a ban on setting coin prices was re-imposed,
stipulating that one liǎng of silver should not exchange for less than one thousand coins.
However, the coin price ultimately could not be stabilized.
In later years, one liǎng of silver exchanged for eight hundred eighty to seven hundred seventy coins.
Therefore, the five urban areas were ordered to sell grain at stable prices, exchanging coins for silver to stabilize their value.
Since the prohibition on old coins was re-emphasized,
and as Mǐn (Fújiàn) was remote,
miscellaneous standard coins were still in circulation there.
In the twenty-fourth year [of Kāngxī],
Governor Jīn Hóng spoke about it,
and Grand Academician Xú Qiánxuè submitted a memorial stating:
"Since ancient times, old and new coins have always been used concurrently,
allowing people convenience."
He then recounted historical precedents from previous dynasties,
saying,
"Since the Wǔzhū (五銖) coins of the Hàn dynasty,
there has never been a case where old coins were abolished and only new ones were used.
The Suí dynasty melted down old coins,
and in the post-Tiānqǐ (天啟) era of the Míng dynasty, all old coins were rounded up for recasting—
this was a change in coinage policy.
Moreover, when the currency system is flawed,
old coins can be utilized to clarify and eliminate [problems],
hence, they were still allowed to circulate after dynastic changes.
What's more, Mǐn is located beyond the ridges,
so it should be allowed for the people to use them."
The emperor approved his words,
completely lifting the prohibition on old and abolished coins.
