In that year, the penalties for private minting and private melting for those in the banner households were set according to the law.
In the forty-first year [of Kāngxī],
due to the reversion to the old system of lighter coins,
private minting resurged.
Court officials requested to abolish the small standard coins,
and to cast coins weighing one qián and four fēn (four-tenths of a qián) again.
New and old coins were temporarily allowed to circulate concurrently.
One thousand new coins were to be equivalent to one liǎng of silver,
and old coins to seven qián.
An imperial edict approved this.
However, private minting could not be stopped after all.
In the forty-fifth year [of Kāngxī],
Shāndōng requested to mint large coins.
At that time, private minting was discovered in Chángshān.
The emperor believed that private minting was not limited to large coins,
and that there must be much private melting.
It was advisable to collect first and then prohibit.
Thus, it was ordered that two thousand coins be collected for every liǎng of silver due for taxes and provisions.
When the coins ran out,
bronze vessels were to be collected instead.
The Board of Revenue, finding the new coins insufficient,
requested to postpone the melting of old coins for five years.
Two years later,
privately minted coins from Xiāngyáng were secretly stored in grain transport boats and entered the capital.
Grand Minister of Justice Tǎjìntài (塔進泰) was ordered to investigate jointly.
He submitted a memorial requesting a strict prohibition on collection and melting,
stating that those who committed private minting or private贩运 again would be punished according to the law.
Boatmen and transport officials would receive the same punishment as private minting.
If local officials were aware,
they would be beheaded,
and their families confiscated;
if they failed to detect,
they would be stripped of their posts.
The laws became even stricter.
For official mints, copper [supply]
started to include products from Diān (Yúnnán) from the forty-fourth year [of Kāngxī].
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
Governor Yáng Míngshí requested that Yúnnán copper be transported to the capital annually.
The court deliberated that minting at the source was more convenient.
Thus, four mints were opened in Dàlǐ and Zhānyì in Yúnnán,
to mint and transport coins to the capital.
The inscription was
"Yúnquán" (雲泉).
The emperor, considering coins as national treasures,
renamed it
"Bǎoyún" (寶雲),
and ordered that the mints in all provinces
have the character
"Bǎo" (寶)
at the beginning,
followed by the province's name,
entirely in Manchu script.
Subsequently, the minting and transport of coins to the capital were sometimes carried out, sometimes suspended.
In the second year of Qiánlóng,
as the coin price had been unstable for a long time,
an order was issued to Dàxīng and Wǎnpíng to establish official brokers for coin exchange to stabilize coin prices.
The emperor, realizing that private melting was particularly harmful,
intensified the prohibition on bronze vessels.
Officials below the third rank were not permitted to use them.
Existing bronze vessels had to be submitted to the government within three years.
Exceeding the deadline would be treated as illegal possession of prohibited items.
If prohibited items were still manufactured,
the crime would be considered accessory to illegal minting.
A general order was then issued to prohibit the manufacture of bronze vessels.
Soon after, restrictions were further tightened;
only officials of the first rank were permitted to use them,
and all others were prohibited.
Concealment or private use
would be judged as violating the prohibition.
In the twelfth year [of Qiánlóng],
the emperor, noting that heavy coins led to private melting and
light coins led to private minting,
ordered a return to the old standard of one qián and two fēn.
In the thirteenth year [of Qiánlóng],
the crime of clipping coin edges was set as "strangulation with a stay of execution."
Previously, Minister Hǎi Wàng, finding the copper prohibition detrimental to the people,
submitted a memorial outlining four disadvantages.
Gāozōng (高宗) approved it,
and consequently abolished the orders prohibiting copper and collecting copper.
Furthermore, as coin prices in the capital were high,
with one liǎng of silver only exchanging for eight hundred coins,
an imperial edict was issued to release coins from the Ministry of Works' Jiéshèn (節慎) treasury to stabilize prices.
Censor Táo Zhèngjìng submitted a memorial arguing that the instability of coin prices
was due to brokers corrupting the currency system,
and immediately ordered their abolition.
Zhèjiāng Provincial Administration Commissioner Zhāng Ruòzhèn stated that the high cost of coins was due to private melting.
If copper and lead were mixed,
with a little tin added,
to cast "green coins,"
then those who melted them would have no profit.
This was tested and proven effective.
Therefore, his suggestion was adopted,
and these coins were minted and circulated alongside "yellow coins."
A prohibition was established for privately minted lead coins:
the ringleaders and artisans would be "strangled with a stay of execution,"
while accomplices and those who knowingly bought and used them
would have their punishment reduced by one degree.
The prohibition on trafficking and hoarding standard coins was reiterated and tightened.
Anyone accumulating more than one hundred thousand coins
would be considered in violation of regulations.
The emperor instructed his court officials, saying:
"Those who speak of prohibitions today
are merely remedying superficial problems and curing minor ills,
not addressing the root cause.
The fixed value of goods is based on silver, not coins,
yet both officials and common people find coins more convenient than silver.
Those driven by profit
exploit the fluctuations in value for gain—
how is this not an inversion of importance?
Henceforth, the use of silver should be emphasized.
All official construction projects in the provinces
and major private purchases of goods
shall be paid in silver."
In the twenty-second year [of Qiánlóng],
Governor-General of Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī, Lǐ Shìyáo, requested a ban on old coins and counterfeit coins.
The emperor, noting that people were mixing in the counterfeit coins of Wú Sānguì
"Lìyòng" (利用),
"Hónghuà" (洪化),
and
"Zhāowǔ" (昭武),
merely allowed people to voluntarily turn them in,
and the government would exchange them for recasting.
Old coins were still permitted to circulate.
In the twenty-fourth year [of Qiánlóng],
after the pacification of the Huí (Muslim regions),
a pattern was issued to Yè'ěrqiāng (Yarkand),
to mint "Qiánlóng Tōngbǎo" (乾隆通寶) coins.
Each coin weighed two qián,
with Yè'ěrqiāng's name inscribed on the back,
Manchu script on the left,
and Hui script on the right,
using red copper.
Old "Pǔ'ěr" (普爾) coins were also melted down for recasting.
Two years later,
Ākèsū (Aksu) requested to mint coins
following the Yè'ěrqiāng example.
Permission was also granted for Xīzàng (Tibet) to mint silver coins
in two denominations: one qián and five fēn.
The inscription read "Qiánlóng Bǎocáng" (乾隆寶藏),
with Tangut script on the reverse,
and the year inscribed on the rim.
These two types of coins
were only circulated in the Huí and Zàng (Tibetan) regions,
not in the interior.
In the twenty-ninth year [of Qiánlóng],
it was ordered that coins minted in the Huí region
should permanently bear the Qiánlóng reign title.
By the middle period,
Qián Zhí'áng,
the directly administered provinces all increased their furnaces and expanded casting,
and prices temporarily trended toward stability.
However, copper transport was delayed,
and market brokers hoarded goods, raising prices,
harming the currency system.
An imperial edict was issued to governors-general and governors, forbidding them from lightly requesting the suspension of furnaces or reduction of production.
In later years, private minting increased,
with Sìchuān, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu as its centers,
spreading to Jiāngnán (Jiāngsū and Zhèjiāng).
Even Yúnnán and Guìzhōu official coinage was halted due to poor quality.
Although private minting was strictly prohibited,
it was often leniently treated through buybacks,
which opportunistic commoners relied on for fraud,
leading to a ceaseless emergence of private coins.
In the 57th year [of the Qiánlóng reign, 1792],
Húguǎng Governor-General Bì Yuán requested the purchase of coins without setting a deadline.
The Emperor stated that Húběi was the main hub of private minting,
and instead of trying to stop it, they were premeditating how to shirk responsibility.
He ordered strict investigation of private trafficking,
and still granted a two-year extension.
In the 59th year
due to the intermingling of official and private coins,
which made money cheap,
casting in the directly administered provinces was temporarily suspended.
Private coins were given a one-year limit for surrender,
but clerks and yamen runners used this as an opportunity for corruption.
In the 1st year of Jiāqìng
casting in the directly administered provinces was resumed.
By the 10th year
the directly administered provinces had not fully restored production,
and money became expensive again.
An imperial edict instructed all governors-general and governors to resume full-scale minting according to production quotas.
However, thereafter, official mints and private mints sprung up in succession.
The coins from the capital mints became indistinct, brittle, and thin in their rims and characters.
"Bǎo Sū"
coins were mixed with sand,
shattering upon impact,
while private minting flourished in Guìzhōu and Húguǎng,
and the official and private mints in Jiāngsū operated secretly.
By the Dàoguāng era,
Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng circulated mixed
"Guāng Zhōng",
"Jǐng Zhōng",
"Jǐng Xīng",
"Jiā Lóng"
and other foreign coins.
Treacherous commoners profited from this
and often imitated them.
The official mints in Guìyáng and Dàdìng also separately cast large base coins,
and the currency system further deteriorated from then on.
At this time, there was trade between China and foreign countries,
exchanging goods for silver.
Foreign ships violated prohibitions,
and millions of taels leaked out annually,
which censors Huáng Zhōngmó and Zhāng Yuán both spoke about.
Various types of foreign silver coins, such as "Big Bun", "Small Bun", "Shaggy Hair", "Bat", "Double Column", and "Horse Sword",
also secretly flowed into the interior to seek profit,
circulating from Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng to south of the Yellow River.
Foreign merchants further carried them to coastal ports in various provinces,
ostensibly buying goods but secretly trading for silver,
leading to an increasing amount of foreign silver
and a decreasing and more expensive supply of traditional silver ingots.
The Emperor was troubled by this
and ordered the Governor-General of Guǎngdōng to strictly enforce prohibitions,
but these prohibitions did not extend to foreign silver coins.
The imitation cast coins, such as Guǎngbǎn, Fúbǎn, Hángbǎn, Wúzhuāng, and Hángzhuāng,
continued to deplete Chinese silver as before.
Censor Huáng Juézī requested a joint prohibition on their export,
and the establishment of special regulations,
with severe penalties.
In the 17th year
an imperial edict instructed governors-general and governors along the rivers and coast, and customs superintendents,
to order their subordinates to strictly investigate smuggling,
determine merits and demerits,
and implement rewards and punishments.
However, domestic silver was ultimately exhausted,
and each tael often exchanged for as much as two thousand [cash].
Court officials debated ways to strengthen the currency to curb the power of silver,
but their proposals were blocked and not implemented.
Earlier, in the mid-Dàoguāng period,
silver flowed out and became expensive,
and both the court and the public wished to issue large denomination coins to remedy this.
Guǎngxī Governor Liáng Zhāngjù submitted a memorial advocating its benefits.
Upon Emperor Wénzōng's ascension,
Sìchuān Education Commissioner Hé Shàojī strongly requested the issuance of large denomination coins to restore ancient practices and save the current situation.
The Emperor initially disagreed,
but eventually allowed the circulation of official notes (guānpiao) and treasury notes (bǎochāo).
Treasury notes had been issued in the 8th year of Shùnzhì
with 128,000-odd pieces produced annually.
They were abolished after ten years.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
Grand Tutor Cài Zhīdìng requested the issuance of notes.
In the 2nd year of Xiánfēng
Fújiàn Governor Wáng Yìdé also made such a request.
The court deliberation deemed it difficult to implement due to obstacles,
and rejected it.
At this time, silver was deficient, and money was scarce and valuable,
while military expenses and river conservancy funds consumed twenty to thirty million taels.
Those planning the national economy
mostly requested the issuance of official notes.
The following year,
the Board of Revenue was ordered to convene a discussion.
Prince Huì and others requested the Board to manufacture paper notes and silver notes to circulate concurrently.
The notes were made of thick paper,
with the title
"Hùbù Guānpiao" (Board of Revenue Official Note)
in Manchu on the left and Chinese on the right,
both in double columns.
The center indicated "X taels of pure silver, 2 taels flat,"
and below it read
"Hùbù Zòuxíng Guānpiao" (Board of Revenue Memorialized and Issued Official Note).
All those wishing to exchange official notes for silver or money
were treated the same as silver,
and they were also permitted to use them to pay official dues according to regulations set by the Board.
Counterfeiters would be punished according to the law.
The border text [was like a dragon pattern].
The title of the treasury note was
"Dàqīng Bǎochāo" (Great Qīng Treasury Note),
with Chinese characters arranged horizontally.
The center indicated "X standard cash,"
and the eight characters on the side were
"Tiānxià Tōngbǎo,
Píngzhǔn Chūrù" (Circulating Treasure Under Heaven, Stabilizing Receipts and Expenditures).
Below it read
"This note shall circulate as a substitute for standard cash,
and is also permitted for paying land tax, grain tribute, all taxes, duties, and donations.
All treasuries in the capital and provinces shall accept and remit it."
The border text was like that of the notes.
Large denomination coins ranged from 1,000 cash to 10 cash,
in five denominations,
weighing from two taels down to four mace four fen.
The 1,000-cash and 500-cash coins
were cast from pure copper,
purple in color;
the 100-cash, 50-cash, and 10-cash coins
were cast from a copper-lead alloy,
yellow in color.
Coins of 100 cash and above were inscribed
"Xiánfēng Yuánbǎo" (Original Treasure of Xiánfēng),
and those below were inscribed
"Zhòngbǎo" (Heavy Treasure),
with the mint name in Manchu on the reverse.
In the 4th year
due to copper shortage, 5-cash iron coins and standard cash were also cast.
Later, lead standard cash was also cast.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
the capital mints used copper from Yúnnán and foreign sources,
but later relied exclusively on Yúnnán supply.
At this time, due to blocked routes and delayed copper,
this was a temporary expedient.
It was decided that one tael of silver note was equivalent to 2,000 standard cash,
and 2,000 treasury notes were equivalent to one tael of silver.
Silver notes and treasury notes were also permitted to be exchanged at this rate.
For commoners paying land tax, grain tribute, taxes, and all official [payments],
50% was permitted to be paid in notes.
The same applied to official [disbursements] from treasuries in the capital and provinces.
Large denomination coins circulated widely like notes,
equivalent to silver at the rate of standard cash.
30% was permitted for official payments.
Iron coins were universally accepted like large denomination coins.
Obstruction was punishable as violation of regulations.
Counterfeiting notes resulted in beheading with a suspended sentence.
Private minting was more strictly suppressed.
An imperial edict ordered the establishment of official money bureaus in the capital and provinces.
Soon after, as directly administered provinces delayed implementation,
it was subsequently proposed to set up treasury note bureaus in each prefecture,
and distribute large denomination coins to businesses and shops,
to facilitate the exchange of money and notes for the convenience of the people.
Land tax and grain tribute could be paid partly in notes,
and for small, petty households, the remaining fractions of silver and notes
could be paid in copper and iron large denomination coins.
All this was first implemented in Zhílì and Shāndōng.
Officials who extorted or bent the law,
and merchants and commoners who traded at unfair prices,
would be severely punished.
In the 7th year
it was ordered that for taxes and grain tribute in all prefectures of Shùntiān and Zhílì,
starting from the busy season of that year,
40% should be paid in actual silver, 30% in treasury notes, and 30% in 10-cash copper and iron large denomination coins.
All expenditures [by the government] were also to be disbursed proportionally.
Soon after, following the Board of Revenue's proposal,
starting from the slack season of that year,
Zhílì was to collect taxes at a rate of 70% silver and 30% notes,
with the 30% for large denomination coins being included within the 30% for notes,
allowing payment in either notes or coins at will.
However, when the banknote system was first implemented,
initially for military provisions,
and subsequently for river conservancy projects,
its distribution and collection were deemed inconvenient by all,
and the public was suspicious and resistant.
When five-tenths of the funds in the directly-administered provinces were to be collected in banknotes,
as it was difficult to use the excessive issue for other allocations,
people gradually became unwilling to accept banknotes for distribution and collection.
When people obtained banknotes,
they accumulated as useless paper.
When people in the capital carried banknotes to the market,
either prices were intentionally inflated,
or goods were hidden.
When banknotes were presented at government agencies or shops,
what they received were all four types of large denomination coins,
which were inconvenient to use.
Thus, the circulation of banknotes brought hardship to both soldiers and civilians, both inside and outside the capital.
Later, in the capital, banknotes were issued at a 70% discount against government-issued coins,
and their value continued to fall.
Even with reduced issuance, it was difficult to cope,
and thus banknotes could no longer circulate.
The large denomination coins, worth one thousand and five hundred,
were the first to be abolished due to their excessively heavy exchange rate.
The coins worth one hundred and fifty were abolished next.
Iron coins were also abolished due to obstruction by private notes,
and only the 'worth ten' (dāng shí) coins were exclusively circulated.
Counterfeiting became rampant,
and even daily reports of death penalties did not stop it.
The quality of the mint-produced coins also gradually deteriorated,
making them indistinguishable from private counterfeits.
Treacherous merchants took advantage of this to discount and pick at coins,
arbitrarily setting their value.
Merchants and vendors, fearing receiving large denomination coins,
all ceased their activities.
The three-tenths collection policy
was merely announced in official documents,
and repeated prohibitions had no effect.
When laws are flawed, many violate them,
and thus it certainly could not succeed.
The dāng shí coins circulated for a particularly long time,
however, one such coin was equivalent to two standard coins (zhì qián),
and it ceased to be accepted once outside the national gate.
In the late period of Xiánfēng,
copper was severely scarce,
and orders prohibiting and collecting copper were issued.
In the early years of Tóngzhì,
the resources for minting coins
were solely commercial copper and scrap copper.
The dāng shí coins were reduced in value to three qián two fēn.
In the ninth year of Guāngxù,
it was again reduced to two qián six fēn.
At that time, Xiàocīn Xiǎn Huánghòu (Empress Dowager Cíxǐ) was keen to restore the old system,
and deliberated with her court ministers.
As the Yunnan copper supply was below quota,
it was decided to temporarily purchase foreign copper
and hand it over to the Jīqìjú (Machinery Bureau) for trial minting.
The Hùbù (Board of Revenue) memorialized about the inconvenience of the Jīqìjú minting coins and the Kōngjú (Capital Bureau) opening furnaces,
but the Yìzhǐ (Imperial Edict) condemned their shirking of responsibility.
Ultimately, Zhílì Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Zhílì) Lǐ Hóngzhāng was ordered to carry it out in Tiānjīn,
with a re-standardized value of one qián.
Then, Táng Jiǒng was granted the title of Xúnfǔ (Governor)
to specifically oversee the copper administration in Yúnnán.
In the fourteenth year,
Guǎngdōng experimented with minting machine-made coins,
marking them with a weight of seven fēn of the treasury standard (kù píng) on the reverse.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the directly-administered provinces were ordered to mint eight-fēn coins.
However, in the capital, due to the scarcity of zhì qián,
dāng shí coins continued to circulate as before.
In the thirty-second year,
copper coins (tóng bì) worth ten were minted,
but the people were not pleased to use them.
Thus, the minting of silver and copper dollars (yín tóng yuán) was initiated,
banks were established,
with the aim of unifying the currency system
to compete with various countries in the East and West.
Initially,
foreign merchants congregated in Yuèdōng (Guǎngdōng),
and large quantities of Spanish and English silver coins were imported.
Zǒngdū Lín Zéxú planned to mint coins himself to resist this,
but it was abandoned as impractical.
Thereafter, México and Japan flooded the market with their national currencies.
In the fourteenth year of Guāngxù,
Zhāng Zhīdòng, as the Governor of Yuè (Guǎngdōng),
first used machinery to mint trial coins according to the standard.
Lǐ Hóngzhāng succeeded him and completed the task.
The inscription read
"Guāngxù Yuánbǎo,
Kù Píng Seven Qián Two Fēn,
Made in Guǎngdōng Province,"
with a coiled dragon on the reverse.
Also minted were four types of smaller silver dollars: three qián six fēn, one qián four fēn four lí, seven fēn two lí, and three fēn six lí.
This marked the beginning of China's own silver currency.
Húběi, Jiāngxī, Zhílì, Zhèjiāng, Ānhuī, Fèngtiān, and Jílín subsequently began minting.
Soon after, the coins minted in Guǎngdōng, Húběi, and Jiāngxī were deemed most convenient for use,
and they were permitted to use funds allocated for remittance to the capital as capital for minting.
Provinces that had not yet started minting
were instructed to undertake supplementary minting.
For collections and disbursements in the capital and other regions,
a three-tenths proportion was allowed.
Therefore, Liú Kūnyī, Zhāng Zhīdòng, and Táo Mú were ordered to deliberate on matters concerning the minting by three bureaus.
It was subsequently approved by the Hùbù.
The scale and fineness of coins minted by the seven provinces varied greatly,
which was unfavorable for circulation.
When the general mint (Zàobì Zǒngchǎng) was completed,
it was proposed to abolish three of them,
and keep Jiāngnán, Zhílì, and Guǎngdōng as branch mints.
Initially, the minting was based on the standard weight of Mexican dollars (mò yuán),
which was widely criticized.
Zhāng Zhīdòng first tried circulating one-liǎng silver coins in Húběi.
The Hùbù also, based on China's traditional accounting,
which had long followed the liǎng, qián, fēn, lí system,
therefore designated the main currency as one kù píng liǎng,
supplemented by five-qián and one-qián small silver coins, as well as copper dollars and zhì qián,
ordering the general and branch mints to produce them according to standard.
Copper dollars (tóng yuán) were first minted in Mǐn (Fújiàn) and Guǎng (Guǎngdōng),
followed by Jiāngsū.
At that time, the capital's mint ceased production,
and each province was ordered to transport hundreds of thousands of coins to the capital,
to be issued by the Hùbù for use.
Provinces along the rivers and coast
were also instructed to raise funds for supplementary minting.
However, while the directly-administered provinces successively began minting,
the Zàobì Zǒngchǎng (General Mint) was completed later.
The Zǒngchǎng planned to mint three types of coins:
gold,
silver,
and copper.
Copper coins were minted first. From a value of twenty standard coins, it was reduced to two;
from a weight of four qián, it was reduced to four fēn,
totaling four types.
The inscriptions were slightly different from those of the directly-administered provinces but largely similar.
The directly-administered provinces had "Guāngxù Yuánbǎo,"
and the Zǒngchǎng initially followed the directly-administered provinces,
later standardizing to "Dà Qīng Tóngbì."
All were marked with the place of minting,
and the reverse side all bore dragon designs,
cast in purple copper,
though the directly-administered provinces occasionally used yellow copper.
All private minting of copper coins and counterfeiting of banknotes
were punished with penalties exceeding those for zhì qián.
Initially, copper dollars were minted
to supplement the shortage of zhì qián.
Soon, attracted by the remaining profits,
new government expenditures all relied on them.
Mints competed to produce and sell them,
even to the point where they could not cover the cost of minting.
Liǎng Jiāng Zǒngdū (Governor-General of Liǎng Jiāng) Zhōu Fú first memorialized about these abuses,
and the Hùbù legislated to restrict them.
Subsequently, with the Zhèngwùchù (Office of Government Affairs), they proposed eight remedial measures.
Soon, as the number of provinces minting reached seventeen,
with two or three bureaus per province,
it was feared that unification would ultimately be difficult.
Thus, Shāndōng was merged with Zhílì,
Húběi with Húnán,
Jiāngnán and Ānhuī with Jiāngníng,
Zhèjiāng with Fújiàn,
Guǎngxī with Guǎngdōng,
and Fèngtiān, Hénán, Sìchuān, Yúnguì were combined into nine factories,
with officials dispatched by the Hùbù to assist in management.
High officials were sent to tour and inspect,
and together with the Hùbù, they planned joint management matters.
However, copper dollars, being inherently cheap,
only achieved half the value of dāng shí coins.
This led to many corrupt practices by both individuals and private bureaus.
For payments due in silver,
the conversion of copper dollars
often resulted in losses,
commodity prices soared,
and people's livelihoods became increasingly impoverished.
Provinces also clashed with each other,
to the point where currencies were not interchangeable.
Shāndōng Xúnfǔ (Governor of Shāndōng) Yuán Shùxūn subsequently listed ten harms.
At that time, the Zǒngchǎng had just begun minting copper coins,
and Bǎoquán (a mint in the capital) still minted six-fēn zhì qián.
Guǎngdōng requested to change to minting one-wén coins,
with the standard to be issued and circulated by the Zǒngchǎng.
In the thirty-fourth year,
all copper dollar mints were ordered to additionally mint new one-wén coins,
in the style of copper dollars.
This was to retain the old one-wén system
and thereby remedy the copper dollar issue.
Thereafter, trade opened up with the various nations of Tàixī,
and the tea business consequently underwent a transformation.
Its major markets numbered three: Hánkǒu,
Shànghǎi,
and Fúzhōu.
The tea from Hánkǒu
came from Húnán, Jiāngxī, and Ānhuī,
and combined with what was produced in the province itself,
it was transported up the Hànshuǐ to Hénán, Shǎnxī, Qīnghǎi, and Xīnjiāng.
That which was shipped to Éluósī
was all brick tea.
The tea from Shànghǎi was even more prosperous;
besides what was produced in the province itself,
there was much tea from Húguǎng, Jiāngxī, Ānhuī, Zhèjiāng, and Fújiàn.
Red and green tea from Jiāngxī and Ānhuī was mostly sold to the various countries of Ōu and Měi.
Shàoxīng tea from Zhèjiāng was shipped to Měilìjiān,
and Níngbō tea was shipped to Rìběn.
Fúzhōu black tea was mostly shipped to Měizhōu and the Nányáng Qúndǎo.
Outside these three markets,
there were also Guǎngzhōu, Tiānjīn, and Zhīfú, three places
where foreign merchants also flocked.
Indeed, tea prefers warmth and dislikes cold,
prefers humidity and dislikes dryness,
and must also avoid fierce winds,
making it most suitable for Zhōngguó.
Although Tàixī commerce was flourishing,
as it was not suitable for their soil,
they could not but rely on our country,
and thus it gradually spread throughout the globe.
Those engaged in this business
included general merchants
and individual merchants.
After receiving permits,
sales each had their designated regions.
There were also those who simultaneously operated with a票法 (piàofǎ, ticket system),
such as Sìchuān, which, after the establishment of the堰工茶票 (yàngōng chápào, weir construction tea ticket) in Qiánlóng fifty-two years,
had numerous designations;
however, it was only implemented in areas with high production or brisk sales,
not extending to all zhōuxiàn.
Only the Gānshāng (Gānsù merchants) were formerly divided into two counters, Dōngguì (East Counter) and Xīguì (West Counter).
Dōngguì mostly consisted of those registered in Shānxī and Shǎnxī,
while Xīguì was staffed by Huímín.
From the middle of Xiánfēng, when Huífěi caused trouble,
followed by a proliferation of bandits,
neither counter had anyone to undertake the duties.
Governor-General Zuǒ Zōngtáng pacified the entire province
and then memorialized to establish regulations,
using tickets to replace permits.
New merchants were selected to procure and transport Hú tea,
which was called Nánguì.
At that time, only over eight hundred tickets were issued.
Subsequently, it was decided that it would be a three-year case,
with tickets allowed to increase but not decrease.
From Guāngxù thirteen years to twenty-seven years,
it increased in each case.
In thirty years,
in addition to Hú tickets, Jìn tickets for sale in Yī and Tǎ were also implemented.
Up until Xuāntǒng two years,
the tea business flourished daily.
Tea and salt
were managed in a somewhat similar way.
However, as salt was a major source of annual revenue,
those in charge of state finances merely attached it to salt and generally reviewed it.
In the beginning, there was only taxation;
except for the fixed permits in Jiāng and Zhè which were collected by various customs houses without a fixed quota,
other provinces collected more than a thousand liǎng annually,
and sometimes only a few hundred liǎng or even tens of liǎng.
Even the so-called biānyǐn (border permits) of Shǎnxī, Gān, and Sìchuān
did not amount to ten thousand jīn.
Since Xiánfēng,
various provinces gradually implemented lí (likin tax).
In Guāngxù twelve years,
Fújiàn reported a registered amount of over one hundred ninety thousand liǎng,
and other provinces' collections also gradually increased,
but soon the revenue decreased again.
According to the Xuāntǒng three years budget table,
tea tax was merely over one million three hundred thousand.
In the initial year of Shùnzhì,
regulations for the tea-horse trade were established.
A superior horse was given twelve chábì (tea combs),
a medium horse was given nine,
and an inferior horse was given seven.
In the second year,
supervising Censor was dispatched to oversee the Wǔ Chámǎ Sī (Five Tea-Horse Administrations).
At that time, many merchants illegally traded across the border,
and the Fān ethnic groups, finding the price cheap, flocked to it.
Furthermore, Fānsēng (Tibetan monks) traveled back and forth by courier,
smuggling private tea out of the passes,
and officials could not question them.
The Hùbù (Board of Revenue) memorialized, saying:
"In Shǎnxī, for exchanging tea for horses,
there was clearly a Ming dynasty precedent of issuing gold plaques and tallies.
These need not be used now,
but only the value should be determined.
As for where Fānsēng travel,
if officials condone and purchase private tea,
let the Xún'àn Yùshǐ (Circuit Censors) investigate and impeach them."
The Chámǎ Yùshǐ (Tea-Horse Censor) Liáo Pānlóng also said:
"The old quota for tea-horses was eleven thousand eighty-eight horses.
In Chóngzhēn three years, an additional two thousand horses were levied.
I request that this be permanently exempted."
Both were approved.
In the fourth year,
one Mǎn (Manchu) and one Hàn (Han) Yùshǐ were appointed to inspect the tea-horse trade.
The area of Zhílì Hé Bǎoyíng was west of Zhāngjiākǒu.
During the Ming dynasty, the È'ěrdūosī (Ordos) tribe had traded tea and horses there,
but it was later closed.
At this time,
the Hùbù dispatched a Lǐshì Guān (Director) to conduct an on-site investigation
and reported the situation.
An imperial edict permitted mutual trade again.
In the seventh year,
based on the old Gānsù precedent,
for dà yǐn bì chá (large permit comb tea),
officials and merchants equally divided it;
for xiǎo yǐn (small permit), three-tenths of the tax went to the government,
and seven-tenths went to the merchants.
An imperial edict stated that thereafter, all permits would be issued by the Board,
following the dà yǐn precedent,
for use with medium horses.
Furthermore, the old precedent attached sixty bì (combs) to dà yǐn,
and sixty-seven jīn (catties) to xiǎo yǐn.
It was stipulated that for every thousand jīn of tea,
one hundred forty jīn would generally be allowed to be attached,
for merchants to sell themselves.
In the thirteenth year,
as Gānsù had enough horses,
an order was issued to sell old tea at a reduced price to supplement military provisions.
In the fourteenth year,
it was again decreed that for the seven horse pastures of Guǎngníng, Kāichéng, Hēishuǐ, Āndìng, Qīng'ān, Wàn'ān, and Wǔ'ān,
private horses and private tea would be confiscated and sold for their value.
What was originally reserved for use with medium horses
was all converted into money to supplement military provisions.
In the eighteenth year,
following the request of the Dálài Lǎma and Gēndū Táijí,
tea was exchanged for horses in Běishèng Zhōu, Yúnnán.
In Kāngxī four years,
the various horse pastures in Shǎnxī were consequently abolished,
and a tea-horse market was opened in Běishèng Zhōu.
In the seventh year,
the Chámǎ Yùshǐ were abolished
and management was assigned to the Gānsù Xúnfǔ (Provincial Governor).
In the nineteenth year,
due to urgent military needs,
the tea tax in Fújiàn was increased by three hundred fifty-nine liǎng of silver;
this was remitted in the twenty-sixth year,
and the newly added tea tax silver in Húguǎng was also abolished.
At that time, Sìchuān produced a lot of tea,
and its use gradually expanded.
The Hùbù deliberated on increasing permits,
and by the end of Kāngxī,
Tiānquán Tǔsī, Yázhōu, Qióng, Róngjīng, Míngshān, Xīnfán, Dàyì, and Guànxiàn all had increases.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Xíngkē Jǐshìzhōng (Supervising Secretary of the Ministry of Punishments) Qiú Yuánpèi stated that the quota tea in Táozhōu and Mínzhōu amounted to over three hundred thousand bì,
which could be exchanged for ten thousand horses.
Old tea sold annually
could also be exchanged for tens of thousands of horses.
He requested that a special officer be dispatched to manage it.
In the thirty-sixth year,
a Board official was consequently dispatched to supervise tea-horse affairs.
In the fortieth year,
due to the prevalence of private tea in Shǎnxī,
strict investigation of passing civilians was ordered.
Anyone carrying less than ten jīn of private tea would not be questioned,
but those transporting more than ten jīn without an official permit would be punished.
In the forty-fourth year,
as unscrupulous merchants relied on previous precedents
and all transported in small, separate batches,
illegal trade increased.
An order was issued to continue arresting them as before,
to suspend the dispatch of Board officials,
and to return management to the Gānsù Xúnfǔ.
Since Kāngxī thirty-two years,
because the tea combs stored in Xīníng Wǔsī (Five Administrations of Xīníng) had rotted due to age,
the Board deliberated and approved their sale.
Later, as there were no horses to be exchanged in Lánzhōu,
the old accumulated tea in Gānzhōu
was distributed according to a ratio of seven parts silver to three parts tea
within the salaries of the Wǔzhèn (Five Garrisons).
Soon after, it was decided to stop exchanging horses in Xīníng and other places.
Each bì of new tea was converted to four qián of silver,
and old tea to six qián,
to supplement military provisions.
By sixty-one years,
tea permits for Xīníng, Zhuānglàng, Mínzhōu, and Hézhōu were again increased,
and all old tea stored in various places
was ordered to be sold.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng
it was then deliberated that starting from the sixty-first year of Kāngxī
for five years, the full amount of actual tea (bensè) should be collected.
After five years, the old tea should be sold off.
Thereafter, old tea was replaced with new,
always at a rate of five years.
In the fourth year
it was decided to regulate the tea trade in Shǎnxī.
The local officials in tea-producing areas were ordered to issue boat tickets,
clearly stating the amount of tea according to the merchants' permits (yǐnmù).
If any merchant carried unapproved tickets beyond the official permits (bùyǐn),
or carried additional tea exceeding the prescribed quota,
they would be prosecuted under the salt smuggling laws.
Officials who failed to investigate or deliberately connived
would all be subject to disciplinary action.
In the eighth year
merchants in Shǎnxī were ordered to transport official tea,
and in addition to the old regulation allowing an extra fourteen catties for every hundred catties,
another fourteen catties of "wear and tear" tea (hàochá) were added.
An edict also stated:
"In Sìchuān, tea taxes are all assessed by garden and by tree.
However, trees vary in size,
and gardens vary in width;
how can they be treated uniformly?
If this is used as the basis for the quota,
it will not be equitable.
Taxes should be collected based on weight.
The provincial governor (fǔ) concerned is hereby ordered to deliberate on this."
Soon after, it was deliberated:
"The old regulation imposed a tax of two lí and five háo per catty.
Now, it only collects four sī and nine hū plus a fraction (yǒuqí),
which is a huge discrepancy.
The amount should be halved.
Regardless of whether it is border (biān), native (tǔ), or interior (fù) permits (yǐn),
all shall pay one lí, two háo, and five sī of silver."
At that time, Sìchuān tea was in demand,
and the permits (yǐn) were insufficient.
Consequently, they were increased again,
with various prefectures (fǔ), departments (zhōu), and counties (xiàn) resuming their issuance.
In the ninth year
the five offices (wǔsī) of Xīníng were ordered to reinstate the 'exchange horses for tea' (zhòngmǎfǎ) system.
In the tenth year
it was again ordered that tea should be issued for the exchanged horses.
At this time, Ānhuī also increased its permits (yǐn),
following the Sìchuān example,
by temporarily storing surplus permits in the provincial treasury (sīkù),
to be allocated for transport
when there was a shortage.
In the thirteenth year
the 'exchange horses for tea' (zhòngmǎ) system in Gānsù was again suspended.
The Yúnnán tea regulations were first established,
with seven catties forming one tube (tǒng),
and thirty-two tubes forming one permit (yǐn),
with taxes collected according to regulations.
In the first year of Qiánlóng
it was ordered that official tea in Gānsù should be collected in monetary equivalent (zhé sè),
with five qián of silver paid per tea comb (bì).
At this time, the old tea in the five offices (wǔsī) of Xīníng was abundant.
It was ordered that the price of each block (fēng) be reduced by two qián,
and sold within a fixed period.
In the second year
as thirty-two prefectures (zhōu) and counties (xiàn) including Nánchāng in Jiāngxī did not produce tea,
and tea sales in Chéngdū, Péng, Guàn, and other counties in Sìchuān were sluggish,
their permits were either suspended or reduced,
and their tax silver was also exempted.
In the seventh year
the tax for areas in Gānsù affected by earthquake was exempted,
and the five offices (wǔsī) of Xīníng were ordered to collect actual tea (bensè).
In the eighth year
the outstanding "surplus and truncated corners" (xiànyú jiécǎo) of Tiānquán Office in Sìchuān before the seventh year of Qiánlóng were remitted,
as were the outstanding silver amounts of Chéngdū, Péng, Guàn, and other counties.
In the eleventh year
Huáng Tíngguì, the provincial governor (xúnfǔ) of Gānsù, reported:
"In the three offices (sī) of Xīníng, Hézhōu, and Zhuānglàng,
Tibetans (fān) and Han Chinese (mín) live intermingled,
and they rely solely on tea.
In recent years, grain has been exchanged for tea,
totaling over sixty-five thousand five hundred blocks (fēng) of tea,
exchanged for over thirty-eight thousand one hundred piculs (shí) of assorted grains.
I request that this be established as a regular practice."
The report was approved.
In the thirteenth year
the amount of tea blocks (cháfēng) to be collected in Gānsù was set:
each year, two tenths (two chéng) would be collected in actual tea (bensè) and eight tenths (eight chéng) in monetary equivalent (zhésè).
The method of verifying permits (yǐn) and truncating corners (jiécǎo) for merchants transporting tea via various land and water routes was also reiterated,
and extended to Ānhuī, Zhèjiāng, Sìchuān, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu.
In the twenty-fourth year
following the suggestion of Wú Dáshàn, the provincial governor (xúnfǔ) of Gānsù,
the tea blocks (cháfēng) of the five offices (wǔsī) of Xīníng
were ordered to be allocated for the pay and rations of various garrisons,
following the regulation of the thirty-seventh year of Kāngxī
In the twenty-fifth year
Wú Dáshàn again reported:
"The Gānsù tea tax was originally established for the 'exchange horses for tea' (zhòngmǎ) system.
Now that the system has been suspended,
although the offices (sī) of Gān and Zhuāng are located in major thoroughfares,
and the offices (sī) of Xī and Hé are near Qīnghǎi,
there are still sales channels.
However, the Táosī Office is remote,
and merchants selling tea
have, over the years, changed to selling in other offices.
Yet, the official tea blocks (guāncháfēng) to be delivered
still go to the Táosī treasury,
often accumulating to hundreds of thousands of blocks,
before a request is made to clear the sales.
The quota of tea permits (cháyǐn) issued to Táosī
should be transferred to Gān and Zhuāng offices for collection from merchants.
Once the tea stored in the Táosī treasury for rations has been exhausted,
the office should be abolished."
In the twenty-seventh year
Yáng Yìngjū, the Governor-General (zǒngdū) of Shǎnxī and Gānsù, again submitted a memorial outlining four matters concerning the clearance of sales:
"Firstly,
official tea should be converted to collecting its monetary equivalent (zhéjià).
It is observed that for official tea stored in Gānsù treasuries,
the practice has been to convert to monetary equivalent (zhésè) if too much accumulates.
Currently, in the five offices (wǔsī) treasuries,
from the seventh year of Qiánlóng
over 1.5 million blocks (fēng) have accumulated.
The former provincial governor (fǔchén) Wú Dáshàn memorialized and received approval for each block (fēng) to be valued at three qián,
and allocated for military pay and rations.
Over four hundred thousand blocks (fēng) have already been allocated.
With an increasing amount of official tea in the market,
it will take no less than ten years
to clear all sales.
Furthermore, merchants are additionally allocated 240,000 blocks (fēng) annually,
and with more merchant tea,
official tea becomes even more stagnant.
It would be better to collect the monetary equivalent of three qián per block for the over 54,000 blocks (fēng) of two-tenths (two chéng) official tea submitted by merchants,
following the regulations,
and then revert to collecting actual tea (bensè) once the old tea has been almost entirely sold off.
Secondly,
merchant tea should be allowed a reduction in allocation.
It is observed that according to the Gānsù tea regulations,
merchants submit fifty catties of tea per permit (yǐn),
which, regardless of whether it is in actual tea (ben) or monetary equivalent (zhé),
constitutes the fixed tax (ékè).
Additionally, there is over 39,000 liǎng of silver for public coffers (chōnggōngyín),
also collected annually,
no different from a regular tax (zhènggōng).
As for the tea blocks (cháfēng) sold by merchants themselves,
each permit (yǐn) should only be allocated fifty catties of main tea (zhègnchá).
Including additional tea (fùchá), a total of over three hundred thousand blocks (fēng) are allocated and sold.
Merchants then pay their tax with the allocated and sold tea.
Wú Dáshàn memorialized and received approval for an increased allocation to ease the burden on merchants,
without any additional tax items.
However, with the increased tea blocks (cháfēng),
and the official tea allocated for military pay and rations,
it inevitably leads to greater accumulation,
making it difficult to avoid capital stagnation and losses.
Currently, merchants are willing to accept only five blocks (fēng) per permit (yǐn).
Within this, 158,316 blocks (fēng) of untaxed tea should be reduced,
making a total allocation of only 409,440 blocks (fēng).
Since the two-tenths (two chéng) actual tea blocks (bensè cháfēng) have been proposed to be collected in monetary equivalent (zhéjià),
there is no need to transport them.
Thirdly,
accumulated old tea blocks (chénjī cháfēng) should be offered to merchants for discounted sales.
It is observed that all offices (sī) have old tea,
with Táosī having the most.
Currently, each block (fēng) is sold for four qián,
discouraging merchants and common people.
I request to revert to the original proposal,
setting the price at three qián per block (fēng),
and inviting merchants to sell it off.
Fourthly,
the interior and Xīnjiāng should be treated uniformly for allocation.
It is observed that in the twenty-fourth year of Qiánlóng
As for tea in Xīnjiāng,
it has historically relied on the interior.
Now, official tea is transported by carts and stations along the route,
eliminating the need for transport fees.
For tea transported from Sùzhōu to various places,
the transport costs are factored into the tea's principal cost,
which is more economical
compared to buying from merchants."
The memorial was submitted,
and the recommendations were approved for implementation.
In the twenty-ninth year,
the post of Gānsù Xúnfǔ was abolished,
and tea affairs were concurrently managed by the Shǎngān Zǒngdū.
In the thirty-fourth year,
as the official tea reserves in Gān Province's treasury gradually diminished,
a further one-tenth was levied in kind.
In the thirty-sixth year,
due to the settlement of the surrendered Tǔ'ěrhùtè and other groups in Yīlí and other places,
they were granted tea seals
and it was still deliberated to levy two-tenths as before.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Liú Bǐngtián, the Sìchuān Zǒngdū, memorialized and received approval for the Tǔsī in Sānzá Gǔ and other places to buy tea,
at a rate of one thousand catties,
such that it would only be enough for their own consumption
and could not be privately resold.
Sìchuān established frontier permits;
merchants would pay taxes, collect permits, and transport tea for sale in Sōngpān and other places.
Whether Tǔsī or indigenous merchants,
all were permitted to go to the frontier to obtain tickets for transport and sale.
In the seventh year of Jiāqìng,
as the official tea permits for Shěnxī Shénmù, which had long been allocated for merchant sale in Gān Province,
were ordered to be exempted from the old designation of "surplus,"
and due to the disturbance by rebel bandits in Sìchuān,
tea taxes were remitted for the five departments and counties of Dàníng, Guǎngyuán, Tàipíng, Tōngjiāng, and Nánjiāng.
In the tenth year,
taxes and levies were again remitted for the four counties and sub-prefectures of Dàníng, Tàipíng, Tōngjiāng, and Wūshān.
In the seventeenth year,
as Gānsù's treasury tea constituted a surplus,
it was stipulated that merchants paying for official tea
should pay entirely in silver equivalent.
In the twenty-second year,
an edict stated:
"Merchants from Mǐn, Wǎn, and Zhè who transport Wǔyí and Sōngluó tea to Yuè for sale
traditionally traveled by inland rivers,
but recently many have been transporting by sea,
smuggling contraband goods for private sale.
It is hereby ordered that tea merchants shall continue to travel by inland rivers,
and oceanic transport for sale is permanently prohibited.
Violators will be punished and the tea confiscated."
In the third year of Dàoguāng,
an edict stated:
"Nàyànchéng memorialized and established regulations for tea trade in Xīnjiāng,
which were deliberated and reported back by the Hùbù.
Brick tea from Wūlǐyàsūtái and Kēbùduō is not allowed to infringe upon the sale in various cities of Xīnjiāng.
Now, General Guǒlēifēng'ā and others have memorialized,
stating that this type of brick tea
has been obtained from Guīhuàchéng and Zhāngjiākǒu with Hùbù permits and tax payments
for over sixty years,
and it is not appropriate to suddenly prohibit it.
However, since Xīnjiāng is an area for official tea permits,
merchant tea ultimately hinders official permits.
It is ordered that from now on, merchants and commoners may annually transport over one thousand chests of brick tea
to Gǔchéng,
still receiving permits as per regulation,
but are not allowed to sell it elsewhere."
In the sixth year,
an edict stated:
"Previously, regarding the transport of tea to various cities in Xīnjiāng,
the former general and others requested permits to attract merchants and levy taxes.
Now, Qìngxiáng and others have memorialized, stating
that there are no wealthy households in the various cities,
and if they are suddenly ordered to serve as official merchants,
both transport and taxes will certainly be jeopardized.
Merchants and commoners from the northern route are to specialize in transporting and selling miscellaneous tea,
and a bureau is to be established in Gǔchéng to collect taxes,
using the silver collected to offset the taxes on Lánzhōu tea merchants.
After a three-year trial period,
the fixed quota will be determined.
As for supplementary tea, it will still be transported and sold by Gān merchants."
In the eighth year,
Imperial Commissioner Nàyànchéng stated:
"Gānsù official tea is
annually expected to export over two hundred thousand seals.
Recently, sales have reached four to five hundred thousand seals,
all due to unpermitted private tea being misrepresented,
and prices have repeatedly increased,
with each seal of supplementary tea
selling for seven to eight taels to over ten taels of silver.
It is requested that from now on, the price per seal be fixed:
Ākèsū shall not exceed four taels,
and Kāshígá'ěr shall not exceed five taels.
Furthermore, bureaus should be established outside Jiāyùguān and in Ākèsū and other places for inspection."
The imperial edict granted the request.
In the ninth year,
it was ordered that Gānsù tea affairs be the responsibility of the Zhèndí Dào for overall inspection,
with Qítái County managing them locally.
In the third year of Xiánfēng,
Wáng Yìdé, the Mǐnzhè Zǒngdū, memorialized requesting the establishment of customs posts to levy taxes on Mǐn Province merchant tea.
In the fifth year,
Lǚ Quánshūn, the Fújiàn Xúnfǔ, further stated:
"Mǐn tea has not traditionally been issued with licenses
or subjected to tax collection.
Since the twenty-ninth year of Dàoguāng,
Nè'ěrjīng'é, the Zhílì Dūchén, observed that Mǐn merchants' transport
made it difficult to distinguish between official and private tea,
and deliberated that licenses should be issued by Chóng'ān County, the tea-producing area.
Upon passing through checkpoints,
taxes would be verified and passage permitted.
Subsequently, because tea was produced in more than one place,
and merchants dispersed to various counties to purchase it,
bypassing routes for sale,
Fǔchén Wáng Yìdé again memorialized, requesting
that beginning in the third year of Xiánfēng,
all tea-producing counties, namely Shā, Shàowǔ, Jiàn'ān, Ōuníng, Jiànyáng, Pǔchéng, and Chóng'ān,
should uniformly collect tea taxes locally,
and issue licenses for transport and sale from their respective counties.
This was successively deliberated and approved by the Hùbù.
The year before last, due to the incursions of the Yuè bandits,
tea merchants from Jiāng and Chǔ did not proceed,
and the sea ban was temporarily relaxed.
Consequently, tea merchants from all routes
transported tea to the province,
without passing through the various checkpoints.
Not only did this reduce taxes in this province,
but Zhè, Yuè, and Jiāngxī also experienced shortfalls.
After I assumed office,
I extensively inquired and found that tea merchants' profits
had more than quintupled compared to before.
Merchant profits are substantial,
while regular revenue is turning into a deficit.
Currently, the Yuè bandits are not yet pacified,
and military expenses are urgent.
All merchants are wealthy,
and taking a tenth of their profits
causes no loss to them.
Moreover, levying from traveling merchants
does not burden the poor,
and collecting from Chinese merchants
avoids entanglements with foreign taxes.
This utilizes the natural benefits of heaven and earth
as a proper contribution to the state,
which is entirely different from increasing land taxes.
However, Mǐn tea is produced in more than just a few counties,
so it is necessary to establish customs posts and increase checkpoints at strategic locations adjacent to the provincial capital,
and issue stamped licenses for verification.
Neighboring provinces
should also establish these uniformly
to prevent evasion.
I request that starting from the fifth year of Xiánfēng,
all tea transported
shall be taxed,
and the collected funds shall be exclusively allocated
and retained for the military pay of this province.
However, as this is a new measure,
the exact amount cannot be predetermined.
After it has been implemented for one or two years,
we will compare and set a fixed quota."
From this point, Mǐn taxes became more stringent.
However, by the tenth year,
it had still not been reported to the Hùbù,
which then urged its submission,
after which it was reported periodically.
In the sixth year,
Zhālāfēntài, the Yīlí Jiāngjūn's request was granted:
Yīlí tea production
would have a bureau established to collect taxes,
to be used for the military pay of Yīlí.
In the eleventh year,
Juéluó Qílíng, the Guǎngdōng Xúnfǔ, memorialized requesting the collection of a "fallen tea" tax.
In the first year of Tóngzhì (1862),
orders were issued to the Governors-General and Governors of Húnán, Húběi, Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, and Fújiàn,
to investigate in detail the tea-producing areas and locations of tea houses in their respective provinces,
and propose appropriate regulations for imperial approval.
In the second year (1863),
Zēng Guófān, the Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, submitted a memorial,
which stated briefly:
"Since the ninth year of Xiánfēng (1859), Jiāngxī
has had regulations for distinguishing between tea lí (likin) and tea juān (contribution).
For every hundred catties, in addition to collecting two qián of lí silver within the province,
and an additional one qián five fēn and some odd amount upon exiting the province,
tea juān was customarily solicited from tea-producing areas and tea houses.
For every hundred catties, a juān silver of one liǎng four qián or one liǎng two qián was collected, varying by location.
Receipts were issued,
and these were allowed to be accumulated and presented for rewards in accordance with the regulations for raising military funds.
Your subject continues to operate according to the old regulations.
This year, according to a detailed report from Cài Jǐnqīng, the acting Superintendent of Jiǔjiāng Customs,
a request was made to comply with the Ministry of Revenue's (Hùbù) approved memorial,
ordering that a unified customs duty be levied on salt, tea, bamboo, and timber.
This began collection in the third month.
Tea transported from Jiāngxī to Jiǔjiāng
is divided into Chinese merchant (Huáshāng) and foreign merchant (Yángshāng) categories.
Foreign merchants, having already paid the half-duty at the 'zǐkǒu' (barrier gate),
are naturally exempt from lí collection.
Chinese merchants, having paid the regular duty at Xún Pass,
also ought not to be made to pay lí again.
Your subject immediately followed the Ministry's regulations
and established a 'landed goods tax' in Yìníng Zhōu.
However, the original memorial's tariff for large chests of pure tea was slightly heavy,
so it has been proportionally reduced.
Referring to the customary tea juān regulations,
for every hundred catties,
one liǎng four qián is levied in Yìníng Zhōu and other places,
and one liǎng two qián five fēn is levied in Hékǒu Zhèn.
These funds are entirely allocated to your subject's military expenses.
Your subject issues printed tax receipts and护票 (hùpiào, transit permits),
collected by appointed commissioners.
Either the proprietors pay themselves,
or tea houses pay the tax and collect the receipts on their behalf.
When it comes time for sale and distribution,
all tax receipts are submitted by the tea houses for cancellation.
Chinese merchants are issued hùpiào,
while foreign merchants rely on their transport permits,
for sale and distribution to various places.
Except for Chinese merchants paying Jiǔjiāng Customs duties and foreign merchants paying the 'zǐkǒu' half-duty,
when passing through the líkǎ (likin barriers) in Jiāngxī and Ānhuī,
they are to be inspected and released.
Such an arrangement
is entirely consistent
with the Ministry of Revenue's original memorial and the Zǒnglǐ Yámén's treaties.
Although tax receipts are handled by tea houses,
the tax silver is actually borne by the proprietors.
Foreign merchants may not use the 'zǐkǒu' half-duty as an excuse
to prevent Chinese proprietors from paying Chinese land tax.
Since Chinese merchants are exempt from lí collection at every barrier,
they will not resort to secretly purchasing transport permits
and falsely claiming to be foreign merchants."
An imperial edict approved the implementation.
In the fifth year (1866),
the Ministry of Revenue memorialized and received approval that, due to the stagnation of permits and suspension of levies in Gānsù Province,
a general government tea store should be temporarily established in the provincial capital of Shǎnxī,
with branch stores in Tóngguān, Shāngzhōu, and Hánzhōng.
Merchants trading tea without permits,
upon arrival in Shǎnxī, should report it.
For superior grade tea, one liǎng of tax silver is collected per hundred catties;
for medium grade, six qián;
for inferior grade, four qián.
The collected funds are to be remitted to Gānsu to make up for outstanding levies.
In the seventh year (1868),
it was approved that merchants from Guīhuà Chéng transporting tea to Qiàkètú,
and passing through Russian territory,
to trade with various Western countries,
should apply for Ministry permits.
Compared to Zhāngjiākǒu, the fee would be halved,
requiring twenty-five liǎng of silver to be paid,
and each permit should not exceed twelve thousand catties.
In the eleventh year (1872),
it was approved that old outstanding levies in Gānsù Province
should still be collected from old merchants.
New merchants recruited would be subject to new levies on a trial basis.
The four categories of miscellaneous levies, yǎnglián (integrity-nurturing fees), confiscations, and official gifts were to be temporarily suspended.
In the thirteenth year (1874),
it was approved that Gānsù Province should emulate the example of Huáinán salt,
using tickets instead of permits.
Regardless of the province of the merchants,
they must first pay the regular tax before
being issued tickets.
Miscellaneous levies were to be consolidated and collected under the lí-tax category.
All other categories were to be abolished.
For tea sold domestically,
in addition to paying the regular tax of three liǎng,
lí-tax was to be paid in the place of sale,
with each ticket limited to one liǎng a few qián,
not exceeding two liǎng.
Exported tea,
however, would be subject to an additional lí collection at border bureaus and barriers,
to differentiate it.
In the tenth year of Guāngxù (1884),
the Ministry of Revenue, in overall financial planning,
briefly stated regarding tea regulations:
"According to the list provided by the Zǒnglǐ Yámén,
in the eighth and ninth years of Guāngxù (1882-1883), tea exports amounted to over 190 million catties.
It is found that during the Dàoguāng era, the tea tax collected by Britain
was approximately fifty liǎng of silver per hundred catties,
while our export tax was only two liǎng five qián,
less than one-tenth.
It is proposed to follow the example of Gānsù tea seals,
collecting three qián of silver from tea garden households for every fifty catties.
With increased levies,
foreigners will have no grounds for complaint.
Alternatively, following the example of Níngxià, Yán, Yú, Suí, and other places where each tea permit is levied three liǎng nine qián of silver,
bureaus should be established in tea-producing areas to inspect tea,
and issue Ministry-approved tea permits.
For every hundred catties on each permit,
three liǎng nine qián of silver would be collected.
When passing through inland customs barriers,
an additional lí-tax would be paid,
and after inspection and stamping of the permit, release would be granted,
with no repeated or disguised levies allowed.
All tea permits
should be applied for in advance from the Governor-General annually,
and the original permits would become void after one year.
Or, tea could be inspected in tea-producing areas and Ministry permits issued.
After paying a tax of three liǎng,
an additional three liǎng nine qián of silver would be collected (doubling the amount),
totaling seven liǎng eight qián.
All miscellaneous fees would be waived.
However, at various customs and border barriers,
any foreign duties payable
would still be collected according to existing regulations.
If tea is sold and transported domestically,
regardless of which province or líkǎ or customs barrier it passes through,
no further collection would be made.
Thus, lí would be converted to 'kè' (tax),
and scattered collections would be centralized,
facilitating inspection
and preventing embezzlement.
However, regarding how to prevent evasion by garden households and merchants,
each province should consider and formulate regulations,
and memorialize for implementation."
In the twelfth year (1886),
because merchants from Shānxī, who obtained permits from the Court of Colonial Affairs (Lǐfānyuàn),
deceptively claimed to transport and sell tea in Měnggǔ (Mongolia),
but actually smuggled Hú tea
and sold it illicitly in the northern and southern routes of Xīnjiāng.
One permit would be used for several years,
circulating repeatedly,
often evading lí and taxes.
The Ministry memorialized and received approval that
henceforth, when permits are issued,
they must be marked with the words
"smuggling of private tea is prohibited."
If one wishes to deal in government tea,
they should go to Gānsù to obtain permits, pay taxes, and settle lí.
If private tea is transported and sold again,
it will be confiscated upon discovery.
At that time, many Western countries were fond of tea.
Japan, India, and Italy envied its substantial profits.
Although their climate and soil conditions were inferior to those of our country,
they meticulously studied and improved cultivation methods,
and their production subsequently increased.
Indeed, India began cultivating tea
in Dàoguāng (道光) fourteen years,
and by Guāngxù (光緒) three years, it had become a major industry.
Sri Lanka and Italy were later adopters.
After France acquired Vietnam,
it also ordered tea cultivation,
establishing gardens such as Dōngshān (東山), Jiànjí (建吉), and Fùhuá (富華).
In Xiánfēng (咸豐) eight years, the United States purchased ten thousand tea saplings from our country,
distributing them to farmers.
Thereafter, they purchased more and more,
annually distributing up to one hundred and twenty thousand tea saplings,
sufficient for their country's needs.
Therefore, before Guāngxù (光緒) ten years, our country's exports were very large,
but soon after, they were gradually overtaken.
Tea from India exported to the United Kingdom
amounted to approximately 732,000 dàn (石) annually,
valued at about 20,040,000 liǎng (兩).
Our country's tea exported there was 898,000 dàn (石),
valued at about 18,680,000 liǎng (兩).
Indian tea was less than Chinese tea,
but its price was higher.
By twenty-two years, our country's exports
had dropped to only about 219,400 dàn (石).
Japanese tea
was mostly sold to the United States,
though some was also shipped to our country.
In Guāngxù (光緒) thirteen years,
our tea exported to Japan was over 12,000 dàn (石),
while their tea imported was over 16,000 dàn (石).
Only Russia exclusively favored and consumed large quantities of Chinese tea.
This was because, since the newly acquired regions of Hāsàkè (哈薩克) and Hàohǎn (浩罕) and others became part of its territory,
its land expanded,
its population grew,
its demand for goods increased,
and tea, in particular, was relied upon.
In Guāngxù (光緒) seven years, a treaty was signed,
agreeing to make Jiāyùguān (嘉峪關) a trade port,
and trade flourished even more.
Ten years later, our country's tea exports
constituted one-third of the total.
In thirteen years,
including miscellaneous goods,
the export value was over 9,020,000 liǎng (兩),
while the import value was only over 118,000 liǎng (兩),
with a total surplus from our exports of 8,900,000 liǎng (兩).
However, in twelve years, tea was scarce and prices were high;
in thirteen years, tea was abundant and prices were low,
and Chinese merchants were already facing difficulties.
Subsequently, they also purchased from other countries,
which drastically reduced the profits from Chinese tea.
Indeed, from ancient times, our country regarded tea as a secondary activity for farming families,
only cultivating it in vacant land.
Moreover, harvesting was not timely,
and processing methods were crude.
It was inevitable
that it would be outcompeted by others.
In thirty-three years,
the Tea Association presented a petition to the Dùzhī Bù (度支部) (Ministry of Finance),
and the customs office also spoke of the decrease in tea tax.
Thereupon, orders were given to devise regularization policies.
In the early years of Xuāntǒng (宣統),
the Nónggōngshāng Bù (農工商部) (Ministry of Agriculture, Industry, and Commerce) proposed to appropriately exempt taxes and levies.
Hànkǒu (漢口) and Fúzhōu (福州) both purchased tea-making machinery from foreign countries,
and also hired skilled instructors from India.
The Jiāngxī (江西) Provincial Governor also planned to extend loans to tea farmers.
From then on, sales to Europe and North Africa became somewhat more prosperous.
The quality of our country's tea is inherently superior to that of other countries;
it often contains fragrance within its astringent taste,
which can leave a sweet aftertaste on the tongue.
Westerners call it
"dǎnniàn" (膽念),
and few products from other countries can match this.
Therefore, even though Japan has tea,
it must buy from us.
The Dutch envoy, Cröber, also stated that Jǐawā (爪哇), India, and Xīlán (錫蘭) teas were far inferior to Chinese tea.
Thus, encouraging and protecting
our natural products, preventing them from being taken over by the efforts of other nations,
is what we must now hope for from those who speak of commerce.
Mining Policy: In the early Qīng (清) Dynasty, learning from the Míng (明) Dynasty's eager pursuit of mining profits,
imperial envoys were dispatched everywhere,
collecting exorbitant taxes and afflicting the people.
Therefore, the people were allowed to extract minerals,
paying taxes to the government,
all at regular rates.
If mining activities interfered with prohibited mountain geomancy,
private fields, homes, or tombs,
or involved gathering crowds to disturb the people,
or in years of poor harvests and soaring grain prices,
mines would immediately be sealed off.
In the early years of Shìzǔ (世祖), silver mines were opened in Shāndōng's (山東) Línqú (臨朐) and Zhāoyǔan (招遠).
In Shùnzhì (順治) eight years, they were abolished.
In fourteen years,
iron mines were opened at Gǔběi (古北), Xǐfēng (喜峯), and other passes.
During the Kāngxī (康熙) reign,
officials were sent to supervise the extraction of silver from Yìngzhōu (應州) in Shānxī (山西), Líntóng (臨潼) in Shǎnxī (陝西), and Láiyáng (萊陽) in Shāndōng (山東).
In twenty-two years,
all were stopped.
An edict also stated that opening mines was not beneficial to the localities,
and thereafter, any requests for mining
would not be permitted.
When Shìzōng (世宗) ascended the throne,
many officials spoke of mining profits.

Guǎngdōng (廣東) Governor Kǒng Yùxún (孔毓珣), Guǎngdōng (廣東) Provincial Governor Yáng Wénqían (楊文乾), Húnán (湖南) Provincial Governor Bùlántài (布蘭泰), Guǎngxī (廣西) Military Governor Tían Jùn (田畯), Guǎngdōng (廣東) Provincial Administration Commissioner Wáng Shìjùn (王士俊), and Sìchuān (四川) Military Governor Huáng Tíngguì (黃廷桂) successively submitted memorials requesting to open mines,
but all were rejected,
or met with severe imperial reprimands.
In thirteen years,
Guǎngdōng (廣東) Governor Èmǐdá (鄂彌達) requested to open mines in the prefectures of Huì (惠), Cháo (潮), Sháo (韶), and Zhào (肇).
This was sent to the Jiǔqīng (九卿) (Nine Ministers) for deliberation.
The emperor stopped it, deeming it to interfere with essential duties.
Indeed, Guǎngdōng (廣東) has many mountains and little arable land,
but its mineral resources are abundant.
Local people were accustomed to mining.
Wherever mining caves were located,
hundreds and thousands gathered,
often forming groups to illegally excavate
and then gathering to plunder.
Therefore, at that time, mining in Guǎngdōng (廣東)
was more strictly prohibited than in other provinces.
In Qiánlóng (乾隆) two years,
an edict permitted the reporting and opening of any copper mines
that genuinely benefited coinage.
However, all gold and silver mines
were sealed.
Prior to this,
in five years, the request by Lǔ (魯) Provincial Governor Zhū Dìngyuán (朱定元) was approved,

to open coal mines in various counties and prefectures: Zhāngqīu (章丘), Zīchuān (淄川), Tàí'ān (泰安), Xīntàí (新泰), Láiwú (萊蕪), Féíchéng (肥城), Níngyáng (寧陽), Téng (滕), Yì (嶧), Sìshuǐ (泗水), Lánshān (蘭山), Yǎnchéng (剡城), Fèi (費), Jǔ (莒), Méngyīn (蒙陰), Yìdū (益都), Línqú (臨朐), Bóshān (博山), Láiyáng (萊陽), and Hǎiyáng (海陽).

However, the request by Gǎochéng (藁城) County Magistrate Gāo Fēng (高崶) to privately fund the opening of silver, copper, and lead mines in Yì (嶧), Téng (滕), Fèi (費), Zī (淄), Yí (沂), Píngyīn (平陰), and Tàí'ān (泰安) was forbidden.
Nevertheless, in Guìzhōu (貴州), Tiānqìng Sì (天慶寺) in Sī'ān (思安) and Zhōngfēng Lǐng (中峯嶺) in Zhènyuǎn (鎮遠);
in Shǎnxī (陝西), Hābùtǎhǎi Hālā Shān (哈布塔海哈拉山);
in Gānsù (甘肅), Zhāmǎtú (扎馬圖), Dūnhuáng (敦煌), and the North and South Mountains of Shāzhōu (沙洲);
in Yīlí (伊犂), Píqiūqìn Shān (皮𩹉沁山), Gǔnèi (古內), and Shuāngshùzǐ (雙樹子);
and in Wūlǔmùqí (烏魯木齊), gold mines in Díhuà (迪化), Kuíténg Hé (奎騰河), Hūtúbì (呼圖壁), Mǎnàsī (瑪納斯), Kù'ěrkālāwūsū (庫爾喀喇烏蘇), and Tíaojīngōu (條金溝);
as well as silver mines in Fǎdū (法都), Píngyǔan (平遠), and Dámó Shān (達摩山) in Guìzhōu (貴州),
and Sānjiā (三嘉), Huílóng (廻龍) in Lìjiāng (麗江), and Lèmǎ (樂馬) in Zhāotōng (昭通) in Yúnnán (雲南),
were successively opened.
In Jiāqìng (嘉慶) four years,
Supervising Censor Míngshéng (明繩) memorialized, stating that commoners Pān Shì'ēn (潘世恩) and Sū Tínglù (蘇廷祿) requested to open a silver mine in Xíngtái (邢臺), Zhílì (直隸).
The emperor said:
"The state's expenditures have regular revenue sources.
Pān Shì'ēn (潘世恩) and Sū Tínglù (蘇廷祿) covet mining profits,
daring to use tax payment as an excuse,
which is truly not keeping to their station."
He ordered them to be escorted back to their hometowns,
and Míngshéng (明繩) was referred to the board for deliberation.
In six years,
Bǎoníng (保寧) for requesting to open the Tǎ'ěrbāhātái (塔爾巴哈台) gold mine,
and Míng'ān (明安) for requesting to open the Píngquán Zhōu (平泉州) copper mine,
both received imperial reprimands.
In the early years of Dàoguāng (道光),
gold mines in Gānsù (甘肅) and silver mines in Zhílì (直隸) were sealed.
At that time, annual revenue was stable,
and profits were not lightly discussed.
Only the silver mines in Nán'ān (南安), Shíyáng (石羊), Lín'ān (臨安), and Gèjiù (箇舊) in Yúnnán (雲南)
paid over 58,000 liǎng (兩) in annual taxes;
other gold mines amounted to only dozens of liǎng (兩) annually,
and silver mines to several thousand liǎng (兩) annually at most.
Moreover, they were frequently opened and then stopped,
their success and failure inconsistent,
and tax revenue was scarce.
Copper and lead profits were crucial for coinage,
so requests for their extraction were often approved,
with some even receiving tax exemptions.
In Guǎngdōng (廣東), mining mountains had been sealed since Kāngxī (康熙) fifty-four years.
By the early years of Qiánlóng (乾隆),
copper and lead mines in counties such as Yīngdé (英德), Yángchūn (陽春), Guīshàn (歸善), Yǒng'ān (永安), Qǔjiāng (曲江), Dàpǔ (大埔), and Bóluó (博羅),
and in the prefectures of Guǎngzhōu (廣州) and Zhàoqìng (肇慶),
were all opened for extraction.
Over more than a hundred years,

the number of reported copper and lead mines opened in Yúnnán (雲南), Guìzhōu (貴州), Húběi (湖北), Húnán (湖南), Guǎngdōng (廣東), Guǎngxī (廣西), Sìchuān (四川), Shǎnxī (陝西), Jiāngxī (江西), and Zhílì (直隸) numbered in the hundreds,
with Yúnnán (雲南) copper mines being particularly prominent among all provinces.
Indeed, for coinage, lead and copper were equally important,
but copper was especially vital.
Shǎnxī (陝西), Húběi (湖北), Sìchuān (四川), Guǎngxī (廣西), Guìzhōu (貴州), and Jiāngxī (江西) all produced copper,
but Yúnnán (雲南) was the most abundant.
The administration of copper from Yúnnán began officially in the 44th year of Kāngxī
and subsequently, the government provided the capital and labor.
In the early years of Yōngzhèng [c. 1723],
the annual output of copper was eight to nine hundred thousand,
and within a few years,
it reached two to three million.
Annually, it supplied the local mints for coinage.
When transported to Húguǎng and Jiāngxī,
it was just over one million.
In the early years of Qiánlóng [c. 1736],
a million taels of silver were allocated annually for copper capital,
and within four to five years,
the annual output reached six to seven million, or even eight to nine million,
with the maximum reaching twelve to thirteen million.
The two boards of Hùbù and Gōngbù,
as well as the nine circuits of Jiāngnán, Jiāngxī, Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Shǎnxī, Húběi, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, and Guìzhōu,
required over nine million annually,
all sourced from there.
The most prominent mining areas were Tāngdān, Lùlù, Dàshuǐ, Màolù, Shīzǐshān, and Dàgōng;
Níngtái, Jīnchāi, Yìdū, Fāgǔshān, Jiǔdù, and Wànxiàng were secondary.
Large mines employed sixty to seventy thousand miners,
while secondary ones had over ten thousand.
More recently, local people traveled as far as Qián [Guìzhōu] and Yuè [Guǎngdōng],
seeking livelihoods from mining profits,
moving continuously.
When the main mining shafts in tónglǎo were exhausted,
subsidiary mines were opened to meet the quota.
Therefore, the copper administration in Yúnnán Province,
having achieved success over successive generations,
was incomparable to other mineral products.
In the 24th year of Dàoguāng
an imperial edict was issued to provinces such as Yúnnán, Guìzhōu, Sìchuān, and Guǎngdōng, stating that
in addition to currently exploited mines,
if there were other mines willing to be exploited,
they would be permitted to operate under the same regulations as existing mines.
In the 28th year
another imperial edict stated:
"The Governors-General and Governors of Sìchuān, Yúnnán, Guìzhōu, both Guǎng Provinces, and Jiāngxī,
shall thoroughly investigate within their respective jurisdictions
and widely publicize this.
The Governors-General and Governors of other provinces
shall also pay attention to investigating
and consider exploitation,
not allowing pretexts for observation and delay.
As for government-operated, privately-operated, or merchant-operated enterprises,
regarding how to uniformly manage, supervise, and inspect them,
the imperial court will not interfere remotely."
At that time, mining restrictions were greatly relaxed.
In the 2nd year of Xiánfēng
to raise military funds,
merchants were invited to exploit gold and silver mines in Rèhé, Xīnjiāng, and other provinces.
In the 3rd year
an edict proclaimed:
"Exploiting mineral resources,
returning the natural bounty of heaven and earth to heaven and earth,
compared to all other expedient and corrupt policies,
does not harm the system
and benefits the people's livelihood.
At this time of vast military expenses
and depleted imperial treasury,
all Governors-General and Governors must weigh priorities
and present proposals for trial exploitation in areas with abundant mineral veins."
At that time, with military campaigns and shortage of funds,
those then exploited
included only the gold mines of Gá'ěr in Xīnjiāng,
Dálātú, Gáshùn, and Hónghuāgōu in Ménggǔ;
the silver mines of Zhūwōshān, Piànshānxiàn, Shìgōu, Tǔcáozǐ, Xīlàpiàn, Niúquānzǐgōu in Zhílì;
Hālějīn, Luóquāngōu, Kùcháshān, Chánghánggōu in Ménggǔ;
and several copper and tin mines in Díhuà, Luóbùnà'ěr, Sāngèshān in Xīnjiāng.
In the 7th year of Tóngzhì
Jílín requested to open coal mines in Huǒshílǐngzǐ and other places,
but as bandits were not yet pacified,
the request was rejected by the Board and not carried out.
In the 13th year
as Yúnnán's mines had long been abandoned due to military conflict,
an edict was issued to order their reopening,
following the request of the Yúnnán Governor Cén Yùyīng.
In that same year, discussions on coastal defense arose,
and Zhílì Governor-General Lǐ Hóngzhāng and Ship Administration Minister Shěn Bǎozhēn requested the exploitation of coal and iron to meet military needs.
The emperor granted their request,
ordering trial operations in Cízhōu, Zhílì, and Táiwān, Fújiàn.
In the 8th year of Guāngxù
Zuo Zōngtáng, Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, also stated that the Northern Seas defense preparations,
manufacturing of ships and cannons,
and the coal and iron needed for machinery and steamships in various provinces
were of great importance.
He requested the opening of the Líguóyì coal and iron mines in Jiāngsū.
This was reported and heard.
Subsequently, with the construction of railways,
coal and iron became even more urgent.
Thus, coal mines were established in Dàshítoudǐngzǐ, Luànnígōu, Bànlāwō, Jīgōu, Èrdàohé, Táojiātún, Shípáilǐng in Jílín;
Tàipíngshān, Cháhàn'áolākǎlún in Hēilóngjiāng;
Kāipíng, Tángshān in Zhílì;
Shàngpíng, Yǒnggù, Cíyáogōu, Nányángzhài in Nèiqiū Xiàn;
Gāngtóu, Shígù, Jiāonígōu, Yángjiāgōu, Xīnzhuāng, Zhúbì, Móucūn, Jiāocūn in Línchéng Xiàn;
Jīmíng, Yùdài, Bābǎosìshān in Xuānhuà Fǔ;
Huīpù Cūn in Fùpíng Xiàn;
Báishígōu, Yěbèicūn in Qǔyáng Xiàn;
Hǎilākǎnshān, Mǎliángēdá in Zhāngjiākǒu Tīng;
Qīnglóngjiàn, Bēijiézǐ in Wǎnpíng Xiàn;
Yúshùgōu in Chéngdé Fǔ;
Yuǎnlāi, Yìhé, Jìnbǎo, Yùshèng, Yǒngshùn, Yǒngyì, Wànlì, Rénhé, Tóngdé, Shùnfā in Hǎilóng Fǔ, Fèngtiān;
Dàyáogōu in Jǐnzhōu Fǔ;
Dàngshígōu in Jǐnxī Tīng;
Wánggāngōu in Běnxī Xiàn;
Mìfēnggōu in Xīngjīng Tīng;
Yáozǐyù in Liáoyáng Zhōu;
Píngxiāng, Yǒngxīn, Yúgàn in Jiāngxī;
Yì Xiàn in Shāndōng;
Guìchí, Guǎngdé, Fánchāng, Dōngliú, Jīng Xiàn in Ānhuī;
Jīngmén in Húběi;
Yǔzhōu in Hénán;
