Píngdìng, Fèngtái in Shānxī;
Tónglú, Yúháng in Zhèjiāng;
Shàngyuán, Jùróng in Jiāngsū;
Xiāngxiāng, Qíyáng in Húnán;
Fùchuān, Hè Xiàn, Fèngyì, Ényáng, Nánníng, Nàpō in Guǎngxī;
Báishuǐ, Chéngchéng, Tóngguān, Yíjūn, Bīnzhōu, Lǒngzhōu, Chúnhuà in Shǎnxī.
Iron mines were in Qiān'ān Xiàn, Luánzhōu in Zhílì;
Dàyě in Húběi;
Yǒngníng Zhōu in Guǎngxī;
Yǒngxīn Xiàn in Jiāngxī;
Kāi and Guǎng Fǔs in Yúnnán;
Qīngxī in Guìzhōu;
all were exploited successively,
and the scattered exploitation by merchants and commoners in Qín [Shǎnxī] and Jìn [Shānxī]
was even more uncountable.
In the 22nd year
an edict ordered the opening of gold and silver mines in various provinces.
From the early years of Guāngxù,
the Yáogōu silver mine in Zhílì was opened,
and aside from the gold mines in Xīníng, Gān, Liáng in Gānsù,
and Mòhé Guānyīnshān, Qíqiánhé in Hēilóngjiāng, nothing else was reported.
After the clear decree was promulgated,
gold mines included Zhuǎnshānzǐ in Píngquán Zhōu, Zhílì;
Jīnchǎnggōu in Jiànchāng Xiàn;
Shuāngshānzǐ in Fúníng Xiàn;
Kuāngōu in Luòpíng Xiàn;
Dàyíngzǐ, Xīniǎnzǐgōu in Fēngníng Xiàn;
Hónghuāgōu, Shuǐquángōu, Guǎibànggōu in Wēngniútè Qí;
and the output from Qiān'ān Xiàn was particularly strong.
Fènghuáng, Āndōng, Liáoyáng, Tōnghuà, Kuāndiàn, Huáirén, Tiělǐng, Kāiyuán, Tōnghuà, Hǎichéng, Jǐn Xiàn in Fèngtiān;
Hèliángōu, Dàxiǎocáo, Niǎngōu, Chúhǔgōu, Zhūjiāgōu, Bǎnqiáozǐ, Zhū'ěrhǔzhū, Kèlènsī, Bùgōng, Tèlèjī, Hālāgénángtú, Kuíténghé, Túshìyètúhàn in Ménggǔ;
Miángōu in Sìchuān;
Píngjiāng in Húnán;
Zhūjì in Zhèjiāng;
Hēihé in Hēilóngjiāng;
Hétián, Yānqí in Xīnjiāng.
Silver mines included Tiānquán, Lúshān, Dàxuéshāntóu in Sìchuān;
all were reported and opened for exploitation.
And mines of copper, tin, lead, antimony, petroleum, sulfur, realgar, etc.,
also emerged one after another.
Copper mines included Tāngdān, Màolù main mines (six),
and subsidiary mines (eleven) in Yídōng, Yúnnán;
Huílóng, Débǎo main mines (eight),
and subsidiary mines (nine) in Yíxī;
Wànbǎo, Shuānglóng belonging to Chǔxióng Yǒngběi and Yúnwǔ;
and various mines in Yǒng'ān Shùnníng, Lín'ān, Kāihuà, Qǔjìng,
all of which recruited merchants for exploitation.
There were also copper mines in Gànzhōu, Jiāngxī;
Zhèn'ān, Shǎnxī;
Suíníng, Húnán;
Báichéng, Kùchē in Xīnjiāng.
Tin mines were in Dānzhōu, Guǎngdōng;
Nándān Tǔzhōu, Fùchuān, Hè Xiàn in Guǎngxī.
Lead mines were in Chángníng, Xiāngxiāng, Línwǔ in Húnán;
Huìlǐ in Sìchuān;
Zhènhǎi, Fènghuà, Xiàngshān, Nínghǎi, Tàipíng in Zhèjiāng.
Antimony mines were in Yìyáng, Shàoyáng, Xīnhuà, Yuánlíng, Cílì, Xiāngxiāng, Qíyáng, Xīn'ān, Wǎnpǔ in Húnán;
Tóngrén in Guìzhōu;
Xiùshān in Sìchuān;
Qǔjiāng, Fángchéng, Rǔyuán in Guǎngdōng;
Nántài, Sìzhèn, Língyángdū in Guǎngxī.
Petroleum mines were in Yáncháng, Shǎnxī;
Yùmén, Gānsù;
Kù'ěrkǎlāwūsū in Xīnjiāng.
Sulfur mines were in Yángqǔ, Shānxī;
Liáoyáng, Jǐnzhōu in Fèngtiān.
Realgar mines were in Cílì, Húnán.
Some were government-operated,
some merchant-operated,
or joint ventures between government and merchants.
Some used traditional methods,
some used Western methods.
In the ninth year,
an imperial edict was issued to each province to invite merchants to raise capital and operate coal mines.
From then on, Yúnnán and Sìchuān both established merchant recruitment and mining bureaus.
Guìzhōu established a Mining Public-Private Bureau,
and Shānxī established a Mining Company.
The copper mines of Qióngzhōu in Yuèdōng,
and the lead mines of Níngbō in Zhèjiāng,
were all opened by inviting merchants to raise capital.
After several decades of operation,
only the coal mines of Kāipíng and Píngxiāng,
and the iron mine of Dàyě,
had grand and far-reaching scales.
Next were the gold mines of Píngjiāng,
the antimony mines of Yìyáng,
and the lead mines of Chángníng,
which still brought benefits to the people.
Although the output of the Mòhé gold mine was abundant,
only 200,000 taels of silver were remitted to the Board annually.
As for Yúnnán copper, since Táng Jiǒng was appointed to supervise its operation in the thirteenth year,
the annual transport of copper to the capital did not exceed one million,
and for provincial minting,
it was still necessary to purchase foreign copper at high prices.
Iron production was for the Hányáng Factory to smelt steel and make rails,
barely meeting the needs of railways.
Although Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, and Shānxī produced abundant iron,
due to imprecise refining,
domestic manufacturing
still largely purchased from British factories.
In the twenty-fourth year,
an imperial edict established the General Bureau of Mining and Railways in Jīngshī,
headed by Wáng Wénsháo and Zhāng Yīnhuán.
Twenty-two regulations were approved by memorial,
allowing Chinese merchants to operate mines,
borrow foreign funds,
and form Sino-foreign joint ventures
to establish companies.
From then on, the Píngxiāng coal mine in Jiāngxī borrowed German funds,
the Dàyě iron mine in Húběi borrowed Japanese funds,
the Bǎochāng Company in Zhèjiāng borrowed Italian funds,
and the Línchéng coal mine in Zhílì borrowed Belgian funds.
When their contracts were agreed upon,
in addition to mortgages and interest,
it was often necessary to employ foreign mining engineers,
and in severe cases, it involved personnel management.
As for the Jǐngxíng coal mine in Zhílì, the Xuānchéng coal mine in Ānhuī,
the Ménpíng, Zé, Lù, and Píngyáng mines in Shānxī,
the Jiāngběi coal and iron mines in Sìchuān,
Tǎchéng in Xīnjiāng,
the Huòjiādì and Chǎngzǐgōu gold mines in Zhílì,
Shàngsī in Guǎngxī,
Zhèng'ān lead and iron mines in Guìzhōu,
Shàowǔ, Jiànníng, and Tīngzhōu in Fújiàn,
Bādàohé in Zhílì,
Wěimíngshān in Fèngtiān,
and the new and old mines in Jílín,
all were operated as Sino-foreign joint ventures.
Once agreements were signed,
disputes frequently arose.
The Fú Company's involvement in the Jìn mines
was particularly egregious.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Yùfēng Company of Hénán, with its exclusive right to operate all mines north of the Yellow River to the left and right of Huáiqìng,
and the Shānxī Commercial Bureau, with its exclusive right to operate the Ménpíng, Zé, Lù, and Píngyáng coal and iron mines,
simultaneously transferred their rights for operation.
One company monopolized the mining affairs of two provinces,
and further proposed building a railway from Shānxī to Biàn.
Due to the mines and railway,
sovereign rights were lost,
and after three years of dispute,
joint operation was finally allowed.
Biàn had already encroached upon the sovereignty of Chinese officials,
and Jìn further interfered with the people's mining activities.
The gentry and people of all Shānxī
insisted on rescinding the agreement.
After a long delay,
it was finally redeemed with over 2.7 million taels of silver.
Other cases, such as the Yáncháng mines in Shǎnxī,
the Fùshùn, Bā, and Wàn oil mines in Sìchuān,
the Lóngwángshān mine in Chángníng, Húnán,
and the Lóngjiǎoshān mine in Xīngguó, Húběi,
all led to diplomatic negotiations
due to private transactions between merchants and commoners.
After the signing of the Jiāojì and Dōngqīng railway agreements,
Chinese people were prohibited from mining within thirteen lǐ of the railway.
Furthermore, the Kāipíng coal mine
and the Guānyīnshān gold mine in Mòhé
were occupied by foreigners due to internal strife.
The Kāipíng coal mine,
since the first year of Guāngxù, had been operated by the Zhílì Governor-General Lǐ Hóngzhāng with the combined efforts of officials and merchants,
and after twenty years of management,
its effectiveness was remarkable.
In the twenty-sixth year,
after the Boxer Rebellion,
the foreign staff member Detring, entrusted by Superintendent Zhāng Yì for protection,
privately signed a sales agreement with mining engineer Hú Huá.
Zhāng Yì also signed and transferred it,
then reported it to the throne as a Sino-foreign joint venture by increasing foreign shares.
As a result, the Tángshān Xīshān, Bànbìdiàn, Mǎjiāgōu, Wúshuǐzhuāng, Zhàogèzhuāng, and Línxī mines,
and the associated Jǐnpíng, Jiànpíng, and Yǒngpíng gold and silver mines in the Qínhuángdǎo port area,
were all controlled by a British company.
A strict imperial edict ordered their recovery,
and a lawsuit was filed in Britain,
but it was ultimately unresolved.
In the thirty-fourth year,
when preparations were made to operate the Luánzhōu coal mine,
the British company obstructed it.
Therefore, the method of forming a business alliance was adopted,
and the Kāiluán General Bureau was jointly established.
The Guānyīnshān gold mine
was also occupied by Russians due to the Boxer Rebellion.
In the thirty-second year,
it was finally redeemed with 12,000 Russian rubles.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the Ministry of Foreign Affairs revised the mining regulations,
stating that Chinese and foreign merchants could operate mines equally,
but approval from the Ministry was required
for it to be valid.
In that year, the Ānhuī Governor Niè Jíguī permitted the Briton John Kelly to operate mining properties in Shè, Tónglíng, Dàtōng, Níngguó, Guǎngdé, and Qiánshān.
Later, for the exclusive operation of Tóngguānshān in Tónglíng,
a contract for a period of one hundred years was signed,
occupying over 384,000 mú of land.
The gentry and people of Ānhuī jointly contested it,
and it was finally redeemed with 400,000 taels of silver for self-operation.
The Frenchman Millot also requested to survey all mines in Yúnnán from the Yúnnán Governor and the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in the same year.
Both rejected him,
but he still obtained mining rights for the prefectures, departments, and sub-prefectures of Chéngjiāng, Lín'ān, Kāihuà, Yúnnán, Chǔxióng, Yuánjiāng, Yǒngběi, etc.
Subsequently, when the British merchant Littleton failed to obtain joint operation of the gold and silver mines in Dōng and Zhāo prefectures,
he invoked Millot's precedent
and demanded mines in the seven prefectures of Guǎngnán, Qǔjìng, Lìjiāng, Dàlǐ, Shùnníng, Pǔ'ěr, and Yǒngchāng.
This was also firmly rejected.
At that time, the entire nation, from top to bottom,
spoke of preserving mining properties.
Thus, Sìchuān established the Bǎofù Company,
to which Sino-foreign operation of Sìchuān province's mines and the matters of purchasing and subleasing land belonged.
Fújiàn established a Commercial Administration Bureau,
and soon proposed establishing a General Mining Company,
to which the authority to review and approve or reject applications for various mining sites belonged.
The Bǎojìn Company of Shānxī
and the General Mining Bureau of Ānhuī
were able to gather wealthy individuals
and raise capital for operations.
Húnán and Húběi,
for their respective mining areas,
surveyed and purchased land to prevent private sales.
In the twenty-fifth year,
Jiāngnán planned to establish schools for agriculture, industry, mining, and railways,
and Húběi and Húnán further planned to establish a Higher Mining School.
In the thirty-first year,
the Ministry of Commerce, seeing foreign merchants privately occupying mining land and mountains,
memorialized to clarify the agreements
to maintain sovereign rights.
Soon after, it proposed establishing provincial mining policy investigation bureaus
to first survey national mining properties and strictly prohibit private sales.
Húběi Governor-General Zhāng Zhīdòng presented seventy-four articles of the main mining regulations,
with seventy-three supplementary articles.
Since the twenty-fourth year,
mining regulations had been repeatedly changed,
and foreign merchants often used mining disputes
as an excuse.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Lǚ Hǎihuán, the minister for commercial treaties, negotiated commercial treaties with various countries,
allowing them the benefit of mining,
but requiring them to comply with Chinese mining regulations.
Chinese mining regulations,
compared with those commonly used by other countries, were to serve as a standard,
and Zhāng Zhīdòng was specially commissioned to draft them.
He consulted and cross-referenced the mining regulations of Britain, America, Germany, France, Belgium, and Spain,
distinguishing between surface and subsurface,
defining mining boundaries and taxes,
analyzing land shares and silver shares,
as well as Chinese and foreign merchants,
with very comprehensive restrictions;
he particularly emphasized Chinese sovereignty,
the livelihood of the Chinese people,
and local governance.
After several years, it was completed,
and submitted to the Ministry for deliberation and implementation,
thus, the Chinese mining regulations finally took shape.
Records, Volume One Hundred, Food and Goods Six, Taxation and Accounting
Taxation
After the rise of the Qīng,
they first abolished cumbersome and harsh taxes.
The customs posts established
mostly followed the Míng system.
Since the opening of maritime trade,
foreign customs houses were established outside the conventional customs,
and the establishment of likin bureaus
and the taxation of foreign opium
also followed.
These three were all unknown in previous dynasties,
and are recorded here.
As for stamp duties and additional taxes on tobacco and alcohol,
they were all tried and then abolished,
and are not fully recorded.
Regular Customs Duties.
In the early years of the Shùnzhì reign,
customs duties for each province were established.
Officials from the Hùbù were specially dispatched to oversee their collection.
For the Eastern and Western Wings [of the capital],
and the Zhāngjiākǒu duties,
senior officials were dispatched to supervise the collection.
At that time, the capital had just been pacified,
so all customs duties were remitted for one year,
and arrears from the late Míng dynasty were also pardoned.
Later, as Zhèjiāng and Mǐn were successively pacified,
the additional taxes imposed in the late Míng,
and the scattered land taxes in various prefectures and counties, were again abolished.
In the third year [of Shùnzhì],
the additional rice tax at Gūxīqiáo and commercial tax at Jīnzhùshān in Táipíngfǔ, which had been imposed in the late Míng, were abolished.
In the fourth year,
it was decided that for the customs posts of the Hùbù and Gōngbù,
Manchu, Han Bannerman, and Han officials would be concurrently dispatched.
In the eighth year,
the number of customs officials was reduced,
and discussions on customs assignments were suspended.
In the ninth year,
the Xīxīnguān and Jiāngníngcāng were combined into one assignment,
and the Dúshíkǒu assignment was suspended.
The prohibition on customs officials being retained or assigned to their native places was strictly enforced.
For all established patrol posts,
uniforms and waist plaques were issued.
In the tenth year,
it was ordered that all customs posts publish fixed regulations,
set up collection counters for taxes,
and not extort surcharges (huǒhào) or demand illicit fees (lòuguī).
Customs runners were also forbidden from monopolizing customs declarations.
In the eleventh year,
acting on the advice of the Grand Supervisor of the Six Boards Dù Dǔhù,
four matters concerning customs malpractice were clarified: one,
reducing clerks and runners;
two,
investigating tax burdens;
three,
customs officials avoiding their native districts;
and four,
verifying approvals within a time limit.
In the sixteenth year,
Pāntáokǒu was moved to Yǒngpíng,
and Gǔběikǒu was moved to Mìyún.
Customs posts were also established to levy timber tax,
taking two-tenths.
In the seventeenth year,
the new customs posts at Yǒngpíng and Mìyún were abolished,
and merged under the joint supervision of Gǔběikǒu.
In the eighteenth year,
it was decided that timber at all passes would be taxed at one-tenth.
The Línqīng brick duty was suspended.
The Bǎnzá tax was handed over to the Běihé Branch Office for collection.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
Héxīwù was moved to Tiānjīn,
and renamed Tiānjīnguān.
It was further decided that each customs post would concurrently assign one Manchu and one Han official as Bǐtiēshì,
who would be selected by lot from candidates sent by the Six Boards.
Mongol and Han Bannerman assignments were suspended.
For the two passes of Zhāngjiā and Shāhǔ,
only Manchu and Mongol officials were specially dispatched.
In the second year,
it was decided that inspection of grain transport boats would be limited to the five customs posts of Yízhēn, Guāzhōu, Huái'ān, Jìníng, and Tiānjīn.
Foreign goods entering Chóngwénmén were exempted from tax.
In the fourth year,
it was strictly forbidden for customs posts to collect taxes contrary to regulations,
and the practice of discussing tax surpluses was permanently abolished.
In the fifth year,
it was ordered that all customs duties be managed by local officials.
Thus, Chóngwénmén went to the Zhìzhōng,
Tiānjīn to the Tiānjīndào,
Lóngquán and others to the Jǐngxíngdào,
Zǐjīng to the Zhílì Shǒudào,
Línqīng to the Dōngchāngdào,
Wāyùntīng to the Tōngjìdào,
Jūyōng to the Chāngmìdào,
Xīxīn to the Zhènjiāngdào,
Wúhú to the Chítàidào,
Yángzhōu to the Yìchuándào,
Hǔshù to the Sūchāngdào,
Huái'ān to the Huáihǎidào,
Běixīn to the Zhèjiāng Bùzhèngshǐ,
Jīng to the Jīngzhōu Tóngzhī,
Jiǔjiāng to the Jiǔjiāngdào,
Gàn to the Jínángàndào,
Táipíngqiáo to the Nánxióng Zhīfǔ,
Yùxiānqiáo and ●guāngchǎng to the Sháozhōu Zhīfǔ,
each overseeing the collection of taxes.
Furthermore, the Gǔběikǒu assignment was abolished and put under the management of Mìyún Xiàn.
Only the Two Wings, Zhāngjiākǒu, and Shāhǔkǒu remained as before.
Only officials from the Hùbù were dispatched,
and an order was issued for customs posts in the directly governed provinces to publish tax regulations.
The tax on goods leaving the capital through Chóngwénmén was abolished.
In the eighth year,
Línqīngcāng was merged into Línqīngguān.
Following the advice of the Grand Supervisor of the Six Boards Sū Bài
that
"local officials concurrently managing customs duties
leads to excessive work,
and they might fear their superiors,
aiming to meet quotas,
thereby burdening merchants and commoners,"
it was again decided that for the customs posts with relatively higher tax quotas—Hǔshù, Wúhú, Běixīn, Jiǔjiāng, Huái'ān, Táipíngqiáo, Yángzhōu, Gàn, Xīxīn, Línqīng, Tiānjīn, and Fèngyángcāng—
Ministry officials would again be dispatched to supervise collection.
The rest remained as before.
In this year, it was decided that when a customs official position became vacant,
senior officials from the Six Boards, based on their salary, would be selected by lot in rotation.
Officials who had previously served in such a capacity
were not allowed to be dispatched again.
A method for assessing customs officials was also established: those with tax arrears of less than half a fen (4.2%) would be fined salary;
from half a fen to four fen (4.2% to 33.3%),
they would be demoted or transferred;
five fen (41.7%) or more, they would be dismissed.
Soon after, it was further decided that those with less than half a fen would be demoted but retained,
while those who fully completed their quota would be recorded.
All Ministry dispatched officials
were not subject to the jurisdiction of Governors-General or Governors.
In the ninth year,
it was decided that Huái'ānguān would concurrently administer Huái'āncāng and the Gōngbù's Qīngjiāng Factory,
and the Two Wings would exclusively dispatch Manchu Bǐtiēshì officials.
In the tenth year,
the Xīxīn Hùguān was abolished and merged into the Lóngjiāng Gōngguān;
the Wúhú Gōngguān was abolished and merged into the Wúhú Hùguān,
each assuming concurrent management.
Later, Fèngyángcāng was assigned to the Fèngyáng Zhīfǔ,
Zhèngyáng to the Tōngpàn,
Línhuái to the Dàshǐ for collection,
and the dispatch of Ministry officials was suspended.
In the seventeenth year,
the Běihé Branch Office was abolished,
and the Línqīngzá tax was concurrently managed by the Jìníngdào.
In the nineteenth year,
the sea ban in Shāndōng was lifted,
and boat owners concealing taxes were ordered to be investigated.
Manchu Ministry officials were dispatched to supervise the collection of Tóngguān and Shānhǎiguān duties,
with Tóngguān also administering the Dàqìngguān and Lóngjūzhài tax offices.
In the twenty-first year,
Jiǔjiāngguān was moved to Húkǒu.
The dispatch of Ministry officials to Tóngguān and Shānhǎiguān was suspended,
and they were returned to local official management.
Fèngyáng still dispatched Manchu officials from the Six Boards.
In the twenty-third year,
the rotation system for dispatching officials from various Ministries and Courts to customs posts was revised.
At this time, the sea bans in Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, and Guǎngdōng were first lifted.
Four maritime customs posts were established at Yúnshān, Níngbō, Zhāngzhōu, and Àomén.
Each customs post had a Superintendent,
and one Manchu and one Han Bǐtiēshì,
who would be replaced annually.
Regulations for maritime taxes were established,
and taxes on bridges and ferries within the sea ports were remitted.
Special officials for tax collection were separately established at the two customs posts of Xīxīn and Lóngjiāng.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Xīxīn was returned to the Hùbù.
Foreign tribute ships were exempted from tax,
and the measurement-based tax on foreign ships was reduced by three-tenths.
In the twenty-fifth year,
punishments for prefecture and county sea boats concealing [goods] were established.
At that time, the sea ban had just been lifted.
Coastal fishing boats,
already paying fishing taxes to prefectures and counties,
were again taxed by maritime customs based on their beam (liángtóu),
which caused great hardship to the people.
The Emperor, acting on the advice of Fújiàn Governor Zhāng Zhòngjǔ,
decided that for fishing boats five feet or longer,
the beam tax would be entirely collected by local officials.
Previously, in the fourth year of Kāngxī, the practice of discussing tax surpluses was abolished.
By the fourteenth year,
it was again decided that based on the amount of surplus,
officials would be promoted and given higher ranks.
By this time,
the Emperor, considering it burdensome and harmful to merchants,
again suspended the discussion of tax surpluses.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Sāng É, the Superintendent of Hǔshù, collected a surplus of over twenty-one thousand taels.
The Emperor, deeming it a disturbance to the populace,
punished him.
The tax quota for Mǐnhǎi was permanently reduced by over six thousand four hundred taels.
In the twenty-eighth year,
taxes on coastal fishing and shrimp boats, and on goods for daily use traded by the common people for their livelihood, were remitted,
and this was made into a decree.
Previously, Shāgōu was merged into Huáiguān in the twenty-sixth year,
and inspections at Ménglóng, Yàdōng, Chàhé, and other places were all exempted.
At this time, since Shāgōu was the confluence of Ménglóng and Yàdōng,
it was deemed inappropriate to add another tax.
Ménglóng was assigned to the Maritime Customs,
Yàdōng to Huáiguān,
and Shāgōu was exempted from tax.
The Xīxīn Hùguān was again merged into the Lóngjiāng Gōngguān.
In the thirty-third year,
officials were again dispatched to supervise the collection of customs duties at Shānhǎiguān,
and the Zhāngjiākǒu duties were concurrently collected by Xuānhuà Fǔ.
In the thirty-fourth year,
the Zhèhǎiguān office was established in Níngbō and Dìnghǎi,
and a supervisor was ordered to patrol there.
In the thirty-fifth year,
for ocean merchant ships from the west that transported rice to Fèngtiān via Tiānjīn,
only the regular tax on goods was collected.
In the thirty-sixth year,
strict prohibitions were enforced against customs officers bringing old servants who had completed their term privately from the capital to occupy positions as heads of the general treasury sections.
In the thirty-seventh year,
the fixed tax quota of Yuèhǎiguān was permanently reduced by 30,200 taels and more.
In the thirty-eighth year,
the Emperor, fearing that customs officials might excessively extort and impoverish merchants,
abolished the collection of additional surplus silver.
The Hé Bǎo Yíng was established,
and officials who had completed their terms were dispatched to supervise the collection of timber taxes from Dàqīngshān.
In the fortieth year,
the commercial tax of Sānyuán Xiàn in Shǎnxī was abolished,
and its collection was transferred to Tóngguān, Lóngjūzhài, and Dàqìngguān.
The Tōnghuìhé Fēnsī was abolished,
and the Tōngzhōu timber yard was placed under the management of Tōngyǒng Dào.
In the forty-first year,
the Dàqīng timber tax was merged with and placed under the jurisdiction of Shāhǔkǒu.
In the forty-sixth year,
Jīnzhōu and Niúzhuāng were handed over to the Shānhǎiguān supervisor for inspection against tax evasion beyond the passes.
The Yúguān was established in Chóngqìng,
and its timber tax was collected by Chuāndōng Dào.
In the forty-seventh year,
officials from the Gōngbù were again dispatched to supervise the collection of Jīngguān duties.
In the fifty-third year,
due to a deficit in the Línqīngguān tax,
its collection was transferred to the Xúnfǔ.
Soon after,
the customs of Fèngyáng, Tiānjīn, Hángzhōu, Jīngzhōu, Jiānghǎi, Zhèhǎi, Huái'ān, Bǎnzá, and Huáiguān
were successively transferred to the various Xúnfǔ for supervision.
The Guāzhōu tax was stopped,
and the tax collection ambassador was abolished.
It was decreed that merchant ships from Jiāng and Zhè and other provinces docking in Táiwān,
if already inspected upon passing Xiàmén, would not be re-taxed.
Fújiàn sugar ships arriving at Xiàmén
were to pay tax at the customs,
but those trading in Jiāng and Zhè were exempt.
The Héngchéng tax station was established,
and its collection was placed under the supervision of the Shānhǎiguān supervisor,
increasing the tax by one thousand taels,
which was set as a fixed quota.
In the sixty-first year,
all barbarian tribes were prohibited from smuggling saltpeter, sulfur, and military weapons out of the border,
but their import taxes were allowed to be lightly reduced.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
the Húkǒuguān was moved to Jiǔjiāng,
and a sub-station at Dàgūtáng was also established.
The additional surplus silver collected by the customs of Huái'ān, Běixīn, Fèngyáng, Tiānjīn, Línqīng, Jiānghǎi, Zhèhǎi, and Jīngzhōu was abolished.
Strict prohibitions were enforced against excessive demands by yamen runners at provincial customs and Chóngwénmén.
In this year, it was decreed that all customs duties were to be managed by local officials,
except for Chóngwénmén, where officials from the Nèiwù Fǔ were still dispatched;
Shānhǎiguān, Liǎngyì,
and the three passes of Gǔběi, Pāntáo, and Shāhǔ,
as well as Dǎjiànlú,
where departmental officials were still dispatched.
The timber tax of Hū'ěrhā Hé in Shèngjīng
was also handed over to the Jiāngjūn and Fǔyǐn, who delegated riverside officials to collect it.
The following year,
Huái'ān still had departmental officials dispatched,
Hǔxù was transferred to the Sūzhōu Zhīzào,
and the Zhōngjiāng tax in Fènghuángchéng
was supervised by Shèngjīng departmental officials.
The grain transport boat fees at Héxīwù
were changed to be collected in Tōngzhōu.
In the third year,
due to Siām's tribute of rice seeds, fruit trees, and other items,
the tax on empty return ballast goods was waived.
Border passes and city gates were prohibited from demanding taxes on Mongolian tribute items,
and those who used false names to evade taxes were punished.
In the fifth year,
Sùqiānguān was merged with Huáiguān for collection,
and the lock tax was handed over to local officials for management.
The timber tax of Hé Bǎo Yíng
was collected by the Shāhǔkǒu supervisor.
The cattle and horse tax of Fèngtiān
was changed to be supervised by departmental officials.
In the sixth year,
the tax on rice, wheat, and miscellaneous grain boats at Línqīngguān was revised.
The tax regulations for all customs were established.
The two customs of Lóngjiāng and Xīxīn
were concurrently managed by the Jiāngníng Zhīzào.
The Siām rice tax was permanently waived.
In the seventh year,
a special commissioner was appointed to supervise the collection at Kuízhōuguān.
The two Xīnxīn customs, North and South, were concurrently collected by the Hángzhōu Zhīzào.
Xúguān of Jīngzhōu was moved to Tiánjiāzhōu,
and renamed Tiánguān.
The Miàowān tax in Jiāngsū was concurrently managed by Huáiguān.
The example of reduced ship tax by measurement at Mǐnhǎiguān was established.
The Gǔběikǒu supervisor was abolished,
and its collection was handed over to Mìyún Xiàn.
As the Tóngguān commercial tax was higher than the departmental regulations,
but had been accepted for a long time,
it was ordered to be
collected according to the current amount.
The main Pāntáokǒu customs was moved to be collected at the two sub-stations of Pānjiā and Táolín.
In the eighth year,
half of the surplus silver at all customs was reduced,
and the additional collection for balance loss at Tiānjīn was abolished.
A regulation for punishing those who excessively demanded land tax was established.
The prohibition against gold export was strictly enforced.
In the tenth year,
a timber yard at Shuǐquántān in Jiāochéng Xiàn was established,
and a tax station was set up in Wǔyuán Chéng for collection.
In the eleventh year,
Tiānjīnguān was transferred to the management of the Chánglú Yánzhèng.
In the thirteenth year,
a tax collection ambassador was established at Jūyōngguān,
and it was decreed that official seals for merchants at Pāntáo, Gǔběi, and Shāhǔ three passes
should also include Manchu, Han, and Mongolian scripts.
In coastal prefectures, counties, and garrisons of Shāndōng, dual-linked seal tickets were issued,
filling in the merchant's age, appearance, native place, ship's name and number, beam length, amount of beans and stones, and date of departure,
distributed to merchant ships,
and checked upon return.
In the first year of Qiánlóng,
the yamen fees and ticket silver at Lóngjiāng and Xīxīn customs were abolished.
Originally,
when foreign plank ships arrived in Yuè,
their cannons were removed
and returned after the transaction was completed.
The tax law collected about two thousand taels of silver per ship based on the beam length,
and goods tax was collected according to regulations.
The additional tax of one percent on goods purchased, collected in addition to the regular tax, was abolished.
The tax on fishing boats in Mǐn Province was set,
divided into three categories: upper, middle, and lower,
excluding excessive additional levies.
Tax regulations for all provinces were established and promulgated.
The three-part tax form system for Jiǔjiāng and Gànzhōu customs was established,
one for the merchant,
one for the Xúnfǔ's office,
and one for the customs office.
Zhāngjiākǒu and Jūyōngguān were permitted to collect "meal money" for goods transported by carts and animals passing through,
to support their livelihood.
Smuggling rice and grain to foreign countries was prohibited,
with varying punishments prescribed.
Tax on single-masted boats used for coastal fishing was waived.
In the second year,
rice and grain taxes were set.
Whenever there was a drought or flood locally,
rice and grain boats were immediately allowed to pass,
and taxes would be collected as before after the harvest.
The rice boat tax for Kāijiàn and Ēnpíng counties in Guǎngdōng was permanently stopped.
In the third year,
the Zhuǎnshuǐ and Bǎidú stations of Hǔxùguān were abolished,
and the Guāzhōu lock tax was transferred to the Liǎnghuái Yánzhèng.
Jiǔjiāng had officials from the Nèiwù Fǔ dispatched,
Wúhú and Fèngyáng had departmental officials assigned,
each managing supervision.
In the fourth year,
the timber tax quota for Guīhuàchéng was set,
and its collection was assigned to Shāhǔkǒu.
In the fifth year,
departmental officials were again dispatched to supervise Jīngguān.
Following the words of Censor Lù Yǐnyào,
the prohibition against making up names to claim customs duties was strictly enforced.
In the sixth year,
the regulation for assessing customs surplus was re-established,
and private increases in ports in outer provinces were investigated.
Taxes on copper, tin, lead, and rice/grain collected with treasury funds were waived,
but boat fees were still collected.
However, as soybeans were not comparable to wheat or millet,
they were still taxed as usual even in lean years.
The land tax for Fēng, Pèi, Xiāo, and Dàng four counties of Sùqiān was changed
to be collected by their respective counties.
The "flying measurement" method for timber tax at Lóngjiāngguān was permanently prohibited.
The surplus of each customs was determined,
and assessed by comparing it with the previous year's figures,
and this was established as a rule.
In the seventh year,
the fixed tax on beans and rice at customs in the directly administered provinces was permanently waived.
Huángcūn, a sub-station of Tōngzhōu,
and the ports of Dézhōu, Wèijiāwān, Jiānzhǒng, and Fánkǒu of Línqīngguān were re-established.
Boat fees at Línqīngguān were waived.
Yángzhōuguān was assigned to the Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū to select officials for collection.
Tax collection at Nánshān Biānkǒu of Mǐnhǎiguān was stopped,
with its sole function being inspection.
In the eighth year,
it was decreed that official grain transport was exempt from boat fees.
In the ninth year,
strict prohibitions were enforced against Mongolians coming to the capital evading tax,
and against illicit transportation of goods for unscrupulous merchants.
In the tenth year,
the rebellion in Jiāozhǐ was pacified.
The collection of the Mǎjiù tax in Yúnnán was reinstated.
The practice of collecting tax on boats by the trip at Sùqiān Guān was prohibited,
and changed to be collected according to the number of *dàn* (piculs).
It was stipulated that one official should concurrently manage two customs barriers;
if their collection quotas showed a surplus in one and a deficit in the other,
they were permitted to offset them.
If there was still a shortfall,
they were still ordered to compensate for it.
The Yǎxī Tax Bureau in Zhào'ān, Fújiàn, was moved to Xuánzhōng.
Because Fújiàn Province previously had Zǐtóu boats that engaged in smuggling,
their manufacture was permanently prohibited.
In the thirteenth year,
the rice and bean tax was reinstated.
In the fourteenth year,
the surpluses of each customs barrier were stipulated,
taking the thirteenth year of Yōngzhèng as the standard.
Those with shortfalls were to be separately deliberated and punished according to the degree,
with punishments varying from salary reduction to demotion.
In the fifteenth year,
the tax station in Níngdé Xiàn, Fújiàn, was moved to Jiǔyǔ.
In the seventeenth year,
the timber tax of Yúguān was merged with and collected by Kuíguān.
In the eighteenth year,
the Yùzhōu Office for tax inspection in Xiàmén was moved to Shíměi.
The Suīyángkǒu for tax inspection at Fèngyáng Guān was moved to Hóng Xiàn,
and the Qīngyáng Zhèn for tax collection in Hóng Xiàn was moved to Suīhékǒu.
In the twentieth year,
the Liújūn Kǒu of Huáinán Guān was moved to Jīnghé.
In the twenty-second year,
the customs tariffs for the two maritime customs of Zhè and Mǐn were additionally stipulated,
following the regulations of the Yuèhǎi Customs.
Soon after, it was again reiterated that foreign ships were not allowed to berth in Zhèhǎi (Zhejiang waters).
If any sailed there,
they were ordered to return to Yuè (Guǎngdōng) to trade and pay taxes.
In the twenty-fourth year,
it was stipulated that the livestock tax in Yè'ěrqiāng and Kāshígá'ěr was one-twentieth,
and the silk, cloth, and hide tax was one-tenth.
Those brought in by foreign traders were taxed double.
The prohibition on exporting raw silk was strictly enforced.
In the twenty-fifth year,
officials were first dispatched to collect taxes on hides, etc., in Duōlúnnuò'ěr.
Tax bureaus were also established in Lālín and Ālèchǔkā in Shèngjīng,
and officials were dispatched to collect taxes,
following the precedent of Nínggǔtǎ and Bódūná.
Irregular fees at Yuèhǎi Customs were abolished,
and converted into public funds and reported.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Shíwù Tax Station was established at Huái'ān Guān.
A General Tax Bureau was also established in Guīhuàchéng,
along with stations in Suīyuǎn, Guīhuà, Hélíngé'ěr, Tuōkètuō, Sàlāqí, Xībāotóu, Kūndūlún, Bāshíjiāzi, and other places.
Two Měnggǔ Bǐtiēshì (Mongolian secretaries) were dispatched
to supervise the collection of livestock tax separately.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Lóngjiāng and Huái'ān passes were assigned to the Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng,
and Hǔshù was assigned to the Governor of Jiāngsū.
Each was to strictly inspect and prohibit accumulated abuses of tax evasion at customs barriers,
and the amount of fines for tax evasion was stipulated.
Chén Hóngmóu, Governor of Jiāngsū, memorialized four abuses at Hǔshù Guān: first,
shops paid taxes on behalf of customers,
engaging in monopolistic speculation,
so merchants were still ordered to pay taxes themselves,
and personally fill out the registers;
second,
when cargo ships arrived at the pass,
they were inspected and taxed,
and only after receiving a ticket were they allowed to pass,
to prevent clandestine passage;
third,
officials were selected to serve as assistant sub-officials,
and replaced every six months;
fourth,
Governors-General/Governors and Customs Superintendents originally assisted each other in administration,
so the amounts collected
should be reported monthly by the Superintendent to the Governor-General/Governor,
and then collectively reported and informed upon the annual memorial.
This was approved.
That year, the prohibition on exporting raw silk was relaxed,
but restrictions were still imposed.
It was stipulated that upon completion of their term, the tax officials of Chóngwén Mén and the two wings
should have their names (Manchu and Mongol Grand Secretaries, Ministers, Commandants, Vice Ministers, Deputy Commandants, and other official titles) listed by the Board,
requesting selection for replacement.
This then became a permanent system.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the tariffs of all ports in Tiānjīn were unified.
It was stipulated that merchants transporting beans and grain from Shāndōng by sea to Zhè (Zhejiang)
were to pay tax according to the regulations for transport to Jiāngnán.
Exported ironware from Zhāngjiākǒu
was to be taxed according to the regulations of Shāhǔkǒu.
Allowances for board for household and labor assistants at Wúhú Guān were abolished,

as were the registration of rejected tickets and issuance of receipts, oil lamp, candle, and meal expenses, inspection fees for holds at Jiānghǎi Customs, and fees for passing through sluices at Yáng Guān.
In the twenty-ninth year,
the regulations for supplementary tax on boats at Línqīng Guān were further stipulated.
It was stipulated that for merchants whose foreign goods reached Huíbù for trade,
one-thirtieth was levied,
and for furs, one-twentieth.
For Huí (Muslim) merchants trading with foreigners,
one-twentieth was levied,
and for furs, one-tenth.
As for livestock and goods that did not meet the fractional levy amount,
they were assessed according to their value.
In the thirtieth year,
the tax quotas for Jílín and other places were further stipulated.
The Superintendent's tax at Pāntáokǒu was abolished and transferred to Zhāngjiākǒu for collection.
Its six subordinate small ports
were transferred to the administration of the Tōngyǒng Circuit.
The following year,
the Pāntáokǒu tax was again changed to be collected by the Duōlúnnuò'ěr Assistant Magistrate.
A bureau was established at Dàhékǒu,
and a departmental official from the Lǐfānyuàn (Court of Colonial Affairs) was dispatched to supervise the collection of Guīhuàchéng tax.
Subsequently, it was changed to be collected by officials selected by the Governor of Shānxī.
Maritime merchant taxes at Bàojiāmǎtóu and other seven ports subordinate to Xiùyánchéng
were transferred to the Shānhǎi Guān Superintendent to establish a bureau and collect.
In the thirty-third year,
Shānhǎi Guān, Zhāngjiākǒu, Bāgōu, Tǎzigōu, Sānzuòtǎ, Wūlánhādá, and Duōlúnnuò'ěr were assigned to the Governor-General of Zhílì.
Shāhǔkǒu and Guīhuàchéng were assigned to the Governor of Shānxī.
The cattle and horse tax and Zhōngjiāng tax in Shèngjīng were assigned to the Vice Minister of the Board of Revenue for Shèngjīng.
The Zuòliáng Tīng was assigned to the Vice Minister of Granaries.
Dǎjiànlú was assigned to the Governor-General of Sìchuān.
Jīngguān was assigned to the Governor-General of Húguǎng.
All were simultaneously responsible for inspection and dispatch.
If any Superintendent engaged in embezzlement or improprieties,
and after impeachment and punishment, could not complete the required amount, the concurrently managing official was immediately ordered to compensate on their behalf.
In the thirty-fourth year,
it was approved that a *liǎng* of regular tax at Jiǔjiāng Guān should have an additional *fēn* surcharge,
to cover meal and food expenses.
The prohibition on foreign ships carrying sulfur into port was lifted,
and made into a regulation.
In the thirty-fifth year,
the public expenses of the two offices/factories in Xún and Wú were abolished and incorporated into the regular tax.
In the thirty-eighth year,
the Superintendent of Duōlúnnuò'ěr was abolished,
and assigned to the Duōlúnnuò'ěr Assistant Magistrate for administration.
The Yóuzhá and Nánbà tax stations were moved to Zhōngzhá.
In the fortieth year,
the Yóucūnyìkǒu in Guǎngxī was closed down,
prohibiting inland merchants and commoners from crossing the pass to trade.
In the forty-first year,
tax collection at the Tōngzhōu Sub-Prefectural Office and Héxīwù, which was based on value, was changed to tax collection based on quantity.
The tax on oil, flour, etc., entering and leaving shops at Zhāngjiāwān was also abolished.
The regulations for collecting tax on merchant goods at Dǎjiànlú by quantity were changed and stipulated.
The following year,
it was stipulated that Dǎjiànlú tax officials,
following the precedent of Shānhǎi Guān,
should be selected from among officials of the Zōngrén Fǔ (Imperial Clan Court) and departmental officials of the Ministries and Censorate.
In the forty-fifth year,
the posting of departmental officials to Jīngguān and Dǎjiànlú ceased,
and was transferred to officials selected by various Governors-General and Governors for administration.
In the forty-sixth year,
the integrity-nurturing allowance for the Jīngguān Superintendent was abolished,
and one official was to be selected from the Jīngyíshī Circuit or the Prefect of Jīngzhōu to supervise collection.
In the forty-ninth year,
it was stipulated that pearls and precious stones at Yuèhǎi Customs were generally not to be taxed,
and this was made into a regulation.
In the fifty-first year,
Hǎoguān and Hǎozhīguān in Jīngzhōu were abolished.
Another station was established at Yuèshì,
and renamed Yuèguān.
Yángguān was moved to Diàoxiánkǒu,
and renamed Diàoguān.
It was stipulated that, except for tribute ships from Xiānluó,
other private ships carrying goods
were to be taxed as per regulations.
In the fifty-second year,
it was stipulated that each customs barrier was to apply for and receive tax record books and files in advance.
If the application was delayed,
the unauthorized use of their own registers would be subject to impeachment and punishment.
Because Ānnán requested enfeoffment,
the prohibitions at Shuǐkǒu and other passes were relaxed.
Four years later,
Miǎndiàn (Myanmar/Burma) showed allegiance,
and was also permitted to open customs for trade.
Export taxes were collected in Yǒngchāng, Téngyuè, and Shùnníng,
and import taxes were collected in Shānmùlóng, Mùfú, and Nánhékǒu.
Ports for ferry crossings were established at Wǔhǔ Mén in Fújiàn and Dànshuǐ Bālǐchà in Táiwān.
Import taxes were collected from Mǐn'ān Zhèn,
and export taxes from Nántáikǒu.
If goods were imported
and then re-transported elsewhere,
they were exempt from re-collection within one month.
However, if exported after the deadline,
or if goods were transferred to another ship within the deadline,
export taxes were to be collected in all cases.
In the 57th year,
it was stipulated that for ships and goods arriving at the Yuèhǎi Guān,
the Dūfǔ were to be held responsible for investigation and verification,
and monthly reports were to be submitted.
At the end of a year,
if the accounts did not match the clean ledger of the Jiāndū,
they would be impeached and dealt with.
In the 58th year,
it was decreed that apart from tribute ships,
other Western merchant ships were not exempt from taxes.
The Hángzhōu Zhīzào was reassigned to the Yánzhèng,
and the two New Guān, North and South, were placed under the administration of the Xúnfǔ.
The Dèshèngkǒu in Shānxī was opened and assigned to the Shāhǔkǒu Jiāndū for tax collection.
At this time, English cargo ships sought to dock and trade in Jiāng, Zhè Níngbō, Zhūshān, and Tiānjīn, Guǎngdōng, among other places.
The emperor did not permit it,
but ordered them to continue trading at Àomén as per custom,
paying duties to the Yuèhǎi Guān,
and also collecting ship's material tax.
In the 2nd year of Jiāqìng,
the left and right wings were merged into one post.
Two years later,
two more officials were specially appointed.
Regulations were established for the Chénguān, Yúguān, Pānjiākǒu, Tōngyǒngdào, and Gǔběikǒu customs barriers.
That year, an order was issued to verify and reduce the surplus quotas of various customs barriers.
Thus, the Hùguān's Zuòliángtīng was set at six thousand liǎng,
Tiānjīn at twenty thousand,
Línqīng at eleven thousand,
Jiānghǎi at forty-two thousand,
Hǔshù at two hundred thirty-five thousand,
Huái'ān at one hundred eleven thousand,
Hǎiguān Miàowānkǒu at two thousand two hundred,
Yángzhōu at sixty-eight thousand,
Xīxīn at twenty-nine thousand,
Jiǔjiāng at three hundred forty-seven thousand eight hundred,
Gànguān at thirty-eight thousand,
Mǐnhǎi at one hundred thirteen thousand,
Zhèhǎi at thirty-nine thousand,
Běixīn at sixty-five thousand,
Wǔchāng at twelve thousand,
Kuíguān at one hundred ten thousand,
Yuèhǎi at eight hundred fifty-five thousand five hundred,
Tàipíng at seventy-five thousand five hundred,
Wúzhōu at seven thousand five hundred,
Xúnzhōu at five thousand two hundred,
Guīhuàchéng at one thousand six hundred,
Shānhǎiguān at forty-nine thousand four hundred eighty-seven,
Shāhǔkǒu at fifteen thousand four hundred fourteen,
Zhāngjiākǒu at forty thousand five hundred sixty-one,
Dǎjiànlú was to collect and remit everything;
for the Gōngguān, Chénguān was three thousand eight hundred liǎng,
Sùqiān seven thousand eight hundred,
Wúhú forty-seven thousand,
Lóngjiāng fifty-five thousand,
Jīngguān thirteen thousand,
Tōngyǒngdào three thousand nine hundred;
for Zhá, Nánxīn, and Yú three customs barriers,
and Pāntáo, Gǔběi, Shāhǔ three passes,
the timber tax had no surplus,
so no further discussion was needed.
In the 5th year,
it was agreed to allow empty grain transport ships to carry an additional twenty shí beyond the sixty shí regular quota,
all exempt from tax.
Strict prohibitions were issued against the extortions of Cóngwénmén, Lúgōuqíáo, and customs runners in various provinces.
As Lǐ Dàměng, the Zhīfǔ of Chénzhōu, collected over ten thousand liǎng in surplus beyond the tax quota,
the matter was sent to the ministry for deliberation.
In the 6th year,
the tax runner for cattle and horses in Shèngjīng was designated,
to be specially appointed from among the five department Shìláng in Shèngjīng.
The regular tax quota for Dǎjiànlú was set at twenty thousand liǎng.
The collection of "2-8 Tiānpíng silver" in Mǐnhǎi was abolished.
In the 7th year,
the collection of timber tax at Gǔběikǒu by Mìyún Xiàn was changed to "collect all and remit all,"
and the original quota supervisor's seal was surrendered and cancelled.
In the 9th year,
the surplus quotas for various customs barriers were re-adjusted:
Zhèhǎi forty-four thousand,
Xīxīn thirty-three thousand,
Jiǔjiāng three hundred sixty-seven thousand,
Hǔshù two hundred fifty thousand,
Huái'ān one hundred thirty-one thousand.
In the 11th year,
the annual collection for Chénguān was set to include an additional 2,770-plus liǎng of "hào silver".
In the 15th year,
the tax regulations for Cóngwénmén were fixed.
Camp and patrol officials were ordered to investigate the malpractice of private release and collection, and impersonation of "white runners" at Cóngwénmén.
In the 22nd year,
all maritime customs were instructed to prohibit goods not allowed for export.
In the 1st year of Dàoguāng,
the Zhèjiāng Yánzhèng was abolished,
and the Hángzhōu Zhīzào was re-established,
concurrently managing the North and South New Guān taxes.
In the 3rd year,
customs in various provinces were ordered to rectify long-standing abuses such as corrupt officials' monopoly and clerks' connivance,
and to strictly prohibit irregular and excessive levies by customs officials and the smuggling of goods by grain transport ships.
The timber tax for Duōlún Nuò'ěr was established.
The tax regulations for the Zhèhǎi Guān were revised.
In the 9th year,
the tax for Huíjiāng was reaffirmed as "thirty to one" (3.33%).
At this time, English dābān and others, due to the closure of foreign trading houses,
owed outstanding merchandise payments,
and their merchant ships were anchored in foreign waters,
delaying their entry.
They often mentioned paying six to seven hundred thousand liǎng in annual taxes at the Yuèhǎi Guān,
using this as leverage.
The Emperor said:
"Foreign merchants privately bring opium into the country,
and secretly buy silver to export;
the gains do not compensate for the losses.
If they deliberately cause difficulties,
they will not be allowed to open their holds.
How much loss would the absence of tax from this one country's goods amount to!
As for the request to differentiate tax payments based on the size of merchant ships,
that can still be flexibly adjusted."
In the 10th year,
it was stipulated that for the surplus silver of various customs, sixty percent would be within the quota,
and forty percent would be extra-quota,
and overages and shortages would be assessed separately for merits and demerits.
Earlier, Yùshǐ Xǔ Nǎijì reported on the extortions by the Cóngwénmén tax bureau,
and an order was issued for the Xúnshì Wǔchéng Yùshǐ to inspect at any time.
By this time,
Yùshǐ Jìnchāng again reported on extortions by patrol runners
and connivance by clerks.
One Manchu and one Han Yùshǐ were specially appointed,
dedicated to inspections,
to be replaced after one year.
In the 11th year,
the Hǔshù surplus was reduced by twenty thousand liǎng,
and Huái'ān by twenty-one thousand liǎng.
Regulations were established for compensating short-collected customs duties,
with varying time limits based on the amount.
Guǎngdōng was ordered to strictly arrest "kuàixiè" boats engaged in smuggling and tax evasion for foreign merchants.
In the 12th year,
the export of white lead was prohibited.
In the 13th year,
various customs' "biāolǐ" (tribute gifts) and "cháchuán xièyí" (inspection gratitude fees),
and "dìgùn bàodān" (local ruffian report forms) and other such items were abolished.
As Huòhǎn repented and showed sincerity,
they were again permitted to trade at the checkpoints,
and were exempt from taxes.
In the 14th year,
the extortions and connivance by customs' private retainers,
and the abuses of clerks monopolizing and local ruffians engaging in illicit activities, were strictly prohibited.
Also, the additional collection of private taxes from foreign merchants by Yuè merchants was investigated and prohibited.
It was stipulated that tribute goods arriving in the capital
would be exempt from tax and allowed through Cóngwénmén.
In the 17th year,
the export of silver ingots was strictly prohibited.
The smuggling and tax evasion by bandit boats and kilns in Yuè Province were investigated and dealt with.
In the 19th year,
Sháozhōu and Dōngjiāng two customs barriers were established,
under the management of the Nánsháolián Dào.
In the 21st year,
the main Jīngzhōu Guān was relocated to Liǔjiājí,
renamed Liǔguān,
and its branch customs was renamed Liǔzhīguān.
In the 24th year,
Siamese ships carrying regular tribute envoys and their goods were exempted from tax.
In the 25th year,
the Lóngjiāng Guān's timber inspection tax bureau was abolished.
In the 2nd year of Xiánfēng,
the rampant smuggling abuses at coastal customs were investigated and prohibited.
In the 3rd year,
due to the Niǎn bandits disturbing Jiāngnán,
Hǔshù, Huái'ān, Wúhú, Fèngyáng, and other customs barriers
all requested to collect and receive as much as possible,
without any limits.
They were ordered to continue collecting according to the established quotas.
In the 6th year,
the tax quota for Dǎjiànlú was set at twenty thousand liǎng.
In the 8th year,
it was stipulated that the surplus tax in Shèngjīng could be paid in copper cash equivalent to silver,
and regulations for fishing boats and large and small cattle boats to pay boat fees were established.
In the 9th year,
the Shāndōng Yāntái tax bureau was established.
In the 10th year,
when scholars entered the capital for the metropolitan examination,
they were to be inspected and released as per custom,
and extortion by Cóngwénmén patrol runners was strictly prohibited.
The tax regulations for Fèngtiān Hǎikǒu were revised,
adding four taxes: soybeans, soybean cakes, bao'tou, and oil drums,
and increasing the surplus by eighty thousand liǎng.
It was also stipulated that if a customs supervisor left office before a year was complete,
the successor would take over collection,
and the full year's accounts would be deducted and reported separately.
The five-day and ten-day limits for passing goods tax at the North New Guān's North and South entrances were abolished.
That year,
Russia was permitted tax-free mutual trade in Hēilóngjiāng.
In the 2nd year of Tóngzhì,
taxes in Bā'ěrcǔkè were waived,
and the regular tax in Yè'ěrqiāng was increased.
In the 3rd year,
the Dǎgǒu Kǒu (Takao Port) Customs House in Táinán, Fújiàn, was established,
under the administration of the巡撫 (xúnfǔ, Provincial Governor).
Tax collection at Běixīn Guān was temporarily suspended.
In the 4th year,
tax collection at Lóngjiāng, Xīxīn Guān, and Hǔshù Sānguān was temporarily suspended.
For bamboo and timber taxes at Húběi Xīnguān,
one member of the 本省道府 (běnshěng dàofǔ, provincial Daotai or Prefect) was selected to oversee collection.
Previously, the fixed levy at Yuèhǎi Guān (Guangdong Maritime Customs)
did not differentiate between regular and overseas trade.
From this point,
goods transported by Chinese ships were designated as regular tax,
with a fixed levy of over 56,500 liǎng,
and a surplus of 100,000 liǎng;
any further surplus
was to be fully collected and remitted.
That year, various unauthorized fees from civil and military offices at Tàipíng Guān were abolished,
and Yuèhǎi Guān was instructed to strictly investigate smuggling and concealment at various ports.
The supervisor of Shānhǎi Guān was dismissed,
and the position was replaced by the Fèngjǐn Shānhǎiguān Dào to oversee collection.
In the 7th year,
it was decreed that Tàipíng Guān would be exclusively managed by the Nánsháolián Dào,
while its four sub-factories' commissioners
would still be appointed by the xúnfǔ.
In the 8th year,
it was reiterated that tribute goods remitted to the capital
should be allowed to pass through Chóngwén Mén,
and no obstruction or extortion was permitted.
In the 11th year,
the practice of handling tasks for Huáiguān in Jiāngsū was suspended.
In the 2nd year of Guāngxù,
Wúhú and Fèngyáng Guān were reopened.
In the 3rd year,
regulations for assessing and evaluating various customs houses were strictly established.
In the 4th year,
the tax affairs of Huīfā, Mùqīn, and other places, as well as Nínggǔtǎ and Sānxìng,
were all to be collected by commissioners appointed by the Jílín Jiāngjūn.
The timber tax in Jiāochéng Xiàn, Shānxī,
was to be collected by the Zhīxiàn (Magistrate) at an office established in Wǔyuánchéng Gùjiāo Cūn.
In the 8th year,
the tax quota for Wúhú Guān was set at over 136,000 liǎng.
In the 9th year,
the tax affairs of Zhōngjiāng were transferred to the Dōngbiāndào for collection.
In the 13th year,
the taxation of Huángjiāng Chǎng in Guǎngdōng was changed to be managed by a dedicated commissioner,
and the titles of Chǎngshū, Qiānzi, Guānfáng, and Zǒngsànfáng were abolished,
along with the elimination of seven malpractices: unauthorized extra flat fees, official money for expenses, lítoú (brokerage fees), boat fees, market boat fees, black money, and contract money,
which were publicly announced.
The surplus of Wú and Xún Chǎng was set at 60,000 liǎng.
Hùwěi and Dǎgǒu Guān were placed under the supervision of the Táiwān Xúnfǔ.
In the 25th year,
the various Jiāngjūn and Dūfǔ were instructed to review the amounts of illicit gains and malpractices at various customs barriers,
allocate a suitable portion to public funds,
and report within a set deadline.
In the 34th year,
the tax on Chinese merchants at Chóngwén Mén was reduced to 3% of the value,
following the example of foreign merchant taxes;
taxes on daily necessities like vegetables were waived.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng,
the Jílín Shěng Shuìwùchù (Jilin Provincial Tax Office) was established,
with four sections: Jīzhēng (Collection), Shùwù (General Affairs), Zhīyìng (Expenditure), and Héxiāo (Verification and Write-off);
all bureaus, offices, and companies related to taxes and donations were abolished and merged.
Regulations for collecting taxes at Sìchuān Chángguān and rules for their implementation were revised.
The establishment of foreign customs houses
began with the opening of the five treaty ports.
Before this, although foreign merchants came to Guǎngdōng for trade,
they merely paid taxes to the regular customs according to regulations.
In the 19th year of Dàoguāng,
there was the incident of receiving opium on hulks.
That autumn, all merchant ships coming to Guǎngdōng
were obstructed by British warships,
preventing their entry.
The tax revenue of Yuèhǎi Customs,
which largely depended on foreign goods,
consequently suffered a deficit.
In the autumn of the 22nd year,
the British demanded treaty ports,
and permission was granted to open Guǎngzhōu, Fúzhōu, Xiàmén, Níngbō, and Shànghǎi along the coast for trade.
The following year,
the foreign goods tariff was set at 5% of the value,
and trade first opened in Guǎngzhōu and Shànghǎi.
Foreign goods entering the country
paid duties according to the tariff.
Subsequently, when transported inland by Chinese merchants,
at customs barriers passed,
taxes were levied only based on the estimated value,
with no more than a certain fen per liǎng added.
In the 24th year,
a treaty with French merchants was established: 1.
French ships going to the five treaty ports for trade
were not allowed to enter other ports or privately trade along the coast;
violators' goods would be confiscated. 1.
French merchants entering and exiting the five treaty ports
would pay goods tax and tonnage dues according to the tariff,
and no other fees would be collected. 1.
If a merchant ship entering port
failed to submit its manifest and cargo list within two days,
and the consul notified the customs,
a fine of 50 silver yuan would be imposed for each day overdue,
but not exceeding 200 yuan.
If a ship, without obtaining a customs permit,
unauthorizedly opened its hold and unloaded goods,
a fine of 500 silver yuan would be imposed,
and the goods would be confiscated. 1.
If a ship entered port but did not unload goods,
it could proceed to another port within two days,
and pay taxes at that port. 1.
If a ship entered port and fully paid tonnage dues after two days,
ships over 150 tons would pay 5 qián of silver per ton,
and those below would pay 1 qián per ton. 1.
For valued goods that were damaged,
the tax silver could be reduced after verification. 1.
A ship entering port would pay duties according to the quantity of goods unloaded;
if the remaining goods were taken to another port for unloading and sale,
taxes would be paid at that port.
In the 25th year,
a commercial treaty with Belgium was established,
with taxes and dues paid according to regulations.
In the 27th year,
commercial treaties with Sweden and Norway were established,
with taxes and dues also similar.
In the 4th year of Xiánfēng,
Jiānghǎi Guān was established in Shànghǎi.
In the 8th year,
a new treaty with Britain was established: 1.
Niúzhuāng, Táiwān, Dēngzhōu, Cháozhōu, Qióngzhōu, and other ports
were permitted to open for trade. 1.
For goods taxed at 5% of their value,
many of which had declining value,
the old tariff should be revised.
If this newly established tariff
was to be revised,
a ten-year limit was set,
and six months' notice had to be given beforehand;
otherwise, payment would be made according to the previous regulations,
and another ten years would pass. 1.
Inland transit tax (zǐkǒu shuì) would be 2.5% of the value;
if a one-time payment was desired,
after foreign goods at import and native goods at the first customs barrier paid tax and received a ticket,
no further collection would occur at other ports. 1.
After British ships paid tonnage dues and received a permit,
no re-collection would occur within four months. 1.
If a cargo ship entered port for two days,
all tonnage dues would be paid. 1.
For British merchants' private boats,
if they carried goods subject to tax according to regulations,
tonnage dues would be paid once every four months. 1.
After merchant goods paid tax,
if they were transported to another port,
and were in their original packaging,
they would be exempt from re-collection.
That year,
French merchants were permitted to trade in Cháozhōu, Qióngzhōu, Dànshuǐ in Táiwān, Dēngzhōu, and Jiāngníng,
with taxes and tonnage dues the same as for other treaty nations.
In the ninth year,
the Yuèhǎi Customs (粤海關) was established in Guǎngzhōu (廣州).
It was permitted for Russians to trade at seven ports: Shànghǎi (上海), Níngbō (寧波), Fúzhōu (福州), Xiàmén (廈門), Guǎngzhōu (廣州), Táiwān (臺灣), and Qióngzhōu (瓊州).
Tariffs were to be determined according to the regulations of other nations.
The agreement with the United States was also set similarly,
and it was further permitted to open markets at the two ports of Cháozhōu (潮州) and Táiwān (臺灣),
paying duties and taxes according to the new regulations.
In the tenth year,
the Cháohǎi Customs (潮海關) was established in Shàntóu (汕頭).
It was permitted for Englishmen to trade in Hànkǒu (漢口) and Jiǔjiāng (九江).
Robert Hart (李泰國) was appointed Inspector General of Customs,
assisting in customs administration at various ports.
Ministers of Trade for the three ports of Tiānjīn (天津), Niúzhuāng (牛莊), and Dēngzhōu (登州) were established.
In the eleventh year,
the Zhèhǎi Customs (浙海關) was established,
under the supervision of the Níngshàotái Circuit Intendant (寧紹台道).
The Jīnhǎi Customs (津海關) was placed under the jurisdiction of the Minister of Trade.
Additionally, the Mǐnhǎi (閩海), Zhènjiāng (鎮江), and Jiǔjiāng (九江) Customs were established.
The foreign duties for all nations were set to begin from August of the previous year,
with reports submitted quarterly,
and accounts settled once every four reports.
Britain and the United States opened ports in Jiǔjiāng (九江) and Hànkǒu (漢口),
and Russia also traded in Hànkǒu (漢口).
Therefore, regulations for trade along the Chángjiāng (長江) and at various ports were established.
When foreign goods entered the river,
they were to pay the regular duty and transit duty in Shànghǎi (上海).
When domestic goods were exported,
they were to pay export duty.
Upon re-importation,
a regular duty was to be paid,
with a 20% deduction allowed.
If half duty was paid,
the 20% deduction was not applicable.
If they re-entered the interior,
they were still subject to internal transit duties.
Additionally, a commercial treaty with Germany was established,
its tariff provisions being the same as those with Britain.
In the first year of Tóngzhì (同治),
the Xiàmén Customs (廈門關) was established.
The commercial affairs of the five ports were placed under the concurrent administration of the Minister of Trade.
In the second year,
the Dōnghǎi (東海), Táinán (臺南), and Dànshuǐ (淡水) Customs were established.
Foreign goods in British concessions were exempted from internal transit duties,
and it was permitted to open four additional ports: Yíchāng (宜昌), Wúhú (蕪湖), Wēnzhōu (溫州), and Běihǎi (北海).
Along the river, Dàtōng (大通), Ānqìng (安慶), Húkǒu (湖口), Wǔxuè (武穴), Lùxīkǒu (陸溪口), and Shāshì (沙市)
were all permitted for temporary mooring of British steamers,
with cargo loaded and unloaded by civilian boats.
Except for foreign goods with half-duty certificates to be inspected according to regulations,
domestic goods were only allowed to be loaded onto boats,
not unloaded and sold.
Furthermore, if British merchants purchased domestic goods themselves,
unless transported out to sea,
they could not invoke the half-duty transit duty rule.
In this year, commercial treaties with Denmark and the Netherlands were established,
with payment of duties and taxes following the British precedent.
In the third year,
the Shānhǎi Customs (山海關) was established in Niúzhuāng (牛莊).
Spanish tariffs were set,
following the regulations of various nations from the eighth year of Xiánfēng (咸豐).
The following year,
an agreement with Belgium was established,
and duties and taxes were also similar.
Regulations for French vessel duties were also revised: For merchant ships that had entered port and paid duties,
when proceeding to other ports,
and when traveling to and from various French ports in Ānnán (安南),
and nearby Japanese wharves,
a certificate would be issued by the Customs,
and duty would be paid again after four months.
Initially, the Yuèhǎi Customs (粵海關) duties did not distinguish between regular and foreign goods,
but it was then determined that goods transported by foreign ships were subject to foreign duties.
In the fifth year,
commercial treaty duties and taxes with Italy were established.
If merchant ships entering port concealed or misrepresented goods,
the shipmaster would be fined five hundred taels,
otherwise, it was as per the French treaty.
In the eighth year,
commercial treaty duties and taxes with Austria were established,
all similar to the Italian treaty.
Additionally, a commercial treaty with Russia was established:
Firstly, those trading within one hundred li of the border and in various Mongol leagues
were exempt from duties.
Secondly, when Russian goods reached Tiānjīn (天津),
they would pay a duty reduced by one-third, following the Tiānjīn Customs (天津關) regulations.
For goods temporarily kept at Zhāngjiākǒu (張家口), the regular duty would be paid.
If then transported to Tōngzhōu (通州) or Tiānjīn (天津),
no further levy would be imposed,
and the extra portion of duty paid at Zhāngjiākǒu (張家口) would be refunded.
Thirdly, when Russian goods were transported from Tiānjīn (天津) to other ports,
the reduced duty portion had to be made up.
No further levy would be imposed at other ports.
If re-entering the interior from other ports,
an additional half transit duty would be paid.
Fourthly, when domestic goods and foreign goods entered by water,
duties would be paid according to the regulations of other nations.
Fifthly, when domestic goods were transported from Tiānjīn (天津) or Tōngzhōu (通州) back to Russia by land,
the regular duty would be paid as per regulations,
with no further levy,
and sales along the way were prohibited.
Sixthly, when re-imported domestic goods were transported from Tiānjīn (天津) back to Russia by land,
after paying duties,
they had to be shipped within one year,
with no further levy,
and the re-import duty would be refunded.
Sales along the way were prohibited.
Seventhly, when goods of other nations were transported from Tiānjīn (天津) or other ports back to Russia by land,
if regular duty and transit duty had been paid,
no further levy would be imposed.
If only regular duty had been paid,
the transit duty should be made up.
Eighthly, the tariff regulations were agreed upon
and implemented on a trial basis for five years.
If modifications were desired upon expiration,
notification had to be given six months in advance.
In the ninth year,
the Jiānghàn Customs (江漢關) was established.
The three Ministers of Trade were abolished.
The Dōnghǎi (東海) and Shānhǎi (山海) Customs were both placed under the jurisdiction of the Governor-General of Zhílì (直隸).
A Jīnhǎi Customs Intendant (津海關道) was separately established,
to supervise the Xīn (新) and Chāo (鈔) Customs.
In the third year of Guāngxù (光緒),
the Wúhú (蕪湖) and Yíchāng (宜昌) Customs were established,
under the supervision of the Huīníngchítàiguǎng Circuit Intendant (徽寧池太廣道) and the Jīngyíshī Circuit Intendant (荊宜施道) respectively.
The Qiónghǎi (瓊海) and Běihǎi (北海) Customs were concurrently managed by the Yuèhǎi Customs (粵海關).
Additionally, the Ōuhǎi Customs (甌海關) was established in Wēnzhōu (溫州).
In the sixth year,
the commercial treaty with Germany was renewed:

Firstly, China permitted, in addition to the previously opened ports of Yíchāng (宜昌), Wúhú (蕪湖), Wēnzhōu (溫zhōu), Běihǎi (北海) and the riverine locations of Dàtōng (大通), Ānqìng (安慶), Húkǒu (湖口), Wǔxuè (武穴), Lùxīkǒu (陸溪口), and Shāshì (沙市) that were already used for loading and unloading passengers and cargo,
German vessels to anchor at Wúsōngkǒu (吳淞口)
for loading and unloading goods.
Secondly, upon arrival of a plank vessel,
if it moored for fourteen days,
it should pay half of the tonnage dues.
Thirdly, if there was concealment or misrepresentation in the declaration of ship or cargo,
the shipmaster should be fined,
not exceeding five hundred taels.
Fourthly, if German merchants transported domestic coal for export,
a regular duty of three qián (錢) per ton would be paid.
Fifthly, unlicensed individuals falsely claiming to be pilots
would be fined up to one hundred taels of silver.
Sixthly, damaged vessels
were permitted to be repaired at various ports.
If pretexts were used to evade or conceal,
a fine of double the amount of the tonnage dues sought to be evaded would be imposed.
Seventhly, if Chinese vessels flew German flags with the knowledge of Germans,
or if German vessels flew Chinese flags with the knowledge of the cargo owner,
all goods would be confiscated by the government.
In this year, a commercial treaty with the United States was established,
with duties and taxes following the regulations of other nations.
In the seventh year,
the Jiāyù Pass (嘉峪關) Customs was established,
under the supervision of the Ānsù Circuit Intendant (安肅道).
The Russian overland commercial treaty was revised:
Firstly, when Russian goods reached Jiāyù Pass (嘉峪關),
they would pay a duty reduced by one-third,
following the Tiānjīn Customs (天津關) regulations.
If then transported to the interior,
duties would also follow the Tiānjīn (天津) regulations.
Secondly, if goods reaching Tiānjīn (天津) did not match the original certificate,
they would be confiscated.
If merely found to have bypassed inspection,
a fine would be imposed, requiring payment of one regular duty.
Thirdly, when domestic goods were transported from Tōngzhōu (通州) back to Russia,
the export regular duty would be paid.
When transported back from Zhāngjiākǒu (張家口),
and when domestic goods were transported from the interior to Tōngzhōu (通州) or Zhāngjiākǒu (張家口) back to Russia,
all would pay transit duty,
and sales along the way were prohibited.
The rest was the same as the previous treaty.
In the twelfth year,
the Sino-French Commercial Treaty was revised: 1.
China agreed to open two trading locations in Běiqí [Tonkin],
where customs would be established to collect duties. 2.
Foreign goods entering Yúnnán and Guǎngxī through their border passes
would pay one-third of the regular duty, reduced by half. 3.
Foreign goods paying duty at this pass,
then transshipped to another pass,
would not be re-taxed within thirty-six months.
If transshipped to other ports,
a separate regular duty would be paid.
Native goods paying duty at this pass and then transshipped to another pass
would only be subject to a re-entry duty.
If transshipped to other ports,
a separate regular duty would be levied.
Entry into the interior would still incur a likin duty. 4.
If import or export goods arrived at the customs and were not declared within eighteen hours,
a fine of fifty liǎng would be imposed per day,
but not exceeding two hundred liǎng.
If omissions or false declarations were found,
the goods would be confiscated.
The rest of the agreement remained as before.
In the thirteenth year,
France was permitted to open Lóngzhōu in Guǎngxī and Méngzì and Mánhào in Yúnnán
as treaty ports for trade.
Import duties on foreign goods were reduced by three-tenths,
and export duties by four-tenths.
Mánhào was later changed to Hénèi,
and Sīmáo in Yúnnán was added as a port.
When native goods were transported from treaty ports to these four ports,
a full ten-tenths of the regular export duty was levied.
Upon arrival at the four ports, a re-entry half-duty was levied, reduced by four-tenths of the ten-tenths.
A treaty with Portugal was also concluded,
its duties, levies, and penalty clauses aligning with the previous year's French treaty.
That year, the Gǒngběi Customs was established in Àomén [Macau],
and the Jiǔlóng Customs in Xiānggǎng [Hong Kong],
both supervised by the Yuèhǎi Customs Superintendent.
The taxes in Táinán and Dànshuǐ were placed under the supervision of the Táiwān Provincial Governor.
In the fifteenth year,
the Zhènnán and Méngzì Customs were established.
In the sixteenth year,
the Chóngqìng Customs was established.
In the twentieth year,
the Yàdōng Customs in Xīzàng [Tibet] was opened,
permitting British trade.
Except for prohibited goods,
import duties were exempted for five years
from the date of opening.
After the period expired, new tax regulations would be set and followed.
It was also agreed that for goods transported via the Mányǔn and Zhǎnxī routes,
import duties would be reduced by four-tenths for six years.
In the twenty-first year,
the Sīmáo Customs and the Měngliè and Yìwǔ sub-customs were established,
administered concurrently by the Sīmáo Prefectural Magistrate.
In the twenty-second year,
the Sino-Japanese Commercial Treaty was concluded: 1.
Import and export goods were subject to the same regulations as other nations,
paying only import or export duties. 2.
For goods already imported and then transshipped to other ports,
regardless of the nationality of the owner, carrier, or ship,
all duties, likin, and miscellaneous levies were entirely exempted. 3.
For goods transported into the interior,
a further likin duty would be paid.
For exempted goods,
a duty of 2.5% of the value was levied. 4.
Native export goods,
after paying regular and likin duties,
were to be transported abroad within twelve months.
If they were items prohibited from export overseas,
only the regular duty was paid upon export. 5.
Foreign goods that had paid import duty,
if re-exported within three years,
would not be re-taxed. 6.
Ship tonnage dues were subject to the same regulations as other nations.
That year, the Hángzhōu, Sūzhōu, and Shāshì Customs were established.
The following year,
the Wúzhōu and Sānshuǐ Customs were established,
along with the Gānzhú and Jiāngmén sub-customs.
The regulations for British trade on the Chángjiāng [Yangtze River] were revised: 1.
Steamships trading on the Chángjiāng
would be issued a special license by the Shànghǎi Customs Commissioner,
to be renewed annually,
or could be renewed in Hànkǒu or Yíchāng.
Tonnage dues would be paid at the customs issuing the license.
Violators would be penalized,
and repeat offenders would have their special licenses revoked. 2.
The practice of simultaneously collecting regular export duty and re-entry half-duty was abolished.
For Chángjiāng steamers with special licenses,
export and re-entry duties would be paid in installments at the loading and unloading ports, according to the regulations of each port.
The loading, transshipping, and unloading of goods
would also follow the regulations of each port.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Yuèzhōu Customs and the Wúsōng sub-customs of the Jiānghǎi Customs were established.
The following year,
the Jiāozhōu Customs was established.
Tax collection methods were jointly agreed upon with Germany: 1.
A customs house would be established in Qīnghǎi,
and Germans should be appointed as Customs Commissioners. 2.
Goods imported by sea would not be taxed.
If transported from the Jiāozhōu boundary into the interior,
import duty would be levied.
However, exit from the Jiāozhōu boundary without a maritime customs permit was prohibited. 3.
If native goods were transported by land into the leased territory
and then by water to other ports,
export duty would be levied.
However, native goods and produce originating within the leased territory,
and goods manufactured from materials imported by sea,
would not be taxed upon export. 4.
Native goods imported and then re-transported into the interior
would pay duty according to the treaty. 5.
Native goods that paid export duty,
if re-transported to another port, would pay half duty.
Regulations for Korea [Hán] and Mexico [Mòguó] regarding duties, levies, and various fees
were also set to follow the customs regulations.
That year, the Jīnlíng Customs was established.
The Fúhǎi Customs was also established in Sān'ào.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the Téngyuè Customs and the Mányǔn and Nòngzhāng sub-customs were established.
In the twenty-seventh year,
it was decided that for regular customs posts located within fifty lǐ of a treaty port,
duties would be collected concurrently by the foreign customs.
In the twenty-eighth year,
the Qínhuángdǎo sub-customs was established.
Formerly, Shèng Xuānhuái and Niè Jīguī and other grand ministers of trade talks stated,
that Customs Commissioner Hè Dé (Robert Hart) proposed to levy import duties on foreign goods,
following the method of simultaneously levying tax and *líjīn* on foreign opium.
After assessing the current market value,
and applying the regular duty and *zǐkǒushuì* (barrier tax) at a ratio of 7:2.5,
the *líjīn* would be uniformly doubled,
making the total 15 out of every 100 *wén* of value.
This would be collected by the Maritime Customs,
to avoid obstruction and confusion from various *líjīn* bureaus,
allowing goods to circulate freely,
and foreign merchants might agree to it.
It was also proposed that *tǔhuò* (native goods) previously subject to half-duty for export
be changed to pay *líjīn*,
to offset the *líjīn* and other duties on foreign goods being transferred to the Maritime Customs for collection,
which would also not harm the *líjīn* revenue of various provinces.
The emperor believed that this matter involved significant gains and losses,
and ordered the Grand Ministers of the Northern and Southern Oceans and various governors-general and governors to consider the situations in their respective provinces
and submit well-considered proposals.
By this time,
an agreement on tariff reduction and tax increase was finally reached with Britain: One,
when the agreement came into effect,
China agreed to abolish all *líkǎ* (likin barriers) and similar *líjīn*-like collection points
that had been established, in addition to the existing regular customs houses.
All would be abolished.
Two,
Britain agreed to an additional tax on imported foreign goods, amounting to one and a half times the current effective 5% ad valorem duty,
to offset the abolition of *líjīn*, *zǐkǒushuì*, and various other duties.
The total export duty on *tǔhuò*
should not exceed 7.5% ad valorem.
Three,
existing regular customs houses would remain.
For places with a Maritime Customs but no regular customs,
and non-treaty ports along the coast and border,
regular customs houses could be added.
If a new treaty port required a Maritime Customs,
a regular customs house could also be established.
Four,
the import and export duties paid by civilian junks and other vessels for transporting goods
