should not be less than the total of the regular import duty and additional duty for steamers.
*Tǔhuò* transported to the first regular customs house
would be subject to an additional export duty according to Maritime Customs regulations,
and a certificate would be issued.
Within one year, regardless of which customs house they exited through,
no further duties would be levied.
If transported outside the concessions for sale,
a sales tax should be paid.
Five,
for *tǔhuò* exports,
in addition to the regular duty,
a half-duty would be levied
to compensate for the abolition of *líjīn* and other duties.
The regular export duty on raw silk
should not exceed 5% ad valorem.
Six,
for goods previously not exported,
a sales tax would be levied at the point of sale.
For *tǔhuò* transported by civilian boats to a port and intended for local sale,
regardless of the nationality of the owner,
a sales tax would be levied.
However, it would not be collected within concessions.
Seven,
Chinese and foreign merchants manufacturing yarn and cloth with machinery in the interior
would only pay a factory exit tax,
with all other taxes exempted.
All machine-woven foreign goods of a similar nature would be treated likewise.
However, the Hányáng Dàyě Ironworks,
and other state-owned tax-exempt factories,
as well as items produced by manufacturing bureaus and dockyards established later,
were not included in this exemption.
Soon after, similar agreements were concluded with the United States, Japan, and various Atlantic countries.
However, due to the cost of investigation,
it could not be implemented.
In the 29th year of the Guāngxù reign,
an agreement was reached with Russia to provisionally implement customs regulations for Northern Mǎnzhōu: One,
railway-transported goods would pay two-thirds of the tax.
Designated boundaries would be set,
varying from ten *lǐ* to five or three *lǐ* from the four sides of each station, depending on its size.
If transported outside the designated boundaries,
the full regular tax should be made up,
and processed according to the regulations for transporting goods into the interior.
Two,
the reduction in price for railway-transported goods
was a special agreement between China and Russia.
Except for Russian goods,
goods from other countries transported via the Eastern Province Railway would be allowed this reduction.
Three,
if any tax items in the regulations needed to be changed,
they would be renegotiated after one year.
Further supplementary regulations for trade and import were also established: One,
for imported foreign goods not listed in the tariff schedule,
they would be valued at 5% ad valorem,
based on market price,
with the market value converted to customs value,
and deducting expenses,
to arrive at the actual value of the goods.
Two,
if goods were sold to a Chinese merchant before customs declaration,
the total value of the contract would be considered the market price.
Three,
if the value estimated by the Maritime Customs did not agree with the merchant,
the Maritime Customs would, together with the merchant's national consul
and the senior consul,
each appoint one person to make a joint decision.
If it was found that the merchant's declared value was less than 24 *liǎng* per hundred,
the regular tax would be levied based on the estimated value,
and four times the declared regular tax would be imposed as a fine.
Four,
foreign ships exclusively carrying tax-exempt rice and other grains would still pay tonnage dues.
That year, a sub-customs house was established in Àomén.
In the 30th year,
an agreement was reached with Germany to establish customs and levy taxes in Qīngdǎo,
with an appendix.
Regardless of whether they were Chinese or foreign steamers,
when navigating inland ports,
they should obtain a customs permit,
renewable annually.
The initial permit fee was ten *liǎng*,
and renewal only two *liǎng*.
Tonnage dues were paid once every four years.
The following year,
the method of tax collection in Qīngdǎo was revised with Germany: One,
the port of Qīngdǎo was reformed.
Generally, it would be tax-exempt,
but a specific area within the designated tax boundary would be chosen as a duty-free zone,
and taxes would be levied in all other areas.
Two,
all goods manufactured outside the duty-free zone
would pay export tax,
which should not exceed the tax payable on the raw materials transported.
The customs house at Jiāngmén in Sānshuǐ was upgraded to a main customs house.
In the 33rd year,
Nánníng and Dàlián customs houses were established,
and also the Āndōng customs house and the Dàdōnggōu sub-customs house.
In the 34th year,
the Bīnjiāng customs house and the Mǎnzhōulǐ and Suīfēnhé sub-customs houses were established.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
the Àihuī and Sānxìng sub-customs houses were established.
In the second year,
the Húnchūn customs house and the Yánjí sub-customs house were established.
In the third year,
the tariffs for various ports under the Dōnghǎi Customs were revised to 2.5% ad valorem,
plus an additional 1.25% for interior donations,
and all regular fees were abolished.
Since the abolition of the Táinán, Dànshuǐ, and Hànchéng customs houses in the 22nd year of Guāngxù,
there were 27 customs houses.
In the third year of Xuāntǒng,
Nánníng, Wúzhōu, Sānshuǐ, Yuèzhōu, Fúhǎi, Wúsōng, Jīnlíng, Jiāohǎi, Téngyuè, Jiāngmén, Āndōng, Dàdōnggōu, Dàlián, Bīnjiāng, Mǎnzhōulǐ, Suīfēnhé, Àihuī, Sānxìng, Húnchūn, and Yánjí were added,
making a total of 47 customs houses.
Previously, all taxes on native opium were included in import duties.
In the 12th year of Tóngzhì, a special schedule was first established,
which calculated the total annual taxes collected by the foreign customs.
In the last years of Xiánfēng,
it was only over 4.9 million.
By the last years of Tóngzhì,
it had increased to over 11.4 million.
In the 13th year of Guāngxù,
with the concurrent collection of *líjīn* on foreign opium,
it increased to over 20.5 million.
In the 34th year,
it increased to over 32.9 million.
In the last years of Xuāntǒng,
the total was over 36.17 million,
making it a major source of annual revenue.
*Líjīn* collection,
initially created in the Yángzhōu area,
was later extended nationwide.
In the third year of Xiánfēng,
Léi Yǐchéng, Right Vice Minister of the Board of Punishments, while commanding troops in Yángzhōu,
first initiated *líjīn* collection in towns such as Xiānnǚmiào.
That year, Sūzhōu and Chángzhōu repeatedly fell,
and land and grain taxes could not be collected.
Thus, *líjīn* bureaus were established in Shànghǎi
to provide financial support.
Additionally, *líjīn* collection was set up north of the Jiāng River,
managed by the grand camp's grain office.
In the fifth year,
Jiāngxī established 65 bureaus and barriers,
Húběi established over 480 bureaus and barriers,
Húnán also established main and sub-bureaus inside and outside cities.
In Jiāngsū, under the prefectures of Yángzhōu, Chángzhōu, and Zhènjiāng, five new bureaus were added at Xiǎohékǒu, Pǔ'ān, Xīngǎng, Sānjiāngyíng, and Héhuāchí.
Censor Zōng Jìchén said:
"Too many barriers are set up north and south of the Grand River,
and the collection of duties is too chaotic."
Luó Dūnyǎn, Left Vice Minister of the Board of Punishments, also said:
"The officials, gentry, officers, and soldiers of the Xiānnǚmiào *líjīn* bureau in Tàizhōu
are obstructing and extorting."
The emperor ordered them to consider reducing and merging them,
and strictly forbade and investigated misconduct.
In the sixth year,
Shèngjīng levied commercial goods and grain donations.
One percent was collected for every hundred units of value,
and Jílín followed suit.
Tǔlǔfān in Wūlǔmùqí also levied cotton customs duties (líjīn).
In the seventh year,
the Húběi Líjīn General Bureau was established.
In the eighth year,
it was decided that in Yùshěng (Henan Province), apart from water pipes, medicinal materials, and tea leaves,
no other líjuān (likin donations) would be levied.
The bureaus and checkpoints at Shǎnzhōu, Jīngzǐguān, and along the river were also abolished.
In the same year, Fújiàn and Guǎngxī both established bureaus and checkpoints
to levy commercial likin.
In the ninth year,
bureaus were established at the seaports belonging to the three prefectures of Dēng, Lái, and Qīng to levy likin.
Shānxī established a Chóuxiàngjú (Bureau for Fundraising),
collecting medicine taxes from traveling merchants and likin donations on all goods,
with seven main checkpoints and various sub-checkpoints set up at different passes.
In the tenth year,
due to poor management of líjīn in Zhāngjiākǒu,
an incident was provoked,
and all civil and military officials involved received severe reprimands.
Zēng Guófān, Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, requested the establishment of an East Expedition Bureau (Dōngzhēngjú) in Chángshā
when the Xiāng Army provided aid to È (Húběi),
with the provision that for each area recovered,
bureaus and checkpoints would be appropriately added
to supplement military provisions.
All goods, in addition to the provincial líjīn, would have an extra half percent levied.
This was granted.
At this time, bureaus and checkpoints were also established in Bālǐpù in Jiāngběi and Sháoguān and Zhàqìngfǔ in Guǎngdōng to levy likin.
In the eleventh year,
the medicine likin for traveling merchants in Shānxī was changed to a tax.
Ānhuī began levying líjīn,
establishing main checkpoints.
The provincial bureau had four subordinate ones,
and the Wǎnnán and Huáiběi bureaus each had three subordinate ones,
with fifty-nine sub-checkpoints for patrolling.
Guìzhōu also established commercial likin bureaus in areas adjacent to Chuān (Sìchuān) and Chǔ (Húběi).
At this time, there were too many likin bureaus in various provinces,
and the Emperor feared they would burden merchants and the populace.
He ordered that, apart from important passes on main thoroughfares in each province,
all other bureaus and checkpoints be abolished.
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
due to corruption and harm to the populace by Guangdong officials and gentry in managing líjuān,
Yàn Duānshū, a metropolitan official of the third rank, was specially ordered to be stationed in Sháoguān
to oversee the líjīn in Guǎngdōng.
Luò Bǐngzhāng, Governor-General of Sìchuān, also spoke of the long-standing abuses of líjuān in Yuèshěng (Guangdong Province).
The Emperor admonished Duānshū, saying,
"Líjuān was originally a last resort,
with the sole aim of benefiting military provisions
without violating public sentiment."
Censor Dīng Shàozhōu said,
"The various commissioners for líjuān only enrich themselves,
and popular resentment is boiling."
He ordered the dismissal of all commissioners
and the centralization of management under local officials.
For busy líjuān matters in major cities and towns,
Dàofǔ and other officials were assigned to handle them,
and they were to be clearly itemized according to Board regulations
and posted in public thoroughfares.
In the same year, the Dàshèngguān likin checkpoint was established in Jiāngníng.
Yǔzhōu, Shǎnzhōu, Hénèi Xiàn, and Qīnghuà Zhèn in Hénán all established sub-bureaus for medicinal material líjīn,
with Yǔzhōu also collecting likin on all goods.
The Yálí General Bureau of Qúzhōufǔ was moved to the provincial capital of Zhèjiāng.
Apart from Hángzhōu, Jīnhuá, and Yánzhōu prefectures,
the other eight prefectures all established sub-bureaus and sub-checkpoints.
The Zhōukǒu and Sānhéjiān likin tax bureaus were established.
In the second year,
Fù Míng'ā, Manchu Commander assisting in Yángzhōu military affairs, said:
"In the Xiàhé area,
over a hundred donation checkpoints have been set up by the northern and southern grain depots.
There are several checkpoints in one location,
and one checkpoint divided into several bureaus.
Monthly bureau expenses are at least two hundred gold,
and up to over a thousand gold.
Commissioners are numerous,
and bureau expenses are especially excessive."
The Emperor, knowing that Jiāngběi was like this and other provinces could be inferred,
strictly ordered all governors-general and governors to merge and abolish them,
and to select capable local officials for management.
Soon after, Yán Shùsēn, Governor of Húběi, said:
"Hú Línyì initiated the Húběi líjīn,
emulating Liú Yàn's method of using scholars instead of clerks,
which has achieved lasting success.
If it is transferred to local officials,
there will be many obstacles."
He then enumerated eight弊
and requested to revert to the old system.
He also said:
"Húběi líjīn annually collects 1.34 million,
entirely relying on the establishment of small bureaus
to investigate smuggling and evasion,
only then can the collection of large bureaus thrive,
making it difficult to abolish the smaller checkpoints.
Moreover, with the financial resources of one province,
assisting the military provisions of several provinces largely depends on líjīn,
so lightly proposing changes
might drastically reduce revenue."
Both requests were granted.
In the same year, the Jiāngběi Líjuān General Bureau was established,
merging various checkpoints,
retaining twenty-six checkpoints including Dàshèngguān.
Jiāngsū also established the Yálíjuān General Bureau,
merging various checkpoints,
retaining fourteen checkpoints including Sūchéng.
Zhèjiāng set the likin donation on all goods at nine percent of value.
In Zhèdōng, there were "two checks and two inspections,"
with intermediate checkpoints collecting.
For goods worth one thousand cash,
thirty cash were collected at the first checkpoint,
half was reduced at the inspection checkpoint,
and if the donation was sufficient for "two checks and two inspections," it would not be collected again.
In Zhèxī, there was "one check and one inspection,"
collected by the first checkpoint,
and all others were for verification and release.
In the third year,
Zhílì established the Tiānjīn Shuāngmiào checkpoint.
Huáinán also established checkpoints to collect likin on private goods from neighbors.
Zhèjiāng set the silk tax.
Hénán, due to the disturbances by the Niǎn rebels,
suspended the Yǔzhōu líjuān,
but it was later restored.
At this time, Guān Wén, Governor-General of Húguǎng, said:
"The líjīn in provinces like Zhílì, Shāndōng, Shānxī, Hénán, Shǎn (Shǎnxī), Gān (Gānsù), Yún (Yúnnán), Guì (Guìzhōu), and Guǎngxī is not much,
and once military affairs are concluded,
its abolition can be discussed.
The líjīn in other southeastern provinces
should not be rashly abolished,
but kept as a fund for post-war rehabilitation."
Zēng Guófān, however, requested the suspension of Guǎngdōng líjīn upon the recapture of Jiāngníng.
The Emperor feared that military funds would be insufficient
and did not permit it.
In the fourth year,
the Húnán Dōngzhēngjú was abolished,
and the Jiāngběi General Bureau was renamed the Jīnlíng Líjuān General Bureau.
Fújiàn established the Shuìlí General Bureau,
collecting likin on all goods and tea.
In the sixth year,
Húběi retained eighty-six líjīn sub-bureaus and checkpoints after abolition.
Húnán merged its sub-bureaus,
collectively naming them the Líjīn Yánchá General Bureau.
In the seventh year,
it was stipulated that líjīn reports be submitted to the Board,
following the format of the Liǎnghuái salt líjīn,
twice a year.
At this time, as military affairs gradually settled,
governors-general, governors, and censors repeatedly suggested abolishing líjīn.
The Emperor ordered each province to retain major ones
and abolish scattered sub-bureaus.
Consequently, Húběi again abolished fifty-four bureaus and checkpoints,
and Zhèjiāng merged sixteen checkpoints.
In the eighth year,
Gānsù began levying likin donations on all goods, salt, and tea.
It was decided that in Guǎngdōng Shěngchéng (provincial capital) and flourishing places like Fóshān, Jiāngmén, and Chéncūn,
an additional "sitting likin" on all goods would be levied,
managed by merchants.
In the ninth year,
Guǎngxī reduced líjīn,
changing it to the "Western Tax."
In the tenth year,
following the advice of Censor Huáng Huáissēn,
the practice of "gang fees" (bāngfèi) by Guǎngdōng líjīn bureaus was prohibited and abolished,
and clerks were also purged.
Zhílì changed the Tiānjīnfǔ Donation and Righteousness Bureau (Juānshū Yìguǎn) to the Líjīn Bureau for All Goods,
establishing four sub-checkpoints: Dōnghé, Xīhé, Nánhé, and Hǎihé.
A foreign medicine líjīn bureau was also established at Dōngguān.
In the thirteenth year,
the Líjīn Bureau of Línyú Xiàn in Shānhǎiguān was abolished.
The Yálí General Bureau was established in Yúnnán Shěngchéng (provincial capital),
with twenty-three sub-bureaus in various prefectures,
and various well-salt líjīn bureaus.
In the first year of the Guāngxù reign,
Zhèjiāng again consolidated and eliminated fourteen *kǎ*,
leaving sixty-five *kǎ*.
The *líjīn* on rice and grain in Húběi was abolished.
In the second year,
Ānhuī implemented reforms.
The Wúhú and Fèngyáng customs posts separately abolished *líkǎ*,
permanently exempting the *líjīn* on rice and grain transported and sold within Húnán province.
For those transported out of the province,
the *líjīn* was still paid once at the first *kǎ*.
In the third year,
Shānxī suffered a great famine,
and commercial goods were unsellable.
The newly established branch *kǎ* along various routes were consolidated.
Jílín levied a seven percent goods tax at Shuāngchéngbǎo and Nóng'ānchéng.
In the fourth year,
Guìzhōu reduced its goods *líjīn* collection by 25 percent.
In the seventh year,
Grand Secretary Liú Ruìqí stated that the *líjuān* was of no benefit to the national economy,
and ordered various Governors-General and Governors to consider retaining a portion.
Shānxī, due to a reduction in *líjīn* collection,
reinstated various branch *kǎ*.
In the eighth year,
Jiāngnán and Yángzhōu abolished one branch *kǎ* and two patrol *kǎ*.
The Hùlí Bureau consolidated the Bùhuòjuān Bureau,
and the Mǐn-Guǎng Sānbāng Záhuòjuān Bureau along with the Dōnggōu Sìlíkǎ,
and also abolished the Gǔshān and Shuǐqiáo patrol *kǎ*.
The following year,
the Hù Bureau again abolished the Dōnggōu and Dàjīng patrol *kǎ*.
In the tenth year,
Shǎnxī abolished and retained twenty-eight *kǎ*.
In the thirteenth year,
Guìzhōu added twenty-five branch bureaus.
Previously, various provinces had bureaus and *kǎ* standing "like trees in a forest,"
harassing the people and harming merchants.
Though repeatedly ordered to consolidate,
Jiāngxī province alone still had over seventy bureaus.
Censor Zhèng Sīhè again spoke on the matter,
leading to a factual review and reduction.
In the twenty-third year,
the Ministry of Revenue memorialized, stating:
"The *lí* bureaus in various provinces are plagued by embezzlement,
the problem being that the officials in charge are unwilling to reveal everything.
In various provinces, expenses that are not normally allowed but are deemed necessary,
are often defrayed from *lí* taxes as 'subsistence funds,'
known as 'external expenses.'
The ministries and departments generally have records,
so it is not originally for personal enrichment.
However, once there are 'external expenses,'
there are also funds that are concealed from reporting.
Otherwise, how are they scraped together?
No wonder there is widespread public rumor,
all saying that the actual revenue of various provinces
is several times the amount reported to the Ministry.
Currently, the problem of embezzlement
has been addressed by an imperial edict ordering all Generals and Governors-General to earnestly rectify it,
so it should not continue as before.
However, if the amount of 'external expenses' is not fully disclosed,
this Ministry, which controls all expenditure,
will ultimately be unable to properly audit
income and expenditure for the year.
Even if the categories of 'external expenses' cannot be completely abolished immediately,
they should still be reported to this Ministry,
to weigh the urgency,
and with internal and external acting as one,
to overcome the current difficulties together.
It is proposed that the most essential categories of 'external expenses'
be clearly declared,
and a suitable amount be approved for expenditure,
to avoid inconveniencing public use.
If there is any further concealment after this,
or even the creation of clever pretexts,
falsely claiming income does not cover expenditure,
then the officials in charge
cannot escape blame."
This was submitted to the Grand Secretaries and court officials for discussion.
Two years later,
the Emperor adopted the officials' recommendations,
ordering all Generals and Governors-General to thoroughly audit,
determining how much of the illicit gains and embezzlement would be eliminated,
and how much would be appropriated for public use,
and to report within a deadline.
As for the categories of 'external expenses,'
they should be allowed to be itemized and reported to the Ministry,
to ensure verification.
Regarding all water and land main and branch bureaus and *kǎ*,
how they should be managed according to local conditions,
with both officials and gentry appointed,
should be observed and handled accordingly.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Jiāngxī Governor Kē Féngshí stated:
"The accumulated malpractices of the *lí* bureaus in Jiāngxī are too deep.
They should be reformed into a consolidated tax system,
where all goods that have paid the consolidated tax
and have stamps affixed,
will not be taxed again."
This was reported and heard.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
Sìchuān, in order to implement the prohibition of opium,
and to make up for various taxes and *lí* on native opium,
doubled the collection of meat *lí*,
which was approved.
In the second year,
Guìzhōu's Sānjiāng Lí Bureau was reformed into a Wood Consolidated Tax Bureau.
Shǎnxī's Hundred Goods Lí Tax was also reformed according to the consolidated tax method,
reduced to twenty-seven bureaus.
Foreign Opium.
In the early years of Dàoguāng,
large British ships moored year-round at Língdīngyáng, Dàyǔshān, and other places,
called "receiving ships" (*dǔnchuán*).
All who trafficked opium to Yuè (Guǎngdōng)
first unloaded it to the receiving ships,
before it entered.
The bulk buyers in the provincial capital called them *yáokǒu*.
Having agreed upon the price,
they would go together to the foreign ships to exchange currency and receive a voucher,
then hire fast boats to the receiving ships,
and take the opium upon presentation of the voucher.
These fast boats were called "fast crabs" (*kuàixiè*),
fully equipped with weapons and cannons,
traveling like flying,
and military ships could not pursue and capture them.
As it flowed into the interior,
the more it was prohibited, the more it increased.
Various other goods
were also often privately sold from the receiving ships.
The outflow of silver bullion
and the evasion of customs duties
mostly resulted from this.
Repeated imperial edicts ordered their expulsion and strict apprehension,
but the receiving ships continued to moor and the "fast crabs" continued to smuggle as before.
In the eighteenth year,
Hónglú Qīng Huáng Juézī stated:
"Since opium entered China,
corrupt merchants in Yuè colluded with naval officers and soldiers,
transporting silver out of the country
and transporting opium into the country.
It was found that in the early years of Dàoguāng,
several million taels of silver were leaked annually;
before the fourteenth year,
over twenty million taels were leaked annually;
in recent years, over thirty million taels were leaked annually.
In addition, combining other seaports, it amounted to tens of millions.
Year after year,
where will this end?
The large amount of silver depletion
is due to the flourishing opium trade.
The flourishing opium trade
is due to the large number of opium smokers.
To truly prohibit it,
the penalties should be made heavier."
The Emperor approved his words,
and specifically appointed Lín Zéxú as Imperial Commissioner,
to go to Yuè to investigate and handle the matter.
The following year,
over 20,880 chests of opium from receiving ships were intercepted,
and burned.
At that time, regulations for opium prohibition were set,
stating that anyone who opened *yáokǒu* or opium dens,
or engaged in trafficking or consumption,
whether Chinese or foreign,
would all be sentenced to capital punishment.
In the second year of Xuāntǒng,
the Dùzhī Bù (Board of Revenue) memorialized, saying:
"The collection of native opium tax has decreased in various provinces,
and the branch offices for the consolidated native opium tax in Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Shāndōng, and Shānxī have been successively abolished.
As for the two Hú provinces (Húbĕi and Húnán), Shănxī, Gānsù, and the two Yuè provinces (Guǎngdōng and Guǎngxī),
there is still a small amount of revenue,
which should be promptly wound up.
However, whether a tax bureau should be abolished
is determined by whether there are tax items to collect,
and whether the consolidated tax should be suspended
is measured by whether the land produces opium."
Thereupon, clerks were dispatched
to various provinces for investigation.
The following year,
it was again memorialized, saying:
"Although it is currently proposed to abolish the native opium consolidated tax branch offices,
the method agreed upon by the various provinces
for dispatching personnel to take over has not yet been reported.
However, regarding the import of foreign opium,
a treaty has already been concluded with Britain,
where both tax and líjīn are levied.
An additional two hundred and fifty liǎng are collected per hundred liǎng.
Native opium must also be proportionally taxed at the same time.
It is found that the value of native opium is less than two-thirds of foreign opium.
If the purpose of the tax is to prohibit,
the tax may be slightly heavier.
Calculating based on the foreign opium tax,
it is decided to levy an additional two hundred and thirty liǎng for every hundred jīn of native opium.
Wherever transportation is not yet prohibited, or where it is produced and sold locally,
this will be collected according to the new regulations."
This was adopted.
At that time, it had been agreed with Britain
that opium prohibition would be progressively reduced,
and three years had already passed.
If, within the remaining seven-year period,
native opium was completely prohibited,
then the import of foreign opium would also be prohibited.
With the implementation of the additional tax on foreign opium,
various other levies were to be stopped.
Accounts. In the early part of Shùnzhì's reign,
the three levies of the late Míng dynasty had been abolished.
The southern provinces were not yet fully pacified,
so annual revenue was initially small.
However, years of warfare,
managing affairs in all directions,
and constant provisions were immense,
making annual expenditures even greater.
By the ninth year,
the realm was largely pacified.
Annual revenue from land and poll taxes amounted to over twenty-one million two hundred and sixty thousand liǎng of silver,
salt taxes yielded over two million one hundred and twelve thousand liǎng of silver,
customs duties and other silver amounted to over one million liǎng,
and taxes in kind (rice, wheat, and beans) totaled over five million six hundred and twenty thousand dàn.
Annual expenditures included over thirteen million liǎng for military pay across various routes,
over two million liǎng for stipends of princes and officials, and other expenses,
and over three million liǎng for provincial retained expenses such as courier stations.
Subsequently, military pay increased to twenty-four million liǎng,
and land and poll taxes also reached over twenty-five million liǎng.
In the early part of Kāngxī's reign,
the Revolt of the Three Feudatories occurred.
Annual revenue from land and poll taxes
decreased from over twenty-six million to over twenty-one million.
In the twenty-first year,
the Three Feudatories were suppressed.
Annual revenue from land and poll taxes again reached over twenty-six million three hundred and forty thousand liǎng of silver,
salt tax silver also reached over two million seven hundred and sixty thousand liǎng,
customs duties and other silver amounted to over two million liǎng,
and taxes in kind (rice, wheat, and beans) amounted to over six million three hundred and forty thousand dàn.
In the early part of Yōngzhèng's reign,
the Dùzhī Bù was reformed,
and revenue significantly increased.
By the thirty-first year of Qiánlóng,
annual revenue from land and poll taxes was over twenty-nine million nine hundred and eleven thousand liǎng,
from hàoxiàn (wastage allowance) over three million liǎng,
from salt taxes over five million seven hundred and seventy-four thousand liǎng,
from customs duties over five million four hundred thousand liǎng,
from reed and fishing taxes over one hundred and forty thousand liǎng,
from tea taxes over seventy thousand liǎng,
from land transactions and miscellaneous taxes over eight hundred and fifty thousand liǎng,
from deed taxes over one hundred and ninety thousand liǎng,
from brokerage and pawnshop taxes over one hundred and sixty thousand liǎng,
from mining taxes with fixed quotas over eighty thousand liǎng,
and from customary contributions over three million liǎng.
This constituted a grand total of over forty million liǎng in annual revenue,
excluding interest on foreign sales and various allocated contributions.
Annual expenditures included over seventeen million liǎng for Manchu and Hàn military pay,
over nine hundred thousand liǎng for stipends of princes and officials,
over one hundred and twenty thousand liǎng for stipends of frontier princes,
over three million four hundred and seventy thousand liǎng for yǎnglían (integrity-fostering stipends) for civil officials,
over eight hundred thousand liǎng for yǎnglían for military officials,
over one hundred and forty thousand liǎng for public expenses and meals in various central government yámen,

five hundred and sixty thousand liǎng for the Nèiwù Fǔ (Imperial Household Department), Gōngbù (Board of Works), Tàicháng Sì (Court of Imperial Sacrifices), Guānglù Sì (Court of Imperial Entertainments), and Lǐfān Yuàn (Court of Colonial Affairs) for sacrifices and guest provisions,
over one hundred and twenty thousand liǎng for purchasing pigments, timber, copper, and cloth,
over one hundred and forty thousand liǎng for weaving,
over one hundred thousand liǎng for materials and labor at the Bǎoquán and Bǎoyuán Mints,
over eighty thousand liǎng for salaries of clerks and yamen runners in various central government yámen,
over eighty thousand liǎng for fodder for official horses, cattle, sheep, and elephants in the capital,
over three million eight hundred thousand liǎng for annual repairs of the Eastern and Southern Rivers,
and over six million liǎng for various provincial retained expenses such as courier stations, sacrifices, ceremonial expenses, official stipends and staff salaries, examination hall provisions, etc.
Not all of this was spent annually.
An additional sum of approximately one million two hundred thousand liǎng was annually required for grain transport boats.
This constituted a grand total of over thirty million liǎng in annual expenditures,
excluding the unfixed amounts for annual stipends and allowances for imperial clansmen, and various expenses for banner troops in grain transport,
and provincial foreign sales.
From this period until the end of Dàoguāng's reign,
the expenditures for military supplies, river works, disaster relief, and indemnities,
as well as the opening of various precedents,
and the allocated collection from salt merchants' contributions for river works,
all constituted large sums for irregular income and irregular expenditures.
These amounts were all significant.
However, the fixed annual revenue and expenditure
still followed the old system of Qiánlóng.
Thus, in the fifty-sixth year of Qiánlóng,
annual revenue was forty-three million five hundred and ninety thousand liǎng of silver,
and annual expenditure was thirty-one million seven hundred and seventy thousand liǎng of silver.
In the seventeenth year of Jiāqìng,
annual revenue was forty million thirteen thousand liǎng of silver,
and annual expenditure was thirty-five million ten thousand liǎng of silver.
In the twenty-second year of Dàoguāng,
annual revenue was thirty-seven million fourteen thousand liǎng of silver,
and annual expenditure was thirty-one million fifty thousand liǎng of silver,
all with odd amounts.
In the early part of Xiánfēng's reign,
the Yuè Fĕi (Taiping Rebellion) suddenly arose,
followed by the Niǎn and Huí (rebels),
causing a great deficit in state finances.
By Tóngzhì,
the main sources of annual revenue
had shifted to líjīn and foreign customs duties,
while the major items of annual expenditure
were for post-war reconstruction and defense preparations.
In the eighth month of the fifth year of Guāngxù,
Wáng Xiānqiān, a Shìdú of the Hànlín Yuàn, memorialized:
"Of the old revenue sources,
such as land and poll taxes, miscellaneous taxes, salt administration miscellaneous funds, etc.,
which totaled forty million,
only twenty-seven to twenty-eight million are now collected.
Of the new revenue sources,
there are twelve million from foreign customs duties
and three million from salt líjīn.
Of the old expenditures,
such as military pay, river works, capital tribute, and provincial retained expenses totaling forty million,
only twenty-four to twenty-five million are now spent.
New expenditures include
approximately ten million for the Western Expedition and Tiānjīn Defense armies,
and approximately ten million for provincial defense armies."
In the 17th year,
the Ministry of Revenue presented a revised plan for annual expenditures and revenues,
based on the detailed ledger of annual expenditures and revenues from the 7th year of the Guāngxù reign.
It stated:
“As the ministry responsible for the aggregate of money and grain,
formerly, expenditures and revenues had fixed quotas.
Revenue sources were merely land tax (dìdīng), customs duties (guānshuì), salt tax (yánkè), and surcharges (hàoxiàn)—a few items;
expenditures were merely capital sustenance (jīngxiǎng), military pay (bīngxiǎng), retained funds (cúnliú), and allocated aid (xiébō)—a few matters,
which was most concise.
However, since the military campaigns began,
expenditures and revenues could not follow the established system.
Revenue items such as deductions for regularization (kòuchéng), reductions for equalization (jiǎnpíng), remittances (tíjiě), and refunds (tuìhuí)
were all derived from expenditures.
Expenditure items such as supplementary allocations (bōbǔ), repayment arrangements (chóuhuán), transfers (yíjiě), and reserve funds (liúbèi)
were all returned to revenue items.
Consolidating them was truly not easy.
The ledgers handled this time

took land tax (dìdīng), miscellaneous levies (záfù), land rent (dìzū), grain commutation (liángzhé), grain transport commutation (cáozhé), grain transport items (cáoxiàng), surcharges (hàoxiàn), salt tax (yánkè), regular taxes (chángshuì), and interest (shēngxī) as ten items for regular collection;
likin (líjīn), foreign customs duties (yángshuì), new customs duties (xīnguānshuì), and grain-based subsidies (ànliángjīntiē) as four items for new collection;
and continued payments (xùwán), donations (juānshū), paid contributions (wánjiǎo), and deducted savings (jiékòu) as four items for this year's receipts.
Excluding various amounts exempted, deferred, or unpaid,
the total actual silver revenue collected was 82,349,198 liǎng,
which constituted the silver receipts.

It took imperial tomb provisions (língqǐn gōngyìng), silver remitted to the capital (jiāojìn yín), sacrifices (jìsì), ceremonial expenses (yíxiàn), stipends and rations (fèngshí), examination expenses (kēchǎng), military dry rations (xiǎnggān), postal stations (yìzhàn), granary rations (lǐnshàn), rewards and pensions (shǎngxù), repairs (xiūshàn), river works (hé gōng), procurement (cǎibàn), grain transport management (bàncáo), textile manufacturing (zhīzào), integrity and frugality (gōnglián), and miscellaneous expenses (zázhī) as seventeen items for regular expenditure;
military and auxiliary forces' payroll (yíngyǒng xiǎngxū), customs bureaus (guānjú), foreign funds (yángkuǎn), and loan repayments with interest (huánjiè xīkuǎn) as four items for new expenditures;
supplementary payments for old arrears
and advance disbursements as two items for supplementary and advance expenditures;
and remittances to various yámen in the capital as one item for remitted expenditures.
Excluding various amounts unpaid or unreported,
the total actual silver expenditure disbursed was 78,171,451 liǎng,
which constituted the silver disbursements.
The original memorial also covered cash receipts, grain receipts, cash disbursements, and grain disbursements,
which was truly clear and verifiable.
Now, according to the ledgers of annual revenue and expenditure for the 17th year,
revenue items were: land tax (dìdīng) 23,666,911 liǎng,
miscellaneous levies (záfù) 2,810,144 liǎng,
rent and interest (zūxī) 141,672 liǎng,
grain commutation (liángzhé) 4,262,928 liǎng,
surcharges (hàoxiàn) 3,004,887 liǎng,
salt tax (yánkè) 7,427,605 liǎng,
regular taxes (chángshuì) 2,558,410 liǎng,
likin (líjīn) 16,316,821 liǎng,
foreign customs duties (yángshuì) 18,206,777 liǎng,
deducted savings (jiékòu) 2,964,944 liǎng,
continued payments (xùwán) 7,128,744 liǎng,
donations and contributions (juānjiǎo) 1,875,576 liǎng,
all with odd amounts.
The total annual revenue was 89,684,800 liǎng and odd.
Expenditure items were: imperial tomb provisions (língqǐn gōngyìng) and other items totaling 130,559 liǎng,
remittances to the capital (jiāojìn) 180,000 liǎng,
sacrifices (jìsì) 336,733 liǎng,
ceremonial expenses (yíxiàn) 74,879 liǎng,
stipends and rations (fèngshí) 3,841,424 liǎng,
examination expenses (kēchǎng) 105,270 liǎng,
military dry rations (xiǎnggān) 20,356,159 liǎng,
postal stations (yìzhàn) 1,734,709 liǎng,
granary rations (lǐnshàn) 112,029 liǎng,
rewards and pensions (shǎngxù) 525,216 liǎng,
repairs (xiūshàn) 2,209,748 liǎng,
procurement (cǎibàn) 4,033,903 liǎng,
textile manufacturing (zhīzào) 1,034,915 liǎng,
integrity and frugality (gōnglián) 4,575,783 liǎng,
miscellaneous expenses (zázhī) 303,278 liǎng,
auxiliary forces' payroll (yǒngxiǎng) 18,268,313 liǎng,
customs bureaus' expenses (guānjú jīngfèi) 3,144,616 liǎng,
foreign funds (yángkuǎn) 3,861,051 liǎng,
supplementary payments (bǔzhī) 12,775,525 liǎng,
advance disbursements (yùzhī) 1,742,073 liǎng,
various expenses for food and supplies remitted to capital yámen (jiě Jīng gè yámén fànshí jīngfèi gèxiàng zhīkuǎn) 3,472,533 liǎng.
The total annual expenditure was 79,355,241 liǎng.”
Three more years passed, it was the Jiǎwǔ year (1894),
the Joseon (Cháoxiǎn) war erupted,
military expenditures were enormous,
and foreign and merchant loans were incurred.
After peace was settled,
loans were again taken from Russia (É), France (Fǎ), Britain (Yīng), and Germany (Dé) to pay Japan's (Rìběn) indemnity,
increasing the apportioned silver from various provinces and customs by 12,000,000 liǎng,
further augmented by principal and interest from various loans like HSBC (Huìfēng), Kassa (Kèsà), and Chinese merchants (Huáshāng),
as well as new military pay for Sòng Qìng and others,
totaling 8,000,000.
Thus, annual expenditures increased by 20,000,000 over the previous amount.
By the Gēngzǐ year (1900),
military disaster again brewed.
When the Xīnchǒu Protocol was concluded,
there was a huge sum of 450,000,000,
of which over 18,000,000 liǎng was allocated to the various provinces.
In the 29th year,
for training new armies,
training expenses were again apportioned to the provinces,
and as the provinces began to train new armies,
and manage police and education,
they also had funds to raise locally.
The police expenses for Fèngtiān province alone reached over 3,000,000 liǎng.
Húběi province allocated 600,000 liǎng from the money price of its land tax (dìdīng qiánjià) to fund education.
The system of donations (juānlì) was halted in the 27th year,
reopened for military training,
and then halted again in the 32nd year.
New revenue sources added after the Gēngzǐ year
were largely grain donations (liángjuān),

such as additional donations based on grain (ànliáng jiājuān), restoration of collected land tax and grain transport money prices (guīfù zhēngshōu dīngcáo qiánjià), restoration of corvée (guīfù chāiyáo), and additional surcharges (jiāshōu hàoxiàn);

salt donations (yánjuān) such as increased price per catty of salt (yánjīn jiājià), additional tax on salt certificates (yányǐn jiākè), additional tax on local salt (tǔyán jiāshuì), and port donations for salt trade (xíngyán kǒujuān);

official donations (guānjuān) such as officials' voluntary contributions (guānyuán bàoxiào), discretionary appropriation of surplus from land tax and grain transport (zhuótí dīngcáo yíngyú), and discretionary appropriation of surplus from good and poor posts (zhuótí yōuquē yíngyú);

additional likin and taxes (jiālì jiāshuì) such as additional likin and tax on tobacco, alcohol, and native opium (yānjǐu tǔyào zhī jiālì shuì), conversion of various goods tax to consolidated tax (bǎihuò shuì zhī gǎitǒngjuān), and additional levy on transfer deeds (shuìqì jiāzhēng);
miscellaneous donations (zájuān) such as lottery donations (cǎipiào juān), shop donations (fángpù juān), fishing household donations (yúhù juān), and entertainment household donations (lèhù juān);

savings (jiéshěng) such as cuts to Green Standard Army stipends and rations (cáijié lǜyíng fèngxiǎng), savings in river works expenses (jiéshěng hé gōng jīngfèi), auditing and deducting postal station expenses (hékòu yìzhàn jīngfèi), and savings in various government office expenses (jiéshěng gè shǔjú jīngfèi);
and industrial enterprises (shíyè) such as railway (tiělù), telegraph office (diànjú), and postal (yóuzhèng) income,
as well as surplus profits from banks (yínháng), silver and copper coin bureaus (yín tóngyuán jú), and government-run factories and commercial bureaus (guānbàn gōngchǎng shāngjú).
Besides indemnities, military training expenses, and costs for education, police, and judiciary,
new expenses for various government offices also constituted a major portion of expenditures.
In the second year of Xuāntǒng,
the Dùzhī Bù proposed a trial budget for the third year of Xuāntǒng.

In December,
the Zīzhèng Yuàn reviewed and approved,
with increases to revenue
and reductions to expenditure.
The following year saw a change in the form of government,
hence there was a budget but no final accounts.
From the thirty-third year of Guāngxù,
the Dùzhī Bù had already memorialized and received approval to instruct central government offices in Jīngshī and all provinces to report their actual annual revenues and expenditures,
and also established finance supervisors in each province to oversee them.
All funds previously disbursed externally,
along with various irregular donations and illicit levies,
and newly established expenses for education, justice, industry, military administration, and foreign debt,
were all entered into account books and periodically reported.
Thus, the income and expenditure were more than ten times that of Shùnzhì and Kāngxī.
This is recorded here to show the gains and losses of a dynasty's finances.
Among the large expenditures for military provisions, river conservancy, relief efforts, and indemnities:
The first Jīnchuān campaign in the early years of Qiánlóng:
over 20 million taels.
The Zhuǎnhuí campaign:
over 33 million taels.
The Myanmar campaign:
over 9 million taels.
The second Jīnchuān campaign:
over 70 million taels.
The Guō'ěrkā campaign:
10.52 million taels.
The Táiwān campaign:
over 8 million taels.
The Jiāqìng campaign against sectarian rebels in Chuān, Hú, and Shǎn:
200 million taels.
The Hóng Miáo campaign:
Húnán province requested to write off 10.9 million taels.
The campaign against foreign bandits:
Guǎngdōng province requested to write off 3 million taels.
The first Huíjiāng campaign in the early years of Dàoguāng:
over 11 million taels.
The second Huíjiāng campaign:
7.3 million taels.
The British campaign:
over 10 million taels.
The campaign against Cantonese rebels in the early years of Xiánfēng:
27 million taels.
Thereafter, the Jiāngnán Grand Army needed 500,000 taels per month,
and the Huī-Níng defense camps needed 300,000 taels per month,
making it 10 million taels per year.
Húběi supplied the needs of the eastern expedition,
over 4 million per year,
and Húnán's contribution was also considerable.
The costs of military campaigns in the northern route and southwestern provinces were not included.
In the middle of Tóngzhì,
Zēng Guófān memorialized for the fourth and fifth cases of the Xiāng Army,
combined with military provisions for suppressing the Niǎn rebels,
totaling over 30 million taels.
Lǐ Hóngzhāng memorialized for the first and second cases of Sū-Hù,
combined with the two cases of the Huái Army's western expedition,
totaling over 17 million taels.
Zuǒ Zōngtáng memorialized for the two cases of the western expedition,
totaling over 48.2 million taels.
In addition, there were military provisions for Fújiàn's aid to Zhèjiāng,
combined with military provisions for its own province and Táiwān,
which by the third year, sixth month,
had exceeded 6 million taels.
Sìchuān and Húnán's aid to Guìzhōu's military provisions
were about 4 million taels per year,
accumulating to 20 million taels over five years.
Yúnnán, from the second year of Tóngzhì to the twelfth year of Tóngzhì,
requested to write off over 14.6 million taels in military provisions.
And in Gānsù, officials, gentry, merchants, and commoners collectively donated over
50 million taels of silver and grain for military provisions.
Adding the various provincial expanded quotas,
the total would not be less than hundreds of millions.
In the middle of Guāngxù,
only the Sino-French War cost over 30 million taels.
As for the funds for the western expedition
and coastal defense,
these were already included in the annual expenditures
and no longer listed separately.
River conservancy works
became increasingly crucial for the Southern River (Nánhé) starting in the middle of the Kāngxī reign.
The major repair project in the sixteenth year
cost 2.5 million liǎng of silver.
The initial estimate was 6 million liǎng.
Later, the project at Xiāojiādù
cost 1.2 million liǎng of silver.
From the eighteenth year of Qiánlóng,
due to the breaches at Gāoyóu, Shàobó, and Chēluóbà on the Nánhé,
2 million liǎng of silver were allocated.
In the forty-fourth year,
to block the breach at Yífēng,
5.6 million liǎng of silver were allocated.
In the forty-seventh year,
to block the breach at Lányáng,
beyond the conventionally required materials and labor,
the price was increased to 9.453 million liǎng.
For the repair of the sea wall in Zhèjiāng,
over 6 million liǎng of silver were allocated.
For the repair of the dikes along the Jiāng River in Jīngzhōu,
2 million liǎng of silver were allocated.
Generally, for a major project,
the cost was often over 10 million,
and at least several million.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
for instance, the cost for the Héng project increased to 7.3 million liǎng.
From the tenth to the fifteenth year,
the annual maintenance, emergency repairs, and other special projects on the Nánhé
totaled 49.9 million liǎng of silver,
not including the major project at Mǎjiāgǎng.
In the twentieth year, upon completion of the Suī project,
the cost increased to over 3 million liǎng.
During the Dàoguāng reign,
beyond the annual maintenance for the Eastern River (Dōnghé) and Nánhé,
for other special projects,
the Dōnghé generally received over 1.5 million liǎng,
and the Nánhé generally received over 2.7 million liǎng.
Over ten years, this amounted to over 40 million.
In the sixth year,
silver for the Wángyíng dam construction and weirs, and the large dikes at Xū on the Nánhé,
totaled 5.17 million liǎng.
In the twenty-first year,
5.5 million liǎng of silver were allocated for the Xiáng project on the Dōnghé.
In the twenty-second year,
6 million liǎng were allocated for the Yáng project on the Nánhé.
In the twenty-third year,
5.18 million liǎng were allocated for the Móu project on the Dōnghé,
with further additions later.
In the early Xiánfēng reign,
the Fēng project also received over 4 million liǎng.
During the Tóngzhì reign,
Shāndōng had the Hóu project and the Jiǎzhuāng projects,
costing over 2 million liǎng.
In the thirteenth year of Guāngxù,
the major project at Zhèngzhōu in Hénán
requested 12 million liǎng.
Afterward, Shāndōng frequently experienced river overflows,
but the expenditure was less than one-tenth of that during Dàoguāng.
For relief efforts,
during the Kāngxī reign,
to relieve the disaster in Shǎnxī,
over 5 million liǎng of silver were used.
In the seventh year of Qiánlóng,
due to major summer and autumn floods in Jiāngsū and Ānhuī,
for relief, official relief, and additional relief,
Jiāngsū provided over 1.56 million dàn of rice to affected soldiers and civilians,
and over 5.05 million liǎng of silver.
Ānhuī provided over 830,000 dàn of rice to affected soldiers and civilians,
and over 2.33 million liǎng of silver.
In the eighteenth year,
due to the breach of the Gāoyóu Canal,
1.1 million dàn of rice and grain,
and 4 million liǎng of silver were allocated
to relieve the disaster in Jiāngsū.
This was the largest sum.
Later, for disasters in Zhílì, Shāndōng, Jiāngsū, Hénán, Húběi, and Gānsù provinces,
funds were disbursed from the treasury, grain transport was diverted, and donations were solicited,
too numerous to list.
In the early Jiāqìng reign,
for disasters in Cáo and Shàn counties of Shāndōng,
the total relief in silver and rice amounted to 3 to 4 million liǎng.
In the sixth year,
due to floods in Zhílì,
1 million liǎng of relief silver were allocated,
and 600,000 dàn of grain transport were diverted.
For disaster relief in Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Shāndōng, and Hénán provinces,
successive expenditures from the treasury
each amounted to no less than several hundred thousand to millions.
Funds from donations,
such as for the disasters in Jiāngsū and Ānhuī in the nineteenth year,
reached 2 to 3 million liǎng.
In the eleventh year of Dàoguāng,
over 1 million liǎng of silver were allocated for relief in Jiāngsū.
In the twenty-seventh year,
over 1 million liǎng of silver were used for relief in Hénán.
In the twenty-eighth year,
1.38 million liǎng of silver were used for relief in Hébĕi.
In the twenty-ninth year,
1 million liǎng of silver were allocated for disaster relief in Jiāngsū and three other provinces.
Meanwhile, Ānhuī and Zhèjiāng retained funds for relief efforts,
each close to 1 million,
and Jiāngsū alone retained over 1.4 million.
Besides these, there were many more,
not including donations from officials, gentry, merchants, and common people.
In the early Guāngxù reign,
for disasters in Shānxī, Hénán, and Shǎnxī,
allocations from the treasury and diverted grain transport were substantial,
and the total of official relief, charitable relief, and donated silver
was no less than several tens of millions of liǎng.
When the river breached at Zhèngzhōu,
relief for Hénán cost over 2.5 million liǎng of silver.
At that time, whenever various provinces suffered from floods or droughts,
requests were made to initiate donation drives for relief.
Zhílì, from the floods in the sixteenth year to the tsunami in the twenty-first year,
spent over 7 million liǎng of silver.
Shāndōng, from the eleventh year onwards,
experienced annual river overflows,
and by the twenty-fifth year,
spent over 7 million liǎng of silver.
Jiāngsū, from the floods in the fifteenth year to the disasters in Huái, Xú, and Hǎi in the twenty-fourth year,
spent over 5 million liǎng of silver.
For the disasters in Qín and Jìn in the twenty-seventh year,
donations from actual officials were opened to aid,
amounting to over 7.6 million liǎng.
Indemnities
began with the Jiāngníng Treaty in Dàoguāng Rén Yín,
for 21 million liǎng.
The treaty of Xiánfēng Gēng Shēn,
16 million liǎng.
The Yīlí Treaty of Guāngxù Xīn Sì,
over 6 million liǎng.
The Sino-Japanese Treaty of Yǐ Wèi,
including the return of Liáonán,
230 million liǎng.
Finally, the Xīn Chǒu Protocol
peaked at an indemnity of 450 million liǎng.
Calculated with interest,
it actually amounted to over 900 million liǎng.
Regarding the amount of land tax collected during the Qīng dynasty,
in the thirty-first year of Qiánlóng,
it was over 8.3177 million dàn of grain.
Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Shāndōng, Hénán, Zhèjiāng, Jiāngxī, Húběi, and Húnán eight provinces,
besides the annual grain transport to the capital,
retained funds for provincial expenses.
Zhílì, Fèngtiān, Shānxī, Shǎnxī, Gānsù, Fújiàn, Sìchuān, Guǎngdōng, Guǎngxī, Yúnnán, and Guìzhōu entirely used the collections for provincial expenses.
In the tenth year of Guāngxù,
Xīnjiāng was converted into a province,
annually collecting over 271,000 dàn of grain,
which was also entirely used for provincial expenses.
Jílín and Hēilóngjiāng, which collected rice, did the same.
Officials and soldiers of the Banner Garrisons and Green Standard Army soldiers in various provinces all received monthly rice.
All funds retained for provincial expenses
were largely used to supply the monthly rice and beans for the Banner and Green Standard armies.
Any surplus was reported for sale in exchange for silver, awaiting allocation, it is said.
Monograph 101, Rivers and Canals, Yellow River
The Yellow River's troubles
have been well-documented throughout history.
The Qīng dynasty, from its beginning, prioritized river management,
exploring the river's source to understand the root of the water calamity.
Early in the reign of Shèngzǔ,
he ordered the Imperial Bodyguard Lāxī to find the river's source.
He reached Èdūntǎlā,
which is Xīngxiùhǎi.
Gāozōng later sent the Imperial Bodyguard Āmǐdá,
who traveled three hundred *lǐ* west beyond Xīngxiù
and found it at Ālèitǎn Gádásūlǎo Shān.
No ancient exploration of the river's source
was as detailed and accurate as this.
However, this was still the upper source.
As for its primary source,
it emerges from Cōnglíng,
consistent with the *Hàn Shū*.
It flows eastward as the Kāshígáěr Hé,
then further east converges with the Yèěrqiāng and Hétián rivers,
forming the Tǎlǐmù Hé,
which empties into Luóbùnàor.
It then flows southeast, underground through sandy deserts for fifteen hundred *lǐ*,
re-emerging as the Ālèitǎn Hé.
When this subterranean flow first appears,
it often has a golden color,
and the Mongols call gold
"Ālèitǎn,"
hence its name.
This is the river's secondary source.
It flows northeast, joining the waters of Xīngxiùhǎi,
traveling two thousand seven hundred *lǐ*,
reaching Hézhōu Jīshíguān to enter China proper.
Flowing through mountains,
it cannot cause great harm.
Once it emerges from Lóngmén,
eastward of Xíngyáng,
the land is flat and wide,
relying solely on dikes for containment.
However, those who managed it often disregarded the water's nature,
defied its势,
contending with the water for land,
and even exploiting it for profit,
leading to frequent breaches,
immeasurable expense and effort,
and untold suffering.
Since Lǐ Zìchéng breached the river to flood Biànliáng at the end of the Míng dynasty's Chóngzhēn era,
it was repeatedly blocked and breached thereafter.
In the summer of Shùnzhì first year (1644),
the Yellow River returned to its old course,
passing through Kāifēng, then Lán, Yí, Shāng, Yú,
and reaching Cáo, Dān, Dàngshān, Fēng, Pèi, Xiāo, Xúzhōu, Língbì, Suīníng, Pī, Sùqiān, Táoyuán,
then eastward through Qīnghé to merge with the Huái,
and entering the sea via Yúntīguān.
In autumn,
it breached at Wēnxiàn.
The Emperor appointed Yáng Fāngxīng, a scholar of the Inner Secretariat, as Director-General of River Affairs,
stationed at Jìníng.
In the summer of the second year (1645),
it breached at Kǎochéng,
and again at Wángjiāyuán.
Fāngxīng stated:
"Since the invasion by the Chǔang rebels,
officials have fled and laborers have scattered;
there has been no one to guard.
During the autumn and spring floods,
Xiǎosòng and Cáojiākǒu on the north bank were entirely breached,
and many fields and dwellings south of Jìníng were submerged.
It is advisable, while the water level is slightly lower,
to urgently recruit workers and build."
The Emperor ordered the Board of Works to select officials to investigate, discuss, and assist in construction.
In July,
it breached at Liútōngjí,
one branch heading towards Cáo, Dān, and Nányáng to enter the Grand Canal,
another towards Tǎérwān and Wèijiāwān,
silting up the canal route,
and the lower reaches at Xú, Pī, and Huáiyáng also suffered many breaches.
That year, the river near Hǎizǐ Cūn to Dùkǒu Cūn in Mèngxiàn was clear for two days.
An imperial edict conferred the title "Xiǎnyòu Tōngjì Jīnlóng Sì Dàwáng" upon the River God,
and ordered river officials to offer sacrifices.
The following year,
Liútōngjí was blocked,
and the entire river flowed downstream,
its current turbulent,
breaching at Wénshàng and entering Shǔshānhú.
In the fifth year (1648),
it breached at Lányáng.
In August of the seventh year (1650),
it breached at Jīnglóng Zhūyuánzhài,
flowing directly to Shāwān,
breaking the canal dikes,
and carrying the Wèn River into the sea via Dàqīnghé.
Fāngxīng, following the advice of river official Fāng Dàyóu,
first built a long, continuous dike upstream
to check the incoming current,
then built smaller long dikes.
In the eighth year (1651),
it was blocked.
In the ninth year (1652),
it breached at Fēngqiū Dàwáng Miào,
destroying the county seat,
the water flowing from Chángyuán towards Dōngchāng,
damaging the Píngān Dī,
and entering the sea to the north,
greatly obstructing the grain transport canal.
Tens of thousands of laborers were dispatched to manage it,
but it breached as soon as it was built.
Staff Supervisor Xǔ Zuòméi,
Censor Yáng Shìxué, and Chén Fěi submitted memorials urging an investigation into the ancient course of the Jiǔ Hé
to allow the river north of the Yellow River to flow into the sea.
Fāngxīng stated:
"The Yellow River has been a common affliction throughout history,
but river management methods have varied historically.
Before the Sòng dynasty, river management
only ensured a path to the sea,
which could be either south or north.
From the Yuán and Míng dynasties up to our current dynasty,
the grain transport in the southeast,
from Qīngkǒu to Dǒngkǒu, over two hundred *lǐ*,
must rely on the Yellow River for transit.
Therefore, managing the river is managing the grain transport;
it can only go south, not north.
If the water were allowed to flow north,
not only would grain transport be cut off,
but there is also fear that the breached water would rush east and west,
becoming uncontrollable.
Now to seek Yǔ's old traces
and extensively dredge it again
would necessarily require building new long dikes,
the difficulty of which, compared to raising low areas and strengthening weak ones,
is clear.
Moreover, the river carries sand;
if confined to one channel,
the water will be swift and carry sand;
if dispersed into nine,
the water will be slow and deposit sand.
After a few years,
the river will again change course,
how then can it benefit transport?"
The Emperor agreed with his words,
and so a channel was dug at Dīngjiāzhài to divert the flow
and reduce the water's force.
That year,
it breached again at Pīzhōu,
and again at Xiángfú Zhūyuánzhài.
Assistant Minister of the Board of Revenue Wáng Yǒngjí and Censor Yáng Shìxué both stated:
"To manage the Yellow River, one must first manage the Huái River;
to guide the Huái, one must first guide its sea outlets,
for the Huái is the lower reach of the Yellow River,
and the coastal prefectures and counties are the lower reaches of the Huái.
We humbly request that high officials for river and grain transport affairs
be ordered to thoroughly dredge any sea outlets that have been blocked by corrupt people.
The canal dikes and sluice gates should be opened and closed according to the season,
and then the work should proceed upstream along the flow.
As for the river itself,
it should be cleared of shallows and silt,
making the river deeper,
sufficient to hold the water."
None of these proposals were implemented.
In the eleventh year (1654),
it breached Dàwáng Miào again.
Staff Supervisor Lín Qǐlóng impeached Fāngxīng for embezzlement,
and the Emperor relieved Fāngxīng of his post,
sending Grand Justice Wú Kùlǐ and Left Staff Supervisor of the Board of Works Xǔ Zuòméi to investigate.
Qǐlóng was found to have made false accusations,
and Fāngxīng was reinstated.
In the thirteenth year (1656),
Dàwáng Miào was blocked,
at a cost of eight hundred thousand *liǎng* of silver.
In the fourteenth year,
Fāng Xīng begged for retirement,
and Zhū Zhīxī, then Left Vice-Minister of the Ministry of Personnel, replaced him.
In this year, the Huái Gēdān at Xiángfú was cut through,
and then immediately dammed.
In the fifteenth year,
Yáo Jiāwān at Yángchái Gōu was cut through,
and then immediately dammed.
The Mùjiā Lóu at Yángwǔ was cut through again.
In the sixteenth year,
the Guīrén Dī was cut through.
Before this, Censor Sūn Kěhuà had submitted a memorial discussing the dike works of the Huái and Huáng rivers,
and the matter was referred to the Governor-General of River Conservancy.
Zhīxī said:
"The Fèijiā Zuǐ at Táoyuán and the Wǔkǒu at Āndōng have been silted up for a long time;
the work required is extensive and the cost immense.
Moreover, the Yellow River is proverbially called 'the Divine River,'
and there is no guarantee that it will not silt up again immediately after being dredged.
The only recourse is to put more effort into repair and defense,
and to redress defects and alleviate problems."
Zhīxī presented the advantages and disadvantages of the two rivers,
and itemized eight abuses concerning engineering projects, equipment, labor, and materials.
He also said:
"To utilize talent according to its capabilities
is an urgent necessity for employing people.
However, for the work of river conservancy,
one must be impartial and detached to endure the toil of wind and rain;
one must be meticulous to discern the principles of protection;
one must combine benevolence with decisiveness to maximize the strength of the multitude of laborers;
and one must be courageous and straightforward to respond to sudden exigencies.
Therefore, pre-selecting river officials is indispensable."
He then presented two methods for pre-selection: one was recommendation,
and the other was talent storage.
And two methods for proficiency: one was long tenure,
and the other was handover.
He also itemized ten matters of river administration: one was to discuss increasing labor in Hénán;
one was to equalize the allocation of labor for Huái River projects;
one was to inspect and deliberate on the Tōnghuì River projects;
one was to establish willow gardens;
one was to strictly eliminate abuses;
one was to scrutinize and verify wasted funds;
one was to be prudent in official duties;
one was to clearly define specialized river conservancy positions;
one was to reiterate the major decrees for encouragement and reward;
and one was to deliberate on the allocation and replenishment of laborers.
All were approved for implementation.
In the seventeenth year,
Guōjiā Bù at Chénzhōu and Luójiā Kǒu at Yúchéng were cut through,
and then immediately dammed.
In the fifth month of the first year of Kāngxī,
Shíxiāng Lú at Cáoxiàn, Dàcūn at Wǔzhì, and Mèngjiā Wān at Suīníng were cut through.
In the sixth month,
Huángliàn Jí at Kāifēng was cut through,
inundating seven counties: Xiángfú, Zhōngmóu, Yángwǔ, Qǐ, Tōngxǔ, Wèishì, and Fúgōu.
In the seventh month,
the Guīrén Dī was cut through again.
The river current had already reversed into Qīngkǒu,
and it also carried the waters of the Suī and Hú rivers from the breach,
connecting with Hóngzé Hú,
and directly flowed towards Gāo Yàn,
breaching Zhái Jiā Bā.
It formed nine major torrents,
and from that year on, Huáiyáng suffered from disasters annually.
In the second year,
Wǔguān Yíng and Zhūjiā Yíng at Suīníng were cut through.
In the third year,
Qǐxiàn and Yánjiā Zhài at Xiángfú were cut through,
and Zhūjiā Yíng was cut through again,
and then immediately dammed.
In the fourth month of the fourth year,
the river breached upstream,
inundating Yúchéng, Yǒngchéng, and Xiàyì,
and also breached Máoliáng Kǒu at Āndōng.
In the fifth year,
Zhīxī died,
and Yáng Màoxūn, then Governor-General of Guìzhōu, was appointed Governor-General of River Conservancy.
In the sixth year,
Yāndūn at Táoyuán and Shíjiāngjūn Miào at Xiāoxiàn were cut through,
and dammed a year later.
Huángjiā Zuǐ at Táoyuán was also cut through;
it was dammed but breached again.
All the prefectures and counties along the river suffered from floods,
with Qīnghé being particularly submerged.
Below Sānchà Hé, the water was no longer above the shins.
As the lower reaches of the Yellow River were blocked,
all the water flowed into Hóngzé Hú.
The water level at Gāoyóu reached nearly twenty *zhàng*,
the city gates were blocked,
and tens of thousands of villagers drowned.
Officials were dispatched to remit taxes and provide relief.
In winter,
Míngzhū and others were ordered to inspect the river mouth,
and open the gates of Tiānfēi, Shítà, and Báijū.
The stele erected by corrupt commoners at Báijū to close the gates was destroyed.
In the eighth year,
Sānchà Kǒu at Qīnghé was cut through,
and Qīngshuǐ Tán was also cut through.
Vice-Censor-in-Chief Mǎ Shàozēng and Salt Censor Lǐ Táng jointly impeached Màoxūn for dereliction of duty,
and he was dismissed.
Luōduō was appointed Governor-General of River Conservancy.
In the ninth year,
Niúshì Tún at Cáoxiàn was cut through,
and Qiáolóu Sì at Shànxiàn was also cut through,
inundating the county seat of Qīnghé.
In the fifth month of this year, there was a severe storm,
and both the Huái and Huáng rivers overflowed,
damaging and washing away more than sixty sections of the Gāo Yàn stone works,
and breaching it for over five *zhàng*.
Lakes such as Gāo and Bǎo were affected by the combined force of the Huái and Huáng floods,
Gāo Yàn almost collapsed,
and Huáiyáng was in imminent danger.
Supervisor in the Ministry of Works Lǐ Zōngkǒng submitted a memorial stating:
"As the waters converge from various breaches and pour into the lake,
Jiāngdū, Gāo, and Bǎo annually reinforced and raised their dikes,
rising with the water.
With thousands of *lǐ* of tumultuous water
attacking a single, isolated high dike,
when the west wind stirs up waves,
it spreads across ten thousand *qǐng* in an instant.
East of Jiāng, Gāo, Bǎo, and Tài, there are no fields,
and north of Xīnghuà, there are no cities or dwellings.
Other lakes like Lùyáng and Píngwàng are shallow and narrow and cannot hold the water.
The various rivers and canals are not dredged in a timely manner,
the sluice gates below Fàn Gōng Dī have long been abandoned,
and the estuaries entering the sea are all blocked.
Although high officials have jointly inspected,
and strictly ordered the opening of gates to discharge water,
due to the great age and scale of the work,
the cost is immeasurable.
Moreover, it is obstructed by corrupt salt makers along the coast,
and ultimately not carried out.
The water detours to the Miàowān Kǒu in the northeast to enter the sea,
and the fields and houses of seven counties are submerged,
often for years.
Just as the stagnant water recedes,
the new year's overflow arrives again."
Censor Xú Yuè also said that Gāo Yàn should be greatly repaired and built during the low-water season in winter.
Therefore, from Táoyuán in the east to Lóngwáng Miào,
an additional great dike of over three thousand three hundred and thirty *zhàng* was built on the old foundation.
After the twelfth lunar month, the ice thawed and the river overflowed,
along the river, villages, houses, and forests were almost completely washed away.
In the spring of the tenth year,
the river overflowed at Xiāoxiàn.
In the sixth month,
Wǔbǎo at Qīnghé and Chénjiā Lóu at Táoyuán were cut through.
In the eighth month,
Qīlǐ Gōu was cut through again.
Wáng Guāngyù was appointed Governor-General of River Conservancy.
Guāngyù requested to restore the three dams built by Pān Jìxùn of the Míng dynasty, including Cuībà Zhèn,
and to move the Jì Tài Bā to the old riverbed at Huángjiā Zuǐ,
to divide and dissipate the force of the water.
In this year,
Máoliáng Kǒu was dammed.
In the autumn of the eleventh year,
Liǎnghé Kǒu at Xiāoxiàn and Tángchí Jiùchéng at Pīzhōu were cut through,
and Yúchéng also overflowed.
Scholar Guō Tíngzuò and others were dispatched to inspect the site.
In the twelfth year,
Qīlǐ Gōu at Táoyuán was dammed.
In the thirteenth year,
Xīnzhuāng Kǒu and Wángjiā Yíng at Táoyuán were cut through,
and it also breached north of Zhèngjiā Kǒu on the Xīnhé River.
In the fourteenth year,
Pānjiā Táng at Xúzhōu and Càijiā Lóu at Sùqiān were cut through,
and Huāshān Bā at Suīníng was also cut through,
again inundating the Qīnghé county seat,
and many commoners became displaced.
In the summer of the fifteenth year,
due to prolonged rain,
the river flowed backward into Hóngzé Hú.
Gāo Yàn could not hold,
and thirty-four breaches occurred.
The漕dike collapsed.
Qīngshuǐ Tán at Gāoyóu,
and Dàzé Wān at Lùmàn Gōu,
together breached for over three hundred *zhàng*,
and all of Yáng's territory was flooded,
with countless drowned.
The emperor dispatched Minister of Works Jì Rúxī and Vice-Minister of Revenue Yī Sāng'ā to investigate the advantages and disadvantages.
In this year, Báiyáng Hé and Yújiā Gāng at Sùqiān,
Zhāngjiā Zhuāng and Wángjiā Yíng at Qīnghé,
Xíngjiā Kǒu and Èrpù Kǒu at Āndōng,
and Luójiā Kǒu at Shānyáng were also cut through.
Xīnzhuāng at Táoyuán was dammed.
In the sixteenth year [of Kāngxī's reign],
Rú Xī and others reported on the dire condition of the damaged riverworks.
Guāng Yù was dismissed from office for investigation.
Jìn Fǔ, the Governor of Ānhuī, was appointed River Commissioner (hé dū).
Fǔ stated:
“River management must consider the overall situation.
It is essential to integrate the riverways and the Grand Canal as one system,
only then can management be free of problems.
The changes in the riverways
are primarily due to those who manage the rivers focusing their efforts on areas where grain transport boats pass,
while other breaches
are considered irrelevant to the canal and are viewed with leniency,
leading to the daily deterioration of the riverways,
and the consequent daily obstruction of the canal.
The river water carries sand as it flows,
relying entirely on clear water from various places to help scour it,
only then can it rush to the sea.
The reason the riverbed is becoming shallower day by day
is entirely due to the failure to promptly block breaches such as those at Guīrén Dī in the past.
From Qīngjiāng Pǔ to the river mouth,
approximately three hundred *lǐ* long,
the river surface used to be below the stone structures of Qīngjiāng Pǔ;
now, the stone structures are level with the ground.
The riverbed used to be two, three, or four *zhàng* deep;
now, the deepest parts are no more than eight or nine *chǐ*,
and the shallowest are only two or three *chǐ*.
When the river silts up, the canal also silts up.
Now, the battlements of Huái'ān city are lower than the riverbed.
The canal has silted up,
and Qīngjiāng and Lànníqiǎn are completely silted.
Now, the bottom of Hóngzé Hú is gradually becoming dry land.
Since the riverbed has been raised to such an extent,
and the muddy yellow water, laden with sand, comes from the northwest
day and night without ceasing,
as soon as it reaches Xú, Pī, Sù, and Táo,
it slows down, weakens, and disperses.
I have personally observed that river sand accumulates daily,
and the riverbed rises daily.
If major repairs are not undertaken,
not only will Hóngzé Hú gradually become dry land,
but the Grand Canal to the south,
and the area downstream from Qīngjiāng Pǔ to the east,
will suffer increasingly severe silting.
Soon, it will be obstructed on three sides,
and the river will have no outlet,
inevitably leading to internal collapse and flooding.
Hénán and Shāndōng will both face the disaster of being submerged and drowned.
At that time, even if tens of millions of gold coins were spent,
it would be difficult to provide timely remedies.”
He then listed eight major repair proposals: first, to take earth to build dikes
to make the river wider and deeper;
second, to open Qīngkǒu and the guide channels (yǐnhé) at Lànníqiǎn
to draw Huái River water to scour the Yellow River;
third, to reinforce the dikes and embankments of Gāojiāyàn;
fourth, the thirty-four breaches from Zhōoqiáo Zhá to Zhái Jiābà
must be blocked in sequence;
fifth, to deeply excavate the canal from Qīngkǒu to Qīngshuǐtán
and reinforce the east and west dikes;
sixth, to levy a river repair tax on fields in Huáiyáng and on merchant ships and goods;
seventh, to consolidate river officials to centralize responsibility;
eighth, to station soldiers every *lǐ* [along the dikes]
and assign them sections of the dikes to guard.
The court deliberated and decided that since military affairs were not yet concluded,
the large number of laborers needed for major repairs
should be temporarily suspended.
The memorial was submitted again,
but only the method of transporting earth was changed from human labor to vehicle transport;
the rest remained as requested.
Thereupon, all projects were launched simultaneously.
Qīngkǒu and the four guide channels at Lànníqiǎn were extensively excavated,
as well as the riverway from Qīngkǒu to Yúntī Guān.
More than eighteen thousand *zhàng* of water-constraining dikes were newly built outside the pass.
Sixteen major breaches at Yújiā Gāng and Wǔjiā Dūn were blocked.
Also, crescent dikes (yuè dī) were built at Lányáng, Zhōngmóu, Yífēng, and Shāngqiū, as well as Zhōujiā Dī at Yúchéng.
The next year,
two diversion dams (jiǎnshuǐ bà) were newly built at Wángjiāyíng and Zhāngjiāzhuāng.
Twenty-five *lǐ* of dikes were built at Zhōoqiáo and Zhái Bà.
The long dike at Gāojiāyàn was reinforced.
All major and minor breaches along both banks of the Yellow River in the three counties of Shān, Qīng, and Ān,
and at the lake embankments, were sealed.
An imperial edict praised these achievements.
In the eighteenth year,
a stone diversion dam was built on the south bank at Dàngshān Máochéngpù, and another on the north bank at Dàgǔ Shān,
to reduce the force of the upstream current.
In the twentieth year,
Yángjiāzhuāng was blocked,
which had been breached for five years.
That year, eight new roller dams (gǔnshuǐ bà) were built north and south of Gāoyóu,
and a crescent dike of 1,689 *zhàng* was added outside the great dike of Chángfán, Xúzhōu.
By this time, the major repairs had been underway for three years,
but the river had not fully returned to its old course.
Fǔ impeached himself.
The Board (Bù) proposed his dismissal,
but the Emperor ordered him to remain in office.
In the twenty-first year,
a breach occurred at Xújiāwān, Sùqiān,
and was subsequently blocked.
Another breach occurred at Xiāojiā Dù.
Previously, the riverbed was merely a single channel.
Fǔ had completely blocked Yángjiāzhuāng,
intending to constrict the water to scour it.
However, the guide channels were shallow and narrow,
and the silt and scouring were in fierce contention.
When it encountered the low dike at Xújiāwān, it breached;
when the soil at Xiāojiā Dù was loose, it breached again.
At this time, Cuī Wéiyǎ, an acting provincial administration commissioner (bùzhèngshǐ), submitted a preliminary proposal (chúyì) for river defense,
listing twenty-four items,
and requested a complete change from Fǔ's previous methods.
The Emperor sent Shàngshū Yīsāng'ā and Shìláng Sòng Wényùn to conduct an on-site investigation,
ordering Wéiyǎ to accompany them.
Wéiyǎ wished to completely destroy the diversion dams
and plan for alternative excavation and construction.
Yīsāng'ā and others stated that although the projects built by Fǔ were indeed often not strong,
rebuilding might not necessarily succeed.
Fǔ also argued,
“The projects are about to be completed in sequence;
it is not advisable to make any changes.”
The matter was then submitted for court deliberation.
Fǔ was summoned to the capital.
Fǔ stated,
“Xiāojiākǒu can be clearly blocked;
Wéiyǎ's proposal is impractical.”
The Emperor agreed
and ordered him to return to work.
In the spring of the twenty-second year,
Xiāojiā Dù was blocked,
and the river returned to its old course.
The next year,
the Emperor made a southern tour to inspect the river
and bestowed a poem in praise.
In the autumn of the twenty-fourth year,
Fǔ stated that Hénán province was upstream,
and if Hénán suffered,
the riverways in Jiāngnán would be silted up in no time.
Therefore, he built dikes at Kǎochéng and Yífēng, 7,989 *zhàng* long,
a large crescent dike at Jīnglóngkǒu, Fēngqiū, 330 *zhàng* long,
and *sǎo* works at Xíngyáng, 310 *zhàng* long.
He also excavated four diversion sluices (jiǎnshuǐ zhá) at Lónghǔ Shān on the south bank of Suīníng.
The Emperor, concerned that the overflowing lakes in Gāoyóu and other prefectures were inundating people's fields,
ordered Yú Chénglóng, the Provincial Surveillance Commissioner (ànchásǐ) of Ānhuī, to repair and manage the river mouth and the Lower River (xiàhé),
subject to Fǔ's supervision.
Soon, Fǔ and Chénglóng were summoned to the capital for a joint deliberation.
Chénglóng strongly advocated for dredging the river mouth.
Fǔ stated that the Lower River's mouth was five *chǐ* higher than the inland areas,
and a long dike, one *zhàng* and six *chǐ* high, should be built
to constrict the water and guide it to the sea.
Their views were in disagreement.
The matter was referred to court ministers for deliberation,
who also held differing opinions.
The Emperor, knowing that Lecturer (jiǎngguān) Qiáo Lái was from north of the Jiāng [River],
summoned him for questioning.
Lái stated that Fǔ's proposal was incorrect.
Consequently, Shàngshū Sàmùhā and others were sent to investigate and deliberate,
and they reported back that opening the river mouth would be useless.
At this time, Tāng Bīn, the Governor of Jiāngníng, entered the capital as a Shàngshū.
When questioned,
Bīn stated that if the river mouth were opened, accumulated water could be discharged,
but the people of Gāoyóu and Xīnghuà feared the destruction of their homes and ancestral graves, which would be inconvenient.
Thereupon, Sàmùhā was dismissed,
and two hundred thousand taels from the imperial treasury were allocated.
Shìláng Sūn Zàifēng was ordered to oversee the project.
At this time, there was also a proposal that the diversion dams should be blocked first before undertaking repairs to the Lower River.
The Emperor did not allow it.
Fǔ was summoned for an imperial audience.
Fǔ stated that if the southern dams were permanently blocked,
he feared that the Huái River's weakness would not be able to contend with the Yellow River's strength.
Therefore, a double dike (chóng dī) should be added outside Gāojiāyàn
to intercept the water and direct it out through Qīngkǒu, not into the Lower River,
and projects at Dīngxī and other places should be suspended.
Chénglóng, who was then Governor of Zhílí (Zhífǔ),
was shown Fǔ's memorial and still maintained that the Lower River should be dredged,
and that building double dikes would be a laborious and useless expense.
The discussion remained undecided.
Shàngshū Fólún and others were again sent to investigate and deliberate.
Fólún supported Fǔ's proposal.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Censor Guō Xiù impeached Fǔ for his lack of achievement in river management.
Internal and external officials also submitted memorials criticizing him.
Consequently, the construction of the double dikes was halted.
Fǔ was relieved of his office,
and Wáng Xīnmìng, the Governor-General (zǒngdū) of Mǐn-Zhè, replaced him,
