still overseeing the repair of the Lower River.
Sūn Zàifēng was demoted,
and Xuéshì Kǎiyīnbù replaced him.
The following year,
the Emperor went on a southern tour,
inspecting Gāojiāyàn.
He said to his ministers:
"This dike is quite strong,
but it should not be without diversion dams to prevent major breaches when the water is high.
However, Jìn Fǔ's desire to build a secondary dike outside the old one
is truly useless."
He also praised Fǔ for constructing diversion dams in dangerous sections,
allowing the water flow to slow down,
which was very good.
When the imperial entourage returned to the capital,
Fǔ's official position was restored.
In the 31st year,
the newly appointed official was dismissed,
and Fǔ was again made River Governor.
Fǔ declined due to illness and frailty,
so Xu Tíngxǐ, the Shùntiān Prefectural Administrator, was appointed as his deputy.
Fǔ requested that willows be planted and grass sown on both banks of the Yellow River,
and that more culverts be installed,
all of which were approved.
That winter,
Fǔ died.
Upon hearing this, the Emperor
sighed and grieved,
bestowing upon him the hereditary position of Cavalry Commandant.
Yú Chénglóng was appointed River Governor.
Two years later,
the Emperor summoned Chénglóng and asked:
"Can the diversion dam really be blocked?"
He replied:
"It should not be blocked.
It should continue to be managed according to what Fǔ built."
The Emperor said:
"If this is the case,
why didn't you explain it earlier?
It is easy for you to frame others,
but difficult to take responsibility as the Director-General of Rivers.
Is this not clear proof?"
In the 34th year,
Chénglóng suffered the loss of his father,
and Dǒng Ānguó, the Grain Transport Governor, replaced him.
The following year,
there was a great flood,
breaching Zhāngjiāzhuāng.
The Huánghé, Dān, and Qìn rivers converged, pressing against Xíngzé,
and the administration moved to Gāobù.
It also breached Tóngjiāyíng in Āndōng,
and the water flowed into Shèyánghú.
That year, the Lánhuáng Dàbà (Yellow River Barrier Dam) was built,
and a diversion canal of over 1,200 zhàng was dug at Yúntīguān.
Outside the pass, at Mǎjiāgǎng, the Yellow River was diverted eastward via the Náncháohé into the sea.
The obstructed outflow
made upstream breaches likely,
and river disasters became more frequent.
In the 36th year,
Shíjiāmǎtóu breached.
The following year,
Chénglóng was again made River Governor.
In the spring of the 38th year,
the Emperor went on a southern tour,
personally inspecting Gāojiāyàn and other dikes.
He said to his ministers:
"The best policy for river management
is to deepen the riverbed.
If the riverbed is deepened,
the water from Hóngzéhú will flow directly into the Yellow River,
and Xīnghuà, Yánchéng, and seven other prefectures and counties will be free from flooding,
and agricultural land will naturally dry out.
If the source is not managed,
managing the flow will ultimately be of no benefit.
Currently, the confluence of the Yellow and Huai rivers is too straight.
The dikes of the river and Huai should each be extended eastward, curving and widening,
making them meet at an angle,
so that the Yellow River will not backflow."
The following year,
Chénglóng died.
Zhāng Pénghè, the Governor-General of the Two Jiāng, was appointed River Governor.
That year, Shíjiāmǎtóu was sealed.
Following Pénghè's earlier request to dredge the estuary,
the Lánhuáng Dam outside Yúntīguān was completely dismantled
and named Dàqīngkǒu.
A stone sluice was built on the north bank of Sùqiān at the outer mouth of the Yellow River,
and a moon dike was built on the south bank of Xúzhōu from Yángjiālóu to Duànjiāzhuāng.
In the 41st year,
the Emperor said that the stone dikes of the Yǒngdìnghé were very beneficial
and wished to extend them to both banks of the Yellow River,
building stone dikes from Xúzhōu to Qīngkǒu.
Pénghè stated,
"Building stone works
requires a solid foundation.
However, the river's nature is unpredictable,
with loose and shifting sand and soil.
Stone dikes involve complex work and huge costs,
and their completion is difficult to predict."
Thus, it was abandoned.
In the 42nd year,
the Emperor went on a southern tour,
inspecting the river works,
and composed a "River Official Admonition" to bestow upon Pénghè.
In the autumn,
the outlet of the Central River was relocated to Yángjiālóu,
forcing the current southward.
The clear water flowed smoothly to resist the Yellow River,
the estuary opened wide,
the riverbed deepened daily,
and there was no worry of the Yellow River backflowing.
The Emperor praised Pénghè's achievements
and promoted him to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
In the eighth month of the 46th year,
Wújiāzhuāng in Fēngxiàn breached
and was subsequently sealed.
The following year,
Pénghè was appointed Minister of Punishments,
and Zhào Shìxiǎn replaced him.
In the sixth month of the 48th year,
the dikes at Léijiājí in Lányáng, Hóngshàowān in Yífēng, and Zhāngjiāzhuāng at Shuǐyì all breached.
In the eighth month of the 60th year,
Zhānjiādiàn, Mǎyíngkǒu, and Wèijiākǒu in Wǔzhì breached.
The main current shifted northward,
flowing into Huáxiàn, Chángyuán, and Dōngmíng,
seizing the Grand Canal,
reaching Zhāngqiū,
and entering the Yánhé via Wǔkōngqiáo to return to the sea.
Since the completion of the river works,
the Yellow River had followed its course,
remaining peaceful for over ten years,
but at this point, Pénghè and others were dispatched to investigate.
In the ninth month,
Zhānjiādiàn and Wèijiākǒu were sealed;
in the eleventh month,
Mǎyíngkǒu was sealed.
Shìxiǎn was dismissed,
and Chén Péngnián was appointed acting Director-General of River Conservancy.
In the first month of the 61st year,
Mǎyíngkǒu breached again,
flooding Zhāngqiū,
and rushing into the Dàqīnghé.
In the sixth month,
the Qìn River swelled,
collapsing the north and south dike platforms of Qínjiāchǎng and the Dàbà of Dīngchuánbāng.
At that time, the Wángjiāgōu diversion canal was completed,
guiding the current from the southeast to meet Xíngzé and enter the main river,
so the Mǎyíng dike remained intact.
Péngnián again dug a diversion canal of over 140 zhàng at Guǎngwǔshān Guānzhuāngyù to divide the water flow.
In the ninth month,
the south dike of Qínjiāchǎng was barely sealed
when the north dike breached again,
and Mǎyíng also overflowed;
in the twelfth month,
it was sealed.
In the sixth month of the first year of Yōngzhèng,
Shílǐdiàn and Lóujiāzhuāng in Zhōngmóu breached,
flowing south from Liújiāzhài into the Jiǎlǔhé.
At this point, Péngnián died.
Qí Sūlè became Director-General of Rivers.
Fearing that the water flowing into the Jiǎlǔhé
would exceed the capacity of the dikes near the lake at Shānxū and Gāoyàn,
it was urgent to block it as circumstances dictated.
The Emperor ordered Jī Zēngyún, Vice Minister of War, to rush there to deliberate.
In the seventh month,
Liángjiāyíng and Zhānjiādiàn breached.
Grand Secretary Zhāng Pénghè was again sent to assist in repairs,
and they were sealed that month.
In the ninth month,
the civilian dike at Láitóngzhài in Zhèngzhōu breached.
The people of Zhèng excavated the old dike of Yángwǔ to drain the water,
and also breached the official dike at Yángqiáo in Zhōngmóu,
which was soon sealed.
That year, east and west water-constricting dams were built at Qīngkǒu to control the Yellow River and store clear water.
In the second year,
Jī Zēngyún was made Assistant Director-General of Rivers,
stationed at Wǔzhì,
overseeing river affairs in Hénán.
The division of the Eastern River administration began from this point.
In the sixth month,
Dàzhài in Yífēng and Bǎnqiáo in Lányáng breached.
They were sealed more than a month later.
In the sixth month of the third year,
a breach was made at Zhūjiāhǎi in Suīníng,
flowing eastward into Hóngzéhú.
In the fourth month of the following year,
before the breach was sealed,
the river water rose sharply,
collapsing the embankment on the eastern bank.
Suīníng, Hóng, Sì, Táoyuán, and Sùqiān were all inundated.
The Grand Governor of Liǎngguǎng, Kǒng Yùxún, was ordered to rush to inspect and assist in defense.
The breach was sealed in the twelfth month.
In that month, the river cleared,
from Fǔgǔ, Shǎnxī, to Táoyuán, Jiāngnán.
In the fifth year,
Qísūlè, considering Zhūjiāhǎi to be strategically important,
added a parallel embankment (jiābà), a crescent-shaped dike (yuèdī), and windbreaks (fángfēngsào).
Moreover, at the point where the main current strongly impacted, he had the steep bank cut into a slope,
and hung dense-leaved large willows on the slope,
to resist the scouring of the current.
After a long time,
the main current returned to the central channel,
and the willow branches, collecting mud and silt,
all became sandbanks,
transforming danger into safety,
with little labor and great cost savings.
Therefore, he requested that wherever river banks were steep,
this method should be imitated.
In the sixth year,
Zēng Yún was transferred internally to become the Shàngshū of the Lǐbù.
His position as Deputy Grand River Administrator remained unchanged.
Yǐn Jìshàn, then acting Ànchásǐ of Guǎngdōng, was ordered to assist in the river affairs of Jiāngnán.
In the seventh year,
the title of Hédào Zǒngdū was changed to Jiāngnán Hédào Zǒngdū,
stationed at Qīngjiāng.
Kǒng Yùxún was appointed to this post,
and the position of Deputy Grand River Administrator was abolished.
Zēng Yún was appointed Shāndōng Hédào Zǒngdū,
stationed at Jìníng.
The Emperor recalled that Pān Jìxún, a minister of the Míng dynasty, had proposed raising the dikes by five inches each year,
and that Jìn Fǔ had also advocated this previously,
estimating the annual cost at no more than thirty or forty thousand.
He submitted this to the two Hédào Zǒngdū for discussion.
Yùxún and others requested to adjust it based on urgency,
doubling the effort by rotating years,
estimating an annual need of over twenty thousand gold.
This was submitted to the appropriate board for implementation.
In the eighth year,
Yùxún died.
Zēng Yún was transferred to oversee the Southern River.
Tián Wénjìng concurrently served as the acting Zǒngdū of the Eastern River.
In the fifth month,
the imperial decree to build the Hèyuán Shénmiào outside Hézhōukǒu was completed,
and additional titles were conferred.
In that month,
the river cleared,
from Jīshígān to Sālāchéng Zhāhànsī.
In that year, breaches occurred at Sùqiān and Shěnjiāzhuāng in Táoyuán,
but were promptly sealed.
At Jīnglóngkǒu in Fēngqiū, the main current was redirected to open the Hēigāngkǒu to Liǔyuánkǒu引河 for three thousand three hundred and fifty zhàng.
In the tenth year,
the reinforced stone dike at Gāoyàn was completed.
In the eleventh year,
officials from various ministries and academies were selected to study at the Southern River,
for a period of three years.
Zēng Yún was appointed Wénhuádiàn Dàxuéshì and concurrently Lìbù Shàngshū,
continuing to oversee the Southern River as before.
Gāo Bīn, the salt administrator of Liǎnghuái, was ordered to learn river affairs.
Zēng Yún subsequently suffered a mother's mourning.
Bīn acted as the Zǒngdū of the Southern River.
In the fourth month of the first year of Qiánlóng,
the river water rose greatly,
surging southward through the gatelocks at Máochéngpù, Dàngshān.
Many dikes were breached,
and at Pānjiādàokǒu, the water was three to five chǐ deep on flat ground.
The Emperor noted that the lower reaches were mostly in the prefectures and counties of Xiāo, Sù, Líng, Hóng, Suīníng, Wǔhé, etc.,
and that the current discussion only concerned dredging the upper reaches without a strategy to clear the lower reaches,
which would leave the water with no outlet.
He ordered the governors and grand administrators of Jiāngnán and Hénán, along with the two Hédào Zǒngdū, to conduct an inspection and hold a conference,
and to move the Southern Deputy Grand River Administrator to Xúzhōu to focus on supervision.
Soon after, Gāo Bīn requested to dredge the river channel from Máochéngpù downwards,
passing through Xú, Xiāo, Suī, Sù, Líng, Hóng, to the Ànhé Dǒumén in Sìzhōu,
a winding but direct route of over six hundred lǐ,
to reach Hóngzéhú,
and then exit through Qīngkǒu to join the Huánghé.
However, Xià Zhīfāng and other officials from Huái and Yáng argued against its convenience.
The following year,
Bīn was summoned for questioning.
Bīn presented a map for inspection,
which revealed that Zhīfāng's statements were inaccurate.
He was ordered to work with Zǒngdū Qìng Fù to make a precise estimate and finalize the plan,
and to inform the people of Huái and Yáng that the dredging would be beneficial and harmless.
Initially,
Bīn dredged the Máochéngpù waterway,
opening a new mouth and blocking the old one,
to prevent the Yellow River from backing up.
By the autumn of the third year,
the river overflowed into the Grand Canal,
and many blamed the newly opened canal mouth.
Bīn said:
"After the tenth month, the Yellow River water will recede,
the lake water will flow freely,
and the new silt will be flushed away by the current,
so there will be no fear of shallowness."
In the fourth year,
Bīn again stated
"last year, the clear water was weak,
and it coincided with an unusual rise in the Yellow River water,
it was not caused by opening the new mouth."
But southerners' complaints did not cease.
The Emperor dispatched Dàxuéshì È'ěrtài to investigate,
who also said the new mouth should be opened.
The following year,
the Yellow River current still pressed southward towards Qīngkǒu,
so imitating the method of Chén Yáozài of the Sòng dynasty,
two wooden dragons were constructed,
to guide the current northward.
In the sixth year,
Bīn observed that from Sùqiān to Táoyuán and Qīnghé, a distance of over two hundred lǐ,
the river flowed rapidly,
with only six thread dikes (lǚdī) on the north bank,
and no distant dikes (yáodī).
Moreover, it encroached upon the Grand Canal.
He proposed to build up and thicken the thread dikes on the south bank of the Grand Canal,
making them serve as the distant dikes for the north bank of the Yellow River,
and further to strategically add nine grid dikes (gédī) within the thread dikes.
Before completion,
Bīn was transferred to oversee Zhílì.
Wányán Wěi succeeded him.
Previously, the Emperor, concerned that the river current was pressing against Qīngkǒu,
causing backflow problems,
decreed to follow the old traces from the Kāngxī period,
to open the Táozhuāng Yǐnhé,
to guide the Yellow River northward,
and dispatched È'ěrtài to conduct a joint investigation.
As soon as the plan was settled,
work was halted due to a sudden rise in floodwaters,
and Bīn also left his post.
At this point,
Wányán Wěi, fearing that the diverting canal might not be effective,
placed wooden dragons west of Qīngkǒu, on the south bank of the Yellow River,
to divert the current northward,
and thus the plan for the diverting canal was abandoned.
Forty-one years later,
the Emperor decided to open it,
and the project was completed the following year.
The new river flowed directly to Zhōujiāzhuāng,
joining the Qīng River downstream,
and the problem of backflow was permanently resolved.
In the seventh year,
dikes at Fēngxiàn’s Shílín and Huángcūn burst,
diverting the current eastward.
The dikes at Pèixiàn’s Lǚtí also burst,
but were subsequently plugged.
Wányán Wěi was transferred to supervise the Eastern River,
and Bái Zhōngshān was appointed Governor-General of the Southern River instead.
When the Fēngxiàn and Pèixiàn dikes first burst,
Grand Secretary Chén Shìguān went to inspect,
and had two additional stone dams built to release floodwater, at the sites of the natural North and South Dams,
to divert the water flow.
In the tenth year,
dikes at Fùníng’s Chénjiāpǔ burst.
At that time, the Huái River and Yellow River both rose,
and the prefectures and counties along the river were flooded.
Cáo Dū Gù Cóng said:
“Chénjiāpǔ is close to the river mouth,
and for over ten *lǐ* downstream, there have never been any dikes.
Whenever the water rises,
it is allowed to spread out naturally.
If we still block it here,
it means contending with the water for land,
with great expense and little benefit.
We should build a remote dike upstream to contain the water flow.”
The matter was referred to Nàqīn and Gāo Bīn,
who still discussed plugging the old breach.
In the eleventh year,
Zhōngshān was dismissed,
and Gù Cóng provisionally managed the Southern River.
He built three wooden *long* at Āndōng’s West Gate,
forcing the current southward.
Above the wooden *long*, everything became silted sandbanks,
transforming danger into safety.
In the thirteenth year,
Cóng was transferred to supervise the Eastern River.
The emperor decreed Grand Secretary Gāo Bīn to manage affairs of the Southern River.
Bīn noted that the two channels below Yúntīguān had swollen with sandbanks,
and the main current was moving southward,
directly threatening the dikes at Tiānfēi Gōng’s Xīnjiādàng.
He opened a diversion channel,
and repaired the cracked stone dikes outside Xúzhōu’s East Gate.
Cóng also noted that the south bank of Xiángfú’s Nineteenth Fort was silting up daily,
and the main current was moving northward, pressing against the base of the dike.
He built North and South Dam platforms,
and drove piles to strengthen the dams from the outside.
In the sixth month of the sixteenth year,
dikes at Yángwǔ burst.
Bīn was ordered to the site,
to coordinate with Cóng in blocking and building.
It was plugged in the eleventh month.
In the seventeenth year,
the emperor noted that outside the main dikes on the river banks in Hénán Province, there was a great relief dike,
connecting Zhílì and the east.
It had deteriorated over the years.
For the section in Zhílì,
Fāng Guānchéng was ordered to inspect and repair.
For the section within Shāndōng’s border,
Ōu Róng’ān was ordered to investigate and repair any erosion or damage.
Ōu Róng’ān reported that the great relief dikes in Cáoxiàn and Shànxiàn had three thousand four hundred and thirty *zhàng* of damage, large and small,
and were additionally weak and thin.
More than three hundred and thirty *zhàng* of breaches were repaired,
and the drainage ditches south of the dikes were dredged to release floodwaters.
In the autumn of the eighteenth year,
dikes at Yángwǔ’s Thirteenth Fort burst.
In the ninth month,
dikes at Tóngshān’s Zhāngjiā Mǎlù burst,
collapsing the inner dike and overflowing the Lǚyuè dike for over two hundred *zhàng*.
The water flowed southward into the various townships of Língbì and Hóngxiàn,
entering Hóngzé Hú,
and diverting the Huái River downstream.
Yǐn Jìshàn was appointed Governor-General of the Southern River,
and Minister Shūhèdé was dispatched with Bái Zhōngshān to rush there and assist.
Tóngzhī Lǐ Dùn and Shǒubèi Zhāng Bīn misappropriated funds and delayed work,
and were impeached by Fùlèhè, who was learning river management as a Provincial Administration Commissioner.
The accusations were verified,
and they were brought to justice.
Gāo Bīn and Assistant Manager Zhāng Shīzài were arrested for negligence,
and bound to await execution.
That winter,
the river was plugged.
When the Tóngshān breach first occurred,
the matter was debated in court.
Minister of Personnel Sūn Jiāgàn alone advocated for opening diversion channels to lead water into the Dàqīng Hé,
saying briefly:
“Since the reigns of Shùnzhì and Kāngxī,
nine out of ten river breaches have occurred on the north bank.
When the north bank breaches,
half the time the grain transport is flooded, half the time it is not.
All the channels of these breaches
lead into the sea via the Dàqīng Hé.
The Dàqīng Hé’s southeast consists of the foothills of Tàishān,
and its course has been stable and
unchanged since ancient times.
When the river previously divided into north and south branches,
it already received half of the river’s flow.
And when Zhāngqiū breached,
it received the entire river’s flow,
yet there were no reports of cities being inundated or people drowning.
This is sufficient proof that this river is beneficial and not harmful.
Now, the Tóngshān breach cannot be successfully closed,
and the accumulated water in two or three dozen prefectures and counties of the upper and lower Jiāng cannot be drained.
Therefore, I propose opening diversion channels.
If the upstream flow is reduced, the downstream flow will be diminished,
the breaches will be easier to plug,
and the accumulated water will recede earlier.
However, the river flow is rapid;
if diversion channels are opened and the main current is diverted,
this must be guarded against.
Therefore, I propose diverting it into the Dàqīng Hé.
Several existing diversion channels
are not far from the Dàqīng Hé.
Counting the prefectures and counties through which the Dàqīng Hé flows,
there are only Dōng’ē, Jìyáng, Bīnzhōu, and Lìjīn—four or five.
Even if there is overflow,
it would only be a partial disaster.
Enduring a partial disaster in four or five prefectures and counties
can reduce the accumulated water in two or three dozen prefectures and counties of the two Jiāng,
and also alleviate the urgent difficulties of Huái’ān and Yángzhōu Prefectures.
The advantages and disadvantages, the gravity of the situation,
do not require a wise person to understand.
After the diversion channels are opened,
passing through two or three prefectures and counties,
there might be overflow.
Build earthen embankments to defend against it.
Once it enters the Dàqīng Hé,
the riverbed is deep and wide,
and very few places on both banks need to be built up.
The estimated cost would be no more than one or two hundred thousand,
while the savings from the construction costs of downstream breaches,
and the relief funds and grain,
would be at least one or two million.
The gains and losses, the quantity of difference,
also do not require a wise person to understand.
No plan is more convenient than this.”
The emperor, concerned about geographical obstacles,
could not adopt it.
After the Tóngshān breach was plugged,
the accumulated water inside the crescent dike was still seven or eight *chǐ* to eighteen or nineteen *chǐ* deep.
The emperor ordered another diversion channel to be opened south of the intake channel’s weir,
so that the new works would not be impacted by the current.
In the twenty-first year,
dikes at Sūnjiājí burst,
and were immediately plugged.
In the second month of the following year,
the emperor made a southern tour and inspected the wooden *long* at Tiānfēi Zhá.
At that time, Zhōngshān was transferred to manage the Southern River,
and together with the Governor-General of the Eastern River, Zhāng Shīzài, said:
“The north and south banks of Xúzhōu are very close to each other,
and whenever there is a great flood, breaches frequently occur.
We request to dredge the silted shallows,
build up the dikes,
and also plug the branch rivers on the north bank,
as a strategy for both north and south.”
The proposal was approved.
In the twenty-third year,
Gāo Jìn, Governor of Ānhuī, was ordered to assist in managing the Southern River.
In the seventh month of autumn,
the newly built earth dam at Dòujiāzhài burst,
flowing directly into Máochéngpù,
and overflowing the Jīnmén earth dam.
Jìn said:
“The earth dam was too high,
obstructing the water flow,
leading to its blockage and bursting,
so there is no need to rebuild it.”
The emperor disagreed,
and also ordered the opening of the Jiǎngjiāyíng and Fùjiāwā diversion channels to re-introduce water into the Yellow River.
In the seventh month of the twenty-sixth year,
the Qìn and Yellow Rivers both rose,
and Wǔzhì, Xíngzé, Yángwǔ, Xiángfú, and Lányáng simultaneously burst at fifteen places.
Yángqiáo in Zhōngmóu breached several hundred *zhàng*,
and the main current flowed directly into the Jiǎlǔ Hé.
Grand Secretaries Liú Tǒngxūn and Gōng Zhàohuì were dispatched to inspect urgently.
Governor Cháng Jūn requested to build the south bank first.
The emperor stated that since the river was diverting its current,
Yángqiáo should be immediately plugged.
Jūn’s statement was greatly mistaken,
so he was transferred to be Governor of Jiāngxī,
and Hú Bǎoxuán was appointed Governor of Hénán.
Gāo Jìn was also ordered to Hénán to assist.
It was plugged in the eleventh month.
The emperor was greatly pleased upon hearing this,
and ordered a River God Temple to be built at the construction site.
In the 30th year,
the emperor made a southern tour,
offering sacrifices to the River God,
and inspecting the Hùijì Sluice of the East Dam wooden dragon at Qīngkǒu.
In the 31st year,
a breach occurred at Hánjiātáng in Tóngpèitīng,
which was soon closed.
In the 33rd year,
Āsīhā, the Governor of Yù, requested to use the silver saved from Yù's construction projects to reinforce dikes and embankments.
The Grand River Superintendent, Wú Sìjué, stated:
"The river surface in Yù province is wide,
and the current is unpredictable in its ebb and flow,
rapidly becoming dangerous and then calm.
If the earth barriers were designated as a fixed number,
I fear that various project officials would consider this an annual customary expenditure,
thereby encouraging the弊 of fraudulent claims for construction work."
The proposal was thus dropped.
The following year,
Sìjué stated:
"The current at Tóngwǎxiāng pushes against the embankment,
and the major project at Yángqiáo, from the fourth or fifth earth barrier to the twenty-first, all directly bears the brunt of the current.
I request that repairs and dismantling be undertaken before the peach blossom flood season arrives,
adding layers of earth and fascines,
pressing them down firmly.
Outside the major dikes on both banks, there are many branch rivers with accumulated water.
When the flood season arrives,
these divert the current to impact the dikes.
It is advisable to build more earth dams to block them."
The emperor approved all his requests.
In the 37th year,
Yáo Lìdé, the Governor-General of the Eastern River, stated:
"The previously constructed earth dams,
which secured the dike foundations, have brought peace from floods for several years,
showing clear efficacy.
I request that during the idle time of winter and spring,
earth dams be built up,
and willow saplings be densely planted,
so that in a few years, the channels will be silted up and leveled,
thereby permanently securing the dike foundations."
The emperor greatly praised him.
In the fifth month of the 38th year,
the river overflowed at Cháoyì,
rising to twenty-five feet,
and many civilian homes were submerged.
In the eighth month of the 39th year,
a breach occurred at Lǎobàkǒu of the Southern River.
The main current flowed down from Shānzǐhú into Mǎjiādàng and Shèyánghú, reaching the sea.
Bǎnzhá and Huái'ān were both submerged,
but it was soon closed.
In the 41st year,
Sìjué stated that the Yellow River water flowed backward into Hónghú and the Grand Canal,
and that dredging the diversion channel at Qīngkǒu might be ineffective.
He was then transferred to another post.
Sàzài took over as acting Grand River Superintendent of the South.
The emperor commanded him to deliberate with Gāo Jìn, the Governor-General of Jiāngnán.
Gāo Jìn and others stated:
"Your servant Gāo Jìn has been working on these projects for over twenty years,
experiencing numerous backflows.
The only solution is to dredge the Qīngkǒu connection to the lake's diversion channel,
allowing a smooth flow,
where the Yellow River water converges and flows eastward,
jointly scouring the sand.
Then the Yellow River will deepen without further dredging,
and the estuary will clear itself without further intervention.
To correct deficiencies and remedy弊,
this is the only method."
They further stated:
"The wooden dragon built west of Qīngkǒu
was originally intended to divert the current northward,
scouring the accumulated earth at Táozhuāng,
to prevent the Yellow River from encroaching upon the Qīng River.
However, it is difficult to scour it completely in a short time.
It is advisable to open a diversion channel north of the accumulated earth at Táozhuāng,
so that the Yellow River is further away from Qīngkǒu,
and meets the Qīng River at Zhōujiāzhuāng to flow eastward.
Not only can this prevent backflow,
but the silted sand can also be gradually scoured,
and the dikes and embankments will also be secured.
This is what is meant by 'governing the Huái River is governing the Yellow River'."
In the second month of the following year,
the diversion channel was completed.
The emperor rejoiced at the completion of this grand project,
which was a single effort for lasting peace,
and could abolish the centuries-old saying of "using the Qīng to oppose the Yellow."
He ordered the construction of a River God temple at the new outlet's stone dam,
and personally composed an inscription for it.
In the 43rd year,
a breach occurred at Xiángfú,
which was closed in ten days.
In the intercalary sixth month,
a breach occurred at the sixteen forts of Yífēng,
more than seventy *zhàng* wide.
The location was upstream of various outlets,
where the current was swift and turbulent,
flowing through Suīzhōu, Nínglíng, Yǒngchéng, directly to the Huái River via the Guōhé River at Bózhōu.
He commanded Gāo Jìn to lead experienced river officials and officers to Yù to assist in blocking the breach,
allocating 500,000 taels of salt tax silver from Liǎnghuái and 300,000 *shí* of Jiangxi tribute grain to relieve the victims,
and also dispatching Grand Secretary Yuán Shǒudòng to investigate and handle the matter.
In the eighth month,
the upstream surged repeatedly,
and an additional two hundred twenty *zhàng* collapsed.
The sixteen forts, once closed, breached again.
It was closed again in the twelfth month.
The next day,
the east and west dams of Shíhéyì successively collapsed.
He dispatched Grand Secretary Gōng Āguì to rush and investigate.
In the fourth month of the following year,
the northern dam collapsed again for over twenty *zhàng*.
The emperor was deeply concerned about the Yí project,
and remembering the ancient custom of offering jade disks in river rituals,
he specially issued a white jade sacrificial text,
commanding Āguì and others to go to the project site to perform the sacrifice.
It was closed in the second month of the 45th year.
This operation
lasted two years,
costing over five million taels,
and required five attempts to block it before it held.
He ordered a stele to be erected at the Táozhuāng River God temple to commemorate it.
In the sixth month,
a breach occurred at Guōjiādù in Suīníng,
and also at Kǎochéng and Cáoxiàn,
all of which were soon closed.
In the eleventh month,
Zhāngjiāyóufáng was closed but reopened.
In the fifth month of the 46th year,
a breach occurred at Wèijiāzhuāng in Suīníng,
and the main current flowed into Hóngzéhú.
In the seventh month,
a breach occurred at Yífēng,
with over twenty breaches.
The entire force of the water from the northern bank flowed into Qīnglónggāng.
In the twelfth month,
it was about to be closed but collapsed again,
and the main current entirely flowed down from the breaches.
In the 47th year,
it was blocked twice,
but both times it collapsed again.
Āguì and others requested to build an additional southern dike outside the great dam of the three forts of Lányáng,
opening a diversion channel over one hundred seventy *lǐ* long,
to guide the water downstream,
and return to the main river from Qībǎo in Shāngqiū,
making the entire current return to the old course,
then the breaches at Qǔjiālóu could naturally be blocked.
The emperor followed their advice.
In the second month of the following year,
the diversion channel was completed,
and it was closed in the third month.
In the eighth month of the 49th year,
a breach occurred at the two forts of Suīzhōu.
Āguì was again dispatched to the site to supervise,
and it was closed in the eleventh month.
Previously, the emperor, concerned about the repeated overflows in the Yù projects over the years,
and the lack of discharge routes outside the dike defenses,
wished to build flood relief dams where appropriate,
so that during major flood seasons, there would be an outlet for diversion.
He sent Āguì and the river and gubernatorial officials to investigate and deliberate.
At this time,
Āguì and others stated:
"For the dike projects in Yù province,
the soil at Xíngzé and Zhèngzhōu is high and firm,
and it is close to Guǎngwǔshān,
so there is no need to set up flood relief dams.
Below Zhōngmóu,
the sand and earth are mixed,
or entirely sand,
and building dams there cannot guarantee stability.
As for the various rivers draining water south of the dikes,
only the Jiǎlǔhé River is a critical drainage route.
It passes through Zhèngzhōu, Zhōngmóu, Xiángfú, Wèishì, Fúgōu, Xīhuá, and enters the Shāhé River at Zhōujiākǒu.
Also, Hùijì is a branch of the Jiǎlǔhé River.
These two rivers are narrow and silted up.
If the Yellow River water needs to be diverted,
they should be greatly dredged,
which would be enormously expensive,
and cannot be accomplished in a short time.
However, the river course at Lán, Yí, and Gāojiāzhài is winding.
If it were dredged and straightened,
guiding the current northward,
the river channel could flow smoothly."
The emperor agreed.
In the autumn of the 51st year,
a breach occurred at Sījiāzhuāng and Yāndūn in Táoyuán,
which was closed in the tenth month.
In the summer of the following year,
a breach occurred again at Suīzhōu,
which was closed in the tenth month.
In the twelfth month,
the Yellow River in Shānxī was clear for twenty days,
stretching for thirteen hundred *lǐ* from Yǒngníng downwards.
In the summer of the 54th year,
a breach occurred at Zhōujiālóu in Suīníng,
which was closed in the tenth month.
In the 59th year,
a breach occurred at Qǔjiāzhuāng in Fēngběi,
and it was soon closed.
In the sixth month of the first year of Jiāqìng's reign (1796),
the Fēng Xùn's (丰汛) six dikes burst.
The Yújiāzhuāng (余家莊) dike on the Grand Canal was breached,
and the water from Fēng (丰) and Pèi (沛) flowed north into Jīnxiāng (金鄉) and Yútái (魚臺) in Shāndōng (山東),
overflowing into the Zhāoyáng (昭陽) and Wēishān (微山) lakes,
passing into the Grand Canal,
and inundating both banks.
Shānyáng (山陽) and Qīnghé (清河) in Jiāngsū (江蘇) were largely submerged.
Lánxídì (蘭錫第), Governor-General of the Southern River (Nánhé Zǒngdū, 南河總督), directed the water into the Lìnjiāshān (藺家山) dam,
and the diversion channel from Jīngshān Qiáo (荊山橋) branched out to the various lakes near Sùqiān (宿遷).
He also opened the Zhúlù (竹絡) dam at Shíjiāhé (十家河) and the Gùjiāzhuāng (顧家莊) dike at Táoyuán (桃源) in Sùqiān,
allowing the water to drain downstream into the main river.
Additionally, he dug out an old riverbed southwest of the breach,
guiding the current eastward into the main river.
He submitted a map along with his report.
The emperor ordered that the channel be straightened towards the south and then east,
widened and excavated,
so that the current would flow directly into the main river,
which would be more effective.
He commanded Sūlíng'ē (蘇淩阿), Governor-General of Líangjiāng (兩江 Zǒngdū), and Kāngjītián (康基田), Provincial Administration Commissioner (Bùzhèngshǐ) of Shāndōng, to jointly inspect and plan the work.
In the eleventh month,
due to ice floes (língxùn, 淩汛), the dam body collapsed again for over twenty zhàng.
At the time, Sūlíng'ē was serving in Jiāngxī (江西),
so Lǐfènghàn (李奉翰), Governor-General of the Eastern River (Dōnghé Zǒngdū, 東河總督), was instead appointed to oversee the project jointly.
It was blocked the following year in the second month.
Fènghàn was given the title of Grand Guardian of the Heir Apparent (Tàizǐ Tàibǎo, 太子太保),
transferred to serve as Governor-General of Líangjiāng,
and concurrently managed Southern River affairs.
In the seventh month of that year,
the river overflowed at Cáoxùn (曹汛), breaching twenty-five dikes.
In the spring of the third year,
the dam construction suffered another collapse due to ice.
Fènghàn impeached himself.
The Grand Secretary (Dàxuéshì, 大學士) Líuyōng (劉墉) and Minister (Shàngshū, 尚書) Qìngguì (慶桂) were dispatched to inspect the situation,
and to interrogate Fènghàn and others for their dilly-dallying.
Yōng and others stated that the breach had already formed a pool,
and with the ice floe season approaching,
they requested to postpone the work until after autumn.
In the eighth month,
it overflowed at Suīzhōu (睢州),
and the water flowed into Hóngzé Hú (洪澤湖).
As the water flow upstream was diverted,
the Cáogōng (曹工) project was completed and blocked in the tenth month.
The following year, in the first month,
the Suīgōng (睢工) project was also blocked.
In the third month,
Wú Jǐng (吳璥), Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hénán (河南), was appointed acting Governor-General of the Eastern River.
Jǐng said:
"The dikes on both banks in eastern Hénán have been heightened,
but the siltation remains the same.
The problem lies in Fēng (豐), Cáo (曹), and Suī (睢) having repeatedly overflowed.
Although they were blocked and the water flow became smooth and stable afterwards,
the diversion channels could not be widened.
Furthermore, the Xúchéng (徐城) river is narrow,
and too much water drains from its sides,
leading to a blockage in the middle.
The method for removing silt
is solely to confine the water to scour the sand,
using dikes to restrict the water.
I heard that Kāngjītián (康基田), the river official in Jiāngnán (江南), is very serious about constructing and reinforcing dikes.
It should be ordered that he assess the condition of the dikes and fascines,
guard the gates and dams,
and regulate the discharge.
Then, it will naturally deepen day by day."
The emperor commanded him to discuss and handle it with Jītián.
In the eighth month,
the Shàojiābà (邵家壩) at Dàngxùn (碭汛) burst.
In the twelfth month,
it was blocked but leaked again.
Furthermore, the materials boats were not guarded,
and they were almost entirely burned down.
Jītián was stripped of his office but retained for the work.
Jǐng was transferred to oversee the Southern River.
Wáng Bǐngjiàn (王秉韜), Provincial Administration Commissioner of Hénán, was appointed Governor-General of the Eastern River.
Eastern River materials were quickly transferred to aid the Southern River.
In the winter of the fifth year,
the Shàojiābà (邵家壩) was blocked.
In the ninth month of the sixth year,
it overflowed at Tángjiāwān (唐家灣) south of Xiāo (蕭),
and was blocked in the eleventh month.
In the ninth month of the eighth year,
it burst at Héngjiālóu (衡家樓) in Fēngqiū (封丘).
The main current surged,
flowing northeast from Fànxiàn (范縣) to Zhāngqiū (張秋),
crossing the Grand Canal and moving eastward into the Yánhé (鹽河),
and entering the sea via Lìjīn (利津).
Chángyuán (長垣), Dōngpíng (東平), and Kāizhōu (開州) in Zhílì (直隸) were all affected by the floods.
The emperor ordered Provincial Administration Commissioner Zhānzhù (瞻住) to provide relief and consolation.
He also dispatched Hónglú Qīng (鴻臚卿) Tōng'ēn (通恩) and others to manage the relief efforts.
Nàyànbǎo (那彥寶), Vice Minister of War (Bīngbù Shìláng, 兵部侍郎), went to the project site
to jointly block and construct with Jīchéngzhì (嵇承志), Governor-General of the Eastern River.
It was blocked the following year in the second month.
In the intercalary sixth month of the tenth year,
Tiěbǎo (鐵保), Governor-General of Líangjiāng, stated:
"Regarding the problems of river defense,
some say the estuary is unfavorable,
some say Hóngzé Hú (洪澤湖) is silted,
and some say the riverbed is too high.
These three theories can all be disregarded.
We should only focus on dredging Qīngkǒu (清口),
extensively repairing the various gates and dams,
using lake water to scour the sand, and the river will be regulated.
With a path for lake water to enter the Yellow River,
there will be no worry of blockage,
and the lake will also be regulated."
The emperor praised his clear and concise statement.
"As for the argument that clear water contends with yellow water,
the dispute is about height, not depth,
which is true,
but if the lake is not deep,
how can it store much water?
It must be deepened to have the power to contend with the Yellow River.
After the major flood season,
consult with Xúdūan (徐端), Governor-General of the Southern River,
and quickly implement construction on the five dams of Gāoyàn (高堰)
and the branch rivers of the various gates and dams,
as appropriate."
At that time, there was a proposal to divert the river from Wángyíng Jiǎnbà (王營減壩) via the Liùtánghé (六塘河) into the sea.
Tiěbǎo, along with Dàijūnyuán (戴均元), Governor-General of the Southern River, reported:
"The new river dike is four hundred *lǐ* long,
and the middle section is widely inundated.
It is difficult to construct urgently,
requiring two to three years
and an estimated cost of three to four million.
Blocking and constructing the diversion dam
would only take two to three months,
costing just over two million.
Moreover, the old river has a known course to follow,
making construction easier."
The emperor agreed.
In the fourth month of the eleventh year,
Wú Jǐng (吳璥), Vice Minister of War, once again oversaw the Eastern River.
In the sixth month,
the position of Southern Assistant Governor-General of the River (Nán Fùzǒnghé, 南副總河) was reinstated,
and Xúdūan was demoted to this position.
In the seventh month,
the Zhōujiālóu (周家樓) at Sùqiān burst.
In the eighth month,
the Guōjiāfáng (郭家房) burst.
Both were subsequently blocked.
In the twelfth year, sixth month,
the Māshān, Ānmǎgǎngkǒu, and Zhāngjiāzhuāng,
branches flowed from Guànkǒu into the sea.
The sluice gates were closed.
In the seventh month,
the flood broke through Chénjiāpǔ outside Yúntīguān,
and more than half of the flow entered Shèyánghú from Wǔxīnggǎng, draining into the sea.
In the thirteenth year, second month,
Chénjiāpǔ was blocked.
Tiěbǎo and others requested the restoration of the stone dam at Máochéngpù and the diversion dam at Wángyíng,
the reinforcement of the great dikes on both banks,
the continued construction of a long dike outside Yúntīguān,
and the raising of the earth slopes behind the Gāoyàn and Shānxū dikes.
Grand Secretary Chánglín and others were dispatched to inspect the situation urgently.
Mò Zhānlù, the Taìpúsì Qīng, stated:
“When the river enters Jiāngnán,
it relies solely on the Huái River for defense.
The Huái collects the waters of seventy-two rivers, converging at Hóngzé,
which are then confined by five dams (stone dikes) at Yàn and Xū,
directing them to exit at Qīngkǒu, merge with the Yellow River, and flow into the sea.
This is the method of confining water to attack silt.
Now, in regulating the Southern River,
it is essential to first manage Qīngkǒu
and protect the five dams.
If the five dams are not easily opened for discharge,
then the lake water can collectively scour the Yellow River.
If the Yellow River does not backflow,
the Grand Canal can naturally be dredged.
Currently, the river officials propose to continue constructing a long dike of over two hundred *lǐ* outside Yúntīguān;
then, at the points where the meandering turns are straightened,
it will be necessary to add *sǎo* sections for protection.
Once repairs and defenses are established,
it will be necessary to add offices and garrisons,
and deploy more officials and soldiers.
This will only lead to increased expenditure
and may not achieve the desired effect of confining and scouring.
As for restoring the rolling dam at Máochéng and dredging Hóng and Suī,
to reduce unusual floods of the Yellow River
and protect Xúchéng, that is permissible.
However, to rely on this to aid the Qing River and benefit transport is not.
Since the Yellow River water enters the lake and deposits silt,
the water flow is turbulent,
and even the five dams at Yàn and Xū are difficult to defend.
How can it then be made to flow smoothly out of Qīngkǒu?
Therefore, by reinforcing the five dams
to allow the lake water to flow freely,
exerting full effort to resist the Yellow River,
and flowing directly downstream,
the river channel can be scoured
to enter the sea.”
Censor Xú Liàng said:
“Among the various repair and defense matters proposed by Tiěbǎo and others,
only regarding the originally proposed stone-slab slope at Gāoyàn,
which did not consider storing clear water to scour the Yellow River,
but focused solely on reinforcing Gāoyàn,
is truly the key to the entire river.
Using softness to control hardness,
this method is the best.
When wind and waves impact,
they are calmed by the slope.
If the entire weir is protected by the slab slope,
then the five dams can be permanently closed,
the clear water can fully scour the Yellow River,
and Huáiyáng can enjoy lasting peace.
This is a plan for ten thousand generations and an urgent task for the present.
The estuary is
the tail-end.
Qīngkǒu is
the throat.
Gāoyàn is the heart and abdomen.
Effort should first be focused on
these vital areas.”
Jìng also agreed with these words.
Chánglín and others reported in response:
“The Máochéng dam is prone to breaching,
so it should not be discussed.
The water accumulated at the Wángyíng diversion dam is too deep,
making construction difficult.
We request to rebuild a rolling dam to its west,
and also add a stone dam.
As for the crushed stone-slab slope,
the section is long,
and it is difficult to complete suddenly.
We will build an earth slope first.”
The rest followed Tiěbǎo’s suggestions.
Jūnyuán was dismissed due to illness,
and Duān again became Governor-General of the Southern River.
Initially,
when Chénjiāpǔ overflowed,
it flowed beside Shèyánghú into the sea.
Tiěbǎo and others, considering the huge cost of digging a river,
and that a direct route from Shèyánghú to the sea was closer than the main river,
therefore proposed a change of river course.
By this time,
Jìng and others were ordered to conduct an on-site inspection.
Jìng and others stated:
“The historical paths of the Guàn River entering the sea during the former Míng and Kāngxī eras
are all still traceable.
Currently, the overflowing water where the North Tidal River merges with Mǎgǎngkǒu and Zhāngjiāzhuāng is still present,
and the silt accumulation is visible.
The exit is not smooth,
and it is also unable to scour the river channel.
Besides this, there is no other way to open a new estuary.
We still request to restore the old channel,
continue constructing the great dike outside Yúntīguān,
and confine the water to flow eastward.”
The Emperor approved their suggestion.
In the sixth month of that year,
the flood breached Qiāngēnqígān and Héhuātáng opposite Tángzi,
and a brick sluice gate over a hundred *zhàng* long leading to the lake was opened,
but the opposite bank of Tángzi and Qiāngēnqígān were immediately blocked,
and Héhuātáng, once blocked, re-sealed.
Duān was again demoted to Vice Governor-General,
and Jìng was made Governor-General of the Southern River.
It was blocked in the first month of the following year.
In the winter of that year,
a crushed stone-slab slope was built at Gāoyàn.
In the fifteenth year, eighth month,
Duān again became Governor-General of the Southern River,
and the Vice Governor-General position was abolished.
In the eleventh month,
strong winds and surging waves
breached over three thousand *zhàng* of brick and stone dikes at the Rén, Yì, and Zhì three dams belonging to Shānxū,
and over one thousand seven hundred *zhàng* of brick and stone dikes belonging to Gāoyàn.
Duān initiated the opening of the Dàbà at Gāoyóu Chēluó and various gates and dams downstream leading to the Jiāng River,
and first blocked the Rén and Zhì dams to release the water flow.
At that time, Jìng was recovering from illness at home,
and the Emperor sought his advice on the course of action.
Jìng stated that the Yì dam should be uniformly blocked,
and the stone works at Gāoyàn especially needed to be completed before the great flood season next year.
The Emperor praised his pertinent remarks.
Soon after,
the Rén, Yì, and Zhì three dams and Mǎgǎng were all blocked,
and the river returned to its main channel into the sea.
In the fourth month of the following year,
Mǎgǎng breached again.
In the fifth month,
the Wángyíng diversion dam collapsed.
In the seventh month,
the flood breached Miánguǎishān in northern Pī and Lǐjiālóu in southern Xiāo.
In the twelfth month,
the Wángyíng diversion dam was blocked.
In the seventeenth year, second month,
Lǐjiālóu was also blocked.
In the eighteenth year, ninth month,
the flood breached Suīzhōu and Xuějiālóu in southern Suī, and Dīngjiāzhuāng in northern Táo,
and Lǐ Hēngtè, the Governor-General of the Eastern River, was stripped of his position,
replaced by Jūnyuán.
In the first month of the following year,
Jūnyuán was recalled to the capital,
and Jìng was again appointed Governor-General of the Eastern River
to manage the works at Suī.
It was blocked in the second month of the twentieth year.
In the twenty-third year, sixth month,
it overflowed at Yúchéng.
In the twenty-fourth year, seventh month,
it overflowed at Yífēng and Lányáng,
then again at Xiángfú, Chénliú, and Zhōngmóu,
and Yè Guāncháo was stripped of his position,
replaced by Lǐ Hóngbīn as Governor-General of the Eastern River.
Jìng, then Minister of Personnel,
went with him to consult on the arrangements.
Soon after,
Chénliú, Xiángfú, and Zhōngmóu were all blocked,
but the Lǚdī at Wǔzhì breached,
and Guāncháo successively blocked five channels.
Then the Mǎyíng dam breached,
and the current flowed eastward,
cutting through the Grand Canal to the Dàqīnghé,
dividing into two branches to enter the sea.
The breach at Yífēng soon dried up.
The Emperor ordered Guāncháo to be paraded in a cangue at the river bank.
Jūnyuán, as Grand Secretary, together with Minister Nàyànbǎo, conducted an inspection.
Nàyànbǎo remained to supervise the works at Mǎyíng dam.
For a long time,
the dam foundation remained unstable,
and Hóngbīn was reprimanded,
then resigned, claiming unfamiliarity with river affairs.
The Emperor, enraged,
stripped him of his position,
and Guāncháo again became Governor-General of the Eastern River.
In the twenty-fifth year, third month,
the Mǎyíng breach was blocked,
and the River Gods Jīnlóng Dàwáng, Huáng Dàwáng, and Zhū Dàwáng were given additional titles.
In that month, Yífēng again overflowed and collapsed,
and Guāncháo and Qíshàn, the Governor of Yù, were stripped of their positions.
When Xuānzōng ascended the throne,
Jìng and Nàyànbǎo were again ordered to the site to manage the works,
which were blocked in the twelfth month.
In the first year of the Dàoguāng reign (1821),
Wú Xuǎn, the Right Vice Minister of the Board of Rites, stated:
“According to a letter from Censor Wáng Yúnjǐn,
last winter, when he returned to his native place and crossed the river,
he observed that in the Yuánwǔ and Yángwǔ areas,
the dikes were as high as ridges,
while the land inside the dikes was very low.
Previously, the dikes were about one zhàng and eight chǐ higher than the shoals.
Since the breach at Mǎyíngbà,
the shoals have silted up,
and the dikes are now only eight or nine chǐ higher than the shoals.
If the dikes are not urgently raised,
it is feared that during the summer floods,
there will inevitably be a risk of the dikes being overflowed.”
The Emperor ordered Zhāng Wénhào, the Grand Canal Governor, to jointly inspect the situation with Yáo Zǔtóng, the Governor of Hénán.
In the third year (1823),
Sūn Yùtíng, the Grand Canal Governor of Jiāngnán,
and Lí Shìxù, the Grand Canal Governor, reinforced the large dikes on both banks of the Southern River,
ordering them to be four to five chǐ higher than the high-water mark of the flood season.
Except for places where work was ongoing or at critical junctures where the dike tops were to be separately assessed for widening,
the rest were to be standardized at one zhàng and five chǐ or two zhàng.
The work was completed in the fifth month.
In the eleventh month of the fourth year (1824),
a great wind
caused breaches at the thirteen fortresses of Gāoyàn and
destroyed over eleven thousand zhàng of stone dikes at Xīlàng'ān near Zhōoqiáo in Xúyí,
stripping Wénhào of his post.
Yán Lǎng was appointed to oversee the Southern River,
and Grand Secretary Wén Fú and Wāng Tíngzhēn were dispatched to rush to the site for inspection.
Pān Xī'ēn, a侍講學士 (Shìjiǎng Xuéshì), stated:
“Storing clear water to combat yellow water
is a long-standing established method.
When a major flood is imminent,
the Yùhuángbà (Yellow Water Dam) is urgently blocked
to force the yellow water to flow eastward with full force.
Now, Wénhào delayed blocking this dam,
causing the Yellow River to backflow,
resulting in such a huge disaster.
Furthermore, if one wants to reduce the discharge,
it should be done downstream.
Yet, he rashly opened the Xiángfú floodgate
to discharge yellow water into the lake.
With the dam mouth already being inundated from below,
and the floodgate mouth again being inundated from above,
the yellow water had no outlet,
and the lake bed became extremely high,
causing unspeakable harm.”
Soon after, Wén Fú and others also made the same argument.
Wénhào was exiled.
Yùtíng was stripped of his post but retained in office.
In the twelfth month,
the breaches at the thirteen fortresses and Xīlàng'ān were both plugged.
In the tenth month of the fifth year (1825),
Zhāng Jǐng, the Governor-General of the Eastern River, stated:
“From ancient times, during the summer and autumn floods,
river officials would rush about frantically,
unable to cope with rescue efforts.
Once the water receded,
they would consider the present situation safe,
no longer seeking strategies to dredge the river channel,
gradually leading to the clear water being unable to flow smoothly,
and the riverbed rising daily.
The dike body would increasingly grow,
leaving cities, towns, and residents
all below the water level.
They relied solely on accumulated annual funds
to elevate the river in the highest places.”
The Emperor praised his words for striking at the heart of current弊病 (bìbìng).
Initially,
Qí Shàn and others had proposed changing the river mouth to reduce yellow water and using stone slopes to retain clear water.
By this time,
Jǐng stated that the mouth of the Guànhé had been changed and breached repeatedly,
so it should not be altered lightly.
Even regarding the crushed stone flat slopes,
there were discussions about their potential drawbacks.
It was
especially necessary to deliberate carefully.
That month, the reinforcement of the dikes, weirs, dams, and revetments of the thirteen offices in Hénán, and the Cáo River and Liáng River two offices in Shāndōng,
were all undertaken at Jǐng’s request.
In the spring of the sixth year (1826),
the river flooded again.
The Emperor ordered Jǐng to jointly inspect the river mouth with Qí Shàn and Lǎng.
Qí Shàn and Lǎng knew that the river mouth could not be changed,
so they presented five proposals,
all temporary remedial measures.
Jǐng stated:
“Upon inspection of the downstream,
the river suffered from being overly full,
with silted shoals blocking it and being difficult to dredge.
The river mouth could not be altered.
I request that a new dike be built on the north bank below the Dōngmén works at Āndōng,
changing the north dike into a south dike,
separated by eight to ten lǐ.
A diversion channel should be dug in between,
guiding the river along the north side of the old river to Sīwǎngbīn before entering the sea.
The river water level inside the dike is one zhàng and five or six chǐ higher than the shoals.
If the diversion channel is dug one zhàng deep,
the difference in water levels would be nearly three zhàng,
making the situation favorable.
From the Dōngmén works to the Yùhuángbà is sixty lǐ.
With the outlet now clear,
the upstream water level could drop by four or five chǐ.
Once the yellow water recedes, the Yùhuángbà can be opened.
By confining the clear water with dams
and diverting it,
it can be used to scour the yellow water,
eroding all the bottom silt.
The yellow water level could drop by over one zhàng.
With seven or eight chǐ of water stored in the lake,
it would already be at a commanding height,
making the stone works easier to maintain.”
The Emperor approved his plan.
Consequently, Lǎng was held responsible for the obstruction and removal of the new works at Yàn and Xúyí,
demoted to a third-rank official, and transferred to act as Governor of the Eastern River.
Jǐng was appointed Governor of the Southern River,
with Pān Xī'ēn, the Intendant of Huáiyáng, as his deputy,
to manage these affairs.
However, Qí Shàn, believing that changing the river was not a good plan,
requested the opening of the Wángjiāyíng diversion dam,
to deeply dredge and clear the main river,
release clear water for scouring,
and then block the dam again to guide the yellow water back to the main river.
This was already approved for implementation,
when Yáng Xuān, a Supervising Censor, stated:
“During the Jiāqìng reign, when the Wángjiāyíng diversion dam was opened,
both upstream and downstream prefectures and counties suffered disasters.
If it only reduced yellow water without diverting the current,
why would there be a request for relief and compensation?
Now, the proposal to open the diversion dam
even anticipates matters of relief and blocking the mouth,
which is no different from the previous situation.
Blockage downstream and collapse upstream must be prevented.”
The matter was referred to the Grand Canal Governor of Jiāngnán and the Grand Canal Governor for discussion.
Jǐng's initial proposal to change the river at Āndōng
was at the time obstructed by those who said that there were old scattered stones outside the Dōngmén works’ fascine,
right at the 'throat',
which might cause obstruction.
Jǐng argued that at the stony areas, over a thousand square units of Wú workmanship scattered stones could be cleared,
and as long as it was cleared above and below,
it would certainly not impede the entire river.
However, the objectors remained doubtful.
When Jǐng saw Xuān’s memorial,
he reiterated:
“During the Jiāqìng period, after the diversion dam encountered water,
the yellow water still backflowed the following year.
Now the riverbed is silted up by one zhàng and four or five chǐ,
not as deeply clear as it was then.
Furthermore, there are many hidden dangers in the stone works of Hónghú.
In the second month of this year,
with a water depth of one zhàng two chǐ eight cùn,
many parts were already dislodged by the wind.
After autumn, the lake water can only be stored up to three zhàng.
In winter, it depletes without increasing.
When the heavy transport passes next year,
the yellow water will surely only be two zhàng eight or nine chǐ,
with the clear water only one chǐ higher than the yellow.
If the yellow water rises higher,
it will immediately cause backflow.
The riverbed outside the Yùhuángbà has risen,
silting up transport routes and the lake,
causing no small harm.
Moreover, the accumulated water in Hǎizhōu has not receded,
and the distant dike of the Yán River is high,
making the outlet not smooth.
After opening the dam, the river will surely rise,
only deepening the disaster for the four prefectures
and doing nothing to remedy the entire river’s problem.
I request that a north dike be built outside the Lǐgōng distant dike of Shān'ān Hall,
above the Āndōng Dōngmén works, below the diversion dam,
sloping eastward,
and still connecting with the previously proposed river alteration dike project,
extending it by over seven thousand zhàng,
and diverting the river to enter the main river at Bātào.
The old dike from Lǐgōng to Bātào is forty-one thousand zhàng long.
By building a straight dike,
it would only be thirty-two thousand odd zhàng long,
which would avoid the obstruction of the scattered stones at Dōngmén.
With the river channel lowered and the clear water level raised,
grain transport would naturally benefit.
The Grand Canal Governor insists that since the opening of the diversion dam has already been decreed,
he cannot simply change plans based on a bystander’s words,
and he listed seven difficulties to refute my proposal.
I have already responded to each point.”
When the memorial was submitted,
the Emperor ultimately considered changing the river a novel undertaking,
and followed Qí Shàn’s proposal.
In the seventh month of the eleventh year,
the Yánghé Tīng's fourteen forts and Mǎpéngwān were breached.
In the twelfth month, they were closed.
In the eighth month of the twelfth year,
Xiángfú was breached.
In the ninth month,
Chén Ruì, a rogue villager from Táoyuán, taking advantage of the overflowing river water,
gathered a crowd to steal and dig open the large dike at Yújiāwān,
to let the silt fertilize their fields.
This caused a wide breach,
diverting the entire flow into the lake.
Tián Ruì, the Táonán Sub-Prefect, and others were stripped of their posts and banished to the frontier.
In the same month, Xiángfú was closed.
In the first month of the following year,
Yújiāwān was closed.
In the fifteenth year,
Lì Yùměi was appointed Governor-General of the Eastern River.
At that time, the Yuánwǔ flood-diversion channel received water over three hundred *zhàng* wide,
flowed for more than forty *lǐ*,
and then re-entered the main river at the tail of the Yángwǔ flood-diversion channel,
where it converged with the Qìn River and the waters from Wǔzhì and Xíngzé shoals, all flowing under the dike.
The two channels had no previous engineering works,
thus there were no straw materials.
With water on both the north and south sides of the dike,
it was impossible to get earth to build it.
Yùměi tried the method of throwing bricks,
forming dams by throwing bricks at the points of impact.
Scarcely had more than sixty dams been completed
when a great storm arrived.
The branch river's head and tail breached,
but the dams remained intact.
Repeated trials all proved effective.
He then requested to reduce the straw and stone silver and allocate funds for brick prices,
ordering residents along the river to set up kilns to burn bricks.
Each cubic *shí* of stone could purchase two cubic *fāng* of bricks.
After several years of implementation,
the treasury saved over 1.3 million,
and the works became more solid.
However, some who found this inconvenient
raised objections.
Thereupon, Censor Lǐ Chún requested to stop burning bricks.
The Emperor dispatched Chún to accompany Grand Secretary Jìngzhēng for an on-site inspection.
Ultimately, it was decided that bricks could not be relied upon when the current was deep and swift,
and so the practice was stopped.
In the nineteenth year,
Yùměi again argued that brickwork was effective and cost-saving,
and it was then permitted to purchase five thousand *fāng* of bricks each for the Mǎyíng and Xíngyuán dikes on the north bank,
and the Xiángfú Xiàxùn and Chénliú Xùn on the south bank, for future use.
In the sixth month of the twenty-first year,
Xiángfú was breached,
the main current was entirely diverted,
and the provincial capital was surrounded by water.
River Governor Wén Chōng requested to follow the example of the Suī project's breached mouth and temporarily postpone the closure and construction.
Grand Secretary Wáng Dǐng and Commissioner of the Office of Transmission Huìchéng were dispatched to investigate and deliberate.
Wén Chōng further requested to relocate the provincial seat,
and the Emperor ordered him to consult with Henan Governor Niú Jiàn for investigation and deliberation.
At that time, the river flow turned from Guīdé and Chénzhōu into the Wō River, converging with the Huái River and flowing into Hóngzé Hú,
dismantling and extending the Yùhuáng and Shùqīng dams,
which was still insufficient for discharge.
The Lǐ, Zhì, and Rén dams were also extended,
and the Yì River was also opened for discharge.
In the eighth month,
Jiàn stated that since the Báilù festival had passed,
the water level was gradually falling,
and the city walls would be safe.
It was therefore inappropriate to lightly discuss relocation.
Dǐng and others said:
"River courses change with time,
and there has never been a perfect strategy since ancient times.
However, there is absolutely no logic in a breach remaining unclosed, or in a closure not being expedited.
As Wén Chōng said,
waiting one or two years to close it,
and moreover citing the Suī project as evidence—
upon investigation, if the Yellow River water flowing through Ānhuī converges into Hóngzé,
and discharge is insufficient,
then Gāoyàn would be endangered,
and Huáiyáng would become a vast flood.
Furthermore, where the new river passes,
new dikes must be built,
and the costs are immeasurable.
Even if the project were fortunately completed,
during this period of one or two years,
hundreds of thousands of people in dozens of prefectures and counties would be displaced.
How can such a thought be entertained?
Moreover, the Suī project's breached mouth is different from this.
The river official's proposal
is absolutely unfeasible."
Upon receiving the memorial,
Wén Chōng was dismissed from his post,
and paraded in a cage by the river.
Zhū Xiāng succeeded him.
In the twenty-second year,
Xiángfú was closed,
using over 6 million in treasury funds.
Dǐng was promoted to Grand Tutor of the Crown Prince.
In the seventh month,
Táoyuán's fifteenth fort and Xiāojiāzhuāng were breached,
and the current flowed through the canal via the Liùtánghé.
Before long,
the fifteenth fort accumulated silt,
and the Xiāojiāzhuāng breach widened to over one hundred ninety *zhàng*,
diverting the main current
and cutting off the flow of the main river.
River Governor Lín Qìng intended to change the course of the river.
Grand Secretary Jìngzhēng and Liáo Hóngquán were dispatched to investigate.
Jìngzhēng and others stated that
changing the river course would impede the transport route.
The only option was to seasonally block the breach,
guide the water back to its original course,
and after the military ships returned empty next year,
build a dam to close the breach.
This was adopted.
In the eleventh month,
Pān Xī'ēn, Vice Minister of Personnel, was appointed Governor-General of the Southern River.
In the twenty-third year,
Censor Léi Yǐchéng stated that
there was no need to close the breach,
and requested to turn the old course into a branch
to facilitate the transport route.
This was sent to Xī'ēn for investigation and deliberation.
Xī'ēn stated that the irrigation mouth was not a suitable place for a river,
and there was no reason to change the river course on the north bank.
He dared not lightly discuss major changes,
and the grain boats should continue to pass through the Middle River and irrigation ponds.
The Emperor agreed,
and further ordered Vice Minister Chéng Gāng and the Prefect of Shùntiān, Lǐ Dé, to jointly investigate.
In the sixth month,
Zhōngmóu was breached,
and the water flowed towards Zhūxiānzhèn,
passing through Tōngxǔ, Fúgōu, and Tàikāng to enter the Wō River and converge with the Huái River.
Jìngzhēng and others were again dispatched for investigation,
and Zhōng Xiáng was appointed Governor-General of the Eastern River,
with Hóngquán supervising the works.
Soon after, Grand Secretary Lín Kuí replaced Jìngzhēng.
In the first month of the twenty-fourth year,
there was a great wind,
and the dam works were disturbed.
Soon the eastern dam lost five sections consecutively.
Lín Kuí and others were demoted and dismissed in varying degrees,
but remained to supervise the works.
In the seventh month,
the Emperor, noting that military expenses and river works were concentrated at the same time in recent years,
and funds were strained,
intended to postpone construction until the autumn of next year.
Zhōng Xiáng and others strongly argued against this.
In the twelfth month, it was closed,
using over 11.9 million in treasury funds.
In the sixth month of the twenty-ninth year,
Wúchéng was breached.
In the tenth month,
Vice Minister Fú Jì was ordered to investigate
and jointly manage the closure.
In the intercalary eighth month of the first year of Xiánfēng,
Fēngběi Xiàxùn's three forts were breached,
the main current was entirely diverted,
and the main river flow was cut off.
At that time, Vice Minister Ruìcháng was overseeing the provincial examination in Jiāngnán.
He was ordered to proceed to investigate after the examination.
Chá Wénjīng, Provincial Surveillance Commissioner of Fújiàn, was also ordered to rush to assist.
In the first month of the third year,
Fēngběi's three forts were closed.
An imperial decree ordered the construction of a river god temple,
following the request of River Governor Yáng Yǐzēng.
In the fifth month, there was heavy rain,
and the water rose with a swift current.
The Fēngběi Great Dam again collapsed by over thirty *zhàng*.
The Emperor held Yǐzēng and the responsible construction officials accountable, ordering them to pay double compensation.
In the fifth year, sixth month,
the Lányáng copper tile embankment was breached.
The flow diverted through Chángyuán and Dōngmíng to Zhāngqiū,
piercing the Grand Canal to enter the Dàqīng Hé and flow into the sea,
while the main river ceased to flow.
The emperor, mindful that military affairs were not yet settled
and military provisions were insufficient,
thought that if the situation could be exploited to guide the Yellow River,
allowing its flow to smoothly enter the sea,
then the Lányáng breach could be temporarily left unrepaired.
The matter was sent down to the Director-General of River Conservancy, Lǐ Jūn, for investigation and report.
Jūn then presented three proposals:
"Firstly, constructing dikes along the river.
To build dikes spanning over a thousand *lǐ* from east to west
would incur immeasurable costs;
how could such a proposal be lightly made?
Except for areas where the river approaches city walls, where dikes and dams must be built for defense,
for the rest, I propose to determine the locations for dikes
based on the extent of the overflowing water,
and encourage the populace to construct them.
They should be no more than three *chǐ* high.
When the water is low, they will serve to obstruct it;
when the water is high, it will be allowed to flow over.
Dispersed water has less force,
and as it overflows, it deposits silt,
gradually raising the ground level
and transforming sandy wasteland into fertile soil.
Secondly, cutting off bends and sandbars.
The river naturally tends to form bends,
and whenever the water rises,
it surges violently at the bends and frequently breaches its banks.
Therefore, facing the bends,
the populace should be encouraged to cut away the sandbars
to widen the river channel.
When the water rises, it can then scour the channel straight,
making the downstream flow smoother,
and preventing the risk of the river eddying around sandbars and causing breaches.
Thirdly, blocking off tributaries.
Currently, the Yellow River is overflowing,
and since it is impossible to construct strong dikes to confine its flow,
nor to dredge diversion channels to reduce its force,
it is advisable, taking advantage of the weaker water flow and calmer currents in winter,
to encourage the populace to build dams to block the flow.
Then, across the downstream channels and gullies, construct earthen grids
rising several *chǐ* high.
When the overflowing water re-enters,
it will have no source from above
and no outlet below,
hopefully leading to its gradual siltation into flat land."
The Governor of Shāndōng, Chóng'ēn, also made similar remarks.
The emperor ordered the Directors-General and Governors of Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Hénán to handle the matter appropriately and encourage its implementation.
In the eleventh year,
Censor Xuē Shūtáng stated:
"Since the Yellow River changed its course,
there are no longer any works to repair in the southern part of the river.
I request the abolition of the Director-General of the Southern River and related officials."
The matter was sent down for deliberation by court officials.
Vice Minister Shěn Zhàolín stated:
"River guidance began with Dà Yǔ.
The old channels of the Nine Rivers were all in Shāndōng,
with the entry to the sea at present-day Cāngzhōu.
Thus, the river mentioned in the *Yǔ Gòng*
indeed flowed northeast into the sea.
Since the Hàn dynasty, during Wáng Mǎng's time, the river shifted to enter the sea at Qiānchéng,
and Yǔ's old channel was lost.
From the Eastern Hàn through the Suí and Táng dynasties,
there were no changes.
During the reign of Sòng Shénzōng,
the river divided into northern and southern branches flowing in parallel,
with the northern branch entering the sea via the Běiqīng Hé.
This is the present-day Dàqīng Hé.
During the Zhìyuán era of the Yuán dynasty,
the Huìtōng Hé was completed,
and fearing that the northern flow of the river would obstruct transportation,
the northern flow was blocked.
For the past five or six hundred years,
whenever the river breached to the north,
it was always diverted back to the south.
Those who argue that once the river enters the Grand Canal,
it will inevitably carry mud and sand into the sea,
and the canal itself will silt up,
thus, in accordance with the river's nature, a northern course is advisable.
In the Qiánlóng reign,
Sūn Jiāgàn's memorial requesting the opening of a flood diversion channel into the Dàqīng Hé
explained this in great detail,
sufficient to dispel doubts about the northern flow obstructing transportation.
If the river enters the Dàqīng Hé,
flowing into the sea via Lìjīn,
this is precisely the course the Yellow River has now adopted.
Currently, east of Zhāngqiū,
from Yúshān to the Lìjīn estuary,
all civilian dikes have been constructed.
Only north of Lányí and south of Zhāngqiū,
where the river broke its banks,
it captured the Zhàowáng Hé and the old diversion channel,
flooding the plains,
and fields and homes have long been submerged.
The old dike at Gāojiālín in Zhāngqiū
is severely damaged,
making its repair a monumental undertaking.
For Dōngmíng, Chángyuán, Hézé, and Yùnchéng,
the repair and construction are easier than at Zhāngqiū.
It is advisable at this time to follow the nature of the water,
allowing it to flow into the sea via the Dàqīng Hé,
and instruct local gentry and commoners to carefully plan and implement measures,
whether it involves opening diversion channels
or constructing dikes and dams,
all to commence when the water recedes.
When the river follows a smooth course,
the people will joyfully cultivate their fields,
the land tax deficit can be recovered,
and annual relief efforts can be ceased.
By thereupon abolishing the Director-General of the Southern River and related officials,
hundreds of thousands of taels of annual treasury funds can be saved,
and the thousands of *lǐ* of land in the Guīdé, Xú, and Huái areas
can all be transformed into fertile soil,
gradually allowing for planting and tax collection.
This seems to be a single action achieving multiple benefits."

The matter was sent down to Director-General of Zhílì Héngfú, Governor of Shāndōng Wényù, Governor of Hénán Qìnglián, and Director-General of the Eastern River Huáng Zàntāng for investigation and deliberation.
In the sixth month,
the Director-General of the Southern River was abolished,
along with the various departmental offices of Huáiyáng, Huáihǎi, Fēngběi, Xiāonán, Sùnán, Sùběi, Táonán, and Táoběi.
In their place, the Huáiyáng Xúhǎi Military Preparation Circuit was established,
also overseeing river affairs.
In the second year of Tóngzhì (1863),
the five sub-prefectures of Lányí, Yísuī, Suīníng, Shāngyú, and Cáokǎo were again made provincial.
In the sixth month,
all the sub-prefectures under Shàngnán were inundated,
with water flowing down from Lányáng.
Villages that had emerged dry in Zhílì and Dōng provinces
were submerged again.
Water reached the city walls in the prefectures and counties of Hézé, Dōngmíng, Pú, Fàn, Qíhé, and Lìjīn.
Acting River Governor Tán Tíngxiāng memorialized, saying:
"The river has already shifted northwards.
Only civilian dikes can hold back the water.
There has never been any discussion about dredging,
and I fear that silt will gradually accumulate.
If the estuary experiences even slight obstruction,
the situation will become even more difficult.
I have investigated that there was an old golden dike in the Pú and Fàn area.
When a former minister served as the Governor of Dōng,
methods were devised to repair and build it,
but it was soon breached again.
Upstream, at the point where it connects to Kāizhōu in Zhílì, there were also breaches.
If Kāizhōu is not repaired,
building in Pú and Fàn will be useless.
The dikes in Dōng and Cháng,
and the embankments in Kāi and Pú,
must be repaired by raising funds and supervising the populace,
so that cities can be protected and ancestral tombs preserved.
Furthermore, since no dedicated river officials have been appointed,
it is crucial for local officials along the river to supervise repairs,
and to encourage fundraising and collection
to supplement the insufficient efforts of the people.

I request that the Governor-General of Zhílì and the Governor of Dōng be instructed to promptly assign officials to cooperate with the respective prefectures and counties to properly manage the areas inundated downstream of Lányáng."
This was approved.
In the twelfth month, he memorialized again, saying:
"This year, the summer and autumn rains were continuous,
and the source flow was
extraordinarily abundant.
One current flowed directly to Kāizhōu,
another veered towards Dìngtáo, Cáo, and Shàn.
Hù province, having dikes and dams,
fortunately remained intact.
Zhílì and Dōng, however, had none,
and could not but let the waters overflow.
Half a year has passed,
but no plans have been heard from Zhílì.
The breach in Kāizhōu
has also not been addressed with construction.
As for Shāndōng, the damage was particularly severe.
Whether to build up dikes and embankments,
or to dredge branch rivers,
no definite plan has been agreed upon.
The golden dike in Púzhōu
also could not be built
because Kāi had not started work.
The spring flood season is fast approaching;
how will it be defended against?
Your subject dispatched the Canal Daotai Zōng Jìchén to survey,
going all the way to Tiěmén Guān in Lìjīn,
to measure the water flow.
It was as deep as six or seven *zhàng*,
indicating that the outflow was not obstructed.
Yet upstream, water still overflowed everywhere,
meaning that the Dàqīnghé riverbed is too narrow to contain it.
Breaches in civilian dikes in Pútái, Qídōng, Jìyáng, Chángqīng, Píngyīn, and Féichéng,
wide by several *zhàng* or dozens of *zhàng*,
number no less than thirty or forty places.
If they are not repaired,
next year will see the same inundation.
Therefore, to ensure lasting stability downstream,
branch channels must first be opened to reduce the floodwaters,
only then can efforts be successful.
The nearby Túhài and Mǎjiá rivers must be dredged by all means,
so that water can be diverted.
Then, all breaches can be blocked,
and dams built to protect the nearby city walls from the water.
This is what must be attended to first for the downstream of Dàqīnghé.
As for the golden dikes in Kāi and Pú, and Shǐjiā Dī connecting to Hézé,
they must first be blocked and built up,
and old embankments reinforced,
selecting key areas for repair.
This is what must be planned first for the upstream of Dàqīnghé."
This was again referred to Governor-General Liú Chángyòu of Zhílì and Governor Yán Jìngmíng of Dōng for joint deliberation.
In the third month of the following year,
as Púzhōu was directly impacted by the river,
Jìngmíng's request was granted
to relocate the administration to the old city
and build dikes for defense.
In the seventh month of the fifth year,
the Hújiātún of Shàngnán Sub-prefecture was breached.
Chángyòu said:
"The current flows heavily towards the northwest,
and the newly built golden dikes
were entirely scoured away.
Kāizhōu saw several branch rivers breached,
from Dùjiāzhài in Kāi and Huá to Chénjiāzhuāng at the Kāi and Pú border,
five dangerous sections,
totaling over nine thousand six hundred *zhàng* in length,
all need to be thickened and heightened
to provide defense.
