However, the upstream is in Yù,
and the downstream is in Dōng;
this cannot be handled by Zhílì province alone.
The three provinces should jointly plan for comprehensive repairs,
then establish patrol stations,
allocate funds and prepare materials,
to ensure lasting peace with one effort.
Since the river changed its course,
the dike works in Zhílì should also fall under the jurisdiction of the River Governor,
making him the River Governor for the three provinces of Yù, Zhílì, and Dōng,
to centralize responsibility."
Upon receipt of the memorial,
River Governor Sū Tíngkuí was ordered to survey
and deliberate with the Governors-General and Governors of the three provinces.
In the sixth month of the seventh year,
the Shíbǎo in Xíngzé was breached,
and Wǔzhì's Zhàofán Cūn was also inundated.
The water flowed down to Yǐng and Shòu, entering Hóngzé Hú.
Vice Minister Hú Jiāyù said:
"It is not advisable to merely block the new Xíngzé mouth and dredge the old Lányáng mouth.
Instead, one should emulate the ancient method of deploying troops for river management.
Instruct all generals to supervise the dredging of the old river in sections,
ensuring uniform depth throughout.
Then, release the upstream water,
drawing the current eastward.
This way, the disaster in Hénán will not shift to Hébĕi,
and river management will also be canal management."
This was referred to Governor-General Zēng Guófān of Zhílì, Governor Lǐ Hànzhāng of È, Governor Mǎ Xīnyí of Jiāng, Grain Transport Governor Zhāng Zhīwàn,
and the River Governor, as well as the Governors of Jiāngsū, Hénán, Shāndōng, and Ānhuī for proper deliberation.
Guófān and others said:
"Considering the current circumstances,
there are three reasons why the river cannot be immediately restored to its former course.
The breach at Lányáng has existed for fourteen years.
From Tóngwǎxiāng down to Yúntīguān,
the dikes on both banks extend for over a thousand *lǐ*.
Due to long neglect of repairs,
the dikes have collapsed and the river has silted up.
If we now wish to dredge it deep and build it high as before,
it would probably require tens of millions of *jīn* to complete.
Moreover, sub-prefectural and battalion offices have long been abolished,
and soldiers and laborers dispersed.
To re-establish them all
would require storing materials,
constructing *sǎo* and dams,
and planning for disaster prevention costs,
which would again require millions of *jīn* annually.
At a time when military affairs have just settled,
and the treasury is empty,
how can such a huge sum be raised?
This is the first reason.
Xíngzé is located upstream;
in terms of strategic position, Xíngzé should naturally be blocked first,
making it difficult to undertake the Lán project simultaneously.
If the Xíng mouth could draw away the entire Yellow River,
then the Lán project could proceed in dry conditions.
However, the Xíng mouth diverts little flow,
and the main current still flows directly from the Lán mouth into the sea at Lìjīn.
The width of its water surface,
the depth of its pools,
and the difficulty of construction
are several times greater than the Xíng project.
There is no foreseeable date for blocking the Xíng project,
and even less certainty for the Lán project.
The original memorial's proposal to open the old river
and draw the current eastward
seems too simplistic.
Moreover, spring is rapidly approaching, making construction already difficult.
This is the second reason.
The Han breached at Suānzǎo,
then again at Hùzǐ,
which marked the beginning of deploying troops for river management.
During the Yuán and Míng dynasties, tens of thousands of able-bodied men were conscripted for labor.
Currently, in Zhílì, Dōng, Jiāng, and Yù, the Nian rebels have just been suppressed,
but bandits and disbanded soldiers still require constant vigilance everywhere.
The remaining brave battalions
certainly cannot all be sent to the riverbanks,
nor would they be sufficient for the dredging work.
If hundreds of thousands more able-bodied men were to be recruited,
gathered along thousands of *lǐ* of the Yellow River,
improper management
could lead to further incidents,
which is even more concerning.
This is the third reason.
We should wait until the national treasury is full
before discussing such a large undertaking.
Adapting to the times,
the only course of action is to urgently block the Xíng project,
as a plan to preserve the downstream areas of Yù, Wǎn, and Huái-Yáng."
The Emperor approved this.
In the first month of the eighth year,
Xíngzé was blocked.
In the eighth month of the tenth year,
the Houjiālín breach in Yùnchéng was opened.
It flowed east into Nánwàng Hú.
Then, via the Zhào Wáng and Niúláng rivers in Wénshàng, Jiāxiáng, and Jìníng,
it flowed directly southeast,
entering Nányáng Hú.
At this time, Tíngkuí was summoned back to the capital,
and the new river director, Qíao Sōngnián, was ordered to collaborate with the Eastern Governor, Dīng Bǎozhēn, to investigate and manage the situation.
Bǎozhēn was on leave due to illness,
so he accompanied Acting Governor Wén Bīn to the site to inspect the works.
Wén Bīn said:
"The river minister is far away in Yùshěng (Hénán Province).
If we have to consult back and forth,
I fear it will delay this crucial project.
One approach is to send an urgent dispatch to the river minister to select and appoint dam managers,
along with officers and clerks to manage the primary and miscellaneous material factories,
as well as skilled officers, soldiers, and artisans familiar with engineering works.
They should bring their tools
and arrive in the east within the year.
Another approach is for your minister to procure the necessary materials
to ensure they are readily available."
The Emperor admonished Sōngnián to start the work on schedule.
Sōngnián replied that he had already instructed the original estimation committee members and personnel familiar with the project to go east and await orders,
and also ordered the procurement of bamboo cables
and the hiring of bundled and reinforced boats to be ready for use.
However, as Lìchūn (Start of Spring) had already passed,
and spring waters would surge momentarily,
there was little certainty in carrying out the work.
He also sent a letter to Wén Bīn to take charge of the matter.
Wén Bīn could not decide.
Bǎozhēn, despite his illness, attended to his duties.
He said:
"The river minister's duty is to oversee riverways,
and a frontier minister's responsibility is to govern the locality.
Both bear inescapable responsibilities.
Yet Sōngnián indiscriminately shifts all responsibility to the locality,
I do not understand his intention.
Lìchūn has already passed.
If we wait for his definite word to decide what to do,
I fear it will delay this crucial project.
Furthermore, if this breach is not plugged,
it will inevitably flood over ten prefectures and counties in Cáo, Yǎn, and Jì.
If it continues to flow south,
then the lower reaches of Qīng, Huái, and Yǔ will be even more critically affected.
Since Sōngnián has deliberately intended to shirk responsibility,
if your minister avoids the suspicion of 'transgressing one's authority' (yuè zǔ),
and procrastinates,
it truly will be an irreversible situation.
Therefore, I must, despite my illness, cancel my leave,
personally proceed to the worksite,
select a date to commence work.
Once the officers and clerks dispatched by Sōngnián arrive at the site,
I will immediately hold them responsible for managing the project entirely,
to complete the work on schedule
and preserve the overall situation.
I request an exceptional commendation
to inspire and encourage others.
Should anyone dare to outwardly comply but inwardly defy,
intentionally cause delay,
once verified,
I request that appropriate action be taken,
and that such officers and clerks be executed at the worksite,
as a warning to those who deceive superiors and harm the populace."
The Emperor praised his courage in undertaking the responsibility,
and also admonished Sōngnián to cooperate sincerely,
and not to be too quick to blame.
In the second month of the eleventh year,
Houjiālín was sealed,
and Bǎozhēn was granted a generous reward.
Previously, Assistant Magistrate Jiǎng Zuòjǐn had memorialized about river and transport matters,
and the court greatly approved his suggestions,
referring them to the river, grain transport, and provincial governors for deliberation and memorialization.
Soon after,
the Houjiālín breach occurred,
and Sōngnián and Bǎozhēn's opinions clashed.
After Bǎozhēn sealed Houjiālín,
Sōngnián memorialized:
"What Zuòjǐn presented
shows outstanding insight
and can be adopted."
He further stated that "the yellow waters in the eastern region are becoming increasingly widespread,
and the transport routes are becoming increasingly silted.
It is advisable to build dikes to confine the Yellow River,
first blocking the various breaches at Huòjiāqiáo,
and also repairing the long dikes on the north and south banks,
so that the Yellow River flows towards Zhāngqiū to aid transport.
Dredge the silted sections north and south of Zhāngqiū
and repair the gates and dams
to facilitate grain transport."
The Emperor considered Sōngnián's intention to guide the situation effectively,
not without merit,
and ordered Bǎozhēn and Wén Bīn to deliberate in detail,
and not to stubbornly cling to their own views.
They soon replied, stating:
"Currently, the methods for managing the Yellow River
are either to block Tóngwǎxiāng to restore the old Huái-Xú channel,
or to build dikes in Dōngshěng (Shāndōng Province) so that it directly enters the sea via Lìjīn—these are the two policies.
However, among these two,
to consider 'building dikes to confine the Yellow River' as superior,
while delaying both upstream and downstream efforts, your minister truly does not see its feasibility.
From Tóngwǎxiāng to Mǔlìzuǐ,
a distance of over 1,300 lǐ,
to build two new dikes on the north and south,
with a calculated distance between them
of approximately ten lǐ,
excluding the currently flooded areas,
would still require abandoning tens of millions of qǐng of land,
with untold hundreds of millions of residents within.
How would they be resettled?
This is the first detriment to revenue and resources.
In Dōngshěng, along the river, there are no fewer than ten counties,
ranging from two or three lǐ to seven or eight lǐ from the water.
If Qíhé, Qídōng, Pútái, and Lìjīn
are all close to the water,
building dikes would necessitate relocation.
This is the second difficulty in construction.
The Dàqīnghé is close to the foothills of Mount Tài,
and all the water on the shady side of the mountain flows north.
Except for Xiǎoqīng and Liūmí rivers which can flow directly into the sea,
all others use Dàqīnghé as their outlet.
After constructing dikes to confine the Yellow River,
the water level would rise.
At places where water previously drained,
leaving gates risks backflow,
while blocking them leaves the water with nowhere to go.
This is the third impediment to water conservancy.
The salt fields of the Eastern Salt Administration
are located in Lìjīn, Zhānhuà, Shòuguāng, Lè'ān, and other counties,
situated on both banks of the Dàqīnghé.
Since the Yellow River flows into the sea via Dàqīng,
salt boats heavily laden,
traveling upstream against the turbulent current,
are greatly hindered.
Furthermore, the tidal flats are intermittently flooded,
causing a daily decrease in salt production,
and the sea beaches are heavily silted by the Yellow River,
making it very difficult for tides to enter.
The Eastern Salt Administration will inevitably collapse,
and private smugglers will consequently rise.
This is the fourth impediment to the salt administration.
Your minister, Bǎozhēn, responsible for the locality,
should certainly speak frankly without reservation regarding matters concerning the overall situation of the entire province.
However, if there truly were certainty in managing grain transport,
then the imperial granaries, being fundamental to the utmost plan,
should still weigh the severity of gains and losses,
and make appropriate adaptations.
Your ministers, after careful consideration and deliberation,
truly do not see its reliability,
and deeply feel its cause for concern.
It seems still best to block and close Tóngwǎxiāng to restore the old Huái-Xú channel as the correct approach."
They also presented four conveniences.
Censor Yóu Bǎichuān also stated that river and transport management should be carried out simultaneously,
and that detailed planning and proper execution were necessary.
When the memorial was submitted,
the court deliberation could not reach a decision.
Since the breach at Tóngwǎxiāng (銅瓦廂) to the east,
the Yuè (粵) and Niǎn (捻) rebels have frequently harassed Cáo (曹) and Jǐ (濟),
almost without a single day's respite.
Unable to cross the river even a step,
the defense of the north bank has a reliable basis,
which will moreover be a benefit to the Gīfǔ (畿輔) for a hundred generations.
Comparing these two situations,
although the river in the east does not require urgent treatment and the future troubles are slightly lighter,
the river returning south, even if it can be greatly managed, the future troubles will be extremely severe—this is the actual situation.
In recent times, river management has also involved canal management,
leading to a dilemma
and ultimately no lasting strategy.
Your servant humbly believes that the national grain revenue
largely comes from Sū (蘇) and Zhè (浙),
and the security of the state
especially emphasizes coastal defense.
Currently, foreign ships are gathered along the coast,
a situation unprecedented in history,
and it is no longer possible to close the country and govern ourselves.
It is perfectly fine to leverage the convenience of sea transport
to gradually expand it,
thereby broadening trade routes and augmenting military provisions.
The grain tribute from Sū (蘇) and Zhè (浙)
is now entirely transported by sea.
Your servant previously invited Chinese merchants to purchase and build steamships for transport,
which has gradually shown results,
and shipping by sea to Jīn (津)
is more convenient and faster.
As for the fact that the sea route is not always smooth,
river affairs cannot be entirely abandoned.
At this time, the method of river management
is nothing more than the ancients' saying: "Where there is water,
increase and establish dikes and embankments."
Upon inspection, north of Zhāngqiū (張秋) on the north bank,
there is the ancient Dàjīntí (大金堤) to rely on for solidity.
South of Zhāngqiū (張秋),
where the bank is high and the water deep,
the Eastern Governor should be instructed to continuously order the protection and reinforcement of the civilian dikes.
As for the civilian dikes above and below Hóujiālín (侯家林), they should follow the method of official dikes,
uniformly raising and thickening them,
which would be a more long-term plan.
Furthermore, at the breach of Tóngwǎxiāng (銅瓦廂),
the water current is eroding eastward day by day,
and in time it will surely overflow and flow south.
Please instruct Sōngnián (松年) to observe the terrain,
construct dikes and embankments accordingly,
and connect them with the dikes of Cáozhōu (曹州),
so as to provide comprehensive defense and ensure a stable course.
Regarding the old course of the South River, stretching over a thousand *lǐ*,
residents have occupied and cultivated it with abundant harvests.
Please also investigate and assess taxes
to avoid the troubles of private reclamation and disputes."
After the memorial was submitted,
the decision was made.
In the summer and autumn of that year,
breaches occurred at Jiāochū (焦丘) in Kāizhōu (開州) and Lánzhuāng (蘭莊) in Púzhōu (濮州).
Another breach occurred at Yuèxīnzhuāng (岳新莊) and Shízhuānghù (石莊戶) civilian dikes in Dōngmíng (東明).
The flow diverted towards Jīnxiāng (金鄉), Jiāxiáng (嘉祥), Sùqiān (宿遷), Shùyáng (沭陽), entering the Liùtánghé (六塘河).
Bǎozhēn (寶楨) surveyed the area and constructed a dike to block it from Zhāngjiāzhīmén (張家支門) in Yùnchéng (鄆城).
He then requested leave to visit his ancestral tomb.
In the spring of the thirteenth year,
the flow veered further south,
overflowing and becoming uncontrollable.
The Governor-General of Jiāng (江) repeatedly memorialized about the disaster.
In September,
Bǎozhēn (寶楨) returned to his post
and changed the plan to build a dam at Jiázhuāng (賈莊) in Hézé (菏澤).
Construction began in December.
In the third month of the first year of Guāngxù (光緒),
the Dōngmíng (東明) breach was blocked,
and a south dike of 250 *lǐ* was built from Lǐliánzhuāng (李連莊) downwards.
At that time, the River Governor Zēng Guóquán (曾國荃) requested the establishment of seven offices on the south bank.
The Board deliberated that it would be decided after Zhí (直), Dōng (東), and Yù (豫) had raised funds for flood defense.
In the spring of the second year,
the acting Eastern Governor Lǐ Yuánhuá (李元華) stated:
“The south dike of the Yellow River,
from Jiázhuāng (賈莊) to Dōngpíng (東平), over 200 *lǐ* in length, is complete and solid.
However, the upstream section, bordering Zhí (直) and Yù (豫),
from Xièzhài (謝寨) in Dōngmíng (東明) to Kǎochéng (考城), over 70 *lǐ* in length,
has no dikes.
This project cannot be delayed.
In previous years, the Hóujiālín (侯家林) breach was blocked,
but later, fearing high costs,
it was neglected,
leading to the Jiázhuāng (賈莊) breach.
Although the dike below Jiázhuāng (賈莊) is now solid,
if the upstream section is not repaired,
should an overflow and breach occur,
not only would all previous efforts be wasted,
but Hénán (河南), Ānhuī (安徽), and Jiāngsū (江蘇) would still suffer,
not to mention Shāndōng (山東) being the first to bear the brunt.
Your servant proposes to deploy troops
and also hire civilian laborers
to build this dike of over 70 *lǐ*.
Fearing a lack of coordination,
I have already consulted with the Governor-General of Zhí (直) and the Governor of Yù (豫) to jointly assist in the effort.
As for the people of Pú (濮) and Fàn (范),
since the Yellow River changed its course,
they have been submerged for over ten years.
After the Jiázhuāng (賈莊) breach,
there was a glimmer of hope,
but with the Jiázhuāng (賈莊) blockage,
they suffered as before.
Upon inspection, the south dike is 60 to 70 *lǐ* from the northern Jīntí (金堤).
While it can shield the capital,
it cannot protect the villages and fields of Pú (濮) and Fàn (范).
The gentry and people there wish to repair the north dike,
but their resources are insufficient.
I request appropriate subsidies.
Once completed,
officers and soldiers will be dispatched to uniformly maintain and defend it.
Over a thousand *qǐng* of land in the five counties of Pú (濮), Fàn (范), Yánggǔ (陽穀), Shòuzhāng (壽張), and Dōng'ē (東阿) can be reclaimed.
Furthermore, above Pú (濮) and Fàn (范),
there are two branches of Yellow River water.
It is proposed to draw two diversion canals
at the tail end of the new river within Shòuzhāng (壽張) and Dōng'ē (東阿) territories,
hoping to merge them into one channel.
North of the south dike and south of the Yellow River,
a small dike will be erected to constrain the water,
which can reclaim another thousand *qǐng* of land.
As for the upstream section of the north dike, eight *lǐ* of it are under Kāizhōu (開州) jurisdiction.
If it is not uniformly repaired,
not only will the north dike be in vain,
but even the Gīfǔ (畿輔) will be difficult to protect from its harm.
I have already consulted with the Governor-General of Zhí (直) to dispatch officials to assist
and complete the work properly and quickly.
However, the land occupied in Zhí (直) and Yù (豫) provides little benefit to the local residents,
while the people of Shāndōng (山東) benefit immensely.
Therefore, Shāndōng (山東) should compensate for the land value.
With the upstream section narrowed,
the downstream water flow will be swift,
which must be guarded against.
From Dōngpíng (東平) to the Lìjīn (利津) estuary, over 900 *lǐ*,
I have already instructed the prefectures and counties along the river to reinforce the civilian dikes,
providing appropriate subsidies
and using work as a form of relief.
All items combined are estimated to cost over 20 million.
This is the proposed plan for the major section of the Yellow River.”
The matter was referred to the relevant ministries.
In the fifth year,
the Saigōu in Lìchéng was breached.
The following year,
it was breached again.
In the eighth year,
the Táoyuán in Lìchéng was breached,
and it was plugged in the eleventh month.
In the ninth year,
Chén Shìjié, as the Eastern Governor, oversaw the construction of large dikes on both banks below Zhāngqiū.
At that time, Shāndōng frequently suffered from river disasters,
and court officials repeatedly raised concerns.
The Emperor dispatched Assistant Minister Yóu Bǎichuān to rush there for a joint investigation.
Bǎichuān stated:
"Those who have discussed the river hitherto
are divided between the southern course and the northern course theories.
After my detailed observation of the terrain,
it is not impossible that in the future, when faced with severe flooding in autumn and winter,
it might turn east again
and find its old channel.
If we try to divert it with human effort,
the difficulties will be insurmountable.
Firstly, after the breach of the northern dike,
it has been completely scoured away.
To build a dike and occupy that space,
the work involved is already immense.
Moreover, with the main current of the entire river flowing north,
to block the middle stream in an attempt to close the breach
would certainly cause extraordinary tremors,
and there is absolutely no certainty in managing it.
Secondly, the sand dunes beside the old channel are extremely difficult to excavate.
Furthermore, in the Xú and Hǎi area, the riverbed has dried up, exposing over a thousand *lǐ* of silted land,
which the people have fully cultivated.
If they are suddenly driven away,
how could the people willingly lose their livelihoods?
Thus, the theory of the southern course should not be deliberated upon.
As for the Dàqīnghé, it was originally the confluence of the Wén and Jǐ rivers.
Since the Yellow River water flowed into it,
at first the water still flowed within the land.
But now the riverbed is silted up and elevated,
and it suffers from the water being unable to drain.
From the upper and lower reaches of the Jǐhé,
to the north are Jǐyáng, Huìmín, Bīnzhōu, Lìjīn;
to the south are Qīngchéng, Zhāngqiū, Lìchéng, down to Zōu, Cháng, Gāo, Bó;
breaches have occurred in eleven places.
I humbly believe that the Yellow River has entered the Jǐdú for twenty-eight years.
Initially, the error was that Shāndōng had no established plans for river management,
which led the people to build dikes and embankments themselves.
Even though breaches occurred frequently,
they were unwilling to report them in memorials,
causing the disaster to reach this point.
Now, it floods for hundreds of *lǐ*,
drowning hundreds of villages.
Having traveled throughout the disaster-stricken areas,
it is a heart-wrenching and tragic sight.
I respectfully propose three methods.
First,
dredge the river channel.
When the Yellow River first entered the Jǐ,
it could still accommodate it.
But the silted deposits grow higher day by day,
and the estuary becomes even more severely blocked.
With sand silting the riverbed,
human effort is difficult to apply.
The only method is to use many boats,
each equipped with iron rakes and 'river-mixing dragons' (dredges),
to drag and scour upstream and downstream,
preventing silt from accumulating
and gradually deepening the channel.
It seems no better method of dredging exists than this.
Second,
divert and reduce the Yellow River flow.
Once the Jǐ receives the Yellow River,
its situation is precarious and cannot last.
To the north of the Dàqīnghé,
the Túhài is the closest,
the Mǎjiá is further away,
and the Líjīn is even further north.
The closest point between the Dàqīnghé and the Túhài is at Báilóngwān in Huìmín,
about ten *lǐ* apart.
If a diversion dam is built and opened here,
to divert water into the Túhàihé,
it would be relatively convenient.
Furthermore, if methods are devised to dredge the Shāhé, Kuānhé, Túnmínhé, and other rivers in between,
and introduce them into the Mǎjiá and Líjīn,
and then distribute the flow into the sea,
there should be no further worry of overflow.
Third,
urgently build longitudinal dikes.
The longitudinal dikes built by the common people
are close to the riverbank,
many do not conform to standards,
and are generally thin and weak,
also intermittent,
repeatedly collapsing.
They build them again and again,
exhausting the people's strength.
Now, it is proposed to build longitudinal dikes first on the north and south banks from Chángqīng to Lìjīn,
and then build reinforced dikes at the most critical points.
This would be about six hundred *lǐ* long.
Still utilizing the people's labor,
with additional subsidies,
it can be completed within days
to protect the people from disaster,
and the people will willingly comply.
As for the saying that river management should not contend with water for land,
no method surpasses universally building distant dikes.
However, in the two prefectures of Jǐ and Wǔ,
the land is narrow and the population dense.
Most of it occupies cultivated land,
and the common people losing their livelihoods
is precisely what is not desired.
Moreover, the countless villages, towns, houses, and graves in between,
combined with Qíhé, Jǐyáng, Qídōng, Pútái, and Lìjīn, all having cities located on the riverbank—
to force them to actually be in such a situation,
the public sentiment would inevitably be alarmed.
To purchase people's land
would require no less than four to five million in funds.
The work would be difficult and the cost enormous,
so it can be planned for later.
This is why I request the construction of longitudinal dikes to address the immediate need,
and dare not lightly advocate the distant dike proposal."
Shìjié held a differing opinion.
At that time, Censor Wú Xún of Hǎifēng suggested that the two diversion canals of Túhài and Mǎjiá should not be lightly opened.
The Emperor ordered Zhílǐ Governor Lǐ Hóngzhāng to conduct a joint investigation with Shìjié,
and they also agreed with Xún's statement.
Thus, the decision was made to build long dikes on both banks.
In this year, Lìjīn Shísìhù was breached,
and it was plugged in the third month of the tenth year.
In the intercalary fifth month,
the Hétàoquān and Huòjiāliū in Lìchéng were breached,
along with Lǐjiā'àn, Chénjiālín, Xiāojiāzhuāng in Qíhé,
and Zhāngjiāzhuāng, Shísìhù in Lìjīn.
They were all plugged one after another.
In this year, the large dikes on both banks were completed,
each several hundred *zhàng* from the river.
These were the longitudinal dikes.
However, the people in the east still maintained the embankments close to the river,
and officials also instructed them to first defend the people's embankments.
If these embankments breached, they should then defend the large dikes.
But there was no discussion of relocating the villages and houses within the dikes.
When a major flood exceeded the channel,
the fields and houses were all submerged,
so the residents breached the dikes to release the water.
Officials could not forbid it.
Thereafter, only the embankments were defended, not the large dikes.
In the eleventh year,
Xiāojiāzhuāng and Saigōu were breached again,
and Zhàozhuāng in Qíhé was also breached.
In the twelfth month,
Saigōu and Zhàozhuāng were plugged.
In the second month of the following year,
Xiāojiāzhuāng was plugged.
In the sixth month,
Hétàoquān was breached again,
and Wángjiāquān in Jǐyáng, Yáojiākǒu in Huìmín, Héwángzhuāng in Zhāngqiū, and Xújiāshāwō in Shòuzhāng were also breached.
Only the work at Wángjiāquān was slow,
the rest were all plugged within the year.
Although the river in the eastern region breached repeatedly,
these were all diversions with little loss of flow.
Each time a breach was plugged,
it cost tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands,
at most one or two million,
which was much less than what was spent during the time of the Southern River.
The submerged land area was also smaller,
due to the flat terrain and gentle current.
In the thirteenth year, sixth month,
the Yellow River breached at Kāizhōu’s Dàxīnzhuāng,
inundating the eastern borders.
Pú, Fàn, Shòuzhāng, Yánggǔ, Dōng'ē, Píngyīn, and Yǔchéng all reported disasters.
In the eighth month,
the Yellow River breached at Zhèngzhōu,
and the current diverted through the Jiǎlú Hé into the Huái Hé,
flowing directly into Hóngzé Hú.
The main river ceased to flow,
and the dry breach at Wángjiā Quān was thus plugged.
As Zhèngzhōu had already breached,
many deliberators argued that it was unnecessary to plug it,
and that this opportunity should be used to restore the old course.
Hùbù Shàngshū Wēng Tónghé and Gōngbù Shàngshū Pān Zǔyīn jointly memorialized:
“Since the time of Dà Yǔ,
the river flowed in the northern regions for over three thousand six hundred years.
Its southward flow has been for no more than five hundred years.
Therefore, the river entering the sea via Yúntī Guān
cannot be truly called its old course.
Even if it were designated as the old course,
the current flow into Hóngzé Hú,
with its terrain higher in the north and lower in the south,
makes it impossible to guide it out through Qīngkǒu.
It is still over a hundred *lǐ* away from the old course,
and its restoration is absolutely impossible.
Some say that as Shāndōng has frequently suffered from floods,
they consider the river flowing through Hénán as fortunate.
They do not realize that the river naturally favors a northern course.
Since the reign of Jīn Zhāngzōng,
though the river has split its flow,
throughout the Míng dynasty,
there were fourteen northern breaches
and five southern breaches.
In our dynasty, since Shùnzhì and Kāngxī,
there have been nineteen northern breaches
and eleven southern breaches.
Moreover, the Huái has no existing channel for its flow.
If the Yellow River enters the Huái, where will it find an outlet?
If the lower reaches cannot be drained,
the upper reaches will certainly breach again.
If it breaches, it will still enter the eastern territories,
and Shāndōng’s troubles will still not be alleviated.
As for the Yellow River flowing south,
there are two great dangers and five concerns.
The Yellow River flows into Hóngzé,
and the mouth of the Huái is silted up,
having been impassable for a long time.
Only the引河 at Zhāngfúkǒu,
no more than a few *zhàng* wide,
channels the great current eastward,
using the Grand Canal as its outlet.
It relies solely on the Eastern Dike for protection,
which is already in a precarious state.
Now, with the sudden addition of the Yellow River,
it certainly cannot be maintained.
This is the first great danger.
Hóngzé is silted up,
and the Gāojiāyàn has been unreliable for a long time.
The Yellow River’s force is fierce,
and after entering the lake, it is hard to guarantee that it won't collapse immediately.
If it doesn't rush eastward to the Xiàhé,
it will flood Yángzhōu to the south.
If the Jiāng, Huái, Hé, and Hàn merge into one,
the overall situation in the southeast,
how can one even imagine it!
This is the second great danger.
The Xiàhé region is a rice-producing area.
If it is unfortunately submerged,
how will the grain tribute be procured?
This is the first concern.
Even if the grain tribute remains as before,
it might be unable to be transported due to the Yellow River carrying sand and silting up the canal.
Or, due to accumulated water overflowing,
the towpath might be nonexistent,
and the grain barges would be stalled.
Moreover, Shāndōng originally relied on the Yellow River to aid transport.
With the Yellow River now far away,
and the Yí and Wèn rivers becoming weak,
where will the water come from?
River transport will certainly be abolished.
This is the second concern.
The salt fields of Liǎnghuái
are all east of the Fàngōng Dī.
If the Fàn Dī cannot be preserved,
and the salt fields are submerged,
how will national taxes be collected?
This is the third concern.
In Yǐng, Shòu, Xú, and Hǎi,
people are prone to aggression and violence.
If the common people are displaced and scattered,
it is hard to guarantee that incidents will not arise.
This is the fourth concern.
When the Yellow River floods combine with the Huái,
they will not be confined to the lake.
They will certainly seek another path to the sea,
and a sudden transverse current will arrive,
leaving the residents of the riverine region no guarantee for their immediate future.
This is the fifth concern.
As for the water entering the lake,
plans for its discharge must also be made early.
The terrain of the Xiàhé region
slopes downward from northwest to southeast.
It is advisable to follow this natural slope,
from north of Xīnghuà,
passing through Ménglóng and Fùjiāwù into the old river,
avoiding the silt at Yúntī Guān,
dredging the Dàtōngkǒu to the north,
entering the Cháo Hé to reach the Huái Hé,
and then taking a direct route to the sea mouth.
The terrain is convenient,
and the expenditure will not be too great.”
The Emperor ordered Jiāngdū Zēng Guóquán and Cáodū Lú Shìjié to deliberate and propose solutions.
Coincidentally, Guóquán and Shìjié also stated:
“Defending the river and combining it with the Huái to flow eastward
is a hundred times more dangerous than usual.
Upon examination, water conservancy relies on two strategies: discharge and defense,
and the use of discharge is even more critical.
There are two outlets for Hóng Hú,
both through the Canal into the Jiāng.
Now that a great calamity has arrived,
it is imperative to plan for more outlets upstream of the lake,
to divide and discharge the water,
and to gather various opinions.
In Táoyuán, there is the Chéngzǐ Hé,
which connects to Hóng Hú in the south
and the old river in the north,
and further north is the Middle Canal.
If the Chéngzǐ Hé is dredged,
to connect to the old river
and directly reach the Middle Canal,
and dikes are built on both banks,
then the overflow can be diverted from Yángzhuāng Old River to Yúntī Guān to enter the sea.
This is a newly opened outlet upstream of Hóng Hú.
In Qīnghé, there is the Suìshí Hé,
which connects to Zhāngfúkǒu in the west,
and its 引河 reaches the old river to the east.
If it is greatly dredged and excavated,
it can also divert the overflow from Yángzhuāng Old River to Yúntī Guān to enter the sea.
This is a newly opened outlet downstream of Hóng Hú.
When asked, the elders
unanimously agreed that there was no other good method.
Therefore, your servants have decided to immediately survey, estimate, and commence work,
not daring to adhere rigidly to old rules,
and to delay,
thereby missing the opportune moment.”
The Emperor approved it,
and also dispatched former Shānxī Bùzhèngshǐ Shào Xián, demoted Zhèjiāng Ànchásǐ Chén Bǎozhēn, and former Shāndōng Ànchásǐ Pān Jùnwén to quickly proceed to the Zhèng construction site,
to assist Hédū Chéng Fú and Yùfǔ Ní Wénwèi in managing river affairs.
At this time, funds for construction and relief were urgently and greatly needed.
The Hùbù submitted six proposals for fundraising: one,
reduce the long-term laborers of the defense camps;
two,
suspend the purchase of military equipment, ships, and machinery;
three,
stop converting rice rations into silver for Beijing officials and soldiers;
four,
appropriately dispatch nearby defense troops to assist in the work;
five,
order salt merchants to donate and reward them;
six,
pre-collect tax silver from pawnshop and remittance house accounts.
Upon deliberation,
an imperial edict was issued to reduce long-term laborers,
solicit donations from salt merchants, and pre-collect tax silver.
The rest were not approved.
In the ninth month,
Lǐbù Shàngshū Lǐ Hóngzǎo was ordered, together with Xíngbù Shìláng Xuē Yǔnshēng, to promptly investigate,
and Hóngzǎo remained to supervise the work.
At this time, the Yellow River overflowed,
and many prefectures and counties in Hénán, such as Zhōngmóu, Wèishì, Fúgōu, Yānlíng, Tōngxǔ, Tàikāng, Xīhuá, Huáiníng, Xiángfú, Shěnqiū, and Lùyì, were inundated.
The water depth ranged from four or five *chǐ* to one or two *zhàng*.
One hundred thousand *tài* from the imperial treasury were specially disbursed,
and three hundred thousand *tài* of Beijing grain funds were intercepted for relief.
As funds for river works were urgently needed,
the requests of Yùshǐ Zhōu Tiānlín and Lǐ Shìkūn were granted,
and a new donation system for Zhèng works was specially opened.
Chéng Fú was dismissed from his post,
and Lǐ Hènián was appointed acting Hédū.
In the tenth month,
the Eastern Governor Zhāng Yào (張曜) stated: "The Yellow River in Shāndōng (山東) is heavily silted, and the tides are high.
It is truly difficult to contain the yellow current.
I request to take this opportunity to restore the old course of the Southern River."
The matter was referred to Hóngzǎo (鴻藻) and Hènián (鶴年) for deliberation.
Hóngzǎo (鴻藻) and others then requested to be instructed to swiftly organize and undertake the project jointly.
The emperor stated:
"Regarding the plan to restore the old course of the Yellow River,
although it has been repeatedly memorialized by my ministers,
the work is enormous and the expenditure vast.
It is absolutely impossible to carry it out simultaneously
before the breach is plugged.
This memorial, concerning the restoration of the old course,
only presents the principle in abstract terms,
with brief words and a vague meaning.
All the advantages and disadvantages, their relative importance,
the elevations of the terrain,
the vastness of the engineering work,
and the urgency of the timeframe
have not been comprehensively considered,
nor explained in detail in the memorial.
For such a major undertaking,
how can the court base its decisions and resolve doubts
on these few brief words?
The proposal for the old course
can temporarily be postponed.
As for all the works mentioned,
to be initiated downstream,
what is the current situation of the old course of the Southern River?
Can the project be started quickly?
Can the funds be raised immediately?
Are there any obstructions?
Guóquán (國荃), Shìjié (士杰), and Sōngjùn (崧駿) are ordered to swiftly estimate and memorialize."
Guóquán (國荃) stated:
"The yellow current flows eastward,
and the lands north and south of the Huái (淮) are situated downstream.
It is advisable to devise a plan for diversion.
I request to dredge the old river for over two hundred *lǐ* (里) below Yángzhuāng (楊莊),
to divert the waters of the Yí (沂) and Sì (泗) rivers,
freeing up the Middle Grand Canal,
in preparation for the heavy floods of the Yellow River,
which would carry the yellow current northward,
making it capable of containment.
This would provide an outlet for the upper reaches.
As for the Huái (淮) River, flowing directly eastward from the Sānhébà (三河壩),
the canal embankment would be under extreme pressure.
It would be impossible not to open the dam for discharge,
causing the lower river regions to be like the bottom of a boiling pot.
However, there are many branch rivers.
If they are dredged beforehand,
allowing the water to flow smoothly,
then the fields, dwellings, and people's lives can also be preserved.
What Tónghé (同龢) and Zǔyìn (祖蔭) said
truly captures the tendency of water to seek lower ground.
An officer has already been dispatched for an on-site inspection,
and I also request to transfer Zhāng Fùnián (張富年), the Jiāngsū (江蘇) Judicial Commissioner, who is familiar with river works, to supervise the matter."
The imperial order was approved.
Previously, Vice Minister Xú Fú (徐郙) had submitted a memorial proposing a comprehensive plan for the Yellow River.
Wénwèi (文蔚) stated:
"The proposals by Fú (郙) regarding opening a diversion canal at the upstream north bank of the river mouth,
dredging a '川' (chuān) shaped river within the river below the Upper Southern Office,
and constructing a drainage dam—
these three are all essential tasks for Hénán (河南),
and are methods that have proven effective in the past.
My earlier request to cut through shoals and dredge silt in wide sections of the river body
is precisely in line with Fú's (郙) idea of opening diversion canals and a '川' (chuān) shaped river.
River officials believe that the river's condition has recently changed slightly,
requiring new measures,
and there is also a view that diversion canals should not be dredged.
However, these laborers
are all people in need of relief.
Regardless of the specific work,
it is all necessary to be undertaken.
In the future, whether it is assisting in dredging the canal
or assisting in building the river embankment,
arrangements should be made by consulting with the river officials for timely deployment."
This was reported and noted.
In the twelfth month,
Guóquán (國荃) and Shìjié (士杰) stated:
"The 'two calamities and five concerns' presented by Tónghé (同龢) and others
are as if they had personally experienced them,
conveying what we wished to say
to the imperial ear.
Officers have been dispatched to conduct separate on-site inspections.
From Fùjiāwù (傅家塢) entering the old Yellow River,
passing Yúntīguān (雲梯關) to Dàtōngkǒu (大通口),
the terrain was surveyed.
The north side is one *zhàng* (丈) five to seven *chǐ* (尺) higher,
which, when considered against the tendency of water to seek lower ground,
is quite unsuitable.
We dare not but strictly obey the imperial instruction
to plan for alternative dredging within the territory of Xīnghuà (興化).
Upon investigation, among the river channels entering the sea in the lower river,
Xīnyáng (新陽) and Shèyáng (射陽) rivers are the most important,
followed by Dòulónggǎng (鬬龍港).
It is only that the branch rivers are blocked,
preventing smooth flow.
Upon investigation, Dàwéizhách (大圍閘) in Xīnghuà (興化) prefecture and Gǔhékǒuxiǎohǎi (古河口小海) in Dīngxīchǎng (丁溪場) prefecture
are extremely silted and shallow.
After dredging,
if the dam at Gāoyóu (高郵) is opened,
it is hoped that all water will flow smoothly
and discharge into the sea via Xīnyáng (新陽) and other rivers.
For sluice gates that are too narrow for smooth water passage,
additional diversion canals will be dug to their left and right,
to allow for a continuous, direct flow.
Beyond this, various main and branch rivers
will be successively selected for dredging,
to ensure smooth flow section by section.
This approach, though differing in specific proposals from Tónghé (同龢) and Zǔyìn's (祖蔭) memorial, achieves the same objective."
In the first month of the fourteenth year,
Guóquán (國荃) and others further stated:
"Xú Fú's (徐郙) memorial on a comprehensive plan for the river situation
states that Huái'yáng (淮揚) truly has no place to position the Yellow River,
and it is advisable to first plan for means of discharge,
and then seek methods for blockage.
This is indeed a precise and pertinent point.
As for the request to dredge the Tiānrán (天然) and Zhāngfúkǒu (張福口) diversion canals,
these are inherently the throat for the Huái (淮) to enter the Yellow River.
The ancients' proposals for guiding the Huái (淮)
all began with these diversion canals.
However, Zhāngfú (張福) is too high due to siltation,
and if not dredged properly,
there is a fear of backflow from the Yí (沂) and Sì (泗) rivers.
Moreover, the Shùnqīng Hé (順清河) is the source for the three sluice gates of Qīngjiāng (清江),
and in the past, it was dammed for self-protection.
Since the Yellow River shifted northward,
this dam has long been abandoned.
Now that the Huái (淮) is to be diverted into the Yellow River,
it is still necessary to build the Shùnqīng (順清) dam,
so that the three sluice gates can be kept safe.
Our officers have inspected the riverbed
and, although it is higher in the north and lower in the south,
by increasing the depth of dredging,
it can still be leveled.
Although the Shùnqīng Hé (順清河) has deep water and a swift current,
with ample materials and earth,
it can also be dammed.
Furthermore, our officer Shìjié (士杰) has conducted an on-site inspection
and found that a diversion canal can be opened at Chénjiāyáo (陳家窰),
connecting upstream to Zhāngfúkǒu (張福口) and downstream to Wúchéng (吳城) Qībǎo (七堡),
which has the same function as the Suìshí Hé (碎石河).
Dredging began in sections in the tenth month,
starting from Zhāngfúkǒu (張福口) and Nèiyáo Hé (內窰河),
and ending at Shùnqīng Hé (順清河),
with a depth of one *zhàng* (丈) four *chǐ* (尺) to two *zhàng* (丈),
hoping that for every portion of water discharged from the upstream,
the lower river will suffer one portion less disaster.
In these work sections, patrolling soldiers are also intermittently assigned to assist with dredging
to supplement the shortage of civilian laborers.
The above measures
are in unintentional agreement with several of the points proposed by the said Vice Minister for Jiāngnán (江南)."
Previously, the emperor, considering that the river would eventually flow north again,
had issued an edict
to "take advantage of the sudden decrease in the turbulent flow
to dredge the Dōngmíng (東明) long embankment,
excavate the river channel in Kāizhōu (開州),
and reinforce the dikes and levees."
At this point,
Hóngzhāng (鴻章) stated:
"The Yellow River within Zhí (直) province is eighty to ninety *lǐ* (里) long.
To dredge it uniformly would involve immense work and vast expense.
Even if only a few northern sections are selectively dredged,
it would still require two to three hundred thousand [coins].
The riverbanks on both sides are one to two *zhàng* (丈) higher than the average flood level,
so the river channel can still contain water.
However, the southern embankment of Dōngmíng (東明) has been eroded over the years
and urgently needs selective repair.
We have already dispatched the Dàmíng (大名) trained troops, Chūnróng (春融), to the site,
and recruited civilian laborers to work simultaneously.
The entire embankment of Kāizhōu (開州) is severely dilapidated,
and officers have also been dispatched to estimate repairs.
As for the small embankment on the south bank of Chángyuán (長垣),
it is relatively far from the river
and can be handled later.
For the civilian dikes on the north bank,
we have instructed and persuaded the populace to repair them,
without forcing the river channel
and thereby hindering the overall situation."
In the sixth month,
Xiǎoyángzhuāng was sealed.
In this month,
Hóngzǎo reported on the two dams of the Zhènggōng project,
which had a combined advance of 614 zhàng.
There remained a mouth opening of over 30 zhàng,
and due to the summer and autumn deluges,
it was difficult for human effort to be applied.
He requested to await the autumn flood to subside slightly
before continuing the work.
The Emperor issued a stern imperial edict, severely reprimanding them,
stripping Hènián of his post,
and banishing him and Chéngfú to military outposts.
Hóngzǎo and Wénwèi were both demoted three ranks but retained in their posts.
Wú Dàchéng, Governor of Guǎngdōng, was appointed acting Director-General of River Conservancy.
Dàchéng stated:
"A physician treating an illness
must investigate its cause,
and a patient taking medicine
must seek a prescription that matches the symptoms.
When I was daily by the river,
consulting with elders from the villages about past events,
and verifying them with records of previous generations,
I realized that the river calamities in Hénán Province are not incurable;
the disease lies in not treating them.
Building dikes without good strategies,
and reinforcing with fascine dikes is not a long-term solution.
The key lies in building dams to channel the current
and force the current to scour the sand.
When the current flows into the mid-stream,
the river does not impinge on the dikes,
thus the dike body naturally stabilizes,
and the river calamities naturally lessen.
Older staff members in the prefectural office
unanimously stated that in the early Xiánfēng reign, Xíngzé still had over twenty brick and stone dams.
Beyond the dikes were all shoals,
and the river current was far from the dikes.
Fascine dikes were built near the dams to prevent danger,
and there were very few fascine works at the base of the dikes.
Since the old dams fell into disrepair,
they were almost completely abandoned within a few years.
The river's force approached closer and closer,
and the number of fascine dikes increased more and more.
The prefectural staff were too busy salvaging to cope,
neglecting one thing for another,
and whenever there was dangerous work,
it often turned into a major disaster.
River officials considered reinforcing with fascine dikes their main task,
but when the main current formed a fixed whirlpool,
they would reinforce and then be submerged again,
almost reaching a state of helplessness.
I personally supervised the circuit and prefectural officials in hastily throwing down stone mounds.
For a strong current three or four zhàng deep,
throwing down just one or two chǐ of stones
would make the current shift outward.
Only then did I realize that where the water is deep and the current strong,
only throwing down stones can provide emergency relief,
its effectiveness being ten times that of fascine works.
Using stones to protect the current,
the current slows down and the fascine dikes stabilize.
River officials of past dynasties, such as Pān Jìxùn, Jìn Fǔ, and Lì Yùměi,
all advocated building dams to channel the current;
they were truly not mistaken.
Currently, these vital projects that have been abandoned for decades,
and dozens of major dams that ought to be repaired,
cannot be completed in a single day.
The only option is to rigorously economize from the funds for the Zhènggōng project.
If ten thousand can be saved,
an additional ten thousand's worth of stone mounds can be purchased.
If one hundred thousand can be saved,
an additional one hundred thousand's worth of dam works can be done.
Although these are follow-up measures,
taking advantage of the dry river to construct them
makes human effort easier.
Otherwise, after the Zhènggōng project is joined,
should danger arise next spring and summer,
it will surely lead to being caught unprepared.
Though I dare not say that one treatment will immediately cure the illness,
it is certainly better than no treatment, which only causes the illness to worsen daily.
If medicine can truly be applied to the symptoms,
there will be small effects in one year,
and significant effects after three to five years."
The Emperor commended him.
Dàchéng further stated:
"In the past, when constructing dams and mounds,
strip bricks and broken stones were always used.
Whenever there was a major flood with a swift current,
the dam base would be scoured deeper day by day,
and not only would bricks easily scatter,
even large heavy stones would collapse with the current.
I have heard that in the West, there is 'cement earth'
which, when mixed with sand, binds together
and is not bothered by water intrusion.
Taking advantage of the diversion channel not yet being opened,
and as various places require the construction of training dams,
which is precisely when the riverbed is dry,
I propose to try applying and filling 'cement earth'
into the brick surfaces and stone crevices,
to consolidate the scattered into a whole.
This could make the dam base form a single piece,
sufficient to withstand the river current,
using fewer stones while ensuring the work is strong.
This also seems to be a method for lasting benefit."
This was reported and heard.
In the twelfth month,
the Zhènggōng project was sealed.
It used 12 million taels of national treasury funds.
Dàchéng was formally appointed Director-General of River Conservancy.
An imperial edict ordered the establishment of a River God Temple at the construction site,
and also the construction of a temple for King Huáng Dàwáng,
bestowing an inscribed plaque.
He and General Dǎng were both granted additional titles.
In the seventh month of this year,
the dike at Fànzhuāng in Chángyuán burst.
It was sealed shortly after.
In the sixth month of the fifteenth year,
the dikes at Dàzhàizhuāng and Jīnwángzhuāng in Zhāngqiū burst,
with the diverted flow entering the sea via the Xiǎoqīnghé River.
The dikes at Zhāngcūn in Chángqīng and Xīzhǐfāng in Qíhé also burst,
and many prefectures and counties along the river in Shāndōng were inundated.
These were sealed in this winter.
In the second month of the sixteenth year,
Zhāng Yào, Governor of the East, stated:
"Previously, the Southern Director-General of River Conservancy oversaw over 900 lǐ of river works,
and the Eastern Director-General of River Conservancy oversaw over 500 lǐ.
Since the breach at Tóngwǎxiāng,
when the river entered Shāndōng,
the Southern Director-General was abolished,
and the Eastern Director-General's jurisdiction comprised only over 200 lǐ of river works.
Now, the Eastern River spans 900 lǐ,
silting up and rising daily,
and relies entirely on dikes for protection.
This year, I was stationed at the works for over 200 days,
supervising repairs and defenses,
with no time to spare.
I request that the river section from Hézé to the mouth of the Grand Canal, over 200 lǐ long,
be placed under the jurisdiction of the Director-General of River Conservancy,
making it equal in mileage to his original jurisdiction."
The Board deliberated that this section of the project
had always been supervised by the Governor, who concurrently managed local officials,
and feared that the Director-General of River Conservancy might not receive timely responses.
Yào further stated:
"Previously, the prefectures and counties along the river
were originally concurrently administered by river officials,
and vacancies were still reported by river officials for appointment.
In cases of merit or demerit,
river officials were also responsible for recommending or impeaching,
so there was no concern about a lack of timely responses.
I request that this matter also be submitted to the Director-General of River Conservancy for deliberation."
Earlier, Dàchéng had dispatched officials to survey and map the entire river in Zhíli, Shāndōng, and Hénán,
and by this time the maps were completed and presented.
In the fifth month,
the dike at Gāojiātào in Qíhé burst,
but was sealed shortly after.
In the sixth month of the eighteenth year,
the Huìmín Báimáo Fén was breached,
diverting the current northward,
directly flowing into the Túhài River and then the sea.
Breaches also occurred at Lìjīn Zhāngjiā Wū, Jìyáng Sāngjiā Dù, and Nánguān and Huībà,
all converging with the overflowing waters from Báimáo Fén and flowing into the Túhài River.
In the seventh month,
the Hújiā Àn in Zhāngqiū was breached,
causing a vast expanse of water
within the Jiāhé River.
Over 33,200 households of disaster victims were relocated from eight counties: Lìchéng, Zhāngqiū, Jìyáng, Qídōng, Qīngchéng, Bīnzhōu,
Pútái, and Lìjīn.
Initially,
the River Governor, Xǔ Zhènyī, requested that twelve thousand (taels) be allocated to the River Defense Bureau
from the annual quota of six hundred thousand (taels)
to raise funds for additional stone materials
and prevent problems in advance.
This was to be presided over by the River Governor.
At this point, the Board ordered it to be submitted and accounted for in separate cases.
Zhènyī stated:
"The great danger of river works
relies more on human effort than on strict adherence to regulations.
If we were to discuss it in terms of strict adherence to regulations,
then the precedents for reporting and accounting,
known to the Board of Works
and also to the river works administration,
have never been deemed non-compliant,
even with the millions of taels annually added and reported for Zhènggōng.
If we discuss it in terms of human effort,
I have recently changed the system and acted accordingly.
In recent years, despite numerous major dangers arising,
repairs and reinforcements have been carried out in an orderly manner,
fortunately achieving tranquility.
Regarding the addition of materials and stones,
there are indeed instances that do not entirely conform to precedents.
My original intention in establishing the River Defense Bureau
was twofold.
Firstly, I feared that officials might shirk responsibility when danger struck,
claiming a lack of money or materials.
Therefore, this large sum was allocated for proactive prevention.
Secondly, I feared that officials might be insincere or incomplete in their work.
Therefore, additional gentry were appointed for immediate relief and assistance,
with the twelve thousand (taels) strictly used for work on site,
not a single cent allowed into the bureau,
and no salaries to be paid.
Officials, gentry, civil servants, and common people in Hénán are all aware of this.
For example, to protect against the great dangers this year,
the purchase of stones alone
has already cost over one hundred eleven thousand taels.
The remainder was used to repair the cracked dikes of the Jīnmén at Zhènggōng.
These cannot be accounted for in separate cases.
Furthermore, stones were purchased from various sources
and used for immediate blockage everywhere.
If the danger had not subsided, more would have been thrown in;
if the danger had passed, work would stop.
These cannot be documented with maps and detailed explanations."
The Emperor acted according to the request.
In that year, all breaches at Báimáo Fén were closed.
In the sixth month of the twenty-first year,
breaches occurred at Shòuzhāng Gāojiā Dàmiào and Qídōng Zhàojiā Dàdī.
Shortly after,
breaches occurred at Jìyáng Gāojiā Zhǐfáng, Lìjīn Lǚjiā Wā, Zhàojiā Yuán, and Shíliù Hù.
These were successively closed that winter.
In the sixth month of the following year,
breaches occurred at Lìjīn Xīhánjiā and Chénjiā.
Censor Sòng Bólǔ memorialized on the accumulated abuses of the Eastern River: Firstly,
fraudulent claims and concealed expenditures should be severely punished;
secondly,
measures should be established to inspect the receipt and distribution of materials;
thirdly,
the old regulations for compensation and repair should be reaffirmed
to prevent arbitrary name changes;
fourthly,
military officers should conscientiously patrol.
An imperial edict ordered the Eastern Governor to thoroughly eliminate the accumulated abuses,
and also instructed all governors and governor-generals responsible for river affairs to investigate.
Should any incompetent officials be found,
they were to be impeached and punished severely.
In the first month of the twenty-third year,
breaches occurred at Lìchéng Xiǎoshātān and Zhāngqiū Hújiā Àn,
which were subsequently closed.
In the eleventh month, during the ice flood,
breaches occurred at Lìjīn Jiāngjiā Zhuāng and Hùjiā Tān,
with the water flowing through Zhānhuà into the Jiànghé River and then the sea.
In the sixth month of the twenty-fourth year,
the Hēihǔ Miào in Shāndōng was breached,
allowing water to flow east through the canal
and return to the main river.
Breaches also occurred at Lìchéng Yángshǐ Dàokǒu, Shòuzhāng Yángjiā Jǐng, Jìyáng Sāngjiā Dù, and Dōng'ā Wángjiā Miào,
diverting water into the Túhài and Xiǎoqīng rivers, which then flowed into the sea.
Hóngzhāng was dispatched to accompany River Governor Rèn Dàoróng and Eastern Governor Zhāng Rǔméi for a joint investigation.
Shortly after,
the post of Governor-General of the Eastern River was abolished,
then later reinstated.
In the second month of the twenty-fifth year,
Hóngzhāng and others reported:
"Since the Yellow River in Shāndōng changed its course from Tóngwǎxiāng to the Dàqīnghé,
it was a time of military campaigns,
and there was no leisure for repairs.
In the last years of Tóngzhì's reign,
overflows gradually occurred,
and so the south dī in the upper reaches was built.
After the eighth year of Guāngxù, overflows occurred frequently,
leading to the universal construction of large dī on both banks.
However, the common people had previously built small niàn along the riverbanks,
pressing tightly against the Yellow River flow.
After the large dī were completed,
people were further encouraged to maintain the niàn,
and some were even converted to official maintenance.
Thus, the dī were neglected for a long time.
Whenever there was a flood and the niàn broke,
the water would rush down like a torrent,
and the dī would also break,
this has been the root cause of past failures.
In the upper reaches, within the jurisdictions of Cáozhōu and Yǎnzhōu, the north and south dī combined measure over four hundred lì in length.
The two dī are twenty to forty lì apart.
If a民 niàn occasionally breaks,
the water flows back into the main river within the dī.
If there is a major breach, the dī themselves cannot be preserved.
There are twenty-four north and south niàn projects in total.
Since Tóngzhì,
only four or five breaches have occurred.
This is the situation in the upper reaches.
In the middle reaches, within the jurisdictions of Jìzhōu and Tàizhōu, both banks have half dī and half niàn,
totaling five hundred lì in length.
The upper section of the south bank, being adjacent to the mountains, has no dī.
The lower section maintains niàn.
The upper section of the north bank maintains dī,
while the lower section maintains niàn.
The arrangements are varied and inconsistent,
all due to the difficulty of relocating villages within the dī,
as a provisional measure for their preservation.
In the lower reaches, within the jurisdictions of Wǔchéng and Dìngxiàn, the south bank entirely maintains dī,
and the north bank entirely maintains niàn,
totaling over five hundred lì in length.
The terrain becomes flatter,
and the water flow becomes stronger.
There are over seventy dangerous spots.
In the past twenty-five years,
twenty-three breaches have already occurred.
This is the situation in the middle and lower reaches.
River management and defense in the Eastern Province were originally makeshift.
Although some projects were undertaken,
they were all due to financial constraints
and did not follow established river management methods.
The former governor Lǐ Bǐnghéng repeatedly elaborated on the harm suffered by Shāndōng from the river
and the difficulty of river management,
stating that there was almost no year without breaches,
and no year without multiple breaches.
The court repeatedly spent huge sums of money,
but the common people never had a peaceful year.
If we do not carry out extensive repairs according to established rules,
how can we respond to the imperial intention of loving and nurturing the populace?
Your ministers have carefully studied ancient methods of river management.
Only Jiǎ Ràng of Hàn relocated the people living in the path of the water,
ceding land to the water,
which was truly the best strategy.
The former governor Chén Shìjié constructed large dī on both banks of the middle and lower reaches,
totaling a thousand lì in length.
The two dī are five to six lì to eight to nine lì apart.
Reinforcing and maintaining these seems to be a moderate strategy.
However, there are places where dī were abandoned and niàn maintained,
such as above and below Luòkǒu on the south bank,
where niàn are maintained for one hundred ten lì.
The upper section, near the provincial capital, sixty lì,
is a hub for merchants,
and the dangerous spots are somewhat flat,
so expansion will be temporarily postponed.
The lower section has many critical dangers.
In the past ten-odd years,
nine breaches have already occurred.
It is proposed to relocate over twenty villages outside the niàn,
abandon the niàn and maintain the dī.
Being a little further from the water,
defense will be easier to secure.
This is the proposed method for relocating people and abandoning niàn on the south bank.
As for the dī projects on the north bank,
from Chángqīng to Lìjīn, four hundred sixty lì,
there are hundreds of villages outside the niàn and inside the dī.
The long niàn press close to the turbulent flow,
the river channel is too narrow,
there is no place without a bend,
and no bend without danger.
The river lips are heavily silted,
and the land outside the niàn is like the bottom of a cauldron.
The various villages absolutely cannot remain safe for long.
Moreover, if the niàn breaks, the dī will surely break.
Wishing to protect the hundreds of villages outside the niàn
while simultaneously subjecting thousands of villages outside the dī to disaster
is even more ill-advised.
However, common people are attached to their land and reluctant to move.
Repeatedly suffering from floods,
they are unwilling to move far away.
This cannot be decided overnight.
It is now proposed that on the north bank, from Guānzhuāng in Chángqīng to Qíhé, over sixty lì,
the river channel is still wide.
From Lìjīn to Yánwō, over seventy lì,
the land is all saline and alkaline,
making it inconvenient to relocate people.
In both cases, the niàn will be converted into dī,
and the people outside the niàn
need not be relocated.
There are still three hundred twenty lì from Qíhé to Lìjīn
where the civil niàn press tightly against the river bank,
some even less than one lì apart.
The situation necessitates abandoning the niàn and maintaining the dī.
But the north dī are mostly incomplete and dilapidated,
leaving no place to retreat to.
Moreover, the required funds are excessively large,
and relocating people is even more difficult.
Therefore, the old niàn should be temporarily maintained.
This is the plan for separately maintaining niàn and converting them into dī on the north bank,
and discussing the abandonment of niàn and maintenance of dī again in the future.
As for the large north and south dī,
they are of the utmost importance for river works.
Since they are everywhere low and weak,
it is proposed that both the dī converted from niàn
and the temporarily designated civil niàn
be uniformly repaired and reinforced according to the old style of river works,
with the general aim of being able to withstand flood surges.
As for the downstream estuary into the sea,
it is especially crucial for the entire river system.
It is found that the old channel of Tiěménguān still spans over eighty lì.
The further downstream, the wider and deeper it becomes,
leading directly to the sea mouth.
Its configuration is more favorable than Sīwǎngkǒu and Hánjiāyuán,
and the construction cost is also relatively lower.
However, building a large dam across the river,
dredging a diversion canal, and constructing large dī on both banks
will require considerable expense.
If the lower mouth is not managed,
the entire river will suffer.
Therefore, a thorough survey and cost estimate must be made.
This is the method for reinforcing the dī works on both banks and rectifying the lower mouth.
It is estimated that the construction cost will be over 9.3 million,
and it can be completed in five or six years."
The imperial court approved the request,
first allocating one million taels
to be overseen by the Governor of Shāndōng, Yùxián.
Yùxián stated:
"The methods for managing the Yellow River
are indeed as the ministers have stated:
widening the river channel,
constructing and reinforcing dī bodies, and dredging the estuary are the key points.
Upon investigation, the harm from the estuary
is worst at Tiěbǎnhé.
The entire river carries sand and mud,
and upon reaching here, it has nowhere to be confined.
It disperses without force,
and with winds and tides,
it becomes solidified like iron.
If the flow is not smooth, the outlet is blocked, and lateral flows increase.
Therefore, there is no river that does not suffer every ten years.
It is proposed to build a long dī directly to the silted shoals,
to protect against winds and tides.
Even if it cannot directly reach the sea,
each step further brings an additional benefit.
As for the low and weak dī and niàn,
when reinforcing them,
the earthwork must be sufficient,
the ramming must be firm,
and special attention must be paid to maintenance.
At the bends,
each bend is a danger,
such as Jiǎzhuāng and Sūnjiālóu in the upper reaches,
Jióngjiā'àn, Huòjiālìu, and Sāngjiādù in the middle reaches,
and Báilóngtán, Běizhènjiājí, and Yánwō in the lower reaches.
These are all famous major dangers,
and there are many other dangers.
It is indeed impossible not to straighten the bends.
However, the terrain must also be assessed,
and the upstream mouth of the diversion channel must be able to meet the flow, and the downstream mouth must go straight into the river heart to be effective.
From Wèijiākǒu west of Pútái to Sòngzhuāng eastwards,
about forty lì long,
the river water divides,
taking one-third of the main river's flow.
If dī and dams are built and channels dredged along the existing terrain
to divert it to the North River,
and if the main river silts up,
the city walls of Pútái will be permanently free from floods.
This is the most beneficial way to straighten a bend,
and it is proposed to survey and undertake it immediately."
This was reported and heard.
In the 26th year,
the Boxer Rebellion broke out.
Requests for funds were not renewed.
Thereafter, as the situation became increasingly difficult,
there was no time to discuss river defenses.
That year, during the winter flood season,
the embankment at Zhāngxiàotáng jiā in Bīnzhōu breached.
It was repaired in the third month of the following year.
In the sixth month,
the embankments at Chénjiāyáo in Zhāngqiū and Yángjiā Dàtí in Huìmín breached,
and were subsequently repaired.
When the Yellow River first shifted north,
Zhōng Qīnwáng Sēnggélínqìn requested the abolition of the post of Director-General of Rivers.
Later, the Eastern River was put under the concurrent jurisdiction of the governor,
and River Governor Qiáo Sōngnián reiterated the request.
By this time,
River Governor Xīliáng stated:
"The river works of Zhílǐ and the Eastern River have long been under the jurisdiction of the governor-generals and governors.
The Governor of Hénán already has the responsibility of concurrently managing river affairs.
I request that, following the precedent set in Shāndōng,
the management be transferred to concurrent jurisdiction,
and the post of Governor-General of the Eastern River be abolished."
The emperor approved the decree.
In the summer of the 28th year,
the embankment at Féngjiāzhuāng in Lìjīn breached.
In autumn,
the embankment at Liúwàngzhuāng in Huìmín breached.
In the second month of the following year,
Liúwàngzhuāng was repaired.
In the sixth month,
the embankment at Nínghǎizhuāng in Lìjīn breached,
and was repaired in the twelfth month.
In the first month of the 30th year,
during the winter flood season,
the embankments at Wángzhuāng, Hùjiātān, Jiāngzhuāng, and Mǎzhuāng in Lìjīn breached,
and were subsequently repaired.
In the sixth month,
the river overflowed at Gāolán in Gānsù,
inundating over twenty villages along the banks.
It also breached at Bózhuāng in Lìjīn, Shāndōng,
inundating over twenty villages and salt pans.
Before this, Shāndōng had repeatedly suffered from river disasters.
Those in charge all built dikes along the water,
following every bend and curve,
which prevented the water from flowing smoothly.
Below Zhāngqiū,
the dikes were low and the river narrow,
and there were no stone works to protect them.
Below Lìjīn,
the estuary shifted south,
making the situation even more unfavorable.
Governor Zhōu Fù requested three million taels of treasury funds
for minor repairs and reinforcement,
but the Board Minister Jìn did not grant them.
Having no choice,
he raised 200,000 taels himself to purchase additional stone materials,
and also provided funds to relocate the residents of Lìjīn's lower reaches who were in the path of the flood,
but not all residents were moved.
Furthermore, large dikes were added south of the existing dikes,
to ensure that if the old dikes broke, the residents would have new homes to return to.
When Bózhuāng breached,
the water flowed northeast via the Túhài Hé into the sea.
Zhōu Fù stated:
"The old riverbed has silted up into flat land.
If we were to restore it to its original state,
it is estimated to require over 900,000 taels,
a huge sum difficult to raise.
Moreover, after restoration,
there would be no guarantee of defense.
Below the breach,
the water depth ranged from over one *zhàng* to two or three *zhàng*,
rushing and vast,
flowing swiftly downstream.
After entering the Túhài Hé,
the current became even wider and deeper,
flowing more smoothly than at Tiěmén Guān, Hánjiā Yuán, or Sīwǎng Kǒu.
Rather than going against the nature of the water,
wasting useless money,
and trying to save the people but ultimately failing to do so,
it is better to relocate the people to avoid the water,
not to contend with the water for land,
and allow both the water and the people to find their proper place.
If this is implemented,
there will be three benefits: the estuary will be clear,
the flow smooth, and erosion reduced —
benefit one;
boat navigation will be convenient,
and trade goods will circulate —
benefit two;
the river will be straight and smooth,
risks reduced, and expenses saved —
benefit three.
The savings in construction costs are not even included.
However, remedial measures also incur three types of expenses: first,
the cost of relocating people;
second,
the cost of building embankments;
third,
the cost of relocating salt pans.
Approximately 500,000 gold taels will be needed,
which is three-quarters less than the cost of restoration,
with greater benefits."
The emperor approved the decree,
and thus no restoration was undertaken.
Thereafter, the Eastern River was calm,
without a single breach for several years.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
the embankment at Mèngmínzhuāng in Kāizhōu breached.
It was repaired the following year.
In the third year,
Governor Sūn Bǎoqí of the Eastern Province stated:
"Since the Yellow River entered the Eastern Province,
the river channel has been deep and clear,
initially without need for repair or defense.
Over time, it silted up and overflowed,
leading to the construction of civilian dikes,
which constricted the Yellow River's flow.
Subsequently, large dikes were universally built,
and then people were ordered to guard the civilian dikes.
If a dike breached,
officials received no punishment;
this was the established practice in both Zhílǐ and the Eastern Province.
In the first year, the Kāizhōu breach occurred,
and the water flowed downstream outside the civilian dikes but inside the main dikes in the upper reaches of the Eastern Province,
only returning to the main channel in the middle reaches.
Pú, Fàn, and Shòuzhāng suffered severe damage.
Your minister conferred with the Governor-General of Zhílǐ,
dispatched officials to assist with funds for repairs,
and only last year was it successfully completed.
If a comprehensive plan could be made,
with separate surveys and treatments,
and the responsibility for guarding the upper reaches' lateral breaches transferred to officials,
how could the disaster be imagined!
Your minister once accompanied Lǐ Hóngzhāng to survey the river in the East;
at that time, the engineers suggested building dikes extending deep into the sea as the most crucial method,
but it was not carried out due to the enormous cost.
If the chief administrators could centrally manage funds,
build dikes over several years,
using the confinement of water as a strategy to scour sand,
and then appropriately purchase foreign dredging vessels
to regularly dredge,
the estuary could be expected to become deep and clear,
and the entire situation would benefit.
River engineering is a specialized field;
without extensive experience,
one cannot grasp its intricacies.
It is urgent to follow the established regulations of Hénán Province,
and redefine the quotas for civil and military officials as lifelong appointments,
with mutual transfers among the three provinces.
Last year, your minister established a river engineering research institute,
recruiting students to study river affairs,
originally to cultivate river management talent;
if directorates and patrol stations are established,
these graduating personnel can be assigned to probationary positions,
which will greatly benefit the engineering works.
The above four points
must be implemented.
Your humble minister believes that a high-ranking Director-General of Rivers should be appointed,
to conduct surveys and consultations,
and the annual expenses of several millions from the three provinces
should be consolidated for use.
Once a major management plan is agreed upon,
funds should be allocated as needed,
to prevent obstruction and achieve success."
Upon submission of the memorial,
an imperial edict instructed consultation with the Governor-General of Zhílǐ and the Governor of Hénán for a comprehensive plan.
Before a response could be discussed,
the Wǔchāng Uprising occurred,
and the matter was consequently dropped.
Records 102: Waterways II - The Grand Canal
The Grand Canal extends from the capital (Jīngshī) through Zhígū and Shāndōng,
reaching the mouth of the Yángzi Jiāng,
spanning over two thousand *lǐ* from north to south.
It also extends from Jīngkǒu to Hángzhōu,
about eight hundred *lǐ* from end to end.
It is collectively referred to as the Grand Canal.
In the Míng dynasty, there were distinctions such as Bái Cáo, Wèi Cáo, Zhá Cáo, Hé Cáo, Hú Cáo, Jiāng Cáo, and Zhè Cáo.
In the middle of the Kāngxī reign of the Qīng dynasty, Jìn Fǔ opened the Central River,
avoiding the dangers of the Yellow River's currents.
Grain boats only travelled a few *lǐ* on the Yellow River
before entering the Central River.
Consequently, the one hundred eighty *lǐ* of Hé Cáo were abolished.
As for Bái Cáo, which relied on the Bái Hé,
Wèi Cáo, which channeled the Wèi Shuǐ,
and Zhá Cáo and Hú Cáo, which received waters from various lakes in Shāndōng and Jiāngnán,
they were no different from those in the Míng dynasty.
In the final years of the Jiāqìng reign,
the river repeatedly burst its banks,
and the transport route became silted up.
Therefore, the Yellow River's water was borrowed to aid transport.
In the early Dàoguāng reign,
sea transport was attempted.
In the twenty-eighth year,
due to saving on assistance fees,
it was used for transport once more.
By the Xiánfēng reign,
the Yellow River had shifted northwards,
and the Central Plains faced many troubles,
interrupting the transport route.
Throughout the Qīng dynasty,
sea transport thus became the norm.
When the Yellow River flowed south,
the Huái River was the first to suffer.
When the Huái River suffered, the transport also suffered.
Hence, the three strategies of river management, Huái River channeling, and transport aid
were concentrated in the single corner of Huái'ān and Qīngkǒu.
The diligence in construction,
the vast expenditure of funds,
and the frequent annual suffering of the people's fields and homes
were unparalleled.
Indeed, the corner of Qīngkǒu
was intended to store clear water to resist the Yellow River.
However, if the Huái River was strong, it could indeed scour the Yellow River,
but if it was too strong, the transport dikes could not be preserved.
If the Huái River was weak, it could not aid transport,
and there was also the danger of the Yellow River's currents backflowing.
This was unlike Bái Cáo and Wèi Cáo, which merely engaged in dredging silt and blocking breaches,
or Zhá Cáo and Hú Cáo, which only aimed for appropriate storage and discharge.
As for Jiāng Cáo and Zhè Cáo,
they were reputed to be easy to manage.
Jiāng Cáo travelled from Húguǎng and Jiāngxī along the Hàn, Miǎn, and Póyáng rivers downstream,
all entering the Yí Hé,
and then sailed upstream.
South of Jīngkǒu,
the Grand Canal only required dredging at townships like Tú, Yáng, and Yángwǔ from time to time;
south of Wúxī,
straight to Sūzhōu,
and the canals of Jiā and Háng,
were all naturally clear-flowing and smooth,
requiring no human effort.
Now, this chapter records the parts that suffered the most and involved the largest projects.
In the summer of Shùnzhì four years, there was prolonged rain,
breaching the Jiāngdū transport dike,
which was subsequently repaired.
In the summer of six years,
the Gāoyóu transport dike breached for several hundred *zhàng*.
In seven years,
the transport dike burst,
