carrying the Wèn Shuǐ through the Yán Hé into the sea.
In eight years,
civilians were recruited for large-scale dredging of the Grand Canal.
In fourteen years,
the River Superintendent, Zhū Zhīxī, said:
"Nánwàng is one hundred twenty *chǐ* higher than Táizhuāng to the south,
and ninety *chǐ* higher than Línqīng to the north.
The standing regulations should be followed:
the gates should not be opened unless the water accumulates to six or seven *chǐ*,
to prevent drainage and drying up.
If the lower gates are closed and
the upper gates are opened,
the water will be deep when still;
if the upper gates are closed and
the lower gates are opened,
the water will be shallow when flowing strongly.
Heavily loaded boats should not open the gates easily;
empty return boats should not close the gates easily."
This was followed.
In fifteen years,
Dǒngkǒu became silted.
Zhīxī opened a new canal two hundred fifty *zhàng* south of Shípáikǒu,
connecting it to the main river,
to facilitate swift towing.
Previously, in nine years, the Zhāng Shuǐ flowed north from Qiū Xiàn,
passing through Qīng Xiàn into the sea.
By the transition between spring and summer of seventeen years,
the Wèi Shuǐ was weak,
and grain transport was impeded.
Consequently, the Zhāng Hé's water, which irrigated agricultural fields, was dammed
and diverted into the Wèi River to aid transport.
At that time, the area north of the Yellow River had suffered severe drought for several years.
Department official Jiāng Tiānshū said:
"In the past, Qīanshì Jiāng Liángcái wished to divert the Yellow River into the Wèi River to add a transport route.
Now, why can we not borrow his idea and reverse its application to divert the Wèi River into the Yellow River?"
Zhīxī followed his suggestion,
and also appointed a Chief Clerk for the Wèi Hé,
making it a regulation.
In Kāngxī one year,
the time limit for Grand Canal repair and construction was set: if breached within three years,
the construction officials would be impeached;
if after three years,
the defense officials would be impeached;
if there was no protection,
leading to a breach,
all would be impeached and dealt with.
In the autumn of four years,
Gāoyóu experienced a great flood,
breaching the transport dike.
In five years,
the Grand Canal from Yízhēng to Huái'ān became shallow due to siltation.
The county magistrate, Hé Chónglún, recruited civilians to dredge it.
The Grain Transport Superintendent, Lín Qǐlóng, said:
"Grain boats going north are obstructed by gates and shallow water everywhere.
I request that river officials be ordered to inspect the various lakes such as Ānshān and Mǎtà,
as well as all the cabinet gates, subsidiary dikes, lock gates, and riverbanks,
and the springs of Dōngpíng and Wènshàng,
to check for blockages,
and to ensure that springs are dredged and lakes are cleared
to facilitate the transport route."
In six years,
the Grand Canal breached at Lùjīnsi, Jiāngdū.
The following year,
it was repaired.
In ten years,
it breached at Qīngshuǐtán, Gāoyóu.
The following year,
it breached again,
and was only repaired in thirteen years.
In fourteen years,
it breached at Shàobózhèn, Jiāngdū.
In the summer of fifteen years,
due to prolonged rain,
the transport dikes collapsed.
Qīngshuǐtán and Lùmàngōu in Gāoyóu,
and Dàtánwān in Jiāngdū,
breached for a total of over three hundred *zhàng*.
In sixteen years,
Jìn Fǔ was appointed River Superintendent.
At that time, water disasters in the southeast deepened,
and the transport route became shallower.
Fǔ said:
"The river and transport ought to be treated as one entity.
The obstruction of the transport route
is often caused by changes in the river course.
Previously, those who discussed river management
mostly focused their efforts on the areas where grain boats travelled,
regarding other breaches
as irrelevant to the transport route and therefore treating them lightly,
which led to the daily deterioration of the river course
and consequently the daily obstruction of the transport route.
Therefore, related areas cannot be treated differently.
Furthermore, the Grand Canal from Qīngkǒu to Qīngshuǐtán,
approximately two hundred thirty *lǐ* long,
has been elevated by siltation of its bed due to the Yellow River's inward flow,
causing constant suffering to residents from flooding
and frequent obstruction of transport boats.
I request that all governors be ordered
to ensure that the grain tribute to be transported this year
is entirely passed over the Huái River by the third month of next year.
Once the grain boats have passed,
the Tōngjì sluice gate should be sealed,
and laborers should be gathered
to undertake a major dredging of the Grand Canal,
with a top width of eleven *zhàng*,
a bottom width of three *zhàng*,
and a depth of one *zhàng* two *chǐ*.
This will require three thousand four hundred seventy-odd laborers daily,
and will be completed in three hundred days.
Additionally, six breaches at Qīngshuǐtán and Dàtánwān
and breaches from Zháijiābà to Wǔjiādūn must be blocked,
requiring ninety-eight thousand-odd *tǎng* of funds."
He further said:
"Previously, due to the silting of the riverbed,
there were countless difficulties from obstruction and exploitation.
If Qīngkǒu is uniformly deepened,
boats can travel smoothly,
saving a great deal of expense.
Therefore, it is ordered to measure the saved expenses
and use them for river management.
I request that once the Grand Canal is deepened and
boats can pass,
all passing cargo boats should be charged a few *fēn* of shallowing silver,
which will be stopped after one year."
All requests were granted.
The following spring,
the Emperor made a southern tour
to inspect river works.
Arriving at the Zhīhé kǒu (Branch River Mouth),
he said to his ministers:
"The river channels are crucial to grain transport and the people's livelihood.
The terrain and water conditions
require adaptation as circumstances change.
Now, observing this river, it is narrow
and very close to the Yellow River bank.
Should the Huánghé (Yellow River) embankment burst,
and we fail in our defense,
the Zhōnghé (Central River) and Huánghé will become one.
After this river was opened,
merchants and common people praised its convenience,
but who knows what the future holds?"
Túnà and Mǎqí said:
"When Your servants surveyed the river,
it was a time of great floods.
Fearing that the narrow river could not contain all the water,
we therefore proposed building three diversion dams along the remote dike to the north,
allowing the water to enter the sea via the old river course."
Fǔ said:
"Your servant's intention in opening this river
was to concentrate the water for its entry into the sea.
And after the dredging was completed,
grain vessels could also navigate it.
If we now increase the remote dike
to secure the Huánghé embankments,
there should be no worries."
The River Governor Wáng Xīnmìng said:
"At Zhīhé kǒu, there is only one Zhènkǒu sluice gate.
The waters from Wēishān Hú (Lake Weishan) are immense,
and in the event of continuous heavy rains, it cannot cope,
inevitably leading to a breach.
If a diversion dam is built at Luòmǎ Hú (Lake Luoma),
allowing floodwaters to enter the Huánghé,
and then Tánchéng Yǔwáng Tái (Yu King Terrace at Tancheng) is reinforced,
to block the water flowing into Luòmǎ Hú,
directing it into the Shùhé,
then the Zhōnghé will be safe."
The Emperor deemed it permissible to continue opening the Zhīhé,
and the Huánghé shipping route
should also be maintained, not abolished.
Previously, Yùshū and others had requested to close the Lánmǎ Hé (Block Horse River).
The matter was referred to the Director-General of Rivers,
and now Xīnmìng said:
"Lánmǎ Hé was originally intended to discharge excess Huánghé water during floods.
It seems it should remain.
When the water rises, open it;
when the water level is normal, close it,
to prevent siltation in the Zhōnghé.
Regarding the three diversion dams at Luòmǎ Hú,
Yùshū and others proposed leaving two within the dike,
diverting water into the Zhōnghé.
However, there is concern that the Zhōnghé cannot accommodate it,
so they planned to build diversion dams at Xiāojiā Dù, Yángjiā Zhuāng, and Xīnhé kǒu to the east to discharge water.
Your servant argues that since the Zhōnghé cannot accommodate it,
why bother letting the water from these two dams enter the Zhōnghé,
only to build dams at Xiāojiā Dù and other places again,
adding unnecessary complications?
It would be better to keep all three dams outside the remote dike,
allowing the water to enter the sea via the old river course.
At the three locations of Xiāojiā Dù, leave two gaps,
and manage their opening and closing according to the water conditions.
There was previously a Yǔwáng Tái at the mouth of the Shùhé in Tánchéng,
obstructing the water flow.
The confluence of the Báimǎ Hé and Yíhé waters into Luòmǎ Hú
makes the overflow even more uncontrollable.
It is necessary to block the flow at the old foundation of the terrace, at the point facing the water,
so that the water can flow into the sea via its original course."
This was submitted to the accompanying ministers for careful deliberation.
Only the Luòmǎ Hú diversion dams adopted Yùshū and others' original proposal;
the rest followed Xīnmìng's recommendations.
In the thirty-second year,
the Zhílì (Directly Controlled Area) Grand Canal burst at five places, including Lǐjiā Kǒu in Tōngzhōu,
and eight places, including Shuǎ'ér Dù in Tiānjīn.
The Wèihé (Wei River) was feeble,
relying solely on the Zhānghé for water supply,
which diverted at Guǎntáo to aid transport.
During the Míng (Ming Dynasty) Lóngqìng and Wànlì eras,
the Zhānghé shifted northward into the Fǔyáng Hé,
and the flow at Guǎntáo ceased.
Now, in the thirty-sixth year,
it suddenly diverted again,
once more entering the Wèihé via Guǎntáo to aid transport.
In the thirty-eighth year,
the court deliberated and decided to convert the Gāoyóu diversion dam and six other dams, including Máojiā Yuán, into spillway dams,
and to increase the stone work of the Gāoyàn (High Embankment) by five chí (Chinese feet).
In the thirty-ninth year,
the Emperor, noting the daily siltation at Qīngkǒu,
feared it would impede grain vessels.
Sea transport to Tiānjīn was also extremely perilous.
He proposed using sand boats to carry grain,
starting from the Jiāng (Yangtze River) into the sea,
and at the mouth of the Huánghé where it enters the sea,
transport it into the Zhōnghé,
thus making sea transport not far.
This was referred to the River Governor Zhāng Pénghé for consideration.
Pénghé stated that the breaches in the Grand Canal had been repaired,
and clear water had already been diverted out,
so grain boats should be able to pass smoothly.
If sand boats were used instead,
hiring sailors
would only lead to increased expenditure.
Furthermore, going from the Jiāng into the sea,
and then from the Huánghé estuary into the Zhōnghé,
with unpredictable winds and waves,
would truly be difficult to navigate.
This advice was followed.
Earlier,
River Governor Yú Chénglóng, finding the Zhōnghé too close to the Huánghé to build embankments,
therefore abandoned the lower section of the Zhōnghé from Táoyuán Shèngjiā Dàokǒu to Qīnghé,
and excavated a new channel sixty lǐ (Chinese miles) long,
named Xīn Zhōnghé (New Central River).
Now,
Pénghé observed that the Xīn Zhōnghé was shallow and narrow,
and the river head at Shèngjiā Dàokǒu was winding,
making towing difficult.
Therefore, he built a cross-river dike at Sānyì Bà (Three Righteousness Dam),
combining the upper section of the old Zhōnghé and the lower section of the Xīn Zhōnghé into one river,
which was heavily repaired and dredged,
making the transport route convenient.
In the fortieth year,
as clear water had already flowed out of Húkǒu (Lake Mouth),
a method for regulating discharge should be devised.
Pénghé's request was granted
to open another intake river between Zhāngfú Kǒu and Péijiā Chǎng's two intake rivers,
to jointly resist the Huánghé.
If the Huánghé floods after grain vessels have passed,
block the Huánghé dam
to prevent backflow;
if it floods during navigation,
close the Péijiā Chǎng intake river mouth,
and divert clear water into Sānchà Hé (Three-Prong River) to Wénhuá Sì (Wenhua Temple) to aid transport.
That year, a stone sluice gate was built on the south bank of Zhōnghé Kǒu.
In the forty-second year,
because the clear water outlet at Zhòngzhuāng Zhá (Zhongzhuang Sluice)
forced the current southward,
obstructing the transport route,
an imperial edict moved the Zhōnghé transport mouth to Yángjiā Zhuāng,
which was the old course of the Dà Qīngshuǐ (Great Clear Water River),
benefiting both grain transport and salt trade.
The following year,
an order was also given to build the Yángcūn diversion dam on the Zhílì Grand Canal to divide the water flow.
In the forty-fourth year,
the Emperor stated that if the Gāoyàn and the Grand Canal diversion dams were not opened,
the dikes and embankments would be endangered.
If they were opened to discharge water, the farmlands would be flooded and damaged.
Therefore, rivers should be dug and dikes built below the three spillway dams of the Gāoyàn,
to channel the water into Gāoyóu, Shàobó, and other lakes.
Below the diversion dams, rivers should also be dug and dikes built,
to channel the water through Chuànchǎng Xī (Chuanchang Stream) into Báijū, Dīngxī, Cǎoyàn, and other rivers, leading to the sea.
The Directors-General of the Jiāng (Yangtze River), Caoyun (Grain Transport), and Rivers were ordered to survey and estimate,
and officials were dispatched to oversee the construction.
From then on, all prefectures in Huái'yáng were spared the calamity of overflowing.
In the forty-fifth year,
Pénghé built two temporary dams on the cross-dike of the Zhōnghé
and one temporary dam at the Bāojiāyíng intake river,
opening and closing them as needed
to prevent siltation in the Zhōnghé.
Furthermore, due to the rising water in the Grand Canal,
which the embankments could not contain,
a stone sluice gate was built at Wénhuá Sì.
Below the sluice, an intake river was opened,
extending from Yángjiā Miào and Dānyáng Kǒu to Báimǎ Hú (White Horse Lake),
measuring over fourteen thousand eight hundred zhàng (Chinese rods) in length.
When water rose, it was opened into the lake;
when water receded, it was closed.
That year,
Zhāng Bóxíng of Jìníng Circuit requested to divert the Zhānghé from Chéng'ān Bǎisì Yíng's new river connecting to the Zhānghé,
connecting it to Guǎntáo's Shāhé (Sand River),
which was what the ancients called the Mǎjiá Hé (Horse Mane River).
He proposed dredging its siltation
to allow smooth flow into the Wèihé.
The proposal was not yet implemented.
Two years later,
the entire Zhānghé flowed into Guǎntáo.
The Zhānghé and Wèihé merged, and their force became violent and swift,
causing harm to the exposed areas of Ēn and Dé.
Therefore, dams were built at Dézhōu Shàomǎ Yíng and Ēnxiàn Sì Nǚ Sì,
and branch rivers were opened to mitigate their force.
Sixty years later,
the Governor of Shāndōng, Lǐ Shùdé, requested the excavation of a new canal at Péngkǒu.
Previously, a certain official of Jǐníng Circuit had said,
“In the area of Péngkǒu, there are Zhaoyáng, Wēishān, and Xīhú lakes.
Sand discharged into the Sāndòngqiáo causes frequent blockages,
which are cleared only to be re-blocked,
hindering grain transports.
A new canal should be dug to avoid the sand discharge
and clear the transport route.”
At this time,
Shùdé repeated this proposal.
The Emperor said:
“The Grand Canal in Shāndōng
receives water from Xīhú Lake.
In the past, the common people opened it when they thought it should be opened,
and closed it when they thought it should be closed.
What was the intention behind opening it?
What was the intention behind blocking it?
The reasons must be fully understood
before a decision can be made on whether to open it or not.
Otherwise,
it will be a waste of resources.”
He also said:
“The Grand Canal in Shāndōng
relies entirely on lakes and springs for its transport capacity.
Now, many paddy fields have been opened,
diverting upstream water for irrigation.
Naturally, the lake waters have no place to accumulate and store,
so how can they sustain transport?
In past years, the people of the east wanted to dig a new canal;
I feared downstream flooding,
and forbade it.
Now, they are again requesting to dig a new canal.
This area is bordered on one side by Wēishānhú Lake
and on the other by the mountains of Yìxiàn.
From where else can it be excavated?
When Zhāng Pénghé arrives in the east,
he shall convey this imperial decree in detail to the Governor,
instruct the local authorities,
survey the spring sources,
and accumulate lake water,
so that grain transport is unimpeded.
This will be easy enough.”
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
the Director-General of Rivers, Qí Sūlè, along with the Director-General of Grain Transport, Zhāng Dàyǒu, stated:
“For water storage to aid transport in Shāndōng,
there are the lakes of Nánwàng, Mǎtà, Shǔshān, Ānshān, Mǎchǎng, Zhaoyáng, Dúshān, Wēishān, and Xīshān.
When water rises, river water is diverted into the lakes;
when dry, lake water is diverted into the channel.
By collecting and storing water as needed,
to supply the Grand Canal,
the ancients called them ‘water cabinets.’
Over the years,
Zhaoyáng, Ānshān, and Nánwàng have mostly been privately reclaimed and cultivated by residents.
Except for fields already established which will not be reclaimed,
the rest, after the water recedes, will be measured,
boundary markers erected,
permanent prohibitions against encroachment enforced,
and methods for water collection devised.
As for Mǎtà, Shǔshān, Mǎchǎng, and Nányáng lakes,
they originally had sluice gates
which, with the addition of earthen dams,
can achieve deeper and wider storage,
to provide resources for next year’s transport.
However, Dúshān Lake
borders the Grand Canal,
with only a thin small weir,
and many breaches.
Considering the water situation,
when river water rises significantly, it should be allowed to flow into the lake;
when the lake and river levels are equal,
a weir should be built to block it;
when river water falls slightly,
not a drop of lake water should be allowed to escape.
Should the Grand Canal become shallow or blocked,
lake water can then be released downstream,
thus making replenishment convenient.
As for the sluice gates of the various lakes,
they should continue to follow old regulations,
filling ponds to accumulate water,
opening and closing them at appropriate times.
Then the lake waters will be deep and wide,
and the transport route will be clear.”
This was sent to the relevant department for discussion and implementation.
In the second year,
Qí Sūlè, observing that the eastern bank of Luòmǎhú Lake was low-lying and prone to leakage,
and the old dam was insufficient to withstand it,
built a diversionary overflow dam at the high ground west of Níngqiáo Bridge on the Lùtánghé River, east of the lake.
He then built another water-blocking dike six hundred zhàng long,
with a mouth thirty zhàng wide,
to facilitate discharge.
He also reinforced the embankment of the Dìdòngkǒu on the west bank of the Grand Canal for five hundred ten zhàng,
and the embankments on the east and west banks of Gāobǎo and Jiāngnán for five thousand twenty-four zhàng,
and the fascine work on the western dike of Báoyìng, from Qīlǐzhá southward to Liǔyuántóu, for five hundred seventy zhàng.
In the fourth year,
Qí Sūlè relocated the old Péngkǒu, south of Zhǒngjiādù, to the Shízìhé River,
but the sand accumulation at Péngkǒu remained as before.
Previously, Vice Minister Jiǎng Chénxī had submitted a memorial on matters concerning grain transport.
The Emperor ordered Grand Secretary Hé Guózōng and others to inspect the transport route in Yùdōng.
At this time, they reported:
“The Grand Canal in Shāndōng must rely on lake water for replenishment.
We request that Ānshānhú Lake be dredged and embankments built;
the dikes of Nánwàng and Mǎtà, and the Guānjiābà Dam, all be heightened and thickened,
and stone sluice gates built for timely opening and closing;
below the sand hills on both banks of the diversion outlets,
a water-constricting dam be built at each;
the Dàicūnbà Dam south of the Wènshuǐ River should be reinforced;
a Kǎnhé stone dam should be built north of the Wènshuǐ River;
a diversion dam should be built at Sìnnǚsì in Ēnxiàn;
on the west bank of the Zhuānpíng Grand Canal, two inlet gates should be repaired,
and on the east bank, an overflow dam built;
at the confluence of the Shāhé River and Zhàowánghé River in Púzhōu,
there was an old earthen dam for diverting water, which should be repaired and dredged.
As for the counties west of the river,
the people should be allowed to open waterways
to converge into the Shāhé River,
which will benefit
both the transport route and the livelihood of the people;
at Wǔchéng and on the north bank of Ēnxiàn,
one diversion canal should be dug at each location.
The Grand Canal in Hénán, from Běiquán southward,
passes through the five sluices of Rén, Yì, Lǐ, Zhì, and Xìn,
which block water for lateral flow.
There are inevitably abuses by ignorant people who intercept water.
We request the removal of the five sluices
and the construction of a stone weir at the southern mouth of Quánchí Pond,
with three opening gates,
divided into three channels,
and small dikes built to prevent lateral leakage;
one channel each to be opened on the east and west,
each channel to have five sluices,
to irrigate private fields.
The Xiǎodānhé River from Qīnghuàzhèn should be dredged and small dikes built.
One li east of the river, a water pond should be opened,
with three stone sluices,
divided into three channels.
The Xiǎodānhé River should be the official channel,
with one each on the east and west as people’s channels.
The stone dams on the Huánhé River are all abandoned
and should be reinforced as diversion dams.
The various spring sources should each be deepened and widened
to enter the Wèihé River for transport purposes.”
This was sent to the relevant department for discussion and implementation.
In the fifth year,
the Governor of Shāndōng, Sāilēng'é, observing that the Liǔchánghé River was progressively silting up and becoming shallow,
and although it was connected in one continuous stretch,
there was the Jīnqiánlǐng Ridge separating it in the middle,
specially opened two diversion canals:
one from north of the ridge flowing into Ānshān Lake,
the other from south of the ridge exiting the sluice gate to supply transport.
In the eighth year,
the Director-General of Rivers, Jī Céngjūn, stated:
“At Sùqiān, Luòmǎhú Lake previously had the Shízìhé River mouth,
which drew lake water to aid transport
and also to scour the Yellow River.
Later, as the lake water became weak,
fearing the Yellow River might flow backward,
the river mouth was blocked,
and a lake-blocking dam was also built west of Xīníngqiáo Bridge.
Consequently, the lake water could not flow through,
and transport relied solely on the Yellow River,
causing the water in the Middle River to carry sand and silt.
This autumn, mountain waters surged,
the outlet was blocked,
and it overflowed widely.
I request the restoration of the old Shízìhé River mouth
to allow lake water to enter the Middle River,
deepening the transport route,
and that the lake-blocking dam be widened appropriately
to allow upstream water
to enter the sea via the Liùtánghé River.”
This was granted.
In this year, for the first time, embankment guards (bǎofū) were established along both banks of the Yellow River and the Grand Canal,
with one fort (bǎo) every two li,
and two guards per fort,
who resided on the embankment and patrolled,
providing mutual support regardless of distance.
In the 9th year [of the reign],
Hé Tiánwénjìng, who was concurrently in charge of river management, stated:
"The Wèn River flows south to join the Grand Canal.
Previously, there were three weirs: Línglóng, Luànshí, and Gǔnshuǐ.
During the autumn floods,
water flowed from the Gǔnshuǐ weir into the Yánhé River,
and sand, along with the water, rushed through the openings of the Línglóng and Luànshí weirs.
Since Hé Guózōng constructed additional stone weirs within these three weirs,
not a single drop could pass.
With no tail-race to drain water [from the river]
and no openings to clear silt,
this caused the Wèn River to carry sand into the Grand Canal,
leading to ever-increasing accumulation of silt.
I request that the weirs be changed into sluices,
with fifty-six piers (jīxīn) constructed,
leaving fifty-five water gates in between,
and sluice boards installed to facilitate drainage.
Furthermore, since they cannot be opened and closed [at will],
a separate earthen embankment should be built
and named Chūnqiūbà."
The request was granted.
In the 11th year,
Yuè Jùn, the Governor of Shāndōng, stated:
"The water reservoirs in Shāndōng Province
previously included the four abandoned sluices of Ānshānhú Lake in Dōngpíng.
Since Hé Guózōng proposed restoring the Ānshānhú Lake reservoir,
the Línhé and Quānhú embankments were rebuilt,
and the Hú and Shégōu sluices were repaired.
Additionally, between the two abandoned sluices at Bālǐwān and Shílǐpù, a stone sluice was constructed,
named Ānjìzhá.
Although all these were completed,
they still could not store water to aid the Grand Canal.
This is because the lakebed soil is porous,
and the surrounding embankments cannot effectively contain the water.
All these should be repaired and protected.
As for the breaches in the Quānhú embankment,
all construction to repair them should be halted
to avoid waste."
This was approved.
In the 12th year,
Lǐ Wèi, the Governor-General of Zhílì, noted that Gùchéng was adjacent to Dézhōu and Wǔchéng in Shāndōng,
which was a turn in the river where it flowed eastward.
Previously, there were no dikes or embankments,
and floods often overflowed.
He encouraged the common people to raise funds to repair the earthen embankments,
providing them with a measured amount of rice
as relief in exchange for labor.
Yuè Jùn, the Governor of Shāndōng, observed that the river current at Dézhōu directly impacted the bank.
He had a new river channel dug on the east bank and a rolling weir built,
with remote dikes constructed on both sides,
and culverts opened as appropriate
to facilitate drainage.
In the 2nd year of Qiánlóng,
Censor Mǎ Qǐyuán stated:
"The Grand Canal in Zhílì and Shāndōng
has recently become severely silted."
Minister Lái Bǎo stated:
"For the Wèi River to supply water to the Grand Canal and irrigate fields,
I request that an order be issued to thoroughly investigate the terrain,
so that grain transport is not obstructed,
and people's fields can also be irrigated."
The Emperor ordered Vice Minister Zhào Diànzuì and Imperial Guard Ān Níng,
in conjunction with the three Governor-Generals of Zhílì, Grain Transport, and River Management,
and the two Governors of Hénán and Shāndōng, to investigate and report.
The Ministry's deliberation concluded:
"All four hundred thirty-nine springs in Shāndōng Province
have been dredged,
and the sluices and weirs are also sound.
However, at the various sluices of Dàimiào, Qījí, Liǔlín, Xīndiàn, Shīzhuāng, Zǎolín, Wànnián, and Dùnzhuāng,
some have collapsed wing walls,
or cracked face stones.
For the sluice gates and culverts on both banks,
there are cases where the wing walls of the Mǎnjiā Sānkōngqiáo bridge are sunken,
and the stone sluice face is too low.
These should be handed over to the River Governor for repair.
Furthermore, the lakes of Mǎtà, Shǔshān, Mǎchǎng, Dúshān, and Wēishān
are strictly forbidden from being used for planting reeds.
The reservoirs of Nánwàng, Nányáng, and Zhāoyáng lakes
are only suitable for draining water.
The Xiǎoqīnghé River has been silted for a long time.
All these should be repaired in due course.
As for the Wèi River supplying water to the Grand Canal and irrigating fields,
a water gauge should be established at Guǎntáo and Línqīng respectively,
to measure depth [and determine when to]
open and close them at the appropriate times."
Qǐyuán also stated that
the river channel from Tōngzhōu to Tiānjīn was largely shallow and silted,
making grain transport difficult.
The Emperor ordered Diànzuì to investigate and deliberate with Gù Cóng.
Soon after, it was deliberated that upstream from Tiānjīn,
though there were soldiers and officers,
there was no official in charge.
Therefore, an additional Assistant Magistrate (Cáoyùn Tōngpàn) should be appointed,
stationed at Zhāngjiāwān,
specifically to oversee dredging;
two Captains (bǎzǒng)
and four Sergeants (wàiwěi)
should be placed under the Assistant Magistrate's command.
Also, the four sluices including Pǔjìsì belong to Tōngzhōu,
so an additional Clerical Officer (lìmù) should be appointed.
The seven sluices including Qìngfēng belong to Dàxīng,
so an additional Registrar (zhǔbù) should be appointed.
When dredging is required,
they should report to the Zùoliángtīng to verify and carry out the dredging.
Following È'ěrtài's suggestion,
a rolling weir was built on the east bank of Dúliú,
and a diversion channel was opened,
leading into Zhōngtángwā,
to prevent the risk of overflow in Jìnghǎi
and reduce the contention of currents at the Sānchàkǒu in Tiānjīn.
That year,
the Huái and Yáng sections of the Grand Canal were extensively dredged,
from the entrance of the canal to Guāzhōu, over three hundred *li*.
In the 3rd year,
Bái Zhōngshān, the River Governor, stated:
"The flow of the Wèi River
is solely dependent on opening and closing [the sluices] as circumstances dictate.
The two water sluices at Guǎntáo and Línqīng, previously proposed by Diànzuì,
may not need to be established.
Hereafter, when rainfall is even,
the hundred springs and various sluices and channels will be used by officials and commoners as before.
Should the water be shallow and difficult to navigate,
the commoners' channels and sluices should be temporarily closed to benefit grain transport.
If the river water is abundant
and grain boats have passed early,
the officials' channels and sluices may also have their boards lowered as appropriate to irrigate the commoners' fields."
That year,
the Sānjiàotáng overflow weir was repaired,
and the silted tributary channels were dredged
to allow water to discharge into the Mǎjiáhé River.
Also, an overflow weir was repaired at the old site of Sānkōngqiáo,
and tributary channels were again dredged
to allow water to discharge into the Túhàihé River.
Two new culverts were constructed southeast of Péijiākǒu,
and the upstream and downstream embankments at Fángjiākǒu, the earthen dike at Mǎjiāzhá,
and the eight hundred *li* towpath of the Grand Canal embankment from Yìxiàn Táiwāng to Línqīng Bǎnjiá,
were repaired to protect the fields and houses along the river.
Previously, when dredging the river channel at Máochéngpù,
Gāo Bīn, due to the backward flow of the Yellow River,
moved the canal entrance over seventy *zhang* upstream,
connecting it to the Sānchàhé River.
The following year,
the Yellow River still flowed back into the canal,
and many argued that this was caused by the newly opened canal entrance.
The Emperor specifically ordered Grand Secretary È'ěrtài to investigate.
He soon reported:
"The canal entrance directly faces Qīngkǒu.
Lake water flows from the Péijiāchǎng diversion channel northeast directly to Qīngkǒu,
and the water entering the canal is still a calm, back-flowing current;
however, the newly excavated weir outside the new entrance is slightly short.
When the clear water is abundant,
the channel might become too wide.
It is advisable to build a longer weir,
and there is no need to revert to the old opening.
However, the old river is direct,
while the new river is winding.
Since the newly constructed sluices and weirs are not yet open,
grain boats should use the old river
to facilitate towing.
For the new river, two sluices, Tōngjì and Fúxīng, should be rebuilt below the Tiānfēizhá sluice,
to be opened and closed as needed.
Each year, after the grain boats have passed,
if the river water is abundant,
then the new river should be opened to divide the water flow.
If the lake water overflows,
then both the old river and the new river sluices should be closed to await the subsidence of the water,
so that the old and new rivers can be used interchangeably."
È'ěrtài again said:
“After detailed investigation of the old course of the Zhānghé River,
one path goes north from Wèixiàn County, Zhílì,
passes west of Qiūxiàn County city in Shāndōng,
reaches Xiàokǒukūn Village to meet the Fǔyánghé River,
enters the Dàlùzér Marsh,
then meets the Zǐyáhé River downstream,
and flows into the sea via Tiānjīn.
Another path goes north from Wèixiàn County via the old Shāhé River,
passes Pān'ěrzhuāng and east of Qiūxiàn County city,
goes through Qīnghé, Wǔchéng, Jǐngzhōu, Fùchéng and other places,
crosses Qiānqǐngwā,
and enters the Grand Canal to the sea.
The old course west of Qiūxiàn County city is quite far from the Wèihé River,
and its old traces are already submerged,
making reopening it very difficult.
Moreover, if the Fǔyánghé River meets the Zǐyáhé River downstream,
the entire Zhānghé River's water would be hard to contain.
Only the old Shāhé River, which is the ancient Mǎjiáhé River,
has a wide riverbed.
If we dredge and restore the old course here,
starting from the east of Hé'ěrzhài Village, following the northward turn of the Zhānghé River,
and opening it up to Zhāngdòngcūn Village,
it would rejoin the old river,
making the current smooth and saving labor.
A sluice gate should be built at the point where the newly dredged river heads east into the Wèihé River.
If the Wèihé River water is low,
it can be opened to assist transport;
if the Wèihé River water is sufficient,
the gate should be closed to let the water return to its old course.
Furthermore, another dam should be built below Qīngxiàn County as appropriate,
which would prevent silting in the canal north of Línqīng,
and permanently prevent flooding of fields and houses below Qīngxiàn County.
Orders should be given to the Zhílì and Shāndōng provinces to jointly survey and estimate repairs.”
In the fifth year,
the Shāndōng Waterway Administration was changed to the Canal Administration,
specifically tasked with water storage, discharge, dredging, and sluice gate affairs,
while still managing river treasury,
following Bái Zhōngshān's request.
In the twenty-second year,
an additional stone dam was built on the eastern embankment of Gāoyóu,
and water regulations were set,
determining the opening and closing based on the volume of water.
Hǎi Míng, the Cáo-yùn Gěishìzhōng, said:
“In the Jiāngnán Grand Canal,
only the ancient city's sandy and gravelly shoals at Táoyuán,
and the accumulating sand in the curved shoals, are problematic.
South of the Huánghé River,
only the section between Yángzhōu's Wāntóu Gate and the Fàn Gōng Cí, over three thousand three hundred zhàng long, is shallow and obstructed.
Both should be dredged.
The stretch from Zhènjiāng to Dāntú and Chángzhōu
originally has no source,
relying on tidal flow from the river for irrigation,
so it becomes shallow when tides are small in winter and spring.
Coupled with daily tidal silting,
and the loose soil on both banks that easily erodes,
it should be extensively dredged once every six years;
otherwise, sections must be shallow-dredged every three years.
Below the two gates of Dāntú,
and in Wǔjìn and other counties of Chángzhōu,
there are also intermittent shallow and stagnant sections,
all of which should be dredged uniformly.”
An imperial edict stated:
“Dredging rivers easily leads to corruption,
so regular inspections should be carried out,
and it should not be left to commissioners.”
In the twenty-fourth year,
Hǎi Míng, River Superintendent Zhāng Shīzài, and Shāndōng Governor Ā'ěrtài were ordered to jointly survey the Zhílì and Shāndōng sections of the Grand Canal.
Initially,
when the Grand Canal waters rose, they overflowed into places like Dézhōu,
and roads in the Jǐngzhōu area were blocked by silt.
At this time,
Hǎi Míng and others said:
“The Zhānghé and Wèihé rivers
experience high floods in autumn and winter,
so additional diversions should be made to their sides.
From Línqīng to Sìsì, 250 li away in Ēnxiàn County,
the river course is winding.
On the east bank of Línqīng Tǎwān, there was originally a Shāhé River,
which was a remnant of the Huánghé River,
flowing through Qīngpíng, Dézhōu, and Gāotáng into the Mǎjiáhé River to the sea.
We request to open it up and build a spillway stone dam,
allowing the Wèihé and Wèihé (likely meant Wènshǔihé) to merge,
to divert the water flow.
The two branch rivers at Sìsì and Shàomǎyíng
were originally channels for the Wènshǔihé and Wèihé rivers to discharge into the sea.
We request to widen their narrow sections
to prevent overflow in downstream areas like Dézhōu.”
In the twenty-fifth year,
Yào Hǎi, the Cáo-yùn Gěishìzhōng, together with Shīzài, said:
“North of Nánwàng, there is only Mǎtà Lake,
which is insufficient for water needs.
Dúshānhú Lake has the Jīnxiàn Gate, whose water only flows south,
but the Lìjì Gate's water can flow north.
We request to move the Jīnxiàn Gate to the north of Liǔlín Gate,
so that all lakes in Dúshānhú can supply water to the northern Grand Canal.”
This was approved.
In the twenty-seventh year,
because there were two existing spillways north of Xīnzhuāng Bridge in Yútái,
and their openings were deeply scoured,
making regulation difficult,
Shīzài and others' request to rebuild a spillway dam was approved.
In that year,
a diversion canal was dredged on the opposite bank of Xīfāng'ān in Dézhōu,
from Wèijiāzhuāng to Xīnhétóu,
forty zhàng long.
The Qi family village's scouring dam was built,
and the eastern and western dams of Qīngkǒu were extended,
and Lǐjiāwù stone sluice gate was repaired.
In the twenty-eighth year,
following Ā'ěrtài's proposal,
five diversion canals were opened near villages along the Línqīng Grand Canal
to distribute the water flow.
In the thirty-third year,
when the Huánghé water entered the Grand Canal,
Grand Secretary Liú Tǒngxūn and others were ordered to open the Línhuáng Dam
to release the high floodwaters,
and to dredge the Grand Canal's silted and shallow sections.
In the thirty-seventh year,
River Superintendent Yáo Lìdé said:
“A stone dam was originally built at Dǒngjiākǒu in the lower reaches of the Sìhé River to divert water.
Now the Sìhé River flows south,
and the stone dam has become a hindrance.
We request to dismantle it
and widen the old stone bridge at Mèngjiāqiáo.”
The request was granted.
In the fiftieth year,
Grand Secretary Āguì was ordered to inspect river works.
Āguì said:
“When I first arrived here,
I consulted Sàzài, Lǐ Fènghàn, and river officials,
most of whom advocated for diverting Huánghé water to fill the lakes.
This year, the lake water is extremely low;
not only is the Huánghé water turbid and the clear water weak,
but after June,
not a drop of clear water could be discharged.
At the same time, the Huánghé water was in full flood,
flowing backward into the Grand Canal,
reaching directly to Huái'ān and Yángzhōu.
The only plan is to use the already supplied Huánghé water to send empty boats back,
and store the weak clear water to assist heavy transport.
It is observed that this year's second batch of grain ships entered the Huáihé River,
relying entirely on the Huánghé water for buoyancy,
only then able to cross the Huáihé and Huánghé rivers.
Therefore, even if the Huánghé water subsides when empty boats return,
empty boats draw little water,
so if a way to manage it is found,
it seems they can proceed in quick succession.”
Using Huánghé water to supply the Grand Canal
began from this point.
In the fifty-first year,
the Grand Canal experienced high floods,
which caused the bottom wall of the Jīnghé River's sluice gate on the eastern bank below Huái'ān to collapse,
making it difficult to operate.
Five years later,
the gentry and common people of Shānyáng and Bǎoyīng repaired it.
In the first year of Jiāqìng,
the river burst its banks during a summer flood,
scouring open the Shéjiāzhuāng embankment of the southern Grand Canal,
and flowing north from Fēngxiàn and Pèixiàn into Jīnxiāng and Yútái,
then spreading into Wēishān and Zhāoyáng lakes,
penetrating the Grand Canal,
and overflowing both banks.
That winter,
the breach was closed,
but it collapsed again during the ice flood.
The following year,
both the eastern and western dams collapsed,
and construction was only completed in February.
Since the breach at Fēngxiàn,
there were scarcely any years without breaches, such as at Cáoxī, Suīxiàn, and Héngshuǐ.
In the ninth year,
due to the shallow and blocked Shāndōng Grand Canal,
extensive dredging was carried out;
also, water from Wēishān and other lakes was pre-stored to aid canal transport.
However, from then on,
the Huánghé River water was higher than the clear water,
and grain boats began to rely on the Huánghé water for buoyancy,
causing daily accumulation of silt,
which brought one benefit but a hundred harms.
In the twelfth year,
Déwén, the Vice Minister of Granaries and Stores, and others requested to dredge and repair the main river at Zhāngjiāwān,
and to block and build up Kāngjiāgōu to restore the canal,
while Censor Jiǎ Yǔnshēng requested to dredge the diversion canal.
Both requests were sent to Zhílì Governor Wēn Chénghuì for investigation and handling.
Chénghuì requested to dredge the upper reaches of the Wēnyúhé River.
The emperor ordered Vice Ministers Tuōjīn and Yīnghé to re-inspect with Déwén and others.
They soon reported:
“In recent years, grain transport has relied on the backflow from the lower reaches of the Wēnyúhé River,
which has caused silt accumulation.
If deep dredging is carried out from the upper reaches,
straight to the stone dam, it would truly be leveraging the situation for advantage.
However, due to varying elevations,
detailed surveys are required to ensure the entire river is completely unobstructed.”
This was approved.
In the thirteenth year,
Tōngzhōu experienced great floods.
The dam at Kāngjiāgōu was breached, forming a river,
and the river channel at Zhāngjiāwān subsequently became silted up.
Dáqìng (達慶), a junior minister of the Granary Administration, requested that grain boats for the following year try using Kāngjiāgōu for one year,
and that the dredging and restoration of the Zhāngjiāwān river channel be temporarily postponed.
The Emperor ordered minister Wú Jǐng (吳璥) to investigate,
and his deliberations with Dáqìng (達慶) concurred.
The request was then granted.
The following year,
censor Shǐ Hù (史祜) stated that
the Kāngjiāgōu river channel was difficult to navigate,
and requested the restoration of the main Zhāngjiāwān river.
The matter was referred to direct supervisor Wēn Chénghuì (溫承惠).
Chénghuì (承惠) reported:
"The current in Kāngjiāgōu is swift and turbulent;
upriver progress for grain boats is extremely arduous
and requires great effort in towing.
The terrain there is quite elevated,
and it is feared that in years of drought,
the river water would drain away completely,
making grain transport even more difficult.
However, the banks of Zhāngjiāwān are sandy,
making it difficult to establish dam foundations,
and the main river has been silted for a long time,
so dredging is also very difficult."
The Emperor again sent minister of public works Dài Jūnyuán (戴均元) to investigate,
who also reported that dam foundations were difficult to establish,
and that time was pressing.
He feared that the river channel would not be restored
before the grain transport season arrived.
He requested that traffic continue via Kāngjiāgōu,
and that a decision be made after another year of observation.
The request was implemented.
At this time, the Huái-Yáng (淮、揚) section of the Grand Canal, over three hundred *lǐ* long, was shallow and obstructed.
Ākèdāng'ā (阿克當阿), salt commissioner for the two Huái (淮) prefectures, requested that after the grain boats had passed through in September,
the three dams at Qīngjiāng (清江) be closed,
dams be built to block the flow,
and the section from Qīngjiāng (清江) to Guāzhōu (瓜洲) be dredged in segments.
The matter was submitted to the Ministry for deliberation.
The reply stated:
"The shallowness and obstruction of the Grand Canal in recent years
are certainly due to repeated breaches,
and the cause of these breaches
is the backflow of Yellow River water.
The cause of the backflow
is the raised riverbed,
which obstructs the clear water.
It is unavoidable to borrow Yellow River water to aid transport,
which leads to silting and breaches,
causing numerous problems.
Thus, the Grand Canal is the afflicted area,
not the root cause of the affliction.
If the clear water could flow freely to counter the Yellow River water
and also be diverted to aid transport,
then new silt within the canal's entrance would not settle,
and old silt could also be scoured away.
If the root cause of the backflow is not removed,
and efforts are hastily made to dredge the canal,
it is feared that it will silt up as soon as it is dredged.
The deeper the canal is dredged,
the fiercer the backflow will become,
causing dikes to break and currents to be drawn,
leading to more widespread harm."
The Emperor ordered minister Tuōjīn (托津) and others to investigate and handle the matter with the River Supervisor.
In the eighteenth year,
Cáo Dū Ruan Yuán (阮元) reported that the Pī-Sù (邳、宿) section of the Grand Canal had too few sluice gates,
resulting in shallow water and sand accumulation.
He requested the construction of two additional gates above and below the Huìzé (匯澤) gate.
The matter was submitted to Jiāng Dū Bǎilíng (百齡) for review and report.
In the first year of Dàoguāng (道光),
the rivers, lakes, and mountains in Shāndōng (山東) all flooded simultaneously.
The dikes and embankments north of Dàicūncùn (戴村) dam were breached for over sixty *zhàng*,
and the grass works scoured for over thirty *zhàng*.
There were three places on the south bank of the Sì Nǚ Sì (四女寺) tributary river where the Wènshuǐ (汶水) overflowed.
Following the advice of巡撫 Yáo Zǔtóng (姚祖同),
a channel was dug within the old river course beside the main river to guide water for transport,
while also considering the lakes and reservoirs.
In the third year,
the waters overflowed into Wángjiāzhuāng (王家莊) in Zhílì (直隸),
and the various *tīng* and *xùn* were responsible for compensation and repairs.
That year, four crushed stone dams were added to the north official dike of Dàicūncùn (戴村) dam.
In the fourth year,
Imperial Lecturer Pān Xī'ēn (潘錫恩) presented a memorial on the disadvantages of borrowing Yellow River water for transport,
stating briefly:
"Storing clear water to counter Yellow River water
is a long-standing method.
This year, Zhāng Wénhào (張文浩) delayed blocking the Yu Huáng (禦黃) dam,
leading to backflow and silting,
causing
calamity.
If Yellow River water is further diverted into the canal,
the river channel will be completely silted,
and everywhere will be blocked and overflowing,
potentially leading to breaches."
The matter was submitted to minister Wénfú (文孚) and others for careful deliberation.
Since the end of Jiāqìng (嘉慶),
the Yellow River had repeatedly flooded,
causing the Grand Canal to become increasingly silted.
Although yearly borrowing of Yellow River water for transport
was known by observers to be an inadequate plan,
there were proposals for sea transport.
In the fifth year,
the Emperor, due to the deliberations on sea transport by Cáo Dū Wèi Yuán Yù (魏元煜) and others,
found that while most considered it difficult and impractical,
Grand Secretary Yīnghé (英和) alone had a comprehensive plan for the entire Grand Canal and river system:
temporarily chartering sea vessels to alleviate delayed transport,
and adjusting the grain tribute quota to fund river management.
The plan was submitted to the relevant departments and Governors-General for careful planning.
Ultimately, as the Yellow River and Grand Canal were deeply afflicted
and could not be dredged and managed overnight,
an imperial edict was issued to temporarily implement sea transport once in the following year.
The newly appointed Governor-General of the Two Jiāng (江) provinces, Qíshàn (琦善), stated:
"Upon arriving at Qīngjiāng (清江),
your servant immediately went to inspect each dam of the Grand Canal, Jìyùn (濟運), and Shùqīng (束清).
Since the policy of borrowing Yellow River water for transport was implemented,
the bottom of the Grand Canal has risen by over ten *chǐ*,
the two banks are wide and thick with accumulated silt,
and the central channel is like a thin line.
What used to be a river surface three to four *zhàng* wide
is now only ten *chǐ* to five or six *chǐ* wide, varying.
Where the river bottom was one *zhàng* five or six *chǐ* deep,
there are now only three or four *chǐ* of water,
and some places have less than five *cùn* of water.
Boats are stuck everywhere in shallow waters,
making movement in either direction difficult.
Although the lake water stored at the Jìyùn (濟運) dam is gradually increasing,
the water flow downstream is no more than three *cùn*,
unable to flow freely.
The same applies to the over thirty *lǐ* stretch at Huái'ān (淮安),
and the condition of the Grand Canal above Gāo-Bǎo (高、寶) which entirely relies on lake water,
can be well imagined.
I request that the two ministers for river and grain transport be ordered to dredge the silted areas of the river surface to increase its width and depth,
then release lake water
to aid in towing,
so as not to miss the deadline for northbound travel."
The Emperor stated:
"Borrowing Yellow River water for transport
was originally a temporary measure.
Sūn Yùtíng (孫玉庭) observed the difficulty of towing grain boats
but did not promptly report and propose changes.
Wèi Yuán Yù (魏元煜), in his previous tenure as Cáo Dū,
and Yán Jiǎn (顏檢) stood by and watched the situation deteriorate,
tolerating it in silence,
wasting state funds and afflicting the people.
What were their intentions?
Order that all silted areas of the Grand Canal be dredged deep,
and the cost be borne proportionally by Yùtíng (玉庭), Yuányù (元煜), and Jiǎn (檢)."
Qíshàn (琦善) further stated that
since the blocking of the Yu Huáng (禦黃) dam,
the silting of the Grand Canal had not increased again,
and the clear water of Hónghú (洪湖) had accumulated to over one *zhàng*,
allowing all boats to be floated.
He dared not rashly proceed with dredging.
The engineering cost would exceed one million,
and even if Yùtíng (玉庭) and others exhausted all their possessions,
they would certainly not have such an amount of family wealth.
What is more concerning is that
to dredge the Grand Canal,
one must first block the Shùqīng (束清) dam,
cutting off the water source,
before the bottom can be exposed for dredging.
Currently, the lake water flows down rapidly,
and the pool outside the Shùqīng (束清) dam is very deep.
Moreover, it is clear water
and cannot carry silt to close and block the flow.
If dredging were to commence,
and the Shùqīng (束清) dam were to collapse,
then the work would be abandoned halfway,
and the funds would be wasted.
He requested to halt the dredging work on the Qīng-Yáng (𩹉、揚) section of the Grand Canal
to avoid rash actions and save unnecessary expenses.
The request was granted.
That year,
the Guǒqú Cūn (果渠村) dam and dikes were built on the upper reaches of the Wēnyú Hé (溫榆河).
In the seventh year,

Eastern River Governor-General Zhāng Jǐng (張井) and Deputy River Administrator Pān Xī'ēn (潘錫恩) requested the repair of the Liú Lǎo Jiàn (劉老澗) stone roller dam on the Northern Grand Canal, the south towing dike of the Zhōnghé (中河) Office, the east and west towing dikes of the Yángliáng (揚糧) two offices, and the stone work outside the dikes,
as well as the relocation of the Zhāoguān (昭關) dam.
The Emperor sent Yīnghé (英和) and others to investigate,
and it was decided to relocate the Zhāoguān (昭關) dam to the south of Sānyuán Gōng (三元宮) to its north.
The rest was carried out as requested.
In the eleventh year,
the Gāoyóu Hú (Lake) river overflowed Mǎpéngwān and Shísìbǎo.
The lake and river became one.
The Governor-General of Jiāngnán, Táo Shù, requested that, following the precedent from the Jiāqìng reign,
when the Grand Canal burst its banks,
empty grain ships should all detour via the lake.
In the eighth month,
Shísìbǎo was blocked.
In winter,
Mǎpéngwān was blocked.
Previously, when Shù was Governor of Sūzhōu,
he noted that the Zhènjiāng section of the Grand Canal had no water source
and relied solely on tidal currents from the river to float boats.
As the lower Liànhú (Lake) had been silted up for a long time,
he relocated and built the Huángnízhá (Yellow Mud Sluice) at Zhāngguāndù to serve as the lake's outlet,
allowing it to hold back the lake's flow,
causing it to ebb and flow,
thus somewhat supplementing the insufficient river tides.
This had achieved notable success.
By the fourteenth year, he was transferred to become Governor-General of Jiāngnán.
He then, together with Governor Lín Zéxú, inspected the area
and constructed two double-tiered water-storage dams at Huángjīnbà near Húdǐngchōng and at Dōnggāng.
They also reinforced 2,880 zhàng of dikes and embankments,
allowing water to enter the lake.
Additionally, two overflow stone dams were built on the eastern bank of the lake
to discharge floodwaters during deluges.
At the entrance to the canal, the ancient Niànsījiā Hán (Twenty-seven Family Culvert) was repaired
to serve as a water gate,
and a stone sluice was built to release water to aid navigation.
The project was completed that winter.
Water drawn from the culvert
could surprisingly flow backward upstream for several tens of lì,
allowing military vessels to follow one another southward.
Two years later,
the water current changed,
and the river's shape became winding.
The Huángnízhá was relocated and rebuilt 200 zhàng upstream,
and changed into two sluices, Zhèng and Yuè.
A central pier was built.
Furthermore, the Lǚchéngzhá, sixty lì downstream from Zhāngguāndù, was also changed into two sluices, Zhèng and Yuè,
to facilitate grain transport.
In the fifteenth year,
the Nángshā Yǐnqú Shābà (Sack Sand Diversion Channel Sand Dam) was relocated and built outside Xīhéchún
for water retention,
following the request of the Governor-General of the Eastern River, Wú Bāngqìng.
In the eighteenth year,
the Grand Canal became shallow and obstructed.
Acting on the advice of River Governor Lì Yùměi,
the Línqīngzhá (Sluice) was temporarily closed.
Nine straw dams were added outside the sluice,
holding back water in sections.
A large river-blocking dam was built upstream of the Hánzhuāngzhá (Sluice), south of Zhūjīzhuāng,
to divert all upstream springs and southbound waters of the Grand Canal
into Wēishānhú (Lake).
Six regulations for water storage and canal navigation were established.
In the nineteenth year,
Yùměi noted that the Dàicūnbà (Dam) was too low,
causing much of the Wènshuǐ (River) to spill sideways,
and ordered it raised according to the old system.
Initially,
Censor Chéng Guān had stated that the Huái and Yáng Mángdàozhá (Sluice) and Rénzìhé (River) should not have dams built,
as this would block the water's path.
This was submitted to Táo Shù and others for deliberation.
By this time, it was reaffirmed:
"This dam has been used for water storage for a long time
and does not block the flow of all waters to the river.
It should not be lightly altered."
This was followed.
At that time, the Wèihé (River) was shallow and stagnant,
making it difficult to aid navigation.
The Governor of the East, Jīng’èbù, requested a change to the rule of using the river for navigation for three days and for irrigation for one day.
An imperial edict ordered all official canals and sluices of Bǎiménquán (Spring) and Xiǎodānhé (River) to be fully opened,
temporarily avoiding civilian canals and sluices.
If any irregularities such as selling water, obstructing transport, or illegal dredging occurred,
severe punishment would be immediately imposed.
The following year,
Grain Transport Governor Zhū Shù again stated:
"The Wèihé (River) cannot flow southward,
which obstructs the transport route."
River Governor Wén Chōng and Governor of Hénán, Niú Jiàn, were ordered to investigate.
Wén Chōng and others reported:
"The time when the Wèihé (River) needs water
is precisely when the civilian fields await irrigation.
Food is the people's heaven;
it is impossible to ignore the wilting of crops.
Henceforth, if rainfall is delayed
and the Wèihé (River) is weak, causing a slight delay in boat travel,
there is no need to change the old regulations.
However, if there is severe drought
and grain ships are delayed for a long time,
as grain transport is more crucial than civilian fields,
civilian canals and sluices should be temporarily closed
to facilitate grain transport."
This was followed.
In the first year of Xiánfēng,
the Gānquánzhá (Sluice) river-supporting dike collapsed for over thirty zhàng.
The river burst its banks in Fēngxiàn,
Shāndōng was flooded,
and the Grand Canal overflowed.
Grain ships were rerouted via the lake and embankment.
Earlier, Minister of Revenue Sūn Ruìzhēn had stated that the Shízìhé (River) was detrimental to all grain transport.
If a new, wider canal were dug west of the river,
using the old river for sediment retention,
and a rolling dam built at Péngkǒu
to take in muddy water and discharge clear currents,
grain ships would not be obstructed,
and 200,000 in loading and unloading fees could be saved.
This was submitted to the Governor-General of the Eastern River, Yán Yǐyù, for deliberation.
By this time, Yǐyù stated:
"There is no certainty in the matter of digging a new canal;
it should not be lightly altered."
This was reported.
In the second year,
the Běiyùnhé (Northern Grand Canal) dike at Běisìzhuāng burst.
Minister Jiǎ Zhēn and Vice-Minister Lǐ Jūn were ordered to inspect and block the breach.
It was also decided that the next year's grain tribute would be transported to Tiānjīn by sea.
From then on, sea transport became regular.
After Tóngzhì,
steamships were used for sea transport,
saving costs and speeding up the journey.
Although some grain from north of the river was tried on the river transport route,
only one-tenth was transported this way,
merely to maintain the transport route.
In the fifth year,
the Tóngwǎxiānghé (River) burst its banks,
cutting through the canal eastward,
and dikes and embankments were washed away.
At that time, military affairs were pressing.
Only the breaches on both banks north of Zhāngqiū were blocked and built up.
At the remaining damaged sections of civilian dikes,
wrapped-head protective revetments were first constructed,
and dams were built to contain the backflowing yellow current.
There was no time for other considerations.
In the tenth year,
the Huáiyáng Mǎpéngwān burst.
In the fifth year of Tóngzhì,
Qīngshuǐtán burst.
In the eighth year,
the river burst its banks at Lányáng,
and floodwaters flowed downstream,
further damaging the Grand Canal's dikes and embankments.
North of Zhāngqiū,
there was no other water source.
For years, navigation relied solely on the Yellow River.
In the ninth year,
Grain Transport Governor Zhāng Zhīwàn requested that strong dikes be built on both the north and south sides where the Yellow River crossed the canal,
leaving a suitable canal mouth as an entry and exit point for grain ships,
and also building a straw dam
to block it during normal times to prevent backflow.
This was submitted to the relevant officials for deliberation.
Zhāng Zhīwàn was soon transferred to be Governor of Jiāngsū.
His successor, Zhāng Zhàodòng, stated that
"since dikes are built to contain water and leave an opening,
and a dam is also built to block it,
water flow might be slightly delayed.
If the upstream water rushed in continuously,
the newly built dikes and sluices might not withstand the impact.
If it were to divert northward,
Dōngchāng, Línqīng, Tiānjīn, and Héjiān
would inevitably be submerged,
and the northern section of the Wèihé (River) would also be ruined.
The only way is to block the Yellow River's eastward flow in the Yùnchéng Jǔhé (River) area,
which would protect the southern transport route.
At Zhāngqiū, Bālǐmiào, and other places, clear the silt from the Grand Canal
to facilitate northward grain transport.
Compared to building dikes to contain water,
this is more practical."
The emperor approved this.
In the tenth year,
the Hóujiālín River burst its banks,
flowing directly into Nányáng and Zhāoyáng Lakes,
and Yùnchéng nearly became a land of marshes.
The Grand Canal Superintendent, Sū Fèngwén, said:
"North of Ānshān,
the Grand Canal relies entirely on the diverting flow of the Wèn River;
it is only above Línqīng
that it receives assistance from the Wèi River.
Now the Yellow River lies across the middle,
carrying the Wèn River eastward,
leaving the area north of Ānshān without any source.
Therefore, at the points where the Wèi River enters the Grand Canal and where Zhāngqiū's Qīnghé meets the Yellow River,
a gate should be constructed at each,
to raise and store the Wèi River's water,
allowing it to flow southward.
Once the grain boats have passed Qí,
the new gate at Línqīng should be opened,
to allow the Wèi River to flow northward again,
to assist with floating and transport.
Furthermore, at the silted-up areas in Zhāngqiū, the channel should be dredged by more than a zhàng,
and south of Ānshān, it should also be uniformly dredged.
Thus, before the Yellow River's waters rise,
the Grand Canal will be deep,
and navigation will naturally be easier."
The Governor-General of Jiāngnán, Zēng Guófān, said:
"River transport is difficult everywhere.
For example, at Dàfànkǒu in Yìxiàn, sand has accumulated and blocked the channel,
where the water depth is less than two chǐ.
It must be dredged to a depth of four or five chǐ,
and the nearby stone piles on the shoals should be removed,
to level them with the riverbed,
only then will navigation be convenient.
To the north, the crucial waterway entering the lake at Xīshān Kǒu in Téngxiàn
is shallow and narrow.
At Wángjiālóu, Mǎnjiākǒu, and Ānjiākǒu on Wēishān Lake,
at Lìjiàn Zhá on Dúshān Lake,
at Xīndiàn Zhá, Huájiāqiǎn, and Shífó Zhá north of Nányáng Lake,
at Liúlǎokǒu and Yuánkǒu Zhá, north of the Nánwàng Zhá water-dividing Lóngwáng Miào,
everywhere is silted and shallow,
in places extending from several dozen zhàng to over a hundred zhàng.
All of these must be uniformly dredged.
These are the obstructions before crossing the Yellow River
that should be prepared for in advance.
As for where the Yellow River cuts through the canal,
gradually shifting southward,
the fifty-five lǐ of canal embankments from Ānshān to Bālǐ Miào
have been completely damaged by the Yellow River's waters.
Moreover, Shílǐpù, Jiāngjiāzhuāng, and Dàorénqiáo are all extremely shallow and silted.
It is advisable to dredge them on one hand,
and on the other hand, to drive wooden piles into the breaches,
connecting them with large ropes,
so that boats have something to rely on and pull themselves along when passing.
These are the difficulties in transport when crossing the Yellow River
that should be prepared for in advance.
After crossing the Yellow River,
from Zhāngqiū to Línhé, over two hundred lǐ,
the riverbed has varying elevations;
it must be excavated to be uniform.
When the Yellow River's floodwaters have not yet receded,
close the gates to store water,
to prevent depletion.
Alternatively, an earthen diversion dam could be built east of the Píngshuǐ Nán Zhá,
to draw Yellow River water into the canal.
These are the measures for preventing the canal from drying up after crossing the Yellow River
that should be prepared for in advance.
West of the Dōngpíng section of the Grand Canal is the Yán River,
which is a vital route for salt boats in the eastern province.
If grain boats enter the Yán River near Ānshān
and return to the Grand Canal at Bālǐ Miào,
the journey is over a hundred lǐ,
but compared to directly crossing the Yellow River,
which has large currents at breaches upstream
and scattered rocks and tree stumps downstream,
the difference in difficulty is vast.
If, upon reaching Ānshān,
the Yellow River current is too strong,
it is advisable to flexibly change the route,
and markers should first be surveyed and established as guidance.
This is another instance of changing routes when crossing the Yellow River
that should be prepared for in advance."
The Director-General of River Conservancy, the Grand Canal Superintendent, and the Governor of Shāndōng conferred on the matter.
In the eleventh year,
the Director-General of River Conservancy, Qiáo Sōngnián, requested the construction of a gate at Zhāngqiū
to divert Yellow River water to supplement the Grand Canal.
The Assistant Department Magistrate, Jiǎng Zuòjǐn, proposed diverting Wèi River water to supplement the Grand Canal.
The Emperor consulted the Governor-General of Zhílì, Lǐ Hóngzhāng.
Lǐ Hóngzhāng said:
"The silting of Qīngkǒu in previous years
was precisely the problem caused by diverting Yellow River water to supplement the Grand Canal.
Now, the river at Zhāngqiū is only a few zhàng wide;
if the heavy, turbid Yellow River water is introduced and regulated by a gate and dam,
the water level will rise,
and the silting will accelerate manifold.
As for Jiǎng Zuòjǐn's proposal to divert the Wèi River,
it stems from the fact that there is no clear water source for the canal north of Zhāngqiū,
hence this proposal.
If the full force of the Huái River
could not withstand the Yellow River,
still leading to backflow and silting,
how could a shallow and clear Wèi River
possibly resist the Yellow River and supplement the canal?
His intention is likely to adopt the method of supplementing the canal with various rivers in Shāndōng.
However, to the south of Tài Shān,
all waters flow westward.
By following the natural gradient,
the waters from one hundred and eighty springs,
with abundant sources and numerous branches,
are sufficient to supplement the canal.
The Wèi River is weak,
and its natural flow is northward.
Now, it must be forced to curve and flow southward,
dividing one river into two, which will lead to many inconveniences.
If the Qìn River were diverted into the Wèi River to boost its source,
the Qìn River's waters are strong and turbid,
and once released, they are difficult to control,
a clear warning about which has been left by predecessors.
In modern times, river management has also involved discussions on facilitating transport,
which has led to a dilemma,
and ultimately no long-term solution.
When things reach an impasse, they change;
when they change, they find a way through.
Currently, along thousands of lǐ of coastline,
ocean-going vessels are gathered in large numbers,
creating an unprecedented situation throughout history.
It is indeed permissible to use sea transport for transshipment,
from Hù to Jīn,
which is more convenient and faster."
Upon receiving the memorial,
an imperial edict was issued that the grain for the Jiāngnán and Ānhuī Grain Circuses, approximately one hundred thousand dàn annually, would still be transported via the Grand Canal,
while the remainder would be transported by sea.
In the third year of Guāngxù,
the Governor of Shāndōng, Lǐ Yuánhuá, presented a three-tier proposal for the Grand Canal's upper, middle, and lower sections.
He also stated that considering the financial resources of Shāndōng province,
he proposed using the middle-tier plan,
which involved thoroughly dredging the northern Grand Canal,
restoring it to its original course,
and constructing a northern gate.
As it was a year of famine,
relief was provided through public works,
making it as economical as possible.
The estimated cost was over three hundred thousand.
The proposal was submitted to the appropriate departments for deliberation.
In the fifth year,
there were requests to restore river transport.
The Governor-General of Jiāngnán, Shěn Bǎozhēn, stated:
"Considering the general trend,
our predecessors, in dealing with river transport,
all resorted to it only as a last resort.
The Hàn and Táng dynasties had their capitals in Cháng'ān,
the Sòng dynasty had its capital in Biànliáng.
There was no other option but river transport.
However, it repeatedly encountered dangers and obstacles,
causing distress to both officials and common people.
Eventually, granaries were built mid-route,
and supplies were transferred at opportune moments,
after which mishaps were fewer.
The Yuán dynasty exclusively used sea transport,
hence there were no river disasters throughout the Yuán era.
It was only after the Míng dynasty
that there was an eagerness for river transport.
Consequently, efforts had to be devoted to river defense.
No sooner was the transport system regulated
than the river suddenly changed its course.
As river channels constantly shifted,
the grain transport administration had to adapt accordingly,
and our dynasty followed suit.
The former Governor-General proposed the idea of sea transport;
when the grain transport administration faced utter destitution,
it was sustained by this to prevent its collapse.
Critics argue that the Grand Canal connects north and south,
and grain boats rely on it for transit,
and also to protect agricultural land.
They believe that if the transport route exists, water conservancy also exists;
if the transport route is abandoned, water conservancy is also abandoned.
I believe it is easier to discuss water conservancy apart from the transport route,
but difficult to plan water conservancy while incorporating the transport route.
Agricultural land and the transport route are fundamentally incompatible.
When there has been no rain for more than ten days,
the people want to open sluice gates to irrigate their fields,
but officials must close them to keep the boats afloat.
When the Grand Canal overflows,
officials then open sluice gates to protect the dikes,
and the agricultural land below the dikes immediately becomes submerged,
making farming even more impossible.
Critics also lament the lack of funds
and insufficient number of boats,
which led to the failure of river transport.
I believe that even if the annual repair funds and government-built boats from the Dàoguāng era
were all still intact today,
it would be unfeasible to conduct grain transport on a river that 'borrows Yellow River water to aid transport.'
It would not be feasible.
In recent years, the boats hired north of the Jiāng
are less than half the number of former grain boats,
yet they must wait for the Yellow River floods to swell,
and exhaust the efforts of thousands of brave men to pull them,
and after a few dozen boats pass, silt accumulates again.
The silt accumulated today
must be worse than yesterday,
and today's expenses
will not benefit tomorrow.
Even if there were many large boats,
how could their skills be applied?
Recently, due to successive years of drought in the northwest,
the Yellow River's source flow has been weak,
leading to a casual disregard.
However, extremes reverse.
If the flow is diverted for transport,
and it moves north, the Jīfǔ region will suffer;
if it moves south, the Huái and Xú regions will suffer.
What then of the people's livelihoods?
What then of the national economy?"
In the eighth year,
during the autumn great flood,
a new section of the Zhāngjiāwān Grand Canal, from Sūzhuāng to Yáoxīnzhuāng, was breached,
measuring over seven hundred zhàng in length.
Both its upper and lower ends connected to the old river.
Its course was straight and smooth,
and the main current flowed down it.
The old river, from its upper to its lower end,
measured over six thousand four hundred zhàng,
had already stopped flowing.
However, since the new river channel was self-breached,
it was not uniformly deep throughout.
The following year,
the Governor-General of Zhílì, Lǐ Hóngzhāng, ordered the manufacture of new-style iron-edged large dredging boards,
to be dragged along both banks,
to ensure uniform patency.
In the twelfth year,
the Píngjiātuan section of the Cháobái River in Tōngzhōu overflowed,
diverting eastward into the Jiàngàn River.
Soon after,
the old course of the Grand Canal was blocked and restored.
In the thirteenth year, sixth month,
it again overflowed, breaching the small eastern dike at Běishìzhuāng, downstream of the new Píngjiātuan works,
and the old dike also collapsed for over a hundred zhàng,
forming a continuous breach.
Eighty percent of the current diverted eastward.
It was soon blocked.
In that year,
the river burst its banks at Zhèngzhōu,
and the Yellow River flow in Shāndōng ceased.
Grain boats could not proceed south,
and those who had previously "borrowed Yellow River water to aid transport"
were now helpless.
Immediately, the accumulated silt at Línkǒu was dredged,
allowing empty boats to enter the canal from the Yellow River.
In the fifteenth year,
the Governor of Shāndōng, Zhāng Yào, stated:
"River transport cannot be suspended for long.
I request that the twenty thousand piculs of grain transport, converted to sea transport, be reverted to river transport."
This was approved.
In the sixteenth year,
following the advice of the Governor-General of Jiāngnán, Zēng Guóquán,
repairs were made to the dikes, sluices, and culverts of the southern Grand Canal in Yángzhōu Prefecture,
as well as the brickwork around cities and towns.
Also, following the advice of the Director-General of Grain Transport, Sōngchūn,
the Grand Canal in Pī and Sù was dredged.
In the nineteenth year,
the Cháobái River overflowed,
with over seventy breaches along both banks of the transport dike,
and seven breaches in the upstream Wùguān Bureau.
All were blocked that winter.
In the twentieth year,
the Grand Canal sections in Jìníng, Wénshàng, Téng, Yì, Chípíng, Yánggǔ, and Dōngpíng Prefectures were dredged.
The following year,
over two hundred lǐ of the Grand Canal from Táochéngbù to Línqīng were dredged.
In the twenty-fourth year,
Attendant Reader Xuéshì Ruìxún stated that converting southern grain transport to payment-in-lieu
was beneficial and without harm.
He requested that the commutation price be raised annually to purchase rice in Tiānjīn to fill the granaries.
Censor Qín Kuíyáng also stated that river transport was excessively arduous and costly,
and requested the suspension of river transport north of the Jiāng.
Both requests were denied,
and orders were reiterated to earnestly dredge
and continue transport as usual.
In the twenty-sixth year,
the allied forces entered Jīngshī,
and all granaries were occupied.
Not a single grain of stored rice remained.
River transport north of the Jiāng, reaching Dézhōu,
was then switched to land transport for Shān [xī] and Shǎn [xī].
In the twenty-seventh year,
Prince Qìng, Yīkuāng, and Grand Secretary Lǐ Hóngzhāng stated:
"The storage of grain tribute
is half dependent on transport operations.
Adapting to the times,
we request an imperial decree for all provinces to convert all grain tribute to payment-in-lieu.
Matters of procurement, transport, remittance, receipt, and storage
should be separately instructed to the grain transport officials and granary officials for planning."
From then on, river transport was abolished,
and the water conservancy of the Grand Canal was also independently managed by the various provinces.
Annals 103: Rivers and Canals (3) – Huái River, Yǒngdìng River, Seawall
The Huái River's source is in Tóngbó Shān.
It flows southeast through Suízhōu,
then turns north past the east of Tóngbó,
traversing Xìnyáng, Quèshān, Luóshān, Zhèngyáng, Xī, Guāngshān, Gùshǐ, Fǔyáng, Huòqiū, and Yǐngshàng.
Its confluent tributaries merge and flow eastward,
reaching Zhèngyáng Guān.
Below it are the Shā River, the East and West Féihé Rivers, the Luò River, the Ěr River, the Qiàn River, and the Tiān River,
all flowing into the Huái.
Passing Fèngyáng,
there are also the Wō River, the Xiè River, the East and West Háohé Rivers, and the Chōng, Kuài, Tuó, and Tóng rivers,
all converging into the Huái and flowing into Hóngzé Hú.
Further northeast,
it passes Qīnghé, Shānyáng, and Āndōng,
entering the sea via Yúntī Guān.
It flows through Húběi, Hénán, Ānhuī, and Jiāngsū provinces,
for over one thousand seven hundred lǐ.
The Huái itself was not a menace.
Since the Yellow River shifted south in the Northern Sòng dynasty,
usurping the lower course of the Huái and entering the sea,
the Huái suffered from this.
When the Huái suffered, all the rivers flowing into it overflowed everywhere,
and both Jiāng [sū] and Ān [huī] provinces suffered.
Indeed, when the lower reaches are obstructed, the upper reaches overflow;
this is the nature of water.
Therefore, governing the river is governing the Huái,
and governing the Huái begins with governing the river.
Throughout the Qīng dynasty,
efforts were made in the area where the Huái and Yellow rivers converged,
with extremely diligent work
and enormous expenditure.
By the Xíanfēng era,
the Tongwǎxiāng breach occurred,
and the Yellow River flow shifted north.
The river course that had existed since the Sòng and Yuán dynasties was thus transformed.
However, with the river shifting and silt remaining,
the task of guiding the Huái could not be abandoned.
Here, the source, course, divisions, and convergences of the Huái River,
as well as the storage and discharge at Qīngkǒu,
and the construction of weirs and dams at Hóngzé Hú,
are all listed in detail.
In the sixth year of Shùnzhì, summer,
the Huái River overflowed at Xīxiàn,
destroying people's fields and homes.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
the people of Xūyí and Sìzhōu illegally cut eight small channels, starting from the ancient Gǔgōu town in the south and ending north of Gǔjiāqiáo,
causing a strong half of the Huái River's water to drain into the various lakes of Gāoyóu and Bǎoyìng,
while the Huái River at Qīngkǒu became weaker,
powerless to contend with the Yellow River.
Within six or seven years,
the Huái River swelled greatly,
breaching Gǔgōu and Zháijiādūn,
and flowing directly from the lakes of Gāoyóu and Bǎoyìng into the Grand Canal,
breaching Qīngshuǐtán,
and also overflowing Wǔjiādūn and Gāoliángjiàn,
submerging Qīngkǒu and causing the Yellow River to breach upstream.
In the fifteenth year,
the Huái River again swelled greatly,
combining with the waters of Suīhú to surge eastward,
breaching twenty-six wooden structures at Gāoliángjiàn,
and seven stone structures at Gāoyàn,
not a single drop exiting Qīngkǒu.
The Yellow River, in turn, took advantage of the high water to breach in four directions,
one entering Hóngzéhú,
and joining the Huái River through the breaches at Gāoyàn,
all converging at Qīngshuǐtán,
further silting up the downstream.
The Director-General of Rivers, Jìn Fǔ, said:
"The downstream of Hóngzéhú,
from west of Gāoyàn to Qīngkǒu, approximately twenty *lǐ*,
was originally a vast expanse of water,
where the entire Huái River met the Yellow River.
Since the Huái River breached to the east and the Yellow River flowed inward,
the entire lakebed gradually became dry land,
with only a small river remaining, about ten-plus *zhàng* wide and five or six *chǐ* to one or two *chǐ* deep,
with tens of thousands of *qǐng* of silt,
making dredging very difficult.
The only way is to dig a diversion channel
on each side, about twenty *zhàng* from the water's edge,
to allow the water to scour separately,
so that the Huái River's downward flow
can clear the silt,
rush directly to Qīngkǒu,
join the Yellow River to scour away sand,
and avoid the worry of obstruction and dispersion."
Fǔ also said:
"Once the downstream is regulated,
the Huái River can flow directly to join the Yellow River and scour away sand.
However, the dikes along the lake,
except for the breaches,
are all damaged and thin,
posing a dangerous threat.
Wooden structures are certainly prone to damage, and even stone structures collapsing are countless.
