However, beneath the dikes are gentle earthen slopes,
which are not easily eroded even by great floods.
Now, to save costs and ensure strong construction,
the only method is to build earthen slopes outside the dikes near the lake.
For every *zhàng* of dike,
a five *chǐ* wide slope should be built,
densely planted with grass roots and seeds on top,
so that when they grow luxuriantly,
the earth will become even firmer.
As for the stone structures at Gāoyàn,
earthen slopes should also be built around them,
embedding the stone structures within,
making them more stable.
Compared to using timber, stone, or bundles of brushwood,
this can save more than two hundred and ten thousand [taels],
and avoid the trouble of erosion and collapse."
He also said:
"From Zhōujiāzhá, passing through Gǔgōu and Tánggěng to the south of Zháijiābà,
it is estimated that thirty-two *lǐ* of dike need to be built,
and the nine channels originally breached here should be blocked,
as well as thirty-four large and small breaches at Gāoliángjiàn, Gāojiāyàn, and Wǔjiādūn.
This would cost more than seven hundred and five thousand [taels],
all using bundles of brushwood,
which would rot away
in no more than three years.
Your servant has considered alternatives:
except for the edges and headings which must use bundles of brushwood,
the rest should be built with densely placed pile foundations,
with many planks and cables added,
using cattail to wrap earth,
tied with ropes and filled in.
This can save half the cost,
and be more durable.
It is now proposed to change from using bundles of brushwood to wrapped earth,
and still build earthen slopes."
The emperor approved.
In the eighteenth year,
Qīngkǒu, Lànníqiǎn, Péijiāchǎng, and Shuàijiāzhuāng diversion channels were greatly dredged,
allowing all Huái River water to exit at Qīngkǒu,
joining the Yellow River downstream to the east.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Director-General of Rivers Dǒng Ānguó, based on the proposal of Mò Zhīhàn, the prefect of Sìzhōu,
requested to open the Yǔwáng River at Shèngrénshān in Xūyí,
to guide the Huái River into the Jiāng River,
stating briefly:
"The ancient Yǔwáng River,
from Shèngrénshān in Xūyí, passing through Hēilínqiáo, Tóngchéngzhèn, Yángcūn, Tiānchángxiàn to Bālǐqiáo in Lùhé,
each has varying river forms, streams, and ridges.
If opened to divert water into the Jiāng River,
then the various tributaries and streams of Tiāncháng, Yángcūn, and Tóngchéng
would not enter Gāoyóuhú during high water,
preventing the lake from overflowing,
and reducing the water in the lower river.
As for the mouth of the ancient river,
it is currently not connected to the Huái River,
so a gate must be built.
When the water is low, the gate should be closed to aid navigation,
and when it floods, the gate should be opened to release water,
which might reduce the surging force of the Huái River."
The proposal was rejected by court deliberation.
The following year,
there was an imperial edict to block the Gāoyànbà.
Two years later,
Director-General of Rivers Yú Chénglóng submitted a request to block six dams.
He died of illness during this time,
and did not complete his work.
That year, the water again rose greatly,
and the three dams already blocked
were quickly swept away by the torrent.
In the thirty-ninth year,
Zhāng Pénghè became Director-General of Rivers,
and completely blocked them,
ensuring no leakage from the Huái River,
and all water returned to Qīngkǒu;
he also opened seven diversion channels: Zhāngfú, Péijiācháng, Zhāngjiāzhuāng, Lànníqiǎn, Sānchà, as well as Tiānrán and Tiāncì,
guiding the Huái River to scour Qīngkǒu;
he also widened the Qīngkǒu diversion channel, which was only thirty-plus *zhàng* wide,
insufficient to effectively discharge all the lake water.
Consequently, the clear flow, which had been interrupted for over ten years,
suddenly surged out,
with the Huái River more than a *chǐ* higher than the Yellow River.
In the fortieth year,
the great dike at Gāoyàn was built.
In the forty-fourth year,
Shèngzǔ made a southern tour,
inspected the Gāoyàn dike project,
and issued an edict to dredge channels and build dikes below the three dams,
to confine the water into the lakes of Gāoyóu and Shàobó.
Furthermore, as the water in Hónghú swelled,
Sìzhōu and Xūyí both suffered from floods,
so dikes should be built at the affected areas to confine the water.
In the forty-fifth year,
the Governor-General of the Two Jiāngs, Āshān, and others, proposed to open another channel at the Liúhuáisào in Sìzhōu,
to reach Zhāngfúkǒu directly,
to divert the force of the Huái River,
estimated to cost over three million one hundred thousand [taels].
The Board deliberated and rejected it.
Court officials also considered the river project significant,
and requested the emperor to personally inspect and instruct.
The following year,
the emperor made a southern tour to inspect the rivers,
and issued an edict saying:
"Upon detailed investigation, the terrain of Liúhuáisào is very high;
even if a channel were dug,
it could not reach Qīngkǒu directly.
Moreover, many of the marker poles were placed on graves.
If a river were opened according to this,
not only would it destroy fields and homes,
but it would even damage tombs.
Why bother with such an unnecessary endeavor?
If Liúhuáisào is to be opened now,
mountains must be excavated and ridges pierced,
which would not only be extremely difficult to succeed,
but also, in case of flood,
if it does not flow into Hónghú,
it will surely breach the Grand Canal."
He ordered the removal of the marker poles,
and reprimanded Āshān, Pénghè, and others accordingly.
The emperor also said:
"The Huái and Yellow Rivers during the Míng Dynasty were completely different from today.
In the Míng Dynasty, the Huái River was weak,
hence there was a risk of backflow.
Now, the Huái River is strong and the Yellow River is weak.
Instead of opening the useless channel at Liúhuáisào,
it would be better to further dredge and widen the outlets of Hónghú,
allowing the clear water to flow even more freely,
which would be of no small benefit."
In the forty-ninth year,
the project of extending the Western Dike for flood control was increased,
at the request of the River Director Zhào Shìxiǎn.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng's reign,
the east and west water-retaining dams at Qīngkǒu were rebuilt in front of the Fēngshénmiao to store clear water,
each over twenty zhàng long.
In the third year,
the Director-General of Rivers, Qísūlè, due to the breach at Zhūjiāhǎi,
which caused siltation at the bottom of the lake,
feared that the Gāoyàn dam would be difficult to maintain.
He lowered the thresholds of the three dams by one chi and five cùn to release lake water,
and remedy a temporary emergency.
Unbeknownst to him, the lower the water fell,
the more difficult it became for the Huái River to flow out.
Its strength was too weak to contend with the Yellow River,
leading to backflow for years,
with the diversion directly rushing through.
Lǐ Wèi somewhat disapproved of this.
Previously, the stone work of the Gāoyàn dam had not been uniformly strong and thick.
By the winter of the seventh year,
a million táels were allocated,
and the Director-General of Rivers, Kǒng Jìxún, and the Governor-General, Yǐn Jìshàn, were ordered to demolish and rebuild the weak and dilapidated sections of the embankment,
ensuring uniform solidity.
In the autumn of the tenth year,
the stone work of the Gāoyàn dam was completed.
In the second year of Qiánlóng's reign,
following the advice of the Director-General of Rivers, Gāo Bīn,
an order was given to dredge the river channel from Máochéngpù downstream,
passing through the various zhou and xiàn of Xú, Xiāo, Suī, Sù, Líng, and Hóng,
to the Ānméndǒu River in Sìzhōu,
a winding route of over six hundred lǐ,
to reach Hónghú Lake,
and exit at Qīngkǒu.
However, the imperial officials from Huáiyáng, Xià Zhīfāng and others, stated its inconvenience.
The matter was referred to the various governors-general and governors, and the Director-General of River Conservancy and Director-General of Grain Transport for deliberation,
and Gāo Bīn was summoned for questioning.
When Bīn arrived,
he presented maps and explained the situation,
and it was then understood that what Zhīfāng and others had said did not reflect the current circumstances,
so Bīn's proposal was ultimately adopted.
The following year,
the Máochéngpù river channel project was completed.
In the fourth year,
Emperor Gāozōng, considering that the three dams of Gāoyàn had been lowered,
and there was sufficient water flow to drain across the banks,
followed the advice of Grand Secretary È'ěrtài,
and permanently prohibited the opening of the two Tiānrán dams.
In the autumn of the fifth year,
a strong westerly gale caused
raging lake waves,
which struck the old embankment of the eighth fort of the Gāoyàn patrol,
causing fourteen sections to collapse.
Repairs were promptly made.
In the sixth year,
Bīn said:
"The Sānchàhé River in Jiāngdū is the mouth of the Guā River and Yí River.
The Guā River has a low terrain,
so the amount of Huái River water flowing into the Guā River is small,
thus the current is slow and cannot scour deeply,
causing the river channel to gradually silt up.
A dam should be built to block the old mouth of the Guā River,
and a new diversion channel should be dug downstream from the Yángzǐqiáo barracks,
to reduce the amount of Huái River water entering the Guā River,
so that the Yí River can divert and scour away silt.
Also, the old diversion channel of the Guāzhōu Guǎnghuì Gate should be blocked,
and a new diversion channel should be opened below the gate,
to equalize the water flow between the gate and the two diversion channels,
thereby slowing the direct flow of the Huái River into the Yangtze River,
which would be even more beneficial for the transport route."
In the seventh year,
both the river and the lake rose,
and some argued that all the upper waters of the Huái River converged into Hónghú Lake,
and therefore more outlets into the Yangtze River should be opened below Shàobó.
Bīn also advocated this.
Consequently, the old Shíyánggōu River was dredged to flow directly into the Yangtze River,
and a forty-zhàng spillway dam was built.
Additionally, the three river channels at Dǒngjiā Yóufáng below Mángdàozhá Gate and Kǒngjiā Hán in Báitǎhé were opened,
and more spillway dams were built,
to ensure the smooth and unobstructed flow of Huái River water.
In the eighth year,
the Huái River suddenly rose by over a zhàng,
threatening Línhuáichéng City,
so the river management was relocated to Zhōuliángqiáo.
In the sixteenth year,
the Emperor, considering that the Tiānrán dam was the tail end of the Gāoyàn dam,
and its frequent opening during floods
caused suffering to the downstream zhou and xiàn,
ordered a stone tablet to be erected to permanently prohibit its opening.
Following Bīn's advice,
the Zhì and Xìn dams were added outside the three dams,
to assist in drainage.
In the seventh month of the eighteenth year,
the Huái River overflowed at Gāoyóu,
damaging the Chēluódà dam and the two Shàobó gates,
submerging many fields and homes in the lower river region.
In the twenty-second year,
given that the lake water flowed out of Qīngkǒu,
relying on the east and west dams to confine it,
and together scour the Yellow River,
if the lake water was too great,
overflowing the Wǔbà (Five Dams),
it was also feared that it would cause disaster for the lower river region.
Therefore, a regulation was established: when the water level at the Wǔbà exceeded one cùn,
the east dam should be widened by two zhàng,
and so on, with this incremental widening
inscribed on a stone tablet at the east dam.
Subsequently, whenever the lake water rose,
the east dam was widened to discharge the floodwaters,
some being widened by as much as sixty or seventy zhàng.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Emperor stated:
"In the lakeside regions of Jiāngnán,
during every major flood season,
heavy rains pose a concern.
Hóngzé Lake, in particular,
is a crucial valve and key.
For the safety of the water-logged areas,
nothing is better than broadly dredging Qīngkǒu,
which is the most important task for now.
Currently, the Wǔbà of Gāoyàn is more than seven chǐ above the water surface,
and the Qīngkǒu mouth is thirty zhàng wide.
A plan should be immediately formulated based on this.
In the future, when the water level at the two dams rises by one chǐ,
Qīngkǒu will be widened by ten zhàng.
As the water level continues to rise,
the mouth will be progressively widened,
following this rate."
In the sixth month of that year,
the water level at the Wǔbà exceeded one chǐ.
The Director-General of Rivers, Gāo Jìn, complied with the imperial decree and widened Qīngkǒu by ten zhàng,
allowing for very smooth drainage.
In the thirty-second year,
the Director-General of Southern Rivers, Lǐ Hóng, stated:
"The old water gauge at Sānguānmiào in Zhèngyángguān,
when examining water marks, shows that the reported rises and falls this year
do not match those downstream.
I request that one additional water gauge each be installed between Jīngshān and Túshān and at Línhuáizhèn,
to verify the rises and falls of the various waters."
This was approved.
In the thirty-fourth year,
the Emperor, fearing that the earthen barrier on top of the Wǔbà of Gāoyàn would not be sufficient to withstand winds and waves,
ordered appropriate additions of stone work.
Gāo Jìn and others stated its inconvenience,
so brushwood and willow branches were used instead.
In the fortieth year,
major repairs were made to the dams at Yàn and Xū, as well as the brick and stone work along the river.
Previously, the Emperor, concerned about the backflow at Qīngkǒu,
issued an edict to dredge the old course of the Táozhuāng diversion channel, opened during the Kāngxī reign by Zhāng Pénghé,
to divert the Yellow River northward.
He dispatched È'ěrtài and Bīn to survey it,
but they stopped due to the sudden arrival of floodwaters.
Subsequently, Wányán Wěi succeeded Bīn as Director-General of Rivers,
and fearing that the diversion channel would be difficult to establish,
adopted Bīn's proposal
to set up wooden guide structures west of Qīngkǒu
to direct the current northward,
but the Táozhuāng plan was ultimately not dared to be discussed.
The following year,
the Director-General of Southern Rivers, Wú Sìjué, was summoned to the court,
and strongly argued against the harm caused by backflow.
Sàzài, who succeeded him,
also advocated for changing the river mouth.
The Emperor then decided to proceed with the opening.
Consequently, the foundations of the east and west dams at Qīngkǒu were moved downstream by one hundred and sixty zhàng to a flat platform,
and a yellow-river-blocking dam one hundred and thirty zhàng long was built.
Additionally, a diversion channel was opened north of Táozhuāng,
to keep the Yellow River farther from Qīngkǒu,
allowing the clear water to flow smoothly,
and powerfully scour away silt.
In the second month of the following year,
the diversion channel was completed.
The Yellow River flowed directly into Zhōujiāzhuāng,
where it met the clear water flowing eastward,
and Qīngkǒu was spared the trouble of backflow for nearly ten years.
In the 50th year [of the reign],
Hóngzé Hú dried up,
and the yellow flow silted up to Qīngkǒu.
Orders were given to Bì Yuán, the Governor of Hénán, to offer sacrifices to the Huái River god,
and to dredge the Jiǎlǔ and Huìjì rivers and others to assist the clear flow.
The lake water still did not flow out,
and the yellow water flowed back in.
The Emperor wished to open the spillways at Máochéng Pù and Wángjiā Yíng.
He referred the matter to Grand Secretary Ā Guì and others for deliberation.
Ā Guì said:
"To cure the problem at Qīngkǒu,
one must remove the silt below the old spillway works,
and especially lower the Yellow River water [level],
allowing the clear water to flow out freely to scour away the sand.
There is no need for self-management."
Thereupon, the four diversion rivers at Zhāngfú Kǒu were closed,
the lake's tributary rivers were dredged and cleared,
clear water was accumulated to more than seven *chǐ*,
the Wángyíng Dam was opened to release yellow water,
all rivers were fully opened,
the clear water flowed out from Qīngkǒu to scour the sand,
the Qīngkǒu water-blocking dam was repaired,
and its name was changed to Shùqīng Bà.
The east and west water-constricting dams in front of Huìjì Cí were moved three hundred *zhàng* to in front of Fúshén Xiàng,
the east dam was lengthened to resist the yellow water,
the west dam was shortened to let out the clear water,
and its name was changed to Yùhuáng Bà.
In the 1st year of Jiāqìng,
the lake water was low,
the clear water was more than a *zhàng* lower than the yellow water,
and the Huái River was blocked and could not flow out.
When the Huái River rose, the five dams at Shānxū and the seven forts at Wúchéng were opened.
When the Yellow River rose, water was sometimes released into the lake,
to prevent backflow at Qīngkǒu.
In the 5th year,
following the advice of Fèi Chún, the Governor-General of Jiāngnán, and Wú Jǐng, the Director-General of River Conservancy,
a diversion channel was opened at the seven forts of Wúchéng,
to allow lake water to flow into the Yellow River,
to reduce the peak flood.
In the 8th year,
the Yellow River flow into the sea was not smooth,
and it directly poured into Hóngzé Hú.
Jǐng went to the estuary to survey the situation,
and requested to forcefully close all dams at the Yùnkǒu,
leaving only the main opening.
Even if the clear water was too weak to flow out,
the yellow water would also not be able to flow back in.
In the 7th month,
the Huái River rose,
and Gāoyàn was in great danger.
The Xìn and Yì dams were opened to release water.
A strong westerly wind blew,
damaging the Rén and Zhì dams,
and the Huái River rushed south towards Qīngkǒu.
The Emperor blamed Jǐng,
and he was subsequently dismissed.
In the spring of the 9th year,
the lake water slightly increased,
but the summer flood of the Yellow River still flowed back.
Xú Duān, the Director-General of River Conservancy, said that because the Shùqīng Bà was north of the Yùnkǒu,
a branch flow entered the canal,
making it unable to withstand the Yellow River.
He requested to relocate and build it south of the Húkǒu.
This was granted.
In the 11th year,
Tiě Bǎo, the Governor-General of Jiāngnán, said:
"Pān Jìxún and Jìn Fǔ managed the rivers,
focusing their efforts on Qīngkǒu,
because if Qīngkǒu flows out smoothly,
then the riverbed will be scoured deep,
the estuary will also be clear,
and Hóngzé Hú will not overflow.
For the current plan,
we must extensively repair the sluices and dams,
use clear water to scour sand,
and cannot but store more lake water.
We also cannot but protect the stone dikes,
and especially cannot but urgently devise an outlet."
He then, along with Xú Duān, presented several matters regarding the river works: first,
Fāngjiā Mǎtóu and Sānlǎobà in the Outer River Office are vital defenses for Huái and Yáng,
and should be filled and protected with crushed stones;
second,
the Yì Bà should be blocked and built up;
third,
the four dams of Rén, Zhì, Lǐ, and Xìn, which are damaged, should be dismantled and repaired.
The court deliberated and approved the requests.
The Emperor feared that repairing all four dams at once would lead to excessive release of clear water,
and ordered them to be carried out in stages.
In the 10th month of the 15th year,
strong winds and surging waves
caused the Yì Bà to break,
and more than a thousand *zhàng* of the Yàn and Xū works collapsed.
Some suggested building a crushed stone gentle slope,
but it was not carried out due to the huge cost.
Jǐng and Duān requested to reinforce the two dikes built by Jìn Fǔ outside the great dike,
to serve as a double gate of protection,
but this was also rejected by court deliberation.
When Chén Fèngxiáng became the Director-General of the Southern River,
he reiterated the request for the two dikes.
This was referred to Bǎilíng, the Governor-General of Jiāngnán, for deliberation.
Bǎilíng said it was better to reinforce and repair the great dike.
In the 17th year,
Sōngyún, Acting Grand Secretary, was dispatched to inspect,
and he also sided with Bǎilíng's proposal.
Thereupon, a sub-weir of the great dike was built,
extending from the end of Shùqīng Bà to the south of Xìn Bà.
Fèngxiáng, for failing to accumulate clear water in the lake before the rise,
and opening the Zhì and Lǐ dams prematurely,
which led to the collapse of Lǐ Bà,
flooding downstream,
and depletion of clear water,
thereby hindering the entire river,
was impeached by Bǎilíng,
deprived of his post, and banished.
In the 18th year,
Bǎilíng and Lí Shìxù, the Director-General of the Southern River, stated that the Rén, Yì, and Lǐ dams had been opened repeatedly,
damaging their foundations and scouring the pools.
They requested to relocate and build the three dams south of Jiǎngjiā Bà near the mountain ridge,
each with its own diversion channel,
and to first build the Rén and Yì dams.
Due to the foundation of Lǐ Bà, a temporary dam was built instead,
ready for release this year.
The Emperor ordered to first build the Yì Bà,
and if the regulation and release were appropriate,
then the others would be repaired in successive years.
In the 23rd year,
the second Shùqīng Dam was added north of the original Shùqīng Bà,
to collect lake water.
In the 2nd year of Dàoguāng,
the stone works of Gāoyàn were reinforced and repaired.
In the winter of the 4th year,
the river rose,
and Hóngzé Hú accumulated water to a depth of one *zhàng* and seven *chǐ*.
It was still about a *chǐ* lower than the Yellow River.
The tops of the dikes at the thirteen forts of Gāoyàn were loosened by the great water,
and the Xīlàng'ān at Zhōuqíao, Shānxū, was also submerged by eight or nine *chǐ* of water,
and all dams suffered damage.
The Emperor dispatched Wén Fú and Wāng Tíngzhēn, Ministers, to inspect,
and dismissed Zhāng Wénhào, the Director-General of River Conservancy, from his post.
The breaches at the thirteen forts were immediately sealed.
Zhū Shìyàn, an Imperial Censor, said:
"All officials involved in the Gāoyàn stone works
only focused on saving costs
and handled matters carelessly.
Also, due to the rush to build the great dike,
soil was taken from the nearby two dikes,
and no reinforcement was done afterwards.
As for the five dams at Shānxū,
which released the great floods of Hóngzé Hú,
they failed to strictly follow the old regulations
and open them according to circumstances,
leading to the dislodgement of the stone works."
The matter was also referred to Wén Fú and others for investigation and verification.
In the spring of the following year,
following the advice of Wén Fú and others,
the earthen gentle slope of the lake dike was changed to crushed stone,
and stone roller dams were added at the former sites of the Rén, Yì, and Lǐ dams,
to prevent unusual floods.
In the 8th year,
the Emperor, noting that the Yùhuáng Bà was silted up by more than a *zhàng* both upstream and downstream,
preventing much clear water from being stored,
and that the Yùhuáng Bà could ultimately not be opened,
referred the matter to Zhāng Jǐng, the Director-General of the Southern River, and others for deliberation.
Jǐng and others said:
"During the Qiánlóng reign, the lake was seven or eight *chǐ* or even more than a *zhàng* higher than the river.
In summer, the Yùhuáng Bà was dismantled and expanded
to release clear water and scour silt,
and was only closed in winter.
During the Jiāqìng reign,
due to river silting,
it was changed to close in summer and open in autumn.
However, when the Yellow River water occasionally rose,
it would immediately flow back.
Now, with prolonged silting,
even if clear water can flow out,
it is only a few *cùn* or a little over a *chǐ* higher than the yellow water.
Opening it temporarily and then closing it immediately
only prevents backflow,
and cannot achieve the effect of scouring silt."
The Emperor was displeased,
and said:
"Using the past to prove the present,
it has already become an incurable situation.
Those who are Directors-General of River Conservancy
only know how to release clear water to protect the weir,
close the Yùhuáng Dam to prevent backflow,
increase work and request funds,
only considering the present,
without thinking of long-term sustainability.
What about the national economy?
What about the people's livelihood?
What about the future?"
In the tenth year,
Jǐng Yán
said: "The path of the Huái River to the sea is not smooth.
I request that two canals be obliquely dug, one at the Bātǎpù of Yángliángtīng and another at Shāngjiāgōu,
to converge and flow into the Jiāng River,
thereby diverting high waters.
Additionally, the east and west sluices of the Mángdào River should be dismantled,
and the silted shoals dredged.
This would serve the purpose of opening a new river."
This was approved.
In the twelfth year,
the Xìn Dam was relocated and rebuilt at Xiàjiāqiáo.
In the fourteenth year,
as the Yìzì Canal had deepened by three or four zhàng,
making it difficult to block,
permission was granted for River Governor Lín Qìng's request
to re-dig the head of the Yìzì River.
In the twenty-first year,
the river breached at Xiángfú,
and its flow plunged into Hóngzé Hú.
As the Jiāng River's tide rose greatly,
it again caused back-pressure.
Consequently, the Yùhuáng, Shùqīng, and the Lǐ, Zhì, Rén dams were dismantled and expanded.
Additionally, the Chēluó and other dams were opened
to drain the lake water.
In the twenty-third year,
the river breached at Zhōngmóu,
and its entire flow poured into Hóngzé Hú.
Over four thousand zhàng of the stone works of the Gāoyàn were dismantled.
The Shùqīng, Yùhuáng, Zhì, and Xìn dams were successively dismantled and expanded.
Additionally, the Shùnqīng, Lǐ, Yì, and other rivers were opened.
The Jīnwān Old Dam and the East and West Wān Dams were simultaneously opened
to divert water into the Jiāng River.
In Xiánfēng's fifth year,
the river again breached at Tóngwǎxiāng,
flowing eastward into the Dàqīng River and thence to the sea.
Since the Huáng River's breach at Huázhōu during the Northern Sòng dynasty,
and its subsequent breach at Chánzhōu,
it had diverted southeast,
joining the Sì River to enter the Huái River.
For over 770 years, the lower reaches of the Huái River had been usurped by the Huáng River.
When the Huáng River was troubled, the Huái River was also troubled.
Now, with its northward shift,
the calamity in the Jiāngnán region ceased.
Scholars and common people repeatedly requested the restoration of the Huái River's old course,
and such requests were heard annually.
In Tóngzhì's eighth year,
Jiang Governor Mǎ Xīnyí dredged the Zhāngfúkǒu diversion canal,
whereupon the Huái River flowed from Qīngkǒu to the Canal.
Later, the silted Huáng River below Yángzhuāng was also dredged
to drain the great floods of the Central Canal.
In the ninth year,
Xīnyí and others stated:
"After surveying the river channel below Yúntīguān,
and the lake center around Chéngzihé, Zhāngfúkǒu, and Gāoliángjiàn,
we learned that the bed of the Huáng River is one zhàng to one zhàng, five or six chí higher than the bed of Hóng Hú.
It is imperative to first extensively dredge the silted Huáng River
so that the Huái River can flow smoothly into the sea.
Then, Qīngkǒu should be opened,
guiding the water into the Old Huáng River.
Next, the Sānhé should be blocked
to prevent lateral leakage and facilitate storage.
However, unless the stone works of Yàn and Xū are repaired
and the two embankments of the Canal are solidly built,
we dare not immediately block the Sānhé and open Qīngkǒu.
Considering all these projects comprehensively,
they cannot be accomplished without several million gold taels.
We propose to prioritize and arrange them in sequence,
not seeking great profit,
but merely aiming to reduce calamity,
as a plan of gaining an inch at a time,
achieving gradual progress.
In Guāngxù's seventh year,
Jiang Governor Liú Kūnyī stated:
"I have recently traveled throughout the rivers and lakes
and learned that the water conservancy of Huái and Yáng is crucial to the nation's livelihood.
The previous proposal to guide the Huái River
must not be abandoned midway.
Below Yángzhuāng, the Old Huáng River has become silted up,
meaning the waters of Shāndōng's Zhāoyáng, Wēishān, and other lakes
flow directly from the Central Canal to the Southern Canal.
Between summer and autumn,
the Three Sluices become heavily strained.
Since Hóngzé Hú has become shallow due to silting,
the Huái River waters cannot converge into a single flow.
The north is higher than the south,
so not much water diverges into the Zhāngfú Diversion Canal.
The main flow
rushes directly through the Lǐ River to Gāo Hú and Bǎo Hú.
After dredging the Old Huáng River last year,
the floodwaters from Shāndōng repeatedly burst forth,
and were thereby diverted into the sea.
After building the Lǐ Dam,
the lake waters deepened,
and a considerable amount flowed into the Canal entrance via the Zhāngfú River.
This shows that dredging the Old River and building the Lǐ Dam were not without slight effect.
However, the Zhāngfú River is shallow,
and the lake waters still tend to rush through the heavy Lǐ River over the dam,
which remains a concern.
Should the lake waters flood,
even if the Lǐ River does not overflow its dam,
it will be difficult to divert the water.
The Xìn and Zhì dams would certainly have to be opened,
allowing water to flow through Gāobǎo Hú into the Southern Canal.
Also, the Chēluó, Nánguān, and other dams would certainly have to be opened,
allowing water to flow through the Yúxià River to the sea,
inundating fields and dwellings along the way,
causing no small damage.
My current proposal is to excavate the Zhāngfú River to be wide and deep
to draw water from Hóngzé Hú,
and also excavate the Suìshí River
to divert water from the Zhāngfú River,
converging at Wúchéng Qībǎo into the Shùnqīng River.
If the water volume is small, it will flow into the Canal via Shùnqīng,
a circuitous route that somewhat eases the pressure.
If the water volume is large, it will flow into the sea via the Old Huáng River,
a direct route that naturally ensures smooth flow.
It is estimated that it can be completed in three or four years,
and the cost will not be too great.
Some might argue that guiding the Huái River to the sea
would completely drain Hóng Hú's water,
which would hinder official transport and civilian farming.
I believe that opening another diversion canal
might indeed lead to such a problem.
However, by following the old courses of the Zhāngfú River and Suìshí River to return to the Shùnqīng River,
unless the Huái River rises by one or two zhàng,
how could the water of the Shùnqīng River be higher than the Central Canal,
and overflow into the Old Huáng River?
If the Huái River were to surge,
there would indeed be a risk of breaching.
The fear is that the water has no outlet;
this is precisely the original intention of guiding the Huái River.
Some might argue that drawing more lake water into the Canal
might cause the Three Sluices to fail.
They do not consider that before Hóng Hú silted up,
its waters were level on all sides,
and it accumulated deep and vast amounts of water.
Beyond Zhāngfú,
there were four diversion canals to aid grain transport.
At that time, the Huáng River had not yet shifted northward,
and whenever grain boats passed through the sluices,
clear water was even accumulated to resist the turbid Huáng River.
With all five diversion canals flowing into the Canal entrance,
the Three Sluices stood firm.
Now, with just the Zhāngfú River,
there is absolutely no reason for the Three Sluices to be damaged.
Moreover, after the Old Huáng River was cleared last year,
it has already diverted some water from the Central Canal,
with only three or four tenths flowing into the Southern Canal.
Although the lake water has increased,
it is roughly similar to before.
Even in the event of great floods,
with the Old Huáng River available for diversion,
the water will not solely exit through the Three Sluices.
Some critics might also say that while this approach
to guiding the Huái River has no drawbacks,
it also has no benefits,
so why waste state treasury funds?
This argument is not entirely correct.
Indeed, the way of water governance
requires comprehensive planning
and also anticipating changes.
Hóng Hú has the Lǐ River to its south
and the Zhāngfú River to its north,
both serving to divert Huái River water.
However, as water flows downwards,
the Lǐ River often suffers from excessive water.
The Lǐ River Dam was built to retain Zhāngfú's water,
and the Zhāngfúkǒu was dredged to protect the Lǐ River's embankment.
They are mutually dependent.
If the Lǐ River were to bear the full impact of the entire lake,
the new dam might not be able to withstand it.
Further repairs would be extremely costly,
and neglecting repairs would cause even greater harm.
The lower areas would become even lower,
and the higher areas even higher,
and the Zhāngfú River would gradually become blocked.
Moreover, the purpose of guiding the Huái River
was originally to prevent severe floods from raging.
If the lake water is drawn from Zhāngfú to Shùnqīng,
using the Old Huáng River as the outlet to the sea,
should there be occasional overflows,
that area is vast and sparsely populated,
making escape relatively easy.
However, if Zhāngfú is not smooth,
the entire lake's water would turn and flow southward.
Then, the prosperous regions of Huái and Yáng,
with countless lives,
would lament being turned into fish.
The benefits of guiding the Huái River
that are visible now are minor,
but those visible in the future are great."
After the memorial was submitted,
it was brought to the attention of the Ministry.
In the eighth year [of the reign],
the Grand Governor of Jiāngnán, Zuǒ Zōngtáng, stated:
“Dredging the Yí and Sì Rivers to serve as the vanguard route for diverting the Huái River
is indeed a sound proposition.
However, downstream from Yúntīguān for over two hundred *lǐ*,
the riverbed is high,
and there are old sandbars.
What could not be cleared in the past even with the full force of the Huáng River,
now attempting to use the Yí and Sì Rivers to clear it,
is indeed very difficult.
Dàtōng is located over ten *lǐ* below Yúntīguān,
on the old northern bank of the Huáng River.
It was an overflow in the Jiāqìng period,
flowing northeast for over forty *lǐ*
to Xiǎngshuǐkǒu,
connecting to the Cháohé River,
and then entering the sea at Guànhékǒu.
Widening and deepening it here
would make it easier to reach the sea.
The sources of the Yí and Sì Rivers
should be greatly diverted and reduced.
Even if the Huái River is not yet restored, the Grand Canal route could be somewhat stabilized,
and once the Huái River is restored, there would be no fear of obstruction in its return to the sea.
This dredging of the lower reaches,
to channel the Yí and Sì Rivers,
is truly the vanguard route for diverting the Huái River,
and preparations must be made urgently.
The Huái River, carrying numerous streams,
converges into Hóngzélake,
which originally was a vast expanse of water in Jiāngnán and Ānhuī.
Since the Dàoguāng period, it has been silted up by the Huáng River,
with the north rising and the south falling,
flowing from Lǐhé towards Gāobǎohú to enter the Grand Canal for nearly thirty years.
Now, to guide it back to its former state
is no less than trying to pull it upstream against the current.
From Zhāngfúkǒu, passing Dàtōng and Xiǎngshuǐkǒu to enter the sea,
over three hundred and fifty *lǐ*,
it is obstructed at every turn.
Unless its downstream path is cleared,
and its upstream leaks are plugged,
it is quite clear that it cannot abandon the lower, higher route and flow into the Huáng River to the sea.
Upon investigation, Zhāngfúkǒu and Tiānrán Yǐnhé
both trend north towards Dàchōng at Chénjiājí,
then to Suìshíhé to reach Wúchéng Qībǎo,
and further north to Shùnqīnghékǒu,
connecting to the old Huáng River at Yángzhuāng.
The width of Zhāngfúhé is over sixty *zhàng*;
it should be widened and deepened.
Tiānrán Hé needs even more dredging.
The Wúchéng Qībǎo area is one *zhàng* six or seven *chǐ* higher than the bottom of Zhāngfúhé;
it must be greatly excavated and dredged,
so that the lake water can flow into the Huáng River.
Only then can Lǐhé be blocked
to cut off its diversionary outlet,
and Shùnqīnghé be blocked
to prevent its diversion of the Grand Canal.
This project to guide the Huái River to the sea
should be undertaken in sequence.
If the lake water is not high,
it cannot enter the Huáng River.
If it is too high,
not only would the stoneworks at Yàn and Xū be concerning,
and the Grand Canal entrance gates and dams difficult to sustain,
but it would also harm the farmlands near the lake in Xūyí and Wǔhé.
It is proposed to repair the Zhì and Xìn dams to discharge the lake's overflow,
and furthermore build a gate at Dàchōng,
so that the manipulation of lake water is controlled by people,
with more entering the Huái River and less entering the Grand Canal.
This is another pre-planned measure to ensure its success.”
In the thirty-fourth year,
the Grand Governor of Jiāngnán, Duān Fāng, jointly surveyed the old course of the Huái River,
forcefully articulating four difficulties in diverting the Huái River.
Consequently, a bureau was established at Qīngjiāngpǔ,
and gentry were selected to deliberate.
After a long time, no progress was made,
so the bureau was dissolved.
In the first year of Xuāntǒng,
when the Jiāngsū Provincial Assembly opened,
Governor-General Zhāng Rénjùn submitted the matter of diverting the Huái River for discussion,
and it was decided to establish the Jiānghuái Water Conservancy Company,
to first conduct surveys,
to ensure the Huái River is restored to its old course,
and flows exclusively to the sea.
In the second year,
Yùn Yùdǐng, a Grand Academician, noting the worsening flood disasters along the Huái River,
memorialized:
“From the Wèi and Jìn dynasties onwards,
farmlands along the Huái River
have mostly diverted water and dug canals,
and irrigation has made them fertile.
Recently, however, prefectures and counties along the Huái River
annually report floods,
inundating cities and towns,
and submerging fields and houses.
From Zhèngyáng to Gāo and Bǎo,
all have become a land of water,
due to the fact that in the past century,
the river channel has silted up,
the lower reaches are blocked,
the water has nowhere to go,
and has become a widespread flood.
This is the harm caused by the Gāoyàndàbà.
In earlier times, when the Huáng and Huái Rivers merged,
there was a tendency to flow south.
Those who managed the river wished to confine the Huái River to resist the Huáng River,
thus they specifically built a strong Gāoyàndàbà dam head,
forcing the Huái River to pass through Tiānfēizhà to supply the Grand Canal.
Now, the Huáng River has long shifted northward,
and the dam is no longer useful.
A separate route to the sea should be planned.
There are two routes;
the one via Qīngkǒuxībà and Yánhé to Běicháohé is more convenient.
Once the outlet is cleared,
and the water has a place to go,
not only will Yǐng, Shòu, Fèng, and Sì be forever free from deep-seated disasters,
but Gāo, Bǎo, Xīng, and Tài will also rest easy for a hundred years.”
The matter was sent to Grand Governor Zhāng Rénjùn of Jiāngnán, Governor Chéng Déquán of Sūzhōu, and Governor Zhū Jiābǎo of Ānhuī for deliberation.
Zhāng Rénjùn and others stated:
“Surveying is currently underway;
once the survey and examination are completed,
officials will be selected to commence operations.”
This was reported and heard.
In the third year,
Censor Shí Chángxìn stated:
“The undertaking of diverting the Huái River
is indeed a commonly agreed-upon plan.
The American Red Cross also intends to send engineers to China for investigation.
Thus, our own foresight and prevention
cannot be delayed.
Since the Jiāngsū Water Conservancy Company has agreed to allocate funds from the board,
Ānhuī should also establish a bureau for surveying,
as a plan to eliminate this great disaster.”
This was sent to the board for deliberation and approved.
The project to divert the Huái River
began in the sixth year of Tóngzhì.
At that time, Zēng Guófān, who was the Grand Governor of the Two Jiāng,
once said:
“Regarding the great benefit of restoring the waterway,
I dare not say it will happen quickly;
regarding the great harm to the Huái and Yáng regions,
one cannot but consider reducing it somewhat.”
By the time the Huáng River shifted northward,
more people spoke on the issue,
with the main points not exceeding two proposals.
One suggested blocking the Sānhé River,
opening Qīngkǒu,
dredging the old river,
and clearing Yúntīguān,
so that it would enter the sea via its old course.
The other suggested that the diversion of the Huái River should start from the upper reaches.
Hóngzélake is the termination of the Huái River,
not its source.
A new channel should be opened in the upper reaches,
following the Suī and Biàn Rivers northward,
so that half of the Huái River is discharged midway
before it even enters the lake.
Then, from Chéngzǐhé at Táoyuán, it would cut through the old Huáng River,
pass through the Shuāngjīnzhà of the Zhōnghé River into the Yánhé River,
and enter the sea at Āndōng,
thereby dividing the entire Huái River into two channels, north and south,
taking in less and discharging more,
which would alleviate the Huái River disaster.
These two theories held different views.
However, since the Tóngzhì and Guāngxù periods,
the dredging of Chéngzǐ, Suìshí, Yí, and Sì Rivers,
and the clearing of the old course from Yángzhuāng down to Yúntīguān,
had already provided a small initial test.
Ultimately, the Huái River, silted by the Huáng River
for several centuries,
no longer had a navigable channel.
Flowing into the Jiāng River via the Grand Canal
was very difficult to reverse completely.
By the time of the national upheaval,
it ultimately achieved little success.
The Yǒngdìng Hé (永定河) is also known as the Wúdìng Hé (無定河),
which is the lower reaches of the Sānggān (桑乾).
Its source is in Tiānchí (天池) in Tàiyuán (太原), Shānxī (山西).
It flows underground to Shuòzhōu (朔州) and Mǎyì (馬邑), where it resurfaces,
collecting many streams.
It passes through Xīníng (西寧) and Huáilái (懷來) in Xuānhuà (宣化), Zhílì (直隸),
then flows southeast into Shùntiān (順天) Prefecture's Wǎnpíng (宛平) county.
Passing below Lúshī Tái (盧師臺),
it first becomes known as the Lúgōu Hé (盧溝河).
Further downstream, it merges with the Fèng Hé (鳳河) and flows into the sea.
Because it joins the Hún Shuǐ (渾水) in Dàtóng (大同) and flows northeast,
it is also called the Hún Hé (渾河).
In the Yuán Shǐ (元史), it is called the Xiǎo Huáng Hé (小黃河).
From ancient times, no official management was ever established for it.
The name Yǒngdìng (永定),
however, was bestowed during the Kāngxī (康熙) reign.
The Yǒngdìng Hé (永定河) collects waters from beyond the frontier,
carrying silt and flowing rapidly downstream.
Because it is flanked by layers of mountains,
it rarely burst its banks.
But south of Shíjǐng Shān (石景山), forty *lǐ* (里) west of the capital,
passing the Lúgōu Qiáo (盧溝橋),
the terrain is steep and the soil is loose,
causing it to meander widely,
constantly shifting course,
and causing considerable harm.
Thus, the construction of dikes and dams,
the dredging of diversion channels,
and flood prevention work became urgent.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì (順治) (1651),
the river shifted from Yǒngqīng (永清) to Gù'ān (固安),
merging with the Báigōu (白溝).
The next year,
the breach was finally sealed.
In the eleventh year (1654),
it merged with the Qīng Shuǐ (清水) at Xīgōng Cūn (西宮村) in Gù'ān (固安),
passed east of Bàzhōu (霸州),
and flowed out into the Qīng Hé (清河).
It also burst its banks at Jiǔhuātái (九花臺) and Nánlǐ (南里),
turning the southwest of Bàzhōu (霸州) into a vast flood.
In the seventh year of Kāngxī (康熙) (1668),
the Lúgōu Qiáo (盧溝橋) dike burst.
Vice Minister Luóduō (羅多) and others were ordered to build it up.
In the thirty-first year (1692),
because the river course gradually shifted north,
Yǒngqīng (永清), Bàzhōu (霸州), Gù'ān (固安), and Wén'ān (文安) were frequently affected by floods.
Following the proposal of Zhílì (直隸) Governor Guō Shìlóng (郭世隆),
the old channel northeast of Yǒngqīng (永清) was dredged
to allow the water to flow smoothly into the *diàn* (淀) (lake/marsh).
In the thirty-seventh year (1698),
because the waters south of Bǎodìng (保定) converged with the Hún Shuǐ (渾水),
the volume became unmanageable,
leading to frequent overflows.
The Holy Ancestor (Emperor Kāngxī) personally inspected it.
Governor Yú Chénglóng (于成龍) proposed a combination of building and dredging.
Starting from the old river mouth at Lǎojūn Táng (老君堂) in Liángxiāng (良鄉),
passing through Shílǐ Pù (十里鋪) north of Gù'ān (固安) and Zhūjiā Zhuāng (朱家莊) southeast of Yǒngqīng (永清),
it joined the Lángchéng Hé (狼城河) in Dōng'ān (東安),
flowed out through Liǔchà Kǒu (柳岔口) into the Sānjiǎo Diàn (三角淀) in Bàzhōu (霸州),
and reached Xīgū (西沽) to enter the sea.
The river was dredged for 145 *lǐ* (里),
and north and south dikes were built for over 180 *lǐ* (里).
It was given the name Yǒngdìng (永定).
From then on, the Hún (渾) flow was diverted northeast,
and it did not shift for nearly forty years.
In the thirty-ninth year (1700),
the Lángchéng Diàn Hé (郎城淀河) became silted and shallow,
and the upper reaches were blocked.
River Superintendent Wáng Xīnmìng (王新命) was ordered to open a new river,
changing the south bank to the north bank.
The west dike was extended from the south bank,
starting from Guōjiā Wù (郭家務).
The east dike was extended from the north bank,
starting from Hémázǐ Yíng (何麻子營).
Both extended to Liǔchà Kǒu (柳岔口).
In the fortieth year (1701),
a remote dike of pile foundations was added to the south bank,
and the Jīnmén Zhá (金門閘) was repaired.
In the forty-eighth year (1709),
it burst at Wánghǔ Zhuāng (王虎莊) in Yǒngqīng (永清),
but was quickly sealed.
In the fifty-sixth year (1717),
the sandy dikes and major dikes on both banks were repaired.
It burst at Hèyáo Yíng (賀堯營).
In the sixty-first year (1722),
it burst again at Hèyáo Yíng (賀堯營),
and was immediately sealed.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng (雍正) (1724),
the major dike at Guōjiā Wù (郭家務) was repaired,
the crescent dike at Qīngliáng Sì (清涼寺) was built,
the Jīnmén Zhá (金門閘) was repaired,
and the breach in the south dike at Táng'èrpù (堂二鋪) in Bàzhōu (霸州) was mended.
In the third year (1725),
due to the sudden narrowing of both banks below Guōjiā Wù (郭家務),
Yǒngqīng (永清) suffered particularly severe damage.
Yī Qīnwáng Yǔnxiáng (怡親王允祥) and Grand Secretary Zhū Shì (朱軾) were ordered
to divert the Hún Shuǐ (渾水) by another route to the sea,
preventing it from entering the *diàn* (淀).
Thus, a new lower mouth was opened slightly north of Liǔchà Kǒu (柳岔口),
and a new river was dug from Guōjiā Wù (郭jiā Wù) to Chángcháo Hé (長●河),
a total of seventy *lǐ* (里).
It passed through Sānjiǎo Diàn (三角淀) and reached Jīn (津) to enter the sea.
A围 dike was built around Sānjiǎo Diàn (三角淀)
to prevent overflows to the north.
A south dike was also built from Wǔjiā Zhuāng (武家莊) to Wángqìng Tuó (王慶坨),
and a north dike from Hémázǐ Yíng (何麻子營) to Fànwèng Kǒu (范甕口).
The dike work from Bīngjiào (冰窖) to Liǔchà Kǒu (柳岔口) was consequently abandoned.
In the twelfth year (1734),
breaches occurred at Liánggèzhuāng (梁各莊), Sìshèng Kǒu (四聖口), and other places, spanning over three hundred *zhàng* (丈).
The river flow at Huángjiā Wān (黃家灣) was entirely diverted,
and the water flowed under the walls of Yǒngqīng (永清) county into Jīnshuǐ Wā (津水窪) in Bàzhōu (霸州), returning to the *diàn* (淀).
Governor-General of Rivers Gù Cóng (顧琮) supervised soldiers and laborers to seal it.
In the thirteenth year (1735),
breaches occurred at Zhūjiā Zhuāng (朱家莊) on the south bank and Zhàojiā Lóu (趙家樓) on the north bank.
The water returned to Sānjiǎo Diàn (三角淀) via the small dike at Liùdào Kǒu (六道口).
In the second year of Qiánlóng (乾隆) (1737),
Governor-General of Rivers Liú Xiǎng (劉勷) surveyed and repaired the north and south dikes,
opened diversion channels at Huángjiā Wān (黃家灣), Qiúxián Zhuāng (求賢莊), and Cáojiā Xīnzhuāng (曹家新莊),
and dredged Shuāngkǒu (雙口), Xiàkǒu (下口), and Huánghuātào (黃花套).
In June,
the water overflowed and submerged over forty villages on the south bank, such as Tiěgǒu (鐵狗), and on the north bank, such as Zhāngkè (張客).
The flow was diverted through the breach at Zhāngkè (張客) and downstream to the Fèng Hé (鳳河).
Minister of Personnel Gù Cóng (顧琮) was ordered to investigate.
He requested to adopt the method of building remote dikes as used for the Huáng Hé (黃河).
Grand Secretary È'ěrtài (鄂爾泰) disagreed,
proposing
"to dig a new river north of the northern intercepting river dike,
making the north dike the south dike,
following it eastward downstream,
and constructing several sections of spillway dams downstream.
Furthermore, four stone roller dams would be built separately on the north and south banks,
each opening a diversion channel: one at the Zhāngjiā Shuǐkǒu (張家水口) on the north bank, where a dam would be built,
and the scoured channel itself would serve as the diversion channel,
converging eastward with the Fèng Hé (鳳河);
one at Sìtái (寺臺) on the south bank, where a dam would be built,
using the old sluice channel that enters the Xiǎoqīng Hé (小清河) as the diversion channel;
one at Jīnmén Zhá (金門閘) on the south bank, where a dam would be built,
using the old course of the Hún Hé (渾河) that connects to Hūniú Hé (●牛河) as the diversion channel;
and one at Guōjiā Wù (郭家務) on the south bank, where a dam would be built,
using the old riverbed itself as the diversion channel.
Separating the clear from the turbid,
the management would become clear."
An imperial edict approved his request.
In the fourth year (1739),
Zhílì (直隸) Governor Sūn Jiāgàn (孫嘉淦) requested to move the Sìtái (寺臺) dam to Cáojiā Wù (曹家務)
and the Zhāngkè (張客) dam to Qiúxián Zhuāng (求賢莊).
He also requested to add temporary dams at Jīnmén Zhá (金門閘) and Cháng'ān Chéng (長安城),
setting the water flow at four-tenths (of the total volume).
Gù Cóng (顧琮) stated
that the water flow at the Jīnmén Zhá (金門閘) and Cháng'ān Chéng (長安城) dams could only be discharged through one river,
fearing it would be insufficient during floods.
He proposed to divide the diversion channel into two branches:
one flowing through Nánwā (南窪) into the Zhōngtíng Hé (中亭河),
and the other through Yángqīng Kǒu (楊青口) into Jīnshuǐ Wā (津水窪).
He also stated that there were old remote rivers at Guōjiā Wù (郭家務), Xiǎoliáng Cūn (小梁村), and other places, totaling 1,700 *zhàng* (丈),
which had been silted up for years,
and requested funds for their repair.
All requests were granted.
In the fifth year (1740),
Sūn Jiāgàn (孫嘉淦) requested to open the double dike at Jīnmén Zhá (金門閘),
dredge the west diversion channel,
open the south dike,
and let the water resume its old course.
In the sixth year (1741),
the ice flood overflowed,
inundating many areas in Gù (固), Liáng (良), Xīn (新), Zhuō (涿), Xióng (雄), and Bà (霸) prefectures.
Following È'ěrtài's (鄂爾泰) proposal,
the new diversion channel was blocked,
Shuāngkǒu (雙口) and other rivers were widened,
the riverbed of Gěyú Chéng (葛漁城) was dredged,
the crescent dikes at Zhāngkè (張客) and Cáojiā Wù (曹家務) were built,
and the dams at Guōjiā Wù (郭家務) and other places were rebuilt.
In the eighth year (1743),
the lower mouth of the new river,
as well as the Dǒngjiā Hé (董家河) and Sāndào Hékǒu (三道河口), were dredged,
and the south bank of the new river and the dikes east of the Fèng Hé (鳳河) were repaired.
More than twenty *lǐ* (里) from Mùjiā Kǒu (穆家口) downstream to Dōngxiāo Zhuāng (東蕭莊) and the Fèng Hé (鳳河) riverbank were also dredged.
In the ninth year (1744),
because the area below Fànwèng Kǒu (范甕口) used the Shā Diàn (沙淀) and Yè Diàn (葉淀) as its outlet,
and most of the water during the two flood seasons flowed into the Yè Diàn (葉淀),
the route to Shā Diàn (沙淀) was dredged,
and the old north and south diversion rivers were also dredged to return to the Fèng Hé (鳳河).
In the fifth month of the fifteenth year,
the river water suddenly rose,
breaking out from the fourth ditch on the south bank,
flowing directly past Gù'ān [固安] city down to Niútuó [牛坨],
and following the Huángjiāhé [黃家河] into the Jīnshuǐwā [津水窪].
One branch flowed into the Niúhé [●牛河] and then into the Zhōngtínghé [中亭河].
The Assistant Minister Sānhé [三和] was ordered to jointly oversee the blocking and defense efforts,
and a diversion channel was dug below the breach,
blocking the flow and building a dam
to prevent the water from overflowing south,
forcing it back to its old course.
In the sixteenth year,
the ice-jam flood occurred,
and the entire river rushed towards the Bīngjiàokǒu Dīkǒu [冰窖隄口].
A diversion channel was immediately opened south of Wángqìngtuó [王慶坨],
guiding the flow into Yèdiàn [葉淀]
to accommodate the water's nature.
In the nineteenth year,
the Nánniàn [南埝] overflowed its dike top,
breaching the old dikes east and west of the Xiàkǒu [下口],
and rushing south,
inundating the old pond of Shèngfāng [勝芳],
passing through Wǔjiāchǎng [武家廠] and Sānshèngkǒu [三聖口] in Yǒngqīng [永清],
and entering Xìn'ān [信安] in Bàzhōu [霸州].
The following year,
Gāozōng [高宗] personally inspected the site,
and the downstream section was altered to flow into the sea via Diàohétóu [調河頭].
A diversion channel over twenty *lǐ* was dug,
and the embankment body was reinforced by over two thousand two hundred *zhàng*.
In the twenty-first year,
the Director-General Fāng Guānchéng [方觀承] requested to build a remote dike outside the Běiniàn [北埝],
reserving it as a floodway.
The east dike of the Fènghé [鳳河] was also extended to the end of the remote dike.
This was approved.
In the twenty-fourth year,
heavy rains caused
all the rivers in Zhílì [直隸] to swell simultaneously.
The downstream waters all flowed into the ponds,
and the Dàqīnghé [大清河] could not discharge them,
instead flowing back through the Fènghé [鳳河],
obstructing the turbid currents,
and causing the dikes of the four southern works to breach.
The Imperial Guard Hè'ěrjǐng'é [赫爾景額] was ordered to coordinate with the Director-General to block and repair the breaches within a specified timeframe.
In the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years,
the dikes on both banks breached repeatedly.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Minister Gāo Jìn [高晉] and Qiú Yuēxiū [裘曰修], along with Director-General Zhōu Yuánlǐ [周元理], were ordered to conduct a survey.
They memorialized, saying:
"Since the Yongdìnghé [永定河] was diked in the Kāngxī [康熙] period,
it has changed course six times.
The method to rectify the problems
is only to dredge the central flood channel, dig out the lower mouth
to smooth the rapid flow, build bank dikes to prevent erosion,
and excavate diversion canals to divide the major floods."
Consequently, a major project was launched,
costing over one hundred forty thousand *nǔ*.
From then on, the water flowed from Diàohétóu [調河頭] directly through Máojiāwā [毛家窪] and Shājiādiàn [沙家淀] to Jīn [津] and into the sea.
In the thirty-eighth year,
Diàohétóu [調河頭] became silted,
and its clear water dispersed downstream,
diverting through Xiǎngshuǐcūn [響水村] in Dōng'ān [東安] directly to Shājiādiàn [沙家淀].
In the fortieth year,
the northern three works and the Nántóugōng [南頭工] breached.
In the forty-fourth year,
a new northern dike was extended and built,
the old Yuyuedī [越隄] was reinforced,
and the old riverside dike was abandoned
to widen the river channel.
In the forty-fifth year,
the west bank of Lúgōuqíao [盧溝橋] overflowed,
and the Běitóugōng [北頭工] breached,
overflowing from Qiánguānyíng [前官營] in Liángxiāng [良鄉] and flowing into Qiúxiáncūn [求賢村] diversion canal, then to Huánghuādiàn [黃花店].
Thereupon, a diversion ditch eight hundred *zhàng* long was opened
to guide the flow back to the river.
In the fifty-ninth year,
the Běi'èrgōngdī [北二工隄] breached,
and the flow rushed into the Qiúxiáncūn [求賢村] diversion channel,
reaching the lower reaches of the Yongdìnghé [永定河] and entering the sea.
Immediately, the flow ceased,
and then the Nántóugōngdī [南頭工隄] overflowed again.
The water flowed from Lǎojūntáng [老君堂] and Zhuāngmǎtóu [莊馬頭] into the Dàqīnghé [大清河].
Over one hundred *zhàng* of the southern dike were built.
A water diversion dam was also built in front of Yùhuángmiào [玉皇廟].
In the sixth year of Jiāqìng [嘉慶],
four stone dikes and eighteen earth dikes on the east and west banks of Lúgōuqíao [盧溝橋] breached.
Assistant Ministers Nàyànbǎo [那彥寶] and Gāo Qǐ [高杞] were ordered to be stationed separately to block and build,
and to dredge the downstream,
mobilizing over fifty thousand laborers for the work.
The Emperor composed "River Breach Sigh" [Hé Jué Tàn 河決歎],
and promulgated it to his officials.
The work was completed in over two months.
In the fifteenth year,
both banks of the Yongdìnghé [永定河] simultaneously breached.
Director-General Wēn Chénhuì [溫承惠] was stationed at the site to block and close them.
In the seventeenth year,
the river trended north,
and Gěyúchéng [葛漁城] became silted.
The water flowed down from Huánghuādiàn [黃花店].
Thereupon, a diversion channel was dug in the old silted riverbed,
and a brushwood dam was built upstream
to guide the flow eastward.
A separate ring dike was built to prevent widespread flooding.
In the twentieth year,
the civilian dike on the east bank of the Fènghé [鳳河] was demolished to remove the downstream blockage.
In June, heavy rains caused
the northern seven works to overflow and collapse by over thirty *zhàng*.
A diversion channel was opened,
slightly south of the old riverbed,
reaching Huánghuādiàn [黃huādiàn],
and extending eastward to Xīzhōu [西洲],
with a length of five thousand six hundred and nine *zhàng*.
In September,
the water returned to its old course.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the northern two works overflowed,
followed by the first work.
It overflowed laterally at the breach for over three hundred *zhàng*,
inundating villages belonging to Dàxīng [大興] and Wǎnpíng [宛平].
In September, the breach was plugged,
and the northern upstream diversion channel was re-dredged.
In the third year of Dàoguāng [道光],
the river breached south at the end of the southern eight works dike,
flowing directly towards Wāng'érdiàn [汪兒淀].
In the fourth year,
Assistant Minister Chéng Hánzhāng [程含章] surveyed and proposed dredging and restoration,
but it was not carried out.
In the tenth year,
Director-General Nàyànchéng [那彥成] requested to open a diversion channel at Dàfànwèngkǒu [大范甕口],
and to heighten and thicken the southern remote dike of the new dike.
This was approved.
In the spring of the eleventh year,
the river flow changed direction to the northeast,
passing through Dòudiàn [竇淀],
and going through Liùdàokǒu [六道口],
flowing into the Dàqīnghé [大清河].
The Wāng'érdiànkǒu [汪兒淀口] was then plugged,
and the water returned to the old course of Wángqìngtuó [王慶坨] via the new channel at Fànwèngkǒu [范甕口].
In the fourteenth year,
breaches occurred in the Běizhōng [北中] and Běixiàxùn [北下汛] sections within Wǎnpíng [宛平] territory.
Water flowed from Pánggèzhuāng [龐各莊] along the old diversion channel to Huánghuādiàn [黃花店] in Wǔqīng [武清],
then returned to the main river's tail-end and entered the sea.
A breach occurred in the southern two works within Liángxiāng [良鄉] territory.
Water flowed from the Jīnménzhá [金門閘] diversion channel into the Qīnghé [清河],
and through Báiqōuhé [白溝河] to the Dàqīnghé [大清河].
Thereupon, a diversion channel was dug,
extending downstream from the breach to Shānjigōu [單家溝],
with intermittent sections repaired for over twenty-seven thousand four hundred *zhàng*.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the southern seven works breached.
Taking Héxīyíng [河西營] about three *lǐ* to the north as the river's head,
a diversion channel over seventy *lǐ* long was dug,
reaching directly to the Fènghé [鳳河].
In the fifth month of the thirtieth year,
mountain water flowed down from upstream,
and the river suddenly swelled.
The northern seven works overflowed by over thirty *zhàng*,
flowing from the old diversion channel through Mǔzhūpō [母豬泊] into the Fènghé [鳳河].
A diversion channel was surveyed and opened north of Fēngjiāchǎng [馮家塲]'s river bend,
and was completed in October.
During the Xiánfēng [咸豐] period,
the northern and southern dikes breached four times.
At that time, military affairs were pressing,
and funds for works were reduced,
so only patching and mending leaks were done.
In the third year of Tóngzhì [同治],
because the river gradually shifted north
and its path became shallow due to silting,
a dam was built at Liǔtuó [柳坨]
to block the northern flow,
and guide it back to the old river.
The river channels at Zhāngtuó [張坨] and Hújiāfáng [胡家房] were widened and deepened,
flowing through Dōng'ān [東安], Wǔqīng [武清], and Tiānjīn [天津] into the sea.
After the sixth year,
breaches occurred from time to time.
In the eighth year,
Director-General Zēng Guófān [曾國藩] requested to build a large water interception dam at the southern seven works,
and to build ring dikes on both sides,
as well as dredging the central flood channel
and clearing the lower mouth
to prevent blockages and breaches.
This was approved.
In the tenth year,
the stone dike on the south bank overflowed,
and the flow rushed through Liángxiāng [良鄉] and Zhuōzhōu [涿州] into the Dàqīnghé [大清河] and out to sea.
The following year,
Director-General Lǐ Hóngzhāng's [李鴻章] request was granted
to repair the Jīnménzhá [金門閘] dam,
and dredge the diversion channel,
flowing from Tóngcūn [童村] into the Xiǎoqīnghé [小清河].
The stone dike breach was plugged.
In the twelfth year,
the southern four works overflowed,
flowing eastward from Bàzhōu [霸州]'s Niúhé [●牛河].
Thereupon, the diversion channel was extended,
and another water diversion dam was built.
In the second year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1724),
the Emperor, considering the urgency of the dikes,

ordered Zhū Shì, Minister of the Board of Civil Office, to consult with Fǎhǎi, Governor of Zhèjiāng, and Hé Tiānpéi, Governor of Sūzhōu, to survey and estimate the dike projects in Hángzhōu, Jiāxīng, Húzhōu, and other prefectures.
This required over 105,000 taels of silver.
For the dike projects in Huá, Lóu, Shànghǎi, and other counties of Sōngjiāng Prefecture,
over 190,000 taels of silver were needed.
The Board deliberated and approved it.
In the sixth year (1728),
Lǐ Wèi, the Circuit Inspector, requested that urgent projects that could not be delayed
be repaired first,
and then reported to the throne.
The term "搶修" (qiǎngxiū, emergency repair)
began from this time.
In the eleventh year (1733),
the Emperor ordered the Grand Minister of the Interior Hǎiwàng and the Governor-General of Zhílì, Lǐ Wèi, to inspect the sea dikes in Zhèjiāng.
The imperial edict stated:
"If the engineering truly ensures permanent stability
and can protect the livelihoods of the people,
then even spending tens of millions of taels of silver is not to be begrudged."
Soon after, they requested to build a stone dam to block water between Jiānshān and Tǎshān,
and to convert the existing grass dikes and dikes made of dressed stones and rough stones into large stone dikes.
Furthermore, an additional protective dike (上備塘, shàngbèitáng) was to be constructed within the old dikes.
In the twelfth year (1734),
due to the long delay in blocking the Jiānshān water outlet and excavating the Zhōngxiǎowěi diversion canal,
Chéng Yuánzhāng, Governor-General of Zhèjiāng, and others were reprimanded for ineffective supervision.
Lóngshēng, Deputy Commander of Hángzhōu, was appointed to take overall charge,
with Yùshǐ Piānwǔ assisting him.
The project was completed in the fifth month.
In the thirteenth year (1735),
Jī Céngyún, Governor of the Southern River, was ordered to take overall charge of the dike projects.
Jī Céngyún said:
"Outside the south gate of Hǎiníng, it directly faces the river and the sea.
I request to first build a fish-scale stone dike of over 500 zhàng [approx. 1665 meters]
to protect the city."
The court officials deliberated and approved it.
In the first year of Qiánlóng's reign (1736),
Gù Cóng, acting Governor of Sūzhōu, requested the establishment of a maritime defense circuit (海防道, Hǎifáng Dào)
to be solely responsible for the annual repair of sea dikes.
Jī Céngyún requested to appropriately construct fish-scale large stone dikes of over 6,000 zhàng [approx. 19,980 meters] in Rénníng and other areas.
Both requests were granted.
The following year (1737),
a large fish-scale stone dike of over 5,900 zhàng [approx. 19,659 meters] was built from Pǔérdōu in Hǎiníng to Jiānshāntóu.
In the fourth year (1739),
Lú Zhuó, Governor of Zhèjiāng, requested permission
to build the Jiānshān Great Dam, which was granted.
The project was completed in the autumn of the following year (1740),
and the Emperor personally composed an essay to commemorate it.
In the sixth year (1741),
Liú Tǒngxūn, Censor-in-Chief of the Left, said:
"Previously, Dé Pèi, Governor-General of Mǐnzhè, requested to convert the brushwood dikes from Lǎoyáncāng to Zhāngjiā'ān into stone dikes,
which the court deliberated and approved.
My humble opinion is that the conversion of brushwood dikes need not be overly urgent,
but the dike projects on the north and south banks should certainly not be delayed.
For the general situation of the dikes,
the tide at Hǎiníng still flows back and forth, scouring,
whereas the tide at Hǎiyán
directly impacts head-on.
Its large stone dikes, having aged, are prone to leaks,
and should be repaired early.
I estimate roughly
that with an expenditure of 700,000 taels of silver,
the entire dike can be as solid as bundled mulberry branches."
Upon receiving the memorial,
the Emperor ordered Liú Tǒngxūn to investigate with Dé Pèi, Governor-General of Zhèjiāng, and Cháng'ān, Governor of Zhèjiāng.
Soon after, they reported:
"Converting to stone construction
is indeed a long-term plan,
but it requires ample time,
at a rate of 300 zhàng [approx. 999 meters] per year."
In the seventh year (1742),
Governor-General Nàsūtú requested to first build stone cages in segments at the most dangerous sections,
and once the foundations were solid,
then construct stone dikes.
Two years later (1744),
Shàngshū Nàqīn was dispatched to inspect.
His memorial stated:
"The brushwood dikes in Rénníng and two other counties are stable.
If there is concern that the protective sands may collapse and swell unpredictably,
one merely needs to dredge the old channels of Zhōngxiǎowěi,
allowing the tidal waters to enter and exit regularly,
and both the upper and lower dikes will be secure."
Thus, the proposal to convert to stone construction was dropped.
In the seventh month (1742),
Chén Dàshòu, Governor of Sūzhōu, said:
"Bǎoshān borders the sea,
and the earthen dikes at Yuèpǔ are being scoured by the tide.
I request to build a single stone dam,
with an outer addition of pile-stone slopes, each 170 zhàng [approx. 566 meters] long,
and also connect and build sand dikes
to link them with the earthen dikes,
with culverts set in the middle for drainage."
The Board deliberated and approved it.
In the eleventh year (1746),
Cháng'ān said:
"North of Shǔshān, there are accumulated sands four to five hundred zhàng [approx. 1332-1665 meters] long,
lying horizontally in the middle.
Previously, four channels were dug at the sand spit
to draw the tidal water to scour it.
Now, the summer flood season has passed,
the southern sands have almost completely collapsed,
Shǔshān is already in the water,
and the tides are gradually moving southward.
If the autumn flood season does not bring new sand,
then the main current will completely flow through Zhōngxiǎowěi."
This was reported to the throne.
In the twelfth year (1747),
Cháng'ān appointed commissioners to dredge the Shǔshān area,
using the method of cutting sand for scouring.
On the first day of the eleventh month,
the Zhōngxiǎowěi diversion canal burst open overnight,
the main current flowed through its old course,
and both the north and south banks, with their distant waters and long sands,
all became clear passages.
In the thirteenth year (1748),
Grand Secretaries Gāo Bīn and Nàqīn were successively ordered to inspect the dike projects.
Gāo Bīn requested to add earthen embankments behind the eastern and western brushwood and stone dikes
to protect against the tidal bore.
In the fourth month,
Nàqīn memorialized on post-disaster arrangements,
and Fāng Guānchéng, the Circuit Inspector, was ordered to deliberate on them.
Fāng Guānchéng requested that at the old channel of Běidàwěi on the North Dike,
and at Sānlǐqiáo, Duózhuǎnmiào, and other places,
bamboo-cage rolling dams be installed
to block the tidal channels.
The Dàxiǎoshān embankments were to be converted into rough stone dikes.
For all projects on the South Dike,
protective measures were to be planned in advance.
Additionally, officers and soldiers of the Right Battalion were to be deployed
to patrol and garrison by turns during flood seasons.
The court deliberated and approved it.
In the sixteenth year (1751),
Yǒngguì, the Circuit Inspector, requested permission to convert the earthen dike at Sòngjiālóu in Shānyīn into a stone dike,
which was granted.
A submerged bank (坦水, tǎnshuǐ) was also added.
In the seventeenth year (1752),
Yǎěrhāshàn, the Circuit Inspector, said:
"The Zhōngwěi mountain pass is only six lǐ [approx. 3 km] wide,
and floating sand easily silts it up.
Moreover, at the foot of Wéntángshān on the south bank, there is a sand spit of over 130 zhàng [approx. 433 meters],
which diverts the current northward.
Outside Hézhuāngshān on the north bank, there is also a sand spit of over 50 zhàng [approx. 166 meters],
which considerably obstructs the main current of Zhōngwěi.
Currently, the accumulated sand at both locations is being dug and cut to clear the passage,
to prevent blockage."
An imperial edict of commendation was received.
In the nineteenth year (1754),
as the dike projects in Zhèjiāng Province were not in danger,
the maritime defense circuit (海防道, Hǎifáng Dào) was abolished.
In the twenty-first year (1756),
Kāěrjíshàn said:
"The water current is moving southward,
and the North Dike is stable,
but the dangerous sections are in the Shàoxīng area.
I propose to construct 400 zhàng [approx. 1332 meters] at Sòngjiālóu and Yángliǔgǎng,
following the style of the Hǎiníng fish-scale large dressed stone dike."
This was approved.
In the twenty-third year (1758),
the sea dike in Zhènhǎi County was further extended.
In the twenty-sixth year (1761),
Chén Hóngmóu, Governor of Sūzhōu, said
that in the coastal areas of Chángshú and Zhāowén,
earthen dikes were constructed, connecting from the border of Tàicāng Prefecture.
Later, the Báimáohé and Xúliùjīng two estuaries were opened,
and gates were built for opening and closing.
In the present year, the tide surged,
and the stone walls collapsed.
He requested to convert them into rolling dams.
An imperial edict was received, granting approval.
In the twenty-seventh year,
the Emperor made a southern tour
and inspected the seawall works in Hǎiníng.
An edict stated:
"We believe the seawall is the primary safeguard for Yuèzhōng.
In recent years, the tidal currents have gradually shifted towards Běidàiwěi,
which seriously affects the interests of Hǎiníng, Qiántáng, and other counties.
It was planned to convert the brushwood dikes in the Lǎoyáncāng area into stone,
but opinions among the deliberators were divided.
When We personally inspected it yesterday,
We found that the brushwood dike had sandy and silty soil,
making stone construction impossible.
Therefore, the only option is to vigorously repair the brushwood dike,
which is a strategy to remedy its defects.
Careful management should be undertaken,
with annual repairs to solidify the dike's foundation,
and the addition of submerged stone baskets to provide protection."
Another edict stated:
"Between Jiānshān and Tǎshān,
there used to be a stone dike.
We now see that it transversely intercepts the sea,
directly facing the main current,
and is a crucial point for the seawall.
Judging by the current situation,
it would be best to use more bamboo baskets for reinforcement,
or to switch to arranging timber caissons.
Should the sand gradually advance further in the future,
it would be appropriate to immediately rebuild it as a slab-stone dam,
so that it stands firm like a central pillar,
and the seawalls on the north bank will forever be protected.
Let the said governors-general and governors thoroughly comprehend Our intention,
allocate funds for the undertaking,
and engrave a stone on Tǎshān
to commemorate it permanently."
In the twenty-eighth year,
Su-fǔ Zhuāng Yǒugōng said:
"In the coastal areas of Sōng and Tài in Jiāngnán, the soil is prone to collapse.
The previously built submerged slopes in Huátíng and Bǎoshān
are all unreliable.
It should be rebuilt with block-stone baskets, emulating the Lǎoyáncāng in Zhèjiāng."
An imperial decree was issued as requested.
In the spring of the thirtieth year,
the Emperor made a southern tour
and inspected the Hǎiníng seawall.
An edict stated:
"The stone dike encircling the city
is indeed a safeguard for the entire city.
The submerged slope beneath the dike
is only built in two layers,
and the tidal current seems to hit it directly.
If a third layer were added,
it would be even more beneficial.
Let the four hundred sixty odd zhàng that ought to be built be uniformly added."
The work was completed in the third month.
In the thirty-fifth year,
Xúnfǔ Xióng Xuépéng requested to rebuild the fish-scale stone dikes in Xiāoshān, Shānyīn, and Kuàijī.
The Emperor, considering that the tidal current was trending towards Běidàiwěi
and was irrelevant to the south bank,
rejected it.
In the thirty-seventh year,
Xúnfǔ Fùlèhún reported on the situation of the pilot channel in Zhōngdàiwěi,
briefly stating:
"The main tidal current
flows one way from Shǔshān directly into the pilot channel,
and another way from Yánfēngxī obliquely into the pilot channel,
meeting at the mid-section of Hézhuāngshān,
where they collide with each other,
then divide into two routes heading west.
Officers were immediately ordered to excavate more than twenty diversion ditches in the mid-section of the pilot channel
to guide the tidal current,
so as to restore the old course of Zhōngdàiwěi."
An edict stated:
"The migration of tidal currents
is a natural phenomenon of ebb and flow.
If a pilot channel is excavated,
it might be a futile effort.
It is only proper to diligently protect the embankments
and await their return to their old course naturally.
There is no need to insist on digging ditches to divert the current,
wishing to overcome the sea tide with human effort."
In the forty-third year,
Zhè-fǔ Wáng Dànwàng submitted a memorial detailing the seawall situation,
and the Emperor ordered Jiāng-dū Gāo Jìn to jointly assess it.
Soon, a memorial stated:
"For the five hundred zhàng of brushwood works in the Zhāngjiā'ān area
and the three hundred zhàng of brushwood dike in front of the Cháoshénmiào,
bamboo baskets should be added,
and two layers of piles should be arranged to prevent displacement."
This was followed.
In the forty-fifth year,
the Emperor made a southern tour
and visited the Hǎiníng Jiānshān to inspect the seawall.
In the twelfth month,
Grand Secretary Ā Guì and Nánhédū Chén Huīzǔ were ordered to Zhèjiāng for an on-site investigation.
A memorial stated:
"For the seawall project,
two thousand two hundred zhàng of stone dike should be built.
If changed to slab-stones,
construction would be easier and completion quicker,
estimated to be finished in about three years."
It also stated:
"To manage the fish-scale stone dikes,
following the example of the Dōngtáng,
depending on the terrain's elevation, sixteen to eighteen layers should be used,
requiring approximately three hundred thousand."
The Emperor ordered Gōngbù Shìláng Yáng Kuí to be stationed there to assist with the work.
The project was completed in the eighth month of the following year.
In the forty-ninth year,
the Emperor visited Hángzhōu
and inspected the seawalls.
An edict stated:
"The old brushwood dike at Lǎoyáncāng,
to which four thousand two hundred odd zhàng of stone dike were uniformly added,
was completed last year.
Naturally, submerged slopes should have been built to protect it.
However, the said governors-general and governors did not consider this.
If an extraordinary high tide occurs,
how could it withstand it?
The earth behind the brushwood dike should be sloped gently downwards,
and willows should be planted on it,
so that their roots interlace.
Then the stone and brushwood will form a continuous barrier,
using the brushwood dike as the submerged slope for the stone dike.
As for the Fàngōngtáng area,
stone works must also be connected and built there
to adequately consolidate the provincial capital.
Five million taels of silver are allocated,
to be handed over to the said governors-general and governors for accounting,
and to be constructed in phases over several years."
The project was completed in the fifty-second year.
In the fourth year of Jiāqìng,
Zhè-fǔ Yùdé requested to convert the earthen dike in Shānyīn into a brushwood dike.
In the thirteenth year,
Zhè-fǔ Ruǎn Yuán requested to convert the earthen embankment in Xiāoshān into a brushwood dike.
In the sixteenth year,
Zhè-fǔ Jiǎng Yōuxiǎn requested that all earthen dikes in Shānyīn be uniformly constructed as brushwood dikes;
Su-fǔ Zhāng Xù requested that the earthen dike in Huátíng be reinforced with two layers of single dams.
All were approved.
In the fifth month of the thirteenth year of Dàoguāng,
Xúnfǔ Fùníyáng'ā memorialized, stating
"For the eastern and western seawall projects,
the most precarious sections should be chosen first for repair, requiring over five hundred twelve thousand taels of silver."
In the eleventh month,
he again stated
"all works within and beyond the limits have collapsed,
requiring over one hundred ninety-four thousand taels of silver."
In the twelfth month,
he again stated
"within the eastern dike's boundary,
a new fish-scale dike of over two thousand six hundred zhàng should be built between the front and rear dikes,
requiring nine hundred twenty-two thousand taels of silver."
All were referred to the Board for deliberation and implementation.
In the fourteenth year,
Xíngbù Shìláng Zhào Shèngkuí and former Dōnghédū Yán Lǎng were ordered
to jointly investigate and assess the necessary repairs with Fùníyáng'ā.
Soon, a memorial stated:
"For protecting the outer dike's foundation,
nothing is better than submerged slopes.
It is proposed to add three headlands from Niànlǐtíng Xùn to Zhènhǎixùn,
and convert over three thousand three hundred zhàng of brushwood dike;
as for the western dike east of Wūlóngmiào,
fish-scale stone blocks should be connected and built;
the Hǎiníng city-encircling stone dike
should be raised by two layers of slab-stones.
This will be continued during next year's major flood season."
Zuǒdūyùshǐ Wú Chūn was dispatched to inspect,
and remained in Zhèjiāng to assist with the work.
The project was completed in the third month of the sixteenth year,
with a total of over seventeen thousand zhàng of works repaired,
costing over one million five hundred seventy thousand taels of silver.
In the thirtieth year,
Xúnfǔ Wú Wénróng reported breaches in the seawall's stone works,
and was ordered to quickly organize emergency repairs.
The work was completed in the tenth month.
In the eighth month of the seventh year of Xiánfēng,
the seawall's brushwood structures and various works were suddenly breached by storms and tides.
In the twelfth month,
they were successively blocked and repaired.
In the third year of Tóngzhì,
Yùshǐ Hóng Yànchāng reported on the collapse of the Zhèjiāng seawall
and requested urgent funding for repairs.
The Board deliberated and allocated taxes from the Zhèjiāng Customs and other sources.
In the fifth year,
