Nèigé Shìdú Xuéshì Zhōng Pèixián memorialized, stating that the seawall affected the overall situation of the Southeast,
and presented four harms and three concerns.
Xúnfǔ Mǎ Xīnyí was ordered to investigate in detail
and repair over two hundred sixty zhàng of Hǎiníng's fish-scale stone works.
In the sixth year,
due to the enormous cost of the Zhèjiāng seawall project,
it was decided to repair it by priority,
with completion scheduled in ten years.
In the seventh year,
Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū Zēng Guófān and others requested to repair the protective dam of the Huátíng stone dike,
and thereafter, dike works were repaired annually.
In the third year of Guāngxù
the northern stone embankment of Bǎoshān was repaired to protect the land.
Various dams for protecting the embankment and blocking water were built,
as well as over 1,300 zhàng of fishtail-scale stone embankments in Rénhé and Hǎiníng.
In the tenth year
embankments, dams, and stone sloped ramps in Zhāowén, Huátíng, Bǎoshān, and other places were repaired.
In the twelfth year
Liú Bǐngzhāng, the Governor of Zhèjiāng, stated,
the originally built stone embankment in Hǎiyán, measuring over 4,600 zhàng,
had collapsed by more than half over the years.
It was proposed to selectively undertake important repairs:
500 zhàng to be buried and paved,
and 460 zhàng to be rebuilt.
This would require 200,000 liǎng of silver.
It was approved.
In the eighteenth year
Liú Shùtáng, the Governor of Zhèjiāng, memorialized,
the stone embankment encircling Hǎiníng was increasingly collapsing.
He requested to add and build a sloped ramp for water,
and to use the accumulated surplus from the silk tax levied for embankment works to begin the project immediately,
with funds to be raised subsequently for phased repairs.
This was approved.
In the nineteenth year
151 zhàng of piled stone sloped ramps at Xīnjīngkǒu in Tàicāng were repaired,
200 zhàng of piled stone at Yánglínkǒu in Zhènyáng,
200 zhàng of double-piled and stone-reinforced protective dams from Shījiāqiáo to Lǎorénbīn in Zhāowén,
and 46 zhàng of purely stone sloped dams on the outer embankment of Huátíng.
In summary of the embankment works in the two provinces,
since the major repairs in the mid-Dàoguāng period,
they suffered from military destruction
and half of them fell into disrepair.
Until the early Tóngzhì period,
large-scale projects were undertaken.
As treasury funds were insufficient,
donations for sea embankments were initiated,
and silk merchants in the two provinces were urged
to pay an additional
silk tax for embankment works beyond the regular tax,
and were given tickets as rewards.
This was subsequently stopped.
In the thirtieth year of Guāngxù
Niè Jíguī, the Governor of Zhèjiāng, requested the reinstatement of the old donation system
to assist crucial projects.
This was because after the twenty-seventh year
the tides were fierce,
and moderately dangerous areas became extremely dangerous.
It was proposed to clear and rebuild all brushwood fascine works from the bottom up.
Without raising a large sum of money,
they could not be consolidated for long, he said.
Gazetteer, Volume 104: Waterways, Canals, Four Zhíshěng Water Conservancy
During the Qīng dynasty, the suffering of the people was deeply felt,
and water management was urgently repaired.
Beyond the Yellow River (Huánghé), Huái River (Huáihé), Grand Canal (Yùnhé), Yǒngdìng River, and sea embankments,
all water conservancy projects in the zhíshěng [provinces directly under central government]
were undertaken with unsparing effort.
These matters can be listed.
In the fourth year of Shùnzhì
Liáng Wéi, a Censor, requested to reclaim wasteland and develop water conservancy,
and his memorial was sent to the relevant department.
In the eleventh year
an imperial edict stated:
"The southeastern regions, rich in taxes and revenues,
have always been known as fertile land.
In recent years, floods and droughts have caused disasters,
and the people's lives are in great distress.
This is all due to the disrepair of water conservancy facilities,
which has hampered agriculture and industry.
The Governors-general and Governors are hereby instructed to hold local officials responsible for diligently studying [the situation],
clearing waterways,
building dikes and embankments,
and regulating storage and discharge in a timely manner,
so that there may be no worries about floods and droughts,
and the people may live in peace and prosperity."
In the first year of Kāngxī
the Lóngxīng Weir in Jiājiāng was rebuilt,
and a large canal was dug to expand irrigation.
In the second year
the Tóngchéng Weir in Hézhōu
and the Lóngshǒu and Tōngjì canals were repaired.
When the Cíwǎ River in Jiāochéng flooded,
the water invaded the city,
so dikes were built to protect it.
In the third year
the Nánmù Weir in Jiādìng was repaired.
In the ninth year
the Jīn Canal and Níngqū water conservancy in Méixiàn were repaired.
In the twelfth year
the Wǔmén Weir in Chénggù was rebuilt.
In the nineteenth year
the Báimáogǎng in Chángshú and the Mèngdúhé in Wǔjìn were dredged.
In the twenty-third year
the Nánhú Dike and Dam in Wǔhé were repaired.
In the twenty-seventh year
the Yúliáng Dam in Huīzhōu was repaired.
In the thirty-seventh year
the Director-general of Rivers Wáng Xīnmìng was ordered to repair water conservancy in Jīfǔ.
In the thirty-eighth year
Emperor Shèngzǔ made a Southern Tour.
Upon reaching Dōngguāng,
he ordered Lǐ Guāngdì, the Governor of Zhílì, to survey the old courses of the Zhāng River (Zhānghé) and Hūtuó River (Hūtuóhé).
He memorialized in response, stating:
"In the areas belonging to Dàmíng, Guǎngpíng, Zhēndìng, and Héjiān,
wherever the two rivers flow,
they should be dredged and cleared,
and enter the Grand Canal (Yùn) via Guǎntáo.
The Old Zhāng River should merge with the tributary at Shānjiāqiáo
and return to the Grand Canal (Yùn) at Bàojiāzuǐ,
which can divide the force of the Zǐyá River (Zǐyáhé)."
In the thirty-ninth year
the Emperor inspected the dike of the Zǐyá River (Zǐyáhé),
and ordered the construction of a stone sluice gate between Yán and Liú villages,
to be opened and closed as needed.
Censor Liú Héng stated,
in the areas near the river in Yǒngpíng and Zhēndìng,
water should be directed into the fields for cultivation.
The edict stated:
"The benefits of paddy fields
should not be pursued too hastily.
If all are undertaken at a fixed time,
it will surely lead to difficulties.
Only after the projects are completed,
and the common people know their benefits,
will they naturally be encouraged to follow suit,
and the matter will surely succeed."
In the fortieth year
Lǐ Guāngdì stated:
"The Zhāng River (Zhānghé) divides into four branches;
three branches that return to the Grand Canal (Yùn) are all weak,
while one branch that returns to the Lake (Diàn) is uniquely strong.
When the water level is high,
methods such as diversion dams should be used
to make the water flow in different directions,
so that the north does not carry the Hūtuó River (Hūtuóhé) to flood fields,
and the south does not combine with the Wèihé to harm the Grand Canal (Yùn)."
This was carried out as requested.
In the forty-third year
the old diversion channel at Yángcūn was dredged.
Previously, when the diversion channel at Guǎngfúlóu on the Zǐyá River (Zǐyáhé) was opened,
the people of Wén'ān and Dàchéng considered it beneficial,
while the people of Qīngxiàn considered it inconvenient,
and gathered along the riverbank to lodge mutual complaints.
By now, the river was completed,
and the people of all three counties considered it convenient.
Lán Lǐ, the Commander-in-chief of Tiānjīn, requested to reclaim paddy fields in Fēngrùn, Bǎochí, and Tiānjīn.
This was sent to the Board for deliberation.
Subsequently, an edict stated:
"In the past, Lǐ Guāngdì made this request,
but I believed it should not be undertaken lightly,
because the nature of the soil and water in the north is vastly different from that in the south.
At that time, the water was abundant,
and it was thought that paddy fields could be planted,
but one did not know that suddenly rising water
dries up very easily.
Observing the waters of the Liúlí River (Liúlíhé), Mángniú River (Mángniúhé), and Yì River (Yìhé),
they all dry up in summer, which is understandable."
The following year, the ministers of the Board still requested reclamation.
An edict stated that this matter should be temporarily set aside,
and Lán Lǐ could be ordered to experiment with opening paddy fields in Tiānjīn,
awaiting inspection after winter.
In the forty-eighth year
the old course of the Jiǎlǔ River (Jiǎlǔhé) in Zhèngzhōu was dredged,
from Dōngzhào to Xīnzhuāng at the Yánghé Yákǒu.
One sluice gate was built at Dōngzhào,
and one brushwood dam and one stone sluice gate were built at Yánghé Yákǒu.
Shūtú, the Governor of Gānsù, stated:
"The mouth of the Táng Canal is higher than its body,
so the water flow is not smooth.
The water from the Yellow River (Huánghé) should be diverted to converge into Sòngchéngbǎo.
If the water is insufficient,
further upriver, near the Yellow River (Huánghé), a channel should be opened to divert water,
and sluice gates and dams should be built as appropriate
to store and discharge water."
This was approved.
Yú Zhǔn, the Governor of Jiāngsū, stated:
"Dānyáng Liàn Lake (Liànhú) discharges water in winter and spring to aid the Grand Canal (Yùn),
and in summer and autumn irrigates the people's fields.
Since corrupt people sought profit,
they leased and taxed the land in the lower lake,
and all the people's fields became barren.
I request that water be accumulated in the lake again,
to provide irrigation."
This was approved.
In the fifty-seventh year
as Péixiàn had been inundated for consecutive years,
Zhào Shìxiǎn, the Director-general of Rivers, was ordered to investigate.
Shìxiǎn stated:
"The water from Jīnxiāng and Yútái
flows through Zhāoyáng Lake (Zhāoyánghú) in Pèi to Wēishān Lake (Wēishānhú),
and exits from Jīngshān Pass into Māo'érwō to enter the Grand Canal (Yùn).
Recently, due to siltation in the Shízìhé at Jīngshān Pass,
low-lying fields have been submerged.
The silt should be dredged and cleared,
and a brushwood dam should be built upstream on the Shízìhé.
If the Grand Canal (Yùnhé) water is shallow,
it should be immediately blocked,
so that all the water returns to Wēishān Lake (Wēishānhú),
exiting through the lake's sluice gate to supply the Grand Canal (Yùn).
This way, both the people's fields and grain transport will benefit."
This was approved.
During the reign of Shìzōng,
much planning was devoted to water conservancy in Jīfǔ.
In Yōngzhèng three years (1725),
Zhílì experienced severe floods.
Yí Qīnwáng Yǔnxiáng and Dàxuéshì Zhū Shì were ordered to survey and manage the repairs.
Consequently, they petitioned to dredge and regulate the Wèi Hé, Diàn Chí, Zǐyá Hé, and Yǒngdìng Zhū Hé.
Furthermore, in Jīngdōng's Luán and Jì,
and Jīngnán's Wén and Bà,
special officials for agricultural reclamation (yíngtián) were appointed
to plan and manage the boundaries.
Experienced farmers were recruited
to advise on irrigation and cultivation.
In the fourth year (1726),
four agricultural reclamation bureaus were established,
and a Shuǐlì Yíngtián Fǔ (Water Conservancy and Agricultural Reclamation Office) was set up.
Yí Qīnwáng was appointed to oversee its affairs,
and one Guāncháshǐ (Inspector) was appointed.
From the fifth year (1727), when the bureaus were established, until the seventh year (1729),
over six thousand qǐng of irrigated fields were reclaimed.
Later, due to the erratic nature of water levels,
half of them fell into disuse and neglect.
In the same year, Shìláng Tōngzhì and Shān Chóushū were ordered
to work with Chuān Dū Yuè Zhōngqí
to open the Huìnóng Qú at Zháhàntuōhù
to benefit the frontier garrisons.
The Jiànchāngrùn Qú was then constructed to the northeast of the Huìnóng Qú.
In the sixth year (1728),
the Wénshuǐ Jìnfén Hé Qú was dredged
to irrigate民tián.
The Yánglín Hǎi in Sōngmíng Zhōu was opened to drain water and create fields.
In the eighth year (1730),
the emperor, noting that the water conservancy in Níngxià relied on the Dàqīng, Hàn, and Táng Qú,
which had long fallen into disrepair,
ordered Tōngzhì to survey and repair them together with Guānglù Qīng Shǐ Zàijiǎ.
In the same year, the Xīng'ān Líng Qú in Guǎngxī was repaired
to benefit agricultural fields
and facilitate boat traffic.
The ditches and canals in Chén and Xǔ Zhōu were dredged.
In the tenth year (1732),
Yúnguì Zǒngdū È'ěrtài stated:
"The water conservancy of the Diān province entirely depends on the Kūnmíng Hǎikǒu.
It has now been dredged and repaired,
and fertile land is gradually emerging.
However, the Pánlóng Jiāng, Jīnlíng, Yínlíng, Bǎoxiàng, and other rivers are all close to the Hǎikǒu,
and it is urgent to construct dams and platforms."
He also said:
"The Yánglín Hǎi water flows freely,
and the surrounding marshlands can all be opened up for cultivation by settlers.
The old riverbed at Jiāngtóu Cūn in Yíliáng has a slightly higher terrain,
so a new waterway should be opened for irrigation.
The solid rock of the Xúndìng Hé is difficult to excavate,
so a new sandy river should be dredged
to allow smooth flow.
North of Dōngchuān Chéng, the sea has receded,
and fields have emerged as the water subsides,
which can also be opened for cultivation."
All these suggestions were adopted.
In the twelfth year (1734),
Yíngtián Guāncháshǐ Chén Shíxià reported:
"In the area bordering Wén'ān and Dàchéng, over 1,500 zhàng of transverse dikes have been repaired,
and 48 qǐng of reclaimed fields have yielded bumper harvests.
However, there is concern that if the water dries up, they will become dry fields.
I request the construction of a stone sluice gate southeast of the great dike
and the installation of more culverts on the north bank
to facilitate drainage."
This was adopted.
In Qiánlóng first year (1736),
Dàxuéshì Jī Zēngyún requested the dredging of water conservancy works in Háng and Hú.
Liǎngguǎng Zǒngdū Èmǐdá stated:
"In the Guǎng and Zhào prefectures, the embankments (jīwéi) along the river
affect people's fields and dwellings,
and are often breached.
I request that in critical areas, earth be replaced with stone,
and construction proceed gradually."
This was submitted to the board for discussion and implementation.
Heavy rains flooded Jiāngnán,
and Huái yáng was submerged.
Orders were given to dredge the waterways of Sùqiān, Táoyuán, Qīnghé, Āndōng, and Gāoyóu, Bǎoyìng.
In the second year (1737),
Zǒngdū Yǐn Jìshàn was ordered to plan water conservancy in Yúnnán.
Regardless of whether they connected to Yuè, Chuān, or were within the province's rivers and seas,
all those concerning the people's food supply
were to be repaired in a timely manner.
Shǎnxī Xúnfǔ Cuī Jì proposed the digging of wells to irrigate fields to aid water conservancy.
An imperial edict ordered thorough planning
so as not to disturb the populace.
In the third year (1738),
Dàxuéshì Guǎn Chuánshǎn Zǒngdū Shì Zhā Láng'ā stated:
"Guāzhōu has much land but little water,
and the irrigation for the people's fields
relies solely on the Shuōlè Hé, which is a small river.
It is observed that north of Jìngnì Wèi, there are the Chuānběi and Gǒngchāng two lakes,
named Mógu Gōu.
To its west are the Sāndào Liǔtiáo Gōu,
which flow north into Bǎidài Hú.
I request that a sluice gate be built in the middle,
whose waters merge into one,
diverting the waters of both gulleys entirely into the canal,
to benefit the irrigation of the Huímín's fields."
Guìzhōu Zǒngdū Zhāng Guǎngsì requested the opening of waterways in the Qián province,
from Dūyún through the old Shī bǐng to connect with the Qīngshuǐ Jiāng, reaching Húnán Qiányáng,
and directly to Chángdé.
Also, from Dúshān Sānjiǎotún to Gǔzhōu,
reaching Guǎngxī Huáiyuǎn,
and directly to Guǎngdōng,
harnessing the natural benefits of heaven and earth.
All these were submitted to the board for discussion and implementation.
In the fourth year (1739),
Ānhuī Bùzhèngshǐ Yàn Sīshèng stated that
in Jiāngběi, Fèng and Yǐng relied on the Suī Shuǐ as their main artery,
and Lúzhōu relied on Cháohú as its main vein.
Other areas like Liù'ān had existing dikes and weirs,
and Chú and Sì also had many streams and gullies.
All should be repaired and dredged promptly with public funds.
This was adopted.
Chuánshǎn Zǒngdū Èmǐdá and others stated:
"The Xīnqú and Bǎofēng in Níngxià
were previously submerged due to an earthquake and surging water,
and the administrations of both counties were ruined.
We request that the arable land be assessed,
and the tail end of the Hàn Qú be extended to facilitate irrigation.
However, the Hàn Qú is over 190 lǐ long,
and there is not much residual water at its tail end.
If the entrance of the abandoned Huìnóng Qú were repaired to draw water,
allowing the Hàn Qú's tail to be extended,
several thousand qǐng of good land in Xīn and Bǎo could be irrigated."
The emperor commended them.
In the fifth year (1740),
Hédū Gù Cóng stated:
"Previously, Zǒnghé Bái Zhōngshān memorialized, saying that 'if the Zhāng Hé returns to its old course,
the Wèi Hé will not overflow, which would be a one-time effort for lasting peace.'
Your subordinates have thoroughly investigated and found that
from Hérzhài East to Bāojiāzuǐ in Qīng Xiàn, where it enters the Grand Canal,
the distance is over 600 lǐ.
The riverbed is shallow and silted,
and residents on both banks are densely populated.
If the entire water of Zhāng is added,
it will be difficult to accommodate.
Then, if it is diverted to its old course,
Zhílì will inevitably suffer.
However, if it does not follow its old course,
Shāndōng will also inevitably suffer.
The only solution is to divert and defend,
so that neither province is harmed,
which would be a long-term plan."
Zǒngbàn Jiāngnán Shuǐlì Dàlǐ Qīng Wāng Méng stated:
"The Dōngtáng Hé in Yánchéng, and the various waterways in Fùníng and Shānyáng,
the lower reaches of Gāoyóu and Bǎoyìng,
as well as the Chuànchǎng Hé and Zhēntóng Hé,
are all shallow and silted
and should be dredged.
The Fàndī of the Chuànchǎng Hé
and the embankments of the Pīnchájiǎo two salt fields
are close to the seacoast
and should be widened and thickened.
The various sluices and dams in Yángzhōu should be cleared and constructed,
to be completed within three years."
All were implemented as requested.
Ānhuī Xúnfǔ Chén Dàshòu stated:
"Water conservancy in Jiāngběi is crucial for agricultural work.
The former Fānsī Yàn Sīshèng proposed repairs,
estimating over 400,000 liǎng of silver.
I believe that while water conservancy indeed prepares for droughts and floods,
urgency and priority
must be carefully considered.
As reported by various prefectures and counties,
large-scale projects such as river dikes, lakes,
and long canals
are extensive,
and the people's strength alone cannot accomplish them;
thus, the government should manage them.
As for other scattered ponds and embankments,
there are existing proprietors
who originally dredged them themselves.
How can the court use limited funds and grain
to undertake shoveling and digging for the common people?"
The emperor approved this.
Hénán Xúnfǔ Yǎ'ěrtú stated:
"Among the water conservancy projects in the Yù province,
only the estimated construction of dikes and dams in Shàngcài
is for preventing unusual floods in the Cài Hé.
As for the dikes and weirs of the Rǔ Hé and Zhì Hé,
landowners should be ordered to repair them themselves.
Regarding the dredging of the Rǔ Hé, Yǐng Hé, and other projects,
I request their suspension to save expenses."
This was reported and heard.
In the sixth year, in spring,
Yǎ'ěrtú言:
"Yǒngchéng's low-lying land accumulates water.
South of the city, there was an old canal over 31,000 zhàng long,
connecting to the Huìhé River.
Over the years, it has become silted up and shallow.
Now, taking advantage of the agricultural slack season,
I urge gentry and commoners to dredge it,
so that the water may have an outlet."
He further said:
"Previously, by imperial decree,
the Gānyáhér River in the provincial capital was to be dredged,
and a new river was to be opened in Zhōngmóu,
to divert the force of the Jiǎlǔhé River's water.
It was to join the Gānyáhér River via the Shāhé River,
reaching the Wōhé River in Jiāngnán and flowing into the Huái River.
It is over 65,000 zhàng long,
and is now complete."
It was granted the name Huìjì.
In the ninth year,
Cáocháo Shēng, a censor, said:
"The northern terrain is flat and extensive,
with existing rivers, canals, lakes, and waterways that can be traced.
If left to naturally fill and drain,
there will be water but no benefit, only harm.
I request that a high official be dispatched with funds to undertake repairs."
The Minister of Personnel, Liúyúyì, was ordered to go to Báodìng,
and together with the Governor-General Gāobīn,
supervise the work.
Soon after, a request was made to sequentially commence work on the old dikes and canals in Wǎnpíng, Liángxiāng, Zhuōzhōu, Xīnchéng, Xióngxiàn, and Dàchéng,
along with the planned new river channels,
and also dikes, embankments, culverts, bridges, and sluice gates.
The matter was submitted for court deliberation,
and proceeded as requested.
Earlier, Censor Zhānghàn had submitted a memorial on water conservancy in Húguǎng.
The Governor-General Èmǐdá was ordered to investigate.
At this point, a memorial stated:
"In methods of water control,
there are situations where one must not contend with water for land,
and situations where one cannot abandon land for water.
The waters of Sānchǔ,
with hundreds of branches and a thousand streams,
have undeveloped land along the rivers and lakeshores.
Private construction of small embankments must be strictly forbidden,
so that water has a place to converge,
to slow its flow.
This is what is meant by 'must not contend.'
For the fertile land already cultivated along rivers and lakes,
dikes and embankments must be diligently protected,
so that the people have a basis for their livelihood.
This is what is meant by 'cannot abandon.'
At points where various jurisdictions face strong currents and impacts,
long dikes should be connected,
and orders given to raise and thicken them annually,
incorporating dredging within the process of damming and building."
This was reported and noted.
In the eleventh year,
Grand Secretary and Acting River Governor Liúyúyì and others memorialized on matters concerning the continued investigation and dredging in Qìngyún and Yánshān.
It was submitted to the Board for deliberation and action.
The Míhé River in Qīngzhōu overflowed,
breaching a dike over a hundred zhàng long.
It was promptly blocked.
Accumulated water in Bóxīng and Lè'ān
was channeled into the Liūhé River.
In the twelfth year, in summer,
the Liùtánghé River in Sùqiān, Táoyuán, Qīnghé, and Āndōng,
and the Shùhé River in Shùyáng and Hǎizhōu,
overflowed due to mountain floods,
and the local area was submerged.
Grand Secretary Gāobīn and Governor-General Yǐnjìshàn were ordered
to jointly investigate with River Minister Zhōuxuéjiàn.
It was decided to widen and straighten dangerous sections,
build stone bridges,
and open diversion canals,
with officials and commoners cooperating in protection.
This was followed.
In the thirteenth year,
Péngshùkuí, the Provincial Governor of Húběi, said:
"In the Jīngxiāng area,
rivers and lakes extend over a thousand lǐ.
Whenever there is an unusual flood,
surplus land is needed to accommodate it.
When Mènggǒng was the prefect of Jiānglíng during the Sòng Dynasty,
he built three lakes and eight reservoirs to store water.
However, the water is turbid and easily silts up.
Opportunistic commoners
therefore intercept flows in many ways at the edges of banks and in the middle of lakes,
causing siltation.
They then, by borrowing on water grain and fish taxes,
build dikes all around to form polders.
People contend with water for land for profit,
which leads to water contending with people for land, causing disaster.
The only way is to prevent this in the future:
the number of existing polders
should be fixed as a definite figure,
and no private increase beyond this will be allowed."
This was reported and noted.
In the fourteenth year,
Tú'ěrbǐng'ā, the Provincial Governor of Yúnnán, due to his excellent work in dredging the bottom of the Jīnshājiāng River,
compiled the Jīnshājiāng Zhì (Annals of the Jīnshājiāng River).
In the seventeenth year,
Zhuāngyǒugōng, the Provincial Governor of Jiāngsū, said:
"The Fúshāntánghé River in Sūzhōu
and the Liúhé River in Tàicāng
are crucial for the water conservancy of Chángshú and seven other prefectures and counties.
They have not been maintained for years,
leaving them unprepared for droughts or floods.
I request that contributions be collected based on acreage
from areas along both banks of the rivers that benefit from water conservancy,
to fund construction and repairs."
An imperial decree of commendation was received.
In the eighteenth year,
Huángtíngguì, the Governor-General of Shǎnxī and Gānsù, said:
"From Jiānshānzi in Bālǐkūn to Kuísù,
the land within a hundred-odd lǐ all uses water from the Southern Mountains.
Beyond the mountain pass,
much of it seeps into the sandy desert.
Wooden troughs must be used to draw the water
for it to flow smoothly.
I request that a thousand military colonists from Gānzhōu, Liángzhōu, and Sùzhōu be dispatched
to go and dredge it."
This was followed as requested.
As Jiāngnán, Shāndōng, and Hénán had been flooded for years,
and the waters of Shāndōng converge in the Huái and Xú areas,
and the waters of Hénán reach Fèngyáng and Yǐngshàng,
it was necessary to manage it by coordinating the overall situation of the three provinces.
Assistant Ministers Qiúyuèxiū and Mènglín were ordered to travel to inspect,
and consult with the Provincial Governors of Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, and Hénán.
Soon after, Yuèxiū said:
"The Bāo and Huì Rivers, at the border of Sùzhōu and Yǒngchéng,
are vital channels for water discharge and commerce.
Within Ānhuī province, there are six stone bridges
that should be widened.
The Hónghé and Suīhé Rivers, along with Bǎijiāhé River in Hóngxiàn, Línzihe River in Xiàjiāng, and Luōjiāhé River,
should have their small weirs repaired.
The Yìgōu, Hēiháo, and Jīngní Rivers in Fèng tái
should be deepened,
allowing them to flow unimpeded into the Huái River."
Mènglín said:
"Dàngshān, Xiāoxiàn, Sùqiān, Táoyuán, Shānyáng, Fùníng, and Shùyáng together have over twenty branch rivers,
which should be distinctly dredged."
Both proposals were followed.
In the twenty-third year,
the dredging of river channels in Yùshěng (Hénán province) was completed.
Acceding to the request of the gentry and commoners,
a Wànsuì Pavilion was built in Yǒngchéng,
and an imperial inscription commemorated it.
Ā'ěrtài, the Provincial Governor of Shāndōng, said:
"Jìníng, Wénshàng, and Jiāxiáng are adjacent to Shǔshānhú Lake,
with about a thousand qǐng of land submerged.
It is proposed to operate the Jīnxiàn and Lìyùn two sluice gates,
so that lake water assists transport,
and slope water returns to the lake,
allowing all the submerged land to be drained."
An imperial decree of commendation was received.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the moats of the capital and the rivers around Yuánmíngyuán were dredged.
Censor Lǐyíqīng requested the dredging of water sources in Jīfǔ (the capital region).
Fāngguānchéng, the Governor-General of Zhílì, was ordered to present a detailed proposal.
Guānchéng said:
"The thousand-lǐ long dikes of the Eastern and Western Dikes
are the remains of the weir built by the Sòng official Héchángjǔ.
The situation now is different from then.
If we adhere to old practices,
the harm will be irremediable.
If we speak of the benefits of the dikes,
then the water villages and products within three hundred li
are more abundant than in the past.
However, when faced with drought and seeking to connect the rain and moisture to the earth's qi,
then human effort must be fully expended."
Kāità, the Governor-General of Sìchuān, said:
"The Dūjiāng Dàyàn in Guànxiàn irrigates the fields of various prefectures in Chéngdū and the two prefectures of Méizhōu and Qióngzhōu.
South of Níngyuǎn there is the Dàdùhé River,
from Miǎnníng to Huìlǐ, with three outlets,
merging with the Jīnshājiāng River.
Numerous branch rivers emerge,
and there are many weirs and dams,
all of which should be repaired and dredged as appropriate."
The Board deliberated and agreed.
Initially,
Censor Wú Péngnán petitioned for the provincial governors to take responsibility for initiating and managing hydraulic engineering projects.
The various governors-general and provincial governors were ordered to plan them.
Zhejiāng Provincial Governor Zhuāng Yǒugōng stated that there are five great benefits of water:
rivers (jiāng), lakes (hú), sea (hǎi), canals (qú), and springs (quán).
Other provinces might possess two or three of these,
but Zhèjiāng indeed had all of them.
In the three prefectures of Jīn, Qú, and Yán,
there were mountain springs and stream-gullies,
which flowed into canals,
and weirs, dams, ponds, and reservoirs
were all present.
However, the upper and middle markets of Rénhé and Qiántáng, Sānhéyuàn, Qūtáng, Tiáoxītáng,
Hǎiyán's Báiyánghé, Tāngjiāpùmiào, Jīnghé,
Chángxīng's Dōngxīnánlóugǎng,
and Yǒngjiā's Qīdōu Xīnzhōu Dǒumén, Jiǔdōu Shuǐqiū, and Sānshísìdōu Huángtiánpǔ Dǒumén
were truly in need of repair and construction
to realize their existing benefits.
As for Hángzhōu's Língpíng Hú and Shàoxīng's Xiàgài Hú,
which held great importance for agricultural fields,
methods should be devised to dredge and clear them,
or tenants could be invited to reclaim and cultivate them.
Further on-site investigation and management were required."
This was approved.
In the 25th year [of the Qiánlóng reign],
Ā'ěrtài reported in a memorial:
"The water conservancy works in the eastern province [Shāndōng]
have the primary objective of aiding transport,
and their ultimate destination is the sea.
The old Huánghé, Mǎjiá, Tuhài, and other rivers in Jì, Dōng, Tài, and Wǔ [prefectures],
and the Guāng, Sù, and other rivers in Yǎn, Yí, and Cáo [prefectures],
totaling over sixty channels,
have all been dredged and made unobstructed.
The civilian embankments along the Grand Canal, extending over seven hundred lǐ,
have also been repaired and reinforced.
In the sub-prefectures and counties of Lè'ān, Píngdù, Chāngyì, Wéixiàn, Gāomì, etc., belonging to Qīng and Lái [prefectures],
over thirty branch rivers needed dredging,
all of which were completed in succession.
The Jiāolái Hé in Láizhōu
receives waters from various upstream rivers.
Gāomì has the Jiāo Hé,
which also flows towards Jiāolái,
easily causing overflow.
It should be diverted into Báimàihú
to distribute the water flow.
The twenty-five channels, including Wǔchéng Gōu Hé, that needed to be opened in the Lán and Tán territories of Yízhōu,
and the subsequent twenty-five channels, including Xiǎngshuǐ Gōu Hé, that were dredged,
diverting water from low-lying areas through Pīzhōu in Jiāngnán into the Grand Canal,
have also been completed."
The Emperor commended him.
In the 26th year,
Hédōng Salt Commissioner Sàhāndài reported:
"The salt pans are low-lying,
relying entirely on the Yáo Xiànqú for drainage.
Recently, due to the channel bed rising day by day,
water has overflowed and inundated the area within the northern and southern dikes and retaining walls.
The Hēihé, which is the source of salt production,
has become shallow and prone to overflow over the years.
The land west of the Sùshuǐhé is higher in the north and lower in the south;
should floods surge south,
the salt pans would be even harder to protect.
Wǔxìnghú is where all waters converge,
and there is a fear of obstruction downstream,
leading to backflow and causing problems.
All these require timely dredging and clearing."
This was approved.
The following year,
the Emperor made a southern tour
and issued an edict:
"In the riverside areas of Jiāngnán prone to waterlogging,
there is concern about continuous heavy rains,
and the mechanism for storage and discharge downstream,
especially Hóngzé Hú, is crucial.
From Shàobó downwards,
the sluices at Jīnwān and Dōngxīwān
have been arranged step by step,
specifically to serve as diversion channels for the three lakes.
However, tracing the source to the essentials,
nothing is better than widely dredging Qīngkǒu;
this is the most important task for now.
As for the Lìutánghé's estuary, which crosses the Yánhé to reach the sea,
all matters of repair and defense
should be carefully discussed and reported by the said governor-general, provincial governor, and river commissioner, in conjunction with the salt commissioner."
In the 28th year,
as Tiānjīn, Wén'ān, and Dàchéng had repeatedly suffered from continuous heavy rains and accumulated water that had not receded,
the Emperor ordered Grand Secretary Zhàohuì to oversee the management.
Also, seeing that Qiú Yuēxiū's previous work on water conservancy in Hényù province had been effective,
he ordered him to rush there for a joint inspection,
and further ordered Āguì to work with Governor-General Fāng Guānchéng to deliberate and implement measures.
Āguì and others reported that
"The Zǐyáhé, from Zhāngjiāzhuāng in Dàchéng downwards,
divides into two rivers: the main river and a branch river.
The tail of the branch river re-enters the main river,
making the configuration unfavorable.
They requested to dredge a river for over twenty lǐ from the south of Zǐyáhé Village, diagonally northeast;
the Yīchéng Hé in Ānzhōu serves as the outlet into the marsh [diàn],
and should be dredged for over two thousand two hundred zhàng;
the Cáohé in Ān and Sù [counties]
should be dredged for over three thousand seven hundred zhàng.
At its upstream location, Jiāngnǚmiào,
a rolling stone dam should be constructed
to allow water to flow into the marsh via the main river.
The area around Hánjiānian in Xīn'ān
is where all waters from the northwest converge,
and a diversion channel of over thirteen lǐ should be dredged."
This was carried out as proposed.
In the 29th year,
the stone sluice gate of Huìjìhé was rebuilt.
The ten-lǐ long dike at Xīzhèn in Húběi was repaired,
as well as the river dikes in Guǎngjì and Huángméi.
Jiāngdōu Yàn was dredged,
and one branch river was opened,
allowing floodwaters to flow directly into the outer river.
In the 32nd year,
the dikes of Diànhé were constructed,
extending for over two thousand seven hundred zhàng from Wén'ān Sāntānlǐ to Dàchéng Zhuāng'értou.
Shāndōng Provincial Governor Cuī Yìngjiē reported:
"Wǔdìng, being low-lying and close to the sea,
relies entirely on the Tùhài and Mǎjiá rivers
to discharge water into the sea whenever floods occur.
The terrain downstream of Tùhài, reaching the point where it enters the sea at Zhānhuà,
rises,
making large-scale dredging difficult to propose.
An old breach and river course at Bàshàngzhuāng were surveyed,
and the terrain was found to be favorable,
so a branch river should be opened
to allow the two channels to drain separately."
Jiāngsū Provincial Governor Míngdé reported:
"Sūzhōu receives water from the mountains of Zhèjiāng via Tàihú from the south,
and from the Yángzǐjiāng via Zhènjiāng into the Grand Canal from the north.
When autumn floods occur,
it often leads to widespread overflow.
I request to repair the pond-paths in the ten counties including Wújiāng and Zhènzé."
Both proposals were approved.
In the 33rd year,
the Hútuó water level rose,
threatening the base of Zhèngdìng city wall.
A new dike of over five hundred seventy zhàng was added to the southwest of the city,
and five diversion dams were built to the east of the return-water dike.
An eighty-zhàng fish-scale dam was built in front of the River God's temple.
On the northeast sides of Gǎochéng,
the Hútuó river flowed around,
and a three hundred sixty zhàng fascine dike was built along the bank,
with an earthen embankment added behind it.
In the 35th year,
the river channels entering the sea from Sūjùn were dredged:
Báimáohé, from Zhītángzhèn to Gǔnshuǐbà,
was over six thousand five hundred thirty zhàng long;
Xúlìujīnghé, from Chéndàngqiáo to Tiánjiābà,
was over five thousand nine hundred ninety zhàng long.
In the 36th year,
the four rivers in Háizhōu, namely Qiángwēi, Wángjiākǒu, Xiàfángkǒu, and Wángjiāgōu, were dredged.
Due to flooding in Zhílì,
Vice Ministers Yuán Shǒudòng and Décéng were ordered to go to various places to supervise the dredging and drainage.
Minister Qiú Yuēxiū was responsible for the overall coordination and management
of these affairs.
Shāndōng Provincial Governor Xú Jì investigated the situation of Xiǎoqīnghé
and requested to dredge it from Wànzhàngkǒu to Huánhékǒu,
totaling forty lǐ,
to allow the main and diversion rivers to flow separately,
from the river into the marsh,
and from the marsh through a ditch to the sea.
The imperial edict approved the proposal.
Guǎngxī Provincial Governor Chén Huīzǔ reported:
"Xīng'ān's Dǒuhé originates from Hǎiyáng Shān,
and at Fēnshuǐtán,
a 'plow-share' structure was previously built to divide the water flow:
seven-tenths into Xiāngjiāng as the North Ditch,
and three-tenths into Líjiāng as the South Ditch.
Inside the intake of the ditch, large and small Tiānpíng [weirs] were built in the north and south
to facilitate storage and discharge,
and then Méiyángpíng was built
to block the overflowing old channel
and also to irrigate agricultural fields.
Recently, due to continuous rain, these structures have been damaged by erosion.
I request to repair all the earth and stone works."
This was forwarded to the Board for action.
In the 38th year,
the Luòhé in Yǔchéng and the Bǎimàihú Yǐnhé in Gāomì were dredged.
In the 40th year,
the Jīnhé Zhōu in Wǔchāng provincial city and the riverside stone embankment of Tàiyǐgōng were repaired.
There was a drought in Jiāngnán,
and both Gāo and Bǎo suffered poor harvests.
Governor-General Gāo Jìn,
River Governor Wú Sìjué, and Sà Zài jointly submitted a memorial, stating:
“Henceforth, the water level of Hónghú should
be based on the markers at Gāoyàn.
The various sluices, dams, and culverts should be opened and closed as appropriate,
always ensuring that the Grand Canal retains five chǐ of water to aid grain transport,
with the surplus water flowing to the lower river for irrigation.”
This was adopted.
In the 41st year,
over 1,100 irrigation channels and weirs in 47 zhou and counties of Xī'ān were repaired.
Governor-General Gāo Jìn reported:
“The Cházǐgǎng embankment outside Guāzhōu city, connected to the Huílánbà,
suddenly developed cracks in the river bank in June,
collapsing into the river for about a hundred zhàng.
The southwest city wall also collapsed for over forty zhàng.
Now that the water level has receded,
it is proposed to move Guāzhōu inward,
ceding land to the river,
and build an earth embankment along the bank to open a towpath.”
An imperial decree ordered proper management.
In the 42nd year,
the Shanxī Provincial Governor Juéluó Bāyánsān reported:
“To the west of Tàiyuán is Fēngyùkǒu,
surrounded by large mountains.
After heavy rains, mountain water rushes down into the county seat,
making it difficult to defend against suddenly.
I request that from Yùkǒu,
a river channel be dug,
leading directly to the Fénshuǐ.
Only forty-plus mǔ of civilian land will be occupied,
but the entire city of Tàiyuán can be assured of no future flood disasters.”
In the 43rd year,
72 lúgǎng in Húzhōu were dredged.
The sea embankment in Chāngyì was repaired,
and residents reclaimed over 1,200 qǐng of abandoned land within the embankment.
The Liúhé in Zhènyáng was dredged,
from the upstream of Xīchénménjīng
to Wángjiāgǎng.
In the 44th year,
the stone dam on the Liǔchuānhé outside Xuānhuà city was rebuilt,
and a stone slope was added.
The Shāzhuāngbà in the lower reaches of the Zhānghé burst,
inundating Chéng'ān and Guǎngpíng,
with no outlet for the water.
An earth levee over 1,100 zhàng long was built
from Bǎisìyíng in Chéng'ān to Dùmùyíng.
In the 47th year,
the Yúnnán Provincial Governor Liú Bǐngtián reported:
“The Míqúhé in Dèngchuān
flows upstream to Làngqióng
and downstream into Èrhǎi,
dividing into eastern and western lakes in the middle.
The eastern lake flows into the sea via the river,
but the river is higher than the lake,
so whenever there are floods in summer and autumn,
water flows back into the lake,
submerging nearby farmlands.
Gentry and commoners advocated donations
to block the entrance of the lake tail into the sea
and open a new branch river
to lead the eastern lake water directly to Èrhǎi.
Also, from Qīngshíjiàn to Tiāndòngshān,
a long embankment was built and a stone sluice constructed,
making the river flow within the embankment
and the water exit through the sluice.
Over 11,200 mǔ of land that had been submerged for years
were completely drained.”
An imperial commendation was received.
He further reported:
“The Lóngchuānjiāng in Chǔxióng originates in Zhènnán
and flows into the Jīnshājiāng.
In recent years, the river current has pressed against the city.
I request deep dredging near the Zhènshuǐtǎ
to redirect the river current back to its old course.
Also, downstream of Fǔxiānhú in Chéngjiāng,
there are one Qīngshuǐhé and one Húnshuǐhé.
The Niúshéshíbà on the Húnshuǐhé was breached,
causing its waters to merge into the Qīngshuǐhé,
thereby causing harm.
I request that a new branch river be opened east of Niúshébà
to divert the Húnshuǐhé
and straighten the river course,
allowing the Qīngshuǐhé to flow unimpeded.”
The Emperor praised and encouraged him.
In the 50th year,
the Hénán Provincial Governor Hé Yùchéng reported:
“The Wèihé flows through the four counties of Jí, Qí, Huá, and Jùn.
Farmers along the riverbanks
built dikes to prevent flooding,
but could not divert the river for irrigation.
Huīxiàn's Bǎiquán area is low-lying,
while counties like Huòjiā are higher,
making winding diversion difficult.
The remaining counties of Jíxiàn and Xīnxiāng have no spring sources,
so digging wells is the only method.
This can both irrigate fields
and facilitate the flow of subterranean qi.
Officials have already been dispatched to trial-dig.”
The Jiǎlǔ and Huìjì rivers were dredged.
The Hàn yán, Tánglái, Dàqīng, and Huìnóng four canals in Níngxià were repaired.
In the 51st year,
merchants from Shāndōng donated funds to dredge the Yánhé,
and eight sluices were built in Dōng'ē, Chángqīng, Qíhé, and Lìchéng.
In the 53rd year,
the Wànchéng embankment in Jīngzhōu burst,
and water entered through the northwest gates.
Grand Secretary Āguì was ordered to investigate.
He subsequently submitted a memorial, stating:
“This time, the flooding was severe.
Local people mostly attribute it to the silting up of Jiàojīnzhōu downstream, which forced the current,
fearing that opening and dredging a diversion channel
would cause the river to become stagnant without force,
leading to re-silting.
I request that an earth embankment be first built against the levee on Yánglínzhōu on the opposite bank,
then a Jīzuǐ stone dam be successively built,
progressing step by step,
to push the current southward.
Once the concave area of the island is scoured into a curved bay,
a diversion channel can then be appropriately dredged,
which would be more effective.”
This was reported and noted.
In the 54th year,
the Tōnghuìhé, the city moat outside Cháoyángmén, and the Wēnyúhé were dredged.
In the 55th year,
the Qiānlǐ Chángtí was reinforced,
as were the embankments of the Zhūlónghé, Dàqīnghé, Lúsēnghé, etc.,
the eastern embankment of Fènghé,
and the stacked roads of Xīgū, Náncāng, Hǎihé, etc.
The stone works of the eastern and western embankments of Fēngchéng were rebuilt.
The old Xiānrén embankment in Qiánjiāng, over 1,280 zhàng long, was built.
The Hónghé in Yǒngchéng was dredged.
In the 57th year,
the Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, Shūlín, and others reported:
“Guāzhōu's dikes are all made of brushwood,
and the river current is swift,
making it impossible to consolidate by successively building stone jetties.
We request that outside the old Huílánbà,
crushed stones be thrown
to protect the base of the fascine,
and from the old city site where the bank had collapsed at the bend,
crushed stones also be thrown,
with fascines laid on top.
In the future, with annual dredging,
it is hoped that the current will gradually move away.”
An imperial decree approved this.
They further reported:
“The river course in Wúwéizhōu forms a curved bay.
The Yǒngchéng Wéibà should be heightened and widened.
It is proposed to excavate a river mouth thirty zhàng wide at Mǎtóugěng,
and the old river from Zēngjiānǎo to the Dōngwéibà also be widened by thirty zhàng,
to allow the river to flow smoothly.”
The Emperor approved this.
The Héhuāchí embankment in Xiāoshān was converted to stone work,
a river breach within the civilian weir, over fifty zhàng wide, was blocked,
and the stone embankment on the Jiāng'àn in Fēngchéng was repaired.
In the 59th year,
the Dàbà in Shāshì, Jīngzhōu,
due to the rushing river current,
was exposed and eroded at the top,
so a grass dam was added.
In the 5th year of Jiāqìng,
the Bòniúhé, Huángjiāhé,
and the river channels of the eight zhou and counties of Xīn'ān, Ān, Xióng, Rènqiū, Bà, Gāoyáng, Zhèngdìng, and Xīnlè were dredged.
In the 6th year,
after continuous heavy rains in Jīngshī,
the imperial treasury allocated funds to dredge
the river channels inside and outside the Forbidden City and within the greater city,
as well as the diversion channels around Yuánmíngyuán.
Wén'ān was flooded,
and the Zhílì Governor-General Chén Dàwén was ordered to deliberate in detail.
He memorialized, stating:
“Wén'ān is extremely low-lying,
receiving shallow water,
and the land is level with the river.
Since its establishment,
there have been no specific dredging regulations.
However, the Guǎng'ān horizontal embankment on the Dàchénghé
serves as a safeguard for Wényì,
and to its south is the Qiānlǐ Chángtí of Héjiān,
which can provide external protection.
Between these two embankments,
a new sluice gate has been built
to discharge the overflow water from Héjiān.
Furthermore, at Lóngtánwān, where the terrain is slightly lower,
a ditch can be dug and dredged,
which may prevent prolonged inundation.”
This was adopted.
Censor Chén Yún疏陳 (submitted a memorial) regarding the water conservancy of the Jīfǔ area,
requesting that repairs be carried out according to urgency.
Grand Secretary Zhāng Yuánmó requested that a bridge be opened south of Liánqiáo at Zhàoběikǒu,
using the ancient Zhàohé River as an diversion canal,
and also dredging the Běilúsēnghé River,
to divert and reduce the exclusive flow of the Báigōu River.
The emperor ordered Jiāngxī Governor Chéng Hánzhāng to act as Vice Minister of Public Works,
to manage the water conservancy of Zhílì,
and to conduct a joint inspection with Jiǎng Yōuxiān.
Hánzhāng requested to first manage the major outlines,
and undertake nine major projects.
Such as dredging the sea outlet of Tiānjīn,
dredging the Dōngxīdiàn and Dàqīnghé Rivers,
and surveying the lower mouth of the Yǒngdìnghé River,
dredging the accumulated water of the Zǐyáhé River,
restoring the old system of the Nányùnhé Canal,
estimating repairs for the Běiyùnhé Canal,
and building up the Qiānlǐ Chángdī embankment,
which should be selected and managed first.
Beyond these, other old rivers such as the Sānzhī, Hēilónggǎng, Xuānhuì, and Hūtúo,
the Shā, Yáng, Míng, Zī, Xiáo, Táng, Lóngfèng, Lóngquán, Zhūlóng, ●niú, and other rivers,
and the embankment works of Wén'ān, Dàchéng, Ānzhōu, Xīn'ān, and other places,
should be managed sequentially over several years.
He further stated that after surveying and determining the rivers to be dredged,
the collapsed river and marshland of Chéngliùjiǎnhé,
which extends down to Qīlǐhǎi,
requires widening of the Zēngkǒuhé River to drain the waters of the Běiyùn, Dàqīng, Yǒngdìng, and Zǐyá four rivers into the marshland.
Then, the Xīdī Yǐnhé diversion canal should be dredged,
and an additional cǎobà (weir made of bundled grass and mud) constructed,
to drain the marshland water into Qīlǐhǎi,
dredging Xíngjiātúo,
to drain the Qīlǐhǎi water into the Jìyùnhé Canal,
reaching Běitáng and entering the sea.
As for Dōngdiàn and Xīdiàn, they are crucial water storage areas for the entire province,
and the Shí'èrlíanqiáo (Twelve Connected Bridges) is a main thoroughfare connecting north and south,
and should also be selected for important repairs.
All were carried out as requested.
The Yúchéng Huìmíngōu was dredged,
as were the Xiàyì Bāqīnghé and Yǒngchéng Jiǎnshuǐgōu.
Yùtíng said:
"The water conservancy of the Sānjiāng (Three Rivers),
such as Qīngpǔ, Lóuxiàn, Wújiāng, Zhènzé, and Huátíng, which receive water from Tàihú Lake,
and flow down into the Huángpǔ River,
have shallow and stagnant tributary rivers blocked by silt,
and urgently need to be repaired and built.
The Wúsōngjiāng River is the main river flowing from Tàihú Lake,
exiting through a sluice in Shànghǎi,
and merging with the Huángpǔ River to enter the sea.
Because the outlet is blocked,
the flow is not smooth,
and it should be extensively dredged at the thickest silted areas."
An imperial decree granted approval.
In the fifth year,
Shǎnxī Governor Lú Kūn memorialized on the completion of dredging works for the Lóngshǒu Qú of Xiánníng,
the Cānglónghé River of Cháng'ān,
the Qīng and Yě two rivers of Jīngyáng,
the Láo and Yù rivers of Zhōuzhì,
the Jǐngtián and other canals of Méixiàn,
the Shítouhé River of Qíshān,
the Lìmín and other canals of Bǎojī,
the Fāngshān and other rivers of Huázhōu,
the Yúxīhé and Qínhé rivers of Yúlín,
all of which were completed,
restoring over a hundred to several hundred qǐng of paddy fields.
Repairs were made to the Jiānlì Jiāngdī embankment and
the Xiāngyáng Lǎolóng Shídī stone embankment.
The disgraced censor Jiǎng Shíjìn submitted a hundred volumes of the Jīfǔ Water Conservancy Gazetteer.
Zhílì Governor-General Jiǎng Yōuxiān submitted a memorial regarding matters concerning the defense and post-disaster management of the Qiānlǐ Chángdī embankment,
which was reported and noted.
The Guǎngrùnpí pond of Ānyáng and Tāngyīn,
having been repeatedly silted up by breaches of the Zhānghé River,
the emperor ordered Governor Chéng Zǔluò to dispatch officials to conduct a thorough investigation and dredge the canal,
to divert the accumulated water into the Wèihé River,
so that it could dry up and be restored as early as possible.
The Míndī embankment at Déshèngtái in Jīngzhōu was constructed.
In the seventh year,
Mǐnzhè Governor-General Sūn Ěrzhǔn stated:
"The Mùlánpí weir in Pútián receives water from various canals upstream,
and blocks sea tides downstream,
irrigating over two hundred thousand mú of flat land in the north and south.
Recently, due to repeated floods,
silt has accumulated,
and the sluice gates and stone embankments have been damaged,
leading to frequent poor harvests in recent years.
Currently, I have led officials and common people to donate funds to repair and build up the stone works on both the north and south banks, which are now completed."
An imperial decree bestowed commendation.
The waterways of Hànchuān Cǎlqiáokǒu and Xiāowōhúkǒu were dredged.
Censor Chéng Dérùn stated that Wángjiāyíng in Jīngshān frequently breached,
causing continuous disasters in the downstream prefectures and counties.
He requested an order to survey and construct repairs.
The emperor ordered Húguǎng Governor-General Sōng Fú to deliberate,
who then requested to emulate the method of cutting sandbanks used in the Huánghé River projects,
to flatten the direct flow of the current,
and then to open diversion canals in the downstream sandbanks,
breaking their encirclement,
to straighten the main flow.
The emperor feared that this would contend with the water for land,
resulting in useless expenditure,
and ordered Minister of Punishments Chén Ruòlín and others to investigate.
They reported:
"The Jīngshān breach is over three hundred twenty zhàng wide,
and the Zhōngxiáng breach is over one hundred seventy zhàng wide.
The main river has flowed for over two hundred years,
and a different old course should not be sought.
Only by dredging the sand accumulation at Hú Lǐwān,
first clearing the downstream outlet,
and then constructing a moon-shaped embankment at the Jīngshān river mouth,
widening the waterway,
and at the Zhōngxiáng river mouth, after blocking it,
adding two stone dams,
to protect the embankment and clear sand."
The emperor approved this,
and ordered Sōng Fú to oversee the project.
In the eighth year,
Hénán Governor Yáng Guózhēn stated:
"The Tānghé and Fúdàohé rivers, along with the Yǒuhé and Xīnhuì and other rivers upstream of the Guǎngrùnpí pond,
have always converged into the Wèi River.
Due to the old course having been long silted up,
they have frequently overflowed for years.
Now, for a plan that provides lasting peace,
by following the terrain and guiding the flow,
all should be made to flow smoothly.
Furthermore, the Báihé River in Nányáng and the Dānjiāng River in Xīchuān have vast and surging waters,
both closely approaching the city walls,
and urgently require the construction of over twenty dams made of crushed stone and millstones,
to divert currents and resist them separately."
All were carried out as requested.
The silted channel of Dōnghǎizǐ in Jìzhōu was dredged,
using work as relief.
In the ninth year,
the river banks of various rivers in Sùqiān were repaired,
as were the sluice gates and dams of Xiàliànhú Lake in Dānyáng.
The Kuíhé River in Sùzhōu was dredged.
The river banks along the new city of Kāshígá'ěr were constructed.
Liǎngjiāng Governor-General Jiǎng Yōuxiān stated:
"The waterways of Xúzhōu,
such as the Lóngshānhé River in Xiāoxiàn,
the Báitánghé River on the border of Pīzhōu and Suīníng,
the Mínbiànhé River in the old city of Pīzhōu,
the Lìmín and Yǒngdìng two rivers in Dàngshān,
and also the embankment works in Pèixiàn,
the Mínniàn (private embankment) on the Yíhé River in Pīzhōu,
and the Tàixíngdī embankment in Fēngxiàn,
are all crucial works.
I request that they be estimated and dredged sequentially."
This was followed.
In the tenth year,
the river banks of the provincial capital of Húběi were repaired,
and additional stone dams were built.
The old course of the Zhānghé River was dredged.
The river channels outside Nánguān in Bǎodìng were repaired,
as were the Xúhé Shíqiáo bridge and the Chénjiāmén embankment in Héjiān.
The Xiǎoqīnghé River in Dōngpíng was dredged,
as were the Ānliú and Lónggǒng two rivers.
The Gōng'ān and Jiānlì embankments were repaired.
In the eleventh year,
the wéidī (dikes) of Nánchāng, Xīnjiàn, and Jìnxián were repaired,
as were the river embankments of Héjiān and Xiànxiàn,
and the embankment works on the south bank of the Hànshuǐ River in Tiānmén.
Tóngzǐ was flooded,
and the Dàijiāgōu river channel was opened and dredged.
The emperor ordered Minister of Public Works Zhū Shìyàn to investigate the water damage in Jiāngnán,
who then submitted a memorial requesting the construction of Jiang dams in Wúwéi and Tónglíng.
Grand Secretary Shào Zhènghù stated that the increasing occupation and cultivation of sandbanks in rivers and lakes was worsening.
An imperial edict ordered Liǎngjiāng Governor-General Táo Shù and Húguǎng Governor-General Lú Kūn and others to instruct their subordinates to investigate thoroughly.
For sandbanks that did not obstruct waterways,
the people were allowed to claim and cultivate them.
Otherwise, strict prohibitions were to be implemented.
In the twelfth year,
the silt in Liáohuāchí in Xīngzǐ was dredged and removed,
the channels were cleared,
and a sand-blocking trench dam was built.
The wéidī (dikes) of Nánchāng and Xīnjiàn were repaired and built,
and the earthen embankment in Fēngchéng was converted to stone.
In the thirteenth year,
Nà'ěrjīng'é, the Governor-General of Húguǎng, requested the repair of the Lǎolóng and Hànyáng city-protection stone embankments in Xiāngyáng,
and the river embankments along Wǔchāng and Jīngzhōu.
Táo Shù, the Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, requested the repair of the Shuāngchéng and Guǒhé two dikes in Liùhé,
the dredging of the Mèngdú, Déshèng, and Wānggǎng three rivers,
and the construction of sluice gates.
All were carried out as proposed.
The Board of Revenue requested the undertaking of water conservancy and city engineering projects in Zhílì.
The Governor-General Qí Shàn was ordered to thoroughly investigate the canals, ponds, and reservoirs of the nearby farmlands,
select the essential ones for repair,
and provide relief through labor.
Censor Zhū Kuíjí reported,
Húběi has been flooded for several consecutive years.
He requested the dredging of the branch rivers of the Jiāng River,
to allow them to flow south into Dòngtíng Hú;
the dredging of the branch rivers of the Hàn River,
to allow them to flow north into Sāntái and other lakes;
and the dredging of the branch rivers of both the Jiāng and Hàn Rivers,
to allow them to flow separately into Yúnmèng
and the Qīzé wetlands, so that the dikes and defenses could be solidified,
and the water disaster could be alleviated.
Censor Chén Yì reported,
the riverside dikes and embankments of Ānlù were breached, causing harm.
He requested the construction of five sluice dams
and the dredging of river channels
to release the water.
Upon receiving the memorials,
Nà'ěrjīng'é, Yǐn Jìyuán, Wú Róngguāng, and others were successively ordered to select officials for detailed investigation.
In the fourteenth year,
the river channels and bridge seats in Liángxiāng were repaired.
The Tiānmén and Niútí branch rivers in Miǎnyáng were dredged,
as was the Tōngshùn branch river in Hànyáng,
and various embankments along the Jiāng and Hàn Rivers were repaired and built.
The branch rivers in Shíshǒu, Qiánjiāng, and Hànchuān were dredged;
the Wànchéng Great Embankment in Jīngzhōu was repaired,
as were the various official and civilian polders in Huáróng and other counties that had been damaged by water.
The Lìmín and Yǒngdìng two rivers in Dàngshān were dredged.
The flood-prone dikes and polders in the eight counties of Nánchāng, Xīnjiàn, Jìnxián, Jiànchāng, Póyáng, Dé'ān, Xīngzi, and Déhuà were constructed.
The collapsed embankments along the river in the six prefectures and counties of Qiánjiāng, Zhōngxiáng, Jīngshān, Tiānmén, Miǎnyáng, and Hànyáng were repaired,
providing relief through labor.
The dikes and earthen embankments along the Yí River in Pī and Sù two prefectures and counties, and projects such as Wángfānhú, were repaired.
Tàicāng, Qīpǔ, and the lower reaches of Tàihú, Mǎodiàn, were dredged,
and the Nántáng Bàodàijiáo in Yuánhé was repaired.
In the sixteenth year,
the Yáo Xiān Qú in Hédōng was dredged.
The river embankments and dams in Kùchē were repaired.
The river channels in Hǎiyán were dredged.
Additionally, silver from the Jiāngsū Provincial Treasury was loaned to dredge the Pídàhé in Yánchéng and the Shùndíhé in Fēngxiàn,
and to repair and build embankments,
as requested by Lín Zéxú, the Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, and others.
Grand Secretary Mùzhāng'ā, Commandant of the Gendarmerie Qíyīng, and Minister of Works Zàiquán were ordered
to inspect and estimate the costs of the river channels and ditches within and outside the capital city that needed repair.
In the seventeenth year,
the riverside stone embankments in Wǔchāng were repaired,
as were the Liúgōng'ān and Héjiātán old dikes in Zhōngxiáng,
the earthen dikes outside Qiánjiāng city,
and the earth and stone embankment projects in Fēngchéng,
and small port stone sluice gates and stone weirs were built.
In the eighteenth year,
the Huángméi embankment was repaired.
The Hēilónghé in Fēngrùn and Yùtián were dredged.
In the nineteenth year,
the river embankments outside Bǎo'ānmén in Wǔchāng,
the garrison dike in Qízhōu,
and the riverside stone embankment in Hànyáng were repaired.
Ēntèhéng'é, the Assistant Amban of Yè'ěrqiāng, reported on the situation of land reclamation for military colonies in Bā'ěrchǔkè.
Previously,
the Emperor had approved the request of Tèyīshùnbǎo, the General of Yīlí,
to reclaim land for military colonies in Bā'ěrchǔkè.
Subsequently, Jīn Hé, acting Assistant Amban, memorialized on its inconvenience.
Ēntèhéng'é was again ordered to deliberate in detail.
At this time,
his memorial stated:
"The main canal in that area is only a little over 328 lí long.
With the embankments on both sides reinforced,
the water flow is very strong,
sufficient for irrigation.
Military colonists have been assigned to guard it in sections,
and when the water rises,
there are grassy lakes alongside the canal to discharge it,
preventing flooding of important roads."
An edict stated:
"Handle it properly as before,
and ensure it is truly beneficial for military colony affairs and border defense."
Guān Fú, the General of Yīlí, reported by memorial
that in Tǎshíbìtú, within the territory of the Èlǔtè'àimàn,
a main canal of over 25,700 zhàng,
amounting to over 140 lí, was opened,
reclaiming over 164,000 mǔ of land,
which was truly fertile,
and the diverted water was sufficient for irrigation.
An imperial edict praised and encouraged him.
This year, the Hàn River rose greatly,
and the dikes and polders in Hànchuān, Miǎnyáng, Tiānmén, and Jīngshān burst.
In the twentieth year,
Governor-General Zhōu Tiānjúe memorialized on the situation of the Jiāng and Hàn Rivers,
proposing six measures for dredging and blocking: One,
construct a diversion dam upstream of the sandbar,
to direct water into the lake entrance,
and then build a sand embankment on its exterior
to block lateral leakage.
One,
on the south bank of the Jiāng River, change the eastern branch dike at Hǔdùkǒu to a western dike,
and add a new eastern dike,
leaving a wide waterway of over four lí,
extending downstream to Huángjīnkǒu,
to flow into Dòngtíng.
Also, at Tiáoxiánkǒu in Shíshǒu, leave a marshy area of thirty to forty lí,
to discharge into Dòngtíng.
One,
on the north bank of the Jiāng River, the old sluice gates
should be converted into rolling dams,
opened in winter and closed in summer.
One,
upstream of Xiāngyáng, construct more spur dikes,
allowing water to flow outwards,
and then at dangerous locations,
add protective dikes and bank reinforcements.
One,
along the four-sided embankments of the Xiāngyáng River,
more steep gates should be built with bricks and stones,
to be opened and closed as appropriate in summer.
One,
as the Xiāng River has a mighty flow,
more rolling dams should be built,
opened in winter and closed in summer,
and canals should be dug to divert water
into low-lying areas on both banks.
These were submitted to the relevant authorities for deliberation and implementation.
This year, the official and civilian dikes and polders in the four counties of Huáróng, Wǔlíng, Lóngyáng, and Yuánjiāng were repaired.
Also, the Great Embankment in Jīngzhōu was repaired,
as were the embankment projects in the four counties of Gōng'ān, Jiānlì, Jiānglíng, and Qiánjiāng.
In the twenty-second year,
the breach in the Wō River at Lùyì was blocked.
Previously,
the Yellow River had breached,
and the main current rushed directly into the Wō River,
causing the dikes at Guānwǔjí, Zhèngqiáo, Liúwāzhuāng, Gǔjiāqiáo on the south bank, and Yánjiākǒu, Wújiāqiáo, Xújiātān, Lóujiālín, Jìjiālóu in Huáiníng, to be submerged and collapse.
The farmlands in Tàihé were all submerged,
and Fǔyáng and subsequent prefectures and counties were also flooded.
At this point,
Chéng Màocǎi, the Governor of Ānhuī, stated:
"The Hénán project is nearing completion of closure,
if the breach in the Wō River is not repaired in time,
the downstream areas will suffer even more deeply.
I request an imperial order to the Hénán Governor to swiftly plan for its blocking and construction."
This was approved.
Yùtài, the Governor-General of Húguǎng, and others memorialized on the high rise of the Jiāng River,
which had washed away the Wújiāqiáo sluice gate above the Wànchéng embankment,
and breached the Dàdī at Shàngyúbùtóu downstream,
directly inundating Jīngzhōu City,
where warehouses and prisons were all submerged.
After the water receded,
the breach at Bùtóu was quite wide,
making it difficult to connect and build directly.
It was proposed to repair one winding dike,
and first build one transverse dike each upstream and downstream.
This was carried out as requested.
The Kùlún embankments and dams were repaired and built,
as were the civilian weirs at Hénghékǒu and Lǐjiāhékǒu in Zōuxiàn.
In the twenty-third year,
Nà'ěrjīng'é, the Governor-General of Zhílì, memorialized on the difficulty of undertaking military colony and water conservancy projects in Zhílì,
briefly stating:
"From Tiānjīn to Shānhǎiguān,
the population is dense,
and there is no unused land.
The places where no one reclaims land
are coastal beaches,
where the tidal water is salty and brackish,
insufficient for irrigation.
As for the water conservancy of the entire province,
wetland cultivation has been attempted repeatedly throughout history,
often succeeding and then failing,
primarily because the water and soil conditions in the north and south differ,
and it is mostly inconvenient for the people.
And opening sources, dredging lakes, building sluice gates, and repairing ponds
all require substantial funds,
so I dare not lightly propose trials.
However, it is advisable to timely clear the ditches and channels in various areas,
to be prepared for both drought and flood,
or to dig wells and springs,
and use waterwheels to draw water,
which would also be beneficial for agricultural work."
This was carried out as proposed.
The embankments at Liáogēgōng, Hékē, and Zhúqítóu in Hǎiyáng were repaired.
In the twenty-fourth year,
the Jiāngxià jiāngdī (dikes on the Jiāng River in Jiāngxià) were repaired.
The Shù Hé in Hǎizhōu was dredged.
In the seventh month,
the Jiāng River in Jīngzhōu swelled and overflowed.
The inner dike at Lǐjiābù breached,
and water inundated the city.
Many dikes along the Hǔdùkǒu Xùnjiāng tributary in Jiānglíng also overflowed.
A decree was issued to Grand Secretary Yùtài to raise funds for repair and construction.
In the ninth month,
the Wànchéng Dàdī was closed.
Yīlí Jiāngjūn Bùyàntài and others reported:
"The abandoned land east of Huìyuǎn City, Āqíwūsū, can be reclaimed into more than one hundred thousand Mǔ of fertile fields.
It is proposed to divert water from the Hāshí Hé for irrigation,
widen the existing channels of the Tǎshíwòsītán farm,
open new channels,
introduce water to the eastern boundary of Āqíwūsū,
and appropriately dig branch rivers at intervals."
They also reported:
"The land of Yīlālìkè and the pasturage of the Kālāshāěr Mongols are separated by mountains.
A river there
flows out from the east side of the mountain,
still separated from the pasturage by another mountain,
which poses no obstacle to the livelihood of the Mongols,
and is suitable for cultivation.
We request to dredge the main channels, branch channels, and spillway channels,
and use water from the Yīlālìkè Hé."
They further reported:
"The Kuítún area is vast,
with a river
formed by the melting snow from the southern mountains of Kùěrkālāwūsū.
Land near the water has long been cultivated by military colonists and households.
Additionally, there are more than ten thousand Mǔ of barren land in Sūqìn,
with fertile soil,
which only requires digging channels to divert water,
and can all become fertile land."
All requests were granted.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Jiǎlǔ Hé was dredged,
and the Mǎtà Hú Mínyàn (folk weirs of Mǎtà Lake) in Wénshàng were repaired.
Kālāshāěr Bànshì Dàchén Quánqìng was ordered to investigate the water conservancy of Héěrhǎn.
He memorialized:
"The land of Héěrhǎn is inherently fertile.
It is advisable to connect and divert water from the Xīběi Hālāwūzhāshí water channels and the Dōngnán Hésèrèwǎtè main channels,
which can be used for cultivation.
The large and small sand dunes in between
have already been excavated.
It is advisable to build stone revetments and drive piles at critical points
to prevent the sand and soil from collapsing,
so that the channels deepen daily,
sufficient for irrigating fertile fields."
He also reported:
"The Yīlālìkè land is located west of the Tuǔlǔfān-governed Tuōkèsùn Military Station.
The soil is fertile,
called Bǎntǔ Gēbì (slab-soil Gobi),
with Shāshí Gēbì (sandy-rock Gobi) to its west.
After more than two hundred Lǐ,
at the spring source at the mountain pass,
there are two waters, Dà Ālāhún and Xiǎo Ālāhún,
which converge to form a river.
Before the channels were opened,
the water was uncontrolled.
Once it reached the Shāshí Gēbì,
it dispersed into the sand,
and the Bǎntǔ Gēbì received no water flow,
turning into barren flats.
Now, the westernmost water is guided eastward.
Three large channels have been dug in the Shāshí Gēbì,
and many branch channels have been opened in the Bǎntǔ Gēbì,
so that even during major floods,
the water has a regulated path.
Furthermore, most of the land in Tuǔlǔfān relies on digging wells to extract spring water,
known as Kǎjǐng (card wells),
which are interconnected for irrigation,
providing great benefit.
However, it is difficult to draw water upstream to high ground.
Households should be permitted to dig wells themselves.
During low water periods in winter and spring,
this can supplement the supply."
The memorial was submitted to the court officials for discussion and implementation.
In the twenty-sixth year,
Wūlǔmùqí Dūtǒng Wéiqín requested the repair of the Kālāshāěr channels, dams, and dikes,
and presented four regulations.
Yīlí Jiāngjūn Sàyíng'ā was ordered to review them.
As there were no apparent malpractices,
an imperial edict was issued to implement them as requested.
The Lùtáng Hé dikes were breached,
and various prefectures and counties were flooded for consecutive years.
The Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū Bìchāng and others were ordered to investigate and handle the matter.
They reported
that within Hǎizhōu, the Lùtáng Hé and Qiángwēi Hé were silted and breached,
inundating fields and houses.
This was greatly related
to the defense of the transport route.
Loans should be promptly sought for dredging and construction.
This was approved.
The Guǒqú Cūn dam and brushwood fascines of the Wēnyú Hé were repaired.
In the twenty-seventh year,
Zásàkè Jùnwáng Bóxīěr presented his privately cultivated land,
which included over four thousand eight hundred and thirty Mǔ of raw land.
Two new channels were dredged,
and two branch channels were added
to facilitate divided irrigation.
In the twenty-eighth year,
Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū Lǐ Xīngyuán requested the repair of the Pèixiàn míndiàn sāobà (folk dikes and brushwood fascine dams in Pèixiàn).
Yùtài requested the repair of the Jiāngxià dígōng (dike works in Jiāngxià) and the outer embankment of Liáojiādiàn in Zhōngxiáng.
Zhílì Zǒngdū Nàěrjīng'é requested the construction of the Wànquán hùchéng shíbà (stone dam protecting Wànquán city).
All were granted as requested.
Censor Yáng Tóngrú impeached Hénán Fǔchén for having excavated the breach of the Jiǎlǔ Hé three times,
spending millions,
without success.
He requested an imperial order for investigation.
An edict was issued to strip Òshùn'ān and others of their positions.
The newly appointed Xúnfǔ Pānduó memorialized:
"The key to repairing the Jiǎlǔ Hé project lies in restoring Zhūxiān Zhèn.
However, the river channels within Zhūxiān Zhèn and north and south of its streets are most severely silted.
It is now proposed to add brushwood fascine works
to prevent silt accumulation on both banks.
For the deepest silted areas,
dredging is more difficult.
An alternative dry land route of several Lǐ will be selected
to divert the old river,
and officials will be held responsible for compensatory repairs,
to be completed within forty-five days."
This was followed.
In the twenty-ninth year,
Jiāngsū Xúnfǔ Fù Shéngxūn reported:
"Continuous overcast and rainy weather
caused accumulated water to have no outlet,
resulting in the breaching of many dikes and polders in Jiāng, Huái, Yáng, and other prefectures.
I request to emulate the method of 'guìtián' (cabinet fields) from the Nóngzhèng Quánshū,
using earth to protect fields,
building them sturdy and high.
Internal water can then be easily drained by pumps.
I encourage the people to carry this out,
using labor for relief,
and also to investigate river mouths
and excavate sluice gates for water discharge."
The emperor praised and encouraged him.
In the thirtieth year,
the Lǎolóng Shídī in Xiāngyáng was repaired,
as well as the dikes and dams in Hànyáng,
the stone embankments along the river in Wǔchāng,
the earthen dikes in Qiánjiāng, and Gāojiādī in Zhōngxiáng.
Censor Wāng Yuánfāng attributed the Zhejiang floods
mostly to mountain cultivation by shed-dwelling people
and subsequent silting of waterways.
He memorialized to prohibit this practice.
An edict was issued to Xúnfǔ Wú Wénróng to strictly investigate,
and to the Governors-General and Governors of Jiāngsū, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, and Húguǎng to uniformly inspect and handle the matter properly.
In the first year of Xiánfēng,
Zhejiāng Xúnfǔ Cháng Dàchún memorialized on the situation of clearing out mountain-cultivating shed-dwelling people.
He briefly stated:
"Regarding water conservancy in Zhèxī, Yúháng and Nánhú are difficult to dredge and restore immediately.
Branch rivers should first be opened and stone sluices repaired
to facilitate storage and discharge.
If the upstream is regulated, the downstream problems can also be somewhat alleviated.
In Zhèdōng, outside the Sānzhákǒu of Shàoxīng,
and the rivers and streams of Yínxiàn and Xiàngshān,
dredging plans are currently being made."
This was reported.
In the third year,
Tàichángqīng Táng Jiàn presented the Jīfǔ Shuǐlì Bèilǎn (Compendium of Water Conservancy in the Metropolitan Region).
It was ordered to be given to Zhílì Zǒngdū Guìliáng for review,
and to be properly handled
after the military campaigns were concluded, taking into account the circumstances.
In the first year of Tóngzhì,
Censor Zhū Cháo requested the opening of water conservancy in Jīfǔ,
and that the success or failure of land management
be used to determine the best or worst performance of prefectures and counties.

Zhílì Zǒngdū Wényù and others were ordered to thoroughly investigate the mountains, springs, rivers, bridges, lakes, and areas suitable for opening channels and diverting water within their jurisdiction,
and to properly discuss regulations.
Soon after, they reported:
"Where implementation is feasible,
whether hindered by boundaries
or limited by resources,
or requiring digging wells and manufacturing waterwheels,
or needing to dig ditches and build polders,
all efforts will be made to encourage and promote
the full realization of benefits."
In the third year,
Jiāngsū scholars and commoners Yīn Zìfāng and others stated:
"The Shìhé, Shízìhé, and Xiǎoshìhé in Shānyáng and Yánchéng wind for hundreds of Lǐ,
flowing eastward into Mǎjiādàng.
Thousands of Qǐng of civilian land along the river
rely on it for irrigation during droughts,
and for discharge during floods.
Since the major dredging in the sixth year of Qiánlóng,
over a hundred years have passed.
The rivers are silted and fields abandoned,
making both droughts and floods easily disastrous.
We earnestly request to dredge and build polders,
and divert water from the Yùnhé into the Shìhé
to alleviate the people's hardship."
Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū and Jiāngsū Xúnfǔ were ordered to investigate and handle the matter.
In the fifth year,
Censor Wáng Shūruì reported,
regarding the water conservancy of Zhèjiāng,
besides the sea dikes,
there were also drainage channels (lóu gǎng).
Wūchéng had thirty-nine drainage channels,
and Chángxīng had thirty-four.
Since the rebel bandits' harassment,
silt and sand had accumulated,
and the mouths of the channels were blocked.
He requested that methods be devised to dredge them.
He also stated that the various prefectures of Sū and Sōng, though having different branches, converged with Háng, Jiā, and Hú.
Húzhōu was at the most crucial upstream position,
while Sū and Sōng and other prefectures were at the most crucial downstream positions.
If the upstream was blocked,
then Húzhōu would suffer harm;
if the downstream was blocked,
then Sū and Sōng would suffer harm,
and Háng, Jiā, and Hú would also be affected.
He requested that Jiāngsū be ordered to conduct a joint survey and management.
This was approved.
In the sixth year,
the diversion canal at Zhāngfúkǒu of the Qīng Hé was dredged.
In the eighth year,
Ānhuī Governor Wú Kūnxiū reported
that the Nángǔ Hé, bordering Yǒngchéng and Sùzhōu,
had long been silted up,
and downstream it connected to Língbì,
which was low-lying like a cauldron.
It had long become a vast inundation,
with no outlet for the water.
He proposed to investigate and plan for its management.
This was approved.
In the ninth year,
the Báimáo Hé waterway was dredged,
and a new stone sluice gate near the sea was built.
The gentry and common people of Jiāngsū requested the dredging and restoration of the old course of the Huái water.
The Governor-General of Liǎngjiāng, the Governor of Jiāngsū, and the Director-General of Grain Transport were ordered to jointly plan.
A memorial was submitted in reply, stating:
"To return the Huái to its old course,
it is first necessary to extensively dredge the silted Yellow River (Huáng Hé)
to clear its path to the sea,
then open the Qīngkǒu
to guide it into the Yellow River,
and then block the three rivers of Chéngzǐhé, Zhāngfúkǒu, and Gāoliángjiàn
to prevent lateral leakage.
Work should be undertaken in stages according to urgency,
hoping for effectiveness within a few years."
It was submitted to the Board for deliberation,
and approved.
In the same year, Zhōng Pèixián, a Shìdú Xuéshì of the Grand Secretariat, also requested the dredging of sea ports.
Thereupon, Zhèjiang Governor Yáng Chāngjùn reported:
"The drainage channels have been silted up for many years.
After investigating the most important and secondary projects,
and estimating repairs separately,
it is proposed to take advantage of the winter slack season
to first expedite the work on the nine channels including Sìqiáo and the two drainage channels of Zhū and Shěn.
The remaining projects and the Bìlàng Hú project
will be planned in sequence,
and should be dredged simultaneously with the Chángqiáo of Wújiāng and the various outlets of Tài Hú."
An imperial decree granted approval.
In the tenth year,
the old canal of Lóngdòng was repaired,
and a new canal was opened to divert the Jīng water.
Jiāngsū Governor Zhāng Zhīwàn requested the establishment of a Water Conservancy Bureau
to undertake water conservancy projects in the Sān Wú region.
Thereupon, the various projects including the bridge sluices of Yuánhé, Wúxiàn, Wújiāng, and Zhènzé were repaired.
The largest was the downstream section of the Wúsōng Jiāng up to the new sluice gate, one hundred and forty zhàng long,
which was dredged separately by machine boats.
All the Qīpǔ Hé of Tàicāng,
the Xúliùjīng Hé of Zhāowén,
the Fúshān Gǎng Hé of Chángshú, the Chángzhōu Hé,
the Mèngdú and Chāopiáo Gǎng of Wǔjìn,
the Huángtián Gǎng of Jiāngyīn, the river channels and dike sluices, the Túyáng Hé, and the branch channels of Dāntúkǒu,
the Xiǎochéng Hé of Dānyáng,
and the Jīngkǒu Hé of Zhènjiāng,
were successively dredged year by year.
It took nearly ten years
to finally complete the work.
Previously, there was a breach at Hóujiālín.
River Superintendent Qiáo Sōngnián considered the season to be too late,
and requested to undertake the work in the winter of the following year.
At this point,
Governor Dīng Bǎozhēn reported that
if this breach was not stopped,
it would surely inundate over ten prefectures and counties in Cáo, Yǎn, and Jì.
If it continued to flow southeast,
then the area around Qīngjīn and Xiàhé would be even more severely affected.
He requested to personally supervise the work of blocking and building.
An imperial edict praised and encouraged him.
