In the twelfth year,
due to frequent river disasters in Zhílì,
Governor-General Lǐ Hóngzhāng was ordered to emulate the established methods of the Yōngzhèng reign
to plan for the repair of water conservancy in Jīfǔ.
Soon, it was decided that all the rivers in Zhílì
would use the淀 (diàn) ponds for storage and discharge.
The hundreds of li of river channels in Xīdiàn
were a major key to the people's livelihood.
First, the breach at Zhàocūn was blocked,
and the southern dikes of the Cí Hé and Zhūlóng Hé were built
to defend against external water.
The Lúsēng and Zhōngtíng rivers were dredged,
to reduce the flow of the Dàqīng Hé,
to prevent backflow.
The Zhàowáng Hé waterway was also cleared,
and sluice gates were built on the large dike above Gǒugèzhuāng and at the Yīngzuǐ Dam at the lower mouth.
In the autumn of this year,
the dikes of the Zhílì Grand Canal breached.
Grand Secretariat Scholar Sòng Jìn requested to selectively repair various rivers and canals
and provide relief through labor.
This was approved.
In the thirteenth year,
a diversion canal was dredged from Chénjiāgōu in Tiānjīn to the edge of Tāhédiàn, over three thousand seven hundred zhàng long.
Additionally, a new canal, over fourteen thousand one hundred zhàng long, was opened from Tāhédiàn, following the old course of the Jīnzhōng Hé, sloping into the Jìyùn Hé,
so that
all rivers in the province could diverge and flow into the sea via Běitáng.
A breach occurred at Shízhuànghù,
diverting the flow southward.
Bǎozhēn was ordered to quickly plan for blocking and building.
Soon, as it was difficult to work on the breach immediately,
he requested to build a dam at Jiázhuāng downstream to block it,
and simultaneously build long dikes on both the north and south banks.
And upstream of Púzhōu on the north bank was Kāizhōu,
and the Governor-General of Zhílì was also ordered to jointly plan.
In the first year of Guāngxù,
the Wén'ān Shèngfāng Hé was dredged,
and the long dike on the south bank of Jiázhuāng in Hézé and the Jīn Dī on the north bank were repaired.
In the second year,
the old and new Sī Hé at Zhāngjiāqiáo were dredged.
In the third year,
the Shízì Hé south of Xiàzhèn in Jìníng was dredged.
Investigating Censor Xià Xiànxīn requested the repair of water conservancy to enrich the people's livelihood.
An imperial edict instructed the various governors and governor-generals to assess the situation
and meticulously plan.
In the fourth year,
the old dike along the river from Huángbòshān to Fánkǒu, forty li long, was repaired,
and a stone sluice gate was built inside Fánkǒu.
In the fifth year,
the Dūjiāngyàn dike was repaired,
and over eighty-two thousand mǔ of formerly submerged land in Guànxiàn, Wēnjiāng, and Chóngqìng were restored to dryness.
In the 20th year [of the Guāngxù reign],
the coastline of Chóngmíng was eroded by tides,
approaching the city walls.
Four anti-water dams were erected on the east and west sides of Qīnglónggǎng,
wooden bridges were added,
and stones were stacked
to defend against the wind and tide.
In the 21st year,
Zhāng Zhīdòng, acting governor-general of the Liǎngjiāng region, stated:
“The Jiǎnwěi River and the Hóng River, branches of the Yellow River,
from Yúchéng, Xiàyì, and Yǒngchéng, passing through Dàngshān and Xiāoxiàn,
reach Suīhé in Sùzhōu, Língbì, and Sìzhōu,
and flow into Hónghú Lake.
Numerous lakes and channels diverge in between,
all flowing down into Suīhé.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
because Suīhé could not contain the water,
the water was diverted into three channels:
the Northern Branch, the Middle Branch, and the Southern Branch.
The Middle Branch was the main course of Suīhé.
In the early Xiánfēng reign,
the Yellow River became increasingly silted,
gradually shifting its course,
and the various rivers in Yù, Jiāng, and Wǎn were also gradually blocked,
causing harmful floods.
Yǒngchéng, Xiāoxiàn, and Dàngshān were particularly severely affected.
In the Tóngzhì reign, proposals were made to dredge the rivers,
but due to the excessive scale of the projects,
they were repeatedly discussed and then abandoned.
Now, a plan for diverting the rivers is proposed:
to guide the water from the Northern Branch River to Yuèhé in Língbì,
and to guide the water from the Middle Branch and Southern Branch rivers to converge and flow into Yùnliánggōu in Sùzhōu,
reaching Huìhé.
However, the Yùnliánggōu channel alone may not be able to accommodate it;
Túhéliánggōu should be managed to restore its former condition,
so that the waters of all rivers flow smoothly into Hónghú Lake
without overflowing.
Then the water calamities in all prefectures will cease permanently.”
The emperor decreed that it be carried out as requested.
In the 22nd year,
Imperial Censor Huá Huī submitted a memorial listing eight matters for hydraulic engineering: namely, drawing springs,
building dikes,
opening canals,
connecting lakes,
digging wells,
storing water,
using waterwheels,
and filling with stones.
It was sent to the relevant departments for deliberation.
In the 24th year,
Liúhé in Tàicāng was dredged,
from Yīnggǎngmén to Pǔjiāgǎngkǒu, a distance of over 4,100 zhàng.
In the 28th year,
Lǐ Xīngruì, governor of Jiāngxī, stated:
“In recent years, water calamities have been frequent,
all due to Póyánghú Lake becoming increasingly shallow,
and the Yangzi River, once wide, now narrow.
Upon sudden heavy rains,
drainage is insufficient,
leading to widespread flooding and disaster.
I request that during the dry winter when the water is shallow,
several dredging machines and steamboats be purchased and manufactured
to dredge the entire lake in sections.
The upstream river channels should also be uniformly dredged at key points.
This is not only for the prevention of water calamities,
but also as a foundation for promoting commerce.”
This was approved.
The northern dike of Húběi provincial capital was repaired from Hóngguān to Chūnshān, eight sections;
the southern dike from Báishāzhōu to Jīnkǒu, ten sections,
to defend against floods from the outer river.
Several stone sluice gates were built
for the drainage of inner lakes.
Additionally, along the river for more than ten lǐ adjacent to the city walls,
stone embankments were uniformly repaired and reinforced.
Xiǎoqīnghé was dredged,
and Túyánghé was opened for over 120 lǐ.
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng,
Nà Tóng, acting governor-general of Zhílì, stated:
“The dikes of Niányúgōu in Tōngzhōu
breached in the 9th year of Guāngxù,
flowing into Gǎnggōu and then to Fènghé.
Thereafter, they were repeatedly blocked and then breached again.
In the great flood of the 24th year, it breached again
and has not been blocked since,
resulting in the repeated inundation of hundreds of villages in Wǔqīng.
It is now proposed to temporarily build a rolling weir in Niányúgōu
to prevent the entire flow from diverting sideways.
Should there be a severe flood,
the earthen embankment will be removed
to facilitate diversion.
At the same time, the upstream dikes and dams will be repaired and reinforced,
the channels leading to Qīnglóngwān and other places will be dredged
to reduce severe floods,
water-blocking embankments will be built to defend against turbid flows,
and Gǔlóngfènghé will be repaired to drain accumulated water.
The rolling weir project should be undertaken immediately.
The repair of dikes and dredging of diversion channels
should be planned after autumn this year
and construction begun in the second month of next year.
The water-blocking embankments and Lóngfènghé
should be planned after autumn next year
and construction begun in the second month of the year after that.
All are to be reported completed before the summer flood season.”
It was sent to the ministry for deliberation and implementation.
Chén Kuíloóng, governor-general of Húguǎng, requested the repair of breaches in Jiāng and Xiāng,
briefly stating:
“Among the various dikes in Jiāng and Xiāng, Yuánjiāyuè Dī in Qiánjiāng is the most crucial.
During this breach,
the dike body was scoured away,
dropping by over 400 zhàng,
and the return current was swift,
turning nearby areas into a marsh.
It should be promptly rebuilt.
In addition, the breached dikes at Guōjiāzuǐ and Yǔwángmiào,
as well as the dike projects at Tiānmén Hēiniú dù, Miǎnyáng Lǚméngyíng, Gōng'ān Gāolǐgōng, Sōngzī Yángjiānǎo, and Jiānlì Hélóngmiào,
are all proposed to have officials dispatched to supervise and plan their repair
to ensure their solidity.”
This was approved.
The Manchu garrison in Níngxià reclaimed wasteland at Mǎchǎng.
First, Tángqú Canal was managed
to enrich the water storage area.
Over 120 lǐ were dredged,
named the Main Canal.
From Jìngyìbǎo, a branch was opened,
diverting water northwest for over 40 lǐ into a ditch,
named the New Canal.
Along the canal, forty small outlets were arranged,
carrying water to the fields,
named Branch Canals.
West of Tángqú Canal,
it had become a marsh,
and without ditches to drain it, no success could be achieved.
Starting from Xìngzihú Lake,
a ditch was dug for over 280 lǐ,
and forty-two large and small stone and wooden sluice gates were built,
along with thirty-three stone and wooden bridges.
Construction began in the ninth month of the previous year
and was completed in the eighth month of this year,
named Zhàn'ēnqú Canal.
Approximately 200,000 mù of fertile land were created.
In the same year,
the Governor-General of the Three Eastern Provinces and the Governor of Fèntiān jointly requested the repair of Liáohé River.
First, they started with the Shuāngtáizihé River dike,
and the following year continued with the Yādǎo and Lěngjiākǒu projects,
and also dredged the sandbar blocking the river mouth at the sea,
carrying it out simultaneously with the Liáohé River project.
The ministry was informed of this.
Record 105, Military 1
The Qīng dynasty established its rule over All Under Heaven through military prowess.
Tàizǔ Gāohuángdì rose in the east,
first establishing the Banner Soldier system,
where every son of the Eight Banners served as a soldier,
as if the entire nation were an army.
Tàizōng conquered the vassal tribes,
Shìzǔ pacified the Central Plains,
and the Eight Banner forces were the strongest.
Shèngzǔ pacified the south,
Shìzōng conquered Qīnghǎi,
Gāozōng pacified the Western Regions,
with the Banner soldiers as the main force,
supplemented by the Green Standard Army.
Rénzōng suppressed the sectarian rebels,
Xuānzōng repelled foreign invaders,
using both frontier guards
and aided by local militias.
Wénzōng and Mùzōng successively suppressed the Yuè and Niǎn rebellions,
the Xiāng Army first rose,
followed by the Huái Army,
and the achievements of trained volunteers became prominent.
By this time, the military system had undergone several changes.
After the Dào and Xián reigns,
the maritime prohibitions were largely lifted,
and Dézōng re-established the navy,
both inland and offshore,
operating alongside the water forces.
Then the trained armies and regular armies also successively rose,
causing turmoil for several years,
eventually leading to the New Army Mutiny.
Those who rose by military force
ultimately fell by military force.
Alas,
was this not fate?
Now, a military record is made: first, the Eight Banners;
second, the Green Standard Army;
third, the Frontier Guards,
with the Regular Army appended;
fourth, the Local Militia;
fifth, the Indigenous Troops;
sixth, the Water Force;
seventh, the Navy;
eighth, Border Defense;
ninth, Coastal Defense;
tenth, Training;
eleventh, Manufacturing;
twelfth, Horse Administration.
All are described in separate sections.
Eight Banners
In the early Qīng dynasty,
Tàizǔ rose with thirteen suits of old armor.
As more people pledged allegiance,
four banners were established:
namely, the Bordered Yellow (Zhènghuáng), Bordered White (Zhèngbái), Bordered Red (Zhènghóng), and Bordered Blue (Zhènglán).
Then four more banners were added:
namely, the Plain Yellow (Xiānghuáng), Plain White (Xiāngbái), Plain Red (Xiānghóng), and Plain Blue (Xiānglán).
These commanded the Manzhōu, Ménggǔ, and Hànjūn forces.
The system of the Eight Banners (Bāqí) began from this point.
Each banner had three hundred men forming one Níulù,
led by a Níulù èzhēn.
Five Níulù were
led by a Zhálán èzhēn.
Five Zhálán were
led by a Gùshān èzhēn.
For each Gùshān, there were two Méilè èzhēn, one for the left and one for the right.
In the fifth year of Tiānmìng (1620),
all Níulù èzhēn were changed to Bèiyùguān.
In the eighth year of Tiāncōng (1634),
the official names for the Eight Banners were finalized:
the Zǒngbīng became Āngbāng Zhāngjīng,
the Fùjiàng became Méilè Zhāngjīng,
the Cānjìang became Jiǎlā Zhāngjīng,
each divided into three ranks.
The Bèiyù became Níulù Zhāngjīng.
The Shízhǎng became Zhuāndá.
Also, the Gùshān èzhēn's expeditionary cavalry was designated Ālǐhā Chāohā,
later known as the Xiāoqíyíng.
The advance scouts of the Bāyǎlāyíng were designated Gábùshíxián Chāohā,
later known as the Hùjūn and Qiánfēngyíng.
Troops stationed in Shèngjīng were called Shǒubīng.
Reserve troops were called Yuánbīng.
Troops in various cities and fortresses were called Shǒubiānbīng.
The old Ménggǔ Left and Right Battalions were called Zuǒyìbīng and Yòuyìbīng.
The old Hàn forces were called Wūzhēn Chāohā.
Kǒng Yǒudé's Tiānyòubīng
and Shàng Kěxǐ's Tiānzhùbīng
were incorporated into the Hànjūn.
In the ninth year (1635),
the captured Cháhā'ěr tribesmen and Kālāqìn able-bodied men were divided into the Ménggǔ Eight Banners.
Their system was the same as that of the Mǎnzhōu Eight Banners.
In the second year of Chóngdé (1637),
the Hànjūn were divided into two banners,
with Left and Right Wings established.
In the fourth year (1639),
they were divided into four banners,
named Pure Black (Chúnzào), Black Bordered Yellow (Zào Xiānghuáng), Black Bordered White (Zào Xiāngbái), and Black Bordered Red (Zào Xiānghóng).
In the seventh year (1642),
the Hànjūn Eight Banners were established,
with a system similar to that of the Mǎnzhōu.
When Shìzǔ established his capital in Yānjīng,
he arrayed the Mǎn, Méng, and Hàn Eight Banners within the imperial city.
Subsequently, the military system was refined.
The imperial guards broadly fell into two categories: the Lángwèi
and the Bīngwèi.
Regarding the Lángwèi system,
there were six Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén,
two each from the Plain Yellow (Xiānghuáng), Bordered Yellow (Zhènghuáng), and Bordered White (Zhèngbái) Banners.
There were six Nèi Dàchén.
The number of Sǎnzhì Dàchén was not fixed.
Shìwèi were divided into four ranks.
There were also Lánlíng Shìwèi.
All Yùqián Shìwèi and Gānqīngmén Shìwèi were selected from the three banners,
while Hàn Shìwèi were selected from Wǔ Jìnshì,
all without fixed numbers.
Initially,
the Plain Yellow (Xiānghuáng), Bordered Yellow (Zhènghuáng), and Bordered White (Zhèngbái) Banners
were personally commanded by the Emperor.
Their sons and younger brothers were selected as Shìwèi.
All who served in the palace courts
were commanded by the Lǐng Shìwèi Nèi Dàchén.
Those on night duty at the Gānqīngmén, Nèiyòumén, Shénwǔmén, and Níngshòumén were considered the Inner Shift (Nèibān),
while those on night duty at the Tàihémén were the Outer Shift (Wàibān).
They all accompanied the Emperor during his travels and stopovers.
Their retinue included
two rear guards,
ten front escorts,
and sixty Leopard Tail Banner (Bàowěibān) Shìwèi.
Regarding the Zuǒlǐng personal guards,
the Plain Yellow (Xiānghuáng) Banner had eighty-five Mǎnzhōu Zuǒlǐng
and twenty-eight Ménggǔ Zuǒlǐng,
with two personal guards per Zuǒlǐng.
The Bordered Yellow (Zhènghuáng) Banner had ninety-three Mǎnzhōu Zuǒlǐng
and twenty-four Ménggǔ Zuǒlǐng.
The Bordered White (Zhèngbái) Banner had eighty-six Mǎnzhōu Zuǒlǐng
and twenty-nine Ménggǔ Zuǒlǐng.
Sixty personal guards from these three banners were selected to serve as Shìwèi,
while the rest were on night duty.
During imperial tours, the Yùqián Dàchén Shìwèi and Gānqīngmén Shìwèi all accompanied the Emperor.
During encampments, they were arranged in two wings,
the rest at the corners of the tent city,
forming a circular guard.
In the twenty-ninth year of Kāngxī (1690),
Wǔ Jìnshì with superior skills were chosen to be Shìwèi,
serving night duty alongside the three banners.
In the eleventh year of Yōngzhèng (1733),
personal guards who had served for less than ten years
were selected to be vanguards.
Each of the Left and Right Wings of the Mǎn and Hàn Eight Banners had one Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng,
to prepare for imperial travel and night guard duty.
Within the Shìwèi ranks were the Shàngsìyuàn Shìwèi,
responsible for reins and saddles.
Other Shìwèi who also served in the Shàngyú, Yīngyáofáng, Húfáng, Shíwǔ Shànshè, Shèhú, and Shànpū departments
were all within the quota of the three banners,
and their numbers were not fixed.
The Luányíwèi were also armed attendants.
One Zhǎngwèisī Nèi Dàchén,
three Luányí Shǐ,
ten Guānjūn Shǐ,
and varying numbers of Yúnhuī Shǐ, Zhìyí Zhèng, and Zhěngyí Wèi were established,
specifically responsible for imperial carriages and ceremonial processions.
The Xiàowèi selected from the Imperial Household Department were Qíwèi,
and those selected from the Five Cities were Mínwèi.
This was the system of the Eight Banners Lángwèi.
Regarding the system of military guards,
at the beginning of the establishment of the dynasty (dìngdǐng chū),
the Three Upper Banners were immediately assigned to guard the Forbidden Palaces (Zǐjìn Gōngquè),
led by the Commander of the Household Guards (Hùjūn Tǒnglǐng), the Company Commander (Cānlǐng), and the Commander of the Vanguard (Qiánfēng Tǒnglǐng).
The Gabušihyan Čooha (gábùshíxián chāohā) of the Manchu (Mǎnzhou) and Mongol (Ménggǔ) Eight Banners (Bāqí) were divided into left and right wings for night watch.
For the Three Banners of the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ Sānqí),
each established three Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng),
four Flag-Drum Company Commanders (Qígǔ Zuǒlǐng),
and the Bordered Yellow Banner (Zhèng Huángqí) established one Korean Company Commander (Cháoxiǎn Zuǒlǐng).
For every two able-bodied men, one cavalryman (mǎjiǎ) was appointed.
Each Company Commander (Zuǒlǐng) had six squad leaders (lǐngcuī) and fifteen guards (hùjūn),
all led by the Grand Minister of the Imperial Bodyguard (Lǐngshìwèi Nèidàchén).
The officers and soldiers of the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ) guarding the imperial traveling palaces (xínggōng),
were divided into three routes: east, west, and north,
and were assigned varying numbers of chiliarchs (qiānzǒng) and other officers and soldiers.
The Jehol Traveling Palace (Rèhé Xínggōng) followed the same system.
As for those guarding the imperial tombs (língqǐn),
in the early Shunzhi (Shùnzhì) reign,
the Yongling (Yǒnglíng), Fuling (Fúlíng), and Zhaoling (Zhāolíng) tombs each had Cloud Cavalry Commanders (yúnqíwèi) and Cavalry Commanders (qídūwèi).
Later, for the Three Tombs of Shengjing (Shèngjīng),
Grand Administrators (zǒngguǎn), Defenders (fángyù), and Commanders of the Agile Cavalry (xiāoqíxiào) were added.
The system for the Eastern and Western Tombs (Dōngxī Líng) in the capital (Jīngshī) was also similar.
The agile cavalry (xiāoqí) of the various subordinate banners (qí) differed.
In the eighth year,
a system was established for princes (qīnwáng) down to auxiliary dukes (fǔguógōng),
who were sequentially assigned chief secretaries (zhǎngshǐ), bodyguards (hùwèi), and other officials.
In the seventeenth year,
the Chinese (hànzì) official names for the Eight Banners (Bāqí) were standardized:
Gūšan Ezhen (gūshān ézhēn) was called Dūtǒng (dūtǒng);
Meile Janggin (méilè zhāngjīng) was called Fùdūtǒng (fùdūtǒng);
Jala Janggin (jiǎlā zhāngjīng) was called Cānlǐng (cānlǐng);
Niru Janggin (niúlù zhāngjīng) was called Zuǒlǐng (zuǒlǐng);
Amban Janggin (ángbāng zhāngjīng) was called Zǒngguǎn (zǒngguǎn);
Ujen Cooha (wūzhēn chāohā) was called Hànjūn (Hànjūn).
From all the Manchu (Mǎn), Mongol (Méng), and Han (Hàn) Banners (qí), a total of 4,800 men were selected as "nurtured soldiers" (yǎngyùbīng)
to be trained in various skills.
Subsequently, the number of soldiers repeatedly increased.
In the middle of the Qianlong (Qiánlóng) reign,
the Manchu (Mǎn) and Mongol (Méng) nurtured soldiers (yǎngyùbīng) reached over 20,300.
In Shengjing Dasing Ula (Shèngjīng Dǎshēng Wūlā),
Grand Administrators (zǒngguǎn), Assistant Leaders (xiélǐng), and Company Commanders (zuǒlǐng) were appointed,
who commanded the hunting soldiers (dǎshēng bīngdīng).
The ginseng-collecting households (cānhù) of Jilin (Jílín),
the honey-collecting households (mìhù),
the fishing households (yúhù),
the hunting households (lièhù),
and the households specializing in eagles, foxes, otters, and cranes (yīng, hú, tǎ, guàn zhūhù),
were all subordinate to the Imperial Household Department's (nèifǔ) Three Banners (sānqí).
The patrol camps (xúnpǔ yíng) guarded the outer seven city gates,
with twenty-five infantry garrisons (bùbīng xùn) established above them.
Outside the city, they were divided into three camps: central, south, and north,
with varying quotas for cavalry (mǎbīng) and infantry garrisons (bùbīng xùn),
all commanded by Brigade Generals (cānjìang) and Guerrilla Generals (yóujī), etc.
The guards of the Changchun (Chàngchūn), Yuanming (Yuánmíng), Jingming (Jìngmíng) and other gardens (yuán)
were commanded by Defensive Commanders (shǒubèi).
In the early Kangxi (Kāngxī) reign,
it was decreed that wherever the emperor sojourned (zhùbì zhī dì),
the Eight Banners' (Bāqí) Household Guards (hùjūn) would patrol and keep watch in left and right wings.
When the emperor departed (qǐbì), the camp commanders (yíngzǒng) of the Three Banners (sānqí) and the Company Commanders of the Household Guards (hùjūn cānlǐng) would follow.
In the thirteenth year,
the Eight Banners' (Bāqí) infantry (bùbīng) were set at over 21,000 men,
and the musket infantry (diǎoqiāng bùbīng) at a total of 1,737 men.
It was also decreed that gate lieutenants (chéngmén xiào) be set up for the Inner Nine Gates (nèi jiǔmén) and Outer Seven Gates (wài qīmén),
commanding the gate soldiers (ménjūn) of the sixteen gates.
The infantry garrisons (bùjūnyíng xùn) within the Imperial City (Huángchéng) were exclusively staffed by Manchus (Mǎnzhou),
while the garrisons (xùn) outside the city were staffed by both Mongols (Ménggǔ) and Han Chinese (Hànjūn).
Soon after, it was decreed that when the emperor resided in a garden (shàng zhù yuán),
the two wings of the Eight Banners (Bāqí),
with each wing divided into seven garrisons (xùn),
would take turns for night watch.
The vanguard (qiánfēng) and musket household guards (diǎoqiāng hùjūn) on duty each day totaled 720 men.
In the twenty-first year,
it was decreed that three imperial hunts (tiánliè) be held annually,
with selected vanguard military officers (qiánfēng jūnxiào) from each of the Eight Banners (Bāqí) accompanying.
In the twenty-second year,
the schedule for imperial tours (chējià xúnxìng) was set.
The Eight Banners' (Bāqí) Agile Cavalry Camps (xiāoqíyíng) increased their garrisons (xùnsuǒ) in both the inner and outer cities.
In the twenty-third year,
skilled archers (jīngqíshè) and tiger hunters (shàn shāhǔ zhě) presented by Heilongjiang (Hēilóngjiāng) were organized into the Tiger Spear Camp (Hǔqiāngyíng).
In the thirtieth year,
the Firearms Camp (Huǒqìyíng) was established.
In the first year of Yongzheng (Yōngzhèng),
the Patrol Camp (Xúnpǔyíng) was established,
with fifteen cavalry garrisons (mǎbīng xùn)
and fifty-two infantry garrisons (bùbīng xùn).
During periods of imperial audiences (cháohuì qī),
Battalion Commanders (xiéwèi) and Vice Battalion Commanders (fùwèi) would lead the infantry (bùjūn) in patrols and security.
In the second year,
an imperial decree ordered the selection of 4,800 "teaching and nurturing soldiers" (jiàoyǎngbīng) from all banners (qí)
to practice various skills such as long spears and polearms.
In the fourth year,
the Eight Banners' (Bāqí) vanguards (qiánfēng) were ordered to practice archery (shè) six times a month.
Those exclusively responsible for fire prevention were called "prevention soldiers" (fángfànbīng).
In the ninth year,
the guards (hùjūn) and cavalrymen (mǎjiǎ) of the five banners' (qí) gate garrisons (ménxùn) were ordered to return to their respective camps for drills.
The three banners (sānqí) were ordered to increase their trained soldiers by 2,000,
organized into two camps.
In the thirteenth year,
the quota for cavalrymen (mǎjiǎ) was set at 5,250,
with combined drills (hé cāo) in spring and autumn.
In the fourteenth year of Qianlong (Qiánlóng),
one camp of ladder soldiers (yúntībīng) was established.
Also, on Kunming Lake (Kūnmíng Hú), "chasing and pulling boats" (gǎnzēng chuán) were set up,
for vanguard soldiers (qiánfēng jūn) to practice naval warfare.
In the twenty-fifth year,
the Hui people (Huírén) who came to the capital (Jīng) were organized into a company (zuǒlǐng),
commanded by a Khoja (Hézhuó) as the company commander (zuǒlǐng),
and this precedent was followed thereafter.
In the thirty-ninth year,
for grand reviews (dàyuè), the first隊of vanguard soldiers (qiánfēng) of the Eight Banners (Bāqí) was organized
into eight teams (duì),
each team having eight small flags (xiǎoqí)
and four conch shells (hǎiluó),
serving as rearguard soldiers (diànhòubīng).
In the forty-first year,
the Fanzi (Fānzi) who came to the capital (Jīng) were treated like the Hui people (Huírén),
organized into a company (zuǒlǐng),
subordinated to the Bordered White Banner (Zhèng Báiqí) of the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ).
In the forty-sixth year,
the capital's (Jīngshī) infantry (bùjūn) added two camps, left and right,
combining with the south, north, and central camps to make five camps,
divided into twenty-three garrisons (xùn),
commanding 10,000 soldiers,
chosen from among the strong men of the Eight Banners' (Bāqí) Han Chinese (Hànjūn), Èrbù (èěrbù), foot soldiers (bùjiǎ), and unemployed.
In the fourth year of Jiaqing (Jiāqìng),
it was decreed that of the five patrol camps (xúnpǔ wǔyíng), the central camp would serve as the main brigade (tíbiāo),
managing the five garrisons (wǔxùn) of the Yuanmingyuan (Yuánmíngyuán).
Four Brigade Generals (cānjìang)
would separately manage the four camps: north, south, left, and right,
totaling eighteen garrisons (shíbā xùn),
subordinated to the two Wing Commanders-in-Chief (liǎngyì zǒngbīng).
In the seventeenth year,
the newly established Jianrui Camp (Jiànruìyíng) was assigned to the left wing,
and the Outer Firearms Camp (Wài Huǒqìyíng) to the right wing,
making a total of thirty-six camps when combined with the Eight Banners' (Bāqí) vanguard, inner firearms camp, and agile cavalry camp.
In the third year of Xianfeng (Xiánfēng),
an imperial decree stated that the capital's (Jīngshī) various banner (qíyíng) soldiers numbered over 149,000.
The commanding ministers (tǒngbīng dàchén) would personally review them in shifts.
Cavalry (mǎ), infantry (bù), and firearms (huǒqì)
must be meticulously trained and in good order,
and should not be filled with arbitrarily recruited soldiers.
In the tenth year,
following Shèng Bǎo's (Shèng Bǎo) request,
the Eight Banners' (Bāqí) soldiers were ordered to intensify training in firearms and grappling with guns (qiāngpào āijiāng).
In the fourth year of Tongzhi (Tóngzhì),
an imperial decree ordered Prince Chún (Chún Qīnwáng) to train the Shenji Camp (Shénjīyíng),
and the banner (qí) and Green Standard (lǜyíng) camps
were also to be inspected regularly.
In the twenty-fourth year of Guangxu (Guāngxù),
the cavalry (mǎduì) and infantry (bùduì) of the Shenji Camp (Shénjīyíng) were selected and trained,
with 10,000 men forming the vanguard (xiānfēngduì),
practicing firearms (qiāngpào) and battle formations (xíngzhèn zhànfǎ).
This was the system of the Eight Banners' (Bāqí) military guards (bīngwèi zhì).
The garrison troops of the Eight Banners (Bāqí zhùfáng zhī bīng)
were broadly of four types:
first, the garrison troops in the Metropolitan Area (Jīfǔ zhùfáng bīng),
which included the assimilated populations from the tributary states (fānbù nèifù zhī zhòng)
and those under the jurisdiction of the Imperial Household Department (Nèiwùfǔ) and the Court of Colonial Affairs (Lǐfānyuàn) in the capital;
second, the garrison troops in the Three Eastern Provinces (Dōng Sānsheng zhùfáng bīng);
third, the garrison troops in the various directly administered provinces (gè zhíshěng zhùfáng bīng),
which included the garrison troops in Xinjiang (Xīnjiāng zhùfáng bīng);
and fourth, the troops of the tributary states (fānbù bīng).
The military system for garrisons in the Jīfǔ (Capital Region):
In the early Shuùnzhì reign,
a defender (fángyù) or two were stationed at Dúshíkǒu, Zhāngjiākǒu, Shānhǎiguān, Xīfēngkǒu, and Gǔběikǒu.
In Cǎiyùlǐ and Gù'ānxian, garrison commandants (fángshǒuwèi) and defenders (fángyù) were appointed, varying in number.
In the fourteenth year of Kāngxī's reign (1675),
for the Eight Banners of Cháhā'ěr,
each banner was allotted one general superintendent (zǒngguǎn),
one assistant general superintendent (fùzǒngguǎn),
three commanders (cānlǐng),
with varying numbers of company commanders (zuǒlǐng), cavalry commanders (xiāoqíjiao), and guard commanders (hùjūnjiao).
Each banner also had two bandit-catching officials (bǔdàoguān),
two imperial guards (qīnjūn) and two vanguards (qiánfēng),
seventeen guards (hùjūn),
four corporals (lǐngcuī),
and twenty-five cavalrymen (xiāoqí).
The Mongolian military governor (Dūtǒng) in the capital concurrently administered them.
Shānhǎiguān had one general superintendent (zǒngguǎn),
eight defenders (fángyù),
and over seven hundred Manchu, Mongolian, and Han soldiers.
Later, one general superintendent (zǒngguǎn) was established at Zhāngjiākǒu,
with seven defenders (fángyù),
and over one hundred thirty soldiers.
Dúshíkǒu and Gǔběikǒu each had two additional defenders (fángyù),
Xīfēngkǒu had two defenders (fángyù),
Lěngkǒu and Luówényù each had one defender (fángyù),
with soldiers ranging from sixty-eight
to as few as twelve.
In the third year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1725),
one naval commander (shuǐshīyíng dūtǒng) was established at Tiānjīn,
with six assistant commanders (xiélǐng),
thirty-two company commanders (zuǒlǐng), defenders (fángyù), and cavalry commanders (xiāoqíjiao) each,
one thousand six hundred banner soldiers (qíbīng),
and four hundred Mongolian soldiers (ménggǔbīng),
divided into left and right wings.
In the third year of Qiánlóng's reign (1738),
two thousand additional garrison soldiers were stationed at Rèhé,

with varying numbers of vanguard commanders (qiánfēngjiao), vanguards (qiánfēng), corporals (lǐngcuī), musket corporals (niǎoqīang lǐngcuī), cavalrymen (mǎjiǎ), musket cavalrymen (niǎoqīang mǎjiǎ), artillerymen (pàojiǎ), and archers (gōngshǐjiàng).
One thousand four hundred soldiers were stationed at Rèhé,
four hundred at Kālāhétún, and two hundred at Huáyúgōu.
In the eighth year (1743),
the general superintendent (zǒngguǎn) of Shānhǎiguān was changed to an assistant military governor (fùdūtǒng),
with additional assistant commanders (xiélǐng), company commanders (zuǒlǐng), and other subordinates,
comprising a total of eight hundred Manchu, Mongolian, and Han soldiers,
divided into left and right wings.
In the twenty-sixth year (1761),
one military governor (dūtǒng) of Cháhā'ěr was established,
stationed at Zhāngjiākǒu,
to manage the nomadic Eight Banners
and concurrently administer the garrison soldiers.
Two assistant military governors (fùdūtǒng)
were stationed at the borders of the left and right wing nomadic territories.
In the forty-fifth year (1780),
two thousand Manchu and Mongolian garrison soldiers were established at Mìyún.
In the third year of Jiāqìng's reign (1798),
an assistant military governor (fùdūtǒng) for the Rèhé hunting grounds was added.
In the ninth year (1804),
it was changed to a general superintendent (zǒngguǎn).
In the fifteenth year (1810),
it was changed to one military governor (dūtǒng).
After the surrenderers from the Ōirats, Dášīdáwǎ, were resettled in Kēbùduō,
their subordinates were subsequently divided into three banners,
and general superintendents (zǒngguǎn), assistant general superintendents (fùzǒngguǎn), company commanders (zuǒlǐng), cavalry commanders (xiāoqíjiao), etc., were established.
They were later moved to Rèhé
and served as regular soldiers.
Previously, in the Kāngxī reign,
the Summer Mountain Resort was built at Rèhé,
and general superintendents (zǒngguǎn), garrison commanders (shǒubèi), and captains (qiānzǒng) were appointed to guard the various imperial lodges.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
additional imperial lodges were built,
and one or two captains (qiānzǒng) or acting captains (wěishǔ qiānzǒng) were established,
with soldiers ranging from six to ninety-eight.
Mùlánwéichǎng had one general superintendent (zǒngguǎn).
In the last years of Kāngxī,
eight defenders (fángyù) and over one hundred Manchu and Mongolian soldiers were stationed there.
By the middle of the Qiánlóng reign,
two left and right wing chiefs (zhǎng) were added,
eight cavalry commanders (xiāoqíjiao),
with a total of eight hundred garrison soldiers.
Each soldier was granted one qǐng and twenty mù of land;
if the land was unsuitable for cultivation,
they were instead given cattle and sheep.
The land of Mùlán
was enclosed by a wooden fence as its boundary,
with eight barracks (yíngfáng)
and forty guard posts (kǎlún).
Each of the Eight Banners was assigned five guard posts (kǎlún),
and each was guarded by banner soldiers.
In the fourth year of Dàoguāng's reign (1824),
an edict was issued that banner soldiers stationed in the capital,
in intercalary months, would be awarded military rations (jiǎmǐ),
a precedent not to be followed by other provinces.
This was the garrison system of the Jīfǔ.
The military system for garrisons in the Three Eastern Provinces (Dōngsānsheng):
There were forty-four garrisons in total,
with over thirty-five thousand three hundred soldiers.
All soldiers, such as vanguards (qiánfēng), corporals (lǐngcuī), cavalrymen (mǎjiǎ), gate and treasury guards (shǒuménkù),
infantrymen (bùjiǎ), night patrols (yèbǔshǒu), artisans (jiàngyì), "nurturing" soldiers (yǎngrùbīng), musket cavalrymen (niǎoqīang mǎjiǎ), corporals (lǐngcuī), and sailors (shuǐshǒu),
were established or not,
and their numbers varied
according to the needs of the stationed locality,
with adjustments made accordingly,
having no fixed limits initially.
In Shèngjīng,
garrisons were first established at Niúzhuāng and Gàizhōu during the Tiāncōng reign,
with ninety-six soldiers.
In the first year of Shuùnzhì (1644),
Shìzǔ was about to move to Yānjīng,
and established the Eight Banner garrisons in Shèngjīng,
with Hélùohuì, an inner minister (nèidàchén) of the Bordered Yellow Banner, as their general commander (zǒngtǒng).
A deputy commander (mèilèzhāngjīng) of the Bordered Yellow Banner commanded the left wing,
and a deputy commander (mèilèzhāngjīng) of the Plain Red Banner commanded the right wing.
Each banner had one Manchu assistant commander (xiélǐng),
four company commanders (zuǒlǐng),
and one Mongolian and one Han company commander (zuǒlǐng) each.
A city commandant (chéngshǒuguān) was established at Xióngyuè,
with three Manchu company commanders (zuǒlǐng) under him,
and one Han company commander (zuǒlǐng).
Jǐnzhōu, Fènghuángchéng, and Níngyuǎn each had a city commandant (chéngshǒuguān),
with two Manchu company commanders (zuǒlǐng) each under them,
and one Han company commander (zuǒlǐng).
Xīngjīng, Liáoyáng, Niúzhuāng, Xiùyán, and Yìzhōu each had a city commandant (chéngshǒuguān),
with one Manchu company commander (zuǒlǐng) each,
and Gàizhōu and Hǎizhōu each had one Manchu and one Han company commander (zuǒlǐng),
who together commanded the garrison soldiers.
In the first year of Kāngxī's reign (1662),
the Angban Zhangjing of Shèngjīng was changed to the General (Jiāngjūn) guarding Liáodōng and other places,
and the two deputy commanders (mèilèzhāngjīng) were changed to assistant military governors (fùdūtǒng),
who commanded the assistant commanders (xiélǐng), company commanders (zuǒlǐng), and cavalry commanders (xiāoqíjiao).
In the fourth year (1665),
the General of Liáodōng was changed to the General of Fèngtiān.
In the fourteenth year (1675),
a city commandant (chéngshǒuwèi) was established at Jǐnzhōu and Yìzhōu each,
with varying numbers of company commanders (zuǒlǐng) and cavalry commanders (xiāoqíjiao).
A defender (fángyù) was placed at each border gate.
Later, three defenders (fángyù) were established at Kāiyuán,
and one defender (fángyù) at Jīnzhōu,
with varying numbers of soldiers and constables.
In the fifty-fifth year (1716),
a naval garrison camp was established at Jīnzhōu,
with ten ships,
five hundred soldiers,
and one hundred sailors.
In the fifth year of Yōngzhèng's reign (1727),
one assistant military governor (fùdūtǒng) was established at Xióngyuè,
one assistant military governor (fùdūtǒng) was established for Guǎngníng, Yìzhōu, Jǐnzhōu, Níngyuǎn to Shānhǎiguān,
and one assistant military governor (fùdūtǒng) was established for Fùzhōu, Nánjīnzhōu, Fènghuángchéng, Xiùyán, Lǚshùn, and other places,
each administering banner soldiers.
In the twelfth year of Qiánlóng's reign (1747),
the General of Fèngtiān was changed to the General guarding Shèngjīng.
The total fixed number of soldiers in Shèngjīng was over fifteen thousand.
As for Jílín:
In Shùnzhì 10th year (1653),
one Àngbāng Zhāngjīng of Nínggǔtǎ was established,
two Méilè Zhāngjīng,
and eight Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each.
In the 18th year (1661),
the Jílín Marine Division camp was established.
In Kāngxī 1st year (1662),
the Nínggǔtǎ Àngbāng Zhāngjīng was changed to a Jiāngjūn (General),
and the Méilè Zhāngjīng to a Fùdūtǒng (Brigadier General).
In the 3rd year (1664),
various Water Division camp Zǒngguǎn (Commanders) were established.
In the 7th year (1668),
two Xiélǐng (Assistant Commanders) were added to Nínggǔtǎ.
In the 10th year (1671),
one Nínggǔtǎ Fùdūtǒng,
eleven Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each,
and seven hundred soldiers
were moved and stationed in Jílín.
Additionally, eight Jílín Xiélǐng were added,
twelve Zuǒlǐng, Fángyù (Defenders), and Xiāoqíjào each,
and six hundred soldiers.
Soon after, fifteen Fángyù were added.
In the 15th year (1676),
the Nínggǔtǎ Jiāngjūn was moved and stationed in Jílín,
the Fùdūtǒng was left in Nínggǔtǎ,
and one Jílín Fùdūtǒng was added.
In the 31st year (1692),
two Bódūnnà Xiélǐng were established,
thirty Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each,
and eight Fángyù.
In the 53rd year (1714),
one Sānxìng and Húnchūn Xiélǐng were established,
and the numbers of Zuǒlǐng, Xiāoqíjào, and Fángyù varied.
In Yōngzhèng 3rd year (1725),
one Ālèchǔkā Xiélǐng was established,
and five Zuǒlǐng, Xiāoqíjào, and Fángyù each.
In the 10th year (1732),
one Sānxìng Fùdūtǒng was established.
Soon after, one Jílín Bird-Musket Camp Cānlǐng (Lieutenant Colonel) was established,
eight Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each,
and one thousand bird-musket soldiers.
In Qiánlóng 13th year (1748),
the Dǎshēng Wūlā soldiers were ordered to be concurrently governed by the Jílín Jiāngjūn.
Previously, during the Shùnzhì era,
two Dǎshēng Wūlā Xiélǐng were established,
and also one Zǒngguǎn,
who supervised the Zhūxuān tribal leaders,
and the households engaged in ginseng, honey, fishing, and hunting,
specializing in various collecting and hunting duties.
Later, eight Zuǒlǐng and Fángyù were successively added,
ten or eight Xiāoqíjào,
and a quota of one thousand soldiers.
By this time, as they were within the Jílín territory,
they were ordered to be concurrently governed by the Jílín Jiāngjūn.
In the 21st year (1756),
one Ālèchǔkā Fùdūtǒng was established.
In Dàoguāng 6th year (1826),
with Shuāngchéngbǎo moved to accommodate the left and right wings of the capital's banners,
two Zǒngtúndá (Chiefs of屯) and Fùtúndá (Deputy Chiefs of屯) were established for each.
Subsequently, one banner was divided into five tún (settlements),
and six Zǒngtúndá and Fùtúndá each were added.
As for Hēilóngjiāng:
In the early Kāngxī years,
the Marine Division camp was moved from Jílín to be stationed at Qíqíhā'ěr and other places,
with over one thousand sailors.
The able-bodied men of Shèngjīng who were scattered about
were organized into the Eight Banners as needed.
The Bā'ěrhū people and Xībó people lived near Jílín,
the Guàlèchá people lived near Bódūnnà,
the Kù'ěrkā people lived near Húnchūn,
and Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào were established to be stationed there separately.
The farthest to the northeast were
the Suǒlún and Dáhú'ěr two tribes.
Between Tiānmìng and Tiāncōng eras,
they successively submitted.
Later, they were divided to serve as quota soldiers in various cities.
As for the Èlúnchūn, they lived even farther away.
The horse-riding and deer-riding divisions were scattered in the mountains and forests,
engaged in sable hunting.
All households were carefully tallied and men registered,
and enrolled in the military.
In the 22nd year (1683),
the Hēilóngjiāng Jiāngjūn was first established.
The original Marine Division Zǒngguǎn and others were all subordinate to it.
Two Fùdūtǒng were established,
four Xiélǐng,
twenty-four Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each,
eight Fángyù,
one thousand Mǎnzhōu soldiers,
and five hundred Suǒlún and Dáhú'ěr soldiers,
stationed in Āihuī City.
In the 23rd year (1684),
one Dǎshēngchù Zǒngguǎn was established,
two Fùzǒngguǎn (Deputy Commanders),
and Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào were established from the able-bodied Suǒlún and Dáhú'ěr men.
Soon after, garrison soldiers were stationed in Mò'ěrgēn City.
In the 29th year (1690),
the Jiāngjūn was moved and stationed in Mò'ěrgēn,
and four more Xiélǐng were added,
seven Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each,
and over four hundred Suǒlún and Dáhú'ěr soldiers,
with one Fùdūtǒng commanding the troops stationed in Āihuī.
Soon after, over one thousand soldiers were stationed to garrison Qíqíhā'ěr.
In the 38th year (1699),
the Jiāngjūn moved again from Mò'ěrgēn to be stationed in Qíqíhā'ěr.
In the 49th year (1710),
one Mò'ěrgēn Fùdūtǒng was established.
In Yōngzhèng 6th year (1728),
three Dǎshēngchù Zǒngguǎn were added,
sixteen Mǎnzhōu, Suǒlún, and Dáhú'ěr Fùzǒngguǎn,
and sixty-two Suǒlún and Dáhú'ěr Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each.
In the 10th year (1732),
one Hūlúnbèi'ěr Tǒnglǐng (Commander) was established,
two Suǒlún and Bā'ěrhū Zǒngguǎn and Fùzǒngguǎn each,
fifty Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào each,
and three thousand soldiers;
soon after, over two thousand more soldiers were added.
One Èlútè Zǒngguǎn and Fùzǒngguǎn each.
In Qiánlóng 8th year (1743),
the Hūlúnbèi'ěr Tǒnglǐng was changed to a Fùdūtǒng.
In Jiāqìng 9th year (1804),
the military colonists (Mǎjiǎ) cultivating official fields at Qíqíhā'ěr and other places were returned to their respective banners.
The newly reclaimed land
was changed to be cultivated by additional Yǎngyùbīng (Nurturing Soldiers).
In Xiánfēng 8th year (1858),
one thousand Hēilóngjiāng Mǎjiǎ were added.
In Guāngxù 8th year (1882),
Jiāngjūn Wénxù requested to establish seven stations from Hēilóngshěng to Màoxìng,
and five platforms from Màoxìng to Hūlán,
totaling sixty station personnel.
One Zhǎnglùjì Fángyù (Road-Keeper Defender) was appointed,
two Xiāoqíjào,
and six Lǐngcuī (Corporals),
subordinate and disciplined separately.
The Hēilóngjiāng Eight Banners soldiers were roughly divided into five categories: the former were Qiánfēng (Vanguard),
totaling one hundred and forty-six men,
who carried quivers,
bore banners,
and served as guides;
the latter were Lǐngcuī,
responsible for accounting and writing,
and were chiefs of the Mǎjiǎ,
totaling seven hundred and forty-eight men;
the next were Mǎjiǎ,
also called Pījiǎ,
totaling nine thousand two hundred and thirteen men;
the next were Jiàngyì (Artisans),
who were artisans for bird-muskets, bows, iron, and saddles,
totaling one hundred and fifty-two men;
the last were Yǎngyùbīng.
In the final years of Kāngxī,
banner soldiers began to cultivate military farms.
By the middle of Jiāqìng,
the military farm Mǎjiǎ were changed to Yǎngyùbīng,
totaling eight hundred men.
There were also those not enrolled in the army called Xīdān,
translated as "horse-controlling servants,"
who were not allowed to participate in military campaigns.
This describes the garrison system of the Three Eastern Provinces.
As for the garrison system in other direct provinces:
In Shùnzhì 2nd year (1645),
the Left Wing Four Banners of Jiāngníng, Jiāngnán, were first established,
and the Right Wing Four Banners of Xī'ān, Shǎnxī.
Both had two thousand Mǎn (Manchu) and Méng (Mongol) soldiers,
twenty-eight bow artisans,
and fifty-six iron artisans.
In the 6th year (1649),
garrison soldiers of the Zhènglán and Xiānglán Two Banners (Manchu and Mongol) were established in Tàiyuán, Shānxī,
as well as nomadic Cháhār soldiers.
Initially,
Tàizōng personally led a campaign against Cháhār,
and the multitude of the Tǔmòtè surrendered.
Later, they were organized into two banners,
with a left and right wing established,
and the Dūtǒng (General) and his troops could jointly handle affairs.
Subsequently, the Dūtǒng position was abolished,
and banner affairs were entrusted to the Jiāngjūn and Fùdūtǒng,
equivalent to the Inner Eight Banners.
By this time,
the nomadic Cháhār were thus listed under the Shānxī garrison.
In the 11th year (1654),
the Xiānghuáng and Zhènghuáng Two Banners (Manchu and Mongol) Lǐngcuī, Mǎjiǎ, and bow and iron artisans were established in Dézhōu, Shāndōng.
In the 15th year (1658),
twenty-eight Xī'ān Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjào were added,
and one thousand Xiāoqí (cavalry).
Manchu and Mongol Eight Banners Mǎjiǎ, Bùjiǎ (infantry), and bow artisans were established in Hángzhōu, Zhèjiāng,
as well as Hànjūn (Han Army) Mǎjiǎ, Bùjiǎ, and iron artisans,
and Manchu and Han cotton-armored soldiers,
totaling over four thousand men.
Subsequently, Zuǒlǐng, Xiāoqíjào, and Xiāoqí were added to each banner.
In the 16th year (1659),
one Zhènhǎi Jiāngjūn for the Jīngkǒu garrison was established,
two Fùdūtǒng,
and varying numbers of Xiélǐng, Cānlǐng, Fángyù, Zuǒlǐng, and Xiāoqíjào.
Soon after, one thousand Bùjiǎ each were added to Jiāngníng and Xī'ān.
In the thirteenth year of Kāngxī
a thousand Manchu and Mongol cavalry (mǎjiǎ) were added to the Four Banners of the Right Wing in Xī'ān,
fourteen bowmen and blacksmiths,
Han military cavalry (Hànjūn mǎjiǎ), etc.,
and a thousand cavalry (mǎjiǎ) in Jiāngníng.
Later, two thousand additional troops, as well as bowmen and blacksmiths, etc., were added to each.
In this year, a thousand infantry (bùjiǎ) were added to Jīngkǒu.
In the fifteenth year
Manchu and Mongol banner captains (lǐngcuī) were established for the Eight Banners in Níngxià, Shǎnxī,
cavalry (mǎjiǎ),
infantry (bùjiǎ),
bowmen, and blacksmiths.
In the nineteenth year
Han military banner captains (Hànjūn lǐngcuī), cavalry (mǎjiǎ), infantry (bùjiǎ), and blacksmiths were established for the Four Banners of the Left Wing in Fúzhōu, Fújiàn,
as well as Manchu and Mongol infantry (bùjiǎ).
In the twentieth year

Han military banner captains (Hànjūn lǐngcuī), cavalry (mǎjiǎ), artillerymen (pàojiǎ), and bowmen were established for the Bordered Yellow, Plain Yellow, and Plain White Upper Three Banners in Guǎngzhōu, Guǎngdōng.
In the twenty-second year
Manchu and Mongol banner captains (lǐngcuī) were established for the Eight Banners in Jīngzhōu, Húguǎng,
cavalry (mǎjiǎ),
infantry (bùjiǎ),
bowmen, and blacksmiths,
totaling more than two thousand eight hundred,
soon increased to four thousand men.
In this year, a General (Jiāngjūn) was added to Xī'ān,
one Manchu Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) for the Left Wing and one for the Right Wing were added,
the Han military Left Wing and Right Wing also did the same,
eight Manchu and Mongol Deputy Lieutenants (Xiélǐng) for the Eight Banners,
and various numbers of Han Deputy Lieutenants (Xiélǐng), Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng), Defenders (Fángyù), and Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao).
A total of seven thousand Manchu, Mongol, and Han soldiers,
seven hundred Manchu and Mongol infantry,
as well as bowmen and blacksmiths, etc.
In the twenty-third year
Han military soldiers were successively established for the Bordered White, Plain Red, Bordered Red, Plain Blue, and Bordered Blue Five Banners in Guǎngzhōu.
One General (Jiāngjūn) was established,
two Deputy Lieutenant-Generals (Fùdūtǒng),
eight Deputy Lieutenants (Xiélǐng) and eight Colonels (Cānlǐng) respectively,
forty Defenders (Fángyù) and forty Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao) respectively,

and more than three thousand total for Eight Banner arquebusiers (niǎoqiāng lǐngcuī), arquebus cavalry (niǎoqiāng xiāoqí), banner captains (lǐngcuī), cavalry (xiāoqí), artillery cavalry (pào xiāoqí), bowmen, and blacksmiths.
Simultaneously, four Green Standard Army (Lǜqí) battalions were established for the left, right, front, and rear wings,
with eight commanders,
and more than three thousand four hundred soldiers.

Soon after, arquebusiers (niǎoqiāng lǐngcuī), arquebus cavalry (niǎoqiāng xiāoqí), banner captains (lǐngcuī), and cavalry (xiāoqí) were separately established in varying numbers in Fúzhōu, Jīngzhōu, Níngxià, Jiāngníng, Jīngkǒu, and Hángzhōu.
Within the Jīngkǒu infantry, quotas were also established for arquebusiers, bowmen, archers, spearmen, rattan shield bearers, etc.
In this year, three thousand two hundred Manchu, Mongol, and Han soldiers were added to the Eight Banners garrison in Hángzhōu.
In the thirty-second year

Manchu, Mongol, and Han guards (hùjūn), banner captains (lǐngcuī), cavalry (mǎjiǎ), and blacksmiths were established for the Eight Banners of the Right Guard (Yòuwèi) in Shānxī, totaling more than five thousand six hundred.
They were commanded by a General (Jiāngjūn),
with forty-eight personal guards (suíjiǎ)
and six secretaries (bǐtiēshì).
In the thirty-sixth year
the Green Standard Army (Lǜqí) naval commander (shuǐshī zǒngbīng) in Jīngkǒu was abolished,
and a Vice-General (Fùjiàng) was established in Jīngkǒu,
divided into two battalions, left and right.
Eight commanders, from Mobile Corps Commander (Yóujī) downwards, were established,
with one thousand nine hundred soldiers.
In the fifty-ninth year
Manchu and Mongol banner captains (lǐngcuī) were established in Kāifēng, Hénán,
arquebusiers (niǎoqiāng lǐngcuī),
cavalry (mǎjiǎ),
arquebus cavalry (niǎoqiāng mǎjiǎ),
bowmen, and blacksmiths.
In the sixtieth year
one Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) was established in Chéngdū, Sìchuān,
four Deputy Lieutenants (Xiélǐng),
Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng), Defenders (Fángyù), Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao), arquebusiers (niǎoqiāng lǐngcuī), arquebus cavalry (niǎoqiāng xiāoqí), cavalry (xiāoqí) and infantry (bùjūn),
bowmen, archers, and blacksmiths.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng
all Han military infantry (Hànjūn bùbīng) in the Fúzhōu garrison were changed to cavalry (mǎbīng).
In the second year
five hundred soldiers were added to each of the Tàiyuán and Dézhōu garrisons.
In the sixth year
one Deputy Lieutenant (Xiélǐng) for the Fúzhōu garrison naval battalion was established,
two Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng) and two Defenders (Fángyù) respectively,
six Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao),
and five hundred naval forces.
In the seventh year
a naval battalion was established in Zhàpǔ, Zhèjiāng garrison.
One General (Jiāngjūn) and one Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) were established for the Qīngzhōu garrison,
four Deputy Lieutenants (Xiélǐng),
sixteen Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng), Defenders (Fángyù), and Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao),
as well as Eight Banner Manchu and Mongol soldiers, bowmen, and blacksmiths.
One Deputy Lieutenant (Xiélǐng) was established for the Guǎngzhōu garrison naval battalion,
two Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng) and two Defenders (Fángyù) respectively,
and varying numbers of Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao) and Eight Banner Han military naval banner captains (Hànjūn shuǐshī lǐngcuī).
In the eighth year
due to the dilapidation of Han military battalions (Hànjūn yíngwǔ) in various provincial garrisons,
the resident General (Jiāngjūn) was ordered to train them.
Two thousand Eight Banner Manchu soldiers were established for the Qīngzhōu garrison.
Five hundred soldiers were added to the Right Guard (Yòuwèi) garrison,
from the General (Jiāngjūn) and the Deputy Lieutenant-Generals (Fùdūtǒng) of both wings downwards,
establishing Deputy Lieutenants (Xiélǐng),
Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng),
Defenders (Fángyù),
Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao),
Manchu and Mongol vanguards (qiánfēng),
Manchu, Mongol, and Han banner captains (lǐngcuī), etc.,
and more than three thousand cavalry (xiāoqí).
In the thirteenth year
a total of two thousand Eight Banner Manchu, Mongol, and Han soldiers were established in Liángzhōu, Gānsù.
A total of one thousand Eight Banner Manchu, Mongol, and Han soldiers were established for the Zhuānglàng garrison.
In the second year of Qiánlóng
a garrison was established in Suíyuánchéng,
with two thousand four hundred Manchu, Mongol, and Han household retainers (kāihù jiādīng) from the campaign against the Dzungar,
one thousand Rehé garrison soldiers,
and five hundred Mongol soldiers from the Right Guard (Yòuwèi),
totaling three thousand nine hundred men.
One General (Jiāngjūn) and one Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) were established in Liángzhōu,
Manchu, Mongol, and Han Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng), Defenders (Fángyù), Cavalry Commandants (Xiāoqíjǐao), Infantry Lieutenants (bùjūn wèijí) and two thousand Eight Banner cavalry (xiāoqí),
and six hundred infantry (bùjūn).
Also, one Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) was established for the Zhuānglàng garrison,
Manchu, Mongol, and Han Deputy Lieutenants (Xiélǐng), Company Commanders (Zuǒlǐng), Defenders (Fángyù), Infantry Lieutenants (bùjūn wèijí) and one thousand Eight Banner cavalry (xiāoqí),
and four hundred infantry (bùjūn).
In the fourth year
six hundred Níngxià garrison infantry (bùjiǎ) were changed to养育兵 (yǎngyùbīng) [maintenance soldiers].
Four hundred maintenance soldiers (yǎngyùbīng) were added to Jīngzhōu.
In the tenth year
maintenance soldiers (yǎngyùbīng) were established for the Jiāngníng garrison.
In the twenty-first year
it was decreed that the Kāifēng City Commandant (chéngshǒuwèi) would be under the jurisdiction of the Governor (Xúnfǔ).
In the twenty-second year
the Jīngkǒu General (Jiāngjūn) was abolished,
and the Green Standard Army (Lǜqí) Left and Right Battalions were transferred to the Jiāngníng General (Jiāngjūn).
In the twenty-fifth year
the garrison troop quota for the Suíyuánchéng General (Jiāngjūn) was changed,
with four hundred infantry (bùjūn) and four hundred maintenance soldiers (yǎngyùbīng) respectively,
totaling two thousand four hundred banner captains (lǐngcuī), vanguards (qiánfēng), and cavalry (xiāoqí).
In the twenty-eighth year
the Two Tǔmòtè Banners were placed under the jurisdiction of the Suíyuánchéng General (Jiāngjūn).
One Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) was established in Guīhuàchéng.
In the thirty-ninth year
one hundred twenty-eight Hángzhōu garrison infantry (bùjūn) were changed to maintenance soldiers (yǎngyùbīng).
In the forty-first year
one General (Jiāngjūn) was established for the Chéngdū garrison.
In the forty-ninth year
one Deputy Lieutenant-General (Fùdūtǒng) was added to Xī'ān.
In the twelfth year of Jiāqìng
it was ordered that Generals (Jiāngjūn) should not fill troop quotas with the old and weak.
This was the garrison system for the various direct provinces.
The military defense system in Xīnjiāng
began to be discussed in the 25th year of Qiánlóng (1760 CE)
to establish troops for stationing in Xīnjiāng.
Āguì was ordered to lead 500 elite cavalry of Mǎnzhōu and Suǒlún,
100 Green Standard Army soldiers,
and 200 Huí people
to Yīlí to search for and capture Mǎhāqìn,
to conciliate and pacify the Èlǔtè,
and to build cities and establish agricultural garrisons.
Afterwards, agricultural garrison troops were successively augmented from the interior, reaching 2,500 people.
They were replaced every five years,
with 500 people assigned to duties and patrols,
and 2,000 people to cultivate land.
They were divided into 25 agricultural garrisons,
with a Túntian Zǒngbīng (Commander-in-Chief of Agricultural Garrisons) appointed.
The following year,
Āguì submitted a memorial proposing the establishment of 15 Kǎlún (border post) guards,
and an increase of 1,500 cavalry for the Yīlí garrison,
bringing the total number of original troops to 2,500.
In the 27th year (1762 CE),
5,000 garrison troops from Liángzhōu and Zhuānglàng,
along with their households, were relocated to Yīlí.
Soon after Xīnjiāng was pacified,
a garrison military system was established.
All Kǎlún troops were led by Shìwèi (guards),
Túntian (agricultural garrison) troops were led by Dū-tún Wǔzhí (military officials supervising agricultural garrisons),
garrison cavalry were led by Zuǒlǐng (company commanders),
and Green Standard Army troops were led by Yíngyuán (camp officers).
A Jiāngjūn (general) was specially appointed to oversee them all.
The Shìwèi, Zhāngjīng (officers), and others were rotated annually.
In the 29th year (1764 CE),
1,000 Green Standard Army soldiers were transferred
to build Huìyuǎnchéng (Huìyuǎn City) on the banks of the Yīlí River.
To manage the city-building troops,
one Fùjiàng (vice-general),
two Shǒubèi (defensive commanders),
two Qiānzǒng (captains),
and eight Bǎzǒng (lieutenants) were appointed.
1,800 households of Cháhā'ěr relocated troops were organized into two Àngjí (banners),
led by a Lǐngduì Dàchén (leading minister),
with twelve Zuǒlǐng established,
divided into two wings, left and right.
Each Zuǒlǐng commanded 200 soldiers.
1,000 households of Hēilóngjiāng relocated troops were organized into one Àngjí,
with six Zuǒlǐng established,
led by a Lǐngduì Dàchén.
Additionally, 1,000 Xībó soldiers, 1,000 Rèhé Mǎnzhōu and Ménggǔ soldiers each,
and 500 Dáshídáwǎ Èlǔtè soldiers
all relocated to Yīlí with their families.
It was stipulated that cavalry would be permanently stationed,
while Green Standard Army soldiers would be rotated every five years.
In the 30th year (1765 CE),
the surrendered Èlǔtè people were organized into one Àngjí,
and together with the Dáshídáwǎ people, formed the Èlǔtè Àngjí,
led by a Lǐngduì Dàchén.
The original Èlǔtè soldiers formed the Èlǔtè Right Wing.
From the Lǐngduì Dàchén downwards,
the number of second and third-class Shìwèi and Lánlíng Shìwèi (Blue Feathered Guards) was not fixed.
In the 31st year (1766 CE),
it was decided to establish a Bànshì Dàchén (Resident Minister) and Xiébàn Dàchén (Assistant Minister) in Wūlǔmùqí,
to oversee the garrison troops and working officials and soldiers,
and to appoint officials for managing Xīnjiāng's trade and inspecting Kǎlún (border posts) and Tái zhàn (relay stations).
In the 32nd year (1767 CE),
the six Zuǒlǐng of the Left Wing Èlǔtè were designated as the Upper Three Banners,
and the ten Zuǒlǐng of the Right Wing Èlǔtè were organized into the Lower Five Banners.
In the 34th year (1769 CE),
one Lǐngduì Dàchén for Mǎnzhōu soldiers in Huìníngchéng was added.
In the 37th year (1772 CE),
the surrendered Shābǐnà'ěr people and others were incorporated into the Lower Five Banners Èlǔtè,
and four additional Zuǒlǐng were established to command them.
In the 20th year of Jiāqìng (1815 CE),
one Fù Zǒngguǎn (Deputy General Commandant) was added within the four Shābǐnà'ěr Zuǒlǐng.
In the 10th year of Dàoguāng (1830 CE),
given that there were over 4,600 Mǎnzhōu soldiers in Huìyuǎnchéng
and over 2,100 Mǎnzhōu soldiers in Bāyàndài,
the Jiāngjūn (general) and others were ordered not to propose increasing the troop quota.
In the 6th year of Tóngzhì (1867 CE),
due to the eastern incursions of the Hāsàkè people,
Lǐ Yúnlín was ordered to train Èlǔtè and Ménggǔ soldiers to defend against them.
A Bùlúntuōhǎi Bànshì Dàchén was added,
to supervise the lamas,
establish an office for affairs,
and also appoint one Bāngbàn (assistant).
These belonged to the northern route of Xīnjiāng.
For the defensive troops on the southern route,
Wūshí had one Zǒnglǐ Huímù Cānzàn Dàchén (Minister Counsellor for Muslim Affairs) and one Xiébàn Dàchén (Assistant Minister),
overseeing Mǎnzhōu, Green Standard Army, and agricultural garrison officials and soldiers,
and also supervising the garrisons of Ākèsū, Sàilǐmù, and Bàichéng.
Subordinate officials included Shìwèi (guards), Zhāngjīng (officers), and others.
The Mǎnzhōu battalion had two Lǐngduì Shìwèi (leading guards),
stationed with one Yìzhǎng (wing commander) and one Cānlǐng (colonel),
two Fù Cānlǐng (lieutenant colonels) and Wěishǔ Cānlǐng (acting lieutenant colonels) each,
and six Qiánfēng Xiào (vanguard captains).
The Green Standard Army battalion had eighteen officials from Yóují (guerilla commander) downwards, and eighteen officials from Túntian Fùjiàng (vice-general of agricultural garrisons) downwards.
Ākèsū had one stationed Zhāngjīng,
and one Green Standard Army Yóují.
Sàilǐmù had one stationed Yìzhǎng,
also overseeing the Bàichéng garrison.
Yè'ěrqiāng had a stationed Bànshì Cānzàn Dàchén (Resident Minister Counsellor) and a Lǐngduì Dàchén,
overseeing the Mǎnzhōu battalion's Lǐngduì Fù Dūtǒng (leading vice-general), Shìwèi, Cānlǐng, Fù Cānlǐng, etc.,
following the example of Wūshí.
Hétián and Kāshígá'ěr also had stationed Bànshì Dàchén and Lǐngduì Dàchén,
overseeing the Mǎnzhōu battalion's Shìwèi, Zhāngjīng, Lǐngduì Shìwèi, Cānlǐng, Fù Cānlǐng, etc.,
as well as Green Standard Army Zǒngbīng (commanders-in-chief) and Cānjiàng (brigade generals), etc.
Kùchē had a stationed Bànshì Guān (Resident Official),
overseeing Green Standard Army officials from Dūsī (regional commander) downwards,
and also managing Shāyǎ'ěr affairs.
Hālāshā'ěr had a stationed Bànshì Guān,
overseeing the Green Standard Army's city defense,
and Túntian garrison troops.
Pìzhǎn had one stationed Lǐngduì Dàchén,
overseeing Xiélǐng (assistant commanders), Zuǒlǐng (company commanders) and below, as well as infantry and Green Standard Army soldiers.
After the 24th year of Qiánlóng (1759 CE),
a Bànshì Dàchén was stationed in Wūshí,
one Bànshì Dàchén and one Xiébàn Dàchén each in Ākèsū,
two Bànshì Dàchén in Yè'ěrqiāng,
along with Zhāngjīng, Kǎlún Shìwèi, etc.
The Mǎnzhōu battalion established one Fù Dūtǒng (vice-general),
overseeing Jiànruìyíng (Elite Camp) Qiánfēng Cānlǐng (vanguard colonels), Fù Cānlǐng, etc.,
Ānxī Mǎnzhōu battalion Zuǒlǐng (fifth-grade officials), Suǒlún (fifth-grade officials), Cháhā'ěr Zuǒlǐng, etc.,
and Green Standard Army Zǒngbīng (commanders-in-chief), Yóují (guerilla commanders) and below.
Also, a Lǐngduì Zǒngbīng Guān (leading commander-in-chief) and Yóují and below were stationed in Hétián.
And Kāshígá'ěr had one stationed Zǒngbīng, Lǐ Huíjiāng Shìwù Dàchén (Minister for Muslim Affairs), and Xiébàn Dàchén each.
The Mǎnzhōu battalion established one Fù Dūtǒng,
and two Lǐngduì Shìwèi.
The Lǐngduì Shìwèi also oversaw Suǒlún soldiers.
Suǒlún established two Wěishǔ Fù Zǒngguǎn (acting deputy general commandants) and two Zuǒlǐng each.
Cháhā'ěr had one Zǒngguǎn (general commandant),
two Fù Zǒngguǎn,
and Hùjūn Xiào (battalion commanders) and below.
The Green Standard Army established Tídū (provincial commanders) and officials from Dūsī (regional commander) downwards.
Yīng'āsà'ěr had one stationed Lǐngduì Zǒngbīng Guān,
also overseeing Suǒlún, Cháhā'ěr, and Green Standard Army soldiers.
Also, Bànshì Dàchén were stationed in Kùchē, Hālāshā'ěr, and Pìzhǎn.
Initially, for the reorganization of Tái zhàn (relay stations),
there were six stations belonging to Pìzhǎn.
Each station had one Wàiwěi Qiān (thousand-man outer sergeant) and one Bǎzǒng (lieutenant).
Yè'ěrqiāng had six Kǎlún (border posts) on its western and southern routes,
each with one Zuòkǎ Shìwèi (stationed guard).
The eastern, western, and southern routes had a total of 21 stations,
each with one Bǐtiěshì (clerk).
Shāyǎ'ěr had one Kǎlún on its southern route.
From Kùchē's eastern route to Hālāshā'ěr's west, there were ten stations.
Each station had one Bǐtiěshì.
Each station and Kǎlún (border post) was garrisoned with defensive soldiers,
with as many as ten people,
or as few as one,
all with ten households of Huí people providing services.
Soon, all officials and soldiers were consolidated into Wūshí and Ākèsū,
with only one Zhāngjīng and Yóují and below stationed.
Later, it was changed to station Xiébàn Dàchén and Lǐngduì Shìwèi, etc.
The Zǒnglǐ Dàchén (Minister-in-Chief) of Kāshígá'ěr was relocated to Yǒngníng in Wūshí,
and soon after, two Bànshì Dàchén were established.
In the 31st year (1766 CE),
Suǒlún soldiers were withdrawn,
and 900 Jiànruìyíng soldiers were dispatched instead for defense rotation.
One Jiànruìyíng Yìlǐng (wing commander),
eighteen regular and acting Fù Wěishǔ Cānlǐng (vice-commissioned colonels),
and twenty-four Hùjūn Xiào (battalion commanders)
were ordered to command the troops and be stationed in various Muslim cities.
In the 44th year (1779 CE),
the Pìzhǎn Bànshì Dàchén was abolished,
and a Lǐngduì Dàchén was established instead.
Soon, Túlǔfān Túntian Dūsī (agricultural garrison regional commanders) and lower officials were established.
In the 8th year of Dàoguāng (1828 CE),
Ākèsū was designated as a central location on the southern route,
and 1,000 soldiers were added.
500 defensive troops from Kē'ěrpíng were moved to Ākèsū,
and officers and soldiers from Bàichéng Cānjiàng (brigade general) downwards were abolished.
The total number of old and new defensive troops became 2,200,
excluding soldiers assigned to guard Kǎ (posts),
leaving 1,300 soldiers for training,
to control all routes.
In the 9th year (1829 CE),
eight Kǎlún (border posts) with officers and soldiers were added on the border of Kāshígá'ěr.
Soon, among the eight Kǎlún, Kālàngguī, Túshūkètǎ, and Wūpāilātè were vital routes leading to Huòhàn.
A fortress was built at Míngyuēluò,
with one Dūsī (regional commander) and 200 Green Standard Army soldiers stationed there.
Fortresses were built at three Ā'ěrhú horse farms,
with 200 or 60 soldiers stationed.
Yè'ěrqiāng had seven subordinate Kǎlún,
with Liànggē'ěr and Kùkùyǎ'ěr being important passes against "barbarians."
Yīngjísā'ěr had five subordinate Kǎlún,
with only Wūlǔkè being a vital route.
All built earthen forts and barracks,
with Qiānzǒng (captains) appointed,
and below them Bǎzǒng (lieutenants) and Wàiwěi (outer sergeants).
The number of stationed soldiers was up to 60 for those with many,
and as few as 15 or 10 for those with fewer.
Bordered Yellow Banner Mongols:
one Dū Tǒng,
two Fù Dū Tǒng,
one Yìnwù Cānlǐng,
two Cānlǐng,
two Fù Cānlǐng,
four Yìnwù Zhāngjīng,
twenty-eight Zuǒlǐng and Xiāoqíjiao each,
four Yìnwù Bǐtiěshì,
totaling seventy-two people.
One hundred forty Lǐngcuī,
four hundred ninety-seven Mǎjiǎ,
twenty-eight Suíjiǎ,
five hundred ninety-two Yǎngyù Bīng,
four Qīnjūn Jiào,
fifty-two Qīnjūn,
one Gōngjiàng Zhǎng,
twenty-seven Gōngjiàng,
and other positions such as Chánghào Dá, Chánghào, Kuījiàng, Ānjiàng, Wǎnghù, Yuànjiǎ, Chéngchāi, Chuánshì Bīng, Tíngbīng, etc., from one to six persons each,
totaling one thousand three hundred sixty-three people.
Plain Yellow Banner Mongols:
