Record 106: Soldiers 2: Green Standard Army
The regulations for the Lǜyíng (Green Standard Army)
originated in the former Míng dynasty.
At the beginning of the Qīng Shùnzhì reign,
with the realm already settled,
the provincial garrison systems were established.
The Lǜyíng system
included Mǎbīng (cavalry), Shǒubīng (garrison troops), and Zhànbīng (combat troops).
Both combat and garrison troops were infantry.
Extra-establishment Wàiwěi (External Sergeants) were all cavalry.
The total number of regular troops throughout the realm was six hundred sixty thousand.
Ānhuī had the fewest,
Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng had the most due to their navies,
and Gānsù was next.
Among the Lǜyíng, those belonging to the Forbidden Army
were only the infantry of the Jīngshī Wǔchéng Xúnzǎo Yíng (Five City Patrol and Arrest Battalions of the Capital).
Only in Sìchuān did a Jiāngjūn (General) also command the Lǜyíng.
Only Húnán and Guìzhōu had Túnbīng (farming-soldiers).
The Lǜyíng garrisons in Xīnjiāng
began in the twenty-fifth year of Qiánlóng,
with troops gradually transferred from Shǎnxī and Gānsù for stationing.
The regulations for the Biāobīng (Provincial Troops) in each province
could be revised by the Dūfǔ (Governors-General and Governors) as needed.
Regarding Lǜyíng military achievements,
from the Kāngxī campaign against the Sānfān (Three Feudatories),
a total of four hundred thousand Qí (Banner) and Lǜ (Green Standard) troops were employed.
In the mountainous regions of Yúnnán and Guìzhōu,
the Lǜyíng infantry led the way,
followed by the Qíbīng (Banner Soldiers),
achieving victory wherever they advanced.
Subsequently, in the pacification of Zhǔnbù, Huíjiāng, and Jīnchuān,
they all performed meritorious service.
In the forty-sixth year of Qiánlóng, troops were increased,
but during the campaign against the Chuān-Chǔ Jiàofěi (Sichuan-Hubei Sectarian Rebels)
and the Anglo-French Commercial War,
their military strength was inferior to before.
When the Yuèkòu (Guangdong Rebels) rose,
the Guǎngxī Lǜyíng had an authorized strength of twenty-three thousand,
and fourteen thousand Tǔbīng (local irregulars),
but they crumbled at the enemy's approach.
Long years of peace
had allowed decadence to set in.
From Tóngzhì to Guāngxù,
after repeated reductions and eliminations,
the Lǜyíng system
barely survived.
For the Jīngshī Xúnzǎo Wǔyíng (Five Patrol and Arrest Battalions of the Capital),
one Bùjūn Tǒnglǐng (Commander of Infantry) was established,
commanding the Zuǒ-Yòuyì Zǒngbīngguān (Brigadier-Generals of the Left and Right Wings) and the Shíliùmén Ménqiānzǒng (Gate Lieutenants of the Sixteen Gates),
with various ranks such as Fùjiàng (Vice General) or Shǒubèi (Garrison Commander) stationed at Hǎidiàn, Chàngchūnyuán, Shùcūnxùn, Jìngyíyuán, and Lèshànyuán,
commanding a total of three thousand soldiers.
For the nine inner gates and seven outer gates of the capital city,
each gate had two Qiānzǒng,
ten or twenty Ménjiǎ (Gate Guards),
and forty Ménjūn (Gate Soldiers).
The Zuǒyì Zǒngbīng commanded the patrol officers of the Nán (South) and Zuǒ (Left) Battalions of the Bùjūn Yíng (Infantry Camps),
totaling over three thousand six hundred soldiers.
The Yòuyì Zǒngbīng commanded the patrol officers of the Běi (North) and Yòu (Right) Battalions of the Bùjūn Yíng,
totaling over two thousand five hundred soldiers.
For the garrison systems of the various provinces,
in the first year of Shùnzhì,
the regulations for Zhílì (direct control) officials and soldiers were established,
with a Zhílì Xúnfǔ (Zhílì Governor) appointed.
The Biāobīng were divided into Zuǒ and Yòu Battalions,
with eight officers from Yóují (Major) downwards.

Six Zhènhuà Zǒngbīngguān (Brigadier-Generals) were established at Xuānfǔ, Zhēndìng, Jìzhōu, Tōngzhōu, Tiānjīn, and Shānhǎiguān, along with Zhènbiāo Shǒubèi (Brigade Garrison Commanders), Yóují, and others.
Seven Xié Fùjiàng (Sub-Generals of Brigades) were established at Zǐjīngguān and other passes, along with Xiébiāo Guānbīng (Brigade Officers and Soldiers).
Seventeen Cānjìang (Colonels) were established at Gǒngjí Chéng (Gǒngjí City) and other places,
Yóují for Shānyǒng and other garrisons,
and Shǒubèi, Dūsī (Commandants) at Gǒnghuá Chéng (Gǒnghuá City) and other locations,
to command the troops of their respective garrisons.
Established the regular system for the Shāndōng officials and soldiers,
established a Hédào Zǒngdū,
its banner troops divided into three battalions: center, left, and right,
established eight officers ranging from Fùjiàng or Yóují downwards,
with a total of three thousand soldiers,
for river defense and escorting transport.
The Shāndōng Xúnfǔ's banner troops were divided into two battalions, left and right,
with eight officers from Yóují downwards,
and a total of two thousand soldiers.
Established Zǒngbīngguān for the two garrisons of Línqīng and Yízhōu, along with eight officers,
with a total of two thousand four hundred odd soldiers.
Established Cānjìang or Shǒubèi for the three battalions of Dézhōu, Qīngzhōu, and Wǔdìng, with eight or six officers,
and a total of two thousand two hundred odd soldiers.
Established a Shǒubèi for the Dēngzhōu naval battalion,
and four Yóují or Shǒubèi for the battalions of Dēngzhōu, Láizhōu, Línqīng, and Jǐnán,
with a total of one thousand two hundred odd soldiers.
Initially,
Shāndōng, along with Zhílì and Hénán, shared one Zǒngdū.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
a Shāndōng Tídū was established,
but was soon entirely abolished,
the post being concurrently held by the Xúnfǔ.
The regular system for the officials and soldiers of Shānxī, Jiāngnán, and Shǎnxī,
was all established in the second year of Shùnzhì.
In Shānxī, a Xuāndà Zǒngdū and a Xúnfǔ were established,
the Zǒngdū's banner troops divided into three battalions: center, left, and right,
and the Xúnfǔ's banner troops divided into left and right battalions,
each with eight officers,
and a total of two thousand soldiers.
Established Fùjiàng for the two brigades of Tàiyuán and Píngyáng, along with their brigade banner officials and soldiers.
Established Cānjìang, Yóují, and Shǒubèi for the Fénzhōu and other battalions,
who separately commanded the battalion soldiers.
In the thirteenth year,
the Xuāndà Zǒngdū was abolished.
In the first year of Kāngxī,
a Shānxī Tídū was established,
repeatedly abolished and reinstated,
until it was again abolished in the ninth year of Yōngzhèng,
the post being concurrently held by the Xúnfǔ.
In Jiāngnán, a Cáoyùn Zǒngdū was established,
along with two Xúnfǔ for Jiāngsū and Fènglú,
with their banner troops and left and right battalions as regulated,
nine or eight officers,
and a total of four thousand odd soldiers,
and also established a Qíbīng Yíng and a Yóubīng Yíng.
Established a Jiāngnán Hànbīng Tídū,
divided into five battalions: center, left, right, front, and rear,
with eight officers separately established,
and a total of four thousand soldiers.
Established Zǒngbīngguān for the eight garrisons of Sūzhōu, Zhènjiāng, Pǔkǒu, Ānqìng, Chítài, Dōngshān, and Guǎngdé,
along with their garrison banner troops and officers.
Established Fùjiàng for Lángshān and seven other brigades,
Cānjìang, Yóují, and Shǒubèi for the Jīnshān and Chángzhōu battalions,
who separately commanded the battalion soldiers.
At the beginning of the dynasty, a Jiāngnán Jiāngxī Hénán Zǒngdū was established.
Afterwards, its divisions and amalgamations were inconsistent.
During the Kāngxī reign,
it was settled as the Liǎngjiāng Zǒngdū.
The Fènglú Xúnfǔ was also abolished and merged into Jiāngsū.
A Sūsōng Tídū was established.
Soon after, it was settled as the Jiāngníng Tídū,
and an Ānhuī Tídū was added,
to separately administer battalion affairs.
Later, the Ānhuī Tídū was again abolished,
and changed to the Jiāngnán Shuǐlù Tídū,
commanding all officials and soldiers in the province.
Previously, a Cāojiāng Xúnfǔ was established,
administering Ānqìng and five other prefectures,
and the soldiers of Chú, Hé, and three other departments.
Later, it was changed to the Ānhuī Xúnfǔ,
with all the Fènglú soldiers also placed under its jurisdiction.
Shǎnxī originally established a Chuānshǎn Zǒngdū,
who also administered the Sìchuān soldiers,
with banner troops divided into five battalions.
Separately established four Xúnfǔ for Xī'ān, Yánsuí, Gānsù, and Níngxià,
each with banner troops divided into left and right battalions,
and officers roughly like those in other provinces.
Established Zǒngbīngguān for the six garrisons of Yánsuí, Gùyuán, Língǒng, Fèngxiáng, Hànqiāng, and Gānsù,
whose garrison banner troops were also divided into five battalions,
with officers like those.
Yánsuí also had two brigades separately established, East and West.
Established Fùjiàng for Xī'ān, Qìngyáng, and eight other places,
Cānjìang, Yóují, Dūsī, and Shǒubèi for Yíjūn, Jiēzhōu, and other battalions,
who separately commanded the battalion soldiers.
During the Kāngxī reign,
the Chuānshǎn Zǒngdū was repeatedly altered,
and also administered Shān, Shǎn, and Gān.
Soon after, it was changed to the Chuānshǎngān Zǒngdū.
During the Qiánlóng reign,
a Zǒngdū was separately established for Gānsù,
the Sìchuān Zǒngdū concurrently administering Shǎnxī soldiers,
and becoming the Chuānshǎn Zǒngdū.
Later, it was again changed to the Shǎngān Zǒngdū.
At the beginning of the dynasty, a Gānsù Xúnfǔ was established,
while the Níngxià and Yánsuí Xúnfǔ were successively abolished.
Níngxià reverted to Gānsù,
and Yánsuí reverted to Shǎnxī.
Later, the Gānsù Xúnfǔ was again abolished,
the Shǎngān Zǒngdū concurrently commanding the Xúnfǔ's banner troops.
In Gānzhōu, a Gānsù Zǒngbīngguān was established,
but soon after it was changed to establish a Gānsù Tídū.
Initially, a Shǎnxī Hànbīng Tídū and a Níngxià Tídū were established,
divided into five battalions,
each with eight officers,
and a total of four thousand soldiers.
Later, it was changed to the Xī'ān Tídū,
and then relocated to Gùyuán,
changed to the Gùyuán Tídū.
In the third year of Shùnzhì,
the regular system for the officials and soldiers of Hénán, Jiāngxī, and Húguǎng was established.
In Hénán, a Xúnfǔ was established,
whose banner troops were divided into left and right battalions,
with eight officers,
and two thousand soldiers,
the system being the same as above.
A Hénán Tídū was established,
whose banner troops were divided into three battalions: center, left, and right,
with officers established to command them separately.
Established Zǒngbīngguān for the three garrisons of Héběi, Nányáng, and Kāiguī,
each with banner troops divided into left and right battalions,
the number of officers and soldiers being the same as the Xúnfǔ's banner system.
Established seven officers for Kāifēng from Fùjiàng and Shǒubèi downwards,
with one thousand soldiers,
and Cānjìang and others for the Wèihuī, Rǔníng, and Guīdé battalions in Hénán,
each with one thousand soldiers.
Established a Dūsī for the Cízhōu battalion,
with five hundred soldiers,
which later belonged to the Shǒubèi of Sōngxiàn and two other battalions in Zhílì,
with three hundred or two hundred soldiers.
Previously, Hénán, along with Zhílì and Shāndōng, shared one Zǒngdū,
who concurrently administered Hénán's officials and soldiers.
Afterwards, sometimes a Hénán Zǒngdū was specially established,
or it was abolished or altered.
Until the thirteenth year of Yōngzhèng,
it remained the Hénán Xúnfǔ.
Jiāngxī initially established a Xúnfǔ and a Nángàn Xúnfǔ,
whose banner troops were divided into left and right battalions,
with five officers established,
and a total of one thousand five hundred soldiers.
Established a Jiāngxī Tídū,
whose banner troops were divided into five battalions,
each battalion with eight officers established,
and a total of five thousand soldiers.
Established Zǒngbīngguān for the two garrisons of Nángàn and Jiǔjiāng,
with banner troops divided into five battalions,
each with officers from Yóují downwards,
and the number of soldiers being the same as the Tídū's banner troops.
Established Fùjiàng for Yuánzhōu and four other brigades,
divided into left and right battalions,
each with eight officers,
and a total of two thousand soldiers.
Established Cānjìang for Guǎngdé and other battalions,
Shǒubèi for each naval battalion in Fǔzhōu,
with six hundred soldiers,
and Shǒubèi for Nánkāng and other battalions with three hundred soldiers.
In the early years of Kāngxī,
the Nángàn Xúnfǔ was abolished,
and its banner troops were placed under the Jiāngxī Xúnfǔ.
In the seventh year,
the Tídū was abolished.
In the thirteenth year,
it was re-established.
Subsequently, a Fǔjiàn Tídū was added,
but was soon abolished,
and the Jiāngxī Tídū was also abolished,
the post concurrently held by the Xúnfǔ.
In Húguǎng, a Zǒngdū was established,
whose banner troops were divided into center, left, and right battalions,
each with eight officers,
and a total of three thousand soldiers.
Established a Húběi Xúnfǔ, a Yúnyáng Xúnfǔ, and a Piānyuán Xúnfǔ,
each with Xúnfǔ's banner troops divided into left and right battalions,
the officers and soldiers being the same as the Jiāngxī Xúnfǔ's banner regulations.
Established a Húguǎng Tídū,
whose banner troops were divided into five battalions,
the officers and soldiers being the same as the Jiāngxī Tídū's banner regulations.
Established Zǒngbīngguān for the three garrisons of Jīngzhōu, Yúnyáng, and Chángshā,
and a Fùjiàng for the Chénzhōu brigade,
each with banner troops divided into center, left, and right battalions,
each with eight officers established,
and a total of three thousand soldiers.
Established Fùjiàng for the three brigades of Huángzhōu, Chéngtiān, and Chángdé,
each brigade's banner troops with seven officers established,
and a total of one thousand two hundred soldiers.
The Chéngtiān brigade was later changed to the Ānlù Yíng.
Established Cānjìang for Hànyáng and other battalions, each with four officers,
and six hundred soldiers.
Yóují for Yílíng and other battalions, each with three officers established,
and four hundred soldiers.
Established Shǒubèi and Bǎzǒng for Sānjiāngkǒu and other battalions,
each with two hundred soldiers.
In the early Kāngxī reign,
the Húguǎng Zǒngdū was combined into the Chuānhú Zǒngdū.
Afterwards, the Sìchuān Zǒngdū did not administer Húguǎng,
and the Húguǎng Zǒngdū was re-established.
The Yúnyáng Xúnfǔ was abolished,
the Húběi Xúnfǔ administering its banner troops.
In the fourth year of Shùnzhì,
the military organization for civil and military officials in Sìchuān was established.
A Xúnfǔ of Sìchuān was appointed,
with the standard troops divided into left and right battalions.
Each had eight generals,
totaling 1,300 soldiers.
Zǒngbīngguān were appointed for the four garrisons of Jiànchāng, Bǎoníng, Yǒngníng, and Kuízhōu.
Their standard troops were divided into three battalions,
with eight generals appointed,
totaling 2,000 soldiers.
Fùjiàng were appointed for the three commanderies of Sōngpān, Chéngdū, and Chóngqìng.
Their commandery standard troops were divided into two battalions,
with generals and officers from Yóují downwards appointed.
Cānjìàng, Yóují, and Shǒubèi were appointed for the various battalions such as Wēimào,
to lead the battalion troops.
Initially, Sìchuān only had a Xúnfǔ,
stationed in Chéngdū Fǔ.
The Chuānshǎn Zǒngdū was stationed in Shǎnxī,
overseeing Sìchuān for fourteen years concurrently.
Subsequently, a Sìchuān Zǒngdū was appointed,
stationed in Chóngqìng Fǔ.
During this period, sometimes it was merged into the Chuānhú Zǒngdū,
stationed in Jīngzhōu for nine years,
then moved to Chóngqìng for nineteen years.
Sometimes it was called Chuānshǎngān,
sometimes Chuānshǎn,
with frequent changes.
Until the Qiánlóng period,
it was fixed as the Sìchuān Zǒngdū.
In the fifth year of Shùnzhì,
the military organization for civil and military officials in Zhèjiāng was established.
A Zǒngdū was appointed,
with standard troops divided into three battalions,
and eight Fùjiàng or Yóují generals,
totaling 3,000 soldiers.
A Zhèjiāng Xúnfǔ was appointed,
with two battalions of standard troops,
eight generals,
totaling 2,000 soldiers.
The Zhèjiāng Tídū's standard troops had three battalions,
each with eight generals,
totaling 3,000 soldiers.
Zǒngbīngguān were appointed for the two garrisons of Dìnghǎi and Qúzhōu.
Their standard troops all had three battalions,
each with eight generals,
totaling 3,000 soldiers each.
The Qiántáng Water Division had two battalions,
the Táizhōu Water Division had three battalions,
each with eight generals,
totaling 3,000 soldiers each.
Qúzhōu appointed Zǒngbīngguān for the left and right routes of the Water Division.
Their standard troops had three battalions,
with generals from Yóují downwards leading the battalion troops.
Fùjiàng were appointed for the seven commanderies including Qúzhōu, Húzhōu, and Jiāxīng.
Their standard troops all had three battalions,
each with eight generals,
totaling 2,500 to 2,600 soldiers per commandery.
Fùjiàng were appointed for the three commanderies of Jīnhuá, Yánzhōu, and Chùzhōu.
Their standard troops had two battalions,
with eight generals each,
totaling 1,600 soldiers each.
Shǒubèi and Cānjìàng were appointed for the various battalions such as Jí'ān,
to lead the battalion troops.
Previously, a Zhèjiāng Zǒngdū was appointed,
later renamed Mǐnzhè,
concurrently overseeing Fújiàn.
The abolitions and reappointments were not constant.
During the Yōngzhèng period,
it was fixed as the Mǐnzhè Zǒngdū.
In the seventh year of Shùnzhì,
the military organization for civil and military officials in Fújiàn was established.
A Fújiàn Xúnfǔ was appointed,
with two battalions of standard troops,
eight generals,
totaling 2,000 soldiers.
A Fújiàn Shuǐlù Tídū was appointed,
with three battalions of standard troops,
each with eight generals,
totaling 3,000 soldiers.
Zǒngbīngguān were appointed for the three garrisons of Dīngzhōu, Quánzhōu, and Tóngshān,
as well as the Yuánjiǎo Zǒngbīngguān and Zhōnglù Zǒngbīngguān.
Their standard troops each had two battalions,
each with eight generals,
totaling 2,000 soldiers.
Fùjiàng were appointed for the three commanderies of Fúzhōu, Zhāngzhōu, and Jiànníng.
Their standard troops had three battalions,
each with eight generals,
totaling 3,000 soldiers.
The Fúzhōu Water Division,
and the standard troops of the seven commanderies' Fùjiàng of Dīngzhōu, Xīnghuà, Shàowǔ, Yánpíng, Mǐn'ān, and Tóng'ān,
each had eight generals,
totaling 2,000 soldiers.
The Fúníng Commandery Fùjiàng had two battalions,
seven generals,
totaling 1,800 soldiers.
Cānjìàng were appointed for battalions such as Quánzhōu, and Yóují for battalions such as Chánglè.
Each had eight generals,
totaling 1,000 soldiers each.
In the eighth year of Shùnzhì,
the military organization for civil and military officials in Liǎngguǎng was established.
Guǎngdōng appointed a Xúnfǔ,
with two battalions of standard troops,
eight generals,
totaling 2,000 soldiers.
A Guǎngdōng Tídū was appointed,
with five battalions of standard troops,
eight generals,
totaling 5,000 soldiers.
A Guǎngdōng Shuǐshī Zǒngbīngguān was appointed,
with 6,000 standard troops,
divided into left and right commanderies,
and central, left, and right battalions.
The two commanderies appointed Fùjiàng,
further divided into two battalions,
with eight generals,
totaling 1,500 soldiers.
The three battalions of the Water Division
each had eight generals,
totaling 1,000 soldiers each.
Zǒngbīngguān were appointed for the three garrisons of Zhàoqìng, Cháozhōu, and Qióngzhōu.
Their standard troops had two battalions,
eight generals,
totaling 2,000 soldiers.
Fùjiàng were appointed for the four commanderies of Sháozhōu, Huìzhōu, Gāozhōu, and Nánxióng.
Their commandery standard troops all had two battalions,
each with eight generals,
totaling 2,000 soldiers each.
Only Nánxióng had 1,600.
Cānjìàng were appointed for the Zhàoqìng and Gāozhōu Water Divisions and battalions such as Wúchuān,
and Yóují for the various battalions of the Zhèlín Garrison.
Each had seven generals,
totaling 1,000 soldiers each.
Generals from Shǒubèi downwards were appointed for prefectures and counties such as Dōngguǎn and Shǐxīng,
with varying numbers of soldiers from 200 to 500.
Guǎngxī appointed a Xúnfǔ,
with two battalions of standard troops,
eight generals,
totaling 1,500 soldiers.
The Guǎngxī Tídū's standard troops were divided into five battalions,
with eight generals,
totaling over 4,000 soldiers.
Zǒngbīngguān for the left and right wings were appointed,
as well as the garrisons defending Guìlín and Nánníng cities.
In the ninth year,
generals from Fùjiàng downwards were added for the three commanderies of Xúnwú, Liǔqìng, and Sī'nán,
each with 1,200 soldiers;
generals from Cānjìàng downwards for the three battalions of Yùlín, Xīntài, and Héchí,
each with 600 soldiers;
generals from Cānjìàng downwards for the two battalions of Yǒngníng and Zhāopíng,
each with 400 soldiers;
generals from Shǒubèi downwards for the two battalions of Shàngsī and Sānlǐ,
each with 200 soldiers;
and a Shǒubèi for the Hèxiàn battalion,
with 100 soldiers.
In the tenth year,
the standard troops of the Liǎngguǎng Zǒngdū were fixed into five battalions.
The central battalion had eight generals,
the left, right, front, and rear battalions had a total of eight generals,
totaling 5,000 soldiers.
In the early days of the dynasty, a Liǎngguǎng Zǒngdū was established.
In the second year of Kāngxī,
it exclusively oversaw Guǎngdōng.
In the fourth year,
it concurrently oversaw Liǎngguǎng.
In the first year of Yōngzhèng,
it again exclusively oversaw Guǎngdōng.
In the thirteenth year,
it again concurrently oversaw Liǎngguǎng.
In the 16th year of Shùnzhì,
the established military system for the officials and soldiers of Yúnnán and Guìzhōu was finalized.
A Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander of Yúnnán and Guìzhōu (Yún-Guì Zǒngdū) was established.
The banner soldiers were divided into four camps: Central, Left, Right, and Front.
The Central Camp had eight generals and officers (jiànglǐng).
The other three camps also had eight generals and officers,
totaling four thousand soldiers.
A Provincial Governor of Yúnnán (Yúnnán Xúnfǔ) was established.
The banner soldiers were organized into two camps,
with eight generals and officers,
totaling one thousand five hundred soldiers.
One year prior,
a Provincial Governor had been established in Guìzhōu,
and its camp system was similar.
At this time, a Provincial Commander-in-chief of Guìzhōu (Guìzhōu Tídū) was established.
The banner soldiers were divided into four camps: Left, Right, Front, and Rear.
The Left Camp had eight generals and officers.
The other three camps also had eight generals and officers,
totaling three thousand soldiers.
Four Brigade-Generals (Zǒngbīngguān) were established for Dàdìng, Qiánxī, Zhènyuǎn, and Wēiníng.
Each had three banner camps,
eight generals and officers,
and over two thousand soldiers.
A Deputy General (Fùjiàng) was established for the Guìyáng City Guard Brigade (chéngshǒu xié) and five other brigades: Píngyuǎn, Dìngguǎng, Tóngrén, Píngyuè, and Ānnán.
Each had two banner camps,
with generals and officers from Mobile Corps Commander (yóujī) downwards.
Assistant Commanders (cāncānjàng), Mobile Corps Commanders, and Battalion Commanders (shǒubèi) were established for the Sīnán Camp and other locations,
to separately command the officials and soldiers.
In the early Qing dynasty, the Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander of Yún-Guì
resided alternately in the two provinces.
In the 1st year of Kāngxī,
separate Grand Coordinators and Regional Commanders were established for the two provinces.
Thereafter, they were sometimes reformed or merged.
By the middle of Qiánlóng’s reign,
it was again fixed as a single Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander of Yún-Guì.
This was the initial system for the Green Standard Army in the directly administered provinces.
In the 4th year of Yōngzhèng,
the General Who Pacifies the Rebels (Jìngnì Jiàngjūn) Fùníng'ān established eight large and small checkpoints (kǎlù) in Hāmì.
The Brigade-General of Xī'ān, Pān Zhīshàn, established sentry posts and courier stations in the southwest passes of Shāzhōu to defend against "barbarians."
In the 5th year,
due to the weakness of the Zhèjiāng Green Standard Army,
sturdy soldiers were selected from Shānxī, Shǎnxī, and Gānsù and transferred there.
In the 10th year,
given the vastness of the Miáo territory,
Guìzhōu had its Brigade-Generals and Mobile Corps Commanders reorganized
to command the Dānjiāng, Táigǒng, and other camps,
as well as the Tóngrén, Zhènyuǎn, and Shíqiān brigades.
Also, newly established camps and brigades for Shàngjiāng and Xiàjiāng,
subordinate to Gǔzhōu,
were set up to keep order.
In the 11th year,
an imperial edict instructed all Brigade-Generals to inspect their troops.
In the 5th year of Qiánlóng,
acting on the words of the Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander of Húguǎng, Nàsūtú,
a decision was made to abolish non-existent warships,
eliminate privately established courier stations (títáng),
and rectify the abuses of fraudulently claiming rations.
In the 16th year,
the system for the garrison troops in Hāmì was established.
Over twenty generals and officers were dispatched from the four commands of Ānxī, Gānsù, Liángzhōu, and Sùzhōu,
along with two thousand soldiers to be stationed there.
They were relieved every two years.
In April and August, half of the troops were alternately rotated,
with new and old soldiers interspersed
to facilitate training.
Upon returning to their original camps,
the regional commanders (zhènchén) would evaluate their diligence,
and promote them accordingly.
In the 18th year,
the Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander of Shǎnxī-Gānsù, Yǐn Jìshàn, submitted a memorial on the defense of the western frontier,
suggesting that military talent for Ānxī should be carefully selected,
more firearms and ammunition prepared,
provisions and grain stored in advance,
city walls constructed,
and livestock chosen.
This was approved.
In the 24th year,
the Provincial Commander-in-chief of Ānxī was changed to the Provincial Commander-in-chief of Bālǐkūn.
Eight generals and officers, from Deputy General of Hāmì downwards, were established,
with eight hundred soldiers.
The rest were abolished or reformed with variations.
Soon after, a Brigade-General of Wūlǔmùqí was established,
divided into Central, Left, Right, and City Guard camps,
subordinate to the Provincial Commander-in-chief of Bālǐkūn.
All generals, officers, and soldiers of Bālǐkūn and Wūlǔmùqí
were placed under the overall command of the Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander of Shǎnxī-Gānsù.
In the 41st year of Qiánlóng,
after Dà-Jīnchuān and Xiǎo-Jīnchuān were pacified,
and newly incorporated into the empire's territory,
troops were stationed there.
The system was similar to that of the interior.
Camps like Màogōng, Suíjìng, Chónghuà, Fǔbiān, and Qìngníng were established.
Officers such as Mobile Corps Commanders and Battalion Commanders were appointed,
with a total of over two thousand six hundred soldiers.
In the 49th year,
based on the advice of the Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander of Shǎnxī-Gānsù, Fúkāng'ān,
Gānsù originally had a quota of fifty-six thousand six hundred soldiers,
and Shǎnxī had a quota of thirty-four thousand five hundred ninety soldiers.
After repeated transfers, reductions, and mergers,
only fifty-five thousand nine hundred or so soldiers remained,
less than half of the original quota.
Subsequently, over twelve thousand seven hundred soldiers were added,
bringing the total to seventy thousand soldiers including the old quota.
However, the military strength in the outposts (dūnshù) of the prefectures and counties was still insufficient.
It was requested to increase the soldier quota in prefectures and counties such as Píngliáng,
and to establish forty-four beacon towers.
Soldiers were to be selectively transferred from various banner troops to garrison them.
This was approved.
Soon after, it was deliberated to add another three thousand soldiers.
It was also proposed that the soldiers of the Shǎnxī and Gānsù camps practice archery, musketry, and horseback gunnery/archery.
They were to practice their skills daily in their own camps.
Small joint drills were to be held every five days,
and large joint drills every ten days,
performing the "Nine Advance, Ten Linked Rings" formation,
training thirty thousand elite troops.
In the 53rd year,
an edict prohibited Provincial Commanders-in-chief and Brigade-Generals from privately appointing positions such as flag-bearers (qípái) and attendants (bàndāng)
to avoid encroaching upon the soldier quota.
In the 4th year of Jiāqìng,
due to the suppression of rebellious bandits,
the quota soldiers from various provinces were dispatched in all directions,
and each province was ordered to recruit replacements.
In the 5th year,
a Brigade-General for the Níngshǎn Command (Níngshǎn Zhèn Zǒngbīng) and officers from Deputy General downwards were established in Shǎnxī,
all according to the former system.
In the 10th year,
an edict instructed all Grand Coordinators, Provincial Governors, Provincial Commanders-in-chief, and Brigade-Generals
to train the Green Banner soldiers using the method for training local militias (xiāngyǒng).
In the 5th year of Dàoguāng,
an edict instructed Zhílì to prepare over fifteen thousand three hundred combat soldiers,
and practice chariot and artillery formations.
This was soon after decided to be cut.
In the 16th year,
an edict instructed the Zhílì camp soldiers that 40% should practice archery,
20% should practice both infantry rifles and cavalry rifles.
For the two skills of swords and spears,
the rattan shield soldiers (téngpáijūn) were ordered to master them completely.
In the 22nd year,
a Brigade-General for the Tōng-Yǒng Command (Tōng-Yǒng Zhèn Zǒngbīngguān) was newly established at Lútái in Zhílì,
to command the fifteen camps including Běitáng and Hǎikǒu.
It was divided into three camps,
with generals and officers such as Mobile Corps Commanders and Battalion Commanders.
The new command's banner soldiers totaled over five thousand four hundred,
specifically for practicing aquatic and land skills.
In the 8th year of Xiánfēng,
the Guīdé Camp (Guīdé Yíng) in Hénán was promoted to a command (zhèn),
establishing a Brigade-General, Left and Right Camp Major-Generals (dūsi), Mobile Corps Commanders, and other officers.
There were five hundred eighty cavalry,
and over one thousand one hundred infantry.
In the 1st year of Tóngzhì,

an edict stipulated that in Zhílì, Jiāngnán, Sìchuān, Gānsù, where a Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander was solely established, and Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, Húběi, where the Grand Coordinator and Provincial Governor resided in the same city, military affairs were to be jointly supervised by the Grand Coordinator and Regional Commander and the Provincial Commander-in-chief.
For the troops of various commands in Jiāngsū, Zhèjiāng, Ānhuī, Jiāngxī, Shǎnxī, Húnán, Guǎngxī, and Guìzhōu,
they were to be supervised by the Provincial Governor nearby.
In the 4th year,
a Brigade-General for the Wǎnnán Command (Wǎnnán Zhèn Zǒngbīngguān) in Ānhuī was added,
with generals, officers, and soldiers established according to the system.
In the 6th year,
an edict stated that the Níngxià Command's Green Standard Army originally had a quota of seven thousand,
and the Dìngbiān Brigade (Dìngbiān Xié) in Shǎnxī originally had a quota of one thousand.
After the Hui bandit rebellion,
few remained.
All were ordered to be replenished.
In the 9th year,
the Chìxī Camp (Chìxī Yíng) in Guǎngdōng was converted into a naval force,
subordinate to the Yángjiāng Command,
modifying the old regulations for patrolling.
Also, the Wǔchāng City Guard Camp (Wǔchāng Chéngshǒu Yíng) in Húběi was relocated to guard Jīnkǒu and Páizhōu two outposts.
In the 12th year,
one thousand soldiers were selected from the Northern and Southern Commands of Shānxī,
divided into two camps,
and generals and officers were appointed to train them.
In the 11th year of Guāngxù,
given that the southern border of Guǎngxī stretched over two thousand li,
and originally had one hundred nine passes (ài)
and sixty-six checkpoints (kǎ),
the military strength was still insufficient.
Important areas were divided into three routes:
The Zhènnánguān pass, the front pass (guānqián'ài), and Píngxiáng Indigenous Prefecture (píngxiáng tǔzhōu) formed the Central Route.
The passes east of the Zhènnánguān formed the Eastern Route,
and the passes west formed the Western Route.
The existing twenty-two defense camps were reorganized into twenty-four camps.
Twelve camps were dedicated to defending the Central Route,
and the remaining twelve camps were divided to defend the Eastern and Western Routes.
The Provincial Commander-in-chief of Guǎngxī was relocated from Liǔzhōu to Lóngzhōu.
The City Guard Camp there established Mobile Corps Commanders and Battalion Commanders.
A Brigade-General for the Liǔ-Qìng Command (Liǔ-Qìng Zhèn Zǒngbīngguān) was added,
stationed in Liǔzhōu.
The additions and reductions to the Green Standard Army regulations over the years
are generally as described.
As for their relocations, reorganizations, and reforms,
the specific details cannot be exhaustively elaborated.
As for the numbers of those cut:
Starting in the mid-Shùnzhì period,
over four thousand bìng soldiers from Shānxī were cut,
forty-eight generals from Shǎan and Gān,
over ten thousand six hundred soldiers,
five hundred from Hénán,
five thousand from Húguǎng,
three thousand from Jiāngxī,
eight generals,
over nineteen thousand from Jiāngnán,
and one hundred seventeen generals.
These were the largest cuts.
For the others, Hǎizhōu had one xié,
with seven generals cut
and over six hundred soldiers.
Línqīng had one zhèn,
with five generals cut
and one thousand soldiers.
Three battalions had five hundred soldiers.
Yízhōu zhèn had nine generals cut.
Línqīng Chéngshǒuyíng had five generals
and three hundred soldiers.
Shòuzhāngyíng had two hundred soldiers.
Also cut were two battalions of officers and soldiers from the fǔbiāo of Jiāngxī and Nángàn,
and two battalions each from the fǔbiāo of Sìchuān, Húběi, and Yúnjiāng.
The numbers varied.
In the eighth year of Kāngxī,
the Zǒngbīng of Chéncháng zhèn was cut,
and the Chénzhōu Xiébiāo officers and soldiers were established.
In the twenty-third year,
the Tídú of Chóngmíng was cut,
and the Chóngmíng Shuǐshī Zǒngbīng was established,
with a fixed system for three battalions and the Qíbīngyíng.
After the thirty-fourth year,
the total number of bìng soldiers cut included
over one thousand from Nángàn zhèn,
over nine hundred from Jiǔjiāng xié,
and over eight hundred soldiers from Tónggǔyíng, which were the most.
The rest were from four or five hundred down
to as few as six or seven people.
In the Qiánlóng period,
two newly established fǔbiāo battalions were cut.
Among other cuts, the most was over three hundred,
and the least was ten or nine people.
In the nineteenth year of Jiāqìng,
an edict stated that the authorized strength of each bìng unit was over six hundred twenty-four thousand soldiers.
Compared to the increases since Yōngzhèng and Qiánlóng, this was indeed excessive,
and Dūdù, Fǔdiàn, Tídú, and Zhènzong were ordered to moderately reduce them.
Consequently, over fourteen thousand were gradually reduced.
In the twenty-fifth year,
another edict instructed all provinces not to waste funds on maintaining excess soldiers.
In the Dàoguāng period,
over three thousand six hundred cavalry from the Lǜyíng of Shǎan and Gān were cut.
Also cut were the fǔbiāo of Shāndōng and Shānxī,
and the three zhèn units including Yǎnzhōu,
the two zhèn units of Tàiyuán and Dàtóng,
the Dōnghé Hébiāo,
the authorized strength of Dūdù, Fǔdiàn, Zhènzong, and Xiéjiāng bìng units in Yún and Guì,
as well as various land and naval battalions in Fújiàn,
cavalry and infantry in Zhèjiāng,
and cavalry, infantry, and garrison troops in Liǎngguǎng, Jiāngsū, and Ānhuī, all with varying numbers.
In the first year of Xiánfēng,
Zēng Guófān memorialized, saying:
"The elite forces of the Bāqí
have more than half guarding the capital
and less than half garrisoning the country.
Strategic mountain passes
are often fully staffed,
but their authorized number is usually no more than three hundred fifty thousand.
The Lǜyíng soldiers are nominally over six hundred thousand,
but in reality, there are always sixty or seventy thousand vacancies.
In the mid-Qiánlóng period,
the proposal to increase troops arose.
The practice of 'empty names drawing rations'
was completely abolished,
and in one fell swoop, over sixty thousand soldiers were added.
Expenditures dramatically increased,
and Grand Secretary Ā Guì argued against it without success.
By the Jiāqìng and Dàoguāng periods,
seeing the gradual depletion of the treasury,
and recalling Ā Guì's foresight,
special edicts were issued to cut troops,
but only sixteen thousand were cut in two attempts.
I request that all provinces be ordered to retain the strong and dismiss the weak,
restoring the system of early Qiánlóng."
The edict was issued as requested,
ordering all Dūdù and Fǔdiàn to restore the old authorized strength over three years.
The numbers cut
were to be reported at the end of the year,
and the malpractice of 'empty rations' was not to recur.
In the fourth year,
over five thousand eight hundred cavalry, infantry, and garrison troops from Shānxī were cut,
and over three thousand nine hundred infantry and garrison troops from Yúnnán.
In the eighth year of Tóngzhì,
the naval battalions of Jiǔjiāng, Dòngtíng, Yuèzhōu, and Jīngzhōu were cut,
and converted into Chéngshǒuyíng,
with some land patrols established.
In the fifth year of Guāngxù,
Zuǒ Zōngtáng and Yáng Chāngjùn memorialized, saying:
"The military campaigns have not achieved the desired effect of controlling troops,
because the pay is low and the numbers are high,
making it impossible to train them effectively in a timely manner.
Untrained soldiers are equivalent to no soldiers,
and poorly trained soldiers are equivalent to untrained soldiers.
Gānsù has little revenue but many soldiers,
its military supplies relying on other provinces.
When funding is slightly scarce,
it easily leads to trouble.
It is urgent to moderately reduce the soldiers that can be cut,
to save military expenses.
By adding the saved military expenses to the remaining soldiers,
they can then be held accountable for diligent training.
In the Yōngzhèng period,
Gānsu's authorized troop strength was higher than that of the interior.
Although continuously cut later,
there are still over fifty-seven thousand cavalry, infantry, and garrison troops.
This must be divided and further reduced."
In the sixth year,
Dīng Bǎozhēn said:
"Since the military campaigns in Sìchuān,
recruitments of yǒng have increased,
with few cuts and many additions.
In the Tóngzhì period,
yǒng from Chǔ, Qián, and Chuān reached over sixty thousand.
They were gradually disbanded,
and currently, over two thousand nine hundred yǒng remain,
of which one-tenth can still be cut."
In that year,
over four thousand three hundred officers and soldiers from various battalions and land and naval defense yǒng in Húnán were gradually cut,
over three thousand two hundred were cut in Húběi,
and about nine thousand were continuously cut in Ānhuī.
In the eighth year,
Zhāng Yào memorialized, saying:
"Cutting yǒngdìng
can restore the authorized troop strength and
transform the battalion system,
which alone can ensure permanent border defense."
In the ninth year,
Zhāng Zhīdòng proposed to reorganize the Lǜyíng trained forces in Shānxī,
cutting one thousand regular yǒng from the Xiāng Army.
Funds were raised for their dismissal,
and subsequently further cuts were made,
totaling about six thousand soldiers cut before and after.
At that time, Guìzhōu's regular troops were cut by twenty percent,
with over three thousand two hundred garrison troops cut,
and over two thousand nine hundred combat troops.
Jiāngxī's authorized strength was over eleven thousand nine hundred soldiers.
Recently, regular troops were used as trained forces,
but long-term training
led to the abuses of fraudulent substitutes,
resulting in
the ridicule that
"though the soldier is still one,
the person has changed three times."
Therefore, it was decided that the fǔbiāo xuǎnfēng would continue their original drills,
and the trained troops drawn from various external battalions
were all returned to their original posts.
In the eleventh year,
an edict ordered the direct provinces to cut the Lǜyíng.
Biàn Bǎodì said:
"Guǎngxī has twenty-three thousand authorized soldiers
and fourteen thousand native soldiers.
When the Cantonese rebellion first started,
there were no more than two thousand rebels.
Yet, with this huge number of soldiers,
they could not defeat a small number of bandits.
If Guǎngxī is like this,
others can be inferred similarly.
Afterward, with the rampant disturbances of the Fà, Niǎn, Huí, and Miáo,
the Lǜyíng had no known battle achievements.
Now, it is advisable to gradually transform the battalion system,
cutting authorized numbers and consolidating rations,
to pay two rations for one soldier.
For example, if there are ten thousand authorized soldiers,
divided into twenty battalions,
half would be stationed,
and half would patrol.
When there is no trouble, they would drill and guard daily;
when there is an alert, they would respond as needed.
The entrenched habits of the Lǜyíng
must not be allowed to persist."
In the twenty-second year,
an edict stated:
"Recently, the Hùbù requested to cut troops,
proposing to cut seventy percent of the Lǜyíng
and thirty percent of the Yǒngyíng.
Since the general edict,
only Shāndōng has clearly stated its intention to cut fifty percent over five years.
Beyond this, actual cuts have been negligible.
In total, the soldiers and yǒng of all provinces still exceed eight hundred thousand,
with annual expenses totaling over thirty million.
The Lǜyíng's entrenched idleness
has long made them a mere empty setup.
At this time, when the need for borrowing is pressing,
to abandon useful funds
to maintain useless soldiers
causes the nation to be poor and the people distressed.
All Jiāngjūn, Dūdù, and Fǔdiàn must urgently set deadlines and make tangible cuts and report them."
In the 24th year [of Guāngxù],
following the suggestions of Hú Yùfēn and others,
the Green Standard Army (Lǜyíng) and drilled local militias (Liànyǒng) were merged,
and new drills were trained.
At that time, about three-tenths of the military quotas in Shāndōng had already been successively reduced.
By this point, it was deemed insufficient for deployment,
so the remaining two-tenths that had not yet been cut,
were kept from being cut.
Thereupon, Shānxī, finding that the reduced military quotas were insufficient for guarding passes,
requested to increase the training of several new army (Xīnjūn) battalions.
Gōngshòu also stated that the Green Standard Army's弊 (bì) were deep-seated,
and despite repeated reductions, they became weaker.
Therefore, civilian strength was needed to supplement them,
and local militias (Tuánliàn) should be urgently implemented.
In the 27th year,
Liú Kūnyī and Zhāng Zhīdòng memorialized for the reduction of the Green Standard Army,
stating:
"The officers of the Green Standard Army are all selected and appointed,
and the soldiers are all local residents.
Soldiers are not recruited by their immediate subordinates (biàn),
nor are immediate subordinates (biàn) trusted by their generals (jiàng).
Without benevolence or loyalty,
it is naturally difficult to command and control them.
To have transient officers
command hereditary soldiers,
is like district magistrates dealing with their clerks and runners.
To expect them to be disciplined, transformed,
and to follow instruction and example,
is simply impossible.
Moreover, Green Standard Army generals (jiàng) and immediate subordinates (biàn),
having been imbued with official habits,
even the officers (guānbiàn) are not easy to teach,
let alone the soldiers!
Layers of accumulated abuses
have become deeply entrenched.
They are both extremely arrogant and stubborn,
and exceedingly tired and weak.
It is inherently difficult to train them into usable soldiers,
and therefore, they must be reduced and eliminated.
The only strategy is to gradually reduce them year by year,
without distinguishing between cavalry, infantry, combat, or garrison units.
One-twentieth shall be reduced each year,
meaning five out of every hundred men,
to be completed within twenty years.
The salaries saved
shall be successively written off,
and the savings from these salaries
shall be used for the patrol and arrest (Jīnbǔyíng Chásuǒ) units.
However, regarding the Zhèngān Sub-Prefecture (Zhèngān Zhèn) in Húnán,
it was a case of 'reforming indigenous officialdom and integrating it into the imperial administration' (Gǎitǔ Guīliú),
with no native farming households.
Except for Míao (Miáo) produce,
the land was all military colonies (túntián),
and the people were all registered as soldiers.
The Suíjìng Sub-Prefecture (Suíjìng Zhèn) was also like this.
We request that the military quotas for these two sub-prefectures not be further reduced,
but that the Green Standard Army be reformed into local militias (Yǒngyíng).
The reduced generals (jiànglǐng),
if capable, should be transferred to the local militias (Yǒngyíng);
those unable to lead militias (yǒng),
should be dismissed or reassigned to civil posts.
This would prevent the abuses of military officials (wǔzhí) holding exclusive power,
and unite all soldiers nationwide under the single path of local militias (Yǒngyíng).
Their camp names should be revised
to match their actual designation. "
In the 29th year,
following the suggestions of Xú Shìchāng and others,
the Green Standard Army was re-designated as patrol police (xúnpōlǐng).
In the 1st year of Xuāntǒng,
the Office of the Commander of the Infantry (Bùjūn Tǒnglǐng Yámén) memorialized, stating:
"The five patrol and arrest battalions (xúnbǔ wǔyíng)
were originally established with 10,000 cavalry and combat soldiers.
Subsequently, due to repeated reductions and mergers,
the Central Battalion (Zhōngyíng) currently has 1,500 soldiers,
comprising 540 cavalry,
860 combat soldiers,
and 100 specially assigned combat soldiers.
The Southern Battalion (Nányíng) has 1,250 soldiers,
comprising 320 cavalry,
330 combat soldiers,
and 100 specially assigned combat soldiers.
The Left Battalion (Zuǒyíng) has 800 soldiers,
comprising 320 cavalry,
380 combat soldiers,
and 100 specially assigned combat soldiers.
The Right Battalion (Yòuyíng) has 700 soldiers,
comprising 300 cavalry and 300 combat soldiers,
and 100 specially assigned combat soldiers.
However, after patrol police were established in the Southern Battalion's (Nányíng) patrol area,
duties became simpler.
We request to transfer 375 soldiers from the Southern Battalion (Nányíng) to the Northern, Left, and Right Battalions (Běi, Zuǒ, Yòu Sānyíng),
with each battalion having 365 cavalry
and 410 combat soldiers. "
That same year,
the two sub-prefectures of Zhèngān and Suíjìng, which had been exempted from reduction,
were definitively reorganized into the Reserve Army (Xùbèijūn).
Additionally, the various detachments (xié) of Qiánzhōu, Yǒngsuí, Chángdé,
and the battalions (yíng) of Héxī, Bǎojìng, etc.,
retained three to four hundred soldiers each,
shedding the name of Green Standard Army,
adopting the regulations of local militias (Yǒngyíng),
and serving as Reserve Army (Xùbèijūn).
The battalions (yíng) of Yuèzhōu, Lǐzhōu, etc.,
each had their generals (jiàngbiàn) reduced,
retaining sixty-four to ninety-three soldiers.
The remaining battalions (yíng) under provincial governors (fǔ), provincial commanders-in-chief (tí), brigade generals (zhèn), and colonels (xié),
each had their commanding generals (tǒngjiàng) reduced,
with one general in the same city concurrently commanding the remaining soldiers.
For the entire province of Húběi,
one of five brigade generals (fùjiàng) was removed,
two of seven colonels (cānxing) were removed,
five of seventeen majors (yóují) were removed,
three of eleven captains (dūsī) were removed,
and ten of thirty-three lieutenants (shǒubèi) were removed.
The various battalions (yíng) under the provincial governor's (fǔ) command were not yet fully reduced,
awaiting phased reductions.
That year,
the two left and right vanguard battalions of the Jiāngběi old service guard soldiers were reduced.
The Guìzhōu Green Standard Army had already been reduced by two-tenths.
Subsequently, all officers below brigade general (fùjiàng) were reduced,
and four battalions (yíng) were merged,
then appropriately reorganized into six battalions (yíng).
However, those border defense strongholds beyond the reach of the Assistant Defense Army (Zuǒfángjūn) were slowly reduced.
In the 2nd year,
after the reduction of the Zhèjiāng Green Standard Army,
there still remained 399 generals (jiànglǐng)
and over 7,000 soldiers.
All were completely reduced,
their horses and weapons confiscated,
and they were reorganized into eight battalions (yíng) of patrol and defense units (xúnfángduì).
The Sìchuān Green Standard Army was gradually and completely reduced,
and strong and robust men were selected and retrained as defense army (fángjūn).
Seven-tenths of the Húguǎng (Húguǎng) battalions (yíng) had already been reduced.
Within one or two years,
they could be completely reduced.
Since the 8th year of Xiánfēng, Húběi had reduced cavalry and converted them to infantry.
In the 8th and 9th years of Tóngzhì,
a total of over 2,100 land and naval troops were reduced,
along with over 200 horses.
Since the 11th year of Guāngxù,
another over 2,900 troops were reduced,
including over 7,600 cavalry, infantry, combat, and garrison soldiers,
and over 880 horses.
There actually remained over 7,000 cavalry, infantry, and garrison soldiers,
and 1,660 horses,
to be completely reduced in successive years.
Subsequently, for the Hànyáng detachment (xié), Xīngguó and other battalions (yíng) in Húběi,
and the Héngzhōu detachment (xié), Bǎojìng and other battalions (yíng) in Húnán,
all officers below brigade general (fùjiàng)
ceased to be replaced.
The Fújiàn Green Standard Army was reduced,
and was entirely cut by the 6th year of Xuāntǒng.
Currently, there remained 380 generals (jiànglǐng) and over 5,900 infantry, combat, garrison, helmsmen, and logistical soldiers.
The Zhílì Green Standard Army
was reorganized into drilled army (liànjūn) during the Tóngzhì period.
Since Guāngxù,
the Tōngyǒng and other sub-prefectures (zhèn) were gradually reduced year by year.
By the 29th year,
there actually remained over 26,000 cavalry, infantry, combat, and garrison soldiers.
Its Tiānjīn city garrison and the eleven battalions (yíng) of Gégū, Tōngyǒng, Tōngzhōu, Běitáng, etc.,
during the Gēngzǐ Incident,
were completely dispersed and destroyed,
and thus all were abolished.
In addition, all other battalions (yíng) were reduced by three-tenths,
and another 314 generals (jiàngbiàn) were reduced.
The six Dàgū battalions (yíng),
having suffered heavy casualties during the Gēngzǐ year,
were also entirely abolished
and reorganized into patrol police (xúnjǐng).
In the 3rd year,
the Zhílì Green Standard Army still had over seven hundred officers
and over six thousand six hundred soldiers.
They were to be demobilized,
but the Huái, Liàn, and Xúnfáng battalions
temporarily retained their original status.
The border troops originally stationed outside the passes in Sìchuān,
who had always been allocated from the Green Standard Army,
totaling thirty-nine posts,
along with their officers and soldiers,
were all to be abolished.
For the Fújiàn Green Standard Army,
a deadline for complete demobilization was set.
The funds saved
were to be used to train Xúnfáng teams.
Jiāngxī also planned to completely abolish its Green Standard Army.
In the strategic border areas of Gānsù,
the Lùjūn had not yet formed into garrisons,
and only over seventeen thousand cavalry, infantry, and guard soldiers remained
to maintain defense and control;
their demobilization was temporarily delayed.
Little of the Shānxī Green Standard Army remained,
and it was to be completely demobilized over three years.
The same applied to the Jiāngnán Green Standard Army,
though the Xúzhōu Garrison's banner force was demobilized slowly.
In Shāndōng, the complete abolition of the Green Standard Army faced obstacles,
so a delay in demobilization was requested.
For the Guǎngdōng Green Standard Army,
the Sānjiāng and Yázhōu brigades,
the Dānzhōu battalion,
and the Dūbiāo Central Battalion were all exempt from demobilization.
Of the remainder, four tenths were reduced.
Among the over five hundred generals,
except for those in strategic border areas and dual-defense battalions whose vacancies were slowly abolished,
all other appointments were suspended,
and they were retrained as Lùjūn.
As for the Guǎngxī Green Standard Army,
after its demobilization in the 29th year of Guāngxù,
only five or four generals from the Fǔbiāo and Tíbiāo remained,
along with forty or fifty soldiers.
The Zuǒjiāng and Yòujiāng garrisons each had two generals
and twenty soldiers each.
This generally reflects the troop reductions throughout previous dynasties.
The Green Standard Army had accumulated power
over several centuries.
After the Tóngzhì Restoration,
border officials and military commanders,
learning from past mistakes,
gradually reformed by training militias and Xúnfáng units.
During the Guāngxù and Xuāntǒng eras, reductions were repeatedly made.
In the 3rd year of Xuāntǒng,
when the Wǔchāng Uprising occurred,
the Lùjūn Bù memorialized, stating that the situation was critical,
and that all provincial Green Standard Army units and Xúnfáng teams should have their demobilization delayed.
Thus, the system of the Green Standard Army
began and ended with the Qīng dynasty.
