In the sixth year,
the warships built by Zēng Guófān in Jiāngxī were
the most effective.
Fú Jì was ordered to select officers
and lead artisans to Lúzhōu to replicate them.
The foreign cannons required
were to be allocated and shipped from Shànghǎi.
In the sixth year,
Hú Línyì, noting that the Chángjiāng naval forces,
after returning to garrison Wǔhàn in the spring of the fifth year,
had few warships,
consulted with Luò Bǐngzhāng.
They jointly supervised the officers of the Ship and Artillery Bureau
to exert themselves in planning,
and the navy was revitalized.
The ships and weapons produced by the Húnán gentry bureau
and delivered to the camps included
over three hundred large and small warships,
over 400,000 catties of gunpowder,
and 1.4 million catties of cannonballs.
All other armaments were also prepared.
They requested an imperial edict to commend this effort.
Naval power primarily relied on artillery positions.
Two hundred foreign cannons were transported from Guǎngdōng,
followed by another six hundred,
to be distributed among various naval vessels.
From Wǔhàn to Jiǔjiāng,
wherever they went, they achieved victories.
However, in naval battles on the Chángjiāng,
the situations upstream and downstream differed.
Above Wǔhàn,
light and agile warships were advantageous.
Below Xúnwǎn,
where the river surface gradually widened,
large warships were advantageous.
In autumn and winter, when winds were strong, large warships were suitable;
in spring and summer, small boats were suitable.
The size of ships and cannons
should be adjusted according to the season and location.
It was requested that the Governors-General of Liǎngguǎng
continue to purchase large and small foreign cannons,
ranging from 400 catties to 1500 catties,
totaling eight hundred cannons,
to entirely replace the old-style artillery positions,
in order to facilitate the eastern campaign.
In the eighth year,
considering that the naval force originally established in Tiānjīn
had been successively abolished
during the Dàoguāng reign,
its re-establishment was planned
to strengthen coastal defense.
The provincial governors of Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng were ordered
to each dispatch large warships,
fully equipped with cannons and weapons,
to sail to Tiānjīn via the sea route,
and establish a naval force of three thousand men.
In the tenth year,
the Qīnghuái Defense Bureau was ordered to raise funds
for the annual expenses of the Húshuǐ naval force.
The Huái-Yáng naval camp was added
to protect the salt fields of Liǎnghuái
and assist the army.
Wúhú was isolated in the water.
Zēng Guófān was ordered to plan the establishment of the Níngguó naval force
to attack Wúhú,
as a foundation for conquering Jīnlíng.
The Tàihú naval force was added
as a foundation for conquering Sūzhōu.
In the second year of Tóngzhì,
an imperial edict instructed coastal governors-general to recommend talented naval commanders.
Zēng Guófān's inland river naval force
and Dū Xīng'ā's Yángfáng naval force,
if they had officers capable of commanding external naval forces,
were each to recommend them for imperial consideration.
In the fourth year,
in Shāndōng province, following the design of Chángjiāng warships,
long-dragon boats and sampans were built,
which were suitable for navigating the currents of the Huánghé.
As the navy was stationed on the Huánghé and Yùnhé,
to block fleeing rebels,
it was necessary to guard sections,
but the terrain was extensive,
and there were insufficient forces for deployment.
Therefore, more long-dragon boats were built in Shāndōng,
along with ten additional sampans,
to be led by high-ranking military officials for patrol and defense.
In the fifth year,
thirty Red Flag Guǎng-style boats at the Jiāngnán river mouth were refitted,
making a total of forty Guǎng-style boats,
to be distributed for defense of the river mouth.
In the sixth year,
the coastal defenses of Fújiàn and Táiwān were reorganized,
and additional Lóngcháo and other vessels were procured.
In the seventh year,
Zēng Guófān proposed reforms to the naval system.
The Jiāngnán naval force
had traditionally been divided into two branches: external sea and inland river.
The external sea naval force had 6,776 men
and 118 military officers.
The inland river naval force had 8,021 men
and 133 military officers.
Regarding the number of ships, based on the old Jiāngnán regulations from the twenty-fourth year of Dàoguāng,
there were 275 naval vessels,
most of which were rotten.
An additional 135 sampans
and 12 large ** boats were built.
In total, these vessels could only carry a few thousand troops,
yet the authorized troop strength
was still over ten thousand men.
This was a waste of funds,
having the name of a navy
without the reality of ships.
It was advisable to make significant changes
and pursue practical solutions.
The Jiāngsū naval force's
camp system and pay regulations
were all to imitate those of the Chángjiāng naval force.
The pay for the Red Flag Guǎng-style boats of the external sea
was also slightly increased.
Lǐ Hóngzhāng, Dīng Rìchāng, and other officials collaborated in planning this,
aiming to address both external defense and internal banditry,
and to balance old systems with new regulations.
Once the regulations were finalized,
the naval forces of Fújiàn, Guǎngdōng, and other coastal provinces
could also adopt them as appropriate.
In the eighth year,
the Board officials reached a consensus
to adopt Zēng Guófān's proposals,
reorganizing the Jiāngsū naval force into three major branches: internal ocean, external sea, and the Wú river system,
to facilitate control.
The Wú river naval force
was to consist of the originally established Commander-in-Chief's Right Battalion,
Tàihú Left Battalion, Tàihú Right Battalion, and the newly added Sōngběi and Sōngnán Battalions, forming five battalions,
under the direct command of the Admiral.
The number of sampans in each battalion varied,
but all were to be repaired
without shortages.
All seven Tàihú battalions
were reorganized into the five Wú river battalions,
with their reduced personnel merged and supplemented by the Commander-in-Chief's corps.
Mǎ Xīnyí and others subsequently proposed
that the Jiǔjiāng naval camp be converted into a city defense camp,
establishing four land patrol posts.
The Póyáng camp was converted into two land patrol posts.
The Dòngtíng naval camp was converted into the Lóngyáng city defense camp.
The Yuèzhōu naval camp retained a suitable number of sailors
under army command.
The Jīngzhōu naval camp retained a suitable number of officers and soldiers.
In the ninth year,
Dìng'ān and others were instructed, due to the difficulty of transporting provisions for the Nínglíng armies,
to build more gunboats
for transport via the Huánghé.
All thirty-two large and small warships
were organized into one battalion,
with commanders and other officers appointed.
In the tenth year,
Shěn Bǎozhēn, with the external sea warships completed,
suggested that competent military officials should be selected to supervise their training.
Subsequently, Lǐ Chéngmóu, the Fújiàn Naval Admiral, was appointed commander of the warships.
That same year,
Zēng Guófān initially proposed fourteen regulations for the Jiāngnán naval force.
Later, Mǎ Xīnyí and others increased them to twenty-five,
which were then edited and consolidated into twenty-one articles.
The six external sea battalions
were to patrol in sequence.
The five internal ocean battalions
were assigned patrol areas.
The five Wú river battalions
were assigned patrol areas.
The Sōngnán Battalion, Sōngběi Battalion, Tàihú Left Battalion, and Tàihú Right Battalion were to have their warships increased appropriately.
The land patrol posts left by naval camps
were to be merged and retained for defense.
The land patrol posts and artillery embankments of the three Jīngkǒu battalions
were assigned separate jurisdictions.
Revised jurisdictions for battalions
and retained garrison commanders were set,
with important strategic points retaining more land troops.
Regulations for the punishment of generals and officers were established.
The number of ships for each battalion was specified.
The number of external officials was determined.
The reduction in vacant salaries and provisions was determined.
The locations for battalion commanders' yamen,
the number of command ships for each battalion,
the authorized number of officers and soldiers,
the number of clerks,
expenses for awnings and banners,
rations for officers and soldiers,
the number of firearms and cannons for each ship,
and the amount of gunpowder, firearms, and cannonballs for each ship
were all comprehensively calculated in terms of funding.
These proposals were submitted to the relevant authorities for review and implementation.
In the eleventh year,
Dīng Bǎozhēn allocated the Ānlán steam warship produced in Fújiàn province to patrol the seas off Shāndōng.
Ruìlín allocated a small warship from Fújiàn province to patrol the sea mouth of Fèngtiān.
In the fourth year of Guāngxù
over 2,300 sailors and marines of the tugboat patrol in Guǎngdōng were disbanded.
In the fifth year
as various provinces were establishing navies,
naval steamships were successively stationed in Fèngtiān, Zhílì, Shāndōng, Jiāngsū, Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, and Guǎngdōng,
forming a navy.
However, the coastal provinces had different geographical conditions,
and their training methods could not be uniform.
Since Wúsōngkǒu was an intermediate point for the northern and southern sea frontiers,
Lǐ Cháobīn, the Tídū of Jiāngnán, was appointed commander of the offshore naval steamships,
to supervise and lead naval steamships of all sizes from various provinces,
to conduct regular joint exercises at Wúsōngkǒu.
In the sixth year
finding the newly acquired mosquito gunboats convenient and useful,
several tens more were purchased from abroad.
Able-bodied men from the coastal areas of Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng were recruited for the navy,
and stationed at various northern coastal ports.
In the seventh year
as the existing Banner garrisons at Lǚshùnkǒu, Fèngtiān,
had dilapidated boats,
and their officers and soldiers were weak,
they were all disbanded,
and assigned to army patrols.
Instead, quick-firing cannons were used for coastal defense.
At this time, Dīng Rúchāng returned to China from England leading warships,
marking the beginning of the Chinese navy sailing in the open sea.
Therefore, Dīng Rúchāng was promoted to Nàvy Tídū.
In the eighth year
considering the geographical situation of Jiāngnán,
which was "sea first, then river,"
the court deliberated on positioning the Chángjiāng Navy Tídū at Wúsōngkǒu,
with the three garrisons of Lángshān, Fúshān, and Chóngmíng subordinate to it.
The Jiāngnán Tídū was to be moved to Huái-Xú,
and the Fújiàn Navy Tídū was to be renamed Mǐnzhè Navy Tídū.
Soon, Zuǒ Zōngtáng and Péng Yùlín submitted their revised proposal,
stating that naval defense consisted of two aspects: offense and defense.
For offense, it was advisable to concentrate military strength;
for defense, it was advisable to set up defenses according to the terrain.
It was better to follow the old system.
After the Fújiàn Navy's troop reductions and pay increases,
there were actually over 6,900 naval personnel,
and over 300 Banner garrison naval personnel.
There were actually 40 warships of various sizes, including tugboats, dragon boats, and fast boats, in various battalions.
Táiwān and Pénghú had six warships.
There were ten naval steamships of various sizes.
It was advisable to combine with the Zhèjiāng Province navy for joint exercises.
The official system should remain unchanged.
In the ninth year
as the Zhàoqìng river section of the Guǎngdōng inland rivers spanned over 600 *lǐ*,
there were only over 20 small patrol boats,
which were insufficient for distribution.
The waters of Jiǔlóng were shallow,
making it difficult for large ships to navigate.
Therefore, shallow-draft naval steamships were added at both locations.
In the tenth year
attempts were made to build sampan boats with pointed bottoms,
and distribute them at sea entrances.
However, due to the boats' weak quality and small size,
the project was abandoned.
In the eleventh year
Péng Yùlín, seeing the increasing urgency of coastal defense,
proposed establishing a Navy Commander-in-Chief at Wúsōng,
with two divisions: one stationed at Dàgū, Zhílì,
to which all warships from the sea entrances of Shèngjīng, Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Jiāngnán would be subordinate;
and one stationed at Xiàmén, Fújiàn,
to which all warships from the sea entrances of Zhèjiāng, Fújiàn, Táiwān, and Guǎngdōng would be subordinate.
The two divisions would patrol the sea entrances annually,
and rendezvous for inspection at Wúsōng.
This was the beginning of the proposals for the Northern and Southern Ocean Navies.
In the twelfth year
a reduction of the Zhèjiāng coastal navy was discussed.
Soon, Liú Bǐngzhāng, the Governor of Zhèjiāng, stated that of the original quota of over 250 warships,
less than half had been purchased or built after the Cantonese bandit rebellion.
In the eighth year of Guāngxù
thirteen naval vessels were disbanded,
and three old ships were taken out of repair,
already meeting the 30% reduction in troops.
However, the eleven red-sailed patrol boats
were not included in the fixed reduction quota.
In the fourteenth year
as the territory of Táiwān expanded daily,
the Ánpíng Naval Fùjiàng was changed to Táidōng陸路Fùjiàng,
and the Lùgǎng Yóují was changed to Ánpíng Naval Yóují,
to serve as garrison officers for newly established areas.
In the fifteenth year
of the Fújiàn inland river navy's original quota of 98 gunboats,
due to frequent disbandments,
only 30 remained.
Each boat was staffed with six naval personnel,
dedicated to patrolling and inspecting the inland waters.
In the sixteenth year
the Hǎitán Navy of Fújiàn was relocated to garrison Fúqīng County,
to suppress pirates.
In the seventeenth year
from the middle, front, rear, left, and right battalions of the Húnán Xiǎnfēng Navy,
over 1,600 men were allocated
to garrison the provincial capital and Yuèzhōu and other places.
Over 400 men from the Chángshèng and Yì'ān Navies were allocated
to garrison Chénzhōu, Yuánzhōu, Chángdé and other places.
Over 300 men from the Chéngxiāng Navy were allocated
to garrison Héngzhōu and other places,
to ensure specific responsibilities.
In the same year,
as the lower reaches of the Liáohé River in Fèngtiān had existing patrol boats,
but the upper reaches only had army patrols,
there was no navy.
Therefore, one Long Dragon gunboat
and eight sampan boats were added.
Officers and men were selected from the trained army
to patrol the upper and lower Liáohé River and the Yánghé River south of the provincial capital.
In the nineteenth year
Tídū Huáng Yìshēng was ordered to review the five battalions of the Chángjiāng Tídū's personal command,
thirteen battalions of the Upper River,
and four battalions of the Lower River.
Regulations for training and discipline were established:
prohibiting land residence,
warning against bad habits,
diligently practicing skills,
and discarding superficial formalities.
They were not to fall into the customs of the Green Standard Army,
which would lead to idleness over time.
The frontier officials of Mǐn and Zhè deliberated,
stating that Zhèjiāng Province had the two naval steamships Yuánkǎi and Chāowǔ,
and Fújiàn Province had the three naval steamships Fúbō, Chénháng, and Jìngyuǎn,
which would cooperate with the coastal navy in suppressing and apprehending.
However, after the Zhèjiāng navy ships were reduced,
only over 50 remained.
After the Mājiāng Battle, Fújiàn Province
had only 29 boats remaining.
Therefore, eight red-sailed and other ships were leased at the Níngbō estuary,
with officers and men appropriately assigned,
to suppress pirates.
In the twenty-fourth year
the four branches of the Jiāngsū Province navy—offshore, inland, Yúhé, and Tàihú—
were all ordered to proportionally reduce their naval personnel.
In the twenty-fifth year
as the river defenses of Ānhuī Province in the lower reaches were Dōngxī Liángshān,
where cannon embankments and gun batteries had been built,
and in the upper reaches were Lánjiāng Jī Qiánjiāngkǒu and the Jiāngxīnzhōu of the provincial capital,
all of which had gun batteries,
but lacked a navy,
twenty-five gunboats from the Chéngqīng Battalion
and the Wúhú, Yùxī, Dàtōng, Ānqìng, and Huáyáng battalions of the Chángjiāng Navy were allocated
to coordinate defenses.
Furthermore, the Governors-General and Governors of the five Chángjiāng provinces were ordered
to each dispatch generals,
without regard to administrative divisions,
to establish strict defenses.
In the twenty-sixth year
as the coastal area of Fènghuángtīng, Fèngtiān,
had long been known as a pirate den,
naval steamships from the Northern Ocean had been dispatched for patrol.
In its branch ports,
it was advisable to station naval forces.
Therefore, three warships were built at each of the three ports—Dàgūshān, Tàipínggōu, and Shāhé—
and naval personnel were appropriately assigned for patrol and inspection.
In the thirty-fourth year
as the forces for suppressing bandits in the three prefectures of Háng, Jiā, and Hú in Zhèjiāng were insufficient,
one Yóují team was selected and trained from the existing navy
to be stationed at Jiāxīngfǔ.
Three additional Yóují teams were trained
and distributed among the river ports of Jiāxīng and Húzhōu.
A small Yóují team was stationed at Hángzhōu provincial capital.
Ten small steamers were leased from merchants in Shànghǎi
to tow armed shuttle boats to patrol waterways,
to ensure swiftness.
Four shallow-draft naval steamships were built at the Nányáng Shipyard,
equipped with eight quick-firing cannons.
Jiāngsū also built four shallow-draft naval steamships
to assist the inland river navy.
Following the regulations of various European countries,
they were organized into combined units
for defense and suppression.
This is a general overview of the navy's reorganization.
The increase or decrease in troop strength,
and the allocation of ships and weapons,
were determined by each province as needed.
The offshore navy,
from Shèngjīng in the north
to Mǐn and Guǎng in the south,
included tugboats, red-sailed ships, and other vessels.
The inland river navy
included patrol sampans and other boats from various provinces.
The naval ships of Fèngtiān, Zhílì, Shāndōng, and Fújiàn all belonged to the offshore navy.
The naval ships of Jiāngxī and Húguǎng all belonged to the inland river navy.
The naval ships of Jiāngnán, Zhèjiāng, and Guǎngdōng were divided between offshore and inland river.
Other trained forces
included the lake patrol navy, salt patrol navy, imperial guard battalions, and trained army battalions.
After Tóngzhì,
the systems of the Chángjiāng Navy and Tàihú Navy were established and augmented,
becoming more detailed than the old system.
The regulations for their patrols were as follows:
The Outer Seas Naval Forces patrolled Shèngjīng,
with a xié lǐng as the chief patroller,
and zuǒ lǐng, fáng yù, and xiāo qí xiào as sub-patrollers.
For the coastal provinces such as Zhílì,
a zǒng bīng guān served as the chief patroller,
and fù jiàng and below served as sub-patrollers.
Each, within their respective jurisdictions,
led the naval forces along the coast, up and down,
rotating back and forth,
interrogating criminals and suppressing violence.
At places where two jurisdictions met,
they would hold a joint inspection meeting at a scheduled time
to report on the patrol and investigation situation
to their respective jiāng jūn, zǒng dū, and tí dū,
who would then dispatch officials for inspection.
If delayed by wind,
each post would report the day of their arrival at the border.
Their annual schedule
began in the second, fourth, and fifth months,
and concluded in the ninth month, when they returned to camp.
Those who evaded patrol
or whose patrols were not thorough
would be punished according to military law.
As for the system of Inner River Naval Forces patrols:
The Cháng Jiāng, from Wūshān in Sìchuān eastward,
exited Sānjiāngkǒu,
reaching the border of Húguǎng,
passing through Yuèzhōu, Wǔchāng, Xīngguó to the border of Jiāngxī,
passing through Jiǔjiāng, Jiāngníng, Jīngkǒu and other places,
eastward to the sea.
The jiāng jūn, zǒng dū, tí, and zhèn of each province would separately appoint flag-bearing officers and soldiers
to patrol along the river,
returning upon reaching the border.
After Kāngxī's reign,
large ships were utilized for the outer seas,
while light boats were used for the inner rivers.
Therefore, ship designs were repeatedly altered,
and due to the vastness of the territory,
the number of naval personnel
increased from time to time.
In the event of war,
even more ships were added.
During the campaign against Wú Sānguì,
Shàngshàn was ordered to lead naval forces into Dòngtíng Hú to capture Yuèzhōu.
Later, Ènài commanded the naval forces,
building an additional one hundred niǎo chuán and
four hundred thirty-eight shā chuán,
establishing a naval force of thirty thousand men.
During the campaign against Táiwān,
Wàn Zhèngsè was ordered to oversee two hundred warships from Húnán and Zhèjiāng,
proceeding by sea to Fújiàn.
Yáo Qǐshèng also repaired three hundred warships,
with a naval force of twenty thousand men.
Shī Láng's victory at Pénghú
used three hundred warships
and twenty thousand naval personnel.
Shī Shìbiāo's suppression of Zhū Yīguì
used over six hundred large and small warships.
During the Qiánlóng era,
during the campaign against Miǎndiàn (Burma),
shipwrights from Húguǎng were ordered to build ships in Mánmù (Bhamo),
taking the Jīnshā Jiāng route to attack Miǎndiàn,
and naval forces from Fújiàn and Guǎngdōng were also dispatched to assist.
Lǐ Chánggēng's suppression of sea pirates
involved building thirty large ships in Fújiàn,
named Tíng Chuán,
equipped with four hundred cannons.
With the full strength of the Fújiàn and Zhèjiāng naval forces,
they fought across vast oceans,
and subsequently subdued Cài Qiān.
After Dàoguāng's reign,
naval threats frequently arose,
and the old wooden ships were no match for the sturdy and superior ironclad ships from abroad.
In the fifth year of Tóngzhì (1866),
shipyards were established in Fújiàn province to manufacture steamships,
modeled after European warships.
Jiāngsū initially set up four steamships.
In the eleventh year (1872),
Guǎngdōng and Shāndōng each set up one steamship,
and Fèngtiān set up one small steamship,
all of which were assigned to the naval forces.
Thereafter, coastal provinces purchased warships,
with annual increases,
and old-style naval warships were gradually phased out.
By the middle of Guāngxù's reign,
the total number of existing naval vessels for the outer seas and inner rivers across all provinces was as follows:
Fèngtiān had ten zēng chuán for the outer seas.
Zhílì had two cháng lóng chuán for the outer seas,
and forty-eight xiān fēng shānbǎn chuán.
Shāndōng had fourteen tuō zēng chuán for the outer seas,
and six shào chuán for the inner rivers.
Jiāngsū had two lún chuán for the outer seas,
eight tǐng chuán,
two lún chuán for the inner seas,
sixty shānbǎn chuán,
three hundred eighty-five shānbǎn chuán and tǐng chuán for the inner rivers,
seventy-six shānbǎn chuán for the Cháng Jiāng,
seven dū zhèn shānbǎn chuán,
ten cháng lóng chuán,
and one hundred twenty-eight xún shào shānbǎn chuán.
Ānhuī had two hundred eighty-two shānbǎn chuán,
fifteen cháng lóng chuán,
one bā tuán chuán,
ten qiāng huá,
fifteen hù kǎ xún chuán,
seven dū zhèn shānbǎn chuán,
and two lún chuán.
Jiāngxī had fifteen cháng lóng chuán,
two hundred sixty-three shānbǎn chuán,
six dū zhèn shānbǎn chuán,
and one lún chuán.
Fújiàn had one cháng lóng chuán for the outer seas,
nineteen shānbǎn chuán,
fourteen xiǎo tǐng,
fourteen shào chuán,
two lóng záo chuán,
one tuō záo chuán,
and thirty pào chuán for the inner rivers.
Zhèjiāng had twenty-seven diào chuán for the outer seas,
twelve tǐng chuán,
seventeen lóng záo chuán,
two shào chuán,
one kuài chuán,
fifty-eight dà shānbǎn chuán for the inner rivers,
eighty-four zhōng shānbǎn chuán,
forty-nine fēi huá chuán,
two hundred thirteen cháng lóng chuán zuò chuán,
eight qiāng chuán,
and five pào chuán.
Húběi had eight dū zhèn dà shānbǎn chuán,
twelve cháng lóng chuán,
and one hundred eighty shānbǎn chuán.
Húnán had four dū zhèn dà shānbǎn chuán,
four cháng lóng chuán,
and sixty shānbǎn chuán.
Guǎngdōng had twenty-two large and small lún chuán for the outer seas,
fourteen xún chuán,
ten tuō chuán,
one cháng lóng chuán,
one pá chuán,
one liǎng lǔ jiǎng chuán for the inner rivers,
one lǔ chuán,
forty jiǎng chuán,
one hundred ninety-six xún chuán,
fifteen jí tiào chuán,
two píng dǐ jiǎng chuán,
two kuài shào chuán,
fourteen kuài chuán,
seven kuài jiǎng chuán,
four [gōu] záo chuán,
and two lǔ chuán.
The warships of each province
were all assigned to biāo yíng,
berthed in selected locations,
and held joint inspections at regular times.
Outer seas naval vessels,
as naval regulations were gradually established,
were only responsible for coastal bandit suppression.
The inner river naval vessels of each province
all imitated the style of the Cháng Jiāng naval shānbǎn chuán.
However, patrol and inspection boats,
which patrolled branch rivers and small harbors,
utilized their lightness and agility,
so their design differed slightly.
The system of Cáo and Hé Naval Camps
began during the Lóngqìng reign of the Míng Dynasty.
The Qīng Dynasty slightly modified its system.
Garrison soldiers (wèi zú) were solely responsible for towing and transporting grain tribute,
while camp soldiers (yíng bīng) were solely responsible for escorting the grain tribute,
and separate chéng shǒu yíng were established to guard cities.
The Cáo Yuàn and the Xúnfǔ were divided into two.
Under the command of the Cáo Yùn Zǒngdū,
he had jurisdiction over the Left, Right, and Middle three camps, as well as the four Chéngshǒu camps,
stationed in the territory of Shānyáng and key areas for grain transport,
with troops deployed accordingly.
Huáijùn was formerly the confluence of the Huáng and Huái Rivers,
where two large sluices were specially built,
guarded by river troops and fort caretakers.
Thus, the River Camps became as important as the Grain Transport Camps,
each having officers such as fù jiàng, cān jiàng, yóu jí, and shǒu bèi.
The promotion system for River Camps
was equivalent to military merit,
and they were solely responsible for the construction and repair of dikes and defenses,
while the responsibility for investigation and capture was not included.
In the Qing dynasty, the naval prowess reached its peak,
defending Dòngtíng Lake and pacifying the Wú rebels,
fighting on the high seas and annihilating Cài Qiān,
descending the Cháng Jiāng and suppressing the Yuè bandits.
For thousands of Lǐ across the southeast,
its might was manifest through drums and gongs.
Diligent officials and valiant generals
achieved glorious deeds,
surpassing previous eras.
When maritime trade was widely opened,
and ironclad ships sailed across the seas,
the old naval system,
being weak, could not withstand the strong,
and thus lost all its reliance.
This was due to the adverse times,
not a defect in planning.
The old quotas of ships and the defense system for the various provinces are
listed below: the Three Eastern Provinces (Dōng Sān Shěng),
Zhílì,
Shāndōng,
Jiāngnán (Jiangnan),
with the attached Tàihú Lake and Cáo Biāo (Grain Transport) naval forces,
Zhèjiāng,
Fújiàn,
Guǎngdōng,
Guǎngxī,
Húnán,
Húběi,
Ānhuī,
and the Cháng Jiāng naval forces.
Among the coastal ports of the Three Eastern Provinces,
Jīnzhōu and Lǚshùn Kǒu were particularly important.
The naval system was established early in the Qing dynasty.
The Sōnghuā Jiāng and Nèn Jiāng rivers flow through the heartland of Jílín and Hēilóngjiāng provinces.
The naval camps and stations established
extended from Jílín north to Mò'ěrgēn (Mergen) and the Hēilóngjiāng (Amur River) region.
By the Guāngxù reign,
Lǚshùn had built a naval port,
where ironclad ships were stationed,
differing significantly from the former system.
On the Túmén River and Húntóng Jiāng (Amur River) in the eastern part,
Russian warships sometimes encroached,
which the old-style naval ships,
with their weak armaments and sparse troops,
could no longer control.
The established naval forces are listed hereafter:
At Lǚshùn Kǒu in Fèngtiān (Fengtian),
a naval camp was established in the early Shùnzhì years.
Ten Shāndōng趕繒 (gǎnzēng) ships were assigned to it,
beginning the organization of camps and stations.
In the 15th year of Kāngxī (1676),
two naval Xié Líng (Assistant Commanders),
two Zuǒ Líng (Company Commanders),
four Fángyù (Defenders),
eight Xiāoqí Xiào (Cavalry Officers),
and five hundred naval soldiers were established.
In the 53rd year (1714),
six large warships were built by the shipyards of Zhèjiāng and Fújiàn provinces,
which traveled by sea to Fèng Shěng (Fengtian Province),
to be stationed at the estuary.
The Jīnzhōu naval camp was subordinate to the Chéngshǒuwèi (City Commandant),
with one hundred naval soldiers.
The Jílín naval camp,
during the Shùnzhì reign,
had officials of the fourth, fifth, and sixth ranks.
In the 14th year of Guāngxù (1888),
one Zǒngguǎn (Director) and
two officials of the sixth rank were added.
The Qíqíhā'ěr naval camp,
in the 23rd year of Kāngxī (1684),
had one Zǒngguǎn,
two officials of the fourth rank,
two officials of the sixth rank,
one shipbuilding official each of the fourth, fifth, and sixth ranks,
eight Lǐngcuī (Foremen),
and two hundred sixty-eight naval soldiers,
later increased to five hundred sixty-eight.
It had two large warships
and fifteen second-class warships.
In the 40th year of Kāngxī (1701),
ten ships were transferred to Hēilóngjiāng.
During the Yōngzhèng reign (1723-1735),
six ships were transferred to Mò'ěrgēn,
leaving twenty-five large and small warships,
five riverboats,
and ten rowboats.
The Mò'ěrgēn naval camp,
in the 23rd year of Kāngxī (1684),
had one official of the fourth rank,
and one Lǐngcuī,
concurrently administered by the Xié Líng of the city.
It had six warships
and forty-three naval soldiers.
During the Yōngzhèng reign, six warships were added.
The Hēilóngjiāng naval camp,
in the 23rd year of Kāngxī (1684),
had one Zǒngguǎn,
two officials of the fifth rank,
two officials of the sixth rank,
eight Lǐngcuī,
thirty warships,
and four hundred nineteen naval soldiers.
In the 40th year (1701),
ships were transferred from Qíqíhā'ěr to supplement it,
resulting in ten large warships,
forty second-class warships,
ten riverboats,
and ten rowboats.
The Zhílì province naval force
began in the fourth year of Yōngzhèng (1726),
with the establishment of the Tiānjīn naval camp,
with one Dūtǒng (Commander-in-Chief),
stationed in Tiānjīn,
solely for coastal defense.
The naval force numbered two thousand men.
All rivers within the province
were assigned to land garrisons,
with no inland river naval force.
In the eighth year of Qiánlóng (1743),
one Fù Dūtǒng (Deputy Commander-in-Chief) was added,
along with one thousand naval soldiers,
twenty-four large and small趕繒 (gǎnzēng) ships,
and eight ●仔 (huázǐ) boats.
In the 32nd year (1767),
since the sea lanes were peaceful,
and it was a waste of provisions,
the entire force was disbanded.
In the 21st year of Jiāqìng (1816),
a naval force of one thousand men was re-established.
Subsequently, Dàmíng Zhèn (Daming Garrison) was established,
and the naval Zǒngbīng (Brigade General) was merged into Dàmíng,
with one Shǒubèi (Battalion Commander),
one Cāncóu (Assistant Commander),
two Qiānzǒng (Captain of a Thousand),
three Bǎzǒng (Captain of a Hundred),
and four hundred ninety-one naval soldiers.
In the 19th year of Jiāqìng (1814),
Nà Yànchéng (Na Yancheng), the Governor-General of Zhílì, stated in a memorial that the officers and soldiers were nominal,
and most of the warships were rotten,
and requested their abolition,
merging them back into Dàmíng Zhèn.
In the eighth year of Xiánfēng (1858),
due to frequent alarms on the sea frontier,
six additional coastal camps were established.
On the north and south banks of Dàgū,
forts were constructed,
comprising five large forts,
ten flat forts,
ninety-nine large cannons,
and three thousand naval soldiers.
Five hundred men formed one camp,
divided into six left and right camps.
In the ninth year (1859),
this was changed to one thousand eight hundred men.
In the eighth year of Tóngzhì (1869),
Governor-General Lǐ Hóngzhāng (Li Hongzhang) memorialized to appropriately determine the camp system,
establishing a Dàgū Xié Fùjiàng (Dagu Assistant Brigade General),
stationed at Xīnchéng (Xincheng) estuary,
to defend the forts.
In the first year of Guāngxù (1875),
Lǐ Hóngzhāng constructed additional forts at Dàgū, Běitáng, and other places,
purchased European ironclad fast ships, ram ships,
and torpedo boats,
commanded by naval officers,
not subordinate to the old Xié Biāo (Battalion of the Assistant Commander) system.
The inland river naval ships
began during the Tóngzhì reign,
following the model of the Cháng Jiāng naval force,
establishing a Dūbiāo Shuǐshī Zhōngyíng (Governor-General's Naval Central Camp),
with one Guǎndài Guān (Commander),
thirty-two Shàoguān (Patrol Officers),
four hundred seventy-six naval soldiers,
and thirty-two sampan warships,
stationed at the Sānchà Hékǒu (Sancha River Estuary).
One Qīnbīng Zǒngshàoguān (Chief Patrol Officer of the Governor-General's Guard),
fourteen Shàoguān,
two hundred two naval soldiers,
and fourteen sampan warships
were stationed at the Xīgū Hékǒu (Xigu River Estuary).
